"...And Peer Aloft to Glimpse Some Fragment" is a prose poem short story by Ruthanna Emrys featured in the anthology "Azathoth: Ordo ab Chao." It explores themes of beauty and chaos, intertwining modern conversations with a cosmic narrative.

### Synopsis
The story follows a group of characters who navigate a world filled with cosmic horrors and existential dread. They are drawn together by their shared experiences and the mysteries of the universe. As they confront their fears and the unknown, they grapple with the fragility of beauty in a chaotic world.

"'‘Twas the Night Before Madness" is a festive Cthulhu Mythos poem by author S. Alessandro Martinez. It was published in the Jesse Dedman/William C. Marchese-edited anthology Cthulhu Christmas Special and Other Lovecraftian Yuletide Tales in November 2017.

### Synopsis
The twelve four-line verses describe how, at Christmas time, a cultist conducts a murderous ritual to summon the Old Ones to our plane of existence. As they return to the material realm, they grant him incredible knowledge, but shatter his sanity in the process.

### Trivia
* The entities summoned by the cultist include Yog-Sothoth, Dagon, Hastur, Yig, Gla'aki, Cthulhu, Ithaqua, Nyarlathotep, and Cthylla.

'Umr at-Tawil (عمر الطويل) is a fictional entity from the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was first described by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price in their short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".

### Background
'Umr at-Tawil is an entity who stands beside the Ultimate Gate, meeting any who traverse the first Gate via the Silver Key. He appears as a heavily cloaked figure with no organs or features discernible beneath his garb. It is somewhat humanoid in shape, but "half as large again as an ordinary man", and moves about by gliding or floating over the ground.

Abdul Alhazred, in the Necronomicon, identifies this entity as "the Most Ancient One" and "the Prolonged of Life", and cites the Book of Thoth's claim about a "terrific" price to be paid by those who glimpse at it.

Believed to have originated as a prehistoric Earth creature that inhabited the planet long before the dawn of humanity, 'Umr at-Tawil is the leader of the Ancient Ones, which are manifestations of the All-in-One and One-in-All, speculated to be Yog-Sothoth by Randolph Carter. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key") 

At least one ancient book claimed that 'Umr at-Tawil and the Ancient Ones were agents of Yog-Sothoth, identified as the All-in-One and One-in-All, and that they "dream forever of that time when once again they shall rule to whom rightfully belong Earth and the entire universe of which it is a part". (: "The House on Curwen Street")

### Pathfinder
'Umr at-Tawil appears as a Great Old One in the role-playing game Pathfinder, under the name Tawil at'Umr.

In the Pathfinder multiverse, Tawil at'Umr is a servant of Yog-Sothoth, operating as the physical projection of its will and working towards its agenda across the dimensions. Tawil at'Umr is theorized on Golarion to being the side of effect of Yog-Sothoth's contact with the material plane. Its knowledge about reality is vast, including how one may access the Dimension of Time, but one acquires such knowledge at a terrible cost.

When it comes to its appearance, mortals see a cloaked humanoid figure which is somewhat larger than the observer. Its true form under the cloak is that of a protoplasmic mass which can take varying shapes, some of which should not be capable of existing.

### In Other Media
*Deus Machina Demonbane: After the Demonbane trio entered the gate and reached a bloody space of countless doors, they were guided by 'Umr at-Tawil to the next location.
*Fate/Grand Order: The mobile game features the Foreigner-class Servant Abigail Williams, who is possessed by Yog-Sothoth. In her Second Ascension, Summer Abigail's outfit has some resemblance to 'Umr at-Tawil.

The 'Ygirothians are a fictional species created by Walter C. DeBill, Jr. for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "In 'Ygiroth".

### Description
Often known as "beast-men", 'Ygirothians are a humanoid species which inhabit the city of 'Ygiroth, in the forested valley of the river Skai where Ulthar, Nir and Hatheg are located, in the Earth's Dreamlands. They are shorter and hairier than the average human, have prominent brows and beady eyes, and move silently on their broad feet. Their language has been likened to "coarse whispering". They worship an avatar of Nyarlathotep known as the Thing in the Yellow Mask.

'Ygirothians hunt with stone spears and wear necklaces made of wolves' teeth. Although they haven't managed to fully domesticate the Kyresh, they use the semi-feral beasts as hounds and steeds to hunt down Buopoths, the flesh of which they eat uncooked. Many 'Ygirothians perish in these hunts, usually slain by the very Kyresh they attempt to ride.

Every Walpurgis and Yule, the 'Ygirothians abduct young women from Ulthar, Nir, and Hatheg to be sacrificed in undisclosed rituals. The rest of the year, they occasionally take "plump" men and women, possibly as food. (: "In 'Ygiroth")

### History
Nyarlathotep, in the form of the Thing in the Yellow Mask, taught the 'Ygirothians how to make stone spears and ride the wild Kyresh, and ordered them to build 'Ygiroth "to honor It and Its unseen brothers". It also taught them the Aklo language, and revealed "secrets which could have made them masters of all Dreamland and perhaps even of the waking world", although, fortunately, the 'Ygirothians had neither the courage not the means to exploit these secrets.

The 'Ygirothians were destroyed when their god, Nyarlathotep, played a cruel "joke" on them, as they tried to summon him to fend off the armies of Ulthar, Nir, and Hatheg, which had gathered to invade 'Ygiroth. Instead of answering their prayers, the god decided to send down his "half-brother and other face", an entity that spreads out fear and panic "like a poisonous vapor". Predictably, the 'Ygirothians abandoned their city and ran straight into the spears of their enemies. (: "In 'Ygiroth")

"Ashcan" Pete Washburne, the Drifter, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos content. He made his first appearance in the Core Set of Arkham Horror Second Edition.

### Description
Pete is a drifter, travelling the country with his trusty dog Duke and his guitar. He has roamed the length and breadth of the United States, but his nightmares have finally led him to the New England town of Arkham, where he hopes to put an end to the bad dreams.

### Quotes






### Appearances
Since his debut in Arkham Horror Second Edition, Pete has appeared in a number of Arkham Horror Files works, including the Arkham Horror: The Card Game expansion The Dunwich Legacy, the Eldritch Horror expansion Cities in Ruin, and the Mansions of Madness expansion Recurring Nightmares. He also made a cameo appearance in Graham McNeill's 2011 novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic, and in 2010 a pre-painted plastic miniature of the character was released as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line.

"Skids" O'Toole, the Ex-Convict, is a fictional character conceived by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-relates games and fiction.

### History
Whilst Skids had never really wanted to be a criminal, needs must when the devil calls, and he was in desperate need of cash. Never really seeing himself as a bad person, Skids did what it took to come up with the money; protection rackets, robbery, even bank jobs were not out of the question, but he prided himself on the fact that he’d never actually killed anybody.

When the law finally caught up with Skids and he explained that he needed the dough to finance treatment for his sick mother, the cops simply laughed in his face and booked him anyway. Clearly, that excuse had been used one too many times.

After his Ma died from her illness when Skids was only two years into his time, he didn’t get any other visitors. To keep himself from going stir crazy, he decided to make real friends with his cell mate, a strange fellow named Brad Hollins. Brad constantly muttered and rambled about how the “Old Ones” were coming and told stories of the things he had learned of in his dreams, but Skids stuck with him anyway and the two became real friends.

Then one night Skids woke up to the sound of chanting and the smell of smoke: looking over at Brad, he saw the man burst into flames, screaming in terror. Although the law wanted to pin this on Skids, they really didn’t have anything to hang it on, and so Skids was paroled right on time.

The first thing he did was travel to one of Brad's old haunts in a city called Arkham. There, he thought, he could maybe find out what had really happened to his old friend.

### Behind the Mythos
Whilst initially created for their Second Edition release of Arkham Horror, Fantasy Flight have since included him as a playable character in Mansions of Madness, Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. In addition, a fully-painted plastic miniature of Skids was released in 2010 as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures collection, but this is now discontinued.

### Trivia
*Skids' real first name remains unknown, as Fantasy Flight Games have never issued any material containing it.

"(S)Exit" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Davie Yates. It was published in the James Ward Kirk Publishing thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
Presented in a jarring combination of present tense, flashback, and flash-forward, "(S)Exit" tells the life story of a sex addict, from his first experience, to marriage and the birth of his child, to how the addiction costs him everything. It culminates with the unnamed narrator meeting a mysterious woman who offers him sweet oblivion through the tender mercies of unmentionable creatures, an offer which he accepts.

### Synopsis
After being driven nearly insane by the mind-altering effects of a small statue of Cthulhu, Captain Nemo reflects upon his childhood in 1840s India. While his brother went slowly mad - presumably from reading a mysterious book gifted to him by his uncle - Nemo attempted to break free from the stifling palace life in which his royal family existed.

### Behind the Mythos
20,000 Leagues Into Madness: Chapter 1 is based on an audio podcast, also created by Brian del Rio and issued through his Mobili Comics Audio label .

fullContent:
"20,000 Years Under the Sea" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story featuring Captain Nemo and the Nautilus from the works of Jules Verne. It was written by Kevin J. Anderson and published in the 2015 anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume Two.

This story uses the same backstory for Nemo that Anderson invented for the novel Captain Nemo: The Fantastic History of a Dark Genius. It differs considerably from Verne's own backstory for the character, as presented in 20,000 Leagues Under the Seas and The Mysterious Island.

### Synopsis
After suffering considerable damage from a giant squid attack, the submarine Nautilus heads towards an island off the coast of Antarctica for repairs. The crew and the captain, Nemo, are former war prisoners who built the Nautilus for the tyrannical caliph Robur, before rebelling against and killing him. They now travel the world's oceans with no destination, sinking warships from all imperialistic nations, and fighting against all forms of oppression.

While leaving his second-in-command, Harding, in charge of repairs, Nemo explores the island and is surprised to find the ruins of a strange city, with disorienting angles, dark obelisks carved with unknown symbols, and a toppled statue of a tentacled octopoid being. He also sees images of the extinct inhabitants of the city: barrel-shaped creatures with starfish-like heads.

Back in the Nautilus, Harding tells Nemo that they found another city, this one entirely submerged and perfectly preserved. The captain and four other crewmen don their diving suits and explore the sunken city, finding that it belonged to the same species of star-headed creatures, but was also inhabited by a race of amoeboid beings that served them. Nemo sees some symbols that he finds familiar. One of the men, Louart, comments on the absence of sea-life, except for some coral and anemones growing on specific places, evidently as decoration. It looks as if someone is tending to the city, and keeping it preserved exactly as it was when inhabited. The image of the octopoid entity is also present on a large domed building, and seems to have some disruptive effect on Nemo's mind, as he becomes fascinated by the mighty alien being, and figures that it holds the power to end all wars for good.

Louart accidentally knocks down a spire and is promptly attacked by one of the amoeboid servants of the city's long-gone builders. Nemo and the others hurl their harpoons at it, but can't do any damage to the creature's amorphous flesh, and it brutally crushes Louart to death by contracting itself around him. After killing him, the creature simply swims away, ignoring Nemo and the others.

That night, after Louart's funeral, Nemo spends time in the Nautilus library and finds the symbols from the ancient city in a book he stole from the caliph: the Necronomicon, by Abdul Alhazred. fullContent:
24 Views of Mt. Fuji, by Hokusai is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by the late American author Roger Zelazny, which was first published in the July 1985 edition of Issac Asimov's Science Fiction Magazine.

### Overview
The story uses mythos elements as a background device for establishing atmosphere rather than as a key plot element, a short background vignette about Shinto priests discovering a far older religion and the sunken city of R'lyeh. No revelations that most readers have not seen before, but we get it mentioned and done in one page, rather than occupying an entire story, which is more focused on the relationship between an AI and his wife.

### Publication History
24 Views of Mt. Fuji, by Hokusai, has been reprinted numerous times over the years, most notably to this wiki in the 1995 Arkham House collection Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology. It has also been translated into French.

"A Body in the Library" is a short Cthulhu Mythos/Thomas Carnacki crossover story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
After noted occultist Thomas Carnacki stumbles across a formula which will allow him to open a portal to the Outer Darkness, his professional curiosity drives him to make the attempt. Unfortunately, the portal he opens allows the entry of a Hound of Tindalos which injures him before he manages to imprison it within a mystical gaol. 

As luck would have it, Carnacki had arranged one of his frequent dinner parties for that very evening, and with the assistance of his friends is able to kill the creature using electricity.

### Characters
*Thomas Carnacki, a man possessed of tremendous mystical knowledge.
*Dodgson, the narrator and Carnacki's friend.
*Arkwright, another friend of Carnacki's.

### Publication History
"A Body in the Library" was published in Carnacki: Starry Wisdom and Other Stories, a collection of William Meikle's Thomas Carnacki stories, by Dark Regions Press as an ebook in March 2021.

### Trivia
*In "A Body in the Library", Meikle states that the Cŵn Annwn, the mythical Welsh hounds of the underworld, are in fact the Hounds of Tindalos.

A Call To Cthulhu is a children's book with some comic elements, published by Titan Nova in 2023. It was written and illustrated by Norm Konyu. 

### Synopsis
Cthulhu receives a phone call in the middle of the night, with the unknown caller insulting him and various stories from the Cthulhu Mythos. Afterwards, Cthulhu gets annoyed and decides to change his number again, so that no more humans can bother him.

The stories referenced in this book include:
*"The Rats in the Walls" 
*"The Nameless City"
*The Shadow Over Innsmouth 
*"Nyarlathotep" 
*"The Colour Out of Space"
*"The Cats of Ulthar" 
*At the Mountains of Madness 
*"The White Ship" 
*"History of the Necronomicon" 
*"The Terrible Old Man" 
*"The Dunwich Horror" 
*"Dagon"
*The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath
*"The Call of Cthulhu"

### Behind the Mythos
Although some parts of the book do come off as a more lighthearted parody, it appears to have been primarily written due to the author's distaste towards H. P. Lovecraft's racism.

fullContent:
"A Case of Royal Blood" is a sci-fi mystery short story by Steven-Elliot Altman first published in the 2003 anthology Shadows Over Baker Street. The story is set in the Cthulhu Mythos and features the great detective Sherlock Holmes joining forces with sci-fi and horror author H. G. Wells to investigate an alleged case of poltergeist activity.

### Synopsis
In 1888, H. G. Wells receives a message from Sherlock Holmes asking for his assistance in a very important case concerning the royal family of the Netherlands. The detective requests Wells' help due to the author's skeptical but profound knowledge of myth and folklore, as it's been claimed that the eight-year-old Princess Mina has been attacked by a poltergeist.

Holmes and Wells travel to the Netherlands and are greeted by Captain Jan Gent and Her Majesty the Queen Emma. They learn that the apparition who attacked young Mina takes the form of a teenage girl bearing a close resemblance to the Princess herself. At the time of the attack, Mina was reading a book in her room, which was locked from the inside. Captain Gent heard her screams and broke down the door, only to find the Princess unconscious, with blood on her throat and clothes, although there were no wounds. The Queen admits that she has also sighted the phantom girl on another occasion, as did several members of the staff. The Princess presents Wells and Holmes with a pair of silver rings blessed by the Pope, to protect them from evil.

After interviewing the servants and the King, who claims he has no enemies, Holmes instructs Wells to see Princess Mina again and tell her a bedtime story while Holmes is out investigating. Her choice of story reveals that she likes horror tales. This doesn't surprise Holmes, as he found that the book the young Princess was reading the night of the attack was far from appropriate for her age. It was in fact the Necronomicon, a grimoire that belonged to the Princess' late older half-brother, Prince Alexander, who was a freemason. Holmes deduces that Mina found the book and read it out of curiosity, which explains why she locked the door of her room, so her mother wouldn't see it. After he goes to bed, Wells has a nightmare in which he sees tentacled extraterrestrial creatures colonising Earth in the distant past and creating a race of protoplasmic monsters as slaves. These in turn would start hunting the fauna of primitive Earth and acquire a taste for blood before rebelling against their masters.

The next morning, Holmes, Wells, and Captain Gent visit an asylum to talk to a woman named Elisabeth Cookson, who was once Prince Alexander's lover and was arrested after threatening the King with a dagger. She mentions the "Dark Things", the same creatures that Wells saw in his nightmare, and wears a locket with a picture of her daughter, Sarah, who Gent recognises as the "phantom girl". fullContent:
"A Christmas Carnage" is a short story by author James S. Dorr, published in the Jesse Dedman and William C. Marchese collection Cthulhu Christmas Special and Other Lovecraftian Yuletide Tales in November 2017. It is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos by the narrator's offhand comment of being a former Miskatonic University student.

### Synopsis
A mentally-unstable man returns to his home at Christmas time to find the ghost of his great aunt Carol - a woman whom he has harboured a deep-seated sexual desire for ever since seeing an ancient pornographic Daguerrotype of her during childhood - awaiting him. She tells him that if they are to be together, then he must claim a toll in blood, one which will cost many, many lives. Taking up his chainsaw, the man embarks on a murderous spree, killing everyone in his building before moving on to other houses in the street.

When he returns to his rooms, Carol, now seemingly entirely corporeal, makes good on her promise, and the two spend a night of carnal bliss together.

When the police, investigating the brutal slayings which the man has perpetrated, break down his door the following morning, they find the man in bed, covered in blood, and embracing the corpse of a woman dead for over a century.

fullContent:
A Colder War is an English-language alternate history novella by Charles Stross written c. 1997. The story originally appeared in Spectrum SF No. 3 in 2000. It was one of Locus Online's 2000 "Recommended Reading" novelettes.

### Overview
The story fuses the Cold War and the Cthulhu Mythos by exploring the consequences of a follow-up to the expedition in H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness. "It's the Oliver North/Guns for Hostages scandal, seen from the viewpoint of a CIA bureaucrat, in a universe in which the entire Cthulhu Mythos is real," Teresa Nielsen Hayden said on Making Light.
Stross described the story's genesis:Back in 1997 when I began to explore this area, I started with a novelette titled "A Colder War", which made it pretty explicit. ACW was set in the future of Lovecraft's "At the Mountains of Madness" –- a future in which Nazi Germany, the USSR, and the USA had all found their uses for the ancient alien technologies found by the Pabodie expedition to Antarctica. It all ends in tears (and a fate worse than global thermonuclear annihilation -– the point of that story was to inject some horror back into Lovecraftiana by linking it implicitly to something truly horrifying, to anyone who grew up during the Cold War), but not before a Senator in a congressional hearing gets to utter the words, “Mister President, we cannot allow a Shoggoth Gap to emerge." Although the story has similarity to the later Stross novel The Atrocity Archives, they are set in different universes. "The online story 'A Colder War' is not part of the Bob Howard/Laundry series, but is an earlier short story along a similar vein, but far more serious (and deadly); there is no humor at all in this shorter story," says [http://scienceblogs.com/principles/2006/12/charles_stross_the_jennifer_mo.php#comment-299720 Marty Halper], Stross' editor on the relevant stories.

### Publication history
Following its original appearance in 2000, the story was later reprinted in Gardner Dozois's The Year's Best Science Fiction and in Stross' collections Toast: And Other Rusted Futures (in 2002) and Wireless: The Essential Charles Stross (2009). In late 2011, it appeared in two Cthulhu-themed anthologies: The Book of Cthulhu by Night Shade Books, and New Cthulhu: The Recent Weird by Prime Books.

### Synopsis
The Soviet Union has developed a superweapon called Project Koschei for use against NATO. (Koschei the Deathless is an evil immortal in Slavic mythology.)  Located at Chernobyl, Koschei is based on captured Nazi German research into an underwater city in the Baltic Sea. The Soviets have also deployed smaller weapons, called servitors, as found in the Kitab Al-Azif, in their occupation of Afghanistan.

Doing so violates the Dresden Agreement, a secret multinational treaty signed in 1931 after an expedition to a strange Antarctic plateau that appears on no maps. Even Adolf Hitler adhered to the treaty, which hides the existence of the supernatural entities from the publi

fullContent:
"A Creak in the Floor" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Providence, Rhode Island author Victoria Dalpe, published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
When Charlie, a young man from out of town, is invited by his old friend Pete to come stay with him for a while, he finds the home an enormous warehouse-like slum inhabited by dozens of colourful characters, and his friend missing.

Throughout a series of conversations with the residents, Charlie realises that the majority consensus between them is that Pete and his girlfriend had uncovered a nest of ghouls living beneath the streets and were killed by them. Unnerved by this story, he nevertheless follows one of the tenants to the expansive basement when she tells him she knows where Pete is. As shapes begin to stir through a hole in the basement wall, she explains that the stories are in fact true, and that Charlie himself now poses a problem to the creatures he has seen…

### Characters
* Charlie, a young man looking for a new start in a new town.
* Dally, a resident who appears to function as something of a superintendent for the building.
* Bernadette, a resident heavily implied to be a ghoul herself.
* Mal, another resident who claims to have been attacked by the creatures some years previously.

fullContent:
"A Crusader to Protect" is a short story, written by Natsume Akatsuki as part of his KonoSuba light novel series. It was originally released as a special booklet that came with a Blu-ray disc for the anime adaptation in 2016 and was later featured in the first volume of the Yorimichi anthology series, published by Kadokawa in 2020.

### Synopsis
Kazuma and his companions investigate a large forest located towards the south of Axel, after finding out about a mysterious high-bounty monster that is said to be lurking there. Although they managed to escape the monster when Megumin blasted it with her Explosion spell during their encounter, it was still able to put a curse on Darkness that made her physically weak. The others were forced to take care of Darkness for a while until the monster was hit by a second Explosion, finally destroying it and breaking the curse.

### Behind the Mythos
The monster that the protagonists encountered was clearly meant to be Nyarlathotep, as it is explicitly referred to by the aliases "The Mighty Messenger" and "Crawling Chaos". Its physical description also recalls certain avatars of Nyarlathotep, being a humanoid creature with tentacles and no visible eyes. However, it should be noted that the Cthulhu Mythos is a fictional story in the KonoSuba universe and the entity was an earth spirit that got its appearance from scanning the thoughts of the first person it met, meaning that it technically isn't the actual Nyarlathotep. Additionally, Nyarlathotep was stated to be "an evil god that is associated with the earth", referencing August Derleth's Elemental classification.

fullContent:
"A Dormant Sense of Strangeness" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Henry V. O'Neil, writing as Vincent H. O'Neil. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 1 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in April 2018.

### Synopsis
Andrew Lippman is a man who has been browbeaten and forced into a life of drudgery for years by family and partners alike. One day, while watching graffiti artists work their magic on an adjacent bridge structure, he finds his passion for painting reignited, and embraces it wholeheartedly.

As he begins to rediscover himself, he notices furred, shadowy creatures watching him as he paints. Visiting his old family mausoleum - a place where he recalls seeing a similar being as a child - he is confronted by a pack of the creatures, who accept him as one of their own.

The story concludes with Lippman taking a photograph of one of the creatures to paint for his father: one whom he notes his father has not seen since it was a baby…

### Behind the Mythos
The premise of an artist discovering his roots as a graveyard-dwelling monster and resolving to paint them is clearly intended to parallel H. P. Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model." Although the stories show different methods in the artist's becoming one with their "tribe" or "clan" the similarities are obvious, and the resemblance of the creatures in "A Dormant Sense of Strangeness" to Pickman's ghouls is striking.

fullContent:
"A Fatal Exception Has Occurred at..." is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Alan Dean Foster, first published in the 2002 anthology The Children of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
A man named Wilbur, who has managed to gain access to the Necronomicon, has scanned the entire book and threatens to post it online unless the American government pays him ten million dollars. FBI agent Bob Hayes explains to his superiors that this would be disastrous, as it would mean public access to spells that can summon monumentally dangerous entities. Wilbur, in fact, has already claimed responsibility for an earthquake in Denver and a ship sinking in Pohnpei. Despite the Bureau's skepticism, they decide to send Hayes off to investigate along with another agent named Spitzer.

The agents visit a man named Herman Rumford, who has great knowledge of occult matters, and who is already talking to Wilbur online, although he hasn't been able to track his location. Wilbur demands the money, and tells the agents to turn on the TV set in a few hours to convince them that he's serious. When they do so, they see the news that the National Aquarium in Baltimore has collapsed into the sea. Wilbur reveals that he's been in contact with the forces of Cthulhu, and plans on summoning the minions of Ithaqua next, so new disasters will keep piling up until they pay him.

Hayes and Spitzer debate what to do, as the FBI still hasn't been able to track down Wilbur's location. Rumford suggests that he might be able to help, but won't proceed without authorization, which the agents grant him. Half an hour later, Rumford announces that his idea has worked, and initiates another chat with Wilbur, warning him not to post the Necronomicon, or there would be consequences. Wilbur shrugs this off, so Rumford inserts a flash drive into his computer and starts hacking. When he's done, Wilbur sends increasingly desperate messages, demanding to know what's going on, and then suddenly stops mid-sentence.

The agents deduce that Rumford sent Wilbur some kind of malware that erased the latter's files and wrecked his machine. Rumford muses about the kinds of things that "can be digitized these days", but refuses to elaborate on what exactly he sent Wilbur. However, he does makes a copy of his flash drive and gives it to the agents, along with instructions on how to use in case something like this ever happens again. The instructions begin with the words "To download Shoggoth".

"A Feast of Death" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Lee Clark Zumpe.

### Synopsis
A group of British prisoners of war during the First World War are transferred from Turkish hands to a German labour camp in the Taurus Mountains. There the camp commandant, an accomplished occultist, is using the detainees as slave labour to dig his way into a hillside in order to uncover the entity that sleeps within. However, the creature awakens before the commandant is ready for it, and only a single survivor escapes the ensuing carnage.

### Characters

*Lieutenant Cyril MacReady, British POW.
*Corporal Guy Blacklock, British POW.
*Corporal Wyndham Hutchison, British POW.
*Oberstleutnant Waldemar von Edelsheim, labour camp commandant.

### Publication History
"A Feast of Death" was published in the Brian M. Sammons/Glynn Owen Barrass-edited anthology World War Cthulhu in 2014.

shortDefinition: "A Finger's Worth of Coal" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Richard Dansky. It was first published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.  ### Synopsis When the firemen aboard the legen...
fullContent:
"A Finger's Worth of Coal" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Richard Dansky. It was first published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.

### Synopsis
When the firemen aboard the legendary passenger train the Orient Express begin to suffer from inexplicable madnesses, a young scholar by the name of Walters, a man with two crippled fingers on one hand, conducts his own investigations. During the course of these, he and another passenger are unexpectedly transported into the distant past by an unknown force, where they encounter a bizarre, inhuman creature; Walters is returned to the present in time to avoid a grisly fate, but the other man is not so fortunate.

Realising that the utterances made by the deranged fireman translate from Magyar to "coal," Walters decides to look into the train's fuel stocks. There, he uncovers a body, preserved in the strata for untold aeons- and holding a strange, futuristic weapon in a hand with two twisted fingers. In the aftermath, Walters once again finds himself transported into the past, which he now believes to be the Carboniferous period, and resolves to hunt down the monstrous creatures which he believes to be responsible for his current predicament.

### Behind the Mythos
"A Finger's Worth of Coal" contains no direct references to the Cthulhu Mythos or the works of H. P. Lovecraft, however the description of the monstrous beings encountered by Walters in the Carboniferous is clearly intended to evoke Lovecraft’s Yithians: "huge … wet gray cone that rose up to a series of four odd points. What only could be described as tentacles drooped from these, and Walters could not fail to note that the two extended in his direction ended in lurid claws clutching odd silvery objects. A third blossomed into a cluster of bright red mushrooms, while the fourth was festooned with bulging, inhuman eyes." Another mention of books on the subject detailing "pre- and post-human civilizations" would appear to support this.

### Publication History
* Madness on the Orient Express (2014)
* A Meeting in the Devil's House (2023)

"A Forty Grain Weight of Nephrite" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and comic book creator Steven Philip Jones. Taking place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting, it was published in the thematic anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022.

### Synopsis
When a valuable artefact known as the Xiamen Bi, Kymani Jones, a private investigator specialising in high-end art thefts, is called to San Fransisco to investigate. Quickly uncovering the method by which the Bi was taken - a sophisticated alteration to the building's basic structure which was clearly planned years in advance - they set out to locate its whereabouts.

Tracking the Bi to Chinatown, Kymani joins forces with another who is on its trail: a man known only as Shibing, who works for the mysterious order known as the Foundation. Shibing tells Kymani that the Bi has been taken by the Red Coterie, an organisation dedicated to collecting items of power for their own reasons. Finding the Bi's hiding place beneath a disused housing block in Chinatown, they face down the Lady with the Red Parasol - a powerful member of the Coterie - and Shibing spirits the Bi away, leaving Kymani to report their failure to locate the artefact.

### Connections
The Foundation, Red Coterie, and Lady with the Red Parasol are all recurrent elements in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting, with the Foundation and Coterie most often being placed at odds with one another.

"A Gentleman from Mexico" is a short story by Mark Samuels that originally appeared in Summer Chills: Tales of Vacation Horror (Carroll & Graf, 2007). It tells the story of a London literary agent who meets a man in Mexico who acts, speaks, and writes exactly like H. P. Lovecraft--yet insists that he is merely a lunatic who is under the delusion that he is Lovecraft.

### Characters

* Víctor Armstrong: A London literary agent who specializes in anthologies featuring "tales depicting the weird and uncanny."
* Juan San Isidro: A "so-called underground poet specialising in sinister verse written in the Náhuatl language," rumoured to have "links with the narcosatánicos." A "notorious drunk" in his mid-thirties who is "scarcely ever sober," he is a "huge bear of a man" with an "immense bulk," shoulder-length "lank black hair," and "a shaggy goatee beard." He looks "twice his actual age."
* Felipe López:  He was once "a fanatical devotee of Lovecraft’s life and work," one of those "freaks who adhere to the outlandish belief that, rather than writing fiction, Lovecraft had unconscious access to ultramundane dimensions." Since March 15, 2003, he has (as he puts it) "been subject to a delusion whereby the identity of Lovecraft completely supplanted my own." His fiction resembles "a previously undiscovered work written by Lovecraft himself," with "the same sense of nightmarish authenticity as the best of the Providence author’s tales." López has "an olive complexion" and "the features of a mestizo," is "perfectly clean-shaven with "short black hair...parted neatly on the left-hand side," and is "about forty years old." He has a "slight stoop," and his speech and accent is "pure, authentic New England Yankee."

### Publication History
The story has been repeatedly reprinted, including in The Mammoth Book of Best New Horror Volume Nineteen (Running Press, 2008), The Book of Cthulhu II (Night Shade Books, 2012), and A Mountain Walked (Centipede Press, 2014).

"A Gift from the Stars" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Sheldon Woodbury. It was first published in the thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark by James Ward Kirk Publishing in November 2015.

### Synopsis
Told in the form of a letter from H. P. Lovecraft to Clark Ashton Smith, "A Gift from the Stars" describes how Lovecraft's mother slowly devolved into insanity, whispering the secrets her broken mind had learned to her son during his formative years.

It culminates with Lovecraft as an adult attending his mother's deathbed in an insane asylum, where Lovecraft himself is exposed to the horrific truth of her ravings, and his belief that he is to suffer the same fate as she.

"A God's Eye View" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in the collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
Wendell Willis, now incarcerated in the Hillsdale Asylum, an institution for the criminally insane, attempts to escape by communing with the dark god Chor-Tal. The divinity agrees to aid him by magically disguising the man as a security guard, but upon his escape, Willis is attacked and presumably killed by the jealous husband of a woman with whom the guard had been having an affair.

### Trivia
*Both Wendell Willis and Chor-Tal are semi-recurrent characters created by Ron Shiflet for his Cthulhu Mythos fiction: the former made his first appearance in "When in Leng…" (1998), the latter in "The Last Laugh" (1997).

fullContent:
A Guide to the Cthulhu Cult is a pseudo-factual book based on the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published by Armitage House in 1998, written by Fred L. Pelton and edited by Pierre De Hammais. 

The original title of the work, as embossed on its cover is "A Complete Survey of the Cthulhu Mythos by Fred L. Pelton". It was written as a labor of love. Pelton himself typed the entire manuscript on book paper and had it bound in black cloth, similar to the Arkham House books. The original book measures 6 5/8" x 10 1/2" x 7/8", and has the title THE CTHULHU MYTHOS stamped on the spine in gold. 

Interestingly, although A Guide to the Cthulhu Cult contains numerous quotes from "The Sussex Manuscript", the extant incomplete copy of that other Pelton work does not agree with the quotes used in the Guide. Since there is a lineage for "The Sussex Manuscript", with a copy used by Lin Carter and Edward P. Berglund, and a separate copy delivered to August Derleth and never returned, it is possible that a different and unseen version of The Sussex Manuscript exists or once existed, in the possession of Derleth.

A Handful of Dust: The Witch Cycle Part 2 is a scenario supplement for the Delta Green setting of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. Written by Australian author and games designer David Conyers, it was published by Call of Cthulhu licensee Yog-Sothoth.com in 2003.

### Overview


The story was originally written as a tournament game for the Melbourne, Australia tournament Conquest 1994, hosted by The Cthulhu Conglomerate. As this predated any mainstream release of Delta Green material (that setting being confined to fanzine releases in The Unspeakable Oath at the time) the original story was devoid of any references to the setting. When it was published in 2003 by Yog-Sothoth.com, the original plot - which involved the players taking part in an FBI investigation - was transplanted into a Delta Green background.

*Amongst the occult tomes consulted by the McCalls during their experiments were "a particularly worrisome text said to have been written by a mad Arab", most likely intended to be the Necronomicon, and "a copy of Prinn’s tome on spells and Saracenic rituals", a reference to De Vermis Mysteriis.

fullContent:
"A Honeymoon in Averoigne" is a short story by author Trevor O. Childers, linked to the Cthulhu Mythos through its setting of Averoigne, a fictional French province created by Clark Ashton Smith. It was published in the Halloween 2018 edition of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press.

### Synopsis
American tourists Greg and Stephanie, on their honeymoon in the rural province of Averoigne, decide to take a day trip to the ancient chapel at Perigon. Although somewhat disconcerted by the atmosphere surrounding the ruins, they have an enjoyable day. Things take a turn for the worse, however, when a storm rolls in, and dark forces conspire to lose them in the woods, eventually bringing them out on the steps of the malignant Chateau Faussesflammes.

Seeking refuge in the building, they find it strangely unaffected by the ravages of time and, exploring further, discover a freshly-laid banquet, although nobody in attendance to partake. As the evening progresses, Greg notices that Stephanie has become enchanted with the place, seemingly losing herself entirely in the haunting charm that Faussesflammes exudes.

Later, Greg wakes up alone and, investigating, finds Stephanie in the grand ballroom dancing with someone who is not there. Shaking her out of her trance, the two attempt to escape but are hindered at every turn by the dark forces which now inhabit the Chateau. Using their flare gun to clear the final stretch before the great doors, Greg emerges into the sunlight, only to find that Stephanie is no longer by his side. With grim determination he turns around and prepares to re-enter the ruins…

### Behind the Mythos
A number of elements of Clark Ashton Smith's Averoigne are mentioned in the story, such as the ones previously mentioned, as well as the city of Vyones. In addition, the events of several of his stories - "The Disinterment of Venus," "A Rendezvous in Averoigne," "The Colossus of Ylourgne," and "The End of the Story" - are all referenced.

"A Lovecraft Movie/Television Show to be Proud of" is a short non-fiction piece by author Patrick Crocker. It was published in the Edward P. Berglund-edited online fanzine Nightscapes in March 1999.

### Overview
The work describes the author's view of a perfect film adaptation of one of H. P. Lovecraft's stories, complete with ideas on cast and director, and uses "The Call of Cthulhu" as a case study. 

It then moves on to question why Lovecraftian elements are not more common in television shows, with a particular emphasis on why The X-Files, one of the most-watched shows in the world at the time of publication, is a prime example of how easy it would be to integrate the Cthulhu Mythos into popular television.

fullContent:
"A Madness from the Vaults" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Ramsey Campbell. It is set on the planet Tond, first mentioned in "The Inhabitant of the Lake".

Two different versions of "A Madness from the Vaults" are known to exist. In the introduction to his collection Cold Print, Campbell explains that he wrote the first version in 1962, but felt at the time that it was "too fantastic" for inclusion in The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, so it ended up being published in a fanzine instead. In 1971, when asked if he could contribute a story to the Lovecraft-dedicated anthology HPL, Campbell decided to submit "A Madness from the Vaults", but felt upon rereading it that the tale contained an excessive amount of "sadism". Unsatisfied, he reworked it into what he described as "virtually a new story under the same title". The two versions have since been published together in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu #43 (Hallowmass 1986).

### Synopsis
### 1972 version
On the planet Tond, the city of Derd was built by the Yarkdao atop the ruins of a far more ancient civilisation. Underneath the city is a vast labyrinth of vaults, the original purpose of which is unknown to the Yarkdao, who are unwilling to explore them due to old legends. At one point, Opojollac, the cruel and tyrannical governor of Derd, decretes that all crimes will be punished by casting the criminal into the underground vaults.

One day, a Yarkdao administrator announces to Opojollac that the body of a Yarkdao, crushed and trampled beyond recognition, has been found near one of the vaults' entrances, along with the tracks of an unknown beast with an "ill-matched number of limbs". Further investigations reveal several other cases of citizens killed by the beast, which seems to be moving along the many entrances to the vaults, closer and closer to Opojollac's palace. Reluctantly, the governor decides to seek help from the Globes of Hakkthu, alone because language is power on Tond, and only Opojollac has the language to converse with such powerful beings.

After traveling through the white desert, Opojollac enters a cloud of sand and speaks to the Globes, who have come to Tond from the depths of space at the time of the world's formation. They in turn explain that the vaults were built to contain a monstrous avatar of Azathoth. As the beast has finally found its way from the center of the labyrinth to its entrances, the Globes instruct Opojollac to enter the vaults and move a lever that will contain the monster once again.

By the time Opojollac returns to Derd, he finds the city empty, and concludes that it has been abandoned during his absence. Inside the vaults, a line of light appears to guide him to the deepest chambers, where the lever is located. fullContent:
"A Mountain Walked" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan. It first appeared in the September 2012 issue of Sirenia Digest.

The title comes from a passage from H. P. Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu", in a description of the titular entity: The Thing cannot be described -- there is no language for such abysms of shrieking and immemorial lunacy, such eldritch contradictions of all matter, force, and cosmic order. A mountain walked, or stumbled.

### Synopsis
The story is presented as "Excerpts from the Field Journal of Arthur Lakes During His Explorations for Saurians and Fossil Remains in the Wyoming Territory (June 1879)"; Lakes was a historical geologist, as was William Hallow (or Harlow) Reed, and they both worked for famed paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh; Marsh really did visit their excavations in 1879, and did butt heads with Lakes' "bone sharp" William Holland Reed. 

In the story, Lakes and Reed first hear "a most peculiar booming" in the sky. Then while digging, they strike a spring that produces "water foul and oily," with a "most noisome odour as if from decaying vegetation"; later they find the water has "an oily iridescent sheen".  

When Marsh arrives, he finds an "Indian stone fetish or lithic artefact which could be, at a casual glance, taken for the effigy of some winged demon as from the illustrations of Gustave Doré." Reed insists that taking the figurine will cause unnecessary trouble with the Sioux or Cheyenne, and he and Marsh have an escalating quarrel over it. The meat of wild game turns tainted, a blood-red ring is seen around the Moon, a dust storm lasts for days.  

Finally, one night, a mysterious figure appears at the camp: A nude woman, seven or eight feet tall, "her skin and hair...as white as a fresh snowfall.... [T]he lankiness of her arms and legs gave her a faintly insectile semblance...both grotesque and unspeakably beautiful." Behind her "a titanic form stood, blotting out both the stars and moon." She silently demands the return of the figurine; Reed threatens to shoot Marsh if he does not comply. He acquiesces, and it disappears from his hand and reappears in hers, leaving a spot of frostbite behind. 

No one talks again about the experience, but Lakes says he is compelled to write it down: What was witnessed, for all its horror, I cannot wish to forget as it hints at a world even more distant and ultimately impervious to our understanding than the bygone ages and their fauna hinted at by our diggings. 

### Behind the Mythos
The winged fetish recalls similar statuettes in "The Call of Cthulhu", from which the story takes its title. The iridescent water and tainted meat recalls the contamination from the meteorite in "The Colour Out of Space".

Ruthanna Emrys suggests that the "titanic form" seen at the campsite is not Cthulhu, but rather an unnamed entity in "The Call of Cthulhu" that escapes from R'lyeh just before Cthulhu's emergence--"a darkness almost material" that "burst forth like smoke from i

fullContent:
A Night in the Lonesome October is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by the late American author Roger Zelazny. First published by AvoNova/William Morrow in August 1993, it was the last book published before Zelazny's death in 1995, and was nominated for the Nebula Award for Best Novel in 1994.

### Overview
A delightful panache of archetypical characters from the realm of classic horror and suspense, including Jack the Ripper, Dracula, the Wolf Man, Frankenstein, and Sherlock Holmes, along with assorted witches, clergy, druids, mad monks, Hermetic occultists and their animal familiars (most of the story being told through the eyes of Jack's demon-dog Snuff) of a month spent to open or defend the world from the coming of the Elder Gods. In the interim, we get a trip to the Dreamlands, with a cat for a guide no less. No particularly unique insights to the Mythos, but generally a lot of fun.

### Publication History
Since its first printing, A Night in the Lonesome October has been reissued numerous times, including by The Easton Press (1993), Orbit (1994), J'ai Lu (1995, French-language edition), Avon/HarperCollins (2007), Chicago Review Press (2014), Farrago (2016), and Edizioni Hypnos (2020, Italian-language edition).

"A Noble Endeavor" is a short story by American author Lucy A. Snyder.

### Synopsis
Set in an alternate timeline where clockwork men are replacing human labourers and flying machines dot the skies, a young black slave girl is called to help one of her plantation masters in his laboratory. The man, who has a dark vision of eugenics, plans to use the fruits of his labour to travel through time, but an accident summons forth a powerful entity which grants the girl a wish; she uses this wish to wipe the dark side of human nature from history, but her course of action has a drastic effect on the dominant lifeforms of Earth…

### Characters

*Mariette, a young slave on a Deep South plantation.
*Dr. Bronson, a twisted scientist with a goal of racial annihilation.
*Ylem, a cosmic entity of seemingly limitless power.

### Publication History
"A Noble Endeavor" has appeared in the anthologies Steampunk Universe (2018), Garden of Eldritch Delights (2018) and the Weirdbook Annual 2 (2019).

shortDefinition: "A Note on the Cthulhu Mythos" is a short non-fiction essay by August Derleth, included as an appendix in his 1962 collection The Trail of Cthulhu.  ### Contents In the essay, Derleth lays down his interpretation of the mythology created by his late ...
fullContent:
"A Note on the Cthulhu Mythos" is a short non-fiction essay by August Derleth, included as an appendix in his 1962 collection The Trail of Cthulhu.

### Contents
In the essay, Derleth lays down his interpretation of the mythology created by his late friend H. P. Lovecraft, its basic themes and most important deities, and how the system has been developed gradually. Although he cautions that there is "no hard and fast line separating Lovecraft's Dunsanian tales from the stories which are definitely part of the Mythos", Derlerth defines the latter as consisting primarily of 13 Lovecraft stories: "The Nameless City", "The Festival", "The Call of Cthulhu" (in which he claims the Mythos gained "its first indication of shape"), "The Colour Out of Space", "The Dunwich Horror", The Whisperer in Darkness, "The Dreams in the Witch-House", "The Haunter of the Dark", The Shadow Over Innsmouth, The Shadow Out of Time, At the Mountains of Madness, The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, and "The Thing on the Doorstep".

Controversially, Derleth ascribes to Lovecraft the idea that the Mythos revolves around an age-old conflict between the Elder Gods, which represent order, and the Great Old Ones, their enemies, which represent "the forces of evil". In truth, this concept is not explicitly present anywhere in Lovecraft's works, although it is present in Derleth's own Mythos stories, some of which were published while Lovecraft was still alive and the two authors corresponded frequently.

On a less controversial note, Derleth also defends Lovecraft from the attacks of Colin Wilson and other critics, and ensures that the author saw his work for what it was: fiction, intended "for his own entertainment" as well as his readers'. He also points out that Lovecraft himself "freely borrowed trivial but colorful details from other writers--Poe, Machen, Lord Dunsany, Ambrose Bierce, Robert W. Chambers" and encouraged others to likewise partake from his own creations.

"A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin" is a tragic poem of romance by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Written circa 27 May 1918, its first known publication was in the collection The Ancient Track by Night Shade Books in 2001.

### Overview
Taking place around the town of Appleton, Wisconsin, USA, the piece concerns the romantic feelings possessed by a small group of people for each other, and their actions in pursuing these interests.

After a woman named Chloe rejects his advances, Strephon instead takes up with a woman named Hecatissa. Chloe, now jealous that Strephon has found another, spitefully steals the man away. Hecatissa, despondent at this turn of events, attempts to take her own life by casting herself into the Fox River; however, the god of the river takes pity on her and refuses to take her soul, casting her back onto its banks.

fullContent:
"A Photograph From Life" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and Lovecraft scholar Robert M. Price. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
Detective Thomas Malone is assigned to investigate the disappearance of the eccentric Bostonian artist Richard Upton Pickman. After interviewing his associate Thurber (whose first name Price gives as Ethan) the two take a trip to Pickman's studio, and the two investigate a suspicious well in the basement. Traversing the seemingly-endless stairs contained within, they find themselves in the Dreamlands, and quickly happen upon Pickman himself. For an unexplained reason, Pickman transforms himself into a ghoul and kills Thurber, though Malone manages to escape and presumably make his way back to the waking world.

### Behind the Mythos
Thomas Malone is possibly the character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1927 short story "The Horror at Red Hook", although this is never confirmed. If this is the case, whether the story takes place before or after the events described in "The Horror at Red Hook" is uncertain, although it seems likely to be the latter.

"A Pickman Original" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Logan Noble. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
Wealthy art lover Walter, a man with an obsessional interest in the vanished artist Richard Upton Pickman, learns that a previously-unseen collection of Pickman's works has come up for sale. He quickly contacts the seller and buys the works, one of which is wrapped in protective paper and accompanied by a note warning of dire consequences should anyone look upon it.

When Walter gets the piece home, he peels off the covering and admires at the work, titled The Witch of Copp's Hill, which shows a picture of a pack of ghouls cavorting in a cemetery no more than a mile from Walter's home. As he looks on, the picture begins to change, with the ghouls tearing a victim to pieces and prostrating themselves in front of a mysterious woman, before turning to stare directly at him.

Determined to prove to himself that what he had just witnessed was a hallucination, Walter makes his way to the cemetery. However, upon his arrival he discovers to his horror that what he witnessed was no mere hallucination, but a vision of his fate.

One morning, two young children, Harry and Kaylee, receive a parcel in the mail from their Uncle Howard containing a map to the Antarctic. Hopping into their parents' biplane, they follow the directions and discover an abandoned camp and an ancient city, before having a picnic with some very special penguins. Before they can do any more, they are frightened off by an overly inquisitive Shoggoth, who only wanted to meet the newcomers.

"A Pleasure in Madness" is a short story by American author C. J. Henderson, and forms the final chapter in the Arkham Detective Agency series begun with "The Idea of Fear".

### Synopsis
After the events of the disastrous Pabodie Expedition described in At the Mountains of Madness reached the outside world, the US government established a research facility in the Antarctic with the goal of investigating the catacombs concealed beneath the surface.

After many decades of governmental restriction, a delegation of scientists from Massachusetts' Miskatonic University are invited to lend their expertise to the expedition, with Frank Nardi  accompanying the group as security. However, unknown to all, the facility has been infiltrated by an ancient enemy with its own designs on mankind. Nardi and one of the other scientists, Professor Knight, are able to put a stop to the scheme and destroy the facility, but are driven insane in the process.

### Characters

*Frank Nardi, former New York cop turned Private Detective.
*Professor Piers Knight, curator at the Brooklyn Museum, New York.
*Harold Clemmens, president of Miskatonic University, Massachusetts.

### Publication History
"A Pleasure in Madness" was written by C. J. Henderson before his death in 2014, but did not see publication until the release of Arkham Detective Agency, edited by Henderson's friend Brian M. Sammons, in 2017.

### Mythos Connections

*The primary antagonists of the story are the ancient Shoggoths created by H. P. Lovecraft himself.
*The main setting for the story is the subterranean city described in At the Mountains of Madness.
*Miskatonic University and some of its faculty are featured, and the Pabodie Expedition, William Dyer, and Danforth are all made mention of.

When 21-year-old Paul Pennywell discovers that he is not as alone in the world as he thought, he travels to England to meet the surviving members of his family. shortDefinition: Against the Grain is a novel written by Joris-Karl Huysmans, published in French as À rebours in 1884. It was also translated into English as Against Nature. Its title in English would literally translate as "Backwards." The current translation into ...
fullContent:
Against the Grain is a novel written by Joris-Karl Huysmans, published in French as À rebours in 1884. It was also translated into English as Against Nature. Its title in English would literally translate as "Backwards." The current translation into English is that of Robert Baldick.

In both its style and its subject, the work epitomizes the decadence of late 19th-century French elite culture. As such, and as one of H. P. Lovecraft's favorite novels, one can see this work as foundational to both Robert W. Chambers' The King in Yellow but also to Lovecraft's Cosmicism and also in particular to the doomed protagonists of his short story "The Hound". The grave robbers in The Hound are decadent aesthetes who rob graves to assuage their ennui, not for any profound reason, good or bad, at all.

Such books as Against the Grain were seen in Paris as lascivious or forbidden and were wrapped in yellow paper to alert the reader to their lascivious content. In Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray (1891), a major corrupting influence on Dorian is "the yellow book" which Lord Henry sends over to amuse him after the suicide of his first love. This "yellow book" is understood by critics to be A Rebours. The resemblance to The King in Yellow is obvious.

The protagonist of Against Nature, Des Esseintes, exhibits the debilitating symptoms of neurasthenia, a generalized psychosomatic disorder that came into vogue during that period. In this respect he of course overlaps with the very real nerve condition suffered by Lovecraft due to the psychological and verbal abuse inflicted upon him by his mother.

The condition Des Esseintes embraces necessitates his temporary retirement from Paris to his country estate at Fontenay. Once there, he sets his course “against the grain” of ordinary life. Cloistered in luxury, Des Esseintes contrives a regimen of exquisite sensualism. He devises a “mouth organ” from which he sips “harmonic” combinations of liqueurs. He cultivates exotic flora and arranges to have the shell of a live tortoise inlaid with jewels. His overly refined tastes encompass perfumes, monastic music, visionary painting, and the poetry of Stéphane Mallarmé. Unchecked indulgence only deepens his malaise, however, prompting his doctor to order him back to Paris. The story ends there, with an appeal by Des Esseintes for pity from a God he only vaguely believes in. Although the author intended the work for a select group of readers, it has become a sourcebook on fin-de-siècle aestheticism.

shortDefinition: "A Redress for Andromeda (2001)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in October Dreams: A Celebration of Halloween (Cemetery Dance Publications, 2000). It begins Kiernan's Dandridge Cycle, a series of interconnected stories abo...
fullContent:
"A Redress for Andromeda (2001)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in October Dreams: A Celebration of Halloween (Cemetery Dance Publications, 2000). It begins Kiernan's Dandridge Cycle, a series of interconnected stories about a mysterious house on the coast of Northern California and the sacrifice hidden beneath it.

This story introduces the Dandridge House, built in 1890 on the Northern California coast by someone named Dandridge, a "tall gabled house with its turrets and lightning rods." In the 1960s, "it was one of those places that hippies and occultists liked to haunt." In 2001, Tara, an ichthyologist at the Monterrey Bay Aquarium, is invited to a Halloween party there, by her friend Darren Quince, that turns out to be a strange annual ritual. Given a silver coin, she joins a procession down stairs cut into the rock below the house, down to a grotto where a woman, like Andromeda in the myth of Perseus, is chained to a rock in a pool of seawater. The "thing that was a woman once" has "pulpy cheese-white skin," "crimson tentacles between her alabaster thighs," and barnacles encrusting her legs.

“She keeps the balance," Darren tells Tara. "She stands between the worlds.... She watches all the gates.” He tells her to drop her coin into the pool: "It helps her hold the line.”

The story ends with Tara knowing that she is now bound to be part of the ritual every year.

### Publication History
"A Redress for Andromeda" was reprinted in The Weird: A Compendium of Strange and Dark Stories (Corvus, 2011; Tor, 2012). It also appears in Kiernan's collections To Charles Fort, with Love (Subterranean Press, 2005) and Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018; Subterranean Press, 2019).

shortDefinition: "A Reminiscence of Dr. Samuel Johnson" is a short story written in 1917 by horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in the September 1917 issue of The United Amateur, under the pseudonym Humphrey Littlewit, Esq.  The story is a s...
fullContent:
"A Reminiscence of Dr. Samuel Johnson" is a short story written in 1917 by horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in the September 1917 issue of The United Amateur, under the pseudonym Humphrey Littlewit, Esq.

The story is a spoof of Lovecraft's antiquarian affectations. Littlewit, the narrator, is born August 20, 1690–200 years to the day before Lovecraft's birthdate—making him nearly 228 years old as he writes a memoir. As the title indicates, the narrative consists of anecdotes about Littlewit's friendship with the famous 18th century English writer, linguist and literary critic Dr. Samuel Johnson.

Critic Daniel Harms writes, "While not one of the most inspired of his pieces, it at least shows that HPL realized his pretensions... of being an older, cultured gentleman of an earlier era, and could make fun of himself."

fullContent:
"A Rendezvous in Averoigne" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, first published in April/May 1931 issue of Weird Tales. It is part of Smith's cycle of stories set in Averoigne, a fictionalized province of Medieval France.

It was the title story of a collection of Smith's fantastic fiction published by Arkham House in 1988.

### Characters

* Gérard de l’Automne, a professional troubadour "of much note and merit" who is the guest of the Comte de la Frênaie. He is enamored with Fleurette Cochin.
* Fleurette Cochin, the daughter of a well-to-do mercer named Guillaume Cochin, noted for her "blond piquancy." She has agreed to a rendezvous with Gérard de l’Automne in the forest of Averoigne.
* Sieur Hugh du Malinbois, the master of Château des Faussesflammes. A notorious sorcerer who has been an undead vampire for some 200 years. He is described as "inordinately tall and cadaverous,,,dressed in black garments of a superannuate mode. His lips were strangely red, amid his bluish beard and the mortuary whiteness of his face."
* Agathe du Malinbois,  the chatelaine of Château des Faussesflammes. Like her husband, a sorceress turned vampire. She is "clad in a gown of emerald green that matched her eyes; in her face was the pallor of dead things, together with a faery beauty; and her lips were dyed as with the scarlet of newly flowing blood."

### Publication History
After its initial appearance, it was reprinted by Weird Tales in the January 1939 issue. It was also featured in the February 1971 issue of the Magazine of Horror.

It has been included in several collections of Smith's fiction, including Out of Space and Time (Arkham House, 1942), A Rendezvous in Averoigne: The Best Fantastic Tales of Clark Ashton Smith (Arkham House, 1988), The Emperor of Dreams (Gollancz/Orion, 2002), and The Door to Saturn: Volume Two of the Collected Fantasies of Clark Ashton Smith (Night Shade Books, 2007), as well as the Averoigne anthologies The Averoigne Archives (Pickman's Press, 2019) and The Averoigne Chronicles (Hippocampus Press, 2021).

It frequently appears in anthologies of vampire stories, such as A Feast of Blood (Avon, 1967), Vampires (Doubleday, 1987), The Penguin Book of Vampire Stories (Penguin Books, 1988), and Weird Vampire Tales (Gramercy Books, 1992), as well as The Oxford Book of Gothic Tales (Oxford University Press, 1992).

"A Shop in Go-by Street" is a short story by Lord Dunsany that first appeared in his Tales of Three Hemispheres (John W. Luce, 1919). It is a sequel to Dunsany's story "Idle Days on the Yann," and has been cited as a key inspiration for H. P. Lovecraft's conception of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
The narrator from "Idle Days on the Yann" wants to return to the Yann to see his friends from the ship Bird of the River. But he hasforgotten the way to those little cottages on the edge of the fields we know whose upper windows, though dim with antique cobwebs, look out on the fields we know not and are the starting-point of all adventure in all the Lands of Dream.So he goes to "the shop of a dreamer who lives not far from the Embankment in the City"; it is on a street "that has never been seen before; it is named Go-by Street and runs out of the Strand if you look very closely." At this shop, you must ask for something that the old man who runs it doesn't have, though he stocks many unlikely things. So he asks for "Abama and Pharpah, rivers of Damascus.... Two and a half yards of each, to be delivered to my flat." 

When the old man admits he is out of these rivers, the dreamer asks the way to those little cottages the look out upon the fields we know not. The shopkeep takes him to "a dingy lumber-room full of idols," which he calls "the heaven of the gods who sleep." "All those," he explains, "that are not worshipped now are asleep." ""Then does Time not kill the gods?" the narrator asks, and is told, "No. But for three or four thousand years a god is worshipped and for three or four he sleeps."

Asked about those "that teach us of new gods," the old man says: "They hear the old ones stirring in their sleep being about to wake, because the dawn is breaking and the priests crow. These are the happy prophets: unhappy are they that hear some old god speak while he sleeps still being deep in slumber, and prophesy and prophesy and no dawn comes.The shopkeep reluctantly tells the narrator the way to the cottages: "You go out by the back door and turn to the right." From the back, the shop appears to be of an incredible age, with a thatched roof; it bears an ancient sign, "Licensed to sell weasels and jade earrings." He walks down a grassy street lined with similar houses until he comes to open fields and the cottages he seeks. Flowers rise up from these gardens as he watches and burst into purple bloom, singing softly; he asks about them of a "very old witch" who comes out of one of the cottages. "Hush! Hush!" she said, "I am putting the poets to bed. These flowers are their dreams." He finds they are "singing of my own childhood and of things that happened there."

He looks out the window to see the mountains of faëry, and "the old gap in the blue-grey hills...whence one sees the Lands of Dream." He leaves the witch "knitting a splendid cloak of gold and green for a king that had been dead a thousand years." (When he asks what use

"A Sister's Love" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Stephen Hernandez. It was published in the sword-and-sorcery anthology Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights by Rogue Planet Press in January 2017.

### Synopsis
Beautiful serving girl Genie recruits the assistance of wandering barbarian Vidric when her younger sister is captured by the Tsathoggua-worshipping Voormi, hoping to save the child before she can be violated and eaten alive. The two battle wandering bands of raiders before reaching the Voormi temple, where they are able to infiltrate the main chamber, killing all within and rescuing those poor captives who have yet to succumb to the attentions of their captors.

### Behind the Mythos
The story purports to be told by Ec'h Pi El, an immortal sorcerer who once acted as guardian and mentor to Vidric. He claimed to have viewed the events through the use of magic and the psychic link the two shared via a longevity potion.

A Solstice Carol is a Dark Adventure Radio Theatre Production by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, a festive edition of the series containing adaptations of "The Festival", "Pickman's Model", and "The Outsider", linked by a tale based on Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol.

### Overview


As with all of the DART productions, A Solstice Carol is presented in the style of a 1930s radio drama and comes complete with a set of period-authentic props to enhance the immersive experience. These include:

*The obituary of Mason Farley, one of the ghosts in the wraparound story.
*A cover of Astonishing Tales magazine.
*A rejection letter from True Terror magazine addressed to one Howard B. Lovecraft.
*An exhibit listing containing the works of Richard Upton Pickman.
*A page of the Necronomicon which details the ritual depicted in "The Festival".

"A Song for Granite Khronos" is a short Lovecraftian story by American author Aaron Besson.

### Synopsis
A veteran sewer worker inducts a new start into the secrets which lie below the streets, explaining how they must work as caretakers of the bodies of dead primordial giants which lie petrifying in the bowels of the Earth.

### Publication History
"A Song for Granitte Khronos" was published in the thematic anthology Chthonic: Weird Tales of Inner Earth in February 2018.

### Behind the Mythos
Although containing no direct references to either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the entities described in "A Song for Granite Khronos" and their negative effect on humanity even while in a death-like slumber is highly reminiscent of certain of Lovecraft's works, particularly "The Call of Cthulhu".

shortDefinition: "A Study in Emerald" is a short story by Neil Gaiman that first appeared in Shadows Over Baker Street, a collection of stories that combine the worlds of Sherlock Holmes and the Cthulhu Mythos. Gaiman's story, whose title is a reference to A Study in...
fullContent:
"A Study in Emerald" is a short story by Neil Gaiman that first appeared in Shadows Over Baker Street, a collection of stories that combine the worlds of Sherlock Holmes and the Cthulhu Mythos. Gaiman's story, whose title is a reference to A Study in Scarlet, the Arthur Conan Doyle novel that introduced Holmes, transposes the characters from Doyle's fiction into an England where the Great Old Ones have ruled for 700 years. The story won the Hugo Award for Best Short Story in 2004.

"A Study in Emerald" was reprinted in Gaiman's 2006 collection Fragile Things.

### Adaptations
In 2018 a comic book adaptation by Rafael Albuquerque was released by Dark Horse Comics.

### External Links

shortDefinition: A Study in Emerald is a comic book adaptation of Neil Gaiman's alternate-history Cthulhu Mythos short story of the same name.  ### Synopsis A man identified only as "The Detective" investigates the brutal murder of one of the German ruling family in ...
fullContent:
A Study in Emerald is a comic book adaptation of Neil Gaiman's alternate-history Cthulhu Mythos short story of the same name.

### Synopsis
A man identified only as "The Detective" investigates the brutal murder of one of the German ruling family in an alternative Victorian England, which has been ruled in the name of the Great Old Ones for seven hundred years. Taking his housemate, a man referred to as "The Major", along for the ride, he discovers the identity of the killers of the inhuman royal, men who belong to a group dedicated to reclaiming mankind's destiny. However, the killers, one of whom is later named as a John or James Watson, outwit both the Detective and the police, and are never caught.

### Characters

* The Detective: a brilliant investigator, and London’s only detective-for-hire.
* The Major: a former army soldier who bears the scars of a terrible tour of duty in Afghanistan. His initials are revealed to be S. M.
* Inspector Lestrade: a loyal and diligent, if somewhat unimaginative, police officer.
* "Sherry Vernet"/"Rache": a member of the radical humanist movement "The Restorationists" posing as theatre player.
* John/James Watson: a former army surgeon and Restorationist.

### Behind the Mythos
The final revelation that one of the Restorationists was in fact Watson implies that "Rache," who managed to outwit the Detective, is actually Sherlock Holmes. From this, and a statement made in a letter by Rache to the Detective in which he calls him "a worthy adversary," it may be inferred that the Detective was Professor James Moriarty, Holmes's nemesis in the Arthur Conan Doyle stories.

### Publication History
A Study in Emerald was adapted into the comic book format by Rafael Scavone, Rafael Albuquerque and Dave Stewart. It was published by Dark Horse Comics in June 2018.
