shortDefinition: "A Thing About Cars!" is a Cthulhu Mythos-connected short story by Brian Lumley that first appeared in his collection The Caller of The Black (Arkham House, 1971). It makes reference to Ramsey Campbell's Severn Valley Mythos setting, one of the first...
fullContent:
"A Thing About Cars!" is a Cthulhu Mythos-connected short story by Brian Lumley that first appeared in his collection The Caller of The Black (Arkham House, 1971). It makes reference to Ramsey Campbell's Severn Valley Mythos setting, one of the first stories not by Campbell to do so.

### Synopsis
After a pair of automobile-related tragedies destroys a man's life, his brother visits the midlands village of Boresby to make sure that he's all right.

### Setting
The story is set in Boresby, a Midlands village noted for its "tall, gnarled oaks letting through only a minimum of sunlight to weirdly dapple the road":

The village proper is "no more than a quarter mile in length, a single street wherein the oaks in their turn gave way to high, stark garden walls of buttress-like outer proportions suggestive of immense thickness." Beyond "shady gates" can occasionally be seen "steeply sloping, thatched roofs." "Many of the great walls, moss- and ivy-grown, leaned perilously towards the road with no sidewalks lining them, so that the trees overhanging from the unseen gardens" give the impression of "immense jaws ready at any moment to snap shut."

The "ancient village post-office" offers one of the few opportunities to encounter a living creature. A mile or so outside of the village is a "great forest" officially closed to motor traffic, and an abandoned quarry filled with junked cars.

Boresby is located "between a certain triangle of ancient but updated towns in the Midlands," in "an area of some hundred square miles simply abounding with tiny villages of hoary antiquity exuding an ancient nastiness." The village has a sense of "a lurking and centuried outsidedess." a "feeling of dark, oppressive effusions...as if all the poisons of unknown centuries had found a temporary outlet in that soul-disturbing region."

The village is cited as an example of a "quiet backwater surviving modernity, defying time and sometimes, when the setting is just right, radiating an aura out of tune with the day and age which...might in certain perspective appear ominous and even frightening." 

It's compared to similar places "in the Severn Valley—Goatswood and Temphill spring unpleasantly to mind—and others in the North and North-East, like Harden on the coast and Tharpe-Nettleford on the North Yorkshire border." Boresby is "one of those places, like Temphill or Harden, where almost anything might happen; an area literally exuding strangeness, to which all manner of strangeness might therefore be expected to be drawn."

Goatswood and Temphill are creations of Ramsey Campbell, introduced in "The Moon-Lens" and "The Church in High Street," respectively. Harden appears in Lumley's own "Aunt Hester," "Dagon's Bell," and "Rising with Surtsey."

### Publication History

"A Thousand Young" is a short story by American author and Lovecraft scholar Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
A man who believes that only sexual experience can grant him spiritual fulfilment succeeds in tracking down a group which professes to believe the same, and is willing to teach him their ways. After completing a series of increasingly-depraved initiation rites, he is finally allowed to participate in one of their orgiastic rituals. However, when the lights are turned on, he finds that he has been tricked into engaging in congress with the Outer God Shub-Niggurath.

### Characters

*The Unnamed Narrator, a man on a quest to find inner completeness.
*Marilyn, the narrator's girlfriend.
*The Priest, leader of a cult called the Libertines.
*Shub-Niggurath, an Outer God.

shortDefinition: "A True Telling of the Terror That Came to Red Hook" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.  ### Synopsis The story tells of two previously unknown participants of the events recounted in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The ...
fullContent:
"A True Telling of the Terror That Came to Red Hook" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
The story tells of two previously unknown participants of the events recounted in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Horror at Red Hook". These men discover the shocking truth of Robert Suydam's occult activities and work towards bringing about his downfall. This involves spiriting him away from the ship aboard which his wife was murdered and killing the creature he had become in the catacombs beneath New York before blowing up the shrine found therein.

### Characters
* The Unnamed Narrator, a colored trumpeter with a strong sense of social justice.
* Botan, a small-time Kurdish business associate of the narrator.
*Robert Suydam, a man in service to a dark power.
* Thomas Malone, a police officer.

### Behind the Mythos
As one of the most xenophobic of Lovecraft's works, "The Horror at Red Hook" has received a great deal of criticism, with a number of collections going as far as even omitting the story in its entirety. "A True Telling of the Terror That Came to Red Hook" is ,therefore, an attempt to reconcile the bigoted depictions of the original story (and generally of the racist legacy of Lovecraft himself)  by centering its narrative on two protagonist belonging to the same marginalized groups that were originally often demonized by Lovecraft in his fiction, with both from backgrounds given little-to-no value by the society of the time. However, in contrast, it also highlights the brutality of Malone's police forces when dealing with the local minorities and immigrants.

### Publication History
"A True Telling of the Terror That Came to Red Hook" was first published in the 2016 anthology Heroes of Red Hook by Golden Goblin Press. It was also included in the collection of Meikle’s own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in 2019.

### Trivia
* "A True Telling of the Terror That Came to Red Hook" provides explanations for parts of the original story which Lovecraft had left vague, such as what fate actually befell Robert Suydam, and why the basement of his house collapsed at the climax.

### Synopsis
A short prologue describes a group of astronauts salvaging a derelict shipyard who bear witness to the manifestation of a group of pallid yellow beings before being utterly destroyed by the newcomers.

The main story tells of a magician who has devoted years to serving the King in Yellow. When the truth of the entity is finally revealed to him, his mind is shattered and his body annihilated.

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance in 2016, "A Visage of Great Truths" has appeared in an independently-produced chapbook to which it lends it name (2017), and the collection Brian Barr's King in Yellow (2019).

### Synopsis
A disgraced New York police officer leaves town and finds employment as a private investigator with the Arkham Detective Agency. On a an apparently-routine assignment he stumbles across a conspiracy involving a murderess in league with dark powers and a secret society of former Miskatonic University alumni dedicated to the occult.

### Characters

* Andrew, a former officer with the NYPD forced out because of negative press in the aftermath of a mob shooting.
* Annabelle "Cookie" Morganfield, an ambitious socialite who gains supernatural powers after a visit to Egypt.
* Candice "Candy" Anderson, Andrew's girlfriend, who works in the Miskatonic University admissions department.

### Publication History

term: A Wisdom That Is Woe, a Woe That Is Madness
shortDefinition: "A Wisdom That Is Woe, a Woe That Is Madness" is a short story by E. Catherine Tobler, originally collected in the Kickstarter crowdfunded anthology A Mythos Grimmly. It is a combination of prose and prose poetry describing thirteen different refract...
fullContent:
"A Wisdom That Is Woe, a Woe That Is Madness" is a short story by E. Catherine Tobler, originally collected in the Kickstarter crowdfunded anthology A Mythos Grimmly. It is a combination of prose and prose poetry describing thirteen different refractions of the same basic event. It incorporates elements of the Rapunzel folk tale into the narrative but operates on several levels of simile, through the use of the interspersed prose poetry.

### Synopsis
Ismail begins his quest in a library, where he first hears of a princess, trapped in a tower. Crossing many miles and many worlds, he arrives at a salt lake desert in which an iron prison in the form of a tower rises from the corrosive wastes.

Climbing the tower with the help of the brambles-like hair of the princess, he finally reaches her. 

Still under the effects of powerful hallucinations caused by breaching the various dimensional barriers, his perceptions are warped beyond understanding. At the same time as he lies down on the beautiful bed where the princess waits for him he sees intermittent and probably more truthful glimpses of a rotting ruined chamber and its iron walls.

As he continues to try and achieve union with the princess, the princess physically invades his body in her true jet-black shapeless and tentacular form, finally parastically taking over his physical shell from the inside. It is at this point that we have revealed to us that the princess is Nyarlathotep, and that, finally concealed within the flesh of a human being, he/she/it can now escape its prison.

shortDefinition: "A World of Silence" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Steven J. Alvarez. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long running zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .  ### Synopsis In a far future in which huma...
fullContent:
"A World of Silence" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Steven J. Alvarez. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long running zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
In a far future in which humankind has discovered not a single trace of extraterrestrial life anywhere in the cosmos, a corporate analyst visits a far-flung colony world to conduct a study on profitability; there, they discover a complex seemingly devoid of all life. When they access the computer system's database, they find that the colonists unearthed an ancient tablet which released some form of infection on the inhabitants and their technological systems, transforming them into cyborg abominations.

Although the creatures attack, the analyst makes their escape, but their ship is crippled in the process. While they drift helpless in space, they see that the entities have somehow managed to construct themselves a device which will allow them travel between the stars, granting them access to an unsuspecting human race…

### Behind the Mythos
Although the story contains no direct references to H. P. Lovecraft's work, the language spoken by the first scientists to unearth the tablet bears a striking similarity to R'lyehian, the cosmic language used by many entities in the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Trivia
*While no background is given on the scientist's discovery, it is implied that the lack of life in the universe was a result of the predations of whatever entity inhabited the ancient tablet, everything having been wiped out by the mysterious intelligence.

Alfred Angelo Attanasio, born on September 20, 1951, in Newark, New Jersey, is an author of fantasy and science fiction. His Lovecraftian short story "The Star Pools" (1980) was included in the anthology New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos. 

Attanasio has written a handful of Lovecraftian stories; his second published work, "The Elder Sign," appeared in the 1972 tribute collection HPL. Other stories with a Lovecraft connection include "Glimpses" (1975), "A Priestess of Nodens" (1995), and "Time in the Hourless House" (2003); together with "The Star Pools," these were rewritten into a unified narrative called "Thirteen Raptures of the Black Goat," which appeared in his 2006 collection Twice Dead Things. 

His first novel, published in 1981, was in the science fiction genre; Radix won the Prix Cosmos 2000, a French literary award, and was also nominated as best novel for the 1981 Nebula Awards. He produced three more novels  in the Radix Tetrad, In Other Worlds, Arc of the Dream, and The Last Legends of Earth. 

He has written novels in multiple genres, including historical fiction (Wyvern and Kingdom of the Grail: Servant of Birds), Arthurian epics (The Perilous Order), paranormal romance (The Moon’s Wife), a Paleolithic saga (Hunting the Ghost Dancer), crime drama (Silent), science fiction (Solis, Centuries), Wiccan adventure (Killing with the Edge of the Moon), and Young Adult (The Conjure Book). 

Attanasio wrote the Dominions of Irth fantasy trilogy under the pseudonym Adam Lee, and the children's fantasy The Moon's Prophecy as Jonathan Sparrow.

His short fiction has been published in three collections: Beastmarks (1985), Twice Dead Things (2006), and Demons Hide Their Faces (2020).

Alpheus Hyatt Verrill (1871 - 1954) was an American archaeologist, explorer, inventor, photographer, illustrator and author. In the 1920s and 30s, he was a frequent contributor to the science fiction magazine Amazing Stories, to which he wrote many tales in the "lost world" subgenre, such as the 1926 novella Beyond the Pole. He traveled extensively through South America and the West Indies, and authored numerous books on natural history.

Verrill was one of the many pulp authors who were spoofed in the comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century", by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. In the story, Verrill and George Allan England are mentioned briefly as a pair of adventurers named "A. Hijacked Barrell and G. A. Scotland".

Albert Roanoke Tilburne, better known by his professional name A. R. Tilburne, was an American pulp illustrator whose work first appeared in The Big Magazine in 1935 before selling his services to Weird Tales in 1938 and Strange Stories in 1939. He continued to draw interior story illustrations for Weird Tales throughout the 1940s.

Having had a full time job as a building manager and apartment rental agent he listed his official occupation as "illustrator" for the first time on April 24, 1942 when he reported for draft.

He painted the cover for Avon paperback books 1947 publication of "The Lurking Fear."

In 1950 he retired from illustration and devoted his time to paintings of the Old West until his death in 1965.

Abbith, a.k.a. the World of Seven Suns, is a fictional planet that revolves around seven stars beyond Xoth. It is inhabited by Metallic Brains, wise with the ultimate secrets of the universe. Nyarlathotep dwells or is imprisoned on this planet.

### Behind the Mythos
While the "world of Seven Suns" was referenced as the abode of Nyarlathotep by H. P. Lovecraft (: The Whisperer in Darkness) and August Derleth (: "The Dweller in Darkness"), the name Abbith was created by Lin Carter.

A place called Cytharion of the Seven Suns is mentioned by Lovecraft in "The Crawling Chaos". However, in spite of its title, that story doesn't feature Nyarlathotep.

In Carter's works, Abbith is also identified as a world revolving around Algol, which is the abode of Zvilpogghua in "The Feaster from the Stars". However, this identification only occurs in the revised version of the story, as published in The Book of Eibon. In the version published in the Crypt of Cthulhu magazine, the Algolian world inhabited by Zvilpogghua is instead identified as Ymar, whereas another story identifies it as Yrautrom.

In "The Thing in the Pit", Ymar is mentioned as being in the same star cluster as Abbith and Xoth.

Abdul Alhazred, also known as the Mad Arab, is a fictional character from the Cthulhu Mythos. He was first mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Nameless City", and is frequently cited as the author of the fabled Necronomicon, a fictional occult text containing knowledge from beyond the Earth.

### Quotations



### Name
Abdul Alhazred is not an Arabic name. The more proper Arabic form might be Abd al-Hazred or simply Abdul Hazred, although these are still anomalous, as Hazred is not one of the 99 Names of God. In Arabic texts, his name has appeared as Abdullah al-Ḥaẓrad (عبدالله الحظرد). 

Al-Hazrad roughly translates as "The Banned" or "The Ban", although whether this is intentional is up for speculation. 

Various writers have theorised on Alhazred's true name, with one theory being that his name was originally Abd Al-'Uzza. (: Ex Libris Miskatonici) 

The term "Mad Arab" in reference to Alhazred is always capitalised and used as a title, and the term can actually be used in lieu of Alhazred's name.

Abhoth (The Source of Uncleanliness) is a fictional entity in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his 1934 short story "The Seven Geases".

Abhoth would later be incorporated into Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, where it has been variously described being a Great Old One or Outer God.

### Overview
Abhoth resides in the cavern of Y'quaa beneath Mount Voormithadreth. It is a horrid, dark gray protean mass and is said to be the ultimate source of all miscreation and abomination.

Obscene monsters constantly form in Abhoth's gray mass and crawl away from their parent. No two of Abhoth's children are alike. In general, they are complex life forms, but the majority of them are simple-minded, acting on impulse. Their forms can be anything from amorphous blobs and singular body parts, to queer humanoids and monstrous mutants. Abhoth's tentacles and limbs grab many of them, pulling them back and devouring them. Most of those that escape simply wander off, only a few of them tend to their sire's needs. Abhoth has a twisted and cynical mind, and can communicate telepathically with others near him.

### Notes 
*Abhoth is also mentioned in Colin Wilson's The Mind Parasites.
*Abhoth is one of the Ancient Ones in the "Dunwich Horror" expansion of the Arkham Horror board game.
*Abhoth is one of the Ancient Ones in the "Under the Pyramids" expansion of the Eldritch Horror board game.
*In Gary Myers's short story "The Snout in the Alcove", Atal goes looking for Abhoth, believing he can gain from him the runes of the Elder Gods in order to prevent the second coming of Nyarlathotep. The story suggests that Abhoth and Ubbo-Sathla might be the same entity.

Abigail Foreman is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
A library intern at Arkham's Miskatonic University, Abigail discovered something unusual in an old book in her care: the pages changed when significant events occurred, but the text always indicated a countdown to a certain date. Joining forces with sailor Silas Marsh, the pair were able to uncover a plot by the folks of Innsmouth to awaken a dread entity and thwart it (: The Deep Gate).

### Appearances
Abigail Foreman has appeared in several Cthulhu Mythos contributions by Fantasy Flight, including the Arkham Horror expansion The King in Yellow, Chris A. Jackson's novella The Deep Gate and Arkham Horror: The Card Game.

### Behind the Mythos
Abigail made her first appearance in The King in Yellow expansion for Arkham Horror, where she appeared as a Blight card representing characters harmful to the "heroes" of the game. Despite this, she is portrayed as very much the secondary protagonist in the novella The Deep Gate.

Abigail "Abbie" Prinn is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft's friend and protégé Henry Kuttner for his 1937  Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Salem Horror".

### History
A witch in the town of Salem, Massachusetts, around the time of the infamous Witch Trials, Abbie boasted that she was the high priestess of some unnamed dark god which dwelt deep in the mountains of New England. She was said to make sacrifices to a "worm-eaten, crescent-horned image of dubious origin," and it was these activities which led to her execution in 1690.

Abbie had laid a curse on the town before her passing, however, and when a man named Carson moved in to her decrepit old house three centuries later and discovered her secret "Witch Room" hidden in the basement, the curse was brought to fruition.

Abbie's desiccated corpse rose from the grave and made its way to the Witch Room, attempting to summon the Great Old One known as Nyogtha to destroy the town, but was ultimately thwarted by an occultist named Michael Leigh who knew of the Witch Room and had deduced that it was a portal between our world and another. Leigh recited a passage from the cursed Necronomicon and used an arcane elixir to cast both Abbie Prinn and the partially-materialised Nyogtha back through the portal, presumably killing Abbie for good. (: "The Salem Horror", Henry Kuttner)

She is related to Ludvig Prinn, author of the occult grimoire De Vermis Mysteriis, with Abbie being an unspecified descendant. (: "Wilbur Whateley Waiting", Robert M. Price)

### Trivia
*Although Abbie is said to have been executed during the Salem Witch Trials in 1690, the Trials did not actually begin until 1692.

The Reverend Abijah Hoadley is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror".

### In Lovecraft's Works
Hoadley is mentioned briefly in the opening chapter of "The Dunwich Horror", where it is mentioned that he delivered a sermon to the Congregational Church at Dunwich Village in 1747, having recently arrived in town. Soon after giving his oration, he disappeared. A copy of the sermon, printed in nearby Springfield, has managed to remain intact. It reads as follows:



### In the Expanded Mythos
In Robert M. Price's short story "Young Goodwife Doten", Reverend Hoadley features as a secondary character. Here, he is shown to be a duplicitous parson, offering condolences to the titular goodwife Doten on the loss of her child one moment, whilst spreading rumours of her heretical practices to others at other times. He is also an enthusiastic participant in the burning of the Dotens at the story's conclusion.

The Aboleths are an aberrant race from the fictional universes in Dungeons & Dragons and the Pathfinder pencil-and-paper roleplaying games.

### Aboleth of Dungeons & Dragons
The Aboleths are fish-like amphibious aberrations whom reside in the desolate waters of the Far Realms and the dark depths of the Underdark. Whose form resembles that of a mutated 20-40 ft long eel. Possessing a horrifying lamprey-like mouth and several tentacles near its head. Whose bodies are constantly exuding (rewrite) a slimy mucus, without which they cannot breathe. On land, they will quickly dry up, entering a state of suspended animation, and form a tough waterproof membrane.

Possess incredible psionic abilities, which gives them the ability to manipulate and control lesser beings. They are nearly immortal, as neither disease or age kills them, though they can still be killed. It's mucous has a horrifying effect on land-dwellers, turning their skin into a water-breathing membrane and their consciousness into a mindless servant. Aboleths also had perfect racial memory, with each member inheriting the memories of all its ancestors. In addition the memories of those they consumed were assimilated. Spending their time in the memories of their ancestors, was a favorite pastime.

Originally they came from the Far Realm, though a long time ago many of them migrated to the Prime Material plane, setting in the Underdark. Most of Toril's aboleths reside in the Underdark, though some of them are found elsewhere, usually at old temples, deep lakes, or ruins. Some of them are served by the kuo-toa. Their cities are full of strange and weird architecture, and are mostly located deep underwater. The largest known city is the Shape of Water, the main residence of their race's leaders and where they hold council. Which is located in the Glimmersea, in the Underdark.

Xxiphu is the flying city of the Aboleth. Home of the Abolethic Sovereignty which is ruled by the Eldest, a massive Aboleth of incalculable age and incomprehensible malevolence. The city originated in the Far Realm and arrived on Abeir-Toril when the world was young. When the sundering split it into two worlds, Abeir and Toril, the city ended up in Abeir. It was later transported to Toril during the Spellplague. It's inhabitants were at first attacked by the startled Aboleth of Toril. Now they live in uneasy peace with each other, though those of Toril avoid the city. The city itself is an colossal obelsik which has tentacles stretching from its walls, an eternal storm wrapped around it, and glyph inscriptions which depict thousands of constantly changing images. Any mortal mind that can comprehend the full meaning of those inscriptions would go insane. Xxiphu alters reality in its vicinity, periodically spawning Far Realm aberrations into the Prime Material Realm.

shortDefinition: Abraham Merritt (January 20, 1884 – August 21, 1943), who published under the byline A. Merritt, was an American editor and author of works of fantastic fiction. Born in New Jersey, he moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 1894. Originally trained ...
fullContent:
Abraham Merritt (January 20, 1884 – August 21, 1943), who published under the byline A. Merritt, was an American editor and author of works of fantastic fiction. Born in New Jersey, he moved to Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, in 1894. Originally trained in law, he turned to journalism, first as a correspondent, and later as editor. He was assistant editor of The American Weekly from 1912 to 1937 under Morrill Goddard, then its editor until his death. As editor, he hired the unheralded new artists Virgil Finlay and Hannes Bok, and promoted the work done on polio by Sister Elizabeth Kenny.

His fiction was only a sideline to his journalism career, which might explain his relatively low output. One of the best-paid journalists of his era, Merritt made $25,000 per year by 1919, and at the end of his life was earning $100,000 yearly—exceptional sums for the period. His financial success allowed him to pursue world travel—he invested in real estate in Jamaica and Ecuador—and exotic hobbies, like cultivating orchids and plants linked to witchcraft and magic (monkshood, wolfbane, blue datura—and peyote and marihuana).

Merritt married twice, once in the 1910s to Eleanore Ratcliffe, with whom he raised an adopted daughter, and again in the 1930s to Eleanor H. Johnson. He maintained an estate in Hollis Park Gardens on Long Island, where he accumulated collections of weapons, carvings, and primitive masks from his travels, as well as a library of occult literature that reportedly exceeded 5,000 volumes. He died suddenly of a heart attack, at his winter home in Indian Rock Keys, Florida, in 1943.

### Writings
His reputation has not stood well over the years among speculative fiction fans and critics (with the singular exception of The Ship of Ishtar, a universally hailed classic of the fantasy genre), but he was an influence on H. P. Lovecraft, who considered his story "The Moon Pool" (1918) one of the ten best stories in weird fiction. Merritt was also highly esteemed by his friend and frequent collaborator Hannes Bok, by then a noted SF illustrator.

Merritt's stories typically revolve around conventional pulp magazine themes: lost civilizations, hideous monsters, etc. His heroes are gallant Irishmen or Scandinavians, his villains treacherous Germans or Russians (depending on the politics of the time), and his heroines often virginal, mysterious, and scantily clad.

What sets Merritt apart from the typical pulp author, however, is his lush, florid prose style and his exhaustive, at times exhausting, penchant for adjective-laden detail. Merritt's fondness for micro-description nicely complements the pointillistic style of Bok's illustrations, and often serves to highlight and radicalize the inherent fetishistic tendencies of pulp sf.

In 1917, he published his first fantasy, "Through the Dragon Glass", in Argosy All Stories Weekly. This was followed by many more tales, including "The People of the Pit" (1918), The Moon Pool (1918; expanded into a novel, 1919),

The Abyss of Yhe, also known as the Land of Yhe or simply Yhe, is a fictional location created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. Situated somewhere in the Pacific Ocean, it was first referenced in his novella The Shadow Out of Time.

### In Lovecraft's Works
When Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee had his mind swapped with a member of the Great Race of Yith, one of the other abducted minds he conversed with was an archmage from "vanished Yhe in the Pacific". (: The Shadow Out of Time)

### In August Derleth's Works
A passage from the Necronomicon mentions "the land of Yhe" along with several other locations in which the Elder Sign could be used to protect one against the minions of the Great Old Ones. (: "The House on Curwen Street")

### In Other Works
The Abyss of Yhe is the location where the Elder Gods imprisoned Ythogtha, the son of Cthulhu. (: "The Thing in the Pit")

fullContent:
"Academic Legacies" is a novelette by C.T. Phipps in the Cthulhu Mythos genre. It was first published in Time Loopers in 2023. It is part of the Cthulhu Armageddon series.

### Synopsis
Mercy Halsey-Mason is a student at Miskatonic University who is the student of Chester Winfield and dating Tommy Tillinghast as a research assistant. A Goth Girl, she has an interest in sorcery and the occult. Doctor Winfield is a former victim of the Yith who has made use of the Windlass app to construct a variant of the Tillinghast Device. It turns out that Doctor Winfield intends to use it to summon the Flying Polyps to attack the Yith in the distant past for revenge upon his violation. This is tied to the larger Time War being fought between the shoggoths and Yith.

### Behind the Mythos
"Academic Legacies" is a loose sequel to "From Beyond" and "The Shadow out of Time." It is also a prequel to the Cthulhu Armageddon series, taking place before the Rising and destruction of the world.

"Acceleratrix," also published as "Accelatrix,"  is a Lovecraftian short story by British author Glynn Owen Barrass, first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2021.

### Synopsis
American scientists attempting to create a black hole inadvertently open a gateway to another dimension. Through this portal emerges a destructive entity which takes the form of the Hindu goddess Kali the Destroyer. Although the head scientist manages to push the being back and closing the gate, it costs her her life.

Six months later however, boffins at CERN's Large Hadron Collider achieve the same result with their experiments, and the being emerges once more…

### Trivia
*"Acceleratrix" was included in the 2023 anthology The Best of Lovecraftiana, under the title "Accelatrix."

### Publication History
*Lovecraftiana Vol 5, Issue 4 (2021)
*The Best of Lovecraftiana (2023)

Achtung! Cthulhu is a roleplaying game designed for Cthulhu Mythos gaming in a World War II setting. Originally a series of supplements created by Modiphius Entertainment for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu system, after Modiphius cut ties with its licenser, the company developed the setting into its own stand-alone game using their in-house 2D20 system.

### Overview
Achtung! Cthulhu is set during the Second World War and details a "secret war" going on behind the scenes where various governmental factions either attempt to use the powers of the Cthulhu Mythos to turn the tide of the war, or thwart the other side from doing so. Likely as a result of the popular belief in the association between Nazism and occultism , the Axis powers are usually the antagonists and the ones most likely to employ Mythos means to reach their goals.

Since its launch in 2021, a quick-start set and several expansion books have been released, largely in the form of scenario supplements.

### Books

* Forest of Fear (2022)

Achtung! Cthulhu is a series of historical setting and scenario supplements originally designed for use with Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. It was first published by third-party content provider Modiphius Entertainment after a successful Kickstarter campaign ; Modiphius have since seemingly cut tied with Call of Cthulhu and re-released the setting as a stand-alone roleplaying game.

The setting was launched with Sarah Newton's short Zero Point campaign books, Three Kings and Heroes of the Sea, in 2012 .

### Premise
Achtung! Cthulhu tells the story of secret agents from various shadowy government organisations as they combat elements of the Cthulhu Mythos during the Second World War. These cults and monsters are often found employed by the various combatants in an attempt to swing the tide of war in their own favour. As a western publication, it is weighed heavily towards playing Allied agents battling against Axis secret projects, with the mythology of Nazi occultism featuring strongly in the narrative.

fullContent:
Achtung! Cthulhu is a horror fiction role-playing game setting inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos, which blends historical elements from the Second World War with the cosmic horror of the Mythos. Written by Lynne Hardy, Chris Birch and others, it was published by Modiphius Entertainment after a successful Kickstarter project; the first supplement was released in 2012. Achtung! Cthulhu was originally designed to be compatible with both the sixth edition of Call of Cthulhu and the Savage Worlds game systems; later it would be adapted to use Modiphius's system-agnostic 2D20 ruleset.

### Call of Cthulhu/Savage Worlds
The Achtung! Cthulhu setting was first introduced in 2012 as a setting supplement for the Call of Cthulhu and Savage Worlds game systems.


### 2D20 System
In 2023, Modiphius released a stand-alone horror roleplaying game for the Achtung! Cthulhu setting, with this edition no longer being affiliated with Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu game.


### Expansions
Since its launch, Achtung! Cthulhu has spawned numerous supplements, miniatures games, an (unreleased) cooperative board game, and even a video game.

### Setting
The game takes place in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos, during World War II. One can find himself (or herself) right in the middle of a battle in a city, in the arid deserts of North Africa, a steaming jungle in the Pacific Ocean, the freezing cold of Russia during the winter, in an air battle, or in a naval battle. On the other hand, you can be part of an expedition to the Antarctica, some forgotten island, a lost city in the desert, or some other location searching for ancient technology or occult artifacts. You can be playing a game of espionage and counter-espionage, investigating a murder or mystery, as part of a partisan unit, or some other activity behind enemy lines or in home territory. It's a setting that combines total war, espionage, mystery, adventure, detective work, small unit level combat, magic, alien technology, super science, and of course entities and races of the Mythos.

It is a multi-sided conflict, which is mostly in the shadows. The German Mythos factions battle their counterparts among the Allied powers (Soviet Union, Great Britain, and the United States) in Europe, Africa, and elsewhere. The Japanese Mythos faction battles its Allied counterparts in the Far East and Pacific Ocean. Within the Nazi Empire of the Germans, the Cult of the Black Sun battles with its rival the Nachtwölfe. In the Soviet Union, a similar conflict occurs between the Institute 21 and Otdel MI.

### Main Factions   
*Cult of the Black Sun: The Die schwarze Sonne (the Black Sun) was founded by the sorcerer Reinhardt Weissler. Black Sun is a name that strikes fear among the Nazis, a name which is feared by even the Einsatzgruppe death squads. Achtung! Cthulhu Tactics is a turn-based tactical video game which takes place in Modiphius Entertainment's Achtung! Cthulhu historical horror setting. Developed by Auroch Digital it was published by Modiphius and Ripstone Games in October 2018 .

### Overview


The game involves the player taking control of a squad of four special forces operatives who must fight the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos behind enemy lines, in the Nazi-held territory of the Forest of Fear. Progress allows the customisation and upgrading of the various officers under the player's command.

### Reception
Achtung! Cthulhu Tactics holds a critic score of 56 and a 6.0 user score on review aggregate site Metacritic, indicating mixed or average reviews. The main issues the game draws criticism over are the repetitive level designs, with one critic stating that "Achtung! Cthulhu Tactics has the most primitive levels I have ever seen in a turn-based strategy game" .

fullContent:
"Acquired Through Deaccession" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Lee Clark Zumpe. It was published in the Lammas Eve edition of Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
When head of Collections Management Norton Schubert is appointed to the Miskatonic University library under somewhat dubious circumstances, many of the senior faculty are troubled, believing his cost-cutting measures to be less than genuine. Using a meeting to discuss these concerns as cover, the former head librarian and members of the campus security break in to Schubert's house and discover that he has been stealing works of great occult significance.

In retribution, some of the more enlightened faculty members enact a ritual to summon a pack of Hunting Horrors, ensuring that Schubert will never be able to unleash unspeakable horrors on the planet, and that the authorities will never ask any awkward questions about his disappearance.

fullContent:
"Acrewood" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Jude Reid, published in the April Moon Books anthology The Call of Poohthulhu in May 2022. Despite its inclusion in this collection, it bears little relation to A. A. Milne's creations, barring a handful of re-used names.

### Synopsis
Jo, her husband Richard and son Christopher travel to a remote farming cottage for a weekend break. On their second night, Christopher disappears; Jo and Richard find him in the nearby forest with the farm's owners, ready to be sacrificed to the ancient bear-like entity which ensures prosperity for the locals. Although the creature kills and devours Richard, Jo strikes a bargain with the cultists: in return for allowing herself to be used to introduce new - monstrous - blood into the community, they will spare her life, and that of her son.

Adam Scott Glancy is an American traditional games designer, author and former attorney. He is perhaps best known for designing the Delta Green setting for Call of Cthulhu with John Scott Tynes and Dennis Detwiller, although he has written numerous other works set in the Cthulhu Mythos, including gaming supplements and fiction. In 2001 he was appointed president of the Mythos-focussed games publisher Pagan Publishing.

Glancy has also been a guest attendee at the H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival every year since 2013 .

Dr. Adele Kramer is a character who features in Troy Young's Nyarlathotep Cycle of Cthulhu Mythos stories. 

### Description
A woman in her early 30s, Adele Kramer is a marine biologist, formerly working at Dalhousie University, currently employed in the service of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena, an agency which stands in opposition to "The Other": a catch-all term given to the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos. 

After an encounter with an entity and its human thrall in the Canadian Arctic Circle on her first assignment for the agency, Adele was wounded: she later sported a bite scar across her cheek and was missing the ends of her left ring and pinky fingers. 

Adele briefly possessed a wide range of extremely powerful psychic powers as a result of spending time in proximity to Azathoth, but saw this as more of a curse than a blessing. These abilities were later removed by the Outer God Yog-Sothoth as a reward for her service. 

### History
Adele participated in the investigation of a bizarre sea-creature at Gallou Cave with the assistance of law enforcement officer Joe Mills; after the subsequent appearance of its mother, she was recruited into the Department by a man named Harjit Singh. 

Her first assignment was in the Canadian Arctic Circle, where she met Sergeant Pete Ivalu of the Canadian Army Rangers, the two of them confronting and defeating a minion of Cthulhu. 

A second assignment whilst supposedly on an R&R period saw her encounter and destroy a captive Shoggoth. 

A few weeks after her last assignment saw Kramer meet once again with Mills and Ivalu, and the three returned to Gallou Cove to investigate a cave uncovered since the town's closure. There, both of her companions were killed, and Adele's soul was dragged off by an avatar of Nyarlathotep to serve in the choir of Azathoth. 

Adele later awoke from her coma with powerful abilities and the knowledge of how to defeat Great Cthulhu, who was on the verge of awakening due to the manipulations of Nyarlathotep. She, along with Harjit Singh, Malcolm Mayweather, and Charlene Hines, travelled to the rising city of R'lyeh in the South Pacific to stop the Great Old One; although successful in their mission, only Adele survived the encounter.

Adolf Hitler (also known as the Fuhrer) was a German politician, military leader, and dictator whose actions led directly to the outbreak of the Second World War. Universally reviled for his genocidal pogroms, he has become one of the most hated figures in history.

### In Real Life
H. P. Lovecraft mentioned Adolf Hitler in his correspondence, considering him as a lesser evil chosen by Germany over Bolshevism, managing to galvanise its people efficiently, but remained doubtful about the future, (: Selected Letters 4.648) and considered him "a clown". (: Letter to Wandrei,  8 November 1936)

### In the Mythos
According to one account, Hitler was actually an avatar of Nyarlathotep. (: Persona 2: Innocent Sin)

Another account held that Hitler was birthed as a result of a ritual carried out by W.W. Westcott in the guise of Jack the Ripper at the direction of Nyarlathotep, who wished to see him bring the Holocaust to fruition in order to consume the life energy of the murdered Jews. (: "April 20th, 1889", Kthulhu Reich) He was a devotee of the occult and a follower of the Tibetan mystic Teppa Tsanpo. (: "Dies Irae", Kthulhu Reich) After his suicide in 1945, Hitler was reincarnated as a Japanese man named Hirata and went on to become the head of the majority party in the Japanese Parliament. (: "The Corporal's Self-Portrait", Kthulhu Reich)

Adolphe Danziger De Castro, also known as Gustav Adolf Danziger, Adolph Danziger, Adolphe Danziger and Adolphe De Castro, (November 6, 1859 – March 4, 1959) was a Jewish scholar, journalist, lawyer and author of poems, novels and short stories. Two of his stories were revised by H. P. Lovecraft for republication in Weird Tales.

### Life
Adolphe Danziger De Castro was born Abram Dancygier, the son of Symcha Jakub Dancygier and Chaja Szarka, near Dobrzyń nad Wisłą, Congress, Poland. He claimed that the ancestor of the family Dancygier was a Portuguese sephardic Jew named Israel De Castro who migrated from Portugal to the Netherlands in the 16th century, and whose descendants settled in Danzig, whence the surname Danziger originated.

Danziger De Castro also claimed that he had received the rabbinical ordination by Rabbi Israel Jehoszua Trunk called 'R. Shiele Kutner' (1820–1893) around 1877 and had obtained a Ph.D. in oriental philology at the university of Bonn in 1882. 

In 1883 he emigrated to the United States, where he first lived as a journalist and teacher in St. Louis and Vincennes (IN), before settling in San Francisco in November 1884, where he practiced as a dentist and freelance journalist until 1900. There he married Bertha M. Levy (b. 1867), and had the children Beatrice Danziger (1891–1974, married to William K. Dolan) and Nathan Danziger (1894–1965), who changed his name to Nathaniel Dolan. 

In 1900, de Castro moved to New York City to get a book published, abandoning his first wife and their children. In 1903-04 he served as vice-consul of the United States in Madrid. Since that time he worked as an attorney at law. In 1904-05, he lived in Aberdeen, Scotland; between 1905 and 1921, in California. In 1907, he got married for a second time -- without having been divorced from his first wife --  to Georgina Sterling McClellan (1880–1935).

On February 1, 1920, he was one of the thirty-nine founders of the Sephardic Community of Los Angeles (La Comunidad Sefardi), and was elected the first president of the congregation. Between 1921 and 1926 he spent some time in Mexico, between 1927 and 1936 he lived in New York City, since 1936 in Los Angeles.

De Castro corresponded with H. P. Lovecraft between 1927 and 1936. Lovecraft wrote of De Castro: "Old Dolph is a portly, sentimental, & gesticulating person given to egotistical rambling about old times & the great men he has intimately known. … he entertained everybody with his loquacious egotism & pompous reminiscences of intimacies with the great. … [He] regaled us with tedious anecdotes of how he secured the election of Roosevelt, Taft, & Harding as Presidents. According to himself, he is apparently America’s foremost power behind the throne!"

After his second wife's death in 1935, De Castro was married for a third time, to Maria Paez Urquidi.

Adolphe Danziger De Castro died at almost 100 years in Los Angeles, California, on March 4, 1959.

fullContent:
Adrian M. Kleinbergen He was born in Edmonton, Canada in 1961. He is an artist, author and poet who has contributed a number of works to H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. 

Along with drawing and paint­ing, he does jewelry design and manufacture, sculpture, caricature, writ­ing, costuming, and even magic. He started in comics in 1987, penciling, inking and coloring Starstone and Darkewood for Aircel Publishing in Ottawa, Canada. He ran his own comic publish­ing com­pany, Ground Zero Graphics, which published The Shadowalker Chronicles in 1991. Adrian is the primary artist and a column­ist for the national magic maga­zine The Servante. He was one of the original artists for On Spec and Neo-opsis magazines, doing both covers and interior art. Adrian's latest project is a graphic novel, Frontiers, written and drawn by him and published by MU Press. He has worked on a number of MU Press and Antarctic Press projects, inking various penciller's works (Chuck Melville, Oscar Marcus and Steve Gallacci), pin-ups, and full art jobs for books such as Cyberkitties, Albedo, and Mousearella.

Adrian has also worked as a professional comics inker for a variety of magazines and artists and has displayed and sold artwork in a number of venues and galleries.

His written works have been published in fanzines such as Nightscapes and Dark Legacy, while his Mythos-related art includes images for Red Sonja.

Adumbrali (The Living Shadows) are a fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by Robert A. W. Lowndes for his short story "The Abyss", and were later expanded upon by Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

### Description
The Adumbrali are creatures that appear as shadows who dwell in the Abyss, sending out Seekers to capture souls for them to torture and devour. They are documented in the Song of Yste.

These monsters, like the Beings of Xiclotl and the Death Vines, are obscure creatures not well-known even among the most learned scholars. They are described as being two-dimensional beings of shadow that can only move in horizontal movement and are known to hunt humans with cruel delight until slaying them outright. Other accounts describe them as a type of shadow elemental of the malicious variety that can teleport into different realms and can shoot out shadow-like tendrils that suck the engulfed victim's body fluids, leaving nothing but a dried-up corpse once it's done.

Aforgomon is a fictional entity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Chain of Aforgomon".

### Description
Aforgomon is believed by some to be a god of time (: "The Chain of Aforgomon"), and may be an avatar of Yog-Sothoth. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

A necromancer used "avorgomon" as part of an incantation. (: "The Dark Eidolon")

### In Other Media
*Aforgomon appears in the mobile game Tower of Saviors, as a servitor of Yog-Sothoth. After being sealed into a magical barrier by Zeus, Yog-Sothoth summoned a bug and transformed it into a creature composed of water elemental power, thus creating Aforgomon to interact with the outside world.  Taking advantage of the false hope Zeus gave to humans, Aforgomon spread the legend to convince people that ascending the Enochian Tower was the only way to save the human realm from catastrophe, eventually finding a man who could see through the god's deception and break through the Seals of the Enochian Tower, freeing Yog-Sothoth and allowing Aforgomon to reunite with his master.
*Aforgomon appears in the mobile game Card Monsters.

fullContent:
"Afraid of Dobermans" is a short story inspired by the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft. It was written by American author and comic book creator Chad Fifer.

### Synopsis
A man with a fear of Doberman dogs hatches a plan to kill his neighbour, who he feels has stolen his moment in the spotlight. Confronting his fear with a view to set the animals upon the woman, he eventually overcomes it and becomes a much better person for it. Not only does he adopt and train two Dobermans, he eventually obtains both a book deal and even a television show devoted to his dog training.

Years later, he decides to see what his neighbour has been doing over the years, only to discover that she is incarcerated in an asylum, convicted of killing many, many children. Realising that if he had only gone through with his original plan to kill her the children would still be alive, his world is shattered.

### Publication History
"Afraid of Dobermans" was published in the anthology of H. P. Lovecraft-inspired fiction Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.

fullContent:
"After the After Party" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author M. Stern, first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2021.

### Synopsis
Lyle, a man besotted with a just-married woman, goes to save his beloved, believing that she is to be a sacrifice in her husband's bizarre ritual. However, he has misread the situation, and both of the newlyweds are willing participants in a plan to unite themselves in blissful eternity. Lyle arrives just in time to be a part of the rituals' completion, and bears witness to the birth of two powerful entities with a complete disdain for the human race.

### Mythos Connections
The components involved in the ritual included a book written by Von Junzt and a sacrificial knife referred to as the "dagger of Sothoth".

fullContent:
"Afterburn" is a short Lovecraftian story by author Carlton Herzog.

### Synopsis
A man recounts the devastation which occurred when his town was cursed by an infestation of flying, fire-breathing extra-dimensional entities. Despite being thrown back by the National Guard, the long-reaching consequences are severe, with mutated vegetation, deformed newborns, and madness consuming the town.

At story's conclusion, he reflects on whether the incursion was a one-off event, or the precursor to a full-scale invasion.

### Publication History
"Afterburn" was published in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2020.

### Trivia
* The deformed offspring of the townsfolk are dubbed "Wilbur Whateleys" by the outside world, implying that H. P. Lovecraft and his works exist in this fictional world.

Afterlife with Archie is an ongoing series from Archie Comics that has 10 issues.

### Synopsis
While attempting a to perform a resurrection with the Necronomicon the witch Sabrina accidentally releases a plague of flesh-eating zombies controlled by Cthulhu, and the survivors of Riverdale struggle to survive.

After the ceremony her aunts Hilda and Zelda are turned into ghouls. They banish Sabrina to the nether-world without her powers as punishment for using the forbidden text.

By Issue 6 Sabrina has been admitted as a patient at a mental institution run by H. P. Lovecraft after her aunts are supposedly killed in a house fire. Lovecraft tells her that she only believes herself to be a witch as a coping mechanism. In reality Lovecraft and her aunts are grooming her to be the Bride of Cthulhu by planting dreams of being led to cliffs. 

In issue 9 her possessed form confronts her former friends alongside Cthulhu himself.

fullContent:
Age of Ishtaria is a Japanese mobile game released by Silicon Studio in October 2014. The gameplay is a battle RPG featuring an array of units, allowing the player to mix and match devastating attacks to create their own powerful combos, such as launching enemies into the air and slamming them right back down, or debuffing tough bosses and charging at them head on. The units featured in the game are based on entities from various mythologies, including the Cthulhu Mythos.

The storyline takes place in the kingdom of Ishtaria, which stood at the brink of destruction from a malevolent force known as STORM, threatening to end the world of man in a time far past. After a group of heroes harnessed the power of the God Stones, the darkness was shattered and peace returned. Over time, the horrors faded from the hearts and minds of people, until the day that STORM had returned. Now, the player must command an army of powerful warriors to save Ishtaria.

fullContent:
Agents of Dreamland is a novel by Caitlin R. Kiernan, the first book of their Tinfoil Dossier trilogy. It follows two agents from rival occult intelligence agencies as they investigate a cult being used by the Fungi from Yuggoth (from H. P. Lovecraft's "The Whisperer in Darkness") to instigate a fungal apocalypse.

### Organizations 
* Albany: A secret intelligence agency, said to be all about "hiding the damage". So called because its headquarters are in Albany, New York, in the subbasement of the Erastus Corning Tower, but it has an extensive underground facility at Groom Lake, Nevada, in the military base known as Area 51. Also known as Dreamland. Its agents include the Signalman, Vance, and Jack Dunaway.
* Y: Referred to as Barbican Estate, or as London. A British organization with offices in Dubai. Jack Dunaway complains they "spent the last hundred years keeping us in the dark." The Signalman admires its lack of "skeptical, rationalist mumbo jumbo". The agent we meet is Immaculata Sexton.
*Moonlight Ranch: A cult on the shore of the Salton Sea in California. They use alien spores and messages sent via TV snow to turn themselves into the seeds of a fungal apocalypse.

### Characters
*The Signalman: An agent of Albany and an alcoholic. Born in 1960, he is 55 at the time of the story but looks at least ten years older. Gets his nickname from the silver railroad-style pocketwatch he carries. Known as "the one who never flinched". Has an apartment in the Santa Monica Hills.
*Immacolata Sexton: An agent of Y. The Signalman refers to her as a "ghoul dressed up like a woman". She is active for well over a century, and experiences past, present, and future simultaneously.
* Jack Dunaway: A hated colleague of the Signalman, 40 years old. He was recruited out of MIT. Recognizable by his "ferrety eyes and crooked nose, the thin lips and jutting chin".
*Agent Vance: Another colleague of the Signalman. Becomes infected with the alien fungus seven days after exposure.
*Drew Standish: The leader of the Moonlight Ranch cult. He is an agent of the Fungi from Yuggoth.
*Madeline Nightlinger: Standish's partner in the cult, "a former Facebook executive who’d been missing since January 2013."
*Chloe Stringfellow: A former heroin addict recruited into Standish's cult when he finds her in an alley in Westmont, California. Thinks of herself as Standish's favorite. She kills the other cult members with a shotgun out of jealousy that they were taken by the fungus before she was.

### Timeline
*352 B.C.: The Black Book placed in a tomb in Persia.
*1839: Eli Davenport writes a monograph on the folklore of the White and Green mountains that includes oral traditions of the Fungi from Yuggoth.
*1859: Alfred Russel Wallace identifies the fungus Ophiocordyceps unilateralis in Brazil.
*1888: The Signalman's watch is manufactured.
*November 1927: Immaculata Sexton dissects a Fungus from Yuggoth in Townsend, Vermont.
* 1934: James Whale makes The Star Maiden. Five weeks later,

Agnes Baker, the Waitress, is a fictional character who first appeared in Fantasy Flight Games' Second Edition of Arkham Horror, but who has since gone on to feature in other Arkham Horror Files lines of Cthulhu Mythos-related games and fiction.

### History
Once nothing more than a waitress at a small-time Arkham diner, when changing a light bulb one day, Agnes fell from the ladder and hit her head, an event which changed her life forever.

Upon awakening at the hospital, she found that the trauma to her head had unlocked memories of a past life untold millennia ago in a strange place called Hyperborea. There, she had been a powerful spellcaster, able to bend the winds of magic to her will. However, the memories also told her that she had been eventually slain by a creature of nightmares.

Finally plucking up the courage to try out one of the spells for herself, to her astonishment she found out that they actually worked. Afterwards, Agnes spent her time quietly developing these new abilities, although she was always careful to do so well away from the prying eyes of others.

Then one night after finishing up at the diner, Agnes stepped out into the street only to be struck by a premonition telling her that the thing which had bested her all those centuries ago was on her trail, and intended to put an end to her once again.

### Behind the Mythos
Initially included as an Investigator character for the Innsmouth Horror expansion for Arkham Horror, Agnes has also made appearances in Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game, both companion games to the original. A pre-painted plastic miniature was released in 2010 as part of Fantasy Flight's Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, but this has since been discontinued (all ). She was also included as an investigator character in Jonathan Green's 2024 gamebook The Darkness Over Arkham.

Ahtu is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by David Drake for his short story "Than Curse the Darkness".

### Description
Ahtu is one of Nyarlathotep's countless avatars, worshipped mainly in central and southern Africa. It manifests in the form of a black column of viscous matter, around fifty feet in diameter, erupting from below the ground. Several golden tentacles sprout from its central mass. 

Dame Alice Kilrea likens this entity to a "cancer" that permeates and mutates its environment into an imitation of life which, if allowed to grow unchecked, would eventually cover the entire Earth and transform the planet into "a ball of viscid slime hurtling around the sun", and then stretch its tentacles towards Mars. (: "Than Curse the Darkness")

It is believed that Ahtu can be called only at certain special locations in Africa, such as in the Congo Free State, although others may exist. To contact Ahtu with a spell, a special golden amulet depicting a three-lobed eye wreathed by flames is necessary. (: Arkham Unveiled)

Some have suggested a link between Ahtu and the Cambodian god Angka. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

### Worshipers
Ahtu's worshipers are usually deformed or mutilated natives, but there are some handicapped Europeans. The Ahtu cult was once a revolutionary organization opposing the Belgian overlords. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana) 

### In Other Media
*In the anime series Haiyore! Nyaruko-san, Ahtu is one of the many avatars of Nyarlathotep documented in the Great Library of Celaeno.
*The role-playing video game Final Fantasy XI features a monster named after Ahtu, whose species is based on the Treants from Dungeons & Dragons.

The Aihai are a species of alien created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his 1932 short story "The Vaults of Yoh-Vombis", and later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by other authors.

### Overview
Aihai are tall creatures, measuring over six feet in height. They possess a tough, leathery hide, a triple-nostrilled nose, sunken eyes, twin sets of sharp teeth, four-jointed fingers, and satyr-like legs. Some are birthed with a vestigial, atavistic third arm which sprouts from their angular chest. Unlike their ancestors, the Yorhi, the Aihai are not proficient in the use of advanced machinery, although occasionally one can be found operating ancient technology beyond the capabilities of human science, such as disintegrator rays.

The Aihai inhabit a collection of subterranean cities on Mars, modest in terms of size and architectural scope. They are a largely peaceful race, and are for the most part quietly friendly to the humans who encounter them.

### Vulthoom
The Aihai are aware of the powerful alien known as Vulthoom which dwells in the subterranean city of Ravormos, and in the distant past fought a vicious war against it and its followers; in the modern age, they see it as something akin to the Christian Satan. Despite this, one radical sect of Aihai has fallen to the worship of this creature, due in no small part to its granting them virtual immortality through the drinking of a mysterious elixir.

### The Dweller in the Gulf
One particular sect of blind subterranean Aihai worship the ancient Martian being known as the Dweller in the Gulf, although they appear to be a minority group and conduct their practices in secret.

### In the Call of Cthulhu Roleplaying Game
The Aihai are a peaceful sentient race which is indigenous to Mars. Its society revolves around culture and trade. The typical Aihai stands about ten feet tall and has a bulging chest and multiple many-angled arms. The race coexists uneasily with the warlike Martians and has as little to do with them as possible. Aihais live in subterranean cities though in the future they will built great and beautiful cities on the surface, once contact is made with humans. A faction resides in a great underground complex with their master, the Great Old One Vulthoom.

Aeons ago, when Vulthoom arrived on Mars, a civil war erupted between Vulthoom and his followers and the ruling Aihais. Vulthoom was defeated and it and its followers fled underground, where they slumbered in suspended animation for centuries. Now they build spacecraft to carry Vulthoom and its followers across the cosmos to conquer new worlds, with Earth being the first target. Among the weapons its followers possess are disintegrator guns capable of melting rock and metal and instantly dissolving organic matter .

Aiueb Gnshal (The Eyes Between Worlds) is a fictional entity created by Kevin T. McKinnon and Dylan K. Sharpe for the Call of Cthulhu scenario "The Eyes Between Worlds", which was published in the monograph Strange Tales of Dread & Wonder.

### Overview
Aiueb Gnshal is a mysterious Lesser Other God who has made his home in a long-lost temple in Bhutan, as well as many other temples. He appears as a formless black void with seven orb-like eyes. It is mainly worshipped by Ghouls who worship him in a defiled cult spoken of in the Cambuluc Scrolls of the wizard Lang-Fu. Looking into the eyes of this horrid being, after a disgusting and awful ritual, will allow you to see into the Court of Azathoth, in which he resides simultaneously as he does across his temples.

It is said that the Mongolian warlord Temujin, better known as Genghis Khan, had the favour of Aiueb Gnshal.

Akachi Onyele, the Shaman, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Files range of Mythos-related content.

### History
Trained by one of the elders of her small Nigerian village from a young age to be the tribe's next shaman, Akachi learned English along with the ways of the outside world from a Christian missionary. Whilst she ignored his attempts to convert her - she already knew far too much about the world which is hidden from the eyes of most mortals - she took all of his other teachings in her stride.

Finally, upon reaching adulthood, the elder called her to him, telling the young woman "Akachi, I have seen that a great trial is coming for you. You must go to the United States, to a city called Arkham. There, you will have to face one of the old creatures, using the things that I have taught you." Thus Akachi made her way to America, finally landing on the shores of New England, and preparing for her greatest test.

### Eldritch Horror
The backstory given in Eldritch Horror varies from that given in Arkham Horror. Rather than being sent to Arkham, Akachi travelled Africa teaching others the ways of the shaman, before beginning her quest in Cape Town.

### Behind the Mythos
Akachi debuted in the Innsmouth Horror expansion for the Second Edition of Fantasy Flights' board game of Lovecraftian horror, Arkham Horror. She has since made appearances in Eldritch Horror, Mansions of Madness and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. A now-discontinued plastic miniature of the character was released in 2010 as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line.

Aklo is a fictional language, first mentioned by Arthur Machen (: "The White People") and incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in "The Dunwich Horror" and "The Diary of Alonzo Typer".

It appears as a key element of Alan Moore's Mythos work The Courtyard and his comic book series Providence.

### The White People
In Arthur Machen's "The White People", a girl's journal includes the passage:

I must not write down the real names of the days and months which I found out a year ago, nor the way to make the Aklo letters, or the Chian language, or the great beautiful Circles, nor the Mao Games, nor the chief songs. I may write something about all these things but not the way to do them, for peculiar reasons.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror" (1928) includes a quotation from Wilbur Whateley's journal:Today learned the Aklo for the Sabaoth...which did not like, it being answerable from the hill and not from the air.... I wonder how I shall look when the earth is cleared and there are no earth beings on it. He that came with the Aklo Sabaoth said I may be transfigured, there being much of outside to work on.After Robert Blake, the protagonist of "The Haunter of the Dark" (1935), discovers a cipher in the abandoned Starry Wisdom Church, he finds that the text is "in the dark Aklo language used by certain cults of evil antiquity, and known to him in a halting way through previous researches." 

Aklo comes up repeatedly in the revision tale "The Diary of Alonzo Typer" (1938). First Typer notes that a presence in the Van der Heyl house "towers like a colossus, bearing out what is said in the Aklo writings." Then he writes, "Later I ascended to the attic, where I found several chests of strange books—many of utterly alien aspect in letters and in physical form alike. One contained variants of the Aklo formulae which I had never known to exist." Finally, referring to the presences in the house, he writes, "I know now that the third Aklo ritual—which I found in that book in the attic yesterday—would make such beings solid and visible."

### Description
The Aklo language and script was first used by the Serpent Men some 1.5 million years ago, during the Pleistocene epoch. To this day the Aklo language is still employed in certain spells and rituals.

### Usage
Although Aklo can be used for communication, its primary usage is in incantations and prayers. Below is a list of some of the magical rites that Aklo is employed in.

### Aklo Unveilings 
:The Aklo Unveilings are a collection of 48 revelations recorded by the Aklo. There is said to be a 49th Unveiling, which mankind will only learn when Glaaki calls humanity to him.

### Aklo Formulae
: The Aklo Formulae are a collection of incantations connected with the summoning, banishing and controlling of certain extradimensional beings. The Third Aklo Formula can be used to make invisible and immaterial entities reveal their physical form.

Aku-Shin Kage (悪 心 影, meaning "malicious shadow" and with alternate spelling "Akushin Kage", "Aku-Shin-Kage" or "Akushin-Kage") is one of the avatars of Nyarlathotep. Its first appearance was in the Secrets of Japan supplement for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

Its field of action is the territory of Japan. During the history of the country, it has caused many wars and confrontations. In fact, it is believed that the warlord Oda Nobunaga was one of his human incarnations know as the "Dark Warlord", and also known precisely as "ghost of Nobunaga". It it said to have dictated the work known as "Kuragari no shūkai" (in English, "Manual of the Shadows") to a ninja clan with supernatural powers that would carry out a multitude of killings and served the Dark Warlord from the late 12th century to the early 18th century. In more modern times, due to a long and close affinity with Oda in life, it can take on the human form of the ghost of Nobunaga, appearing age 40. In this guise, the avatar of Nyarlathotep urges on one or more deranged leaders of ultra-right nationalist groups. Nowadays, it resembles a Yotsubishi Heavy Industries businessman advocating a golden age for the Japanese empire in boardrooms. 

In his usual form, he appears dressed in a full suit of blackened samurai o-yoroi armor. Where unprotected parts of the body would normally be seen, like the upper arms, legs and head, it is instead an amorphous shadow that shifts within the suit. Those who are brave enough to look into the hooded helmet will see a black void with dozens of tiny mouths bearing sharp gnashing teeth. Blood constantly drips from cracks in the armor.

### Veneration and invocation
The Aku-Shin Kage was worshiped by the Japanese before the 20th century as a kami-sama of chaos and war. Worshipers hoped its summoned fury would be unleashed upon the enemy. Eventually, it became known how unpredictable the being was, so this practice declined. Now, it is worshiped by power-mad modern cultists like Buddha’s Tears and the Dugpa sect of degenerate Buddhists (the Green Caps), hoping to gain occult knowledge or to destroy a foe. This can be done with a spell or reciting texts from the book "Rock Garden on Infinity". Invocations take place on the night of a new moon or deep within a cavern where no sun can reach. If it contacts the caster, usually among a group of worshipers, it will appear as the shadow of an armored samurai on a wall. Someone present, but not the caster, will begin to bleed profusely from all orifices, eyes, ears and even fingernails, causing the victim and witnesses to lose sanity. Until it leaves, the avatar speaks through the bleeding victim in harsh unnatural whispers. The host/victim loses vitality until the avatar departs. However, the avatar partially animates the victim and keeps him or her standing erect like a puppet until the contact ends, even if the victim dies (though the limbs and head loll about limply).

Al-Azif was a short-lived Cthulhu Mythos-focused periodical.

### Overview
Containing a selection of Mythos-related short fiction and poetry, Al-Azif was edited by Peter A. Worthy who also provided the interior illustrations. Cover art was by Stanley C. Sargent for the first three issues, and Mike Minnis for the fourth and final issue.

### Publication History
Al-Azif was published by Yhtill Press for a total of four issues between January and December 1998 (Jan/Feb 1998, March/April1998, May/June 1998, with the last issue being simply named #4).

### Trivia
*Al-Azif was named for Abdul Alhazred's Necronomicon, Al-Azif being Alhazred's original title for the work.

fullContent:
"Alabaster" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-hunter. On March 18, 2003, Kiernan conceived of the story and completed a version of it in one day--"something I've never done before," they wrote on their online journal. The thousand-word short-short was published as "chapette" by Camelot Books in 2003. It was expanded into a full-length short story in 2004, which appeared in print for the first time as the title story of Kiernan's 2006 Subterranean Press collection Alabaster.

"Alabaster" is set five days after the events of "Bainbridge," and occurs before the story "Waycross." It tells the story of Dancy's encounter with a wizard who runs a Texaco station somewhere in Georgia, and with a shapeshifting panther woman that he keeps in a cage out back. The story gives one of the most detailed descriptions of Dancy's angel, referred to as one of the Seraphim.

### Publication History
The story also appeared in The Mammoth Book of Angels and Demons (Robinson/Running Press, 2013).

fullContent:
Alan Dean Foster is an American sci-fi and fantasy author whose works include the Pip & Flinx series and the Icerigger trilogy, both set in his Humanx Commonwealth universe. He also wrote the novelizations of famous films such as Star Wars (1976) and Alien (1979). Some of his stories are set in the Cthulhu Mythos.

Foster's first professional sale was the Mythos pastiche "Some Notes Concerning a Green Box," which appeared in the Summer 1971 issue of The Arkham Collector. In his introduction to that story in the collection With Friends Like These..., Foster recounts that he didn't have publication in mind when he wrote it, but sent the story to August Derleth anyway, hoping that the latter would find it amusing. He was surprised when Derleth actually offered to buy it.

In his introduction to another Mythos story, "A Fatal Exception Has Occurred at...", in his collection Exceptions to Reality, Foster reveals that he once taught a seminar about H. P. Lovecraft's works at the University of California.

### Selected works

*"The Horror on the Beach" (1978)

*"The Door Beneath" (2015)

Alan Moore (born 18 November 1953) is a prolific British comic book creator and prose writer whose work has at times explored the Cthulhu Mythos.

For the comic book genre, he has written several works set in and around the Cthulhu Mythos, including the hugely popular linked series Neonomicon and Providence. His League of Extraordinary Gentlemen series has also incorporated the Mythos in a supporting role.

Moore has written short stories connected to the Mythos, including "The Courtyard", whose adaptation in comic book format was the inspiration for Providence.

Albert N. Wilmarth is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Whisperer in Darkness". He has since made other appearances in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos.

### Biography
Albert Wilmarth is a folklorist and professor of English at Miskatonic University in Massachusetts. When, after the historic floods in Vermont in 1927 the isolated sightings of strange bodies in the rivers are discussed in public, Wilmarth first takes part offering rationalizations, which quickly makes him one of the most well-known spokesmen in the debate.

Only after the arrival of the letters of the local hermit Henry Wentworth Akeley and closer inspection of the sightings and myths of the area he changes his point of view increasingly. By continuing to contact Akeley, Wilmarth quickly becomes convinced that the myths are true and that the mountains are inhabited by aliens.

After a local commemoration of the scene and the subsequent disappearance of his friend Akeley, Professor Wilmarth, who continues to teach at Miskatonic University, despite the lack of evidence, points to the authenticity of ancient Indian legends about the Mi-Go. (: "The Whisperer in Darkness")

At some point prior to the Pabodie Expedition, Wilmarth has shared his knowledge of the Cthulhu Mythos with fellow professors Dyer and Lake. After seeing the Elder Things' city, Dyer regrets having had such conversations and describes Wilmarth as an "unpleasantly erudite folklorist". (: At the Mountains of Madness)

Wilmarth is a popular figure among the students at Miskatonic, and is known for his love of automobiles. He keeps several pet cats and is a friend of Danforth and Lovecraft. (: "The Terror from the Depths")

In the Expanded Mythos, Wilmarth is the founder of the Wilmarth Foundation. (: The Burrowers Beneath)

fullContent:
Alberto Breccia (15 April 1919-10 November 1993) was a South American comic book artist. He has provided artwork for a number of adaptations of H. P. Lovecraft stories, most of which have yet to be translated into English.

His somewhat tragic life was best encapsulated by his work on his masterpiece The Eternaut which is outside the Mythos.

Breccia completed ten adaptations of Lovecraft’s stories, the majority of them between 1972-1974, six of them from scripts developed by his collaborator Norberto Buscaglia. 

The first six stories were published in the Italian comic magazine Il Mago, but were translated and reprinted in other languages, such as the Métal Hurlant/Heavy Metal/Metal Extra Lovecraft Special.

Multiple collections of these comic stories have been published over the decades, although ironically, few of Breccia’s influential Lovecraft adaptations have been published in English. While the first nine are relatively well-known and widely republished, after Breccia’s death a new collection of adaptations was published, Sueños Pesados (2003, “Heavy Dreams”). These are painted, in color, and contain one additional Lovecraft adaptation.

### Selected Bibliography

* The Shadow Over Innsmouth (1973)
* The Nameless City (1974)
* The Haunter of the Dark (1975)
* The Dunwich Horror (1979)

### Collections
