The Albino penguins are a fictional species from the Cthulhu Mythos, which first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's novella At the Mountains of Madness.

### Overview
The albino penguins are a species of penguin described by explorer William Dyer, as standing six-feet-tall, making them larger than even the Emperor Penguin, and thus the tallest and heaviest of all living penguin species. The modern Albino Penguins discovered by Dyer and Danforth in Antarctic mountains near the Elder Thing city are concluded through sculptures to be descendants of archaic penguins bred by the Elder Things. When Antarctica became glaciated, the penguins retreated to a heated underground abyss, although years of evolution in these depths "destroyed their pigmentation and atrophied their eyes to mere useless slits." Despite being incredibly large, they are harmless, calm and apathetic towards humans. Having lived side by side with the Elder things, they learned to be unbothered by their horrible stench. However, the smell of the shoggoths will put them in a frenzied panic.

### In the Expanded Mythos
In his short story "The Fillmore Shoggoth", Harry Turtledove gives their Latin name as Aptenodytes miskatonensis. Specimens are kept as exhibits in San Fransisco zoo, the only zoo in the world to have successfully bred them. They were brought back from the Antarctic by the Starkweather-Moore exploration team which followed the disastrous Pabodie expedition.

In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, the albino penguins are alluded to when Al Azif claims that her pet shoggoth Dunsany's favorite food is penguin meat from the South Pole.

Aldebaran is one of the brightest objects in the night sky, a giant red star about 65 light-years away from our Solar System. Seen from Earth, it appears to be part of the Hyades, although it is in fact much closer. It was used by Robert W. Chambers in his work The King in Yellow.

August Derleth identifies it as the "place where the dark stars hang", the abode of Hastur (: "The Return of Hastur").

Aldebaran appears in the short story "Polaris" by H. P. Lovecraft. The unnamed narrator observed Aldebaran from the city of Olathoë in the Arctic region of Lomar in the Dreamlands. The red star never set but crawled low around the horizon during the extended polar night.

Aldebaran is visible in the sky above Kingsport during the events of "The Festival" by H. P. Lovecraft, making the narrator shiver as the star seems to balance itself on the spire of the church. The Byakhee, which debuted in that story, are revealed to be servants of Hastur in Derleth's The Trail of Cthulhu.

### Overview
Also known as the Eye of the Bull, Aldebaran lies in the constellation of Taurus and is said to be the star of the Great Old One Hastur, who inhabits the Lake of Hali on a planet circling a nearby dark star. The Celaeno Library might also be located here (although it should be noted that Celaeno is a different star).

### Notes
Aldebaran as it appears in the Cthulhu Mythos may be connected with Marion Zimmer Bradley's Darkover novels, which also incorporate the Hastur myth.

"Aldebaran Apocalypse" is a short Yellow Mythos story by American author Brian Barr. The fourth and final of his King in Yellow stories, it was independently published in both print and digital formats in May 2019.

### Synopsis
In 400BC Anatolia, a young Greek woman is inducted into a cult of the Yellow King known as the Cult of the Carians, receiving the mark of her new master.

In the modern day Robbie, a man completing his PhD on the cult, is is slowly consumed by his thirst for knowledge on the subject while simultaneously coming to realise that he may have unwittingly drawn the King's attention to him. Following the lead of a beautiful Greek woman who appears in his dreams, he begins to experiment with magical rituals. Unfortunately for the inhabitants of planet Earth, his work results in the opening of a breach in reality, allowing the armies of Hastur to pour through and begin their conquest.

### Publication History
Since it’s release, "Aldebaran Apocalypse has also been included in the June 2019 collection Brian Barr's King in Yellow.

### Trivia
*The fleet of ancient ships used by Hastur's army is the one described in Barr's earlier story "A Visage of Great Truths".

fullContent:
Aleister Crowley (born Edward Alexander Crowley, 12 October 1875 - 1 December 1947) was an English author, occultist, artist, and practicing magician, perhaps best known for the proliferation of works he produced in the esotericism and occult literature genres, as well as his personal life and sexual proclivities, issues which were very much taboo during his lifetime.

Crowley has intersected with the Cthulhu Mythos on several occasions, mostly in a fictional aspect, although he was for a time a member of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn, the organisation which was the (loose) inspiration for the Order of the Silver Twilight.

### In the Mythos
*Call of Cthulhu: Lam, the alien entity purported to have been in contact with Crowley in 1919, was incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu supplement Malleus Monstrorum.
*Deus Machina Demonbane: The main antagonist Master Therion, Grandmaster of the Black Lodge, was named after one of Crowley's aliases. His characterization features many references to the real-life Crowley, including his grimoire the Pnakotic Manuscripts having a humanoid manifestation named Etheldreda, derived from Crowley’s pet dog; as well as piloting the Deus Machina known as Liber Legis, taken from Liber AL vel Legis, the sacred book about Thelema written by Crowley himself.
*Herald: Lovecraft and Tesla: Crowley is a secondary villain in the comic and has genuine magical abilities.
*Simon Necronomicon: H. P. Lovecraft and Aleister Crowley were said to have undergone a meeting of minds in Sumeria, both being described as prophets of a new age.
*Minky Woodcock: The Girl Called Cthulhu: Cynthia von Buhler's risqué comic book sees Crowley as an antagonist in a World War II story of espionage and murder.
*White Darkness: in David A. McIntee's 1993 Doctor Who novel, Crowley once owned a copy of the forbidden Necronomicon, which contained illustrations by Nicholas Roerich.
*The Womb of Time: it is mentioned that Crowley was a member of the Golden Dawn along with Arthur Machen, Algernon Blackwood, and others. However, main character Richard Halsted dismisses Crowley as a "famous charlatan".

The Alert is a fictional yacht used by the Cthulhu cult, and later by the crew of the Emma, which originated in Dunedin, New Zealand. It first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Background
The Alert was a heavily armored steam yacht which originated in Dunedin, New Zealand, and at one point was manned by "a queer and evil-looking crew of Kanakas and half-castes," in addition to being members of the Cthulhu cult. The crew of the Alert was slain in retaliation for attacking the schooner Emma, and upon being discovered by the Vigilant, the Alert was towed to Sydney, Australia where it was sold for commercial use. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

### In Other Media
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, Cthulhu headed towards the coordinates 47'9" South and 126'43" West in the southern Pacific Ocean, the location of R'lyeh. During the briefing about Cthulhu, Hadou Ruri recalls the Alert incident on March 23, 1925, where the crew of the armed yacht encountered something strange and unexplainable from the waves in the same region of the ocean. Subsequently, her grandfather investigated the incident with great interest.
*In the 2007 film Cthulhu, while Russell is speaking to Zadok, a yacht named the Alert can be seen moored in the background.

Aletheia is a fictional deity created by comic book author Tiziano Sclavi for Dylan Dog issue #374 "La Fine dell'Oscuritó" (Sergio Bonelli Editore, November 2017).

### Description
Aletheia appears as a large loosely interconnected grouping of enormous hands in the sky, jutting out of clouds and darkness, with each hand having a large eye in the center of its palm. Untold amounts of much smaller but thick cords or threads of metallic flesh extend from the surface of its hands and fingers - the threads of Aletheia.

A thread of Aletheia will interconnect with a human victim at the base of their spine. Attempting to remove the thread - which is about as thick as the spine it attached itself to -  with sufficient force will cause the entire spine of the victim to be violently pulled out, leading to an explosively gory demise.

Once connected, a being will at some point experience the call of Aletheia, approaching its summoning point, which will be engulfed in blinding light. Those not called, at Aletheia's disgression, are violently expelled with a painful, but non-lethal searing burn, which flings them back from the light.

The criteria Aletheia uses seem mysterious, but its cult interpretes this selection as rejecting those who are sane - ones who bend the truth with their own logic. Those that are instead accepted by Aletheia will either remain with the entity or return back into the world: the latter fundamentally changes the person's perception and they will lack any recollection of Aletheia that does not fit into their worldview; they will henceforth both see and interprete the world with their senses and prior beliefs: their experienced world will not only entirely conform to those beliefs, but the people within them will never begrudge them their beliefs either.

Furthermore, those affected by Aletheia can be confronted with people and visions of their past, through which it seems to be able to indirectly communicate with its victims in vague hints, though it will not adress them specifically in any conversational way itself. A cultist implies that certain affected may also be able to sense some things about one another - their current status or perhaps even how they perceive the world.

Aletheia's reach may or may not be of a global scale. It furthermore has the ability to emit highly powerful energy beams, strong and large enough to level entire cities. It may also be the case that Aletheia does not connect itself to all people, but due to its perception-warping abilities, this may not be so.

### Worshippers
The Sons of Aletheia are a cult that was active in Westminster, London. Their only known activity was to cause a massacre in the subway system which was a mix of the wanton ritual slaughter of innocent bystanders as well as suicide by the cult members themselves, claiming a total of 233 lives. This was instrumental in calling Aletheia to earth.

Alex Shvartsman (born 19 November 1975) is an award-winning Ukrainian-born American author and editor who is best known for his light-hearted short fiction. His Cthulhu Mythos output includes the 2013 short story "Explaining Cthulhu to Grandma," which won the WSFA Small Press Award for Short Fiction the year after its publication, and he edited the 2018 anthology The Cackle of Cthulhu.

Shvartsman's non-Mythos output includes a series of short fiction based around the conceit that pioneering science fiction author H. G. Wells was in fact a secret agent. He is also a world-ranked player of the fantasy card game Magic: The Gathering.

Dr. Alfred Schuyler Clarendon is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft and Adolphe de Castro for their short story "The Last Test".  

Clarendon is a famous physician, "one of the greatest biologists and physicians" of the 1890s, he is an authority at twenty-five and an international figure at thirty." He is said to be researching a "basic antitoxin combating the whole febrile principle at its very source...ensuring the ultimate conquest and extirpation of fever in all its diverse forms."

A native of New York City, he is the son of Old Clarendon, "a Wall Street pirate of the ruthless elder breed," and Frances Schuyler Clarendon, known for her gentleness. His only sibling is his sister Georgina. The family lived in an old mansion on East 19th Street.

His closest friend from childhood, who called him "Little Alf", was James Dalton, his protector at Phillips Exeter and Columbia University. 

He travels throughout the world to study diseases, including to North Africa, the Middle East, India, and China, including Tibet. In Tibet's U-Tsang, he acquires a team of eight servants of "skeletonic leanness" and "grotesque" aspect, whom he dresses in "the loose black silk robes of Bonpa priests". In the Hoggar Mountains of Algeria, he meets the mysterious Surama, who becomes his chief factotum and clinic-man.

On his travels, he picked up a considerable amount of eldritch knowledge. "I didn’t go to China for nothing," he warns Surama--that's where he "heard an old man...calling on Yog-Sothoth"--and he "talked in Yemen with an old man who had come back alive from the Crimson Desert," who "had seen Irem, the City of Pillars, and had worshipped at the underground shrines of Nug and Yeb." He was familiar with "Alhazred’s Azif", which contains lore unknown in Atlantis. He claims to be able to call on the "Nemesis of Flame", and to be able to appeal to Shub-Niggurath.

After relocating from New York to San Francisco, he reconnects with his friend Dalton, who has been out of touch for ten years, since Old Clarendon refused his request to marry Georgina. In the meantime, Dalton has risen in California politics to the point of becoming governor, a position that allows him to appoint Clarendon to become medical director of California's San Quentin Penitentiary. This appointment is seen as bringing prestige to the state.

Clarendon is described as "lean and ascetic, with steel-rimmed pince-nez and pointed brown beard". He lives with Georgina in "the gloomy old Bannister place near Goat Hill, overlooking the bay...a rambling, French-roofed relic of mid-Victorian design and gold-rush parvenu display." (Goat Hill is better known today as Portrero Hill.)

Alfred Delapore is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his horror short story "The Rats in the Walls".

### Biography
Delapore's only child, Alfred was born in 1894, apparently in Bolton, Massachusetts. His mother died at some point, either during his birth or childhood, and when he was ten, his paternal grandfather passed away as well. In 1917, he fought in World War One as an airplane pilot in England, where he befriended Captain Edward Norrys, whose family had come to own the Delapores' ancestral estate of Exham Priory. Alfred wrote letters to his father, telling him the horrific stories about their ancestors, some of which rumoured to have been murderers and devil-worshipers; stories which Norrys didn't take seriously and Alfred found merely amusing.

In 1918, Alfred was gravely wounded and sent back home as a "maimed invalid". His father left his business to the care of partners and dedicated 100% of his time to take care of Alfred, who passed away two years later. The trauma of losing his son to the war contributed in part to Delapore's own mental collapse in 1923. (: "The Rats in the Walls")

fullContent:
Alfred Galpin (8 November 1901-5 March 1983) was a writer, literary academic and musical composer, as well as a long-time friend and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft's.

### Overview
First making Lovecraft’s acquaintance while still in high school, the two met through the United Amateur Press Association, an organisation which Lovecraft spent a great deal of time involved with. There, Galpin served two terms as vice president, the appointment being made by Lovecraft himself. They also wrote a series of round-robin pieces with fellow author Maurice W. Moe; most of these pieces are no longer extant.

Although Galpin and Lovecraft corresponded for decades, they only met in person once, when the latter visited Galpin and Samuel Loveman in Cleveland, Ohio in July 1922.

When hearing of Lovecraft’s death in 1937 Galpin dedicated the last in a series of four musical pieces, which he was in the process of completing, to his old friend: "Lament for H. P. L."

Later in life Galpin would write a memoir titled "Memories of a Friendship"; August Derleth included the work in the Arkham House anthology The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces in 1959. This volume also featured the first printing of Lovecraft's cautionary short story "Old Bugs", in which a fictionalised version of Galpin who succumbed to the lure of alcohol became a drunken destitute.

Sir Alfed Jermyn is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family".

### Background
Alfed Jermyn was the son of Nevil Jermyn and the father of Arthur Jermyn. His mother, an unnamed dancer with whom Nevil eloped in 1849, died when Alfred was an infant. Nevil and Alfred returned home to Jermyn House the following year to live with Nevil's father Robert Jermyn.

When an explorer named Samuel Seaton visited the Jermyn home in 1852 with a manuscript of notes collected in Africa, Robert discovered to his horror that there was a simian strain in his own family originating from a union between his grandfather Wade Jermyn and a female member of a race of African white apes. The unhinged Robert murdered Seaton along with his own three children including Nevil, but the two year old Alfred survived. 

Sir Alfred became a baronet before his fourth birthday, but his tastes never matched his title. At the age of twenty he joined a band of music hall performers, and at thirty-six he deserted his wife and son to travel with an itinerant American circus. His death was particularly brutal after developing a fascination and kinship with a trained circus gorilla. One morning in Chicago as Alfred and the gorilla were rehearsing a performative boxing match, the gorilla delivered a blow more forceful than usual, hurting both the body and the dignity of the amateur trainer. The enraged Alfred attacked the gorilla which defended itself. Alfred was killed and his body was left beyond recognition.

shortDefinition: "Alfredo: A Tragedy" is a satirical stage play by the late cosmic horror author Howard Phillips Lovecraft.  Many of the play's characters are based on real people: the titular Alfredo is Alfred Galpin, Rinarto is Rheinhart Kleiner, Teobaldo is Lovecr...
fullContent:
"Alfredo: A Tragedy" is a satirical stage play by the late cosmic horror author Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

Many of the play's characters are based on real people: the titular Alfredo is Alfred Galpin, Rinarto is Rheinhart Kleiner, Teobaldo is Lovecraft himself (who frequently used "Theobald" or "Theobaldus" as a pseudonym), and Mauricio is Maurice W. Moe.

### Synopsis
The play is a parody of Alfred Galpin’s high school romances, written in the form of an Elizabethan tragedy.

Alfredo (Galpin), the Prince Regent, yearns for Margarita (Margaret Abraham), but she claims to find him too studious for her “airy will”; nevertheless, she becomes jealous when she sees him spending much time studying with Hypatia. She and Hecatissa (an unattractive woman previously scorned by Alfredo) plot together to gain revenge. During the presentation of a play in which Alfredo and Hypatia, now engaged, act in the presence of King Rinarto (Rheinhart Kleiner), Alfredo and Hypatia drink from a goblet that has been poisoned by Hecatissa; they lie dying. In a rage, Gonzago perceives the trickery and kills Hecatissa; her father, Olero, kills Gonzago; Teobaldo (HPL), Alfredo’s tutor, kills Olero; Margarita kills Teobaldo; Alfredo, in his death throes, manages to stab and kill Margarita; Rinarto, in grief, drinks from the goblet and dies, leaving Mauricio (Maurice W.Moe), a Cardinal, to lament the tragedy and count his beads.

### Publication History
Alfredo: A Tragedy is a verse drama of 411 lines. The original manuscript for this work is dated September 14, 1918, as by “Beaumont and Fletcher” (i.e., John Fletcher [1579–1625] and Francis Beaumont [c. 1585–1616], the Jacobean dramatists). It was first published nearly 30 years years after Lovecraft’s death in the collection The Dark Brotherhood and Other Pieces in 1966, a volume edited by his friend and contemporary August Derleth through his Arkham House label. It has since been reprinted several times.

Algernon Henry Blackwood (14 March 1869 - 10 December 1951) was an English author, journalist and radio broadcaster who worked in the horror, fantasy and weird fiction genres.

### Overview
One of the most prolific horror writers of all time, Algernon Blackwood's work has been described as "more consistently meritorious than any weird writer's except Dunsany's."  He has had an enormous influence on the development of the Cthulhu Mythos, with Lovecraft himself claiming him as both an inspiration and one of his favourite authors. Other weird fiction writers to cite Blackwood as a source of inspiration include Frank Belknap Long, Clark Ashton Smith and Ramsey Campbell.

Similar to some of his own characters, Blackwood was known for his interest in both occultism and outdoor activities, such as camping and hiking. He was also one of the most eminent and well-established authors of supernatural fiction to contribute original stories to the American magazine Weird Tales.

Blackwood's interpretation of the legendary Wendigo was incorporated into the Mythos by August Derleth, who associates it with his own creation, Ithaqua.

Algernon Harris is a fictional character created by Frank Belknap Long for his Cthulhu Mythos novel The Horror from the Hills.

### Biography
Despite being only 26 at the time of the novel, Algernon Harris has post-graduate degrees from Yale and Oxford, and has recently succeeded the late Halpin Chalmers as Curator of Archaeology in the Manhattan Museum of Fine Arts.

Dressed unassumingly, with a genial and jovial disposition, Harris is often mistaken for a subordinate, and there's nothing in his aspect that gives away his scholarly inclinations. He is very enthusiastic about his work and well regarded by the Museum's field workers, who have ventured into the remotest corners of the globe to bring back new artifacts. Despite his young age and generally informal attitude, Harris is very capable of speaking with authority if needed.

When Harris' friend, Clark Ulman, returned from a lone expedition into the inhospitable Plateau of Tsang, bringing along what appeared to be a statue of Chaugnar Faugn, Harris was horrified to find out that Ulman had been inexplicably disfigured and was suffering from physical and mental stress. However, he didn't believe in Ulman's claim that the supposed statue of Chaugnar Faugn was actually Chaugnar itself in a dormant state, and that his disfigurement had been the result of Chaugnar periodically feeding on his blood. Harris did believe in Ulman's claim to have met the cult of Chaugnar in the Plateau of Tsang, but assumed that the high-priest Chung Ga had implanted hypnotic suggestions on Ulman and that Ulman's disfigurement was the result of some unknown hormonal treatment and/or surgical procedure. At this point, however, Ulman started to convulse as if being attacked by an invisible assaulter, and died before Harris could do anything to help him.

The coroner attributed Ulman's death to heart failure, and reluctantly accepted Harris' hypothesis about the unfortunate man's disfigurement. However, Harris himself was less inclined to believe in his own explanation after witnessing how Ulman's body putrefied abnormally fast, and how his elongated nose kept moving even hours after death. Pressed by reporters and public interest, Harris agreed to put the Chaugnar Faugn "statue" on display in the museum.

A few days later, Harris took a bus and came across his boss, George Francis Scollard. While talking about Ulman's fate, the two noticed a large crowd gathered around the museum and found that the watchman, Cinney, had been killed and mutilated beyond recognition, with nothing of his face remaining. Cinney's body was also entirely drained of blood, while Chaugnar Faugn's mouth, trunk and tusks were covered in it.

Algol, the Daemon-Star, is a double (and possibly quintary) star mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's shorty story "Beyond the Wall of Sleep", described as being the sidereal home of a demonic shining entity made of light. 

### Overview
After the death of Joe Slater, the luminescent being trapped in his physical body was freed, becoming completely incorporeal to have a final battle with its nemesis Algol, the Daemon-Star. (: "Beyond the Wall of Sleep") 

In the works of Lin Carter, Algol is orbited by a world inhabited by Zvilpogghua, the son of Tsathoggua. However, the name of this world varies from one tale to the next. In "The Feaster from the Stars", Carter identifies it as either Ymar (in the Crypt of Cthulhu version) or Abbith (in the Book of Eibon version), the latter being Carter's name for the World of Seven Suns from which Nyarlathotep can be summoned (as mentioned in Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness and August Derleth's "The Dweller in Darkness"). Conversely, in "Strange Manuscript Found in the Vermont Woods", the Algolian world where Zvilpogghua dwells is named Yrautrom.

In "The Thing in the Pit", Abbith and Ymar (and therefore possibly Algol) are located in the same star cluster as the binary green star Xoth.

### In Other Media
*The mobile game Crash Fever features a female character named after and based on Algol. Seeking to get revenge on Cthulhu for conducting some horrible experiments, with her brother being one of the victims, Algol threatened to destroy the data storage area of the labs but was quickly interrupted by Wendigo.

### Gallery

Algol (Crash Fever).jpg|Algol (Crash Fever)
Algol (Crash Fever) 2.jpg|Algol (Crash Fever)


### Behind the Mythos
The name Algol is derived from an Arabic phrase meaning "the demon's head" (Ra's al Ghul) and concordantly occupies a place in the constellation of Perseus often assigned to the head of Medusa.

Although believed to have been a binary star at the time of Lovecraft's writings, recent research suggests that it may in fact be a cluster system of as many as seven separate stars.

"Alhireth-Hotep the Prophet" is a very short (five line) prose poem by Lord Dunsany appearing in his story anthology The Gods of Pegāna, first published in 1905.

The story is redolent with names that would become very familiar in style and content for Cthulhu Mythos devotees. It had a significant influence on H. P. Lovecraft, and through him on his legion of collaborators and imitators. It was later featured in Chaosium's anthology The Nyarlathotep Cycle, as one of the works that served as inspiration for the Outer God known as Nyarlathotep.

Alice, (: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland)  fully named Alice Liddle (: Return to Wonderland, Alice in Wonderland) is the mother of Calie Liddle and Johnny Liddle.

### Background
Alice was sacrificed to Wonderland by Charles Dodgson (a.k.a., Lewis Carroll), thereby maintaining his youth. There she encountered the Jabberwocky, who let her return to Earth, but tricked her and made her leave part of her aspect behind, leading others on Earth to perceive her as being crazy. Despite having a bit of madness within her, she was able to have a normal life with her high school sweetheart whom she married and had children.

Her aspect back in Wonderland grew up to be an adult known as "Lacie", whose willpower eventually made her powerful in Wonderland. Back on Earth, Alice was eventually driven to suicide by the White Rabbit with her husband's infidelity pushing her over the edge. In Wonderland, Lacie continued to exist and helped her daughter Calie when she was brought to Wonderland. Alice's spirit would later be found by "The Maker", a godlike being. Who reincarnated her as "Love", making her one of "The Keepers", a group of celestial beings.

### Behind the Mythos
Alice was created by Lewis Carroll in 1865, first appearing in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. 

In 2008, she first appeared in Zenescope Entertainment's highly sexualised Grimm Fairy Tales fictional universe, in the issue #0 of the 1st volume of Grimm Fairy Tales: Return to Wonderland. The series also incorporated elements from the works of H. P. Lovecraft, and also featured Lovecraft himself as a character.

Alice Liddle's name is based on the name of Alice Liddell, one of the children of Lewis Carroll's friend Henry Liddell, to whom he told stories.

Alicia Y (『アリシア・Y』) is a Cthulhu Mythos manga series, written and illustrated by Juan Gotō. It was originally published as a serialized story by Tatsumi Publishing, before being collected into a trade paperback volume by Akane Shinsha in 1994. It was later released as an e-book on Amazon Kindle and Manga Library Z, which also featured two bonus chapters.

The story appears to be primarily written as a sequel to "The Dunwich Horror", while also incorporating many elements from H. P. Lovecraft's other works.

### Synopsis
### Chapter 1: "Jack the Ripper in the 111th year"
While performing a human sacrifice in London, a cult of fishmen are interrupted by a mysterious girl who tries to interrogate them about the gate to R'lyeh. The cult members attack her but are quickly defeated, with the girl introducing herself as Alicia Y Armitage, the one who will unseal the Gate to the Netherworld. Alicia tries to force the only surviving member to reveal the one who gave them information regarding the Seal; however, he quickly dies from spontaneous combustion, leading to Alicia realizing that she's being watched. Elsewhere, an old man is watching Alicia from his crystal ball, coming to the conclusion that he needs to find out her true identity, as well as targeting her friends.

Meanwhile, a woman named Satsuki is at the airport where Alicia was supposed to pick her up. A dark-skinned man named Nyar explains to Satsuki that Alicia could not make it because she had some urgent business, before an airplane crashes into the building.

### Chapter 2: "The Magician of Crystal"
A man named Inumaru saves Satsuki from getting caught in the plane explosion, followed by him scolding Nyar for not doing anything to help her. In response, Nyar demonstrates his powers by causing both of them to fall and catches them before they can hit the ground, causing Inumaru and Satsuki to float in midair.

Meanwhile, at the British Library, Alicia gets confronted by the old man, who is the head of the cult from earlier. While seemingly under a hypnotic spell, Alicia explains that she is a descendent of Henry Armitage, the man who thwarted the summoning of Yog-Sothoth. After getting that information, the old man tried to use his hypnosis to kill Alicia; however, she was actually immune to the spell and was just faking it the whole time. Alicia then attempted to force the old man to identify himself, only for him to quickly retreat.

With no more threat in sight, Alicia lets Satsuki enter the room, along with Inumaru and Nyar. Inumaru reveals that he is a Japanese journalist who was investigating recent events but claims that the occult-ish story would be unusable for the newspaper, unless a giant monster went on a rampage throughout London. Alicia tells him that it could actually happen, as there was an incident in 1925 where a volcanic eruption awakened Cthulhu for a short period of time, causing people to suffer from mental illness around the world. ### Background
Alicia Y Whateley is the daughter of Yog-Sothoth, making her a half-breed between god and human. She was originally created by the Whateley family to get revenge on Henry Armitage, the man who thwarted their ancestors' plan to summon Yog-Sothoth; using spellcraft to make the offspring of Armitage give birth to Alicia. After being enrolled at Miskatonic University, Mr. Whateley ordered Alicia to steal the research results left by her mother's great-grandfather, in order to avenge the Whateley household; however, Mr. Whateley ultimately died from using an incorrect summoning technique. Despite initially sharing the Whateley's resentment towards the world, Alicia changed her ways after meeting Nyar (also known as Nyarlathotep), who took the role of her guardian, as well as changing her name to "Alicia Y Armitage".

Alicia would later confront John Dee, a man who attempted to assimilate himself with Yog-Sothoth; however, Alicia ended up being the one who took the role of Yog-Sothoth, after her consciousness shifted during Dee's summoning of Cthulhu. Upon reaching Yog-Sothoth's domain, Alicia took Dee to the grave of the London Tower, in order to kill his past counterpart while he was still sleeping, as well as subjecting his spirit to never-ending agony. Back in the mortal world, Alicia returned to London and professed her love for Nyar. (: Alicia Y)

Due to her being a descendent of the Great Old Ones, Alicia has been shown to have several supernatural abilities.

In combat, Alicia can summon lightning bolts to destroy her opponents. She can also destroy objects with the Trapezohedron by warping the closed space-time, encircling the entire surrounding space with negative light; however, the Trapezohedron's power was cut off after being confined by a giant star-shaped stone. When removing her eye patch, Alicia can fire a powerful hypnosis beam from her right eye.

fullContent:
Alien, also referred to frequently and inconsistently as Aliens, is a multimedia franchise begun with the gritty 1979 science fiction/horror film Alien, directed by Ridley Scott and written by Dan O'Bannon. Since it’s release, the franchise has expanded to include numerous feature films, a television series, original fiction, comic books, toys, and much more. The series has also crossed over with other popular properties, including The Terminator, Marvel Comics' The Avengers, Vampirella, Judge Dredd, D.C. Comics' Batman and Superman, Buffy the Vampire Slayer, and Predator. The latter, launched in 1990 by Dark Horse Comics in Dark Horse Presents #36 and supported by an Easter egg in the film Predator 2 the same year, has established itself as a long-term interaction between the two properties.

Although featuring little in the way of specific references to either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos in general, the Alien franchise was intended to have a more direct connection from its inception, with writer Dan O'Bannon's early screenplay showing the titular aliens as having a connection to the Outer God Yog-Sothoth. Despite this having been written out in the final draft, the finished film has been cited as a prime example of cosmic horror in cinema, and over the course of its history the property has also included numerous nods and homages to the Mythos, although often in a subtle and easily-overlooked way.

### Elements and Themes
Central to the franchise's stories are the titular aliens, most commonly referred to as Xenomorphs since the release of the first sequel film, Aliens, in 1986. These creatures are multi-stage, insect-like parasitic lifeforms which require a living host in which to gestate; birth invariably results in the death of the host. The Xenomorphs are highly-aggressive, lethal predators who will do anything to protect their hive colonies, and possess a defence mechanism in the form of acid blood, meaning that even in death, a Xenomorph has the potential to eliminate its opponent.

Another core element of the property is "Big Business," with the stories frequently featuring ruthless and avaricious megacorporations, which in the setting are monolithic organisations with vast amounts of political capital who wish to capture and study the Xenomorphs, usually for the purpose of bioweapons research. These ventures almost invariably end in disaster, and are often fatal for the poor innocents who have found themselves between the corporations and their objectives. The most well-known of these companies, and the one most frequently featured in the franchise, is Weyland-Yutani, a British/Japanese conglomerate which was first introduced in the original 1979 film.

### Background
Alien Intelligences are monstrous supernatural beings that are evil incarnate. Which are theorized as being related in one form or another to the Old Ones. They come in a wide variety of forms, but the majority have bodies consisting of fleshy pulsating mounds with slimy tentacles.

Many of them are gargantuan monstrosities, the largest being as massive as skyscrapers. They may straddle dimensions, sending shards of their lifeforce into worlds to spread hate, murder, fear, and madness. Which can possess sentient beings, creating monstrous or beautiful avatars which are as powerful as demigods.

"All Moon-Beasts Amorphous and Mephitic" is a comedy short story by Peter Cannon which features veterinarians James Herriot and Siegfried Farnon from the All Creatures Great and Small franchise setting up practice in H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands. The story was first published in 1995 in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu, and is also included in Cannon's 2011 collection Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches.

### Synopsis
James Herriot is a veterinary surgeon working in the Dreamlands who has treated all sorts of species, from Ghouls to Wamps. One day, King Kuranes calls him to look at his beloved Moon-beast, Matilda, a strong and healthy racer, now suddenly looking ill, with her pink tentacles turned to a sickly shade of green. Herriot prescribes an ointment, but with little success: a few days later, a distressed Kuranes appears in the clinic with Matilda looking worse than before.

Herriot and fellow doctor Siegfried Farnon try to get the Moon-beast to consume the prescribed medicine by offering it inside the body of a tasty Zoog. When Matilda can still smell the remedy inside the Zoog, they try to give it to her in a wide-mouthed ruby merchant, but still with no success. Finally, remembering Kuranes' earlier remarks about Matilda's favourite treat, Herriot offers the medicine in a bowl of fried fungi, which the animal devours eagerly. With Kuranes now pleased and Matilda on the road to recovery, the vets ponder about what to do with the wide-mouthed ruby merchant once he awakens from his drug-induced coma.

All-Consuming Fire is a Doctor Who novel by Andy Lane. It was published in 1994 as part of the franchise's New Adventures series. Serving as a three-way crossover between the world of Doctor Who, the Sherlock Holmes series by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, and the Cthulhu Mythos, All-Consuming Fire sees the Doctor and his companions Bernice Summerfield and Ace teaming up with Holmes and Watson to battle against a cult of Azathoth worshipers and their minions.

In addition to several references to the lore of all three franchises, the novel also mentions characters from other works that likewise exist as real people in-universe, including Sax Rohmer's infamous Dr. Fu Manchu, Kim Newman's Charles Beauregard of the Diogenes Club, and Doyle's own Prof. Challenger and Lord John Roxton from The Lost World and its sequels.

### Frame story
The bulk of the narrative is presented as a journal written by Dr. John Watson, and edited into a novel by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. It is stated that "Sherlock Holmes" and "John Watson" are not the actual names of the detectives, but merely pseudonyms ascribed by Doyle to protect their real identities. Some chapters are taken from Bernice Summerfield's journal instead of Watson's, and some brief interludes are narrated by Ace. In the epilogue, Bernice quips that either Watson or Doyle took a lot of liberties with the story, thus casting doubts about the veracity of some of the events narrated.

### Synopsis
In 1887, the detective Sherlock Holmes and his friend and roommate Dr. John Watson are hired by the Pope to investigate the disappearance of certain books in the secret Library of St John the Beheaded in London: a repository of tomes and documents banned by the Catholic Church and other authorities. Provided with a list of the library's most recent visitors, which include a mysterious man without address who presents himself as "the Doctor", Holmes examines the crime scene and tests the library's rigid security system by unsuccessfully attempting to steal a rare copy of De Vermis Mysteriis, by Ludvig Prinn.

Back in their apartment on Baker Street, Holmes and Watson are visited by the Doctor, who proves to be an eccentric, but also a shrewd and resourceful man who, although aware of his own status as a suspect, is willing to assist in the investigation.

Watson and the Doctor visit the first suspect, Kate Prendersly, who went to the library to investigate the death of her husband, as she believes he was assassinated after learning something from the occult books he had been consulting. While in the library, she claims to have seen the shadow of a man swallowing a book whole, shedding light on how the theft might have been accomplished. Shockingly, Prendersly dies, as her body spontaneously bursts into flames before the incredulous eyes of Watson and the Doctor.

fullContent:
"Allan and the Sundered Veil" is a horror-fantasy short story written by Alan Moore and illustrated by Kevin O'Neill, set in their League of Extraordinary Gentlemen universe. It features the character Allan Quatermain, from the works of H. Rider Haggard, joining forces with three other heroes: John Carter from Edgar Rice Burroughs' Barsoom series, Randolph Carter from H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos (who is depicted here as John Carter's grandnephew), and the Time Traveler from H. G. Wells' The Time Machine. It also features the spatial anomaly from Jorge Luis Borges' story "The Aleph".

Despite being a prose story, "Allan and the Sundered Veil" was published in Moore and O'Neill's graphic novel The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen, Volume I, where it serves as a prequel to the comic's narrative.

### Synopsis
Three years after faking his own death to escape his fame, the British adventurer Allan Quatermain visits the dilapidated castle of his friend, Lady Ragnall, to partake of the taduki drug, which allows one to experience visions of past lives. As soon as Quatermain inhales it, however, he finds himself (or, more properly, his astral self) falling into a cosmic abyss, and transported to a strange realm made out of fluid shapes and colours. Gradually, the environment solidifies into an alien landscape of polypous vegetation under a starless sky. Quatermain sees two men sitting by a fire and asks for information, but finds that the two are just as lost as him, and came from different points in time.

The younger man is Randolph Carter, from the twentieth century: an experienced dreamer who admits to having ventured into a part of the Dreamlands completely unknown to him. The other man is his granduncle, John Carter, sill dressed in his American Civil War uniform, who recounts how he was standing at the entrance of a cave in the 19th century, staring at the planet Mars in the sky when his astral projection took place and he was transported to this mysterious land.

Suddenly, the three men notice the approach of large, menacing, centipede-like creatures with gelatinous flesh and a dozen eyes. John Carter takes up his sword while Quatermain grabs a burning stick from the fire, and Randolph admits to not being much of a fighter. Before the fight starts, however, the monsters are startled by the approach of a metallic vehicle piloted by a man who introduces himself as "the Time Traveler". He urges the others to jump onboard, as the creatures won't stay frightened for long.

The Time Traveler takes Quatermain and the Carters to a distant future, at the location where London once was, to the interior of a sphinx that he has turned into his base of operations, its entrance activated by a trapezohedron. He explains that he was looking for them, hoping to recruit their help to fight against a threat to all of spacetime. Somehow the fabric of reality has been ruptured, and a mighty race of eldritch beings from another universe are pouring through.

Dr. Allan Halsey is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his story "Herbert West--Reanimator", in which he serves as the dean of the medical school of Lovecraft's imaginary Miskatonic University. He made his first appearance in the February 1922 issue of the amateur press publication Home Brew.

Halsey becomes in effect a zombie after being subjected to Herbert West's experiments in reanimation.

The character appears in adaptations of Lovecraft's story--notably the 1985 film Re-Animator, where he is portrayed by Robert Sampson.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Lovecraft introduces Halsey as "the learned and benevolent Dr. Allan Halsey, whose work in behalf of the stricken is recalled by every old resident of Arkham." The story suggests that Halsey, the dean of Miskatonic's medical school,  is of the  “professor-doctor” type—"kindly, conscientious, and sometimes gentle and amiable, yet always narrow, intolerant, custom-ridden, and lacking in perspective."

Halsey naturally comes into conflict with West, a Miskatonic student obsessed with using science to raise the dead. Even as an undergraduate, "West clashed disagreeably with Dr. Halsey...in a wordy dispute that did less credit to him than to the kindly dean in point of courtesy." After "the scientific slaughter of uncounted small animals" to further his "freakish work",  West was "debarred from future experiments" by the "sceptical dean". 

By the summer of 1905, West has graduated from Miskatonic and is taking post-graduate medical classes when Arkham, the town where Miskatonic is located, is hit with a typhoid epidemic. During the crisis Halsey "distinguished himself in sacrificing service, applying his extreme skill with whole-hearted energy to cases which many others shunned because of danger or apparent hopelessness." The "fearless dean" becomes a "popular hero," though he "struggled to keep from collapsing with physical fatigue and nervous exhaustion."

On August 14, 1905, Halsey himself succumbs to typhoid. His "hasty funeral" is attended on the 15th by Misktatonic's students, who buy "an impressive wreath" that is "quite overshadowed by the tributes sent by wealthy Arkham citizens and by the municipality itself" in honor of the "public benefactor". West is "shaken by the death of his chief opponent", but sees Halsey's death as an opportunity to vindicate his "notorious theories". On August 16, about 3 a.m., West brings Halsey's corpse back to his boardinghouse, where it is reanimated; the revivified Dean attacks West, escapes through a window, and goes on a killing spree, starting with the watchman of Christchurch Cemetery, who is "clawed to death in a manner...too hideous for description".

Allen is a fictional character from the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald.

### Biography
In the 1920s, Allen was the head factor at the small trading post of M'gonga, close to the Ugandan border. In January 1929, when the post's physician Dr. Thomas Slauenwite was at a loss about how to treat the hunter Mevana, who had been bitten by a devil-fly, Allen suggested that Slauenwite contact his predecessor, Dr. Lincoln, who "had a profound knowledge of the local sicknesses". Lincoln's suggestion of applying intramuscular injections of tryparsamide proved effective and resulted in Mevana making a full recovery.

Later on, Slauenwite organised a party led by Mevana to travel to the area in which the devil-flies lived so he could capture some for study. Slauenwite convinced Allen to authorise this by claiming that the trip was "in the interest of local health work".

Slauenwite had dinner with Allen on November 17, the same day that Batta died. (: "Winged Death")

Allen Koszowski (born 27 June 1949) is a professional American artist who has illustrated thousands of Cthulhu Mythos-related publications, especially covers and panel illustrations for short stories, since 1973.

Koszowski was a cover artist for Crypt of Cthulhu during its lengthy run as well as illustrating newsletters, zines and website publications from EODapa. As per his website, he is said to be "one of the most prolific artists in his field, having published more than 2,500 illustrations for hundreds of genre publications," and this is easy to believe since any cursory image search will display hundreds of his black and white ink drawings of Mythos subjects. 

Koszowski is also a member of The Association of Science Fiction and Fantasy Artists. He is a past winner of the L. Ron Hubbard Illustrators of the Future Award and won Best Artist (and other categories) in the Small Press Writers and Artists Organization each year over a ten year period.

fullContent:
Alone Against Nyarlathotep is a sprawling and ambitious solo-play adventure module released by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game under the Miskatonic Repository third-party supplement publishing scheme. It is one of a series of solitaire role-playing game books in the "Alone Against..." series but in this case the basic premise is expanded upon greatly.

### Overview
As with other solo-play scenarios, Alone Against Nyarlathotep offers an adventure in the choice-tree style of the Choose Your Own Adventure or Fighting Fantasy books. It is a stand alone game that does not require, although it is based on, the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game seventh edition rules. It also incorporates the use of both a hardcover physical book, a PDF and downloadable pre-generated characters and handouts making it somewhat more complex in terms of logistics than previous offerings. It has also been provided with a short summary of how to turn it from a solitaire game to a more conventional Keeper-plus-players gaming experience.

Alone Against Nyarlathotep is a huge Call of Cthulhu 7th Edition, solo campaign, set in Classic 1925 England. 3 times larger than other "Alone Against..." titles this sandbox game has hundreds of locations. Dozens of NPC's, tens of items and numerous horrors to battle. The solo game, allows traditional TTRPG gameplay, but without several players, or a Keeper.

Game mechanics allow for vast exploration and tracking of time, in a complex web of plots and intrigue. The setting is real and perfect for Lovecraftian horror. There are numerous vehicles to use, animals to ride, trains to alight and boats to sail, Mythos tomes to study, weapons to acquire, from nitro express elephant guns to deadly axes. Government agencies, private organisations and law enforcement, all have an interest in your case. 

It is also noted that although this is also an involved and serialized adventure where Nyarlathotep is the main antagonist, it is not connected to nor any form of adaptation of the better known Masks of Nyarlathotep."Can you thwart the cosmic horrors and fiendish puzzles, to overcome the evil? Can you stave off insanity and stay out of the asylum? Can you overcome the eternal horror and save the world, from downfall? Only you can decide, once you are Alone Against Nyarlathotep.

340 pages of solo Call of Cthulhu investigation, horror and combat. Totalling 1185 entries, numerous maps, several towns and villages, numerous farms, several pubs and more. includes 8 PRE GEN characters and more that can be recruited in the adventure. Expect to lose some along the way in this campaign of attrition, not for the feint hearted.

This is perhaps the most difficult Alone Against title, but there are many endings and ways it can play out, depending on your chosen lines of investigation. Alone Against the Dark: Defying the Triumph of the Ice is a solo-play adventure module for Chaosium's Lovecraftian horror roleplay game Call of Cthulhu. It is one of a series of solitaire role-playing game books in the "Alone Against..." series.

### Overview
Designed in a style reminiscent of the Fighting Fantasy gamebooks popular in the 1980s, Alone Against the Dark provides a complete adventure for one player. Included is a party of five pregenerated characters with which to play, along with a selection of player aids. As the core rules for Call of Cthulhu are available for free on Chaosium's website, all a player need bring to the table is paper, pencil and dice.

Alone Against the Dark was written by Matthew J. Costello and Mike Mason with cover art provided by Petr Štovik, and runs to a total of 102 pages.

### Publication History
First released in April 2018, Alone Against the Dark is available in both physical print and digital PDF versions.

Alone Against the Flames is a solo-play introductory adventure for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. It is one of a series of solitaire role-playing game books in the "Alone Against..." series.

### Overview
Designed in a similar way to the Fighting Fantasy and Choose Your Own Adventure books popular in the 1980's, Alone Against the Flames is intended to teach new players the basics of Call of Cthulhu whilst giving a taste of the games' atmosphere. As both the core rules and Alone Against the Flames are available as free downloads on the Chaosium website, all players need supply is a pencil, paper and dice.

It is meant to be rudimentary, and it is; this is the free adventure available as a free hyperlinked download with seventh edition Call of Cthulhu RPG. However the PDF does provide a map of Emberhead, the small village in which one arrives, and almost all of the sections are hyperlinked making it much easier to use.

### Synopsis
In a short series of challenges, your lone player character Investigator explores the village of Emberhead. Central to the village is a massive black iron scorched and seemingly part melted sculpture, due to be lit in a bonfire at the festival in two days time. After cursory exploration, and very abruptly if one has failed most of one's previous rolls, an abduction by a cult precipitates the climax of the adventure.

### Publication History
Alone Against the Flames was first released in August 2016 and is available in both print and free digital (PDF) versions.

### Overview
Written in a similar style to the Fighting Fantasy gamebooks popular in the 1980s, Alone Against the Frost requires the player only supply a pencil, paper and dice, as the basic rules for Call of Cthulhu are available as a free download on Chaosium’s website. The story allows a single player to take control of a small party of investigators as they travel through Canada's Northwest Territories in search of the fabled Sasquatch.

Written by Glenn Rahman and released as Alone Against the Wendigo in 1985, this updated release was revamped by British game designer Gavin Inglis for the seventh edition of Call of Cthulhu. It features a full-colour cover by Veronica Anrathi with black-and-white interiors. The title was changed due to fears of accusations of cultural appropriation.

Alone Against the Tide is a solo-play adventure module for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, written and produced by Nicholas Johnson and first released through the Miskatonic Repository player-driven resource initiative in 2018.

### Overview




As with other solo-play scenarios, Alone Against the Tide offers an adventure in the choice-tree style of the Choose Your Own Adventure or Fighting Fantasy books. The adventure involves the player travelling to the quiet lakeside town of Esbury to investigate a series of bizarre events, and allows for custom character creation using the Core Rules, although a pre-generated character, Miskatonic University's Dr. Woods, is included in the 2nd edition for quick-start play.

### Publication
In 2020, Chaosium released a revamped edition of Alone Against the Tide featuring new cover art by M. Wayne Miller, which was published in a solely digital format. Polish, German, and Russian editions have also been released.

In November 2025, a licensed app version of the scenario, with a focus on providing audio immersion into the setting, was released by Sound Realms AB.

"Along Came Cthulhu" is a children’s Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Dawna Flowers. It was first published in the collection Deep in the Forest through her independent label Under the Moon Publishing via Amazon's digital Kindle platform in January 2012. It later received a digital chapbook release.

### Synopsis
When young Augustus and his family temporarily move into his grandfather's rural home , he discovers strange papers and a mysterious amulet hidden in the attic. Using these artefacts, he accidentally activates a ritual which summons dread Cthulhu from the nearby lake; luckily for the boy his grandfather, who has experience with such matters, takes notice, and is able to abort the summoning before any harm can be done.

### Behind the Mythos
The chapbook edition of "Along Came Cthulhu" features cover art by Flowers' son Thoren inspired by H. P. Lovecraft’s original sketch of Cthulhu, and includes Alfred Lord Tennyson's poem "The Kraken", often cited as an inspiration for both "The Call of Cthulhu" and its titular antagonist.

Alos is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1920 short story "Polaris".

### Overview
Alos is the commander of the army of the city of Olathoë in the Dreamlands. He was considered the last hope for the kingdom of Lomar against the invading hordes of the Inutos. Alos was described by the unnamed narrator of "Polaris" as not only a friend but "a true man and patriot".

The Alskali are a species of inhuman creatures created by Theatre of the Mind for their Pursuit to Kadath expansion for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Description
Enormous humanoids with hypnotic powers, the Alskali are about ten feet tall with squat, heavily-muscled bodies. They are hairless, with dead-grey skin and huge hands and feet. Each has a single black glossy eye in the centre of their otherwise human faces. This single eye appears to be multiple eyes due to the magical effects possessed by its owner. 

In the modern day, the surviving Alskali worship Nyarlathotep, although in the past they were followers of many of the Outer Gods and Great Old Ones. A secret Turkish sect known as Erkek KardeÕ Göz - which translates to The Brothers of the Eye - worship these one-eyed giants as gods, and work to keep their existence hidden from the rest of mankind.

### History
The Alskali are a race of intelligent beings who evolved entirely apart from the human race. These giants have entered into human folklore as the Cyclops, amongst other traditional giants. In prehistory they built huge dwellings out of the sides of mountains, and from these citadels communicated and became affiliated with the entirely alien Outer Gods. Eventually, the Alskali were driven out of their great cities and into new dwellings deep in the earth. This migration had the effect of producing evolutionary change in the giants, making them smaller in size (although still huge in comparison to humans).

Altuan is an ancient island-continent created by American author James Ambuehl as the primary setting for his Lu-Kthu Cthulhu Mythos story cycle. It was first referenced in the 1997 short story "The Stalker in the Snows".

### Description
Although the exact nature of Altuan is somewhat ambiguous, it is likely a large island-continent which plays host to the cities of Amas-Nath, Xammad and Ibtand. A place inhabited by the Serpent People, it might appear in the Sussex Manuscript under the corruption "Altorn" (the singular form of "Altornos"). It may also be a kingdom or district of the Mesozoic continent of Shuggon or even an alternative name for the same place. It might also be the same as Altuas.

Altuas is a fictional region created by American author James Ambuehl for his 1997 short story "The Stalker in the Snows".

### Overview
Altuas is an ancient land which was old even when Atlantis itself was young. The villages of Zendosh and Thom-Raballos, and the wind-swept Plateau of Shung all lie in Altuas. All in the ancient land of Altuas feared Parthias the Conqueror.

It seems likely that it is the same location as Altuan, and possibly an alternative name for Shuggon although it is not clear that it is a Serpent People colony.

Alyda Winthrop is a character created by Jean-Paul Ouellette for the 1988 film The Unnamable and its 1993 sequel The Unnamable II: The Statement of Randolph Carter. She is loosely based on the titular creature from H. P. Lovecraft's original short story "The Unnamable".

In the first film, Alyda was played by Katrin Alexandre. In the second film, her human body is separated from the creature possessing her, with the former played by Maria Ford and the latter by Julie Strain.

### Biography
Alyda Winthrop was born in 17th century Arkham to the wizard Joshua Winthrop and his wife. Physically, she was a gargoyle-like creature with pale skin, hoofed feet, legs covered in white fur, bat-like wings on her back, scaly hands with taloned fingers, pointed ears, sharp teeth, and horns on her head. She was sensitive to the light and preferred to flee from it. Her behaviour was animalistic and violent, as she produced screeching noises and would try to brutally kill anyone who came near her.

Alyda's mother died in childbirth, as Alyda "ate through her body". As a result, the child was raised by Joshua, who was forced to keep her locked up in the attic. Unable to control his daughter, Joshua consulted grimoires such as the Necronomicon, and successfully cast a spell that prevented Alyda from leaving the house. However, he was aware that the wooden walls would rot someday, and thus planted trees around the property, hoping to find ways to communicate with the tree spirits that he believed could help him. (: The Unnamable)

In 1704 (: The Unnamable II), Joshua was killed by Alyda, and the house was abandoned for over 300 years, during which Alyda remained alive and confined to the house by her father's spell (: The Unnamable). However, the spell didn't prevent her from burrowing under the ground, which gave her access to the nearby graveyard. Over the centuries, she built a system of subterranean tunnels and survived by feeding on human corpses (: The Unnamable II).

When a group of students from Miskatonic University came to explore the Winthrop House, Alyda attacked and killed several of them, until Randolph Carter found the means to summon the spirits of the trees planted by Joshua. The trees outside the house became animated by the spirits, and reached inside with their branches to capture Alyda and drag her away, saving the lives of Howard Damon and Tanya Heller. (: The Unnamable)

Dragged to the underground tunnels, Alyda was bound by the tree roots. She was later found in that state by Randolph Carter and Prof. Warren when they were exploring the passages.

A blood sample taken by Warren revealed that Alyda's cellular structure was a mix of human cells intertwined with those of an unknown creature. Warren deduced that Alyda was in fact a human who had been possessed her entire life by a being that could occupy the s

Amanda Sharpe, the Student, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Cthulhu Mythos setting.

### History
A 2-year student at Arkham's prestigious Miskatonic University during the late 1920s, Amanda has been having nightmares of an ancient entity sleeping beneath the waves. These dreams were sparked by the sight of a painting hanging in the university’s halls, and have had a negative impact on her schoolwork.

### Ghouls of the Miskatonic
In Graham McNeill's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic, Amanda and her friend and roommate Rita Young were kidnapped by a cult of Cthulhu worshippers who intended to feed the pair to their pet ghouls. Fortunately, the two were saved by an unlikely band of heroes, including Rex Murphy and Finn Edwards.

### Behind the Mythos
First introduced in Fantasy Flight's Arkham Horror Second Edition Core Set, Amanda Sharpe has since appeared in several other of the company's releases, including Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and a plastic model of Amanda was created for the Arkham Horror Premium Figures series. Her character was expanded on significantly in Graham McNeill's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic, and she was included as a playable investigator character in Jonathan Green's 2024 gamebook The Darkness Over Arkham.

### Trivia
*In one piece of flavour text released by Fantasy Flight, Amanda is mentioned to work as a bank teller. Whether she used this to help fund her university course, or she was intended to have left her studies in favour of a steady job is unknown.
*The "Personal Story" mechanic introduced in the Innsmouth Horror expansion for Arkham Horror tells of how Amanda is possessed of Deep One heritage; it should be noted that no previous mention of this condition had been made. Although it is possible for her to transform fully into an aquatic form (automatically losing the player the game), it is also possible to prevent her transformation through gameplay.
*In Ghouls of the Miskatonic it was revealed that she was born in Muncie, Indiana, and was a friend and roommate of Rita Young at Miskatonic's Dorothy Upman Hall.

### Background

Amazing Stories, launched in 1926 by Hugo Gernsback, was the first magazine devoted to science fiction. Its September 1927 issue featured H. P. Lovecraft's "The Colour Out of Space"; after Lovecraft's death, his collaboration with Henry S. Whitehead, "Bothon", appeared in the magazine's August 1946 issue.

Amazing Stories is considered to have had an enormous impact on the development of the science fiction genre; writers whose first stories appeared in the magazine include  John W. Campbell, Isaac Asimov, Ursula K. Le Guin, Roger Zelazny, and Thomas M. Disch.

fullContent:
"Ambler's Inspiration" is a Cthulhu Mythos-connected short story by Brian Lumley that first appeared in his collection The Caller of The Black (Arkham House, 1971). It mentions Oakdeene Sanitarium, which appears repeatedly in Lumley's Mythos tales, and compares its central character, a writer of weird fiction, to H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
A horror writer visits a fellow author and finds that the question "Where do you get your ideas?" has a horrific answer....

### Characters
* Mr. James: The story's narrator, a horror fiction writer and member of the London Mystery Writers Society. Author of Four Faces of Fear and Bentley’s Barrier.
* Biron Ambler: A horror writer who caused a sensation with stories like In the Yellow Moss, The Burning Man, and Edges of Mist. At the time of his death he was working on a story called The Darker Dark; when he died, the magazine Grotesque published a special memorial issue. He called himself a “haunter of the dark”; his father, whom he lived with on the outskirts of Durham City, said he was the "pasty, listless type and very highly strung." Physically, he "was a small man...mousey-haired, bespectacled, pale and nervous."
* Professor Ernest Ambler:  A scientist engaged in electroencephalography, or the study of brain-waves; his research involved preserving animal brains in vats of soup-like "feeder-fluid." He was "a small, bald-headed man," physically the "very duplicate of the 'mad scientist'” with his "white smock...thick-lensed spectacles and...ruby-red lips."
* William Barnstable: the "one-time Governor of Oakdeene Sanatorium," and "a very good friend of Professor Ambler’s." He once aided the professor's experiments by sending him the brain of "one of the more violent inmates of Oakdeene."

### Publication History
The Caller of The Black, which was reissued in 2019 by Crossroad Press, is the only English-language text that features "Ambler's Inspiration." It was translated into French in 1989 as " L'inspiration d'Ambler."

Ambrose Gwinnett Bierce (June 24, 1842 – circa 1914) was an American short story writer, journalist, poet, and Civil War veteran. He disappeared in Mexico around 1914.

He notably wrote the short stories "Haïta the Shepherd" and "An Inhabitant of Carcosa", which introduced the names of Hastur and Carcosa, later expanded upon by Robert W. Chambers, H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth.

### Major Works

### Military Service
Bierce served in the Union Army during the American Civil War, enlisting in 1861. He fought in several key battles, including:

* Battle of Shiloh
* Battle of Chickamauga
* Battle of Kennesaw Mountain

He was wounded in battle, which influenced his later writings.

### Disappearance
In 1913, Bierce traveled to Mexico during the Mexican Revolution, seeking firsthand experience. He disappeared in early 1914, and his fate remains a mystery, with speculation that he may have been killed during the conflict.

Doctor Ambrose Dexter  is a character who is first mentioned in the the 1936 H. P. Lovecraft short story "The Haunter of the Dark", but plays a more developed role in Robert Bloch's 1950 sequel, "The Shadow From the Steeple".

### History
Dexter is unnamed when he first appears toward the beginning of Lovecraft's story, which concerns the death of the writer Robert Blake after he encounters an artifact called the Shining Trapezohedron in the deserted Starry Wisdom Church in Providence: A "reputable physician with a taste for odd folklore" is said to have been "moved to fanatical extremes" when he "threw into the bay the curiously angled stone and its strangely adorned metal box found in the old church steeple." This doctor is said to be among those "inclined to take much of Blake’s diary at its face value." 

Toward the end of the story, Lovecraft names "superstitious Dr. Dexter, who threw the curious box and angled stone...into the deepest channel of Narragansett Bay."

When Bloch wrote a sequel--continuing a sort of literary game, as the Lovecraft story was itself a sequel to Bloch's "The Shambler from the Stars"--he expanded this brief mention into a full-fledged character. Giving the doctor the first name of Ambrose and a house on Benefit Street, he describes the physician as "Providence-born, a lifelong resident, forty years of age [in 1935], unmarried, a general practitioner, [and] member of several medical societies". Bloch wrote that Dexter "had left town immediately following his dramatic theft and disposal of the 'Shining Trapezohedron'."

The protagonist of the story, a friend of the late Robert Blake named Edmund Fiske, searches for Dexter for several years before finding a reference in an astrophysics journal to Dexter "delivering an address on 'Practical Applications in Military Technology'" at Princeton University in 1945. In 1948 he is listed among "investigators in the field of nuclear physics" in a national newsmagazine. News accounts in 1949 connect him to research on the H-bomb.

When Fiske finally catches up with Dexter, who returns to the house on Benefit Street in 1950, he finds him "a tall, thin, immaculately dressed man who may have been fifty but who scarcely looked thirty-five; a man whose wholly natural grace and elegance of movement concealed the sole incongruity of his aspect--a very deep suntan."

Dexter admits to Fiske that after Blake's death, he went to to the Starry Wisdom Church and removed the stone as well as the sect's collection of forbidden books--including De Vermis Mysteriis, the Liber Ivonis and the Necronomicon itself. Subsequently, he says, "during the past decade or more, I have been working on problems relative to atomic energy and nuclear fission"--including an unnamed project he took part in with Albert Einstein.

The American Project was an event which happened in the Titus Crow story cycle created by Brian Lumley.

### Overview
Little is known about the American Project other than that it was directed by the Wilmarth Foundation in conjunction with the Great Britain Project, and that it was designed to drive the forces of the Cthulhu Cycle Deities from the Americas. Although the foundation achieved a greater measure of success than they had anticipated, the operation was far from a total victory.

### Behind the Mythos
What little was given away on the specifics of the American Project was told in the novel The Burrowers Beneath, the first in the Titus Crow series of stories.

"Amid the Sands of Deepest Time" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Jason Brick, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Synopsis
In Egypt during the Second World War, a pair of highly-skilled thieves are coerced by a shady organisation into stealing an unspecified cargo from the British army.

In the aftermath, the pair fall asleep only to inexplicably awaken in the bodies of Yithian rebels waging a war against the totalitarian ruling faction which they believe to be a threat to all other species in the universe. After a while they escape back to their own time through the death of their Yithian hosts.

In the aftermath, one of the thieves kills itself, unable to cope with what he has seen, while the other falls back into the hands of the shadowy organisation and is interrogated by its leader, the mysterious Yellow Man.

### Mythos Connections
During their flight from the Yithian secret police deep beneath the alien city, the group of rebels pass a door behind which can be heard a cry of "tekeli-li." This noise terrifies the Yithians, implying that it originated from a Shoggoth, a species of voracious creature created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella At the Mountains of Madness.

### Behind the Mythos
The Yellow Man is implied to have been the leader of the dictatorial Yithian leadership, or at least a member of his species in service to it.

Ammutseba, also known as the Devourer of Stars or the Daughter of Isfet, is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Ann K. Schwader for her short story "Lost Stars", and later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Secrets of Kenya)

### Description
Ammutseba is described as a dark black vapor cloud with wispy, black, misty tentacles that floats in the sky and absorbs falling stars and all lights. (: Secrets of Kenya)

She has also been represented as a woman-shaped black hole. (: "Lost Stars")

She is said to be the daughter of an entity named Isfet, who is the abstract representation of chaos in Egyptian mythology. Egyptologist Martin Stanley inferred this to be Azathoth. (: "Lost Stars")

### In the Mythos
Ammutseba was worshiped by the Stygian civilisation during the Hyborian Age, and then by a sisterhood in the very early days of Ancient Egypt. Nowadays, cults that revere her are normally restricted to women-only ones, who incorporate Egyptian magic in their rituals. A prophecy in the tome The Gate of All Lost Stars foretold that one day Ammutseba, guided by her favorite priestess Sesh'tet, will return to devour the stars and all light. (: Secrets of Kenya)

"Amoeboid" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
The scientists of the Rocket Research Group must track down and destroy an alien being which is highly reminiscent of the titular entity from 1958 creature-feature The Blob.

### Characters

### Behind the Mythos
Although containing no direct references to either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Meikle's inclusion of "Amoeboid" in the collection Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates his belief that the piece is in the spirit of such writings.

### Trivia
*The Prof, George Thornton and the Rocket Research Group also appeared in Meikle's short story "The Invisible Menace".

Amon-Gorloth is a fictional deity created by David Calvo for the Call of Cthulhu scenario "Les Yeux d'Amon", featured in issue #101 of the French role-playing magazine Casus Belli.

### Description
Amon-Gorloth is a mysterious Great Old One who once dwelled in a great palace known as Gz-eh, close to the Valley of the Kings. His dreaming force had the ability to reshape reality, making the Nile Valley flourish 3,000 years ago until the stars ceased to be right. Amon-Gorloth was entombed beneath the ground in the Sahara Desert. His cult is similar to that of the Egyptian god Amun, and his loyal priests built secret mausoleums to access the entity's body, where they sacrifice cattle to please him.

Among the pictures are these: is a short essay written by Ramsey Campbell and included in his 1985 collection of short horror fiction Cold Print.

### Overview
Little more than a handful of pages composed of single-paragraph descriptions of his early sketches written in truncated sentences, Campbell said in 1984 of Among the pictures are these::  
Whilst many of the sketches apparently portrayed a high degree of surrealism, the influence of H.P. Lovecraft on the young Campbell can be seen shining through in several others.

It should be noted that, while Among the pictures are these: includes descriptions of Campbell's artwork, the sketches themselves were never published.

### Publication History
Although written in 1973, Among the pictures are these: did not see publication until 1981 in the March 16th edition of Nyctalops Magazine. It was later reprinted in the Scream/Press release of Cold Print, and it's 1987 and 1993 reprints by Tor Books and Headline, respectively.

fullContent:
"An Account of Ozgamuun" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Frank Forte. It was published in the collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
When his uncle dies, a man comes into possession of the old man's journal. Within it he finds an account of how Laurens can Ginneken, the uncle, crossed paths with an ancient evil in the fjords of Sweden, and how this encounter wrought a horrendous change on his mind and body. 

The journal further tells of how this evil was later washed into the ocean by Swedish authorities and causes the man to wonder just what repercussions this may have for the human race in the future…

An Epicure in the Terrible: A Centennial Anthology of Essays in Honor of H. P. Lovecraft is a non-fiction collection edited by S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz.

### Overview
Containing thirteen essays on a range of topics from Lovecraft's life, career, works and legacy, An Epicure in the Terrible was released in 1991 to coincide with the 100th anniversary of his birth. Running to a total of 347 pages, it was published by Fairleigh Dickinson University Press and edited by leading Lovecraft scholars S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz. A revised and updated version, running to 380 pages, was released by Hippocampus Press in June 2011.

All of the essays included were original to this collection.

### Contents
*Introduction, S. T. Joshi.
*"The Parents of Howard Phillips Lovecraft", Kenneth W. Faig, Jr.
*"The Cosmic Yankee", Jason C. Eckhardt
*"Lovecraft and the Pulp Magazine Tradition", Will Murray
*"On Lovecraft’s Themes: Touching the Glass", Donald R. Burleson
*"Letters, Diaries, and Manuscripts: The Handwritten Word in Lovecraft", Peter Cannon
*"Outsiders and Aliens: The Uses of Isolation in Lovecraft’s Fiction", Stefan Dziemianowicz
*"Lovecraft’s Cosmic Imagery", Steven J. Mariconda
*"From Microcosm to Macrocosm: The Growth of Lovecraft’s Cosmic Vision", David E. Schultz
*"Landscapes, Selves, and Others in Lovecraft", Robert H. Waugh
*"Lovecraft’s “Artificial Mythology”", Robert M. Price
*"Lovecraft and the Tradition of the Gentleman Narrator", R. Boerem
*"The Artist as Antaeus: Lovecraft and Modernism", Norman R. Gayford
*"Synchronistic Worlds: Lovecraft and Borges", Barton Levi St. Armand
