"An Evening at Mount Baldy" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Mark Brandon Allen. It was published in the thematic James Ward Kirk Publishing anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
Two curious men, investigating the catacombs revealed by a sinkhole, encounter a bizarre and malevolent creature lurking within. The being kills the men, but not before violating them in a most horrible way first.

fullContent:
An Exchange of Souls is a horror novel by the late British author Barry Pain. First published by Eveleigh Nash in 1911, it was later reprinted by Hippocampus Press in an omnibus edition with Henri Béraud's Lazarus as part of Lovecraft's Library, a series which republishes stories H. P. Lovecraft was known to have read and admired.

### Synopsis
The story revolves around a scientist who creates a machine which allows him to swap his consciousness with another; he uses it on his fiancé, with horrific consequences.

### Behind the Mythos
An Exchange of Souls has been suggested as a possible inspiration for H. P. Lovecraft's short horror story "The Thing on the Doorstep".

shortDefinition: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia is a reference work written by S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz. It covers the life and work of American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft.  ### Overview The book provides entries on all of Lovecraft's stories, com...
fullContent:
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia is a reference work written by S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz. It covers the life and work of American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview
The book provides entries on all of Lovecraft's stories, complete with synopses, publication history and word counts. People from Lovecraft's life, including selected writers who influenced his work, are also included.

Fictional characters from Lovecraft's work are given brief entries, but most Cthulhu Mythos-related subjects are not referenced. "The 'gods' themselves, with rare exceptions, do not figure as 'characters' in any meaningful sense in the tales, so there are no entries on them," the authors explain.

### Authors
S. T. Joshi is the author of H. P. Lovecraft: A Life and the editor of several collections of Lovecraft's work, including the corrected Arkham House editions.

David E. Schultz is the editor of a critical edition of Lovecraft's Commonplace book (1987). With Joshi, he has edited several volumes of writings by Lovecraft and Ambrose Bierce.

### Publication History
First published in 2001 by Greenwood Publishing Group, it was reissued in a slightly revised paperback edition by Hippocampus Press.

shortDefinition: "An Idol for Emiko" is a Lovecraftian short story by Travis Heermann. It was first published in the thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press in 2011.  ### Synopsis In 17th century Japan, a small village is brought to ruin by pu...
fullContent:
"An Idol for Emiko" is a Lovecraftian short story by Travis Heermann. It was first published in the thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press in 2011.

### Synopsis
In 17th century Japan, a small village is brought to ruin by punishing taxes imposed by the Tokugawa Shogunate and a drastic drop in the productivity of their fishing grounds. In an effort to alleviate their problems, the villagers strike a deal with a "hairy barbarian" who promises them abundance and wealth in exchange for one of their young women.

Immediately the fisheries begin producing a wealth of strange fish, far more than the townsfolk can eat, and beautiful gems and golden trinkets wash in with the tide. One young woman, Emiko, is promised to the son of the man who made the life-changing deal but refuses, and runs off to a nearby settlement. However, her furious family drag her back, pregnant and shamed, and Emiko becomes a recluse, giving birth to an idiot child and shunning the wealth and sustenance of the ocean.

Over the years, Emiko and her son Taro become targets of ridicule, and the villagers who partake of the ocean's strange bounty begin to change, becoming more and more fish-like in appearance. After the disappearance of some of the village's children, a labourer witnesses Taro dragging a small girl off into the forest; the townsfolk track Taro down and catch him feeding on the child's corpse, but the boy is able to make his escape. When Emiko is approached by an angry mob, she tells them that she will deal with the problem, and Taro is never seen again.

In the aftermath, Emiko lives an even more solitary existence. She begins to change in the same manner as the townsfolk, implied to be the result of a golden statue gifted to her by her sister. When she finally takes to the sea, her family discover the body of Taro, desiccated and with his skull crushed, laid to rest for decades in the family home.

### Behind the Mythos
The appearance of the townsfolk after eating the strange fish is very like the description of the Innsmouth Look, and the odd golden trinkets washed ashore bear similarities to the jewellery of the Deep Ones in The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Trivia
* The discovery of Taro's mummified corpse in Emiko's home after her death was stated by the author to have been inspired by William Faulkner's "A Rose for Emily." "An Idol for Emiko"'s title would also appear to have drawn influence from the story.

### Publication History 
* Historical Lovecraft (2011)
* Beneath the Waves (2017)
* Into the Briny Deep (2022)

### References

fullContent:
"An Incarceration in Bh'Yhlun" is a short story by author Ian Davey. It forms the second part of his Bh'Yhlun series of post-apocalyptic Mythos fiction.

### Synopsis
A survivor of the return of the Old Ones, a young girl who has dubbed herself Glyph in the new world, has been captured and imprisoned in the living tower of Bh'Yhlun. There, she meets a mysterious man named Stanley, and the two escape by using a magical incantation from Francesci's Cult of the Necronomicon which allows them to hide in the bowels of a guardian Shoggoth. Not trusting Stanley, Glyph ditches the man and heads off on her own, using a newfound ability to see ley lines to navigate her way towards an unknown destination.

### Characters

*Glyph, a young orphan girl alone in the insanity caused by the return of the Old Ones.
*Stanley, a mysterious man with a command of the occult information contained within Francesci's Cult of the Necronomicon.
*Nyarlathotep, the otherworldly messenger of the Old Ones and lord of Bh'Yhlun.

### Publication History
"An Incarceration in Bh'Yhlun" was first published in the online zine Nightscapes #3 in September 1997, and received a printed release in Dark Legacy #5 in May 1995.

shortDefinition: "An Inhabitant of Carcosa" is a short story by Ambrose Bierce, first published in 1886. Elements of the story, including the setting of Carcosa and the name Hali, were later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos.  Bierce's story first appeared in the ...
fullContent:
"An Inhabitant of Carcosa" is a short story by Ambrose Bierce, first published in 1886. Elements of the story, including the setting of Carcosa and the name Hali, were later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos.

Bierce's story first appeared in the San Francisco Newsletter of December 25, 1886. It was later reprinted in Bierce's collections Tales of Soldiers and Civilians and Can Such Things Be?.

### Synopsis
A man from the "ancient and famous" city of Carcosa, pondering the words of a philosopher named Hali, wanders through a deserted wilderness, not knowing how he got there. He notes that it is cold but does not feel it. He notices the remains of gravestones and tombs, like the "burial-ground of a prehistoric race of men whose very name was long extinct." He comes across a lynx, and then a stranger dressed in skids, but neither acknowledges him. He can see stars in the sky, but he can see around him as though it were day. He eventually finds a well-preserved gravestone that bears his name and the dates of his birth and death, and realizes that he is dead, and that he is in the ruins of Carcosa.

### Connections to the Mythos

### Carcosa
Robert W, Chambers borrowed the name "Carcosa" for the setting of his fictional play The King in Yellow, which appears in much of his weird fiction.  Though Lovecraft doesn't incorporate Carcosa into his own fiction, he does, in his essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature", mention "primordial Carcosa" as an element in Chambers' fiction. He notes, "It is worth observing that the author derives most of the names and allusions connected with his eldritch land of primal memory from the tales of Ambrose Bierce."

### Hali
Bierce's story begins with a quote from an otherwise unidentified Hali:

The quote, particularly the last sentence, prefigures the claim Lovecraft attributes to Abdul Alhazred that "with strange aeons even death may die."

Hali also appears in Chambers' fiction as the Lake of Hali, on whose shores Carcosa is located. In "The Whisperer in Darkness", Lovecraft mentions "the Lake of Hali" among the "names and terms that I had heard elsewhere in the most hideous of connexions".

### The stars are right
When the narrator notices the stars, he says, "Looking upward, I saw through a sudden rift in the clouds Aldebaran and the Hyades!" Aldeberan is repeatedly mentioned in Lovecraft's fiction, while in August Derleth's "The Gable Window," it's speculated that the Hyades might be the source of the glass in the titular window. 

### External Link

* "A Family Way" by Oscar Rios: sex crimes and their aftermath in New York.
*"Fire Without Light" by Helen Gould: racism and mob violence in Oklahoma.
*"They Are From Away" by Charles Gerard: the depredations of the Ku Klux Klan in Maine.

fullContent:
"An Item of Supporting Evidence" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, featuring the occult investigator Titus Crow. It first appeared in the Summer 1970 issue of The Arkham Collector (#7).

### Synopsis
Titus Crow is taken to task by weird artist Chandler Davies for writing a piece of Lovecraftian fiction that blatantly contradicts known history. Crow defends himself by producing an object that proves that his fiction is grounded in fact.

### Characters
Titus Crow: He appears in this story as a writer of weird fiction, though he maintains that all my stories have at least a tenuous basis in established fact, some more definitely than others, and that I have never chronicled anything which I believe could not possibly have happened or which has not, in some way or other, directly involved myself.His most recent piece, a short story called "Yegg-ha's Realm," which appeared in the magazine Grotesque, was based on an incident recorded in the Lollius Urbicus' Frontier Garrison, written c. 138 AD--and verified by Crow's own archaeological investigations.

Crow lives in Blowne House, which is surrounded by a "curious aura of foreboding."

Chandler Davies: A "weird-artist" who maintains that "Mythological-Fantasy was ‘out,’" that the Cthulhu Mythos and the Hyborian Age "should have been allowed to die a sad but certain death along with their respective originators," and that writers who follow in such literary footsteps were "weakening the impact of the original works."

### Mythos Connections
Davies is impressed by Crow's library, which includes of "an original copy of Geoffrey’s People of the Monolith," as well as "Feery’s Original Notes on the Necronomicon, the abhorrent Cthaat Aquadingen, [and] a literally priceless Cultes des Goules."

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Arkham Collector, "An Item of Supporting Evidence" was reprinted in Lumley's collections The Caller of The Black (Arkham House, 1971) and The Compleat Crow (W. Paul Ganley, 1987).

fullContent:
"Anadhan" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Kieran Judge. It was first published in Vol 5, Issue 3 of the Lovecraftiana zine in October 2020.

### Synopsis
A man begins to have nightmares about a dark city, a future version of his own in which mankind is enslaved and consumed by bizarre monstrosities. Soon the dreams begin to bleed into reality, and he realises that the enslavers have followed him into his world in an attempt to make him keep his silence. Coming to the conclusion that everyone he knows has been assimilated by these beings and that he cannot escape their clutches, he throws himself from the window of a high-rise building.

fullContent:
"Ancient" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Armand Rosamilia. It forms the first part of his Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Synopsis
When a young man and his wife visit Keyport, New Jersey to settle his grandfather's affairs, they discover a town full of odd citizens with a dark secret and a decrepit old house with something living in one of its locked rooms. As night falls, the wife is whisked off by the Esoteric Order of Dagon, and rowed out to the bay to be sacrificed to a creature which sleeps beneath the waves.

### Characters
*Harrison Marsh, a young man with a dark genetic history.
*Nicole Marsh, Harrison's wife.
*Sylvia Smoltz, Keyport's town realtor.
*Jeb Marsh, Harrison's grandfather, now almost completely devolved.

### Publication History
"Ancient"was first published in the chapbook Ancient: A Keyport Cthulhu Tale in 2012, and was later included in the collection Keyport Cthulhu in November 2013. Both were released by Rimfyre Books through Amazon's digital Kindle platform.

fullContent:
"Ancient Astronauts" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Cynthia Ward.

### Synopsis
In 1979 Maine, when a teenage boy is kidnapped by a deranged cult and forced to undergo a mind-transference, his two best friends must devise a plan to rescue him. Although the cultists are successful in calling forth an Elder Thing from the depths of the Earth, the teens manage to defeat it and save their friend.

### Characters

*Joanna Saltonstall, a teenager from Penobscot County, Maine.
*Mike Francis, Joanna's friend.
*Bradley Greenwood, Joanna and Mike's friend, and intended cult victim.
*Harold Waite, an Innsmouth man who was the nephew of Ephraim Waite, and also a cult leader.

### Publication History
"Ancient Astronauts" was published in the Wildside Press anthology Weirdbook Annual 2 in 2019.

The Ancient Ones are fictional beings created by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price for their short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".

In Price's first draft of the story, which has been published as "The Lord of Illusion", the Ancient Ones take the form of bearded men, but are not actually human, being nothing but manifestations of a supreme pluridimensional entity. In the final version, their physical appearance is concealed by the hooded cloaks they wear.

The Ancient Ones dwell in an "extension" of planet Earth, in a realm where time has no meaning. Randolph Carter met these beings when he used the Silver Key to cross through the First Gate. At first, Carter perceived them as "cloaked, ill-defined Shapes" standing on hieroglyphed quasi-hexagonal giant pedestals. They are led by 'Umr at-Tawil, who is known as the Most Ancient One, a vaguely humanoid being believed to have once been a creature that inhabited the Earth long before the rise of humankind. As Carter soon learns, the Ancient Ones are, in fact, manifestations of the All-in-One and One-in-All, the Supreme Archetype, which he believes to be Yog-Sothoth.

When Carter approached the Ultimate Gate, the forms of the Ancient Ones became clearer and more human-like to him, even though Carter was aware that they were not human. They appeared to wear strangely coloured mitres over their cloaked heads, and carried oddly carven scepters. At this point, Carter "guessed what they were, whence they came, and Whom they served; and guessed, too, the price of their service". Under the guidance of 'Umr at-Tawil, the Ancient Ones were instructed to sleep, so that their dreams could open up the Ultimate Gate to Carter. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

At least one ancient book claimed that 'Umr at-Tawil and the Ancient Ones were agents of Yog-Sothoth, identified as the All-in-One and One-in-All, and that they "dream forever of that time when once again they shall rule to whom rightfully belong Earth and the entire universe of which it is a part". (: "The House on Curwen Street")

Although Randolph Carter was aware of grimoires which characterised the Ancient Ones as dangerous and "malignant", he dismissed these warnings as libel. As he followed 'Umr at-Tawil towards the Ultimate Gate, the Ancient Ones radiated a telepathic message saluting Carter, whose courage, they claimed, made him one of them. This might suggest that the Ancient Ones were originally travelers who ventured through the Gates. That they are described as manifestations of the Supreme Archetype is not inconsistent with this idea, as Carter learned that all the great wizards, scholars and artists of the universe are facets of this Archetype, including Carter himself. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

fullContent:
Anders Fager (b. 1964) is a Swedish horror writer and game designer who has described his fiction as "what would happen if James Ellroy took on H. P. Lovecraft." He is best known for his short-story collection Svenska kulter (2009), issued in English translation as Swedish Cults (Valancourt International, 2022).

He began his game career in 1982 at the age of 18, when he traveled around Sweden to demonstrate the first Swedish role-playing game, Drakar & Demoner. For that game, he wrote Spindelkonungens pyramid, the first role-playing game adventure published in Swedish. He later wrote supplements for such role-playing games as Call of Cthulhu, Kult, Twilight: 2000, and Tales from the Loop.

He made his literary debut in 2009 with the publication of Svenska kulter, whose stories place Mythos horrors like Shub-Niggurath and Ithaqua in Swedish settings, mostly in the present day. His Swedish Mythos milieu, known as "The Cult's World," has been turned into a role-playing game, as well as being incorporated into the Swedish edition of the Call of Cthulhu game.

In 2022, Dark Horse Comics published The Crows, a graphic novel written by Fager with art by Peter Bergting.

Dr. Andrew Doran is a character created by American author Matthew Davenport for his Cthulhu Mythos series to which he lends his name. An action-archaeologist in the style of Indiana Jones, he made his first appearance in the novel The Statement of Andrew Doran in 2013.

### Description
An athletic man with a thick crop of unruly brown hair and matching beard, Doran is a proficient user of magic, although he claims that his internal reserves are small and exhausting to use. He is an alumni of Miskatonic University who, at the series beginning, is working as a field archaeologist in Mexico, but later returns to his alma mater to take up the position of Dean.

### Olivia
Doran is accompanied by a "woman" named Olivia who is stated to be an aspect of his psyche self-manufactured to protect him from the horrors which he has witnessed. Through Olivia, he is able to perform actions which would shatter the sanity of a normal person: this would seem to suggest that rather than an aspect of Doran's psyche, she is an entirely separate personality, or has perhaps even become her own entity.

### History
Prior to 1941, Doran had spent a year living amongst a tribe of Night Gaunt-worshipping natives named the Night Watchers in Mexico. For some unspecified reason, they sentenced him to death, but were unsuccessful in their execution (: The Statement of Andrew Doran).

In 1941, he was tasked by the serving Dean of Miskatonic University with recovering their copy of the Necronomicon, which had been stolen by the Traum Kult, an occult group in service to the Nazis. In the aftermath of the expedition, he is appointed the new Dean of Miskatonic (: The Statement of Andrew Doran).

fullContent:
"Andromeda Among the Stones" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan, part of their Dandridge Cycle. It first appeared as a chapbook accompanying the anthology Embrace the Mutation (Subterranean Press, 2003).

### Synopsis
The story reveals the history of the Dandridge family: how Machen Dandridge found “a hole in the world" on the California coast and built a house there; how his wife, Ellen Douglas-Winslow Dandridge, died trying to stop the demons from "squeez[ing] in through the tear"; how their son Avery Dandridge tried to close the gate, even though "the one who wields the key cannot be a man," and was spit back "twisted and insane"; and finally how their daughter Meredith Dandridge becomes the creature on the rock who holds the line against "the moment when the stars wink out one by one and the sea heaves its rotting belly at the empty, sagging sky."

### Publication History
"Andromeda Among the Stones" was reprinted in The Mammoth Book of New Terror (Robinson/Carrol & Graf, 2004) and The Book of Cthulhu (Night Shade Books, 2011). It also appeared in Kiernan's collections To Charles Fort, with Love (Subterranean Press, 2005), Two Worlds and In Between: The Best of Caitlin R. Kiernan (Subterranean Press, 2011), Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018), and The Very Best of Caitlín R. Kiernan (Tachyon Publications, 2019).

Angelo Ricci is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1921 short story "The Terrible Old Man". He was a literary representation of the animosity felt by Lovecraft towards the non-white immigrants of the time, who he believed were polluting the genetic pool of the United States.

### Overview
Ricci, along with fellow criminals Joe Czanek and Manuel Silva, intended to rob the titular Terrible Old Man of Kingsport, an elderly recluse reputed to be extremely wealthy. What they did not bargain on was the man's true nature, and the gang's corpses were found washed ashore, horribly mutilated, shortly afterwards.

Ricci was one of the more thuggish of the trio, appearing entirely willing to cause the old man any bodily harm necessary to persuade him to give up the location of his fortune. (: "The Terrible Old Man")

shortDefinition: "Angels We Have Heard on High" is a short story with Cthulhu Mythos connections by author Tyson West. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 2 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana in July 2018.  ### Synopsis Father McGorski, a ...
fullContent:
"Angels We Have Heard on High" is a short story with Cthulhu Mythos connections by author Tyson West. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 2 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana in July 2018.

### Synopsis
Father McGorski, a discontented Catholic missionary priest in a remote rural parish in India, must deal with his parishioners and assistants, some of whom are committing suicide after having their faith shaken to the core and believing their god to have deserted them.

As the faith of his congregation deteriorates one of the nuns, Sister Cathleen, disappears, and is later discovered in the ruins of an ancient and forbidden temple, seemingly possessed by a dark force. Although McGorski is able to free the Sister, it costs him his life, though it appears to others to be a suicide.

In the aftermath, a monkey is born at a local temple, one whose mind bears memories which seem to echo the fondest ones of the late Father McGorski…

### Mythos Connections
One of Father McGorski's closest confidants is a man named Nimcarb, a Priest of the Temple of Azathoth. Unusually, neither he nor his church are depicted as being in any way malevolent, and in fact he and his flock actively assist McGorski in locating the missing Sister Cathleen.

### Behind the Mythos
"Angels We Have Heard on High" would appear to suggest that the Christian faith is a false worship, as Father McGorski's faith in his god is never shown to waver throughout the course of the story, yet he is still reincarnated (as believed in the Hindu religion) rather than going to Heaven (as would be expected by a good Christian).

### Background
Angerboda is a descendant of the Elder God Set. She is the offspring of Varcolac and Set's granddaughter Echidna. Angerboda is a giantess of Jotunheim, who is also a witch. She mated with Loki the Asgardian trickster god, and like her mother and grandfather, gave birth to several monsters of legend. Siring both the Midgard Serpent and the Fenris Wolf, and its alleged Hela, the Asgardian goddess of death.
In addition to her magical knowledge, she possesses superhuman strength and is able to shapeshift into animals.

"Anglo-Saxendom" is a short non-fiction piece by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in The Conservative, Volume 4, Number 1 , in July 1918 .

### Overview
The text relates Lovecraft’s firm belief that the United States and England are uniquely connected by a heritage of "race, language and culture."

### Behind the Scenes
"Anglo-Saxendom" showcases Lovecraft’s racist leanings, as seen with the lines concerning a "pernicious fallacy, fostered by and for the unthinking immigrant rabble," and "the detestable contamination caused by alien blood."

The Animiculi are fictional entities created by Charles and Janyce Engan for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu tabletop roleplaying game. They made their first appearance in the scenario supplement Beyond the Mountains of Madness in 1999. 

### Description
The Animiculi are severed pieces of a deceased Outer God or Great Old One caught in something called the "God Trap", a mystical device located somewhere in the Antarctic. Animiculi who manage to worm their way out of the God Trap become abraded to the point that they appear to be little more than black opal-like cysts. These cysts can reform into Animiculi when exposed to heat.

The Animus is an extraterrestrial life form created by the BBC for Doctor Who in 1965. It was later retconned into being a Great Old One during the period when Virgin Books tie-in novels related to Doctor Who were being published in the 1990s.

### Background
The Animus is a Great Old One from the Lloigor race. It was the only one of its race to cross into the physical universe, establishing itself at Vortis and turning the formerly lush planet into an acidic wasteland. It manifested itself within the Carsenome, an organic self-healing palace. The Animus is capable of taking over anything living which came into contact with gold. It resembled a hybrid created by crossing a spider or plant with an octopus. It could generate a fungus-like sustenance which grew into Carsenome, its fortress. The Animus could also create webbing with which it ensnared its victims. It consumed organisms via direct mental adsorptions and its tentacles spread out like roots, absorbing matter and generating webbing.

Dividing the Animus resulted in fission, creating two Animus. If it was dying, the Animus would create a seed of itself, that would grow into a new Animus complete with the memories of the old one. A single tendril could regrow to an Animus. It generated a light which weakened or hypnotized individuals. The Animus communicated telepathically with its Zarbi slaves, siphoned water from the planet, and drew power from the planet itself. It was capable of creating force fields, could fly, projected gravity beams, and could draw other planets and moons toward Vortis. It created incredibly resilient four-armed webbed beings.

During the Last Great Time War, a conflict between the Time Lords and the Daleks, the Animus was destroyed, with its "carsenome walls crumbling".

fullContent:
Anna Helen Crofts (22 December 1889 - 13 April 1975) was a writer, poet and teacher who is best known for her collaboration with H. P. Lovecraft on "Poetry and the Gods". She published some other short stories in various other amateur press magazines. There was false speculation for a time that Crofts may have been a pseudonym for Winifred V. Jackson, or Lovecraft himself.

### Biography
Crofts was born Anastasia Crofts to Nicolas M. Crofts (a physician and surgeon) and Julia B. Crofts on December 22 1889. She had a brother Edmond and is still listed as living with her family in the 1920 census, though she is incorrectly listed as 27 years of age (she would have been 31). She was elected Eastern Manuscript Manager at UAPA's Columbus, Ohio convention in July 1920 (this was the same convention which elected Lovecraft as Official Editor of the United Amateur).

In the North Adams directory, she is listed as a school teacher beginning in 1919, and it is likely that she corresponded and collaborated with Lovecraft during this period. Records indicate that she taught from at least 1919-1944, and at Haskins School for some, if not all of this time.

It is unclear how they first came to work together or why Lovecraft chose to collaborate with her. Faig proposes that Lovecraft may have been fond of the block of blank verse that likely appeared in the first draft. However, Faig notes that the poem was lifted in pieces from the poem "Sky Lotus" by Elizabeth J. Coatsworth. It is likely Lovecraft was unaware of this plagiarism. It is also speculated that Lovecraft may have become aware of Crofts work through her poem "Le Silent", which appeared in the same issue as Lovecraft's poems, "A Winter Wish" and "Laeta: A Lament".

Crofts published several articles in Vocational Guidance magazine, the official communication of the National Vocational Guidance Association, one entitled "Guidance versus Knights of the Road" (1932).

She additionally published the following works:
*"Le Silent", (short story), The Tryout Feb 1918.
*To Autumn", (poem), The Vagrant Jun 1918.
*"War Literature", (article), The Tryout Apr 1919.

"S.T. Joshi credits Miss Crofts with at least one further story in the amateur press, "Life" (United Amateur, June 1921)"

"Annals of the South Part Two" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author John C. Adams. It was published in the Gavin Chappell-edited anthology Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights by Rogue Planet Press in January 2017.

The title of the story refers to the name of a fictional book, and not to its position in a series.

### Synopsis
Ambitious King Gortah mounts an expedition to steal a book which he has been told will tell him the secrets of his future. When he finally lays hands on the book, his party are attacked by a colossal cephalopod-like creature which kills the others and shows Gortah what became of the long-lost land of Lomar. Although unable to recall exactly what he has seen, the young monarch is forever after haunted by the dreams of what he witnessed.

Annie Knowby is a fictional hero in the Evil Dead franchise. The character was originally created by Sam Raimi for the 1987 horror/comedy film Evil Dead 2, and would later be featured in the comic book series Army of Darkness. 

### Background
Annie Knowby arrived at her parents cabin with her boyfriend and two locals, to show them lost pages of the Necronomicon that she found, only to find evidence of a slaughter and a bloody Ash Williams. At first they believed Ash to be the murderer, but soon discovered the horror of the Deadites. One by one the members of her party were killed, till only she and Ash remained. As she read the Necronomicon to banish the Deadites, she was mortally wounded by Evil Ash's dismembered hand, dying as she spoke the final words of the incantation.

An alternate version survived the events in the Cabin and ended up in hell when it swallowed the cabin. With the help of a simulacrum of Ash, she freed her parents souls. After the two of them escaped from Hell, they would go on killing Deadites back on Earth. Eventually they would end up in the Mirror Dimension.

When Hyperborean sorcerer Eibon recovers a tattered copy of the Noctuary of Vizooranos from an ancient tomb, he inadvertently brings the owner's soul home with it. fullContent:
"Another Terrible Old Man" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by authors Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
Chased by a group of bigots, Veronica finds herself saved by a strange old man in whose house she has sought refuge. In the aftermath, the man shares a mysterious drink with her, and explains that many years ago he survived a confrontation with the Great Old One Cthulhu whilst aboard the steam yacht Alert, and distilled the brew from the ectoplasm left behind from the encounter. The magical properties of the drink begin to take effect, and the two transform before indulging in their carnal desires.

### Characters
*Ambrose, a man claiming to have survived the events related in "The Call of Cthulhu".
*Veronica/Victor, a trans woman experiencing trouble with intolerant locals.

### Publication History
"Another Terrible Old Man" was published in the 2019 collection The House of the Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares.

### Trivia
*Although Ambrose claims to have been present on the Alert during the events of "Call of Cthulhu", this directly conflicts with Lovecraft's story in which only two men survived the encounter, neither of whom shared his name. It's possible he is simply using an alias.

Antarctica is the southernmost continent on the planet Earth. H. P. Lovecraft had a long-running fascination with Antarctica and one of his most famous stories, At the Mountains of Madness, has ensured it a central place in the Cthulhu Mythos.

The fabled Plateau of Leng is rumoured to be situated somewhere in the Antarctic (although sources conflict on this), and a ruined Elder Thing city is located there. At the Mountains of Madness also heavily implies that some undisclosed monstrosity inhabits the plain beyond the barrier mountains and Elder Thing city.

### Stories with Antarctic Settings

### Inhabitants of Antarctica

*Albino penguins (: At the Mountains of Madness)
*At least one Chthonian (: "Big Nasty")
*Elder Things (: At the Mountains of Madness)

### Other References
*Prof. Harold Hadley Copeland's papers contain references to a primordial city of "the Yuggoth-spawn" in Antarctica (: "Out of the Ages"). It's not known whether "Yuggoth-spawn" refers to the Mi-Go or a different species from Yuggoth.

Dr. Anton Zarnak, whose surname is derived from Zhar-Nak, meaning the Mouthpiece of Zhar, is a character created by Mythos author Lin Carter. He is a supernatural detective in the style of others such as William Hope Hodgson's Thomas Carnacki.

### Description
Zarnak appears to be Eurasian of descent, with a high forehead and jet black hair shot through with a central zigzag of grey. He may be independently wealthy, and lives in a fair degree of luxury with his faithful manservant Ram Singh. 

He appears to possess a degree of magical power, which includes the ability to mesmerise others and to detect whether certain objects have been tampered with.

According to "Dope War of the Black Tong", Zarnak was once the high priest of Zhar and Lloigor amongst the Tcho-Tcho people on the remote Plateau of Sung, although the temptations offered by the Black Lotus drug resulted in him being ousted from his position. 

He has multiple doctorates, at least one of which (in metaphysics) was obtained from Miskatonic University, and his expertise has earned him a consultancy position with the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities.

### Library
Anton Zarnak possesses an extensive collections of occult writings, including:
*The Black Rituals of Koth-Serapis
*The Dhôl Chants
*The Ponape Scripture

The Anton Zarnak series is a collection of occult detective stories centred around the character from which it takes its name. 

### Overview
Fully integrated into the Cthulhu Mythos, the Anton Zarnak series follows the titular character and his loyal manservant Ram Singh as they battle supernatural threats to humanity, including gods, monsters, evil cults, and insane sorcerers.

### Behind the Mythos
Created by Mythos stalwart Lin Carter for his 1988 short story "Dead of Night", the tales of Anton Zarnak have been expanded upon by several other authors, including Robert M. Price (who was also Carter's literary executor), C. J. Henderson, Pierre Comtois, and Joseph S. Pulver, Sr.

Aphoom-Zhah (The Cold Flame) is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Lin Carter for his short story "The Acolyte of the Flame", depicting the entity as a cold and grey version of Cthugha.

### History
Aphoom-Zhah was spawned by Cthugha on "a dim world" in orbit around the star Fomalhaut. After the Elder Gods imprisoned Cthugha, Aphoom-Zhah fled to the Solar System, first dwelling on Yaksh (a.k.a. Neptune) and then moving on to Earth in Hyperborea (: "The Acolyte of the Flame"). There, Aphoom-Zhah was worshipped as a god. This put him in direct competition with other polar gods, Rhan-Tegoth and Rlim Shaikorth, which began to dispute with him for devotees.

This situation remained stable for some time until the Elder Gods arrived to destroy them. Rhan-Tegoth was sunk in a comatose state and Rlim Shaikorth was thrown to the sea aboard an iceberg. However, when they were about to apprehend Aphoom-Zhah, it reacted with such violence that it froze the regions of Hyperborea, Lomar and Zobna, giving rise to the North Pole.

This history is collected in the Pnakotic Manuscripts.

Aphoom-Zhah likely spawned the Gnoph-keh, Rhan-Tegoth, and Voorm. Though no human cult worships this being, Aphoom-Zhah is revered by the Gnoph-keh, the Voormi and his own race of minions: the spectral Ylidheem.

### In Other Media
*In the anime Haiyoru! Nyaruani, Kuuko summons Aphoom-Zhah to help cool off Mahiro's cheesecake.
*In the manga series Dandadan, Kashimoto can channel the power of Aphoom-Zhah to freeze his opponents.
*In the mobile game Yurudora, Aphoom-Zhah appears during the Cthulhu Festival event.
*In the strategy RPG game Codename: Bakery Girl (a predecessor of Girls' Frontline), the Secret Documents and Confidential Files feature many familiar names from the Cthulhu Mythos, including Aphoom-Zhah.

fullContent:
Aphra Marsh is the protagonist of the Innsmouth Legacy books by Ruthanna Emrys. She is a Deep One woman who has lived in San Francisco since her release from an Oklahoman concentration camp after World War II. She works in a bookstore and, less officially, for the FBI. She is the leader of a small magical coven, known as a confluence, following the Aeonist teachings she was raised in. 

### Appearance
Aphra is a woman in her late thirties that consistently refers to herself as "ugly." She has the "bulging eyes, thick neck, and receding hairline" associated with her Innsmouth heritage. Despite this, cover art and several characters show attraction to her in-universe. She is assumed to be of a white ethnicity despite the mixed heritage of the Deep Ones. 

### Biography
Aphra Marsh was born in 1910 in Innsmouth, Massachusetts to Kezia and Silas Marsh. She was ten years old when the Innsmouth Raid occurred and she was interred along with her family, far away from the ocean. Despite this, she was already fluent in both Enochian (the language of the Yithians), English, and R'leyian (the language of the Deep Ones). While interred, their camp was later filled with Japanese victims of the real-life Executive Order 9066. While the majority of Deep Ones and Innsmouth residents died as a result, Aphra and her brother, Caleb Marsh, survived and were released with the Japanese residents in 1946.

Aphra would live with a Japanese family, the Kotos, in San Fransisco until 1949. She would work as a bookstore clerk for a minor occultist named Charlie Day. Aphra would keep her true nature secret from him even as she helped him in translating some of the occult works there. Later, she would be recruited by FBI agent, Ron Spector, to investigate Aeonist activity. While initially extremely reluctant, the FBI agent sharing the documentation of her mother's torture and dissection by the US government convinces her to cooperate. Aphra would investigate a minor Cthulhu cult led by Osmin Wilder and companion, Mildred Bergman, who had unwittingly been drowning their members by sending them out in parodies of the Deep Ones return to their homelands. She reluctantly has Ron Spector send the leaders of the cult to asylums for their safety. Aphra also takes her boss on as a magical apprentice. (: "The Litany of Earth")

She comes to Miskatonic University to help the FBI learn whether mind-transfer magic may have been learned by the Soviets--but also to get back in touch with her Deep One family in Y'ha-nthlei. Aphra makes contact with a Yithian possessed professor, Trumbull, as well as several students investigating the occult. She also reunites with her brother Caleb, who has been unsuccessfully trying to regain Innsmouth artifacts and books from the University. Aphra takes on an additional apprentice in Audrey Winslow and runs afoul of a rival FBI agent to Ron Spector, George Barlow. Appleton is a city in eastern Wisconsin, United States, the seat of Outagamie County, resting on the banks of the Fox River, a major tributary of Green Bay. Originally the domain of native Ho-Chunk and Menominee cultures, the area was settled by European colonists in the early 1800s; the city proper was established in 1857.

Although receiving minimal representation in the works of H. P. Lovecraft, the city nevertheless possesses a number of connections which intersect with the topic of this wiki.

### In Lovecraft's Works

### "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin"
Lovecraft's farcical romantic poem describes the events surrounding a group of young Wisconsinites and their attempts to win each others' affections. (: "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin")

### In Real Life
Lawrence Appleton was a pseudonym used by Lovecraft himself when publishing in the amateur journal The Tryout. In addition, Maurice W. Moe and Alfred Galpin, both friends and literary correspondents of Lovecraft, were born in Appleton. Harry Houdini was also a resident as a child when his family first moved to the States.

shortDefinition: "Aptenodytes Albus" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by California, USA-based author Chris W. McGuinness. It was published in the online splatter/extreme horror zine Carnage House in 2025.  ### Synopsis Two years after the ill-fated Pabodie Expedition...
fullContent:
"Aptenodytes Albus" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by California, USA-based author Chris W. McGuinness. It was published in the online splatter/extreme horror zine Carnage House in 2025.

### Synopsis
Two years after the ill-fated Pabodie Expedition to the Antarctic wilderness, the director of Arkham Zoo Dr. Burtram De Vries orders head zookeeper Arlo Hollis to prioritise the care of his newest acquisitions, a small waddle of enormous, albino penguins. Although disgusted by his new charges, Hollis acquiesces to his superior's wishes, lamenting the neglect of the other animals under his care.

Six weeks later, and Hollis can still barely tolerate the sight of the new arrivals. After an evening of heavy drinking, he resolves to poison the penguins, believing that to do so would be a mercy for all involved. As he sneaks into the enclosure, he comes to the realisation that he is not the only one present: De Vries and a group of cultists are also there, stripped naked and worshipping the penguins as the Earthly representatives of the Elder Things. Although Hollis attempts to run, he is easily caught and forced by the cult into partaking of their dark communion.

### Behind the Mythos
In his writer's commentary for "Aptenodytes Albus," author Chris W. McGuinness says that "Lovecraft’s fiction is full of horrors and abominations of all shapes and sizes. The creatures I find more unnerving the more I think about them are the giant, blind albino penguins forever wandering the lightness depths beneath the dead, cyclopean city in At The Mountains of Madness. I wanted to write something explicitly Lovecraftian without falling into pastiche, so I leaned into the disgust these creatures triggered in me and the result was this story."

fullContent:
"Aquadingen" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
An apprentice occultist believes he has disposed of his mentor by betraying her to the local witch-hunters and, stealing her copy of the Cthäat Aquadingen, travels to the banks of the Rhine in order to use its power to make himself rich. Using a passage from the book, he summons what he believes to be a water nymph, and is captivated by its charms. Whilst he is distracted his mentor, alive and well, takes up the book and reads a spell from its pages, and the "nymph" reveals itself to be a servitor of Cthylla before dragging him down to the depths.

### Characters

* Hrothbard, a greedy occultist.
* Old Magda the Crone, Hrothbard's mentor.

### Publication History
"Aquadingen" was published in Blasphemies & Revelations, a collection of Price's works from across his career, in November 2008.

shortDefinition: Arabia is an archaic name for the Arabian Peninsula, much of which is occupied by the current nation-state of Saudi Arabia. The use of the term Arabia has overtones of exoticism and orientalism not appropriate in modern sensibilities but which were t...
fullContent:
Arabia is an archaic name for the Arabian Peninsula, much of which is occupied by the current nation-state of Saudi Arabia. The use of the term Arabia has overtones of exoticism and orientalism not appropriate in modern sensibilities but which were typical in Lovecraft's time and which only added to the desired aura of mystery of many of the stories set there.

In the Cthulhu Mythos, Arabia or this region appears many times with a number of notable appearances. Only Asia as a general region has more references within the Mythos, both representing the Other in an old fashioned and in some respects implicitly colonialist and racist sense.

### In Lovecraft's Works
Arabia is a fundamental part of the Mythos and has appeared in many stories, as well as giving us Abdul Alhazred, the supposed author of the Necronomicon. Many of the non-Earthly settings and concepts of the broader Cthulhu Mythos are infused with the trappings of the One Thousand and One Nights and other Arabesque stories. Ironically of course some of the most famous of these influences were themselves the inventions of Europeans simply appropriating and creating pastiches of Middle Eastern society and culture. However, the influence on Lovecraft and his works is strong. The use of hallucinogens to obtain visions especially of other worlds or of meaningful dreams was commonplace in Arabesque stories of the late nineteenth century through the first half of the twentieth century and this is also present in the works of Lovecraft and his Circle. This crosses over into similar dated attitudes to China and its use of opiates in popular fiction.

Arabia was popular in contemporary fiction, cinema, novels and plays, and was used as one of those "unknown" regions in a manner similar to Tibet or China, where to a sheltered Western mind the impossible became more plausible and "barbaric" splendor was readily available as a backdrop. The cultural insensitivity and othering of the local people and culture was irrelevant to the exigencies of telling a story.

### References and Name-checks
* Abdul Alhazred: author of the dreaded Necronomicon
* Al-Azif: this is an invented "Arabian sounding" name created by Lovecraft and explained as the original Arabic name for the book later known as the Necronomicon.
* Azathoth is referred to as the Daemon Sultan, a term for a kind of Middle Eastern ruler in Islamic cultures.
* The aging cultist Castro believed "the center [of the Cthulhu cult] lay amid the pathless deserts of Arabia, where Irem, the City of Pillars, dreams hidden and untouched." (: "The Call of Cthulhu")
* Constantinople, now Istanbul, is given as the location where the Necronomicon was transcribed into Greek.
* Damascus is given as the location where the Necronomicon was first committed to writing.
* Ghouls: taken directly from Arab folklore, the Ghoul as realized by Lovecraft blends the malevolent spirit of folklore with the real corpse eating ogre-like physical entity from other stories and add

fullContent:
"Arcanum Miskatonica" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Australian author Mike Adamson, first published in Vol 3, Issue 1 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction magazine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in April 2018.

### Synopsis
Rick Coleman, a research fellow at Miskatonic University's School of Biological Sciences, is assigned to sort and catalogue a collection of ancient specimens stored haphazardly in the school's basement archives. Amongst the detritus, he comes across a jar containing what appears to be a biological specimen labelled "Unidentified tissue sample recovered from Lake’s camp 76˚15’ S,  113˚10’ E, January 26th, 1931." 

Intrigued, he contacts his superiors and arranged for access to a portion of the restricted records regarding the 1931 Antarctic expedition, and is stunned when he learns that what he has uncovered may be a tissue sample from a previously-unknown entity so alien that all records of its existence have been suppressed. 

After consulting with his supervisor Dave Tremont, Coleman and the pair decide that the only course of action as scientists is to analyse the sample to see what they are dealing with. Predictably, their meddling awakens the dormant tissue which begins to grow at an exponential rate; they are able to activate a sterilisation system which destroys the majority of the now-huge - and voracious - Shoggoth, but decide to retain a cryogenic sample for future study.

### Publication History
Since its initial publication, "Arcanum Miskatonica" has also been included in the Lovecraftian anthology The Nameless Songs of Zadok Allen (JayHenge Publishing, 2023), and as an audio reading on the podcast Psuedopod (Escape Artists, Inc., 2023).

fullContent:
"Archons" is a short story by Cody Goodfellow that first appeared in Rapture of the Deep and Other Lovecraftian Tales (Hippocampus Press, 2016). It has also been translated for the German-language collection Tiefenrausch (Festa, 2022).

### Overview
Goodfellow uses the Iraq War as the setting for a Cthulhu Mythos story that examines the roots of human violence. The plot involves a secret war within the war, between a for-profit private military operation whose roots go back to the Crusades and a sect of snake worshippers who are "older than the dinosaurs." The story's protagonist, a combat-hardened Marine, is recruited by the former and gradually comes to identify with the latter.

### Behind the Mythos
The mention of unimaginable antiquity and snake worshippers recalls Set and his Serpent People.

Arcturus is a red giant star in the constellation Boötes in the northern sky. It is the fourth brightest star in the night sky, and the brightest in the northern celestial hemisphere. One easy method of finding Arcturus from the northern hemisphere is by following the curve of the handle of the Big Dipper.

### In the Mythos
Arcturus is first mentioned in the story "Polaris" by H. P. Lovecraft, where the unnamed narrator observes the star as it shines redly from above a cemetery on a low hillock.

The cosmic entity that inhabited the body of Joe Slater and his "brother of light" have voyaged to "the worlds that reel about the red Arcturus", while their human host bodies remained asleep. (: "Beyond the Wall of Sleep")

The double planet Kythanil, or Kythamil, once revolved around Arcturus. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", : "The Dweller in Darkness")

Asa Sandwin believed that Lloigor could only appear on Earth when Arcturus was above the horizon (: "The Sandwin Compact"). Zhar can also be summoned from Arcturus (: "The Dweller in Darkness").

According to the Unaussprechlichen Kulten, Nyogtha was sired by Ubbo-Sathla on Earth, but was at some point banished to a lightless world near Arcturus. (: "The Horror in the Gallery")

shortDefinition: The Argosy is credited as the first "pulp" magazine: a periodical printed on cheap (pulp) paper and sold at a low cost but in vast numbers. It was also the instigator of the entire genre of pulps and a print industry revolving around their publicatio...
fullContent:
The Argosy is credited as the first "pulp" magazine: a periodical printed on cheap (pulp) paper and sold at a low cost but in vast numbers. It was also the instigator of the entire genre of pulps and a print industry revolving around their publication. 

It was the creation of Frank Andrew Munsey, a Western Union telegraph manager. Munsey moved to New York City in September 1882. Following several months of financial hardships and entrepreneurial uncertainty, he published the first issue of The Golden Argosy on December 9, 1882. After several years, the drawbacks of producing a paper specifically for juvenile readers led Munsey to rethink his targeted audience. Juvenile audiences continuously outgrew the medium, and they lacked disposable incomes of their own that would attract advertisers. Following this reasoning, the all-new Argosy appeared in October 1896; the magazine was now intended for an adult audience, and was produced on less-expensive pulpwood paper, allowing for a substantial increase in page numbers and content. The use of pulpwood paper caused the coining of the term "pulp" for both the medium and the content of publications of this type. This new type of periodical, the pulp magazine was a runaway success.

Argosy was a showcase for popular fiction of every genre imaginable. Western, romance, adventure, war, crime, and science-fiction stories all found their home in Argosy. 

### Cthulhu Mythos and related features in Argosy
Weird Tales was the main forum in which the Cthulhu Mythos and works of the Circle took their life, but some writings of H. P. Lovecraft and others did appear in Argosy, including:

* "Ad Criticos: Liber Secundus" (H.P. Lovecraft letter to the editor, February 1914)

fullContent:
Ark Order is a Chinese mobile game developed by Mingchao Interactive Technology Co. Ltd. in September 2018, and later ended its service in May 2021. The game was also available in Taiwan, Japan and Korea. The gameplay involves collecting divine humanoids who originate from various mythologies, with the battle system being primarily based on the characters' attributed categories, such as certain elemental powers countering others. Many of the divine humanoids are female versions of familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos.

Taking place in the technologically advanced year of 2353, the storyline involves competitive spirits modeled after those from mythology sweeping through society, making human life become richer and more vibrant; however, the breakthrough of humanity's tangible technological boundaries could either result in a more advanced civilization or end up being destroyed for defying the laws of nature. The player must search for more divine humanoids and discover the world's secrets, in order to become the ark of salvation, granting humanity a glorious new future.

Arkham is a fictional town set in the US state of Massachusetts, invented by H. P. Lovecraft. It frequently appears in his horror fiction and in the work of other writers in the Cthulhu Mythos, particularly as the home of Miskatonic University, making it a key location in the Lovecraft Country setting.

Arkham is the namesake of Arkham House, the publishing house that promoted Lovecraft's work after his death. 

### Lovecraft Mythos
Lovecraft first mentions Arkham in the story "The Picture in the House", written in December 1920; the town remains offstage in this tale. The narrator relates:I had been travelling for some time amongst the people of the Miskatonic Valley in quest of certain genealogical data.... Now I found myself upon an apparently abandoned road which I had chosen as the shortest cut to Arkham; overtaken by the storm at a point far from any town, and confronted with no refuge save the antique and repellent wooden building which blinked with bleared windows....The strange house's odd resident  remarks, "I hain’t seed many folks ’long this rud sence they tuk off the Arkham stage,” and the narrator "replied that I was going to Arkham." One gets the sense in these references that Arkham is a rather remote town in a rural part of "backwoods New England"; the state of Massachusetts is not specified in this first appearance. This is the first of several instances where Lovecraft uses Arkham to establish another location--a role that comes to make the town the central point of Lovecraft Country.

Arkham is fleshed out a bit more in "Herbert West--Re-Animator", written between late 1921 and mid-1922. Here it's established as the home of its most famous institution: "We were in the third year of our course at the Miskatonic University Medical School in Arkham." The story also mentions Christchurch Cemetery, a hotel or restaurant called the Commercial House, a Crane Street near the Miskatonic campus, and a Meadow Hill on the outskirts of town where Herbert West and his colleague used a deserted farmhouse known as the Chapman house as a laboratory. The story notes that Arkham was devastated by a typhoid outbreak in 1905. 

The story describes Bolton as "a factory town near Arkham", where the "Bolton Worsted Mills are the largest in the Miskatonic Valley." Bolton is a real town in Massachusetts, located about 30 miles west of Boston--not in Essex County to the northeast of Boston, where Arkham is often thought to be located.

### 'Witch-Haunted'
Lovecraft returns to Arkham in "The Unnameable", a story written in September 1923

The Arkham Advertiser is a fictional newspaper created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Overview
The Arkham Advertiser is a local newspaper which, as its name might suggest, services the city of Arkham. Whilst it does not play any appreciable role in Lovecraft's works, other contributors to the Mythos have expanded upon it.

### Expanded Mythos

### Arkham Horror (Fantasy Flight Games)
Shown to have an extensive archive, the Arkham Advertiser has covered its fair share of Mythos-related stories, but has also shown a propensity to cover up the more fantastical of disturbing elements of these incidents. Whether this is on purpose as part of a conspiracy or merely an attempt to protect their journalistic reputation from ridicule is unknown.

Arkham Asylum is a fictional institution in the Cthulhu Mythos inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft. Located in the city from which it takes its name, it is a sanatorium which exists for the treatment of the mentally ill.

Some sources posit that the asylum is not as innocent as it likes to appear: according to these, Dr. Herbert West used/uses the facility to continue his attempts at perfecting the re-agent (: Feeders from Within, Army of Darkness Vs. Re-Animator).

### Behind the Mythos
It should be noted that the name Arkham Asylum is only used by later contributors to the Cthulhu Mythos: in Lovecraft's work Arkham Sanitarium is the city's mental health institution. As different sources show the two to be in existence at roughly the same time, there are several possible solutions:  

*the institutions have been conflated
* they are the same institution which was renamed at some point
* more recent authors have confused the institution with the D.C. Comics facility (see trivia, below).

The Arkham Detective is a fictional character created by American author and filmmaker Byron Craft for his eponymous series of Cthulhu Mythos stories. The Detective, whose name is never revealed, made his debut appearance in the 2015 novella Cthulhu's Minions.

### Overview
A hard-boiled detective in the employ of the Prohibition-era Arkham Police Department, the Detective spends his time working for the department's Mythos Division, a subdivision of that agency dedicated to combatting the many and varied supernatural threats which plague the small New England city of Arkham. Despite his lack of jurisdiction outside of his home town, he has been known to travel to other notable Lovecraft Country locations, including Innsmouth and Dunwich. He has been stated to have lost two different partners in the twelve months leading up to the first story.

The Detective was once married with a son but, due to the long hours he spent on the job and with his drinking buddies in the town's many Speakeasies, his wife left him, taking the child with her. He has not spoken to either of them since.

During one of his investigations, a murder-kidnapping which took him to the coastal town of Innsmouth by the sea, the Detective rescued a seven-year-old girl named Allison. The terrors they experienced that night created a strong bond between the two, and he soon adopted the girl. While he is at work his landlady, an elderly, good-natured woman by the name of Mrs. Trumble, takes care of Allison, and has even gone so far as to convert her spare room into a play area for her.

The Detective later met and married a woman named Nora Bishop and, together with Allison, Mrs. Trumble, and an adopted dog named Robber, proceeded to carve out a new family life for himself. Later still, his biological son Elijah was dumped on him by his first wife for reasons unspecified, and he took in Alvin Nash, a street urchin who had assisted him in the past.

In Who Stole the Necronomicon?, we learn that the Detective left the force and set himself up as a private investigator using some of the fortune he came across in The Dunwich Dungeon. He had also decided to embark on a carrer in amateur writing, using his past experiences with the occult as the basis for his stories.

### History
The first case we see the Detective investigating involved ferocious creatures dubbed Pilot Demons which were attempting to awaken an ancient entity slumbering beneath the streets of Arkham. He defeated the monsters, but his house was destroyed in the process (: Cthulhu's Minions).

A short while later, he was assigned the case of a murdered down-and-out, which soon expanded to include a kidnapping by Deep Ones and a plot to summon an abomination from beneath the Innsmouth coast. It was during these events that the Detective met and adopted Allison (: The Innsmouth Look).

Arkham Detective Agency: A Lovecraftian-Noir Tribute to C. J. Henderson is a collection of short pulp horror stories set in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
Focusing around author C. J. Henderson's Arkham-based private eye Franklin Nardi, Arkham Detective Agency includes four stories from Henderson himself, plus a selection of tales based on the character by other authors.

### Behind the Mythos
The idea for Arkham Detective Agency was originally pitched to editor Brian M. Sammons by Henderson shortly before his death in 2014, the premise being that of requesting other authors to submit stories based around protagonist Frank Nardi's investigations into the supernatural in the sleepy Massachusetts town of Arkham. Sammons agreed to this suggestion, but the finished work was not published until after Henderson's passing, with Sammons lamenting "I only wish that the publishing world didn't move so slowly and that C.J. could have seen this book."

### Publication History
First released in November 2017 by Dark Regions Press, Arkham Detective Agency received a Second Trade Paperback Edition in 2018. The volume has also been released as an ebook on Kindle.

The Arkham Detective Agency is a fictional business created by American author C. J. Henderson as a plot device for his Arkham Detective Agency series of short stories. It has since been expanded upon by other authors.

### Overview
Upon retirement from the New York Police Department, former detectives Frank Nardi, Tony Balnco, Mark Berkenwald and a man whose name is only given as Galtoni formed their own private investigations firm, choosing the New England town of Arkham as their base of operations as no other company offered those particular types of services in the area. Shortly afterwards, the partners began to awaken to the fact that not all was exactly as it seemed in Arkham, and in a bid to capitalise on the wealth of the local populace started to accept contracts with a more supernatural twist to them; for example, performing house cleansing services for homeowners, and the acquisition of occult artefacts for collectors.

The Arkham Gazette is a fictional newspaper created by H. P. Lovecraft for his Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Overview
The newspaper was created to service the fictional town of Arkham, Massachusetts. Although Lovecraft created the Arkham Gazette, it plays no appreciable part in his stories. Later authors have included it in their works, however. 

The Gazette has been in circulation since at least the 1880s. In Lovecraft's works, it is only mentioned in "The Colour Out of Space", which is set in 1883. In stories set in the early 20th century, such as "The Dunwich Horror", The Whisperer in Darkness, and At the Mountains of Madness, the Arkham Advertiser is mentioned instead.

In the works of August Derleth, it is confirmed that the Gazette still exists in the 1930s, as Andrew Phelan, while seeking information about his employer Prof. Shrewsbury, "sought the newspaper files of both the Arkham papers, the Gazette and the Advertiser". (: "The House on Curwen Street")

### Employees
*Willard Peck, editor (: Bones of the Yopasi)

### Trivia
*Named for the newspaper, The Arkham Gazette is a sporadically-released real-world zine created to supplement Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. It ran for only four issues between August 2013 and November 2021.

Arkham Horror is a series of board games based in the universe of the Cthulhu Mythos whose first edition was published by Chaosium, with subsequent editions being developed and released by Fantasy Flight Games.

### Overview
While actual gameplay varies wildly from edition to edition, all versions of the game involve a group of up to six players each taking control of one or more characters whose mission is to destroy roaming monsters and close inter-dimensional portals. These events take place within the city of Arkham with the base games, and as of the Second Edition throughout other famous locations from the Mythos via the purchasing of certain expansion sets.

### First Edition
The original Chaosium edition of the game was designed by Richard Launius and had a production run from 1987 until 1991. Each player selects a pre-made character from a deck and must travel the streets of Arkham, visiting notable places from the Mythos while closing inter-dimensional portals which spew out a variety of creatures featured in the works of H. P. Lovecraft. Victory is achieved by closing all active portals on the board before a certain number of portals have opened. Should the players fail to do this, then the game automatically ends in defeat.

### Second Edition
The Second Edition of Arkham Horror, first released in 2005, saw the publisher changing from Chaosium to Fantasy Flight Games, and while it retained many of the features of the original, was given a fairly major overhaul by games designer Kevin Wilson. Most notable of the changes was the introduction of Great Old Ones as antagonists which must be fought if the players are unable to close all of the portals before a pre-determined series of events leads to their awakening.

This edition also saw the release of several expansion sets, a handful of which contained additional boards which allow the players to travel to other locations of note such as Dunwich and Innsmouth, along with more Investigators, Monsters, Equipment, Spells and Great Old Ones to choose from. Each expansion typically introduced a new mechanic which changed the way the game was played in some way or other.

### Third Edition
The 2018 edition of Arkham Horror marks a fairly radical departure for the franchise, being the first to feature modular boards and branching decision trees. A series of expansion sets are planned for release from the second half of 2019 onwards.

Arkham Horror Fiction is a line of novels, short stories and art books set in the Arkham Horror iteration of H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Overview
Designed with an eye to expanding on the characters created for inclusion in Fantasy Flight Games' Cthulhu Mythos games, Arkham Horror Fiction began as a handful of novel-length publications of fiction (including a pair of trilogies) but has since expanded in scope to encompass an ongoing series of hardback novellas, each of which centres upon a specific character from their games, and a coffee table-sized book showcasing the associated artwork.

Initially produced by Fantasy Flight under their Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos-related content, the rights for Arkham Horror Fiction have since been licensed to Aconyte Books, the fiction imprint of games manufacturer Asmodee, since their acquisition of Fantasy Flight in 2014.

It should be noted that much of the content in these stories outright contradicts events which occur to minor characters during the course of the various games; for example, many of the Blights which feature in Arkham Horror were never driven insane by watching the play The King in Yellow.

The Arkham Horror Premium Figures line was a range of pre-painted miniatures released by Fantasy Flight Games as a part of their Arkham Horror Files range.

### Overview
Designed by Fantasy Flight as alternatives to using the cardboard tokens provided in their games of Arkham Horror, Eldritch Horror and Mansions of Madness, the complete range featured sculpts of most of the investigator characters for these games, along with a large selection of the most popular Monsters to go along with them. First released in 2010, originally only the Investigator figures were available, but from 2012 the Monsters made their appearance, being released in a succession of waves over the course of several months.

One of the design features of the Monster miniatures was a slotted base, which enabled players to insert the relevant Monster card into the base, so as to easily be able to view pertinent game information without consulting additional sources. This feature could not be adapted for the Investigator miniatures, as their play cards were far too large to allow.

These figures, whilst still listed on Fantasy Flight's website as of July 2019, are all marked as out of stock, and the company has not announced any plans to reissue them.

The Arkham Horror Second Edition Core Set was the first edition of the game to be issued by Fantasy Flight Games after its First Edition printing by Chaosium. It first run was released in 2005.

### Overview
The Second Edition Core Set had been quite drastically overhauled from the First Edition, with many major changes such as the removal of randomised movement rates and the addition of Ancient Ones to serve as final "bosses" for the Investigators. These entities increased the difficulty of the game by a large factor, but a confrontation could be avoided if the players closed all open portals on the board within a certain time limit. 

It was also the first edition to be supplied with expansion packs, add-ons which featured additional equipment, skills, spells, encounters, Investigators and Ancient Ones, to play with, with most featuring optional game mechanics to change the way the core set is played, and a handful even containing additional game boards to expand the area of action beyond Arkham.

Arkham Horror: The Card Game is a card-based investigative adventure game published by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-related products. It was designed by Nate French and Matthew Newman.

### Overview
Replacing Fantasy Flight's first Mythos card game, Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game, Arkham Horror is a fairly major departure from its predecessor. Instead of being a player-versus-player game (as was Call of Cthulhu), Arkham Horror is intended to be cooperative in nature, with players taking on the roles of Investigators attempting to find out more about the supernatural events which plague Arkham, and put a stop to them.

### Gameplay
Players start by choosing which Investigator they wish to play, and then build their deck from there. Each Investigator comes with a small number of unique cards which they are required to incorporate into their decks (which affect gameplay in ways which other Investigators do not), but are otherwise free to choose from a large selection of cards which drastically affect the way they are able to play the game.

Instead of facing off against other players, the Investigators play against an Agenda Deck, which dictates the events and actions perpetrated by their Mythos opponents. The Agenda Deck advances the goals of the enemy each turn, and should the Investigators take too long to complete their goal, they will automatically lose the game.

### Expansions
In addition to the core set, a large number of expansions have been released for Arkham Horror: The Card Game. Each of these adds new elements to the basic game, and new adventures for the Investigators to play through. The expansions have generally been released in waves (referred to as "cycles," with each cycle being thematically linked, and normally containing one deluxe expansion and a number of smaller packs.

shortDefinition: Arkham House was a publishing house specializing in weird fiction founded in Sauk City, Wisconsin in 1939 by August Derleth and Donald Wandrei to preserve in hardcover the best fiction of H. P. Lovecraft. The company's name is derived from Arkham, Lo...
fullContent:
Arkham House was a publishing house specializing in weird fiction founded in Sauk City, Wisconsin in 1939 by August Derleth and Donald Wandrei to preserve in hardcover the best fiction of H. P. Lovecraft. The company's name is derived from Arkham, Lovecraft's fictional New England city. Arkham House editions are noted for the quality of their printing and binding. The colophon for Arkham House was designed by Frank Utpatel.

### Under August Derleth
August Derleth was the guiding force behind Arkham House, financing the company and, after Wandrei resigned his interest in the firm after World War II, serving as sole editor and publisher.

In addition to volumes of H. P. Lovecraft's fiction, Arkham House published a five-volume edition of Lovecraft's Selected Letters that gives an overview of Lovecraft's correspondence to peers, friends, and family--including Arkham House founders Derleth and Wandrei. (Arkham House's volumes of Lovecraft's letters are highly abridged; unabridged volumes of Lovecraft's letters to individual correspondents have been issued progressively by Hippocampus Press).

Arkham House also published horror and fantasy fiction by many of Lovecraft's contemporaries, including Ray Bradbury, Robert E. Howard, Frank Belknap Long, Clark Ashton Smith, Robert Bloch, and Derleth himself; classic genre fiction by authors such as William Hope Hodgson (under the prompting of Herman Charles Koenig), Algernon Blackwood, H. Russell Wakefield, Seabury Quinn, and Sheridan Le Fanu; and later writers in the Lovecraft school, such as Ramsey Campbell and Brian Lumley to whom Derleth gave their earliest publication in hardcover.

Despite the wealth of talented writers who appeared under the Arkham House imprint, it was not a financial success. Derleth wrote in 1970, "[T]he fact is that in no single year since its founding have the earnings of Arkham House met the expenses, so that it has been necessary for my personal earnings to shore up Arkham House finances."   Robert Weinberg, a later editor at the publishing house, wrote that "intense competition from the SF (science fiction) small presses as well as slow sales of certain titles put August Derleth in a precarious bind. Only a generous loan from Dr David H. Keller prevented Arkham from going bankrupt during a period of cash flow problems. 

After Derleth's death in 1971, Wandrei briefly acted as editorial director, but declined to resume his interest in the firm permanently.

Prior to the 1980s, Arkham House did not generally reprint its books (with some exceptions, such as Someone in the Dark and Night's Yawning Peal: A Ghostly Company, and the core Lovecraft collections issued in the 1960s -- Dagon and Other Macabre Tales, At the Mountains of Madness and Other Novels and The Dunwich Horror and Others). Arkham House Books: A Collector's Guide is a non-fiction work by Leon Nielsen.

### Overview
Intended as a reference guide for every book published by Arkham House up until 2004, A Collector's Guide contains a chronological list of the works featuring details such as editions, reprints, value, etc, and includes titles from the imprints Mycroft & Moran and Stanton & Lee. It is fully illustrated with dust jacket covers, and also includes a history of Arkham House and a biography of its first editor and co-founder, August Derleth.

It should be noted that although the values of works given within were correct at the time of going to press, they are likely out of date in the current year.

### Publication History
Compiled by Leon Nielsen, Arkham House Books: A Collector's Guide was first published by McFarland & Co. in 2004.

Arkham House: The First 20 Years is a non-fiction work which, as it’s name might suggest, takes an in-depth look at the history of publisher Arkham House's first twenty years. 

### Publication History
Compiled by Lovecraft's friend and contemporary August Derleth, Arkham House: The First 20 Years was published in paperback format by Arkham House in 1959 in a run of only 815 copies. It has not been reprinted. The cover was designed by long-time Mythos artist and former correspondent of Lovecraft, Frank Utpatel. 

### Trivia
*As can be seen from the front cover, Arkham House: The First 20 Years was marketed with an RRP of only $1.
