Arkham is one of the most iconic elements of the Cthulhu Mythos and is synonymous with H. P. Lovecraft; as a result, it has appeared in or been referenced by countless other works in popular culture. The following is a non-comprehensive list of media that either includes Arkham or contains references, allusions or themes relating to it.

### Comic Books & Manga
*DC Comics: Arkham Asylum is a high-security asylum for the criminally insane which has been the subject of story arcs and graphic novels (A Serious House on Serious Earth, The Last Arkham). In the fictional universe, it was built and operated by the Arkham family, who gave it its name.
*Ghost Reaper Girl: manga series featuring an organisation named the Arkham Bullet, dedicated to exterminating evil spirits that cause mischief.
*The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen: Arkham is mentioned in Allan and the Sundered Veil, The New Traveller's Almanac and The Black Dossier. 

### Film & Television
*Arkham Sanitarium: both the name and the setting of a film currently in post-production (as of March 2022) by UK production company Survivor Films Ltd.
*Die, Monster, Die!: movie based on "The Colour Out of Space", Arkham is the setting, although here the town is located in England.
*The Haunted Palace: 1963 movie based on Lovecraft's "The Case of Charles Dexter Ward". Arkham appears.
*The Real Ghostbusters: The episode "The Hole in the Wall Gang" takes place in Arkham, Massachusetts. In the episode "The Collect Call of Cathulhu", the Ghostbusters go to Miskatonic University in order to get information on how to stop Cathulhu.

### Games
### Board Games
*Arkham Horror: a cooperative adventure board-game themed around H. P Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. The game has players exploring the town of Arkham as they attempt to stop unmentionable horrors from spilling into the world.

### Video Games
*The Batman Franchise: Batman: Arkham Asylum, Batman: Arkham Origins, Batman: Arkham City, and Batman: Arkham Knight are all related to the fictional asylum (see Comics, above).
*Bioshock Infinite: first-person roleplaying game whose main character, Booker Dewitt, is stated to come from Arkham.
*Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth: roleplaying game in which the main character, private detective Jack Walters, is admitted to the Arkham Mental Institution after seeing Yithians and going insane during a raid on a Boston home.
*Deus Machina Demonbane: visual novel which takes place in Arkham for most of the story.
*Penny Arcade Adventures: On the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness: roleplaying game which features the city of New Arcadia which is a parody of Arkham.
*Shadow Hearts: From the New World: features a visit to the fictional Arkham University, based in Boston, Massachusetts. Lovecraft himself appears as a professor at the university, conjuring demons for the heroes to fight at their request.
*Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened: a mystery game that combines the Cthulhu Mythos with Sherlock Holmes. The main villa

The Arkham Police Department is the primary law enforcement division for the city of Arkham. It has featured in many Cthulhu Mythos stories over the years.

### Expanded Mythos Works

### Arkham Detective Agency
In the Arkham Detective Agency anthology, the APD is used by a secretive branch of the government to keep tabs on the Agency. At least one investigator was also recruited by Frank Nardi from their ranks.

### Casefile: Arkham
In the altered timeline of the pulp/noir graphic novels, the APD is depicted as a profoundly corrupt organisation who seem more intent on clearing cases from their desks than seeking actual justice.

### Fall of Cthulhu
In Michael Alan Nelson's comic book series, the Arkham Police Department is headed by Sheriff Raymond Dirk. They suffered a number of deaths at the hands of the Gray Man, a supernatural entity in search of the young thief Lucifer.

### Fantasy Flight Games
Fantasy Flight have included the APD several times in their Mythos-related works. In this iteration, the department appears to have been infiltrated by the Silver Twilight Lodge who use it to cover up their activities and keep tabs on "undesirables."

### Known Employees

* Sheriff Engle: the department's head, Engle has appeared in several of Fantasy Flights' Arkham Horror games and stories.
* Officer Galeas Morgan: a promising young policeman, Morgan has seen the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos up close, and has proven himself a capable and resourceful individual.

Arkham Relic Hunt is a Call of Cthulhu-based card game from Squamous Studios, produced on licence from Chaosium.

### Overview
A competitive card game in which players take on the roles of cultists, the aim being to collect relics and recruit acolytes, with different achievements awarding varying levels of points. The player who has accumulated the most points by the end of the game is declared the winner. Arkham Relic Hunt is designed for 2-4 players aged 14 and over, and a game is estimated to take 45 minutes to an hour.

### Publication History

shortDefinition: Arkham Unveiled, subtitled Adventures and Background in the Home of Miskatonic University, is a supplement book by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu RPG. It provides extensive details on Arkham, Lovecraft's most famous fictional Massachusetts town, ...
fullContent:
Arkham Unveiled, subtitled Adventures and Background in the Home of Miskatonic University, is a supplement book by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu RPG. It provides extensive details on Arkham, Lovecraft's most famous fictional Massachusetts town, and 4 scenarios for keepers.

The book was revamped and re-released as The Compact Arkham Unveiled in 1995; this new edition did not include the scenarios, and changes were made to the maps included .

### Overview
Arkham Unveiled introduces the town Arkham on October 1928, as seen from a Call of Cthulhu RPG point of view. Most information was drawn from materials written by Lovecraft, with additional entries came other authors: August Derleth, Brian Lumley, Ramsey Campbell, Lin Carter, Robert E. Howard, Robert Bloch, and Clark Ashton Smith. Original materials are also included to "fill in the blanks". Buildings, people, business, relationships, history, grimoires, even the weather are described in detailed in the supplement.

A chronology deriving only from Lovecraft's stories is included for reference. Also included is a map of the center of Arkham, with a note that it differs considerably from Lovecraft's notes and drawing in Marginalia.

4 scenarios are included in the supplement:
* "A Little Knowledge": derived from "Herbert West--Reanimator", this scenario features a Miskatonic University student trying to recreate the work of Herbert West, and how the other students could stop him.
*"The Hills Rise Wild": the investigators attempt to find the site where a bolide, a meteorite of significant size, is presumed to have landed. Their area of search is the back-country northwest of Dunwich, Massachusetts, where they encounter a dangerous family and their god.
*"The Condemned": the investigators face off against an 18th century sorcerer, who intends to murder the 7 descendants of the 7 men who sealed him in 1752.
*"Dead of Night": a human skeleton discovered in a partially demolished mansion sets off a re-discovery of the truth of a crime long forgotten, which may or may not be related to a mysterious man trying to recover jewelry from the police's custody.

Arkham: Reanimated is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author Brandon Berntson, the second in his Lovecraft Mysteries series. Running to a total of 168 pages, it was independently published in February 2020; both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Synopsis
Millie Von Clydesburgh and Devlin Macky decide to take a day trip to the countryside, but become stranded in the near-derelict tumbledown that is Arkham. There, they encounter hostile locals, reanimated corpses, abominable experiments, and even an Outer God in their efforts to find out what secrets haunt the mysterious town.

### Plot
### Chapter 1
Private investigator Devlin Macky and his secretary/romantic interest Millie Von Clydesburgh decide to take a romantic day trip into the nearby countryside. Unfortunately for them, a storm moves in, and as the rural backroads become waterlogged, their gets bogged down near the mysterious and dilapidated town of Arkham.

### Chapter 2
As Macky and Millie try to make the best of their situation, they begin to realise that they are not alone in the countryside. A strange creature apparently made from stitched-together body parts attempts to gain access to their vehicle, but Macky is able to kill it using a gun which Millie keeps in her purse for protection.

### Chapter 3
Millie and Macky are rescued from their predicament by a friendly Arkham resident and local hotelier Theodore "Tiki" Bannister, who put the two up for the night.

### Chapter 4
The following morning, one-armed local mechanic Joseph Douglas "Duckie" Abercrombie drives Millie and Macky out to retrieve their stricken coupe. While there, Macky checks for the body of the creature he shot the previous night, but instead of the expected corpse, all he finds is a vile residue. As Duckie begins to work on their car, the two take a trip to Miskatonic University's near-derelict library on a fact-finding mission. There, the cranky Dr. Henry Armitage begins to fill them in on the activities of one Dr. Herbert West and the curse that hangs over Arkham.

### Chapter 5
After a tour of Christ's Church Cemetery during which they discover a number of opened  graves missing their occupants, Macky and Millie discover that Duckie has his malevolent, reanimated arm hidden away in a box in his office.

### Chapter 6
When Duckie informs them that their car will take at least another day to repair, Millie and Macky do a little more investigating, and come to the realisation that there are other reanimated creatures in Arkham, including a former occupant of the Christ's Church Cemetery who has been dead for decades.

### Chapter 7
Back at the Bannister Inn, Tiki and his wife let Millie and Macky in on the secret experiments performed by Dr. West on his return from the war, explaining how West had attempted to set things right with the locals by bringing their loved ones back to life, but eventually falling to obsession with his reanimation serum. Arkham's Masters of Horror: A 60th Anniversary Anthology Retrospective of the First 30 Years of Arkham House is an anthology of horror and fantasy by the late American author Peter Ruber. Running to a total of 444 pages, it was published in a hardcover limited run of 4,000 copies by Arkham House in 2000. A Spanish translation, titled Maestros del horror de Arkham House, was released by Valdemar in 2010 .

Each story was prefaced by an introductory piece on the author by Ruber, and attracted a degree of criticism from the community for the hostility displayed to some of the writers in these essays, which included the suggestions of H. P. Lovecraft being "a schizoid personality" and "a genuine crackpot"

Armandra is a fictional character created by the late British author Brian Lumley for his Titus Crow series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Overview
Daughter of the Great Old One Ithaqua, Armandra is a powerful sorceress and priestess who wages war against her parent. She uses magic, but is also telepathic. A highly strung but heroic character, she assists the human protagonists of the Titus Crow and other interlinked stories against Ithaqua and other Mythos entities until final victory. She has an important role in Lumley's novel "In the Moons of Borea".

Army of Darkness is a 1992 comedy horror film from director Sam Raimi. It is the final instalment in his original Evil Dead series, with a semi-sequel/reboot taking 21 years to make its appearance.

### Synopsis
Department store clerk Ash Williams once again faces off against the demon contained in the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis, which casts him back in time. In medieval England, he must battle an evil version of himself at the head of the titular army of undead, and keep the Necronomicon from destroying the world.

### Trivia
*Although Army of Darkness features a grimoire called the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis as a central plot device, it is important to note that this is not intended to be the same book as Lovecraft's Necronomicon, and is in fact a tome possessed by a malevolent spirit, written in ancient Sumerian, and bound in human skin.

fullContent:
"Around the Corner" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. 

### Synopsis
A man who had been a member of a cult as a young child begins to experience strange happenings in his apartment block after a mysterious woman and her group of friends move into the building. As the angles of space and time begin to lose all meaning and the madness infects his mind, the man begins to remember his suppressed past and a chanting begins, opening doorways to another plane of existence. 

### Characters
*Franklin, a lonely man who experienced a dark childhood.
*Reyna, a cult-member who has recently moved into Franklin's building.

### Mythos Connections
Reyna's cultists speak use Naacal for their ceremonies, a language proposed by British author James Churchward as the language of the lost continent Mu and later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price in their short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".

Additionally, the description of one entity, recalled from a book shown to Franklin by his mother during childhood, is a clear nod to the Great Old One Cthulhu: "a seated creature or entity with a bulbous head bearing three eyes on either side, and many long tentacles where a nose and mouth would be in a human".

### Publication History
"Around the Corner" was first published in the anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror in 2017. It was later included in the collection of Thomas's own works The Coming of the Old Ones in 2019.

fullContent:
Sir Arthur Charles Clarke (16 December 1917 - 19 March 2008) was a British author, inventor, explorer and television personality. He is widely regarded as one of the most influential science fiction writers of all time, his Rama and Space Odyssey series being considered classics of the genre. He also wrote the screenplay for the film 2001: A Space Odyssey, a critically-acclaimed piece of modern cinema, based on his novels and directed by Stanley Kubrick.

In 1948, Clarke sent Irish author Lord Dunsany, one of H. P. Lovecraft's literary inspirations, a copy of The Arkham Sampler containing a segment of The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. Dunsany was appreciative of the piece, stating "I see Lovecraft borrowed my style, & I don't grudge it to him" .

fullContent:
Arthur Machen was the pen name of Arthur Llewellyn Jones (born March 3, 1863, Caerleon, Monmouthshire, Wales.—died  Dec. 15, 1947, Beaconsfield, Buckinghamshire, England), a leading Welsh author of the 1890s. Best known for his influential supernatural, fantasy, and horror fiction, he was a major influence on the weird fiction of H. P. Lovecraft.

His long story The Great God Pan made him famous and controversial in his lifetime, but The Hill of Dreams is generally considered his masterpiece. He also is well known for his leading role in creating the legend of the Angels of Mons.

Machen’s work was deeply influenced by his childhood in Wales and his readings in the occult and metaphysics. As a child he encountered the findings of local archaeologists, who in the 1870s were digging up strange pagan sculptures and inscribed stones dating from the Roman occupation of the region. Machen's grandfather who was a local clergyman had found Roman inscriptions and carvings in his own churchyard at Caerleon, and the boy's imagination was captured early on in his life by the sense that the ground itself was haunted with a tangible and pagan strangeness. This sense of archaic survivals and suggestive inscriptions and remnants inflected all of his stories of the weird and occult. The temple of the Romano-British god Nodens was excavated at Lydney Park close to where Machen spent his boyhood years, and it is notable that this "Celtic" deity urns up in some of his most memorable horror fiction.

He lived most of his life in poverty as a clerk, teacher, and translator. In 1902 he became an actor with Benson’s Shakespearean Repertory Company. In 1912, approaching his 50th birthday, he joined the staff of the London Evening News.

fullContent:
Arthur S. Koki (1937–1989) was an academic who wrote a master's thesis on H. P. Lovecraft at Columbia University in 1962. It is the first detailed account of Lovecraft's life, and remains one of the most substantive scholarly examinations of the writer's life and work. It was published as H. P. Lovecraft: An Introduction to His Life and Writings by Hippocampus Press in 2022. 

Koki, whose parents were born in Albania, wrote an honor's thesis on Lovecraft at Clark University in 1960. Koki went on to study with Hart Crane scholar John Unterecker  at Columbia, and later became a professor at Pennsylvania's Kutztown University in Pennsylvania.

Koki's master's thesis was based on extensive original research, including interviews with Lovecraft correspondents Donald Wandrei and Wilfred B. Talman, and his second cousin Ethel Phillips Morrish, among others.

Koki's paper was a significant source for  L. Sprague de Camp’s Lovecraft: A Biography (1975).

Arwassa, also known as the Silent Shouter on the Hill, is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Randy McCall for the Call of Cthulhu scenario "The Asylum", featured in the gaming supplement The Asylum & Other Tales. Arwassa's first appearance would later be re-printed in the Cthulhu Casebook: A Plethora of Plots and Adventures and The Asylum 40th anniversary edition by Chaosium on Kickstarter.

Arwassa was also featured the short story "Saucers from Yaddith" by Robert M. Price.

### Overview
Arwassa is a Great Old One that floats around the hills of the old mottes and baileys of Europe, driving the men stationed there to insanity. It is described as having a humanoid torso but with tendrils instead of limbs, and a short neck that leads to a toothless, featureless mouth.

### In Other Media
*Arwassa appears in the mobile game Tower of Saviors, as a higher entity who was dedicated to creation and partnered with Daoloth.
*In the strategy RPG game Codename: Bakery Girl (a predecessor of Girls' Frontline), the Secret Documents and Confidential Files feature many familiar names from the Cthulhu Mythos, including Arwassa.
*Arwassa is revealed to be the antagonist of the graphic novel Fight or Flight, accompanied with the cooperative board game Cthulhu: Death May Die.

Asenath Waite is a character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Thing on the Doorstep".

### Biography
She was born in 1905 to Ephraim Waite and an unnamed mother who "always went veiled." A native of Innsmouth, Asenath's home was generally avoided due to the boarded attic windows and "strange sounds sometimes floated from within as evening drew on."

After the "death" of her father, Ephraim, Asenath attended the all-girls school, Hall School, in Kingsport. She later enrolled in Miskatonic University - becoming the only known female student to attend the institution - where she studied medieval metaphysics. It is at university, during a gathering in the student rooms, where she met Edward Pickman Derby, who became almost instantaneously infatuated with her. They soon married and purchased a house in Arkham, Asenath brought with her three unpleasant servants from her home in Innsmouth and a hoard of ancient tomes and books.

Years pass, and it is noted that Asenath ages incredibly, producing "premature crow's feet". Less and less is seen of both Asenath and her husband throughout this time. Edward tells of strange stories about Asenath and her father:



It is during their marriage that Asenath attempts to exploit her husband's weak will by "exchanging personality". After apparent months of mental abuse at the hands of Asenath, Edward finishes their relationship after but a few years of marriage. Edward dismisses her servants and burns most of her books, including her copy of the Necronomicon.

Asenath is eventually "killed" by her husband after he "smashed her head in" with a candlestick. However, Asenath's presence still lingers, even after Edward buries her body beneath a mound of boxes in the cellar, and Asenath eventually succeeds in "exchanging" with her husband - transferring her spiritual essence into his body, and vice versa. However, her husband was admitted to the Arkham Sanitarium and thus, Asenath was confined to a cell there. She manages to persuade those at the Sanitarium that Edward's "reason has suddenly come back," however, she is unsuccessful in persuading his best friend, Daniel Upton - who sees that it is not Edward's true personality.

Edward - now inhabiting Asenath's putrefying corpse - manages to deliver a letter to Daniel that reads:



At his friend's request, Daniel Upton went to the Arkham Sanitarium and shot Edward Pickman Derby - effectively killing Asenath and cremating the remains.

According to one account, she is the alter ego of Elspeth Waide created by Howard Phillips Lovecraft based on Robert Black's Commonplace Book. Elspeth is the daughter of Edgar Waide, and they were both possessed by an older ancestor whose first stolen body was Mathilde Roulet, presumably making this entity her husband Etienne Roulet. Ashley Joanna Williams (aka, Ash Williams) is a fictional hero in the Evil Dead franchise. The character was originally created by Sam Raimi for the 1981 film, and would later go on to become the main protagonist of the sequels and related media.

### Background
Ash Williams is a hero that is reckless and a braggart. The definition of macho, a chauvinistic pig who tries to "sleep" with every "hot" woman he meets, and something of an idiot. He first encountered the evil of the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis on a weekend excursion with his girlfriend and friends to a cabin, that ended up in the deaths of all but Ash. Since then he has fought demons and Deadites, was pulled centuries into the past, sent back to his own time, and decades later has found himself once more in the middle of things.

Another version of Ash has experienced far more adventures. Traveling repeatedly into the past and into the future, ending up in the Mirror Dimension, and in alternate realities. He has battled not only demons and Deadites, but also sorcerers, vampires, werewolves, aliens, and super-powered beings (zombies and werewolves). He has failed to prevent the end of the world at least twice, and both times managed to alter events in the past to prevent the post-apocalyptic future. This Ash also once prevented the return of the Dark Ones to Earth.

"Ashes" is a horror short story by American authors H. P. Lovecraft and C. M. Eddy, Jr. It first appeared in the March 1924 issue of Weird Tales. It is one of the few short stories by Lovecraft that has a happy ending.

### Synopsis
The narrator, identified only as "Prague", is paid a visit by his dear friend Malcolm Bruce who proceeds to recount a harrowing ordeal that he has just experienced.

Malcolm has recently been the lab assistant to Professor Arthur Van Allister, a former teacher of Prague's and an independent chemist who works from a home lab. Bruce is introduced to Van Allister's secretary and assistant, Marjorie Purdy, who proves to not only be a beautiful and capable secretary, but also a capable amateur chemist. She and Brice develop a friendship as the Professor becomes more and more withdrawn in his own secret project.

Eventually, Van Allister reveals his completed chemical invention in a rather gruesome fashion. He pours his chemical formula, a colorless liquid, on a live rabbit subject in a glass box. The rabbit is instantly reduced to a "fine white ash". He then funnels the ash into a small vial for storage. He describes his plan to implement the chemical as a military weapon of mass destruction. All of this is too much for Marjorie's constitution and she flees the room, followed by Bruce.

Once outside, she faints and Bruce catches her. As she falls into his arms, he is overcome by his emotions and he begins to kiss her. She awakens with his kiss and the two proceed to "make love" there in the lab. Once they get a hold of their emotions they realize the professor could find them at any time and they compose themselves to complete their workday. That night they resume their passion filled exercises and Bruce proposes.

After two days of this torrid romance, Marjorie disappears while Bruce has stepped out of the lab. Her hat and coat are gone, but the servants of the household report that do not know where she has gone. In a state of stress, wondering what could have become of his beloved, the professor calls him to his private lab. There he sees a casket sized glass vat of the deadly liquid, and a new vial of white ash. To his horror he sees Marjorie's coat and hat on a chair in the corner.

In horror and rage at the death of his fiancé, he overpowers the professor and it is unclear whether he has killed or simply rendered Van Allister unconscious. He then proceeds to place the body in the vat of the chemical, reducing the body to ash and consuming the mysterious liquid.

Horrified at his actions, he rushes to Prague's house to find someone to confess his guilt to.

The narration returns to the present and Prague presses Bruce on whether or not he was certain that the ashes were those of Marjorie. In doubt they return to the house and lab and eventually find Marjorie locked in a wooden chest. "Asphinxiation" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Frank Forte, first published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
Miskatonic University resercher Dr. Darius believes himself to be writing a cautionary work about the extraterrestrial dangers facing mankind, and relates the tale of how, after discovering a copy of the fabled Necronomicon, he was led to a chamber hidden below the Great Sphinx of Giza. Beneath the chamber he discovered a portal to the ruined city of R'lyeh, within which terrible forces were beginning to stir. Driven half mad, he fled before collapsing into unconsciousness.

The story concludes with the revelation that Darius is in fact incarcerated in a mental health facility, and in his insanity believes that the doctors are his peers, come to hear his dire warnings.

Asteroth is a cosmic demon appearing in Marvel Comics. The character appeared in the final four issues of Stormbreaker: The Saga of Beta Ray Bill, issues #3-6 in 2005. Asteroth was a Great Old One or a Lesser Old One. (: Official Handbook of the Marvel Universe A-Z #3)

### History

She claimed to have been born from the chaos of the universe's creation. She once visited the home reality of the main Marvel Comics stories (Earth-616) but sometime later became trapped in another dimension, imprisoned by the race from which she emerged. During the fight between the Korbinite Beta Ray Bill and the Cosmic Herald Stardust, a dimensional warp was opened by Stardust who attempted to send Beta Ray Bill into a cosmic hell. A monstrous tentacle surged forth from the warp and seized Beta Ray Bill. A blast from Stardust severed the tentacle right before it closed, leaving behind the fragment.

This fragment then transformed into a feminine semi-humanoid form who planned to consume order throughout the universe, remaking it in its image by permitting chaos to reign supreme. After this she planned to move on to the next universe, consume it, and move on to the next, and so forth, until chaos overcame all of the Multiverse after which it would move on to the Omniverse. During battle with both Stardust and Beta Ray Bill, Asteroth was suddenly attacked by Alpha Ray, the Korbinite android sent by Galactus.

Asteroth was taken close enough to a Black Hole to be pulled in, but was able to send her essence into Beta Ray Bill's Meta-Orb which contained the lifeforces of the Korbinites who had been collected by Stardust. Upon arriving at his ship, it began to absorb power from the vessel. When he arrived at Asgard in the aftermath of Ragnarok, it emerged from the Meta-Orb in a new more beastly humanoid form, having fed on the Korbinite life forces. An enraged Beta Ray Bill fought Asteroth once more, and this time emerged victorious, apparently killing her.

### Powers of Asteroth
A small fragment of the entity was powerful enough to incapacitate a Cosmic Herald (Stardust) and a champion of Asgard, Beta Ray Bill, with a single blast. She was able to obliterate a planet when smashed into its core by the combined assault of Beta Ray Bill and Stardust, and emerged unharmed. Asteroth was able to re-direct a black hole's gravity well. It's an entity that thrives on destruction, feeding on order and life. It can feed on worlds and then galaxies, using them to increase it power and once she became powerful enough, she would feed on the universe.

shortDefinition: Astounding Stories was the leading science fiction magazine of the pulp magazine era. It published two of H. P. Lovecraft's most highly regarded works: At the Mountains of Madness, which was serialized in the February, March, and April issues of 1936...
fullContent:
Astounding Stories was the leading science fiction magazine of the pulp magazine era. It published two of H. P. Lovecraft's most highly regarded works: At the Mountains of Madness, which was serialized in the February, March, and April issues of 1936, and "The Shadow Out of Time", which appeared in the June 1936 edition.

Founded in 1930 by William Clayton, Astounding was bought in 1933 by the Street & Smith publishing company after Clayton went bankrupt. Street & Smith hired F. Orlin Tremaine as editor; Tremaine's policy of printing stories that he liked without being overly concerned about how closely they fit the genre of the magazine led him to accept Lovecraft's Antarctic horror story when it was submitted in 1935 by Lovecraft's agent Julius Schwartz.

The typographical errors, alterations and omissions in Astoundings version of Madness outraged Lovecraft, who referred to Tremaine as "that god-damn'd dung of a hyaena" in a letter to R. H. Barlow.

"Astral and Arcane Science" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author S. J. Leary. It was published in Tomorrow's Cthulhu: Stories at the Dawn of Posthumanity by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator and their partner Alice, private investigators specialising in industrial cases, are engaged by genetic self-help company Andyne to look into possible corporate misconduct in one of their research facilities. They uncover a cooperative effort between the scientists - both those at this particular facility and others worldwide - and an insectile alien species named the Mi-go to "improve" the human species on a genetic level. Stunned and disgusted by this revelation, the two investigators kill the lead scientist and his latest half-human creation before reporting their findings in the hopes that something may be done to stop the global conspiracy.

In the aftermath, the investigators suffer terrible blows to their sanity, and Alice is committed to a mental health facility. In the news, the narrator begins to see signs that the conspiracy may not have been exterminated as he had hoped, and he worries that the Earth will soon be little more than a Mi-go colony.

fullContent:
"Astrophobos" is a poem by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview
The subject of the poem is a stargazer suffering the replacement of his original visions of splendour inspired by looking at the starry night sky with visions of horror and of cacodaemons which must be fluttering around unknown stars. The change in viewpoint is matched by the change in colours of the stars he looks at, from glittering golden to muted fiery red.

### Publication History
"Astrophobos" was first published in The United Amateur, 17, No. 3 (January 1918). It has since seen inclusion in a number of collections, particularly those with a focus on poetry.

### Behind the Mythos
At one point in his life, at the age of 12, Lovecraft imagined nothing finer or more inevitable that spending his life as a professional astronomer. It is interesting comparing Lovecraft at 12 publishing pamphlets on astronomy with Lovecraft at 21, publishing weird horror poetry.

shortDefinition: Whether called an insane asylum, sanitarium or madhouse, institutions for the treatment of the mentally ill play a prominent role in Cthulhu Mythos fiction, reflecting the sanity-sapping effects of many Mythos entities, creatures, and tomes.  ### In ...
fullContent:
Whether called an insane asylum, sanitarium or madhouse, institutions for the treatment of the mentally ill play a prominent role in Cthulhu Mythos fiction, reflecting the sanity-sapping effects of many Mythos entities, creatures, and tomes.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction

### Arkham Sanitarium
Edward Pickman Derby is committed here after a breakdown in "The Thing on the Doorstep"; Daniel Upton kills his body there.

### Sefton Asylum
Allan Halsey, former dean of Miskatonic's medical school, is committed there after a cannibal rampage in "Herbert West--Reanimator".

### Danvers Hospital for the Insane
A government or business man who "went crazy" after a visit to Innsmouth is held there in "The Shadow over Innsmouth". Thurber, in "Pickman's Model", says Richard Upton Pickman espoused "art theories and philosophic speculations wild enough to qualify him for the Danvers asylum." 

[Danvers State Hospital, also known as the State Lunatic Hospital at Danvers or the Danvers Lunatic Asylum, was a real institution, operating from 1878 until 1992 in Danvers, Massachusetts.] 

### Essex County asylum
Nahum Gardner, in "The Colour out of Space", declines to send his disturbed wife there.

### Conanticut Island
Charles Dexter Ward is committed to a private hospital for the insane there in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. The hospital is run by Dr. Waite.

### Canton sanitarium
Lawrence Williamson, Robert Olmstead's cousin, is sent here in "The Shadow Over Innsmouth".

### Guthrie insane asylum
The progeny of Yig is kept there in "The Curse of Yig".

### Huntingdon madhouse
Sir Wade Jermyn is placed there in 1765 because of his wild tales of Africa in "Arthur Jermyn". He dies there three years later.

### Synopsis
After a chance encounter with a mysterious and sinister man during a work night out, Valerie, a shy young office worker, begins to suspect the man is following her. Her suspicions increase as her colleagues notice him loitering in odd places, and Valerie uncovers evidence that he is responsible for the sudden disappearance of her flatmate. The story concludes with Valerie pondering what she should do when the dark man inevitably comes for her…

### Mythos Connections
"At First Sight" is set in the fictional town of Brichester, a locale created by Campbell for many of his Cthulhu Mythos stories.

shortDefinition: At the Mountains of Madness is a novella by American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in February and March 1931 and originally serialized in the February, March, and April 1936 issues of Astounding Stories. It has been reproduced in numerous c...
fullContent:
At the Mountains of Madness is a novella by American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in February and March 1931 and originally serialized in the February, March, and April 1936 issues of Astounding Stories. It has been reproduced in numerous collections since Lovecraft's death. Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi describes the novella as representing the decisive "demythology" of the Cthulhu Mythos by reinterpreting Lovecraft's earlier supernatural stories in a science fiction paradigm.

### Plot


The story is written in the first-person perspective by the geologist William Dyer, a professor from Miskatonic University. He writes to disclose hitherto unknown and closely kept secrets in the hope that he can deter a planned and much publicized scientific expedition to Antarctica. On a previous expedition there, a party of scholars from Miskatonic University, led by Dyer, discovered fantastic and horrific ruins and a dangerous secret beyond a range of mountains taller than the Himalaya.

The group that discovered and crossed the mountains found the remains of fourteen ancient life forms, completely unknown to science and unidentifiable as either plants or animals, after discovering an underground cave while boring for ice cores. Six of the specimens seem to be badly damaged, the others uncannily pristine. Their highly-evolved features are problematic: their stratum location puts them at a point on the geologic time scale much too early for such features to have naturally evolved yet. Because of their resemblance to creatures of myth mentioned in the Necronomicon, they are dubbed the "Elder Ones".



When the main expedition loses contact with this party, Dyer and the rest of his colleagues travel to their camp to investigate. The camp is devastated and both the men and the dogs slaughtered, with only one of each missing. Near the camp, they find six star-shaped snow mounds, and a damaged Elder One buried under each. They discover that the better-preserved life forms have vanished and that some form of experiment has been done, though they are only able to speculate on the subject and the possibility that it is the missing man and dog. Dyer decides to close off the area from which they took their samples.

Dyer and a student named Danforth fly an airplane over the mountains, which they soon realize are the outer wall of a huge, abandoned stone city of cubes and cones, utterly alien to any human architecture. By exploring these fantastic structures, the men are able to learn the history of the Elder Things or Old Ones, by interpreting their magnificent hieroglyphic murals: The Old Ones first came to Earth shortly after the Moon was pulled loose from the planet and were the creators of all Earth life. They built their cities with the help of "Shoggoths", organisms created to perform any task, assume any form, and reflect any thought. As more buildings are explored, a fantastic vista opens of the history of races beyond the scope of man's understanding

At the Mountains of Madness and Other Novels is an anthology of stories by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Publication History
First released in 1964 by Arkham House, At the Mountains of Madness and Other Novels collects eight of Lovecraft’s works together with an introduction by friend and contemporary August Derleth, with this edition receiving four reprints. It was later revised in 1986 by S. T. Joshi, with the new edition replacing Derleth's introduction with two new ones, one by Joshi himself and another by Jim Turner. This version, titled the "corrected printing" was reissued a further four times.

fullContent:
"At the Mountains of Murkiness, or, From Lovecraft to Leacock" is a short story by the late British author Arthur C. Clarke. A parody of H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, it was first published in the March 1940 edition of fanzine The Satellite.

### Synopsis
The sole remaining survivor of an expedition to the Antarctic tells of how his group stumbled across the ancient civilisation of the Elder Ones, existing quietly for millennia beneath Mount Morgue. Although at first believing their hosts to be cultured and genial, the party soon come to the realisation that the Elder Ones wish to destroy the human race. Making a bid for freedom, they are pursued by the unspeakable creatures which serve the Elder Ones, but manage to effect their escape with the aid of a shoddily-repaired main gateway which buys them time to flee.

### Behind the Mythos
"At the Mountains of Murkiness" contains many elements from Lovecraft's works, all of them altered or exaggerated for comedic effect. These include a creature which fits the description of a Shoggoth, ancient bas-reliefs which are hard for the human mind to look at, an ill-fated Antarctic expedition, and the Elder Ones themselves- who are mentioned to own a half interest in pulp magazine Weird Tales. Also included is a little creature named Slog-Wallop, the Elder Ones' Inspector of Outhouses and Public Conveniences, who bears something of a resemblance to Brown Jenkin from "The Dreams in the Witch-House".

"At the Root" is a short non-fiction piece by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. It was first published in The United Amateur, 17, No. 6 in July 1918.

### Synopsis
In "At the Root", Lovecraft sets out his beliefs for the base cause of the First World War: the tendency of human populations to revert to an atavistic state of aggression when confronted with the denial of their desires. He also expresses his belief that only the consistent and ongoing vigilance of armed states will prevent such conflicts in the future.

Atal is a fictional character from the Cthulhu Mythos, who first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Cats of Ulthar".

### Background
Atal is a denizen of the Dreamlands. The son of an innkeeper he was brought up in the town of Ulthar and was a witness to the strange event that led to the law that forbade killing cats in the town. (: "The Cats of Ulthar")

As a young man he became a priest and the apprentice of Barzai the Wise, loyally accompanying him on his doomed climb to the top of Mount Hatheg-Kla to see the gods. (: "The Other Gods")

Having survived his ill-fated master he returned to Ulthar and was eventually visited by Randolph Carter, by which time he was well over 300 years old and the patriarch of the Temple of the Elder Ones. Despite his age he was "still very keen of mind and memory" and, knowing the danger, initially refused to divulge information on Kadath. However after many drafts of moon-wine from Carter, he drunkenly reveals a key piece of information that points towards the mysterious fortress. As befits his age and station, Atal sports a long beard. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

### Behind the Mythos
Atal is also the synonym of a person who portrays braveness and determination. Most people with this name are believed to be highly knowledgeable and creative. The name also indicates a strong sense of selectiveness.

Athammaus is a fictional character created by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith for his Hyperborean Cycle series of fantasy stories. He appears in "The Testament of Athammaus", first published in the October 1932 issue of Weird Tales.

### Overview
The chief headsman (a Hyperborean title for executioner) of Commoriom in its final days, Athammaus was the latest in a family which had held that title for generations. He was proud of his abilities, and carried out his work diligently.

When the entity Knygathin Zhaum was brought to the city only to prove unkillable, he believed that he had failed in his duty, and was the last of the citizenry to leave when it was decided to abandon Commoriom. However, he did continue in public service for many years after a new capital was established at Uzuldaroum.

Near the end of his life, Athammaus wrote his testament, describing the events that led to Commoriom's abandonment.

"Atishfishan" is a contemporary Cthulhu Mythos story by Australian author Brian Craddock. It was published in the first issue of short-lived horror periodical The Asylum Files by Oscillate Wildly Press in May 2019.

### Synopsis
A Western reporter and his local guide and lover travel to an archaeological site in Pakistan to cover the proceedings. Nearby, the archaeological team discover an ancient and colossal fortification beneath which sleeps an army of vicious, intelligent beings which belch fire and have a penchant for flaying men alive; defeated many years ago and sent to slumber beneath the sands, the creatures awaken and begin their assault upon the human race.

The reporter and his lover, having joined consciousnesses and inhabited the same body through some unknown mental process, bear witness to the battle which rages between the creatures and the Pakistani army for the next three weeks. As the humans finally defeat their opponents through the use of heavy artillery strikes, the beings retreat back below the ground. The gestalt creature which the two men have become resolves to remain hidden in the caves nearby, watching the sleeping beings and ready to warn humankind should they ever begin to stir.

### Mythos Connections
The reporter remarks at one point that he attended Miskatonic University in his younger days, and studied under one Professor Wingate Peaslee.

### Behind the Mythos
"Aatish-fishaa.n" is a Sanskrit word which translates to "scattering fire, fire spewing volcano, fiery, [or] fire-spitting" .

Atlach-Nacha is a fictional deity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Seven Geases"; it has since been referenced and elaborated upon by August Derleth, Colin Wilson, Brian Lumley, Lin Carter, Laurence J. Cornford, James Ambuehl, Ran Cartwright and many others.

### Description
Atlach-Nacha resembles a giant spider with an anthropomorphic face capable of some human expression. It dwells in a cave system beneath Mount Voormithadreth, in the now extinct Arctic kingdom of Hyperborea. There, it spins a great web, bridging the many caverns of the underworld together. In its original appearance in the short story "The Seven Geases", Atlach-Nacha dwelt between the lairs of Tsathoggua and the antehuman sorcerer Haon-Dor. 

According to later Chaosium material, Atlach-Nacha's web is a bridge between the Dreamlands and the waking world. It is believed that when the web is complete, the end of the world will come.

According to the fiction of Lin Carter, it is served by the "Gray Weavers". A burial ritual in the Book of Eibon references this god.

### In Other Media
*Doom: in the megawad Strange Aeons, the Spinner in Darkness is revealed to be the primary antagonist, tricking the player character into traveling across the Dreamlands to free it from its prison.
*Sundered: Atlach-Nacha is referenced by name in the Thunder Lotus-produced game; when the player corrupts an ability that allows them to run up walls they will then instead turn into a purple anthropomorphic spider and climb the walls instead. This corrupted ability is known as "Atlach-Nacha's Grip"
*World of Horror: Alternately referred to as "Atorasu-Nasa" and "Cthac-Atorasu," this iteration appears as one of the game's possible Old God major antagonists threatening to cross the veil into the player character's reality in the city of Shiokawa, Japan. Its mere presence as the active Old God in a given playthrough disables the player's option to flee from any combat encounter, and should the "Doom progress" bar representing the enemy cult's summoning ritual be filled completely, the player character will be unable to prevent the ritual in time, and Cthac-Atorasu's "insatiable hunger" will be unleashed upon the hapless residents of the seaside city.

"Atlachnaphobia" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Ambuehl.

### Synopsis
A man with a lifelong fear of spiders visits a psychiatrist with a very peculiar set of skills. Despite receiving a certain degree of help, he eventually falls prey to the depredations of Atlach-Nacha, the Spider Goddess.

### Characters 

*Jim Campbell, a regular fellow whose deathly fear of spiders is negatively affecting his day-to-day life.
*Dr. Raymond Thulask, a psychiatrist with knowledge of the occult.
*Atlach-Nacha, a Great Old One.

### Publication History
"Atlachnaphobia" was first published in the small-press horror periodical Cthulhu Cultus #9 in January 1998, a magazine edited by Tani Jantsang and James Ambuehl himself.

The Atlanta Radio Theatre Company is a Georgia, US-based acting troupe who focus on the science fiction, horror and fantasy genres. Founded in 1984, the ARTC have both recorded studio adaptations and performed at live venues including NecronomiCon; they have adapted several of Lovecraft’s stories into audio dramas in the style of the golden age of radio, and have even written some original Mythos material. Many of these are available as CD and digital download through their website.

It seems in more recent years they have primarily focused on their episodic radio drama style performances "Mercury" about a radio station that helps survivors of a zombie apocalypse.

Atlantis is a legendary lost continent, usually supposed to have been located in the North Atlantic Ocean. It was believed to have hosted an ancient civilization that was destroyed and sunk beneath the ocean in a cataclysmic event. The myth of Atlantis was incorporated as a background element by H. P. Lovecraft and other Cthulhu Mythos authors; Robert E. Howard and Clark Ashton Smith, among others, set stories in pre-cataclysm Atlantis.

### H. P. Lovecraft
Though rarely the focus of Lovecraft's stories, Atlantis is mentioned numerous times.

The kingdom of Atlantis thrived for thousands of years. At its prime, it was a mighty empire, with a respected naval fleet. The Atlanteans enslaved ape-like creatures known as Gyaa-Hua and had diplomatic relations with the mother-continent Mu, which turned sour when the Atlantean General Bothon's army besieged the Muvian capital of Alu to abduct the Emperor's niece. (: "Bothon")

Alien gods were worshiped in Atlantis (: "The Last Test") and there are rumours that the cult of Ghatanothoa was present in it. (: "Out of the Aeons")

In addition to the island itself, the Atlanteans also spawned colonies in Africa, which survived after the sinking of their parent kingdom. The Saharan Tuareg people are their descendants. (: "The Last Test")

Priests and sorcerers of Atlantis, most notably Surama, have found means to preserve their bodies in a death-like state that resembles mummification, but from which they can be revived even after several millennia. (: "The Last Test")

The Shining Trapezohedron was in Atlantis at the time of its sinking. (: "The Haunter of the Dark")

When Thomas Olney visited the strange house atop a cliff near Kingsport, the mysterious man who lived there told him stories about "how the Kings of Atlantis fought with the slippery blasphemies that wriggled out of rifts in the ocean's floor, and how the pillared and weedy temple of Poseidonis is still glimpsed at midnight by lost ships, who know by its sight that they are lost". (: "The Strange High House in the Mist")

Lt. Commander Karl Heinrich of the submarine U-29, which sank to the bottom of an oceanic abyss in 1917, found the ruins of a city that he believed to be Atlantis, the location of which he estimated as N. Latitude 20º, W. Longitude 35º. There, Heinrich saw the temple of a god shining with a mysterious light and felt the mental influence of the entity that had driven his fellow crew members to madness and death. (: "The Temple")

When Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee mind-swapped with a member of the Great Race of Yith, one of the other Yithian victims he met was a priest of Atlantis' middle kingdom. (: The Shadow Out of Time)

Dead Atlantean cities remain in the Hoggar region of the Sahara. The secret of Cthulhu and the Elder Ones was nearly wiped out when Atlantis sank, but was kept half alive in hidden traditions and allegorical myths and furtive, midnight cult-practices. (

"Atonement" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It functions as a follow-up to H. P. Lovecraft's "Herbert West-Reanimator".

### Synopsis
The narrator from "Herbert West-Reanimator" moves to Townsend, Illinois to help his ageing uncle with his medical practice. Only a short while passes, however, before he discovers that Dr. West has survived the attack by his reanimated monstrosities, and is now working at the Townsend morticians, where he continues his unholy experiments. After confronting West and demanding that he leave town, the narrator and his former partner fight. Although West gains the upper hand, one of his vengeful creations emerges from the vault, and drags him off into the woods, presumably to be killed.

### Characters

* The Narrator, the unnamed narrator from the original story, now a small-town physician in Illinois.
* Dr. Herbert West, a deranged scientist who believes that he can create a serum to defeat death.
* Dr. Norris Whitman, the narrator's uncle and town doctor in Townsend, Illinois.

### Publication History
"Atonement" was published in the Ron Shiflet anthology They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in June 2018.

In the 1990 Arkham Unveiled supplement for Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, his first name is given as Donald, whereas in the animated film Howard Lovecraft and the Kingdom of Madness, it is Jaswant.

Aucturn (the Stranger), also called the Newborn, is a Great Old One created by Paizo Inc for the Pathfinder role-playing game in 2007. It is in Paizo Inc's Starfinder roleplaying game that Aucturn was fully developed. In the Second Edition of Starfinder, Aucturn "hatches", fully developing into an Outer God with a profound grudge against Nyarlathotep for his attempted enslavement of it.

### Background
Aucturn is a newly born or created Great Old One. It is a living planet with an inhospitable geography, one that is mutable. Landmasses consist of chalky stone or rubber soil from which stunted, mutated vegetation grows. Unseen leviathans swim through the black sludge of its oceans. The atmosphere consists of poisonous gases, which vary depending on the place, from clinging soupy neurotoxin in one area to a thin hallucinogenic mist at another. From its yellow sky, acidic rain pours on the land. Its geography is in a state of flux, morphing and twisting as the planet heaves and contracts. Rivers are drained and mountain ranges of flesh-like hummocks are created. Usually these changes happen over months or years, but sometimes they occur within moments.

Most of the planet's lifeforms are both vicious and monstrous, which include Shoggoths and Gugs. The most common lifeform are the Orocorans, semi-intelligent predators considered by most to be nuisances, but which pose a threat when gathering into large swarms. On the planet, there is an ongoing feud between the followers of the Outer Gods who dominate the world and the scattered cells of the Dominion of the Black. It is a lawless place, where evil runs rampant. Among the world's residents, no topic of study is forbidden and no act is taboo. Great factories produce illegal drugs outside of the reach of the law, revolutionaries plot against the governments of their homeworlds, slavery is common, and scholars research the forbidden arts so they can warp reality. The unofficial leader of Aucturn is the mysterious Carsai the King, who is suspected of being an avatar of Nyarlathotep.

In the leadup to Starfinder Second Edition, it is revealed that Nyarlathotep was actually attempting to corrupt Aucturn and enslave it to his will, rather than assist in its midwifing as it fully developed in its planet-shaped egg. However, Shelyn, the goddess of love, and her brother, Zon-Kuthon the god of despair, discovered this and set aside their feud to stop him, with Zon-Kuthon sacrificing his life to save his sister. This disrupted Nyarlathotep's ritual to take command of Aucturn's gestation, and its hatching proceeded normally, destroying its planet-form (and leaving behind a massive asteroid belt) but allowing itself to become the Newborn, the Outer God of cosmic horrors, paradigm shifts, and renewal while banishing Carsai from the Pact Worlds. fullContent:
Audrey Driscoll is a Canadian writer who has written several novels centered on the character of Herbert West from H. P. Lovecraft's Herbert West--Re-Animator.

Driscoll's first novel, The Friendship of Mortals, retells the story of West at Miskatonic University, focusing on his relationship with his assistant--called Charles Milburn in Driscoll's version, and depicted as a Miskatonic librarian. Books two and three, Islands in the Gulf: The Journey and Islands in the Gulf: The Treasure, take West to Bellefleur Island, on the West Coast of North America, where he's working as a country physician under the name Francis Dexter. Hunting the Phoenix, which concludes the series, journalist Alma Halsey, an old adversary of West's and a former lover of Milburn, confronts them both in Providence, Rhode Island.

Driscoll wrote two sequels to the series, She Who Comes Forth and She Who Returns, centering on the character France Leighton, a young archaeologist. The former is set in Egypt and the latter at Miskatonic, where Leighton is a student.

Driscoll also published a collection of short stories, Tales From the Annexe, several of which tie in to her Herbert West series.

She has worked as a librarian at the University of Saskatchewan and the Greater Victoria Public Library in British Columbia.

fullContent:
August Derleth (February 24 1909 - July 4 1971) was an American writer and anthologist. Though best remembered as Howard Phillips Lovecraft's literary executor and for his own contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos genre of horror, Derleth was a prolific writer in several genres, including historical fiction and detective fiction.

### Life
The son of William Julius Derleth and his wife Rose Louise Volk, he grew up in Sauk City, Wisconsin. At the age of 16, he sold his first story to Weird Tales magazine. Derleth wrote all throughout his four years at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and received a B.A. in 1930. During this time he served briefly as editor of Mystic Magazine.

In the mid-1930s he organised a Ranger's Club for young people, served as clerk and president of the local Board of Education, served as a parole officer, organised a local Men's Club and a Parent-Teacher Association. He also lectured in American Regional Literature at the University of Wisconsin.

Derleth was awarded a prestigious Guggenheim Fellowship in 1938 for his Sac Prairie Saga, a series of novels focused on Wisconsin history. His sponsors included the novelist Sinclair Lewis and the poet Edgar Lee Masters.

In 1941 he became literary editor of The Capital Times newspaper in Madison, a post he held until his resignation in 1960.

Derleth was married April 6, 1953, to Sandra Evelyn Winters; he was 44 and she was 18 at the time. When the couple divorced six years later in 1959, Derleth retained custody of their two children, April Rose and Walden William. In 1960, Derleth began editing and publishing a magazine called Hawk and Whippoorwill, dedicated to poems of man and nature.

He died on July 4, 1971, and is buried in St. Aloysius Cemetery in Sauk City.

### Contributions

Derleth was a contemporary and friend of H. P. Lovecraft — when Lovecraft wrote about "le Comte d'Erlette" in his fiction, it was in homage to Derleth. Derleth invented the term Cthulhu Mythos to describe the fictional universe described in the series of stories shared by Lovecraft and other writers in his circle. Derleth's own writing emphasized the struggle between good and evil, in line with his own Christian worldview and in contrast with Lovecraft's depiction of an amoral universe. Derleth also treated Lovecraft's Old Ones as representatives of elemental forces, creating new entities to flesh out this framework.

When Lovecraft died in 1937, Derleth and Donald Wandrei put together a collection of that author's stories and tried to get them published. With existing publishers showing little interest, they founded Arkham House in 1939 to do it themselves. The name of the company comes from Lovecraft's fictional town of Arkham, Massachusetts, which featured in many of his stories.

Following Lovecraft's death, Derleth wrote a number of stories based on fragments and notes left by Lovecraft. These were published in Weird Tales and later in book form, under the byline "H. P. Lovecraft and Au

After H. P. Lovecraft's death, August Derleth wrote and published numerous stories under his own and Lovecraft's bylines, described as "posthumous collaborations". They were mostly based on story ideas from Lovecraft's Commonplace Book, and occasionally incorporated fragments written by Lovecraft, but overwhelmingly consisted of Derleth's own prose.

Lovecraft scholar  S. T. Joshi commented:




### The 16 Stories
The 16 stories that S. T. Joshi has separated apart, which have been in the past uncritically attributed to both Derleth and Lovecraft as co-authors, or even to Lovecraft alone, are
*The Lurker at the Threshold (1945)
*"The Survivor" (1954)
*"The Ancestor" (1957)
*"The Gable Window" (1957)
*"The Lamp of Alhazred" (1957)
*"The Peabody Heritage" (1957)
*"The Shadow Out of Space" (1957)
*"Wentworth's Day" (1957)
*"The Fisherman of Falcon Point" (1959)
*"The Shuttered Room" (1959)
*"Witches' Hollow" (1962)
*"The Shadow in the Attic" (1964)
*"The Dark Brotherhood" (1966)
*"The Horror from the Middle Span" (1974)
*"Innsmouth Clay" (1974)
*"The Watchers Out of Time" (1974, unfinished before Derleth's death in 1971)

S. T. Joshi's scholarship confirmed what was known privately for many years, that none of the above works are by H. P. Lovecraft. All of them are properly to be considered entirely the works of August Derleth. 

This has no relevancy to any praise or criticism of these stories based on their merits; this is a matter completely related to authorship.

### Posthumous Collaboration: A Mythos Tradition?
Given the enormous love many authors have for the works of other Mythos writers, and further given that from the very inception of what amounts to an open-ended shared universe Lovecraft freely intermingled his own ideas with those of other authors, the basic idea of the "posthumous collaboration" has antecedents going back to the beginning of the Mythos.

Nor is it restricted to Lovecraft's story notes and fragments. Lin Carter mined Clark Ashton Smith in the same way for example in the "collaborative" short story "The Stairs in the Crypt" and other authors have similarly taken one-line notes or stray mentions from correspondence as their inspiration. While sometimes it is done to add a patina of legitimacy or add the shine of a more popular author to the work of another, oftentimes in the context of the Mythos it really is done to supply the relentless appetite for new stories and fresh takes that the audience desires.

The controversy's central point is that a deceased author cannot genuinely give permission or approval for such a collaboration nor edit or modify the use made of their work. This makes the claim of "collaboration" spurious, insofar as at best what is being done is an authorized continuance. It also muddies the distinction between the works of Lovecraft, the works of Lovecraft's Cir

fullContent:
"Aunt Hester"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley. Written in December 1971, it was first published in the anthology The Satyr’s Head (Corgi Books, 1975). Lumley acknowledges the story's debt to H. P. Lovecraft’s “The Thing on the Doorstep” (1937).

### Synopsis
Hester Lang tells her favorite but long-separated nephew Peter about times when she and her twin brother George--now living in Australia--exchanged bodies. When they were 12, she unconsciously switched with George in order to rescue their younger sister from a swimming mishap. A year or two later, when George was anxious about an exam, they again switched identities without meaning to; Hester as George got high marks on the exam, while George as Hester was thought to be delirious for claiming that she wasn't herself. 

Hester used her mind-swap power intentionally for the first time soon after she and George turn 19, when he had a girlfriend he refused to tell Hester anything about. When the couple was out on a date, Hester projected into George's mind in order to see her--but ended up running away in a panic. Six months later, after George warns a boy away from Hester, she plans to retaliate by taking over his body to sabotage his relationship--but when she made the switch, George jumped through a glass window, putting her in the hospital. He moved to Australia soon afterward. 

After telling Peter this history, she convinced him to help her attempt a switch one last time--supposedly so she could see a niece and nephew she has never met. She makes the transfer when she expects him to be asleep--and ties up her own body, just in case. But when George's mind is in her body, she undergoes a horrific transformation--"purple tongue...protruding from frothing lips"--and her body dies, of an apparent heart attack.

Peter then learns that George had died and was buried three weeks earlier. When Peter finds himself in a "numb, black, silent void," he realizes that Hester is trapped in George's body, and is trying to force her way into Peter's.

### Characters
Hester Lang: The title character of the story is a 54-year-old woman, the "black sheep" of her family, who is "a bit on the psychic side" and belongs to a "séance group." She was "a bookish kid" and "very plain" as a teenager, and "terribly jealous of [her] brother" George, her twin.  

Peter Norton: The son of Hester's younger sister. He is close to his aunt, going to her house after school to drink cocoa and talk about "things of interest to small boys," until his family moves to London when he was 12. He is out of touch with her until he visits her out of the blue when he is 20.

George Lang: Hester's twin brother. He was a "handsome lad...long and lean and a natural for the girls," though "not strong" and "not...too bright."

### Setting

fullContent:
Australia is a nation and a continent in the Southern Hemisphere. It features in the fiction of H. P. Lovecraft (most notably in the story "The Shadow Out of Time") and in the stories of other Cthulhu Mythos writers.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction

### The Shadow Out of Time
The most notable appearance of Australia in Lovecraft's fiction is in the story "The Shadow Out of Time" (1936), in which the formerly mind-swapped Miskatonic professor Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee travels to the island continent looking for the remains of the prehistoric non-human city he dreams that he was held captive in. He is drawn there by a letter from Robert B. F. Mackenzie, a prominent Australian mining engineer based in Pilbarra, Western Australia, which tells him that ruins resembling the city in his dreams exist in the Great Sandy Desert, located at latitude 22° 3′ 14″ South, longitude 125° 0′ 39″ East. (Mackenzie also links the Australian ruins to an Indigenous legend "about Buddai, the gigantic old man who lies asleep for ages underground with his head on his arm, and who will some day awake and eat up the world"--which is a genuine Aboriginal tradition.)
These ruins turn out to be the Cyclopean remains of the archive city of the Yithians--a city that is unnamed in Lovecraft, but is identified by Lin Carter as "Pnakotus"--source of the Pnakotic Manuscripts.

The glimpses the story provides of Australia are not enticing: "I need not tell how the sight of the low, sandy West Australian coast depressed me," the narrator Peaslee writes, "and how I detested the crude mining town and dreary gold fields." 

"The Shadow Out of Time" also mentions, among the minds abducted to the Yithian city, "the Australian physicist Nevil Kingston-Brown, who will die in A.D. 2518."

### The Call of Cthulhu
Australia appears more incidentally in "The Call of Cthulhu" (1928). The chance discovery of a report in the Sydney Bulletin informs Francis Thurston about the arrival of the Vigilant in Sydney's Darling Harbour, towing the derelict steamship Alert and carrying Gustaf Johansen and his tale of an encounters with cultists and a mysterious island. The stone idol he carries baffles experts at "Sydney University, the Royal Society, and the Museum in College Street." When Thurston travels to Sydney to seek more information, he sees the Alert in commercial use at Circular Quay in Sydney Cove, and observes the Cthulhu figurine at the Australian Museum on Hyde Park.

### Other Mentions
In "The Little Glass Bottle" (1897), the crew of a fishing vessel are tricked into travelling to Australia in search of treasure as part of a practical joke. Harry Houdini is on his way to Australia for "a tour of Australian theatres" when he stops off in Egypt in "Under the Pyramids" (1924).  "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" (1934) mentions Pickman Carter, a relation of Randolph Carter "who in the year 2169 would use strange means in repelling the Mongol hordes from Australia." Autophagia: Fear & Infection in from the High Seas is a third-party adventure supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview




Containing a complete adventure revolving around the quarantined ocean liner Essexia, Autophagia: Fear & Infection in from the High Seas contains a set of handouts as well as layout blueprints for the ship and a complete cast of non-player characters, although pre-generated investigators are not included. It was written by Tyler Omichinski, edited by Chitin Proctor, and features artwork by Stephanie McAlea. It was published by third-party content creator Stygian Fox, and runs to a total of 36 pages.

### Synopsis
The investigators must find out the cause of an inexplicable contagion which has taken root aboard a luxury passenger liner currently held under quarantine in New York. What they uncover is a well-meaning but misguided scientist who has attempted to incorporate Shoggoth DNA into human hosts in an effort to breed a species which will help the human race fight back against any malevolent forces which may try to destroy it.

Avaloth is a fictional monster created by Richard F. Searight for his short story "The Sealed Casket". It is also mentioned alongside Cthulhu and Tsathoggua in "The Warder of Knowledge".

### Description
Avaloth is an invisible creature with slender tentacles, strong enough to break every bone of a man's body, and drain its victims of blood. It also has the ability to absorb heat and drastically lower the temperature of its environment. Conversely, a great source of heat, such as fire, might destroy it.

In the "Elder Time", Avaloth used its abilities to generate ice and snow and threatened to cover the entire Earth in an ice sheet, but was imprisoned inside a sealed casket by the great wizard Om Oris before it could do so. After its imprisonment, the ice-covered regions returned to their previous verdant state. Many ages later, Avaloth was released by Wesson Clark and killed him, but was itself destroyed when Clark's house was engulfed in flames. (: "The Sealed Casket")

### Behind the Mythos
Avaloth is similar to the Star Vampire from Robert Bloch's "The Shambler from the Stars". Both are invisible monsters who kill victims in the exact same manner: crushing the body to death with their tentacles while draining all the victim's blood. Coincidentally, both stories were first published in 1935 in the magazine Weird Tales, and both end in a house fire.

On a different note, Avaloth is also similar to Aphoom-Zhah, from Lin Carter's "The Acolyte of the Flame", as both entities have been responsible for creating a giant ice sheet that spread southwards, covering vast areas of formerly green land with ice.

In "Wrath of the Wind-Walker", by James Ambuehl and Robert M. Price, it is suggested that Avaloth is just another name for Ithaqua, and possibly Aphoom-Zhah as well.

An avatar (: "The Haunter of the Dark") (/ˈævəˌtɑr, ˌævəˈtɑr/; Hindustani: [əʋˈt̪aːr] from Sanskrit अवतार avatāra "descent") is a concept originating in Hinduism. It is a deliberate descent of a deity to Earth, or a descent of the Supreme Being (e.g., Vishnu for Vaishnavites), and is mostly translated into English as "incarnation", but more accurately as "appearance" or "manifestation".

Within the Cthulhu Mythos, an avatar generally holds the same meaning. An Elder God, Great Old One, or an Outer God may decide to appear in a physical or spectral manifestation to humans or their inhuman brethren. The reasons for why an otherworldly entity may need to manifest an avatar are varied. Most deities and entities of power in the Cthulhu Mythos do not or cannot exist in mundane, three-dimensional space. Alternatively, they may be otherwise separated by vast distances of space, sequestration in a secret location, or by virtue of living in another universe or dimension. Manifesting an avatar is often the only way such a being can communicate and interact with its worshippers or have physical agency in a particular location.

An avatar is exponentially weaker but requires a considerable effort of will on the part of its deity to manifest. Avatars may be capable of being harmed, killed or confounded by mortals, though to a cosmic entity, such interference is likely less than the buzz of a fly.

The Avengers are a fictional team in the mainstream prime reality of the Marvel Universe by Marvel Comics.

### Background
The Avengers are a team of superheroes whose membership has included humans, mutates, robots, aliens, and mutants. It's a team which has been around for decades, protecting the United States from both foreign and domestic threats, and the world from global, extra-dimensional, and alien threats. It has operated on Earth, the Moon, elsewhere in the Milky Way galaxy, neighboring galaxies (Shi'ar, Andromeda, etc), and other dimensions. Some of them have traveled in time or visited other realities. The team has battled aliens, demons, and gods. Some of them have been participants in universal scale events.

The Avengers are a team that has had a long history of conflict with Chthon, an Old One. This is due to the history that the Scarlet Witch has with the demonic entity and the ongoing struggle between mutant and Old One always ends up involving the Avengers. 

Most recently, Chthon conquered the Earth, temporarily remaking it in his image, before what he did was reversed. 

Some time ago, they clashed with the supervillain Grim Reaper who was empowered by Lloigoroth, another Old One.

Averoigne is a fictional province in France, created by Clark Ashton Smith as a setting for a series of horror fantasy stories set in a pre-modern era. The fictional land appears to based on the historical province of Auvergne. The frequent references to Lovecraftian deities, often in transparently altered terms (Sodaqui for Tsathoggua, Iog-Sotôt for Yog-Sothoth, the Ram With a Thousand Ewes for Shub-Niggurath), establish Averoigne as a part of the Cthulhu Mythos.

In addition to Mythos entities and their worshippers, Smith populates Averoigne with malign and dangerous creatures like vampires ("Rendezvous in Averoigne"), lamias ("The End of the Story", possibly "The Enchantress of Sylaire"), and satyrs ("The Satyr").

### Stories
Smith used Averoigne as the setting for the following stories:

*"The End of the Story" (Weird Tales, May 1930)
*"A Rendezvous in Averoigne" (Weird Tales,  April/May 1931)
*"The Satyr" (La Paree Stories, July 1931)
*"The Maker of Gargoyles"  (Weird Tales,  August 1932)
*"The Mandrakes" (Weird Tales,  February 1933)
*"The Beast of Averoigne"  (Weird Tales, May 1933)
*"The Holiness of Azédarac" (Weird Tales, November 1933)
*"The Colossus of Ylourgne" (Weird Tales,  June 1934)
*"The Disinterment of Venus" (Weird Tales, July 1934)
*"Mother of Toads" (Weird Tales,  July 1938)
*"The Enchantress of Sylaire" (Weird Tales, July 1941)
*"Averoigne" (poetry) (Challenge, Spring 1951)

These stories are collected in The Averoigne Archives: The Complete Averoigne Tales of Clark Ashton Smith, an ebook published by Pickman's Press in 2019.

### Geography
Smith places Averoigne near the center of France, in the highland region known as the Central Massif. The northern half of the territory is dominated by the walled city of Vyônes, site of an impressive cathedral. In the southern half is located the town of Ximes. The main road of Averoigne runs between Ximes and Vyônes, straight through the thick, dark forest that blankets the province. A river called Isoile flows from the mountains in the northern part of the province to feed into a swamp in the south.

Other Averoigne towns and villages mentioned by Smith include Moulins, Les Hiboux, La Frenâie, Sainte Zenobie, and Périgon. In the forest can be found haunted ruins, such as the Chateau des Faussesflammes and the stronghold of Ylourgne.

In The History of Averoigne, Glenn Rahman suggests that Vyônes might be identified with Clermont-Ferrand in the real world's Auvergne, Ximes with that province's St. Flour, and Périgon with La Chaise Dieu, which also had a prestigious abbey. Aylesbury is a fictional town created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft, first appearing in the 1928 short story "The Dunwich Horror." It is also mentioned in the sonnet sequence Fungi from Yuggoth.

### In Lovecraft's Writing
Considered part of New England's "Lovecraft Country", Aylesbury from its mentions in "The Dunwich Horror" appears to be located in the Miskatonic River valley somewhere between Arkham and Dunwich: One must traverse the "wrong fork" of the Aylesbury Pike junction to reach the latter from the former. Another small and obscure town, Dean's Corners, is located nearby.

Old Whateley of Dunwich declares that his daughter Lavinia's mate is "as good a husban’ as ye kin find this side of Aylesbury." When there are tremors in Dunwich in 1915, "even the Aylesbury people felt" them.

According to "The Dunwich Horror," Aylesbury has a court-house, an office of the Massachusetts state police, and  a newspaper, the Aylesbury Transcript. When the Whateley family needs medical help, they call on Dr. Houghton of Aylesbury.

Fungi from Yuggoth suggests that Aylesbury is near Zaman's Hill, as sightseers from the town come out to gape when the village at the hill's foot disappears. The poem cycle also refers to the "Aylesbury town farm," which a character named John Whateley is supposed to be taken; town farms were New England institutions that "served as nursing homes, mental wards, and homeless shelters."

### The Derleth Mythos
August Derleth makes frequent references to Aylesbury in his "posthumous collaborations" with Lovecraft: 
* Wilbur Akeley in "The Gable Window" lives "in a pocket of the hills off the Aylesbury Pike." 
* "The Survivor"'s Jean-Francois Charriere has a file of clippings from the Aylesbury Transcript in his library.
* Abner Whateley has to go to Aylesbury to hire workers willing to tear down his mill in "The Shuttered Room."
* Uriah Garrison of "The Shadow in the Attic" lives in a "gambrel-roofed house on his gambrel-roofed house on Aylesbury Street, in that part of Arkham south of the Miskatonic River." 
* In "The Watchers Out of Time," when "the country around Dunwich" is discussed, it's noted that "in Aylesbury they call it ‘Whateley country.’"

### In Popular Culture
*The 2015 horror film We Are Still Here is set in a fictional Massachusetts town called Aylesbury. The film stars Barbara Crampton, who has starred in several films based on and inspired by Lovecraft’s work.
