Azathoth, sometimes called "The Blind Idiot God", the "Nuclear Chaos", and the "Daemon Sultan", is a fictional deity in the Cthulhu Mythos--portrayed as an Outer God and a supreme omnipotent being.

### Description
There can be no definite description of Azathoth, because everybody envisions him differently and he is always changing.

For example Ronald Shea enters a temple after visiting the forest near Goatswood and discovers a twenty-foot idol that "represented the god Azathoth--Azathoth as he had been before his exile. Outside, It consisted of a bivalvular shell supported on many pairs of flexible legs. From the half-open shell rose several jointed cylinders, tipped with polypous appendages; and in the darkness inside the shell I thought I saw a horrible bestial, mouthless face, with deep-sunk eyes and covered with glistening black hair." (: "The Insects from Shaggai")

Later Shea sees "something ooze into the corridor--a pale grey shape, expanding and crinkling, which glistened and shook gelatinously as still-moving particles dropped free; but it was only a glimpse". (: "The Insects from Shaggai")

Most mortals can't withstand the sight of Azathoth. It's been claimed that "even the slightest glimpse" of it would result in the "utter and complete destruction to the beholder". (: "Hydra")

According to some accounts, it is a huge sentient black hole. (: Russell's Guide to Interdimensional Entities)

The Necronomicon states that "The fire of Azathoth is all brightness and heat as it devours." (: Antonius Quine Necronomicon)

Azathoth reproduces asexually by fission, giving birth to other gods such as Cxaxukluth. While Azathoth itself might be genderless, its offspring are more accurately described as androgynous. (: "The Family Tree of the Gods")

### In the Necronomicon
Azathoth is a significant malign presence in the Necronomicon, as both Albert Wilmarth (: The Whisperer in Darkness) and Walter Gilman (: "The Dreams in the Witch-House") are horrified at the mere mention of its name, having both read about it in the occult tome.

"Azathoth" is the name assumed by a giant slug-like alien creature who posed herself as a goddess and was imprisoned on the icy planet Ry'leh, guarded by a legion of Shlangii mercenaries. The Doctor initially suspected her to be an avatar of one of the Great Old Ones, but once he came face to face with her, came to the conclusion that she was merely using the name of a far more powerful entity to back up her claim of goddesshood.

This creature originates from the crossover novel All-Consuming Fire, by Andy Lane. In the audio play adaptation by Big Finish, her name is changed to Azazoth and she's played by Samantha Béart.

### Description
Physically, "Azathoth" resembles a massive swollen slug or worm, with purple skin marked with irregular black spots. She has no visible eyes or limbs, only a large toothless mouth which produces a viscous cobweb-like substance.

Although the Doctor is certain that she isn't really one of the Great Old Ones, "Azathoth" does have undeniably powerful psychic abilities, which allow her to easily enter the minds of any species, ranging from humans to Shlangii to sapient robots, speaking to them as a benevolent deity and promising love and happiness. It takes a lot of will to resist her telepathic influence. Those who are converted become her loyal worshipers and are eventually transformed into crustacean-like beings called the rakshassi.

The Doctor has speculated that "Azathoth" might be the larval form of her species, and that the adult form might resemble the rakshassi. (: All-Consuming Fire)

### Trivia
*The name "Azazoth" has also been used in the Cthulhu Mythos novel Strange Eons, by Robert Bloch.

shortDefinition: "Azathoth" is the beginning of a never-completed novel written by H. P. Lovecraft in June 1922. It was published as a fragment in the journal Leaves in 1938, after Lovecraft's death. It is the first piece of fiction to mention the fictional being Aza...
fullContent:
"Azathoth" is the beginning of a never-completed novel written by H. P. Lovecraft in June 1922. It was published as a fragment in the journal Leaves in 1938, after Lovecraft's death. It is the first piece of fiction to mention the fictional being Azathoth, one of the major entities in Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos, though the entity only appears in the title.

### Inspiration
Lovecraft described his planned novel as a "weird Eastern tale in the 18th century manner" and as a "weird Vathek-like novel", referring to a novel of Arabia written by William Thomas Beckford in 1786. Suggesting that his story would involve "material of the Arabian Nights type", he wrote that



Though Lovecraft likely never got past the 480-word fragment that survives, he later wrote a novel with a similar theme: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Plot summary
The story begins by describing how the modern world has been stripped of imagination and belief in magic. The protagonist is an unnamed man who lives in a dull and ugly city. Every night for many years the man gazes from his window upon the stars, until he comes over time to observe secret vistas unsuspected by normal humanity. One night the gulf between his world and the stars is bridged, and his mind ascends from his body out unto the boundless cosmos.

### Behind the Mythos
"Azathoth" as it survives has something in common with Lovecraft's story "Polaris" and his poem "Astrophobos" -- and indeed with the A Princess of Mars, the original John Carter novel by Edgar Rice Burroughs, in which the hero stares at the planet Mars, in the form of a red star, and is then transported there astrally.

"Azathoth Awakening" is a short Mythos story by American author Ran Cartwright writing as R. S. Cartwright.

### Synopsis
A woman's dream awakens the sleeping Azathoth, summoning it into our universe. As it comes to claim its prize, all of existence devolves into madness and chaos from its mere presence. Finally arriving at Sol, it takes the woman and consumes her before destroying all of creation. It then retreats back into slumber, while dreaming a dream of a new universe.

### Characters
*Joyce, an woman who, in her madness, is destined to become sustenance for Azathoth.
*Azathoth, the Daemon-Sultan, an Outer God.

### Publication History
"Azathoth Awakening" was first published in Cthulhu Cultus #17 in 2000. It was later reprinted in a handful of periodicals before being included in A. J. French's anthology The Shadow of the Unknown in August 2011. Ran Cartwright then included it in his own collection, Of Gods & Aliens, in October 2011.

"Azathoth in Analysis" is a horror comedy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It is the fourth installment of Peter Cannon's six-part novella Forever Azathoth, which serves as a humourous sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep".

"Azathoth in Analysis" was originally published in the August 1998 issue of the magazine Tales of Lovecraftian Horror. The entire series would later appear in Cannon's collections Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (1999) and Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches (2011).

### Synopsis
(Continued from "The House of Azathoth"...)

Part four of the series is narrated by Arkham Sanitarium psychoanalyst Dr. Zimmerman, who treated Azathoth House editor Vartan Bagdasarian (referred to in this story as "patient Aa" due to doctor-patient confidentiality) after the latter came to him claiming that he couldn't remember anything from the past ten years. After learning of Bagdasarian's lifelong devotion to the works of the late Edward Derby, the doctor comes to the conclusion that his patient has found an abstract father figure in the poet, and an even more abstract one in Azathoth, an ancient deity that figures prominently in Derby's works. Bagdasarian also confides that he has dreamed about a tunnel that leads to a pit of shoggoths: protoplasmic amoeboid creatures that are usually almost brainless, but capable of developing high levels of intelligence, as Bagdasarian claims to have learned by communicating telepathically with one of them.

After Bagdasarian disappears, leaving a note about seeking "the House of Azathoth", Dr. Zimmerman joins forces with Azathoth House lawyer Judge Hand and the teenager Eph Upton, who is very attached to the editor, to try to figure out his whereabouts. The three of them travel to the woods of Chesuncook, Maine, where the incident that triggered Bagdasarian's amnesia took place. They camp in the woods close to the house of Jacob Derby, the inventor. When Zimmerman wakes up in the morning, however, he sees no sign of Hand or Eph. When he does find them, Hand is injured, dazed, and incapable of speech, with the only explanation offered by Eph being that he tripped and hit his head. They seek help from Jacob, who contacts the local asylum. There, Hand is diagnosed with brain damage and starts repeating the words "Azathoth... the pit of the shoggoths...".

Almost six months pass by before Zimmerman receives a letter from Bagdasarian apologising for having disappeared and explaining that he found work editing the manuscripts of another late author, Robert Blake, and won't be returning. Zimmerman, in the meantime, has started to court Wendy and assumed Judge Hand's duties as a member of the board of directors of Azathoth House, whereas Eph opts to abandon high school to become the House's new editor.

(...The story continues in "Bride of Azathoth".)

fullContent:
"Azathoth in Arkham" is a horror comedy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It is the first installment of Peter Cannon's six-part novella Forever Azathoth, which serves as a humourous sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep".

"Azathoth in Arkham" was originally published in the 1995 anthology The Azathoth Cycle along with the next installment, "The Revenge of Azathoth". The entire series would later appear in Cannon's collections Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (1999) and Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches (2011).

### Synopsis
At the beginning, the story is narrated by Daniel Upton's son Edward Derby Upton, named after the poet Edward Derby, who was Daniel's best friend before tragedy struck. Daniel confessed to the murder of his friend, while on the doorstep outside the house, his butler Soames found the decomposed corpse of Derby's estranged wife, Asenath, holding a note begging Daniel to commit the crime. Released on bail, Daniel attended the double funeral of Derby and Asenath, but collapsed in the middle of the service and was committed to an asylum, seemingly no longer able to recognise his wife or son. For the next years, he received no visitors, except for the faithful Soames.

Meanwhile, Edward Derby Upton grows up wealthy, as the Uptons inherited Derby's money after a brief legal battle against Asenath's relatives from Innsmouth. Eventually, Edward becomes interested in Derby's work, including his most celebrated book, Azathoth and Other Horrors. When he visits Miskatonic University to try to learn more about Derby, librarian Henry Armitage informs him of a student group called the Dead Edward Derby Society. Edward not only joins the group, but becomes a sort of unofficial leader, owning in part to his seniority compared to the others, as well as being the son of Derby's best friend (even if said friend was also his murderer). At the anniversary of Derby's death, the group visits the poet's grave at night to pay respect, but the ceremony is interrupted by a girl from Innsmouth who insists that Asenath was a greater artist than her husband, for she could master the art of mind transference, even from beyond the grave.

The next morning, Edward receives a message from the asylum informing him that his father's behaviour has changed, as he now claims to be his butler Soames. The narrative voice switches mid-sentence, signalling that Edward's own body is taken over by the mind of Asenath's father, Ephraim Waite, a magician skilled at mind transference who stole the body of his daughter, then Derby's, then Daniel Upton's, and then Soames', before finally moving to Edward's body, thus leaving the real Edward stuck in Soames' body, and the real Soames stuck in Daniel's (the real Daniel having presumably perished when his mind was transferred to Derby's already interred body).

shortDefinition: Azathoth's Answer is an extremely rules-light table top roleplaying game, either solo or for a group. It is written by Tobias Deißler with art licensed from clipart artist CRODEART. It is published by Pyromancer Press. It is a "pay what you want" tit...
fullContent:
Azathoth's Answer is an extremely rules-light table top roleplaying game, either solo or for a group. It is written by Tobias Deißler with art licensed from clipart artist CRODEART. It is published by Pyromancer Press. It is a "pay what you want" title with a suggested price of one dollar. Its stated ethos is to provide almost the opposite rules experience from the "heavy" Cthulhu Mythos game, by implication the designer is referring to Chaosium and their seminal Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

Originally written and published in German as Azathoths Antwort, in keeping with the rest of Pyromancer's output it was then translated into English and offered as an English-language version with little modification from the original German version. It is part of the "minimalist" approach to roleplaying game writing where there are virtually no games mechanics other than very simple dice rolls to determine success or failure. This approach puts the entire burden on the imagination and storytelling of the players and referee which can in some cases be exactly what is desired but does not lend itself to what one might call the "Monster Manual" or Dungeons & Dragons rules-heavy approach.

Despite the game's name there is no relevant specific focus on Azathoth.

### Design & Gameplay

### Statistics
Azathoth's Answer features four statistics for all characters, Mind. Body, Soul and Speed. Each player assigns points to each of these four statistics from a points pool, with a typical human character having 5 points to assign at the start of play and with a normal mortal required (presumably) to have at least one point in each although it is allowable not to. All points must be used however. A maximum of 20 points is allowed to be assigned between them within the indicated limits to create the most powerful types of playable characters. 

### Skills
These characteristics are then used in conjunction with Skills. Each character has six Skills defined by the players and associated with a characteristic of their choice, with a maximum of three skills for a characteristic, and two secondary characteristics, Wounds and Madness. Wounds is the overall status of the character's physical state; Madness is the overall status of the character's mental state. The normal maximum for Wounds is equal to the character's Body score; the normal maximum for Madness is equal to the character's Soul (not Mind) score. The Madness score being higher the better the Soul score seems counter-intuitive to some since "Madness" to some players is understood to be better when lower in the sense of "less Mad" however this is not the rationale used in the game.

### Taking Actions
Actions are performed by rolling a 10-sided die, which must yield a result lower than the characteristic in play. In other words a basic saving throw or "roll less than" system.

Aži Dahāka is a demonic entity in ancient Persian folklore. It was later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the Call of Cthulhu supplement Cthulhu Invictus.

### Background
Azi Dahaka is a Great Old One which has three heads, each with six reptilian eyes and three fanged mouths. For a millennium it ruled over Babylon's seven kingdoms, until it was defeated by the hero Feredum. Now Azi Dahak lies bound within a cave in Mount Damavand. Waiting for the day when the celestial bodies are aligned so it can rise and take back what belongs to it, the lands of ancient Persia and Mesopotamia.

### Behind the Mythos
Azi Dahaka is based directly on Zahhak or Zohhak, an evil being in Zoroastrian religious beliefs. Azi Dahaka is the idiomatic name given to this being by non-Zoroastrian Persians in Persian folklore.

The meaning of dahaka is uncertain. Among the meanings suggested are "stinging" (source uncertain), "burning" (cf. Sanskrit dahana), "man" or "manlike", "huge" or "foreign". Aži Dahaka is the source of the modern Persian word azhdaha or ezhdeha, meaning "dragon", often used on a banner of war.

Azhi Dahaka was created by Angra Mainu (the cosmic god of ultimate evil in Zoroastrianism) through a mating with Autak, to oppose goodness and truth. Literally made of the unclean khrafstra, animals such as snakes, toads, scorpions, frogs and lizards, this dragon embodied corruption and entropy.

Aži Dahaka is the most significant and long-lasting of the ažis of the Avesta, the earliest religious texts of Zoroastrianism. He is described as a monster with three mouths, six eyes, and three heads (presumably meaning three heads with one mouth and two eyes each), one thousand senses (almost omniscience and unable to be surprised), cunning, strong and demonic. But in other respects, Aži Dahaka has human qualities, and is never a mere animal.

Zahhak was also the name of a stern, unforgiving and to some regional dwellers, evil, king in Persia. Thus there is also the possibility Azi ("snake" or "dragon") Zahhak was an insult curse addressed to this king: "Zahhak you snake!" or "Zahhak you destroying dragon-like monster!"

Azoth, Azotharoth, or Azotheroth, is a fictional Outer God (mistaken often enough to be considered as Great Old Ones) who was created by writers Gerry Conway and Roy Thomas for Marvel Comics.

The character first appeared in Conan the Barbarian: The Horn of Azoth (issue #59 of the first volume of Marvel Graphic Novel) in April 1990, which was inspired by the original script of the 1984 movie, Conan the Destroyer. The movie's main antagonist, Dagoth, was renamed Azoth in the graphic novel, among other things, to distance it from the movie.

### Background
Azoth is a God of Pain and Hate, the Dreaming God. Before the emergence of man, it warred with other gods, and was defeated when his horn was torn from his forehead. He slipped into a deep sleep and could only be awakened upon the alignment of the stars in a specific pattern.

For a millennia the monks used the poor and the dead to sustain the Dreaming God with a river of blood, unknown to the inhabitants of Shadizar, the capital of Zamora. When awakened, its horn absorbed the blood and flesh of those impaled, leaving only bones. The priests of Azoth retrieved his horn and put it on his forehead at the moment the stars were perfectly aligned. He awakened and began to slaughter all those near him, including the priests. Conan was able to tear his horn off, destroying its body in the material plane.

### Notes
*It has been hypothesized that Azotharoth might be Azathoth.

B'Moth is a fictional sea god created by Bertram Russell in the story "The Scourge of B'Moth". Henry Hasse listed the creature (as "Beh-moth") among Mythos entities in a quote from "The Guardian of the Book". The name evokes Behemoth, a giant  monster mentioned in the Bible. 

Chaosium later presented B'Moth as an avatar of Cthulhu.

### The Cult of B'Moth
Whilst B'Moth is worshipped the world over, its cultists appear to be most numerous in South America and Africa. These mortals believe that the earth should be returned to a wilder, more primitive state, and have faith that their god will one day return rise to bring about the fall of humanity and the planet's regression. Their worship includes wild rites which include sex and violence elements, and they are known to offer blood sacrifice by feeding their victims to sharks and crocodiles, likely in response to B'Moth's affinity for water (: Ye Booke of Monstres II).

### Description
The Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement Ye Booke of Monstres II describes B'Moth as a glowing, fog-like entity. It has no direct control over the physical realm, and must rely on its - admittedly extensive - mental abilities to exert its influence. However, this lack of a tangible physical presence works both ways, and it is almost immune to harm in this world.

B'Moth primarily uses its psychic abilities to control the minds of others to achieve its goals, although it is also known to wantonly spread madness through dreams and waking nightmares wherever it goes. Its power also seems to increase in proximity to large bodies of water.

"Baby Rhyme Time: Youngsters Enjoy Initiation at Innsmouth Public Library" is a tongue-in-cheek Cthulhu Mythos story by U.K.-based author Deborah Walker.

### Synopsis
Written in the style of a local newspaper article, the story describes some of the activities undertaken by Innsmouth children on a visit to the Innsmouth Public Library, including singing English translations of R'lyehian and reading Mythos-related picture books.

### Publication History
First showcased on the Innsmouth Free Press website in 2009, it was given an ebook release in the Kat Rocha-edited anthology Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be in October 2015.

fullContent:
"Back to the Black Bog" is a short story which blends Lovecraftian horror with A. A. Milne's beloved children's character Winnie-the-Pooh. Written by American author Lee Clark Zumpe, it was published in the April Moon Books anthology The Call of Poohthulhu in May 2022.

### Synopsis
When a strange meteor crashes to earth in Hundred Acre Woods, nihilistic donkey Eeyore attempts to hide it from the other inhabitants, fearing that it contains something evil. Unfortunately though, his efforts are in vain, and Christopher Robin and Owl discover the artefact, dragging it back to their laboratory. Before long, the meteor has corrupted all of the plants and animals for miles, turning the once-harmless creatures of the forest into ravening monsters.

Although Eeyore eventually manages to return the rock to its landing site, somehow undoing the evil it wrought, the outside world has been changed, darkened. The poor donkey slowly comes to realise that although the worst might have been averted for Hundred Acre Woods, things may not be exactly as they seem…

### Behind the Mythos
The transformative properties of the meteorite can be compared to those effected by the titular creature in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Colour Out of Space", although the entity in "Back to the Black Bog" is depicted as being actively malevolent in nature, a characteristic not implied in Lovecraft's story.

### Trivia
*A brief reference to an encounter Eeyore had with "a curiously well-dressed toad", a mole, and a badger, would appear to be a reference to another British children's book of the early 1900s, Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows.

fullContent:
Bad Medicine is an audio production by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, released as part of their Dark Adventure Radio Theatre series.

### Overview


Somewhat unusually for a DART production, Bad Medicine is not a single story but a short anthology of three stories. Two are by Lovecraft: "Cool Air" and "The Picture in the House", and one by Poe , "The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar". Available in both Compact Disc and digital download formats, it runs to just over 77 minutes. As with other releases, it is presented in the form of a 1930s-style radio broadcast, and comes with a series of period-authentic props to enhance the immersive experience. These include:

*An article from the New York Amsterdam News regarding the happenings in Harlem.
*A medical leaflet extolling the virtues of hypnotism.
*An Edison electrical bill covered in notations.
*A page from the Latin text Regnum Congo regarding the Anziques.

Baharna is a mighty port city on the island of Oriab. 

### Description
Coming in from the Southern Sea the porphyry wharves are flanked by the gleaming beacons of Thon and Thal and a million mellow lights shine from the windows of its great stone terraces behind them. Further in the streets steps weave under and around the buildings with some structures linked by bridge. The original part of the town is home to an ancient tavern and stepped alleys built from brick and resembles the nameless ruins on the far bank of Yath.

Beneath the city, a tunnel with granite gates funnels the canal inland towards the lake of Yath.

### Geography
*The rear half of the city reaches as far as the sloped banks of Yath.
*Eleven days by ship from Dylath-Leen.
*Two days' zebra-ride from Mount Ngranek.

shortDefinition: "Bainbridge" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-hunter. It was written in December 2005/January 2006, and was published for the first time in Kiernan's collectio...
fullContent:
"Bainbridge" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-hunter. It was written in December 2005/January 2006, and was published for the first time in Kiernan's collection Alabaster (Subterranean Press, 2006). 

"Bainbridge" takes place shortly before the events of "Alabaster," in an abandoned church on the banks of the Flint River near Bainbridge, Georgia. There Dancy is accosted by a host of shadow creatures, and then confronts and defeats a creature called Elandrion, known as the demon of Hopekill Swamp. This narrative is interspersed with descriptions of Julia Flammarion, Dancy's mother, running away to Pensacola Beach, Florida, as a 15-year-old. She tries to commit suicide to escape the demands of the angel that hounded her the way it would later haunt Dancy; there's a suggestion that the angel relents in its attempts to make Julia its instrument in exchange for the rights to her unborn child, who was presumably conceived with one of the men Julia sleeps with during her escape to Pensacola.

The story belongs in continuity after "Highway 97," a story that was the original opening scene of "Bainbridge," which Kiernan says they "cut for some reason entirely lost to me now."

Barnabas Marsh is a fictional character, who appears as the head of the semi-human Marsh family in H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth. In Lovecraft's story, he is the most powerful figure in the sinister town of Innsmouth.

Also known as Old Man Marsh, Barnabas owns the gold refinery that is Innsmouth's main industry; he's said to be "richer'n Croesus". He is the grandson of Captain Obed Marsh, the New England sea captain who made an alliance with the undersea Deep One civilization that involved breeding with nonhuman mates. Due to his Deep One ancestry, Barnabas is functionally immortal, though he may still be killed through violent means. This heritage also means he will gradually mutate into an undersea creature. 

Barnabas' father was Onesiphorus Marsh, Obed's eldest son, the child of his human first wife; Barnabas' Deep One heritage comes from his mother, who "was another o’ them as wa’n’t never seed aoutdoors," in the words of Zadok Allen, the alcoholic human resident of Innsmouth who provides most of the information about Barnabas in the story. (Barnabas Marsh never appears directly in the story's action.) Barnabas is married to a human woman from the nearby town of Ipswich, a choice he made against the wishes of the town's hybridized power structure; "they nigh lynched Barnabas when he courted her fifty odd year’ ago," Allen says.

At the time of the story, Barnabas' transformation had progressed to the point where he had not been seen in public for ten years; he is said to have "developed some skin disease or deformity late in life that makes him keep out of sight." He sometimes comes to the refinery in a "closed, curtained car", but mostly leaves the management of the works to a younger generation. Later we learn that he is no longer able to shut his engorged eyes. He is still able to wear clothing; it's noted that "he still wore the frock-coated finery of the Edwardian age, curiously adapted to certain deformities."

Barnabas was presumably either killed or imprisoned during the federal government's attack on the town in February 1928, or else escaped to Innsmouth's underwater sister city of Y'ha-nthlei.

Barnabas is the great-uncle of Robert Olmstead, the protagonist of The Shadow Over Innsmouth; Olmstead is unaware of the relationship at the time of his fateful visit to Innsmouth, and its unclear whether the Marsh family knows of the connection.

### In Other Media 
*Barnabas Marsh appears as an antagonistic monster in Fantasy Flight Games' Lovecraft-inspired board game Arkham Horror.
*Barnabas Marsh appears as one of the antagonists of the comic Rick and Morty vs. Cthulhu. He was a cultist in Innsmouth whose goal was to summon Dagon The Deep.

fullContent:
"Barren" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Armand Rosamilia. It forms the second part of his Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Synopsis
A man named Bones, who is on the run from his former partners in crime, comes through Keyport on his way to parts unknown. Meeting up with Harrison Marsh and Father Rocco, the three decide to do something about the evil which lurks in the small town, and perhaps get Harrison's wife back in the process.

Unfortunately for them, an attack by the Esoteric Order of Dagon leaves only Harrison, the other two being drawn into a magical prison.

### Characters
*Bones/Bobby Anderson, a former motorcycle thug.
*Father Rocco Ignacio, a devout priest.
*Harrison Marsh, a man cursed with a dark genetic legacy.

### Publication History
"Barren" was first published as a chapbook in July 2012, and was also included in the collection Keyport Cthulhu in November 2013. Both were released in digital format by Rimfyre Books.

Barren is a Cthulhu Mythos chapbook by American author Armand Rosamilia.

### Overview
Containing only the Keyport Cthulhu series story "Barren", the book runs to a total of 29 pages including author notes. It was released solely as a digital download on Amazon's Kindle platform by Rymfire Press in July 2012.

Although Barren is no longer available as an individual book, the story is contained in the collection Keyport Cthulhu, again only through Amazon Kindle.

Barry Eric Odell Pain (28 September 1864 – 5 May 1928) was a British author and journalist active in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, perhaps most famous for his work on the now-defunct satirical magazine Punch. His 1911 novel An Exchange of Souls, published by Eveleigh Nash, has been suggested as an inspiration for H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Thing on the Doorstep". The book was reprinted in May 2007 by indie publisher Hippocampus Press as part of Lovecraft's Library, a series focusing stories which Lovecraft was known to have read and admired .

The Basalt Pillars of the West are a pair of pillars of gargantuan size made of basalt (a dark volcanic rock) that rise from the ocean in the Dreamlands on the western edge of the world. The pillars form the gate of a monstrous cataract whose swift, resistless waters spill over the edge into the "abysmal nothingness" of planetary space. The pillars are shrouded in mist so that none may see beyond them until one sails through the pillars and the mists are lifted, at which point the current becomes too strong to escape. (: "The White Ship"), (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

Basil Elton sailed through the Basalt Pillars aboard the White Ship on his search for the fabled land of Cathuria but never found it. (: "The White Ship")

Randolph Carter was taken to the Moon as a prisoner aboard a ship that sailed through the pillars and over the edge. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

Basatan is a sea god of Zothique. His appearance is unknown, but most likely he has tentacles and fins.

There's a magic ring associated with him that gives its owner the powers to control sea winds and creatures. 

It's possible that the people of Zothique know Cthulhu or Dagon by the name of Basatan. 

### Behind the Mythos
Basatan was created by Clark Ashton Smith for the non-Mythos Zothique tale "The Master of Crabs". 

There is a common misunderstanding that Basatan is "The Master of Crabs" and so must look like a gigantic crab. However, in the story, he is not described at all. "The Master of Crabs" is the sorcerer Sarcand, who used Basatan's ring to rule the crabs for there were a lot of these creatures in his palace.

By the look of the ring "with the tentacles of a kraken clasping the orb-like gem" and the visions that one of the characters sees in the orb "swirling as of tides and of shadowy fins and tentacles far down in its glimmering greenness" we сan assume that he has tentacles and/or fins.

### In Popular Culture
*In the game Deep Black there is a boss called Basatan, which is a crab-like mech.
*A gigantic crab and a magic ring feature prominently in the Dungeons & Dragons adventure module White Plume Mountain, which has other faint echoes of the Zothique stories.
*Basatan appears in the mobile game Card Monsters.

Basil Frederick Albert Copper (5 February 1924-3 April 2013) was an English author and editor.

### Overview
Beginning his career as a journalist and newspaper editor, Basil Copper decided to become a professional author around 1970. He established long-lived relationships with both August Derleth and Arkham House, who published many of his works, perhaps the most famous being his continuation of Derleth's Solar Pons series of Arthur Conan Doyle pastiches; Copper not only wrote more short works, but also edited a collection of Derleth's original Pons stories, although the changes he made were poorly received by the fanbase. 

In addition to his other stories, and as might be expected by his close ties to Derleth and Arkham House, Copper also wrote several short stories set in the Cthulhu Mythos established by the late H. P. Lovecraft.

### Selected Bibliography

* Beyond the Reef (1994)
* "Voices in the Water" (2005)

fullContent:
Basilisks are a species of extra-dimensional entity created by American games manufacturer Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. It was inspired by the real-world legends of the Basilisk, a creature known in European mythology since at least the beginning of the first century AD .

### Description
Basilisks resemble some kind of scaled avian, with a sinuous, snake-like tail and expansive wings decorated with bright plumage. Their head sports a striking crest and vicious fangs .

Basilisks are a highly venomous species found only in Earth's Dreamlands. Their toxin is so potent that any area they inhabit soon becomes a desolate, inhospitable wasteland as the venom seeps into the very ground, and rivers are polluted for leagues downriver whenever the creatures sate their thirst. Needless to say, this poison is instantly fatal to most living creatures, and there are even accounts of the effects transferring from one affected creature to another in physical contact .

An unusual capability of the Basilisk is its ability to transfer its venom to its prey through simply making eye contact; only a second or two is required for this process to complete, again resulting in the near-certain death of the victim .

### Appearances
*H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands
*S. Petersen's Field Guide to Creatures of the Dreamlands

Bast, a.k.a. Bubastis, is the Egyptian goddess of cats and in legend the daughter of Isis (: "The Brood of Bubastis"). Queen of all cats, including those of Mars, Saturn, Jupiter and Uranus. Also spelt Bubaste and Ubaste. Bast is sometimes connected with the goddess Sekhmet and occasionally linked with the goddess Mut. Bast is also linked with ghouls by some Saracen sorcerers, who call her "the Chewer of Corpses". A ghoul-cult to Bast fled from the Middle East to Cornwall where they established a secret temple.

### Trivia
*It is speculated(by who?) that Bast qualifies as an Elder God due to H.P. Lovecraft's feline obsession and because of hints given in Lovecraft's "The Cats of Ulthar".(what hints?) She appears as a female human with a cat's head or a regular cat in Egyptian mythology. Robert Bloch clearly inserts this goddess into the Mythos in his fiction.
*Another spelling of her name is Bastet, but due to the way the Egyptian language works it does not change the pronunciation. The additional 'et' ending is added merely to emphasize the t in her name which denotes that she is female.

shortDefinition: Batman: The Doom That Came to Gotham is a three-issue comic book miniseries published in 2000-2001 that puts Batman in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos. It was written by Mike Mignola and Richard Pace, with art by Troy Nixey (pencils) and Dennis Janke...
fullContent:
Batman: The Doom That Came to Gotham is a three-issue comic book miniseries published in 2000-2001 that puts Batman in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos. It was written by Mike Mignola and Richard Pace, with art by Troy Nixey (pencils) and Dennis Janke (ink). It was published as part of DC Comics' Elseworlds line, for stories that are not part of the regular DC continuity. 

The title combines H. P. Lovecraft's "The Doom that Came to Sarnath" with Batman's Gotham City, the plot riddled with Lovecraft references.

### Synopsis
Having witnessed his parents' brutal murder as a child, Bruce Wayne traveled across the world for twenty years in search for answers behind the criminal mind. But everything changes when he and his wards travel to the Antarctic to find an expedition crew led by eccentric socialite Oswald Cobblepot. What Bruce finds there, Cobblepot wandering the frozen wilderness while his surviving crewman Grendon became an animated frozen corpse digging out a creature from the ice, compels him to return to Gotham with the latter in his custody. But against the crime-ridden backdrop of The Roaring '20s, Bruce delves into a connection of the city's dark past with his father, his parents' killer, and a murdered scientist named Kirk Langstrom who claimed to speak to bats. Furthermore, Bruce learns that only he could stop the Cult of Ghul from bringing about the end of Gotham and the world, which requires him to die and sacrifice his humanity to do so.

### Allusions 
*Ra's al Ghul is given aspects of Abdul Alhazred as a Mideastern sorcerer who wrote a book of dark magic while visiting an ancient city, and was also torn to pieces by an invisible entity in Damascus.
*The lizard creature supporting the Cult of Ghul is named Ludvig Prinn.
*While Grendon resembles DC villain Mr. Freeze in appearance and power - and is even referred to as Mister Freeze by Dick Grayson at one point - his nature as a corpse that would decompose into slime if not exposed to cold temperature is a homage to Muñoz from Lovecraft's short story "Cool Air".
*Iog-Sotha, an extra-dimensional dark god that Ra's al Ghul tries to summon in order to end all of humanity, is a pastiche of Yog-Sothoth.

### Adaptations
*On 28 March 2023, Warner Bros. Animation and DC Studios released an animated adaptation of the story, whose cast included, amongst others, Jeffrey Combs, an actor with a long history of involvement in screen Mythos productions.

Batman: The Doom That Came to Gotham is an animated film based on Mike Mignola and Richard Pace's comic book series of the same name. Produced by Warner Bros. Animation and DC Studios and directed by Christopher Berkeley and Sam Lui, it was given a direct-to-video release on 28 March 2023 .

### Behind the Scenes
Amongst the cast are American actor Jeffrey Combs, who has had a long and illustrious involvement with Cthulhu Mythos screen productions, including perhaps his most well-known role, that of Dr. Herbert West in the Re-Animator film series. Dr. West is also featured in The Doom That Came to Gotham, but does not appear to have been voiced by Combs in this feature .

### Reception
The Doom That Came to Gotham holds a 6.1/10 rating on IMDb . Rotten Tomatoes gives it a 77% critic score, but only a 48% audience score .

fullContent:
"Bats in the Belfry" is a short Cthulhu Mythos/Thomas Carnacki crossover story by British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
Paranormal investigator Thomas Carnacki discovers a portal to the Outer Darkness located inside an ancient church and opened by the ringing of its bells. He is successful in closing it and beating back its guardian - the Outer God Yog-Sototh, or perhaps one of its avatars - with the aid of a mysterious entity in the guise of a large ginger tomcat.

### Characters
*Thomas Carnacki, occult detective extraordinaire.
*The Ginger Tom, a guardian of the portal disguised as a housecat.
*Reverend John Wilkinson, a rural priest who appears to have a certain affinity for the supernatural.
*Mrs. Wilkinson, John's wife.

### Publication History
"Bats in the Belfry" was first published in Tails of Terror by Golden Goblin Press in 2018. It was later included in the collection of Meikle's own works Carnacki: Starry Wisdom and Other Stories in March 2021.

Batta is a fictional character from the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald.

### Biography
Batta was a domestic servant who worked for Dr. Thomas Slauenwite at the small trading post of M'gonga, close to the Ugandan border. In 1929, Slauenwite coldly decided to use Batta to test the lethality of his hybridised devil-flies, which he intended to use to kill Dr. Moore. On August 10, Slauenwite secretly arranged for one of the flies to get loose and bite Batta. Soon afterwards, he recaptured the fly alive and placed it back in its cage. He gave Batta some iodine for the pain, for which Batta was grateful.

On August 25, Batta started to feel pain on his back, where he had been bitten. One week later, he was already showing signs of lethargy and claiming that "his back aches all the time". Over the next week his condition deteriorated and he correctly guessed that the fly that bit him was a devil-fly. Slauenwite only pretended to treat him, as he wanted to see how the disease would develop. Batta, who believed in the local legends about the devil-fly's ability to "steal" the soul of its victims, asked Slauenwite to kill the insect, but Slauenwite lied to him that it had already perished.

When Batta died on November 17, his consciousness was transferred to the body of the devil-fly. As soon as Slauenwite entered the laboratory, he saw that the fly was acting frantic, but stopped once it noticed the doctor's presence and stared at him "in the oddest way". When Slauenwite returned after dining with Allen, he saw that the fly had beaten itself to death on the sides of its cage. (: "Winged Death")

fullContent:
Battle Spirits is a Japanese trading card game created by Bandai and Sunrise, Inc. in September 2008, which would later spawn a multimedia franchise including several anime, manga and video games. In August 2009, the card game received a limited run in North America, with only six sets being released. In April 2023, the card game saw much more success in the West, under the name Battle Spirits Saga, and is still active to this day. It remains one of the most popular Japanese card games of all time.

Battle Spirits is a two-player game with each player setting up five core on their life, three on their reserve, and one soul core. The game mechanics involve summoning spirits, placing nexuses, and casting magic with the goal of depleting the opponent's five lives. In order to perform any action, cores are needed to generate each turn; however, the number of color Spirits/Nexuses specified on the top left of the card can be used to reduce costs.

Relevant to this wiki, several of the cards are based on familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos.

The Beast of Averoigne is a fictional monster created by Clark Ashton Smith for his eponymous short story.

### Background
The Beast is an extraterrestrial creature, whose arrival coincided with the sight of a mysterious red comet in the year 1369, on the French province of Averoigne. The comet remained visible in the sky for several weeks, during which time the Beast ran loose each night, brutally tearing apart people and animals to feed on their spinal marrow. It is estimated to have killed over forty people: men, women and children, in addition to stags, wolves, horses and oxes.

As an alien life form, the Beast couldn't interact with anything on Earth in its natural form, which was described as "impalpable and powerless". To be able to feed, it made itself tangible by inhabiting the body of a human host: the Abbot Theophile, who was himself unaware of the possession. Every night, the Beast assumed control of the Abbot and transformed him into a black reptilian creature with an elongated body, undulating limbs, a sinuous neck and flat serpentine head, small lidless red eyes, and serrated teeth, and surrounded by a luminous color-changing aura. Despite being as large as a man, the Beast's reptilian form moved swiftly and silently, and was capable of running on vertical surfaces like a spider.

The Beast was killed by a fiery demon released from the ring of Eibon by the wizard le Chaudronnier. (: "The Beast of Averoigne")

### In the Demonbane Mythos
In the novel Zanma Taisen Demonbane, the Beast of Averoigne (also known as the Beast of Gévaudan, or La Bête d'Averoigne in French) appears as a techno-organic demon beast, under the name Demonbane Diabolos. Hailing from the stellar world, this giant robotic beast is piloted by the Bewitching King Phantom of Opera, one of the Five Werewolf Kings and the strongest Werewolf. Its control system is the Ālaya-vijñāna System, neurally linked with the spinal cord of the pilot, and since the system itself puts a massive strain on the operator, normal humans cannot pilot the Beast or they will immediately die. Only Werewolves with powerful vitality can withstand the burden, and that is none other than Phantom himself. 

Diabolos is summoned via the Ring of Eibon, made from an ancient super metal. Additionally, the ring can function as the grimoire known as the Book of Eibon, with Phantom chosen to be its pilot. Both Diabolos and Phantom are planned to be the final bosses of the Auseil city arc in Zanma Taisen Demonbane.

Diabolos' design is based on the mecha from the Zoids franchise and Zinogre from the Monster Hunter series.

Beecher Smith, full name Drayton Beecher Smith, II, is a retired attorney known for being Elvis Presley's personal lawyer and has published various works, including fiction in the science fiction, fantasy, and horror genres. He is also recognized for his novel The Guardian: Dracula’s Destiny and has received awards for his writing. Relevant to this wiki, he wrote the Cthulhu Mythos story "The Burrower From the Bluff".

In 2007, he was convicted and jailed on child pornography charges. Following his release, he retired from public life.

Beecher Smith lives in Memphis, Tennessee. He studied at Millsaps College, where he majored in English literature before graduating and going to the University of Tennessee to earn his law degree. He distinguished himself in the practice of law as Elvis Presley's personal attorney, probated the late entertainer's will, and chartered Elvis Presley Enterprises. He rezoned Graceland to become a world-class museum. After a near-fatal hunting accident in 1986, he returned to writing poetry and fiction, for which he has received numerous awards.

The Poetry Society of Tennessee elected him its Poet Laureate in 1995. That same year he was also inducted as a fellow Laureate Man of Letters by the United Poets Laureate International and the World Congress of Poets.

"Before the Storm" is a short story written by British fiction author Ramsey Campbell. It was published in his collection of short horror, Cold Print.

### Synopsis
An unnamed man stumbles into a tax office, seeking shelter from the sun's rays, clearly insane and apparently unable to communicate with those inside. As some of the employees try to ascertain what is the matter with him, the reader is told in a flashback the story of how the man became involved with a group called the Society, before being inducted into the mysteries of the occult. At one point, he made a bargain with the Great Old One known as Eihort, a bargain which allowed him to travel the universe by switching bodies, but drove him into madness.

Eventually, the man decides that the employees are all servants of Eihort, come to drag him into the light, and makes a break for it, opening the door to the rooftop fire escape. As the door opens, the lone employee close enough to see the man observes the light grabbing hold of his body and dissolving it into a mass of what appears to be fat, white spiders.

*Unnamed Man, the main character.
*Joan, tax office employee.
*Robert, tax office employee.
*Bernard "Bernie" Cohen, tax office employee.
*Mr. Weedall, tax office supervisor.

"Behind the Mask" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, first published in the May 1987 issue of the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu. It serves as a direct sequel to August Derleth's short story "The Return of Hastur".

### Synopsis
In 1928, the library at Miskatonic University receives a collection of rare occult books from the recently deceased Amos Tuttle, donated as per the dead man's request. Librarian Cyrus Llanfer delegates the cataloging of the items to his assistant, Bryant Hoskins, who is quick to notice a copy of the exceedingly rare R'lyeh Text, bound in human skin and written in the R'lyehian language.

Studying Tuttle's notes and letters, Hoskins finds references to the Plateau of Leng, and to a region of Tibet described as "Tcho-Tcho country", where some kind of document was to be delivered to "the Tcho-Tcho lama". Hoskins consults one of his teachers, a folklorist named Wilmarth, who informs him that the Plateau of Leng is the location from which the Great Old Ones once ruled the world, according to the Necronomicon of Abdul Alhazred. Due to a curse placed by the Elder Gods (the Great Old Ones' enemies), it is now a barren land where nothing human could live. The Tcho-Tchos, however, are not human, and while their civilisation is centered in the Plateau of Sung in Burma, they are also found in other parts of Asia and are known to worship the Great Old Ones, therefore a Tcho-Tcho lama in Leng wouldn't be out of place.

Hoskins notices that some passages of the R'lyeh Text have been translated by Tuttle, and searches the man's papers for a glossary that would allow him to translate the rest of the book. Meanwhile, he finds more information about Leng in the Necronomicon, according to which the location of the plateau might be in central Asia, the South Pole, or the Dreamlands. Alhazred believed that Leng functioned as a bridge between worlds, and speaks of an Elder Hierophant wearing a mask of yellow silk. That night, Hoskins actually sees the plateau in his dreams.

After searching extensively through Tuttle's documents, Hoskins finally locates the "R'lyehian Key", and takes the R'lyeh Text home to start working on its translation. He works through the entire night and sleeps through the next day, once again dreaming of Leng. This time, however, he notices that the sky is filled with unfamiliar constellations, and sees a stone tower with a high circular window from which a light flashes out, like a lighthouse.

Over the next days, as Hoskins continues to work on the text, the meaning of words and phrases seem to become intuitively clear to him, and he learns all he can about the Great Old Ones and their servitor races. His dreams of Leng persist, always showing the stone tower with the light beam flashing from its upmost window. As his unrestful dreams prevent him from getting proper sleep, Hoskins seeks help from a physician, Dr. Ephraim Sprague, who also alerts Llanfer. "Behold, I Stand at the Door and Knock" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
A young man who fancies himself something of an occultist jumps at the chance to buy an edition of Volume I of The Revelations of Glaaki from a door-to-door salesman. However, once he begins to read, he realises that he has been tricked, and must now become a herald for the dark power or face a dire punishment…

### Characters

*Sid Hingley, an aimless man in a dead-end life.
*Errol Undercliffe, an apparently-ordinary travelling salesman offering a 12-volume set of The Revelations of Glaaki.

### Publication History
"Behold, I Stand at the Door and Knock" was first published in the Chaosium anthology Cthulhu's Heirs in March 1994, and was later included in a collection of Price's own works, Blasphemies & Revelations, in November 2008.

### Trivia
*The story takes place in Lower Brichester, a location created by British author Ramsey Campbell as part of his Severn Valley Mythos setting.
*Sid Hingley works in an establishment named the Black Goat, a clear reference to Shub-Niggurath, the Black Goat of the Woods with a Thousand Young.

Bel Yarnak was a fictional city created by H. P. Lovecraft's friend Henry Kuttner for his 1937 short story "The Eater of Souls".

### Description
Once a city on a nameless world beyond Betelgeuse and the giant suns around which Iod is worshipped, Bel Yarnak was the primary city of this world, and some scholars use the city's name to reference the planet. It was possessed of many silver spires and a single Black Minaret within which dwelled the wizards who acted as the priesthood of the city. The reptilian gorlaks were used as beasts of burden, and the city was famed for its necromancers and hydromancers. It was ruled by the benevolent alien being known as Sindara, a worshipper of the Elder God Vorvadoss. 

The city was destroyed when the priests of the Black Minaret evoked the god Droom-avista who caused all substances in the city to transmute to iron. Forever after, Bel Yarnak would be known as Dis, the City of Iron.

fullContent:
Belasco is a supervillain in the fictional Marvel universe, who was created in 1982 and has been an enemy of the X-Men throughout his history.

### Background
Belasco is one of Earth's most powerful sorcerers with an encyclopedic knowledge of occult spells from a number of books. He has a superhuman demonic form, is immortal, and has superhuman durability. He was a 13th century sorcerer from Florence, Italy who contacted the Elder Gods and made a pact with them. He kidnapped Dante's beloved, took her to Pangea, and raped her to produce a new race of demons. When she died giving birth, an enraged Dante attacked him and during the fighting he ended up being placed in suspended animation.

In the late 20th century, the volcanic mountain became active, releasing Belasco. During his attempt to repeat history with Ka-Zar's wife Shanna, he ended up trapped in Limbo when Ka-Zar hurls the Bloodstone locket into the volcano. Belasco conquered the demonic pocket dimension of Limbo and then kidnaps 7-yr old Illyana Rasputina (Magik), to use her mutant powers to open a gateway to the Elder Gods and make her his apprentice. The X-Men attempted to rescue her but failed and she remained trapped in Limbo, where he turned her into a demon sorceress. She turned on him, drove him from Limbo and became its ruler.

Belasco became the ruler of the Cat People and later regained control of Limbo. He attempted to wipe out mankind, but his pawn was killed by the Punisher. He later had a contest with the fear-demon D'Spayre to see if they could corrupt the mutant Cable but failed. Later with the aid of the N'Garai, Belasco fought the X-Men but they emerged victorious with Magik's assistance. He later returned to Limbo and regained his domain. Belasco is obsessed with Magik, not only because of her powers but because he has also fallen in love with her.

* Tommy Hubbard, showrunner of The Cryptid Files.

When three adventurers on a trek to the South Pole encounter a mysterious stranger, it does does not take them long to discover that it is in fact an alien creature disguised as a human. ### Synopsis
A man awakens, amnesiac, naked and hairless, in a cavern deep under the Mountains of Madness in Antarctica. He encounters a cavern where a protoplasmic red blob surround by smaller blobs resides, and after further explorations discovers a machine creature, a Shoggoth, edible crustaceans in a large rock pool, and ultimately four other men like himself, frozen to death, all of whom have his own face. Like him, they have no signs of any past life such as scars or other marks, and it is implied that he, and they, are in fact creations of the protoplasmic entity in the cavern near where he awoke.

"Beneath the Tombstone" is a short story by American author and Lovecraft scholar Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
A man inherits his distant uncles' expansive property in the remote countryside and discovers a host of ancient grimoires in the study and slaughtered livestock in the basement, indicating that he was practicing some kind of black magic. After perusal of some of the books, the man unwittingly utters a phrase from one, condemning his uncle's soul to the monsters from which he had thought himself protected.

### Characters

*William, a young man who has recently come into possession of his eccentric uncles estate.
*Absalom Mueller, William's deceased uncle.

*Amongst the tomes included in Absalom Mueller's library were the Book of Iod and the R'lyeh Text.

Benjamin Adams (born 1966) is a Bram Stoker Award-nominated American author and editor based in Phoenix, Arizona, who has had a hand in a number of Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos works. He has written tie-in pieces for the popular British science fiction franchise Doctor Who, as well as the Mythos-set roleplaying game Delta Green .

Adams' Lovecraftian output includes editorial duties on the anthology The Children of Cthulhu (2002,  Del Ray/Ballantine, with John Pelan), and his short fiction has appeared in anthologies such as Singers of Strange Songs (1997, Chaosium) and Delta Green: Dark Theatres (2001, Armitage House), as well as the fanzine Cthulhu Codex.

Beowulf is an Old English epic poem. It’s exact date of writing is unclear, but the earliest known manuscript dates from the late 10th/early 11th century. 

### Synopsis
The story follows Swedish warrior Beowulf as he ascends to become king of the Geats, battling a series of supernatural threats along the way. It culminates with the death of Beowulf and his people entering a period of mourning.  

### Behind the Mythos
Beowulf appears to have been an influence on H. P. Lovecraft, as he mentions the poem in his essay Supernatural Horror in Literature as an example of how elements of horror have been an integral part of folklore throughout history.

fullContent:
Bernard Austin Dwyer (1897 - 1943) was an American poet, artist and woodcutter from West Shokan, New York. His poem, "Ol' Black Sarah", was published in the October 1928 issue of Weird Tales. His letters also appeared multiple times in the magazine, praising the writings of Clark Ashton Smith, Seabury Quinn, and especially H. P. Lovecraft, who was regarded by Dwyer as the greatest author in the field.

Dwyer became a friend of Lovecraft, first by correspondence, then by meeting him personally, including at least one occasion in which Lovecraft visited and stayed with him for a few days.

In a 1928 letter to Frank Belknap Long, Lovecraft described Dwyer as an intelligent man with "an imagination of the utmost sensitiveness, delicacy, and picturesqueness". Physically, he also referred to Dwyer as a "near-giant—a mighty woodcutter and athlete". (: Selected Letters 2.319)

In the comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century", by Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow, Dwyer is represented as "Knockout Bernie, the Wild Wolf of West Shokan", who competes in a fighting match against "Two-Gun Bob, the Terror of the Plains", both being described as "renowned champions of the strange-story firmament".

fullContent:
"Beside Myself" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
A down-on-his-luck security guard who has inherited a collection of mystical grimoires - including the notorious Unausperechlichen Kulten [sic]- from his eccentric uncle accidentally summons a doppelgänger one night while drunk. At first, this seems like a godsend to him, as the double takes over the daily drudgery of work and household chores, but things soon begin to change, and the being becomes increasingly abusive towards his it’s supposed master.

As things get worse, the man realises that the creature intends to kill him, and begins to put into action a plan to get rid of the malevolent being. He eventually manages to uncover the spell he needs in the Unausperechlichen Kulten, and summons a Shoggoth, which consumes his duplicate in a bloody frenzy. Although he loses his house in the ensuing carnage, the man's life soon returns to the mundane grind that it had been prior to his accidental brush with magic.

### Trivia
* One of the books bequeathed to the narrator is The Ohm-Dhari Chronicles. The Ohmdari are a slug-like species of eldritch abomination who are referenced in a number of Shiflet's works.

The six lines describe in brief a date-rape scenario intended to allow a juvenile Shoggoth to be smuggled through customs inside the unsuspecting victim's womb. Betelgeuse, a.k.a. Alpha Orionis, is a red giant believed to be located about 650 light-years from Earth. It is the brightest star in the constellation of Orion and one of the largest stars in our galaxy. Such massive stars are relatively short lived, and Betelgeuse is no exception, believed to be only about 10 million years old, yet already entering the final stages of stellar life.

In the works of August Derleth, the Elder Gods dwell in the vicinity of Betelgeuse, which they refer to as Glyu-vho (: "The Return of Hastur", : "Out of the Ages") or Glyu'uho (: "The Horror from the Bridge").

The name Glyu-Vho was suggested to Derleth by his friend H. P. Lovecraft, who pointed out that it would be unrealistic for alien beings to refer to the star by its English name. (: Selected Letters 4.599)

Bethmoora is a fictional city created by Lord Dunsany for his fantasy book A Dreamer's Tales. It is mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness and Hugh B. Cave's "The Isle of Dark Magic", although in the latter it seems to refer to a being, as opposed to a place (cf. Hastur, Yian, and Yuggoth).

### History
Standing next to a desert and beyond the snowy Hills of Hap, Bethmoora is a long-abandoned city whose gates of green copper are open and castigated by sand storms. In its prime, it was separated from the desert by a narrow strip of fertile land, in which the locals planted vineyards and purple flowering bushes. The grapes were crushed in vats to make the syrabub, which was traded for turquoises and emeralds with the people of Oxuhahn. When the harvest was good, the natives celebrated by dancing and playing instruments such as the kalipac, the tambang, the tittibuk, and the zootibar.

One day, three men mounted on mules arrived at the gates and delivered a message to the people of Bethmoora which caused them to abandon their homes in silent panic, set fire to their vineyards and escape the city to never return. Some European travelers who were present at the occasion heard the message, but couldn't understand the language. Therefore, the reason for the sudden and drastic evacuation is unknown.

Many ideas have been proposed, some claiming the message came from the unseen emperor Thuba Mleen, or even from the gods themselves, either friendly gods issuing a warning or hostile ones issuing a threat. Some speak of a plague, or even assume that the three men were not messengers at all, but suffering from the gnousar sickness, which scared the population away. The most popular idea, however, is that the message came from the desert itself, which desired to claim Bethmoora.

At least one man has claimed to have visited Bethmoora in hashish dreams and to know the nature of the message. According to him, it was sent by the cruel emperor Thuba Mleen. (: A Dreamer's Tales)

Bettie Page is a comic book hero, based on the historical pin-up model of the same name. The character first appeared as the girlfriend of the protagonist in Dave Steven's comic The Rocketeer and it was Dave who was responsible for lifting her from obscurity to become, once more, not only a sex symbol but a pop culture cottage industry until her death in 2008. She also appeared in the Bettie Page Comics one-shot by Dark Horse Comics in 1996, and later came back in 2017 for her own series by Dynamite Entertainment.

In 2018, The Fantasy World of Bettie Page was released by TidalWave Comics as a four issue limited series. In the storyline, Bettie Page is a secret agent for the US in 1955. The work was developed in the 1990s but put on hold by rights disputes unconnected to the Bettie Page project specifically; however, it prevented the publication of a whole raft of completed comics for the better part of eight years. Bettie Page was a casualty of that unrelated rights legal dispute.

### Background
Bettie Page is a model who works as a secret agent for a secretive American spy agency in the early 20th century which deals with various threats including extraterrestrials, monsters, the supernatural and mad scientists. During one of her missions, she had to save Earth and the entire multiverse from the Great Old Ones, who were breaking out of their dimensional prison. (: "The Crisis on Infinite Betties")

fullContent:
"Between Angels and Insects" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Simon Bestwick. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
When Heald Jones's 12-year-old sone kills himself after an extensive and apparently motiveless campaign of cyber-bullying, he throws himself into his work - designing a nanotechnology which can alter chemical imbalances in the brain - as a coping mechanism. When this fails to have any effect on his emotional state, he decides other means are necessary, despite his program being a resounding success.

Engaging the services of a private detective agency, he tracks down the nine of the bullies; of these, three are in a catatonic state, while five have died by their own hands. The remaining one, a man named Rogers, owns a small waxwork museum in Blackpool which specialises in the entities created by H. P. Lovecraft.

When Jones confronts Rogers, Rogers suffers a psychological breakdown and reveals that the two were both unwitting pawns in a scheme by Cthulhu to bring about the return of the Great Old Ones: Rogers was employed as one of the bullies whose campaign would result in Jones's sons' suicide, an outcome which the Great Old One knew would precipitate Jones's creation of the nanobot system, a technology which is capable of uniting every human brain on the planet into an organism which may be of use to Cthulhu. 

### Mythos Connections
Aside from Cthulhu, other entities which had waxwork depictions on view at the Lovecraftiana Museum included a nightgaunt and Yog-Sothoth. Another exhibit was titled Innsmouth Tableaux, but it is uncertain what this display depicted.

Paxwell immediately attempts to flee with his wife and child, but his pursuers catch up with them them and kill his wife. Threatening to destroy his brain if his demands for a better life for his child are not met, he secures a deal with his hunters; although the bargain is honoured to the letter, the consequences for his daughter are horrific.

fullContent:
Beyond the Reef is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by Basil Copper first published in the 1994 anthology Shadows over Innsmouth.

### Synopsis
In 1932, the coastal town of Innsmouth is hit by a massive storm. This, however, is only the latest of a series of unusual events that have been going on since a rare book was stolen from the library at Miskatonic University in the nearby town of Arkham in 1929. The following year saw a great tidal bore which swept up the Manuxet River, concurrent with a whirlwind and a mysterious phenomenon that the locals referred to as "white lightning". A fire resulted in the loss of several priceless records at Arkham Public Library.

At the university, strange occurrences pile up, as locked doors are inexplicably found opened, footsteps are heard in the corridors, taps turn on and lights switch on and off by themselves. All of this culminates in a more serious incident, in which a large stone cross memorial falls down and almost kills the dean, Dr. Darrow, who is fortunately pulled away from danger by some students. Scientific analysis reveals that the interior of the memorial was damaged as if it had "rotted away": an absolute impossibility, as it is made of granite. Soon afterwards, a janitor named Jeb Conlay, who had been missing for a few days, is found dead in a pond with his face inexplicably corroded away to almost nothing.

While looking over the area where the memorial fell down, surveyor Andrew Bellows discovers an underground complex of tunnels apparently connecting Arkham to Innsmouth all the way to the sea. Marks on the dusty floor suggest that someone has been dragging some kind of object along, while inscriptions on the walls remind Dr. Darrow of symbols he has seen in some of the library's rare books. Bellows and Dr. Darrow explore the tunnels and see signs that someone has been there recently. They come across a passage that has been sealed by rocks, at which point Darrow is scared by the sight of squirming creatures with flat snake-like heads, which can apparently pass through the solid walls at will.

Back in his office, Darrow tells Bellows about a brilliant cryptographer named Jefferson Holroyd, who is trying to decode the symbols in the library's books. As soon as they call him, Holroyd invites them to see his progress. However, they arrive in the library to find that Holroyd's deciphering machine has been melted down and wrecked. His papers are inexplicably blank, with all the annotations gone, and even Holroyd's memory seems to have been somehow altered, as he can no longer remember the phrases he had already translated.

Meanwhile, Captain of Detectives Cornelius Oates is baffled by the faceless corpse of Jeb Conley, for which the police surgeon, Dr. Ewart Lancaster can offer no proper explanation. At Dr. Lancaster's suggestion, Oates goes to Innsmouth to investigate rumours about strange sea creatures. fullContent:
"Beyond the Threshold" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by August Derleth, first published in the September 1941 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
A Miskatonic librarian is summoned by a cousin to the house of their grandfather in Wisconsin, who has become obsessed with the papers of his uncle. The uncle had trafficked with the Great Old Ones, and left a warning to "not pass beyond the threshold, for fear of dire consequences." The grandfather finds that the house conceals "a rocky opening leading into the depths of earth"; he crosses that threshold, and is taken away by a Great Old One.

### Setting
The story takes place in September 1940--three years after H. P. Lovecraft's death. It's set in a "lonely house deep in the forest places of northern Wisconsin," "the old house grandfather owned in the heart of the forest and lake country of northern Wisconsin." It was built in the 1850s by Leander Alwyn, who specified that it have a "curious windowless room" that serves as a study.

The house is near "the village of Harmon, deep in the forest country of Wisconsin—a place of great natural beauty, not far from the shores of Lake Superior."

### Characters 
*Leander Alwyn: He is "one of the seafaring Alwyns of Innsmouth." He was "afflicted with that curious facial change which overtook so many of the inhabitants of accursed Innsmouth"; his nephew remarks, "There does not exist even a likeness of Uncle Leander, but the old-timers around Harmon told me years ago that he was a very homely man, that he reminded them of a frog.” He was "apparently a wicked man," as evidenced by his willingness to collaborate with "elemental forces of evil." 
*Josiah Alwyn: A nephew of Leander, he is an explorer of "remote corners of the world": "Tibet, Mongolia, the Arctic regions, and certain little-known islands in the Pacific." He is described as "a barrel-chested old man, with a heavy, full face, decorated with a closely clipped moustache and a small beard to soften the hard line of his square jaw. His eyes were dark, not overlarge, and his brows were shaggy; he wore his hair long, so that his head had a leonine appearance." In his early seventies in 1940, so born in the late 1860s.
*Frolin Alwyn: Grandson of Josiah Alwyn, cousin of Tony. In his late thirties in 1940, though he looks a decade younger. Has "hot, intense brown eyes, and a soft, sensitive mouth that belied his inner hardness."
*Tony Alwyn: Grandson of Josiah Alwyn, cousin of Frolin. He is the assistant librarian at Miskatonic University.
*Hough: He and his wife have been Josiah's servants since about 1920.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Weird Tales, "Beyond the Threshold" was reprinted in Derleth's Arkham House collection Something Near (1945). It was then included in the Lovecraftian anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1969).

It appeared in the horror anthologies Beware More Beasts (Manor Books, 1975) and A Treasury of American Horror Stories (Bonanza Books, 1985).

"Beyond the Wall of Sleep" is a short story by American writer H. P. Lovecraft written in 1919 and first published in the amateur publication of Pine Cones in October 1919. It would eventually be reprinted in Weird Tales in March of 1938.

### Inspiration
Lovecraft said the story was inspired by an April 27, 1919 article in the New York Tribune. Reporting on the New York state police, the article cited a family named Slater or Slahter as representative of the backwards Catskills population.

The nova mentioned at the end of Lovecraft's story is a real star, known as GK Persei; the quotation is from Garrett P. Serviss's Astronomy with the Naked Eye (1908).

The title of the story may have been influenced by Ambrose Bierce's "Beyond the Wall"; Lovecraft was known to be reading Bierce in 1919. Jack London's 1906 novel Before Adam, which concerns the concept of hereditary memory, contains the passage, "Nor...did any of my human kind ever break through the wall of my sleep."

### Synopsis
 (Weird Tales)]]
An intern at a mental hospital relates his experience with Joe Slater, an inmate who died at the facility a few weeks after being confined as a criminally insane murderer. He describes Slater as a "typical denizen of the Catskill Mountains region, who corresponds exactly with the 'white trash' of the South", for whom "laws and morals are nonexistent" and whose "general mental status is probably below that of any other native American people". Although Slater's crime was exceedingly brutal and unprovoked he had an "absurd appearance of harmless stupidity" and the doctors guessed his age at about forty. During the third night of his confinement, Slater had the first of his "attacks". He burst from an uneasy sleep into a frenzy so violent it took four orderlies to strait-jacket him. For nearly fifteen minutes he gave vent to an incredible rant. The words were in the voice and couched in the paltry vocabulary of Joe Slater but the onlookers could construe from the inadequate language a vision of:

As an undergraduate, the intern had built but never tested a device for two-way telepathic communication. The device was designed around his principle that thought was ultimately a form of radiant energy. Heedless of any ethics, he attached himself with Slater to the device as Slater lay near death. With the device switched on, he received a message from a being of light whose experiences had been what were transmitted through the medium of Joe Slater. This being explained that, when not shackled to their physical bodies, all men are light beings. The thought-message went on to explain that, as light beings within the realm of sleep, humans can experience the vistas of many planes and universes which remain unknown to waking awareness.

Beyond the Wall of Sleep is a collection of fantasy, horror and science fiction short stories, poems and essays by American author H. P. Lovecraft. It was released in 1943 and was the second collection of Lovecraft's work published by Arkham House. 1,217 copies were printed. The volume is named for the Lovecraft short story "Beyond the Wall of Sleep".

The stories for this volume were selected by August Derleth and Donald Wandrei. The dust jacket art was a collage of photographs of sculptures by Clark Ashton Smith.

Beyond the Wall of Sleep is a comic book adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft short story of the same name. Bh’Yhlun is a fictional structure created by the Old Ones in Ian Davey's Bh’Yhlun series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Description
Created upon the return of the Old Ones, Bh’Yhlun was formed from both the debris of the city of London and the living organic matter of its residents. It is a colossal tower which soars many miles into the sky, and across its visible surfaces can be seen the remains of the sentient creatures whose souls compose its veins and arteries, caught in an eternal agony.

The interior of Bh’Yhlun is honeycombed with passageways and cells, and patrolled by servitor Shoggoths.

### Purpose
Bh’Yhlun is ruled by the Outer God Nyarlathotep who keeps an unknown number of humans prisoner within its walls to use as his personal playthings. It is also suggested that the tower is at least in part responsible for the changes in biosphere and atmosphere occurring since the return of the Old Ones, creating a more hospitable environment for the Earth's new masters.
