The Bhlemphroim are an extraterrestrial species which first appeared in Clark Ashton Smith's 1932 short story "The Door to Saturn".

### Description
Hairless humanoid beings roughly the same size as a human, the most distinguishing feature of the Blemphroim is their lack of a head. Instead, the heads of the Blemphroim have slowly fused with their torsos over the millennia; this has since become a source of racial regret for these intelligent creatures.

### Conceptual information and role
They are indigenous to the planet Cykranosh. Its main city, Vhlorrh, is surrounded by mineral vegetation. In "The Door to Saturn", it is said of them that they are "singular, meritorious and virtuous", being always respectful. They have a system of ideas, beliefs and customs. While they worshiped gods like Zhothaqquah in the past, they no longer did, and they had forgotten their language (unlike the Ydheems). Despite this, they speak of them with respect.

They are a practical and unimaginative breed: despite having a certain level of technology, they have little interest in advancing their knowledge beyond growing edible mushrooms (which they eat raw, boiled, or roasted) and domesticating for cargo a type of large, tough-skinned, multi-legged beast on which they also feed and reproduce. Regarding this last point, the Bhlemphroim choose a single woman to be the mother of an entire generation of Bhlemphroim. This matriarch, called "djhenquomh", is fed special mushrooms until she reaches gigantic proportions. At that point, a committee elects a small group of men to father the next generation. Once they had fulfilled their function, they were cooked for the female as ragu. It is possible to see a statue of the matriarch on the road that crosses the border of the territories of this breed.

### Stories
In "The Door to Saturn", Eibon and Morghi are the guests of the Bhlemphroims during several months of the planet, visiting the next matriarch. Eibon quickly learns their language. For their part, the Bhlemphroims were not impressed by the magic of the two men from Hyperborea or that they came from so far away, but they saw them as ideal exemplars of cephalic evolution by possessing a differentiated head, to the point that they were selected to marry and have children with the matriarch in order to have descendants with heads. At first, Eibon and Morghi used their vows of celibacy as an excuse. When Eibon asked what the marriage would entail, they replied that it was of little consequence, as all husbands including them would be served to the queen. Diplomatically, Eibon agreed to the request for both of them, but, as soon as the bhlemphroims fell asleep, the two left the place where they were staying. The Kingdom of Bhutan is a mountainous landlocked country in South Asia, bordered by China to the north and India to the south . Although never referenced in H. P. Lovecraft's writings, it has appeared in the Cthulhu Mythos work of other authors.

### The Call of Cthulhu Roleplaying Game
In Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu "Eyes Between the Worlds" scenario, Bhutan is home to a long-lost temple which houses the obscure Outer God Aiueb Gnshal and its cult of ghoul worshippers. The scenario was written by Kevin T. McKinnon and Dylan K. Sharpe, and included in the Monograph supplement Strange Tales of Dread and Wonder #1 in 2006.

### The CthulhuPunk Roleplaying Game
In the Steve Jackson Games tabletop roleplaying game CthulhuPunk, Bhutan has been incorporated into the Chinese bloc as one of its satellite states, primarily to provide a buffer for China against its political and military opponents.

"Big Nasty" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Josh Reynolds writing as Joshua Reynolds. It was published in the online zine Pulp and Dagger Fiction in 2003.

### Synopsis
A small team of researchers from Miskatonic University uncover a frozen Chthonian at the old Starkweather-Moore Antarctic Expedition Site. When the worm defrosts, they face a frantic battle for survival.

* Molly Quinn, grad student.
* Cooper Marley, grad student.
* Carmen Hart, grad student.
* Harlan West, grad student.

### Publication History
Since its first publication in 2003, "Big Nasty" has also appeared in the December 2006 edition of E. P. Berglund's online zine Nightscapes.

### Trivia
* In At the Mountains of Madness, the narrator William Dyer was telling his tale in an effort to stop the Starkweather-Moore Expedition from going ahead; according to this story, he was unsuccessful.

fullContent:
"Big Trouble in Billy's Basement" is an episode from the first season of the animated television series The Grim Adventures of Billy & Mandy.

### Synopsis
Shortly before giving Mandy a pedicure, Grim warned Billy not to read The Bad Book. Despite this, Billy decided to read it anyway, leading to him getting possessed by the extra-dimensional entity Yog-Sothoth, who wanted to open a portal from the mortal realm to his dimension and destroy the world. Now under Yog-Sothoth's power and influence, Billy beat up Grim and stole his Scythe, using it to open up the portal in his basement, transforming his house into an eldritch location in the process. Teaming up with Hoss Delgado, Grim and Mandy find out that the only way to close the portal is to throw The Bad Book into it. After Billy swallowed the book, Mandy pushed him into the portal, ending the threat of Yog-Sothoth. However, the Outer Gods didn't feel like dealing with Billy for an eternity and decided to send him back to the mortal realm.

### Behind the Mythos
*Although it's never explicitly stated, The Bad Book is most likely meant to be the Necronomicon.
*A much later episode "Prank Call of Cthulu" features a similar premise with Cthulhu being the antagonist.

William "Bill" Sweetan ("my friends call me Ace") is a recurrent character in the Cthulhu Mythos fiction of American author Ron Shiflet. He made his first appearance in the short story "The Scales of Justice", published in the 2008 collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir.

### History
Sweetan earned his nickname of Ace in school, when his friends discovered that he was a skilled baseball pitcher.

During the Second World War, Sweetan served in the armed forces, although in what capacity is unknown. He was captured by the Japanese and spent much of the duration of the war in a prison camp, having survived an unspecified death march at the hands of his captors, and remaining interred on the Philippine island of Corregidor until its liberation in 1945.

Sweetan later set up his own private detective agency in the small city of Arkham, where he primarily conducted background checks for some of the region's larger organisations, and developed a special relationship with Miskatonic University.

While in Innsmouth on a case, Sweetan met an Idahoan woman named Molly Connors, who he subsequently employed as his secretary. Although Sweetan and Connors appear to harbour romantic feelings for each other, no actual relationship between the two has yet come to be realised.

### Cases
*Arkham: Sweetan investigated the case of amateur herpetologist Warren Peasley who had been receiving mysterious letters demanding he "Return the child". The case ended in the death of Peasley at the hands of the Great Old One Yig.
*Innsmouth: in 1952, while investigating the disappearance of a young woman, Sweetan and Connors bore witness as she embraced her Deep One heritage.

### Behind the Mythos
In his story notes for the 2017 edition of Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir, creator Ron Shiflet states that "The truth is that there was an ongoing mental tussle at the time as to whether I should focus on Sweetan or Wade Kearney as an ongoing character in my fiction. They are pretty much the same person but I eventually seemed to settle on Kearney."

### Appearances

*"Looking for Darla" (2008)

fullContent:
"Billy's Oak" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Brian Lumley, first published in the Winter 1970 issue of The Arkham Collector. It marks the print debut of the character Titus Crow, although the 1987 short "Inception" saw his earliest in-universe timeline appearance.

### Synopsis
A writer named Gerald Dawson is doing research for a book about black magic and wishes to consult the infamous Cthäat Aquadingen. To that end, he contacts occultist Titus Crow, who possesses a copy of the rare volume.

Crow allows Dawson to see the book, but warns him that the parts that contain instructions for spells and rituals have been removed for safety. Surprised by Crow's genuine belief in the supernatural, Dawson challenges him to produce evidence. In response, Crow draws attention to a creaking sound that can be heard coming from his garden. He claims the sound is made by a tree called Billy's Oak, after the wizard Billy Fovarque was hanged there in 1675, and the branch continues to creak with the hanged man's weight to this day. Crow also claims that a previous owner of the house went almost mad trying to figure out the sound's origin.

Unimpressed with the story, Dawson offers that the branch creaks because of the wind, and opens up the window to see the tree. He is shocked, however, to find that there's nothing there, as Crow informs him that Billy's Oak was cut down seventy years ago, yet the sound is still heard.

### Characters
Titus Crow: In his first appearance, Crow is introduced as "a London-dwelling collector of obscure and eldritch volumes"--including a 400-year-old copy of the Cthäat Aquadingen, bound in human skin. He is engaged in unspecified "studying," largely nocturnal, because "he was better able to concentrate at night." He professes to  "believe in ghosts and fairies, in ghouls and genies, in a certain mythological ‘prop’ [i.e., the Necronomicon], and in the existence of Atlantis, R’lyeh, and G’harne.” Physically, he is described astall and broad-shouldered and it was plain to see that in his younger days he had been a handsome man. Now, though, his hair had greyed and his eyes, though they were still bright and observant, bore the imprint of many a year spent exploring—and often, I guessed, discovering—along rarely trodden paths of mysterious and obscure learning. The Bimini Glyphs are a series of occult carvings which exist in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos begun with the works of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview
A series of petroglyphs carved on a wall of the offshore construction known as the Bimini Wall, located near the Bimini Islands from which they take their name, the Bimini Glyphs are stated to have been carved in a larger scale than that which might be achieved by a human hand. The only translation of these engravings was by Larry Stanton, accomplished with the aid of the R'lyeh Text, but his work was later destroyed by his mentor Professor Maitland, who deemed the information too dangerous to be allowed to exist.

### Appearances
*"Down in Limbo" (1995, Robert M. Price)

The Bimini Islands are an island chain in the North Atlantic east of Florida that feature in stories of the fictional Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Description
Located near the Bahamas in the West Indies, Bimini comprises three islands, North Bimini, South Bimini and East Bimini. According to certain Mythos stories, advanced underwater constructions have been discovered off the coast of Bimini, leading some to speculate that it is home to a previously undiscovered - or perhaps extinct - intelligent species.

### The Bimini Road
A long series of stone blocks which create an undersea causeway, the Bimini Road has been carbon dated to be between six and twelve thousand years old, although Professor Sheldon believes them to be much older.

"Bitter Shadows" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Lisa Morton. It was published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.

### Synopsis
Georges Méliès, an aging filmmaker on a trip to try and rediscover his passion for life, meets a beautiful and enigmatic woman named Helen aboard the legendary passenger train the Orient Express. Helping her escape the attentions of a group of would-be assailants, after the men are apprehended by the authorities it emerges that Helen is in fact an international thief hired to steal an ancient totem, a carving of the monstrous Shaurash-Ho.

Coming to the realisation that the men, members a cult from Greenland whose origins date back to the age of Hyperborea, were actually trying to prevent the summoning of Shaurash-Ho, Helen takes her leave of Georges, and resolves to take her revenge on the deceitful client, but not before a bizarre occurrence causes the entity to notice Georges' involvement with the statue.

### Trivia
* Georges Méliès, full name Marie-Georges-Jean Méliès, was a real-life French filmmaker whose long and varied career did suffer a crisis during the time period in which the story is set. The causes for this included falling revenues from his films, the death of his first wife, and the destruction of many of his films at the hands of the French government during World War I.

Bizaamo is a kaiju in the fictional universe of the Ultraman Tiga television series by Tsuburaya Productions. 

### Background
Bizaamo is a genetically engineered life form which was originally created by extraterrestrials to save their world from the current depletion of oxygen. As an amoeba/plant hybrid, Bizaamo was able to convert the polluted atmosphere into oxygen and save the planet from extinction. Bizaamo used electricity to multiply itself and eventually developed intelligence but ended up going against its original purpose due to an error from its creation (the lack of "heart"). Due to the entity's ability to self-reproduce, the Bizaamos wiped out all life on the planet, reducing it to a dead world where even the Bizaamos were forced to go into a state of suspended animation, as a result of having no electricity to feed on. (: Forest of the White Fox) 

After the destruction of its homeworld, one of the Bizaamos arrived on Earth, where it was discovered in the South Pole. The specimen was taken to the GUTS headquarters, initially presenting itself as a benevolent entity who wanted to help humanity. However, this turned out to be a ruse, as Bizaamo's true intentions were to wipe out and replace all life on Earth, as Bizaamo was devoid of any compassion. Bizaamo kidnapped the GUTS member Horii and held him hostage, while draining electricity out of their base to multiply itself. After Horii sent the secret password to his teammates that allowed the base to use a backup source, the Bizaamos no longer had any power to feed off of. Although most of the Bizaamos were destroyed by the GUTS members, one of them managed to escape using the GUTS Wing 2, the fighter jet that was piloted by Rena. The Bizaamo headed towards an energy plant and absorbed enough electricity to transform into a more complex kaiju-like life form but would be defeated by Ultraman Tiga. (: "The Attacked GUTS Base")

### Notes
*Before they went extinct, it was stated that the inhabitants of Bizaamo's home planet wanted to benefit other worlds by sending Bizaamos into outer space. However, the Bizaamo that appears in the episode claims to have left after its home planet was destroyed, making it unclear how it arrived on Earth.
*It being named deliberately after its own home planet had been a staple for alien beings that appeared in the Ultraman Series, usually the naming sense being "Alien (home planet name)". However, Bizaamo is an artificial life form who wasn't a true native to its own home. It adopted the name of its home planet under orders from its creator so that those who discover the creature would know the name of its home planet.
*Its absorption of electricity to grow, multiply and even attaining a corporeal monster form is a carryover trait from its creator's race, who are also electricity-feeding beings and that his namesake planet was one where electricity current flow in

Bizarre Adventures Vol 1 #33 is an issue of the anthology series published by the Marvel Magazine Group in October 1982. It is notable to this wiki for two of the five stories contained within; the first being an original Cthulhu Mythos story, and the second introducing a character who would later be incorporated into the Mythos.

### "Tales of the Zombie!: Damballah's Deeds"
The story involves anti-hero Simon Garth, aka "The Zombie", tackling a pair of murderers in possession of a magic amulet which can control the dead. Among the Mythos elements made mention of are Von Juntz, Yog, and R'lyeh; Clarkashton and HPL are also both name-dropped.

### "Tomb of Dracula: The Blood Request"
The entity known as Varnae lays the groundwork for Dracula to become the future Lord of the Vampires

fullContent:
"Black Eons" is a short story by American author Robert M. Price with Robert E. Howard.

### Synopsis
A pair of archaeologists, Allison and Brill, unearth a temple in the Egyptian desert which Allison believes dates from the Hyborian Age. Later that evening, Allison dreams that he is a warrior sacking the city in which the temple once stood, and killing its high priest, a devotee of Gol-goroth who curses his immortal soul to be reincarnated until the priest may take his vengeance.

Awakening to find himself within the tomb, Allison realises that he is the owner of the warrior's soul, destined to once again face down the priest. His friend Brill attacks him, having been possessed by the priest, but Allison manages to kill him and destroy the priest's desiccated body before claiming the inner peace that has been denied him for millennia.

### Characters
* James Allison, a much-reincarnated soul currently in the body of a scholarly archaeologist.
* Bane, a Vanir tribesman in search of glory during the fall of the Stygian empire during the Hyborean Age.
* Koth-Serapis, a sorcerer-priest in the service of Gol-goroth during the Hyborian Age.
* Brill, an archaeologist and unwitting pawn of Koth-Serapis.

### Behind the Mythos
"Black Eons" was an unfinished and untitled fragment by Howard which was completed and named by Price. The protagonist, James Allison, is a recurrent character in the works of Howard.

The story contradicts other James Allison stories by Howard and others. In "Black Eons", Bane the Reaver is said to have been Allison's first life, whereas "The Valley of the Worm" takes place long before the Hyborian Age. Also in this story, Allison dies in the 1930s, while in Ghor, Kin-Slayer he survives into the 1960s or 70s.

* Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2009)

The Black Fan is a fictional artefact in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was created by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu RPG. It is described as an enchanted fan used to change the wearer's appearance. (: Masks of Nyarlathotep)

### Description
The Black Fan is used by the Bloated Woman, an avatar of Nyarlathotep in China, and is the namesake of her other name "Goddess of the Black Fan". When the enchanted fan is held under the Bloated Woman's eyes, her appearance changes to that of a slim and beautiful Chinese maiden. The fan can conceal even the massive bulk of her true form, and also draw all viewers' attention towards her eyes only. (: Masks of Nyarlathotep)

Black Forbidden Things: Cryptical Secrets from the “Crypt of Cthulhu” , published in 1992 by Starmont House, is a collection of material from the Lovecraftian fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu. Like the publication itself, it was edited by Robert M. Price. It serves as a sequel to the 1990 collection The Horror of It All.

The volume features literary criticism from leading Lovecraft scholars like Price, S. T. Joshi, Will Murray, and David E. Schultz. Two essays by Price that originally appeared in the publication Tekeli-li were included as complements to other pieces. The collection contains some fiction pieces, inclduing the original version of stories by William Lumley and Adolphe de Castro that were revised by Lovecraft. 

The title comes from a passage in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Haunter of the Dark": "They were the black, forbidden things which most sane people have never even heard of, or have heard of only in furtive, timorous whispers."

The Black Galleys are ominous trading ships that sail the Southern Sea of the Dreamlands under the power of triple banks of oars. They function as the cosmic link to the moon between the Basalt Pillars of the West. 

### Crew
The traders that interact with human merchants are Men of Leng, almost human slaves disguised with turbans to cover their two horns and shoes to extend their hooved feet. Despite this their wide mouths and sinister reputation lead to distrust in the human population. They are also responsible for the lighter jobs like steering and cooking.

Unknown to the humans the galleys trade with the officers, navigators and remarkably efficient rowers are all toad-like moon-beasts. At ports such as Dylath-Leen they remain below decks for weeks without buying any provisions and only emerge through the ship's hatches when they return to the moon.

### Trade
They give unique rubies to the bazaars of Dylath-Leen in exchange for gold and "fat black men of Parg whom they bought by the pound" which they took back with them to the moon. 

### Appearances
*The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, by H. P. Lovecraft
*The Clock of Dreams, by Brian Lumley

fullContent:
Black Helicopters is a novella by Caitlin R. Kiernan, part of her Tinfoil Dossier trilogy. It was first published as a Subterranean Press chapbook in 2013, then released in a considerably expanded form by Tor.com in 2018--so it may be considered either the first or the second book in the series, preceding or following Agents of Dreamland. 

The story involves the conflicts among secret agencies in the occult world over an outbreak of eldritch horror in Deer Isle, Maine, and over a weird science experiment involving twins.  

### Organizations
*Y: A secret agency fighting occult threats. Also known as Barbican Estates, named for a residential development in Central London. Its leader is the Commissioner; Ptolema is an agent for them.
*X: A shadowy organization known for the "miasma, the muddling aura that surrounds every last agent of the X." Seemingly more interested in creating occult threats than in fighting them.  They are described as quasi-Buddhist, mongrel Hindu, cyber-Shinto, Gnostic Thelemite worshippers at the shrines of Castaneda, Crowley, Camus, Blavatsky, Robert Anton Wilson, Velikovsky, Berlitz, Charles Fort, ad infinitum, a congregation based, possibly, in Saigon, or Calcutta, or Buenos Aires, or, more likely, nowhere at all.Led by a woman called Julia Set. They are responsible for Twisby's twinning experiments, and also apparently for turning Sixty-Six into an assassin.
*Albany: An agency that "has no official or unofficial title," though it's once referred to as the Other American Group. Called "Albany" because its headquarters are in the subbasement of the Erastus Corning Tower in Albany, New York: a "labyrinth of fluorescent lights and numbered doors" sometimes referred to as "the Ant Farm". They are "the men in black suits and tinfoil hats who answer to no one," "faceless, hollow men who crouch in the shadows beneath an Albany skyscraper and are ever on standby when this sort of s*** goes down". The Signalman is a high-ranking agent there.

### Characters
*Lizbeth and Elle Margeride: A set of twins (and also lovers), albinos with pale skin, "cornsilk hair", and "startling blue eyes". They are prodigies in paleontology as well as chess; in chess, Elle always plays white. They are also known as Ivoire and Bête, though which is which is unclear; obedience comes easily to Ivoire, unlike turbulent, seditious Bête". It's Ivoire who is sent to Deer Isle to combat the shoggoth invasion, and who develops a heroin addiction to cope with chronic pain. Both twins have psychic abilities; Bête manifests hers through origami. Later there is only one twin, who goes by a multitude of names, but she is sometimes known as the White Woman. She suggests she may be the "Second Coming of Jesus Christ. Or, it may be I’m the Anti-Christ. Shiva. Maitreya."
*Twisby: Also known as Thisby, her real name is Dr. Lane Dunham, PhD, MD; her degrees are in neurology and biopsychiatry, from Oxford and Yale. She had a high profile in the American Psychiatric Assoc

fullContent:
"Black Hill" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Orrin Grey, first published in the anthology Historical Lovecraft (2011, Innsmouth Free Press) .

### Synopsis
A successful American oilman purchases a plot of land believed by the indigenous people to be the home of something dark and sinister. Despite what he tells his workforce - that he expects to quickly strike a rich deposit of black gold - he shares the belief of the native people, and is determined to confront whatever lurks beneath the surface. Unfortunately for the man, the colossal entity tears open a rip in the bedrock, swallowing him whole before sealing itself back up in its subterranean lair.

### Mythos Connections
In his earlier life, the oilman claims to have met a deranged preacher who attempted to destroy one of his drilling operations; after killing the preacher, he found an ancient book in the man's possession. One of the lines in the book read in part "That is not dead which can eternal lie…", a famous quote of H. P. Lovecraft's often used when referring to creatures of the Cthulhu Mythos.

shortDefinition: "Black Letter Day" is a short story by author Ian Davey. It is the first part of his Bh'Yhlun series of post-apocalyptic Mythos fiction.  ### Synopsis In a post-apocalyptic future where the Old Ones and their Shoggoth servants rule the world, a survi...
fullContent:
"Black Letter Day" is a short story by author Ian Davey. It is the first part of his Bh'Yhlun series of post-apocalyptic Mythos fiction.

### Synopsis
In a post-apocalyptic future where the Old Ones and their Shoggoth servants rule the world, a survivor named Lucy recalls how the end of the world came about while attempting to make her way to Glastonbury, rumoured to be a place of great power and a refuge for survivors.

Through Lucy's musings we are told how her boyfriend Georgio, a filmmaker, came across a copy of Feery's Notes on the Necronomicon and, combined with pages from a copy of the original book held in the British Museum, devised and distributed a leather-bound promotional screenplay (titled Francesci's Cult of the Necronomicon), before filming a visual translation with Hollywood funding. When the film was screened, many of the viewers were driven insane, and their collective insanity caused the rebirth of the Old Ones.

The story ends with the revelation that the city of London, along with many of its inhabitants, has been transformed into a colossal living tower named Bh'Yhlun, whose purpose appears to be to "terraform" the Earth into a place more comfortable for the Old Ones.

### Characters
*Lucy, one of the few survivors of the apocalypse, now using a combination of narcotics to retain control of her sanity.
*Giorgio Francesci, a visionary filmmaker, subsumed into Bh'Yhlun at the end of days.
*Professor Stanley Pickman, a veteran cultist who aids Francesci in the creation of his work.

### Publication History
"Black Letter Day" was first published in Nightscapes #1 in June 1997, and later appeared in Dark Legacy #3 in January 1999.

### Trivia
*The mention of a riot during which many people disappeared in the Crouch End suburb of London is likely a nod to Stephen King's Mythos story "Crouch End".
*Although the servitors of the Old Ones are named Shoggoths, the creatures themselves bear little resemblance to the beings described by Lovecraft, being engineered by the Old Ones rather than the Elder Things, and seemingly having little to no ability to change their shape.

The Black Lotus is a fictional plant created by the late American author Robert E. Howard for his Hyborian Age stories featuring Conan the Cimmerian. It was first mentioned in "The Tower of the Elephant", but only as a source of poison. Its oneirogenic properties originate from the 1933 short story "The Slithering Shadow". The plant itself first appears in "Queen of the Black Coast", where Conan describes it as "the black lotus, whose juice was death, and whose scent brought dream-haunted slumber".

### Description
A mysterious plant with hallucinogenic and esoteric properties, the Black Lotus was notably cultivated in ancient Xuthal (: "The Slithering Shadow", Robert E. Howard), and prior to that in Acheron and Stygia (: "Dreams of the Black Lotus", Lin Carter). According to at least one source, it is still grown by the Tcho-Tcho People on the Plateau of Sung (: "Dope War of the Black Tong", Robert M. Price).

fullContent:
"Black Lotus" is a horror short story by Robert Bloch first published in 1935 in the magazine Unusual Stories. It was one of Bloch's earliest stories, and is connected to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Thousands of years ago, "in the days of the griffin and the fleet-winged unicorn", a Sultan named Genghir ruled over an ancient kingdom. Being a man of scholarly inclinations, he spent his days studying, and the nights in hedonistic pleasures, so that the actual governing was left to his Vizier, Hassim el Wadir, whose abuses and corruption led to chaos and revolt only made worse by the arrival of a plague that claimed the lives of two thirds of the population. Even then, Genghir remained indifferent to all that happened outside his palace. Eventually, nearly all the remaining subjects abandon him for other lands, taking all the treasures they can carry, and leaving Genghir alone in the middle of an empty city, where he retreats into a world of opium-induced dreams. When enough time passes and even opium proves unsatisfactory to relieve his ennui, he finds in one of his occult books a formula for a new drug derived from the mysterious black lotus, which can induce dreams so vivid as to "surpass reality, or blend with it in new and unhallowed ways".

Ignoring the book's warnings about the dangers posed by this drug, Genghir orders his three remaining servants to journey to the distant swamps where the black lotus grows and bring back a few samples. Only one of the three returns, now wearing a veil over his face for unrevealed reasons. A pleased Genghir extracts the drug from the lotus and promptly starts smoking it. His first dream seems to last centuries, as Genghir finds himself dead inside a tomb, feeling the passage of every second while his body slowly decomposes and his bones crumble to dust, leaving him as a disembodied consciousness trapped for what feels like an eternity. When he finally awakens, he consults the book and finds a passage claiming that "the first dream shall foretell that which is to come".

Despite this terrible experience, Genghir's lust for new sensations soon overcomes his fear and common sense, so he smokes the black lotus again. This time, he dreams that his head is swelling, giving him unbearable pain, and continues to swell impossibly until it bursts open like a rotten fruit, at which point he smells the fragrance of black lotuses. When he awakens, Genghir reads from the book that "the second dream shall show what might have been".

When he smokes for the third time, Genghir finds himself staring at a giant black lotus flower. Feeling danger, he reaches for the dagger that he carries on his belt. The black flower extends a petal and attacks him, grabbing him by the throat, so Genghir uses the dagger to cut it off. He wakes up just in time to realise that he has sliced his own throat and dies, while blood pours from his throat onto the pages of an open book that contains the sentence "the third dream brings reality".

The Black Man is an avatar of Nyarlathotep who coerces people into signing the Black Book of Azathoth. It has a prominent role in The Dreams in the Witch-House. 

### Appearance
The Black Man is usually portrayed as a dark-skinned bald man dressed in a robe. When traveling in the fourth dimension he looks like a large wisp. He leaves half-circle-shaped prints behind him, suggesting that he has hoofed feet. he can also appear as a pale-skinned man with very dark hair and dressed in a suit and top hat. The protagonist of the story "The Peabody Heritage" describes him as a "monstrous black man, not a black man, but a man of blackness such that he was literally darker than night, but with blazing eyes, as if they were made of fire".

### The Book of Azathoth
The main mission of the Black Man is to recruit acolytes by having them sign the Book of Azathoth with their blood. Those who do this swear eternal allegiance to Azathoth and Nyarlathotep, then being obligated to serve them until the end of days.

To gather acolytes, this avatar of Nyarlathotep enlisted the help of the witch Keziah Mason and Brown Jenkin, Keziah's animalistic familiar.

Another method of attracting greater numbers of less faithful acolytes used by the Black Man is to gather large masses of people captivating them with shows and modern gadgets and then brainwash them by showing them miracles and resorting to demagoguery.

### The Black Man of Witchcraft and Folk Lore
Keziah Mason references The Black Man in the H.P. Lovecraft short story "The Dreams in the Witch House."

As a witch herself and clearly one steeped in the Lovecraftian version of the Salem Witch Trials, Mason is referring to the figure from folklore and putative 'black magic' occultism in which a dark or black figure of a man appears during orgies or rituals. This figure either conducts the ceremonies or is present to witness or carry out the signing over of a witch's soul to the Devil or other dark malevolent non human intelligence in return for the granting of status in the witchcraft cult or magical power.She had spoken also of the Black Man, of her oath, and of her new secret name of Nahab. Then she had drawn those devices on the walls of her cell and vanished.

-The Dreams in the Witch House, H.P. Lovecraft

### The Great Horned One
In Ramsey Campbell's story "The Faces at Pine Dunes," a character known as "The Great Horned One" is featured. He is also associated with covens and witches and seems to be linked in some way to the Black Man. However, this similarity could be a simple coincidence, as there is no clarification on this point. It is possible, however, that he is related to another of Nyarlathotep's avatars, The Horned Man (source/reason?).

"Black Man with a Horn" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author T. E. D. Klein.

### Synopsis
An ageing and unnamed member of Howard Phillips Lovecraft's circle one day has a chance encounter with a former missionary to Malaysia. The man relates his dealings with the remote Tcho-Tcho tribesmen, and how his contact with them led him to become the target of a supernatural being.

When the man later turns up dead, the narrator decides to investigate, and discovers that many of the people who had come into contact with the missionary have met their end. As whatever the evil is closes in on him, he sits down to write his account and await his fate…

### Characters
* The Unnamed Narrator, an elderly author who has spent his career in Lovecraft's shadow.
* Ambrose Mortimer, a religious man who has fallen foul of dark forces.
* Maude, the narrator's sister.
* Shugoran, an avatar of Nyarlathotep.

### Publication History
"Black Man with a Horn" was first published in the Ramsey Campbell-edited anthology New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos by Arkham House in 1980. It has since been reprinted many times, and has also been translated into German, French and, Finnish.

fullContent:
Black Noon is an unfinished novella by the late American author C.M. Eddy, Jr. 

### Synopsis
Black Noon has as its central conceit a fictionalized version of Eddy ("Biff Briggs") and H. P. Lovecraft ("Robert Otis Mather" or "ROM" for short) seeking (but not finding) a town called Granville, during which search the H. P. Lovecraft stand-in faces death several times. His near-death "accidents" are not really accidents at all and it is clear, before the unfinished work ends, that something means to frustrate their quest.

### Behind the Mythos
Black Noon was based on the real-life search for the legendary location known as The Dark Swamp, undertaken by Eddy and Lovecraft in August of 1923. The Dark Swamp was one of the inspirations for the early part of Lovecraft's story "The Colour Out of Space".

### Publication History
Black Noon was included in the anthologies Exit into Eternity: Tales of the Bizarre and Supernatural (1973, 2000) and Acolytes of Cthulhu (2001).

### Trivia
*The story features Eddy's fictional town of Fenham which is also used in some of his other stories, chief among them "The Loved Dead".

The Black Rites are a fictional text invented by Robert Bloch, attributed by Bloch to his character Luveh-Keraphf, a thinly veiled allusion to Bloch's friend H. P. Lovecraft.

The Black Rites are first mentioned in Bloch’s "The Suicide in the Study" (1935), where a copy is owned by the wizard James Allington. They are described as being written by "the mad poet Luveh-Keraphf, priest of Bast."

The book comes up again in "The Grinning Ghoul" (1936), where Bloch refers to it as "the grotesque Black Rites of mystic Luveh-Keraph, the priest of cryptic Bast."

The Black Rituals of Koth-Serapis is an ancient compendium of evil magic written by the Hyperborean sorcerer Koth-Serapis during the days of Acheron.

### Contents
The majority of its contents are unknown, but its study was frowned upon during the Hyperborean age, and still is in modern times.

### Known Contents
* Details on the usage and benefits of the Black Lotus as a narcotic.

### Copies

### Hyperborean Age
*The sorcerer Eibon was known to possess a copy written on papyrus scrolls.

### Others
*In the modern day, occult detective Anton Zarnak keeps a copy in his library, although how faithful to the original it may be is unknown, as it is bound as an actual book and written in Egyptian hieroglyphics.

The Black Sphinx, also known as the Unknown God of the Dead, is a fictional monster created by H. P. Lovecraft for the short story "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs", ghostwritten for Harry Houdini.

### Overview
The Beast is a huge being similar to a sphinx, with an indescribable face. Originally, the Sphinx of Giza had the face of this creature, but it was re-sculpted by Khephren. Its size is phenomenal, a single paw being as large as a hippopotamus. The paws are covered in yellowish fur and have five toes with retractable claws.

The Beast inhabits the underground of the Great Pyramid, where it is venerated by the sect of the Children of the Sphinx, led by Khephren and Nitocris.

In the story "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs", the magician Harry Houdini observes the immense paw of this creature, receiving offerings from the Children of the Sphinx. Initially, Houdini mistakes the paw for a faceless monster, with five jaws distributed asymmetrically from which retractable rigid tentacles or beaks emerge. It is only after he catches a glimpse of the entire creature that he realizes that the "monster" was just one of its paws, and the five "heads" with rigid tentacles were merely five toes with claws. He ends up convincing himself that the entire experience was nothing more than a nightmare.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite the reveal at the end of the story, that what the protagonist mistook for a five-headed monster was nothing more than the paw of the Black Sphinx, the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu depicts this creature as actually having a mouth at the tip of each toe. The game makes a distinction between the Black Sphinx and the Beast, which is an avatar of Nyarlathotep associated with the Sphinx.

The Black Sphinx is identified as one of the Million Favoured Ones. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

Black Star Magic is a gamebook supplement for Pelgrane Press's Yellow Mythos roleplaying game The Yellow King. Written by Robin D. Laws, Sarah Saltiel, Gareth Ryder-Hanrahan, and Ruth Tillman, it was published in both print and digital editions.

### Overview


Black Star Magic introduces advanced rules for using magic in The Yellow King, along with a large selections of spells. Additionally, four complete stand-alone scenarios are included.

### Scenarios
*"Dancer at the Bone Cabaret": Parisian artists face off against evil nightlife.
*"A Casket at Le Thil": paranormal warriors venture into a village with a dark underworld.
*"Memories of a Dream Clown": revolutionaries must face a dark memory.
*"Love Wears No Mask": a mobile app has a sanity-shattering effect.

fullContent:
"Black Tallow" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Edward M. Erdelac.

### Synopsis
When Raymond, a specialist in translating ancient texts, is contacted by his old friend Paul, a successful businessman who wishes to pay him seven million dollars to translate a ritualistic text, he jumps at the chance.

However, while translating the text at Paul's house, Raymond slowly comes to the realisation that in preparation for enacting the ritual - which he believes will allow him to commune with Yog-Sothoth and Azathoth amongst others, and grant him ultimate knowledge of the universe - Paul has murdered his wife and daughter, and rendered them down into tallow for devotional candles.

In the meantime, Paul takes the translation but imperfectly completes the rite, and is consumed by an entity from beyond. 

### Characters

*Raymond, a scholarly but poor man in his middle age.
*Paul Woodson, Raymond's former college roommate, now head of a successful multinational.

### Publication History
"Black Tallow" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu by April Moon Books in March 2014.

fullContent:
"Black Veins" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Carlton Herzog. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long-running horror magazine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
After a highly-successful crime spree, a petty criminal taking Brooklyn's G line home witnesses a bizarre conflict between the servitors of two opposing dark masters. One is an obese yet extremely agile man with a frog-like visage and prehensile tongue, while his opponents are a pair of clawed humanoids with heads resembling octopuses. The frog-man wins the battle, dispatching both of his opponents through use of a magical amulet, while the criminal quickly takes his leave.

Shortly afterwards, the man navigates the city streets to complete his journey and bears witness to several acts of insanity which he believes goes above and beyond usual occurrences in New York. He begins to speculate that perhaps the creatures were the cause of these events, a "trickledown effect from some greater cosmic conflict."

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos, the appearance and abilities of the entities which battled aboard the subway train would seem to imply that they were servitors of the Great Old Ones Tsathoggua and Cthulhu.

The Black Whore (also known as Abigail Dexter) is a fictional character created by American author Kevin L. O'Brien for his 2006 short story "October Surprise".

### History
After merging with Doctor Ambrose Dexter and turning him into a new avatar for himself, Nyarlathotep impregnated Dexter’s wife with his own seed; the resultant child, Abigail Dexter, would therefore be Nyarlathotep's avatar from birth.

As an adult, Abigail earned her doctorate in nuclear physics and took a post with the United States government. She then masterminded a plot to detonate a nuclear weapon underwater to destroy a Deep One city; this fulfilled the schemes' primary goal of cracking an Elder Sign which held the Great Old One Cthaeghya in imprisonment. (: "October Surprise")

Abigail Dexter's current whereabouts are unknown.

fullContent:
"Blacked Out" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by British horror writer Ramsey Campbell.

### Synopsis
A man named Lamb travelling across the German countryside takes a room in a picture-perfect village with one small quirk: all of the lights are on, even though it’s daytime. As night begins to descend, the villagers stage a honey trap to lure Lamb out into the street before locking all of their doors to prevent him from going inside. Soon Lamb sees a blanket of darkness extinguishing the lights, and travelling in his direction. He has no choice but to risk a long dash through the pitch-black fields in the hope that the light of the moon, shining on a nearby ridge, will be his salvation.

### Characters
* Lamb, an English-speaking tourist on a road trip through Germany.
* The girl, a pretty young villager who uses her charms to lure Lamb outside.

### Publication History
"Blacked Out" was first published in Ramsey Campbell's Mythos collection Cold Print in 1985.

Blandot is a fictional character who appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's 1921 short story "The Music of Erich Zann."

### Overview
Blandot was a landlord who ran a boarding house on the liminal street known as the Rue d'Auseil in an unnamed French city. The musician Erich Zann and the unnamed narrator of the story both resided at the boarding house before the entire street and its inhabitants mysteriously vanished as though they never existed, including Blandot. The narrator himself only barely escaped.

What Blandot's ultimate fate was remains a mystery.

The Blasted Heath is a fictional locale created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1927 short science fiction/horror story "The Colour Out of Space."

### Description
Located somewhere to the west of Arkham, Massachusetts, prior to the events related in "The Colour Out of Space," the Blasted Heath was an area of land centring on a functioning farm owned by one Nahum Gardner, who lived there with his wife and three sons. The farm appeared to produce mostly fruit and vegetables, such as pears, apples, melons, and tomatoes.

Post-"Colour," Lovecraft described the Blasted Heath as "five acres of grey desolation that sprawled open to the sky like a great spot eaten by acid in the woods and fields." (: "The Colour Out of Space")

### History
In June 1882, the Gardner farm became the subject of much local gossip and a degree of scientific interest when an unusual meteorite made planetfall there.

In the wake of the landing, the land, as well as the plants and animals which inhabited it - including the human residents - began to undergo bizarre changes. In the case of the vegetation, this resulted in oversized crops which outwardly appeared to be lush and delicious, but were rendered inedible by their foul taste, described as being "bitter and sickish;" the fauna underwent physical changes which made them appear deformed and perhaps even frightening to behold; while the humans devolved into hideous creatures tainted by madness. In the aftermath, the area became shunned by the locals, and was henceforth known as the Blasted Heath.

Decades later, the area was surveyed as a site upon which to construct a new reservoir to provide Arkham with its drinking water; whether this came to pass is not confirmed in Lovecraft’s story, but it would appear likely, as no objection which might be accepted by reasonable men of science was offered by the narrator of the tale. (: "The Colour Out of Space")

The Blemmyes are part of Greco-Roman mythology, the names given to them meaning Headless Men. Chaosium first used them in 2009 for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Background
The Blemmyes are children of Y'golonac, whom during the times of the Romans were found in the lands of Kush, Numidia, Egypt, and Africa Proconsularis. Blemmyes are a nomadic race of warriors, that expanded the cult of Y'golonac and sacrificed those that resisted.

### Behind the Mythos
Similar creatures named Bhlemphroims inhabit the planet Saturn in Clark Ashton Smith's Hyperborea story "The Door to Saturn".

The Young of the Black Goat or Gof'nn hupadgh Shub-Niggurath, also known as Blessed of Shub-Niggurath or goblins, are a fictional race from Ramsey Campbell's 1964 short story "The Moon-Lens". They were expanded on by Chaosium in 1994 for their Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

### Overview
Servants and priests of Shub-Niggurath, the Gof’nn Hupadgh are a mutant race, resembling satyrs of myth. Indeed, historically, they have been associated or mistaken for the hedonistic pagan god Pan. As such, these creatures have formed the basis of many myths and legends, including those concerning woodland goblins and other fairy-type folk. Communities of Gof’nn Hupadgh may be found hidden living apart from civilization, with those seeming more human treating with nearby villages while the less than human elements of such groups remain hidden. Thus, a community can exist at the fringes of society, allowing them to conduct their unholy rites to Shub-Niggurath free from constraint.

Separate but kin to the Gof ’nn Hupadgh are those who were once human but who have been transformed by tasting of the milk of Shub-Niggurath. Unlike the Gof ’nn Hupadgh, these are usually lone individuals or small groups, rather than the bloodlines of entire communities. Such changelings tend to be known as “satyrs” rather than Gof ’nn Hupadgh. Once the milk of Shub-Niggurath has been consumed by a human, it enters the bloodstream and provokes changes at a cellular level, triggering the mutation. The person is changed into a half-human-half-monstrous thing. Depending on the blessing granted by Shub-Niggurath, satyrs may take a greater or lesser form. Most often, as the physical mutation takes hold, the person gains certain animalistic features, such as that of a goat, bird, pig, dog, or other animal, and tend to act in manner commensurate with the animal they manifest as. Such hybrids of humanity and animal may account for the folklore concerning creatures like werewolves, the Jersey Devil, Skunk Ape, and so on. As the mutation reaches fruition, the human mind sinks into madness while the body mutates into a mass of riotous flesh. At this point, such folk are no longer recognizable as human or animal in any way, being utterly insane and devoid of purpose other than to consume and reproduce. While lesser satyrs may retain some human aspects of appearance, greater satyrs tend to be monstrous aberrations.

The Bloated Woman, also known as the Goddess of the Black Fan, is a fictional entity created by American games designer Scott David Aniolowski for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. She made her first appearance in the critically acclaimed 1984 scenario supplement Masks of Nyarlathotep.

### Overview
An avatar of Nyarlathotep active in and around China, the Bloated Woman is described as "a 600 pound, seven-foot-tall being vaguely resembling an obese human female, with tentacles in place of arms and nose, five perfect cupids-bow mouths made hideous by clusters of protruding tangs, and wearing a yellow-and-black tunic of a material resembling fine silk, in the belt of which hang six sickles and the mystic Black Fan". However, the fan allows her to project the appearance of a beautiful young Asian woman: without it, she reverts to her "natural" appearance.

### Cult


She is worshipped by the Order of the Bloated Woman, a historical organisation which has been in her service for millennia.

"Bloodborn in Sarandë" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Patrick Garratt which takes place in Modiphius Entertainment's Achtung! Cthulhu horror roleplaying setting. It was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius in 2015.

### Synopsis
A British diver-turned-spy during the Second World War embarks on a secret mission to the Mediterranean, but is inexplicably drawn to the coast of Albania where the Greek army is laying seige to entrenched elements of the Albanian armed forces.

On site, he meets up with a cabal of Black Sun sorcerers in league with Nazi Germany and his father, and discovers that he is the intended victim in a sacrifice to their dark god. When the ritual is complete, a horde of tiny demons called Bloodborn are unleashed upon the unsuspecting Greeks. Fortunately for them, a band of Albanian partisans are on hand, and manage to destroy the diminutive creatures by shooting the tanks of the Greek's flamethrowers and burning them to cinders.

In the aftermath, the leader of the cabal is able to make his escape and report his failure to his masters. Sadly, their inability to route the besieging forces causes the Führer to sign orders which will unleash the full fury of the Nazi war machine on the Greeks, resulting in over three years of fascist occupation.

shortDefinition: Bloodborne is an action role-playing game (RPG) developed by FromSoftware and published by Sony Computer Entertainment. Released exclusively for the PlayStation 4 in March 2015, Bloodborne is renowned for its challenging gameplay, intricate world-bui...
fullContent:
Bloodborne is an action role-playing game (RPG) developed by FromSoftware and published by Sony Computer Entertainment. Released exclusively for the PlayStation 4 in March 2015, Bloodborne is renowned for its challenging gameplay, intricate world-building, and deep, enigmatic lore. Directed by Hidetaka Miyazaki, the game is a spiritual successor to FromSoftware's Dark Souls series, but it distinguishes itself with a faster-paced combat system and a setting heavily inspired by Gothic horror and Lovecraftian themes.

### Setting and Story
Bloodborne is set in the decrepit, Gothic city of Yharnam, a place afflicted by a mysterious blood-borne disease that has turned many of its inhabitants into horrific beasts. The player assumes the role of a Hunter, who arrives in Yharnam in search of a cure for their affliction. The story unfolds as the Hunter delves deeper into the city's secrets, uncovering a dark history filled with ancient blood rituals, nightmarish creatures, and cosmic horrors.

The narrative is deliberately obscure, told through environmental storytelling, item descriptions, and cryptic dialogues with non-player characters (NPCs). As the Hunter explores Yharnam and its surrounding areas, they discover that the blood disease is connected to eldritch beings and the pursuit of forbidden knowledge by scholars and churches, leading to a layered and complex story that players must piece together.

### Gameplay
Bloodborne features a third-person perspective with an emphasis on exploration, combat, and character progression. The gameplay shares similarities with FromSoftware's Dark Souls series but introduces several key differences:

* Combat: Combat in Bloodborne is fast-paced and aggressive, encouraging players to take the initiative rather than adopting a defensive playstyle. The game emphasizes dodging, quick reflexes, and precise timing. The absence of shields, a staple of Dark Souls, reinforces the need for offensive tactics. The "Rally" mechanic allows players to regain lost health by striking back immediately after taking damage, further incentivizing aggressive gameplay.
* Weapons: Players can equip a variety of melee weapons, many of which have "trick" forms, allowing them to switch between two different modes (e.g., a one-handed sword that transforms into a two-handed greatsword). Firearms, typically used in the off-hand, play a crucial role in parrying enemies and interrupting their attacks.
* Exploration and Level Design: Yharnam and its surrounding areas are intricately designed, with interconnected levels that encourage exploration and reward players with shortcuts, hidden items, and lore. The game features multiple branching paths, secret areas, and optional bosses, enhancing replayability.

Blupes are a fictional species created by Sandy Petersen and featured in the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, in which they're classified as a lesser servitor race.

### Description
Blupes are translucent creatures that float through the air and glow faintly in the dark. Their bodies are elliptical in shape, with rubbery fin-like protuberances giving them a "wingspan" of about 3 ft (~ 91 cm). They produce a distinctive "clean odor", similar to the smell associated with storms and heavy rains. In terms of disposition, they have been described as "friendly".

Blupes originate from the Dark Dimension, an otherworldly realm described as "an opaline plane where light radiates as blackness and shadows have wavelengths". Within the Dark Dimension, they inhabit the Cire Enicar area, where the atmosphere is composed almost entirely of water vapour.

While they can be summoned to both the Waking World and the Dreamlands, Blupes are extremely vulnerable to dehydration, and rarely survive for more than 10 to 15 days away from their natural habitat. Although keeping them in humid areas or underwater will allow them to last longer, Blupes can neither feed nor breed outside of the Dark Dimension.

Blupes are naturally drawn towards fire, which is extinguished as soon as the Blupe touches it, dousing the flames upon contact. However, the Blupe itself might also be destroyed in the process of extinguishing the flames. While harmless to most species, contact with a Blupe can be fatal to some forms of life, such as the Fire Vampires and the Minions of Karakal. (: S. Petersen's Field Guide to Creatures of the Dreamlands)

"Boat Trip" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author David A. Riley. It was first published in The 3rd Spectral Book of Horror Stories by Tickety Boo Press in 2016.

### Synopsis
Two down-on-their-luck fisherman and their boat are hired by a pair of Jesuit priests from a secretive order dedicated to combatting the insidious Esoteric Order of Dagon. Travelling to the middle of the English Channel, they succeed in delivering a biological weapon into a nest of fish-like humanoids.

Days later, dying from whatever horrific contagion has been released upon them, the oceanic monstrosities track down the ship's captain and his wife, murdering the two as a small measure of vengeance.

Bob Eggleton (born 1960) is an American artist known for his science fiction and fantasy illustrations, and has provided the cover art for numerous Cthulhu Mythos anthologies.

A fan of giant monsters in general, Eggleton's work often features dragons, dinosaurs, or other similar creatures. In addition to the Cthulhu Mythos, he has illustrated books and comics for the Godzilla franchise, and created the cover art for dozens of novels and collections by authors such as Brian Lumley, Alan Dean Foster, Edgar Rice Burroughs, Robert A. Seaman Bohm is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Temple".

### Overview
Bohm served aboard the German submarine U-29 under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich during the First World War. As a result of the supernatural events experienced by the crew, both Bohm and Seaman Schmidt became sick and lapsed into violent insanity. Their constant ravings concerning a "terrible curse" upon the submarine led Heinrich to execute them in order to maintain discipline. (: "The Temple")

Bokrug, The Great Water Lizard, is a fictional deity created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1920 short story "The Doom That Came to Sarnath", which is considered part of his Dream Cycle.

In the expanded Mythos, Bokrug is sometimes portrayed as a Great Old One (: Call of Cthulhu), or as a Lesser Old One subservient to the Great Old One Mnomquah (: "Something in the Moonlight", "Behind the Mask").

### Description
Bokrug is the lake-dwelling god of the semi-amphibian Thuum'ha ("Voiceless Ones") of Ib in the land of Mnar. The deity sleeps beneath the calm waters of a lake that bordered Ib and the city of Sarnath. When the humans of Sarnath cruelly slaughtered the populace of Ib and stole the god's idol, the great deity stirred. Each year thereafter, strange ripples reportedly disturbed the otherwise placid lake. On the one-thousandth anniversary of Ib's destruction, Bokrug rose up and utterly destroyed the city of Sarnath, so completely that not even ruins remained. Afterwards, the Thuum'ha race recolonised Ib and thenceforth lived undisturbed.

### In the Expanded Mythos

In Brian Lumley's "The Sister City" and Beneath the Moors, Bokrug is reinterpreted as a species, rather than a single deity. According to these tales, the Bokrug came to colonise Earth in ancient times, bringing along the voiceless Thuun'ha who worshiped them. The Bokrug life cycle is similar to that of the Ghouls, as they send their children to the surface world to be raised by humans. Like Deep One hybrids, the Bokrug look mostly human until they reach a point in their lives in which they start mutating and develop an urge to abandon the human world and rejoin their own species.

### In Other Media 
*Bokrug (given the alternate spelling of "Bokrag") appears as a water-based kaiju in the Japanese television series Ultraman Gaia. Like its namesake, Bokrag takes the form of a reptilian creature; thanks to his body being mostly water, he also has the ability to regenerate from almost any attack, as well as being invisible to radar.
*Bokrug appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
*Bokrug appears in the trading card game Battle Spirits, under the name Bokrugar.

Bolton is a town in Massachusetts that is mentioned in the fiction of H. P. Lovecraft. While there is a real Bolton in central Massachusetts, Lovecraft's Bolton is often thought to be a separate, fictional town located in Lovecraft Country.(by who?)

### In the Real World
The real-world town of Bolton is Massachusetts' Worcester County, to the west of Boston and a considerable distance from the real and imaginary communities in Essex County that constitute Lovecraft Country. It was incorporated in 1738 and has never been a large place; the censuses from 1900 to 1940 each recorded a population in the 700s. An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia notes that "in HPL's day Bolton was a tiny agricultural hamlet with no industries of significance."

The location of the real Bolton features in the debate over whether Lovecraft originally conceived of Arkham as being in central Massachusetts before placing in the northeastern part of the state.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Bolton appears first and most prominently in Lovecraft's "Herbert West--Re-Animator," where it's introduced as a "neighbouring town" to Arkham, where a circus manager denies that any of his animals could be responsible for the rampages that turn out to be the work of the reanimated Allan Halsey.

Later, after Herbert West and the narrator have graduated from Miskatonic University's medical school, they set up practice in Bolton, described as "a factory town near Arkham, the seat of the college." It's home to the Bolton Worsted Mills, "the largest in the Miskatonic Valley," and the new doctors set up shop in the factory district, as the mill's "polyglot employees are never popular as patients with the local physicians." 

They move into "a rather run-down cottage near the end of Pond Street" with no close neighbors, conveniently located near a source of material for West's experiments: It's "separated from the local potter’s field by only a stretch of meadow land, bisected by a narrow neck of the rather dense forest which lies to the north."

Boxing was outlawed in Bolton, due to "the prevailing spirit of Puritanism," but secret and illegal bouts were common there. Nevertheless, it's said that "Bolton had a surprisingly good police force for so small a town," a fact that gave West and his companion no little worry.

Bolton comes up again in "The Rats in the Walls," where it's the hometown of the narrator, Delapore, the New England business owner who restores Exham Priory. The mill town is representative of "the greyness of Massachusetts business life" that is Delapore's immediate background.

Lovecraft's final reference to Bolton comes in "The Colour Out of Space," where the phosphorescence of the Gardner farm is first noticed by "a timid windmill salesman from Bolton who drove by one night in ignorance of the country legends." The Bolton Worsted Mills are fictional industrial facilities created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his 1922 short story "Herbert West--Reanimator".

### Overview
A  group of textile manufacturing plants in the fictional factory town of Bolton, Massachusetts, the Mills were located near Arkham (worsted refers to a type of cloth). They were the largest such mills in the Miskatonic Valley. The immigrant workers were described as a rough and tumble bunch, and enjoyed competing in secret boxing matches since the sport was outlawed in Bolton. One of the workers, a man named Buck Robinson, was killed in one of these secret matches. His body was used by Herbert West as a test subject for his experiments involving the reanimation of the dead. (: "Herbert West--Reanimator")

"Bonanza" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Sam Gafford. It forms part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by the late C. J. Henderson.

### Synopsis
When ex-cop and former Arkham Detective Agency employee Mike Dolan is tricked into hunting down the Shining Trapezohedron for a dangerous hoodlum, a monstrous creature breaks into our dimension before being beaten back by the intervention of the Agency.

### Characters

*Mike Dolan, a down-on-his-luck man who has an unhealthy obsession with Anna. Is re-hired by Frank Nardi at the story's conclusion.
*Anna Eliza Cordell, a femme fatale and girlfriend of Big Phil.
*Frank Nardi, a private detective and senior partner in the Arkham Detective Agency.
*"Big Phil" McGurk, a gangster who collects mystical artefacts for unknown reasons.
*Wilson Monahan, an elderly man who was for a time in possession of the Shining Trapezohedron.
*Tony Balnco (reference only), a former partner in the Agency, deceased at the time the story takes place.

### Publication History
"Bonanza" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited thematic anthology Arkham Detective Agency (for which it was written) in November 2017.

Bones (real name unknown, but used the alias of Bobby Anderson) is a character created by American author Armand Rosamilia for his Keyport Cthulhu series of Mythos stories.

### Description
A heavy-set former gang member, Bones has a tremendous capacity for violence, but has also displayed great compassion when dealing with those in need. He possesses a seemingly supernatural ability to judge the character of others, although he believes it only works on around 25% of those he meets.

### History

### Keyport Cthulhu
In the first book of the series, Bones stole a mysterious artefact which his biker club had been hired to obtain before going on the run from his former associates under a false identity. He eventually found himself in the degenerate town of Keyport where he discovered the sinister Esoteric Order of Dagon, which was trying to awaken the Great Old One Cthulhu. Joining forces with a ragtag group of people who were fighting back against the cult, he succeeded in saving a girl named Tina from becoming a human sacrifice, but his own life was hanging in the balance at the book's conclusion.

### Appearances

Bones of the Yopasi is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by British author Graham McNeill, the second in his Dark Waters trilogy, which takes place in the Arkham Horror setting. Running to a total of 345 pages, it was published by Fantasy Flight Games in August 2012.

### Overview


### Synopsis
When news of a Cthulhu cultist's attempt to retrieve a mystical artefact known as the Eye of Infinite Stars in an attempt to raise his dark master from his sleep reaches them, Professors Oliver Grayson and Alexander Templeton must reunite with reporter Rex Murphy to combat the threat. Travelling to the decrepit fishing village of Kingsport, they are aided in their quest by Silas Marsh, a fisherman and near-pariah due to his unusual appearance, and the elderly scholar George Gammell Angell. There, the group hears of a recent phenomena which has been occurring off the coast: the wrecks of long-sunken ships inexplicably rising to the surface.

During their investigations, they are approached by Luke Robinson, a man returned from the Dreamlands who brings a message from former colleague Henry Cartwright, who he believes is dying yet possesses the knowledge to aid them in their quest. Travelling to the Dreamlands, the group restore Cartwright's sanity in the waking world, but are unable to contact him upon their return to reality due to other pressing concerns.

Hiring a small fishing vessel, the group make their way to the last sighting of the mysterious lights and risen ships; sure enough, when they arrive, the ocean is littered with risen reefs and rotten hulks. Locating and boarding the one they believe to be the resting place of the artefact the require, they are shocked to discover that Templeton, a man long thought to be their ally, is in fact the cultist, and he makes off with the Eye atop a bizarre creature, leaving the others to their fate at the hands of a horde of Deep Ones. Although the crew of the fishing boat are slaughtered, the others are saved at the last moment by a white ship from the Dreamlands.

In the aftermath, the survivors go into hiding, determining anonymity to be their greatest asset while they decide their next moves.

### Mythos References
Bones of the Yopasi is littered with references to the Arkham Horror setting and the Cthulhu Mythos in general. These include:

*Lighthouse keeper Basil Elton, who plays a supporting role, and finally finds forgiveness and a place aboard the White Ship, allowing him return to the Dreamlands.
*A trip to Miskatonic University during which Henry Armitage allows the investigators to read a passage from the Necronomicon.
*When dreamer Luke Robinson is attacked by eldritch entities spawned from a green flame, he names his assailants as the "worms of Tulscha."
*Luke also mentions that he was trained in the art of dreaming by one Randolph Carter.
*Ma's Boarding House and St. Mary's Hospital, both recurrent locations in the Arkham cityscape, are made mention of.

fullContent:
"Boojum" is a short story by Elizabeth Bear and Sarah Monette that first appeared in the anthology Fast Ships, Black Sails (Night Shade Books, 2008). It is the first of three stories in the Boojumverse, a series that blends the Cthulhu Mythos and the bestiary of Lewis Carroll in a space opera setting.

"Boojum" tells the story of the boojum Lavinia Whateley--an enormous spacefaring creature that serves as a liveship for a crew of (mostly) human space pirates--and Black Alice Bradley, a member of her engineering crew who comes to love her. Trouble comes when the pirates loot a cargo of Mi-Go brain cannisters; when the owners come to reclaim what's theirs, Black Alice is forced to make a desperate choice.

### Boojums
“‘But oh, beamish nephew, beware of the day,

If your Snark be a Boojum! For then

You will softly and suddenly vanish away,

And never be met with again!’"

--Lewis Carroll, "The Hunting of the Snark"Boojums are a gigantic race of "deep-space swimmer[s]"; they "evolved in the high tempestuous envelopes of gas giants, and their offspring still spent their infancies there, in cloud-nurseries over eternal storms." They don't name themselves, so are given names by the humans who use them as liveships. 

The Lavinia Whateley (named for the mother in "The Dunwich Horror") was born over Uranus. She looks "like a vast spiny lionfish to the earth-adapted eye. Her sides were lined with gasbags filled with hydrogen; her vanes and wings furled tight. Her color was a blue-green so dark it seemed a glossy black unless the light struck it; her hide was impregnated with symbiotic algae." Vinnie, as she is affectionately known to her crew, has many teeth, "the diamond edges worn to a glitter," and "dozens of bright sapphire eyes"; she bears "an ugly ring of scars where the Henry Ford had bitten her." Her interior smells of ozone and nutmeg.

Another Boojum mentioned in the story--besides the bitey Henry Ford--is the Marie Curie, who is reputed to have eaten her crew.

Boojums are named for the creatures in Lewis Carroll's "The Hunting of the Snark"; They have "big wet eyes" and communicate through "fingersigns" and other gestures.

### Characters
* Black Alice Bradley: After "working in the sunstone mines on Venus," she signed up with crew of the Lavinia Whateley "back in ’32, after the Venusian Riots." She is considered "reliable," since "she didn’t smoke hash and she didn’t cheat at cards." As she "couldn’t hit the broad side of a space freighter with a ray gun," she works in Engineering. She is a mostly self-taught engineer, whose "implants were second-hand, black market, scavenged, the wet work done by a gilly on Providence Station."  And she "loved her ship."
*Captain Song: The captain of the Lavinia Whateley. She is widely feared; everyone remembers how she keelhauled a crewmember, and after since a fellow pirate captain double-crossed her, she's kept his head in a jar.  She is a pragmatist; she "didn’t mind other people worrying about souls, s

The Boojumverse is a fictional setting for a series of short stories written by Elizabeth Bear and Sarah Monette. The stories combine elements of the Cthulhu Mythos with the bestiary of Lewis Carroll in a space opera setting.  

### Stories
*"Boojum" (2008)
*"Mongoose" (2009)
*"The Wreck of the Charles Dexter Ward" (2012)

### Creatures
Bear and Monette's Boojumverse features a number of alien creatures, some derived from the Mythos, some with names from Lewis Carroll, and at least one monster combining both.

### Boojums
Boojums, introduced in the short story "Boojum", are titanic creatures at home in outer space, used by humans as living spaceships. The gigantic race of "deep-space swimmer[s]" "evolved in the high tempestuous envelopes of gas giants, and their offspring still spent their infancies there, in cloud-nurseries over eternal storms." They don't name themselves, so are given names by the humans who use them as liveships.

The Lavinia Whateley (the liveship featured in "Boojum") looks "like a vast spiny lionfish to the earth-adapted eye. Her sides were lined with gasbags filled with hydrogen; her vanes and wings furled tight. Her color was a blue-green so dark it seemed a glossy black unless the light struck it; her hide was impregnated with symbiotic algae." Vinnie, as she is affectionately known to her crew, has many teeth, "the diamond edges worn to a glitter," and "dozens of bright sapphire eyes". Her interior smells of ozone and nutmeg.

Other Boojum liveships mentioned are, in "Boojum," the Henry Ford, who tends to bite, and the Marie Curie, who is reputed to have eaten her crew; in "Mongoose," the Manfred von Richthofen, Erich Zann, Harriet Tubman, and possibly the Arthur Gordon Pym; and in "The Wreck of the Charles Dexter Ward," the titular Ward, a derelict hospital ship, and the Richard Trevithick.

Boojums are named for the creatures in Lewis Carroll's "The Hunting of the Snark"; they are the kind of Snark you don't want to hunt, as those who do tend to vanish forever.

### Toves
Interdimensional vermin with sluglike, segmented bodies, a little short of a meter long, introduced in the story "Mongoose". They often attach themselves to ceilings with a foul-smelling secretion; a tove infestation can be identified by itd "sharp stink...ammoniac and bitter." They hunt by dangling glowing, sticky lure-tongues, half a meter long, which they use to catch prey which they then attack with "flesh-ripping pincers".

Despite this, toves are less a threat than a nuisance, "with their tendency to use up valuable oxygen, clog ductwork, eat pets, drip goo from ceilings, and crunch wetly when you stepped on them." They are lazy creatures--or "energy efficient"--"never crawl[ing] farther than was necessary to find a usable anchoring point." Their real danger is that they weaken the barriers between dimensions, attracting raths, their natural predators--and worse things.

The Book of Dzyan is a text that Theosophist Helena Petrovna Blavatsky claimed to have seen in Tibet. It was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft, and has been subsequently cited by other Mythos writers.

According to Blavatsky, she saw the manuscript, which was guarded by an occult brotherhood, while studying esoteric doctrines in Tibet. It was written on "a collection of palm leaves made impermeable to water, fire, and air, by some specific unknown process." Their language is Senzar, an otherwise unknown tongue that may be Atlantean in origin. 

The word "Dzyan", according to Blavatsky, is pronounced "djan" and signifies "to reform one's self by meditation and knowledge". He tips his hat to Theosophy in a backhanded way when he includes the Book of Dzyan in the library of "mildewed, disintegrating books" Robert Blake discovers in the Starry Wisdom Church in "The Haunter of the Dark" (1936):


"The Diary of Alonzo Typer" (1935), a story Lovecraft wrote in conjunction with William Lumley prior to "The Haunter of the Dark", gives further background on the Book of Dzyan, in the form of lore learned from a manuscript written by 16th century occultist Claes van der Heyl: 


### Other Writers
August Derleth picked up on Lovecraft's inclusion of the Book of Dzyan in the library of "black, forbidden things". In Derleth's "The Gable Window" (1957), the narrator finds a copy in his late cousin Wilbur Akeley's house, alongside the "Pnakotic Manuscripts, the R’lyeh Text, the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt, the Book of Eibon, the Dhol Chants, the Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan, Ludvig Prinn’s De Vermis Mysteriis, the Celaeno Fragments, the Cultes des Goules of the Comte d’Erlette," and "a photostat copy of the Necronomicon".

In The Lurker at the Threshold (1945), Winfield Phillips borrows a copy from Prof. Seneca Lapham.

### In Other Media
*In the Real Ghostbusters episode "The Collect Call of Cathulhu", the Ghostbusters consult the Book of Dzyan to learn more about the Cult of Cathulhu.
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, Nya owns a bookstore that contains many grimoires, including the Book of Dyzan.
