The Book of Eibon, also known as the Liber Ivonis or Livre d'Eibon, is a fictional grimoire created by Clark Ashton Smith. Part of Smith's Hyperborea setting, he attributed the book to the magician Eibon of Mhu Thulan, and the French translation to Gaspard du Nord of Averoigne.

One of Smith's stories, "The Coming of the White Worm", is presented as a chapter of the Book of Eibon.

H. P. Lovecraft mentioned the Book of Eibon repeatedly in his own fiction. Other members of the Lovecraft circle, such as Robert Bloch and August Derleth, mentioned it in their Mythos stories as well.

Brian Lumley mentions the book in his story, "The Second Wish".

The book was passed down by secret cults to the present day. Never printed until the 20th century, there are many editions which vary widely, from tablets to scrolls. It is a key text in the Tsathogguan Cycle.

### Editions
*The Kishite Version
*The Punic (1600 B.C.)
*The Greek Edition
*The Latin Liber Ivonis (10th-11th century)
*Livre d'Ivon (13th century)
*The only printed version, the Adkins and Jones Edition of the Latin text (A.D. 1937)

### Contents
Among other topics, the book includes:

*A spell for the emanation of Yoth that requires a child's blood (: "The Man of Stone")
*A method of giving people the Green Decay (: "The Man of Stone")
* The third part is entitled "Papyrus of the Dark Wisdom," and consists of a treatise of considerable length on theogony. It discusses "the hidden origins of the Earth, the creation of the first of the Old Ones, the cause of their rebellion against the Elder Gods, the war between the two groups of divinities, the flight into this dimension of space /time by the Old Ones, and so on--a capsule history of the Elder World." The Book of Ending is a fictional eldritch book created by Vertigo Comics for their miniseries The Trenchcoat Brigade. 

### Background
In the mid-17th century, the Book of Ending was held by the Ukrainian Leshy whose city was protected by the "Eye of the World", which hid them from the world. Princess Elliana was betrayed by her Cossack lover who sneaked into the castle, killed her father, stole the Eye of the World and led the Cossacks against her city; slaughtering and enslaving its inhabitants and scattering the survivors across the land.

Seeking revenge, Elliana took the book and her hand was infected by M'nagalah, who kept her alive and young over the centuries to influence her. At the turn of the 20th century, she managed to bring M'nagalah to Earth. Having seen a future where all life on Earth had been consumed by M'nagalah, the Trenchcoat Brigade arrived to prevent his entry to the world. Realizing that she was being used by M'nagalah, Elainna changed her mind and destroyed the book, thereby preventing his return.

The Book of Iod is a fictional book created by Henry Kuttner and expanded upon by Lin Carter and Robert M. Price. It first appears in Kuttner's short story "The Bells of Horror" (1939). The book provided the title for a collection of Kuttner's Mythos-related fiction, The Book of Iod: Ten Tales of the Mythos.

H. P. Lovecraft had told Kuttner that he planned to mention the tome in his writings, but he died before he was able to do so.

### Description
Kuttner describes the tome as an "abhorrent and monstrous volume of ancient esoteric formulae about which curious legends still cling." It was originally "written in the pre-human Ancient Tongue," and only one copy of that original text is said to exist. 

Even the little-known expurgated English translation by Johann Negus is referred to as "forbidden" and "hellish." The Huntington Library in San Marino, California, has a copy of the Negus translation.

The Book of Iod describes an entity called Zushakon, known to the Mutsune Indians as Zu-che-quon. Presumably, it also discusses the being called Iod the Hunter.

The Book of Thoth is an Ancient Egyptian text referenced by Abdul Alhazred in the Necronomicon who claims it warns of the "price of a single glimpse" of what lies beyond the Ultimate Gate.

### Behind the Mythos
In reality the Book of Thoth is a name given to many ancient Egyptian texts supposed to have been written by Thoth, the Egyptian god of writing and knowledge usually depicted as Baboon writing on a scroll or an Ibis headed humanoid figure holding a knotted rope symbolising memory or a stylus symbolising the craft of the scribe. The Book of Thoth became a phrase in the ancient world simply meaning any of a wide variety of texts that were in most cases fictional, almost similar to the books and texts referred to in Mythos stories. One book in particular is referred to in a surviving ancient Egyptian adventure story, and this Book of Thoth was a spellbook similar to a more modern grimoire.

The fictional Book of Thoth appears in an ancient Egyptian story from the Ptolemaic period. The book, allegedly written by "Thoth", is said to contain two spells, one of which allows the reader to understand the speech of animals, and one of which allows the reader to perceive the gods themselves. It is worth noting that the original ancient Egyptian word "hekare", the name for what is usually translated as "god", actually means wonder worker, or magician.

According to the story, the book was originally hidden at the bottom of the Nile near Coptos, where it was locked inside a series of boxes guarded by serpents. The Egyptian prince Neferkaptah fought the serpents and retrieved the book, but in punishment for his theft from Thoth, the gods killed his wife Ahwere and son Merib. Neferkaptah committed suicide and was entombed along with the book. Generations later, the story's protagonist, Setne Khamwas (a character based on the historical prince Khaemwaset), steals the book from Neferkaptah's tomb despite opposition from Neferkaptah's ghost. Setne then meets a beautiful woman who seduces him into killing his children and humiliating himself in front of the pharaoh. He discovers that this episode was an illusion created by Neferkaptah, and in fear of further retribution, Setne returns the book to Neferkaptah's tomb. At Neferkaptah's request, Setne also finds the bodies of Neferkaptah's wife and son and buries them in Neferkaptah's tomb, which is then sealed.

The story reflects the Egyptian belief that the gods' knowledge is not meant for humans to possess. That, at least, is a concept solidly rooted in the Mythos.

### References
*H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price (1934). "Through the Gates of the Silver Key ".

The Book of Yng is an occult text created by author and editor Fred C. Adams for his Translations from the Book of Yng series.

### Overview
The exact origin of the Book of Yng is unknown, but it can be deduced to predate the time of Classical Greece by some margin. The text is stated to have been translated by Fred C. Adams himself whose copy was written in Arabic, although it is unclear if this was an original version or was itself translated from some earlier tongue. The book contains some of the stories which inspired the mythology of Ancient Greece.

It must be noted that when translating the text Adams had to employ a degree of guesswork, as acknowledged in the following note:



Thus, some of the meaning of the contents may have been either lost or unknowingly twisted to fit a more modern worldview.

fullContent:
"Boots on the Ground" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Jeff C. Carter. It was first published in Tomorrow's Cthulhu: Stories at the Dawn of Posthumanity by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
In the near future, a revolutionary technology which allows the user to "pilot" another person's body through use of connected neural networks is utilised by the USA's Central Intelligence Agency to combat terrorism in the mountain wildernesses of Afghanistan.

As fortune would have it, the latest "Remotely Piloted Civilian" is betrayed by a rival tribe during the course of his mission, and is sold out to a shadowy group which inhabits the caves beneath the rocky terrain. As the group prepares the poor unfortunate for sacrifice, the pilot witnesses the object of the group's worship - a colossal entity half-buried in a rock face - and is driven insane, tearing out his own eyes before embarking upon a murderous spree and, ultimately, dying at the hands of military police.

The story ends with the project's director demanding that Afghanistan be flooded with RPCs in an effort to discover how the group "hacked" his precious software, and to track down the mysterious object of their veneration…

### Mythos Connections
The group which abduct the RPC are named as the Abd-Al-Hazred, which the CIA translate as "The Servants of the Great Lord." Near the story's conclusion, they are heard to chant "N’yarlathotep rabb thal’a Nazara!" which the computer translates as Arabic, meaning "Look upon the face of {non-standard/named entity: Nyar lath otep}.

Boris Hurtta (born 8. December 1945 in Turku, Finland) is a Finnish author who is one of main early contributors to Finnish Cthulhu Mythos together with S. Albert Kivinen and others.

Hurtta edited an anthology of Lovecraftian & Cthulhu Mythos stories written by Finnish authors named Kultainen Naamio (The Golden Mask) published in 1993 and wrote many Mythos stories for the Science-fiction magazine Portti and others.

On top of his other Mythos stories Hurtta wrote a long-running series of stories about the bibliophile bookshop owner Valdemar Rydberg and his friend and assistant Nils Hermelin. In stories such as Pirunkirjojen kintereillä and Perkeleitä Broadwaylla the heroes hunt for books such as The Necronomicon and visit Arkham. S. Albert Kivinen also features as a character in some of Hurtta's stories.

"Born Again?" is a story in issue #90 of Marvel Comics' long-running superhero comic Doctor Strange, Sorcerer Supreme. Written by J. M. DeMatteis, it was published in May 1996 .

### Synopsis
The human/demon hybrid Victoria Montesi, hero and member of supernatural protectors the Darkhold Redeemers, is about to give birth to the Elder God Chthon, and Doctor Strange must prevent his return to Earth while saving Victoria's life. After a failed attempt to defeat Cthon in its home dimension, Strange is ultimately successful when facing down the entity fortified with Montesi's purity of heart .

shortDefinition: Born of the Winds is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by Brian Lumley. It first appeared in the December 1975 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction (#295). It was also collected in the author's miscellany anthology Fruiting Bodies and Other Fu...
fullContent:
Born of the Winds is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by Brian Lumley. It first appeared in the December 1975 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction (#295). It was also collected in the author's miscellany anthology Fruiting Bodies and Other Fungi (Roc UK/Tor, 1993).

The story was nominated for a World Fantasy Award; Lumley calls it "one of my personal favourites."

The story relates the efforts of a meteorologist, recuperating in a remote area of Canada, to help a woman find her son, whom she believes has fled into the Manitoba wilderness. It develops that the son's father is the air elemental Ithaqua; their attempt to retrieve the son brings them into conflict, first with the entity's cult, and then with the Wind-Walker himself.

The story is a sequel to August Derleth's "The Thing That Walked on the Wind," and prefigures later Lumley stories that detail the action-adventure struggles of heroic humans against Ithaqua. The concept of Ithaqua having offspring was developed in Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game as the creatures known as the Spawn of the Winds.

### Ithaqua
The entity that drives the stories plot is Ithaqua, the Wind-Walker, "perhaps the very greatest of the mythical air-elementals." According to the the eccentric scholar Samuel Bridgeman, Ithaqua "made war against the Elder Gods in the Beginning; for which ultimate treason He was banished to frozen Arctic and interplanetary heavens to ‘Walk the Winds Forever.’" He appears as "a dark outline against the sky, anthropomorphic, a manlike yet bestial silhouette...with carmine stars for eyes”--but "the very sight of Him means a freezing and inescapable death for the unfortunate observer."

Bridgeman links Ithaqua to the legend of the Wendigo, and to Native American deities like the Iroquois wind spirit Gaoh,  and Negafok, the "Eskimo cold-weather spirit," as well as to mythological figures like the Norse god of thunder Thor, and Enlil, the Babylonian storm god. (Tha-thka, the "Hittite god-of-the-storm," appears to be Lumley's invention.)

### Characters
David Lawton: An American meteorologist, on extended holiday in Manitoba to recuperate from a "debilitating chest ailment." He describes himself as "addicted to mysteries, as curious as a cat."

Judge Jason Andrews: A "retired New Yorker of independent means," a somewhat reclusive widower, and "something of a professional anthropologist all his life." An old friend of David's father, he offers to let David stay at his home in Navissa, Manitoba, while he recovers from his ailment. The judge is also a longtime friend of Lucille Bridgeman, and was close to her late husband as well. Andrews is described as "a man who liked his facts straight on the line, undistorted by whim or fancy"--but he says that "near the end of a lifetime, I’m no closer now than I was fifty years ago to being able to say what is and what isn’t."

Lucille Bridgeman: A widow who is searching for her missing son. An encounter with Ithaqua 20 years earlier

fullContent:
Boston, the largest city and capital of Massachusetts, and the cultural and financial center of New England, plays a prominent role in H. P. Lovecraft's fiction.

The city was founded in 1630 by Puritans who named it for their hometown in England. It played a central part in the American Revolution, the scene of key events like the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party and the Battle of Bunker Hill, and home to notable figures like Paul Revere and John and Samuel Adams.

Writers like Ralph Waldo Emerson, Henry David Thoreau, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Nathaniel Hawthorne, and Louisa May Alcott made Boston a cultural hub in the 19th century.

### Lovecraft's Visits
Lovecraft made repeated visits to Boston, the nearest large city to Providence. In 1919, he saw Lord Dunsany speak at Boston's Copley Plaza hotel, an event that had a major impact on Lovecraft's writing. His attendance at the 1921 National Amateur Press Association convention in Boston was similarly impactful, as it was there that he met his future wife, Sonia Greene.

Lovecraft went to Boston with Donald Wandrei in 1927, with Samuel Loveman in 1929, and with W. Paul Cook in 1931, among other visits.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction

### Richard Upton Pickman
In "Pickman's Model", the narrator Thurber declares, "Boston never had a greater painter than Richard Upton Pickman." “The place for an artist to live is the North End," Pickman insists:Don’t you realise that places like that weren’t merely made, but actually grew? Generation after generation lived and felt and died there, and in days when people weren’t afraid to live and feel and die.... I can shew you houses that have stood two centuries and a half and more; houses that have witnessed what would make a modern house crumble into powder.... Look here, do you know the whole North End once had a set of tunnels that kept certain people in touch with each other’s houses, and the burying-ground, and the sea?...

Why, man, out of ten surviving houses built before 1700 and not moved since I’ll wager that in eight I can shew you something queer in the cellar. There’s hardly a month that you don’t read of workmen finding bricked-up arches and wells leading nowhere in this or that old place as it comes down—you could see one near Henchman Street from the elevated last year.There were witches and what their spells summoned; pirates and what they brought in from the sea; smugglers; privateers....

What do maps and records and guide-books really tell of the North End? Bah! At a guess I’ll guarantee to lead you to thirty or forty alleys and networks of alleys north of Prince Street that aren’t suspected by ten living beings outside of the foreigners that swarm them.... [T]hese ancient places are dreaming gorgeously and overflowing with wonder and terror and escapes from the commonplace....Pickman has a more public studio on Newbury Street in Boston's Back Bay, which he dismisses as a parvenu set of artificial streets on made land. Back Bay isn’t Bo

fullContent:
"Bothon" is a short story by Henry S. Whitehead written in 1930 but first published in the August 1946 issue of Amazing Stories, as well as the Arkham House collection West India Lights.

Some sources regard this story as a collaboration between Whitehead and H. P. Lovecraft, although it is unknown whether and to what extent the latter was involved in its writing.

The title character, Bothon, previously appeared in a minor role in Whitehead's story "Scar-Tissue", which is part of the Gerald Canevin series.

### Authorship
According to S. T. Joshi, Lovecraft and Whitehead collaborated on devising the plot of the story, originally titled "The Bruise", for which Lovecraft wrote a synopsis. The authorship of the final version is unclear, although Joshi's analysis of the text concludes that it was not written by Lovecraft.

Lin Carter, while agreeing with Joshi's judgment, points out that the names of the Muvian provinces in "Bothon" bear more than a passing resemblance to names mentioned in "Out of the Aeons", a story ghostwritten by Lovecraft for Hazel Heald which also features the continent of Mu.

### Synopsis
After bruising his head, Powers Meredith, a man from the time when the story was written (1930), starts hearing sounds of cataclysm and chaos that nobody else can hear, and is captivated by ever more vivid dream states in which he is Bothon, a general from Atlantis serving in his home province of Ludekta.

Called upon to act as Atlantean ambassador to Aglad-Dho, in the continent of Mu, Bothon travels to the Muvian imperial capital of Alu, where he falls deeply in love with Lady Ledda, the Emperor's niece. Despite his prestige as a general, the Atlantean remains a commoner, unfit to marry Ledda in the eyes of the royals, and thus is sent back to Atlantis to prevent a scandal.

Following a rebellion staged by the ape-like creatures known as the Gyaa-Hua, Bothon leads an extraordinarily successful counter-strike that earns him the acclaim of his people, and organises a fleet to invade Alu and capture Ledda so the two can elope together. Although the siege of Alu is successful, he loses three-quarters of his army when cataclysmic earthquakes strike the city for the first time. His army defeated, Bothon ends up a prisoner in the deepest dungeon of the capital.

Meredith discovers that other people of his own waking world have had similar experiences and used words from the Naacal language spoken in his dream, which seem to be the effect of ancestral memories awakening, if not part of a shared dream or hallucination of ancient times.

Returning to Atlantis in dream state, Meredith, as Bothon, escapes from the dungeon amidst the surrounding chaos and rescues his beloved Ledda. Together, they flee to the high mountains of A-Wah-Ii and watch as the continent of Mu is annihilated under an enormous lethal green tidal wave, ending the civilisation.

Buddha is a historical figure from ancient India who is part of the Buddhist cosmology which was first used by Chaosium in 2005 for its Call of Cthulhu role-playing game as an Outer God. However, it is stated that this classification should be taken loosely and used as a basis of comparison with Cthulhu Mythos entities.

### Background
The Cosmic Buddha is a timeless entity who exists beyond time and space, where it appears as a statue. Changes such as a facial expression or a new hand position are instantaneous with no visible movement from the old to new position. On Earth a mortal on a path to enlightenment awakened to the cosmos true nature. He became the Cosmic Buddhas's physical incarnation on Earth, the Body of Manifestation (Nirmâna-Kâya), the Living Buddha. Upon his death, he ascended to the Outer Realm of Nirvana, where he merged with the Cosmic Buddha's Absolute Body (Dharma-Kâya).

Just as the multiverse has an infinite number of dimensions, so there are an infinite number of Buddhas, each of which watches over a specific dimension. Every 3000 years, a mortal becomes the Living Buddha thereby renewing the teachings of Dharma on Earth. After which it ascends to merge with the Cosmic Buddha. When the Lord Buddha manifests on Earth, it is usually to those whom are on the path to enlightenment, appearing as glowing man who is in the lotus seating position. Behind the hovering man is a spectral purple flame. Often the unmoving man is surrounded by a court of swirling devas and bodhisattvas.

The Bouda are part of Ethiopian folk religion. Chaosium first used them in 2009 for their Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. (: Cthulhu Invictus)

### Background
The Bouda are race of shapeshifters who at will are able to change from their human forms to hyenas, usually doing so at night. In their beast form, they look exactly like hyenas, except larger and heavier, being up to a foot taller and at least fifty pounds heavier. 

They have a complex social structure and are fiercely loyal to each other. Bouda have worked for a number of Cthulhu Mythos deities, but are aligned and loyal to none. They have roamed across Africa for over 20 million years, and are a race skilled in magic and famous for their proficiency in metalworking.

### Trivia
*A version of this mythological creature appeared in an episode of Buffy the Vampire Slayer (Season 1, Episode 6 "The Pack"), and a different version appeared in the Monster Manual for Dungeons & Dragons Second Edition.

"Bound for Home" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Christopher Golden. It was first published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.

### Synopsis
Legendary illusionist Harry Houdini is lured aboard the luxurious passenger locomotive the Orient Express with a challenge from a group of men claiming to wish to test his abilities. Houdini must escape from being chained to a platform bolted to the roof of one of the carriages while blindfolded, in the few short minutes before the train passes through a low-ceilinged tunnel, with death being the price of failure.

Unfortunately for him, the men are in fact inhuman cultists in the service of one Abdul Reis el Drogman, the villain from "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs," returned to claim Houdini's life essence in an attempt to open a portal which will guide the Old Ones into our world. He is able to defeat the villains by escaping his chains and leaping from the train, but not before they sacrifice a young reporter in a hideous and agonising ritual and murder his publicist.

* Fantastic Tales of Terror (2018)

Brad Hollins is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games as part of the backstory for Investigator "Skids" O'Toole in the board game of Lovecraftian Horror, Arkham Horror.

### History
While doing time for the murders of nine people, Brad made the acquaintance of small-time criminal "Skids" O'Toole due to the fact that the two were cellmates. While Skids was mostly harmless, Brad was crazy as a junkyard dog, claiming that aliens made him do what he had done, and constantly ranting and raving about the Ancient or Old Ones. Where he came about this knowledge is anybody’s guess - he sometimes claimed it came to him in dreams - but Brad was determined to get to Argentina to put a stop to them.

All of this came to an end, however, the night Skids heard his cellmate chanting in a strange tongue. Looking over, he was just in time to see Brad's body erupt into a blazing inferno, killing him instantly.

It was this experience which prompted Skids to travel to Arkham upon his release in order to get to the bottom of what had happened to Brad.

### Behind the Mythos
Brad Hollins was first mentioned in the flavour text for Investigator "Skids" O'Toole in the Arkham Horror Second Edition expansion Innsmouth Horror, although he has since been mentioned in at least one of their other games, Eldritch Horror.

The Bran cult is a fictional religion centered around the deified figure of Bran Mak Morn, the ancient king of the Picts in the works of Robert E. Howard.

### Overview
The Bran cult was mentioned by the 19th century occultist Friedrich von Junzt, who attested that it still existed. The cult worships the Dark Man, a statue of Bran Mak Morn, who ruled the Picts at the time of the Roman occupation of Britain. Carved by a master sculptor at the time Bran was still alive, the statue is located inside a "great nameless cavern" to which every Bran cultist makes a pilgrimage once in his or her life.

The cultists, who are themselves descendants of Bran, believe that one day the statue will come to life and rebuild the Dark Empire of the Picts that existed at the time of the Romans, which was itself a revival of an even older prehistoric Pictish empire that conquered Britain and drove the Children of the Night to the underground. (: "The Children of the Night", "Worms of the Earth")

Bran Mak Morn is a fictional barbarian hero created by Robert E. Howard. He is the last king of the Cruithni Picts. The character lived in Roman times during the period when Rome had invaded but not entirely subdued the southern British Isles. 

Following Bran Mak Morn's death, he is  worshipped as the demigod the "Dark Man" or "Dark One" by Scottish and Irish tribesmen of Pictish descent. In Howard's story "The Children of the Night" (1931) set in then-contemporary times, a "Bran Cult" is thought to survive among relict populations descended from the Picts.

### Connection to the Cthulhu Mythos
Bran Mak Morn is central to the shared universe in a way that Conan (in the original writings by his creator) never was. Bran and his adventures take place in the shared universe of the Cthulhu Mythos as it was being developed by members of the Lovecraft Circle and H. P. Lovecraft himself.

In the Howard-penned Bran story "Worms of the Earth," explicit mention is made of black gods of R'lyeh, resting place of Cthulhu. In the earliest known draft of Worms, Cthulhu himself is mentioned but this was later changed to Nameless Gods in the final version. Also mentioned is Dagon.

Lovecraft in turn references "Bran" in his story The Whisperer in Darkness, which is interpreted by Clark Ashton Smith to be either Bran Mak Morn or possibly Brân the Blessed of Celtic mythology. (: Selected Letters of Clark Ashton Smith #209)

"Breaking Point" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author Sam Stone.

### Synopsis
In a ruined post-apocalyptic city, a pair of women are forced to submit to the carnal attentions of hybrid Old One monstrosities in order to earn food with which to feed their "children": in actuality the hellish offspring of these couplings.

*Kerys, a strong-willed survivor of the return of the Old Ones.
*Mai, Kerys' friend, a woman on the verge of losing her sanity.

### Publication History
"Breaking Point" was included in the Dark Regions Press anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror in 2017.

Brian Lumley (born 2 December 1937 - January 2024) was an English horror-fiction writer and a major contributor to the Cthulhu Mythos, inventing a number of new Great Old Ones, Elder Gods, grimoires, and Mythos locations.

Born in County Durham, England, Lumley discovered the Cthulhu Mythos at age 13 or 14, when he read Robert Bloch's "Notebook Found in a Deserted House".

He joined the British Army in 1958, and was well into a 22-year career there when he began corresponding with Arkham House's August Derleth. Derleth selected two of his first stories, "Cement Surroundings" and "The Sister City", for inclusion in the 1969 anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos. Arkham House later published two collections of Lumley's short fiction, The Caller of The Black (1971) and The Horror at Oakdeene and Others (1977), as well as his first novel, The Burrowers Beneath (1974).

Many of Lumley's Mythos stories fall into three main series: one featuring the occult investigator Titus Crow, another taking place in Lovecraft's Dreamlands, and the Primal Land stories taking place in prehistoric Theem'hdra. 

Lumley later achieved mainstream success with the Necroscope and Psychomech books.

On 28 January 2024, Lumley's wife Barbara Ann announced his death earlier in the month via social media platform Facebook .

fullContent:
Brian John McNaughton (23 September 1935 - 13 May 2004) was an American author of both novels and short fiction whose focus was the horror and fantasy genres. Many of his pieces include references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, and Robert E. Howard amongst others, and he has contributed several stories to the Cthulhu Mythos. A selection of his works have been published in their original formats by Wildside Press.

Born in Red Bank, New Jersey, McNaughton began his career writing for fanzines while in high school. He attended Harvard, but did not graduate. He worked as a reporter for the Newark Evening News for ten years. He later worked for ten years as the night manager at a "decrepit seaside hotel." 

### Mythos Writing
McNaughton's Mythos writing is characterized by black humor, considerable gore, and frank sexuality; "every character in [his] novels of any significance has a sexual identity and has thoughts and actions regarding sex and potential partners," critic Bobby Derie notes. H. P. Lovecraft often appears as a background element in McNaughton's stories, writing fictionalized accounts of "real" Mythos entities.

McNaughton wrote a series of sexually explicit "romance" novels under the pen name Sheena Clayton, "all of which to greater or lesser extent contain references to the Mythos."

Brian Michael Stableford (25th July 1948 - 24 February 2024) was a prolific British science fiction and horror author who wrote numerous stories set in the Cthulhu Mythos. These include several which were written as sequels to the stories of H. P. Lovecraft, which were collected together in the anthology The Legacy of Erich Zann and Other Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos.

Graduating from university with a degree in biology, he spent many years in the research field before moving his focus to sociology, a subject he would go on to lecture in, along with creative writing; subsequent to this, he became a full-time writer. Stableford passed away on 24 February 2024 .

fullContent:
Brichester is a fictional town invented by Ramsey Campbell, the main community of his Severn Valley environment. It is the setting of several of his Mythos-related short stories.

Campbell depicts it as an ordinary town where the weird is always threatening to break through: "These days Brichester has an impressively mundane surface," he writes in "The Franklyn Paragraphs", "but I still sense that it may crack."

In "The Enchanted Fruit", Campbell describes "the daily press of Brichester, the false harsh rainbow of packed cars", and "churches robbed of dignity by plummeting iron balls" (though the protagonist also recalls "streets where some lone house had struck him speechless with its silent pride, the noble bearing of its age and history"). 

Brichester is said to have a wide variety of media outlets, including a daily newspaper, The Brichester Herald, advertised as "Brichester's Evening Voice", and a radio station, Radio Brichester.  It also has a weekly paper,  the Brichester Weekly News. Ingels, a reporter for the Herald, complains that the town lacks a television studio.

Brichester's Ultimate Press published an important manuscript by the medieval heretic Johannes Henricus Pott, a new 12th volume of the Revelations of Glaaki, and an entire line of bondage-related pornography. Brichester also has the True Light Press, though this is merely cultist Roland Franklyn's self-publishing operation.

Errol Undercliffe notes of Brichester Central Library,  "You couldn't get farther from a Lovecraft setting." It does, however, carry a copy of Roland Franklyn's We Pass From View—as well as Ramsey Campbell's "The Inhabitant of the Lake". an allusion to Campbell's story "The Mine on Yuggoth".)  Brichester also has a Co-operative Social Club.

The main green area of the town is the Brichester Central Park.

### Brichester University
Brichester has a sizable university, where, Campbell says, "they were familiar with things whose existence is not recognized by science." 

While in "The Enchanted Fruit,"  Campbell mentions "the hard bleached University smashing and swallowing ornate facades", in The Darkest Part of the Woods, Brichester University's architecture is depicted as more traditional, with a "long, lofty Gothic facade, and high pointed windows." 

The library once kept copies, in a locked case, of "the Necronomicon, Revelations of Glaaki, De Vermis Mysteriis, and other titles as ominous", but in the 1960s "a Muslim student... spray(ed) them with lighter fluid and set fire to them", destroying them completely. 

There is a science-fiction shop, Worlds Unlimited, near the University campus "in the dilapidated Victorian streets which have become the student quarter."  In the same neighborhood is the Scholar's Rest: "Beneath a jauntily sagging slate roof the squat sandstone building faced the university campus... Brichester University is a fictional school created by Ramsey Campbell, part of his Severn Valley setting for Cthulhu Mythos stories. It is located in Campbell's invented town of Brichester; as Brichester was created as an analogue to Lovecraft Country's Arkham, Brichester University is Campbell's analogue to Miskatonic University.

### Overview
In the introduction to The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, Campbell notes that while most sorcerers in Brichester "practise their arts secretly...there still is a regrettable cult among students at the university".

One of the first mentions of Brichester University is in "The Horror From the Bridge", where it's said "they were familiar with things whose existence is not recognized by science."  The story notes that "the staff at the University often met with terrors which they had never thought could exist, for they were sometimes called by the frantic inhabitants of various localities to quell phenomena which were rising from hiding." A librarian at the university, Philip Chesterton, is instrumental in foiling the eldritch plans of Lionel Phipps.

In "The Mine on Yuggoth", Brichester native Edward Taylor enrolled in the university in 1918, where he "led a witch cult."  All members, including "the artist, Nevil Craughan, and the occultist, Henry Fisher", were expelled.

"The Inhabitant of the Lake" describes the "red-brick houses and steeples which surround the central white University building" in Brichester. A manuscript apparently left by cult leader Thomas Lee at Lakeside Terrace admits that he "dabbled in the forbidden practices at Brichester University." Professors from the university in that story find that the mysterious metal spine that killed artist Thomas Cartwright was "composed of living cells."

"The Plain of Sound" tells the story of three Brichester University students who find a mysterious cottage on the way back from Severnford; it used to be the home of Arnold Hird, a Brichester professor who war "asked to leave the university because he attacked someone when they disagreed with him", and said "he'd return and astonish everybody some day".

While "The Enchanted Fruit" mentions "the hard bleached University smashing and swallowing ornate facades", in The Darkest Part of the Woods, Brichester University's architecture is more traditional, with a "long, lofty Gothic facade, and high pointed windows."

In Scott David Aniolowski's short story "I Dream of Wires", the Tick-Tock Man manifested in the Dughall Computer Lab, located at Brichester University.

The Brick Cylinders of Kadatheron are a collection of ancient writings created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Doom That Came to Sarnath".

### Description
The Cylinders are never actually described in the story. However, it can be assumed that due to their name and antiquity they are comprised of several cylindrical stamps designed to be used to roll images, glyphs or text onto another medium, possibly wet clay. Their number, provenance and current whereabouts were never given by Lovecraft, although they presumably originate from Kadatheron.

### Contents
The Cylinders, at least in part, describe the physical properties of the Beings of Ib, as well as they and their city's descent to Earth from the moon. Whether they contain any other information is unknown.

### Behind the Mythos
H. P. Lovecraft mentions the Brick Cylinders of Kadatheron in a single passage at the beginning of his short story "The Doom That Came to Sarnath":



The closeness of the Cylinders' title of Kadatheron may also suggest a connection to another of Lovecraft's creations: the city of Kadath. Kadath has been postulated to have existed in both the real world and the Dreamlands, although Lovecraft himself never specifically stated which.

fullContent:
"Brick Row", a.k.a. "The East India Brick Row", is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft in December 1929 as a tribute to a set of warehouses located in South Water Street, Providence, Rhode Island, which were at the time threatened with demolition. Lovecraft stood publicly against this plan, as he regarded the buildings to be a charming component of the city's landscape that ought to be preserved. The poem was published in 1943 in the Arkham House collection Beyond the Wall of Sleep.

Unfortunately, Lovecraft's campaign to save the warehouses was unsuccessful and the Brick Row was indeed demolished.

Joseph Payne Brennan regarded "Brick Row" as the best of Lovecraft's poems.

"Bride of Azathoth" is a horror comedy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It is the fifth installment of Peter Cannon's six-part novella Forever Azathoth, which serves as a humourous sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep". The series was published in Cannon's collections Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (1999) and Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches (2011).

### Synopsis
(Continued from "Azathoth in Analysis"...)

Part five of the saga is narrated by Miss Holden, an elderly woman from Kingsport who became Asenath Waite's legal guardian following the death of her father Ephraim Waite. Miss Holden laments that the brilliant and precocious Asenath grew up to marry an "overrated poet" named Edward Derby, and how the marriage resulted in Asenath's untimely death. Decades later, Miss Holden comes to befriend Wendy Upton, whose sister worked for Asenath as a domestic servant, and who has since become the sole heir to Derby's literary estate and owner of a publishing company named Azathoth House. Wendy's admiration for the late Asenath helps to cement her friendship with Miss Holden.

One day, Miss Holden witnesses an accident involving Wendy's son Eph (named after Ephraim Waite) and family friend Dr. Zimmerman while the two are horse-riding. Their horses are scared by a dog named Fearless, causing both men to fall to the ground. A horrified Miss Holden watches as Eph, Zimmerman, and Fearless are all seized by convulsions. Eph recovers, while the dog runs off in panic, but the most badly affected is Dr. Zimmerman, who loses his ability to speak or communicate coherently, shows great difficulty with walking upright, and becomes prone to chasing after rabbits and other animals. He is committed to Arkham Sanitarium, but escapes and dies when he is hit by a car while chasing after a deer.

In the meantime, a relative of Edward Derby named Jacob, who lives in Chesuncook, Maine, threatens to sue Azathoth House over the rights to the Edward Derby estate, which infuriates Eph. Taking Miss Holden's advice, Wendy agrees to meet with Jacob without Eph and try to get to an agreement. Jacob, who works as an inventor, appears to be less concerned with money and more concerned with trying to convince Azathoth House to make some grammatical changes and other minor corrections in future editions of Derby's stories, which were brought to his attention by former editor Vartan Bagdasarian. After he leaves, a surly Eph arrives with the news that another publisher is going to release an unabridged paperback edition of the Necronomicon, which Eph regards as a potentially dangerous move.

Wendy, who has had terrible luck with her previous lovers, starts dating Jacob, and eventually decides to marry him. Eph is predictably furious, but agrees to act as best man, while Miss Holden will be the maid of honour. Bride of Re-Animator is a 1990 comedy horror film and the second in Brian Yuzna's Re-Animator series. Like its predecessor, it is (very) loosely based on Howard Phillips Lovecraft's short story "Herbert West--Reanimator".

### Synopsis
The two male leads of the previous film, Doctors West and Cain, attempt to construct a body to resurrect Cain's deceased fiancée. Predictably, things go horribly wrong, and a horde of zombies and dismembered body parts attack, burying West in an old crypt and presumably killing him.

### Behind the Mythos
Produced and directed by Brian Yuzna, who also had a hand in the screenplay, Bride of Re-Animator starred Jeffrey Combs, Bruce Abbott and David Gale, who reprised their roles from the first film. It ran to a total of 96 minutes, and was filmed on a budget of $2.5 million.

The Bride of Slorioth is a fictional item in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 1994 in issue 15 of volume one of the Secret Defenders comic series.

### Background
The Bride of Slorioth was a mystical statue related to the Great Old One, Slorioth. Which permitted the ex-Avenger Dr. Druid to transform Shadowoman's soul into a shadow-form, which had various superhuman abilities. Unknown to Dr. Druid, it also claimed a portion of his own soul, corrupting it into a dark soul.

fullContent:
Brindlewood Bay is a tabletop role-playing game (TTRPG) in which the players take on the role of retired old ladies or other "cozy" community based amateur detectives, in a setting combining comfy detective mysteries as seen on TV with the Cthulhu Mythos, in a small New England town.

Brindlewood Bay is a game that combines Murder, She Wrote with H. P. Lovecraft. In it, you play a group of elderly women, members of the local Murder Mavens Mystery Book Club, who help the authorities solve murder cases in a picturesque New England Town. Over the course of their investigations, they become aware of a dark occult conspiracy that connects the cases, and will eventually have to face that conspiracy in order to save their community.

Brindlewood Bay has had several expansions, third party adventures and related materials published. Many of them steer away from most of the Mythos elements in favor of light hearted comedy murder mysteries. However the underlying Mythos conspiracy is central to the setting whether present in every "episode" played or not.

fullContent:
"Bring the Thunder" is a Lovecraftian black comedy short story by U.K.-based author Chris Lynch, first published in his linked horror collection Welcome to Neverbury in June 2023.

### Synopsis
When paramedic Danielle arrives at the scene of a suspected heart attack, she attempts to use a defibrillator on the dying man. As she activates the paddles, time halts and an all-but-forgotten thunder god named Taranis appears to her. Taranis informs Danielle that the victim is in fact a disloyal high priest of his who is being punished for his crimes. Furthermore, he informs the medic that, should she wish to save the man, she must become his new high priest as payment.

Danielle, by now somewhat annoyed with Taranis, requests that her own god give her an audience. To Taranis' horror, the sky opens up and something tentacled - and far older than the petty thunder god - descends from the heavens to consume him.

### Behind the Mythos
"Bring the Thunder" was written as part of an online writing challenge which gave story prompts from H. P. Lovecraft's Commonplace Book. This, combined with Danielle's description of her god - who is never named -  as being "rather well-known, in a sense, although most people think it’s just a story … my god has really become quite popular. Books, films, t-shirts. even stuffed toys" may suggest Lynch's intent that this entity be taken by the reader to be Cthulhu.

Britannia & Beyond is a licenced supplement for the 7th edition of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game, published by Golden Goblin Press in 2023.  

### Overview
Britannia & Beyond is a setting guide detailing the Roman Province of Britannia and the barbarian lands of Caledonia (Scotland) and Hibernia (Ireland) for Cthulhu Invictus. Available in both PDF and print (softcover and hardcover) editions, it was written by Stuart Boon with William Adcock, Fred Norton, Oscar Rios and Richard Watts.

The British Museum is a cultural institution in London, England, established in 1753, that collects and displays artefacts from around the world. Until 1973, it was also home to the British Library, the largest library in the world. It plays a role in the Cthulhu Mythos as one of just five libraries in the world that H. P. Lovecraft named as being in possession of a copy of the Necronomicon. (The British Museum alone is said to have a copy of the earlier, 15th century printing of the Latin translation.) Other Mythos writers have made use of the Museum to lend authenticity to eldritch lore. 

### In the Real World
The museum was established by an act of Parliament in 1753, establishing a museum based on the collection of curiosities bequeathed by Sir Hans Sloane, an Anglo-Irish physician and naturalist. It was initially housed in Montagu House, a grand mansion in London's Bloomsbury neighbourhood, and opened to the public in 1759. The building that currently houses the museum occupies the same site, greatly expanded; its earliest wing dates to 1827 and its last major reconstruction was in 2000. 

The museum houses cultural artefacts from around the world, brought back by British archaeologists and adventurers from Capt. James Cook to T. E. Lawrence. Some of its most famous holdings, like Egypt's Rosetta Stone and Greece's Parthenon sculptures, are regarded as stolen property by their nations of origin. 

The museum's natural history collections were spun off into a new British Museum of Natural History in 1887 (which was not legally separated from the museum until 1963). The British Library was part of the British Museum until 1973, and was not moved into its own building until 1998; the library's Reading Room at the British Museum has been a haven for writers like Mark Twain, Arthur Conan Doyle, Rudyard Kipling, Bram Stoker, H. G. Wells, George Orwell, George Bernard Shaw, Oscar Wilde, Virginia Woolf, and Arthur Rimbaud, and political figures like Karl Marx, Sun Yat-sen, Mahatma Gandhi, Vladimir Lenin, Marcus Garvey, and Friedrich Hayek. It has perhaps the largest collection of books in the world today, rivaled only by the US Library of Congress; it holds a vast collection of rare books, including the only surviving manuscript of Beowulf. 

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In "History of the Necronomicon", composed in 1927 to provide a consistent background for his favorite tome, Lovecraft wrote: Of the Latin texts now existing one (15th cent.) is known to be in the British Museum under lock and key, while another (17th cent.) is in the Bibliothèque Nationale at Paris. A seventeenth-century edition is in the Widener Library at Harvard, and in the library of Miskatonic University at Arkham. Also in the library of the University of Buenos Ayres. fullContent:
"Broadsword" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by prolific British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
“Stop this war. Or you will die.” With these words and the destruction of Turin, the alien Mi-Go launch a bid for domination of the Earth in 1940. In response, Berlin and London each send small teams of highly-trained men into the Andes to investigate the suspected site of the aliens' deadly weapon and neutralise it. Although the German team is captured by the Mi-Go, the British soldiers are successful, and call in a bombing raid which destroys the alien base.

### Characters

*Sandy, the narrator and British team member.
*Captain Dave Collins, leader of the British expedition.

### Publication History
"Broadsword" was first published in the thematic anthology World War Cthulhu in 2014, and later appeared in the collection of Meikle's own work Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in 2019.

### Trivia

*The name of the mountain on which the Mi-Go base is located, the Trollenburg, is possibly a nod to the 1958 sci-fi horror B-movie The Trollenberg Terror, which features a Lovecraftian creature on a mountain of the same name.

"Broken Sleep" is a short story by Cody Goodfellow that first appeared in Black Wings IV, edited by S. T. Joshi (PS Publishing, 2015). 

### Overview
The story explores the dreams of Tre (real name: Andre Kellogg), a young man locked up in a juvenile prison and subjected to sleep experiments. He's told by a woman he dreams of, who calls herself Ariadne:

It becomes impossible for Tre to know what is dream and what is reality. At one point, he's told that he's "in a secure ward at MU Hospital. You’ve been an inmate at a private juvenile correctional institution, and you’ve been under sedation for most of the last fourteen months." Later, he's told that he's "only been in solitary for forty-eight hours."

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in Goodfellow's collection Rapture of the Deep and Other Lovecraftian Tales (Hippocampus Press, 2016).

The Brood are an extra-galactic race and cosmic horror element in the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. They are very similar to the Xenomorphs from the Alien franchise, except with the added bonus of being sentient, having technology, possessing a civilization, and being a spacefaring species. They are one of the X-Men's most formidable foes and the antagonists of their classic space opera storyline "The Brood Saga".

### Background
The Brood are a reptilian-like demonic insectoid race which reproduces by infecting sentient lifeforms with their eggs. They are an evil race which enjoys the suffering of their hosts and believe it's their destiny to conquer the cosmos, known for enslaving races and working them to their death (including the sentient, miles-long, faster-than-light whale ships called Acanti), and consuming them. The Brood are ruled by an empress, who is in constant telepathic communication with the hundreds of hive worlds spread across the cosmos, and the Brood Queens who rule the hives (some of which are super hives, controlling sectors of space). Though they are infamous for their living starships (the Acanti whaleships and the non-FTL fighter-like Space Sharks), they possess conventional technology including faster-than-light conventional starships, directed energy weapons, and computers.

The Broodlings of Chthon are a fictional Amazonian race created by Marvel Comics, which first appeared in the comic book Carnage Vol 2 #11. They are a pastiche of the Deep Ones.

### Background
The Broodlings of Chthon were created from mud by Chthon and live in the shadowy corners of the world, as they pray and wait for the return of their master. Broodlings are a race of reptilian humanoids, frog-like creatures, whose species consists mostly of females.

They serve and worship Chthon, as well as the Great Old Ones (Chthon was mentioned as one of the Great Old Ones). To propagate the species, they capture human males and rape them, after which they are sacrificed to Chthon. They are technologically primitive (e.g. spears and blades), but have access to Chthonic magic.

The Broodlings of Eihort are a fictional species created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "Before the Storm". They were later incorporated into Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Overview
Broodlings are gestalt beings made up of millions of the tiny white spidery brood of Eihort. When combined, broodling looks like a deathly pale, hairless human of average size. In such a form, the entity is capable of a guttural speech and (with a little disguise) may walk among humans indetected. It is not until a broodling suffers some sort of physical damage that its true nature become apparent.

When attacked, each damage causes bits of broodling to come apart, falling off as globby masses of the white spidery brood. If its form is "killed", a broodling melts down into millions of individuals white spiders that creep and wriggle away.

Like the children of other Great Old Ones, the Broodlings of Eihort live to serve their sire and prepare the way for the coming of the Great Old Ones.

"Brother Bound" is a Cthulhu Mythos novelette by Australian author Jason Fischer, which takes place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting. It was published in the thematic anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022.

### Synopsis
When young Cuban student Desi discovers that his brother Javier is prominent name on the local criminal scene and, worse, that he has stumbled across a mystical organisation in search of a magic blade, he is launched into a deadly battle with American mafiosos determined to get their hands on the weapon. After Javier is brutally murdered by the gangsters' sorcerous leader, Desi flees to his brother's mountain hideout in search of the artefact, the Americans hot on his heels.

Inside the cave, Desi locates the blade, which possesses him and gives him the power to not only slay his pursuers, but erase them from existence. In the aftermath, he is approached by two enigmatic characters, the Claret Knight and Tzu San Niang, representatives of a secretive organisation known as the Red Coterie. They induct him into their ranks with the promise that he will be allowed to keep the blade and use it as he sees fit.

### Behind the Mythos
The Red Coterie, Claret Knight, and Tzu San Niang - also known as the Lady with the Red Parasol - are recurring elements in the Arkham Horror setting.

The Brotherhood of Sahb Delanzar is a fictional cult which appeared in Marvel universe in 1986, making its first appearance in issue #125 of the 1st volume of the Savage Sword of Conan.

### Background
The Brotherhood of Sahb Delanzar was a Mythos cult in Zamora during the Hyborian Age. The cult had been kidnapping babies to sacrifice to Shub-Niggurath (aka, Sahb Delanzar). Once they sacrificed 1000 young, he would return to Earth and rule over the world. It was led by the wealthy Lissandra who was its priestess. The cult also used assassins. Conan of Cimmeria interfered in her plans, which resulted in Shub-Niggurath consuming her and her husband rather than their child.

The Brotherhood of the Beast is a fictional organisation that worships The Beast, an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep (: Masks of Nyarlathotep).

### History
The Brotherhood was founded by two men (Baron Hauptman and Lang-Fu) in the 12th century with the intention of making Nephren-Ka's prophecy come true. Lang-Fu, the leader of a cult of the Deep Ones in southern China, befriended Hauptman in Damascus when both were studying astrology. Lang-Fu possessed a fragment of the Kitab Al-Azif that he claimed had been brought to him by a dark, winged being, and which came from a city buried under the sand in Arabia. The fragment told of the prophecy and the Royal Family waiting in G'harne. Together they traveled to central Africa to find the miserable remains of the priest's descendants, more animals than humans after centuries of isolation. These descendants resisted contact with the two men until Hauptman transferred his mind to the body of his chief, and as tribal leader led these people north to the Mediterranean coast, where they began to mix with normal people, extending their genetic line east towards Muslim lands and north towards Europe.

When Lang-Fu returned to China, Hauptman established the Brotherhood's headquarters in Europe and began to create a network of agents drawn from among the descendants of Nephren-Ka, to help him track the genealogy of the families who possessed the said genes. These agents are not usually aware of the Brotherhood's activities, but they know that they are part of a family with a specific destiny and are benefiting financially from the situation due to Hauptman's constant machinations. Throughout these centuries, Lang-Fu has laid the foundation for much of the Brotherhood's spiritual and political guidelines.

The original plans of the Brotherhood were to establish a kingdom in Eastern Europe, but both attempts were made in failure. The first was due to a political revolt in Poland and the second, to the accidental death of the chosen child at the hands of a misguided being. With the advent of the twentieth century, constantly changing world conditions have once again altered their plans. Using Lang-Fu's ability to summon spirits, much like Paul LeMond's, they got in touch with the spirit of the centuries-dead priest, and the three of them devised a desperate plan for world domination, much like the one Nephren-Ka intended to use against the pharaoh.

The Brotherhood of the Black Pharaoh is a sect of wealthy Egyptians and Sudanese, most of whom hold positions of power, and who worship Nyarlathotep, specifically his avatar of the Black Pharaoh. Dedicated to carrying out their will on Earth, they are relentless in their dealings with those who stand in their way. They meet at irregular intervals to perform rituals in the desert near the pyramids in Saqqara and in the network of caves below the Sphinx of Giza.

### Organisation
### London
Originally made up of Egyptian servants, almost equally depraved Hindus, Arabs and whites now form part of it; the sect is small, and the hierarchy is still largely Egyptian. The name of the sect comes from a form of Nyarlathotep who in dynastic Egypt was said to be a dark or invisible master who, like the night, was both everywhere and nowhere.

The Brotherhood serves the Penhew Foundation here; Sir Aubrey Penhew accompanied the Carlyle Expedition. The sect uses various venues outside London to carry out its rituals, and two important leaders reside in the capital: Edward Cavigan, the director of the Foundation, and Tewfik al-Sayed, who runs a small spice shop not far from Soho. They are both smart, dangerous, and absolutely insane. The sect's characteristic ritual weapon is a short staff with a spike; As payment for certain crimes, the sectarian is allowed to try to break the victim's bones with the stick before stabbing him in the heart. They never leave identifying runes on victims, and it is very rare for them to use weapons later. The Brotherhood does not accept women in its ranks. Relatively recently, a New York artist belonging to the sect has sculpted an ankh (or tapered cross) with the top broken or bent, which may perhaps indicate that the Cult of the Bloody Tongue and the Brotherhood tend to converge.

### Notable members
### Egypt
*Omar Shakti: chief priest of the sect, wealthy cotton farmer and landowner, who owns a large estate in the Fayum.

### London
*Edward Gavigan: prestigious 55-year-old British Egyptologist, current director of the Penhew Foundation and high priest of the Brotherhood of the Black Pharaoh in London.
*Tewfik al-Sayed: owner of a spice shop in London and a member of the Brotherhood of the Black Pharaoh in the city. Associated with Edward Gavigan, about once a month he visits the Misr House, in Essex, owned by Gavigan, in the company of a couple of dozen men. He also has a means of killing someone from a distance, if he gets his/her blood, known as the Mirror of Gaal.

The Brotherhood of the Skin, also referred to as the Brothers of the Skin, are a secret society of fanatical malicious killers. They first appeared in the Horror on the Orient Express supplement for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. This cult revolves around the Skinless One (an avatar of Nyarlathotep) in light of Sedefkar's scrolls and their powers.

### Members and History
It was founded by Selim Makryat and his followers in the 19th century. By the 20th century, the power of the discreet sect was considerable, having developed in Istanbul. Among other places, they took over the Red Mosque, an abandoned place of worship. In time, it came to be known as the Shunned Mosque among those who knew what was going on within its red-stained walls.

This first point gave rise to minor cults in Europe, such as the branch in Milan led by Arturo Faccia. Faccia owns some factories on the outskirts of Milan, run by other brothers, exploiting the workers to the maximum. Its members are in search of the different parts of the Sedefkar Simulacrum to enjoy its glory and, thanks to their adoration of the skinless being, live forever. Both Selim and Arturo have an obsession with prolonging their life. Mehmet Makryat, for his part, has obeyed his father but is a heretic who believes that the Sedefkar Simulacrum must be recovered in order to provide the Brotherhood of the Skin with more power in the world.

### Practices and Purposes
The Acolytes of the Skinless One one carried their terrible cult practices away from the gaze of the rest of the citizens, which included skinning and mutilating in order to gather enough material to invoke their deity successfully. In the end, the Skinless One transferred a part of his power to them in the form of spells, and, in the case of his most devoted acolytes, created the so-called Skin Beasts in order to defend their interests.

The Brotherhood of the Yellow Sign, also referred to as the Brothers of the Yellow Sign and the Cult of the Yellow Sign, is an evil fanatic cult of Hastur in its King in Yellow form. There are conflicting reports about its origin; some say it started among the Serpent Men of Valusia, but it seems more likely that it started in the underground land of K'n-yan. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

### Symbol
They identify each other by hand gesture or by wearing rings and earrings with a yellow stone.

### Members
The Brothers are led by a group of immortal humanoid alien beings from the blue-litten K'n-yan. These immortals possess advanced technology, as well as a number of telepathic powers, including the ability to dematerialize, read minds, and paralyze and hypnotize their victims. The Brothers have a small number of followers among the inhabitants of the surface.

### Actions
Occasionally they gather to destroy Mi-Go outposts and to worship Hastur and Shub-Niggurath.

It has been suggested that the Brotherhood of the Yellow Sign has founded all the religions that have passed through the world to strengthen the Great Old Ones, but it sounds highly unlikely.

In the video game The Baby In Yellow, they provided an adoption and babysitting service, though all of the babies they provided for adoption are identical to each other as they came from The King's tree, and they go under the name "Crown Childcare". Their enemy in The Baby in yellow is The seekers of The Jaundice Court, "Bane of the yellow sign".

Brown Jenkin is a fictional entity created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dreams in the Witch-House". The character is depicted as being a rat-like creature with a human-like face, who is a familiar to the witch Keziah Mason.

### Description
Brown Jenkin is "a small white-fanged furry thing", "no larger than a good-sized rat", whom for years haunted the witch house and the town of Arkham in general, "nuzzl[ing] people curiously in the black hours before dawn".



### History
When Walter Gilman managed to kill Mason, Jenkin replied in kind by burrowing though his chest and eating his heart.

Brown Jenkin's bones were later found with those of Mason and several small children by workers tearing out a slanting wall.

### In Other Media
Brown Jenkin has been showcased as a creature in a number of films and television shows, most notably in the television adaptation of "The Dreams in the Witch House" for Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities. The episode of the series features the creature heavily. Although the plot of the episode is different from that of Lovecraft's story, Brown Jenkin plays the same role assisting the witch Keziah and ultimately kills Walter by bursting out his chest then possessing his body. Within the episode, the character is instead named as "Jenkins Brown".

### Behind the Mythos
The origins of Brown Jenkin are subject to debate. Perhaps the most popular theory is that he is the child of Keziah and Nyarlathotep, the Lovecraftian deity she presumably serves. This is rather likely, considering that Lavinia Whateley mated with Yog-Sothoth, and that in The Lurker at the Threshold (posthumously published and co-written with August Derleth) there is a quote that reads: "'She affirm'd, and her good neighbours likewise, that it had been borne to her, and took oath that she did not know by what manner it had come upon her, for it was neither Beast nor Man but like to a monstrous Bat with human face.'" Another theory, proposed by Weird Tales columnist Kenneth Hite, is that Brown Jenkin was a higher dimensional servitor of Nyarlathotep who was rewarded as being a familiar. However, as he was in the third dimension, he could only appear as a third-dimensional interpretation of what he was (this being similar to the vistas of Hyperspace in the story).

Brown University is an Ivy League college located in Providence, Rhode Island. It was H. P. Brown is believed to be the main model for Lovecraft's fictional Miskatonic University (source?).

Bryan Katz is a fictional character created by author and artist Dean Wirth. He made his first appearance in the 2020 short story "The Dewey Mine Attack", published in Lovecraftiana Vol 5, Issue 1.

### History
Katz decided to wander his home country of the United States, believing that somewhere along the way he would find his goal in life. Overindulging in alcohol one evening he was robbed: this necessitated taking a back-breaking job working in Oregon's Dewey Mine.

Katz took well to the job, but soon came to realise that something was not right with the strange bands of shadow which appeared to roam the mountainside periodically. One night, he and his friends, again under the influence of rotgut, shot at the bands: the retaliation was instant and overwhelming, the creatures which lived inside these shadow-bands emerging and slaughtering the entire 100-strong workforce. Only Katz and two others managed to escape, making it to a nearby river and heading downstream.

Washing up on a deserted island off the West coast, the three were pursued by the entities which claimed the lives of two of the men, only Katz managing to evade them. He eventually made his way to civilisation, where he was suspected of perpetrating the atrocity and incarcerated in a the Oregon Hospital for the Insane, remaining there from 1886 - 1898.

Upon his release, Katz headed to Los Angeles, where he made something of a name for himself in the nascent silent movie industry. However, the advent of "talkies" and his lack of an acceptable speaking voice put an end to this, and he was forced to take employment as a janitor in a tough inner-city school. 

During this time, Katz made the acquaintance of a woman named Mina Luddox, whose husband, while serving aboard the USS Connecticut of the coast of Maryland in 1919, had been killed by the same creatures encountered by Katz in Oregon. The pair attempted to alert the world to the dangers these beings posed, but were met with nothing but derision. Following an interview with reporter Randy Oswald in 1945, Katz was urged by Mina to let the entire matter rest. Whether he took this advice remains unknown.

### Appearances

*"The Randy Oswald Story" (2020)

"Bug of the Stars" is a short Lovecraftian story by author Evan Rodenhausen.

### Synopsis
Ever since childhood a man has been visited by a mysterious buglike being which has imbued him with great knowledge, which allows him to make enormous strides for mankind but simultaneously curses him to a life of solitude and misery.

In his old age, the man devises a plan to rid himself of the bug's understandings, and is successful. However, in order to survive, the bug and it’s kind require a mortal with which to share their knowledge. Without such a vessel they begin to die, and the great darkness from beyond the stars from which they have been hiding the human race is revealed.

### Publication History
"Bug of the Stars" was published in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2020.

Buopoths are a species of extra-dimensional creature created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Description
Buopoths are large herbivorous animals with a passing resemblance to terrestrial tapirs. Native to the otherworldly dimension known as the Dreamlands, their preferred habitat is tropical forest, and they are generally peaceful creatures who much prefer to run and hide than confront any potential aggressor.

The courtship and mating rituals of the Buopoths are vigorous and noisy, yet pleasing to the ear: for this reason, they are found to be mimicked in the song and dance of many Dreamlands cultures which are aware of the creatures.

"Bus Ride Into Dreamlands" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Danny Nicholas. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long-running horror genre magazine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
While en route to Kadath Sports Camp, a prestigious summer camp purporting to be a facility for athletically-gifted children, a school bus blows a tyre. As the clearly-terrified driver attempts to fit the spare, he is consumed by a colossal sentient eyeball. Scholarship student Randy Upton manages to finish the job, and attempts to navigate the bus on the long drive back to civilisation.

Along the way they are accosted by all manner of bizarre entities, with most of the other students being taken by shapeshifting beings which enthral their minds with visions of salvation. Eventually the entire bus is swallowed by something lurking beneath the ground, and Randy and Warren, the only other surviving child must take to the woods to escape. Warren, however, his mind broken by the strain, makes too much noise and is taken by an unseen predator. 

Randy finally realises that he has somehow become turned around during his travels, and finds himself at the gates of Camp Kadath where he is imprisoned by the sinister councillors who begin his indoctrination into their cult. 

### Mythos Connections
*The name from which the summer camp takes its name, Kadath, is one of the central elements in H. P. Lovecraft's Dream Cycle series, also referenced in the story's title.
*Randy Upton's name would appear to be a nod to Richard Upton Pickman, the subject of Lovecraft’s short story "Pickman's Model." Like Pickman, Randy would also go on to become an inhabitant of the Dreamlands.
*The character's name of Warren is a clear reference to Harley Warren, one of the main characters in "The Statement of Randolph Carter," as illustrated when Randy questions the head councillor on his friend's whereabouts; he receives only the reply "You fool, Warren is dead."
*The siren-like beings which lure the majority of the children from the bus in a manner similar to the entities from Greek mythology  appear to do this using the psychic cry of "tekeli-li": the call of the Shoggoths in the novella At the Mountains of Madness.
*At one point, the bus is held up by a group of cats on the road, which Randy recognises to be "the meanest and most dangerous animals in these woods, no matter how small or cute or normal they appeared."
*At another point the boys encounter a hitchhiker resembling "[a] man-sized cucumber with wings and a star-fish head," which would appear to resemble one of the Elder Things from At the Mountains of Madness.
*The rituals Randy is forced to undertake at Camp Kadath include the worship of "a world devouring, unholy octopus man," likely a nod to the Great Old One Cthulhu.
*Camp Kadath's head councillor is shown to be a brain in a jar, a procedure carried out by the alien Mi-Go to preserve the intellects of promising individual

Butterfly-Dragons are a species of creature which originate from the magical dimension known as the Dreamlands.

### Description
Possibly named for their expansive wings which are brightly patterned like those of a butterfly, Butterfly-Dragons are found almost exclusively  in the land of Sona-Nyl in Earth's Dreamlands . Prized as pets, they are peaceful creatures which feed upon silence and the most choice aromas. They are possessed of a unique defence mechanism: when threatened, a Butterfly-Dragon will release a cloud of pheromones which render those they infect profoundly deaf. This effect is so powerful that it can even cross worlds, with those affected in the Dreamlands still suffering from hearing loss upon awakening.

"By the Way, Whatever Happened to the Dagons?" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Ambuehl.

### Synopsis
When an Innsmouth resident attends a reunion concert for one of his old favourite bands, he has no idea that the new member of the group has not only convinced them to change their name, but has taken them in a decidedly different direction. Unfortunately, this direction has little to do with music and everything to do with summoning a dark deity, and the concert awakens something terrible.

Byagoona (The Faceless One) is a fictional entity created by James Ambuehl for his short story "The Bane of Byagoona".

### Description
Byagoona is a Great Old One and the offspring of Lu-Kthu. He arrived on Earth during the reign of the Atlaus civilization. During their reign he was revered as a god of the dead and reanimated the deceased to sustain itself on their life force. It is theorised that Byagoona is not its own entity but is, in fact, an avatar of Nyarlathotep, though this is unconfirmed.

Byakhee are fictional creatures in the Cthulhu Mythos. They are predators who are known to travel in the vacuum of interstellar space. If one has the means by which to survive the myriad threats space presents, then one could ride a Byakhee to anywhere in the cosmos. When travelling beyond the speed of light, the creature's metabolism is greatly increased. When descending to the surface of any given planet, it is usually to feed, at which point it is best avoided.

### Overview
This interstellar race is believed to serve Hastur the Unspeakable and may be summoned to partake in rituals. Composed of conventional matter, they are vulnerable to ordinary mundane weapons but possess cunning intelligence and guile, and some are able to cast spells. 

Dwelling in interstellar space, Byakhee do not have bases on Earth (although the Nameless City serves as a sort of harbour for them), but may be summoned to perform deeds or to serve as steeds, carrying riders through interstellar space - such riders may need to partake of the revered Space Mead to survive such cold journeys. Some suggest that Byakhee do not fly through space but rather fold space around themselves, allowing near-instantaneous transport between two points.

### Locomotion
Byakhee have a hune organ attuned to the magnetic field of the galaxy, capable of providing ease of movement in both vacuum and within atmosphere by generating a "keim" field to travel through. Located in the thorax of the creature, it allows them to travel at 400 times the speed of light. (: S. Petersen's Field Guide to Cthulhu Monsters)

While on the earth's surface, Byakhee can fly at speeds up to 70 kph. The "hune" also allows them to hover on a planet's surface, using their wings for directional movement.

It has been theorized that the Byakhee's "hune" is paramagnetic in nature; that is in fact attuned to the galactic magnetic field, and is propelled by the flux. If this is true, than it may explain the creature's uncanny ability to hover while planetside, as it could easily manipulate the earth's natural magnetic field to achieve such an effect.

Byatis, The Berkeley Toad or the Serpent-Bearded Byatis appears as a gigantic, multicolored toad with a single eye, claws similar to a crabs and a beard of tentacles.

### Summary
Byatis has been associated with "Yig" and "Han", as among the "gods of divination".

An 18th-century document relates that a statue of the creature. Later the document says the monster is "somewhat like a Spider, somewhat like a Crab, and somewhat like a Horror in Dreams." It reports that the "Romans found it behind a stone Door in a Camp which was here long before the Invasion."

De Vermis Mysteriis reads:



The creature is depicted as incredibly large - one of its facial tentacles is as thick as a man - which makes it about the size of the castle that it is trapped beneath. Byatis can be repelled by the Elder Sign.

### History
In ancient times, The idol of Byatis was brought down to earth by the Deep Ones. Some time later, under unknown circumstances, Byatis itself was sealed behind a stone door in what would later become the Severn Valley. Most likely, the Elder Gods were responsible. When the Romans conquered Britain, a small group of soldiers formed a cult to the god, which was annihilated upon Byatis' short-lived escape. Centuries later, a Norman castle was built over the spot where Byatis was trapped, near what would later become Berkeley and Severnford.

During the 18th century, Byatis came under the control of the warlock Sir Gilbert Morley, who trapped the monstrous creature in the dungeon of the castle, and used its powers to enhance his own. He fed it by setting it loose during the night to devour the townsfolk, then returned it to the castle and locked it away once more. However, with each living thing it ate, Byatis grew larger. Eventually, Byatis became too big for its prison, and finally trapped itself when it consumed its keeper. This event and the memory of the Great Old One's earlier escapes, developed into the legend of the Berkeley Toad.

### Robert M. Price
In the Robert M. Price short story "The Beard of Byatis", the creature is capable of turning others to stone through the use of its facial tentacles and disguising itself as a human being.

### Behind the Mythos
Byatis was first mentioned in Robert Bloch's short story "The Shambler from the Stars", originally published in the September 1935 issue of Weird Tales. It plays a central role in Ramsey Campbell's 1964 short story "The Room in the Castle".
