fullContent:
Curtis Charles Senf (1873 - 1949) was a Prussian-American artist who worked extensively for Weird Tales, regularly providing covers and interior art for the magazine from 1927 to 1932. During this period, he illustrated dozens of stories, including H. P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness, Frank Belknap Long's "The Hounds of Tindalos" and The Horror from the Hills, Robert E. Howard's "The Children of the Night", and several tales by Clark Ashton Smith, among others.

Senf's parents, Constantin Ernst Senf and Rosette "Rosa" Senf, moved to the United States in June 1881 with their four children. Senf was born in Alsace-Lorraine which had recently been added to the greater German Empire at the time. Senf and his family settled in Chicago and that is where Senf himself spent the balance of his life. He opened an art agency called Senf & Company with a business partner Fred S. Gould.  They sold illustrations to the Chicago newspaper advertising industry. His younger brother Robert Senf also worked for them as a staff artist.

Outside of Weird Tales, his career was mostly focused on newspaper advertising and professional lithography.

fullContent:
Charles John Thompson (March 17, 1923 - February 11, 1991) was a pulp writer who used the pen name C. Hall Thompson. He wrote at least two well-regarded Cthulhu Mythos stories, though he reportedly faced resistance to his Mythos writings from Arkham House publisher August Derleth.

Thompson graduated from South Philadelphia High School for Boys in June 1942. Even before graduating, he had begun using his pseudonym--a tribute to his mother.  He published four stories in Weird Tales, including the Mythos stories "Spawn of the Green Abyss" (Nov. 1946) and  "The Will of Claude Ashur" (July 1947). As the blog Tellers of Weird Tales reports:Thompson sold nearly four dozen stories to Adventure, Argosy, Dime Western Stories, Frontier Stories, North-West Romances, 10 Story Western Magazine, and other titles, mostly Westerns, over the next six years. He also broke into the slicks with stories in Collier's and Esquire.Some Lovecraft scholars have read not only a proprietary attitude but also jealousy into Derleth's actions. Robert M. Price writes thatthe story goes that August Derleth intimidated Thompson into dropping the Lovecraft pastiche hobby, apparently because Thompson was working Derleth’s side of the street (and selling a better product).S. T. Joshi also criticizes Derleth's approach:It is not surprising that August Derleth apparently badgered Thompson to give up the idea of any further pastiches—not because Thompson had failed and was somehow tainting Lovecraft’s reputation, but precisely because he had succeeded, and succeeded far better than Derleth himself in any of his own Lovecraftian imitations.

fullContent:
Catherine Lucille Moore (January 24, 1911 – April 4, 1987) was an American science fiction and fantasy writer, who most often used the pen name C. L. Moore. She was among the first women to write in either genre (though earlier woman writers in these genres include Sophie Wenzel Ellis, Clare Winger Harris, Lilith Lorraine, Greye La Spina, Francis F. Stevens, Leslie F. Stone, and Everil Worrell). Moore's work paved the way for many other female speculative fiction writers. She and her first husband Henry Kuttner were prolific co-authors under their own names and three pseudonyms.

### Biography
### Early life
Moore was born on January 24, 1911 in Indianapolis, Indiana. She was chronically ill as a child and spent much of her time reading literature of the fantastic. She left college during the Great Depression to work as a secretary at the Fletcher Trust Company in Indianapolis.

### Writing career
Her first stories appeared in pulp magazines during the mid-1930s, including two significant series in Weird Tales, then edited by Farnsworth Wright. One features the rogue and adventurer Northwest Smith wandering through the Solar System; the other features the swordswoman/warrior Jirel of Joiry, one of the first female protagonists in sword-and-sorcery fiction. Both series are sometimes named for their lead characters.

The most famous Northwest Smith story is "Shambleau", which was also Moore's first professional sale. It originally appeared in the November 1933 issue of Weird Tales,

Included in that collection were "Judgment Night" (first published in August and September 1943), the lush rendering of a future galactic empire with a sober meditation on the nature of power and its inevitable loss; "The Code" (July 1945), an homage to the classic Faust with modern theories and Lovecraftian dread; "Promised Land" (February 1950) and "Heir Apparent" (July 1950), both documenting the grim twisting that mankind must undergo in order to spread into the Solar System; and "Paradise Street" (September 1950), a futuristic take on the Old West conflict between lone hunter and wilderness-taming settlers.

Moore met Henry Kuttner, also a science fiction writer, in 1936 when he wrote her a fan letter under the impression that "C. L. Moore" was a man. They married in 1940 and thereafter wrote almost all of their stories in collaboration—under their own names and using the joint pseudonyms C. H. Liddell, Lawrence O'Donnell, and Lewis Padgett—most commonly the latter, a combination of their mothers' maiden names.

In this very prolific partnership they managed to combine Moore's style with Kuttner's more cerebral storytelling. Their works include a classic, "Mimsy Were the Borogoves" (February 1943), the basis for the film The Last Mimzy (2007), and "Vintage Season" (September 1946), the basis for the film Timescape (1992). They also collaborated on a story that combined Moore’s signature characters, Northwest Smith and Jirel of Joiry: "Quest of the Starstone" (1937)

Clifford Martin Eddy Jr. (C. M. Eddy Jr.; January 18, 1896 – November 21, 1967) was a writer of weird fiction best remembered now for his friendship with H. P. Lovecraft and in some circles for his writing "The Loved Dead", a story of energy vampirism and necrophilia co-written by Lovecraft.

In addition to "The Loved Dead", Eddy and Lovecraft also collaborated on "Ashes", "The Ghost-Eater" and "Deaf, Dumb, and Blind". All four stories were published in Weird Tales and credited solely to Eddy. Later in life, Eddy wrote the short story "Black Noon" (1973), which was included in the anthology Acolytes of Cthulhu.

Eddy introduced both Houdini and Hazel Heald to Lovecraft amongst others and so was instrumental in widening the Mythos as it would come to be reconstructed or interpreted, through the collaboration and ghost writing work for which Lovecraft was commissioned by these and other authors.

His grandson, Jim Dyer, is the founder, owner and publisher of Fenham Publishing, a small press publisher that has published collected works of C. M. Eddy, Jr. as well as other related publications by both Eddy and his wife Muriell Eddy and his daughter Ruth Eddy relating to their personal reminiscences of H.P. Lovecraft.

Christopher P. Webster, known professionally as C. P. Webster, is a British author born in Runcorn, Cheshire. He was a lecturer of Fine Art at Aberystwyth University in Wales for 25 years before taking early retirement from teaching in 2020 to focus on writing fiction. Much of his work is inspired by H. P. Lovecraft and his circle, and Webster's own writing often incorporates aspects of the Cthulhu Mythos.

Webster’s short stories have been published widely both in the UK, the USA, and the rest of the Anglosphere, and he is a regular contributor to both The Bizarchives and Aegeon: Science Fiction Illustrated.

Two of his mythos related stories have appeared in the fanzine Lovecraftiana, including "The Reliquary" (Volume 5, Issue 1), and "At the Foot of the Stair" (Volume 10, Issue 3).

"Cabal" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Armand Rosamilia. It forms the third part of his Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Synopsis
When reporter Elizabeth Marsh travels to Keyport, New Jersey as part of a routine filler piece, she learns that her missing father was born in the town. When she decides to look into her ancestry, she discovers that the town - and her family name - carries with it a dark secret.

Unfortunately, her investigations lead her to stumble into a supernatural prison, where she meets fellow captives Bones and Father Rocco. Although the two are able help Elizabeth escape, she is quickly torn to pieces by the prison's malevolent guardians.

### Characters
*Elizabeth Marsh, a small-time reporter on assignment.
*Harrison Marsh, a scion of the Keyport branch of the Marsh family.
*Bones, a former gang member.
*Father Rocco Ignacio, an elderly priest.
*Dylan Murphy, local bar owner and leader of the Keyport branch of the Esoteric Order of Dagon.
*Nicole Marsh, Harrison's catatonic wife.

### Publication History
"Cabal" was first published in chapbook format in December 2012. It was later included in the collection Keyport Cthulhu in November 2013.

The Cabot Museum of Archaeology is a fictional institution located in Boston, created by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald in the story "Out of the Aeons". It is part of the Cthulhu Mythos. 

Originally designed as a mansion by Bullfinch in 1919,  the small museum specialises in objects from ancient and unknown civilisations. Before interest in the ancient Pacific mummy in 1932 it held little public interest, but had widespread recognition in scientific circles. The mummy's presence caused a surge of occult visitors and break-ins, leading to the death of a guard and two intruders on the 1st of December 1, 1932.

### Collection
By 1931 the Hall of Mummies on the second floor of the West Wing is said to be the finest collection of its kind in America, housing:
*Egyptian Mummies from Early Sakkarah through to the 8th century Coptic period.
*Prehistoric Indian examples from the Aleutian Islands.
*Several petrified citizens from the ruins of Pompeii.
*"Natural" mummies from people trapped in mines around the world.
*The mummy of T'yog, which entered the collection in November 1879.
*Preserved bodies from the crypts of Château Fausses-flammes in Averoigne, France, obtained in Spring 1931.
The Museum also has a basement library of books on lost cultures that also contains T'yog's scroll.
### Staff
*Curator Pickman - The curator in 1879.
*Richard H. Johnson Ph.D. - The curator in the early 1930s.
*Wentworth Moore Sc.D. - The museum taxidermist in the early 1930s.
*Lawrence Cabot and Dudley Salton - Museum trustees in the early 1930s.
*Drs Mason, Wells and Carver - Museum staff in the early 1930s.

"Cahokia" is a short story by Cody Goodfellow that first appeared in Horrors Beyond: Tales of Terrifying Realities (Elder Signs Press, 2005). It was later reprinted in Goodfellow's collection Rapture of the Deep and Other Lovecraftian Tales (Hippocampus Press, 2016).

### Synopsis
Set in the 22nd century, "Cahokia" tells the story of a Marine unit that calls themselves the Plague, whose mission is pillaging alien artifacts reached through interdimensional space. On their final mission, they find an asteroid that resembles Cahokia, the mysteriously abandoned Native American city in downstate Illinois. The space they stumble into what appears to be the refuge of "all the vanished peoples of the earth whose fabled ruins had eluded conquistadors."

shortDefinition: Caitlín Rebekah Kiernan (26 May 1964 - present) is an Irish-born American author of weird fiction, much of which includes Lovecraftian themes. They have published over 10 novels in the science fiction and dark fantasy genres, along with more than 250...
fullContent:
Caitlín Rebekah Kiernan (26 May 1964 - present) is an Irish-born American author of weird fiction, much of which includes Lovecraftian themes. They have published over 10 novels in the science fiction and dark fantasy genres, along with more than 250 shorter pieces of fiction and a series of comic books. Kiernan is a two-time recipient of both the World Fantasy and Bram Stoker awards. They are also a published paleontologist.

Saying that "too many people are obsessed with Lovecraft’s monsters, tentacles and polyps and shuggoths," Kiernan has cited the elements of Lovecraft that have had the greatest influence on their own work: "the importance of atmosphere, the found manuscript as a narrative device, and his appreciation of what paleontologists and geologists call deep time": Deep time is critical to his cosmicism, the existential shock a reader brings away from his stories. Our smallness and insignificance in the universe at large. In all possible universes. Within the concept of infinity. No one and nothing cares for us. No one’s watching out for us. To me, that’s Lovecraft. They also cite John Steinbeck as a "tremendous formative influence," who "taught me invaluable lessons about characterization; that stories, novels, are not about events. They’re about people.... Steinbeck also introduced me to the importance of profoundly flawed characters." Other writers who play important roles in Kiernan's fiction include Lewis Carroll and Charles Fort.

Kiernan's novels Threshold (2001), Low Red Moon (2003), and especially Daughter of Hounds (2007) explore the subterranean world of ghouls as envisioned in Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model". Their Tinfoil Dossier series--Agents of Dreamland (2017), Black Helicopters (2018), and The Tindalos Asset (2020)--mix the Cthulhu Mythos with the shadowy world of government conspiracies, a la The X-Files.

Kiernan's 2019 collection Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales includes many of their shorter Lovecraftian fiction pieces.

Kiernan is the publisher of Sirenia Digest, billed as "A Monthly Journal of the Weirdly Erotic", where much of their short fiction has first appeared since 2005.

### Selected Works


### Novels

Caliber Comics is an American independent publisher best known for its comic book output, but which also publishes a small amount of written content.

### Overview
Established in 1989 by Gary Reed, Caliber Comics is still publishing as of October 2022, despite a lengthy hiatus between 2000 and 2015, and Reed's death in 2016. Caliber's primary interest to this wiki is its Worlds of H. P. Lovecraft series by Steven Philip Jones, in which he has adapted a number of Lovecraft's stories into the comic book format.

Caliber also publishes a certain amount of prose work under the label Caliber Books; these works are usually published in both paperback and digital editions.

Carroll Ann Liddle was created by Raven Gregory and Daniel Lester in 2007, first appearing in issue #1 of the 1st volume of Grimm Fairy Tales: Return to Wonderland by Zenescope Entertainment. She is the primary protagonist of the Wonderland saga, appearing as the protagonist in the majority of the story arcs and mini-series.

### Background
Carroll Ann Liddle is Alice Liddle's daughter who grew up with a mother who slowly but steadily went insane. One day, Calie was given the task of watching her mother (to guard against the threat of suicide) but her mother demanded that she find a white rabbit which had escaped. Calie searched for the rabbit and eventually found it in the basement, in a previously unknown hole in the basement floor.

She fell through and her own adventures in Wonderland began. Calie would end up fighting and running from the Madness of Wonderland for decades, both in the Realm of Nightmares and on Earth. Fighting alongside her mother's aspect in Wonderland (Lacie) against the madness of Wonderland, battling her insane brother Johnny Liddle, trying to change Wonderland for the better, defending Earth from its madness, and trying to save and then protect her daughter Violet Liddle.

Calie evolves throughout the three series, and her evolution is tied to her own abilities, and especially those in Wonderland. Upon her second trip to Wonderland, while seeking to reclaim her daughter Violet, her physical abilities are all enhanced dramatically. Once the portal is destroyed she reverts to her ordinary capabilities as this was a result of her learning that she had control over the dimension by learning she had control over the madness which sought to infect her. In this mentality, she also proves adept with using martial weapons, most often a sword or a battle ax.

shortDefinition: California is a state in the Western region of the United States. It is the setting of H. P. Lovecraft's revision tale "The Last Test," and is mentioned elsewhere in his fiction. It frequently appears as a setting in later Cthulhu Mythos fiction.  Ca...
fullContent:
California is a state in the Western region of the United States. It is the setting of H. P. Lovecraft's revision tale "The Last Test," and is mentioned elsewhere in his fiction. It frequently appears as a setting in later Cthulhu Mythos fiction.

California was originally inhabited by Indigenous peoples, including the Yurok, Pomo, Miwok, and Chumash, among many others. Starting in 1769, the area was colonized by the Spanish Empire; when Mexico gained its independence in 1821, Alta California became a territory of the new nation. It was seized by the United States in 1846 during the Mexican-American War, and became a state in 1850. Since 1962, it's been the most populous state in the union.

Sacramento is the capital of California, and Los Angeles its largest city. Other prominent cities include San Francisco and San Jose in the Bay Area, and San Diego near the southern border with Mexico.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
"The Last Test," a story Lovecraft wrote with Adolphe de Castro, is set in California; one of its characters, James Dalton, is in fact governor of the state. The story's central character, Dr. Alfred Clarendon, lives in San Francisco after being appointed the medical director of the California State Penitentiary at San Quentin. His arrival makes California "a centre of medical scholarship with earthwide influence and reputation."

The narrator of Lovecraft's story "Dagon" wakes up in a San Francisco hospital after his encounter with the giant on the risen sea floor.

"The Call of Cthulhu" names California as one of the areas where Cthulhu's influence is felt in the spring of 1925: Among George Gammell Angell's notes are a "despatch from California [that] describes a theosophist colony as donning white robes en masse for some 'glorious fulfilment' which never arrives."

In The Whisperer in Darkness, Henry Wentworth Akeley has a son, George Goodenough Akeley, in San Diego, California; Henry plans to relocate to his son's home when he begins to fear for his life from the Mi-Go.  Later he despairs: "They don’t mean to let me get to California now—they want to take me off alive, or what theoretically and mentally amounts to alive."

### Other Mythos Writers
"The Return of the Sorcerer" (1931), by Clark Ashton Smith, is set at John Carnby's house in the suburban hills of Oakland, California. Smith's "The Hunters from Beyond" (1932) takes place at the studio of Cyprian Sincaul in San Francisco.

Henry Kuttner's "The Invaders" (1939) takes place in Michael Hayward's "isolated cottage on the beach north of Santa Barbara." His "Bells of Horror" (1939) is set in the fictional town of San Xavier, not far from Los Angeles. The main action of Kuttner's "Hydra" (1939) takes place in Hollywood, with the fatal book purchased in San Pedro, a seaport neighborhood of Los Angeles.

Fritz Leiber set his story "The Terror from the Depths" (1976) in Vulture's Roost, a fictional community in the Hollywood Hills above Los Angeles. The story describes Southern

fullContent:
Caligo Accedendum Tournament: An Adventure for Cthulhu Dark Ages is a scenario supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
Caligo Accedendum Tournament consists of three stand-alone adventures along with all of the necessary handouts and a set of pre-generated investigators to allow for quick-start games.

### Scenarios
*"Island of the Damned" by Michael Patty, in which Vikings fall prey to the entities of the Cthulhu Mythos.
*"Risam Vellere" by Deanne P. Goodwin, involves the deciphering of an ancient grimoire.
*"The Innocent" by Bob Geis, a human-interest story based within the Mythos.

### Behind the Mythos
The scenarios contained in Caligo Accedendum Tournament were first used for demonstration games at traditional gaming convention Gen Con 2004. It was published by Chaosium as part of their Monograph series of supplements in both print and digital formats, but both versions are currently unavailable.

### Trivia
*The Latin portion of the title roughly translates as "the approaching darkness".

fullContent:
"Call and Response" is a short story by Scottish-born author William Meikle. It crosses over the Arkham Detective Agency created by C. J. Henderson with Meikle's own Midnight Eye Files, another hardboiled series which includes supernatural elements. It was written by Meikle at the request of Brian M. Sammons for a story involving Henderson's hard-boiled private investigator Frank Nardi, and was first published in the anthology Arkham Detective Agency by Dark Regions Press in November 2017.

### Synopsis
Private Detective Frank Nardi follows a trail of clues to Glasgow, Scotland, where he joins forces with fellow PI Derek Adams. Together, the pair help to decipher a mysterious code coming from somewhere far out in the universe.

### Characters 
*Frank Nardi, a former NYPD detective turned private eye.
*Derek Adams, a Glaswegian private investigator.
*John Logie Baird, a Scottish inventor.
*Dr. Piers Night, a boffin from Arkham.

### Mythos Connections
*Both Frank Nardi and Dr. Night reside in the town of Arkham created by H. P. Lovecraft himself.
*The Great Old One Cthulhu is referenced, albeit tangentially.

### Behind the Mythos
Although Scottish inventor John Logie Baird appears as a character in "Call and Rssponse", the Arkham Detective Agency continuity takes place in a roughly contemporary setting despite its noir overtones; Baird, however, died in 1946 .

### Publication History

fullContent:
Call of Cthulhu is a horror fiction role-playing game based on H. P. Lovecraft's story of the same name and the associated Cthulhu Mythos. The game, often abbreviated as CoC, is published by Chaosium. The game was first released in 1981, and eighteen editions (mostly fairly minor revisions) have been published to date. 

The game makes use of Chaosium's Basic Role-Playing (BRP) system, first seen in the game RuneQuest, but with special rules for Sanity. It is notable among roleplaying games for its longevity and also for remaining largely unchanged for most of its history, with only the most recent seventh edition making significant changes to the rules.

In October 2024, Call of Cthulhu was inducted into the ENNIEs hall of fame, only the second inductee since the Hall was established the previous month. The award was presented to 7th edition co-authors Mike Mason and Paul Fricker at the 2025 Gen Con event in Indiana, USA.

### Setting
The game takes place in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos, by default in 1920s Lovecraft Country. Supplements published by Chaosium and others supported other settings, such as 1890s England (Cthulhu by Gaslight), the modern day (Cthulhu Now),  World War II (Achtung! Cthulhu), 11th century Europe (Cthulhu Dark Ages), Ancient Rome (Cthulhu Invictus), and the 23rd century (Cthulhu Rising).

### Supplements


### Miskatonic Repository


### Video Games
Since its release, a number of video games carrying the Call of Cthulhu branding have been released. These games are of the horror survival, adventure and mystery-solving type.

*Shadow of the Comet (1993)
*Call of Cthulhu: Prisoner of Ice (1995)
*Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth (2006)
*Call of Cthulhu: Destiny's End (cancelled)

*Call of Cthulhu (2018)

### See also
*Achtung! Cthulhu - A Mythos-based RPG set during World War II.
*CthulhuTech - A Mythos-based RPG set in the late 21st century, in which humans use advanced technology to fight off Lovecraftian threats.
*Trail of Cthulhu - A later Mythos-based RPG which uses the GUMSHOE system, focusing on investigation and interpreting clues.
*Delta Green: The Role-Playing Game - An alternate contemporary setting based on the Mythos, originally set in the 1990s but later updated to the 2010s.
* Cthulhu Live - A live-action Mythos-based RPG.

fullContent:
Call of Cthulhu is a survival-horror video game developed by Cyanide and published by Focus Home Interactive in 2018. The game is based on the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game by Chaosium, and follows an original story loosely inspired by The Shadow Over Innsmouth and "The Call of Cthulhu" by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Summary
Alcoholic World War I veteran turned private investigator Edward Pierce is summoned to the whaling town of Darkwater on the island of the same name in order to investigate the case of the Hawkins family, who perished in a mysterious fire. While investigating a nightmarish painting made by artist Sarah Hawkins, Edward finds himself hunted by a Dimensional Shambler, also earning himself the ire of the local rum-running crime syndicate and cultists who worship the Leviathan and its progenitor Cthulhu.

### Characters

* Edward Pierce - A member of the Lost Batallion and WW1 veteran who joined the Wentworth Detective Agency before degenerating into alcoholism. He is hired to find out the truth behind Sarah Hawkins, her mysterious paintings, and the fire that supposedly killed her along with her family. He is the "Chosen One" necessary to awaken Cthulhu.
* Sarah Hawkins - A painter of mysterious and macabre paintings that are, nevertheless, extremely desired as well as famous. She was mentally ill and saw visions. Supposedly, she started a fire that killed her, her husband, and her young son. She is actually alive and working with the cult of Cthulhu to revive her dead child.
* Charles Hawkins - A failed importer and exporter who inherited all of his money. He is Sarah's husband and survived the fire that supposedly killed him by becoming an unholy fusion of man as well as Star Spawn. He is a Cthulhu cultist and working for the Leviathan.
* Catherine "Cat" Baker - the female head of the local gang of bootleggers and smugglers that run Darkwater Island (or at least think they do until the cult of Cthulhu proves otherwise). She is hardy enough to resist most of the supernatural shenanigans going on.
* Thomas Fuller - The head doctor at the Riverside institute. He has been experimenting on the patients at his hospital using the samples of the Leviathan's DNA he's acquired. He is wildly respected in his field and seemingly capable of resurrection.
* Marie Colden - A beautiful doctor at the Riverside Institute that believes Doctor Fuller is engaged in unethical medical experimentation but is unaware of the existence of the supernatural. She becomes Pierce's ally despite this.
* Captain Fitzroy - The captain of the sole remaining functional boat in Darkwater Island as well as the head of the docks. He is also secretly the head of the cult of Cthulhu and over a century old. Despite being head of the cult, he has very little control and both Pierce as well as Sarah Hawkins have far larger importance to Leviathan's plans.
* Ethan Bradley - A Darkwater Island police officer who is well meaning but woefully incompetent at his job.
* Leviathan

fullContent:
The Call of Cthulhu Keeper Screen , originally launched as the Keeper's Screen, is a play aid for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. First released by Chaosium in 1985, it has since undergone a number of revamps featuring rules updates and errata, as well as new artwork and extras .

The concept of the "screen" in table top roleplaying games (TTRPG) is for the referee, judge, storyteller or in the case of Call of Cthulhu RPG, the Keeper, to conceal dice rolls or maps and other periphera from the inquisitive gaze of their players, thus allowing suspense and mystery. It also allows the "fudging" of dice rolls by the Keeper should they need to insure the players' character survive a little longer. Finally, TTRPG screens most often contain tables, charts and even combat flow charts to help the person running a game maintain order and keep focused whilst preventing wasted time while a book is cracked open to look up rules.

### Overview
First released as a play aid in 1985, the Keeper Screen at its core consists of a hard-stock cardboard screen in a 3xA4 sized format, printed with a selection of most-commonly referenced rules, tables, and guidelines. It has been revised and updated several times over the years, with new editions seeing print in 1988, 1991, 1992, 2000, 2010, and 2016. These editions have featured numerous extras including new artwork, rules clarifications, scenarios, and more .

fullContent:
End Time is a horror fiction role-playing game based on the Cthulhu Mythos. The game is published by Chaosium and was released in 2001.

### Setting
The game takes place in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos, though in the mid 22nd century. The Great Old Ones have returned to Earth, turning it into a nightmarish world in which most of humanity has gone mad and been enslaved by the Great Old Ones and/or their servitor races. On Mars are two small human colonies struggling to survive.

### History of Earth
In 2034, Domaag T'eel is temporarily freed by his servant, Dr. Tensler. The Mi-Go and humans were able to imprison it again at the cost of the human outposts on the Moon. Domaag T'eel is an entity that the Mi-Go had been growing on the Moon to use against the Great Old Ones. Dr. Tensler's contact with it changed things, as it wanted its freedom.

In 2038, the moon starts to shift its orbit, causing weather disruptions and coastal flooding. As the influence of the Great Old Ones increased, the crime rate grew and so did the rate of insanity. The islands of Ghatanothoa and R'lyeh become exposed. Inexplicable strange events began to happen on a regular basis. Massive fear and madness induced riots hit the major cities. Deep Ones took over many small coastal communities and inland many small communities fell to Mythos entities. Aircraft and ships vanished from the sky and seas. Cities turned into war zones and those governments that remained declared martial law.

By 2054, not a single human government remained intact. In 2055 Domaag T'eel finally broke free of the containment field that the Mi-Go used on it, after which it moved the Moon's orbit enough to free the Great Old Ones. Nuclear warheads were fired at the remaining cities from the orbital battle satellites, denying the Great Old Ones the ability to prolong their rule by a ritual mass sacrifice of the human race.

### History of Mars
2036-2055 China and the United States worked together to build space stations and colonies on Mars. China took the lead in these projects (e.g. being first to launch rockets) due to political resistance in the US due to the cost. As chaos, insanity, and warfare slowly but steadily spread across the world, their efforts to build the space stations and colonies accelerated.

By 2049 they were joined by Japan and the European Economic Community which launched their own rockets. In 2056 the colonies lost contact with Earth. On Mars, by 2057 there were 500 humans on the Mars colony. They lost contact with the satellites in Earth orbit in 2091. The population of Mars reached 645 by 2094 and 700 by 2112.

### Earth
*Geography: Many parts that used to be submerged are now dry land, including R'lyeh, and many parts that were once dry are now submerged. Parts of the world are now radioactive wastelands, including New York.

Call of Cthulhu: Beyond the Mountains of Madness was a planned video game based on the roleplaying game scenario of the same name.

### Overview
Announced in November 2002, Beyond the Mountains of Madness was developed by Headfirst in parallel with their Dark Corners of the Earth release. It was ultimately cancelled in 2006 after Headfirst were unsuccessful in securing a publisher; this cancellation was a major contributing factor in the bankruptcy of the company.

### Premise
Stated to have been a first person shooter survival horror, it was set in the 1930s. The player was to assume the role of globetrotting Miskatonic University archaeologist Robert Naples, recalling the character of Indiana Jones.

fullContent:
Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth is a video game released in 2005 for the Xbox and 2006 for PC platforms, developed by Headfirst Productions and published by Bethesda Softworks. The game is based on the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game by Chaosium and loosely follows the plot of H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Summary
The main character is Jack Walters, a private investigator suffering from amnesia following a mysterious case in 1915. The majority of the plot takes place seven years later in the seaside town of Innsmouth, Massachusetts. Jack travels to Innsmouth to solve a missing person case, encounters the Esoteric Order of Dagon and their idols of worship and, as the game reaches its conclusion, eventually learns the truth about himself and some of the things that live in the dark corners of the earth.

Announced in November 2002, Destiny's End was developed by Headfirst in parallel with their Dark Corners of the Earth release. Call of Cthulhu: Prisoner of Ice is a video game based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. It is a sequel to the game Call of Cthulhu: Shadow of the Comet.

### Overview
A single-player puzzle solving game, Prisoner of Ice begins on a pre-WWII British submarine departing a German military base built atop the ruined Elder Thing city described in At the Mountains of Madness. The plot later moves to Argentina where it ties in with its predecessor game Shadow of the Comet.

### Release
First released by Infogrames in the US and UK in 1995, Prisoner of Ice received a Japanese release in 1997, where it was also ported to the Sega Saturn and PlayStation.

### Tie-Ins
Three French comic books were released to tie into Prisoner of Ice,  La Geôle de Pandore (Pandora's Jail), Le Glaive du Crépuscule (The Dagger in the Dusk) and La Cité des Abîmes (The City of the Depths).

Call of Cthulhu: The Wasted Land is a single-player tactical roleplaying Cthulhu Mythos video game.

### Premise
In 1915, a scholar and a British army officer battle a German Army cult who are using the stolen work of Dr. Herbert West to create a legion of undead soldiers to fight the war in France. However, the cult's ultimate goal is later revealed to be the summoning of a Star-spawn of Cthulhu, which will eliminate mankind in its entirety and pave the way for a new species of Star-spawn/human hybrids.

### Release
The Wasted Land was released for iOS and Windows in January and May 2012 respectively, and for Android in July of the following year.

Set in 1934, the story follows Norah Everhart as she searches for her missing husband on an island in the South Pacific, slowly discovering a connection to Dagon and the Deep Ones.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Norah Everhart is on a mission to find her missing husband, Harry, who went to a mysterious island in the Pacific that he has gone to in order to find a cure for her mysterious illness. This includes strange growths on her hands, dreams of swimming underwater, and fatigue. The Everhart Expedition seems to have suffered a terrible series of tragedies as well as madness. The island is also full of bizarre technology as well as weird fish motif art and structures. Norah Everhart gradually discovers that she isn't sick at all but undergoing a strange transformation that she must either embrace or reject, knowing it will kill her.

fullContent:
Call of Wonderland is a seven-issue comic book mini-series written by Raven Gregory in 2008-2009 which was published by Zenescope Entertainment. 

### Synopsis
With both the Jabberwocky and Queen of Hearts defeated, Wonderland has been thrown into chaos. The Red Knight is going to unleash the Old Ones thereby destroying both Wonderland and Earth. Back on Earth, a forgotten secret is discovered by Julie Sands, a literary student who obtains a journal written by her favourite author, H. P. Lovecraft. After Julie and Salome Gray decapitate a monster in self-defense, only for it to revert to human form upon death, they find themselves pursued by both the police and the Red Knight's forces.

### Connections
*The Lovecraft journal was donated to the library of Julie's university as part of a collection of rare books from the estate of Francis Wayland Thurston of Boston.
*The creature summoned from Wonderland by Jacob Hall's magic is a Moon-beast, identified as such by Lovecraft himself, who has seen the species in his dreams.
*The Jabberwocky is identified as one of the Old Ones who was spared in the ancient war by the triumphant Keepers. While the other Old Ones were trapped for eternity in a sleep-like stasis (as actually destroying them would be impossible), the Jabberwocky was still young, and the Keepers hoped that placing it in the Realm of Dreams would cleanse it of its evil. Instead, the Jabberwocky corrupted its environment and turned it into the Realm of Nightmares, while plotting to form a link strong enough to escape into the waking world and destroy it.
*The detective who investigates the murder of Mai Lee is named Emma Legrasse, likely as an homage to John Raymond Legrasse from "The Call of Cthulhu". She would go on to play a bigger role in Madness of Wonderland.

Its leader Jimmy Cruz was a monsignor within the Catholic Church who desired to destroy Satan and his forces. He was willing to use whatever means were necessary to accomplish that goal. Therefore turning to the N'Garai for power and their assistance. It's members summoned demons and both extracted and bound souls. They tried to kill Satana, the heroic rebellious daughter of Lucifer, only to die at her hands.

Camp Hollow Lake is a short scenario supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Written by Danny Stephens, it was published under licence by DriveThruRPG as part of their Miskatonic Repository player-driven resource initiative in July 2023.

### Overview




The scenario consists of a sandbox-style adventure which takes place in a remote summer camp for teens, four of whom possess a dark secret - although they are unaware of each others' involvement. It contains no direct references to the Cthulhu Mythos.

The plot involves a lonely girl who, after her amorous advances were spurned by her best friend and the subsequent mockery she endured at school, was plied with liquor and assaulted by a boy who saw in her an easy target; she is soon presumed dead. However, as circumstances would have it, she survived the attack and a pact with an ancient spirit known as a Wendigo, and is now intent on taking her revenge on those she deems most responsible: the player characters.

shortDefinition: Camside is a fictional town in England, created by Ramsey Campbell as part of his Severn Valley setting.  In the introduction to his collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, Campbell describes the place as "a rather unimportant...
fullContent:
Camside is a fictional town in England, created by Ramsey Campbell as part of his Severn Valley setting.  In the introduction to his collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, Campbell describes the place as "a rather unimportant town between Berkeley and Severnford, once visited by a man intent on seeking out the god Byatis, but otherwise undistinguished." By "unimportant", Campbell appears to mean that is the home of relatively few horrific entities; it is the location of several institutions that seem to play vital roles in the everyday life of the Severn Valley region, but it often appears in Campbell's stories to contrast its relative normalcy with the weirdness going on around it. 

Camside is first mentioned in passing in "The Church in High Street" as one of a number of Severn Valley towns where "the actual worship of trans-spatial beings [is] still practiced"; it also has a hospital where narrator Richard Dodd wakes up after his attempts to flee from Temphill. 

Camside plays a slightly larger role in "The Room in the Castle", the story that Campbell alludes to when he says that Camside was visited by a seeker after Byatis; the narrator of that story learns of that ancient entity from his friend Scott, who lives in the town. But the ruined castle where the main action of the story occurs is located across the river from Severnford.

Helping Scott with an article he is writing for the Camside Observer is what gets the narrator interested in Severn Valley lore in the first place--so Camside is at least large enough to support a newspaper. The paper is mentioned again in "The Render of the Veils" and "The Plain of Sound". 

"The Render of the Veils" may record the one genuinely uncanny event in Campbell's fiction that takes place in Camside. The occultist Henry Fisher, who ropes Kevin Gillson into a disastrous summoning of the Outer God Daoloth in that story, lives in a block of flats on Tudor Drive (or Tudor Street) in that town; it's the chief of police of Camside who investigates what seems to be the resulting double murder.

Other mentions of Camside in Campbell's fiction include:

*in "The Horror from the Bridge", Camside is the hometown of James Phipps, until he was expelled in 1800 for practicing weird science, resettling in Clotton.
*When a meteorite falls in the woods near Goatswood in the 1600s, searchers come from both Camside and Brichester to look for it without success, in "The Insects from Shaggai".
*In "The Mine on Yuggoth", Edward Taylor is committed to the Camside Home for the Mentally Disturbed in 1924, after his ascent of the Devil's Steps.
*The undertaker who handles the funeral of Brichester resident Robert Shorrock in "The Return of the Witch" came from Camside; afterwards he "suddenly left his profession and took to drink." (Brichester is certainly large enough to have its own funeral parlours; it's possible that undertakers closer to hand knew enough to refuse the Shorrocks' business.)

Canada is a first-world country which occupies the northern portion of the North American continent and is the second largest country by landmass in the world, although it is relatively sparsely populated. It borders the United States to the south, while its northern territories stretch far into the Arctic Circle.

Canada as it exists in the modern day began life as a series of European colonies, primarily those of the British and French. Although it has long since thrown off its colonial ties, as a result of the nature of its genesis, Canada's history and culture has been extensively influenced by that of Europe.

### Overview

### In Lovecraft’s Works
Although Lovecraft's works feature few mentions of Canada, some notable exceptions are given below.

### "Herbert West--Reanimator"
In "Part V: The Horror From the Shadows" of Lovecraft's hokey 1922 science fiction/horror story, the narrator, his friend Dr. Herbert West, and Sir Eric Moreland Clapham-Lee all serve with the Canadian army surgical corps from 1915, during the early years of World War I before US involvement in the conflict. They conducted experiments into human reanimation, using the violence of the war to conceal their activities. (): "Herbert West--Reanimator")

### "Waste Paper"
A line of Lovecraft’s satirical poem mentions "the Governor-General of Canada … Lord Byng." (: "Waste Paper")

### Commonplace Book
The first entry of 1935 in a notebook which he used to jot down notes for his work, Lovecraft copied the following newspaper article:

: Commonplace Book)}}

### In the Works of Lovecraft's Circle
Clark Ashton Smith's 1932 short story features two characters, Henry and Arthur Chaldane, who reside in Canada. (: "The Nameless Offspring")

### In the Real World
Two of Lovecraft’s correspondents, Henry George Weiss and Vincent Starrett, were Canadian by birth.

Cancerverse is a fictional universe in the Marvel Multiverse, one of the realities conquered by the Many-Angled Ones. It appeared in The Thanos Imperative mini-series in 2010.

### Background
In this reality, Death was defeated by Life. A dying Captain Mar-Vell was seduced by the Many-Angled Ones into making a pact with them, who cured him of his cancer. After convincing his closest allies and friends to join him, twisting and corrupting them, they killed Thanos, the Avatar of Death. As a result of that ritual, which also destroyed that universe's cosmic aspect of Death, Life itself became an Eldritch abomination. Without Death to keep Life in check, it absorbed everything that would otherwise have been destroyed or killed and it grew like a cancerous tumor.

This unnatural "eternal life" was fueled by the power of the Many-Angled Ones, and Lord Mar-Vel, as the Cancerverse's Avatar of Life,  was determined to spread the plague of undeath throughout the Multiverse. His first target was the Prime Reality (Earth-616), which he assaulted through a tear in reality known as the Fault. They would have succeeded if not for the actions of 616's Thanos and the Guardians of the Galaxy, who brought their universe's Death into the Cancerverse, temporarily weakening it and crippling the invasion. As the entity Death had to return to their reality, the Cancerverse was able to recover.

The Cancerverse features corrupted versions of the Marvel Universe's leading super teams, including the Revengers (Avengers), the Defenders of the Realm (Defenders), the Ex-Men (X-Men) and the Ftaghn Four (Fantastic Four).

Canis Mysterium: A Scenario With Bite is an adventure supplement for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Published by Chaosium in May 2013, it was written by Scott Haartman and edited by Meghan McLean with cover art supplied by Colin Nitta and interior work by Eric York . Both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Overview


The storyline involves psychotic gravedigger Tobias Lurtz - heavily implied to have come from Ghoul stock - and his Ghoul companion as they attempt to use a forbidden text to raise an army of the dead and exact vengeance on the townsfolk of Coldwater Falls, who Lurtz believes have done him many grave injustices over the course of his life.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite the back cover claiming that a copy of H.P. Lovecraft's Arkham would be helpful in running this scenario, Arkham plays no appreciable role in the story - the vast majority of the action taking place in Coldwater Falls, a town located some 60 miles from Arkham  - and could easily be edited out entirely by the simple expediency of substituting a reason not involving Miskatonic University for the investigators to be pursuing a case in small town New England.

fullContent:
"Captain Marvel Battles the Vampire" is a golden age comic book story from Captain Marvel Adventures issue #1, published by Fawcett Publications. It is a sixteen-page story in which Captain Marvel's human child alter ego Billy Batson, a radio reporter and newsboy, is given an assignment to interview Doctor Deever. In a way slightly reminiscent of Herbert West, Deever has created a process to restore the dead to life. It is notable not for Mythos allusions or pastiche but because H. P. Lovecraft himself appears as a character, in the form of the writer of the authoritative work on vampires of the world in which the story takes place. 

### Synopsis
The doctor takes Billy to a cemetery and succeeds in raising a corpse back to life. The dead man is Bram Thirla, and once resurrected, proves to be a bloodthirsty vampire. In the process of raising the vampire, Doctor Deever is killed by the creature. Thirla then runs amok, killing people who themselves turn into vampires. Captain Marvel initially believes the vampires are destroyed since they all seem to die at sunrise.

Captain Marvel must figure out a way to defeat his unholy foe before more people become its victims. Returning to his child form as Billy Batson, he goes to the local library and checks out a book to aid him in his cause: "The Vampire Legend" by H. P. Lovecraft. In this universe, Lovecraft is quite the expert on vampires. Billy discovers that garlic does indeed drive off vampires but that they return from the dead each sunset and can only be permanently killed by a white thorn wooden stake. He prepares one and destroys Thirla and his minions permanently.

### Trivia
*The name Bram Thirla is obviously inspired by the author of Dracula, Bram Stoker.

Carcosa is a mystical ancient city created by Ambrose Bierce for his short story "An Inhabitant of Carcosa". It is a central element of the horror fantasy story cycle The King in Yellow, by Robert W. Chambers, who places it in an apparently extraterrestrial landscape complete with two suns, strange moons, and black stars. In some of Chambers' stories, it is stated that the towers of Carcosa can rise behind the moon, as if the city itself was a celestial place - or perhaps a theatrical stage. 

The King in Yellow also associates Carcosa with Aldebaran and the Hyades, as well as Hastur (originally the name of a god created by Bierce).

While the mythology of The King in Yellow was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in The Whisperer in Darkness, Carcosa itself was referenced in the Mythos stories of August Derleth and Donald Wandrei.

### Description
Carcosa is often described to have:
*Black stars on a bright sky
*Twin suns
*The Lake of Hali
*Black soaring towers
*Wet winds

### Pathfinder
In the Pathfinder universe, Carcosa is a highly magical planet which contains a living city that is also called Carcosa. It's the home of Hastur, who resides in the monstrous Lake of Hali. When the light from Carcosa's star shines on another world's night sky, Hastur's power increases on that world. Carcosa is continuously expanding, absorbing the societies and cities of other worlds, serving as the fuel for Hastur's eventual ascension into the ranks of the Outer Gods, at which time he will consume and absorb Carcosa and its inhabitants. The city of Carcosa is a vast patchwork of the cities which it absorbed over the eons, each individual patchwork is a nexus, which may retain some of the properties of their original worlds. Some of the known nexuses include Neruzavin (flying polyp city), Bohlvari (shoggoth inhabited elder thing city), a technologically advanced city of skyscrapers (inhabited by robots and aliens), and an underwater city (inhabited by the undead).

Cards of Cthulhu: A Deckbuilding Game, also known as Cthulhu Deckbuilder, is a competitive card game from Duel Grounds.

### Overview
Based on the works of H. P. Lovecraft and the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Cards of Cthulhu: A Deckbuilding Game was designed by Paul Davis and released in 2015 after a successfully-funded kickstarter campaign.

### Gameplay
Designed for between two and five players, Cards of Cthulhu involves players taking on the role of one of seven types of investigator, each of which have their own special abilities. The objective of the game is to build the best possible deck through gameplay, and use it to score points whilst avoiding the effects of insanity caused by cards such as Cthulhu, Azathoth and Hastur. The player with the most points at the games' conclusion wins.

fullContent:
Carl Richard Jacobi (10 July 1908 – 25 August 1997) was a pulp fiction writer who contributed frequently to Weird Tales. Three collections of his short stories were published by Arkham House. His story "The Aquarium", which first appeared in Arkham House's Dark Mind, Dark Heart (1962), was later included in Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos (Fedogan & Bremer, 1992).

In addition to Weird Tales, Jacobi wrote horror fiction for pulp outlets like Thrilling, Thrilling Wonder Stories, Ghost Stories, Startling Stories, and Strange Stories. He also wrote pulp adventure and crime stories for Thrilling Adventures, Complete Stories, Top-Notch, Short Stories, The Skipper, Doc Savage and Dime Adventures Magazine. He wrote some stories in the space opera genre for science fiction magazines like Planet Stories.

He wrote under a variety of pseudonyms, including Philip Spayne, King Marling, James K. Vermont, Richard Carle, Matthew South, Stephen Benedict, and Jackson Cole.

Born in Minneapolis, Jacobi was an English major at the University of Minnesota from 1927-1930, where he met Donald Wandrei. In 1931, Wandrei introduced him to August Derleth, with whom he would correspond for 40 years. 

Jacobi began writing professionally while still in college; his short story "Mive", which won a campus writing contest and was published in the college's Minnesota Quarterly (Fall 1928) before being resold to Weird Tales (January 1932), caught the attention of H. P. Lovecraft.  He wrote to Jacobi, "I told [[Farnsworth Wright|[editor Farnsworth] Wright]] that I was glad to see at least one story whose weirdness of incident was made convincing by adequate emotional preparation and suitably developed atmosphere."

An omnibus collection of the best of Jacobi's weird fiction, edited by S. T. Joshi, was published by Centipede Press in 2014. A two-volume selection of Jacobi's work, also edited by Joshi, came out from Weird House Press in 2021.

### Bibliography

### Collections
* Revelations in Black (Arkham House, 1947)
* Portraits in Moonlight (Arkham House, 1964)
* Disclosures in Scarlet (Arkham House, 1972)
* East of Samarinda (Bowling Green State University Popular Press, 1989)
* Smoke of the Snake (Fedogan & Bremer, 1994) 
* Masters of the Weird Tale: Carl Jacobi (Centipede Press, 2014)
* Mive and Others: Best Weird Stories of Carl Jacobi Volume 1 (Weird House Press, 2021) 
* Witches in the Cornfield: Best Weird Stories of Carl Jacobi Volume 2 (Weird House Press, 2021)

Karel "Carl" Kolchak is a fictional character created by American author Jeff Rice. He is the protagonist of two made-for-television movies, one season of television episodes, numerous novel and short story adaptations. and several comic books. Due to the production order of the various media associated with Kolchak's genesis, his creation is often attributed to Richard Matheson; however, Kolchak is the original creation of author Jeff Rice, who wrote the novel The Kolchak Papers which kickstarted the franchise.

There have also been in more recent times several series of comic book adaptations and new stories published in novel form, most notably by Moonstone Books.



It is mainly in the comic book stories that Kolchak encounters creatures and cults that would fit easily into the Mythos and that are in a few cases directly stated as being linked to Mythos entities.

Screenwriter, producer, and director Chris Carter has repeatedly mentioned the Kolchak series as having had a significant impact on the creation of his wildly popular science fiction/supernatural franchise The X-Files .

Carl Sanford is a fictional character from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. He appears in Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game, and in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files-related content.

### Description
The High Priest of Arkham's Silver Twilight Lodge, Sanford is a tall, slim man with an air of breeding about him. An antiquarian by trade, he holds a degree of influence in nearly every organisation in the city. Despite his standing in the community, there are many who fear the man, and rumours abound regarding the unwholesome deeds perpetrated in both his name and that of the Lodge.

### Call of Cthulhu RPG
Sanford was first introduced in Shadows of Yog-Sothoth as the central antagonist, working behind the scenes of the Order of the Silver Twilight, and using other "Lords of the Silver Twilight" to raise the island of R'lyeh and possibly to even wake Cthulhu, depending on the player's intervention. Canonically, this fails, but Sanford escapes and then reappears in Masks of Nyarlathotep as a secondary antagonist in the China chapter. In Cults of Cthulhu, he is listed as an example "Deathless Master" (a leader of the global Cthulhu cult, coequal to the "deathless Chinaman" of The Call of Cthulhu, whom the book names Hui Qiang), or maybe even a direct agent of Cthulhu, but the book leaves the exact interpretation up to the Keeper.

### Feeders from Within
During the events of the novel, Sanford inducted Phillip Avery into the Lodge as a way to gain the services of the Mi-Go known as Mr. Stone and his Byakhee servants. (: Feeders from Within)

### Behind the Mythos
Carl Sanford's name is a nod to games designer Sandy Petersen, whose full name is Carl Sanford Joslyn Petersen, the man behind the original Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

Carl T. Ford (? - 13 November 2017) was a British Fantasy Award-winning editor, publisher, and occasional author who specialised in the Lovecraftian genre. Perhaps best known for being the driving force behind gaming/weird fiction fanzine Dagon, he was also a contributor to Robert M. Price's long-running fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu. Ford's short fiction appeared in periodicals such as Tales After Dark, and anthologies including The Fourth Black Book of Horror (2009, Mortbury Press).

Carnacki: Starry Wisdom and Other Stories is a thematic collection of short works by British-born author William Meikle.

### Overview
Containing a selection of Meikle's Thomas Carnacki stories (although by no means all of them) Carnacki: Starry Wisdom and Other Stories contains several tales which cross over William Hope Hodgson's occult detective with the Cthulhu Mythos created by H. P. Lovecraft and expanded upon by many others. Although not all of the tales directly reference the Cthulhu Mythos, some of those which do not could be considered to be Lovecraftian in nature.

Consisting of thirteen works, nine of which are new to this collection, and running to a total of 170 pages, Carnacki: Starry Wisdom and Other Stories was published in ebook format by Dark Regions Press in March 2021.

Carnacki: The Lost Cases is an anthology of Thomas Carnacki short stories, a number of which are loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. Edited by the late American author and editor Sam Gafford, it was published by Ulthar Press in June 2016. Both paperback and digital formats were released.

*"The Shadow Suns" by John Howard

*"The Dark Trade" by John Linwood Grant

Carolyn Fern, the Psychologist, is a character created by Chaosium as an investigator character for their Cthulhu Mythos-inspired board game Arkham Horror.

### Biography
Gaining her degree at Rhode Island Hospital during the 1920s, Carolyn spent a further year training as an allopathic psychiatrist at Butler before taking up a residency position at the Lemarchand Institute under the supervision of physician Dr. Spencer. (: Feeders from Within)

When one of her patients, one Malachai Farrow psychologically damaged by experiences he underwent while in the US Army, was murdered in exactly the same way he had been dreaming of, Carolyn took a leave of absence from the hospital and travelled to Arkham to look into Farrow's psychological history. (: Feeders from Within)

What she found there was a plot by both human cultists and the alien Mi-Go to bring madness to the world. Fortunately, Carolyn made the acquaintance of Henry Armitage, Mark Harrigan and Diana Stanley, unique individuals with knowledge of the occult, and the group were able to thwart the conspiracy against mankind. (: Feeders from Within)

### Behind the Mythos
Carolyn Fern made her debut appearance in the first edition of Chaosium's board game of cosmic horror Arkham Horror and has appeared in every iteration of the game since, despite the licence transferring to Fantasy Flight Games. She has also featured in other Fantasy Flight games including Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, Mansions of Madness and Elder Sign. In addition, a prepainted plastic miniature of Carolyn was released under the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, and she appeared as a main character in Fantasy Flight's Mythos fiction novel Feeders from Within.

### Trivia
*The name of the Lemarchand Institute attended by Carolyn for her residency is a possible nod to Clive Barker's Hellraiser body horror franchise, which appears to have been influenced to a certain degree by the Cthulhu Mythos.

The Carolyn Fern Sanitorium is an institution created by author Sebastian Greaves for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "Have You Seen the Yellow Sign?" 

### Overview
Located in the city of Arkham, Massachusetts, the Carolyn Fern Sanitorium dominates the local skyline, situated as it is in a large, 16-story tall building with a small attached parking lot. It’s purpose appears to be the treatment of mental-health disorders on a large scale, although some of its staff may also be complicit in the worship of certain ancient entities, including Cthulhu. 

### Known Patients
*An unnamed publisher who was unfortunate enough to witness the aftermath of an incursion by the King in Yellow.
*Alan Drashing, a Cthulhu cultist who appeared to have only been incarcerated as part of a ruse to lure one Constance Ashford into becoming the cult's next sacrificial victim.

### Appearances
*"Have You Seen the Yellow Sign?"
*"Great Cthulhu"

### Behind the Mythos
Greaves likely named the facility after the Fantasy Flight Games investigator Carolyn Fern, a character created for their Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos content.

"Carry Me Softly Into the Land of Dreams" is a short Cthulhu Mythos comic book story written by Bruce Brown and illustrated by Renzo Podesta. It was published in the Arcana Comics horror anthology Velvet Rope in November 2010.

### Synopsis
A young Howard Phillips Lovecraft is present at the moment a malevolent entity comes to claim the soul of his insane father Winfield. Begging the entity to release his father, the two strike a bargain: Howard must spend his life writing of the horrors which lurk just out of sight of humankind, or his father's immortal soul shall suffer eternal torment.

fullContent:
Carsai the King is the leader of the Citadel of the Black. It is an enigmatic being who's always covered in smoke and whose clothes or burning eyes are rarely seen. He frequently invites people to the place, whether they are victims, followers of the Great Old Ones, or people from Golarion who simply grab his attention. It is a neutral zone between the Old Cults and the Dominion of the Black, and Carsai attends to both sides.

### Starfinder
The powerful immortal leader Carsai the King is the closest thing the planet-god Aucturn has to a ruler and whose true form and nature are unknown. A High Priest of Nyarlathotep, he has ruled the Citadel of the Black for centuries. However, he does so autocratically, and the citadel is not a theocracy. He is suspected of being an avatar of the Empty Traveler, who is in turn an avatar of Nyarlathotep. There are also those who comment that it could be the Black Pharaoh.

He tends to appears in public frequently. Each of his appearances gathers multitudes of cultists who esteem him. His charismatic speeches are often broadcast on the Pact Worlds, frequently causing jubilant screams and spontaneous ecstatic suicides. Aucturn's defense facing the Dominion of the Black and his being a reasonable figure on an alien planet caused the Pact Council to accept Aucturn as a protectorate of the Pact Worlds, if only out of necessity and proximity. While this means that he may have a representative on the council (usually Carsai or his associates), he does not have much power on planets or moons in the system.

Interestingly, the media leader's portrayal of an anti-hero (a handsome rebel protecting the Pact Worlds from terrible horrors) has increased devotion to Nyarlathotep and the Outer Gods in the Pact Worlds.

All the ichor lords recognize the authority of Carsai the King and see him as the prophet of their god, referring to him as the "first dreamer".

Carter & Lovecraft is a novel by Jonathan L. Howard, published in 2015 by Thomas Dunne Books, that combines the noir and Cthulhu Mythos genres. The story teams Daniel Carter, a former homicide detective turned PI, with Emily Lovecraft, a Providence bookstore owner and the last descendant of H. P. Lovecraft--whose works turn out to be far from fictional.

It was followed by a sequel, After the End of the World.

"Case of the Missing Grimoire" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
When tough Arkham private detective Wade Kearney takes on the case of a missing grimoire, he finds himself embroiled in a complex web of antique book dealers, monstrous duplicates, avaricious sorcerers, secret societies, and duplicitous clients. Despite the odds, Kearney emerges unscathed, and with his pockets full of hard cash.

### Trivia

* The book which Kearney is hired to locate is the Rituals of the Ohmdari Priesthood. The Ohmdari are a slug-like species of eldritch abomination who are referenced in a number of Shiflet's works.
* Wade Kearney is a recurrent character in Ron Shiflet's fiction.

Casefile: Arkham- Her Blood Runs Cold is a 2018 graphic novel written by Josh Finney, illustrated by Patrick McEvoy and edited by Kat Rocha. It is a reimagining of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep", but aside from character names little remains faithful to the original.

### Synopsis
Asenath Waite hires private investigator Hank Flynn on the pretext of having him track down a manuscript belonging to her dead husband, Edward Pickman Derby. However, she is actually using him to track down those responsible for her husband's death and as a weapon in her battle against her father's newly-embodied spirit. Once Flynn realises his role as little other than a pawn in her schemes, he walks away from the case, while his girlfriend Glynda exposes Asenath and her father to the tabloid press.

A subplot explaining Glynda's backstory is also present, but has little bearing on the main storyline.

### Characters
*Henry "Hank" Flynn, a former marine turned private detective.
*Glynda, a white witch and Flynn's partner.
*Asenath Waite, a beautiful young Innsmouth woman who has been taught the secrets of magic by her father.
*Edward Pickman Derby, Asenath's husband, deceased.
*Detective Billy Sinclair, a jaded APD officer.
*Ephraim Waite, Asenath's dead father, now inhabiting Derby's body.
*Dan Upton, a former friend of Derby's responsible for his fall into madness and, ultimately, death.

Casefile: Arkham- Nightmare on the Canvas is a Cthulhu Mythos graphic novel which acts as a follow-up to H. P. Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model". Written by Josh Finney, illustrated by Patrick McEvoy and edited by Kat Rocha, it was published by 01Publishing in 2016; both softcover and digital download editions were released.

### Synopsis
Arkham, 1946: amidst a spree of killings perpetrated by the Arkham Slasher, private eye Hank Flynn is hired by a wealthy woman to find missing artist Richard Upton Pickman. Interspersed with flashbacks of Flynn's wartime service, the investigation leads him to cross paths with psychics, Deep One hybrids and Ghouls, before culminating in a showdown with the murderous Pickman.

### Characters
*Henry R. Flynn, a former U.S. marine now working as a private investigator.
*Glynda, a woman with a deep knowledge of the occult, and Hank's love interest.
*Richard Upton Pickman, a former artist driven to madness and murder.
*May Derlith, a wealthy socialite who has an obsession with Pickman and his works.
*Thurber, a man driven to the verge of insanity through his historic association with Pickman.
*Detective Billy Sinclair, a police officer in the Arkham Police Department working on the Slasher case.

### Trivia
*Nightmare on the Canvas is littered with references to many of Lovecraft's works, not only those which feature Pickman.
*Despite the original story apparently being set at around its time of writing in 1926, Nightmare on the Canvas is set only a few weeks after Pickman's disappearance in post-WWII 1946.

"Casino Carcosa" is a short story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A dying funeral director who secretly murdered his wife embarks on a bucket list trip to Las Vegas after pocketing a trinket from a body in his care. However, the Tattered King wants what is his, and after a nightmarish hallucinatory journey through a very special casino, the man is found dead, although how it occurred is left ambiguous.

Cassie Hack is a horror victim whose mother was a serial killer who murdered those who bullied her daughter. She later returned as a "slasher", an undead serial killer. Cassie has dedicated herself to hunting down "slashers" and ending their rampages. She will come into conflict with the Neflords, Lovecraftian entities known for violating and impregnating human virgins. Cassie would end up battling the Army of Darkness, side by side with Ash Williams.

Cassilda, occasionally referred to as the Queen of Carcosa, is a fictional character created by the late American author Robert W. Chambers for his 1895 short story "The Repairer of Reputations". Her concept was later taken by Paizo, Inc. and incorporated into their Pathfinder roleplaying game, a universe which takes many inspirations from Cthulhu Mythos-related works.

### History
### In the Pathfinder Roleplaying Game
Queen Cassilda is the former queen of the city of Yhitll. She is a beautiful woman who was transformed into a life-sized hollow porcelain doll. Her tragic story is one of horror and defiance against the fate befallen her people.

During a time of upheaval on her world, her city was visited by Hastur's servant, the Pallid Mask. Whom claimed that he could help them avoid the prophecy that foretold their doom by Hastur. The nobility of Yhtill were deceived into attending a masquerade where the Yellow Sign was present, thinking themselves immune. At the given time, all of the attendants removed their masks, at which the Pallid Mask revealed his deception. He called upon the Yellow Sign, and the city of Yhtill was struck by a wave of madness, resulting in its consumption by Carcosa.

Cassilda looked away, and therefore was neither driven mad nor was she enslaved. She absorbed a portion of her peoples' tortured souls into herself, preserving their lifeforces so that one day her people may be restored. Their memories and personalities are contained within her imperial diadem. She became Carcosa's first denizen and acquired a form of immortality. As long as Hastur existed, she would continue to reform, no matter how many times she is killed. She lives for the day that Hastur is permanently destroyed and both her and Hastur are ever destroyed within 24 hours of each other, the souls contained within the diadem will either be resurrected in a new Yhtill or they will move on to the afterlife.

### In Other Media
*In the video game The Baby In Yellow, Cassilda is the adoptive mother of one of the many babies and the main caller of the first 3 acts.

fullContent:
"Cassius" is a horror short story by Henry S. Whitehead based on one of the entries of H. P. Lovecraft's commonplace book. It was published in the November 1931 issue of Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror.

This story is part of the Gerald Canevin series (which also includes the Lovecraft collaboration "The Trap"), and features the return of two other characters, namely Dr. Pelletier and Arthur Carswell, both introduced in "Passing of a God". It also marks the debut appearance of Canevin's dependable house-man, Stephen Penn, who would go on to appear in several more entries in the series, as well as the minor characters of Colonel Lorriquer, his family, and Mrs. Squire, all of whom would return in "Mrs. Lorriquer".

### Synopsis
Gerald Canevin is a writer of supernatural stories living in St. Thomas, in the Virgin Islands. His house-man Stephen Penn, who presides over the staff, convinces Canevin to hire Penn's friend, Brutus Hellman, who has recently lost his job. Canevin is pleased by Hellman's work, so when Hellman reveals that he needs surgery to remove some kind of tumor, Canevin contacts his friend, Dr. Pelletier. The doctor performs what he describes as a very simple operation and Hellman's growth is removed.

While Hellman is recovering, Canevin finds an object that looks like a miniature hut in the yard outside the man's cabin. Assuming that the thing must be a toy that belongs to the young son of his washer, Canevin playfully places a coin inside it to surprise the kid. At this moment, his finger is bitten by some small creature. Canevin makes a mental note to ask Penn to remove the animal from the toy, so it wouldn't hurt the child, but afterwards forgets about the incident.

Canevin and his friend Carswell hear a scream coming from Hellman's cabin. Once inside, they find a terrified Hellman with an open wound on his leg. While Canevin bandages him, Hellman asks about the "thing" that bit him. Canevin and Carswell catch sight of a strange creature, about the size of a rat or mongoose, scurrying away from under the bed towards the yard. Although they can't find the thing, Canevin comes across the body of a rat that has been viciously torn apart, and Hellman himself notices that the bite mark on his own leg is similar to that on the rat's throat, suggesting that the thing that bit him also killed the rat.

On the next day, Hellman is targeted again when the creature tries to enter his room by the window. He fires a shot and hits it, as indicated by a blood stain, but the thing manages to escape. Hellman describes the creature as small and frog-like. Canevin finds a liana tied with loop knots, which the thing used to climb to the window -- a testimony to its intelligence. He sends a sample of the animal's blood to be analysed in the lab, but the analysis shows that the blood belongs to a human being.

Castle Freak is a 1995 low budget horror film. Stuart Gordon (who was given a free hand in virtually all aspects of the film, but only a $500,000 budget) directed, Dennis Paoli and Gordon screenwrote, with Mythos stalwart Jeffrey Combs starring in the lead male role and Barbara Crampton in the lead female role. The four of them had previously worked together on both Re-Animator and From Beyond, partial film adaptations of H. P. Lovecraft's short stories "Herbert West--Reanimator" and "From Beyond", respectively.

The film was remade in 2020, although this version adds in specific references to elements of the Cthulhu Mythos, establishing itself as more of an Expanded Mythos work (see main article (Castle Freak (2020 film)).

A grieving American family inherits a 12th-century castle in Italy, unaware that a homicidal and deformed man lies chained in the dungeons. When the man breaks loose, the family faces a fight for survival.

Castle Freak is a 2020 remake of the 1995 film of the same name. It was directed by Tate Steinsiek from a script by Kathy Charles, based on H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Outsider" ("The Dunwich Horror" is also a major inspiration).

### Synopsis
The film centers on Rebecca Riley, a young American woman blinded in an accident caused by her boyfriend John's drunk driving. She inherits a castle in Albania from her biological mother, Lavinia Whateley, who gave her up for adoption when she was a baby. It turns out that Rebecca has a monstrous twin living secretly in the castle--and that both she and her sister are the daughters of Yog-Sothoth. Her friend, the Professor, reads a copy of the Necronomicon that Rebecca discovers in the castle, and he urges her to join hands with her sister to open a gate for the Great Old Ones.

In a post-credits sequence, the Professor addresses a man called West who has a vial of glowing green liquid on his desk--and West calls the Professor "Armitage".

### Connections
John and Rebecca's accident happens on I-95 near Dunwich, Massachusetts.

The Professor speculates that Rebecca's Necronomicon might be the one stolen from Miskatonic University in the 1920s. At one point, he is seen wearing a Miskatonic T-shirt.

### Trivia
* Barbara Crampton, star of the original 1995 Castle Freak and several other Lovecraftian films, worked as a producer on the remake.

"Castle of Circles" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Mike Lee. It was published in the sword-and-sorcery anthology Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights by Rogue Planet Press in January 2017.

### Synopsis
Petty criminals Law Pferzonne and Valzarum find themselves indebted to the powerful sorcerer Umma Xatha, a former apprentice to the great wizard Eibon, who enlists the pair in a scheme to retrieve a complete and annotated copy of his former master's greatest work, the fabled Book of Eibon. 

After travelling to the tower containing their prize Xatha betrays the thieves, attempting to sacrifice them to the minor god Kathatana which dwells within. Fortunately for the two men, Kathatana bears them no ill will, having only designs for Xatha, and they are able to escape while the vengeful deity consumes their treacherous partner.

Castro is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who makes his first appearance in the 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Description
He is an "immensely aged mestizo [...] who claimed to have sailed to strange ports and talked with undying leaders of the Cthulhu Cult in the mountains of China." Castro was arrested on November 1, 1907 during a New Orleans police raid on a cult ceremony in Louisiana. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

### Behind the Mythos
Robert M. Price believes that Castro's name is based on that of Adolphe de Castro–born Adolph Danziger–an author of "unbelievably bad fiction" who hired Lovecraft as a ghostwriter. Joshi and Schultz, however, report that Lovecraft did not become acquainted with DeCastro until late 1927, whereas "The Call of Cthulhu" was completed in 1926.

Cats are often featured in the Cthulhu Mythos and play a prominent role in the writings of H. P. Lovecraft, who in real life was greatly fond of cats.

The plot of the Dreamlands story "The Cats of Ulthar" is an explanation of why in the village of Ulthar it is against the law to kill a cat.

Another Dreamlands tale, The Dream Quest of Unknown Kadath, reveals that there are sapient cats living in the Earth's Dreamlands which the protagonist, Randolph Carter, has befriended. The story includes a sequence where Carter is abducted by the Men of Leng and brought to the Moon, but is rescued by the cats, who are able to transport themselves back and forth between the Earth to the Moon by leaping. The cats of the Dreamlands are a noble race, friendly towards humans, and inimical towards the Zoogs and the alien Cats from Saturn.

Delapore, the protagonist and narrator of "The Rats in the Walls", has several cats; the name of his favorite, N-----man, is a famous example of the casual racism in Lovecraft's stories. Similarly, in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, the Ward family cat has a name that seems to be a shortened version of the name of Delapore's cat.

Lovecraft's poem "The Cats" emphasizes the disquieting aspect of cats:


Lovecraft also wrote poems to cats, including at least two Christmas Greetings to Felis, the cat of his friend and correspondent Frank Belknap Long.
