Cathriona "Cat" Tobin is an Irish games designer and publisher based in West Cork. She is the current co-owner and only full-time employee of Pelgrane Press, where she oversees design, development, production, marketing, and sales. Tobin's Cthulhu Mythos-related output includes work on games such as Trail of Cthulhu, The Yellow King, and The Fall of Delta Green, while her non-Mythos credits include Dungeons & Dragons and Pathfinder books. 

Described as a "rising star of RPG publishing … [s]ince joining Pelgrane, the company has seen the number of events it runs at Gen Con skyrocket from fewer than 10 to over 150. The company had a $120,000 Kickstarter, and won 15 ENnies, all while Tobin “worked hard to build a Pelgrane community that engages fans, and acknowledges the vital part they play…in our team,” she says."

"Catch of the Day" is a Lovecraftian short story by Irish author Ed Nobody, first published in Vol 5, Issue 3 of the Lovecraftiana zine in October 2020.

### Synopsis
A man hears the tale of how the captain of a fishing boat and his crew claims to have encountered an eldritch horror while out making their living. The octopoid abomination became tangled in the boat's nets, nearly sinking it and driving the captain to the brink of madness - or perhaps even causing the very fabric of reality to unravel - before he was able to slay it with a kettle full of boiling water.

The listener is understandably sceptical, but soon changes his mind when the captain shows him the corpse of the beast pinned to a nearby building.

The Caterpillars were a species of creature which appeared in Brian Lumley's Mythos novel The Transition of Titus Crow.

### Description
Originating billions of years in the future on planet Earth in its dying days, not much is known about the Caterpillars. Small animals measuring no more than eight to nine inches in length, they had a thick coating of fur and no discernible features. Moving in a way reminiscent of modern-day caterpillars, hence their name, they were attracted to heat, as the Earth of the future was a much colder place than it is today. At one point a group were seen “feeding” from small, withered bushes, although the manner in which they did this was unknown as they possessed no visible mouths. The Caterpillars appeared to be non-sentient.

### History
Nemesis of the Great Old Ones, cosmic time-traveller Titus Crow encountered several of these creatures during his first journey aboard the time machine De Marigny’s Clock, although he paid them little heed. Titus did, however, ensure that one specimen which had tried to gain access to his Time Clock got back to its fellows in a place that looked suitable for the creature.

A fabled land of otherworldly beauty that is thought to exist by many of those who live in the Dreamlands, Cathuria is regarded as a legend and is said to lie beyond the Basalt Pillars of the West. "Scream for Jeeves; Or, Cats, Rats, and Bertie Wooster", later published as "Cats, Rats, and Bertie Wooster", is a horror comedy short story by Peter Cannon, first published in 1990 in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu. A crossover between the worlds of H. P. Lovecraft and P. G. Wodehouse, the story is a partial retelling of "The Rats in the Walls" featuring Wodehouse's famous characters Jeeves and Bertie Wooster.

It was followed by two more crossovers in the same vein: "Something Foetid", which builds upon "Cool Air" and the Randolph Carter series; and "The Rummy Affair of Young Charlie", which builds upon both "The Music of Erich Zann" and The Case of Charles Dexter Ward.

### Synopsis
Bertie Wooster, a well-meaning but not particularly bright British socialite, receives a telegram from his old friend, Captain Edward Norrys, requesting assistance. An American businessman named Delapore, who is the father of Norrys' late comrade, has restored and moved to his family's ancestral property of Exham Priory, where he is being tormented by bizarre dreams. Meanwhile, Delapore's cats have been acting strangely as well. Norrys asks Wooster to come over to Exham Priory and bring his astute valet, Jeeves, "the only one who can get to the bottom of this mystery". On their way, Jeeves impresses Wooster with his knowledge of certain legends concerning Exham Priory, which was built on top of a prehistoric temple that dates from the time of the Druids or earlier.

As soon as they arrive, Norrys explains that Delapore is suffering from delusions, and asks Wooster to "humour" him while Jeeves tries to figure out the cause of the problem. They also get confirmation that the nine cats of the house have all been restless, chasing after something within the walls. At dinner, Delapore talks at length about the terrible stories told about his ancestors. The next morning, he relates a dream involving a monstrous swineherd and his entourage of flabby beasts. Wooster, on the other hand, has slept splendidly. The next night, however, he is awakened by the noise made by the agitated cats and finds his host awake in the corridor, rambling about the sound of rats, which Wooster cannot hear. They are joined by Norrys, Jeeves, and Delapore's servants, and jointly decide to investigate the Roman vaults underneath.

By the time they arrive at a ceremonial chamber, most of the cats have calmed down, except one, who paws at the bottom of the stone altar. Jeeves notices a draught of air that indicates the existence of an even deeper vault beneath this one. The party retreats, unsure about how to proceed, until Jeeves suggests that they return to London to gather a group of archaeologists and other scholars, which Norrys and Delapore agree to. While Wooster is relieved to get away from the place and tries to "beg off" the subsequent expedition, Norrys insists that he and Jeeves come along until they reluctantly agree.

The Cavern of Flame is a fictional location created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Description
The Cavern of Flame is a gateway to the Dreamlands and dwelling of Nasht and Kaman-Thah. At one time a natural formation, it has since been worked and smoothed, with painted bas-relief sculptures carved into the walls. These are depictions of the Earth Gods.

To enter the Dreamlands one must first find a stairway descending into the earth in his dream. This is known as the Seventy Steps of Lighter Slumber, and if he descends it, he soon finds himself emerging into a Cavern of Flame. The dreamer arrives naked, even if he had been clothed. He also arrives alone, even if he descended with others. This last has been violated only once in the entire history of the Dreamlands.

Nasht and Kaman-Thah act as judges of the soul of any newly arrived dreamer. Whenever a new dreamer appears, they examine the dreamer's soul to determine if he or she is worthy. If not, or the dreamer is so foolish as to attack them, the dreamer will immediately awaken in their own bed, and is never able to find the Seventy Steps again.

If, however, the dreamer is worthy, they are welcome. They can then answer any question on the Dreamlands the dreamer asks, though their answers may seem evasive or couched in riddles. If the dreamer decides to leave the Cavern of Flame, the way back to it can be found again whenever needed. However if the dreamer chooses to enter the Dreamlands, the priests direct the dreamer towards the back of the Cavern of Flame. 

There, the Sacred Pillar of Fire stands in the middle of an opening into a back chamber. The dreamer can pass the pillar unscathed, and will find a small vestibule with two tables of green malachite. On one lies clothing and weapons, on the other food and supplies. Anything the dreamer might desire, within reason, is available, and the dreamer is free to choose whatever seems best to them.

At the back of the vestibule is the Seven Hundred Steps of Deeper Slumber, and once the dreamer is dressed and equipped, the dreamer can descend them.

One of the stars of the Pleiades, between Alcyone and Electra on one side, and Maia and Taygeta on the other. In astrology, it forms part of the constellation of Taurus.

The name comes from Greek mythology, and means "the dark one", or "black". In Greek mythology it is the name of an Amazon and one of the seven Pleiades, daughter of the Titan Atlas and the ocean nymph Pleion. Celaeno was also used by the Roman poet Virgil as the name of one of the Harpies, and it's through this association that the name first enters the Cthulhu Mythos.

In an epigraph to "The Dunwich Horror", H. P. Lovecraft quotes a passage from Charles Lamb's "Witches and Other Night-Fears" (1821), which refers to "dire stories of Celaeno and the Harpies", along with "Gorgons, and Hydras, and Chimaeras", as archetypes of terror.

August Derleth took up the name and put it to use in its astronomical sense in the Mythos. In his Trail of Cthulhu series, the fourth planet around the star Celaeno is the site of the Great Library of Celaeno, a vast repository of galactic knowledge. Based on his research at the library, Derleth's protagonist Laban Shrewsbury writes the Celaeno Fragments.

The Celaeno Fragments are a fictional series of occult writings created by H. P. Lovecraft’s friend and contemporary August Derleth for his series The Trail of Cthulhu.

### Overview
Consisting of a ream of nearly fifty handwritten pages, the Fragments were submitted to Miskatonic University by their author Dr. Laban Shrewsbury at some point during 1915. The doctor wrote the Fragments from memory after a series of visits to the Great Library of Celaeno, located in a star system in the Pleiades.

### Known Contents

*Descriptions of Azathoth, Yog-Sothoth, Nyarlathotep, Cthulhu, Ithaqua and Cthugha.
*Several spells, including one for creating an Elder Sign and others for summoning Cthugha or a Byakhee.

fullContent:
"Celephaïs" is a fantasy story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in early November 1920 and first published in the May 1922 issue of the Rainbow. "Celephaïs" was next republished in 1970 by Del Rey Books in a short story collection called The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

The title refers to a fictional city that later appears in Lovecraft's Dream Cycle, including his novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath (1926).

### Inspiration
Like many of Lovecraft's stories, Celephaïs was inspired by a dream, recorded in his commonplace book as "Dream of flying over city." (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

The story resembles a tale by Lord Dunsany, "The Coronation of Mr. Thomas Shap" in The Book of Wonder, in which the title character becomes more and more engrossed in his imaginary kingdom of Larkar until he begins to neglect business and routine tasks of daily living, and ultimately is placed in a madhouse. The imagery of the horses drifting off the cliff may derive from Ambrose Bierce's "A Horseman in the Sky" (1891). (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

"Celephais" is a regularly constructed coined word in Ancient Greek, cel- hidden; eph from epi, throne or seat; ais, of or from or by, impliedly a place to which one will come or from which one has come.

In related linguistics, related in the sense of being also derived from prehistoric PIE language, Cel was the Etruscan goddess of the earth, a cthonic deity of the Earth who was concealed or covered ie hidden by the Earth that she ruled.

### Synopsis
Celephaïs was created in a dream by Kuranes (which is his name in dreams—his real name is not given) as a child of the English landed gentry. As a man in his forties, alone and dispossessed in contemporary London, he dreams it again and then, seeking it, slowly slips away to the dream-world. Finally knights guide him through medieval England to his ancestral estate, where he spent his boyhood, and then to Celephaïs. He became the king and chief god of the city, though his body washes up by his ancestors' tower, now owned by a parvenu.

In The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, Randolph Carter pays a visit to Kuranes, finding that the great dreamer has grown so homesick for his native Cornwall, he has dreamed parts of Celephaïs to resemble the land of his boyhood. Kuranes advises Carter, on a mission to find his own dream-city, to be careful what he wishes for—he might get it.

Although the name of the protagonist is not provided, his body is eventually found on the rocks below the cliffs where his ancestral home is located, and the name of that home is given. Since it is named "Trevor Towers" it is possible that Trevor is the last name of Kurane's earthly form. However, this might also be the name given to the building by its nouveau riche new owner.

### The City

The Celestial Toyroom is a dimension created by the BBC in 1966 for Doctor Who.

### Background
The Celestial Toyroom is the realm of the Great Old One, the Celestial Toymaker, a remnant of its original universe and an integral part of the entity. The Celestial Toymaker could not survive long outside of this reality, due to the rules which were set down in his own home universe. He resides in the "Toy Shop" which unlike the rest of the realm is actually connected to him. Everything else can be destroyed except for the Toy Shop. A void surrounds the Toy Shop and anyone who attempts to leave, find themselves in a loop reentering it.

Interestingly, several of the entities appearing within the Celestial Toyroom seem to be fictional creations with their own independent "life", similar to Dreamlands entities.

fullContent:
"Cells" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the September 1993 issue of Deathrealm by TAL Publications.

### Synopsis
Dr. Carl East and his terminally-ill wife Violet attempt to enact a plan which will allow her to transcend her physical form and inhabit an artificially-created protoplasmic mass - dubbed a Shoggoth - which they believe she will be able to sculpt to meet her own needs. Using excerpts from the blasphemous Revelations of Glaaki and Carl's extensive medical expertise they put their scheme into action, making sure to create several of the inert Shoggoths in case the first try is unsuccessful.

On the night of Violet's death, when Carl sees no evidence of his wife's manifestation in the new bodies, he flies into a rage and attacks all of the inert husks, smashing his equipment in the process. When later he hears noises from the destroyed lab and his wife's voice calling his name, he returns with hopes of seeing his wife happily inhabiting one of the masses, but something has gone horribly awry: her consciousness has been scattered throughout all of the entities, unable to manifest properly in any and in terrible pain. When she begs him for a merciful release, he pours gasoline over them both and prepares to light a match.

### Behind the Mythos
Another of the authors whose works the Easts are said to have read in preparation for their mind transferral are those of Colin Wilson, who has written extensively on the subject of existentialism, and has also authored his own Cthulhu Mythos fiction.

### Publication History
Since it’s debut in Deathrealm in 1988, "Cells" has also appeared in the collection of Thomas's own works Unholy Dimensions in October 2005.

fullContent:
"Cement Surroundings" is a short story in the Cthulhu Mythos genre by Brian Lumley. Written in June 1967, it was first published in Arkham House's 1969 collection Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos. It was later incorporated into Lumley's first novel, The Burrowers Beneath.

### Synopsis
An author reads his archaeologist uncle's notes and realizes that his uncle was done away with by subterranean horrors--and worries that he will be next.

### Characters
Sir Amery Wendy-Smith: An "antiquarian and archaeologist," noted for his "foresight and inquisitiveness" and "strange wanderings to foreign lands." He "deciphered or translated...a handful of decaying, centuried shards known in archaeological circles as the G’harne Fragments," then discovered the site of G'harne itself. The discovery left him with an intense fear of underground spaces and a "sudden fascination for seismography." While prior to his G'harne expedition, he was "straight and strong, for a man his age, with jet hair and a constant smile," afterwards he had "a pronounced stoop and had lost a lot of weight. His hair had greyed and his smile had become rare and nervous." He disappears in September 1933 when his cottage on the Yorkshire moors collapses.

Paul Wendy-Smith: Sir Amery's nephew, an author by profession. His account of the Chthonian threat, pieced together from his uncle's notes, is mistaken by police for a fiction writer's fantasy. He disappears in October 1933 when his home is similarly destroyed. 

### Setting
The story introduces G'harne, a lost pre-human city somewhere in Africa. The location is othewise unspecified ("I did not wish to know—not even remotely—the whereabouts of dead G’harne," the narrator Paul Wendy-Smith notes), but the tendency of Cthonians to travel in straight lines suggests a West African location.  

G'harne is "a legendary city which Sir Amery believed had existed centuries before the foundations were cut for the pyramids.... Man’s primal ancestors were not yet conceived when G’harne’s towering ramparts first reared their monolithic sculptings to pre-dawn skies." Sir Amery refers to it as “a buried land where Shudde-M’ell broods and bubbles, plotting the destruction of the human race and the release from his watery prison of Great Cthulhu…” 

Most of the story takes place in Yorkshire, where Sir Amery had a cottage that his nephew Paul came to stay at near the town of Radcar. (Radcar also features in Lumley's story "The Sister City.") It's noted as the home of the Radcar Recorder newspaper, whose sub-editor Mr. McKinnen is said to be "particularly helpful."  

The cottage is also said to be "nearby" to Marske; a motorist who witnesses its destruction speeds into Marske to report it. Paul takes a new house "on the outskirts" of Marske in order to be close if his uncle should reappear--but this house too is destroyed. 

There are two villages named Marske in Yorkshire: one in Richmondshire near the center line of the island, and the other, known as Marske-by

Census Issue 4 is the fourth issue of short-lived supernatural comic book Census. Created by Marc Bernardin, Adam Freeman, and Sebastian Piriz, the series followed the adventures of Liam Malone, an average Joe with a slacker streak, as he takes on a new job: conducting a census on behalf of the bureaucracy of hell on the numbers and locations of demons living in New York City.

The book was published in January 2023 by Dazzling Urbanite through Amazon as part of their Comixology line of digital comic book originals.

### Mythos Connections
As part of a plan to free a group of trapped ghosts, Malone enlists the help of the Great Old One Cthulhu, who he had previously encountered through his information-gathering duties, to redirect a parade making its way through the streets of New York City. During the course of their scheme Cthulhu is inexplicably given the code name "Reggie". This version of Cthulhu is a much more personable entity than the one more familiar to Mythos enthusiasts, being described as "incredibly low-maintenance" and "a congenitally lazy miscreant." When questioned on its activities, it states that " [I] split my time between here [New York] , the underwater city of R'lyeh, and my place on the vineyard."

fullContent:
The Ceph are an eldritch-like extra-galactic race and a cosmic horror element in the fictional universe of the Crysis video game.

### Background
The Ceph are cephalopod-like in form, which is the reason humans call them "Cephs" (Cephalopod). Pure-strain Cephs are approximately 2 meters long with a bluish/purple color. With five tentacles coming from the torso, several red eyes, and two arms. They required a special suit to survive on Earth. The human-derived strain of the Ceph have three tentacles coming from their back, vary in height, and are a pink or red color.

It's a race whose language is so far beyond human understanding that all mankind can do is speculate about the species and their motives.
They possesses a billion-year old interstellar civilization. Which is organized into several vast over-hives. Each one consisting of countless ships, planets, and colonies. In the local group of galaxies, the Ceph dominate several galaxies. Completely controlling the Triangalum galaxy (M33, over 2.7 million light years away) and most of the Milky Way galaxy.

Their technology lets them adapt to any environment and most of them combat equipment consists of autonomous or semi-autonomous machines, usually using anti-gravity technology. Which are equipped with energy-based and ice-based weapons, and are able to drain energy from nearly any source that is in close proximity. Machines which are able to repair themselves. Ceph interstellar ships, range from the mountain-sized scout / seedling ship to the squid-like planetoid warship that was the size of a continent or moon.

### History
The Ceph arrived on Earth over 65 million years, in several seeding ships. They were responsible for the mass-extinction event at the time, thereby ending the age of dinosaurs. Now they wage a genocidal war against humanity, the reason which remains a mystery to the human race. It's speculated that since they are so technologically advanced that they are virtually able to create anything that comes to mind, the only thing the Ceph are interested in is in what they are unable to think of, which is organisms and proteins that evolve over millions of years. Therefore the Ceph who have been stationed on Earth for millennia, periodically wake up on schedule to scout the world and collect scientific data. Acting as its gardeners, nurturing life and observing its evolution. The reason they are waging a war of extermination against mankind is the see them as pests or weeds in the "garden".

Cgfthgnm'o'th is a fictional monster created by Brian Lumley for his novel The Burrowers Beneath.

### Description
A creature of gargantuan proportions, Cgfthgnm'o'th's actual appearance was unknown, although it is described as a Chthonian and thus presumably resembles the other members of its species. From underground soundings conducted on the area where its body dissolved was estimated to have been nearly a quarter of a mile long and a third that distance in width. It was known to have been capable of extruding enormous grey tentacles with crimson mouths at the tips, which it used to consume any humans unfortunate enough to come within its reach. 

### History
When the Wilmarth Foundation, a group of humans with knowledge of the Cthulhu Cycle Deities and who were dedicated to destroying them, launched the Great Britain Project, their telepaths located Cgfthgnm'o'th in an undisclosed locale beneath the British countryside, possibly somewhere in Scotland. Cgfthgnm'o'th, a child of Ubbo-Sathla and one of the lesser minions of the Great Old Ones who appeared to be directly affiliated with Cthulhu himself, had been imprisoned there aeons ago by the Elder Gods, who held it there through the use of their Star Stones.

The Wilmarth Foundation planned to use an enormous modified drilling rig with an explosive-tipped harpoon to reach and destroy the creature deep in its subterranean lair and, although their plan was ultimately successful, lost a great deal of their equipment and a number of their personnel during the operation, including one of their valuable telepaths, a man named Gordon Finch.

Upon its demise Cgfthgnm'o'th, like many of the Cthulhu Mythos creatures, rapidly decomposed into little more than a foul-smelling putrescent goo.

### Powers
Cgfthgnm'o'th possessed several powers which it was able to use despite the fact that it was held captive in the web of Star Stones left behind by the Elder Gods. These powers included:

### Mental Strength
*It was able to possess psychic Gordon Finch, an act which ultimately turned the poor man into a babbling lunatic. It also demonstrated an extremely powerful "psychic shriek," which was strong enough to incapacitate even mildly-receptive individuals, and send the residents of local lunatic asylums into a frenzy. 

### Elemental Mastery
*Cgfthgnm'o'th showed the ability to summon a mighty storm when under the Foundation's attack, including the power to call down highly-accurate lightning strikes upon the humans.

### Tentacle Extrusion
*As stated above, the thing could extend tentacles from its body which were equipped with fang-filled maws at the tips. The maximum number and length of tentacles that Cgfthgnm'o'th was capable of producing is unknown.

Chad J. Bowser is an accomplished American freelance games designer based in Kernersville, North Carolina.

### Overview
Chad Bowser has written for a number of roleplaying games and systems, not least of which is Chaosium's popular Call of Cthulhu system. He has written material for nearly every time period which that game supports, but appears to have a particular affinity for the Cthulhu Invictus setting, and has worked on the game for not only Chaosium, but also third-party content providers Cubicle 7 Entertainment and Modiphius Entertainment.

Challengers of the Unknown (Vol 1) is a long-running comic book series which had a two-part story featuring M'nagalah in issues #82-83, written by Gerry Conway and published by DC Comics in 1977. 

### Synopsis
### Issue #82: "The Lurker Below"
When founding member Prof Haley was infected by M'nagalah, the team of heroic scientist-adventurers headed for Perdition, a mining town in Pennsylvania, in hopes of saving his life. The group's efforts to cure Haley brought them into the sights of Dr. Heathcliff Monroe, who was quickly revealed to be in league with M'nagalah. When the Challengers began to fight back, Monroe and his cult took their member June Robbins as a hostage, threatening to feed her to their god.

### Issue #83: "Seven Doorways to Destiny!"
Now forced to obey him, Monroe attempted to use the Challengers to help him open the Seven Doorways that would free the Elder Gods, allowing M'nagalah and his kind to take over Earth. With the aid of the supernatural monster the Swamp Thing, the team managed to stop Monroe's plan and defeat M'nagalah.

### Behind the Mythos
When the team was starting to get suspicious of Dr. Heathcliff Monroe, they discovered that his library contained a huge collection of occult books, including the works of Friedrich von Junzt, Abdul Alhazred and Ludvig Prinn.

Chandler Davies is a fictional character created by Brian Lumley. The character is a British weird artist who first appears in Lumley's Titus Crow story "An Item of Supporting Evidence" (1970). He is subsequently mentioned in a handful of Lumley stories, making one more brief appearance in "The Fairground Horror" (1976). 

### 'An Item of Supporting Evidence'
Davies, though introduced in "An Item of Supporting Evidence" as a "weird-artist," originally appears as a skeptic of the idea that there is a reality behind the eldritch horrors in Lovecraftian fiction. He is invited by Titus Crow to Blowne House after writing a letter "commenting upon the negative effect which [Crow's] short story 'Yegg-ha’s Realm' had had on him." 

As a "gourmet of such tales," Davies objects that the story--a "Lovecraftian piece" published in the magazine Grotesque that was "set during the time of Rome’s rule over England and involving the worship of an 'outside God'”--had depicted “so thoroughly unbelievable a God” as "existing in such a well-known period of England’s history that even an average student of our country’s antiquities could hardly miss the obvious impossibility." "I must admit that blunders like yours irk me considerably," Davies complains.

More generally, Davies insists that "Mythological-Fantasy was ‘out;’ that the Cthulhu Mythos’ fabled lands and creatures and Cimmeria’s scintillating citadels and dark demons should have been allowed to die a sad but certain death along with their respective originators." The "constant culling from those tales...was weakening the impact of the original works," Davies feels.

Davies changes his tune after being presented with archeological proof that Yegg-ha actually existed. The artist even promises to illustrate Crow's next book.

### In Other Stories
"An Item of Supporting Evidence" is placed in Crow's chronology before "Billy's Oak," which is set in 1955. The next time Davies appears in Lumley's fiction, things have taken a turn for the far worse.

In "Rising with Surtsey," published in 1971, there is a list of disturbing happenings that occur in May 1962. Among them: "Chandler Davies, who later died raving mad at Woodholme, painted ‘in a trance of sheer inspiration’ an evil black and grey G’harne Landscape, which his outraged and frightened mistress set on fire upon its completion."

In "The Thing From the Blasted Heath," another story published in 1971 (in the same collection, The Caller of The Black), a regretful collector says he once had a "collection of ten nightmare paintings by Pickman, Chandler Davies and Clark Ashton Smith," but these "now belong to an avid American collector."

Davies' art is also referenced in Lumley's 1974 novel The Burrowers Beneath (1974), set in 1968, in which Henri-Laurent de Marigny muses that
there were also a number of painters whose works, I knew, had from time to time feature

"Changing of the Guard" is a short story by American author Peter Rawlik. Portions of the story read like a laundry list of Mythos names and grimoires.

### Synopsis
In 1928 two people, with the partial knowledge and consent of the senior faculty of Miskatonic University, attempt to protect the human race from the horrors of the Cthulhu Mythos. While one instructs the entire library staff in a safety protocol regarding access to the restricted library, the other steals newer documents which they believe to be more dangerous and throws them in the university furnace.

### Characters
*Detective Robert Peaslee, a police officer examining library security at the request of Miskatonic University staff.
*Megan Halsey, Peaslee's accomplice.
*Dr. Henry Armitage, Miskatonic University library director, recovering from a bereavement.
*Dr. Cyrus Llanfer, acting director of the library.

### Publication History
"Changing of the Guard" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu by April Moon Books in March 2014.

### Trivia
* Megan Halsey, Peaslee's partner in "Changing of the Guard, shares her name with Barbara Crampton's character in Stuart Gordon's 1985 comedy horror film Re-Animator, based on the H. P. Lovecraft short story for which it is named.

shortDefinition: Chaosium is a publisher of tabletop role-playing games established by Greg Stafford in 1975. Its first game was a wargame called White Bear and Red Moon, which was later reworked to become Dragon Pass and its sequel, Nomad Gods. White Bear and Red Mo...
fullContent:
Chaosium is a publisher of tabletop role-playing games established by Greg Stafford in 1975. Its first game was a wargame called White Bear and Red Moon, which was later reworked to become Dragon Pass and its sequel, Nomad Gods. White Bear and Red Moon is notable for containing the first published material about Glorantha, later used as the primary setting for the role-playing games RuneQuest, Hero Wars and HeroQuest. Chaosium is the publisher of Call of Cthulhu, based on the stories of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Background
The rules of RuneQuest, Chaosium's first role-playing game, were distilled down into a generic, genre-neutral format known as Basic Role-Playing (BRP). These generic rules formed the basis of many of Chaosium's later RPGs, such as Call of Cthulhu, Stormbringer, Nephilim, and Ringworld.

Chaosium and Greg Stafford are also responsible for Pendragon, an Arthurian RPG now published by White Wolf, Inc.'s ArtHaus imprint after a spell with Green Knight Publishing. Other games of note include Thieves' World, Mythos, Elfquest, Worlds of Wonder, Superworld, Hawkmoon, Stormbringer, and Prince Valiant: The Story-Telling Game.

Several notable RPG authors have written material for Chaosium, including Steve Perrin, Sandy Petersen, Lynn Willis, Keith Herber, David Conyers, Ken St. Andre, Mike Mason, and Arduin creator David A. Hargrave.

### New directions
In response to collectible card games' popularity after the emergence of Magic: The Gathering, Chaosium released the now discontinued Mythos CCG.

In the late 1990s, Chaosium effectively split up into various successor companies, each maintaining its focus on a few of the company's products. Green Knight Publishing formed to focus on Pendragon, Chaosium "proper" retained Call of Cthulhu, Stormbringer, and Mythos, while Greg Stafford (who left Chaosium in 1998) founded Issaries, Inc. to publish HeroQuest and focus on bringing new Glorantha related material into print. Also, Wizard's Attic (no longer in business) was formed in order to act as a fulfillment house.

Chaosium continues to release roleplaying supplements for its Call of Cthulhu and BRP product lines. In 2012, Cthulhu by Gaslight won two Ennie awards at GenCon Indian;, Gold for Best Supplement and Silver for Best Cover Art. Later that year Cthulhu by Gaslight also won the Diehard GameFAN award for Best Re-Make/Re-release. Chaosium successfully funded a kickstarter for a re-release of the box-set campaign, Horror on the Orient Express.

In June of 2015, Chaosium announced the return of both Greg Stafford and Sandy Peterson to the the firm. According to their announcement:

Chapelwaite is a 2021 television series adaptation of Stephen King's Cthulhu Mythos short story "Jerusalem's Lot" (which also serves as a prequel to his non-Mythos novel 'Salem's Lot). It stars Adrien Brody as Captain Charles Boone, who inherits a house called Chapelwaite in the town of Preacher's Corners, Maine, in the year 1850.

### Synopsis
### Episode 1: "Blood Calls Blood"
Directed by Burr Steers
Written by Jason Filardi & Peter Filardi

As a child in 1817, Charles Boone is attacked by his insane father, who tries to kill him while rambling that "the Worm" is coming and that "blood calls blood". His life is saved when his father is shot by his mother, who tells the boy to go far away and never return. 33 years later, Charles is now the captain of a whaling ship, and married to a Japanese woman with whom he has three children: Honor, Loa, and Tane. When his wife dies from a disease contracted by spoiled meat (which also results in one of Loa's legs being crippled), he takes his children to America and settles in his family's ancestral home of Chapelwaite, inherited recently from his cousin Stephen, who hanged himself after the death of his own daughter, Marcella.

The Boones arrive at the town of Preacher's Corners, Maine, where Chapelwaite is located, only to find that the townsfolk shun and hate the Boone family, blaming Stephen Boone for a mysterious plague that causes lapses of memory, fatigue, and eventually death. Not everyone is entirely hostile, however. While most of the employees at the family's sawmill do little to hide their hatred, one named Able Stewart proves himself to be far more loyal. Similarly, an aspiring writer named Rebecca Morgan, whose late father worked for the Boones, offers her services to the family as a governess, despite the fact that the elder Morgan was terrified of his boss.

While trying to make his children comfortable, Charles deals privately with his own demons, as he experiences nightmarish hallucinations about earthworms, and hears the sounds of rats inside the walls, even after a man hired to exterminate them insists that there are none. The family also finds out that Stephen, his father Phillip, and daughter Marcella, are all buried in the house's yard, as opposed to the cemetery. In Preacher's Corners, a man named Edward Mallory, whose daughter Susan is suffering from the plague, decides to sneak into Chapelwaite at night and burn down the place. Before he can do so, however, he is attacked by a mysterious figure who cuts his throat and collects his blood in a bucket.

Written by Jason Filardi & Peter Filardi

Charlene Hines is a fictional character created by Canadian author Troy Young for his Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Description
A twenty-eight year old woman with an extensive criminal record, at the time of her introduction Charlene is serving a lengthy jail sentence for murder. Her only distinguishing feature is a mole on her chin, which she rubs when she is anxious.

### History
Once a promising student from a wealthy family, Charlene's life was destroyed after she was abducted by a clan of inbred cultists who promised her as a bride to the Great Old One Hastur. Despite making an escape, she ran away from home, falling into a life of drugs and prostitution on the streets. After her pimp mistreated her once too often, she killed him, and was sentenced to prison time.

After five years in jail, Charlene was approached by Harjit Singh of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena at the suggestion of Adele Kramer. Singh recruited her into the organisation and partnered her with senior investigator Malcolm Mayweather.

On one mission, Charlene encountered the spirit of long-dead sorcerer Pierre Girault, which briefly possessed her. Although she believed it to have left her completely, it was later revealed that a small part of it remained locked within her mind.

In 2019, Charlene, in company with Kramer, Mayweather, and Singh, embarked on a mission to the South Pacific to prevent Great Cthulhu from awakening. Although the mission was a success, the psychic emanations emitted by the Great Old One were sufficient to shatter Charlene's psyche and destroy her body, allowing Girault to reclaim and reconstitute what remained, claiming it as his own.

### Missions
The following is a list of Charlene's missions by in-universe chronology.

*Montreal, Canada: her first mission. Was briefly possessed by an ancient spirit, but ultimately came through apparently unscathed (: "The Shade of Pierre Girault").
*Cambridge, Canada: she and Malcolm Mayweather investigated the appearance of a long-lost painting by Richard Upton Pickman (: "The Misplaced Masterpiece of Richard Upton Pickman").
*Windsor, Canada: she and Mayweather tracked down an immortal spirit murdering those who had wronged her in the past (: "The Curse of the Windsor Witch").
*Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, Canada: embarked solo on a previously-aborted mission to destroy a cell of Hastur cultists, in an effort to free herself of the psychological legacy of her own abduction (: "The Bride of the Yellow King").
*South Pacific Ocean: along with Mayweather, Harjit Singh, and Adele Kramer, Charlene traveled to R'lyeh in an attempt to prevent the awakening of the Great Old One Cthulhu (: "In the Depths of R'lyeh).

Charles Dexter Ward is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, the title character of his novel The Case of Charles Dexter Ward.

### Overview
Ward is a young man from a prominent Rhode Island family, born in 1902--making him 26 in 1928, when the story takes place. He develops an obsession with his great-great-great-grandfather, Joseph Curwen, a reputed wizard who is Ward's physical double. Ward searches for his ancestor's grave and attempts to duplicate his Qabalistic and alchemical feats. He eventually uses this knowledge to physically resurrect Curwen.

### Behind the Mythos
Though considered one of Lovecraft's autobiographical characters, some details of the character seem to be based on William Lippitt Mauran, who lived in the Halsey house and, like Ward, was "wheeled...in a carriage" in front of it. Like the Wards, the Maurans also owned a farmhouse in Pawtuxet, Rhode Island. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

 Charles Dodgson is a fictional character loosely based on the historical figure Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (who is better known as Lewis Carroll), the the writer of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There. In the fictional Grimm Fairy Tales universe, he first appeared in 2008 in issue #6 of the 1st volume of Grimm Fairy Tales: Return to Wonderland. The character was created by Joe Tyler, Raven Gregory, & Ralph Tedesco.

### Background
Charles Dodgson is a wealthy man who has been involved with Wonderland for over a century. Born in the early 19th century, he contracted an incurable disease. To prevent his death, he made a pact with the Jabberwocky. In exchange for the restoration of his youth and health, making him immortal, he sacrificed humans to Wonderland, usually children and the majority of them having come from his extended family.

During the early 21st century, guilt overwhelmed Charles as he witnessed the devastation that Wonderland inflicted on the real world. Charles went into Wonderland, committing suicide by provoking Johnny Liddle into murdering him.

Dodgson also appears in the series' Cthulhu Mythos crossover Call of Wonderland, where he is an antagonist-turned-ally of H. P. Lovecraft. Dodgson's son, Howard Philips Dodgson, first appeared in issue #3 of Beyond Wonderland, and seems to have been named after Lovecraft.

shortDefinition: Charles Hoy Fort (1874 – 1932) was an American author famous for his non-fiction books that document unexplained phenomena. Before terms like "UFO" and "cryptid" were coined, Fort's works dealt with the subject of extraterrestrial visitors and undisc...
fullContent:
Charles Hoy Fort (1874 – 1932) was an American author famous for his non-fiction books that document unexplained phenomena. Before terms like "UFO" and "cryptid" were coined, Fort's works dealt with the subject of extraterrestrial visitors and undiscovered animals, as well as psychic abilities, mysterious disappearances, meteorites with unusual properties, cases of animals or unidentified substances raining from the skies, etc. His influence was such that the word "Fortean" has become virtually synonymous with the unknown.

In The Whisperer in Darkness, by H. P. Lovecraft, the main character Albert Wilmarth, initially skeptical about the existence of extraterrestrial creatures from local folklore, mentions how the defenders of such ideas have cited the books of Charles Fort as evidence to back up their claims. In the 2011 movie adaptation of the story, Fort appears as Wilmarth's opponent in a public debate, played by the film's co-writer and co-producer Andrew Leman.

In his 1919 work The Book of the Damned, Fort proposes that some disappearances could be the result of extraterrestrial beings laying down "dragnets" to capture people or animals. This idea might have inspired the concept of the Fishers from Outside, especially how they're described in The Horror from the Hills, by Frank Belknap Long.

### Behind the Mythos
It's hard to overestimate or exaggerate the debt owed by Lovecraftian horror to Charles Fort. Not only did his books such as Lo! And The Book of the Damned begin a subversive subgenre of conspiratorial and anti-orthodoxy critical thinking, but his recording and promulgating of very real but completely unexplained phenomena set the scene for the whole oeuvre of Lovecraft and Mythos fiction. His recorded phenomena attested to by independent sources include unexplained discoveries in coal beds, ostensibly hundreds of millions of years out of place; lumps of jade and granite falling from the sky, discovered to be inscribed with characters in no known language; islands appearing and disappearing; unexplained animals (and even plants) and what would later be called UFO or UAP observations and encounters but which in those pre-UFOlogy days sound very much like encounters with entities from the Mythos.

As much as Lovecraft was influenced by his favorite past writers of suspense and horror he was also a voracious reader of scientific and pseudoscientific literature, and Charles Fort was one of the leaders and indeed the originator of the "Silly Season" news items - albeit those with a clear basis in reality.

Of note in terms of possible direct influences on the Mythos are the following concepts first found in Fort:

* Antarctica being the home of a lost civilization of great antiquity and great advancement, with survivals to modern times; (At the Mountains of Madness, et al)
* Astronomical observations of stars that suddenly, unexpectedly and dramatically change color at the exact time of an event on Earth; (Astrophobos; Beyond the Wall

shortDefinition: Charles Hoffman is known for his contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos, particularly through works like "Herbert West—Reanimated," which serves as a sequel to H.P. Lovecraft's "Herbert West—Reanimator." His writing often explores themes of horror and t...
fullContent:
Charles Hoffman is known for his contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos, particularly through works like "Herbert West—Reanimated," which serves as a sequel to H.P. Lovecraft's "Herbert West—Reanimator." His writing often explores themes of horror and the supernatural within this shared universe. He was a prolific contributor to Crypt of Cthulhu as well as contributing many online essays related to Conan and the Robert E. Howard universes.

Whilst Hoffman was an obvious fan of Lovecraft's fiction, he was also outspoken, even against popular apologists, about Lovecraft's racism and unflinchingly brought criticism of it and exposure of its details to any debate.

Hoffman co-wrote with Marc A. Cerasini a major article providing criticism and examination of Colin Wilson entitled “The Transition of Colin Wilson,” which also fed into Hoffman's ongoing critique of the views of Lovecraft and of the need to clearly differentiate writers from their work. One of the ongoing themes of Hoffman's cultural and artistic criticism is the contrast between the optimistic or existential writers such as August Derleth or Wilson and the pessimism, Cosmicism and outright hatefulness he sees behind the writings of Lovecraft, and the middle ground shot through with sexuality of some of Wilson's work and of the writings of Clark Ashton Smith. It is clear that Hoffman prefers the lusty and existential adventure storytelling of Robert E. Howard but it is also clear that despite his brutal honesty about his views on Lovecraft's character he finds much to admire in the man's work.

In more recent years he has drifted out of Mythos related work entirely, focusing on writing "dark erotic fiction" instead.

Charles Le Sorcier is an antagonist from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Alchemist". After his father was wrongfully murdered by the ancestor of Count Antoine de C-, he cursed the family line, stating that no member in Comte de C- bloodline would live past the age of 32.

Charles Le Sorcier then drank an elixir of eternal life and set up a lab in the hidden confines of the castle ruins where de C- lived. He then carried out the curse by personally murdering each male in the lineage on or before the age of 32. The method of assassination varied between poison, arrows, to dropping a dislodged stone.

Count Antoine de C-, would have been the last member of the line to be assassinated by Le Sorcier if he were to be successful. However he failed in the assassination attempt and ended up being burned alive by Count Antoine. Despite being charred beyond recognition, Le Sorcier is possibly still alive within the ruins as the elixir of eternal life would perhaps have saved him.

### Notes
It is unknown if he is related to Hippolyte Le Sorcier, ancestor of Clark Ashton Smith in the family tree of Azathoth since the Count Antoine de C- was unaware of Charles having descendants.

Charles St. Cyprian is a character created by Josh Reynolds as the protagonist of a series of occult detective stories begun with "Krampusnacht" in 2011. The character has a number of peripheral connections to Lovecraftiana, and has appeared in at least one story directly tied to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
Occupying the post of Royal Occultist in the early 20th century - a position first held by noted scholar and alchemist John Dee - Charles St. Cyprian is a man steeped in mysticism. He is known to have been the protégé of esteemed occultist Thomas Carnacki in the years before his appointment to the crown, and is served in his office by a highly trained combatant by the name of Ebe Gallowglass. He is also acquainted with a number of prominent occultists.

### Selected Appearances
St. Cyprian is the protagonist of his own series by Reynolds, and has appeared in well over thirty stories. These stories include:

Charles David George Stross (born 18 October 1964) is a British science fiction and fantasy author, several of whose works were directly inspired by the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft. 

Of particular note is The Laundry Files series, which centres on The Laundry, a British secret agency dedicated to fighting extra-dimensional threats. Stross's mix of the Lovecraftian science fiction and spy thriller genres is reminiscent of the Delta Green setting for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, although the two are not related or set in the same universe. (Stross has stated that he was unaware of Delta Green when penning The Laundry Files.) Stross's Laundry Files stories also have an ample helping of office comedy.

Charlie Kane, the Politician, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for inclusion in their Arkham Horror Files line.

### Overview
Charlie Kane is a man on a mission, a politician determined to clean up Arkham. Like many politicians, he made whatever promises he needed to to get elected, but unlike most, he actually did what he could to help the city once he came to power. Charlie has had to do things that he doesn’t like to think about, but all of his actions have most definitely been for the public good.

Being a man with his finger on the pulse, Charlie's contacts slowly began to feed him the parts of a sinister picture in Arkham, one which he didn’t like one bit. However, he couldn’t tell anybody about it; nobody would believe him for one thing, and for another he couldn’t be causing panic in the streets. So, gathering his meagre evidence together, Charlie went to see an old acquaintance, Professor Grant, at Miskatonic University.

Standing dumbfounded over Professor Grant's horribly mutilated corpse in a university office whose walls were stained crimson, Charlie took his first steps down the road to ridding the streets of whatever threat has befallen them, whatever the cost.

### Behind the Mythos
Whilst the character of Charlie Kane was originally created by Fantasy Flight as an Investigator for inclusion in the Second Edition of Arkham Horror, he has since made appearances in their other product lines, including Eldritch Horror and the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line (all ).

He is visibly based on Charles Foster Kane from Citizen Kane, himself considered based on William Randolph Hearst.

The Arkham Horror Fiction novel Lair of the Crystal Fang establishes that he is the mayor of Arkham.

Charlie Krank (born 1957 in San Francisco, California, USA) is an American games designer, artist, and editor who has a long association with Call of Cthulhu publisher Chaosium. Beginning work for the company in around 1978, he worked on many of their Cthulhu Mythos publications from 1981 onwards, and eventually rose to become president after Greg Stafford left in 1999. This lasted until mid-2015, when Stafford and Sandy Petersen returned to head up the firm.

Chaosium suffered considerable financial losses due to their investment in the Mythos card game and the subsequent collapse of the trading card market in the late 1990s; in an interview with Yog-Sothoth.com, he states that his management of the company during this time kept it afloat;

In the same Yog-Sothoth.com interview, Krank claims to "have been involved in some form in many, but not quite all, of the titles that Chaosium has released," including "game design, game development, editorial and writing, sales and marketing, advertising, art assignments, map drawing, cover layout, project conception and execution, bookkeeping, accounts payable and receivable."

"Chasing Sunset" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author A. C. Wise.

### Synopsis
A man on the run from his sorcerous father flees a across country, believing that only by reaching the ocean will his father's psychic tormenting cease. When he reaches the coast, he realises that he is mistaken, and that all the while the old man was calling him to that very spot. Fortunately, an idol which the man purchased from a sailor in Innsmouth proves to be his salvation, and the use of it summons a colossal monstrosity from beneath the waves which consumes his father.

### Publication History
"Chasing Sunset" was first published in the Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in 2013.  It was also included in the October 2015 anthology The Monstrous.

### Trivia
* The description of the aquatic leviathan would suggest that the entity is intended to be Cthulhu, or perhaps one of the Star-Spawn.

Chaugnar Faugn (The Feeder) is a Great Old One in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Frank Belknap Long for his horror novel The Horror from the Hills.

The entity is a vampiric elephant-like humanoid horror with a leech-like mouth on the end of his trunk. When he hungers, Chaugnar moves very quickly for his size and uses his trunk to drain the blood from his victims, hence his nickname, "The Feeder".

### Description
An impossibly ancient being, Chaugnar Faugn originates from a higher dimension and came to Earth over two billion years ago (: The Horror from the Hills). Before Earth, it dwelt in another world, inside a glowing cone at the edge of a crater, and had a different form, with ropy arms that extended down to the pools of lava below to suck nutrients while the creature slept and dreamed (: "When Chaugnar Wakes").

Chaugnar's Earth form resembles a bipedal reptilian elephant. Its long flexible proboscis ends in a disk-shaped mouth like a lamprey's, which is used to suck its prey's blood. Its ears are webbed and tentacled, its hands are human-like, and its long interlocked tusks are crystalline and translucent. The alien's body is made of an unknown material which is neither organic nor mineral, but allows it to easily pass off as a stone statue by remaining immobile. (: The Horror from the Hills)

Chaugnar can change its own size at will, but tends to become less solid when it increases. Its body and footprints can also give off a phosphorescent glow. Its actual form is unguessable by humans, given its "hyperdimensional" nature. The creatures referred to as the Brothers of Chaugnar Faugn are actually parts of its body which operate as individuals, but are linked to Chaugnar in a way that tridimensional beings cannot see. Despite this, Chaugnar's Brothers function as mentally distinct beings, capable of conversing with Chaugnar (by "thought-transference") and even disagreeing with it. (: The Horror from the Hills)

Chaugnar and its Brothers can appear to humans in dreams, and send telepathic messages (: The Horror from the Hills, "When Chaugnar Wakes"). Those unfortunate enough to be captured by Chaugnar Faugn meet a horrible end, as the deity is a messy eater who not only sucks blood, but also mutilates the bodies of its prey, destroying their faces and rendering their corpses unrecognizable. Conversely, victims who are kept alive by Chaugnar so that it can feed on them repeatedly will experience a gradual transformation, as their facial features deform, the nose and the ears become grotesquely elongated, and the psychic connection develops to such an extent that Chaugnar can influence them and even kill them by telepathy if it chooses to. (: The Horror from the Hills)

The Cheshire Cat was created by Lewis Carroll in 1865, first appearing in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. In 2008, it first appeared in Zenescope Entertainment's Grimm Fairy Tales fictional universe, in the issue #0 of the 1st volume of Grimm Fairy Tales: Return to Wonderland.

### Background
The Cheshire Cat is a house cat that was thrown through the Mirror to Wonderland by the scientist Henry Allen in the late 19th century, where it was transformed into a malicious beast who became Johnny Liddle's companion as he pursued his sister Calie Liddle. The Cheshire Cat was later killed by Calie, but due to the power of Wonderland it returned. Infiltrating a dorm room at a college, where it killed its new master's perceived enemies.

While they can be befriended by humans, they are also rumoured to be related to the Hounds of Tindalos.

Chester Chase is a character who has appeared in the Lovecraft-related works of the late American author Michael Shea.

### Description & History
In his younger years, Chester was a cocky, well-built construction worker who married a woman named Emily. Although he had a few dalliances with other women over the years, their marriage appears to have been a mostly happy one. 

By the time of his appearances, Chester is an ageing widower of 75. He was supported until just prior to the events described by his late sister, but is facing homelessness and destitution at his introduction.

### Mr. Cannyharme
In the novel Mr. Cannyharme, Chester is torn from his body by the evil Mr. Cannyharme, his soul finding a temporary home in the body of former addict Britt, who he helps to survive in the brutal underbelly of 1980s San Francisco. He later leaves her body, his essence contentedly scattering to the cosmic winds.

### "The Recruiter"
In the short story "The Recruiter", Chester is also taken from his mortal shell to perform a task for his malign neighbour, but in this version - which is a rewrite of sections of Mr. Cannyharme - he manages to find his way back, and resolves to do what he can to combat the evil lurking in the city.

Chiaki J. Konaka (born 4 April 1961 in Tokyo, Japan) is an influential Japanese writer and filmmaker whose works have been heavily inspired by the Cthulhu Mythos begun with the stories of H. P. Lovecraft. His Lovecraftian output includes a one-hour made-for-television adaptation of The Shadow Over Innsmouth, and other references can be found littered throughout his other works, for example the title of Armitage III, an OVA inspired by "The Dunwich Horror". He was also the head writer for many episodes of Ultraman Tiga, which features Ghatanothoa as the main antagonist.

In 2018, Konaka appeared as the guest of honour at the Portland, Oregon H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival.

The Children of Abhoth (also known as the Spawn of Abhoth) are a fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Seven Geases", and later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

### Background
The Children of Abhoth are the creatures which sloughed off the Outer God's bulk. They are complex life forms, although some do not appear to be "finished", with vestigial limbs and half-formed bodies, while others seem fully realized. No two offspring are alike: they range in looks from prehistoric creatures to singular body parts, weird humanoids, monstrous mutants, unfinished bodies, amorphous blobs of living flesh, and so on. Most of them are simple-minded, reacting and acting on impulse, but a few seem to demonstrate intelligence and cunning. Therefore, their abilities are equally varied: depending on their bodies, they may fly, crawl, swim, run, or be immobile. Some of them are re-absorbed by Abhoth whilst some remain with their sire, tending to its needs. Those that scurry away to dark corners can mature into larger manifestations. A few eventually find the angles to be transported to the the Dreamlands and other dimensions .

The Children of Tsathoggua are a fictional race created by Robert E. Howard for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Thing on the Roof", although the story does not identify them by name or link them to Tsathoggua. They were adapted for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by J. Todd Kingrea in 1995, when they appeared in the monster-manual supplement Ye Booke of Monstres II .

### Background
The Children of Tsathoggua are a race of extraterrestrial toad-things that were brought to Earth by Tsathoggua. Greasy, enormous, and bloated creatures that have dozens of tentacles, a pair of huge membranous wings, and four or more thick legs that end in mastodonic hooves. Dripping slime covers their ebony black blubbery skin, the eyes are milky white, and extending from their mouth's bony ridges are curved fangs.

The Children of Tsathoggua live in the temples and caverns where their creator is worshiped, acting as the guardians of the shrine and accepting sacrifices. Thieves are mercilessly tracked down and killed, the stolen items retrieved and returned. Some of them were worshiped by early man. It's a race knowledgeable in magic.

### Behind the Mythos
In addition to "The Thing on the Roof", the monster featured in Howard's "The Fire of Asshurbanipal" is almost identical to this species, with the only difference being that its feet have claws rather than hooves.

The sourcebook Ye Booke of Monstres II also implies that the Master of the Monolith from Howard's "The Black Stone" might be a member of this species.

The Children of Yog-Sothoth are a species inspired by Wilbur Whateley, one of the main antagonists in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror".

### Background
The Children of Yog-Sothoth are mortal creatures infused with the Outer God Yog-Sothoth's essence. Most of them can pass for a prominent member of a specific species (relating to the mother) if they wear clothing that hides the monstrous elements in its body. These features include tentacles, eyes, and tails, along with extra maws in places where joints or vertebrae would be expected. They notably emanate an unpleasant scent, typical among old ones and relations. They have a fundamental understanding of magic, easily expanded upon provided with basic tutoring. They are not born evil and have complex morals, but since nearly all of them are raised by the cults that create them, they almost always have evil tendencies manifesting in passive malevolence in the good of their respective cult group. Creating a Child of Yog-Sothoth involves a blasphemous ritual in which a humanoid or animal is used as an incubator, the child's seed combined with the blood of a member in a pact of Yog-Sothoth. The mother dies upon giving birth and usually gives birth to twins, a Child of Yog-Sothoth and a Spawn of Yog-Sothoth. If twins are not produced, the offspring are still birthed. Children of Yog-Sothoth mature much faster than their mother's species; however, they have an extended life span by age, prone to health complications.

fullContent:
"Chimera" Is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Sam Gafford.

### Synopsis
When an abused Arkham youth enters a sleep-study program, he meets a group of cultists who plan on using the Outer God Yog-Sothoth to open a gateway which will bring about the return of the Old Ones. Discovering that he is the herald of these beings by virtue of his bloodline, the boy takes up his birthright as a pair of enormous gates on a Pacific island open …

### Characters
*William Byers, the product of a union between a human woman and a celestial being, likely Yog-Sothoth.
*Lieutenant Jeff Byers, William's sadistic stepfather.
*Dr. Munroe, head of the sleep-study program at Miskatonic University.

### Publication History
"Chimera" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Trivia
A reference to one of the former study group subjects, a boy named Alex Kintner who dreamed about being attacked by sharks, is a clear reference to the novel Jaws by Peter Benchley and the subsequent film adaptation by Steven Spielberg, in which a young boy of the same name is eaten by the titular beast.

fullContent:
China is a region in Earth, which is also a nation-state and a civilization. In the Cthulhu Mythos, it is presented as a center of cult activity, particularly that of Cthulhu. The Plateau of Tsang and the Plateau of Leng have both been suspected of being in China.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
When the Louisiana cultist Castro gives Inspector Legrasse information about the Cthulhu Cult in "The Call of Cthulhu", he claims that the source of his knowledge is his talks with the "undying leaders of the cult in the mountains of China." These "deathless Chinamen" instruct him about "Cyclopean stones on islands in the Pacific" and "double meanings in the Necronomicon".

Dr. Alfred Clarendon, in "The Last Test", also claims to have gotten eldritch knowledge from China: "I didn’t go to China for nothing," he boasts, and declares that it was there that he once "heard an old man...calling on Yog-Sothoth."

In "Out of the Aeons", China is said to be one of the places where the "hidden and detested cult of Ghatanothoa" had penetrated--and it is said to still survive in "the Far East".

The Deep One's 1846 purge of Innsmouth, according to The Shadow Over Innsmouth, was covered up with rumours of a plague from China.

### Lovecraft Circle Writers
Frank Belknap Long, in "The Hound of Tindalos", describes the Liao drug as having been "used centuries ago by Chinese alchemists", and to have been used by the Chinese philosopher Lao Tze" to vision the Tao.  

### Call of Cthulhu Roleplaying Game
Supplements connected to the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game have offered background material on China.

### Secrets of Japan

Taoism, Confucianism, Buddhism, and Islam are all practiced within China, but in a low-key manner. Officially athiesm is the "religion" of the People's Republic of China. Within China are many Mythos secrets. The Plateau of Leng is possibly located within the Xinjiang region. The plateau is the Tcho-Tcho peoples' center of power, and the Lama of Leng is a Tcho-Tcho. Somewhere within China is the city of Yian, the home of the Kuen-Yuin (Oriental sorcerers), and it's likely the center of a Cthulhu Cult. Inside China is also a cult dedicated to Ghatanothoa. The Plateau of Tsang is believed to be in Tibet and has a significant population of Tcho-Tcho and the Miri Nigri, their predecessors. Nyarlathotep's avatar in China is known as the Bloated Woman, the Outer God Yidhra has her avatar Madame Yi, and the Chinese know Hastur as Kaiwan. Within China is also the Brotherhood of the Black Lotus, a cult founded in China during the 6th century BC dedicated to Hastur (through the Emerald Lama, an avatar) and whose influence is global, and which directly or indirectly controls the Chinese Triads and the Golden Triangle drug trade.

Chloe is a fictional character created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his 1918 poem "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin."

### Description
Little is known of Chloe, although from her actions, she can be inferred to be a spiteful, covetous person. Although she initially turned him down, she later married Strephon.

### History
Chloe became jealous after Strephon, whose advances she had previously rejected, entered into a relationship with a woman named Hecatissa. Out of apparently nothing but spite, she stole Strephon away from Hecatissa who, despondent at the loss of her love, attempted to take her own life. (: "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin")

The Chorazin is an avatar of Cthulhu created by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Description
The psychic manifestation of Cthulhu's will, the Chorazin appears as an ethereal representation of its "parent" entity, but can only make its presence known through the dreams and nightmares of those nearby. Using this method to spread madness and chaos, the Chorazin will slowly absorb the insanity it creates and, once it reaches a critical mass, explodes into our dimension in a flash of raw energy. This mass will gestate over the course of the next twelve hours, until finally a full-size representation of Cthulhu with all of its powers and abilities emerges. Once manifested in this way, the Chorazin is only vulnerable to electricity and certain types of magic.

Chorazin was a community in Biblical Palestine, located in what is now modern Israel. It appears in the New Testament, was associated in tradition with the Antichrist, and was mentioned in the horror fiction of M. R. James. Presumably because of this connection, H. P. Lovecraft used it as the name of an unwholesome village in "The Diary of Alonzo Typer".

### In the Real World

Chorazin was a village in Galilee, one of the divisions of Palestine in Roman times. It was located some 2.5 miles north of  Capernaum, a town that features prominently in the Gospel story. Chorazin was later the site of an Arab village, Khirbat Karraza, that was depopulated during the 1947-48 civil war in Mandatory Palestine. Today a nearby Israeli village, Korazim, is named for the ancient site.

In the gospels of Matthew ([https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Matthew+11%3A20%E2%80%9324&version=NRSVUE 11:20-24]) and Luke ([https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Luke+10%3A12%E2%80%9316&version=NRSVUE 10:12-16]), Jesus curses the towns that heard his message and did not repent, in parallel passages that begin, "Woe to you, Chorazin!" Capernaum and Bethsaida are also singled out for condemnation, leading the Apocalypse of Pseudo-Methodius, an apocryphal religious text, to comment that the Antichrist "will be conceived in Chorazin, be born in Bethsaida, and begin to rule in Capernaum."

### In M. R. James
Because Chorazin is not otherwise mentioned in the Gospels, whereas the other two places are the hometowns of eight of the 12 Apostles, this prediction had a worse impact on Chorazin's reputation. This sinister association led to Chorazin's appearance in the M. R. James story "Count Magnus" (1904), a story that Lovecraft greatly admired.

The title character of the story, a sinister and supposedly long-dead aristocrat, is said to have gone on a "Black Pilgrimage" to Chorazin, and to have "brought something or someone back with him". The Count leaves behind a note saying, "If any man desires to obtain a long life, if he would obtain a faithful messenger and see the blood of his enemies, it is necessary that he should first go into the city of Chorazin, and there salute the prince...." The last words appear to be "of the air".

### In Lovecraft
Lovecraft uses the name Chorazin for the location of the Van der Heyl mansion in the revision tale "The Diary of Alonzo Typer"-- a "straggling village...populated by Indians and later by renegades from the surrounding country." The "decadent Chorazin villagers" are noted for their "stupidity and taciturnity,"

Lovecraft's Chorazin is located in upstate New York, about a six-hour walk from the town of Batavia.

### Other Writers
The Lovecraftian writer Darrell Schweitzer also uses the name Chorazin for a horror setting, this one "inspired by long drives to Niagara Falls" when he regularly attended a convention called Eeriecon:You do notice on such trips how

fullContent:
The Chorazos Cult (erroneously called "Choronzon Cult") is a religious cult dedicated to the worship of Yog-Sothoth. It appears in the Encyclopedia Cthulhiana, a supplement to the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. The cult gets its name from the founder, a man of supposed gypsy descent who welcomed cultists from various parts of the world.

This enigmatic and fanatical cult was founded in the mountains of Romania in the late 16th century, but moved to Elizabethan England. Although they owned a temple in Finchley with royal approval, an investigation by John Dee forced them to leave the place. It was then that they settled in a house, but a year later the locals set it on fire, with which they cursed the place and left. It was then that Chorazos and his followers arrived in Scotland. Although King James IV opposed what he saw as witchcraft, the cult developed a good reputation due to its alleged healing powers, but was eventually disbanded again by the villagers as its true nature was revealed.

The cult returned to the present day in the United States. Its goal is to awaken Yog-Sothoth.

### Curiosities
*The name of this fanatic cult could be an allusion to Choronzon, a demon that appears in the writings of the occultists John Dee and Edward Kelley, and that again would be referenced in those of Aleister Crowley.

Chris A. Masters (real name Chris Anagnostopoulos, 1961 - 5 January 2022) was an Australian author and editor who worked on a number of weird fiction projects during the course of his career. He is perhaps best known for his editorial work on the Lovecraftian fanzines Shoggoth (1992 - 1993) and EOD (1991 - 1994), both of which he founded and edited for their complete run. In addition to these, Masters also wrote a handful of short stories and non-fiction pieces around the genre, the majority of which were published in the aforementioned zines.

fullContent:
Christian T. Petersen is a Danish-American game designer and publisher best known as the founder of Fantasy Flight Games (FFG) and the creator of the acclaimed strategy board game Twilight Imperium. Over the course of his career, Petersen became one of the most influential figures in modern tabletop gaming, guiding FFG to international success and later overseeing Asmodee North America.

### Early Life
Christian T. Petersen was born in the United States but spent much of his childhood in Denmark. While still in high school, he founded Pegasus Spil Import, a small company that imported Avalon Hill titles into Scandinavia. During the same period, he also established Games Weekend, the second gaming convention ever held in Denmark.

In 1991, Petersen returned to the United States and began studying economics at St. Olaf College in Northfield, Minnesota. His years of education, paired with his European experiences in gaming and publishing, laid the groundwork for his future endeavors.

### Founding of Fantasy Flight Games
After completing his studies, Petersen launched Fantasy Flight Publishing in June 1995. His first ambition for the company was to republish European comics in English. He acquired rights to several major series, including Lucky Luke, Spirou & Fantasio, and Percevan.

Recognizing demand, Petersen expanded into importing and distributing beloved European titles such as Asterix and Tintin. This venture soon grew into Downtown Distribution, which quickly gained momentum in the comics market.

However, Petersen’s passion for games led him to shift focus. Inspired by his love of strategy and his earlier experiences in Denmark, he designed and released Twilight Imperium in 1997. By 1998, Petersen sold off the comics side of his business and rebranded his company as Fantasy Flight Games, concentrating entirely on tabletop gaming.

### Rise of Fantasy Flight Games
Under Petersen’s leadership, FFG became a powerhouse of innovative game design. A longtime fan of Lovecraftian horror, Petersen secured a license from Chaosium to create a line of Call of Cthulhu supplements. Alongside Darrell Hardy, he co-authored the Nocturnum adventure trilogy (Long Shades, Hollow Winds, and Deep Secrets), establishing FFG’s reputation in the role-playing market. He also co-designed and released the board game Mansions of Madness which is directly based on the Chaosium version of the Cthulhu Mythos. In 2004 he secured the publication rights for a re-release of the 1987 game of Lovecraftian monster-hunting Arkham Horror, which underwent a major overhaul before being released by FFG.

As CEO, Petersen personally guided both the business strategy and the creative direction of FFG. He was directly involved in the design of many landmark titles, including:

* Twilight Imperium (all editions)
* A Game of Thrones: The Board Game
* World of Warcraft: The Board Game
* The Lord of the Rings Trivia Game

He also co-designed numerous other projects, such as Diskwars and Vor

"Christmas Day" is a festive Cthulhu Mythos story by author DJ Tyrer. It was published in the Jesse Dedman/William C. Marchese-edited anthology Cthulhu Christmas Special and Other Lovecraftian Yuletide Tales in November 2017.

### Synopsis
While visiting family on Christmas Eve, Louie receives a present intended for him by his recently-deceased uncle. Opening the gift, he finds it to be a play called The King in Yellow, and he falls asleep while reading it. Awakening into a strangely disturbing dream, he meets his cousin Connie, apparently having the same dream. Suddenly, a figure clad in tattered yellow robes appears, and traps the two in their nightmare. As he begins to relive the same Christmas Day for all eternity, he realises that it had all been planned by his uncle, Connie's father.

Chronicles of the Cthulhu Codex, also The Cthulhu Codex and simply Cthulhu Codex, was a sporadically-released zine which focused on the Lovecraftian horror genre.

### Overview
Running to a total of 17 issues, Chronicles of the Cthulhu Codex underwent a surprisingly large number of name changes throughout its limited run. The first issue was released in January 1985 by Fungoid Press and under the editorship of Pierre Comtois, and it remained under his direction until 1988. In 1989, Henry J. Vester, III took the helm for issue #5, after which it lapsed into hiatus. In 1994, Vester returned along with Ron Hilger to produce issue #6, renaming it simply The Cthulhu Codex, after which it once again briefly lapsed. 1996 saw veteran editor Robert M. Price revive the zine through Necronomicon Press, again simplifying the title, this time to Cthulhu Codex. Joseph S. Pulver, Sr. edited for a single issue (#16) in 1999, and Comtois returned for the final issue in December 2000, once again under the Fungoid label and reverting the title back to Chronicles of the Cthulhu Codex.
