"Confession in Darkness" is a horror short story by Gerald W. Page set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in 1979 in the magazine Weirdbook 14.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator is a sorcerer who has extended his life with dark rituals. He relates his story to a journalist in an unlighted room at night. Without any hint of shame, he tells the interviewer about his first murder, committed in Victorian England over a century prior. The victim was a young woman named Marie Ostroff. The narrator killed her while practicing an elaborate ritual found in the Book of Eibon, which took several days to complete. When she finally expired, he went to his mentor, Leffler, to give him the news.

Leffler, despite his enviable knowledge about the Great Old Ones, Mi-Go, Deep Ones, and other creatures, was only a "theoretical" sorcerer, having given up the practice after an incident in which he summoned something that terrified and traumatised him. He was, moreover, a cannibal, and afflicted with another recurring fear: that his enemies might devour his body after death. In exchange for his teachings, Leffler made the narrator promise to stand with him when he died, arrange the funeral and the burial in graves that could never be found, and make sure that no ghouls would eat him. The narrator takes a perverse delight in revealing that he has betrayed Leffler and devoured him himself, doing so as a part of a ritual to increase his own power.

After that, the narrator spent a year and a half in Scandinavia, sometimes in the form of a werewolf, sadistically hunting animals (including regular wolves) and humans. However, after being threatened by locals who might have had access to silver bullets, he gave up his lycanthropy and moved to France in human form. There he met a beautiful sorceress named Catherine, who had made a pact with an entity named Ptar-Axtlan that granted her eternal youth. Initially infatuated, the narrator eventually got tired of her and tried to figure out a way to dump her while securing his personal safety in the war that was threatening to break out in Europe. At the same time, a dealer in occult books named Jerome found a bone that belonged to Leffler's left leg, complete with bite marks, and tried to blackmail the narrator by threatening to show this evidence to some powerful friends of the deceased occultist.

Seizing the opportunity, the narrator murdered Catherine and Jerome, cut their bodies into small pieces with a meat-cleaver, and set fire to the apartment, then moved to America to escape the war. He made acquaintances with the Deep Ones in Innsmouth and used a spell found in Von Junzt's Unaussprechlichen Kulten to visit Y'ha-nthlei. However, only three months later, he was forced to move again, as the military occupied Innsmouth. Confessions of the Mad Monk Clithanus, or simply The Confessions of Clithanus, is an occult text created by August Derleth for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "Passing of Eric Holm".

### Overview
Penned by a Christian monk named Clithanus in Rome sometime in the late 4th/early 5th century, not much is known about the Confessions. However, it has been stated to contain information on subterranean catacombs beneath Hydestall Cathedral, England, and the oceanic horrors which lurk beneath the waves thereabouts. It also tells of an encounter which Clithanus and Saint Augustine of Hippo had with the titular "Something" from Derleth's short story "Something from Out There", during which the entity was defeated and sealed away.

fullContent:
"Conglomerate" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the November 1996 edition of the Robert M. Price-edited fanzine Midnight Shambler.

### Synopsis
When a crazed vandal kills himself after defacing a company's icon - an enormous, rock-like sphere - head of security Colin James decides to look into the man's motives. What he discovers is that his city was once the site of a titanic battle, one in which Yog-Sothoth was rendered inert by cosmic powers. Furthermore, his company - which he now realises is far more expansive and insidious than he had ever imagined - is responsible for buying the land containing the inactive spheres of the Outer God, linking them together in an attempt to revive the being.

The story concludes with James realising that even though there is little he can do against the forces ranged against mankind, he must try before the megacorporation achieves their goal.

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance, "Conglomerate" has also been included in the collections Unholy Dimensions (2005) and Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012, German translation).

fullContent:
The Congregation of the Earth Mother is a fictional organisation in the CthulhuTech pencil-and-paper role-playing game by Wildfire LLC.

### Background
The Congregation of the Earth Mother is an ancient cult, that has existed for millennia. That spread throughout the nations of man and wielded great power. It's a fertility cult that has taken various forms across history. Recently it has been decimated by the NEG and is a shadow of what it once was. The true initiates are gone and so are most of the Dark Young, therefore it's members have forgotten the true purpose of the cult and believe that their goddess, Shub-Niggurath is a benevolent entity who will bring balance to Earth and turn it into a paradise. 

Across the world are small pockets of the cult, with good sized numbers in the jungles of Africa, the primordial forests of the Pacific Northwest, and South America's remaining rain forests. It recruits environmentalists and uses the "Horned Ones" to attract recruits. Who are introduced to herbalism, narcotics and hallucinogenics, fertility rituals to increase crops, wanton sex and orgies, and ritualistic sex. Recently they've regrouped and gained powerful allies, the support of the Chrysalis Corporation.

Convicts & Cthulhu: For the Term of His Preternatural Life is a sub-setting for Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, set in Colonial Era Australia. It was launched by third-party content provider Cthulhu Reborn with the release of the Convicts & Cthulhu sourcebook in 2016.

Although marketed for use with Call of Cthulhu, alternative versions of the various supplements designed as generic supplements for any Cthulhu Mythos-related roleplaying game have also been released, and a book dedicated for use with The Cthulhu Hack was published in the same year as the original supplement.

"Cool Air" is a short story by the American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in March 1926 and published in the March 1928 issue of Tales of Magic and Mystery.

### Summary

The story is set up as the narrator's explanation for why a "draught of cool air" causes him more discomfort than one would expect.

The tale opens up in the spring of 1923 with the narrator looking for housing in New York City, finally settling in a converted brownstone on West Fourteenth Street. Eventually, a chemical leak from the floor above reveals that the inhabitant directly overhead is a strange, old, reclusive doctor. One day the narrator suffers a heart attack, and remembering that a doctor lives directly above, heads there, culminating in his first meeting with Dr. Muñoz.

The doctor shows supreme medical skill and saves the narrator with a concoction of drugs, resulting in the fascinated narrator returning regularly to sit and learn from the doctor, his new friend. As their talks continue, it becomes increasingly evident that the doctor has an obsession with defying death through all available means.

The doctor's room is kept cold at approximately 56 degrees Fahrenheit (13 degrees Celsius) using an ammonia-based refrigeration system, the pumps driven by a gasoline engine. As time goes on, the doctor's health declines and his behaviour becomes increasingly eccentric. The cooling system is continuously upgraded, to the point where some areas are at sub-freezing temperatures--until one night when the pump breaks down.

Without explanation, the panic-stricken doctor frantically implores his friend to help him keep his body cool. Unable to repair the machine until morning and without a replacement piston, they resort to having the doctor stay in a tub full of ice. The narrator spends his time replenishing the ice, but soon is forced to employ someone else to do it. When he finally manages to locate competent mechanics and the replacement part however, it is too late.

He arrives at the apartment only to see the rapidly-decomposed remains of the doctor, and a rushed, "hideously smeared" letter. The narrator reads it, and to his horror, finally understands the doctor's peculiarities: Dr. Muñoz was undead, and has been for the past 18 years. Refusing to give in, he has kept his body going past the point of death using various methods, including perpetual coldness.

After being treated by Muñoz, his upstairs neighbor, he becomes "a disciple and devotee of the gifted recluse".

term: Copyright status of works by H. P. Lovecraft
shortDefinition: There is controversy over the copyright status of some of the fiction works of American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft. His writings published in 1928 or earlier are automatically in the public domain; his work published in 1929 or later may also be i...
fullContent:
There is controversy over the copyright status of some of the fiction works of American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft. His writings published in 1928 or earlier are automatically in the public domain; his work published in 1929 or later may also be in the public domain.

In the United States, the copyright on works published before 1978 expires after 95 years. This means that as of 2025, all works published before 1930 are in the public domain, so no permission or payment is needed to reprint or adapt them. This category includes many well-known Lovecraft stories, including "The Rats in the Walls" (1924), "The Festival" (1925), "The Colour Out of Space" (1927), "Pickman's Model" (1927), and "The Call of Cthulhu" (1928).

Works published after 1930 and before 1964, which would include all the remainder of Lovecraft's fiction, may still be in copyright if they were originally published with a copyright notice, and if that copyright was renewed by the copyright holder after 28 years. It is unclear whether any of Lovecraft's fictional work meets both criteria.

Questions center on who exactly owns or owned the copyrights, and whether the copyrights for the majority of Lovecraft's works published post-1928 — including such prominent pieces as At the Mountains of Madness — were renewed as required.

Regardless of the legal disagreements surrounding Lovecraft's works, Lovecraft himself was extremely generous with his own works, and actively encouraged others to borrow ideas from his stories, particularly with regard to his Cthulhu Mythos. By "wide citation" he hoped to give his works an "air of verisimilitude", and actively encouraged other writers to reference his creations, such as the Necronomicon, Cthulhu and Yog-Sothoth. After his death, many writers have contributed stories and enriched the shared mythology of the Cthulhu Mythos, as well as making numerous references to his work.

The Open Cthulhu Mythos project relying on the extreme scholarship of the German Lovecraft Society have prepared a complete and exhaustive list of all Lovecraft works and elements that are beyond question in the public domain as of 2024 and after.

### Copyright Ownership
Lovecraft had specified that the young R. H. Barlow would serve as executor of his literary estate, though these instructions had not been incorporated into his will. Nevertheless, his surviving aunt, Annie Gamwell, carried out his expressed wishes, and Barlow was given charge of the massive and complex literary estate upon Lovecraft's death.

Barlow deposited the bulk of the papers, including the voluminous correspondence, with the John Hay Library at Brown University. However, as a young writer with no legal training, his efforts to organize and maintain Lovecraft's other writing stood little chance of success. August Derleth, an older and more established writer than Barlow, vied for control of the literary estate. One result of these conflicts was the legal confusion over who owned what copyrights.

"Cordelia's Song from The King in Yellow" is an addition to The King in Yellow by Vincent Starrett, first published in Weird Tales in 1938.

It adds to the original work by expanding the fragments of the fictional and eponymous play with an entire new song, and a new character in the person of Cordelia. It is not identified as belonging to either of the two known Acts of the play.

"Cordelia's Song from The King in Yellow" was also published in the anthology The Spawn of Cthulhu.

"Corpse Candles" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the Hallowmas 1998 edition of the Cthulhu Codex fanzine.

### Synopsis
Detective Grange is given a glimpse into the world of the occult when he is called to attend an incident where an elderly man apparently self-combusted, although he survived the event. What he uncovers is a decades-long feud between two brothers, each of whom worship a seperate deity: one a being named only as N, the other likely Cthulhu. The story concludes with the death of both brothers, each having summoned lesser minions of their patrons to destroy the other.

### Behind the Mythos
Amongst the Cthulhu Mythos elements mentioned are the Spawn of C_ (a globster washed up on the Florida coastline) and Cthugha (stated to have been responsible for the Great Chicago Fire and the American Midwest fires of 1871).

One of the specimens encountered by Detective Grange was labelled as having been sent by one S. Sargent. This is likely a nod to Stanley C. Sargent, a noted Mythos author contemporary to the publishing of "Corpse Candles".

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance in Cthulhu Codex, "Corpse Candles" has been seen in the collections Unholy Dimensions (2005) and Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012, German translation).

"Correlated Contents" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and editor James Ambuehl, part of his Lu-Kthu story cycle.

### Synopsis
In a letter to a member of the Miskatonic University faculty, a man describes a series of artworks created by a blind painter. These pieces portray the Great Old Ones of the Lu-Kthu Cycle, and just the simple act of looking at them appears to drive mortals insane.

### Characters

* Davis Rault, a faculty member at Braving, Minnesota'sRoyceton University, and the author of the letter.
* Dr. Eben Stone, a faculty member at Arkham, Massachusetts' Miskatonic University, and the letter's addressee.

### Publication History
"Correlated Contents" was first published in an anthology of stories by James Ambuehl, also called Correlated Contents; this collection was released by Mythos Books in December 1998.

### Trivia

* The title of the story appears to be a reference to a line from "The Call of Cthulhu" (): "The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents."
*A line makes reference to Toad Lake, the setting for Ambuehl's 1997 story "The Terror of Toad Lake".

The Cosmic Abstracts are eldritch cosmic entities of the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. Entities that are neither benevolent or malevolent, which most mortals or "godlings" are unable to grasp their existence much less their purpose or whatever agendas they may have.

### Background
The Cosmic Abstracts are nigh-omnipotent beings which are the embodiment of concepts of the universe and the Multiverse (e.g. time and space). Entities of such incalculable power that they make "gods" like Thor seem like flies, annoying pests at best. They are witnesses to universal and multiversal events. Guiding, shaping, protecting, destroying, and reshaping universes. Humans and other sentient lifeforms are incapable of comprehending their true forms. When manifesting in the material universe, they take one of the fractal beings of the Dimension of Manifestations, to provide them with a "shell" of sorts that can take infinite forms. Entities that are so alien, that when the spacefaring team of superheroes known as the "Guardians of the Galaxy" unknowingly found themselves on a cosmic abstract they perceived themselves as being on a checkerboard like planet.

The Multiverse has a pantheon of sorts, consisting of various multiversal abstracts. Each of whose power vastly eclipses that of the most powerful entity in each universe within the Multiverse. Whenever there is a major multiversal event they are either involved as participants or as observers.

* One Above All = The master of the Multiverse. It is a mysterious supreme being who permits virtually anything to happen in its multiverse, from the birth and creation of new realities to the corruption or destruction of old realities.

* Living Tribunal = Balance in the multiverse is maintained by the Living Tribunal a being whose power is eclipsed only by the One Above All and whom answers only to the One Above All.

* Eternity = Similar to how Yog-Sothoth in the Mythos contained within it every universe, likewise the multiversal version of Eternity also contains within it every universe in the multiverse.

* The Firmaments = Are the beings who embodied the previous multiverses, with the current Eternity being the 8th Cosmos (Multiverse).

Each of the universes within the Multiverse has its own pantheon of sorts, consisting of various cosmic abstracts and in some cases a single nigh-omnipotent entity. Each of whose power vastly eclipses that of the most powerful "god" on Earth. Whenever there is a major universal-scale event they are either involved as participants or as observers. As the planet Earth is currently the most important point in the Prime Reality (Earth-616), they occasionally involve themselves with matters on Earth, likewise as either participants or as observers. There are dozens of cosmic abstracts, including Eternity and Infinity, Master Order and Lord Chaos, the Queen of Nevers, and Death.

fullContent:
"Cosmic Aggressions" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Chad Eagleton, first published in Vol 3, Issue 1 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana in April 2018.

Unusually for an Expanded Mythos story, "Cosmic Aggressions" deals with the indirect effects of a hostile universe on the vulnerable psyches of bystanders, rather than the mind-shattering revelations or gruesome ends caused by Mythos entities more often depicted.

### Synopsis
Ty Whitcomb, a student at Miskatonic University, consults one of the school's councillors about a deep-seated sense of cosmic persecution and discontent which has been ruining his mental health. The councillor, a man named Ezra Gaskell, is, in addition to his duties concerning the school body, a member of clandestine group the Dunwich Committee on Student Safety, an organisation dedicated to ensuring that the eldritch entities which infest the university and its environs cause as little disruption to the unsuspecting city of Arkham as possible.

Taking Whitcomb to a specialist campus unit dealing with these kind of traumas, Gaskell reflects that perhaps it is not too late for the boy, but that the number of cases just like Ty's are beginning to take their emotional toll on him as well.

### Mythos Connections
"Cosmic Aggressions" features numerous references to aspects of the Cthulhu Mythos. These include:

* Ty Whitcomb is stated to come from "just south of Dunwich"
* The Dunwich Committee of Student Safety, "founded in the wake of the terrible incident that occurred almost 90 years ago over in Dunwich," has been involved with several Mythos-related events, such as:
**an incident at the Pickman Exhibition
**an issue with a swimmer from Innsmouth
**a student production of "the Queen in Purple," a likely nod to Robert W. Chambers' The King in Yellow
**a local metal band named Krawling Kaos
**and a "disastrous Edward Pickman Derby recitation"
* The story concludes with Gaskell receiving a smartphone alert informing that "someone had just filed a library request for both De Vermis Mysteriis and The Ludwig Prinn Confession."

fullContent:
### Concept
Much has been written at length about the horror subgenre of "Cosmic Horror", and it remains an important and vital subgenre that H.P. Lovecraft and his contemporaries might take great pride in having introduced to the horror genre.

The term "Cosmic Horror" can be applicably defined Lovecraftian Horror and Cosmicism, and cosmic horror is heavily influenced by the philosophical notion of existential nihilism and philosophical pessimism, as well as the desolate quality of the natural world, and the cosmos in general.

### Themes
### Cosmic Indifference
Thematically, the primary attribute of the cosmic horror story is the idea that human beings are insignificant and inconsequential in the scope of cosmic reality. Humanity is at best a nominal footnote in the history of the universe, and at worst deserves no notice whatsoever. 

While the stories themselves seem essentially pessimistic, Lovecraft himself believed that the negative connotation of "pessimist" was improper, preferring "indifferentist".

### Alienation
The fear of the Other, the alien, and the unknown are central tenets that underscore the terror in the cosmic horror story. The xenophobia and racist overtones in many of Lovecraft's stories are unarguable, but the underlying fear of what one does not understand remains the pervasive note. One might argue that the enduring nature of Lovecraft's work is not in spite of his racism, but precisely because his racism allowed him to tap into every reader's deepest irrational terror of the Other.

This alienation further extends to the self. There is often an alien nature to a character's ancestry and personal relationships, with questions of alien or supernatural parentage and sinister personal acquaintances. Furthermore, the characters are often loners, and isolated people without close personal ties.

### Sanity
The characters of cosmic horror stories often skirt the line of rationality and sanity. Sanity is displayed as a fragile and tenuous thing, with the experience of the horrors of the true nature of reality being enough to drive one to madness. 

### Tropes
The themes of cosmic horror stories express themselves in many ways, but are frequently seen in a number of tropes: 

*The Eldrich Abomination -- This type of antagonist is a common trope in the cosmic horror story. Always horrific in appearance, and occasionally beyond human description or comprehension, these monsters threaten the boundaries of reality. At best their motives are inconceivable or in disregard of humanity, at worst they are a malevolent force actively seeking to subvert or corrupt human society. The various "gods" of the Mythos are counted in this category.

*The Cult -- This other common antagonistic force frequently seek to act as agents of Eldrich Abominations or other malevolent/alien forces. The reach of their sinister network is unknown, but is suspected to influence many powerful men and women.

*Secret Knowledge -- Whether it's the forbidden tome

fullContent:
Cosmicism is a philosophy and literary movement developed by H. P. Lovecraft and his followers through their stories. When applied to horror fiction, it forms one of the bases of Lovecraftian Horror.

Lovecraft was a writer of philosophical horror that included phenomena related to the occult on Earth and the secrets of the universe. The themes of his and others' stories contributed to the development of this philosophy. Lovecraft's cosmos does not revolve around the human being. All of Lovecraft's work is sustained under the watchful eye of alien entities from beyond reality that, when they awaken in our world, corrupt and destroy everything that exists that is real to human beings: human beings are a very insignificant presence in the general scheme of the universe, a small species but whose arrogance makes us believe that they have a significant or total power as a source of existence in the universe, but nevertheless they can be eliminated at any moment by forces of which they even ignore their existence.

### Bases of cosmicism
Lovecraft argues that there is no perceptible divine presence, like a god in the universe, and that humans are particularly insignificant on the great map of intergalactic existence: just a small species projecting its own mental idolatries into the vast cosmos, always susceptible to be removed from existence at any time.

Cosmicism shares many characteristics with nihilism, although one important difference is that cosmicism tends to make clear the inconsistency of humanity and its actions rather than summarily rejecting the possible existence of a higher purpose (or purposes). In Lovecraft's stories it is not the absence of the meaning of things that causes horror to its protagonists, it is their discovery that makes them realize their human inability to change the indifferent and incomprehensible universe that surrounds them.

Lovecraft's cosmicism was the result of his dislike for all religious concepts and his feeling of the existential impotence of humanity in the face of what he called "infinite spaces" opened by scientific ideas, a terror towards the finiteness of being in the infinity of space and our ignorance. In his works of fiction, these ideas are expressed in different ways (Herbert West--Reanimator, The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, The Call of Cthulhu, among others). Recurring elements related to Lovecraft's cosmicism in fiction are humanity's insignificance in the universe and the search for wisdom ending in disaster.

Lovecraft once observed that the supreme being in the universe has no likelihood of being the human being, and could more likely to be imagined to be a glowing gas floating around a distant star.

Despite the frequent use of expletives and imprecations invoking the Christian God in the Mythos stories, at least in the case of Lovecraft it is clear that his atheism and nihilism meant that he did not in any way think that the God so called upon would ever or could ever intervene. And in

Cotoaahd is a fictional monster created by Philip José Farmer for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Freshman".

### Overview
According to the folklore of the extinct Tamsiqueg people who inhabited the Miskatonic River area, Cotoaahd was the chief of a group of "evil giants" who battled against the heroes Mikatoonis and Chegaspat. After Chegaspat was killed, Mikatoonis turned the giants into stone with a magical club, thus creating the Tamsiqueg Hills that now stand next to Arkham's Miskatonic University. One of these "curiously shaped" hills is known as Cotoaahd.

It is also said that every few centuries, Cotoaahd manages to free himself from the spell and walk around for a while, before returning to his "rocky slumber". A colossal creature, he can flatten houses and trees under his feet. When Roderick Desmond summoned Cotoaahd with a spell to kill his mother, witnesses reported that the house his mother was in collapsed suddenly "like a giant foot stepped on it", but no one reported seeing the monster, which might suggest that Cotoaahd is invisible.

Miskatonic University's Committee of the Occult Arts and History Department (COTOAAHD), at one point headed by the wizard R. Layamon, appears to be named after this entity. (: "The Freshman")

### Behind the Mythos
The idea of a giant invisible monster who can flatten houses and kill the inhabitants inside is similar to H. P. Lovecraft's classic Mythos story "The Dunwich Horror", in which the titular entity crushes the house of Elmer and Selina Frye.

fullContent:
Cotton Mather (12 February 1663 – 13 February 1728) was a Puritan minister perhaps best known for his involvement in the Salem Witch Trials of the late 17th century. He has intersected with various aspects of this wiki, both in the real world and as a fictional character.

### Real Life
Howard Phillips Lovecraft was known to read the writings of Cotton Mather, and drew a germ of inspiration from a quotation in one of his works. This quotation, from one Dr. Pierre Borel, led in part to his writing The Case of Charles Dexter Ward.

### In Lovecraft's Works
In one of his books, Mather wrote about the birth of a mysterious creature known as "the thing with the blemished eye", but failed to provide any information about what became of it ("The Unnamable").

Mather was present at the time accused witch Keziah Mason disappeared, and was at a loss to explain the mystical sigils which were all that remained in her cell ("The Dreams in the Witch-House").

Richard Upton Pickman's four-times-great-grandmother was hanged as a witch with Mather in attendance during the Salem Witch Trials ("Pickman's Model").

Just before their Sabbat at Hallow-Mass, 1693, the devil-worshipping coven of Roodsford used dark magic to make Cotton Mather sick with colic, thus ensuring that he wouldn't interfere with their plans ("Satan's Servants").

### In Other Works
The Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. short story "In The Chapel Of Ghattambah" tells of how Azmael, the High Priest of Ghattambah, was a one-time associate of Mather's.

shortDefinition: "Count Magnus" is a short horror story by M. R. James. H. P. Lovecraft cites it in Supernatural Horror in Literature as one of James' best stories, calling it "a veritable Golconda of suspense and suggestion." (Golconda is an Indian fort famous for i...
fullContent:
"Count Magnus" is a short horror story by M. R. James. H. P. Lovecraft cites it in Supernatural Horror in Literature as one of James' best stories, calling it "a veritable Golconda of suspense and suggestion." (Golconda is an Indian fort famous for its wealth of diamonds.)

The story of "Count Magnus" was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Brian Lumley, who refers to it in "The House of the Temple".

### Synopsis
Set around 1863, the story describes the contents of a manuscript written by an English travel writer named Wraxall, who had been researching a book in the Vestergothland region of Sweden. In a town called (but not actually named) Raback, he learns of a family referred to as De la Gardie, and in particular of a sinister ancestor named Count Magnus, a tyrannical landlord with an interest in alchemy; poachers on his land years after his death have met horrible fates, one found with the flesh of his face "sucked away off the bones". 

Magnus is said to have gone on a "Black Pilgrimage" to Chorazin (a village in Palestine associated with the Anti-Christ), and to have "brought something or someone back with him." In a note labelled  "Liber nigrae peregrinationis"--"The book of the black pilgrimage"--Magnus wrote, "If any man desires to obtain a long life, if he would obtain a faithful messenger and see the blood of his enemies, it is necessary that he should first go into the city of Chorazin, and there salute the prince...." The last words appear to be "of the air".

Wraxall is fascinated by Magnus' mausoleum, which he visits repeatedly. The lid of the count's sarcophagus, which is sealed with three locks, bears a scene of a man being hunted by a hooded dwarf with the "tentacle of a devil-fish," as a cloaked man looks on with interest. Wraxall remarks out loud three times that he wishes he could see Magnus, and each time one of the locks drops off. After the third time, he hears the lid of the sarcophagus creaking open, and flees in terror; Wraxall writers, "I only know that there was something more than I have written that alarmed me, but whether it was sound or sight I am not able to remember."

Returning to England, he is obsessed with two fellow passengers on a canal boat: One "a man in a long black cloak and broad hat, and another a ‘short figure in dark cloak and hood’". He is convinced that he is being followed after landing at Harwich, and races to the village of Belchamp St Paul in Essex, where he sees his pursuers again.  

So ends Wraxall's manuscript. The story notes that Wraxall was found dead, in an undisclosed state that caused seven jurors at the inquest to faint; his death was ruled a "visitation of God". The narrator closes by noting that he found the account in a cottage he was having torn down.

"Country Mouse, City Mouse" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Nick Mamatas.

### Synopsis
The fates of two identical twins are juxtaposed: whilst one participates in social activism and the 2011 Tottenham Riots, the other becomes a victim of the Great Old One Glaaki, compelled to carry out his master's will for eternity. Both, however, seek to change the order of establishment in their own ways.

### Characters
*Maria, a woman transitioning from male to female in early 21st century London and a proponent of social change.
*Yiannis, Maria's brother who chose to move to the Severn Valley to tend to goats as a way to spite his overbearing father.

### Publication History
"Country Mouse, City Mouse" was published in the 2017 thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki: A Tribute to Ramsey Campbell's Great Old One by Dark Regions Press in January 2017.

fullContent:
The Court of Azathoth is a place mentioned in the Cthulhu Mythos. Sometimes it is called "the Final Void". According to some accounts, it awaits behind the last of the Gates.

### Location
The Court of Azathoth is located, presumably, in the place beyond the angular space, in which all dimensions come together.

### Description
The Court stands on a plane beyond space and time, serving as the abode for the lobotomized Azathoth, "the foolish Daemon Sultan." There, the almighty Outer God remains dormant by the sounds sung by amorphous flute players. Both Nyarlathotep and Yog-Sothoth are known to visit the Court of Azathoth to review the state he is in after some time.

As for its appearance, it can be said that the Court of Azathoth represents the pure essence of chaos: anything strange and surreal that one can imagine has a place in that world that goes beyond logic.

### Inhabitants
The Court of Azathoth is inhabited by amorphous flute players, accompanied by a large group of Outer Gods and Lesser Other Gods. Those confirmed are found below:

Outer Gods:

* Azathoth
* Ghroth
* K'thun
* Noth-Yidik
* Nyarlathotep
* Tru'nembra
* Tulzscha


Lesser Other Gods:

* Aiueb Gnshal
* Cloud-Thing
* Crackling Energy Mass
* Luminous Transparency
* Roiling Gas-Cloud
* Shimmering Liquid
* Singer of Dhol
* Suc'naath

### Behind the Mythos
There are a number of entities which may reside at the court of Azathoth which have been said to originate from "the center of the universe" or a similarly named place, which also have a Lesser Outer God or Lesser Other God status (see The Blackness from the Stars and Shabbith-Ka).

### In Other Media
*The name of the final boss of the video game Kirby Star Allies is translated into Spanish as "Final Void". It does not seem to be a coincidence, since the creature in question is a mindless and amoral god of chaos and destruction that remains sealed in a state of torpor, which makes him very similar to Azathoth himself.

fullContent:
Courting Madness is an anthology collection of material for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Compiled by Pagan Publishing for GenCon 1992 - from which it was ultimately banned as a result of the suggestive nature of Blair Reynolds' cover art - the book contained resources collected from issues 1 - 3 of gaming magazine The Unspeakable Oath, all of which was first published in 1991.

The production team for Courting Madness included Brian Bevel, John Tynes, and Brian Appleton; cover art was provided by Blair Reynolds, with interior panels by Reynolds, Jeff Barber, and Charlie Mitchell.

### Contents
*Introduction: "The Dread Page Of Azathoth" (by John Tynes)
*"Yeah, But What Does It Look Like?" (by Chris Klepac)
*"A Chip Off The Old Blob" (by Scott David Aniolowski and Kevin A Ross)
*"A Tale Of Terror: Grim Portrait" (by Steve Hatherley)
*"A Tale Of Terror: Little Death" (by Steve Hatherley)
*"Grace Under Pressure" (by John Tynes & Jeff Barber)
*"You Are Cordially Invited" (by Thomas Stratman)
*"The House On Stratford Lane" (by John Crowe)
*"The Travesty" (by Chris Klepac)

### Trivia
*In 1993, the scenario "Grace Under Pressure" was reprinted in its own book as part of Pagan's sporadic series The Resurrected, which published rare and out-of-print material from The Unspeakable Oath.

The Crackling Energy Mass is a fictional entity created by American author and games designer Kevin A. Ross for the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. It first appeared in "Thunder in the Blood", a scenario included in the supplement End of the World (Triad Entertainments, 1994).

### Overview
The Crackling Energy Mass is one of five Lesser Other Gods from the Court of Azathoth that appeared during a summoning of Azathoth near San Lucas. It appears as a large mass of crackling black energy from which ebony lightning lashes out. (: End of the World)

Craig Paul Alexander Hinton (7 May 1964-3 December 2006) was a British writer best known for his work on various spin-offs from the British Broadcasting Corporation Television series Doctor Who.	His Doctor Who spinoff novel Millennial Rites made overt and prolific use of concepts and characters from the Cthulhu Mythos and combined the continuity of Doctor Who with that of the Mythos, reconciling details between the two.

He also wrote articles for various science fiction magazines, and was the Coordinator of the Doctor Who Appreciation Society. He most recently lived in London, where he taught mathematics. Hinton was found dead in his home on 3 December 2006. The cause of death was given as heart attack.

fullContent:
Crash Fever is a Japanese mobile game created by Wonderplanet Inc. in May 2015. The global version was released in October 2016, and later ended its service in December 2023; however, the Japanese server is still active as of this writing. The gameplay features a combination of puzzle-burst mechanics with RPG character leveling and collectible units, as the player matches coloured beads on a tap-based puzzle to activate their attacks, with the continuous combo chains generating high damage and allowing usage of different skills from various units.

The storyline takes place in the near future, where almost everything has been connected to the virtual world of ALICE, leading to cybercrime becoming too rampant for the government to handle. In retaliation, the super-AI known as the QUEEN of Hearts was created by the Superior Seven, a group of avatars, in order to manage everything. Shortly afterwards, there was an increase of attacks from various groups of hackers and crackers, attacking both each other and the Queen. This leads to the QUEEN believing that all humankind is evil, and attempting to eradicate all of humanity to preserve peace in ALICE; however, there was a failsafe that prevented her from destroying everyone. When the QUEEN began to wage war on ALICE, it caused many real-world services to become buggy or defunct. 

The player, a special avatar known as the Adapter, must use their special ability to create clones of units, joining them in the battle against the QUEEN's makeshift army and other enemies. The units featured in the game are based on characters from various sources, including the Cthulhu Mythos.

Crawford Tillinghast is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "From Beyond".

### Description
The best friend of the story's narrator, Tillinghast is a researcher of the "physical and metaphysical". Characterized as a man of "feeling and action", the narrator describes his physical transformation after he succeeds in his experiments: "It is not pleasant to see a stout man suddenly grown thin, and it is even worse when the baggy skin becomes yellowed or grayed, the eyes sunken, circled, and uncannily glowing, the forehead veined and corrugated, and the hands tremulous and twitching."

### History
Tillinghast was the creator of a machine which could open gateways between worlds, allowing humans to interact with entirely alien entities. Unfortunately for him, his experiments ended in disaster when his friend destroyed the machine, an act which inadvertently resulted in Tillinghast's death. (: "From Beyond")

### Behind the Mythos
In the first draft of the story, Lovecraft called the character Henry Annesley; he replaced that name with one composed of two old Providence surnames. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) In The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, Lovecraft mentions "the seasoned salts who manned...the great brigs of the Browns, Crawfords, and Tillinghasts"; James Tillinghast and Eliza Tillinghast are minor characters in that story.

The Crawling Dead was an eldritch abomination from the fictional universe of Marvel from Marvel Comics.

### Background
The Crawling Dead lived in the abandoned ruins of an Atlantean city during the Thurian Age. It was a fleshy throbbing mass of living putrescence with a brain. Centuries earlier, the city's inhabitants had dumped their dead into a communal tomb. Where eldritch forces kept the falling flesh alive, and eventually the corpses began to meld and grow. Until an eldritch abomination arose, one with a brain which was insatiably hungry for more flesh, to further expand. 

It used a spell to lure King Kull of Valusia to its lair. The enchanted Kull saw and followed a beautiful women into the city's dark catacombs. Lorkar his bestial humanoid companion was unaffected by the spell and saved Kull's life, at the cost of his own as he was enveloped and digested by the mass. It then tried to consume Kull whom killed the abomination.

The Crawling Ones are a fictional race developed by Chaosium in 1994 for their Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. They were based on entities which appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Festival," written in 1923.

### Overview
In past times, good folks were wise to burn the bodies of evil wizards, lest their "essential fats" be eaten and consumed by grave worms and the like. As Lovecraft notes in "The Festival", such worms may be "instructed" and form corruption "horrid life springs". Which is to say, the consciousness of a dead wizard or witch could be consumed (when laid to rest) by worms, maggots, and other crawling things, imprinting the wizard's mind upon them and creating a new form of life intent on carrying on the ambitions of dead wizard. Thus, a crawling one is a union of such creatures, forming a human-like mass, able to disguise itself to pass as human and work its malign intent. The "ingested" will of the wizard effectively drives the mass to work collectively to perform deeds and actions. 

Despite their ghastly appearance, a Crawling One is not undead, for the worms that compose its form are living creatures. While the injuries it suffers may kill individually roaches or spiders, this merely inconveniences the "whole" monster, as over time the vermin breed replacements.

Normally, Crawling Ones cannot speak but can use tools, and, thereby, write messages - some may use magical means to create a voice with which to communicate, and are able to learn or remember differing languages. It is unnecessary for crawling ones to use spoken words in performing spells or when communing with their alien overseers or creatures from beyond. In many cases, Crawling Ones are driven to continue the work of their "forbear" wizards, which could be magical experimentation, the adoration of Mythos Gods, or the culmination of a horrific ritual that in life they were unable to complete.

### Summary
Thousands of maggots and worms make up a Crawling One. Each of the squirming creatures is individually alive and is constantly moving, though the general shape of a human is maintained. Because of the soft resilient quality of the body they create, normal weapons inflict the most minimum of damage.

Crawling ones are unable to speak but they are capable of writing messages. They are all able to use magic and in close combat they use hand-held weapons as they are unable to make physical attacks.

Creatures & Cultists, which features the tagline The Furiously Fuggly Card Game is a card-based combat game centred on the Cthulhu Mythos established by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview
Created by Jeff Barber and John Tynes with supplementary material by Dennis Detwiller and Jonathan Tweet, Creatures & Cultists featured card art by J. Todd Kingrea. It was issued as a book containing rules and player sheets, with the cards themselves needing to be cut out after purchase.

Gameplay involves each player assembling a cult which they then use to battle other cults. Once a set number of points have been achieved through winning battles, the player may then attempt to summon their dark god and win the game.

### Publication History
First appearing in 1990 in issue #4 of Mythos gaming magazine The Unspeakable Oath, at that time edited by John Tynes, Creatures & Cultists was later released through Tynes' label Pagan Publishing as a stand-alone game in 1993. It is currently out of print.

Creighton Capshaw is a fictional character created by American author Brandon Berntson for his Lovecraft Mysteries trilogy of Cthulhu Mythos stories. He made his debut appearance in the first book in the series, 2018's The Night of Dagon.

### Description
The curator of Innsport's Natural History Museum, Capshaw is described as "a short, portly man with a salt and pepper beard and mustache" with "tiny round spectacles on a boyish, cherubic face … his eyes … beady but bright blue."

Capshaw has an inveterate interest in ancient artefacts, which is likely what brought him to the academic position which he holds in the series.

### History
Before the events of The Lovecraft Mysteries, Capshaw had been a long-time friend of the wealthy antiquarian Mordred Haddonfield, but over the years their relationship deteriorated into a bitter rivalry. At the beginning of the series, Capshaw's museum came into possession of the Silver Bluebell, also known as the Shadow of Dagon. Haddonfield, by this time a devoted cultist of that dark god, hired private eye Devlin Macky to steal the artefact from Capshaw's office (EXP: The Night of Dagon).

After Macky realised his deadly mistake and put an end to the threat to the world, Capshaw destroyed the Shadow and dumped its remains into the deep blue sea, despite the - possibly supernatural in nature - longing he felt to keep it for himself (EXP: The Night of Dagon).

When Macky accidentally initiated a plot to bring about the return of the Outer Gods, Capshaw travelled through time and space and witnessed the fall of the fabled city of Sarnath; he later again crossed dimensions and assisted in closing the portals which would allow the Outer Gods and their minions to destroy the human race (EXP: The Lurker at the Threshold).

### Appearances
*The Night of Dagon (2018)
*The Lurker at the Threshold (2021)

The Crimson Desert is a region in southern Yemen, Arabia, famous for the blood-red local sand and the gory legends invented to explain the landscape's appearance. The region is called Abyan, or Abyan of the Crimson Sands. The scientific explanation for the red sand is that it is basically dust composed of iron oxide, but local folklore insists that a great war was once fought there resulting in so much spilled blood that it is still welling up and discoloring the ground.

This location is referred to in the H. P. Lovecraft and Adolphe de Castro collaboration "The Last Test".

The Crimson King is a Lovecraftian-like demonic entity in the fictional universe of the Dark Tower horror novels by Stephen King.

### Background
The Crimson King is a demonic entity born from chaos, born from a union between a human male and the Crimson Queen, a female elder demon of the primordial "Prim". His goal is to destroy the multiverse by taking down the Dark Tower, so he can remake the multiverse in his image. Due to a prophecy stating that he will be one day killed, he becomes increasingly paranoid and insane as time goes on. He had a variety of powers, including telekinesis, shapeshifting, necromancy, elemental powers, dark magic, weather control, and the "Deadlights" (an eldritch type of energy).

Crom Cruach (The Bloody Crooked One) is a god from Irish mythology, an inspiration for Robert E. Howard's fictional Cimmerian god Crom. Crom Cruach himself was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Brian McNaughton in his novel Downward to Darkness.

Chaosium has also featured the entity in its role-playing games. Laurence J. Cornford suggested the connection to Pan and other similar gods as the public face of Crom.

### Description
Crom Cruach is presented as a giant worm or dragon-like creature. A god mentioned in Dr. Dee's Necronomicon as a lesser concubine (or facet?) of Shub-Niggurath, Crom Cruach is said to lie under Stonehenge. His cult believe him to be all-knowing. According to the Necronomicon, Crom Cruach can grant eternal life to its worshippers in a ritual involving the sacrifice of human infants. 

In the Hyborian Age, the grim god Crom (who is probably the “public face” of Crom Crauch) was worshipped in Cimmeria. Later he was worshiped by the Celts in Ireland. It's said that its worship was ended by St. Patrick, who destroyed the cult sign with a hammer. It posed as a pre-christian deity to obtain the souls of children and deceived his followers.

Sources connect Crom Cruach with Pan (which allegedly means "feeder") in ancient Greece. Also called "The Horned Ram," "Khnum," "The Lord of the Wood" (possibly this is also a name for Nyarlathotep/Ahtu?) and "Delcarnon" ("Lord of the Two Horns").

shortDefinition: "Crossing Stars" is a short story by author and games designer M. J. Newman. Taking place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror iteration of the Cthulhu Mythos, it was published in the thematic anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022...
fullContent:
"Crossing Stars" is a short story by author and games designer M. J. Newman. Taking place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror iteration of the Cthulhu Mythos, it was published in the thematic anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022.

### Synopsis
Professor Luciana Diallo, a historian at the University of Barcelona, is recruited by a mysterious woman who gives her name only as Amaranth. En route to their destination, Amaranth relates to Diallo the story of the 11th century sorcerer Razin Farhi and his consort Haresah Izem as they sought out a kisra, one of many "mysterious relics left behind by those who came before."

Travelling to the deep desert on a tip from their scouts, Farhi and Izem located a subterranean cave complex protected by living vines and the meat puppets created by the poor unfortunates who had previously succumbed to their attentions. Fighting their way past these threats, the group finally entered the central cavern, where the vines' controlling intelligence dwelt. Although Izem was successful in claiming the sentient flower from its resting place, her entire party was killed, and in the aftermath the flower bonded with Izem, claiming her memories and body for itself.

After finishing her story, Amaranth reveals that she is the sentient flower, and has survived the centuries by claiming a new human body whenever her old one wears out. However, her memories of Izem's enduring love for Farhi have compelled her to seek out his desiccated corpse so that the two may spend eternity together, a task for which she requires Diallo's assistance - whether the professor is willing to assist or not…

### Mythos Connections
Aside from the Arkham Horror milieu, "Crossing Stars" mentions that Izem and Farhi are members of a "scarletbound cabal," which would suggest that they belong to a historical version of the Red Coterie, a mystical organisation which features as a recurrent element in the setting. Although it is not directly stated in the story, it is implied (through numerous mentions of her attire and the accoutrements of her entourage) that Amaranth retains at least some affiliation with the group.

At one point during their quest, when faced with a horde of living dead, Farhi casts a spell to incinerate their enemies. Part of his invocation includes the line "Cthugha, The Living Flame, Kathigu-Ra; Fthaggua, Seeker of Fire; Aphoom-Zhah, burning progeny."

### References

Crossroad Press is a United States-based horror and science fiction publisher formed in 2009 as Macabre Ink Digital by David Niall Wilson. It publishes re-releases of out of print horror classics, audiobooks from individuals such as Clive Barker and Brian Lumley, as well as new releases from independent authors. It has produced numerous Cthulhu Mythos and Lovecraftian works over its history, including the Titus Crow series of audiobooks, CT Phipps' Cthulhu Armageddon, the Harry Stubbs series, Andrew Doran books, and the Books of Cthulhu anthologies. Its non-Lovecraft related works include re-publishing the Stargate SG-1 series and Vampire: The Masquerade novels.

fullContent:
"Crouch End" is a short story by popular horror writer Stephen King.

### Synopsis
Young couple Lonnie and Doris Freeman are on their way to a dinner party when they find themselves lost in the London suburb of Crouch End, a place where the barriers between dimensions has been rubbed thin. As they make their way through an increasingly-bizarre world, Lonnie is taken by a nightmarish creature, while Doris barely manages to escape with her life.

### Characters
*Leonard "Lonnie" Freeman, a young lawyer.
*Doris Freeman, Lonnie's wife.
*PC Robert Farnham, an officer at the Crouch End police station.
*PC Ted Vetter, a veteran officer assigned to the station.

### Publication History
First published by Arkham House in New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in 1980, "Crouch End" was later included in a slightly edited version in King's own collection Nightmares and Dreamscapes in 1993.

### Mythos Connections
*Several Mythos entities are made reference to, including Cthulhu Kryon (Cthulhu), Yogsoggoth (Yog-Sothoth) and Nrtesn Nyarlahotep (Nyarlathotep). Lonnie is heavily implied to have been taken by The Goat with a Thousand Young (Shub-Niggurath).
*Cthulhu's resting place of R'yeleh (R'lyeh) is mentioned.
*A sign on a decaying warehouse reads Alhazred, a clear reference to Abdul Alhazred, the crazed author of the Necronomicon.

### Adaptations
*An audiobook version of Nightmares & Dreamscapes was released with a reading of "Crouch End" by actor Tim Curry.
*The story was adapted into an episode of Nightmares and Dreamscapes: From the Stories of Stephen King by television network TNT.

### Trivia
*H. P. Lovecraft himself is mentioned by PC Vetter when he is explaining the nature of dimensions to Farnham.
*Crouch End is a real life location in north-west London described as an "urban village." It was voted best place to live in London in 2023.

### References

Crouch End is an episode of Nightmares & Dreamscapes: From the Stories of Stephen King, and is based on King's short work of the same name.

### Synopsis
A young American couple on their way to a colleague's dinner party become stranded in the seemingly-idyllic London suburb of Crouch End. However, Crouch End is a place where the barriers between dimensions have rubbed thin, and as their sanity begins to unravel, the husband is snatched by a horror from the beyond.

### Characters

*Lonnie Frehman, a successful lawyer.
*Doris Frehman, Lonnie's wife.
*Archibald, a London cab driver.

### Behind the Mythos
Crouch End is based on the Stephen King short story of the same name, and remains largely faithful to the original, the main deviation being the removal of the police officers as a source of exposition, this being left to the character of Archie the cab driver. Lonnie's ultimate fate is also given an additional twist, as he is apparently transformed into one of Crouch End's cats, rather than being simply swallowed by the eldritch entity.

The episode was released by TNT in July 2006 as episode 2 of Nightmares and Dreamscapes: From the Stories of Stephen King. It stars Claire Forlani and Eoin Bailey as Doris and Lonnie Frehman.

### Mythos Connections

*Several Mythos entities are made reference to, including Cthulhu Kryon (Cthulhu), Yogsoggoth (Yog-Sothoth) and Nrtesn Nyarlahotep (Nyarlathotep). Lonnie is heavily implied to have been taken by The Goat with a Thousand Young (Shub-Niggurath).

shortDefinition: "Cruelty" is a short story by American author C. J. Henderson and the first in the Arkham Detective Agency series.  ### Synopsis Private Detective Frank Nardi is called by one of his clients, the world-renowned Miskatonic University, to resolve a sit...
fullContent:
"Cruelty" is a short story by American author C. J. Henderson and the first in the Arkham Detective Agency series.

### Synopsis
Private Detective Frank Nardi is called by one of his clients, the world-renowned Miskatonic University, to resolve a situation involving a mysterious and dangerous stranger who has gained unauthorised access to their Exhibit Museum's new Egyptian display. Despite a horrific encounter which leaves Nardi's partner dead, he manages to secure the safety of the University.

### Characters
*Frank Nardi, a private investigator specialising in supernatural cases.
*Harold Clemmens, the president of Miskatonic University.
*Tony Balnco, one of Frank's partners in the Arkham Detective Agency.
*The Stranger, a magically-powerful interloper with unclear goals.
*The Hacker, a man who gains access to the University's security network.

### Behind the Mythos
Cruelty was written by C. J. Henderson shortly before his death in 2014. It was first published in the compilation Arkham Detective Agency in 2017, and has since also received an ebook release.

### Mythos References
*The story is set in Miskatonic University, Arkham, an institution created by H. P. Lovecraft himself.
*Frank Nardi makes reference to "the enclaves of fishfolk all up and down the Massachusetts coast," a clear nod to the Deep Ones featured in "The Shadow Over Innsmouth."
*Although never explicitly stated, the Stranger is heavily implied to be Nyarlathotep; a man of apparently Middle-Eastern descent, after Nardi calls him "one goat-sucking son'va bitch," the Stranger replies with "Now I suppose I have a thousand and one names."

shortDefinition: Crypt of Cthulhu was a fanzine devoted to the writings of H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published as part of the Esoteric Order of Dagon Amateur Press Association for a short time, and was formally established in 1981 by Robert M. Pr...
fullContent:
Crypt of Cthulhu was a fanzine devoted to the writings of H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published as part of the Esoteric Order of Dagon Amateur Press Association for a short time, and was formally established in 1981 by Robert M. Price, who edited it throughout its subsequent run.

Described by its editor as "a bizarre miscegenation; half Lovecraft Studies rip-off, half humor magazine, a 'pulp thriller and theological journal,'" it was a great deal more than that. Lovecraft scholarship was always a mainstay, with articles contributed by Steve Behrends, Edward P. Berglund, Peter Cannon, Stefan Dziemianowicz, S. T. Joshi, Robert A. W. Lowndes, Dirk W. Mosig, Will Murray, Darrell Schweitzer, Colin Wilson and Price himself. 

The magazine published stories and poems, too: resurrected, newly discovered, or in a few cases newly written, by Lovecraft and other such Weird Tales veterans as R. H. Barlow, Robert Bloch, Hugh B. Cave, August Derleth, C. M. Eddy, Jr., Robert E. Howard, Carl Jacobi, Henry Kuttner, Frank Belknap Long, E. Hoffmann Price, Duane W. Rimel, Richard F. Searight, Clark Ashton Smith, and Wilfred Blanch Talman. It also had stories and poems by newer writers paying tribute to the old, including Ramsey Campbell, Lin Carter, John Glasby, C. J. Henderson, T. E. D. Klein, Thomas Ligotti, Brian Lumley, Gary Myers, and Richard L. Tierney. Several issues were devoted to showcasing one or another of such authors. 

Its contents were illustrated by such artists of the fantastic as Thomas Brown, Jason C. Eckhardt, Stephen E. Fabian, D. L. Hutchinson, Robert H. Knox, Allen Koszowski, Gavin O'Keefe, and Gahan Wilson. Its reviews covered genre books, films and games.

### Publication History
The magazine's initial run encompassed 108 issues over a span of 20 years. The first 75 issues (dated Hallowmas 1981 through Michaelmas 1990), were published by Price under his own Cryptic Publications imprint. The next 26 issues, dated Hallowmas 1990 through Eastertide 1999 and numbered 76 through 101, were published by Necronomicon Press. The next seven issues, dated Lammas 1999 through Eastertide 2001 and numbered 102 through 108, were published by Mythos Books. The covers were illustrated by D. L. Hutchinson.

From 2001 through 2017, the magazine was inactive; it returned from 2017 to 2019 with Price once returning to the helm, and Necronomicon Press again the publisher. This incarnation ran from issue 108 (dated Hallowmas 2017)  to #113 (Lammas 2019). 

In 2022, Price restarted the publication under the aegis of a resurrected Cryptic Publications, starting with #114 (St John's Eve 2022).

### Collections
Material from Crypt of Cthulhu has been republished in two general collections,  The Horror of It All (1990) and Black Forbidden Things (1992), and in a collection of Price's essays, H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos (1990).

Crypt of Cthulhu is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author Jack Ryan. Consisting of four shorts connected by a wraparound story, it was independently published in October 2018. Both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Synopsis
Dr. Gestalt, a supervising physician at Arkham Asylum, is mystified when four of his most promising patients suddenly slump into a catatonic state for no apparent reason. When the mysterious Dr. Ng arrives with a revolutionary device, the two delve into the patients' dreams, witnessing first hand their recurrent nightmares regarding the evil entities Cthulhu, Dagon, Yog-Sothoth, and Nyarlathotep. 

At the story's conclusion it is revealed that Dr. Ng is in fact Nyarlathotep himself, and that accessing the minds of the comatose patients was a way to decipher the clues left by Cthulhu on how to awaken him and the other slumbering gods. Gestalt is able to thwart the Outer God's plans, but must sacrifice his own life to do so.

Crypt of Cthulhu Michaelmas 1983 is the sixteenth issue of Robert M. Price's long-running Lovecraftian fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu. Edited by H. P. Lovecraft scholar Price, it ran to a total of 62 pages in an A5 format and was self-published in September 1983. Cover artwork was supplied by Stephen Fabian, and it featured an interior piece by Jason C. Eckhardt.

The issue was humorously titled Tales from the Crypt of Cthulhu, and the cover was styled in the same manner as the comic book Tales from the Crypt, a horror anthology series popular in the early 1950s. Unusually for earlier issues, it was devoted exclusively to fiction content, with all of the stories coming from authors who had known Lovecraft in some capacity.

shortDefinition: The Cryptic Events Evaluation Section, also known as the Cryptic Events Evaluation Taskforce, is a fictional secret government organization created by writer Will Murray as a backdrop for his Cthulhu Mythos stories. Depicted as part of the real world...
fullContent:
The Cryptic Events Evaluation Section, also known as the Cryptic Events Evaluation Taskforce, is a fictional secret government organization created by writer Will Murray as a backdrop for his Cthulhu Mythos stories. Depicted as part of the real world's National Reconnaissance Office, the CEES is tasked with investigating "events"--"any unexplained or unclassifiable phenomenon"--often using paranormal means.

Murray's stories that feature the CEES form a loosely connected series. He introduced the organization in the story "To Clear the Earth" (1994).

### Behind the Mythos
Murray explained the creation of the CEES (or CEET) in the introduction to the first volume of The Wild Adventures of Cthulhu:For “To Clear the Earth,” I created a secret government agency in the grand tradition of the Man from U.N.C.L.E., Marvel’s S.H.I.E.L.D., and the Destroyer series’ CURE, which was dedicated to thwarting the Great Old Ones in their ongoing efforts to overrun the Earth and replace mankind. I hadn’t planned to create a series around this cadre, the Cryptic Events Evaluation Taskforce, which debuted in “To Clear the Earth” and which soon returned in “Rude Awakening.” But as I was increasingly invited to contribute to various Mythos anthologies, they made excellent protagonists for story purposes. Murray notes that CEES agents tend to have short lifespans, both in-universe and as fictional characters:Since most of the field agents perished during the performance of their duties, I had to create fresh ones to undertake the next foredoomed mission. So no central heroic figure ever emerged. Most often, they were snuffed out by forces greater than they. Appropriately, I think, for a Lovecraftian series.

### Appearances
* "To Clear the Earth" (1994)
* "Rude Awakening" (1995)
* "The Sothis Radiant" (1996)
* "The Eldridge Collection" (2003)
* "What Brings the Void" (2010)
* "The Hour of Our Triumph" (2011)
* "Dark Redeemer" (2015)

Primarily used to publish Lovecraftian fiction and scholarly work in a fanzine format, it also released a handful of science and weird fiction works. shortDefinition: The Crystal Company is a fictional organisation featured in the science fiction short story "In the Walls of Eryx", by H. P. Lovecraft and Kenneth Sterling.  ### Overview In the future, as Earth starships have landed on Venus and discovered the spher...
fullContent:
The Crystal Company is a fictional organisation featured in the science fiction short story "In the Walls of Eryx", by H. P. Lovecraft and Kenneth Sterling.

### Overview
In the future, as Earth starships have landed on Venus and discovered the spheroid crystals, the Crystal Company is the corporation responsible for gathering them and shipping them to the home planet, to tap into the enormous energy they contain. Stationed at the post of Terra Nova (the only human settlement on Venus), the Company sends out lone operatives to locate and bring back the crystals. The native Venusians originally left the humans alone, but turned hostile once they started taking the crystals, which have a religious significance in the Venusian culture. After the discovery of the invisible labyrinth in the plateau of Eryx and the death of operatives Dwight and Stanfield, the Crystal Company decided to employ an army to exterminate the Venusians. (: "In the Walls of Eryx")

### Equipment
Crystal Company operatives are provided with the following equipment:
*Leather suits, worn without any undergarments due to Venus' uncomfortably hot and humid climate.
*Oxygen mask and helmet.
*Crystal-detector.
*Canteen.
*Knife to cut through leathery vegetation.
*Flame pistol to battle the Venusians.
*Electric lamp to see at night.
*A decay-proof record scroll to write logs, made of a thin metallic material that cannot tear.

The masks employed by operatives are of a model known as the Carter oxygen mask, equipped with tubes and an electrolyser that produces oxygen when replenished with potassium chlorate cubes. Operatives are provided with a supply of such cubes, as well as food tablets, which can be slipped through the mask. A similar supply of lacol tablets can also be used to keep a man alive if the canteen is empty, although they've been described as "a poor substitute for water".

Operative Kenton J. Stanfield has commented that the Carter oxygen masks are exceedingly heavy, and offered that "a Dubois mask with sponge-reservoir instead of tubes would give just as good air at half the weight". The reasons why the Company prefers to use Carter masks over Dubois masks are unknown.

### Known Operatives
*Anderson
*Bailey
*Frederick N. Dwight
*Koenig
*Markheim
*Wesley P. Miller
*Kenton J. Stanfield

### Trivia
*Other characters who may of may not be affiliated with the Crystal Company include the pilot Matsugawa, who mapped the plateau of Eryx 50 years before the story is set; and the scientists Fogg, Ekberg, and Janat, who proposed the idea that the movement of the Venusians' two pairs of pectoral tentacles serves as a form of communication.

The Crystals of the Elder Things are fictional artefacts in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were created by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu RPG (which book?). They are described as containers constructed to harness power. (: Call of Cthulhu)

### Description
The Elder Things constructed large crystalline storage containers to store magical power so that they can then be used to bind shoggoths to their will. Only the Elder Things have the knowledge and ability to imbue them with magical power, but other creatures may access the power inside by becoming attuned to the vibrations of the crystal when in contact. (: Call of Cthulhu)

In their dormant state, the crystals remain at ambient temperature, but the more magical power they store inside, the colder they become. (: Call of Cthulhu)

The Crystallizers of Dreams are fictional artefacts in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were first mentioned in "The Render of the Veils" by Ramsey Campbell and then expanded by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu RPG. They are described as being able to transport the consciousness of a person to another dimension. (: "The Render of the Veils")

### Description
A Crystallizer looks like a yellow egg having a diameter of about a foot. It periodically emits a strange intermittent whistling (: "The Render of the Veils"). It sounds hollow when tapped and looks fragile, but actually weights about twenty pounds. The Crystallizers require no magical source and automatically act on the closest person sleeping near them within ten yards. (: The Keeper's Companion)

If a person sleeps near a Crystallizer, the consciousness of that person will automatically be transported to distant lands such as Yuggoth and Tond, the Dreamlands, or even other dimensions (: "The Render of the Veils"). The dreams are so realistic, the dreamers can even interact with that world, bring back items to his or her own world, or even be killed in the dreams (: The Keeper's Companion).

The Crystallizers of Dreams belong to the Elder God Hypnos and are not intended to be used by anyone but him, so there is a 10% chance of attracting his attention anytime someone uses a Crystallizer. Once noticed, Hypnos will send the guardians of the Crystallizers of Dreams to retrieve the Crystallizers and severely punishes the users by trapping their souls forever in the court of Hypnos, never to be awakened again. (: The Keeper's Companion)

### In the Mythos
The Crystallizers of Dreams are mentioned in both the Necronomicon (: "The Render of the Veils") and The Revelations of Glaaki (: "The Inhabitant of the Lake").

The Cthäat Aquadingen (trans. Things of the Water) is a fictional grimoire created by British author Brian Lumley.

### Overview
A combination of occult reference work and spell book, the Cthäat Aquadingen has a focus on entities associated with water, and Ubbo-Sathla in particular. It is unknown who penned the original text, but since its first appearance in Germany around 400 AD, a number of translations have surfaced including a Latin version in the 11th or 12th century and a Middle English one in the 1300s.

It was possibly first written at least partially in R'lyehian.

In the Demonbane Mythos, Caligula owns a copy that he uses to pilot Kraken. (: Deus Machina Demonbane) Although it does not appear in the actual series, an official illustration depicts his grimoire as taking the form of a human girl. (similarly to Al Azif, Etheldreda and the R'lyeh Text)

### Known Contents

*Lengthy discourses on the Great Old Ones Bugg-Shash and Yibb-Tstll.
*A series of rituals and spells concerning Ubbo-Satthla.
*Instructions on how to create an Elder Sign.

Cthaeghya is a fictional entity created by Kevin L. O'Brien for his short story "October Surprise", depicting the character as the sister of Cthulhu and responsible for spawning the Cthulhi.

### Background
According to The Book of Merlin, Cthaeghya was birthed by the Outer God known as Cxaxukluth on a black star in the center of a grand nebula, along with her brothers Ghizguth, Hzioulquoigmnzhah and Rahb, and their sisters Zstylzhemghi and Klosmiebhyx. Cthaeghya and her family journeyed to Yuggoth, where Rahb mated with the infertile Cthaeghya. They were forced to flee when Cxaxukluth began feeding off its progeny, with Cthaeghya and Rahb fleeing to Xoth. There, Rahb began mating with Idh-yaa, who bore his three sons: Ghatanothoa, Ythogtha and Zoth-Ommog. In a fit of rage, Cthaeghya destroyed Idh-yaa and then headed towards Magmhel.  

During their attack on Xoth, the Elder Beings managed to kidnap Rahb, with his sons escaping to Magmhel in order to tell Cthaeghya about their father's capture. Journeying to Xoth, Cthaeghya successfully freed Rahb; however, the servitors of the Elder Beings followed them back to Magmhel, leading to the destruction of the planet and Rahb being caught again, with Cthaeghya and the Sons of Rahb fleeing to nearby Aihai. The servitors split Rahb into two, creating Cthulhu and Hastur; the latter of which was imprisoned on a dark world in the Hyades. Cthulhu was in the keeping of Ousir and his company, until the servitors betrayed Ousir, allowing Cthulhu to escape. 

Fleeing to Aihai, Cthulhu was reunited with Cthaeghya, while still weakened by the division. Taking pity on him, Cthaeghya gave the greater portion of her power to Cthulhu, who preceded to rape her, resulting in Cthaeghya giving birth to their servitors known as the Cthulhi, the spawn of Cthulhu. Eventually arriving in the world of man, on the ancient landmass of Mu, Cthaeghya ruled over the lost continent Lemuria, until the cosmological cycles of this universe forced her to fall into a state of hibernation. Placed in a tomb, Cthaeghya laid dormant in a submarine mountain drowned beneath the Pacific Ocean. Blocking the opening, a grouping of massive stone blocks, which formed the Elder Sign, was placed on top of a huge plug, preventing Cthaeghya from being freed.

About 286 million years later, Abigail Dexter detonated a nuclear weapon that cracked the Elder Sign, releasing Cthaeghya from her imprisonment, causing people all over the world to go insane. Abigail's goal was to use Cthaeghya in order to free Cthulhu and the other Old Ones, allowing them to ravage the world and eventually destroy the entire universe; however, Cthaeghya and her allies seemingly left humanity alone, waiting until the split between Cthulhu and Hastur is healed, which would reform Rahb and restore their knowledge to a complete state. (: "October Surprise")

Finally fed up with the bullying and abuse, she decides she will do anything to make herself normal. Emi Lenox's return to the Black Hammer World! Ties directly into the Eisner-Award winning Black Hammer comic books series and is written by Jeff Lemire.Cthu-Louise is a half-human hybrid, the spawn of a possessed emissary of Cthulhu and a human. Surreally, she goes to school as if a normal teen school girl but is relentlessly mocked due to her bizarre appearance. Cthu-Louise struggles about being teased at school due to her monstrous appearance. Finally fed up with the bullying and abuse, she decides she will do anything to make herself "normal." The tension comes from her being relatively normal in outlook but driven to extreme methods in a comic book universe where not only malevolent Mythos gods exist but many other powerful and countervailing self interested cosmic forces.

Cthugha (also known as The Living Flame) is a fictional deity in the Cthulhu Mythos. Originally created by August Derleth, the character was first mentioned in his short story "The House on Curwen Street" (1943) but did not appear until "The Dweller in Darkness" (1944).

### Background
Cthugha is one of the Great Old Ones that opposes the Elder Gods. As the elemental spirit of fire, Cthugha takes the form of a giant fireball located near Fomalhaut, who is served by the Flame Creatures. The entity can be summoned to Earth if the chant "Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthugha Fomalhaut n'gha-ghaa naf'l thagn! Iä! Cthugha!" is repeated three times when Fomalhaut appears over the horizon. Laird Dorgan summoned Cthugha to destroy an avatar of Nyarlathotep in the Wood of N'gai, a forest in northern Wisconsin. (: "The Dweller in Darkness")

Other writers have contributed to the lore of Cthugha. In John Glasby's short story, Cthugha was sealed away in Korvaz, a small star in the vicinity of Fomalhaut. (: "The Black Mirror") However, in the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game, Korvaz is depicted as just being another name for Fomalhaut itself. (: Delta Green) In The Stars Are Right!, André Bishop depicted the Zoroastrian prophet Nestar Mobedan Mobed as the leader of a cult to Cthugha during the 6th century AD. Although the cult seemingly died out after Nestar was killed, the surviving members have continued to maintain their activities in secret, with their goal to summon Cthugha in San Francisco and engulf the entire city in flame. (: "This Fire Shall Kill") In The Unbound Book, Bret Kramer introduced an Egyptian cult that worshipped Cthugha, under the name Kathigu-Ra. (: "Baggage Check") In one of his essays, Richard L. Tierney also speculated that Cthugha may be equated with Huehueteotl, the fire-god of the Aztecs. (: "Cthulhu in Mesoamerica") In C. T. Phipps' novel series, Cthugha is mentioned and characterized as being a "living sun". (: Cthulhu Armageddon)

Aphoom-Zhah is the offspring of Cthugha, who was worshipped as a god in Hyperborea. (: "The Acolyte of the Flame") Fthaggua, regent of the Fire Vampires, may also have a connection to Cthugha. Although it is not entirely clear, it has been speculated that Fthaggua is either a servant or an avatar of Cthugha. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)
