The Cthulhi (also known as the Cosmic Octopi, Star-spawn of Cthulhu, and as Xothians) are a species that have a physical similarity with their leader, the Great Old One known as Cthulhu, but are of far smaller size. They came to Earth at some point in the Paleozoic Era and have been known to make war against the Elder Things. Despite their cephalopod appearance, they are actually land-based, not aquatic, and built their cities on dry land before they were sunk by a cataclysm. (: At the Mountains of Madness / : "Papyrus of the Dark Wisdom", Lin Carter)

### Description
Initially described as "a land race of beings shaped like octopi and probably corresponding to the fabulous pre-human spawn of Cthulhu," (: At the Mountains of Madness) the Star-Spawn are also described as being "composed of matter more widely different" than that which is native to our universe. And their physicality so malleable that they might to some small degree be called shapeshifters, for "They were able to undergo transformations and reintegrations impossible for the Elder Things."

This aspect is even contrasted against the Elder Things descriptions as "strictly material" and native to "the known space-time continuum", implying an origin with perhaps vastly different governing laws of nature to limit the Star-Spawn.

### History
Originating on the planet Xoth (: "Papyrus of the Dark Wisdom"), it's said that the Star-Spawn came to Earth from an unknown region of space and began to wage war against the Elder Things, which already had been inhabiting the Earth. After an unknown period of time, peace was established between the two races, with the Star-Spawn retaining all the exposed lands and the Elder Things retreating to inhabit all the oceans of the Earth. (: At the Mountains of Madness)

The R'lyehian language was brought to Earth by the Star-spawn of Cthulhu. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

After a period of peace and apparent prosperity during which many cities were built, the lands on which the Star-Spawn cities had been built sank into the sea for reasons unknown, including the city of R'lyeh, at which time all the Star-Spawn present on Earth either perished or went into a death-like sleep similar to their apparent forebearer Cthulhu (in "The Call of Cthulhu", it's stated that the Great Old Ones could not live while the stars were wrong). It is unclear at this point whether Cthulhu was present at the time when R'lyeh sank, or if he joined it at the bottom of the ocean some later time. Cthulhu is a fictional cosmic entity created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Call of Cthulhu". First appearing in the February 1928 issue of the pulp magazine Weird Tales, he is depicted as an octopoid Great Old One of enormous power who lies in a death-like slumber in his sunken city of R'lyeh beneath the Pacific Ocean. He is the namesake and the best-known element of the Cthulhu Mythos, appearing in the works of numerous authors following Lovecraft and frequently referenced in popular culture.

### Description
The most detailed descriptions of Cthulhu are based on statues of the creature. One, constructed by the young artist Henry Anthony Wilcox after a series of baleful dreams, is said to have "yielded simultaneous pictures of an octopus, a dragon, and a human caricature [...] A pulpy, tentacled head surmounted a grotesque and scaly body with rudimentary wings." Cthulhu is a 2007 film loosely inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth. The film is notable for having a gay protagonist, exploring LGBTQ themes seriously for the first time in a film with a Cthulhu Mythos backdrop.

### Synopsis
A young college professor returns to his small seaside hometown after the death of his mother. There, he discovers that his father, the leader of a mysterious cult, is engaged in bringing about the return of an ancient deity named Cthulhu. As people begin to disappear, he discovers that preparations are being made to enact a ritual, and while he is tempted by the cult, his sexuality offers him some small protection against their charms. Ultimately, however, he is forced to choose between the man he loves and his father.

### Behind the Mythos
Cthulhu was directed by Dan Gildark, who co-wrote the screenplay with Grant Cogswell. It premiered at the Seattle Film Festival on 14 June 2007. Filmed on an estimated budget of $750,000, it was a commercial flop. It received mixed reviews, with a 62 percent fresh score from Rotten Tomatoes and an average rating of 41 (out of 100) from Metacritic.

### Mythos Connections
*The protagonist's family name in this version of The Shadow Over Innsmouth is Marsh.
*At one point in the film, while Russell is speaking to Zadok, a yacht named the Alert can be seen moored in the background. The Alert was a ship crewed by members of the Cthulhu Cult in "The Call of Cthulhu".
*At another point, an image of an octopoid creature is clearly visible on a manhole cover, an obvious nod to Cthulhu himself.

### Sexuality
Critic Bobby Derie calls Cthulhu, which explores a gay subtext sometimes seen in The Shadow Over Innsmouth, a film with "a lot of firsts for Cthulhu cinema: the first homosexual protagonist, and the first film to make a character’s sexuality an important aspect of the narrative." Cthulhu Armageddon is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by C. T. Phipps, and the first in his series of Cthulhu Armageddon. It was published by Crossroad Press in 2016.

### Overview


### Synopsis
The world has been destroyed by the rising of the Great Old Ones and turned into a monster-filled wasteland. Even the laws of physics and time no longer obey the same rules as they did before. The story follows John Henry Booth and his companion, Mercury Takahashi, after they are exiled from their post-apocalypse city-state New Arkham. John survived the destruction of his squad of New Arkham Rangers only to be branded a monster due to the suspicious nature of his loss. Having nothing left, John proceeds to track down the mysterious Black Cathedral in hopes of discovering who killed his companions and gaining the only thing he has left: revenge.
### Characters

*John Henry Booth - A New Arkham Ranger of African American descent. He is a soldier trained in Wasteland survivor with an extensive history of fighting supernatural entities. He bears the Mark of Nyarlathotep on his left soldier.
*Mercury Takahashi - A medical doctor forced to perform interrogations and torture for the government of New Arkham, she flees after murdering her abusive husband. She later takes an interest in sorcery, believing herself already doomed for her actions.
*Alan Ward - A former New Arkham scientist and scholar of the occult, he has taken to practicing Wasteland sorcery and become leader of the local branch of the Cult of Cthulhu.

### Mythos Creatures
*Byakhee - A powerful interstellar predator that threatens the protagonists.
*Deep One - Human fish hybrids that now live in Kingsport as gangsters.
*Dhole - A giant extra-dimensional worm.
*Elder Thing - A pre-human race of advanced aliens that have since fled to the Dreamlands.
*Ghoul - A race of doglike humanoids that are not particularly hostile to humanity.
*Nyarlathotep - The messenger of the Other Gods who has a strange interest in John.
*Shoggoth - A protoplasmic shapeshifting creature.

### Behind the Mythos
Cthulhu Armageddon was first published in 2016 by Crossroad Press.

fullContent:
Cthulhu Britannica is an adventure sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game.

### Overview
Containing five stand-alone scenarios set in England, Cthulhu Britannica covers a range of time periods, from the height of the British empire in the Victorian era through to the far future. Each scenario was contributed by a different author and comes complete with player handouts and a set of pre-generated characters to allow for quick-start games. The book runs to 172 pages in total and was available in both hardback and paperback editions.

### Contents
*"Bad Company" Bad Company concerns a missing son of a peer of the realm. The investigators must watch their step as they descend into a Victorian world of greed, insane desire and death.
*"Darkness, Descending" Darkness, Descending takes place in the 1930s amongst the splendid greenery of the English countryside. Archaeologists come to unearth relics from Britain's dawn find themselves at the centre of strange goings on. A simple case of theft? Or the foreshadowing of something far darker to come?
*"Wrong Turn" Wrong Turn is a contemporary tale set in a long abandoned radio telescope installation. A television production crew must spend the night amidst the cobwebs and dust. The investigators would be advised to tread carefully lest they wake the ghosts of the past, present and future.
*"King" King takes place in the near future at the private hospital. The investigators awake from surgery to realise that in the kingdom of the blind the one eyed man is king.
*"My Little Sister Will Make You Suffer!" Set during the end of days in an insane future is My Little Sister Will Make You Suffer! In a galaxy gone mad, where cruelty and entertainment go hand in hand, the investigators must run the gauntlet if they are not to meet their end.

### Publication History
Cthulhu Britannica was published by third-party content provider Cubicle 7 Entertainment in 2009, but is currently out of print.

fullContent:
Cthulhu by Gaslight is a supplement for Chaosium's popular roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu. 

### Overview
Giving options for play in Victorian England, Cthulhu by Gaslight was first published as a boxed set in 1986. It included details of all aspects of life during Victorian times, a map of London, character sheets and a complete period-appropriate adventure, The Yorkshire Horror. 

A second edition was released in 1989, this time in book-only format. This release saw the addition of an article on world politics of the era, extra maps and a guide to cockney slang, amongst other things. 

In 2012, a third edition was released, edited by Kevin Ross and featuring additional content by Ross, Scott David Aniolowski, Dave Hallett and Glyn White. As noted in the introduction to the third edition, this saw the book expanded by almost 50%, losing most of the Sherlock Holmes material and adding new material about the Victorian world, crime, politics, personalities and more, including new sections on the Cthulhu Mythos in Britain (such as Ramsey Campbell's Severn Valley setting) and a gazetteer of British myths and legends. The third edition also included two new scenarios, "The Night of the Jackals" by Kevin Ross and "The Burnt Man" by Richard Watts. First released in print, it is currently only available in PDF and ebook formats. 

A fourth edition of Cthulhu by Gaslight was published for Chaosium's 7th edition Call of Cthulhu in 2024, starting with the Cthulhu by Gaslight: Investigators Guide, released globally on 20 November 2024 after pre-release copies were made available at a number of gaming conventions. The latest edition was written by Keris McDonald and Mike Mason with contributors including William A. Barton and Kevin Ross, and provides expanded information about the British class structure (including playing working class investigators), information about death and mourning in the Victorian age, LGBTQI+ life in the Victorian age, and science, pseudoscience and the occult. The Gaslight Investigators' Guide also expands the game setting to include the British Empire and the USA in the Gaslight period, with an appendix summarising the 7th edition Call of Cthulhu rules to facilitate game play in the setting. An accompanying Cthulhu by Gaslight Keepers' Guide is due for release in early 2025.

The Cthulhu Companion is a Call of Cthulhu supplement from roleplaying games manufacturer Chaosium.

### Overview
A compilation of articles from a wide variety of writers, the Cthulhu Companion contains additional skills, details on prison systems of the 1930s world, an expansion of the Sanity condition, a selection of gods and monsters, and three ready-to-play scenarios. Along with poetry by H. P. Lovecraft himself, it features cover art by Chris Marrinan.

### Publication History
First released in 1983, the Cthulhu Companion has since gone out of print, but is currently available as a digital PDF download direct from Chaosium.

The Cthulhu Cult, alternately referred to as the Cult of Cthulhu, are the mortal worshipers of the Great Old One Cthulhu.

### Origin & Beliefs
The cult believes that their worship will one day result in the return of Cthulhu, and that when he awakens they will be able to throw all notions of morality and compassion aside, transforming the world into a landscape of violence and bloodshed. They claim to possess carven idols given to them by the Great Old Ones in times long forgotten, and their high priests use these to keep the memories of their masters alive.

### Organisation
According to a Louisiana cult elder named Castro, he had "talked with undying leaders of the cult in the mountains of China." He believed that "the centre" of the cult, however, "lay amid the pathless deserts of Arabia, where Irem, the City of Pillars, dreams hidden and untouched." Small "cells" of the cult exist in remote parts of the world; many of their members are seamen who travel from port to port, and thus can be found in nearly any location.

Several cells have been identified by both the authorities and individual investigators, and for the most part their members appear to be humans, although often they are deformed from extended interbreeding, and possibly their spiritual closeness to their god.

### Greenland
Discovered by Professor Webb of the American Archaeological Society in 1860 on the west coast of Greenland, this group were described as a group of "diabolist Eskimos". They were feared and reviled by the other tribes of the area.

### Louisiana
Hidden away in the backwoods of Louisiana, these deformed humans came to the attention of Inspector Legrasse of the New Orleans police after reports surfaced of the disappearance of several locals. The cult was smashed by law enforcement officers who killed five and captured 47 (two of whom were later hanged) of the estimated 100 worshippers, who were believed guilty of mutilating and sacrificing the abductees in orgiastic rituals to their dark god, represented by a white polypous thing that dwells yet deeper in the swamps.

### The South Pacific
A small group of cultists described as "a curious group of half-castes" with an "evil reputation" operated the Alert, a heavily-armed steam yacht, out of Dunedin, New Zealand. They were all killed when they attacked the crew of the Emma after they refused to comply with the Alerts demands.

### In the Expanded Mythos

* "The Hidden": Scott T. Goudsward's short story depicts a cult who call themselves The Hidden enacting a ritual to awaken Cthulhu.
* Cults of Cthulhu: A sourcebook for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game focused on the Cthulhu Cult in various eras and settings. The book also expands on the undying leaders of the cult, using the collective label, "the Deathless Masters."
*Ghouls of the Miskatonic: Graham McNeill’s novel tells of a Cthulhu

Cthulhu Cultus is a now-defunct American small press horror magazine.

### Overview
Running to a total of 18 sporadically-released issues between 1995 and 2001, Cthulhu Cultus was published by P. Marsh with Tani Jantsang as editor and James Ambuehl as associate editor. Its purview was weird, supernatural and horror fiction, with a particular focus on the Cthulhu Mythos established by H. P. Lovecraft. As Ambuehl himself described it:


While earlier issues consisted of submissions from only a handful of authors - with Jantsang herself providing a significant portion of the content - later editions rectified this, featuring a far more diverse range of talent. Writers whose works were showcased during the course of the zine's run include Robert M. Price, Ran Cartwright, Ron Shiflet and Franklyn Searight.

shortDefinition: The Cthulhu Cycle was a collection of Cthulhu Mythos anthologies published by Chaosium as an accompaniment to their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. Robert M. Price was the series editor, and the editor of many of the individual volumes.  Most of th...
fullContent:
The Cthulhu Cycle was a collection of Cthulhu Mythos anthologies published by Chaosium as an accompaniment to their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. Robert M. Price was the series editor, and the editor of many of the individual volumes.

Most of the books are thematic, focusing on works related to a particular Mythos-related entity, local, or tome; or else collecting the work of a particular author. The series also includes two general Mythos anthologies--one featuring original stories, the other a reprint of a 1976 collection--and an encyclopedia of Mythos-related information.

As of 2023, all of these volumes are out of print.

### Books
*The Hastur Cycle: 13 Tales that Created and Define Dread Hastur, the King in Yellow, Nighted Yuggoth, and Dire Carcosa (October 1993, June 2006)
*Mysteries of the Worm, by Robert Bloch (October 1993)
*Cthulhu's Heirs: Tales of the Mythos for the New Millennium, by Thomas M. K. Stratman, ed. (March 1994)
*The Shub-Niggurath Cycle: Tales of the Black Goat with a Thousand Young (July 1994)
*Encyclopedia Cthuliana , by Daniel Harms (December 1994, June 1998)
*The Azathoth Cycle: Tales of the Blind Idiot God (March 1995)
*The Book of Iod, by Henry Kuttner (May 1995)
*Made in Goatswood: New Tales of Horror in the Severn Valley, by Scott David Aniolowski , ed. (July 1995)
*The Dunwich Cycle: Where the Old Gods Wait (November 1995)
*The Disciples of Cthulhu: Second Revised Edition , by Edward P. Berglund, ed. (February 1996)
*The Cthulhu Cycle: Thirteen Tentacles of Terror (July 1996)
*The Necronomicon: Selected Stories and Essays Concerning the Blasphemous Tome of the Mad Arab (November 1996)
*The Xothic Legend Cycle: The Complete Mythos Fiction of Lin Carter (1997)
*The Nyarlathotep Cycle: The God of a Thousand Forms (May 1997)
*The Innsmouth Cycle: The Taint of the Deep Ones in 13 Tales (February 1998)
*Nameless Cults: The Cthulhu Mythos Fiction of Robert E. Howard (January 2001)

shortDefinition: Cthulhu Dark is a rules-light Lovecraftian tabletop role-playing game by Graham Walmsley. Full rules are available for free on the author's website. It has two small supplements, Cthulhu Dark Tales and Dark Depths, also available for free.  One very ...
fullContent:
Cthulhu Dark is a rules-light Lovecraftian tabletop role-playing game by Graham Walmsley. Full rules are available for free on the author's website. It has two small supplements, Cthulhu Dark Tales and Dark Depths, also available for free.

One very different but very appropriate Mythos element is that there is no combat. If you fight anything you meet in Cthulhu Dark, you die. Rolls are only allowed to hide, or escape. This stands in dramatically stark contrast to the "Dungeons and Dragons but you throw dynamite at Cthulhu" approach of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu.

Another element, one popular in  many cooperative games is that other players can attempt to impose an outcome on your character, unless your character is carrying out a step essential to the adventure. Competing dice rolls resolve the conflict.

Cthulhu Dark is also available to use for writing one's own adventures, after receiving email permission from the author.

shortDefinition: Cthulhu Dark Ages is a horror fiction role-playing game based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set during the 10th Century AD. The game is published by Chaosium and was published in 2003. It was based on an earlier iteration of the game setting ca...
fullContent:
Cthulhu Dark Ages is a horror fiction role-playing game based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set during the 10th Century AD. The game is published by Chaosium and was published in 2003. It was based on an earlier iteration of the game setting called Cthulhu 1000AD by Stephane Gesbert, which was published by German company Pegasus Spiele in a special edition of their magazine, Cthuloide Welten. A new edition of Cthulhu Dark Ages by Chad Bowser and Andi Newton, and now set in Anglo-Saxon England in 950-1050 AD, was published by Chaosium in 2020.

### Setting
The game is set during the Dark Ages, right before the start of the Crusades. It's in a world of superstition, poverty, famine, and disease. Where most men and women are peasants who work the land for their feudal lords, the Church is possibly the most powerful institution in Europe, kings and their feudal lords are vying for power with each other, and barbarians raid their lands and sack their towns. Within it are hidden cults that worship the Great Old Ones or Outer Gods. As the setting introduction notes, the Al Azif has been translated and renamed the Necronomicon in 950 AD meaning that in this period before the Necronomicon becomes proscribed and banned, it is passed around, copied and used. This in turn means that in this setting monstrous beings proliferate, haunting the wilderness environment and awaiting the turn of history to overwhelm humanity.

### Mythos Organizations
Cult of Magna Mater: Which is perhaps 1000s of years old, and can be traced to Rome as far back as 205 BC. Magna Mater (the Great Mother) is worshiped mostly by women. Everywhere that the Romans had a presence, remnants of the once powerful cult exist. Usually the cult builds its temples near caves, where the women will sleep in the hope of being touched by the goddess and given healing powers. In reality the cult is worshipping Shub-Niggurath. It was at the peak of its power during the 1st and 2nd centuries AD. Between the 4th and 10th centuries, they were hunted by the Brothers of Chrysostom, whose monks waged war against them across the empire. Now the cult of Manga Mater is experiencing a resurgence.

The Pastores: It's a fertility cult of pre-Roman and perhaps pre-Celtic ancestry. Which had commerce with K'n-Yan, a subterranean civilization. Like them they worshiped Yig, Tsathoggua, and Shub-Niggurath and received from them breeding stock. Over the millennia the cult survived and intermarried with those who invaded their lands. When they were strong the bred openly and when weak, they hid underground. Eventually their matrons and priests would end up joining the Roman religious establishment, and their nobility ended up intermarrying with Roman aristocracy. When Roman authority collapsed in the 3rd century, the cult revived its open breeding in the slave plantations though it was brought to a halt by Emperor Diocletian. Constantine and the Christian emperors that followed forced its members to fake their con

fullContent:
Cthulhu Dice is a tabletop dice game by Steve Jackson Games inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.



### Overview
A generic dice game with a Mythos skin, players take turns rolling the dice in an effort to remove all of their opponents' sanity, represented by glass beads. The game came packaged with a custom-designed 12-sided dice, 18 glass tokens and a rules sheet. Available accessories included dice in a variety of designs, materials and sizes, and a plush dice bag, but all of these - including the core set - have been discontinued.

Lovecraft and his correspondents; "Cthulhu Universalis", an index of "characters, places, Gods, books, et al.," in such stories;  and the "Librarium Cthulhuvius: Classic Mythos Stories Online", "an online repository of public domain Cthulhu Mythos stories by the first generation of Mythos writers".

The image seen in the infobox has been adopted as something of a mascot for the site.

fullContent:
Cthulhu for President is a satirical political campaign run by Chaosium during the United States presidential elections since 1996. It is known for its slogan "Why settle for the lesser evil?"

### Overview
Begun by Chaosium in 1996 as a marketing campaign, Cthulhu for President has been run in every US presidential election since. The campaign is accompanied by the release of various items of merchandise, including buttons, t-shirts, stickers, mugs, and posters. In 2012, Cthulhu was given a running mate in the form of Dagon.

In 2010, the campaign was held for the Polish presidential elections, and in 2011 for the Spanish general elections.

In 2016, the campaign was endorsed by Mexican filmmaker Guillermo del Toro, while horror writer Stephen King passed comment on a resemblance between one of the candidates' resemblance to the Great Old One.

### Tie-In Game
In 2004, 9th Level Games in association with Chaosium produced a roleplaying party game based on the campaign, where the players attempt to install Cthulhu in the US presidency.

### In Other Media
*In the Robot Chicken episode "The Unnamed One", Cthulhu appears as a presidential candidate. In the segment, Cthulhu promotes his candidacy on The Oprah Show but ends up killing Oprah, after she questioned if he was eligible to run due to him being a resident of R'lyeh. Although the audience is upset at first, Cthulhu wins back the crowd by giving everyone a free car.

### Synopsis
After being kicked out by his parents for spending his whole life lying around sleeping, Cthulhu finds himself a job in fast food joint Burger Czar. Although he is completely unsuited for this type of work, the promise of sexy cultists hanging out in the restaurant, and a liberal dose of mind-control thrown in to boot, ensures the Great Old One steady employment- despite the occasional death which his mind-shattering powers tend to cause in those nearby.

"Cthulhu in the Comics Part One: The Superhero Books" is a short non-fiction work by American authors  James Ambuehl, Boyd E. Pearson and Dan Ross. It was published in the Edward P. Berglund-edited online fanzine Nightscapes in December 1997.

Despite its title, no follow-up articles were ever published.

### Overview
As its title states, the piece offers a brief history of Cthulhu Mythos and Lovecraftian elements in the comic book medium. It is divided into four parts, with the first three being devoted to the DC Comics Company (which is incorrectly stated as being founded by Lovecraft's former literary agent Julius Schwartz), Marvel Comics Group, and independent comics, with a special section devoted to Marvel Comics' occult superhero Dr. Strange.

Cthulhu Invictus is a period setting supplement and sub-game for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Setting
The game takes place in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos, though in the time of the Roman Empire. It mixes the Cthulhu Mythos with the mythology of the ancient Greeks, Romans, Celts, Germans, Egyptians, and so on. With such classical monsters and creatures like the Satyr and Harpy included in the setting along with the monsters and entities of the Cthulhu Mythos. Scenarios run the gamut from conspiracies in the Imperial capital (Rome) to sinister cults in the outskirts of the empire.

Cults that worship the Great Old Ones or Outer Gods may be outlawed and therefore operating underground, or officially tolerated or supported by the Imperial authorities. Barbarian tribes often worship one of the Mythos entities and the cults operate in foreign kingdoms. Orgies and human sacrifice in their name happens both within the cities and on the frontier. Deep Ones trade and interbreed with some of the coastal communities. Outside of the cities, it's the Roman soldiers that investigate and hunt down the cults and do battle with the monsters when encountered or their barbarian worshipers (if they don't get slaughtered first).

### Major Organizations
*Fishmen of Lierganes: It's a fishing village in Hispania on the Mediterranean, whose inhabitants hundreds of year ago made a pact with the Deep Ones. In return for worshipping Dagon and allying with the Deep Ones, they would receive more fish each day than they catch per month. As the years passed, their children began to change. Deep one hybrids eventually outnumbered the untainted. Now they capture women to use as breeding stock and raid Roman trading vessels.
*Daughters of Isolation: Which is an all-female cult in Antioch (a Hellenic colony in modern-day Turkey) whom follow the Great Old One Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her who lives in the caverns below. Twice a month, they wear masks which are made of flayed human skin and wear sheer gowns. The women lure men to the Paradise of Daphne, promising that they will fulfill their most outrageous sexual desires. The orgy is a cover, and three victims are taken underground, whom have been drugged, becoming unable to either speak or move while still being semi-conscious. They are both raped and flayed before being fed to Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her.
*Followers of Dagon: Consists of a hundred humans and deep one hybrids living in Tyre (Phoenicia) who worship Dagon. Underwater caverns and tunnels connect the Mediterranean sea to the temple, which the Deep Ones use to travel to the temple for mating and worship. The Deep One city raids grain shipments from Egypt. From the ships they take slaves and breeding stock, and give salable items (e.g. grain) to the temple which can be sold to human traders.

The Cthulhu Monsters Series is a Japanese Cthulhu Mythos-themed toyline produced by Pogona Toys and released in collaboration with Marmit, designed by special effects artist Tetsuya Yoshida. The line features soft vinyl figures that are approximately in the 10-inch scale. 

The toyline reimagines the Mythos entities as what they would be like if they were depicted in a tokusatsu series.

In 2021, the first wave consisted of Cthulhu, Nyarlathotep, Shub-Niggurath, Azathoth, the Dark Young, and Yog-Sothoth. The figures were available through Marmit's official website. Soon afterward, the black variants of the figures were released later that year.

In 2022, the glow-in-the-dark versions of the figures were released during the Wonder Festival Winter 2022 event. The following year, the glow-in-the-dark figures were temporarily available again during the Graveyard Glow Festival.

fullContent:
|Selected Letters 2.284}}

The Cthulhu Mythos encompasses the shared elements, characters, settings, and themes found in the works of H. P. Lovecraft and several horror fiction writers who are associated with him. Together, they form the mythos that authors writing in the Lovecraftian milieu have used — and continue to use to this day — to craft their stories. The term itself was coined by the writer August Derleth. Although this legendarium is also sometimes called the Lovecraft Mythos, most notably by the Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi, it has long since moved beyond Lovecraft's original conception.

### Development
Robert M. Price, in his essay "H.P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos", sees two stages in the development of the Cthulhu Mythos. The first stage, or the "Cthulhu Mythos proper" as Price calls it, took shape during Lovecraft's lifetime and was subject to his guidance. The second stage occurred under August Derleth, who attempted to categorize and expand the Mythos after Lovecraft's death. Writer Richard L. Tierney later applied the term the "Derleth Mythos" to distinguish between Lovecraft's works and Derleth's later stories.

### The First Stage (The Cthulhu Mythos Proper)
During the latter part of Lovecraft's life, there was much borrowing of story elements among the authors of the "Lovecraft Circle", a clique of writers with whom Lovecraft corresponded. This group included Clark Ashton Smith, Robert E. Howard, Robert Bloch, Frank Belknap Long, Henry Kuttner, August Derleth, Duane W. Rimel, Richard F. Searight and others.

Lovecraft recognized that each writer had his own story-cycle and that an element from one cycle would not necessarily become part of another simply because a writer used it in one of his stories. For example, although Smith might mention "Kthulhut" (Cthulhu) or Iog-Sotôt (Yog-Sothoth) in one of his Hyperborean tales, this does not necessarily mean that Cthulhu is part of the Hyperborean Cycle. Whether or not this is the case is a matter of interpretation. A notable case of an entity being well integrated into another author's story-cycle is Smith's Tsathoggua, which Lovecraft mentioned in no less than 10 stories (one of them unfinished), starting with The Whisperer in Darkness. In his revision of Zealia Bishop's The Mound (1940), Lovecraft effectively connected Smith's creation to his story-cycle by placing Tsathoggua alongside such entities as Tulu, Yig, Shub-Niggurath and Nug and Yeb in subterranean K'n-yan.

Many of the elements of Lovecraft's Mythos were not a cross-pollination of the various story-cycles of the Lovecraft Circle, but were instead deliberately created by each writer to become part of the Mythos — the most notable example being the various arcane grimoires of forbidden lore. So, for example, Robert E. Howard has his character Friedrich von Junzt reading Lovecraft's Necronomicon in "The Children of the Night" (1931) and Lovecraft, in turn, mentions Howard's Unaussprechlichen Kulten in both "Out

Cthulhu Mythos Anthology, which has confusingly also been called Mythos Cthulhu: An Anthology Part One and Mythos Cthulhu Anthologies Book 1, is a collection of short Cthulhu Mythos stories by author Sebastian Greaves. 

### Overview
Containing a total of five short stories and running to 50 pages in length, Cthulhu Mythos Anthology was published on Amazon's digital Kindle platform. It is aimed at readers of the Young Adult level and above.

### Contents
*"Have You Seen the Yellow Sign?"
*"The Eye of Horus"
*"Great Cthulhu"
*"The Blind Idiot Godhead"
*"Nyarlathotep: The Man With No Face"

fullContent:
Audio adaptations of H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos have been made since at least 1945, when "The Dunwich Horror" was adapted for the radio series Suspense. Since then, a number of Lovecraftian works have been turned into audio dramas, including continuing projects to bring the Providence writer's stories to life through sound alone. Many Mythos stories by Lovecraft and others are available as audiobooks, which are not noted here unless otherwise noteworthy.

### Audio

* 19 Nocturne Boulevard: a podcast anthology series by Julie Hoverson that produced a loose audio drama adaptation of the "The Picture in the House" in 2009, and in October 2011 released an adaptation of "The Dunwich Horror" in a 4-part miniseries. Each episode was roughly 30 minutes long.
* The Atlanta Radio Theatre Company, a Georgia-based acting troupe that focuses on the science fiction, horror and fantasy genres, has  adapted several of Lovecraft’s stories into audio dramas in the style of the golden age of radio, and has written original Mythos audio dramas (The Dancer in the Dark and Special Order).
* Caedmon Records, an American recording label that specialises in spoken-word and other literary productions, released three albums in the 1970s featuring Lovecraft works read by British actor David McCallum.
* Catchers: Ben Rock and Bob DeRosa's 2022 audio drama tells the story of two animal control officers - one a rookie, the other on the verge of retirement - who are called in to deal with what is first thought to be a feral dog, but laters turns out to be an infestation of previously-unknown subterranean creatures. A running joke throughout the story is that most people when confronted with the monsters guess them to be aliens, to which one of the main characters will always reply "Not an alien." At one point when this happens, another character responds with "More like a Cthulhu or something," despite the fact that nothing in the (admittedly vague) description of the beasts seems to resemble the Great Old One.
* Dark Adventure Radio Theatre, a project of The H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, has produced numerous audio adaptations of Lovecraft stories, along with a few original Lovecraftian audio dramas.
* Edwards, Colin: The writer and director adapted "The Dunwich Horror" into an "audio horror movie" in 2010 with sound company Savalas. Recorded in 5.1 Surround Sound to essentially create a movie without pictures, it premiered at the Filmhouse cinema in Edinburgh on 23 June 2010 as part of the 64th Edinburgh International Film festival. Edwards was in attendance along with cast members Greg Hemphill, Innes Smith and Vivien Taylor and sound designer Kahl Henderson.
* HorrorBabble is an indie production company dedicated to creation of audio horror, including recordings of classic stories by writers like Lovecraft and Algernon Blackwood, and original weird audio dramas.

Comic books and manga have frequently been influenced by H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos. Some comics have adapted Lovecraft or other Mythos writers' works, more or less faithfully; other projects have been original works set in a Mythos or Mythos-adjacent universe. Other graphic stories have Lovecraftian themes without directly referencing the Mythos, while other times comics creators drop Mythos names as an homage to Lovecraft.

### Comic Books

### John Coulthart
British artist John Coulthart has created several Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos works, including:
* The Call of Cthulhu (1988): published in The Starry Wisdom in 1994.
* The Haunter of the Dark (1988)
* The Dunwich Horror (1989): unfinished adaptation published in 1999.

### DC Comics
*Arkham Asylum: Living Hell: Cthugha (also known as the "Arbiter of Hell") appears in issue #6, taking the form of a squid-like entity who speaks in rhyme.
*Batman: Arkham Asylum is the name of a heavily fortified insane asylum located on the outskirts of Gotham City in the various Batman media. There are also the video games Batman: Arkham Asylum, Batman: Arkham Origins, Batman: Arkham City, and Batman: Arkham Knight. In the DC universe, it was run by the Arkham family, namely Amadeus Arkham, giving it its name.
*Batman: The Doom That Came to Gotham (2000; Mike Mignola): an Elseworlds story which combines the character Batman with various elements of the Cthulhu Mythos, and takes its name from "The Doom that Came to Sarnath".
*Batman/Aliens II (December 2002-February 2003): Ian Edginton and Staz Johnson's 3-issue crossover miniseries features a man obsessed with life beneath the Antarctic ice who embarks on an expedition to the pole in 1928, recalling the plot of At the Mountains of Madness. Further reinforcing the Cthulhu Mythos connection, at one point a small statuette resembling the one described in "The Call of Cthulhu" can be glimpsed on his study desk.
*Constantine: The Hellblazer: a reboot series of the gritty 1980s occult series. In the second issue, after absorbing an enormous amount of magical energy, protagonist John Constantine remarks that "I could stop Cthulhu in his tracks with a simple lock-sigil".
*El Diablo: Ghatanothoa appears as a Mesopotamian demon in issue #6 of Volume 3. He is the son of the goddess Ninhursag and the fallen angel Chutriel, who was born in a cave in New Mexico. Despite being destined to unite Hell and Earth, Ghatanothoa betrayed his original purpose by devouring his mother. Later, Ghatanothoa attempted to recruit the metahuman El Diablo as a general in his war against the world; however, Ghatanothoa was ultimately stabbed to death by El Diablo, after rejecting his offer.
*iZombie: the Lovecraftian monster Xitalu was heavily inspired by Cthulhu.
*Justice League vs. Godzilla vs. Kong: In Issue #3, the Monsterverse Titan Scylla is compared to Cthulhu by the Flash and Cyborg.

Film and television productions have frequently been influenced by H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos. Some productions have adapted Lovecraft or other Mythos writers' works, more or less faithfully; other projects have been original works set in a Mythos or Mythos-adjacent universe. Other films and TV shows have Lovecraftian themes without directly referencing the Mythos, while other times screenwriters drop Mythos names as a homage to Lovecraft.

### Adaptations
### Film
*13:de mars, 1941 (2004; Robert P. Olsson): based on "The Statement of Randolph Carter".
*Arkham Sanitarium (post-production as of May 2022; Andrew G. Morgan): an anthology of three of Lovecraft's short works connected by an original 'wraparound' story.
*Banshee Chapter (2013): loosely adapts the short story "From Beyond" and the 1986 Gordon film, with a similar plot involving the drug Dimethyltryptamine instead of Ultraviolet. At one point Lovecraft's short story is explicitly mentioned.
*Bride of Re-Animator (1989): begins with material from the last two episodes of the original story before veering off into Bride of Frankenstein territory.
*The Call of Cthulhu (2005; Andrew Leman): A silent adaptation by The H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, attempting to make a film that could have been released the same year as the short story.
*Castle Freak (1995; Stuart Gordon): A direct-to-video horror film, loosely based on "The Outsider".
*Castle Freak (2020; Tate Steinsiek): A straight-to-video remake of the 1995 film, which draws from "The Dunwich Horror" as well as "The Outsider".
*Color Out of Space (2019, Richard Stanley): an adaptation of the short story starring Nicholas Cage.
*Cool Air (1999, Bryan Moore): an adaptation that's part of the H.P. Lovecraft Collection.
*Cthulhu (2000, Onara Films): a Mythos story loosely based on The Shadow Over Innsmouth.
*Cthulhu (2007): Another film loosely inspired by The Shadow Over Innsmouth. 
*The Curse (1987): based on "The Colour Out of Space" and starting Claud Akins.
*Curse of the Crimson Altar (1968): based on "The Dreams in the Witch-House" and featuring Christopher Lee and Boris Karloff.
*Dagon (2001, Stuart Gordon; written by Dennis Paoli): a loose adaptation of "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" set in a Spanish town called Imboca.
*Die, Monster, Die! (1965): A loose adaptation of "The Colour out of Space" featuring Boris Karloff.
*The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath (2003, Edward Martin III): The art of Jason Thompson's comic adaptation of the novel was used as the basis for an animated feature film, with Thompson drawing additional art and help coming from volunteers and Lovecraft fans from around the world. The film premiered on October 11, 2003, at the H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival and was later released on DVD. In 2004, the film's composer Cyoakha Grace O'Manion released a concept album featuring the film's original soundtrack with extended tracks and additional music, called Unknown M

fullContent:
H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos have had a significant influence on the world of games, including board games, card games, and particularly video games (including visual novels). Some games (notably Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game) attempt to replicate the shared Mythos universe in game form; others contain references or allusions to Lovecraft's fiction.

### Board Games
*Arkham Horror is a series of board games based in the universe of the Cthulhu Mythos whose first edition was published by Chaosium, with subsequent editions being developed and released by Fantasy Flight Games.
*Carcosa (2017): One Free Elephant's tile-placement board game revolves around Robert W. Chambers' The King in Yellow and the manifestation of his city on Earth.
*Cthulhu: Death May Die (2019): a cooperative board game produced by CMON.
*Final Girls (Van Ryder Games, 2021): The Mystery Boxes for Series 1 and Series 2 are Mythos-themed. For Series 1, the Mystery Box is designed to look like the Necronomicon. For Series 2, the Mystery Box is called "The Otherworldly Mirror" and has a Cthulhu-influenced motif around the edge of the frame.
*King of Tokyo (2011): a kaiju-themed tabletop game featuring pastiches of popular monsters, such as "The King" and "Kraken"; however, the later expansions would incorporate the actual versions of the characters, including King Kong and Cthulhu respectively.
*Smash Up (2012): has an expansion centered around the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Card Games
*Battle Spirits: features several cards based on familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos.
*Force of Will: features the Cthulhu as a race of evil creatures in the fictional universe of the game.
*Gwent: The Witcher Card Game: features Dagon as a leader card. His ability allows him to create harmful weather effects on the opponent's side of the board.
*Hecatomb: features Nyarlathotep as the Thing Outside Time and Space.
*Magic: The Gathering (1993):
**There are cards named Library of Leng and Candles of Leng.
**The mysterious being Marit Lage is depicted similarly to a Lovecraftian being. It is an extremely large, tentacled creature frozen in ice. Players in-game can free it by using mana to thaw the ice.
**The eldrazi are beings from the spaces between the planes of existence (comparable to universes) that are able to warp reality with an unnatural form of magic. The most powerful eldrazi, known as titans, are comparable to Great Old Ones. They appear in the Zendikar and Battle for Zendikar blocks. They also appear in Eldritch Moon in a slightly different form; rather than entirely alien creatures, in this set they are mutated forms of creatures already found on Innistrad, such as humans, werewolves, and angels; this mutation being the work of the eldrazi titan Emrakul.
*Munchkin: has an edition titled "Munchkin Cthulhu" which features many parodies of Lovecraftian lore.
*Twilight of the Gods: features the Elder Gods as one of the pantheons.
*Yu-Gi-Oh!: The Entity Extra Deck monste

Music has frequently been inspired by the Cthulhu Mythos and other works of H. P. Lovecraft, going back at least to the 1960s psychedelic rock band H. P. Lovecraft. The heavy metal genre in particular has often drawn imagery and themes from Lovecraft's work.

The following is a non-comprehensive alphabetical list of musical and audio works that contain references, allusions or themes that have their origin with Lovecraft, or appear likely to have been inspired by his fiction.
### Examples

*Adams, Ryan (alt-country musician): wrote a song called "Arkham Asylum," which he and The Cardinals have performed live since September 18, 2006.
*The Arkhams (psychobilly band):
**"The Road to Arkham" 2007 album;
**"The Valley of the Arkhams" 2010 album.
*Arzachel (English Acid-Rock/Heavy Metal band): Their 1968 self-titled debut EP contains a song "Azathoth"; a hymn-like piece with lyrics praising the Outer God, that descends into a repetitive rhythm with slow pounding drums and droning, dissonant guitar and organ parts, much like the "maddening beat of vile drums" and "the whine of accursed flutes"
* Blue Oyster Cult:
** "In the Presence of Another World" is a track from the 1988 album Imaginos;
** "The Old Gods Return" is a track from the 2001 album Curse of the Hidden Mirror;
** "The Alchemist" is a track from the 2020 album The Symbol Remains.
* Ballif, Claude (French composer): wrote stage music by the name "Erich Zann".
*Bejelit (Italian heavy metal band): recorded a song titled "The Haunter of the Dark," based on the story of the same name, for their Bones and Evil EP.
*Black Dahlia Murder (death metal band): recorded a song inspired by "The Call of Cthulhu" titled "Thy Horror Cosmic." Lyrics include: "“For vast aeons has slept, lurking 'neath the haunted deep / Sea soaked perversion, arise / Named of the foulest tongue, his will ebbs within me / Beckoning -- what was shall once more be.”
*Black Sabbath (metal band): The song "Behind the Wall of Sleep" on their self-titled debut album evokes Lovecraft's "Beyond the Wall of Sleep".
*Burning Star Core (band): The song "Nyarlathotep" is on their album The Very Heart of the World.
*Common Market (hip hop collective): wrote a song called "Escaping Arkham" one of five songs on the album "The Winter's End EP".
*Conan (British doom metal band): The music video for their song "Foehammer" depicts Nyarlathotep.
*Congress (Belgian metalcore band): has a song intro titled "Nyarlathotep" on their Angry With the Sun album.

The following is a non-comprehensive alphabetical list of written fiction that, while not direct adaptations of Lovecraft's works, contain references, allusions or themes that have their origin with Lovecraft, or appear likely to have been inspired by his writings.

For other examples of prose fiction related to the Cthulhu Mythos, please refer to :Category:Novels and :Category:Anthologies.

*'Salem's Lot (Stephen King): 1975 vampire horror novel set in the same continuity as his short story "Jerusalem's Lot." Lovecraft is mentioned twice in passing, once in the published novel, and again in a scene which was edited from the final draft. Edgar Allan Poe and Arthur Machen are also made mention of.
*A Certain Magical Index: New Testament (Kazuma Kamachi): In volume 14 of the light novel series, Patricia Birdway gets her body infested by a parasite known as "Sample Shoggoth". The creature was discovered during a research mission in Antarctica (a reference to At the Mountains of Madness).
*A Song of Ice and Fire (George R. R. Martin): has several Lovecraftian elements in its lore.
**The Black Goat of Qohor is a nod to Shub-Niggurath, the Black Goat of the Woods with a Thousand Young.
**The Drowned God is a nod to Cthulhu.
**Citizens of Carcosa are said to exhibit fish-like physical features much like those of the townsfolk in The Shadow Over Innsmouth.
**The Many Faced God could be equated to Nyarlathotep.
**Lord Dagon Greyjoy was ruler of the Iron Islands. The symbol of his people is a kraken and the chant of their baptism is "What is dead may never die, but rises again, harder and stronger", all references to the Mythos.
** Martin published a [http://grrm.livejournal.com/140797.html short story] pitting Jaime Lannister against Cthulhu on his blog.
*"The Adventure of Exham Priory" (F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre): a short story in the anthology Shadows Over Baker Street.
*"The Adventure of the Death-Fetch" (Darrell Schweitzer): a short story featured in the anthology The Improbable Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, a mystery revolves around an expedition to the Plateau of Leng.

H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos have had a significant influence on later works in a wide variety of media. The following is a non-comprehensive alphabetical list of stage productions that, while not direct adaptations of Lovecraft's works, contain references, allusions or themes that have their origin with Lovecraft, or appear likely to have been inspired by his fiction.

*HP Lovecraft's The Shadow over Innsmouth: January 2012, the Cape Cod based Provincetown Theater announced a reading of a full-length play of the story, entitled HP Lovecraft's The Shadow over Innsmouth, adapted for the stage by Bragan Thomas.
*The Rats in the Walls (2006): Tim Uren adapted the Lovecraft story into a one-man play of the same name which was performed at the 2006 Minnesota Fringe Festival.
*The Rats in the Walls (2007): Dave Walsh adapted and performed the one-man play at Shakespeare by the Sea, Newfoundland Festival.
*H. P. Lovecraft's The Dreams in the Witch House (2008): "The Dreams in the Witch House" was brought to the stage by WildClaw Theatre Company in Chicago, in conjunction with Weird Tales Magazine's 85th anniversary. It was adapted and directed by WildClaw Artistic Director Charley Sherman.
*The Dunwich Horror (2011): the Lovecraft story was adapted by David Dawkins of Ororo Productions for the inaugural London Horror Festival. The production retained a great deal of the language from the original story and was both praised and criticised for this, though reviews were generally positive.
*The Picture In The House (September 2011): the Cape Cod-based Provincetown Theater Company announced that an adaptation of the Lovecraft story would be performed live onstage at the November 2011 Fall Playwright's Festival in Provincetown, Massachusetts. This is believed to be the first such adaptation of this particular tale.
*The Dunwich Horror (October 2013): The Company (a Yorkshire amateur dramatics society) produced a stage play adaptation of the Lovecraft story at the University of Sheffield's Drama Studio.

The World Wide Web has been home to original works that evoke the imagery and themes of H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Examples
*The Adventures of Lil Cthulhu: an animated short film by Zooboo Child. 
*The Angry Video Game Nerd: In the episode for Super Mario Bros. 3, it was speculated that the "N" on the Tarrot cards stood for "Necronomicon", as one of the many Satanic messages in the game. A sentient version of the Necronomicon is later seen amongst Satan's army but was quickly destroyed by the Nerd. 
*The Church of the SubGenius: the parody religion includes some aspects of the Cthulhu Mythos, such as the Elder Gods who are led by Yog-Sothoth.
*Creepypasta:
**The Rake is a hideous being, difficult to describe, but usually described as a slim, hunchbacked creature with grayish skin. The purpose of this being is to corrupt the human mind: it begins to visit you daily, tormenting you at bedtime, causing you severe depression and psychosis.
**Physically speaking, Slender Man is very reminiscent of certain Nyarlathotep avatars, due to its elongated profile, its lack of facial features and its tentacles.
***There is also the Slender Man webseries Dark Harvest, which takes a lot from Lovecraftian lore. Here, the Slender Man is an extra-dimensional entity named Gorr'Rylaehotep, which was invoked into our universe through a gateway opened via a ritual found in some Egyptian tablets. It is worshipped by a cult named "The Order", who believe Gorr'Rylaehotep can give them godhood. 
**Smile.dog is an image that just seeing it leads to loss of sanity. Those who see it begin to be tormented by a dog in their nightmares, to have delusions, seizures and hallucinations. This creepypasta is very similar to the effect that different objects in the Mythos produce.
**Zalgo is a chaotic entity associated with destruction and madness. It cannot be named or described, and the only descriptions given of it are only metaphors and allegories. It is an entity that just evoking it leads to madness itself. It tells the story that it has seven mouths and with the seventh it will sing the song of the end of the world. It is the one who waits behind the wall. His story itself is very similar to that of Azathoth or Cthulhu. 
***It should be noted, however, that the original creator claimed Zalgo had nothing to do with Lovecraft (it went as far as that Zalgo could only warp comics and similar kinds of media). It would be later sources and stories, like the "Zalgo Invocation", which would rise Zalgo into the status of a world ending entity more in the line of the Great Old Ones.
**Y'golonac appears as the main antagonist in the short story "The Defiler", where he tries to manipulate the narrator with forbidden literature.
**Eihort is the overarching antagonist of the Creepypasta "Vicksburg" where he is the master of the story's main antagonist Narcissa Witwe and is fully responsible for the eponymous town's dilapidated state.

fullContent:
Cthulhu Now is a sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. It was the first concerted attempt to update the basic game, set during the Roaring Twenties, to a contemporary setting. Two editions were released, in 1987 and 1992 respectively; although the books are long out of print, the original edition has been made available as a digital download through roleplaying game website DriveThruRPG. 

Both editions contain information on contemporary equipment, weaponry, skills, and scientific techniques, as well as a selection of stand-alone scenarios and all necessary player handouts.

Cthulhu Rising is a horror fiction role-playing game based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set during the 23rd century. The game is published by Chaosium and was published in 2008.

### Setting
The game is set during the 23rd century, as man has colonized the Solar System and has been establishing colonies beyond the Earth, dozens of light years away. It is a world in which there is a world government, though its member states would still have a lot of autonomy and compete with each other. Within the human race, conspiracies of the Mythos continue in the shadows and the threat of the Great Old Ones returning is ever present, though unknown to most of the public.

### Human Government
* United Earth Federation - Which governs the human interstellar sphere (which extends 40 light years from Earth). It's power is enforced by the United Earth Armed Forces (UEAF) and the FLEA (Federal Law Enforcement Authority).
* Interstellar Colonial Authority - It governs a sphere of influence that is 20 light years in radius from Sol. The UEF has reserved the right to annex any colony within 50 light years and to expand the sphere.
* United Earth Armed Forces - Which consists of the fleet and planetside ground forces. One of its elite units are the Marines. The UEAF has a variety of ships, vehicles, technologies, and weapons, including power armor, plasma-based weapons, rail guns, smart missiles.

### Major Terran States
* Chinese Consortium - Which is an authoritarian socialistic state that has a population of 1.88 billion on Earth and 168 million in space, and a GDP of E$91.4 trillion. It was established in 2086 AD by China and most of Southeast Asia. The Chinese Consortium emerged from the Pacific Rim War as the largest and most powerful state within the United Earth Federation (UEF). It was also the largest contributor to the world's economy. The Chinese Consortium now has incorporated parts of Russia since then. In it the main languages are Chinese, Russian, and Vietnamese. Together with the United Americas, they are at the leading edge of the UEF interstellar colonization.
* United Americas - It's a federal republic with a population of 512 million on Earth and 164 million in space. With an economy which is the most technologically powerful in the world and the second largest. They are the second most powerful state within the UEF. It was established in 2084 and consists of the United States, and parts of Mexico, Canada, and Central America. Within the UA, the corporations hold much of the real power. Due to the rampant consumerism, religious conservatism is on the rise.

shortDefinition: "Cthulhu Rising" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Heather Graham. It was published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 by Titan Books in October 2017.  ### Synopsis Decades after the Depression-era l...
fullContent:
"Cthulhu Rising" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Heather Graham. It was published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 by Titan Books in October 2017.

### Synopsis
Decades after the Depression-era liner Guinevere disappears, it mysteriously reappears, somewhat weathered but no worse for wear- and missing the entire 900 souls who had been aboard during its last voyage. The owners sail her across the Atlantic to Miami, where they intend to return her to service as a hotel ship and tourist attraction. However, rumours that the ship is haunted prompt them to employ two groups, one of scientists and one of paranormal investigators, to stay aboard the Guinevere during her final voyage, to look into the claims and hopefully drum up some publicity.

During the course of the trip, the two groups fall for a ruse by the ship's owners, believing the crew have vanished along with several of their own number. This is quickly discovered to be part of a publicity stunt orchestrated by an avaricious lawyer who has commissioned a reality television show in which the group members are the unwitting stars.

Soon, however, the crew does begin to vanish, along with several of the investigators. Clues lead the remaining investigators to the conclusion that they have fallen victim to the depredations of a Shoggoth which has lain hidden in the bowels of the vessel since its discovery. This is confirmed when the creature attacks, and the survivors attempt to reach the Guinevere's lifeboats and flee. Finally, two are able to make their escape, and as they row away from the ship get a glimpse of a colossal creature, Great Cthulhu himself, as it briefly breaches the surface.

The story concludes with the two survivors speculating that H. P. Lovecraft’s stories were based on factual accounts told by others who had encountered elements of the Cthulhu Mythos, and subsequently monetised as fiction. They wonder if perhaps their story will be picked up by some aspiring writer later in life and given the same treatment.

Cthulhu Tales is a horror anthology comic book series published by Boom! Studios. Begun as a pair of specials, The Rising two-parter and Tainted, issued in December 2006 and September 2007, respectively, it was later relaunched as a monthly series running for 12 issues between March 2008 and March 2009. Four collected editions were also released, as were a pair of omnibuses.

The series features both Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos stories, with artwork and writing from a wide range of contributors.

Cthulhu Tales #1 is the first issue of the horror anthology comic book series Cthulhu Tales. It was published by Boom! Studios in March 2008.

### Stories

### "The Eyes of Madness"

### Synopsis
A blind stranger who wanders into the rural New England town of Mason is accused of killing a dozen of the local children, claiming that they were the disciples of the Great Old Ones. While awaiting execution after conviction in a kangaroo court, he shows the town preacher a ritual to perform upon the blind man's death, the results of which show the preacher the horrors lurking just out of sight of the human race…

### Creative Team
* Story: Steve Niles
* Art: Chee
* Letters: Marshall Dillon
* Colours: White Rabbit

### "The Farm"

### Synopsis
A group of children sneak onto a nearby body farm - an area designated for research into various external conditions on the human body post-mortem - in search of cheap thrills. While there, they encounter an undead monster which is feeding upon the bodies in situ; fortunately they are saved by the local sheriff and his men who kill the beast and let the boys off with a warning.

### Creative Team
* Story: Michael Alan Nelson
* Art: Sunder Raj
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "Exactly the Right Word"

### Synopsis
The coach of the baseball team the Maine Cheetahs conducts a mystical ritual which involves sacrificing seven devoted fans to the dark god Cthulhu. Its goal: to ensure that the Cheetahs win their first World Series in 72 years.

### Creative Team
* Story: Tom Peter
* Art: Chee
* Letters: Marshall Dillon
* Colours: Ben Hunzeker

### Behind the Mythos
In "The Farm," a remark by one of the sheriff's men, "Looks like the doc’s reanimating kids now, too," may be a reference to the necromantic science practiced by one Dr. Herbert West.

fullContent:
Cthulhu Tales 10 is the tenth issue of Boom! Studios' Lovecraftian comic book anthology series. Featuring three short strips (one of which was the first in a multi-part series), it was published in January 2009.

### Overview


### Stories

### "Rite to Life"

### Synopsis
A social worker for the Washington State Child Protection Services is tipped off about a child of the Marsh family who may be in danger. Removing the child - who will only repeat phrases in R'lyehian - from his family, the worker discovers that his new charge is a key and a gateway, and his family intend to sacrifice the boy to bring about the return of the Old Ones. Although the Esoteric Order of Dagon slaughter the entire CPS staff, the worker is able to hide the boy away, averting the disaster that would befall humankind should their plans have been brought to fruition.

### Creative Team
* Story: Mark Rahner
* Art: Unai
* Colorist: Digikore
* Letterer: Dillon Marshall

### "Comeback Tour"

### Synopsis
A light-hearted story in which the band "Cthulhu, Shub-Niggurath, Nyarlathotep, and Yog-Sothoth" face an uncertain future in an airport departure lounge when two of the members, Cthulhu and Shub-Niggurath, seem unable to get along. Ever the mediator, Nyarlathotep steps up to the plate and sacrifices a pair of unruly children, calming the two and allowing them to make their peace with each other and continue with their epic tour.

### Creative Team
* Jeff Lester, Chee, and Marshall Dillon

### "Where Am I?" (Part 1)

### Synopsis
In the wake of the God War, a cleaner discovers a living human brain encased in a jar hidden beneath the ruins of the Arkham Boarding House - known to have been owned by Nyarlathotep in his human guise. Turning the brain over to an accomplished scientist, the doctor proceeds to implant it into a cadaver in an effort to find out what went on in the lead up to the war.

This story marks the beginning of a story which takes place in Michael Alan Nelson's Fall of Cthulhu setting.

### Creative Team
* Story: Michael Alan Nelson
* Art: Aritz Eiguren
* Colors: Digikore Studios
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### Behind the Mythos
In "Rite to Life," the social worker was alerted to the child's peril by one Randolph Carter; a police officer makes a remark about Carter being trouble to follow up on. This panel is a nod to Lovecraft's character and his life-changing transition into the Dreamlands. Later in the story, the worker contacts the Innsmouth Child Protection Services during his research into the boy's plight.

### Trivia
* In "Comeback Tour," Shub-Niggurath plays the part of a flamboyant lead singer willing to pander to a crowd, while Cthulhu takes on the role of the angst-ridden lead guitarist dedicated to his craft.

Cthulhu Tales #2 is the second issue of the monthly horror anthology comic book series Cthulhu Tales. It was published by Boom! Studios in April 2008.

### Stories

### "The Hiding Place"

### Synopsis
When a criminal which he has been pursuing for the last decade takes his own life, a detective attends the autopsy in an attempt to gain some closure. Unfortunately, the criminal had left a curse hidden within his own corpse which activates during the procedure, and the cop is shown a vision of the Great Old Ones…

### Creative Team
* Story: Steve Niles
* Art: Shane Oakly
* In assist: Suzanne O'Brien
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "Katrina"

### Synopsis
A convict on cleanup duty in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina stumbles across a journal in which the author recounts his mid-storm experience of bizarre monster-headed creatures which are returning to lay their claim on the world. Reading its contents proves too much for the man, and he subsequently dies muttering the word "Cthulhu."

### Creative Team
* Story: Eric Calderon
* Visuals: Jon Schnepp
* Inks: Dik Pose
* Colours: Dan Bigelow
* Letters:Marshall Dillon

### "How to Get Ahead in the Occult"

### Synopsis
A student who believes herself to be a practitioner of magic takes her roommate to a keg party whose organisers purport to be a cult of Cthulhu. Later that night, the roommate wakes screaming, reciting bizarre phrases in both English and R'lyehian, and expressing an urgent desire to visit the seaside.

At the shore, Great Cthulhu rises from the depths and claims the roommate as a sacrifice, proclaiming the sorceress to be his new High Priestess of New England.

### Creative Team
* Story: Christine Boylan

Cthulhu Tales #3 is the third issue of the horror anthology comic book series Cthulhu Tales. It was published by Boom! Studios in May 2008.

### Stories

### "Alimentary, My Dear Cthulhu"

### Synopsis
A surrealist story in which Lieutenant Pickman of the Providence Police Department and his psychic friend Charles Dexter Pigeon are called to investigate a murder during a seance at the Polaris mansion, where the victim has been partially transformed into a Great Old One/Elder God.

During the course of their investigations, reality begins to break down; finally, the pair confront the insane scion of the Polaris family, Howard, who explains that dimensions are merging. He then recites the infamous R'lyehian "Cthulhu fhtagn" passage, before somehow transforming into a god-monster.

### Creative Team
* Script: William Messner-Loebs
* Art and colours: Andrew Ritchie
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "On the Wagon"

### Synopsis
Young Ken drinks because he believes that doing so is the only thing which keeps the demon living inside him in check. His worried family stage an intervention and Ken agrees, only to find that all along they were cultists who wish only for him to release the dark entity from within…

### Creative Team
* Written by: Michael Alan Nelson
* Drawn by: Eduardo Ferigato
* Coloured by: Pablo Quiligotti
* Lettered by: Marshall Dillon

### "The Cruise of Cthulhu"

### Synopsis
A tongue-in-cheek infomercial on the benefits of Alhazred Cruises' Nature Cruise. Highlights include the Lovecraft Lounge, a casino with slots named Cthulhu Cash, the Old Ones Inn (which serves drinks such as the Tentacle Twist, Shot of R'lyeh, and Cthulhu Woo-woo), a sightseeing trip to Greenland (where one can watch whales be consumed by the "local" wildlife), and daily services on-deck - conveniently conducted in R'lyehian.

### Creative Team
* Written by: Todd Lepre
* Drawn by: Chee
* Coloured by: Renato Faccini
* Lettered by: Marshall Dillon

### Behind the Mythos
"Alimentary, My Dear Cthulhu" is a play on words, combining Sherlock Holmes' famous catchphrase "Elementary, my dear Watson" with the cosmic horror implications of "alimentary" (meaning sustenance or nourishment) alongside the mention of Great Cthulhu.

The story also features a number of names which relate to characters from Lovecraft’s works, such as Lieutenant Pickman (Richard Upton Pickman or Edward Pickman Derby), Charles Dexter Pigeon (Charles Dexter Ward), and both Phillip Horne and Howard Polaris (Howard Phillips Lovecraft), as well as the family name Polaris itself, which is a nod to Lovecraft’s 1918 short story.

"The Cruise of Cthulhu" also features a prominent Mythos name in Alhazred Cruises, the "Mad Arab" Abdul Alhazred being the author of the cursed book which would one day become known as the Necronomicon.

### Trivia

* In "Alimentary, My Dear Cthulhu" the character design of Phillip Horne bears a remarkable resemblance to Marvel Comics' Doctor Stephen Strange.

Cthulhu Tales #4 is the fourth issue of the Lovecraftian comic book anthology series Cthulhu Tales. It was published by Boom! Studios in June 2008.

### Overview


### Stories

### "In the π of the Beholder"

### Synopsis
After Professor Binder , a university mathematics teacher, reads a copy of the infamous Necronomicon sent to him anonymously, he develops a disturbing condition whereby he sees all those around him - and eventually even himself - as possessed of heads resembling vile octopuses.

Unable to get help for this malady, he seeks answers in the ancient book, and slowly begins to develop mathematical formulae which he believes will "bridge our reality to the higher dimensions." While visiting his psychiatrist, the doctor suggests that his condition may not be psychological, but rather some form of cosmic warning against his course of action.

Taking this advice to heart, Binder decides to burn all of his research and the copy of the Necronomicon;  instantly all of his terrifying symptoms disappear: it appears that the psychiatrist had hit the nail on the head.

### Creative Team
* Story: Mark Waid
* Art: Chee
* Colour: Andrea Barreto
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "There Will Be Blood"

### Synopsis
During the 2003 invasion of Iraq, Hassan Alhazred, a distant descendant of the infamous Abdul and curator of the Iraqi Museum for Heretical Antiquities, is abducted by US military contractors intent on having him translate a page from the Necronomicon and reveal the location of the Nameless City, which they mistakenly believe is a source of oil ripe for the taking.

Despite the tortures he undergoes, Alhazred refuses to give them what they want, and the contractors make the decision to kill him. However, he casts a powerful spell invoking Y'ha-nthlei, Sarnath, and Dagon which allows him to kill the thieves, although he pays a terrible price in return, becoming the very danger to the world that his family has sworn to protect against.

### Creative Team
* Written by: Mark Sable
* Drawn by: Sergio Carrera
* Coloured by: Andrew Dalhouse
* Lettered by: Marshall Dillon

### Trivia
* "In the π of the Beholder" is a play on words, with the mathematical symbol for pi being substituted in the saying "in the eye of the beholder." The play is fitting given the story's mathematical premise and the condition suffered by Professor Binder.
* One panel in "There Will Be Blood" depicts a crate labelled as containing the Ark of the Covenant resting in a warehouse somewhere beneath the United States. This is a reference to the 1981 action-adventure film Raiders of the Lost Ark, in which the final scene shows the Ark being placed in storage.

### Synopsis
An operative known as a "Doorman" working for a shadowy agency is assigned a new partner after the death of his old one. The agents' job: to locate and block portals which form between our reality and others. However, when the veteran is captured and consumed by an entity from beyond, the rookie must take over his mantle of "Doorman."

March 1903, Chamber's Notch, New England: when Dr. Nyarlathotep, The Wizard of Lightning, arrives in town, local businessman Howard Cartwright is captivated by his electrical achievements, and invests everything he has in the doctor's venture. "The Current Chaos" involves several characters with names connected to the Mythos: the main character Howard Cartwright (Howard Phillips Lovecraft), a worker named Carter (Randolph Carter), and a site manager named West (Dr. Herbert West).

Cthulhu Tales #6 is the sixth issue of the horror anthology comic book series Cthulhu Tales. It was published by Boom! Studios in September 2008.

### Stories

### "Cthulhu House"

### Synopsis
The tongue-in-cheek story of a reality television series in which contestants, organised into Teams Squamish and Nyarlathotep, compete to contact the Elder Gods. After a few hiccups - in which several members of Squamish burn themselves to death through accidental misuse of the Pnakotic Manuscripts, and a field trip to Innsmouth which results in the death of two others at the hands of giant leeches - contestant Brian unearths a copy of the Necronomicon in the Miskatonic University Restricted Collection; attempting to summon Cthulhu, he is instead possessed by the entity, which the other housemates dub Cully. Although popular with the surviving contestants, he is voted out of the house due to lacking the killer instinct to survive the series' run. However, in his post-eviction interview, Cully says that the experience has made him feel better about himself.

### Creative Team
* Story: William Messner-Loebs
* Art: Drew Rausch
* Colors: Drew Berry
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "A Stranger Comes to Night Hill"
### Synopsis
A mysterious traveller makes his way to the town of Night Hill, where he enters the local church which is in the midst of worship. Although the minister is welcoming, the man immediately turns into a winged, tentacle-faced monstrosity and murders the entire congregation as blasphemers. The story concludes with others of his type making their way ashore and reciting a chant to their dark master: "Ia! Ia! Cthulhu Fhtagn!"

### Creative Team
* Story: John R. Fultz
* Art: Mark Dos Santos
* Colors: Andrew Dalhouse
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "One of Those Days"

### Synopsis
An IT technician working for a large firm discovers that an unusual piece of software has infiltrated the company's computers, something called the Cthulhu Virus. Although he does his best to ascertain the nature of the problem, even staying back far beyond business hours, he is murdered by another employee, his body dragged off to who knows where.

### Creative Team
* Writer: Glen Cadigan
* Artist: Chee
* Colorist: Renato Faccini
* Letterer: Marshall Dillon

### Trivia
* In the penultimate panel of "Cthulhu House," one of the housemates, Devon, who had earlier been seen in bed with Cully, is shown to be holding a small baby who looks remarkably similar to the Elder God…
* In "A Stranger Comes to Night Hill," the story initially suggests that the Stranger is perhaps something of an avenging angel and the parishioners servants of an ancient evil, but the reverse proves to be true.
* Whether the murderous employee in "One of Those Days" was attempting to prevent the technician from releasing Cthulhu or covering up the activities of its worshippers is left open to debate.

Cthulhu Tales #7 is the seventh issue of the horror anthology comic book series Cthulhu Tales. It was published by Boom! Studios in October 2008, and was later collected in the volume Cthulhu Tales Vol. 3: Chaos of the Mind in April 2009.

### Overview


### Stories

### "The Empire of Ants"

### Synopsis
The story relates the journal of one Lt. Colonel Henry Dinsmore Boothby of the 3rd Bombay Cavalry, as he undertakes a resupply mission to another unit in India during April 1887. Along the route, his wagon train happens upon an overgrown temple which, he is informed by one of his local guides, is ancient beyond belief.

In his arrogance, and hoping to find it full of abandoned riches, Boothby enters the building; inside, an unknown force shows him the complete history of the Earth, which was visited by powerful alien entities in its distant past, shaped by their presence, and ultimately theirs for ever more. In his despair, Boothby kills himself, realising that, for all their achievements, in the face of these cosmic powers mankind is nothing more than an empire of ants.

### Creative Team

* Writer: Brian Augustyn
* Artist: Milton Sobreiro
* Colorist & Letterer: Felipe Sobreiro

### "The Awakening"

### Synopsis
A disillusioned nurse leaves her job and takes up with a biker named Mike who introduces her to his group, a cult to the Great Old One Cthulhu, who introduce her to their rituals of drug abuse and human sacrifice. Attempting to conduct their own ritual, the former nurse steals a baby from a local hospital, but realises that she cannot go through with the act; killing Mike, she takes the baby to raise as her own and disappears into anonymity.

At age 16 the child, who has been named Sarah, gets pregnant. The woman decides that it is time to take up her old mantle in service to Cthulhu and plans to sacrifice the newborn; fortunately for the child, at the last moment Sarah realises what is happening and kills her adoptive mother instead, the woman realising at the last that she is the true sacrifice to her dark god.

### Creative Team
* Writer: Glen Cadigan
* Artist: Clint Hilinski
* Colorist: Renato Faccini
* Letterer: Marshall Dillon

### Trivia
* While under the influence of LSD, the former nurse sees her fellow cultists as Cthulhu-faced abominations. Whether this is intended to be a manifestation of their devotion or simply an effect of the perception-altering drug is unclear.
