Cthulhu Tales #8 is the eighth issue of Boom! Studios' Lovecraftian horror anthology series Cthulhu Tales. It was published in November 2008.

### Overview


### Stories

### "The Elite"

### Synopsis
When FBI agent Kenneth Gardner Pruitt, the last living descendant of the ill-fated Gardner family, investigates the case of a missing anthropologist in an area known to the locals as the Blasted Heath, he hears the story of how, decades past, a meteor landed in the area, the effects of that which it contained causing genetic chaos amongst the flora and fauna.

When he locates Dr. Andrews, he finds her to be possessed by a remaining element of the alien entity; the being communicates with Gardner through the doctor, offering to share the knowledge of the universe with him, if only he will join with it. Knowing that all of his forebears have devolved into madness at age 38, and that his own 38th birthday is that very day, he accepts.

### Creative Team
* Story: Christine Boylan
* Art: Axel Medellin Machain
* Colors: Andrew Dalhouse
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "Theater of the Empty Eye"

### Synopsis
During experimental research into wormhole technology, astronaut Alexander Shatiskiy is sent on the first mission brought one of these deep-space anomalies. Upon returning, ground control are unable to reestablish contact with Shatinskiy, and his craft, now violently out of control, crash-lands in Siberia. When a recovery team goes to investigate, they find the remains of Shatinskiy, now a betentacled monstrosity, animating from the wreckage of the ship…

### Creative Team
* Story: Matthew McLean
* Art: Drew Rausch
* Colors: Drew Berry
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### Behind the Mythos
The story related to Agent Gardner during "The Elite" is that told in H. P. Lovecraft’s pioneering 1927 science fiction/horror story "The Colour Out of Space."

In "Theater of the Mind's Eye," the scientists monitoring the mission recorded a strange feedback noise resembling the piping of distant flutes during Shatinskiy's translation through the wormhole. This would seem to suggest that the poor astronaut was transported to somewhere in the vicinity of Azathoth.

### Trivia
* Gardner's family's existence in "The Elite" is explained by his grandfather, a son of Nahum Gardner, being a difficult child, sent to live with family in Wales in an attempt to correct his behaviour.
* At one point during the story, Dr. Andrews recites Lovecraft’s famous "That is not dead which can eternal lie, and with strange aeons even death may die" quote.

Cthulhu Tales #9 is the ninth issue of Boom! Studios' Lovecraftian comic book anthology series. Featuring three short strips, it was published in December 2008.

### Stories

### "The Zoo"

### Synopsis
At a bar, the night security guard at a research facility relates how earlier in the evening he witnessed a doorway opening to another realm, an unspeakable monster emerging and absorbing the test chimps before rampaging through the laboratory. In his panic he fled the building and made his way to get a much-needed drink.

However, the entity must have followed his scent to the bar and breaks in, beginning its gruesome absorption process on the unfortunate customers…

### Creative Team
* Story: Raven Gregory
* Art: Sergio Carrera
* Colors: Drew Berry
* Letters: Marshall Dillon

### "It Must Have Been Something You Ate"

### Synopsis
A gluttonous man, desperate to experience new sensations in taste, visits a dealer in exotic meats. The bizarre creature whose flesh he purchases delights the man's palate, but he quickly finds out the truth of the matter: these creatures, which come from another dimension, are unable to reproduce normally in our world, and must painfully parasitise a living host in order to birth their young…

### Creative Team
* Written by: Sam Costello
* Drawn by: Axel Medellin Machain
* Colored by: Digikore Studios
* Lettered by: Marshall Dillon

### "Face of the Competition"

### Synopsis
A genius architect is hired by an avaricious billionaire to design a new installation which he believes will make him even more rich. The architect, apparently in service to some dark god, builds an underwater facility resembling a ruined temple and, as the gates of the temple open, the monstrous, tentacled deity emerges and consumes the client and his unfortunate lawyer.

### Creative Team
* Story: Robert Tinnell
* Art: Milton Sobreiro
* Colors & Letters: Felipe Sobreiro

### Trivia
* The extra-dimensional monsters depicted in "It Must Have Been Something You Ate" resemble the creature dubbed the "Space Jockey," as depicted in the 1979 Lovecraft-inspired science fiction/horror film Alien (the comic was released several years before the true appearance of the Jockeys - whose species was known to humans as "Engineers" - was clarified in the 2012 film Prometheus). Additionally, the method of reproduction used by the creatures recalls the fate suffered by the Jockey in the film.

A mass murderer committed to the oceanside Howard Psychiatric Lunatic Asylum watches in horror as his fellow inmates begin to turn into monster-headed creatures before his very eyes. As this and the sound of the crashing waves drives him insane, he begins to accept the call of the ocean.

"Cthulhu War: Genesis" is a short story by Michael Carter, featuring in the March 1999 edition of E. P. Berglund's digital anthology magazine Nightscapes.

### Synopsis
Set in 2083 it briefly summarizes a reality where H. P. Lovecraft and other authors of his Circle are proven to have created fictitious situations and human characters but who had done no more than chronicle reality when describing the Old Ones and other Cthulhu Mythos entities.

The story begins by describing the arrival of a nebula sized mass of alien insects crossing interstellar space from the direction of Betelgeuse. After this insect plague arrives on the future Earth it first darkens the skies and causes global cooling before unleashing a stinging horde of ferocious insectoids worldwide. While humanity is still recovering from this, the tnataths, gargoyle-like creatures with tentacular heads. In an escalating series of apportations more and more hostile creatures of the Mythos appeared on Earth accompanied by the human race suffering powerful hypnotic dreams and nightmares.

The short story concludes with the narrator preparing an assault, having provided us with the background of how the war against the Mythos began.

fullContent:
Cthulhu Wars is a Cthulhu Mythos-based board game in which a group of players take control of a Great Old One and their cults, and battle for power over a map. The game is usually won by completing the "Doom Track". The game makes extensive use of Mythos elements, as well as making its own assumptions and connections.

It was originally released by Petersen Games in 2015, followed by various expansions.

### Background
On Earth, mankind had the polluted the air, water, and land. Famine, wars, and plague spread like a cancer across the Earth. There were those few foolish but kind-hearted souls who tried to reverse the damage inflicted on the world, but it was a lost cause. The Old Ones had plans for Earth, and through the eons guided the world toward a destination which was to their liking. By the time the end came, the conflicting but compatible agendas of the various Old Ones were complete. The waste, poison, and irradiation made the Earth more hospitable to the Old Ones, pleasing them greatly. Their influence grew as the stars aligned, speeding up the sickness in the world.

Then the Wars erupted on Earth. All it took was psychic nudge to set things off and mankind did the rest. Wars exploded and spread from the Third World to the First World, engulfing the streets of their cities. Massacres became the norm in the towns and cities of the First World. The combatants developed strange new weapons, but no one could gain a decisive advantage. Humans ran on the streets, burning and killing, shouting and destroying. Never in human history had blood flowed like this. As the world burned in a holocaust of freedom and ecstasy, the Old Ones finally rose from their eons long slumber.

### Core Game
### Factions
Each faction is composed of a Great Old One (or two, rarely), eight to ten monsters, and six cultists. The players start the game with their cultists, and must unlock their monsters and Great Old Ones, and use spellbooks to enhance their abilities.

### Green Faction - Great Cthulhu
*Great Old One: Cthulhu
*Monsters
**4 Deep Ones

**2 Starspawn

### Blue Faction - Crawling Chaos

### Red Faction - Black Goat

### Yellow Faction - Yellow Sign
*Great Old One: Hastur, The King in Yellow (secondary)
*Monsters

**4 Byakhee

### Maps
### Earth
Earth is the base map with no additional features changing gameplay. Great Cthulhu starts in the South Pacific, Crawling Chaos starts in Asia/South Asia, Black Goat starts in Africa/West Africa, Yellow Sign starts in Europe, Sleeper starts in North America, and Windwalker starts either in the Arctic Ocean or Antarctica.

fullContent:
Cthulhu: Death May Die is a cooperative board game produced by CMON Global Limited. Designed by Rob Daviau and Eric M. Lang, the core set was released in 2019.

In 2023, the game received a second edition release titled Cthulhu: Death May Die - Fear of the Unknown. An upcoming third edition titled Cthulhu: Death May Die – Forbidden Reaches is also scheduled for 2026.

### Gameplay
A group of players (up to 5) work together to stop a group of Old One worshiping cultists who are attempting to awaken an Elder God. To achieve this, they will need to fight through various monsters and cultists, disrupt the ritual of the cultists, and deal with the Elder God when it inevitably awakens. 

The game has a series of episodes, each one provides a different map, set of monsters, and methods of disrupting the ritual. The base game comes with six episodes. 

The base game comes with two Elder Gods: Cthulhu and Hastur. Each has different mechanics that can affect the players and monsters, both before and after the ritual is disrupted.

### Sets

### Core Sets
To date, two editions of Death May Die have been released, the first in 2019 and the second in 2023; as well as an upcoming third one in 2026.

*Cthulhu: Death May Die (2019)
*Cthulhu: Death May Die - Fear of the Unknown (2023)
*Cthulhu: Death May Die – Forbidden Reaches (2026)

Since its launch, there have been several expansions released, each bringing something new to the game. Some introduce a new Elder God, others bring new episodes, investigators, and monsters.

Xothic Wars is a sci-fi horror tactical miniature board game set over 250 million years ago, before man evolved on Earth. The game is published by GobboTown Games which also produces the miniatures. The game was first released in 2017.

### Setting
Earth is invaded by Eldritch beings from another dimension, the Xothians. Standing in their way of universal conquest are the world's dominant lifeform, the Elder Things. War erupts between the two for control of the Earth. It's the twilight of the Permian Period, right before the dawn of the Triassic Period, when the greatest mass extinction in Earth's history would occur, known as the "Great Dying".

### Factions
* Xothians: At the twilight of the Permian period, in approximately 250 million BC, Earth is invaded by extradimensional aliens, the Xothians. They arrive in this universe intending to establish a power base for Cthulhu, an entity from their home dimension. Cthulhu has the ambition of becoming a higher being. In the dimension he comes from, the higher beings prevented him from joining their ranks. Earth will be turned into a location where Cthulhu will ascend to greater godhood upon the completion of a ritual. The forces of the Xothians are divided into tyrants, priests, greater terror beasts, and lesser terror beasts.
* Qhrell: The Elder Things were already on Earth when the Xothians invaded the world. Only they stand in the way of their plans and Cthulhu's ascension. A war rages on Earth between the Qhrell and the Xothians. The Qhrell are masters of genetic engineering and possess directed energy weapons. It's a race that is 7 ft tall and can survive freezing temperatures, the vacuum of outer space, and the pressures of the deep ocean. Their army deploys in battle against the Xothians, the Shoggoth.

shortDefinition: "Cthulhu? Gesundheit!" is the third story featured in issue #19 of The Simpsons' Treehouse of Horror series by Bongo Comics. It was written by Len Wein and illustrated by Dan Brereton.  ### Synopsis At Springfield Elementary School, Principal Skinner...
fullContent:
"Cthulhu? Gesundheit!" is the third story featured in issue #19 of The Simpsons' Treehouse of Horror series by Bongo Comics. It was written by Len Wein and illustrated by Dan Brereton.

### Synopsis
At Springfield Elementary School, Principal Skinner punishes Bart and his friend Milhouse by forcing them to catalogue all the books in the school's abandoned old library, leading to Bart finding a copy of the Necronomicon. Taking the book back home, Bart explains to Milhouse that it can be used to summon the Great Old Ones to do his bidding and recites the chant "Yog-Sothoth Demonicus Cthulhu". Meanwhile, Homer was washing his face in the bathroom until one of Cthulhu's tentacles clogs the sink faucet. At first, Bart uses Cthulhu to get revenge on his enemies, such as killing Skinner and some bullies. Shortly afterwards, Cthulhu goes out of control and starts eating everyone throughout the town. Fearing that it will be the end of the world, Bart and Milhouse go back to the Necronomicon to find a way to stop it. Unfortunately, a demonic version of Bart's pet dog, Santa's Little Helper, eats the only page that can banish Cthulhu back to where it came from. Realizing that he screwed up big time, Bart begins to break down into tears, before getting knocked out by a giant tentacle. Sometime later, Bart wakes up, assuming that it was all just a dream. However, this turns out to be not the case, as it's revealed that the entire Simpson family has been transformed into Lovecraftian monsters, including Bart himself. At the dinner table, Marge serves a "Roast Milhouse" to her family for dinner, with Bart proclaiming that he'll never read another book again.

### Trivia
*Towards the end of the story, an issue of Cthulhu Tales can be seen in Bart's bedroom.

### Reprints
*Simpsons Comics #229 (UK) (2014)
*The Simpsons Treehouse of Horror Ominous Omnibus Vol. 2: Deadtime Stories for Boos & Ghouls (2023)

The Great Old One known as Cthulhu has gone by many names since its first appearance in the 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu", published by the Weird Tales magazine. While many of these are undoubtedly little more than alternate spellings for a name never intended to have been uttered by human vocal chords, a sizeable portion are entirely new monikers. This page offers a guide to the many and varied names of Cthulhu, arguably the most iconic of H. P. Lovecraft's creations, and includes the avatars employed by this eldritch abomination.

### Lovecraft's Works
*Cthulhu ("The Call of Cthulhu", 1928)
*Cthulhutl ("The Electric Executioner", 1930)
*Clulu ("Winged Death", 1934)
*Clooloo ("Medusa's Coil", 1939)
*Tulu (The Mound, 1940)

### Lovecraft Circle Works
*Kthulhut ("Ubbo-Sathla", 1933)
*Him Who Is to Come ("The House on Curwen Street", 1944)
*Shooloo ("The House on Curwen Street", 1944)
*Kthulhu ("The Gorge Beyond Salapunco", 1949)
*Kulu ("The Gorge Beyond Salapunco", 1949)
*Great Old One ("The House in the Valley", 1953)
*Him Who Lies Dreaming ("The Seal of R'lyeh", 1957)
*Him Who Will Rise Again ("The Seal of R'lyeh", 1957)
*Thooloo ("Innsmouth Clay", 1971)
*Cutlu ("The Terror from the Depths", 1976)
*Kutullu ("Dead Giveaway", 1976)
*Mark Dixon (Strange Eons, 1978)

### Expanded Mythos
*B'Moth (Call of Cthulhu, Ye Booke of Monstres II, 1995)

*Cthyhni ("In His Daughter's Darkling Womb", 1997)

Cthulhu's Heirs is an anthology of  Cthulhu Mythos fiction edited by Thomas M. K. Stratman and published by Chaosium in March 1994. Stratman describes it as "more than 20 writers' visions into the landscape of Lovecraft Country."

The stories mostly appeared for the first time in the collection, with the exceptions of  Hugh B. Cave's "The Death Watch" (1939), Ramsey Campbell's "The Franklyn Paragraphs" (1973), Michael D. Winkle's "Typo" (1987), and Arthur William and Lloyd Breach's "The Return of the White Ship" (1989). 

Cthulhu's Heirs won the Origins Award for Best Game-Related Fiction of 1994.

fullContent:
Cthulhu's Minions is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author and filmmaker Byron Craft. The first in his Arkham Detective series, it was independently published as a chapbook in September 2015; both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator, a hardboiled detective in 1930s Arkham, is assigned to solve the case of a series of murders in which the victims - including his former partner - have had their faced ripped off. His investigations lead him to a scholarly priest who informs him that the perpetrators are in fact a breed of monstrous creatures known as Pilot Demons, whose function is to pave the road for the return of their masters, the Old Ones.

Tracking the creatures to the grave of Joseph Curwen, into which they have broken and stolen a quantity of the resurrection powder for which he was famed. Realising that the Pilot Demons will need holy water to complete their ritual, the Detective and a beat cop make their way to St. Matthew's church in time to prevent them from claiming their prize, but too late to save the elderly priest.

Making his way home for some much-needed rest, the Detective discovers that the Pilot Demons have tunnelled beneath his house to where the Old One rests. Hijacking a petrol truck, he uses it to destroy his home, the swarming Pilot Demons, and the slowly awakening Old One.

### Publication History
Since it’s first publication, Cthulhu's Minions has also appeared in the collection The Arkham Detective Collection Volume 1 in September 2017.

fullContent:
CthulhuPunk is a sci-fi horror role-playing game based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set during the mid 21st Century. The game is published by Steve Jackson Games and uses the GURPS system. It combines the Call of Cthulhu and Cyberworld, a cyberpunk game released earlier in 1993 by Steve Jackson Games. The political, economic, and social background of Cthulhupunk is that of Cyberworld and so is the technology used, requiring the use of that game in conjunction with CthulhuPunk. Steve Jackson Games first released CthulhuPunk in 1995.

### Setting
CthulhuPunk is set in the mid 21st century in a dystopian cyberpunk future. The United States is no longer the land of the free but a dictatorship. Global climate change has gotten worse, a plague devastated the world, and another plague turned Australia into a graveyard. Cyberwear is commonplace and netrunners use neural interfaces to link to cyberspace. It's a world in which man-portable laser and gauss weapons are new to the market. Geo-politically it's a multi-polar world and the United States is no longer a superpower much less a hyperpower. There are megacorps that are more powerful than many nations and several global criminal syndicates whose power can compare to that of a megacorp. The masses are entertained by gladiatorial sports, virtual reality, sensory chips, drugs, gambling, sensationalist news, pornography, and the suicide of snuff artists. In the background, hidden in the shadows is the Mythos. Outer Gods, Great Old Ones, and various races and cults that are corrupting human society, manipulating mankind, and/or bringing madness, terror, and/or death.

### History of Cyberworld

### World
*1997-2001 Tolliver's Disease, a retrovirus which between 1997-2001 infects over a third of humanity and kills over 1 billion.
*2006 - Global depression brought about by the "Grand Slam". Resulting in the crash of stock markets and the total collapse of weak economies, ending in 35-50% global unemployment.

### United States
*1998 - Hurricane Abner, the most powerful hurricane in recorded history devastate the American Southeast, the Caribbean, and Cuba.
*2000 - Hurricane Marko follows the same path as Abner and is equally destructive, bringing the reality of global warming.
*2007 - Martial law is imposed on a third of the United States as civil unrest is worsened by a record heat wave.
*2017 - The National Emergency Resource Coordinating Commission (NERCC) is established by President Patterson to suppress dissent in the United States.
*2024 - Flash riots erupt in the US, resulting in the declaration of martial law. President Patterson takes advantage of the unrest to establish a dictatorship, suspending presidential elections which have remained suspended 20 years later.
*2026 - Alaska becomes virtually autonomous, defying the US by establishing the Alaskan Free State.
*2027 - US peacefully annexes most of Mexico, though the five southernmost states oppose annexation.

fullContent:
CthulhuTech is a sci-fi horror role-playing game based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set during the 21st Century. The game is published by Sandstorm Productions. The game was first released in 2007. A revised edition using Kickstarter funding was released in July 2025.

### Setting
The game takes place in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos, in the late 21st Century (starting in 2085 AD). It is a setting which combines the horror and paranormal of the Cthulhu Mythos with science fiction (both the cyberpunk genre and the mecha and space opera of Japanese anime). It has borrowed elements from Cyberpunk 2020, Shadowrun, Guyver, Macross, and Neon Genesis Evangelion. The setting includes not only cybernetics (weapons, fashion, sensors, etc) and cyberspace (hackers, virtual reality, etc) but also robots of various sizes with pilots. Directed energy weapons of varying types are employed. Psionics, superhuman abilities (e.g. super strength), and magic-like powers are available. Strange, bizarre, or nightmarish beings (sentient and semi-sentient) and creatures from alien worlds and dimensions can be summoned. Monsters from the Mythos are faced in battle or encountered due to someone opening a portal. It is a horror game where humanity is fighting a desperate war for survival, one that they are losing and badly. Every human knows it at one level or another and they either live in despair and/or terror, escape the horror of the reality using drugs or other forms of entertainment, hold on desperately to the faith or hope, are living in denial, or rage against the night and refuse to go quietly.

### Factions
### Geo-political Factions
*New Earth Government: Is the human faction in this conflict. They are the only remaining human government in the world. All of the remaining nation-states, government agencies, and military forces are under its command. Due to the aliens and cults that pose an existential threat to humanity, the government has evolved into an oppressive one. Big brother is watching and the government manipulates its citizens. Among its citizens, they range from the fabulously rich and incredibly powerful to the dirt poor and barely surviving. Cthuloide Welten, which translates into English as Cthulhu Worlds, was a long-running German-language gaming magazine which focused on Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, which was published by Pegasus Spiele over the course of a decade .

### Overview
Published by traditional games manufacturer and distributor Pegasus Spiele, Cthuloide Welten ran for 21 regular issues and one special between 2001 and 2011 before being discontinued .

After its discontinuation, the vacuum left by Cthuloide Welten was taken up by its fan base who founded the zine Cthulhus Ruf (Cthulhu's Call), a publication created by many of its predecessors' contributors, and which would become the official publication for the Deutsche Lovecraft Gesellschaft (German Lovecraft Society) in 2014 .

Cthylla (also known as The Kraken or The Secret One) is a Great Old One from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was first mentioned in Brian Lumley's novel The Transition of Titus Crow.

### Background
Cthylla is the youngest progeny of Cthulhu and his androgynous mate Idh-yaa. She came from the star Xoth, but now dwells on Earth in Yhe, where she is guarded by Cthulhu's minions. Cthylla is destined to give birth to Great Cthulhu again after he is destroyed in the distant future. She is considered essential for Cthulhu's plans, and is thus vigilantly guarded by countless Yuggya and Deep Ones.

She is also called "The Secret One" because the cult tries to hide all information about the goddess, most famously by defacing the Columns of Geph. Her legend is dimly recorded in Greek Myth as "Scylla".

Project X is used in an attempt to kill Cthylla with a subterranean atomic bomb. She is wounded and escapes, and Cthulhu's retribution is a vastly magnified repeat of the events in the short story "The Call of Cthulhu". (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

Cthylla has the appearance of a gigantic, red-bodied, black-ringed, and six-eyed octopus with small wings. Like her father, she is able to alter her body-proportions at will, such as by enlarging her wings to enable her to fly. While she normally has eight arms like any octopus, she can extrude or retract additional ones at will (she has been known to sport as many as twelve arms). Each arm is equipped with dozens of razor-sharp claws, each about five inches in length. (: "In His Daughter's Darkling Womb")

Cthylla was captured by researchers who mistakenly believed her to be a rare specimen of a previously undiscovered octopus species. For the sake of preserving and studying the species, they attempt to impregnate her through artificial self-insemination. (: "In His Daughter's Darkling Womb")

Cthylla also appeared in a more humanoid form or avatar as a possible bride for Hastur. (: "In the Hall of the Yellow King")

### In Other Media
*Cthylla is a playable character in the fighting game Chaos Code, taking the form of a magical girl. She is described in-game as Cthulhu's daughter and the queen of the sea. Her attacks are named "Phantom of Yog-Sothoth", "The Hound of Tindalos", "Wind-Walking Ithaqua Upper", "The Ring of Papaloi", "Tulzscha", "Interstellar Flight Hastur", "Game of Shoggoth", "Flame of Fire Vampires", "Shadow of the Dagon", "The Black Goat's Sabbath", "Incarnation of Darkness" (which summons Nyarlathotep), and "The Call of Great Father".
*Cthylla is the main catalyst of the Lovecraft-based open world game The Sinking City, in which she slumbers beneath the flooded fishing town of Oakmont, not too distant from Innsmouth.
*Cthylla's name inspired that of a character in the Digimon franchise, Cthyllamon.

fullContent:
Cubicle 7 Entertainment is an Irish publishing company specialising in roleplaying games, although they also produce a handful of card and board games. Established in 2006, Cubicle 7 publish a wide range of tie-in roleplaying games, from Warhammer to Doctor Who to The One Ring, and also provide production and distribution services for several small press companies, including Arc Dream Publishing.

With regards to this wiki, Cubicle 7 are most notable for the supplements for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game which they produced under licence, foremost among them the Cthulhu Britannica line which focuses on the Mythos in the British Isles, and World War Cthulhu, which covers adventures taking place during World War II. In 2010, Cubicle 7 released the eNnie Award-winning The Laundry, a game based on Charles Stross's series of Mythos/spy thriller novels. They have also released a small amount of tie-in fiction.

Cubicle 7's licence to produce Call of Cthulhu material expired in 2017. Since then, the rights to all of their Call of Cthulhu sourcebooks have reverted to Chaosium . As of January 2024, these books remain out of print.

The Cult of Glaaki is a fictional group of humans and undead created by Ramsey Campbell for his 1964 short story "The Inhabitant of the Lake".

### Overview
Established at some point before 1865, whether the Cult of Glaaki is an actual cult in the strictest sense of the word is up for debate, as the group has been for the most part mentally enslaved by the Great Old One Glaaki in order to have them do his bidding. Their main purpose appears to be the recording of the wisdom of their master in the collected volumes The Revelations of Glaaki, and "recruiting" small numbers of new members and zombie-like automatons. They appear to be in contact with the Tomb-Herd, another cult based in nearby Temphill.

The "leader" of the cult is one Thomas Lee, who ordered the construction of a small row of houses in a remote part of the Severn Valley which was then named Lakeside Terrace. This was to be their base of operations, close to the side of the unnamed lake which plays host to Glaaki. Dotted around the surrounding countryside are a number of stone sarcophagi which contain the undead servitors of Glaaki, former cultists who have fully succumbed to the Green Decay and are now unable to venture forth into the sunlight. 

### Outside of the Severn Valley
Although primarily associated with Ramsay Campbell's Severn Valley, according to some sources Glaaki is capable of manifesting in other bodies of water across the globe, and presumably some of these locales also support their own cult cells. 

### The Sesqua Valley
A cell of worshippers led by an ancient woman named Siobhain Cleary exists in the Sesqua Valley; Cleary is possibly also an avatar of Glaaki.

The Cult of Mhar is a religious organization introduced in the "Wake of the Watcher" supplement to the Pathfinder RPG.

### Information
Acolytes of the god Mhar congregate near volcanic areas and active fault lines, seeking to initiate geological events that open the correct rift. They believe that the birth of Mhar can be predicted by an increase in earthquakes and volcanic activity. They claim that when this occurs, Mhar will cover northern Avistan and eventually the entire Golarion with fire and ash.

Mhar's followers are rivals of Rovagugs, as they see them as brutish and myopic.

Its sacred colours are black and orange. Its symbol is a shattered triangular rune.

fullContent:
"Cult of Panacea" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Greek author Konstantine Paradias.

### Synopsis
A group of drones in service to Gla'aki maintain his city-starship whilst trading memories to while away the time. When a facet of the God-Cancer breaks through from another dimension and attempts to consume Gla'aki's home, the drones sacrifice themselves in an effort to allow their master time to retaliate. 

In the aftermath of the battle, the drones are rewarded with a home in The Green, a gestalt consciousness which plays host to all of the countless drones who have served Gla'aki over the previous millennia.

### Characters
* The Unnamed Narrator, a drone in service to Gla'aki.
* Tom-C, another drone, this one something akin to a priest to the others.
* Ralph-L, another drone.

### Publication History
"Cult of Panacea" was published in the thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Trivia
* The character of Tom-C May be intended to be artist Thomas Cartwright, one of the main characters in Ramsey Campbell’s short story "The Inhabitant of the Lake", the first appearance of Glaaki. In this story, Cartwright was pierced by one of Glaaki's spines before his death: this means that it is entirely possible that he was reanimated to serve the Great Old One after the conclusion.
* Unusually, "Cult of Panacea" portrays Gla'aki as being if not actually benevolent, at least not actively malicious, and suggests that it may in fact be keeping other, worse, entities at bay. Of course, this could also be interpreted as Gla'aki wishing to save the conquest of humankind for himself.

The Cult of the Bloody Tongue is an ancient African cult that worships the God of the Bloody Tongue, one of the avatars of Nyarlathotep (: Call of Cthulhu: Masks of Nyarlathotep).

### Description
This cult began its activity in western Kenya, but it spread throughout the continent and there is even the possibility that it has a presence in other places on Earth. While it is usually closed to non-African people, all Nyarlathotep worshipers are welcome to worship.

Anthropologist Nigel Blackwell wrote a book called Dark Cults of Africa in which some details about this cult are discussed. Thanks to this text, it is known that they perform rituals on the Mountain of Dark Wind, in the Aberdare Mountains, which include murders of people kidnapped in the vicinity, as well as beheadings and scarifications with the emblem of the cult. It is for this reason that the people who lived near the cult centers were terrified, especially when the colonial governments (back in 1928) ignored the matter, putting it down to simple tribal brawls.

The most important of its celebrations is the orgiastic ritual once every five years, in which its deity manifests itself, causing terrible storms in the area. These rituals are led by a high priestess, chosen at age 14 and trained in the magical arts on Mountain of the Black Wind itself by inhuman servants of Nyarlathotep. As for the followers, those who perform the sacrifices wear a red headscarf as a reference to their god, using a machete as a weapon.

### The Cult in New York
Many of its members are Kenyan illegal immigrants who have forged American citizenship documents. However, in recent years, their ranks have swelled from degenerate elements of New York's slums, and race is no longer a major prerequisite for membership. The name of the sect comes from one of the aspects of Nyarlathotep in which it shows a blood-red tentacle instead of a face. They have headquarters in a Harlem store that sells African tribal paraphernalia. The rites take place in the cellar, which has been suitably enlarged for such use. The shop is run by Silas N'Kwane, while the sect's sorcerer is Mukumga N'Dari. Assassins of the Bloodtongue often use the pranga (an African long machete) in their attacks, although American members have sometimes used pistols. The assassins or executioners of the sect wear a terrifying-looking cap, with a red band that hangs from the forehead.

* Mukunga M’Dari: High Priest of the Cult of the Bloody Tongue in his New York branch. This powerful enemy enjoys the unspeakable eliminating the adversaries of his god. The Cult of the Darkhold, also known as the Chthonic Brotherhood and the Darkholders, is a fictional organisation in the Marvel universe.

### Organization
The Cult of the Darkhold is made up of men and women of power and position, who joined to acquire power and/or wealth, and stay in the organization to keep what they have acquired or get more of it. During meetings, the upper tier of/inner circle wears robes and demonic-looking masks which may have built-in weapons.

The cult has access to secret bases, all types of vehicles (land, air, and sea), and cutting edge technology (e.g., laser blasters). It employs heavily armed security teams (with body armor), hit squads, teams of ninjas, and contract killers.

### Background
The Cult of the Darkhold traces back to the Thurian Age, as early as 18,500 BC. It started out as the followers of the dark sorcerer Thulsa Doom. After his death, they used the Darkhold to create the first vampire, Varnae, though they were unable to control him. Varnae turned several of the Darkholders into vampires. The survivors were able to escape with the Darkhold before Atlantis sank.

Its members worship the Elder God Chthon (their allies, the Broodlings of Chthon, worshiped him as part of and along with the Great Old Ones) and/or they have joined the cult to achieve wealth or power. The powerful medieval sorceress Morgan le Fay is a member of the organization and the legendary 500+ year old Romanian vampire, Dracula, is likewise an ally.

In the modern era they have been opposed by the Darkhold Redeemers, the Avengers, the Midnight Sons, the X-Men, Spider-Man, Thor, Wolverine, and Captain America.

The Cult of the Sand Bat is a racially organized sect for the worship of the Father of All Bats, an avatar of Nyarlathotep feared in Australia since ancient times by Aboriginals. This cult had become extinct, but investigations carried out have come to the surface the knowledge necessary for the resurrection of the sect.

The Father of All Bats is a horror that arises from the Dream Time and is one of the enemies of the Rainbow Serpent. It is said to manifest in the form of a sandstorm arising from a cave in the sky; among the Kartudjara, in whose original territory lies the city of the Great Race of Yith, the black silhouette is known as the Dark Wing. Further east, the Bindubi refer to this being as the Face Eater.

For the most part, sectarians are recruited from the slums of Sydney and Melbourne; based on the original works, there is a subtle personality test that, conducted by trusted assistants, must be passed by every aspiring sectarian. There is also a small Aboriginal clan in Australia that is in charge of spying on all intruders approaching the city of the Great Race and of getting innocent victims from among the aborigines living west of the Pilbarra gold mines. In total, there are several hundred cultists of the Sand Bat throughout Australia. (: Call of Cthulhu: Masks of Nyarlathotep).

### Symbol
The symbol of the cult is an open spiral. A regular part of the rites is that their members meditate and are hypnotized before a representation of the open spiral that is being rotated by the acolyte who directs the ritual. There is also a sign of recognition: both hands open, palms extended outward and thumbs cross and arch, mimicking wings and fangs.

### Notable members
*Robert Huston: psychiatrist who participated in the Carlyle Expedition and priest of the Sand Bat.

### Actions
The crimes are carried out with the club of the cult, a polished bar of eucalyptus wood covered with sharp nails. Aboriginals carry clubs embedded with thorns, teeth, and bat claws. The founder of the sect, a megalomaniac, is the only priest. He has created half-priests (acolytes), each of whom may use a few spells. The acolytes are responsible for making psychological reports on the applicants.

Cult of the Spider Queen is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author and editor S. A. Sidor. It is the fifth volume of the Arkham Horror Fiction series. It was published on December 7th, 2021. It is a standalone novel. Paperback, digital and audio editions were released. It was adapted by Graphic Audio into an audio production with an entire cast of voice actors.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Andy Van Nortwick is a cub reporter working for the Arkham Advertiser when he steals an unmarked package that reveals former silent screen star turned director, Maude Brion, is still alive. She disappeared in the Amazon searching for the elusive Spider Queen supposedly worshiped by natives. What follows is a dark and steamy trip with female adventuress Ursula Downs as well as an untrustworthy crew. Human greed and treachery prove as much an impediment as the forces that hail not from this universe.

### Characters
*Andy Van Nortwick: A reporter for the Arkham Advertiser who interviewed Alden Oakes from The Last Ritual. Stealing a package not meant for him, he sees his chance to become a big reporter in arranging an expedition to rescue Maude Brion. However, he quickly finds himself over his head.
*Iris Bennett Reed: A female anthropologist who lost her husband on a previous expedition to try and find the Spider Queen. She manipulates Andy's desire for fame to fund a second expedition. She alone suspects that the Spider Queen may not be of this Earth.
*Maude Brion: A silent screen star turned adventuress, she ventured down to the Amazon to create a documentary about the mythical Spider Queen. Disappearing and presumed dead, an unmarked film reel indicates that she, in fact, survived.
*Ursula Downs: The famous Explorer card from the Arkham Horror game. She is the world's greatest adventuress and the one that Iris Bennett Reed hires to head the expedition.
*Jake Williams: The companion to Ursula Downs and her closest ally in exploring the world. He is more cautious and conflict averse than her, frequently warning her against rash action.

Cultes des Goules, or Cults of Ghouls, is a fictional book of black magic. In the Cthulhu Mythos, it is said to have been written by François Honoré-Balfour (Comte d'Erlette) in 1702. It was published in France and later denounced by the Church. Only a handful of copies are in existence. One of the known copies was kept for 91 years in an arcane library of the Church of Starry Wisdom in Providence, Rhode Island. After Robert Blake's mysterious death in 1935, Doctor Dexter removed the grimoire and added it to his library.

### Description
The book, a 600-page quarto, goes into details about the existence of necromancy and necrophilia in France at the beginning of the 18th century. According to the author, there was a society of tomb robbers and grave robbers, with various blasphemous rites and practices. Members of the society called themselves "goules". A person wishing to join the society must perform necrophagy at the initiation ceremony. Other acts include divination by reanimating the dead and necrophilia. (: The Keeper's Companion)

The French witch covens are also mentioned, along with their ties to a secret society of subhumans (ghouls) inhabiting the catacombs of Paris. The Great Old One Nyogtha is also referred to frequently, as is the Outer God Shub-Niggurath, who is described as being linked to werewolves and other lycanthropes (: The Keeper's Companion). There are also tales of the Yeti (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana).

Also included are some prophecies, a few necromancy spells and ways to contact different beings such as Nyogtha, Shub-Niggurath and her dark youngs, ghouls and byakhees. Simple phrases in ghoul's language are translated and included. The Voorish Sign is also mentioned. Reading the book frequently may alter the physiology of the reader to be more ghoul-like. (: The Keeper's Companion)

The book was written based on an earlier manuscript by a d'Erlette predecessor, Antoine-Marie Augustin de Montmorency-les-Roches, who due to his involvement in the Affair of the Poison was vanished by the king's order in 1681 (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana). The manuscript was copied and distributed secretly since 1865 (: The Keeper's Companion).

### History
Cultes des Goules was written by François Honoré-Balfour in 1702, then privately printed and circulated in Paris in the early month of 1703. shortDefinition: "Curiosity" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by author Adam Heine. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.  ### Synopsis A manned mission is sent to distant Mars to investigate imagery sent ba...
fullContent:
"Curiosity" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by author Adam Heine. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
A manned mission is sent to distant Mars to investigate imagery sent back by the Curiosity rover which suggests evidence of an ancient civilisation. On the outward journey, the crew are beset by nightmarish dreams and an unexplained space walk accident which drives one member insane and leaves the ship with a depleted power supply, forcing them to continue to their destination. 

Upon arriving on the planet, the lander is attacked by a bizarre creature, but the landing party is able to repel the beast. Making their way into a series of caverns which run beneath the surface of Olympus Mons in search of the rover and its power supply, they encounter a vast chamber filled with what appears to be the statues of three-legged tree people. Glyphs carved into the cavern walls depict the history of these entities who believed themselves to be the children of some great Mother which pushed them from world to world, consuming all in their path before encountering Earth and a species of "tubular beings on spindly legs, like a bacteriophage," who successfully repelled their assaults. 

At this point, the tree statues begin to animate, and herd the survivors deeper into the catacombs, towards an enormous maw. Fortunately, the distraction caused by the reappearance of the creature which attacked the lander and the subsequent battle between it and the tree people allows the two remaining crew to escape, although they are forced to leave the power cell behind. They manage to launch the lander off-planet, but realise that they will soon die from lack of power and oxygen. Their final act is to send a transmission begging those listening on Earth to stay away from the Red Planet. 

### Behind the Mythos
When the first crew member is driven insane, she repeatedly chants a phrase of seeming gibberish containing the phrase Shub-Niggurath. Additionally, although never directly named as such, the tree people are implied to be the Dark Young, and Olympus Mons is strongly hinted to be the Outer God itself. 

The "tubular beings on spindly legs, like a bacteriophage" would appear to resemble descriptions of the Elder Things. This is reinforced by the abilities of the creature which attacked the lander, which recalls the protoplasmic mimicking powers possessed by Shoggoths, a species which spent long years in service to the the Elder Things. 

### Trivia
* The Curiosity rover is a real-world space venture launched by NASA in November 2011, making Martian planetfall in August 2012. Despite having only been designed for a two-year mission, as of December 2025 the vehicle is still active and collecting data.

The Curse Whistle is a fictional artefact in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was created by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu RPG. It is described as a magical musical pipe that can induce horror and madness through sound. (: The Grand Grimoire of Cthulhu Mythos Magic)

### Description
The Curse Whistle is a musical pipe made from owl bones, but sometimes human bones are used instead. It is created not by craftsmanship, but through a spell that lasts at least a night. The spell can only be cast on the first full moon following the Summer Solstice. (: The Grand Grimoire of Cthulhu Mythos Magic)

Otherworldly tunes can be played from the pipe, causing nearby creatures within earshot to go insane. The player of the pipes, while having a much smaller chance, can also go temporary insane and be locked into playing the tunes non-stop. The pipe can also be used to cause visual and auditory hallucinations on a single target. (: The Grand Grimoire of Cthulhu Mythos Magic)

Cxaxukluth (Ksaksa-Kluth, Illimitable Androgynous Desire) is an Outer God and is the offspring of Azathoth by spontaneous fission. According to at least one genealogical chart, its progeny are Hziulquoigmnzhah, Ghisguth, and Tulu. It is described as an androgynous being, capable of reproducing asexually. Via Ghisguth, it is the grandparent of Tsathoggua.

Cxaxukluth dwells on Yuggoth. Its immediate family lived with it for a while, but soon left because of its cannibalistic appetites.

The Second Epistle of Eibon unto his Disciples, or The Apocalypse of Eibon reports that Cxaxukluth divided itself into a masculine and feminine aspects, the masculine was called Nug, the feminine being called Yeb, and then produced their various offspring together. This text also refers to Cxaxukluth as the "Illimitable Androgynous Desire" prior to the split.

There is additional speculation that Ptmâk and Cxaxukluth may have only been the Hyperborean names for Nug and Yeb. Cxaxukluth is probably Yeb (: "The Second Epistle of Eibon unto his Disciples, or The Apocalypse of Eibon" , Robert M. Price is included in The Book of Eibon (Chaosium, 2002)). Ptmâk has been identified as the immediate parent of Cthulhu (a.k.a. Tulu), which might mean that Ptmâk and Cxaxukluth either mated with each other to spawn Cthulhu, or are merely different names or avatars for the same entity.

### Behind the Mythos
The creature was invented, outside of fiction, in the letters by Clark Ashton Smith to Robert H. Barlow, and published in the article "The Family Tree of the Gods" in The Acolyte fanzine (issue 7, Summer 1944). It was also featured in the works of Richard L. Tierney.

fullContent:
Cy Morgan is a character created by American comic book creator Michael Alan Nelson for his Boom! Studios Cthulhu Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. He made his debut appearance in the first issue in 2007.

### Description
Cy is an average American man who as an adult studied at Arkham's Miskatonic University. He previously lived with and was engaged to a woman named Jordan, but their relationship ended with her supernaturally-motivated suicide.

### History
Cy and his sister Sarah were raised by their uncle Walt after the death of their parents at a young age, and was fortunate enough to be accepted to study at Miskatonic University.

Later in life, Walt killed himself in front of Cy and his fiancé Jordan, leaving little but questions and a stack of occult artefacts in his wake. This prompted Cy to investigate what had happened to Walt, a journey which took him to the Dreamlands, led to a confrontation with the evil Mr. Arkham and, eventually, resulted in insanity and incarceration in a mental health facility : Fall of Cthulhu Volume 1: The Fugue).

Later, Cy was freed by the Harlot and Lucifer, and was directly responsible for putting an end to Nyarlathotep's scheming, although this involved travelling to the Court of Azathoth, an action which ultimately resulted in his death (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 4: Godwar; Fall of Cthulhu Volume 5: Apocalypse).

Cyäegha is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Eddy C. Bertin for his short story "Darkness, My Name Is".

### Background
Cyäegha, also known as The Destroying Eye or The Waiting Dark,  is a deity characterized by its supreme nihilism and utter contempt for all things. The entity appears as a great, black-bodied, green eye surrounded by a mass of tentacles. Cyäegha is served by toad-like monsters known as the Nagäae (possibly a derivative of "Nagae").

Cyäegha has existed since the dawn of time and sleeps in a vast cavern under the mountain Dunkelhügel, the "Dark Hill", in Germany. The inhabitants of the nearby farming village of Freihausgarten are descended from cult that once worshipped Cyäegha. Cyäegha's worshippers draw upon the deity for vitality but also greatly fear awakening the god for its wrath is said to be terrible.

### Cult
Cyäegha's cult became active in the town of Freihausgarten in the 17th century and remained so well into the 19th century. In 1860, the cult was disbanded by a young priest who died while battling it. Even so, once a month on the night of the full moon, the descendants of the former cultists are drawn to Dark Hill by a hypnotic, telepathic pull from Cyäegha. Once there, they are compelled to climb Dark Hill and perform a ritual that both appeases and binds Cyäegha. However, despite performing this ritual every month without fail, the villagers are not even aware that they practice the rite, and continue to fear the mountain and ordinarily avoid it.

### The five Vaeyen
Cyäegha is both protected and imprisoned by five lesser demons known as the Vaeyen. They are "The Green Moon", "The White Fire Which Is Darker Than The Night", "The Winged Woman", "The White Dark Which Is More Red Than The Fire" and "The Black Light". The spirits of these guardians are contained in five vulturine statues which Cyäegha's worshippers use to keep their god in check.

### Other aspects
Cyäegha is an earth elemental and is said to be a cousin to Nyogtha, another earth elemental. Cyäegha is also believed to be related to the Great Old One Othuyeg, because each appear alike and have similar habits. Like all the other earth elementals, Cyäegha is adversely affected by the Ankh or Crux Ansata, the Vach-Viraj ritual, and the Tikkoun Elixir. References to Cyäegha are found in the Necronomicon, the Unaussprechlichen Kulten, the R'lyeh Text and its German translation Liyuhh, the Cthäat Aquadingen, and a few more obscure grimoires.

### In Other Media
*Cyäegha appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
*Cyäegha appears in the mobile game Yurudora, during the Cthulhu Festival event.
*In the television series Ultraman Taiga, the kaiju Night Fang appears to be at least partially inspired by Cyäegha.
*In the Mighty Morphin Power Rangers Anniversary

Cybil is a hero in the fictional Army of Darkness universe which expands the world of the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was created in 2009 by Mike Raicht. She first appeared in issue #22 of the 2nd volume of Army of Darkness by Dynamite Entertainment.

### Background
Cybil is a woman who was adopted as a child and in her early teens became possessed by a demon which used her as a gateway for other demonic spirits who had escaped hell and possessed others in her community. She was incarcerated in an asylum along with the other possessed patients. Ash Williams and the werewolf Brad searching for the Protectors of the world, identified her as a fellow Protector. They were able to free her and the others from demonic possession.

Cybil joined them in their mission to find other Protectors, becoming a member of the League of Light. Alongside her fellow superheroes, she fought the forces of the Necronomicon. Having failed to prevent the Apocalypse and the end of mankind, the team built a time machine to send two members back in time (Cybil and Brad) with Ash's spirit. They were successful in preventing the possession of Ash by Hell's Prophet thereby altering the timeline. Cybil and Brad disappeared, and the new timeline's Cybil was freed of her demon and the asylum years earlier by this timeline's Brad.

Cynothoglys (also known as The Mortician God and She Whose Hand Embalms) is a fictional entity created by Thomas Ligotti for his 1986 short story "The Prodigy of Dreams".

### Overview
Cynothoglys being appears as a shapeless, multiform entity with a single arm used for catching those who summoned her, and bringing them a painless, ecstatic death. 

In ancient times, she once held a small cult in Italy, which paid her homage rather than worshiping her, since actual worship would be the same as summoning the god. They considered her to be no mere Cloacina (a Roman goddess of sewers and purification, associated with Venus), but the mortician of all creatures, even the gods themselves.

Cytharion, also known as Cytharion of the Seven Suns, is a mystical realm located somewhere "beyond the Milky Way and the Arinurian Streams", mentioned in the story "The Crawling Chaos" by H. P. Lovecraft. Cytharion is somewhere adjacent to the realm of Teloe, both of which are described as beautiful utopias inhabited by benevolent deities and favored mortals.

Cytharion and Teloe were part of an apocalyptic vision of the future experienced by the unnamed narrator of the story under the influence of opium, so their literal existence may or may not be taken for granted in the context of the Mythos.

### Behind the Mythos
According to The Whisperer in Darkness and other sources, Nyarlathotep also dwells in a "world of Seven Suns", which is named Abbith in the expanded Mythos. However, Nyarlathotep is not mentioned in "The Crawling Chaos" (despite the story's title matching one of his most common aliases).

shortDefinition: The D-Void is a Lovecraftian extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of the Transformers comics by IDW Publishing, appearing as a major antagonist in the Heart of Darkness storyline. As an eldritch tentacle monster trapped in an alternat...
fullContent:
The D-Void is a Lovecraftian extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of the Transformers comics by IDW Publishing, appearing as a major antagonist in the Heart of Darkness storyline. As an eldritch tentacle monster trapped in an alternate dimension, it appears to be at least partially inspired by some entities from the Cthulhu Mythos, including Cthulhu himself. 

### Background
The D-Void is a malevolent undead entity that lives in the Dead Universe, the only inhabitant in that realm which lurks on the far side of every living world. D-Void is the personification of the Dead Universe, whose form is that of a vast mass of giant tentacles and huge eyes. It consumes other universes to satisfy its hunger and to expand the borders of the Dead Universe, giving it more life to feed upon. It is an incredibly powerful being that is able to control the minds of sentient robots, return the spark to a deceased Cybertronian, and feed on Cybertronians by draining their energy. 

His universe can be accessed by various points, all of which are related to death and decay. Anyone who crosses over from a living universe to the Dead Universe becomes undead themselves, unable to survive for long outside of the Dead Universe. D-Void itself is unable to leave the Dead Universe without external assistance, which it does by tricking sentient beings into entering his realm (e.g. a trans-dimensional portal disguised as a lake) or an aspect of it in the material universe, the Heart of Darkness (the Matrix of Leadership's dark mirror).

In its assault on Cybertron, it entranced Galvatron's Sweeps and Megatron's Decepticon forces to merged into the "Deceptigod" (All-Who-Are-One), a monstrous titan which was capable of only a single thought: to destroy. With a single sweep of its arm, it destroyed Omega Supreme's rocket section. The only Decepticons that were able to resist the summon to merge where Megatron and Shockwave, who helped hold off the colossus, while Optimus Prime and the Autobots moved against Galvatron. Megatron was able to defeat the titan.

Optimus Prime tried to stop Galvatron from using the Heart of Darkness to destroy Cybertron but actually had the planet be used as a portal into the living universe. Galvatron succeeded and D-Void arrived in the universe, only for Optimus Prime to use the Matrix of Leadership to destroy D-Void and save the universe.

Desmond Francis Lewis (born 18 January 1948) is a prolific British horror author and editor who has written several works of Lovecraftian fiction. He was a regular contributor to the now-defunct fanzine Cthulhu Cultus, and has had numerous collections of his works released through various publishing houses.

Amongst his editorial credits is the magazine Nemonymous, a science fiction, fantasy and horror anthology series. It was unusual in that it did not credit the stories until the following issue, a setup intended to remove the reader's prejudices against particular authors .

fullContent:
Daryl Hutchinson (born November 28, 1955) is a Michigan-based illustrator and designer who has produced book covers, illustrations, and album covers. The majority of his work is based on the writings of H. P. Lovecraft. His most notable work is The Lovecraft Tarot first published in a limited edition of 500 copies in 1997 by Mythos Books. A second edition of 1000 copies was published on October 31, 2002. With the dissolution of Mythos Books, a third edition was published by Black Moon Publishing in 2024. Each edition features different art.

His first art sale was to Easyriders biker magazine in 1977. As a graphic artist, he worked for Ford Motor Company and several graphic art studios, creating illustrations for educational books for children. Although never a full time artist in the horror and fantasy field, he has supported small press publishers such as “Crypt of Cthulhu”, “Cyaegha” and others.

In 1988, Fantagraphics Press published the Edgar Allan Poe-inspired magazine The Tell Tale Heart, a collaborative effort with his artist brother Joe. Daryl and Joe created cover art for the Detroit tabloid Fun Magazine in the 1980s. Lovecraft-inspired works include the 1991 comic H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu: The Whisperer in Darkness, by Millennium Publishing. In 2002, Daryl worked with close friend and noted Mythos writer Stan Sargent to create cover art for Sargent’s books The Taint of Lovecraft, and Ancient Exhumations. Artwork based on the writings of Clark Ashton Smith and Robert E. Howard remain unpublished with plans for an art portfolio in the future.

In 2023, Daryl worked with Oniricous lead singer and guitarist Joaquín Granero on cover art for the album Los Cultos del Ghoul, by the Spanish death metal band Oniricous, born from the ashes of GHUL. The band is devoted to the works of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
### Case No. 01: "The Haunting"
While hanging out in a classroom, Azana Hatsumi had a discussion with her friends Muu and Kurumi Kuruya, involving an urban legend about a faceless killer living in the abandoned hospital on the outskirts of Y City; leading to them investigating the area. Upon breaking into the hospital, the faceless killer seemingly murdered Muu by impaling her head with a katana before facing off against Kurumi. Failing to run away, Azana tripped over and tried to call the police but was interrupted by a faceless version of Muu grabbing her arm. The faceless killer saved Azana by impaling Muu's head again, taking off his mask to show that he is a man with a face underneath.

Muu quickly recovered, revealing her true identity to be Yoguruma Mugen, a Freak known as "Infinite Chromata" that possesses the power of the evil god Yog-Sothoth, who had been tampering with Azana's memories. Kurumi was also being manipulated by Mugen, transforming into a monstrous form and using his tentacles to attack the man, whose real name was Narukami Chikage. In retaliation, Narukami used the Mask of Nyarlathotep to take the form of the Haunter; defeating Kurumi shortly afterwards. Meanwhile, Azana discovered the Asylum, a medical institution for the prevention of "Hell Hazards".

Amongst the Freaks was Kurumi, who had been infected by the "Color" of the sea god Cthulhu and turned into "Spawn of the Deep". Meanwhile, Narukami got into a fight with Mugen; although Narukami managed to chop her head off, Mugen was unfazed and initiated her ability "Embryo Phantasm" by opening her left eye.

Sent back to the classroom where it all began, Azana and Mugen were reliving the conversation they had earlier before being interrupted by Narukami, restoring Azana's memories of everything that just happened. Narukami explained that Mugen used her ability to warp time and space to drag them into her dimension, as well as adapting Azana's past to her needs. Once sealed away by the Asylum, Mugen broke free with her 13 Relics of Evil Gods, also known as "Artifacts" that reproduced "Color", being scattered throughout Y City. Although Narukami managed to retrieve Kurumi's Artifact, the Asylum's goal was to defeat the remaining twelve Freaks hidden in the city and collect all the Artifacts.

Despite only having access to the arm of his Deus Machina, Crow continued to fight the dragon using the Scimitar of Barzai, with the dragon transforming into a smaller flying form in retaliation. Crow fires the power of Cthugha from his pistol but the dragon was too fast to get hit by the attack, leading to Crow using Ithaqua instead, which was able to home in on the target and seemingly destroy it. Shortly afterwards, the dragon regenerated due to the woman using a revival incantation from the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis.

D'endrrah, also known as The Divinity, is a fictional entity created by Pierre Zaplotny for the Call of Cthulhu scenario "La Terza Bocca di D'endrrah", featured in issue #46 of the French role-playing magazine Casus Belli. The character also played a pivotal role in Bryn Fortey's 2021 short story "Beneath the Pimple", published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine.

### Overview
D'endrrah is a shape shifting Outer God who possesses a great hunger for living worlds. It often manifests in the form of a gigantic squid-like monster or a cloud of heavy, smoky, organic matter with millions of teeth, which wanders the cosmos endlessly to devour any world it stumbles across.(source?) 

D'endrrah was defeated by Cthulhu when it threatened to devour Earth sometime before the time of ancient Egypt. Stories are also told of the Egyptian god Ra, the god of the sun, who fought this monster in its guise as Apep from his flying chariot.(source?)

Another story tells of how D'endrrah acted on behalf of Yog-Sothoth in a plan to expose and imprison the duplicitous god Olkoth, sealing it beneath a hill in rural Wales. (: "Beneath the Pimple")

The entity is heavily inspired by C. L. Moore's short story "Shambleau", in which a being or race of beings from another time or dimension appear to people in the shape of a beautiful woman to feed on them, heavily hinted to be the origin of both the myths of medusa and vampires.(source?)

### In Other Media
*"Voice of D'endrrah" was a card in the now-defunct Hex: Shards of Fate digital battle card game.

fullContent:
"Daddy, Daddy" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Australian games designer and author Penelope Love. It was published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014. It is one of the few stories in the collection to feature a contemporary setting.

### Synopsis
An unnamed young woman, under the partial control of her deceased father, must travel aboard the faded Orient Express to Istanbul in order to enact a ritual which will result in her father's resurrection. The woman has come to the realisation that this will involve the man taking possession of her body while her consciousness is relegated to the dead saltes which sustain him, but his strength of will is, for the most part, too much for her to overcome.

Many years of forced study under the insane man, however, has given her the inkling of an idea on how to avoid this horrible fate, and she has been working on concealing her innermost thoughts from him. Although she realises that there may be a price to pay for her act, upon reaching the site of the intended ritual she offers up her father's saltes as a sacrifice to the dark being, and escapes into the night. 

Thinking herself free, as the woman attempts to leave Istanbul and begin her life anew, she is horrified to see the Skinless One appear and demand it’s payment for helping to free her from her father's control… 

### Mythos Connections
In addition to the obvious similarities with H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Thing on the Doorstep" - an evil magician attempting to exchange bodies with his daughter to prolong his own lifespan - the story is prefaced with a quote from the story: "Why did he curse that his daughter wasn’t a son? […] what devilish  exchange was perpetrated in the house of horror where that  blasphemous monster had his trusting, weak-willed, half-human  child at his mercy?" The Essential Saltes utilised by the protagonist's father appeared in another of Lovecraft’s stories about practitioners of the dark arts, The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, in which they are used to resurrect the dead.

The Skinless One is an avatar of Nyarlathotep created for Chaosium's Horror on the Orient Express supplement for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game; its obsidian blade, the Mims Sahis, which the entity uses to take its payment, is also featured.

### Trivia
* The title of the story is taken from the final line in Sylvia Plath's poem "Daddy," "Daddy, daddy, you bastard, I’m through" which is included as a preface to "Daddy, Daddy."

Dagon is a deity from Mesopotamian mythology who was incorporated into H. P. Lovecraft's fiction in the short story "Dagon", eventually becoming a prominent element of the Cthulhu Mythos, where he is often referred to as Father Dagon. In the stories of Lovecraft and others, he presides over the Deep Ones, a hidden amphibious humanoid race that resides in the Earth's oceans, and is worshipped by the Esoteric Order of Dagon, a secret cult based in Innsmouth.  He is the consort of Mother Hydra.

In the real world, Dagon or Dagan was a deity worshipped in Mesopotamia, particularly in what is now Syria. He may have been connected with fertility or grain. He appears in the Hebrew Bible as a leading god of the Philistines, notably in Judges 16, where Samson brings down the temple of Dagon where he is being held captive. The similarity of Dagon to the Hebrew word dag ("fish") led to a depiction of the deity as half man, half fish, like a merman, and to a misconception in Western culture of Dagon as a kind of sea god.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In the Lovecraft story "Dagon," written in 1917, the narrator finds ancient carvings that depict humanoid creatures with webbed hands and bulging eyes, at least one of whom is almost as large as a whale. He then sees a similar  creature like that in the flesh--a "vast, Polyphemus-like...monster of nightmares," with "gigantic scaly arms." The creature is never identified as Dagon in the story, though he does seek out a "celebrated ethnologist" to ask "peculiar questions regarding the ancient Philistine legend of Dagon, the Fish-God."

The people of Innsmouth in The Shadow Over Innsmouth worship at the Esoteric Order of Dagon, and according  to Zadok Allen are required to take the three Oaths of Dagon. (Allen at one point rants about "Dagon an’ Ashtoreth—Belial an’ Beëlzebub—Golden Caff an’ the idols o’ Canaan an’ the Philistines.") The faithful in the order, Allen says, will not die but instead "go back to the Mother Hydra an’ Father Dagon what we all come from onct." To which he adds, "Iä! Cthulhu fhtagn!". Additionally, Robert Olmstead comes to believe that someday the Deep Ones will "rise again for the tribute Great Cthulhu craved [...] a city greater than Innsmouth next time". This suggests that Dagon functions as a deity in the Innsmouth community, but whether he is supposed to be a distinct entity or merely Cthulhu referred to with a biblical name is unclear.

### In the Expanded Mythos
In the works of Lin Carter, Dagon and Hydra are identified as the Lesser Old Ones who serve Cthulhu, and lead all the Deep Ones who serve him. (: "The Horror in the Gallery", "Behind the Mask")

In "Dagon's Bell", by Brian Lumley, the character David Parker claims that Cthulhu is merely another name for Dagon (and so is Neptune).

Dagon is a 2001 Spanish film loosely based on H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Synopsis
When two couples are shipwrecked off the coast of Spain, one of the couples is taken by Deep Ones while the other, Paul and Barbara, both make it to shore. Once there, Barbara is also taken, and although Paul manages to track her down - discovering a dark family secret along the way - he is unable to save her. Ultimately attempting suicide by fire, he is dragged off into the depths by a seductive hybrid, where he begins to realise his destiny.

### Behind the Mythos
Directed by Stuart Gordon with a screenplay from Dennis Paoli, Dagon was produced by Brian Yuzna, among others. It premiered in Spain on October 31 2001, 

### Trivia
*While The Shadow Over Innsmouth takes place on the shores of 1920s New England, Dagon moves the story to a more contemporary setting and takes place in Spain, the town being named Imboca in this interpretation of the story. The name Imboca is a subtle nod to Lovecraft’s Innsmouth, as the word in Spanish literally translates to "in your mouth."
*South African filmmaker Richard Stanley, writer and director of the 2019 adaptation Color Out of Space, made an appearance in Dagon as an uncredited Fish Monster.

fullContent:
"Dagon" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Armand Rosamilia. It forms the fourth part in his Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Synopsis
After young Tina and her boyfriend have an argument and split up while on a date in Keyport, she stumbles into Father Rocco, who enlists her in the battle against the Esoteric Order of Dagon. Together, the two rescue former biker thug Bones from the ruined basement in which he was trapped.

Elsewhere, the Order once again attempt to sacrifice Nicole Marsh in an attempt to awaken mighty Cthulhu and Matthew DiNardo, Tina's date, is captured by the deformed children which inhabit the tunnels beneath Keyport.

### Characters
*Tina, the highly-religious daughter of a church minister.
*Matthew DiNardo, a struggling author and Tina's devious boyfriend.
*Father Rocco, a devout priest.
*Harrison Marsh, a young man desperate to save his wife.
*Dylan Murphy, leader of the Keyport branch of the Esoteric Order of Dagon.
*Bones, a somewhat-reformed former criminal.
*Nicole Marsh, Harrison's wife.

### Publication History
"Dagon" was first published in the collection Keyport Cthulhu in November 2013.

shortDefinition: Dagon is a Lovecraftian extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of the Ben 10 animated television series. Despite its name being taken from that of Dagon, it is clearly more closely based on Cthulhu.  ### Background Dagon is a demonic en...
fullContent:
Dagon is a Lovecraftian extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of the Ben 10 animated television series. Despite its name being taken from that of Dagon, it is clearly more closely based on Cthulhu.

### Background
Dagon is a demonic entity from another dimension, an interdimensional conqueror who has conquered 100 dimensions. Its true form resembles that of a giant octopus with the face being mostly covered by brownish armor and its red eyes being framed by hooked projections. It has other forms including one of a giant serpentine octopus with a gigantic tentacle coming out of its back like a tail and another form in which it manifests itself as a huge dragon, complete with claws and wings. Its dragon form battled Sir George in ancient times, before he defeated it by cutting its heart out with the sword Ascalon and banishing Dagon to its home dimension.

As it is a being whose substance consists of power, it sees itself as a god who has the right to rule all other lifeforms, making him not only power hungry but arrogant, talking down to others and seeing most as nuisances at best. He does possess some honor, but only when dealing with the strong and likewise respects those with power. With a heart that possesses the power to reshape a universe, he is a nigh-omnipotent being. Among his powers are super strength, levitation, shapeshifting, weather control, breathing fire, optical laser beams, regeneration, teleportation, power bestowal, and transforming others. It can dominate others via mind control, resurrect the dead, and is knowledgeable when it comes to magic. Serving it are the Lucubra and, for a time, the galactic warlord Vilgax. As a supernatural entity, it is bound by the rules of magic.

### Lucubra
The Lucubra are animalistic creatures from Dagon's world that somewhat resemble lizards, who have a gelatinous body that is greyish green and whose faces have reddish teeth-like markings. They use their tentacles to feed off their victim's thoughts and to communicate with others. Once a person has been fed upon, they become their mindless servants which the Lucubra can send telepathic commands to. Lucubra are able to crawl up walls, have enhanced strength and agility, fire optical laser beams, and are immune to radiation. They vary in size, with the smallest being the size of a large dog and the largest being much larger than a human.

fullContent:
Dagon was a British fanzine which was released between 1983 and 1990, and ran for a total of 27 issues. Edited by the late Carl T. Ford, it initially focused on gaming content for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game; it later expanded to cover all forms of Lovecraftian and weird fiction, but never forgot it’s Call of Cthulhu roots.

Dagons run ended in June 1990, with Ford citing time constraints imposed by his day job as the main reason. Although there were rumours of relaunching the magazine (or perhaps another Lovecraft-related publication, the source is unclear) this never came to pass .

During the course of its run, Dagon was nominated for the British Fantasy Award in the Small Press/Independent category four times, achieving three wins in 1988, 1989, and 1990.

Contributors to Dagon included authors such as Neil Gaiman, Thomas Ligotti, Ramsey Campbell, T. E. D. Klein, Peter Cannon, Robert M. Price, S. T. Joshi, and artists such as Allen Koszowski, Dave Carson, and Gahan Wilson.

Dagon is a novel by Fred Chappell, first published in 1968. It blends the Southern Gothic and Lovecraftian elements--the latter signaled by the novel's epigraph, "Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthulhu R'lyeh wgah'nagl ftagn." Ultimately, whether the evil abundantly on display in the book is supernatural or not is left to the reader's imagination.

### Publication History
Dagon was first published in hardcover by Harcourt, Brace & World in 1968, and in paperback by St. Martin's Press in 1987. In that same year, St. Martin's included it as part of the hardcover edition of The Fred Chappell Reader, a paperback version of which was released by the publisher in 1990. Other paperback editions were published by Louisiana State University Press (2002) and Boson Books (2009). 

### Awards
Dagon was named best foreign book of the year by the French Academy in 1971.
