"Dagon" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft, written in July, 1917. It is one of the first stories he wrote as an adult, and was first published in the November 1919 edition of The Vagrant (issue #11). Later, in October of 1923, Dagon was published in Weird Tales, the first Lovecraft story to be published by the magazine. To some people, "Dagon" is one of Lovecraft's most forward-looking stories. (: The Call of Cthulhu and Other Dark Tales) It has many elements that foreshadow future stories, such as The Call of Cthulhu and The Shadow Over Innsmouth, and the title is an allusion to Dagon, a deity who would appear in subsequent works, occasionally identified as a Great Old One.

### Inspiration
After reading Lovecraft's juvenilia in 1917, W. Paul Cook, editor of the amateur press journal The Vagrant, encouraged Lovecraft to resume writing fiction. That summer, Lovecraft wrote two stories: "The Tomb" and "Dagon".

The story was inspired in part by a dream he had. "I dreamed that whole hideous crawl, and can yet feel the ooze sucking me down!" he later wrote.

Critic William Fulwiler indicates Lovecraft was influenced by Irvin S. Cobb's "Fishhead", a story about a strange fish-like human. Fulwiler has also suggested that Lovecraft took the story's theme of "an ancient prehuman race that will someday rise to conquer humanity" from Edgar Rice Burroughs' At the Earth's Core (1914).

The story mentions Piltdown Man, which had not been exposed by the scientific community as a hoax at the time of writing.

### Synopsis

The story is the testament of a tortured, morphine-addicted man who plans to commit suicide over an incident that occurred early on in World War I when he was a merchant marine officer.

In the unnamed narrator's account, his cargo ship is captured by a German sea-raider in "one of the most open and least frequented parts of the broad Pacific." He escapes on a lifeboat and drifts aimlessly across the sea "somewhat south of the equator" until he eventually finds himself inexplicably stranded on "a slimy expanse of hellish black mire which extended about me in monotonous undulations as far as I could see.... The region was putrid with the carcasses of decaying fish, and of other less describable things which I saw protruding from the nasty mud of the unending plain." He speculates that this land mass could be "a portion of the ocean floor... thrown to the surface" by a volcanic upheaval, "exposing regions which for innumerable millions of years had lain hidden under unfathomable watery depths."

After waiting three days for the seafloor to dry out sufficiently to walk on, he strikes out on foot to find the sea and possible rescue. After two days of walking, he reaches his goal, a "hummock" that turns out to be a mound on the edge of an "immeasurable pit or canyon". shortDefinition: "Dagon and Jill" is a short parody story written by American writer, animator and producer John P. McCann which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos.  ### Synopsis Taking place in a contemporary setting (as evidenced by the references to Harry Pott...
fullContent:
"Dagon and Jill" is a short parody story written by American writer, animator and producer John P. McCann which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Taking place in a contemporary setting (as evidenced by the references to Harry Potter and email) the story is written in the form of letters between a publisher and his client, who has recently sold a trio of books to the Los Angeles Unified School System to promote cultural and religious diversity and acceptance.

As the correspondence progresses, it quickly becomes clear that Whateley (the client) is a deranged cultist intent on bringing about the return of the Great Old Ones by disguising occult texts as children’s books, while Gelb-Crispling (the publisher) is extremely naive and willing to interpret Whateley's volumes through a veil of political correctness.

The story concludes with the first sign of the end times predicted by Whateley - a six-hour long lightning storm - coming to pass.

### Characters
*Ezra Whateley, a Dunwich occultist whose aims are to return the Great Old Ones to dominance on Earth.
*Martin Gelb-Crispling, a Santa Monica publisher working for Whitman Press.
*Hank Armitage, an FBI special agent determined to put a stop to Whateley's activities.
*Shannon, Martin Gelb-Crispling's daughter and unwitting cultist.

### Behind the Mythos
Dagon and Jill was first published in Necrotic Tissue Magazine #13 in 2011, and received an eBook release in The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack by Wildside Press LLC in 2012.

### Mythos References
* Ezra Whateley is a direct parody of Old Whateley from The Dunwich Horror, whilst his son's body dissolving into a puddle of black liquid after death references Wilbur Whateley.
*The One That Dwells Below, mentioned by Whateley in two of his letters, is intended to represent the Dunwich Horror itself.
*Hank Armitage is a parody of Professor Henry Armitage from The Dunwich Horror.
*Whateley's books (Dagon and Jill, The Shadow Over Humpty Dumpty and A Children's Necronomicon (with pop-up section)) are clear nods to Mythos elements crossed with children's books ("Dagon"/Jack and Jill, The Shadow Over Innsmouth, and the Necronomicon respectively. Cthulhu and Nyarlathotep are both mentioned as being in the texts.
*References to the Deep Ones and their golden jewellery are made in two of the correspondences.

### Publication History
In 1972, J'ai Lu took over publication of Dagon et autres récits de terreur. They released a second edition in 1972 featuring cover art by Philippe Druillet, which was reissued in 1973. A third edition, with new art by Druillet was released in 1978; this was reissued in December 1982 and February 1984. March 1989 saw a fourth edition with another cover by Druillet. Druillet's final image for the publication was launched with the book's fifth edition in December 1992; reprints were released in April 1993 and March 1997. Richard Guérineau supplied the cover for the sixth and final edition in March 2003; reprints were published in January 2006 and July 2007.

Dagon: War of Worlds is a Dark Adventure Radio Theatre production by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society. Taking Lovecraft's short story "Dagon" and the events of The Shadow Over Innsmouth, it expands upon the history of conflict between humankind and the Deep Ones.

### Overview


As with all DART productions, Dagon: War of Worlds was released in compact disc and digital formats, with the former including a set of period-authentic props to enhance the immersive experience. These include:

*A U.S. Navy internal circular regarding an incident in the Pacific Ocean
*A page from the Portsmouth Daily Herald
*The prison records of a human/Deep One hybrid
*A classified government memorandum
*A teletype news bulletin (pre-orders only)

"Dagon's Bell" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, written in 1983 and first published in Weirdbook 23/24 (1988).

### Synopsis
Moving into an ancient farm on the North Sea coast has a deleterious effect on a young couple's health and sanity.

### Publication History
Following its initial appearance in Weirdbook, "Dagon's Bell" was reprinted in the anthology Shadows Over Innsmouth (Fedogan & Bremer, 1994) and served as the title story of Lumley's collection Dagon's Bell and Other Discords (New English Library, 1994). It also appeared in Lumley's Beneath the Moors and Darker Places (Tor, 2002) and Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008).

### References

shortDefinition: "Dagoniad" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.  ### Synopsis A supernatural killer stalks the streets of San Francisco, feeding upon the drug users who hear the whispering of its dark master. When two women accid...
fullContent:
"Dagoniad" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
A supernatural killer stalks the streets of San Francisco, feeding upon the drug users who hear the whispering of its dark master. When two women accidentally eat marijuana-laced cookies, they face their end at the hands of the creature but fight back, showing its bay-dwelling liege that not all of humankind will lie down and submit to its depredations.

### Characters
* Dee, a 55-year-old owner of a bookstore named Treefrog. She has "vigorous gray hair worn neck-length," a "strong face" with "seamed cheeks," "wide intelligent gray eyes," and a "mobile mouth." She carries a walking stick she calls Rod, "a stout yard of hardwood headed with a brass knob and tapering to a weighty ferrule...weighted with a core of iron." She also appears in Shea's story "Tsathoggua."
* Scat, a young prostitute whose way of life has yet to break her spirit. A "nervy little minx, bright as a button," she describes herself as "a hooker that reads"--particularly fantastic fiction. She resembles "a cute little raccoon in her bandit mask of mascara and shadow, her black hair short and sleek as fur."
* Susy, a happy-go-lucky drug dealer and Dee's former lover.
* Babs, the co-owner of Dee's bookstore.

### Connections
* Parts of the story take place in the fictional Hyperion Hotel and Gin and Beer It bar, both recurring locations within Michael Shea's Mythos contributions.
* As the story's title suggests, the creature that lurks beneath the waves of the bay is identified as Dagon,  based on Scat's reading of the works of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Publication History
"Dagoniad" was included in the collections of Shea's own works Copping Squid and Other Mythos Tales (2009) and Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea (2017).

### Synopsis
The story charts a day in the life of a psychiatrist who treats people who have glimpsed what lies beneath the veneer of reality which coats our world. What nobody knows is that she has an extensive knowledge about that dark truth, and now must work for the forces which lurk just out of sight to keep the masses ignorant and compliant, for if she does not, a horrible fate awaits her and her loved ones.

 Daisy Walker, the Librarian, is a fictional character from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. She was created by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files range.

### History
A quiet and unassuming young woman, Daisy had been an avid reader her whole life, being particularly enthralled by tales of horror, and consumed everything she could lay her hands on with eager abandon. These stories were in stark contrast to her real life, in which she despised violence of all kinds.

One day however, Daisy happened across the John Dee edition of the Necronomicon, that most evil of tomes and, at first believing it to be just another work of fiction, dived right in. She quickly came to the realisation that this was not simply another imaginary tale, and the thought that the beings and practices contained within could be real filled her with a deep sense of dread. Repulsed yet determined to learn more, she sought out other books on the subject, familiarising herself with De Vermis Mysteriis and the Cultes des Goules among others, with each new revelation causing her fear to grow.

Then one night, when Daisy was alone in the library, the Thing materialised, a creature straight from the pages of the Ponape Scripture. Managing to escape, the realisation dawned on her that if the Thing was real, then so too could be the other monstrosities she had read about, and so she quietly went to work, using her extensive knowledge of the occult to try and devise a way to put an end to the horror.

### Behind the Mythos
Daisy was first created by Fantasy Flight as an Investigator character to be included in the Kingsport Horror expansion for the Second Edition of adventure board game Arkham Horror, but has since made appearances in both Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. Additionally, the company released a prepainted plastic miniature of her in 2010 as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures range, but this has since been discontinued (all ).

The Dakini are a fictional species created by Chaosium in 2005 for the  Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement Secrets of Tibet.

### Background
The Dakini are mystical creatures whose enlightened form is that of a beautiful human female, Dakini. They have been used as messengers or to test the willpower of a monk, the latter may happen simply because the entity feels like doing so. They can be summoned and bound by sorcerers. Dakini can entrance human males with their seductive dance, freezing in place a person or group. It is agile, can fly, and is known to fight with blades. 

The unenlightened form is the flesh-eating demon, Khandromas, which can also be summoned and bound by sorcerers. It appears as a tall, muscular humanoid with leathery black wings, glowing eyes, claws, a tough hide, and fangs. This form is skilled at ambushing human prey whom they carry off to devour.

Damballah is a fictional character from Marvel Comics. He was created in 1975 by Roy Thomas, Gerry Conway, and John Buscema and Made his first appearance in issue #152 of the 1st volume of the Avengers comic book series.

### Background
Damballah, is the offspring of the Elder God Set. He had worshipers in Zembabwei during the Hyborian Age and in modern day Haiti. When in spirit form, Damballah can travel to Earth where it manifests as a humanoid serpent or a huge snake. It is able to possess serpents and transforms them into versions of its form, and is also able to control snakes. It is able to possess or control others, even those with training in the mystical arts.

The Dame De Blois is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his narrative poem "Psychopompos: A Tale in Rhyme".

### Overview
The Dame De Blois lived in a castle that belonged to her husband, the Sieur De Blois, in the historical French province of Auvergne. The couple had no children and kept only elderly servants whose families had been with the De Blois ancestors for generations. They were rarely seen and were shunned by their neighbours. Secretly, the Sieur De Blois was a werewolf, while the Dame De Blois was a different kind of shapeshifter, able to assume the form of a reptilian beast.

The Dame was twice as feared as her husband and laughed at those who tried to guess her ancestry. Her physical appearance isn't described in detail, but her eyes were said by some to be "too bright by half", and her laughter was known to scare some nervous children. (: "Psychopompos")

### Biography
One year on Candlemass Eve, the Dame stopped by the bailiff's house and smiled evilly at the bailiff's young son, Jean. On the next day, the strong and healthy boy fell inexplicably ill and died. That night, while a storm raged outside, the child's mother saw that a reptilian monster had entered her house and climbed the table where the coffin was set, intending to devour the boy's corpse. Before it could do so, the grieving mother armed herself with an axe and struck the beast's head with it, causing the injured monster to flee into the night.

The Dame De Blois was never seen again after this incident until the snows melted and her human corpse was found with her skull split open. Her body was delivered to the Sieur, who waited until the next winter for his revenge. On Candlemass, he transformed himself into a wolf and gathered his pack to attack the bailiff's residence. However, the bailiff was able to strike the transformed Sieur with the same axe his wife had used to kill the Dame earlier. The wounded lycanthrope fled from the scene, only to die in the quicksand swamp nearby. (: "Psychopompos")

fullContent:
Daniel Thomas "Dan" O'Bannon (30 September 1946 – 17 December 2009) was an American writer, actor and filmmaker who directed the 1991 film The Resurrected, adapted from H. P. Lovecraft's novel The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, and co-wrote the screenplay for the 1997 film Hemoglobin, based on Lovecraft's short story "The Lurking Fear".

His writing credits also include Lovecraftian blends of horror and science fiction, such as the 1979 film Alien, which introduces the Xenomorph species, and the 1985 film Lifeforce, adapted from Colin Wilson's novel The Space Vampires.

O'Bannon has also worked with special effects on various films, such as the 1977 space opera Star Wars.

### Influences
O'Bannon has stated in several interviews how the works of H. P. Lovecraft have been an influence on his own. At age 11 or 12, he first discovered Lovecraft through the short story "The Colour Out of Space"; he later sought out more of his fiction, as it had had such a profound effect on him.

He has also claimed that when writing the screenplay for Alien, he had intended for there to be a direct connection between the Xenomorphs and the Outer God Yog-Sothoth; this was removed from the final draft. His claim is perhaps recognised in the finale of the prequel movie Alien: Covenant, when the antagonist removes human embryos from storage and replaces them with Xenomorph embryos, to the tune of Wagner's "Das Rheingold" (popularly known in English as "Entry Of the Gods Into Valhalla").

Dancy Flammarion is a fictional character created by Caitlin R. Kiernan, an albino teenager from the backwoods of Florida who hunts monsters at the direction of a Lovecraftian angel. First appearing in the novel Threshold (Roc/New American Library, 2001), Dancy was subsequently featured in a series of short stories collected in the volumes Alabaster (Subterranean Press, 2006) and Comes a Pale Rider (Subterranean Press, 2020). She also appears in a number of graphic novels written by Kiernan.

### Inspiration
In their notes for Threshold, on September 16, 1998, Kiernan mentions a “creepy little ‘Boo Radley’ albino girl”--their earliest reference to the character who became Dancy Flammarion. (Boo Radley is a reclusive, offputting, ultimately heroic character from Harper Lee's novel To Kill a Mockingbird.) The name Dancy comes from a small town in Alabama, in Pickens County near the Mississippi state line, that Kiernan passed through while collecting Upper Cretaceous fossils in July or August 1998; "the name stuck in my head, as names often do," they later wrote.

Danforth is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who makes his first appearance in the 1936 novel At the Mountains of Madness. He is described as "a great reader of bizarre material", and makes allusions to Edgar Allan Poe and the Necronomicon. 

### History
Danforth is a graduate student at Miskatonic University. As part of the Pabodie Expedition, he accompanied Professor William Dyer on a survey flight over the "Plateau of Leng" and went insane escaping from the Shoggoth that was residing deep within the mountain. The thing that broke Danforth's mind was never fully explained, as he vowed to keep it a secret from everyone, but according to Danforth, it was something he saw in the reflection of the sky, as they left the mountain range of the Plateau. (: At the Mountains of Madness)

According to Fritz Leiber's account, Danforth later recovered after being treated with experimental drugs developed by one Professor Morgan, though he never recalled the horror he saw on the plateau. Afterward, he became a professor of psychology at Miskatonic University. (: "To Arkham and the Stars") The recovered Danforth takes care of Albert Wilmarth's cats while Wilmarth is traveling. (: "The Terror from the Depths")

### Expanded Mythos
In Christopher Michael's Danforth series, he has since recovered from his horrific experiences but has become obsessed with finding the answers to the occult at any cost. After the United States joins World War II, Danforth is recruited to the Office of the Coordinator of Information (COI) – soon to become the Office of Strategic Services (OSS). He is tasked with finding out the goals of the Third Reich and their mission to seek the unknowable. (: Danforth: Eldritch Tales of WWII)

fullContent:
Danforth: Eldritch Tales of WWII is a modern historical–cosmic horror novel series that follows the character of Danforth from H. P. Lovecraft's novella At the Mountains of Madness. Written by Christopher Michael, the series blends elements of World War II espionage with themes and entities drawn from the Cthulhu Mythos.

The series presents Danforth as an intelligence operative whose prior exposure to incomprehensible cosmic forces during the Antarctic expedition has left him psychologically scarred and uniquely vulnerable to further encounters with forbidden knowledge.

### Premise
Set during the Second World War, the series follows Danforth as he becomes involved in covert intelligence operations intersecting with occult phenomena. Drawing upon historical events and locations, the narrative situates Mythos elements beneath real-world wartime espionage, portraying cosmic horror as an unseen force operating in the shadows of history.

Throughout the series, Danforth struggles with trauma, nihilism, and the lingering effects of his earlier encounter with the alien city in Antarctica.

### Mythos Connections
Danforth: Eldritch Tales of WWII incorporates numerous established elements of the Cthulhu Mythos, including references to the Necronomicon, Nyarlathotep, Yog-Sothoth, Ghatanothoa, and many others. These entities and concepts are presented in a manner consistent with Lovecraftian themes of cosmic indifference and the limits of human understanding.

The series is a derivative literary work inspired by the writings of H. P. Lovecraft and later Mythos authors. It is not part of Lovecraft’s original canon. The series expands upon Lovecraft's work and can be seen as an unofficial direct sequel to At the Mountains of Madness.

### Installments
* Volume I: Tomb of the Black Pharaoh (2025)
* Volume II: The Horror in the Lamplights (upcoming)

### Reception
The series has received extremely positive attention within modern horror and Lovecraftian fiction circles, including recognition on award recommendation lists and coverage by genre reviewers.

fullContent:
"Danger Nazi U.X.O." is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Will Salmon, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Synopsis
An unspecified point during the Second World War in London, England: when the Nazis use an experimental V rocket to deploy a voracious abomination deep into the heart of Great Britain's capital city, a team of special investigators from shadowy government organisation Section M are called in to deal with the problem. Agents Snaith and Lockwood's research uncover information from a former deep-cover spy who conducted a mission to the Mittelwerk rocket factory in Germany: that a pair of similar entities had annihilated the entire workforce and escaped into the surrounding countryside. Lockwood concludes from his studies that the creatures are a part of what he names a "polypous race."

Commandeering a small portable generator and a sturdy cage the unit attempt to lure the creature out, using themselves as bait, and capture it in an electrified prison. Underestimating the speed and ferocity of the being, it proves too much for them and kills the two soldiers assigned to assist the agents. The subsequent detonation of a V-2 rocket close to their position then destroys the cage. Fortunately, just as the creature is about to kill Snaith, an injured Lockwood recovers enough to recite a spell of temporary binding, stalling it and giving Snaith just long enough to plunge a live cable from the damaged generator into its amorphous body, destroying it utterly.

At the funeral of one of the fallen soldiers, Lockwood and Snaith resolve to head to Germany; there is, after all, at least one more of these entities still on the loose…

### Mythos Connections
The "polypous race" which act as the primary antagonists of "Danger Nazi U.X.O." are possibly intended to be Flying Polyps, which first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft’s novella The Shadow Out of Time. Supporting this are their amorphous shape, ability to fly without external assistance, and predatory nature, as well as the fact that Lockwood identifies them as "[e]xtra-terrestrials" that "originally came to Earth … hundreds of millions of years ago at the very least." Points against them being Flying Polyps would be their near-mindless behaviour and resultant lack of interest in any form of technology or tool use, as well as their seeming inability to manipulate the elements in any way, shape, or form.

### Behind the Mythos
Mittelwerk was a real-life underground forced-labour factory which did construct V weapons for the Third Reich during World War II. Some evidence of other experimental weapons programs undertaken at the facility does exist; however, this is far from conclusive. The plant was evacuated after an attack by the British RAF Bomber Command.

Daniel "Dan" Cain is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1922 short story "Herbert West--Reanimator", although, being the narrator of the work, his name never entered into the text. He was first given the name Dan Cain in Stuart Gordon's 1985 low-budget film adaptation Re-Animator; since then, many authors have adopted this as his de facto title.

### In Lovecraft's Work
In "Herbert West--Reanimator", the narrator is the assistant to gifted medical student (later medical practitioner) Herbert West. Himself a qualified physician, Cain accompanies West for many years, even going as far as to follow him into the armed forces and on to the fighting in France during World War I, witnessing all of West's triumphs and setbacks and, eventually, his apparent downfall.

### In the Expanded Mythos

### Re-Animator Franchise
Cain was a struggling medical student forced to take in lodger Herbert West. As time passed, he became involved with West's experiments and was instrumental in defeating an uprising of reanimated corpses, although he lost his fiancé in the process. He attempted to revive her using the reagent, and was apparently successful, but dire complications were suggested (: Re-Animator).

Later, Cain and West attempted to give Megan, the deceased woman, a proper reanimation, but after a successful procedure discards his former love for a new girlfriend. After battling another horde of zombies, Cain and partner escape; he is never seen again, and what became of him later in the series is unknown (: Bride of Re-Animator).

Daniel Cain was portrayed by American actor Bruce Abbott.

### Peter Rawlik
In Peter Rawlik's Reanimator writings, Cain's life follows the same path as it did in the events of "Herbert West--Reanimator", and he later spent a period of time in a mental health institution after witnessing his friend's abduction by animated corpses. Later, when West returns from his sojourn amongst the living dead, he injected his assistant with a sample of the reagent, causing a drastic change in the man. (: Reanimators)

Daniel Harms is an American writer, author, games designer, and librarian living in upstate New York. 

His main interests are the works of H.P. Lovecraft, role-playing games and books of magic (fictional and real).

Harms is best known for the books The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana: A Guide to Lovecraftian Horror and The Necronomicon Files, as well as The Long-Lost Friend: A 19th Century American Grimoire. 

Harms work has appeared in publications such as The Journal for the Academic Study of Magic, Abraxas, Fortean Times, and Paranoia. He was the originator of The Shadow Over Usenet, a detailed online discussion of the works of H. P. Lovecraft. 

He was a lecturer on Lovecraft Circle literature and occult films and history, and his blog Papers Falling from an Attic Window provides commentary on these and other topics.

Harms's Cthulhu Mythos gaming material has appeared in dedicated journals such as The Unspeakable Oath, and in compendiums including Island of Ignorance: The Third Cthulhu Companion.

Daniel Upton is a fictional character and the narrator of H.P. Lovecraft's short story "The Thing on the Doorstep". He is an architect and the best friend of the story's protagonist, Edward Pickman Derby.

### Overview
Daniel Upton is mentioned as having designed Miskatonic University's new Administration Building and its Pickman Nuclear Laboratory, as well as Arkham's Polish Quarter apartment development. Albert Wilmarth remarks that Upton "has had a distinguished career ever since he was given a clean bill of mental health and discharged with a verdict of ‘justified homicide’." Danny O'Bannion is a fictional character created by Keith Herber for the first edition of Arkham Unveiled, published by Chaosium in 1990 for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game, where he is presented as the owner of Lucky Clover Cartage Company, a front for O'Bannion's bootlegging operations. O'Bannion's name is Herber's homage to the American screenwriter and director Dan O'Bannon (who co-wrote the screenplay of Dark Star (1974) and wrote the screenplay of Alien (1979) among other films), according to correspondence between Herber and fellow Call of Cthulhu writer Richard Watts during the development of Arkham Unveiled. Most recently, O'Bannion reappears in Chaosium's Arkham (2023), the first of several releases planned for the 'Arkham Unveiled' line (formerly known as 'Lovecraft Country') for the 7th edition of the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

O'Bannion has also appeared in publications from Fantasy Flight Games (establised 1995) for their Arkham Horror Files series of Cthulhu Mythos-related releases. Although primarily appearing in the now-discontinued Call of Cthulhu Living Card Game, he has also been referenced in other media, such as Peter J. Evans' franchise tie-in novel Feeders from Within.

### Overview
Danny O'Bannion is a major player in the shady underworld of 1928 Arkham, heading the organised crime coalition dubbed The Syndicate, a powerful group with an interest in every illegal activity in town. Conducting much of his business from the Clover Club, a shady den of iniquity, his group is at constant war with the Sheldon gang, bootleggers plying their trade in opposition to the Syndicate.

O'Bannion has a daughter, a beautiful young woman named Naomi, who also works for the Syndicate.

Daoloth is an Outer God in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Render of the Veils".  

### Background
Daoloth is an entity that dwells beyond the three dimensions known to humans. Worshipped on Yuggoth and Tond, and formerly in Atlantis, his astrologer-priests are said to be able to see the past and the future, and even how objects extend into and travel between different dimensions.

Daoloth's indescribable shape causes viewers to go mad at the sight of him; thus, he must be summoned in pitch-black darkness using the Daoloth formula, and is known to take a small amount of blood from the summoner. If not held within some kind of magical containment, such as the Pentacle of Planes, he continues to expand and expand — perhaps even to an infinite size. Those enveloped by the god are transported to utterly bizarre and remote worlds, usually perishing as a result. Daoloth's worship is rare on Earth.

One request that can be made to Daoloth, magically contained, is to view things as they really are, not as our veiled senses perceive them. The sight is usually more than one can bear. (: "The Render of the Veils")

### In Other Media
*In the Demonbane Mythos, Daoloth was briefly mentioned as one of the Evil Gods who was destroyed by Demonbane's Big Bang Impact in the short story "Lost World" from Storm War.
*In the mobile game Tower of Saviors, Azathoth gave birth to Daoloth at the beginning of the universe. Daoloth was initially just a white slime that drifted aimlessly, before it gained consciousness and transformed itself into a metallic irregular body with limbs. The entity's instincts drove it to bring fertility to the desolate universe, creating countless planets populated with lifeforms. Daoloth later teamed up with Arwassa, another higher entity who was devoted to creation. In contrast to Daoloth, Arwassa created things with its emotions, rather than instinct. This helped Daoloth's creations become much more diversified but the worlds they created were unfortunately doomed to die off. Unbeknownst to Daoloth, its actions had disturbed the slumber of Azathoth who, once awoken, set its sights to interfere with Doaloth's plans in every possible way. Despite this, Daoloth became more eager to create than ever, which eventually led the creation of the sky and the Earth. Ghatanothoa and Atlach-Nacha are the offsprings of Daoloth, with the latter ultimately being corrupted by Azathoth's influence.
*In the light novel series Ultimate Antihero, Sumika Hoshikawa can channel a portion of Daoloth's power with a grey bullet. After being fired, the target will be removed from the universe entirely, eternally frozen in a place where there is no light, no distance, no space and no time; only absolute nothingness. Daoth-Yhol is an enigmatic figure created by Ross F. Bagby for his short story, "The Arctic Stone". Older than R'lyeh, it has lived on Earth long before Zagguwa arrived and the Ubbo-Sathla sloughed, and it is considered to be Cthulhu's deadly enemy. It can be summoned by an elliptical grey stone, which was stolen by a shaman from a dark tower run by three-toed eyeless creatures. This stone was eventually inherited by his great-grandson, the shaman of an Inuit tribe in the West Greenland coast that worshipped Cthulhu, whom kept it in a box out of fear and regarded it as an object of taboo. (: "The Arctic Stone")

"Darghud's Doll" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, featuring the occult investigator Titus Crow.  It first appeared in The Horror at Oakdeene and Others (Arkham House, 1977).

### Synopsis
When writer Gerald Dawson asks for an example of "imitative magic," Titus Crow offers a tale of a British doctor in Africa whose life is first threatened and then accidentally ended by means of a magical doll.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Horror at Oakdeene, "Darghud's Doll" was reprinted in Lumley's collection The Compleat Crow (W. Paul Ganley, 1987).

"Dark Cell" is a short Cthulhu Mythos horror story by American authors Brian M. Sammons and Glynn Owen Barrass.

### Synopsis
A highly-specialised Central Intelligence Agency operative recruits a former arms dealer when he learns that an Irish Republican Army cell plans to summon a Dark Young of Shub-Niggurath to use as a terror weapon. The two manage to stop the creature, but at a price.

### Characters
* Jacob, a former arms dealer spending time detained at Her Majesty's pleasure.
* Jordan, a CIA agent who specialises in combatting the creatures of the Mythos.
* Patrick, an IRA cell leader who has in his possession a book of ancient knowledge.

### Publication History
"Dark Cell" was published in the war-themed anthology World War Cthulhu by Dark Regions Press in August 2014. The anthology was also edited by Brian M. Sammons and Glynn Owen Barrass.

The Dark Giants are a fictional race of extra-dimensional entities in the DC Comics Multiverse, appearing as the primary antagonists in the latter half of the 14-issue Secret Six (Vol. 4) comic book's run. It was also in that series where they were given the name of the "Dark Giants", as entities like M'nagalah were referred to as Elder Gods in earlier comics. 

### Background
On Earth, there is a cosmic doorway which provided the Elder Gods the ability to roam the cosmos at will. One billion years ago, their rivals for control of the universe, the "Golden Ones", banished them. Millions of years ago, Earth was plagued by their kind, though as to whether they returned to this universe or not all of them had been banished is unknown. Earth was a playground to them, its life both vermin and entertainment. They fed on its life forms, receiving pleasure from their fear and pain. One of their kind (M'nagalah) claimed to be responsible for the rise and evolution of life on Earth. Upon the ascent of mankind, the "One Over All" (the Multiversal God), banished them again (either the whole race or those that had remained behind).

Despite their banishment, the Dark Giants continued to influence mortals in the universe and searched for ways to get back to that reality. It was the Dark Giants who gave the human race violence and evil. M'nagalah had been observing the universe since before man emerged and has shown an interest in Earth for millennia. On occasion they would reach out and influence learned men, and with their visions twist their intellects and corrupt their souls. M'nagalah had been successful in establishing a physical beachhead on Earth, and several of his brethren have made similar attempts (e.g., Koth-Shugoth and Thrumm). At least one of them was imprisoned on Earth within a mystical crystal, the entity Syththunu.

shortDefinition: Dark Gods is a collection of Lovecraftian novellas by T. E. D. Klein, published by Viking in 1985. It comprised three previously published stories by Klein, along with the original "Nadelman's God."  A review on Signal Horizon calls the collection "a...
fullContent:
Dark Gods is a collection of Lovecraftian novellas by T. E. D. Klein, published by Viking in 1985. It comprised three previously published stories by Klein, along with the original "Nadelman's God."

A review on Signal Horizon calls the collection "a missing link between where horror was and where it is today...pushing the genre to new expanses by exhuming the old and refracting it through a new lens." Caitlin R. Kiernan credits reading Dark Gods, along with Klein's novel The Ceremonies, with rekindling their youthful fascination with the Cthulhu Mythos.

Klein points out in an author's note to the PS Publishing edition (2021) that three of the four stories are set in New York City, "with the fourth an evening's drive away." As justification, he quotes novelist John Updike: "The true New Yorker secretly believes that people living anywhere else have to be, in some sense, kidding." 

### Contents
*"Children of the Kingdom" (1980)
*"Petey" (1979)
*"Black Man with a Horn" (1980) 
*"Nadelman's God" (1985)

### Publication History
After its initial publication by Viking in hardcover in July 1985, Dark Gods was issued in paperback by Bantam Books in July 1986. A British edition was published by Pan Books in January 1987. PS Publishing reissued the collection as a trade paperback in November 2021.

A German translation was released by Goldmann in 1987 under the title Verschwörung der Götter ("Conspiracy of the Gods").

Dark Legacy was a sporadically-released Lovecraftian fanzine with a focus on works set in and around the greater Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
Running for 14 issues between 1998 and 2005 (with issue #12 appearing to have never been published, resulting in the final issue being numbered 15), Dark Legacy was released on an irregular basis. Edited by Ron Shiflet (1998-1999), Ran Cartwright (2000-2001), and Lee Clark Zumpe (2004-2005), each issue ran to 58 pages.

In 2015, Cartwright compiled a collection titled Dark Legacy - The Poetry, which gathered all of the poetry from the fanzine's run, while 2016 saw the release of Volume 1 and Volume 2 The Best of Dark Legacy.

The Dark Man is a character created by American author Ron Shiflet for his Cthulhu Mythos fiction. He made his first appearance in the short story "The Dark Man's Assassin", published in the April 1998 edition of Edward P. Berglund's online fanzine Nightscapes.

### Description
The Dark Man manifests as a looming figure made entirely out of a black, smoky substance, standing in excess of seven feet in height. Although its only consistently-visible facial details are a pair of fiery red eyes, it occasionally reveals the barest hints of shifting features, and is possessed of a smile which chills the recipient to their very core.

Although the Dark Man likes to enact Byzantine schemes to gain material power, he also appears to be a somewhat capricious creature, occasionally granting boons to mortals in exchange for their service, and visiting upon them a terrible vengeance when they betray him.

### Known Activities
*The Dark Man attempted to install a pawn of his, Senator Wilson, into the seat of the US presidency, but was thwarted by a cabal of Miskatonic University occultists and a former psychiatric patient (: "The Dark Man's Assassin")
*He granted a disgraced 1950s music star a second chance at fame, then took it away again in a fiery wrath when the man reneged on his deal (: "The Jealous God")

### Appearances

*"The Jealous God" (2008)

In the role-playing game Cthulhu Dark Ages, the Dark Ones, or Dark Folk, are a species of subterranean creatures who serve Nyarlathotep (a.k.a. Loki) and the Magnum Innominandum. They are usually encountered in groups of ten or more.

### Overview
The Dark Ones correspond to the dwarfs of Norse and Germanic mythology, and due to their alliance with Nyarlathotep, have been speculated to correspond to the Million Favoured Ones as well. Their real form is unknown, as they are in fact parasitic creatures that inhabit the dead bodies of other beings, which they are capable of reanimating. When their current host becomes too decayed, the Dark Ones must find themselves a new one to inhabit. As such, they are particularly prone to inhabiting mummified bodies for convenience, as these will last much longer. According to legends, they originally lived off the bodies of dead Great Old Ones. Their advanced science (speculated to be provided by Nyarlathotep) compensates for their complete inability to use magic.

### Behind the Mythos
The Dark Ones from Cthulhu Dark Ages are also known as the "Miri Nigri" and share traits in common with them: descending from the hills twice a year to abduct people and offer them as blood sacrifices to their deity. However, they are not related to the Miri Nigri as developed by Frank Belknap Long for his novel The Horror from the Hills. The reason for the shared lore is that Gesbert's Dark Ones and Long's Miri Nigri are both based on the same letter by H. P. Lovecraft, describing one of his dreams, which also forms the basis of the short story "The Very Old Folk".

shortDefinition: The term "Dark Ones" has multiple meanings within the Cthulhu Mythos.  The wizard John Carnby claimed that his brother and fellow sorcerer Helman Carnby was "more favored by the Dark Ones". As he identifies himself and his brother as being "in the se...
fullContent:
The term "Dark Ones" has multiple meanings within the Cthulhu Mythos.

The wizard John Carnby claimed that his brother and fellow sorcerer Helman Carnby was "more favored by the Dark Ones". As he identifies himself and his brother as being "in the service of Satan and of Those who were before Satan", it's possible that these beings include the Dark Ones. (: "The Return of the Sorcerer")

In the R'lyeh Text, as translated by Bryant Hoskins, the Dark Ones are the servitor race that serves Ghatanothoa, under the leadership of Yeb (: "Behind the Mask") Therefore, it's possible that they might be the Lloigor species, which have likewise been identified as Ghatanothoa's minions (: "The Return of the Lloigor").

Other uses of the term:
*Dark One (Cthulhu Dark Ages)
*Dark One (Dynamite Entertainment)

The Dark Ones are a race or group of demonic-like Lovecraftian beings in the Army of Darkness / Evil Dead / Reanimator multiverses of Dynamite Entertainment / Space Goat Publications and the Ash vs Evil Dead cable program which are based on the Old Ones of the Cthulhu Mythos. They are the primary antagonists in the story, the power behind the Necronomicon and the Deadites.

### Background
The Dark Ones are a race of godlike beings who are the projection of the universe's dark minds. Who in the distant past roamed the Earth till they were banished to another dimension, where they are kept at bay. In one reality it was the first Chosen One who banished them to the Mirror Dimension, and in another they were betrayed by the necromancer Kaya who banished them to the Deadlands.

The Dark Ones are beings of vast size and power, with incomprehensible forms that would drive a human mad. In one reality they can shapeshift into humanoid entities that are taller than humans that are covered in hooded cloaks, and one of them (Ruby Knowby) could shapeshift into a human form.

### Powers of the Dark Ones
It's stated that the Dark Ones are beings possessing unfathomable power, and in the comics some of that great power is shown. In the mainstream (canon) reality, the Dark Ones appear to possess far less power than the versions shown in the comics. Either they are nowhere near as powerful or their manifestations on Earth possess only a fragment of their power.

Dark Regions Press was a small press publisher which focused on horror and dark fiction, but also produced fantasy and science fiction content. 

### Overview
Established in 1985 by Joe Morey as the fanzine Dark Regions, Dark Regions Press soon expanded to produce chapbooks and novels. It later specialised in deluxe hardcover collectors editions, but continued to publish regular novels, anthologies, magazines and ebooks. Winning several awards over the years, management of the company later passed to Morey's son Chris.

On 21 July 2024, Scottish author William Meikle, who published several of his works through Dark Regions, announced its closure. The blog stated that "the website is down, the company is up for sale … and Chris Morey, the owner, is incommunicado."

The Dark Sargassum is a fictional monster from the Cthulhu Mythos featured in the role-playing game supplement The Bermuda Triangle.

### Description
Classified as a "Unique Entity", the Dark Sargassum is a colossal organism spread over a large area within the Bermuda Triangle, in the Atlantic Ocean. This marine terror originated as a Dark Young of Shub-Niggurath which sank with the lost continent of Atlantis and adapted itself to a new environment, mimicking the form of seaweed and feeding off marine life in the area. Now over 11,000 years old, it has grown into a humongous beast that looks and smells like a floating mass of sargassum.

Hidden within its body are over a hundred rope-like tentacles, which are used to capture prey and drag it towards the creature's toothed maw, located near its centre. Due to its size, the Dark Sargassum can encircle and crush ships weighing up to 200 tons. Few people are aware of the monster's real nature, save for the local Deep Ones and the organisation known as the Cult of Sargath, the latter of which congregates every All Hallow's Eve to offer human sacrifices to it. (: The Bermuda Triangle)

"Dark Waters of Sin" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Chuck Buda. It is set in Keyport, a fictionalised version of a real town, created by Buda's friend Armand Rosamilia.

### Synopsis
A father in desperate financial straits strikes a bargain with an ancient entity lurking beneath the waves of Keyport Bay. The deal means that he will never again struggle to catch fish in those dark waters, but he and his daughter are changed to better serve the being…

### Characters
*Kenny, a devoted father struggling to make ends meet.
*Charlene, Kenny's unhappy daughter.

### Publication History
"Dark Waters of Sin" was first published in the Revised and Expanded edition of the collection Keyport Cthulhu in 2017.

### Trivia
*Although the entity in the story is never specifically named, judging by its - admittedly vague - description, and what has previously been written of the Keyport setting, it can be reasonably assumed that it is intended to be Cthulhu.

The Dark Young of Shub-Niggurath, sometimes abbreviated simply to Dark Young, are a fictional species first mentioned by H. P. Lovecraft in the short story The Whisperer in Darkness through Shub-Niggurath's title, "The Goat with a Thousand Young", but are seldom described further.

They properly first appeared in the short story "Notebook Found in a Deserted House", by Robert Bloch, although the story's narrator refers to them as "shoggoths". The "Dark Young of Shub-Niggurath" alias originates from the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu.

### Description
The Dark Young of Shub-Niggurath are horrifying, pitch-black monstrosities, seemingly made of ropy tentacles. They stand as tall as a tree on stumpy, hoofed legs. A mass of tentacles protrudes from their trunks where a head would normally be, and puckered maws, dripping green goo, cover their flanks. The monsters roughly resemble trees in silhouette — the trunks being the short legs and the tops of the trees represented by the ropy, branching bodies. The whole mass of these things smells like an open grave. They usually dwell in woodlands wherever Shub-Niggurath's cult is active. The Dark Young are usually called upon to preside over cult ceremonies. One means for summoning them is found in the Book of Eibon and requires a blood offering. The ritual may only be performed in the deepest of woodlands at the darkest of the moon, and the victim must be sacrificed over a stone altar. Dark Young act as proxies for Shub-Niggurath in the accepting of sacrifices and the worship of cultists, in the devouring of non-cultists, and in the spreading of their mother's faith across the world.

The Bermuda Triangle sourcebook for Call of Cthulhu mentions a rare aquatic variant of the Dark Young called Dark Sargassum.

### In Other Media
*The Dark Young appear in the Japanese light novel series Overlord, along with the anime based on it, when five of them are summoned by Ainz Ooal Gown after the sacrifice of 70,000 humans.
*The Dark Young appear in the mobile game Card Monsters.
*The Dark Young are featured in the Greek indie developer Ares Dragonis video game The Shore.
*A Dark Young makes an appearance as the main antagonist and final boss in the 2024 survival horror video game Alone in the Dark.

fullContent:
Darkest Dungeon is a roguelike horror roleplaying game at least partially inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft. The core game was first released by indie developer Red Hook Studios on 19 January 2016; since then, several DLC add-ons have been issued, including "The Color of Madness", an expansion which takes its cue directly from "The Colour Out of Space".

### Overview
Gameplay involves the exploration of various procedurally-generated dungeons with a roster of heroes chosen from a hub location, during which the player will battle various enemies of increasing levels of difficulty. The plotline involves an ancient being trapped beneath the surface of the Earth, and the player-characters attempts to prevent it from awakening and destroying the world.

### Behind the Mythos
Director Chris Bourassa had listened to audio recordings of H. P. Lovecraft's works prior to commencement of design: these influenced the game, imparting a Lovecraftian horror aspect to it which may not have otherwise been present .

### See Also

The Darkhold, also known as the Shiatra Book of the Damned, is a fictional grimoire which first appeared in Marvel Comics in the 4th issue of the 1st volume of Marvel Spotlight in 1972.

### Background
The Darkhold is a volume which consists of the scrolls of Chthon. Hundreds of millions of years ago, when Chthon and the other Elder Gods were corrupted,  and began practicing forbidden arts, he recorded his dark knowledge on indestructible parchment.

As the coming defeat and annihilation of the Elder Gods at the hands of the Demigorge, a god-eating being created by Gaea to cleanse Earth of their evil Chthon fled into a parallel dimension of his own creation, leaving the Darkhold behind on Earth to provide him a link back to his homeworld.

The Darkhold appears in the final episode of the Disney+ streaming service series "Wandavision" where it is said to have predicted the appearance of a natural witch, known as The Scarlet Witch.
### Contents

The chaotic magic of the Darkhold can create disastrous effects across the Earth, and when used by Chthon himself, it can reshape the planet. Its necromantic spells have been used to create vampires, zombies, and werewolves. Various dark cults and sorcerers have used these powers down through the ages, including Atlantean sorcerers who became the world's first vampires.

Certain pages contain spells for summoning demons and monsters or hold imprisoned demons (e.g. Wish-Demon).

### The Necronomicon
In the Marvel stories, the Necronomicon -which seems to have been the inspiration for the Darkhold- is said to be based on the Darkhold, and only contains within it a small fraction of the dark knowledge of the Darkhold itself. (: "If Not for Love" [Marvel Team-Up Vol 1 76])

The Darkhold Redeemers were a fictional team in the prime reality of the Marvel universe of Marvel Comics.

### Background
The Darkhold Redeemers was a short-lived team of humans and mystics led by Victoria Montesi that operated for a few years. It dedicated itself to fighting the Elder God Chthon by stopping others from using the pages of the Darkhold and minimizing the effects once someone used one of the pages. Though the team eventually disbanded after taking major losses, the surviving members continued the fight against the Old Ones, with Victoria Montesi joining the Midnight Sons.

The Darkness (also known as Magnum Tenebrosum) is an Outer God from the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was first mentioned by H. P. Lovecraft in the Selected Letters, described as being the progenitor of Shub-Niggurath. 

### Behind the Mythos
Lovecraft placed Darkness as an offspring of Azathoth, with Nyarlathotep and the Nameless Mist being Darkness' siblings, in a 1933 family tree that he wrote for a light-hearted letter to James F. Morton. Shub-Niggurath is placed as a child of Darkness on the tree. (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft 4.617)

The Nameless Mist was identified with the Magnum Innominandum by some later writers, notably Lin Carter and the Call of Cthulhu RPG.  For this reason, Darkness is sometimes known as "Magnum Tenebrosum", or "The Great Darkness", as a parallel to its sibling. (Some readers still believe the Magnum Innominandum to be a term for Yog-Sothoth.)

In Lovecraft's novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, Randolph Carter is described as falling through endless voids of "sentient blackness". It's unknown if this is related to the entity named Darkness, though much of the language used to describe the realms outside of existence such as the Ultimate Void and the Court of Azathoth relates to blacknesses, darkness, "spiral black-vortices" and such (and the Ultimate Gods are described as "tenebrous").

Darrell Hardy is a games designer who specialises in writing the flavour text or "fluff" for roleplaying games, card games and digital card games for mobile and desktop computer games. His main contribution to the Cthulhu Mythos was the Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game for which he provided writeups, flavour text and summaries to tie the world of the cards together.

The Daughters of Atlach-Nacha are a fictional species of arachnid horrors created by Keith Herber for the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Spawn of Azathoth.

### Overview
The Daughters of Atlach-Nacha are enormous venomous spiders that are nearly completely black, the only exception being the green and gold streaks on their abdomen. Every one of them started out as human, women chosen to become companions of the Great Old One, had survived the bite of a lethal spider and now bear "the mark of the spider". 

Atlach-Nacha's  servants coerce or kidnap these women into the Spider God's service. Eventually the women undergo a nightmarish transformation, as they shed their skin and change into a giant spider, after which they join Atlach-Nacha in its lair, helping it weave the Great Web.

Human devootes who bear the mark of a venomous spider bite are particularly revered by the god's cult priestesses, who regard the subject as "favored", and a candidate for transformation by their god. Such candidates may already be initiates, although many are not aware of the spider cult. These unwitting people are either coerced or kidnapped so they may be indoctrinated into the cult. Successfully inducted candidates are later presented to Atlach-Nacha, with the god deciding wether to bless and transform or simply devour the hopefuls. The process of transformation begins with the human shedding their skin, which in turn forms a sack-like cocoon around it. Within this "egg sack", the rebirthed human's flesh peels away while their body mutates into a massive, spider-like creature. Within a few hours, the transformed daughter breaks free of the cocoon, ready to undertake Atlach-Nacha's bidding.

fullContent:
Daughter of Hounds is a 2007 novel by Caitlin R. Kiernan that explores the subterranean world of New England ghouls, as envisioned in H. P. Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model". Published by Penguin-Putnam, it includes characters first encountered in Kiernan's Threshold (2001) and Low Red Moon (2003).

Daughter of Hounds tells the stories of Soldier, a changeling woman who works as enforcer for the ghoul warrens of Providence, Rhode Island, and Emmie Silvey, a strange yellow-eyed girl living on the city's surface. Each has a secret origin that binds their fates together, and a special power that makes them a target of subterranean forces.

### Characters
*Soldier, changeling, works as an assassin for the Bailiff. An alcoholic.
*Emma Jean Silvey, a eight-year-old with yellow eyes who lives with her father on Angell Street in Providence.
*Pearl/Hester, human, the daughter of a wizard. Lives in an extra-dimensional attic on Benefit Street. Has been 12 years old for 78 years.
*The Bailiff, human who acts as an agent for the warrens' aboveground affairs. A magician and a pedophile.
*Madame Terpsichore, ghoul, the High Dame of the ghoul warrens of Providence.
*Deacon Silvey, human, father of Emma. Dr. Chance Silvey's widower. He is an alcoholic who owns a used bookstore. 
* Sadie Jasper, human, stepmother of Emma. A writer and a witch. Lives on St. Marks Place in New York City.

David Gerrold (born 1944 in Chicago, Illinois) is an American science fiction author whose work includes the War Against the Chtorr and Star Wolf series, as well as several other novels and short stories. He is also known for writing numerous scripts for television, including episodes of Star Trek, Land of the Lost, and Babylon 5.

Gerrold wrote two episodes of the animated series The Real Ghostbusters, one of which, "The Hole in the Wall Gang", takes place in the town of Arkham, Massachusetts. It was one of three episodes of the show to incorporate elements of the Cthulhu Mythos, along with Michael Reaves' "The Collect Call of Cathulhu" and J. Michael Straczynski's "Russian About".

shortDefinition: David Henry Keller, M.D. (1880 - 1966) was an American author of horror, fantasy, and science fiction, as well as a practicing psychiatrist. Born in Philadelphia, he wrote purely as a hobby for decades until he sold his first sci-fi tale, "The Revolt...
fullContent:
David Henry Keller, M.D. (1880 - 1966) was an American author of horror, fantasy, and science fiction, as well as a practicing psychiatrist. Born in Philadelphia, he wrote purely as a hobby for decades until he sold his first sci-fi tale, "The Revolt of the Pedestrians", which appeared in the February 1928 issue of Amazing Stories. Hugo Gernsback was impressed by Keller's unique handling of sci-fi concepts and encouraged him to write more. For the next decade, Keller contributed frequently to Amazing Stories, Weird Tales, and other magazines, and published a number of novels.

Outside of his literary career, Dr. Keller served in the US Army Medical Corps during both World Wars, and used his knowledge of psychiatry to treat those afflicted with shell shock. He wrote articles on sex education and acted as editor to Gernsback's magazine Sexology.

Keller contributed to the Cthulhu Mythos with the satirical story "The Final War", first published in 1949, which describes the apocalyptic war waged by Cthulhu against humanity.

Keller's essay "Shadows Over Lovecraft", published in the Summer 1948 issue of Fantasy Commentator, attempts a psychiatric analysis of the late H. P. Lovecraft.

Arkham House published two collections of Keller's stories: Tales from Underwood in 1952, and The Folsom Flint and Other Curious Tales in 1969. During a period of financial instability for the publishing house, Keller spontaneously wrote a check in the amount of $2,500 and sent it to August Derleth as a loan at 3%. This act of generosity helped keep Arkham House afloat during this difficult period.

Keller was one of the many pulp authors who were spoofed in the comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century", by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. The story pairs him with Miles J. Breuer (another author who, like Keller, was also a medical doctor) and portrays the two as a pair of surgeons named "Drs. D. H. Killer and M. Gin Brewery", who treat those who partook of the cream-puffs sold by a certain "Wladislaw Brenryk".

David Hambling is a British science fiction and horror author from London, England, who also works as a freelance journalist. He is the author of several Cthulhu Mythos series, including Harry Stubbs, William Blake, and Age of Monsters, the first two of which take place in a post-World War I Britain, with the latter two being loosely linked together.

In addition to his solo forays into the Cthulhu Mythos, Hambling has also collaborated with other genre authors, such as C. T. Phipps, David Niall Wilson, Matthew Davenport, David J. West, Byron Craft, Mark Howard Jones, and Peter Rawlik.

Outside of his Mythos work he's a senior contributor for Forbes.

David Niall Wilson (born 1959) is an American horror author, two time Stoker Award winner, and editor. He is the CEO and founder of Crossroad Press, a publishing house for horror and science fiction. He is the author of "Of Dark Things and Midnight Planes", The Call of Distant Shores, and a participant in the Books of Cthulhu series. His Lovecraftian fiction has appeared in anthologies including Cthulhu's Heirs (1994, Chaosium), Tales of the Al-Azif, Tales of Yog-Sothoth, and Tales of Nyarlathotep (2019, 2019, 2023 respectively, Crossroad Press). 

Wilson's non-Mythos related books include The Grails Covenant Trilogy for Vampire: The Masquerade, Dark Age Clan Novel: Lasombra, Star Trek: Voyager: Chrysalis, Gideon's Curse, Deep Blue, and This is my Blood.

Wilson cites Edgar Allan Poe, Stephen King, and Neil Gaiman as amongst his influences .

shortDefinition: Rev. David Van Bush (1882 - 1959) was an American poet, actor, Congregational pastor and pop psychologist who hired H. P. Lovecraft and James F. Morton to revise many of his writings during the 1920s. His first published book was Peace Poems and Saus...
fullContent:
Rev. David Van Bush (1882 - 1959) was an American poet, actor, Congregational pastor and pop psychologist who hired H. P. Lovecraft and James F. Morton to revise many of his writings during the 1920s. His first published book was Peace Poems and Sausages (1915). His books on psychology anticipate what would later become known as the self-help movement, including titles such as The Power of Visualization: How to Make Your Dreams Come True (1922), Psychology of Healing (1924), and Psychology of Sex (1924). 

Born in Pennsylvania, Bush came from a poor rural background. At the age of six, he moved to Philadelphia and, according to Lovecraft, made a living "selling loads of papers too heavy for him to carry". He later found work as a trick cyclist in a circus, an actor, a preacher, and finally a psychologist. His books and lectures were financially quite successful.

Lovecraft regarded Bush as an unintelligent person who wrote abysmally bad poetry, but also described him as "a harmless, likeable chap" who "means well, and undoubtedly believes much of what he preaches". Bush was also, in Lovecraft's estimation, a capable speaker with good pronunciation (which Lovecraft jokingly attributes to Bush's wife being a former teacher), a "natural orator", a "very fair actor", and "an undeniably efficient organiser and business-man". (: Selected Letters 1.105)

fullContent:
David Hattersley Warner (29 July 1941 – 2022) was an English actor who had portrayed multiple characters in Cthulhu Mythos productions. He played Amos Hackshaw in Cast a Deadly Spell, Chancellor Thayer of Miskatonic University in The Unnamable II: The Statement of Randolph Carter, and Dr. Richard Madden (a character based on Dr. Muñoz from H. P. Lovecraft's "Cool Air") in Necronomicon: Book of the Dead. He also performed a great number of characters in the Doctor Who franchise, both in television and audio plays, up to and including (but not limited to) the Doctor and the Grace.

A member of the Royal Shakespeare Company, Warner had a distinguished and varied career encompassing theatre, film, television, and audio productions. While particularly well known for his villainous roles, which include Ra's al Ghul in Batman: The Animated Series and the Lobe in Freakazoid!, he has also played more sympathetic characters such as Prof. Jordan Perry in Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Secret of the Ooze, St. John Talbot and Chancellor Gorkon in the Star Trek franchise (although he was also the cruel inquisitor Gul Madred in Star Trek: The Next Generation), and Aldous Gajic in Babylon 5. Some of his most notable film credits include Nicholas Meyer's Time After Time, Terry Gilliam's Time Bandits, James Cameron's Titanic, and Disney's Tron.

shortDefinition: Dawnward Spire, Lonely Hill is a collection of the letters between H.P. Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith covering the period 1932 to 1937.  The letters were edited and compiled by David E. Schultz with assistance from S. T. Joshi.  ### Publisher's Su...
fullContent:
Dawnward Spire, Lonely Hill is a collection of the letters between H.P. Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith covering the period 1932 to 1937.

The letters were edited and compiled by David E. Schultz with assistance from S. T. Joshi.

### Publisher's Summary
"In this second volume of the correspondence of H. P. Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith, we find the two authors in the prime of their careers. Smith was publishing frequently in the weird and science fiction pulps of the day, compelled to earn money to take care of his ailing parents. Lovecraft had suffered some painful setbacks—the rejection of his work by Putnam’s, Knopf, and other book publishers—but he was continuing to develop his Cthulhu Mythos, and Smith was making distinctive contributions to it. 

And yet, dark clouds were on the horizon. Smith’s parents died in 1935 and 1937, and as a result his output of fiction declined significantly. Lovecraft kept his own ailment—cancer of the intestine—a secret from Smith and most other colleagues, so that his California friend was stunned to hear of his passing on March 15, 1937.

### Notable Contents

### Salem Witchcraft
Lovecraft makes reference to having received a letter from an unnamed direct descendant of one of the Salem Witches, Mary Eastey:

"By the way—that tale has just earned me a highly interesting letter from a curious old lady in Boston, a direct lineal descendant of the Salem witch Mary Easty, who was hanged on Gallows Hill Aug. 19, 1692. She hints at strange gifts & traditions handed down in her family, & asks me if I have access to any ancient secret witch-lore of New England. Also, she wants to know if Dunwich & Arkham are real places! I shall answer the letter, & see if I can get the good old soul to relate some of the whispered witch-traditions! A story of Salem horror based on actual “inside dope” from a witch-blooded crone would surely be a striking novelty!"

—H. P. Lovecraft to Clark Ashton Smith, 22 Mar 1929, Dawnward Spire, Lonely Hill at page 171

fullContent:
The Dchichi are a fictional race of bird-like creatures created by Brian Lumley as part of his Titus Crow series of novels.

### Overview
A species of humanoids which bear several similarities to terrestrial birds, the Dchichi possess avian heads, raptor-like feet and a beautiful, multicoloured plumage. Normally attired in garments woven from a fine golden mesh, they are a highly intelligent race famed for their natural understanding of the communication forms of other beings, be it vocal or through body language, and are strongly implied to be amongst the chosen of the Elder Gods.

The Dchichi are known to inhabit a floating mountain-island in Elysia powered by antigravity discs, although whether this is their point of origin is as yet unknown. The many eyries and honeycombed tunnels contained within this island are decorated like the richest of homes, and play host to thousands upon thousands of Dchichi eggs. Each of these eggs is spoken to and taught as if it were a thinking, sentient being; in fact they are, and each hatchling has heard and absorbed the lessons given to it by its tutor througout its incubation. By the time a Dchichi hatches, it is already capable of speaking and understanding more languages than any human could learn in a lifetime, and is a connoisseur of the arts, architecture and sciences of uncountable races.

### Notable Dchichi
* Esch, The first Dchichi to encounter Titus Crow.

fullContent:
De Horrore Cosmico is a a scenario supplement book for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview


De Horrore Cosmico contains six stand-alone adventures set in the Cthulhu Invictus time period of Call of Cthulhu. Each scenario is based upon a different story by Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Also included are an article providing tips for both players and keepers, and a selection of six ready-to-use non-player characters. The scenarios are:

*"The Vetting of Marius Asina" by Jeffrey Moeller
*"Doom" by Chad Bowser
*"Murmillo" by Oscar Rios
*"Kith and Kine" by Phredd Groves
*"The Devil’s Mouth" by Stuart Boon
*"The Case of Tertius Orestius Sedonius" by Penelope Love and Mark Morrison

### Behind the Mythos
Running to a total of 166 pages, De Horrore Cosmico was launched through a successful Kickstarter campaign. Published by licensed third-party content provider Golden Goblin Press in June 2015, it was initially released in print but is currently only available as a digital download.

De Marigny's Clock is a fictional artefact created by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price for their short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key". The concept was greatly expanded upon in Brian Lumley's Titus Crow series of Cthulhu Mythos novels and short stories, which portray the machine as a creation of the Elder Gods.

### Description
In the original story, de Marigny's clock is a mysterious coffin-shaped grandfather clock that Etienne-Laurent de Marigny acquired from a Yogi who claimed to have been to the city of Yian-Ho. Its dial contains "baffling hieroglyphs" and its four hands move in a way that doesn't match any time system known on Earth, ticking in an irregular alien rhythm. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

### In the Expanded Mythos
Disguised as a grandfather clock shaped somewhat like a coffin, the Clock is in fact an incredibly advanced ship with the ability to traverse time, space and, with the correct pilot, dimensions as well. It features a door on the front body which is large enough to admit a full-grown human. Upon stepping inside, pilot and passengers will become enveloped in a white mist which cushions their bodies perfectly, presumably to protect them from any manoeuvring stresses.

Controlling the Clock's direction of travel - either in the material universe or through time - requires nothing more than the mental concentration of the pilot, who may use the advanced sensors to view his surroundings out to a tremendous distance. It is capable of travelling at faster than light speed both in and out of an atmosphere (although it features inbuilt safeguards to prevent most collisions), is capable of moving through time at the speed of thought, and can be outfitted with a variety of sensor and weapon packages depending on the requirements of the user. As a device created by the Elder Gods, the weapon systems are powerful enough to physically harm (though not destroy) entities as powerful as a Great Old One, as seen when Titus Crow used the Clock's energy beam against Ithaqua.

### Trivia
*De Marigny's Clock is not a unique device; Titus Crow observed a great hall full of them when he first arrived on Elysia, one of which was utilised by the alien Dchichi named Esch.
*Ran Cartwright presents a very different version of the clock in his short story "De Marigny's Clock", this one being more of a mystical artefact, and seemingly malevolent in nature.
*Lumley's depiction of de Marigny's Clock shares several similarities with the TARDIS from the Doctor Who franchise. Both are living machines that can travel through time, space and other dimensions. fullContent:
"De Marigny's Clock" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ran Cartwright.

### Synopsis
Told in a series of diary entries, the story covers the last few days of missing author Joseph Ward who, seeking inspiration for his writing, has taken up residence in the abandoned Chateau de Marigny. Over the course of several nights, he gradually begins to detect the return of an ancient clock - in actuality a gate between worlds - which begins to drive him insane with fear. In Ward's final entry, he writes that he intends to destroy the clock.

### Characters
*Joseph Ward, a writer seeking an atmospheric location to inspire his work.

### Publication History
*Dark Legacy #4 (1993)
*Nightscapes #13 (2000)
*Thirteen Stories #12 (2003)
*Of Gods & Aliens (2011)

### Trivia
*The story is spun off from H. P. Lovecraft's and E. Hoffman Price's short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".
*Although sharing de Marigny's clock as a plot device with the Titus Crow series, Cartwright presents it as a much more sinister object, likely the cause of Ward's doom, rather than the technological artefact portrayed in Brian Lumley's work.

shortDefinition: De Marigny's Clock is a short story by Brian Lumley, first published in the Arkham House collection The Caller of the Black, in 1971. It features Lumley's recurring character Titus Crow and the mysterious clock from the story "Through the Gates of th...
fullContent:
De Marigny's Clock is a short story by Brian Lumley, first published in the Arkham House collection The Caller of the Black, in 1971. It features Lumley's recurring character Titus Crow and the mysterious clock from the story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price.

### Synopsis
Eccentric occultist and psychic Titus Crow wakes up to find himself threatened by a pair of burglars, who demand to know where he keeps his money. The ruffians refuse to believe in Crow's claim that there is no money in the house, and proceed to search for it amidst his collection of books and antiquities, much to the occultist's despair. At last, they come to a coffin-shaped grandfather clock which previously belonged to American occultist Etienne-Laurent de Marigny.

The mysterious clock functions without any visible mechanism, its hands moving irregularly, and emits strange sounds. For years, Crow has been trying to make sense out of its functioning, but hasn't been able to open it. One of the burglars, Pasty, who has untrained psychic abilities, senses danger, but his colleague, Joe, is convinced that the money is inside the clock.

Being a master safecracker, Joe manages to open a panel from the machine and sticks his arm inside, only to scream in horror as something on the other side grabs him. Pasty rushes to help him, but when he temporarily manages to pull Joe back from what turns out to be a spacetime portal, he sees that Joe's skin has been horribly corroded by acid and loses his balance, resulting in both men disappearing inside the mechanism. Crow faints in terror and the clock's panel closes again automatically.

When he wakes up, Crow remembers the horrifying psychic impressions he had received from Pasty as the two thugs plunged into the Lake of Hali on a world in the Aldebaran system and were devoured by strange aquatic predators.

De Vermis Mysteriis, or Mysteries of the Worm, is a fictional grimoire created by Robert Bloch, first mentioned in his Cthulhu Mythos story "The Secret in the Tomb", and featured in many subsequent stories by Bloch, H. P. Lovecraft, and others. It is described as containing "spells and enchantments", particularly those that can summon strange entities. (: "The Shambler from the Stars")

### Ludvig Prinn, Author


### Description
A folio-sized printing in black ink over 700 pages long, the earlier of the 16 chapters of the book discuss ghosts, zombies, and the like. Later parts of the book detail the author's travels among the Saracens of Arabia, Egypt, Syria, and Libya, and of his encounters with djinn and efreet. There is much material regarding the summoning and binding of different "demons". The last chapter contains the formula for a drug that allows one to travel through space and time (Liao/Plutonian drug). (: The Keeper's Companion)

Prolonged readings of the book could cause unexpected spontaneous summoning of maggots and snakes close by, or hallucinations that something is crawling beneath one's skin. (: The Keeper's Companion)

Being a grimoire of great importance and one of the most famous in the entire Mythos, the contents of De Vermis Mysteriis have since been expanded in numerous stories and materials.

### Chapters
* A chapter specifically dealing with familiars (: "The Shambler from the Stars").
* "Saracenic Rituals", a chapter that "revealed the lore of the efreet and the djinn, the secrets of the Assassin sects, the myths of Arabian ghoul-tales, the hidden practices of dervish cults" and "the legends of Inner Egypt", providing backstory on the cults of Bubastis (: "The Brood of Bubastis"), the cults of Sebek (: "The Secret of Sebek"), and on the Pharaoh Nephren-Ka's worship of Nyarlathotep (: "Fane of the Black Pharaoh"). It also contains info regarding the worm-wizards of many-columned Irem (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana).
* A chapter on divination (: "The Sorcerer's Jewel").
