fullContent:
Dead Boarder is an introductory scenario supplement for the Call of Cthulhu investigative horror roleplaying game. Written by Todd Gardiner and Mike Mason, it was published by Chaosium in 2016.

A single-scene scenario, rather than being designed as a one-shot to insert into a existing campaign, Dead Boarder is intended to give new players an introduction to both the themes and mechanics of Call of Cthulhu.

### Overview




### Synopsis
In 1931 Depression-era Providence, Rhode Island, a group of investigator characters - all with different motivations - assemble at the apartment of one James Gardiner, who has apparently committed ritual suicide. Gardiner had been previously cut off from the Dreamlands and, desperate to reconnect with that fantastical realm, embarked upon a course of action which he discovered in a mystical tome named The Book of Dreams. However, he was unaware that the ritual was a trap designed to open the caster's body to possession from outside entities; during the course of their investigations, the group is attacked by Gardiner's resurrected corpse, now home to the mind of an ancient, evil, and utterly insane sorcerer.

### Mythos Connections
* The ritual utilised by Gardiner invokes the Outer God Yog-Sothoth.
* A hideous, sanity-draining statuette discovered in Gardiner's room is implied to depict the Great Old One Cthulhu.
* Gardiner's room is situated in Ma's Boarding House, a recurrent location in the Arkham Horror/Call of Cthulhu setting.
* Patrolman/Officer Malone, a character who makes a brief appearance at the scenario's climax, is likely a nod to Detective Thomas Malone, the narrator of H. P. Lovecraft’s "The Horror at Red Hook."

### Design Team
* Written by: Todd Gardiner and Mike Mason
* Artwork by: Todd Gardiner and Nicholas Nacario
* Production staff: Mike Mason and Nicholas Nacario

### Trivia
* The unfortunate victim of the scenario, James Gardiner, shared the same last name with its lead writer, Todd Gardiner.

fullContent:
"Dead Deal" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Drew Nicks. It was published in the first issue of short-lived horror magazine The Asylum Diaries by Oscillate Wildly Press in May 2019.

### Synopsis
Baker Martin, a small-time private investigator in debt to the mafia, is recruited by Santino Sforza, a tough mob enforcer with an interest in black magic, to retrieve a valuable book of ancient lore. After witnessing a mysterious woman annihilate a barroom full of hoods, Martin is approached by a shady-looking man who offers him the book, along with a piece of paper with a star-shaped symbol for protection. Giving the book to Sforza, Martin bears witness to the gangster's demise at the hands of the three entities which manifest upon its opening: the mysterious woman, the shady man, and an enormous, eldritch abomination.

### Mythos Connections
*The book which Tini Sforza is in search of is stated to be the Kitab Al-Aazif [sic], an ancient name for the Necronomicon.
*The mysterious woman's name is given as Lucy Delapore, a reference to the main character from H. P. Lovecraft's 1924 short story "The Rats in the Walls". Whether Lucy is intended to be a relative to Lovecraft’s Delapore or simply a throw-away nod to the authors work is not clarified.

Dead Light: Surviving One Night Outside of Arkham is a survival horror adventure supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
Designed as a stand-alone scenario which can alternatively be slotted in to a longer campaign, the story of Dead Light involves a party of Investigators encountering a series of strange occurrences and a dangerous entity whilst travelling through the backwoods on a dark and stormy night. It also contains a small selection of non-player characters along with maps and schematics depicting the areas of play.

Although Dead Light was designed for Call of Cthulhu 7th edition, it includes an appendix containing basic conversion rules to allow it to be played with earlier editions.

### Publication History
Dead Light was released alongside the 7th Edition Call of Cthulhu core rules in both softcover print and digital PDF formats.

### Overview
A book themed around encounters whilst travelling across country, Dead Light & Other Dark Turns contains two ready-to-play scenarios, six pre-generated characters, a set of player handouts, and plot seed ideas for Keepers to create their own adventures. It runs to 88 pages and features full-colour cover art by Wayne Miller with black and white interiors.

*Saturnine Chalice, by Matthew Sanderson.

### Publication History
Dead Light & Other Dark Turns was released in 2020 and was made available in both softcover and digital PDF formats.

"Dead Man's Tongue" is a short story by American author Josh Reynolds.

### Synopsis
When Harley Warren and Randolph Carter are asked by the local police to help in a bizarre murder case, they must face down a Rolang- a desiccated, undead servitor with a killer temperament.

### Characters
*Randolph Carter, a mild-mannered author.
*Harley Warren, Carter's friend.

### Publication History
"Dead Man's Tongue" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu by April Moon Books in March 2014.

### Trivia

* This story, centring on an encounter with a Rolang, may have been inspired by an entry in H. P. Lovecraft's Commonplace Book:  "Thibetan ROLANG—Sorcerer (or NGAGSPA) reanimates a corpse by holding it in a dark room—lying on it mouth to mouth and repeating a magic formula with all else banished from his mind. Corpse slowly comes to life and stands up. Tries to escape—leaps, bounds, and struggles—but sorcerer holds it. Continues with magic formula. Corpse sticks out tongue and sorcerer bites it off. Corpse then collapses. Tongue become a valuable magic talisman. If corpse escapes—hideous results and death to sorcerer".

fullContent:
"Dead of Night" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, featuring his occult investigator character Anton Zarnak. It was first published in the April 1988 edition of Crypt of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
A wealthy young woman named Teresa de Rivera consults Anton Zarnak, an occult detective based on River Street, New York. She asks Zarnak to help her uncle, Don Sebastian, formerly a strong and healthy man, who has become weak and prematurely aged by a debilitating fear of the dark.

Seven years before, Don Sebastian had opened up the tomb of a Mutsune shaman in a burial mound and found several artifacts, including a pectoral pendant made of obsidian. Following this incident, he started to avoid the darkness, sold all his lands and moved with Teresa to New York, where he keeps the lights on all night in his room (which is filled with lamps and flashlights), and fears every shadow and dark corner.

Consulting excerpts from the Book of Iod, Zarnak confirms his suspicions that the monster that Don Sebastian fears is in fact Zushakon, a subterranean creature that manifests only in darkness and is kept at bay by light.

On the next day, Zarnak visits the de Riveras, introduced by Teresa as an antiquarian interested in Don Sebastian's collection of relics. When shown the obsidian pendant, Zarnak recognizes the image of Zushakon and privately recalls that artifacts depicting the Great Old Ones can be used to summon these same beings. He copies down the symbols depicted in the pendant, and returns home to study them, finding them to be letters of the Aklo language. From the translation, he learns that the pendant was supposed to be kept in perpetual darkness, and that Zushakon will consume anyone who dares expose it to light.

Zarnak tries to call the de Riveras to warn them of the danger, but the house is temporarily out of reach. The radio announces that sudden electrical storms threaten to cause blackouts in certain parts of the city.

Zarnak takes a taxi and arrives there to find a desperate Don Sebastian filing his room with candles. A sudden icy wind blows out all the candles, and the presence of Zushakon is felt inside the room. Zarnak tries to keep the creature at bay with a five-pointed star-stone and utters an incantation to Cthugha to light the room with fire. When the power returns and the room is illuminated again, Zushakon retreats and vanishes. However, Zarnak and Teresa realize that Sebastian has died of fright.

### Characters
*Dr. Anton Zarnak, an occult investigator.
*Ram Singh, Zarnak's loyal servant.
* Don Sebastian de Rivera, a wealthy man, formerly a rancher, with an interest in archaeological relics.
*Dona Teresa de Rivera, Don Sebastian's niece who seeks out Zarnak's help for her uncle.
*Carmelita, a maid who works for the de Riveras.
*Zushakon, a creature of darkness.

"Dead Thing" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Frank Forte, first published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
When an inquisitive young boy discovers the carcass of a bizarre creature deep in the forest, his investigations result in a strange substance squirting out to cover his arm.

Over the next few years, whatever he had been infected by claims his entire body, forcing him into the life of a recluse, and claiming the lives of his parents.

Eventually, the larvae which he had been impregnated with emerge from his mutated body, and he finds himself transformed into a "mother" creature for these new beings.

fullContent:
"Deadfall in the Parking Lot" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Francis Erdman, first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of fanzine Lovecraftiana in 2021.

### Synopsis
An inmate at Arkham Asylum relates the tale of how his friend, a talented artist, inexplicably vanished. The pair were on their way to a budget supply store in Kingsport when a deadfall of logs appears in front of them. The artist climbs the deadfall and finds a small village full of fish-like humanoids. Travelling back across the deadfall to say farewell to his friend, the man then heads back across the log pile, never to be seen again.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite being included in a magazine dedicated to Lovecraft-inspired fiction, "Deadfall in the Parking Lot" appears to draw more on Stephen King's Pet Sematary, the 2019 film version of which is specifically mentioned in the story.

Deadites are fictional entities which first appeared in The Evil Dead, a low-budget supernatural horror film written and directed by Sam Raimi, and released in 1981.

### Background
Deadites are demonic spirits and zombies which are controlled by the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis. They are able to possess both the dead and the living. Their animating spirits are from the Deadlands, a shadowy dimension that is a mirror image of the real world. Deadites "consume" the souls of their victims after which they take over their bodies. They are connected to each other via a hive mind. It's a species which is both sadistic and comedic, demons with a mood that is both angry and childish.

Deadites possess enhanced strength and endurance, inhuman dexterity, and are able to camouflage themselves as normal humans. While they can be killed, if their severed head is re-attached, it resurrects the Deadite. They can infest and/or possess humans via physical contact or injuries which they inflict.

"Deaf, Dumb and Blind" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and C.M. Eddy, Jr.

### Synopsis
Richard Blake, a deaf, mute, and blind World War I veteran who was once a vivacious and imaginative poet, lives alone in a rural home and faces malevolent forces. A growing smell of smoke that becomes a sulfurous hell-like stench, and a freezing cold so powerful it burns strike him. He is typing a manuscript, and when his corpse is found the next morning, it is this typed message that the delegation sent to discover what has transpired reads:


### Publication History
"Deaf, Dumb, and Blind" was first published in the April 1925 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into both French and German.

Dean Engelhardt is a prolific roleplaying games designer and artist who has worked on many horror roleplaying games, particularly those with a Lovecraftian leaning. These include contributions to Cthulhu Reborn's Apocthulhu and Cthulhu Eternal, Pelgrane Press's The King in Yellow and The Fall of Delta Green, the German-language Fhtagn, and Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu, in several of the games' settings, including Classic (1920s America), Convicts & Cthulhu (1800s colonial Australia), Cthulhu by Gaslight (Victorian Britain), and Cthulhu Invictus (Roman Empire-era), as well as publishing a small amount of material through DriveThruRPG's Miskatonic Repository player-driven initiative.

Engelhardt's work has also seen publication in a handful of gaming magazines, such as The Arkham Gazette, Bayt al Azif, and Cthulhus Ruf.

fullContent:
Robert Dean Stockwell (5 March 1936 - 7 November 2021) was a prolific American film and television actor whose career spanned over sixty years. Although he had been acting for 35 years by the time of its release, he is perhaps best remembered for his role as Admiral Albert "Al" Calavicci in the popular science fiction drama series Quantum Leap; he also appeared in the television adaptation of Expanded Mythos author Stephen King's The Langoliers.

Stockwell starred in two adaptations of the H. P. Lovecraft short story "The Dunwich Horror", nearly forty years apart, playing very different characters in each: in the 1970 adaptation, he portrayed the malevolent Wilbur Whateley, while in the 2008 production he was instead protagonist Dr. Henry Armitage.

Dean's Corners is a fictional town created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft, which was first mentioned in his short story "The Dunwich Horror," published in 1929.

### Overview
First referenced in the short story "The Dunwich Horror," little was said of Dean's Corners in Lovecraft's works. Located somewhere along the Miskatonic River Valley in the fictional region of New England most commonly referred to as 'Lovecraft Country', it can be reached via the Aylesbury Pike junction when travelling from Arkham (the other turnoff leading to the backwards and degenerate township of Dunwich).

Another small and obscure township, Aylesbury, is located nearby.

fullContent:
"Death Is an Elephant" is a horror short story by Robert Bloch (credited by his pen name "Nathan Hindin"), first published in the February 1939 issue of Weird Tales. It is the second story in the Stellar Brothers Circus series, following "Fangs of Vengeance", and incorporates elements from the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
As with "Fangs of Vengeance", the story is narrated by the press agent for the Stellar Brothers Circus, who claims that the events are true, although he had to alter the names of those involved in order to get it published.

At the end of 1936, the circus owner and the press agent travel to Singapore, and are told that they might find a new attraction for next year's show in the nearby principality of Jadhore. This small nation, although under the jurisdiction of the British Empire, is ruled by a rajah who, according to Hindu tradition, possesses a magnificent and sacred white elephant. While the rajah refuses to sell the animal, he agrees to rent it to the circus for a season, provided that he himself comes along to guarantee the safe and proper treatment of the holy animal. Also accompanying them is Leela, the high-priestess of the temple of the god Ganesha.

Aboard the ship, the rajah reveals himself to be a genial and educated man, but warns the circus men to be cautious around Leela, who disapproves of the whole enterprise. The rajah tells them that the white elephant is in fact an incarnation of the primal god Ganesha, who has also been worshiped under the name Chaugnar Faugn in Tibet, and Lord Tsathoggua in prehistory. As high-priestess, Leela is the god's consort, and presides over human sacrifices whenever those are needed to placate the deity. Later on, a ship passenger who had spent too much time staring at the elephant kills himself by jumping into the sea.

After the arrival, the rajah befriends the circus performers, particularly Captain Dence, the elephant trainer, but the artists show fear of Leela, who never leaves the stall where the elephant is kept. The rajah is increasingly worried and has seconds thoughts about the ordeal. At one point, both the rajah and Captain Dence show up drunk and plead the circus owner to forget about the contract and allow the elephant and Leela to be returned to Jadhore. Two days later, Dence's body is found hanging from a rope, having committed suicide.

Despite the somber atmosphere, the narrator notices that some of the artists spend a lot of time in the stall, whether fascinated by the majestic elephant, the beautiful Leela, or both. An acrobat named Alonzo Corbot, a clown named Jim Dolan, the equestrian director Rizzio, and the knife-thrower Captain Blade are all frequent visitors. On the opening day's performance, Corbot falls to his death in the middle of the show, and his partner later claims that "his eyes were dead" right before it happened. Death on the Arkham Express is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author and screenwriter Byron Craft, the fifth in his Arkham Detective series of hardboiled detective fiction. It was self-published in May 2019; both paperback and digital editions were released. Cover art was supplied by Marko Serafimovic.

### Overview


### Synopsis
On the once-luxurious but now sadly neglected Arkham Express - returning from an assignment escorting a prisoner to New York - the Arkham Detective finds himself investigating a series of gruesome murders aboard the train, where the victims have been decapitated. His investigations lead him to an alien being disguised as a human, who reveals herself to be a kind of cosmic police officer, attempting to save the Earth from an accidental incursion of voracious Doels.

Despite his lack of jurisdiction, and with the alien's assistance, the Detective manages to destroy the Doels who have made their way to Earth and seal the portal which allowed them access, but is unable to save all of the passengers or the alien from their depredations.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, Death on the Arkham Express has also appeared in the 2022 collection The Arkham Detective Collection Volume 2.

"Deconstruction" is a very short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Harris Coverley. It was published in the Lammas Eve edition of Rogue Planet Press zine Lovecraftiana in July 2020.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator, one of the few humans aware of what is happening, watches as an event called "the Crunch" destroys the universe and everything in it. Of particular irony is that Great Cthulhu chooses that moment to awaken and begin his reconquest of the globe, seconds before he is obliterated along with everything else. The final sentient creatures in existence are the Great Race, but even they are consumed by the end of the cosmos.

### Behind the Mythos
Among the other Mythos entities mentioned are the Elder Things, the Hounds of Tindalos, and the Vampires of Fire, all of which are mentioned to have fled this reality ahead of the coming destruction.

Dee is a recurrent character in the Cthulhu Mythos works of the late American author Michael Shea.

### Description
An attractive 55-year-old gay woman, Dee is described in her first appearance as having



She often carries a heavy walking stick, although she acknowledges that this is for aesthetic and self-defence purposes, rather than as a result of any mobility issues. She has given it the ironic nickname of "Rod".

Dee enjoys walking in the hills surrounding her home in San Francisco, where she has taken in a lodger, a young woman who calls herself Scat. She is also the co-owner of a small independent bookstore named Treefrog - where she first came across Scat - and drives an aged Volkswagen Bug when she needs to.

### History
Dee first encountered the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos after she was accidentally given cookies laced with cannabis by her former partner, a woman named Susy. Ingesting the drug caused her and Scat to come to the attention of a supernatural reaper in service to Dagon, and while the two managed to destroy their assailant, they were forever changed by the experience. Dee now spends her time attempting to find ways to combat the powers she has come to know are active in our world while simultaneously recruiting those who have also come into contact with them.

The Deep Ones are a fictional species of ocean-dwelling humanoids, created by H. P. Lovecraft for his story "Dagon", although not identified by name until the novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth, in which Lovecraft presents them as having an affinity for mating with humans.

Lovecraft's novella tells of how the Deep Ones entered a contract with the people of Innsmouth to keep the fish plentiful in their area, and provide them with a supply of gold artifacts of inhuman design. The Deep Ones are presented as worshipping the Cthulhu Mythos entity Father Dagon and his consort Mother Hydra. (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth)

In addition to Innsmouth, human/Deep One hybrids are known to inhabit other coastal cities around the world. (: "The Keeper of the Key")

### Overview
The Deep Ones are an amphibious race that primarily serve the two beings known as Father Dagon and Mother Hydra, but also have strong ties to Cthulhu, and are known to employ Shoggoths as servants (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth, : The Return of the Deep Ones). Locked in the timeless depths of the sea, their alien and arrogant lives are coldly beautiful, unbelievably cruel, and effectively immortal. They are a marine race, unknown in freshwater environments, and globally have many cities, all submerged beneath the waves; one is off the coast of Massachusetts, near Innsmouth, called Y'ha-nthlei, while other sites, such as Y'lu-Y'loa (off the British Isles), K'toch (off Northern Europe), and Y'ha-gom-loa (off Antarctica) are said to exist.

Deep Ones are immortal until slain (so are any hybrid offspring), and may be worshipped by humans. From time to time, the Deep Ones establish and foster relationships with isolated human communities, offering to trade golden treasures from the depths of the sea, along with bountiful fish catches, in return for certain promises. Since their official debut in H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth, the Deep Ones have had numerous appearances and references throughout popular culture. 

Arguably, their influence is seen in films with the theme of mutation and miscegenation in Humanoids from the Deep (1979) and the period action horror film Island of the Fishmen (1979), as well as the Gill-man from The Creature from the Black Lagoon (1954). It is worth noting that the much later film Dagon shows some influences from the much earlier Island of the Fishmen, for example, in the architecture of the sunken city and in the head dress and general appearance (from the waist up at least) of the high priestess. 

The Creature from the Black Lagoon series also features references to the prehistoric survival of a prehuman species (the eponymous Creature) and its sequels show an implied connection between the Creature and humanity as the Creature sheds its overtly amphibian or fish-like features to become radically more human-like. 

There are also many Expanded Mythos or Mythos-Adjecent works featuring the Deep Ones, as well as other direct references, including the following. 

### Books/Stories
*13 Monsters: In Eric S. Brown's novel, a character compares the mermen he encounters to the Deep Ones which he had read about in Lovecraft's fiction in his youth.
*Cthulhu Armageddon: Deep Ones have been orphaned by the fact that Cthulhu did not notice him or bless him when he arose. They have since had civil war and conflict over why their religion was wrong.
*The Innsmouth Legacy: In her series of novels, Ruthanna Emrys uses and subverts the mythology of the Deep Ones and their involvement with the town of Innsmouth.
*Where the Deep Ones Are: a children's book, published by Atlas Games.

### Comic Books & Manga
*Alicia Y: in the first chapter, a cult of Deep Ones attempt to perform a human sacrifice, but are quickly defeated by Alicia Y Armitage.
*Hellboy: Deep One-like creatures appear frequently in the series, with one of its protagonists, Abe Sapien, being a member of a race called Icthyo Sapien. There is also a race of creatures referred to only as "Frog Monsters," which were created in imitation of Icthyo Sapien and closely resemble Deep Ones.
*Infestation 2: In the Transformers segment, the Deep Ones appear as the minions of an Elder God.
*Marvel Comics: features several pastiches of the Deep Ones.
**In Marvel Premiere #4-6, the Serpent Men were created by and worship Sligguth.

fullContent:
Deep Time is the concept of geological time that spans billions of years, providing a framework for understanding Earth's formation, evolution, and the development of life. It was first developed in the 18th century and has significantly influenced various scientific fields, including geology and evolutionary biology.

### Standard Definition of Deep Time
Deep time refers to the vast geological time scale that spans billions of years, far exceeding human experience. It provides a framework for understanding the Earth's formation, the evolution of life, and the slow processes that shape our planet. In terms of the Cthulhu Mythos, this span of aeons is the setting for hundreds of significant world-changing events whose evidence has largely been erased or gone unnoticed by the sheer passage of time between the time when they occurred and the present day.

### Historical Context
The concept was first developed in the 18th century by Scottish geologist James Hutton, who proposed that geological formations undergo continuous transformation over long periods. The term "deep time" was popularized in the 20th century by writer John McPhee in his book Basin and Range (1981).

### Importance in Science
Deep time is crucial for various scientific fields, including:

* Geology: It helps explain the Earth's history and the processes that have shaped its surface.
* Evolutionary Biology: The concept provides the necessary timescale for understanding evolutionary changes and the development of biodiversity.
* Climate Science: Studying deep time allows scientists to understand past climate changes and their implications for current and future environmental conditions.
* Extinction: Deep Time can be seen as the underlying process of change that oversees the extinction of all life. From the Great Race of Yith and the Elder Things to humanity and whatever follows us, all are ultimately consumed by the passage of time itself. This concept is adjacent to the Decadent movement of nihilism and embracing of meaninglessness, as exemplified by the Fin de Siecle stories in The King in Yellow.

### Cultural and Philosophical Implications
Deep time challenges human-centric views of history and encourages a broader perspective on our impact on the planet. It promotes "deep time literacy," which helps individuals grasp the significance of long-term environmental changes and the need for sustainable practices.

### Behind the Mythos
Deep Time is central to a contemporary concept of Cosmicism. Whether through the Keynsian "on a long enough timeline everyone dies" concept of reducing humanity to a blip on the cosmic radar and our history to insignificance, or by emphasizing the enormous geological forces that reshape the planet and in the process bury, drown or erase past civilizations.

A strong element of the Mythos is of course those preternatural, supernatural or godlike beings that stand outside the passage of time or who defy Deep Time's effects by placing themselves or being

fullContent:
For the Cthulhu Mythos concept of deity and deity classification is particularly confusing and contentious, even among those with a large knowledge of the Cthulhu Mythos. However, a deity within the Mythos can be generally defined as any being, entity, or intelligence that wields power and influence beyond what humans can perceive or comprehend. One thing all deities of the Mythos share is that one or more group or cult offer the entity worship or veneration, whether in an active sense associated with an organized religion, or in a general sense of respect for an enormously powerful creature.

### Cthulhu Mythos Deities
In general, Cthulhu Mythos deities differ substantially from notions of deity in real world religious and spiritual traditions.

As with the rest of the Mythos, the deities are generally based in a materialist philosophy. This is to say, that the "gods" of the Mythos are not essentially supernatural. Rather, they are physical beings that hold to the natural laws of the entirety of the Mythos, what Lovecraft called the "cosmos-at-large". (: Selected Letters 2.284)

However, many of these laws are strange and unknown to humankind. These laws, as they apply to the gods of the Mythos, include psychic communication, inter-dimensional travel, the existence of parallel universes, pocket universes, extra-universal realms, and transcendent realities.

All of these aspects of the nature of the Mythos, and the presence of the deities themselves, add to the over-all concept of cosmic horror. To the deities of the Mythos humanity is insignificant, ignorant of the true nature of reality, and barely worthy of notice. Humans are often used as proxies to impact global events, undermine the plans of competing deities, or as playthings to torment for their own amusement.

### Deity Classification
From story to story, there is a great deal of inconsistency in terms of the classification of the various entities termed "gods" of the Mythos.

However, over the course of Lovecraft's writings and the subsequent additions to the Mythos by August Derleth, a certain order has been asserted.

The deities have been generally placed into four basic categories: Outer Gods/Other Gods, Elder Gods, Great Old Ones, and Great Ones.

### Outer Gods


Within the Mythos, the Outer Gods are seemingly older, perhaps predating the universe or the creators of the universe itself. They are often referred to as "ruling gods", and seem to transcend the boundaries of time and space. They are vastly more powerful and have influence on a much larger cosmic scale.

The Outer Gods are generally portrayed as being without real personality or intelligence, called "mindless blasphemies," with the exception of Nyarlathotep. Nyarlathotep is portrayed as acting as an intermediary between the Outer Gods while apparently despising them, and descends to direct his malign intellect to serve the will of the Great Old Ones and actively meddle in the lives of mortals.

Delapore is the main character and narrator of "The Rats in the Walls", a 1924 short story by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Biography
Born c. 1857 on a plantation on the banks of the James River in Virginia, Delapore after the Civil War moved with his family to Massachusetts, his mother's home state. He grew up a "stolid Yankee", making a fortune in manufacturing. He lived in the town of Bolton with his one son, Alfred Delapore.

After World War I took Alfred to England as a flyer, his father bought Exham Priory, the family's ancestral home in England, in 1918. When Alfred was maimed in the war later that year and died two years later, the bereaved father decided to relocate to Exham. He began restoring the ruin in 1921, and moved in on July 16, 1923.

fullContent:
Delta Green is a roleplaying game setting originally created for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu, but which has since been expanded into its own stand-alone game.

### Premise
Delta Green is a top-secret, black-ops organisation dedicated to combatting the threats presented by various Cthulhu Mythos creatures and cults from the shadows. Originally taking place in a 1990s setting, it has since been updated to reflect contemporary times, equipment and issues, and expanded to cover other time periods, such as the Vietnam War.

### Development
Created by John Scott Tynes, Dennis Detwiller and Adam Scott Glancy, the very first appearance of Delta Green was in a roleplaying game scenario in the Cthulhu Mythos gaming fanzine The Unspeakable Oath, by Pagan Publishing. The scenario was titled "Convergence" and was released in 1992. Pagan followed this up in 1997 with a complete sourcebook for the setting, which itself spawned a series of expansions. In 2016, Arc Dream Publishing released a stand-alone roleplaying game based on Delta Green, which was also accompanied by a wealth of satellite books. In 2018, Pelgrane Press acquired a licence to produce The Fall of Delta Green roleplaying game, a stand-alone setting adapted for the GUMSHOE system which details the group's activities in the decade before it was closed down in 1970.

Delta Green is a setting supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, written by Dennis Detwiller, John Scott Tynes, and Adam Scott Glancy. It was published by third-party content provider Pagan Publishing in 1997.

### Overview
Delta Green is a contemporary setting for Call of Cthulhu, and involves players taking on the roles of agents of the shadowy government organisation from which it takes its name. The organisation is dedicated to combatting any paranormal threats which present themselves to humanity, and ensuring that the nature of these threats remains unknown to the general public.

The setting was developed from a single scenario printed in The Unspeakable Oath, a Pagan Publishing fanzine dedicated to Call of Cthulhu, titled "Convergence". Delta Green has since become one of the most popular Call of Cthulhu settings, and now boasts its own stand-alone game system (albeit one which is still compatible with other editions), a host of supplements spanning an in-universe time period of several decades, and dedicated fiction. These have all been published through the Pagan label.

Delta Green: Need to Know was the first release for Arc Dream Publishing's stand-alone roleplaying game Delta Green: The Role-Playing Game.

### Overview


Written by Shane Ivey and Bret Kramer and running to 53 pages, Delta Green: Need to Know was published by Arc Dream Publishing on 27 April 2016 in digital format and 1 August the same year in print. It contains a set of basic rules, six pre-generated agents and a short scenario to allow a quick start to games of Delta Green.

shortDefinition: Delta Green is a stand-alone Cthulhu Mythos roleplaying game published by Arc Dream Publishing.  ### Overview Updating the original Call of Cthulhu supplement Delta Green from the 1990s into a post-9/11 environment, Delta Green continues with the the...
fullContent:
Delta Green is a stand-alone Cthulhu Mythos roleplaying game published by Arc Dream Publishing.

### Overview
Updating the original Call of Cthulhu supplement Delta Green from the 1990s into a post-9/11 environment, Delta Green continues with the theme of a covert United States government agency devoted to combatting supernatural threats. It also advances the story of the fictional group.

Gameplay involves the players taking on the role of Delta Green agents who are assigned to investigate and, if necessary, contain or destroy any threat to humankind by any means necessary. This includes the influences of the Cthulhu Mythos, and also more traditional supernatural forces. The game uses a modified version of Chaosium's Basic Role-Playing (BRP) system, allowing it to be used in conjunction with many Call of Cthulhu supplements with little to no adaptation.

### Design and Publication
Designed by Dennis Detwiller, Adam Scott Glancy and John Scott Tynes, the team behind the creation of the original Pagan Publishing supplement, a quick-start book titled Delta Green: Need to Know was released by Arc Dream Publishing on 27 April 2016. A host of additional supplements have been released since.

### List of Supplements


### Fiction
In addition to the gaming supplements published for Delta Green, a small amount of fiction has been released for the setting. These include:

* Denied to the Enemy (2004)
* Tales from Failed Anatomies (2014)
* Delta Green: The Way it Went Down (2018)

### See Also
*Delta Green (1997), the original supplement, still relevant to the stand-alone game as it provides much of the organisation's backstory.

"Demiurge" is a short story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
A powerful entity awakens to the modern world and proceeds to insert its consciousness into every living organism in its vicinity. As it becomes more aware of the greater world around it, is comes into contact with another of its kind, a creature which inhabits the nearby bay. The two are finally able to connect, at which point they mate.

### Characters
* Grunt, a small-time criminal.
* James Deuce, a substitute teacher.
* Lionel, another criminal, deceased.

### Publication History
"Demiurge" was published posthumously in the collection Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea in December 2017.

### Behind the Mythos
Although containing no references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, "Demiurge" is considered to be a part of this shared universe by Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi, as evidenced by his inclusion of the work in the collection to which it lends its name.

The story also appears to be unfinished, with no conclusion offered to the human aspects of the story. As it was published three years after Shea's death, it seems likely that it was being worked on at the time of his passing, or was an abandoned project.

fullContent:
"Demon in Glass" is a Lovecraftian short story by author E. Dane Anderson. It was published in the Salomé Jones-edited anthology Cthulhu Lives! by Ghostwoods Books in August 2014.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator, a photographer during the waning days of the 19th century who occasionally assists with mortuary pictures, relates the story of one Dr. Rachel Lamarche, formerly of New Orleans, who has since moved to town and established her own "health sanitarium." However, it is soon revealed to the man by government officials that Dr. Lamarche is under investigation, suspected of murdering her wealthy clients by starvation and appropriating their assets.

As time goes on, the photographer begins to look more closely at the images he had previously taken of some of Dr. Lamarche's deceased patients. He comes to the terrifying conclusion that some of these pictures show not a body in peaceful repose, but a damned soul tormented by some hellish force.

Soon, news reaches the photographer that Dr. Lamarche's resort has burned to the ground, seemingly resulting in many deaths; he is called upon in his official capacity to document what is presumed to be a crime scene. As the investigation progresses, the true extent of Lamarche's crimes are unveiled, with scores of corpses uncovered. The police also discover an unusual idol in one of the huts, prompting the media to speculate about possible devil worship. Of the doctor herself, there is no sign.

Later, when developing his plates, the photographer sees that every single image of a corpse shows the poor soul's essence writhing in torment; in another, a spectral Lamarche can be clearly seen waving mockingly at the camera. After ridding himself of the cursed images, the man resolves never to take another photograph again.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never directly named, the description of the statue discovered at the former health spa would seem to suggest that the entity being worshipped by Lamarche and her followers was in fact the Great Old One Cthulhu: "the distorted image of some blubbery bipedal creature with bat-like wings and extended digits. The figure was sitting on a throne, one that was covered in arcane symbols. Its head resembled that of a squid or octopus, being bulbous and altogether misshapen, and ending with a thick mass of disgusting tentacles."

### Trivia
* The story’s title, "Demon in Glass," is a reference to the glass plates used to capture images in the early days of photography.

The Demon Lord of the Dark Valley is a Lovecraftian-like demonic entity from the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. The character first appeared in Conan the Barbarian Vol 1 45 "The Last Ballad of Laza-Lanti". It has heavy overtones of H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Dunwich Horror".

### Background
The Demon Lord of the Dark Valley was a demonic being in Koth which ruled over the Dark Valley during the Hyborian Age which seized the mortal dancer Timara, and violated her. She gave birth to twin sons and apparently fell in love with the monster, becoming its concubine. Timara continued to visit the Demon Lord bringing it food such as cattle and raised one of the sons in the valley while sending the other one to the Druids to be educated.

Over the intervening years, the creature maintained Timara's youth and beauty. Mistakenly thinking the girl was going to be sacrificed to the monster, it was later attacked by Conan and her son Laza-Lanti who was unaware the creature was his father. As Conan fought it head-on, Laza attacked from above and was able to strike a killing blow. Distraught, Timara told the story to a stunned Conan and Laza, before plunging a dagger into her chest to join the creature in death. Overcome with grief at this revelation, Laza asked Conan to leave the area before committing suicide as well. (: "The Last Ballad of Laza-Lanti")

Demon Spawn are a fictional species created by Craig Digregorio in 2018 for the STARZ series Ash vs Evil Dead.

### Background
Demon Spawn are summoned by the Necronomicon Ex Mortis. When summoned they need to inhabit human host bodies. Physically they are black skinned humanoid demons with sharp teeth and black hole-like eyes. Their bodies are extremely flexible which gives them remarkable maneuverability. Demon spawn are great climbers, and are stealthy, using the shadows.

They can negate one's immortality, turning you into a mortal. They are able to elongate their body parts, including their claws. If injured, the flesh repairs itself and they can only be killed by supernaturally forged weapons. They are able to transform and mimic the shadows of other individuals.

Demons by Daylight is an anthology of short horror stories by British author Ramsey Campbell. It is divided into two thematically-linked sections, Nightmares and Relationships, and contains several stories linked to the larger Cthulhu Mythos.

### Publication History
First published in 1973 by Arkham House, Demons by Daylight had originally been scheduled for a 1971 release; however, the death of the company's co-founder and chief editor August Derleth that year caused a two-year delay. In 1979, a revised edition was published by Jove/HBJ with "The Second Staircase" removed and replaced with two other stories, "Reply Guaranteed" and "The Telephones," but the 1980 Star reprint restored the original story line-up. It was reissued by Carroll & Graf in 1998, and by Lume Books in 2017, who included a digital version with their release.

Demons by Daylight has also been translated into German under the title Dämonen bei Tag, although it retains "Demons by Daylight" as an English tagline.

fullContent:
"Demons Dreaming" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Cody Goodfellow, which is loosely linked to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.

### Synopsis
After British foreign agent Captain Glendower extracts his old friend Lieutenant Roland Morrison from the chaos of the crumbled Ottoman Empire, the two make good their escape aboard the luxurious passenger train the Orient Express. Unfortunately for Glendower, Morrison has been co-opted by the sinister Hashishim and, using a mystical narcotic, transports his consciousness to a nightmare desert realm where he offers the captain a choice: become a servant of the cult, or die in the inhospitable land.

Using his superior skills and training, Glendower is able to overcome every obstacle put in his way by the cult, including the harsh terrain, a horde of undead warriors, and a dream-version of his former friend. Eventually managing to shake himself from the drug-induced trance he begins to awaken, but as he does so comes to the horrific realisation that the desert lake from which he slaked his thirst is in fact the limpid eye of some enormous entity across whose colossal face the events of the last few hours have unfolded…

### Mythos Connections
Despite containing little in the way of direct connections to the Cthulhu Mythos, "Demons Dreaming" contains themes familiar to any reader of Lovecraftian horror; namely an ancient god too vast and incomprehensible for the human mind, and a secretive cult in service to that god.

The story's sole link to the Cthulhu Mythos is contained in a single line concerning the entity encountered by Glendower in the nightmare realm: "Of all the Outer Gods, only He has deigned to walk among men. He ruled over ancient Egypt as the Daemon Sultan." While this would appear to conflate the Outer Gods Nyarlathotep and Azathoth, this can potentially be explained by positing that Nyarlathotep - the Messenger of the Outer Gods and Azathoth’s servant - is simply enacting its "father's" will on Earth using Azathoth's own epithet.

### References

fullContent:
"Demons of Cthulhu" is a short story by Robert Silverberg (using the pen name Charles D. Hammer) set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in the magazine Monster Parade #4 in March 1959.

### Synopsis
Two men who work in the library at Miskatonic University plot to steal the rare and priceless book known as the Necronomicon. The older of the two, Theophilius Vorys, has a strong interest in the occult. His young colleague, Marty, knows nothing about such things, and only agrees to participate in the scheme for 10 dollars, as Vorys needs his help to accomplish the theft unnoticed. However, after getting hold of the book, Marty double-crosses Vorys and takes the grimoire home, reasoning that he can sell it himself and keep all the money, as Vorys won't be able to accuse him without implicating himself as well.

With the book on hand, Marty starts reading, finding that most of the text is concerned with witchcraft and ancient gods. His curiosity is piqued when he learns about an entity named Narrathoth, who will do one's bidding when summoned. The ritual to summon Narrathoth is comparatively easy, requiring only a few ingredients, a pentagram drawn with chalk, and the chanting of certain words in a mysterious language.

Vorys arrives at Marty's house and confronts him, insisting that Marty has no clue of what he's doing, and that messing with the Necronomicon is dangerous, but Marty dismisses his concerns and kicks him out. Alone again, he performs the ritual and summons Narrathoth, taking care to enunciate the sentence that would force the entity to obey him. He asks Narrathoth for a banquet and dancing girls, which the creature duly conjures out of thin air. After he eats and watches the girls dancing, Marty asks questions about Narrathoth's masters and kin, and learns about the likes of Cthulhu, Yig, Azathoth, and more, which makes him shudder with fear. At last, he tries to cast the spell that would send Narrathoth back to its own dimension. But instead of vanishing, the entity starts to grow and laugh, as Marty watches in awe and terror.

Vorys returns and informs Marty that the sky above the house is dark, and a gateway is opening up. Whether by an unfortunate accident or Narrathoth's subtle trickery, it turns out that Marty had looked at the wrong page and didn't pronounce the spell to send Narrathoth back, but rather one to summon Yog-Sothoth. A gigantic tentacle breaks through the window and erases the chalk pentagram, freeing Narrathoth. Vorys recites some chants, but is unable to send back Yog-Sothoth before it grabs Marty with one of its tentacles and devours him.

### Publication History
*Monster Parade #4 (1959)
*Crypt of Cthulhu Michaelmas 1988 (1988)
*The Necronomicon: Selected Stories and Essays Concerning the Blasphemous Tome of the Mad Arab (1996)

Dennis Detwiller (born 12 July 1972) is an American traditional and video games creator, author, editor, and occasional artist.

### Overview
Beginning his gaming career by volunteering at Pagan Publishing on The Unspeakable Oath magazine, Detwiller subsequently became the company's art director, and co-created the award-winning Delta Green roleplaying setting with Adam Scott Glancy and Pagan founder John Scott Tynes.

After leaving Pagan Publishing, Detwiller co-founded Arc Dream Publishing with Shane Ivey; Arc Dream acquired the license for The Unspeakable Oath and revived it, and still produces books for the Delta Green roleplaying game (the original book having been a setting supplement for Call of Cthulhu).

Detwiller has since mostly left the traditional games industry and now works as video games designer, although he does contribute the occasional book to the Delta Green roleplaying universe.

Denys Barry is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Moon-Bog".

### Background
Denys Barry was an American man who moved to the fictional village of Kilderry, Ireland in County Meath to purchase and restore the old ancestral castle that had belonged to his Irish family in generations past.  

When the restoration was complete, he declared his intent to drain a bog on his property that was said to be haunted, despite the strong warnings against this by the local villagers. Barry remained steadfast in his decision to empty the bog, and eventually the guardian spirits that dwelt in the bog took vengeance against him. They lured Barry and his team of workers into the bog at night beneath the moon where they were never seen again.

The workers and household servants were transformed into bloated green frogs, while Barry was drawn writhing and struggling into the night sky along a pale moonbeam, as if pulled upward by "unseen demons." (: "The Moon-Bog")

The Department of Extraordinary Phenomena is an organisation created by Troy Young for his Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Purpose
The sole purpose of the Canadian government's Department of Extraordinary Phenomena is to protect humankind from "The Other", a term used by Harjit Singh to describe the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos.

They are known to eliminate those whose contact with The Other has irrevocably damaged them, a policy implemented to prevent causing a panic amongst the general populace. 

### History and Organisation
The Department of Extraordinary Phenomena was founded in 1928 after two law enforcement officers and a scholar uncovered cult activity which resulted in the summoning of a malevolent being. In the aftermath, the officer in charge of the investigation petitioned the Canadian government who agreed with his assessment and established the new organisation. 

In the modern day, the Department employs an unknown number of field agents along with an extensive network of consultants and support staff, the majority of whom are unaware of the exact nature of their work, a precaution designed to both maintain secrecy and protect these valuable assets. They are also known to be in contact with their counterpart agencies from other countries, a policy intended to allow for a global coverage of Other incursions. The heads of these agencies meet twice annually to compare notes and keep up to date.

### Recruitment
In order to spare the lives and sanity of the innocent, the Department recruits only from those individuals who have had previous encounters with The Other. Even amongst those with prior contact, only individuals who have shown an exceptional degree of resourcefulness and open-mindedness are considered as candidates.

As a "black" organisation, the Department usually employs its agents in a mundane government agency and has them seconded to an unspecified project. This ensures that it’s activities cannot be traced. For example, Dr. Adele Kramer ostensibly works for the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, but in reality her on-paper superiors have no idea of her actual line of work.

Due to the unfortunate fact that the record for an agent's career combatting The Other is a mere eight years before their sanity is too degraded to continue functioning, the turnover of field staff is high.

Deputy Dingby is a character who features in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files series of games and fiction. He was a member of the Arkham County Sheriff's Department.

### Arkham Horror ()
A number of Encounter cards from Arkham Horror Second Edition feature interactions with the Deputy, in which he is usually portrayed as more than a little inept.

### Feeders from Within ()
Dingby assisted Sheriff Engle in his interview with reformed cultist Diana Stanley after she attempted to break her ties to the Silver Twilight Lodge. His subsequent disappearing act hints that he may have been in league with the cult, or perhaps on their payroll.

### Ire of the Void ()
When Professor Norman Withers informed Sheriff Engle of the abduction of his colleague Claus Schmidt by a Hound of Tindalos, Dingby investigated the scene, finding a torn-off fingernail.

fullContent:
"Der Alptraum" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in Modiphius Entertainment's Achtung! Cthulhu horror roleplaying setting. Written by J. E. Bryant, it was published in the tie-in fiction anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius in 2015.

### Synopsis
During the Second World War, a unit of German engineers led by Lieutenant Christian Gruber and his second Feldwebel Ernst are assigned duty under a Black Sun officer, Oberst Eckhart. The group is joined by blind Romanian Cosmina Stafie, a woman with very special abilities who is collaborating with the Nazis in order to save her family. Loading up their pack animals, the detachment make their way deep into the primal German forests.

Guided by Eckhart, the engineers arrive at a ruined temple deep into the woodlands. Eckhart directs the men to erect a bizarre-looking construction resembling a cage, the specifications for which cause unease and a sense of psychological discomfort in those working on the project.

When the structure is complete, Eckhart and his small group of Black Sun men use Cosmina's abilities to enact an awful ritual, summoning a terrifying creature from a different reality. Horrified by what they see, Gruber and Ernst sabotage the ritual and rescue Cosmina. While the Black Sun operatives die at the claws of whatever monstrosity they summoned, the engineer unit flees into the forest and safety.

fullContent:
"" is a short story by Robert E. Howard that first appeared in the Fall 1967 issue of Magazine of Horror, more than three decades after Howard's death. The story's narrator is named Kirowan; whether he is the same character as the John Kirowan who appears in several Howard stories is open to interpretation.

The Kirowan in this story has gone to Galway in Ireland in hopes of finding some sort of solace for the death of his beloved twin sister, Moira Kirowan. He rehears a story that he knew as a child, about Dermod O’Connor, known as the Wolf, an Irish chieftain around the time of the Norman invasion. He was "a red-handed reaver" who "preyed alike on Norman and Celt." He was mortally wounded by Sir Michael Kirowan and hanged from the tree ever after known as Dermod's Bane. He is remembered as a "giant of a man" with a "great black beard and ghastly eyes and boar tushes.” 

The latter-day Kirowan has a ghostly encounter with him--in wolf form, in his own monstrous human form, and in the guise of Moira, who almost leads him off a cliff to his death. His life is saved by the hand of Moira's true ghost--which comforts him with the knowledge that he and his sister will someday be together again.

### Behind the Mythos
A character named Kirowan confronts Mythos horrors in Robert E. Howard's stories "The Children of the Night" (1931), "The Haunter of the Ring" (1934), and "Dig Me No Grave" (1937). If the similarly named protagonist of "Dermod's Bane" is considered to be the same character, that story provides him with a backstory and a family background. 

While the horror elements in "Dermod's Bane" are not connected to the Mythos, the story's theme of ancestral enmity is one that appears in several of Howard's Mythos tales.

The Greater and Lesser Desh are an extradimensional species created for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. They first appeared in the supplement Adventures in Arkham County in the adventure "The Dark Wood" written by Fred Behrendt. 

### Description
The Desh are a beings categorised into two varieties: The Lesser Desh, which resemble large silvery tadpoles with beady eyes and long limbs, and the Greater Desh, which were fish-like with sharp teeth and large eyes. 

Both species were native to a parallel dimension, but were summoned to our reality through methods utilising a human brain. Despite appearing to move slowly, the Desh were actually very fast and were able to leap through the air.

Larry "Deuce" Richardson is an author and online critic who works in the horror and fantasy genres. He is passionate fan of and writer and editor of works related to Sword and Sorcery. His own work in the genre is often published by DMR Books. He is also moderator at the Official Robert E. Howard Forum as of 2007. In June 2007 he presented a scholarly paper on Robert E. Howard’s Thurian Age at Howard Days in Cross Plains. 

He has contributed articles and stories to several anthologies most of the external to the Mythos although he has written extensively on Rober E. Howard, Fritz Leiber both online and in published collections. His main writing focus is barbarian fantasy, in particular Conan the Barbarian when not writing more general fiction.

He resides in Pittsburg, Kansas.

Deus Machina Demonbane, also known as Zanma Taisei Demonbane (斬魔大聖デモンベイン) in Japanese, is the first installment of the Demonbane Mythos franchise by Nitroplus. It was released on April 25, 2003, as an eroge visual novel for PC. The game was later localized into English by JAST USA and released on May 13, 2011.

An all-ages remake version that removes all the H-scenes with newly written content was released on July 1, 2004 for the PlayStation 2. It was later ported to the PC on April 26, 2019.

### Synopsis
The main premise revolves around Daijuuji Kurou, a poor detective living in Arkham City. One day, he received a request from Hadou Ruri of Hadou Financial Group to search for a grimoire called the Necronomicon. While he initially refuses, Ruri offered him a large sum of money upon completion of her request, which leads Kurou to accept. As Kurou searches for the book, he unexpectedly runs into Al Azif, a pretty girl who is actually the humanoid manifestation of the Necronomicon. They forge a contract with each other, bestowing Kurou with powerful magic. Soon afterwards, Al also activated Demonbane, a Deus Machina owned by the Hadou Financial Group, to combat the menace from the occultist terrorist organization known as the Black Lodge, beginning the war between them. However, unbeknownst to all of them, the events and actions of the story are secretly being manipulated by a mysterious malevolent entity behind the shadows for their own personal agenda that threatens creation itself.

fullContent:
Devil Maker: Tokyo is a Korean mobile game developed and released by Palmple Inc. in March 2013, and later ended its service in October 2015. Featuring a traditional turn-based CCG gameplay, combined with RPG elements, the player was able to collect over 700 Devils based on entities from various mythologies, including many familiar Great Old Ones and Outer Gods from the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
10 years ago, the city of Tokyo was ravaged by the Devil War, enveloping the place with darkness. You formed a contract with the sun-goddess Amaterasu, in order to defeat the legendary serpent Yamatano Orochi and help the woman that you're trying to save. After defeating Orochi, Amaterasu decides to absorb Orochi's powers, granting her the power of all the light and darkness in the world, ending the contract. The end of the war causes you to black out and lose your memories.

In the present, you repeatedly wake up from the same nightmare, hoping that it'll stop bothering you. Attempting to figure out your identity, you start working as a private investigator, eventually receiving a Devil named Yuki as a client, who requests you to find her master. Yuki reveals that you made a contract with her master ten years ago, despite you having no memories of doing so. With the goal of finding Yuki's master and regaining your memories, you have to investigate the darkness remaining in the world by making contracts with other powerful Devils.

Devil Reef is a location first mentioned in the H. P. Lovecraft story The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

It is an offshore rock formation located a mile and a half out to the sea near Innsmouth, Massachusetts. Most of the time it juts out of the sea and is only thinly covered at high tide. Rumours abounded that the rocks are home to a legion of devils and imps or a hidden pirate hoard.

At the time in which the story was set and in earlier years, during the day Innsmouth natives held constant swimming races to the reef, while at night fully fledged Deep Ones would move back and forth between the rocks and the town.

### History
The reef was used by Captain Obed Marsh as a meeting point when contacting the Deep Ones of Y'ha-nthlei from around 1838.

In 1846, after a sacrificial ritual at the reef, Captain Marsh and several members of the Esoteric Order of Dagon were arrested by Selectman Mowry. No formal charges were made as Mowry and his supporters were soon killed during the Innsmouth riots.

According to one account, it is the literary equivalent to Misery Island near Salem. (: Providence)

### Y'ha-nthlei
Beyond the reef the water descends into an immeasurably deep trench known as Y'ha-nthlei, home of the Deep Ones. 

It was torpedoed during the government raid of 1928, but not destroyed.

The devil-fly is a fictional type of insect featured in the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald. These flies are notable for "stealing" the soul or consciousness of those who die after being bitten by them.

### Overview
Entomologists identify the so-called devil-flies of Uganda as Glossina palpalis, a relative of the common tsetse fly (Glossina marsitans) of South Africa. Science dictates that the devil-fly is dangerous for its habit of feeding off the blood of crocodiles, antelopes, and other animals infected by Trypanosoma gambiense, a parasitic microbe and cause of a potentially fatal disease when transmitted to humans. The first symptoms show up weeks after being bitten, while the illness itself lasts for months and is fatal if not treated.

However, the people who live in and around the jungles inhabited by these insects are also aware of another reason to fear them, as the devil-flies have the supernatural ability to "steal" the consciousness of those they have bitten. The reason for this is unknown, although the phenomenon is believed to be connected to the monolithic ruins of the outposts of the Fishers from Outside and their gods, Tsadogwa and Clulu. Whatever the cause, it has been observed that those who die after being bitten will have their minds transferred to the body of the insect responsible. The only known way to avoid this fate is if the fly perishes before its victim.

In their natural state, devil-flies are "as stupid as they are deadly", as Thomas Slauenwite puts it. They can be captured by the simplest fly-traps and are easy to swat or catch. However, if a person who has been bitten dies while the fly is still alive, the fly will acquire the consciousness of the deceased, including their human intelligence, memories, and personality, thus making them potentially more dangerous.

It's not known whether the curse of the devil-fly is related to the Trypanosoma infection. Slauenwite died from a heart attack before the disease could kill him, but still suffered the same fate as the other victims, finding his mind transferred to the body of the fly after death. On the other hand, it is possible that those who have been successfully treated and survived the disease, such as Mevana, will be able to avoid the curse by simply outliving the flies that bit them, although the fact that the devil-flies live longer than ordinary flies might cast some doubts about this.

### Slauenwite's hybrids
The devil-fly (Glossina palpalis) is genetically compatible with the Southern African species that Slauenwite refers to as the tsetse fly (Glossina marsitans). When crossbred in captivity, the two species produce fertile hybrid offspring. These hybrids are known to inherit their parents' infectiousness, as well as their ability to acquire the consciousness of the people they kill.

"Devil's Bathtub" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author and editor Lois H. Gresh. It was first published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu in October 2014.

### Synopsis
Iris is a neglected ten-year-old girl who lives on a remote Antarctic research station with her workaholic father. When her dog goes missing, she resolves to find it, but discovers that it has been assimilated by creatures from the nearby "Devil's Bathtub", beings known as Shoggoths. Her father attempts to bring her back, but the two fall into the clutches of the Shoggoths; while Iris embraces her new family in their collective consciousness, her father is driven to insanity by his condition.

### Publication History
Since its debut appearance, "Devil's Bathtub" has also been included in Cult of the Dead and Other Weird and Lovecraftian Tales, a 2015 collection of Gresh's own works.

Devilarium: The Mythos Merchant is a supplement for Zgrozy, the Polish-language spinoff of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG.

### Synopsis
Devilarium details a new Mythos creature which will trade information or items of use to Investigators in return for something precious to the Investigators, in the same way that traditional folklore and occult pacts with the Devil or other supernatural contracts were said to work.

### Behind the Mythos
Zgrozy is an imprint for Polish players of Call of Cthulhu, more recently translated into English for the general audience. Available in print and digital in Polish, Zgrozy as of mid 2021 is available only in digital formats for the English speaking audience. "Zgrozy" is an old Polish word of archaic usage, meaning "Horrible" or "Terror". The Zgrozy range is part of the Miskatonic Repository range of third party community products released under Chaosium and DriveThruRPG' licensing initiative.

Devlin Fredelin Macky is a fictional character created by American author Brandon Berntson for his Lovecraft Mysteries trilogy of Cthulhu Mythos novels, for which he is the series protagonist. He made his debut appearance in the first book in the series, The Night of Dagon.

### Description
A private investigator in the East Coast city of Innsport, Macky is used to taking on any kind of job just to pay the bills, usually missing persons cases, or looking into spouses suspected of cheating. He operates a small office for his business in one of the more nondescript areas of the city, and drives a somewhat beaten-up, but still perfectly serviceable, coupe. He has an aversion to fire, deep water, heights, guns, and dogs, although none of these are crippling fears. Macky also drinks and smokes too much, character flaws which he freely admits to.

### Relationships

### Veronica Macky
Macky was married in the past, to a woman named Veronica, who he nicknamed Posh-posh. Sadly, Veronica was diagnosed with cancer a month after their first meeting; she died two years later, after losing her battle against the disease. 

### Millie Von Clydesburgh
Macky and his secretary Millie Von Clydesburgh have something of a complicated relationship: despite having shared a few kisses, Macky seems reluctant to commit, despite Millie having been quite blunt about her feelings for him.

### Newt Bardhoff
Macky is also good friends with Innsport Police Department Lieutenant Newt Bardhoff, having saved his life at least once, and even introduced Bardhoff to his future wife, Amelia.

### Bradley "Boom-boom" Denton
A contact of Macky's from years ago, Boom-boom is a good-natured criminal with an unhealthy obsession with explosives. He is one of the few people in the series to have met Macky's deceased wife.

### History
After stealing an artefact from the Innsport Natural History Museum, Macky found himself embroiled in a plot to raise the monstrous Dagon. Despite opposition from deranged cultists, undead chauffeurs, and an angry Great Old One, and with more than a little help from Millie and Boom-boom, he was able to thwart the scheme and save the world (: The Night of Dagon).

When on a day trip to Arkham, Macky and Millie faced down an army of mutants, abominations, and even the Outer God Shub-Niggurath when attempting to thwart the schemes of Eric Moreland, who was attempting to find a new body for his deceased wife (: Arkham: Reanimated).

When he accidentally came into possession of the Necronomicon and initiated a series of events which would result in the return of the Outer Gods, Macky travelled through dimensions to enlist the aid of the Elder Gods and save his beloved home town (: The Lurker at the Threshold).

*The Lurker at the Threshold (2021)

The Dhôl Chants, or Dhol Chants, is the name of two fictional books in the Cthulhu Mythos, both described as containing spells in the form of musical chants. The original Dhôl Chants was created by H. P. Lovecraft in his story "The Horror in the Museum," ghostwritten for Hazel Heald and published in 1933.

### Description
### Leng book
The Dhôl Chants contains 555 chants of various natures, mostly to command spirits. There is one chant named "Blue Glow". The beneficial spells are noted to be often ineffectual, while the spells of vengeance usually work only after the death of the caster. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

There is a link, proven by metaphysical research, between this manuscript and the Dholes. Whether they influenced its text remains uncertain. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

### German book
Written in German, the Dhôl Chants deals with similarities between the music of the Caribbean and West Africa, and songs and chants that in truth are various kinds of magical spells. Because of their microtonality, the chants can only be performed by either singing or playing with an unfretted stringed instrument such as a violin. (: Arkham Unveiled)

Contains in the book are chants to contact Ahtu and Veerla (: Arkham Unveiled). Also mentioned are a pair of binoculars capable of viewing other dimensions (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana).

Zimmerman's volume may have incorporated material from the original Dhôl Chants (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana).

### History
### Leng book
Not much is known about the Dhôl Chants from Leng. There is a Chinese copy in an Asian monastery discovered in 1650, and also several English copies in existence, one of which is in Miskatonic University. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

### German book
The German Dhôl Chants was written by Heinrich Zimmerman in the 1890s. By careful studying West African music and discovering the odd similarities to Caribbean music at the time of Columbus, Zimmerman professed that he had discovered spells in the form of chants and recorded them in the book. (: Arkham Unveiled)

Dholes, also called bholes, are huge, slimy worm-like creatures, at least several hundred feet long. Because they avoid daylight and are covered in viscous goo, their features are nearly impossible to discern. They exist in the Vale of Pnath in the Dreamlands, and are also known to inhabit the planet Yaddith, where they have fought and emerged victorious against the native Yaddithians.

Dholes are featured in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" and The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, although in some editions of the latter, they are called "Bholes". It's been speculated that they might be the same as the "Dôls" mentioned in Arthur Machen's "The White People".

### Overview

Dholes are gigantic worm-like burrowing horrors. They are not native to Earth and none seem to be brought here for more than brief periods - fortunately, for they seem to have riddled and laid waste to other worlds, consuming them from within. It is unknown how they reach new worlds, but theories include magical summoning to "swim" through space. Some speak of Dholes traveling via the the Dreamlands, forcing their way through the inter-dimensional fabric of dream to reach distant places. 

They are rarely seen in daylight, and then only on planets that they have thoroughly conquered, as they dislike direct light, though it does not visibly harm them. Likewise, water does not affect them as it does some other worm-like Mythos entities (like Chthonians).

### Behind the Mythos
*In "The White People" by Arthur Machen, there is mention of "Dôls", but no description is given.
**The name is also similar to the Doels, although these appear to be distinct, as Frank Belknap Long has described the Doels as tiny flesh-eating creatures, whereas Lovecraft identifies the Dholes as massive worm-like creatures.
*In the works of Lin Carter, the Dholes are giant worms with white skin and porcine snouts, and are worshipers of Shub-Niggurath.
*In "The Illuminatos! Trilogy" both the Dôls of Machen and Dholes of Lovecraft are mentioned as being references to mythical creatures associated with the Illuminati.
*Dholes appear to be related to (or perhaps identical with) chthonians and their vermiform god, Shudde M'ell. Like dholes, chthonians are huge, worm-like creatures covered in viscous slime who live deep underground.
*In Ire of the Void () by Richard Lee Byers, the protagonists are confronted by a Dhole after escaping the Hounds of Tindalos, but manage to destroy it using dynamite.

Dhumin is a fictional entity created by American author Beecher Smith for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "The Burrower From the Bluff."

### Description
Dhumin is hinted at by Chief Russell Two Bears as being a Great Old One, or perhaps a species of colossal worm unknown to modern science (see "Behind the Mythos," below). (: "The Burrower From the Bluff")

One description given by Chief Two Bears is of Native American legends telling of Dhumin being "the most terrible" of the Uktena, "a great snake of the underworld" with "antlers like a deer and wings like an eagle." These creatures are said to inhabit "the deep waters, high places, and caverns beneath the earth … bor[ing] like the earthworm, and travel[ling] freely between the land of the living… and of the dead." (: "The Burrower From the Bluff")

The entity has a dislike of the sun and light in general, although it is only stated to be truly afraid of fire. (: "The Burrower From the Bluff")

### History
Whatever the origin of Dhumin, it has inhabited the Earth since before the time of men. When humans migrated to the Americas they worshiped it for as long as it left them in peace. However, when it began to prey on families and even entire clans, the tribes United in their outrage. A great horde of braves gathered their torches and herded the creature into the hard rock beneath the bluff, where it became trapped. (: "The Burrower From the Bluff")

Many years later, a corrupt lawyer related the story of how amoral developers paid him to push through a legal appeal which would allow them to relocate the mounds which contained Dhumin, freeing the creature and giving it free reign to prey on humankind once more. (: "The Burrower From the Bluff")

### Behind the Mythos
Smith's classification of Dhumin in "The Burrower From the Bluff" is inconsistent. At first described as a Great Old One - a species largely banished back to the stars by the Elder Gods - the same character later refers to it as a member of the Uktena, a species of subterranean beast of which Dhumin is "the most terrible."

Of course, this may also be attributable to either an unreliable narrator or confusion resulting from Native American oral history; either way, the entity's provenance remains ambiguous.

The Diabolique is a fictional character in the prime reality of the Marvel universe of Marvel Comics. Diabolique was created in 1993 by Chris Cooper and Rurik Tyler, first appearing in issue #9 of the 1st volume of Darkhold: Pages from the Book of Sins.

### Background
Diabolique is a demon/human hybrid that has ties to both the Darkhold and the Cult of the Darkhold. It appears as a 6 year old child, but is far older though she acts as a bratty child, a twisted sadistic one. She is constantly seeking out surrogate parents, who she later kills when she decides to move on to a new set of parents.

The demonic child possesses a number of magical powers. She gains the form of those she kills and their bodies and souls are fused into an entity called Playmate. Which at it's smallest is the size of a mouse which can grow to massive size and slaughters everything that's in its path, growing in power as the number of victims that it absorbs increase. It smothers, renders, strangles, and engulfs its victims. The entity projects heads, tentacles, and limbs with claws and teeth. Diabolique's power increases as the power of the Playmate grows, but if it's destroyed she is temporarily made powerless.

At full power, she can open dimensional portals, manipulate and absorb hellfire, tear apart victims, mentally control others, and practice sympathetic magic (e.g. voodoo dolls). She uses a spider called Zoroaster, which is the size of a small tarantula and she treats as a pet (Zoro). It is immune to hellfire, possesses superhuman strength, is able to regenerate it's limbs, and can increase its size to that of an automobile.
