Diana Stanley, the Redeemed Cultist, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-related content.

### History
Diana was raised on the family farm, but after her father died she sold it and moved to the city of Arkham in 1924. Using the proceeds from the sale, she bought the failing Emmie's Boutique and made a success of the business, eventually renaming it Huntress Fashions (the play being that Diana was the Roman goddess of the hunt).

Quickly establishing herself in the local community, Diana joined the Chamber of Commerce, the Women's League and the Historical Society, seeing membership in these institutions as a way to promote and advance her financial interests. After a while she was invited by prominent local businessman Carl Sanford to join the elite Silver Twilight Lodge and, believing it to be nothing more than an exclusive social club, happily accepted.

However, the further she progressed up the ranks of the Lodge, the more bizarre and horrific their practices became, and she was introduced to the rites of animal sacrifice and demon-conjuring. Sickened by this, Diana came to the conclusion that she must put a stop to the activities of the Lodge.

At this point, Diana's backstory diverges into two differing accounts.

### Eldritch Horror ()
In this version (which was written first) it is stated that Diana decides to topple the Silver Twilight Lodge from within. Carl Sanford sees a certain promise in the young woman and sends her on a mission to Panama as part of their grand scheme.

### Feeders from Within ()
Richard Lee Byers' 2013 novel Feeders from Within recounts Diana's attempt to expose the Lodge by going to the authorities about their activities, but unfortunately the police are in Sanford's pocket, and she barely survives an attempt on her life by the Lodge and their otherworldly allies.

The morning after her escape, she is admitted to Arkham Asylum, half mad and raving. She is treated by psychologist Dr. Carolyn Fern who is visiting on other business, but one night she undergoes an unspecified treatment by unconventional physician Dr. Herbert West, following which she develops two distinct personalities. The first is little more than her old self, terrified of what she has seen and done and wishing nothing but an end to the horror, while the second is that of a borderline psychopath whose goal is to rid the world of the evil forces manipulating it. 

Disappearing shortly after her procedure, Diana later joins up with Carolyn and ex-soldier Mark Harrigan who have uncovered a plot by the Silver Twilight Lodge to bring madness and chaos to the world using the entities known as Feeders from Within. Die Offenbarungen des Glaaki is a collection of German-language translations of works by Ramsey Campbell, mostly those from The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants.

### Overview
Containing nine short stories and running to a total of 313 pages, Die Offenbarungen des Glaaki (which translates as The Revelations of Glaaki) was published in June 2014 by Festa as part of their H. P. Lovecraft's Bibliothek des Schreckens (H. P. Lovecraft's Library of Horrors) series. Cover and interior artwork was supplied by Giorgio Grecu.

*"Die Kammer im Schloss" ("The Room in the Castle")
*"Das Grauen von der Brücke" ("The Horror from the Bridge")
*"Der die Schleier zerreißt" ("The Render of the Veils")
*"Die Insekten aus Shaggai" ("The Insects from Shaggai")

*"Das Lied des Strandes" ("The Voice of the Beach")
*"Ein unheimlicher Drang" ("The Tugging")

Die, Monster, Die! or Monster of Terror is a film based on the plot of H.P. Lovecraft's The Colour Out of Space.

### Plot Summary
Stephen Reinhart, an American scientist (Nick Adams), pays a visit to the estate of his British fiancée's family. He finds a scorched area of countryside near an enormous crater. Local townspeople are hostile toward him and refuse to either drive him to his destination or talk about the family that lives there. The source of all these problems is later revealed to be a radioactive meteorite kept hidden in the basement by his girlfriend's father, Nahum Witley (Boris Karloff), who has been using the radiation to mutate plant and animal life, with horrific consequences to his subjects and to members of his family. Nahum's wife, Letitia, mutated by the meteorite and driven insane, dies in an attack on Steve and Susan. After Helga, a maid who has been mutated and driven mad by radiation, comes after Nahum, he is mutated after his attacker falls on the meteorite and is killed. The Nahum monster attacks Steve and Susan, but falls from a balcony and bursts into flame when he hits the floor, setting the entire Witley mansion ablaze. Steve and Susan escape from the burning mansion, and never look back.

### Reception
In their book Lurker in the Lobby: A Guide to the Cinema of H. P. Lovecraft, Andrew Migliore and John Strysik call Die, Monster, Die! a "textbook example of the walking-around-endlessly-in-a-big-house school of filmmaking". G. Noel Gross, writing for the DVD review website DVD Talk, writes: "The plodding plot would be more painful if the flick were longer, but the intriguing meld of gothic horror and contemporary sci-fi is hard to pass up".

### Adaptions

* Die, Monster, Die! (March 1966): a Dell Movie Classic comic book.

fullContent:
Different Worlds Issue 45 is the March/April 1987  issue of the long-running roleplaying game magazine Different Worlds. It was published by Sleuth Publications.

The issue was advertised as a "Cthulhu Special," although it contained a limited amount of material which was directly related to H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos.

Featured articles included:

* "Scary Monster Horror Picture Show Role-Playing Game" by Brian J. Underhill: a rules-light, B-movie-esque horror roleplaying alternative to the Call of Cthulhu game
* "Call of Cthulhu in the Eighties" by Michael Szymanski: a brief piece offering a rundown of playing Call of Cthulhu in a contemporary setting
* "Occult Organisations in the 1920s" by Richard Kaczynski: a rundown of the state of real-world occult groups during the Roaring 20s. Although the introductory paragraph describes the piece as being useful for Call of Cthulhu, the article could be used for any roleplaying game in which the characters encounter an occult organisation
* "The Lights of Madness" by Richard Launius: a 1920s adventure scenario for Call of Cthulhu featuring a cult dedicated to Yog-Sothoth
* A review of Stuart Gordon's Lovecraft film adaptation From Beyond

"Dig Me No Grave" is a short story by American fantasy and horror writer Robert E. Howard, published in the February, 1937 issue of Weird Tales. It was also published as "John Grimlan's Debt".

It is part of a series of stories by Howard that are set in H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Characters
*Professor John Kirowan
*John Conrad
*John Grimlan
*Malik Tous, the Prince of Darkness / the veritable Satan / Sathanas / Beelzebub/ Apolleon / Ahriman, the old Serpent

### Also mentioned:
*Professor Von Boehnk
*Yog-Sothoth
*Kathulos
*Nameless One
*Elder Ones 
**unnamed lord

### Adaptations
The story was adapted by Roy Thomas and Gil Kane in Marvel's horror comic Journey into Mystery, with some variations, including the change of some of names:

*Only Grimlan is named John (in the original story, both Grimlan and Conrad are named by their first name). John Conrad is only named "Professor Conrad", and John Kirowan became "Dan Kirowan". Those changes were possibly made for the sake of clarity and to avoid the repetition.
*The names-droppings mentions "Shuma-Gorath" (the first mention of that name -created by Robert E. Howard-, and later developed in Marvel comics as the lord of the Great Old Ones), instead of "Yog-Sothoth" and "Kathulos" in the original story, ignore a mention to the "black cyclopean walls of Koth", and replace "Yuggoth" by "Acheron".

Digital Pinball: Necronomicon was a 1996 video game for the now-defunct Sega Saturn games console.

### Overview
As its name indicates, Digital Pinball: Necronomicon consists of a series of three digital pinball tables which draw their inspiration from the works of H. P. Lovecraft. It was a Japan-exclusive release, although all text and vocal effects were included in English.

### Trivia
* Tracks included on the musical score include "Arkham Multiball", "Cult of the Bloody Tongue Multiball", "Dreamlands Multiball", "Keeper of the Silver Gate" and "Moon Beast".

"Dilution Solution" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Adrian Simmons. It was published in the Jason Andrew-edited thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods by Simian Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
In a subterranean city on an Earth besieged by the forces of madness and chaos, a Patroller - men and women designated to travel the world in search of vital supplies for the colony - is brought to a rehabilitation centre suspected of being infected by the pervasive insanity he has witnessed in the world above.

Over the following weeks, he is treated by a genius doctor, one who came from outside and is reputed to know everything about the cause of the madness. He and his fellow inmates are slowly indoctrinated into the doctor's cult, before leaving the city to spread their unique form of madness to the next colony in line…

shortDefinition: The concept of different dimensions is present throughout the writings of H. P. Lovecraft and the cosmic horror genre as a whole. The term is often used to describe universes or planes of existence different from our own, usually very alien in nature...
fullContent:
The concept of different dimensions is present throughout the writings of H. P. Lovecraft and the cosmic horror genre as a whole. The term is often used to describe universes or planes of existence different from our own, usually very alien in nature or following different laws and having different matter than our own universe. For example Cthulhu is from a different universe/dimension as he is described as being made of a different type of matter, as well as the Mi-Go. The Dreamlands are a famous example as well.

Dimensions can also be interpreted as higher spatial dimensions, which as seen in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", go up until "archetypal infinity". Gates are a series of highly transcendental planes of existence which themselves surpass the very concept of higher dimensions. An unknown amount of gates exist, but there is stated to be a "multitude". The Ultimate Gate transcends all dimensions, universes and planes of existence and is where the Court of Azathoth is located in the "Ultimate Void", where the Outer Gods reside.

Fictional dimensions are often treated as places similar to "parallel worlds" or pocket dimensions, small and finite bounded other worlds. However sometimes the term is used less accurately or more poetically in Mythos works. For example the entities in "From Beyond" are visible when an attunement takes place. This attunement is treated as accessing a different dimension by most authors using it in their own pastiches. However, the original story deals with vibrations or frequencies so in that sense treating different frequencies as different dimensions is not correct. This is why some later writers deliberately obscure the intended nature of the "other dimensions" by using poetical or literary terms such as "realm" or "world" rather than "dimension". Dimension is the most scientific sounding of the common terms and in later Lovecraft, for example "The Dreams in the Witch-House", when magic-as-unknown-science has more or less replaced the supernatural, the term "dimension" is used in its applicable meaning from physics.

The Dimensional Shamblers are a race of monsters from a different dimension that first appeared in H.P. Lovecraft's story "The Horror in the Museum". They might also be the same as the eponymous entities described in Clark Ashton Smith's story "The Hunters from Beyond"; the publication of which predates Lovecraft's tale by a year.

### Overview
Little is known about these beings who seem capable of walking between the planes and worlds of the cosmos, never spending much time at any location. It is unknown whether they are a distinct interdimensional species or constructs created in the deep passages of time to serve a higher power, but are now free to roam where they will. Rumours suggest that these entities occasionally serve the Outer Gods and Great Old Ones, yet their individual motivations and purpose remain a mystery.

### Description
These "hunters from beyond" appear as short crouching creatures with tight grey mummy like skin. Its head is semi ape like and semi canine, and has crooked stained fangs. Its eyes are recessed in deep eye holes and appear as yellow slits. It has long arms with huge claws. Though it has the appearance of being material the Dimensional Shamblers originate from a different dimension, making it immaterial in our world. It is intangible, making it unable to touch or be touched.

### Origins
The Shamblers come from a lower dimension described as "a long, gray, oozing plain, beneath skies where the fumes of Hell were writhing like a million ghostly and distorted dragons." In this dimension thousands if not more Dimensional Shamblers live. Humans sucked into this dimension sink into the gray ooze to have their minds and souls eaten by the Shamblers.

### Powers
The Shamblers can be called to our dimension with certain spells or pure will power, the Shamblers being keen on hunting victims. When they have chosen a victim they will attempt to suck them into their own dimension calling as many of their cohorts as needed. While they do seem to grab at the victim they actually use a form of hypnosis that can be broken by a strong willed person. Its possible that a larger amount of the Shamblers can be more powerful. When they try to suck a victim in it will seem as if the place around the Shambler disappears behind it and their own dimension will become visible.

Dire Documents is a player aid for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, published by Chaosium in 1993, and running to a meagre nine pages in length. It is currently out of print, and likely to remain so due to the ease of replicating similar contents digitally in the current age.

### Overview
Dire Documents contains a selection of blank player handouts for use by keepers to enhance the immersion of Call of Cthulhu games, as well as a novelty form to award the player whose character died in the most entertaining way.

### Contents
*Arkham Sanitorium inpatient admission form
*Arkham Sanitorium letterhead
*Award for Meritorious Service
*Near East Treasure Import letterhead
*Eye of Amara Society letterhead
*Dewey Cheatham & Howe Attorneys at Law letterhead
*Miskatonic University letterhead
*Formal invitation
*Keeper's Choice Award for Superlative Demise.

Dr. Yōzan Dirk W. Mosig (born 1943) is, amongst many other things, a leading scholar of Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Born in Germany, he emigrated to the United States where he attended the University of Florida; he currently teaches psychology at the University of Nebraska.

S. T. Joshi, to whom Mosig has offered a degree of mentorship in the field, has said that "Dirk Mosig is the key transitional figure in Lovecraft studies; and if the history of this field is ever written, he will have to occupy a central role."

### Selected Works
*"H. P. Lovecraft: Myth-Maker" (1976)
*""The White Ship": A Psychological Odyssey" (1980)

### Trivia

*The Lammas 1985 edition of Robert M. Price's long-running Lovecraftian fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu was devoted to the works of Dirk W. Mosig, and included some complementary works by fellow scholars including S. T. Joshi and Peter Cannon.

The Disciples of Dagon is a fictional organization in the Marvel universe whose first appearance was in 1990 in issue #176 of the 1st volume of the Savage Sword of Conan series.

### Background
The Disciples of Dagon is a cult dedicated to Dagon which exists in the Hyborian Age. It consists of Deep Ones and humans whom have been transformed into fish people. In one of the possible futures that Conan of Cimmeria saw, he was the sole survivor of a wrecked ship. Who ended up in a sinister fishing town that was desolate and inhabited by fearful people. He was told that things had drastically changed for the worst in the last couple of months, with people disappearing.

He discovered that the Disciples of Dagon had infiltrated the town, when they attempted to kill or capture Conan and the barmaid he was with, sleeping in his room. They seized her and he pursued them underground, down the stairs. Where they were calling to Dagon, about to offer her to their god. He attempted to intervene but both Conan and the barmaid were taken by Dagon. Afterwards, his vision showed both of them now thralls of Dagon, physically alive but having experienced death of the mind.

The Disciples of the Rapine Storm is a fictional organization in the CthulhuTech pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Wildfire LLC.

### Background
The Disciples of the Rapine Storm is a cult under the control of Hastur which emerged from the Plateau of Leng. The Disciples of the Rapine Storm consists of cannibals and insane psychopaths (many of them self-mutilated), who murder, rape, torture, mutilate, and consume those that fall into their hands. A terrifying horde that lays waste to all in front of it. Marching along with the heavily armed bloodthirsty crazed horde are monsters, including alien beasts from other dimensions or worlds which they have summoned to Earth.

Its armies have destroyed and depopulated huge swaths of Asian and European territory. Starting out in Tibet or possibly Central Asia, they have reached as far west as the eastern borders of Europe, have marched south into Pakistan and northern India, overran all of China and Southeast Asia, and have reached northwestern Australia. Despite the NEG's superior conventional firepower, it has prevailed due to it's extensive use of zoners, dream magic, ancient monsters, and offensive parapsychics and its cooperation with the Disciples of Death's Shadow. In desperation, the NEG has used nuclear weapons, which at best has only slowed them down.

Discovering H. P. Lovecraft is a collection of non-fiction works compiled and edited by Darrell Schweitzer.

Consisting of eighteen works - including several from those who actually knew him and one from H. P. Lovecraft himself - and running to 172 pages, Discovering H. P. Lovecraft was compiled and edited by Darrell Schweitzer, and published by Wildside Press in August 2001.

The majority of the included pieces were previously collected in Schweitzer's 1976 anthology Essays Lovecraftian.

fullContent:
"Discovery of the Ghooric Zone -- March 15, 2337" is a short story by Richard A. Lupoff, first published in the anthology Chrysalis (Zebra Books, 1977).

### Synopsis
In the year 2337, a trio of cyborg space explorers make the first visit to the Solar System's tenth planet. As their arrival takes place on the 400th anniversary of H. P. Lovecraft's death, the travellers name the planet for the writer's invented planet Yuggoth, naming its moons for other worlds in Lovecraft's mythology: Nithon, Zaman, and the twins Thog and Thok. Detecting what appear to be structures on Thog--the first signs of extraterrestrial life in the Solar System--the party lands there to explore, finding a passageway that lead down to an inner world that they decide is the Ghooric zone written of in Lovecraft's "Fungi from Yuggoth" sonnet sequence--complete with  a "foul lake/Where the puffed shoggoths splash in doubtful sleep." There they find a platform on which rests the body of Lovecraft himself. When the explorers try to return to the surface, they find they are trapped in the Ghooric zone forever.

The story is intercut with a series of sketches of life in 2337, 2237, 2137, 2037, and 1937--giving a brief future history of Earth over the next four centuries.

### Characters
Njord Freyr, the male member of the crew, represents the Laddino Imperium that rules Earth's Western Hemisphere. He is the least modified of the team. 

Sri Gomati, the female crewmate, comes from Khmeric Gondwanaland, the government of the Eastern Hemisphere. 

Shoten Binayakya, the nonbinary participant in the voyage, is "fitted with multiply-configurable genitalia" and is "ambiguous as to his or her own origin."

### Publication History
The story was later reprinted in the revised edition of Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1990). It was also included in Lupoff's collection Claremont Tales (Golden Gryphon Press, 2001).

shortDefinition: "Dispatches from the Providence Observatory: Astronomical Motifs and Sources in the Writings of H.P. Lovecraft" is a non-fiction summary and review by T. R. Livesey of the influence of astronomy on and in the works of H. P. Lovecraft. It formed part ...
fullContent:
"Dispatches from the Providence Observatory: Astronomical Motifs and Sources in the Writings of H.P. Lovecraft" is a non-fiction summary and review by T. R. Livesey of the influence of astronomy on and in the works of H. P. Lovecraft. It formed part of the non-fiction anthology Lovecraft Annual No. 02 published by Hippocampus Press in 2008.

In 1902 at the age of 12, Lovecraft discovered his aunt's astronomy reference books and from that point on for several months was obsessed with the idea of a career as an astronomer. Although this passed, as the author notes Lovecraft was growing up, and then writing, at a time when constant astronomical discoveries and theories in physics were not merely undermining anthopocentrism but abolishing it. Seen in this context, Lovecraft's cosmicism was the logical outcome of his exposure to the scientific theories supporting astronomy.

fullContent:
Dispersing Vibrato (산란 비브라토) is a community-created but fully licensed supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG. It is a creation of Korean fans of the system and setting and forms a "foreign language" (from the point of view of English speakers at least) contribution to the crowd sourced and fan authored material collected and sold as the Miskatonic Repository, a truly immense collection of gaming material.

### Adventure Overview
With an estimated playtime of 4 to 5 hours, this adventure serves as a potential introduction for a new campaign or a stand alone adventure for pre-generated characters of the Keeper's choosing. The adventure is recommended for 2 to 4 players maximum. This scenario features a created mythical creature. 

### The Story
Recently, violinist and former conductor of the Arkham Philharmonic Orchestra Gerard Perkins went missing. He was reported missing by his housekeeper. Gerard had not been seen at his home for several days and since this felt strange to the housekeeper she reported it. The police who received the report found handwritten writings suggesting a crisis while searching his home, but they found no trace of Gerard anywhere. At the start of the adventure the police have temporarily closed the investigation. Not satisfied with this outcome, Leslie Woods, the sister of the missing Gerard and a famous violinist, looks for someone to entrust with the task of finding her missing brother.

### Behind the Mythos
The first of three adventures in a series of crowd sourced and community contributed stories, together with Red Nectar, Les Parasites and Double Walkers aka Doppelgangers.

P. Lovecraft and many others. These have been included in anthologies such as Swords Against Cthulhu, Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights, Corporate Cthulhu, The Averoigne Legacy,  Steampunk Cthulhu: Mythos Terror in the Age of Steam, Kill Those Damn Cats, Cthulhu Christmas Special and Other Lovecraftian Yuletide Tales, and The Idolaters of Cthulhu.

In addition to his fiction credits, Tyrer wrote an introduction for the Lovecraftian board game Carcosa by One Free Elephant in 2017 .

Tyrer is also the founder and chief editor of the small press Atlantean Publishing, a Southend-on-Sea, England-based publishing house established in 1996. The press publishes a range of material, including zines and chapbook collections .

term: Documents in the Case of Elizabeth Akeley
shortDefinition: "Documents in the Case of Elizabeth Akeley" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Richard A. Lupoff, a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness. It first appeared in the March 1982 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction.  ### Synopsis...
fullContent:
"Documents in the Case of Elizabeth Akeley" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Richard A. Lupoff, a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness. It first appeared in the March 1982 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction.

### Synopsis
A federal agency investigates a cult headed by the great-granddaughter of a man who vanished under mysterious circumstances a half century earlier. Evidence suggests that the great-grandfather may be returning, improbably enough--but what is his hidden agenda?

### Characters
*Elizabeth Akeley: Radiant Mother of the Spiritual Light Brotherhood. Aside from her position in the church, she lives "a normal life for a young woman of her social and economic class." She lives at 176 Pleasant Street in National City, a residential suburb of San Diego, California.
*Marc Feinman: Elizabeth's boyfriend. Works as a computer systems programmer with an avocation as a musician. He was "born and raised in the Bronx, New York." He lives in "a pleasant apartment on Upas Street near Balboa Park."
*Vernon Whiteside: Sexton of the church, "a nondescript looking Negro." He was infiltrated into the church by a federal agency to keep tabs on its doings.
*Ezra Noyes: President of the Vermont UFO Intelligence Bureau and editor of the Vermont Unidentified Flying Object Intelligencer. Nineteen years old, he lives with his parents in Dark Mountain, Windham County, Vermont.
*Henry Wentworth Akeley: Elizabeth's great-grandfather, born in 1871.
*Sh’ch’rrru’a: An entity from Aldebaran, Henry's lover. Also known as Sheera.

### Akeley Family
Lupoff creates an extensive family history for the Akeleys, presented as one of the documents that make up the story. Highlights include:

1607: Beelzebub Akeley sails on the caravel Worthy from Portsmouth, England, to Kingsport, Massachusetts.

1618: Beelzebub establishes the Akeley dynasty in Townshend, Windham County, Vermont.

The Akeleys line continues in Windham County for the next two centuries, "producing numerous clergy, academics, and other genteel professionals in this period."

1832: Birth of Abednego Mesach Akeley, "the last of the Vermont Akeleys to pursue a life of the cloth."

1868: Death of the Rev. Samuel Shadrach Solomon Akeley, Abednego's father, who ordained him. On rising from assistant pastor to pastor, Abednego "transferred the affiliation of his church from its traditional Protestant parent body to that of the new and suspect Starry Wisdom sect.

1871: After Abednego's death at the age of 39, "the remnants of his congregation moved as a body to Providence," Rhode Island. Later that year, Henry Wentworth Akeley is born to Sarah Elizabeth Phillips, a formerly a servant in the  Akeley household, "fathered by Abednego mere hours before his death."

1901: Henry's wife gives birth to their only child, George Goodenough Akeley, "succumbing two days later to childbed fever."

Henry has a successful academic career and returns to Windham County to retire.

Early 1920s: George Akel

Doels are a fictional species from another dimension created by Frank Belknap Long.

In Howard Phillips Lovecraft: Dreamer on the Nightside, Long describes the Doels as tiny, flesh-devouring creatures "who inhabit an alien dimension shrouded in night and chaos".

It's been speculated that they might be the same as the Space Eaters.

### In the Mythos
Halpin Chalmers made contact with the Doels at some point after consuming the Liao drug, and has seen "their maker" in dreams. He later mentions the Doels and the Satyrs as creatures that might help the Hounds of Tindalos break into his room. (: "The Hounds of Tindalos")

Albert Wilmarth learned about the Doels and the Hounds of Tindalos from a creature masquerading as Henry Wentworth Akeley. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

### Behind the Mythos
It's possible that the Doels might be related to, or synonymous with, the Dôls mentioned in "The White People", by Arthur Machen.

The Doel Chants mentioned in Robert Bloch's "The Mannikin" might be the same as the Dhôl Chants mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Horror in the Museum".

The name is also evocative of the Dholes, which are massive predators that inhabit Yaddith and the Dreamlands in Lovecraft's fiction.

fullContent:
The Dominion of the Black, also referred to as Dominions of the Black and the Black Truth, is a sinister intergalactic organization controlled by Lovecraftian-like entities in the fictional universe of Pathfinder a pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Paizo Inc.

### Background
It's a intergalactic conglomeration of races who serve a group of vast and powerful alien intelligences. These alien intelligences are similar to the Great Old Ones but do not use magic and they are beings of the material plane. Entities which are at least as powerful as the Great Old Ones and perhaps more, who have vast psychic powers. One of which is Tychilarius, a massive abomination created by the fusing of thousands of smaller abominations in the center of a black hole. The Dominion of Black is not a state but a network of worlds controlled by them, which are used as facilities to produce weapons and servitor races by using bio-mechanical technology, cybernetics, and genetic engineering.

Worlds are conquered to provide their biotech fleshfarms with more input. Their forces include monstrous servitor races and are equipped with interstellar starships with faster-than-light capability and directed energy weapons. Its members view humanoids as inferior, good only as raw material, to experiment on, and to manipulate their genes. Scholars state that the Dominion of the Black is in actual opposition to the Elder Mythos. No one knows their agenda, but it's rumored that their ultimate goal is the extermination of all life in the cosmos and/or its replacement with something else from another reality.

Don Diego de la Vega, better known as the hero Zorro, was created by Johnston McCulley in 1919, first appearing in The Curse of Capistrano. In 2019, he became the protagonist in the Lovecraftian pastiche Zorro: Rise of the Old Gods by American Mythology Productions.

### Background
Don Diego de la Vega is a wealthy landowner who takes up the masked identity of Zorro to "to avenge the helpless, to punish cruel politicians, to aid the oppressed". He lives a double identity in which Zorro is a man of action, a courageous hero with the mind of a fox. Originally, his civilian identity was that of a proud young man who cared little for the poor, was not a man of action, and was perceived by women as lacking passion. One version of Zorro has battled the forces of the Mythos.

fullContent:
"Don't Monkey With a Monkey" is a tongue-in-cheek Cthulhu Mythos short story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in the collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
Tough Arkham private detective Wade Kearney is hired by former Miskatonic University researcher Horace Wilkins to retrieve a laboratory monkey which has gotten loose. Tracking the beast to a local bar, he finds that it has been given a secret formula which has increased its size, strength, and aggression. During a fight between several bar patrons, local mobsters, law enforcement, and the monkey, a number of people - including Wilkins - end up dead, and the creature collapses drunk. Kearney returns to his office minus his fee, but with an incredible story to tell.

### Behind the Mythos
In the story, Wade Kearney, a recurrent character in Shiflet's Mythos fiction, mentions another private eye, one "Sweetan over at Discreet Investigations". This would appear to be a reference to Bill Sweetan, another of Shiflet's characters, despite his statement in the story notes for the 2017 edition of Looking for Darla that "[Kearney and Sweetan] are pretty much the same person."

Donald Allen Wollheim (1 October 1914-2 November 1990 ) was an American author, editor, publisher, and early promoter of the concept which would (much later) come to be known as "fandom."  He wrote a number of works which intersect with the purview of this wiki, including a hoax review of a non-existent translation of the fabled Necronomicon , and a real-world eulogy for H. P. Lovecraft himself, published only two months after the author's death , as well as being responsible for the first professional printings of some of Lovecraft's works, including "The Nameless City" (Fanciful Tales, Fall 1936).

American novelist F. Paul Wilson, who has cited Lovecraft as one of his major influences, cites Wollheim as the catalyst for his fascination with Lovecraftian horror .

Donald Richard Burleson (born 1941) is a fiction writer, literary critic, professional mathematician, and UFO researcher. He has written extensively on the work of H. P. Lovecraft and has contributed numerous stories to the Cthulhu Mythos. 

His literary criticism includes the books H. P. Lovecraft: A Critical Study (1983) and Lovecraft: Disturbing the Universe (1990). 

His Mythos and Mythos-related fiction has appeared in such collections as The New Lovecraft Circle, The Azathoth Cycle, The Cthulhu Cycle, Made in Goatswood, Acolytes of Cthulhu, Black Wings of Cthulhu, Black Wings of Cthulhu 3, and Gothic Lovecraft.

### Overview
Burleson studied at several universities, including Yale and the University of Massachusetts at Amherst. He has master's degrees in English and mathematics, and a PhD in English literature. (His dissertation was on Lovecraft.) He was on the mathematics faculty of Eastern New Mexico University.

Burleson is New Mexico state director of the Mutual UFO Network (MUFON). His nonfiction books about UFOs include The Golden Age of UFOs, UFOs and the Murder of Marilyn Monroe, and UFO Secrecy and the Fall of J. Robert Oppenheimer (all from Black Mesa Press).

He is married to Mollie L. Burleson, who has also written Mythos fiction. Meeting at a horror convention in Providence in 1979, they were both also members of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts and scholars active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s.

Donald Tyson (born 12 January 1954) is a Canadian author who has written more than a dozen nonfiction books on the Western esoteric tradition, some of which are connected to H. P. Lovecraft. Tyson has also written fiction in the Cthulhu Mythos genre, including two novels that focus on the character of Abdul Alhazred. He lives in Halifax, Nova Scotia.

Tyson's 2010 book The Dream World of H. P. Lovecraft: His Life, His Demons, His Universe is both a biography of Lovecraft and an exploration of his work from an occult perspective. S. T. Joshi blurbed it as "a thought-provoking and intellectually stimulating book...a must-read for Lovecraftians. 

In The 13 Gates of the Necronomicon and Grimoire of the Necronomicon, both published in 2008, Tyson attempted to use the Cthulhu Mythos as a framework for ritual magic. With artist Anne Stokes, Tyson produced the Necronomicon Tarot in 2007 featuring Mythos imagery.

fullContent:
Donald Albert Wandrei (April 20, 1908 – October 15, 1987) was an American science fiction, fantasy and weird fiction writer, poet and editor. He was the older brother of science fiction writer and artist Howard Wandrei. He had fourteen stories in Weird Tales, another sixteen in Astounding Stories, plus a few in other magazines including Esquire. He was the co-founder (with August Derleth) of the prestigious fantasy/horror publishing house Arkham House.

He contributed three stories to the Cthulhu Mythos: "The Fire Vampires" (1933), "The Tree-Men of M'Bwa" (1933), and "The Lady in Gray" (1933).

### 1920s
He attended Central High in St. Paul, Minnesota, from 1921–24, during which he published short compositions in the school newspaper and avidly read the magazine Science and Invention. In 1923 he began work part-time as a "page-boy" in the circulation room of the Saint Paul Public Library, filling reader's requests for books from the storage stacks; this expanded his access to, and reading of, a wide variety of literature. In 1923 and 1924 he also worked evenings at the Hill Reference Library.

He attended the University of Minnesota. While there, he was a student editor and regular columnist on the student newspaper The Minnesota Daily, and was also associated with the Minnesota Quarterly Magazine, as well as contributing pieces (often unsigned or pseudonymous) to the campus humour magazine Ski-U-Mah, which was edited by classmate Carl Jacobi. At that time he was enormously influenced by a reading of Arthur Machen's novel The Hill of Dreams. Wandrei graduated in 1928, with a BA in English.

At the age of 16, Wandrei completed his short story "The Red Brain", in which a mysterious Cosmic Dust sweeps through the universe, obliterating the stars. Only Antares, inhabited by a race of viscous Brains, survives -– and this last remnant of universal sentience entrusts its fate to the unique, laboratory-created Red Brain, in a compelling fable that leaves behind the concerns of the human aquarium to revel in the cosmos and the ultimate terror waiting there.

Wandrei started writing professionally in 1926, and his writing career took off around 1932. In late 1927 he hitchhiked from Minnesota to Rhode Island to visit H. P. Lovecraft. Lovecraft conducted him on a grand antiquarian tour of Providence, and then on to similar tours in Boston, Salem and Marblehead. There was also an excursion to Warren, Rhode Island, later made famous by Wandrei's reminiscences in the Arkham House volume Marginalia (1944), during which Wandrei, Lovecraft and James Ferdinand Morton each sampled twenty-eight different flavors of ice cream at Maxfield's ice-cream parlour.

In 1925, Wandrei gave Clark Ashton Smith $50, so the Auburn poet could see Sandalwood through the press.

Donovan is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu". 

### Overview
Donovan was a member of the schooner Emma of Auburn, although his role is uncertain. When the crew discovered Cthulhu's vault in R'lyeh, William Briden failed to find its opening. Donovan proceeded to feel "over it delicately around the edge," press "each point separately as he went," and was the one who successfully opened the immense door, after climbing atop the structure. However once the door had been opened, Cthulhu emerged, killing Donovan, Guerrera and Angstrom. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

### Trivia
*Donovan is one of only three known characters in Lovecraft's fiction to be slain by Cthulhu itself.

fullContent:
Doors to Darkness is an adventure supplement for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium.

### Overview
Consisting of five standalone scenarios, Doors to Darkness is specifically designed to help ease new Keepers into running games of Call of Cthulhu. All of the maps and handouts necessary to play are provided, as well as a set of ten pre-generated Investigators to enable quick-start games. Also included is an article by veteran games designer Kevin Ross featuring a range of hints and tips on being a successful Keeper. Doors to Darkness runs to a total of 144 pages.

### Scenarios

*"The Darkness Beneath the Hill" by Christopher Smith Adair: “A house renovation in Providence, Rhode Island lures the investigators into ancient earthly secrets.”
*"Genius Loci" by Brian Courtemanche: “The investigators explore the Danvers State Asylum in a desperate attempt to help a friend in need.”
*"Servants of the Lake" by Glynn Owen Barrass: “Pursuit of a missing friend finds the investigators sequestered in a roadside motel where not all is as it seems.”
*"Ties That Bind" by Tom Lynch: “Strange rock formations appear in the fountain of a wealthy Arkham resident, leading to a wellspring of forbidden knowledge.”
*"None More Black" by Brian M. Sammons: “The death of a Miskatonic University student leads the investigators into unsavory neighborhoods and dark business dealings.”

### Publication History
First published by Chaosium in 2016, Doors to Darkness was released in both full-colour hardback and digital PDF editions.

"Dope War of the Black Tong" is a short story by American author Robert M. Price. It continues the Anton Zarnak series created by Lin Carter, for whom Price acted as literary executor.

### Synopsis
Steve Harrison, a private detective on a mission to clean up the city's dark underbelly, stumbles across an incursion of Tcho-Tcho criminals who have allowed a consignment of the drug Black Lotus to reach the streets. 

Recruiting the aid of famed occultist Dr. Anton Zarnak the two, with the aid of Zarnak's capable manservant Akbar Singh, track down the cult and put a stop to their nefarious scheme. Despite the fact that Zarnak is seemingly killed during the confrontation, Singh believes him to have magically transported himself to the Plateau of Sung.

### Characters
*Steve Harrison, a hard-bitten private eye.
*Anton Zarnak, a man with a mysterious past and a deep understanding of the occult.
*Akbar Singh, Zarnak's faithful manservant and bodyguard.

### Publication History 
*The Disciples of Cthulhu: Second Revised Edition (February 1996)
*Lin Carter's Anton Zarnak: Supernatural Sleuth (June 2002)
*Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2008)

fullContent:
Dora McCain is a character created by American author Ron Shiflet for his short story "Seduced".

### Description
Dora is a beautiful young girl with long blonde hair who is apparently in her middle teens. She dresses in cheap, dirty clothes, is poorly educated (at least by the standards of the modern world), and lives in a rickety old country shack with her father and at least four siblings.

### History
A typical backwoods hillbilly from a degenerate West Virginia family, Dora's mother died when she was aged twelve, and a few weeks later she made the acquaintance of Mother Shub, a crazy old woman who lived deep in the forest and was widely believed to possess magical powers. Over the years, Mother Shub taught her how to mix potions, make prophecies and even command the animals of the woods on occasion.

When she was around fifteen, Dora was raped by three boys, brothers from a neighbouring family. She went to Mother Shub for help, who gave Dora her own power before passing on. Gathering her strength, Dora assembled the ingredients for a dark elixir and cast the spell she had been taught. Answering her call, Shub-Niggurath sent its servants to slaughter the brothers for her.

Dora now seems to spend her time roaming the backwoods in search of lone men to seduce and sacrifice in the name of The Black Goat of the Woods.

### Appearances
This is a list of the stories in which Dora has appeared, arranged by her in-mythos timeline.
*"Out of the Frying Pan" (2009)
*"Out of Her Gourd" (2018)
*"Seduced" (1998)
*"Mother's Little Helper" (2008)

Dorieb is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The White Ship".

### Background
Dorieb is a legendary king who rules the fabled land of Cathuria according to the beliefs of many who live in the Dreamlands. He is even said by some to be a god or demigod. Upon the walls of his high palace are many turrets of marble. In his wide halls many multitudes assemble, and there hang the trophies of the ages. The roof is of pure gold, set upon tall pillars of ruby and azure, and having such carven figures of gods and heroes that he who looks up to those heights seems to gaze upon the living Olympus. The floor of the palace is of glass, under which flow the cunningly lighted waters of the River Narg with its colorful varieties of fish not found outside Cathuria. (: "The White Ship")

Dorothy Charlotte Walter (27 April 1889 - 1967) was, amongst other things, a teacher, researcher, editor, and archivist. Dividing much of her time between Vermont and Providence, Rhode Island, she was an alumni of Brown University; she subsequently spent some time working the Brown archives, including those regarding Howard Phillips Lovecraft. 

Walter also wrote a small number of non-fiction pieces on Lovecraft, which have been published in collections such as The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces, Rhode Island on Lovecraft, and Lovecraft Remembered.

Dositheus is a fictional character, based on the historical figure Dositheos, who is a recurring character in the Simon of Gitta stories of Richard L. Tierney. His first appearance was in "The Sword of Spartacus", published in Swords Against Darkness #3, published in 1978.

Dositheus appears as a Samaritan wizard who serves as a mentor to Simon of Gitta, though at times Simon has to rein in Dositheus when his plans for revenge against Rome go too far. Dositheus has an apprentice named Menander and a crow familiar named Carbo.

### The Historical Dositheos
Dositheos, who probably lived in the first century AD, was the founder of a Samaritan religious sect with Gnostic teachings. He is said to have known John the Baptist and to have been either a teacher or a rival of Simon Magus, the figure that Simon of Gitta is based on.

### In the Simon of Gitta Series
Dositheus appears in Tierney's stories "The Sword of Spartacus", "The Fire of Mazda", "The Seed of the Star-God" and "The Throne of Achamoth", and in his novel The Drums of Chaos. His death is referred to in Tierney's story "The Dragons of Mount Fractus".

fullContent:
"Down in Limbo" is a short story by American theologian and author Robert M. Price which is set in H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
The story follows young university lecturer Larry Stanton who is finishing his dissertation on a translation of the scroll known as The R'lyeh Text, aided by the recent discovery of a set of undersea carvings dubbed the Bimini Glyphs.

Stanton and his girlfriend Barb later visit a past-life regression channeler, where Barb is regressed using lines from the original script of The R'lyeh Text and remembers an existence in a world which she does not recognise.

In the meantime, Stanton completes his translation and passes it on to his mentor Professor Maitland who has dedicated his life to attempting to decipher the runes, and then leaves to speak to the past-life channeler, Dr. Waite. After Stanton leaves, Maitland reads the translation and, terrified by what he sees there, burns all records of it (including the original parchment) and takes his own life.

When Stanton speaks to Waite, the man channels a creature from the future, who recounts his people's efforts to regress themselves in order to recover the translation which has been lost in their time. With that, the entity tells him that Stanton's own session is over, and he awakens in an alien body under a ruined sky. As his body chants the translated texts, a chasm opens beneath him and something begins to awaken.

### Characters
*Larry Stanton, a university lecturer at the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities whose focus is undersea archaeology. He is later revealed to be some kind of creature from a ruined future Earth.
*Barbara Gilbert, Stanton's girlfriend, and a student of Marine Biology. She is possibly of the same future species as him, and may have been an Atlantean priestess in a past life.
*Professor Maitland, Stanton's mentor and a senior faculty member at the Sanbourne Institute.
*Dr. Waite, an occult channeler.

### Publication History
"Down in Limbo" was first published in Deathrealm #24 in June 1995. It was later included in a collection of Price's own works, Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2011, and again in the eBook anthology The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack by Wildside Press in 2012.

### Mythos Connections
*Several entities from the Cthulhu Mythos are mentioned in the story, including Ghatanothoa, Ythogtha and Mother Hydra. A line which refers to the "Dead King of the Old Ones" is likely intended to mean Cthulhu.
*The Mythos locations R'lyeh, Mu, Atlantis and the Bimini Islands are all referenced.
*In addition, the occult sources The R'lyeh Text, The Unter Zee Kulten and the Cthäat Aquadingen are all stated to have been read by Larry Stanton.

fullContent:
Downward to Darkness is a Cthulhu Mythos novel written by Brian McNaughton. It was originally published in 1978 as Satan's Mistress (Carlyle Books), and released under McNaughton's preferred title in 2000 by Wildside Press. It was followed by a sequel, Worse Things Waiting (aka Satan's Seductress). 

### Synopsis
When teenager Patrick McLaughlin's family moves into an old mill once owned by an ancestor in Mt. Tabor, Connecticut, he begins having vivid and powerfully erotic dreams about a mysterious red-haired woman. The dreams turn out to be part of his ancestor's plot to return to the world of the living by possessing a descendant--a plot that disrupts not only Patrick's family but the entire community of Mt. Tabor. 

### Characters
* Mordred Glendower: A Welsh wizard born in 1560 who kept himself alive by "incarnating himself in a new body each generation." He was "secretary to Dr. John Dee in the reign of Elizabeth I." He walked with a limp due to his "ineptly set leg, broken during his headlong flight from Salem, Massachusetts, in 1692." He lived as a miller in Mt. Tabor, Connecticut, until he was blamed for a series of infant disappearances in 1847 and neighbors burned him to death in his home.
* Mirdath Hodgson: Mordred's daughter, and "a partner in his deviltry." She was hanged from an oak tree after her father's killing; her son changed his name to Glenn, moved to California, and became the ancestor of Rose McLaughlin. Mirdath has "straight, long hair of a particularly dark-red shade," "her skin [is] as smooth and as white as the flesh of an egg," and her "nose was long and straight and suggestive of a classical goddess."
* Patrick McLaughlin: A 15-year-old boy who is "even more awkward and shy than most of his contemporaries; he had neither charm nor good looks."
* Frank McLaughlin: Patrick's father, a successful commercial artist. He had a "large knees," a "large face" and a "large belly." He attended Harvard, but likes to wear a Syracuse sweatshirt as a "badge of reverse snobbery."
* Rose Glenn McLaughlin: Patrick's mother and Frank's wife, she has a Ph.D. in English. Described as "handsome," she has "freckles and prominent upper teeth": "Her dark hair, pulled back from her angular face, held streaks of gray that she didn't try to conceal."
* Dr. Howard Ashcroft: The leader of an esoteric cult near Mt. Tabor. He was "written up in one of those grocery-store tabloids as a wizard who practices the Black Mass." He has a "neat, salt-and-pepper Vandyke."
* Jane Miniter: A real estate agent and a friend of Rose's; Frank refers to her as "Mrs. Minotaur." Twenty years earlier, she "had been the prettiest girl in Mt. Tabor" (according to George Spencer, who had an affair with her), but grew "coarse and mannish in middle age." She "always looked as if she'd just tramped in from a day's rough shooting on the moors."
* Amy Miniter: Jane's daughter, whom she calls "stolid."; Patrick sees her as "a plain, awkward girl, even less socially acceptable

Doyle Jeffries is a fictional character who appears in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos-related games and fiction. He is the editor of the Arkham Advertiser, Arkham's local newspaper in the Fantasy Flight Games version of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Arkham Horror
Doyle Jeffries first appeared in the Arkham Horror Second Edition expansion The King in Yellow as a Blight, a character which imparts negative effects onto the players.

### Ire of the Void
In Richard Lee Byers' 2018 novella Ire of the Void, Professor Norman Withers approached Jeffries at the offices of the Advertiser requesting access to their archives in an effort to find others which had suffered the same fate as his friend Claus Schmidt, who had been abducted by a Hound of Tindalos. Jeffries obliged this request, on the condition that Withers later give him an exclusive interview on the event. Jeffries did indeed get his exclusive, but it was a heavily-edited version of the tale which featured no supernatural events.

"Dr. Dexter" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Llewellyn M. Cabos. It made its first appearance in Randall D. Larson's Threshold of Fantasy #1 in March 1982.

### Synopsis
British secret agent John Blake pursues international criminal Szasz, a man suspected in the murder of several people. The trail leads Blake to Arkham's Miskatonic University where he learns that Szasz is in fact Nyarlathotep, who is inhabiting the body of Ambrose Dexter while attempting to awaken the Great Old One Cthulhu using the power of a "fiery messenger from the heavens called Zindarak."

When Dexter/Nyarlathotep steals the Necronomicon, Blake and his Allie’s track him to Innsmouth, but he has already made good his escape and embarked for the coordinates of R'lyeh. Summoning whatever help he can muster, Blake heads to the newly-risen island where he kills Dexter's body, forcing Nyarlathotep into an incorporeal form. Fleeing R'lyeh, an American naval taskforce pounds the island with its advanced weaponry, causing it to once again sink beneath the waves.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Dr. Dexter" has also been published in the January 1998 edition of Edward P. Berglund's online zine Nightscapes.

### Trivia
*John Blake is a thinly-veiled pastiche of Ian Fleming's spy James Bond (more accurately, of the popular film series version of the character) complete with Walther PPK handgun and Aston Martin sports car.

Dr. Fo-Lan is a fictional character created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer for their short story "The Lair of the Star-Spawn".

### Biography
Doctor Fo-Lan was a famous Chinese scientist and philosopher who resided in Peiping. By the time he met Eric Marsh, Fo-Lan was an old, white-haired man. He is slightly over 6 ft tall (~ 1.83 m) and speaks English fluently. Like Laban Shrewsbury, Dr. Fo-Lan is incredibly knowledgeable in the matters of the Cthulhu Mythos and has even mastered the art of astral projection, although he refers to it as "telepathy".

At the end of the nineteenth century, Fo-Lan was abducted from his home in Peiping by the Tcho-Tcho people, who brought him to their hidden city of Alaozar, in the Burmese Plateau of Sung. Fo-Lan's brother was killed, presumably disfigured to prevent identification, and left in Fo-Lan's place, leading the world to believe that the doctor himself had been murdered.

For the next three years, the captive Fo-Lan reluctantly helped the Tcho-Tchos and their leader E-Poh to dig deeper into the heart of the Plateau, until they found the chamber where Lloigor was imprisoned. Unbeknownst to his captors, Fo-Lan spent all his spare time trying to use astral projection to contact the Elder Gods in the Orion Belt. When the Tcho-Tchos captured an American explorer named Eric Marsh and brought him to Alaozar, Fo-Lan convinced them to spare the man's life by claiming that Marsh could help them.

Fo-Lan told Marsh the story of how the Elder Gods imprisoned Zhar and Lloigor in prehistory, and how the Tcho-Tcho people were formed from "seeds" left by the latter and now live to serve their masters, seeking to free them from their subterranean prisons. Fo-Lan enlisted Marsh's help by asking him to stand guard over his body while he was busy trying to contact the Elder Gods or their allies in Rigel. At last, their plan succeeded and the Star-Warriors of Orion descended from the stars to destroy the twin monstrosities and their servants, followed later by the Elder Gods themselves, one of which transported Fo-Lan and Marsh to safety.

A Tokyo newspaper later published the news about Fo-Lan being still alive.

By the time Eric Marsh wrote his narrative, he told readers that they could seek out Fo-Lan in the village of Bangka, in the province of Shan-si, if they wanted to confirm the veracity of the events narrated. (: "The Lair of the Star-Spawn")

fullContent:
Dr. Herbert West & Astounding Tales of Medical Malpractice is a children’s horror graphic novel written by Bruce Brown and illustrated by Thomas Boatwright. Running to a total of 78 pages, it was published by Arcana Comics in September 2019; both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Overview


### Synopsis
After the West family relocate to the city of Providence, Rhode Island, an unfortunate accident leaves the town doctor permanently incapacitated. Taking over the reigns, child prodigy Herbert West uses his unique intellect to serve the needs of the people, and for a while his great brain is occupied with the challenge.

However, perhaps inevitable for one such as he, apathy sets in and he begins to seek other ways to stimulate his mind- including his greatest endeavour to date, an attempt to bring the dead back to life.

Unfortunately for the people of Providence, West accidentally drops a few crumbs from his sweet treat into the serum he is developing; this not only prevents the risen dead from falling back into their eternal slumber after a certain time, it also bestows upon them an insatiable appetite … for sugar.

Enlisting the aid of "Dean" Allen Halsey (in actuality a Miskatonic University janitor who sells fake degrees from his office in a broom cupboard), West and his younger sister Elizabeth cook up a plan to deal with the rampaging zombies. Stealing a cart loaded with sacks of sugar, they lure the undead into chasing them to the banks of the river where they drive the whole cart into the water. The zombies, unable to resist their cravings, follow and the town is saved.

### Trivia
* The book features a foreword by Jeffrey Combs, an actor with a long history of involvement with Cthulhu Mythos-related film, and who played the role of Dr. West in Stuart Gordon’s 1985 comedy-horror adaptation Re-Animator.
* Although the character is consistently referred to as Allen Halsey (itself a slight variation on the naming of Allan Halsey in Lovecraft’s story) the plaque on his desk is spelled "Hasley".

Dr. Pelletier is a recurring character in the Gerald Canevin series of supernatural stories by Henry S. Whitehead.

### Biography
A good friend of Canevin, Dr. Pelletier is the Chief Surgeon of the Naval Station Hospital in St. Thomas, in the US Virgin Islands. He is described as a large, portly man, and is highly esteemed for his surgical skills. He is also known for his scientific knowledge and open-minded willingness to accept extraordinary, even potentially supernatural explanations for events, provided that they fit the evidence at hand. (: "Passing of a God", "Cassius")

He has traveled to China, Haiti, and continental Central America. (: The Great Circle)

Dr. Jonas Reid is a fictional character created in 1926 by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his iconic short story "Pickman's Model," although he is given little more than a passing mention in the story.

In the original story, he is only referred to as Dr. Reid. His first name, Jonas, originates from the story "The Truth About Pickman", by Brian Stableford.

### Background
Dr. Jonas Reid (: "The Truth About Pickman") was a well-educated man who possessed a morbid interest in what many would describe as the more unsavoury side of science, perhaps even the occult. He was tutored at the Cabot Museum by the skilled taxidermist Will Minot (: "The Studies of Dr. Reid"), a character who debuted in "Out of the Aeons".

### History

### In Lovecraft's Works
Dr. Reid's initial mention tells only that Reid was one of the "fussy old women" described by Thurber as being responsible for Richard Upton Pickman's pariah status among the Bostonian artistic community, a result of the morbid nature of his paintings. At the time, Reid had taken up comparative pathology classes, and observed that Pickman's "features and expression were slowly developing in a way he didn't like; in a way that wasn't human" ("Pickman's Model").

### In Other Works
Peter Rawlik expands upon the character in his short story "The Studies of Dr. Reid," explaining that Reid had not in fact cast aside Pickman as originally believed, but simply wished to distance himself from the young artist after an extended period spent in close contact (the issue of social propriety is also implied).  

However, Reid continued to watch Pickman, and eventually bore witness to his liaisons with the ghouls which he was so fond of painting: this revelation prompted Reid's study of taxidermy.  

Later, Dr. Reid brought Pickman with him to the lair of some ghouls, in the hope that he would be of assistance in acquiring a specimen for dissection. Whether this endeavour was successful or not is unknown, but unlikely.

Dragon Kings are a fictional species created by Lin Carter for his Thongor series, which first appeared in the 1965 fantasy novel The Wizard of Lemuria. They were later adapted by Marvel Comics in 1973, making their debut appearance in issue #26 of Volume 1 of the Creatures on the Loose comic book series by Val Mayerik and Gardner Fox.

### Background
The Dragon Kings are descendants of the Elder God Set. It's a race which was sired by his son Sligguth, spawned a million years ago (together with the race known as the Serpent Men). Half a million years ago, in the time of elder Hyperborea, the Dragon Kings ruled the Earth (including the continent of Lemuria). It was the Age of Dragons, when reptilian kings and necromancers ruled the land, studying dark magic and building monolithic cities of black stone. Masters of science and technology, unlike any seen on Earth.

They worshiped the Lords of Chaos, including Iao Thamungazoth.

The Dragon of the Moon is an eldritch Lovecraftian entity from the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. It was created in 1984 by Peter B. Gillis and Don Perlin, making its first appearance in issue #138 of the Defenders comic book series.

### Background
The Dragon of the Moon originated on Earth, The offspring of the Elder God Set, it originated on Earth, but later headed out into space to explore the cosmos and spread its evil beyond Earth. The Dragon has claimed to be responsible for committing various evils but it is a great liar, and thus many of its claims are difficult to verify. It is most infamous among the superhumans of Earth for corrupting the hero Moondragon.

The Dragon has the power to reshape reality and can manipulate forces on a planetary scale. If a mortal is worthy, it will offer them its power, seducing them by appealing to their insecurity and/or greed. The greater the acceptance of the victim, the greater the Dragon's power within the material universe. The Dragon of the Moon manifested as an amorphous centipede-like presence, which grew in tandem with its power.

"Drawing No. 8" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas, which takes place in his futuristic Punktown setting. It was first published in the collection Haunted Worlds by Hippocampus Press in August 2017 .

The story forms the first part in a short series (later collected in The Summoning of the Old Ones), which describes an alien cult's efforts to summon an avatar of malevolent extra-dimensional god Ugghiutu.

### Synopsis
Struggling artist Maxim Komaroff is commissioned by the enigmatic Kalian Nhil to recreate the final painting in a series of religious images, the original having been destroyed by a woman who believed herself to be acting in the interests of preventing an imminent apocalypse.

As Komaroff works, he begins to dream of an ancient and powerful entity named Ugghiutu, which he comes to believe will be summoned with the completion of the artwork. However, too prideful to leave his masterpiece unfinished, he delivers the final piece to Nhil, and sets in motion a series of events which will rock Punktown to its roots.

### Publication History
Strangely, "Drawing No. 8" did not receive a release until three years after the final part of the trilogy, "Wunderwaffe", had seen print .

*Haunted Worlds (2017)
*Punktown (2018)
*The Summoning of the Old Ones (2019)

fullContent:
Drawn from Life is a short story by prolific British author John Glasby which is set in H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos. It bears similarities to both Lovecraft's The Music of Erich Zann and Pickman's Model.

First published in the Michaelmas 1989 edition of Crypt of Cthulhu magazine, "Drawn from Life" received an eBook release with the Wildside Press publication of The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack in 2012.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator is writing a book concerning obscure contemporary artists, and to this effect is trolling London's art shops to gather material for his work. In a small shop off the beaten track, he discovers a piece by acclaimed violinist Antonio Valliecchi that depicts an alien landscape in incredible detail. He purchases the painting and searches for others, finding another two, both of which are of bizarre worlds and painted with such an eye for detail that they seems to the narrator to almost have a life of their own. 

The man then contrives to meet Valliecchi after one of his concerts in order to discuss the pieces with him. Valliecchi at first denies having made any paintings, but then tells the narrator to come to his home on Mewson Street later that night.

When the narrator visits Valliecchi -- who lives in an area of London which seems to have been unchanged for hundreds of years -- he finds that the man has created many other paintings in the same vein as the ones he bought. Valliecchi then whips back a large curtain from the wall, revealing what appears to be a window before beginning to play his haunting melodies on the violin; as he does so, the window begins to display scenes from the paintings, although what is seen appears to be actual visions of these places. Finally, a blackness descends on the window, and an amorphous creature extends a tentacle through the glass and drags the screaming Valliecchi through, never to be seen again.

### Characters
*The Narrator, a writer and connoisseur of fine art.
*Antonio Valliecchi, a violin supremo whose music connects him to malevolent otherworldly entities.

The Dreamlands (also known as the Dream Realm) are a fictional setting created by H. P. Lovecraft for a series of stories, known as the Dream Cycle, set in a world that people enter through their dreams. It is a vast, alternate dimension or universe, with lands, seas, creatures, civilisations, and an extensive Underworld. 

### Description
The Dreamlands are for the most part a mirror-image of our waking universe, having, as far as can be determined, the same planets, stars, and other cosmic geographical features. However, there are numerous races, civilisations, and beings existing in the Dreamlands that do not exist in the waking universe, such as the Zoogs, Gugs, Ghasts, moon-beasts, and others.

In keeping with the dimension's nature as the consensus of Earth's dreams, it is easier to travel to distant places including other planets or the Moon than it would be in the physical waking world. The journey may still be long or have requirements to be met but travel to distant "locations" in the Dreamlands is a relative commonplace.

Also, the Dreamlands usually refers to the Dreamlands of Earth; however the overarching Dream realm includes a "Dreamlands" for every world inhabited by intelligent life. For example if Mars still had intelligent life, as some writers suggest, it too would have a Dream realm of its own and those falling asleep and dreaming on Mars would enter the same Dreamlands but in a vastly distant and presumably different set of entry points to those of Earth's Dreamers.

### The North
*The Plateau of Leng—Home to man-eating spiders and the satyr-like "Men of Leng".

### The East
*Celephaïs—A city dreamt into being by its monarch Kuranes, greatest of all recorded dreamers.
*Serannian—A city-state floating in the clouds in the sky of the Dreamlands, close enough to Celephaïs to trade with it.
*The Forbidden Lands.

### The West
*Steps of Deeper Slumber (accessed via the "Cavern of Flame").
*The Enchanted Woods—the place where many enter the Dreamlands, which is home to the Zoogs.

### Geographical features
*Hatheg-Kla—A "high and rocky" mountain in the "stony desert" 13 days' walk from the village of Hatheg, for which it is named. It is one of the places where the "gods of earth" once dwelt, and sometimes return to when they are homesick. (: "The Other Gods")
*Thurai—A white-capped mountain where the gods of earth used to dwell. It is said that at Thurai, men mistake the tears of the gods for rain. (: "The Other Gods")
*Lerion—Another mountain formerly inhabited by the gods, where the "plaintive dawn-winds" are in fact their eternal sighs. (: "The Other Gods") Lerion is later

fullContent:
"Dreams in the House of Weir" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, first published in the licensed Weird Tales anthology Weird Tales #1.

### Synopsis
The story is set in 1931 and consists of extracts from the diary of a linguist named Hareton Paine. To be able to concentrate on his translation work, Paine rents a house on the British countryside. The place is called Delaware House after its builder, a 13th century nobleman named Ranulf de la Weir, so Paine refers to it as the "House of Weir".

In spite of the complete silence, Paine still finds himself unable to concentrate. His wife, Elaine, is similarly agitated, particularly after seeing some kind of white animal in the woods outside their window. To make things worse, Paine starts to experience strange dreams of being Kzoora, an insectoid alien living on a world named Yaddith, with metallic high towers and five suns in the sky. In his dreams, Paine is aware that Kzoora is a wizard trying to find ways to combat the burrowing Dholes, which are enemies of the insectoid Yaddithians, even though both species are followers of the same goddess, Shub-Niggurath.

One day, Paine finds Elaine reading a manuscript called Visions from Yaddith, which catches his attention, as he thought the word "Yaddith" had originated from his dreams. The book turns out to be a collection of poetry from an author named Ariel Prescott, who died interred in an asylum, and Paine is shocked to find several terms and descriptions that perfectly match his dreams. Elaine reveals that she saw a huge white creature with a porcine snout outside the window, which Paine dismisses as probably just a boar, but recalls that Prescott's poems also describe the Dholes as "swine-snouted worms".

Following another nightmare of Yaddith, in which Kzoora and the others debate about whether to abandon the planet and settle in some other world, Paine reads from Prescott's verses that even that wouldn't be a guarantee of safety, as the Dholes could track them through their dreams and follow them. Paine then visits the local vicar, Dr. Minge, who confirms that Ariel Prescott did live in the Delaware House before she went mad. On his way back, Paine sees something that looks like a giant white worm with a porcine snout moving through the woods, and reasons that his dreams must be affecting him. Two days later, he sees another one, this time very clearly, and faints.

The last entry reveals that the Dholes are now trying to get into the house. Paine has barricaded himself and killed Elaine to spare her of being devoured by the creatures. He plans to kill himself when they break in, but not before finishing the narrative and urging that the house and its psychic link to Yaddith must be destroyed somehow.

fullContent:
Dreams in the Witch House is a 2023 open world horror adventure game, based on the short story "The Dreams in the Witch House" by H. P. Lovecraft. The gameplay involves guiding Walter Gilman as he prepares to face the dreaded May-Eve witch ritual in the legend-haunted city of Arkham. 

### Description
Arkham, Massachusetts, 1929. Walter Gilman, a promising math student, has just moved to the city and is starting his studies at Miskatonic University. The Dombrowskis' boarding house where he resides has a bad reputation, but Walter doesn’t mind the old rumors... until the dreams start. A hideous scheme is underway, and if Walter is not careful, it could cost him more than his life. It could cost him his soul.

### Gameplay
Dreams in the Witch House combines role-playing and survival game elements with traditional point-and-click adventure gameplay. Players can choose to study for exams, research occult tomes, or focus on Walter’s physical and mental well-being. Time progresses in the background, and the nightly horrors intensify as the May-Eve climax approaches.

The game features multiple endings that reflect the consequences of Walter’s actions. Unlike in the original story, it’s possible to achieve a “good ending” and defeat the occult menace.

"Dreams of a Diseased Mind" is a short Cthulhu Mythos piece by the late author, artist and editor Steve Lines. It was published in Ron Shiflet's short-lived fanzine In Lovecraft's Shadow by Tenoka Press in March 2007.

### Overview
Part Cthulhu Mythos story, part biography, "Dreams of a Diseased Mind" reads as more akin to an author's description, the likes of which frequently precede published works. It gives a fictional account of Lines' childhood, which purportedly included encounters with a Polynesian Cthulhu cult and the government agency Delta Green, as well as sojourns in the Severn Valley and Innsmouth, before describing his real-world pursuits as an adult: mentions include his editorial work, musical achievements, and history as a publisher.

"Dreams of the Docent" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Lee Clark Zumpe. It was first published in the July 2015 edition of Tales of the Talisman (Hadrosaur Productions) , and was later voted by the fanbase to be included in the anthology The Best of Lovecraftiana (2023, Rogue Planet Press) .

### Synopsis
When car trouble finds the unnamed narrator stranded in the small Floridian town of Shady Haven, he is forced to spend the weekend at the only hotel, where he makes the acquaintance of owner Mose Lipscomb. Lipscomb tells the man of how, many years ago, famed horror writer H. P. Lovecraft spent an evening at the hotel, and his vile dreams are now blamed by the remaining townsfolk for the town's decline, believing Lovecraft to have "fiddled with the dial on the cosmic radio … opened the channel and initiated the transmission."

During his stay, the narrator experiences nightmares of the "blind and mindless Daemon Sultan at the very heart of Ultimate Chaos", as well as visions every bit as horrendous as those experienced by Lovecraft, and takes his leave as soon as possible. However, despite his most fervent wishes, it appears that the dreams will not diminish with distance, and that the illusion of realities merging may be with him for the rest of his life.

### Trivia
*Amongst the bedside reading material to be found at Lipscomb's hotel are old copies of pulp magazines Weird Tales and Thrilling Wonder Stories, containing fiction by Robert Bloch, August Derleth, and Henry Kuttner.

Dreams of Yith, by Duane W. Rimel, is a series of sonnets that were much admired by H.P. Lovecraft; they were first published in the June 1934 issue of The Fantasy Fan. In an uncredited revision of the poem, Lovecraft changed the title, noting that the original name "Yid" accidentally was a derogatory name for Jewish people. The poem cycle is the first mention of the fictional planet Yith, which Lovecraft adopted as the home planet of his Great Race of Yith in The Shadow Out of Time.

Lovecraft's well-documented views", while accusing Cthulhu of being antisemitic; however, Cthulhu denies this allegation, claiming that he is a progressive and forward-thinking being who is disdainful for all of humanity equally. Furthermore, Cthulhu did not even want to destroy anyone at the moment, but was awoken by a battle between Godzilla and the kaiju from Pacific Rim.

fullContent:
"Drunk on Dream" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the Cody Goodfellow/Joseph S. Pulver, Sr.-edited anthology New Maps of Dream by PS Publishing in July 2021 .

### Synopsis
In the aftermath of a messy breakup, the unnamed narrator turns to alcohol in an effort to forget about his former lover. After a while it dawns on him that, while passed out, his consciousness visits another plane of existence in which he can control the landscape. During one of these nighttime excursions, he believes he glimpses his ex and, upon waking, resolves to seek her out on future trips in an effort to rekindle their romance.

Unfortunately for the man, he soon comes to the realisation that the alcohol is his only vector for entering this other realm and, in a drunken stupor one evening, accidentally causes a car crash which results in his death.

### Behind the Mythos
Although "Drunk on Dream" contains hints but no explicit references to H. P. Lovecraft's works, the realm the man visits is intended to be the Dreamlands: this was made clear in the publisher's description for the chapbook collection The Offspring of Nightmares (2022, Forma Street Press) . Some of the elements described in the story include large creatures possessing vertical mouths full of teeth, presumably Gugs, and flying humanoid monstrosities with blank faces, most probably Night-gaunts.

fullContent:
Duane W. Rimel was an American science fiction, fantasy and erotica writer most well known for his collaborations with American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft.

Lovecraft was a close friend who mentored him in his early writings as early as 1934. The following year, Rimel collaborated with writer Emil Petaja to create The Fantaisiste's Mirror a fan magazine to continue the serialization of Lovecraft's essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature" where the magazine The Fantasy Fan left off. However, the magazine never made it to print.

Lovecraft and Rimel collaborated on several pieces, such as "Dreams of Yith", "The Tree on the Hill" and "The Disinterment", the latter published in Weird Tales. After Lovecraft's death, Rimel continued to write Mythos stories, such as "Music of the Stars".

He was also co-editor (with Francis T. Laney) of the early fanzine The Acolyte (1942-1946) which published several notable Lovecraft pieces including the first glossary of the Cthulhu Mythos.

He went on to write numerous other fantasy, science fiction and detective stories.
