Duckthulhu is a fictional monster from the Darkwing Duck comic book storyline "F.O.W.L. Disposition", featured in issues #9-12 of the 2010 series by Boom! Studios. 

### Background
Duckthulhu is an "elder being" from beyond the stars, older than time itself. He takes the form of a gigantic, green anthropomorphic duck with tentacles coming out of his beak and wings on his back. Seeking to enter this reality, Duckthulhu has the power to not only enslave the world, but to destroy all of existence. The ancient texts prophesied that a "purple pawn" would arrive of his own volition, in order to satisfy Duckthulhu's appetite for a character of high spirits and exaggerated self-image.

When the terrorist organisation F.O.W.L. began losing to Quackwerks Corporation, the three shadowy figures known as the High Command of F.O.W.L. started planning to summon Duckthulhu so that they could use his power to remake the world in their image. Steelbeak, one of the top agents for F.O.W.L., seemingly defected after thinking that they were going too far, and teamed up with the superhero Darkwing Duck to foil their plans. Meanwhile, Darkwing refused to tell anything about the mission to his girlfriend, a powerful sorceress named Morgana, who was upset over being stuck babysitting his daughter, Gosalyn. Using her crystal ball, Morgana received a message about the rising of Duckthulhu, and then went to Darkwing's trusted sidekick, Launchpad, for assistance. As Duckthulhu's power began drawing closer, Morgana and Launchpad observed that a crowd of people had been transformed into octopus-like monsters, mindlessly chanting "Duckthulhu F'Sure". Before Morgana could cast a protection spell, Launchpad succumbed to the effects as well, leading to Morgana using a transformation spell to disguise herself with a tentacled-form, following the others to meet Duckthulhu while her mind was still intact. 

Eventually reaching the heart of F.O.W.L., Darkwing and Steelbeak discovered Duckthulhu's altar, which had a torture cross and a large statue of Duckthulhu. Steelbeak immediately betrayed Darkwing, bounding him to the torture device, so that the High Command can use the "purple pawn" to perform their ritual. Feeding on Darkwing's arrogance and selfishness, the statue comes to life and manifests itself as Duckthulhu. By the time Morgana and her team arrived, Duckthulhu was already fully awoken. The High Command were unable to control Duckthulhu's power, leading to them suffering the consequences of their god's judgement. Morgana projected a forcefield to protect Darkwing and their allies, before activating a magic scroll to transform all of reality.

Inspector Duke Givens is a fictional character created by American author Brandon Berntson for his Lovecraft Mysteries trilogy of Cthulhu Mythos novels. He made his debut appearance in 2018's The Night of Dagon.

### Description
A "portly man with jowls", Givens prefers to dress in suits which are always clean and neatly pressed. An inspector in the Innsport Police Department, he is married to an unnamed woman, and has a love/hate relationship with the protagonist of The Lovecraft Mysteries, private investigator Devlin Macky.

### History
After being assigned the case of an artefact stolen from the Innsport Natural History Museum, Givens and his partner Lieutenant Newt Bardhoff found themselves investigating a missing persons case on the estate of cultist Mordred Haddonfield. Captured by Haddonfield and his undead servant Borgas, they were destined to be sacrificed to the recently-awoken Dagon: the timely intervention of Macky and Millie Von Clydesburgh saved them from this fate, and the pair returned to Innsport to begin an evacuation ahead of Dagon's murderous rampage (: The Night of Dagon).

Later, Givens was heavily involved in the battle against the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred, the Outer Gods, and their legions of monstrous minions after Macky accidentally kickstarted Alhazred's plot to bring about the return of his dark masters (: The Lurker at the Threshold).

fullContent:
Dungeons & Dragons is a tabletop fantasy roleplaying game co-created by Gary Gygax and Dave Arneson in 1974. Originally published by Tactical Studies Rules, Inc. (TSR), the brand is now owned by Wizards of the Coast, a division of Hasbro.

Gygax acknowledged H. P. Lovecraft as one of the writers of "particular inspiration" to him that he offered as recommended reading to people running the game. Other Cthulhu Mythos-connected writers on the list of 29 recommendations include August Derleth, Robert E. Howard, and Lord Dunsany.

Lovecraft's influence can perhaps most obviously be seen in the game's inclusion of imaginary gods who can be invoked to obtain esoteric powers; one of the main evil deities in the game's original Greyhawk setting was Hextor, whose name echoes Hastur. Some of the deity-like archdemons, who represent Chaos as well as Evil, have a Lovecraftian feel to them, such as Juiblex the Faceless Lord, a formless slime who resembles Ubbo-Sathla, and Demogorgon, whose image combines elements of reptile and octopus in a Cthulhu- or Wilbur Whateley-like way.

The central trope of the game, in which characters explore an underground realm in search of mystery, occurs in a surprising number of Lovecraft stories, from "The Transition of Juan Romero" to "The Statement of Randolph Carter" to At the Mountains of Madness, as well as in the revision story "The Mound".

Some of the monsters intended to be encountered by players have Mythos antecedents, like the sahuagin, a deep sea-dwelling species of reptilian humanoids who resemble deep ones. The mind flayer, an ancient civilization of evil humanoids with cephalopod-like heads and mind control powers, could be inspired by the spawn of Cthulhu; Gygax says he was inspired by the cover of Brian Lumley's The Burrowers Beneath. The ghast, an undead creature resembling a ghoul, seems to take its name from The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. The lich may be influenced by the "liche" Clark Ashton Smith's "The Stair in the Crypt," although Gygax credited Gardner Fox's "The Sword of the Sorcerer" (1969).

In the 5th edition of the game, players can choose the Warlock class, which requires them to make a deal with an "otherwordly patron" to gain magical powers. One type of patron suggested is a Great Old One, with "Great Cthulhu" offered as an example.

The Dunwich Horror is a fictional entity created by H. P. Lovecraft for his eponymous short story. 

### Background
The Dunwich Horror is the inhuman child of Lavinia Whateley and Yog-Sothoth, who was conceived to free the Great Old Ones so that they may reclaim the Earth. Its existence was kept secret by its grandfather, mother and eventually its twin brother, Wilbur Whateley. It fed on cattle growing up, draining them of blood before devouring them completely. The intense stench of the abomination kept away most passersby.

On September 9th 1928, the creature broke free from the Whateley farmhouse, littering the hillside with wooden planks soaked with an odd viscous substance. Barrel-sized tracks were found leading to a meadow where over half a herd of cows were drained of blood.

In its natural state the being is invisible to the human eye, but a special powder can render it visible for a few seconds. A distant relative of the monster, Curtis Whateley, was immensely disturbed by the hideous sight of it and was barely able to form a sentence to describe it. Curtis described it as bigger than a barn, made of wiggling strings that are tied together and shaped like a chicken egg. He noted it to appear gelatinous rather than solid. The creature possessed dozens of legs as big as barrels, had big eyes all over it and ten or twenty grey mouths of trunks on its side with blue or purple rings over them that were as big as oven pipes. On top of the creature, there was half a face, which lacked a chin, had red eyes and white, frizzly albino hair. The face looked just like the face of Wilbur Whateley's grandpa. Curtis also described it as something like a squid, a centipede or a spider.

Its final words were a cry of help to its father, after which the creature was destroyed for good by the spell cast by Henry Armitage and his colleagues, its essence banished back to the realm of its father. (: "The Dunwich Horror")

The Dunwich Horror Deluxe Expansion was the second expansion released for the Second Edition of Fantasy Flight Games' board game of Lovecraftian adventure, Arkham Horror.

### Overview
First published in July 2006 as a large-box expansion, Dunwich Horror included a host of additional Location, Spell and Item cards to add variety to the base game along with extra tokens and other game paraphernalia; it also features four new Ancient Ones and eight new Investigators to add further diversity. Despite these extras, it is most notable for being the first expansion to introduce an additional game board, the town of Dunwich. This board allowed the players to travel from Arkham to Dunwich, opening up new locations to explore, and new encounters to be had.

Dunwich is a fictional town created by the late Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror".

### Overview
Located in the northeast American state of Massachusetts, Dunwich is one of the country’s oldest settlements, with no village in thirty miles even nearing its age. The region has many hills, several of which bear large stone columns of unknown origins. The most recently constructed building is a mill at the falls which, like much of Dunwich, has fallen to ruin. A notable point of this town is Sentinel Hill.

### Population
Whilst the exact population of Dunwich is unknown it is undoubtedly small, with a number of extended families scattered haphazardly throughout the nearby countryside. Due to its remoteness, by 1928 the inhabitants have become somewhat degenerate and inbred (: "The Dunwich Horror"); by the mid-1980s, they have become so isolated from the outside world that not even a resurrected Wilbur Whateley raises any unibrows amongst the locals (: "Wilbur Whateley Waiting").

### Notable Features
### Sentinel Hill
One of the many strangely-rounded hills in the nearby countryside, Sentinel Hill is a place with a dire reputation. It is crowned by a circle of incredibly ancient standing stones, surrounding a rock shaped somewhat like a sacrificial altar. 

It was atop Sentinel Hill that a group of men led by Professor Henry Armitage defeated the monstrous Dunwich Horror in 1928 (: "The Dunwich Horror").

### The Covered Bridge
While not actually a part of Dunwich, the covered bridge provides the means to cross a ravine on the only road into town. In the modern day, it has been neglected to such a degree that the bottom has fallen out of it (apparently caused by the weight of a crossing automobile which lies on the ravine bed below) rendering the bridge unusable (: "Wilbur Whateley Waiting").

Dust 1947 is a sci-fi horror, tactical miniature board game. Set during an alternate World War II during the mid 20th Century. It originally was mainly a dieselpunk-style wargame with some horror elements (for example, zombies). Recently the Cthulhu Mythos has been added to the setting. The game is published by Dust Studio, which also produces the miniatures. The game was first released in 2016. A rules-light roleplaying version called Dust Adventures is published by Modiphius Entertainment.

### Setting
Vril-Kultur (VK) is a newly discovered energy source, which appears to be of extraterrestrial origin. The first to harness VK were the Germans who gave it it's name. The extraordinary properties of VK have enabled the development of powerful new weapons of war by the great powers. On the modern battlefield, marching alongside the tanks and soldiers are massive walkers, armored fighting vehicles with two or more mechanical legs. VK has also led to the development of directed energy weapons. The deployment of these new weapons has resulted in the breaking of alliances and the formation of new ones. The major powers have formed three blocs; the Axis, the Allies, and the Sino-Soviet Union (SSU). Only a small number of nations have been able to remain neutral during this global conflict. Recently a new player has joined the global conflict. From the ancient land of Mesopotamia, an army of cultists has emerged. Fanatical worshipers of the dark eldritch deities of the Mythos, supported in the battlefield by strange aliens and monstrous creatures.

### History

### Prehistoric Earth
Approximately 12,000 years ago, Earth was visited by the Annunaki who established colonies. They used humans to mined gold to shield them from the radiation caused by their VK-based technology. The humans may have been genetically modified by the Annunaki and over time they developed their own technological civilization which flourished under the Annunaki. Eventually the intergalactic war between the 
Annunaki and their enemies the Vril reached Earth, which had significant amounts of VK and therefore was worth fighting over. It was a centuries long battle over Earth which was remembered by humans in such stories as the war between Hell and Heaven in the Bible and in the Hindu tradition as the war of the gods. Both sides used VK to power their destructive war.

Circa 10,000 BC, the Vril developed a new devastating weapon powered by VK, which launched meteors toward planetary targets. During the
conflict an asteroid was launched toward Earth by the Vril, targeting the Pacific Ocean. Destroying nearly all of the Annunaki and the human civilizations which were being guided and manipulated by them. The night sky was illuminated by the asteroid's impact, which melted the glaciers and caused the rising of the seas, generating unimaginably high tsunamis. Mankind remembers this event in its great flood myths. The war between the two is still raging across the cosmos, a war that is mil

fullContent:
"Dust of the Gods" is a science fiction short story by C. L. Moore, featuring her recurring character Northwest Smith. It was first published in the August 1934 issue of Weird Tales.

This story is notable for providing information about Pharol, an ancient god that up to this point had only been mentioned briefly in previous Northwest Smith tales. Pharol was first incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Henry Kuttner in "Hydra".

### Synopsis
In a Martian tavern, Earth smuggler Northwest Smith and his Venusian partner Yarol are approached by a mysterious man, who hires them to retrieve the dust of Pharol: an entity so ancient that its name has become a virtually meaningless exclamation. Uncountable ages ago, however, Pharol's name wasn't spoken aloud at all, in fear of the god's might. Native to another realm, the deity inhabited a corporeal body on a planet that once existed between Mars and Jupiter, believed to be the original cradle of humanity. When this planet was destroyed (forming the Asteroid Belt), Pharol migrated to Mars and continued to be worshiped for generations. Although Pharol itself cannot die, the body that it used to interact with its subjects is now dead and long turned to dust. The man wishes to retrieve this dust, as he believes he can use it to summon Pharol.

Before accepting the job, Smith and Yarol talk to the two men who were originally hired to do it: a pair of hunters with a reputation for being tough, but now reduced to nervous wrecks, permanently scared of something they saw inside a cave. In spite of this, Smith and Yarol decide to take the job, purely because they're out of money.

Taking an airplane to the Northern saltlands of Mars, Smith and Yarol explore the mountains and find the cave where their predecessors saw the apparition. Soon, complete darkness engulfs them. While the heat of the lenses tells them that the torches are still functioning, something seems to be absorbing the light before it reaches their eyes. Amidst this darkness, they see a faceless white creature gliding through the solid floor of the cave. Smith tries to shoot the monster with his heat-gun, but finds that the beam passes through it. Realizing that the creature is starting to affect their minds in some way, and remembering the fate of their predecessors, Smith and Yarol force themselves to step forward, passing straight through the white monster's body, and leaving the darkness behind to continue along the tunnel. They exit the cave and find themselves in the ruins of a city that dates back to millions of years ago, when Mars was a lush green world.

Carving an entrance with their heat-guns, Smith and Yarol venture inside the ruins and through underground passages, where they come across a door marked with the sign of Pharol. The Dust-Men are a fictional species of beings created by Robert Horowitz for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. They made their first appearance in the Malleus Monstrorum bestiary supplement in 2006. 

### Description
Native to the Dreamlands, Dust-Men appear as humanoid figures in the Dreamlands, and spend their time moving piles of dust or sand around in the waking world. The inhalation of a dust-man in the waking world causes nightmares in those unfortunate enough to have done so. They are rumoured to have been created by Abdul Alhazred. 

### Behind the Mythos
The Dust-Men were created as a result of a competition held by Chaosium, where the top three entries would feature in their new monster manual Malleus Monstrorum. The Dust-Men came third, losing the top spots to the Pallid Dancers and Father-of-All-Sharks .

The Dwarf is a fictional demon in the prime reality of the Marvel universe of Marvel Comics who was created in 1992 by Chris Cooper and Richard Case, first appearing in issue #28 of the 3rd volume of Ghost Rider.

### Background
The Dwarf is a demon which serves the Elder God Chthon. It delivers pages of the Darkhold in black envelopes to people, sometimes giving them little to no inkling of what it contains or what it's for and other times promising much if they use the page. 

It can magically transport itself to anywhere it wants. Usually appearing wherever a Darkhold page is found. To get people to use a Darkhold page and thereby damn their souls, it influences them. The Dwarf prefers manipulating others to directly attacking them.

The Dweller is a mechanical eldritch entity from the fictional universe of Transformers by Hasbro and TakaraTomy. 

### Background
In the G1 cartoon, the Dweller was one of the Trans-Organics, the first lifeforms ever created by the Quintessons to be their slaves. When the Dweller proved to be far too destructive, it was sealed away in a Hibernation Chamber below the depths of the planet Cybertron. Millions of years later, the Quintessons hatched a scheme to conquer Cybertron by manipulating Galvatron into awakening the Dweller and the rest of the surviving Trans-Organics. Free and unencumbered, the Dweller went on a rampage and drained the life-force of the Cybertronians that it encountered, turning them into mindless "Energy Vampires". The Autobots eventually ejected the Dweller into space, where it attacked the Quintessons' ship.

Another incarnation of the Dweller appears in Cyberverse, where it was depicted as being an ancient Titan who laid dormant in the Argon Sea. Once awoken, the Dweller attempted to use the cityspeaker Windblade to spread his psychic mind control and enslave all of Cybertron.   

### Mythos Connections
*The Dweller is a pastiche of Cthulhu, being an ancient evil entity who was sealed away in the depths below. This is made even more prevalent with his Cyberverse incarnation, bearing a strong physical resemblance to the Great Old One.
*The Trans-Organics' backstory recalls the relationship between the Shoggoths and the Elder Things.

The Dweller Beneath is an insane Lovecraftian-like entity in the fictional universe of the Rifts pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium.

### Background
The Dweller Beneath is a monstrous eldritch entity, an alien intelligence with an insane plan which is to consume all life, not only in the cosmos but throughout the Megaverse, both physically and pyschically. It estimates that his plan will take another million years to achieve his goal, but he is patient. It's because of this plan that it orchestrated the successful uprising of one of the Splugorth's minion races, the Kreeghor, whom have unknowingly been serving the entity ever since.

The warrior race has carved for itself a totalitarian intergalactic empire in the "Three Galaxies", the Trans-Galactic Empire (TGE). Only one individual in the empire knows the dark truth, the Kreeghor Emperor. When its time to pass control of the empire to his successor, the chosen Kreeghor is brought to the Dweller Beneath before he assumes the throne. Where he learns the terrible truth and it bestows a tiny fraction of its power on him. The Dweller Beneath feeds on the psychic suffering of the trillions under the boot of the TGE.

### The Dweller Beneath
The Dweller Beneath is an incredibly ancient entity, one that has been around for a million years. A skyscraper-tall pillar of moldy flesh topped with a gigantic cyclopean eye and greenish hair like growth in the upper part. It's a psychic empire which feeds on the suffering of sentient lifeforms. 

Which has vast magical and psionic powers, including being able to telepathically communicate up to galactic distances. It is able to regenerate and can survive a 19 megaton nuke, though with grievous wounds. The entity can send out fragments of its essence which have the ability to take any form and maintain telepathic communication with the core. Each of which is extremely durable, able to take up to x8 as much damage as late 20th century main battle tank. The Dweller Beneath itself can shapeshift into any form up to 2 stories in height. It's able to bestow an insignificant sliver of its power on a minion who becomes the Kreeghor Emperor, giving him super powers, including the ability to survive a 280 kiloton nuke.

The Dwellers in the Depths are a fictional race created by Chaosium in 1994 for its Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game which were based on Ramsey Campbell's "The Horror from the Bridge".

### Overview
Said to be associated with entities like Great Cthulhu, Dagon and Mother Hydra, and the cursed Star-Spawn, these creatures appear to be amphibious, with some suggesting they are a larger, more powerful, and advanced strain of Deep One. Inhabititing places beneath the ocean as well (as certain great freshwater lakes), the dwellers may also be found in Deep One cities. On occasion, individuals rise to the surface and walk on land, causing havoc where they go. The Cult of Cthulhu holds the dwellers in great regard and reverence.

Their rubbery, half-gelatinous flesh grants immunity to most physical harm and, in death, a dweller's body quickly decomposes, leaving behind nothing more than a foul-smelling stain.

### Summary
Dwellers in the Depths are amphibious creatures that serve the Great Old Ones, usually those associated with water, whom are theorized to be Deep Ones, a mutant strain that is larger, more powerful, and possesses tentacles.

They live in their underwater cities, occasionally coming to the surface to feed and wreak havoc. Their semi-gelatinous rubbery flesh is immune to most types of physical attacks, and if slain quickly decomposes, leaving a foul smelling stain.

The Dweller in the Gulf is a fictional entity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his eponymous short story.

### Background

It is served and worshiped by a cult of Martians who have been captured and blinded by the Dweller, which is equipped with two proboscides for the extraction of eyes. The cult periodically gathers around a strange figure of the Dweller (the Eidolon of the Blind) which induces a drug-like ecstasy in anyone who touches it; while they are thus drugged, the Dweller claims one as a living sacrifice.

The Dweller-in-Darkness, also known as He Who Dwells in Darkness, is a fictional entity created by Marvel Comics, who first appeared in Thor Vol 1 #229 "Where Darkness Dwells, Dwell I!". The character is known for being one of the Fear Lords and an adversary of Doctor Strange. 

### Biography
The Dweller-in-Darkness is a demon, allegedly sired by Cthulhu himself, hailing from the dimension Everinnye, similar to the demon Nightmare. He was ostracized by his own kind for adhering to "The Way of the Shamblu." Like Nightmare, the Dweller draws strength and sustenance from the fear of living beings. In a previous universe, he caused a rupture in the M'Kraan Crystal with the aim of destroying the universe and feeding on the resultant fear. However, just before the crystal's destruction, the Phoenix Force intervened telepathically, uniting all life in peace and thwarting the Dweller's plan. As a result, the current Marvel Universe was created.

In this new universe, when the Dweller-in-Darkness first arrived on Earth, he fed on the fear generated by the conflict between the Atlanteans and the Lemurian Deviants. The Atlantean sorceress Zhered-Na discovered the Dweller's presence and, with the aid of Agamotto and the Atlantean god Valka, banished him. After Atlantis sank, the Dweller absorbed the fear of the survivors and used it to create D'Spayre, instructing him to exact revenge on Zhered-Na. D'Spayre manipulated a tribesman into killing Zhered-Na, and her student, Dakimh the Enchanter, would spend the following millennia battling D'Spayre as he sought to generate enough fear on Earth to release his creator. During this period, the Dweller also created other beings with similar goals, including the demoness Spite. Despite this, D'Spayre remained his most formidable creation.

In the 20th century, the Dweller began appearing in the dreams of numerous people, promising them eternal life if they died. Many of these individuals committed suicide, only to become Shade Thralls—powerful beings loyal to the Dweller but weak against light. His scheme was thwarted by the gods Thor and Hercules, who battled and defeated the Shade Thralls. Additionally, he influenced Zoltan Drago to take on the role of the first Mister Fear.

### Powers and Abilities
The Dweller has the power to instill fear in other living beings, which both sustains and strengthens him, enabling him to generate even more fear. He also possesses other mystical abilities: he can create independent entities from fear, such as D'Spayre, and transform humans who die under his influence into Shade Thralls—shadowy beings with superhuman strength. These thralls can be killed or banished by strong light.

The Dweller is immortal and does not age. Even the sorceress Zhered-Na, with the help of powerful allies like Agamotto and Valka, could only banish him rather than destroy him.

Dwellers in the Depths is a fictional book created by Carl Jacobi, part of a set of books dealing with undersea horrors that are mentioned in his 1962 short story "The Aquarium". Jacobi says that the book was written "by Gaston Le Fe who, the foreword stated quite blandly, had died insane."

The other eldritch aquatic books named by Jacobi are Hydrophinnae and Unter Zee Kulten; all three texts are frequently mentioned by Brian Lumley to indicate an unwholesome interest in oceanic secrets, in such stories as "The Cypress Shell," "Rising with Surtsey", "Dagon's Bell", "De Marigny's Clock", "Lord of the Worms", and "The House of the Temple".

fullContent:
Dwellers in the Mirage is a fantasy novel by A. Merritt first published in 1932.

### Publisher summary
Leif Langdon was suddenly ripped from the 20th century and plunged into the ancient world of The Mirage. But his entrance into this awesome land awakened the slumbering Dwayanu, who in this strange incarnation was also Leif. Thus, two-men-in-one battle with the beautiful witch-woman Lur and the ethereal beauty Evalie for the glory of The Mirage.

### Contents
The novel concerns American Leif Langdon who discovers a warm valley in Alaska. Two races inhabit the valley, the Little People and a branch of an ancient Mongolian race. In a debased cult setting, they worship  Khalk'ru, an evil extra-dimensional monstrosity resembling the Scandinavian kraken which they summon from another dimension to offer human sacrifice. The inhabitants recognize Langdon as the reincarnation of their long dead hero, Dwayanu. Dwayanu's spirit possesses Langdon and starts a war with the Little People. Langdon eventually fights off the presence of Dwayanu and destroys the Kraken.

### Connection to the Mythos
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia notes that Dwellers in the Mirage "may be a homage to HPL in its use of extra-dimensional octopus demon Khalk'ru (an analogue to Cthulhu?)."

fullContent:
The Dybbuk are a fictional species created by Chad Bowser and Andi Newton for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. They made their first appearance in the historical setting supplement Cthulhu Invictus in 2009.

### Background
The Dybbuk are a race from an alien planet whom have a gaseous form. They arrived on Earth, millennia ago, fleeing the Mi-Go, where they discovered they were unable to complete the simplest tasks, but if a human inhaled them, their consciousness could replace that of the host. Though reluctant to abandon their hosts, occasionally one is convinced to do so. The host has no recollection of its possession.

### Behind the Mythos
The Dybbuk would appear to be inspired by creatures from Jewish mythology with whom they share their name. These entities are believed to be the disembodied spirit of a dead person which possesses the body of a living being in order to accomplish a specific goal.

### References

Dylan Murphy is the primary human antagonist in Keyport Cthulhu, the first book in Armand Rosamilia's Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Description
A bald, heavyset man, Dylan has a mean temper. He is the head of the Keyport branch of the Esoteric Order of Dagon and the eldest son of his family, at least the ninth to take the name of Dylan Murphy. He owns the Broad Street Pub, the de facto headquarters of the Order.

Dylan may or may not be a human/Deep One hybrid; his appearance is suggestive of such ancestry, but his contempt for the deformities present in others of this kind suggests otherwise.

### History
While growing up, Dylan saw the mistakes that his forbears had made in their attempts to awaken great Cthulhu, and new that he could do better.

As an adult, he made the same mistakes as the others, but eventually found a woman whom he believed would make the perfect sacrifice. Unfortunately, his attempt to enact the ritual met with failure, and he died in Tina's place, killed by the former biker known only as Bones.

Dylath-Leen is a bustling trading port and one of the largest cities in the Dreamlands. As well as the usual boats, mule caravans and two wheeled carts that stream constantly through the gates and docks, Dylath-Leen is famous for the comings and goings of the mysterious Black Galleys.

### Description
The thin angular towers that line the dark streets of Dylath-Leen are built of black basalt and from a distance could be compared to the stones of the Giant's Causeway. 

### Geography
*On the coast of the Southern Ocean, near the mouth of the River Skai
*7 days ride up river from Ulthar.

### Residents
The streets and sea taverns along the wharves are filled with oddly robed sailors from across the earth and beyond. Though most of the locals' conversation is taken up with rumours about the Black Galleys they can be coaxed to help travellers like Randolph Carter who arrives looking for passage to Oriab.

### The Black Galleys

A source of fear and superstition from across the Southern Sea. Though the rubies they bring are essential to the port's economy they are an unwelcome presence and it's this avenue of trade that keeps the people of Ulthar from ever going there. Many smoke thagweed to cover the smell of the ships.

shortDefinition: "Dylath-Leen" is a Dreamlands short story by Brian Lumley, first published in his 1971 Arkham House collection The Caller of the Black . It was later incorporated as part of Lumley's Titus Crow novel The Clock of Dreams.  ### Synopsis Grant Enderby h...
fullContent:
"Dylath-Leen" is a Dreamlands short story by Brian Lumley, first published in his 1971 Arkham House collection The Caller of the Black . It was later incorporated as part of Lumley's Titus Crow novel The Clock of Dreams.

### Synopsis
Grant Enderby has visited the Dreamlands city of Dylath-Leen three times in his life. In his first visit, at age 18, he lodges with a local basalt quarrier named Bo-Kareth, and falls in love with his daughter, Litha. Enderby spends several weeks in Dylath-Leen, and makes it his mission to warn the locals against trading with the strange ruby merchants who travel in black galleys, as he is convinced that they are not human. Nevertheless, the rubies are sold for a very affordable price, and since the trade has been going on for years, the gems can be found in practically every house in Dylath-Leen at this point. Eventually, Enderby wakes up from the dream and thus returns to the Waking World.

Several years pass before Enderby visits the Dreamlands again. When he does, at age 30, he finds himself instantly transported to Dylath-Leen. He quickly notices that the city has been dominated by the ruby merchants, who are indeed not human, but the horned creatures known as the Men of Leng. When he gets to Bo-Kareth's house, he finds that a much longer time has passed in the Dreamlands compared to the Waking World, as Bo-Kareth has aged at least 20 years to Enderby's 12. He also learns that, a few years before, the Men of Leng brought a gigantic ruby as a gift to the people of Dylath-Leen, which was exposed in the city's main square. At night, the giant ruby was observed to glow, and the common rubies of all sizes everywhere in the city glowed in response as well. The light had a drowsing effect on the humans, and it was easy for the Men of Leng to take over the city and start to simply abduct people instead of buying slaves (which have been in short supply for a while). Many people have since left Dylath-Leen for the nearby Ulthar, including Litha, who now has a husband and children of her own. Pursued by the horned Men of Leng after sneaking out to see the giant ruby, Enderby manages to escape from the city just in time and wakes up.

At age 43, Enderby experiences his third and final visit to the Dreamlands. Finding himself at the outskirts of Ulthar, he learns that no one goes to Dylath-Leen anymore. Seeking to find the means to liberate the city, Enderby visits the Temple of the Elder Ones to talk to the wise priest Atal. The aged priest listens to the story about the ruby and finds a book which reveals that the great gem was carved in Yuggoth, and contains an entity known as the Fly-the-Light, which is the one responsible for mesmerising the people. To release it from the ruby would result in the most horrible death of everyone at the monster's reach, including its own allies, the Men of Leng. Enderby insists that he is willing to face the risk if it would avenge Dylath-Leen and prevent other cities from having the same

Dythalla, also known as the Lord of Lizards, is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by American author James Ambuehl for his 1985 poem "Dythalla".

### Background
Dythalla is a Great Old One that takes the form of a giant reptilian creature with a long serpentine mass of sucker-disced tentacles crowned around its head. Worshipped as a god in the ancient land of Altuas, a temple for worship was built in a courtyard west from the gates of Temme-Kiroth. The temple has an eighteen-foot-tall stone statue of Dythalla, with numerous lizards squirming and scurrying upon every inch of the floor. 

During one of his conquests, a ruthless military despot called Parthias the Conqueror raided the temple, torturing and killing the priests on their altar. Further mocking and taunting their god, Parthias urinated on the statue of Dythalla; however, the foul-smelling stream was absorbed into the stone, causing the statue to glow a yellowish hue and transform into a living creature with flesh. Shortly afterwards, Dythalla chomped off Parthias' head, drenching his body in gore. (: "Lord of Lizards")

E-poh is a fictional character created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer for their short story "The Lair of the Star-Spawn".

### Biography
E-poh is a Tcho-Tcho sorcerer from the fabled city of Alaozar in the Plateau of Sung, Burma, and leads his people in worship of Zhar and Lloigor. He is "slightly taller" than the typical four-foot-tall Tcho-Tcho, and "disfigured by a hump on his back". He is said to be  over 7,000 years old. (: "The Lair of the Star-Spawn")

According to the works of Lin Carter, he is the prototype of the Tcho-Tcho people, the first member of his species to be created. (: "The Descent into the Abyss")

shortDefinition: Edward Frederic Benson (July 24, 1867 – February 29, 1940) was an English novelist, biographer, memoirist and short story writer, known professionally as E. F. Benson. His friends called him Fred.  ### Life E.F. Benson was born at Wellington Co...
fullContent:
Edward Frederic Benson (July 24, 1867 – February 29, 1940) was an English novelist, biographer, memoirist and short story writer, known professionally as E. F. Benson. His friends called him Fred.

### Life
E.F. Benson was born at Wellington College in Berkshire, the fifth child of the headmaster, Edward White Benson (later Chancellor of Lincoln Cathedral, Bishop of Truro and Archbishop of Canterbury), and Mary Sidgwick Benson ("Minnie"), who was described by William Ewart Gladstone as the 'cleverest woman in Europe' and after her husband's death set up a lesbian household with Lucy Tait, daughter of the previous Archbishop of Canterbury, Archibald Campbell Tait .

Benson was the younger brother of A. C. Benson (Arthur Christopher Benson), who wrote the words to Land of Hope and Glory, Monsignor Robert Hugh Benson, author of several novels and Catholic apologetic works, and Margaret Benson (Maggie) an amateur Egyptologist. Two other siblings died young.

E.F. Benson was an excellent athlete, and represented England at figure skating. He was a precocious and prolific writer, publishing his first book while still a student. Nowadays he is principally known for his Mapp and Lucia series about Emmeline "Lucia" Lucas and Elizabeth Mapp.

The principal setting of four of the Mapp and Lucia books is a town called Tilling, which is recognizably based on Rye, East Sussex, where Benson lived for many years and served as mayor from 1934 (he moved there in 1918). Benson's home, Lamb House, served as the model for Mallards, Lucia's home in some of the Tilling series. There really was a handsome 'Garden Room' adjoining the street but, unfortunately, it was destroyed by a bomb in the Second World War. Lamb House attracted writers: it was earlier the home of Henry James, and later of Rumer Godden.

In London, Benson also lived at 395 Oxford Street, W1 (now the branch of Russell & Bromley just west of Bond Street Underground Station), 102 Oakley Street, SW3, and 25 Brompton Square, SW3, where much of the action of Lucia in London takes place and where English Heritage placed a Blue Plaque in 1994.

Benson died in 1940 of throat cancer in University College Hospital, London.

### Works
Benson's first book was "Sketches from Marlborough". He started his novel writing career with the (then) fashionably controversial "Dodo" (1893), and he followed it with a variety of satire and romantic melodrama. The Mapp and Lucia series, written relatively late in his career, consists of six novels and three short stories.

Benson was one of the most prestigious writers of his generation to contribute original stories to the American magazine Weird Tales.

Lovecraft himself spoke highly of Benson and his following short stories.
*"Negotiam Perambulans"
*"The Horror-Horn"
*"The Man Who Went Too Far"
*"The Face"

fullContent:
Everett Franklin Bleiler (30 April 1920 – 13 June 2010) was an American editor, bibliographer, and critic. Over the years he wrote many pieces on the works of the late Howard Phillips Lovecraft, many of which have drawn unfavourable conclusions.

### On Lovecraft's Works
*On "From Beyond": "very interesting, despite stiff, immature writing".
*On Marginalia: "The guest memoirs and essays are of varying interest", but that "Lovecraft's fiction is juvenile or minor. His essays are more significant".
*On "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family": "actually, the story is a metaphor for his extreme bigotry and social snobbery; the motifs of expiating ancestral evil and committing suicide on discovering 'racial pollution' occur in other of his works."
*On "The Lurking Fear": "digressive and clumsily written, perhaps because it was written for serial publication".
*On "Herbert West--Reanimator": a "wretched work".

fullContent:
E. Hoffmann Price (July 3, 1898 – June 18, 1988) was an American writer of popular fiction (he was a self-titled 'fictioneer') for the pulp magazine marketplace. He collaborated with H. P. Lovecraft on "Tarbis of the Lake" and "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".

### Biography
Price was born in Fowler, California.

Originally intending to be a career soldier, Price graduated from the United States Military Academy at West Point; he served in the American Expeditionary Force in World War I, and with the American military in Mexico and the Philippines. He was a champion fencer and boxer, an amateur Orientalist, and a student of the Arabic language; science-fiction author Jack Williamson, in his 1984 autobiography Wonder's Child, called E. Hoffmann Price a "real live soldier of fortune".

In his literary career, Hoffmann Price produced fiction for a wide range of publications, from Argosy to Terror Tales, from Speed Detective to Spicy Mystery Stories. Yet he was most readily identified as a Weird Tales writer, one of the group who wrote regularly for editor Farnsworth Wright, a group that included Lovecraft, Robert E. Howard, and Clark Ashton Smith. Price published 24 solo stories in Weird Tales between 1925 and 1950, plus three collaborations with Otis Adelbert Kline, and his works with Lovecraft, noted above.

His first sale was to Droll Stories in 1924, followed almost immediately by the first of scores of acceptances by Weird Tales, "The Rajah's Gift" (Jan 1925).


Some of Price's stories aroused controversy; "The Stranger from Kurdistan" (1925), a story which featured a dialogue between Christ and Satan, was criticised by some readers as blasphemous, but proved popular with Weird Tales readers. (Lovecraft professed to find it especially powerful). "The Infidel's Daughter" (1927), a satire on the Ku Klux Klan, also angered some Southern readers, but Wright defended the story.

Price worked in a range of popular genres—including science fiction, horror, crime, and fantasy—but he was best known for adventure stories with Oriental settings and atmosphere. Price also contributed to Farnsworth Wright's short-lived magazine The Magic Carpet (1930–34), along with Kline, Howard, Smith, and other Weird Tales regulars.

Like many other pulp-fiction writers, Price could not support himself and his family on his income from literature. Living in New Orleans in the 1930s, he worked for a time for the Union Carbide Corporation. Nonetheless he managed to travel widely and maintain friendships with many other pulp writers, including Kline and Edmond Hamilton. On a trip to Texas in the mid-1930s, Price was the only pulp writer to meet Robert E. Howard face to face. He was also the only man known to have met Howard and also H. P. Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith (the great 'Triumvirate' of Weird Tales writers) in person. fullContent:
Earth is a terrestrial world and the third planet in the Solar System. It is the homeworld of humanity, although it has been inhabited and ruled by numerous other species across time as well.

Over the course of Earth's history, the planet has been colonized by several extraterrestrial races that struggled with each other for dominance, including the Elder Things, the Cthulhi, the Great Race of Yith, the Flying Polyps, and the Mi-Go, as each held some territory on Earth for a time. (: At the Mountains of Madness, The Shadow Out of Time)

### History
At some point in time, Yog-Sothoth's species, which the Necronomicon refers to as the "Old Ones", ruled over the Earth. (: "The Dunwich Horror")

According to the history presented in the Unaussprechlichen Kulten, the Earth was originally located in another dimension and ruled by the Elder Gods, who created the Old Ones as their slaves, the first two of which were Azathoth and Ubbo-Sathla. Eventually, the Old Ones rebelled against their masters, and in the ensuing conflict, the Earth was plunged into our universe. (: "The Horror in the Gallery")

### Prehistory
Shortly after Earth's formation four and a half billion years ago, Cthugha and the Fire Vampires arrived and dwelt in the molten ruins. (: "Timeline of the Cthulhu Mythos," Shannon Appelcline)

Some primitive life may have evolved on Earth a little under four billion years ago, accompanied shortly by the arrival of Tsathoggua and Chaugnar Faugn. (: "Timeline of the Cthulhu Mythos," Shannon Appelcline)

Roger Little speculated that Chuagnar Faugn might have created the Miri Nigri about 2 billion years ago, molding them "from the plankton-like swarms of small organisms which must have drifted with the tides through the ancient oceans". (: The Horror from the Hills)

More than a thousand million years ago, the Elder Things came to Earth, settling on the area that would eventually come to be known as Antarctica. This was not long after the formation of the moon, at a time in which the entire surface of the Earth was submerged, so their first settlements were aquatic. However, as the continents started to emerge, the Elder Things began to colonize land as well. They created the Shoggoths and other artificial bio-forms which would eventually evolve into Earth's vertebrates, including Humans. (: At the Mountains of Madness)

The first species to challenge the Elder Things for supremacy on Earth were the Cthulhi (a.k.a. Spawn of Cthulhu or "Cosmic Octopi"), which arrived with their leader, Cthulhu, after the emergence of the first continents (: At the Mountains of Madness). However, some believe that the Cthulhi were already present in the South Pacific since before the formation of the moon (: The Transition of Titus Crow).

600 million years ago, the Flying Polyps came to Earth, preyed upon the inhabitants, and built windowless basalt cities. (: The Shadow Out of Time)

350 million years ago, the Deep Ones may have helped build the city of R'lyeh. (:

fullContent:
The Earth is the primary setting in the Prime Reality (Earth-616) within Marvel Comics' fictional universe. Whose publication history dates as far back as during the wartime patriotic comics of World War 2, starring Captain America. Most of the comic series mostly occur on Earth and to a lesser degree one of the pocket dimensions adjacent to Earth. The Cthulhu Mythos has been part of its history, publication wise since the 1970s with the 3rd volume of Journey into Mystery.

When it comes to its fictional history, its relation to the Cthulhu Mythos dates far into its primordial age, during the time of the dinosaurs (tens of millions of years ago) in flashback and within the stories as far back as the Thurian Age during the reign of Kull the Conqueror of Valusia, over ten thousand years ago. Several Old Ones were active on Earth as far back as the Hyborian Age during the time of Conan the Barbarian. There have been several cosmic horror stories (or stories with such elements) in which the primary if not sole setting was on the Earth of the modern era, including "Wraith War" (1984-85 - Dire Wraith aliens), "Atlantis Attacks!" (1989 - Set the Elder God), "Planet of the Symbiotes" (1995 - Klyntar aliens), "Earth's Mightiest" (2009 - Chthon the Elder God), "Fear Itself" (2011-2012 - The Serpent), and "Monsters Unleashed" (2017 - Kaiju).

### Old Gods & New Gods
On the planet Earth, there have existed eldritch entities since before life began. The first such entities were the Elder Gods, all of whom except for one (Gaea) became corrupted, twisted, and dark. Most of them were destroyed by her son Demogorge, though some managed to escape to other dimensions (e.g. Set and Chthon). Some time afterward the Old Ones, or Many-Angled Ones (e.g. Shuma-Gorath), established their reign over the Earth, hundreds of millions of years before the emergence of man. A few of them remained on Earth as recently as during the time of Conan of Cimmeria during the Hyborian Age, over 12,000 years ago.

Afterwards new gods emerged, whose power paled in comparison to those that came before. Gods that appeared human and established their dominions in pocket dimensions adjacent to Earth, whose pantheons were worshiped by the various human civilizations. They still maintain contact with Earth, and some of its members (e.g. Thor and Hercules) interact with humans today. Ruling these pantheons are the "Skyfathers", the most powerful among the new gods, who have formed a sort of council of godheads to deal with existential threats. At the same time, man is plagued by the corruption and evil spread by the Hell Lords. Demons and dark gods who rule over realms of the dead and/or damned, usually in opposition to the Skyfathers. They too have established their own council.

### Eldritch Locations
There are several Eldritch locations on Earth, some of them were created by Mythos entities or connected to them. Others had other origins, one of them evolutionary.

fullContent:
The Earth is a planet in the fictional universe of the Rifts pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium.

### Background
Earth is a post-apocalyptic dystopian world, which has been invaded or infiltrated by extra-terrestrial beings, demons, extra-dimensional beings, gods, and alien intelligences.  It's a world that in the early 21st century experienced the cataclysmic return of magic, resulting in the death of billions and the annihilation of most of human civilization. The geography of the Earth itself was reshaped. It was followed by a dark age that lasted centuries during which several alien invasions and demon plagues hit the world.

Today on Earth, a third of mankind uses or accepts magic and psionic abilities, and have accepted the aliens among them. A third of mankind is now living in primitive barbarism. Another third of mankind has rejected magic and sometimes psionic abilities, fear those whom are not human, and destroy that which they don't understand. Throughout the world are human and alien empires and city-states, most of which are a shadow of the empires of mankind's past, in territory and population. Dozens of malevolent and sadistic alien intelligences have established strongholds on Earth, the three greatest with dominions spanning 1000s of sq miles. 

Demons have carved out their own empires on Earth, the greatest being that of the Yama Kings whom have divided among themselves most of historical China, east of Tibet and south of Mongolia. In Europe, the Gargoyles a lesser race of demons have conquered much of mainland Europe, west of Germany and the Brodkils a lower race of demons have allied with the cybernetic Mindwerks corporation and conquered Poland. Naut'Yll invaders from another dimension have established a growing undersea empire in the southern Atlantic Ocean. The Horune another extra-dimensional race, plague the seas of Earth as pirates. North America is threatened by another extra-dimensional race, the Xiticix, insectoids who found themselves transported to Earth and have been rapidly expanding their domain. The greatest power on Earth though is Atlantis, the island-continent which has returned to Earth after several millennia. Ruled by a Lord Splynncryth, a young and ambitious Splugorth.

Hidden under China is the vast subterranean civilization of Geofront, descended from the People's Republic of China. Based in Germany is the New German Republic, bastion of humanity in Europe which has established its dominance over Central Europe. In what used to be Russia are feudal human kingdoms ruled by warlords known as Sovietski. Over in South America, are several human states of varying sizes, most of them in what used to be Argentina. In North America is the fascist and genocidal Coalition States which is the greatest power in what used to be the continental United States, and further north is the isolationist Republic of Quebec.

### Background
In this world there are no living humans or none are visible. The world is run by a totalitarian regime, in which "civilians" require permits for a variety of things. It's inhabitants included vampires, werewolves, ghosts, mummies, zombies, spider humanoids, fish-like humanoids, and squid-like beings. They prayed to or swore by, the Old One Shuma-Gorath and the Hell Lord Mephisto. Its superhuman defenders were the Undead Avengers.

Their god is an Undead Celestial (space god) and their objective is to spread the undead across the universe. Who possessed the Orb of Necromancy which they planned to us to help them in their goal of bringing the dead back to life throughout the cosmos. It was feared that if the rest of the cosmos found out about their agenda, they would come and destroy their planet. Located on their world was Shuma-Gorath's Ego Maze, or at least access to it via a portal.

shortDefinition: "Earthworms" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Cody Goodfellow. It was first published in the November 2011 edition of Midnight Echo magazine.  ### Synopsis After the fall of civilisation, the last remaining member of a doomsday cult i...
fullContent:
"Earthworms" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Cody Goodfellow. It was first published in the November 2011 edition of Midnight Echo magazine.

### Synopsis
After the fall of civilisation, the last remaining member of a doomsday cult is taken to the stars by the arrival of their long-awaited alien saviours. He awakens prematurely in a cryogenic capsule, virtually unable to breathe due to the toxic atmosphere. When one of the aliens approaches him, it informs the man that his species have been used as living terraformers for countless millennia, the manner in which they pollute and destroy their environments rendering them near-perfect for the aliens. The only stumbling block appears to be the length of time that humans take to annihilate each other.

The man is later transplanted on to a virgin world, a new paradise. The religious fanatics he has been dropped with are already busily tearing down their environment in order to create their new cities.

### Publication History
Since its debut in Midnight Echo, "Earthworms" has also been included in the Jason Andrew-edited thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods.

### Trivia
*In the introduction to Apotheosis, editor Jason Andrew states that hearing Goodfellow give a reading of "Earthworms" was the catalyst for beginning work on that anthology.

fullContent:
"East and West Harvard Conservatism" is a short non-fiction piece by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. It first saw print in an unknown publication, likely in 1922.

The piece shows examples of Lovecraft’s now-infamous racist leanings through his mentions of immigrants "all but conceal[ing] the dominant heritage."

### Synopsis
In the piece, Lovecraft’s discusses the differences between the well-established society of New England and the relative newness of more westerly locales. He goes on to lament the staid traditionalism of American higher leaning institutes in general, and Harvard University in particular, while praising what he perceives as a more liberal educational culture in Europe.

### Text
The Bush campaigns in New England presented the paradox of giving two distinct and opposite impressions. To Dr. Bush and his staff, accustomed to the street, filling crowds and vociferous audiences of the West, enthusiasm seemed relatively mild; yet to the people of Worcester and Boston, the two cities visited, the campaign appeared as a record-breaking event. Auditoria were filled each night to their capacity, and the speaker was undoubtedly accorded a more remarkable demonstration than that received by any other orator during recent years. In Worcester, indeed, it was freely estimated that nothing of equal magnitude had taken place during the city’s history.

The cause of this paradox lies deep in the fundamentals of American geography—specifically, in the unique traditions and mentality of New England. This region, of which the writer is undeniably a more or less typical product despite more cosmopolitan philosophical tendencies, has behind it influences totally non-existent in the West; and of these nearly all operate against the enthusiastic reception of new and orally presented ideas. That any psychological speaker should achieve marked success, is a striking testimonial to his individual ability and personality.

New England is old. Unlike the West, it has a background of three hundred years of continuous history as a white, settled country; so that today it has lost every trace of that youth which characterises America as a whole. It is, in a sense, European—it has acquired a degree of experience and sophistication which forbids it to thrill at novelties. Like all old regions, it is impressed more by the samenesses than by the varieties of life. With age come ennui and weariness; the languor which not only distrusts the new, but which questions its value even if it is genuine. This sense of futility is hard to combat—in very old regions, like the countries of Asia, it becomes a dominant philosophical characteristic. In the larger cities one does not see the old age of New England so readily. There we find an exterior of modern architecture and a conspicuous immigrant class which all but conceal the dominant heritage. Ebenezer Holt is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Picture in the House".

### Background
Ebenezer Holt was the captain of a merchant ship out of Salem, Massachusetts during the 18th century. During his travels he obtained a copy of the real world book Regnum Congo, concerning the history and geography of the Congo region of Africa, written by Filippo Pigafetta and published in 1591. 

In the year 1768 Holt traded the book to the unnamed old man from the story. It was the Regnums depiction of the Anzique cannibals of Africa that created in the old man a desire for the taste of human flesh, a dietary habit that somehow imbued him with exceptionally long life. Holt himself was killed in the Revolutionary War. (: "The Picture in the House")

shortDefinition: Echidna is part of Greek mythology. Echidna is a monster in Greek mythology, depicted as half-woman and half-snake, known as the "Mother of Monsters." She was the mate of Typhon and the mother of many famous mythical creatures, including the Hydra an...
fullContent:
Echidna is part of Greek mythology. Echidna is a monster in Greek mythology, depicted as half-woman and half-snake, known as the "Mother of Monsters." She was the mate of Typhon and the mother of many famous mythical creatures, including the Hydra and Cerberus, representing chaos and danger in ancient stories.

While there is no direct reference to Echidna in the Cthulhu Mythos created by H.P. Lovecraft and later authors, several parallels can be drawn.

### Similarities in Theme

# Monstrous Lineage:
#* Echidna is known as the "Mother of Monsters," giving birth to various fearsome creatures. Similarly, the Cthulhu Mythos features a pantheon of monstrous beings, including Cthulhu, Nyarlathotep, and others, often described as having bizarre and terrifying forms. These entities, like Echidna, are also arranged in (joking or not) family trees in which monstrosities claim ancestry to other eldritch horrors.
# Chaos and Destruction:
#* Echidna and her offspring often embody chaos and destruction, much like the entities in the Cthulhu Mythos, which often bring madness and despair to humanity. The themes of existential dread and the insignificance of humanity in the face of these beings are prevalent in both mythologies.
# Hybrid Forms:
#* Echidna's half-woman, half-snake form resonates with the Cthulhu Mythos' frequent use of hybrid creatures, such as Deep Ones, Serpent People and other beings that blur the lines between species. This blending of forms emphasizes the alien and incomprehensible nature of the entities in Lovecraft's works.

### Marvel Mythopoeia
The Marvel adaptation was created in 2014 by Cullen Bunn and William Sliney and made her first appearance in issue #11 of the 1st volume of the Fearless Defenders comic book series. Due to the long publishing history of Marvel comics and its predecessors and the relentless agglomeration of characters from myth and from works in the public domain as well Conan when used under license by Marvel, Echidna becomes not merely the Mother of Monsters of Greek myth but an overarching progenitor mother figure of entities from the myths of Ancient Greece, Egypt, China, Arabia and any other location touched upon in Marvel stories. Thus although there is a totally different lineage for Echidna from Greek myth, in Marvel comics she descends from an Egyptian god.

### Marvel Origins
Echidna is the granddaughter of the Elder God Set born to his son Phorcys who mated with Ceto, a sea monster. She has sired many of the monsters of Greek mythology, most of which the heroic demi-god Hercules has battled. Most of them were sired with Typhon, one of the Titans, except for Angerboda who she sired with Varcolac and the Snakes of Many Colors.

fullContent:
"Echo of a Distant Scream" is a short story by American author Lee Clark Zumpe.

### Synopsis
Tisha Hewitt agrees to dinner with private eye Frank Nardi as part of a consultancy, and their conversation awakens old emotions about the unexplained disappearance of her brother many years ago. After re-examining the evidence, she uncovers a pattern of similar occurrences stretching back many years, which the locals seem to have swept under the rug.

A final investigation of the area where her brother and several of the other vanished townsfolk were last seen grants Tisha a glimpse of the ultimate fate of the missing and, perhaps, an element of closure.

### Characters
*Tisha Hewitt, a former reporter for a major Chicago newspaper turned ghost-tour guide and writer.
*Frank Nardi, a private investigator.
*Winston Moss, a childhood friend of Tisha and her brother.

### Publication History
Written by request from Brian M. Sammons as a piece involving C. J. Henderson's fictional character Frank Nardi, "Echo of a Distant Scream" was published in the 2017 collection Arkham Detective Agency.

fullContent:
"Echoes in Porcelain" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Greek author Konstantine Paradias, first featured on the Bizarrocast podcast in September 2013.

### Synopsis
Post-R'lyeh rising, the Earth seems surprisingly unchanged aside from the integration of a species of Deep One-like creatures known as Drownies into human society, albeit as second-class citizens. 

When one morning elderly Gladys's house is invaded by tiny but intelligent humanoid pests from the toilet, she tries everything she can to get rid of them, but nothing works. Eventually seeking help from a sympathetic Drownie, she unleashes a squid-like cat-hybrid creature upon the critters, a solution which sorts out the problem nicely.

### Publication History
Following its debut on Bizarrocast, "Echoes in Porcelain" was included in the Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be in October 2015.

shortDefinition: Edgar Allan Poe (19 January 1809 - 7 October 1849) was an American writer, editor, and literary critic. Poe is best known for his poetry and short stories, particularly his tales of mystery and the macabre. He is widely regarded as a central figure o...
fullContent:
Edgar Allan Poe (19 January 1809 - 7 October 1849) was an American writer, editor, and literary critic. Poe is best known for his poetry and short stories, particularly his tales of mystery and the macabre. He is widely regarded as a central figure of Romanticism in the United States and of American literature as a whole, and he was one of the country's earliest practitioners of the short story. He is generally considered the inventor of the detective fiction genre and is further credited with contributing to the emerging genre of science fiction. He was the first well-known American writer to earn a living through writing alone, resulting in a financially difficult life and career.

### Influence On Lovecraft
H. P. Lovecraft was famously inspired by Poe's morbid literature. In Lovecraft's essays, poems and letters, Poe is mentioned multiple times. Lovecraft wrote "When I write stories, Edgar Allan Poe is my model" and "But Poe was my God of Fiction" in his letters to Rheinhart Kleiner.

The Shoggoth's cry of "Tekeli-li! Tekeli-li!" from At the Mountains of Madness is a direct reference to Poe's only novel The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, where the same cry is said by the natives and the birds at the end of the novel. Both of these works are also thematically similar.

Along with Arthur Gordon Pym, An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia cites "Berenice", "The Masque of the Red Death", "The Fall of the House of Usher", and "Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar" as having particularly influenced Lovecraft. Critic Bobby Derie also points to "The Fall of the House of Usher", and adds "Ligeia" as another influential Poe story.

shortDefinition: Edgar Rice Burroughs (1 September 1875 – 19 March 1950) was a prolific American writer of fantasy, science fiction and adventure stories. Perhaps best known for being the creator of the Tarzan and John Carter of Mars series, he is an inductee into th...
fullContent:
Edgar Rice Burroughs (1 September 1875 – 19 March 1950) was a prolific American writer of fantasy, science fiction and adventure stories. Perhaps best known for being the creator of the Tarzan and John Carter of Mars series, he is an inductee into the Science Fiction and Fantasy Hall of Fame.

Despite the acclaim Burroughs has received for his work, and in a similar fashion to H. P. Lovecraft himself, he was vocal in espousing the tenets of eugenics and scientific racism, and included instances of these in some of his most popular works. Again similarly to Lovecraft, he was also something of an Anglophile.

### Influence on Lovecraft
Critic William Fulwiler has suggested that Burroughs' At the Earth's Core was the inspiration for "The Nameless City" and "Dagon". Additionally, he has suggested that "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family" was influenced by The Return of Tarzan and Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar.

Scholar Robert M. Price has put forward the possibility that the Barsoom (John Carter of Mars) books were a template for The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, although others have pointed out the lack of similarities between the protagonists.

Comparisons have also been drawn between Lovecraft's "The Temple" and The Land That Time Forgot.

shortDefinition: Edith May Dowe Miniter (1867 - 1934) was an American amateur journalist who also authored poems, short stories, and at least one novel, Our Natupski Neighbors (1916). A friend and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft, she wrote the first known parody of ...
fullContent:
Edith May Dowe Miniter (1867 - 1934) was an American amateur journalist who also authored poems, short stories, and at least one novel, Our Natupski Neighbors (1916). A friend and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft, she wrote the first known parody of his work, the horror comedy "Falco Ossifracus: by Mr. Goodguile", inspired chiefly by "The Statement of Randolph Carter". Lovecraft seems to have taken it in good sport, as he remained friends with Miniter for several years afterwards.

Miniter was born in Wilbraham, Massachusetts. Her mother, Jennie E. T. Dowe, was a poet, and her father a mathematician. Her career in amateur journalism started in 1883. For the next decades, she edited several papers, including The Muffin Man and Aftermath.

It was from Miniter that Lovecraft first heard about the myth that some windows can "slowly absorb and retain the likeness of those who habitually sit by them, year after year" (: "Mrs. Miniter - Estimates and Recollections"), an idea that Lovecraft would incorporate into his short story "The Unnamable".

During an eight-day visit to her house in Wilbraham, Lovecraft also learned from Miniter about the legend of the whippoorwills, according to which these birds can capture the souls of the departed (: "Mrs. Miniter - Estimates and Recollections"). This too would be incorporated into one of his stories, namely "The Dunwich Horror".

According to Lovecraft, despite her great knowledge of folklore, Miniter didn't care much for supernatural fiction, and once declined an offer to revise Bram Stoker's then still unpublished novel Dracula. (: "Mrs. Miniter - Estimates and Recollections")

Edmond Moore Hamilton (21 October 1904-1 February 1977) was a prolific American science fiction, horror, and fantasy author active throughout the middle of the 20th century . He was one of the most frequent contributors to pulp magazine Weird Tales, having a total of 79 of his stories published within its pages. In addition to his prose work, Hamilton also wrote early stories for comic book superhero properties such as Superman and Batman .

Hamilton's first published short story "The Monster-God of Mamurth" (Weird Tales, August 1926) was cited by author Kenneth Sterling as at least a partial inspiration for his original draft of "In the Walls of Eryx," before it was presented to H. P. Lovecraft for revision.

Edward Hutchinson is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. 

### Overview
Hutchinson is the friend and associate of the seventeenth century alchemist Joseph Curwen. He is another alchemist with life-prolonging powers, who lives in Salem-Village (latter-day Danvers), where he had "a house well out toward the woods, and it was not altogether liked by sensitive people because of the sounds heard there at night." 

Hutchinson relocates to Transylvania, where he adopts the name Baron Ferenczy. 

As Baron Ferenczy, this character is greatly expanded upon in the Mythos-adjacent writings of Brian Lumley in his Necroscope series of novels and connected short stories. In Lumley's works, Hutchinson / Ferenczy is an outright vampire cut from similar cloth to the movie version of Count Dracula.

Captain Edward Norrys is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his horror short story "The Rats in the Walls".

### Biography
Described as a "plump, amiable young man", Captain Edward Norrys was a pilot who served in the Royal Flying Corps during World War One. While in service, he became a friend of Alfred Delapore, whose family's ancestral estate of Exham Priory had been incorporated into the lands of Norrys' uncle.

Norrys told Alfred about the sinister history of the Delapores, including superstitious claims of murder and devil-worship. Norrys himself didn't believe in these tales, but Alfred found them amusing.

Following Alfred's death in 1920, the elder Delapore moved to England, having purchased Exham Priory from Norrys' uncle. Norrys himself assisted Delapore with the restoration and with gathering information about the Delapore family's history.

Norrys was with Delapore when he found evidence of deep pre-Roman vaults underneath the priory, and also accompanied Delapore and the five scholars who descended these vaults to explore them. Unfortunately, the expedition ended in tragedy when Delapore's mind was overwhelmed by the revelations about his ancestors who practiced cannibalism. This, combined with the previous trauma of losing his son, costed Delapore's sanity. In a fit of madness, Delapore killed Norrys and was feeding on his corpse when the others located him. After being interred in Hanwell Asylum, Delapore insisted that it was the rats who had eaten Norrys, not him. (: "The Rats in the Walls")

### In Other Media
According to one source, Edward Norrys was a friend of Bertie Wooster, who knew him by the nickname "Tubby". (: "Cats, Rats, and Bertie Wooster")

Edward Pickman Derby is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Thing on the Doorstep".

### Background
Edward Pickman Derby was a poet and the husband of Asenath Waite. Derby's body was killed by Daniel Upton, his best friend, while confined to a sanitarium in Arkham; Derby, however, was already dead at the time, his body having been possessed by the spirit of Ephraim Waite, Asenath's father. (: "The Thing on the Doorstep")

Derby was a child prodigy, writing poetry at the age of seven "of a sombre, fantastic, almost morbid cast which astonished the tutors surrounding him." After the murder, Upton described his friend's over-protected childhood: 

Derby's best-known work, a collection of "nightmare-lyrics"  called Azathoth and Other Horrors, caused a sensation when it was published when Derby was 18. He was a correspondent of Justin Geoffrey, "the notorious Baudelairean poet."

Derby's marriage to Asenath Waite led to increasingly bizarre behavior and his eventual confinement to the Arkham sanitarium--a commitment that lasted until his physical death.

### Behind the Mythos
Lovecraft's depiction of Derby's childhood is considered to be in large part autobiographical. It is considered unlikely, however, that the typically self-deprecating Lovecraft was thinking of himself when he described Derby as a child prodigy and young literary sensation.

The title of Derby's book suggests that Lovecraft had Clark Ashton Smith in mind, who won acclaim at the age of nineteen when he published a book of poetry called The Star-Treader and Other Poems (1912). Another possible model is Alfred Galpin, a friend of Lovecraft's who was eleven years his junior, whom he described as being "immensely my superior" in intellect.

In writing that Derby's "attempts to grow a moustache were discernible only with difficulty", Lovecraft evoked his protégé Frank Belknap Long, whom he frequently teased for the same reason.

Like Upton, Pickman and Derby are both old Salem names. There is a suggestion in Lovecraft's fiction that the three families are closely allied; Richard Upton Pickman is the title character of "Pickman's Model", while the Nathaniel Derby Pickman Foundation underwrites the Antarctic expedition in At the Mountains of Madness.

Peter Cannon notes that the protagonist's character drives the plot of "The Thing on the Doorstep" more than in most Lovecraft stories. "Where cosmic forces usually overtake the typical Lovecraft hero such as Peaslee by chance, here Derby has only his own weak personality to blame for his falling victim to his wife's nefarious designs."

Dr. Edward Pretorius is a fictional character created for the 1986 film adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's short story "From Beyond". He is the main antagonist in the film, with most of the action taking place in his mansion. He is played by actor Ted Sorel.

### Biography
Edward Pretorius is a brilliant scientist who, with the help of his assistant Crawford Tillinghast, invented an electrical device called the Resonator, which stimulates the pineal gland of anyone in its proximity. This allows them to see and be seen by a variety of creatures that move through the air, invisibly to normal humans.

Pretorius is a cruel, hedonistic man whose main goal is to find new ways to stimulate himself, hiring women to participate in sadomasochistic activities. Believing that the ordinary five senses aren't enough for him, he tries to use the Resonator as a means to experience new sensations. His first successful experiment led to him being decapitated by an invisible predator, with Tillinghast blamed for his death and confined to an asylum, as the authorities wouldn't believe his story.

However, it turns out that Pretorius' mind had been assimilated by the creature, and his consciousness transferred to its amorphous body, invisible and incapable of interacting with humans unless the Resonator is turned on.

When Tillinghast returns to Pretorius' house, accompanied by his psychiatrist Dr. Katherine McMichaels and policeman Bubba Brownlee, he uses the Resonator again and proves to them that the creatures are real, but is shocked to see Pretorius alive in front of him.

At first, Pretorius appears exactly as he looked like in life, but reveals his amorphous nature when Tillinghast touches him. In his subsequent appearances, he shows up increasingly deformed and monstrous, with an eyestalk protruding from his forehead to represent the hyperstimulated pineal gland.

Pretorius enjoys his new existence and is delighted by the chance of experiencing what he comes to regard as the ultimate pleasure: dominating someone completely by assimilating their minds. He becomes obsessed with trying to consume McMichaels and Tillinghast. However, when he does finally consume the latter, his body is torn apart as Tillinghast's mind fights against Pretorius' in an effort to save McMichaels, who manages to escape as the bomb she planted earlier detonates and kills the composite creature.

### Gallery

EdwardPretorius1.jpg|Human
EdwardPretorius3.jpg|Mutated


### Behind the Mythos
Edward Pretorius was created specifically for the film and is not present in the original story, in which his role is fulfilled by Tillinghhast himself. The presence of Pretorius allows the film version of Tillinghast to be portrayed in a more positive light, as a protagonist who uses the machine reluctantly.

fullContent:
Edwin Baird was the first editor of Weird Tales, the pioneering pulp magazine that specialized in horror fiction, as well as Detective Tales.

### Career
Baird, hired by Weird Tales publisher J. C. Henneberger, put out the magazine's premiere issue, dated March 1923. Over the course of the next year, Baird published some of the magazine's most famous writers, including H. P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, and Seabury Quinn.

Baird—in marked contrast to his successor—accepted everything that Lovecraft submitted to the magazine, including "The Hound", "Arthur Jermyn", "The Statement of Randolph Carter", "The Cats of Ulthar", "Dagon", "The Picture in the House", "The Rats in the Walls", "Hypnos" and "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs". He did, however, insist that Lovecraft retype his first submissions using double spacing, causing the author to remark, "I am not certain whether or not I should bother."

Under Baird's editorship, Weird Tales lost a considerable amount of money—estimated at $51,000. After the April 1924 issue, Henneberger fired him and offered his job to Lovecraft. When Lovecraft declined, the publisher made Farnsworth Wright, until then Baird's assistant, the editor of Weird Tales, a position he held until 1940.

Baird remained as editor of another of Henneberger's titles, Detective Tales. In this post, he rejected Lovecraft's "The Shunned House" in July 1925. Detective Tales was sold off, and Baird remained editor when it retitled as Real Detective Tales.
