Eric Marsh is a fictional character created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer for their short story "The Lair of the Star-Spawn".

### Overview
Marsh was the sole survivor of the Hawks Expedition, which was massacred by the Tcho-Tcho people in the hinterlands of Burma in the early 20th century. In the process, he came across the city of Alaozar in the Plateau of Sung, where he fell into the captivity of the Tcho-Tchos. While there, he met a fellow prisoner, Doctor Fo-Lan, with whom he eventually escaped. Ultimately Marsh and Fo-Lan were the sole survivors when the Elder Gods and the Star-Warriors came down from Orion to lay waste upon Alaozar. Upon his return to the United States he kept silent about the events of which he was part. The publication of his papers after his sudden death no more than a month after his return resulted in the entire story then being made known. (: "The Lair of the Star-Spawn")

Eric Marsh was an explorer and aide de camp to the explorer Hawks. He was with Hawks when the latter along with the rest of his expedition were slaughtered by the Tcho-Tcho. Marsh survived in an injured condition and eventually through his own offers of violence and heroic efforts escaped captivity and made his way back to civilization. The events however gave him permanent phobias and left his expanded mind, already affected by exposure to the entities Zhar and Lloigor, permanently damaged.

Sir Eric Moreland Clapham-Lee is a character created by H. P. Lovecraft in his episodic story "Herbert West--Reanimator." A military surgeon on the Western Front during the Great War, Clapham-Lee is first a supporter of Herbert West in his reanimation experiments, and then--after he is used as a guinea pig in those experiments--becomes West's nemesis. 

Clapham-Lee is a major in the Canadian army during the Great War; he is described by West's associate (and Lovecraft's narrator) as "the greatest surgeon in our division." He received the Distinguished Service Order, a British military decoration awarded for meritorious actions by individual officers during wartime.  

He had at some point "secretly studied the theory of reanimation to some extent under West"; he was a "friend and fellow-scholar" who "knew about his experiments and could have duplicated them." Clapham-Lee used his influence to help get West his commission. 

In 1915, in response to heavy fighting, Clapham-Lee was transferred to the St. Eloi sector, where West and his associate were working. (Known in English at St. Eloi, Siint-Elooi is a village in Belgium where there was intense combat in March 1915, and again in March-April 1916; it was actually the 1916 battle that involved Canadians.) His plane was shot down just as it was arriving, however, killing both Clapham-Lee and his pilot, the "intrepid" Lieut. Ronald Hill; the crash "yielded up the great surgeon in a nearly decapitated but otherwise intact condition." 

Rather than trying to bring his friend back to life, West sees this as an opportunity to test his theory that consciousness, reason, and personality can exist independently of the brain—that man has no central connective spirit, but is merely a machine of nervous matter, each section more or less complete in itself.  In Clapham-Lee, West had the remains of "a man at once physically powerful and of such high mentality that a sensitive nervous system was assured." He finished severing the head, placing it in a vat of "reptile embryo tissue" he kept in his surgery tent, in order "to preserve it for future experiments." West then closed off the neck wound,  using "engrafted skin from an unidentified specimen which had borne an officer’s uniform," and then "injected his reanimating solution into the arm of the headless body." The experiment seems to be a success: The arms stirred disquietingly, the legs drew up, and various muscles contracted in a repulsive kind of writhing. Then the headless thing threw out its arms in a gesture which was unmistakably one of desperation—an intelligent desperation apparently sufficient to prove every theory of Herbert West. But then West and his associate hear a sound that called into question West's interpretation: Clapham-Lee's severed head, crying out from the "hellish vat of pulpy reptile-tissue": “Jump, Ronald, for God’s sake, jump!”

Eric Stokes Brooks (aka, Blade) is a superhero in the fictional Marvel universe, who was created in 1973. He's a B-list hero with several comic book series.

### Background
Blade is a human/vampire hybrid who was born to a woman bitten and killed by a vampire (and turned into a vampire herself). He grew up into a vampire hunter, dedicating himself to hunting down and exterminating all vampires. Along the way he has also fought other supernatural threats. To help him hunt down and kill Dracula, he joined other vampire hunters in a team of vampire hunters, the BorderLine Investigative Services (The Nightstalkers).

Currently he is a member of the Midnight Sons a team of supernatural superheroes and recently joined the Avengers. In his war against vampires he has clashed with their allies, the Cult of the Darkhold and once came under the influence of the Elder God Chthon.

Erich Zann is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Music of Erich Zann".

### Background
Erich Zann is a German musician who, at the end of his life, lived in a tenement on Rue d'Auseil, in an unspecified French city. Of his early life nothing is known. He is completely mute and earns his living by playing the viol as part of a small theater orchestra.

Zann resides in the attic room of a large boarding house. The window of his room is the only place in the entire Rue d'Auseil high enough to allow him to see the landscape behind the wall that occupies the end of the street. Every night, Zann plays strange music, usually of his own composition, that apparently serves either to soothe or to counteract the influence of a mysterious cosmic entity.

Physically, Erich Zann is described as a short, lean, nearly bald old man with a curved posture, blue eyes, and a satyr-like face. His room is unkempt, almost bereft of furniture, and his clothes are also described as "shabby".

The story's narrator, a student of metaphysics, meets Erich Zann after renting a room in the boarding house's otherwise empty fourth floor. Unable to sleep at night due to the bizarre music, the narrator is nonetheless fascinated by it and recognizes Zann's composition as the product of a creative genius. Despite Zann's reclusive and eccentric attitude, the narrator is able to befriend him and asks him to play some of his pieces.

While the narrator enjoys Zann's music, they are disappointed to hear none of the "weird notes" that had so fascinated them in the nights before. Once the narrator mentions the fact and whistles some of the notes, Zann reacts violently, covers the narrator's mouth with his hand, and casts a terrified glance at the window as if expecting someone to be there, despite the great height and absence of other nearby buildings. When the narrator tries to peek through the window themself, Zann becomes even more agitated, to the point of physically restraining them and gesturing them to leave the room. However, as the narrator reacts angrily to this, Zann calms down and writes a note in broken French. In this note, Zann asks the narrator to forgive his behaviour, citing nervous disorders that make it impossible for him to bear playing his "weird harmonies" to another or hear them from another. He assures the narrator that he was pleased by their visit and would be glad to play his other compositions, but asks the narrator to rent a different room from which they would no longer be able to hear Zann's "weird" pieces, and offers to pay the difference in rent, to which the narrator agrees.

Erlik Khan is a fictional entity in the Marvel Universe, who first appeared in 1987 in issue #6 of the Strange Tales Vol 2 comic book series.

### Background
Erlik Khan is either a Great Old One or a Lesser Old One, who has five arms on each side, of which four pairs are of much smaller than the main pair. He is able to animate the dead, can cross dimensional barriers, and is able to teleport.

He was one of the agents of Shuma Gorath, the lord of the Great Old Ones.

Sometime in the past, the Ancient One was able to imprison him. During the late 20th century, upon the weakening of the mystical barriers protecting Earth, he sent his servants known the Khats to Earth, who then confronted Dr. Strange and his servant Wong.

Ermengarde Stubbs is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Sweet Ermengarde". While Lovecraft is far more well known as a writer of horror and fantasy, "Sweet Ermengarde" is a rare example of a comedy with no supernatural elements. As a parody of a romantic narrative character, Ermengarde subverts the genre's conventions by starting out as a typical love interest who is kidnapped by the villain, then revealing herself as a shameless opportunist who turns every situation to her advantage at the end.

### Biography
Ethyl Ermengarde Stubbs was raised on a farm in Hogton, Vermont. She is the daughter of Hiram Stubbs, a farmer and alcohol smuggler, and his wife Hannah. After the prohibition, her father asked her to drop her first name as the word "ethyl" made him thirsty (the products he sold contained mostly methyl rather than ethyl alcohol). Although naturally brunette, she dyed her hair blonde, and claimed to be 16 even when she was actually 30.

At about the same time, two men coveted Ermengarde's affection, albeit for different reasons. The rich and dastardly 'Squire Hardman, who had a mortgage on the Stubbses' farm, had recently discovered gold there and hoped to marry Ermengarde as a means to claim it. Meanwhile, Ermengarde's childhood friend, the far less privileged Jack Manly, finally gathered courage to confess his love for her, which she at this point reciprocated.

After overhearing Ermengarde and Jack's plans to get married, 'Squire Hardman took more drastic measures by talking directly to the Stubbses, asking for their daughter's hand, and threatening to foreclose the mortgage if they refused it. When Jack learned about this scheme, he promised Ermengarde to resolve the situation by moving to "the great city", gaining his own fortune and freeing the Stubbses from their financial dependence on Hardman's mortgage.

While her beloved was out in the city, Ermengarde was kidnapped by 'Squire Hardman with the help of two hired thugs, but was duly released once Hardman came to his senses and realized that he could get the farm and the gold by simply foreclosing the mortgage, and thus didn't need to marry Ermengarde at all. Yet soon after Hardman gave up his original plot, another man named Algernon Reginald Jones discovered the gold while out hunting and came up with almost the same plan, deciding that he must marry Ermengarde.

No more than a week after meeting Algernon for the first time, Ermengarde agreed to elope with him. However, once he fell asleep on the train, she found a love letter from another woman among his belongings and promptly pushed him out of the train's window, only regretting the fact that she forgot to steal his money first.

Ernest B. Aspinwall, Esq. (1863 - 1932) is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, first mentioned in his fantasy short story "The Silver Key". The character appeared for the first time in that story's sequel, "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", co-authored by Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price.

### Overview
A lawyer by trade, Aspinwall scoffed at any notion of mysticism and the supernatural which so fascinated his distant maternal cousin, Randolph Carter. At the age of 69, Aspinwall was described as "keen as a youth in forensic battles". Physically, he was a portly man with white hair and sideburns.

Carter was on first name basis with him. However, it is possible that their relationship wasn't entirely amiable, as Aspinwall described Carter as being "half-crazy". (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

### Biography
Born in 1863, Aspinwall was ten years older than Carter. Despite being distantly related, he had enough contact with Carter during his youth to vividly recall how the younger boy changed after a visit to the Snake-Den in the autumn of 1883. From this point on, Carter developed a sense of precognition, displaying occasional knowledge of events that were to take place in the future, although never further than 1928. Unbeknownst to Aspinwall, this happened because the adult Carter of 1928 used the Silver Key to go back in time and revert to his child self in 1883. (: "The Silver Key")

In 1932, Aspinwall was present in a meeting to decide the destination of Carter's estate following his mysterious disappearance. The other men present were Etienne-Laurent de Marigny, Ward Phillips, and the Swami Chandraputra, who claimed to have proof that Randolph Carter was still alive, but trapped in the body of an alien creature called Zkauba, following an astral journey enabled by the Silver Key, which took place after the aforementioned return to his childhood. Aspinwall, more than any of the others, was extremely skeptical of the Swami's claims and openly called him a charlatan. As it turns out, the Swami was nothing more than a disguise used by Carter himself to hide his alien appearance. Once Aspinwall noticed that the Swami's face was a mask, he assaulted the mystic and forcibly removed it, only to die of fright at the sight of the inhuman visage of Zkauba. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

Baron Ernst Kant is a fictional character created by Brian Lumley as a recurring background element in his Cthulhu Mythos stories. He is first mentioned in Lumley's story "The Mirror of Nitocris" (1971). 

Kant is described as a "witch-hunter" or "the witch-hunting Baron." He was the putative owner of a silver-plated revolver accompanied by silver bullets, later sold to occultist Henri-Laurent de Marigny; there is an "ornately inscribed 'K' on the weapon’s butt," but de Marigny acknowledges that there is not "a single shred of evidence" that the pistol actually belonged to Kant.

Kant is said to be the father of occultist Joachim Feery--though Feery was "illegitimate," Bedlam." According to "a comparatively modern work on singular foreign mental cases," Kant believed that "his every insane action [was] controlled by a creature he called Yibb-Tstll," which he described as “huge and black with writhing breasts and an anus within its forehead, a black-blooded thing whose brains feed upon its own wastes….”

Esch is an extraterrestrial avian creature who appears in Brian Lumley's Titus Crow series of novels, making his first appearance in the 1975 novel The Transition of Titus Crow.

### Description
Like the rest of his species, the Dchichi, Esch is a tall humanoid with the head and lower limbs of a terrestrial bird. He sports a beautiful set of feathers similar to that of a bird of paradise, and wears a cloak and shoes crafted from fine gold mesh. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

### History
When Titus Crow first set foot outside of his Time Clock upon Elysia, he was greeted by Esch. At first Esch attempted to communicate with him in alien languages which the Earthman did not understand, but as soon as Crow tried to tell him this, Esch replied in plain English. Esch then informed Crow that there was a Lithard on its way to collect Crow, before disappearing into a Time Clock of his own. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

The Esoteric Order of Dagon is a cult which features prominently in many Cthulhu Mythos works, especially those involving Innsmouth and the Deep Ones.

### History
### Lovecraft's Works
The Order was founded by Captain Obed Marsh in Innsmouth using the practices learned from the inhabitants of a Polynesian island. The people of Innsmouth carried out ritual sacrifices on Devil Reef to appease the Deep Ones. In 1846 during one of these sacrifices Captain Marsh and several members of the Order of Dagon were arrested, though no formal charges were made. It was disbanded when the United States government launched an attack on the town in 1928. (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth)

### Expanded Mythos Works
### CthulhuTech
The Esoteric Order of Dagon is an organisation controlled by the Deep Ones and their hybrid agents. Prior to the 21st century, they spread their influence across the world and recruited humans. Their ultimate objective is to free Cthulhu from his imprisonment, and therefore are searching for R'lyeh. Meanwhile they breed with willing cultists or unwilling captured humans in rape camps (mostly the latter) to increase their numbers. At their disposal are mecha, the Star-Spawn of Cthulhu, monsters of the deep, and servitors of Cthulhu. They control the oceans and most of the coastal regions of the world, having complete naval supremacy. (: CthulhuTech)

### Providence
According to one account, it is the literary equivalent of the Friends of Oannes, based in St Jude's parish in Salem. (: Providence)

### The Sinking City
In his quest to find the cause of the flood and madness plaguing Oakmont, Massachusetts, Charles Reed infiltrates a local chapter of the Esoteric Order of Dagon. Posing as a charity called "Everyone's Obvious Duty," they initially appear to be helping the people of the city, such as feeding the poor and residents affected by the flood with stockpiles of fish, but have much more sinister intentions.

### Behind the Mythos
Fans of Lovecraft eventually made an amateur publication association named the Esoteric Order of Dagon.

There exist a real occult order called the [http://esotericorderofdagon.net/ Esoteric Order of Dagon] (E.O.D) that works with Yog-Sothothery, mainly from a pure Lovecraftian approach.

Another occult society also named the Esoteric Order of Dagon (E.'.O.'.D.'.) exists in real life, mixing concepts from the writings of Lovecraft and the occultist author Aleister Crowley, among other things.

The Esoteric Order of Dagon amateur press association (EODapa) is an amateur press group very similar to those that first published H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview
EODapa was established in 1973 by Roger Bryant. Its focus is that of a fan group, concerning itself with both nonfiction research and fictional creations related primarily to the author H. P. Lovecraft and his circle, though also focussing on the wider weird and horror field of literature and film. EODapa has generated an enormous amount of material across the years. Copies of all quarterly mailings are deposited with the Lovecraft collection at the John Hay Library at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island. 

EODapa still produces its zines and mailings in hardcopy form. The Official Editor issues an 'umbrella'  zine listing the titles of the zines within a given mailing, the number of pages of each contribution, and the names and addresses of each mailing. Under Roger Bryant and Mollie Burleson as Official Editors, this zine was titled The Cry of the Cricket. 

Lovecraft scholar and editor S.T. Joshi has been the Official editor of EODapa for over thirty years, with his 'umbrella' zine being titled Nuclear Chaos and his personal zine What Is Anything?

fullContent:
Etepsed Egnis is a short story by British author D. F. Lewis written as a parody of cosmic horror stories like those of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Plot summary

The narrator, Halizbuk, climbs into a small box through the curtained window, using themselves as a ladder, to find a naked contortionist in the darkness licking them self clean. Halizbuk has been searching for this man and hopes to learn more about his trade. In his head he runs through a ringmasters calls, describing a list of impossible feats that closes with him turning inside out.

Still dreaming of fame he sees another man in the room before running to the window, describing the room and its occupants to a crowd of reporters who watched him come in. As he does so the two men begin to graphically merge together from opposite corners, a tendril fusing with Halizbuk before he rips it off in disgust. Eventually the hair, flesh and bones of the men cover the walls of the room and as one they announce them self as Etepsed Egnis.

The Press soon lose interest as Etepsed Egnis fails to appear and Halizbuk joins a family circus.



The ragged circus sets up in a modern housing estate as Halizbuk, now a magician, rehearses with a familiar curtained box. As local children watch he calls forth Etepsed Egnis which erupts out with a bone white claw "And a wild wicked flashpoint of wrinkled, rippling skin ridden with writhing lengths of jaws 'n claws entered fist 'n fury nova, a hypernuclear prestidigitation of supermeshed sky and dogfight.". The creature escapes and wheels over the surrounding TV antennae as the children somehow grow by drawing up strength from the soil.

### Connections
Etepsed Egnis reappears in "A Core Unto Itself" and "The Gemstone From Out of Space".

Etepsed Egnis is a fictional entity created by D. F. Lewis for his eponymous short story.

### Description
Whilst almost nothing is known of Etepsed Egnis, it has been described as a vast, amorphous blob composed of an unidentifiable material. The only recognisable feature of this mass is the single great arm which protrudes from its disgusting form.

The appearance of Etepsid Egnis seems to be very similar to that of the Great Old One Cynothoglys, The Mortician God, although whether these two beings are somehow related - or even the same entity masquerading under different names - has yet to be established.

"Eternal Life" is the forty-fifth episode of the Japanese tokusatsu television series Ultraman Tiga, which first aired in 1997. It was directed by Shingo Matsubara and written by Masakazu Migita. 

The plot involves humanity being threatened by self-destruction through the effects of Gijera, a servant of the evil god Gatanothor.

### Synopsis
After detecting strong plasma readings, with seeming nothing there, the defense team GUTS decides to send their members, Daigo Madoka, Rena Yanase and Tetsuo Shinjoh, to investigate the field, while the vice-captain, Seiichi Munakata, is currently on vacation. Upon arrival, Rena notices some mysterious flowers in the field, which end up awakening the ancient memories lying latent in Daigo Madoka's DNA. In his mind, Daigo recalls that the flowers were tied to the destruction of an ancient civilization, coming to a conclusion for the plasma. Investigating further in a nearby forest, Daigo is interrupted by a young girl wearing a blue cloak, with one of the flowers in her hair. Daigo asks what that flower is, and the girl identifies it as "Gijera".

Beneath the forest, a massive plant with numerous vines began emitting pollen through the flowers, putting both Rena and Shinjoh in a drug-like state. The girl proclaims that it's starting, and wonders why Daigo isn't going to the dream world. Daigo tries to snap the others out of it, but the girl informs him that no one wants to come back once they've seen the dream world, claiming that they should enjoy it since they're all bound for destruction anyway.

Daigo takes his two fellow officers, Rena and Shinjoh, back to the main base of GUTS, along with the girl, who is named Terra, the only key to the riddle of Gijera. Masami Horii identifies the flowers as a new species to Earth; however, Terra claims that Gijera bloomed on the Earth a million years ago, having learned from her father that Gijera would bloom whenever the destruction of humanity draws near. When asked what her father does, Terra reveals that he is searching for new land, leading to Daigo remembering the message from the time capsule, where a hologram of Yuzare spoke of ancient voyagers leaving the Earth. Soon afterward, Jun Yazumi reports that Munakata had also succumbed to the effects of Gijera, unable to respond to a call from Megumi Iruma, who zooms into the monitor to see that one of the flowers is in Munakata's room. Revealing that the field is not the only place Gijera grows, the flowers are now blooming all over the world, including Moscow, Washington, Paris and Beijing.

Horii began examining Gijera, coming to the conclusion that their composition is the same as plants on Earth. While Yazumi goes after Munakata, Iruma asks what would happen to humanity if the flowers kept spreading their pollen, with Terra claiming that they will enjoy a painless destruction. Etienne Roulet is a fictional character in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Shunned House". It is suggested in the story that he is a relative of the historical figure Jacques Roulet, who was tried as a werewolf in France in 1598.

The story relates that Etienne Roulet and his wife had moved to from Caude in France to East Greenwich, Rhode Island, in 1686, "after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes." (The Edict of Nantes, in which King Henry IV granted tolerance to French Protestants in 1598, was repealed by his grandson Louis XIV in 1685, leading to a Protestant exodus from France.)

The Roulets were unpopular in East Greenwich, for reasons that rumour said "extended beyond mere racial and national prejudice". Claiming religious persecution, they asked to move to Providence, and despite some hostile whispering, the town fathers allowed them to do so in 1696. Etienne was "given a clerical post in the warehouse at Pardon Tillinghast’s wharf"--Tillinghast being a historical figure, a successful merchant and a pastor of the Baptist Church of Providence.

In 1697, the family leased a small tract of land, where they built a one-story cottage with an attic. Behind it they laid out a graveyard--on land that later became the site of the Shunned House. The narrator notes that "no record of any transfer of graves existed."

Etienne Roulet is described as "swarthy"--almost always a red flag in a Lovecraft story--and "less apt at agriculture than at reading queer books and drawing queer diagrams." The entire family is said to have "possessed an abnormal affinity for outer circles of entity—dark spheres which for normal folk hold only repulsion and terror." But the worst of them was said to be Etienne's son Paul.

### References

Étienne-Laurent de Marigny is a fictional character invented by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffman Price, and later referred to in other Cthulhu Mythos stories, including the works of Brian Lumley.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In his first appearance, in the co-authored story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", de Marigny is identified as a "distinguished Creole student of mysteries and Eastern antiquities," and as North America's "greatest mystic, mathematician and orientalist". Physically, he is described as "slim, dark, handsome, mustached, and still young".

The story takes place in 1932 in de Marigny's New Orleans home, where he is serving as the executor of Randolph Carter's will.  He and Carter met in France during World War I, when they both served in the French Foreign Legion. They bonded over their "similar tastes and outlook", and sealed their friendship when de Marigny took Carter to Bayonne, where de Marigny "had shown him certain terrible secrets in the nighted and immemorial crypts that burrow beneath that brooding, eon-weighted city". Carter made de Marigny both his literary and financial executor.

"Through the Gates of the Silver Key" also introduces de Marigny's clock, "a curious, coffin-shaped clock whose dial bore baffling hieroglyphs and whose four hands did not move in consonance with any time system known on this planet".

Lovecraft uses de Marigny again in his revision tale "Out of the Aeons", where he is described as "the famous New Orleans mystic Etienne-Laurent de Marigny". In this story, he writes "a highly learned article" for The Occult Review about the scroll held by the Cabot Museum, linking its designs to "certain ideographs of horrible significance" reproduced in von Junzt's Nameless Cults.

### Other Appearances
In "The Secret of Sebek", by Robert Bloch, de Marigny makes a cameo appearance as a member of the Coffin Club, a New Orleans occult society. 

Elsewhere, de Marigny is credited with the book The Tarot: A Treatise and a translation of the Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan (source?). 

Brian Lumley makes de Marigny the father of his recurring character Henri-Laurent de Marigny. In Lumley's The Clock of Dreams, the elder de Marigny has become a Dreamer, one whose dreams "have carried him beyond hither to undreamed of regions -- not only in Earth's Dreamlands but in those of distant worlds and dimensions."

"Euchred", which has also been published as "Eucred", is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Kevin L. O'Brien. It was first published in Ron Shiflet's short-lived fanzine In Lovecraft's Shadow in March 2007.

### Synopsis
Police officer Matthew Cardigan enlists the aid of his good friend, Professor Arthur Templeton of Miskatonic University, in the case of multiple murders in which the victims have had their hearts ripped out and consumed.

Their investigations lead them to a crazed Iraqi occultist who has taken it upon himself to summon a minion of Cthulhu, dubbed an alu, to eliminate his competition in an attempt to gain more material power over the town of Arkham. Cardigan and Templeton are able to defeat the crazed man and his demonic servant by summoning their own spirit, a winged bull shedu.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Euchred" has also appeared in the October 2006 edition of Edward P. Berglund's online zine Nightscapes, where it was titled "Eucred".

Eva is a hero in the fictional Dynamite universe, who was created in 2006 by James Kuhoric. She is Dracula's daughter, who has fought against him her whole life.

### Background
Upon the death of Vlad Tepes's wife, he made a pact with what he believed to be god's envoy in exchange for her life. In reality a demon, Vlad Tepes was turned into a vampire and his wife didn't return to life as he was promised, but a part of her returned as Eva, his baby daughter. Who was deliver by wolves to a monk. Eva possesses a preternatural ability to find evil influences among men and wipe it out, and has been destroying Dracula's influence ever since.

Eva fought alongside Ash Williams against her father and his army of monsters, when he tried to use the Necronomicon to bring about eternal night on Earth. She later was part of a coalition of warriors and supernatural beings which included her father Dracula, that fought against the Hyborian sorcerer Kulan Gath in the early 21st century. In one possible post-apocalyptic future, she was allied with Ash Williams, her father, and the remnants of the human, witch, vampire, and werewolf races against the Deadites.

fullContent:
Even Death Can Die is a scenario supplement for Pelgrane Press's Cthulhu Mythos roleplaying game Cthulhu Confidential. Written by Robin D. Laws, Chris Spivey, and Ruth Tillman, it was published by Pelgrane in both print and digital formats.

### Overview


The book contains nine stand-alone scenarios for Cthulhu Confidential, a one-on-one game system designed for more intimate gaming sessions consisting solely of a gamesmaster and a single player. Of the included scenarios, six had been previously released as digital downloads, with the remaining three being original to this volume. The three new scenarios are:

*"Preacher Man Blues": Langston Wright investigates a traveling fire and brimstone preacher spurring the black community to action. The police want him silenced. Local churches want him to move on. What do those slaughtered animals have to do with it? 
*"Boundary Waters": Vivian Sinclair’s third cousin, society heiress Tabitha “Tabby” Sinclair hosts a benefit gala aboard a gambling ship. Vivian accepts her invitation to cover the gala, keen to investigate rumors about the boat’s other international activities. But under this swell affair skitters something creepy and crawly .
*"Skin and Teeth": The Revelstock hotel, on South Normandie near Pico, is a place where the shady go to hide out and/or ply their trades. But one of the maids found something so terrible under a bed while cleaning that even the mob-connected owner Hal Cade is sweating. The answer lies in a shocking disaster of the recent past—and something older still .

This is a timeline of events as they take place in the fiction of American horror author H. P. Lovecraft.

It is comprised mostly, or entirely, from the canon events established in Lovecraft's own work, and the Lovecraft Circle. It does not take from the Expanded Mythos. Where other writers have contributed to the timeline, there will be a footnote that details which writer has contributed the information.

### Prehistory

Unknown (possibly 2.5 Billion B.C. ca)

145 Million B.C. ca
*Elder Things build a vast city in the Mountains of Madness in the early Cretaceous to replace an even vaster one destroyed in a cataclysm.

2.5 Million B.C. ca
*Elder Thing city in the Mountains of Madness abandoned long before the opening of the Pleistocene. Dyer places this at 500,000 years ago, but modern scientists place it much earlier.

1587
*Nicholas Van Kauran, ancestor of "Mad" Dan Morris, is hanged as a wizard in Wijtgaart, the Netherlands.
*Pigafetta’s Regnum Congo printed at Frankfort.

*The Roulet family moves from France to East Greenwich, Rhode Island.

shortDefinition: This is a timeline of significant events in the life of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.  ### 1890  * August 20: Howard Philips Lovecraft born at 454 Angell Street, Providence, Rhode Island.  ### 1893  * April 25: Winfield Scott Lovecraft, H. P. Lovecraft'...
fullContent:
This is a timeline of significant events in the life of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### 1890

* August 20: Howard Philips Lovecraft born at 454 Angell Street, Providence, Rhode Island.

### 1893

* April 25: Winfield Scott Lovecraft, H. P. Lovecraft's father, committed to Butler Hospital in Providence after suffering a psychotic break at a hotel in Chicago. Howard will not see his father again.

### 1897

* Lovecraft writes "The Little Glass Bottle," his earliest surviving fiction.

### 1898

* Lovecraft begins attending Providence's Slater Avenue School in 1898. He discovers Edgar Allan Poe the same year.
* July 19: Winfield Scott Lovecraft dies at Butler Hospital.

### 1904

* Lovecraft begins attending Providence's Hope Street High School in 1904.
* March 4: Whipple Van Buren Phillips, Lovecraft's maternal grandfather, dies. Lovecraft and his mother move to 598 Angell Street, where he will live for the next 20 years.

### 1905

* April 21: Lovecraft writes "The Beast in the Cave."

### 1908

*Lovecraft has a nervous breakdown that forces him to leave high school without graduating. He spends the next five years as a virtual hermit.
*Lovecraft writes "The Alchemist."

### 1913

*Lovecraft writes a letter to Argosy mocking the romance writer Fred Jackson, prompting a spirited debate (largely in verse, on Lovecraft's end) that gets Lovecraft noticed by Edward F. Daas, president of the United Amateur Press Association.

### 1914

* January 1: Lovecraft begins writing an astronomy column for the Providence Evening News that will continue until 1918.

### 1915

* April: The first issue of Lovecraft's amateur press journal, The Conservative, appears.

### 1916

* November: "The Alchemist" printed in The United Amateur, Lovecraft's first published fiction. 

### 1917

* Lovecraft returns to fiction writing by writing two humour pieces, "A Reminiscence of Dr. Samuel Johnson" and "Sweet Ermengarde," sometime in 1917.
* May: Lovecraft attempts to enlist in the Rhode Island National Guard, and later the U.S. Army, but is rejected by both.
*June: Lovecraft writes "The Tomb."
*July: Lovecraft writes "Dagon."

### 1918

*Lovecraft writes "The Green Meadow" with Winifred V. Jackson sometime in 1918 or 1919.
*May: Lovecraft writes "Polaris." (Month is approximate.)

### 1919

fullContent:
Evil Dead is a multimedia comedy-horror franchise created by American filmmaker Sam Raimi. Launched with the 1981 low-budget horror film The Evil Dead, it has since expanded into five feature films, a live-action television series, numerous computer games, several comic book tie-ins/franchise crossovers, and an off-Broadway musical. As of May 2024, two more spin-off films and an animated series are also in development.

World-renowned horror writer Stephen King has been at least partially credited with the series' initial success; after attending a screening of The Evil Dead at the 1982 Cannes Film Festival, the rave review he wrote garnered sufficient industry attention to interest larger distributors.

### Premise
The original trilogy (The Evil Dead, Evil Dead II, and Army of Darkness), the live action series, and the majority of the computer games and comic books follow the escapades of former sales clerk Ashley Joanne "Ash" Williams (played by Bruce Campbell) as he battles the forces of the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis, a demon-possessed book bound in human skin. Since his initial battles with the "Deadites" - mutated undead humans created and conjured by the book - in the Tennessee backwoods, Ash's adventures have taken him across space and time in an effort to free the world from the demon's curse.

### The Necronomicon Ex-Mortis
The Necronomicon Ex-Mortis, the focal point for the antagonistic forces ranged against Ash and his allies, was first imagined by Sam Raimi while studying at Michigan State University. Its physical design was realised by special effects artist Tom Sullivan, who has also provided artwork for several of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplements.

Ex Libris Miskatonici: A Catalogue of Selected Items from the Special Collections in the Miskatonic University Library is a pseudofactual bibliography of the eldritch tomes that are supposedly found at Miskatonic University, written by Joan C. Stanley and published as a chapbook by Necronomicon Press in 1993.

The book provides an in-universe examination of the major (and some minor) imaginary occult books of the Cthulhu Mythos, including origins, translations, publication histories and physical descriptions.

The book is divided into sections on the Stone Library, covering the Pnakotic Manuscripts, the Eltdown Shards and Celaeno Fragments, and the G'harne and "Sussex Fragments"; the Department of Eastern Antiquities, including the Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan, the Book of Dzyan, the R'lyeh Text and the Dhôl Chants, and the Ponape Scripture; and the Darby Collection, which comprises the Codex Dagonensis, Les Cultes des Goules, De Vermis Mysteriis, the Liber Ivonis, and Die Unaussprechlichen Kulten. Though the Necronomicon is described as part of the Darby Collection, it is given its own section.

shortDefinition: "Ex Oblivione" is a prose poem by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in late 1920 or early 1921 and first published in The United Amateur in March 1921, under the pseudonym Ward Phillips.  ### Inspiration An H. P. Lovecraft Encyc...
fullContent:
"Ex Oblivione" is a prose poem by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in late 1920 or early 1921 and first published in The United Amateur in March 1921, under the pseudonym Ward Phillips.

### Inspiration
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia suggests that the theme of "Ex Oblivione"—that nothingness is preferable to life—was derived from Lovecraft's reading the philosopher Arthur Schopenhauer. Lovecraft expressed similar sentiments in non-fiction work at the time, writing in In Defense of Dagon, "There is nothing better than oblivion, since in oblivion there is no wish unfulfilled."

### Synopsis
The story is written in first person and tells of the dreams of a presumably dying man. In his dreams, the man is walking through a valley and encounters a vine-covered wall with a locked bronze gate therein. He longs to know what lies beyond the gate.

Then one night, the man dreams of the dream-city Zakarion, in which he finds a yellowed papyrus written by wise dream-sages who exist only within the dream world. The papyrus tells of the gate, with varying accounts of what lies beyond: some of the dream-sages tell of immense wonders, while others tell of horror and disappointment.

Despite this lack of unanimity, the man still wishes to see for himself, even knowing that whichever of these is true, there will be no return. Thus he reads further into the papyrus and learns of a drug which will unlock the gate.

The next night he swallows the drug and returns to the gate which is now ajar, but upon entering, he discovers that indeed both accounts within the papyrus are in a sense true: beyond is the wonderment of forever being free from the pain of the real world and the happy surprise that nothing lies beyond the gate but the infinite void that is death.

Exham Priory is a fictional location in England that features prominently in the H. P. Lovecraft short story "The Rats in the Walls". In the story, it is the ancestral home of the De la Poer family, whose last surviving heir restores it and moves there following World War I. It is located some three miles from the equally fictional village of Anchester.

Lovecraft describes Exham prior to its restoration as "a jumble of tottering mediaeval ruins covered with lichens and honeycombed with rooks’ nests, perched perilously upon a precipice, and denuded of floors or other interior features save the stone walls of the separate towers."

### History
Lovecraft writes, "Exham Priory stood on the site of a prehistoric temple; a Druidical or ante-Druidical thing which must have been contemporary with Stonehenge"--which was constructed between 3000 and 2000 BCE. In its earliest recorded incarnation, "indescribable rites had been celebrated there."

These rites continued when the Roman Empire conquered Britain beginning in 43 CE, and Exham became a temple of Cybele, "the Magna Mater whose dark worship was once vainly forbidden to Roman citizens." This temple "was splendid and thronged with worshippers who performed nameless ceremonies at the bidding of a Phrygian priest." (Phrygia is a region in Asia Minor, now Turkey.) Inscriptions evoking Cybele were visible in the priory's sub-cellar into the 20th century. The "orgies at the temple" continued unchanged after Rome officially Christianized in 380 CE.

Nor did the collapse of the Empire change Exham: "Saxons added to what remained of the temple, and gave it the essential outline it subsequently preserved, making it the centre of a cult feared through half the heptarchy"--referring to the period between the 5th and 9th centuries CE. Around 1000 CE, a chronicle calls it "a substantial stone priory housing a strange and powerful monastic order".

In 1261, after an apparent decline in its power, Exham was granted by Henry III to Gilbert de la Poer, First Baron Exham. Though the family had an unblemished reputation before that point, by 1307 a chronicler refers to a de la Poer as “cursed of God”. The de la Poers built a castle on the foundations of the temple and priory, and village legend recalls villagers occasionally disappearing into it over generations. It was believed that "a legion of bat-winged devils kept Witches’ Sabbath each night at the priory" at this time. 

One notable de la Poer of the era was Lady Margaret Trevor from Cornwall, who married Godfrey de la Poer, the second son of the fifth baron; she was "a favourite bane of children all over the countryside, and the daemon heroine of a particularly horrible old ballad not yet extinct near the Welsh border". fullContent:
"Exham Priory" is a short story by American author Robert M. Price. It is a direct sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Rats in the Walls".

### Synopsis
After the death of Thomas de la Poer in the institution to which he had been sent at the end of "The Rats in the Walls", three of the surviving members of the first expedition, Brinton, Trask and Pettijohn, return to Exham Priory to search for Thayer (another survivor whom Pettijohn believes has returned already) and to document the caverns beneath the manor before they are destroyed by the local authorities.

Beneath the Priory they encounter Thayer, who has made contact with the degenerate denizens of the deepest caverns, and been accepted as one of their own due to a birthmark which signifies that he carries their blood in his veins. He relates to them snippets of the creature’s culture and appearance, but states that he wishes to remain amongst them, though he will not stop them if they decide to explore deeper, which the three do.

After a while, the group chances upon a gallery hung with tapestries which seem to indicate that the ancestors of the creatures which dwell in the depths were in fact beings from a distant star. However, at this point the treacherous Thayer attacks them accompanied by a group of degenerates, with only Brinton escaping to tell the story.

### Characters
* Sir William Brinton, a renowned archaeologist.
* Dr. Francis Abelard Trask, an equally-renowned anthropologist.
* Dr. Randolf Holmes Pettijohn, a psychiatrist.
* Professor Andrew Powys Thayer, a folklorist.

### Publication History
"Exham Priory" was first published in Crypt of Cthulhu #72 in May 1990. It later appeared in the Robert M. Price collection Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2008.

Exo III is a fictional planet created by Robert Bloch for the episode "What Are Little Girls Made Of?" of the science fiction television series Star Trek. While not explicitly linked to the Cthulhu Mythos, the episode contains references to an ancient humanoid race known as the "Old Ones".

Exo III was subsequently incorporated into the Doctor Who universe, and referenced in the Mythos crossover novel White Darkness as a world formerly inhabited by the Great Old Ones.

### History
Rock carvings depicting the Great Old Ones have been found in the tunnels of Exo III, dating back to millions of years. (: White Darkness)

About half a million years ago, a humanoid species known as the Old Ones lived on the planet, and moved to the underground as the sun began to cool and the surface became increasingly inhospitable. As a technologically advanced race, they built sapient androids in their image, and were eventually destroyed by their creations. (: "What Are Little Girls Made Of?")

Circa 59,000 BC, the androids of Exo III were part of the interstellar empire of the Gubbage Cones. (: The Crystal Bucephalus)

By the time of the 23rd century, Exo III was a harsh, inhospitable world covered in ice, and the androids themselves were practically extinct. (: "What Are Little Girls Made Of?")

### Behind the Mythos
In the Star Trek episode, the Old Ones of Exo III were a humanoid species. In the Cthulhu Mythos, several species have been known as the "Old Ones", including at least one humanoid extraterrestrial race, the K'n-yanians, which worshiped Cthulhu.

"Experiments…" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by authors Sergio Palumbo and Ernesto Canepa. It was published in Vol 5, Issue 3 of the Lovecraftiana zine in October 2020.

### Synopsis
Robert Andberg is approached by an alien disguised as a human who tells him of monstrous creatures named Dimensional Shamblers which he says prey on the human race in the shadows. The alien then explains that he is in possession of technology which would allow the man to change his body at will, granting him the power to fight these beings.

After a short time spent killing the Shamblers, Andberg realises that he has been lied to: the humans which they kill are in fact more aliens in disguise, and he has been tricked into becoming a pawn in an inter-species war. Murdering the alien who gave him his powers, he vows to track down any others who may have been changed in the way he has been.

### Trivia
*The inspiration for the genetic technology modifications gifted to Robert Andberg is clearly drawn from Extremis, a 2005/6 storyline in Marvel's Iron Man comic book property.

Franklin Lee Baldwin (1913 - 1987) was an amateur weird fiction author from Asotin, Washington, and a correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft. He struck up a friendship with fellow Asotin resident and Lovecraft correspondent Duane W. Rimel, as the two shared interests not only in weird fiction but also in music. Rimel's Cthulhu Mythos story "Music of the Stars" features a character named "Frank Baldwyn". Similarly, the comedic story "The Battle that Ended the Century", by Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow, affectionately spoofs Baldwin as the "Maestro Sing Lee Bawledout".

The Faceless God is an avatar of Nyarlathotep described in a homonymous story by Robert Bloch. It is one of the multiple avatars of Nyarlathotep related to the Sphinx.

### Appearance
This avatar is shown as a three to five meter tall black stone sphinx, with vulture wings, the body of a hyena and a human head devoid of a face. When this being becomes enraged, two eyes of fire appear in the void of his face that usually cause madness to those who look at them.

### Cult
This avatar was revered by a branch of the Brotherhood of the Black Pharaoh. The rituals were performed around large black stone idols erected in the Egyptian desert and representing the Faceless God. Little is known about the kinds of rites they performed, but they probably included human sacrifice. When the celebration was over, the faceless god would reward his devotees by sending them forward or backward in time.

Given the perverse nature of this being, his cult ended up being forbidden and his effigies abandoned in the desert, where they remain buried.

### The Curse of Nyarlathotep
If someone commits the imprudence of unearthing one, the contained fury of the Faceless God will fall upon him and the buried effigies will come to life to start harassing him until he gives up and decides to face his fate. One of the punishments that the Faceless God can inflict on his victims is to bury them and let them be devoured by vultures.

### Trivia
* Many of the nicknames of the Faceless God have been mistakenly interpreted as names of avatars of Nyarlathotep, although in reality they are only other names given to this same being.

shortDefinition: "Fact and Fancy" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. It was first published in The Tryout No. 3 in February 1917.  ### Poem  * How dull the wretch, whose philosophic mind * Disdains the pleasures of fantastic kind; * Whos...
fullContent:
"Fact and Fancy" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. It was first published in The Tryout No. 3 in February 1917.

### Poem

* How dull the wretch, whose philosophic mind
* Disdains the pleasures of fantastic kind;
* Whose prosy thoughts the joys of life exclude,
* And wreck the solace of the poet’s mood!
* Young Zeno, practic’d in the Stoic’s art,
* Rejects the language of the glowing heart;
* Dissolves sweet Nature to a mess of laws;
* Condemns th’ effect whilst looking for the cause;
* Freezes poor Ovid in an ic’d review,
* And sneers because his fables are untrue!
* In search of Truth the hopeful zealot goes,
* But all the sadder tums, the more he knows!
* Stay! vandal sophist, whose deep lore would blast
* The graceful legends of the story’d past;
* Whose tongue in censure flays th’ embellish’d page,
* And scolds the comforts of a dreary age:
* Would’st strip the foliage from the vital bough
* Till all men grow as wisely dull as thou?
* Happy the man whose fresh, untainted eye
* Discerns a Pantheon in the spangled sky;
* Finds Sylphs and Dryads in the waving trees,
* And spies soft Notus in the southern breeze;
* For whom the stream a cheering carol sings,
* While reedy music by the fountain rings;
* To whom the waves a Nereid tale confide
* Till friendly presence fills the rising tide.
* Happy is he, who void of learning’s woes,
* Th’ ethereal life of body’d Nature knows:
* I scorn the sage that tells me it but seems,
* And flout his gravity in sunlit dreams!

"Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family", also known as just "Arthur Jermyn" or "The White Ape", is a short story in the horror fiction genre written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1920, and first published in the amateur press journal The Wolverine in 1921. The themes of the story are tainted ancestry, knowledge that it would be best to remain unaware of, and a reality which human understanding finds intolerable.

### Inspiration
Both of Lovecraft's parents died in a mental hospital, and some writers have seen a concern with having inherited a propensity for physical and mental degeneration reflected in the plot of his stories, especially his 1931 novella, The Shadow Over Innsmouth, which shares some themes with "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family". As in many of his stories, the mind of a narrator deteriorates as his investigations uncover an intolerable reality, a central tenet of Cosmicism which Lovecraft outlines in the opening sentence of "The Call of Cthulhu": "The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents." In a letter, Lovecraft described the impetus behind "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family":

: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)}}

While Lovecraft claimed that he intended to describe the most horrible family shadow, E. F. Bleiler declares that "actually, the story is a metaphor for his extreme bigotry and social snobbery; the motifs of expiating ancestral evil ands committing suicide on discovering 'racial pollution' occur in other of his works." 

### Publishing history and possible influences
The story was first published in the journal The Wolverine in March and June of 1921. To Lovecraft's distaste, the story was retitled "The White Ape" when it appeared in Weird Tales in 1924; he commented: "If I ever entitled a story 'The White Ape', there would be no ape in it". (: Selected Letters 1.160) Subsequent reprintings titled it "Arthur Jermyn" until the corrected publishing in Dagon and Other Macabre Tales in 1986. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

Critic William Fulwiler suggests that the plot of "Arthur Jermyn" may have been inspired by Edgar Rice Burroughs' novels The Return of Tarzan (1913) and Tarzan and the Jewels of Opar (1916), in which the lost city of Opar is "peopled by a hybrid race resulting from the matings of men with apes." E. F. Bleiler, too, has commented that it "undoubtedly owes much to Edgar Rice Burrough's Opar in his Tarzan series".

The story begins by describing the ancestors of Sir Arthur Jermyn, a British nobleman. His great-great-great-grandfather, Sir Wade Jermyn, had been an early explorer of the Congo region, whose books on a mysterious white civilization there had been ridiculed. fullContent:
"Facts in the Case of H. P. Lovecraft" is a short non-fiction piece by author and scholar Barton L. St. Armand.

### Overview
Running to only eight pages in length, "Facts in the Case of H. P. Lovecraft" was published in the S. T. Joshi-edited collection H. P. Lovecraft: Four Decades of Criticism by Ohio University Press in 1980. Its original publication was in the January 1972 issue of the journal Rhode Island History.“A rather unusual assortment of readers may have been stirred by a minor item in The New York Times Book Review, May 17, 1970. Included under the heading of “Revivals” in the “European Notebook” of Mark Slonim, it announced to its American audience that…

   A most striking phenomenon in France, Italy and Spain is the number of translations (mostly very good) of the American science-fiction writer H.P. Lovecraft.  Not only are they widely read in Paris, Rome, and Madrid, but Lovecraft is also hailed by the leading critics as superior to Poe. The Spanish essayist Jose Luis Garcia recently included Lovecraft in a list of 10 best writers of the world, and the French sophisticated periodical L’Herne dedicated a special large issue to the greatest American master of supernatural literature.”Among a lot of disparagement of both Lovecraft and two of the three groups identified as having a reawakened interest in him - fanatical student fans and foreign art critics - the paper acknowledges that Lovecraft's work had a deep if peculiar vitality and energy that had been lacking in fiction after Poe.

The paper is also notable for providing a photo of Lovecraft as a young child.

fullContent:
"Falco Ossifracus: by Mr. Goodguile" is a horror comedy short story by Edith Miniter first published in April 1921 in The Muffin Man. The story is a parody of "The Statement of Randolph Carter" and other tales by H. P. Lovecraft, who was a friend and correspondent of Miniter. Far from being offended by it, he remained on good terms with her for several years afterwards.

"Falco Ossifracus" is the earliest known Lovecraft parody ever published, predating Arthur C. Clarke's "At the Mountains of Murkiness" by almost two decades.

### Synopsis
The story is narrated by Mr. Goodguile (a fictionalized version of Lovecraft), who starts paradoxically enough by denying any knowledge of the events he is about to relate. He also denies the rumour that he and John Smith (his best friend for the past 18 years, known to Goodguile by the fancier name Iacchus Smithsonia) have morbid tastes, despite admitting that they have been frequently seen in graveyards.

One November evening, Goodguile and Smith are visiting a cemetery. Goodguile loses sight of Smith, but thinks little of it, as it is a common occurrence in their adventures. Soon, his attention is caught by an animated skeleton passing by, with blue blood streaming from its nonexistent nose. Goodguile accidentally offends the skeleton by asking about its ribs. A second one appears moaning, which Goodguile acknowledges as another contradiction, given that skeletons have neither lungs nor a windpipe. This second apparition tells him that Smith is cleaning out Tomb 268. Sure enough, Goodguile finds his friend there, wearing pennies over his eyes as he is prone to, while holding the thigh bone of one of his ancestors, surrounded by six grinning wraiths.

Smith urges Goodguile to leave, as this isn't a place for someone with "cold feet" like him. When Goodguile hesitates, Smith makes an undisclosed gesture that causes Goodguile to understand why the second skeleton fled the scene. After that, Goodguile loses track of the many aeons he spent wandering among the graves, before returning to his boarding house in time for breakfast. Inside, he is shocked to find that Smith hasn't returned. Goodguile notices that the napkin is still in the exact same place and position that Smith left it last evening. This realisation makes him so scared that he shivers and knocks down several items over the table. Before he faints, he hears the voice of the landlady explaining Smith's absence: "You fool, he's got indigestion from a supper of Grilled Bones!"

Fall of Cthulhu is a long-running Cthulhu Mythos comic book series written by Michael Alan Nelson. The first issue was published by Boom! Studios in 2007, with the first story arc running for 15 issues, later collected into three volumes. Since then, three four-issue miniseries have been released (Godwar, 2008; Apocalypse, 2009; and Nemesis, 2010); In 2009, a two-part strip set in the universe was published in the anthology series Cthulhu Tales. Additionally, a limited series and ongoing series, both titled Hexed, have been spun off from the original comic. 

In 2015, the complete series was collected into an omnibus edition, although the spin-off series were not included.

### Overview
Fall of Cthulhu tells a tale in which the Outer God Nyarlathotep orchestrates an apocalyptic war between the Elder Gods and Great Old Ones. Many Mythos entities are referenced or make appearances, and the Dreamlands plays a significant role in the storyline.

shortDefinition: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 1: The Fugue is a comic book omnibus collecting the first five issues of Michael Alan Nelson's Cthulhu Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. First published by Boom! Studios in February 2008, both trade paperback and digital editions ...

Fall of Cthulhu Volume 1: The Fugue is a comic book omnibus collecting the first five issues of Michael Alan Nelson's Cthulhu Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. First published by Boom! Studios in February 2008, both trade paperback and digital editions were released.

### Synopsis

### Prologue
In eighth century Damascus, the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred is executed for writing the fabled Al-Azif. In the present day his corpse is retrieved and reanimated by Mr. Arkham.

### Issue 1: "Harlot"
Cy Morgan, a student at Arkham's prestigious Miskatonic University, meets his uncle, who hands him a duffel bag of occult notes and makes him promise to put a stop to an unspecified something before killing himself.

Later that night, Cy unwittingly travels to the Dreamlands where he meets the enigmatic being known as the Harlot, and begins to learn that his uncle may not have been as crazy as he first believed.

The next day, Cy visits his uncle's old apartment - in a boarding house run by Mr. Arkham - and discovers a statue to Cthulhu concealed in the closet.

### Issue 2: "The Black Chorus"
As Cy's relationship with his girlfriend Jordan begins to break down, he discovers a cultist in his uncle's apartment; the man kills himself before providing any answers. Later, a friend whom Cy had tasked with deciphering some of his uncle's notes is found nearly dead with his jaw torn off.

During another trip to the Dreamlands, The Harlot begins to explain the nature of the Cthulhu Cult.

### Issue 3: "The Hunt"
As Cy and Jordan's relationship continues to deteriorate, Mr. Arkham tries to convince him that the recent events are down to the malice of the human spirit rather than anything supernatural.

Back in the Dreamlands, Cy bargains with the Harlot for knowledge; she puts him in touch with a cult to the Elder God Nodens.

### Issue 4: "Lucky"
Nodens' cultists attempt to kill Cy, resulting in a confrontation with some Nightgaunts and a standoff between the Harlot and the Elder God.

Desperate to make things right with Jordan, Cy gifts all of his uncle's belongings to Mr. Arkham, but when he returns home discovers that Jordan has killed herself.

### Issue 5: "The Conductor"
Devastated by the loss of Jordan, Cy comes to the realisation that Mr. Arkham is not who he appears to be, a revelation which drives him to madness and incarceration in a mental health institution. Mr. Arkham subsequently retrieves an artefact required to enact his plan.

As Cy's mind retreats to the Dreamlands, he begs the Harlot for release; she takes his soul and grants him paradise.

shortDefinition: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 2: The Gathering is a comic book omnibus collecting issues 5 - 10 of Michael Alan Nelson's Cthulhu Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. First published by Boom! Studios in July 2008, both trade paperback and digital editions were rel...
fullContent:
Fall of Cthulhu Volume 2: The Gathering is a comic book omnibus collecting issues 5 - 10 of Michael Alan Nelson's Cthulhu Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. First published by Boom! Studios in July 2008, both trade paperback and digital editions were released.

### Synopsis
The overarching plot of this book involves Mr. Arkham gathering the beings known as the Horsemen of Nyarlathotep to his service.

### Part I: "Sysyphyx"
Mr. Arkham's assistant Connor leads an expedition into the Arctic to retrieve a mysterious chest buried in the ice for over a century. Returning it to his master, he lures in an unsuspecting victim before opening the chest; the creature contained within - a creature named Sysyphyx - murders the victim and inhabits her body.

### Part II: "Happy Birthday"
Sysyphyx uses her charms to corrupt the soul of a young boy, turning him increasingly more vicious and sociopathic. Eventually the big kills his father and enters a cocoon-like state, emerging soon after as the monstrous Gnruk of Vol'kunast.

### Part III: "Vessel of Gith"
Connor descends into the Dreamlands where he has his soul removed by a bizarre priest before assuming the role of the Vessel of Gith, killing the creature which previously used that name.

This issue features cameos from both the Harlot and Nemesis.

### Part IV (untitled)
The Masked Mute, a small girl who hides a deadly secret behind her many masks, dances her way through the Dreamlands and into the service of Mr. Arkham.

### Part V (untitled)
After retrieving a jar of a toxic substance received from the old Gardner farmstead, Connor makes a mistake which may cost him his sanity. The four creatures are united in purpose under Mr. Arkham.

fullContent:
Fall of Cthulhu Volume 3: The Gray Man is a comic book omnibus collecting issues 11 to 14 of Michael Alan Nelson's Cthulhu Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. The individual issues were first published by Boom! Studios between March and June 2008, while the collected edition was released in December of that year. Both trade paperback and digital editions were released.

The volume also includes two short Cthulhu Mythos stories, "The Call" by Pete W. Roncoli and "The Rockets' Red Glare" by David C. Roncoli. These stories were the winning entries in a competition run by Boom! Studios.

### Synopsis

### Chapter 1
Young thief Lucifer is arrested in connection with a gruesome double murder. When the real perpetrator, the enigmatic Gray Man, comes in search of her, he slaughters all of the officers at the station, although Lucifer is able to shield herself from him through the use of protective wards.

### Chapter 2
Sheriff Raymond Dirk, who had been investigating the murder during the time of the Gray Man's attack, returns to the station and confronts the creature. Although injured during the ensuing showdown, he is saved by Lucifer's wards.

Later, after breaking the girl out of jail, she begins to tell him the nature of the threat facing Arkham. Under her direction, he enters the Dreamlands and meets with the Harlot.

### Chapter 3
After trading with the Harlot for information on how to save Arkham, Sheriff Dirk returns to the waking world, where he and Lucifer break into the Arkham Boarding House and steal the Gray Man's dagger, which had been in the possession of Mr. Arkham. Despite a run-in with both Mr. Gray and Gnruk, the two make good their escape and set of in search of an artefact with which to defeat their enemy.

### Chapter 4
At the remote hiding place where Lucifer has stashed her secret weapon, she and Sheriff Dirk face off against a group of Cthulhu cultists who have tracked them down. Defeating the cultists, they are confronted by the Gray Man, who retrieves his knife from them, but is subsequently trapped in Lucifer's stolen artefact - one of the Harlot's boxes, from which there is no escape, even for a being of his power.

The story concludes with Lucifer leaving Arkham to prepare for the coming Godwar.

Fall of Cthulhu Volume 4: Godwar is a comic book omnibus collecting issues 1-4 (15-18 in the overall series) of Godwar, a limited-run instalment of Boom! Studios' Fall of Cthulhu series. Written by Michael Alan Nelson and featuring artwork by Mat Santolouco, the individual issues were published between July and October 2008, with the omnibus collection being released in April 2009.

Despite the title of Godwar, the collection focuses on the movement of the main players into the eleventh hour of the preparations, with the beginning of the war left as a cliffhanger.

### Synopsis

### Chapter 1
The Harlot releases Cy Morgan's soul from its box and instructs Lucifer to free him from Arkham hospital, where he has been a patient since shortly after his fiancé Jordan's suicide. Meanwhile, Mr. Arkham has the Horsemen of Nyarlathotep hard at work spreading chaos and devastation across the globe.

### Chapter 2
Lucifer enlists the help of Raymond Dirk, and the group visit Miskatonic University to learn the location of R'lyeh. A confrontation with Mr. Arkham ends with the three falling into his hands, and Sysyphyx assuming the guise of Cy's dead fiancé to ensure his cooperation.

### Chapter 3
The madness infecting the world increases as various Cthulhu cults add their own brand of violence, while Mr. Arkham tortures Lucifer and Dirk for his own amusement. Later, Arkham takes the entire group to the recently arisen R'lyeh, where Abdul Alhazred begins the rituals of summoning.

### Chapter 4
Alhazred offers a potted history of the activities of Cthulhu cults across the globe and throughout human history. Nyarlathotep and Nodens come face-to-face on R'lyeh as Cthulhu begins to rise from his sleep.

fullContent:
Fall of Cthulhu Volume 5: Apocalypse is a comic book omnibus collecting issues 1-4 (19-22 in the overall series) of Apocalypse, a limited-run instalment of Boom! Studios' Fall of Cthulhu Mythos series. Written by Michael Alan Nelson and featuring artwork by Mateus Santolouco, the individual issues were first published between November 2008 and February 2009, with the collection being released in March 2010. Both physical and digital editions were issued.

Apocalypse marks the conclusion of the main story arc of Fall of Cthulhu, although a prequel of sorts, Nemesis, was later released, along with two spin-off series focusing on the character of Lucifer, both titled Hexed.

### Synopsis

### Chapter 1
As the world descends into chaos, Lucifer, Raymond Dirk and Cy Morgan attempt to find a way to sink R'lyeh. Cthulhu begins to emerge from beneath the waves and Nyarlathotep and Nodens do battle in the risen city. The Harlot emerges through the portal into the waking world.

### Chapter 2
Dirk defeats Sysyphyx while Lucifer manages to wrest the Al-Azif from Abdul Alhazred. Nodens weakens beneath Nyarlathotep's onslaught. Under Nyarlathotep's orders, Morgan travels through the dimensional rift to the Court of Azathoth.

### Chapter 3
Lucifer defeats the Masked Mute, and Dirk kills Gnruk before it can attack her. Nodens falls to Nyarlathotep. Lucifer and Dirk use the Al-Azif to send R'lyeh back beneath the waves, while the Harlot raises her army of lost souls to face down Nyarlathotep.

### Chapter 4
Abdul Alhazred witnesses the final stages of the war from a sinking R'lyeh, while the Harlot and Nyarlathotep do battle. As ordered by the Harlot, Morgan signs Nyarlathotep's name in Azathoth's book instead of his own, ending his plans for Earth. 

In the aftermath, the Harlot reveals to Lucifer the true puppet master: a small girl dressed in yellow, who is heavily implied to be Hastur. The Harlot has the girl mark Lucifer as the successor as lord of the Dreamlands.

Fall of Cthulhu Volume 6: Nemesis is a comic book omnibus collecting issues 1-4 of Michael Alan Nelson's Nemesis arc from Boom! Studios' Fall of Cthulhu series. It was originally published between March and July 2009, and later collected as a graphic novel in November of that year.

Despite being billed as the conclusion to Fall of Cthulhu, the story has virtually nothing to do with the main series, being instead a character exploration of Mr. Arkham's pet cat Nemesis, a character who played almost no part in the original run.

### Synopsis
In ancient Atlantis, King Levin is being slowly driven to insanity by the presence of a cult to Nyarlathotep in his capital city, an event which he believes to be linked to a prophecy regarding the downfall of civilisation. Entrusting the destruction of his cult to his brother, the D'harin or high priest of Atlantis, he simultaneously embarks upon a war with the people of Athens.

As events progress, the D'harin comes to realise the true mental state of his brother, and consults the Oracle, a creature known as Sysyphyx, who tells him of his destiny: to be the last Atlantean, and become as a god. This inspires him to plot against the king, and after much scheming the D'harin overthrows his brother, throwing him to the baying crowd to be torn to pieces.

However, the D'harin had underestimated the power of Nyarlathotep's cult, and had been deceived by the Outer God, who had manifested personally in order to oversee the destruction of Atlantis for his own amusement. As he summons an enormous tentacled sea creature (implied to be Cthulhu) to sink the once-mighty continent, he transforms the D'harin, now the last of his people, into an immortal cat, stating that this makes him as a god.

"Family Snapshots" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American authors Ron Shiflet and Peter A. Worthy. It was published in the first (and only) issue of short-lived fanzine In Lovecraft's Shadow, also edited by Shiflet, by Tenoka Press in March 2007.

### Synopsis
An impoverished and petty-minded art collector named Jared Whalmsey manages, after much hard work, to get his hands upon the last painting by vanished artist Richard Upton Pickman, a virtually unheard-of piece titled Taking Communion. The picture depicts a priest strung up in his own church, being drained of his blood before a pack of hungry ghouls.

Later that night, Pickman and his pack break into Whalmsey's home to reclaim Taking Communion. As the story concludes, the old collector begins to realise that he is to suffer the same fate as the priest in the painting…

fullContent:
"Family Tradition" is a short Mythos story by American author Edward Morris.

### Synopsis
Denny Whateley visits Frank Nardi and relates the story of how his family raised his younger brother, a creature created through an unholy union with a dark god. Unfortunately, Junior has escaped and Whateley asks for the assistance of the Arkham Detective Agency. The story ends with the investigators preparing to put a stop to Junior's dark magic.

### Characters

*Mark Berkenwald, a former NYPD detective-turned-private investigator.
*Dennis W. "Denny" Whateley, a Dunwich resident who has had prior contact with Frank Nardi.
*Frank Nardi, one of Berkenwald's business partners, also a PI.
*Johnny Thunstone, an Arkham Detective Agency employee.
*Galtoni, another partner in the Agency.

### Behind the Mythos
"Family Tradition" was written by Edward Morris after a request by Brian M. Sammons for pieces centred around C. J. Henderson's Arkham Detective Agency. It was published in the collection Arkham Detective Agency by Dark Regions Press in November 2017.

### Mythos Connections

*The Arkham Detective Agency offices in which the story is set are based in Arkham, Massachusetts.
*The events related in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Horror at Red Hook" are briefly recalled by Berkenwald.
*Both the Whateley family and Dunwich were created by Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror."
*Denny Whateley makes mention of Olaus Wormius, a translator of the Necronomicon, De Vermis Mysteriis, a tome of ancient knowledge, and both R'lyeh and Ktulu-ili-mo'ku.

### Trivia

*The story which Denny Whateley relates is a partial rewrite of Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror."
*The story mentions Tony Balnco and Madame Renee, a deceased partner in the Agency and its psychic consultant, respectively.

fullContent:
Fanciful Tales of Time and Space was is a one-off magazine published by Wilson Shepherd and Donald A. Wollheim in the fall of 1936. The venture folded due to lack of financial backing. It features stories by H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth amongst others. Wollheim was the driving force behind it but he ran out of money after only one issue and parted ways from Shepherd and the latter's publishing company.

In some respects this was an early version of Lin Carter's much later Kadath offering in that it was more professional than a fanzine but nowhere near the level of finish of Weird Tales. It is sometimes described as a "semi-pro" zine or simply a failed magazine.

The cover illustration was by Clay Ferguson, Jr.

### Contents
* Page 2: A Word from the Editor by Donald A. Wollheim
* Page 3: "The Nameless City" by H. P. Lovecraft
* Page 3: "The Nameless City" interior artwork by Duane W. Rimel
* Page 19: "Umbriel" by Donald A. Wollheim
* Page 21: "The Forbidden Room" by Duane W. Rimel
* Page 21: "The Forbidden Room" interior artwork by Duane W. Rimel
* Page 26: "Solomon Kane's Homecoming" by Robert E. Howard
* Page 28: "The Typewriter" by David H. Keller, M.D.
* Page 34: "The Man from Dark Valley" - by August W. Derleth
* Page 39: "The Globe" by William S. Sykora
* Page 40: "The Globe" interior artwork by Duane W. Rimel
* Page 41: "The Electric World" by Kenneth B. Pritchard
* Page 45: "Fanciful Tales of Time and Space" interior artwork by Duane W. Rimel

### Further Publication
A fascimile edition was privately printed in 1977. Its circulation of 750 numbered copies was over double that of the original semi-pro zine.

shortDefinition: "Fane of the Black Pharaoh" is a short story by Robert Bloch that appeared in the December 1937 issue of Weird Tales. One of Bloch's Egyptian tales, it elaborates on the hints dropped in H. P. Lovecraft's fiction about the Black Pharaoh Nephren-Ka.  ...
fullContent:
"Fane of the Black Pharaoh" is a short story by Robert Bloch that appeared in the December 1937 issue of Weird Tales. One of Bloch's Egyptian tales, it elaborates on the hints dropped in H. P. Lovecraft's fiction about the Black Pharaoh Nephren-Ka.

### Synopsis
The story focuses on Captain Carteret, an archaeologist who is given a chance by a mysterious Egyptian stranger to see the legendary temple-tomb of Nephren-Ka, which has been hidden for thousands of years below the surface of what is now Cairo. 

Nephren-Ka, according to the story, wasthe last and greatest of that Egyptian cult of priest-sorcerers.... The tale goes that Nephren-Ka, on the throne, renounced all religion save that of Nyarlathotep. He sought the power of prophecy, and built temples to the Blind Ape of Truth. His utterly atrocious sacrifices at length provoked a revolt, and it is said that the infamous Pharaoh was at last dethroned. According to this account, the new ruler and his people immediately destroyed all vestiges of the former reign, demolished all temples and idols of Nyarlathotep, and drove out the wicked priests who prostituted their faith to the carnivorous Bubastis, Anubis, and Sebek. The Book of the Dead was then amended so that all references to the Pharaoh Nephren-Ka and his accursed cults were deleted. The story further cites the Saracenic Rituals chapter of Ludvig Prinn's De Vermis Mysteriis, which says of Nephren-Ka thatbefore he died down in the darkness, he conjured up the earthly image of Nyarlathotep in a final gigantic sacrifice; and that the god granted him his desires. Nephren-Ka had stood before the images of the Blind Ape of Truth and received the gift of divination over the 
gory bodies of a hundred willing victims. Then, in nightmare manner, Prinn recounts that the entombed Pharaoh wandered among his dead companions and inscribed on the twisted walls of his tomb the secrets of the future. In pictures and ideographs he wrote the history of days to come, revelling in omniscient knowledge till the end.

### Publication History
After its appearance in Weird Tales, "Fane of the Black Pharaoh" was reprinted in Avon Fantasy Reader No. 5 (1947). It was included in the original Mysteries of the Worm (Zebra, 1981) and both subsequent editions (Chaosium, 1993, 2009). It was featured in both Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos (Fedogan & Bremer, 1992) and The Nyarlathotep Cycle: The God of a Thousand Forms (Chaosium, 1997).

It was translated into French as "Le sanctuaire du pharaon noir", published in L'embarquement pour Arkham (1994), the French edition of Mysteries of the Worm.
