Fantasica is a Japanese mobile game developed by Silicon Studio and published by MyNet in June 2012, before ultimately ending its service in March 2019. The gameplay combines elements of CCG, RPG, and tower defense adventure games, featuring the player taking on the role of a hero using a collection of illustrated cards that gives him power, in order to defeat his enemies and complete various quests. The combat is based on using strategy carried out in real time. 

The game features over 200 quests to improve the player's skills, as well as receiving rewards including gold, new cards and event items. It also includes a social component, which allows the player to ally with their friends, or compete with them in battle. 

Relevant to this wiki, several of the cards are based on familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos.

shortDefinition: Fantasy Flight Games, usually abbreviated to simply FFG, is a relatively new games developer and publisher from the United States whose primary interest to this wiki is their Arkham Horror Files line of products, which deal with games and fiction rel...
fullContent:
Fantasy Flight Games, usually abbreviated to simply FFG, is a relatively new games developer and publisher from the United States whose primary interest to this wiki is their Arkham Horror Files line of products, which deal with games and fiction related to H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
Founded in 1995 by CEO Christian T. Petersen, Fantasy Flight enjoyed a swift rise to prominence primarily through its releases of popular board games. In 2004 however, they secured the publication rights for a re-release of the 1987 game of Lovecraftian monster-hunting Arkham Horror, which underwent a major overhaul before being released. 

Due to the major success of Arkham Horror, since that time, Fantasy Flight have expanded the scope of their Mythos products to include more board games set in the universe, Living Card Games, dice-and-card based cooperative strategy games, a range of miniatures to replace the cardboard counters included in their board games, and a series of novels centered on some of the characters featured in their other products. These have all been released under their Arkham Horror Files label.

### List of Arkham Horror Files Products
*Arkham Horror: A board game set in Arkham, Massachusetts, where the players must stop the evil forces of the Ancient Ones from awakening and destroying the world.
*Arkham Horror: The Card Game: A Living Card Game inspired by Arkham Horror, replacing Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.
*Mansions of Madness: A board game wherein a small group of investigators uncover the dark secrets of an eerie old house.
*Eldritch Horror: A streamlined version of Arkham Horror whose events are set on a global scale.
*Arkham Horror Fiction: a series of novelisations designed to expand on the events featured in Fantasy Flight's other games.
*Elder Sign and Elder Sign: Omens: Dice-and-cards game set in the Arkham universe, with Omens being the App version of the game.
*The Investigators of Arkham Horror: A collection of stories to give some flavour to the characters featured in-game.
* Arkham Horror Premium Figures: Pre-painted miniatures to replace the games cardboard counters with three-dimensional models. Now discontinued.
*Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game: Another Living Card Game set in the Mythos universe. Now discontinued and replaced by Arkham Horror: The Card Game.
*Arkham Horror: Final Hour: A board game involving an incursion of monstrous beasts in Miskatonic University.
*Unfathomable: A betrayal-style board game set aboard a luxury steamer beset by Deep Ones.

fullContent:
Fanucci Editore is an Italian publishing house based in Rome which specialises in genre fiction, particularly science fiction, fantasy, and horror. Founded in 1971 by Renato Fanucci, the company operated under his direction until his death in 1990, when operations were taken over by his son Sergio.

Between 1985 and 1991, Fanucci published a 38-volume series of books titled I Miti di Cthulhu, or The Myth of Cthulhu, which consisted mostly of anthologies translating English-language works with scattering of original stories. Despite the title of the series, not all of these books were Mythos-related, or even Lovecraftian, in theme, with some instead focusing on a particular horror topic, such as werewolves.

Starting in 1994, the company began releasing Italian translations of tie-in novels for the wildly popular The X-Files supernatural science fiction franchise.

shortDefinition: "Far Below" is a short story by the late American author Robert Barbour Johnson.  ### Synopsis A man relates the history of a covert war waged in the New York subway tunnels between an elite division of law enforcement and the flesh-eating ghouls whi...
fullContent:
"Far Below" is a short story by the late American author Robert Barbour Johnson.

### Synopsis
A man relates the history of a covert war waged in the New York subway tunnels between an elite division of law enforcement and the flesh-eating ghouls which burrow their way up from the depths. The conclusion of the story reveals that the man, and all those who work in the division, is slowly devolving into one of the creatures due to a supernatural aura which seems to infect those in proximity to them.

### Characters
*Professor Gordon Craig, a former primatologist and head of the Special Subway Division for 25 years.

### Publication History
"Far Below" was first published in the June-July 1939 issue of Weird Tales, and has since been reprinted numerous times.

### Mythos Connections
*Gordon refers to the stretch of subway haunted by the ghouls as a "mad Nyarlathotep-world".
*Gordon also tells of how he learned much from H. P. Lovecraft, and vice versa, implying that this fictionalised version of Lovecraft had somehow come into possession of knowledge on the subject.

### Possible Inspiration
A possible inspiration for the story is an image described in "Pickman's Model", painted by the titular character. This image shows a pack of ghouls attacking a subway station: a similar event happens in "Far Below" when the survivors of a train crash are fed upon by a number of the beasts.

### Adaptations
"Far Below" was loosely adapted as an episode of the anthology TV series Monsters, which aired in 1990. The episode was written by Michael McDowell and directed by Debra Hill. It was one of two Mythos stories adapted for the series, the other being "The Space-Eaters".

fullContent:
The Far Realm is a Lovecraftian-like eldritch dimension from the fictional universe of the Dungeons & Dragons pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Wizards of the Coast.

### Background
The Far Realm is a plane of madness, which is very far from the material plane. Which consists of an infinite number of layers of finite size. Layers that are very thin from a mile in thickness at most to an inch at the thinnest, with 10 ft separating each layer. Which are transparent and highly morphic. Entities and landmarks within the Far Realm are multidimensional, simultaneously existing on multiple layers at once.

It's a plane with forests of tentacles vegetation, viscously syrup-like air, drifting colossal multi-layer beings with the smallest being city-sized, falling globes that burst releasing horse-sized ticks, rivers of mikly white fluids, etc. Neither time or gravity exists in the Far Realm. Inhabited by a number of species including Aboleth, Illithid, Beholder, kaorti, and carrion crawlers. Many Aberrations are also created here. Visitors usually go mad and all are twisted into gruesome creatures. It threatens all of the realities in the Multiverse. The rulers of the Far Realm are the Uvuudaums, whose very presence would make most creatures insane.

shortDefinition: Farnsworth Wright (1888-1940) was the editor of the pulp magazine Weird Tales during the magazine's heyday.  Wright, a veteran of World War I, was working as a music critic for the Chicago Herald and Examiner when he began his association with Weird ...
fullContent:
Farnsworth Wright (1888-1940) was the editor of the pulp magazine Weird Tales during the magazine's heyday.

Wright, a veteran of World War I, was working as a music critic for the Chicago Herald and Examiner when he began his association with Weird Tales, founded in 1923. At first serving as chief manuscript reader, he replaced founding editor Edwin Baird in 1924 when the latter was fired by publisher J. C. Henneberger.

Wright's editorship of the magazine, which lasted until 1940, is considered the magazine's golden age, when it was regularly publishing such authors as H. P. Lovecraft, Robert E. Howard and Clark Ashton Smith. Yet Wright had a strained relationship with all three writers, rejecting major works by them such as Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness and The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Howard's "The Frost Giant's Daughter" and Smith's "The Seven Geases" (which Wright dismissed as just "one geas after another").


Wright (nicknamed "Plato" by his writers) was also noteworthy for starting the commercial careers of three important fantasy artists: Margaret Brundage, Virgil Finlay, and Hannes Bok. Each of the three made their first sale to, and had their work first appear in, Weird Tales.

Robert Bloch, who wrote frequently for Wright, recalled him as a tall thin man with a small, thin voice. The latter, together with a persistent palsy, was probably due to the effects of Parkinson's disease, an affliction which had plagued him since wartime military service. An authority on Shakespeare and a former music critic, this soft-spoken, balding, prematurely aged man seemed miscast as editor of a publication featuring bimbos uncovered on its covers and horrors concealed within its pages.Wright developed Parkinson's disease in 1921; by 1930, he was unable to sign his own letters. His failing health forced him to step down as editor in 1940, and he died later that year.

### Wright and Lovecraft
While Wright's predecessor, Edwin Baird, had published everything Lovecraft had submitted, Wright was more particular; his  rejection of "The Shunned House" was the first the writer had received from the magazine. "Wright tended to accept HPL's more conventional tales and to reject his more aesthetically challenging ones," An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia notes. After the necrophilia of "The Loved Dead" almost got the magazine banned in Indiana, Wright was reluctant to publish work from Lovecraft that he considered too gruesome, turning down "In the Vault" and "Cool Air" for that reason. Sometimes Wright would initially reject stories and then reconsider, as he did with "The Call of Cthulhu" and "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".

Lovecraft was particularly rankled by Wright's turning down At the Mountains of Madness, a story he was particularly proud of. For the next five years, Lovecraft submitted only one story to Wright--"In the Vault", which was rejected; when August Derleth showed The Shadow over Innsmouth and "Dreams in the Witch-House" to Wright

"Faster, Vampussy … Kill, Kill!" Is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Alex S. Johnson. It was published in the Roger Cowin/James Ward Kirk thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
A private detective with a Miskatonic University degree in Occult Arts is hired by a femme fatale who has inadvertently drawn the attentions of malevolent supernatural entities. Tracking down a copy of the Necronomicon, they attempt to conduct a ritual which will throw the creatures off her trail, but they are too late; the woman is killed by the creatures and her contractor gives up the life of a PI.

fullContent:
"Fat Face" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
A working girl in Los Angeles, California harbours a fantasy about the strange occupant of the building opposite the hotel from which she plies her trade. As bizarre and horrific events occur all around her, she plucks up her courage to fulfil her desire, but the man is harbouring a dark secret: he is in fact the head of an enclave of evolved Shoggoths who have been preying on the strays of the city, both animal and human.

### Characters
*Patti, a Californian sex worker lacking meaning in her life.
*Sheri, Patti's best friend, also a prostitute.
*Fat Face, a Shoggoth capable of mimicking the human form in order to blend in.
*Arnold, a street vendor who may or may not be one of Fat Face's clan.

### Publication History
"Fat Face" was first published as a chapbook by Axolotl Press in 1987. It appeared in The Year's Best Horror Stories: XVI (DAW Books, 1988) and The Year's Best Fantasy: First Annual Collection (St. Martin's Press, 1988). It was included in Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology (Arkham House, 1995) and The Book of Cthulhu (Night Shade Books, 2011). It appears in Shea's collections The Autopsy and Other Tales (Centipede Press, 2008), Copping Squid and Other Mythos Tales (Perilous Press, 2009), and Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea (Dark Regions Press, 2017). It has been translated into Dutch, German, and Finnish.

### Trivia
*The Shoggoths in "Fat Face" were later developed into a sub-species of monsters dubbed Shoggoth Lords for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.(which book?)

fullContent:
Fate of Cthulhu is a Cthulhu Mythos roleplaying game which was published by Evil Hat Productions in 2019. It utilises the system-agnostic Fate roleplaying ruleset, which emphasises roleplaying over rolling dice.

### Premise
Fate of Cthulhu involves players taking the roles of characters from the present day as well as time travellers from the future who have lived through the awakening of the old gods. Forewarned and forearmed against the coming apocalypse, they must make a stand and attempt to avert the horrors which are about to befall the human race.

### Publication
Fate of Cthulhu was launched with the core rulebook after a successful Kickstarter campaign in 2020; of a $20,000 goal, a total of $93,894 was pledged. Since its inception, numerous supplements have been released (see "Supplements" below).

### Supplements
The supplements released each introduced a separate future timeline for the investigators to prepare against, most of them involving the coming of a different old one. These include: 
*The Rise of Azathoth (2021)
*The Rise of Hastur (2021)
*The Rise of the Basilisk (2021)
*The Rise of the Quiet (2021)
*The Rise of Yig (2021)
*The Rise of Yog-Sothoth (2021)
*The Zombie Apocalypse (2022)
*The Ascellan Conspiracy (2023)
*The Rise of Tsathoggua (2024)

### Behind the Scenes
On 17 January 2020, Evil Hat Productions caused controversy after posting a page from the Fate of Cthulhu core rulebook stating the design team's stance on H. P. Lovecraft's racial views; this sparked an online debate - which included input from the Evil Hat publicity team - which became increasingly hostile on all sides before subsiding.

Father Michael is a fictional character who appears in several of Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files series of Cthulhu Mythos-related games and fiction. He is the pastor at Arkham's South Church, and works alongside investigator character Sister Mary.

### Arkham Horror
Father Michael first appeared as a Blight card in the Arkham Horror Second Edition expansion set The King in Yellow, although he was mentioned on Sister Mary's Investigator card from the Core Set.

### Ire of the Void
In the novella by Richard Lee Byers, Father Michael made a brief appearance when the protagonists, Professors Norman Withers and Claus Schmidt, visited South Church as part of their research.

### Trivia
* Father Michael holds meetings of the Arkham Chapter of the teetotaller organisation named the Lincoln-Lee Legion at South Church. This is possibly a nod to H. P. Lovecraft's own abstinence from drink.

The Father-of-All-Sharks is an avatar of Cthulhu created by Bruce L. Priddy for the 2006 edition of Malleus Monstrorum, a monster manual supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror role-playing game. Priddy created the creature as part of a competition run by Chaosium, with the top three entries being included in the book; the Father-of-All-Sharks came in second place.

### Description
The Father-of-All-Sharks manifests as a colossal glowing white shark resembling the ancient extinct species Megalodon, but twice the size. It has been theorized to have been the inspiration for the biblical Leviathan.

The Deep Ones know the correct rituals required to summon the Father-of-All-Sharks, but are wary of doing to, as their mystical skill does not include the knowledge on how to control the being once it has manifested: thus, they only ever resort to deploying the creature during the direst of circumstances, such as when one of their cities is under threat, or some terrible transgression must be punished.

### Worship
The Deep Ones are known to worship the Father-of-All-Sharks, and some other non-human species are believed to do so as well. It has no human cult as such, although various Polynesian and Hawaiian islanders venerate the creature, having made sacrifices to it in the past in hopes of appeasing the beast and avoiding its terrible attentions.

Fauns are a liminal species originating from Greek and Roman mythology, in which they are portrayed as playful creatures of the woods, with the upper body of a human and the lower body of goat, as well as goatish ears and horns.

### In the Mythos
Fauns and Satyrs are associates of the god Pan and the rest of the Greek pantheon. When Hermes appeared to a young woman named Marcia to tell her of the incoming return of the Greek deities, he mentioned that Pan is currently sleeping, but "wishful to wake and behold about him the little rose-crowned fauns and the antique Satyrs". Later, Zeus himself tells Marcia that when the gods return, "Fauns and Dryads shall haunt their accustomed groves in beauty". (: "Poetry and the Gods")

In ancient Arcadia, the sculptor Kalos would often spend the nights in the woods of Mount Maenalus conversing with Fauns and Dryads, which provided inspiration for his art. (: "The Tree")

Prior to his correspondence with Henry Wentworth Akeley, the folklorist Albert Wilmarth dismissed reports about alien creatures in the Vermont woods as being comparable to "those universal legends of natural personification which filled the ancient world with fauns and dryads and satyrs, suggested the kallikanzarai of modern Greece, and gave to wild Wales and Ireland their dark hints of strange, small, and terrible hidden races of troglodytes and burrowers". (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

"Fear and Loathing in Innsmouth: Richard Nixon's Revenge" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jason Andrew.

### Synopsis
While on the trail of a story which he hopes will derail Richard Nixon's presidential re-election campaign, journalist Hunter uncovers a plot by Innsmouth's Esoteric Order of Dagon, led by one Ephraim Waite, to call forth Mother Hydra and Father Dagon. Fortunately, a call to the police claiming the cult is involved in the illegal narcotics trade saves Hunter and his companion, but they are left in no doubt that continuing to investigate will result in their brutal deaths.

### Characters
*Hunter, an investigative journalist.
*Rooster Brown, a violent Hell's Angel.
*Ephraim Waite, leader of the Esoteric Order of Dagon.

### Publication History
"Fear and Loathing in Innsmouth: Richard Nixon's Revenge" was published in the Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in 2013.

### Trivia
*The journalist Hunter is likely intended to be Hunter S. Thompson, a counterculture journalist prominent in the 1960s and 70s. Jason Andrew had previously written a story about this fictionalised version of Thompson in which he encountered Dracula.
*Several surnames associated with the Mythos are used in the story, including Marsh, Akeley and the aforementioned Waite.

"Fear of the Knight" is a short story by author Carl Fox, first published in the Rogue Planet Press anthology Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights in 2017.

### Synopsis
A recluse offers hospitality to a knight of an ancient order who is on his way to a gathering of his peers. When, shortly after, the knight returns horribly aged and disfigured, he recounts the story of a disastrous encounter with the disciples of Cthulhu, and how he barely escaped with his life.

The story concludes with the knight passing and the hermit becoming aware that the cultists of Cthulhu are now watching him. Writing down the knight's tale, his existence passes from recorded history.

fullContent:
"Feast with a Few Strangers" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author and editor Edward P. Berglund. It was first published in the Fred C. Adams-edited chapbook anthology Spoor Anthology by Fort Necessity Press in 1974.

### Synopsis
Writer George Drury, seeking inspiration for his works in a decaying old graveyard, encounters a trio of hobos who invite him to dine with them before regaling him with tales of their encounters with the supernatural. As the last one finishes his story, the three men begin to change into horrific monsters, and reveal that, rather than joining them for a meal, Drury is to be their supper for the evening.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite being encountered in a graveyard and consuming human flesh, the creatures which the three men transform into do not resemble the common depiction of ghouls, being described thusly: "Their beards were gone. In fact, there was no hair anywhere on their faces, not even eyebrows or eyelashes. The skin of their faces looked sort of rubbery, as if it just hung on their skulls". Further, "their teeth … had been sharpened to razor-sharp points".

### Mythos Connections
One of the men mentions that if Drury was one of their kind, he "would have to give a blessing to Mordiggian before the meal".

### Publication History
Since its first appearance in Spoor Anthology, "Feast with a Few Strangers" a slightly altered version was also included in the first issue of abortive Cthulhu Mythos zine In Lovecraft's Shadow, edited by Ron Shiflet and published by Tenoka Press in March 2007.

Fedogan & Bremer is a publishing house specializing in weird fiction based in Minneapolis, Minnesota. It has published many titles related to the Cthulhu Mythos and Lovecraftian fiction.

Founded by by Philip Rahman and Dennis Weiler, the company takes its name from the two partners' college nicknames.

Launched in 1987, the house's first offering was an audio cassette of H. P. Lovecraft's poem Fungi From Yuggoth read by actor John Arthur.

The house won a special World Fantasy Award for non-professional book publishing in 1998.

The Feeders from Within were the titular creatures from the 2013 novel Feeders from Within by Peter J. Evans.

### Description
What the Feeders actually looked like is unknown, but they were stated to be parasitic entities which caused a slow, painful death in their host creature over a period of months, all the while broadcasting infectious thoughts of psychic insanity to others in the vicinity. They may have been servants of the Great Old One Tsathoggua, as they were said to dwell with him in N'kai.

### Feeders from Within ()
As part of an unspecified plot, alien Mi-Go Mr. Stone and a number of Silver Twilight Lodge members travelled to N'kai with the intent of "harvesting" the Feeders from Within. The group were foiled by the combined efforts of Mark Harrigan, Diana Stanley and Carolyn Fern.

Feeders from Within is a novel set within the fictional Cthulhu Mythos. It was written by Peter J. Evans and published by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Fiction line. The story features several characters from Fantasy Flight's associated games and fiction.

### Synopsis
### Prologue
Mark Harrigan, a soldier in the United States Army, is sent with a detachment of troops to Mexico to hunt down the Villistas, a group of Mexican revolutionaries. His squad is separated from the main group and, pursued by a large group of Villistas, discovers a cave inside which are a group of Mi-Go working on a strange machine. The Mi-Go attack, but the squad are able to destroy the machine and apparently dispatch all of the Mi-Go; however, in the fight all but two of the squad - Harrigan and a man named Farrow - are killed. The pair subsequently escape.

### Main Story
Years later, psychiatrist Carolyn Fern travels to Arkham in search of information about one of her former patients (Farrow) who was apparently murdered after leaving her care. Meeting with Dr. Hardstrom, the head of Arkham Asylum, she is given access to Farrow's medical reports, where she discovers that he had been having disturbing dreams about strange creatures coming for him.

At the same time, businesswoman Diana Stanley, who had over the past several months become unintentionally involved with a bizarre cult named the Silver Twilight Lodge, visits the police department in an effort to expose their sickening and highly-illegal blood rituals. Realising that the police were implicit in the cult's activities, she attempts to flee Arkham, but is kidnapped by one of the cult's henchmen and taken to see Phillip Avery, a priest in the Lodge. Confronted by Avery and a Mi-Go dubbed Mr. Stone, Diana is shot and falls into the Miskatonic River.

The following morning, Carolyn returns to Arkham Asylum in order to obtain more information, and while there Diana is brought in, hysterical and bleeding, having been fished from the river. Fern manages to calm her down and gain some information about the monster which attacked her.

Over the course of the next few days, Carolyn tracks down Harrigan who agrees to meet her in Arkham. The two visit Diana who has since become catatonic. Later that night, Diana disappears. Harrigan decides to look for answers from Phillip Avery, while Carolyn visits Miskatonic University's Orne Library to find out more on the monsters.

While looking for Avery, Harrigan is accosted by a pair of Byakhee who carry him off to Avery and Mr. Stone. Avery reveals that he is actually Sergeant Johnathan Orton, one of Harrigan's old squad thought dead but reconstructed by Mr. Stone. Mr. Stone extracts shards of the machine left embedded in Harrigan's leg from the encounter in Mexico, but Harrigan is saved by the appearance of Diana who had fled the hospital after undergoing a radical personality change. The pair escape Avery's goons and kill the two Byakhee.

The Fendahl is an extraterrestrial entity in the continuity of the Doctor Who television series and related media. It was part of an entire species known as the Fendahleens, but is now the last of its immensely powerful kind. It originated on a planet that has long since been destroyed, leaving behind the Solar System's Asteroid Belt as its only remnant. The Fendahl is introduced in a Doctor Who story entitled, appropriately, Image of the Fendahl.

According to Chaosium, the Fendahl and Fendahleens are not part of the Cthulhu Mythos themselves but can easily be used in the setting. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Overview
Palaeontologists uncovered a 12-million-year-old human skull, which when X-rayed revealed a pentagram in the bone of the scalp. This impossibly ancient skull was psychic, and a focus for a horrific godlike alien creature known as the Fendahl. The Fendahl is an entity so terrible that it used to give the Doctor nightmares. 

The Doctor’s people, the Time Lords, believed that they had sealed the Fendahl away aeons ago by trapping its world in a time-loop, but the creature sent this skull to Earth and through its malign influence guided the whole of human evolution in order to bring about its return. This it eventually did with the usual repertoire of possessions, cultists, human sacrifice at pagan altars, pentagrams and its tentacular slug-like servitor race, the Fendahleen. The Fendahleen phase into existence as the Fendahl increases in power in a manner similar to the way interphased creatures appear and affect the physical world in the H. P. Lovecraft story "From Beyond." Thirteen physically separate organisms made up the Fendahl, twelve Fendahleen and the core. Additionally, a High Priestess of the Fendahleen would merge with them to complete the Fendahl creature.

Fendahls are psychevores, meaning they fed on psychic energy. The Fendahl could drain all the spectrum of energy from their prey, effectively sucking out their souls. Even the skull nicknamed Eustace, the fossil remnants of a Fendahl core twelve million years dead, had the power to drain the life force of the Fourth Doctor. The core could create Fendahleens from living beings with the correct genetic inheritance and in some cases could create the Fendahleens out of pure energy. If the core was destroyed, the Fendahl was killed. 

All of the parts of the Fendahl could telekinetically control people, but the core had many more psychic powers such as mind control and astral projection.

Fenric is a fictional cosmic entity created by the BBC for the Doctor Who franchise. The Doctor has described it as a force of evil that was present at the birth of the universe, before space, time and matter were formed (: The Curse of Fenric). He later identified it as one of the Great Old Ones, and another name for Hastur. (: All-Consuming Fire)

### Description
As one of the most powerful creatures ever featured in Doctor Who, Fenric's powers are immense; it can manipulate time and space so as to "cause things to happen" i.e. manipulate history, it can bring mortal beings (for example the Haemovores) from their native time period to its physical location when it has manifested an avatar, and it can kill with a touch. Individuals who are possessed by Fenric can appear with glowing yellow eyes.

Fenric is obsessed with strategy and with chess in all its variants in particular. Once engaged in a game of chess it will not be free to act with full power until it wins the game (or is defeated).

The Fenris Wolf (also known as Fenrir) is a giant wolf deity from Norse mythology. It was first mentioned in the anonymous narrative poem collection Poetic Edda, which describes the entity as the one destined to kill the god Odin during Ragnarök. The Marvel Comics incarnation was created in 1965 by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby, making its first appearance in Journey into Mystery Vol 1 #114.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The 17th century Danish sorcerer Axel Holm learned about "Loki the Sly One and the accursed Fenris-Wolf" in his occult studies. (: "The Trap")

### In the Marvel Multiverse
The Fenris Wolf is a descendant of the Elder God Set and the offspring of Set's great granddaughter, the giantess Angerboda, after she mated with the Asgardian god Loki.

It is an Asgardian Wolf God, approximately 15 ft tall, which has the intelligence of a human and is capable of shapeshifting, to a large-sized wolf or a wolf-like humanoid. It also possesses god-like strength, speed and regenerative abilities.

### In Other Media
In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, Mh'ithrha has some resemblance to the Fenris Wolf. (: Unseen Masters) 

The cosmic entity Fenric, from the science fiction series Doctor Who, was inspired by the Fenris Wolf legend. According to the Doctor, the entity truly has no name, but the name "Fenric" was attributed to it by the Vikings. Its followers are known as the Wolves of Fenric (: The Curse of Fenric). In the Doctor Who expanded universe, this entity is equated with Hastur the Unspeakable, who is one of the Great Old Ones. (: All-Consuming Fire)

Dr. Ferdinand Ashley is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1936 novella The Shadow Out of Time, and also featured in "The Horror in the Gallery", by Lin Carter. In both tales, he has a minor role.

### Biography
Dr. Ferdinand C. Ashley works at the Department of Ancient History at Miskatonic University. He was already a member of the department in 1929. (: "The Horror in the Gallery")

In 1935, Ashley was one of the Miskatonic staff members who joined an expedition to excavate the ruins of a prehistoric Yithian city in the Great Sandy Desert in Australia, along with William Dyer, Nathaniel Peaslee, Wingate Peaslee and Tyler M. Freeborn. (: The Shadow Out of Time)

fullContent:
"Festival", also titled as "Yule Horror" in some publications, is a seasonal horror poem by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. First published in the December 1926 edition of popular pulp magazine Weird Tales, it has since been reprinted numerous times in many different publications, and has also been translated into French and Italian.

### Poem 
: There is snow on the ground,
: And the valleys are cold,
: And a midnight profound
: Blackly squats o’er the wold;
: But a light on the hilltops half-seen hints of feastings unhallow’d and old.

: There is death in the clouds,
: There is fear in the night,
: For the dead in their shrouds
: Hail the sun’s turning flight,
: And chant wild in the woods as they dance round a Yule-altar fungous and white.

: To no gale of earth’s kind
: Sways the forest of oak,
: Where the sick boughs entwin’d
: By mad mistletoes choke,
: For these pow’rs are the pow’rs of the dark, from the graves of the lost Druid-folk.

: And mayst thou to such deeds
: Be an abbot and priest,
: Singing cannibal greeds
: At each devil-wrought feast,
: And to all the incredulous world shewing dimly the sign of the beast.

### Adaptations
*In 2023, Canadian comic book creator Nick O'Gorman published an adaptation of "Yule Horror" through his Target Destroyed Comics label. This version was later included in the omnibus collection HPL Vol. 1: Comic Adaptations of the Works of HP Lovecraft.

The Fhtagn are a fictional race from the Marvel universe, which first appeared in Ben Reilly: Scarlet Spider Vol 1 #9 by Marvel Comics, but would not be identified until the next issue.

### Background
The Fhtagn are extra-dimensional eldritch entities which are able to bend the laws of physics and feed on evil. The vocalizations of the fhtagn are painful to humans; however, some individuals can withstand it if they have an evil soul. It's difficult to injure a fhtagn, even for superhumans.

Their appearance is that of a mass of tentacles surrounding a large fang-lined mouth with multiple prehensile tongues and a single telescopic eye-stalk. Its home dimension has not been seen yet, but the fhtagn seems to enjoy the bottom of the ocean; an area that is pitch dark, extremely cold, and with a high pressure.

One specimen got into a confrontation with the superheroes known as the Scarlet Spider and Ricochet, when it was summoned by their adversary Hornet. After the artifect used to summon and control it was destroyed, the fhtagn nearly invaded the Prime Reality but was thwarted by the heroine Dusk, who teleported the fhtagn to the Marianas Trench, where it found a new home. (: Ben Reilly: Scarlet Spider Vol 1 #9 & #10)

### Mythos Connections
The Fhtagn would appear to take their name from the notorious R'lyehian phrase quoted in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Call of Cthulhu": "Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthulhu R'lyeh wgah'nagl fhtagn", or "In his house at R'lyeh, dead Cthulhu waits dreaming". The chant is often abbreviated to "Cthulhu fhtagn".

Final Space is an animated science fiction series that ran for three seasons from  February 26, 2018 to June 14, 2021, first on TBS and later on Cartoon Network's Adult Swim. The series featured Lovecraftian Horror elements.

Invictus, the main antagonist of the series, is based on the Christian Satan, but some elements of Invictus' character were inspired by the titular alien from the cosmic horror short story "The Colour Out of Space". Like Invictus, the Colour Out of Space is a cosmic entity of pure energy that infects all life all around it. After it arrived on Earth, it infected the Gardners' farming community, mutating and corrupting humans, plants and animals, and water in the area, which is very similar to how Invictus corrupted the Titans' minds, turning them against their creators upon its imprisonment.

The seventh and eighth episodes of the first season depict a Titan resembling Cthulhu, with an octopoid head and winglike appendages sprouting from its back. Another creature is a Lovecraftian mass of tentacles, eyes, and mouths.

"Finding God(s)" is a short tongue-in-cheek Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Ambuehl.

### Synopsis
The story is written as a series of postcards from three sisters - all living in the Miskatonic Valley - to each other, with each describing how they have found a new god, and how that god has blessed them with an unusual child.

### Characters
*Sarah, who birthed a child similar to Wilbur Whateley to the Outer God Shub-Niggurath.
*Janet, who was gifted a hybrid Deep One baby by the Great Old One Dagon in exchange for her husband Dale.
*Marsha, who gave herself to Outer God Yog-Sothoth and subsequently spawned a creature not unlike the Dunwich Horror.

### Publication History
First published in fanzine Cthulhu Cultus #8 in March 1997, "Finding God(s)" was later included in Nightscapes in September 1997.

Finn Edwards, the Bootlegger, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games who appears in several of their expanded Cthulhu Mythos lines.

### History
The advent of Prohibition was nothing less than a godsend for small-time drifter Finn Edwards: until that point, he had been simply meandering through life, scratching out a living wherever he could, but the new demand for alcohol on the streets of America gave him the opportunity to make some serious money and, more importantly, feed his craving for danger.

All of this ended one night when, after a botched supply run, Finn found himself tearing through the woods one moonlit night, just a little ahead of the deranged cultists who wanted to sacrifice him to their dark god.

Narrowly escaping, and shaken to his core, Finn gathered up all the cash, firearms and supplies he could lay his hands on, resolving to make those lunatics pay for giving him the fright of his life.

### Ghouls of the Miskatonic
Edwards' character is expanded upon in Graham McNeill's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic. In the story, Finn joins forces with other investigator characters from the Arkham Horror Files line, including journalist Rex Murphy, to rescue Amanda Sharpe and Rita Young, students who have been kidnapped by an evil cult. During the course of their journey, Edwards and the others travel to other dimensions and must face monstrous ghouls, but eventually emerge triumphant.

### Behind the Mythos
Conceived as an Investigator character for their Innsmouth Horror expansion of adventure board game Arkham Horror, Finn Edwards has also made appearances Fantasy Flight's Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and Mansions of Madness lines. A now-discontinued plastic miniature was released as a part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures issue in 2010, which was designed to replace the cardboard tokens included with the games (all ).

The Fire Vampires of Fthaggua are a fictional alien species created by Donald Wandrei for his short story "The Fire Vampires". They were later incorporated into H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.

The Fire Vampires are often conflated with the Flame Creatures of Cthugha. The two species were first identified as synonymous in "The Horror in the Gallery", by Lin Carter, and the identification was popularized by the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu and The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana.

### Overview
The Fire Vampires are living extensions of the cosmic entity known as Fthaggua. Traveling the cosmos in their interstellar ship, the comet Ktynga, they appear as reddish electrical discharges resembling lightning. All the Fire Vampires are red, save for Fthaggua itself, which is blue. They feast upon the life energy of sentient creatures. The victim will burst into flames during this process, with the Fire Vampires consuming their essence and memories using heat instead of internal metabolization. These stolen memories are added to Fthaggua's gestalt consciousness, allowing them to learn better and adapt to consuming more.

After Fthaggua came to Earth in the year 2339, it was destroyed by the scientist Gustav Norby and the Fire Vampires died with it (: "The Fire Vampires").

Fireworms are a fictional species created by Sandy Petersen for Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. They first appeared in the gaming supplement H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands (1986).

### Overview
Originating in the Parg forests of the extra-dimensional realm known as the Dreamlands, Fireworms are a species of large armoured annelid whose biology seems to revolve around the utilisation of extremely high temperatures, emitting occasional puffs of smoke from their body and even possessing the ability to burst into flames on command. They have a fifty-year breeding cycle, and during these periods infest the land in a frenzy of destruction before seemingly disappearing for a full decade, possibly entering a state of hibernation or simply hiding away while their young gestate.

Fischbuch is a fictional book featured in the Cthulhu Mythos stories of Brian Lumley, first mentioned in "Name and Number".

### In the Mythos
Authored by Konrad von Gerner in 1598, Fischbuch is a tome of "oceanic lore and legend", comparable to Gaston le Fe's Dwellers in the Depths and Gantley's Hydrophinnae. Occultist Titus Crow owns a copy (: "Name and Number"), as does the wizard Julian Carstairs (: Lord of the Worms).

### Behind the Mythos
The name of the book's author, Konrad von Gerner, is similar to the real 16th century naturalist Conrad Gessner, who did author a book named Fischbuch, although not in 1598.

The Fishers from Outside are entities that serve the Great Old One Groth-Golka, first appearing in the "The Outpost", by H. P. Lovecraft.

### In Lovecraft Circle Works
In prehistoric times, the Fishers from Outside built outposts on many planets, including the Earth, where abandoned ruins of their settlements are still found in the jungles of Africa. (: "The Outpost", "Winged Death")

Occult detective Roger Little refers to them as "malignant and unknowable entities". Over the course of his career, Little has investigated several cases of men and women abducted in broad daylight by the Fishers from Outside, who produce invisible webs or tentacles to capture their victims. Once captured, "a shadow seems to pass over them, to envelop them for an instant and then they are gone". (: The Horror from the Hills)

### In the Expanded Mythos
Sometimes confused with Shantaks and even prehistoric Pterosaurs, the Fishers from Outside are a distinct species believed to serve the Great Old One known as Groth-Golka. Called down from the spaces between and beyond the stars, the Fishers sometimes act as proxies, accepting and devouring human sacrifices while also metering out the divine will of their master. As such, cultists of Groth-Golka regard the Fishers as the manifestation of their god's will. 

Whether the Fishers were created by Groth-Golka or somehow recruited is unknown, although their evolution over time has certainly been tailored or affected by the Great Old One. Viewing or handling a representational image of a Fisher from Outside is akin to viewing an image of Groth-Golka, causing humans to experience horrific nightmares. 

### Behind the Mythos
The Fishers from Outside might have been inspired by Charles Fort's ideas about alien abduction. In his typical humorous style, Fort claims:



In "Synchronicity or Something", by Brian Lumley, the character Paynter mentions "Charles Fort and his fishers from outside".

Robert M. Price, in his introduction to The Ithaqua Cycle, also claims that the Fishers from Outside were inspired by Fort.

In the works of Lin Carter, the Fishers from Outside are synonymous with the Shantaks, which Carter portrays as winged reptilian predators with a single eye and a single leg. (: "The Fishers from Outside")

The Flame Creatures of Cthugha (also known as the Minions of Cthugha) are a fictional extraterrestrial species created by August Derleth for his short story "The Dweller in Darkness" (1944). 

The Flame Creatures are nowadays most commonly conflated with the Fire Vampires that debuted in Donald Wandrei's 1933 story of the same name. The two species were first identified as synonymous in "The Horror in the Gallery", by Lin Carter, and the identification was popularised by the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu and The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana.

### Overview
The Flame Creatures are extraterrestrial entities made of living flame which dwell in the star Fomalhaut with their master, the Great Old One fire elemental known as Cthugha. They resemble living dots of bright light which set fire to anything they touch. They can be summoned to Earth when Fomalhaut is visible in the night sky by the repetition of the sentence "Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthugha Fomalhaut n'gha- ghaa naf'l thagn. Iä! Cthugha!". (: "The Dweller in Darkness")

One may cross stones, then swamps, followed by snow, and then sands; in which the snow burns like fire and the stones bleed. The only thing that is constant in the dimension is danger. It also contains the dimension of the N'Garai, which is full of demons.

The Floating Horror is an avatar of Nyarlathotep which is usually associated with Haitian voodoo.

### Appearance
The Floating Horror appears as a colossal airborne jellyfish shot through with scarlet veins. During its incubation phase it parasitically occupies the body of a living human being.

### Behavior
This avatar of Nyarlathotep can be summoned by using voodoo magic to make the offering of a human host body. Once the ritual is complete, the Floating Horror will enter the body of the "chosen one" and begin its incubation period. Once this phase is complete, the host will die and the Floating Horror will emerge to begin its work: the capture and consumption of living human beings.

Flying Polyps are a fictional extraterrestrial race in the Cthulhu Mythos. The creatures first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Shadow Out of Time.

### Description
The precise nature of the Flying Polyps is unclear; the records kept by the Great Race of Yith are notably evasive, making fearful references but shying away from actual description. They are capable of flight, although they lack wings or other appendages to facilitate this, and they were capable of controlling air currents for offensive and manipulative purposes. Although airborne, they seem to make some contact with the ground during movement, as they leave behind five-toed radial footprints wherever they go.

Unlike animals or plants, the Polyps are entities that twist and form a dark plastic flesh, cancerous with strange growths amidst multiple eyes and mouths. They are semi-material, elements or portions seem to phase between visible and invisible.

### History
To humanity, these strange species are (mostly) known as Flying Polyps, although their true name is unknown. They traveled across space and found Earth around 750 million years ago. On arrival, they constructed bizarre basalt cities wherein numerous high and windowless towers were raised. Rumours speak of the Polyps also raising cities on three other planets in the solar system, with speculation pointing to Mars, Neptune, and Venus.

Having arrived on Earth, the Polyps warred with the Great Race of Yith, but were eventually defeated and driven underground. Around 70 million years ago (during the Cretaceous era), the Polyps rose from their subterranean haunts to exact revenge by exterminating the Yithians in one fell swoop.

In the intervening years to the modern era, the Polyps left the planet en masse, although many remained and again sought out deep places to dwell, and seem content to remain there, annihilating anything that chanced upon their rest. The entrances to their dwellings are mostly below the ground, sometimes within ancient ruins or great wells now sealed over with stone, while others have taken to the deep oceans. For what purposes or reason these polyps remained on Earth is unknown, with numerous tomes speculating on a variety of factors. Such tomes also tells of the Polyps' great powers concerning the manipulation of the elements, particularly the wind and air, which can be brought to bear upon enemies and cause terrible devastation. (: The Shadow Out of Time)

### In Other Media
*The Flying Polyps appear in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.

fullContent:
Folklore is a background sourcebook produced by Cubicle 7 Entertainment as part of their Cthulhu Britannica line of Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplements. 

### Overview
Written by Stuart Boon, James Desborough and others as part of Cubicle 7's Cthulhu Britannica line, as it’s name might suggest, Folklore focuses on the legendary aspects of the British isles and how this interacts with the beings and events of the Cthulhu Mythos. It runs to 136 pages in a softcover binding. 

The book contains a new character profession, a bestiary of folkloric creatures and how they relate to the Mythos, the use of folkloric or hedge magic, a calendar of significant dates, and a selection of nine stand-alone proto-scenarios (including non-player characters but no handouts or pregenerated characters). 

### Publication History
Folklore was published by third-party content provider Cubicle 7 Entertainment in 2013. As Cubicle 7 no longer hold a license to produce Call of Cthulhu material, it is currently out of print.

Fomalhaut is the brightest star in the constellation Piscis Austrinus and one of the brightest stars in the sky. It is a class A star on the main sequence approximately 25 light-years (7.7 pc) from Earth as measured by the Hipparcos astrometry satellite. Since 1943, the spectrum of this star has served as one of the stable anchor points by which other stars are classified. It is classified as a Vega-like star that emits excess infrared radiation, indicating it is surrounded by a circumstellar disk. Fomalhaut, K-type star TW Piscis Austrini and M-type star LP 876-10 constitute a triple system even though the companions are separated by several degrees.

Fomalhaut holds a special significance in extrasolar planet research, as it is the center of the first stellar system with an extrasolar planet candidate (Fomalhaut b) imaged at visible wavelengths. The image was published in Science in November 2008. Fomalhaut is the third brightest star known to have a planetary system (as viewed from Earth), after Pollux and the Sun.

### In the Mythos
Fomalhaut is the abode of the fiery Cthugha, who can only be summoned to Earth when the star is visible in the night sky (: "The House on Curwen Street", "The Dweller in Darkness"). It is also the birthplace of Cthugha's son, Aphoom-Zhah, who later settled on Neptune and finally Earth (: "The Acolyte of the Flame").

In the Doctor Who universe, it is orbited by the planet Veltroch, one of the worlds that harbours legends about the Great Old Ones. (: White Darkness)

"Fond Regards––N" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author J. L. Royce. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long running magazine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
Bruce, a senior executive at a highly-successful technology company specialising in cloud software, is drawn to the firm's newest motivational speaker, a man named Daniel Nyarlat. As his obsession with the enigmatic newcomer increases, he finds himself desperate to spread the mysterious Message being preached by Nyarlat, and is eventually selected as one of his chosen few.

### Trivia
*Daniel Nyarlat uses the website domain name Nyarlat.hot.ep, confirmation (if any were needed), that he is at the very least an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep.

"Footprints in the Snow" is a Lovecraftian short story by author June Violette. It was published in the Jason Andrew-edited thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods by Simian Press in October 2015.

### Synopsis
In a degenerate future world where the night is ruled by alien abominations, an aging trader witnesses the arrival of a strange young girl in her town. The girl explains that she is on her way to the nearby mountains in search of a hidden valley, where rests a being who might make all right with the world again. Although the trader wishes to join the girl on her quest, she is too old to make the trip, and the girl's fate remains unknown.

"For Susannah" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tom Lynch. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
A descendant of Richard Upton Pickman, himself a talented yet struggling artist, one evening meets a beautiful woman who inspires him to paint his greatest work ever. Creating a masterpiece which transcends time and space, he pours so much of himself into the canvas that it kills him, his aged body being discovered later, along with a note dedicating the piece to his muse.

For the Greater Good is a deluxe expansion for Fantasy Flight Games' Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

### Overview
Following the standard format of deluxe expansions, For the Greater Good focuses on one particular faction (in this case The Agency) with the majority of cards being specific to that faction. Also included are the usual handful of new cards for the other factions and non-specific cards usable by any faction. It contains a total of 165 cards, 55 unique cards in duplicate sets of three, and was released in 2015.

For the Greater Good was discontinued when Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game was replaced by Arkham Horror: The Card Game, likely due to licensing considerations.

shortDefinition: "Forces of Change" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author J. B. Lee, first published in the now-defunct webzine NetherReal in 1999.  ### Synopsis Kat and Dren are a pair of prodigies, Kat specialising in all things mathematical, while Dren is capa...
fullContent:
"Forces of Change" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author J. B. Lee, first published in the now-defunct webzine NetherReal in 1999.

### Synopsis
Kat and Dren are a pair of prodigies, Kat specialising in all things mathematical, while Dren is capable of absorbing, analysing, and collating vast amounts of written material. When one day they stumble across a bizarre entity in an abandoned house filled with esoteric books, they decide to bring it home and study it.

As the weeks go by, they discover that the entity - which they now know to be named Gtuhanai - is an extra-dimensional visitor likely to have been on the planet for millennia. Fascinated by its ability to absorb all forms of metals into its body, they fail to realise that they have been slowly corrupted by its presence before it is too late.

The story concludes with Kat and Dren, now fully-assimilated devotees to Gtuhanai, accidentally releasing their dark god into the world, dying in the process.

### Mythos Connections
"Forces of Change" features numerous connections to the Cthulhu Mythos and its contributors, including:

* A line referring to chaos theory which states: "A butterfly flits through a cemetery in Providence, Rhode Island, coming to rest on a famous author's tombstone" is a likely nod to H. P. Lovecraft and his burial site.
* The story features locations named for various Cthulhu Mythos authors: Berglund's Furniture Co (Edward P. Berglund), Clore and Price, Inc (Dan Clore and Robert M. Price, respectively), and Ambuehl Street (James Ambuehl).
* The abandoned building explored by Kat and Dren has copies of The Golden Bough, Von Junzt's Nameless Cults in the Golden Goblin edition, and several volumes of The Revelations of Glaaki. Later, they purchase a commercial edition of the Necronomicon for five dollars, which Dren describes as "worthless." Dren also mentions having read Gustav Johansen's diary, and commenting that "He didn't know what they found, out there in the Pacific."
* One section states "A famous violinist … was found in his hotel room, completely mad, babbling about bells and the music of the spheres. This was the precursor to a series of mental breakdowns among the artists, poets and musicians of the city, all of whom claimed to be besieged by terrifying visions." This is a clear nod to Henry Anthony Wilcox and the events described in the first section of "The Call of Cthulhu," "The Horror in Clay."
* Hyperborea is referenced as the possible site of Gtuhanai's emergence into our world.
* Cthulhu, Yog-Sothoth, Glaaki, the "invisible lloigor" and "many-legged gharoides," the latter of which is a species created by author J. B. Lee, are also mentioned in passing.

shortDefinition: Forever Azathoth is a horror comedy novella by Peter Cannon and a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Thing on the Doorstep". It consists of six stories, each written one year apart, and each narrated by a different character. The first two ...
fullContent:
Forever Azathoth is a horror comedy novella by Peter Cannon and a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Thing on the Doorstep". It consists of six stories, each written one year apart, and each narrated by a different character. The first two installments were published for the first time in the Chaosium anthology The Azathoth Cycle: Tales of the Blind Idiot God, before reappearing along with the remaining four segments in Cannon's collections Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (1999) and Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches (2011).

### Stories
*"Azathoth in Arkham"
*"The Revenge of Azathoth"
*"The House of Azathoth"
*"Azathoth in Analysis"
*"Bride of Azathoth"
*"Son of Azathoth"

### Characters
*Edward Derby Upton: the son of Daniel Upton, named after his father's friend, the poet Edward Pickman Derby. He first appeared in "The Thing on the Doorstep", by H. P. Lovecraft. Part one is narrated by him.
*Soames: the old British butler of the Upton family. He might be the same Soames from "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family", but is more likely a son or relative, given that the original Soames was already described as "aged" in 1913, and Forever Azathoth sees him still active in the 1940s.
*Henry Armitage: the elderly librarian at Miskatonic University. He first appeared in "The Dunwich Horror", by H. P. Lovecraft.
*Wendy Babson: a woman from Innsmouth whose older sister Eunice worked for Derby's wife Asenath before being fired by Derby. By the end of each story, starting with part two, she has a new husband or boyfriend: Edward Upton in part two, Vartan Bagdasarian in part three, Dr. Zimmerman in part four, Jacob Lamar Derby in part five, and the (unnamed) dean of Miskatonic in part six.
*Vartan Bagdasarian: a fan of Derby's works, one of the founders of the Dead Edward Derby Society, who becomes the first editor of Azathoth House, a publishing house created specifically to publish the works of Derby. Part two is narrated by him.
*Judge Hand: originally Upton's lawyer, who later becomes a member of the board of directors at Azathoth House. Part three is narrated by him.
*Ephraim "Eph" Upton: the son of Edward Upton and Wendy Babson, named after Asenath Waite's father Ephraim Waite.
*Jacob Lamar Derby: an inventor by trade and a distant cousin of Edward Derby who inherits the Derby cabin in the woods near Chesuncook, Maine. He first appeared in "The Pit of the Shoggoths", by Stephen Mark Rainey.
*Dr. Zimmerman: psychoanalyst working at the Arkham Sanitarium. Part four is narrated by him.
*Miss Holden: retired headmistress of the Hall School at Kingsport where Asenath studied. She became Asenath's legal guardian after the death of Ephraim Waite. Part five is narrated by her.
*Fearless: a foxhound dog from the Foxfield Hunt Club.
*Vartan Bagdasarian Jr.: the son of Vartan Bagdasarian and Belinda Blake, who inherits his father's love for the works of Derby. Part six is narrated by him.
*George Holden: great-nephew of Miss

Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches is a collection of humourous stories set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was written by Peter Cannon and published by Subterranean Press in 2011, with cover art by Jason C. Eckhardt.

The book is divided in three sections, consisting of the six-part novella Forever Azathoth, the Scream for Jeeves trilogy that places P. G. Wodehouse's characters in the world of H. P. Lovecraft, and a third part collecting other assorted tales, most of which written as a pastiche or parody of one specific author.

While some of the stories are recycled from the earlier, similarly-named Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (Tartarus Press, 1999), others are new to this collection.

The Formless Spawn are fictional creatures in the Cthulhu Mythos, originally created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Tale of Satampra Zeiros".

### Description
These black, protean beings may be found in temples dedicated to the Great Old Ones or in deep sunless caverns, often acting as guardians and protectors of secrets. They may accompany or herald the arrival of a Great Old One or stand in the god's stead, or simply lie motionless for years at a time, like some quiet dark pool waiting to be disturbed by the unwary. Whether they are born of a specific entity or magically created is unknown.

True to their name, Formless Spawn are polymorphic entities made of black ichor and look like amorphous goo. Similarly to Shoggoths, they have the ability to change their form and shape into any conceivable form. Being a living viscous liquid, they can ooze through small cracks, usually finding a way through any obstacle, while also able to cast spells, and can form vocal organs to issue strange sounds - no record exists suggesting they have ever communicated with words a human could understand.

### Background
The Formless Spawn were found resting in a great basin beneath an idol of their god Tsathoggua by the thief Satampra Zeiros and his companion Tirouv Ompallios. Described as "a torrent of black quicksilver" and "an undulant ophidian form which immediately developed more than a dozen short legs", the creature attempted to devour the interlopers. (: "The Tale of Satampra Zeiros")

The people of the subterranean world of K'N-Yan had once worshipped Tsathoggua, until a scientific expedition exploring N'Kai encountered the Formless Spawn. Those who escaped had all the images of Tsathoggua destroyed, and his temple re-dedicated to Shub-Niggurath. (: The Mound)

It was also stated that "[a] few daring mystics have hinted at a pre-Pleistocene origin for the fragmentary Pnakotic Manuscripts, and have suggested that the devotees of Tsathoggua (including the Formless Spawn) were as alien to mankind as Tsathoggua itself." (: At the Mountains of Madness)

### In Other Media
*In the Demonbane series, Vespasianus has the ability to summon the Formless Spawn. They attempted to consume Daijuuji Kurou and Al Azif but were ultimately destroyed by Laban Shrewsbury.
*The Formless Spawn makes an appearance in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, under the name "Formless Terror". 
*The Formless Spawn appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X, under the name "Eldritch Spawn". 
*The Formless Spawn appear as adversaries in the video game Quake. Their design was based on an illustration from S. Petersen's Field Guide to Creatures of the Dreamlands

shortDefinition: Forrest James Ackerman (November 24, 1916 – December 4, 2008) was an American magazine editor, science fiction writer and literary agent who lived and worked in Los Angeles California. He was a principal founder of science fiction fandom and the conc...
fullContent:
Forrest James Ackerman (November 24, 1916 – December 4, 2008) was an American magazine editor, science fiction writer and literary agent who lived and worked in Los Angeles California. He was a principal founder of science fiction fandom and the concept of a modern organised fandom. He was a leading expert on both the professional exponents, production and minutiae of genre films covering science fiction, horror and fantasy.

He was considered by some to be the world's most passionate collector of genre books and film memorabilia, for example on the 1970s travel programme Whicker's World. Despite his passion for collecting his enormous collection, which filled his 18 room mansion in Los Angeles, was never categorized or listed and many irreplaceable pieces were lost or stolen.

Ackerman founded the first science fiction fan group (The Boys’ Scientifiction Club) in 1929, and wrote for the genre’s first fanzine (The Time Traveler) in 1932. He created and coined the term "Sci-Fi" to describe science fiction. He became a professional publisher of science fiction and fantasy in 1926. 

He collaborated with C. L. Moore on the story "Nymph of Darkness", part of Moore's Northwest Smith series, which appeared in the December 1939 issue of Weird Tales.

Working with publisher James Warren, Ackerman created the iconic comic book character Vampirella in 1969. 

Ackerman appeared in more than 210 films, including parts in genre films Dracula vs. Frankenstein, The Howling, The Aftermath, Scalps, Return of the Living Dead Part II, Innocent Blood, The Time Travelers, Future War, Amazon Women on the Moon, The Wizard of Speed and Time, Curse of the Queerwolf, Transylvania Twist, Hard to Die, Nudist Colony of the Dead, Attack of the 60 Foot Centerfold and at least one major music video Michael Jackson's Thriller.

Ackerman was, like H. P. Lovecraft, a confirmed atheist and skeptic. Despite this, after his death it is alleged there were four attested contacts "from beyond the grave" involving people who had been close to him in the final phase of his life.

In "In the Walls of Eryx", by Lovecraft and Kenneth Sterling, the Venusian efjeh-weeds and akmans are named after Ackerman.

### Posthumous Allegations
Forest J Ackerman has, since his death, been publicly outed as a serial sex pest and unconvicted sex offender, preying on young women relentlessly. Lucy Chase Williams was brave enough to post her personal experience but it stands for many more. Ackerman's behaviour was well known, and ignored or excused by many in the industries in which he worked.

The Fosterlings of the Old Ones are a fictional race expanded on  in 1994 by Chaosium for its Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, and which were based on Ramsey Campbell's "The Faces at Pine Dunes."

### Background
The Fosterlings of the Old Ones are mutants born to humans whom have mated with a Great Old One or an Outer God. In a special ceremony, the entity projects dreams that reach the pregnant woman's womb altering the unborn fetus DNA. The resulting offspring, a Fosterling, lives for years as a normal human, until the day it mutates.

Its transformation happens in one evening. The Fosterling becomes something that more closely resembles its parent deity. Two or more of these creatures may merge into one Fosterling. Mutations borne by Fosterlings are passed down genetically, with each generation becoming more like the alien parent. The Fosterlings are destined to be the chosen servants of the Great Old Ones when they return, in effect a form of long term colonisation of the Earth.

fullContent:
"Found in a Trunk from Extremadura" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by French author Meddy Ligner. It was first published under its French title of "Manuscrit trouvé dans une malle d'Estrémadure" in the anthology HPL 2007 in September 2007.

### Synopsis
The story follows two threads, one in which Spanish conquistadors encounter terrifying entities in the jungles of South America, and another in which a man meets a fictionalised version of Howard Phillips Lovecraft, who is promptly consumed by an unknown entity.

### Behind the Mythos
Cthulhu Mythos elements made mention of include Cthulhu, the Necronomicon, the Pnakotic Manuscripts, the Book of Dzyan, and Ulthar, although none of these play any appreciable part in the narrative, being relegated to little more than a laundry list.

### Trivia
* The H. P. Lovecraft featured in the story was accepted into the United States army and was injured in the knee during World War I. 

### Publication History
* HPL 2007 (2007)
* Historical Lovecraft (2011; translated by Paula R. Stiles)

The Foundation is a fictional organisation created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Cthulhu Mythos setting. Several of the stories in Aconyte's 2022 anthology Secrets in Scarlet involved the group.

### Overview
The Foundation are a secretive government department whose goal is to protect humankind from the horrors presented by the Cthulhu Mythos; this usually involves keeping those eldritch entities existence hidden in their entirety. Unfortunately for the Foundation, their activities often put them in opposition to the Red Coterie, a faction dedicated to acquiring powerful magical artefacts known as "Keys" for an unknown purpose.

### Known Members & Agents
* Commissioner Qiana Taylor: a government official whose job appears to be to contain outbreaks of Mythos-related activity amongst the general populace (: "The Man in the Bubble")
* Archibald Hudson: aide-de-camp to Taylor (: "The Man in the Bubble")
* Valeria Antonova: aide-de-camp to Taylor (: "The Man in the Bubble")
* Li Flint: an operative working in the Asian theatre, determined to find those who murdered his partner (: "City of Waking Dreams")
* Shaw: Nanjing chapter operative, deceased (: "City of Waking Dreams")
* Chen Guiying: Nanjing chapter operative (: "City of Waking Dreams")
* Kymani Jones: a private investigator specialising in the theft of precious artefacts; not a member of the Foundation, but has worked with them in the past (: "A Forty Grain Weight of Nephrite")
* Shibing: a Chinese operative assigned to San Fransisco. Last seen on his way to sacrifice his own life to keep a Key known as the Xiamen Bi secure. (: "A Forty Grain Weight of Nephrite")

### Appearances

* "City of Waking Dreams" (2022)

"Foundling" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tim Waggoner.

### Synopsis
A recently-bereaved woman travels to a site where an abortive magical ritual once took place in the hope that something might remain which she can use as a bargaining tool to regain her lost family. What she finds is a small part of a Great Old One, severed when the ritual ended, which takes her body to use as a birthing shell for its new form.

### Characters
*Mary Carter, a grieving woman who has recently lost her husband and daughter in a horrific road accident.
*Josiah Mast, a struggling farmer from Ohio who attempted to bargain with a Great Old One in 1957.

### Publication History
"Foundling" was first published in the online Mythos magazine Nightscapes in September 1997, and later in the anthology The Truth Is Out There in February 2016.

### Trivia
*Originally written as a Cthulhu Mythos story, "Foundling" was later incorporated into The X-Files universe in the anthology The Truth Is Out There, although the original text contains no tangible relation to that franchise.

A group of heroic investigators must gather their powers, carry out research and hope that favorable astral alignments will help them survive as they race to stop a cult which, when the stars are right, will meet to summon eldritch horror to Earth in the form of the Great Old Ones, plunging the world into chaos and ultimately leading to the destruction of the human race.

fullContent:
"Four O'Clock" is a horror short story by Sonia H. Greene, based on an idea suggested to her by H. P. Lovecraft. Written in 1922, it was published for the first time in the 1949 Arkham House collection Something About Cats and Other Pieces. It was later reprinted in The Horror in the Museum and Other Revisions.

### Synopsis
The narrator lies wide awake in bed at night, anticipating with dread and horror the approach of four o'clock. At some point in the past, a man placed a curse on them, which would take place on this exact date at 4 a.m., the same day and hour in which some undisclosed tragedy befell the man, although the narrator claims to be blameless. The fact that the man is now dead does little to placate the narrator's fears. On the contrary, from their window, the narrator can see the cemetery in which the man was buried, and wonders why they chose to sleep in this very house on this very date.

From the direction of the cemetery rises a mist-like substance which seeps through the narrator's window and takes up the form of a giant clock's dial. From the empty dial protrude four claws on the place where the numeral 4 would be. As the monster gradually emerges from the dial, the narrator sees that each claw ends in a cluster of wriggling tentacles. At this point, every sound coming from outside is intensified unbearably, and the cricket's chirping seems to endlessly repeat the words 'four o'clock". The bedroom's wall comes alive with images of dancing demons of various sizes, each with the face of a clock showing four. When the narrator turns back to the tentacled apparition, the creature reveals itself as a hellish being made of fire, and with a face reminiscent of the deceased man who cursed the narrator.

The Fox River is a significant watercourse located in the state of Wisconsin in the United States. It’s interest to this wiki is its mention in H. P. Lovecraft’s 1918 poem "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin."

### Overview
Flowing from its headwaters in south-central Wisconsin, the Fox River deposits into Green Bay, and is the largest of the bay's tributaries to do so. By extension, it is also the largest tributary of the inland sea known as Lake Michigan.

### In Lovecraft’s Works
In Lovecraft’s 1918 romantic poem, a woman named Hecatissa, jilted by her love, attempted to end her life by throwing herself into the Fox River. However, the god of the river took pity on the girl and refused to take her, "cast[ing] her back again." (: "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin."

Foxfield is a fictional town set in the US state of Massachusetts, created by H. P. Lovecraft. 

### Overview
Despite being mentioned in his letters, Foxfield was never used in any published works by H. P. Lovecraft. The town was later used by Miskatonic River Press in their anthologies of adventure scenarios for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role playing game, New Tales of the Miskatonic Valley: Further Adventures in Lovecraft Country (2008) and More Adventures in Arkham Country (2010), where it is a hotspot of Mi-Go activity.

*New Tales of the Miskatonic Valley
**Proof of Life, by Keith Herber, where strange creatures get involved in the small town's affairs.

*More Adventures in Arkham Country
**The Crystal cavern, by Brian Courtemanche, where the players investigate strange attacks in an ancient quartz mine.

### History
Located about 40 kilometers North-west from Arkham, Foxfield was founded in 1729 on the Fox river, a tributary of the Miskatonic River. Starting out as a small farming community, the small town entered the industrial age in 1843 when the Pickering family of Salem built a modern woolen mill. The venture was a wide success that attracted many immigrant workers, especially after the textile boom of the Civil war when demand for fabric skyroketed to manufacture army uniforms. Despite occasional frictions between locals and newcomers, the town prospered until the end of the 19th century, when business slowed down and caused layoffs among the work force. The final blow was a disastrous fire in 1911 that completely destroyed the factory, ending its activity for good as the Pickerings deemed it unprofitable to rebuild and left the town for good. With its economical power house now gone, most of the immigrant workers left the town and Foxfield became a small farming community once again.

The Fractal Creatures are a fictional extra-dimensional race created by Scott David Aniolowski for the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Ye Booke of Monstres II (1995).

### Background
Fractal creatures live in the fractal dimension which can only be accessed via a gate created by a computer. They manifest in the material plane as beings of pure energy which drift in the air in search of energy. There are various sub-species among the fractal creatures. Some of them are like herbivores, grazing on the energy provided by civilisation's electrical networks. Others are more predatory, feeding on the energy of living beings. Some of them are not much different from animals and others are intelligent lifeforms.

In the material plane their energies dissipate within 24 hours, forcing them to feed on a daily basis. Physical weapons are unable to harm them but energy attacks will harm fractals (e.g. microwaves, lasers, electricity, and ultra-sound). The race consists of numerous different sub-species. In their home dimension they serve the Outer God Yog-Sothoth.

The Fractal Yog-Sothoth (also known as Lord of the Fractal Realm) is a fictional entity created by Scott David Aniolowski for Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, depicted as being an avatar of the Outer God known as Yog-Sothoth. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

### Description
Appearing as an agglomeration of coruscating rainbow-coloured geometric shapes surrounding a central mass of tentacles, the Fractal Yog-Sothoth is rarely encountered in the real world; nevertheless it is occasionally stumbled across by unwitting computer users. When its bizarre dimension is accessed, the Fractal Yog-Sothoth immediately forces its way through the user's now-destroyed computer screen and grows to a terrifying size, lashing out with its appendages: any living being touched by the Fractal is instantly absorbed by it.  

Being an entity composed entirely of energy, the Fractal Yog-Sothoth cannot be harmed by any physical means. However, it is vulnerable to energy-based weapons and effects, and the switching off or restarting of the computer which it used as a gateway may act to cast it back to its own dimension. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

It has been suggested that entities other than Yog-Sothoth possess fractal avatars in this other dimension, although if any of them have been encountered by humans there have been no survivors left to tell the tale. 

### Behind the Mythos
The Fractal Yog-Sothoth is remarkably similar to the Saraquezel entity created by Craig Hinton for his Doctor Who tie-in novel Millennial Rites in 1994.
