fullContent:
France is a country in Europe whose colonialism and cultural heritage have spread its language and influence across the globe. The nation features in the fiction of H. P. Lovecraft and in other Cthulhu Mythos writers, particularly the Averoigne stories of Clark Ashton Smith. 

French history traces back to 507, when the Merovingian dynasty of Franks took over the province of Gaul from the collapsing Roman Empire. The Frankish King Clovis I made his capital at Paris in 508, which has ever since been the center of France's political and cultural life. 

France established itself as one of the great powers of Europe, under leaders from Charlemagne to Napoleon. It seized colonies in Canada, Louisiana, the Caribbean, West Africa, and Southeast Asia, among other places. France's regicidal revolution of 1789, with its ideals of liberty, equality, and fraternity, was an inspiration to many and a warning to others around the world. 

France had a bitter rivalry with England that lasted centuries, but found itself on the side of Britain in two world wars. (For Americans of Lovecraft's generation, "France" could be used synonymously with the "Great War", or World War I.) In the post-World War II world, France has maintained a sometimes contentious alliance with the United States. 

### French Weird Literature
Lovecraft praises several French writers in his survey of Supernatural Horror in Literature, though noting that France has produced relatively few great writers who focused on specifically supernatural horror. Thus both Victor Hugo and Balzac are said to "employ supernaturalism...generally only as a means to some more human end, and without the sincere and daemonic intensity which characterises the born artist in shadows." Gustave Flaubert "but for a strong realistic bias might have been an arch-weaver of tapestried terrors."  

Lovecraft credits "the powerful and cynical Guy de Maupassant" with "suggesting with marvellous force the imminence of nameless terrors, and the relentless dogging of an ill-starred individual by hideous and menacing representatives of the outer blackness." But Lovecraft suggest these are more "the morbid outpourings of a realistic mind in a pathological state than the healthy imaginative products of a vision naturally disposed toward phantasy and sensitive to the normal illusions of the unseen." 

Lovecraft says of the Symbolist and Decadent schools that their "dark interests really centre more in abnormalities of human thought and instinct than in the actual supernatural." The writing team Erckmann-Chatrian create "a shuddering midnight atmosphere...despite a tendency toward natural explanations and scientific wonders." Writers like Villiers de l’Isle-Adam and Maurice Level are devoted to "the so-called conte cruel, in which the wrenching of the emotions is accomplished through dramatic tantalisations, frustrations, and gruesome physical horrors. 

In short, argues Lovecraft, "the French genius is more naturally suited to thi

shortDefinition: "Francesci's Cult of the Necronomicon: An Interlude" is a short story by author Ian Davey first published in 1998. It is the third entry in his Bh'Yhlun series of Cthulhu Mythos fiction.  ### Synopsis The story follows a filmmaker named Francesci who...
fullContent:
"Francesci's Cult of the Necronomicon: An Interlude" is a short story by author Ian Davey first published in 1998. It is the third entry in his Bh'Yhlun series of Cthulhu Mythos fiction.

### Synopsis
The story follows a filmmaker named Francesci who becomes obsessed with the Necronomicon, an ancient and forbidden text associated with the Cthulhu Mythos. As he delves deeper into the book's dark secrets, he unwittingly attracts the attention of a cult that worships the cosmic entities described within its pages. Francesci's journey leads him to confront the terrifying realities of the cult's beliefs and the consequences of his obsession. The narrative explores themes of madness, the allure of forbidden knowledge, and the thin line between creativity and destruction. Ultimately, Francesci's pursuit of artistic inspiration becomes a harrowing experience, revealing the dangers of engaging with forces beyond human comprehension. It is the incorporation of these  all too familiar Mythos trappings into the world of a filmmaker that elevates the story somewhat.

### Publication History
"Francesci's Cult of the Necronomicon: An Interlude" was published in the March/April 1998 issue of short-lived fanzine Al-Azif.

His poem "To Howard Phillips Lovecraft", written in honour of his late friend, was published in the March 1938 issue of Weird Tales.

He also co-authored a handful of stories with Forrest J Ackerman.

Professor Francis Morgan is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror".

### Overview

### Lovecraft's Work
Professor of Medicine and Comparative Anatomy (or Archaeology) at Miskatonic University. The story refers to him as "lean" and "youngish". Together with professors Henry Armitage and Warren Rice he succeeds in defeating the plans of the Whateleys and destroying the Dunwich Horror.

### Other Works
In Fritz Leiber's "To Arkham and the Stars"—written in 1966 and apparently set at about that time—Morgan is described as "the sole living survivor of the brave trio who had slain the Dunwich Horror". According to Leiber, Morgan's "research in mescaline and LSD" produced "clever anti-hallucinogens" that were instrumental in curing Danforth's mental illness.

Morgan also appears in several of Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files products including Arkham Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game.

Francis Wayland Thurston is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu". 

### Overview
Thurston was a Bostonian anthropologist, the grandnephew of George Gammell Angell and the sole heir and executor of his estate. While going through the late Professor Angell's papers, he discovered the secret of the Cthulhu Cult, a revelation that likely sealed his doom.

### Behind the Mythos
* Thurston's name appears only in the story's subtitle, which originally appeared in Weird Tales but was dropped from later reprints until the 1981 Arkham House edition.
*"Thurston" is an old Providence family name, while Francis Wayland was the name of the fourth president of Brown University, who did much to build up the institution.

Frank T. "Kiz" Sronce is an American game designer and critic. He is the author and game designer of Hyberborean Mice, a pastiche role-playing game of grim Swords & Sorcery action... as portrayed by talking mice and rats. The ecology of the forest replaces the milieu of Conan and Hyberborea, with "giant" predators (the owls, foxes, wolves and so on) replacing mythical monsters and prehistoric horrors.

An infrequent contributor to Crypt of Cthulhu as a correspondent, he and his wife ran a now-defunct publishing and gaming website. He relocated to Washington state to work for Amazon for several years but is now devoting his time to game design and writing.

Frank Belknap Long (April 27, 1901 - January 3, 1994) was a prolific American writer of horror fiction, fantasy, science fiction, poetry, gothic romance, comic books, and non-fiction. Though his writing career spanned seven decades, he is best known for his horror and science fiction short stories, including early contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos. During his life, Long received the World Fantasy Award for Life Achievement (at the 1978 World Fantasy Convention), the Bram Stoker Award for Lifetime Achievement (in 1987, from the Horror Writers Association), and the First Fandom Hall of Fame Award (1977).

### Biography
He was born in Manhattan, New York City, on April 27, 1901. He grew up in the Harlem area of Manhattan. His father was a prosperous dentist and his mother was May Doty. The family resided at 823 West End Avenue in Manhattan. A lifelong resident of New York City, he was educated in the New York City public school system. He developed his interest in the weird by reading the Oz books, Jules Verne, and H.G. Wells, as well as Ambrose Bierce and Edgar Allan Poe.

As a boy, he was fascinated by natural history, and wrote that he dreamed of running "away from home and explore the great rain forests of the Amazon."  Though writing was to be his life's work, he once commented that as "important as writing is, I could have been completely happy if I had a secure position in a field that has always had a tremendous emotion and an imaginative appeal for me—that of natural history."

In his late teens, he was active in the United Amateur Press Association (UAPA) after winning a prize from The Boy's World (around 1919) and thus discovering amateur journalism. His first published tale was "Dr Whitlock's Price" (United Amateur, March 1920). Long's UAPA story "The Eye Above the Mantel" (1921) caught the eye of H. P. Lovecraft, sparking a friendship and correspondence that would endure until Lovecraft's death in 1937.

Long studied journalism at New York University from 1920 to 1921, later transferring to Columbia but leaving without a degree. In 1921, he suffered a severe attack of appendicitis, leading to a ruptured appendix and peritonitis. He spent a month in New York's Roosevelt Hospital, where he came close to dying. Long's brush with death prompted him to leave college to pursue a freelance writing career.

In 1923, at the age of 22, he made his first sale of a short story, "The Desert Lich", to Weird Tales magazine. Throughout the next four decades, Long was to be a frequent contributor to pulp magazines, including two of the most famous: Weird Tales (under editor Farnsworth Wright) and Astounding Science Fiction (under editor John W. Campbell). Long was an active freelance writer, also publishing many non-fiction articles. 

His first book, the scarce volume A Man from Genoa and Other Poems, was published in 1926 by W. Paul Cook. The poems in this collection won praise from a great variety of writers, among them Arthur Machen, Cliffor

Frank Elwood is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "The Dreams in the Witch-House."

### "The Dreams in the Witch-House"
An attendee at Arkham's Miskatonic University, Elwood is the only fellow student of Walter Gilman's to live at the decrepit boarding house known locally as the "Witch House." He tried to help Gilman through his somnambulism, and listened to his deathbed confession. After witnessing Gilman's death, he was institutionalized for a year.

### In the Expanded Mythos
Elwood appeared as a minor character character in Peter Rawlik's 2013 novel Reanimators, and returned in his 2014 sequel The Weird Company, where he assisted a group of other characters assembled from some of Lovecraft's most popular stories to save the world from destruction by an army of voracious Shoggoths.

Franklin "Frank" Nardi is a fictional character who appears in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. He was originally created by author C. J. Henderson for his short story "The Idea of Fear", but has since been expanded upon by others including Josh Reynolds and Robert M. Price.

### Description
Originally of Italian descent, Frank is outwardly a stereotypical hard-boiled New York detective, although he possesses a strong moral compass and is fiercely loyal to his friends. He is somewhere in his late middle age and, although still solidly built for a man of his years, has gained a certain amount of excess weight since leaving the force.

### History
After serving with the New York Police Department - where he attained the rank of detective - Frank chose to take early retirement. Subsequently, he contacted three other former police officers and partnered with them in the Arkham Detective Agency, a private-investigations firm which they established in the supposedly-sleepy town of Arkham, Massachusetts. 

Soon after setting up business the group realised that, far from being an ordinary place, Arkham was in fact home to many strange and inexplicable occurrences. In order to exploit this, the Agency branched out from regular detective work into paranormal investigations, a side business which has proven to be extremely lucrative, if at times hazardous.

### Behind the Mythos
C.J. Henderson originally created the character of Frank Nardi, whom he used as the protagonist for four short stories before his death in 2014. Before his passing, Henderson pitched the idea of a collection of short stories by contemporary authors based on the character to his friend and editor Brian M. Sammons, who agreed to the suggestion. This eventually became Arkham Detective Agency; however, due to the speed at which the industry processes work, the book was not published in Henderson's lifetime.

Frank H. Pabodie is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who makes his first appearance in the 1936 novel At the Mountains of Madness.

### Description
Pabodie is a member of Miskatonic University's engineering department, and the inventor of a drill "unique and radical in its lightness, portability, and capacity... to cope quickly with strata of varying hardness," used in the disastrous Pabodie Expedition to Antarctica in 1930–31. He also added "fuel-warming and quick-starting devices" to the expedition's four aircraft. (: At the Mountains of Madness)

### Behind the Mythos
Lovecraft chose "Pabodie" as "a name typical of good old New England stock, yet not sufficiently common to sound conventional or hackneyed." (: Selected Letters 5.830)

It is an alternative spelling of "Peabody", a name Lovecraft was familiar with through the Peabody Museum in Salem.

He does not seem to be connected with the real life palaeontologist Frank Elmer Peabody (1914-1958).

fullContent:
Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus is an 1818 gothic horror novel by English author Mary Shelley. The book has since become one of the most influential stories ever in the speculative fiction genre, and has been cited as an early example of science fiction.

### Synopsis
The book tells the story of brilliant scientist Doctor Victor Frankenstein, a man obsessed with uncovering the secrets to the creation of life. Using stolen body parts, over many years he finally manages to perfect the process and animate a new, living being, but is disgusted with his creation. Abandoning the wretched being, he attempts to leave his researches behind him, but is pursued across the globe by the creature, who merely wishes acceptance from its creator and the world at large.

### Inspiration
In his letters, author Howard Phillips Lovecraft stated that his short story "Herbert West--Reanimator" was written as a parody of Frankenstein. S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz have also suggested the book as an inspiration for "The Outsider."

Ellsworth Franklyn Searight (5 August 1935 - 8 December 2020) was the son of Richard F. Searight, Weird Tales author and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft and the grandson of silent movie actor Frank Searight. He is an accomplished Cthulhu Mythos author in his own right, having written several short Lovecraftian stories and two lengthy series of Mythos poetry. 

Although the elder Searight invented the evocative Eltdown Shards, and was occasionally employed by Lovecraft himself, he made no great effort to carry on the Cthulhu Mythos tradition. Franklyn however wrote numerous Mythos stories especially in a productive period in the 1970s.

Frederick Lee Pelton (29 August 1921-22 September 1950) was an American author who has penned a handful of works which intersect with the purview of this wiki. These include a fictional text purporting to be an ancient grimoire which describes the history of Cthulhu Mythos forces on Earth, and a pseudo-factual work on the history and practices of the Cthulhu Cult.

He was a keen wargamer while attending college at the University of Nebraska and anticipated both the cosplay and the role-playing elements eventually pioneered by David Weseley and David Arneson in the activities of his own wargaming group. Had he lived, we may well have seen the emergence of table-top roleplaying decades earlier than in our own history.

Freddy Krueger is a slasher in the fictional Nightmare on Elm Street universe, who was created in 1984 and has been the franchise's antagonist. He has appeared in comic book series by Marvel Comics, Innovation Publishing, Trident Comics, Avatar Press, and most recently Wildstorm Productions.

### Background
Born to a nun who was raped by the inmates of an asylum, (: A Nightmare on Elm Street III) Freddy Krueger was bullied in his youth and as an adult murdered the children of those whom bullied him and who formed a mob, hunted him down, and burned him alive. (: A Nightmare on Elm Street) As he was burning to death, he made a pact with dream demons, becoming one himself. (: A Nightmare on Elm Street VI)

Since then he has preyed on the teenagers living on Elm Street and those whom descended from the original families, terrorizing and killing them in their dreams. He cannot be killed in the dreamworld but if pulled to the real world, he can be killed. (: A Nightmare on Elm Street) When killed he goes to hell but has returned repeatedly. He would encounter and battle both Jason Voorhees and Ash Williams at Crystal Lake, and afterwards would use the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis to try to take over the world. (: Freddy vs. Jason vs. Ash, Freddy vs. Jason vs. Ash: The Nightmare Warriors)

Friedrich von Junzt (1795-1840) is a fictional character created by Robert E. Howard for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Children of the Night". He was also mentioned in several other stories by Howard, H. P. Lovecraft and others. 

Howard described von Junzt as a "German eccentric" who "spent his entire life...delving into forbidden subjects"; his magnum opus was the infamous Unaussprechlichen Kulten (Nameless Cults) or Black Book, published in 1839. Shortly thereafter,  he was found dead in a locked and bolted room with the marks of taloned fingers on his throat. He had written another book just before his death, but his closest friend, after reading the manuscript, burnt it and then slit his own throat. (: "The Black Stone", Robert E. Howard).

Robert Anton Wilson, in his Schrödinger's Cat trilogy, writes that von Junzt made a translation of the Necronomicon titled Das Verichteraraberbuch from an unknown Greek copy, and that this was published in Ingolstadt in 1848.  (: Schrödinger's Cat trilogy, Robert Anton Wilson).

fullContent:
Fritz Leiber was an American author of science fiction, fantasy, and horror. He was also a correspondent of Howard Phillips Lovecraft in the year before Lovecraft's death. An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia writes, "Leiber wrote some of the most distinguished science fiction, fantasy, and horror literature of the century, and is perhaps the only one of HPL's colleagues who can rival him in literary substance."

Much of Leiber's early fiction shows Lovecraft's influence; some of this work was published in Leiber's Arkham House collection, Night's Black Agents (1947), and other pieces were collected in Fritz Leiber and H. P. Lovecraft: Writers in the Dark (Wildside Press, 2003). Another early novella with "strong Lovecraftian elements", The Dealings of Daniel Kesserich, was published in 1993 by Tor.

Very little of Leiber's work has overt connections to the Cthulhu Mythos. One such story, "The Terror from the Depths", was begun in 1937 in the wake of Lovecraft's death and not completed until 1975, in time to be published in Edward P. Bergland's Disciples of Cthulhu the next year. Another story, "To Arkham and the Stars", which revisits Lovecraft's Miskatonic University setting and includes many of his characters, was published in 1966 in Arkham House's Dark Brotherhood.

Leiber wrote for Weird Tales under the editorship of Dorothy McIlwraith (beginning in April 1940). His greatest fame is as the creator of Fafhrd and Gray Mouser and their Lankhmar setting in the Swords series of novels and stories, which created an ironic and almost post-modern twist on the Sword and Sorcery genre. 

Lovecraft read a draft of the first story in the Swords series, "Adept's Gambit", and gave Leiber substantial feedback. The story originally contained Mythos elements, but these were removed before publication. 

### In Other Media
Created in "The Terror From the Depths", the Tunnelers Below were later expanded upon by Chaosium in their Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

The Frog Monsters are recurring antagonists in the Hellboy-universe, who are inspired by the Cthulhu Mythos race of the Deep Ones.

### Overview
The Frog Monsters were all once humans, who had been turned into creatures by the Ogdru Hem.

The creatures were first met by Hellboy, Abe Sapien and Liz Sherman in Cavendish Hall in the 1990's, where Sadu-Hem had turned four humans into these creatures. The were all killed by the B.P.R.D. agents.

The Conqueror Worm also turned people into Frog Monsters, which were then consumed by the Worm.

Katha-Hem also turned people into Frog Monsters during the apocalypse.

### Trivia
* Besides the Deep Ones, these creatures are also likley based on the second plague of Egypt (Ex. 7:25-8:15) and "three impure spirits that looked like frogs" from the End times (Revelation 16:13).

shortDefinition: "From Arkham" is a Lovecraftian short story by Australian author S. Gepp. It was published in the Candlemas 2019 edition of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in January 2019.  ### Synopsis When the f...
fullContent:
"From Arkham" is a Lovecraftian short story by Australian author S. Gepp. It was published in the Candlemas 2019 edition of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in January 2019.

### Synopsis
When the freight ship Arkham is shipwrecked offshore in 1887 during a particularly violent storm, some of the citizens of the burgeoning colony of Adelaide, Australia are determined to claim its cargo as salvage- despite the dire warning issued by the crew's sole survivor, a man driven to the brink of insanity from his long exposure to what lies within, named Howard Phillips.

Phillips relates to the men the story of how the ship agreed to transport a single metal-encased chest from Newport, Rhode Island to Liverpool, England. During the course of the journey, the ship was beset by storms and the men tormented by an unseen force. As they began to fear sleep, the crew took their own lives one by one until only Phillips was left, alone and adrift until the Arkham was wrecked on the Australian coast two years later.

Despite these warnings, the locals are determined to salvage the chest, which they believe must be extremely valuable if an entire ship was chartered to transport its contents. However, once they open the chest a dark force escapes, heading straight for town and dooming the inhabitants to become the playthings of whatever once dwelt within.

### Behind the Mythos
Although the creature which was imprisoned within the Arkham's chest is never named, some parts of the story hint that it may have been intended to be a Star-Spawn of Cthulhu. For example, when recalling his dreams, Howard Phillips describes the entity which haunts them as possessing "the wings of a bat as huge as any sea vessel ever built, tentacles like a squid hanging about a mouth I could not see;" later, when the being emerges from the ruptured casket, we are given the following description: "its full height, fully two times the size of Lincoln … bat-like wings … the scaled talons of a dragon … [t]he head was bulbous ... [t]here was no nose … and the mouth was invisible beneath a beard of writhing tentacles." All of these elements are compatible with common depictions of the Cthulhi, although not entirely with H. P. Lovecraft's original description.

fullContent:
"From Between" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
In post-World War I Britain, the narrator responds to a request for help from his old university friend, who bids him to travel to his ancestral home. There, he finds his friend in a terrible state, his experiences in the trenches having impacted him tremendously.

The friend has discovered a chamber beneath his manor which is inscribed with strange and seemingly-indecipherable runes, which he requires aid in translating. The narrator quickly determines them to be musical notes and as he plays, the two are swept off into the incomprehensible universe of a sleeping god. Although the narrator manages to bring himself back, his friend does not, remaining drifting in the other realm with all thoughts of the War happily forgotten.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, a learned scholar.
*Roger, the narrator's close friend.

### Publication History
"From Between" was published in the collection Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in April 2017.

### Trivia
*Although not explicitly referencing either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos, Meikle's inclusion of "From Between" in Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates that he believes it to be in the spirit of these works. Additionally, the premise of the story, that of an ancient sleeping god from outside of our reality whose dreams call to us, is very much Lovecraftian in nature.
*The story is very similar to another of Meikle's works, "Carnacki: The Larkhill Barrow"; indeed, one short passage describing the carven chamber is almost word-for-word identical. This leads to the question of whether the less-developed "From Between" was an original draft of the Carnacki story.

fullContent:
"From Beyond" is a short story by writer H. P. Lovecraft. It was written in 1920 and was first published in The Fantasy Fan in June 1934 (Vol. 1, No. 10).

### Synopsis
The story is told from the first person perspective of an unnamed narrator and details his experiences with a scientist named Crawford Tillinghast. Tillinghast creates an electronic device that emits a resonance wave, which stimulates an affected person’s pineal gland, thereby allowing them to perceive planes of existence outside the scope of mundane reality. 

Sharing the experience with Tillinghast, the narrator becomes cognizant of a translucent, alien environment that overlaps our own recognized reality. From this perspective, he witnesses hordes of strange and horrific creatures that defy description. Tillinghast reveals that he has used his machine to transport his house servants into the overlapping plane of reality. He also reveals that the effect works both ways, and allows the denizens of the alternate dimension to perceive humans. Tillinghast's servants were attacked and killed by one such entity, and Tillinghast informs the narrator that it is right behind him. Terrified beyond measure, the narrator picks up a gun and shoots it at the machine, destroying it. Tillinghast dies immediately thereafter as a result of a stroke. The police investigate the scene and it is placed on record that Tillinghast murdered the servants in spite of their remains never being found.

### Characters
### Crawford Tillinghast


### Reaction

The book Science-Fiction: The Early Years describes the concepts of "From Beyond" as "very interesting, despite stiff, immature writing". S. T. Joshi judges it "unlikely that 'From Beyond'...will ever be regarded as one of Lovecraft's better tales", due to "its slipshod style, melodramatic excess and general triteness of plot".

Joshi also considers Crawford Tillinghast's references to the pineal gland to be a joke at the expense of René Descartes, who proposed that this gland was the point of mediation between the material body and the immaterial soul. Despite Joshi's somewhat eccentric interpretation, a more likely explanation is the influences of  Theosophy and fringe Egyptology. The Third Eye or Prophetic Eye is located ...in the pineal gland.

### Connections
*Joshi points out that "From Beyond"'s theme of "a reality beyond that revealed to us by the senses, or that which we experience in everyday life", is continued in later Lovecraft tales, such as "The Shunned House" (1924), "The Colour Out of Space" (1927), "The Dreams in the Witch-House" and others.
*A narrator says that "scientific study and reflection had taught us that the known universe of three dimensions embraces the merest fraction of the whole cosmos of substance and energy." (: "The Shunned House")

fullContent:
From Beyond is a 1986 low budget horror film from director Stuart Gordon. It is an adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft's short story of the same name.

### Overview
Directed by Gordon and co-written by him with Dennis Paoli and Brian Yuzna, From Beyond stars Mythos screen regulars Jeffrey Combs and Barbara Crampton in the lead roles (Combs and Crampton had previously worked with Gordon on the 1985 film adaptation Re-Animator). It was filmed in Italy with a local crew to keep production costs down.

About one minute of footage was cut prior to From Beyond's original 1986 release in order to secure an "R" rating; this footage has since been restored and the film re-released in an extended director's cut.

### Trivia
*The film's tagline is "Humans are such easy prey".
*A sequel miniseries titled The Resonator: Miskatonic U, written and directed by William Butler, was released in 2021.

One of the more popular of H. P. Lovecraft's short stories, "From Beyond" has been referenced numerous time in popular culture. This page offers a non-comprehensive alphabetical list of these.

### Music
*Manilla Road: The American heavy metal band adapted the story to a song of the same name featured in their 1990 album The Courts of Chaos.
*Massacre: The American death metal band released a largely Lovecraft-themed album of the same name in 1991.
*Nox Arcana: The dark ambient and Halloween-themed duo based their 2009 album Blackthorn Asylum on this story, with some twists of their own.
*Ripping Corpse: The death metal band's song "Beyond Humanity" is clearly directly inspired by the Lovecraft story and the Gordon film.
*Sleep: The American stoner doom metal band and Lovecraft devotees included a song of the same name on their classic 1992 album Sleep's Holy Mountain.

### Film & Television
*Banshee Chapter: movie which features a similar plot involving the drug Dimethyltryptamine instead of Ultraviolet. At one point Lovecraft's short story is explicitly mentioned.
*From Beyond (1986): A 1986 film adaptation of the short story directed by Stuart Gordon; written by Dennis Paoli, Gordon and Brian Yuzna; and starring Jeffrey Combs and Barbara Crampton.
*Star Trek: The Next Generation: the episode "Phantasms" features inter-phasic parasites, undetectable under normal conditions, that feed off of cellular matter, and are perceived by Data as surrealistic objects during his dream program. Individuals experiencing elements of the world beyond our own through dreams and visions is a common theme in Lovecraftian literature.
*Stargate SG-1: in the episode "Sight Unseen", an alien device is accidentally activated that allows members of SG-1 to see, but not interact with, strange insect-like creatures who inhabit a dimension parallel to our own. Though originally confined to the Cheyenne Mountain Complex, the phenomenon of this "second sight" is also spread by touch. It quickly spreads to nearby populations, mostly by way of a "sight-infected" conspiracy theorist who stumbles upon a real government conspiracy concerning aliens and the SG-1. Parts of Colorado and Wyoming are "quarantined" until the process can be reversed. Hallucinogenic gas is used as cover-up story.

### Prose
*"Immotor": a short story written by Chiaki J. Konaka, featuring a "perpetual motion machine" which causes several people to mysteriously disappear. By the end of the story, it is revealed that the machine makes people immortal by taking them to an extra-dimensional location, inhabited by a hideous deep sea fish-like creature. This is possibly a homage to Lovecraft's story.
*The Jennifer Morgue: Charles Stross novel that features an electronic device known as a "Tillinghast resonator", which allows the user to see otherwise invisible entities.

fullContent:
"From Cabinet 34, Drawer 6" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first in 2005's Weird Shadows Over Innsmouth. It revolves around the discovery of an impossible fossil, Grendelonyx innsmouthensis--"Grendel's claw from Innsmouth"--in a storage cabinet in a museum. The story was reprinted in Kiernan's collections Two Worlds and In Between (2011) and Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (2019).

Kiernan's story was inspired by both H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth and the 1954 film The Creature From the Black Lagoon. She relates in the afterward to Weird Shadows Over Innsmouth:


### Locations
The Pratt Museum was a real museum located at Amherst College in Massachusetts; since a 2006 move on campus, it's been known as the Beneski Museum of Natural History. It houses the largest collection of dinosaur tracks in the world.

The discovered fossil bears a label "from Naval dredgings, USS Cormorant (April, 1928), Lat. 42°40'N., Long. 70°43'W, NE. of old Innsmouth Harbor, Essex Co., Mass. ?Devonian." The coordinates are about 1,000 feet from the entrance to Essex Bay, near Coffin Beach.

Kiernan provides explicit directions to the fictional location of Innsmouth: From Ipswich, "take Argilla Road out of town and stay on it all the way down to the river." Unfortunately, in the story, these directions lead to "a locked gate and chain-link fence crowned with loops of razor wire." In real life, the directions would take you to the Castle Neck River Reservation, owned by the Essex County Greenbelt Association.

### Characters
*Lacey Morrow, a paleontologist who discovers a fossilized claw in a cabinet at the Pratt Museum
*Dr. Solomon Monalisa, head of a secret organization that preserves and conceals evidence of Earth's true history. He is described as a "grinning scarecrow of an old man in a blue fedora and a shiny gabardine suit, blue bow tie to match his hat.... [H]is violet-grey eyes sparkle like amethysts and spring water." He first appeared in Kiernan's short story "Onion".
*Dr. Jasper Morgan, Morrow's boss at the Pratt.
*Dr. Mary Hanisak, a colleague at the Pratt's zoology department who specializes in the evolution of rodent teeth. Described as "chubby little Dr. Hanisak like a storybook gnome". Has a secret connection to Monalisa.

fullContent:
"From the Parchments of Pnom" is a text created by combining excerpts of two letters written by Clark Ashton Smith to R. H. Barlow in 1934, the first of which had previously been published as "The Family Tree of the Gods". In these letters, Smith answers some of Barlow's questions about the Cthulhu Mythos while genially pretending to have consulted occult sources such as the fictional Parchments of Pnom, thus acting as if dealing with a historical mythology. In addition to his own stories, Smith also references the works of H. P. Lovecraft, Lord Dunsany, and James Branch Cabell.

"From the Parchments of Pnom" was published in The Tsathoggua Cycle: Terror Tales of the Toad God. Editor Robert M. Price introduces it as "not strictly speaking a story", but "nonetheless an important piece of fiction".

### Content
Viewed as a work of fiction, "From the Parchments of Pnom" presents a fragmentary narrative in which an unnamed scholar (Smith) answers questions from an unnamed correspondent (Barlow) about the myths surrounding Azathoth, Tsathoggua, and other deities. His main source, albeit not the only one, is an ancient text called the Parchments of Pnom. The time period is unknown, although the scholar mentions a type of whiskey that is "imported from Mars".

He starts out by revealing that, while Azathoth's androgynous children reproduced asexually like their parent, many of their offspring were single-gendered. For instance, the androgynous Cxaxukluth spawned at least two male sons: Hziulquoigmnzhah and Ghizguth, the latter which married Zstylzhemgni and fathered Tsathoggua. He also mentions a descendant of the gods named Knygathin Zhaum, who regained the Azathothian ability to spawn amorphous children after "the stress of his numerous decapitations", and hints of another legend that he hasn't translated yet. For details concerning a deity named Tulu or Cthulhu, the author recommends that the correspondent contact a certain Ech-Pi-El, who can provide more information.

Although Cxaxukluth's sons were born far away from the Solar System, the entire family eventually came to reside on Yuggoth, where Cxaxukluth remains to this day. To escape his parent's cannibalistic inclinations, Hziulquoigmnzhah moved on to Yaksh, where the natives worshiped him, then onto Cykranosh, followed aeons later by his nephew Tsathoggua. The encounter of Eibon with Hzioulquoigmnzhah many ages later is mentioned.

From Cykranosh, Tsathoggua traveled interdimensionally to Earth, first appearing in the lightless subterranean country of N'kai, and then moving to caves closer to the surface, where he was venerated by the natives until "the coming of the ice" forced him to retreat. The author speculates that the natives of Yoth and K'n-yan might have misunderstood or forgotten parts of the legend, thus explaining any potential contradictions told in the narrative of Zamacona.


Moving on to other questions, the scholar reveals that Tsathoggua's wife was known by names such as Chus

Fthaggua is a fictional entity created by Donald Wandrei for his short story "The Fire Vampires". It was first incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Lin Carter in his short story "The Horror in the Gallery", which portrays Fthaggua as a Lesser Old One who serves Cthugha.

### Background
The King Regent of the Fire Vampires, Fthaggua appears as a great flickering ball of cold blue flame. It dwells with the Fire Vampires within an enormous edifice upon the surface of the reddish-blue comet Ktynga, a celestial body which Fthaggua can guide across the cosmos and which is possessed of many strange properties, not least the incredible heat that it radiates or the fact that it can exceed the speed of light.

Fthaggua was killed by the human scientist Gustav Norby in the year 2339 after it attempted to subjugate the Earth. (: "The Fire Vampires")

The entity may have a connection to the Great Old One known as Cthugha. Although it is not entirely clear, it has been speculated that Fthaggua is either a servant or an avatar of Cthugha. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

In the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game by Chaosium, Fthaggua is mentioned as a being that serves Cthugua and has the potential to evolve into the Old One. It reforms in 50 days after it is defeated. (: Malleus Monstrorum: Cthulhu Mythos Bestiary Volume II)

### The Fire Vampires of Fthaggua


### In Other Media
*In the mobile game Tower of Saviors, Fthaggua was originally an insignificant piece of stardust with no self consciousness until the power and influence of Azathoth transformed it into an entity of raging flames with a desire to cause destruction. Unlike most depictions, this version of Fthaggua has orange flames instead of blue, as well as resembling a more dragon-like creature.
*In the mobile game Fate/Grand Order, the Foreigner-class Servant Yang Guifei is used as a vessel by Cthugha. Despite this, the depiction appears to be at least partially based on Fthaggua due to Guifei's blue flames and ability to summon Fire Vampires.

fullContent:
Fungi from Yuggoth is a sonnet sequence by supernatural horror writer H. P. Lovecraft that constitute a continuous first-person narrative. It concerns a person who obtains an ancient book of esoteric knowledge that allows one to travel to other planets and strange parts of the universe. The title is a term for the Mi-Go, an alien race the narrator encounters, which are fungoid beings resembling crustaceans which hail from the planet Yuggoth, to which the narrator has unwittingly traveled.

### Plot
### I. The Book
In the tangled alleys of a seaside town, the narrator searches a bookshop for tomes and grimoires, and finds a strange book.  He wants to buy it, but can't see the shopkeeper, hearing only a disembodied laugh.

### II. Pursuit
The narrator flees the shop, hiding the book under his coat. Despite not being seen stealing it, he can't shake the laugh from the shop, and the sound of approaching footsteps as the path ahead grows more and more unusual.

### III. The Key
Making it home and bolting the door, the narrator reveals his intention to use the book to bridge dimensions in order to explain his unusual visions of sunset spires and twilight woods.

### IV. Recognition
The narrator enters a vision of the "strange, grey world" of Yuggoth, where a victim on an altar to the Nameless One is being feasted upon by inhuman creatures. When the body shrieks at him with a "dead cry," the narrator recognizes it as himself!

### V. Homecoming
A daemon tells the narrator that he was going to take him "home," and escorts him through a seaside city and into the sunset-lit sky, taking him to a black gulf he said "was his home when he had sight."

### VI. The Lamp
The narrator enters "hollow cliffs" where "frightened hieroglyphs" warn all Earth creatures away. There he finds nothing but a lamp containing "traces of some curious oil" and embossed with "symbols hinting vaguely of strange sin." Ignoring "the fears of forty centuries," he takes the lamp back to his tent, and when he lights it, the "vast shapes we saw...seared our lives with awe."

### VII. Zaman's Hill
Zaman's Hill, near Aylesbury, had a reputation for two centuries for mangling animals and losing boys. Then one day the village at its foot disappears, houses and people alike, and a mailman is thought mad for saying the hill had greedy eyes and wide-stretched jaws. 

### VIII. The Port
The narrator sets off from Arkham, and ten miles later reaches the trail that follows the cliff above Boynton Beach; he hopes to reach a ridge that overlooks Innsmouth by sunset. He sees a sign  but seeing a reaches a seaside port ten miles off of Arkham as the sun set, as a sailboat from his destination of Innsmouth sailed by, which the narrator did not wave to when he feels that Innsmouth was a very oddly gray and unsettling town.

fullContent:
Futurama is an American animated science fiction sitcom created by Matt Groening of The Simpsons fame. It has spawned a series of spin-off comics, numerous direct-to-DVD movies, and endless merchandise.

### Premise
The story follows a 20th-century delivery boy, Philip J. Fry, who is accidentally frozen in a cryogenic tube. Awakening in the 31st century, he gains employment with interplanetary delivery company Planet Express, which is owned and operated by one of his descendants. The majority of plotlines involve Fry and his two best friends, fellow Planet Express employees Turanga Leela, a one-eyed mutant, and Bender, an entirely amoral former industrial robot. A host of recurrent characters also feature.

### Mythos Connections
Many Lovecraftian staples have been nodded to or made cameos during the course of the franchise, including R'lyeh, the Great Race of Yith, and even Cthulhu himself. In addition, several original entities which could be considered Lovecraftian have appeared in the show, including the Being of Inconceivable Horror, a three-eyed octopoid creature who purchases the Milky Way at auction.

G. W. Thomas (born 1963) is a published Canadian author with an extensive career dating back to 1987 with the publication of his Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game scenario "The City in the Sea" in the supplement Cthulhu Now (co-written with Lynn Willis). He lives and works in Athabaska, Alberta, Canada. 

His work has appeared in Writer’s Digest along with other magazines such as The Writer, The Armchair Detective, The Mystery Review and Black October Magazine. In 1999 he received an Honorable Mention from Years’ Best Fantasy & Horror for “Waking Dream” (Flesh & Blood #4, June 1999). Currently he is focused on writing Mythos Noir with his Book Collector series, as well as sword and sorcery fiction.

He is the owner and operator of RAGE machine Books (stylised in his way) and the Dark Worlds Quarterly website which functions as his promotional site as well as his personal blog.

Gahan Allen Wilson (18 February 1930-21 November 2019) was an American cartoonist, illustrator and author.

### Overview
In addition to his work as a cartoonist, Wilson also contributed cover art for books such as The Horror in the Museum and Other Revisions. In 1975 he created a bust of H. P. Lovecraft for the World Fantasy Awards; this bust was used as a trophy given to winners of the award for the next forty years, until controversy over Lovecraft’s racist leanings caused it to be retired in favour of a less culturally-offensive design.

Officer Galeas Morgan is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Fiction series of Cthulhu Mythos stories. He made his first appearance in the 2017 novella Hour of the Huntress by Dave Gross.

### Description
A junior officer in the Arkham Police Department, Morgan is a tall fellow but almost painfully thin, to the point where Jenny Barnes, on their first meeting, guessed that he skipped meals. Although prone to a certain social awkwardness, he has shown himself to be a brave and resourceful individual. (: Hour of the Huntress)

Morgan appears to be in a developing relationship with tomboy mechanic Lonnie Ritter, Lonnie seemingly possessing deep feelings for the officer, feelings which may not be entirely reciprocated. (: Hour of the Huntress)

### History
Morgan assisted globetrotting dilettante Jenny Barnes in her quest to find her missing sister Izzie in the town of Arkham. Along with Lonnie Ritter and Miskatonic University anthropology professor Tilde Félix, Morgan fought a cult dedicated to the Outer God Shub-Niggurath, facing down and banishing the Dark Young which they had summoned during a sacrificial ritual. (: Hour of the Huntress)

Morgan was also briefly seen during lecturer Norman Withers' attempts to rescue his missing colleague, German physicist Claus Schmidt. (: Ire of the Void)

* Ire of the Void (2018)

Gamba is a fictional character from the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald.

### Biography
Gamba was a messenger who worked for Allen, the head factor of the small trading post of M'gonga, close to the Ugandan border. In 1929, Dr. Thomas Slauenwite secretly used him as part of an experiment to test the lethality of the hybridised devil-flies that he intended to use to kill Dr. Moore.

On August 17, Slauenwite arranged so that one of his flies would get loose and bite Gamba, having previously arranged a similar incident for Batta. Slauenwite killed the fly and treated Gamba, for which the latter was grateful. Unbeknownst to all but him, his experiment involved giving actual medicine to Gamba while only pretending to medicate Batta. Accordingly, Batta perished, while Gamba made a full recovery. (: "Winged Death")

fullContent:
A gambrel roof is an architectural feature frequently cited in the fiction of H. P. Lovecraft. A roof with a steeply sloping section below a section with a gentler slope--think of the profile of the classic barn--the style is characteristic of 17th and 18th century architecture, an era for which Lovecraft had a great fondness.

### In Lovecraft
"The Unnamable" (1923):The crumbling slate slabs, the patriarchal trees, and the centuried gambrel roofs of the witch-haunted old town [of Arkham] that stretched around, all combined to rouse my spirit in defence of my work...."The Festival" (1923):I saw Kingsport outspread frostily in the gloaming; snowy Kingsport with its ancient vanes and steeples, ridgepoles and chimney-pots, wharves and small bridges, willow-trees and graveyards; endless labyrinths of steep, narrow, crooked streets, and dizzy church-crowned central peak that time durst not touch; ceaseless mazes of colonial houses piled and scattered at all angles and levels like a child’s disordered blocks; antiquity hovering on grey wings over winter-whitened gables and gambrel roofs; fanlights and small-paned windows one by one gleaming out in the cold dusk to join Orion and the archaic stars."The Ghost-Eater" (1924, with C. M. Eddy, Jr.)“Then he sent to Mayfair[, Maine] for the Count—his name was Feodor Tchernevsky and he had bought the old gambrel-roofed Fowler place up State Street—to come out and see him....""He" (1925):About me in my exhaustion I could see  [in New York City] only strange walls and windows and old gambrel roofs."The Silver Key" (1926):Then he went back to Arkham, the terrible witch-haunted old town of his forefathers in New England, and had experiences in the dark, amidst the hoary willows and tottering gambrel roofs, which made him seal forever certain pages in the diary of a wild-minded ancestor....

[Coming upon the old Carter place outside Arkham:] And dogs barked as the yellow light of small-paned windows shone out at the farther turn, and the Pleiades twinkled across the open knoll where a great gambrel roof stood black against the dim west."The Strange High House in the Mist" (1926):Granny Orne, whose tiny gambrel-roofed abode in Ship Street [in Kingsport] is all covered with moss and ivy, croaked over something her grandmother had heard at second-hand....

Games Workshop is a British wargames manufacturer based in Nottingham, England, the largest of its type in the world. They are best known for their Warhammer Fantasy Battles/Age of Sigmar fantasy and Warhammer 40,000 science fiction settings.

Founded in 1975 by Steve Jackson, Ian Livingston, and John Peake, Games Workshop started out selling traditional gaming accessories such as game boards through a mail order service. The company gained traction in the gaming industry after landing U.K. distribution rights for TSR, Inc.'s fantasy roleplaying game Dungeons & Dragons, and followed up on this success by obtaining licenses to publish material for other roleplaying properties, including Chaosium's Runequest and Iron Crown Enterprises' Middle-earth Role Playing, as well as wargames and miniatures for Doctor Who and various 2000AD properties.

During the early- to mid-1980s, Games Workshop produced a number of supplements for another of Chaosium's franchises, Call of Cthulhu, and published further material in their monthly magazine White Dwarf. During the early 1990s, they began to eliminate all properties which they did not own from their catalogues, focussing solely on their own products; they have maintained this business model in the years since.

Set in the Peruvian Andes and at the Yanacocha gold strip mine there, it tells the story of the awakening of an Elder Thing known as the Scientist after 100 million years, and the efforts of US special forces soldier Lt. The Garuda Birds are a species of extra-dimensional avian created by Jason Williams for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement Secrets of Tibet.

### Background
Garuda Birds reside in the Dreamlands and occasionally cross over into Tibet's western regions. Enormously strong and agile creatures, they can be summoned and if bound are capable of understanding simple commands. They can carry up to four individuals and are capable of interstellar flight.

### Behind the Mythos
The name of the Garuda is taken from a steed of the god Vishnu from the Hindu religion .

Gary Clayton Myers (born 15 August 1952) is an American writer of fantasy and horror, as well as an occasional artist. He is a resident of Fullerton, California. His first book, The House of the Worm, was a collection of Cthulhu Mythos stories in the fantasy manner of H. P. Lovecraft and Lord Dunsany; it was published by Arkham House in 1975. His second book, Dark Wisdom: New Tales of the Old Ones, was a collection of Cthulhu Mythos stories in a more contemporary horror mode; it was published by Mythos Books in 2007.

Myers is the illustrator for most of his books.  He contributed ten black-and-white interior illustrations to the Mythos Books edition of Dark Wisdom. He also contributed cover illustrations to his self-published editions of The Country of the Worm, Dark Wisdom, Gray Magic, Lovecraft's Syndrome, Myers's Folly and The Last Offering.

What may be his final written work, as the title may suggest, was The Last Offering: A Horror Play. This was his first and only play, a late return to the fantasy manner of Lovecraft and Dunsany; it was self-published through Kindle Direct Publishing in 2024.

"Gate of the Gods" is a Lovecraftian poem by author Oliver Smith. It was published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of digital zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in 2021.

### Synopsis
The story tells of a monstrous creature known as the Dreamer who falls to earth amidst the "ruins of another world". It then goes on to detail how the nascent human civilisation bound the being to its will before it rose against them and crushed its former jailors.

### Behind the Mythos
Cthulhu is often referred to as "The Dreamer" in Mythos fiction; however, primitive humans besting a creature such as this and taking "his crown" would not seem to fit with the most common interpretation of a Great Old One.

"Gathering Forces" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement Punktown by Miskatonic River Press/Chronicle City in 2018 .

The story is the second in a short series set in Thomas's dystopian sci-fi setting of Punktown, which charts the summoning of an ancient and malevolent got named Ugghiutu.

### Synopsis
As the Kalian extremists from "Drawing No. 8" begins the ritual to summon an avatar of Ugghiutu, two former gang members begin to realise that something is wrong in their habitation block. While the seed of the avatar grows and starts to consume the neighbourhood, what remains of old gang reform, ready to face the threat with whatever weapons they have to hand.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite being the second story in a trilogy, delays in the publication of Punktown  meant that "Gathering Forces" did not see print until three years after "Wunderwaffe", the final part, was published.

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance in Punktown, "Gathering Forces" has also appeared in the 2019 collection of Jeffrey Thomas's own works, The Summoning of the Old Ones .

Gatsby and the Great Race is a Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game scenario book written by Paul Fricker and published by Chaosium as part of their Monograph line of supplements. First released in October 2005 in a paperback format, it is currently out of print.

### Overview


Taking place in a 1920s setting, Gatsby and the Great Race is unusual for a roleplaying game scenario in that it is able to be played by a single small group, multiple groups playing individually with several keepers to keep the game coordinated, or a large group of up to 32 players.

The plot involves the heir of a grand old mansion whose foolish actions have caught a group of partygoers in a Groundhog Day-style time loop.

Gazira is a fictional monster created by Michael Dziesinski for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

### Background
Gazira is a colossal monster whose existence and activities the Japanese government has kept a secret, resulting that most believe it to be a fictional monster created by the media (known to the West as Gadzella). Nuclear radiation wakes it from hibernation, as does strong seismic activity. It's a courageous beast though not a particularly intelligent one.

After going on its rampage, Gazira returns to its hibernation site. Its rampages are covered up as the result of typhoons or earthquakes, with the locals generously paid off. It considers Japan to be its turf and will battle creatures which are of similar size, including various Great Old Ones. The being has the ability to exhale a column of radioactive fire. (: Secrets of Japan)

### Behind the Mythos
Gazira is a clear nod to the iconic kaiju Godzilla, with its nuclear and seismic plot devices being identical to those portrayed in the original run of films. Even the names Gazira and Gadzella are near-carbon copies of the real world names given to the creature (Gojira and Godzilla, respectively).

Gedney is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his horror sci-fi novella At the Mountains of Madness.

In the short story "Gedney", by Laurence J. Cornford, he is given the first name Leonard.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In 1930, Gedney was a graduate student at Miskatonic University who joined the Pabodie Expedition to Antarctica. Specifically, he was part of the group that accompanied Prof. Lake in his quest to find the remains of a prehistoric organism responsible for certain fossilised tracks. This led to the discovery of fabulously well-preserved specimens of a previously unsuspected species.

However, the exciting discovery turned tragic when it transpired that some of the specimens weren't dead, but dormant. The revived creatures were attacked by the dogs and felt threatened by the men (not helped by the sight of the dissected remains of their companions). In the ensuing chaos, they butchered Lake's entire group, after which they gave a proper burial to their comrades and proceeded to dissect the dogs and men in order to learn more about them. When they departed, they took with them the bodies of Gedney and one of the dogs, along with several other items piled up in the sledges, and headed towards their nearest city.

On January 25, 1931, Prof. Dyer and his party found the remains of the massacre. Seeing as there was no sign of Gedney, they were forced to conclude that he might have been responsible. The next day, Dyer and Danforth took an airplane to try to survey the nearby mountain range. This led them to discover the Elder Things' city, where they eventually did find the sledges containing the body of Gedney, as well as the missing dog and the other items, next to the bodies of the Elder Things themselves, decapitated by a Shoggoth. (: At the Mountains of Madness)

### In the Expanded Mythos
Laurence J. Cornford wrote a story called "Gedney", which takes place after the events of Lovecraft's novella. It involves the discovery of a man claiming to be Gedney, the identity of whom cannot be confirmed. The story's narrator concludes that he might be an organic replica created by the Elder Things, although he does allow the possibility that the replica might house the reanimated brain of the original Gedney, which would explain why he seemed so convinced of his identity.

### In Other Media
The Zenescope Entertainment comic Madness of Wonderland includes a subplot inspired by At the Mountains of Madness, in which the members of an underground expedition are found dead, apparently killed by a Shoggoth, with one of the men absent. The missing man is named Gedney as a nod to Lovecraft's novella.

"Gedney" is a horror sci-fi short story by Laurence J. Cornford which serves as a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's novella At the Mountains of Madness. It was published in the 2015 anthology Beyond the Mountains of Madness.

### Synopsis
The story takes the form of a letter addressed to "Edward Lyle of Brown University", who is apparently interested in creating a website where the photographs and journals of the Starkweather-Moore Expedition to Antarctica could be made available. The narrator advises Lyle to avoid making too much mention of the previous Miskatonic Expedition led by Prof. William Dyer, who is generally believed to have suffered a "mental collapse", as his account of the Antarctic discoveries mention a pre-human civilisation and a mountain range taller than the Himalayas, which Starkweather-Moore and others failed to locate.

However, the narrator concedes that Starkweather-Moore did report some odd things, from the inexplicably mutilated bodies of penguins to the sounds of airplanes flying at night when none of their own were being used. Perhaps strangest of all was the discovery of a living man in the frozen continent who claimed to be Leonard Gedney, a member of the Miskatonic Expedition initially reported as missing after the mysterious massacre that claimed the lives of several men, but whose body Dyer claimed to have found inside the allegedly pre-human city amidst the mountains. From this point on, the narrator reveals that they have conducted their own investigation about the Gedney case and came to some conclusions that cannot be made public.

For one thing, the identity of the man who claimed to be Gedney could never be verified in the following decades. The story he told was that the leader of his group, Prof. Lake, had gone mad and killed the others, but that Gedney managed to escape and find shelter inside a cave, where he survived for the next three years on a diet of penguin meat and lichens, in addition to the few supplies he could salvage. The veracity of this was deemed dubious, in part due to the man's physical appearance, which was similar, but not identical, to the available photographs of Gedney. People who had known Gedney were not positively sure that it was him, and while he did get many facts right about Gedney's life, he also made basic mistakes. Since the evidence pointed towards an impostor, while the man himself remained fully convinced of being Gedney, he was eventually committed to Arkham Asylum, from which he escaped in 1943 and was never seen again.

Intrigued by the story, the narrator recounts how he went to Arkham and studied the files personally. The patient had been subjected to a full medical exam, complete with x-rays that revealed a piece of metallic wire wrapped around his spinal cord, which no conceivable explanation could account for. Gemma Files (April 4, 1968) is a Canadian horror and dark fantasy writer. Her work has appeared in numerous anthologies of Lovecraftian fiction, including A Mountain Walked, Lovecraft Unbound, Lovecraft's Monsters, Autumn Cthulhu, Dreams From the Witch House, Cthulhu's Daughters, and Black Seas of Infinity.

Files was born in London, England, to actors Elva Mai Hoover and Gary Files. The family relocated to Toronto, Ontario, where Files still resides. A graduate of Ryerson University, she reviewed film for Toronto's eye Weekly from 1993-2001, and taught at the Toronto Film School from 2001-2008.

She is the author of over 100 short stories, five short-story collections, and five novels, including Experimental Film, which won the 2015 Shirley Jackson Award for best novel. Her short story, "The Emperor's Old Bones", won the International Horror Guild Award for Best Short Story of 1999. Five of her short stories were adapted by the Canadian horror anthology TV series The Hunger. Files has also published three collections of poetry.

Gene Rodman Wolfe (7 May 1931 - 14 April 2014) was a prolific American author widely regarded as one of the finest genre writers of his day, winning several awards and receiving nominations for many more. Although his works largely focus of the science fiction and fantasy genres, he also wrote a number of Lovecraftian pieces, such as "Lord of the Land", which was included in anthologies such as Lovecraft's Legacy (1990, Tor), Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology (1995, Arkham House), and The Book of Cthulhu (2011, Night Shade Press).

"Genuine Article" is a short story by mythos author J. B. Lee.

### Synopsis
A woman researching New Age philosophy for a book uncovers a copy of the Necronomicon which possesses her and attempts to force her to recite a series of incantations which will bring about the return of Yog-Sothoth. The woman's will is strong, however, and she is able to destroy the book, although the effort involved kills her.

### Characters

*Shana Anne McEwan, a successful Christian author researching material for her new book.
*Curtis Daniels, Shana's boyfriend.
*Tara Moonfire/Cynthia Atkinson, a New Age bookstore owner.

### Publication History
"Genuine Article" was published in the fanzine Nightscapes in April 1998. It appeared in Dark Legacy magazine in October of the same year, and was included in the anthology The Best of Dark Legacy, Volume 2 in September 2016.

### Trivia

*The character Le Novar is referenced by Shana McEwan as being author of one of the source books she read for her research.

Geoff Gillan is games designer and occasional author best known for his work on the classic Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game campaign supplement Horror on the Orient Express. He has written extensively for the Call of Cthulhu system in the years before and since, and was the co-creator of the Convicts & Cthulhu sub-setting for the game. He has also contributed to a number of Cthulhu Reborn's Cthulhu Eternal system. His short fiction has appeared in Chaosium's tie-in anthology Madness on the Orient Express.

Gillan is also the founder of Mutant Brainchild, a small press publisher specialising in genre fiction, which he runs with help from his wife, Cathie, and daughters Lucille and Abigail.

fullContent:
George Allan England (1877 - 1936) was an American explorer, poet, and author, known for his science fiction stories. Born in Fort McPherson, Nebraska, he later moved to Maine, where he ran for governor in 1912. Politically, he was a socialist, which is reflected in some of his novels, such as The Air Trust (1915), which portrays a world in which capitalist moguls charge people for the very oxygen they breathe. Some of England's stories have been adapted as films.

England's short story "The Thing from — Outside" was included in the Cthulhu Mythos anthology The Ithaqua Cycle. The story was first published in Hugo Gernsback's magazine Science and Invention in 1923, and reprinted in the very first issue of Amazing Stories in 1926. It is an early example of cosmic horror, which Richard L. Tierney argues might have influenced August Derleth's creation, Ithaqua. Derleth himself included England's story in his 1948 anthology Strange Ports of Call.

England was one of the many pulp authors who were spoofed in the comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century", by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. In the story, England and A. Hyatt Verrill are mentioned briefly as a pair of adventurers named "A. Hijacked Barrell and G. A. Scotland".

George Barnaby, the Lawyer, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games as a playable Investigator for their Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-related content.

### History
Always one with a strong desire for control over his situation, George spent a month in prison for a crime of which he was innocent. The experience instilled in him a need for justice, and this pushed him into the decision to become a lawyer.

Being a highly charismatic and intelligent man, he proved to be extremely well suited to his chosen profession and, after a long and successful career, retired to spend time with his wife Maria. Their dream was to buy a boat and sail the seven seas in their old age.

However, George's life was shattered when, not long after retiring, Maria was murdered by assailants who wore occult jewelry. Vowing revenge, he tracked the men down to the small city of Arkham, where he prepared his final act of justice.

### Behind the Mythos
Originally conceived as an Investigator character for the Innsmouth Horror expansion to Arkham Horror Second Edition, George was also included as a playable character in the similar Eldritch Horror board game. In 2010, Fantasy Flight released a pre-painted plastic miniature of him as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, but this has since been discontinued (all ).

### Trivia
*George's character biographies from Arkham Horror and Eldritch Horror differ slightly. In the first, he had only just retired before the men broke into his house, killed his wife and burned it down, while in the second they had bought a boat and sailed to Bombay, where he took a quick trip to shore before returning to find Maria's body surrounded by occult symbols.

George Birch is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his horror short story "In the Vault". Unlike the typical Lovecraft protagonist, he is noted to be a remarkably "calloused" man who remains practical-minded and unaffected by situations that would likely scare a more sensitive person, such as being stuck inside a tomb with several corpses. Even so, like many other Lovecraft characters, the events he experiences still end up permanently costing him his peace of mind.

### Biography
George Birch worked as an undertaker in the small town of Peck Valley, where he was widely regarded as a crude man with little in the way of ethics or professional standards. Whenever a body didn't quite fit the coffin he had carved for it, Birch would simply arrange its limbs in the best possible configuration, unperturbed by the lack of dignity and respect for the deceased. This wasn't done out of malice, but rather a careless attitude that didn't put too much weight to such matters. On one occasion, he mistakenly buried the coffin of Judge Capwell under the headstone of Hannah Bixby, which was only discovered after Bixby's relatives decided to move her to a different cemetery.

Despite his thoughtless attitude, Birch wasn't without friends. In 1876, when he went bankrupt, a kindly old man named Matthew Fenner was very generous to him and helped him get through that period.

In the cold winter of December 1880, the ground of Peck Valley Cemetery froze solid, which forced Birch to store all the bodies in the town's receiving-tomb to wait to be buried in spring. Nine of the town's inhabitants died during that winter and had to be stored together, including nonagenarian Darius Peck, kindly old Matthew Fenner, and the rancourous Asaph Sawyer, who died of fever. At first, a disinterested Birch carved a very crude and imperfect casket for Fenner, but changed his mind as he remembered how Fenner had helped him before and decided to make a better, more comfortable resting place for him. The crude casket he used for Asaph Sawyer, who had been spiteful and vengeful in life, and for whom Birch felt no sympathy. Since Sawyer had been considerably taller than Fenner, Birch secretly cut off Sawyer's feet to make his body fit inside the casket.

On a windy Good Friday afternoon on April 15th, 1881, a not entirely sober Birch drove his horse wagon to the receiving-tomb to pick up Fenner's casket for burial, having previously buried Peck's body earlier that week. Birch, who cared not for superstition, didn't think much of the date. When he was inside, the wind shut the door closed and the latch broke, trapping him with only eight corpses for company. Birch, as befitting his personality, was more annoyed than unnerved by the situation.

George C. Titteridge is a fictional character from the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald.

### Overview
George C. Titteridge was the proprietor and manager of the Orange Hotel in Bloemfontein, South Africa. On January 24, 1932, he was called by the hotel's clerk after one of the guests was found dead inside his room. Words were written in black ink on the ceiling, even though there was no possible arrangement of furniture or other means by which a man could reach it. A dead blue-winged fly floated inside a bottle of ammonia, and a notebook that belonged to the deceased guest revealed that his real name was Thomas Slauenwite.

Titteridge was one of the men present, along with constable Ian De Witt and coroner Johannes Bogaert, when Dr. Cornelius Van Keulen read aloud the contents of Slauenwite's notebook. All four men reacted with shock and horror to the events narrated and the significance of the words on the ceiling. (: "Winged Death")

George Gammell Angell (1834–November 23, 1926) is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who makes his first appearance in the 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Description
Angell is Professor Emeritus of Semitic languages at Brown University who was "widely known as an authority on ancient inscriptions, and had frequently been resorted to by the heads of prominent museums." Angell died suddenly after "a careless push" from a sailor "on a narrow hill street leading up from an ancient waterfront," while returning from the Newport boat. At the time of his death, at age 92, he was a childless widower. His research notes on the worldwide Cthulhu cult were discovered after his death by his nephew, Francis Wayland Thurston.

### Behind the Mythos
*"Angell" is an old Providence family name, as well as the name of the street where Lovecraft's childhood address was situated. The author also had an uncle named Gamwell, whose name was pronounced with a silent W.

George Julian Houtain (26 November 1884-21 August 1945 ) was an American amateur journalist and President of the National Amateur Press Association (1915-17) who established the Home Brew magazine with his wife E. Dorothy MacLaughlin. 

As the editor of The Zenith, Houtain met H. P. Lovecraft in July 1920 at a Boston amateur convention. He wrote the article "20 Webster Street: Lovecraft" for the January 1921 Issue before meeting Lovecraft in Boston again on February 22, 1921.

He went on to establish Home Brew and was the first person to commission Lovecraft for a professional work of fiction (Herbert West--Reanimator).

George Rogers is the main antagonist of H. P. Lovecraft's revision story "The Horror in the Museum". He runs a wax museum of horrors in the Southwark borough of London, and insists that some of the figures on display are actual specimens of eldritch creatures. 

### Description
Rogers is described as "tall, lean, and rather unkempt, with large black eyes which gazed combustively from a pallid and usually stubble-covered face."

### History
Rogers had previously worked for Madame Tussaud's, but he was discharged amidst "aspersions on his sanity and tales of his crazy forms of secret worship". He started his own museum in a basement of Southwark Street, where he was able to fully indulge his passion for "teratology and the iconography of nightmare." 

A "person of disconcertingly wide scholarship in dark and dubious fields," Rogers consulted "forbidden books like the Necronomicon, the Book of Eibon, or the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt," and even "such monstrous and half-fabulous books as the prehistoric Pnakotic fragments and the Dhol chants attributed to malign and non-human Leng," for ideas for displays. 

He took "mysterious trips to Thibet, the African interior, the Arabian desert, the Amazon valley, Alaska, and certain little-known islands of the South Pacific" to gather not just suggestions for wax figures, but actual specimens that he would put on display. 

Most notably, he acquired on a trip to Alaska a grotesque hibernating creature named Rhan-Tegoth.  Rogers proclaimed himself "High Priest of Rhan-Tegoth", and began to offer animal sacrifices to the creature in hopes that it would fully revive. 

Rogers met Stephen Jones, a connoisseur of bizarre art, and dared him to spend the night in the museum--hoping to make him another sacrifice to Rhan-Tegoth. Rogers dresses up in the hide of a Dimensional Shambler to surprise Jones, but Jones manages to subdue Rogers and flees, leaving Rogers to himself become a sacrifice to the alien god.

George Rogers' Wax Museum is, as the name implies, a private collection of waxworks opened in a basement by George Rogers after his dismissal from Madame Tussaud's. In addition to the usual grizzly models popular at the time, the museum also houses a curtained off alcove displaying an array of pieces too horrifying for the general public.

Some of them are actually bodies sealed in wax.

### Collection

*Madame Demers - Possibly Melina Masse, murdered by her husband Napoleon Demers in Montreal, 1895.
*Rizzio - The Private Secretary to Mary Queen of Scots who was murdered in 1566.
*Lady Jane Grey - The English "Nine Days' Queen" who was executed by Mary I in 1554 for the threat she posed to the throne.
*Several maimed soldiers and revolutionaries
*Gilles de Rais - A 15th century French nobleman famous for a series of child killings.

George T. Wetzel (1 June 1921 - 10 November 1983) was an American author, editor and early Howard Phillips Lovecraft scholar who wrote a number of works on both Lovecraft's works and his personal life. He also edited several collections of non-fiction on these subjects .

Wetzel has been reported as having been a member of the Esoteric Order of Dagon amateur press association, and is reputed to have been something of a "difficult character," having allegedly sent malicious letters to the employers of those he took a dislike to .

George Willard Kirk (1898 - 1962) was a bookshop manager and book publisher from Akron, Ohio, who lived in Pelham, New York. He was a friend of Clark Ashton Smith and a member of the Kalem Club alongside Rheinhart Kleiner, Arthur Leeds, Frank Belknap Long, H. P. Lovecraft, Samuel Loveman, Henry Everett McNeil, and James F. Morton.

In 1925, Kirk and Lovecraft were living in the same apartment building at 169 Clinton Street, Brooklyn. However, a few months later, Kirk moved to a different apartment in Manhattan. Lovecraft helped him with the move and used the new building as inspiration for the setting of his horror story "Cool Air".

Kirk died at age 63 in Manhattan General Hospital after a battle with cancer.
