Gerald Canevin is a fictional character created by Henry S. Whitehead for a series of supernatural stories, first appearing in the 1926 tale "The Projection of Armand Dubois". One of these stories, "The Trap", was co-written by H. P. Lovecraft. As with many other collaborations, Lovecraft revised Whitehead's draft and rewrote it into the final version, receiving no credit for it during his lifetime. Another Canevin story, "Cassius", was based on one of Lovecraft's plot outlines from the commonplace book.

Most of the Canevin stories were published in fantasy themed magazines such as Weird Tales and Strange Tales, although the last one, "Scar-Tissue", was published in the science fiction themed Amazing Stories. This story is also notable for introducing the Atlantean character Bothon, who would have a much larger role in the Lovecraft-Whitehead collaboration "Bothon", thus connecting that yarn to the Canevin series, even though Canevin himself is absent.

### Biography
In the series, Gerald Canevin is an American writer of supernatural fiction who spends most of his time in the US Virgin Islands, alternating between Santa Cruz (a.k.a. St. Croix) and St. Thomas. The earlier stories tended to take place in Santa Cruz, while later ones more commonly find him in St. Thomas. Some tales move away from the Caribbean and take place in other locations, such as the continental USA (: "The Trap", : "The Chadbourne Episode"), Mexico (: The Great Circle), and even the United Kingdom (: "The Shut Room", "The Napier Limousine").

Canevin is always the first person narrator in his series. However, while most stories were experienced by Canevin himself as the main character, there are also some that he heard from his acquaintances and merely relates to the reader, acting only as a narrator rather than a participant. The latter includes Canevin's debut story, "The Projection of Armand Dubois", as well as "The People of Pan".

The first two stories in the Canevin series ("The Projection of Armand Dubois" and "West India Lights") are not part of the same continuity as the rest. The first story takes place in 1881 and presents Canevin as an established author, whereas all the others take place in the 1920s, and some have him as "a young fellow" and not yet known as a writer (: "The Tree-Man").

In "West India Lights", Canevin falls in love with a woman named Gertrude Maclane and the two get married, his marriage having been mentioned in passing in "The Projection of Armand Dubois" as well. This is never mentioned again in the series

Gerald Wilburn Page (born August 12, 1939) is an American writer and editor. His oeuvre has consisted of short stories and articles related to fantasy, science fiction, mystery and horror, particularly weird horror.  

He sold his first story to the magazine Analog where it appeared in 1963.

Page acquired Coven 13 magazine from Arthur H. Landis and retitled it Witchcraft and Sorcery. The retitled magazine lasted for six issues. Page acted as editor with Jerry Burge serving as art director.

In 1969 he joined the editorial staff of TV Guide.

He edited DAW Books's anthology series The Year's Best Horror Stories from 1976 to 1979.

His Mythos story "Worldsong" appears in the anthology Nameless Places (Arkham House, 1975) of which he was also the editor.

fullContent:
The German Lovecraft Society (Deutsche Lovecraft Gesellschaft) is an inclusive, non-commercial association dedicated to the culture around Howard Phillips Lovecraft as well as weird and horror fiction in general. It is officially a "club." 

The club was born out of DIY culture by people who published a German fanzine and people who ran a convention dedicated to horror roleplaying, predominantly Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG. Since then, many different projects were added, like publishing a free and accessible roleplaying system by the name of FHTAGN, regional meet-ups, running a webzine, supporting artists, filmmakers and writers, running workshops and more. Studying Lovecraft's work is part of the club's mission and they are very open that they feel obliged to do this critically and unapologetically. By doing this they wish to avoid glorifying the writer's problematic views that they frequently and openly speak out against.

The club published Cthulhus Ruf (Cthulhu's Reputation / Chtulhu's Call) and its webzine, Lovecrafter.

The club is a non-commercial association according to German law and its charter states that its goal is establishing and fostering an open and creative community of people who like horror fiction and gaming. The focused aim is to encourage everyone to take the interesting parts of cosmic horror and become inspired to form innovative and new things or to take part in cultural activities with other people. The club has approximately 380 members as of August 2025.

The German Lovecraft Society is dedicated to promoting projects involved in the cultural heritage of H. P. Lovecraft and other authors. The association not only supports the ethics surrounding the topic of Cthulhu Mythos with advice and action, but can also be a helpful partner in areas such as planning, financing and implementation of projects. In the area of cooperation, models can also be found after joint agreement, which are helpful for both sides. The aspect of art and culture, as it is also enshrined in the association's statutes, is always the focus of the activities of the association.

The single most momentous and far reaching achievement of the Deutsche Lovecraft Gesellschaft is in its thorough and painstaking research to compile the only complete and authoritative list of all public domain Lovecraftian stories, characters, concepts and items. The public domain status is cross indexed by jurisdiction and was provided gratis (at no cost) to the people creating The Open Cthulhu Mythos project.

Gerrit Martense is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his story "The Lurking Fear" (1923).  He is the progenitor of the Martense family whose hideous devolution is the subject of the story.

Martense was "a wealthy New-Amsterdam merchant who disliked the changing order under British rule", and in 1670 built the Martense mansion on Tempest Mountain in the Catskill Mountains of upstate New York--a "magnificent domicile on a remote woodland summit whose untrodden solitude and unusual scenery pleased him." 

After moving to his new estate, his only disappointment with it was the "prevalence of violent thunderstorms in summer"; realizing that "the locality was especially liable to such phenomena," he built a storm cellar "into which he could retreat from their wildest pandemonium."

Martense raised his descendants "in hatred of the English civilisation, and trained [them] to shun such of the colonists as accepted it." Their social isolation led to them "intermarrying with the numerous menial class about the estate"; this inbreeding was said to make them "heavy of speech and comprehension," and gave them "a peculiar inherited dissimilarity of eyes; one generally being blue and the other brown."

Ghadamon is a character invented for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Description
Ghadamon is described as being a bluish-brown larval Great Old One made of slime that lives in the stagnant Underworld Sterile Lake east of the Fungus Forest with a colony of its minions. A series of deformed heads can be seen floating and peering from within its form. Its long tentacles give it limited movement over ground by pulling itself along on nearby objects. It emits and absorbs a mix of noxious gas and slime through an ever shifting cycle of pustules and orifices.

### Followers and beliefs
Despite having no established cult, its attempted incursion into the waking world was supported by the Deep Ones. It is referenced in the Book of Eibon as a creature "...spawned on the flesh of human brains and secreted beneath a great lake in a fearsome world of darkness where it would lie for eternal ages, feeding, growing, and waiting. This man did claim that Ghadamon is coming and coming soon."

The grimoire of an unnamed sorceress prophesied that in the lake "...Ghadamon shall lie until one shall come for him and Ghadamon shall pass into another realm and there take his place beneath the sea, to grow and wait for the Day. On this day He Who Waits to Spawn will leave his nest and find his terrible cold mate who has awaited him forever. These days, when the Beast shall rampage and dark R'lyeh rise from its watery crypt will see the passage of great Cthulhu..."

### Minions of Ghadamon
Ghadamon's minions are large black cone-like fish with huge jaws and heads that taper back sharply to a narrow snake-like tail. They are 3-4 feet long and have yellow eyes that stare horribly. Eating one of the pale-blue, purple veined mushrooms that grow by the lake allows one to enter the lake unharmed by the creatures.

The Gharoides are a fictional species of parasitic insectoid creatures created by author J. B. Lee for his 1998 short story "Genuine Article." 

### Description
Gharoides are small, carnivorous creatures with three eyes, three fur-covered antennae and a long proboscis. They secrete a deadly venom, and lay their eggs in a living host to provide a food source for the hatchlings.(: "Genuine Article")

The Gharoides are known to be servants of the Outer God Kaalut, which they worship in the dimension known as K'gil'mnon.(: "Genuine Article")

A line referring to "the many-legged gharoides in the ancient land beneath the earth" may imply that they are subterranean creatures, although it is more likely to suggest that they inhabit a subterranean realm.(: "Forces of Change")

### Background
The only known appearance of the Gharoides to date is in the short story "Genuine Article," in which a Christian evangelist, Shana McEwan, summons one to murder a New Age bookseller. However, there is a clear reference to the Gharoides in the line "Kaalut and it’s swarming insect servants" from Lee's short story "His Hour Upon the Stage," and they are briefly mentioned in "Forces of Change."

Ghasts are a fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos, who were originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Overview
Ghasts are humanoid creatures who dwell in the vaults of Zin, where they are often hunted by the Gugs. Their language appears to consist of "coughing gutturals". They also appear to travel in packs, as Randolph Carter meets a group of fifteen. Together they seemingly manage to bring down a Gug.

Ghasts may be encountered in places where sunlight never comes, such as underworld labyrinths, cavern networks, and deep tunnel systems. They shun light and are fearful of the sun, as when they are exposed to direct sunlight they sicken and may eventually die. Like the ghouls, the ghasts have sharp hooves for feet, although they are larger and move around by hopping. Their faces are eerily humanoid, but have neither a nose nor a forehead.

Often living in groups of 10 to 20 members, some ghast communities can accommodate up to 60 or more individuals. Ghasts prefer to go about either singly or in pairs but may hunt in larger packs, making the best use of their knowledge of underground networks to herd and trap prey. Close relationships between ghasts are rare, as they are cannibalistic in nature, happy to prey on one another as well as other beings that enter their domains. In some cases, wizards (human or otherwise) have been able to utilize ghasts as guardians as they have a tendency to be fairly docile and amenable to command, although their primitive and savage nature does carry a risk of brooding resentment if left to their own devices, which can cause them to attack and eat “allies” considered to be particularly tasty.

Given that the vaults of Zin might be located in the mysterious red-litten Yoth (: The Mound), it is possible that the semi-human quadrupeds ridden by the morally degenerate inhabitants of the inner world of K'n-yan may be distant relatives of ghasts. 

Should this conjecture prove true, it suggests that the origin of the ghasts may stem from genetic experimentation by the sapient quadrupedal reptiles that formerly inhabited Yoth (which in turn might be related to the serpent people).

### In Other Media
*Ghasts feature as monsters in the role-playing game Dungeons & Dragons, where they appear as an advanced form of ghoul.
*Ghasts appear in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.

Ghaszaszh Nyirh is a fictional character in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 1987 in issue #9 of the 2nd volume of the Strange Tales comic book series.

### Background
When the mystical barriers protecting Earth from the Old Ones weakened, GHaszaszh Nyirh set up shop in a famine stricken part of Africa. There, he ruled as a god, providing the starving locals with food and warping their bodies. The price for his help was human sacrifices and surrendering their souls to him.

His temple was made of living flesh. It could fire mystical optical energy blasts with pinpoint accuracy, could change form, and had the the ability to create (create what?). Dr. Strange confronted the entity, and was successful in banishing him.

Ghatanothoa (also known as The Dark God) is a fictional entity in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character first appeared in the 1935 short story "Out of the Aeons", ghostwritten by H. P. Lovecraft for Hazel Heald.

### Background
In Lovecraft's original story, Ghatanothoa is depicted as a gigantic abomination whose appearance is so hideous that anyone who gazes upon it or its image is petrified into a living mummy. The monster is described as a "hellish god or patron daemon" brought to Earth in prehistoric times by aliens from Yuggoth (identified elsewhere as the home planet of the Mi-Go). They built a colossal fortress atop the mountain Yaddith-Gho in K'naa in the lost continent of Mu, and sealed Ghatanothoa below it beneath a vast trapdoor. When humans arose after the departure of the aliens, they too worshipped the monster out of fear of its frightful power, offering it sacrifices lest it emerge from its crypt and wreak havoc. 

Though Ghatanothoa is said to be indescribable, it appears to combine aspects of an octopus and an elephant, and to be both scaly and wrinkled while remaining amorphous. 

Victims of Ghatanothoa are permanently immobilized, their skin taking on the consistency of leather; their internal organs are preserved indefinitely, with the brain remaining fully aware. Only the destruction of the subject's brain or the application of a magic scroll can free it from its hellish prison, though the unfortunate is likely to be incurably insane long before the welcomed release. 

Ghatanothoa's cult was immensely powerful in K'naa, though opposed by the priests of Shub-Niggurath. After Mu sunk beneath the Pacific Ocean, traces of its worship could be found in "Egypt, Chaldaea, Persia, China, the forgotten Semite empires of Africa, and Mexico and Peru in the New World", and in modern times can still be found in the Far East and the Pacific islands. (: "Out of the Aeons") 

Lovecraft attributes much of his invented history of Ghatonothoa and its followers to the fictional book Nameless Cults, originally created by Robert E. Howard.

Other writers have contributed to the lore of Ghatanothoa. In the works of Lin Carter, Ghatanothoa is classified as a Great Old One and the firstborn of Cthulhu, spawned by Idh-yaa on the planet Xoth. (: "The Thing in the Pit") In Colin Wilson's short story, Ghatanothoa was the ruler of the Lloigor, a race of flying reptilian creatures. (: "The Return of the Lloigor")

### In Other Media 
*Ghatanothoa (Ghat) appears in the 2022 horror/comedy movie Glorious, voiced by J.K. Simmons, as a god inhabiting a rest

Ghattambah, the Insect-God, is a fictional entity created by Mark McLaughlin with input from Michael Sheehan, Jr. for the Cthulhu Mythos humor and bawdy tales collection Best Little Witch-House in Arkham.

### Description
Ghattambah is described as being

: "Shoggoth Apocalypse"}}

Ghattambah exists outside of time and space, and is said to be able to gift those it deems worthy with fantastic powers.

The High Priest of Ghattambah's human cult, Azmael Mondrago, has shown no compunction in destroying those who trespass within its chapel, and is suspected of being responsible for the disappearance of several children in his time, suggesting that Ghattambah requires blood sacrifice (: "In The Chapel Of Ghattambah").

At some point in Earth's future Ghattambah served Nyarlathotep in the Outer God's plots to lay waste to the human race. (: "The Spawn Of Ghattambah").

### Gat
: "The Horror In The Water Tower"}} 
: "The Hungry One Must Feed"}}
Gat is an avatar of Ghattambah that begins its life as a cat-like creature which feeds on the psychic energy of lust and violence. When it has consumed a sufficient amount, it enters a chrysalis-like stage which hatches into an insectile monstrosity with a hunger for more tangible sustenance. This stage is capable of intelligent communication and also reproduction, which it achieves by laying its eggs in living human flesh.

It is said that Gat visited Ancient Egypt in the past, although what form it took is unknown. (: "The Hungry One Must Feed")

### History
In ancient prehistory, Ghattambah was worshipped by the native Martians before the coming of the Elder Things. His worship ended when the servile Shoggoths rose up against their masters and devastated the planet, the Elder Things draining the world of its water supplies in an effort to wipe out their former slaves (: "Shoggoth Apocalypse").

In more modern times, Ghattambah somehow established its worship on Earth, with the Mondrago bloodline acting as it’s priests since at least the 1400s. They have maintained the Chapel of Ghattambah in their expansive mansion to this day (: "In The Chapel Of Ghattambah", "Shoggoth Apocalypse").

There also exists an ancient temple to Ghattambah somewhere in Peru. This temple includes sacred pools which were home to at least one extra-dimensional larva of an unknown species (: "The Horror in the Water Tower").

The Ghorii are a fictional species created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his 1934 short story "The Tomb-Spawn."

### Overview
A species of devilish undead that infest the wild desert regions of Zothique, the Ghorii are gaunt, jackal-like creatures. They have long muzzles and double rows of teeth, and have a savage bite. They run on all limbs, but can use their taloned forelimbs for grasping. Their sole source of moisture is the blood of their victims, so they devour both the living and the dead, including fallen Ghorii.

Ghorii arose in the desert of Zothique and like Ghouls may once have been living humans. However it is also possible for a powerful sorcerer to use magic to create Ghorii from jackal bones and animal skins. Their general appearance is broadly similar to a desert version of the Ghoul.

They are usually the color of the local soil, and hide very well, except for the stench which reveals their presence. They prefer to travel in large bands or hordes pursuing prey including intelligent beings such as the humans of Zothique relentlessly and ravenously tearing them to pieces if they catch them.

It is implied that they are actually undead, since they can be created through necromancy, but their bite may also convert victims into a Ghorii if the victim survives their brutal predations.

Ghost Reaper Girl (GHOST GIRL ゴーストガール) is a Japanese manga series written by Akissa Saiké and published by Shueisha. Beginning in July 2020, it was released as a serialized story in the Shōnen Jump+ platform. So far, the chapters have been collected into four paperback volumes, which were later translated to English by Viz Media. Although the series is still ongoing, it has gone on hiatus a few times, due to the author's poor health. The series went on hiatus in May 2022, and temporarily resumed publication in October 2023, until going on an indefinite hiatus again in March 2024.

The storyline incorporates many elements from the Cthulhu Mythos, including some familiar names and characters.

Ghost Reaper Girl, Vol. 1 is a manga volume that collects chapters #1-4 of Ghost Reaper Girl. It was written by Japanese manga creator Akissa Saiké and published by Shueisha in 2020. An English translation was later published by Viz Media in 2022. 

### Synopsis
### Chapter #1: "May I Come In?"
After the seal of the Abyss has been broken, the trapped evil spirits escape from their eternal prison, while a suited man wearing a chain sets his sights on pursuing them. Meanwhile in Yokohama, a producer named Sudo is interviewing an unknown actress who wants to be in his movie. The actress identifies herself as a 28-year-old named Chloé Love, but accidentally put her age as 20 on her resume; however, the producer thinks to himself that she looks much younger. When asked what roles she had played so far, Chloé tells the producer that she had the starring role in a horror action show called Ghost Reaper Girl, with Sudo thinking that she's scraping the bottom of the barrel. Sudo begins to get haunted by a voice in his head, claiming that Chloé will be an exceptional vessel. An evil spirit then bursts out of the producer's mouth, attempting to possess Chloé's body. Despite remembering her boss threatening to fire her if she gets into another fight, Chloé kicks the producer in the face, knocking him out and running away. When the other employees arrived to check on Sudo, several more spirits began to burst out of his mouth.

Outside, Chloé worries that her boss will never believe her, coming to the conclusion that she will be fired for sure. Remembering how she grew up in a slum, being forced to steal and fight in order to survive, Chloé laments how she wants to live a shining life. The group of spirits catches up to Chloé and nearly possess her body, until she is rescued by a man who dismembers the spirits with his chains. The man quickly recognizes her, claiming that she is his idol, before finishing off the spirits by slicing them again. Shortly afterwards, the man introduces himself as Kai Iod from the realm of Hades. Chloé is surprised that he recognizes her, with Kai explaining that he is a huge fan who watches everything that she's in, including minor roles. Kai figures out that Chloé's genetic makeup is a Spirit Medium, someone who can communicate with spirits and whose body can be possessed by any type of spirit. After the huge jailbreak in Hades, a number of evil spirits escaped into the real world, looking for compatible bodies for them to possess and control, meaning that they will likely attack Chloé again. Kai began to set his sights on Chloé, claiming that she is the girl of his dreams, making her think that he was a pervert. Due to him being a spirit as well, Kai had a hard time maintaining his human form, asking Chloé to let him inside her body, leading to Chloé punching away Kai.

Ghost Reaper Girl, Vol. 2 is a manga volume that collects chapters #5-13 of Ghost Reaper Girl. It was written by Japanese manga creator Akissa Saiké and published by Shueisha in 2021. An English translation was later published by Viz Media in 2022.

### Synopsis
### Chapter #5: "Catfight"
After Chloé transformed into a catgirl, Nyarlathotep expresses interest in recruiting her, offering Chloé to work as her subordinate. Exclaiming that Noel is weak and useless, Nyarlathotep attempts to persuade Chloé by insisting that she will make her shine even brighter, due to her being the director of the Arkham Far-East Branch. Chloé refuses the offer, considering Nyarlathotep to be her enemy until she apologizes to both Kai and Noel for hurting them. Refusing to let her go, Nyarlathotep summons a gang of ghosts to attack Chloé, leading to her jumping much higher than expected, due to cats being light on their feet. Appearing as a cat coming out the end of her tail, in order to communicate with her, Noel explains that his true body is inside of Chloé, much like when Kai used her as a vessel. Using her superhuman speed, Chloé quickly overwhelms the ghosts, and then seemingly defeats Nyarlathotep by clawing her face.

Kai apologizes for the actions of his old friend, claiming that she has a bad habit of wanting to test people, as well as having sadistic tendencies which get worse depending on her opponent's power, with there being no escaping her once you've caught her eye. As Chloé began to get scared, Nyarlathotep got back up and hugged her, overjoyed that she had finally found someone of Chloé's raw talent. Chloé is confused at first, but according to Kai, it would take at least a thousand slashes to kill Nyarlathotep, due to how tough she is. Finally, Nyarlathotep apologizes for what has happened, followed by asking for a favor, requesting Chloé to use her abilities in order to investigate the strange corpses being seen all over town.

### Chapter #6: "Code Name"
Inviting Chloé and her friends to the director's room, which looks like a hospital room, Chloé thinks that Nyarlathotep is taking the roleplay too far, with Nyarlathotep asking to do a checkup, telling Chloé to take off her clothes. Getting down to business, Nyarlathotep informs Chloé about the number of murders and violent crimes greatly increasing in the real world, due to the prison break orchestrated by unknown forces, leading to a huge number of evil spirits escaping from Hades. Using the nickname given to Chloé since that video was uploaded, Nyarlathotep registered it as her code name, giving her a smartphone license full of tools necessary for the job, making her an official member of Arkham Bullet, referring to her as the "Ghost Reaper Girl". Not appreciating working in the shadows, Kai questions if Nyarlathotep really knows nothing, asking if the identity and objective of what broke into the abyss is actually unknown. The Ghostbusters are a fictional team of paranormal investigators created by Dan Aykroyd and Harold Ramis for the 1984 supernatural comedy film Ghostbusters. The success of the film led to the creation of sequels, video games, animated series, comic books, and spin-offs.

In the cartoon series The Real Ghostbusters, the team had some run-ins with the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
Based in New York City, where they operate from a former firehouse, the group consists of Drs. Egon Spengler, Ray Stantz, Peter Venkman, and Winston Zeddemore. The former three started out as discredited parapsychologists who decided to put their occult knowledge to practical use and start their own company, whereas Winston was hired afterwards. Together, they opperate as the supernatural equivalent of a pest control agency, capturing ghosts for hire and freeing houses and commercial establishments from the apparitions that haunt them. Secretary Janine Melnitz and a gluttonous ghost named Slimer sometimes assist the team.

The Ghostbusters drive around in the Ectomobile, a.k.a. the Ecto-1. Their equipment includes P. K. E. (Psychokinetic energy) Meters that detect traces of spiritual activity, Proton Packs to immobilize the ghosts, and specially-designed traps to contain them.

In the films, Ray and Egon are played by the franchise's creators Aykroyd and Ramis, respectively, while Peter, Winston, Janine and Slimer are played by Bill Murray, Ernie Hudson, Annie Potts, and director Ivan Reitman (who directed the first two films). The Real Ghostbusters features an entirely new cast, with Ray and Slimer voiced by Frank Welker, and Egon voiced by Maurice LaMarche. In the first two seasons, Peter was voiced by Lorenzo Music, Winston by Arsenio Hall, and Janine by Laura Summer. Dave Coulier and Kath Soucie took over from Music and Summer starting on Season 3, while Buster Jones took over from Hall on Season 4.

### Trivia
*In the episode "The Haunting of Heck House", Egon claimed the Whateley House in Arkham (a reference to "The Dunwich Horror") is one of the most haunted houses on record, with a total of thirteen ghosts.
*In the 2024 film Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire, Ray seeks help from a folklorist named Dr. Hubert Wartzki, who is also the tri-state treasurer of the H. P. Lovecraft Society.

Ghoth the Burrower is a fictional entity created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his tongue-in-cheek "Family Tree of Azathoth".

### Overview
According to a fictional family tree provided by Lovecraft, Ghoth is a descendant of Cthulhu and an ancestor of Lovecraft himself. It is referred to as "one of the Little People", and mated with a Roman noblewoman named Viburnia, something which Lovecraft described as "a hellish and nameless tragedy".

### In Other Media
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, Daijuuji Kurou mentioned the vile and tragic marriage of Viburnia and Ghoth, while he fled away from Cthugha and Ithaqua in the monochrome world.

Ghouls are a species of cannibalistic humanoids featured in several of H. P. Lovecraft's works, where they feed principally (but not exclusively) on the bodies of the dead. They are first mentioned in "The Hound", although ambiguously, as the word "ghoul" in that story might be intended as just a synonym for "graverobber". The story also mentions a corpse-eating cult based on the Plateau of Leng.

Ghouls are first patently depicted in the short story "Pickman's Model", where the eponymous main character meets with the beings regularly to paint them in various poses and activities. It is revealed in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath that Pickman is in fact a partial or full-blooded ghoul, and now resides with them in the Dreamlands as a chieftain.

Like the zoogs, ghouls know passages between the Waking World and the Dreamlands that allow them to cross from one realm to another, rather than visiting the Dreamlands while asleep like humans do. In combat, ghouls are known to use items such as headstones and were unfamiliar with other types of weaponry up until their battle with the Moon-beasts. It was here that they first discovered, and quickly mastered, the use of spears and of javelins. With this newfound technology, they were able to annihilate the garrison of Moon-beasts on the nameless rock off the coast of Sarkomand in the Dreamlands.

### Overview
The word "ghoul" or "ghul" originates from Arabian folklore, where it denotes a creature that dwells in graveyards and devours corpses, sometimes considered a type of jinni. Due to the association with graveyards, many writers have come to use the word in connection with the undead, including Lovecraft himself (: "The Outsider"). However, the creatures most often referred to as "ghouls" in Lovecraft's fiction are mortal beings: a species of canine-like humanoids with rubbery skin, scaly claws, and hoof-like feet, which live in groups and scavenge for corpses, but also hunt live prey occasionally (: "Pickman's Model", The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath).

In Lovecraft's works, the ghouls are an independent faction that have no allegiance to Nyarlathotep and the Outer Gods. Instead, they have treaties with the Night-gaunts who serve Nodens, and side with them in battle against Nyarlathotep's forces (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath). Conver

fullContent:
"Ghoulmaster" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Brian McNaughton. It first appeared in the anthology Miskatonic University (DAW Books, 1996).

### Synopsis
Felix Aubrey, a man who in his younger days wrote a whimsical book on the folklore of ghouls in the city of Arkham, thereby earning himself the contemptuous nickname of "Ghoulmaster", finds that his young niece Sarah has fallen in with a group which he later discovers to be a cult devoted to these cannibalistic beasts.

Although he succeeds in spiriting Sarah away from the cult, the two are followed by a pair of their goons who ambush them to snip the girl's little finger off. Felix, realising that this is part of a ritual to absorb the sum of her memories, gives chase.

Arriving at the medical school in which the cult hold court, he fails to prevent the finger from being eaten by one of the ghouls, but maims the cult leader before making his long and arduous escape through the catacombs beneath Arkham.

Upon returning to his niece's home, he finds that the ghoul has got there first, and has murdered the girl before assuming her form. He is never again able to locate the tunnel system which leads to the ghouls' lair.

### Characters

*Dr. Felix "Ghoulmaster" Aubrey, a learned, if somewhat absent-minded, medical doctor.
*Mrs. Kilpatrick, the sorcerous leader of a ghoul-cult.
*Roger Kilpatrick, Mrs. Kilpatrick's son, now fully transformed into a ghoul.
*Sarah Hazard, Felix's wayward niece.

### Publication History

*Miskatonic University (November 1996)
*Even More Nasty Stories (February 2000)
*The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (April 2012)

Ghouls of the Miskatonic is the first book in the Dark Waters trilogy by Graham McNeill.

### Synopsis
The vicious murders of several young women in the town of Arkham bring together a disparate group of people intent on solving the mystery of who is behind the atrocities. Throughout the course of their investigations, they uncover a deranged cult of Cthulhu worshipers deep in the heart of Arkham academia, and use the powers of their enemies against them.

### Characters
*Professor Oliver Grayson, lecturer in anthropology at Miskatonic University.
*Professor Alexander Templeton, a lecturer in Ancient Religions at Miskatonic University.
*Rex Murphy, a reporter for the Arkham Advertiser.
*Finn Edwards, a small time criminal and bootlegger.
*Minnie Klein, a photographer for the Arkham Advertiser.
*Gabriel Stone, a private detective who’s daughter was one of the murdered girls.
*Amanda Sharpe, a student at Miskatonic University.
*Rita Young, a student at Miskatonic University.
*Kate Winthrop, a research assistant at Miskatonic University.
*Henry Cartwright: a former professor now incarcerated at Arkham Asylum.
*Spencer Osborne, a senior at Miskatonic University and Cthulhu cultist.
*Wilson Brewster, a senior at Miskatonic University and Cthulhu cultist.
*Marie Lambeau (cameo)
*Jim Culver (cameo)
*Tommy Muldoon (cameo)
*"Ashcan" Pete (cameo)

### Behind the Mythos
Ghouls of the Miskatonic is the first book in the Dark Waters trilogy by Graham McNeill, and is part of Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Fiction line of Mythos-related literature. It was first published in paperback format in August 2011, and has also received an ebook release.

Ghroth is an Outer God in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Tugging", which depicts the entity as being a living planetoid.

### Background
Ghroth is an Outer God that resembles a rust-colored moon with a single gigantic red eye that it closes to avoid detection. It's made up of molten iron, ash and gas, and splitting the surface are cracks or faults. Below its crust are vast seas, which are used to form a giant eye.

It drifts throughout the universe while singing its siren song, The Music of the Spheres. Any Great Old Ones or Outer Gods sleeping on a planet it passes is awakened by its call. Ghroth destroys planets as well and has destroyed the home of Baoht Z'uqqa-Mogg, forcing it to flee and take up residence on Earth. As Ghroth gets closer to a world, the planet experiences natural disasters in the form of erupting volcanoes, tidal waves, earthquakes, changing tides, and horrific storms.

### In Other Media
*Ghroth appears in the mobile game Tower of Saviors, as a sentient void that was spawned by Azathoth. Due to it being a formless entity, Ghroth compressed itself into a planetoid body to interact with lower dimensions. 
*Ghroth appears in the mobile game Card Monsters, under the name Nemesis Star.
*In the role-playing video game World of Horror, Ath-Yolazsth was based on Ghroth.
*In the role-playing video game Persona 3, Nyx Avatar's Moon body has a strong resemblance to Ghroth.
*In the manga Magi: The Labyrinth of Magic, the Medium (a crystalized entity composed of hatred and malice) has a strong resemblance to Ghroth.
*In the manga Hellstar Remina, the titular antagonist appears to be heavily inspired by Ghroth.
*The arcade game Pump It Up Phoenix features a boss song named after Ghroth, with a BPM of 212.
*In the mobile game Neural Cloud (a spin-off of Girls' Frontline), an Entropic entity named after and visually based on Ghroth appears in chapter 12.5 "Irradiant Awakening". It is the Entropic Core of one of the allied characters after it has been corrupted by Entropy, but is ultimately destroyed.

### Behind the Mythos
The Death Star, one of Ghroth's many aliases, is also the name of the planet-destroying space station constructed by the Galactic Empire from the Star Wars franchise.

Gi-Hoveg is a fictional cosmic entity created by James Ambuehl for his Lu-Kthu Cycle.

Ambuehl classifies Gi-Hoveg as a Great Old One in "The Advent of Uvhash", and as an Outer God in "The Stalker in the Snows".

### Description
Known as the Aether-Anemone, Gi-Hoveg is a giant spherical being with spongy flesh and spikes protruding from its body, as well as numerous eyes set between its spikes. It is the arch rival of Uvhash, the Blood-Mad God of the Void. (: "The Advent of Uvhash")

Nobody knows where Gi-Hoveg dwells, but some believe "he exists everywhere". (: "The Stalker in the Snows")

Gianni Pilo (born 10 August 1939 in Tripoli, Italian Libya) is an Italian editor, author, and former director of Fanucci Editore. He has worked on numerous publications which intersect the topic of this wiki, perhaps most notably Fanucci's I Miti di Cthulhu series of weird fiction anthologies. He has also been involved with the release of anthologies focusing on the fiction of authors including H. P. Lovecraft, Robert E. Howard, Clark Ashton Smith, Arthur Conan Doyle, E. F. Benson, M. R. James, Ambrose Bierce, William Hope Hodgson, Algernon Blackwood, Robert Bloch, and Brian Lumley, amongst others.

"Gifts" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Robert Stahl, published in the Kat Rocha-edited anthology Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be by 01Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
Pianist Jakob Zann, the last descendant of Erich, is tasked with the duty to play his music in order to keep dark entities from ravaging our world. After stopping his medication and being jilted by a girl he has fallen for, he decides to send her a gift: his severed fingers. No longer kept in check by the genius of Jakob's music, something malevolent begins to seep through…

Gilles Grenier is a fictional sorcerer created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Mandrakes".

In the story, Gilles Grenier and his wife Sabine are 15th century sorcerers who move to the French province of Averoigne, where they set up a shop selling love potions made from the roots of mandrakes. Although these potions were their most popular product by far, they also dealt in charms and divination, and Gilles in particular was notable for his ability to "read infallibly the dictates of the stars". He was rumoured to come from a family of werewolves, and his hands and face were singularly hirsute, with a beard that grew almost to his eyes.

H. P. Lovecraft established Gilles Grenier as a descendant of Nush the Eternal, and an ancestor of both Hippolyte Le Sorcier and Smith in his Family tree of Azathoth. However, Lovecraft labels Grenier as "Lord of Averoigne", which suggests that this might be a different character. The Gilles Grenier from Smith's story never had such power over Averoigne, being executed for the murder of his wife Sabine five years after arriving at the province.

"Ginger Snap" is a short story by Michael Wentela, originally collected in the Kickstarter crowdfunded anthology A Mythos Grimmly. It is combination of the expanded Mythos version of Nyarlathotep and a grotesque inversion of the Little Red Riding Hood folktale.

### Synopsis
A copywriter living in Arkham stumbles over a fourteen year old red-headed homeless girl and becomes completely obsessed by her. Becoming a financial donor to her, he resists her various hints and overtures, and is apparently in fact not sexually attracted to her or of any bad intentions.

However, the same can not be said for the girl, who is actually an avatar of Nyarlathotep and who, seemingly from sheer malice, entraps her good samaritan in her lair where she has drained the life from countless teens. The police believe they have saved "Ginger" from a child predator. The victim of her scheme is not believed when he relates how, before the police she has already called arrive in her basement lair, she shifts to several of the more notorious forms that Nyarlathotep can take out of his "thousand forms."

"Give Me That Old Time Religion" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Lee Finney.

### Synopsis
A hillbilly con-artist who has made a living preaching his faux religion across the country finds a true calling before returning to his roots. There, he enacts a sacred ritual designed to awaken the Great Old One Cthulhu, although he is grievously injured in the process.

### Characters
* Zebulon "Zeb", a poverty-stricken backwoods moonshine distiller.
* Caleb, a backwoods charlatan with a newfound purpose,
* Bertha Jean, Caleb's sister and Zeb's wife.

### Publication History
"Give Me That Old Time Religion" was published in the H. P. Lovecraft-inspired anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.

Glaaki, sometimes spelled Gla'aki, is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Inhabitant of the Lake". It is known to dwell in a lake near the fictional town of Brichester, in the Severn Valley, located in the West Midlands of England.

### Description
As old as the stars themselves, Glaaki has a vast reservoir of knowledge, not only of the supernatural entities that exist on Earth, but of those which predate it. Whilst he is aquatic in nature, in his physical form Glaaki resembles nothing so much as an enormous slug with slender spines which appear to be made of matte metal, but which are in fact organic in nature. These quills can inject a substance to ensure its victims' compliance. Those skewered in such a way are granted Glaaki's gift of everlasting life, albeit as an undead puppet. In addition, it is capable of forming tentacles tipped with eyes, so as to keep its true nature hidden whilst observing the world from beneath the water's surface.

Interestingly, although Glaaki is believed to have landed on Earth in the Severn Valley, sightings of it have been reported from many other bodies of water across the globe. How Glaaki is able to achieve this is unknown.

### The Cult of Glaaki
Glaaki's cult, a group of depraved humans both mortal and undead, wrote a series of scriptures known as The Revelations of Glaaki. What these writings contain is for the most part unknown, though it cannot be anything good.

### Behind the Mythos
In 2017, an anthology of works focused on Glaaki, titled The Children of Gla'aki, was published by Dark Regions Press. It contained Glaaki's first appearance in "The Inhabitant of the Lake" along with 17 stories by contemporary Mythos authors, and an afterword commentary by Ramsey Campbell.

fullContent:
Glenn Arthur Rahman (born 1949) is an author and games designer. He is known for his collaborations with Richard L. Tierney and for co-creating what's been  "the first successful transference of H. P. Lovecraft’s style of supernatural literature into a modern role-playing format." 

### Overview
Rahman was born in 1949, one of six children, and for grade school attended a one-room country schoolhouse in Minnesota. In high school, he mainly read history, mythology, and comic books like Conan the Barbarian, Howard the Duck, and Tomb of Dracula. In college, he discovered pulp fiction, devouring authors like Edgar Rice Burroughs and Robert E. Howard, and a little later H. P. Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith. He graduated from Minnesota's Winona State College with a BA in Geological Science. 

Rahman has written a number of stories for a variety of genres, although he specialises in fantasy, and his output includes contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos through his work on Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. 

Rahman has co-written stories featuring Simon of Gitta with Simon's creator, Richard L. Tierney. These include "The Wedding of Sheila-Na-Gog" (1985), The Gardens of Lucullus (2001) and the unpublished Path of the Dragon. He wrote a solo novel set in the Simon of Gitta continuity, Heir of Darkness (1989). 

With his brother Philip (co-founder of the publishing house Fedogan & Bremer), Rahman published "The Lovecraft Variant" in the Summer 1980 issue of Sorcerer's Apprentice, a set of rules for running Lovecraftian scenarios with the Monsters! Monsters! roleplaying system. It was later described as "a full system for investigating strange occurrences and uncovering ancient secrets, all while struggling to maintain the characters' sanity in the face of unimaginable terrors." The Summer 1981 issue of Sorcerer's Apprentice included a sequel, "The Monsters of the Cthulhu Mythos." The two pieces were packaged together as The Lovecraft Variant by Bolt Thrower Press.

Gloon, the Corrupter of Flesh, Master of the Temple, is a fictional deity created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Temple". 

### Description
Gloon is described as great limacene or slug-like abomination, though it usually hides its true nature through the glamour of a beautiful statue resembling the Greek god Dionysus. 

### History

### In Lovecraft's Work
In "The Temple," the crew of a World War I German submarine come into possession of a statue of a deity, which proceeds to drive most of the crew insane before dragging the sole survivor, the submarine's captain, down to the entity's temple on the ocean floor. 

### In Other Works
Later authors expanded that this deity was a Lesser Old One named Gloon, who has been imprisoned in his temple since long before the sinking of Atlantis. (: "The City in the Sea," G. W. Thomas & Lynn Willis) 

Gloon appears (though is unnamed) in author Molly Tanzer's novelette "The Infernal History of the Ivybridge Twins" (citation needed) - in this tale he is served by dolphins (which were long-associated with Dionysus).

Gloria Goldberg, also known simply as The Author, is a fictional investigator character created by Richard Launius for Chaosium's Cthulhu Mythos board game Arkham Horror in 1987. Since Fantasy Flight Games' acquisition of the property in 2005, they have significantly expanded on her history and exploits. However, it is possible that Chaosium still hold rights to the character, as Gloria does not appear in the latest edition of Arkham Horror (third).

### Overview
Unlike many of the investigator biographies from Arkham Horror, Gloria Goldberg's backstory has remained largely consistent over the years. She has suffered from nightmarish, apocalyptic visions of sinister entities from beyond our reality destroying the world for as long as she can remember. Over the years, medical and psychiatric treatment has helped her channel these dreams into her fiction, and this has earned her a reputation as a highly-inventive horror writer with a successful career. 

### History

### Bones of the Yopasi
In Graham McNeill's 2012 novel Bones of the Yopasi, Gloria is encountered by a group of investigators on the trail of a Cthulhu cultist while on tour in Kingsport promoting her latest book. Although the group keep her in the dark about their true agenda, an invitation to her latest reading - at a local historical society - allows the others to examine occult materials which they would not have otherwise had access to.

### Behind the Mythos
Since her first appearance in 1987, Gloria has appeared in most Arkham Horror-related work, including Eldritch Horror, the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, and Arkham Horror Fiction. A more complete list is given below.

* Arkham Horror (first and second edition core sets)
* Arkham Horror Premium Figures
* The Dreamlands (Eldritch Horror expansion)
* Mansions of Madness (core set)
* Bones of the Yopasi (novel)
* Dark Revelations (novella)

### Trivia
The depiction of Gloria writing about the terrors she witnesses in her dreams recalls an element of the real-life writing process of H. P. Lovecraft: many of his stories and entities were taken directly from dreams he himself experienced.

Glynda (second name undisclosed) is a fictional character created by Josh Finney for his Casefile: Arkham Mythos stories. She made her first appearance in the 2016 graphic novel Casefile: Arkham- Nightmare on the Canvas.

### Description
Glynda is a beautiful woman of indeterminate age whose body has been modified by the Outer God Shub-Niggurath to make her more appealing to the opposite sex. She owns and operates a shop named Rare Books which deals in antique books, and has a sideline in occult writings. She is currently in a relationship with private eye Hank Flynn.

As a former devotee of Shub-Niggurath, Glynda possesses certain magical powers, and her abilities specialise in protective invocations. 

### History
Given by her mother to the service of Shub-Niggurath at a young age, Glynda underwent a mystical transformation at the hands of her god which was intended to give her physical characteristics desirable to men. She was then sent out into the world under orders to seduce and have children with as many men as possible; these children were then sacrificed as a blood offering to the Black Goat. 

Despairing of this life, Glynda invoked the power of the Elder God Nodens, with whose aid she was able to break ties with Shub-Niggurath, and left her service to lead a more mundane life.

Eventually, Glynda came to Arkham where she established Rare Books and met Hank Flynn, with whom she fell in love and began a relationship. Since then, she has assisted Flynn with his more mystically-inclined cases, and has likely even saved his life during their acquaintance.

### Appearances

Glyph (real name unknown) is a primary character and main protagonist in Ian Davey's Bh'Yhlun series. She made her first appearance in "An Incarceration in Bh'Yhlun," published in the September 1997 edition of Edward P. Berglund's online fanzine Nightscapes.

### Description
A 13-year-old British girl, Glyph found herself orphaned in the aftermath of the coming of Bh'Yhlun. She has spent the time since then living by any means necessary in the ruins of the world, dodging the various monstrosities which patrol the now-twisted countryside.

### History
After a brief period of imprisonment in the living tower of Bh'Yhlun, Glyph began the long journey to Glastonbury when some previously-unsuspected magical ability told her that her destiny lay in that ancient place (: "An Incarceration in Bh'Yhlun").

Glyph subsequently joined up with an older couple named Helen and Aaron and, later, a pregnant woman named Lucy who had borne witness to the genesis of this new world. Eventually arriving at Glastonbury, the group were confronted by Stanley Pickman, an avatar of Nyarlathotep. When the Outer God fully manifested, a magical ritual was able to banish it, and restore the world to the way it was before the coming of Bh'Yhlun (: "The Epiphany of Dissolution").

### Appearances
*"An Incarceration in Bh'Yhlun" (1997)
*"The Epiphany of Dissolution" (1998)

The Gn'icht' Tyaacht are a species of African tree spirits created for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror role-playing game. They first appeared in Pete Tamlyn's scenario "The Horror of the Glen", included in the 1987 Games Workshop anthology collection Green and Pleasant Land. 

### Description
The Gn'icht' Tyaacht are spirits who inhabit the black-leaved Nuwanda trees of West Africa, emerging mostly in their childhoods to hunt for food. They have been tamed over the years by native witch-doctors, who feed them dried human flesh when young, a process which allows them to be controlled through the use of magic (: Green and Pleasant Land).

At one point in their history, the Gn'icht' Tyaacht were forced into slavery by the visiting Great Old One Cthugha; although they are now free of its influence, they nurse an ancient grudge against the malevolent cosmic being (: Green and Pleasant Land).

"Gnashing Whispers: A Lost Archivist Story" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author David Kenney. Forming part of his Lost Archivist series, it was published in Vol 5, Issue 2 of Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
Chief Archivist of the Miskatonic University forbidden archives Wendell Hunt is tasked with uncovering a thief and murderer who has been targeting those involved with one of the most dangerous areas of the subterranean vaults: Storage Area B. His investigations in the facility, while driving him to the brink of madness, uncover a jealous professor using necromancy and other forbidden arts to steal occult manuscripts. Although Hunt is able to defeat the perpetrator and his undead minion, it comes at the cost of his ear, chewed off by the zombie during the conflict.

Gnoph-keh, also known as Gnoph-Hek are sharp-horned, coarse-haired beings with six long-limbs, found in Greenland and the Arctic Circle. Empowered with blizzard summoning and reducing temperatures. Connected with Rhan-Tegoth (whom they seem to worship) and possibly Ithaqua, Zhar and Lloigor (god). In early texts (such as the Book of Eibon) it is a race of vicious cannibals who were driven from Lomar by mankind and the Voormis, but in later texts it appears as a lone creature, sometimes called "the Hairy Thing" and is confused with Rhan-Tegoth. Some texts call them "reptilian" although hairy reptiles are far from common. It is now on the brink of extinction and only encountered in ones. The Gnophkeh are either creatures of air or water. 

### Overview
The Gnoph-keh are a race of beings who appear to inhabit cold places, notably Greenland, northern Canada, and other isolated wintry wildernesses. Legend purports that the Gnoph-keh are the remnants of a lost tribe who turned from earthly gods to serve the Great Wind-Walker, Ithaqua, and in doing so became something other than human.

Other tales speak of the creatures as earthly extensions of alien powers, always at the periphery, waiting and watching in the vast wilderness to pounce on those who would forsake the safety of civilization. Some tomes recall the attack of the gnoph-keh upon doomed Lomar. Whatever their true origin, gnoph-keh are territorial, individualistic, and rarely encountered. Seemingly, their solitary existence is broken only occasionally, when two or more gather to form a pack for unknown reasons—perhaps when they sense the arrival of Ithaqua or some other manifestation of the Great Old One. Especially harsh winters may bring them down into lowland regions and closer to humanity. 

Feared by those who are aware of their existence, there are a few isolated communities who have turned their fear into a form of worship, venerating the gnoph-keh as harbingers of icy fate and, in doing so, some have been touched by the mind of Ithaqua and turned their devotions to the Great Wind-Walker. Such communities soon turn to the terrible delights of cannibalism and consort with the gnoph-keh in blasphemous ceremonies. 

### Behind the Mythos
The Gnoph-keh appear in H. P. Lovecraft's early Dunsanian tales. Lin Carter incorporated them into the Cthulhu Mythos and they were eventually developed further by Laurence J. Cornford and John Glasby.

### Trivia
* Edgar Rice Burroughs' Barsoom series of popular science fiction books features a species of Martian animal called White Apes, which bear certain similarities to the Gnoph-keh, although lacking the horn. Gnophkehs are brutish humanoids are enemies of both the voormis and early Hyperborean human tribes.

### Description
They are humanoid cannibals described as being covered in coarse, matted hair with large protruding ears and proboscidean noses. They originally lived in Hyperborea and worshiped the Great Old One Rhan-Tegoth (: "The Scroll of Morloc"). But Rhan-Tegoth eventually forgot them when he entered a stone-like hibernation state. They were invaded and driven to the land of Lomar by the Tsathoggua-worshipping Voormis.



Later on they were again invaded by humans from Zobna and driven even further up north. It was there that Ithaqua, the wind-walker, appeared, to whom the Gnophkhehs transferred their allegiance. They started to harass the Voormis again as they grew in power contributing to the demise of the Voormi civilization.

The Gnophkehs in Lomar were eventually destroyed when Ithaqua and Aphoom-Zhah brought about the Ice Age along with the remnants of the Voormis in Hyperborea and the human civilization in Zobna.

Goatswood is a fictional town invented by Ramsey Campbell, part of his Severn Valley setting for Cthulhu Mythos stories.

First described in the short story "The Moon-Lens", Goatwood is an isolated town in the Severn Valley, surrounded by woods to the east of Brichester. The narrator of that story is struck by the town's atmosphere: "The close-set dull-red roofs, the narrow streets, the encircling forests—all seemed somehow furtive." As in Lovecraft's Innsmouth, the residents of Goatswood have a distinctive, offputting appearance; a typical resident is described as "revoltingly goatlike," resembling "a medieval woodcut of a satyr," and clad in "grotesquely voluminous" garments. Instead of worshiping a race of monsters from the sea (the Deep Ones), however, they worship Shub-Niggurath.

The most prominent feature of Goatswood is the titular Moon-Lens: A "metal pylon, 50 feet high, rose from the center of the square. At the top [is]... a large convex lens surrounded by an arrangement of mirrors, and all hinged on a pivot attached to the ground by taut ropes." It's said, by a perhaps unreliable character, to have originally been built by the Romans.

Goatswood is sometimes an unavoidable connection on the train route from Exham to Brichester. The infrequent visitors to Goatswood, "The Moon Lens" reveals, eat at the Station Cafe and stay at the Central Hotel.

In a later story, "Made in Goatswood", the village has more to offer to outsiders: a curiosity shop with a toad-like proprietor whose "hands were brown and crinkled as the paper in which he wrapped the parcels," selling disturbing lawn ornaments; a fruit stand in a "canvas stall like a shrine" where fruit resembling peaches are offered by a girl whose "eyelids lowered wickedly." There's even a red light district, Fitzroy Street, on the edge of town:

"The Franklyn Paragraphs" mentions a number of places visited by "the circle of young men" around occultist Roland Franklyn; Goatswood is among them.

In the "woods toward Goatswood" is a clearing, according to "The Insects from Shaggai", where a meteorite once fell in the 17th century; a coven that subsequently worshiped there was executed by real-life witchfinder Matthew Hopkins. Within the clearing is a mysterious gray cone, home to the titular creatures; the story "The Moon-Lens" also alludes to this artefact.

These woods are also featured in "The Enchanted Fruit", whose protagonist at first finds them enticing; "Each corridor of trees seemed made to be explored, each green shadow promised mystery;" and later forbidding; "A screen of leaves seemed secretive; parted, it revealed only vistas of dim branches." In the forest, he finds a tree whose "rich trunk, dark yet warm, stood alone on a mound of autumn built high from the edge of the glade;" he eats the fruit of this tree, "large as apples, soft and shaped as peaches", to his immediate delight and eventual regret.

Goatswood Gnomes are fictional creatures  created by Ramsey Campbell in the story "Made in Goatswood", and later used by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.(which book?) They are living statues that resemble malicious garden gnomes. 

### Overview
Found in many gardens across Europe, the British Isles, and North America, the garden gnome is thought to be a comic and endearing character, designed to liven up and decorate front and back yards. These stone or concrete-created “elves” are, in the main, inanimate; however, some are in fact ugly little creatures brought to life by magic and alien design. Some believe the Dark Mother with a Thousand Young, Shub-Niggurath, or her children imbue life into these vessels, which lie dormant during daylight hours but can spring to life at night to carry out vile and devious acts.

The awakening of these small, stone monsters may be linked to the cycles of the moon, and they may be able to function only at specific times such as full or new moons, with much depending on the magic used to enchant them or the source of that magic. Acting as scouts, with watchful eyes, or going forth to carry out strange or vile acts, these “Goatswood” gnomes bring nightmares and fear to the unwary who might see them about their business during darkness. Rumors tell of those witnessing the gnome’s antics as being marked, should they be seen by the gnomes, and liable to expect some form of revenge from the spiteful little folk. Such “revenge” may be minor but might also lead to a horrific death, should the gnomes deem their target to have seen “too much.”

Apart from some affinity to Shub-Niggurath, reports suggest that certain wizards and witches may have uncovered the necessary spell or spells to conjure life into such vessels for their own ends, using gnomes to carry out tasks and meter out harm as directed.

Known as Goatswood Gnomes (to those in the know), due to the fact that it was in the Goatswood area of the Severn Valley in England (to the east of Brichester)—where the mysterious Moon-Lens (a curious 50-foot/15 m metal pylon) is positioned in the center of the town square—where their appearance was first noted. 

### Summary
Goatswood Gnomes are statues of small, ugly men animated through an unknown source possibly relating to Shub-Niggurath. They inhabit Goatswood and the surrounding area.

### Trivia
*John Goodrich's short story "Tribute Band" features a metal band named the Goatswood Gnomes, whose frontman was obsessed with the Revelations of Gla'aki.

Goblins are legendary creatures from the folklore of medieval Europe. They were later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Ye Booke of Monstres.

### Background
Goblins are creatures of the Dreamlands, who appear to be deformed humanoid fairies of short stature. No two goblins are alike in form, with variations such as pointed or round ears, noses of varying lengths, tusks, humped backs, more than one head, legs of varying lengths, etc. Goblins are known for stealing children, playing cruel pranks, and selling magic food to unwary humans. For combat, they use melee weapons.

### Behind the Mythos
Chaosium appears to have adapted the concept of goblins as delineated by Christina Rossetti from her poem "Goblin Market".(source?)

### Synopsis
An orderly in a hospital psych ward notices one of his colleagues whispering into the ears of several patients shortly before their inexplicable deaths. Confronting the woman outside of work, he is overcome by an inhuman rage and murders her; at the moment of her death something dark passes between them, and the orderly heads out into the larger world to carry on the work of this malevolent entity.

The God of the Bloody Tongue (also known as The Howler of Darkness) is a fictional entity in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft and J. Chapman Miske for their short story "The Thing in the Moonlight"; however, it would not be properly identified until later on.

The entity was later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, depicted as being an avatar of Nyarlathotep. (: Masks of Nyarlathotep)

### Overview
The Bloody Tongue takes the form of a giant humanoid monster that has clawed appendages and three legs, with a single blood-red tentacle where its face should be. The tentacle can stretch forward while howling at the moon.

The god was worshipped by an African cult that originated from Kenya, but would later expand into other territories, including the United States. The cult members will head towards the Mountain of the Dark Wind, in order to perform monthly rituals to honor their god. Every five years, the Bloody Tongue will manifest itself on the mountain, feeding off the sacrifices that were offered to it and generating a terrible storm around the ritual sight.

### In Other Media
*This avatar of Nyarlathotep appears in the video game Persona 2, under the name "Moon Howler".
*In the Haiyore! Nyaruko-san series, Nyaruko's ahoge was designed to resemble the Bloody Tongue.
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, after Daijuuji Kurou reached the Shining Trapezohedron in Leica Crusade's route, Nya briefly transformed into a "three-legged monster".

### Behind the Mythos
Despite having very little prominence in Lovecraft's works, the Bloody Tongue is arguably the most iconic incarnation of Nyarlathotep, with many other artistic depictions featuring the tentacle-like head.

The God-Machine is Lovecraftian-like entity from the fictional universe of the Chronicles of Darkness pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by White Wolf.

### Background
The God-Machine is an eldritch entity, which has created the idea of technology, giving human a reasons to create parts of it. It is neither cruel, nor malevolent, or mindlessly destructive and which is totally apathetic toward humans. The entity is deeply embedded in reality, mystically connected to what man takes for granted - energy, gravity, probability, the seasons, etc - which it maintains to ensure its own continued existence. 

Due to a number of reasons, the God-Machine has to deal with reality at the human level. Therefore manipulating humans or keeping them from interfering. It is an incomprehensibly vast entity, with a consciousness that comprehends the conjunction of primal forces and the movement of galaxies. With the power to extinguish constellations and destroy worlds. To deal with issues at the human level, it created the Angels, beings which operate at the human level. Beings of great power, relatively speaking compared to other beings on Earth, whom are immortal, never aging or getting sick, and are extremely difficult to kill. Expendable tools whom exist only to complete the missions given to them and whom are recycled by the God-Machine. Some of whom have rebelled against such a fate and defected, forming a resistance known as "demons".

The Gods of Ragnarok are extradimensional entities created by the BBC in 1988 for Doctor Who. They were later identified as Great Old Ones by the Doctor (: All-Consuming Fire).

### Background
The Gods of Ragnarok are a trio of Great Old Ones who appear to sentient beings as stone statues. They are entertained by the suffering of others. The Time Lord Rassilon was the one who named them Raag (Father Ragnarok), Nah (Mother Ragnarok), and Rok (Little Girl). He theorized that they created and destroyed numerous universes, even destroying their own. The Gods of Ragnarok kidnap those with individuality and imagination, and force them to entertain them endlessly, demanding bigger and better acts each time. They can fire thunderbolts and create rain, reanimate the dead, manifest simultaneously in different time-phases, and reduce their victims to ashes in a clash of thunder and blinding light.

### Behind the Mythos
"Ragnarok" from Old Norse literally means "Reign Wreck", the wrecking of the reign of a king or more broadly in a cosmic sense the destruction of cosmic order and the bringing of utter chaos and ruin.

Gods of the Deep, which features the tagline "A New Depth of Fear", is a low-budget British Lovecraftian horror film written and directed by Charlie Steeds and released in February 2024.

### Synopsis
When a new deep sea trench is discovered at the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean - the deepest ever recorded at 37,000 feet - a large corporation designs a revolutionary new submersible craft and recruits a crack team of experts to explore this hidden new world. However, when they uncover a colossal sleeping creature, avaricious executives demand a tissue sample, revealing that they had expected the existence of such a being all along.

As the monstrous entity begins to awaken, insanity starts to claim the minds of the crew, and the sample begins to grow, adding its own power to the waves of madness washing through the ship.

### Mythos Connections
*The name of the company which funds the expedition is the Pickman Corporation, a clear nod to the titular character of "Pickman's Model", but with no substantial connection to the story.
*The main character is stated to have attended Miskatonic University, although the one mentioned in Gods of the Deep is located in London, England rather than Lovecraft's New England.
*Although never directly named, the entity which awakens, an enormous winged humanoid with tentacles in place of its lower face, is clearly intended to be Cthulhu.

### Other Connections
*The character of Jed Pickman, owner of the Pickman Corporation, was played by actor Chris Lines. Lines had previously played the part of the titular character in the 2017 short H. P. Lovecraft's The Terrible Old Man.

### Reception
Gods of the Deep has received mostly negative reviews, holding a 3.2/10 rating on iMDB (below average user experience)

Godzilla (ゴジラ, Gojira) is a fictional kaiju, who first appeared in Toho's 1954 film of the same name. The character was later incorporated into the cooperative board game Cthulhu: Death May Die and appears in the tie-in comic Godzilla vs. Cthulhu: A Death May Die Story.

### Overview
In the original film, Godzilla was a prehistoric reptile who laid dormant in the ocean for millions of years, before being awoken and mutated by a hydrogen bomb. The giant monster preceded to go on a rampage to get revenge on humanity, most notably destroying the Japanese city of Tokyo, until he was finally killed by a superweapon known as the Oxygen Destroyer. Shortly afterwards, a second Godzilla would emerge to be featured in the rest of the Showa era films. Although this Godzilla was initially antagonistic and destructive like the first one, he would slowly become more of a heroic character, protecting the Earth from various threats.

Godzilla has since gone through many different iterations in various films, comics, novels, animated series and video games. However, most of the incarnations have a similar backstory, with them being either inspired by or even directly connected to the original film.

### Trivia
*Godzilla was planned to fight Cthulhu in an unmade 1994 Heisei film and the Infestation 2 crossover comic story, but both instances were scrapped.
*The Japanese reference book World Kaiju Encyclopedia features an illustration of Cthulhu, which was inspired by Godzilla in terms of design.
*In the children's book Dreidel of Dread: The Very Cthulhu Hanukkah, Cthulhu is awoken by a battle between Godzilla and the kaiju from Pacific Rim.
*In the film Shin Godzilla, the character Goro Maki used to be a professor at Miskatonic University.
*In the novel GODZILLA: Monster Apocalypse, the American nuclear submarine Seawolf made contact with the kaiju Dagahra at the coordinates 47°9′S 126°43′W, which is the same location as R'lyeh.
*In the comic Godzilla in Hell #5, the God-demon has a strong resemblance to Yog-Sothoth.
*In the comic Godzilla: Here There Be Dragons II - Sons of Giants #2, Hedorah's design has a strong resemblance to Cthulhu.
*The Monsterverse Titan Scylla has some resemblance to Cthulhu. In the comic Justice League vs. Godzilla vs. Kong #3, she is compared to Cthulhu by the Flash and Cyborg.
*In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, Gazira was heavily inspired by Godzilla.
*In the television series Ultraman Tiga, Gatanothor has a slightly modified version of Desghidorah's roar, and the Zoiger have a modified version of Rodan's roar.

Gog-Hoor (Eater of the Insane) is a fictional entity created by Weston Ochse for his short story "A Spectacle of a Man". The character was later incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

### Description
Gog-Hoor is a Great Old One that lives in a reverse dimension and can only be visible to humans through reflective surfaces, including puddles of water and mirrors. It is described as being a monster with a bullet-shaped head attached to a body that is inconceivably huge, presumably infinite in size. Gog-Hoor feeds on humans with mental disorders, using its numerous tentacles to drag them into its own dimension and devour their souls. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

Gol-goroth (The Forgotten Old One) is a fictional deity created by Robert E. Howard for his Cthulhu Mythos stories, and later incorporated into the tales of Lin Carter as a Great Old One. He is first mentioned in Howard's "The Children of the Night", where Professor Kirowan refers to "nameless and ghastly gods and entities as Cthulhu, Yog Sothoth, Tsathoggua, Gol-goroth, and the like." Howard explores the idea further in "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth", where Gol-Gororth is preeminent among the titular entities.

### Background
Gol-goroth appears as a titanic, black toad-like monstrosity with an impossibly malevolent glare, or a tentacle covered, scaly, bat-winged entity. However, its physical form may alter to fit the worst nightmares of whoever is viewing it (spider-like to an arachnophobic person, etc.). (: "Dagon Manor")

It is a dark god of Bal-Sagoth (: "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth") and Hyboria, with some modern cults centering around Britain (: "Dagon Manor") and might also be named as the god of the Black Stone in Hungary (: Ye Booke of Monstres), although other sources have challenged this claim (: Ye Booke of Monstres II). It may have been worshipped in Atlantis under the name Golgor in connection with other Atlantean deities such as Valka, Hotah, and Honen (: "The Moon of Skulls").

In the first printing of "The Fishers from Outside", by Lin Carter, Gol-goroth is mentioned in the Book of Eibon as dwelling under Mount Antarktos, at the South Pole, and being the master of the Fishers from Outside (which Carter equates with the Shantaks). However, this has been rectified in more recent printings, as Carter intended to refer to Groth-Golka, not Gol-goroth, having simply confused the names of the two deities.

A remark by Kirowan implies that the Nameless Cults contains information about the Gol-goroth cult. (: "The Children of the Night") Kirowan later encountered the cult personally, implied to be hybrids of humans and Little People, and witnessed them summoning the god. An explosion killed the cultists and supposedly destroyed Gol-goroth himself. (: "Dagon Manor")

### In Other Media
*In the Marvel Multiverse, the events of "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth" occurred during the Hyborian Age of Conan, with Gol-goroth being worshipped as the god of darkness.
*Gol-goroth appears in the mobile game Devil Maker: Tokyo.
*Gol-goroth appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
*Gol-goroth appears in the trading card game Battle Spirits, under the name Gel-Goroth.
*Gol-goroth appears as a Hive Ogre and the second boss in the video game Destiny: The Taken King.
*In the survival horror video game Fear & Hunger, the final boss to reach Ending B is named "Gro-goroth", an Old God of destruction and human sacrifices who seeks to have blood spilled in his name, while embodying the concepts of death, chaos, and war.

shortDefinition: Golarion is a planet created by Paizo Inc in 2007 under its GameMastery imprint in a generic OGL module and 2 months later it became the primary setting for the Pathfinder roleplaying game. Because Pathfinder takes so much from the Cthulhu Mythos, Go...
fullContent:
Golarion is a planet created by Paizo Inc in 2007 under its GameMastery imprint in a generic OGL module and 2 months later it became the primary setting for the Pathfinder roleplaying game. Because Pathfinder takes so much from the Cthulhu Mythos, Golarian is influenced affected by Mythos concepts and creatures.
### Background
Golarion is a planet of numerous lifeforms, both sentient and non-sentient. A magic heavy world, with sorcerers, witches, and necromancers. There are dozens of sentient species inhabiting the planet. Which includes both native species and those whom have immigrated to the world or unwillingly ended up on the world (e.g. brought to the world by their former masters). Races which include dragons, elves, giants, krakens, lizardmen, merfolk, elementals, serpentmen, kitsune, etc. Humans are one of the primary races, but they did not originate on Golarion. Legends speak of a homeworld called Earth, and the ethnic groups among the humans are reminiscent of those of Earth (e.g. Chinese).

Golarion is part of a solar system that has a number of inhabited worlds, each of which has more than one sentient species, some of them native and others alien. Like Golarion, they are all magic-heavy worlds. Technologically these worlds range from the bronze age level to the Renaissance period, and societies range from cave-dwelling hunter-gatherer cultures to continent spanning bureaucratic empires. There is also sophisticated alien technology (robots, directed energy weapons, etc) which are the remnants of crashed starships or lost alien settlements, and are therefore rare and treated as artifacts.

The Outer Gods and Great Old Ones have servants and followers on Golarion, though they are in the minority. Among these races are Deep Ones and Neothelids. Cults which worship the Old Ones and/or the Dark Tapestry (Outer Gods) are considered blasphemous by most races and therefore suppressed. The planet has a few Great Old Ones, including Orgesh who was born on Golarion, Mhar who is imprisoned in that world, and Yig. Its sorcerers have visited other worlds under the influence of the Old Ones, as well as the Dreamlands within the Dimension of Dreams.

The golden mead is a fictional substance created by August Derleth for his Cthulhu Mythos series of short stories The Trail of Cthulhu.

### Description
The golden mead is a consumable liquid noted for its strong but pleasant taste and its soporific quality that causes the user to fall asleep until the mead's effects start to manifest. Such effects consist of a heightened sensory awareness, which also enables the user to separate their consciousness from their body, the latter which is kept in a state of suspended animation while the consciousness is free to travel through space by means of astral projection. (: "The House on Curwen Street", "The Gorge Beyond Salapunco")

According to the Celaeno Fragments, the golden mead is a product of the Elder Gods. While it's not known how he got access to it, Laban Shrewsbury carries vials of golden mead with him, and has used it to travel by Byakhee to the Nameless City, where his body remained preserved and unaging while his astral self traveled to the Great Library of Celaeno from 1915 to 1935. (: "The House on Curwen Street", "The Keeper of the Key")

The golden mead is also available as pellets that can be swallowed. (: "The Watcher from the Sky")

### In Other Media
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, Daijuuji Kurou screamed for his golden mead when Al Azif sent him flying in the bathroom.
