Gompa Bkgo-tu is a fictional monastery created in 2013 by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Background
Gompa Bkog-tu (aka, the Home of the Dawn), is a monastery located in southern Tibet near the Nepalese border. Within are 300 hundred monks of the Yellow Hat (Gelug) sect. Most of whom are warrior-monks who are skilled in the martial arts, the bow and arrow, and the spear. It's the stronghold of an ancient organization, predating Buddhism and the Tibetan Bon religion. Known as "The Dawn", it's believed to have been founded before the Hyperborean period and been active ever since. A dozen of its members reside in the monastery, and others operate elsewhere gathering intelligence or operating as its messengers. A few woman have been recruited into the Dawn.

The monastery was built in such a way that it can withstand a siege for many months. Within is a library containing mystic books, many of which contain information about the Mythos. The members of the Dawn have taken oaths in which they have given their absolute obedience its the orders's leadership and their total commitment to defend Tibet at any cost. The senior members of the Dawn are knowledgeable in spells that banish or destroy the Old One's minions and in the crafting of weapons that can be used against them.

Professor Gordon Walmsley, often known as Gordon Walmsley of Goole, is a fictional character created by Brian Lumley, frequently referred to in his Cthulhu Mythos tales. An expert of translating ancient texts, Walmsley is first mentioned in Lumley's "The Sister City" (1969); the work most often attributed to him, Notes on Deciphering Codes, Cryptograms, and Ancient Inscriptions, appears first in "Billy's Oak" (1970). Walmsley's most extended appearance is in "In the Vaults Beneath" (1971).   

Walmsley is described in "In the Vaults Beneath" as a "stout, balding, bespectacled little professor."   

### Biography
Gordon Walmsley comes from Goole in Yorkshire, a town he is so identified with that he is repeatedly referred to as "Gordon Walmsley of Goole."   

The professor achieves fame with his "feats of antiquarian deciphering," becoming an "expert on the Phitmar Stone—that contemporary of the famous Rosetta Stone with its key inscriptions in two forms of Egyptian hieroglyphs—and the Geph Columns Characters." Titus Crow acknowledges him as "the country’s greatest paleographer"--the only one who surpasses himself--and includes him among a select group of "notable gentlemen students of matters concerning things not usually apparent or open to the man in the street." Wingate Peaslee calls Walmsley "the greatest ever in his field." Hamilton Tharpe, on the other hand, denounced him (along with Sir Amery Wendy-Smith) as "mere dabblers" who "only scratched the surface."   

In 1952, Walmsley is curator at the Radcar Museum in Radcar, Yorkshire, where he studies a green figurine discovered in a Yorkshire stream and dates it as being over 10,000 years old.   

Sometime before 1955, he publishes Notes on Deciphering Codes, Cryptograms, and Ancient Inscriptions, the work for which he is best known.   

In October 1962, Anderson Tharpe seeks Walmsley's help in translating a text, but the professor is away at the Buenos Aires Museum of Antiquities, "busily translating the hieroglyphs on certain freshly discovered ruins in the mountains of the Aconcaguan Range near San Juan."

The Gorgons are a trio of sisters in Greek mythology: the two immortals Stheno and Euryale and the mortal Medusa. Who had living venomous snakes for their hair, turning those who viewed their visage into stone.

They first appeared in Marvel Comics in U.S.A. Comics #6 (December, 1942), written and penciled by Syd Shores and Al Avison.

### Background
According to Cthulhu cultist Hamilton Tharpe, the Gorgons were Cthulhu's priestesses "in the old world". (: "The Fairground Horror")

They are avatars of Our Ladies of Sorrow. (: Our Ladies of Sorrow, Malleus Monstrorum) 

The Gorgons are a mystical race that descends from the Elder God Set. Sired by Set's son Phorcys who mated with the sea monster Ceto. They have green-skinned serpentine bodies, a feminine humanoid face, two mammary glands (breasts), snakes for hair, and fangs. Some of them have a green-skinned humanoid body with snakes for hair.

### Notes
*The Witches and Other Night-Fears excerpt about Gorgons is the preface to "The Dunwich Horror" ().

Gorlaks are a species of creature created by H. P. Lovecraft’s friend and correspondent Henry Kuttner for his 1937 short story "The Eater of Souls."

### Description
The garlaks inhabited, and presumably originated on, an unnamed planet orbiting a star beyond Betelgeuse. A domesticated reptilian species, they are fast-moving, but described as possessing a "repugnantly shaped" body form. (: "The Eater of Souls")

A gorlak was used by the Sindara, ruler of the city of Bel Yarnak, in his quest to end the deaths of his people at the hands of the monstrous Eater of Souls. (: "The Eater of Souls")

Gou Tanabe is a Japanese manga creator, best known for adapting the stories of H. P. Lovecraft into the comic book format. His adaptations have proven so popular that they have been translated into English, French, German, Spanish and Italian.

Tanabe has noted how Lovecraft's characters "lose all hope and appetite for life. It is this common thread in Lovecraft's stories that particularly struck me."

According to Junji Ito, a famous horror manga artist, he had considered adapting Lovecraft's stories until Tanabe did it first.

The Grace are Great Old Ones from the fictional universe of Doctor Who by Big Finish Productions.

### Description
The Grace are a benevolent group of Great Old Ones who created the Key to Time. The Black and White Guardians are their agents. They exist outside of time and space, in a state of non-existence. This collective works at keeping the universe together, and when necessary enters reality to prevent its collapse. Beings which are too big to enter normal time and space, the Doctor imagined them as "big, peaceful, pan-dimensional creatures with enormous power". They are in fact entities who can stop time for brief periods and crush the Doctor with a thought. (: The Chaos Pool)

In their native realm, the Grace appear as impish boneless creatures. (: The Prisoner's Dilemma)

Despite their association with the Mythos as putative Great Old Ones, their goodness puts them at odds with the cosmicism of Lovecraft and aligns them more with the benevolent Elder Gods of the Derleth version of the Mythos.

fullContent:
The Graeae ("Gray Ones") are three Titan sisters in Ancient Greek mythology. They are hags or witches in Greek mythology.  They were described as sharing only one eye, one tooth and one tongue, having to share use of these three grisly detachable body parts to communicate or take action.

In the Marvel fictional universe it is mentioned they are the offspring of Echidna but they have not yet made an appearance in Marvel Comics.

### Background
In the Marvel fictional universe, the Graeae are granddaughters of the Elder God Set, as the offspring of Set's son Phorcys who mated with Ceto, a sea monster. The sisters are witches that look like ancient women (hags) and they share one eye and one tooth. Whose names are Enyo, Deino (or Dino), and Pemphredo (or Pephredo).

They have also been called the Grey Ones of Hellas and were individually known as Pephredo, Enyo and Deino. In this version they are an avatar of Our Ladies of Sorrow. (: Our Ladies of Sorrow) They were the oracle of men, but that role was then taken over by the keeper of secrets. They tried to retake that role through their daughter, clashing against the Harlot. (: Hexed: The Harlot and the Thief)

Graham Masterton  (born 16 January 1946) is a British horror fiction author. His debut novel, The Manitou (Neville Spearman, 1975), featured as its villain Misquamacus, a character from H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth's The Lurker at the Threshold. Masterton went on to write a series of novels featuring Misquamacus.

### Manitou Series
Masterton's novels featuring Misquamacus and/or the protagonist Harry Erskine include:

* The Manitou (1976)
* Revenge of the Manitou (1979)
* Burial (1993)
* Manitou Blood (2005)
* Blind Panic (2009)
* Plague of the Manitou (2015)

Misquamacus is also featured in Masterton's 1996 short story  "Spirit Jump."

The Manitou was made into a 1978 film of the same name, starring Tony Curtis, Susan Strasberg, Burgess Meredith, and Michael Ansara. Masterton was said to have "liked it a lot".

fullContent:
"Gramma" is a short story by Stephen King, first published in Spring 1984 in Weirdbook #19. It also appeared in the 1985 collection Skeleton Crew. It is one of a handful of King stories that makes direct allusions to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
The story concerns a boy in his early teens who must look after his bedridden grandmother while his mother is away. The old woman dies, but then resurrects herself long enough to pass something evil on to the boy.

### Mythos Connections
In an attempt to lay his gramma to rest, the boy invokes the name of Hastur after being prompted to do so by his aunt. One of gramma's spells also mentions "Gyaagin" and "Yos-soth-oth".

### Adaptations
"Gramma" was the basis of a 1986 episode of The Twilight Zone, with a screenplay by Harlan Ellison. The voice of Gramma was provided by Piper Laurie.

In 2014, a feature film called Mercy was based on the short story.

Grandma Gilman is a Cthulhu Mythos novelette by author Bryan Whitehead, published digitally through Amazon's Kindle platform by 8sails Press in January 2013 .

### Publishers Description 


### Synopsis
When her maternal great-aunt Rebeccah "dies", apparently lost at sea, 12-year-old Sarah Upton and her parents travel to Innsmouth to attend the passing ceremonies. There, she learns of the Innsmouth Look, it’s implications for her and her extended family, and the secret that her grandmother, reputedly sequestered in her home for 20 years, is ready to claim her birthright in the ancient city of Y'ha-nthlei.

### Behind the Mythos
Grandma Gilman portrays the Deep Ones in a far more sympathetic light than is the norm: while not exactly depicting them as benevolent creatures, certain parts of the story suggest a sense of community and belonging absent in most other works.

### Trivia
*The cover of Grandma Gilman, which depicts a dinosaur skull partially obscured by lace fabric, is unrelated to the story.

"Graveyard Rats" is an episode of the Netflix original television show Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities. It is an adaptation of Henry Kuttner's 1936 short story "The Graveyard Rats".

### Overview
Whilst remaining largely faithful to the original, the episode adds some backstory involving Masson, the sticky-fingered graveyard caretaker, having to steal from the corpses in his charge in order to repay a debt owed to a dangerous criminal, as well as a segment on the mortician who aids him in his activities. The end is also slightly altered, with Masson being devoured by the hungry rats rather than suffering a heart attack.

Adapted for the screen by Guillermo del Toro, directed by Vincenzo Natali, and starring David Hewlett in the role of Masson, "Graveyard Rats" was released on the Netflix streaming service on 25 October 2022.

The Gray Man is a supernatural character created by American comic book creator Michael Alan Nelson for the Fall of Cthulhu story arc named for the character. The Gray Man made his first appearance in issue #11 of that series in March 2008.

### Description
A seemingly unkillable creature of unknown origin, the Gray Man manifests as a humanoid male dressed in the manner of a stereotypical Hispanic gangster, complete with tailored suit and Portuguese language. He possesses a ceremonial knife which he prefers to use to kill his victims, but is not necessary for use on mortal beings. However, it has been hinted that this artefact is intended for use against targets far more powerful than mere humans…

### History
The Gray Man was summoned by persons unknown to kill an unidentified target. Although the young thief Lucifer stole his knife and spirited it away to Arkham, the Gray Man tracked it down and embarked on a murderous rampage in his efforts to retrieve it. Although several civilians and police officers died during the slaughter, Sheriff Raymond Dirk and Lucifer managed to imprison him in one of the Harlot's boxes, saving Arkham, at least for a short while.

fullContent:
The Great Britain Project was a series of operations conducted by the Wilmarth Foundation against the Cthulhu Cycle Deities which occurred as the culmination of events in Brian Lumley's 1974 novel The Burrowers Beneath.

### Overview
In the 1960's, the Wilmarth Foundation, a secretive group of humans from across the globe who were aware of and dedicated to destroying the Cthulhu Cycle Deities, became aware of a major incursion by the subterranean Shudde M'ell and his kin. Responding only after several years' research into the strengths and vulnerabilities of these underground creatures, the Foundation eventually made its move, but not before recruiting occult authorities Titus Crow and Henri-Laurent de Marigny into their ranks.

Having discovered that most tactics employed against the Cthulhu Mythos deities would only work once as these creatures communicated telepathically, transmitting their experiences to each other on or during death, the Foundation coordinated the efforts of the Great Britain Project to coincide with the assaults of the American Project, a similar campaign designed to rid the American continents of the same threats.

The Wilmarth Foundation's strategy consisted mainly of sinking deep shafts into the ground baited with captured female Chthonians, then blasting any of that species which came to rescue their kin with high-powered jets of water; as water acts like a powerful acid upon Cthonic biology, this was thought to have been a perfect weapon to use once the ambushes were sprung.

Ultimately, the Great Britain Project was successful, cleansing the whole of the British Isles of the Cthonic menace, although it was not without setbacks, notably when Professor Wingate Peaslee attempted to destroy Cgfthgnm'o'th, a lesser minion of Cthulhu, with an explosive mining drill. While this did kill the beast, much of the Foundation's equipment and several of their personnel were lost in the carnage unleashed by the dying monstrosity. Also, at the height of the Project's success, the by-then fleeing Cthonians discovered that by pooling their mental resources, they could bypass the magical defences employed by Peaslee's men, and their psychic "invasions" resulted in several suicides and so-called accidents. However, this too was only a stalling tactic, and the Foundation overcame it through the profligate use of Star Stones, artefacts which were anathema to the Cthonics, and whose protections the subterranean creatures were unable to breach.

"Great Cthulhu" is a short Mythos story by author Sebastian Greaves. It is aimed at the Young Adult demographic.

### Synopsis
A pair of Cthulhu cultists, secretly conducting rituals in Miskatonic University, concoct an elaborate plan to lure in a fresh sacrifice. As their plot unfolds, the Great Old One Cthulhu begins to awaken …

### Characters
*Constance Ashford, a "professor-turned-curator", specialising in ancient artefacts.

*Michael Rochester, a lawyer and secret Cthulhu cultist.

### Publication History
"Great Cthulhu" was published in the collection Cthulhu Mythos Anthology on Amazon's digital Kindle platform.

### Trivia
*The name of the mental health institute involved in the cult's scheme, the Carolyn Fern Sanitorium, is likely a nod to a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Files series of Cthulhu Mythos works.

The Great Intelligence is a fictional cosmic entity created for the science fiction TV series Doctor Who in the 1967 serial The Abominable Snowmen. Some sources in the Doctor Who expanded universe equate this entity with Yog-Sothoth. (: All-Consuming Fire, Millennial Rites)

### Overview
The Great Intelligence is a malevolent disembodied intelligence perhaps originating from another dimension or universe, although in its original appearances it is explicitly extraterrestrial in origin, "floating about in space". It can take over the bodies of humans and manifest itself as a web-like material. Although its exact motivations are unclear, it desires to conquer Earth, and has employed armies of Robot Yeti to try to subjugate humanity. These robots contain metallic spheres inside their bodies, which provide a direct link to the mind of the Intelligence.

The physical manifestation of the Great Intelligence in our universe (outside of its Robot Yeti and the people whose minds have been possessed by it) usually takes the form of a web-like substance that can be generated on land, sky, or outer space, and is even capable of immobilising a Time Lord's TARDIS in mid-flight. This web also seems to have the biological properties of a fungus.

Additionally, the Great Intelligence can also manifest itself as a slime-like fluid, a dense fog that can engulf and absorb victims, or even as information in a computer network. (: The Abominable Snowmen, The Web of Fear, Downtime)

### History
In the 17th century, the Tibetan High Lama Padmasambhava made contact with the Great Intelligence while astral-traveling. The Intelligence took over his body and kept him alive for centuries until 1935, using him to create an army of Robot Yeti. Once defeated by the Doctor, the Intelligence was banished from Earth, thus allowing the High Lama to finally die in peace. (: The Abominable Snowmen)

More than 30 years later, however, the reactivation of one of the Robot Yeti provided the Great Intelligence with another opportunity to manifest itself on Earth and try to complete its transition into a fully corporeal form, which appeared as a web-like substance generated in space and in the London sewers.

Once again, the Intelligence took over a human host, in this case Staff Sergeant Arnold. This time, however, it intentionally lured the Doctor towards it with the ultimate goal of draining his mind and taking over his body. The Doctor, upon learning this, tried to reverse the process and destroy the Intelligence by draining its own mind instead, but the process was interrupted by Jamie, who destroyed the Intelligence's control spheres to save the Doctor. This resulted in the Great Intelligence being simply banished from Earth again, but not destroyed permanently as the Doctor hoped. (: The Web of Fear)

The Great Intelligence Institute was an organisation created by the BBC in 2012 for Doctor Who.

### Background
The Great Intelligence Institute was founded in London, Great Britain during the 19th century by Walter Simeon. It was established with the goal of creating a physical form for the Great Intelligence. The Institute manipulated snow so that it could be imbued with the Great Intelligence's essence. It took the institute decades to achieve its goal, resulting in the rising of snowmen on Christmas Eve, 1892, to which the Doctor put an end.

The Great Library of Celaeno is a fictional extraterrestrial library created by August Derleth for his Cthulhu Mythos short story series The Trail of Cthulhu.

### Description
As its name indicates, the library is located on a world orbiting the star Celaeno, and contains "books and hieroglyphs stolen from the Elder Gods". (: "The House on Curwen Street")

It is a vast, ancient stone structure of gigantic proportions, as if built by a species much larger than humans, including at least one colossal round window and a number of monolithic columns and shelves, holding equally enormous books with strange hieroglyphs. (: "The Gorge Beyond Salapunco")

### In Other Media
*Demonbane: The Great Library of Celaeno appears as one of the worlds where Demonbane and Liber Legis fought through during their final battle at the Outerverse. The Library was described to be filled with many arcane tomes, including books about the Elder Gods, with bat-winged creatures that could be seen flying in the distance.
*Haiyore! Nyaruko-san: The Great Library of Celaeno appears in the episode "Celaeno Library War", where it is stated to have the largest collection of books in the universe, containing any and all wisdom including the rarest grimoires known to exist. Zhar and Lloigor infiltrated the library to steal the Evil Deity’s Memo Pad for the "Nonexistent Deity Plan", in order to receive more funds for their sketchy environmentalist group by creating new endangered species to protect.

The Great Old Ones are a group of unique, malignant beings of great power in the fictional cosmology of the Cthulhu Mythos. Cthulhu, H. P. Lovecraft's famous creation, is described as a Great Old One. They reside in various locations on Earth, and once presided over the planet as gods and rulers.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Lovecraft uses the phrase "Great Old Ones" in just two of his stories. Unlike his successors, Lovecraft uses the term to refer to the races later writers would identify as the Cthulhi and the Elder Things, not to his pantheon of alien gods.

In "The Call of Cthulhu," it's how the captured Cthulhu cultists refer to the entities they worship:

More information on the Great Old Ones comes from Old Castro, one of the few sane members of the cult:

Castro looks forward to a time when humanity will "become as the Great Old Ones; free and wild and beyond good and evil, with laws and morals thrown aside and all men shouting and killing and revelling in joy."

In At the Mountains of Madness, the discovery of traces of evolutionarily advanced creatures in Antarctic sediments a billion years old prompts the Miskatonic University biologist Lake to "whimsically recall the primal myths about Great Old Ones who filtered down from the stars and concocted earth-life as a joke or mistake."

Dyer, the story's narrator, later declares that the starfish-headed crinoids known as the Elder Things are: 


### Classification
In the broader Cthulhu Mythos, the Great Old Ones are often distinguished from the more cosmically placed entities such as Azathoth, Nyarlathotep, and Yog-Sothoth--known as the Outer Gods--and from alien but less godlike creatures such as the Chthonians, the Deep Ones, the Elder Things, and the Mi-Go. Yet this distinction is unclear at times, in part because the terminology is not always consistent; for instance, Nyarlathotep, despite his marked interest in Earth and its culture, is generally considered to be one of the Outer Gods instead of a Great Old One. On the other hand, Hastur has several avatars and is generally based in outer space, but he is still considered a Great Old One. There are conflicting views on the proper classification for Shub-Niggurath.

Very few people dispute that Azathoth and Yog-Sothoth are Outer Gods instead of Great Old Ones, although some accounts make them ancestors of a few Great Old Ones. This has led to the theory that "Great Old One" is the term for everything younger than Cthulhu and Tsathoggua, and "Other God" or "Outer God" to be everything older.

The Great Old Ones are a pantheon of malevolent entities in the Doctor Who universe. The Great Old Ones were first introduced to Doctor Who in the 1993 novel White Darkness, by Virgin Publishing, with Cthulhu as the primary antagonist, although he wasn't identified by name until All-Consuming Fire. In 1994-1995, old enemies of The Doctor (e.g. Animus) were retconned into being Great Old Ones in the novels All-Consuming Fire and Millennial Rites.

### Background
The Great Old Ones are entities which existed before the universe. Beings whom, in the race memory of mankind, were its worst nightmares. Entities that spread chaos, evil, and destruction wherever they were. They couldn't be killed within the material universe. The language of the Old Ones was quantum mnemonics, which was their equivalent of Block Transfer Computations, giving them the ability to rewrite reality. They saw the Time Lords as a threat.

In their home universe, the Old Ones had physical bodies. When they entered N-Space, they got new bodies; some of them lost their new bodies when forced to flee from the Fendahl, abandoning their new forms. Afterwards, for brief periods of time, the Old Ones were able to assume physical forms, as their new state of being was as collective consciousnesses. The Old Ones created planes and universes between the dimensions, which became their new home.

It's theorized that the Old Ones were the Time Lords of their universe. The Great Old Ones most active in the universe were known as the Elder Gods, who played cosmic games with each other, using the dimension known as the Board. The powers displayed by the Great Old Ones varied depending on the individual, including re-animation of the dead, extending an individual's lifespan, time travel, manipulating and relocating timelines, creating thunder and lightning, simultaneously existing in multiple time zones, stopping a TARDIS in fight, and generating fog, fungus and webbing.

The Old Ones could not die within the material dimension, simply reappearing if killed--since their bodies were composed of energies that didn't belong in the material universe. If they decayed, those energies would tear apart space and time. The only places that an Old One could safely die were either in its own universe or the Board, causing the Time Vortex to turn inside out. TARDIS sensors revealed that the amount of energy in an Old One's body was the equal of 20 billion nukes.

### Departure from Canon
In the Doctor Who universe, there are no Outer Gods. Entities which are generally considered Outer Gods in the Cthulhu Mythos (e.g. Yog-Sothoth) are instead regarded as Great Old Ones. The Great Ones (also known as the Gods of Earth) are fictional entities created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Other Gods". 

### Overview
The so-called "gods" of the Dreamlands, the Great Ones are not as powerful as the Great Old Ones and are not even as intelligent as most humans. However, they are protected by the Outer Gods, particularly Nyarlathotep.

While they once lived on peaks across the world they were driven off of lower mountains by the spread of humanity until they had to leave Earth entirely, leaving only a mark on Mount Ngranek. The Great Ones now rule from their hidden fortress of Kadath, whose location in time and space is unknown. As well as occasionally returning to white capped Thurai, Lerion and Hatheg-Kla on cloud ships under the cover of a light mist, they abandoned Kadath for a brief period for the "sunset city" that Randolph Carter conjured in his dreams.

In the past, the Great Ones often married human women, so many human inhabitants of the Dreamlands have Great One blood in them. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

In H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands, a distinction is made between the Great Ones and "Lesser Dreamlands Deities", such as Oukranos, which aren't part of the pantheon.

### List of Great Ones

The Great Race of Yith (also known as Yithians) are a fictional species of sapient extraterrestrial entities, created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Shadow Out of Time. Their most notable feature is an ability to coercively exchange minds with individuals of other species, even across great spans of time and space. 

They are often depicted as large cone-shaped invertebrates, the form of a prehistoric Earth species whose bodies the Yithians projected their minds into. In this incarnation, they built a flourishing civilization about two hundred million years before the present day.

Their civilisation as it existed in Earth's distant past was eventually wiped out by a race of even more ancient extraterrestrial (possibly extradimensional) beings known as the flying polyps, which the Yithians had already fought several terrible wars with. However, the Yithians themselves survived by again projecting their minds en masse, into a future insectoid race that will one day inherit the Earth long after mankind has ceased to be.

### Description
The shape of the original forms the Great Race had on Yith is unknown; after migrating to Earth, they housed themselves in a species native to our planet, beings resembling large cones with a muscular foot for locomotion and four extensible arms or tentacles projecting from the apex. Two of these arms ended in claws or pincers, the third terminated in four clustered trumpet-like organs, and the fourth was topped with a spherical yellow "head" with three dark eyes, four stalked flower-like hearing organs on top, and a number of green tentacles dangling beneath. Their blood was dark green and very thick.

The Great Race spoke using their pincers to produce a series of clicks and scraping sounds, probably also with some form of telepathy, and wrote using their head tentacles. They ate and drank using their red, trumpet-like organ, the food described as an almost liquid, grey substance. The Great Race shared only two senses with humans, hearing and seeing, but possessed other senses inaccessible to other species inhabiting a Yithian body.

The Great Race was sexless and reproduced via seeds laid in water; however, due to their longevity, which could last several thousands of years, reproduction rarely happened.

### Mind control
Yithians gained very advanced and evolved minds that allowed them to project their consciousnesses across time and space, taking over the minds of other creatures from not only other time periods but other planets and universes. While the Yithian inhabited the body, the captive mind was projected into the body of the inhabiting member of the Great Race; though the difference in personality of the target of the mind-exchange was usually noticeable and the person affected considered oddly repu

Green is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu". 

### Overview
Green was the first mate of the Emma of Auburn. En route to Callao, the Emma encountered the heavily armored steam yacht Alert, who ordered the schooner to turn back. Captain Collins refused, leading the Alert to fire upon the Emma using a brass cannon. In retaliation, the crew of the Emma managed to board the Alert and slay all of its members, although Green and Collins were killed in the battle, leaving Second Mate Gustaf Johansen in command of the crew.

fullContent:
Green and Pleasant Land is a regional sourcebook for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Produced by American roleplaying game manufacturer Chaosium in collaboration with British wargaming/roleplaying company Games Workshop, it was compiled by Pete Tamlyn and includes work from an ensemble cast of writers including Brian Lumley, Graeme Davis, and Marc Gascoigne. Running to a total of 80 pages, it was published in 1987.

### Overview
Green and Pleasant Land contains real-world background information on the culture, politics, and influential personages of Great Britain during the 1920s and 30s, as well as fictional information on the occult factors present throughout the British Isles. Also included are a trio of stand-alone scenarios set across the country, as well as a short story by the late British author Brian Lumley.

### Reception
Green and Pleasant Land holds an approval rating of 5.6/10 based on 6 reviews on review aggregate site RPG.net, indicating an "Average" to "Above Average" score.

The Green God is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Horror Under Warrendown" (although it is unnamed), and later incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu horror role-playing game. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Description
Residing in the underground labyrinth beneath Warrendown in the Severn Valley of England, the Green God appears as a giant statue of a head, similar to those found on Easter Island; however, it is composed entirely of vegetable matter and is capable of extruding lengthy vine-like appendages which it uses to ensnare potential victims or to offer communion to the degenerate cult of mutants who worship it.

An unusual feature of the Green God is its ability to transmute those who eat its flesh. Any who consume the vegetable matter which forms its body will slowly transform into a disgusting, rabbit-like creature, whose sole purpose is to expand the Horror's cult by offering seemingly-innocent vegetables to normal humans, in turn changing them into one of their own.

*Ei'lor, another Great Old One who shares many similarities with the Green God.

Greenland, the largest island on Earth, lies to the east of North America off the coast of Canada. It is mentioned in Cthulhu Mythos stories by H. P. Lovecraft, and is thought to be at least part of the location of Clark Ashton Smith's Hyperborea.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In "The Call of Cthulhu", Princeton anthropology professor William Channing Webb tells a gathering of archeologists about his 1860 visit to Greenland, in which "high up on the West Greenland coast [he] had encountered a singular tribe or cult of degenerate Esquimaux whose religion, a curious form of devil-worship, chilled him with its deliberate bloodthirstiness and repulsiveness." Their religion, rejected by other Esquimaux, "had come down from horribly ancient aeons before ever the world was made." It required human sacrifice, as well as "certain queer hereditary rituals addressed to a supreme elder devil or tornasuk"; in a formula provided by "an aged angekok or wizard-priest," their deity is addressed as "dead Cthulhu". A fetish "around which they danced when the aurora leaped high over the ice cliffs" closely resembled one retrieved by Inspector John Raymond Legrasse in the Louisiana swamps.

The revision story "The Horror in the Museum" alludes to "the sharp horn of Gnoph-keh, the hairy myth-thing of the Greenland ice, that walked sometimes on two legs, sometimes on four, and sometimes on six."

### Clark Ashton Smith
Clark Ashton Smith, in his story "Ubbo-Sathla", writes of the Crystal of Zon Mezzamalech: "A geologist found it in Greenland, beneath glacial ice, in the Miocene strata.... It may have belonged to some sorcerer of primeval Thule. Greenland was a warm, fertile region, beneath the sun of Miocene times."

Chief Grey Eagle is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop. He has a minor role in "The Curse of Yig", and a comparatively small but important role in The Mound.

### Biography
Grey Eagle is a Wichita chieftain from Oklahoma. In 1928, his age was estimated as being close to 150. A young ethnologist from Virginia suspects that his longevity might be related to the medallion he carries with him, made from an unknown metal that was brought to Earth by Cthulhu. The object was inherited by Grey Eagle from his father, who in turn inherited it from Grey Eagle's grandfather, and so on. All his ancestors who bore the medallion lived for over a century and died only in battle.

As a chief, Grey Eagle is widely regarded as a wise and benevolent man, respected by his own people as well as by many others. He and his family have preserved knowledge of how the people of K'n-yan once lived on the surface and used to trade and bear children with humans, but isolated themselves in the underground after the cataclysmic floods that sank many of the Earth's landmasses. (: The Mound)

In 1889, Walker Davis asked questions about Yig to the Wichita shamans and chiefs, including Grey Eagle, who told Davis that Yig's appearance was humanoid enough to be mistaken for a man if seen from some distance. (: "The Curse of Yig")

In 1916, Grey Eagle was the only Wichita to offer any advice to Joe Norton and Rance Wheelock when they were investigating the death of Capt. George E. Lawton, who had disappeared into a local mound and returned mutilated and traumatized, dying soon afterwards. Grey Eagle advised the two men to stay away from "those people". Twelve years later, he gave the same advice to the Virginian ethnologist who sought to investigate the legend of the two "ghosts" (a man and a headless woman) who patrol the mound. When the ethnologist decided to explore the mound anyway, Grey Eagle presented him with his medallion, which would confer protection against the K'n-yanians, as they would recognize it as a symbol of their gods.

After the man returned following a terrifying encounter with the reanimated remains of one of the K'n-yanians' victims, he asked and obtained permission from Grey Eagle to have the medallion examined by authorities, who found that the metal it was made of didn't occur anywhere on Earth. Afterwards, the medallion was returned to Grey Eagle. (: The Mound)

Grimm Spotlight: Lovecraft's Legacy is a comic book story written by Joe Brusha and featuring artwork by Juan Francisco Mota. It was published digitally by Zenescope Entertainment in June 2023; a variety of variant covers were created .

### Overview


### Synopsis
As part of his scheme to rouse the sleeping god Cthulhu, Dagon tasks Hastur, the King in Yellow, to hunt down the great grandson of fames horror writer and prophet H. P. Lovecraft, who he believes holds the secret of the Nameless City - location of the dread Necronomicon - in the depths of his unconscious.

Although Hastur is easily able to track down Professor Henry Jones - the last of Lovecraft's line - the timely intervention of Sherlock Holmes's descendant Spencer and goddess of death Keres proves too much for the King. With assistance from a fortuitously-discovered box of magical artefacts, the group are able to defeat Hastur and retire to plan their next move.

Grimoires are books of great importance or power and are the source of much of the forbidden knowledge that illuminates the darkest recesses of the world. These books contain forbidden knowledge and discoveries about the Great Old Ones or of many occult topics. Oftentimes, these discoveries of forbidden truths end up either driving the reader insane or leading to their ruin in one way or another.

Grimoire of the Aristocracy (Гримуар аристократії) is a Ukrainian-language anthology translated by Solomiya Kurylo and published by Propala hramota (Пропала грамота). This book contains Lovecraft's non-fiction works and reveals his worldview and ideological beliefs. It will discuss aristocracy, thoughts on conservatism, and reflections on the decline of civilization, inspired by Oswald Spengler.

fullContent:
“Grinding Rock” is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Cody Goodfellow that first appeared in Book of Dark Wisdom #5 (2005). It tells the story of a firefighter battling a wildfire near San Diego and the price he learns must be paid for California's paradise.

The title refers to a type of Native American artifact commonly found in the region:


### Characters 
*Tim Vowles: A San Diego firefighter who comes across an ancient ritual being consummated while battling a wildfire.
*Calvin Loomis: A 69-year-old "retired U.S. Geological Survey engineer afflicted with Alzheimer’s" who carries out a sacrifice that must be made every 20 years to protect California from disaster. He is described as having "soft, sunny, Elmer Fudd features, white crew-cut hair, and freckled, ruddy skin."

### Setting
The places mentioned in the story--Mission Trails Regional Park, Mount Fortuna, the Golden West Concrete quarry,  the Navy golf course, the "upscale pseudo-villas and palatial townhouses" of Tierrasanta--are real locations in San Diego County.

### Connections
When offering the sacrifice, Loomis mentions N'kai--a fictional underground realm below K'n-yan in H. P. Lovecraft's revision tale "The Mound"--and Ubbo-Sathla, the polymorphous Outer God created by Clark Ashton Smith. Later in the story, an entity that seems to be Ubbo-Sathla manifests:


### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Book of Dark Wisdom, "Grinding Rock" was reprinted in The Weird Fiction Review (Fall 2010). It was included in the anthology New Cthulhu: The Recent Weird (Prime Books, 2011) and in Goodfellow's collection Rapture of the Deep and Other Lovecraftian Tales (Hippocampus Press, 2016).

The Grioth are a fictional race created by Paizo Inc. in 2013 for the Pathfinder roleplaying game.

### Background
The Grioth are a malevolent race that worships Nyarlathotep. They are enemies of the Dominion of the Black. They inhabit rogue worlds, residing in dark spire cities that are ruled by elders. Grioth use portals to travel to other worlds, to pillage them for resources. Physically they are batlike humanoids with four narrow eyes and a long ratlike tail. Many of them have been mutated by the Dark Tapestry into deformed or lumbering beings. The Elder possess unusual psionic powers, which aids the Grioth against their mortal enemies, the Dominion of the Black.

Groth-Golka is a fictional creature created by Robert E. Howard for his story "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth", originally depicted as being a giant flightless bird worshipped as a deity. In the expanded Cthulhu Mythos, Lin Carter identified it as a Great Old One and the lord of the Fishers from Outside, although in a case of mistaken identity, the first printing of "The Fishers from Outside" featured Gol-goroth in the place of Groth-Golka.

It has subsequently appeared in the Conan stories of Marvel Comics, and as a monster in the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. It is sometimes represented as resembling a pterosaur. 

### Background
In its debut story, Groth-Golka was identified as the last member of a species of prehistoric bird, who has lived for centuries and is worshiped as a god by the people of Bal-Sagoth. The creature's mortality, however, is demonstrated by its death at the hands of the protagonists. (: "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth")

However, in Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, Groth-Golka is now said to reside beneath Antarctica, indicating that it is still alive. Furthermore, one theory adds the interpretation that Groth-Golka and Mnomquah are brothers. (: Malleus Monstrorum: Cthulhu Mythos Bestiary Volume II)

### In the Marvel Multiverse
In the Marvel Universe, the events of "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth" occurred during the Hyborian Age of Conan. Groth-Golka was the last of the Lizard-Gods, and was killed by Fafnir.

Growleywogs are a fictional species of fabulous creatures featured in the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu.

### Description
Like most fabulous creatures, Growleywogs are native to the Dreamlands, where they can be found in swamps and humid areas, such as the Forest of Parg and the Jungles of Kled. They resemble giant toads, and nest in pools of water. These carnivorous beasts capture prey with a long, sticky, prehensile tongue. The prey is dragged towards the beast's mouth and held in place with needle-like teeth, as the Growleywog submerges in water and drowns its unfortunate victim. The name "Growleywog" comes from the low growling sound they make, which is similar to that of a large cat. (: H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands)

### Behind the Mythos
Growleywogs share their name with a species from the Wizard of Oz universe created by L. Frank Baum.

Gtuhanai the Insatiable is a fictional entity created by author J. B. Lee for his 1999 short story "Forces of Change."

### Description
Manifesting as a whirling conglomeration of helical metal structures, Gtuhanai is capable of absorbing any metals in its vicinity into its body, in turn increasing its own mass and power. What the upper limits to this ability are remain unknown, but are implied to perhaps be limitless. (: "Forces of Change")

According to the Necronomicon, Gtuhanai is worshipped by a species of metal beings known as the Aartna, which inhabit the region of space around the Pleiades star cluster. (: "Forces of Change")

### History
Gtuhanai is the "brother" of Cthulhu and the "son" of Yog-Sothoth; it has also been described as being somewhat similar to Glaaki, although whether any "familial" relationship exists between the two entities is unknown. It was first summoned to Earth by the sorcerer Mezamalek (perhaps the same being as Zon Mezzamalech of Hyperborea) who used its power on his enemies, obliterating all who stood against him before the entity turned on Mezamalek and consumed him. (: "Forces of Change")

In the modern day, Gtuhanai was discovered living in a small glass case in an old abandoned laboratory by a pair of young prodigies, Kat and Dren. The two brought Gtuhanai home with them and studied it, slowly becoming corrupted by its malignant presence before unleashing its full power on an unsuspecting world. (: "Forces of Change")

The Guardians of the Crystallizers of Dreams are a species of creature which appear in the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. 

### Description
Servants of the entity known as Hypnos, the Guardians originate on a plane of existence separate from our own. Appearing as ethereal floating jellyfish-like creatures with a pair of luminous amber eyes, they manifest in this dimension when one of the Crystallizers is used incorrectly or is taken from its owner. They will attack the offending entity with their long tentacles and drag them back to their own dimension, and due to their insubstantial form are immune to all physical attacks. 

### Behind the Mythos
The Guardians of the Crystallizers of Dreams were first mentioned in the Ramsey Campbell short story "The Render of the Veils" and were later expanded upon by Scott David Aniolowski for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement Ye Booke of Monstres II in 1995.

The Guardian Pillar is a fictional avatar created by Chaosium for the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. It is loosely inspired by the description of the Elder Gods in "The Lair of the Star-Spawn", by August Derleth and Mark Schorer, as well as the "pillar of flame" featured in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Description
The Guardian Pillar is a living flame, identified as an avatar of the Elder Gods, which dwells in the Cavern of Flame with the bearded priests Nasht and Kaman-Thah. It guards the gates to the Dreamlands, and enables Nasht and Kaman-Thah to contact the Great Ones, which are the only beings capable of commanding the Guardian Pillar to leave the Cavern of Flame. (: H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands)

### Behind the Mythos
The portrayal of the Guardian Pillar as an avatar of the Elder Gods which is controlled by the Great Ones might be a reference to the Dreamlands stories penned by Gary Myers, in which the Elder Gods and the Great Ones are actually the same species. However, this interpretation is not supported by the Call of Cthulhu RPG in general. In most iterations of the Mythos, the Great Ones are allied with the Elder Gods' enemies, the Outer Gods.

Guerrera is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu". 

### Overview
Guerrera was a member of the schooner Emma of Auburn, although his role is uncertain. After Donovan was successful in opening the vault discovered by the crew in R'lyeh, Cthulhu emerged, killing Guerrera, Donovan and Angstrom. This slaughter is the only mention of Guerrera in the story. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

### Trivia
*Guerrera is one of only three known characters in Lovecraft's fiction to be slain by Cthulhu itself. The Cthulhi, an extraterrestrial race who follow the deity and bear its image, were once at war with the Elder Things, but it is uncertain if Cthulhu was personally involved in the battle.

Gugs are a fictional extra-dimensional species in the Cthulhu Mythos. They originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Description
Gugs are large, black-furred beasts with vertically-opening fanged jaws. Their two eyes protrude from either side of their head, and their limbs bifurcate at the elbows, giving them four separate forearms. They are worshippers of the Great Ones, the gods of Earth who reside in Kadath. Gugs are estimated to reach around sixteen feet in height and weigh in at nearly 2,000 pounds.

### Behind the Mythos
Fantasy Flight Games have used Gugs as antagonists in several of their Arkham Horror Files lines of Mythos games, and even released a pre-painted plastic miniature as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures series of gaming aids.

### Gallery

S'glhuo is a fictional dimension which first appeared in Ramsey Campbell's short story "The Plain of Sound".

### Description
S'glhuo is another dimension that only exists in our dimension as sound. In certain places, such as the plain in the Severn Valley, the dimension overlaps into our own, creating the effect of walking through jelly. Sounds from our world correspond to objects in S'glhuo, and sounds in our world can create things both living and non-living in S'glhuo. The location in the Severn Valley corresponds to a city of pillars on a planet composed of sound. It is implied there are other planets made of sound in S'glhuo and that the dimension is home to Tru'nembra, an Outer God made from pure sound. In S'glhuo, our dimension is only perceptible as odor. Details on S'glhuo are given in The Revelations of Gla'aki, along with plans for a machine to contact the S'glhuoans.

### Inhabitants
It is not known if the blue skinned reptilians that live near the Severn Valley are the only type of S'glhuoans, but it is likely that the dimension is home to other life forms. The denizens of S'glhuo may be friendly or hostile, but seem to have knowledge of both advanced science and the Mythos. In their own world they are blue skinned, tall, boneless reptiloids, but in ours they are beings of pure sound.

Gustaf Johansen is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Overview
Johansen was a Norwegian sailor "of some intelligence," and the second mate of the Emma of Auburn, whose home address was in Oslo's Old Town. En route to Callao, the Emma encountered the heavily armored steam yacht Alert, who ordered the schooner to turn back. Captain Collins refused, leading the Alert to fire upon the Emma using a brass cannon. In retaliation, the crew of the Emma managed to board the Alert and slay all of its members, although Collins and First Mate Green were killed in the battle, leaving Johansen in command of the crew. He died shortly after his return from the South Pacific in 1925; his papers, found posthumously, provided the only first-hand account of Cthulhu in Lovecraft's fiction. His report was written in English to spare his wife, who could not speak the language, from learning the horror of Cthulhu. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

### Behind the Mythos
*Robert M. Price suggests that Johansen's nationality is a tip of the hat to the Draugen, a creature from Norwegian folklore, for helping to inspire Cthulhu. (: "The Other Name of Azathoth")

"Gut Shot and Coyote Eaten" is a short story by American author Ron Shiflet which is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
When small-time criminal Rafe's cousin Josh is shot in a double-cross, he takes the injured man to the new medical practitioner in town, Dr. Billingham, for treatment. However, although Billingham's procedure at first seems to works wonders for Josh, it soon becomes apparent that he has implanted some kind of abomination into him, one which is slowly taking control. Although Rafe is able to put the man out of his misery, he is captured by the doctor in the process and subjected to the same procedure himself.

### Behind the Mythos
At one point, Dr. Billingham mentions to Rafe that he learned his craft in Arkham, before reflecting to himself upon how his peers ostracised him for his unethical practices.

The Gyaa-Hua are a fictional species created by H. P. Lovecraft and Henry S. Whitehead for their short story "Bothon".

### Description
The Gyaa-Hua are ape-like creatures noted for their remarkable strength. In prehistoric times, they were employed as slaves by the human inhabitants of Atlantis (: "Bothon") and Mu (: "The Red Offering").

### Behind the Mythos
In the original story, the name of this species appears four times but with different spellings: twice spelled as "Gyaa-Hua" and twice as "Gyaa-Hau". This creates some uncertainty about which is supposed to be correct. Lin Carter, in "The Red Offering", opted to use Gyaa-Hua.

It's not known whether they're related to the similarly-named Gyaa-yothn from Lovecraft's The Mound. However, the fact that the Gyaa-yothn are hybrids created by cross-breeding the reptilian natives of Yoth with an unspecified mammalian species suggests that the mammals in question might have been the Gyaa-Hua.

Atlantis being home to ape-men is also present in "The Hyborian Age", by Robert E. Howard.

The Gyaa-yothn (singular: Gyaa-yoth) are a fictional species created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Mound.

### Description
The Gyaa-yothn are unnatural hybrids created by the men of the K'n-yan city of Tsath to act as horse-like mounts and perform physical labour. These quadrupeds combine aspects of reptiles and mammals. They have pale skin with black fur on their backs, a single horn on their heads, and vaguely humanoid faces. Though carnivorous, they are considered to be harmless.

### Creation
The Gyaa-yothn are the result of forcibly breeding the defeated races of K'n-yan with the creatures discovered in Yoth.

Despite the similarities of their names, it's not known whether they're related to the Gyaa-Hua.

### Purpose
They are used in a similar way to horses in the world above, for transport or pulling ploughs. However, in the former case, they can be ridden without saddles or guidance with a clumsy but regular pace. They are also capable of almost human farmwork.

Gyyagin is a fictional monster created by Stephen King for his short story "Jerusalem's Lot". A giant extraterrestrial worm that transforms its human followers into undead servitors, Gyyagin is itself identified as a servant of "Yogsoggoth" (possibly Yog-Sothoth), and is heavily implied to be the titular Worm that the grimoire known as De Vermis Mysteriis (English: Mysteries of the Worm) alludes to.

### Description
Gyyagin is a massive worm that burrows under the ground in the area around the town of Jerusalem's Lot, Maine. Descriptors and sobriquets include "the Worm from beyond space", "Star-Eater" and "Blinder of Time". Its body is segmented, at least 5 ft. wide, grey in colour, and produces black slime as it moves around its tunnels. Wherever it crawls over, the ground's vegetation withers and turns white. Its mere proximity seems to have a noxious effect on the local inhabitants, precipitating the birth of eyeless or noseless children.

Like many Mythos deities, Gyyagin demands bloody sacrifices. Its victims are apparently killed by constriction, as the gargantuan worm squeezes them until their blood vessels are ruptured.

Gyyagin is perhaps most notable for transforming its human followers into undead creatures (referred to at one point as nosferatu) which live in its tunnels with it. Blood relatives of these cultists seem to be subtly attracted to the area that the Worm inhabits, but it is not known whether this psychic link is formed by Gyyagin or by the undead relatives themselves.

Additionally, Gyyagin is known to have some kind of connection to the grimoire known as De Vermis Mysteriis, to the point that burning the book will force the deity to retreat and abandon pursuit of its target, at least for the time being. (: "Jerusalem's Lot")

### Behind the Mythos
The town of Jerusalem's Lot first appeared in Stephen King's 1975 novel 'Salem's Lot. In the novel, the vampire Kurt Barlow establishes himself in the town by making a pact with a powerful undisclosed entity, offering a child named Ralphie Glick as a sacrifice to it. Given Gyyagin's domain over the same town, penchant for demanding sacrifices, and association with undead / nosferatu, it would not be too much of a stretch to assume that the being that Barlow made a pact with might have been Gyyagin.

Herman Charles Koenig (28 November 1893 - 6 July 1959) was a laboratory manager at the Electrical Testing Laboratories in New York City. He was a friend and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft, who visited his laboratory in 1935 along with Frank Belknap Long and R. H. Barlow.

Lovecraft and Barlow included a reference to Koenig in their comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century" as the lighting effects supervisor "H. Kanebrake". A Crystal Company operative named Koenig is also mentioned briefly in "In the Walls of Eryx", by Lovecraft and Kenneth Sterling.

A massive fan and collector of fantastic literature, Koenig helped to popularise the work of William Hope Hodgson in the USA. He wrote the introduction to the Arkham House collection of Hodgson stories, The House on the Borderland and Other Novels (1946).

He also penned a short non-fiction piece, "The Favorite Weird Stories of H. P. Lovecraft," which first appeared in the October 1934 edition of The Fantasy Fan, and was later included in S. T. Joshi's The Annotated Supernatural Horror in Literature.

Herbert George Wells (1866 - 1946) was a British author who contributed to a variety of genres, but is most famous for his huge influence in science fiction. The Martian invaders and their tripod machines from his 1898 novel The War of the Worlds were later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, and by Don Webb's crossover story "To Mars and Providence".

The unnamed protagonist of Wells' The Time Machine was one of the heroes who teamed up with Randolph Carter in "Allan and the Sundered Veil", by Alan Moore.

### Themes
Wells' stories (sci-fi and otherwise) often show a preoccupation with social themes such as socialism, feminism, the stratification of classes, and the influence of new technologies, some of which he anticipated (his story "The Land Ironclads" predates the invention of actual tanks by over a decade). Perhaps his most famous story, The Time Machine, was the first major work of science fiction to depict a time-traveling device. Other novels that explore the consequences of scientific experiments and human nature include The Invisible Man and The Island of Dr. Moreau. 

Some of Wells' story lines and themes are paralleled in the Cthulhu Mythos. In The War of the Worlds, the Martians can't be communicated or reasoned with, as their mentality is completely different from man's, and they view humans in the same way as most humans view animals. The actions of humans are for the most part inconsequential, as far as the Martians are concerned. At the end, the invaders perish due to their vulnerability to Earth's bacteria, meaning that mankind is saved by pure chance. This portrayal of a non-anthropocentric universe and the insignificance of civilisation when faced with an outside threat is comparable to H. P. Lovecraft's cosmicism.

Other stories by Wells also showcase ideas that would later be explored by Lovecraft. In "A Moth – Genus Novo", a scientist is tormented by an insect animated by the spirit of his deceased rival, as in "Winged Death"; whereas "The Story of the Late Mr. Elvesham" anticipates "The Thing on the Doorstep" in its depiction of an old man's attempt to circumvent death by transferring his consciousness to the body of a much younger person. "In the Abyss" features the discovery of a sapient species of deep sea humanoids with gills, which bear some resemblance to Lovecraft's Deep Ones.

Howard Phillips Lovecraft (August 20, 1890 – March 15, 1937), of Providence, Rhode Island, was an American author of fantasy, horror, and science fiction.

Lovecraft's major inspiration and invention was cosmic horror, the basic premise of which is that the true workings of the universe are beyond human comprehension and that humanity's place in the cosmos is terrifyingly insignificant. A key feature of many of his stories is the existence of powerful, extraterrestrial or supernatural entities that influence or threaten the human world in subtle ways, and whose mere perception by human observers often drives the latter to madness.

Lovecraft has become a cult figure for his Cthulhu Mythos, a series of loosely interconnected fictions featuring a pantheon of human-invalidating entities, as well as the famed Necronomicon, a grimoire of magical rites and forbidden lore. His works were deeply pessimistic, fabricating a mythos that challenged the values of the Enlightenment, Romanticism, and Christianity.

Although Lovecraft's readership was limited during his life, his reputation has grown over the decades, and he is now commonly regarded as one of the most influential horror writers of the 20th Century, exerting widespread and indirect influence, and frequently compared to Edgar Allan Poe in the tone of his writing style.

One author theorized that Lovecraft had used the pseudonym Paul H. Lovering, based on an introductory note stating "author of When the Earth Grew Cold and The Color Out of Space [sic], etc.", when the story "The Inevitable Conflict" was published. However a word analysis of this story showed that it significantly deviates from Lovecraft's known corpus of text. Others have attributed "When the Earth Grew Cold" (1929) and "The Inevitable Conflict" (1931) to Paul Henry Lovering (1880-1943).

### Biography
### Early life

Lovecraft was born on the 20th of August 1890, at 9:00 a.m. in his family home at 194 (now 454) Angell Street in Providence, Rhode Island. The house would be torn down in 1961. He was the only child of Winfield Scott Lovecraft, a traveling salesman of jewelry and precious metals, and Sarah Susan Phillips Lovecraft, a woman who could trace her ancestry in America back to the Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1630. His parents married, the first marriage for both, when they were in their thirties. This was unusually late in life, given the time period. 

In 1893, when Lovecraft was three, his father became acutely psychotic in a Chicago hotel room while on a business trip. He was brought back to Providence and placed in Butler Hospital, where he remained until his death in 1898. Lovecraft was informed that his father was comatose during this period. It is now almost certain that Winfield Scott Lovecraft died from tertiary syphilis.

Lovecraft thereafter was raised by his mother, his two aunts (Lillian Delora Phillips and Annie Emeline Phillips), and his maternal grandfather, Whipple Van Buren Phi

shortDefinition: H. P. Lovecraft was an American psychedelic rock band named for horror writer Howard Phillips Lovecraft, formed in Chicago, Illinois, in 1967. The band's repertoire included two songs inspired by Lovecraft stories, "The White Ship" and "At the Mounta...
fullContent:
H. P. Lovecraft was an American psychedelic rock band named for horror writer Howard Phillips Lovecraft, formed in Chicago, Illinois, in 1967. The band's repertoire included two songs inspired by Lovecraft stories, "The White Ship" and "At the Mountains of Madness".

The band formed around George Edwards, a folk singer/songwriter, and Dave Michaels, a classically trained vocalist and keyboardist. They were joined by Tony Cavallari on lead guitar, Michael Tegza on drums, and Jerry McGeorge (later replaced by Jeffrey Boyan) on bass.  
Music promoter George Badonsky played a key role in putting the band together. Rock journalist Nick Warburton writes:A fervent reader of H.P. Lovecraft’s literary works, Badonsky had befriended another Lovecraft fan, local musician, music business attorney and producer, Bill Traut and together they had formed the production company, Dunwich (named after H.P. Lovecraft’s short story "The Dunwich Horror").Edwards was one of Dunwich's acts, and the band grew out of Badonsky's attempts to promote Edwards' solo career. When Michaels was brought in to provide harmony for Edwards' cover of "Any Way That You Want Me" (a Chip Taylor song that was a recent hit for the Troggs), the single was released not under Edwards' name but as the first recording from H. P. Lovecraft.

Michaels later recalled the genesis of the name:I remember being with George Badonsky, Bill Traut and George Edwards in Badonsky’s apartment above the club Mother Blues. The record company had sent the producers a list of possible group names…We were all groaning at how none of the names fit us [and] then started talking about other things. The name of Badonsky’s dog (a Yorkshire terrier called Yuggoth) came up, along with the name H.P. Lovecraft. We all leaped at the idea of naming the group after the author. Who the first one was to suggest H.P. Lovecraft is anyone’s guess [but] all our minds clicked on it right away. The fact that it was unusual, catchy, and had the word ‘love’ in it, sealed our collective fate.Traut knew August Derleth, who was managing the Lovecraft estate, and secured his blessing for the use of the name.

The fictional version of Howard Phillips Lovecraft has appeared in various conflicting accounts, usually having a small role but he has been the protagonist in several. The earliest appearance of him in fiction was in August Derleth's 1948 poem "Providence: Two Gentlemen Meet at Midnight", which tells of a fictional meeting between Lovecraft and Edgar Allan Poe. In 1979, Lovecraft appeared as a character in the Heavy Metal Magazine.

While innumerable pastiches have put Lovecraft in the role of adventurer or even action hero, more commonly he is portrayed in the role of sage or scholar. Post-modern pastiches have begun to accentuate his racialist outlook and in those works he has become a simplistic caricature.

### Background
In his own works, Lovecraft appeared as the thinly-veiled Teobaldo (: "Alfredo: A Tragedy"), Randolph Carter (: "The Statement of Randolph Carter", "The Unnamable", "The Silver Key", The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", "Out of the Aeons"), Ward Phillips (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key"), and Horse Power Hateart (: "The Battle that Ended the Century").

Also, in the "Family Tree of Azathoth", Lovecraft names himself as a distant descendant of the Great Old Ones.

Other authors have referenced H. P. Lovecraft as a real person within the fictional universe of the Cthulhu Mythos. For example, in "The Children of the Night", by Robert E. Howard, he is mentioned as the author of "The Call of Cthulhu", even though Cthulhu himself is also mentioned as an actual deity in-universe.

In "The Hunters from Beyond", by Clark Ashton Smith, the sculptor Cyprian Sincaul claims that he wanted to achieve in sculpture what Poe, Lovecraft and Baudelaire achieved in literature.

In The Trail of Cthulhu series by August Derleth, H. P. Lovecraft is mentioned as one of the men who met an untimely death as a result of meddling in the affairs of the Cthulhu Cult, since he wrote about real events by disguising them as fiction. Lovecraft is also mentioned by name in several other Mythos stories by Derleth, including "The Thing That Walked on the Wind", "The Return of Hastur", "Beyond the Threshold", and "The Dweller in Darkness".

### Overview
The highlights of the H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival calendar are a series of events held in Portland, Oregon (annually) and Providence, Rhode Island (biannually), although it also organises more ad hoc screenings across the United States on request when time and funds allow.

Many low-budget and indie films have been shown at the H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival, and the organisers frequently release collections of their most popular screenings on DVD and Blu-ray, along with a range of other merchandise.

### Trivia

*The Providence event is held biannually so as not to clash with NecronomiCon, which takes place on the years when the Film Festival is showing.

term: H. P. Lovecraft: Against the World, Against Life
shortDefinition: H. P. Lovecraft: Against the World, Against Life (originally published as H. P. Lovecraft : Contre le monde, contre la vie) is study of H. P. Lovecraft and his oeuvre by French author Michel Houellebecq.  First published by Éditions du Rocher in 1991...
fullContent:
H. P. Lovecraft: Against the World, Against Life (originally published as H. P. Lovecraft : Contre le monde, contre la vie) is study of H. P. Lovecraft and his oeuvre by French author Michel Houellebecq.

First published by Éditions du Rocher in 1991, it has since been reprinted many times by many different publishing houses, and has also been translated into both English and Portuguese.

It is a comparison between what Houellebecq sees as Lovecraft asexual and anti-materialist existentialism and his own embrace of the philosophy of Schopenhauer.

Houellebecq quite correctly identifies Lovecraft's hatred of modernity and the increasingly diverse contemporary America in which he lived, and noted that "not a single allusion to two of the realities to which we generally ascribe great importance: sex and money."

Houellebecq attributes Lovecraft's racism to the two years Lovecraft spent in New York City amongst its diverse population and also noted how often Lovecraft would conjure up the image in his prose of a great city teeming with intimidating or frightening beings. At its base, suggests Houellebecq, Lovecraft experienced chronic deep seated fears, and these informed his work and his audience.

fullContent:
H. P. Lovecraft: Tales is a 2005 collection of Lovecraft's fiction edited by Peter Straub and published by the Library of America, a nonprofit publisher that says it "champions our nation’s cultural heritage by publishing America’s greatest writing in authoritative new editions":

Lovecraft's inclusion in a roster that includes the likes of Henry James, Edith Wharton, and Herman Melville was taken as a sign of his literary acceptance; the Los Angeles Review of Books cited the Library of America volume as evidence that "literary critics...are finally beginning to pay attention to this defiantly unfashionable writer." 

Not everyone was pleased with Lovecraft getting this recognition. Newsweeks Malcolm Jones offered him as exhibit A in his argument that "the Library of America is running out of writers": "maybe it's cruel to label H. P. Lovecraft a second-tier writer, but maybe not so mean to call him a fringe author." Other examples Jones gave of dubious choices were Philip K. Dick and Shirley Jackson, a "writer mostly famous for one short story." 

Lovecraft was not the first writer of weird fiction to be included in Library of America's canon, however; previous volumes had been dedicated to Nathaniel Hawthorne and Edgar Allan Poe, both featured prominently in Lovecraft's Supernatural Horror in Literature.

fullContent:
H. P. Lovecraft's Dunwich: Return to the Forgotten Village is a supplement for Chaosium’s horror roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu.

### Overview
As it’s name might suggest, H. P. Lovecraft’s Dunwich is a sourcebook which focuses on the degenerate town of Dunwich, Massachusetts made famous in the novella The Dunwich Horror. Included in the supplement are maps of both Dunwich itself and the surrounding landscape, the town's history and inhabitants, details on several non-player characters, and two quick-start scenarios, "Return to Dunwich" and "Earth, Sky, Soul", for which player handouts are provided.

H. P. Lovecraft's Dunwich was written by Keith Herber with cover art provided by Philippe Bouveret, and runs to a total of 192 pages plus fold-out map.

### Publication History
H. P. Lovecraft's Dunwich was first published in August 2002. It is available in softcover print and digital (PDF) editions, both of which consist of full-colour cover art with black and white interiors.

H. P. Lovecraft's Magazine of Horror was a short-lived periodical whose focus was, as its name might suggest, the horror genre.

### History
Initially advertised as a quarterly publication, H. P. Lovecraft's Magazine of Horror was nevertheless issued in an irregular schedule by Wildside Press. The first issue, published in March 2004, was edited by Marvin Kaye, who would continue to edit the series for its entire (limited) run. After the first five issues (including #1.5, a free interim issue for subscribers only), the series was “indefinitely suspended” before the publication of Issue #5 in 2009, after which it was merged with the new Weird Tales, also printed by Wildside Press.

H. P. Lovecraft's Museum of Madness is an American series of collectible statues released by PCS Collectibles in 2018. The statues were designed by Jerry Macaluso, in collaboration with concept designer Conceptopolis, sculptor Joe 'Dopepope' Lucchese, and painter Bobby Sutton. 

The series consists of a 22-inch Cthulhu statue released as three different versions: the Retail Version, the PCS Exclusive, and the Bronze Exclusive. The Retail Version is a standard statue with no LED light-up features. The PCS Exclusive includes a light-up LED lighthouse and volcano. The Bronze Exclusive has an exclusive "Faux" Bronze deco and no LED features.

shortDefinition: Harold Warner Munn (1903 - 1981) was an American fantasy and horror fiction author and poet, a friend of H. P. Lovecraft and W. Paul Cook, and a recurring contributor to Weird Tales. His work notably includes the Tales of the Werewolf Clan series, as...
fullContent:
Harold Warner Munn (1903 - 1981) was an American fantasy and horror fiction author and poet, a friend of H. P. Lovecraft and W. Paul Cook, and a recurring contributor to Weird Tales. His work notably includes the Tales of the Werewolf Clan series, as well as an Arthurian fantasy trilogy consisting of King of the World's Edge, The Ship from Atlantis, and Merlin's Ring. He was born in Athol, Massachusetts, and would move to Tacoma, Washington, in the latter half of his life.

The idea for Munn's first published story, "The Werewolf of Ponkert", stemmed from a Lovecraft letter to Weird Tales in which the Providence author wondered why there seemed to be no werewolf stories narrated by the werewolf himself. Munn and Lovecraft would go on to become friends through correspondence and meet each other in person. Munn's book The Werewolf of Ponkert (consisting of the original story along with its novella-length sequel, The Werewolf's Daughter) is dedicated to Lovecraft.

The name of Wladislaw Brenryk, the protagonist of "The Werewolf of Ponkert", was later used by Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow as the name of a cream-puff vendor in their comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century".

Later in life, Munn wrote a short story trilogy set in the Cthulhu Mythos, consisting of "The Merlin Stone", "The Stairway in the Sea", and "Wanderers of the Waters". These stories depict a global war between humans and Deep Ones, and posit an evolutionary origin for the latter, according to which the Deep Ones are an aquatic offshoot of the Worms of the Earth, themselves descended from humans.

fullContent:
"H.P.L." is a short story by Gahan Wilson, originally published Lovecraft's Legacy in 1990 before being reprinted in the anthology Cthulhu 2000. French and German translations have also been released.

The story is a comedic Mythos work offering the conceit that H. P. Lovecraft in fact did not die in 1937 due to the intervention of a Great Old One.

### Synopsis
Edward Haines Vernon, obscure fantasy-horror author, is invited to visit H.P. Lovecraft in Providence in 1990. Lovecraft is by 1990 is nearly 100 years old  and has become a very wealthy man due to the contemporary popularity of his stories.  He's bought up, refurbished, and expanded his grandfather's old home on Angell St., complete with secret rooms and passages. He's got a Rolls Royce, and a strangely familiar chauffeur/housekeeper with a Mythos-related skin condition.

Edwardius, as Lovecraft refers to his visitor, is given a tour of the home and is given a bedroom to use during his stay. In the bedroom, Edwardius experiences strange, Lovecraftian dreams.  He realizes that the chauffeur/housekeeper is familiar because he is, in fact, Clark Ashton Smith.  This is all a confusing since Smith was also meant to have died some time ago.  Smith explains that Lovecraft brought him back from the dead, because he was lonely and Smith was one of his few peers.  Lovecraft tells Edwardius that they want him to assist them in some ongoing project, for which they consider him uniquely qualified.  He takes his guest to his library and shows him an actual copy of De Vermiis Mysteris.  When Edwardius states incredulously that it was his belief that this was a fictional invention of Lovecraft and Robert Bloch, Lovecraft explains all that has transpired.

As he lay dying in 1937, Lovecraft discovered that the Great Old Ones were quite real, and that he could open gateways to them by sheer will and concentration alone.  He allowed Shub-Nuggurath to cure him of cancer, carried on with his career, and became a rich and famous author.  He also discovered that the characters and events of his fiction were manifesting in the real world ( in a manner similar to that described in the more recent movie In The Mouth Of Madness).  He and his fellow authors had not imagined the Lovecraftian world, they had discovered it.

With his newfound wealth and freedom, and with the dark magic of his fiction now quite efficacious, Lovecraft resurrected Clark Ashton Smith for company using the method described in "The Case of Charles Dexter Ward". And then the pair carried on, gradually working to open the way for the Great Old Ones. Part of this process involved making human sacrifices - usually literary critics and authors who wrote bad pastiches of Lovecraft's fiction. This selection of sacrifices, being inexhaustible, their plan was relatively foolproof.

The Haemovore are a species created by the BBC in 1989 for Doctor Who. They are servants of Fenric, a cosmic entity who would later be identified as one of the Great Old Ones, specifically Hastur.

### Background
The Haemovores (Homo haemovorax) are vampiric humanoids that serve Fenric and feed on blood, humans being their food source. They are a possible future evolution of mankind, half a million years into the future. The inhabitants of a polluted Earth, mutated by its chemical slime, Haemovores possess great strength, are resistant to bullets, have razor-sharp claws, their hands can weld metal, they can easily climb sheer surfaces, and are able to survive in sea water. Psychic barriers can stop them, including those generated by holding an object of religious significance to the holder, and the only way to kill one is via a stake to the heart. They communicate with each other telepathically and are able to telepathically control humans. They only hunt in the mist or fog. Haemovores all began as humans whom were changed by other Heamovores, the result of a cyclical paradox as the "first" Haemovore was actually the last member of the species, transported from the distant future by Fenric. Once they are killed, they quickly decay into charred bones and slime.
