fullContent:
"Haggopian" is a short story in the Cthulhu Mythos genre by Brian Lumley. It was written in mid-1970 and first published in the June 1973 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction.

Lumley later incorporated this story as the sixth chapter of his novel The Return of the Deep Ones.

### Synopsis
The story, narrated by journalist Jeremy Belton, centers on Richard Haggopian, an Armenian millionaire with his own Aegean island--called Haggopiana, naturally--who is "perhaps the world’s greatest authority on ichthyology and oceanography". Belton interviews Haggopian, who reveals a dark secret about his past involving a monstrous hagfish, confirming that this story is a sequel to H.P. Lovecraft's "The Shadow Over Innsmouth". The denouement occurs when Haggopian reveals his transformation into a parasitic horror in a version of the transformation of someone with the Innsmouth Look into a Deep One.

### Publication History
Since its debut, "Haggopian" has been reissued many times, and has been translated into German, Italian and French.

### Behind the Mythos
Haggopian and Other Stories is the title of Lumley's 2008 collection published by Subterranean, which showcased Lumley's favorites of his short Mythos fiction.

### Description
Haiogh-Yai is a monstrous, amorphous, whirling entity who took his abode within a wandering black hole called Vix'ni-Aldru in the Elder Lore. It also hosts a city made of titanic blocks called T'halu, inhabited by mysterious creatures named Voorlak, resembling either worms or lizards. (: "Correlated Contents")

fullContent:
A short story by Ambrose Bierce (first published in Wave (San Francisco) January 24, 1891, also published as part of Tales of Soldiers and Civilians & Can Such Things Be?).

Haïta is a naive shepherd who prays at the shrine of Hastur, god of shepherds, and knows nothing of his origin. When great storms threaten to drown the cities of the valleys, he threatens to abandon his worship, blackmailing Hastur into saving them by transforming the water into the sea. He cares for a holy hermit living an hour away and he enlightens him as to the identity of the maiden he has met – Happiness. Sadly, he never has her for more than a moment...

This story is the ultimate source of the name Hastur, which has gone on to take a much greater significance, though much altered in context, in the Hastur Mythos in general and in the Cthulhu Mythos.

fullContent:
Haiyore! Nyaruko-san (Nyaruko: Crawling with Love or Nyaruko-san: Another Crawling Chaos, literally Crawl Up! Miss Nyaruko) is a series of light novels, manga, and anime published in Japan that incorporates elements from the Cthulhu Mythos. The novels, written by Manta Aisora and illustrated by Koin, were published in 12 volumes by Soft Bank Creative under its GA Bunko imprint between April 2009 and March 2014. 

A flash-animated straight-to-video adaptation titled Haiyoru! Nyaruani was released from October 2009 to March 2010, with nine episodes mostly running two minutes long. (however, the last episode was six minutes) Another series, Haiyoru! Nyaruani: Remember My Mr. Lovecraft, was released from December 2010 to February 2011, with 12 episodes of about four minutes each.  An animated TV series was released in two seasons from 2012 to 2013, with 12 half-hour episodes per season.

Two different manga series were released starting in 2011.

### Mythos Connections
*The premise involves a human boy named Mahiro Yasaka becoming roommates with several extraterrestrial entities from the Cthulhu Mythos, including Nyarlathotep (Nyaruko), Cthugha (Kuuko) and Hastur (Hasuta). Additionally, Nyaruko has a pet Shantak.
*Hasuta's dad is the owner of the Carcosa Computer Entertainment corporation.
*Luhy Distone is a Cthulhi, who was a former employee at the Cthulhu Corp. gaming and entertainment company.
*R'lyeh is a theme park that has intergalactic contraband and human trafficking. Nodens is one of the space smugglers there, who uses Night-gaunts to kidnap his victims.
*Dagon is the R'lyeh express water taxi.
*Tamao Kurei (a human friend of Nyaruko) gets possessed by a Yithian named Isuka.
*Ghatanothoa appears in episode 11 and 12 of the TV series, taking the form of a little girl named Ghutatan. She is accompanied by Roy Fogger, who is later revealed to be an evil Lloigor that seeks to steal all of Earth's eroge games. A gang of Shoggoths also try to attack Ghutatan.

Haiyoru! Nyaruani is a Japanese series of flash-animated shorts, directed by Azuma Tani and produced by DLE. It is the first anime adaptation of the light novel series Haiyore! Nyaruko-san and was followed by a second season titled Remember My Mr. Lovecraft.

fullContent:
"Hallow Eve" is a horror comic book story starring FBI agents Fox Mulder and Dana Scully from the supernatural sci-fi franchise The X-Files. The story is partially set at Miskatonic University. It was written by Stefan Petrucha, illustrated by Charlie Adlard, and published in the first issue of The X-Files Annual in August 1995.

### Synopsis
At an excavation site in Africa, a scientist named Jonah Brockford has a nocturnal encounter with a spectral woman and collapses in a fit of madness. The same ghost is also sighted by a pilot flying through a storm near Florida, who crashes his plane as a result. After the black box recording reveals the pilot's encounter with the apparition, Mulder and Scully are assigned to investigate the crash site. Before the departure, Scully has a vision of her late father warning her to be careful.

In Florida, the agents learn that the plane was transporting bones from an archaeological site to Miskatonic University, Arkham, Massachusetts. That night, the truck driver transporting the bones picks up a mysterious hitchhiker who tells him to leave her at the graveyard. Startled by her sudden disappearance, the driver crashes the truck.

The next day, Mulder and Scully find out about the deaths of Jonah Brockford and the truck driver. Mulder tells Scully that Brockford was in Africa trying to find the bones of "Eve", the hypothetical maternal ancestor of all humanity, and speculates that he might have disturbed her spirit. At Miskatonic, the agents speak to the scientist's widow, Prof. Meredith Brockford. While she's explaining the "Eve Theory", a sudden sound blast shatters the room's windows.

The agents learn that Jonah Brockford's first love, Lilith Moore, suffered from a terminal genetic disease called Huntington's Chorea, but committed suicide before the illness could kill her. Jonah believed that Eve's genes might harbour a cure for the disease. When Scully examines the bodies of Jonah, the pilot, and the trucker, she finds that all three died from heart failure. Meanwhile, Mulder investigates the graveyard where the truck crashed and finds the tomb of Lilith Moore, but is attacked by an unknown assailant. He wounds his aggressor by shooting at them and collects a sample of their blood. The same night, Prof. Brockford finds evidence of an apparition or intruder in her house and drives away, only to die as the ghost woman appears in front of her car, causing her to lose control of the vehicle.

When Scully analyses the blood sample, she finds that the person who attacked Mulder suffers from Huntington's Chorea. However, even assuming that Lilith Moore might have faked her suicide, she couldn't be alive, as those afflicted by the disease never live past their twenties. Therefore, the agents get permission from Dr. Beech, the president of Miskatonic, to hold a séance, during which the ghost of Eve manifests herself. fullContent:
"Hallowe'en in a Suburb" is a poem by H. P. Lovecraft. During his life, it was published in The National Amateur in March 1926, there named simply "In a Suburb". It was later published in the Arkham House collection Beyond the Wall of Sleep in 1943, and in the magazine Weird Tales in September 1952.

### Synopsis
The poem describes a supernatural village that exists only in nightmares, lit by the light of the moon, and infested with flying vampires, harpies, ghouls lurking on graveyards, and all types of undead creatures. The poet muses that the world of sunlight will eventually join this morbid scenery, as "the hounds of Time" claim everything.

### Trivia
*Although most likely a coincidence, the "hounds of Time" are evocative of the Hounds of Tindalos.

"Hallowed Rock" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Franklyn Searight. It was published in the first issue of Ron Shiflet's short-lived Lovecraftian fanzine In Lovecraft's Shadow by Tenoka Press in March 2007.

### Synopsis
The story is told from the point of view of a sacrificial altar, located somewhere deep in the backwoods, which has long been used as a place of worship by the cult of Nyarlathotep, and has become sentient due to the release of so much dark energy.

After a period of long and lonely disuse, the rock perceives to its delight the return of the cultists with a fresh victim; it’s elation is short lived however, as the cultists notice a small tree in the shape of a cross which has begun to grow from the rock. Believing this to be an ill omen, the group departs the clearing, leaving the rock to its eternal solitude.

Halpin Chalmers (1891–July 3, 1928) is a fictional character created by Frank Belknap Long in the 1929 short story "The Hounds of Tindalos". He is notable for being the first victim in literature of the titular creatures, among the most prominent in the Cthulhu Mythos bestiary.

In the story, Chalmers is depicted as a  journalist and "the author of several recondite books on occult themes," including The Secret Watcher, published by London's Charnel House Press. He is said to have "the soul of a medieval ascetic", one that has "always scoffed at modern science". He describes himself as "a rebel, a champion of originality and lost causes"--one with a "superhuman" intellect.

Physically, Chalmers is described as having a "long nose and slightly receding chin".

Said to be originally from Brooklyn, at the time of the story Chalmers lives in the town of Partridgeville, where he has an apartment at 24 Central Square, above the Smithwick and Isaacs jewelry store. It is there he enlists his friend Frank--evidently Frank Belknap Long, the author appearing in his own story--to record his experiences with the esoteric drug liao, in an effort to prove that "time is an illusion and does not exist". His successful psychic journey to before the beginning of time unfortunately attracts the attention of the Hounds of Tindalos, leading to his gruesome death on July 3, 1928--deemed an unsolved homicide by the Partridgeville police. (: "The Hounds of Tindalos")

In his 1931 novel The Horror From the Hills, Long mentions "the late Halpin Chalmers" as having retired from the position of curator of archaeology at the Manhattan Museum of Fine Arts in New York City. He was succeeded by the young Algernon Harris. (: The Horror from the Hills)

Hammerheads were a hostile species that rose during the apocalypse of the Ogdru Jahad.

### Overview
It is speculated that the hammerheads are creatures produced by the scourge of the Ogdru Hem.

They are very large pseudo-hexapods with a bone-white exoskeleton. This armour could hold off most small arms fire, but explosives could break through. Direct shots in the mouth we’re also capable of killing the creature.

The Hammerheads could survive in a variety of habitats, from the frozen tundra to scorching deserts.

shortDefinition: Hammers on Bone is a 2016 novella by Cassandra Khaw, the first of two works in their Persons Non Grata series that combine the Cthulhu Mythos with the hard-boiled detective genre. Published by Tor.com, it was a finalist for best novella in the 2017 L...
fullContent:
Hammers on Bone is a 2016 novella by Cassandra Khaw, the first of two works in their Persons Non Grata series that combine the Cthulhu Mythos with the hard-boiled detective genre. Published by Tor.com, it was a finalist for best novella in the 2017 Locus Awards and British Fantasy Awards.

The novella features John Persons, a private detective working in London who is an alien entity wearing a human form. He is hired by an eleven-year-old boy to kill his stepfather: "You’re the only one who can help,” the boy Abel says: “Because you’re a monster too.”

The stepfather, McKinsey, turns out to be a shoggoth, as evidenced by his cry of “Tekeli-li” during a final confrontation. Persons is a Yithian who failed to make the mind-leap into the bodies of the Coleopterans: "I don’t like bugs,” he says. "I can’t imagine existing in a world of endless darkness, dirt, and Yithian academics."

Persons has an ambivalent relationship with a waitress, Sasha, who has reasons of her own to want Persons to confront McKinsey. She is revealed to be a cultist of Shub-Niggurath, who makes a brief appearance speaking through Sasha's body--described as "the All-Mother, black as pitch and bigger than worlds, Her Many Eyes blinking like headlamps between the tree line."

Hammers on Bone was included in the Tor omnibus Reimagining Lovecraft. It was followed by A Song for Quiet.

Hank Samson, the Farmhand, is a ficitonal character created by Fantasy Flight Games as a part of their Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos-related content.

### History
Never the most cerebral of men, Hank has spent his whole life life working on the farm. When one day in the fields he spotted a colossal bird attacking the cattle, he didn’t think twice before picking up the nearest thing he could use as a weapon and killing it.

Since news got out about the incident, things have started to go bad for Hank: his Pa has disappeared, and word has reached him that a mysterious man is on his trail.

### Arkham Horror vs Eldritch Horror
Arkham Horror states that Hank worked his whole life on the family farm, whilst Eldritch Horror has him as an itinerant worker.

fullContent:
Wayne Francis Woodard (1914 - 1964), better known as Hannes Bok, was an American speculative fiction artist and author, most well known for the distinctive style of his illustrations. His pen name is derived from the famous composer Johann Sebastian Bach.

### Biography
Born in Kansas City, Missouri, Bok started contributing art to fanzines in 1932. In the late 1930s, he shared an apartment in Los Angeles with Lovecraft correspondent Emil Petaja. Together, Bok and Petaja struck up friendships with the likes of Ray Bradbury, Henry Kuttner, and Forrest J Ackerman, among others.

In 1939, Bok moved to New York City and started to provide covers and interior art for Weird Tales, continuing to do so until the magazine ended its run in 1954. He also worked for Fantasy Magazine and Stirring Science Stories, and drew the cover art for numerous books, including Arkham House collections of Clark Ashton Smith (Out of Space and Time), Robert E. Howard (Skull-Face and Others), Frank Belknap Long (The Hounds of Tindalos), and William Hope Hodgson (The House on the Borderland and Other Novels).

While in New York, Bok was a member of the science fiction society known as the Futurians, the ranks of which included Donald A. Wollheim, Robert A. W. Lowndes, Frederik Pohl, James Blish, and Damon Knight.

Bok was also a friend and an admirer of Abraham Merritt, and even completed a couple of Merritt's unfinished novels after his death.

In his later years, Bok dedicated himself to the study of astrology and occultism. Tragically, he died in poverty at the age of 49.

### Behind the Mythos


Hanwell is a real world asylum.

Lord Dunsany mentioned it in : "The Coronation of Mr. Thomas Shap".

Hanwell Asylum's full title was the Middlesex County Asylum at Hanwell.

Hanwell was the first pauper lunatic asylum for the county of Middlesex. It opened in June 1831, originally to take 500 patients, but the building was enlarged in 1831, 1837, 1857 and 1879 to cope with the increasing demand for beds. In 1888 the Asylum had 1891 patients. Hanwell achieved great prominence in the field of psychiatric nursing due to the work of two of its first Medical Superintendents. Dr (later Sir) William Ellis, the first Medical Superintendent at Hanwell (1831-1838) introduced his idea of "Therapy of Employment", which encouraged patients to use the skills and trades which they had acquired before entering the Asylum, to occupy themselves, for the benefit of the Asylum and as an aid in their treatment by restoring their self respect and by reviving an aspect of their lives from before their illness. This diversionary therapy, intended to distract patients from the causes of their madness and reduce their emotional reactions, led to some cures and speedy results considered almost miraculous. However, there were also several cases where inmates, having armed themselves with tools as weapons, carried out atrocities on themselves and others. Work became closely supervised and "productive".

This was the forerunner of occupational therapy and industrial therapy. In time the system was somewhat abused and patient labour was used to provide some of the essential services of the Asylum, so reducing its running costs.

In 1889 the Asylum was taken over by the newly formed London County Council and became the London County Asylum, Hanwell. In 1918 it became a County Mental Hospital. In 1937 its name was changed to St Bernard's Hospital. From 1948 to 1974 it was part of the North West Metropolitan Region with its own hospital management committee. In 1974 it became part of North West Thames Regional Health Authority and was within Ealing Health District. In 1980 it was absorbed into Ealing Hospital and is now known as the Psychiatric Unit, St Bernard's Wing, Ealing Hospital. It still functions as a psychiatric and psycho-geriatric hospital for long stay patients. It currently has 950 beds.

Haon-Dor is a fictional character created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Seven Geases".

### Description
Described as an "antehuman" sorcerer, Haon-Dor belongs to an unknown species that predates humankind. He currently lives as a recluse in a labyrinthine palace of stone deep inside Mount Voormithadreth, beyond the gulf inhabited by Atlach-Nacha. The entrance to his palace is a staircase guarded by a giant rattlesnake. The interior is decorated with statues of polycephalic monsters, illuminated by floating lamps that burn with "inverse flames", and inhabited by scores of carnivorous mist-like familiars that crawl and slither upon the walls.

Haon-Dor himself seats upon a throne so high that it appears to be reachable only by levitation or flight. He speaks in an unknown language, but has the power to make himself understood by any listener. He is an ally of the scholarly Serpent People, and also seems to have an amicable relationship with Atlach-Nacha. (: "The Seven Geases")

Happyology is a Lovecraftian-like cult in the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics.

### Background
In the rebooted Marvel Comics, Happyology is a cult which was founded by McTavish on the Internet, dedicated to the undergod Uluath. They took a private yacht to the Pacific Ocean to awaken their deity, with a ritual ceremony. Uluath was awakened and the City Below the Seas rose to the surface, but he was defeated and sent back into slumber by one of Kid Kaiju's creations.

Hardboiled Cthulhu: Two-Fisted Tales of Tentacled Terror is a thematically-linked anthology of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Overview
Combining the grittiness of the hardboiled genre with the fantastical horror of the Cthulhu Mythos, Hardboiled Cthulhu contains a total of 22 stories. It was first published on July 15th 2006 by Elder Signs Press, was edited by James Ambuehl, who also contributed two pieces to the collection, and runs to 332 pages.

Harjit Singh is a fictional character created by Troy Young for his Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos stories. He made his first appearance in the short story "It Slumbers Beneath the Ice".

### Description
A slight man with dark skin, a winning smile, and a ruthless streak, Singh works for the Canadian Department of Extraordinary Phenomena, an agency whose sole purpose is to protect humankind from the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos, which Singh has dubbed "The Other." Within this organisation, he functions as a handler for an unknown number of field agents, a position he has held for six years.

### History
Singh's first encounter with The Other was on an oil field outside Fort McMurray, where his group was splashed by an anomalous material, Singh being the only one to avoid contamination. In the following days, one of the men snapped and murdered his entire family, and the Department stepped in, euthanising the others and recruiting Singh.

Knowing the potential for insanity through contact with The Other, Singh divorced his wife without explanation, although he still keeps tabs on them through resources provided by the Department.

Singh received a gunshot wound to the leg while investigating a suspected manifestation on a remote island, but the injury was not life-threatening.

He was killed while on a mission to prevent the awakening of Cthulhu in the South Pacific, his human mind unable to cope with the psychic emanations of the stirring god.

Harley Warren is a major character in the Dream Cycle series, he's a friend of Randolph Carter. He was a fictional counterpart of H. P. Lovecraft's real life close friend Samuel Loveman.

He was mentioned several times in the Dream Cycle series, but it was revealed that he died in "The Statement of Randolph Carter".

He is also made reference to in "The Silver Key". In "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by Lovecraft and E. Hoffman Price, he is called "the South Carolina mystic whose studies in the primal Naacal language of the Himalayan priests had led to such outrageous conclusions".

The Harlot is a character created by American comic book creator Michael Alan Nelson for the Boom! Studios Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. She made her debut appearance in the very first issue in 2007.

### Description
The Harlot is a large humanoid creature who dresses in a gaudy burlesque style offset by her appearance, which appears to be degenerate to the point of resembling a corpse. A resident of the Dreamlands, she operates a brothel of sorts, trading her secrets for less savoury payments, such as body parts or memories.

The Harlot is a powerful creature in control of her own dream-realm, and has been seen to destroy several Nightgaunts with little effort. Although she is not a match for a being such as the Elder God Nodens, she has stated that she would be capable of making him work for his victory, should such a confrontation come about.

### Overview
The Harlot chose to help the bereaved dreamer Cy Morgan, even to the point of challenging the Elder God Nodens for the possession of him. She later imprisoned him in one of her boxes at his own request, as he wished to forget the death of his fiancé, which he believed to have been his own fault (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 1: The Fugue).

Later, the Harlot was instrumental in thwarting Nyarlathotep's plans to bring his army from the Dreamlands to devastate Earth, releasing Morgan from her box and using him as a tool to banish Nyarlathotep to Azathoth's Court, as well as summoning her own army of lost souls to delay the Outer God's forces long enough for Lucifer and Raymond Dirk to send Cthulhu back into his slumber. These acts were revealed to have been performed under the guidance of an entity heavily implied to be Hastur; her reward was to become the new Lord of the Dreamlands, and to have Lucifer marked as her successor in the event that she should fall (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 4: Godwar; Fall of Cthulhu Volume 5: Apocalypse).

Prof. Harold Hadley Copeland is a fictional character created by Lin Carter for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Dweller in the Tomb".

### Biography
Prof. Copeland was an eminent archaeologist, one of the world's leading authorities on ancient civilisations of the Pacific area. He co-founded the Pacific Area Archaeological Association and was, at some point, president of it, prior to his compulsory resignation in 1911. While his earlier works were lauded as brilliant, Copeland's interest in unorthodox hypotheses, such as touching upon the existence and worship of Cthulhu and particularly about the existence of the lost continent of Mu, led to the gradual decline of his reputation.

His Prehistory in the Pacific: A Preliminary Investigation with Reference to the Myth Patterns of Southeast Asia (1902) was universally admired and acclaimed. Polynesian Mythology, with a Note on the Cthulhu Legend Cycle (1906) was more controversial, but still regarded as "a massive work of scientific research". However, after reading the Ponape Scripture, Copeland became obsessed with finding the tomb of Zanthu, a hierophant who escaped the destruction of Mu, and the legendary Zanthu Tablets. His next published book, The Prehistoric Pacific in the Light of the Ponape Scripture (1911), resulted in his being asked to resign from the Pacific Area Archaeological Association.

After his academic fall from grace, Copeland organised the Copeland-Ellington expedition to central Asia, which penetrated the Plateau of Tsang in 1913 to search for the tomb of Zanthu. Ellington died of red-water fever only a few days after the party's departure from Sangup-Koy, leaving Copeland as the solo leader. Deep into the inhospitable deserts of Tsang, other members of the expedition deserted or were taken one by one by the Mi-Go. Copeland felt an inexplicable familiarity with the Plateau, as if he had seen it before in a previous life or in dreams. When confronted by a Mi-Go, he was even more surprised to find that the creature appeared to recognise him, and it was the Mi-Go who was scared of him, rather than vice-versa.

Copeland ended up as the only survivor of the expedition and successfully found the tomb, containing the Zanthu Tablets and the hierophant's mummified body. The sight of Zanthu's visage, still preserved enough to be recognisable, traumatised Copeland and explained his feelings of déjà-vu, as he saw that Zanthu looked exactly like him (: "The Dweller in the Tomb"), possibly implying that the professor might be the hierophant's descendant and/or reincarnation.

Three months after Ellington's death, Copeland was found in a delirious state, almost dead from starvation, having made his way to the dunes beyond the Russian meteorological outpost at Kovortny, on the borders of the Mongolian province of Chian.

Harpies are a legendary species of winged female creatures from Greek mythology. Traditionally, their physical appearance is that of a human-sized bird of prey with the head of a woman, or a female humanoid with avian legs and wings.

Harpies are featured in H. P. Lovecraft's poem "Hallowe'en in a Suburb", and mentioned in the opening quote of "The Dunwich Horror", which is from "Witches and Other Night-Fears", by Charles Lamb.

### In the Mythos
According to the Pict warrior Brule, before humanity became the dominant species on Earth, the early humans warred for centuries against several enemy races, including "the bird-women, the harpies, the bat-men, the flying fiends, the wolf-people, the demons, the goblins" and the Serpent People. By the time Kull became king of Valusia, most of these foes had been extinct and forgotten, with only the Serpent People and a few of the Wolf Men remaining. (: "The Shadow Kingdom")

In De Vermis Mysteriis, Ludvig Prinn claims that mysterious beings, "half-beast, half-man", once roamed the world, and became worshiped as gods, including the snake-like Set and the animal gods of Egypt. A writer of weird fiction who has read Prinn wondered if the harpies could be related to the avian god Thoth, and werewolves to the canine Anubis. (: "The Secret of Sebek")

While under the mental influence of a Sea-dweller, Graham Dean experienced nightmares about the sea, which included visions of soaring Harpies, monstrous Gorgons and sea serpents. Dr. Makoto Yamada would later mention these same mythical creatures as evidence that the human mind cannot completely suppress the horror of the Sea-dwellers, even as it tries to depict them as lovely Mermaids or Nereids. (: "The Black Kiss")

Harrison Marsh is a character created by American author Armand Rosamilia for his Keyport Cthulhu series of Mythos tales.

### Description
At the beginning of the cycle, Harrison appeared as a youngish man with no distinguishing features. As his Innsmouth heritage began to assert itself, he gradually came to resemble his kinfolk, losing most of his hair and his skin taking on an unhealthy pallor.

It is worth noting that although Harrison comes from Innsmouth stock, he is considered of "weak blood" by those of the Esoteric Order of Dagon. Why this might be the case is not explained.

### History

### Keyport Cthulhu
After coming to Keyport with his wife Nicole to settle his grandfather's estate, Nicole was abducted by the local chapter of the Esoteric Order of Dagon and used as a sacrifice to awaken Great Cthulhu. Despite Harrison's best efforts, he was unable to rescue her, and quickly began to assume the traits of his blood, the proximity to others of his kind apparently being the catalyst.

After a while, Nicole was returned to Harrison, being an unsuitable offering and with her sanity in tatters. When the Order began the final ritual to summon their god, the two settled down to watch the end of the world together.

Harry Houdini (born Erik Weisz, later Ehrich Weiss or Harry Weiss; March 24, 1874 – October 31, 1926) was a Hungarian-American illusionist and stunt performer, noted for his sensational escape acts. He first attracted notice in vaudeville in the US and then as "Harry Handcuff Houdini" on a tour of Europe, where he challenged police forces to keep him locked up. Soon he extended his repertoire to include chains, ropes slung from skyscrapers, straitjackets under water, and having to escape from and hold his breath inside a sealed milk can.

In 1904, thousands watched as he tried to escape from special handcuffs commissioned by London's Daily Mirror, keeping them in suspense for an hour. Another stunt saw him buried alive and only just able to claw himself to the surface, emerging in a state of near-breakdown. While many suspected that these escapes were faked, Houdini presented himself as the scourge of fake spiritualists. As President of the Society of American Magicians, he was keen to uphold professional standards and expose fraudulent artists. He was also quick to sue anyone who pirated his escape stunts.

Houdini made several movies, but quit acting when it failed to bring in money. He was also a keen aviator, and aimed to become the first man to fly a plane in Australia.

In 1924, Houdini wrote essays for the magazine Weird Tales, which made the covers of the March and April issues of that year. He also hired H. P. Lovecraft to ghostwrite a story for him, called "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs", which was the cover of the May issue. Houdini enjoyed the story so much that he hired Lovecraft to collaborate with him on a book to be called The Cancer of Superstition, a project that C. M. Eddy, Jr. was also involved with, but which was discontinued and never completed after Houdini's death.

### Early life

Harry Houdini was born as Erik Weisz in Budapest, Austria-Hungary, on March 24, 1874. His parents were Rabbi Mayer Sámuel Weisz (1829–1892), and Cecília Weisz (née Steiner; 1841–1913). Houdini was one of seven children: Herman M. (1863–1885) who was Houdini's half-brother, by Rabbi Weisz's first marriage; Nathan J. (1870–1927); Gottfried William (1872–1925); Theodore "Theo" (1876–1945); Leopold D. (1879–1962); and Carrie Gladys (born 1882–1959) who was left almost blind after an accident that occurred during her childhood.

Weisz arrived in the United States on July 3, 1878, on the SS Fresia with his mother (who was pregnant) and his four brothers. The family changed the Hungarian spelling of their German surname to Weiss (the German spelling) and Erik's name was changed to Ehrich. Friends called him "Ehrie" or "Harry".

They first lived in Appleton, Wisconsin, where his father served as Rabbi of the Zion Reform Jewish Congregation.

shortDefinition: Rev. Harry Kern Brobst (1909 - 2010) was an American psychologist and minister. During the 1930s, he worked as a psychiatric nurse at Butler Hospital in Providence, Rhode Island, and was a close friend of H. P. Lovecraft.  Born in Wilmington, Delawar...
fullContent:
Rev. Harry Kern Brobst (1909 - 2010) was an American psychologist and minister. During the 1930s, he worked as a psychiatric nurse at Butler Hospital in Providence, Rhode Island, and was a close friend of H. P. Lovecraft.

Born in Wilmington, Delaware, Brobst was a weird fiction fan and admirer of Lovecraft's stories long before he met him personally circa 1932, when he moved to Providence and started out his training as a nurse. When Lovecraft himself became terminally ill and was committed to Butler Hospital, Brobst visited him frequently.

After Lovecraft's death, Brobst attended the University of Pennsylvania and became a doctor of psychology. In 1947, he became one of the founding members of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Stillwater, Oklahoma, and was eventually ordained as a minister.

He lived to the age of 100, and may have been the last person alive to have known Lovecraft personally.

The Harry Stubbs series is a Cthulhu Mythos story cycle by David Hambling, begun with The Elder Ice in 2018. It is published by Crossroad Press.

### Premise
Harry Stubbs is an ex-boxer and World War One veteran who is always struggling to stay afloat when he ends up taking a job that results in him uncovering the secret nature of the universe. Unfortunately, once you are aware of the supernatural, it becomes harder and harder to avoid it thereafter. 

The Harry Stubbs series is focused more on the occultism surrounding the stories rather than the actual monsters. Harry often deals with cultists, lunatics, and weird science but rarely anything resembling the undeniably supernatural until the final section of each story when the full reality of the horror is he facing appears in all its eldritch magnificence. 

The stories are firmly set in historical South London and draw on characters such as Madame Blavatsky and Ernest Shackleton who lived there. 

Stubbs also appears in short stories featuring Captain Cross (who appears in some of the Stubbs stories) and William Blake  as part of a larger universe.

Harry Norman Turtledove (born 1949) is an American author and historian who has contributed a handful of stories to the Cthulhu Mythos, and wrote the novel Conan of Venarium, featuring Robert E. Howard's character Conan in his teenage years.

While prolific in the fields of fantasy, historical fiction, and science fiction, Turtledove is most well-known for his numerous works of alternate history, a genre that he helped to popularise. His oeuvre notably includes the Worldwar series, in which World War II was derailed by an alien invasion in 1942, and the Crosstime Traffic series, in which each book features a protagonist transported to a divergent timeline.

In addition to stories where characters have incidental discussions about Lovecraft, Turtledove has written a number of short pieces which are either set in the Mythos or serve as a spoof of it.

Harvard University, founded in 1636, is an Ivy League university situated in Massachusetts, the oldest and one of the most prestigious in the United States. It was mentioned a handful of times in the fiction of Howard Phillips Lovecraft, where it is generally perceived to be in the same class as the world-renowned Miskatonic University, for which it was likely one of the models.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Charles Dexter Ward is mentioned to have been conducting antiquarian research at Harvard's Widener Library at Cambridge.(: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward)

Professor Chambers, who analysed the rock-like metallic object which landed off the coast of Potowonket, Maine on 13 August 1913, was an alumnus of Harvard.(: "The Green Meadow")

Harvard is said to possess an incomplete seventeenth century copy of the Necronomicon.(: History of the Necronomicon)

It is mentioned that the "Whateleys and Bishops still send their eldest sons to Harvard and Miskatonic, though those sons seldom return to the mouldering gambrel roofs under which they and their ancestors were born." The two schools are said to be the most popular for the Massachusetts "Old Gentry," at least in the 1920s.(: "The Dunwich Horror")

Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee, the scholar whose body was "appropriated" for their research into human culture by the Great Race of Yith, was a post-graduate student of economics at Harvard.(: The Shadow Out of Time)

### Non-fiction Works
In a 1922 philosophical essay, Lovecraft lamented the traditionalist nature of American universities in general, and Harvard in particular, comparing them to what he perceived as a far more liberal higher education culture in Europe.(: "East and West Harvard Conservatism")

### Other Connections
* H. P. Lovecraft's close friend James F. Morton earned both Bachelor and Masters degrees from Harvard, where he was also a member of the Independent Order of Good Templars, an anti-alcohol temperate organisation. 
* Lovecraft's co-author Henry S. Whitehead was a graduate from Harvard, where he also played football. 

### External Links
* [https://www.harvard.edu/ The Harvard University website]
* [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University Harvard University] at Wikipedia

Harvey Walters, also known as simply The Professor, is a fictional character created by Chaosium for their Cthulhu Mythos boardgame Arkham Horror in 1987. Since their acquisition of the property in 2005, his background has been significantly expanded on by Fantasy Flight Games. However, Chaosium appear to still hold at least some rights to the character, as Walters has been used as an example for character creation in the core rules of Call of Cthulhu since its inception in 1981, and does not appear in the latest (third) edition of Arkham Horror.

### History
Walters is consistently described as possessing more occult knowledge than any other - sane - person on the planet. However, as is usually the case with Arkham Horror Files characters, there are discrepancies between the histories given for him. The various iterations are given below.

### Arkham Horror
A visiting professor at Miskatonic University, Harvey Walters possesses doctorates in both History and Archaeology. Over the course of a long and noted career, he has come into the knowledge that humankind is beset on all sides by supernatural threats which - for the most part - it doesn’t even know exist. He has long since chosen to use his arcane insight to protect the human race, and possesses a wealth of experience and resources, along with a vast trove of occult knowledge, with which to go about his task.

### Eldritch Horror
After obtaining his Masters degree in Journalism from Miskatonic University, Harvey Walters became a roving reporter. During the course of his assignments, he encountered many mystical and psychic phenomena, which in turn prompted him to pursue doctorates in History and Archaeology. He has now returned to Arkham, where he intends to pursue his struggle against the outer darkness.

### Behind the Mythos
Since his first appearance, Walters has appeared in most Arkham Horror-related material, including Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line. A more complete list is given below.

* Arkham Horror (first and second edition core sets)
* Arkham Horror Premium Figures
* Under the Pyramids (Eldritch Horror expansion)
* Recurring Nightmares (Mansions of Madness expansion)
* Harvey Walters Investigator Starter Deck (Arkham Horror: The Card Game expansion)

### Trivia
* In the short story "Strange Things Done," included in the 2022 anthology Secrets in Scarlet, investigative reporter Rex Murphy remarks to himself that a fellow passenger on his ship reminds him of Professor Walters.

"HashtagDreaming", stylised as "#Dreaming" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
The user @greatcthulhu grows in popularity on the social media platform Twitter. The more attention it receives, the more those who follow it feel the urge to promote its message, and are gifted with dreams of a god who sleeps beneath the waves. As it’s popularity increases, so the time to the gods' awakening begins to count down…

### Characters

*Darren, a regular internet user.

### Publication History
"#Dreaming" was published in the collection of Meikle's own works Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in April 2017.

fullContent:
Hastalÿk is a Great Old One in the Cthulhu Mythos. Its only appearance is in Chaosium's supplement Malleus Monstrorum for their Call of Cthulhu RPG.

### Description
Hastalÿk is a gestalt entity composed of millions of microbial parts. It sweeps from planet to planet, amplifying and altering existing contagions as well as causing cellular mutations. It is neither a disease nor carry any disease, but a "mutating force" that forces native species to mutate uncontrollably, enabling diseases to spread throughout the planet.

Humans who caught a disease mutated by Hastalÿk may experience delusional fevers or fevered visions and dreams about other cosmic horrors. In rare cases, their body and voice may be possessed and controlled by Hastalÿk or another Old One.

Not much fact is known about Hastalÿk, only conjectures from scholars and scientists. Whether the mutation and spreading of disease are its goal or only side effects of its presence, as well as whether it moves throughout the galaxy or actually spreads itself on all worlds while remaining dormant on most, are highly contentious. A few scholars even suggest that Hastalÿk's consciousness may be active in many locations at once with varying scopes, thereby causing either global or only local outbreaks.

Interaction with Hastalÿk is difficult because its thoughts are beyond human comprehension, though it might be possible with advanced species such as the Mi-Go.

### Worshipers
There are no known organized human cult of Hastalÿk, only certain affiliated groups or individuals exist that want to summon Hastalÿk to Earth to serve their own goals.

### In the Mythos
Some researchers claimed that Hastalÿk was responsible for accelerating certain outbreaks on Earth, such as the 14th century's Bubonic Plague or the 20th century's Great Influenza epidemic.

When a Great Old One awakens, Hastalÿk could potentially be awakened as well, mutating nearby life forms to better serve the Old One.

Hastur the Unspeakable is a fictional deity in the Cthulhu Mythos. Although the being is associated with H. P. Lovecraft, it is only mentioned in one of his novellas, The Whisperer in Darkness. It was originally the creation of Ambrose Bierce, whose short story "Haïta the Shepherd" describes Hastur as a god of shepherds. Hastur is the name of a city in the Robert W. Chambers short stories "The Yellow Sign" and "The Repairer of Reputations", which appeared in his short story collection The King in Yellow.



### Hastur in the Cthulhu Mythos
:|The Whisperer in Darkness}}
Hastur is defined as a Great Old One, spawn of Yog-Sothoth, the half-brother of Cthulhu, and possibly the Magnum Innominandum (). In this incarnation, Hastur has several avatars:  

*The Feaster from Afar, a black, shriveled, flying monstrosity with tentacles tipped with razor-sharp talons that can pierce a victim's skull and siphon out the brain (: "The Feaster from Afar", The Hastur Cycle (2nd ed.), pp. 272-82 [Joseph Payne Brennan]).
*The King in Yellow.

The Carcosa Foundation is a Stockholm-based coterie that worships Hastur.
(: Anders Fager, "Samlade Svenska Kulter")

Hastur is amorphous, but he is said to appear as a vast, vaguely octopoid being similar in appearance to his half-niece, Cthylla.

### Behind the Mythos
### Inspiration
In Bierce's "Haïta the Shepherd", which appeared in the collection Can Such Things Be?, Hastur is more benevolent than he would later appear in August Derleth's mythos stories. Another story in the same collection ("An Inhabitant of Carcosa") referred to the city Carcosa and a person named Hali, names which later authors were to associate with Hastur.

In Chambers' The King in Yellow (1895), a collection of which some are horror stories, Hastur is the name of a potentially supernatural character (in "The Demoiselle D'Ys"), a place (in "The Repairer of Reputations"), and mentioned without explanation in "The Yellow Sign". The latter two stories also mentioned Carcosa, Hali, Aldebaran, and the Hyades, along with a "Yellow Sign" and a play called The King in Yellow.

The Great Old One Hastur has appeared in and been referenced by numerous other works in popular culture. The following is a non-comprehensive list of media that either includes Hastur or contains references, allusions or themes relating to him.

### Comic Books & Manga
*Murcielago: ongoing Japanese manga with a protagonist by the name of Kuroko. Kuroko is translated to 'black lake' and is a reference to the Lake of Hali where Hastur reigns.
*Providence: In the comic by Alan Moore and Jacen Burrows, the meteorite from "The Colour Out of Space" is identified as the Shining Trapezohedron, which is said to be "an abstraction ... of Hastur. Hastur is the thing itself, that cannot be described." It was called down to Earth by the secret society of the Stella Sapiente, appearing to absorb the "orgone energy" released when protagonist Robert Black has sex with another man in its presence in issue #9, and seems to be connected to Nyarlathotep manifesting in reality in the next issue. Hastur, as the Trapezohedron, reappears in the final issue as an "important dignitary" carried by a Mi-Go to witness the birth of Cthulhu.

### Film
*Tummbad: 2018 Hindi movie based on the work of Marathi author Narayan Dharap which features an entity named Hastar. The work in question was heavily inspired by Stephen King's work "Gramma" and Dharap was among the first to introduce readers in the Marathi language to the mythos.

### Literature
### Light Novels
*Aisora, Manta: features Hastur as one of the main characters, along with Nyarlathotep and Cthugha, in the light novel and anime series Haiyore! Nyaruko-san.

### Miscellaneous
*Olshevsky, George: named the nonconvex snub polyhedra after several of the Great Old Ones, with the small snub icosicosidodecahedron dubbed "Hastur".

### Television
*Haiyore! Nyaruko-san: anime based on the light novel series which features Hastur as one of the main characters.
* True Detective: makes mentions of the King of Yellow and Carcosa.

### Video Games
*20 Minutes Till Dawn: Hastur appears as a playable character, added in V0.8.0, whose ability involves periodically summoning tentacles from the ground to attack enemies. There is no yellow imagery, but this is likely due to the artstyle of the game consisting solely of greens and reds. They are unlocked by beating the game once on the Temple map. Additionally, Hastur also appears as the main boss of the Temple map, appearing once 15 minutes have elapsed in a run. He boasts an immense health pool, and drops a tome on defeat.
*The Baby In Yellow: Hastur appears in the game, and you babysit his son (also named Hastur). There are many other references in the game, and it's established to be in the universe of the Cthulhu Mythos.
*Devil Maker: Tokyo: Hastur appears in the mobile game. 
*El Viento: A cult seeks to summon Hastur to bring forth the end of the world.

Hasuta (also known as Hastur) is an extraterrestrial entity from the fictional universe of the Haiyore! Nyaruko-san series.

### Background
Hasuta was a childhood friend of Nyaruko and Kuuko. His father is the owner of the Carcosa Computer Entertainment corporation and Hasuta was initially sent to Earth to help their gaming company win the extraterrestrial console wars. Although, after he failed the mission, Hasuta joined the Space Defense Agency and remained on Earth to help protect a human boy named Mahiro Yasaka. Hasuta quickly fell in love with him and, despite Mahiro not being interested in him romantically, the two of them are generally in good terms. Kuuko initially wanted them to be together so she can have Nyaruko all to herself, until she set her sights on having a threesome with both Mahiro and Nyaruko. 

Hasuta takes the form of a young feminine boy with blond hair, however, he is capable of transforming into his "King in Yellow" super mode where he appears to be more masculine and mature. His species was the inspiration for the character "Hastur" from the Cthulhu Mythos. He is physically stronger than Nyaruko and Kuuko, and in combat, he uses the power of wind manipulation.

The Haunter of the Dark is an avatar of Nyarlathotep who appears in the eponymous story by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Appearance
The Haunter is a gigantic black entity, similar to a bat. Its body is only partially material, being composed of a corrosive substance capable of dissolving human skin on contact. Its most characteristic feature is its brilliant trilobed eye.

### History
The Haunter of the Dark is linked to a cursed item, the Shining Trapezohedron. The Shining Trapezohedron appears to come from a very remote location, possibly another planet, although the first testimony related to the Trapezohedron's presence in our world placed it in Valusia. From there it went to Lemuria, Atlantis and finally Egypt. In this last place it had to be summoned by Nephren-Ka and later by Nitocris, who benefited on multiple occasions from his contact with Nyarlathotep.

The Trapezohedron would be rediscovered in 1843 by archaeologist Enoch Bowen, who would use it as the sacred object around which he would create the Church of Starry Wisdom. Using the Trapezohedron, the Haunter of the Dark was led to Providence, specifically into the interior of the ancient church where the Sect was based. Since the Haunter does not withstand light, it made his dwelling in a dark corner of the building and, even after the official closure of the Sect in 1877, the creature would remain there, remaining with the passage of time practically forgotten. However, in 1936 a notable stir was formed by the death of Robert Harrison Blake, caused by the Haunter of the Dark and, feeling threatened by the expectation generated, the creature escaped from the church possessing the body of Dr. Ambrose Dexter. Later it would take advantage of the influence of this scientist to quickly close the investigation of death and keep the population away from the truth of the case.

In parallel, the Haunter of the Dark would have been worshipped in Australia by the Cult of the Sand Bat, linked to the Aboriginal people. These referred to the Haunter of the Dark as "Father of All Bats", who believed that at the beginning of time it had faced the Rainbow Serpent, avatar of the god Yig. They also say that the Father of all Bats manifests as a sandstorm that arises from a cave that is in the sky.

Other names given to this being by the Aboriginal people are Dark Wing and the Face Eater, the latter being related to the ability of this creature to melt human skin only on contact, which would allow it to decompose the faces of its victims, giving the impression of having devoured it.

"Have You Seen the Yellow Sign?" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Sebastian Greaves. It is aimed at the Young Adult demographic.

### Synopsis
After an author accidentally glances at a copy of a strange book with a yellow symbol on its cover at the local library, horrifying dreams of the King in Yellow begin, and she descends into mental chaos.

When her publisher visits her home to check on the client, she sets eyes on what the author had written in the throes of madness, and also loses her grasp on sanity.

### Characters
*The unnamed narrator, a successful author living in a small town.
*The publisher, the narrator's business agent.

### Publication History
"Have You Seen the Yellow Sign?" was published in the collection Cthulhu Mythos Anthology on Amazon's digital Kindle platform.

### Trivia
*The name of the institution to which the publisher is sent, the Carolyn Fern Sanitorium, is likely a nod to a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Cthulhu Mythos works.

Hawkins is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Overview
Hawkins was a member of the Emma of Auburn, although his role is uncertain. When Donovan successfully opened Cthulhu's vault in R'lyeh, the "quick-eared" Hawkins was the first to hear the creature's "nasty, slopping sound." As the crew continued to listen, Cthulhu emerged, killing Donovan, Guerrera and Angstrom. Hawkins' fate isn't made explicit, but as he did not escape the island with Gustaf Johansen and William Briden, his death by Cthulhu may have simply gone unwritten, or he might have been swallowed with Cthulhu when R'lyeh re-submerged. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

fullContent:
Hazel Drake Heald was an American horror and weird fiction author from Somerville, Massachusetts. She is best known as a revision client of H. P. Lovecraft. Lovecraft revised several of her stories, many of which were published in Weird Tales and credited solely to Heald.

### Stories revised by Lovecraft

* "The Man of Stone"
* "Winged Death"
* "The Horror in the Museum"
* "Out of the Aeons"
* "The Horror in the Burying-Ground"

### Relationship with Lovecraft
There are few details of her time working with Lovecraft. It is documented that she and Lovecraft began corresponding in 1932, and it is possible they met once in person. Colleague C. M. Eddy stated once that he believed Heald harbored romantic feelings for Lovecraft.

Leaving aside any personal relationship aspects, it is interesting to speculate as to the order of the revisions, based on the use of the dialect in "The Horror in the Burying-Ground" compared to that he used in "The Dunwich Horror".

"Hazuth-Kleg" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gary Myers.

### Synopsis
A man named Sliph approaches a locked gate looking for Cathuria leaving from Providence. He came across an elderly woman in black robes and a sack speaking of the stars. He ran off in fear and ends up following her advice to follow a star brighter than the others. He found a peculiar destination as three figures followed him, one wearing a yellow robe with hieroglyphs. They spoke tersely that it was surely time and Sliph followed them toward the star.

He lost them in an alley of the city of Tobacconists, called Hazuth-Kleg, where he walked through the disturbing buildings and found a small iron gate meeting the Watcher who was performing a ritual. Behind the Watcher’s shoulder, Sliph noticed the black-cloaked old woman approaching a bejeweled house. He followed her directly to a mysteriously opening door as she vanished. He saw her on the fifth floor of the building on a hoary dais with ‘Azathoth’ wrought in emeralds with the entrails of a sacrificed child with the three figures from before present in the ritual. He was invited to dine with them before sleeping.

A charwoman appeared to Sliph’s home in Providence and was horrified at what she found there. 

### Publication History
"Hazuth-Kleg" was published in the collections The House of the Worm (1975) and The Country of the Worm: Excursions Beyond the Wall of Sleep (2013).

fullContent:
"He" is a short story by American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft. Written August 1925, it was first published in Weird Tales, September 1926. (: H. P. Lovecraft: Tales [Peter Straub])

### Plot summary
The story tells of an unnamed poet narrator, who has moved from New England to New York City and greatly regretted it. One night, while wandering an older part of Greenwich Village, he happens upon a man strangely dressed in garments from the eighteenth century. The man offers to show the narrator the secrets of the town.

After bringing the narrator to his home, the man tells him the story of a squire who bargained with Native Americans for the secrets of their rituals concerning time and space which were practiced on the land where that squire had recently taken up residence. After learning their secrets, the squire gave the Native Americans "monstrous bad rum," so that within a week all of them were dead and only he was left with the knowledge. The man then proceeds to show the narrator visions of the city's past and future so terrifying that the narrator begins to scream wildly. The screams rouse the spirits of the Native Americans to take vengeance on the man, who is that same squire from 1768.

### Inspiration
The story "He" was written after an all-night tour of the remnants of Old New York; by 7 a.m. the next morning, Lovecraft had reached Elizabeth, New Jersey, by ferry, where he bought a dime composition book and wrote the story in Elizabeth's Scott Park. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

Lovecraft had moved to New York City in March 1924 for his short-lived marriage to Sonia Greene. He moved back to Providence, Rhode Island in April 1926, having developed a thorough aversion to New York. The opening paragraphs of "He" are believed to be largely autobiographical, (: "Lovecraft's New York Exile", Black Forbidden Things [David E. Schultz]) expressing Lovecraft's own feelings about the city:



Lovecraft's disgust for New York stemmed in large part from his racist attitudes, which are also reflected in "He"'s narrator:



The court off Greenwich Village's Perry Street actually exists; Lovecraft learned of its existence in a New York Evening Post article of August 29, 1924. The stranger's house is apparently based on a mansion on the block bounded by Perry, Bleecker, Charles and West 4th streets, built as early as 1744 and demolished in 1865. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia, p. 108)

A suggested literary model for "He" is Lord Dunsany's The Chronicles of Rodriguez, in which a wizard displays visions of past and future wars in successive windows. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia, p. 108)

### Adaptations
* Lovecraft Anthology: Volume II (2012): the story was adapted for the comic book format by Dwight L. MacPherson and features artwork from Paul Peart-Smith.

Lovecraft's most famous works: "The Colour Out of Space", "The Call of Cthulhu", "The Dunwich Horror", The Shadow Over Innsmouth and At the Mountains of Madness are all included, in that order. Each verse ends with the line "Lovecraft knew."

"He Shall Put on the Semblance of Man" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by prolific American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the Simon Brake-edited anthology N, published by Stygian Fox in May 2021 .

### Synopsis
In a world where many cities have manifested colossal, ephemeral Sphinx-temples to an unknown god, a man named Merino ponders the nature of the god’s mysterious messengers as all around him society polarises into two factions: those who have heard the Message, and those who wish to be rid of its influence.

A blooming relationship with his coworker Estefania ends with the woman taking Merino into the interior of one of the temples; there, he witnesses the true glory of the god, and is instantly converted to his cause- whatever it may be…

### Behind the Mythos
Although "He Shall Put on the Semblance of Man" contains hints but no explicit references to H. P. Lovecraft's works, the god is intended to be the Outer God Nyarlathotep: this was made clear in the publisher's description for the chapbook collection The Offspring of Nightmares (2022, Forma Street Press) . Elements of the story, such as the god's preference for Egyptian-style imagery, lay subtle implications to this in the text.

### Publication History
*N (2021, Stygian Fox)
*The Offspring of Nightmares (2022, Forma Street Press)

"Head Like a Jar" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Edward M. Erdelac, which crosses the worlds of Howard Phillips Lovecraft with that of children's character Winnie-the-Pooh. It was published in the April Moon Books anthology The Call of Poohthulhu in May 2022.

### Synopsis
Christopher Robin, now living under the name of Billy Moon in an attempt to escape the legacy of his father's books, has a valuable grimoire stolen from him. Tracking the perpetrator down, he comes across the man conducting a sinister ritual, one resulting in the summoning of an eldritch being which proceeds to attack Moon. In an effort to evade the beast, he retreats into a small corner of the Dreamlands: Hundred Acre Woods.

Appearing in this fantasy world as the character of Piglet, Moon encounters his childhood friends as well as a small Zoog who tells him that the land is being devoured by a creature which feeds the rewards of its feasting to the Sleeper of R'lyeh. Recruiting the aid of Pooh Bear and the dreamer A. A. Milne, the group destroy the being, saving Hundred Acre Woods and restoring all that was lost.

### Behind the Mythos
The book stolen from Billy Moon was said to have been created from parts of "The Liber Ivonis, The Book of Karnak, The Testament of Carnamagos, the Ponape Scripture, de Vermiss Mysteriis, and the Scroll of Thoth-Amon".

"Hear My Call" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by American author Mark A. Mihalko. It was published in the James Ward Kirk Publishing thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
The poem is written in a first-person narrative, and tells of a devotee to the Great Old Ones calling on sleeping Cthulhu to return in the face of unbelieving cultists.

### Behind the Mythos
Amongst the Mythos elements made reference to in "Hear My Call" are the Necronomicon, Innsmouth and Dagon.

fullContent:
"Hear the Squidman Speak" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mike Minnis.

### Synopsis
The story is told as an interview between a man incarcerated in a lunatic asylum for killing a former movie star and a second, unknown party; although the man first denies the murder, he confesses at the conclusion.

Artie Ashbourne has dreamt of Cthulhu and the coming of the Old Ones his entire life, and has spent years trying to shut the insidious voices out of his head. One of the distractions he uses is the release of the movie theatre, and this is where he first discovers his hero, a B-movie actor named Geoff Tucker.

Tucker's career is covered in brief, from his glory days, through succumbing to his addictions, subsequent rehabilitation and return to the screen, to his final fall from grace and retirement to his hometown of Arkham. In an effort to revive Tucker's career, Ashbourne writes a screenplay for him based on his dreams, but Tucker believes him to be nothing more than another crackpot groupie.

However, the screenplay has come to the notice of the Deep Ones of Innsmouth who do not like what they have read: soon a group of Innsmouth heavies abduct Ashbourne and show him a Shoggoth, telling him that he will be fed to the creature if he does not kill Tucker (the exact reason for their desire to see Tucker dead is not explained). He complies with their demands and is convicted of the murder, serving his sentence in a lunatic asylum.

### Characters
*Arthur "the Squidman" Ashbourne, a man who developed an inexplicable connection to Cthulhu after investigating an abandoned house as a child.
*Geoffrey Tucker, a disgraced former low-budget movie star.

### Publication History
"Hear the Squidman Speak" was published in the E. P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes #9 in September 1998.

"Heart of the Highlands" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Will Shadbolt. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long-running horror magazine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
A pair of Arkham businessmen, on the run from creditors, flee the country and take refuge in the small Scottish hamlet of Wickton.  Unfortunately, they fall foul of the village's inhabitants, descendants of the legendary cannibal clan of Sawney Bean and modern-day worshipers of the dark god Zath-Illia. One of the men becomes a meal for this malevolent monstrosity, whilst the other is sent out into the world to recruit more victims for Zath-Illia's insatiable appetites.

### Trivia
* Although Zath-Illia's priest refers to his god as "probably the weakest god among this elder race’s number," it is mentioned alongside the names of such beings as Cthulhu and Yog-Sothoth, which makes this assessment somewhat questionable on a meta-scale.

The Heavenly Realms has historically been part of Buddhist cosmology. The Heavenly Realms of the Cthulhu Mythos was created by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game in 2005.

### Background
The Heavenly Realms are located above Mount Semura, and can only be reached via specific spells and portals. The heavens are stacked in infinite dimensional layers. It's not a place for either the living or the dead, and humans are rarely welcomed with open arms by the gods residing there. Like humans, the gods of the Heavenly Realms have emotions and desires. Therefore depending on the mood of the god, a human guest may be struck by an angry god or seduced by a lustful one. Living in the Heavenly Realms are the gods of ancient China and Japan, the Taoist Immortals, and avatars of the Mythos (e.g. Aku-Shin Kage, one of Nyarlathotep's forms). It's a dimension which is either adjacent to the Dreamlands or completely separate.

It is not yet clear what if any connection may exist between the gods of the Heavenly Realms and the old gods of Earth now known as the Great Ones who reside in the Dreamlands.

Hecatissa is a fictional character created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his 1918 poem "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin."

### Description
Little is known of Hecatissa, although she is described as "fair," and from "an Eastern scene."

### History
When he was spurned by the object of his affection, a woman named Chloe, Strephon used Hecatissa's feelings for him to make Chloe jealous by taking up with her. This ploy worked, and Chloe and Strephon were soon together and wed. Hecatissa, distraught at this cruel treatment, attempted to take her own life by throwing herself into the Fox River; fortunately for her, the god of the river took pity on her soul and cast her back upon its banks. (: "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin")

Hecuba is a Great Old One created by Big Finish Productions in 2013 for Doctor Who.

### Background
Hecuba is the sister of the Celestial Toymaker who ensnares sentient beings in time related games forcing them to stake their freedom on the outcome.

She has powers similar to the Celestial Toymaker's and appears as a very beautiful woman in a luxurious ballgown. A giant timepiece, the Grand Chronometer, which can manipulate time, stabilizes her pocket universe. She is coy and flirtatious, but takes her amusement from the pain and fear of her victims.

fullContent:
Heir of Darkness is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by Glenn Rahman set in the era of Ancient Rome, published in 1989. It is considered a Simon of Gitta story, despite not featuring that character, as it is a prequel to the Simon of Gitta novel The Gardens of Lucullus, co-written by Rahman and Richard L. Tierney.

### Synopsis
As the Roman Empire passes from the hands of the hated Tiberius to the untested Gaius--better known as Caligula--three spellcasters vie for control of the ring Andvaranaut, an enchanted item that brings great power--and certain doom.

### Publication History
After writing The Gardens of Lucullus with Tierney in 1981, Rahman got his co-author's approval to write a solo novel set in the same continuity. Started in 1982, the prequel novel was published in 1989 by New Infinities, a short-lived publishing house founded by Gary Gygax, co-creator of Dungeons & Dragons. (Gardens of Lucullus would not see print until 2001.) Heir of Darkness was reissued by Pickman's Press in July 2023.

Helen V. Sully (1904 - 1997), also known as Helen Sully Trimble, was an American musician from Auburn, California. She was a close friend of Clark Ashton Smith, as were her sister Marion and mother Genevieve.

In 1933, Helen travelled through the Panama Canal and visited several locations, including Cuba, New York, Providence, Rhode Island, Newport, Gloucester, and Quebec. It was during this trip that she met and befriended a number of Smith's fellow authors, including H. P. Lovecraft, Frank Belknap Long, and Donald Wandrei. She and Lovecraft corresponded for the remainder of his life.

Hellboy, a.k.a. Anung Un Rama, is a fictional character created by Mike Mignola for his dark fantasy comic book series of the same name, which debuted in 1994 and was published by Dark Horse Comics.

In the series, Hellboy is a cambion (i.e. half human, half-demon hybrid) brought to Earth as a child by a gateway opened in 1944 by the mad monk Grigori Rasputin, and adopted by Prof. Trevor Bruttenholm of the Bureau for Paranormal Research and Defense. As an adult, Hellboy works as one of the Bureau's agents, defending mankind from supernatural threats, including some which are Lovecraftian in nature. These range from apocalyptic cosmic entities like the Ogdru Jahad, to humans transformed into Frog Monsters. His allies include Abe Sapien, an ichthyoid humanoid; and Johann Kraus, an ectoplasmic spirit in a containment suit. His adventures also regularly involve witches, vampires, fairies, and other folkloric elements.

A live action movie adaptation was released in 2004, followed by a sequel, Hellboy II: The Golden Army, in 2008. Both films were written and directed by Guillermo del Toro and feature creature designs by Wayne Barlowe. Hellboy was played by Ron Perlman, who would later voice a shoggoth in the animated film Howard Lovecraft and the Frozen Kingdom.

The Hellboy movies feature a number of references to the Cthulhu Mythos. The first film opens up with a quote from [[De Vermis Mysteriis|Des [sic] Vermis Mysteriis]], while The Golden Army mentions Bethmoora (a creation of Lord Dunsany, incorporated into the Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft) and features a pair of Elder Things in a brief background appearance, most likely as an Easter egg reference to del Toro's unmade adaptation of At the Mountains of Madness.

In the 2024 film Hellboy: The Crooked Man, Hellboy speculates that the supernatural occurrences in the Appalachian Mountains might be due to a dimensional rift, which he describes as a "Lovecraft type scenario".

### Trivia
* The graphic novel Hellboy: Seed of Destruction features an introduction by Lovecraft’s friend and protégé Robert Bloch; in the introduction to "Goodbye, Mister Tod," Mike Mignola also mentions his "continuing fascination with H.P. Lovecraft monsters."

Hellstar Remina is a living planet and the cosmic horror element in the fictional universe of the Hellstar Remina manga by Junji Ito. It bears a strong resemblance to Ghroth, an Outer God from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Description
Hellstar Remina is a neptune-sized living planet that consumes planetary bodies. It has a huge mouth full of needle-like sharp teeth, a long tongue, and multiple eyes. The planet's surface is acidic, poisonous, and hostile to life. It is likely sentient and at minimum aware, being able to sense when it was being observed light years away.

### History
A Japanese scientist with a telescope discovers a planet in the galaxy, one that consumes worlds. It turns its eye to him and upon learning Earth's location begins to head toward the planet, taking the quickest route to Earth. The living planet reaches the Solar System, eating every one of the planets on its way toward Earth.

Humanity went mad with terror and turned on the scientist who discovered the entity and his daughter Remina, whom he named the world after. In their madness, they wanted to murder Remina to appease the "angry" Hellstar. Mobs chased Remina and eventually caught her, murdering her father along the way. They then hung her on a cross, along with a bum they caught by her.

Meanwhile, astronauts are sent to Hellstar Remina, to determine if it was friendly and/or if the human race could survive its arrival. Once there, they discover that its otherworldy environment was incredibly hostile to human life. One-by-one, each astronaut was killed in extremely horrible ways. Later, Japan's leaders launched into space, attempting to survive on Hellstar Remina itself, only to die horrible deaths like the astronauts before them did.

The Hellstar licked the Earth with its tongue, causing the planet to spin like a top. Realizing that flight was now possible, the bum grabbed Remina and escaped the mob. The mob took flight and pursued the two across the world. They finally escaped the mob and took shelter within a nuclear fallout shelter, owned by the bum's family from whom he had been estranged from. Along with the two are a few other survivors, none related to each other. Hellstar Remina devoured the Earth, and the only humans left were those in the fallout shelter as it floated in space.

Helman Carnby is a fictional character created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "The Return of the Sorcerer."

### Description
A tall, thin man in life, Carnby was a man who exuded a certain power even in old age. He was possessed of strong, aquiline features and a great mane of hair. In death, he appeared as a corpse which was in the early stages of decomposition.

### History
Helman Carnby and his brother John were once powerful sorcerers. They worshipped dark gods, and in return were gifted with great power and the services of many demonic familiars. However, as the years went by and the pair grew older, John became jealous of his brother, whom he knew was the more powerful magician of the two, and held in greater favour by the fell beings which they revered. Finally, the envy became too much to bear, and John killed Helman, dismembering his body with a surgeon's saw and scalpel then burying the pieces in various locations across his estate. The head, however, he kept locked in a cabinet in his library, fearful that his brother would rise from the grave to take his revenge.  

John's fears were well founded, and for the next nine nights Helman's severed limbs crawled through his house, terrorising the magician despite his attempts to use passages from the cursed Necronomicon to banish their animating magic back to whence it came. 

On the tenth night, the limbs and torso united and smashed down the door to John's bedroom before killing the man and doing to him what he had done to his brother. Once the deed was done, Helman's head burst forth from the cabinet, smiling, before the whole cadaver disintegrated once more into its component parts, dead for good this time, its vengeance complete.

This final event was witnessed only by one Mr. Ogden, John Carnby's secretary, who subsequently ran screaming in terror from the house. (: "The Return of the Sorcerer")

fullContent:
Henri Béraud (21 September 1885 – 24 October 1958) was a popular French author and journalist, as well as a Nazi collaborator during the Second World War. His novel Lazarus (1925, The MacMillan Company) has been cited as an inspiration for H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Shadow Out of Time.

Béraud was sentenced to death in 1945 for his work with the Vichy French government during World War II; the sentence was later commuted to life imprisonment by President Charles de Gaulle, but he served only 5 years of his term before being released for health reasons .

### Selected Bibliography

### Novels
*Lazarus (1924)

### Behind the Mythos
Béraud was a rabid Anglophobe, a fact H. P. Lovecraft was unlikely to have been aware of when reading Lazarus. How Lovecraft, himself a confirmed Anglophile, would have reacted to this is an interesting topic for debate.

fullContent:
Henri-Laurent de Marigny is a fictional character created by Brian Lumley as a companion for Titus Crow, a time-travelling adventurer engaged in a long war with the Cthulhu Cycle Deities about whom Lumley wrote an extensive series of stories. Lumley presents him as the son of a character featured by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".

### Biography
Born to noted occultist Etienne-Laurent de Marigny some time in 1923, upon the death of his father Henri inherited an extensive library of mystic knowledge amongst other things. After making the acquaintance of Titus Crow, another man with a deep understanding of the occult, the pair proceeded to embark on a course of action which would bring them into direct conflict with many Mythos entities (which they refer to as the Cthulhu Cycle Dieties), Ithaqua in particular appearing to consider them something of a nemesis.

Throughout the course of their conflict with these beings, de Marigny has fought several Mythos beings -- alone, by the side of Crow, and as part of the Wilmarth Foundation -- has travelled to places unknown to the general populace, including Earth's Dreamlands, and has mastered the use of the time travelling device left to him by his father known as de Marigny's Clock.

Although an accomplished occultist in his own right, de Marigny is usually overshadowed by the understanding possessed by his companion Crow; however, this does not seem to overly concern him. The only Lumley story in which de Marigny serves as a main character without an appearance by Crow is "The Mirror of Nitocris".

Henrik Sandbeck Harksen is a Danish author, editor, independent publisher, and occasional critic who works in the horror genre, and specialises in Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos fiction. His publishing label, H. Harksen Productions, has released at least two collections of Lovecraftian horror, and he has written a handful of fiction and non-fiction pieces on the genre.

"Henry" is a short story by author Lance Axt. It is inspired by the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
After a bullied schoolboy discovers an ancient text in a seedy bookstore, he is confronted by a mystical being which offers to grant him the power to destroy his enemies. Accepting the offer, the boy begins to plot his revenge.

### Characters
*Henry, a mistreated young boy who loves to read.
*The Great One, a mysterious entity willing to offer Henry a way out of his situation.

### Publication History
"Henry" was published in the anthology of H. P. Lovecraft-inspired fiction Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.
