Henry Anthony Wilcox is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who makes his first appearance in the 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu". 

### Overview
Wilcox is an art student studying sculpture at the Rhode Island School of Design, and lives alone at the Fleur-de-Lys Building near that institution. He is described in terms that somewhat recall Lovecraft himself, as a "thin, dark young man of neurotic and excited aspect [...] The youngest son of an excellent family [...] a precocious youth of known genius but great eccentricity, and had from childhood excited attention through the strange stories and odd dreams he was in the habit of relating. He called himself 'psychically hypersensitive', but the staid folk of the ancient commercial city dismissed him as merely 'queer'." (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

### Trivia
*The Fleur-de-Lys Building is an actual building that still stands in Providence. Bernard K. Hart, a Providence Journal columnist who lived in the building, took mock-offense at its appropriation by Lovecraft, and threatened in print to send a ghostly visitor to Lovecraft's own address. Lovecraft's sonnet "The Messenger" is his response to this threat.
*"Wilcox" is a name from Lovecraft's own family tree. 
*A very similar character named "Henry Antonio Wilcox" appears as a potential NPC in the Masks of the Mythos supplement for the Scion roleplaying game.

Dr. Henry Armitage is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror". He has since made numerous appearances throughout the Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
### Lovecraft's Work
Armitage was the head librarian at Miskatonic University who retired around 1936 due to failing health. As a young man, he graduated from Miskatonic in 1881 and went on to obtain his doctorate from Princeton University and his Doctor of Letters degree at Johns Hopkins University. He became interested in the occult in 1882 after hearing of a strange meteorite that fell to Earth near Arkham, this event prompting him to read Miskatonic's copy of the Necronomicon. Years later, and with the help of professors Warren Rice and Francis Morgan, Armitage used this work to defeat the Dunwich Horror. (: "The Dunwich Horror")

### Expanded Mythos Works
Armitage assisted Dr. Carolyn Fern in her research on the Mi-Go and Feeders from Within, before giving the three protagonists shelter at the house of his friend, Professor Albert Wilmarth. (: Feeders from Within)

According to one account, Armitage is Lovecraft's literary equivalent of Hank Wantage, the librarian of St. Anselm's College, based on Robert Black's Commonplace Book. (: Providence)

### Death
Conflicting accounts are given for Armitage's demise. In one account, he was killed in 1939 by a fire in the library when he tried to save Miskatonic's Rare Book collection. In another account, he died of a heart attack outside the library in 1946 after being frightened by a guard dog. Before his death, Armitage published two books on the occult: Notes toward a Bibliography of World Occultism, Mysticism, and Magic (Miskatonic University Press, 1927) and Devils and Demons in the Miskatonic Valley.

### Behind the Mythos
Lovecraft noted that while writing "The Dunwich Horror", "[I] found myself identifying with one of the characters (an aged scholar who finally combats the menace) toward the end". (: letter to August Derleth, September 1928; : An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia).

Henry C. Imbert is a fictional character created by Frank Belknap Long for his Cthulhu Mythos novel The Horror from the Hills.

### Biography
Dr. Henry C. Imbert, F.R.S., F. A. G. S., is a renowned American ethnologist, introduced as one of the foremost authorities in his field. His appearance isn't described in detail, save for the fact that he wears spectacles.

About two years prior to the events of the novel, Imbert helped the police to identify the toxin in a poisoned arrow used to kill an old woman, recognizing it as the same one traditionally used by a certain African culture.

When the supposed "statue" of Chaugnar Faugn revealed itself as the actual living god and killed a watchman in the Manhattan Museum of Fine Arts, the museum's curator Algernon Harris sought help from his friend, Dr. Imbert, who in spite of his knowledge was unable to offer any clue about the ancient god's nature. Instead, Imbert advised Harris to seek help from a retired occult detective named Roger Little.

Little showed Harris and Imbert the entropy-reversing machine he had invented, prompting Imbert to react with skepticism, believing that the fourth-dimensional image produced by the machine proved only that Little had hypnotized them. However, he was convinced after Harris used the machine to pulverize a wall. Together the three men mounted the machine on Little's car and followed Chaugnar Faugn to the Jersey coast, where the exposure to the machine's entropy-reversing beam sent the primal being back to the higher dimensions it had originally come from. (: The Horror from the Hills)

fullContent:
Henry Everett McNeil (1862 - 1929) was an American film scenographer, scriptwriter, and author of children's adventure books. Born in Stoughton, Wisconsin, he lived in New York in the 1920s and was a member of the Kalem Club, along with George Willard Kirk, Rheinhart Kleiner, Arthur Leeds, Frank Belknap Long, H. P. Lovecraft, Samuel Loveman, and James F. Morton. However, some members of the club didn't attend meetings hosted at McNeil's house, as they regarded him as "tiresome". Lovecraft, however, didn't share this opinion and never failed to attend the meetings at McNeil's.

A letter from McNeil was published in the January 1925 issue of Weird Tales, after the magazine asked readers to elect their favourite story from the November 1924 issue. McNeil voted for Frank Belknap Long's tale, "The Desert Lich".

shortDefinition: Henry Fuseli (7 February 1741-17 April 1825), born Johann Heinrich Füssli, was a Swiss-born artist, draughtsman and artistic commentator and critic. His paintings, which frequently featured elements of the supernatural and diabolical, were highly inf...
fullContent:
Henry Fuseli (7 February 1741-17 April 1825), born Johann Heinrich Füssli, was a Swiss-born artist, draughtsman and artistic commentator and critic. His paintings, which frequently featured elements of the supernatural and diabolical, were highly influential in the British art scene of the time, and later made an impact on American horror writer Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### In Lovecraft's Works

### "The Colour Out of Space"
Lovecraft describes the titular alien entity in the line "It was a scene from a vision of Fuseli, and over all the rest reigned that riot of luminous amorphousness, that alien and undimensioned rainbow of cryptic poison from the well—seething, feeling, lapping, reaching, scintillating, straining, and malignly bubbling in its cosmic and unrecognisable chromaticism."

### "Pickman's Model"
When describing the paintings of artist Richard Upton Pickman, Lovecraft compares his work to that of several artists including Fuseli. "I don’t have to tell you why a Fuseli really brings a shiver while a cheap ghost-story frontispiece merely makes us laugh," his narrator says.

### Commonplace Book
In a 1924 entry, Lovecraft writes "Art note—fantastick daemons of Salvator Rosa or Fuseli (trunk-proboscis)."

### In Other Works

### Pickman's Gallery
Matthew Carpenter's 2018 anthology of stories about and inspired by "Pickman's Model" features cover art by Fuseli.

shortDefinition: Henry Kuttner (1915-1958) was a prolific American author of science fiction, fantasy, and horror. A friend of H. P. Lovecraft's as well as of Clark Ashton Smith, Kuttner contributed several stories to the Cthulhu Mythos genre invented by those author...
fullContent:
Henry Kuttner (1915-1958) was a prolific American author of science fiction, fantasy, and horror. A friend of H. P. Lovecraft's as well as of Clark Ashton Smith, Kuttner contributed several stories to the Cthulhu Mythos genre invented by those authors (among others).

Kuttner's first published story, "The Graveyard Rats," which appeared in the March 1936 issue of Weird Tales, caught H. P. Lovecraft's eye, evoking as it did "moribund, inhuman life that was said to exist in forgotten burrows in the earth...where forgotten pagan rites were still celebrated in defiance of law and sanity." The two became correspondents, with Lovecraft encouraging him to incorporate Mythos elements into his work, which Kuttner did, in pieces like "The Salem Horror" (1937) and "Hydra" (1939). "The Salem Horror" would be included in the seminal anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1969).

Lovecraft also encouraged Kuttner to write to another correspondent of his, C. L. Moore; though Kuttner's first letter to the pulp writer Catherine Lucille Moore was addressed to "Mr. Moore," the two soon became romantic partners as well as literary collaborators, and were married in 1940. Their relationship produced a large body of co-written work, largely science fiction published under joint pseudonyms like Lewis Padgett and Lawrence O'Donnell.

Kuttner's contributions to the Mythos include the entities Iod ("The Secret of Kralitz"), Vorvadoss ("The Eater of Souls"),  Nyogtha ("The Salem Horror"), and Zuchequon ("The Bells of Horror"). "Hydra" introduced the treacherous Mythos tome On the Sending Out of the Soul, and "The Bells of Horror" the Book of Iod. 

The latter work provided the title to a collection of Kuttner's Lovecraftian work, The Book of Iod: Ten Tales of the Mythos. Editor Robert M. Price suggest in his introduction that "Henry Kuttner's own private corner of the Cthulhu Mythos was...apparently derived in about equal measure from Lovecraft, Bloch, Zoroastrianism, and Theosophy."

Kuttner died of a heart attack in Los Angeles, California, the city of his birth, on February 3, 1958. He was just 42 years old.

Dr. Henry Sargent Moore is a fictional character from the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald.

### Overview
Henry Sargent Moore, Ph. D., was a renowned biologist who specialised in the study of African insects. He was a Professor of Invertebrate Biology at Columbia University and authored the book Diptera of Central and Southern Africa, which is used in Columbia, Harvard, and the University of Wisconsin. (: "Winged Death")

### Biography
Born in Brooklyn, New York, Moore studied at Columbia University, and was a close friend of Thomas Slauenwite for many years in both America and Africa. Slauenwite later claimed that he was the one who "coached and inspired" Moore throughout his career, even going as far as to claim responsibility for Moore's book on African dipterans, crediting his own suggestions as "responsible for half its strong points": a statement that may or may not be true, given that the story is only told from Slauenwite's point of view.

While Slauenwite's research focused on medicine, Moore specialised in entomology. Nevertheless, it was Moore who became a correspondent of the great Mombasan physician Sir Norman Sloane. After Sir Norman's death, Slauenwite found the late doctor's papers. Soon afterwards, he published a revolutionary theory about the transmission and development of remittent fever, which Moore recognised as Sir Norman's work. In spite of their friendship, Moore openly accused Slauenwite of plagiarism, which put an end to Slauenwite's promising career.

In early June 1930, Moore received a package containing living specimens of an unknown species of flies sent from Ukala, along with a typewritten letter from a purported Londoner entomologist who claimed that the insects were harmless. As a result, Moore wasn't too careful when handling them. On June 19 he was bitten on the back of the neck by one of the flies.

Unbeknownst to Moore, the fly that bit him was a devil-fly / tsetse hybrid, with its wings artificially dyed blue to avoid identification, and infected with a deadly pathogen by Slauenwite, who wanted to kill Moore for ruining his career. Over the next several months, Moore fell violently ill, and correctly guessed that Slauenwite was responsible. His condition deteriorated for a year, and by August 1931, he was in a coma.

When Moore died on September 20, 1931, his mind and memories were supernaturally transferred to the body of the fly that had bitten him. Once he found himself in the fly's body, Moore flew all the way from his house in Brooklyn and entered the room of his colleague, Dyson, possibly in an attempt to tell him about what happened. Dyson was awakened by the fly's buzzing, but it flew out of the window before he could do anything. For the next months, the fly traveled all the way to South Africa, where it managed to locate Slauenwite on January 15, 1932.

Henry R. "Hank" Flynn is a character created by American writer Josh Finney for his Mythos/noir Casefile: Arkham comic book stories. He made his first appearance in the graphic novel Casefile: Arkham- Nightmare on the Canvas in February 2016.

### Description
Flynn is a cynical New Englander who works as a private investigator to pay the bills. A former marine, he sustained an injury amidst ancient ruins on an unspecified island, seems to have given him some connection to a mystical force which he can tap into in times of great stress, although he seems entirely unable to control its effects. He is in love with a woman named Glynda, a self-styled witch with a deep, if bookish, knowledge of the occult.

### History
Flynn served as a marine in the Pacific theatre during the Second World War where he suffered head trauma from an artillery blast which left him with a piece of shrapnel embedded in his skull. After being invalided out of the service, Flynn returned to his home town of Arkham, where he set himself up as a private investigator.

In 1946, Flynn was hired by a woman named May Derlith to find missing artist Richard Upton Pickman, to whom she was both benefactor and lover. However, Pickman had gone insane, murdering those who had in his human life denied his talent, and eventually turned his rage on Derlith before being shot and killed by Flynn.

Three months later, Flynn was hired by Asenath Waite under the pretext of tracking down a manuscript belonging to her dead husband, Edward Pickman Derby. He soon came to realise that she was using him as a pawn in her quest to track down those responsible for Derby's death and as a tool to kill her father. He refused to cooperate any further with Waite, and Glynda ended the charade by exposing both to the public.

shortDefinition: Henry St. Clair Whitehead (5 March 1882 – 23 November 1932) was an American writer of horror fiction and fantasy. He co-wrote two short stories with H. P. Lovecraft, "The Trap" (published in 1931) and "Bothon" (1946).  ### Biography Henry S. Whitehea...
fullContent:
Henry St. Clair Whitehead (5 March 1882 – 23 November 1932) was an American writer of horror fiction and fantasy. He co-wrote two short stories with H. P. Lovecraft, "The Trap" (published in 1931) and "Bothon" (1946).

### Biography
Henry S. Whitehead was born in Elizabeth, New Jersey, on March 5, 1882, and graduated from Harvard University in 1904 (in the same class as Franklin D. Roosevelt). He led an active and worldly life in the first decade of the 20th century, playing football at Harvard, editing a Reform democratic newspaper in Port Chester, New York, and serving as commissioner of athletics for the AAU.

He later attended Berkeley Divinity School in Middletown, Connecticut, and was ordained a deacon in the Episcopal Church in 1912. From 1918 to 1919 he was Pastor of the Children, Church of St. Mary the Virgin, New York City. He served as acting archdeacon of the Virgin Islands from 1921 to 1929. 

While there, living on the island of St. Croix, Whitehead gathered the material he was to use in his tales of the supernatural. A correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft, Whitehead published stories from 1924 onward in Adventure, Black Mask, Strange Tales, and especially Weird Tales; in his introduction to Jumbee, R. H. Barlow would later describe Whitehead as a member of "the serious Weird Tales school". Whitehead's supernatural fiction was partially modelled on the work of Edward Lucas White and William Hope Hodgson. Whitehead's "The Great Circle" (1932) is a lost-race tale with sword and sorcery elements.

In later life, Whitehead lived in Dunedin, Florida, as rector of the Church of the Good Shepherd and a leader of a boys group there. Barlow collected many of his letters, planning to publish a volume of them; but this never appeared, although Barlow did contribute the introduction to Whitehead's Jumbee and Other Uncanny Tales (1944). Lovecraft was a particular friend of Whitehead's, visiting him at his Dunedin home for several weeks in 1931. Lovecraft said of him: "He has nothing of the musty cleric about him; but dresses in sports clothes, swears like a he-man on occasion, and is an utter stranger to bigotry or priggishness of any sort."

Lovecraft expressed admiration for Whitehead's work, described his story "The Passing of a God" as "perhaps representing the peak of his creative genius". Stefan Dziemianowicz describes Whitehead's West Indian tales as "virtually unmatched for the vividness with which they convey the awe and mystery of their exotic locale".

Whitehead died in 1932 of an apparent gastric problem.

*"The Trap" (1931) (with H. P. Lovecraft) Strange Tales
*"Bothon" (1946) (with H. P. Lovecraft) West India Lights

Dr. Henry Stephenson Blaine is a fictional character created by Lin Carter for his Xothic Legend Cycle.

### Biography
Henry Stephenson Blaine, Ph.D., was the curator of the Manuscripts Collection at the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities in Santiago, California (: "The Dweller in the Tomb"). He once studied Semitic Languages under George Gammell Angell (: "Out of the Ages").

In 1928, Dr. Blaine was in charge of making an inventory of the collection of artifacts and manuscripts that formerly belonged to the late Prof. Harold Hadley Copeland. Among Copeland's possessions was a carved jade idol of Zoth-Ommog and a copy of the Yuggya Chants. The idol gave Blaine nightmares and affected his mind, showing him images of the submerged Zoth-Ommog and trying to influence Blaine to remove the Elder Sign that kept the god imprisoned. At night, Blaine was afflicted with episodes of somnambulism in which he would walk to the beach at Wexton Pier with a paper containing an incantation copied from the Yuggya Chants. One night, he was found sleepwalking into the sea. Upon being awakened by the cops who located him, Blaine caught sight of at least one Yugg diving into the water. After that episode, Blaine was committed to Mercy Hospital Psychiatric Emergency under the care of Dr. Robinson Dambler. For the next two months, Blaine spoke nothing other than repeating the word "Yugg" and tried to blind himself 11 times. (: "Out of the Ages")

He was succeeded as curator by his friend and former assistant Arthur Wilcox Hodgkins. (: "Out of the Ages", "The Horror in the Gallery")

### Personal Life
Blaine was a pipe smoker and a self-confessed fan of thrillers, including Richard Marsh's The Beetle. He lived on Curwen Street with his housekeeper, Mrs. Wilkins. (: "Out of the Ages")

### Trivia
*The Curwen Street that Dr. Blaine lived in is located in Santiago, and thus not the same Curwen Street that Prof. Laban Shrewsbury lived in in the works of August Derleth, which is located in Arkham, Massachusetts (: "The House on Curwen Street").

Henry Wentworth Akeley (1871–1928) is a character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Overview
A farmer residing at the Akeley farm on Black Mountain, Vermont, Henry Akeley is a correspondent of Professor Albert Wilmarth. He is also an amateur student of folk lore who takes it upon himself to investigate the Bostonian man Noyes and several locals during their interaction with the Mi-Go. During his investigations, he manages to ship a black stone which originated on one of the Mi-Go worlds to Professor Wilmarth, as well as a phonograph record of a dark ceremonial incantation of theirs and several wax rubbings, photographs and other research notes. Wilmarth eventually destroys these though.

He is later found out to be investigating these people and is beset by several home invasions and killed by these outer beings from Yoggoth. Whilst his fate remains slightly ambiguous, we know the following of his end. His brain is placed inside of a Mi-Go brain case and his body parts are used as props to lure Wilmarth into staying at the Akeley farm overnight. Whilst Akeley may not be fully dead, his body is no longer organically alive.

He has one documented relative, his son, George Goodenough Akeley, who lives in San Diego.

### Trivia
*A man named William Akeley works for the Dean of Occult Studies at Miskatonic University. According to the Dean "his family has been in Arkham since its founding and has witnessed many strange things firsthand". Akeley is later revealed to be an avatar of Nyarlathotep  (: "It Ends Where It Began").

Dr. Herbert West is the main character in H. P. Lovecraft’s short story "Herbert West--Reanimator", as well as the Re-Animator series of films and comics.

### Appearance
Herbert West is 'a small, slender, spectacled youth with delicate features, yellow hair, pale blue eyes, and a soft voice'. He is a highly intelligent, unconventional and ruthless man. (: "Herbert West--Reanimator") According to more recent accounts, he has brown hair. (: Re-Animator)

### History
### Lovecraft's Work
West is a scientist who creates a formula capable of animating unliving bodies, although his ultimate aim is to bring living creatures back to life, complete with all of their faculties.

### Expanded Mythos Works
### "Atonement"
Ron Shiflet's tale "Atonement" sees West survive the events of Lovecraft's story and set up shop to continue his experiments in small-town Illinois. Although once again dragged off by his creations, the ending is left, like the original, somewhat ambiguous.

### Feeders from Within
In Peter J. Evans' novel Feeders from Within, West unexpectedly appears at Arkham Asylum and conducts an unspecified procedure on recently-admitted inmate Diana Stanley; this results in her developing a multiple-personality disorder.

### Alan Moore's Providence
In this account, he is the literary equivalent of Dr. Hector North, in a gay couple with James Montague. (Providence)

### Reanimator franchise
In the Reanimator franchise, he is an acquaintance of Dr. Daniel Cain and is portrayed by Jeffrey Combs in a modern setting. (Re-Animator, Bride of Re-Animator, Beyond Re-Animator)

### The Demonbane Mythos
In the Demonbane franchise, Doctor West is a guitar-wielding mad scientist who is a member of the Black Lodge. He primarily creates Destroyer Robots to attack Arkham city and tries to collect the missing pages of Al Azif (also known as the Necronomicon) for his leader Master Therion. However, West eventually left the Black Lodge and joined the fight against them, after he was offended by them trying to use the power of Cthulhu to take over the world instead of his inventions. After the death of Al, West reprogrammed Demonbane to be able to function without the use of her, with his robot girl Elsa being Daijuuji Kurou's new copilot, feeding the data from the Necronomicon through Elsa in order to activate Demonbane, until Al's resurrection.  

### "The Thing from the Trenches"
Robert M. Price's short story "The Thing from the Trenches" describes an incident during West's time serving on the Western Front with the narrator. The two unsuccessfully experiment with building a conglomerate warrior from the remains of a French and a German soldier

"Herbert West and the Mammaries of Madness" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Dixie Pinoit. Inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's short story "Herbert West--Reanimator", it was included in the James Ward Kirk Publishing thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
When the unnamed narrator's ravishing new wife Elena is struck dead by a cart in the street, doctors Herbert West and Dan Cain arrive on the scene to administer to her with suspicious speed. Convincing the man that they will be able to reverse her condition, they transport the corpse to West's laboratory.

There, they inject the dead woman with West's signature serum, which inexplicably allows her to extrude tentacles from her nether regions and indulge in carnal relations with all three men at once.

In the aftermath, Elena embarks on a career of sexual indulgence while her husband, repulsed by his wife's new appetites, leaves her.

### Trivia
* The character of Dan Cain is never named in the original story, only being given the name in Stuart Gordon's 1985 film adaptation.

fullContent:
"Herbert West—Reanimator" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. It was written between October 1921 and June 1922. It was first serialized in February through July 1922 in the publication Home Brew. The story was the basis of the 1985 horror film Re-Animator and its two sequels, in addition to numerous other adaptations in various media.

The story is the first to mention Lovecraft's fictional Miskatonic University. It is also notable as one of the first depictions of zombies as "scientifically" reanimated corpses with animalistic and uncontrollable temperaments. It is often cited as one of Lovecraft's most explicitly racist stories. 

### Inspiration
According to his letters, Lovecraft wrote the story as a parody of Mary Shelley's Frankenstein. He drops in numerous Frankensteinian references (even hinting at the poetry of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, as Shelley did).

### Reaction
Lovecraft claimed to be unhappy with the work, writing it only because he was being paid $5.00 for each installment. Moreover, he disliked the requirement that each installment end with a cliffhanger, which was unlike his normal style. He also had to begin each installment with a recap of the previous episode. The book Science-Fiction: The Early Years calls Herbert West–-Reanimator "wretched work".  Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi claims that Herbert West–-Reanimator is "universally acknowledged as Lovecraft's poorest work."

### Publication
Lovecraft originally serialised the story in Home Brew (Vol. 1, No. 1–6), a magazine published by his friend, George Julian Houtain. Lovecraft was paid $5.00 for each installment of the story, the first money he ever received for his fiction.

### Plot summary
### From the Dark
The narrator, a doctor who went to Miskatonic University Medical School with the titular character, informs the reader that Herbert West has recently disappeared.

The narrator goes on to explain how he met West when they were both young men in medical school, and the narrator became fascinated by West's theories, which postulated that the human body is simply a complex, organic machine which could be "restarted." West initially tries to prove this hypothesis, but is unsuccessful. West realizes that he must experiment on human subjects. The two men spirit away numerous supplies from the medical school and set up shop in an abandoned farmhouse. At first, they pay a group of men to rob graves for them, but none of the experiments are successful. West and the narrator then go into grave robbing for themselves. One night, West and the narrator steal a corpse of a construction worker who died that morning in an accident. They take it back to the farmhouse and inject it with West's solution, but nothing happens. Later, an inhuman scream is heard from within the room containing the corpse, which forces the two students to instinctively flee into the night. "Herbert West—Reanimated" is a Cthulhu Mythos round-robin published in the Roodmas 1989 edition of the Crypt of Cthulhu zine. It serves as a sequel of sorts to the H. P. Lovecraft short story "Herbert West—Reanimator".

### Synopsis
The story is told in six chapters, each written by a different writer--until the last chapter, which is, like the first chapter, written by Robert M. Price.

### I. Charnel Secrets
by Robert M. Price

Herbert West returns from the dead, his dismembered body having been stitched together and reanimated by his nemesis, Sir Eric Moreland Clapham-Lee. More maniacal than ever, West embarks on a series of increasingly bizarre experiments, first recreating hybrid creatures from mythology, then temporarily transplanting West's brain into a mummy stolen from Miskatonic University's museum, thereby accessing the memories of a "hieratic sorcerer." He then travels to Egypt with a Miskatonic expedition to retrieve a hidden scroll from a tomb holding secrets of a pre-human civilization. Armed with knowledge from both the mummy and the scroll, West kills and reanimates  his assistant (and or narrator), leaving him with "terrible scar tissue that runs down my face and neck."

### II. The Body from the Bog
by Peter H. Cannon

West and his assistant, now both reanimated, move to New York City's Greenwich Village, where they set up a practice "among the better-off artists and writers." (While there, they consult with Dr. Muñoz, "a gentlemanly recluse with a well-chilled laboratory near us on 11th Street," and meet with a Dr. Allen in Providence, who "promised to teach us miraculous preservation techniques" before disappearing.) West develops a belief in reincarnation, asserting that he has learned from his dreams that he had been "an aristocratic young Celt of the second or third century B.C. associated with a Druidic cult." When "Owlind Man," a preserved corpse from pre-Roman times is discovered in a bog near Anchester, England, West is convinced that this is his past self, and insists on breaking into the British Museum in order to reanimate this mummy. When injected with West's reagent, however, the mummy attacks West, even while informing him through a telepathic bond that his name is Trebor, he belonged to a secret cult of the Old Ones, and he thinks West is the high priest who arranged for his death. West realizes that he is not in fact Trebor's reincarnation, but rather the mummy had been projecting himself into West's dreams in order to trick him into reanimating him. After fighting off the mummy, which promptly dissolves, West loses consciousness, and is taken into custody by the museum's Dr. Richard Steadman--who turns out to be Clapham-Lee, West's nemesis, wearing a waxen mask.

Hermaeus Mora is a Daedric Prince in the fictional universe of The Elder Scrolls video game series. Often referred to as the Daedric Prince of Knowledge by the mortals denizens of Tamriel, his sphere of influence encompasses the scrying of fate, past and future, as well as the vast realm of knowledge itself. 

### Description
Unlike many other Daedric Princes, Hermaeus Mora does not possess a humanoid form. Instead, he is depicted as a monstrous entity, a mass of tentacles and eyes, constantly immersed in a swirling vortex of information. His personality is as enigmatic as his appearance, driven solely by an insatiable hunger for knowledge. He is indifferent to the mortal plane, often manipulating mortals for his own ends without any regard for their well-being. 

Hermaeus Mora has played a significant role in the history of Tamriel. He is often associated with the Dragonborn, a prophesied hero with the power to absorb dragon souls. The first Dragonborn, Miraak, sought out Hermaeus Mora and became his champion, gaining immense power but ultimately succumbing to the Prince's influence.

### Domain and Powers
Mora's realm of Oblivion, called "Apocrypha", is a vast, unending library filled with forbidden knowledge. It's inhabited by the spirits of those consumed by a relentless thirst for learning during their mortal lives. It is a place of immense power, but also of great peril, as the knowledge within can corrupt and consume those who seek it. As the Prince of Knowledge, Hermaeus Mora possesses immense power over information, memory, and fate. His followers, known as Seekers and Lurkers, guard the secrets of the Black Books, ancient tomes containing fragments of his power.

### Trivia
* Hermaeus Mora shares striking similarities with Lovecraftian horror entities. His appearance, characterized by tentacles and an enigmatic nature, closely resembles the god-like creatures in Lovecraft's mythology. Mora's vast knowledge, ability to manipulate others, and corrupting influence on power-holders mirror the malevolent attributes of these cosmic horrors.
* Mora's formless, tentacled body further strengthens the connection to Lovecraftian abominations like Yog-Sothoth, who is also omniscient, and Shoggoths. His appearance strongly resembles Cthulhu Mythos creatures, particularly Cyäegha and Shuma-Gorath. 
* His lore echoes the Lovecraftian concept of dangerous, forbidden knowledge that can drive one mad. Mora’s realm, Apocrypha, is a vast, dark library reminiscent of the Great Race of Yith's knowledge-hoarding spaces. Mora's preoccupation with fate and prophecy shares affinity with the Lovecraftian entity, Daoloth, who also seeks to impart forbidden knowledge.
* The peculiar composition of the Daedric artifact Oghma Infinium recalls the Necronomicon.

"Hideous Interview with Brief Man" is a short story by American author Nick Mamatas. It is told in the form of an interrogation, although the actual questions asked are never revealed, only the responses.

### Publication History
"Hideous Interview with Brief Man" was published in the Lovecraft-inspired anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in 2013.

### Trivia
*H. P. Lovecraft, At the Mountains of Madness, and the Mi-Go are all discussed as if the story takes place in our world rather than a fictional one.

The High Priest Not to Be Described, also known as the Tcho-Tcho Lama of Leng, is a minor character in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath by H.P. Lovecraft. Little is known about the priest as it is encountered only once in the story, and the protagonist, Randolph Carter, fearful of the potential dangers, flees soon after meeting the creature.

### Appearance
The Tcho-Tcho Priest appears as a man covered by a yellow robe and with his face hidden behind a silk mask. Although they are not clearly described, it seems that he has terrifying hands.

### History
Randolph Carter is captured and taken by shantak-bird over the feared Plateau of Leng. Far past there deep inside a labyrinthine tunnel system, he is forced into an audience with the High Priest Not to Be Described. This Tcho-Tcho Priest is the lord of the Plateau of Leng and possibly the sole inhabitant of the Leng Monastery. Sensing how truly dangerous this thing is and gripped with a wild fear, Carter knocks one of his captors into a well-like aperture in the cave floor and flees with no plan of escape. This is the last thing we see of the High Priest Not to Be Described. (: The Dream Quest of Unknown Kadath)

Kuranes, on one occation, barely managed to escape from the High Priest Not to Be Described, who dwells in a prehistoric stone monastery on the plateau of Leng and is said to wear a yellow mask of silk. (: "Celephaïs")

There are also mentions of a Pharo residing in Leng wearing a yellow mask. (: Fungi from Yuggoth: "The Elder Pharos")

According to some accounts, the Lama of Lêng is Lam (: Hecate's Fountain [Kenneth Grant]) but according to some others, he is an avatar of Nyarlathotep, (: Malleus Monstrorum) to some others the Plateau of Leng belongs to the Hastur faction while the character Tcho-Tcho Priest belongs to the Shub-Niggurath faction and physically looks related to Y'golonac, who belongs to the same faction. (: Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game)

He is speculated to be "the greatest of the hooded harbingers", having gained some autonomy. (: Pathfinder)

It is also described as praying to "the Other Gods and their crawling chaos Nyarlathotep."

### Behind the Mythos
When Robert Bloch asked Lovecraft to kill a a fictional version of him in "The Shambler from the Stars" (1935), Lovecraft answered favorably in a letter he "attested" by writers from the Mythos: Abdul Alhazred, Gespard du Nord, Friedrich von Junzt, and the Tcho-Tcho Lama of Leng; the latter possibly being the High Priest not to Be Described. He also jokingly stated in the same letter that Bloch was the "reincarnation of Meinheer Ludvig Prinn, author of De Vermis Mysteriis." (: Selected Letter 5.748)

Very little is known about this creature: we know it is clad in a yellow robe and dwells deep in Earth's Dreamlands, served by the Moon-beasts, shantak birds, and the Men of Leng. Id

"Highway 97" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-hunter. It was published by Subterranean Press in 2006 as a chapbook accompanying Kiernan's collection Alabaster; it was later included in an expanded edition of Alabaster published by Dark Horse Books in 2014.

"Highway 97" takes place just before the events of "Bainbridge," and in fact was the original opening scene of that story, which Kiernan says they "cut for some reason entirely lost to me now."

The story describes Dancy walking toward Bainbridge, Georgia, on a mission from her angel. She is accompanied for a time by a talking dog.

Hippocampus Press is an American publishing house focussing on the horror genre; according to trade magazine Publishers Weekly it is "the world’s leading publisher of books related to horror writer H. P. Lovecraft."

### Overview
Established in 1999 by Derrick Hussey, Hippocampus Press publishes the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft, as well as that of his literary circle and even some of his influences. In addition, they produce a number of periodicals and non-fiction works related to the horror genre, and have published a large selection of work from more contemporary authors such as Franklyn Searight, Ramsey Campbell, Ann K. Schwader and Thomas Ligotti, among others.

Hippocampus also publish a line titled Lovecraft's Library, which reprints "works that Lovecraft himself read and admired, and that he commented upon in his letters or elsewhere". Each of the books also features an introduction and commentary by scholars in the field .

Hippolyte Le Sorcier is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who included him in the Family tree of Azathoth in a 1933 letter to James F. Morton. Le Sorcier is depicted as a son or descendant of "Gilles Grenier, Lord of Averoigne", and an ancestor of Lovecraft's friend Clark Ashton Smith.

It's unknown if Lovecraft intended this character to be related to Charles Le Sorcier, the titular villain from his short story "The Alchemist". In French, "Le Sorcier" means "The Sorcerer", most likely intended as an epithet, as opposed to a surname. In "The Alchemist", Charles Le Sorcier is the son of Michel Mauvais ("mauvais" being a French word for bad or evil), and is specifically noted to have no known descendants.

Hiram is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Tomb".

### Background
Hiram is the elderly servant of Jervas Dudley. Jervas has stated that he was always fond of Hiram, describing him as a simple man but extremely loyal, and who shares Jervas' love of churchyards. 

After Jervas was confined to an asylum, Hiram investigated the abandoned burial vault of the Hyde family discovered by Jervas, and confirmed enough of his story so that Jervas was convinced of his own sanity. (: "The Tomb")

Hiroshi Maruyama is a freelance Japanese illustrator and character designer. Originally from 1992 to 2008, Maruyama used to work for Tsuburaya Production in designing characters, such as the titular heroes of the Ultraman Series and their Kaiju contemporaries.

### Selected Works
### Artist

**Bizaamo
**Gijera

**Ghatanothoa
*Walking to the Abyss - Designer for the Great Old One
*Ultraman Gaia

**Deep Ones (see below)

### Participations
*Cthulhu Mythos exhibit 2014 - Designer of Ghatanothoa

### Gallery

Hiroshi Maruyama 2006.png|Hiroshi Maruyama circa 2006 (Ultraman Mebius Archive Document)


### Trivia
*In Japanese, the term Cthulhu has several Katakana transliterations; namely クトゥルー/Kuturū (one of the many alternates) and クトゥルフ/Kuturufu (frequently used). Maruyama however finds it favorable to pronounce in the latter than the former.
*When designing Ghatanothoa from Ultraman Tiga, Chiaki J. Konaka gave Maruyama various designs of monsters from Cthulhu Mythos. While he had seen their images, but then chose to form his own design by combining shells, octopuses and squids. He admitted that it was very cheeky of him from back then.
**Model maker Shinichi Wakasa (who also participated in Ultraman Tiga) also agreed that Ghatanothoa in that series was more comparable to the Cthulhu Mythos' titular deity than its original namesake.
**Maruyama admittedly also had his own stash of Cthulhu mythos art book from 1990s, which he used for design reference for an undisclosed project in 2012.
*Episodes 49 and 50 of Ultraman Gaia sees the appearances of the Deep Ones, but while Maruyama was indeed the designer of most of the Ultra Kaiju in that series, the Deep Ones are portrayed by repainting the Digon suits from Ultraman Dyna (the preceding series) while adding torn clothes, thus making them a wholly kitbashed Ultra Kaiju that was never designed from ground up. However as the Digons in Dyna were also designed by Maruyama, then Maruyama's participation in the Deep Ones' creation is nevertheless acknowledged, however indirect he may be.

*While no indication had been proven over the extent of Cthulhu Mythos influences to his overall works, Maruyama had at least participated in the 2014 Cthulhu Mythos exhibit, where he designed the subspecies of Ghatanothoa from Ultraman Tiga to a slightly similar and more tentacle-oriented breed of Kaiju. This original design is part of a series which he calls, Cthulhu Tiga Series, as two more are added and hopes that he would design more in the future.
*Being one of the many artists behind Battle Spirits, Maruyama had drawn the Lovecraftian monsters that inspire their Kaiju counterparts during its collaboration with Ultraman Tiga. However, one particular card is Ghatanothoa, which is clearly a redraw and recolor of the illustration of the same entity in Chiaki J. Konaka's Walking to the Abyss short story.

"Hiru Gyamu" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Australian author Gerry Huntman. It was published in the first issue of short-lived horror magazine The Asylum Diaries by Oscillate Wildly Press in May 2019.

### Synopsis
Seventeen year old Isao lands a job chaperoning a group of three young Japanese girls as they spend a little time exploring Sydney, Australia. As the story progresses, he learns that these girls are far from normal, and are in fact cultists of the Great Old One Dagon, in search of a relic which had been stolen from them, and that his family's fate is inextricably linked to theirs.

The girls seduce Isao, before tracking down and brutally torturing one of those responsible for the theft and recovering the missing statue. Making their way to nearby Bondi Beach, they use the artefact to summon Dagon who proceeds to consume the other man who had been in possession of the statue; they then inform Isao that he has been much-honoured, and that now he must walk into the water and feed the risen god. 

### Behind the Mythos
Certain details given about the girls, such as a shimmer to their skin which Isao first mistook for cosmetics, hint that they are intended to be Deep One hybrids; this may be further reinforced by their statement at the finale that they may only mate with certain males, and that they seduced him to ensure that their joint bloodlines would continue.

fullContent:
"His Hour Upon the Stage" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author J. B. Lee.

### Synopsis
Robert Clarke, a man grieving after the loss of his unborn child, makes a deal with Le Novar, who claims to be a cosmic time-traveller, to steal a manuscript from Miskatonic University in return for the chance to travel back and make things right.

After holding up his end of the bargain, Clarke is allowed to use a device called The Clawed Crystal, with the warning that anything he meets on his journey through the time stream will be inimically hostile to him. Whilst travelling, he is detected by a pack of Hounds of Tindalos, but they are chased off by a seemingly-angelic figure.

Reaching his destination, Clarke is successful in altering the timeline, and immediately returns to himself and the blissful life he now has with his wife and child. Back in the time stream, Nyarlathotep, having shed his angelic mien, muses on the suffering the Clarke family are to undergo now that they have a child.

### Characters
*Robert Clarke, a man suffering from deep psychological and physical scars after an automobile accident.
*Nick "Le Novar" Calvert, an alien being living in the shell of a human body.
*Nyarlathotep, an Outer God with a cruel sense of humour.

### Publication History
"His Hour Upon the Stage" was first published in the online fanzine Nightscapes in September 1998. It later appeared in issue 3 of Dark Legacy in January 1999, and was included in the collection The Best of Dark Legacy, Volume 2 in September 2016.

shortDefinition: "History of the Necronomicon" is short piece by H. P. Lovecraft laying out a backstory for his fictional eldritch tome, the Necronomicon, and its author Abdul Alhazred. Lovecraft wrote it in 1927, largely for his own use, to keep his references to th...
fullContent:
"History of the Necronomicon" is short piece by H. P. Lovecraft laying out a backstory for his fictional eldritch tome, the Necronomicon, and its author Abdul Alhazred. Lovecraft wrote it in 1927, largely for his own use, to keep his references to the book consistent; it was published as a pamphlet in 1938, after Lovecraft's death, by The Rebel Press.

The piece provides biographical details about Alhazred, including his origin in Sanaa, Yemen; his travels to Babylon, Memphis, Irem, and the Nameless City; his worship of Yog-Sothoth and Cthulhu; and his "final death or disappearance" in Damascus in 738 A.D., when he was, according to the 12th century biographer Ebn Khallikan,  "seized by an invisible monster in broad daylight and devoured horribly before a large number of fright-frozen witnesses."

The account gives an original Arabic title for the Necronomicon, Al-Azif, and translates it as referring to "that nocturnal sound (made by insects) suppos’d to be the howling of daemons." It lists three translations of the work: into Greek in 950 by Theodorus Philetas of Constantinople (who gave it its current title); into Latin by Olaus Wormius in 1228; and into English by Dr. John Dee. The Greek translation was printed in Italy in first half of the 16th century, though no copy has been reported since one was burned in Salem in 1692. The Latin version was printed twice, in the 15th century ("evidently in Germany") and 17th century ("prob. Spanish"). The book has been banned at least twice, by Patriarch Michael in 1050 and Pope Gregory IX in 1232.

Lovecraft's sketch lists five libraries known to have copies: The British Museum, which holds the 15th century edition, and Paris's Bibliothèque Nationale, Harvard's Widener Library, Miskatonic University at Arkham, and the University of Buenos Ayres. It notes that are probably private copies held in secret, including a 15th century Latin edition rumored to be "part of the collection of a celebrated American millionaire." A Greek text was whispered to belong to the Pickman family of Salem until Richard Upton Pickman's disappearance in 1926.

### Continuity
*Lovecraft would expand some parts of the history in his correspondence (Selected Letters 2.307, letter to James Blish & William Miller 13 May 1936)
*"Azif" is the name of insects noise attributed to howling of daemons (: Selected Letters 2.307, : Vathek note by Henley)

fullContent:
"Hobstone" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author G. K. Lomax. It was published in the Salomé Jones-edited anthology Cthulhu Lives! by Ghostwoods Books in August 2014.

### Synopsis
Making his way home one night somewhat the worse for wear, London architectural student James Belmont notices something wrong with the dimensions of his shared house: the outside seems to be somewhat larger than the inside would suggest. Succumbing to the effects of the alcohol, he puts these thoughts to one side and collapses into bed. 

Awakening the next morning, Belmont remembers his conclusions from the trip home, and begins to look into the mystery. Coming to the conclusion that his drunken observation was correct, he starts by peeling back the wallpaper. When this results in chunks of plaster coming off the decaying walls too, revealing a small section of inscribed stone, this further fuels his curiosity and prompts him to remove more. 

Over the course of the next few days, his curiosity turns to obsession, and he ends up tearing the entirety of the false wall down, brickwork and all, until the complete stonework is revealed, along with an inset gem which begins to glow. When Belmont touches it, clouds of billowing green smoke erupt from the building, and he hears a a thunderous voice in his head chanting the words "We are the Eternal, the All-in-One, the One-in-All. We are the Way, and the Gate, and the Keeper of the Gate. We are Yog-Sothoth. Yog-Sothoth is the Way and the Key and the Gate. Yog-Sothoth is the Was and the Now and the Will Be. Yog-Sothoth is the all-seeing and the all-knowing. Life eternal in the Tawil-at’Umr. Yog-Sothoth h’leth mn’gar rRhann y’law y’law. Yog-Sothoth calls. Yog-Sothoth calls – and you answer. You answer  – and you shall know All." After a moment, James Belmont is no more. 

In the aftermath, unidentified government representatives assume control of the situation. Quietly buying up the property and sealing it off, they proceed to silence - through both bribery and force - anyone who speaks about the incident, and the world forgets about the strange stone buried within a suburban house's walls.

fullContent:
Home Brew was an American humour and horror fiction pulp magazine. The magazine was set up by George Julian Houtain and his wife E. Dorothy MacLaughlin.

It was known for its slightly racy nature and was dedicated to challenging gender roles, moral codes and prohibition.

H. P. Lovecraft was paid $5 each for a series of "Grewsome Tales" which became "Herbert West--Reanimator" and later the magazine published "The Lurking Fear" as a four-part serial. Lovecraft regarded it as a "vile rag" for which he produced "artificial hack-work".

It was renamed "High Life" before closing in 1924.

"Home From the Sea" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
When a large whaling vessel founders outside the harbour, a group of locals sets out into the storm to render assistance. What they find is a dead crew and a ship swarming with bloodsucking tentacular horrors, which had been incubating inside the latest catch, a sperm whale. 

Whilst most of the party are brought down by the creatures, two survivors manage to reach the last lifeboat, and set the ship ablaze as they leave. Although they are nearly overwhelmed by the creatures as they attempt to reach port, the newly-hatched monstrosities are called back to sea by their colossal mother, freshly risen from the depths.

### Publication History
*Daylight Dims: Volume 1 (2013)
*Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2017)

fullContent:
Hong Kong is a region and city in the Asian country of China, located along the southeast coastline. Once a colony of Great Britain, ceded as spoils after the end of the First Opium War, it remained a British territory for over a century and a half, prospering immensely under foreign rule. It was returned to Chinese jurisdiction in 1997. In the modern era, it stands as one of the worlds biggest financial powerhouses, and is one of the most densely populated areas on the planet

As the city once known as "the Pearl of the Orient," Hong Kong has had its share of interactions with the Cthulhu Mythos and Lovecraftian fiction. These include such diverse storytelling devices as short fiction and roleplaying games, both directly connected to the mythos and more indirectly inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Notable Individuals
* Yun Shatu: a smuggler and opium den operator in the employ of the undying sorcerer Kathulos of Atlantis (: Skull-Face)

### Appearances
* Masks of Nyarlathotep Companion (2013): Call of Cthulhu supplement which includes guides for, amongst other places, Hong Kong
* "City of Waking Dreams": in Davide Mana's Arkham Horror Fiction story, once main character Li Flint exhausts all of his option in Shanghai, he moves his investigation to Hong Kong

### External Links

"Honor Among Thieves" is a Cthulhu Mythos novelette by American author Carrie Harris which takes place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting. It was published in the thematic anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022.

### Synopsis
In Buenos Aires, Argentina, high society thieves Rosa and Mila Varela are blackmailed by a mysterious figure into stealing a set of historic clothing from an exhibition at very short notice. Their blackmailer, a man named the Sanguine Watcher, is much feared by the locals, and reputed to be a sorcerer of great power.

During the course of the heist, Rosa has cause to put the clothes on, and discovers that the jacket grants her the ability to teleport. While she is able to make her getaway, her sister Mila is murdered by a vengeful and corrupt politician.

Attempting to find out more about the properties of the jacket, Rosa meets with the Sanguine Watcher and, although he attempts to take the artefact from her and use her in his vile experiments, she is able to escape.

Back at her safe house, Rosa is approached by the Red-Gloved Man, a member of the secretive organisation known as the Red Coterie. He recruits her into their ranks with the promise that her activities need never involve another member of the group, the Sanguine Watcher. She is then given a new name: La Chica Roja, or the Girl in the Crimson Coat.

### Behind the Mythos
The Red Coterie is a recurrent element in the Arkham Horror setting, a secret society dedicated to obtaining mystical artefacts known as "Keys."

The Hooded Harbingers are a fictional race created by Paizo Inc in 2016 for the Pathfinder roleplaying game.

### Background
The Hooded Harbingers are Hastur's faceless messengers. Clad in a tattered yellow hood and rags, they resemble humanoid mummies. They emit a musty carrion stench and carry themselves with a stooped posture. If you pull the hood back, the head is covered by the same layers of rags. Peal them off, and you find more layers. Eventually after pulling off dozens of layers the unraveller sees his own face. They possess several abilities including teleportation, plane shift, and bloodless touch (in which the victim's blood flow is restricted). Hooded Harbingers have lightning reflexes and slash with their claw-like hands. They originate from Carcosa and it is rare to encounter more than one at a time.

fullContent:
Horror on the Orient Express is an adventure supplement for Chaosium's horror roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu. Two editions were issued, a boxed set in 1991, and a revised hardcover release in 2013.

### Synopsis
Set in the classic era Call of Cthulhu of the 1920s and primarily located aboard the prestigious Orient Express, the plot involves a journey from London across Europe en route to Constantinople, with the investigators looking into the death of three identical men while attempting to assemble the pieces of an artefact and simultaneously avoiding the deadly attentions of the Brothers of the Skin.

### Editions

### First Edition
The first edition, released in 1991, came packaged as a boxed set containing the following:

*four campaign books totalling 205 pages in length
*32-page "Strangers on the Train" booklet
*16 pages of player hand-outs
*17” × 27” map
*four 11” × 17” cardboard cut-out train car blueprints
*11” × 17” cardboard cut-out of the Sedefkar Simulacrum artefact
*11” × 17” cut-out of the Scroll of the Head
*four passport forms
*two luggage stickers
*11” × 15” Chaosium Inc. poster

### Second Edition
The second edition was released in 2013 as a pair of deluxe hardcover books. The handouts, maps, blueprints, etc. were all included, although not as separate items as in the previous edition. This edition was also released in digital format.

### Spin-offs
In July 2023, Chaosium announced a board game spin-off of Horror on the Orient Express. The Kickstarter was launched in April 2024, with a projected release date of 2025. It raised 1.6 million dollars from 13,201 backers and fulfilment finally began as of August 16, 2025.

HorrorBabble is an indie production company which specialises in audio and ebook horror.

### Overview


Founded by Ian and Jennifer Gordon, HorrorBabble produces audio readings of both classic stories and more contemporary ones, including many written by Gordon himself. Their output includes many of Lovecraft's original stories, as well as connected tales by his contemporaries. Although not exclusively set in the Cthulhu Mythos or even Lovecraftian in nature, the more recent stories tend to lean towards the weird fiction genre, and the Weird Tales-era style in particular.

HorrorBabble runs a limited publishing operation, with their releases to date being confined to the digital format, and releases audio works through Amazon's Audible platform.

### Selected Releases

*The Call of the Old Ones: An Annotated Cthulhu Mythos Collection (2023)

The Four Horsemen of Nyarlathotep, also known as simply the Horsemen of Nyarlathotep, are a demonic quartet of supernatural beings who serve the messenger of the Outer Gods, Nyarlathotep. They are part of the "Million Favoured Ones". They are supporting antagonists of Fall of Cthulhu, a supernatural horror comic book series published by Boom! Studios in 2007.

### Members

*Sysyphyx: known as the "Scourge of Atlantis", she was an oracle of that civilization. Once a bloated woman with auburn hair, she is now a multi-eyed worm-like shapeshifter who, after beheading a victim and modifying their spine with her own, can take the form of the victim. She was on the brink of death in the Arctic after being thrown into a chest that was scheduled to be blown up, but the intense cold froze the wick. In the comic, she takes different bodies.
*Gr'nuk of Vol'Kunast: known as the "Devourer of the Royal Corpse of Thuln", it is a disembodied essence in an empty box. Whoever opens the box will be possessed by the essence and transformed into a corpse-eating monster. In the comic, Sysyphyx offered it to a seven-year-old boy named Jacob, whose personality and body changed until the boy's eventual transformation, who then proceeded to murder and eat his parents. The more corpses it eats, the more it transforms.
*The Masked Mute: known as the "Sister of the Lost Abyss", she manifests herself as a young girl covered in endless masks with which she expresses her emotions. It is said that her true face could kill even the greatest beings in the Dreamlands.
*Gith: known as the "Father of Pestilence" and the "Champion of Damnation", it is an irrational force found on the mountain of Kundai'i, in the Dreamlands. Under certain rites which include vomiting one's own soul and wearing a jackal's head, as well as undergoing brain surgery and bonding using the colour out of space, it can possess a human. Its appearance is that of a mummy from which purple-blue fire appears where the eyes and mouth should be.

Little is known about the titular creature from the H. P. Lovecraft short story "The Hound". It is not known whether the hound is one of a race of hounds or a unique mutation of another race, although the narrator links it to the Plateau of Leng. The beast appeared to have had a particular affinity for an ancient amulet buried with the body of a 15th century Dutch graverobber.

This creature appears like a giant winged hound or sphinx with a canine face, and is accompanied by a swarm of unusually large bats. The Necronomicon, by Abdul Alhazred, refers to it as the symbol of a corpse-eating cult from the Plateau of Leng in Central Asia, and as a "supernatural manifestation of the souls of those who vexed and gnawed at the dead".

The hound was first encountered by St. John and his companion in a graveyard in the Netherlands. After this first encounter, it apparently followed the pair all the way back to their native England, where it brutally killed St. John. (: "The Hound")

The Hounds of Tindalos are a fictional extra-dimensional species in the Cthulhu Mythos, originally created by Frank Belknap Long for his eponymous short story.

According to some sources, the Outer God known as Mh'ithrha is the master of their species. (: Unseen Masters) 

### Description
The Hounds of Tindalos are extra-dimensional predatory creatures, capable of materializing at any point in space and time to feed upon victims. They are said to inhabit the "angles" of time; in contrast, humans and other earthly lifeforms live within the "curves" of time. Little is known about their appearance, as few victims survive their attacks; however, they are known to have hollow proboscises used for feeding, and are associated with a blue pus-like substance.

Hounds may appear wherever angles or corners may be found, especially those sharper than 120 degrees. When breaking through into the universe, their arrival is preceded by the appearance of smoke pouring from the corner, followed by their head and body.

### In Other Media
*Alone in the Dark: The Hounds of Tindalos appear in the survival horror game. They are the stronger equivalent of the enemies known as the Dogs of Darkness. 
*Battle Spirits: The Hound of Tindalos appears in the trading card game, under the name Tindalo-Hound.
*Deus Machina Demonbane: In the visual novel, Al Azif described herself as being more persistent than the Hounds of Tindalos, while refusing to leave Daijuuji Kurou alone. Much later in the story, Master Therion summoned multiple dog-like creatures that emerged from every angle of the world leaders' conference room to slaughter them.
*Haiyore! Nyaruko-san: In episode 4 of the anime television series, Nyaruko offers to share her "Tindalos dog" with Mahiro, presumably a hotdog made using Hound of Tindalos meat. Mahiro tells her to "Go hit your head on the angles of time!".
*The Incredible Hulk (1996): In the episode "Mind Over Anti-Matter", Doctor Strange attempted to cast a spell while falling from a great height, exclaiming "By the Hounds of Tindalos, I summon forth the power of..." before being interrupted and rescued by She-Hulk.
*Re:Creators: In episode 6 of the anime television series, Magane Chikujoin steals a monster manual for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. After the store owner asked her to pay for the book, Magane summoned a Hound of Tindalos to kill him.

fullContent:
"Houndwife" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Caitlín R. Kiernan that first appeared in the March 2010 issue of Sirenia Digest (#52).

### Synopsis
The story is a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Hound" and "The Haunter of the Dark," with the amulet from the former tale being found in a Savannah curiosity shop by a young woman, who subsequently becomes a willing sacrifice for the Church of Starry Wisdom. It's also a continuation of Kiernan's story "Les Fleurs Empoisonnées," which is set in Savannah.

### Publication History
The story was republished in the anthology Black Wings II (PS Publishing, 2012). It later appeared in Beneath an Oil-Dark Sea: The Best of Caitlín R. Kiernan (Volume Two) (Subterranean Press, 2015), and in Kiernan's collection Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Subterranean Press, 2019).

shortDefinition: Hour of the Huntress is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author Dave Gross, first published in a hardcover format by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Fiction line in October 2017; digital and Russian-language editions have also b...
fullContent:
Hour of the Huntress is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author Dave Gross, first published in a hardcover format by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Fiction line in October 2017; digital and Russian-language editions have also been released.

### Overview


### Synopsis
When her little sister Izzie goes missing, globetrotting socialite Jenny Barnes travels to Massachusetts - the last place she was seen - to try and bring the young woman home. In the town of Arkham, she enlists the aid of motorbike-riding tomboy Lonnie Ritter, Miskatonic University professor Tilde Félix, and sympathetic Arkham Police Department officer Galeas Morgan.

Using clues from Izzie's letters, gleaned from vicious gangsters in a seedy speakeasy, and found on a protective amulet retrieved from an archaeological dig in Italy, the group discover that one of Arkham's wealthiest families are operating a cult to the Outer God Shub-Niggurath. The villains have coerced the terrified girl into assisting them in raising one of the Dark Young using human sacrifice. Although Jenny and her new friends are successful in stopping the ritual and banishing the creature, Lonnie's father pays the ultimate price, and the cult's High Priestess escapes, taking Izzie with her.

### Publication History
Since its first release, Hour of the Huntress has also been included in the omnibus collection Dark Origins by Aconyte, released in October 2021.

### Trivia
*Sheriff Engle, Father Iwanicki, and Professor Henry Armitage are all mentioned in the story, but make no actual appearance. Similarly, newspaper the Arkham Advertiser is remarked upon by Jenny Barnes in passing, but plays no part in the story.

### External Links
*[https://www.fantasyflightgames.com/en/news/2017/10/13/your-investigators-in-action/ Your Investigators in Action] at the Fantasy Flight Games website

"House of the Rising Sun: Innsmouth, USA" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Ken Ichigawa.

### Synopsis
A pair of sexually-jaded brothers from Providence, Rhode Island are made aware of a bordello in Innsmouth which will give them everything they desire. Travelling there, the two unknowingly bed Deep One-hybrid prostitutes in the rundown brothel. Whilst one is disgusted by the experience, the other finds a deep satisfaction in the act, and perhaps even a hint as to his own heritage.

### Publication History
"House of the Rising Sun: Innsmouth, USA" was published in the E. P. Berglund-edited Mythos zine Nightscapes in May 2000.

"Houses Under the Sea" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan, originally published in the 2007 anthology The Mammoth Book of Best New Horror: Volume 18. It takes the form of a journalist's reminiscences about his affair with Jacova Angevine, a cult leader who led a mass suicide into the Pacific Ocean.

The story was reprinted in Thrillers 2 (2007) and Lovecraft Unbound: Twenty Stories (2009). It was included in Kiernan's collections Two Worlds and In Between: The Best of Caitlin R. Kiernan (2011) and The Very Best of Caitlin R. Kiernan (2019). It is the title story of Kiernan's Lovecraftian collection, Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (2018).

Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales is a collection of the best of Caitlin R. Kiernan's short Lovecraftian fiction, released by Subterranean Press in 2019, though a limited edition was published by Centipede Press in 2018. "Lovecraft and I", a keynote address they gave at the 15th annual HPL Film Festival in Portland, Oregon, in 2010, serves as an introduction.

fullContent:
"How the Gods Bargain" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author William Browning Spencer. It was first published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu by Titan Books in October 2014.

### Synopsis
A senior Miskatonic University researcher whose name is given only as Jerry relates the tale of how he lost his childhood girlfriend Marissa to genius freshman Harley James. In the aftermath, the three teens discovered a mysterious building in the woods: Elder General Store, an eldritch structure whose interior does not obey the laws of space. After a time exploring, Jerry kills Harley in a jealous rage; shortly afterwards, the building disappears.

Many years later the building manifests once again. Jerry and Marissa decide to investigate and encounter Harley James - or a being impersonating him. While Harley and Marissa embrace, Jerry flees in terror, and once again the store dematerialises.

### Publication History
Since its debut in 2014, "How the Gods Bargain" has also been included in the collection of Spencer's own works, The Unorthodox Dr. Draper and Other Stories, published by Subterranean Press in July 2017.

"How to Frame a Dying Art" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Mike Lee.

### Synopsis
A man visiting the unnamed capital of his homeland meets an artist who takes him on a tour of the less-seen quarters of the city. In one particularly seedy bar, the man bears witness to a terrifying scene whereby a seemingly-deceased dancer entertains with the "truth of the Worm". Horrified and disgusted, the man flees, but suspects that his turn to provide "entertainment" may come soon…

### Publication History
"How to Frame a Dying Art" was published in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine.

fullContent:
Howard Lovecraft is a series of Cthulhu Mythos comic books created by Bruce Brown and published by Arcana Studio, begun with Howard Lovecraft and the Frozen Kingdom in 2009. Despite the setting and names, many of the Mythos elements incorporated into the series have been modified to such an extent that they are nearly unrecognisable from their original incarnations.

Three animated films based on the series have been produced by Arcana Studio since 2016.

### Premise
The series follows a young Howard Lovecraft and his pet monstrosity, a creature he refers to as Spot for the sake of convenience, as they explore the worlds of the Cthulhu Mythos. Their adventures take them to such far-flung places as Antarctica and R'lyeh, and meet such Mythos alumni as Dagon and Herbert West.

### Characters
*Howard Lovecraft: a fictionalised version of the real-world author, Howard's father Winfield has been driven insane by what he has witnessed. Left a book written by Winfield, Howard inadvertently uses its contents to travel through dimensions and, occasionally, as a makeshift weapon.
*Spot: a creature who gives its name as Thu Thu Hmong, which Howard saved from certain death and has subsequently sworn his service to the boy. Creator Bruce Brown has confirmed in an interview that Spot is in fact Cthulhu .

Howard Lovecraft and the Frozen Kingdom is a Cthulhu Mythos graphic novel published by Arcana Studio, the first in their Howard Lovecraft series. Written by Bruce Brown and featuring artwork by Renzo Podesta, it was released in February 2010. Both trade paperback and digital editions were issued.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Howard Lovecraft, a small boy traumatised by his father Winfield's insanity, inherits a book of magic from the old man, and is transported to a realm of ice filled with strangeness. Saving the life of a creature named Spot who pledges its services to him, the boy is subsequently tricked into helping the people of R'lyeh: a city cursed by its former inhabitants to remain a frozen wasteland for all eternity for the crime of attempting to raise Cthulhu.

Defeating a Jinn named Dagon and returning a spellbook to the king of R'lyeh, Howard is quickly prepared as a sacrifice in the ritual to awaken Cthulhu. Although Spot manages to save the boy and cast him through a portal which returns him home, Spot's fate is left untold.

### Adaptations
In October 2016, Arcana Studio released an animated film adaptation of the comic. Starring Ron Perlman, Christopher Plummer, Jane Curtin, and Doug Bradley, distribution was handled by Shout! Factory.

Howard Lovecraft and the Kingdom of Madness is a Cthulhu Mythos graphic novel published by Arcana Studio, the third in their Howard Lovecraft series. Written by Bruce Brown and featuring artwork by Thomas Boatwright, it was released in November 2013. Both trade paperback and digital editions were released.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Since the events of the previous book, young Howard's father, Winfield, has somehow become possessed by an evil entity. In an effort to cure the old man, Howard, Spot, and Constable Smith travel to Antarctica to enlist the aid of Dr. Herbert West. In a trip to some underground caverns and encounters with angry Shoggoths, the group are successful in freeing Winfield from the spirit, but Smith is seemingly killed in the endeavour. Although he returns to sanity for a brief period, Winfield's old madness soon reasserts itself.

### Adaptations
In December 2018, Arcana Studio released an animated feature film adaptation of Howard Lovecraft and the Kingdom of Madness. Starring the vocal talents of Christopher Plummer, Mark Hamill, Finn Wolfhard, Jeffrey Combs, and Doug Bradley, distribution was handled by Shout! Factory.

### Synopsis
In an effort to claim young Howard Lovecraft's magical book, the Outer God Azathoth kidnaps the boy's family and begins to transform them into Deep Ones, while imprisoning Spot in an inescapable cell. Enlisting the aid of his deranged father Winfield, the heavily-armed Constable Smith, and housecat Beastie, Howard travels to distant Yuggoth in his quest to defeat the Lord of the Outer Gods. The boy foils Azathoth's scheme by tricking its servant, former ruler of R'lyeh King Abdul, into accepting the wrong book in place of his own grimoire.

### Adaptations

Howard Lovecraft & the Undersea Kingdom is a 2017 animated feature film adapting the graphic novel of the same name.

### Synopsis
After conquering R'lyeh and the Frozen Kingdom, young Howard Lovecraft must now travel to the Undersea Kingdom in order to free his captured family, protect three mysterious magical books, and prevent the impending wrath of Cthulhu.

Before he becomes the famed horror writer H. P. Lovecraft, young Howard Lovecraft is a curious and imaginative boy living with his mother, because his father is locked up in Arkham Sanitarium. But after his mother unwittingly gave Howard the legendary Necronomicon, Howard went to a dangerous and frozen land where he saved and befriended a monstrous creature he named  Spot. Howard thought that was behind him, but now there is a new threat, and only Howard and Spot can save the day. Howard’s mother has been kidnapped and evil forces are turning Howard into a fish creature. Howard will have to find his father’s old journals if there is any hope to save his mother and himself!

"Howard Phillips Lovecraft" is a tribute piece written by author and publisher Donald A. Wollheim for the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. Although dated May 1937, a mere two months after Lovecraft's death, it does not appear to have been published until its appearance in Operation: Phantasy: The Best from The Phantagraph thirty years later in 1967 , although this discrepancy may simply be due to to the fact that Wollheim was himself the publisher, and included the piece in one of his magazines without credit.

term: Howard Phillips Lovecraft and Sex: or The Sex Life of a Gentleman
shortDefinition: "Howard Phillips Lovecraft and Sex: or The Sex Life of a Gentleman" is a short monograph by R. Alain Everts, originally published in Nyctalops 2, No. 2 (July 1974).  Everts obtained several interviews with Sonia Greene, including tape recorded exchan...
fullContent:
"Howard Phillips Lovecraft and Sex: or The Sex Life of a Gentleman" is a short monograph by R. Alain Everts, originally published in Nyctalops 2, No. 2 (July 1974).

Everts obtained several interviews with Sonia Greene, including tape recorded exchanges. In them the subject of H. P. Lovecraft's sexuality, sex life and his orientation were discussed, as brought up on various occasions by Greene. She made it plain that Lovecraft was a studious and satisfying lover and although he had been brutalized verbally by his mother and traumatized by her demeaning language used to him, and by his "puritanical" upbringing, he had been a normative husband and lover, indeed a satisfying one even though he was unusually passive.

Of note to the genesis of Lovecraft's weird tales and their themes was his father's suffering from syphilis and the insanity it caused. At the commencement of his marriage to Sonia Greene his aunt Annie Gamwell had told Sonia that she and Lovecraft could not - not should not, could not - have children, due to the disease in his blood.

This disturbing monograph shows the sheer trauma and personal hell that tormented H. P. Lovecraft but at the same time busts several myths about him and shows how Victorian in mode and manners America still was in the 1920s and 1930s.

Howard Phillips Lovecraft: A Bibliography is a non-fiction piece by American author Jack L. Chalker.

### Overview
The work is most notable for the controversy it generated following publication, with George T. Wetzel accusing Chalker of plagiarising his own 1955 Lovecraft bibliography. Although never formally settled, there appears to have been some grounds for these claims.

### Publication History
Howard Phillips Lovecraft: A Bibliography was first published in the collection The Dark Brotherhood and Other Pieces by Arkham House in 1966.

shortDefinition: Howard Vachel Brown (1878 - 1945) was an American science fiction artist who provided the original illustrations for H. P. Lovecraft's novellas At the Mountains of Madness and The Shadow Out of Time, both published in the magazine Astounding Stories ...
fullContent:
Howard Vachel Brown (1878 - 1945) was an American science fiction artist who provided the original illustrations for H. P. Lovecraft's novellas At the Mountains of Madness and The Shadow Out of Time, both published in the magazine Astounding Stories in 1936. He also illustrated stories by Frank Belknap Long, Donald Wandrei, Jack Williamson, and others.

Brown started working as a professional artist in the 1900s. Some of his early work includes illustrating Katharine Elizabeth Dopp's The Tree-Dwellers (a non-fiction book about life in prehistory) in 1904, and H. G. Wells' feminist novel Ann Veronica in 1909.

In the 1920s, he provided the cover art for several issues of Hugo Gernsback's magazine Science and Invention, whereas the interior art was done by Frank R. Paul. In the 1930s, Brown was the main cover artist for Astounding Stories and Thrilling Wonder Stories.

### Trivia
*One of Brown's illustrations for The Shadow Out of Time showcases several alien creatures. Included as an Easter egg are two species that Brown had previously illustrated for Astounding: an Elder Thing from At the Mountains of Madness and a Centaurian from Murray Leinster's "Proxima Centauri".
