shortDefinition: Howard Elmer Wandrei (1909 - 1956) was an American artist and author of weird fiction, detective fiction, and science fiction. He was the younger brother of Donald Wandrei and a friend and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft.  Born in St. Paul, Minnesot...
fullContent:
Howard Elmer Wandrei (1909 - 1956) was an American artist and author of weird fiction, detective fiction, and science fiction. He was the younger brother of Donald Wandrei and a friend and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft.

Born in St. Paul, Minnesota, Howard Wandrei was arrested for burglary at the age of 18 and spent three years in a reformatory. In 1931, he illustrated his brother's poetry collection, Dark Odyssey, and soon started publishing stories of his own, contributing numerous yarns for Weird Tales, Astounding Stories, and Spicy Mystery Stories. Like many other pulp authors, he frequently used pseudonyms, including Robert A. Garron and Robert Coley. He also provided the cover art for two Arkham House collections of his brother's fiction: The Eye and the Finger (1944) and Strange Harvest (1965).

"Howling Synchronicities" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Greek author Konstantine Paradias.

### Synopsis
A man who has been used his whole life as a tool to aid in the return of the Old Ones watches from orbit as the world devolves into madness. However, he also witnesses the sparks of sanity which hide away to one day resurrect the human race, and makes the ultimate sacrifice to stop his puppeteers from learning of these small hopes.

### Characters
*Anatoly, a ruthless soul who has nevertheless been manipulated into aiding dark powers.

### Publication History
"Howling Synchronicities" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Trivia
*Amongst the things witnessed by Anatoly is the lonely death of a fisherman on the shores of a recently-risen R'lyeh.

Hsieh Ho is a fictional character created by Frank Belknap Long for his Cthulhu Mythos novel The Horror from the Hills.

### Biography
Hsieh Ho is a Chinese laundry shop owner living in Manhattan. Like Roger Little, he is an individual of above-average psychic sensitivity, which led him to experience a dream about the incoming return of the monstrous Chaugnar Faugn.

In his dream, Hsieh Ho saw "big green animals" descending from mountains and devouring people, and was ordered by Gautama Siddhartha to head to the Manhattan Museum of Fine Arts, where Chaugnar himself would be waiting. He also saw the museum's curator of archaeology, Algernon Harris, and despite not knowing his identity, somehow also knew that that man would help him.

Following his prophetic dream, Hsieh Ho visited the museum, where he remained hidden after closing hours. When Chaugnar awakened, it didn't go after Ho, but preferred to feed on the museum's night guard, Cinney, whose corpse was found horribly mutilated and exsanguinated. Having witnessed the death of Cinney, Hsieh Ho hid himself behind a large statue of Venus Erycine.

The next day, the police found and arrested Hsieh Ho, believing him to be the murderer, but Algernon Harris (who was aware of Chaugnar Faugn's nature) intervened on his behalf. Seeing that the officers were planning to use force to interrogate Ho until he confessed, Harris threatened to take legal action. The police sergeant reluctantly agreed to treat Ho only as a witness for the moment. (: The Horror from the Hills)

Hugh Barnett Cave (11 July 1910 – 27 June 2004) was a prolific American writer of pulp fiction, best remembered for his horror and science fiction stories, but also writing in the Western, crime, romance, and other genres. He wrote and published at least 800 stories in such outlets as Weird Tales, Astounding, and Black Mask. 

His Cthulhu Mythos fiction includes "The Isle of Dark Magic" and "The Death Watch". Though he corresponded with H. P. Lovecraft (the letters do not survive), the two never met, despite both living in Rhode Island in the 1930s. (Cave lived in Pawtuxet,) Lovecraft complained in a letter to Robert H. Barlow that Cave "uses our own evil pantheon in a way which plays the deuce with the 'style-sheet.'" 

Cave also had a long correspondence with weird fiction writer Carl Richard Jacobi.

shortDefinition: Hugh Doak Rankin, born Hugh Dearborn Copp (1878 - 1956) was an American artist who produced an extensive amount of illustrations for Weird Tales, particularly between 1927 and 1930. As such, he provided the original art for dozens of stories by H. P....
fullContent:
Hugh Doak Rankin, born Hugh Dearborn Copp (1878 - 1956) was an American artist who produced an extensive amount of illustrations for Weird Tales, particularly between 1927 and 1930. As such, he provided the original art for dozens of stories by H. P. Lovecraft, Frank Belknap Long, Robert E. Howard and others whose work formed the foundation of the Cthulhu Mythos.

Stories originally illustrated by Rankin include, but are not limited to, "The Call of Cthulhu", "The Curse of Yig", "The Dunwich Horror", "The Electric Executioner", "The Last Test", "Out of the Aeons", "Pickman's Model", "The Shadow Kingdom", "The Silver Key", Skull-Face, "The Space-Eaters", "Tarbis of the Lake", and "Two Black Bottles".

### Biography
Hugh Copp was born in Loda, Illinois. His mother, Ellen Rankin Copp, was a celebrated sculptor, and Hugh followed her footsteps from an early age, drawing attention from the local newspapers for his sculptures while still 14. As a teenager, his mother took him to study art in Germany for a year.

In 1897, when Hugh was graduating from high school, the family became the target of far less desirable publicity, as Hugh's father attacked his wife's parents and sister and was arrested for attempted murder. As a result, young Hugh cut all ties with his father and changed his name to Hugh Doak Rankin.

The following year, Rankin and his mother moved to Indianapolis, where he started selling illustrations to newspapers. After the death of his mother and maternal grandfather, Rankin returned to Chicago to live with his maternal grandmother, aunt and uncle, and was employed as an artist by the same newspaper for which his uncle worked. Later in life, he moved to Los Angeles along with his aunt and uncle.

Hugo Gernsback (born Hugo Gernsbacher, 16 August 1884 – 19 August 1967) was a prolific editor and magazine publisher. Born in Luxembourg City, Luxembourg, he later emigrated to the United States where he became a naturalised citizen and established his name in the burgeoning publishing industry.

Gernsback was referred to as "Hugo the Rat" by both H. P. Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith as a result of his tendency to pay authors both poorly and late for their submissions. 

### In Fiction
*In "The Battle that Ended the Century", the character Ivor K. Rodent was a private jab at Gernsback.
*"In the Walls of Eryx" contains a species of creature dubbed Ugrats, a reference to his nickname of Hugo the Rat.

### External Links

Huitloxopetl is a fictional entity created for the round-robin story to which it lends its name.

### Overview
Huitloxopetl is the false lure or trickster. It is described as an angel who lures dead souls into its realm (The False Haven). The souls believe they are lead to the afterlife, but they face a horrible truth, and that is a pit of utter darkness. His true form is a demon with four tentacles, horns, wings, goat-like legs, and a head.

In the pit lies the unknown who hungers for souls.

fullContent:
Huitloxopetl is a round robin novella administered by the Nightscapes online magazine in 1998. It was contributed to by many authors, most of them members of the Esoteric Order of Dagon amateur press association (EODapa).

### Synopsis
The story varied wildly, as is the way of round robins where short passages are contributed. Huitloxopetl is a Great Old One worshipped in Medieval Mexico as a god, but it and its fellow Old Ones are returning for a feast of blood. Sllytha, an alien entity from the dark planet Yaar-Kyth and a devout worshipper of the Elder Gods, possesses the form of a young woman called Susan and acts to help the human race against the threat of the Old Ones.

### Behind the Mythos
This round robin story featured a lot of namechecking and syncretism- the attempt to reconcile different versions of entities and concepts from the Mythos into coherent wholes. Overall, it was a race against time story similar to an adventure from the Chaosium Call of Cthulhu RPG.

Huitzilopochtli was the Aztec sun god and patron god of the city of Tenochtitlan. It is also a god of war and associated with hummingbirds, its name originating from the Nahuatl words for "hummingbird" and either "south" or "left". It's commonly represented as a humanoid figure, sometimes blue-skinned, wearing a feathered hummingbird helmet, and holding the fire serpent Xiuhcoatl. Human sacrifices were performed to Huitzilopochtli, as the Aztecs believed that blood gave it strength and nourishment.

Huitzilopochtli (spelled as "Huitzilopotchli") was mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's early story "The Transition of Juan Romero" and first incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos in "The Electric Executioner", a collaboration between Lovecraft and Adolphe de Castro. In the works of August Derleth, this entity is associated with Cthulhu.

### In the Mythos
Juan Romero, while entranced by an inexplicable force or spell, repeatedly cried out this god's name as he descended into a deep chasm inside a mine shaft. On the next day, Romero was found dead in his bunkhouse, with no signs of having left it during the night, and the entrance to the abyss disappeared during a massive cave-in caused by a storm. (: "The Transition of Juan Romero")

The deranged inventor Arthur Feldon believed that Huitzilopochtli and the other Aztec gods were about to return, and that Feldon would rule the world with them with the power of his invention: a portable electric executioner. When another man pretended to be an emissary of Huitzilopochtli in order to play along with Feldon's mania, the inventor was so impressed that he pledged his servitude while mentioning the names of Tonatiuh-Metztli and Cthulhutl. (: "The Electric Executioner")

Prof. Laban Shrewsbury suggested that Huitzilopochtli might be another name for Cthulhu, pointing out how the god has been represented with serpents issuing from various parts of his body, similar to how Cthulhu has tentacles over his body. (: "The House on Curwen Street")

Humankind in the Cthulhu Mythos differs from its real-world counterpart in a number of ways, perhaps most importantly its origins, and its ability to interbreed with vastly different beings (usually referred to as "miscegenation" in Lovecraft's writings). This page aims to cover these variations.

### History
According to the history depicted in the murals found by Prof. Dyer and Danforth in Antarctica, humankind arose - like most life on Earth - as a result of natural evolution acting on the distant descendants of fauna engineered as servants and sustenance by Elder Things at around the time their empire was coming to its end. In these far-distant days, proto-human simians were regarded as sources of amusement and food by the Elder Things (: At the Mountains of Madness). Conversely, the K'n-yanians, an extraterrestrial humanoid species brought to Earth by Cthulhu in prehistory, have also claimed to be the ancestors of humanity (: The Mound).

Some believe that the ancestors of modern humans might have originated from the original fifth planet of the Solar System, a world that once stood between Mars and Jupiter until it was destroyed by a cataclysm and reduced to an asteroid belt (: "Dust of the Gods", "From the Parchments of Pnom").

It is possible that the first human beings inhabited Mu (: "The Invaders") and/or Lemuria (: "The Haunter of the Dark").

At some unspecified point in their history, humans mastered the art of magic, although this was limited to a very few learned individuals, and is widely believed to be a myth in the modern age. A possibly-related trait is the ability of certain humans to travel to the alternate dimension known as the Dreamlands in their sleep (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath).

At some point in the future, humankind will become extinct (: "Memory") and a civilisation of sapient beetles will emerge as the Earth's next dominant species (: The Shadow Out of Time).

### Interbreeding and Hybridisation
Lovecraft established that humans are capable of mating and producing fertile offspring with a number of beings without even the remotest of biological relation. These beings include creatures such as the Deep Ones (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth), the Great Ones (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) and White Apes (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family").

In addition, it has been shown that entirely alien or even interdimensional entities such as Yog-Sothoth are capable of breeding with humans, and may in fact use their offspring to gain access to our own reality (: "The Dunwich Horror"). In the past, the Elder Gods have also interbred with humans (: The Transition of Titus Crow).

### Devolution
As well as evolving, humankind has on occasion been seen to devolve into a more feral, bestial state, such as with the creatures portrayed in "The Beast in the Cave", "The Lurking Fear", and "The Rats in the Walls". The causes for this may vary, but in the examples given appears to be d

"Hunters from Beyond" are an alien species of interdimensional predators. (: "The Hunters from Beyond")

### Description
These horrific creatures are native to a world ordinarily unreachable by human senses, but are capable of crossing over into our realm and even leaving physical traces, such as saliva. Their strong putrefying smell is also indicative of their presence. However, they're not capable of interacting with anything physically, and the way they move around is not fluid, but rather resembles a series of instantly-shifting images.


Their physical appearance is similar to a pale-grey hairless ape, with a slouched posture and vaguely canine jaws, as well as long fangs from which their greenish slime-like saliva is often seen dripping. The talon-like claws on their hands are comparable to those of a hyena. The shriveled skin is marked by etiolated rings, which also give them a trace of worm-like aspect. Their deep-sunken eyes glow with a bright yellow phosphorescence.

These "Hunters from Beyond" have been so-named by the sculptor Cyprian Sincaul, who eventually mastered the ability to summon them from their native realm, without having to resort to spells or incantations. The appellation is more than adequate, given that these creatures are predators, although not in the traditional sense. They feed on the minds of living prey, converting their victims into mindless non-responsive automatons. Their hunting method consists of using a form of mesmerism to tempt victims to cross into the Hunters' own realm, where the prey becomes tangible to them. Strong-willed individuals are capable of resisting it with some effort.

The Hunting Horrors are a fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, and were later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Description
The hunting horrors are a servitor race of flying serpent-like creatures that serve Nyarlathotep, capable of travelling through the cosmos and other dimensions to undertake their master's bidding, as well as breaking into the dreams of humanity in order to bring fear. Sometimes acting as messengers, the hunting horrors may spread the word of Nyarlathotep to certain cultists. If a sorcerer knows the correct spells and signs, the hunting horrors can be summoned to perform various tasks, such as exacting revenge. Fueled by pure rage, the hunting horrors are relentless when going after their object of desire, smashing through brick walls or ripping apart metal casings until reaching the target. However, the hunting horrors can be dispelled by strong daylight and other intense light sources.

### Notes
*The hunting horrors being depicted as bat-winged serpentine creatures are based on the works of August Derleth, who describes them as "great viperine creatures, which had curiously distorted heads, and grotesquely great clawed appendages, supporting themselves with ease by the aid of black rubbery wings of singularly monstrous dimensions". (: The Lurker at the Threshold) However, in Lovecraft's original story, the hunting horrors were stated to be "formless"; presumably an amorphous monster, similar to the Formless Spawn and Shoggoths.

The Hyades is a real-world star cluster located in the constellation of Taurus. As the nearest star cluster to our own solar system, it is one of the most thoroughly studied.

The name Hyades is a collective noun originating from Ancient Greek myth. In the myth, the Hyades are Nymphs who bring rain to the fields to make the crops grow and nourish the forests and fields where animals graze. The Hyades are often depicted as nurturing figures. The most common version of the Hyades states that there are five Hyades, named Ambrosia, Phthia, Coronis, Lycaon, and Polyxo. Each of these nymphs has her own unique attributes and stories, but together they symbolize the nurturing aspect of nature.

The Hyades are also associated with the "Seven Sisters" of the Pleiades, who are considered to be their sister nymphs. The Pleiades are celestial nymphs considered to be gorgeously beautiful; the Hyades, whilst still possessing godlike beauty as nymphs are tied closely to fertility, water and the living earth. Pleiades are thus sky oriented, the Hyades nymphs of the fields and living things, on an elemental basis. In their use before being syncretized into the Cthulhu Mythos, the Hyades were referenced in the context of a shepherd god or of other more pastoral, dreaming or acquiescent decadence, and possibly as being rather than the typical Mythos identification of the Hyades as a place. Even on the basis of being a physical location, the Mythos usage is problematic; the Hyades is a constellation, not a coherent localized area.

### In the Mythos
In August Derleth's short story "The Gable Window" (one of his controversial "posthumous collaborations" with Lovecraft) one of the characters remark that the glass from which the titular window is made with glass from "Leng… possibly Hyadean in origins". This suggests that the fabled Plateau of Leng, whose location has long been a topic of debate, may in fact be situated somewhere in the Hyades star cluster.

The Hyborian Age is a fictional time period created by Robert E. Howard which first appeared in "The Phoenix on the Sword", the first of his Conan the Barbarian stories, which was published in 1932 in Weird Tales. It is the setting for Conan, Red Sonja, many of James Allison's past lives, and other tales. In both Marvel Comics and the Conan: Adventures in an Age Undreamed Of roleplaying game of Modiphius Entertainment, the Mythos is involved in its history.

In many derivative works, the fictional supercontinent that makes up most of the setting is referred to as Hyboria. However, it should be noted that Robert E. Howard never used this term. He used the term "Hyborian" to refer specifically to the northern civilized folk of his fictional world, for example as Conan uses the term when speaking to the Aquilonian character Balthus in the story "Beyond The Black River." Hyborians in that story are distinguished from other civilized folk, the Stygians and Shemites. 

Variants used in the Cthulhu Mythos include Hyborea (used by Brian Lumley) and Hyborios (used by Richard L. Tierney).

### Overview
The Hyborian Age is a "forgotten" era of mankind's existence which lasted for thousands of years, taking place after the Pre-Cataclysmic Age of the Thurian Continent (the setting of Howard's Kull of Atlantis series), but before all recorded history.

During the Hyborian Age, the configuration of the continents was different, with the world dominated by an enormous landmass combining much of today's Eurasia and Africa, with an inland sea in the middle known as the Vilayet Sea. In Howard's stories, this continent is unnamed. The Hyborians are an ethnic group divided among many different kingdoms (Aquilonians, Brythunians, Corinthians, Gundermen, Hyperboreans, Kothians, Nemedians, etc.), all originating from the original Hybori people, named after their deified chief Bori.

It should be noted that Conan's people, the Cimmerians, are not Hyborians, although Conan did become king of Aquilonia, a Hyborian nation. This is similar to Howard's earlier character, Kull, a barbarian from precivilised Atlantis who seized the throne of Valusia at the time of the Thurian Continent. The similarity is due to the fact that the first Conan story ("The Phoenix on the Sword") was a partial rewrite of an unsold Kull story ("By this Axe I Rule!").

Some elements of the Hyborian Age are based on preexisting myths, such as the rival kingdoms of Asgard and Vanaheim, continuously at war with each other. The names of many Hyborian nations come from unrelated historical sources, e.g. Aquilonia was the Roman name for the Italian comune of Lacedonia. Howard intentionally chose names derived from ancient history to suggest an era which, although long forgotten, did influence our world's (pre)history. fullContent:
In biology, a hybrid is the offspring that results when individuals of different species reproduce with each other. The concept of interbreeding between humans and inhuman beings is a common theme in the Cthulhu Mythos, being central to stories such as "The Dunwich Horror", "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family" and The Shadow Over Innsmouth. It is likewise present in the Mythos-adjacent works of Arthur Machen, such as The Great God Pan and "The Novel of the Black Seal", which have influenced the writings of H. P. Lovecraft and Robert E. Howard, among others.

### Overview
In Lovecraft's fiction, hybridization is one of the paths that might lead to what he regarded as degeneration. Although it is, in a sense, the opposite of inbreeding (in which the two parents are genetically too close to each other, rather than too far apart), Lovecraft depicts both processes as potential ways to spawn aberrations and monsters.

It should be noted that Lovecraft often used the word "hybrid" in a more colloquial sense as an adjective to describe beings that combine traits of different creatures. For example, he referred to Pan as a "hybrid man" ("To Pan"); to the white apes as "hybrid creatures" and "jungle hybrids" ("Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family"); to the Byakhee as "hybrid winged things" ("The Festival"); to the Children of the Sphinx as "hybrid blasphemies" ("Imprisoned with the Pharaohs"); to Joseph Curwen's resurrected monsters as "nameless hybrids" (The Case of Charles Dexter Ward); to the creatures that inhabited Europe 200,000 years ago as "hybrid entities" ("Out of the Aeons"); and to the Swine-Things as "hybrid anomalies" (Supernatural Horror in Literature). He also used the word to describe a heterogeneous group of people in "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Hybrid creatures in the Mythos
The Gyaa-yothn were created by hybridization, resultant from cross-breeding a species of horned reptilian quadrupeds from Yoth with a mammalian species enslaved by the K'n-yanians. (: The Mound)

In 1929, an American biologist named Dr. Thomas Slauenwite successfully cross-bred the legendary devil-flies of Uganda with another fly species, creating a hybrid insect that was just as lethal and also retained the devil-fly's mysterious trait of "stealing" the consciousness of those who die from its infection. (: "Winged Death")

A dog named Wolf, that belonged to 19th century Oklahoma settlers Walker and Audrey Davis, had coyote ancestry (: "The Curse of Yig"), meaning that either he or one of his ancestors was a coydog or dogote.

The Deep Ones seem actively interested in hybridizing with humans. A population of human-Deep One hybrids used to inhabit Walakea's island in the South Pacific, until being wiped out by another group of islanders in 1838. Another population was formed in the American town of Innsmouth in 1846 (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth), and several others are known to exist in other coastal cities around the world (: The

The Hydra is a fictional creature created by American author Henry Kuttner for his short story "Hydra".

### Overview
An extra-dimensional being which feeds on the life essence of its victims, the Hydra requires a portal to be opened to enter universes other than its own; at least as far as the human race is concerned, it utilises cultists who lay honey-traps which grant the ability to project one's astral self. Once the ritual is enacted and the person has projected, a gateway to the Hydra's realm is opened, allowing it to enter our universe and claim its victim, which it does by beheading some poor unfortunate. This person's consciousness is then held in eternal torment whilst the Hydra takes its sustenance from him.

The Hydra appears to dwell in the same plane of existence as the slumbering Outer God Azathoth; indeed, it is entirely possible that the two were intended by Kuttner to be one and the same.

The Hydra is a fictional entity whose origins lie within Classical Greek mythology. It has been mentioned in a number of Cthulhu Mythos stories, as well as in other related works through its real-world aspect.

### Background
The Hydra is a creature that lurks in the deepest parts of the Mesopotamian Sea. It takes the form of a many headed serpent that harbours a bitter hatred for surface dwellers, spitting acid and poisonous venom at unsuspecting travellers.(source?)

### In Marvel Comics
The Lernean Hydra was a descendant of the Elder God Set, sired by Set's granddaughter and mother of many prominent mythological monstrous figures Echidna, who mated with the Titan Typhon.

The Hydra was multi-headed reptilian monster who could grow two heads when one was removed, and whose blood was venomous. The Hydra became stuff of legends in Greece, and was one of the "labours" assigned to the demigod Hercules.

### Other Mentions
*In his poem "To Greece, 1917" a tribute to the people and mythology of Classical Greece, H. P. Lovecraft briefly mentions the Hydra as a foe of gods, heroes, and men.
*In Witches and Other Night-Fears, Charles Lamb mentioned the Gorgons, Hydras, and Chimaeras, as "dire stories of Celaeno and the Harpies". The excerpt is quoted as a preface in "The Dunwich Horror" ().

fullContent:
"Hydra" is a short story by American author and friend of H. P. Lovecraft's Henry Kuttner, originally published in 1939.

### Synopsis
Two amateur occult enthusiasts, Paul Edmond and Robert Ludwig, stumble upon a pamphlet with instructions on astral projection; their experiment results in Kenneth Scott, their mentor in the supernatural, being captured by a transdimensional entity. A rescue attempt results in Ludwig's being trapped by the same creature; when Edmond refuses to put his own soul at risk to save Scott, the elder occultist returns to our plane of reality to wreak a hideous revenge.

### Characters
*Kenneth Scott, a "noted Baltimore author and occultist" who "possessed one of the best occult libraries in America".  A "strange man" who "spent most of his time in an old brownstone house in Baltimore", he is described as "slender, sharp-eyed, and taciturn". He becomes a victim of Hydra as a result of Ludwig's and Edmond's experiment.
*Robert Ludwig,  a young man whose "correspondence with Scott was well known in literary circles". He appears to live in New York City. Like his friend Edmond, he is a dabbler in witchcraft and demonology; on a visit to California to visit Edmond, he purchases On the Sending Out of the Soul in a San Pedro bookstore. He becomes a second victim of Hydra.
*Paul Edmond, another occult dilettante who lives in Hollywood. He keeps a diary that describes many of the events of the story. He is killed not by Hydra but by Scott's decapitated head.
*Russell Hodgkins, "California’s most noted bibliophile", who insists that On the Sending Out of the Soul is not a real book.
*Perry L. Lewis, a professor and a "recognized expert on dream-phenomena". He provides a psychological explanation for the experiences described in Edmond's diary.

### Mythos Entities

The story describes two godlike beings who are disastrously encountered through astral projection:
*Hydra, a "vampiric entity, living not on the blood of its victims but on their heads—their brains." It appears as a "sea of gray slime, protoplasmic and featureless," whose "fluctuating leaden surface was dotted and speckled with round dark blobs," which are the innumerable heads, of human and inhuman form, that have been incorporated into the being. This entity is generally distinguished from the Mother Hydra worshiped by the Deep Ones.
*Azathoth, the "Lord of All Things," through whose thoughts "all that exists was created." The slightest glimpse of this entity "would mean utter and complete destruction to the beholder."

### Publication History
First published in the April 1939 edition of Weird Tales, "Hydra" was not reprinted again (except for a 1979 French translation) until 1986, when it appeared in the Lammas 1986 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu (#41). It was subsequently included in two Chaosium books from 1995, The Azathoth Cycle: Tales of the Blind Idiot God and The Book of Iod.

Hyperborea is a fictional prehistoric land created by Clark Ashton Smith as a setting for the Hyperborean Cycle of stories which intersect with the Cthulhu Mythos. The name, meaning "Beyond the North Wind", is taken from Greek mythology, where it appears as a land far to the north. In Smith's fiction, it is more or less identifiable with the island of Greenland, though in his stories, set in the Pleistocene epoch, it is mostly ice-free. 

Millennia later, the name of Hyperborea was given to the northernmost kingdom of the Hyborian Age in what later became Europe. There is no connection between the two Hyperboreas aside from their shared northern latitude.

### Locations
### Mhu Thulan
Mhu Thulan is a province in northern Hyperborea, famous for its sorcerers like Eibon and Zon Mezzamalech.  (: "Ubbo-Sathla").

### Polarion 
Polarion is a region in northern Hyperborea, separated from the rest of the realm by a mountain range. It is home to the White Sybil. (: "The White Sybil")

### Eiglophian mountains
The Eiglophian mountains, mentioned in Smith's "The Seven Geases", are a terrifying range of ebon peaks, said to be "glassy-walled", and are believed to be honeycombed with hidden tunnels. The Eiglophian mountains cross the middle of the Hyperborean continent, with one range stretching to the south and another to the east.

### Mount Voormithadreth
Mount Voormithadreth, the tallest peak in the Eiglophian mountains, is a four-coned extinct volcano. Its exterior is inhabited by the Voormis; beneath it is the dwelling place of various horrors, including the toad-god Tsathoggua and the spider-god Atlach-Nacha.

### Y'qaa
The gray-litten cavern of Y'qaa the entrance to which is below Voormithadreth, is the dwelling place of the enigmatic Ubbo-Sathla, and possibly also Abhoth, the Source of Uncleanliness. It is in fact an interdimensional hub connected to multiple worlds, and indirectly connected with the Cavern of Archetypes. Atlach-Nacha originated here.

### Cavern of Archetypes
The cavern of the Archetypes is a vast cavern inhabited by the spectral archetypes of all life on this earth. Nug and Yeb reside here.

### Commoriom
Commoriom was the first seat of power in Hyperborea, established by the pre-human migrants from the south. In its heyday, Commoriom was a grand city, built of marble and granite and marked by a skyline of altitudinous spires.

Legend has it that the populace fled Commoriom when the White Sybil of Polarion foretold of its destruction. However, Athammaus, headsman of C

fullContent:
Hyperborea is sword-and-sorcery table-top role-playing game based on Hyperborea as described or informed by the fantastic literature of Robert Ervin Howard, Howard Phillips Lovecraft,  and Clark Ashton Smith. It uses the original Dungeons & Dragons rules options from 1974, and is part of what has come to be called the Old School Revival (OSR) movement in table-top role-playing.

It is published by North Wind Adventures. The first edition was released in 2012 and the game is now supported online and has print on demand versions of some of its earlier releases. In 2013, the first full year of its original release, it received nominations (but did not win) in the following competitions:

*North Texas RPG Con 2013, Three Castles RPG Design Award
*ENnie Awards 2013, Best Game
*ENnie Awards 2013, Best Production Values
*ENnie Awards 2013, Product of the Year

The game made some effort to be faithful to the original source material in the works of the Lovecraft Circle authors but balance that with playability and more than passing reliance on the Marvel Comics conceptualisation of Conan the Barbarian from its many years of publishing what was essentially a pastiche of the original tales.

The Hyperborean cycle is a series of short stories by Clark Ashton Smith that take place in the fictional prehistoric setting of Hyperborea (present-day Greenland). Various elements in Smith's cycle have been borrowed by H.P. Lovecraft, most notably the "toad-god" Tsathoggua. (: "The Tale of Satampra Zeiros", : "The Mound", "The Whisperer in Darkness")

|Selected Letters 3.383}}

Because Smith in turn borrowed numerous Lovecraftian elements, the cycle itself may be regarded as a branch of the Cthulhu Mythos.

: Selected Letters of Clark Ashton Smith 244}}

The Hyperborean cycle mixes cosmic horror with an Iron Age-style setting. Adding to the peril is the rapidly approaching ice age, which threatens to wipe out all life on the Hyperborean continent. A host of other deities play important roles in the cycle; foremost is the toad-god Tsathoggua, who dwells in Mount Voormithadreth.

### Hyperborea
Hyperborea is a legendary continent in the Arctic. Before it was overwhelmed by the advancing ice sheets of the Pleistocene age, Hyperborea was warm and fertile with lush jungles inhabited by the last remnants of the dinosaurs. A race of yeti-like bipeds known as the Voormi once populated Hyperborea, but were wiped out by the pre-human settlers that migrated here from the south. These pre-humans built the first capital of Hyperborea at Commoriom. Later they moved to Uzuldaroum when prophesies foretold of Commoriom's doom.

### Gods
### Abhoth



### Atlach-Nacha



### Rlim Shaikorth



### Tsathoggua

The early settlers of Hyperborea at first worshipped the toad-god Tsathoggua, the patron deity of the Voormi. Later, they turned to more conventional deities — primarily, Yhoundeh, the elk-goddess.

### Ubbo-Sathla



### Yhoundeh

In Smith's "The Door to Saturn", Yhoundeh the elk-goddess is the name of the deity worshipped in the waning days of Hyperborea. Yhoundeh's priests also banned Tsathoggua's cult, and her inquisitors punished any heretics. As the Hyperborean civilization drew to a close, Yhoundeh's priests fell out of favor and the people returned to the worship of Tsathoggua.

According to the Parchments of Pnom, Yhoundeh is the wife of Nyarlathotep, avatar of the Outer Gods. (: Clark Ashton Smith letter to Robert H. Barlow, dated September 19, 1934; Will Murray, "The Book of Hyperborea Introduction")

### Geographical locations
For places in the Hyperborean Cycle, see Hyperborea.

### Notable denizens
### Voormi
The Voormi are the bestial humanoids that once occupied Hyperborea. After most were wiped out by pre-human settlers, the most savage Voormi became restricted to caves in the upper slopes of the Eiglophian mountains. Before Hyperborea's fall, the remaining Voormi were hunted for sport.

fullContent:
The Hyperion Hotel is a recurrent location created by the late American author Michael Shea. The Hyperion has two histories which cannot quite coexist, the major difference being the fate of long-term resident Chester Chase.

### Description
Located in  San Francisco's Mission District, the Hyperion is a "shabby old residence hotel," described as "a faded, century-old hotel...a decent but decidedly frayed and funky habitation". It has a "big battered old steel" front door, and its facade features the black Z’s of its fire escape."

Along with short-term room rentals, the Hyperion also plays home to several long-term residents. Those who frequent its ageing corridors are mostly people considered by the bulk of society as the outcasts and down-and-outs.

### Staff
* The Patels (formerly), husband and wife Bill and Phaasri, and 12-year-old daughter Aarti. The family live in and manage the hotel on behalf of wealthy relations.
*Ramdass Patel, manager and another relation of the Patels.
*Jack Hale (formerly), a poet and author who worked the night shift in reception. Here, he did much of his writing. Also a resident.
*Elmer (formerly), the daytime reception clerk, described as a "scrawny old rooster in an undershirt, with thick goggle-glasses and a phlegmy voice". Also a resident.
* Daryl, a construction worker who works the graveyard shift in reception in exchange for room and board.

### Residents
* Chester Chase, a 75-year-old man who has decided to oppose the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos/has discorporated into the ether.
* Mr. Cannyharme/Mr. Cunningham/Mr. Van Haarme/Mr. Canning, an ancient predatory being hiding in plain sight.
*Rich Rasp, a roofing worker with a drug habit.
*Ron Ratchett (formerly, now homeless), a middle-aged alcoholic.
*DeeAnn (formerly, deceased), an upbeat hooker.
*Razz (formerly, deceased), DeeAnn's pimp.
*Bender, a computer worker.
*Brittany aka Britt, a former drug addict.
* Susy (formerly, deceased), a small-time drug dealer.

### Appearances
*"The Pool" (2007)
* "The Recruiter" (2009)
* "Dagoniad" (2009)
*Mr. Cannyharme (2021)

### Trivia

* Although making its first printed appearance in the 2007 short story "The Pool", the Hyperion Hotel was actually created for the novel Mr. Cannyharme which, although not published until 2021, was written in 1981.

fullContent:
"Hypnos" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, penned in March 1922 and first published in the May 1923 issue of The National Amateur.

### Synopsis
Hypnos is a first-person narrative written from the perspective of an unnamed character living in Kent and later London, England. The narrator writes that he fears sleep, and is resolved to write his story down lest it drive him further mad, regardless of what people think after reading it.

The narrator, a sculptor, recounts meeting a mysterious man in a railway station. The moment the man opened his "immense, sunken and widely luminous eyes", the narrator knew that the stranger would become his friend-–"the only friend of one who had never possessed a friend before". In the eyes of the stranger he saw the knowledge of the mysteries he always sought to learn.

From this point on, he would touch his friend and sculpt him daily. At night they would commence their adventures, exploring worlds beyond human comprehension. Over time, the narrator's companion begins speaking of using their ability to transcend into the unknown to rule the universe, via a set of drugs, a thought that scares the narrator (who disavows to the reader any such hubris).

Soon the narrator is off on a foray with his friend, travelling through a void that he explains is beyond human sensation. Passing through several barriers, eventually the narrator comes to one he cannot cross, though his friend does. Opening his "physical eyes", the narrator wakes up and awaits the return of his friend, who awakes severely shaken and reticent, warning only that they must avoid sleep at all cost.

From then on, with the aid of drugs, the two avoid sleep, as each time they succumb, they both seem to rapidly age and are plagued by nightmares that the narrator refuses to explain. The story ends with the narrator explaining that one night, his friend fell into a "deep-breathing sleep" and was impossible to arouse. The narrator shrieks and faints, and awakes surrounded by police and neighbours, who inform him he has never had a friend—all there is in the room is a statue of his friend, engraved with the Greek word ΥΠΝΟΣ (Hypnos).

### Significance
Lovecraft dedicated this story to his longtime friend Samuel Loveman, who featured in the dreams that inspired Lovecraft's "The Statement of Randolph Carter" and "Nyarlathotep". Loveman suggested it was the best thing Lovecraft had ever written up to that point in time, as mentioned by Lovecraft in a letter.

The plot-germ of the story is found in Lovecraft's commonplace book, in an early entry (#23) reading, "The man who would not sleep--dares not sleep--takes drugs to keep himself awake. Finally falls asleep--& something happens."

As in many of Lovecraft's writings, the terror and the world are unknowable. This fits in to Lovecraft's common themes as to the alien and hostile nature of the universe, infinity, and the futility of everything. Even at the end of the story, the f

Hytherion (aka, the Beast of Time) is a multiversal Lovecraftian-like entity in the fictional universe of Transformers by TakaraTomy.

### Background
Hytherion is a hyper-dimensional entity of incredible power that is able to freely travel throughout a universe's timeline. It's made of alterium, a dimensionally-resonant material, and sustains itself on time. Savoring the devouring of worlds and universes' origins, therefore the name "Origin Eater". To lower-dimensional beings the entity is both invisible and intangible. It's a force of nature in the multiverse, consuming universes that have been weakened or damaged, thereby protecting the multiverse from their chaos.

Hziulquoigmnzhah (also known as Ziulquaz-Manzah) is a fictional entity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Door to Saturn".

### Overview
Hziulquoigmnzhah is described as having "ludicrously short legs … exceedingly elongated arms, and [a] round, sleepy-looking head that was pendulous from a spherical body". It is slow-moving, and shows no real interest in either helping or hindering the sorcerer Eibon or his pursuer, the zealot Morghi. (: "The Door to Saturn")

Currently residing on Cykranosh, the planet known as Saturn in the modern day, the Parchments of Pnom tell of Hzuilquoigmnzhah being the "son" of Cxaxukluth, "brother" to Ghisguth and "uncle" to Tsathoggua.

### In Other Media
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, the Anticross Vespasianus uses a spell called "Iqhui dlosh odhqlonqh", which was taken from Hziulquoigmnzhah's words to Eibon in the original story.

fullContent:
"I Am ..." is a short story by John Claude Smith, originally collected in the Kickstarter crowdfunded anthology A Mythos Grimmly. It is a quite graphic and horrifying short story about an irreversible physical transformation.

### Synopsis
A young woman has begun a relationship with a tattooed sadist and would-be alchemist and cultist, who has come into possession of a grimoire of extreme power. At the same time, to add to his occult powers, he has begun to keep the ashes of his past lovers in jars, in the manner of the essential salts used in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward by H. P. Lovecraft.

However, it eventuates that the sadistic occultist is burning his lovers alive in the most hideous imaginable torture to produce the "essential salts."

Accusing his latest lover of trying to steal his secrets and read the grimoire, he douses her in lighter fluid and sets her on fire, causing fourth degree burns and burning her face off.

Awakening in hospital and strangely functional, the latest victim goes back to the apartment she had shared with the occultist to discover the ashes of the past victims mixed with the burned ruins, allowing still to communicate with her. The grimoire has also been reduced to ash.

In the process of her own mutilation by fire, the grimoire has combined with the apparently living victim. She has become a living grimoire: The Necronomicon made flesh.

In 2023, it was voted by the fanbase on social media platform Facebook to be included in the anthology The Best of Lovecraftiana (2023, Rogue Planet Press), where it appeared as the final piece .

The twenty-five lines describe how the tombstone of Howard Phillips Lovecraft bears witness to the return of the Elder Gods.

I Am Providence: The Life and Times of H. P. Lovecraft is a non-fiction work by Lovecraft scholar and critic S. T. Joshi. 

### Overview
Joshi has described this comprehensive biography as his most significant achievement in his long career of studying Lovecraft. I Am Providence is a significantly expanded edition of one of his earlier works, H. P. Lovecraft: A Life, containing an addition 150,000 words which had been cut from the original publication due to length considerations, has been revised to incorporate recent information on Lovecraft, and was released in two separate volumes. 

### Publication History
I Am Providence was released by Hippocampus Press in 2010.

"I Do the Work of the Bone Queen" is a short Lovecraftian story by American author John R. Fultz.

### Synopsis
A crippled man commits suicide to escape the prison of his ruined body. His ghost is subsequently given a fresh corporeal form by an entity known as the Bone Queen, and sent back to run the factory where he had his accident in life. However, the factory has been repurposed, and now functions as an assembly line for bizarre flesh golems which are sacrificed to some unknown abomination.

### Publication History
"I Do the Work of the Bone Queen" was published in the Kat Rocha-edited Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in 2013.

shortDefinition: "'I Had Vacantly Crumpled It into My Pocket . . . But by God, Eliot, It Was a Photograph from Life!'" is a short story written by Joanna Russ, first published in the August 1964 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. The title is a quo...
fullContent:
"'I Had Vacantly Crumpled It into My Pocket . . . But by God, Eliot, It Was a Photograph from Life!'" is a short story written by Joanna Russ, first published in the August 1964 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. The title is a quote from H. P. Lovecraft's story "Pickman's Model"; the story itself does not reference the Cthulhu Mythos directly, but describes an obsessive Lovecraft fan's fatal fascination with a supernatural seductress.

### Characters
* Irvin Rubin: A "bookkeeper in a cheap publishing house" called Fantasy Press. Twenty-eight years old, he has "pale-blue protuberant eyes that should have been nearsighted." He lives in a "furnished room...in the decaying blocks near the rich section of Central Park West." He "never ate without a book propped up in front of his plate," and believes that "Howard Phillips Lovecraft was the greatest writer in the world." 
* June Kramer: Irv's only friend at work, whom he turns to for advice. She lives in the Stuyvesant Town housing development. Her younger sister died when they were girls, some 40 years earlier.
* Irv's Girl:  The woman Irv meets "near Central Park, walking two dachshunds on a leash"; he describes her as a “real lady” and a “glamour girl.” When June sees her, she is struck by her "pale, powdered face": "the thin eyebrows, the expressionless profile," and her "wild, lovely, violet eyes." She appears to be a supernatural predator rather than a human woman--as evidenced by Irv's being found frozen to death in Central Park after an encounter with her.

### Publication History
The story was republished in The Hidden Side of the Moon (St. Martin's Press, 1988), a collection of Russ's fiction, and was later included in Cthulhu 2000 (Arkham House, 1995). It has been translated into French (as "La jeune fille en noir," 1965) and German ("Ich muß sie unwillkürlich abgerissen und eingesteckt haben ... aber bei Gott, Eliot, es war eine Blitzlichtaufnahme nach dem Leben!," 2004).

I Miti di Cthulhu ("The Cthulhu Mythos") is an Italian-language series of collections of Cthulhu Mythos-related horror and other selected stories published by Fanucci Editore between March 1985 and September 1991. The books consist largely of translations of English-language works from a variety of authors, including those of the Lovecraft circle, expanded mythos authors, and writers from whom Lovecraft took inspiration, although a fair portion are more traditional horror anthologies, with these choosing to focus on a specific theme; for example vampires or werewolves. 

Authors who have been published in the series include H. P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, Arthur Conan Doyle, Algernon Blackwood, William Hope Hodgson, Robert Bloch, Arthur Machen, Ambrose Bierce, and many others.

The series was edited by Sebastiano Fusco, Gianni Pilo, Domenico Cammarota, and Luigi Cozzi, and translators included Pilo and Daniela Galdo.

In February 1992, the series was relaunched as I Miti di Cthulhu (Nuova Serie), which was edited solely by Pilo. This series proved short-lived, with only four books receiving a release, all novels, and only one related to the actual Cthulhu Mythos.

I Walk the World's Black Rim is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Mike Minnis.

### Synopsis
The novella recounts the adventures in the Viking Age of a Deep One descendant warrior who quests to destroy an enormous Deep One-type monster called Nindhoggir. 

### Behind the Mythos
"I Walk the World's Black Rim" is notable for its use of what was then a very different setting for a Mythos story and for its deliberate parallelism of (fictional) folklore, providing a reasonably comprehensive list of Viking cognates for familiar Mythos entities. The "Great Kraken" is the Viking lore name for Cthulhu, for example.

### Publication History
"I Walk the World's Black Rim" was first published in the E. P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes in October 1997. It later received a physical release in the October 1998 edition of Dark Legacy.

"I, Cthulhu, or, What's a Tentacle-Faced Thing Like Me Doing in a Sunken City Like This (Latitude 47° 9' S, Longitude 126° 43' W)?" is a humorous short story by Neil Gaiman that purports to be the autobiography of Cthulhu, dictated to a lackey named Whateley. It was first published in 1987 in the 16th issue of the fanzine Dagon under the title "Bloody Peculiar Aeons".

### Synopsis
Cthulhu dictates his memoirs to a human servant named Whateley, who duly writes down everything their master says, including interjections, such as asking if the shoggoth has been fed, or answering Whateley's occasional questions.

Cthulhu reveals that he was born in "the dark mists of Khhaa'yngnaiih", an extradimensional world of swamps and towers, lit by the light of an enormous red moon, and orbiting a faded old sun that eventually exploded. His father was eaten by his mother, who in turn was eaten by Cthulhu as he was born. The young Cthulhu was about 4 ft. long and spent his first millennia lurking in the swamps, ambushing and devouring prey while avoiding larger predators.

One Tuesday, Uncle Hastur visits Cthulhu's part of the swamp to invite him to go out, along with some other relatives, which include the likes of Azathoth, Nyarlathotep, Tsathoggua, etc. Despite feeling a bit disconnected from his cousins, Cthulhu eagerly takes the opportunity to see other worlds. At Yog-Sothoth's insistence, they choose humanity's dimensional plane as their destination, and pass through a gate to dim Carcosa. At first, Cthulhu is scared of humans, but gets along well with the King in Yellow, who finds being worshiped fun and recommends Cthulhu try the same, suggesting a world named Earth. However, he does warn Cthulhu about the Old Ones: a species of barrel-shaped, starfish-headed beings, which oppose this kind of thing.

Cthulhu arrives on prehistoric Earth, where he allies himself with a creature named Dagon and becomes the master of a native species of fish-men. At first, they rule over the seas, but when the star-headed Old Ones start fighting them, they move on to land instead, where they build cyclopean cities and devour all the dinosaurs in a single barbecue. Ironically, thanks to a cataclysm that Cthulhu blames on the Old Ones' messing around with the Earth's orbit, many of the continents sink and Cthulhu's domain of R'lyeh is submerged, while Antarctica (the domain of the Old Ones) freezes.

After that, the story jumps to another point, as a note informs the reader that three pages of the manuscript are missing. Cthulhu tells Whateley that the stars have changed and, as a result, he and his kind cannot live, so they have to stay down and wait for the stars to be right again, at which point Cthulhu will rise and reclaim the Earth. In a distant future, after the Earth has become cold and lifeless, Cthulhu plans to return to his homeworld and estivate. Ian Gordon is a British author, editor, and audio production creator who has worked on numerous releases by and about the late horror writer Howard Phillips Lovecraft and the expanded Cthulhu Mythos which has sprung from his stories.

Gordon's output includes Lovecraftian anthologies and readings, as well as short fiction pieces, several of which feature the character Peter van Melsen, a supernatural sleuth in the vein of William Hope Hodgson's Thomas Carnacki or August Derleth's Solar Pons.

In addition to these works, Gordon is, with his wife Jennifer, the co-owner and founder of the indie publisher/production company HorrorBabble, an organisation which specialises in both classic and original weird fiction.

"Ibid" is a parody by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in 1927 or 1928 and first published posthumously in the January 1938 issue of O-Wash-Ta-Nong. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

### Summary
"Ibid" is a mock biography of the Roman scholar Ibidus (486-587), whose masterpiece was Op. Cit., "wherein all the significant undercurrents of Graeco-Roman thought were crystallized once and for all." The piece traces the skull of Ibidus, once the possession of Charlemagne, William the Conqueror and other notables, to the United States, where it travels via Salem, Massachusetts and Providence, Rhode Island to a prairie dog hole in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

Ibidus, later known as St. Ibid, is a fictional Roman scholar created by H. P. Lovecraft for his comedy short story "Ibid".

In real life, the word "ibid." comes from the Latin ibidem ("in the same place") and is used in academic texts to refer to a source already given, in order to avoid repetition. Lovecraft's comedy is based on the idea of a reader mistaking "Ibid" for the name of an author. Whether this scenario is hypothetical is unknown. However, the story was originally written for Maurice W. Moe, a friend of Lovecraft who was also a teacher, so it is possible that it might have been based on a gaffe that occurred in one of Moe's classes.

### Biography
Ibidus (486 - 587 AD) was an eminent Roman scholar who authored the famous Op. Cit., a work in which "all the significant undercurrents of Graeco-Roman expression were crystallised once for all—and with admirable acuteness". His full name is a matter of debate among scholars:
*Caius Anicius Magnus Furius Camillus Æmilianus Cornelius Valerius Pompeius Julius Ibidus, according to Von Schweinkopf
*Caius Anicius Magnus Furius Camillus Cornelius Valerius Pompeius Julius Claudius Decius Junianus Ibidus, according to Littlewit
*Magnus Furius Camillus Aurelius Antoninus Flavius Anicius Petronius Valentinianus Aegidus Ibidus, according to Bêtenoir

Ibidus was born in the year 486, either in Rome or Ravenna, and educated in the schools of Athens. In 512, he was a rhetorics teacher in Rome. Four years later, he was already a consul along with Pompilius Numantius Bombastes Marcellinus Deodamnatus. When Theodoric the Great died in 526, Ibidus briefly retired from public life to dedicate himself solely to his writings, but was soon summoned to act as court rhetorician for Theodoric's nephew, Theodahad.

When Vitiges usurped the throne, Ibidus was imprisoned. However, he was liberated by Belisarius' army and joined their ranks, fighting bravely to defend the Empire during the first siege of Rome. He was appointed to accompany the Bishop of Milan, Dacius, to Corinth, Greece, and resided with him in 539. Two years later, Ibidus moved to Constantinople, where he lived the remainder of his life as an esteemed public figure. When Ibidus was 101 years old, the emperor Maurice adopted his Op. Cit. as a textbook in the schools of the empire. (: "Ibid")

### Skull of Ibid
Ibidus died in 587, at the age of 102, and his body was taken to Ravenna to be interred. The history of his remains is as turbulent as his life. He was exhumed by the Duke of Spolato, who sent his skull to King Autharis to be used as a drinking bowl. This morbid item was passed from king to king and stolen by Charlemagne during his conquests. Pope Leo III used it to hold the royal unction when he declared Charlemagne Holy Roman Emperor. Ibn Schacabac, often rendered as Ibn Schacabao, is a fictional character mentioned in two stories by H. P. Lovecraft. There is some confusion about the correct spelling of the character's name.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The first mention of Ibn Schacabac is in a quote from the Necronomicon that Lovecraft created to conclude his short story "The Festival," written in 1923. It includes the passage: Wisely did Ibn Schacabac say, that happy is the tomb where no wizard hath lain, and happy the town at night whose wizards are all ashes. Then in his novel The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, written in 1927, Lovecraft presents a letter from Joseph Curwen to Simon Orne that includes the line:  I laste Night strucke on ye Wordes that bringe up YOGGE-SOTHOTHE, and sawe for ye firste Time that fface spoke of by Ibn Schacabac in ye ——.  In both passages, Ibn Schacabac is presented as an authority on occult matters. To be cited by Abdul Alhazred, the character must have lived in the 8th century or earlier. 

### Behind the Mythos
Ibn Schacabac means "Son of Schacabac" in classical Arabic. Schacabac is the name of a character from The Arabian Nights, in the Andrew Lang edition that Lovecraft knew and loved as a child. Schacabac, also known as the Barber's Sixth Brother, is a starving man who appreciates an imaginary meal offered to him by a wealthy man, and is rewarded with a real feast and a job managing the rich man's house. (The rich man's name is Barmecide, and the phrase "Barmecide feast" has come to mean pretended or illusory generosity.)

Both "The Festival" and Charles Dexter Ward were originally published by Weird Tales, and in both original publications the name appears as "Ibn Schacabac." Lovecraft's hand-written manuscript of Charles Dexter Ward likewise says "Ibn Schacabac." When "The Festival" was reprinted by Arkham House, however, the name was rendered as "Ibn Schacabao," while it was printed correctly as "Ibn Schacabac" in Arkham House's Charles Dexter Ward.

S. T. Joshi, while correcting a great many textual errors in Arkham House's Lovecraft reprints, unfortunately "corrected" the Charles Dexter Ward version to conform to the misprint in "The Festival." This mistake has been corrected in Joshi's Variorum Edition.

Icthultu is an extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of the Justice League animated series by DC Comics.

### Background
Thousands of years ago, Icthultu once ruled over Thanagar, where the people of that planet worshiped him as their god. Icthultu helped build the foundations of their entire culture including its agriculture, mathematics and philosophy. However, they eventually grew tired of their many sacrifices to Icthultu and stopped worshipping him. Afterwards, Icthultu and the other Old Ones invaded the Earth, nearly wiping out all of humanity before King Poseidon banished them to their home dimension at the cost of sinking the city of Atlantis in the process.

In the present day, Icthultu attempted to invade the Earth again. While Doctor Fate, Aquaman and Soloman Grundy performed a ritual that would prevent Icthultu's return, it was interrupted by the Justice League, causing Icthultu to nearly escape from his dimensional prison. With Icthultu's banishment only being temporary, the Justice League decided to enter his dimension to fight the threat head-on. Icthultu was eventually defeated when Hawkgirl and Soloman Grundy attacked him from the inside of his body, destroying his brain. (: "The Terror Beyond")

### Behind the Mythos
The show writers originally intended to use Cthulhu but were under the impression that the character wasn't in the public domain, hence creating their own pastiche.

"Iden-Inshi" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Greg Stolze.

### Synopsis
Written as a series of diary entries kept by a kidnapped geneticist, "Iden-Inshi" follows the woman and a fellow scientist as they attempt to create genetically-modified bodies for an unspecified Asian dictator. As they become more desperate to escape, they decide to infect one of themselves with a variant retrovirus which would grant the infected person superhuman abilities. However, the treatment has drastic and unforeseen consequences.

### Characters
* The Unnamed Narrator, a highly-skilled Portuguese geneticist.
* Kiro, a Japanese geneticist and fellow prisoner.

### Publication History
"Iden-Inshi" was published in the anthology of H. P. Lovecraft-inspired fiction Whispers from the Abyss in 2013.

### Trivia
* The creatures whose DNA the two scientists use, the eponymous iden-inshi, appear to share some traits with Lovecraft's Deep Ones, their reproductive methods bearing definite similarities.

fullContent:
"Idle Days on the Yann" is a short story by Lord Dunsany that first appeared in  his collection A Dreamer's Tales (George Allen & Sons, 1910). Set in the "Lands of Dream," it was a major influence on H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands tales, particularly "The White Ship."

### Summary
"Idle Days" tells the story of a dreamer who voyages down the River Yann on the ship Bird of the River. The captain comes from "fair Belzoond," where are "worshipped gods that were the least and humblest, who seldom sent the famine or the thunder." When the sailors laugh at the dreamer for claiming to be from Ireland in Europe, since "There are no such places in all the land of dreams," he tells them that he mostly dreams of a beautiful blue city called Golthoth the Damned," in the "desert of Cuppar-Nombo," they agree that "such places might well be imagined."

When the sailors pray to their various gods, taking care "that no god should hear two men praying to him at once," the dreamer chooses to pray to "Sheol Nugganoth, whom the men of the jungle have long since deserted, who is now unworshipped and alone."

The ship comes to various cities, including Mandaroon, where the citizens sleep lest the gods die and "men may dream no more"; Astahahn, where is found nothing new, for they "have fettered and manacled Time, who would otherwise slay the gods”; Perdóndaris, where the dreamer sees "a huge ivory gate...carved out of one solid piece"; and Nen, which is crowded with Wanderers, "a weird, dark tribe, that once in every seven years came down from the peaks of Mloon." 

Finally the ship comes to Bar-Wul-Yann, the Gates of Yann, where at the river's mouth "two cliffs of pink marble came out into the river, all glowing in the light of the low sun...the fairest marvel that the eye beheld—and this in a land of wonders."

The sailors strike anchor here, "for they were sailors of the river and not of the sea." The dreamer says farewell to the captain, knowing they will never meet again, "for my fancy is weakening as the years slip by, and I go ever more seldom into the Lands of Dream."

### Illustrations
Like many of Lord Dunsany's stories, "Idle Days of the Yann" was illustrated by S. H. Sime, who provided two images: "Bird of the River" and "The Gate of Yann."

Iku-Turso is a fictional sea monster, who is deeply rooted in Finnish mythology, most famously appearing in Elias Lönnrot's epic poem the Kalevala. Mikael Agricola, a Lutheran clergyman and de facto founder of literary Finnish, listed Iku-Turso as god of war, while others have tied him to pestilence.

Iku-Turso was later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Finnish writer Tuomas Saloranta for his 2012 short story "Mahtavat Ammoiset" (Finnish for "Great Old Ones"). The entity is said to reside somewhere in the waters of Finland.

### Overview
Iku-Turso was a Great Old One who ruled over the areas of Finland, until he, alongside Kalanpäinen and the other Old Ones, were sung into the swamps by Finnish sages and poets, who had learned these abilities from the Sámi people. Only myths and some of the Deep Ones remained in the country.

Around the 1930s, author Matts W. Cornelius, who was a correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft, wrote stories in which he compared Iku-Turso with the Great Old One Cthulhu. 

The Deep Ones, especially those who live in Lauttasaari, still seek to awaken the Iku-Turso and the Old Ones, so that they could reclaim the world. (: "Mahtavat Ammoiset")

Iku-Turso is speculated to be involved with the Von Rühnen/Värynen-family, and their ability to continue to exist as spiritual beings after death. (: "Kari Tenho Väyrysen tapaus")

### Trivia
*The Finnish word for octopus (tursas) come from the mythological Iku-Turso.
*Iku-Turso has also been compared to other ancient sea beasts, such as the Leviathan from the Abrahamic faiths and Jörmungandr from Norse Mythology.

fullContent:
"Il Segno Giallo" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by David Dunwoody. It is part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by C. J. Henderson.

### Synopsis
When Frank Nardi receives a call for help from an old musician acquaintance, he hears the story of a genius composer whose music causes those who play it to commit suicide. Ultimately unable to save his friend, a furious Nardi leaves the composer to die by his own hand as an offering for the god to whom his music was dedicated.

### Characters

*Frank Nardi, former NYPD Detective turned private eye.
*Isabella Andora, accomplished cellist and Frank's old friend.
*Gio Pastore, a young and exceptionally gifted composer, but also a practitioner of dark magic.

### Behind the Mythos
"Il Segno Giallo" was written by David Dunwoody at a request by Brian M. Sammons for a story based around PI Frank Nardi. It was published in November 2017 by Dark Regions Press in the anthology Arkham Detective Agency.

### Mythos Connections

*The story is set in H. P. Lovecraft's legendary town of Arkham.
*One of the notes used frequently in Pastore's composition is described as "like an eye with malformed arms splayed about it." This description appears to match that of the Yellow Sign of Hastur; additionally, the title of the story, il segno giallo, translates into English as the yellow sign.

Ilarnek is a city in the land of Mnar on the River Ai in the Dreamlands. It was built by the same wandering tribes that built the Mnaran cities of Thraa, Kadatheron, and Sarnath. Early in their history, an important trade route was established between Sarnath and Ilarnek. Sarnath eventually conquered the neighboring cities and lands (including Ilarnek) and forged an empire. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

After the destruction of Sarnath, the green stone idol of Bokrug, the Great Water Lizard, was found on the marshy lakeshore where the city once stood. The idol, which had been taken by Sarnath from the conquered city of Ib, was enshrined in the high temple at Ilarnek and was subsequently worshipped throughout the land of Mnar. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

Ilarnek is a repository of lore pertaining to the beings of Ib written on papyrus, including their discovery of fire and their use of flame in rituals and ceremonies. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

The Illithids, also known as the Mind Flayers, are an aberrant race from the fictional universe of the Dungeons & Dragons pencil-and-paper roleplaying game.

They were created by Gary Gygax based on a cover of a Brian Lumley's story, claiming it was The Burrowers Beneath, although it more likely was The Caller of the Black instead as the former does not feature any humanoids.

### Background
The Illithids (AKA Mind Flayers) are cephalopod humanoids with two arms, two legs, and a bulbous head with a hideous mouth surrounded by fourth tentacles. Illithids are hermaphrodites whom two or three times in their lives spawn larvae. Said larvae resemble tiny illithid heads or tentacled tadpoles. If they survive to reach 10 years of age, they are inserted into a sapient creature's brain. The hosts are usually humanoids ranging in size from 5'4" to 6'2" in height. Once inside the host, it grows and consumes its, absorbs its body, and becomes sapient. There are some who end up taking on elements of their host's former mind. Illithids feed on brains, using the tentacles which rips out the victim's brain.

Their cities are ruled by creatures known as Elder Brains, which reside in the center of their cities, in a pool of cerebral fluid. Upon their death, an Illithid's brain is extracted and taken to the Elder Brain. Illithids believe they will live on in the Elder Brain, their personalities being incorporated. In reality, only it's thoughts, memories, and experiences are incorporated into the Elder Brain. The God-Brains are incredibly ancient Elder Brains, called such due to their nearly limitless psionic powers. Elder Brains serve as vast troves of knowledge which can be telepathically called upon by Illihids, who in turn receive orders from the Elder Brains. 

Illithids have formidable psionic powers, that ability being an important part of their identity. Powers include levitation, telekinesis, mind control, and even teleporting themselves to other dimensions via plane shifting. They usually communicate with each other telepathically. Illithids for the most part look upon magic with disapproval, though they do tolerate its study, but only to a limited degree and for the purpose of understanding their enemies. They see other races as being inferior and are forever plotting and scheming against them, seeking power and domination. Due to their psionic powers they are respected by the dominant races within the Underdark (e.g. Beholders and Drow) and are feared on numerous worlds across the multiverse.

They are an ancient race, one whose existence predates recorded history and which even the ancient Aboleths with their perfect racial memory, have no idea of their origins.

Illyana Rasputina (aka, Magik) is a superhero in the fictional Marvel universe, who was created in 1975, a B-list hero with a few comic book series.

### Background
Illyana Rasputina is a mutant who also possesses magical abilities. She is the younger sister of Colossus of the X-Men. In her pre-teen years she was kidnapped by the sorcerer Belasco and turned into a demonic sorceress, who overthrew him and took control of his demonic pocket dimension, Limbo.

Ever since she has been its on and off ruler, periodically losing control to Belasco or one of the stronger demons of Limbo, and regaining her throne afterwards. Within the dimension of Limbo she is the Sorceress Supreme. Magik is also a long standing member of the X-Men, having started out as a member of the teenage New Mutants during the 1980s.

"Imprisoned with the Pharaohs" (called "Under the Pyramids" in draft form, also published as "Entombed with the Pharaohs") is a short story written by American fantasy author H. P. Lovecraft in February 1924. Commissioned by Weird Tales founder and owner J. C. Henneberger, the narrative tells a fictionalized account in the first-person perspective of an allegedly true experience of escape artist Harry Houdini. Set in 1910, in Egypt, Houdini finds himself kidnapped by a tour guide, who resembles an ancient pharaoh, and thrown down a deep hole near the Great Sphinx of Giza. While attempting to find his way out, he stumbles upon a gigantic ceremonial cavern and encounters the real-life deity that inspired the building of the Sphinx.

Lovecraft accepted the job because of the money he was offered in advance by Henneberger. The result was published in the May–June–July 1924 edition of Weird Tales, although it was credited solely to Houdini until the 1939 reprint. Despite Lovecraft's use of artistic license, Houdini enjoyed the tale and the two men collaborated on several smaller projects prior to the latter's death in 1926. "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs" has been suggested as an early influence on author Robert Bloch and as anticipating the cosmic themes in Lovecraft's later work, including "The Shunned House".

### Synopsis
Told from the first-person perspective of escape artist Harry Houdini, "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs" is a fictionalized account of an encounter that he claims to have experienced while on vacation in Egypt in January 1910. Enlisting the services of a guide named Abdul Reis el Drogman, Houdini is taken on a tour of Cairo and eventually forced to break up a conflict between his guide and a Bedouin leader by the name of Ali Ziz. Drogman enlists Houdini to help him settle the fight by way of a "custom of great antiquity in Cairo": a boxing match atop the Great Pyramid of Giza. Houdini soon discovers, however, that the entire argument was merely a ruse designed to lure him into the desert at night and kidnap him. The escape artist is tied up, taken to an unknown location, and dropped down an extremely deep pit. at the time the largest sum he had ever been given as an advance. This was a major factor in motivating him to take the job as, after listening to Houdini's story and researching its background, Lovecraft concluded that the tale was completely fabricated and requested permission from Henneberger to take artistic license. After receiving clearance from the editor, he began his writing by spending considerable time researching the setting in books issued by the Metropolitan Museum of Art as well as by frequently visiting the museum's Egyptian exhibits. The work's original title, "Under the Pyramids", is known only from the lost and found advertisement that he placed in The Providence Journal. "In a Sequester'd Providence Churchyard Where Once Poe Walk'd" is a short poem by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. First published in Four Acrostic Sonnets on Edgar Allan Poe by Maurice W. Moe in 1936, it has since been reprinted many times, and has also been translated into French .

### Synopsis
The thirteen lines in two verses describe the graveyard of the Cathedral of St. John in Providence, Rhode Island, and the tragic spirit of Edgar Allan Poe which wanders the plots.

### Behind the Mythos
Written on 8 August 1936 in the graveyard of the Cathedral of St. John in Providence, Rhode Island, USA , "In a Sequester'd Providence Churchyard Where Once Poe Walk'd" was written as part of a contest held between Lovecraft, Robert H. Barlow, and Adolphe de Castro .
