"In Amundsen's Tent" is a short story by John Martin Leahy first published in the January 1928 edition of popular pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has been extensively reprinted in the years since

### Synopsis
The story details Antarctic explorers discovering a tent left by the polar and antarctic explorer Amundsen. An indescribable predatory alien being lurks within and this unimaginable creature is so horrifying that it drives men mad to look at it for any length of time. Leaving the tent and continuing in their explorations, they see that the tent has begun to move as the creature within uses it as camouflage. The creature stalks them and through a combination of causing madness and violence picks the explorers and their sled dogs off until only the narrator remains to write down a record of their experiences.

Whilst no description of the entity is given it is stated as being not native to the Earth.

shortDefinition: "In Art, Truth" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Fadeley which takes place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting. It was published in the anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022.  ### Synopsis In the n...
fullContent:
"In Art, Truth" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Fadeley which takes place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting. It was published in the anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022.

### Synopsis
In the nascent republic of Turkey during the 1920s, scholar of ancient art and history at the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts in Constantinople Ece Şahin begins to believe that her research into ancient Christian art - suspected to lie behind plaster Kariye Mosque - is being monitored by sinister forces.

She and her assistant Haluk quickly arrange to have the work uncovered, and discover an ancient mural depicting, amongst other things, an enormous, shadowy, winged entity, with three eyes. The two quickly document what they have found, but are shortly thereafter chased and run down by a group of cultists; Ece is allowed to live, while Haluk is not so fortunate. The leader of the group then leaves Ece with a terrible warning: "The Haunter watches you." 

### Behind the Mythos
The cultist's reference to a being known as "The Haunter," intended to be the entity depicted on the Mosque's mural, is most likely the Haunter of the Dark, an avatar of Nyarlathotep created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1936 short story "The Haunter of the Dark," as the two share near-identical descriptions: black entities with expansive wings and three eyes.

At one point, Ece consults a fellow scholar from Nairobi, Kenya, one Professor Tuwile Masai. During the course of their conversation, it is revealed that both are members of the secretive Red Coterie, a recurrent faction in the Arkham Horror iteration of the Cthulhu Mythos. Further, Ece is strongly hinted to possess one of the arcane artefacts coveted by the Coterie known as Keys (items invariably associated with the colour red in some variation of shade), as shown in the line "the Coterie let her imbue her hijab with the vermillion gift"; however, what mystical properties her garment may possess is not explored in the story.

* Another member of the Red Coterie, the Claret Knight (who previously appeared in "Brother Bound"), is mentioned to have at one point intervened on Ece's behalf, when a rival group of occultists attempted to recruit her into their own ranks, although he makes no direct appearance in this story.

### Trivia
* Ece's name is stated to be pronounced "Ed-jey," something those without knowledge of regional languages would be unlikely to be aware of. It is also the Turkish word for "queen."

### References

shortDefinition: In Defence of Dagon is actually a collective title. It refers to three essays by H.P. Lovecraft: “The Defence Reopens!” (3,820 words; January 1921); “The Defence Remains Open!” (5,980 words; April 1921); and “Final Words” (2,100 words; September 1921...
fullContent:
In Defence of Dagon is actually a collective title. It refers to three essays by H.P. Lovecraft: “The Defence Reopens!” (3,820 words; January 1921); “The Defence Remains Open!” (5,980 words; April 1921); and “Final Words” (2,100 words; September 1921). Together these were first published in 1938 in fragmentary form but only published in its entirety in In Defence of Dagon (Necronomicon Press, 1985). The complete original essays are available for viewing at Brown University Digital Repository.

The essays were written in response to comments on Lovecraft’s poems and stories submitted to the Transatlantic Circulator, an Anglo-American organization of amateur journalists who circulated their work in manuscript and commented on it. The essays present a strong defense of Lovecraft’s brand of weird fiction. Lovecraft's basic assertion is that the weird tales writer is “the poet of twilight visions and childhood memories, but sings only for the sensitive”, calling upon Oscar Wilde’s critical theories to combat the notion that weird art (or any art) can be “morbid” or “unhealthy.” 

Lovecraft also vigorously defends his atheistic materialism (first expressed in a letter or essay that does not now survive), maintaining that religion has been largely disproven by the sciences of physics and biology and that anthropology has accounted for the origin of religious belief. Thus these essays also explain the basis for Lovecraft's cosmicism and atheism.

fullContent:
In Lovecraft's Shadow was an abortive zine published by American author and editor Ron Shiflet through his Tenoka Press label. Despite containing stories by a number of popular contemporary Cthulhu Mythos authors, it ran for only a single issue which was released in paperback format in March 2007; in December 2017, a digital edition was issued through Amazon's Kindle platform. Artwork was provided by Philip Rogers and Steve Lines.

In the introduction to the first issue, Shiflet stated that the zine would "strive to bring the reader outstanding stories of Lovecraftian horror. It will feature both tales in the Cthulhu Mythos and other Horror tales that convey the mood that Lovecraft evoked in readers. We will also spotlight an outstanding genre artist in every issue."

shortDefinition: "In the Dark" is a story featured in issue #27 of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles Adventures by Archie Comics. It is one of two comics in the franchise to have Innsmouth as a setting, with the other one being Mirage Studios' "Men of Shadow".  ### Synops...
fullContent:
"In the Dark" is a story featured in issue #27 of Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles Adventures by Archie Comics. It is one of two comics in the franchise to have Innsmouth as a setting, with the other one being Mirage Studios' "Men of Shadow".

### Synopsis
While driving to Boston to cover a story about toxic waste, April O'Neil's rental car gets a flat tire, leaving her stranded in the middle of nowhere. After checking her map, April heads over to the town of Innsmouth, where she encounters a police officer who seemingly tries to help, and tells her to wait at the diner down the street while her car was allegedly brought in for repairs At the diner, April drinks a shake that makes her feel very sick. Shortly afterwards, she meets a girl named Beth Ann who tries to help her and warns her about the "Boogey-Men". April tries to escape on her own but is chased down by all the other residents, who appear to be in a zombie-like state and want her to stay in the town forever. Although April manages to successfully run away from them and finds a telephone booth to call the Ninja Turtles for help, Michelangelo dismisses it as a prank call. Fortunately, the other turtles point out that it couldn't be a prank call, as nobody else knows their number, leading to them arriving at Innsmouth after a four-hour drive. With the help of Beth Ann, they manage to find where the kidnappers took her. In the abandoned old house, the "Boogey-Men" (who are actually a group of three mutant animals: a cat, owl and crow) try to force April to drink more of the shake before they are defeated by the Ninja Turtles.

One week later, April explains to the police that the cat, owl and crow were mutated by illegally dumped toxic waste, and they seeked revenge by putting small amounts of waste in the food and water supply for Innsmouth, turning all of the residents into waste zombies. Subsequently, the factory that was responsible for all the trouble got shut down and everything went back to normal.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite taking place in Innsmouth and being thematically similar to The Shadow Over Innsmouth, the story does not have many other references to the Cthulhu Mythos.

fullContent:
"In the Depths of R'lyeh" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young. It constitutes the twentieth and final episode of his Nyarlathotep Cycle, a series begun in 2020 with "It Came from the Sea".

### Synopsis
The newly-awakened Adele Kramer briefs the other members of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena on the information she has gleaned from her time in the Outer Cosmos, revealing that Nyarlathotep intends for them to thwart a plan by Cthulhu to awaken Azathoth and end all of existence.

Developing a device which can mimic the melodies played by the flautists at the Court of Azathoth, Harjit Singh calls in some favours from his international contacts, and they begin to formulate a plan. Kramer and Singh, along with Malcolm Mayweather and Charlene Hines, travel to South America, narrowly avoiding an attack by cultists of Hastur along the way, where they rendezvous with a navy frigate which has been put at their disposal by the Chilean government.

Undertaking the voyage to the centre of the South Pacific, and barely escaping death at the blades of another group of cultists, the group finds that the sunken city of R'lyeh is already beginning to rise, and they hastily board their submersible. As they reach the city, Cthulhu finally awakens; the psychic backlash from this event results in the deaths of nearly all aboard, but the sole survivor, Adele Kramer, is able to activate the device and send Cthulhu back into torpor.

In the aftermath, Kramer is approached by Nyarlathotep who informs her that there was no need for her friends to have died: he only implemented that part of the plan to watch her suffer. However, Yog-Sothoth makes his appearance and rewards the agent for her acts by removing the cursed powers which resulted from her time at Azathoth's Court, simultaneously warning Nyarlathotep that she is now under his protection. When she is returned to the real world, her experience with the Other leads to an offer of the position as the next director of the DoEP, which she accepts.

### Characters
*Adele Kramer, field agent, Department of Extraordinary Phenomena
*Harjit Singh, director, Department of Extraordinary Phenomena

"In the Flesh" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Josh Vogt, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Synopsis
A small group of covert Allied operatives use their unique abilities to infiltrate a German concentration camp during the Second World War. Their goal: to rescue a kidnapped scientist and occultist whose research may prove vital to the ongoing war effort. However, when they locate the man - who is protected by a heavy Nachtwölfe presence - they find that he has fully embraced his position in the Nazi order, and is using his newfound influence to perform horrific experiments on both living and dead subjects.

Thanks to the sacrifice of one of the team, a man with the power to alter the minds of others, the scientist is killed, and the gem which he has been using to extend his life and enhance his experiments is recovered. Although two of the team manage to make their escape, the operative in possession of the gem decides to take his leave and disappear, not trusting himself with the power contained within the artefact and desperate to find a way to destroy it. 

### Mythos Connections
The gem utilised by the evil professor was an artefact of the Outer God Daoloth, an entity created by British author Ramsey Campbell for his 1964 short story "The Render of the Veils."

fullContent:
In the Haunted Darkness is a short story by Michael R. Collings set to the backdrop of H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos. It first appeared in the World Horror Convention 2012, Salt Lake City, Utah, Souvenir Book.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator, who is plagued by debilitating tinnitus, is attempting to catalogue the many noises he hears in and outside of his head while attempting to sleep. In doing so, he somehow manages to project his consciousness outside of his body, travelling through space to the outer fringes of the solar system. There, an unseen - and innately evil - presence tells him that he is not ready to travel so far, and flings him back to Earth to land deep beneath the sea (likely in R'lyeh) where he encounters an entity (intimated to be Cthulhu) which offers him a release from his condition, and learns a ritual which will "restore the Outer Ones to their ancient place within the universe...and condemn humanity to slavery, to torture, and to death."

The story concludes with the narrator awakening and debating with himself whether or not he should enact the ritual and be free of his torment.

### Behind the Mythos
In the Haunted Darkness was released as part of the eBook anthology The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack by Wildside Press in 2012.

shortDefinition: In the Mouth of Madness is a 1994 psychological/supernatural horror film written by acclaimed American director John Carpenter, written by Michael De Luca, and starring Sam Neill.   ### Synopsis The story follows John Trent, an insurance agent tasked...
fullContent:
In the Mouth of Madness is a 1994 psychological/supernatural horror film written by acclaimed American director John Carpenter, written by Michael De Luca, and starring Sam Neill. 

### Synopsis
The story follows John Trent, an insurance agent tasked with tracking down horror writer Sutter Cane, who has gone missing in the midst of a bizarre epidemic. As his investigations lead him to the area of New England in which much of Cane's fiction is set, Trent's sanity begins to fray. Arriving at the town of Hobb's End, a New Hampshire town created by Cane for his stories, revelations uncovered in Sutter's latest manuscript tear at Trent's sanity and destroy his companion Linda Styles' mind. 

Finally escaping the nightmare town of Hobb's end, Trent's experiences lead to a complete mental breakdown, and he is confined to an asylum. The radio announcement that the world has been conquered by ancient monsters frees him from his imprisonment, and the film ends with Trent realising that he is nothing more than a character in the stories of Sutter Cane. 

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing little to directly connect the film to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos, the exploration of the concept of insanity in In the Mouth of Madness is very Lovecraftian, as is the motif of Old Ones returning to reclaim the Earth from humankind.

Additionally, many of the names mentioned in the film are nods to various works of Lovecraft's, such as the titles of Sutter Cane's books-  Haunter out of Time ("The Haunter of the Dark" and The Shadow Out of Time), The Hobbs End Horror, The Thing in the Basement, and The Whisperer of the Dark. The setting of Hobb's End is a nod to a location from Quatermass and the Pit, another film with Lovecraftian influences. A character named Mrs. Pickman also makes an appearance, and the title of the film is a play on the novella At the Mountains of Madness.

Sections of dialog that are supposed to be quotes from Sutter Cane's books are actually direct quotes from the works of Lovecraft, notably "The Rats in the Walls" (when John Trent is reading aloud outside the church) and "The Haunter of the Dark" when Linda Styles reads from Cane's final manuscript as John Trent crosses a dimensional rift back to "reality."

"Do you read Sutter Cane?" is a phrase uttered by various people throughout the film in a way similar to how "Have you seen the Yellow Sign?" is used in the Cthulhu Mythos and the anthology The King in Yellow by Robert W. Chambers.

In September 2025, a novelisation of the film, also called In the Mouth of Madness, was released by Echo on Publications and credited to Sutter Cane- the author from the original film. The digital Kindle edition was purportedly issued by Arcane Publishing, the publishing house which featured in the film, and all editions boasted the cover of the fictional book from the film.

"In the Shadow of Swords" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Cody Goodfellow set in Saddam Hussein's Iraq. It was first published as a chapbook in 2002.

The story's Iraqi setting is shared by Goodfellow's novels Radiant Dawn and Ravenous Dusk, and forms something of a bridge between the two longer works. Written before the US invasion of Iraq in 2003, the story takes as a background assumption that Saddam was concealing an arsenal of weapons of  mass destruction that the invasion revealed to be nonexistent.

### Synopsis
A UN weapons inspection team in Iraq, about to end its mission without finding hard evidence of Saddam Hussein's hidden arsenal of chemical and biological weapons, gets one last chance to bring back proof: An intercepted message from a supposed archaeological dig called Tiamat suggests that secret research there is creating an imminent disaster, giving the UN an excuse to cut through the Iraqi smokescreen. When they arrive, however, they find that the site conceals something far more dangerous than mere weapons of mass destruction.

### Characters

### Inspectors
* Warren Revell, an American, the leader of a United Nations weapons inspection team in Iraq. He was "born and raised in Austin and spent most of his tour with the Army in Panama."
* Skelton, a "lanky British biologist" connected to the team who is "among the most respected savants in the Royal Society." He has a "default state of droll melancholy." He is described in appearance as "a bitter caricature of the stereotypical British phenotype—hooked nose, abominable teeth, watery gray eyes, and tangled eyebrows." His "long, bulging bald skull" is reminiscent of a marabou stork.
* Reinhard Greuel, a German biologist who is "ardently Green, and the most passionate disarmament advocate in the group." He is "short, stout, and alarmingly sunburned," and is said to subsist "on a diet of wheat grass juice, vitamins, and some sulfurous macrobiotic soup."
* Dr. Sofia Texeira, a Brazilian forensics specialist; she has a minor in archaeology. Texeira is described as short, slim and dark; the sun has turned her skin "a robust mahogany and burned an auburn tinge into her long black hair."
* Luscombe, the team's senior communications tech. His "impregnable Oxford-bred good humor" could give the misimpression that he is a "thick-skinned twit."
* Chris Healey, the assistant communications tech.

* Lupo Bertolucci, the medic.

fullContent:
"In the Shadows of the 603rd" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Richard Dansky, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Overview
The 603rd Camouflage Engineers under Captain Henry Rifkin, a highly specialised Allied unit during the Second World War, are seconded to enigmatic Swiss major Heinrich Schiller. The major has them build a replica of a bizarre henge complete with incomprehensible carvings, some of which drive the men to distraction, and a stone altar. Once complete, Schiller instructs the men to retire to their campsite and not to return, no matter what they may hear.  

As night draws in, the soldiers witness what appears to be a ritual being conducted on the far side of the river- one which is answered by a matching event at the site of their recent construction. When Rifkin and his second investigate, they find Schiller and a gaggle of cultists on the verge of sacrificing a terrified woman upon the stone altar. They attempt to intervene, but both men are knocked unconscious before they can make good their rescue.  

Upon awakening, Rifkin is confronted by Schiller who informs him that the woman was a Nazi collaborator whose death has saved the lives of uncounted millions; the ritual they conducted was done in tandem with one attempted by the Order of the Black Sun which was designed to allow a monstrous entity entry into our world. By enacting their own rite, the ritual was neutralised and the threat averted.  

### Behind the Mythos
The 603rd Camouflage Engineers were a real-life unit during the Second World War, part of a larger detachment, the 23rd Headquarters Special Troops, nicknamed the Ghost Army. Their remit was to deceive enemy reconnaissance and intelligence, and they achieved a remarkable amount of success using unconventional tactics such as deploying inflatable ordnance and constructing dummy supply depots.

shortDefinition: "In the Vale of Pnath" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, first published in the 1975 Arkham House anthology Nameless Places.  ### Synopsis In Hyperborea, the wizard Eibon tries to obtain the ingredients for the powerful Ygthar elixir tha...
fullContent:
"In the Vale of Pnath" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, first published in the 1975 Arkham House anthology Nameless Places.

### Synopsis
In Hyperborea, the wizard Eibon tries to obtain the ingredients for the powerful Ygthar elixir that he learned about from the scrolls of Zon Mezzamalech, but cannot complete the recipe without the enigmatic "Glund fluid", the nature of which is unknown to him. Using a crystal to contact the great sorcerer Maal Dweb, from the world of Xiccarph, Eibon learns of a mage named Shuggob who might be able to help him.

Eibon travels to the Dreamlands and reaches the shadowy Vale of Pnath, where he meets Shuggob, a scholarly ghoul who lives in a stone house and offers him a meal that might have been made from human flesh. When Eibon asks about Glund fluid, Shuggob tells him that he has a cauldron of it brewing at the moment, and offers some. Inside the cauldron there is a swollen, wrinkled grey mass with hooked knives buried into it, causing it to produce a slimy fluid. To Eibon's shock, he realises that the thing is the still-living brain of some undisclosed creature. The horrified wizard runs away, never to visit the Vale of Pnath again.

shortDefinition: "In the Vault" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written on September 18, 1925 and first published in the November 1925 issue of the amateur press journal The Tryout.  ### Inspiration "In the Vault" was based on a su...
fullContent:
"In the Vault" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written on September 18, 1925 and first published in the November 1925 issue of the amateur press journal The Tryout.

### Inspiration
"In the Vault" was based on a suggestion made in August 1925 by Charles W. Smith, editor of the amateur journal Tryout, which Lovecraft recorded in a letter: "an undertaker imprisoned in a village vault where he was removing winter coffins for spring burial, & his escape by enlarging a transom reached by the piling up of the coffins". (: Selected Letters 2.196) Lovecraft accordingly dedicated the story to Smith.

### Synopsis
George Birch, undertaker for the New England town of Peck Valley, finds himself trapped in the vault where coffins are stored during winter for burial in the spring. When Birch stacks the coffins to reach a transom window, his feet break through the lid of the top coffin, injuring his ankles and forcing him to crawl out of and away from the vault.

Later, Dr. Davis investigates the vault, and finds that the top coffin was one of inferior workmanship that Birch used as a repository for Asaph Sawyer, a vindictive townsperson whom Birch had disliked, even though the coffin had originally been built for the much shorter Matthew Fenner. Davis finds that Birch had cut off Sawyer's feet to fit the body in the coffin—and that the wounds in Birch's ankles are teeth marks.

### Reaction
The story was rejected by Weird Tales in November 1925; according to Lovecraft, editor Farnsworth Wright feared that "its extreme gruesomeness would not pass the Indiana censorship", (HPL, letter to Lillian D. Clark, December 2, 1925; : An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) a reference to the controversy of C. M. Eddy, Jr.'s "The Loved Dead".

After being published in Tryout, the story was submitted in August 1926 to Ghost Stories, a "very crude" pulp magazine that specialized in "true" tales of the supernatural, which also rejected it. August Derleth urged Lovecraft to resubmit the story to Weird Tales in 1931, which finally published it in its April 1932 edition. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia calls "In the Vault" "a commonplace tale of supernatural vengeance" in which "HPL attempts unsuccessfully to write in a more homespun, colloquial vein."

shortDefinition: "In the Vaults Beneath" is a Cthulhu Mythos story written by Brian Lumley that first appeared in his collection The Caller of The Black (Arkham House, 1971). Largely a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, it features the archaeolo...
fullContent:
"In the Vaults Beneath" is a Cthulhu Mythos story written by Brian Lumley that first appeared in his collection The Caller of The Black (Arkham House, 1971). Largely a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, it features the archaeologist Gordon Walmsley, who is mentioned repeatedly in Lumley's Mythos tales.

### Synopsis
Archaeologist Gordon Walmsley and two amateur colleagues decipher the G'harne Fragments and uncover an undercover complex, known only as The Outpost, built by the Elder Things somewhere in Britain. After nearly unleashing a shoggoth, the explorers withdraw from the site, taking with them a few artefacts, including samples of a mysterious metallic fabric that has the ability to stop clockwork in its vicinity. Before they have a chance to return to the complex, it suddenly disappears along with all the items taken from it--which spells a grisly end for Walmsley, as at the time he was wearing a suit of clothing made from the fabric.

### Characters
* Gordon Walmsley: An archaeologist, professor curator of the Wharby Museum, formerly at the Radcar Museum. He is described as a "stout, balding, bespectacled little professor."
* Simon Guest: The story's narrator, an amateur archaeologist enlisted in Walmsley's project to identify locations mentioned in the G'harne Fragments.
* Arthur Jeffries: Another amateur archaeologist who teams up with Guest on Walmsley's project. He is described as "tall and angular" and "ever the more intrepid member of our group."

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Caller of The Black, "In the Vaults Beneath" has not been released in another English-language collection, although The Caller of The Black was re-released by Crossroads Press in 2019. A French translation (as "L'avant-poste des Grands Anciens") was released in 1986 as the title story of a Lumley collection published by Néo.

shortDefinition: "In the Walls of Eryx" is a short story by the pulp fiction authors H. P. Lovecraft (1890-1937) and Kenneth J. Sterling (1920–1995), written in January 1936 and first published in Weird Tales magazine in October 1939. It is unusual among Lovecraft's ...
fullContent:
"In the Walls of Eryx" is a short story by the pulp fiction authors H. P. Lovecraft (1890-1937) and Kenneth J. Sterling (1920–1995), written in January 1936 and first published in Weird Tales magazine in October 1939. It is unusual among Lovecraft's work as a standard science fiction story involving space exploration in the near future.

### Inspiration
Sterling, a precocious Providence high school student who had befriended Lovecraft the previous year, gave Lovecraft a draft of the story in January 1936. This draft included the idea of an invisible maze—a concept Sterling recalled as being derived from the story "The Monster-God of Mamurth" by Edmond Hamilton, published in the August 1926 issue of Weird Tales, which featured an invisible building in the Sahara Desert. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

Lovecraft thoroughly rewrote Sterling's draft, lengthening the story to 12,000 words (from an original 6,000-8,000). Though the original draft does not survive, most of the prose in the published version is believed to be Lovecraft's. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

### Reaction
The story seems to have been rejected by Weird Tales, Astounding Stories, Blue Book, Argosy, Wonder Stories, and possibly Amazing Stories. After Lovecraft's death, it was resubmitted to Weird Tales and finally published in its October 1939 issue. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

### Synopsis
The story, written in first-person narrative, depicts the life and death of a prospector on the planet Venus who, while working for the Crystal Company, becomes trapped in an invisible maze.

The story takes place in the future, when humanity has developed space travel and begun to explore Venus. There, they discover valuable spheroid crystals that can be used as a source of electrical power, as well as a race of primitive lizardmen who guard the crystals fervently and who attack any humans who try to take them.

The narrator, Kenton J. Stanfield, is one of many explorers employed to collect the crystals. He is equipped with a breathing apparatus fueled by oxygen cubes (as Venus' atmosphere cannot sustain human life) and clad in a leather protective suit, as well as a "flame pistol" to use against lizardmen.

While on a routine mission, the narrator encounters a bizarre structure: a maze whose walls are completely invisible, at the entrance of which is a crystal of unusually large size. The prize is held by a dead prospector. The protagonist, feeling confident he can map out the maze, makes his way to the center after collecting the crystal in order to explore the structure. However, he soon discovers that he has misjudged the maze, and is unable to relocate the entrance point.

Trapped in the maze, the narrator's oxygen and water supply steadily begins to run out, and lizardmen soon begin to gather at the outside of the maze to observe and mock him. Realizing the futility of his situation, the narrator begins to grasp the religious significance of the crystals to the liz

fullContent:
"In Which We Discover the 101st Acre" is a short story by author Robert P. Ottone which blends the world of Winnie-the-Pooh with Lovecraftian horror. It was published in the April Moon Books anthology The Call of Poohthulhu in May 2022.

### Synopsis
In Hundred Acre Woods, long after young Christopher Robin has stopped visiting, Owl begins to notice that their small corner of the world is being encroached upon by a mysterious mist. Investigating, he hears strange noises in the fog, and notices titanic shapes moving around inside its borders.

Alerting the other animals, they try to discern the nature of the miasma, but their attentions seem to increase the rate at which its incursion progresses. Attempting to flee, first Kanga, then Rabbit are swallowed up, and it is not long before Pooh, Piglet and Eeyore are too. Finally only Owl and Roo remain, fearfully waiting for the mist to wash across them too.

The story concludes with Christopher Robin, now a soldier in the British Army, digging through the ruins of his family home, unearthing the remains of his burnt children's toys, and going on with the search for survivors in Blitz-era London.

fullContent:
"Inception" is a short story by British author Brian Lumley. It is the first story in his Titus Crow series, although it was not the first to be written.

### Synopsis
An international thief who specialises in cultural treasures steals an elixir, which is said to be capable of expanding the mind of the pure, from an African cult. In the process he awakens the sect's undead guardian which pursues him across the world on an unstoppable quest to retrieve the liquid.

Upon reaching London, the thief seeks refuge in one of his childhood sanctuaries: an ancient church. Attempting to divert his pursuer, he disposes of the elixir in an unattended bowl of water, but the creature catches and kills him, although it is itself caught in the early morning rays of the sun and destroyed.

The following morning, a baptism takes place in the church, and a child is granted very special powers.

### Characters

*The Fugitive, a daring and accomplished thief.
*The Priest of the Undying Dead, a former Sanusi tribal wizard and the undead guardian of the temple for the past 270 years.
*Titus Crow, a baby who has a long association with the occult ahead of him.

### Publication History

"Incident at Dagon Wells" is a short Cthulhu Mythos/western story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
In America’s old west, a trio of outlaws on the run from hostile natives take refuge in the abandoned outpost of Dagon Wells. What they do not realise is that the waystation lies on the site of a breach between worlds, and as night falls and creatures begin to emerge from beneath the earth, the three become part of a repeating cycle of events.

### Characters
*Lonnie Otwell, outlaw.
*Tom Hawkins, outlaw.
*Jamie "Frog" Jenkins, outlaw.

### Publication History
"Incident at Dagon Wells" was first published in the anthology Frontier Cthulhu: Ancient Horrors in the New World by Chaosium in November 2007. It was later included in the Ron Shiflet collection They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in June 2018.

### Trivia
*Although not explicitly stated, the enormous creature which rises from one of the outpost's wells is implied to be Dagon himself, although why Dagon, a being most often associated with the ocean, would choose to manifest in the middle of the desert is not explained.

"Incident at the Hanford Inn" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Frank Forte, first published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
A journalist in post-civil war America investigates the reports of a missing child at the supposedly-abandoned Hanford Inn. What he finds there is a ghostly innkeeper and a demonic minion who use their dark magic to cloud his mind and cause him to shoot several innocent people who he mistakes for enemies.

The man is soon captured by the vengeful authorities and hung, nobody ever believing his stories about magic and monsters.

Indrid Cold, also known as The Smiling Man or The Grinning Man, is a pop culture figure who has been incorporated into the expanded Cthulhu Mythos by American author Josh Reynolds.

### Description
A tall, thin man with abnormally long limbs and an over-wide smile which never leaves his face, Indrid Cold has pale skin through which can occasionally be seen a wriggling movement or an unnatural twitch. He is also a telepath who appears to be immune to conventional weapons. Indrid Cold's real nature has not been confirmed, but it is heavily implied that he is an extraterrestrial creature from the Cthulhu Mythos in the disguise of a human.

### Behind the Mythos
Indrid Cold is infamous in conspiracy theory circles for being connected to sightings of unidentified flying objects and the Mothman of Point Pleasant, with his appearance being reported since as early as 1966. He is also commonly associated with the so-called Men in Black, a government agency purported to be heavily involved with covering up UFO phenomena. It is in this last guise that Reynolds most closely portrays the Cthulhu Mythos iteration of Cold: an alien entity working with the United States government.

### Appearances

*"The Yoth Protocols" (2014)
*"Those Folk Below" (2017)

The inhabitants of the Nameless City are a fictional species created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Nameless City". In The Keeper's Companion, they are referred to as the Reptile People, a race of quadrupedal reptiles with scaly skin and horns.

In the story, a man finds and ventures into the titular Nameless City, which he believes he is the only human to ever enter. He enters several deteriorated temples before discovering that the largest temple, located far to the south from all the others, has a large corridor that leads extremely far underground. after climbing down for a length of time that he describes as nearly eternal, he encounters a tomb full of caskets containing reptilian creatures. These creatures documented their existence in murals which are shown on the wall of the tomb where the bodies are preserved underground. (: "The Nameless City")

### Depiction
The only available information about the Inhabitants of the Nameless City is taken from images in vast murals found throughout the immeasurably deep cavern beneath the temple where "The Nameless City" takes place in the Nameless City. These murals are displayed above the preserved bodies of the Inhabitants which are kept in casket-like structures lining the narrow passage underground. The paintings can be found through the entire length of an incredibly long hall where the bodies of the creatures are stored. The paintings show the Nameless City when it was prosperous and when it was beginning to decline.

Physically, the inhabitants of the Nameless City are crawling creatures which resemble reptilian seals or crocodiles, albeit with horns on their heads and dexterous digits. They evolved before mankind and built their city over 10 million years ago. The fact that natural deaths are never recorded in their great mural -- which otherwise depicts every aspect of their lives, including death caused by disease or violence -- suggests that these creatures might be biologically immortal and thus never die of old age. (: "The Nameless City")

Early in their history, these creatures were originally aquatic and followers of Cthulhu. (: "The Keeper of the Key")

### Culture
The Inhabitants of the Nameless City are shown to be very cultured beings capable of forming a civilization with distinct societal ranks, the result of which was the prevalence of a city with wealth comparable to Egypt and Chaldaea. The preservation of dead society members shows a sophistication of intelligence and the ability to uphold a race of emotionally perceptive beings with ideals and morals.

Innsmouth is a fictional location introduced in the H. P. Lovecraft story The Shadow Over Innsmouth. It is a seaside town in Essex County, Massachusetts, run by the Esoteric Order of Dagon and their Deep One allies until their destruction in 1928. Since its first appearance, it has appeared in numerous Cthulhu Mythos stories written by various authors.

Another town named Innsmouth (also fictional) is located in England (: "Celephaïs", : "Shoggoth's Old Peculiar"), but this one is mentioned far less frequently.

### Geography & Known Locations
The Manuxet River runs through the centre of town, before turning southward to join the ocean at the end of the harbour's breakwater; Newburyport is an hour's bus ride down the coast.

As it fell into disrepair under the control of the Deep Ones, by 1927, the town lacked a public library or a chamber of commerce. Many of the street signs had also been removed, making navigation difficult for outsiders. In general, the South is less populous, but the north is more dangerous.

### Streets
*Broad, Washington, Lafayette, and Adams: The western streets of grand houses belonging to the town's elite.
*Federal Street: The central thoroughfare of the town. Home to New Church Green and the Hall of the Esoteric Order of Dagon, a former Masonic hall sold to the Order by the Cavalry Commandery.
*Main Street: One of the roads that bridges the dangerous seaward slums and home to the three abandoned Georgian churches. Though some people still lived here in 1927, most houses had been boarded up.
*Fish Street: Another deserted street with well maintained brick and stone warehouses, cut in half by its ruined bridge over the Manuxet.
*Water Street: Similar to Fish Street but broken up by the remains of wharves, its bridge though tottering is still usable.

### Town Square
Home to the Gilman House, a 4+ story hotel, topped with cupolas and covered in peeling yellow paint; a First National chain grocery store and a dozen other shops including a "dismal" restaurant, a drug store, and wholesale fish-dealer’s office; and an office of the Marsh Refining Company.

### The Marsh Refinery
A large building with a white belfry on the northern bank of the river across from the town square.
### The Harbour
A sand-clogged dock behind an ancient stone breakwater once covered by a lighthouse.

### History
Founded in 1643, Innsmouth was noted for ship-building before the American Revolution, after which the civic centre shifted to the present Town Square. It reached its peak as a naval hub after the War of 1812, when many of its privateering sailors were killed. As a result, there was a dip in trade for both the shipping families and local mills.

shortDefinition: "Innsmouth Bane" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late British author John S. Glasby, first published in the Spring 2005 edition of H. P. Lovecraft's Magazine of Horror by Wildside Press. It tells of how the town of Innsmouth came to be as it i...
fullContent:
"Innsmouth Bane" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late British author John S. Glasby, first published in the Spring 2005 edition of H. P. Lovecraft's Magazine of Horror by Wildside Press. It tells of how the town of Innsmouth came to be as it is during the events depicted in Lovecraft's 1931 novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Synopsis
In a document which he hides for his young son to find in hopefully-better times, Jedediah Allen tells the story of how, as a rival trader to the ruthless Obed Marsh during the 1800s, he witnessed the decades-long corruption of Innsmouth and its people at the hands of Marsh and the inhuman Deep Ones.

At first believing that Marsh was, amongst other things, people-smuggling Allen attempted to gather evidence which he and the other town elders could use to bring Marsh down; indeed, he managed to gather sufficient proof which prompted two visiting federal agents aided by a group of citizens to raid the Marsh estate and arrest all of those suspected to have been involved. At the time, all looked well for the town.

However, by that point Marsh had spread both his influence and corruption throughout much of Innsmouth, and those in his sway broke the men loose and proceeded to capture or kill most of the uncorrupted citizens, as well as the two agents. Those who survived were given the chance to join Obed - by taking his five oaths - and live forever, with very few choosing to remain apart, Allen being one of the latter.

Over the next twenty years, Allen watched as the physical condition of the townsfolk degenerated and their devotion to the Esoteric Order of Dagon became more fanatical. While on one of his trips to observe the activities of the monsters, he accidentally witnessed the mighty Dagon swimming in the deep ocean beyond Devil Reef and knew that the cultists would now have no choice but to eliminate him. It was this knowledge which made him resolve to commit his account to paper before taking his own life.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly stated, Jedediah Allen is heavily implied to be the father of Zadok Allen, the main source of exposition in The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Publication History
* H. P. Lovecraft's Magazine of Horror (2005)
* To the Stars and Beyond (2011)
* The Lonely Shadows (2012)
* Weirder Shadows Over Innsmouth (2013, 2015)

### Trivia
* At one point during the story, Allen mentions that he finds it odd that Ephraim Waite, the primary antagonist in the short story "The Thing on the Doorstep," remained uncorrupted during his lengthy time in Innsmouth, despite being one of Obed Marsh's closest allies.

### References

"Innsmouth Clay" is a 1971 short story by August Derleth, one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. It first appeared in the Arkham House anthology Dark Things in 1971.

### Synopsis
The story involves a sculptor named Jeffrey Corey who, upon returning from Paris in the fall of 1927, rents a cottage on the Massachusetts coast south of Innsmouth, a town where his distant relatives live. (The story mentions a great-grandfather named Jethro Marsh.) Corey, in his late 30s, is described by his old friend Ken, this story's narrator, as "not ill-favored in looks": six feet tall with "fine, fresh skin", and "very strong blue eyes" with a "piercing quality". He is clean-shaven with long hair and has a lantern jaw. Overall, there was "a queer quality, almost hypnotic, that informed his fine-featured face". Readers familiar with Lovecraft's "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" will not be puzzled by the one discordant feature in his appearance: "There is a strange, wattled appearance of the skin back from his jaws, under his ears and down his neck a little way below his ears."

The artist spends only a few days in Innsmouth, where he finds "a considerable amount of talk, however guarded", about his Marsh relatives that "suggested all manner of arcane horror" before the events related in the Lovecraft story, which Corey sums up by writing that "a large band of federal officers of some kind descended upon the town and spirited away some of the citizens". He notes that the Navy dropped depth charges off the coast "in the vicinity of what is known as Devil's Reef [sic]" and how "a subsequent storm washed ashore all manner of debris", including "a peculiar blue clay [that] came in along the water’s edge". Seeing this as a potential medium for sculpting, Corey gathers up as much of the Innsmouth Clay as he can and brings it back to his cottage. 

He uses this clay to create a sculpture he calls the "Sea Goddess", which our narrator declares himself as "oddly repelled" by when he first sees it. He describes it as a "lissome" figure with "rather heavier pelvic structure than I thought fitting", and "webbing between the toes". Corey confesses to working on the sculpture in his sleep, ultimately adding gill-like slits onto the statue's neck during one such session. 

In his journal, Corey describes several dreams involving "swimming accompanied by shadowy men and women", which he attributes to from hearing a story at Hammond's Drug Store "of Great-grandfather Jethro living in the sea. Gilled!" Later, he dreams of swimming in the ocean depths and seeing a "sort of city far below. Ryeh or R’lyeh? Something named ‘Great Thooloo’?”

He also dreams that "a woman, naked, slipped into my bed after I had gone to sleep, and remained there all night." "Nothing like it since Paris!" remarks Corey.

Innsmouth Escape is a hidden-movement Cthulhu Mythos board game based on H. P. Lovecraft's classic novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth. Designed by Darrell Hardy, it was published by Twilight Creations, Inc in 2008.

### Overview


### Gameplay
The game is designed for between two and five players ages 12 and over, one of whom takes on the role of the Survivor. This player must sneak around the map - which depicts the town of Innsmouth - collecting items to assist them in their escape. The other players portray Deep Ones, whose goal it is to catch the Survivor and prevent their escape; certain game mechanics may allow them to call on additional villains, such as more Deep Ones, or even a dread Shoggoth, to aid them in their task.

"Innsmouth Harvest" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ran Cartwright writing as R. S. Cartwright.

### Synopsis
Jerry Daniels, who has recently moved to the small coastal town of Innsmouth with his pregnant wife begins to have doubts about his new home. While looking for answers about what his wife really does at the Women's Club, and why his friend has started raving about "fish people", Brian uncovers the dark truth lurking in Innsmouth, and that an ancient god needs not only children, but sacrifice . . . 

### Characters

*Jerry Daniels, an author recently moved to Innsmouth in search of inspiration.
*Carolyn Daniels, Jerry's pregnant wife.
*Brian Abrams, an artist and Jerry's best friend.
*Vicki Abrams, Brian's wife.
*Dagon, Lord of the Deep Ones.

### Publication History
"Innsmouth Harvest" was first published in the October 1997 edition of the Nightscapes zine, then again in Cthulhu Cultus #9 in January 1998. It has since been reprinted in the collections Innsmouth Tales - 2000 (2000), Y'ha-nthlei Rising and Other Tales of the Deep Ones (2006), Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos: Cthulhu's Creatures (2007), and Of Gods & Aliens (2011).

The Innsmouth Horror Deluxe Expansion was a big-box expansion set for Fantasy Flight Games' board game of Lovecraftian adventure, Arkham Horror. It was chronologically the sixth to be released.

### Overview
Included with the Innsmouth Horror set are a host of new Item, Spell and Ally cards for Investigators to choose from, Ancient One cards designed to reflect the realities of an incursion into Innsmouth, 32 Spawn Monsters showcasing the horrors found in that blighted town, 2 new Heralds, 8 new Ancient Ones, 16 new Investigators, and an additional board which enabled the players to access the streets of Innsmouth via Arkham's train station.

This expansion was notable for introducing the Personal Stories concept, and optional set of rules which gave the game more of a role-play feel than was offered under previous versions.

Another new mechanic seen here was the Innsmouth Look, another optional ruleset which represented the players' slow degeneration into becoming a full-blown Deep One.

fullContent:
The Innsmouth Legacy is a Cthulhu Mythos fiction series by Ruthanna Emrys, focusing on the survivors of the government raids on Innsmouth depicted in H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth. Emrys, expanding on Lovecraft's twist ending, presents the deep ones not as inhuman monsters but as sympathetic members of the human family, co-equal with what she refers to as the "people of the air."

In Emrys' series, worship of the Mythos entities is a religion known as Aeonism, one that can be followed by genuine spiritual seekers as well as apocalyptic nihilists.

The books follow Aphra Marsh, a daughter of the Marsh family, who is one of the two survivors of the internment camps that the Innsmouth population was sent to. In this setting, they were released in 1946 alongside the victims of the real-life Japanese internment. Aphra is then recruited by Jewish FBI agent (and closeted gay man) Ron Spector to investigate Aeonist activity across the country. He believes that it is possible to separate the good from the bad among the cults and ritualists while Aphra simply wishes to make contact with those who share her religion. Events will bring them into contact and conflict with multiple Lovecraftian cults and entities with a twist.

Other recurring characters include her brother Caleb Marsh, her friend and employer Charlie Day, a possession victim of the Yith named Trumbull, her adopted sister Neko, and a Miskatonic student named Audrey Winslow.

### Works
*The Litany of Earth (Tor, 2014)
*Winter Tide (Tor, 2017)
*Deep Roots (Tor, 2018)

Innsmouth Magazine, which began its life as Innsmouth Free Press, was a digital horror magazine specialising in Lovecraftian fiction which ran between May 2009 and June 2014. It was published by Innsmouth Free Press, a company which was created for this express purpose, and which later branched out into a small number of other publications.

### Overview
Launched under the title Innsmouth Free Press under the editorship of Paula R. Stiles, the name was changed to Innsmouth Magazine in October 2011. In January 2013, Silvia Moreno-Garcia assumed co-editor duties for the remainder of the magazine's run. In 2012, two collected editions were released.

The publication ended with issue #15 in June 2014 with the statement "[w]ell, it had to happen sometime … [w]e’ve had fun putting together this little zine, but don’t make enough sales to keep it afloat. So, it must go."

### Synopsis
In a future where humankind has been devastated by the rising of the Deep Ones and their command of the oceans, a small group of survivors mount a last-ditch effort to salvage what they can of the species. The operatives, members of an ancient order once dedicated to protecting humanity from supernatural threats, embark on a covert operation to Innsmouth in order to bring back a member of the Deep One royal family who is sympathetic to their cause.

The prince is taken back to the order's secret underground facility, where a team of scientists believe they can reverse the horrors of the hybrid transformation process and, just maybe, use what they learn as a weapon in the war against the Deep Ones.

Innsport is a fictional city created by American author Brandon Berntson for his Lovecraft Mysteries trilogy of Cthulhu Mythos novels. It made its first appearance in the first book in the series, The Night of Dagon.

Innsport was devastated by the manifestation of Cthulhu, Yog-Sothoth, Azathoth, and their legions of monstrous creatures to the extent that it required federal aid in the aftermath in order to recover (: The Lurker at the Threshold).

### Description
Located somewhere on the east coast of the United States, Innsport had a population of 437,962; after an attack by the monstrous creature Dagon, this number is likely to be inaccurate. Described as being home to "[the] regular dregs and seedy nightcrawlers and criminals" found in most major urban areas, "[it is not] much different than any other city in the known universe". Innsport boasts numerous towering buildings, its own police department, and even a Natural History Museum (: The Night of Dagon).

### The Shady District
Located across the bay and accessed via the Buryport Bridge lay the slums of the Shady District. A run-down shambles of an urban sprawl, the shady district occupied an area at least ten city blocks in radius. Home to not only the dregs of Innsport society, but also a large number of fish-like humanoids, the Shady District was largely destroyed by pyromaniac Bradley "Boom-boom" Denton when he activated tons of explosives concealed beneath the streets in his battle against the rampaging Dagon (: The Night of Dagon).

### Castle Hills
Located around thirty miles out of town, Castle Hills is a mostly-wooded rural area bordering on the ocean. It boasted an expansive estate owned by the cultist Mordred Haddonfield before his death at the hands of Devlin Macky (: The Night of Dagon).

### Inhabitants 
*Devlin Macky, a private investigator and the protagonist of The Lovecraft Mysteries.
* Millie Von Clydesburgh, Macky's secretary.
*Inspector Duke Givens, a senior police officer.
*Lieutenant Newt Bardhoff, Givens' partner.
*Creighton Capshaw, curator of the Natural History Museum.
*Bradley "Boom-boom" Denton, a former criminal and pyromaniac.
*Amelia Bardhoff, Newt's wife.
*Gloria Trelane, a poor Spanish widow.
*Lamont Freestone, a friendly car mechanic.
*Carmine Versucci, a miserly Italian restaurateur.
*Mr. Kalabraise, Millie's (female) dog.

### Appearances 
*The Night of Dagon (2018)
*The Lurker at the Threshold (2021)

### Trivia
*The name Innsport is likely a portmanteau of Innsmouth and Kingsport, both prominent locations in the Cthulhu Mythos.
*Although the exact site of Innsport is never given, the fact that Macky and Millie can easily reach Arkham on a Sunday drive would suggest that it is located somewhere in New England (: Arkham: Reanimated).

"Inquisitor" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
Told through the journal of two Spaniards, a ship's captain and an Inquisitorial priest, "Inquisitor" tells the story of how a Shoggoth, revered by the natives as a god, is taken from its temple in South America and transported across the Atlantic, spreading its madness to the crew throughout the voyage. In Spain, the inquisitor assigned to its interrogation believes himself to be breaking through its mental defences, but he is equally as tainted as the unfortunate crew were before him.

### Characters
*Father Fernando, a 16th century Spanish inquisitor.
*Juan Santoro, captain of the treasure-ship Santa Angelo.

### Publication History
"Inquisitor" was first published in the anthology Historical Lovecraft: Tales of Horror Through Time in April 2011. It was later included in the collections of Meikle's own works Samurai and Other Stories (2014) and Home From The Sea: Tales Of Lovecraftian Terror (2017).

### Trivia

* A section of the story was reused in the non-Mythos Thomas Carnacki story "Carnacki: Captain Gault's Nemesis" in 2013.

fullContent:
"Inscrutable" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author and games designer Robin D. Laws. It was published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.

### Synopsis
Phut, an enigmatic bodyguard in the service of British foreign agent Sir Russell, must take violent action to protect his charge from meeting his end under the bullets and fanged jaws of a pair of bestial assassins. His unique talents ensure that he is successful in this task, and the story concludes with him mulling over Sir Russell's imminent fate: a gruesome, painful, and drawn-out death at Phut's own hands in a ritual necessary to save the human species from an unidentified threat.

### Mythos Connections
During Phut's musings on the nature of the assassins, his analysis concludes that they are not "sea-people … features neither fishy nor frog-like," a likely reference to the aquatic Deep Ones. He later concludes that they are semi-human creatures descended from a species of white ape from the depths of the African continent, a clear nod to H. P. Lovecraft’s 1920 short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family."

Phut's own appearance would appear to match that ascribed to the Tcho-Tcho people who first appeared in August Derleth and Mark Schorer's 1932 Cthulhu Mythos story "The Lair of the Star-Spawn"; further reinforcing this is his use of an alchemical compound using ingredients from Leng, a location commonly associated with the Tcho-Tcho.

### References

"Inside Uncle Sid" is a short story by Cody Goodfellow that originally appeared in Dead but Dreaming 2 (Miskatonic River Press, 2011) under the title "Uncle Sid's Collection".

The story is told from the point of view of a young woman who lives with her Uncle Sid, a compulsive hoarder who attracts a group of misfits who "came in hopes of being changed, or just helping Uncle Sid to become something to punish the world."

### Characters

* Sidney Swenson: Known as Uncle Sid, he's "a big, shy loner who drives an ancient primer-gray Ford Econoline van, never been on a date, but a wizard with anything mechanical." He lives near near San Diego State University in California in "a four-bedroom ranch house in the middle of a nice quiet neighborhood" filled with "mounds of exotic forgotten jetsam."
* Dana: Sid's niece, she's been living with him "for three months, since she split up with Tony."
* Ricardo: "Sid’s new friend," he's a "Chilean Allende socialist" who "emigrated to America and became the laziest communist handyman in the free world." He "looks like a bandito gone to seed, with his graying Che mustache and blue bulldog jowls, and his scars."
* The White Man: A character "living in the backyard" who "cooks all their meals." He "looks like a castaway: emaciated, with wild white hair and a Karl Marx beard." He has "the hollow thousand-yard stare and leathery, freckled skin of the terminal homeless, but his white shirt and painter’s pants are always spotless."
* Rhoda: Apparently Sid's girlfriend, a former "mud wrestler and an actress."  She is "emaciated, wiry yellow limbs carelessly swathed in flaking crepe-paper skin, concave except for her absurd artificial breasts and collagen-injected lips," with "bleach-blond fiberglass hair and eyes like runny, infected blue sores."
* Dr. Blythe: He is a "once-respected psychiatrist" who "used to treat all the socialite wives in La Jolla" until "a motorcycle accident left him in a coma for a year." He "looks uncannily like Richard Widmark, if he had a coke problem and a stroke."
* Dolores Zuburan: The former tenant of Sid's house, who Sid insists was a witch. She also rented the storage unit whose contents Sid bought, including a weirdly modified bicycle that seems to bring him into contact with eldritch powers.

### Mythos Connection
The story is more Lovecraftian horror than Cthulhu Mythos, with its theme of an outsider obsessed with secret knowledge (in the form of such books as The Hollow Earth Codex, The Secret Teachings of All Ages, and Phyllis Diller’s Guide to Marriage) undergoing a physical degeneration as the harbinger of apocalyptic destruction. A connection to Lovecraft's shared universe is made when Dana sees Ricardo's message "LAS CANTATAS DEL DHOLEZ" (which she misinterprets as "the songs of sadness") on a notepad. Later Ricardo compares Sid to "the Dholes that eateth the Earth like the worm gnaws the tooth."

fullContent:
Intersect is a science fiction-thriller film featuring time travel, parallel dimensions, and the manipulation of humans by creatures from outside normal time and space. It was released in 2020, written and directed by Gus Holwerda.

### Synopsis
A group of young Miskatonic University scientists invent a time machine, only to learn that they are being manipulated by mysterious, unseen forces from another dimension.

Ryan Winrich (Jason Spisak) is part of a team of young physicists at the Miskatonic University. The group conducts advanced research into creating the ability for humans to send physical objects through time. The advances allowing this are inexplicable, and it emerges that their origin lies outside human consciousness.

After initial success, their teammate Nate decides in a drunken stupor to test the system on himself. Transporting himself through the time portal, killing himself in the process. Gradually, Ryan starts realizing that the current events may somehow be related to the mysterious happenings in his childhood when he saw strange creatures whom nobody else could.

Told in a series of moments that apparently occupy a time loop crossing different parallel worlds, Ryan searches for a missing girlfriend Emma. In some worlds she never existed, in others they were never in a relationship. Trying to find her and also rescue Ryan from another reality is the driver of the plot, although the glacially slow pace of the film and the digressions make this a borderline non-linear story.

Their relationship is explored as Ryan travels between dimensions and encounters other versions of himself, Ryan's close friend Nick is also searching for Emma / Emilia, and their search is interrupted by the repeated appearance of alien entities and cryptic occurrences.

Ultimately, Ryan and Emma / Emilia's relationship and their fate is left open, although it is implied that the shattering of the single universe into parallels was all the plot of the creatures from outside time and space who had planted the seeds of the experiment in the minds of the researchers.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite both the research team and their experiment being based in Miskatonic University, as well as the plot arguably being Lovecraftian in theme, the film does not feature many other references to Cthulhu Mythos.

fullContent:
"Into the Black" is a short story by Scottish author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
When a drilling expedition to the Antarctic breaks through the ice into a millennia-isolated chamber, they accidentally release a viscous and highly aggressive predator. After consuming one of the group and inhabiting the body of another, it takes off into the nearby mountains. Two of the survivors pursue it in the hope of saving their colleague, entering a series of manufactured caverns and passageways culminating in a vast pool filled with the same black, tarry substance which composes the predator, and they flee.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, the expedition's biologist.
*Carruthers, team leader.
*Greer, another member.

### Publication History
"Into the Black" was published in the collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in May 2019.

### Behind the Mythos
"Into the Black" was given a rewrite and published as "Starry Wisdom" in March 2021. This version contains complete passages which are entirely unchanged, but lacks any direct reference to the Cthulhu Mythos and features William Hope Hodgson's occult investigator Thomas Carnacki as it’s protagonist.

### Trivia
*Despite lacking any direct reference to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the entities featured in "Into the Black" bear more than a passing resemblance to Shoggoths, and the bas reliefs encountered by the team in the underground complex are reminiscent of the ones described in At the Mountains of Madness. 
*The story may have also taken its cue from the 1982 sci-fi/horror film The Thing, which features a similar setting and premise.

The Inutos are a fictional race created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Polaris".

### Overview
The Inutos are an Arctic race of humans native to the Dreamlands. They appeared out of the "unknown west" to ravage the far northern kingdom of Lomar as ruthless conquerors. When they sacked the city of Daikos, the way was made clear for them to assault the city of Olathoë. The Inutos are presented as Dreamland ancestors of the real world Inuit. (: "Polaris")

"Invaders of Gla'aki" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Orrin Grey.

### Synopsis
Two boys discover a new arcade game, the titular Invaders of Gla'aki, at their local gas station. Although one of them is disturbed by it, the other develops an obsession. When the latter sneaks out of the house in the middle of the night to play the game he completes the final level, only to be infected by a device concealed within the machine's cabinet.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, an average boy in the early 1990s.
*The Narrator's Friend, another young boy.

### Publication History
"Invaders of Gla'aki" was first published in the thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki by Dark Regions Press in 2017. It was also included in the collection of Grey's own work Guignol & Other Sardonic Tales in October 2018.

### Trivia
*The titles of the individual levels in Invaders of Gla'aki are related to elements of the Cthulhu Mythos.

Iod is a Great Old One in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by the late American author Henry Kuttner for his short story "The Secret of Kralitz", and was later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### In Kuttner's Fiction
The first mention of Iod appears in Kuttner's "The Secret of Kralitz," when Franz Kralitz is learning eldritch lore from his ancestors: "I learned, too, of the unbelievable manner in which Iod, the Source, is worshiped beyond the outer galaxies."

In "The Invaders" (1939), Hayward's experiment teach him that "the first human race dwelt in primal Mu, worshiping strange, forgotten gods"—including "Iod the Shining Hunter."

The most extensive discussion of Iod comes in Kuttner's "The Hunt" (1939), in which the wizard Will Benson "call[s] up an entity which mankind worshiped eons ago as—Iod.  Iod, the Hunter":Man had worshiped Iod in older days, under  other names. He was one of the oldest gods, and he had come to Earth, the tale  went, in pre-human eons when the old gods soared between the stars, and earth  was a stopping place for incredible voyagers. The Greeks knew him as  Torphonios; the Etruscans made nameless sacrifices diurnally to Vediovis, the  Dweller beyond Phlegethon, the River of Flame.

This ancient god did not dwell on Earth,  and a certain apt phrase the Egyptians had coined for him meant, rendered into English, the Dimension Prowler. The evilly famous De Vermis Mysteriis spoke of Iod as the Shining Pursuer, who hunted souls through the Secret Worlds—which, Prinn hinted, meant other dimensions of space.

...It was the human soul, the Flemish magician wrote, which the ancient god  hunted. It was his monstrous pleasure to hunt the soul, as a hound will course  and run down a frightened rabbit; but if an adept took the necessary precautions, he could safely summon Iod, and the god would serve him in certain curious but desirable ways.... Iod's appearance is said to be indescribable--and unsurvivable:
No man could say, moreover, what shape Iod  would assume; it was whispered that he did not always retain the same form.... And for a human being to see the shape of Iod in all its frightful completeness, unprotected by the necessary precautions, meant swift and certain doom.When Iod does appear, he manifests as a "blazing cosmic horror":
It was not a homogeneous entity, this unholy specter, but it partook hideously of incongruous elements. Strange mineral and crystal formations sent their fierce glow through squamous, semitransparent  flesh, and the whole was bathed in a viscid, crawling light that pulsed  monstrously about the horror.

Iranon is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Quest of Iranon". 

### Overview
Iranon is a resident in the Dreamlands. He is a vine-crowned, yellow-haired wanderer dressed in a purple robe. Though he believed himself to be an exiled prince from Aira, he in fact grew up poor in the countryside.

This Adonis or Apollonian youth does not age, unlike his companion. Iranon searched tirelessly for a lost homeland, only to discover that it is a figment of his imagination and that his single-minded focus on his quest deferred the effects of age. Stripped of this illusion, the weight of ages immediately descends upon him and he is withered by old age.

Ire of the Void is a novella written by Richard Lee Byers and published by Fantasy Flight Games under their Arkham Horror Files label. The story revolves around one of the setting's recurrent characters, Norman Withers.

### Synopsis
When renowned physicist Professor Claus Schmidt visited Arkham in 1926 as part of his research, he was befriended by university lecturer Professor Norman Withers, who by that point in his career was considered something of a crackpot by his peers due to his claim that several stars in the sky had simply disappeared overnight. Withers agreed to assist Schmidt in his unconventional task in exchange for having him look at his own work afterwards to see if Schmidt could could cast a new perspective on why the stars had vanished.

The two proceeded to investigate the sites of historical missing persons reports, as Schmidt believed that gravitational anomalies had caused the disappearances, and in the first two locations did indeed obtain some strange results; Withers, however, was plagued by the thought that they were being observed by something malevolent.

Upon reaching the third site, an apparently-disused barn, they found it to have been taken over by a bootlegger who was using it as a storage place for his illegal liquor. After persuading the guard that they posed no threat to the enterprise, they were allowed to conduct their research; however, in the process they disturbed some malign entity which killed the guard and pulled the unfortunate Schmidt through a portal to another dimension.

After Withers escaped, he went straight to the County Sheriff who, whilst not believing the story, knew that Arkham was home to many strange happenings, and accepted that as long as the professor change his statement to something more conventional, then he would initiate a missing persons search.

Withers, unhappy with this turn of events, decided to take things into his own hands. Approaching the editor of the Arkham Advertiser, he agreed to give the man an exclusive interview about the disappearance of Professor Schmidt in exchange for access to the paper's archives. There, he found reference to a man named Jonathon Hobart Stane whose fiancée had been brutally murdered in an apparently motiveless assault. Stane's address had been one on the list possessed by Schmidt.

Upon visiting with Stane, the man informed Withers that his research had uncovered the fact that the disappearances had been perpetrated by creatures known as the Hounds of Tindalos, that he and his wife had also been victims of their predations, and that they were known to return for those that had escaped them.

Immediately after revealing this information, Stane pulled a gun on Withers and informed the professor that he had so far avoided their attentions by kidnapping others and summoning the Hounds before feeding them these unlucky victims in his place. Ireland is an island in Europe, the homeland of the Irish people. For centuries part of the British Empire, the majority of the island gained its independence as the Republic of Ireland in the Irish War of Independence (1919-1921). It figures as a setting in H. P. Lovecraft's fiction, most extensively in "The Moon-Bog". It is also significant to Lovecraft as the home of one of his chief literary influences, Lord Dunsany.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Thomas Malone, the New York detective who is the protagonist of "The Horror at Red Hook," is "a Dublin University man born in a Georgian villa near [Dublin's] Phoenix Park."

In "The Whisperer in Darkness,"  Albert Wilmarth at first dismisses reports of strange creatures in the Vermont hills as akin to the "universal legends of natural personification" that "gave to wild Wales and Ireland their dark hints of strange, small, and terrible hidden races of troglodytes and burrowers." This is an allusion to the Welsh writer Arthur Machen's "The Novel of the Black Seal," in which the legends of "little people" turn out to be based on horrific reality.

Listing the signs of Cthulhu's global influence, "The Call of Cthulhu" notes, "The west of Ireland, too, is full of wild rumour and legendry."

The "strange regularities" of the titular mountain range in At the Mountains of Madness are compared to "the famous Giants’ Causeway in Ireland."

### Expanded Mythos
In 2024, designer Colin Dunlop released a sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game simply titled Cthulhu Ireland, and published through the Miskatonic Repository player-driven resource initiative. The book details the Emerald Isle in the Roaring 20s with elements of the Cthulhu Mythos added as appropriate.

Irem, or Irim, is a legendary city mentioned multiple times in the Cthulhu Mythos stories of H. P. Lovecraft, Robert Bloch, and August Derleth. 

It was the City of Pillars visited by the Mad Arab in the deserts of Arabia.

### In the Mythos
Irem is first mentioned by Lovecraft in "The Nameless City", in which the narrator finds evidence of a sapient reptile species that flourished before mankind and built a city in the Arabian desert. One of the images in their murals depicts a human being torn to pieces by the reptiles. The narrator muses that the man in the picture might have been "a pioneer of ancient Irem, the City of Pillars", thus implying that the reptile inhabitants of the Nameless City might have been enemies of the human inhabitants of Irem.

Abdul Alhazred, the 8th century author of the Necronomicon who worshiped Yog-Sothoth and Cthulhu, claimed to have seen Irem, the City of Pillars, "and to have found beneath the ruins of a certain nameless desert town the shocking annals and secrets of a race older than mankind". (: "History of the Necronomicon")

Alhazred also heard the name of Nyarlathotep whispered "in tales of shadowed Irem". (: "The Faceless God")

An unidentified grimoire that belonged to Abel Harrop contains a passage in which the author claims to have opened a gate in Irem that would allow the Great Old Ones to come through from their realm, although they also point out that such a gate can be opened from anywhere, not just Irem. They also refer to Irem as the City of Pillars, or the City under the Desert. (: "The Whippoorwills in the Hills")

In 1907, when a man named Castro was interrogated by the police about the activities of the Cthulhu Cult, he told them that he believed the centre of the cult was located "amid the pathless deserts of Arabia, where Irem, the City of Pillars, dreams hidden and untouched". (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

At some point, Prof. Laban Shrewsbury believed that one of the eight focal points of activity of the Cthulhu Cult was located near an ancient buried city in a desert in Kuwait. Shrewsbury tentatively identifies this as possibly being Irem, the City of Pillars. (: "The Gorge Beyond Salapunco")

However, Shrewsbury later became convinced that Irem was located in the vicinity of the Nameless City. (: "The Keeper of the Key")

Alfred Clarendon once spoke to an old man in Yemen who claimed to have been to "the Crimson Desert", where he saw Irem, the City of Pillars, and "worshipped at the underground shrines of Nug and Yeb". (: "The Last Test")

The Iron-Bound Books of Shuma-Gorath first appeared in print in "The Curse of the Golden Skull" by Robert E. Howard, which was published in 1967. They were invoked by the sorcerer Rotath before his death and his subsequent curse. Since Rotath menaced both Kull and Conan, the Iron-Bound Books of Shuma-Gorath cross an enormous span of history, from circa 100,000 BC through the time of Conan circa 8,000 BC to close to the present day in the time of the final part of the original story in which they appear.

The Iron-Bound Books were first mentioned in Marvel Comics in 1974 in Conan the Barbarian Vol. 1 #37 and first made a visual appearance in Conan the Barbarian Vol. 1 #258. They have also been mentioned in the role-playing game Conan: Adventures in an Age Undreamed Of by Modiphius Entertainment.

### Background
The Iron-Bound Books of Shuma-Gorath are tomes of mystic lore with which one can become the master of the world. The clasps on it are enchanted and cannot be opened either by sorcery or sword. To unlock its secrets, a key is required. They were magically created by humans long before the first books existed. The book was created from iron plates and rings. It was used by the sorcerers of Pre-Cataclysmic Lemuria to summon magical power for their spells.
