Isaac "Icthyic Ike" Waite is a fictional character which features in the works of American author James Ambuehl.

### Overview
Beginning his career as a radio DJ at Innsmouth's K-FSH FM, Waite later moved on to journalism, becoming the music editor and chief critic for the Innsmouth Courier. He is currently a patient in Arkham Asylum, presumably as a result of believing himself to be a Deep One (which he revealed to his doctor during treatment). His previous encounter with a colossal entity at a rock concert from which he was the only survivor seems to have planted a seed of madness which grew into this delusion: prior to his incarceration, he may have already been showing signs of dissociative identity disorder.

### Trivia

*Waite's surname is likely a nod to Lovecraft's character Asenath Waite, who was implied to have had at least a modicum of Deep One ancestry; when Waite was incarcerated in the institution, he believed himself to have been a Deep One.

The storyline involves a worn out salaryman being sent to the Demon Realm, where he turns into a Demon Prince who rules over the kingdom of Paladina. Beginning his journey, the Demon King must lead his army to conquer all known and unknown, while having the responsibility to protect his people, lead troops to defeat enemies, and expand his demon influence.

Ishiti is a fictional character from Marvel Comics who was created in 1982 by Gil Kane and Bruce Jones. She made her first appearance in issue #134 of the first volume of the Conan the Barbarian comic book series.

### Background
Ishiti is an offspring of the Elder God Set. She had the ability to "freeze" time for everything except serpents and any living being which had been bitten and poisoned by a serpent, and anything that person was carrying. In her serpentine form, she had the body of a giant snake with a humanoid head that had fangs and a gorgon-like spread of writhing serpents.

In her semi-humanoid form, she had the upper torso of a woman and was able to extend her two long snake-like arms which would draw a victim into her dimension. Conventional weapons (for example, swords) were unable to harm Ishiti due to her scaly hide. She could also project powerful mystical blasts from her mouth, which with repeated strikes could turn a human into Serpent Man. Her mouth had fangs and was able to swallow a fully grown man.

shortDefinition: Island M is an island within the Marvel Comics' fictional universe. It first appeared in 1964 in issue #4 of volume 1 of the comic book series X-Men.  ### Background Hundreds of millions of years ago, during the time of the dinosaurs, Shuma-Gorath, t...
fullContent:
Island M is an island within the Marvel Comics' fictional universe. It first appeared in 1964 in issue #4 of volume 1 of the comic book series X-Men.

### Background
Hundreds of millions of years ago, during the time of the dinosaurs, Shuma-Gorath, the ruler of the Old Ones, imprisoned the rebellious Quoggoth in a tomb on Earth. The location where his sepulcher was located would eventually become part of the Bermuda Triangle, an island which came to be known as Island M.

Before mankind developed language, the island was a stronghold of the Ancients, an evil race who once ruled Earth. They were seemingly monstrous cephalopod humanoids with octopus-like heads who committed "unspeakable atrocities" at their citadel. Eventually, they were defeated and bound via the use of black magic and human sacrifice. Millennia afterwards, its stones radiated a malevolence that neither time or effort could ever purge. The citadel was protected by guardians, statues which were made of a crystalline circuitry matrix.

In the mid-20th century the uncharted island, which had sunk to the bottom of the ocean, was raised to the surface by Magneto, who turned it into a base for his team, the Brotherhood of Evil Mutants. The X-Men were temporarily imprisoned on the island, but escaped with the help of the Avengers and defeated Magneto, who they thought killed by the explosion of the base.

Years later, Magneto would re-establish his base on the island, where he built a machine that amplified his powers and permitted him to manipulate the electromagnetic field of Earth, including causing an earthquake in a Russian city in Siberia, complete with lava flows erupting in the middle of the city. The device was destroyed by the X-Men and, during the fighting, the teenage mutant Shadowcat was almost killed, forcing Magneto to reflect on his past actions. In the aftermath, the temporarily stranded X-Men encountered Quoggoth, the imprisoned Old One, who attempted to manipulate and force Cyclops and Shadowcat to free him, but failed as they were rescued by Wolverine.

Decades later, the (temporarily) reformed Magneto, the X-Men, and the New Mutants used the island as a rest-and-relaxation location, as its electronic systems and eldritch nature masked the island from the rest of the world. Being on that evil island made the X-Men uneasy. The Chief Examiner, an alien, activated the statues and unleashed the eldritch horrors on the mutants, whose touch turned their victims into statues, living but inanimate. They were saved by the actions of Magneto and Rogue.

It is a 1986 horror novel by Stephen King. It has been called "by far the author’s most Lovecraftian work", with parallels drawn between Pennywise and H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu.

It tells the story of Pennywise the Clown, a shapeshifting entity that emerges every 27 years to prey on the fears of the residents of Derry, Maine. It is an ancient extradimensional creature that comes from a realm it calls the Deadlights.

### Adaptations
The original story has been adapted to film and television several times, including: 
*The 1990 two-part miniseries It, which aired on ABC. It was directed by Tommy Lee Wallace and features Pennywise portrayed by Tim Curry.
*The Indian television series Woh, directed by Glen Baretto and Ankush Mohla, was loosely based on It, which aired on Zee TV in 1998.
*The 2017 film It and its sequel It Chapter Two, directed by Andy Muschietti and featuring Pennywise portrayed by Bill Skarsgård. The films were later followed by a 2025 prequel television series titled It: Welcome to Derry.
*The animated television series The Simpsons had a 2022 episode titled "Not It", which features the main antagonist as "Krusto the Clown", a parody of Pennywise portrayed by Krusty the Clown.

"It Came from the Sea" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Troy Young. It is the first story in the Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
When a bizarre creature resembling a cross between a squid, shark and lobster washes up on a remote Canadian beach, a marine biologist and a Mountie attempt to uncover the creature's origins. After an investigation which leads nowhere, the creature's mother arrives at the town, destroying the pier and prompting the government to shut the town down, quarantine the area, and bring in a special department which deals with, among other things, biological oceanic anomalies.

### Characters
*Joe Mills, a corporal with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
*Dr. Adele Kramer, a marine biologist at Dalhousie University.
*Cecil Walker, self-proclaimed mayor of Gallou Cove, eaten when the mother arrived to claim its offspring.

### Publication History
"It Came from the Sea" was published in The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 1 in 2020.

### Trivia
* Kramer mentions at one point that she intends to call in help from a colleague at Miskatonic University, Arkham.

"It Ends Where It Began" is a short story by Troy Young. It is the sixth instalment in the Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Synopsis
Adele Kramer, Joe Mills and Pete Ivalu visit Miskatonic University on a fact-finding mission. 

Soon afterwards, they are called to back to Gallou Cove, site of the events in "It Came from the Sea" , which is in the process of being bulldozed by the Canadian government. There, a missing girl's diary leads them to a subterranean shrine to Dagon where Mills is killed by Deep Ones.

Fleeing to the surface, Kramer and Ivalu are confronted by an avatar of Nyarlathotep who murders Ivalu and takes Kramer's soul off to serve in the choir of Azathoth, leaving her body in a catatonic state.

### Characters
*Dr. Adele Kramer, a field agent for the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.

*Sergeant Pete Ivalu, another agent.
*Harjit Singh, senior manager in the Department.
*William Akeley, an avatar of Nyarlathotep.
*Molly Xiao, departmental researcher.

"It Lurks in the Basement" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Troy Young. It is the fifth instalment in the Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
Whilst attempting to get some rest during a brief downtime, Adele Kramer's sensitivity to The Other alerts her to something lurking in a mysterious old house nearby. Encouraged by her handler Harjit Singh to investigate, she discovers an old man whose family have been keeping a Shoggoth captive in the basement for generations. Unfortunately for the man, he is accidentally killed during Kramer's intrusion, and with nothing left to be wary of, she burns the house to the ground, Shoggoth and all.

### Characters
*Dr. Adele Kramer, a field operative for a government branch devoted to paranormal investigation.
*Harjit Singh, Kramer's handler.
*Walter Eddoes, an elderly man whose family have kept a captive Shoggoth in their possession for unknown reasons.

### Publication History

fullContent:
"It Slumbers Beneath the Ice" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Troy Young. It is the second story in his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
Dr. Adele Kramer, now working for a shadowy government organisation, is sent to investigate the disappearance of a tribe of natives from within Canada's arctic circle. Joining up with local liaison Brennan and Army Ranger Ivalu, the group determines the tribe to have been historic Cthulhu worshippers, and that they have moved on to release something from beneath the ice.

Locating the iceberg sought by the tribesfolk, the group discovers that they have almost freed the entity. Although they are able to kill the surviving cultists, Brennan's mind is broken and he is killed when attacking Kramer. As the beast within the ice finally awakens, the other two are able to kill it with the explosives which they had brought for that very task.

The story concludes with Ivalu being recruited into the same organisation as Kramer.

### Characters
*Dr. Adele Kramer, a marine biologist working for a government department whose remit is the removal of "The Other" (a catch-all term for entities of the Cthulhu Mythos) from Earth.
*Scott Brennan, a government liaison to the indigenous tribes of northern Canada.
*Pete Ivalu, a sergeant with the Canadian Army Rangers.
*Harjit Singh, senior representative of the unnamed agency.

### Publication History
"It Slumbers Beneath the Ice" was published in the collection The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 1 in 2020.

### Trivia
*The name of the Coast Guard ship called in to assist the team is the CCGS Howard Phillips, and it was captained by a man named Armitage.
*The entity frozen in the ice was heavily implied to have been a Cthulhi.

Ithaqua, also known as the Wind-Walker or the Wendigo, is a fictional entity in the Cthulhu Mythos. The titular creature debuted in August Derleth's short story "The Thing That Walked on the Wind", which was inspired by Algernon Blackwood's 1910 tale The Wendigo.

### Background
Ithaqua is one of the Great Old Ones and appears as a horrifying giant with a roughly human shape and glowing red eyes. He has been reported from as far north as the Arctic to the Sub-Arctic, where Native Americans first encountered him. He is believed to prowl the Arctic waste, hunting down unwary travelers and slaying them in a gruesome fashion. He is believed to have inspired the Native American legend of the Wendigo and possibly the Yeti.

Ithaqua's cult is small, but he is greatly feared in the far north. Fearful denizens of Siberia, Canada, and Alaska often leave sacrifices for Ithaqua; not as worship but as appeasement.
Those who join his cult are granted immunity to extremely cold temperatures.
He often uses Shantaks, a colossal avian "lesser race", as servitors.

Derleth classified Ithaqua as an elemental of air, alongside Hastur, Zhar and Lloigor. However, in at least one of the many conflicts among the Great Old Ones, Ithaqua seems to have sided with Cthulhu against Hastur and Cthugha. (: "The Black Island")

Friedrich von Junzt's Unaussprechlichen Kulten claims that Ithaqua, Zhar, and Lloigor are the children of Hastur and Shub-Niggurath. (: "The Horror in the Gallery")

Ithaqua might be the same entity as Avaloth, and possibly Aphoom-Zhah (: "Wrath of the Wind-Walker"), although the latter is generally regarded as a child of Cthugha (: "The Acolyte of the Flame").

Ithaqua figures prominently in Brian Lumley's Titus Crow Mythos series, ruling the ice-world of Borea. In Lumley's works, Ithaqua periodically treads the winds of space between Earth and Borea, bringing helpless victims back to Borea to worship him among its snowy wastes.

He frequently attempts to reproduce with humanoid females, hoping to create offspring which can surpass his own limitations, imposed by the Elder Gods, and so help free the rest of the Great Old Ones. It is suggested that Ithaqua has the ulterior motive of desiring offspring to assuage his bitter loneliness, as he is the only one of his kind. None of his surviving offspring to date has accommodated him, all turning against him at some point.

### Followers
* The Secret Order of the Wind-Walker: a Toronto, Canada based cult dedicated to Ithaqua. Little is known of the group. (: Cold Warning, Call of Cthulhu supplement)

shortDefinition: "Ithaqua" is a short story by August Derleth, written in 1933,  that first appeared in the February 1941 issue of Strange Stories. The story further develops the entity Ithaqua, introduced in Derleth's "The Thing That Walked on the Wind" (1933). As t...
fullContent:
"Ithaqua" is a short story by August Derleth, written in 1933,  that first appeared in the February 1941 issue of Strange Stories. The story further develops the entity Ithaqua, introduced in Derleth's "The Thing That Walked on the Wind" (1933). As the tale itself says, it's the "incredible story of a Snow-Thing, the story of a strange god of the great white silence, the vast land where snow lies for long months beneath a limitless, cold sky."

### Characters
*John Dalhousie: Division Chief of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, from temporary quarters at Cold Harbor, Manitoba
*Constable James French: An investigator for the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, looking into the disappearance of Henry Lucas.
*Constable Robert Considine: Sent to Cold Harbor after French's disappearance.
*Henry Lucas: He is the first white man in a string of disappearances. Considered highly popular because of his cheating the Indigenous.
*Randy Margate: Henry Lucas' brother-in-law, who reports him missing.
*One Medicine Three-Hat: A First Nations man who tells French that Ithaqua is something "no man may look upon without worship. Only to see him is death, like frost in the deep night."
*Father Brisbois: An itinerant priest who reported the disappearances of children, and later tells French about Ithaqua.
*Doctor Telfer: A skeptical doctor in Cold Harbor.

### Timeline
*1932: Father Brisbois twice reports the disappearance of Indian children from Cold Harbor, Manitoba.
* February 21, 1933: Henry Lucas disappears from the town of Cold Harbor.
*February 23, 1933: Brother-in-law Randy Margate reports Lucas' disappearance.
*February 25, 1933: Constable James French arrives in Cold Harbor.
*February 27, 1933: French talks to Brisbois about the disappearances, and altars along the old Olassie trail.
*March 3, 1933: French issues his last report.
*March 5, 1933: French's report reached Division Chief John Dalhousie.
*May 7, 1933: French's body is found encased in spun snow.
* May 11, 1933: Dalhousie releases a statement about the Lucas investigation.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Strange Stories, "Ithaqua" appeared in Derleth's collection Something Near (Arkham House, 1945). It later appeared in Windigo: An Anthology of Fact and Fantastic Fiction (Western Producer Prairie Books, 1982). Robert M. Price selected it for his anthologies Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos (Fedogan & Bremer, 1992) and The Ithaqua Cycle: The Wind-Walker of the Icy Wastes (Chaosium, 1998). It's found in two collections of Derleth's Lovecraftian fiction, The Cthulhu Mythos (Barnes & Noble Books, 1998) and In Lovecraft's Shadow: The Cthulhu Mythos Stories of August Derleth (Mycroft & Moran, 1998).

fullContent:
Ivy Town is a fictional city in the DC universe which first appeared in 1961 in issue #34 of the 1st volume of the Showcase comic series.

### Background
Ivy Town was established in 1708 by a group that broke away from the Protestant town of Calvin City. Which by the 1800s became one of New England's major industrial centers. Ivy University was established in 1885. One of America's premiere scientific institutions, a rival of Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

In the late 20th century, Ray Palmer a brilliant physicist discovered white dwarf star matter which he used to discover how to shrink himself down to a subatomic size. He became a costumed super-hero, taking the moniker "The Atom". He worked alongside another brilliant scientist, Alpheus V. Hyatt who developed the technology to travel forward and backward through time using a microscopic quantum singularity he discovered.

The town was gradually transformed by their tampering with the time stream and the Atom's experiments and shrinking technology. The laws of physical nature eroded and broke down, resulting in a town that became a magnet for quantum irregularities and time vortexes. Its neighborhoods have developed their own individual psychoses. Ivy Town is now a critical nexus over which both the forces of magic and science fight over. By the early 21st century, the Dark Giant M'nagalah had relocated to Ivy Town, where it clashed with the Atom.

shortDefinition: Jack Chapman Miske (August 17, 1920 – December 6, 2003) was a fantasy and science fiction fan turned fanzine publisher and critic. An active fan from 1937, he corresponded with several authors including H. P. Lovecraft with whom he collaborated on th...
fullContent:
Jack Chapman Miske (August 17, 1920 – December 6, 2003) was a fantasy and science fiction fan turned fanzine publisher and critic. An active fan from 1937, he corresponded with several authors including H. P. Lovecraft with whom he collaborated on the story "The Thing in the Moonlight." This story was printed, credited solely to H. P. Lovecraft, in Bizarre magazine, a single-issue fanzine created and published by Miske and Walter E. Marconette as a replacement for the pair's fanzine Scienti-Snaps that they published beginning in 1939. Following World War II, Miske worked as editor and eventually editor-in-chief of Foundry Magazine.

Miske was outspoken in his political views, and in his literary criticism, both of which sparked many feuds. His nickname for the Futurians such as Hannes Bok was "The Bolshevik Boys". 

Bob Tucker reported in a 1941 issue of fanzine Le Zombie that Miske was refusing to let copies of Bizarre fall into the hands of British conscientious objectors. 

Miske had an opinionated column in Spaceways called Stardust, which was published under the pseudonym "The Star-Treader" until he was finally threatened with exposure by Robert A. W. Lowndes, who had taken offense to a number of remarks on the subject of Michelism. In response, Miske revealed his identity publicly and continued the column. Stardust had drawn ire from the beginning, beginning almost immediately with an accusation from William L. Hamling that the name Stardust had been stolen from his fanzine, to which Miske countered that Hamling hadn't invented the word "stardust" and many other science fiction works had already used it as a title.

Miske considered leaving fandom entirely, despite having a positive experience at the first Chicago fan convention that surprised everyone after the reputation he'd garnered as The Star-Treader.It would be difficult for me to state in so many words what prompted me to enter fandom, but that which made me think of leaving is easily set forth. I found that fans were not as greatly different from the average person as I hoped. Thus they were different from me, and continued association with them could bear little fruit for me...

J. Chapman MiskeThe passionate but turbulent fan fiction and fanzine scene of which Miske was a part was a significant contributor not only to the survival of H. P. Lovecraft's work after his death but also to its continuous expansion and tradition of literary criticism of which Lovecraft had been a very active part from his adolescence onward.

J. Michael Straczynski (born 17 July 1954) is an American writer most well known for his extensive and acclaimed work in television and comic books, the latter including several titles for DC and Marvel Comics. He is the creator of the science fiction series Babylon 5 and acted as a writer and story editor on the animated series The Real Ghostbusters, for which he wrote the Cthulhu Mythos crossover episode "Russian About".

Straczynski was one of the writers of the classic animated series He-Man and the Masters of the Universe, along with fellow Mythos authors Larry DiTillio and Michael Reaves. Straczynski and DiTillio created the show's equally popular spin-off She-Ra: Princess of Power. He also wrote episodes for the long-running crime series Murder, She Wrote.

fullContent:
J. Scott Vanlester is an American author and artist who has adapted several of H. P. Lovecraft's works into a visual format, and has also illustrated guides to the people, places and entities created by Lovecraft; these have been published independently as part of his Lovecraft Comics series.

In addition to his Lovecraftian output, Vanlester has illustrated a comic book-format adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula, as well as reimaginings of Blue Bolt, a Golden Age comic book superhero, and Winnie the Pooh, A. A. Milne's beloved children's character. He has also written at least one original illustrated story, the science fiction novel Anna's Song.

Vanlester was drawn into the world of writing as the result of a head injury sometime prior to 2018, which necessitated the relearning of his language skills, likely as a result of brain trauma .

Joseph Vernon Shea (August 11, 1912 - February 2, 1981) was an American author and poet who corresponded with Howard Phillips Lovecraft and a number of his circle, including Clark Ashton Smith and August Derleth.

### Overview
Shea contributed a number of works to the greater Cthulhu Mythos, and at age 19 entered into a correspondence with Lovecraft in 1931, this relationship lasting until the latter's death in 1937. He was also a long-term member of the Esoteric Order of Dagon Amateur Press Association, and by the time of his death had become their most prolific contributor, a record he still holds as of October 2022.

In addition to his fiction output, Shea also wrote a number of non-fiction works on Lovecraft; these have been published in a variety of studies and periodicals.

### Selected Bibliography

### Short Fiction

*"The Haunter of the Graveyard" (1969)
*"Dead Giveaway" (1976)
*"The Snouted Thing" (1979)

### Non-Fiction

The Jabberwocky (also known as the Jabberwock) is a fictional creature created by Lewis Carroll for his nonsense poem "Jabberwocky", which was first published in his 1871 novel Through the Looking-Glass.

Zenescope Entertainment later reimagined the Jabberwocky as an Old One for their fictional multiverse, making its first appearance in issue #16 of Grimm Fairy Tales Vol 1.

### Original Text
: "Jabberwocky"}}

### In the Mythos
During the Age of Chaos, a war raged for control of all the realities which threatened to tear the multiverse apart. The Keepers defeated the Old Ones, who were put into a slumber and imprisoned for eternity. Only the youngest of the Old Ones was spared, a child who was placed in the Realm of Dreams. Its real name was unpronounceable, but it became known as the Jabberwocky. It was hoped that it would be cleansed of its evil by the realm of dreams and wonder. They miscalculated and it grew up evil, and eventually doom came to Wonderland, as it twisted the Realm of Dreams into its demented playground, turning it into the Realm of Nightmares. (: Call of Wonderland)

The Jabberwocky has its eyes on Earth, desiring to spread its madness to that world. To prevent this, cults have been offering human sacrifices to the Jabberywocky, children whom are given to him and transformed by Wonderland. Its madness still seeps into the Earth resulting in various atrocities, from serial killers to wars, although refusal to sacrifice a child will cause worse things to happen. In the early 20th century, one father refused to sacrifice his child, and the influence of Wonderland increased on Earth, resulting in the Great Depression and World War Two (: Return to Wonderland). The Jabberwocky has great physical and magical powers, including being able to transform others and make itself as large as a skyscraper, 102 stories high. (: Grimm Fairy Tales)

In the Demonbane Mythos, the Jabberwock was a fantasy character summoned to Arkham City by the Mirror of Nitocris. (: Deus Machina Demonbane)

According to another account, the Jabberwock is an Old One who engages in Nyarlathotep's plot to trap the composite existence created from Lewis Carroll in Wonderland forever as a source of breeding stock and entertainment. While she appears to have some connection with Yhoundeh, she also shows a drastically different appearance as her true form when she is directly confronted. (: Black Souls)

fullContent:
Jack Laurence Chalker (December 17, 1944 – February 11, 2005) was an American science fiction author. He wrote and edited Cthulhu Mythos material and also composed a biography of H. P. Lovecraft.

Chalker worked as a Baltimore City Schools history teacher in Maryland for 12 years. In 1978, he became a full-time professional writer and remained in that career for the rest of his life. He was a member of the Washington Science Fiction Association and was one of the founders of the Baltimore Science Fiction Society.

His co-edited work The Science-Fantasy Publishers: A Bibliographic History, 1923-1998 has been of great use in compiling information for this wiki in the past.

### Selected Works

Jack Russell (aka, Werewolf by Night) is a superhero in the fictional Marvel universe, who was created in 1972, a C-list hero with a few comic book series.

### Background
Jack Russell is a werewolf , the son of a Transylvanian nobleman and baron. One descended from a family which had been cursed by the Elder God Chthon. It was the curse of lycanthropy which remained dormant until his father activated it by reading a passage in the Darkhold. On his 18th birthday, he turned into a werewolf.

Ever since he has been trying to find a cure (and for his sister who also became a werewolf though she was later cured by a sorcerer who took the curse upon himself) and until then ways to control or minimize the curse. An adventurer who lives off the trust fund established by his mother through the sale of his father's estate, he has fought the evil forces of the supernatural (including the Cult of the Darkhold and the Wolf Lord Varcolac) both individually and as a member of the Midnight Sons.

Professor Jacob Maitland is a fictional character created by American author Robert M. Price as part of his Cthulhu Mythos writings. As noted by occult detective Anton Zarnak, he is a highly intelligent man, and later in life develops an extensive knowledge of the forces of the supernatural.

### History
As a young graduate assistant working towards his doctorate at the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities, Maitland aided Anton Zarnak with a matter regarding the acquisition of occult texts.

Later, as a senior faculty member at Sanbourne, with the aid of his star pupil and the Bimini Glyphs, Maitland decoded the mysteries of the R'lyeh Text. Whatever he learned from the translation, it pushed him to destroy the Text to protect humankind.

### Appearances

Jacqueline Fine, the Psychic, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos gaming material.

### History
Plagued by terrible nightmares her whole life, Jacqueline dreams of a time when the world will be plunged into a thousand years of horror by dread creatures from another dimension. Having recently learned to control her "curse", she has discovered that they are in actuality visions of a future not yet come to pass. As a result, she now works to decode the meaning behind the dreams and, perhaps, prevent the coming apocalypse.

### Behind the Mythos
Jacqueline Fine was first introduced in the Arkham Horror supplement Dunwich Horror. She has also appeared in Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. Additionally, a plastic gaming accessory was released as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line in 2010.

fullContent:
Jacques Roulet is a historical figure from 16th century France who is mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's story "The Shunned House"; the story implies that Jacques is the ancestor of the story's fictional villains, Etienne and Paul Roulet.

The story's narrator, discussing the history of Providence's Roulet family, recalls an "ominous item in the annals of morbid horror": the creature Jacques Roulet, of Caude, who in 1598 was condemned to death as a daemoniac but afterward saved from the stake by the Paris parliament and shut in a madhouse. He had been found covered with blood and shreds of flesh in a wood, shortly after the killing and rending of a boy by a pair of wolves. One wolf was seen to lope away unhurt.

Compare this to the nonfiction account given in a blog on social history in central France:One werewolf trial took place in the Touraine in Angers in 1598. In that year two hunters came across two wolves feeding on the body of a dead 15 year old boy. As they chased the wolves into the forest they came across Jacques Roulet with his clothing in tatters, his hands drenched in blood, and with shreds of human flesh under his fingernails.  Roulet was dragged before the court in Angers where he was charged with murder. During his questioning, when he may well have been tortured, Jacques Roulet claimed that he had been a werewolf ever since using a salve his parents had given him years before....

Roulet was sentenced to death on the grounds of murder, werewolfism, and cannibalism. He eventually appealed to the Parliament of Paris and his sentence was revoked and reduced to two years in a mental institution on the grounds that his testimony was taken under duress and during a time that he was not of a sound mind.The narrator notes the "queer significance as to name and place", since the story's Roulet family also comes from Caude. He speculates that  if the "Providence gossips" had "generally known of it...the coincidence of names would have brought some drastic and frightened action."

The Jade Emperor is a deity from the mythology of Chinese traditional religion (aka, Folk Religion) and is part of the Taoist cosmology. The entity was later incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game by Chaosium, appearing as an Elder God in the Secrets of Japan supplement; however, it is stated that this classification should be taken loosely and used as a basis of comparison with Cthulhu Mythos creatures.

### Background
The Jade Emperor is an Elder God who sits on the Jade Throne within the Citadel of the Taoist Immortals. He is at the head of the Taoist court, the personification of Yin (dark) and Yang (light). The cosmic forces which exist in the cosmos. He is an entity of pure Tao, unmanifested reality. He gives breath to all of creation and flows through all life.

The Jade Emperor is an incredibly powerful entity who follows the "way of achieving action through minimal effort", and therefore he rarely intervenes. Being the embodiment of the cosmic force of probability, he is able to alter probability. He can also restore the balance of the primal life force in any being and bestow immortality. (: Secrets of Japan)

The Jade God is a green jade statue of a winged ape. The ape is reclining, and grinning in a hideous and evil way.

The statue was between two and three feet tall. It was also extremely heavy for its size.

The Jade God appears in the short story The Jade God by Robert E. Howard along with his characters Conrad and Kirowan.

When first encountered the statue came to life and attacked, only finally being subdued by being trapped in a pool of tar and set on fire. This burned the creature to death. Kirowan theorised that it was originally a living monkey changed through surgery by Fu Manchu, or even a Tcho-Tcho.

James Allison is a fictional character created by Robert E. Howard as the protagonist for a story cycle titled after him.

### Overview
A Texan man living contemporarily to Robert E. Howard, James Allison has an extensive recollection of his past lives, some of which he narrates over the course of seven stories. In "Marchers of Valhalla", Allison is granted the ability to recall his past lives by the goddess Ishtar. In "Black Eons", a fragment completed by Robert M. Price, Allison discovers the reason for his anomalous memories and breaks the curse of reincarnation which was placed upon him by evil sorcerer Koth-Serapis during the Hyperborean age.

### Appearances
There follows a list of Allison's appearances by the year in which they were published.

The James Allison Cycle is a series of linked short stories set across the ages, most of which were written by Robert E. Howard, although two were fragments completed by other authors.

### Synopsis
James Allison is a Texan man in the 1930s who has memories of his past lives, which span millennia; in each of the stories, he recounts a tale from one of these lives.

In "Black Eons", a story fragment completed by Robert M. Price, Allison is revealed to have been a tribal warrior named Bane during the Hyborian Age. Bane slew a sorceress priest of Gol-goroth named Koth-Serapis, but before he died the priest cursed him to be continually reincarnated and to never know peace until the two meet in another life and he could take his revenge. Allison destroys the priest forever, and subsequently falls asleep never to wake again, having broken the curse.

James Ambuehl is an American writer, poet and editor who has made a number of contributions to the H. P. Lovecraft-inspired Cthulhu Mythos. He has also written under the pseudonym Lew Cthew.

Many of Ambuehl's Mythos works are set in or around the town of Braving, Minnesota, a fictional locale created for this particular purpose.

Although unconfirmed at the time of writing, it would appear likely that he is somehow related to author and poet Tracy Ambuehl, with whom he has written several short stories and poems; in his author biography on The Temple of Dagon website, Ambuehl writes that he is married, but does not include the name of his spouse.

Barry's non-Lovecraftian output includes work on tie-in games for franchises including Fallout, Kung Fu Panda, and Star Trek.

James Benjamin Blish (23 May 1921 – 30 July 1975) was a prominent American author of science fiction, fantasy, and horror. As a teenager in 1936, he and his friend William Miller corresponded briefly with H. P. Lovecraft.

Blish was born in East Orange, New Jersey. In high school, he published a fanzine called Planeteer that ran for six issues. Blish asked Lovecraft to contribute to it, and was sent the poem "The Wood"; the issue that it was to appear in, however, never appeared. Blish also got Lovecraft to clarify some dates in his fictional history of the Necronomicon.

Blish went on to acclaim as a science fiction writer, with his A Case of Conscience winning the Hugo Award for best novel in 1959. His story "More Light," which attempted to provide a version of Robert W. Chambers' fictional play The King in Yellow, was described by writer Elizabeth Bear as "my favorite Lovecraftian story" and "one of the creepiest things I have ever read."

Blish worked as a writer for the Tobacco Institute, a lobby for the cigarette industry. He died of lung cancer in 1975.

fullContent:
James Churchward (27 February 1851 - 4 January 1936) was a British author and engineer whose travels across the Pacific Ocean prompted much of his later writings. These consisted largely of a series of books on a proposed lost continent, which he dubbed Mu. He claimed to have come by this knowledge through his friendship with an Indian priest and discovery of a series of ancient tablets written by the Naacal - the supposed inhabitants of Mu - although his writings have been largely decried as pseudoscience outside of certain fringe groups.

Churchward released his first book on Mu, The Lost Continent of Mu, the Motherland of Men, relatively late in life in 1926, after emigrating to the United States, and followed this with another four volumes. It has been speculated that the entire Mu proposal was something of an elaborate hoax, although there are those who believe that Churchward thought his concept to be a valid one.

### Mythos Connections
Churchward's Mu is mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's short stories "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" (with E. Hoffman Price) and "Out of the Aeons" (with Hazel Heald).

fullContent:
James F. Morton was an anarchist writer and political activist of the 1900s through the 1920s, whose work focused on the single tax system, racism, and advocacy for women. After about 1920, he was beter known as a Bahá'í, a notable museum curator, and an esperantist. He was a close friend of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Biography
### Early years
Morton was born in Littleton, Massachusetts, and lived in Andover, New Hampshire.  His family reached back to the Pilgrims landing in 1620; his grandfather was Rev. Samuel Francis Smith. A newspaper article from 1906 refers a little to his youth -- that he worked as a "newsboy, bootblack, an organ blower, and an employe (sic) in a jelly factory". In 1892, he earned a Bachelor of Arts and a Master of Arts degree from Harvard University,  simultaneously, in Classical Philology, earning a "Gorham Thomas" scholarship, graduated cum laude and was a member of the honors society Phi Beta Kappa. He was a classmate of W.E.B. Du Bois  and carried on some correspondence with him.  He gained skills in Greek, Latin and French. The Harvard Secretary's Report of 1896 noted by then he was in the temperate Independent Order of Good Templars, the animal rights-oriented New England Anti-Vivisection Society, and had campaigned under the People's Party. 

Even at this early period, he was actively involved in the amateur journalism movement, appearing in newspaper coverage of the developing practice in 1891,  and elected president of the National Amateur Press Association (NAPA) in 1896. In his earlier days in New England, he explored a number of alternatives to mainstream culture. 

### Anarchism and the Tour to the West and back
He converted to anarchism, especially as individualist anarchism in the United States, anarchism and issues related to love, sex and freethought ,and went on a cross-country speaking tour in 1899-1900 to the West in support of these ideas. 

By 1901, he was active on the West Coast.

When living in the West, Morton wrote for or edited various anarchist journals  such as Free Society, Discontent, The Demonstrator, Truth Seeker, and Emma Goldman's Mother Earth  and lived at the Home, Washington anarchist commune, which had been raided, though Morton was not arrested,  and was still present when the news of the assassination attempt against US President William McKinley occurred. Morton's writings clarified that he favored a "non-retaliatory" anarchism. In 1904, he made his way back to the East Coast, and a talk of his on anarchist/free-thought and morality was carried in several newspapers.

### Initiatives
As early as 1903, Morton is visibly against racism in his writing for the anarchist Distcontent, campaigned actively for civil rights for blacks, published The Curse of Race Prejudice and challenged productions like Thomas Dixon's The Clansman in 1906. Captain James P. Orne is a fictional character created by Sonia H. Greene and H. P. Lovecraft for their short story "The Horror at Martin's Beach".

### Overview
James P. Orne was the captain of the fishing vessel Alma from Gloucester. On May 17, 1922, his ship was attacked by a 50 ft. long sea creature of a species unknown to science. After 40 hours of struggle, Orne and his crew finally managed to kill the leviathan, the body of which was examined by scientific authorities who proclaimed it to be just a juvenile. They also found that the species had a surprisingly developed brain.

Taking advantage of the ensuing publicity, Captain Orne acquired a new ship, which he converted into "an excellent marine museum", with the taxidermied sea monster as the main attraction. The ship was anchored at the wharf of the Wavecrest Inn, at the "wealthy resort district" of Martin's Beach.

Unfortunately for Orne, his lucrative business didn't last long. On the night of July 19, the ship containing the specimen was lost during a sea storm. Orne, backed up by the scientific community, gathered a fleet of fishing boats from Gloucester to search for the lost vessel, but to no avail. On August 7, he returned to Martin's Beach to officially close down his business.

The next day, an agonising scream was heard at Martin's Beach, coming from the ocean. An air-cushion thrown by the local lifeguards was apparently swallowed by a creature, presumably the vengeful parent of the dead juvenile monster. When several people, including Captain Orne himself, gathered to help pull the rope, the unseen beast exerted some sort of psychic influence which rendered them helpless, unable to let off the rope, as if their hands were glued to it. The surrounding crowd, similarly paralysed by the monster's psychic influence, was only able to watch in terror as Orne and the others were slowly pulled into the sea with the rope, to their deaths. (: "The Horror at Martin's Beach")

James Allen "Jim" Turner was an American editor who worked on several anthologies of Cthulhu Mythos content amongst other works. 

### Overview
Working as the editorial director for Mythos publishing house Arkham House throughout the 1970s and 80s, Jim Turner took over the post from August Derleth after the latter's death in 1971. Whilst there, he worked on several volumes of Mythos-related content with S. T. Joshi, but left in 1996, citing creative differences with co-owner April Derleth, August's daughter. 

After his departure, Turner formed his own publishing house, Golden Gryphon Press, where he worked on similar material to that at Arkham House, and published more Lovecraft-related content.

James Van Pelt (born 1954) is a relatively notable current fantasy, horror, and science-fiction writer. He has been nominee for several awards and was a finalist for the John W. Campbell Award for Best New Writer in 1999. His stories have received nominations for numerous awards in his chosen genres but also nominated in readers' polls, an indication of his popularity with the general readership of the magazines in which he appeared in the 1990s. 

Van Pelt's first collection of seventeen stories, Strangers and Beggars, includes a tale about a teacher who is trapped by a giant spider and begins to see her plight in a transcendent light, and another about a group of sharks feeding on office workers. The book also includes a homage to the H. G. Wells classic The Time Machine.

### Mythos-related works

James Wade (5 January 1930 – 1 August 1983) was an American-born writer and composer who lived much of his adult life in South Korea. He wrote a number of stories set in the greater Cthulhu Mythos, as well as Lovecraft-related non-fiction works and poems. 

After first visiting Korea in 1954 while enlisted in the US Army, Wade returned in 1960 to become a permanent resident. He wrote a column for the Korea Times, "Scouting the City," from 1964 until 1974, and published a book, One Man's Korea, in 1967. He wrote about music for a variety of publications.

His symphonic and chamber music compositions were performed in numerous countries. He wrote an opera, The Martyred, based on a novel by Richard E. Kim.

Wade's work has been collected in Mythos anthologies like Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1969), The Disciples of Cthulhu (DAW Books, 1976), The Hastur Cycle (Chaosium, 1993), The New Lovecraft Circle (Fedogan & Bremer, 1996), The Innsmouth Cycle (Chaosium, 1998), and A Mountain Walked (Centipede Press, 2014).

A collection of Wade's work, Such Things May Be: Collected Writings, was released by Shadow Publishing in 2018, edited by Edward P. Berglund with a foreword by Fritz Leiber.

Janai'ngo is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Crispin Burnham and Edward P. Berglund for their short story "The Thing in the Library".

### Description
Janai'ngo is a crustacean-like, tentacled, half-amorphous marine horror which serves Cthulhu, dwelling in the depths of the Bay of Rhiiklu, somewhere within the eastern coast of the United States. 

Janai'ngo can only be summoned on All Hallow's Eve at the stroke of midnight, if a female virgin is sacrificed while placed on an altar outside the great circle enclosing the pentagram. The entity will manifest from the pentagram using the incantation "Iä! Iä! Janai'ngo! Janai'ngo! Mylrtn yh igpstn y'rgo syh'v gt zn drak'lu smr zn dral'ku smr Rhiiklu! Janai'ngo! Janai'ngo! Ai! Ai!" as the sacrifice's blood starts pouring out. The practitioner can contain Janai'ngo for half an hour. Once the time is up, the practitioner must chant "Iä! Janai'ngo! Mylrtn ys igpstn y'rgo dnlq gt zn drak'lu smr Rhiiklu! I command thee!", in order to send Janai'ngo back to his watery dwelling place. (: "The Thing in the Library")

### In Other Media

Jason Voorhees is the main antagonist in the Friday the 13th horror film series. He has also appeared in many comic books by various publishers including Marvel, Innovation Publishing, Trident Comics, Avatar Press and Wildstorm Productions.

### Background
Jason Voorhees was a mentally disabled child who had a deformed head and face. He was bullied and it was believed that he drowned in Crystal Lake. His mother later went on a killing spree and was decapitated. (: Friday the 13th) In reality, Jason seemingly survived and came back to the summer camp at Crystal Lake, now a serial killer taking revenge for the death of his mother. He killed teenagers at the camp and later the city, until his apparent death. (: Friday the 13th Part 2, III & The Final Chapter)

Jason later returned as an undead serial killer, virtually unstoppable with supernatural powers. (: Friday the 13th Part VI & VII) If his body is destroyed, he can possess a new body after compelling a victim into consuming his heart. The Necronomicon Ex-Mortis was found in Jason's family house, indicating that his mother used it to resurrect him. Due to this, he can only be killed if a member of the Voorhees bloodline stabs him with the Kandarian dagger and sends him to Hell. However, even this is only temporary. (: Jason Goes to Hell: The Final Friday) He clashed with both Ash Williams and Freddy Krueger at Crystal Lake, and is later manipulated by Freddy, while posing as his mother, into helping him try to take over the world with the Necronomicon. (: Freddy vs. Jason vs. Ash: The Nightmare Warriors)

Jeb Marsh is a character created by American author Armand Rosamilia for his Keyport Cthulhu series of Mythos stories. He made his first appearance in the short story "Ancient" in 2012.

### Overview
A distant descendant of the Innsmouth Marshes, Jeb carries the curse of his blood and is now almost completely inhuman. Upon his change, the Keyport branch of the Esoteric Order of Dagon locked him up in his secluded cottage, likely due to their belief that he was not of a like mind with them. However, he has managed to tunnel his way through the basement, and is now able to come and go as he pleases. It is implied that he roams the streets of Keyport at night, attempting to help those who might fall victim to the monstrous creatures which lurk beneath the town.

Jedidiah Mortonson is a character created by author C. J. Henderson as an antagonist in his Frank Nardi series of short stories.

### History
Born over three hundred years ago, Jedidiah Mortonson was hung by the citizens of Arkham for child sacrifice and the practice of black magic, before they appropriated his house to, ironically, convert it into an orphanage. What the locals had failed to realise was that Mortonson had already lived far beyond his natural span through the use of his blood magic, and an extension of the spell allowed him to transfer his consciousness into the walls of his former home upon death.

Mortonson spent the next one hundred and fifty years inhabiting the bodies of those who dwelt within the house, draining their life's essence to fuel his own, until the closure of the orphanage. The departure of the inhabitants caused him to wither, and with no life force to drain, he began to die.

This state of existence continued until the property was purchased by Edward and Julie Douglas in the present day. Mortonson promptly began his psychic draining of the couple, but was eventually thwarted and killed by the intervention of Frank Nardi and the Arkham Detective Agency. Upon his death, the old house imploded, leaving nothing but a great hole in its place.

### Behind the Mythos
The character of Jedidiah Mortonson was created by C. J. Henderson shortly before his death in 2014. He was intended as the first antagonist for his hard-boiled private detective Frank Nardi, and featured in two of the Nardi stories, although his involvement in the first was limited to a short point-of-view section at the end.

Jeffrey "Jeff" Barber is an American games designer and occasional artist who has worked on several Cthulhu Mythos projects through his involvement with third-party content provider Pagan Publishing. Despite his work on Lovecraftian games, he is best known for his science fiction eco-fantasy Blue Planet roleplaying game.

### Overview
Beginning his career at Pagan Publishing as a member of their volunteer staff , during his time there Barber authored several Cthulhu Mythos works, all of which were published through in-house magazine The Unspeakable Oath, with many articles receiving reprints in later years.

When founder John Scott Tynes decided to relocate the company to Seattle, Washington, Barber parted ways with Pagan, moving on to establish his own enterprise, Biohazard Games . This would mark the end of Barber's Cthulhu Mythos publications, although Biohazard would go on to work closely with Fantasy Flight Games, a company with a long history of Mythos output.

Jeffrey Alan Combs (born 9 September 1954) is a prolific American actor who has appeared in a number of screen works with a connection to the Cthulhu Mythos, including playing lead roles in Re-Animator (1985) and From Beyond (1986), and even portraying a fictionalised version of H. P. Lovecraft himself in the 1993 movie Necronomicon: Book of the Dead, as well as derivative character H. P. Hatecraft in the animated series Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated. Having made his name in the low-budget movie industry, he has since worked on more mainstream film productions such as The Frighteners, big-budget television shows including several of the various iterations of Star Trek, and voice-acting roles in cartoon and video game franchises such as Transformers and Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. 

In many of Combs' earlier Mythos roles, he appeared alongside American actress Barbara Crampton, who has also featured in numerous Lovecraftian productions.

Jeffrey Edwin Thomas is a prolific American writer (of both fiction and non-fiction), editor and artist. He has made many contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft in all of these fields.

Thomas is the creator of the expansive Punktown milieu, a dystopian science fiction setting which has been expanded on by many other authors. Punktown has been linked to the Cthulhu Mythos through several short stories, and others which feature Lovecraftian elements.

Thomas was also close friends with the late W. H. Pugmire, and the two collaborated on a collection of Cthulhu Mythos stories, Encounters with Enoch Coffin, in 2013.

shortDefinition: "Jendick's Swamp" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Joseph Payne Brennan, featuring the Great Old One Ithaqua. It is set in the fictional town of Greystone Bay, created by Charles L. Grant for the multi-author anthology of the same name. "Jendick's ...
fullContent:
"Jendick's Swamp" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Joseph Payne Brennan, featuring the Great Old One Ithaqua. It is set in the fictional town of Greystone Bay, created by Charles L. Grant for the multi-author anthology of the same name. "Jendick's Swamp" was first published in the second Greystone Bay anthology, Doom City, in 1987 .

### Synopsis
In Greystone Bay, a writer named Kirk is having a chat with the local constable, Chris Kellington, who tells him about an incident at the nearby Jendick's Swamp. The area is named after the Jendicks, a supposedly extinct family of squatters who lived there, and has a long history of mysterious disappearances, allegedly due to quicksand. According to Kellington, a hunter who got lost in the swamp found the supposedly abandoned Jendick house, and fled in terror after he saw a pair of eyes watching him from the window. The hunter described the eyes as "those of a wild animal", although the silhouette was that of a man.

Kellington convinces Kirk to explore the swamp with him, to see if they can locate the house. He tells Kirk that the Jendicks worshiped a deity named Iththaqua, regarded as a Spirit of the Swamp, who protected its worshipers in exchange for sacrifices. It is told that the Jendicks always took care to capture a living animal in their hunts that they could sacrifice to Iththaqua.

After hours of treading through the swamp, the two men come across a ramshackle house that seems to be about to collapse at any moment, and plagued with a noxious smell of decay. They venture inside anyway, and find a cellar filled with vats, which contain chunks of human flesh and gnawed bones, preserved in brine. Just as they're about to leave, a gaunt white-haired man appears, who calls himself Asa Jendick, and threatens to "pickle" the intruders.

Kirk and Kellington hide in the cellar, and Kirk uses the flashlight to momentarily blind Jendick, while Kellington stabs him with a large skewer. They're both surprised when Jendick removes the skewer from his heart and attacks them. After a brief fight, during which Kirk fatally shoots Jendick, the latter calls out the name of Iththaqua and falls dead, his body immediately decaying and turning into a skeleton. Outside the house, a massive tornado forms, and Kirk and Kellington rush through the swamp to escape it. Looking up, they see the face of a monstrous creature in the sky.

A few days later, Kellington announces that he has found more information about Iththaqua. Apparently, in some cases, the god has been known to grant extraordinary longevity to its loyal cultists. He is convinced that Asa Jendick must have been almost 150 years old, and that all the disappearances were caused by him, as they didn't find any quicksand in the swamp.

### Publication History 
*Doom City (1987, Tor)
*The Ithaqua Cycle (1998, Chaosium)
*Il custode della polvere (2022, Dagon Press, Italian-language version)

fullContent:
Guinevere "Jenny" Barnes, the Dilettante, is a fictional character created by Chaosium for the first edition of the Arkham Horror cooperative board game. Her character has since been extensively expanded on by Fantasy Flight Games after they acquired the Arkham Horror franchise, appearing in both game expansions and Arkham Horror Fiction releases.

### Overview






### Description
A strikingly attractive woman, Jenny is independently wealthy due to a generous allowance given to her by her father, a professor of Arthurian studies. It was as result of her father's vocation that she was named Guinevere, which she dislikes intensely, choosing to be known as Jenny. She prefers to dress in clothes which are the height of fashion, appears to be very up to date with cultural trends, and carries a pair of nickel-plated .45 automatic pistols. She is well-educated, likely as a result of her upbringing and her travels through Europe (: Hour of the Huntress).

### History
During the Roaring Twenties, Jenny spent a long period attempting to help her sister Izzie overcome mental health problems for which she was committed. Finally, after experiencing burnout from her efforts - which she believed were her parents responsibility - she took the plunge and moved to Paris, desperate to start living her own life. Unfortunately, this caused a rift between the sisters, with Izzie believing that her sibling had abandoned her. With time this breakdown began to be repaired, and Jenny and Izzie's correspondence increased as the two embarked on the long process of reforging their former bond (: Hour of the Huntress).

When Izzie disappeared in the New England town of Arkham, Jenny made her way to Massachusetts in search of the missing woman. There, she discovered that Izzie had first been manipulated into joining, then coerced into assisting, a cult dedicated to the worship of the Outer God Shub-Niggurath. With the assistance of a ragtag group of allies, including tomboy mechanic Lonnie Ritter, Miskatonic University professor Tilde Félix, and Arkham PD officer Galeas Morgan, she managed to thwart the cult's efforts to summon a Dark Young, although the High Priestess was able to make her escape with Izzie as a hostage (: Hour of the Huntress).

The Jermyn family and their history is the basis of the story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family" by H. P. Lovecraft.

### History
Little is mentioned of the family's history prior to the birth of Sir Wade Jermyn. However, it's said they were respectable enough and many had portraits, suggesting they have a long history of wealth. Sir Wade Jermyn was a famed anthropologist and explorer who was among the first to explore the Congo region. He kept an extensive collection of unusual artifacts and specimens he acquired in his travels. During one of Wade's expeditions to the Congo he found a lost city controlled by a race of highly evolved white apes. For unknown reasons these creatures make Wade their king. He took one of their females as his bride and after fathering a child with her they returned to Britain. Although Wade kept her hidden from his staff and the outside world, claiming she is an extremely shy Portuguese girl. He gave her a locket with the Jermyn coat of arms on it. In 1765 he was committed to an insane asylum in Huntingdon.

### Notable Individuals 
*Sir Arthur Jermyn, an English nobleman and the final descendant of Wade Jermyn. Lovecraft described him as a poet and a scholar who had come to accept his unusual appearance. After learning of his ancestry he soaked himself in oil and set himself on fire, putting an end to the Jermyn family line.

shortDefinition: "Jerusalem's Lot" is a short story by American horror fiction giant Stephen King. It is part of the Cthulhu Mythos, inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft and Robert Bloch, and features the town of Jerusalem's Lot, created by King as the setting of...
fullContent:
"Jerusalem's Lot" is a short story by American horror fiction giant Stephen King. It is part of the Cthulhu Mythos, inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft and Robert Bloch, and features the town of Jerusalem's Lot, created by King as the setting of his non-Mythos vampire novel 'Salem's Lot.

### Publication History
"Jerusalem's Lot" was first published in the 1978 collection of King's own short stories Night Shift. It has since been reprinted dozens of times in a plethora of different publications, and has been translated into Spanish, Portuguese, French, German, Dutch, Finnish and Chinese.

### Behind the Mythos
*De Vermis Mysteriis features heavily in the story, and the godlike creature Yogsoggoth is mentioned.
*The story functions as something of a follow-on or prequel to King's 1975 vampire novel 'Salem's Lot, linking that tale to the Cthulhu Mythos, although it contains no direct references to it. Taking this story into consideration, it is possible that the undisclosed entity that the villain of 'Salem's Lot makes a pact with might have been Gyyagin, or even Yogsoggoth.

### Adaptations
In 2021, "Jerusalem's Lot" was adapted into a 10-episode television series called Chapelwaite, the main plot of which is fairly faithful to the source material, although some changes are made and new characters and plot lines are added.

Jervas Dudley is the narrator and protagonist of H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Tomb".

### Biography
Born to wealthy parents, Dudley was a daydreamer and would often play alone. One day, he discovered an old family crypt belonging to the well-to-do Hyde family that once lived not far away. For years he was obsessed with the crypt until one day he was able to enter into the tomb.

Once inside, he discovered a sarcophagus with his name on it. Henceforth, he would sneak into the crypt to sleep in this sarcophagus.

One night, during a storm, he found his way to the ruins of the Hyde family. The manor was destroyed after lightning caught the building on fire during a ball, killing one of the family members. However he found the manor alive with activity and very much intact. He decided to attend the ball and spent the night living in debauchery and hedonism. Soon a lightning strike hit the roof and caused the place to once again go up in flames.

He would soon discover the ball was an illusion, and that his father and a watcher discovered him screaming about not being able to be buried in the crypt. His father then committed him to an asylum, where he was diagnosed with monomania. Despite the evidence, he insists he is sane, and that he will some day be buried in the tomb. (: "The Tomb")

Jervas Hyde is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Tomb".

### Background
Jervas Hyde was a member of the Hyde family of Boston, a line that was founded by Sir Geoffrey Hyde after emigrating from Sussex to Boston in 1640. One night while hosting a party marked by great extravagance and hedonism, a bolt of lightning struck the Hyde mansion during a thunderstorm and set it ablaze. The edifice was completely destroyed and Jervas, the only casualty, was burned to such an extent that nothing remained that was fit for burial in the family vault. 

Unable to rest in peace without proper burial, the spirit of Jervas Hyde was reincarnated a century later as Jervas Dudley, who had discovered the abandoned burial vault and became obsessed with unlocking its mysteries. This psychic fixation eventually resulted in his confinement to an asylum, but in the end he was promised that upon his death he would be laid to rest in the vault in the space that had been reserved for Jervas Hyde. (: "The Tomb")

Jill Hand is an American author, former newspaper reporter, and editor who lives in New Jersey. She has edited more than forty books for Whitechapel Press about ghosts, true crime, mysterious disappearances and bizarre creatures like sea serpents and giant birds. Outside of Mythos works she is best known for her novel White Oaks.

She is a member of International Thriller Writers. She is a member of the Horror Writers Association. Her short stories have appeared in dozens of publications and in many anthologies. Her time-travel novella, The Blue Horse, won a Pinnacle Book Award for fantasy and science fiction.

Jim Culver, also known as the Musician, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Files series of Cthulhu Mythos releases. He made his debut appearance in the Dunwich Horror expansion for the second edition of Arkham Horror.

### Overview
A young black man from New Orleans, Jim Culver inherited a trumpet from his father, one which has caused him no end of trouble: despite being a talented trumpeter, playing the instrument allows him to commune with the dead, and even, on occasion, raise them to life. He also appears to be accepted by the graveyard ghouls, and has been known to exchange information with them.

### Behind the Mythos
Since his debut, Culver has appeared in several Fantasy Flight releases, including Eldritch Horror (Horrific Journeys expansion), Elder Sign and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. In 2010 a pre-painted plastic miniature of the character was released as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, but this has since been discontinued.

### Trivia
*Culver made a cameo appearance in Graham McNeill's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic, in which he and Marie Lambeau performed a set at a speakeasy attended by two of the main characters.

The Jinn (singular: Jinni) were part of pre-Islamic Arabia's mythology which were later incorporated into Islamic theology.

R. H. Barlow wrote an anthology called Annals of the Jinns about a humanoid species of ancient times. He suggested that they came from Antanôk, a planet now blown to asteroids, and Yaksh could not be habitable by them. (: Clark Ashton Smith letter to R. H. Barlow, 10 September 1934)

Ludvig Prinn encountered "djinns and efreets" in the years he spent as a captive in Syria, having been captured during the Ninth Crusade. (: "The Shambler from the Stars")

According to occultist Edward Barnes Halpin, the Jinn are alien creatures that ruled the Earth before humanity. On Earth, they became nearly extinct during the ice ages, in part due to the adverse conditions, combined with fighting among themselves. However, some Jinn remained active on the planet until the time of King Solomon, who found a way to magically imprison them in objects, such as jars. Due to fundamental differences in metabolism, it's not possible for a human to actually kill a jinni, so imprisoning them is the only way to defeat them. (: "Out of the Jar")

According to some accounts, the howling daemons from which the Kitab al Azif was named are Jinns.

### In the Call of Cthulhu RPG
In 2009, they were introduced by Chaosium as a fictional race for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

According to Chaosium's Cthulhu Invictus sourcebook, the Jinn are a race of beings from another dimension who were brought to Earth by Taranushi, an Outer God. For a while they treated Earth as a playground, tormenting humans. Upon the death of the sorcerer who summoned Taranushi, they found themselves trapped on Earth, unable to return back home. Enraged, they rebelled against Taranushi, and though their attacks were repelled, he was unable to reestablish his control over them.

Like Taranushi, the Jinn appear as insubstantial beings, as if made of smoke. No two jinn are alike, and the race consists of several sub-species, including the Marid, the Ifrit, the Dalham, the So'la, the Hofafa, and the Ghul. Like their former master, they sometimes take human forms. The various jinn factions claimed territory on Earth, establishing themselves in the ancient Middle East.

During the time of the Romans, the Marid, who were the most powerful of the jinns, claimed the oases, mountains, and seas of Arabia Magna (the Arabian Peninsula) and Cyrenaica (eastern Libya). Huge greyish creatures of great strength and short tempers, they are susceptible to flattery and therefore can be persuaded to show mercy if praised enough.

The Ifrit are the second-most powerful type of jinn. Incredibly cunning beings, they claimed the underground caverns, where they established a great kingdom, only going to the surface to capture human slaves who are lured to ruins.

Joachim Feery is a fictional scholar of the occult, created by Brian Lumley, who frequently cites him as an authority in his Cthulhu Mythos stories. He is first mentioned in Lumley's "Cement Surroundings," which debuted in the 1969 Arkham House anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos. Lumley's fullest discussion of the character occurs in the short story "Aunt Hester" (1975).

Feery appears as the author of limited-edition commentaries on books of eldritch knowledge, such as his Notes on the Necronomicon, which was first referenced in "Cement Surroundings", and Notes on the Cthaat Aquadingen, which Lumley cited in "The Fairground Horror". The existence of a more complete first edition of Notes on the Necronomicon--known as the Original Notes on the Necronomicon--was revealed by Lumley in "Name and Number". Other sources cited by Feery include Unspeakable Cults and De Vermis Mysteriis. 

Feery's books were published in limited editions, mostly at his own expense, and the vast majority of copies were "bought up and destroyed as fast as they appeared" by "religious and other authorities" and Thomas Millwright warns that "Feery’s reconstructions and translations were often at fault or fanciful in their treatment of the original works."  Hester Lang notes that Feery's "quotes, while apparently genuine and authoritative, often differ substantially when compared with the works from which they were supposedly culled," because "Feery claimed that most of his occult knowledge came to him ‘in dreams’!” 

Feery is said to be the illegitimate son of the "witch-hunter" Baron Kant, and to have "died quite mysteriously in 1934 while still a comparatively young man."

fullContent:
Joan Carol Stanley (May 24, 1945-October 16, 2016) was an attorney and the author of Ex Libris Miskatonici, a highly detailed, scholarly mock-catalogue of the Mythos-related special collections of the Miskatonic University library.

Stanley was born in Boston to the former Lucile Duncan, a schoolteacher who moved from Alabama to Boston during World War II to be a welder in the Navy Yard, and John C. Stanley, who joined the Merchant Marine in 1919 to escape lynch mobs in Texas. Her father regretted not being able to attend college, and insisted that his children study hard and watch the nightly news.

In tenth grade, she "fell in love with Lovecraft’s writing by reading At the Mountains of Madness."

Though a member of the National Honor Society, guidance counselors talked her out of applying to college, convincing her to attend clerical school instead. Working as a secretary in a law firm, however, she realized she was at least as smart as the lawyers, and got a scholarship to Howard University, where she graduated Phi Beta Kappa with a degree in philosophy in 1969, and then got a law degree from Northwestern University in 1972.She faced "considerable prejudice within the system" in the early 1970s, wrote Anthony J. Benedetti, chief counsel for the Committee for Public Counsel Services, but persisted with "ardent determination and a noble spirit." 

An avid science fiction and fantasy fan, Stanley was an early member of the Boston Star Trek Association; friends joked that she had a Vulcan attitude toward life. She traveled widely, studying in Japan and France and once going to Australia to attend the World Science Fiction Convention. She loved books, collecting stamps, jazz and classical music, and cats;  an obituary said her sister adopted her cat Miss Kitty. She was a longtime resident of Roxbury.

She was diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis in her early 20s; at times the pain and swelling was so great she was unable to brush her hair without her sister's help. She died from complications of the illness at Boston's Brigham and Women's Hospital at the age of 71.

Joe Czanek is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1921 short story "The Terrible Old Man". He was a literary representation of the animosity felt by Lovecraft towards the non-English immigrants of the time, who he believed were polluting the genetic pool of the United States.

### Overview
Czanek, along with fellow criminals Angelo Ricci and Manuel Silva, intended to rob the titular Terrible Old Man of Kingsport, an elderly recluse reputed to be extremely wealthy. What they did not bargain on was the man's true nature, and the gang's corpses were found washed ashore, horribly mutilated, shortly afterwards.

Czanek was depicted as the least-violent of the three, having asked his associates to use only the means necessary to get the Old Man to reveal the location of his riches, and not to resort to violence if unnecessary. This is further supported by the fact that he acted as the getaway driver, rather than joining the other two in entering the Old Man's home. However, this minor compassion served him no good, as his torn carcass was discovered alongside those of Ricci and Silva. (: "The Terrible Old Man")

Joe Mills is a character created by Troy Young for his Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Description
Mills is a tall, broad-shouldered man somewhere in his early thirties. As a trained law enforcement professional, he generally has a calm demeanour and is able to function well in high-stress situations.

### History
As a Corporal with the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, Mills was sent to investigate a strange creature which had washed up on the shore of a small fishing community in Canada named Gallou Cove. Whilst there, he met marine biologist Dr. Adele Kramer, and the two of them attempted to perform an ad hoc autopsy on the beast. However, when they cracked open its shell, a bizarre side-effect of whatever the creature was composed of awakened a psychic ability in them, allowing them to sense when elements of "The Other" (a catch-all term for the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos) are nearby. Shortly afterwards, the creature's mother appeared, and the town was closed down by a mysterious government organisation which also recruited them into its ranks.

Ostensibly promoted to the rank of Inspector in the RCMP and transferred to the other side of the country, Mills was in fact seconded to the agency under the orders of a man named Harjit Singh, who proceeded to send him on a variety of assignments across the country. He has since encountered (and defeated) several elements of The Other including both a Cthulhu worshipper and his summoned abomination and, in partnership with an agent named Pete Ivalu, an entire cult devoted to the Outer God Nyarlathotep.

When Mills and Ivalu, along with Adele Kramer, were called back to Gallou Cove in response to recent developments, Mills was killed by Deep Ones whilst investigating a subterranean shrine.

Joe Slater is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Beyond the Wall of Sleep".

### Background
Joe Slater was an inmate at a mental hospital in New York State, having been confined there as a criminally insane murderer during the winter of 1900-1901. He died there a few weeks later at the age of forty-two. Slater had previously lived in a backwoods community of generational hill dwellers in the Catskill Mountains, and was regarded by his psychiatric caregivers as a primitive degenerate. 

An intern at the hospital (who is not named) studied the particulars of his case and began to suspect that a higher cosmic intelligence was trapped within the physical confines of Slater's otherwise decadent brain. From the things that Slater ranted about during his manic episodes, the intern learned that this higher soul that inhabited Slater's body during its current incarnation on Earth yearned to break free of its fleshly prison and seek vengeance against a mysterious entity that had perpetrated a terrible wrong against it. This resulted in Slater's extreme mental turmoil which ultimately led to his death. 

Using an experimental telepathic communication device that he designed as an undergraduate, the intern made contact with the soul being inside Slater's mind as Slater lay dying. During their conversation, the intern learned that his "brother of light" would become incorporeal after Slater's death, and finally undertake a last battle with its hated nemesis near the star Algol. Slater died then, and there were no further transmissions. The night after his death, a bright new star was discovered near Algol. Within a week or two it had visibly faded, and in a few months it had become barely discernible to the naked eye. (: "Beyond the Wall of Sleep")

John "Johnny" Bell is a character created by American author Jeffrey Thomas as a recurrent protagonist in his Punktown series of dystopian science fiction stories. He made his first appearance in the 1995 short story "The Bones of the Old Ones".

### Description
Bell is described as "a man of thirty-one, with sandy short hair neatly cut and brushed back from his forehead. His eyes were blue and far-spaced, his lips too full for his taste though his ex-wife had called them sensuous"; "[t]here was to his face, oddly, both a boyish quality and a prematurely wasted, haggard aspect."

When first introduced, he is working as a Detective Inspector for a local police force; later appearances show him to have an affinity for jobs involving the protection of others.

### History
In the extra-terrestrial colony of Paxton, Oasis, Bell was involved in the investigation of mass murders and cult activities which eventually led to his involvement in the thwarting of a scheme to return the Old Ones to this plane of existence (: "The Bones of the Old Ones").

Having been exiled from Oasis for highly illegal activities involving the elimination of more cults, Bell made his way to Earth where he was again instrumental in foiling an attempt by the mutated survivors of the earlier incursion to bring about the return of the Old Ones (: "The Avatars of the Old Ones").

Now a Special Investigator with Colonial Security, Bell is sent to the planet of R'lyeh where experiments in dimensional travel have sparked another incursion event, this time orchestrated by the Old Ones themselves, rather than their minions. Once again he plays a key role in putting an end to the threat (: "The Young of the Old Ones").

### Appearances

*"The Avatars of the Old Ones" (1999)
*"The Young of the Old Ones" (2005)
