John Conrad is a fictional character in the Cthulhu Mythos. He first appeared in Robert E. Howard's short story "The Children of the Night", and is often partnered with Prof. John Kirowan.

### Overview
John Conrad is an erudite man of the early 20th century, his stories taking place around 1930. His "bizarrely fashioned study" contains relics from around the world and includes an eclectic collection of books about witchcraft and demonology, as well as horror fiction by Machen, Poe, and Blackwood. One of the rarest books in his collection is a copy of the Nameless Cults by Friedrich von Junzt. He has also read the Latin translation of Abdul Alhazred's Necronomicon. One of the artefacts he owns is a small prehistoric flint mallet which, unknown to Conrad, belonged to the Children of the Night. Conrad himself carved a wooden handle to fit the mallet, and commented on "how difficult it was to carve it into a shape and balance corresponding with the head". (: "The Children of the Night")

Conrad's strong academic interest in occult matters led him to befriend the sorcerer John Grimlan. However, Grimlan dismissed Conrad as a mere dabbler, too afraid to advance in his studies. Conrad, on his part, eventually came to regard Grimlan as a disquieting man who was only interested in the "dark" aspects of magic and arcana, which Conrad saw as "evil and perverse". Nevertheless, he remained Grimlan's only friend, and was loyal enough to follow Grimlan's instructions after his death, which involved a ritualistic ceremony, during which Grimlan's body was reclaimed by Malik Tous, the entity he had sold his soul to in exchange for 250 years of unaging life and knowledge. After the ceremony was concluded and Grimlan's body disappeared, Conrad and Kirowan fled the house in terror. (: "Dig Me No Grave")

### Trivia
*Conrad's nationality is unknown, but is either British or American of British descent. (: "The Children of the Night")
*In "Dig Me No Grave", Grimlan claims that Conrad has never even heard of Yog-Sothoth and Kathulos. This apparently contradicts "The Children of the Night", in which Yog-Sothoth is mentioned by Kirowan as part of a conversation with Conrad and the context strongly implies that the deity is referenced in the Nameless Cults and/or the Necronomicon, both of which Conrad has read. It is possible that "Dig Me No Grave" might take place before "The Children of the Night". Alternatively, it's also possible that Grimlan simply underestimated Conrad's knowledge of the occult, and Conrad never bothered to correct him.

John Coulthart (born 15 March 1962) is a World Fantasy Award-winning British author, illustrator, and graphic designer. His work has intersected the topic of his wiki on several occasions, most notably through a series of graphic novel adaptations of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu," "The Haunter of the Dark," and "The Dunwich Horror." He has also collaborated on several occasions with comic book creator and author Alan Moore.

Coulthart's non-Mythos output includes book, album, and DVD covers, artwork for the Magic: The Gathering collectible card game, as well as critical reviews for horror film publication Horror: The Definitive Guide to the Cinema of Fear. He has also worked with British author Colin Wilson on at least one occasion.

John Dee was a real-world astronomer, astrologer, occultist and alchemist. In real life, Dee was inducted into the service of the crown when Queen Elizabeth took the throne in 1558, acting as her astrological and scientific advisor.

In the Cthulhu Mythos, Dee is presented as the English translator of the fictional Necronomicon, as mentioned in Frank Belknap Long's "The Space-Eaters" (1928), and H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror" (1929).

### In the Expanded Mythos
In Josh Reynolds' short story "Squatter's Rights", at around the same time he was granted his official positions, Dee was also given the title of Royal Occultist, in reward for an unrecorded act in service to the crown. This title has remained into at least the first half of the twentieth century, where it was occupied by Charles St. Cyprian.

According to the Call of Cthulhu supplement Masks of Nyarlathotep, Dee translated his friend Baron Hauptman's Greek copy of the dread Necronomicon into English, at some unknown point in his carreer. This version is known to be imperfect, but still contains a plethora of functional spells. This version is one of the most commonly referenced in the Cthulhu Mythos.

In the manga series Alicia Y by Juan Gotō, Dee appears as the main antagonist. He used the Necronomicon to become immortal, and would later get into a conflict with Alicia Y Armitage during his quest to reach godhood. Dee created a homunculus named Errol, who served as his henchman until being sacrificed for the awakening of Cthulhu. Dee ordered Cthulhu to destroy everything in London, with Alicia being caught in one of his tentacles. After heading towards Stonehenge, in order to summon Yog-Sothoth, Dee was seemingly destroyed by Inumaru; however, this actually freed Dee from his bodily prison, liberating him from his mortal self that had been bound to this world and allowing him to reach the domain of Yog-Sothoth. Dee attempted to assimilate himself with Yog-Sothoth but quickly found out that Alicia had already taken the role of Yog-Sothoth, when her consciousness shifted during Dee's summoning of Cthulhu. Alicia took Dee to the grave of the London Tower, the place where he had been sleeping for 111 years before being awoken about half a year ago, killing his past counterpart in front of him, as well as tormenting Dee's spirit with never-ending agony while being unable to lose his mind for eternity.

fullContent:
"John Four" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the September 2010 issue of Sirenia Digest (#58).

### Synopsis
The story is set after the return of the Great Old Ones, in a Temple in the last city of humanity, where a woman dispenses solace from a pool of greater darkness.

### Behind the Mythos
The title is a reference to the fourth chapter of the Gospel of John, which includes the story of the Samaritan woman at the well. Jesus asks her for water, and when she fails to give him any, tells her:Everyone who drinks of this water will be thirsty again, but those who drink of the water that I will give them will never be thirsty. The water that I will give will become in them a spring of water gushing up to eternal life.

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in the anthology A Mountain Walked (Centipede Press, 2014).  It later appeared in Kiernan's collection Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Subterranean Press, 2019).

John Gregory Betancourt (born 25 October 1963) is an American author and editor, and is the co-founder of Wildside Press, an indie publication house who have printed numerous works from a wide spectrum of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
Betancourt has worked as both author of science fiction, fantasy and mystery, and editor of various publications at several points in his career. After a stint as assistant editor at Amazing Stories from 1985-87, he co-founded a literary agency along with Darrell Schweitzer and George Scithers where the three licensed the Weird Tales name from Weird Tales, Ltd and revived the magazine. 

Founding Wildside Press in 1989 with his future wife Kim; he published books through the imprint whilst taking a break from editing to care for their first child. In 2005, he acquired Weird Tales in its entirety, which he has published through Wildside ever since.

John Henry Booth is a character created by C.T. Phipps for the eponymous series of Mythos novels Cthulhu Armageddon.

### Appearance
John Henry Booth is a middle aged African American man with grizzled features and is a physically imposing specimen. He prefers to dress in the weather beaten attire of a New Arkham Ranger or those of a cattle rancher.

### History

John is a former Ranger that led Gamma Squadron for the Council of Leaders in New Arkham. He spent many years traveling and charting the Wasteland outside of his city-state in hopes of helping humanity's pockets of survivors. Unlike the majority of his fellow Rangers, John held little animus to mutants or members of human-related races like the Deep Ones or Ghouls.

John was raised as the son of Marcus Booth and Winifred Booth. When he was a boy, his father murdered his mother and attempted to kill him before being killed by John in return. The reason for this was becasue Marcus Booth had discovered John was not his biological son. He was in fact conceived by an unknown inhuman father (at the behest of magician-scientist, Alan Ward).

John would eventually marry a psychic Loyalty Officer, Martha Booth, and had two children, Gabriel and Anita. He would grow to love these children even if the marriage was not a happy one. John would eventually encounter a Color out of Space and go on several other missions with Gamma Squadron, one of them leading to his briefly being enslaved by the Dunwych tribe. He would befriend the Ghoul, Richard Jameson, in the town of Scrapyard.

Eventually, Gamma Squadron would attempt to investigate the widespread abduction of children in the region and this would lead them to the Black Cathedral. It would result in the deaths of half his squadron and John somehow surviving, wandering naked through the desert despite the fact this should have been fatal.

### Cthulhu Armageddon ()
John wakes up imprisoned and sentenced to death in his hometown of New Arkham. His teammates, Gamma Squad, have been killed and he has no memory of how it happened. Interrogator Mercury Takahashi helps him escape in exchange for taking him with her. John has no interest in helping her, though, and plans to gain revenge on whoever is responsible for his teammates' death. 
Journeying to the frontier town of Scrapyard, they encounter the ghoul Richard Jameson who helps John explore the Dreamlands. This leads him to discover one of his fellow Rangers, Jessica O'Reilly, is alive. It also leads him to discover that the person who killed his squad, Alan Ward, is leading the Cult of Cthulhu to kidnap local children. Seeking out the Black Cathedral, John eventually allies with local tribals from Dunwich to assault it.

### The Tower of Zhaal ()

Professor John Kirowan is a fictional character in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Robert E. Howard for his short story "The Children of the Night".

### Background
Professor Kirowan is a son of a titled Irish family and a scholar of the Mythos who traveled widely in search of forbidden knowledge. He is often partnered with the character John Conrad (and on one occasion his brother James Conrad). Kirowan's place of residence is not given; in "The House in the Oaks", it is close enough to upstate New York for a casual day trip, while in "The Jade God", it is close to a cypress swamp, suggesting the southeastern United States.

In Budapest, Kirowan studied with a man called Yosef Vrolok but refused to "descend to the foul depths of forbidden occultism and diabolism to which [he] sank". In revenge, Vrolok used his "vile arts" to turn "the only woman Kirowan ever loved", against him and "debauched" her. In order to have his own revenge, Kirowan traveled the world seeking greater knowledge of the occult but became sickened by what he learned and renounced this knowledge. (: "The Haunter of the Ring")

In later life he joined the Wanderer's Club, "which is composed of the drift of the world, travelers, eccentrics, and all manner of men whose paths lie outside the beaten tracks of life." (: "The Haunter of the Ring")

The story "Dermod's Bane" features a main character named Kirowan whose first name is not given; this Kirowan had a twin sister named Moira who died suddenly, prompting him to visit the family's ancestral home of Galway, Ireland while mourning. It is possible that this is John Kirowan, though no other story mentions him ever having a twin sister. This Kirowan encounters the vengeful ghost of Dermod O'Connell, a vicious outlaw killed by his ancestor, Sir Michael Kirowan. (: "Dermod's Bane")

### Behind the Mythos
"Kirowan" is an alternate spelling of "Kirwan" ("Ó Ciardhubháin" in Gaelic), one of the historical merchant families who ruled the city of Galway in Ireland.

The group of intellectuals Kirowan meets with in "The Children of the Night" and "Dagon Manor" are presumably the Wanderer's Club, though they are not identified as such.

John O'Donnel is a fictional character created by Robert E. Howard for his Conrad & Kirowan series of Mythos-related stories.

### History
A sometime-companion of occultist John Kirowan, John O'Donnel lacks the esoteric learning of his friend.

### "The Children of the Night"
O'Donnel is revealed to possess knowledge of a past life, one in which he was a Pictish warrior in the tribe of the Aryara, or Sword People. He had fallen asleep whilst on watch, causing the slaughter of his tribe; this disgrace prompted him to exile himself and dedicate the rest of his life to tracking down and killing the perpetrators, the Children of the Night.

### "The Haunter of the Ring"
O’Donnel acted as the narrator, and witnessed the downfall of malicious occultist Josef Vrolok at the hands of dead sorcerer Thoth-amon, although he played no appreciable role in the actual events which transpire.

### Trivia
*Although his first name is given as John, one of the secondary characters in "The Haunter of the Ring", Evelyn Gordon, refers to him as Michael- the only time in the story his first name is mentioned.

John P. McCann is an American producer, scriptwriter, voice actor and occasional author. While his television works focus on children’s animation, his literature focuses on horror and dark humour. His Lovecraftian works have appeared in anthologies such as The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (Wildside Press, 2012).

McCann was born in Elmhurst, Illinois in 1952. He relocated to Chicago as a young adult where he began a career as a standup comic. Working as a comedian in Illinois, he met Arsenio Hall and Jay Leno. 

He moved to Los Angeles to take up script writing in 1979 and commenced his scriptwriting and acting career at that time. Subsequent to this, still in Los Angeles, ihe began work in the 1980s as a voice actor and as an independent film producer in the 1990s.

John C. Pelan (19 July 1957 - 12 April 2021 ) was an American author, editor, scholar/critic, and small-press publisher who had a hand in numerous works of Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos fiction over the course of a career which spanned over 40 years, both on his own and in collaboration with others.

Pelan's first novel, The Colour Out of Darkness (1998, Sideshow Press), was heavily influenced by H. P. Lovecraft's 1927 short story "The Colour Out of Space". His editorial credits include the anthologies The Children of Cthulhu, Shadows Over Baker Street (2002 and 2003 respectively, Del Ray/Ballantine), and The Last Continent: New Tales of Zothique (1999, Shadowlands Press), as well as collections by Fritz Leiber, Michael Shea, and James P. Blaylock, while his fiction has appeared in anthologies such as Black Wings IV (2015, PS Publishing) and Robert M. Price's long-running fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu.

Inspector John Raymond Legrasse is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Overview
Described as "a commonplace-looking middle-aged man," Legrasse is the New Orleans police inspector who led the raid on a band of bayou savages on November 1, 1907, and later approached Professor Angell and the American Archaeological Society for help in identifying the cult (: "The Call of Cthulhu").

### In Other Media
*The late American author C. J. Henderson wrote a series of short stories with Legrasse as their protagonist, which were collected under the title The Tales of Inspector Legrasse.
*Legrasse also appeared as a friend and confidant of Justin Sabbath in H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu: The Whisperer in Darkness graphic novel, written by Mark Ellis.
*Legrasse appears as a small mentioned character in the 2024 survival horror game Alone in the Dark, with a story based on his raid on the Cthulhu Cult.

John Richmond is a fictional character from the short story "The Green Meadow" by H. P. Lovecraft and Elizabeth Berkeley. 

### Background
John Richmon was, along with Peter B. Carr and Simon Canfield, a member of the three-man fishing party responsible for dragging a 360-pound metallic rock ashore after it crashed into the water off the coast of Potowonket, Maine.

The object fell from the sky on Wednesday, August 27, 1913, at approximately 8:30 PM. The fishing party retrieved the object the following Sunday, August 31. (: "The Green Meadow")

fullContent:
John Stephen Glasby (23 September 1928 – 5 June 2011) was a prolific British author whose work spanned a range of popular genres. During the 1950s and 1960s, he produced over 300 novels and short stories, most of which were published pseudonymously under the Badger Books imprint.

His contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos are numerous, including several short stories. Collections of Glasby's Lovecraftian horror fiction include The Lonely Shadows: Tales of Horror and the Cthulhu Mythos (Borgo Press, 2012), The Brooding City and Other Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Dancing Tuatara Press, 2015) and Beyond the Rim and Other Tales of Cosmic Horror (Dancing Tuatara Press, 2015). His works have also been included in multi-author Cthulhu Mythos anthologies such as The New Lovecraft Circle, Weirder Shadows Over Innsmouth and The Antarktos Cycle. He was also the author for the novel series The Dark Armageddon Trilogy, although it was not published until after his death.

Glasby's other works can be summarised briefly as follows:

*Approximately 25 speculative fiction novels, using pseudonyms such as "A. J Merak" and the Badger house names "John E. Muller", "Karl Zeigfreid" and "Victor LaSalle".
*More than 30 western novels using the house name "Chuck Adams", and ten as "Tex Bradley".
*34 hospital romance novels written as "D.K. Jennings".
* Two crime novels and six desert adventure novels, all using the "A.J. Merak" pseudonym.
*Six James Bond-style spy novels written as "Manning K. Robertson".
*An unknown number (possibly as many as a hundred) War stories set during World War II and published under a huge range of pseudonyms.
In addition to his fiction writing, Glasby was a chemist and mathematician.

John Sunseri (born 11 March 1969) is an American author and occasional editor from Portland, Oregon, who has written and edited numerous works set in the greater Cthulhu Mythos. Of these, perhaps the most notable are his several contributions to David Conyers' Harrison Peel universe, a military horror setting with extensive Lovecraftian references, and the Cthulhu Unbound anthology series, which he edited with Thomas Brannan. John Taggart is a fictional character created by Richard L. Tierney, a time traveller who works both for and against alien forces inimical to humanity. 

Taggart is Tierney's first series hero, created when the author was still a teenager; he first emerged as a villain in Tierney's story "The Howler in the Dark," published in 1984 but written much earlier. Taggart's first appearance in print was in Tierney's 1975 novel The Winds of Zarr. The character was subsequently featured in several short stories, as well as in the 2008 cross-over novel The Drums of Chaos, where Taggart joins forces with Simon of Gitta.

Johnathan Orton, who later went by the name Phillip Avery, is a character who appears in Peter J. Evans' 2013 Arkham Horror Fiction novel Feeders from Within.

### History
A sergeant in the United States Army, Orton was part of the abortive 1916-17 Pancho Villa Expedition to the Sierra Madres. Whilst separated from the main force, Orton's squad discovered a cave in which a group of Mi-Go were working on a bizarre machine. During the ensuing battle between the soldiers and aliens, he was badly wounded and presumed dead by the survivors.

In the aftermath, the Mi-Go who would come to be known as Mr. Stone rebuilt Orton using parts from both the alien and human dead, and while Orton could now pass as human by concealing his body beneath heavy clothing, his face was hideously disfigured. Orton and Mr. Stone then travelled to Arkham, Massachusetts, where he took the name Phillip Avery.

Establishing a successful import business specialising in esoteric artefacts with the ulterior motive of gathering equipment and supplies for Mr. Stone, Avery became a highly-influential figure in Arkham, and soon joined the Silver Twilight Lodge, a cult dedicated to the service of dark gods.

After finally locating all of the pieces of the Shard of Panestes required by Mr. Stone, Avery was granted his wish by the Mi-Go: to become immortal. However, this wish did not take the exact form he had hoped for, and his brain was transferred into a Mi-Go cylinder.

Following this, Avery, Mr. Stone and several members of the Silver Twilight Lodge travelled to N'kai to harvest the parasitic Feeders from Within as part of their scheme, but were ultimately thwarted by the combined efforts of Mark Harrigan, Diana Stanley and Carolyn Fern. Avery's brain cylinder was left to the tender mercies of the Great Old One Tsathoggua, who had been awakened during the course of their activities.

### Trivia
*Orton was stated to have come from a well-bred Arkham family, but what happened to the others is never revealed. They may simply be living normal lives, unaware that Johnathan had returned as Avery. Alternatively, he may have been the last of his line.
*Although Avery ran the successful Avery Imports, he was also involved in the thriving bootleg liquor trade, and presumably its associated criminal enterprises, given that he was able to easily enlist the aid of organised criminals.

The Mad Hatter was created by Lewis Carroll in 1865, first appearing in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. In 2008, the character was reimagined as Johnny Liddle for Zenescope Entertainment's Grimm Fairy Tales fictional universe, in the issue #1 of the 1st volume of Grimm Fairy Tales: Return to Wonderland.

### Background
Before Johnny Liddle, there were two other men who had the title of the Mad Hatter, with the first being Jack the Ripper and the second was Alice Liddle's brother, Drake Liddle, who corrupted his nephew, Johnny Liddle, molesting the child. He grew up into a sociopath who was fascinated with death and killed small animals. What finally broke his mind was his mother's suicide. After finding out that Alice committed suicide because of his father's infidelities with a prostitute, he murdered his father. Upon learning this, his sister Calie Liddle, sent her brother through the Mirror to Wonderland, where he was transformed into one of Wonderland's most feared inhabitants, an insane killer who sometimes serves the Jabberwocky.

fullContent:
Jonathan Elihu Hoag (1831 - 1927) was an American poet and journalist, and a friend of H. P. Lovecraft.

Born in Valley Falls, New York, Hoag traveled widely through the United States in 1904, when he was already a septuagenarian. In his travels, he visited iconic locations, such as Pike's Peak, and conversed with famous individuals, such as Geronimo. (: Introduction to The Poetical Works of Jonathan E. Hoag)

Lovecraft edited and wrote the foreword to The Poetical Works of Jonathan E. Hoag (1923), expressing his admiration for the older bard and his oeuvre. Two of Hoag's poems included in that book, "To the American Flag" and "Death", were later misattributed to Lovecraft and published under his byline in the 1949 Arkham House collection Something About Cats and Other Pieces.

The Poetical Works of Jonathan E. Hoag also includes an appendix with verses and essays honouring Hoag, which were written by Lovecraft and other fans, such as Winifred V. Jackson and James F. Morton.

### Trivia
*Hoag shares the same years of birth and death with Zadok Allen, a fictional character from Lovecraft's 1936 novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth. However, while Allen was a drunk whose dialogue is rendered in broken English, Hoag in contrast was described by Lovecraft as an erudite man and staunchly opposed to alcohol, even being a member of the Prohibition Party.

Jonathan L. Howard is a British author and videogame creator, best known for his series of books featuring  Johannes Cabal the Necromancer. He is the author of Carter & Lovecraft (2015) and its sequel, After the End of the World (2017), which combine the Cthulhu Mythos and noir detective genres.

In the 1990s, Howard worked on the popular videogame series Broken Sword, a modern-day adventure game featuring a conspiracy connected to the Knights Templar. In 2009. he published Johannes Cabal the Necromancer, the first of a series of novels starring an amoral occultist who bargains with Satan. He wrote two young adult novel, Katya's World (2012) and Katya's War (2013), about submarine warfare on a Russian-colonized alien planet.

Howard describes the Carter & Lovecraft books as "works for hire"; the rights to the characters are owned by Macmillan.

Joris-Karl Huysmans was a French novelist and art critic, born on February 5, 1848, in Paris, and died on May 12, 1907. He is best known for his novel À rebours (1884), which is a key work in the Decadent movement, and his later writings reflect his spiritual journey and conversion to Catholicism.

### Influence On Lovecraft
H. P. Lovecraft's favourite author was Huysmans; his favourite book À rebours. It is a decadent work in which idle pleasure and diversion seekers stray very far from normal paths, and, stripped of its sexual content, this becomes a common form of protagonist in the Decadent Movement influenced works that Lovecraft or on which he collaborated, most notably "The Hound" and "The Loved Dead".

The influence also explains to an extent the easy way in which "The King in Yellow" was borrowed from so freely but with such intent by Lovecraft and then his Circle.

Jormungand is a dragon from Norse mythology, better known as the Midgard Serpent. Which in Norse mythology plays a role in Ragnarok, the apocalypse. The Marvel adaptation was created in 1966 by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. Making its first appearance in issue #127 of the 1st volume of the Thor comic book series.

### Background
Jormungand (aka, the Midgard Serpent) is a descendant of the Elder God Set. It is the offspring of Set's great granddaughter, the giantess Angerboda who mated with the Asgardian trickster god Loki. The Midgard Serpent is an incomprehensibly large serpentine dragon, which is able to wrap itself around Earth.

It exists in ethereal form around the planet, and when it squeezes the world it causes natural disasters such as earthquakes and storms. When manifesting itself in physical form, time freezes on the planet, with only godling races like the Asgardians being unaffected.

Joseph Curwen is a fictional character, the antagonist of H. P. Lovecraft's novel The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. He is resurrected through necromancy by his great-great-great-grandson Charles Dexter Ward, whom he closely resembles, and takes his descendant's place. 

### Biography
Curwen is depicted as a successful merchant, shipping magnate, slave trader, and highly accomplished sorcerer, born in present-day Danvers, Massachusetts, seven miles from Salem, on February 18, 1662. He fled to Providence from the Salem witch trials in 1692. He died, at least temporarily, in 1771, in the course of a raid on his lair by a group of prominent Providence citizens who had gotten wind of only a few of his crimes. He was killed again in 1928, presumably for good, by Dr. Willett, using Curwen's own sorcery.

Curwen perfected a method of reducing the effects of aging to an uncanny degree. He also had the ability to resurrect the dead and converse with them, from either the complete corpse or its "essential saltes" (derived from the ashes of said corpse). This ability is used to obtain privileged intelligence from long-defunct wise men. To this end, his agents scoured the graveyards and tombs of the world for the corpses of illustrious persons, which are then smuggled back to Providence, where Curwen temporarily raised them to torture their secrets out of them. In this endeavour he was assisted by two fellow necromancers and Salem exiles: Simon/Jedediah Orne, alias Joseph Nadek, who lived in Prague; and Edward Hutchinson, who masqueraded as Baron Ferenczy in Transylvania. He was able to summon Cthulhu Mythos entities such as the god Yog-Sothoth to assist him in his magic.

Prior to his first death, Curwen found a way to create a spell that would transcend time and inspire a descendant to become interested in him and his work and attempt to bring him back should he ever be slain. When later resurrected by Ward, Curwen initially appeared in disguise as a bearded, spectacled "Dr. Allen" to avoid suspicion, due to his close resemblance to Ward. The undead Curwen showed vampiric tendencies as a side effect of his resurrection, attacking local travelers and breaking into houses to drink the blood of the inhabitants. Curwen immediately made contact with Orne and Hutchinson, who had been alive and active all the while, and started up his old plots once again. He soon murdered Ward when Ward started having doubts about what they were doing, and assumed his identity.

Curwen never hesitated to stoop to murder, torture, or blackmail to achieve his ends; he also used -- and killed -- vast numbers of living slaves as subjects for his experiments. fullContent:
Joseph Payne Brennan (20 December 1918 - 28 January 1990 ) was an American author of fantasy and horror fiction who wrote a handful of stories set in the Cthulhu Mythos. Born in Bridgeport, Connecticut, his works were almost exclusively set in New England .

Brennan's contributions to the magazine Weird Tales only cover a short period between 1952 and the end of the magazine's run in 1954, but include the story "Slime", which became one of the most famous yarns to ever appear in the pulp's pages. He is also known for a series of tales featuring the occult detective Lucius Leffing.

In addition to writing prose, Brennan was also an accomplished poet and literary critic. In 1952, he authored a biography of H. P. Lovecraft.

Several collections of Brennan's prose and poetry have been published by Arkham House.

### Praise
Brennan's works have received praise from fellow authors and scholars including Stephen King, Don D'Ammassa, and S. T. Joshi, all of whom have strong ties to both the Cthulhu Mythos and New England horror in general .

Josh Reynolds is an author and editor who specialises in horror, science fiction and fantasy. Born and raised in South Carolina, United States, Reynolds has since moved to Sheffield, England. He has written over thirty novels and a multitude of shorter works, including several pieces set in the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. fullContent:
The Journal of Lovecraftian Science is an intermittent but intended to be annual periodical. It approaches the Chulhu Mythos entities in terms of real world biology and other sciences. Each is written by Fred Lubnow, Jr. Ph.D, edited by Scott Jones and usually illustrated by Steve Maschuck.

It is scholarly in that it treats the biological and ecological topics raised by the existence of various Mythos entities in a serious and educational way. It examines them as if they were real and explains and elucidates their biological systems and contextualizes them using real world science.. Each volume is an anthology of a series of short essays on some of H.P. Lovecraft's "biological discoveries". 

The essays in Volume One focus on discussions on the biology of the Elder Things and the Shoggoths, from Lovecraft's novella At the Mountains of Madness, as well as the Mi-Go, from the short story "The Whisperer in Darkness." Specific subjects within the essays include the anatomy and physiology of these organisms as well as their modes of reproduction.

fullContent:
Joyce Carol Oates (born 16 June 1938) is a prominent American writer, the winner of the National Book Award for her 1969 novel them and the author of 57 other novels, as well as numerous short stories and plays. 

She has declared herself to be a longtime fan of H. P. Lovecraft:

She later observed: "Lovecraft is a compulsive, obsessive, hallucinatory & non-paraphrasable prose stylist, a sort of crazed Henry James. [Y]ou read for the bizarre music, not for the bizarre plot."

Her review of S. T. Joshi's H. P. Lovecraft: A Life in The New York Review of Books helped solidify Lovecraft's literary reputation as a "serious" writer. She later edited a collection of Lovecraft's stories, Tales of H. P. Lovecraft (1997), and has included Lovecraft's work in the literary anthologies American Gothic Tales (1996), Telling Stories: An Anthology for Writers (1998), and The Oxford Book of American Short Stories 2nd Ed. (2013). " "I have reprinted Lovecraft tales in anthologies of 'literary' stories in the hope of breaking down the artificial barriers and unfortunate prejudices between genres," Oates has written.

Some of Oates' short stories have been included in anthologies of Lovecraftian fiction, including "Commencement" in Lovecraft Unbound, and "Shadows of the Evening" in Dreams From the Witch House. She wrote a novella, Night-Gaunts (2017), about a weird fiction writer, a fictionalized version of Lovecraft named Horace Phineas Love, Jr.

shortDefinition: Julius Schwartz (19 June 1915 – 8 February 2004) was the literary agent for H. P. Lovecraft and other notable science fiction writers. An enthusiastic science fiction fan, Schwartz went on to have a prominent career as an editor for DC Comics.  Schwa...
fullContent:
Julius Schwartz (19 June 1915 – 8 February 2004) was the literary agent for H. P. Lovecraft and other notable science fiction writers. An enthusiastic science fiction fan, Schwartz went on to have a prominent career as an editor for DC Comics.

Schwartz was born in 1915 in the Bronx, New York City, the child of Jewish Romanian immigrants. In 1932, he founded the fanzine Time Traveller with Forrest J. Ackerman and Mort Weisinger, one of the first science fiction fan publications.  He helped to organize the first World Science Fiction Convention in 1939.

Schwartz launched the Solar Sales Service, a literary agency, in 1934; the business lasted until 1944. In addition to Lovecraft, his clients included Robert Bloch, Ray Bradbury, Albert Bester and Stanley Weinbaum. Schwartz sold two of Lovecraft's stories, At the Mountains of Madness and "The Shadow Out of Time", to Astounding Stories. Schwartz also arranged  for Lovecraft, Robert E. Howard, Frank Belknap Long, Abraham Merritt and C.L. Moore to write the collaborative story "The Challenge from Beyond" in 1935.

In an interview with the fanzine Alter Ego, Schwartz admitted: "I was not a devout Lovecraft fan. I couldn't read them fast enough. I was a fast reader, and you couldn't read Lovecraft fast!" He said he preferred Lovecraft's shorter fiction, like "The Rats in the Walls" and "Pickman's Model". 

Schwartz's client Alfred Bester, who was writing the Green Lantern book for All-American comics, recommended that Schwartz try to get a job there. He was hired, and went on to have a long career at DC comics, which All-American was folded into. In the late 1950s and early '60s, he revived characters like the Flash and Hawkman, and came up with the concept of the Justice League of America. He is credited with helping to return Batman to his gritty origins starting in the mid-1960s. He's been called the "co-creator of the DC Universe".

After his death in 2004, several female comic book figures came forward to describe Schwartz's chronic record of sexual harassment.

Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System, the fifth planet from the Sun. H. P. Lovecraft, an accomplished amateur astronomer, referred to it repeatedly in his fiction.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The mental patient Joe Slater describes his dream travels through time and space in "Beyond the Wall of Sleep",: "You and I have drifted to the worlds that reel about the red Arcturus, and dwelt in the bodies of the insect-philosophers that crawl proudly over the fourth moon of Jupiter." By convention, the fourth moon of Jupiter is Callisto, the outermost of the planet's four major satellites. It is Jupiter's second-largest moon and the third-largest in the solar system, being nearly the size of the planet Mercury.

In "Through the Gates of  the Silver Key", Swami Chandraputra, a disguised Randolph Carter, describes Carter's return from the stars, saying he "learned an untellable secret from the close-glimpsed mists of Jupiter and saw the horror on one of the satellites".

One of the mind-swap victims of the Yithians in "The Shadow Out of Time" is "from an outer moon of Jupiter six million years in the past."

### Other Mythos Appearances
In Joseph L. Pulver's short story "Nightmare's Disciple", Jupiter's Great Eye--the Great Red Spot, a colossal storm system--is the prison of two of Cthulhu's "daughters", Nctosa and Nctolhu.

In Hyperborea, the planet Jupiter was known as Ylidiomph. (: "The Utmost Abomination")

### Background
Jupiter is a malevolent alien intelligence worshiped by man, including the ancient Romans. Its true form is a fleshy mound with a large cyclopean eye and seven smaller ones, and six large tentacles. The entity is able to do magic, can regenerate, and generates a bio-energy field that both protects it and fires energy blasts. It enjoys causing sorrow, death, suffering, destruction, and torture. Jupiter likes tricking and manipulating others. It is able to split his lifeforce into several fragments which it sends to other dimensions and can survive a 5.9 megaton nuclear blast, though with grievous wounds. In its humanoid form it is nine feet tall but is fifteen feet tall and twenty feet in diameter in its true form.

Justin Geoffrey (1898–1926) is a fictional character created by Robert E. Howard for his short story "The Black Stone". He was a poet who wrote The People of the Monolith after visiting the village of Stregoicavar in Hungary.

### History
Geoffrey came from a family of merchants with no interest in art or poetry. As a child, he went to sleep one summer night beside a long-abandoned, sinister-looking farmhouse, an incident that was later marked as the beginning of his insanity. Afterwards, he developed an increasingly violent temper (in contrast to his family's well known friendliness and sociability) as well as the habit of sneaking out of the house late at night to go exploring. Justin left home at the age of 17, after reluctantly completing high school. (: "The House")

He was a friend of Edward Pickman Derby, the husband of Asenath Waite. (: "The Thing on the Doorstep").

After his travel to Hungary and his encounter there with the Black Stone, he was remembered by the villagers of Stregoicavar as acting in an odd manner, with a habit of mumbling to himself. He subsequently died "screaming in a madhouse". (: "The Black Stone")

K'n-yan is a fictional subterranean realm created by H. P. Lovecraft in the revision tale The Mound, located under the US state of Oklahoma. It is depicted as a vast underground nation under a "sky" of glowing blue clouds similar to the Northern Lights, occupied by a hidden race of prehistoric humanoids who sealed themselves away from the rest of the world at some time after the sinking of Mu.

### History
Hailing from a planet much like Earth, the K'n-yanians were supposedly brought across space by Tulu, founding a mighty civilisation spanning as far as the South Pole near the Mountain of Kadath. When the continent of Mu sank, they decided to hole up in their underground shelter, believing survivors on the outside to be in league with space-devils. Though at one point the great expanse had once been home to several races, the men of Tsath managed to conquer and subdue them, going on to forcibly breed them with the creatures of Yoth. After a million years or two, belief in the old legends faded and rare visitors like Zamacona y Nuñez were allowed to enter to be questioned about the world above, but could never leave. (: The Mound)

According to Friedrich von Junzt, the cult of Ghatanothoa might have been present in K'n-yan at some point. (: "Out of the Aeons")

The extraterrestrial Mi-Go have also been to K'n-yan (: The Whisperer in Darkness), although it's not known whether they came as settlers or merely explorers.

### Description
The North of K'n-yan has a dry, temperate climate and a landscape of bare hills and plains made up of grey basaltic soil. A snaking highway leading to the city of Tsath crosses a slow moving river full over an ancient black basalt bridge. By 1541 the road up until this point had lost its paving, but the towns on the other side remained.

Tsath is the last occupied city in K'n-yan and the de facto capital.

All of the information about Yoth's lost civilisation comes from a handful of manuscripts and carvings discovered by K'n-yanian archaeologists in the vaults buried beneath the city.

The K'n-yanians, also known as the People of K'n-yan, are a species of extraterrestrial humanoids who closely resemble the outward appearance of human beings of Earth. They are immortal in the sense that they do not age or die but they can die from misadventure, violence or disease, should any disease be found that can harm them. They live within a mysterious underground city known as K'n-yan that is concealed within an enormous mound similar to those created by the Mound Builder civilization of prehistoric North America. 

They first appeared in The Mound, by Howard Phillips Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop.

### Conceptual information and role
K'n-yanians are extraterrestrial beings possessing amazing mental powers. These powers include telepathy, the ability to phase through solid matter and teleportation. Despite these powers, or indeed perhaps because of them, the K'n-yanians have fallen into decadence. Even though their ancestors had the secret of atomic power and other technological wonders, when encountered in the story they are unable to operate many of their most impressive pieces of technology, having long since forgotten their principles. Similarly the society and culture of the K'n-yanians has collapsed into barbaric splendor, with bloodsport and other similar entertainments replacing their previous intellectual pursuits. 

The natives of K'n-yan are immortal (except by violence or suicide), and have fallen into decline by losing interest in having all their needs met. To survive the boredom, they indulged in grotesque entertainments and the worship of sinister gods they had discovered while exploring the abyss of N'kai (where they had encounters with the Formless Spawn of Tsathoggua). The natives worshiped Azathoth, Nyarlathotep, Ghatanothoa, Nug and Yeb and Shub-Niggurath, as well as Han the Dark. Their titular gods, to whom they dedicate rich shrines and statues, are Yig and Cthulhu, whom they call "Tulu." According to them, Tulu brought with him an alien metal, which they use as currency after they extracted it from ancient cyclopean idols created on other worlds. This metal was shown to be the only substance that could harm or ward off the K'n-Yanians while they were intangible. Tulu also taught them to write in the R'lyeh glyph form, which has evolved over time. Its capital, Tsath, was named after Tsathoggua, who was venerated by the K'n-Yanians until the inhabitants discovered the Old One’s true nature.

They also fervently studied the culture of the serpent people, often descending to the Yoth region to analyze the archaeological remains they left there, such as ruins of temples and idols of Tsathoggua (which were rescued by the snake men from the abyss of N'kai) and Yig (god of serpent people).

The public's fear of Ghatanothoa made his devoted priests the most powerful group in K'naa with the ear of the king. Each of the hundred priests had "a marble house, a chest of gold, two hundred slaves and a hundred concubines, besides immunity from civil law and and the power of life and death over all in K'naa". Kaajh'Kaalbh is a fictional entity created by Jeff Beney for the Call of Cthulhu scenario "Full de Drames", featured in the French fanzine Backstab #9. The character is depicted as being a servant of the Outer God known as Azathoth.

### Description
Kaajh'Kaalbh is an entity of pure chaos, usually dwelling in the realm of Chaos. It has no true stable form, and is brought to the Earth dimension through summoning magic. This summoning by black magic requires the assistance of a Dimensional Shambler to succeed, due to the requirement to find and access the correct dimension of Chaos in which Kaajh'Kallbh dwells.

Once summoned, the form taken by Kaajh'Kaalbh is stable when on Earth. However, what that form may be is random- anything from a colossal puddle of goo to a rocky dinosaur-like monster. Formless and fearless, Kajh'Kaalbh is immensely powerful.

Kaalut is a fictional character created by J. B. Lee for the short story "Genuine Article" (January, 1998).

### Background
Kaalut is a gigantic insectoid larva-like horror, dwelling in the nebulous realm of K'gil'mnon, along with the Gharoides, its parasitic insectoid servants. It also likely has human worshipers.

### Behind the Mythos
Kaalut, the Gharoides, and K'gil'mnon were all created by J. B. Lee before he ever read H. P. Lovecraft. Upon discovering the Cthulhu Mythos, Lee decided to incorporate his inventions into the pantheon, mentioning Kaalut along with Yog-Sothoth, Nyarlathotep, Azathoth and Shub-Niggurath in "Genuine Article" (January, 1998).

Kadath is a mountain crowned by an onyx castle, and the home of the dream-gods of Earth, otherwise known as the "Great Ones".

Created by H. P. Lovecraft, Kadath is mentioned in several of his stories, including both the Dream Cycle series and more "science fictional" pieces, such as At the Mountains of Madness. It was first mentioned in print in "The Dunwich Horror" (written after the Dream Cycle series, but published earlier).

In Lovecraft's fiction, it is most often referred to as "Kadath in the cold waste", a location unknown to humans and other mortal races.

In the works of August Derleth, Kadath in the Cold Waste exists "in time and space conterminously with a portion of Asia". (: "The Whippoorwills in the Hills", "The Seal of R'lyeh")

### Behind the Mythos
Kadath's precise location in the universe is uncertain; there is even confusion over whether it exists in the dream-world or the waking world. The Zoogs couldn't tell whether "the cold waste" is located in the Dreamlands of Earth or another world (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath). However, in Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, it is hinted that the mountain ranges beyond the Antarctic plateau of Leng may hide the location of Kadath. In The Mound, Zamacona y Nuñez's narrative likewise identifies Kadath as a mountain near the South Pole. But in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, Randolph Carter finds it far of north from the Leng and Inganok.

Sylvan Phillips's map places "Kadath in the Cold Waste" in the vicinity of Mongolia, north of the Plateau of Leng in Central Asia, but also explicitly notes it as being "in space-time continua: coterminous". (: "The Seal of R'lyeh")

Another source states that Kadath is neither in the waking world nor part of the Dreamlands, as it's "not truly contiguous with any space men know or dream of". (: "In 'Ygiroth")

In the Doctor Who universe, "Kadath in the Cold Wastes" is a city where the false Azathoth was imprisoned on the planet Ry'leh. (: All-Consuming Fire)

Kadath was an abortive fanzine published by Lin Carter. Only one issue was ever created and it failed on launch.

### Overview
In 1974, Carter created and published one issue of his own fantasy fanzine Kadath, named after H. P. Lovecraft's fictional setting from his eponymous story The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. 3,000 copies were printed however the printer was in a dispute with the binder, who held the copies. While Carter paid the printer, the printer embezzled the money and fled to California. The binder was not paid. When Carter went to see the binder, he was told that the copies had been kept for a while, but then most had been thrown out. Carter believed that only about 30 copies of the issue survived, thus the magazine was restricted radically in terms of its circulation. 

It contained Carter's Cthulhu Mythos story "The City of Pillars" on pages 22 to 25 of the issue under its original title, "In The City of Pillars".

Kadatheron (not to be confused with Kadath) is a city in the land of Mnar on the River Ai in the Dreamlands. It was built by the same wandering tribes that built the Mnaran cities of Thraa, Ilarnek, and Sarnath. Sarnath eventually conquered the neighboring cities and lands (including Kadatheron) and forged an empire. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath") 

Kadatheron is a repository of lore written on brick cylinders pertaining to the city of Ib and its nonhuman inhabitants. The cylinders record how the Ibians arrived on Earth after they descended one night from the moon. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

Kaiju Girls Black is a 2018 Japanese animated film directed by Shuji Katayama and produced by Tsuburaya Productions. It is a sequel to the Kaiju Girls anime, a spinoff of the Ultra Series featuring girls who possess the souls of past kaiju and have the ability to transform into kaiju girls, usually by using a device known as a Soulriser.

### Synopsis
The film starts with a high school girl named Satsuki Hiraga being recruited to join the Black Stars, an evil group of kaiju girls. Led by Commander Black, the Black Stars seek to defeat the GIRLS (a heroic group of kaiju girls) and take over the world. After breaking into the GIRLS' headquarters and nearly getting caught, the Black Stars manage to escape when it's revealed that Satsuki possesses the soul of Alien Pegassa, giving her the power to open vortexes to a pocket dimension known as the Dark Zone.

When they figure out that Satsuki can only activate her ability while feeling negative emotions, Commander Black nearly gets sucked up into the Dark Zone where she finds another kaiju girl who had been inadvertently trapped there earlier in the film. Taking the girl back to their headquarters, the Black Stars find out that she possesses the soul of the evil god Gatanothor, a powerful kaiju who nearly destroyed the Earth at some point. Although they were initially unable to wake her up, the Black Stars find out that Gatanothor regains her strength by consuming chocolates, causing the shell on her head to grow bigger while sprouting two giant snake heads and many tentacles. However, after eating some wine-based chocolate, Gatanothor got drunk and went on a rampage throughout the city with Commander Black being unable to control her. While Gatanothor easily overpowered both the GIRLS and Black Stars, she was eventually defeated when Satsuki traps her back in the Dark Zone and depowers her with the Soulriser.

The film ends with the Black Stars being chased away by the GIRLS due to all the trouble they have caused.

Kalanpäinen is a fictional Great Old One connected with Finland, created by the Finnish writer Tuomas Saloranta for his 2012 short story "Mahtavat Ammoiset" (Finnish for "Great Old Ones"). The author Matts W. Cornelius, a character in the story, compares  Kalanpäinen to Dagon (Kalanpäinen means "fish-head" or "fish-headed" in Finnish).

### Overview
Kalanpäinen was a Great Old One who ruled over the area of Finland, until he, alongside Iku-Turso and the other Old Ones, were sung into the swamps by Finnish sages and poets, who had learned these abilities from the Sámi people. Only myths--and some of the Deep Ones--remained in the country.

Around the 1930's, author Matts W. Cornelius, a correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft, wrote stories that compared Kalanpäinen with the Great Old One Dagon.

The Deep Ones, especially those who live in Lauttasaari, still seek to awaken Kalanpäinen and the Old Ones so they can reclaim the world. (: "Mahtavat Ammoiset")

shortDefinition: The Kalem Club was an informal group that coalesced around American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft during his stay in New York City in the mid-1920s.   It was given its name, in February 1925, from the fact that its members' surnames happened to al...
fullContent:
The Kalem Club was an informal group that coalesced around American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft during his stay in New York City in the mid-1920s. 

It was given its name, in February 1925, from the fact that its members' surnames happened to all begin with the letters K, L, or M, adopted phonetically to spell "Kalem". Lovecraft, however, never called it by that name in his correspondence, referring to it instead as "the gang" or "The Boys." In late 1925, Wilfred B. Talman and Vrest Orton became members, but the name didn't change; these alphabetical outliers attended only "sporadically."

The club initially met on Thursdays, but switched to Wednesdays to accommodate a night class Frank Belknap Long was taking at New York University. When Lovecraft hosted the club, he would serve coffee in a 49-cent aluminum pail from a local deli, and "various desserts on his best china."

The club later had a split between "McNeil" and "Leeds" factions, after Everett McNeil and Arthur Leeds had a falling out over a small loan the latter had made to the former. Several members did not attend the meetings held in McNeil's Hell's Kitchen apartment, because they found McNeil "tiresome," but Lovecraft attended both meetings.

The club did not long survive Lovecraft's move back to Providence in 1926.

fullContent:
Kandar the Destroyer is a fictional demon created by Sean Clements in 2018 for the STARZ series Ash vs Evil Dead.

### Background
Kandar the Destroyer is a demon which was unleashed by the Dark Ones. Prophesied to battle the Prophesied One to test mankind's mettle. It wreaked havoc and not even the US military could stop it despite calling in air strikes and deploying armor against the demon. It was finally killed by Ash who fired the Kandarian Dagger into it's mouth.

It was impervious to all types of attacks (e.g. bullets, explosives), except for the Kandarian Dagger which could kill it. The demon increased its strength by absorbing the damage inflicted by fighter jets and tanks. If a nuclear weapon had been used its strength would have been increased exponentially. The demon could also breathe fire.

shortDefinition: The Kandarian Demon is a fictional demon created by Sam Raimi in 1981 for the movie, "The Evil Dead", though it would not appear in physical form till 1987 in the sequel, Evil Dead 2.  ### Background The Kandarian Demon is the creator of the Deadites...
fullContent:
The Kandarian Demon is a fictional demon created by Sam Raimi in 1981 for the movie, "The Evil Dead", though it would not appear in physical form till 1987 in the sequel, Evil Dead 2.

### Background
The Kandarian Demon is the creator of the Deadites, though it's unknown if it was created by the Dark Ones or they got it to do their bidding. Sometime in the past, it was placed into a slumber by a spell within the Necronomicon. To summon the Kandarian Demon requires the reciting of passages in the Necronomicon. Known sightings of the Kandarian Demon include in medieval England (circa 1300 AD), the United States in Tennessee (1980s), and again in the United States in Michigan (early 21st century).

It is able to turn nearly anything into a Deadite, including plants, humans, and inanimate objects. When it comes to humans, it will focus on a specific target. Going so far as to chase the target, until it "infects" the victim. In its non-corporeal form the Kandarian Demon has the ability to apply physical force, and can fly long distances several feet over the ground.

shortDefinition: The Kappa are part of Japanese folklore. In 2005 they were first used as a fictional race by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.  ### Background The Kappa are a vampiric amphibious species who are up to 3ft tall with sharp bird-like be...
fullContent:
The Kappa are part of Japanese folklore. In 2005 they were first used as a fictional race by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Background
The Kappa are a vampiric amphibious species who are up to 3ft tall with sharp bird-like beak, a thick tortoise-like shell on their back, and lion-like facial features. They have a clammy slimy skin that changes its color to match the ambient surroundings and possess thick fatty deposits which lets them easily survive the extreme cold. Kappa have great strength and agility for such a small species. A Kappa is strong enough to seize a human, drag him underwater, and hold him until he drowns. They consider humans to be a food source, siphoning out the blood of their drowned victim through its entrails.

Most of them live off Japan's coast in underwater kingdoms. Their dominions exist side by side with those of the Deep Ones, and they usually have good relations with each other. Kappa will sometimes capture humans for labor or their amusement. They worship Gol-goroth and Yig and sometimes work for Cthulhu and his Star Spawn. Kappa possess a code of ethics, and if you show a caught Kappa mercy they will repay you with one service. It's a race whose members exact vengeance for any perceived insult.

fullContent:
Karl Edward Wagner (12 December 1945 – 14 October 1994) was an American writer, editor, and publisher of horror, science fiction, and fantasy fiction. He created the character of the immortal swordsman Kane, edited the book series The Year's Best Horror Stories from 1980 to 1994, and published a three-volume set of Robert E. Howard's Conan the Barbarian fiction as it was originally written.

His Cthulhu Mythos-related fiction includes the short stories "Sticks", collected in Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos; "The River of Night's Dreaming", which appears in The Hastur Cycle; and "I've Come to Talk With You Again", found in The New Lovecraft Circle. Other works include novels featuring Robert E. Howard’s characters Conan and Bran Mak Morn.

In the wake of August Derleth's death Wagner, along with David Drake and Jim Groce, founded the publishing house Carcosa out of concern for the future of Arkham House. The press was named for the titular city of Ambrose Bierce's 1886 short story "An Inhabitant of Carcosa."

Karl Heinrich is a fictional character in the story "The Temple" by H. P. Lovecraft. He was a lieutenant-commander in the Imperial German Navy and commanded the submarine U-29 during the First World War. He was ruthless and arrogant, and often resorted to capital punishment against his own men. He regarded himself as culturally and intellectually superior even to his own crewmates, many of whom he regarded as irrational, superstitious, and weak-willed.

As related in the story, the crew fell victim to an apparently divine curse after sinking the British freighter Victory in the North Atlantic Ocean. As a result of this curse the submarine found itself in the grip of an inexorable current that carried the vessel southward and ever deeper. Along the way, the crew experienced supernatural phenomena as well as technical malfunctions, casualties, and an attempted mutiny. 

Heinrich was the only crewman left alive when the U-29 eventually came to rest among the splendid ruins of an underwater city, presumed by him to be a remnant of the lost continent of Atlantis. Putting on his diving suit he explored the ruins and discovered a magnificent temple that glowed from within. Compelled by an unknown force, Heinrich entered the eldritch glow of the temple, never to be seen again. His written account that he had sealed in a bottle before entering the temple was eventually found on the coast of Yucatán, Mexico.

Kassogtha is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Joseph S. Pulver, Sr. for his 1999 novel Nightmare's Disciple. She is depicted as Cthulhu's sister and mate, and the mother of Nctosa and Nctolhu, who takes the form of a writhing mass of tentacles.

### Overview
According to some sources, Kassogtha shares some relationship with Great Cthulhu, with more than one tome speaking of these deities creating or unifying to form or breed the known entities Nctosa and Nctolhu. One reference suggests Kassogtha and Cthulhu are "sister" and "brother" (if such terms are applicable). However, the former has no known association with Xoth, said to be the originating planet of Cthulhu and its kin.

This Old One seems to be more like some cosmic parasite, able to merge or join with other significant entities for periods of time, and thereby cause the creation or birth of an "offspring." Thus, at times, Kassogtha disappears (presumably while inhabiting or merging with another being), giving rise to the general opinion that this Old One is rarely heard of or encountered in Mythos lore. For some, this parasitical behavior posits the notion that this deity is characteristically like a disease, and possibly one unwelcomed by the entities it "preys" on. Indeed, Jedediah Pullington, in his "Visions of Crystal and Blasphemy" (New York, 1889), recounts a drug-induced vision where he witnessed the merging of Cthulhu with Kassogtha, which he describes as "tortuous" and "near lethal" and how it took all of Cthulhu's strength to throw off or cast out the other. If something can give such a report credence, it does support the idea of an invading entity, perhaps drawing off some form of sustenance to enable it to create new or altered life.

When not bound with another entity, Kassogtha appears to dwell in a great body of water (or some other liquid matter), poisoned by its presence. A strong association with disease seems evident, amplified by reports of the illnesses suffered by those in the areas where this Old One has manifested. For many scholars, Kassogtha is like a "cosmic sickness" that seeps into life, corrupting and mutating it in foul ways.

### Cult
Kassoghta has little organized earthly following, seemingly only worshipped by solitary practitioners of magic and those crazed enough to embrace disease as a force for transformation. The (still at large) serial killer known as the "Carrion Murderer" may be an adherent of this Old One. In addition, the New York subway incident of 1921, where somebody released (allegedly) mustard gas, may have originated from the hand of a Kassoghta worshipper. While little is known of the sick rites practiced by this deity's adherents, most guess that ritual murder and torture are vital components.

Kate Winthrop, also referred to as the Scientist, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for the second edition of Cthulhu Mythos board game Arkham Horror, released in 2005.

### History
A researcher in the physics department at Miskatonic University during the late 1920s, Kate's life changed when an experiment ripped a hole in reality, allowing a terrifying abomination through which consumed her partner, the unfortunate Professor Young. Since then she has devoted her time to creating a weapon with which to combat the creatures she now know knows lurk just out of sight.

In Graham McNeill's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic, Kate appears as a minor character who conducts research on a mysterious artefact uncovered by the investigators, but achieves little other than destroying her laboratory.

### Behind the Mythos
Since her debut in Arkham Horror Second Edition, Kate Winthrop has appeared in many of Fantasy Flight's Arkham Horror Files releases including Eldritch Horror and Elder Sign. A pre-painted plastic miniature of the character was also released as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line.

### Trivia
*In the original flavour text for Arkham Horror, Kate developed her device at Miskatonic University. In Eldritch Horror, Arkham's counterpart on the global scene, she conducted her research at the University of Buenos Aires.

Katha-Hem is one of the Ogdru Hem, spawn on the Ogdru Jahad.

### History
Katha-Hem was the third Ogdru Hem to be released on the Earth, and his arrival was the first sign that world would begin to change.

He was summoned by the Black Flame out of the ether and the eldritch entity began to rampage across the Midwestern United States, turning all humans who ventured too close into frog-creatures. He appeared to be immune to artillery fire, and the US government was ready to use nuclear weapons to kill the entity. Luckily Liz Sherman, with the Spiked Cylinder, managed to burn the creature to death.

### Apperance
Katha-Hem, like most Ogdru Hem, bear a resemblance to beings from the Cthulhu Mythos. The entity towered as large as a mountain and stood on tripod of spidery legs. The beings top was tentacled and has numerous green-toothed maws lining down his trunk.

### Appearance
*The creature bears a resemblance to both Shub-Niggurath and Dunwich Horror.

Katherine Pryde (aka Shadowcat) is a superhero in the fictional Marvel universe, who was created in 1980 and has been one of its main superheroes, one of the most popular B-list Marvel heroes and female characters. She has occasionally fought Lovecraftian supervillains.

### Background
Shadowcat is a mutant and long standing member of the X-Men, who is in many ways like an adopted daughter or niece to Wolverine (similar to Jubilee). She was a founding member of the British superhero team Excalibur, and has also been a member of the global intelligence agency S.H.I.E.L.D. and the spacefaring multi-species superhero team, Guardians of the Galaxy. Shadowcat has had a history with the demonic N'Garai, battling them several times and once having to face one of them alone in the Xavier Mansion. Along with Cyclops she also faced Quoggoth, the rebellious creation of Shuma-Gorath.

Kathulos was a fictional character by Marvel Comics and first appeared in Marvel Premiere #8 (May, 1973), written by Gardner Fox and Jim Starlin. Kathulos was also named Kulthas.

Both names were created by Robert E. Howard: The Atlantean sorcerer Kathulos (: "Skull-Face") and the evil deity Kulthas (: "The Curse of the Golden Skull"). Kulthas was invoked in Marvel Comics' Conan stories.

"L'mur-Kathulos" was also listed along with various eldritch entities and locations (: "The Whisperer in Darkness")

It is unknown how and if Kathulos the Slave-Seer is related to the others. (: Savage Sword of Conan #8 "The Forever Phial")

### History
Kathulos/Kulthas was a vegetation-covered planetoid in the service of Shuma Gorath.

When he brought Dr. Strange to the planetoid and battled him, Dr. Strange discovered his weakness and upon ripping out its roots, Kathulos died.

### Powers and abilities
### Powers
He could fire powerful mystical bolts, mesmerize others, and fight its enemies in the Astral Plane. Those it entranced risked having their life force absorbed. It was able to control and physically manipulate the vegetation on its surface.

### Weaknesses
His only weakness was the fact that a giant Venus Fly Trap-like plant contained its life force and, like any other plant, could be injured.

Kaunuzoth is a fictional creature introduced in R. S. Cartwright's story "The Moore Dam Monster", depicted as being a squat, sea cucumber-like monstrosity with five eyes, three-toed, taloned appendages, and a large mouth. He is described as one of Gla'aki's brethren, and dwells within the Moore Reservoir of Vermont, in the United States.

### Behind the Mythos
The Moore Dam in real life is connected to Lake Champlain, home to an alleged lake monster dubbed "Champ". Moore Dam itself was the scene of a reported sighting of a glowing alligator-like monster decades ago, and this may well be the inspiration for this Mythos creature. It has been suggested that the real life Moore Dam Monster was a Northern Pike, a highly aggressive predatory river fish.

The Keeper of the Moon-Lens is an avatar of Shub-Niggurath created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Moon-Lens".

### Description
The Keeper of the Moon-Lens is a massive creature that appears like a towering white mass of gelatinous flesh. Its legs have several joints, and the feet are shaped like circular pads. Instead of arms, it has three spines that can be used to hold onto the ground to facilitate movement. Its head is formed by thick coils of semi-transparent flesh. The face consists of "a huge toothed beak" and a number of yellow eyes that peer in many different directions. It speaks with a sibilant high-pitched voice.

This avatar is worshiped by the inhabitants of the English town of Exham in the Severn Valley, who can summon it using a gigantic lens mounted atop a high pylon to create a beacon of concentrated moonlight and open a door to the interior of a hill, from which the Keeper will emerge. Chosen "sacrifices" will be engulfed by the monster's coils of gelatinous flesh before being expelled. Those who go through this ritual begin to experience a gradual transformation, both physical and mental, turning them into the Goff'nn Hupadgh Shub-Niggurath (a.k.a. the Blessed of Shub-Niggurath). These are creatures reminiscent of the legendary satyrs and dryads, whose flesh, at least in some cases, is tough and wood-like, and who become immortal once the transformation is complete.

Inside the hill, the Keeper inhabits a subterranean world of catacombs built with alien geometry and strange angles. The ancient Romans worshiped it as the Magna Mater, while modern cultists seem to refer to it with male and female pronouns interchangeably, suggesting that the entity might be androgynous. Like many beings associated with the Great Old Ones, the Keeper of the Moon-Lens can be repelled by the star-signs. (: "The Moon-Lens")

The Keepers of the Yellow Sign are a fictional race created by Paizo Inc in 2016 for the Pathfinder roleplaying game.

### Background
The Keepers of the Yellow Sign are cultists who've sacrificed their souls to Hastur, becoming its undead servants. They hunt down unbelievers who have gotten to close to Hastur's secrets, such as seeing the Yellow Sign or possessing an artifact. Most of them do so out of a desire to cause pain and misery, but occasionally they will work for one of Hastur's clerics. The Keepers of the Yellow Sign are attracted to art, usually creations that are decadent and/or weird. They are able to pass off as humans though they have a disturbing aura and some telltale marks such as an unhealthy pale exterior and a swollen face.

Keepers are able to drain the lifeforce of others, and sometimes become enraptured by the act of draining energy. While doing so can kill the victim, they also risk being overwhelmed and destroyed themselves by that lifeforce. Keepers have been known to exist for centuries or millennia, keeping to the fringes of society, thereby remaining unknown to most. They work in macabre fields (e.g. graveyard security or grave digging) or pose as mendicants or beggars, pretending to be insane. They have some magical abilities such as invisibility and bestowing curses.

"Keeping it Under Wraps" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published as a bonus story in the second edition of his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Tenoka Press in 2017.

### Synopsis
Arkham private detective Wade Kearney takes on a case for former Miskatonic University faculty member Professor Kearney, who has accidentally managed to reanimate a murderous mummy during the course of his researches. After tracking the mummy to its hiding place in a pit of quicksand, Kearney is able to destroy the malevolent being by blowing it up with a canister of gasoline.

*Wade Kearney is a recurrent character in the Mythos works of Ron Shiflet, having first appeared in the short story "Unfinished Business" in July 2006.

Daniels died on 18 December 2001 in Ridgecrest, California. His passing was described as "premature."

Keith Donald "Doc" Herber (3 January 1949 - 23 March 2009) was an American game designer, author, editor and musician.

### Overview
A professional bass guitarist who has written both gaming supplements and novels for White Wolf Publishing, Keith Herber's relevance to the Cthulhu Mythos is his work on the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium. Already a freelance writer for Chaosium, he joined the staff in 1989 and worked as the Call of Cthulhu line editor for the next five years until his departure in 1994; however, even after leaving the company Herber continued to provide additional material for the game through until 2008.

Herber was also the co-founder, with Tom Lynch, of the now-defunct Miskatonic River Press, an independent publisher established in 2008 which specialised in Lovecraftian gaming material and fiction.

Ken Asamatsu (born 1956) is a prolific Japanese horror writer and editor who played a key role in popularizing the Cthulhu Mythos with a Japanese audiences. His Lairs of the Hidden Gods anthologies, in turn, have brought Japanese Lovecraftian Horror to the English-speaking public.

Asamatsu encountered the legacy of H. P. Lovecraft when he visited Providence, Rhode Island, as a teenager and read The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. “I was stunned by the way it pulled me in, and its superb structure,” he later told an interviewer. “I felt that Lovecraft would be my mentor and guide in literature for the rest of my life.”

Asamatsu and his friends published a Lovecraft-related fanzine while still in high school. Realizing that not all of Lovecraft's fiction was available in Japanese, Asamatsu and his friends launched a project to translate the missing stories.  Later, working for the publishing house Kokusho Kankokai, he helped oversee an official complete translation of Lovecraft’s work. English-speakers can also read Asamatsu's collection of interconnected Mythos stories dealing with World War II, Kthulhu Reich (Kurodahan Press, 2019).

Asamatsu has published two Mythos-related anthologies, Hishin (1999) and Hishinkai (2002). The latter, which also includes essays on Lovecraftian topics, was published in English as a four-volume series called Lairs of the Hidden Gods, with introductions by Robert M. Price.

shortDefinition: Kenneth Grant (23 May 1924 – 15 January 2011) was an English ceremonial magician and prominent advocate of the Thelemite religion. A poet, novelist, and writer, he founded his own Thelemite organisation, the Typhonian Ordo Templi Orientis later renam...
fullContent:
Kenneth Grant (23 May 1924 – 15 January 2011) was an English ceremonial magician and prominent advocate of the Thelemite religion. A poet, novelist, and writer, he founded his own Thelemite organisation, the Typhonian Ordo Templi Orientis later renamed the Typhonian Order with his wife Steffi Grant.

Born in Ilford, Essex, Grant developed an interest in occultism and Asian religion during his teenage years. After several months serving in India with the British Army amid the Second World War, he returned to Britain and became the personal secretary of Aleister Crowley, the ceremonial magician who had founded Thelema in 1904. Crowley instructed Grant in his esoteric practices, initiating him into his own occult order, the Ordo Templi Orientis (O.T.O.). When Crowley died in 1947, Grant was seen as his heir apparent in Britain, and was appointed as such by the American head of the O.T.O., Karl Germer. Founding the London based New Isis Lodge in 1954, Grant added to many of Crowley's Thelemite teachings, bringing in extraterrestrial themes and influences from the work of H. P. Lovecraft. This was anathema to Germer, who expelled Grant from the O.T.O. in 1955, although the latter continued to operate his Lodge regardless until 1962.

In 1949, Grant befriended the occult artist Austin Osman Spare, and in ensuing years helped to publicise Spare's artwork through a series of publications. During the 1950s he also came to be increasingly interested in Hinduism, exploring the teachings of the Hindu guru Ramana Maharshi and publishing a range of articles on the topic. He was particularly interested in the Hindu tantra, incorporating ideas from it into the Thelemic practices of sex magic. On Germer's death in 1969, Grant proclaimed himself Outer Head of the O.T.O.; this title was disputed by the American Grady McMurtry, who took control of the O.T.O. Grant's Order became known as the Typhonian Ordo Templi Orientis, operating from his Golders Green home. In 1959 he began publishing on the subject of occultism, and proceeded to author the Typhonian Trilogies, as well as a number of novels, books of poetry, and publications devoted to propagating the work of Crowley and Spare.

Grant's writings and teachings have proved a significant influence over other currents of occultism, including chaos magic, the Temple of Set and the Dragon Rouge. They also attracted academic interest within the study of Western esotericism, particularly from Henrik Bogdan and Dave Evans.

fullContent:
Kenneth J. Sterling (1920–1995), was an American medical doctor and science fiction author best known for his collaboration with Howard Phillips Lovecraft in the short story "In the Walls of Eryx". He was a young man when when he first crossed paths with Lovecraft in 1934. 

In January of 1936 Sterling shared his draft of a story with H. P. Lovecraft while he was a medical student in Providence. The story was rewritten and published after Lovecraft's death in the Weird Tales of October 1939. This collaboration would be Lovecraft's only interplanetary science fiction story.

There are numerous indications of a certain attitude that contrasted with Lovecraft's. Sterling insisted that Lovecraft also have a by-line when the story was published — in Weird Tales about two years after Lovecraft's death. As "In the Walls of Eryx" comes to a close the protagonist remarks:

This type of progressive thinking presages the culturally reflective storytelling of the 1950s and 60s, and is extremely out of character for a Lovecraft story. Considering Lovecraft's notorious classist and racist attitudes, such sentiments are stark indeed. Reflecting upon Lovecraft's change of heart regarding socialism, due to his interactions and arguments with Robert E. Howard, it is interesting to imagine what impact an extended correspondence with Sterling might have had on Lovecraft.

As of 1952, Sterling had become a physician and was involved in cancer research.
