shortDefinition: Kenneth W. Faig, Jr. (born 24 August 1948) is an American author and literary critic from Cincinnati, Ohio, who specialises in the life and works of H. P. Lovecraft. and is particularly well known for his in-depth research into the friends and family...
fullContent:
Kenneth W. Faig, Jr. (born 24 August 1948) is an American author and literary critic from Cincinnati, Ohio, who specialises in the life and works of H. P. Lovecraft. and is particularly well known for his in-depth research into the friends and family of Lovecraft, an aspect of Lovecraft scholarship which has otherwise been largely ignored. Active in the field since the 1970s, he has worked extensively with the Esoteric Order of Dagon amateur press association, and has collaborated with fellow scholar S. T. Joshi, who has also published Faig's work in his journal Lovecraft Annual.

Faig first encountered the amateur press community, of which Lovecraft himself was such an active part, in the 1970s. Eventually, Faig won the 2012 Russell L. Paxton Award for his amateur press research related to Lovecraft. In 2014, Faig was made president of The Fossils, the community organization of historians and archivists of the American amateur press publications which he joined in the 1990s. The group is named after the term used for the original founders of amateur press publications in the United States.

In addition to his scholarly work, Faig has written a small number of fiction pieces; these have appeared in Tales of the Lovecraft Collectors and Lovecraft's Pillow and Other Strange Stories, collections of his own stories, as well as the fanzines Eldritch Tales and The Black Book. He was also a semi-regular contributor to the Crypt of Cthulhu letters page.

Faig was the founder of the now-defunct small press Moshassuck Press, group which he published his own work, as well as that of others including Dirk W. Mosig and Duane W. Rimel.

Kenton J. Stanfield is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft and Kenneth Sterling for their science fiction short story "In the Walls of Eryx". The story is set at an unspecified point in the future, 72 years after the first humans landed on Venus.

### Overview
Operative A-49, Kenton J. Stanfield, is a prospector employed by the Crystal Company as one of several agents whose mission is to find and collect the rare spheroid crystals in the poisonous jungles of Venus, clashing with the native Venusians who view the crystals as objects to be venerated, not taken. Stanfield's address is given as 5317 Marshall Street, Richmond, Virginia. He is level-headed, practical, and not the least bit superstitious. His physical appearance isn't described, save for the fact that he has a full head of thick hair.

Stanfield initially dismissed the Venusians as unintelligent creatures, claiming that their cities are merely the equivalent of ant-hills or beaver dams, and expressing frustration over the fact that they defend the valuable crystals without having any use for them outside of their religion, while the humans use them as a power source. His opinion changed after he came upon an invisible solid building in the Venusian plateau of Eryx.

Stanfield ventured inside to explore the building, without realising that it was, in fact, a labyrinth. For the next three days, he tried to map out the invisible structure and escape, but the complexity of the task combined with a dwindling supply of oxygen, water, and food tablets resulted in failure and death, tragically only a few hours before his rescue arrived. In his final log recorded shortly before death, Stanfield pleaded with his fellow humans to stop collecting the Venusian crystals and leave the planet's inhabitants alone, as he felt that humanity had "violated some obscure and mysterious law" in their attempts to take them.

Stanfield's body was retrieved from the labyrinth and buried in the company's graveyard. After his log was examined, the corporation decided to employ armed forces against the Venusians instead of following Stanfield's suggestion, which they interpreted as a dying delirium. (: "In the Walls of Eryx")

Keris McDonald, who often goes by the pseudonym Janine Ashbless, is a British author, traditional games designer, and current associate editor for Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Her Cthulhu Mythos-related output includes material for the games Call of Cthulhu and The Cthulhu Hack, as well as being one of three authors, along with Adam Gauntlett and Adrian Tchaikovsky, whose works are collected in the 2016 Alchemy Press anthology The Private Life of Elder Things.

McDonald's non-Mythos output includes material for Chaosium’s Rivers of London roleplaying game, perhaps unsurprising given her love of the Victorian setting, as well as a number of novels and numerous short stories.

The Kester Library is a fictional institution created by Henry Kuttner for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Salem Horror".

Located in the town of Salem, Massachusetts, the Kester Library is notable for containing a number of rare grimoires, including the Necronomicon (: "The Salem Horror"), although theirs is an incomplete copy from the 15th Century black-letter edition from Germany (: "The Fishers from Outside"), not nearly as valuable as the complete version found in Miskatonic University's library.

The Kester Library also has the original Ponape Scripture found by Captain Abner Exekiel Hoag, as well as the English translation made by Hoag's Deep One hybrid servant, Yogash. (: "Out of the Ages", "The Fishers from Outside")

A copy of the Book of Eibon, apparently in English, can also be found in the library. (: "The Fishers from Outside")

In 1946, the Curator of Manuscripts at the Kester Library was an amiable fellow named Prof. Edwin Winslow Arnold. (: "The Fishers from Outside")

Kevin James Anderson (born 27 March 1962) is a prolific American science fiction author and editor who wrote the Cthulhu Mythos story "20,000 Years Under the Sea", featuring Jules Verne's character Captain Nemo as reimagined in Anderson's novel Captain Nemo: The Fantastic History of a Dark Genius.

With a long and varied career, Anderson has contributed stories in the form of novels, short tales and comic books to a large number of science fiction franchises, including The X-Files, Dune, Star Wars, The War of the Worlds, Star Trek, Titan A.E., Superman, StarCraft, and Predator.

### Overview
Kick-starting his career by sending original Call of Cthulhu material to Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu line editor Sandy Petersen, Kevin Ross was assisted in this venture by the patronage of the now-deceased Keith Herber, another long-time games designer. Although Ross has spent the lion's share of his time devoted to Call of Cthulhu, he has also produced fantasy content in the form of the Conan roleplaying game from Modiphius Entertainment, and has written a small number of fictional works based within the Mythos.

The Keys of the Eternal Gates are fictional items in the Dynamite universe which first appeared in 2019 in the 1st issue of 1st volume of the Bettie Page: Unbound comic book series.

### Background
The Keys of the Eternal Gates are powerful sorcerous artefacts, of which there are five, all of which can fit in the palm of a human's hand, and are attached to a necklace. Each is able to open a portal to summon one of the Great Old Ones. Together they can release them from their dimensional prisons or imprison the Old Ones. They are scattered across time, space, and dimensions with one of them on Earth, the Tunguska Star (aka, The Sorcerer's Star).

Keyport, New Jersey, is a fictionalised town in the United States. It has featured in a number of expanded Cthulhu Mythos stories, and is the primary setting for Armand Rosamilia's Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Overview
A small town on the shore of New Jersey, Keyport's primary industry appears to be fishing. It is a decrepit and backwards place, many of its buildings being rotten and hiding a labyrinthine network of tunnels and cellars beneath the ground.

Keyport is under the sway of the Esoteric Order of Dagon, a cult which came to town from Innsmouth, Massachusetts. Despite the Order's name, they are dedicated to bringing about the return of the Great Old One Cthulhu.

### Places of Note

### Broad Street Pub
A 150-year-old bar that has seemingly not been renovated in decades. It has been in the Murphy family for nine generations, with the eldest son of each generation taking on ownership, along with the name Dylan Murphy.

The Broad Street Pub also functions as the meeting point and perhaps headquarters of the Keyport branch of the Esoteric Order of Dagon, with the current Dylan Murphy being the cult's leader.

### Keyport Bay
Keyport's industrial heart, if such a thing could be said of the town. The bay area incorporates extensive docks and is home to Keyport Fishery.

Keyport Bay is also home to a sleeping leviathan, said to be Cthulhu himself.

### Behind the Mythos
Keyport was created by American author Armand Rosamilia for his short story "Ancient" in 2012. It is a fictionalised version of a real-world location, with the elements of decay and degeneracy exaggerated for dramatic effect.

The first edition of Keyport Cthulhu, published in November 2013, contained the five stories which form the first part of Rosamilia's Keyport Cthulhu story cycle, along with an additional related story, and an unrelated children's story co-written with his daughter.

The Revised and Expanded edition was released in 2017. This featured all of the stories from the original edition along with an additional two from Chuck Buda.

Both versions were released in paperback and digital formats.

Keyport Cthulhu is an expanded Mythos story cycle created by American author Armand Rosamilia.

Begun in 2012 with the publication of the short story "Ancient" Keyport Cthulhu has, as of October 2022, amassed a total of three volumes of stories.

It follows a disparate group of people who band together to put a stop to the Keyport branch of the Esoteric Order of Dagon and their plans to awaken the Great Old One Cthulhu. The final story in this chapter ends on a cliffhanger, with Cthulhu implied to be in the process of awakening.

Keziah Mason is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dreams in the Witch-House". She is depicted as being a witch who studied the secrets of inter-dimensional travel.

### Biography
During the Salem witch trials of 1692, an old woman by the name of Keziah Mason was arrested for her suspicious behavior and seeming insight into other worlds. In her testimony to Judge John Hathorne, she confessed to having signed her name in the Book of Azathoth under the influence of the Black Man, and to taking her secret name of Nahab. During her trial she spoke of "lines and curves that could be made to point out directions leading through the walls of space to other spaces beyond...." and when she later disappeared mysteriously from Salem gaol "curves and angles (were) smeared on the grey stone walls with some red, sticky fluid" that were inexplicable even to Cotton Mather.

It was eventually found that by signing the Book of Azathoth she was able to enter a higher dimension to gain knowledge and serve Nyarlathotep. Student physicist Walter Gilman believed that Mason--"a mediocre old woman of the Seventeenth Century"—had developed "an insight into mathematical depths perhaps beyond the utmost modern delvings of Planck, Heisenberg, Einstein, and De Sitter." When he took a room in her house she revealed to him that same knowledge in the hopes of taking his soul.

She is described as having a "bent back, long nose, and shrivelled chin" and has a "croaking voice".

She has an animal familiar; the rat-creature Brown Jenkin, which she trusts to carry messages between her and the Black Man. She feeds this creature on her own blood.

### Behind the Mythos
Critics have noted with some surprise that Mason is "struck with panic" at the sight of a crucifix. (: The Azathoth Cycle [ Price ]) While some have called this overblown and ridiculous, especially considering that H. P. Lovecraft was a lifelong atheist, some have taken a different perspective, saying that Keziah might've been psychologically damaged by the tortures inflicted upon her by the men of the cloth in her time, or that she was simply surprised to see that a sharp metal object had been thrust towards her face.

Khalk'ru is a fictional extra-dimensional creature created by Abraham Merritt for his novel Dwellers in the Mirage.

### Description
This dark octopoid horror is worshiped as a god by the Uighur people who inhabit the Gobi Desert, and whose ancestors migrated to both Europe (giving rise to the Norse people and their legends of the Kraken) and to Alaska, where they settled within a hidden warm valley, unknown to the outside world.

Khalk'ru can be summoned from its native dimension by a mysterious ring bearing its image. When summoned, it will be offered sacrifices, generally in the form of young women whose bodies are consumed entirely. Although Khalk'ru's followers treat it as a single deity, Leif Langdon speculates that there might be several such creatures, any of which might appear to answer the summoning.

While Langdon has expressed doubts about how powerful Khalk'ru actually is, its followers believe that it is a force of chaos and entropy, antagonistic to the very principle of life, and that it was responsible for turning the formerly lush lands of the Gobi into the desert that it is today. (: Dwellers in the Mirage)

### Connection to the Mythos
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia suggests that Khalk'ru, as an "extra-dimensional octopus demon," may be "an analogue to Cthulhu."

Khephren (c. [tel:2600-2532 2600-2532] BCE) is a real-life pharaoh of Ancient Egypt in the 4th dynasty who was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos via H. P. Lovecraft's fiction (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs"), which took some liberties with the historical facts.

Khephren (also Chephren) is the Greek form of the pharaoh's name, which is more properly Khafre or Khafra.  He is not to be confused with Khephnes, a fictional Egyptian possessed by a Yithian, who by Lovecraft's chronology lived a thousand years later.

Khafre is credited by some with building the Second Pyramid and the Great Sphinx, whose face is thought by some to have been carved in his likeness. His statue in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo is "one of the most important and iconic surviving sculptures from ancient Egypt."

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
According to Lovecraft (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs"), Khephren built the Second Pyramid shortly after 2800 BCE. He restored (rather than constructed) the statue of the Great Sphinx; its face was "probably altered to form a colossal portrait" of Khephren, "that men might look at the colossus without fear." He also built the Temple of the Sphinx, a "yawning gateway temple" in which was found a life-size diorite statue of Khephren that was moved to the Cairo Museum. 

It's said that Khephren still "lives far underground wedded to the ghoul-queen Nitokris and ruling over the mummies that are neither of man nor of beast." 

On one occasion, he posed as a tourist guide named Abdul Reis el Drogman, and under that identity kidnapped Harry Houdini to see if the famed magician's magic tricks could escape more ancient traps than those of modern men.

Khosatral Khel (The Ancient from the Abyss) is a fictional entity created by Robert E. Howard for his short story "The Devil in Iron". The character also appears in the adaptation by Marvel Comics, which was published in Savage Sword of Conan #15.

According to some accounts, Khosatral Khel is the spawn of Dagon. (: Official Handbook of the Marvel Universe A to Z Vol 1 3)

### Background
Khosatral Khel was an extra-dimensional entity that originated from the abyss and darkness, and entered the physical universe. Human flesh was incapable of holding its lifeforce therefore it used matter to create itself a body, a blasphemous form. For millennia, it traveled across the world as humans ineffectually attacked him. It eventually found the primitives living on the island of Dagonia. He brought them civilization and with his assistance they built the city of Dagonia. Human sacrifices were offered to him by the priests. 

Some time later, their was a slave rebellion led by a priest armed with a knife that was forged from a meteor, which negated Khosatral Khel's magic, and when stabbed by it, became immobile and senseless. The slaves slaughtered the Dagonians and took over the city. A fisherman would years later remove the knife from Khosatral Khel, reviving him. Using necromancy it restored the city and its inhabitants. Later it would encounter Conan which killed it, using the magical dagger.

"Kickstarter" is a tongue-in-cheek Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Richard Lee Byers, first published the the anthology Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be by 01Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
As its title might suggest, the story is written as an online Kickstarter campaign in which members of Dunwich's Whateley family are attempting to raise funds to awaken Great Cthulhu. As with genuine Kickstarter campaigns, it includes what the money would be spent on, backer rewards and stretch goals. Only $37 had been raised of the $400,000 goal, with eleven days still to go.

### Publication History
Following its debut in Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2, "Kickstarter" was included in the collection of Byers' own works The Hep Cats of Ulthar and Other Lovecraftian Tales in May 2018.

Kilderry is a fictional village created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Moon-Bog". In Irish Gaelic derived place names, Kilderry is transliterated from the Irish name "Cill Doire," which translates to "church of the oak." The prefix "Cill" means "church," while "Doire" refers to "oak," indicating a historical connection to a church or religious site located in an oak grove. The use of "oak" in the name suggests the importance of oak trees in Irish mythology and history, often associated with strength and endurance.

### Description
Located in County Meath, Ireland, Kilderry was the village to which Denys Barry relocated after emigrating from America. There he bought and restored the old ancestral castle that had belonged to his family in generations past. It was there also that he met his demise at the vengeful hands of supernatural forces when he attempted to drain a haunted bog on his property. Kilderry is located near the village of Ballylough. (: "The Moon-Bog")

Kim James Newman is a prolific British author, editor and film critic whose works fall for the most part into the science fiction, fantasy and horror genres. He has written several full-length novels under the pen name Jack Yeovil, the majority of these as tie-ins for British wargames manufacturer Games Workshop, and frequently collaborates with Stephen Jones in editorial projects. King of Chicago & The Secrets of Marseilles is a scenario supplement book for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. It boasted the tagline "Prohibition, a Gangland Murder, the Casbah of Marseilles, Black Market Weapons."

### Overview
The bulk of the content of King of Chicago is taken up by two stand-alone scenarios thematically linked through interaction with a criminal element, although it also contains a short piece on the state of organised crime in 1920s America and a longer article on the black market, with rules for new weapons.

King of Chicago was edited by Keith Herber and Lynn Willis, and written by Gary Sumpter, Ugo Bardi and Earl Geier. It runs to a total of 64 pages in a softcover black-and-white book.

### Scenarios
* "King of Chicago":  the investigators must solve the murder of a colleague in the criminal underworld of Chicago.
* "The Secrets of Marseilles": where the investigators get caught in the middle of a gangland war in the French port of Marseilles.

### Publication History
King of Chicago was published by Chaosium in April 1994. It is currently out of print.

shortDefinition: The King of Tears is a Lovecraftian-like chaotic entity in the fictional DC universe by DC Comics.  ### Background The King of Tears is the god of the Subtle Realms. Dimensions beyond those which man perceives. Which are inhabited by entities, whom w...
fullContent:
The King of Tears is a Lovecraftian-like chaotic entity in the fictional DC universe by DC Comics.

### Background
The King of Tears is the god of the Subtle Realms. Dimensions beyond those which man perceives. Which are inhabited by entities, whom were cast aside when creation was formalized by the creator. In the mid 20th century he was summoned to Earth by Johnny Sorrow, which the Justice Society of America battled. Not even Spectre could destroy it, though he was able to transform the entity. Capturing its essence which the Green Lantern (Alan Scott) then contained. 

Decades later, Johnny Sorrow summoned it back to Earth again. To enter the universe the entities needed vessels, but Johnny Sorrow was going to make it so that they no longer required that. Manhattan was attacked by a swarm of giant insects which slaughtered and consumed many, until they were stopped by the JSA. Meanwhile the King of Tears manifested on Earth, with skyscraper-sized, tornado like winds surrounding it and creating a steadily expanding labyrinth of skyscraper-tall pillars. He was feasting on everything organic it encountered. Which was stopped by JSA upon their defeat of Johnny Sorrow.

Years later it was once again summoned to earth by Johnny Sorrow and the Injustice Society, who this time planned to enslave the King of Tears. It once again battled the Justice Society of America. Dr. Fate sent Anna Fortune to help the JSA stop the entity and in the process she accidentally released the King of Tears, bringing the Subtle Realms to Earth. It's heart exploded when stabbed by Stargirl.

### King of Tears
Within the Subtle Realms it is nigh omnipotent, the god of the entities who were banished to that dimension. It has the ability to alter reality around it and bestow powers on others. Johnny Sorrow was given an Eldritch power, in which anyone that sees his true face falls dead, thereby requiring him to wear a mask. The King of Tears lacks a soul, has no conscience, and does not feel guilt. A force of pure evil, though a blind, idiot god that without someone to guide was a rudderless god. It can't be killed and it takes nearly godlike power to stop the entity.

Kingsport is a fictional town created by H. P. Lovecraft, an archaic seaside village in Massachusetts that serves as an integral part of Lovecraft Country. It is the setting of many stories, including "The Festival" and "The Strange High House in the Mist".

### Geography
North of Kingsport is a famous stretch of cliffs that break at the Kingsport Head for the mouth of the Miskatonic River before following the coast up just short of the Manuxet in Innsmouth. Other named cliffs include Father Neptune and The Causeway.

### History
In the early 19th century, local fishermen sailed their sloops to Innsmouth, following rumours of fish swarming the harbour, but they never returned. (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth)

### Locations
*Water Street - The seafront home of the Terrible Old Man. (: "The Terrible Old Man")
*Ship Street - A road of tiny gambrel-roofed homes parallel to Water Street.
*Hall School
*The Strange High House in the Mist - An infamous house atop Kingsport Head, visible from both Kingsport and the northern road into Innsmouth.

### Residents
*Granny Orne - An old woman who lives on Ship Street.
*Asenath Waite - A student at the Hall School who later moved to Arkham after marrying Edward Derby.
*Thomas Olney - A professor who spent a summer in Kingsport.
*Basil Elton - A lighthouse keeper who has traveled through the Dreamlands. (: "The White Ship", The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

### Expanded Mythos
*The Kingsport Horror expansion for the board game Arkham Horror centres around players travelling to Kingsport.

### In Other Media
Kingsport is also the name of the supernatural town featured in Carl Jacobi's short story "Chameleon Town", published in the Arkham House anthology Nameless Places. Jacobi's Kingsport is located somewhere in the USA's East Coast, apparently to the south of New York, and is also known by the alternative name Kingsboro. It's unknown if this is intended to be the same Kingsport from the Cthulhu Mythos, but characters who visited it have witnessed scenes from the past (apparently a form of "psychic residue"), similar to what the narrator experiences in Lovecraft's "The Festival".

The Kingsport Horror Deluxe Expansion was the fourth supplement released for Fantasy Flight Games' Second Edition of Arkham Horror, the board game of Lovecraftian adventure.

### Overview
One of the big-box expansions, Kingsport Horror included the standard additional Investigator cards featuring new Items, Skills, Spells and Allies, more Ancient One cards which put a unique spin on the core game, and a host of other tokens and game paraphernalia.

Kingsport Horror was notable for introducing the Guardian mechanic to games of Arkham Horror, representing entities willing to lend their assistance against the awakening Ancient Ones. This functioned in exactly the same way as the Herald mechanic but with beneficial effects for the players, whereas Heralds were actively detrimental.

The most major change offered by the Kingsport Horror expansion however, was the inclusion of an additional game board which allowed players to travel from Arkham to new locations in Kingsport, either via the Train Station, or through using one of a number of vehicles represented by Item cards. This opened up a number of different opportunities to those who had grown weary of Arkham, and radically changed the way the game played overall.

fullContent:
Kishin Houkou Demonbane is the second installment of the Demonbane Mythos franchise by Nitroplus. It was released on July 1, 2004 for the PlayStation 2 and later ported to the PC on April 26, 2019. The game is an all-ages remake version of the first visual novel, removing all the H-scenes and adding newly written content.

A 24-minute special OVA was included in the limited DX and KADOKAWA THE Best version of the PS2 pack. 

### Mythos Connections
Most of the references can be found in Deus Machina Demonbane but this version has some new ones including:
*Chapter 8: THE THING THAT WALKED ON THE WIND
**Daijuuji Kurou and Cthugha are transported to the Wood of N'gai where they encounter three avatars of Nyarlathotep: a formless monster that howls with clawed tentacles that can grow infinitely, the darkness with three burning eyes and a large shimmering tree with golden tendrils. Much like in August Derleth's original story, the forest is eventually destroyed by Cthugha. This scene was completely rewritten as in the original version, Kurou was raped by both Cthugha and Ithaqua. 
**Nyarlathotep is referred to as the "Mighty Messenger", an alias that was used in Robert Bloch's short story "Fane of the Black Pharaoh".
** References to the "Ygnaiih" chant used for Yog-Sothoth, the World of Seven Suns and The Black Goat in the Woods with a Thousand Young can also be heard in the forest. 
*Chapter 15: STRANGE EONS (Al Azif route)
**At the beginning of the chapter, there is a title that reads "The Compleat Daijuuji Kurou FINAL", a reference to Brian Lumley's anthology The Compleat Crow.
**In the original version, the Demonbane trio used the Scimitar of Barzai to trace Master Therion after they entered Yog-Sothoth's gate; however, it was replaced by Zhar and Lloigor in this version.

fullContent:
Kishin Houkou Demonbane is an anime television series based on the Demonbane Mythos. It was produced by Wowow and first aired in 2006. The storyline is an adaptation of the visual novel Kishin Houkou Demonbane, featuring a compressed version of Al Azif's route.

### Synopsis
### Episode 1: I AM PROVIDENCE
While desperate for money living in Arkham City, private investigator Daijuuji Kurou got hired by Hadou Ruri of the Hadou Estate to find a grimoire to activate her Deus Machina known as Demonbane. During his search, Kurou visited a mysterious bookstore where he met the owner Nya. Although Nya couldn't sell any grimoires to him, she informed Kurou that he will find one that is fit for him in the near future. Nya turned out to be correct, as Kurou had an encounter with Al Azif, the humanoid manifestation of the Necronomicon. Weakened without a sorcerer, Al used Kurou to form a pact with her, turning him into a powerful sorcerer and her new master to combat the Black Lodge. Doctor West was one of the Black Lodge members who wanted to capture Al for his master, bringing his Destroyer Robot to attack her and Kurou. In retaliation, Al would summon Demonbane.

### Episode 2: EVIL SHINE
Now piloting Demonbane, Kurou and Al managed to defeat West's Destroyer Robot. After their battle, Kurou abandoned Al by quickly driving off, not wanting to get involved with her conflicts any further. Back at the Black Lodge, Master Therion went out to go search for the new master of the Necronomicon. The next day, Kurou visited the church run by his friend Leica Crusade so he can get a free meal from her. Unbeknownst to him, Al followed Kurou all the way there and the two of them were confronted by Master Therion. When Master Therion attacked Leica, Kurou began to attack him out of rage. After Kurou summoned Demonbane, Master Therion eventually summoned his grimoire the Pnakotic Manuscripts, which took the form of a human girl named Etheldreda, who was able to defeat Demonbane with a single attack due to Al's power being incomplete from her missing pages. Realizing the full extent of the Black Lodge's depravity, Kurou agreed to help Al fight against them before they can hurt anyone else. Meanwhile, Ruri and her butler Winfield found out that it was Kurou who had been using Demonbane without their permission.

### Episode 3: REANINATOR 
Back at his laboratory, West completed his newest invention: an android girl named Elsa. Meanwhile, Kurou and Al began to collect her missing pages, including a fragment that took the form of a spider-woman monster named Atlach-Nacha. However, Ruri scolded them for repeatedly destroying the city during their conflicts, threatening to take away Demonbane if they cause any more collateral damage. Not wanting to continue the argument, Kurou went off with Al to retrieve more of her missing pages so that her power can be at its full potential.

Kishin Houkou Demonbane is a 2004 OVA episode set in the Demonbane Mythos by Nitroplus. It was accompanied with the limited DX and KADOKAWA THE Best version of the eponymous visual novel, taking place at some point during the main story.

### Synopsis
After arriving in Arkham City, aspiring photojournalist Lilli M. Bridge got a job at the Daily Arkham, a newspaper publisher that was looking for pictures of the giant robot Demonbane to include in their articles. Lilli tries to interview several of the residents including Leica Crusade, Lieutenant Stone and Daijuuji Kurou, but has little to no success at getting any information. When she encounters Al Azif in an area that was restricted by the Hadou Financial Group, Lilli discovers a mysterious piece of alloy as well as successfully photographing Al's missing fragments, known as Zhar and Lloigor. Lilli was nearly attacked by the fragments before being rescued by Kurou.

Back at the Daily Arkham, Lilli's boss had no interest in Zhar and Lloigor, referring to it as an "insignificant occult incident" and scolds her for not getting photos of Demonbane instead. However, the alloy that she retrieved was speculated to be created by the Hadou Financial Group, leading to Lilli coming to the conclusion that the organization must have some connection to Demonbane. Partnered with Kurou, Lilli fails to gain more information by questioning the group leader Hadou Ruri, with the Daily Arkham also encouraging her to not pursue any articles involving their organization's activity. Depressed and disappointed, Lilli got drunk while hanging out with Kurou, who warned her to not get any closer to the "dark realm".

Ignoring his warnings, Lilli decides to visit the restricted area again, where she would accidentally get caught in one of Doctor West's traps. Although the trap was actually meant for Zhar and Lloigor, West set his sights on using Lilli for human experiments but was interrupted by Kurou, knocking West out of the way and freeing Lilli. Shortly afterwards, Al arrives to assist Kurou and retrieve her missing fragments before they get into a confrontation with a Destroyer Robot piloted by West and his android girl Elsa. While piloting Demonbane, Kurou and Al defeated the Destroyer Robot by chopping its limbs off with Zhar and Lloigor, before it was completely obliterated by their finishing move Lemuria Impact.

### Mythos Connections
*Lilli M. Bridge's name is derived from Edwin M. Lillibrige. 
*One of the employees at the Daily Arkham was named Blake, a reference to Robert Blake.

The Kitsune (multi-tailed fox spirits) are part of Chinese and Japanese folklore, with the Japanese version (kitsune) being the most well known in the West. In 2005 they were first used as a fictional race by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu RPG.

### Background
The Kitsune first appeared in China and over time migrated to Korea and then Japan. They are elementals spirits from an alien planet that due to the predations of the dholes became a lifeless world. When Mu was destroyed and the dimensional gates were opened, they were drawn to Earth by its teeming lifeforce, where they manifested as animal-like beings. If they manifest in their true form, their unnatural presence becomes a blight on the Earth, draining the lifeforce from neighboring beings.

It's a race which is neither benevolent or malevolent, which has its own code of ethics and usually camouflage themselves with human customs. Mercurial beings who are as likely to antagonize as befriend humans, they never stray from their core personality. To those whom they judge incorrect in their actions, they become malevolent, evil, and destructive. On the other hand, to those whom they judge good, they are helpful, gentle, and polite. They can live up to 900 years and upon dying either reincarnate as a different being or return to the spirit world.

Kitsune have three forms, which are those of a Japanese fox, a lupine humanoid form with a fox head, and that of an extremely attractive human. Their true form is that of a 5f tall stalk that has approximately 20 tentacles, most of which are flattened close to the body like tangled hair. Topping each of the tentacles is a small orb. Kitsune feed on Chi and life force and can possess humans and fox cubs. By rubbing their tails together they can create an energy ball of fire or lightning which is used as a weapon, and they can also breathe fire.

Klarkash-Ton the Hierophant is a character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft as a fictional version of his close friend Clark Ashton Smith.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In The Whisperer in Darkness (1931), Henry Akeley (or a Mi-Go posing as him) mentions that the god Tsathoggua is mentioned in the "Commoriom myth-cycle preserved by the Atlantean high-priest Klarkash-Ton." This is an homage to Smith on multiple levels, in that both Tsathoggua and the Hyperborean city of Commoriom were creations of Smith, who also wrote stories set in Poseidonis, depicted as the last remnant of Atlantis.

The name Klarkash-Ton also appears in "The Battle That Ended the Century" (1934), a parody of boxing reporting Lovecraft wrote with R. H. Barlow, set in the then-distant year 2000. It mentions that an account of the titular boxing match was illustrated by the "well-known artist Klarkash-Ton (who esoterically depicted the fighters as boneless fungi)."

### In Other Writing
In Robert M. Price's short story "The Incubus of Atlantis" (1998), Klarkash-Ton the Heirophant is a high priest of Zhothaqquah in the lost realm of Atlantis. He is engaged by the Philosopher King Pharnabazus to chronicle the history of his land. 

Price depicts Klarkash-Ton as the reincarnation of the powerful Hyperborean magician Eibon--another of Smith's creations--his soul saved over and over by his lord Zhothaqquah in order to continue his service.

Lieutenant Klenze is a fictional character in the story "The Temple" by H. P. Lovecraft. 

### Background
Lieutenant Klenze was a lieutenant and second-in-command serving aboard the German submarine U-29 under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich during the First World War. At the culmination of the supernatural events experienced by the crew of the submarine, Klenze and Heinrich were the only men aboard left alive by the time the disabled U-29 came to rest among the underwater ruins of an Atlantean city. Klenze eventually went mad and took his own life by exiting the submarine. (: "The Temple")

Knull is a fictional entity created by Marvel Comics. The character first appeared in Thor: God of Thunder Vol 1 #6 "What the Gods Have Wrought" (2013), though he was unnamed and served as nothing more than a plot device for how Gorr acquired the eldritch sword known as All-Black. Knull was greatly expanded upon by writer Donny Cates in the fourth volume of Venom (2018), which revealed his backstory and role in the creation of the symbiotes.

### Background
Before the creation of the universe, Knull was a dark Elder God who slumbered in the void. Awakened by the Big Bang, he was enraged to see the Celestials despoiling his kingdom and created the All-Black, a sword made of living darkness, in order to combat them.

As the millennia passed, Knull declared war on the Celestials and their creations, amassing a horde of draconic monsters and symbiotes - amorphous parasites formed from living darkness. Knull lost the All-Black in battle, but discovered he could bond his symbiotes to mortal lifeforms in order to control them. However, his connection to his horde was severed when one of his symbiote dragons, known as the Grendel, arrived on Earth and was attacked by the storm-god Thor Odinson. The symbiotes, freed from his control, rebelled and imprisoned him in the core of Klyntar, an artificial planet formed from billions of themselves.

On Earth, a cult dedicated to reviving Knull was formed, and in the 1960s, the Grendel was unearthed by the government agency S.H.I.E.L.D., which sought to weaponize the symbiotes during the Vietnam War. In the 21st century, Knull seized control of the Grendel and attempted to use it to free himself, but was foiled by the symbiote-augmented antihero Venom. However, a piece of the Grendel was obtained by the cult, who used it to resurrect the symbiote-augmented serial killer Carnage. Pledging himself to Knull, Carnage began hunting down all the former symbiote hosts in order to restore the Grendel symbiote to its full power and awaken the sleeping god. 

Awakened by Carnage's symbiote being absorbed by Venom, Knull destroyed Klyntar and seized control of the symbiotes, resuming his conquest of the universe.

### Powers and Abilities
As a primordial god of darkness, Knull controls a force he calls the "Living Abyss" - which he uses to create his symbiotes and other minions. He is strong enough to decapitate a Celestial, and can slaughter entire armies of gods singlehandedly. His presence corrupts symbiotes, bending them to his will and turning them evil.

### Weaknesses
Knull is vulnerable to a force he calls "the Light", which is embodied by all living things but especially potent in deities. He is also vulnerable to electricity, with Thor's divine lightning and Miles Morales' bioelectric Venom Blast disrupting his control over his symbiotes.

Knygathin Zhaum is a creature created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his Hyperborean Cycle series of fantasy tales.

### Description


This is how Zhaum is first described, but as it continues to be beheaded and resurrects itself, its appearance changes drastically. After the third beheading, it is described thus:



Additionally, the form which Zhaum takes to reunite his torso and severed head appears very similar to that of the Formless Spawn of Tsathoggua: Zhaum is a descendant of the Great Old One, and is the only living entity left in Commoriom at story’s conclusion. Later in the history of of the city, the thief Satampra Zeiros and his companion visit the long-abandoned metropolis and encounter a Formless Spawn, and as Zhaum reproduces by fission, there is perhaps a case to be made for Zhaum being the first of these creatures. 
### History
The child of Sfatlicllp and a Voormi, Knygathin Zhaum was a reaver and cannibal. Upon its capture by the constabulary of Commoriom, headsman Athammaus attempted to execute it by beheading, but because of its preternatural heritage, such attempts proved unsuccessful and only served to temporarily inconvenience the creature. As the folks of Commoriom realised that they stood no chance against this seemingly-unkillable entity, they left the fabulous city to its fate and re-established the capital at Uzuldaroum.

As a descendant of Cxaxukluth, Knygathin Zhaum reproduced by fission and thus created an Azathothian strain among the Hyperborean Voormi, with which it later repopulated Hyperborea after humankind deserted the capital city of Commoriom.

fullContent:
Kolchak: The Night Stalker is a multimedia franchise consisting of two television films, two television series (one a reboot of the original), a pair of novels, and a host of comic books. Created by American author Jeff Rice, the franchise was begun in 1972 with the release of the first film Kolchak: The Night Stalker. 

The character of Carl Kolchak was created for the novel The Kolchak Papers, but was first seen in the film The Night Stalker, the novel having been optioned but unpublished until after the film's release. 

### Premise
Kolchak: The Night Stalker follows the exploits of Carl Kolchak, a talented but struggling reporter, as he chases a variety of bizarre stories which usually turn out to have the involvement of supernatural elements. During the course of his investigations he frequently clashes with his editor Tony Vincenzo, with whom he shares a love/hate relationship, as well as the local authorities, some of whom have even gone to the lengths of running Kolchak out of town in order to cover up the results of his reporting.

### Mythos Connections
Although the original series contained little-to-no references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft, the Cthulhu Mythos, or cosmic horror in general, preferring to focus on classic supernatural entities such as vampires, werewolves, zombies, witches and the like, or cases with a science fiction theme, such as androids or cloning.

Despite this, later writers in the franchise have included elements of Lovecraftian horror and even direct ties to the Cthulhu Mythos. Perhaps most notable amongst these are the contributions of the late American author C. J. Henderson, who wrote an entire collection of short fiction centred around Kolchak and the Mythos.

### Legacy
While Kolchak was something of a failure on its release - usually attributed to its airtime slot - it has gained a cult following in the years since, and has been cited as an influence on many more modern works. Not least among these is Chris Carter's wildly popular X-Files franchise, which he states owes a huge debt of gratitude to Kolchak. Indeed, the producers of the show at one point approached Darren McGavin, the actor who played Kolchak in the original series, in an attempt to persuade him to reprise his character, but McGavin turned the offer down. However, several other references to Kolchak have appeared as Easter eggs in the show.

### Short Fiction

"König Feurio" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Cody Goodfellow.

### Synopsis
During the Second World War, the crew of a crippled German U-boat are picked up by a commerce raider believed to have been lost in the Great War. Aboard, they find a crew composed of human/Deep One hybrids - including one colossal specimen which acts as the ship's engine - and are slowly seduced by the creatures.

The U-boat crew's leader, having managed to break himself from the temptations of their captors, is eventually able to destroy the ship, although by this point it has reached its destination: Devil Reef off the coast of Innsmouth.

The story concludes with the Oberleutnant, the sole human survivor of the ship's destruction, moving to the middle of the Arizona desert, convinced that one day his former rescuers will come to reunite him with his inhuman offspring.

### Publication History
"König Feurio" was published in the collection of Goodfellow's own works Rapture of the Deep and Other Lovecraftian Tales by Hippocampus Press in April 2016, and in the German-language translation of this book, Tiefenrausch, by Festa in October 2022.

Korol i Shut (Король и Шут; English: King and Jester) were a Russian horror punk band from St. Petersburg (Leningrad) active between 1988 and 01.01.2014. They took their inspiration from, amongst other things, the supernatural, folklore, and mythology.

At least two of the band's songs incorporated lyrics from the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft, the short story "Dagon" and the poem "The Messenger." 

### King, Jester and Lovecraft


This is the title of a 2010 article for the magazine Mir Fantasticki:"Despite the fact that in their younger years, the members of the group were quite informal and did not disdain alcohol, drugs and debauchery, in fact they were well-read and versatile people. Yes, almost the entire cast was engrossed in various fiction (up to Winnie the Pooh!): the work of Lovecraft, Edgar Allan Poe and, of course, Tolkien. The cast of The King and the Jester were early Tolkienists, from the era before Peter Jackson's films."

Koth is a fictional city first mentioned in the Conrad & Kirowan stories of the late American author Robert E. Howard. It is also the name of a Hyborian kingdom in Howard's Conan series of sword and sorcery tales, and further expanded upon in this setting by Marvel Comics. Described as a black, cyclopean city, it is believed to be located in the ancient supercontinent of Hyboria.

Despite Howard presenting Koth as a city (: "Dig Me No Grave"), the waters have been somewhat muddied through mentioning it in the same context as such beings as Cthulhu and Yog-Sothoth. This would seem to imply that it is perhaps more than a simple complex of buildings (: "The Fire of Asshurbanipal", Robert E. Howard; : "The Lords of Pain", Richard L. Tierney).

The Tower of Koth, marked with the sign of Koth, is a location in the city of the gugs in H. P. Lovecraft's novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath; these are probably unrelated to Robert E. Howard's Koth.

### Marvel Comics
In the fictional world of Marvel Comics, the being known as Varnae established a lair in Koth, and later clashed with the hero Conan. 

Conan also clashed with the Demon Lord of the Dark Valley in Koth.

Koth-Serapis is a fictional sorcerer who features in Robert M. Price's stories set in Robert E. Howard's James Allison story cycle.

### Overview
An evil magician of the Hyperborean age, Koth-Serapis penned the occult script which came to be known as the Black Rituals of Koth-Serapis when alive.

At the moment of his death, he cursed the Vanir warrior Bane to live forever through multiple incarnations until such time as the two could meet again and he could take his revenge upon the savage. However, in the 1930s Bane, now in the form of a Texan man named James Allison, met the sorcerer and defeated him, breaking the curse and earning his final rest.

After Koth-Serapis' death in Hyperborea, he somehow transformed into a colossal worm-like creature which inhabited the Dreamlands and consumed the souls of the dead. How this fits with his confrontation with James Allison in the 1930s is unclear.

### Appearances
*"Black Eons" (1985)
*"The Burrower Beneath" (1997)

Koth-Shugoth is a fictional entity created by DC Comics for the comic story "Lost in Memory", featured in Spectre Annual Vol 3 #1. The character appears to be inspired by the Shoggoths.

### Background
Koth-Shugoth is one of the Elder Gods, who was banished from the universe by the Presence, the supreme being of the Multiverse. During World War II, the U.S. Government was looking into the supernatural and its potential military uses. Due to Hitler's people looking for the Ark of the Covenant and the Spear of Destiny, the U.S. was attempting to harness the power of the Elder Gods.

They worked with the dark occultist Micah Cole, who betrayed them and opened a portal for Koth-Shugoth to return to Earth, where it engaged in battle against Doctor Fate, the Spectre and the military. Koth-Shugoth was defeated when the Spectre followed it into its home dimension and erased it from existence as a warning to the other Elder Gods, before closing the portal. (: "Lost in Memory")

Kthanid is an Elder God in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by the late British author Brian Lumley for his 1975 novel The Transition of Titus Crow, the second in Lumley's Titus Crow series.

### Description
Reputed to be the “brother” of the Great Old One Cthulhu, Kthanid is physically identical to his sibling - a colossal humanoid with stubby bat-wings and sporting a growth of octopoid tentacles from his lower face - in every way but one: his eyes are a deep gold in colour. Said to be as good as Cthulhu is evil, Kthanid radiates an air of benevolence to all who those in his presence. He is the head of the pantheon of Elder Gods who oppose both the Great Old Ones and Outer Gods, and resides in a vast crystal palace at the centre of the realm of Elysia, home of the Elder Gods.

### History
Kthanid summoned the cosmic time-traveller Titus Crow after the latter became lost in the infinite depths of the multiverse, seeking a champion to aid him in his battle against the Great Old Ones. He then introduced Titus to his daughter Tiania, and the two fell instantly in love.

The Elder God then sent Crow on a mission to Earth’s Dreamlands in order to defeat the threat of the Great Old Ones which had begun to fester there, claiming to be unable to travel to that reality himself.

Titus Crow faced many hazards in the Dreamlands, not least among them the Men of Leng and the Fly-the-Light, but finally came to the source of these threats where he unwittingly opened a portal which would allow the Great Old Ones to spill forth into the Dreamlands, a potentially devastating turn of events for mankind. 

At the last, Nyarlathotep, messenger of the Great Old Ones, manifested to gloat over their victory, but Kthanid was able to use Crow’s dimensional time machine to appear in the Dreamlands himself, and used his great power to banish Nyarlathotep and his evil masters whilst sealing shut the portal for good.

### Powers and Abilities
Whilst as an Elder God Kthanid’s powers are incomprehensibly vast to the human mind, a few are listed below. It should be noted that although these powers appear to be magical in nature, Titus Crow speculates that they are simply a manifestation of technologies far beyond the level of mankind.

*Great Thought: Kthanid could use what he referred to as a Great Thought to project his consciousness nearly anywhere in the cosmos that he pleased. Whilst there, he could communicate and interact with individuals as he pleased.
*Prescience: Using his crystalline viewing monitor, Kthanid could predict how any possible action in any of the many dimensions would affect the future, and used this to make his plans accordingly.
*Banishing Blast: Kthanid used this power to direct a stream of pure energy at both the Great Old Ones and Outer Gods in order to send them back to the planes of reality from whence they had come.

Ktynga, also known as Norby's Comet, is a planetoid which serves as cosmic transportation for the entity known as Fthaggua in Donald Wandrei's 1933 Cthulhu Mythos story "The Fire Vampires".

### Description
An asteroid the size of a small moon, Ktynga is home to the cosmic being Fthaggua, and its extensions the Fire Vampires. It is wreathed in an aura of intense heat, and is described as having an "almost molten surface". Ktynga is capable of traversing the interstellar void at speeds far greater than light, achieving jumps of light-years in incredibly short times - as great as four light years in four days - although its more usual speed was calculated to be in the region of 50,000 miles per second. How its master engineered this performance from a seemingly-inert piece of space debris is unknown.

Ktynga also plays host to "a great darker spot, a fantastic architecture, dream-like, unreal, with curved angles and alien geometry of sinister beauty." The darker spot is later revealed to be a single building "as large as a city", wherein reside Fthaggua and the Fire Vampires.

### History
Ktynga was first observed by human astronomer Gustav Norby on 7th July 2321, around five light-years from the Earth's solar system. 

It transported its residents to Earth in their constant quest for sustenance later that year, and returned in the years 2327, 2332, and 2339. During its final visit, its master Fthaggua was destroyed by Gustav Norby; in the aftermath, Ktynga became an inert satellite of the planet Earth.

Kukulkan, also written K'uk'ulkan, is the feathered serpent creator god of ancient Maya mythology.

He is believed to embody the sky, wind and rain and provides the energy to sustain life.

The name Kukulkan is formed from the Mayan language words feathered (k'uk'ul) and serpent (kan).

In the Cthulhu Mythos, Kukulkan is considered to be another name for Yig.

Kulalu is a fictional entity created by The Asylum for their kaiju film Ape X Mecha Ape: New World Order. The character was inspired by Cthulhu in terms of its name and characterization.

### Background
Kulalu is one of the Great Old Ones, a race of extraterrestrial entities who are known to be world destroyers. Millions of years ago, the first specimen of its kind arrived on Earth in a chrysalis, which was thought to be the meteor that killed the dinosaurs, before being awoken and causing the fifth mass extinction event. The substance known as "Sample 7" is actually the blood of Kulalu, with exposure to it causing other lifeforms to experience accelerated growth.

The Johnson Space Center made contact with Kulalu during a mission where they launched a space capsule containing a chimpanzee named Abraham. The space capsule crashed into Kulalu's body, injuring the creature and causing it to lay dormant in the Pacific Ocean for nearly two decades. Kulalu's blood from the accident was responsible for enlarging Abraham into a monstrous King Kong-like ape.

Kulalu was eventually awoken through human sacrifice by Varda, a secretive group of world leaders who worship the Great Old One as their god. The Varda intended to use Kulalu to end humanity's suffering by bringing forth the apocalypse. During its rampage, Kulalu got into some conflicts with Abraham and Mecha Ape. Although Mecha Ape was destroyed, Abraham ultimately defeated Kulalu by dropping the creature into an active volcano. (: Ape X Mecha Ape: New World Order)

Kulan Gath is a fictional character in the Marvel universe who first appeared in 1972 in issue #14 of the 1st volume of Conan the Barbarian. He also has starred in the Red Sonja line of comics published by Dynamite Entertainment.

### Background
### Marvel
Kulan Gath was an incredibly powerful sorcerer, whose power approached the level of the Sorcerer Supreme, Doctor Strange. His power was amplified by human sacrifices and his N'Garai masters. Kulan Gath was able to transform NY city and its population into Hyborian Age analogs, project mystical lasers, summon demonic entities, and manipulate flesh and bone.

During the Hyborian Age he was Stygia's dominant sorcerer. He waged war with his bitter rival the sorceress Vammatar of Hyperborea, but then formed an alliance with her. They married and attempted to free the imprisoned Shuma-Gorath from Mount Crom. Who they then attempted to subjugated, and were overwhelmed by the Old One. Each though the other dead, and both headed back home. Kulan Gath returned to Stygia where he had been displaced by Thoth-Amon. For a while he apprenticed uner him, but was later forced out of Stygia due to his blasphemous sorcery. He would later clash with the sorceress (and mutant) Selene Gallio, and had multiple encounters with the barbarian Conan in various kingdoms of the Hyborian super continent.

He returned to life in late 20th century Earth by possessing the body of a worker who found his necklace. Kulan Gath transformed NY City and its inhabitants into a city of the Hyborian Age, enslaving the Morlocks, X-Men, New Mutants, and Avengers. While Selene and Kulan Gath restarted their old feud, the heroes regained their memories and turned on him. Using the mutant Magik, Doctor Strange reversed time to undo Gath's spell. Later a fisherman found his necklace and was himself possessed. Kulan Gath traveled the world and ended up in South America where he took over an indigenous village. In his attempt to ascend to godhood, he attempted to sacrifice a goddess his agents captured to the N'Garai. The Avengers foiled his plans therefore the N'Garai feasted on him.

Kull is a fictional prehistoric warrior hero. He was created by pulp author and Lovecraft Circle member Robert E. Howard. Kull is often known as Kull the Conqueror or Kull of Atlantis, since he conquered a civilised kingdom and ruled it by strength of his axe, and he was born and adventured on the continent of Atlantis.

As Kull exists in the same continuity as Conan, he also exists in the same continuity as the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. Notably, he lived at a time further back than most human characters in the expanded Mythos.

### Overview
Howard first brought Kull to the world in three stories published in Weird Tales: "The Shadow Kingdom", August 1927; 'The Mirrors of Tuzun Thune", September 1927; and "Kings of the Night", November 1930. Kull is a barbaric warrior often put at odds with more civilised people and whose strong ethical axis opposes the decadent, treacherous and scheming natures of more civilised folk.

Kull's stories take place around 100,000 BC in pre-cataclysmic Atlantis. The primary antagonists other than treacherous human beings are eventually resolved to be the Serpent-People, a reptilian race predating humanity and serving the entity that will one day become Set of Conan's time (approximately 90,000 years after the time of Kull). 

### Ties to Conan the Barbarian
Conan the Barbarian, Howard's more famous later sword-and-sorcery hero, began life in a story originally written as a Kull tale and re-written for the later character. As many Kull stories and story ideas were eventually reworked by both Howard himself and later writers for use in Conan stories, there is a "echoing" of incidents and opponents shared between Kull and Conan. Kull is more introspective and thoughtful than Conan, and his adventures, although broadly similar, eventually lead Kull to be the barbarian ruler of a thoroughly decadent civilised city-state.

Likewise Kull's main humanoid nemesis, Thulsa Doom, has also been incorporated into the Conan continuity.

Kuranes is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Celephaïs".

### Overview
Kuranes is the dream-name of an Earthly homeless man (his real name is never revealed) who had, as a youth, created the city of Celephaïs in the Dreamlands. As he grew older, he became more desperate to return to that city, eventually resorting to narcotic drugs to grant him more time to search. It wasn't until his death that he would return to his dream-city for the final time to rule over it eternally as King. (: "Celephaïs")

Ironically, King Kuranes became homesick for the common visions of his childhood on Earth. No longer comforted by the unearthly beauty of the Dreamlands, Kuranes used his powers to convert a small part of it into a replica of his childhood home at Cornwall-By-The-Sea. It was here that he received Randolph Carter as his guest during the latter's quest to locate Kadath. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

Kuuko (also known as Cthugha) is an extraterrestrial entity from the fictional universe of the Haiyore! Nyaruko-san series.

### Background
Kuuko was a childhood friend of Nyaruko before they graduated from space school. Many years later, Kuuko was hired by Nodens as a bodyguard for his plans of human-trafficking in the theme park of R'lyeh, where she eventually reunited with Nyaruko and confessed her romantic feelings towards her. Nyaruko rejected Kuuko's advances due to a human boy named Mahiro Yasaka being her true love. Seeing him as an obstacle between them, Kuuko tried to kill Mahiro, leading to Nyaruko defeating her in battle. Despite this, Kuuko later moved to Earth to help protect Mahiro so she can stay close to Nyaruko. Over time, Kuuko also developed feelings towards him, showing interest in having a threesome with both Mahiro and Nyaruko. When her cousin Kuune tried to be in an incestuous relationship with her, Mahiro pretended to be in an engagement with Kuuko in order to convince Kuune to leave her alone. Kuuko continued to try to get together with Nyaruko, much to Nyaruko's annoyance. She is also big into otaku culture and loves playing video games.

Kuuko is capable of shapeshifting and takes the form of a red-haired slender human girl. Her species was the inspiration for the character "Cthugha" from the Cthulhu Mythos, and is considered to be archenemies with Nyaruko's. (likely a reference to August Derleth's short story "The Dweller in Darkness") Although, she is physically weaker than Nyaruko, Kuuko is still a very competent fighter. In combat, she uses the power of pyrokinesis as well as a plethora of weapons including a crowbar, lasers and swords.

The Kyresh is a fictional species created by Walter C. DeBill, Jr. for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "In 'Ygiroth".

### Description
Kyresh are carnivorous creatures from the Earth's Dreamlands which resemble a combination of horse and bloodhound, with an equine body and long muzzle used to scent prey at distance. Their paws are equipped with talon-like claws, and their jaws are filled with irregular fangs to tear apart prey.

Described as a "morbid relic of an older time", Kyresh were already extinct in most of the Dreamlands when the Thing in the Yellow Mask taught the 'Ygirothians how to ride them. Although the beasts were only "half-tamed" and extremely dangerous to handle, the 'Ygirothians used them as both hounds and steeds when hunting for Buopoths. The Kyresh often killed their masters as well, but surprisingly, this didn't bother the 'Ygirothians, as it meant less people to divide the spoils of the hunt, if successful. Alternatively, if the hunt wasn't successful, the fallen hunters themselves would become food for the survivors. (: "In 'Ygiroth")

Kythanil (also Kythamil or Kthymil) is a fictional double planet that once revolved around the star Arcturus. It was created by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price for their short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", and also mentioned by August Derleth in "The Dweller in Darkness". 

Tsathoggua's followers, the Voormi, once lived here, and Zvilpogghua's "daughter," Sfatlicllp, may also have dwelt here. The planet was destroyed in some catastrophe, but not before the Voormis moved to primal Hyperborea.

Ariel Prescott, in her "Visions from Yaddith", implies that the planet Kythamil is still in existence in 1927, although Kythanil was destroyed millions of years before the first hominids.

Lyon Sprague de Camp (27 November 1907 – 6 November 2000), usually referred to as L. Sprague de Camp and who sometimes wrote under the pseudonym Lyman R. Lyon, was an American writer. He wrote science fiction, fantasy, and biographical works, particularly of genre authors; he is the author of Lovecraft: A Biography (Doubleday, 1975).

Although he did not coin the term, de Camp is credited with the first usage of "extraterrestrial" as a noun with the meaning of "alien life," and with coining the abbreviation "E.T." He did so in the first part of his two-part article "Design for Life", which was published in May 1939 in Astounding Science Fiction magazine.

De Camp worked for many years editing and writing fiction in continuation of Robert E. Howard's Conan cycle. He edited a series of anthology publications through the 1960s that renewed and maintained interest in high fantasy and sword and sorcery stories, old and new. His editorial work also spread the works to new audiences. He also worked editorially and wrote with Lin Carter.

L'affaire Charles Dexter Ward is a French-language translation of H. P. Lovecraft's occult horror novel The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. Translated by Jacques Papy, it was first released in a paperback format by J'ai Lu in 1972.

### Publication History
In the years since it’s first released, J'ai Lu have reprinted L'affaire Charles Dexter Ward numerous times, first in November 1975. February 1984 saw another edition featuring new cover art by Michael Whelan; this was reissued twice, in February 1986 and January 1989. In November 1995, another reprinting with new cover art by Philippe Druillet was released; this edition was given reprints in September 1996, March 1997, August 1998, and January 1999. A final edition with yet more new cover art by Richard Guérineau saw print in December 2001; this was reissued in October 2002 and March 2004.

The L'gy'hxians are a fictional alien species created by Ramsey Campbell for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Insects from Shaggai". They were further developed by Chaosium in 1994 for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Description
A race of metallic cuboids around three feet in height, the L'gy'hxians are extremely strong and physically dense creatures. Originating from L'gy'hx, known as Uranus by the human race, they are not a hostile species, once even sharing their home planet with the refugee Shan. However, after discovering the loathsome rites the Shan practiced in worship of Azathoth, the L'gy'hx evicted them from their world.

The L'gy'hx worship Lrogg, an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep, and show their devotion to him by mutilating themselves in bizarre rites.

fullContent:
"La Musique de l'Ennui" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and games designer Kenneth Hite. It was first published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.

### Synopsis
Kristie, a young woman with a deep-seated passion for all things related to The Phantom of the Opera, buys a ticket for a once-in-a-lifetime experience: a trip across Europe on the legendary locomotive the Orient Express, stopping at various historic locations to take in productions of the play. 

As the tour makes its way across the continent, Kristie begins to notice certain oddities manifesting in her fellow passengers, the productions become increasingly bizarre and include more and more elements not featured in the original. When she reaches the final destination, she is confronted by a figure dressed as the Phantom, but when she attempts to remove its pallid mask, is confronted by an entity not of this Earth… 

### Mythos Connections
"La Musique de l'Ennui" is littered with references to the colour yellow, such as the lighting used in some of the productions, and the costumes worn by the performers. She also engages in conversation with a man who shows her a book containing the characters Camille and Cassilda, and the scene of her final confrontation with the entity posing as the Phantom - a "Black Lake" - indicates that it was in fact the Outer God Hastur. Further reinforcing this, its entry in Madness on the Orient Express is prefaced with a quote from The King in Yellow.

Professor Laban Shrewsbury is a fictional character created by August Derleth, who appears as the main protagonist for his The Trail of Cthulhu series of short stories.

### Background
A member of the faculty at Arkham's Miskatonic University, Laban Shrewsbury was the institutions' Professor for Anthropology and Philosophy. For years, he has dedicated himself to the study of the Cthulhu mythic cycle, learning astral projection and how to summon the Byakhee (which are enemies of Cthulhu), hoping one day to be able to defeat or at least temporarily deter the cosmic entity. His studies have taken him beyond the Solar System, to the Great Library of Celaeno.

Shrewsbury's dark glasses conceal the fact that he has no eyes. It's not known whether he was born that way or somehow lost them, but the lack of eyes doesn't seem to impair him in any way. (: The Trail of Cthulhu)

He is the author of An Investigation Into the Myth-Patterns of Latterday Primitives With Especial Reference to the R'lyeh Text, and Cthulhu in the Necronomicon.

### In Works of Other Writers
*In Kevin L. O'Brien's short story "October Surprise", Shrewsbury is depicted as working as an occult consultant for the covert agency Black Omega.

fullContent:
"Labyrinth" is a short story by Thomas Parrott and the fourth story in the anthology The Devourer Below. It is set in the popular Arkham Horror Fiction universe.

### Plot Summary
Joe Diamond, a private investigator in Arkham, is in his office when an unexpected package arrives through his mail slot. Arming himself with a Colt, Joe approaches the door, unlocking it and finds the hallway empty. Whoever delivered the package had left in a hurry and the other offices are empty as it was late in the afternoon and everyone had gone home for the day. Joe locks the, takes the package to his desk and empties its contents over it, which turns out to be pictures and documents. Most of them are photos and police reports of a young woman, Nadia Leandros, who had reached out to the police for help as something was harassing her. She claimed she had seen shadowy figures at night who vanished, heard wings battering against her windows and whispers from the drain of her sink. But the police had dismissed her claims so someone had brought the case to Joe instead. The rest of the file was about an older man who’s body had been found seemingly rotting from the inside before he died, but the coroner had reported it as a death from natural causes. On a picture of the man there is a birthmark on his neck, shaped as a circle surrounded by dark tendrils. When looking back at the other photos of the woman Joe notices she has the same mark on her collarbone. The police report on the man’s death tells that his neighbors and coworkers had described him having paranoid behavior and suffering from an inescapable fear. Joe knows that if he does not act, the woman could end up dead as well. But he needs more information and he leaves for the one source that could give it to him: Miskatonic University.

Joe reaches the library on campus and when entering he is greeted by the librarian Daisy Walker. She had been saved from cultists and ghouls by Joe and in her gratitude had helped Joe get information from the library whenever he needed as it was usually restricted to faculty and students. Joe tells her he needs information and she brings him to a table lit by a single candle. He shows her the pictures of the woman and the body, and Daisy says she has seen something similar to the birthmark but doesn’t believe the victims are cultists and not the same cultists who attacked her. She disappears amongst the bookshelves and when she returns she shows him a leather-bound tome titled “The Labyrinth: The True Tale of the Darkness Below Crete”. Daisy asks Joe if he paid attention to the subject of mythology in school and begins to read from the book.

The Lady with the Red Parasol, whose real name is Tzu San Niang, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Cthulhu Mythos setting.

### Overview
The Lady is a beautiful woman of apparently Asian descent, who is never seen without her signature red parasol, which is likely one of the powerful magical artefacts known as "Keys."  She is a senior member of the Red Coterie, a secret society dedicated to obtaining the Keys as part of an unknown agenda.

Although capable of wielding significant mystical powers, such as the ability to psychically reach through walls and attack her enemies (: "City of Waking Dreams"), she is not immune to magic herself, as seen when a blast from the Key known as the Xiamen Bi left her visibly shocked and unwell (: "A Forty Grain Weight of Nephrite").

The Lady is known to be a formidable figure in the Shanghai criminal underworld, as well as amongst its upper echelons (: "City of Waking Dreams"), but has been seen to operate in as diverse locations as Cuba (: "Brother Bound") and San Francisco, California (: "A Forty Grain Weight of Nephrite").

### Appearances

* "Brother Bound" (2022)
* "A Forty Grain Weight of Nephrite" (2022)

fullContent:
"Laeta: A Lament" is a poem by H. P. Lovecraft first published in February 1918 in The Tryout. It also appeared in the collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems. It is dedicated to Lovecraft's friend and fellow poet Rheinhart Kleiner.

### Synopsis
On a place known as Zulal, the narrator mourns the loss of his wife, Laeta, whom he has known since they were both children playing in the fields and by the streams. He remembers how the Nymphs tried and failed to match Laeta's beauty, yet bore no grudge against her, as they loved Laeta too, and the wind gods Auster and Zephyrus were so charmed by her sweetness that the wind wouldn't mess up her hair.

The narrator married Laeta in a temple, but she passed away in that year's autumn. Now that spring has returned, he notices that the flowers aren't as sweet, the Nymphs no longer show up, and the wind seems subdued as if the gods were mourning too. Seeing all this, the narrator yearns for the next autumn when he too will be dead.

fullContent:
Lagh metal is a fictional extraterrestrial substance featured in the story "Out of the Aeons", written by H. P. Lovecraft for Hazel Heald.

### Description
Lagh metal doesn't occur naturally on Earth, but has been brought to the ancient continent of Mu by alien creatures from Yuggoth. The cylinder that contained the scroll of T'yog was made out of this substance, which defied all kinds of scientific analysis. The metal is further described as iridescent and "impervious to all reagents". (: "Out of the Aeons")

### Behind the Mythos
In The Whisperer in Darkness, the Mi-Go are known to use brain cylinders made of an unknown metal from Yuggoth. Ramsey Campbell's "The Mine on Yuggoth" names this metal tok'l.

The Tulu-metal used by the K'n-yanians from The Mound is also unknown to Earth, having been brought from the stars by Cthulhu, and is similarly used to make cylinders to store important scrolls.

"Lair of the N'Garai" is a superhero comic book story which made its first appearance in Wolverine Annual Vol 1. Written by Larry Hama, it was published by Marvel Comics in August 1995 . 

### Synopsis
The mutant superhero Wolverine encounters and does battle with one of the N'Garai attempting to infiltrate the Xavier Mansion after coming through a dimensional portal called the Cairn.

Wolverine, along with friend and fellow mutant Nightcrawler, then do battle with a horde of demons at the Cairn; upon the demons' defeat, the portal vanishes and the Earth is safe once more.

Lake is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who appears in the 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness.

### Description
A professor of biology at Miskatonic University, Lake was the first to discover the Mountains of Madness as a result of his "strange and dogged insistence on a westward -- or rather, northwestward -- prospecting trip", based on his discovery of strange fossils. He also discovers the ancient extraterrestrial specimens that he dubs "Elder Ones", based on their resemblance to "certain monsters of primal myth" found in the Necronomicon. He reports that his findings in Antarctica confirm his belief "that earth has seen whole cycles of organic life before known one that begins with Archaeozoic cells," and predicts that this "[w]ill mean to biology what Einstein has meant to mathematics and physics." When eight of the Elder Ones turn out to be living creatures rather than fossils, they butcher Lake and the rest of his sub-expedition. For the rest of the story, he is referred to as "poor Lake".

Lake is notable for his "alarmingly radical daring"; he is willing to put the expedition at risk in pursuit of knowledge, asserting that "his new specimens made any hazard worth taking." The narrator Dyer notes at one point that his "excitement had reached the point of mutiny". He is an imaginative personality, as evidenced by his comparison of his first sight of the Mountains of Madness to a "land of mystery in a dream or gateway to forbidden world of untrodden wonder." He is familiar with the Cthulhu cult from "prehistoric folklore things Wilmarth has spoken of".

The Lake of Hali is a cloud-lake near the city of Carcosa, on a world near the star Aldebaran in the Hyades (: The King in Yellow, : "The House on Curwen Street", : "De Marigny's Clock"). Hastur is said to be "the Sleeper beneath the Lake." When the Spawn of Cthulhu wake and thrash about in the lake it is called "the Time of the Frothing". Mists and cloud banks commonly cover the surface of the lake (or else the whole lake is made of mist?), and the ghostly presence of Carcosa can sometimes be seen. There are several lakes in the area, and one text refers to "the black lakes of Hali", however the other lakes have their own names (such as Dehme). Called "The Lake of Hali" as well as just "Lake Hali" and is sometimes termed "the Black Lake."

The Lake of Hali was added to the Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in The Whisperer in Darkness, based on coinage by Ambrose Bierce and Robert W. Chambers; it has been greatly and conflictingly expanded upon since. In Bierce's works, Hali was the name of a character quoted by the narrator of "An Inhabitant of Carcosa".

### In Other Media
*Lake of Hali makes a minor appearance in the ongoing Japanese manga Murcielago in which the main character is named Kuroko, which translates into 'black lake'. 
*The first season of the HBO series True Detective namechecks a lot of the Chambers material from his book The King in Yellow, including the Lake of Hali.
*The Lake of Hali is mentioned in an invocation by Peter Ingram in Hugh B. Cave's short Cthulhu Mythos story "The Death Watch".
*In Providence by Alan Moore, "Hali" is an Anglicization of Khalid ibn Yazid, who is portrayed as the historical inspiration for Abdul Alhazred; the "real" Necronomicon is referred to as "Hali's Book". Later, Nyarlathotep tells the protagonist that all servants of the Mythos are rewarded, and that for authoring his book, Khalid was transformed into a lake of fluorescent gas near a star in Taurus (the location of the Hyades), implied to be the Lake of Hali.
