A lamia is a fantastic creature from Greek mythology and later folklore, usually depicted as a seductive but often bestial woman. They have occasionally appeared in Cthulhu Mythos fiction.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The only appearance of the word "lamia" in Lovecraft's fiction is in the revision story "Medusa's Coil," in which Marceline Bedard is referred to as "that leopardess, or gorgon, or lamia, or whatever she was."

### Clark Ashton Smith
Lamias are a recurring feature of Clark Ashton Smith's fiction, reflecting his interest in the intersection of sexuality and horror. In "The Hunters from Beyond" (1932), Cyprian Sincaul's sculptures include, among ghouls and satyrs, "lamias voluptuously coiled about their victims, and less namable things that belonged to the outland realms of evil myth and malign superstition." Later in the story Sincaul confesses, "These statues of mine—these devils, vampires, lamias, satyrs—were all done from life,"

Lamias are a recurring element in Smith's pseudo-Medieval Averoigne setting, as reflected in his poem "Averoigne":In Averoigne the lamia sings

To lyres restored from tombs antique, 

And lets her coiling tresses fall 

Before a necromantic glass.In "The End of the Story" (1930), set in Averoigne, the student Christophe Morand is warned by the Abbot Hilaire that the Château des Faussesflammes is a "dwelling-place of foul spirits":Some say that the demons are abominable hags whose bodies terminate in serpentine coils; others, that they are women of more than mortal beauty, whose kisses are a diabolic delight that consumes the flesh of men with the fierceness of hell-fire.Undeterred, Morand enters Faussesflammes, and there meets Nycea, "a woman of goddess-like beauty." "Never before had I experienced a passion of such intensity, such all-consuming ardor, as the one I conceived immediately for this woman," Morand declares. He takes her in his arms; "it seemed almost as if the completeness of her yielding was unhindered by the presence of bones in her lovely body."

Nycea's seduction is interrupted by the abbot, who denounces Nycea: "Foul vampire! accursed lamia! she-serpent of hell!” After chasing her off with holy water, Hilaire explains: "the beautiful Nycea who lay in your arms this night is a lamia, an ancient vampire, who maintains in these noisome vaults her palace of beatific illusions." But even knowing what Nycea is does not prevent Morand from returning to her alluring doom.

When Anselme first meets Séphora in Smith's "The Enchantress of Sylaire" (1941), another Averoigne tale,  she is described as "swaying like a lamia." Lamp-efts are a fictional species of "fabulous creatures" from the Dreamlands, as featured in the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu.

### Description
Measuring about 3 ft. (~ 91 cm) long from snout to tail end, Lamp-efts are floating salamander-like creatures with webbed feet, laterally flattened tails and luminous bodies, complete with a pair of globular eyes that emit beams of light like an electric torch. They naturally inhabit the upper atmosphere of the Earth's Dreamlands, and descend to the ground only at night.

Lamp-efts have no mouth and feed solely on the energy generated by all living things. As they require only small amounts of food, they are not usually dangerous. In fact, Lamp-efts are often kept as pets, known for their inquisitive and companionable nature. However, they might be capable of draining the energy of smaller animals to the point of rendering the prey unconscious for several hours, or even an entire day. The light generated by Lamp-efts contributes to their popularity among occultists by providing a line of defense against a number of Mythos entities that can only move about in darkness.

Lamp-efts propel themselves through the air with their feet and tail. Although the organ that allows them to defy gravity is analogous to the hune of the Byakhee, the Lamp-efts' don't share the former's ability to travel through interplanetary space. (: S. Petersen's Field Guide to Creatures of the Dreamlands)

shortDefinition: Lawrence G. DiTillio (February 15, 1948 – March 16, 2019) was an American film, TV series, and tabletop role-playing game writer. His creations include He-Man and She-Ra, and the award winning Masks of Nyarlathotep for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG....
fullContent:
Lawrence G. DiTillio (February 15, 1948 – March 16, 2019) was an American film, TV series, and tabletop role-playing game writer. His creations include He-Man and She-Ra, and the award winning Masks of Nyarlathotep for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG. Not only did this adventure expand the number of players prepared to try that role-playing game, and in the process help to popularise Nyarlathotep and the broader Cthulhu Mythos, it also established a pattern for how the expanded Mythos would be handled for many game designers and writers for decades to come.

Larry DiTillio attended film school at New York University and UCLA. After graduating, DiTillio attempted to make a career as a Hollywood screenwriter. DiTillio wrote for both television and movies in the 1970s before becoming a staff writer for the original He-Man and the Masters of the Universe series and over its two seasons, wrote 17 episodes, more than anyone else. He also directed one episode. He had crucial input into character development. During a writers' strike, DiTillio was forced to find other paid writing work outside Hollywood. Settling on game design, he wrote The Isle of Darksmoke (1984) for the Tunnels & Trolls RPG. Most famously, DiTillio collaborated with Lynn Willis to create Masks of Nyarlathotep (1984), a world-spanning campaign for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu. It won an Origins Award, and is considered one of the best roleplaying adventures of all time. For a few months, DiTillio was also a contributor to Chaosium's Different Worlds magazine, writing about news from the world of film and television in his "The Sword of Hollywood" column. He wrote numerous other Chaosium works including the Call of Cthulhu supplement Terror Australis.

Despite his success in the role-playing games industry, once the screenwriters' strike ended, DiTillio went back to screenwriting.

More recently, DiTillio tried his hand at short fiction, releasing at least one Cthulhu Mythos story, and two set in the Babylon 5 universe created by J. Michael Straczynski.

### Selected Bibliography

### Short Fiction
*"Welcome to Cthulhuville" (2012)

### Gaming Supplements
*Masks of Nyarlathotep (1984, with Lynn Willis)
*Terror Australis (1987, with Penelope Love, Mark Morrison, Lynn Willis, and Sandy Petersen)

The Larvae of the Other Gods (sometimes referred to as the Larvae of the Outer Gods) are a fictional cosmic species which made their first appearance in H. P. Lovecraft's 1943 novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Overview
The Larvae are the product (or perhaps offspring) of the beings which revel in the Court of Azathoth, created when portions of the Other Gods slough off and drift away into the cosmos. These entities vary enormously in every aspect, including intelligence: some are mindless, some possess their own goals and desires. For some unknown reason, the space surrounding Earth's Dreamlands plays host to an unusually high concentration of these creatures. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

fullContent:
"Last Rites" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gael Baudino, writing under the pen name of K. M. Tonso. It was published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 by Titan Books in October 2014.

### Synopsis
Two Miskatonic University faculty members independently come to the conclusion that the events related by disgraced Pabodie Expedition leader William Dyer were in fact true, and had been suppressed by both the university board and those who mounted disastrous follow-up expeditions to the site.

Seizing a university-funded opportunity to travel beneath the ocean to a site which seemingly hosts more of the bas reliefs depicted by Dyer, they encounter a cavern filled with dying Elder Things who are desperately trying to hold closed a portal leading to the ruins of their former city- one which is being assaulted by Shoggoths desperate to find their way into the outside world. As the last of the guardians dies, the men are able to seal the chasm, but one is forced to pay the ultimate price.

### Characters 
*Dr. Paul Dyer, the son of William Dyer and chairman of the Miskatonic University geology board. Dyer is possessed of a lifelong ambition to prove to himself that his father was not the crazed lunatic portrayed by the authorities in the aftermath of the Pabodie Expedition.
*Dr. Alf Marsh, a professor of geology at Miskatonic, and the younger Dyer's protégé.

shortDefinition: "Last Stand at Waltham's Cabin" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.  ### Synopsis As the city becomes more and more lawless Bill Waltham, a retired widower, decides to move to a cabin in the Texas backwoods which he inheri...
fullContent:
"Last Stand at Waltham's Cabin" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
As the city becomes more and more lawless Bill Waltham, a retired widower, decides to move to a cabin in the Texas backwoods which he inherited from his uncle years previously. After only a few days, however, an unidentified beast kills and skins his dog and, discovering what he believes to be the creature's burrow, Waltham empties a can of gasoline into it and lights the torch.

Later that evening, Waltham's cabin is attacked by a pack of vengeful Serpent People. Expending the few shells he has for his shotgun, Waltham decides to go out with a bang, and lights up his final can of gasoline, obliterating himself and the reptilian creatures.

### Characters

* Bill Waltham, an elderly former government employee in search of a peaceful existence.
* Lucas, Waltham's faithful dog, also advanced in age.
* Old Man Dewitt, the local grocery store owner.

### Publication History
"Last Stand at Waltham's Cabin" was published in the collection They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in June 2018.

### Trivia

* Bill Waltham mentions Robert E. Howard, Henry Kuttner and H. P. Lovecraft as being amongst his favourite authors.
* The cabin is mentioned as being near to Tenoka, Texas, a location which has appeared in a number of Shiflet's Mythos stories.

The Last Void is a fictional "location" created by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffman Price for their short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key." It should be distinguished from the distinct and different Final Void, another term for the Court of Azathoth.

### Overview
In "Through the Gates of the Silver Key," Lovecraft and Price refer to the Last Void as that which is beyond all matter, and reality - transcending "all earths" and thus by implication all parallel worlds, alternative histories. The Last Void is thus, in current physics terms, either the Base Reality - or complete nothingness incapable of definition.

In the context of the story, it is clearly something inspiring both awe and fear. The story deals with the annihilation of individuality among many other themes and so it is not inappropriate to see the Last Void as a true baseline in the writings of Lovecraft but also in the broader Cthullhu Mythos, beyond any individual versions of any of the concepts or creatures written about, and since it is also beyond the Dreamlands it forms a kind of hard boundary within which the entirety of all the expanded Cthulhu Mythos takes place. It is the end of all invention, as it were.

Whether the resemblance of the Last Void to the annihilation of the ego and consciousness in Zen, certain Buddhist and Hinduism beliefs and in Jungian philosophy is coincidental or not is unknown.

### Legacy
The likening of the barrier between the Last Void and the rest of consciousness and reality is very similar to the concepts of The Doors of Perception, an essay by Aldous Huxley describing his use of psychedelic drugs published in 1954.

Lavinia Whateley is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror". She appears as the albino daughter of the wizard Old Whateley and the mother of Wilbur Whateley and the Dunwich Horror. The children's father is the entity Yog-Sothoth, summoned by Old Whateley for the purpose of impregnating Lavinia.

Born in 1878, Lavinia loses her mother to an unexplained and violent death when she was 12 years old. She is in her mid 30s at the time of Wilbur's birth. She goes missing on Halloween night 1926, at the age of 48. While no conclusions are spelled out in the story, it is implied Wilbur killed her.

Lavinia is described as an unattractive albino woman with the characteristically weak Whateley chin. She is uneducated except for the bits of ancient lore she gleans from her father's books and his limited tutoring. Her appearance is described as "slatternly," and she is prone to wild daydreams.

A younger version of Lavinia appears in the video game Fate/Grand Order, as a fictional character summoned in a magical version of Salem during the witch trials, together with her grandfather. She is an albino who is connected to the Outer Gods, but being 12 years old, she lacks the implications of her main Mythos counterpart. She is a friend of Abigail Williams, who is possessed by Yog-Sothoth. (: Forbidden Advent Garden Salem)

### Behind the Mythos
She is likely named after the character in Shakespeare's Titus Andronicus, who is horribly mutilated and raped before being murdered by her father.

Lawrence Watt Evans (born 1954) is an American science fiction and fantasy author and editor who has also written commissioned works in franchise properties such as Star Trek. He also wrote as a critic at one point in his career including film reviews and a non-fiction critical work on British fantasy author Terry Pratchett. 

He has often written under pseudonyms including Lawrence Watt-Evans and Nathan Archer.

The majority of his work has nothing to do with the Cthulhu Mythos and consists in large part of science fiction or fantasy books series.

Lazarus is an obscure 1924 novel by the late French author Henri Béraud. It was first published by Alvin Michel, and was later translated into English. Ironically, given its author's extreme Anglophobia , it is more famous in its English translation than it was in its native language.

### Synopsis
After an accident, a man loses his memory and adopts an entirely different persona for the following 16 years.

### Publication History
Lazarus was translated into English and reprinted by The MacMillan Company in 1925, and later included in an omnibus collection along with Barry Pain's An Exchange of Souls by Hippocampus Press as part of their Lovecraft's Library series in May 2007 .

Le Novar is a character created by author J. B. Lee for his Cthulhu Mythos writings. He was first made mention of in the 1998 short story "Genuine Article".

### Overview
Le Novar claims to be a cosmic time-travelling alien from Xandra the Asteroid Planet, currently occupying the body of a human being - an elderly black man named Nick Calvert - although whether this is actually the case is uncertain. He is the author of the fictional book The Stars Are With You!, a "paperback mishmash of [Erich] von Daniken, Madame [Helena] Blavatsky and H. P. Lovecraft", in which he reveals the truth of his origin.

Le Novar owns an artefact, dubbed the Clawed Crystal, which allows its user to travel through space and time, and even to affect events in the past. He has also been shown to be willing to loan the Crystal to others in exchange for favours, as seen when he allowed Robert Clarke the use of its abilities in exchange for the theft of a manuscript from Miskatonic University.

### Possible Origin
Despite there being no mention of Xandra the Asteroid planet in the works of Lovecraft, Le Novar being a body-swapping, time-and-space travelling alien suggests that he may be of the Great Race of Yith.

### Appearances
*"Genuine Article" (1998, mention only)
*"His Hour Upon the Stage" (1998)

The League of Light is a fictional team in the Army of Darkness universe by Dynamite Entertainment.

### Background
The League of Light are a team of superheroes that is made up of Protectors. Legacy heroes whom inherited their powers from bloodlines. Whom are the protectors of their respective continents. The members of the team were brought together by the Chosen One, Ash Williams to fight the Deadites and prevent the apocalypse.

They failed to prevent the conquest of Earth by the Deadites and the extermination of the human race. The two surviving members (Cybil and Brad) along with Ash's spirit, used a time machine to travel to the past to prevent the post-apocalyptic future by preventing Hell's Prophet's infection of Ash. They were successful in re-writing history, with one of the changes being that Cybil was freed from a demonic possession years earlier by Brad.

### Members

shortDefinition: Leaves was a fanzine devoted to weird fiction edited by Robert H. Barlow. Two issues of this mimeographed publication were released, the first in Summer 1937 and the second in 1938. It was published in Leavenworth, Kansas, U.S.A.  ### Overview Barlow...
fullContent:
Leaves was a fanzine devoted to weird fiction edited by Robert H. Barlow. Two issues of this mimeographed publication were released, the first in Summer 1937 and the second in 1938. It was published in Leavenworth, Kansas, U.S.A.

### Overview
Barlow had become an active member in the amateur press scene under the encouragement and mentorship of H. P. Lovecraft, and after obtaining his own printing press for a short period of time create his own fanzines, Dragon-Fly and Leaves. After family issues and lack of money Barlow was forced to discontinue his participation as a publisher.

### Issues
* Leaves #1 (1937) provides items from Clark Ashton Smith, Wandrei, Derleth, A. Merritt, and Edith Miniter. Clark Ashton Smith provided his completion of William Beckford‘s “Third Episode of Vathek.” Wandrei has three works, one a reprint from Weird Tales, but the others are original, one being a sequel to that story. Merritt’s is a reprint. Leaves #1 also included a previously unpublished essay by Lovecraft. The remainder of the volume is dedicated to poetry.
* Leaves #2 (1938) features a previously unpublished work by C.L. Moore entitled the “Were-woman.” It also included short pieces by Lovecraft, including an unfinished collaboration with Barlow. There is also a short work by Barlow. There is a reprint of Henry S. Whitehead's “The Tree-Man” from leading pulp magazine Weird Tales, as well as a listing of his weird fiction. Other works and poetry round out the issue.

shortDefinition: Lee Brown Coye (1907 - 1981) was an American artist who illustrated several stories for Weird Tales starting in 1945, and produced the cover art for a number of Arkham House books, including the original Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos and the H. P. Love...
fullContent:
Lee Brown Coye (1907 - 1981) was an American artist who illustrated several stories for Weird Tales starting in 1945, and produced the cover art for a number of Arkham House books, including the original Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos and the H. P. Lovecraft collections At the Mountains of Madness and Other Novels, Dagon and Other Macabre Tales and The Dunwich Horror and Others. He also provided cover art for collections of stories by Hugh B. Cave, Clark Ashton Smith, and Manly Wade Wellman.

Stories that Coye illustrated for Weird Tales include "The Hog", "The Will of Claude Ashur", "The Whippoorwills in the Hills", "The Master of the Crabs", and "The Gorge Beyond Salapunco".

In 1944, the August Derleth edited anthology Sleep No More: Twenty Masterpieces of Horror for the Connoisseur was released, featuring classics such as "Count Magnus", "The Return of the Sorcerer", "Two Black Bottles", "The Horror in the Burying-Ground", "The Yellow Sign", "The Black Stone", and "The Rats in the Walls", each accompanied by an illustration by Coye.

In 1967, Arkham House released 3 Tales of Horror, featuring three Lovecraft stories ("The Colour Out of Space", "The Dunwich Horror", and "The Thing on the Doorstep") illustrated by Coye.

Coye's illustrations of lattices of sticks (such as featured in the cover of the Clark Ashton Smith collection Other Dimensions) inspired the horror short story "Sticks", by Karl Edward Wagner, which was included in the revised edition of Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos.

fullContent:
The Legend Horror also known as the Kraken is a colossal talking creature resembling an octopus. It battles the Fawcett Comics' superhero Captain Marvel in the final issue of Whiz Comics #155, from 1953. The story uses many Cthulhu Mythos terms such as "gibbering" as well as noting that had the alter ego of Captain Marvel, Billy Batson, been able to make sound he would have screamed in the process of going insane at the sight of the Legend Horror. Very obviously, and given the strong shift to horror content that had recently taken place in American comic books, this was inspired by Mythos stories and in particular the entity Cthulhu.

The Legend Horror is abducting humans then keeping them to devour later by stacking them in a larder resembling a giant frozen food section from a supermarket.

The Legend Horror even has servitors: gigantic intelligent vampire bats that swoop in and easily grab human victims, carrying them off to the lair of the Legend Horror.

Legends of Cthulhu is a range of 3 3/4" action figure line based on similar figures of the late '70s and early '80s such as the original Star Wars figures and the plethora of modern figures in this scale offering toys based on everything and everyone from GI Joe, Deborah Harry and Hellraiser to Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Universal Monsters and Heavy Metal magazine. The Cthulhu range is by Warpo Toys and were first released in January 2016. 

This is the first retro action figure line based on the works of H. P. Lovecraft. These are a range of deliberately retro collectible figures designed in a way aiming to be true to the original flavor of the 1970s to 1980s toy ranges, with appropriate articulation, accessories and deco consistent of the era. The figures in the first wave are based on classic archetypes including the Cultist, Spawn of Cthulhu, the Professor (based on a combination of the police and researcher protagonists of "The Call of Cthulhu"), and the Deep One. Each figure comes with character-specific accessories. The figures also feature retro style blister card packaging.

Legs is a short scenario supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Written by Jim Phillips and featuring artwork by Tobias White, it was published in May 2018 through Chaosium/DriveThruRPG's Miskatonic Repository player-driven resource.

### Overview


The story revolves around a young filmmaker who has stumbled across a number of Dreaming Stones while working in the Amazon rainforest, and has been granted certain occult knowledge as a result. This causes him to enact a ritual at the screening of his new film, Legs, one which transports the convention venue to the Dreamlands while simultaneously calling down the wrath of the Spider God Atlach-Nacha and its deadly brood. Not all of the investigators will survive this encounter.

### Behind the Mythos
The scenario features a handful of Easter eggs, such as the name of the group's favourite weird fiction author Harrison Paul Likenstuff (H. P. Lovecraft), Beckon of Bethsagua, the game based on Likenstuff's works (Call of Cthulhu), and the convention itself, which bears a resemblance to NecronomiCon/The H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival.

shortDefinition: Lemuria is a lost continent that supposedly existed in the Indian Ocean before sinking beneath the waves. Originally proposed by the zoologist Philip Sclater in 1864 to explain the existence of lemurs or their fossils in both Madagascar and India, th...
fullContent:
Lemuria is a lost continent that supposedly existed in the Indian Ocean before sinking beneath the waves. Originally proposed by the zoologist Philip Sclater in 1864 to explain the existence of lemurs or their fossils in both Madagascar and India, the theoretical continent was adopted by occultists like Helena Blavatsky, an exponent of Theosophy who asserted that it was the homeland of human civilization. The notion was adopted into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft and other writers.

### Hypothetical Continent
According to current supporters of the theory of such a lost continent:

"Lemuria was an ancient civilization which existed prior to and during the time of Atlantis. Physically, it is believed that Lemuria existed largely in the Southern Pacific, between North America and Asia/Australia. Lemuria is also sometimes referred to as Mu, or the Motherland (of Mu). At its peak of civilization, the Lemurian people were both highly evolved and very spiritual. While concrete physical evidence of this ancient continent may be difficult to find, many people "know" that they have a strong connection to Lemuria."

Lemuria originated in the Western World in 1864, when the British lawyer and zoologist Philip Lutley Sclater wrote a paper titled “The Mammals of Madagascar” which was published in the The Quarterly Journal of Science. Based on his own observations, Sclater noted that the lemur had far more subspecies in Madagascar than there were in either Africa or India. Based on this contemporary evidence he deduced that Madagascar was the animal’s original homeland.

To explain the diffusion of Lemurs to India and Africa from Madagascar, he postulated the existence of a now sunken continent in the Indian Ocean, roughly triangular in shape. This continent of “Lemuria,” would have formed land bridges with India’s southernmost point, southern Africa, and western Australia. At some point in prehistory, Lemuria sank to the ocean floor.

In 1870, Ernst Haeckel, a biologist, suggested that Lemuria was the original homeland of the human race.

In 1888 as part of her published book The Secret Doctrine, Helena Blavatsky, as part of the Theosophy project, claimed that Lemuria was indeed the homeland of ancestral human forms - albeit four-armed ones.

It should be noted that Sclater merely suggested an ancient land bridge and later subsidence of previous landmasses. It was Haeckel who added the evolutionary biology of humanity to the theorem, and Blavatsky, ever the opportunist, who together with the others working on the Theosophy project added Lemuria, as with so many other more or less random components, to the mix.

Lemuria as a sunken landmass was validated as a theory in 2013 by the finding of geologically recent rocks on the sea floor as well as revising the dating for the formation of islands in the Indian Ocean. fullContent:
"Leng" is a horror short story by Marc Laidlaw set in the mysterious Plateau of Leng. It was published in the 2009 anthology Lovecraft Unbound.

### Synopsis
The story consists of four entries in the narrator's journal documenting what he describes as "the Second Mycological Survey of the Leng Plateau Region". He is following the trail of the Schurr-Perry expedition, in which expert mycologists Danielle Schurr and Heinrich Perry penetrated the Tibetan plateau of Leng in search of new species of fungi and never returned. One of the species speculated to await scientific discovery is Cordyceps lengensis, a native relative of the well-documented Cordyceps sinensis. This parasitic fungus infects the bodies of caterpillars and sprouts out of the insects' heads as a single featureless stalk, which is known for its medicinal properties and thus extremely valued in the local economy.

The narrator and his interpreter, Phupten, talk to a man named Zhang, whose cafe has been visited by Schurr and Perry before they headed towards Bu Gompa, a temple dedicated to Cordyceps sinensis, the name of which might be translated as Temple of the Worm (as it refers to the infected caterpillars). Zhang speaks fondly of the mycologists, but warns the narrator that Chinese authorities have forbidden all passage to Leng, although he fails to elucidate the reason. He also reveals that long after Schurr and Perry's departure, a pair of Tibetan men stopped by asking for them, only to surreptitiously tear off the page of Zhang's Guestbook that the scientists had written on, as if trying to cover up the previous expedition's footsteps.

Three days later, the narrator and Phupten arrive in a village whose inhabitants are both friendly and very enthusiastic about fungi, affectionately nicknaming the narrator Shamu-pa ("Mushroom Man") due to his knowledge. However, only the children acknowledge that Schurr and Perry have passed there. Accompanied by two guides, the narrator and Phupten resume their journey and arrive two days later at the temple, Bu Gompa, which stands at the entrance to Leng. 

The four men are welcomed by the monks, who appear amiable. However, when the narrator intends to give an offering to the temple's god as courtesy, Phupten pushes him aside and comments that the faith of the monks of Leng has been condemned by the Dalai Lama, who declared their god a demon: not a bringer of enlightenment, but of "false wisdom". This doesn't prevent the two guides from giving offerings, however. Soon, the narrator finds one of the monks to be none other than Heinrich Perry himself, who explains that he and Schurr haven't been lost, they both simply decided to join the order. While Perry has never ventured beyond the temple, Schurr has actually penetrated deep into the plateau itself and achieved a much higher level of enlightenment as a result. She now spends her time meditating in a cave.

"Les Fleurs Empoisonnées" (originally published as "In the Garden of Poisonous Flowers") is a novella by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-slayer. Published as a hardcover book by Subterranean Press in 2002, it was the first story Kiernan wrote about Dancy after her initial appearance in the novel Threshold (Roc/New American Library, 2001), but the second to be published, after "The Well of Stars and Shadow" (Gothic.net, 2001).

### Synopsis
Hitchhiking in Georgia, Dancy Flammarion is picked up by a strange traveller with two undead companions, who happens to be going to the same house in Savannah that Dancy has been instructed to go to by her angel. The traveller kidnaps Dancy and offers her as a gift to the sinister women's society based in the Savannah mansion--but his hidden agenda is revealed when Dancy is left alone with a young man in a dress who carries a mysterious bottle.

### Characters
Dancy Flammarion: A teenage albino, she has "talcum-powder skin" and hair like "milk spun into the finest silken thread." She wears "dark wrap-around sunglasses" that hide her "eyes the deep red-pink of pyrope or the pulpy hearts of fresh strawberries." She first appeared in Kiernan's novel Threshold, and went on to be featured in numerous short stories.

The Bailiff: Apparently a human, based in Providence, Rhode Island, he runs supernatural errands across the South. He has green eyes, an "easy smile," and "secretive parchment creases" on "his ancient face." He appears in numerous stories by Kiernan, and figures prominently in their novel Daughter of Hounds.

Dead Girl: A vampire from Providence, accompanying the Bailiff on his errands. Dancy tells her, "I dreamed about you sleeping at the bottom of a cold river," and refers to her as "Mercy Brown"--referring to a historical figure who was posthumously accused of vampirism in Rhode Island in 1892. (Dead Girl angrily rejects this identification.)  Dead Girl is the central character of Kiernan's 2001 short story "So Runs the World Away."

Bobby: Another vampire, Dead Girl's companion. He "might be any six-year-old boy," except that "his silver eyes flash like mercury and rainwater coins." He also appears in "So Runs the World Away."

Samuel: A mysterious figure, described as an "old conjurer," who never appears onstage. Porcelina describes his offer of a supernatural bottle despite Aramat's insistence that his name never be mentioned in her house. He may be one of the people the Bailiff tells Dancy "you best hope you never have to meet face to face.”

Samuel's Boy: An emissary sent with the bottle to the League and Society. He appears as a "pretty boy with star-shine eyes," "tall and very slender," in his late teens, "wearing a black velvet dress with a dark green symbol like an hourglass embroidered over his flat chest." The Lesser Old Ones is a designation coined by Lin Carter to refer to a category of beings who serve the Great Old Ones and lead their servitor races. Apart from their hierarchical rank in the Cthulhu Mythos, a notable difference between Great Old Ones and Lesser Old Ones is that the former have been (for the most part) imprisoned by their enemies, the Elder Gods, while the Lesser Old Ones remain (for the most part) free.

Although the concept appears in several other works, the term "Lesser Old One" is not always used. The role-playing game Call of Cthulhu refers to most of these beings as Greater Servitors, and a few of them as full-blown Great Old Ones. In the Demonbane Mythos, entities like Dagon and Mother Hydra are classified as Lesser Gods.

### Overview
The concept of the Lesser Old Ones appears to be based on the works of August Derleth, specifically The Trail of Cthulhu series, which establishes that the Great Old Ones are served by two kinds of beings. Their ordinary servitors are species such as the Deep Ones, the Mi-Go, and the Tcho-Tcho people, which can be repelled by the five-pointed star-stones of Mnar. The second kind consists of the Great Old Ones' "immediate servitors". These are far mightier creatures, identified as "superior beings [...], against whom the five-pointed star is powerless". At least one of them is described as a giant, tentacled frog-like creature. (: "The Watcher from the Sky")

In the stories of Lin Carter, the expression "Lesser Old Ones" is used by Prof. Copeland (: "The Horror in the Gallery") and Abdul Alhazred (: "Behind the Mask") to denote a group of immortal beings who are several times more powerful than the servitor races they lead, but still nowhere close to the Great Old Ones they serve (: "The Descent into the Abyss"). They thus stand at an intermediary level between the Great Old Ones and their common servitors. Unlike their imprisoned masters, however, the Lesser Old Ones still roam the world, trying to find ways to free their overlords (: "The Horror in the Gallery").

In most cases, the Lesser Old Ones appear to be nothing more than primordial and extraordinarily ancient specimens of the servitor species they lead, corresponding to the "Prototypes" of said species (: "The Descent into the Abyss"). These include beings such as E-poh, leader of the Tcho-Tcho people, or Quumyagga, first among the Shantaks.

Conversely, however, there are also examples of creatures regarded as Lesser Old Ones by Carter which bear no physical resemblance to their corresponding servitor race. For instance, Bokrug and Rlim Shaikorth, who are leaders of the Thuum'ha and the Cold Ones, respectively, but don't appear to belong to these species. Other sources, such as the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, classify Bokrug and Rlim Shaikorth, as well as Nug and Yeb, as actual Great Old Ones.

Letters Lovecraftian is an art book which presents the letters of the alphabet as Lovecraftian illustrations, with each letter being accompanied by a quote from one of H. P. Lovecraft's works. The first 55 copies of the limited 400-copy run were produced in a softcover format, with the remaining copies featuring a spiral-bound plastic spine.

The book is closed with a reprinting of the poem "On the Death of a Rhyming Critic."

Leviathan is the name given by some Inuit cultists to a child of Cthulhu: "...the Other Tornasuks left or went to sleep with Him [Cthulhu], except Dagon his servant-creation and Leviathan his son." (: "The Arctic Stone")

It is also one of the primary antagonists of the 2018 video game Call of Cthulhu by Cyanide Studio, based on Chaosium's role-playing game.

### Description
The Leviathan is a colossal shark-like or serpentine creature, more than fifty feet in length, that is regarded as an offspring or avatar of Cthulhu — though some sources speculate that it could alternatively be a particularly massive Deep One or Star-Spawn, and others consider it part of an unholy trinity alongside Dagon and Hydra. Its powerful jaws are capable of biting through wood, metal, flesh, and bone with ease, and can gape wide enough to swallow creatures almost as large as a Dark Young whole. Despite being most-proficient at swimming, it is capable of moving on land as well. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

In at least one manifestation, the Leviathan resembles a prehistoric fish with four fins pierced by metallic rings, squid-like tentacles framing its jaws, and a long tail for swimming. It is observed to be two to three times the size of a common whale. It preys upon whales and other large marine animals, but is said to never directly harm humans, instead attempting to psychically corrupt and compel them to worship and unleash its progenitor, Cthulhu. (: Call of Cthulhu)

In an alternative timeline in which magic is commonplace, creatures known as Leviathans have been trained to attack ships during World War Two. Modern Leviathans, at least those employed by the American government, have abdominal pouches filled with bat-winged Night-gaunts, which upon orders will "slash their way free of the monster's belly, launch, and fly to their appointed targets with pitiless accuracy and the speed of a tempest". (: "The Unthinkable")

### Worshipers
One notable group that pays tribute to the Leviathan is the Inuit tribe that Professor William Channing Webb deemed to be degenerate devil-worshippers. They celebrated infanticide, ritual torture, acts of profanity, and blasphemy to prove their loyalty to their god Cthulhu, his servant-creation Dagon, and the mighty Leviathan. They first learned the English language from whalers that traveled in search of the oils of the Leviathan before they were killed. The tribe was ultimately wiped out by a summoned Daoth-Yhol. (: "The Arctic Stone")

According to the Malleus Monstrorum, the Leviathan is worshiped by various isolated island and coastal communities, such as Polynesia, Hawaii, and coastal regions of the Arctic. The Leviathan is a Lovecraftian-like eldritch god from the fictional universe of the Hellraiser movies and comics. Although not part of the Cthulhu Mythos, it is similar enough to be used in the RPG setting. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Background
The Leviathan has existed for numerous millennia, ruling over Hell (also known as the Labyrinth) and the Cenobites. The entity is obsessed with law and order. To it the human realm of flesh is chaotic and wrong, and therefore it uses the Cenobites to wage war against it. The Hell of the Leviathan represents the maze of the mind, which is why it takes the form of a Labyrinth. 

Legend says that it is ancient, existing long before the creation of life. Chaotic life spread across the world, until it broke through the walls of Hell, bringing light and life to that realm. Leviathan retaliated and pushed life back, but soon threatened his world again. It decided on a new approach, and reached into the dreams of men. Giving men the desire to dominate and shape the world, to crush and slaughter those whom stood in the way. It whispered to them of machines, weapons, and tolls. Man began to destroy and slaughter, and while the world continued to grow, it was now also dying. The Leviathan then visited man in its dreams again, and influenced them to make their world like his. Covering the land with concrete and erecting monolithic towers that reached the sky.

The Leviathan is the creator of the Cenobites, whom come in many shapes and forms. It is an immortal entity that feeds on the souls of those brought to its realm but were not deemed worthy to be made Cenobites. When its beam of black light hits you, he slips inside, and by the time it passes, he knows more about you than you know about yourself. If your touched by the black light, you feel every sin or wrongdoing you have done throughout your life. His only weakness is the the Lament Configuration which if solved in Hell, temporarily weakens him and causes him to lose some of his power. He reverts into a cube shape, and captured souls flee the Leviathan.

### The Cenobites
The Cenobites are humans who have been brainwashed and mutilated to serve Leviathan. In the Labyrinth they torture humans for all eternity. They are summoned to Earth when someone solves one of Lemarchand's Boxes, the most infamous being the Lament Configuration. Puzzle boxes which promise pleasures. If the individual is deemed worthy by Leviathan, he or she is taken to the Cenobite Transformation Chamber. Where they undergo an alteration that is unimaginably painful, results in a brutally mutilated body with its blood replaced by blue fluid. The end result is twisted version of what you were, without memory of your past life, and often with perverted aspects of your original persona. fullContent:
"Leviathan" is a short story by author Nicholas Almand. It is inspired by the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Off the coast of California, a washed-up and myopic cryptid hunter discovers an enormous, aggressive, beast which has the power to drive those who look upon it insane. Although he is able to kill the creature and retrieve samples for a shadowy organisation to study, his young companion is killed during the endeavour.

### Characters
*Gedeon Vassago, an aging cryptozoologist.
*Ashton Clark, the son of a wealthy businessman and fan of Vassago's.

### Publication History
"Leviathan" was published in the anthology of H. P. Lovecraft-inspired works Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.

### Behind the Mythos
The name of Vassago's young pilot Ashton Clark is a clear nod to Lovecraft's friend and contemporary Clark Ashton Smith.

fullContent:
The Leviathans are a Lovecraftian extra-dimensional race in the fictional universe of the Supernatural television series--incredibly ancient, shoggoth-like shapeshifters who are sometimes referred to as the Old Ones.

### Background
The main villains in Supernaturals seventh season, the Leviathans are shapeshifting monsters, a ravenously destructive race that sees other lifeforms as inferior, to be destroyed or treated as a food source. In their true forms, they are perceived by humans as balls of black goo with powerful jaws. When possessing human hosts, they dislocate their jaw, displaying a forked tongue and large teeth. Their society has a hierarchy based on strength and fear, in which they betrayal is the norm and those who fail or annoy others are eaten. Death referred to the Leviathans as "the Old Ones."

In the show's mythology, they predate the angels. Immortals that are virtually indestructible, they are able to fly, block angels' powers by their physical presence, regenerate from virtually any injury, have enhanced senses, possess venomous blood that can kill angels, and have super strength, agility, and speed.

Lexur'iga-serr'roth is a fictional entity created by John Prescott for his 2011 short story "The Brown Tower."

### Overview
A photophobic bat-winged monstrosity with both a thousand-eyed misshapen head and a huge maw, Lexur'iga-serr'roth's leathery wings and legs have prodigious slimy claws and it also has a powerful tentacle-like prehensile tongue able to grab and hold a human being or even snap their bones.

It attacks its prey (such as humans) in the darkness of the tower in which it dwells, and holds them to eat at its leisure or simply hurls them down to the base of the tower.

Liao is a fictional substance created by Frank Belknap Long for his short story "The Hounds of Tindalos", where it is depicted as a drug that allows the user to mentally "travel" through time and space, seeing visions of ancient places and eras.

### Description
According to Halpin Chalmers, Liao was used by alchemists in China many centuries ago. The great philosopher Laozi used it to see the Tao, which permeates all things. It is practically unknown in the western hemisphere.

The drug is consumed in pellets. The first effect is a sensation of darkness, during which some objects fade from the user's sight while others remain visible. Afterwards, the user is flooded by the sensation of seeing and participating in historic and prehistoric scenes, as if reliving all one's ancestors' lives simultaneously. On the next stage, the user can move through different temporal dimensions, which Chalmers identifies as "curved time" and "angular time". The longer the user remains in trance, the further back in time they can go and the number of "strange angles" increases. If the user peeks through those angles, they might see the creatures that inhabit these dimensions, such as the Hounds of Tindalos, which in turn might become aware of the time-traveler's existence and track them.

Even during a trance, the user remains capable of conversing with other people, and it is possible for the user's consciousness to return to the present if another person violently shakes them.

When he took Liao experimentally in 1928, Chalmers was convinced that the drug itself posed no danger, although he did acknowledge the danger of getting "lost in time" and unable to return without outside help. As he found out, however, the Hounds of Tindalos pose the biggest danger, as they can track the user long after the latter has returned to their own time, and use geometric angles to enter our dimension. (: "The Hounds of Tindalos")

Liao might be derived from the Black Lotus. (: "The Madness Out of Time")

### Behind the Mythos
The effects of Liao are similar to those of the unnamed drug taken by Michael Hayward in "The Invaders", by Henry Kuttner. However, in Hayward's case, the mental time travel attracted the attention of a different kind of extradimensional predators: namely the Ny'ghan Grii, as opposed to the Hounds of Tindalos.

The effect is also similar to that of the crystal from Clark Ashton Smith's "Ubbo-Sathla".

In another Smith story, "The Plutonian Drug", the titular stimulant expands the user's temporal consciousness, but is distinct from Liao in that it only allows the user to see themself a few hours into the past or future, as opposed to seeing one's past lives. Nevertheless, some Mythos works have referred to Liao as the Plutonian Drug (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana).

Liao is also similar to the taduki drug from H. Rider Haggard's Allan Quatermain series, which is featured in the Mythos crossover story "Allan and the Sundered Vei

The Library of St John the Beheaded is a secret library of forbidden texts in the fictional universe of Doctor Who. It is owned by the Catholic Church and contains items they deemed unwise for the general public to know about. As well as evidence of alien activity and lost works by writers Plato, Aristophanes and Shakespeare, it also contains the following Mythos books:

*De Vermis Mysteriis (: All-Consuming Fire)
*The Eltdown Shards (: Millennial Rites)
*The Pnakotic Manuscripts (: Millennial Rites)
*The Book of Eibon (: Millennial Rites)
*Lies and Lives of Yog-Sothoth (: Millennial Rites)

### Behind the Mythos
Although the Library is fictional, St Giles is a real location in the East End of London which was once infamous for its slums and its rookery.

"Light a Candle, Curse the Darkness" is a short story by Paula R. Stiles which forms part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by C. J. Henderson.

### Synopsis
Whilst looking into the history of a piece of land as part of a contract, private investigator Frank Nardi listens to a former paramedic's tale of how an evil witch turned her colleagues into kittens.

### Characters
*Frank Nardi, retired NYPD homicide detective turned private investigator.
*Ms. Johnson, former paramedic, now working as a supernatural investigator.
*Keziah Mason, practitioner of black magic.
*Angela Barrett, former paramedic.
*Josie Kittredge, former paramedic.
*Sam Lee, former paramedic.

### Behind the Mythos
*"Light a Candle, Curse the Darkness" was written by Paula E. Stiles on request by editor Brian M. Sammons. It was published by Dark Regions Press in the anthology Arkham Detective Agency in November 2017.
*The title of the piece is based off of the phrase: "It is better to light a candle than curse the darkness" which is a Chinese proverb meaning it is better to do something about a problem than just complain about it.

### Mythos Connections
*The story is set in the fictional town of Arkham, a major focus of many Mythos stories.
*When disturbed by something he sees, Frank Nardi makes the Elder Sign to ward himself against evil.
*Keziah Mason was originally a character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1932 short story "The Dreams in the Witch-House."

### Synopsis
A man joins Facebook where he signs up to play a mysterious time-killer named The Green God Game. *Fred, unwitting cultist.

### Behind the Mythos
The idea of participants being encouraged to do activities as a lark whilst knowingly or unknowingly helping complete a ritual was previously used in the Fritz Leiber novella Our Lady of Darkness.

"Like Comment Share" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu by April Moon Books in March 2014.

Anyone who is aroused by Lilith will find himself awestruck and dazed and under Lilith's command to do her bidding. She can walk through any obstruction and is known for visiting sleeping men, with whom she then engages in somnambular sex.

Lilith drains them of their energy and takes their semen. She may also observe lovers and, when they fall asleep, take some of their semen, which is used to create monsters and deformed creatures. Her children are the non-Mythos creatures that haunt the night. During the night, she cannot be harmed by physical attacks, but in the daylight she can be harmed normally. Lily Chen, the Martial Artist, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for inclusion in their vision of H.P. Lovecraft’s Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
The day after Lily's birth on mainland China to a pair of impoverished peasants, a group of mysterious monks arrived on the doorstep. Claiming to be searching for a “child of prophecy,” they told Lily's parents that their child was the one they sought. Despite their obvious shock that the babe was female, the monks expressed their desire to take her away and train her for a task of great importance; after receiving assurances that Lily would be well looked after, her parents agreed.

From the time she could take to her feet alone, the monks trained Lily in every combat technique they knew, and even went so far as to bring in instructors from across the globe. Lily absorbed all of their teachings with ease, and in the process achieved a state of harmony between her mind and body that few ever attain.

Then, in 1926, one of the monastery monks leapt from his meditations screaming “the Great Eye is opening! The final days are upon us!” before dropping down dead. Taking this as a sign that her purpose was near at hand, Lily made her way to Arkham, where she searched for clues on how to defeat whatever ancient evil was threatening existence.

### Behind the Mythos
Lily was first introduced in the expansion for the  Second Edition of Arkham Horror, Kingsport Horror, and has since been incorporated into some of their other games, including Eldritch Horror and Mansions of Madness, as well as making appearances in their Mythos fiction. Fantasy Flight also released a plastic miniature of her which was intended to replace the cardboard tokens included in their games, but this has since been discontinued.

shortDefinition: Linwood Vrooman Carter (9 June 1930-7 February 1988) was an American author of science fiction and fantasy, as well as an editor, poet and critic. He usually wrote as Lin Carter; known pseudonyms include H. P. Lowcraft (for an H. P. Lovecraft parody)...
fullContent:
Linwood Vrooman Carter (9 June 1930-7 February 1988) was an American author of science fiction and fantasy, as well as an editor, poet and critic. He usually wrote as Lin Carter; known pseudonyms include H. P. Lowcraft (for an H. P. Lovecraft parody) and Grail Undwin. He is best known for editing the Ballantine Adult Fantasy series in the 1970s, which introduced readers to many overlooked classics of the fantasy genre.

### Life
Carter was born in St. Petersburg, Florida. He was an avid reader of science fiction and fantasy in his youth and became broadly knowledgeable in the field. He was also quite active in fandom.

Carter served in the United States Army (Infantry, Korea, 1951–53), after which he attended Columbia University (1953–54), during which time he attended Leonie Adams's Poetry Workshop.[2] He was a copywriter for some years before writing full-time. He married twice, first to Judith Ellen Hershkovitz (married 1959, divorced 1960) and later to Noel Vreeland (married 1963, while they both worked for Prentice-Hall publishers; divorced 1975). He was an advertising and publishers copywriter (1957–69). From 1969 he was a freelance writer and editorial consultant. During much of his writing career he lived in Hollis, New York.

He was a member of the all-male literary banqueting club the Trap Door Spiders, which served as the basis of Isaac Asimov's fictional group of mystery solvers the Black Widowers. Carter himself was the model for the Mario Gonzalo character. He was also a member of the Swordsmen and Sorcerers' Guild of America (SAGA), a loose-knit group of Heroic fantasy authors founded in the 1960s, some of whose work he anthologized in the Flashing Swords! series. In the 1970s Carter issued his own fantasy fanzine, titled Kadath, after H. P. Lovecraft's fictional setting. Only one issue appeared; it was well-printed but in extremely low numbers, and it was scarcely circulated. The magazine contained Carter's Cthulhu Mythos story "The City of Pillars" (pp. 22–25).

In 1985, his quality of life was severely reduced when he developed oral cancer and had to endure extensive surgery to have it removed. Only his status as a Korean War veteran enabled him to receive treatment, which failed to cure his illness and left him disfigured.

In the last year before his death, he had begun to reappear in print with a new book in his Terra Magica series, a long-promised Prince Zarkon pulp hero pastiche, Horror Wears Blue, and a regular column for Crypt of Cthulhu magazine. Despite these successes, Carter had increased his alcohol intake, becoming a borderline alcoholic and further weakening his body, already ravaged by his cancer and therapy. The disease subsequently resurfaced, spreading to his throat and leading to his death in 1988. He resided in East Orange, New Jersey in his final years, and died in nearby Montclair, New Jersey.

The Lithards are a species of extraterrestrial dragonoid creatures who appear in Brian Lumley's Titus Crow series of Cthulhu Mythos novels.

### Description
Resembling the enormous dragons of Earth mythology, the Lithards are great, scaled, winged creatures with a high degree of intelligence and the ability to converse in English. They are a sociable race who live in communal groups, with a single female dragon assigned to the protection of all the eggs from a given colony. In addition to being capable of flight, Lithards are also very much at home in water, and appear to enjoy raising their hatchlings in large freshwater bodies.

Lithards evolved on a world called Thak'r-Yon, but were relocated to the realm of Elysia by the Elder Gods when Thak'r-Yon's sun went nova. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

### History
When interdimensional time-traveller Titus Crow came to Elysia, he was gifted the services of a Lithard. This creature flew him across the land, showing him the wonders of that strange place, and was delighted when Crow happily played with the hatchlings in their communal lake. It was so enamoured with the man, in fact, that it even allowed him to visit the subterranean nursery where the Lithard eggs were incubated.

### Trivia
*The name "Lithard" may not be the correct term for these creatures: as their reptilian mouths have trouble forming certain syllables in the English language, it is entirely possible that they are simply called "Lizards". However, other species such as the Dchichis (who are renowned as great linguists) refer to them as Lithards as well.

shortDefinition: Little Journeys to the Homes of Prominent Amateurs is a short raconteur monograph providing biographical details of H.P. Lovecraft who was vice president of the United Amateur Press Association (UAPA) at that time. It written by Andrew Francis Lockha...
fullContent:
Little Journeys to the Homes of Prominent Amateurs is a short raconteur monograph providing biographical details of H.P. Lovecraft who was vice president of the United Amateur Press Association (UAPA) at that time. It written by Andrew Francis Lockhart and published in The United Amateur of September 1915. Its title is a play on what was at the time a popular series of biographical books, the "Little Journeys to the Homes of..." series.

According to the summary of Lovecraft's activities and antecedents, which describe Lovecraft as an Anglo-American, Lovecraft joined the UAPA as of April 16, 1914 with his membership application only processed in July of that year. Between that time and the time of the monograph Lovecraft had risen to the position of vice president through acclamation rather than being "a politician."

Of interest are the details that Lovecraft first published his own "fanzine" at the age of 8 and a half years, this being "the Scientific Gazette, a weekly periodical, written in pencil and issued in editions of four carbon copies." Lovecraft devoted the work to chemistry which had been an earlier passion of his. Tongue in cheek or not this reference confirms how early Lovecraft's engagement with amateur press, writing and publishing really was. 

Lovecraft followed this effort with his weekly (later monthly) pamphlet the Rhode Island Journal of Astronomy. This had a run of 25 copies per issue. Compared to some later fanzines containing his own work, Lovecraft was comparable in output, and it helps explain how fond he was of helping younger writers following the same path as him throughout his life.

The Little People are a fictional humanoid species featured most extensively in the works of Arthur Machen and Robert E. Howard. A race of subterranean creatures, they are believed to be the inspiration for the folkloric Fair Folk, or "Fairies".

In Howard's stories, they are also known as the Children of the Night and the Worms of the Earth. Whilst stated to have originally been a tribe of humans, since their banishment underground millennia ago the Worms have devolved into a semi-reptilian race of creatures who fear the light. Their skin appears to be scaly, they have glittering yellow eyes, and they move with the sinuous grace of a serpent.

H. P. Lovecraft referenced this species in The Whisperer in Darkness, a story believed to have been inspired by Machen's "The Novel of the Black Seal". As a result, the Little People share some traits in common with the Mi-Go.

Lovecraft also identifies Ghoth the Burrower, a descendant of K'baa the Serpent, as "one of the Little People".

In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, this species is known as the Degenerate Serpent Folk, portrayed as the result of interbreeding between Serpent People and humans. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

### Description
: "People of the Dark"}}
Despite their reptilian features, the Little People were originally human, being the descendants of a tribe known in prehistoric Britain as the "Children of the Night", who were driven underground by the Picts. For the next thousand years, they "retrogressed" (or evolved) into a new species, adapted to life in a subterranean environment. (: "The Children of the Night", "People of the Dark", "Worms of the Earth")

Ethnologist Prof. William Gregg believes them to be the Fair Folk of myth, called "fair" not because they were in any way beautiful or benevolent, but because humans feared them and wanted to appease them. (: "The Novel of the Black Seal")

)]]
The Little People are small humanoids, less than 4 feet tall, with yellow skin and almond-shaped eyes that can see in complete darkness (: "The Shining Pyramid", : "People of the Dark"). Their mouths are equipped with fangs (: "People of the Dark", "Worms of the Earth"). Their skin is scaly and snake-like, although they still have hair, and their hands are clawed (: "People of the Dark"). Being adapted to a fossorial existence, they can burrow prodigiously fast like moles, and their excavations are said to stretch for uncounted miles beneath the surface of mainland Britain (: "Worms of the Earth").

The Little People speak in hissing, sibilant voices that bear no resemblance to any sound produced by human beings. They hate the sun, and avoid even the light of the moon or the stars. (: "The Novel of the Black Seal", : "People of the Dark", "Worms of the Earth")

"Little Sam Perkins" is a poem by H. P. Lovecraft, written in September 1934 and published posthumously in 1940 in The Olympian.

The poem mourns the passing of Samuel Perkins, a black kitten Lovecraft found at a boarding-house across the street from his aunt's back garden (: Selected Letters 5.714).

Llewellyn M. Cabos (26 June 1954 - ?) was the pen name of R.D. Larson, an American writer. She was an American author and occasional artist who has written a number of Lovecraftian works. These have been included in publications such as Edward P. Berglund's online periodical Nightscapes, Peter A. Worthy's short-lived genre magazine The Black Book, and Fred C. Adams's Spoor Anthology.

All of Cabos's Lovecraftian stories were written when she was in her teens and early 20s. For some of her writing and all of her professional art, she used the pseudonym Lew Cabos.  

Under her own name she has written more than 300 works and provided a biography of herself to Author's Den noting her unusual upbringing.

The Lloigor (also known as The Invisible Ones from the Stars) are a fictional species from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. They first appeared in the short story "The Return of the Lloigor" by Colin Wilson.

### Description
The Lloigor are vortices of living power completely invisible except on occasions when they appear reptilian. They came from Andromeda, first settling in Lemuria and Mu. They used humans as slaves (see the Kthatans), have the power to transform people physically and can adopt corporal bodies if they wish. They are sometimes called "the invisible ones from the stars" and may be the same as the flying polyps. They were ruled by Ghatanothoa possibly through mating with the god Lloigor.

### In Other Media
*In The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen story "Allan and the Sundered Veil", by Alan Moore, the Lloigor species is actually another name for the Great Old Ones in general, including Ithaqua. Moore portrays them as manifestations of a metaphysical plane named Yuggoth, which can be variously perceived as a planet, a deity, or a state of mind.
*An evil Lloigor named Roy Fogger appears in episode 11 and 12 of the anime Haiyore! Nyaruko-san. Lloigor is also one of the components for the BLT sandwich, along with Byakhee and Tsathoggua.
*The Zoiger, a race of Lloigor-based kaiju, appears in the TV series Ultraman Tiga as the harbingers of Gatanothor. A variant of the Zoiger, the human-sized Shibito-Zoiger, later appear in the film Ultraman Tiga: The Final Odyssey, where they are the servants of the Dark Giant Camearra.
*The Zoiger make a brief appearance in Chiaki J. Konaka's short story Walking to the Abyss, again as Gatanothor's servants, though they aren't referred to by name, instead being called the Great Old One's "followers". The Zoiger are described as "countless blood-colored monsters with insect wings", who fly through the gloom of the deep ocean surrounding R'lyeh as if it were the sky, and fire "orbs of bloody light" from their mouths.
*The Zoiger appear in the trading card game Battle Spirits.

Lloigoroth is a fictional entity created by Marvel Comics, which first appeared in Avengers Vol 1 #352-354 "Fear the Reaper".

### Background
Lloigoroth is an Old One who was summoned by the supervillain, the Grim Reaper. Seeking revenge against the Avengers, he made a pact with the Old Ones. He swore to reward their generosity with a feast of decay, corruption, and death. Lloigoth empowered him with supernatural powers, giving him the ability to do things that he could not do before; downing an airliner while in flight, walking away from its crash intact, the ability to manipulate time and space, create holographic projections, and re-arrange matter. He was also able to reanimate and control the dead, including former superhumans, who despite being undead, possessed the abilities they had before. Intelligent zombies who hungered for blood and flesh. When the Grim Reaper lost control of the living dead who then turned on him, Lloigoroth appeared and consumed the Grim Reaper.

### Notes
*Lloigoroth was seemingly inspired by Lloigor, created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer in "The Lair of the Star-Spawn" (1932). possibly to be added to Great Old Ones' (MAO/Lloigor part) and Lloigor/Lloigar's pages -->

"Lockbox" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Armand Rosamilia. Despite being set in his Keyport milieu, it has no connection to the Keyport Cthulhu cycle.

### Synopsis
New York, 1984: a police detective investigating a series of brutal murders finds his inquiries taking him to the strange fishing town of Keyport, New Jersey. There he discovers the murderer, a man who has killed to keep a copy of the Revelations of Gla'aki from reaching the hands of innocents. Possessed by a sudden inexplicable urge, the detective kills the murderer and decides to head to England to see what lies behind the book…

### Characters
*Detective Graeme Kirkpatrick, an English-born New York homicide cop.
*Detective Briggs, Kirkpatrick's junkie partner.
*Brendon Marsh, a Keyport resident and possible Deep One hybrid.

### Publication History
"Lockbox" was published in the Revised and Expanded edition of Keyport Cthulhu by Rymfire Books in 2017.

Lola Hayes, the Actress, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for inclusion in their Arkham Horror Files line of games and fiction set within the greater Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
After her last show - a bizarre play full of ritualistic chanting and disturbing masks - Lola decided to admit herself into a sanatorium; the nightmares had just been too much to bear, and she feared for her mental wellbeing.

However, when she read the article in the newspaper about how the director of that play had hung himself, she decided that she needed to look into things for herself. So, once again securing herself a role in the production, she surreptitiously strapped on her derringer and went back to work.

### Behind the Mythos
Although first created for Fantasy Flight's Kingsport Horror expansion for their Second Edition of the Arkham Horror board game, she has since appeared in other games of theirs related the Mythos, including Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. In addition, a plastic miniature intended to replace the cardboard counters included in the game boxes was released as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, but production of this has since been halted (all ).

### Trivia
*Whilst not explicitly mentioned to be so, the play which drove Lola to commit herself to the institution is heavily implied to have been The King in Yellow.

Lomar is a nation in the Dreamlands besieged by the armies of the Inutos and an encroaching northern ice sheet.

### Notable Features
*Olathoë - A great marble city on the Plateau of Sarkis between the mountains Noton and Kadiphonek. Its people are described as the bravest of the Lomarians for their past battles against the Gnophkehs,
**Thapnen - The site of a watch tower built to keep watch over the narrow path behind Mount Noton.
*Daikos - A city that fell 5 years into the Inutos invasion.
*Zobna - A city lost to the ice sheet before the retreat to Olathoë and presumably the former home of the Zobnarian Fathers.
*Banof - A distant valley visible from the Thapnen tower.

### Notes
After Kadatheron, the wanderer Iranon stopped here for a long time on his travels.

George Rogers claimed that Lomar existed in the arctic circle of Earth, and that Rhan-Tegoth's ruins predated it.

"Long Island Weird - The Lost Interviews" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Charles Christian.

### Synopsis
The story offers a series of vignettes on a long-running and secret war between humanity and a race of undersea creatures, hinted at being the Deep Ones. It is told through eight recovered interviews conducted by a man who is writing a book on the subject, a fragment from a police report, and partial autopsy findings (implied to be on the body of the interviewer).

### Characters
Most of the characters are not named, and are only referred to by their titles.

*The Skipper, a captain running tours for sightseers around Long Island.
*The Ghost Hunter, a professional ghost hunter and author.
*The Lighthouse Keeper, a former Coast Guard working with the U.S. Lighthouse Society.
*The FBI Agent, a Supervisory Senior Resident Agent with the Federal Bureau of Investigation
*The Cryptozoologist, the Professor of Cryptozoology and Teratology at Miskatonic University.
*The Naval Historian, a scholar in the field of naval history.
*The Nazi Conspiracy-Theory Blogger, a fringe-theory internet user.
*The Antarctic Explorer, an expert on the continent of Antarctica.
*The Landlady, a property owner renting to the interviewer.
*The Medical Examiner, a Long Island medical examiner.

### Publication History
"Long Island Weird" was published in the thematic anthology World War Cthulhu by Dark Regions Press in 2014.

"Looking for Darla" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in the collection to which it lends its name Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
In June 1952, Arkham private detective Bill Sweetan takes on a case for Wyatt Sanderson, a Miskatonic University professor whose wife has gone missing. The woman had suffered from a strange, debilitating condition for months before her disappearance, and Sweetan tracks her down to the degenerate fishing village of Innsmouth. After an encounter with the more progressive members of the Marsh family, he is invited to watch a ceremony in which the woman ascends to take her place among the Deep Ones. He returns to Sanderson and, in the interest of giving the man closure, tells him that his wife has committed suicide.

### Behind the Mythos
In the story notes for the second edition of Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir, Shiflet states that when he submitted "Looking for Darla" story to Elder Signs Press editor William Jones for consideration, Jones suggested that perhaps he should spin the piece into a full-length novel. Terrified by the prospect and feeling unready to commit to the project, Shiflet made the counter-proposal of a collection of short stories: the result was Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir.

### Trivia
* Bill Sweetan is a semi-recurrent character in the Mythos fiction of Ron Shiflet, having appeared in at least one other story, "The Scales of Justice".

Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir is a collection of Lovecraftian short stories by American author Ron Shiflet. Although Shiflet states in his afterword that not all of the stories are strictly noir in nature, he believes that they are all sufficiently "hardboiled" to be thematically similar.

### Publication History
Looking for Darla was first published by Elder Signs Press in September 2008. It runs to a total of 236 pages, and features cover art by Christopher Hill.

In 2017, Shiflet re-issued the book in a digital format under his Tenoka Press label. This edition featured new cover art two additional stories not seen in the 2008 release, and story notes from the author.

shortDefinition: Edward John Moreton Drax Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany (/dʌnˈseɪni/; 24 July 1878 – 25 October 1957), was an Irish writer and dramatist, notable for his work, mostly in fantasy, published under the name Lord Dunsany. More than eighty books of his w...
fullContent:
Edward John Moreton Drax Plunkett, 18th Baron of Dunsany (/dʌnˈseɪni/; 24 July 1878 – 25 October 1957), was an Irish writer and dramatist, notable for his work, mostly in fantasy, published under the name Lord Dunsany. More than eighty books of his work were published, and his oeuvre includes many hundreds of published short stories, as well as successful plays, novels, and essays.

Born to the second-oldest title in the Irish peerage (created in 1439), Dunsany lived much of his life at what may be Ireland's longest-inhabited house, Dunsany Castle near Tara. He worked with W. B. Yeats and Lady Gregory, received an honorary doctorate from Trinity College, Dublin, was chess and pistol-shooting champion of Ireland, and travelled and hunted extensively. He died in Dublin after an attack of appendicitis.

The mystical city of Bethmoora, first mentioned in Dunsany's A Dreamer's Tales, was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in The Whisperer in Darkness, and is also mentioned in the Mythos fiction of Hugh B. Cave.

### Behind the Mythos
Dunsany is almost always referenced when people discuss Lovecraft's Dreamlands stories. “There are my 'Poe' pieces and my 'Dunsany pieces' —but alas— where are any Lovecraft pieces?” Lovecraft once lamented. Not only Dunsany's style, but also his naming conventions made an impact on Lovecraft's work, particularly in "Polaris" (1918), "The White Ship" (1919), "The Quest of Iranon" (1921), "The Tree" (1920), "Celephais" (1920), and The Dream Quest of Unknown Kadath (1927). There is also a somewhat aimless, dream-like quality to Dunsany's works, which of course the Dreamlands in Lovecraft's writings overtly imitates. 

Dunsany also populated his fantasy worlds with imaginary gods of various types, as in his first published book, The Gods of Pegāna. The concept of an invented pantheon was a key influence on H. P. Lovecraft, who said he "got the idea of the artificial pantheon and myth-background represented by 'Cthulhu', 'Yog-Sothoth', 'Yuggoth', etc." from Dunsany.

Dunsany also invented creatures, like gnoles and gibbelins, that seem like models for the zoogs and ghasts of Lovecraft's Dreamlands.

In his correspondence, Lovecraft listed some of his favourite works by Dunsany:When I think of Dunsany, it is in terms of The Gods of the Mountain, "Bethmoora", "Poltarnees, Beholder of Ocean", "The City of Never" [sic], "The Fall of Babbulkund", "In the Land of Time", and "Idle Days on the Yann".Another Dunsany piece cited as a particular influence on Lovecraft is "A Shop in Go-by Street".

"Lord Dunsany and His Work" is a short non-fiction work by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Although it was written in 1922, it did not see publication until its appearance in the 1944 Arkham House collection Marginalia , seven years after Lovecraft’s death.

### Overview
The piece is an appreciation of the writings of Lord Dunsany, a prolific Anglo-Irish author whose work was a major influence on Lovecraft. This influence can be most clearly seen in Lovecraft's more fantastical works, such as the Dream Cycle.

*Marginalia (1944)
*Howard Phillips Lovecraft 1 (1991)
*Miscellaneous Writings (1995)

fullContent:
The Lord of the Deep is a malevolent Lovecraftian-like entity in the fictional universe of the Rifts pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium. It is somewhat similar in function to Cthulhu and has some Mythos overtones in its description.

### Background
The Lord of the Deep is a colossal cephalopod-like Eldritch monster, which is thousands of years old. One thats over 500 ft tall and 900 ft in diameter, with numerous tentacles. It's primary ones can stretch 1000s of miles and are almost 100 ft thick with 100s of tentacles at the end. Some believe that is the originator of the Kraken myth of pre-Cataclysmic Earth. 

It's a incredibly powerful entity with great magical and psionic powers, in addition to regenerative abilities and super strength. Capable of surviving a 82 megaton nuke, though with grievous wounds. The Lord of the Deep is a psychic vampire that feeds on the negative emotions which are generated by its dying victims. It's an entity which travels from dimension to dimension, consuming worlds. Its home dimension is a pocket dimension, a realm of water. 

Sometimes it will send out tentacles vast distances to capture victims which it drags back 100s or 1000s of miles back, kept alive by its magic. Which it then kills or turns into abominations.  Using its magic to merge its victims to the lifeforms of the sea, thereby creating monstrous hybrids. Magic, wooden weapons, holy weapons, and runic weapons inflict far greater damage on it than plasma cannons, laser beams, explosives, missiles, or other weapons.

### Background
The Lord of the Deep visited Earth thousands of years ago, before Egypt and Sumeria, when due to the Atlantean cataclysm, magic was disappearing from the world. It had opened a rift to Earth, and right through it came the Lemurians who were fleeing Earth, trapping it on Earth for 1000s of years. It would give rise to the Kraken myth of pre-Cataclysmic Earth. As magic slowly but steadily disappeared, it weakened and eventually went into a slumber. Upon the cataclysmic return of magic to Earth in the early 21st century, he began to slowly awaken. 

Now it terrorizes the sentient inhabitants of the sea and coastal regions along the Pacific Rim. Killing and mutating 1000s, most likely far more. It has established its own dark dominion in the western Pacific, south of Japan, east of China, and north of Indonesia. A domain which is steadily growing, both dimensionally and physically. Which is defended by its army of monstrous abominations, whom terrorize the seas, raid neighboring communities, and kidnap victims. In opposition to it is the time displaced American navy, the seaborne civilization of the Lemurians, and sentient dolphins, orcas, and whales. The Splugorth lord in the island-continent of Atlantis is aware of its existence and is monitoring its activities, and so are the various Vampire Intelligences on Earth.
