fullContent:
"Lord of the Land" is a horror short story by Gene Wolfe featuring his folklorist character Sam Cooper. It was originally published in 1990 in the anthology Lovecraft's Legacy, and was also included in Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology and The Book of Cthulhu, as well as in Wolfe's collection Starwater Strains.

This is the second story in the Sam Cooper series, following "The Nebraskan and the Nereid" (1985).

Although featuring only a tenuous connection to the Cthulhu Mythos, "Lord of the Land" is notable for its use of Lovecraftian horror, blending elements of mythology, folklore, and science fiction in a way reminiscent of some of H. P. Lovecraft's stories such as The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Synopsis
Sam Cooper, a folklorist from Nebraska, is interviewing an elderly Appalachian man named Hop Thacker, who lives with his son Joe and his granddaughter Sarah. Hop tells him a story that allegedly happened to one of his grandfather's friends, but his memory seems sketchy, as he mixes up characters' names and at one point starts referring to one of the characters as "Cooper", apparently confusing him with his interlocutor.

The story concerns a man named Laban Creech who sacrificed an old mule to attract crows so he and his two friends could have a crow-shooting competition. As the day comes to an end, Creech shoots something that he mistakes for a very large crow, only to find that it is a human-like creature known as a soul-sucker. According to local belief, the soul-sucker feeds on the souls of animals and people who fail to move on to the afterlife. When hungry, however, it might prey on the souls of the living. Although it looks mostly human, its mouth is filled with worms. It is also believed that the one who kills a soul-sucker will become a soul-sucker themself.

Having recorded the tale for his studies, Cooper agrees to stay with the Thackers for the night. After dinner, he consults a book called Gods before the Greeks and finds reference to an obscure Egyptian god named An-uat, a jackal-like being also known as "Lord of the Land" and "Opener of the North", who steals the souls of the departed when they refuse to board the boat of the sun god Ra. Cooper finds the parallels between An-uat and the soul-sucker interesting and wonders if an Egyptian legend might have somehow influenced Appalachian folklore.

When he comes downstairs to watch TV, Cooper notices that the Thackers appear to be afraid of something. He finds a handwritten message from Sarah asking him not to tell her father about the story that old Hop told him. Back in his bedroom, he dreams of the ancient Necropolis, the city of the dead that lies beyond the moon, where a jackal feeds upon a corpse that Cooper recognises as his own. At this point, he is awakened by a sound and gets up, only to hear a mysterious voice pronouncing the words "you must come to me".

"Lord of the Worms" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, featuring the occult investigator Titus Crow. Written in 1982, it was first published in Weirdbook 17 in 1983. Lumley says that it is, in his opinion, the best Titus Crow story.

A young Titus Crow, at loose ends after working for the British military during World War II, takes a job organizing the library of notorious occultist Julian Carstairs. He comes to realize that Carstairs actually has a more sinister purpose in mind for him--and finds himself in a battle of wits and will with his very identity at stake.

### Characters
Titus Crow: A 29-year-old man, born  December 2, 1916, whose "bent for the dark and mysterious side of life had early steeped him in obscure occult and esoteric matters." He worked for the British War Department during World War II, when he "advised the Ministry in respect of certain of Der Führer’s supernatural interests," and employed "the skills of the numerologist and cryptographer to crack the codes of his goose-stepping war machine."

Crow's father is an archaeologist; in discussing the "Oriental Institute’s work at Megiddo in Palestine" in 1937, he notes that "only a bout of ill health held me back from accompanying my father out to the site.”

Julian Carstairs: An "eccentric cult- or coven-leader" known as the “Modern Magus,” or “Lord of the Worms,” His "almost spectral face and figure" are "positively dismal." He is described as being "extremely tall and thin almost to the point of emaciation, with a broad forehead, thick dark hair and bushy eyebrows...with sunken cheeks and slightly stooped shoulders." 

Carstairs appears to be at least seventy years old, and possibly older than eighty-five--but in fact he is a collective worm-based entity who was born in 1602, in the Palestinian town of Chorazin, and has inhabited his current body since 1888. His previous incarnations, were, from 1602-68, a "dark, hawk-faced" Arab man; another Middle Eastern man, who wore the "rich dress of a sheik or prince," from 1668-1734; from 1734-90, a "statuesque, high-browed negro of forceful features and probably Ethiopian descent"; a "stern-faced young man in periwig and smallclothes" from 1790-1839; and from 1839-88, a "bearded, dark-eyed man...of unnatural pallor" who wore a monocle.

Taylor Ainsworth:   A friend and a chemist whom Crow "had known and studied with in Edinburgh." His "interests in the more obscure aspects of chemistry had alienated him from both tutors and students alike," with some thinking him "more alchemist than chemist proper."

Harry Townley: Titus Crow's family doctor, born 1896 or earlier. He believed that "hypnotism, homeopathy, acupuncture and such" could be "tremendous aids to more orthodox treatments." In 1946, he is considering retiring from medicine to become a minister.

The Lords of Tindalos are a fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by Frank Belknap Long for his 1984 short story "Gateway to Forever", and were later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Background
The Lords of Tindalos are transcendental creatures which are perceived by humans as having wolf-like shapes consisting of sharp angular pieces. Existing on higher planes, the lords appear to shift and change both their size and contours, which is due to the various segments popping in and out of space-time.

They have been in conflict with Yog-Sothoth from the beginning of time, as the Lords of Tindalos represent angular time and Yog-Sothoth represents curved time. The Lords of Tindalos have powers over time and space. In battle, they use not only their time-space abilities but also their claws, teeth, and tongue.

The Lost Archivist is a series of Cthulhu Mythos short stories by American author David Kenney. It was begun with the story to which it lends its name "The Lost Archivist," first published in Gavin Chappell's long-running horror magazine Lovecraftiana in July 2020.

### Premise
The Lost Archivist follows the exploits of Chief Archivist Wendell Hunt, a senior librarian at Arkham's Miskatonic University, specifically the Armitage Memorial Library, as he deals with various dark forces and departmental infighting while going about his daily duties.

Hunt is aided and directed in his activities by his superior, Dr. Clara Pedrick, and fellow archivist Dr. Shattuck, an elderly professor who keeps a legion of cats and has been driven to the verge of insanity by his experiences in the university vaults.

"Lost Soul" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the Necropolitan Press collection The Bones of the Old Ones and Other Lovecraftian Tales in 1995.

The story's title refers not only to those who were transported to alien dimensions, but to the mental state of one of the main characters, Meredith, who has no direction to her life.

### Synopsis
When thrill-seeking Leonard, his half-sister Meredith, and his girlfriend Andrea come into possession of an occult text - whose author mysteriously disappeared decades ago - they attempt to use the knowledge contained within to open a portal to another dimension. However, opening this gateway summons back the soul of the book's creator, who kills Andrea and sucks Leonard away to another plane of existence. Meredith is able to secure her freedom through trading the book with its former owner, but later resolves to do anything in her power to find another portal and rescue her missing sibling.

### Mythos Connections
The book used by Leonard, Meredith and Andrea, The Book of Awe, is stated to have been compiled from fragments from the Necronomicon, "The Pnakotic Manuscripts, The Book of Dzyan...Der Vermis Mysteriis, The Book of Thoth, Liber Ivonis and The Metal Book".

fullContent:
"Lost Stars" is a horror short story by Ann K. Schwader set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in 2003 in the collection Strange Stars & Alien Shadows: The Dark Fiction of Ann K. Schwader, before being republished in the 2011 anthology The Book of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
A woman named Diane invites her friend Sara to participate in a spirituality group led by the mysterious Egyptian priestess Sesh'tet. Sara works in an art gallery and has been busy organising an Egyptian exposition. Although skeptical, her interest is piqued by the claim that Sesh'tet's religion is older than the cult of Isis. At the meeting, the leader recites excerpts from a book called The Gate of All Lost Stars, which mentions deities with names such as Nyarlat, Assatur, Shuddam-El, Karakossa, and Shuppnikkurat. The principal deity that the text focuses on, however, is the goddess Ammutseba. The priestess Sesh'tet's appearance is peculiar, with disproportionately large eyes and a narrow face. She gives Sara a mystic amulet and instructs her to wear it until their next meeting while focusing her thoughts on whatever goal she wants to achieve.

Sara wakes up in the middle of the night to discover that the amulet has attached itself to her skin like a leech. She tears it off with difficulty and tosses it away. With the lights on, she finds that the silver ankh that she was also wearing is now looking inexplicably old and corroded. Unnerved, she copies the designs on the amulet and sends an e-mail to her former Egyptology teacher, Martin Stanley.

The next day, Sara has lunch with Diane. She notices that her friend is not sticking to her diet, but has nevertheless lost weight, which was Diane's goal when she joined Sesh'tet's group. Diane explains that focusing one's energy is all it takes and insists that Sara start wearing the amulet again before announcing that she will visit one of their fellow group members, who is sick in the hospital. Back home, Sara receives a very unexpected phone call from her ex-husband inviting her for dinner, as well as a call from Martin Stanley, who sounds nervous when he mentions Ammutseba. Stanley asks Sara to send him the amulet, warning her not to touch it again and to stay away from Sesh'tet's group.

Sara visits Diane on the next day after finding out that she's been in the hospital herself. Diane is very sick and has been told that she might have cervical cancer. Sara opens her friend's shirt and sees Diane's amulet all swollen, pulsating and feeding on her blood like a leech. She viciously tears it off and smashes it, although it shatters like ordinary stone rather than the squishy organism it appeared to be. Diane begs Sara to join the group's next meeting, which will be conducted outdoors at night as a healing ceremony under the stars.

"Love Is Forbidden, We Croak & Howl" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the May 2012 issue of Sirenia Digest (#78).

### Synopsis
The story presents a vignette of the impossible love between an Innsmouth deep one hybrid and an Arkham ghoul.

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in the anthology Lovecraft’s Monsters (Tachyon Publications, 2014). It later appeared in Kiernan's collection Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Subterranean Press, 2019).

A German translation, "Liebe ist verboten, so krächzen und jaulen wir," was published in a German edition of Lovecraft's Monsters (Festa, 2020).

Lovecraft and the Stars is a short monograph by E. Hoffman Price. Its main feature is a detailed description of H. P. Lovecraft's astral chart, based on Western astrology.

The American writer E. Hoffmann Price (1898-1988), who knew H. P. Lovecraft personally, and even became a cordial friend of his - in addition to writing in collaboration the story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" - set out to approach the mystery of the Providence master's life from a novel angle: astrology.

It was based on E. Hoffmann Price's own astrological studies of Lovecraft's life, and published in the Spring 1949 issue of The Arkham Sampler magazine.

The Lovecraft Annual was a long-running scholarly periodical published by Hippocampus Press.

### Overview
As its name might suggest, the Lovecraft Annual was a yearly publication, first issued in October 2007 and afterward released every August. It consisted of essays on the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft by a wide variety of modern-day contributors, and was edited by noted Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi.

The publication would appear to now be defunct, with the last issue seeing release in 2020.

### Overview
As a young man of 15, Willis Conover was interested in science fiction. He published a science-fiction fanzine, Science Fantasy Correspondent. This brought him into contact with horror writer H. P. Lovecraft. As an inveterate letter writer, Lovecraft began a communicative and extensive correspondence with Conover. The correspondence between Lovecraft, who was at the end of his life, and the young Conover, has been published as Lovecraft at Last.

shortDefinition: Lovecraft Cocktails (full title Lovecraft Cocktails: Elixirs & Libations from the Lore of H. P. Lovecraft) is a humorous horror fiction recipe guide based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. The book is published by The Countryman Press, copyrighted...
fullContent:
Lovecraft Cocktails (full title Lovecraft Cocktails: Elixirs & Libations from the Lore of H. P. Lovecraft) is a humorous horror fiction recipe guide based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. The book is published by The Countryman Press, copyrighted by Red Duke Games, LLC and illustrated by Kurt Komoda. The illustrated edition was first published on 21 October, 2021 and is available in Hardcover and Kindle.

### Setting
Similar to the Necronomnomnom before it, Lovecraft Cocktails appears to be set in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos. The tome itself is designed as an accompanying "bar book" supplementing the recipes found in Mike Slater's original Necronomnomnom with new drink guides. 

### Main Body
The main body is broken into six sections: Aberrations and Variations Upon Classic Libations, Uncharted Waters, Beer and Fear, Divine Inventions, Caffeinedish Creations, and Virgin Sacrifices. 

Within this section, the recipes are written in-world with accompanying illustrations. Various recipes are presented in the format of either a spell, a ritual, an alchemical process, and even as a poem with each having been collected together as the original Necronomnomnom was.

### Unit Conversion Guide
Unlike the original Necronomnomnom book, there isn't an Appendix; rather there is a Unit Conversion Guide for translating the measurements between Imperial and Metric. This conversion guide continues on with the in-world feel by converting the amounts into "Eldritch", a fictionalized unit of measurement that continues the flavour of the book.

### Design
The main design of Lovecraft Cocktails is presented as a parody, with fictional cooking humor to offer real-world recipes that can be made and enjoyed. The text presents the ingredients as real-world mundane items but with odd "rituals" in embellished format substituted for everyday directions.

Examples of the rituals involved:
*"In a hand cauldron mix the bitter and the sweet with the water" - mixing bitters with sugar and water in a pitcher
*"In a sipping pipe pour the black ichors of Kafe, follow with the nutty amber" - coffee liqueur with amaretto in a cup
*"The juice of moo is poured in the shaking vessel with the sands of awakening and the white crystals" - milk, instant coffee, and sugar in a shaker

Recipe titles will also often have parodies based in the lore of the Mythos, such as
*"Innsmouth Depth Charge"
*"Pink Flami-go"
*"H. Peach Lovedraft"
*"The King in Jello"

### See Also
*The Necronomnomnom: Recipes and Rites from the Lore of H. P. Lovecraft

The novel was adapted in 2020 into a TV series for HBO. A sequel, The Destroyer of Worlds: A Return to Lovecraft Country, will be published in 2023.

The major characters of the novel include Atticus Turner, a Black Korean War vet; his father Montrose Turner; his aunt Hippolyta Berry; his uncle George Berry, Hippolyta's husband; Letitia Dandridge, a neighborhood friend of Atticus; and Ruby Dandridge, Letitia's sister. The book also features Samuel Braithwhite, lodgemaster of the Order of the Ancient Dawn, and his son Caleb Braithwhite.

### Synopsis

### Episode 1: "Sundown"
Director: Yann Demange

Writer: Misha Green

Air Date: August 16, 2020

Atticus Green, a Korean War veteran, returns home to find his father Montrose missing. Among his possessions, he discovers a letter which leads him to believe he may have travelled to the town of Ardham, Massachusetts (which was at first misread as Arkham). Along with his uncle George Freeman and his friend Leti Lewis, Atticus embarks on a road trip to uncover his heritage. After a series of encounters with bigoted locals, the trio are apprehended by a lynch mob and dragged off into the woods. Before the mob has a chance to enact their violence, however, a pack of monstrous creatures attacks the group, seemingly under the control of an unseen benefactor; although the protagonists make their escape, the mob is torn to pieces, and Atticus and his friends find their way to a stately home and its welcoming tenant.

### Episode 2: "Whitey's on the Moon"
Director: Daniel Sackheim

Writer: Misha Green

Air Date: August 23, 2020

Atticus, George and Leti are guests of Samuel Braithwhite and his daughter Christina--who hint that there is a role for Atticus in the forthcoming Sons of Adam ritual. A clue is found to Montrose's whereabouts.

### Episode 3: "Holy Ghost"
Director: Daniel Sackheim 

Writer: Misha Green

Air Date: August 30, 2020

Back in Chicago, Leti and her sister Ruby attempt to turn a ramshackle Victorian mansion into a boardinghouse--facing opposition from neighborhood racists and awakening dormant spirits in the house.

Director: Victoria Mahoney

Writer: Wes Taylor & Misha Green

Air Date: September 6, 2020

Christina mysteriously shows up at Leti's doorstep. Later, Leti, Atticus, and Montrose travel to Boston hoping to find the missing part of a crucial text.

Director: Cheryl Dunye

Writer: Misha Green & Jonathan Kidd & Sonya Winton

Ruby supernaturally visits the other side of the racial divide. Atticus and Montrose have a confrontation.

Sprague de Camp and first published by Doubleday in 1975. Lovecraft: A Biography has been translated into several other languages, and has been extensively reissued, including in the digital medium.

fullContent:
Lovecraft: A Look Behind the "Cthulhu Mythos" is a 1972 non-fiction book written by Lin Carter. It was originally published by Ballantine Books in 1972. The introduction notes that the book is not intended to be a biographical work on H.P. Lovecraft himself but more a social history of the growth of those using his Mythos in their own works.

Lin Carter attempted in this work to define what was and was not "part of" the Mythos. His criteria for inclusion were such that The Colour Out of Space was NOT considered by him to be part of the Mythos. Lin Carter defined his approach thus:

"[T]he mere mention of a Mythos name in an otherwise self-contained story cannot be taken as proof that the story belongs to the Mythos,"

He excludes stories that do not "borrow from or build upon the system of the Mythos" as well as stories that do not "contribute a new portion of background lore to future stories in the Mythos."

Using his own system, he arrives at the following list as being his 'canon' Mythos works:

#"The Nameless City"
#"The Hound"
#"The Festival"
#"The Call of Cthulhu"
#"The Dunwich Horror"
#"The Whisperer in Darkness"
#"The Dreams in the Witch House"
#"At the Mountains of Madness"
#"The Shadow Over Innsmouth"
#"The Shadow out of Time"
#"The Haunter of the Dark"
#"The Thing on the Doorstep"
# "History of the Necronomicon" (short essay)
#Fungi from Yuggoth (poem)

Although his conclusions are wildly at odds with accepted wisdom today, his basic principles in attempting to pin down and create a formula for the Mythos is not especially different from later attempts, most notably in recent decades Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

fullContent:
Lovecraft's Book, by Richard A. Lupoff, is a historical novel originally published by Arkham House in 1985. It wad the first of Lupoff's books to be published by Arkham House.

The plot, set in 1927, involves H. P. Lovecraft being hired by a far-right politician to write an American Mein Kampf, in exchange for the publication of a collection of Lovecraft's horror fiction. The story unfolds to reveal a secret German plot to set up an underwater base for the resupply of submarines off the New England coast. It is obvious that the implication is Lovecraft would go on to incorporate the real-world German conspiracy in fictional form in his later story The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

An expanded version of the novel was published as Marblehead: A Novel of H. P. Lovecraft by Ramble House in 2006.

fullContent:
Lovecraft's Iraq is a military fiction Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author and former recon marine David Rose. Published by Screaming Banshee Press in March 2022 , it was released in paperback and digitally through Amazon's Kindle platform; the digital edition has since been removed from their library.

The book was followed by a short story sequel, "Lovecraft in Lockup," which was included in the 2023 collection Monsters in the Bush.

### Overview


### Synopsis
During the chaos of the Iraq War at the dawn of the 21st century, a squad of United States marines must contend with the re-emergence of the Sect of the Faceless God, an ancient cult dedicated to the Outer God Nyarlathotep. With the aid of a crippled soldier in possession of arcane powers and a mystical text which allows them to employ their own magics, the soldiers battle the cult, its sorcerous leaders, and a host of summoned abominations, paying a heavy price for their victory.

Despite winning this battle, it is later revealed that the cult was not destroyed, merely once more driven underground.

### Behind the Mythos
In addition to Nyarlathotep, other Mythos creatures which appear in the story include Shantaks, Nightgaunts, and Dimensional Shamblers, although unlike their appearance in other media, these creatures are employed as little more than cannon fodder in the battles between marines and cultists.

fullContent:
Lovecraft's Untold Stories is an action-adventure video game developed and published by Blini Games. Released on January 29, 2019, the game is inspired by the works of H.P. Lovecraft and draws heavily from the Cthulhu Mythos. It combines elements of survival horror, roguelike gameplay, and narrative exploration, immersing players in a world of cosmic horror and eldritch secrets. 

The game is also accompanied with a Lovecraft's Untold Stories Artbook DLC, a collection of the most beautiful images and artworks in hi resolution of the game, comprising 70 pages full of colourful elements, both in-game and created by Blini Games artists.

### Gameplay Overview
Lovecraft's Untold Stories features a top-down perspective and incorporates both action and exploration elements. The game allows players to choose from multiple characters, each with unique abilities and backgrounds. Players can explore procedurally generated levels, face off against otherworldly creatures, and unravel the mysteries of Lovecraft's universe.

Key gameplay elements include:

#Character Selection: Players can choose from different characters, including private investigators, occultists, and other archetypes inspired by Lovecraft's fiction. Each character has distinct skills and attributes that affect gameplay.
#Procedural Generation: The game features procedurally generated maps, ensuring that each playthrough offers a new and unpredictable experience. This design choice is intended to enhance replayability and maintain player engagement.
#Combat and Survival: Combat in Lovecraft's Untold Stories involves a variety of weapons and items, with a focus on managing resources and strategic use of equipment. Players must navigate hostile environments, combat supernatural entities, and solve puzzles.
#Sanity Mechanics: Reflecting Lovecraftian themes, the game includes a sanity system where encountering horrific events and creatures can affect the player’s mental state. This system impacts gameplay by altering character behavior and perception.
#Narrative Exploration: The game features a rich narrative that delves into Lovecraftian lore and mythology. Players uncover clues, read notes, and interact with NPCs to piece together the story and understand the cosmic horror elements at play.

### Storyline
The storyline of Lovecraft's Untold Stories centers around a series of mysterious events and eldritch occurrences that disrupt the lives of the characters. Set in a world plagued by supernatural forces and ancient deities, players investigate various scenarios that lead them to confront the horrors of the Cthulhu Mythos. The narrative is driven by exploration and discovery, with each character’s story offering different perspectives and insights into the cosmic threats they face.

### Development and Design
Blini Games, an independent developer known for their work in the action-adventure genre, created Lovecraft's Untold Stories with a focus on capturing the essence of Lovecraftian horror.

shortDefinition: Lovecraft's Untold Stories 2 is a roguelike action RPG developed by Blini Games. It draws heavily from the Cthulhu Mythos, and serves as the sequel to the original Lovecraft's Untold Stories while continuing the blend of Lovecraftian horror with fast...
fullContent:
Lovecraft's Untold Stories 2 is a roguelike action RPG developed by Blini Games. It draws heavily from the Cthulhu Mythos, and serves as the sequel to the original Lovecraft's Untold Stories while continuing the blend of Lovecraftian horror with fast-paced, top-down combat. Released on September 13, 2022, the game is available on multiple platforms, including PC (via Steam), PlayStation, Xbox, and Nintendo Switch.

The game's art style is a mix of pixel art and hand-drawn visuals, giving it a distinct, eerie aesthetic that complements its dark themes. The environments are richly detailed, capturing the atmosphere of dread and decay that Lovecraft's stories are known for. The sound design plays a crucial role in building tension, with a haunting soundtrack and unsettling sound effects that enhance the game's horror elements.

### Gameplay
Lovecraft's Untold Stories 2 builds upon the mechanics of its predecessor, offering a mix of action, exploration, and role-playing elements. The game features procedurally generated levels, ensuring that each playthrough offers a unique experience. Players navigate through various environments inspired by H.P. Lovecraft's stories, facing off against eldritch horrors, solving puzzles, and uncovering dark secrets.

The game introduces three playable characters, each with distinct abilities and playstyles:

*The Detective: A balanced character with a mix of ranged and melee attacks.
*The Witch: Specializes in magic and crowd control.
*The Professor: Utilizes gadgets and ranged weapons.

In addition to combat, the game features crafting mechanics, allowing players to create weapons, gear, and other items to help them survive the challenges they encounter. The game also emphasizes resource management, with players needing to carefully manage their health, sanity, and ammunition.

### Story
The narrative of Lovecraft's Untold Stories 2 continues to draw heavily from the works of H.P. Lovecraft, weaving a tale of cosmic horror and madness. The story takes place after the events of the first game, where the protagonists must once again confront the encroaching horrors from beyond the veil of reality. Players will explore new locations, including ancient temples, desolate cities, and otherworldly dimensions, all while piecing together the mysteries of the Lovecraftian universe.

### Reception
Lovecraft's Untold Stories 2 received mixed to positive reviews from critics and players. While many praised the game for its atmospheric design, challenging gameplay, and faithful adaptation of Lovecraftian themes, some criticisms were directed at its difficulty curve and the repetitiveness of its procedural levels. Despite these critiques, the game has garnered a dedicated fanbase, particularly among fans of Lovecraftian horror and roguelike games.

Lovecrafter is a German-language magazine focusing on Lovecraftian topics, including but not limited to pen and paper roleplaying games. It was launched in September 2016.

### Overview
Lovecrafter is published as the official journal of the Deutsche Lovecraft Gesellschaft e. V. (German Lovecraft Society). It was launched after the demise of Cthulhus Ruf. Each issue contains essays, interviews, and reviews on the respective issue's focal topic (e.g. Lord Dunsany; Lovecraftian Geographies; Dreamlands; etc.). In addition, a significant section of the magazine features pen and paper content, including game materials and scenarios for either the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game or the society's own gaming system FHTAGN.

Lovecraftian Cliff Notes for Ech-Pi-El is a poetry series by the late American author Franklyn Searight.

Ech-Pi-El (with suitable accents over some of the letters) was a psuedonym for H.P. Lovecraft used by, amongst others, Lin Carter and Richard F. Searight, the latter being Franklyn Searight's father. The name is a play on Lovecraft's initials: Ech for "H", Pi for "P" and El for "L."

### Overview
Published between 1998 and 2001, each of the poems in Lovecraftian Cliff Notes for Ech-Pi-El consists of a brief rundown of the plot of one of Lovecraft's short stories. The majority of these pieces were published in periodicals, with the E. P. Berglund-edited online fanzine Nightscapes hosting nearly half of them.

The term Lovecraftian Horror is a sub-genre of horror created by the American writer H. P. Lovecraft in his stories. Lovecraftian horror has been used in literature, art, comics, movies, television, and video games long after the author's death.

### Origin
Lovecraft refined this style to tell stories about his own "Cthulhu Mythos", as it came to be called by his successors, which comprised a set of supernatural, mythological, human, and extraterrestrial elements informed by the author's atheism and cosmicism. His work was deeply inspired by previous authors that Lovecraft constantly read and admired, some of them being Edgar Allan Poe, Algernon Blackwood, and Lord Dunsany. The basis of Lovecraft's work was cosmicism: the philosophy that ordinary human life is tiny and insignificant compared to the vastness and mysteries of the Universe.

In the search for wisdom or understanding the secrets of the vast universe in which we live, the discoveries that are made can end up damaging the sanity of a person, since our mind is not prepared to assimilate them. Lovecraft's stories usually take place in rural New England, that is, in the section of the United States in which the author himself grew up; however, Lovecraftian horror is not restricted to any particular setting, as some of the scenes in Lovecraft's tales do not take place in New England.

Narrations of this genre are usually characterized by the presence of a dark atmosphere that tries to convey to us the idea that there are secrets that man is not destined to know.

### Themes and elements of Lovecraftian Horror
Certain themes and elements are considered basic or essential to compose pieces within the genre of cosmic horror. Said aspects are also commonly found in Lovecraftian works by other authors.
*Anti-anthropocentrism, misanthropy in general. The Lovecraftian genre tends not to focus on the characterization of characters as individuals but rather on the point of view of humanity in general and their insignificant place in the universe (see: cosmicism).
*Preoccupation with strange and unknown substances and textures. The Lovecraftian genre tends to include gelatinous substances unknown to human science rather than elements of classic horror such as blood, bones, or bodies.
*Abominations. Biological in nature, they are detached from specific mysterious events and incomprehensible horrors. They are not explained in any other way or attributed to a specific event.
*Old-fashioned (Victorian) writing style. Even with the technology of his time, Lovecraft tended to use anachronisms and medieval words in his stories. For example, Lovecraft used the term 'man of science' instead of the word 'scientist' and usually spelled 'show' as 'shew' and 'lantern' as 'lanthorne'.

The line features plush toys in the 12-inch scale. The first Cthulhu plush was released in 2015; however, it would not become an official toyline until 2023.

In 2023, the first wave re-released the original Cthulhu plush with the new additions of Deep One, Hastur, Shoggoth, and Howard Lovecraft.

In 2024, the second wave consisted of the Necronomicon, Black Goat, Nyarlathotep, Old Ones, and Silver Cthulhu. 

In 2025, the third wave added Dagon, The Unnamable, and Yog-Sothoth.

Additionally, there are many other variants of the original Cthulhu plush, with most of them also being available in the 6-inch scale.

fullContent:
Lovecraftian: The Shipwright Circle is a short novel by American author and comic book creator Steven Philip Jones. Featuring cover and interior art by Trey Baldwin, it was published by Caliber Comics in August 2019; both paperback and digital editions were released.

Also included in the book is "The Empty House on Harley Street", a short story by Jones written as a prequel to "Herbert West--Reanimator".

### Premise
The story transposes several characters from H. P. Lovecraft's fiction into a contemporary setting, where they must thwart the plans of witch Keziah Mason and Messenger of the Outer Gods Nyarlathotep. These characters include Randolph Carter, Harley Warren, Asenath Waite, Edward Pickman Derby, Walter Gilman, Herbert West, and Henry Armitage.

### Synopsis
### Chapter 1: Memories & Possibilities
The main characters are introduced (sans West), having formed a social group dubbed The Shipwright Circle in Arkham, Massachusetts. Derby rents a very special room in the dilapidated Witch House, as he and Waite begin to become close. Warren and Carter investigate an ancient tomb hidden in the wilderness, but accidentally awaken Nyarlathotep, who kills Warren and assumes his form. 

### Chapter 2: Vague Ghosts of Monstrous Things
As Carter recuperates in an out-of-town institution, a mysterious virus - with symptoms similar to those encountered during the events at the Nahum farmstead years previously - begins to circulate in Arkham. While the town is quarantined and national agencies search desperately for a cure, West continues his trials with the reagent.

### Chapter 3: The Scourge, Grinning and Lethal
Carter receives dream-tutelage from fellow patient Joe Slaader before his release from hospital. Gilman and Pickman investigate an island on the Miskatonic River. At the behest of Dr. Armitage, Derby and Dr. Waldron look into the history of the Nahum farmstead. The Arkham Police Department must deal with a resurrected and cannibalistic Dean Allan Halsey, who is captured and admitted to a psych ward.

fullContent:
Lovecraftiana: the Magazine of Eldritch Horror is a fanzine published by Rogue Planet Press, an imprint of Horrified Press now known as Schlock! (schlock.co.uk). 

It features traditional Mythos works such as Lovecraftian short stories, poetry and art. Lovecraftiana currently as of 2025 is on an intended quarterly publication schedule with issues coming out April 30th, July 31st, October 31st, and January 31st. It  has some intermittently published issues bearing a numerical index as well as yearly volumes named for Candlemas, Lammas and so on.

The zine is known for including stories from established contemporary weird fiction authors, as well as showcasing works from newer or more obscure talent. Payment for authors or artists published in the zine is in the form of exposure and royalties from sales of the zine.

fullContent:
Lovely Lovecraft is a comic written and illustrated by Sara Bardi, based on life and tales of H. P. Lovecraft. It originated as a webcomic but a single paperback volume has been published, and is thus the only part covered by this wiki.

### Plot
In 1936, a middle-aged Howard Phillips Lovecraft is struggling with his latest novel, when he notices a flyer for a performer calling himself "The Great Nyarlathotep". While monologuing about what he knows about said performer, Howard makes his way to an abandoned building where Nyarlathotep is in the middle of giving a speech about the Old Ones to a group of frightened onlookers. Before he can finish, Howard stands up and calls him an impostor.

Nyarlathotep, seemingly enraged, demands the audience leave, leaving him alone with Lovecraft. Alone in the room, Nyarlathotep reveals how pleased he is to see Howard "Again". Howard inquires as to why he was summoned, and if the stars have finally aligned for the old ones return, and Nyarlathotep answers that they are, but not for him and his kin. For Lovecraft. The room is filled up with creatures dressed in yellow, and Nyarlathotep joyfully exclaims "You're going to die, Howard".

Decades earlier, in 1902, a young Howard Philip Lovecraft and his mother are traveling along an old road to Arkham. The driver is bleak, with sharpened teeth and cold, unblinking eyes. Howard inquires his mother about their landlord, the missing Randolph Carter, who went missing after being accused of murdering his friend Warren. When they arrive, the driver helps the mother carry in the lugage, though she shuts the door on him when she notices his unusual features. While she unpacks, Howard notices a draft upstairs, and go to investigate.

Upstairs, he finds Carter's workroom, and picks through a number of old books, eventually. Picking up the Necronomicon (one half of it, anyway). As he reads aloud, a figure looks at him through the window. Tentacles stretch out of the book, and Howard's mind shatters, and he sees his past, present and future, gaining the knowledge that he'll always be an outsider.

Howard wakes up in his bed, where his mother tells him that he slipped on the wet floor, and knocked himself out. She locks him in his room, and tells him that he can't read any more of those horror stories, while reminiscing about Howard's childhood and nightmares. At the same time, a young woman with purple hair awakes screaming in cell AZ-42 in the asylum. The caretakers claim to call her Azaela, after the color of her hair.

As Howard considers the posibility that he dreamed it all up, a small being with bat wings, three short horns, tail and long ears throws the necronomicon at him, calls him cultist, and acuses him of being involved in Carter's disapearance. The thing claims to be Phil'Gwanach, a night gaunt, though Howard doesn't believe it, on account of night gaunts being frightening and faceless, while Phil is kinda cute and rather face... ful. Howard does eventually believe

fullContent:
Low Red Moon is a novel by Caitlin R. Kiernan, published in 2003. Part of their Deep Time sequence of novels, it centers on characters that earlier appeared in Kiernan's Threshold (2001) and reoccur in their Daughter of Hounds (2007). Part of the background of these novels is a secret subterranean world of ghouls, inspired by the H. P. Lovecraft story "Pickman's Model."

In addition to Lovecraft, Kiernan names William Blake, Charles Fort, Tennyson, John Keats, W. B. Yeats, Angela Carter, Joseph Campbell, and Carl G. Jung  among the writers who influenced the story. They credit the title to song of the same name on Belly's 1993 album Star.

### Characters

* Chance Matthews, a scientist, university professor, paleontologist and expectant mother in her mid-twenties, she is married to Deacon Silvey. She is organizing an exhibit at the Fernbank Museum of Natural History in Atlanta when she experiences supernatural things. Since she grew up with grandparents who were both scientists, she finds it hard to believe in Deacon's psychic ability and in any other illogical and paranormal events. She was also known to be a straight-A honor student who focused only on studying and publishing academic papers until she met Deacon Silvey who was the first man she ever dated. The two of them shares a love of reading. (She is a major character in Threshold and features prominently in Daughter of Hounds.)
* Deacon Silvey, Chance Matthews' husband; a psychic who has worked with the Atlanta PD and is asked to help the Birmingham PD. A recovering alcoholic, he "looks a lot more like the hard end of fifty than thirty-nine." He is a stay-at-home husband and he tries hard to stay sober for Chance and their upcoming child. However, he gets involved with the police again when they ask him to use his psychic ability to solve a murder, despite his reluctance and annoyance. He drinks alcohol to deal with the migraines he gets from his abilities. He met Chance when she was still a student and he saved her and her friend one night from a street fight. Deacon and Chance share a love of reading books.  He studied philosophy for two years at Emory. (He is a major character in both Threshold and Daughter of Hounds.)
* Narcissa Snow, daughter of Caroline (and Aldous, apparently); a serial killer and magic-user with a plan involving Deacon Silvey's child. Said to be a werewolf, though whether that involves physical transformation is unclear. She is born December 31, 1975.
* Charles L. Patrick Akeley, Birmingham steel heir who donated his occult books to the library; "the wealthy grandson of a Birmingham steel baron who never married and spent most of his time traveling in Europe and Asia, chasing ghosts and collecting odd books on the occult."
* Elise Alden, a friend of Chance Matthews. She was with Chance when they met Dean Silvey. (She features prominently in Threshold.)

"Loyalty" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by prolific American author John Shirley.

### Synopsis
In the last days of an alien invasion in 2087, the surviving humans enlist the aid of an elderly professor with the aim of awakening Great Cthulhu to destroy the aggressors. However, Cthulhu wants something from humanity in return, and the survivors discover that the cost of salvation is far worse than they had expected.

### Characters

*Dr. Kline, a doctor charged with assuring Cthulhu's awakening.
*Professor Seekley, an old scholar with the knowledge of how to call forth Cthulhu.
*Ihlala Gulahosi, a representative of the United World.
*Cthulhu, a Great Old One and former Lord of the planet Earth.

### Publication History
"Loyalty" was first published in the Brian M. Sammons/Glynn Owen Barrass-edited anthology World War Cthulhu in 2014.

Lrogg is a fictional deity created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Insects from Shaggai", which portrays it as the main god worshiped by the L'gy'hxians, the native inhabitants of the planet L'gy'hx, known to humans as Uranus.

In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, it is identified as an avatar of Nyarlathotep. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

### Overview
Described as a "relatively insignificant deity" (compared to Azathoth), Lrogg is a two-headed bat-like creature worshiped as the main god on L'gy'hx. Its cult is regarded as comparatively agreeable, as Lrogg confers benefits to its believers and demands nothing more than an annual ritual that involves the removal of the limbs of a chosen native. Cultists are willing to tolerate other faiths, if not provoked. Their enemies are executed by having acid poured into their brains. The fact that these practices pale in comparison to the atrocities committed by the cult of Azathoth speaks volumes about the cruelty of the latter. (: "The Insects from Shaggai")

Lu-Kthu, otherwise known as Lew-Kthew or the Birth-womb of the Great Old Ones, is an Outer God whose first appeared in James Ambuehl's short story "Correlated Contents", published in 1998. Ambuehl is an American horror writer who has expanded H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos with the creation of the Lu-Kthu Cycle or Pantheon of Lu-Kthu.

### Overview
Lu-Kthu is described in the book called The Rituals of Glaa-Dith.

The innumerable ovoid pustules on the slimy surface of the enormous creature are both inside and outside these tunnels and are in fact biological incubators. How often the larvae inside the incubators mature and spawn forth is unknown.

Luci Jenifer Inacio Das Neves, who goes by by the name of Lucifer, is a character created by American comic book creator Michael Alan Nelson for the Gray Man story arc of his Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. She made her first appearance in issue #11 in March 2008.

### Description
A pretty young woman in her late teens or early twenties, Lucifer lived her early life as an orphan thief on the streets of Brazil. There, she encountered an occultist named Walter McKinley who took her in, making use of her talents as a thief in exchange for food and board. Under his tutelage, she gained a degree of mystical knowledge, including how to use protective wards and travel to the Dreamlands.

As an adult, Lucifer continues to use her talents to combat the supernatural threats which threaten humanity, despite the recent loss of her mentor.

Lucifer has, during the course of her activities, stolen a precious artefact from the supernatural creature known as the Harlot. Although she has been punished for this transgression, she remains in the Harlot's debt.

### History
After travelling to Arkham in search of McKinley, Lucifer was devastated to discover that her mentor had committed suicide in the face of the horrors which he had witnessed. 

After a series of gruesome murders - including those of several Arkham Police Department officers - Lucifer partnered with Sheriff Raymond Dirk to defeat the supernatural perpetrator, a being known as the Gray Man. After a series of adventures in which she confronted one of the Horsemen of Nyarlathotep, travelled to the Dreamlands and met with the Harlot, and faced off against a Cthulhu cult, Lucifer and Dirk were successful in trapping the Gray Man in an inescapable prison.

### Synopsis
Chuck, a man seemingly in the grip of a midlife crisis, accepts the invitation of a group posing as a social outreach organisation when they offer to take him and a bus full of other discontented people on a road trip, ostensibly to help them all find a little happiness. However, the group are not as they seem - indeed, may not even be human - and open a gateway in the desert to allow Great Cthulhu to pass through and feed on the poor unfortunates.

Lucy is a character created by author Ian Davey as one of the protagonists in his Bh'yhlun series of Cthulhu Mythos stories. She made her first appearance in 1997 in "Black Letter Day".

### Overview
Lucy was, in the time before the coming of Nyarlathotep, a regular woman in a relationship with a man named Georgio, a gifted filmmaker. Georgio decided to create a piece based on an old book he had come across, Feery's Notes on the Necronomicon, and thus began the end of the human race, an event which Lucy was uniquely placed to witness.

After the fall of humankind Lucy, alone and pregnant, preserved her sanity through the careful use of certain drugs while she made her way to Glastonbury, following a psychic pull which promised safety.

Eventually reaching Glastonbury, Lucy, a girl who called herself Glyph, and older couple Helen and Aaron defeated an avatar for Nyarlathotep and managed to restore the world to its former condition- mostly…

Ludvig Prinn is a character created by H. P. Lovecraft's friend and contemporary Robert Bloch. He was first mentioned in the short story "The Secret in the Tomb" in May 1935.

### Description
An alchemist and practitioner of black magic during the Middle Ages, Prinn apparently used his knowledge of dark sorcery to prolong his life for at least two centuries. (: "The Shambler from the Stars")

Prinn is the author of the occult text De Vermis Mysteriis, which would go on to appear in a host of Mythos stories over the years since its creation.

### History
Prinn was captured during the Ninth Crusade in 1271 and held captive in Syria, where he learned much from the sorcerers of that country. He later travelled through Libya and Egypt, before being burned at the stake in Brussels for apparent human sacrifice. (: "The Shambler from the Stars", "Fane of the Black Pharaoh")

In his later years Prinn was attended by a number of invisible creatures he kept as his loyal servants. (: "The Shambler from the Stars")

### Descendants 
*Abigail Prinn, a witch and secret priestess of the being known as Nyogtha who was executed in 1690 (: "The Salem Horror").
*Ezekiel Prinn, a cultist in the modern day (: "Wilbur Whateley Waiting").
*Although never explicitly identified as Prinn, one of Randolph Carter's ancestors was a "flame-eyed Crusader who learnt wild secrets of the Saracens that held him captive". (: "The Silver Key")

Luigi Cozzi (born 7 September 1947 in Busto Arsizio, Lombardy) is an Italian filmmaker, author and editor who has had a hand in a number of Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos works. He has written at least two short Mythos stories and edited a further two anthologies of material translated into his native language, all of which has been published by Fanucci Editore as part of their I Miti di Cthulhu series. In Wikipedia's article on Cozzi, it is claimed that Dennis Fischer's 2011 non-fiction book Science Fiction Directors, 1895-1998 credits him with the creation of a novel, Cthulu Night. Although outside verification for this is lacking, it would appear at least possible that the author has this confused with Cozzi's short story "La notte di Cthulhu," which translates to "The Night of Cthulhu."

Cozzi's filmmaking credits include numerous science fiction, fantasy, and horror productions, several collaborations with legendary horror director Dario Argento, and the supervision of an edited version of the original 1954 release of Godzilla.

Luke Robinson, the Dreamer, is a character who appears in several of Fantasy Flight Games' additions to the expanded Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
Always a great dreamer, years ago Luke discovered the allure of the Dreamlands. He had climbed down the Seventy Steps of Light Slumber, faced the judgment of Nasht and Kaman-Thah, and walked through the Doors of Sleep; from then on he spent every night delving into its secrets. He wandered the sleeping world exploring all that he could, and discussed the reality of the place with its denizens before stumbling across the greatest truth of all: the Dreamlands were a real place, and one could travel there, if one knew how.

Gathering up his meagre possessions and setting his affairs in order, Luke made his way to the portal he had been told of and passed through, thinking that he would never again see the waking world.

However, word came to Luke that something catastrophic was happening in Arkham, that an evil from before time was rearing its ugly head once again. So, collecting his things for a second time, Luke prepared to leave the Dreamlands, to return to the waking world and prepare to defend his old home.

### Bones of the Yopasi
In Graham McNeill's 2012 novel, while living in the city of Oriab, Luke encountered Henry Cartwright, an amnesic dreamer whose body was dying in the waking world. He travelled back and located Cartwright's companions, who made their way to the Dreamlands - with help from the Terrible Old Man - and saved the poor man.(: Bones of the Yopasi)

### Behind the Mythos
The character of Luke Robinson was originally created to be an Investigator for the Kingsport Horror expansion for the Second Edition of Arkham Horror, but has since made appearances in Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and Arkham Horror Third Edition. In addition, Fantasy Flight released a plastic miniature of him in 2010 as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, but this is no longer in production (all ).

### Trivia
* When Luke departed the waking world for the Dreamlands, he left behind an unnamed woman who he loved, a decision he has always regretted.
* Luke claims to have been taught the art of dreaming by no less than the legendary Randolph Carter.
* A gifted artist, Luke once did a stint for the Boston police as a sketch artist; his drawing linked one Frank Wallace to a series of bootlegging murders in Charleston, resulting in a conviction.

Lumens are an odd phenomena/lifeform created by F. Paul Wilson for his 1989 Cthulhu Mythos story "The Barrens". 

### Description
Lumens are glowing lights that appear in "nexus points" where the fabric between reality is thin. Animals and plantlife that inhabit the areas where Lumens manifest mutate into strange forms.

### Behind the Mythos
Lumens appear to draw inspiration from the entity in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Colour Out of Space", which also physically transforms living matter which it comes into contact with.

The Luminous Transparency is a fictional entity created by American author and games designer Kevin A. Ross for the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. It first appeared in "Thunder in the Blood", a scenario included in the supplement End of the World (Triad Entertainments, 1994).

### Overview
The Luminous Transparency is one of five Lesser Other Gods from the Court of Azathoth that appeared during a summoning of Azathoth near San Lucas. It appears as a constantly shifting and self-reconfiguring conglomeration of transparent blue-white pyramid shapes. During this process it encloses nearby objects within itself. (: End of the World)

The Lurker in the Star Pool is a fictional entity created by American author A. A. Attanasio for his 1980 short story "The Star Pools."

### Description
The Lurker in the Star Pool is one of the Million Favoured Ones, beings granted a new form by Nyarlathotep. It is described as a massive translucent blob full of a red gas with multiple heads resembling sharks and squids as well as gangly limbs and bat-like wings. 

It dwells in the Star Pools, a collection of thousands of green ponds in Haiti.

The story tells of how as a child, the narrator took up the task of searching for Howard Phillips Lovecraft's lost cat. He remarks on how unsurprising it is that Lovecraft suffers from night terrors as he returns the thing and claims his dollar reward.

fullContent:
"Lurkers" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author David A. Riley.

### Synopsis
Johnny, a bank robber on the run, decides to cut through a bad area of town in an effort to evade the police officers who are hot on his heels. However, he picks up some new pursuers in the form of a group of hideously deformed youths who chase him into a derelict housing estate. Finding his new hidey-hole to be inhabited by more of the creatures - even more devolved than the others - he attempts to escape through a tunnel, only to emerge in a future Earth overrun by a multitude of hideous abominations, including the dreaded Shoggoths.

Encountering a small group of near-feral humans, Johnny rises to become their leader, hunting other groups who soon become their food source. As the nearby tribes are wiped out and the group begins to starve, he realises that they must attempt to return to his time. Successfully navigating the tunnel, they emerge into a more civilised time only to discover that they have become exactly like the creatures inhabiting the estate.

### Publication History
"Lurkers" was first published in the collection of Riley's own works The Lurkers in the Abyss and Other Tales of Terror by Shadow Publishing in August 2013. It also appeared in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2020.

Lurking Fear is a low-budget horror film from director C. Courtney Joyner. It is very loosely based on the H. P. Lovecraft short story of the same name.

### Synopsis
A former criminal and member of the Martense family attempting to recover a stash of stolen money buried in a cemetery finds himself up against a brood of monstrous creatures.

### Trivia

*Horror movie icon Jeffrey Combs is one of the lead actors in Lurking Fear; Combs was also the star of Re-Animator and From Beyond, other films based on Lovecraft's work ("Herbert West--Reanimator" and "From Beyond").
*Another horror movie icon, Ashley Laurence, the star of Clive Barker's film Hellraiser, a production which has also been cited as Lovecraftian in nature, also appears in Lurking Fear.
*Veteran Cthulhu Mythos artist Pete Von Sholly provided the storyboard for Lurking Fear.

Lynn Willis (died January 18, 2013) was an American game designer and writer.

### Overview
Beginning his career working with Metagaming Concepts, in 1978 Lynn Willis joined Chaosium, the company with which he would make the largest impact on the world of tabletop gaming. Although he worked on several different lines during his time with Chaosium, his contributions to the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game were perhaps his most memorable works. Aside from designing the Masks of Nyarlathotep campaign (one of the most highly praised game expansions of all time) with Larry DiTillio, Willis worked on the design of the fifth and sixth editions of Call of Cthulhu with Sandy Petersen, and took over as line editor for the series after the departure of Keith Herber. He then continued as Chaosium's editor-in-chief from 1998 until 2008, when poor health forced his retirement after more than thirty years with the company.

Lynn Willis died in 2013 after several years suffering from Parkinson's disease.

Lynne Hardy is an award-winning roleplaying games designer and occasional author based in the United Kingdom. Her gaming credits include the core books for Modiphius Entertainment's historical Call of Cthulhu setting Achtung! Cthulhu, as well as material for the main time period of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu, a major influence on horror roleplaying and the modern Cthulhu Mythos in general. Her fiction has appeared in anthologies such as Cthulhu Lives! (Ghostwoods Books, 2014) and It Came from Miskatonic University (Broken Eye Books, 2020).

Hardy is currently Chaosium's Associate Editor for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

Montague Rhodes James, better known as M. R. James, (August 1, 1862 - June 12, 1936) was a British scholar, story teller and writer. He served as provost of King's College, Cambridge (1905–18) and of Eton College (1918–36). 

He is best known for his ghost stories and for developing some of the elements that are still used in that genre. His writings influenced H. P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, Stephen King, Ramsey Campbell and John Betjeman. James also influenced radio, film, television and music works.

He originated the "antiquarian ghost story" sub-genre, where a contemporary setting is juxtaposed with elements, histories or even survivals from a past time, usually tied to the same location as the present day setting.

James was a practising archaeologist and Medieval scholar of some fame and repute within his own life-time, having led excavations and made significant discoveries from the Medieval period.

Most of his ghost stories were originally written to be read aloud to friends.

The M'and Ybula are a fictional race created by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Secrets of Tibet.

It would seem that their name is inspired by or a play on the word "mandibular".

### Background
The M'and Ybula are a race of Deep One/Human hybrids. Intelligent and powerful cephalopod humanoids which were created by the Deep Ones to serve and protect the imprisoned Star Spawn, whose eternal prisons had been elevated far above the sea level by tectonic activities over the millennia. The M'and Ybula have adapted to living on the Tibetan plateau, living close to the salt lakes of Tibet. Over millions of years their numbers have dwindled. As they age at a far slower rate than any other lifeform on Earth, the eldest of them possess great intellect and powerful spells. It's a sophisticated race which is in contact with humans and likely other Mythos races. The M'and Ybula understand and use technology, but prefer using magic. It's rumored that their greatest weapon is an Elder Thing weapon they have somehow acquired: a virus which was developed by the Elder Things to eradicate all humans and shoggoth, and which is their doomsday weapon. It has been used to threaten mankind when they need to force one of their nations or leaders to do their bidding. The oldest and wisest are shapeshifters able to take many forms, including that of human beings.

Unknown to the younger members of the race, the eldest also have the ability to preserve their lifeforce and thoughts for days after their physical form is killed. During which, their "spirit" is able to look for a new host, normally a human baby. The baby will grow like a normal human but with the knowledge and thoughts of the M'and Ybula. Once it becomes an adult, it will take full control and either continue existing as a human for a time or manipulate the body's DNA to transform it into a M'and Ybula. M'and Ybula are naturally stealthy beings and are able to camouflage themselves in a manner similar to cuttlefish. Ancient M'and Ybulas usually are entrenched in mountain fortresses or cavern systems, where they surround themselves with their minion, servants, and slaves (the latter two consisting of humans). Within some of these enclaves are elaborate bureaucracies and their inner circles are rife with Machiavellian politics. The M'and Ybula that walk the land as humans for years do so for a variety of reasons. Some of them enjoy inflicting pain and fear on humans via torture. Others have a clinical mindset, seeing humans as subjects to perform experiments on. Some enjoy mankind's sensual pleasure, engaging in all types of pleasurable and painful activities.

M'bwa is a fictional character created by Donald Wandrei for his short story "The Tree-Men of M'bwa", later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the role-playing game supplement Malleus Monstrorum.

### Description
M'bwa is an undead human being, a reanimated corpse in service of the mysterious God of the Red Flux in a valley beyond the Mountains of the Moon, somewhere between the Congo river and Uganda. He appears as an extremely old man with dark skin and a pasty grey face. He has no voice, no breathing, and no blood. His eyes look completely dead. Despite all this, M'bwa has superhuman strength and moves with supreme speed and agility. This, coupled with his relentlessness and ability to shrug off physical injuries, allows him to overpower any opponent at his master's command. While his body isn't invulnerable, any damage caused by blades or bullets is of no consequence. Even after being decapitated, M'bwa was simply revived by his master, who briefly stepped out of the Red Flux to reattach his severed head to his shoulders.

After subduing his victims, M'bwa pours a burning liquid into the victim's mouth which renders them unconscious, then starts making deep cuts on the victim's legs. When the victim awakes, their legs have become roots which have been planted into the soil. With the passage of time, the victim mutates into a Tree-Man. (: "The Tree-Men of M'bwa")

M'nagalah is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Len Wein for DC Comics and made its first appearance in Swamp Thing Vol 1 #8 "The Lurker in Tunnel 13", depicting the entity as a threat to the entire universe.

Soon afterwards, M'nagalah was introduced to the Mythos proper in Ramsey Campbell's short story "The Tugging", and was later incorporated into the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Background
In prehistoric times, M'nagalah ruled over the Tethys Ocean and was described as being "Cthulhu's right-hand man". (: Nightmare's Disciple) Some drawings of M'nagalah were documented in The Revelations of Glaaki, depicted as being a tentacled mass consisting of ropey intestine-like appendages and numerous eyes. (: "The Tugging")

### In the DC Multiverse
### New Earth
Billions of years ago, M'nagalah and the other Elder Gods were able to roam the universe at will through a cosmic doorway located on Earth, until they were shut off from the cosmos by the Golden Ones. Despite this, M'nagalah and his kind were still able to reach out across the dimensional barriers and touched the minds of learned men, twisting their intellect with visions and corrupting their souls. (: Challengers of the Unknown) M'nagalah claimed to have created all life on Earth and bestowed mankind with the capacity for mindless violence, as well as influencing the minds of some of humanity's greatest scribes, including H. P. Lovecraft, Ambrose Bierce and Edgar Allan Poe. (: "The Lurker in Tunnel 13")

In the year 1684, M'nagalah used the Book of Ending to infect the hand of a Ukranian girl named Elaina and later used his influence on her to conduct a ritual that would allow him to fully manifest in Chernobyl. In an alternate future, M'nagalah consumed all life on Earth, but this was ultimately prevented by the time-traveling efforts of the Trenchcoat Brigade. (: The Trenchcoat Brigade)

By the year 1904, the occult practices of Abraham Monroe allowed M'nagalah to manifest in the town of Perdition, Pennsylvania. Starting off as a growth on his arm, M'nagalah eventually infected Abraham's entire body and consumed many others so that he could gain more mass, dwelling in one of the town's mine shafts named Tunnel 13 and terrorizing the town for over 70 years. During his encounter with the Swamp Thing, M'nagalah attempted to consume the supernatural monster in order to reach his full mass and conquer the entire universe. Although he was seemingly destroyed after the Swamp Thing caused the tunnel to collapse on top of him, a piece of M'nagalah survived and was growing on the arm of Abrah

M'nthster is a Great Old One from the fictional universe of the animated series The Simpsons. The character first appeared in the opening sequence for the episode "Treehouse of Horror XXIV", directed by Guillermo del Toro, when Bart skateboarded on his tentacles that bursted out of the ground. M'nthster was later featured in the mobile game The Simpsons: Tapped Out, as an unlockable character during the "Cthulhu's Revenge 2019 Event".

### Background
M'nthster is the eldest spawn of Cthulhu, who was abandoned by his father as a baby, after being traded in for a pair of designer sunglasses. They continued to be on bad terms for a while, and at least one of their fights resulted in them destroying all of reality. With some help from Marge, Cthulhu was able to eventually patch things up with M'nthster. (: The Simpsons: Tapped Out)

Situated in the town of Arkham, Massachusetts, Ma's Boarding House is located in the Southside neighbourhood. according to Arkham Horror, it is owned by one Ma Mathison, about which little is known; however, the 2016 Call of Cthulhu scenario Dead Boarder states that it is owned by Loretta "Ma" Shanks, an elderly woman who is partially deaf and resides in the building. This "Ma" employs a landlord to run the business in her stead, her age and condition making it unfeasible to do so herself.

Brenda Goff, better known as Madame Renee, is a character who appears in several of the Arkham Detective Agency stories by C. J. Henderson and others.

### History
After a career as a dancer in her younger years, Brenda Goff came to the realisation that the natural shelf-life of a professional dancer would not provide her with a steady income for the rest of her days. Deciding to make use of her natural psychic talents, she changed her name to Madame Renee and cultivated her naturally-Middle Eastern looks along with a faux accent to become a professional medium. 

Since then she has developed a working relationship as a consultant with the Arkham Detective Agency, and Frank Nardi in particular, who she seems to have something of a soft spot for.

At some point in her life, Madame Renee gave birth to an unnamed daughter who is now of college age. She is stated to be worried about being able to afford her daughters university fees.

### Behind the Mythos
Madame Renee was created by C. J. Henderson for his first Frank Nardi story, The Idea of Fear, and has since appeared in several other stories involving the characters by different authors.

### Synopsis
The plot involves Terry Aldrich, a young man from Brichester who travels to neighbouring Goatswood to buy a set of garden gnomes for his girlfriend Kim, thinking they will "bring her garden closer to nature". The Goatswood gnomes turn out to be animate--and malevolent.

"Madeline Marsh's Midlife Crisis" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author K. Z. Morano. It was published in the James Ward Kirk Publishing anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
After his wife Madeline returns home to Innsmouth to be with her love Dagon, a man nicknamed Mister Snow travels to the coastal town to win her back from what he believes to be her small-town lover. When he gets there, he is captured by a group of degenerate Deep Ones attempting to restore their genetic code and used as breeding stock. Although Snow is almost successful in escaping with the help of a young girl, his attempt to rescue his wife results only in him bearing witness to her final transformation and his recapture by the locals.

Madeline Rothleschilde is a hero in the fictional Army of Darkness universe who was created in 2005 by James Kuhoric. She first appeared in issue #1 of the 1st volume of Army of Darkness Vs. Re-Animator.

### Background
Madeline Rothleschilde was a nurse at Arkham Asylum who freed Ash Williams so he could stop Dr. Herbert West and prevent the return of the Dark Ones. After which she became involved in several of his adventures as an ally of Ash, battling Deadites and various supernatural monsters (vampires, werewolves, and mummies). In the aftermath of Ash's defeat of the Four Horsemen, history was re-written and Sugarbaby was now an agent of the T.A.R.D. organization.

The Madness of Wonderland is a four-issue comic book mini-series written by Dan Wickline in 2008-2009 which was published by Zenescope Entertainment. 

### Synopsis
Detective Legrasse investigates the murders that happened in the Call of Wonderland, and the mysterious disappearance of the two murder suspects. In the back-story, Lovecraft's disturbing dreams become ever more real and he finds himself held at gunpoint by Jacob Hall, forced to take part in a subterranean expedition where they encounter an organism unknown to science.

### Connections
*The Lovecraft subplot includes several references to At the Mountains of Madness. For instance, the scientist hired by Jacob Hall to study the new organism is named Dr. Danforth. A character named Gedney is also mentioned, and his involvement is identical to the role the original Gedney played in the novel.

fullContent:
"Madness on the Black Planet" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Darrell Schweitzer. It was first published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
In a future in which humankind is on the brink of an unspecified destruction, three astronauts embark on a mission to a newly-discovered planet in the Kuiper Belt. Their journey culminates in a meeting with the oligarch who dispatched them in the first place, now in the guise of a yellow-masked being whose only motivation seems to be witnessing the end of the human species.

### Mythos Connections
The rich individual who finances the expedition and later turns out to be an otherworldly entity is likely intended to be Hastur, or possibly its avatar, the King in Yellow; the description of his yellow mask combined with the cycle of madness experienced by the astronauts would appear to support this.

One of the astronauts, in the depths of insanity, mentions "Kadath in the Cold Waste, the Gardens of Ynath, and "more distant Shaggai.""

### Publication History

Magic is the practice of feats that defy natural laws, supposedly achieved by supernatural forces or energies, and might involve spells, rituals, signs, potions, etc. As a widespread concept in speculative fiction (particularly but not exclusively in the fantasy genre), magic has been a part of the Cthulhu Mythos since its beginnings, although different authors and works have provided different views on it. Practitioners of magic, sometimes referred to as sorcerers, witches or wizards, often appear as characters in the Mythos.

In the real world, magic has been studied and allegedly practiced by occultists and other scholars, including such figures as John Dee and Éliphas Lévi, among many others. It is distinct from the stage magic performed by entertainers such as Harry Houdini, which is openly based on illusion and skill. Expanded Mythos author Alan Moore is also a practitioner of ceremonial magic.

### In the Mythos
Magic can describe any otherworldly force or energy. It can be manipulated by humans but only with tremendous danger to the user. For some greater magics it even requires the sacrifice of the soul. It is known to be practiced in nearly every part of the human inhabited world. With advanced mathematics and theoretical physics some grasp can be gained over the these forces.

Magic is usually very difficult to wield and requires knowledge and preparation, whether it needs several hours of chants, intricate esoteric circles or sacrifices, it is a very dangerous discipline that no mundane human tends to come across. Many times, cults draw magic from their primal deities, as the practitioners summon their patrons to fuel incantations and spells.

.]]
There are numerous books dedicated to the study and practice of magic, the most infamous likely being the Necronomicon. Objects and even people may be infused with mystical energy. The extra-dimensional being Azathoth is known to supply his followers with magical energy. Most unearthly entities can only exist on our plane through the extensive use of magic. If not constantly charged with this magic they will be destroyed.

An example of an object with magical properties would be the Silver Key, which was forged in Hyperborea (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key"), where sorcerers and wizards seem to have been common (: Hyperborean Cycle). Even in the modern day, some humans have been known to master magic, such as Ephraim Waite (: "The Thing on the Doorstep") or the Carnby brothers (: "The Return of the Sorcerer"). Beyond Earth, other civilisations had their own wizards, such as Zkauba, a Yaddithian who used magic spells to help prevent the Dholes from leaving their burrows (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key").

Magic seems to be a natural ability of some species, such as the Serpent People. (: "The Shadow Kingdom")

Magna Mater is referenced as Cybele in the H. P. Lovecraft story "The Rats in the Walls".

Magna Mater is a Latin phrase meaning 'Great Mother' and was used historically as a title in Ancient Rome for both Cybele, a middle eastern cult with transvestite and eunuch priests and ecstatic public rituals and processions involving ritual slashing and blood spilling, and more generally in ancient syncretic religious beliefs as being the female principle in its highest and most powerful form, that of the giver of life, who impliedly could also take it away. In this sense it is cognate with the "Earth Monster" from South American ancient religion or the Amazonian Yacumama. More simply, a humanoid personification of Mother Nature as both the mother of us all, and the soil to which we will return.

The Magnum Innominandum (also known as the Nameless Mist, Nyog'Sothep or N'yog-Sothep) is a fictional deity from the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first mentioned by H. P. Lovecraft in the Selected Letters.

### Overview
The Nameless Mist is an Outer God, who is the progenitor of several other cosmic entities, including Yog-Sothoth. It is older than everything, except for its creator Azathoth and its siblings, the Unnamed Darkness and Nyarlathotep.

Its powers include possible omnipresence, reality warping, acausality, space-time manipulation, immortality and incorporeality.

### Behind the Mythos
The Magnum Innominandum idea came to Lovecraft during a Roman dream he recalled in three letters, one of those being incorporated into The Horror from the Hills and another posthumously published as "The Very Old Folk". It was also mentioned in The Whisperer in Darkness, alongside many Mythos concepts such as Hastur, the Yellow Sign and Yog-Sothoth. The incantation "Tibi, Magnum Innominandum, signa stellarum nigrarum et bufaniformis Sadoquae sigilum" from De Vermis Mysteriis was penned by Lovecraft for Robert Bloch's "The Shambler from the Stars".

Lovecraft also mentioned the "Not-to-be-Named One" in "The Mound" as husband of Shub-Niggurath (this has led to the theory that the Magnum Innominandum and the Nameless Mist are two separate entities, and the Magnum Innominandum is Yog-Sothoth). He also introduced "Him Who is Not to Be Named" along with other names such as Shub-Niggurath or Nyarlathothep (though Yog-Sothoth is not named in the invocation).

Lovecraft mentioned the Nameless Mist in a Family Tree of Azathoth. The Nameless Mist was given the name "Nyog'Sothep" and "N'yog-Sothep" by later authors.

The Magnum Innominandum and The Nameless Mist were also unified as the same entity by later writers, including Lin Carter and the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.
