fullContent:
"Mahtavat Ammoiset" (Finnish for Great Old Ones) is a 2012 Finnish short horror story written by Tuomas Saloranta, which is tied to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Summary
The story starts around the 1980s when the unnamed narrator, who is an university student in Helsinki, is spending time with Uncle Allan, a long-time family acquaintance, who owns an antiquarian bookshop in the neighbourhood of Punavuori.

Both Allan and the narrator are big fans of the works by H. P. Lovecraft, especially the Cthulhu Mythos.

While drinking, Allan tells the narrator, that the first Finnish author who wrote Lovecraftian tales was not S. Albert Kivinen or Boris Hurtta, but one Matts W. Cronelius, who was a supposed correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft himself. According to Allan, that while Cornelius and Lovecraft had a productive correspondence, it ended in conflicts over the Cthulhu-mythos. Allan claims that it was because of Cronelius that Lovecraft viewed Finnish people as "racially inferior". Matts W. Cornelius would then return to Finland and write a collection of Lovecraft-based short stories, which were never published, but could be very valuable.

Allan then tells the narrator that Matts' only living relative, Albert Cronelius, a rock musician from the district of Lauttasaari, currently owns these stories. He wants that the narrator to meet Albert and buy said books, as he had already tried himself and failed, and believes that the younger narrator could more easily influence the rock musician.

The narrator goes to Lauttasaari, where he meets Cronelius and it is revealed to him slowly that the books are not fiction, but include truth about at least two Great Old Ones that reside in the area of Finland (Iku-Turso and Kalanpäinen), as well as a population of Deep Ones that live in Lauttasaari, who seek to to resurrect their deities using the Cronelius-books.

Albert Cronelius is actually Matts W. Cronelius, who wants to smuggle the books to Allan and out of the grasp of the Deep Ones. It is also implied that ancient Sami-sorcerers, such as the mythical Finnish hero known as Väinämöinen, used to sing the Old Ones to sleep.

The unnamed narrator succeeds in smuggling the books, but gazes upon something he should not have seen, possibly Iku-Turso, which damages his mental health.

While Allan has gotten his books, the narrator drops out of university and starts to live off government-assistance, being paranoid all the time and believing that the Deep Ones are following him.

### Cotent
### Humans
*Narrator: A unknown student who lives in Helsinki. A fan of of the works of H. P. Lovecraft, who is manipulated into something bigger than himself.
*Uncle Allan: An older man who owns an antiquarian bookshop in Punavuori, Helsinki. He has an interest in the works of Matts W. Cornelius.
*Matts W. Cronelius: A supposed correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft, who was the first Finnish author to write stories about cosmic horror in the 1930's, mixing them with Finnish folklore.

Maine is a state in the New England region of the United States. It is featured in Lovecraft's fiction, including in two revision tales, and has been used as a setting by other Cthulhu Mythos writers. Lovecraft appears to have made only one brief visit to the state.

Maine was the last of the New England states to be admitted to the union, in 1820; it is by far the largest, at 35,380 square miles more than three times the size of Massachusetts. Its population in 1930 was 797,423, and 1,362,359 in 2020, making it the least densely populated state east of the Mississippi River. Its capital is Augusta; its largest city is Portland, which had 70,000 residents in 1930.

Lovecraft visited Portland, Maine, in August 1927, visiting Vermont, New Hampshire, and several towns in Massachusetts on the same trip.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Arguably the most notable reference to Maine in Lovecraft's fiction is in "The Thing on the Doorstep" (1937). After his marriage to Asenath Waite, Edward Pickman Derby "talk[s] about terrible meetings in lonely places, of Cyclopean ruins in the heart of the Maine woods beneath which vast staircases lead down to abysses of nighted secrets". Later, his friend Daniel Upton gets a telegram from the town marshal of Chesuncook, Maine, telling him that Derby had "stumbled out of the woods with delirious ravings." 

Chesuncook is a real-world town in the Maine Wilderness; in 1933, it had fewer than 70 residents. Lovecraft describes it, accurately enough, as "close to the wildest, deepest, and least explored forest belt in Maine." Derby's rants depict it as a fearsome site of eldritch horror: The pit of the shoggoths! Down the six thousand steps . . . the abomination of abominations . . . I never would let her take me, and then I found myself there. . . . Iä! Shub-Niggurath! . . . The shape rose up from the altar, and there were 500 that howled. . . . The Hooded Thing bleated ‘Kamog! Kamog!’—that was old Ephraim’s secret name in the coven. . . . I was there, where she promised she wouldn’t take me. . . . A minute before I was locked in the library, and then I was there where she had gone with my body—in the place of utter blasphemy, the unholy pit where the black realm begins and the watcher guards the gate. . . . I saw a shoggoth—it changed shape. . . .While Derby is understandably eager to get out of Maine, he is heard "muttering darkly to himself" when the route home passes through Augusta, and later Portland--"as if the sight of a city aroused unpleasant memories." When the Asenath/Ephraim personality regains control of Derby's body, it tries to explain away the rant about Chesuncook: "There are certain Indian relics in the north woods—standing stones, and all that—which mean a good deal in folklore, and Asenath and I are following that stuff up."

Dr. Makoto Yamada is a fictional character created by Robert Bloch and Henry Kuttner for their short story "The Black Kiss".

### Biography
Dr. Makoto Yamada is an occult investigator, and a friend and associate of Michael Leigh, although he claims that Leigh's knowledge far exceeds his own.

Yamada believes that legends about werewolves and other instances of therianthropy are based on historical accounts of sorcerers who could temporarily transfer their minds to the bodies of animals, as doing so is easier than initiating mind-transference with humans. 

He is described as "a small, slender man," with his "thin face sallow beneath a stiff thatch of gray hair...covered with a fine-spun web of wrinkles." (: "The Black Kiss")

Malachai James Farrow was a character who appeared in Peter J. Evans' 2013 novel Feeders from Within.

### History
Farrow was a soldier who served in the Pancho Villa Expedition of 1916-17 alongside his friend Mark Harrigan. When their squad was separated from the main force and pursued by Villistas, they took refuge on a rocky hillside. While looking for a means to escape, the squad came across an unusual opening in the side of the hill and investigated, hoping to find a route which lead away from the Villistas.

Delving deep into the cave, the group came across a cavern which was home to a bizarre machine attended by a number of Mi-Go who promptly attacked. Fending them off and destroying the machine, Farrow and Harrigan were able to escape, although all of the other soldiers were apparently killed.

Returning to the United States, Farrow was institutionalised in Arkham Asylum where he was treated by Dr. Eric Hardstrom for two years and seven months with little progress. After his discharge he travelled to Providence, Rhode Island, where he lived for a few years before checking himself into the Lemarchand Institute with what little money he had for more psychiatric help. Dr. Carolyn Fern treated him, and slowly discovered his fear of monsters with knives for hands.

After a few months, Farrow once again discharged himself, and three days later was found by the police, mutilated and murdered in an back alley with what appeared to be a multi-bladed knife.

Malcolm Mayweather is a character created by Canadian author Troy Young for his Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Description
Mayweather is a tall, physically fit black Canadian man, likely in his late twenties or early thirties. Since a violent encounter with a magic-using Nyarlathotep cultist, he is missing his left arm. He is capable of utilising minor magic, but the effects of this appear to consist solely of the ability to keep away the effects of the nightmares caused by exposure to the entities of the Cthulhu Mythos.

Mayweather was exposed to radiation in a temple to Nyarlathotep which caused him to develop a highly-aggressive form of cancer. It has been speculated that this is a magical affliction, which Nyarlathotep is capable of accelerating, halting, and perhaps even reversing.

A relationship had begun to form between Mayweather and junior agent Charlene Hines; this was cut short with the death of both parties.

### History
In the mundane world, Mayweather was a firefighter. Attending a call to a burning building (a blaze which had been started by agent Adele Kramer whilst on a mission) Mayweather encountered a Shoggoth, an event which brought him to the attention of Harjit Singh of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.

After being recruited into the department, he was partnered with a senior agent, Mindy Nguyen, who would supervise him on his first mission. He has since embarked on a number of missions without Mindy but has usually been assigned other partners, sometimes from the international investigative community. After Mindy's death - a mercy-killing at Mayweather's hands - he was assigned to mentor new agent Charlene Hines.

Mayweather was killed while on a mission to the South Pacific, with the goal of preventing Cthulhu from awakening, his mind shattered from the psychic emanations emitted by the Great Old One, and his body ceasing to function.

### Missions
In chronological order, Mayweather has been assigned to the following locations: 

*Canada: Mayweather's first mission. He and Mindy Nguyen battled a Saskatchewan cultist with the ability to control rats (: "The Rat King").
*Egypt: as part of an international venture, he explored a recently-discovered pyramid and met an avatar of Nyarlathotep (: "The Pyramid of the Black Pharaoh").
*Scotland: was partnered with a British researcher; the two exposed a cult to Yog-Sothoth in the nation's capital (: "The Druid of Castle Rock").
*Canada: was partnered with a treacherous Norwegian researcher who took his left arm when uncovered (: "The Viking's Doom").
*Canada: he and Mindy Nguyen encountered an entity devoted to spreading pestilence through the city of Winnipeg. Mayweather was forced to kill Mindy as an act of mercy after she was infected by the virus (: "The Tattered Lady").

fullContent:
The Malleus Monstrorum, which is a faux-Latin play on the late medieval text Malleus Maleficarum, is a gaming supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. First released in 2006, it was a revised and considerably updated development of 1998's Creature Companion.

All editions of the book have been "monster manuals": collections of various monsters, deities, spirits, and other creatures, giving background details along with relevant statistics for use in Call of Cthulhu. 

### Editions

### First Edition
The first edition of Malleus Monstrorum was written by Scott David Aniolowski and consisted of the contents of the books Ye Booke of Monstres, and Ye Booke of Monstres II, as well as additional material, some of which was taken from foreign language supplements for Call of Cthulhu.

### Second Edition
The second edition was written by Aniolowski along with Mike Mason and Paul Fricker. This edition was released in a two-volume hardcover set, with the contents divided between "monsters" and "deities".

Deluxe leatherette and digital editions were also released for this printing, and a Keeper Deck, which contained reference cards for 60 of the most popular beings in the game, was issued in accompaniment to the main book.

The Men of Leng are an intelligent species of humanoid which first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, and later featured prominently in Brian Lumley's 1978 Titus Crow novel The Clock of Dreams.

### Etymology
The Men of Leng take their name from the Plateau of Leng, a geographical feature which may or may not be located in the Dreamlands, from which they possibly originate.

### Description
Humanoid creatures with hooves and excessive body hair, the Men of Leng are degenerate creatures with little in the way of moral limitations and a penchant for the consumption of human flesh.

### History
### Lovecraft's Work
When the creatures known as Moon-beasts arrived in the Dreamlands, the Men of Leng initially welcomed them as gods, but the creatures soon turned on the Men of Leng, conquering and enslaving their worshippers. For the most part, they were employed to perform menial tasks, but the Moon Beasts would also take those with the most meat on their bones as a source of food.

Perhaps the most well-known of the Men of Leng are those employed as merchants; these individuals were commonly seen in the Dreamlands port of Dylath-Leen selling the rubies produced by the moon-mines and using the profits to buy more slaves which were sent back to the moon to continue the cycle.

### Expanded Mythos
In Brian Lumley's novel The Clock of Dreams, the Men of Leng are shown to be in the service of the Fly-the-Light, and the rubies which they were trading were in actuality a way to entrance the population of Dylath-Leen and bring them over to its cause. Luckily for the townsfolk, Titus Crow, Henri-Laurent de Marigny and Tiania were able to thwart the scheme and destroy the crystals, killing many of the Men of Leng in the process.

The Man-Bats are a fictional race in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 1983 in issue #153 of the 1st volume of the Conan the Barbarian comic book series.

### Background
The Man-Bats were created by the Elder God Chthon. Whom they serve and by the time of the Hyborian Age, they had existed for eons. Man-Bats worshiped or swore by the Rat and the Great Fanged Bat.

They lived in the floating city of Ur-Xanarryh, which lied in the clouds over Cimmeria. Man-Bats were the ancient enemies of the Bird-Men of the floating city of Akah Ma'at, with whome they waged war with for centuries.

Man-Bats were monstrous humanoids with large bat-like wings, blue skin, claws, fangs, and pointed ears. Many of the males possessed huge fangs. On the bald heads of some of them was a horn-like backward curving projection. Unlike the males, the females were attractive humanoids able to seduce humans, though they still had wings and pointed ears.

It was a cruel and brutish race, whose only ambition was to conquer. In addition to their claws and fangs, they also used spears, shields, and swords though they lacked the sorcery and science of their rivals, the Bird-Men.

Man-Serpents are a race created by Robert E. Howard, first appearing in his story, "The God in the Bowl" published in 1952, sixteen years after his death. The Marvel Comics adaptations were introduced in 1971 by Roy Thomas and Barry Smith, making their first appearance in issue #7 of the first volume of the Conan the Barbarian comic book series.

The creature in the original story is a gigantic black snake with mottled markings and in place of a snake head the head of a male human of unearthly beauty and alien emotional expression.

### Background
In the original Robert E. Howard story, a "child of Set" or "monster-king" is sent by Thoth-Amon of Stygia to kill his rival in another land. It is transported there in its black cylindrical sarcophagus and set free by a would-be jewel thief.

The Man-Serpents are descendants of Elder God Set. It is a race which was spawned by his daughter Ishiti and, prior to the Thurian Age, had splintered from the Serpent Men. The Man-Serpents were a reclusive race, unlike the Serpent Men whom were served by men. When man overthrew the Serpent Men, they thought they exterminated the Man-Serpents. In reality, the survivors went into hiding. Its members clashed with Conan of Cimmeria during the Hyborian Age.

Māna-Yood-Sushāī is a creator deity who slumbers after creating the gods; if his drummer, Skarl, ceases drumming for an instant, he would awaken and destroy the world.

When Chaosium integrated Māna-Yood-Sushāī into the Cthulhu Mythos, they established it as an avatar of Azathoth (: Malleus Monstrorum).

Before that, Māna-Yood-Sushāī was mentioned in Gary Myers' Mythos story "The Gods of Earth".

### Behind the Mythos
Māna-Yood-Sushāī and his ceaseless drummer, Skarl, is the creation of Lord Dunsany in his anthology The Gods of Pegana, which was an inspiration for Lovecraft. Dunsany's Pegana stories are regarded by some as the first example of an author inventing a mythos.

According to Mythos scholar Robert M. Price, Mana-Yood-Sushai was likely the inspiration for the Outer God Azathoth.

The Manhattan Museum of Fine Arts is a fictional institution located in New York City, created by Frank Belknap Long in his novel The Horror from the Hills. In Long's story, the museum becomes enmeshed in horror when it acquires what it thinks is a statue of the entity Chaugnar Faugn.  

### Notable Staff
The president of the museum is Dr. George Francis Scollard; the curator of archaeology is Algernon Harris, who succeeded Halpin Chalmers. 

The museum's field workers have included Richardson, who was tortured to death by the followers of Chaugnar Faugn on the Tsang Plateau, and Clark Ulman, who returned from Tsang as the god's mutilated slave. Other agents of the museum included Symons, a Chang Dynasty specialist who was "obliged to leave his left eye and a piece of his nose in  a Buddhist temple near a place called Fen Chow Fu," and Francis Hogarth, who "lost eighty pounds and a perfectly good right arm somewhere between Lake Rudolph and Naivasha in the Anglo Egyptian Sudan." 

Other employees of the museum include Cinney, a night guard who is slain by Chaugnar Faugn, and Jim Williams, an attendant who discovers Cinney's body. 

### Location
The museum appears to be located on Manhattan's Fifth Avenue; to get to work, Harris gets off the subway at Fifth Avenue and 59th Street, and takes a bus some distance before noticing that it's taking him past the museum. 

Long does not specify whether the bus takes Harris uptown into the Upper West Side or downtown into Midtown. When Chaugnar Faugn leaves the museum to go on a rampage, his first victims are all reported as being between 35th and 48th streets, implying a Midtown location. However, Harris meets his boss Scollard on the bus, who says he "took the first train down"; the commuter train would have taken him to Grand Central Station, on 42nd Street, suggesting that they are on an uptown bus. Several museums are located on the stretch of Fifth Avenue from 82nd to 110th streets, known as Museum Mile; if the Manhattan Museum is located there, it would be directly across the street from Central Park, which is mentioned as one of the places Chaugnar Faugn might hide. 

### Collections
The Manhattan Museum appears to specialize in historical artefacts; the opening line of the novel mentions its "Egyptian, Graeco-Roman, Minoan, and Assyrian antiquities."  

Notable items acquired by the museum during Harris's tenure include mirrors of Graeco-Bactrian design and miniature tiger-dragons or too-tiehs from Central China dating from at least 200 B.C., enormous diorite Sphinxes from the Valley of the Nile, “Geometric” vases from Mycenaean Crete, incised pottery from Messina and Syracuse, linens and spindles from the Swiss Lakes, sculptured lintels from Yucatan and Mexico, Mayan and Manabí monoliths ten feet tall, Paleolithic Venuses from the rock caverns of the Pyrenees, and even a series of rare bilingual tablets in Hamitic and Latin from the s

Manly Wade Wellman (21 May 1903 – 5 April 1986) was a prolific pulp fiction writer, noted for his science fiction and fantasy writing for Weird Tales and other outlets. His Cthulhu Mythos homage "The Terrible Parchment", which featured the Necronomicon trying to make itself real through the power of collective belief, was published in the August 1937 issue of Weird Tales, and dedicated "to the memory of H. P. Lovecraft, with all admiration".

Wellman created the recurring characters Judge Pursuivant and John Thunstone, both psychic detectives, and the backwoods minstrel John the Balladeer.

Wellman's literary executor was the writer and editor Karl Edward Wagner.

Mansions of Madness is a Cthulhu Mythos board game designed by Corey Konieczka and first published by Fantasy Flight Games in 2011. A second edition was released in August 2016.

### Gameplay
The game involves a group of players taking on the roles of investigators (many of whom are characters who appear in other Fantasy Flight lines such as Arkham Horror and Eldritch Horror) who must explore a map and solve a predetermined mystery.

The fundamental difference between the first and second editions was the replacement of the keeper (the player who manages the storyline, encounters, etc. and acts as the antagonist for the other players) with a digital app, giving the game an element of randomness and opening up a solo play option.

Manuel Silva is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1921 short story "The Terrible Old Man". He was a literary representation of the animosity felt by Lovecraft towards the non-white immigrants of the time, who he believed were polluting the genetic pool of the United States.

### Overview
Silva, along with fellow criminals Joe Czanek and Angelo Ricci, intended to rob the titular Terrible Old Man of Kingsport, an elderly recluse reputed to be extremely wealthy. What they did not bargain on was the man's true nature, and the gang's corpses were found washed ashore, horribly mutilated, shortly afterwards.

Silva was one of the more thuggish of the trio, appearing entirely willing to cause the old man any bodily harm necessary to persuade him to give up the location of his fortune. (: "The Terrible Old Man")

The Many-Angled Ones are a race of extradimensional entities from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The term "Many-Angled One" was originally created by Grant Morrison for Zenith, a series published in the science fiction comic magazine 2000 AD by Fleetway Publications. It would later be used for several other works, most notably in Marvel Comics.

### Zenith
The Many-Angled Ones (also known as the Lloigor) exist in a space that contains more dimensions than our universe therefore they appear to humans as "many angled." Therefore when one of them manifests in our universe, it appears to us as the floating disconnected body parts of a larger creature. Unlike most Lovecraftian entities, that often seem to have unknown albeit hostile motivations, the goal of the Many-Angled Ones is to impose on the multiverse a rigid geometrical order thereby making everything run like clockwork.

No matter what host body a Many-Angled One takes, it possesses superhuman strength, reflexes, and speed. It's extremely durable and nearly invulnerable. From the eyes it incredibly destructive beams. Regardless of whether they stole a body or specifically built it to host their lifeforce, they appear to always have these powers.

### Marvel Comics
In the Marvel Multiverse, the Many-Angled Ones (also known as the Great Old Ones) are a group of malevolent entities who exist in the space between the innumerable realities, where they try to spread their corruption and decadence towards those universes. Shuma-Gorath is the most well-known of them all, however, other members include Zvilpogghua, Shub-Niggurath, and Tsathoggua. Despite being one of the Elder Gods of Earth, Chthon is frequently conflated with them. They are referred to as the "Many-Angled Ones" due to them existing simultaneously in many dimensions throughout the Multiverse, and mortals (for example, humans) are unable to perceive their true forms. 

In "Realm of Kings", it is discovered that they offered the powers to the Revengers (the counterparts of the Avengers in a Lovecraftian universe) in exchange for being worshiped. The Iron Man of that universe believes that they have surpassed their reality and are looking for a new place to be worshiped, and this is how they let Quasar know. Back in the land of this, they are opposed by heroes like Vision.

They are also the main antagonists of The Thanos Imperative, where they seek to invade the main universe through "the Fault". (a tear that opens the door to other realities) They hail from a reality known as the "Cancerverse", in which they defeated Death so that nothing dies anymore. Life ran rampant like a cancerous tumor and its inhabitants are determined to spread the influence of these beings to other realities. Here a battle takes place that they end up losing.

Mappo no Ryûjin is a fictional entity created by Michael Dziesinski for the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Secrets of Japan.

### Background
Mappo no Ryûjin is a Great Old One, which is currently bound and slumbering in an eight-pointed Elder Sign in the Muvian ruins near the Japanese isles. Currently, it's active in a semi-corporeal form. The last time it visited Earth was 50,000 years ago, when Yig unleashed it to punish the Serpent Men who were worshiping Ghatanothoa and who had joined forces with the island civilization of Mu to create a new hybrid race of humans and Serpent Men. In one night, most of Mu and parts of Lemuria sank beneath the waves. The last act of the dying Muvian wizards bound Mappo no Ryûjin to the Elder Sign.

It is believed that at the twilight of the age of man, when the celestial bodies are in perfect alignment, it will bring forth an orgy of destruction, as the sixth race emerges to take over the world. The Mother of Yig will devour the sun and darkness will reign for 666 days. It is a 1000 ft. long entity with two skeletal wings, a desiccated oriental dragon head, and 666 pseudopods covering its white skin. Each of the pseudopods looks like a giant albino snake, which are used to swallow and consume living creatures, each thick enough to contain a human victim. They are covered with a slimy mucous containing digestive acids.

fullContent:
"Marble from the Void" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Steven J. Alvarez, first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2021.

### Synopsis
An astronaut performing maintenance work on his ship in the orbit of Saturn encounters a derelict craft. Aboard, he disturbs an entity which opens a portal to another realm, allowing its true form to emerge and unleash its voracious appetites on the galaxy.

### Trivia
*Despite never being explicitly named, the entity's description as a collection of glowing spheres locked out of our dimension along with the narrator's reference to it being "both the gate and its key" would suggest that it is intended to be the Outer God Yog-Sothoth.

fullContent:
Marblehead is a town in Essex County, Massachusetts, USA. Marblehead is a coastal town  known for its rich maritime history and as the birthplace of the American Navy. It features a picturesque harbor, historic homes, and is a popular destination for sailing and recreational boating. H. P. Lovecraft visited Marblehead in December, 1922 and took inspiration there for his story "The Festival".

### Overview
Marblehead is a coastal town located in Essex County, Massachusetts, along the North Shore. It was settled in 1629 and incorporated in 1649. The town has a population of approximately 20,441 as of the 2020 census. Marblehead is known for its picturesque harbor and rich maritime history.

Marblehead is often referred to as the "Birthplace of the American Navy." In 1775, it played a crucial role in the formation of the Continental Navy, with local merchant Colonel John Glover helping to fit out the USS Hannah, the Navy's first vessel. The town was also a significant center for fishing and shipbuilding in the 18th century.

### Historical Sites
* Marblehead Light: A historic lighthouse.
* Fort Sewall: A coastal defense fortification.
* Old Burial Hill: One of New England's oldest graveyards.

### Behind the Mythos
Unlike nearby Innsmouth and Arkham, Marblehead is a real city in Essex County, Massachusetts.

### References

Marc A. Michaud is an American author, editor and scholar whose focus is weird fiction in general, and the works of H. P. Lovecraft in particular. He is also founder of indie publisher Necronomicon Press, which he began in 1976 to distribute those works of Lovecraft which had never previously seen print. The majority of his writings are non-fiction, and he has collaborated with several other scholars in these; his co-authors include S. T. Joshi, Donald R. Burleson and Steven J. Mariconda.

Michaud was also a member of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts and scholars active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s.

Marcus L. Rowland (born 1953) is a former lab technician turned prolific roleplaying games designer from the United Kingdom.

### Overview
A long-time fan of roleplaying games, Marcus L. Rowland began submitting articles to hobby magazines including home-brew supplements and his own opinions on games. He wrote on a wide variety of roleplay games, and in 1985 began to write complete modules for several of these, including Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu, for which he contributed to seven published sourcebooks. Although he continues to write material for RPGs, he ended any association with Chaosium and other game publishers in 1989, and no longer contributes to Chaosium supplements. Since then he originated the modern version of the OGL concept and publishes Forgotten Futures RPG.

Margaret Hedda Brundage (née Johnson, 9 December 1900-9 April 1976) was an American artist best known for her controversial Weird Tales images, a situation exacerbated by the fact that the artist was a woman. She illustrated many of the most memorable covers for the pulp magazine in the later years of its glory days during the 1930s.

Brundage began working for Farnsworth Wright in 1932, when Wright hired her to provide cover art for Oriental Stories, a companion magazine to Weird Tales which proved unsuccessful. Her work on Oriental Stories was so well-received by Wright that he hired her to provide the covers for the far more popular Weird Tales, which she did between 1932 and 1945, although her most prolific years were between 1933 and 1938.

Margaret Alice Murray (13 July 1863 – 13 November 1963) was a multi-discipline researcher into the history and psychology of the human species. Her work intersected with several major tenets of the Cthulhu Mythos, including the study of ancient Egyptian culture and such tropes as the ancient cult lurking just out of sight of an oblivious population. Indeed, H. P. Lovecraft mentioned that he "had just been reading Miss Murray's The Witch-Cult in Western Europe" when he wrote his short story "The Festival" . Another of Lovecraft’s stories likely to have taken inspiration from The Witch-Cult is "The Horror at Red Hook."

Margery Williams Bianco (22 July 1881 – 4 September 1944), born Margery Winifred Williams, was an award-winning American children’s author best known for her popular 1921 novel The Velveteen Rabbit. 

Williams' 1913 novel The Thing in the Woods (which was reprinted in the United States under the pseudonym Harper Williams) a story about lycanthropy in Pennsylvania, has been speculated to have been an influence on H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Dunwich Horror" ; Lovecraft was known to have read the book, and wrote the poem "On The Thing in the Woods by Harper Williams", a piece which remained unpublished until its inclusion in the 2001 Night Shade Books collection The Ancient Track: The Complete Poetical Works of H. P. Lovecraft .

Marginalia is a collection of fantasy, horror and science fiction short stories, essays, biography and poetry by and about the American author H. P. Lovecraft. It was released in 1944 and was the third collection of Lovecraft's work published by Arkham House. 2,035 copies were printed.

### Reception
New York Times reviewer Marjorie Farber said Marginalia "should cause intense satisfaction among the disciples of the late great Master of Necrology", commenting that Lovecraft's "whole career seems an effective protest against 'natural laws', against genuine scholarship and against literary craftsmanship". E. F. Bleiler noted that "The guest memoirs and essays are of varying interest", but that "Lovecraft's fiction is juvenile or minor. His essays are more significant". Lovecraft bibliographer Francis T. Laney described the volume as "a glorified fan magazine in book format. . . . [presenting] an unforgettable composite view of Lovecraft as a man".

Marie Lambeau, also known as the Entertainer and the Smoky Velvet, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos releases. She made her first appearance in the Dunwich Horror expansion for Arkham Horror in July 2006.

### Overview
A young black woman from New Orleans, Louisiana, Marie Lambeau is an extremely talented singer. Her grand-mére was regarded by many as a witch, and some believe that Marie carries a touch of magic in her blood as a result.

Shortly after moving to Arkham, Marie's grand-mére passed, and the girl began to hear songs and rhymes in her head. What they mean, Marie is yet to find out.

### Behind the Mythos
Since her debut, Marie has appeared in several other Arkham Horror Files releases including Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. In 2010, a pre-painted plastic miniature was released as a gaming aid as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, although this is no longer in production.

### Trivia
*In Eldritch Horror, the globally-set counterpart to Arkham Horror, Marie travelled to Borneo to combat an ancient evil after her grand-mére's passing.
*Marie made a cameo appearance in Graham McNeill's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic, playing a gig in an Arkham speakeasy with Jim Culver.

Marinus Bicknell Willett is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, appearing as the protagonist of his novel The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. 

### Overview
Willett, the family physician of Charles Dexter Ward, grows increasingly worried about  Ward's obsession with his ancestor Joseph Curwen, his physical double. Willett investigates the history of Curwen, a notorious necromancer, and grows convinced that the old wizard has plotted to use Ward to resurrect himself, eventually killing his descendant and taking his place. Willett eventually uses the reverse of the resurrection spell to turn Curwen back into dust.

He is described in the novel as "a small man", and as "a trim, blue-eyed, clean-shaven gentleman". 

### Behind the Mythos
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia compares Willett's character to other "valiant counterweight[s]" in Lovecraft such as Thomas Malone in "The Horror at Red Hook" (1925) (EXP: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​ and Henry Armitage in "The Dunwich Horror"; like Willett, Armitage "defeats the 'villains' by incantations, and he is susceptible to the same flaws--pomposity, arrogance, self-importance--that can be seen in Willett." (EXP: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

The Marit Lage is a Lovecraftian-like god from the fictional universe of the Magic: The Gathering collectible card game.

### Background
Marit Lage is an immensely powerful being who is able to move across the planes of the multiverse. It has been associated with black mana, and is said to have been both a mage and a sorceress. Not much is known about the entity, including its origins or history, what it is, and its current status. Centuries before Dominaria's ice age, it devastated the world. During the world's ice age, it somehow ended up frozen in the core of a glacier. No one knows what happened to her or if she is even still alive. Long after her disappearance, she continued to have human followers who believe she is slumbering in the ocean and are awaiting her return (the Brine Shamans and the Acolytes of Marit-Lage).

Mark Harrigan, the Soldier, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games who has appeared in several of their Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-related products.

### Origin Story
There are three separate origin stories given for Harrigan, each one slightly different from the others.

### Arkham Horror ()
The first backstory stated that Harrigan had joined the United States Army and fought in Europe during the First World War, where he saw monsters killing men in the trenches. Upon returning home, he finds that his partner Sophie has one of the monsters inside her, and the creature consumes her soul. 

### Eldritch Horror ()
This version is largely similar to the Arkham Horror story, but Sophie is confirmed to have been Harrigan's wife, and after her death he travels to Helsinki, where he had seen some of the monsters posing as German soldiers during the war.

### Feeders from Within ()
Feeders from Within tells that Harrigan did not in fact fight in the Great War, and was instead a member of the Pancho Villa Expedition of 1916-17. Whilst deployed in the Sierra Madres, his squad encountered a group of Mi-Go working on a bizarre machine. After a short battle, the Mi-Go were defeated but at the cost of the lives of all except Harrigan and one other soldier, the two survivors being shipped home to convalesce. Sophie is still murdered in this version, and he was stated to have grown up "on the wrong side of the tracks in Harrisburg."

### History
The novel Feeders from Within expands on Harrigan's activities after Sophie's death.

Since the events in Mexico, Harrigan has been pursuing his vendetta against the eldritch creatures which he has found to be plaguing much of the world. After being contacted by psychologist Carolyn Fern, who had treated the other survivor from the Sierra Madres incident, Harrigan travels to Arkham where the pair uncover a plot by the Silver Twilight Lodge and the Mi-Go known as Mr. Stone to bring madness and chaos to the world. Joining with former cultist Diana Stanley, the three manage to foil the scheme after travelling to the subterranean realm of N'kai.

Subsequent to these events, Harrigan disappears for a few months, presumably continuing to hunt down supernatural beings. However, after he receives a letter from Diana Stanley asking for their help, he reaches out to Carolyn Fern, and the two prepare to once again face the forces of evil.

### Behind the Mythos
Mark Harrigan was first introduced by Fantasy Flight Games as an Investigator in the Dunwich Horror Deluxe Expansion for Arkham Horror Second Edition. Since then he has made appearances in both Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and a now-discontinued plastic miniature of the character was released as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line. Mark Morrison is an Australian game designer, writer and editor. As of November 2022 he is also a Chaosium employee, focused on the Companions of Arthur community content program for the Pendragon role-playing game.  

### Overview
Morrison's first-ever credit for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game was the scenario "The Land of Lost Dreams" in H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands, since which he has written and edited an array of scenarios and books for the game, including co-writing the first edition of Terror Australis with his partner Penelope Love and leading the development of the Horror on the Orient Express campaign, as well as editing both editions of the campaign to date. Morrison was the line editor for Chaosium's now-axed Stormbringer & Elric! games in the early 1990s and has also written and designed videogames for Atari, THQ and Robot Circus, including the storyline for the Call of Cthulhu computer game developed by Cyanide.

The Marsh Family is a bloodline of humans (and later, hybrid beings) which draws its roots from the small fishing village of Innsmouth in the early days of colonial America. The first individual of distinction in this family was Captain Obed Marsh. Like most of the residents of Innsmouth, he was forced to interbreed with the Deep Ones, Pth’thya-l’yi. This Deep One ancestry means that his descendants will gradually mutate into potentially-immortal, amphibious humanoids. They had three children, two of whom disappeared under mysterious circumstances. The third, an unnamed daughter, was from an early age educated in France, and never knew the dark truth of her conception. The only hint to her ancestry was that her eyes greatly resembled those of the infamous Obed Marsh. Just after the Civil War, she married Benjimin Orne, and they lived together in Arkham. The two had only one child, a daughter. At some point, she moved to Toledo, married, and had three children. Two of her children appeared normal, as their father. Douglas, however, shared his mother's unsettling appearance. He would eventually shoot himself in the head after learning the history of his family. Shortly afterwards, the mother disappeared, presumably returning to the undersea city of Y'ha-nthlei.

The last of the line appears to be Robert Olmstead and his cousin Lawrence. Lawrence is the son of Walter and was committed to a sanatorium in Canton.

Other relatives are James Williamson, Eliza Orne, Enoch Marsh, Lydia Menize, Barnabas Marsh, Old Olmstead, Mr. Cleveland, Alice Marsh.



### Members

*Captain Obed Marsh: The founder of the Esoteric Order of Dagon, and the great-great-grandfather of Robert Olmstead. He died in prison in 1878.
*Pth'thya-l'yi: Obed's second wife and the Deep One great-great grandmother of Robert Olmstead. She currently lives in Y'ha-nthlei, and favors Robert.
*Mrs. Marsh: Obed's first wife and the step-great-great grandmother of Robert Olmstead. Died of illness.

### 2nd generation

* Alice Marsh: Obed's daughter from his 2nd wife, and the great grandmother of Robert. Died of childbirth. She did not know of her mother's lineage.
*Benjamin Orne: Alice's husband, and the great-grandfather of Robert. Lived in Arkham. Possible relation to necromancer Simon Orne.
* Marsh Boys: Obed's two sons, and Alice's brothers who disappeared without a trace.
*Onesiphorus Marsh: Obed's eldest son by his 1st wife, half-brother of Alice, and the great-granduncle of Robert Olmstead.

The Martense Family were created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Lurking Fear". They were once humans, but have devolved into a deformed cave-dwelling race due to decades of isolation and in-breeding. 

### Description
Due to decades of in-breeding, the Martense Family now hardly resembled normal humans. They were misshaped and covered in hair, with their most prominent trait being their heterochromia. 

They not only ate any humans who came across them, but also members of their own family who were not fit enough. 

### History
In the 1670s, the Dutch merchant Gerrit Martense built his family mansion on Tempest Mountain in Catskill, New York. He and his family isolated themselves away there due to their loathing of the British Empire and society as a whole. 

Several year on, they began to inbreed with themselves and their servants. Much of their offspring would spread out to inhabit the local valleys and hills, but the main Martense family stayed in their mansion. 

The only recorded Martense to have left isolation was Jan Martense, who had joined the colonial army. When he returned to Tempest Mountain, his family treated him as an outsider, so he made plans to leave. 

When a friend of his went to see him after he stopped sending letters, he was told that Jan had been struck by lightning. But, after exhuming his grave, he found that Jan's skull had been smashed in. The Martenses were not convicted due to lack of solid proof, but this broke off what little ties to the outside world they had. 

What exactly happened during this period is unknown, but the Martenses seemingly continued to inbreed until that had devolved into a grotesque species that lived in the tunnels below their old mansion. 

In 1921, monster hunters came to Catskill after sightings of the hairy men. After several encounters, the monster hunters have much of Tempest Mountain exploded, seemingly ending the threat of the Martenses.

### Adaptations
In the 1994 film Lurking Fear, the detail about the Martenses having heterochromatic eyes is dropped. The 1997 film Hemoglobin, on the other hand, keeps the heterochromia, but renames them the Van Daam family, founded in the 17th century by a noble Dutch woman named Eva Van Daam, who had an incestuous relationship with her own twin brother.

The Martians are a fictional species created by H. G. Wells for his science fiction novel The War of the Worlds. They were first incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Ye Booke of Monstres II.

### Background
The Martians are tentacled creatures with large eyes and three-lobed pupils. They reproduce asexually by budding. (: "To Mars and Providence")

They are a warlike vampiric race that communicates telepathically. Possessing a large eardrum in the back of the head, they are only able to hear specific tones and sounds. They use long glass pipettes to extract blood from their victims, which they take directly into their systems. Extremely strong beings who are able to move unaided in Earth's heavier gravity, possessing tentacles from which humans rarely escape once they've been caught. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

They operate tripod battle machines that cannot be harmed by anything short of a direct artillery strike. Devastating weapons of war that are a hundred feet tall and can reach 60 mph. They are armed with heat rays, black smoke projectors, and mechanical tentacles. The invisible heat rays ignite buildings up to a mile away. Canisters release the poisonous black smoke which rises up to fifty feet in the air, a viscous, clinging thick smoke. The mechanical tentacles are used to grasp objects, when not carrying the black smoke canister guns or heat ray projectors. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

As with other telepathic species, some Martians are capable of projecting their minds across space and inhabiting the bodies of other creatures. (: "To Mars and Providence")

Their relationship with the Aihai species has been described as "an uneasy truce". (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

### History
The Martians are not native to the red planet, but descend from the same ancestral species from outside the solar system that also colonised Earth in prehistoric Antarctica. However, unlike their Antarctic cousins, the Mars colonists modified themselves physically and mentally. By removing certain glands and enzymes, they eliminated all their emotions except fear (which was deemed necessary for survival), and made themselves biologically immortal and incapable of aging. By eradicating all pathogenic bacteria and sterilising their planet, they no longer had to worry about disease. Without religion, they dedicated their lives to intellectual and aesthetic pursuits, which included building labyrinthine and Cyclopean structures to express aesthetic, mathematical, or metaphysical formulae. They explored other worlds and traded with other civilisations, such as the Mi-Go. Eventually, the Martians discovered an ancient species of long-faced ghoul-like creatures called the Elder Gods, which were even more advanced than them, and used to be the dominant species on Mars before their arrival. Martin's Beach is a fictional beach resort used by H. P. Lovecraft and Sonia Greene as the setting for their short story "The Horror at Martin's Beach". It appears as the venue for the display of a huge sea monster, and then later as the scene of the revenge of the creature's still-more enormous parent.

The story describes Martin's Beach as a "wealthy resort district" that is "popular as watering-place". Its main attraction seems to be the Wavecrest Inn, a "cliff-perched Inn whose imposing towers proclaimed its allegiance to wealth and grandeur." It has a "sumptuous ballroom" and a "high-ceiled and lantern-lighted veranda". The "hotel wharf" mentioned in the story is presumably the Wavecrest's dock.

The story also mentions a "distant cottage colony that rose modestly on a green hill to the north".

### Location
While the story does not specify the location of Martin's Beach, it does provide some clues. First of all, the boat that captures the sea monster is called "the fish smack Alma of Gloucester". That this refers to the Massachusetts fishing town is bolstered by the fact that when it comes time to preserve the creature, the experts who do so are "Boston naturalists"--implying that that is the nearest large city to Martin's Beach.

When Captain Orne installs the monster in a shipboard museum, he is described as then "sailing south to the wealthy resort district of Martin’s Beach". If one assumes that Orne is starting from his home port, that narrows down the possible locations considerably; one can only sail south from Gloucester for a few miles before hitting open ocean; most locations on the shore near Gloucester would be described as being either to the west, east or north. (That Martin's Beach is in the vicinity of Gloucester is again implied when the boat holding the creature disappears, and the search for it is "aided by large numbers of fishing boats from Gloucester.")

In her memoir The Private Life of H. P. Lovecraft, Greene describes the real-world area that inspired the story:

Magnolia, a prosperous beach resort located near and to the south of Gloucester, would answer well as a location for Martin's Beach in Lovecraft Country.

The Martin's Beach creature is a fictional monster created by H. P. Lovecraft and Sonia Greene for their short story "The Horror at Martin's Beach". In the story, the unnamed sea monster was killed in 1922 by Captain James P. Orne, who later exhibited the creature's body at Martin's Beach. However, the monster turned out to have been just an infant, and its presumed parent surfaced months later to exact revenge upon the Captain and numerous other people. 

### Description
Very little is known about this species, except that they bear resemblance to a cyclopic version of the mythological sea serpents, with a single eye on their faces. They also seem to combine aspects of many animal groups, possessing scaly skin, gills, forelegs and six-toed feet in the place where the pectoral fins would be in a normal fish. Scientific examination also reveals that they have highly-developed brains.

The infant specimen killed by Captain Orne and the Alma crew on May 17, 1922, measured close to 50 feet in length (15 m) and 10 feet in diameter (3 m). This ferocious specimen unleashed a seemingly unprovoked attack on the boat, fighting a prolonged and arduous battle that lasted close to 40 hours before the human crew finally emerged victorious. The fact that such a beast turned out to be merely a juvenile gives an idea of the danger that an adult specimen would surely represent; to which one may add their intelligence, their ability to mimic human screams, and to seemingly hypnotize people from a distance.

Two months after the Alma incident, a boat housing the specimen broke free of its moorings during a storm and vanished; presumably sunk by the creature's parent to recover its deceased offspring. A few weeks later, a terrifying scream was heard coming from the sea at Martin's Beach, leading lifeguards on duty to throw an air-cushion tied to a rope. This was promptly swallowed by the adult monster. Once the rope was pulled, a large number of people, including Captain Orne, gathered to try to pull it back. Due to some unknown psychic or supernatural manifestation on the monster's part, the crowd was unable to let go of the rope, feeling as if their hands were stuck to it, and all were slowly pulled into the ocean by the vengeful beast.

fullContent:
Marvel Comics is a brand management company and a wholly owned subsidiary of the Disney corporation. It is one of the two largest comic book publishers in the world and has been around since 1939. Since the 1990s, in most years it has sold the most comics, has had the most popular and profitable characters, and generated the most revenue from its comic books in the comic book industry. Since it was purchased by Disney in 2009, its property has become the most valuable in the movie business with numerous blockbusters. Its property has also been seen in other types of media either produced by Marvel or via license including live-action TV series, animated TV series, roleplaying games, card games, animated movies, paperback novels, console games, arcade games, and smartphone games. There are also toys, models, clothing, bedding, and other products that have licensed their property.

### Background
Marvel Comics, which is now owned by Disney has published a number of comic books starring characters from the Cthulhu Mythos. Which have appeared in comic book series and issues both within the mainstream universe (Earth-616, the Prime Reality) and alternate realities. It was during the 1970s-80s when Mythos characters, entities, and races appeared in Marvel usually in the Conan comics (e.g. Conan the Barbarian, Savage Conan, etc). They also appeared in a number of issues of Journey into Mystery and in Marvel Comics Presents. Afterwards the characters of the Cthulhu Mythos would occasionally appear in one or two comic issues. Recently Marvel published a 3-part mini-series called the "Haunt of Horror: H.P. Lovecraft" under the MAX line of comics (whose market is adults), whose stories do not occur on Earth-616 unlike those of Conan which took place in the distant past of Earth-616.

The fictional Marvel Multiverse, its mainstream universe (the Prime Reality (Earth-616)) and the main setting within (the Earth) are locations in which there exists cosmic deities (multiversal and universal), pantheons of demi-gods called "gods" (both alien and Terran), interstellar and intergalactic empires, multiversal and temporal organizations and empires, superhero and supervillain teams (Terran and Cosmic), and numerous super powered heroes and villains (both Terran and alien). There is super science and ultra technology such as artifacts that can destroy the universe, weapons that can destroy galaxies, scanners and communication systems with ranges in the millions of light years, and interstellar ships able to warp from one galaxy to another one millions of light years away within minutes. Magic and the supernatural exists side by side with the aforementioned, with demons, the undead, and sorcerers among both the humans of Earth and among the aliens. In addition to the Many-Angled Ones of the Mythos there are other Lovecraftian-like multiversal, temporal, cosmic, and Terran demonic-like entities. shortDefinition: The Marvel Multiverse is a fictional multiverse created by Marvel Comics, which is inhabited by the Many-Angled Ones. It is the setting for two ongoing on-again, off-again comic series published by Marvel Comics, the What If? series (1977+) and the E...
fullContent:
The Marvel Multiverse is a fictional multiverse created by Marvel Comics, which is inhabited by the Many-Angled Ones. It is the setting for two ongoing on-again, off-again comic series published by Marvel Comics, the What If? series (1977+) and the Exiles series (2001+). It was also the stage for an epic cosmic horror story which was the "Time Runs Out" event published in 2014-2015, as well as the issues leading up to the event, mainly within New Avengers Vol. 3 (issues #3-6 and 13-22 in 2013-2014).

### Background
The Marvel Multiverse is an infinite one (per the One Above All, who rules the Multiverse), in which each action that an individual takes creates a new reality, even something as simple as scratching your nose (as proven by Thanos and confirmed by the One Above All). In the early 21st century, Earth alone had billions of future timelines and the largest known multiversal temporal government (the Congress of Realities) had representatives from millions of realities. There have been a few known multiversal-level incidents which threatened the Marvel Multiverse or made changes to it, most recently when the Beyonders (a trio of omnipotent beings from a dimension beyond the Multiverse) nearly ended the Multiverse (the "Time Runs Out" event). It was destroyed at the end of the conflict, but was later restored.

The Marvel Multiverse is one of an unknown number of Multiverses that make up the Megaverse, which in turn is one of an unknown number of Megaverses that make up the Omniverse. Other Multiverses that are known to exist to the higher-level beings of the Marvel Multiverse include the DC Multiverse, the Transformers Multiverse, the Doctor Who Multiverse, and the Capcom Multiverse. Sometimes, there is interaction between the Multiverses, which result in temporary new realities or permanent realities that come about due to the merging of a universe from each Multiverse.

### Lovecraftian Multiversal Entities
The Old Ones are scattered across this Multiverse with some living in the positive universes, beings that are powerful enough to pose a threat to a world to those that pose a threat to the entire universe. In the space between the infinite realities is where many of the Old Ones live or exist, from which they attempt to corrupt and conquer those realities. Any world or universe which is conquered by them gradually decays and dies. One such universe was called the Cancerverse, where the abstract entity known as "Death" was killed and nothing died. It was a universe corrupted by the Many-Angled Ones and life ran riot, like a cancer.

The Many-Angled Ones are not the only eldritch entities that operate at the Multiversal stage. At one extreme are those who pose universal-scale threats to the realities they visit and at the other extreme are those who pose threats only to a world. fullContent:
Marvel Super Heroes is a super hero role-playing game based on Marvel Comics which was licensed by TSR. The game was first released in 1984 and game supplements were last published in 1993. It incorporates elements of the Mythos (Shuma-Gorath and Chthon), which were found in the "Realms of Magic" sourcebook (1986) but it was specific to certain campaign types, otherwise it's rare the characters will encounter the Mythos. The game was designed to be easy to understand and use, and the focus was on superhero fights.

### Setting
The setting encompassed all of the Marvel setting, though it was not in the mainstream prime reality of Earth-616. You were able to play the role of the licensed super hero characters or could create one of your own. Campaign settings were either cosmic, on Earth, in New York City or in another dimension. Your campaign could be one that involved traveling through time or visiting different dimensions or realities. The core books and their campaign books were focused on one of four "worlds", that of the X-Men (mutants), the Avengers, the Fantastic Four (time travel & dimensional travel), and the street heroes of NY City.

Marvin Kaye (10 March 1938-13 May 2021) was a prolific author and editor as well as an actor and stand-up comedian. Amongst his editorial credits was the long-running pulp fiction magazine Weird Tales, which he edited from 2012 until 2019. He also edited at least one Weird Tales anthology with his wife Saralee Kaye. Although Kaye edited many Lovecraftian tales, and even wrote non-fiction works on H. P. Lovecraft, he does not appear to have written any Mythos-related works himself.

fullContent:
Mary Wollstonecraft Shelley née Godwin (30 August 1797 - 1 February 1851) was an English novelist best known for her pioneering gothic/science fiction novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. In his letters, H. P. Lovecraft stated that the book was the inspiration for "Herbert West--Reanimator," which he wrote as a parody, and was suggested by S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz as inspiration for "The Outsider."

Although Shelley wrote several novels, these have historically been overshadowed by Frankenstein; however, scholarly interest in her other works has increased in recent years.

fullContent:
Masks of Nyarlathotep: Perilous Adventures to Thwart the Dark God is an expansion for Chaosium’s seminal roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu. It was written by Larry DiTillio and Lynn Willis.

### Overview
As the tagline might suggest, the story involves the players attempting to foil the plots of the Outer God Nyarlathotep through a series of encounters which take them across the globe. Originally consisting of five scenarios, a sixth which had been cut from the first release was later added back in, and in 2018 an all-new seventh scenario was included with a special edition set. The locations visited are New York, London, Cairo, Nairobi, Shanghai, Australia and Peru.

### Editions

### First Edition
Released in a boxed set in 1984, the first edition included a separate booklet for each adventure, reference sheets and a set of player handouts.

### Second Edition
Issued as a single book in 1989 for Call of Cthulhu 4th edition, the second edition included all-new artwork and integrated handouts.

### Third Edition
Released in 1996 for Call of Cthulhu 5th edition and titled The Complete Masks of Nyarlathotep, this was the first edition to feature the missing Australia chapter. A version tweaked for 6th edition was released in 2006.

### Fourth Edition
Published in 2010 with the title returned to simply Masks of Nyarlathotep.

### Fifth Edition
Completely revised for the 7th edition Call of Cthulhu rules, the fifth edition was published as a two-volume slipcase containing handouts. Also included are new artwork and material. This edition contains a new prologue adventure set in 1921 Peru, 8 chapters detailing the main campaign, and 4 appendices of related game material detail, for a total of 666 pages.

Masks of the Mythos is an expansion book for the White Wolf Publishing/Onyx Path Publishing roleplaying game Scion. It was published by Onyx Path in 2022; hardcover and digital formats were released, with the former issued in both standard and premium editions.

Scion is a roleplaying game in which the players take on the roles of the Earthly children of the gods, acting as their agents in various celestial conflicts. Masks of the Mythos introduces players to new characters descended from the gods of the Cthulhu Mythos, allowing for more varied character creation and storytelling possibilities.

fullContent:
Massa di Requiem per Shuggay (Requiem for Shaggai) is a fictional opera in the Cthulhu Mythos. It first appeared in The Unspeakable Oath, a magazine about Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG. It is described as a never-published opera composed by Benvento Chieti Bordighera around 1768 in Italy. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

### Description
The opera describes the flight of the shan from their doomed home world to Earth. Its composition contains lurid and unpleasant scenes depicting torture, incest, and other degradations, and was banned by both the Church and State. (: Malleus Monstrorum) It also details the shan's worship of Azathoth and a being known as Baoht Z'uqqa-mogg. Performing the entire opera will result in the summoning of Azathoth. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

### In the Mythos
Only a single performance was ever given and which resulted in a riot, leading to the opera's ban and to Bordighera's arrest and later execution, although some reports suggest that the composer escaped the Italian authorities by fleeing into France. Bordighera created new musical instruments to be able to play some portions of the works, and due to his apparent death the method used to read and played some musical notes have been lost to history. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

Copies of the opera are kept at the British Museum, Bibliotheque Nationale, and the Vatican Library, and others are held by private collectors in India, Japan, and the United States. The German band Knochen Maschine adapted the piece into a modern format; the two singers hired to perform the main portions died shortly thereafter. (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

The Commonwealth of Massachusetts is a state in the New England region of the United States. It is a very common Cthulhu Mythos setting, for both real-world and invented locations. Essex County, the northeastern corner of the state, forms the heart of Lovecraft Country.

### Locations
The Massachusetts towns and villages invented by H. P. Lovecraft for his fiction include:

*Arkham
*Innsmouth
*Dunwich
*Kingsport
*Aylesbury
*Dean's Corners

Other real-world Massachusetts locations mentioned in Lovecraft's fiction include Boston, Salem, Newburyport, and Cambridge. Bolton is the name of an actual town in Massachusetts that Lovecraft seems to place in a different location.

The Master of the Monolith is a fictional monster created by Robert E. Howard for his short story "The Black Stone".

### Description
The Master of the Monolith is a large toad-like creature, believed to be a remnant from prehuman eras. In the middle ages, it was worshiped by the people of Xuthltan (later known as Stregoicavar) in Hungary, who raided nearby villages and abducted young women and children to offer as sacrifices to it. The rituals also involved a female cultist dancing wildly to the sound of drums, while a male cultist savagely whipped her and danced with her to entertain the Master, who watched the ceremony while perched atop the Black Stone: a monolith marked with symbols of an unknown language.

When Hungary was invaded by the forces of Suleiman the Magnificent in 1526, the Turkish army led by Selim Bahadur was so disgusted by the rituals that they executed the entire village, and destroyed the Master of the Monolith using a combination of fire, steel blessed by Muhammad, and ancient incantations. Before it died, the beast killed ten of Bahadur's men "in ways that Selim would not or could not describe". 

However, in the summer of 1931, the ghost of the Master of the Monolith and its Cultists appeared, and ghosts of Cultists sacrificed a baby and a girl. (: "The Black Stone")

### Behind the Mythos
As a toad-like deity who demands brutal sacrifices to be appeased, the Master of the Monolith is similar to Howard's Gol-goroth.

Ye Booke of Monstres II implies that the Master of the Monolith might have been a Child of Tsathoggua that was mistaken for Gol-goroth.

Matthew Theron Ruff (born September 8, 1965), who publishes under the name Matt Ruff, is a writer of genre fiction, the author of Lovecraft Country (2016) and its sequel, The Destroyer of Worlds: A Return to Lovecraft Country (2023). 

Ruff was born in 1965 in New York City. He attended Stuyvesant High School, a prestigious public school, where one of his teachers was the writer Frank McCourt. He graduated from Cornell University in 1987, and the next year published his first novel, Fool on the Hill, a fantasy based on his college experience.

Other novels by Ruff include the cyberpunk Sewer, Gas & Electric: The Public Works Trilogy (1997), the alternate history The Mirage (2012) , and 88 Names (2020), a thriller set in virtual reality.

Matthew DiNardo is a minor recurrent character in Armand Rosamilia's Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Description
An aspiring young author, Matthew writes extreme horror stories with the intent to shock and disgust. He is a devious character, willing to say or do almost anything to get women to sleep with him.

### History
When Matthew took his new girlfriend Tina out on a date to nearby Keyport, the two had an argument about his writing and broke up. As the Esoteric Order of Dagon were conducting their plans to raise great Cthulhu from his watery slumber, Matthew was not allowed to leave town, and ended up falling into the clutches of the deformed children which roamed the subterranean labyrinth beneath Keyport, where he was tortured and killed.

* "Evil" (2013)

shortDefinition: Maurice Winter Moe (1882 - 1940) was an American teacher, amateur journalist, and poet from Appleton, Wisconsin. Together with Rheinhart Kleiner, Ira A. Cole, and H. P. Lovecraft, he took part in the literary correspondence circle known as the "Kleic...
fullContent:
Maurice Winter Moe (1882 - 1940) was an American teacher, amateur journalist, and poet from Appleton, Wisconsin. Together with Rheinhart Kleiner, Ira A. Cole, and H. P. Lovecraft, he took part in the literary correspondence circle known as the "Kleicomolo": a word composed of the first syllable of the names of each of the four participants. Lovecraft and Moe were also part of the similarly-named "Gallomo", with Alfred Galpin; as well as the "Coryciani", with Natalie H. Wooley. Moe was deeply religious and frequently clashed wits with atheist Lovecraft.

Moe also edited the anthology Four Acrostic Sonnets on Edgar Allan Poe, which collected poems about Poe written by Moe himself, Lovecraft, R. H. Barlow, and Adolphe de Castro. Lovecraft's entry was "In a Sequester'd Providence Churchyard Where Once Poe Walk'd".

The characters Joel Manton ("The Unnamable") and Cardinal Mauricio ("Alfredo; a Tragedy") were both based on Moe.

Meadow Hill is a landmark in the fictional town of Arkham, Massachusetts, invented by H. P. Lovecraft and mentioned repeatedly in his stories.

Meadow Hill is first mentioned in Lovecraft's story "Herbert West--Re-Animator", written in 1921-22, as a place on the outskirts of Arkham where Herbert West and his colleague live in a deserted farmhouse and perform macabre experiments. 

The hill occurs again in 1923's "The Unnamable", where it's mentioned as the site of a long-ago sighting of "a frightful loping, nameless thing". Later, after their encounter with the Unnamable, Randolph Carter and Joel Manton are found "in a lonely field beyond Meadow Hill, a mile from the old burying-ground, on a spot where an ancient slaughterhouse is reputed to have stood."

In "The Colour Out of Space", from 1927, "the McGregor boys from Meadow Hill" shoot a "very peculiar" woodchuck--not on their hill, but near the Gardner farm.

Meadow Hill appears, finally, in "The Dreams in the Witch-House" (1932),  where "beyond Meadow Hill" there is a "dark ravine...where the old white stone stands in a place queerly void of all plant-life."

fullContent:
"Medusa's Coil" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop. It was first published in Weird Tales magazine in January 1939, two years after Lovecraft's death.

It was completed in 1930 but had been universally rejected for publication at that time, not due to its content, but purely on quality of writing. Due to its casual, overt and relentless racism, this story is unlikely to see reprint or adaptation.

### Synopsis
An unnamed narrator is travelling through Cape Girardeau, Missouri, when he seeks shelter in a run-down plantation house. The sole occupant is a hermit, Antoine de Russy, who relays his story.

The plantation is called Riverside, and the de Russys are an old family of Louisiana aristocracy.  de Russy takes an opportunity to reflect fondly of life on the plantation in pre-Civil War days, when around 200 slaves lived and worked for his family: "to hear them singing and laughing and playing the banjo at night as to know the fullest charm of a civilization and social order now sadly extinct." de Russy sadly lost his wife in childbirth, and Denis, his only child, became the centre of his life.

Denis goes to Sorbonne University, France, where a fad for the occult and pseudo devil worship is sweeping the local aesthetes.  There, Denis reunites with a friend named Frank Marsh, and also falls in love with the leader of one of the fad cults, Marceline Bedard.  Calling herself "[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanit Tanit]-[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isis Isis]," Marceline preached that her cult was tied to prehistoric Egypt and to Carthage, and also spouted "a lot of gibberish concerned with snakes and human hair," including references to Medusa, and to the legend of [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coma_Berenices Coma Berenices], where Berenice II of Ptolemaic Egypt sacrificed her hair as part of a rite to save her husband Ptolemy II. While Marsh is a regular attendant, Denis only gets to know Marceline outside her occult life, and falls in love with her. Soon, they marry.

Denis returns home, where Marceline abandons her occult theatrics. Nevertheless, Antoine finds her oddly disturbing, and frequently lapses into morbid fascinations, like that she might indeed be from some ancient civilization, or that her hair – beautiful, jet black hair that Marceline keeps a single braid that goes past her knees – occasionally moves with a life of its own.  Only the servants (all Black men and women) seem to share his disregard, except "Old Sophinisba," who regards Marceline almost worshipfully.

In Summer 1916, Frank Marsh comes for an extended stay. He complains of an artistic dry spell, and asks permission to paint Marceline, admitting that she – and her hair – have haunted him since Sorbonne, and that she may be the spark he needs to create a masterpiece.  "In a sense," he says to Denis, "I'm half doing it for you," promising a "waking-up and a sort of salvation."

"Medusa's Harem" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Magenta Nero. It was published in the James Ward Kirk Publishing thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
The chosen devotee of a cult searches out a being known as the Queen Medusa in an attempt to harness her power for some dark purpose. Locating her in a high mountain cave, he is seduced by her and her followers before being transformed into something powerful and inhuman. The story concludes by telling of the cultist's intent to return to his group and take control of them by force.

fullContent: Megalopolisomancy, or in the revised text of Our Lady of Darkness and The Pale Brown Thing, megapolisomancy, is the (black) magic of giant cities. Megapolisomancy is a fictional occult science created by Fritz Leiber, an influential American writer of fantasy and science fiction. Featured in Leiber's novella Our Lady of Darkness, megapolisomancy is the art of predicting and manipulating the future through the existence of large cities. In Our Lady of Darkness, the primary practitioner of this pseudoscience is fictional occultist Thibaut de Castries, whose seminal work, Megapolisomancy: A New Science of Cities, concerns the physical, psychological and paramental (spiritual) effects of certain substances, including steel, electricity, paper, and so forth as they accumulate in cities. This book was primarily a book of occult theory; De Castries preserved all of his actual methods for practicing megapolisomancy in a second book, which he referred to as his Grand Cipher or Fifty-Book. The latter book contained a series of 50 astrological and astronomical signs and other cryptic sigils.

Meikumi Urushibarao is a fictional entity created by Kouichi Azakawa for his light novel series Makai Shoujo R'lyeh Lulu.

### Description
Meikumi Urushibarao is an avatar of Nyarlathotep, who takes the form of an attractive female human with glasses; however, she has no true form, possessing the ability to exist in multiple different forms at the same time and can summon other manifestations, including the Black Pharaoh and the Great Calamity. As an entity from a transcendent superdimension, Meikumi is not bound by any concepts from all other universes and dimensions, as well as dwarfing gods like Cthulhu and Hastur in terms of power.

Posing as an air-headed Japanese teacher in Rhymegasaki City, Meikumi's true goal is to release chaos and destruction from the Shining Trapezohedron. (: Makai Shoujo R'lyeh Lulu)

shortDefinition: "Memory" is a prose poem by American horror and science fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in 1919 and published in June 1919 in The United Co-Operative.  ### Themes "Memory" uses many of H. P. Lovecraft's common images and ideas, such as relics...
fullContent:
"Memory" is a prose poem by American horror and science fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in 1919 and published in June 1919 in The United Co-Operative.

### Themes
"Memory" uses many of H. P. Lovecraft's common images and ideas, such as relics of the deep past and things "without name". Also, his fondness for vast, monolithic ruins (a favourite with many other Cthulhu and horror writers) is evident in the intricate description found in the page-long story.

Given the story's climax, it is possible to put this short story firmly in the Dying Earth sub-genre of science fiction although the naming conventions used make an equally strong case for this being a Dreamlands story. Since there is nothing in the story to tie it to any specific time or place other than arguably an implied future, we will never really know.

### Overview
This story takes place in the ancient valley of Nis, in vegetation-covered stone ruins described by Lovecraft in great detail. These crumbling blocks of monolithic stone now serve only for grey toads and snakes to nest under. Interspersed in the ruins are large trees that are home to little apes. Through the bottom of this valley runs the great, slimy red river called Than.

"Memory" involves only two characters: "the Genie that haunts the moonbeams" and "the Daemon of the Valley". The Genie inquires of the Daemon who it was that long ago placed the stones that were now the desolate ruin near the river Than. The Daemon replies that he remembers the name of the creatures "clearly," but only because their name rhymed with that of the river: they were called Man. He also remembers "dimly" that they appeared like the small apes that now leap through the ruins. The Genie flies back to his moonbeams, and the Daemon turns to regard an ape in silent contemplation.

### Inspiration
The short piece owes a heavy debt to Edgar Allan Poe, particularly Poe's story "The Conversation of Eiros and Charmion", which also features a dialogue between two supernatural creatures after the extinction of humanity. Poe's "The Valley of Unrest" mentions "the valley Nis".

### Publication History
After its first appearance in The United Co-Operative--an amateur press journal jointly edited by Lovecraft, W. Paul Cook, and Winifred V. Jackson, among others--the story was reprinted many times, including in the Arkham House collections Beyond the Wall of Sleep (1943) and Dreams and Fancies (1962), and the Ballantine paperback The Doom That Came to Sarnath (1971).

"Memory" is a Lovecraftian poem by American author Josh Maybrook. It was published in Vol 5, Issue 2 of Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
The fourteen lines describe a haunting sound almost heard, which appears to emanate from the very cosmos itself, as well as the narrator's inkling that they may not be wholly of the Earth.

### Behind the Mythos
The description of the cosmic music and "ghostly choir" may be a reference to the Outer God Azathoth.
