fullContent:
"Men of Shadow" is a story featured in issue #29 of the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles comic series by Mirage Studios. Set in Arkham, the plot involves the protagonists facing off against Dagon and his vampire cult.

### Mythos Connections
*In his opening editorial, A.C. Farley mentions H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth, the story that this comic was heavily inspired by. 
*The character who fights against the cult is named Clark Ashton Allard, a nod to Clark Ashton Smith. In the prologue, he uses his computer to access some files involving the Necronomicon. The character's last name, Allard, is the last name of the alias of the pulp character, The Shadow (Lamont Cranston) who uses Kent Allard in a manner similar to the Matches Malone false identity of the later character Batman.
*April and Casey are held hostage in a library annex called the "Whatley House", named after the Whateley family from "The Dunwich Horror".
*In the climax of the story, the vampire cult takes Allard to Innsmouth and attempts to use him as a sacrifice. Although they manage to successfully awaken their god, Dagon is banished using the artefact that summoned him before he can destroy humanity like they planned.

Menes is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Cats of Ulthar".

### Background
Menes is a young boy who visited the town of Ulthar in the Dreamlands as part of a caravan of wanderers from the South. Orphaned as a child during a plague, he found comfort in a small black kitten that he kept as a companion. When his kitten went missing the blame was placed on an old man and his wife, residents of Ulthar who were notorious for capturing and killing cats.

Menes prayed to the gods of his people for justice, and after his caravan departed Ulthar, all the cats of the village converged on the house of the old man and his wife and took revenge against them by killing and eating them. Following this incident the town burgesses passed a law against the killing of cats. (: "The Cats of Ulthar")

The Menoptera are a species created by the BBC in 1965 for Doctor Who.

### Background
The Menoptera are a humanoid insectoid race which have human-like faces with large black eyes and antennae. They have four large wings that give them the ability to fly. If removed the wings quickly regenerate though the ability to fly is lost. The secret to their flight was the anti-gravitic power of isocryte, which they consumed in minute traces. Bands of white fur and black skin cover their bodies.

They were a technologically capable race, which possessed weapons and a fleet of spacecraft. Menoptera built their villages and temples in cliff-faces and the nests were usually constructed in trees. They worshipped the Gods of Light and looked down on the wingless.

Menoptera did not originate on Vortis. Dozens of Menopetra were taken from their homeworld and relocated to Vortis by the Gods of Light. Early in the planet's history, the Zarbi waged war against the Menoptera. Whom were forced to withdraw to the moons. Some time afterwards they return to the planet, where they lived a peaceful life, leading simple lives. This situation changed upon the arrival of the Animus, who took over the Zarbi. Once again, the Zarbi waged war against the Menoptera, forcing them to retreat to one of Vortis' moons. The Animus would eventually be defeated with the assistance of the Doctor and his companions.

For many years afterwards, the Zarbi and Menoptera lived and worked in peace together. The world eventually ended up in the nearby Rhumos system, which was the home of a warlike race who turned the Menoptera into slaves, who were simultaneously facing the threat of a resurrected Animus. The Doctor and his companions liberated the Menoperate from slavery, defeated the Animus again, and made the Rhumons declare the planet neutral ground.

The Zarbi would become a threat to the Earth when a Zarbi Supremo evolved and took over the Zarbi. They then used advanced technology to move Vortis to Earth's Solar System, as part of a plan to conquer Earth. The Menoptera built a fleet of spacecraft and attempted to stop the Zarbi. With the assistance of the Doctor and a group of Earth scientists, the Zarbi Supremo was slain and the Zarbi returned to their normal state.

"Messages from a Dark Deity" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Stephen Mark Rainey.

### Synopsis
A reporter who had witnessed some unknown entity during his time covering the war in Iraq begins to see things which others cannot. As the horrific - and largely ignored - murders increase, the daytime stars move into position and the holes in the sky grow larger, while the city begins to quietly burn before all is revealed to a terrified population.

### Characters
*Owen Blair, a somewhat jaded investigative journalist.
*Debra, Owen's devoted partner.

### Publication History
"Messages from a Dark Deity" was published in the 2017 thematic anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror by Dark Regions Press.

### Trivia
*The phrase which Owen overheard a soldier repeat to himself - which he could only interpret as "Ee-eye-ee-eye-oh, cuckoo who’ll fool you, foe tag again, glue a gnarly toe tap" - is a clear phonetic representation of the language of R'lyeh.

The Messenger of Azathoth is a fictional monster created by Gary Myers for his short story "Passing of a Dreamer", where it is encountered by the dreamer Snireth-Ko on the dark side of the Dreamlands' moon.

This creature has also been incorporated into the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, where it is portrayed as a "seed" destined to "fertilize" and destroy the Dreamlands' moon.

### In the Call of Cthulhu RPG
The Messenger of Azathoth is a "seed" drifting through the Dreamlands towards the moon. When it comes in contact with the satellite, it will melt through the ground and lodge itself in its core, where it will begin to grow, boiling the Lake of Ubboth and consuming Mnomquah in the process. While burrowing, it will radiate an intense green light that causes those who come near it to undergo a gradual deterioration until their bodies finally dissolve into living "pools of protoplasm". The Messenger can't be destroyed by physical means, only by magical artefacts. If allowed to reach maturity, it will eventually break free, destroying the Dreamlands' moon with cataclysmic consequences not only for the dream realm, but for the sanity of all the Waking World's population as well. (: H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands)

### Behind the Mythos
In the works of H. P. Lovecraft, Nyarlathotep holds the role of Azathoth's messenger (: Fungi from Yuggoth) and is known to operate from the dark side of the Dreamlands' moon with his Moon-beast allies (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath). It's not known whether Myers intended the creature from "Passing of a Dreamer" to be Nyarlathotep, but the RPG classifies it as a distinct servitor race, apparently unconnected to the Crawling Chaos.

In later books, this entity is said to be one of the Larvae of the Other Gods (: Ye Booke of Monstres II).

shortDefinition: Metallica is an American thrash metal band whose music has repeatedly referenced the Cthulhu Mythos. The band was reportedly turned on to the work of H. P. Lovecraft by Cliff Burton, its bassist from 1982 until his death in a tour bus accident in 198...
fullContent:
Metallica is an American thrash metal band whose music has repeatedly referenced the Cthulhu Mythos. The band was reportedly turned on to the work of H. P. Lovecraft by Cliff Burton, its bassist from 1982 until his death in a tour bus accident in 1986; Burton has been described as "an HP Lovecraft-reading, piano-playing homebody who loved beer, Mexican food, pot and acid." When guitarist Kirk Hammett joined the band in 1983, he and Burton bonded over a mutual interest in the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

The Lovecraft influence first emerged on the 1984 album Ride the Lightning, which closes with a nearly nine-minute instrumental, written by James Hetfield, Lars Ulrich, Burton and Dave Mustaine, called "The Call of Ktulu". The song is said to be inspired not only by "The Call of Cthulhu" but by "The Shadow over Innsmouth" as well. The variant spelling was reportedly intended to make the song title easier to pronounce.



The following album, Master of Puppets (1986), features "The Thing That Should Not Be", whose lyrics (written by Hetfield) contain multiple Mythos references.

Mevana is a fictional character from the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald.

### Overview
A renowned crocodile hunter, it is said that Mevana "knows all Uganda like a book". (: "Winged Death")

### Biography
In November 1928, Mevana was bitten by a devil-fly in the vicinity of Lake Mlolo, in the jungles of Uganda. Over the next months, he became violently sick, with symptoms that included lethargy, low temperature, and convulsions. He was brought to the trading post of M'gonga, where Dr. Thomas Slauenwite treated him. At first, Slauenwite was at a loss about what to do, being completely unfamiliar with the disease. By January 1929, Mevana's condition had deteriorated significantly. Fortunately, Slauenwite gave him tryparsamide at a colleague's suggestion, which proved an effective treatment. Over the next weeks, Mevana recovered and was tended by his wife Ugowe.

On February 3, Slauenwite asked Mevana to guide him to Lake Mlolo so that he could capture devil-flies for study. Despite his fear, Mevana agreed to lead a party consisting of himself, Slauenwite, and five others to the location. On the way, they passed through the ruins of the outposts of the Fishers from Outside and their gods, Tsadogwa and Clulu. The expedition was a success and Slauenwite got a good supply of devil-flies for his studies. (: "Winged Death")

### Personality
Slauenwite regarded Mevana as courageous, but also superstitious. While suffering from the devil-fly's illness, Mevana was afraid that if he died, his soul would pass on to the fly that bit him: a belief that was actually justified, as the devil-flies do in fact acquire the consciousness of the people they kill. After he was cured, Mevana held Slauenwite in high regard, even to the point of believing that the doctor had the ability to "ward off disease as well as cure it". This, in addition to gratitude for saving his life, was the reason why Mevana agreed to guide Slauenwite to Lake Mlolo, despite being afraid to return there.

Mh'ithrha (The Arch-Lord of Tindalos) is an Outer God in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Bruce Ballon for the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Unseen Masters.  

### Description
The master of the Hounds of Tindalos, Mh'ithrha is the mightiest member of that strange species. Although invisible to the human eye, its physical form is said to be that of a gargantuan wolf, somewhat resembling the beast Fenrir from Norse mythology.

Mh'ithrha has been engaged in a war with Yog-Sothoth for all of eternity; stories of this conflict are the stuff of legend in the Cthulhu Mythos, and the fact that it has not been annihilated by such a being gives a hint to the true extent of Mh'ithrha's power. (: Unseen Masters)

Mhar (The World Thunder) is a fictional entity created by Paizo Inc for their role-playing game Pathfinder. The character first appeared in the gaming supplement Spires of Xin-Shalast.

### Background
Mhar is a Great Old One whose shape is that of a living volcano with fangs of lava surrounding its caldera and eight crystalline legs coming out of the base. The lava is constantly erupting, afterwards cooling or melting away, bringing it endless pain. It is currently under one of Golarion's largest mountains, the 31,565 feet tall Mhar Massif. The site of the former capital of the ancient realm of Shalast, known for the great carving it has on its face of Karzoug, the last Runelord of Greed.

It was born when the essence of the Planes of Earth and Fire were made to fuse together by a unique planar rift. To alleviate its pain, it traveled the cosmos, settling on hot, molten planets. It would rest within their cores, but eventually their heat wouldn't be enough to keep it asleep. Resulting in its awakening and the destruction of the planet. Numerous worlds were destroyed like this, until it ended up on Golarion.

When the goddess Sarenrae opened the Material Plane to create the Dead Vault, she attempted to put Mhar out of its misery by killing it. She was unable to permanently destroy him, as he was put into a slumber within Golarion. When it awakened, Mhar found itself trapped within Golarion and went insane. Its madness was intensified by his psychic convulsions which rebounded from the planet's surface. The Kodar Mountain range was created by Mhar's convulsions. If Mhar ever breaks free from its prison, it will cover Golarion with magma. Using it as a focus to open a portal to the Plane of Fire. Consuming the Material Plane in lava so that it can finally know peace.

"Mhuld'enda of the Deep" is a short story by author Tom Bont, first published in Vol 3, Issue 1 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana. It is very loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
After it’s destruction at the hands of a ferocious sea creature - which, as a result of his research at Arkham University Lieutenant Bill Newkirk recognises as the sea monster Mhuld'enda - a small group of survivors from the USS Evermay are washed ashore on a tiny outcropping of land in the middle of the Pacific Ocean.

As they are slowly picked off by tentacles which shoot from the sea, they come to the understanding that they have been guided into a "larder" of sorts: with nowhere to go, they can be consumed at leisure. Resolving to fight back against the creature, they bait it into attacking, and use their sole flare gun to shoot the beast through the eye, killing it. However, in the aftermath, they realise that the creature they have killed is far too small to have been the one which sunk their ship and is only a juvenile, the island being a place where it could hone its hunting skills.

The story concludes with Newkirk, the final survivor, writing the story in his diary while waiting for Mhuld'enda to return and take vengeance for the death of its offspring.

### Behind the Mythos
The premise of a mother monster returning to avenge its dead offspring could draw comparisons to H. P. Lovecraft and Sonia H. Greene's "The Horror at Martin's Beach," although the circumstances leading to the story's conclusion are very different.

### Publication History
* Lovecraftiana Vol 3, Issue 1 (2018)
* Lovecraftiana Volume 3 (2020)

### Trivia
* The mention of Newkirk having attended "Arkham University" would appear to be a reference to Miskatonic University, the only institute of higher learning in Arkham in Lovecraft’s fiction.
* The description of Mhuld'enda would appear to more closely match that of the mythical Kraken of Norse mythology - likely a result of sightings of giant squid  - rather than any "conventional" depiction of an eldritch abomination.

The Mi-Go, also known as the Fungi from Yuggoth, are a fictional alien species first introduced by H. P. Lovecraft in his 1931 short story The Whisperer in Darkness and frequently referenced in other Cthulhu Mythos fiction. They are depicted as an extragalactic species that has colonized numerous worlds, including Yuggoth (which Albert Wilmarth believed to be the dwarf planet Pluto). They are described as winged fungal creatures that resemble crustaceans, with large claws and heads covered in antennae.

The Mi-Go are a scientifically and technologically advanced race, having a particularly sophisticated grasp of surgical techniques and neuroscience. Their name originates from the Mi-Go (in Tibetan standard transliteration, migoi or in earlier times migou) or "Abominable Snow-Men" of Nepalese and Bhutanese folklore, although they're also referred to as the Outer Ones or Outer Beings. To the Pennacook, they are known as the Winged Ones and believed to have come from Ursa Major. Elsewhere they're known simply as "those ones", or "the old ones". (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

### Description
Several types of Mi-Go exist, including winged and wingless variations. Those that have wings use them to fly through the "ether" of outer space (a pre-Einsteinian concept). The wings do not function well on Earth. (: The Whisperer in Darkness) Several other races in Lovecraft's Mythos have wings like these as well, suggesting they are a standard mode of interplanetary travel.

On Earth, the Mi-Go are known to be present in the Vermont hills and the Himalayas. They usually walk on all their limbs, but are also capable of standing on their hindmost pair of limbs and leaving the others free to carry objects with them. They don't have a fixed size, but the most common ones appear to be around five feet in length. (: The Whisperer in Darkness) Some, however, can be as large as a grizzly bear. (: "The Dweller in the Tomb")

The Mi-Go are fundamentally alien with respect to Earthly life, originating from strangely organized abysses beyond our space-time continuum, the human known space-time is described like an atom within theirs. And they have established numerous outposts across the myriad universes (: The Whisperer in Darkness). According to two reports in the original short story, their bodies consist of a form of matter that does not occur naturally on Earth. Similarly, the artwork of the Elder Things of Antarctica depicts both the Mi-Go and the Cthulhi as being made of an unearthly type of matter that originally come from remoter gulfs of cosmic space, while the Elder Things originate within the known space-time continuum. Mi-Go Brain Cylinders are arcane technological devices created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Description
A Brain Cylinder is a cylindrical, medium sized machine used by the Mi-Go to transport humans to Yuggoth. It contains a living human brain, vivisected from its host and preserved in nutrient fluid. The cylinder can be connected with various devices that provide the faculties of sight, hearing and speech to the brain, allowing it to observe and interact with its surroundings.

### Behind the Mythos
The Mi-Go brain cylinders are a literal example of the "Brain in a Jar" thought experiment. The "Brain in a Jar" or "Brain in a Vat" is a philosophical exploration of whether, if all we are is a brain wrapped in meat, if the brain is isolated and only experiences things indirectly, can we be sure that anything we experience is real? The original version of this thought experiment was proposed by René Descartes in 1641 and was based on a human brain trapped inside a demon (a very Mythos concept). The vat/jar version was proposed by Gilbert Harlan in 1973 to update the experiment and remove any moral or supernatural element.

"MIBs" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tim Waggoner.

### Synopsis
After mentioning an odd sighting he made to his ex-wife, a man is driven insane by the attentions of the otherworldly Men in Black. Once his descent into madness is complete, he becomes one of them.

### Characters

* Ian Thompson, a divorced man in his thirties who had a keen interest in the paranormal during his childhood.
* Janice, Thompson's ex-wife.

### Publication History
"MIBs" was published in issue #2 of the E. P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes in August 1997

### Trivia

* The book which Thompson read while a youth, The UFO Prophecies, states the author's belief that the Men in Black are agents of entities such as Cthulhu, Nyarlathotep and Azathoth, with the latter being particularly singled out; the end of the story heavily implies this to be the case.

Michael Cisco (b. 1970) is an author and literary critic who both writes and studies weird fiction. Several of his short stories connect to the Cthulhu Mythos. He has described his writing as "de-genred."

Cisco's first novel, The Divinity Student, won of the International Horror Guild Award for Best First Novel of 1999.  He has since written 12 more novels, including The Great Lover, which was named the Best Weird Novel of 2011 by the Weird Fiction Review.

Author Jeff VanderMeer writes that Cisco "has forged a singular path in creating visionary, phantasmagorical settings, uniquely alienated anti-heroes, and genuinely creepy happenings—while also exhibiting a healthy absurdism and dark sense of humor." Author China Miéville calls him "one of the key figures in the experimental fantastic."

Cisco has a  B.A. from Sarah Lawrence College (1992), an M.A. from the State University of New York at Buffalo (1994), and an MPhil. (2002) and PhD. in English (2004) from New York University. Since 2008, he has taught English at Hostos Community College, part of the City University of New York; one of his courses is "Literature of the Macabre and the Supernatural."

Michael Leigh is a fictional character created by American author Henry Kuttner for his short story "The Salem Horror" (1937). He later appears in "The Black Kiss", by Kuttner and Robert Bloch.

### Overview
Leigh is an occultist with a deep understanding of mystical practices who lives in San Francisco, California. Described as "a lean, tall figure of a man, with thick steel-gray eyebrows overhanging keen gray eyes. His face, although strongly marked and gaunt, was unwrinkled ... His voice was deep, pleasant." Carson, the main character of "The Salem Horror", finds himself liking Leigh as a result of his magnetic personality.

James Michael Reaves (14 September 1950 - 20 March 2023) was an American author who wrote a number of works set in the Cthulhu Mythos, starting with the episode "The Collect Call of Cathulhu" of the animated series The Real Ghostbusters. He contributed stories to the anthologies The Children of Cthulhu and Shadows Over Baker Street, the latter which he co-edited with John Pelan. Reaves also developed the animated series Conan and the Young Warriors, based on the character created by Robert E. Howard.

Reaves' career was largely focused on animation. In addition to The Real Ghostbusters, he wrote multiple episodes for Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Batman: The Animated Series, Gargoyles, Dungeons & Dragons, Godzilla: The Series, Blackstar, Ewoks, and more than one iteration of the He-Man and the Masters of the Universe franchise, among many others. His live action credits include four episodes of the anthology series Monsters, and an episode of Star Trek: The Next Generation co-written with Diane Duane.

The InterWorld novel trilogy was co-written by Michael Reaves with his daughter Mallory Reaves and fellow Mythos author Neil Gaiman.

Michael Shea (3 July 1946-16 February 2014) was an American author who wrote in the horror, fantasy and science fiction genres. A recipient of multiple awards, he won two World Fantasy Awards, and was nominated for a Hugo award, two Nebula Awards, and the British Fantasy Society's August Derleth Award. Possessed of a life-long interest in H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos, Shea wrote several stories within the setting, and two volumes of these were collected and edited by Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi. His works have also been favourably compared to those of Lord Dunsany and Clark Ashton Smith.

Much of Shea's Lovecraftian work is set in his home town of Los Angeles, California.

Michel Thomas (born 26 February 1956), who uses the nom de plume Michel Houellebecq borrowing the surname from his maternal grandmother, is a French film maker, writer, critic, occasional singer, and actor.

His contribution to the field of Lovecraft study is his novella length literary criticism of Lovecraft entitled H. P. Lovecraft: Contre le monde, contre la vie or in English H. P. Lovecraft: Against the World, Against Life. It is a comparison between what Houellebecq sees as Lovecraft's asexual and anti-materialist existentialism and his own embrace of the philosophy of Schopenhauer.

Houellebecq identifies Lovecraft's hatred of modernity and the increasingly diverse contemporary America in which he lived, and noted "not a single allusion to two of the realities to which we generally ascribe great importance: sex and money."

Houellebecq attributes Lovecraft's racism to the two years Lovecraft spent in New York City amongst its diverse population and also noted how often Lovecraft would conjure up the image in his prose of a great city teeming with intimidating or frightening beings. At its base, suggests Houellebecq, Lovecraft experienced chronic deep seated fears, and these informed his work and his audience.

Midnight Shambler was an irregularly-released small press horror fanzine published by Necronomicon Press.

### Overview
Although a publication in the horror genre, Midnight Shambler had a heavy leaning towards the Cthulhu Mythos and Lovecraftian horror in general, and featured work by a wide array of contributors, including both up-and-coming and previously published authors. 

The first two issues, released in 1988, were edited by David Barker, after which it ceased publication until 1996, with a notable issue in November of that year, when it was revived under Robert M. Price's editorship for another eight issues, through 1998. Joseph S. Pulver, Sr. took the helm for the eleventh and final issue in April 1999. 

Cover art was provided by a variety of different artists, including Allen Koszowski.

The Midnight Sons are a fictional team in the prime reality of the Marvel universe of Marvel Comics.

### Background
The Midnight Sons (aka, Children of Midnight) is a supernatural team of superheroes. Whom have dedicated themselves to protect humanity from supernatural threats. They fight supernatural creatures such as vampires and werewolves. It's a team which has been around for over two decades and has included Ghost Rider, Mobius the Living Vampire, Doctor Strange, and Blade.

The team has clashed repeatedly with the Elder God Chthon, its minions (such as the N'Garai), and the Cult of the Darkhold. Blade temporarily came under the influence of Chthon and went on a murderous spree. Recently they pursued the superhuman serial killer Carnage who attempted to bring about the return of Chthon to Earth, stopping him in time and preventing the return of Chthon and the other Old Ones.

shortDefinition: Miles John Breuer, M.D. (1889 - 1945) was an American science fiction author and medical doctor of Czech origin who published stories and medical articles in both English and Czech. Born in Chicago, Illinois, he would later move to Nebraska, where he...
fullContent:
Miles John Breuer, M.D. (1889 - 1945) was an American science fiction author and medical doctor of Czech origin who published stories and medical articles in both English and Czech. Born in Chicago, Illinois, he would later move to Nebraska, where he worked as a physician. During World War One, he served in the US Army Medical Corps.

Breuer's work was most commonly published in Amazing Stories and other magazines geared towards science fiction. However, he did write at least one horror poem, "The Specter", which appeared in Weird Tales. He also co-authored stories with other sci-fi pioneers such as Jack Williamson and Clare Winger Harris.

Breuer was one of the many pulp authors who were spoofed in the comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century", by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. The story pairs him with David H. Keller (another author who, like Breuer, was also a medical doctor) and portrays the two as a pair of surgeons named "Drs. D. H. Killer and M. Gin Brewery", who treat those who partook of the cream-puffs sold by a certain "Wladislaw Brenryk".

When August Derleth was asked to provide a glossary to the nicknames used by Lovecraft and Barlow in "The Battle that Ended the Century", he identified "M. Gin Brewery" as "Miles G. Breuer", apparently mistaking Breuer's middle initial for "G", rather than "J". This error has been corrected in reprints.

Millie Von Clydesburgh is a fictional character created by American author Brandon Berntson for his Lovecraft Mysteries trilogy of Cthulhu Mythos novels. She made her debut appearance in the first book in the series, 2018's The Night of Dagon.

### Description
A perennially upbeat young woman, Millie is strikingly pretty with hair "a bundle of red and orange curls, her skin fair", and dark emerald eyes. Millie has stated her mother to be extremely wealthy, and is given an allowance, which allows her to work on a low, irregular wage for Devlin Macky as his secretary.

Millie has a deep-seated affection for Macky; although the feeling is mutual - the two have shared a handful of kisses, and Millie has been upfront about her feeling for him - Macky seems reluctant to commit to any kind of meaningful relationship.

In the novel Arkham: Reanimated, Millie claims to have attended college, where she majored in "[d]esign, with an emphasis on fashion. Then I took Eastern European History, Ancient Egypt, and Religious Studies. My minor was English Literature with an emphasis on Literary Studies. I also got a Master’s of Physics and Astronomy. And I took Greek and Hebrew", although given that she is relatively young, this would appear unlikely.

Millie also owns a cocker spaniel named Mr. Kalabraise who is, strangely, female.

### History
Amidst a plot by Dagon cultists to raise their monstrous god and bring about first the end of Innsport then, later, the world, Millie was instrumental in freeing two police officers who were to be sacrificed, and initiating the evacuation of the city. She also bore witness to Dagon's final moments as it was destroyed by the tons of explosives detonated by lunatic pyromaniac Bradley "Boom-boom" Denton (: The Night of Dagon).

Millie and Macky, while on a day trip to Arkham, faced an army of mutated creatures and monstrous abominations when they stumbled upon a scheme by Eric Moorland to revive his deceased wife; the sceme involved the participation of the Outer God Shub-Niggurath who dwelt in the catacombs beneath the town (: Arkham: Reanimated).

When Macky accidentally initiated the opening of dimensional gates and the subsequent return of the Outer Gods Millie, through a series of bizarre occurrences, travelled through time and space and for a brief time became the Queen of Sarnath; while there, she witnessed the fall of the once-great city at the hands of monstrous reptilians (: The Lurker at the Threshold).

Mindy Nguyen is a character created by Canadian author Troy Young for his Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Description
A tall, good-looking Asian woman with long black hair which she usually wears tied back, Mindy is trained in the combat techniques of Krav Maga.

### History
Formerly an investigative reporter, Harjit Singh recruited Mindy into the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena around 2018 after her fiancé was tortured and killed by 'winged shrimp with legs' (most likely Mi-Go) whilst on a hiking trip.

A little over a year later, one of her assignments caused her to cross paths with an alien life form and its collection of exotic flora. This encounter left her with a heightened ability to sense the presence of otherworldly entities and influence.

Nine months after that, she was first partnered with rookie agent and former firefighter Malcolm Mayweather. This partnership would only last for two assignments over the course of seven weeks, as Mayweather killed Mindy at her own request after she was infected by a horrific, incurable and fast-acting supernatural disease.

### Known Missions
Mindy has been given the following assignments (listed according to her in-universe timeline):

*Niagara, Canada: Mindy had her encounter with the alien gardener and its sentient greenhouse (: "The Alien Gardener").
*Saskatchewan, Canada: she and Malcolm Mayweather battled a cultist with the ability to control rats (: "The Rat King").
*Winnipeg, Canada: she and Mayweather encountered a being dubbed the Tattered Lady whose goal was to spread contagion through the masses. Was infected by the contagion and died at Mayweather's hands (: "The Tattered Lady").

### Appearances

*"The Alien Gardener" (2020)
*"The Tattered Lady" (2020) final appearance

Minh Thi Phan is an Investigator character created by Fantasy Flight Games for inclusion in their Cthulhu Mythos-related games and fiction.

### History
Minh Thi Phan has had two differing biographies released, one in the Innsmouth Horror Deluxe Expansion to Arkham Horror Second Edition, and the other in Eldritch Horror.

### Innsmouth Horror Deluxe Expansion ()
Minh's family fled their home in Korea to escape persecution from the Japanese; making their way to the United States, the family settled down to build themselves a future. Being hard workers, they were able to pay for Minh to attend community college where, despite experiencing her own share of racism and harassment, she completed her degree before heading out into the wider world to find a job.

Landing a position as secretary at a small firm in Arkham, Minh's main concern was that her new boss might act inappropriately towards her, but luckily Mr. Thompson wasn’t that kind of man, and Minh settled into her new job comfortably.

That was, until Mr. Thompson loaned her The King in Yellow. Minh was utterly repulsed by the contents of the book, and returned it to Mr. Thompson unfinished despite her employer's insistence that the end was the best part.

The very next day, Minh received a telephone call from St. Mary's Hospital saying that Mr. Thompson had died by suicide, and had named her as his next of kin. Collecting up Mr. Thompson's belongings - including The King in Yellow - Minh began to think on what to do next.

### Eldritch Horror ()
After travelling from Vietnam to Seoul in pursuit of business interests, Phan Thi Minh's father paid for an expensive education for the girl. Reaching adulthood and proving to be every bit as business-savvy as her father, Minh changed the ordering of her name to fit Western conventions before taking a secretarial job with a firm who specialised in importing unusual antiquities in Tokyo.

Forming a firm friendship with her boss Mr. Thomas, when the man was murdered Minh resolved to find the culprit and, armed only with a bizarre text left by her employer, set about doing just that.

### Behind the Mythos
Minh Thi Phan was first conceived by Fantasy Flight for the Innsmouth Horror expansion to the Second Edition of Arkham Horror, and has since appeared in other games including Mansions of Madness, Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. A pre-painted plastic miniature of Minh designed to complement these games was released in 2010, but is no longer in production (all ).

The Minions of Karakal are a fictional species created by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, making their first appearance in the 1986 supplement H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands.

### Description
The Minions of Karakal are supernatural beings that resemble floating spheres of electricity native to the Dark Dimension. They are about 3 feet in diameter, red and black in color, with spidery legs shaped like lightning bolts that undulate rhythmically and can deliver lethal electric discharges. As their name indicates, they worship the Great One known as Karakal.

The Minions of Karakal feed on electricity and have an affinity for dry environments, as humidity causes them to gradually dissipate over a period of weeks. Under rainfall, they are destroyed within minutes.

### Behind the Mythos
Created by Sandy Petersen, the Minions of Karakal made their first appearance in the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands in 1986. They have also appeared in S. Petersen’s Field Guide to Lovecraftian Horrors, and their statistics were reprinted in the monster manual Ye Booke of Monstres II.

The Minions of Othuum are fictional creatures created by Brian Lumley for his short story "Rising with Surtsey" and later used by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. 

### Description
The Minions of Othuum appear as miniature versions of their master Othuum, and inhabit the depths of the ocean. They have the ability to swap minds with people, but only when their master is at his most powerful. The telltale sign that a person has been replaced by a Minion of Othuum is their inhumanly swollen red eyes. (: "Rising with Surtsey")

The Minions of Othuum have their own servants in the form of sea-dwelling Shoggoths. (: The Burrowers Beneath)

Minions & Monsters is an American animated horror/comedy film directed by Pierre Coffin and produced by Illumination, currently scheduled for release in July 2026. Part of the long-running film series Despicable Me, it serves as a prequel to the 2010 film Despicable Me and a sequel to the 2022 film Minions: The Rise of Gru, as well as being the seventh film in the franchise overall.

Set in the 1920s, the plot involves the Minions trying to find monsters to cast for their monster movie. In the trailer, the Minions perform a ritual in order to summon Cthulhu; however, they end up freeing a smaller and cuter monster instead (known as "Goomi"). Now assisting the Minions, Goomi decides to take them to see the scariest monsters.

The Miri Nigri are mute semi-human dwarves. They are created by Chaugnar Faugn from the flesh of toads. Their normal behaviour is to serve Chaugnar Faugn without question or hesitation, and in silence. They are usually found crawling over the Great Old One's body.

### Description
Created thousands of years ago, when Chaugnar Faugn dwelled in Western Europe along with his brothers, the Miri Nigri are voiceless and mindless, mentally controlled by their creator. As Clark Ulman puts it, "their thoughts [are] the thoughts of Chaugnar".

Twice a year they descend from the hills to abduct young men and women on whose blood their master can feast. (: The Horror from the Hills)

### Behind the Mythos
Although their first appearance was in The Horror from the Hills, by Frank Belknap Long, the Miri Nigri actually originate from a dream of H. P. Lovecraft. While writing The Horror from the Hills, Long incorporated Lovecraft's description of his dream, with Lovecraft's permission, into the story. The same description would later form the basis of the story "The Very Old Folk", although the name "Miri Nigri" wouldn't be used.

Information about this species is also included in Chaosium's role-playing supplement Malleus Monstrorum.

The Mirror Dimension is a fictional dimension in the Evil Dead universe which was later retconned as first appearing in the 1987 movie Evil Dead II, although it was not identified as the Mirror Dimension at that time. Its subsequent comic book appearance (see below) is its true first appearance and where it received its name.

### Background
The Mirror Dimension is where the first Chosen One banished the Dark Ones and Deadites. The spirits of slain demons and Deadites live in this dimension until someone summons them to Earth, alongside the souls of those consumed by the Deadites. It's unknown as to who created the dimension. Entry to the dimension is via a portal created by a spell in the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis, a Deadite swallowing one’s soul, or being pulled into it by a doppelgänger via a reflective surface.

One can leave the dimension by two ways, a teleportation spell cast by a servant of the Dark Ones or if you were pulled in by the doppelganger, by returning to the same spot and switching places. It's implied that the dimension is somewhat sentient. Changing its appearance, using the "swallowed" souls that joined the group consciousness as inspiration. Those who are pulled into the dimension experience death over and over, in varying ways (e.g. melting, falling apart, being consumed / replaced by worms, etc). When a simulacrum of Ash Williams ended up in that dimension, it experienced or witnessed its death a million times.

"Mirror Fishing" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author John Langan.

### Synopsis
When his babysitter teaches young Pat how to commune with the Great Old One Gla'aki through the art of mirror fishing, the boy is at first delighted. However, when he comes to realise what is required of him and the sacrifices he must make - both in his own life and those of others - he realises that he cannot continue. As he escapes the mirror realm, his babysitter is killed, but Pat has already been touched by Gla'aki…

### Characters
*Patrick, a thirteen year old boy with a miserable life.
*Lisa, a pretty nineteen year old girl in service to Gla'aki.

### Publication History
"Mirror Fishing" was published in the Dark Regions Press thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki in 2017.

The Mirror to Wonderland is a fictional item in the Grimm Fairy Tales universe of Zenescope Entertainment which first appeared in 2007 in the 1st issue of the 1st volume of the Return to Wonderland mini series.

It is loosely based on the titular object from Lewis Carroll's 1871 novel Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There.

### Background
The Mirror to Wonderland accidentally absorbed the energies of the portal to Wonderland due to the actions of the scientist Henry Allen. It became a portal to Wonderland, one that was portable and which has been used often. The mirror has been smashed several times but keeps returning. Being near the mirror has at times permitted the forces of Wonderland to influence those on Earth.

Miskatonic is a five issue Cthulhu Mythos comic book written by Mark Sable and illustrated by Giogio Pontrelli. It was published by AfterShock Comics individually before being compiled into a trade paperback. It had a 51-page sequel with the same name.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Miranda Keller is one of the last female investigators for the Bureau of Investigation with J. Edgar Hoover planning to fire the remainder. She is given a final assignment, though, to investigate a series of mysterious bombings happening in the peculiar area of Arkham, Massachusetts. She is reluctantly teamed up with former New York City detective, Thomas Malone, who tries to warn her away from the supernatural goings on in the area.
### Characters 

*Miranda Keller: A beautiful and intelligent detective who is aware she is being forced out of her chosen profession for her sex. She is not a believer in the supernatural and dismisses Thomas Malone as a crude fool. She swiftly becomes enchanted with Asenath Waite even as she becomes drawn in to the mysterious goings on.
*Thomas Malone: The protagonist of "The Horror at Red Hook". Traumatized by his encounters there, he remains both racist as well as sexist. He is strongly attracted to Miranda Keller and annoyed at her interest in Asenath Waite.
*Asenath Waite: The villain of "The Thing on the Doorstep", she is possessed by the spirit of her father and a manipulative psychopath who takes great amusement in seducing Miranda Keller as well as manipulating her investigation. Her ability to summon storms and possess people allow her several advantages.

shortDefinition: "Miskatonic Contradance" is a short story by Greek author Konstantine Paradias. It forms part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by C. J. Henderson.  ### Synopsis Frank Nardi and Nerea Yeboa (who accompanies Nardi by possessing a series of...
fullContent:
"Miskatonic Contradance" is a short story by Greek author Konstantine Paradias. It forms part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by C. J. Henderson.

### Synopsis
Frank Nardi and Nerea Yeboa (who accompanies Nardi by possessing a series of animals and entities) track a young drug addict who has inadvertently stolen an artefact of great power which was hidden in the trunk of Nardi's car. When the addict accidentally activates the device, a terrifying eldritch entity is able to enter our world, and the two must use every trick at their disposal to banish it back to the beyond.

### Characters

*Frank Nardi, New York cop turned Arkham private investigator.
*Nerea Yeboa, a powerful magic user and member of a mysterious British organisation apparently dedicated to the eradication of Mythos influences from Earth.
*Donnie Kiernan, a thief and a junkie.
*Nancy, a deformed prostitute.

### Behind the Mythos
"Miskatonic Contradance" was written by Konstantine Paradias at the request of Brian M. Sammons. It became part of the Arkham Detective Agency series of short Mythos stories begun by C. J. Henderson, and was published in the 2017 collection Arkham Detective Agency by Dark Regions Press.

### Mythos Connections

*The story is set in Lovecraft's legendary town of Arkham.
*Nerea makes reference to a colleague of hers consulting the Pnakotic Manuscripts.
*Whilst not explicitly stated, the entity encountered by Nardi and Nerea is heavily implied to be the Outer God Azathoth, with Nerea referring to it as the "idiot, all-knowing Sultan at the center of all things."
*The memory of Tommy Malone (the protagonist of Lovecraft's short story "The Horror at Red Hook") flashes through Nardi's mind when Nerea attempts to possess his body.

Miskatonic High is an ongoing comic book series set in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos begun with the works of H. P. Lovecraft. Written by Mike Shea and illustrated by Ryan Mendoza, the first issue made its debut in November 2021; as of February 2024, the series comprised 17 issues, one collection, and a single one-shot spin-off/prequel.

### Premise
The main story follows five Miskatonic High students, Sarah, Alex, Ren, Simon, and Matt, who work together in the same school-run community outreach program. Their various activities bring them into contact with various supernatural and Cthulhu Mythos forces, including Abdul Alhazred, Deep Ones, and demonic Aswang. They also visit locations as exotic and far-flung as Ancient Egypt, the Dreamlands, and Innsmouth,

fullContent:
Miskatonic High: The City of Silence is the first issue in the Miskatonic High series of young adult comic books. Written by Mike Shea and featuring cover art by Ryan Mendoza, it was published by Danger Dads in November 2021; it was released solely in a digital format.

### Synopsis
Five Miskatonic High students attend to some chores for an elderly local woman while volunteering at a school-run community outreach program. In her basement, they are magically transported to ancient Egypt, where they encounter the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred, who is attempting to summon the Elder One Kalib Nargul using the fabled Al Azif. With the help of a talking cat, the group employ the magic contained within the book and are able to defeat the crazed sorcerer and his demonic minion, before returning themselves to their natural place in space and time.

### Trivia
*Although never explicitly named in the story, the crazed sorcerer encountered by the gang is revealed to be Abdul Alhazred in the accompanying production notes.

The Miskatonic Horror Deluxe Expansion is a big-box expansion pack for Fantasy Flight Games' board game of Lovecraftian adventure, Arkham Horror.

### Overview
As the eighth and final expansion set for Arkham Horror, Miskatonic Horror saw a departure from the design of previous add-ons; instead of introducing a new scenario for Investigators to play through, it functioned as an expansion for the previous expansions. To this effect it was comprised of cards and other elements which added to the scope of the earlier expansions, rather than itself providing much in the way of new ways to play.

Despite this, Miskatonic Horror did contain rules and components to add a new mechanic to the base game: Institutions. These represent organisations of individuals who offer the players their patronage for a price, reportedly making Arkham Horror marginally easier to complete.

fullContent:
Miskatonic Repository is a player-driven resource initiative for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, created in partnership between Chaosium and DriveThruRPG. In essence, it allows creators to offer free or for-sale their own resources for the game with the parent company's blessing, in exchange for a percentage of any profits.

### Overview


The Miskatonic Repository offers enthusiasts, and even seasoned games designers, the opportunity to create resources for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game without the worry of securing any licensing involved in self-publishing, with Chaosium essentially offering a limited license to content creators with the stipulation that they follow a specific set of guidelines. For any content which is sold through DriveThruRPG, 50% is payable to the creator, with the other 50% divided between Chaosium and DriveThruRPG.

As part of the service, templates, artwork, background, and various other resources are provided for the creation of spells, non-player characters, in-game organisations, handouts, maps, scenarios, sourcebooks, and anything else one might think useful for a Call of Cthulhu game.

The Miskatonic River is a fictional river in Massachusetts, created by H. P. Lovecraft. It links two of the most important settings in Lovecraft Country--Arkham and Dunwich--and is the source of the name of Miskatonic University.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The first allusion to the Miskatonic River in H. P. Lovecraft's fiction occurs in "The Picture in the House", written in 1920, when the narrator says, "I had been travelling for some time amongst the people of the Miskatonic Valley in quest of certain genealogical data."

The river itself probably appears for the first time in 1926's "The Silver Key", which says of protagonist Randolph Carter:
The river also shows up in  "The Strange High House in the Mist", written in November 1926, where it serves to establish that the titular house exists in the same setting as Arkham and Kingsport from "The Festival". "[N]orth of archaic Kingsport," the story notes, there is "a bleak point jutting in limitless space, for there the coast turns sharp where the great Miskatonic pours out of the plains past Arkham, bringing woodland legends and little quaint memories of New England’s hills." Later the character Thomas Olney reasons that the house "must be tenanted by people who reached it from inland along the easier ridge beside the Miskatonic’s estuary."

The river plays a similar connective role in 1928's "The Dunwich Horror", linking Arkham to the newly introduced Dunwich: "The thin, shining line of the Miskatonic’s upper reaches has an oddly serpent-like suggestion as it winds close to the feet of the domed hills among which it rises."

The river makes its final appearance in Lovecraft in "Dreams in the Witch-House", written in 1932, where it is the location of an ominous island in Arkham visited by Walter Gilman: "He also rowed out twice to the ill-regarded island in the river, and made a sketch of the singular angles described by the moss-grown rows of grey standing stones whose origin was so obscure and immemorial."

Miskatonic University is a fictional university located in Arkham, named after the Miskatonic River which flows through the town. The school appears in numerous Cthulhu Mythos stories by Lovecraft and many other writers.

Lovecraft depicted Miskatonic University as a highly prestigious university, on par with Harvard University; in fact, at least in the 1920s, Harvard and Miskatonic are the two most popular schools for the children of the Massachusetts “Old Gentry”. (: "The Dunwich Horror")

### Etymology
Lovecraft has declared that the word was "a jumble of Algonquin language roots." (: The Lovecraft Lexicon)

### Origins
Miskatonic University is modeled on northeastern Ivy League institutions of Lovecraft's day, such as Harvard University, Yale University, and Dartmouth, and especially Brown University in his hometown of Providence, Rhode Island, which Lovecraft himself wished to attend.

### Campus
Depictions differ as to whether mystical and Mythos studies at the University are covert or overt. In early works by Lovecraft and others, Miskatonic is an apparently ordinary university whose occult undercurrent only occasionally breaks the surface. Some students practice black magic, and have unusual classes, such as Medieval Metaphysics (: "The Thing on the Doorstep", : "The Abyss"). Later works tend towards portraying these strange elements as being openly displayed and an integral part of the campus' cultural identity.

### Facilities
*Medical School: the University boasts a medical school (: Herbert West--Reanimator).
*Miskatonic Museum: located on the University campus, holds a piece of jewelry implied to be a creation of the Deep Ones (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth).
*The Orne Library: Miskatonic University is famous for its collection of Cthulhu Mythos arcane literature and occult books. The library holds one of the very few genuine copies of the Necronomicon. Other tomes include the Unaussprechlichen Kulten by Friedrich von Junzt and the fragmentary Book of Eibon.

### Faculty and Student Body


### Notable students
The university's student body is implied to have been predominantly male throughout the early 20th century, and the only female student mentioned is the infamous Asenath Waite. (: "The Thing on the Doorstep")

Walter Gilman attends classes at the university. (: "The Dreams in the Witch-House")

Miskatonic University: Elder Gods 101 is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author and editor Matthew Davenport, and his brother Michael Davenport. It is tied to Matthew's Andrew Doran series but with a new cast and set during the present day. It is a lighter and softer series closer to Buffy the Vampire Slayer than traditional horror. It was published in August 15, 2022 by Crossroad Press.

### Synopsis
It is a new school year at Miskatonic University, Massachusetts and the barriers between reality are breaking down. Deciding the only way to protect themselves is to use the Scion Cycle, a powerful spell that draws individuals related to the supernatural, the staff of Miskatonic University summon a fresh crop of students that are all tied to the most famous characters of HP Lovecraft's writing. But can they save the world against the individuals who want to destroy it? Or are they more interested in their own concerns like not failing and romance?

### Characters
*Ralph Allen - A Deep One hybrid from a rebuilt Innsmouth who just wants to play football and not have to marry as his parents wants him to. This is due to being gay and it not fitting in with the Deep One's religion.
*Carlos Davies - The most seemingly "normal" of the students and friendliest, Carlos is cursed with visions of the future. He also possesses an ability to read people and know facts no one else can figure out.
*Meredith Johnson - An archaeology student with an interest in the occult due to her family's long association with its dangers. She is a descendant of one of the sailors from Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu".
*Sheryl Mason - A computer science major who loves gaming and is a mathematics prodigy. Unfortunately, she hates math and it is the gateway to nearly unimaginable power in the Mythos. A descendant of Keziah Mason.
*Stephanie West - A veterinary science student who has a particularly infamous ancestor that causes no end of problems for her in Miskatonic University. She also discovers the joys of necromancy herself.

### Trivia 
*Sheryl Mason and Meredith Johnson make a guest appearance in "Academic Legacies" by C. T. Phipps in Time Loopers.

fullContent:
Miskatonic University: The Restricted Collection is a Cthulhu Mythos competitive card game created by prolific German designer Reiner Knizia and published by Chaosium in 2019.

### Overview
The game involves 2-5 players taking on the role of different faculty members and attempting to gather occult knowledge for Dr. Henry Armitage from Miskatonic University's restricted archives. To represent this, the players must collect card sets to score points, while avoiding collecting duplicates. The player with the highest score after 5 rounds is declared the winner.

### Behind the Mythos
To fit with the theme of mystical grimoires and the university library, the box is designed to look like an occult volume; opening the front cover reveals the storage area for all playing pieces.

Misquamacus, also known as Quamis, is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth for their novel The Lurker at the Threshold. While most "posthumous collaborations" credited to Lovecraft and Derleth were entirely written by Derleth, Misquamacus--a Native American leader with great supernatural powers--appeared in a fragment written by Lovecraft and incorporated into a larger narrative by Derleth. The character has since gone on to appear in works by other creators, notably a series of horror novels by the writer Graham Masterton. 

### The Lurker at the Threshold
One of the few fragments Lovecraft wrote that he never worked into a finished story was a simulated excerpt from a fictional Colonial-era book called Of Evill Sorceries Done in New-England of Daemons in No Humane Shape. It introduces Misquamacus, who is variously described as an "antient Wonder-Worker," an "antient Wizard," a  "Wampanaug wise Man," and "head man" of "a Band of Wampanaug Savages." (The Wampanoag are a real-world Indigenous nation that lived somewhat to the south of Lovecraft Country, from what is now the town of Weymouth, Massachusetts, through Cape Cod and to the islands of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard.) Misquamacus lived "when Mr. Bradford was governor"--meaning William Bradford, who was governor of Plymouth Colony off and on from  1621 until his death in 1657.

In the fragment, Misquamacus is the teacher from whom the colonial wizard Richard Billington "had learnt some of his Sorceries." Later Misquamacus tells Governor Bradford that "Billington had done worse Evill than cou'd be well repair'd, and he was no doubt ear up by what he had call'd out of ye Sky."  This is Ossadagowah, a spawn of Tsathoggua, Though unable to dispel Ossadagowah, Misquamacus had managed to imprison it in a ring of standing stones near New Dunnich, i.e. Dunwich. 

In the novel that Derleth expanded from this and a couple of other short fragments, Misquamacus reappears under the name Quamis or Quamas, who is identified as a member of the Narragansett nation. (This is even further afield than the Wampanoag, as the Narragansett are the Indigenous people of Rhode Island.) As Quamis, the character plays a more subservient role--presumably because he was raised from the dead by Billington's descendant Alijah Billington, and the ritual of resurrection sometimes gives the necromancer some power over those they raise. (See The Case of Charles Dexter Ward.) 

In scenes that take place in the late 18th or early 19th century, Quamis acts as a servant to Alijah and a guardian of Alijah's son Laban. In a diary, Laban notes that when he and Quamis visit Arkham, the two are "treated with great respect and marked fear," and Quamis is "not troubled as the Indians sometimes are in the streets of towns."

The Mist Projector is a fictional artefact in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was created by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu RPG. It is described as capable of generating freezing mist. (: Call of Cthulhu RPG Keeper Rulebook 5th edition)

### Description
The Mist Projector was created by the Mi-Go. It is a cluster of twisted metal tubes that, when turned on, slowly disperses a cone of icy mist about ten feet across. The mist is described as thick and intensely cold, so much that even running automobile engines can be frozen upon long exposure. When fully charged, it can disperse the mist twenty times before stopping. (: Call of Cthulhu RPG Keeper Rulebook 5th edition)

### History
The Mist Projector was used by the Mi-Go in the war against the Elder Things on Earth millennia ago. It proved to be particularly effective. (: Eldritch Horror)

Mister Misery is an eldritch abomination from the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics.

### Background
Mister Misery (aka, the Thing in the Cellar) is a magical being that was created by Doctor Stephen Strange. Into the being he deposited all of the pain and suffering caused by his use of magic. They kept it within the basement of his mansion in Manhattan, NY City. During the Empirikul's assault on Earth in their attempt to purge the world of magic, his mansion was razed. 

Mister Misery and Doctor Strange temporarily joined forces and defeated their common enemy, the leader of the Empirikul, Imperator. Freed of Doctor Strange's suffering, to its dismay it didn't experience joy only feelings of nothingness. To feed off the suffering of others, it terrorized citizens and during its confrontation with Doctor Strange, it revealed the name it had taken for itself, Mister Misery.

Mister Ys is a fictional character in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Shadow Out of Time (1936), as the alien entity who transfers minds with  Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee, but appears without a name. He is given the name Ys in Peter Rawlik's novel The Weird Company (2014), and plays a significant role in Rawlik's Mythos stories involving the Peaslee family.

### Overview
Mister Ys is a member of the Great Race of Yith, a species of time- and space-travelling aliens who are capable of inhabiting the bodies of other beings in their quest to view major events from the entirety of the universe's history.

In Mister Ys's case, he appears to be capable of travelling through alternate realities as well, as he appears to have witnessed at least two separate fates of the human race. In one, he and thousands of other Yithians observe the outbreak of a zombie invasion, having made provisions which may allow a select few humans--including Pandora Peaslee--to survive the collapse of civilisation (: "Time Flies"). In another, Mister Ys and the Yithians have taken over the Earth and work with human collaborators in keeping the population under their thumb; in this reality, a resistance movement learns to control the zombie hordes and employs them as an ad-hoc army. Here, mister Ys's human body was destroyed, although whether he was able to relocate his consciousness beforehand is uncertain (: "The Pestilence of Pandora Peaslee").

Mister Ys inhabited the body of Titus Sempronius Blaesus in Ancient Rome, playing the part of the Cigarette Smoking Man in an historical homage to The X-Files (: "Tempus Edax Rerum").

The Mites of Yuggoth are a fictional species created for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game supplement The Bermuda Triangle. They are closely related to the Mi-Go.

### Description
The Mites of Yuggoth are descended from the Mi-Go, an intelligent race of half-fungoid, half-crustacean creatures from the planet Yuggoth. Compared to their ancestors, however, the Mites are much smaller, being about the size of a mouse, and have completely lost their ability to fly. They have also evolved the ability to consume Earth food, something which their ancestors lacked.

The Mites inhabit the area of the Atlantic known as the Sargasso Sea, living in and feeding upon the vast nets of floating sargassum weed. They can swarm in large numbers and devour animals that get entangled in the sargassum. Like their Mi-Go brethren, the Mites hide from the light, change colours to communicate with each other, are invisible to cameras (i.e. they can't be photographed), and their bodies dissolve upon death.

According to legends told by sailors, the Mites of Yuggoth are also capable of swarming over entire ships and devouring everyone on board. It's been suggested that this might be the explanation for the mysterious disappearance of the crew and passengers of the Mary Celeste. (: The Bermuda Triangle)

fullContent:
Mlandoth is a primal entity or force, not dissimilar to the Nameless Mist or Darkness, although it is uncertain if it is a place, conscious being, or an inconceivable maelstrom of unknown forces and properties outside the perceptible cosmos. It is mentioned in Uralte Schrecken as a kind of prime archetype from which all mythical god-heads are derived. It is paired with the equally primordial Mril Thorion.

According to the cycle surrounding these beings, they are a sort of cosmic yin and yang, whose meeting resulted in the creation of all things (although Azathoth is usually attributed to this). Their joinings routinely create and destroy matter and entities. One of the beings created in this way was the inimical Outer God Ngyr-Khorath.

### Behind the Mythos
Mlandoth and Mril Thorion were created by Walter C. DeBill Jr., but were suggested years earlier by Clark Ashton Smith.

shortDefinition: The Mlandoth cycle is a parallel legend to the "Cthulhu cycle". It is the invention of Walter C. DeBill Jr. and, instead of relying heavily on the literary creations of H. P. Lovecraft or his followers, DeBill's stories utilize an entirely new panthe...
fullContent:
The Mlandoth cycle is a parallel legend to the "Cthulhu cycle". It is the invention of Walter C. DeBill Jr. and, instead of relying heavily on the literary creations of H. P. Lovecraft or his followers, DeBill's stories utilize an entirely new pantheon, literary milieu, and different forbidden books.

The cycle gets its name from the creator deity, Mlandoth. Other important deities are Ngyr-Khorath, its avatar or "extension" 'Ymnar, the "nuclear force-creature" Paighon, and the fertility goddess Yidhra. (: "Where Yidhra Walks", Walter C. DeBill, 1976)

The cycle is described in various sources such as the incredibly ancient The Chronicles of Thrang, The Texts of Mloeng and the more recent Uralte Schrecken. (: "Ngyr-Khorath", Walter C. DeBill, 1973 / "The Barrett Horror", 2006)

Mnar is a fictional prehistoric land in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Doom That Came to Sarnath".

### Overview
Mnar is the land where the doomed city of Sarnath was located.

The River Ai runs through the territory. Successive waves of inhabitants have come and gone over its long history.

Originally inhabited by the amphibious Thuum'ha who constructed the city of Ib, these creatures were displaced and then rendered extinct in a deliberate genocide by a race of humans who followed the River Ai into the region. These humans built Sarnath on top of the location of Ib.

### Behind the Mythos
Mnar is often treated as though it is part of the Dreamlands but close reading of the texts does not confirm this. It certainly is ancient, and may have been part of Earth's forgotten prehistory.

The Mnggal-Mnggal is a fictional entity created by Daniel Wallace for Lucasfilm's Star Wars Expanded Universe role-playing game supplement The Unknown Regions. A terrifying and mysterious entity known throughout the Unknown Regions, it was a sentient, shape-shifting organism that was essentially a viral infection, capable of taking over and controlling the bodies of those it infected. This creature existed as a collective consciousness, meaning that every part of it was connected and shared the same mind. The Mnggal-Mnggal's essence was spread across the galaxy, and it could take control of any being that comes into contact with it.

### Description
Mnggal-Mnggal desired nothing more than control, and subsequently sought to spread its body and influence over as many worlds as possible. If possible, it would destroy entire planets as it had with Mugg Fallow, but the idle amusement of torturing and killing other sentients was entertaining as well.

Mnggal-Mnggal delighted in torturing and consuming other beings; indeed, it seemed to thrive more on beings' suffering than on the sustenance their bodies provided. Using its possession abilities, it would create torturous scenarios such as reuniting a grieving mother with the reanimated corpse of their youngling time and time again. It would persuade other beings by playing with their emotions into making deadly decisions such as opening a ship's airlocks or deactivating perimeter fences.

When conversing in its natural form, Mnggal-Mnggal spoke in dreamlike observations, often in verse, metaphors, and riddles. Due to its long life, it also spoke ancient languages and conversed in long-forgotten conventions of speech. Though it told tales of the Celestials, Rakata, and the dawn of the Jedi Order, and seemed to know the current plots of galactic rulers, the locations of lost treasures, and the answers to age-old mysteries, some believed that every word it spoke was a lie.

### Characteristics and Abilities

*Hive Mind: The Mnggal-Mnggal operated with a collective intelligence, meaning all parts of it were aware of the actions and thoughts of any other part.
*Infection and Control: It could infect living beings by taking over their bodies, essentially turning them into zombie-like creatures under its control. Once infected, the original being's consciousness was typically suppressed or destroyed.
*Shapeshifting: It had the ability to take on various forms, depending on the hosts it controlled. This could range from humanoid shapes to more monstrous, grotesque forms.
*Assimilation: It could assimilate other life forms, absorbing their knowledge and experiences into its collective mind.
*Persistence: Mnggal-Mnggal was incredibly difficult to destroy, as it existed across multiple locations at once. Destroying one part of it would not eradicate the whole entity.

Mnomquah is a fictional entity created by the American author Lin Carter for his short story "Something in the Moonlight".

### Description
Mnomquah is a great reptilian creature with a crown of writhing feelers and empty sockets in place of eyes, although somehow it is still able to see. It is trapped inside the Dreamlands' moon, though how it became stuck there is unknown. In Brian Lumley's version of the expanded Cthulhu Mythos, it is the mate of the disgusting Oorn, and when the Great Old Ones awaken to lay waste to our world, then Mnomquah will be reunited with its repulsive bride.

It is called the Lord of the Black Lake because it rules over the Lake of Ubboth, a great body of water which rests beneath the surface of the moon.

Modiphius Entertainment is a U.K.-based traditional games manufacturer who publish a wide range of material for a host of different franchises, with one of their flagship ranges being a highly-popular series of Cthulhu Mythos tabletop games.

### Overview
Founded in 2012/2013  by husband and wife Chris and Rita Birch for the purpose of publishing the first Achtung! Cthulhu supplement for Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game and Pinnacle Entertainment's generic Savage Worlds system , a successful Kickstarter campaign allowed Modiphius to continue with the series and, eventually, to branch out. In 2023, the company cut ties with Chaosium and Pinnacle's properties, reissuing Achtung! Cthulhu as a stand-alone roleplaying game using their in-house 2D20 rules system. They have also published a Roman-era roleplaying game, Cohors Cthulhu, along with tie-in tabletop wargames for both Mythos properties, and even a related video game.

Since these humble beginnings, they have published large amounts of original material and franchise tie-in expansions, including games for such global properties as Dune, Fallout, John Carter, Star Trek, The Elder Scrolls, Airfix, Mass Effect, Thunderbirds, Conan the Barbarian, and Kung-Fu Panda.

More recently, Modiphius have acted as a distributor for Black Cats Gaming's Cursed Captains of Cthulhu roleplaying game, offering digital downloads of the works through their website. Black Cats, an indie games publisher, was founded by two former Modiphius employees.

The Moit of Shub-Niggurath are a fictional race created by Paizo Inc in 2011 for their Pathfinder roleplaying game.

### Background
The Moit of Shub-Niggurath are spawn of the Outer God, Shub-Niggurath. Which start out as "Slugspawn", bloated mucus covered slugs which are as long as a man's forearm. As they are vulnerable to large predators they hide in shadow crevices or dark pools, waiting for the pliant brains and warm flesh that they need. Upon infesting a living body, they borrow toward the skull and wrapped themselves around the lower brain. Where they feed and grow on the energies generated by thought. Though a slugspawn can be killed or removed, the longer it's in the host the more damage to the victim and if not removed soon from the host, the host's life becomes linked to that of the slugspawn. Within 2-12 days, a humanoid host matures into a "Spawning Canker". The slugspawn devours the host's brain and takes over the beheaded body, becoming a spawning canker.

Spawning Cankers are fanatically obsessed with propagating the species. They avoid competing with each other, but if there aren't enough resources, each Canker will attempt to make sure that it's the one that can spawn. If a region experiences an infectious invasion of moits, each Canker becomes increasingly desperate as the number of hosts diminish. Spawning Cankers are as tall as the body they infest plus an additional 2-3 ft of added height due to the wildly whipping tentacles where the head used to be. Inside the body's chest cavity is a squirming heart-like body that is a mass of fetal features with spiny tendrils which have spread throughout the host, controlling its limbs and organs. They give the host superhuman strength and speed, and the ones that extend from outside act as both its feeding tubes and sensory organs. After it has gorged itself, the limbs split and tear from the host as slugspawn. Approximately one percent of the cankers become Dark Young.

Mollie L. Burleson (née Werba) is an American author and poet who has written both prose and non-fiction pieces related to H. P. Lovecraft's works and the greater Cthulhu Mythos. These have appeared in collections such as the anthologies Black Wings: New Tales of Lovecraftian Horror, Black Wings III, Black Wings V: New Tales of Lovecraftian Horror, Gothic Lovecraft, and Return to Lovecraft Country, as well as the periodicals Lovecraft Studies, The Arkham Sampler, Midnight Shambler, and Crypt of Cthulhu.

Burleson is married to author Donald R. Burleson, another prolific Mythos contributor. The two met at a Providence, Rhode Island horror convention in 1979, and were long-term members of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft scholars and enthusiasts active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s.

"Momma Durtt" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
A highly-skilled mob killer uses those he kills as sacrifices to awaken the youngest of the Great Old Ones, a tarry abomination which sleeps in an abandoned mine beneath the mountains of California, in an effort to gain a portion of its power. He is successful, and the creature accepts his offerings but demands that he bring it more...

### Characters
*Sol Lazarian, an underworld enforcer for a powerful mafia family.
*Kimberly Haas, a young but jaded truck driver unwittingly in the employ of the mob.
*Alex, Kimberley's friend.
*Chip, caretaker of the mine, also working for the mob.
*Lou Bonifacio, Lazarian's former East Coast Capo.
*Junior Lee, a mob footsoldier.
*Sonny Beasely, another mob footsoldier.
*Momma Durtt, a Great Old One.
