fullContent:
The Mondrago family is a bloodline created by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. for their Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Overview
Secret worshipper of the insect-god Ghattambah, the Mondragos have been cultists of the Hungry One for untold centuries, their earliest known involvement with it being the early 1400s. In the modern age the - extremely wealthy - family maintain a chapel to Ghattambah in their expansive mansion.

The Mondragos are known for producing an uncommonly high number of successful writers.

### Known Members
*Adrian, a Belgian warlock and author of the 1417 book The Seven Blasphemies of Ghattambah.
*Azmael, the High Priest of Ghattambah and one-time associate of Cotton Mather. He was the author of one of the cult of Ghattambah's bibles, Wyck'd Secrets Of The Infernal Beaste Ghattambah and was likely responsible for a number of child disappearances which occurred around 1700. His current incarnation is as a swarm of insects which may be summoned through the use of a piece of decayed wood kept in Ghattambah's chapel.
*Jupiter, the current patriarch of the Mondrago family, an ancient man with a wildly successful career as an author already under his belt.
*Lydia, one of the current curators of the chapel of Ghattambah.
*Booth "Boo-Boo", Lydia's brother and co-curator.

shortDefinition: "Mongoose" is a short story by Elizabeth Bear and Sarah Monette, part of their Boojumverse setting that combines elements of the Cthulhu Mythos and creatures from Lewis Carroll in a space opera setting. The story first appeared in the anthology Lovec...
fullContent:
"Mongoose" is a short story by Elizabeth Bear and Sarah Monette, part of their Boojumverse setting that combines elements of the Cthulhu Mythos and creatures from Lewis Carroll in a space opera setting. The story first appeared in the anthology Lovecraft Unbound (Dark Horse Books, 2009).

"Mongoose" centers on the relationship between Izrael Irizarry, an exterminator of interdimensional vermin, and Mongoose, an alien creature with whom he has a symbiotic bond; the two are hired to deal with an infestation on a space station, and soon find that they may be over their heads.

### Bestiary
### Cheshires
Small, predatory alien creatures, adapted for vacuum, with the ability to phase between dimensions. They form intensely close bonds with human partners; they are deaf, but can sense and understand speech when in physical contact. They change the colors of their skin for communication and self-decoration--though flat representations mean nothing to them. 

They have wedge-shaped heads on extensible necks, four compound and twelve simple eyes. They have catfish-like barbels and flick their tongues out to taste the air. Their teeth are a "needle-sharp crystalline array".

Cheshires are bred by Arkhamers, a spacefaring culture of knowledge-seekers whom outsiders view with suspicion. There is a theory that cheshires are sub-adult bandersnatches (see below)--“trained and bred and intentionally stunted so that they never mature fully”--though the main cheshire in the story firmly rejects this theory.

The name "cheshire" comes from Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. A cheshire can, like their namesake, disappear slowly, with its grin the last thing visible--but it will likely only do so if they've had Lewis Carroll read to them.

### Toves
Interdimensional vermin with sluglike, segmented bodies, a little short of a meter long. They often attach themselves to ceilings with a foul-smelling secretion; a tove infestation can be identified by their "sharp stink...ammoniac and bitter." They hunt by dangling glowing, sticky lure-tongues, half a meter long, which they use to catch prey which they then attack with "flesh-ripping pincers".

Despite this, toves are less a threat than a nuisance, "with their tendency to use up valuable oxygen, clog ductwork, eat pets, drip goo from ceilings, and crunch wetly when you stepped on them." They are lazy creatures--or "energy efficient"--"never crawl[ing] farther than was necessary to find a useable anchoring point." Their real danger is that they weaken the barriers between dimensions, attracting raths, their natural predators--and worse things.

The name "tove" comes from the "Jabberwocky" poem from Carroll's Through the Looking-Glass. Humpty Dumpty explains to Alice in that book that toves are "something like badgers——they're something like lizards——and they're something like corkscrews."

Monk's Hollow is a fictional village invented by Henry Kuttner, the setting of his stories "The Frog" and "The Hunt."

In "The Frog," it's described as a "quiet, lonely little village" that is "hidden in a secluded valley in the eastern hills." Its exact location is not specified, but it may not be far from New York City, as an artist moves from there to Monk's Hollow to get privacy for his painting. It has a history of witchcraft, which suggests somewhere in New England.

Points of interest include the Witch Stone, the North Swamp, and the Wizard's House.

The Witch Stone, in "The Frog," is  "a roughly chiseled block of gray stone, perhaps three feet high and two feet square, which stood in the flower garden behind" an  ancient, gambreled house...two miles from the village." It served to imprison the frog-thing Persis Winthorp until it was moved by artist Norman Hartley.

The North Swamp, also in "The Frog,"  is a "festering" place "shunned by the villagers" where "witches had worked detestable sorceries."

The Wizard's House, appearing in "The Hunt," is a cabin in "a little canyon two miles from the village of Monk’s Hollow." It is the home of the occultist Will Benson.

fullContent:
Monster Parade was an American horror magazine issued by Irwin Stein’s Magnum Publications. It was only published in 1958 and 1959. It was intended to cash in on the success of Warren’s Famous Monsters of Filmland, however its mix of original horror fiction and reprints of pre-code horror comics, articles, pin-ups and movie coverage didn’t succeed with fans and it ran for just four issues. Issue 4 featured a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Robert Silverberg, "Demons of Cthulhu".

fullContent:
Monster Strike is a Japanese mobile game released by Mixi in August 2013. The game was created by Yoshiki Okamoto, who had previously worked for Capcom. The gameplay incorporates elements from the role-playing, puzzle, physics and strategy genres, centered around collecting monsters and using catapult mechanics to battle others. The game was later released for the Nintendo 3DS in December 2015, as a more traditional role-playing video game. An anime adaptation was also released in 2015, followed by three animated films.

As of 2019, the game grossed a total revenue of over $8.13 billion, making it the highest-grossing mobile app of all time.

Cthulhu first appeared in the 2nd Anniversary Dream Sharl Event. The game would later introduce the Battle of Carcosa series, featuring other familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos.

The Monstrosity is a fictional demon in the prime reality of the Marvel universe of Marvel Comics, created in 1993 by Chris Cooper, first appearing in issue #13 of the 1st volume of Darkhold: Pages from the Book of Sins.

### Background
The Monstrosity is a demon released by the Darkhold, which the press called "Monstrosity". It possessed superhuman strength, durability, and speed. Able to easily life a tall muscular man with both hands above its head and throw him. Its claws could easily tear human flesh and bone, and rip through a car's roof. The demon siphoned the lifeforce of humans via its mouth, killing them. Usually it left a shriveled corpse. 

For every lifeforce that it consumed it gave the one who used the Darkhold page the lifeforce to heal another being. Victoria Montesi for a short period was able to heal her hospitalized lover because she used one of the pages of the Darkhold, not realizing that it released a demon which was killing and stealing their lifeforce for her use. Many were killed before she discovered the truth and rejected the Darkhold.

The Moon-beasts are a fictional species in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, and were later incorperated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Background
The Moon-beasts are pale, squat toad-like creatures living in the Dreamlands' version of Earth's moon, active in the trade of human slaves and gold (in exchange for their rubies) in the port of Dylath-Leen, on Earth's Dreamlands.

They are superhumanly strong and noxious-smelling, having no eyes but instead a mass of pink tentacles at the end of their snout. They are described as sailing Black Galleys between the Moon and the Dreamlands to trade rubies in exchange for slaves and gold in the port of Dylath-Leen, employing Men of Leng disguised in turbans, as to not reveal their true nature. They communicate using flutes, at least to their servants, being otherwise silent even in death. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

### In Other Media
*The Moon-beasts appear in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
*The Moon-beasts appear in the mobile game Card Monsters.
*In the comic book Moon Girl and Devil Dinosaur Vol 1 41 by Marvel Comics, several unnamed creatures resembling the Moon-beasts were depicted as a cameo in Nightmare's Dream Dimension; however, they are never explicitly referenced.

Mordiggian is a fictional deity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his Zothique story "The Charnel God". The entity was later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos as a Great Old One by Scott D. Aniolowski in his Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

Described as swirling darkness, a gigantic shadow, or a worm-shaped column, Mordiggian is worshipped by several human cults and cults of ghouls as a symbol of Death. His name is used in Zothique, Man's last continent, and it is possible that this gigantic creature is the same as Shaurash-Ho or even identical to Cynothoglys. The name may also find its origins in medieval France, being a corruption of the Latin "Mortician" (to do with the dead). There is also at least some faint echo of the Celtic death goddess The Morrigan in the name, especially since one of her epithets was The Crow That Feasts On The Battlefield. 

Mordiggian also seems to be the main subject of The Ghoul's Manuscript and Cultes des Goules. 

In the far future time in which Zothique stories take place, the ghoul-like Ghorii most likely worship Mordiggian as their ghoul-god.(source?)

shortDefinition: "More Light" is a short story by noted science fiction author James Blish, first published in the Anne McCaffrey-edited anthology Alchemy and Academe in November 1970. It is as much a commentary on cosmic horror and fear of the unknown as it is a "st...
fullContent:
"More Light" is a short story by noted science fiction author James Blish, first published in the Anne McCaffrey-edited anthology Alchemy and Academe in November 1970. It is as much a commentary on cosmic horror and fear of the unknown as it is a "straight" Mythos short story.

### Synopsis
The story focuses on the narrator meeting a man who claims to have a copy of the complete King in Yellow play. Reading it is vaguely disappointing due to its pedestrian nature, however what the narrator is struck by is the stipulation by the play's author that almost all the cast of the play should be people of color. The narrator's strong suspicion is that the man who claims to have found this manuscript is in fact its author rather than Robert W. Chambers, the author of the original King in Yellow book.

### Publication History
"More Light" originally appeared in the anthology Alchemy and Academe published in November 1970 and reappeared in The Hastur Cycle, published by Chaosium many years later.

The Morlocks are a fictional species created by H. G. Wells for his classic science fiction novel The Time Machine.

### Overview
The Morlocks are one of the two species descended from humans which the Time Traveler encountered in the year 802,701 AD, the other being the childlike Eloi. While the Eloi live on the surface, the Morlocks have adapted themselves to a subterranean existence. Their bodies are dull-white in color, with abnormally large eyes that are sensitive to bright lights, as well as long flaxen hair covering their heads and backs. Their faces are pale and chinless, and their hands have lanky digits. They appear to be facultative bipeds and are also adept at climbing rocks like a spider. Their diet is carnivorous. The Morlocks feed and clothe the Eloi and tend to their needs, basically raising the Eloi like cattle so that the Morlocks can feed on them. (: The Time Machine)

### In Other Media
In The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen universe by Alan Moore and Kevin O'Neill, the Morlocks are identified as the same species that is also known as the Mi-Go, or the Abominable Snowmen. They can be found in several time periods, not just the distant future, and act as a servitor race of the Great Old Ones from Yuggoth, helping them in their plans to invade our universe. (: "Allan and the Sundered Veil")

### Behind the Mythos
The Morlocks, as depicted in the original novel by Wells, are similar to other subterranean, carnivorous, human-derived anthropoids featured in the works of H. P. Lovecraft, such as in "The Beast in the Cave", "The Lurking Fear", and "The Rats in the Walls".

shortDefinition: Mormo is a shapeshifting female entity known for having three forms: The first form, is a mocking vampire-like maiden who may or may not be wearing Victorian Era style clothing; Second, a gorgon-like creature with tentacles for hair instead of snakes...
fullContent:
Mormo is a shapeshifting female entity known for having three forms: The first form, is a mocking vampire-like maiden who may or may not be wearing Victorian Era style clothing; Second, a gorgon-like creature with tentacles for hair instead of snakes; And lastly, a large toad-like creature with tentacles for a face, akin to her servitors the Moon-beasts.

In the story The Horror At Red Hook, H. P. Lovecraft directly connected Mormo to Lilith. He referenced Hippolytus, but put a more sinister twist upon the worship of Mormo.


In the story "Hydra", Henry Kuttner equates Gorgo, Mormo, the Thousand-Faced Moon and the Magna Mater with Hydra.

In the Trail of Cthulhu roleplaying game, Kenneth Hite says Mormo is Diana, Mab, Lamia, Lilith, Medusa, The Moon, and/or several other Gods, Titans, and Great Old Ones. He links her to vampires, werewolves, and dogs, and says she's an enemy of Bast. As with all of Hite's write-ups of Gods and Titans in that book, the Keeper (GM) is encouraged to decide which of the contradictory elements are true and which are mere myth or misunderstanding.

### Trivia

*In Ancient Greek mythology, Gorgo and Mormo, along with Stheno, are given as names for the Gorgons, of whose form the originally very beautiful Medusa is given the likeness as a curse.

Mother Hydra is a fictional deity created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novel The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Background
Mother Hydra is a creature who, alongside her consort Father Dagon, is said to rule over the race known as the Deep Ones. There is debate as to whether or not they are lesser Great Old Ones or mere grotesquely mutated Deep Ones - though the latter seems more likely as they do not seem to show much in the way of supernatural power outside of their gigantic size and unnaturally long life span. Therefore although considered deities, they are not classified as Great Old Ones.

In the Xothic Legend Cycle, Dagon and Hydra are classified as Lesser Old Ones who serve Cthulhu. (: "The Horror in the Gallery", "Behind the Mask")

fullContent:
"Mother of Serpents" is a short story by Robert Bloch that appeared in the December 1936 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
The Snake-God is the real deity of the obeah cults. The blacks worshipped the Serpent in Dahomey and Senegal from time immemorial. They venerate the reptiles in a curious way, and there is some obscure linkage between the Snake and the crescent moon. Curious, isn’t it—this serpent superstition? The garden of Eden had its tempter, and the Bible tells of Moses and his staff of snakes. The Egyptians revered Set, and the ancient Hindoos had a cobra god. It seems to be general throughout the world—the kindred hatred and reverence of serpents. Always they seem to be worshipped as creatures of evil. Our own American Indians believed in Yig, and Aztec myths follow the pattern.

-"Mother of Serpents"

After her magic has brought him success in the past, the President of Haiti turns on his sorceress who was the secret of his power. Her god, Damballah, confers on her the means of an awful revenge.

### Publication History
After its initial Weird Tales appearance, "Mother of Serpents" has not often been reprinted, mainly due to its racism. It was published as part of a collection of Robert Bloch stories in 1945 in the book The Opener of the Way.

fullContent:
"Mother of Toads" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith. It takes place in his Averoigne continuity but features a toad-like antagonist akin in some respects to a Deep One related human.

### Synopsis
A young apothecary's apprentice, sent to the abode of a witch in a swamp, is ensorceled, seduced and ultimately killed by a giant toad that can take the form of a human woman, or a human witch with an atavistic spirit of a gigantic toad. The toad-witch-woman seduces the young man then unleashes a horde of toads upon him which force him down into the muck of the swamp and carpet him as he drowns.

### Publication History
"Mother of Toads" was first published in the July 1938 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into Dutch, Italian, French, German, and Spanish.

### Behind the Mythos
Unlike H. P. Lovecraft who emphasized heredity, miscegenation and his horror of racemixing, Smith in this short story emphasizes the seductive power of the glamour and illusion magic at the witch's command, opposed to the horrifying reality of her physical form. The sexual aspect of the story is much more mature and balanced than the Lovecraft coldness or the Robert E. Howard adolescent adventurousness of his compatriots and it stands quite apart and unique among the Lovecraft Circle as a whole.

Mother Shub is a fictional character created by American author Ron Shiflet for his short story "Mother's Little Helper". Whether this was the character's name, an affectation, or her title, is unknown.

### Overview
An ancient woman at the time of her death, Mother Shub lived in a ramshackle, single-room hut in the West Virginia forests known to the locals as Shub's Woods. There, she plied her trade as a local witch doctor, providing the nearby hillbilly families with basic medical care and potions with a variety of effects amongst other seevices in exchange for goods and services. She also operated a moonshine still near to her home, and kept a small number of scrawny black goats.

Although the locals feared Mother Shub and the powers she possessed, they appeared to be unaware that she was in fact a cultist devoted to the worship of Shub-Niggurath, from whom she was granted her gifts. When the time came for her to be with her god, she passed her power on to young Dora McCain, a local girl apprenticed to Mother Shub since the death of her ma.

Later, it is shown that rather than die, Mother Shub was instead transformed into a seductive inhuman entity which inhabits another dimension and accepts the gifts of male souls from her former apprentice in the name of her dark god (: "Mother's Little Helper").

### Appearances
A list of Mother Shub's appearances arranged by her in-universe timeline:

*"Out of the Frying Pan" (2009)
*"Out of Her Gourd" (2018)
*"Mother's Little Helper" (2008)

"Mother's Little Helper" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in his 2008 collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press, and in the revised second edition by Tenoka Press in 2017.

### Synopsis
When amoral factory supervisor Bud Womack finds out a dirty little secret kept by one of his new staff, he attempts to blackmail the girl into embarking on a carnal relationship with him. However, what he has not counted on is that the girl is in fact a priestess of Shub-Niggurath, and has engineered the situation to drain Bud's life essence, while her former mentor - now gloriously transformed by her god and inhabiting another plane of existence - claims his soul…

### Characters
*Bud Womack: a lustful man with a lack of any kind of moral compass.
*Dora McCain: a hillbilly girl recently relocated from West Virginia to texas to continue her duties as a priestess of Shub-Niggurath.
*Mother Shub: a former priestess of the Outer God, now transformed into an inhuman monstrosity.

### Behind the Mythos
Dora McCain and Mother Shub are recurrent characters in Ron Shiflet's Cthulhu Mythos fiction, both making appearances in several of his shorts. However, their stories usually take place in the backwoods of the Appalachian mountains rather than the big cities of Texas.

"Moths to a Pallid Flame" is a short story by Ron Shiflet and Glynn Barrass, first published in the June 2011 edition of The Yellow Sign magazine by Rainfall Books.

### Synopsis
A horrific murder in rural Texas following a stage adaptation of The King in Yellow brings together a sheriff's deputy and a specialist from England to put a stop to the spread of the incursion. Despite succeeding in thwarting the creature attempting to break through from another world, a small part of it escapes, and runs off into the woods where it will bide it’s time and heal…

### Characters
* Mark Warren, a Deaconville sheriff's deputy experiencing his first glimpse of the horror which lurks beyond our world.
* Agent Phillips, a member of a shadowy organisation called the Yellow Cross which is dedicated to halting outbreaks of the yellow madness.
* Charles Applewaite, director of the most recent production of The King in Yellow.
* Jane Doggitt, an actress in the play.

### Publication History
*The Yellow Sign (2011)
*They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness (2018)

### Trivia
* The story takes place in Tenoka, Texas a setting created by Ron Shiflet for many of his mythos works.

Mr. Arkham is a character created by American comic book creator Michael Alan Nelson for the Boom! Studios Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. He made his debut appearance in the very first issue in March 2007.

### Description
Manifesting as a well-spoken, distinguished gentleman in his late middle age, Mr. Arkham hides a dark secret: he is in fact an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep. To maintain a cover while he enacts his schemes, he operates the Arkham Boarding House, an antiquated, and somewhat dilapidated, establishment which charges high prices for maintaining its residents' privacy.

Mr. Arkham is served by a human man named Connor, and a creature resembling a common housecat named Nemesis, who is in fact a former Atlantean sorcerer.

### History
Mr. Arkham was responsible for unearthing the corpse of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred, whom he subsequently reanimated as part of his scheme to initiate a cosmic war. He then befriended first Walt McKinley, and later his nephew Cy Morgan, in his schemes to retrieve a mystical dagger, before driving the latter insane with the revelation of who he really was (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 1: The Fugue).

Following these events, Mr. Arkham went on to recruit four monstrous beings for his war, the entities known as the Horsemen of Nyarlathotep (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 2: The Gathering).

Once his plans began to come into effect, Mr. Arkham captured Lucifer, Cy Morgan, and Raymond Dirk, using Sysyphyx to bewitch Morgan into helping him and torturing Dirk and Lucifer for a time. Once he landed on the newly-risen R'lyeh, his captives in tow, he threw off the guise of Mr. Arkham and manifested fully as Nyarlathotep (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 4: Godwar).

Mr. Cannyharme is a novel by the late American author Michael Shea. It is a loose retelling of H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Hound".

### Synopsis
Set in San Francisco during the late 1970s or early 1980s, Mr. Cannyharme follows several characters who live in and around the run-down Hyperion Hotel. An immortal evil lurks within the hotel, and some are seduced by its promise of eternal life, while others take a stand against the horrors it wishes to inflict upon the human race.

### Main Characters
*Jack Hale, an author and poet working desk at the Hyperion to earn some money.
*Brittany/Britt, a young addict with a history of childhood abuse.
*Aarti, the daughter of the hotel managers.
*Mr. Cunningham/Mr. Cannyharme/Mr. Van Haarme, an immortal entity who appears to feed on the basest emotions of humankind.

### Publication History
Mr. Cannyharme was published by Hippocampus Press in August 2021. Both paperback and digital versions were released.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite not seeing publication until 2021, Linda Shea, Michael's widow, states in her introduction that the novel was completed in 1981. In addition, sections of the work were taken and rewritten by Shea himself, being published as the short stories "The Pool" and "The Recruiter" in 2007 and 2009 respectively.

### Trivia
*The Hyperion Hotel is a recurrent location in Michael Shea's Mythos-related works.
*Chester Chase, a secondary character in Mr. Cannyharme, is the protagonist of the short story "The Recruiter", although the outcome for him is very different in these stories.

Mr. Cannyharme, also known as Mr. Cunningham, Mr. Van Haarme, or Mr. Canning, is an antagonistic character created by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Description
Usually appearing as a hunched man of incredible age, Cannyharme walks with a cane and is frequently said to be bent almost double. In his true form, he resembles an enormous hound with oversized jaws and sexual organs. He is in fact an immortal supernatural predator who feeds upon the basest emotions of the human psyche, and has been in existence for hundreds of years.

In the modern day, Cannyharme resides in the Hyperion Hotel, a San Franciscan business which has seen better days. From there, he preys upon the locals, a mix of addicts, homeless people, and outcasts.

Cannyharme is also the leader of an organisation called the Sons of Holland, a group comprised of servants from his homeland who carry out the will of their malignant master.

Mr. Stone was an alien Mi-Go who appeared in Peter J. Evans' 2013 novel Feeders from Within. He was called Mr. Stone as his human associates required a name to reference him with; as Mi-Go have no need for names, he settled upon the first object which caught his attention, a stone.

### History
Mr. Stone was one of the Mi-Go present in the cave encountered by Mark Harrigan's squad during the Pancho Villa Expedition in the Sierra Madres. Although grievously injured in the conflict with the soldiers, he managed to reconstruct both himself and the barely-alive squad leader, Sergeant Johnathan Orton, using parts from the dead troopers and Mi-Go.

Travelling to the United States with Orton (who had changed his name to Phillip Avery), the two allied themselves with the Silver Twilight Lodge with the aim of completing Mr. Stone's task, which was to reassemble the Shard of Panestes in order to travel unmolested into Tsathoggua's domain.

Finally locating the missing pieces, Mr. Stone transferred Avery's mind into a Mi-Go brain cylinder to grant him the immortality he had been promised, before opening a portal to N'kai. 

Reaching N'kai, Mr. Stone attempted to locate the Feeders from Within, a species of parasitic creature which would cause madness and destruction on Earth. The expedition was thwarted by the arrival of Mark Harrigan and Diana Stanley, who destroyed the Shard and in doing so awoke Tsathoggua, who consumed Mr. Stone before the others escaped.

"Mrs. Dakhamunzu" is a short story by authors Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A young man who makes his living by seducing rich old women for their money meets a singularly different mark: a princess of Egyptica who wishes for him to travel back to her realm and raise their unborn child together.

### Characters
*Seth Kendall, a handsome yet manipulative young man.
*Sabah Dakhamunzu, the heir to the throne of Egyptica, apparently on some form of sabbatical on Earth.
*Maggie, Seth's actual girlfriend.
*Dr. Khyan, an Egyptican.
*Umer Horemheb, an Egyptican, deceased.

### Publication History
"Mrs. Dakhamunzu" was first published in the collection The Blasphemy In The Canopic Jar & More Tales Of The Cthulhu Mythos in September 2016, and was later reprinted in Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

"Mrs. Hudson's Fancies" is a Lovecraftian short story set in the extended Sherlock Holmes universe. Written by British author William Meikle, it was published in his collection Inspector Lestrade: The Black Temple and Other Stories by Weird House Press in February 2023.

### Synopsis
Inspector Lestrade agrees to help Sherlock Holmes's landlady Mrs. Hudson when she approaches him with concerns over her bereaved friend's involvement with what she believes to be a phoney medium. Unfortunately, the man's powers turn out to be more real than suspected, and her desperation to speak to her dead husband results in the summoning of an extra-dimensional monstrosity and a tragic demise for the poor woman.

### Behind the Mythos
Although containing no direct references to H. P. Lovecraft’s work or the Cthulhu Mythos in general, "Mrs. Hudson's Fancies" contains a number of elements and themes which feature in Meikle's Lovecraftian writings. These include an other-dimensional entity which resembles a mass of ever-replicating globes reminiscent of descriptions of the Outer God Yog-Sothoth; this connection would appear to be reinforced by the medium referring to the being as, amongst other things, Sototh.

"Mrs. Miniter - Estimates and Recollections" is a short non-fiction piece by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Written on 16 October 1934, it did not see print until Spring 1938, a year after his own death.

It is an essay of 5,210 words first published in The Californian (Spring 1938). This poignant essay traces the amateur career of the recently deceased Edith Miniter, with a discussion of her household (including her cousin Evanore Beebe and numerous pets) at a rural home, Maplehurst, outside of Wilbraham, Massachusetts, which Lovecraft visited in 1928. The essay was intended for a booklet devoted to Miniter, to be published by W. Paul Cook, for which Lovecraft had gathered numerous other articles. Unfortunately the project was never completed. Lovecraft also wrote an elegy, “Edith Miniter” pubished in The Tryout (August 1934).

### Publication History
* The Californian: 1934-1938 (1977)
* Miscellaneous Writings (1995)

Mu is a supposed lost continent that was said to have sunk beneath the waves of the Pacific Ocean. This pseudo-scientific geological history has been incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos.

### In the real world
Mu is the name of a suggested lost continent whose concept and name were proposed by 19th-century traveler and writer Augustus Le Plongeon, who claimed that several ancient civilizations, such as those of Egypt and Mesoamerica, were created by refugees from Mu—which he located in the Atlantic Ocean, and identified with Atlantis.

This concept was popularized and expanded by James Churchward, who asserted that Mu was a different lost continent than Atlantis; he located Mu in the Pacific Ocean. Mu was also adopted into the cosmology and world history of Theosophy as the home of one of Theosophy's Root-Races.

H. P. Lovecraft (1890–1937) featured the lost continent in his revision of Hazel Heald's short story "Out of the Aeons" (1935). Mu appears in numerous Cthulhu Mythos stories, including many written by Lin Carter.

### In the Mythos
It's been claimed that the first human beings inhabited Mu (: "The Invaders"), although other sources claim that they inhabited Lemuria (: "The Haunter of the Dark"), perhaps hinting at some connection between the two continents.

The Muvians mainly worship the ghastly Ghatanothoa (trapped under mount Yaddith-Gho), though there are some who oppose this prevailing religion. Among them are T'yog the high priest of Shub-Niggurath (: "Out of the Aeons") and Zanthu the hierophant. (: Xothic legend cycle, Lin Carter) In trying to free his god Ythogtha and restore his cult, Zanthu accidentally causes the destruction of Mu. (: "The Thing in the Pit")

It's also believed that between 18,000 and 10,000 BC, the Muvians were enslaved by extraterrestrial creatures called the Lloigor, led by Ghatanothoa. (: "The Return of the Lloigor")

The Atlantean General Bothon was appointed ambassador to the Muvian province of Aglad-Dho. After falling in love with the Muvian Emperor's niece, Ledda, the Atlantean raised an army to siege the capital of Alu so he could elope with her. (: "Bothon")

Boatswain Müller is a fictional character in the story "The Temple" by H. P. Lovecraft. He served as a 
boatswain aboard the German submarine U-29 under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich during the First World War. 
Müller was an elderly man and described by Heinrich as a "superstitious Alsatian swine" (the region of Alsace, France 
being under German control during the time period of the story). 

During the supernatural events experienced by the crew, both Müller and Seaman Zimmer went missing. They were presumed 
by Heinrich to have committed suicide by jumping overboard while the U-29 was surfaced, victims of the fear that overcame them.

A mummy is a dead body that has been preserved by natural or artificial processes. Historically, mummification has been widely practiced by the ancient Egyptians and Incans, among other cultures. The concept of undead or reanimated mummies is a common trope in fantasy and horror fiction, tracing back to The Mummy!: A Tale of the Twenty-Second Century (1827) by Jane Webb, and popularized by the 1932 film The Mummy.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
While the ancient Egyptians had a long tradition of mummifying people and animals, it was only in the latter days of their civilization that certain priests started to create "composite mummies" by combining human and animal body parts, in an attempt to imitate their gods. Nowadays, the reanimated composite mummies still inhabit subterranean catacombs ruled by Khephren and Nitokris, and worship the Sphinx. (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs")

Mummification was also practiced by the non-human inhabitants of the Nameless City. (: "The Nameless City")

In 1770, Joseph Curwen acquired a cargo of Egyptian mummies with the purpose of reanimating them and learning their secrets. (: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward)

The greatest collection of mummies in America is located in the Cabot Museum's hall of mummies. The collection includes ancient Egyptian specimens, prehistoric mummies from the Aleutian Islands, citizens of Pompeii preserved by the volcanic ashes, and the naturally-mummified bodies of people who died in mines and excavation shafts. In 1879, Curator Pickman acquired an alleged "mummy" found on a newly-emerged portion of the lost continent Mu. This "mummy" was actually the still-living body of T'yog, a victim of the petrifying glare of Ghatanothoa. (: "Out of the Aeons")

Surama, an Atlantean sorcerer raised from his tomb after thousands of years, is compared to "a Pharaoh’s mummy, if miraculously brought to life." (: "The Last Test")

In 1913, Arthur Jermyn acquired the mummified body of a white ape princess who turned out to be his great-great-great-grandmother. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

St. John's  collection of ghoulish trophies includes "cases of antique mummies" that line the walls. (: "The Hound")

### Other Mythos Writers
Friedrich von Junzt discovered the mummy of a high priest in the Temple of the Toad, in Honduras. (: "The Thing on the Roof")

Simon of Gitta fled from an army of mummies in the crypts beneath the Pyramids. (: "The Treasure of Horemkhu")

The looting of the mummy of a priest of Sebek to New Orleans brought the crocodile-headed god himself to seek vengeance. (: "The Secret of Sebek")

Munchkin Cthulhu is a competitive card game published by Steve Jackson Games. 

### Overview
A thematic version of the popular Munchkin card game, Munchkin Cthulhu is a game in which players compete to gain "levels" in the form of points whilst doing their utmost to prevent the other players from doing the same. Like all Munchkin releases, it is 100% compatible with other sets. 

Munchkin Cthulhu has spawned a series of similarly-themed expansions and sets allowing players additional options without incorporating different themes. A guest artist edition was released in June 2016. 

### Expansions
The sets listed below are not stand-alone games, they require a copy of the Munchkin game to use (although not necessarily Munchkin Cthulhu). 

*Cursed Demo, an introductory pack allowing players with a copy of the core game to "dip-in" and sample Munchkin Cthulhu. 
*Sanity Check, an additional 30 cards to add variety to games. 
*Call of Cowthulhu, an expansion which mixes the Cthulhu Mythos with the farmyard. Features creatures such as Hog-Sothoth, Sheep Ones, Shoggoats, a Doggoth, and the Arkhamster. 
*The Unspeakable Vault, an expansion based on the Lovecraft-inspired webcomic The Unspeakable Vault (of Doom). 
*Crazed Caverns, a thematic expansion representing underground exploration in various Mythos locations including Dunwich and K'n'Yan.

Doctor Muñoz is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. He made his first appearance in the 1928 short story "Cool Air."

### Description
A Spanish physician of "striking intelligence and superior blood and breeding", Muñoz is described as "short but exquisitely proportioned", with a "high-bred face of masterful though not arrogant expression", "a short iron-grey full beard", "full, dark eyes" and "an aquiline nose". He calls himself "the bitterest of sworn enemies to death", and one who had "sunk his fortune and lost all his friends in a lifetime of bizarre experiment devoted to its bafflement and extirpation." Saying he feels a "repugnance" on first meeting Muñoz that "nothing in his aspect could justify", the narrator remarks on "the ice-coldness and shakiness of his bloodless looking hands" and that fact that his breathing was imperceptible. (: "Cool Air")

### Biography
Dr. Muñoz and his mentor, Dr. Torres of Valencia, spent years experimenting and trying to find ways to overcome death. Muñoz believed that "will and consciousness are stronger than organic life itself", and that a human consciousness might be preserved indefinitely, as long as the body frame is properly conserved, even after the irreversible failure of major organs, such as the heart. Although a man of science, "he did not scorn the incantations of the mediaevalists, since he believed these cryptic formulae to contain rare psychological stimuli" that could have "singular effects" on the nervous system.

When Muñoz died in 1905, his body was retrieved and reanimated by Torres, who died himself soon afterwards.

Following his revival, Muñoz moved to the United States, where he rented an apartment in New York. He lived as a recluse and converted part of his apartment into a laboratory, while keeping his room refrigerated by "an absorption system of ammonia cooling", powered by a gasoline engine. His landlady and fellow lodgers believed him to suffer from some kind of illness. In addition to keeping his room at about 55 °F (~ 12.7 °C), Muñoz also took "funny-smelling baths" and used rare spices and Egyptian incense to keep his body preserved and functional.

Although he no longer practiced, Muñoz remained a skillful and compassionate physician, as demonstrated when he fixed the broken arm of a plumber, and successfully treated the narrator's heart condition. While he never left his house, he maintained a correspondence with other scholars, which the narrator describes as "for the most part lettered East Indians, but including a once celebrated French physician now generally thought dead, and about whom the most inconceivable things had been whispered".

Despite all his efforts, Muñoz's body continued to deteriorate slowly. His voice weakened, as did his fine motor skills. With the help of the narrator, he modified his refrigerating machine to keep his room at 28 °F (~ minus 2.2 °C),

Mupp is a character created by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. for their Egyptian Cthulhu Mythos stories. 

### Description
Severely deformed from birth - as a result of interference from the Outer God Nyarlathotep at the time of conception - Mupp is described as "large, red-faced … with an oversized skull, a cleft lip, a slight chin, a stunted arm, and overly large, malformed hips. His crooked spine ended in a vestigial tail. His left foot resembled the flipper of a turtle, while his other foot and hands all featured the wrong numbers of fingers and toes." His most distinctive feature is that he is a cyclops, with a "huge single eye nestled above … flaring cheekbones. Even at birth, a thick arc of black brow curved over the eye, which regarded the world with seething wrath. The iris of this eye was composed of three reddish-gold lobes, centered around the irregular black circle of the pupil." 

He is also a gifted magic user with the ability to cause blood to gush from the ears of others with but a whisper, see in total darkness, and project blasts of green fire from his hands. 

### History
Despite being born to the pharaoh Tutankhamen, Mupp's hideous appearance meant that he was exiled to the catacombs beneath the royal palace. There, he formed his own cult to Nyarlathotep before one day stumbling across the undying followers of Azathoth. He learned from these shrivelled mummies how to reanimate the dead, and commanded them to bring him more corpses with which to create his own army. However, before his plans could come to fruition, he was slain by the creature Setek after displaying a burst of childish petulance. 

In the modern day, Mupp was shown to have somehow survived the ages: or more accurately, his single swollen eyeball had. He used his powers to merge what remained of his physical form with an unsuspecting human before heading off into the night, his fate unknown.

fullContent:
Muriel Elizabeth (Gammons) Eddy (January 19, 1896 - January 30, 1978) was a writer born in Taunton, Massachusetts. She corresponded with H. P. Lovecraft and was married to Lovecraft collaborator C. M. Eddy, Jr.. 

She spent parts of her early life living in California before returning to New England and living the rest of her life in Providence, Rhode Island. 

She married C. M. Eddy in 1918. They began their friendship in an exchange of letters centered on their common interest in amateur writing. Once married, both Muriel and her husband developed their writing careers and began to be published professionally. While working as a writer, Muriel gave birth to three children with her husband. 

Muriel Eddy wrote in many genres, including romance, occult, biography and poetry. She served as president of the Rhode Island Writers' Guild for more than 20 years, and also taught creative writing.

She maintained a voluminous correspondence with authors including H. P. Lovecraft, August Derleth, L. Sprague de Camp, Sonia Haft Greene Davis, Joseph Payne Brennan, Robert Bloch, and Princess Red Wing. 

She made a lasting contribution to Lovecraft scholarship with her biographical work The Gentleman from Angell Street, which also features reminiscences from her husband. This work was first published in 1945 under the title Howard Phillips Lovecraft, and then republished in an expanded 2001 edition. The accuracy of some of her descriptions and remembered incidents has been questioned. 

### Selected Works

fullContent:
"Mushrooms from Ceres" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Harris Coverley. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long running zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
When skinflint tree surgeon Vince Exley turns up a mysterious fungus embedded in one of the plants he is called upon to attend, he decides that the best course of action would be to boil it up and consume it as a home-made remedy to the many ailments from which he suffers. Unfortunately for the unwise man, the fungus is more than a common or garden variety, and the spores infect him before rapidly spreading to engulf the entirety of his home.

When Exley's employee Martyn Hallam discovers the situation, he decides that the best course of action would be to incinerate both his boss and the infected home. As Hallam completes his task, he accidentally touches the fungus and is shown a vision of the fungus's history as part of an interstellar species with designs on planet Earth.

### Behind the Mythos
Although "Mushrooms from Ceres" contains no direct references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos, elements of the story strongly suggest that the creature was a member of the alien Mi-Go; its physical description of a crab-like fungus matches that of the Mi-Go, and Hallam's insights about both it's species' desire to mine the Earth for minerals and a historic war with beings which dwelt in Antarctica are also in accordance.

"Music of the Stars" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Duane W. Rimel. It was first published in the Spring 1943 edition of The Acolyte.

### Synopsis
In 1940, a man named Rambeau visits his friend, Frank Baldwyn, who shares his interests in both occultism and music. Baldwyn claims that he has come across disturbing combinations of tones, which he plays in his piano. Rambeau is shocked to hear it, describing the melody as "eerie and unearthly". When the music is finished, they hear the rustling sound of agitated rats moving inside the wall. Baldwyn claims that his music affects all animals, including humans. He believes he might be close to unveiling "the music of the stars", a song that would literally drive the listener mad.

Rambeau is fascinated and awed by the idea, but also realises the danger, recalling the fate of a certain Erich Zann, as well as "the savage music with which certain tribes in Haiti summon their evil Gods". To guide him in the composition of the "music of the stars", Baldwyn plans to study several passages of the Chronike von Nath, by Rudolf Yergler, a book containing "odd musical rhythm patterns designed to summon certain star-born monsters from the Earth's core and from other worlds and dimensions". According to history, Yergler himself went mysteriously blind and mad after completing his book, and died in an asylum. He was found dead after a thunderstorm, covered in holes that looked like burn marks.

After a week goes by, Rambeau visits Baldwyn again, and is shocked to see how his physical health has deteriorated. Still, Baldwyn claims that he has almost completed his composition, and asks Rambeau to return in the evening. When he does so, Baldwyn confirms that he's succeeded in making the music described by Yergler. He admits that a friend of his named Lancaster, who is extremely knowledgeable in the matters of the occult, has begged him not to play it, claiming that it might summon "a certain thing from the shadows of another dimension". However, Baldwyn dismisses Lancaster's worries and asks Rambeau not to interrupt his experiment.

When Baldwyn starts playing, the entire house seems to shake. The moonlight intensifies until the glass of the windows and the lamps shatter. Rambeau sees a strange shadow appear over Baldwyn and screams, but the scream is lost amidst the cacophonous music, and he can only watch in horror as a monstrous beast starts to materialise. When Baldwyn finally stops playing, the beast envelops him. Rambeau grabs his revolver, but his shots seem to go through the monster and only hit the wall. When the thing is gone, Baldwyn looks like Rudolf Yergler did in death: eyeless and covered in holes that look like burn marks. Still alive, Baldwyn claims that the thing has consumed part of him, and urges Rambeau to kill him before it consumes the rest. The Muvians are a fictional prehistoric human civilisation that inhabited the lost continent of Mu. They were based on the pseudoscientific writings of Augustus Le Plongeon and James Churchward, who equated Mu with Atlantis and Lemuria, respectively. In the Cthulhu Mythos, these three continents are portrayed as distinct nations that coexisted and traded with each other during the same precataclysmic time period (: "The Shadow Kingdom", : "Bothon", : "The Warder of Knowledge").

The Muvians were first incorporated into the Mythos by Hazel Heald and H. P. Lovecraft in their short story "Out of the Aeons".

### In the Mythos

### Religion
The people of Mu worshiped many different deities, including Ghatanothoa, Shub-Niggurath, Yig, Nug and Yeb (: "Out of the Aeons"), Cthulhu, Iod, Vorvadoss (: "The Invaders"), and Ythogtha. Over the course of millennia, the cult of Ghatanothoa gradually became more powerful than the others, to the point that, towards the end of the continent's history, the worship of other deities was forbidden in the Muvian main kingdom of K'naa. (: "The Thing in the Pit").

Every year, the priests of Ghatanothoa sacrificed 12 young warriors and 12 young maidens to their god on the flaming altars of a marble temple at the base of Mt. Yaddith-Gho. The people of Mu believed that, without these sacrifices to appease it, Ghatanothoa would emerge from the mountain and cast its petrifying gaze on all below. Due to their pivotal role in preventing this catastrophe, the priests enjoyed enormous power and riches, hundreds of slaves and concubines, and legal immunity (: "Out of the Aeons").

According to Friedrich von Junzt, the cult of Ghatanothoa was kept alive by Muvian survivors after the continent's sinking and spread secretly to various parts of the world, from the Pacific Islands to Atlantis, to the Plateau of Leng, underground K'n-yan, and several locations in Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas. (: "Out of the Aeons")

Prof. Laban Shrewsbury believed that the worship of certain maritime deities in Mu and Atlantis survived into the 20th century in the Balearic Islands, the Caroline Islands, and the town of Innsmouth, Massachusetts, among other places. (: "The Black Island")

### Society
The Muvians spoke the Naacal language. (: "Out of the Aeons", "Bothon")

The Muvian continent was divided into several provinces or kingdoms, including K'naa (: "Out of the Aeons"), the central eastern province of Ghua, and a confederation of three southeastern provinces named Yish, Knan, and Buathon, which shared the joint-capital of Aglad-Dho. The imperial capital of the continent was Alu, where the Emperor and his family resided. It was a sophisticated commercial center visited by foreign diplomats, artists, philosophers, traders and shipmasters (: "Bothon").

"My Boat" is a short story by Joanna Russ that first appeared in the January 1976 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. It was included in the revised edition of Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1990). The story ties in explicitly to H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands stories.

### Synopsis
A writer, Jim, is in a restaurant, telling his agent Milty a story about two kids he knew in high school in 1952. Cissie is a brilliant but troubled Black student from Brooklyn, bused in to his Long Island high school for desegregation. He and his friend Al initially try to get her kicked out of school for not being "normal," but then become her protectors and soon her admirers. 

Cissie offers to show Jim and Al her boat, named My Boat, tied up at a Long Island marina. The boat appears at first to be a simple weather-beaten rowboat, but becomes bigger and more luxurious every time Jim looks at it. Cissie and Al also transform, from awkward teenagers to heroic characters out of fantasy; they talk of exotic lands they have sailed to on their ship, Cissie mentioning places from African and Mediterranean history, and Atlantis; Al referring to places from H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands stories. Jim hesitates to join them on the ship; when his back is turned, My Boat depart, leaving Jim behind and unable to explain Cissie and Al's disappearance. 

Many years later, Jim sees Al again, still a teenager; he has returned to retrieve a book he left behind, H. P. Lovecraft's The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. As the story ends, Al appears in the restaurant, and Jim finally seems ready to go with him.

### Characters
Jim: A writer who attended Central High on Long Island, New York, "a public high school but very fancy." He was raised "sort-of-nothing Jewish." He looks back on himself as "a damned fool...even considering your run-of-the-mill, seventeen-year-old white liberal racist."

Milty: Jim's agent. He once sold an H. P. Lovecraft film project, but is only interested in the percentage he got from it.

Alan Coppolino: Jim's friend, an "Italian punk" who is "five foot three and so brilliant no other kid could understand half the time what he was talking about." His family is "sort-of-nothing-really Catholic." The "Woody Allen of Central High," he reads "crazy books" like The Cult of Cthulhu, Dagon Calls, and The Horror Men of Leng.

Cecilia Jackson: A "little black girl aged fifteen" from Brooklyn who is "some kind of genius," particularly in drama; she's known as Cissie. She saw her father killed by a white cop when she was five. Her mother is poor and a strict Christian, forbidding Cissie to go to parties, dance, or wear makeup. She spends time briefly in a mental hospital. Jim observes, "I guess her imagination just had to find some way out." She is four foot eleven, weighs 85 pounds, and wears her hair in a "natural."

"My Family" is a short Lovecraftian story by author Matt Spencer, first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine.

### Synopsis
Two men, one whose daughter has run away and the other recently bereaved, travel to a remote much-feared mountain village in search of the missing girl. There it is revealed that the girl, like her mother before her, is a member of a hostile eldritch race. The two men are taken by the beings; one is soon released as a result of the tattooed ward which he bears, while the other, who does not possess such a charm, is less fortunate.

fullContent:
"My Life in Miniature" is a four-part story featured in issues #1-4 of The All-New Atom Vol 1, written by Gail Simone and published by DC Comics in 2006. 

### Synopsis
After the death of his mother, Ryan Choi moves to the New England city of Ivy Town so that he can take up Professor Ray Palmer's old position at Ivy University; however, Ryan's true motivation is to continue Ray's legacy by obtaining his size-altering belt and becoming the superhero known as the All-New Atom. 

Shortly afterwards, Ryan is lured into the sewers by the disappearance of a homeless woman, where he discovers that the town has become the center of a war between the forces of science, led by "The Waiting", and the forces of magic, led by M'nagalah. Both sides attempt to force him to join them in order to turn the tide of the battle but Ryan manages to escape, using his new powers that he has gotten from Ray's Bio-Belt. 

The next day, Ryan goes on a movie date with his fellow professor, Doris Zuell. While watching a double feature at a drive-in, Doris reveals herself to be the super-villain Giganta, who has been infected by M'nagalah. Giganta precedes to trap Ryan in a circular petri dish and swallow him alive, which is quickly followed by M'nagalah and his cult occupying the movie theater.  

Giganta goes on a rampage throughout Ivy Town before she gets into a confrontation with the alien invaders known as "The Waiting". Ryan is able to free himself by causing Giganta to vomit him out, after which the aliens quickly retreat, as they are scared off by Giganta's "biological weapon".

### Trivia
*The movie playing in the theater is based on Swamp Thing Vol 1 #8, "The Lurker in Tunnel 13", the first comic book story to feature M'nagalah.

"My Stalk" is a short story by author and editor Aaron J. French. It is inspired by the fiction of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
A man with the soul of a seeker of knowledge purchases a bag of mushrooms from a reputed witch deep in the forest. When he grows the mushrooms, they begin to allow him to commune with an eldritch deity not of our world, and he dedicates his existence to creating a causeway to allow it to breach realities.

### Characters
*The Narrator, a man in search of meaning to his life.
*The Witch, a forest-dwelling hag.
*Sky-God, an extra-dimensional batrachian entity.

### Publication History
"My Stalk" was first published in the collection of French's own works Aberrations of Reality in September 2014. In November that same year, it was included in the 01Publishing anthology of Lovecraft-inspired works Whispers from the Abyss.

fullContent:
Mycroft & Moran was an imprint of Arkham House, created to publish weird detective stories and August Derleth's Solar Pons series in particular. It was named after two characters from the Sherlock Holmes stories of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, and the imprint's logo featured a deerstalker hat, one of Holmes' iconic accessories.

Mycroft & Moran was retired by Arkham House in 1982, but was briefly revived in 1998 when it was licensed to George A. Vanderburg's Battered Silicon Dispatch Box publishing house which specialises in detective fiction, with a focus on Sherlock Holmes works.

Mynoghra, also known as The She-Daemon of the Shadows, is a fictional entity created by the late American author Edward P. Berglund for his 1975 short story "Wings in the Night".

### Description
Mynoghra is a cosmic entity capable of manifesting in a variety of forms, including that of a beautiful woman, but in its true form possesses a pair of membranous wings and is highly averse to any form of light. Despite this, Mynoghra has shown to be capable of extinguishing any light sources it encounters, and is usually surrounded by a cloud of inky blackness to protect herself from its effect in any case.

A Great Old One mentioned as a cousin of Nyarlathotep in The O' Khymer Revelations, and the Count de Hammais’ Sorcerie de Demonologie states that of all the Great Old Ones, Nyarlathotep and Mynoghra are the only ones not to be "imprisoned beneath the Elder Sign," and that once summoned, a portal to its dimension is created which may only be closed by the person who opened it.

Mynoghra likes to forge pacts with mortals for an unnamed price, although usually this price is the life-essence of the other party, as the entity finds this to be a particularly delicious repast. The remains of the victim are then fed to Mynoghra's Hell-Hounds, demonic entities only vaguely described but which bear some unspecified connection to the Hounds of Tindalos despite being the offspring of Mynoghra and Shub-Niggurath. In exchange, she may offer boons such as artistic inspiration; these pacts are always brought to a close on All Hallow's Eve. (: "Wings in the Night")

### In Other Media
*Mynoghra appears in Hashtag Comics' Carpe Noctem series. She is described as being the daughter of Cthulhu and makes her first appearance in issue 2, when she interrupts an underworld council meeting.  
*Mynoghra appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
*The mobile game Crash Fever features a character named after and based on Mynoghra. 
*In the anime series Haiyore! Nyaruko-san, Mynoghra's name is briefly seen written on the main character's marriage certificate.
*The light novel series Isekai Apocalypse Mynoghra takes place in a fictional country named after Mynoghra.
*In the role-playing video game Black Souls II, Mynoghra appears as a minor character named little sister Alice, based on Alice in Wonderland  by Lewis Carroll. The main goal of Mynoghra is to deceive the player to help Nyarlathotep. She also has a descendant, mad bird Jubjub.

Mysteries of the Worm: Early Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos is a collection of Robert Bloch's Cthulhu Mythos fiction. It first appeared in 1981 in an edition edited by Lin Carter, published by Zebra Books. It was later reissued in a revised and expanded second edition, edited by Robert M. Price and published by Chaosium in 1993 as part of its Cthulhu Cycle series. Another edition was put out by Chaosium in 2009.

The second edition adds three early Mythos tales from Bloch: "The Brood of Bubastis", "The Creeper in the Crypt", and "The Sorcerer's Jewel". In addition, the texts of "The Grinning Ghoul", "The Dark Demon", and "The Secret of Sebek" were slightly revised by Bloch for the second edition.

The third edition also adds "The Opener of the Way", "The Eyes of the Mummy", "Black Bargain", and "Philtre Tip".

### Synopsis
A Roman centurion newly arrived at a garrison in ancient Britain pleads to any god who will listen when his camp is overrun by barbarians. However, the entity which answers has a price for this aid: as the centurion has decided who lives and who dies, he must remain as a servant on earth, forever choosing the fate of those who go to war.

### Characters

* Nyarlathotep, an Outer God.

### Publication History

fullContent:
Mythos was a collectible card game for two or more players published by Chaosium and based on the Cthulhu Mythos and the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. It was first published in 1996, but discontinued in 1997 after a slump in sales. It was succeeded in 2004 by Call of Cthulhu Collectible Card Game, a licensed CCG from Fantasy Flight Games, later transformed into the Living Card Game Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

### Gameplay
Players choose an Investigator, a double-sized card representing a character archetype from the Mythos. Other cards, including Locations, Events, Allies, Artefacts, Tomes and Spells, are played for various game effects. The goal of the game is to score points by completing Adventures, short story cards which specify other cards or card types which must be played to tell the story. Players can also summon Monsters, who may battle each other, though this is a secondary aspect of the game. It is also possible to eliminate other players by reducing their Investigator's sanity to zero.

### Editions
### Limited Edition
The original Limited Edition consisted of starter decks, which included a random investigator card, and boosters released as three themed collections: Expeditions of Miskatonic University, Cthulhu Rising and Legends of the Necronomicon.

### Standard Set
The Standard Set included two pre-configured decks, one "Stalwart" and the other "Corrupt".

### Expansions
Two expansions were published in the game's second year: Dreamlands, which introduced other dimensions, especially elements from The Dreamlands cycle of stories; and New Æon, which added modern-day elements drawn from popular culture, including the Men in Black, aliens and time travel.

Amongst the authors whose works it has published are C. J. Henderson, Stanley C. Sargent, Robert M. Price, Jeffrey Thomas and Richard L. Tierney.

The N'Garai are a fictional elder race in the Marvel universe that first appeared in 1974, in a prose story in issue #4 of the 2nd volume of Haunt of Horror. Their first appearance in a comic was in 1975, in issue #96 of the 1st volume of the X-Men comic book series. In the 1980s, likely due to the Aliens sci-fi horror franchise, the look of the N'Garai was changed to make them look more like the Xenomorphs.

### Background
### Origin, Culture and Society
The N'Garai are a race of demons created by Chthon, one of the Elder Gods (the spawn of the Elder Gods is known collectively as "Elderspawn"). Millions of years ago, they lived on Earth, where they enslaved the human race, treating them as pets, workers, and livestock. Sometime later, they were defeated by an as-yet-unidentified force, and were driven back to their own dimension.

The race is ruled by a king-like demon. Their master and a small number of elite N'Garai are highly intelligent and lead the warrior caste (aka, the lower caste), who make up the rest of the race. The warrior caste are brutally savage and bloodthirsty, and rely on numbers to overwhelm their enemies. They are varied in appearance, such as reptilian or insectoid forms and having things such as wings, tentacles, mandibles, fangs, pincers, claws, etc. The most common type have a bipedal reptilian form with two arms, claws, an elongated head with a mouth full of sharp teeth, and a long tail. It's a race that ranges in size from an average human to multi-story ones.

N'Garai cannot give birth; they are born from the cycle of violence, from the unborn who were conceived and consigned to violence. They possess superhuman strength and durability, being able to tear out a motor vehicle's engine through its hood. N'Garai can go up against a superhuman like the bloodthirsty Sabretooth. One was capable of eliminating a town's entire sheriff's office, and bullets weren't able to noticeably slow it down. The upper caste have various additional powers. These aren't always consistent, but have included regeneration, the ability to mentally control others, casting magical spells, and optical energy blasts.

In 1861, the N'Garai returned to Earth and battled the mutant Apocalypse, who slaughtered an entire tribe of the demons by himself. Recently, they have clashed with the Avengers, the Invaders, Doctor Strange and the Hulk. Their greatest enemies, though, have been the mutant superheroes of the X-Men who have repeatedly thwarted them, with Wolverine doing the most damage to them. On Earth, the N'Garai have their human servants, the Camarilla of the N'Garai, and human allies, the Cult of the Darkhold.

### Camarilla of the N'Garai


The Camarilla of the N'Garai are a group of humans. based in San Francisco, who pledged their service to the N'Garai. (: Issue #4, Volume #2, Haunt of Horror) Its leader, Jimmy Cruz, was a monsignor in the Catholic Church who desired to destroy Sa

The N'Garai Cairns are  fictional artefacts created by Marvel Comics, which first appeared in Uncanny X-Men Vol 1 #96 "Night of the Demon".

### Background
The cairns are used by the demonic N'Garai to cross over into other dimensions. Wherever the walls between dimensions are thin, one of these can appear, thrusting upward from the ground. The number of N'Garai that can come through one of them varies and multiple cairns can simultaneously appear on a world, the start of a N'Garai invasion. One can also travel to the N'Garai dimension via one of these cairns.

One cairn just happened to appear on the grounds of the Xavier Mansion, and was inadvertently destroyed by Cyclops, who impulsively fired a massive optic blast while mourning the death of his teammate Thunderbird. This freed a N'Garai that ran rampant on the mansion grounds; this incident was the first time the X-Men battled one of these demons, and not the last.

N'kai is a colossal underground cavern located beneath the subterranean nation of K'n-yan in H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
Below the ruins of Yoth in K'n-yan is the black realm N'kai, populated with peculiar-sensed beings which had forged great civilisations without any light at all even before the emergence of the people of Yoth. N'kai is the source of the multiple black idols and images of Tsathoggua. The Yothic manuscripts were scoured by archaeologists for references to N'kai, and even singular stone troughs or burrows had excited infinite speculation. Though the manuscript described it as barren, the one expedition from Tsath found that it had been repopulated by a collection of formless black blobs that worshipped onyx and basalt images of Tsathoggua. Much later, a second attempt to access the depths was made, but neither they nor Zamacona y Nuñez were able to find the entrance.

N'kai is known to be the current residence of the Great Old One Tsathoggua and its guardians, the Formless Spawn.

N'tse-Kaambl is an Elder God from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos, who first appeared in Gary Myers' short story "The House of the Worm". 

### Background
N'tse-Kaambl is a powerful Elder God, who is primarily worshipped in the Dreamlands and was responsible for the creation of the Elder Sign. She is known to combat the Great Old Ones and Outer Gods. Although her ultimate goal is to defeat the evil gods, she is indifferent towards humanity as a whole. Referred to as a goddess "whose splendor hath shattered worlds", N'tse-Kaambl usually takes the form of a beautiful woman wielding a spear and shield. Her spear is capable of firing blasts of powerful energy, while her shield is emblazoned with an Elder Sign and protects anything that is behind it. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### In Other Media
*N'tse-Kaambl appears in the anime Haiyore! Nyaruko-san, as a member of the Space Defense Agency's Dreamlands Management Division. 
*N'tse-Kaambl appears in the trading card game Yu-Gi-Oh!, under the name Elder Entity N'tss.
*N'tse-Kaambl appears in the mobile game Yurudora, during the Cthulhu Festival event.

### Behind the Mythos
N'tse-Kaambl was most likely inspired by Athena, a goddess from Greek Mythology.

shortDefinition: Naacal is a language supposedly spoken on the lost continent of Mu, according to the pseudo-science of British author James Churchward. H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price later incorporated Churchward's invented language into the Cthulhu Mythos in...
fullContent:
Naacal is a language supposedly spoken on the lost continent of Mu, according to the pseudo-science of British author James Churchward. H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price later incorporated Churchward's invented language into the Cthulhu Mythos in the short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key". 

### Pseudo-Science
The term "Naacal" first appears in the work of  Augustus Le Plongeon (1825-1908), a 19th century archaeologist who believed that civilization originated with the Mayans of the Yucatan peninsula, then spread via Atlantis to the rest of the world. Le Plongeon called the Mayan adepts who carried civilization across the globe Naacal, which he said meant "exalted". 

Author James Churchward adopted the term in his book The Lost Continent of Mu, Motherland of Man (1926), an ostensibly nonfiction work considered to be pseudo-science, or lacking in proper scientific verification. Churchward used the word "Naacal" to refer to both the people of Mu, a continent that supposedly vanished under the Pacific Ocean, and to their language. Churchward claimed to have learned Naacal in India, where it was still spoken by only three people, allowing him to read Naacal tablets containing the lost history of Mu. 

### Alphabet
Churchward provided a Naacal alphabet (labeled "Mu"), comparing it to Mayan and Egyptian: 
 

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by Lovecraft and E. Hoffman Price, Harley Warren is described as a "South Carolina mystic whose studies in the primal Naacal language of the Himalayan priests had led to such outrageous conclusions." Churchward is name-dropped in the story, as Etienne-Laurent de Marigny says of a parchment found in Randolph Carter's car, "Col. Churchward declares it is not Naacal." (The Swami Chandraputra  later confirms that "the language of those hieroglyphics is not Naacal but R’lyehian, which was brought to earth by the spawn of Cthulhu countless cycles ago.") 

The revision tale "Out of the Aeons", written by Lovecraft for Hazel Heald, describes "a vanished continent...which legend has given the name of Mu, and which old tablets in the primal Naacal tongue speak of as flourishing 200,000 years ago." The scroll created by the High-Priest T'yog for protection from Ghatanothoa is said to be written in "the hieratic Naacal of his order."

### Other Appearances
August Derleth also makes reference to the Naacal language in "The House on Curwen Street" and The Lurker at the Threshold. 

In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, the Naacal Code is used to activate Demonbane's fishing move, the Lemuria Impact.

Naggoob is the Father of Ghouls and the free lead servant of Nyogtha, according to the Unaussprechlichen Kulten. (: "The Horror in the Gallery") As such, he might be related to Nug, Feaster Among the Tombs, who the Book of Eibon identifies as the grandfather of all ghouls who serve Nyogtha. (: "The Descent into the Abyss")

### Behind the Mythos
Naggoob was created by Lin Carter for his 1976 story "The Horror in the Gallery", and classified as one of the Lesser Old Ones.

As the "father of ghouls", Naggoob might be associated with Shaurash-ho, a a descendant of Nug through Cthulhu, and the ancestor of Yogash the Ghoul according to H. P. Lovecraft's Family Tree of Azathoth.

By stating Nug to be grandfather of the same ghouls in his 1980 story "The Descent into the Abyss", Carter might have intended to  harmonise Lovecraft's family tree with his own lore, perhaps suggesting a connection between Shaurash-ho and Naggoob, as both are related to Nug and the ghouls. Several possibilities exist, such as "Naggoob" being simply the Hyperborean name for Shaurash-ho.

Alternatively, it's also possible that Shaurash-ho mated with Naggoob, or with one of his descendants, and gave birth to Yogash the Ghoul, since there is no indication that Naggoob himself descends from Nug, only that the ghouls descend from both.

Naggoob is not to be confused with Nagob, a mysterious character mentioned in "Out of the Aeons" who, in 1932, was believed to be in possession of the genuine scroll of T'yog.

Nahum Gardner (1831 - 1883) is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Colour Out of Space", first published in Weird Tales, March 1937.

### Overview
Gardner was a farmer in the farming land west of Arkham that would come to be known as "the Blasted Heath". He was married to a woman named Nabby who bore him three children, Zenas (? - 1883), Thaddeus (1868 - 1883) and Merwin (? - 1883). He is described as "a lean, genial person of about fifty, living with his wife and three sons on the pleasant farmstead in the valley." The entire family, including Nahum himself, was killed after exposure to the alien Colour Out of Space.

Gardner's best friend was a neighbouring farmer named Ammi Pierce; Pierce bore witness to much of the tragedy which befell the Gardner family. Telling Nahum's story 45 years later, "Ammi had nothing but praise for him after all these years."

### History
In June 1882, a meteorite made planetfall on Gardner's land. Over the following months, whatever alien organism had been aboard proceeded to infect and mutate the surrounding plant and animal life, including the Gardners themselves. Succumbing to the toxic and madness-inducing effects of the Colour, Nabby and Thaddeus lost their minds before their deaths, while Zenas and Mervin disappeared: their remains were later found at the bottom of the well, with the suggestion that they fell victim to whatever presence the Colour exerted down there. Nahum himself was the last to die, falling to insanity before passing. (: "The Colour Out of Space")

fullContent:
"Name and Number" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, featuring the occult investigator Titus Crow.  Written in 1981, it first appeared in the July 1982 issue of the Anglo-Italian fanzine Kadath in a special issue dedicated to occult detectives. 

### Synopsis
Talking to his associate Henri-Laurent de Marigny, Crow claims responsibility for the death of a prominent arms merchant--and insists his intervention saved the world from the greatest threat it had ever faced.

### Characters
Henri-Laurent de Marigny: The story's narrator, he is looking back on events that happened many years earlier, in 1964, before his and Titus Crow's escape from the destruction of Blowne House (dated October 4, 1968) and de Marigny's return (at least eight years later) from Elysia. De Marigny notes that his "deep interest in darkling matters...was probably inherited, sealed into my personality as a permanent stamp of my father, the great New Orleans mystic Etienne-Laurent de Marigny." Henri mentions that "my father sent me out of America as a child in the late thirties"; the chronology suggests that he was born no earlier than the 1920s, making him a decade or so Crow's junior.) The story also refers to de Marigny and Crow's "involvement with the Wilmarth Foundation (that vast, august and amazingly covert body, dedicated to the detection and the destruction of Earth’s elder evil...)." 

Titus Crow: Reintroduced Crow as "one of London’s foremost occultists," de Marigny remarks on his stature, his leonine good looks, and the sheer weight of intellect which seemed invariably to shine out from behind those searching, dark eyes of his. In his flame-red, wide-sleeved dressing-gown, he might easily be some wizard from the pages of myth or fantasy.De Marigny tells him he is “the sanest man I ever met"--a judgement Crow demurs from. He does, however, accept the compliment that he is “one of the country’s greatest paleographers”--“second only to Professor Gordon Walmsley of Goole," he agrees.

At the time of the story, Crow lives in a "bungalow dwelling on Leonard’s Heath known as Blowne House"--Leonard's Heath being a fictional park on the outskirts of London.

Sturm Magruser V: Born 1 April 1921 and died 4 March 1964, almost 43 years old. The head of Magruser Systems UK, a "weapons manufacturing company of world repute," and according to Crow "the greatest peril the world has ever faced!" His company owned 10 manufacturing plants in seven countries, including one outside Oxford. He offered the British military a "secret" national defence system "which will effectively make the atom bomb entirely obsolete." In fact, according to Crow, he “intended to destroy the world, reduce us to savagery, return us to the Dark Ages" and "turn the world into a desert"--and may possibly "have aimed at total destruction—no survivors at all!”
