The Nameless City is a ruined city created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story of the same name. 

### Description
Located somewhere in the Arabian desert, possibly modern-day Yemen, the Nameless City was built in prehistory by a species of quadrupedal reptilian creatures, and thus one of its most distinctive aspects is the proliferation of low ceilings. (: "The Nameless City")

When built, the city had been located deep beneath the ocean, as its saurian inhabitants felt perfectly at home underwater, but the same cataclysm which sank Atlantis and Mu caused it to rise above the surface. This spelt its doom, as the inhabitants were ill-suited to survival beneath the burning desert sun, and the few survivors fled to the deepest subterranean sections of what remained. Currently, the Nameless City is described by Laban Shrewsbury as a "domain of Hastur", and serves as a safe harbor for the Byakhee and their allies. (: "The Keeper of the Key")

### Behind the Mythos
It has been suggested that the real-world abandoned city of Irem was the inspiration for the Nameless City; in his Commonplace Book, Lovecraft had copied out its Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. As a result of the Orientalist fad of the time, Iram was much better known as a folk tale during Lovecraft's career than it is in the twenty-first century, and it can be seen that "The Nameless City" is not the only tale in the Mythos that has taken inspiration from it.

The Islamic holy book "The Quran" mentions Iram by name, "Ubar:, a city of towers or "lofty buildings". Its inhabitants were a people known as the Ad ('Ud), and they were given over to evil, having turned away from holy teachings. A prophet named Hud was sent to try and turn the people back to goodness but he was ignored. As a result, Iram was drowned in a sandstorm that raged for seven nights and eight days. Iram vanished beneath the sands as though it had never existed.

An updated second edition was released in 2023, credited to the same writers, with the main differences being new artwork, player handouts, and maps. Despite being an update, it claims a lower page count than the previous edition at only 202. Hardcover and digital versions both received a release.

Nancy Kilpatrick (b. 1946) is a Canadian writer and editor who works mainly in the dark fantasy and horror genres; she's best-known for her vampire stories. She has contributed to several Cthulhu Mythos anthologies, and in 2023 self-published the collection Thirteen Plus-1 Lovecraftian Narratives, with a foreword by S. T. Joshi.

Kilpatrick has published 21 novels, more than 200 short stories, and six short-story collections. She has edited 15 anthologies, including Nevermore!: Tales of Murder, Mystery, and the Macabre, a tribute to Edgar Allan Poe. She is also the author of the non-fiction The Goth Bible: A Compendium for the Darkly Inclined. In addition to her own name, she also publishes under the pseudonyms Amarantha Knight and Desiree Knight.

Nargis-Hei is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Doom That Came to Sarnath".

### Background
Nargis-Hei was the king of Sarnath at the time of the city's destruction from the vengeance of Bokrug. Nargis-Hei and his nobles had been feasting and reveling in the banquet hall of the royal palace on the thousand year anniversary of the conquest of the city of Ib and the genocide of its nonhuman inhabitants. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath") 

On the night of the celebration, dark shadows were observed descending from the moon into the lake, and Sarnath became shrouded in a green mist. Strange lights were seen on the water, followed by a significant rising of the elevation of the lake. Near the hour of midnight the banquet hall was overrun by a horde of Ibians, and the king and his nobles were no longer among the living. The people fled the city never to return, and Sarnath itself would vanish, leaving nothing but the lakeshore where the city once stood. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

Nasht and Kaman-Thah are a pair of fictional characters created by H. P. Lovecraft for his fantasy novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Description
Nasht and Kaman-Thah are bearded, pshent-wearing priests who guard a cavern-temple where a pillar of flame burns. This Cavern of Flame is located just after the gates that separate the Waking World from the Dreamlands, following a stair of seventy steps that dreamers may descend when they enter the realm of dream. After Nasht and Kaman-Thah's station, there is a much longer stair of seven hundred steps, which dreamers may descend in order to pass through the Gate of Deeper Slumber, leading to the Enchanted Wood.

When Randolph Carter spoke to Nasht and Kaman-Thah about his desire to find Kadath, the priests advised against it, warning Carter that the Gods of Earth would be displeased, and reminding him that no human is aware of Kadath's location. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

In "The Gods of Earth", by Gary Myers, Nasht and Kaman-Thah are themselves identified as Gods of Earth, along with Nath-Horthath.

Nathaire (c. 1230-1281) is a fictional character, the antagonist of Clark Ashton Smith's story "The Colossus of Ylourgne".

He is described as "thrice-infamous", being an "alchemist, astrologer and necromancer". He is noted for "his minikin stature, his deformity and ugliness." There were rumours about his "obscure nativity":People said that he was fiend-begotten...his father being no less a personage than Alastor, demon of revenge; and his mother a deformed and dwarfish sorceress. From the former, he had taken his spitefulness and malignity; from the latter, his squat, puny physique. Before coming to Vyônes in 1275, Nathaire "had travelled in Orient lands, and had learned from Egyptian or Saracenic masters the unhallowed art of necromancy, in whose practice he was unrivalled." 

Through his "remarkable power" of "mesmeric persuasion", Nathaire was able to attract a school of some ten followers, "young men of the most brilliant promise," whom he "plunged into bottomless and ghoulish iniquities," giving him a reputation as "a corrupter of youth." One of those students was Gaspard du Nord, who withdrew from Nathaire's fellowship "after learning the enormities that would attend his further initiation." 

Nathaire is permanently lamed by a cobblestone aimed by a mob in 1278. He mysteriously leaves the town in 1281, absconding with his followers to the fortress of Ylourgne, where they create the Colossus of Ylourgne by reanimating and combining the dead of Averoigne. He merges with this abomination and uses it to go on a grisly rampage across the province, finally assaulting Vyônes where his spree is ended by the counter-sorcery of Gaspard.

Nathaniel Hawthorne (4 July 1804 - 19 May 1864) was an American author, many of whose works, like those of H. P. Lovecraft, centre around his native New England. Lovecraft praised his novel The House of the Seven Gables as "New England's greatest contribution to weird literature" in the essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature", and also discussed Hawthorne's role in the genre.

According to An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia, compiled by leading scholars S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz, several of Lovecraft's stories drew inspiration from those of Hawthorne. These include:

*"The Dreams in the Witch-House" (the unfinished novel Septimius Felton)
*The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath (The Marble Faun, "The Great Stone Face")
*"The Case of Charles Dexter Ward" (The House of the Seven Gables)
*"The Outsider" ("Fragments from the Journal of a Solitary Man")

The writings of Lovecraft's friend and contemporary Robert E. Howard have also been favourably compared to Hawthorne's work.

Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee (born c. 1871) is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, and the protagonist of his horror sci-fi novella The Shadow Out of Time. He is a professor of political economy at Miskatonic University, and, from 1908 until 1913, a victim of the Great Race of Yith.

### Biography
Peaslee was born in Haverhill, Massachusetts, about 1871, the son of Jonathan and Hannah (Wingate) Peaslee. He enrolled in Miskatonic University in 1889, at the age of 18, and after graduation studied economics at Harvard. In 1895, he became an instructor in political economy at Miskatonic, promoted to associate professor in 1898 and becoming a full professor in 1902.

He married Alice Keezar, also of Haverhill, in 1896; their children are Robert K. (b. 1898), Wingate (b. 1900) and Hannah (b. 1903). They lived at 27 Crane Street in Arkham.

### Possession
Peaslee fears he is losing his mind when he unaccountably sees strange vistas of other worlds and of the Yithian library city. He also feels himself being led about by these creatures and experiences how they live. When he is returned to his own body, he finds that those around him have judged him insane due to the actions of the Yithian that possessed his body for the past five years. While he was experiencing a Yithian existence in Earth's ancient past, the Yithian occupying his body was experiencing a human one in the present day.

His son is Wingate Peaslee, also a Miskatonic University professor, and the only family member who doesn't cut ties with Nathaniel. Instead, Wingate uses his knowledge of psychology to try to help his father.

### Behind the Mythos
There are autobiographical aspects to the character. The years of Peaslee's amnesia correspond to the timespan of Lovecraft's adolescent nervous breakdown, which forced him to drop out of high school and withdraw from society. During this period, Lovecraft suffered from facial tics, which may be reflected in the Yithian-possessed Peaslee's inability to control his facial muscles. The feeling Lovecraft described, upon returning to Providence after living in New York City for two years, that he was "awakening from the queer dream about being away from home" has been called "the cornerstone upon which Lovecraft built his masterpiece, 'The Shadow out of Time'." But An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia, which calls Peaslee perhaps "the most thoroughly developed of HPL's characters", notes that there are parallels as well to Lovecraft's father, Winfield Scott Lovecraft, who also displayed eccentric behavior during a five-year period of madness.

fullContent:
"Nathicana" is a narrative poem by H. P. Lovecraft, first published in 1927 in The Vagrant. It has been included in some Lovecraft collections, such as The Doom that Came to Sarnath (1971).

The poem shares themes in common with Lovecraft's Dreamlands cycle.

### Synopsis
The narrative is set in the pale, mist-covered gardens of Zaïs: a place of beauty and tranquility, with white nephalotë flowers, crystalline lakes and silent streamlets running under alabaster bridges. The sky is filled with alien suns and planets, as well as "the crescent Banapis". At night, "the white vapours of Yabon" fall over the landscape.

One night, the narrator meets and falls in love with a mysterious woman, the titular Nathicana. The two spend time together in the gardens and "dream in a world made of dreaming". They live happily until the arrival of the dreaded "season of Dzannin", in which the suns and planets shine red, as do the crescent Banapis and the vapours of Yabon, reddening in turn the flowers, lakes and streamlets, and making even the alabaster bridges seem pink.

The narrator searches for their beloved through the ubiquitous red mist, but seems to find themself in a new world: "a horrible coma call'd living", inhabited by bright hollow "phantoms of beauty". The phantoms, although superficially beautiful like Nathicana, are entirely evil. It is only in dreams now that the narrator is able to find Nathicana.

As the poem ends, the narrator is brewing a deadly potion, hoping that suicide will free them and allow them to return to the white gardens of Zaïs where "the deathless, restor'd Nathicana" awaits them.

"Nation of Disease: The Rise & Fall of a Canadian Legend" is a short story by author Jonathan Sharp. It is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Written as a media article, the story follows the career of a band as the two main members grow more and more obsessed with the occult, incorporating recordings which they believe come from somewhere beyond our own world. As their mania grows, their behaviour becomes increasingly erratic, and culminates in one killing the other in the middle of a particularly deranged concert.

### Characters
* Darren "Krankenheit" Cross, the lead singer of Nation of Disease.
* Stuart "Stahl" Smith, keyboards and electronics for the band, and seemingly the driving force being their degeneration into occultism.

### Publication History
"Nation of Disease: The Rise & Fall of a Canadian Legend" was published in the Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss in 2013.

### Trivia
* Lyrics which appear in one of Nation of Disease's tracks include the repetition of the phrase "Aklo Sabaoth". This is a reference to the ritual invoked by Wilbur Whateley in the H. P. Lovecraft story "The Dunwich Horror". The name of this song is "Dreams In The Witch House", a nod to another of Lovecraft’s stories.

fullContent:
"Necro-Nom-Nom-Nom-I-Con" is an episode of the animated series SpongeBob SquarePants. It was written by Luke Brookshier and first aired in 2024. 

### Synopsis
When SpongeBob was unable to properly make breakfast to serve at the Krusty Krab restaurant, his boss Mr. Krabs sends him to a bookstore to pick up a cookbook titled Breakfast Magic!, which ends up getting mixed up with a spellbook that a witch had ordered. SpongeBob brings the Necronomicon to the kitchen and finds a page about cooking breakfast. Despite listing some weird ingredients (including zombie teeth, dragon's breath and eye of newt), Mr. Krabs happened to have them in the freezer due to him being unable to pass up on a sale. After SpongeBob cooked the ingredients in a cauldron and gave out various breakfast items, all of the customers experienced some supernatural side effects, including sprouting new body parts or being transformed into food-like forms. 

Meanwhile, the witch noticed the mix-up and headed towards the Krusty Krab to retrieve her spellbook. By the time she gets there, the Necronomicon had already combined itself with some breakfast treats to become a monster. The witch tried to fight against it but the monster managed to incapacitate her with syrup. However, she was still able to transfer some of her magic into SpongeBob's spatula. After the monster ate his co-worker Squidward and the customers, SpongeBob defeated it using the power of dinner, freeing all of its victims. 

The episode ends with the witch retrieving the Necronomicon, and Mr. Krabs obtaining another spellbook that summons a giant skeleton and several ghosts.

### Behind the Mythos
The depiction of the Necronomicon in this episode was based on the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis from the Evil Dead franchise.

fullContent:
Necronauts is a horror comic book story written by Gordon Rennie and illustrated by Frazer Irving. It was originally serialised in the magazine 2000 AD from December 13 2000 to February 21 2001.

The story features four historical characters: Harry Houdini, H. P. Lovecraft, Charles Fort, and Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, teaming up against the forces of the Great Old Ones.

### Synopsis

### Part One
In the year 1926, celebrated stage magician and escapologist Harry Houdini practices for a stunt in which he holds his breath in a water-coffin for over seven minutes. Falling unconscious, he experiences a vision of a dark abyss inhabited by monstrous entities which try to seize him. Luckily, he escapes the monsters' clutches just in time to return to his body and regain consciousness. Despite dismissing the experience as a hallucination, Houdini admits to his brother Dash that he is trying to witness what the afterlife is like, and come back alive to tell the world about it.

Meanwhile, a secret coven known as the Illuminati learns about Houdini's activities from one of their psychic agents, who reports that Houdini has travelled deep beyond the Dreamlands and into the void inhabited by the Sleepers (a.k.a. the Great Old Ones), awakening them from their slumber. While Houdini was able to evade them, the other psychics who were secretly following him were all slain. The Illuminati leader murders the surviving psychic for the insolence of refusing to give out his soul to the Sleepers, then orders his men to summon the Tcho-Tchos to track down Houdini by his psychic scent.

In Providence, Rhode Island, horror writer Howard Phillips Lovecraft receives a visit from a talking raven informing him that the Sleepers have been awakened, and that his presence is required in New York.

In England, spiritualist author and physician Sir Arthur Conan Doyle participates in a séance in which the medium delivers him a message, explaining how Doyle's friend Houdini is now in grave danger. Suddenly possessed by one of the Sleepers, the medium tears off his own face in terror and dies, despite Doyle's efforts to save him. The Sleeper reanimates the medium's body and warns Doyle that it is too late: Houdini's life belongs to them already. Nevertheless, Doyle embarks to New York to try to save his friend.

### Part Two
Doyle arrives in New York on October 30, and while Houdini is still skeptical about the danger, he does admit to having experienced strange and unpleasant dreams ever since the water-coffin stunt incident. In these dreams, he invariably finds himself in a lightless realm and feels the presence of the things that dwell there, as well as lesser presences that he understands to be the human servants of these entities.

Houdini and Doyle realise they're being followed by cloaked figures which, when confronted, reveal themselves as faceless inhuman creatures. They attack Houdini with what looks like an orb of energy and warn Doyle to not interfere.

The Necronomicon is a fictional book created by H. P. Lovecraft. It is the archetypal book of forbidden knowledge whose contents threaten one's sanity, and serves as one of the centrepieces of Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. Numerous other authors, including Clark Ashton Smith, Brian Lumley, Ramsey Campbell, and Keith Herber, have added to its contents over the years.

In terms of the elements of Lovecraftian horror, one could suggest that the Necronomicon is as central to the conceits of the sub-genre as cosmic monsters, tentacles, and dreams. The Necronomicon rises from, feeds, and expresses the antiquarian, euhemeristic, occult, and pseudobibliographical elements that are almost universal in Mythos works.

### History
According to Lovecraft's pseudo-scholarly "History of the Necronomicon", the book was written in Damascus in the early 8th century by Abdul Alhazred, a "mad poet" from Sanaa in Yemen. He completed the work sometime before his mysterious death in 738 CE.

It was translated into Greek in 950 CE by Theodorus Philetas of Constantinople, who gave it the title Necronomicon. A Latin translation was made in 1228 by Olaus Wormius. 

It is banned in most countries and all organised ecclesiastics. (: "History of the Necronomicon")

According to Lovecraft's fiction, Robert W. Chambers took inspiration for his King in Yellow concept from rumours he had heard regarding the Necronomicon (: "History of the Necronomicon").

### Known Contents
### Lovecraft's Work 
*The Voorish sign ("The Dunwich Horror")
*A formula for mind transference ("The Thing on the Doorstep")
*Instructions on how to make the Powder of Ibn Ghazi ("The Dunwich Horror")
*A passage about the Crawling Ones and the Green Flame ("The Festival")
*Page 751 of the "complete" version contains a long chant capable of summoning Yog-Sothoth if used at the right time ("The Dunwich Horror")
*A large amount of information on the Antarctic Elder Things (At the Mountains of Madness)
*Stories about a ghoul, one having its conclusion torn off the Harvard volume of the Necronomicon (The Selected Letters of H.P. Lovecraft III)
* A line of asterisks that even the Arabian original used to censor itself (The Selected Letters of H.P. Lovecraft III)
*Page 984 contains a passage in the Naacal; no translation is given

shortDefinition: NecronomiCon is a convention about science fiction and horror, especially cosmic horror. The convention is held biannually (every two years). It has billed itself in recent years as "The International Festival of Weird Fiction, Art, and Academia."  N...
fullContent:
NecronomiCon is a convention about science fiction and horror, especially cosmic horror. The convention is held biannually (every two years). It has billed itself in recent years as "The International Festival of Weird Fiction, Art, and Academia."

NecronomiCon is the major event created and held by The Lovecraft Arts & Sciences Council, a nonprofit organization based in Providence, Rhode Island. They have a [https://www.weirdprovidence.org/ separate website] for their other activities with the motto "Keep Providence Eldritch."

It was founded in 1982,  and became a biannual event in 2018. It was originally held on or around Halloween (31 October) but is now held in late August of the years in which it is organized. It has traditionally featured two or more recognised science fiction authors as guests but has in more recent years featured a more expanded "celebrity" assortment. There is also an exhibitor and merchant area where artists, craftspeople and others offering goods and services can rent a table or booth.

The convention includes and features, subject to the number and length of entries, the H.P. Lovecraft Film Festival, a genre film festival featuring all standard categories (feature, short, animated, childrens, multimedia, new media). The film festival is international, allowing entries from outside the United States. It is also an officially listed film festival on Filmfreeway and IMDB / IMDB PRO.

A "Robert Bloch Award", shaped like the Shining Trapezohedron, is also attributed during the convention.

Finally, the various thesis material and other presentations from the breakout activities, community activities and academic readings and speeches are collected and published by Hippocampus Press.

Confusingly, there are as of 2023 no less than three identically named conventions. There is a roleplaying convention held irregularly, a general pop culture expo and NecronomiCon Providence which is the one that is the subject of this article.

Necronomicon is a 72-page Cthulhu Mythos comic book written by David Wohl and Chas! Pangburn, and featuring artwork from various artists. It was published digitally by Zenescope Entertainment in September 2024; a selection of variant covers were also created.

### Overview


### Synopsis
After the events related in Lovecraft's Legacy, Henry Jones, having taken the surname Lovecraft after his great-grandfather, and Spencer Holmes, a descendant of famed detective Sherlock, make their way to Morocco in search of the Nameless City and the cursed Necronomicon which lies inside. However, they are pursued by Hastur who steals the book from them before summoning a fearsome monster and taking his leave.

Although Lovecraft and Holmes are able to defeat the monster through the use of a variety of mystical artefacts, the Necronomicon remains in the hands of Hastur, and the two must lick their wounds and plan their next move.

The book also includes a subplot showing how the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred came to be involved with the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos, his writing of the Necronomicon, and his ultimate slaughter at the hands of an unknown entity.

fullContent:
Although the Necronomicon is a fictional book invented by H. P. Lovecraft, many publications over the years were named Necronomicon or purported to be the genuine article. Many more releases have used the book as inspiration, plot device or simply as a name-drop. This page aims to offer a guide to these releases.

### Books/Stories
*Alhazred: Author of the Necronomicon (Donald Tyson, 2006): novel.
*Black Velvet Necronomicon (Mike Dubisch, 2010): artbook.
*H.R. Giger's Necronomicon I & II (1977 & 1985): following a short movie, two artbooks with no link to the Mythos, supposedly made to complement the lost manuscript.
*The Illuminatus! Trilogy features references to Cthulhu as well as flashbacks to people reading the Necronomicon including on one such occasion someone looking at the frankly pornographic pages depicting intercourse between a Shoggoth and a human.
*Kolchak: Necronomicon (C. J. Henderson, 2012): illustrated stories.
* Metal Hurlant: "Spécial Lovecraft" (Les Humanoïdes Associés, 1978): contains "Le Necronomicon" by Phillipe Druillet, 2 illustrations were published in Autumn 1966 in Anubis.
*The Lovecraft Necronomicon Primer: A Guide to the Cthulhu Mythos (T. Allan Bilstad, 2011)
* The Necronomicon (J. Vernon Shea): A short story which was annotated by Lovecraft. first published in Dragon & Microchips: Le Seul Fanzine Qui Rêve.
*The Necronomicon Files: The Truth Behind Lovecraft's Legend (John Wisdom Gonce III & Daniel Harms, 2003): a study of the Necronomicon books
*The Necronomicon: Selected Stories and Essays Concerning the Blasphemous Tome of the Mad Arab (Robert M. Price, 2002): an anthology of fiction and essays dealing with the Necronomicon by Chaosium.
*Pseudonomicon: the title of Gavin Chappell’s 2011 "Best Of" anthology for the magazine Schlock! is a clear nod to the Necronomicon.

### Comic Books & Manga
*Fables: in issue #130 of Bill Willingham's modern day fantasy epic, one of the minor characters, a little girl named Junebug, discovers a copy of the Necronomicon while exploring her family's new home in Fabletown.
*Forbidden Scrollery: set in the long-running Touhou franchise, the first chapter features Kosuzu owning the kanji edition of the Necronomicon. Despite the letters being written in kanji, the scribe and language are unknown. Marisa wanted to borrow the book, but it was too expensive.
*Necronomicon (Patrice Wooley, 2007): French graphic novel.
*Necronomicon (William Messner-Loebs, 2008): a four issues comic, art by Andrew Ritchie.
*Savage Pencil's Rock'n'Roll Necronomicon (Savage Pencil, 1992): a collection of Savage Pencil's cartoons.

### Films

*Necronomicon (Richard Driscoll, 2023)
*Necronomicón (Marcelo Schapces, 2018)
*Necronomicon (1993)
*Necronomicon - Geträumte Sünden (Jess Franco, 1968): German erotic film, allegedly based on a story from a Necronomicon book read by Franco.

Necronomicon Press is a small-press publisher of H. P. Lovecraft-related content based in the United States.

### Overview
Established in 1976 by Marc A. Michaud as an outlet for the writings of H. P. Lovecraft, over the years Necronomicon Press have expanded their scope to include other Cthulhu Mythos contributors, as well as critical works from many other authors (generally published in journal form), and at least one biography of Lovecraft's life.

Authors whose works have been published by Necronomicon Press include H. P. Lovecraft, Robert E. Howard, Clark Ashton Smith, Richard F. Searight, Ramsey Campbell, Hugh B. Cave, Brian Lumley, Brian Stableford, and S. T. Joshi

Necronomicon: Book of the Dead is a 1993 horror anthology film based on the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Overview
Consisting of adaptations of three of Lovecraft’s works - "The Rats in the Walls", "Cool Air" and "The Whisperer in Darkness", each of which featured a different director at the helm - connected by an original wraparound story, Necronomicon: Book of the Dead is an English-language film and runs to a total of 96 minutes.

### Segments

*"The Library": starring screen Mythos regular Jeffrey Combs as H. P. Lovecraft himself, "The Library" acted as the wraparound segment and involves a fictionalised Lovecraft reading stories from a copy of the Necronomicon held in a monastery. Directed by Brian Yuzna.
*"The Drowned": purporting to be an adaptation of "The Rats in the Walls", it features a character named Edward De Lapoer, although he is placed in a different setting and storyline. Directed by Christophe Gans.
*"The Cold": a fifty-minute black-and-white take on "Cool Air". Directed by Shûsuke Kaneko.
*"Whispers": adapted from "The Whisperer in Darkness". Also directed by Brian Yuzna.

fullContent:
Necronomicon: The Dawning of Darkness, also known as Necronomicon: The Gateway to Beyond, is a 2001 video game developed by Wanadoo Edition and released for Windows and the PlayStation video game console.

The game shares its engine with a pair of Dracula-themed games previously released by Wanado, Dracula: Resurrection and Dracula: The Last Sanctuary.

### Description
The game is set in 1927, where the ordinary life of William H. Stanton is affected by matters of the occult and darker truths about our world.

### Plot Summary
The plot of the game draws heavily from The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, with some of the characters re-named and repurposed.  The protagonist, William Staunton of Providence, Rhode Island circa the 1920s or 30s, is greeted at the door by a frantic friend, Edgar Wycherly, who shoves a strange, pyramid-like artifact into his hands and tells him not to give it to anyone: "not even to me… especially if I ask for it."  Edgar leaves, but minutes later, William receives another guest: a psychiatrist, Dr. Robert Eagleton, working for Edgar's father. Edgar has recently moved out of the family home after an argument and several strange chemical experiments, and Eagleton wants William to look in on Edgar for the sake of his mental health. William's attempts to find Edgar's new home are disrupted by the unfriendly population of nearby [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pawtuxet_Village Pawtuxet Village], until he finally gets information from a swindling grocer (a situation meant to call to mind The Shadow Over Innsmouth, but with a comic bent).  Finally, he makes contact with Edgar, who initially does not recognize him, but insists that he is fine, and urges William to dissuade Eagleton and his father.  He also introduces Edgar to a new friend, Dr. Owens, a mysterious chemist.

Still concerned for his friend, William begins to investigate Edgar's 18th-century ancestor, Gregor Herschell – Edgar showed a strong interest in Herschell, which may have provoked his change in behavior.  William soon uncovers documents and stories that suggest Herschell's involvement in occult activities, kidnappings, and disappearances (many of these documents are taken directly from The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, with slightly updated English, and Herschell's name substituting for Joseph Curwen). He also learns Herschell may have been burned alive by either a collaborator who learned too much, or by a mob. After discovering several of Herschell's letters in Edgar's home, William reports back to Eagleton, and Edgar is forcibly taken to an asylum.

William eventually locates a bungalow once owned by Herschell, and confirms that Edgar was making use of it. There are extensive caverns below, where William discovers corpses, and pits in the floor that seem to contain unseen, snarling monsters. fullContent:
Throughout its long history, the fictional Necronomicon has been translated and transcribed many times, giving rise to a number of distinct variants. This page aims to give a guide to these variants.

### Variants Originating From The Lovecraft Circle's Works

### The Greek Translation
In AD 950, Theodorus Philétas of Constantinople made a Greek translation named the Necronomicon (Τὸ Νεκρονόμικον) (: "History of the Necronomicon") of the Kitab al Azif. Philétas later translated the Book of Eibon. (: Ex Libris Miskatonici)

In 1050, the Patriarch Michael suppressed the book and had many of its copies burned. In 1232, it was again suppressed by Pope Gregory IX (: "History of the Necronomicon") and put on the Index Expurgatorius. (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft 2.307)

Sometime between 1500 and 1550 in Italy, Philétas' Greek translation was printed (: "History of the Necronomican") or in 1567 (: Miscellaneous Letters) in Italy. Another account claims that this edition was in 1501, and was likely the work of Aldus Manutius, the founder of the Aldine Press. (: Keeper's Compendium)

In 1692, the last known copy was lost in a library fire in Salem and another was rumoured to be owned by Richard Upton Pickman, who disappeared in 1926. (: "History of the Necronomicon")

### The Latin Translation
A Latin translation of Philétas' Greek version was made in 1228 by someone who signed himself Olaus Wormius (: "The Festival", "History of the Necronomicon"), although that was a long time before the more famous scholar of that name, Ole Worm (1588-1654), was born. (: The Womb of Time) According to one account, this Olaus Wormius was a black magician who was burned at the stake. (: "The Necronomicon", Donald A. Wollheim)

Its prefatory note indicates that the original Arabian text was considered lost. (: "History of the Necronomicon")

In 1232, this edition was outlawed by Pope Gregory IX (: "History of the Necronomicon") and put on the Index Expurgatorius, (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft 2.307) after which many copies were destroyed, although it was widely printed until then.

In the 15th century, the Latin translation was printed with black letters by a German publisher. (: "History of the Necronomicon")

It was also printed in Lyons, France in 1472. (: The Illuminatus! Trilogy)

In the 17th century, another printing was made in Madrid (: "History of the Necronomicon") in 1647. (: "The Adventure of the Six Silver Spiders") The title of the opening section is "A Warning To Those Who Peruse This Book." (: "Demons of Cthulhu")

There is one known remaining copy of the German edition locked in the British Museum, and one supposedly owned by an American millionaire. (: "History of the Necronomicon")

Four copies are known to exist of the Spanish edition, in the Bibliothèque Nationale in France, the Widener Library in Harvard, Miskatonic University, and Buenos Aires' university. (: "History of the Necronomicon")

Other secret copies exist: one at a Londo

fullContent:
Necrophosis is a first-person horror adventure game developed by Dragonis Ares and Adonis Brosteanu. Inspired by the works of Polish artist Zdzisław Beksiński, the game was released for PC by Dragonis Games in April 2025.

### Overview
Set in a decaying alternate future, Necrophosis is a "walking sim"-type game, in which the player explores the world and its story as much through the visual clues incorporated throughout the intricately-designed scenery as through the sparse narration.

Puzzle-solving is key in Necrophosis, with, unusually for an exploration game, combat being entirely absent.

### Behind the Mythos
At one point during exploration, the player witnesses a field of stars over which Lovecraft's "death may die" quote from "The Call of Cthulhu" is recited: "That is not dead which can eternal lie, And with strange aeons even death may die."

Prior to the game's release, Dragonis Ares released digital images of a Cthulhu model which was intended for inclusion in the game; whether these renders made it into the final product before release remains unknown at the time of writing.

The Neflords are a Lovecraftian-like race of dark gods in the fictional universe of the Hack/Slash comic book by Devil's Due Publishing.

### Background
Neflords are an eldritch race whose forms are fleshy flying masses of flesh with many tentacles protruding from the bottom. They rule the dead dimension of Nef and its demonic inhabitants, including the humanoid Nefspawn. Despite being powerful gods they cannot create, as they are gods of death and suffering.

To create they need humans, whom are pure, good, and virgin. Neflords find humans (heros) and offer them gifts (music and talents). The humans use those gifts and become famous, earn glory, and receive the love of many. Using the magic they are taught by the Neflords, they send them pure humans, who are violated and impregnated by the Neflords. Once the "hero" has done his part, the gifts leave him. He in turn finds other "heroes" who want the same thing he wanted. Nefspawn are produced from these unions, and have been sent to Earth as assassins against Cassandra Hack.

fullContent:
"Negotium Perambulans" is a short story by British writer E. F. Benson. It was first published in the November 1922 issue of Hutchinson's Magazine.

### Plot

The story details the tale of a man, who, as a child, comes to an isolated fisher village in West Cornwall and is enchanted with it. He stays at his uncles house during this entire time, hearing his uncle (who is a vicar) give sermons that are especially terrifying, mostly when referring to a couple of painted panels, on which is detailed the horrible death of a sacrilegious person at the hands of of a horrible creature. The panel bears the following biblical text:

"Negotium perambulans in tenebris," mistakenly translated as "the pestilence that walketh in darkness" and coming from the ninety first psalm.

When he grows up he eventually moves to London and only when his education is complete, he returns, intending never to leave again.

As he learns from his widowed aunt, the person, who possessed the house, on whose grounds the murder described in the church panel.

The man had died, after one night loosing the light with whose possession he became obsessed and was found dead, as a sack of skin and bones, with all blood drenched from him.

The young man then meets an old acquaintance of his, an artist, who now lives in the cursed house. Everything on him and his drawings repel and also attract the young man and thusly, he visits his home. A short while after, he is found by the young man in darkness, cornered by the horrible thing. The young man tries to fight it of, but he cannot harm it and he cannot prevent it from reducing the artist to but skin and bones.

The young man leaves, resolute never to see his beloved village again.

### Setting

A number of the locations mentioned in the story are real. Both Penzance and Newlyn are towns on the western tip of Cornwall. A road named "The Coombe" (referring to the Combe valley, sometimes steep and narrow, usually without a watercourse) runs through Newlyn, which might have inspired the combe wherein Polearn lies. Southward along the coast from Newlyn is the Penlee Quarry.

Polearn itself doesn't exist. Mousehole lies two miles along the coast road from Penzance, and Mousehole Lane appears to run through a shallow valley, which may be the combe referred to.

Neil Baker is an author, editor and artist based in Ontario, Canada, although he grew up in England. In 2014 he founded the small press publishing house April Moon Books, a company which specialises in horror fiction and continues to publish Cthulhu Mythos material to this day. His Mythos work has been featured in anthologies including World War Cthulhu, The Dark Rites of Cthulhu, and Return of the Old Ones.

In addition to this, Baker has also penned a Cthulhu Mythos children’s book, A Picnic at the Mountains of Madness, and has contributed work to Jeffrey Thomas's Punktown milieu, amongst other things.

Nemesis, whose name as a mortal was Hadron, is a character created by Michael Alan Nelson for his Fall of Cthulhu series of Mythos comic books. Nemesis made his first appearance in the very first issue of Fall of Cthulhu, titled "Harlot", although he played little part in the events of the main story arc, his character being fleshed out somewhat in the prequel spin-off Fall of Cthulhu Volume 6: Nemesis.

### History
Hadron was the D'harin, or high priest of Vesh, in Atlantis in the days leading up to the sinking of that once-proud civilisation. He was blindsided by the Oracle Sysyphyx, who was herself in league with the Outer God Nyarlathotep, and tricked into overthrowing his brother, the King, through a series of complex schemes. 

Ultimately, the Oracle's prophecy bore fruit: Hadron was the last of his people, bore witness to the destruction of his civilisation, and later became immortal like a god when Nyarlathotep transformed him into an undying housecat for his own amusement (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 6: Nemesis).

In the modern day Hadron, now going by the name of Nemesis, assisted Nyarlathotep's avatar Mr. Arkham by stealing the Gray Man's knife from the Arkham Police Department lockup. In the aftermath of the war between Nyarlathotep and Nodens he declared himself the victor, as he was the only "god" left undefeated. However, he played no part in the actual war and, being in effect a housecat, had nothing to gain from this declaration, nor any way to force his will upon the world.

The Nemesis of Flame is a fictional entity featured in the short story "The Last Test" (1928), by Adolphe de Castro and H. P. Lovecraft.

### History
As its name indicates, the Nemesis of Flame is a fiery creature that seems to be made of living flames. At some point, Dr. Alfred Clarendon's studies into occultism taught him how to summon this entity, having possibly learned it from a man in Yemen who had seen the legendary city of Irem.

Clarendon used his knowledge of the Nemesis of Flame to implicitly threaten Surama, and told James Dalton that the Nemesis of Flame might be the only way to destroy Surama, other than a stake through the heart.

After inoculating himself with a deadly extraterrestrial pathogen, Clarendon summoned the Nemesis of Flame to burn down his clinic with flames that "half resembled some nameless, Cyclopean creatures of nightmare". Surama laughed at first, until a bolt of lightning came straight from the sky and destroyed him. After his death, the flames "resumed their normal shape".

### Behind the Mythos
The Nemesis of Flame might take its name from the Algernon Blackwood story "The Nemesis of Fire", published in his 1908 collection John Silence, Physician Extraordinary. H. P. Lovecraft praised the John Silence stories, including "The Nemesis of Fire", in his essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature".

In Blackwood's story, the entity is identified by Silence as a fire elemental, employed in ancient Egypt to guard the tomb of a mummy and punish those who disturb it.

Captain Nemo is a fictional character created by the late French author Jules Verne, a pioneer of the science fiction genre. He first appeared in the 1870 novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas. Given Nemo's history of adventures in the depths of the ocean, it is perhaps unsurprising that the character has found its way into the Cthulhu Mythos in a variety of mediums.

### Overview
First conceived as a member of the Polish aristocracy, editorial pressures regarding international book sales forced Nemo's origins to be revised, his history being obscured in his first appearance; later, he would be described as the son of an Indian raja.

Nemo is a scientific visionary and explorer, as well as - in later iterations by other authors, at least - something of an anti-imperialist freedom fighter. He is a highly intelligent man, well versed in advanced science, able to speak multiple languages, and an accomplished musician. He used his scientific expertise to design and construct a technologically-advanced submarine, the Nautilus, which he used in his exploration of the deep ocean.

### Trivia

fullContent:
"Nemo Me Impune Lacessit" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
At his sprawling mansion, a two hundred-year-old warlock seeks revenge on a group of amoral people who wronged him in the past. Using his powers to invoke Mythos entities, he tailors each one's fate to their individual personality.

### Characters
*Monty, a sorcerer who has lived for over two hundred years, presumably by calling on his knowledge of the Cthulhu Mythos entities. He claims to have "wrested man’s deepest lore from its thousand crypts," but presents himself as an "oddball, bookish...Old World-ly man of late middle age."
*Koboldus, Monty's servant, who appears as an "elderly, thick-set little man." His true form features "scales and talons." He does not speak in front of outsiders, because "that which he is in truth possesses a Voice that may not be disguised."
*Valerie, porn star and ex-wife of Monty's. She has a "long-limbed flamingo strut" and russet hair. Monty describes her as "born to money, and college 'educated,'" and as a "fidgeting, self-adoring gypsy." She dies in a climactic ritual involving the Hounds of Tindalos, a spider-creature called Araknadd, and the Outer God Azathoth.
*Kamin Quartz, porn star and Valerie's new partner. He has "a drifting walk, a cool bodily denial of effort, and ...hold[s] his handsomeness still and unwrinkled." He dies in the same ritual as Valerie.
*Bo Beck, a pornographer with designs on producing snuff films. He is fat--"the teasing, malevolent type of pachyderm"--and "glossy-bearded like a Neronian senator." He is killed by a Shoggoth.
*Natalie, Natalie's sister and production assistant on her porn films; she has an over-inflated sense of her own intelligence and an "aggrieved sense of personal worth." Described as a "leggy stork." She dies under the attentions of carnivorous Yuggothian roses.
*Roger, the producer of Valerie's porn films. He is taken to another dimension by an entity older than the Earth that drains him of his blood.

### Setting
The story takes place at Sternbrucke, Monty's mansion in an unnamed European nation. (The name is German for "Star Bridge.") Its "upper structures are scarcely more than three hundred years old"—the original living quarters having burned down in ""an unfortunate local disturbance at the turn of the seventeenth century"--while the extensive dungeons below "date from the tenth century, if not earlier." Its "ultimate, deepest corridors" were dug by "workers and artisans from the sea, some five miles distant."

### Publication History
"Nemo Me Impune Lacessit" was first published in horror periodical Whispers in March 1982. It has since appeared in the collections of Shea's own works The Autopsy and Other Tales (2008), Copping Squid and Other Mythos Tales (October 2009), and Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea (December 2017). It has been translated into German.

Neothelids were created by Wizards of the Coast in the 2nd Edition of the Dungeons & Dragons roleplaying game in 1998 and are now part of the Forgotten Realms lore, where they are colossal mutated offspring of the Illithids (aka, Mind Flayers) who were hated by all. They became part of the Cthulhu Mythos in Paizo Inc's Pathfinder roleplaying game in 2008, with the earliest mention being in the Darklands sourcebook, in which they were retconned to being the spawn of Shub-Niggurath.

### Physiology
Neothelids are gargantuan creatures with powerful psionic abilities which give them the ability to teleport on the battlefield, communicate with others telepathically, move objects telekinetically, and fly without wings. Their minds are strong enough to overwhelm weaker minds, sometimes fatally, and influence those with weak wills. Neothelids have the ability to ascertain where a target is going to teleport and thereby pursue said target. Physically they are superhumanely strong and have hides which can resist all blows except those of cold iron weapons, in addition to shrugging off spells cast by all but the very powerful. From their maws they exhale a cone of acid at their enemies and within are four barbed tongues which can inflict wounds as well as drag their prey into their mouths which can easily swallow smaller creatures. Biologically they are immortal but Neothelid eggs take centuries to hatch, though they can spawn hundreds of seugathi each month, creating armies within decades.

### Background
Neothelids are a race of powerful and foul worm-like creatures, that are cunning and intelligent. They are massive worms with four barbed tongues, drenched in slime, with incredibly tough hide and whose maws easily swallow smaller creatures. Millions were spawned on Golarion by Shub-Niggurath during the Age of Creation. Who then burrowed deep into the Darklands, establishing a great subterranean empire where they hunted and consumed each other for sport for tens of thousands of years. When other races arrived in the Darklands, they were overwhelmed by these races which bred at faster rates, which forced them to retreat, stopped hunting each other, and reproduce. Centuries later they began to expand their territory, and are currently waging a proxy war with the intellect devourers. They usually live alone and when they rarely do gather, it's in small groups. Seugathi offspring are used as servants, their strongest as bodyguards, and the seugathi speak on behalf of the Neothelids.

Nephren-Ka, "The Black Pharaoh" (also called Nophru-Ka) is a fictional pharaoh of Ancient Egypt. The character was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Outsider", depicted as being a worshipper of the Outer God Nyarlathotep. Later versions of the Cthulhu Mythos presented him as an avatar of Nyarlathotep himself. 

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Lovecraft first mentioned Nephren-Ka in the short story "The Outsider" (written in March-August 1921, and published in April 1926), whose narrator says near the story's close:  Now I ride with the mocking and friendly ghouls on the night-wind, and play by day amongst the catacombs of Nephren-Ka in the sealed and unknown valley of Hadoth by the Nile. I know that light is not for me, save that of the moon over the rock tombs of Neb, nor any gaiety save the unnamed feasts of Nitokris beneath the Great Pyramid.... Nephren-Ka is alluded to briefly in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward (1927/1941), in which necromancer Edward Hutchinson signs one of his letters, "Nephren-Ka nai Hadoth, Edw. H." This seems to be some sort of invocation; his colleague Simon Orne signed a letter "Yogg-Sothoth Neblod Zin, Simon O." 

The most extensive treatment of the character in Lovecraft comes in "The Haunter of the Dark" (1935/1936), where he forms part of the history of the Shining Trapezohedron: The Pharaoh Nephren-Ka built around it a temple with a windowless crypt, and did that which caused his name to be stricken from all monuments and records. Then it slept in the ruins of that evil fane which the priests and the new Pharaoh destroyed, till the delver’s spade once more brought it forth to curse mankind. 

### Appearance
: Fragment of "The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath".}}

### Cult
Nyarlathotep is worshiped in this avatar by the Brotherhood of the Black Pharaoh.

### History
Nephren-Ka was supposedly the last pharaoh of the Third Dynasty of Egypt. He was the one who introduced the cult of the animal-headed gods to that nation and always stood out as a sorcerer. Nyarlathotep was not long in taking an interest in him and, summoning him to the city of Irem, proposed a bloody pact: Nephren-Ka would sacrifice thousands of victims in his honor and Nyarlathotep would give him the gift of prophecy. This was done and Nyarlathotep granted him the power to see the future. He secured the Shining Trapezohedron for Egypt, but after being convinced by the resident Haunter of the Dark, he had a lightless temple created to hold the stone and the deity within. That temple became a center of abominable happenings, and the rites carried out there were so monstrous the temple was destroyed.

The Nestene Consciousness is a Great Old One in the fictional universe of Doctor Who by the BBC.

### Background
The Nestene Consciousness is a hive mind race which is both a singular entity and a disembodied life force. It is the offspring of Shub-Niggurath, which spawned it on the planet Polymos. (: Millennial Rites, Craig Hinton)

Nestene exist as energy that can possess plastic. Described by the Doctor as "ruthlessly aggressive and intelligent". The Nestene Consciousness manifests either as a being of pure energy and force or as a mass of solid plastic. It's natural appearance is that of a many-tangled horror which is sort of a hybrid of a octopus, crab, and spider. Which is large enough to dwarf a radio telescope. Due to the stresses of the Last Great Time War, their biology have drastically changed, resulting in a form that is mostly plastic and manifests in a mostly liquid form possessing a humanoid face.

The Nestene Consciousness is able to exist in various places, various plaes, and various times. They travel across space in energy units, which are hollow plastic meteorites that are 8.5 inches in diameter and move across space in "clusters" which are swarm formations. Landing on worlds where they are collected by Autons and then placed into an environment tank where a plastic body to contain the brain is manufactured. Nestenes can absorb psychic energy from willing humans and covert their bodies into energy. A Nestene which had been absorbed into a human mind demonstrated the ability to project energy barriers, teleport, and materializing Autons.

### Auton
The Autons are robots that resemble plastic mannequins, each of which contains a fragment of the Nestene Consciousness. Their hands conceal wrist-guns which can kill or vaporize targets, and can temporarily disable a weakened Dalek. Some of the Autons can alter the shape of their limbs and features. Autons are extremely effective trackers, finding their targets via their brain-wave patterns.

fullContent:
New England is a region of the United States and the location of Lovecraft Country, the semi-imaginary setting of many Cthulhu Mythos tales.

New England comprises the states of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont, New Hampshire, Maine and Connecticut. The ancestral home of Algonquin Native Americans like the Narragansetts and the Wampanoag, New England was one of the first areas in North America to be colonized by English settlers. Their first colonies were established by religious Puritans at Massachusetts' Plymouth, Boston and Salem. Up through the American Revolution and behind, immigration to New England was dominated by departees from the country that gave the region its name, without the admixture of Dutch and German folk found in the Mid-Atlantic region, or the dependence on enslaved African labor of the Southern colonies.

### Horror
Lovecraft would sometimes suggest that New England was particularly conducive to evoking the feeling of horror that his fiction specialized in. In "The Picture in the House", the story that first mentions the key Lovecraft Country town of Arkham, Lovecraft declares that the true epicure in the terrible, to whom a new thrill of unutterable ghastliness is the chief end and justification of existence, esteems most of all the ancient, lonely farmhouses of backwoods New England; for there the dark elements of strength, solitude, grotesqueness, and ignorance combine to form the perfection of the hideous.Similarly, "The Colour Out of Space" refers to "farms, ancient and rocky, with squat, moss-coated cottages brooding eternally over old New England secrets". In "The Dunwich Horror", Henry Armitage muses: "Unseen things not of earth—or at least not of tri-dimensional earth—rushed foetid and horrible through New England’s glens, and brooded obscenely on the mountain-tops."

Thurber in "Pickman's Model" describes Pickman's "frightful pictures which turned colonial New England into a kind of annex of hell," shewing "a pack of ghouls and witches overrunning the world of our forefathers,"

### Insensitivity
At the same time, Lovecraft also used New England as a byword for a kind of prosaic insensitivity that failed to appreciate the weird: in "The Unnamable", Randolph Carter's friend Joel Manton is described as "born and bred in Boston and sharing New England’s self-satisfied deafness to the delicate overtones of life." When Carter's story "The Attic Window" shocks readers in the South and on the Pacific coast, "New England didn’t get the thrill and merely shrugged its shoulders at my extravagance."

When George Gammell Angell in "The Call of Cthulhu" records people's reactions to the psychic disturbances that accompany (as we learn later) the rising of R'lyeh, he finds that "[a]verage people in society and business—New England’s traditional “salt of the earth”—gave an almost completely negative result, though scattered cases of uneasy but formless nocturnal impressions appear here and there."

fullContent:
New Jersey is a state in the Mid-Atlantic region of the United States. It has been repeatedly used as setting for Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
H. P. Lovecraft visited New Jersey repeatedly; when he lived in New York City, he toured the nearby towns of Elizabeth (in October 1924 and again in June and August 1925) and Paterson (in August 1925). He returned to Paterson, where his friend James F. Morton was curator of the Paterson Museum, in May 1928. In the summer of 1931, he went with Frank Belknap Long to Asbury Park on the Jersey Shore; in summer 1934, he and the Longs returned to Asbury Park and the adjacent Ocean Grove.

But New Jersey features only incidentally in Lovecraft's fiction. One of the unfortunate residents of "The Shunned House" (written in October 1924) is William Harris, Jr., who served during the American Revolution as "a Captain in Rhode Island forces in New Jersey under Colonel Angell." In 1780, "he met and married Phebe Hetfield of Elizabethtown," whom he brought back to Providence and his cursed abode in 1781. Lovecraft was inspired to write "The Shunned House" by a house in Elizabeth, which he described in a letter:On the northeast corner of Bridge Street and Elizabeth Avenue is a terrible old house — a hellish place where night-black deeds must have been done in the early seventeen-hundreds — with a blackish unpainted surface, unnaturally steep roof, and an outside flight of stairs leading to the second story, suffocatingly embowered in a tangle of ivy so dense that one cannot but imagine it accursed or corpse-fed. In "The Call of Cthulhu" (written in 1926), Francis Wayland Thurston happens upon a report of the rescue of Gustaf Johansen while Thurston is "visiting a learned friend in Paterson, New Jersey; the curator of a local museum and a mineralogist of note." (This is a tip of the hat to Morton, who had amassed a renowned mineral collection at the Paterson Museum.)

Dr. Thomas Slauenwite, the narrator of the revision tale "Winged Death," was born in Trenton, New Jersey, on April 12, 1885.

### Other Mythos Writers

### Frank Belknap Long
Frank Belknap Long never specified the state that includes Partridgeville, the setting of his stories "The Space-Eaters" (1928) and "The Hounds of Tindalos" (1929); it's on a seacoast near New York City, which suggests Jersey, but could potentially be Connecticut or even Long Island, New York.

Long's novel The Horror from the Hills (1931), however, definitely has its climax in New Jersey, when Algernon Harris pursues Chaugnar Faugn from Asbury Park (where it committed a massacre) to Atlantic City before cornering it in the Jersey marshlands and dispelling it with an entropy machine.

### C. Hall Thompson

New Orleans is the largest city in Louisiana, a state in the Southern United States. It is notable for its French heritage and for its vibrant Creole culture. The city and state feature as a setting in H. P. Lovecraft's fiction, and in other tales of the Cthulhu Mythos.

New Orleans was for a time the home of Lovecraft's correspondent E. Hoffman Price; Lovecraft visited Price there in the summer of 1932.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction

### "Call of Cthulhu"
Louisiana features prominently in Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu" as a center of Cthulhu Cult activity. Inspector John Raymond Legrasse, a New Orleans Inspector of Police, tells the American Archaeological Society about a 1907 raid on "supposed voodoo meeting" in "the wooded swamps south of New Orleans". The cult gathering takes place in "a natural glade of the swamp", on "a grassy island of perhaps an acre’s extent, clear of trees and tolerably dry." It features "a great granite monolith some eight feet in height", from which a figurine of Cthulhu is recovered.

The gathering raided by Legrasse involved more than 50 cultists, and more apparently escaped into the swamp. They were responsible for some ten human sacrifices.

Legrasse hears reports that further into the swamp there is "a hidden lake unglimpsed by mortal sight, in which dwelt a huge, formless white polypous thing with luminous eyes.... [B]at-winged devils flew up out of caverns in inner earth to worship it at midnight."

Before turning to the American Archaeological Society, Legrasse seeks the advice of "authorities at Tulane University", a private school in New Orleans, about the Cthulhu Cult. They are of no help.

Legrasse lives at 121 Bienville Street--an actual street in New Orleans, though in the 21st century, at least, the address appears to be a parking lot.

### "Through the Gates of the Silver Key"
New Orleans appears again in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", co-written in 1932-33 by E. Hoffman Price, who was living in New Orleans at the time. The story is set in "the New Orleans home of this continent’s greatest mystic, mathematician, and orientalist," Etienne-Laurent de Marigny.  De Marigny is described in the story as Creole, a word signifying descent from those born in the French (and later Spanish) colony of Louisiana. Creoles are often of mixed racial heritage, though they may be of any ethnicity.

When de Marigny makes a cameo appearance in the revision tale "Out of the Aeons", he is described as  "the famous New Orleans mystic".

### "Medusa's Coil"
Though set in Missouri, the revision tale "Medusa's Coil", written with Zealia Bishop in 1930, makes repeated reference to New Orleans and Louisiana. The story's interlocutor, Antoine de Russy, comes from "an ancient, powerful, and cultivated line of Louisiana planters." He went to "a good school in Louisiana," and in 1885 marries "a distant cousin in New Orleans."

fullContent:
New Tales of the Miskatonic Valley: Further Adventures in Lovecraft Country is an anthology of adventure scenarios for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. Originaly created by Miskatonic River Press in 2009, it has been published by third-party content creator Stygian Fox since 2020, after a successful Kickstarter campaign completed in 2018.

The latest volume reprints the scenarios from the original New Tales of the Miskatonic Valley but in full colour, with new art, new maps and play aids, and includes a seventh scenario, "A Mother's Love," by Seth Skorkowsky.

### Contents
*Two Tales of Arkham
**The Reeling Midnight, by Tom Lynch. introduces Investigators to Arkham's truly decadent party scene.
**Wasted Youth, by Christopher Smith Adair, explores the roots of juvenile delinquency, culminating in a wild chase through the wilderness.
*A Tale of Dunwich
**Spirit of Industry, by Oscar Rios, takes Investigators to the village of Dunwich, where they explore old murders and an ancient mystery.
*A Tale of Foxfield
**Proof of Life, by Keith Herber, is a tale of extortion and madness in the Lovecraft Country town of Foxfield.
*Two Tales of Kingsport
**Malice Everlasting, by Oscar Rios, explores Kingsport and old grudges.
**The Night War, by Kevin Ross, sees the author of Kingsport, City in the Mists, revisit his creation when a veteran of the Great War is suddenly haunted by deadly nightmares.
*A Tale of Innsmouth
**A Mother's Love, by Seth Skorkowsky, author of the Valducan series, takes us to the hidden town Innsmouth, with all its squalor, dangers, and dark corruption in a brand new scenario for New Tales of the Miskatonic Valley, 2nd Edition.

New York City, located in New York state, is the largest city in the United States, and the center of its financial and publishing industries. H. P. Lovecraft lived there for a time after his marriage to Sonia Greene, and set some of his Cthulhu Mythos fiction there. Later writers have continued to use it as a Mythos setting.

### Lovecraft in NYC
Lovecraft first visited New York City in April 1922, invited by his future wife to stay with her for six days in her apartment at 259 Parkside Avenue in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighbourhood. He described his first impression of the city to his correspondent Maurice Moe:

I saw for the first times the Cyclopean outlines of New-York. It was a mystical sight in the gold sun of late afternoon; a dream-thing of faint grey, outlined against a sky of faint grey smoke. City and sky were so alike that one could hardly be sure that there was a city – that the fancied towers and pinnacles were not the merest illusions.

He returned to the city to July 1922 and again in August of that year; during the latter visit, a tour of the Dutch Reformed Church in Brooklyn, with his friend Rheinhart Kleiner, inspired Lovecraft's story "The Hound". 

Lovecraft moved to New York on March 2, 1924, marrying Greene the next day at St. Paul's Chapel in Manhattan, the oldest church building in New York City. Lovecraft and Greene moved in 1924 to 259 Parkside Avenue in Brooklyn's Flatbush neighborhood. After Greene relocated to Cincinnati for work, Lovecraft moved to 169 Clinton Street in Cobble Hill, Brooklyn. He described his Clinton Street home in horror terms:I conceived the idea that the great brownstone house was a malignly sentient thing — a dead, vampire creature which sucked something out of those within it and implanted in them the seeds of some horrible and immaterial psychic growth.Lovecraft disliked New York's "crude, foreign hostility and underbreeding", its "vulgar trade spirit and plebian hustle.” He called the city “an Asiatic hell’s huddle of the world’s cowed, broken, inartistic, and unfit.” He moved out of Brooklyn and back to Providence in 1926.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Lovecraft wrote three stories set in New York during his time there: "The Horror at Red Hook", written on August 1-2, 1925, is one of his most virulently xenophobic tales, reserving its choicest bile for the titular neighborhood on the Brooklyn waterfront:Red Hook is a maze of hybrid squalor near the ancient waterfront opposite Governor’s Island, with dirty highways climbing the hill from the wharves to that higher ground where the decayed lengths of Clinton and Court Streets lead off toward the Borough Hall.... The population is a hopeless tangle and enigma; Syrian, Spanish, Italian, and negro elements impinging upon one another, and fragments of Scandinavian and American belts lying not far distant. New York is a state in the United States of America, part of the Midatlantic region, adjacent to but not considered part of New England. While H. P. Lovecraft lived in and wrote repeatedly about New York City (see which), he also had a connection to the expansive, largely rural area to the north and west of the city, known as Upstate New York.

### Lovecraft and Upstate New York
Lovecraft's father, Winfield Scott Lovecraft, was born in Rochester, New York--a fact that was surely meaningful to the writer, given his preoccupation with ancestral taint and his father's descent into madness.

When the younger Lovecraft was living in Brooklyn with his wife Sonia Greene, he made his first visits to the state outside the city--visiting the near-upstate towns of  Yonkers and Tarrytown in September 1925, as well as the Long Island villages of Jamaica, Mineola, Hempstead, and Garden City. After his separation from Greene and his return to Providence, he visited her in Brooklyn in April 1928, during which time he and Frank Belknap Long took a car trip up the Hudson Valley. In May 1928, Lovecraft  visited Wilfred B. Talman in Spring Valley, in New York's Rockland County, returning through Tarrytown and Sleepy Hollow. (The latter village is, of course, the setting of one of America's most famous ghost stories, Washington Irving's "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow", but as Lovecraft notes of Irving in Supernatural Horror in Literature, "most of his ghosts are too whimsical and humorous to form genuinely spectral literature".)

In the spring of 1929, Lovecraft spent several weeks in Yonkers at the home of Vrest Orton. Later that year, Long drove him to West Shokan, N.Y., to visit correspondent Bernard Austin Dwyer. Concurrent tours of the nearby Dutch colonial towns of Kingston, Hurley, and New Paltz led to the travelogue “Travels in the Provinces of America” (1929). His last sojourn in Upstate New York seems to have been in Kingston in June 1930.

"The Lurking Fear" is likewise set in New York's Catskill Mountains, once again portrayed as a region of genetic degenerates. The story centers on Tempest Mountain,

"The Man of Stone", written by Lovecraft for Hazel Heald, switches the location from the Catskills to the Adirondacks, but features as a minor character Sam, a "barefoot old mountain decadent", who would be at home in either of Lovecraft's Catskills stories. 

The story's main antagonist is Daniel "Mad Dan" Morris, the descendant of Dutch settlers; his ancestor, William Van Kauran, settled in the colony of Rensselaerwyck after his grandfather was hanged as a wizard in the Netherlands, later crossing over the Hudson River to Esopus. The Van Kauran family was notorious for its supernatural powers from Kingston to Hurley, N.Y.; one of their enemies, Squire Hasbrouck, was turned to stone in New Paltz in 1834. Newburyport is a town in Essex County, Massachusetts.

### Geography
Newburyport is bordered by the Lower Green and Parker River beyond which is the sea. The coastal highway to Rowley and Ipswich passes Plum Island and a desolate patch of land exposed to the sand by deforestation in 1846. Despite humans being responsible for the deforestation, the locals believed the desolation to be connected to the great evil behind the Innsmouth plague that same year.

Innsmouth is an hour's bus ride down the coast.

### Residents
The people of Newburyport are widely suspicious and refuse to discuss their dreaded neighbours in Innsmouth.
*Miss Anna Tilton - The curator of the Historical Society
*The Ticket Agent - A stout, shrewd-faced employee of the Newburyport train station from Parton, Vermont. As an outsider he is less afraid of discussing Innsmouth but would still never dare go there.

### Landmarks
*Newburyport Public Library - Home to documents on Essex County history.
*Newburyport Historical Society - Home to the mysterious Innsmouth tiara and curated by Anna Tilton.
*YMCA

### Market Square
*Hammond's Drug Store
*Bus stop - Busses for Arkham via Insmouth leave at 10 AM and 7PM.

### State Street
*Rows of old brick buildings
*Pawn Shop -  Obtained an Innsmouth tiara after a drunk (Later murdered) sold it in 1873.

### High Street
*A left turn off of State Street with early republic mansions of the early republic and colonial farmhouses.

### Behind the Mythos
Unlike nearby Innsmouth and Arkham, Newburyport is a real city in Essex County, Massachusetts.

Lieutenant Newt Bardhoff is a character created by American author Brandon Berntson for his Lovecraft Mysteries trilogy of Cthulhu Mythos novels. He made his debut appearance in 2018's The Night of Dagon.

### Description
Bardhoff is a thin man who is usually clean-shaven, who is described as being "pleasant, easy to talk to". A lieutenant in the Innsport Police Department, he is married to a shy bookstore owner named Amelia, and is good friends with the protagonist of The Lovecraft Mysteries, private investigator Devlin Macky. Prior to his marriage, Bardhoff had a "harmless, innocent crush" on Macky's secretary Millie Von Clydesburgh.

Although single at the beginning of the series, at the end of The Night of Dagon Bardhoff is introduced to a shy bookstore owner named Amelia; by the time of the events described in The Lurker at the Threshold, the two have been married for around two years.

### History
After being assigned the case of an artefact stolen from the Innsport Natural History Museum, Bardhoff and his partner Inspector Duke Givens found themselves investigating a missing persons case on the estate of cultist Mordred Haddonfield. Captured by Haddonfield and his undead servant Borgas, they were destined to be sacrificed to the recently-awoken Dagon: the timely intervention of Macky and Millie Von Clydesburgh saved them from this fate, and the pair returned to Innsport to begin an evacuation ahead of Dagon's murderous rampage (: The Night of Dagon).

Bardhoff was heavily involved in the battle against the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred, the Outer Gods, and their legions of monstrous minions after Macky accidentally kickstarted Alhazred's plot to bring about the return of his dark masters (: The Lurker at the Threshold).

### Appearances

*The Lurker at the Threshold (2021)

### Synopsis
The mighty cruise ship Pride of the Sea finds itself lost and without power in a violent Pacific Ocean storm, its passengers and crew subjected to terrible dreams of doom and destruction throughout this ordeal.

As the storm clears and the maintenance team inspect the damage, they find that the propellers are fouled with what at first appears to be an enormous rope, but is soon recognised for what it truly is: a colossal tentacle. As the crew desperately try to cut the tentacle loose and escape, the tentacle's owner, Great Cthulhu himself, rises from the depths and sends the ship and everyone aboard to a watery grave.

Ngyr-Khorath (also known as The Ultimate Abomination, The Dream-Death, and The Mad God of the Void, among other titles) is an entity featured in the Mlandoth Cycle by Walter C. DeBill Jr. It has existed in the area now home to the Solar System since before the Sun and planets formed. It appears as a red or deep blue-green mist which causes a sense of terror as it approaches. Once close, an eye of flame forms within. When life arrived on Earth, it became enraged. A cult to Ngyr-Khorath exists. Its legend (part of the so-called Mlandoth Cycle) appears in the Book of Thoth, The Chronicles of Thrang, the Uralte Schrecken, and The Texts of Mloeng. Von Könnenberg suggests that it is a form of the entity Mlandoth, and itself has an avatar, 'Ymnar.

It spawned by fission the Great Old One (or its avatar) 'Ymnar, and its nemesis is the Elder God Paighon.

Nhimbaloth (also known as The Empty Death) is a fictional entity created by Paizo Inc for their role-playing game Pathfinder. The character first appeared in the gaming supplement In Search of Sanity.

### Background
Nhimbaloth is the Outer God of ghosts, swamps, and despair. This being hunts those who prey on souls, digesting both the predator and prey. Souls which are consumed by her never make it to the afterlife: their fate is oblivion. Nhimbaloth has no form but her passage is thought to be revealed by telltale marks.

The most obvious of these telltale marks is a cluster of seven impeccably positioned sods of crumbling soil on shores, which are thought to be her fingerprints. In any place she has visited local wildlife becomes unusually antagonistic and faceless undead ones haunt the area.

Nicholas Roerich (Russian: Николай Рерих, 1874 - 1947) was a Russian painter, archaeologist, stage scenographer, writer, and spiritual philosopher. He is known for his landscape paintings, his interest in mysticism, hypnotism and Buddhism, his extensive travels through Asia, and his outspoken activism for the preservation of artistic and archaeological artifacts. After the revolution of 1917, Roerich and his family left Russia and spent time in several countries, including Finland, England, the USA, and finally India, where he resided until his death.

### In the Mythos
In the novella At the Mountains of Madness, by H. P. Lovecraft, protagonist William Dyer reminisces that the sight of the Antarctic mountain range discovered by the Pabodie Expedition reminds him of "the strange and disturbing Asian paintings of Nicholas Roerich, and of the still stranger and more disturbing descriptions of the evilly fabled plateau of Leng which occur in the dreaded Necronomicon of the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred". Later on both Dyer and Lake comment on how the architecture of the Elder Things' city remind them of Roerich's Asian paintings.

In the Doctor Who crossover novel White Darkness, an unexpurgated copy of the Necronomicon formerly owned by Aleister Crowley contains passages written in the Eocene language and original illustrations by Roerich.

He has written several original comic books, and has also adapted a number of H. P. Lovecraft stories into the visual format. He is the founder of independent publishing Target Destroyed Comics, through which he publishes these works, usually after obtaining funding via Kickstarter crowdfunding campaigns.

Nicole Marsh is a minor recurrent character in the Keyport Cthulhu series of Mythos stories by Armand Rosamilia.

### Overview
Nicole is the young wife of Harrison Marsh, a descendant of the Keyport branch of the Marsh family.

When she and her husband travelled to Keyport to settle old Jeb Marsh's estate, Nicole was kidnapped and used as a sacrifice to awaken the Great Old One Cthulhu. However, the being found her to be unworthy, and although she was not killed in the process, the encounter left her in a catatonic state.

### Appearances
*"Ancient" (2012)
*"Cabal" (2012)
*"Evil" (2013)

### Trivia
*Nicole is sometimes referred to as Nichole; however, she is most often referred to in the former manner.
