Night Fang is a kaiju in the fictional universe of the Ultraman Taiga television series by Tsuburaya Productions. The character appears to be at least partially inspired by Cyäegha.

In the mobile game Ultra Kaiju Battle Breeders, it was speculated that Night Fang might be a distant relative of the evil god Gatanothor.

### Background
Long ago, on a day with a total solar eclipse, Night Fang descended from outer space and arrived at Kuzuryu Village, causing all sorts of natural disasters. Despite this, the locals were able to protect themselves by offering visitors as human sacrifices. However, other travelers began to hear about this, causing no one to ever visit the village again. The locals had to resort to using themselves as human sacrifices, until the village became empty and off the grid. Night Fang was sealed away in a mountain by a shrine maiden, who wielded a shining sword with the power of Earth. The evil spirits of the locals remained in the village, hoping to free Night Fang from its prison so that they can finally be at peace.

In the present day, the evil spirits eventually succeeded with that goal during another solar eclipse. With the help of Alien Babarue, Night Fang was freed using the psychic powers of the net idol Ai Tennoji, who is the reincarnation of the shrine maiden that originally sealed it away. (: "To the Demon's Mountain!!")

Night Fang headed towards a populated city in order to unleash nightmare-inducing sound waves, feeding off the suffering of the people. Fortunately, the effects were negated by some noise-cancelling waves, freeing all the victims, including Hiroyuki Kudo, who transformed into Ultraman Taiga to fight off Night Fang. Taiga was unable to defeat Night Fang, until Ai Tennoji summoned the shining sword again and transferred Earth's power to him. Gaining a new form called "Photon-Earth", Taiga destroyed Night Fang with the Aurum Strium beam, reducing the evil kaiju's remains to a small ring that contained its power. (: "Defeat the Demon!")

### Mythos Connections
In an interview with director Makoto Kamiya, it was stated that Night Fang is a homage to the Cthulhu Mythos. In particular, Night Fang's characterization strongly resembles the Great Old Ones, being an ancient evil god who was sealed away but still worshipped by a cult in the outside world.

fullContent:
Night Gallery was a horror anthology TV series created by Rod Serling that aired for three seasons on NBC from December 16, 1970, to May 27, 1973. Its episodes included adaptations of H. P. Lovecraft short stories, along with segments that took a more light-hearted look at the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Episodes

### "Miss Lovecraft Sent Me"

The first episode of Night Gallery's Season Two, originally aired September 15, 1971, included a comedy sketch written by Jack Laird and directed by Gene R. Kearney. It stars Joseph Campanella as a vampire father and Sue Lyon (best known for playing Lolita in Stanley Kubrick's adaptation) as Betsy, the babysitter he hires. The most Lovecraftian thing about it is that the agency that sent Betsy to babysit is referred to as "Miss Lovecraft".

### "Professor Peabody's Last Lecture"

The last segment of Season Two's eighth episode, written by Jack Laird and directed by Jerrold Freedman, is a Cthulhu Mythos parody about a college lecture on the Necronomicon that teaches more than is safe to know. First aired November 10, 1971, it stars Carl Reiner as Professor Peabody and Johnnie Collins III, Richard Annis, and Larry Watson as students named Mr. Lovecraft, Mr. Bloch, and Mr. Derleth, respectively.

### "Pickman's Model"
 from Night Gallery's adaptation of "Pickmans' Model".]]
Season Two's 11th episode, first aired December 1, 1971, was an adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's “Pickman’s Model”, directed by Jack Laird from a teleplay by Alvin Sapinsley. It stars Bradford Dillman as Richard Upton Pickman, and Louise Sorel as Mavis Goldsmith, a student of Pickman's who is in love with him. It also features Robert Prohaska as the Ghoul and Jock Livingston and Joshua Bryant in a modern-day framing story. 

### "Cool Air"
Season Two's 12th episode, first aired December 8, 1971, led with an adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's "Cool Air", directed by Jeannot Szwarc from a teleplay by Rod Serling. It starred Henry Darrow as Dr. Juan Muñoz; Barbara Rush as Agatha Howard, a friend and potential love interest of Muñoz; and Beatrice Kay as Mrs. Gibbons, Muñoz's housekeeper.

Director Szwarc commented:As it is written, Lovecraft is impossible to adapt because you can never find a visual equivalent of his style. He describes horrors that chill your bones. It’s the words and way he manipulates those words, and you can’t do that on film because film is almost too literal a form.

### "Last Rites of a Dead Druid"

The 18th episode of Night Gallerys second season, aired January 26, 1972, and directed by Jeannot Szwarc, was written by Alvin Sapinsley as an extremely loose adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft/Hazel Heald story “Out of the Aeons”. "My final version was so far removed from the original short story as to be unrecognizable," Sapinsley says in  Rod Serling’s Night Gallery: An After-Hours Tour. Sapinsley did retain the idea of an ancient priest surprisingly still alive in a rigid form. A more faithful adaptation of the story was written by R

Night Ocean et autres nouvellas is a French-language collection of works by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Running to a total of 250 pages, it was translated by Jean-Paul Mourlon, featured an introduction by Lovecraft scholar S. T. "Night of the Hopfrog" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tim Curran. Somewhat unusually for a Mythos story, it is written in the style of a video transcript.

### Synopsis
The crew of paranormal television show Haunted: Dead or Alive live stream an investigation into the decrepit houses of the Severn Valley's Lakeside Terrace. As the energy their broadcast brings to the old buildings awakens malevolent forces, their minds and bodies are quickly consumed by the servants of both Gla'aki and Byatis before the remains are dragged off to the lake.

### Characters
* Guy, the producer of Haunted: Dead or Alive.
* Annabelle Mathews, the first team presenter.
* Kealan Brightly, the second team presenter, and seemingly the least credulous of the cast members.
* Piers Lyon, second team cameraman.
* Simon McGee, second team cameraman.
* Bert Taylor, mobile unit crew.
* Susan Pealan, mobile unit crew.

### Publication History
"Night of the Hopfrog" was published in the Dark Regions Press thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki in 2017.

Night-gaunts are a species of flying creatures in the Cthulhu Mythos, who first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. They inhabit Earth's Dreamlands and are described as having smooth whale-like skin, long slender humanoid bodies, curving horns, leather bat-like wings, and a blank expanse of flesh where one would expect a face to be.

They revere and worship Nodens as their lord and master.

### Trivia
*The concept of night-gaunts first came to Lovecraft as a young child, in a series of recurring nightmares in which "they would whirl me through space at a sickening rate of speed, the while fretting & impelling me with their detestable tridents". Lovecraft credited the illustrations of Gustave Doré as inspiration for their appearance.
*A pair of night-gaunts are employed as supernatural muscle by the Silver Twilight Lodge in Peter J. Evans' novel Feeders from Within.
*The form of the Night-Gaunt is identical to that attributed in Ancient Greek Myth of Late Antiquity to the sleep and dream related gods Morpheus ("The Shaper") and his siblings the Oneiroi ("Dreams").

shortDefinition: "Nightjar" is a short Lovecraftian story by author Dean Wirth first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2021.  ### Synopsis Told through a series of letter and newspaper articles, the story tells of how a serial killer in the 180...
fullContent:
"Nightjar" is a short Lovecraftian story by author Dean Wirth first published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2021.

### Synopsis
Told through a series of letter and newspaper articles, the story tells of how a serial killer in the 1800s stumbles across a book, The Book of Soul Carriers, Transference and Invasives, and uses it to cheat death, inhabiting various bodies across the centuries while continuing his gruesome work. At an execution in 1957, when he attempts to vacate his borrowed body, a flock of ethereal nightjars mob the execution party and prevent him from leaving.

Despite this, the final letter tells of how the killer's discorporated soul has found a new home, and now plans to go about his business as usual.

### Trivia
* One of the letters mentions how the book was actually one in a series of nine, hinting at the possibility that more evil souls may roam the ether in search of victims.

fullContent:
Nightmare in Norway is a scenario sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, created by third-party content provider Games Workshop in the years before they limited their catalogue to their own products.

### Overview


Called in to assist a powerful politician and shipping mogul in a case of blackmail, the investigators make their way to Norway to solve the crime. During the course of their inquiries, they stumble across a previously-unknown species of humanoid trolls in service to the Great Old One Tsathoggua, and, due to the actions of a particularly heartless NPC, find themselves embroiled in a battle for revenge initiated by the primitive beasts.

Coming complete with all of the necessary handouts and maps in a pull-out centre section, Nightmare in Norway was written by Marcus L. Rowland with cover art by Lee Gibbons, interior art and maps by Tony Ackland, and ran to a total of 36 pages. It was published by Games Workshop under license from Chaosium in 1985, and is currently out of print.

fullContent:
Nightmare World is a Lovecraftian comic series created by writer Dirk Manning and illustrated by a wide variety of artists. It was first published as a weekly webcomic in 2002.

The story consists of 52 short comics running to 8 pages each (9 including title page), published in a non-sequential order. While most of the stories do not directly tie into each other, the elements of each slowly build an overall story, one in which he reader is encouraged to spot the various connections and threads. 

### Synopsis
The overall story arc concerns the fallen angel Lucifer, anlso known as the Morning Star, and his centuries-long grand scheme to wrest control of Creation (in this instance seemingly referring solely to the planet Earth) from God. 

Lucifer's plans involve not only his own legions of the fallen but his allies, the demonic offspring of Lilith, the first woman. Simultaneously, he hatches a plot to awaken Great Cthulhu and the Great Old Ones as well as the monstrous Nephilim, forcing his "father" to join battle on two fronts.

Lucifer's ploy is ultimately successful, with the resultant carnage initiating the biblical Rapture (aided by a coalition of powerful extraterrestrial civilisations) and subsequent Three Days of Darkness. In the aftermath, God seemingly abandons his children on Earth, with those who survived the Armageddon living on in a world ruled by the Morning Star, although life for many seems surprisingly unchanged.

### Mythos Elements

### Cthulhu
Cthulhu's re-emergence forms part of the tactics employed by Lucifer to overwhelm God's angelic hosts and force the abandonment of Creation. Awakened by a deranged man named Brian Carter using the Al-Azif/Necronomicon, Cthulhu and the Old Ones face off against the colossal biblical giants known as Nephilim, leaving the loyal angels no choice but to split their legions to fight both the Nephilim and the spawn of Lilith. 

At the end of battle only Cthulhu remains, the Nephilim utterly destroyed, the Great Old Ones banished from our plane of existence, and the surviving angels unable to match their opponent and fleeing the field. Ultimately, Cthulhu is defeated by a powerful extraterrestrial devoted to protecting the Earth named the Jovian; the Jovian, severely weakened and badly injured after the battle, is in turn dispatched by an evil industrialist named Dan Danforth. 

### The Cthulhu Cult
The Cthulhu Cult's direct involvement is limited to the actions of a single priestess, a seemingly-immortal woman named Vanessa. Vanessa swore her loyalty to Cthulhu in the long-distant past after an encounter with an evil sorcerer caused her lover to turn his back upon her. Her rewards for service include longevity and the ability to extrude tentacle-like appendages from her mouth.

Nightmares of Lovecraft is an American toyline originally released by SOTA Toys in October 2006. It was set for release in 2005, before ultimately getting delayed. The figures are based on familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos, ranging in the 7-inch to 10-inch scale with multiple points of articulation.

The first wave consists of Cthulhu from "The Call of Cthulhu", the Ghoul from "Pickman's Model", and Dagon from The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

The line also featured some collectible statues, including a 14-inch Ultra Cthulhu Statue released in June 2008, and a 12-inch polystone statue of Nyarlathotep released in late 2009.

Nightscapes was a relatively long-running online fanzine dedicated to the Cthulhu Mythos inspired by the works of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview


Edited by noted Mythos author and scholar Edward P. Berglund, Nightscapes contained a mix of stories and poetry from both established authors and up-and-comers. Running for seventeen issues between June 1997 and December 2006 -- with a three-year gap before the final two issues -- it is now defunct, although the back issues are still hosted for free on the website.

### Issues

### 1997
*June
* August
*September

The Nioth-Korghai are a long-lived androgynous, yellow, fungoid, squid-like alien race. They come from the planet Karthis, a water-world, and possessed a highly evolved civilisation millions of years ago. According to them they created the first true hominids, after 700 years of experimenting. Some of the Nioth-Korghai became vampiric (calling themselves "the Ubbo-Sathla") and these were outlawed by the Nioth race. Their relationship with the Cosmic Octopi is unclear. A group of criminals attacked the Earth in the late 20th Century.

### Background in Call of Cthulhu
The Nioth-Korghai are space-faring vampires traveling in a 50-mile long spacecraft while lying dormant within, until they either reach a world with suitable prey or they are contacted by an intelligent life form. These aquatic fungi are capable of possessing sentient life forms, and are able to leave their host and possess a new one. They feed on the lifeforce of sentients by kissing their victims, whom rapidly age as it's drained from them. If only a little is taken, it leaves the victim tired but if all of it is taken, the victim ends up as a dried and withered husk.

Nioth-korgahi can shapeshift to resemble life forms but at great cost to their power, which can be restored by draining a victim's lifeforce. They can revert back to their true form at will, without cost. They cannot be wounded but are instantly killed if impaled in the solar plexus region. They are a species which worships the Outer God Ubbo-Sathla.

### Deviation in the 1985 Movie
In the film Lifeforce, the space vampires were in appearance vastly different than in the Colin Wilson's novel, The Space Vampires. They still fed on the lifeforce of their victims, traveled in a planetoid-size spacecraft, and possessed others. Unlike the octopoid-like star vampires of Colin Wilson, their true form was that of a demonic bat-like humanoid.

### Behind the Mythos
The name Nioth-Korghai was created by Clark Ashton Smith as a minor god in his Zothique stories. Francis Laney listed it as a Mythos god in his Glossary. Colin Wilson picked up the name and applied it to his aliens in the novel The Space Vampires. Chaosium also used them.

Nioth-Korghai is an extraterrestrial character who appears in Clark Ashton Smith's Zothique Cycle story "The Tomb-Spawn".

### Description
When first introduced, Nioth-Korghai was not described, although it was mentioned that young men and women were sacrificed to it.

Later, after dying and merging with the equally-dead Ossaru, it was described thus:



### History
Nioth-Korghai descended from the stars on a fiery comet and befriended one of Zothique's most powerful rulers, to whom he offered advice on a variety of subjects, and dwelt in a specially-constructed chamber beneath Ossaru's palace. After many years, it died of an unknown condition, and was buried in its old living quarters, where Ossaru joined it upon his own death.

When a pair of travellers stumbled across its tomb, they discovered that the two entities had merged, and were promptly murdered by the gestalt creature before it accidentally killed itself.

### Trivia

*Nioth-Korghai was developed by Colin Wilson for his novel The Star Vampires, and by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

Nith is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Cats of Ulthar".

### Background
Nith is a resident of the town of Ulthar where he works as a notary (a legal professional who witnesses the signing of documents). He was one of the town burgesses who helped pass the law that made it illegal to kill cats. (: "The Cats of Ulthar")

The plain of Nith is also the name of a location within the blue-litten subterranean realm of K'n-yan. (: The Mound)

Nitokris or Nitocris was a possibly historical queen of Ancient Egypt, who may have ruled at the end of the 6th Dynasty, from 2184–2181 BC. H. P. Lovecraft incorporated her legend into the Cthulhu Mythos, referring to her as  the "ghoul-queen". (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs")

### In History
Nitocris' historicity is today debated, but she was considered to be real by ancient historians like Manetho, who (wrongly) attributed the building of the Third Pyramid at Giza to her,  and Herodotus, who presents her as the avenger of her brother, whom she succeeded on the throne:He had been the king of Egypt, and he had been put to death by his subjects, who then placed her upon the throne. Determined to avenge his death, she devised a cunning scheme by which she destroyed a vast number of Egyptians. She constructed a spacious underground chamber and, on pretense of inaugurating it, threw a banquet, inviting all those whom she knew to have been responsible for the murder of her brother. Suddenly as they were feasting, she let the river in upon them by means of a large, secret duct.This legend was the basis for a play by one of Lovecraft's favorite writers, Lord Dunsany; The Queen's Enemies premiered in New York City in 1916. Asked by The New York Times where he got the idea for the play, Dunsany replied that the theme of "The Queen's Enemies" I owe to a lady, and not one of those dreamy women who, having got an idea, write a sonnet about it or a play: she did it; she got the motive of drowning her enemies, so she invited them to dinner and drowned them. That is all I know about her.

It was not only easier but more amusing to imagine her character and all the names of her enemies than to be bothered with reading about her.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Lovecraft first mentioned Nitokris in his story "The Outsider," written in 1921 and first published in 1926. The piece refers to "the unnamed feasts of Nitokris beneath the Great Pyramid," in a passage that also evokes the "catacombs of Nephren-Ka" and "the mocking and friendly ghouls on the night-wind."

Nitokris comes up repeatedly in "Under the Pyramids," which was ghostwritten for Harry Houdini in 1924 and published that same year. It invokes both the legend of her drowning her enemies and her connection to the Third Pyramid:Even the smallest of them held a hint of the ghastly—for was it not in this that they had buried Queen Nitokris alive in the Sixth Dynasty; subtle Queen Nitokris, who once invited all her enemies to a feast in a temple below the Nile, and drowned them by opening the water-gates? I recalled that the Arabs whisper things about Nitokris, and shun the Third Pyramid at certain phases of the moon. The story also links Nitokris to the Pharaoh Khephren, telling of rumors that he "lives far underground wedded to the ghoul-queen Nitokris and ruling over the mummies that are neither of man nor of beast."

Nodens (also known as Lord of the Great Abyss) is a healing god from Celtic mythology, incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Strange High House in the Mist". The character is generally depicted as being an inhabitant of the Dreamlands and the master of the night-gaunts, a servitor race of flying creatures.

Later writers, starting with August Derleth, refer to Nodens as an Elder God. (: "A Note on the Cthulhu Mythos") 

### History
Nodens is an "archaic" god served by the night-gaunts. He seems to be somewhat benevolent, opposing the frightening Nyarlathotep, and helping Randolph Carter to find his way back to the waking world, along with S'ngac. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

Nodens is also described with "...the grey and awful form of primal Nodens, Lord of the Great Abyss". He appeared to Thomas Olney and the One, along with the ocean god Neptune and a procession of tritons and nereids. Nodens was riding a "vast crenulate shell" carried by dolphins. He extended a hand to help Olney and the One board the shell carriage and took off "into the limitless aether". (: "The Strange High House in the Mist")

Bas-reliefs in the Dreamlands represent Nodens as an anthropomorphic deity with a beard made of tentacles, "now hunting winged octopi with a trident, now enthroned in a scallop shell". (: "The Summons of Nuguth-Yug")

### In Other Media 
*Battle Spirits: Nodens appears in the trading card game, under the name "The GreatDeepSea Norg-Dens".
*Black Souls II: Nodens appears as a major NPC in the main safe area of the role-playing video game, under the name White Rabbit Node. The game depicts her as a human girl with rabbit ears and she serves the player without questioning their morality. In one of the endings, she reveals the nature of the game as a breeding project for Outer Ones. In the 'true ending', she aids the player in escaping Wonderland and sacrifices herself to do so.
*Crash Fever: The mobile game features a character named after and based on Nodens, who is one of the founding members of the Dream Kingdom. Nodens was a rogue hacker who worked with fellow founding member Nyarlathotep and his childhood friend Zehirete. Along with the new recruit Nightgaunt, Nodens would later fight against Cthugha's attack on the virtual world of ALICE.
*Demonbane: Nodens (also known as the White Ship) appears in the novel Zanma Taisen Demonbane, as one of the Elder Gods who led her fleet against the Vortex Blaster. shortDefinition: "Nor the Demons Down Under the Sea (1957)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the anthology The Children of Cthulhu (Del Rey, 2002). It is part of Kiernan's Dandridge Cycle, a series of interconnected stories about a myster...
fullContent:
"Nor the Demons Down Under the Sea (1957)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the anthology The Children of Cthulhu (Del Rey, 2002). It is part of Kiernan's Dandridge Cycle, a series of interconnected stories about a mysterious house on the California coast and the strange sacrifice hidden beneath it.

The title is a quotation from Edgar Allan Poe's poem "Annabel Lee," in which the poet refuses to allow death to separate him from the young woman he loves.

### Synopsis
Dr. Julia Winter, a professor of marine biology, and her grad student and lover Anna Foley travel up the California coast to visit a haunted house. Julia sees glimpses of the house's haunted past.

### Behind the Mythos
"Nor the Demons Down Under the Sea (1957)" makes mention of the Cthulhu Mythos entities Dagon and Mother Hydra.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Children of Cthulhu, "Nor the Demons Down Under the Sea" was reprinted in The Mammoth Book of Best New Horror Volume 14 (Carroll & Graf, 2003) and in The Book of Cthulhu II (Night Shade Books, 2012). It also appears in Kiernan's collections To Charles Fort, with Love (Subterranean Press, 2005) and Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018; Subterranean Press, 2019).

Norman Withers, the Astronomer, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games, who has made numerous appearances in their various expansions to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
Years ago, when respected astronomer Norman Withers noticed that the little slice of the sky which he had been studying was somehow missing six of its stars, his associates at Miskatonic University simply believed that he had been overdoing things, and dismissed the claim out of hand.

Norman knew, however, that his findings were correct and, after destroying his career in the process of trying to bring this fact to public attention, found a clue in an ancient book of occult knowledge. This tome stated the order in which those stars would disappear and the dates on which it would happen, dates which coincided exactly with Norman's findings. Furthermore, the text contained within prophesied that this event would herald the coming of a great evil to Earth, one which would wipe out Mankind and all of his achievements.

### Ire of the Void
When noted physicist Professor Claus Schmidt visited Arkham on a field research trip, Norman made acquaintance with the fellow and struck a deal with him: in exchange for Withers' assistance in his work, Schmidt would in turn aid him with his own problem, that of the vanished stars.

After the two investigated a series of locations which Schmidt believed to be the sites of gravitational anomalies, Schmidt was abducted by a Hound of Tindalos and carried off to another dimension.

Withers, unwilling to leave his new friend to his fate, did some research of his own into the anomalies, and learned of a man who he believed to have some knowledge on the subject, one Jonathon Hobart Stane. Visiting, Stane, he learned that he had been the victim of an attack by the Hounds in 1917 which had claimed his fiancée. Whilst Stane had survived the attack, it had left him both physically and mentally scarred, and he had sought out all the information he could find on the beasts, while kidnapping Arkham citizens and transients to sacrifice to the Hounds in his stead. He intended to make Withers his next victim, but the Professor was able to turn the tables on his attacker, and the summoned Hound devoured Stane.

Searching Stane's property, he discovered a trove of arcane knowledge, amongst it instructions on how to open a portal to the Hounds home dimension and, after suitably arming himself, set about attempting to rescue Schmidt.

Upon travelling to Tindalos, Withers was able to locate his colleague, and the pair made their escape, narrowly avoiding the attentions of more Hounds and a Dhole, and managed to return to Earth before destroying the portal which they used to claim their victims.

"Norse Blood" is a comic book story featured as one of the strips in Marvel Comics Presents #63, written by Len Kaminski and featuring artwork by Don Heck. The issue was published by Marvel Comics in September 1990.

### Synopsis
During the time of vikings Thor, the Norse god of thunder, is called to protect a small girl in the New World whose colony had been attacked by vampires. Although Thor defeats the vampires and their leader Varnae, he is unable to save the little girl, who eventually travels to the settlement of Roanoke and turns the entire colony into vampires, leaving behind only a single word, "Croatoan," carved into a nearby tree.

### Behind the Mythos
The conclusion of "Norse Blood" is an attempt to tie the Marvel universe into the real-life disappearance of the entire English Roanoke Colony in North Carolina, USA in the late 1580s. The settlers mysteriously vanished at some point before 1590, after attempts to relieve the struggling colony were thwarted by rumours of the Spanish Armada preparing to attack and the actions of greedy sailors attempting to capture Spanish merchant vessels. The ultimate fate of the colonists remains unknown, but speculation on their fate has included everything from integration into local Native American tribes to the unfortunate pioneers being lost at sea during an abortive attempt to return to England.

"North by Due North" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author David M. Hoenig. It was first published in the Jesse Dedman-edited Deadman's Tome anthology Ancient Ones II in March 2018 .

### Synopsis
The story offers a glimpse into the life of the unnamed narrator, a well-connected American man on a mission to thwart the plans of the Old Ones. As he makes his way to the North Pole aboard a Norwegian Coast Guard cutter, the expedition is attacked by enormous tentacled creatures from the deep. Using the firepower carried aboard the ship's two helicopters, they are able to repel the assault, although with heavy casualties, before continuing on with the job at hand. 

### Behind the Mythos
Amongst the Cthulhu Mythos elements mentioned in the stories are Othuum and Shoggoths, as well as the "Windwalker" and the Book of Eibon.

Norway is a Nordic country situated in the extreme northwest of Europe, the vast majority of which lies within the Arctic circle. It has existed continuously for well over 1,000 years, and is a land possessed of a rich history of folkloric tradition.

Although mentions of Norway in the works of H. P. Lovecraft (and indeed, the Cthulhu Mythos in general), some notable exceptions are noted below.

### In Lovecraft's Works

### "The Call of Cthulhu"
In Lovecraft’s seminal short story, the sole survivor of the crew of the Emma, a schooner which had a fateful encounter with the Great Old One Cthulhu, was one Second Mate Gustaf Johansen, a Norwegian émigré to New Zealand. After the events related in his manuscript, Johansen and his wife returned to their home in Oslo; shortly afterwards, he died, the death implied to have been at the hands of Cthulhu cultists. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

### In the Works of Lovecraft's Circle

### "Spawn of the Maelstrom"
August Derleth and Mark Schorer's 1939 short story concerns the investigation into a vampiric entity which has been held imprisoned on the isle of Vömma, off the coast of Norway. The being has been imprisoned on the island for millennia. (: "Spawn of the Maelstrom")

### In Other Works

### "The Kraken"
Alfred Lord Tennyson's 1830 poem regarding colossal sea creature from Norwegian folklore has been cited as a major inspiration on H. P. Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu." (: "The Kraken")

### Nightmare in Norway
Marcus L. Rowland's 1985 supplement for the Call of Cthulhu investigative horror roleplaying game concerns a band of Tsathoggua-worshipping trolls in the fictional town of Vikenberg. (: Nightmare in Norway)

### External Links
* [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway Norway] at Wikipedia

fullContent:
"Notebook Found in a Deserted House" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author and H. P. Lovecraft protégé, Robert Bloch.

### Synopsis
As might be gleaned from the title, the story is presented in the format of an account recovered from an abandoned residence, this one located deep within a forest surrounded by dark legends.

After orphaned Willie goes to stay with his aunt and uncle on their remote farm, strange events deep in the woods begin to haunt him. When his adoptive parents, along with all of their cattle, disappear over the course of a few nights, he tries to walk to the nearest town but encounters a man claiming to be a cousin come for a visit. Willie is suspicious however, and attempts to escape with the mailman on his buggy, but the two are ambushed by a "Shoggoth" and the mailman presumably killed. 

Running off into the forest, Willie stumbles across a sacrificial altar and witnesses a cult murdering his aunt and uncle, and he flees, eventually finding himself back at the deserted homestead.

The story concludes with the boy writing down his account, and the cultists bursting in through the front door.

### Characters
*Willie, a 12-year-old boy who has lost his parents.
*"Cousin Osborne", a man masquerading as family, in actuality a cultist of Shub-Niggurath.
*Cap Pritchett, the local mailman.
*Aunt Lucy, Willie's adoptive mother.
*Uncle Fred, Willie's adoptive father.

### Publication History
"Notebook Found in a Deserted House" was first published in the May 1951 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into French and Finnish.

### Trivia
*The story features the first appearance of the creatures which would later become known as the Dark Young of Shub-Niggurath, but are here referred to as Shoggoths, despite possessing little resemblance to Lovecraft's creations other than a degree of amorphousness.
*"Cousin Osborne" claims to have come from both Arkham and Kingsport, one of the mistakes he makes which rouses Willie's suspicions.
*Despite being told in the form of a discovered written account, "Notebook Found in a Deserted House" could be considered an early example of the "found-footage" genre of horror.

Noyes is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his horror sci-fi novella The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Description
A man of distinguished, cultivated demeanor and mysterious origins, Noyes was one of the human agents employed by the extraterrestrial Mi-Go. On May 1st, 1915, circa 1 a.m., he and a Mi-Go took part in a ritual worship of Cthulhu, Tsathoggua, Shub-Niggurath, and other deities, while Henry Wentworth Akeley secretly recorded their voices in a phonograph.

Compared to Akeley, Noyes is described as "a younger and more urban person, fashionably dressed, and wearing only a small, dark moustache" (as opposed to Akeley's full beard). He speaks with a Bostonian accent. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

### History
After Akeley was captured and replaced by an alien impersonator, the Mi-Go sent a letter in Akeley's name inviting Albert Wilmarth to visit his farm, claiming all the hostilities between Akeley and the Mi-Go had ceased. Noyes was sent to pick up Wilmarth at the station. He told Wilmarth that Akeley was feeling ill, but still wished to talk to him.

When the creature impersonating Akeley showed Wilmarth the brain cylinders, Wilmarth spoke to B-67, who invited him to an interplanetary voyage that he, Akeley, and Noyes were about to make, with the Mi-Go carrying their disembodied brains while their bodies remained preserved in stasis inside Round Hill, waiting for their return.

Later that night, Wilmarth overheard a discussion between Noyes, another human voice, two Mi-Go voices, and a voice coming from a brain cylinder attached to the speech-machine, which he mistakenly assumed to be B-67. Although he couldn't make out what they were talking about, Wilmarth overheard his own name, as well as Akeley's and Nyarlathotep's, and assumed that he and Akeley were in danger.

After the discussion was over and the sound of wings flapping and a car leaving the premises indicated that the others had left, Wilmarth was left with only the sound of a man snoring on the couch, which he assumed to be Akeley. However, when he approached to wake him up, Wilmarth saw that the sleeping man was Noyes, and that the brain cylinder, now disconnected from the speech-machine, was labelled with Akeley's name. When he found the face and hands of Akeley (either genuine or replicas) lying on a chair next to his dressing-gown and scarf, Wilmarth finally realised that the being he had spoken to earlier was an impersonator and fled from the house screaming. Later, he returned with a sheriff who found no sign of Akeley, Noyes, the brain cylinders and speech-machine, or the face and hands.

At some point after the incident, Wilmarth made inquiries about Noyes, but failed to find anyone who knew him in any of the villages surrounding Akeley's farm. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

Nug and Yeb are twin Great Old Ones from the Cthulhu Mythos, who first appeared in the short story "The Last Test" by H. P. Lovecraft. They were born from the mating of Shub-Niggurath with Yog-Sothoth (: Selected Letters 5.875) and T’yog believed them to be friendly to man. (: "Out of the Aeons")

According to another account by Eibon, the androgynous Cxaxukluth split in two, becoming male Nug and female Yeb. This minority interpretation may just be a textual gloss attempting to harmonize conflicting information. (: "The Second Epistle of Eibon unto his Disciples, or The Apocalypse of Eibon" [Robert M. Price and Laurence J. Cornford])

Nug is the parent of Cthulhu and Yeb is the parent of Tsathoggua (: Selected Letters 4.617) via the influence of Yog-Sothoth. Nug might be known by the name Ptmâk in Hyperborea, as Ptmâk corresponds to the "immediate" parent of Cthulhu. (: letter of Clark Ashton Smith to R. H. Barlow, September 10th, 1935) Dr. Dee calls Nug "Father of Ghouls," a title shared with its spawn Shaurash-Ho. Nug might also be the father of Hastur.

They are 10 feet in diameter in their usual appearance. (: Selected Letters 5.875) Both Nug and Yeb closely resemble Shub-Niggurath.

Nug and Yeb are worshipped in K'n-yan (: The Mound), Irem (: "The Last Test") and other places and form a kind of yin and yang symbolically. Other texts refer to the two Great Old Ones as the creator and keeper of the garden where Yig lives. They are entrusted with clearing the earth for the Great Ones' return. Using two devices called the "Furnace of Yeb" and the "Torch of Nug" to accomplish this purpose. Esoteric doctrines of monks in Leng teach that Nug and Yeb are the secret names of Lloigor and Zhar, (: "The Strange Doom of Enos Harker") but they never lived on Earth. (: Selected Letters 4.617) Although they might have appeared at or near Kadath, and Nug and Yeb are said to be in the Cavern of Prototypes beneath Mount Voormithadreth (which may be extra-dimensional). Nug is a god among ghouls, while Yeb is the leader of Abhoth's Unclean Ones alien cult. (: "The Descent into the Abyss" Clark Ashton Smith and Lin Carter)

Yeb (Yeb of the Whispering Mists) may also have been called Cxaxukluth in Hyperborea since Yeb is the "father" of Tsathoggua. (: Family tree of Azathoth) By implication it is male though it may be androgynous. Yeb is connected with the "Black Flame," and the instrument of world destruction, "The Furnace of Yeb" in which the flame resides on Earth.

Nug and Yeb, alongside Shub-Niggurath and Yig, were listed by T'yog as being willing to side with humanity against the hostile Great Old One Ghatanothoa. (: "Out of the Aeons")

### Behind the Mythos
*There is a Biblical town called Yeb.
*The names Nug and Yeb are similar to the names of the Egyptian

Nug-Soth is a fictional character mentioned in the novella The Shadow Out of Time, by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Background
In Lovecraft's original story, Nug-Soth is a magician who served "the dark conquerors" around 16,000 AD. They were the victim of a mind transfer with a member of the Great Race of Yith, and their consciousness was sent back to 150,000,000 BC to meet with Professor Peaslee. Peaslee listed Nug-Soth's name among the other humans he met during his experience, as opposed to the non-human intelligences he mentioned earlier, thus suggesting that Nug-Soth might have once been human. (: The Shadow Out of Time)

In the works of Lin Carter, "Nug-Soth" is the name of Zkauba's species, the tapir-snouted Yaddithians that first appeared in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price. These creatures once lived on Yaddith, and are said to have similar traits to mammals, reptiles and insects. Some of them survived the destruction of the crust of their planet from the Dholes. Most of their civilisation was destroyed by the Dholes, and the survivors of the Nug-Soth have fled to other planets, planes, dimensions and times to hide from the invaders. They used to be the dominant intelligent life on their planet before the arrival of the Dholes. The Yaddithians are known to be a race of powerful wizards and brilliant scientists who were able to create machines that could travel through space and time. (: "Dreams in the House of Weir")

In Colin Wilson's work on the Necronomicon, "Ye Alphabet of Nug-Soth" is the name of an alphabet that was created as some kind of esoteric scripture, to serve the purpose of the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred for his great work, the Necronomicon. It is also used on talismans to help its user to travel through time and space.

The alphabet might have been inspired by the "runes of Nug-Soth" mentioned in Fritz Leiber's 1976 story "The Terror from the Depths".

### Behind the Mythos
In the Necronomicon by George Hay and Colin Wilson, published 1978, various Lovecraft works and names from those works and the broader Cthulhu Mythos are namechecked but recontextualized, as with the use of the name of an alien race, the Nug-Soth, for an alphabet, without any direct connection to imply that this might be the alphabet used by that alien species. One can infer such a thing, but such a statement or inference is not present in the 1978 work. In this sense, Wilson and Hay are really using Mythos names as labels for disparate and in many cases arguably unrelated material.

The Nug-Soth letters are based on the Coelbren inscriptions in Coelbren, Glamorganshire, Wales, and on the allegedly forged alphabet alleged to have been created rather than discovered by Iolo Morganwg, and first described by Iolo Morganwg's son Taliesin ab Iolo in works published in 1840. The Dark Age inscriptions from the sixth century AD and earlier are matters of historical fact.

Using the Coelbren Script, in the form in which it appears on the Dark Age stonework and graves rather than the simplified form from Morganwg, implies several interesting links to the historical King Arthur, ley lines and the Lloigor and was undoubtedly intended to do so given the bent of Wilson's other contributions to the Mythos.

fullContent:
Nunn-Jahad is one of the Ogdru Jahad (the Seven Gods of Chaos) in the fictional universe of Hellboy by Dark Horse Comics.
### Overview
### Origin
Nunn-Jahad was created alongside his six siblings during the begining of  time, made out of mud and fire by the Watchers (angels serving God).

As night fell the seven dragons came to life, filled with the purpose of destruction and subjugation. The spawned 369 Ogdru Hem and started to battle the Watchers. The Dragons were eventually defeated and were imprisoned in a crystal prison in the heart of the cosmos.

Ever since the dragons have seeked to get out and casue the end of the world.
### Hell on Earth
In the 21st Century Nunn-Jahad managed to escape it's imprisonment and arrived on an apocalyptic Earth. With it's arrival the dragon destroyed part of the state of Kansas upon landing and began to spawn hordes of Ogdru Hem.

Despite the efforts of the U.S. military (barrage of nuclear missiles) and the Bureau for Paranormal Research & Defense (B.P.R.D), they were unable to stop his advance. Worldwide other Ogdru Hem were appearing, devastating cities alongside the Frog people and Hammerhead monsters which served them. He was finally stopped by Johann Kraus who sacrificed himself, channeling the infinite power of Vril to kill Nunn-Jahad. After which all the Ogdru Hem on Earth went still and silent.
### Appearance
Nunn-Jahad bears a resemblance to an outdated depiction of the theropod dinosaur [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceratosaurus Ceratosaurus].

### Trivia
*Nu is likely a reference to Nunn, a primordial watery abyss deity from ancient Egyptian religion

"Nutmeat" is a short Lovecraftian story by American author and university professor Martin Hill Ortiz.

### Synopsis
A parasitologist investigating an alleged infestation in rural California realises too late that whatever is infecting the local walnut crop has already made the jump to more mobile lifeforms…

### Characters
* Doctor Hiram Lerner, a plant parasitologist working out of California's Davis University.
* Baskin, a country bumpkin who has become infected by some kind of intelligent body-snatching organism.

### Publication History

fullContent:
Nxla (aka, the Cold and the Darkness, Soul Stealer) is a Lovecraftian-like extra-dimensional entity in the fictional universe of the Rifts pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium.

### Background
Nxla the Harvester of Souls is an alien intelligence of such power, that even the Splugorth fear him. It establishes footholds on worlds where mortals worship power and/or death, accepting it as their master. Whom are recruited and turned into its minions, the Soul Harvesters. Once he physically enters the world, his minions are given immortality, though they can still be injured and killed. The only way to force him back to his home dimension is to destroying most of his physical body, killing or liberating at least half of the Soulless Xombies, and wiping out 60% or more of the Harvesters. 

It's appearance is that of a 800 ft tall living pillar of disfigured flesh, with a dozen 500 ft long tentacles, hundreds of eyes, and a half dozen 200 ft long human-like arms. It is a powerful psionic, is knowledgeable in spell magic and necromancy, can regenerate, is able to animate and control hundreds of the dead, and can survive a 85 Megaton-level nuke though with grievous wounds. Rune and holy weapons inflict twice as much damage as conventional weapons and psionic attacks inflict x10 as much damage.

The Soul Harvesters mutilate and kill their victims, taking their life essence captive within themselves. Which feeds their own power and evil. The victim's soul cannot find peace until the Harvester is killed or they are released via an exorcism. Nxla itself harvests its own souls by sends fragments out to the world. Taking possession of sentient beings which become Soulless Xombies (which are controlled by the Soul Harvesters), as their own souls in turn are torn from their bodies and sucked back into Nxla who enjoys tormenting them as long as they are held within it. The Soulless Xombies can take as much damage as a late 20th century armored fighting vehicle, and are able to regenerate. 

The number of fragments that Nxla can send out into the world, depends on whether or not it is physically on that world, and how many souls it has harvested. If he is temporarily summoned, he can manifest for up to 12 minutes and send out up to 40 fragments. On the other hand if it physically arrives on a world, every day on it the entity will unleash 1000 fragments of its lifeforce. His power increasing as more souls are harvested, and once he harvests 100 million souls he will be creating 10,000 lifeforce fragments a day. Nxla has etablished a foothold on post-apocalyptic dystopian Earth with 1000s of Soul Harvesters and Soul Xombies operating in North America.

The Ny'ghan Grii, a.k.a. Dwellers in the Hidden World, are a fictional race created in 1939 by Henry Kuttner for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Invaders". In 1994, Chaosium incorporated them into the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. As is often the case Chaosium has somewhat departed from the original source material to produce something more compatible with roleplay gaming.

### Background
The Ny'ghan Grii are an extra-dimensional race of luminous spherical creatures with glossy ivory-yellow semi-translucent vine-like appendages ending in raw looking stumps covered in cilia. They posses a single great faceted eye at the top of their rugose bodies, with a puckered orifice below this eye. They move by crawling or floating, accompanied by icy cold and a thick fog.

Originating from another dimension, the Ny'ghan Grii seek entry to other worlds, searching for sacrifices or disturbances in the time/space fabric that will give them entry. They desire to wipe out all life on Earth so that they can colonise the planet. They vocalise in strange bird-like skirling or shrill whistles. They can produce a chilling blast and have the ability to devolve victims into increasingly bestial forms. One of their methods of killing is to flay the flesh from their victims. 

The Nyghan Grii are similar to the Doels and the Mind Parasites. They are probably the Hidden Ones. They fear the Elder God, Vorvadoss.

### Overview
Nya is an avatar of Nyarlathotep, who takes the form of a tall, black-haired woman wearing glasses and a purple dress suit. Depending on the circumstances, she can assume many different forms, such as the Black Pharaoh or Reverend Nye; however, her true form is a burning smile with the three-lobed eye. She owns a bookstore that contains many grimoires including the Key of Solomon, the Lemegeton, the Grand Grimoire, the Black Pullet, the Book of Dzyan, and the Book of Loagaeth. 

Nya's characterization is shown to be cunning and manipulative, as she enjoys toying with everyone. But most of all, she is an Evil God who claims that true evil is no different than love, resulting in her loving humanity but in the most twisted way possible.

She was responsible for creating a time-looped world called the Infinite Spiral, also known as the Klein Bottle, forcing Daijuuji Kurou and Master Therion to relive their battle countless times. Her ultimate goal was to break the Shining Trapezohedron and free the Court of Azathoth, allowing the Outer Gods to consume all of reality and sink everything into primordial chaos. Nyar (also known as Nyarlathotep) is a fictional entity created by Juan Gotō for his manga series Alicia Y.

### Background
Nyar is an avatar of Nyarlathotep, who resembles a dark-skinned man wearing clergy attire. When accompanied by Alicia Y Armitage, he often transforms into a black cat, and can also take the form of the three-lobed burning eye. Nyar has been shown to have several supernatural abilities, including flight and teleportation; however, his powers are limited due to him merely being a projection of a god in this world. In addition to spending time on Earth, he appears to have a secret lair, located in the Cydonia region of the planet Mars.

Thousands of years ago, Nyar was the god worshipped in Egypt, who granted a dying wish to the Great Pharaoh Nephren-Ka, teaching him magic and bestowing him with the power of clairvoyance. Nephren-Ka spent his last days painting future events on the walls of his catacomb, which was concealed in fabric by the priests out of fear, only taking a look into the future little by little. According to Nyar, Nephren-Ka is destined to be resurrected in the future but will suffer in a world where there are no humans left to rule. 

In the present day, Nyar took the role of Alicia's guardian after the death of Mr. Whateley, changing her surname to "Armitage" instead of Whateley. At the behest of John Dee, Alicia was trapped underneath a giant star-shaped stone by a descendent of the priests who guarded the catacomb of Nephren-Ka, a woman claiming to be a servant of Nyarlathotep. Soon afterwards, Nyar got into a confrontation with the woman, ultimately killing the self-proclaimed servant by crushing her head. Nyar eventually figured out that he needed the Silver Key to save Alicia, with Randolph Carter arriving for assistance; despite being on bad terms with Nyar, Carter agreed to help due to the dire circumstances. 

At some point, Nyar had reached the domain of Yog-Sothoth but was disinterested in taking on that role. (: Alicia Y)

### In Other Media
*Nyar makes a cameo in the final volume of the light novel series Haiyore! Nyaruko-san, when Nyaruko summoned an army of infinite Nyarlathoteps from popular culture. He is described as being "a black cat Nyarlathotep". 
*In the manga series Shirley Holmes, which was also written by Juan Gotō, Alicia admits to losing her virginity with Nyar.

Nyarlathotep, known by his epithet The Crawling Chaos, is a fictional Outer God in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft, and made his first appearance in the prose poem "Nyarlathotep" (1920). He is the spawn of Azathoth, and acts as the Outer Gods' "soul and messenger".

Nyarlathotep appears in numerous subsequent stories by Lovecraft, and is also featured in the works of other authors, as well as in role-playing games and other media based on the Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Description
: "The Dreams in the Witch-House"}}
Nyarlathotep differs from the other deities in the Mythos in a number of ways. Most of the Outer Gods are exiled to the stars, like Yog-Sothoth and Azathoth, and most of the Great Old Ones are sleeping and dreaming like Cthulhu; Nyarlathotep, however, is active and frequently walks the Earth in the guise of a human being, usually a tall, slim, joyous man. He has "a thousand" other forms and manifestations, many reputed to be quite horrific and sanity-blasting.

Most of the Outer Gods have their own cults serving them; Nyarlathotep seems to serve several cults and takes care of their affairs in the other Outer Gods' absence. Most Outer Gods use strange alien languages, while Nyarlathotep uses human languages and can easily pass for a human being if he chooses to do so. Finally, most of them are all-powerful yet evidently without clear purpose or agenda, yet Nyarlathotep seems to be deliberately deceptive and manipulative, and even uses propaganda to achieve his goals. In this regard, he is probably the most human-like among the Outer Gods.

Nyarlathotep enacts the will of the Outer Gods, and is their "messenger, heart and soul", "the immemorial figure of the deputy or messenger of hidden and terrible powers". (: "The Dreams in the Witch-House") He has power over the Dreamlands and authority over the Gods of Earth, as well as the Moon-beasts and Shantaks, but seems to be opposed by Nodens. fullContent:
"Nyarlathotep" is a prose poem/short story by H. P. Lovecraft written in 1920, and first published in the November 1920 issue of The United Amateur. It is the first mention in fiction of the Cthulhu Mythos entity Nyarlathotep.

### Synopsis
The story is written in first person and begins by describing a strange and inexplicable sense of foreboding experienced by humanity in general, in anticipation of a great unknown evil.

The story proceeds to describe the appearance of Nyarlathotep as a "man" of the race of the Pharaohs, who claims to have been dormant for the past twenty-seven centuries, and his subsequent travels from city to city demonstrating his supernatural powers. Wherever Nyarlathotep went, the story relates, the inhabitants' sleep would be plagued by vivid nightmares.

The story describes Nyarlathotep's arrival in the narrator's city, and the narrator's attendance at one of Nyarlathotep's demonstrations, in which he defiantly dismisses Nyarlathotep's displays of power as mere tricks. The party of observers is driven away by an infuriated Nyarlathotep, and wanders off into at least three columnal groups: One disappears around a corner, from which is then heard a moaning sound; another disappears into a subway station with the sound of mad laughter; and the third group, which contains the narrator, travels outward from the city toward the country.

The story ends by describing horrific, surreal vistas experienced by the party, in which they realize horror and doom have come to the world.

### Behind the Mythos
Originating in one of Lovecraft's dreams, a source of what some consider to be some of his most moving work, Nyarlathotep has gone on to be one of the central figures in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos, with an almost constant stream of derived works. Many of these works treat Nyarlathotep as inimicably hostile to humanity or even outright "evil". Perhaps this is due to Nyarlathotep being amongst the most apparently understandable and human-like of Lovecraft's creations.

Lost in the ongoing fascination with "Nyarlathotep", which is really a continuous reiteration of the derived version of the character, is the subtlety of his canonical appearances in Lovecraft's original stories. Nyarlathotep acts as the guardian, indeed almost custodian of the ancient and apparently forgotten or abandoned gods of earth in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, and is not always an unsympathetic figure or even an antagonist. Lovecraft's cosmicism would make Nyarlathotep dangerous, elemental and mysterious, but also a transformative figure, as he was in this original appearance. That is often lost or ignored in the Nyarlathotep sequels cottage industry.

### Possible Influence

As one of H. P. Lovecraft's most famous creations and the most "human" of his cosmic horrors, Nyarlathotep has appeared in and been referenced by numerous other works in popular culture. The following is a non-comprehensive list of media that either includes Nyarlathotep or contains references, allusions or themes relating to him.

### Comic Books

*Caballistics, Inc.: the character of Ethan Kostabi has been hinted to be Nyarlathotep.
*Conan the Barbarian: features invocations to "Nyarla Thotep".
*Fall of Cthulhu: Nyarlathotep is the main antagonist in Boom! Studios' series.
*Journey Into Mystery: Nyarlathotep is featured in their adaptations of "The Haunter of the Dark" and "The Shadow from the Steeple".
*The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen: Black Dossier: Nyarlathotep appears as an emissary sent from Yuggoth to negotiate a truce with Prospero of the Blazing World.
*Lovely Lovecraft: Nyarlathotep is the primary antagonist.
*Nyarlathotep: a French comic book by Rotomago and J. Noirel, a literal adaptation of the Lovecraft short story.
*Providence and Neonomicon: Nyarlathotep is an unseen driving force throughout the comic and with his avatar Johnny Carcosa arranging events.
*Serenity Rose: Skarsdayle is the former lead singer of a band named Nyarlathotep.
*Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (Mirage Studios): In issue #43 "Hall of Lost Legends", Loki summons Nyarlathotep, "destroyer of souls, tearer of flesh".

### Film

*Nyarlathotep: a 13-minute short film version was released in 2001, directed by Christian Matzke. It was re-released on DVD in 2004 as part of the H. P. Lovecraft Collection Volume 1: Cool Air.
*The Empty Man: a supernatural horror film released in 2020, directed by David Prior and based on Cullen Bunn and Vanessa E. Del Rey's comic book series of the same name.

### Games

### Traditional Games

* Hecatomb: he appears as the Thing Outside Time and Space in the trading card game. 
* Pathfinder: role-playing game in which Nyarlathotep is the god of conspiracies, dangerous secrets, and forbidden magic.
* WIXOSS: appears in the trading card game, under the name Code Anti Nyarlatho.
* Yu-Gi-Oh: appears in the trading card game, under the name Outer Entity Nyarla. 

### Video Games
* Alone in the Dark (2024): Nyarlathotep appears in the human-like form of the antagonist as The Dark Man. He is also referred to as Nephren-Ka, the Black Sun, the Black Pharaoh, the Crawling Chaos and the Stalker Among the Stars. He made a pact with the central character, Jeremy Hartwood, to stop the awakening of Shub-Niggurath.
* Bloodborne: a 2015 videogame by From Software known for its Lovecraft-inspired story, has an optional final boss, "The Moon Presence", that was likely inspired by and modeled after Nyarlathotep.
* Call of Duty Zombies: a character known as the "Shadowman" (who serves a similar role to the Crawling Chaos) goes by the pseudonym of Tony "Hale" Rapt; an anagram for Nyarlathotep.
* Card Monsters: mobile game featuring Nyarlathotep,

"Nyarlathotep: The Man With No Face" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Sebastian Greaves. It is aimed at the Young Adult demographic.

### Synopsis
The Faceless Man, an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep, travels North America making converts by the townful and inciting terrible acts of violence. At the height of the phenomena, everything inexplicably stops, and the world quickly - if perhaps not entirely explicably - forgets the horrors. However, the movement has simply gone underground, and the Faceless Man still travels the world, leaving violence and bloodshed in his wake.

### Characters
*The unnamed narrator, an average man who witnesses the beginning of the end of the world.
*The Faceless Man, an avatar of the Crawling Chaos, Nyarlathotep.

### Publication History
"Nyarlathotep: The Man With No Face" was published in the collection Cthulhu Mythos Anthology on Amazon's digital Kindle platform.

Nyarlathotep's Half-Brother is a fictional cosmic being created by Walter C. DeBill, Jr. for his short story "In 'Ygiroth".

### Description
Little is known about this entity, which is described as Nyarlathotep's "half-brother and other face", possibly indicating that it might be an aspect of Nyarlathotep himself, as opposed to a literal relative.

It is also described as "a ravenous and by no means sane entity", and has the power to spread fear "like a poisonous vapor", causing all in its proximity to panic in sheer uncontrollable terror. (: "In 'Ygiroth")

### Behind the Mythos
Since Nyarlathotep's only known parent is Azathoth (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft), which reproduces asexually by fission (: "The Family Tree of the Gods"), the idea that he could have a "half-brother" seems unusual, although it opens up the possibility that Azathoth might be able to reproduce sexually as well, and that either Nyarlathotep or his Half-Brother (or both) were born from such a union.

"Nyarlathotep's Way" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Tom Pinchuk, first published in the collection of Lovecraftian fiction Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be by 01Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
Vagrant Serge, desperate to achieve the musical fame which he craves, seeks a boon from a priest of Nyarlathotep at a remote and hidden temple. Seemingly petitioning successfully, he makes his way back to civilisation, ready for the success which he knows must be coming his way.

Howvever, once the man leaves the priest is revealed to be Nyarlathotep itself, who has over the decades engineered Serge's descent into destitution and has in fact granted no boon. This will eventually lead to Serge being consumed by uncertainty and despair, emotions which the Outer God wishes to explore and enjoy.

Nyaruko (also known as Nyarlathotep) is an extraterrestrial entity from the fictional universe of the Haiyore! Nyaruko-san series. 

### Background
Nyaruko is a member of the Space Defense Agency, an alien organization dedicated to stopping intergalactic crimes. Nyaruko was sent to Earth to protect Mahiro Yasaka, a human boy that she fell in love with. Mahiro constantly rejects Nyaruko's advances towards him, usually with violence (i.e. stabbing her with forks) due to her persistence. Despite this, he does genuinely love her back but is often turned off by her behavior. Nyaruko would later be joined by her childhood friends Kuuko and Hasuta, the former of which is madly in love with her despite Nyaruko expressing zero interest in return and the latter is in love with Mahiro, making both of them an inconvenience for Nyaruko's relationship.

Nyaruko is capable of shapeshifting and takes the form of a silver-haired petite human girl, as her true form would cause people to lose their sanity. Her species was the inspiration for the character "Nyarlathotep" from H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. In combat, she uses a plethora of weapons including a crowbar, grenades, swords and chainsaws. 

It is later revealed that, as an incarnation of the character, Nyaruko is protected by the Story of Nyarlathotep, preventing anyone from truly defeating her. The final volume of the light novel series features a parody of Demonbane's Athleta Aeternum, where the Story of Nyarlathotep summons an army of infinite Nyarlathoteps from popular culture to save Nyaruko.

Nycrama is a cosmic entity first mentioned by Clark Ashton Smith in his unfinished story "The Infernal Star" and expanded upon by John W. Patterson. It made its first actual appearance in his Cthulhu Mythos story "Priestess of Nycrama", published in the December 1999 edition of Edward P. Berglund's online fanzine Nightscapes.

### History
Nycrama was once a human brujo, or sorcerer, in Central America who commanded a large following amongst the native peoples. Coming into possession of a powerful alien artefact, he began his descent into darkness, using the stone's power to consume the souls of young men in order to extend his own lifespan. When the creators of the stone discovered this, they destroyed his human body and banished his soul to a small pocket dimension.

Creating a new body for itself, an enormous, disgusting amalgamation of slug and maggot, it proceeded to use its influence over its former followers, coercing them into sending it more souls to increase its power as it sought a way to break free. Eventually, an alien woman named Endura, with the aid of intended human sacrifice Dr. Claude Farnsworth, was able to destroy the creature utterly, this time imprisoning its soul in the centre of the dark star Yuzh.

Nymphs are feminine nature spirits originating from Greek mythology. Beautiful, youthful, and divine, they are the offspring of gods, and often the lovers of gods and mortals.

Several types of Nymphs exist, each associated with a specific aspect of nature: Dryads of the trees, freshwater Naiads, oceanic Nereids, etc.

In "The White People", by Arthur Machen, a practitioner of magic claims that there are two kinds of Nymphs, one "bright" and the other "dark", both of which are described as "very lovely and very wonderful". While some people only see one kind or the other, there are also those who see both.

In H. P. Lovecraft's poem "To Pan", Nymphs and Satyrs dance to the music played by Pan.

Another Lovecraft poem, "Laeta: A Lament", tells of how "the shy Nymphs of the woodland, the fount and the plain" all tried in vain to equal the title character's beauty, yet bore no grudge or envy against her, as Laeta was so pure that the Nymphs loved her.

### In the Mythos
### Sea Nymphs (Nereids)
)]]
Thomas Olney saw Nereids and Tritons accompanying the procession of the gods Neptune and Nodens, and noted that the Nereids made a strange music "by striking on the grotesque resonant shells of unknown lurkers in black sea-caves". (: "The Strange High House in the Mist")

Dr. Makoto Yamada believes that legends of Nereids and Mermaids are actually inspired by the Sea-dwellers. (: "The Black Kiss")

### Wood Nymphs (Dryads)
The ancient sculptor Kalos habitually spent his nights in the woods conversing with Fauns and Dryads, which provided inspiration for his art. (: "The Tree")

As a boy, Jervas Dudley often spent time in the woods and watched the Dryads dance under the moonlight. (: "The Tomb")

Prior to his correspondence with Henry Wentworth Akeley, a skeptical Albert Wilmarth dismissed the stories about winged crustacean creatures of the Vermont woods as being comparable to the legends of Satyrs, Fauns and Dryads. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

A passage from the Necronomicon claims that when the time comes, the Spawn of Shub-Niggurath will "take dominion over all wood nymphs, satyrs, leprechauns, and the Little People". (: "The House on Curwen Street", "The Keeper of the Key")

In "The Moon-Lens", by Ramsey Campbell, it is suggested that satyrs, fauns and dryads are related to the Gof'nn hupadgh Shub-Niggurath: humans who have been transformed by Shub-Niggurath. Roy Leakey, after his transformation, was described by Dr. James Linwood as "half a dryad". Dr. Whitaker, who caught a glimpse of Leakey's hand, described it as clawed and looking like it was made out of wood.

Nyogtha is a Great Old One in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Henry Kuttner for his short story "The Salem Horror".

### Description
Nyogtha is an amorphous mass composed of an unidentifiable sticky black substance. It is capable of extruding tentacles from this mass to manipulate the environment around it. According to the cursed book the Necronomicon, the only way that it can be cast back to its own dimension once summoned is through the use of a ritual combining an ankh, the Tikkoun elixir and the Vach-Viraj incantation (: "The Salem Horror").

Nyogtha is served by a large pack of ghouls which live in the catacombs beneath the city of Arkham. (: "The Anatomy Lesson")

### History
When a man by the name of Carson unwittingly invoked the curse of Abigail Prinn, the body of the witch resurrected itself and attempted to summon Nyogtha through a portal between worlds known as the Witch Room. Luckily, an occultist named Michael Leigh was able to thwart the ritual through use of the method described in the Necronomicon, and both Abbie Prinn and the Great Old One were banished back through the partially opened gateway. (: "The Salem Horror")

Nyogtha was also worshiped for a time by a group of hustlers in New Orleans.

### In Other Media
*Nyogtha appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X. 
*The survival horror game That's Not My Neighbor features a character named after Nyogtha.
*The Ben 10: Omniverse episode "Mystery, Incorporeal" features a food truck known as "HP Lunchkraft", with one of the ingredients being named after Nyogtha.
*In the Adventure Time comic book series by Boom! Studios, the slime-based Cosmic Elemental known as Ng'Zot Aa bears a strong resemblance to Nyogtha, including its name and characterization.

Obed Marsh is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Background
Obed Marsh was a sea captain from Innsmouth. At the height of his career he had command of three ships, the Columbia, the Hetty, and the Sumatra Queen. He learned from the inhabitants of a Polynesian island a ritual to summon the Deep Ones. This was done on Devil Reef before entering into a pact with them, offering human sacrifices in exchange for a constant supply of fish and the occasional golden artefact. Marsh at some point founded the Esoteric Order of Dagon. He died in 1878 and his family continued their control of Innsmouth. He is the great-great-grandfather of Robert Olmstead. (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth) 

Years after his death, a Deep One with his face was seen swimming near Devil Reef, implying that he somehow became one despite not being descended from them. (: "The Watcher from the Sky")

shortDefinition: "Objects from the Gilman-Waite Collection" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and editor Ann K. Schwader, first published in her collection Strange Stars & Alien Shadows (2003, Lindisfarne Press) .  ### Synopsis A man visits an unusua...
fullContent:
"Objects from the Gilman-Waite Collection" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and editor Ann K. Schwader, first published in her collection Strange Stars & Alien Shadows (2003, Lindisfarne Press) .

### Synopsis
A man visits an unusual museum exhibit. The exhibit displays, amongst other things, bizarre golden jewellery with distinctly aquatic motifs. Seeing these items triggers memories of a heinous crime committed by the man during his university days. As the time in the exhibition drags on, his sanity becomes increasingly frayed, and he begins to believe that the attendant is in fact the woman he violated so many years ago, come back to exact the price for his foul deed…

### Behind the Mythos
The artefacts on display in the museum are clearly intended to be pieces created by the Deep Ones, as described in H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth, while the woman's description closely matches most common depictions of the Innsmouth Look. Additionally, the names Gilman and Waite are often associated with the scions of Innsmouth in Cthulhu Mythos fiction.

### Publication History  
*Strange Stars & Alien Shadows (2003, Lindisfarne Press)
*Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos: Cthulhu's Creatures (2007, Rainfall Books)
*The Book of Cthulhu II (2012, 2022, Night Shade Books)

The Obyriths are Lovecraftian-like demonic entities from the fictional universe of the Dungeons & Dragons pencil-and-paper roleplaying games by Wizards of the Coast.

### Background
The Obyriths are ancient demons which predated all other demonic races and even the gods. They rarely have humanoid forms, and mortals who glimpse an obyrith risk going insane. As time passed, some of the Obyrith lords assumed humanoid forms. Their reality was destroyed and most of their kind wiped out during the wars that resulted from the creation of the Abyss. There are only twelve Obyrith lords remaining, the greatest of them being the Queen of Chaos and the Pale Night. A number of Obyrith species have likewise survived.

Occupations are a key characteristic of characters in stories by H. P. Lovecraft and other Cthulhu Mythos writers. Often the heroes of such stories have a profession or other calling that provides a ready-made motivation for seeking the knowledge that leads to horrific revelations.

### Academics

### Professor
]]
Perhaps the archetypal Lovecraftian hero is the professor, whose academic role requires a continual quest for knowledge. The professor's drive to analyze and explain leads to the dreaded correlation of the mind's contents that Professor Francis Wayland Thurston warned against.

Students, like professors, are engaged in the pursuit of knowledge, only on an amateur rather than professional level, and so if anything even more liable to run into trouble.

Closely related to professors, the profession of librarian involves the collection of texts, which in Lovecraftian situations often conceal dangerous knowledge.

"October" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Written in October 1920, it did not see publication until its inclusion in the 1943 Arkham House collection Beyond the Wall of Sleep, six years after Lovecraft's death. It has since been reprinted several times in various collections .

### Overview
The poem, as may be gathered from its title, is an ode to the month of October, in which it was written. Lovecraft also wrote a similar month and seasonal themed poem, "August".

### Publication History 
* Beyond the Wall of Sleep (1943)
*Collected Poems (1963)
*The World of H. P. Lovecraft (1971)
*Fungi from Yuggoth and Other Poems (1971)
*Medusa and Other Poems by H. P. Lovecraft (1986)
*The Ancient Track: The Complete Poetical Works of H. P. Lovecraft (2001, 2013)

fullContent:
"October Surprise" is a 2006 short story by American author and editor Kevin L. O'Brien. It appeared in the October 2006 issue of the online fanzine Nightscapes (#16).

### Synopsis
In the lead-up to the 1980 Carter-Reagan presidential election, a 300,000-year-old man named Hawthorne, currently in charge of a covert government agency, uncovers a plot by a secret cabal to destroy a Deep One city and awaken the Great Old One Cthaeghya. Infiltrating the enemy group, Hawthorne meets the physicist behind the scheme, one Abigail Dexter. However, there is more to Dexter than meets the eye, and despite Hawthorne's best efforts, the plan succeeds. Cthaeghya is set free to release those Great Old Ones that remain imprisoned.

### Characters
*Ethan Oliver Hawthorne/Khuranes, an ancient human who has dedicated his existence to combatting the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos. Currently at the head of the covert agency known as Black Omega.
*Abigail Dexter/The Black Whore, an accomplished physicist and avatar of Nyarlathotep.
*Professor Laban Shrewsbury, a member of the Miskatonic University faculty with extensive occult knowledge.

### Behind the Mythos
Following the 1980 election, the Reagan campaign was accused of negotiating with the government of Iran to delay the release of American hostages held in the Tehran embassy until after the election--an allegation referred to as the "October Surprise".

Odin is a diety in Norse mythology, the ruler of Asgard and chief god of the Æsir tribe of deities. 

A more Lovecraftian-like depiction of Odin appears as the main antagonist of Robert E. Howard's short story "The Cairn on the Headland".

### Background
During the Dark Ages, Odin frequently appeared on Earth to his worshippers, either to accept human sacrifices or assist them in battles as a Norse warrior. Due to him taking the form of a human, Odin was subjected to many of the limitations of humanity and could be harmed by certain weapons. After being fatally wounded in the Battle of Clontarf near Dublin, Ireland, Odin's body was buried with the stones of the cairn by Red Cumal, an Irish warrior who was fighting against the pagan Viking invaders. Thereafter, Christianity became triumphant over his religion, with Odin eventually being forgotten to time. 

Hundreds of years later, Odin was dug up to be resurrected by the touch of holly. The human-like body was altered in horrific transmutation, now taking the form of a "slavering monster" with "shadowy tentacle-like arms outspread." Odin confronted James O'Brien, the reincarnation of Red Cumal, who managed to defeat him with the cross of Saint Brandon, banishing the heathen god back to the stars where it came from. (: "The Cairn on the Headland")

### In Other Media
*Demonbane: Odin appears in the novel Zanma Taisen Demonbane, as one of the Elder Gods who engaged in battle against the Vortex Blaster. He has authority over [Evil-Crushing Truth-Spreading], which gives him the ability to reject a single law and overwrite it with his own.

"Of Circles and Rings" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tom Lynch.

### Synopsis
Pete Jones, an up-and-coming martial artist, thinks he has found in Shun Jian someone who can teach him a new method of fighting which will make him unbeatable. Unbeknownst to Pete, his "teacher" is actually a millennia-old cultist of Yog-Sothoth, and his god requires sacrifice to continue granting Shun eternal youth.

### Characters
* Pete Jones, a young and gifted sportsman.
* Shun Jian, an ancient follower of the dark god Yog-Sothoth.

### Publication History
"Of Circles and Rings" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu by April Moon Books in March 2014.

"Of Gold and Sawdust" is a short non-fiction piece by H. P. Lovecraft’s former friend and contemporary Samuel Loveman, published in the 1975 limited-run collection The Occult Lovecraft.

### Overview
Samuel Loveman was originally a close confidante of H.P. Lovecraft who sponsored him into his own amateur writing world and in return was the beneficiary of Loveman, a bookman, introducing him to ghostwriting clients and other sponsors. 

As interest in Lovecraft grew after his death, Loveman wrote three memoirs of his friend. In 1948 he wrote “Howard Phillips Lovecraft” which was laudatory, the 1958 summary of conversations and table talk “Lovecraft as a Conversationalist” but finally the extremely critical “Of Gold and Sawdust” written in 1975 near the end of Loveman's own life. This final memoir related to Lovecraft went into detail about what Loveman had, in correspondence with Sonia Greene, come to see as Lovecraft's extreme hypocrisy, deviousness and violent anti-semitism.
