Young Melei, a peasant serving girl from the city of Ulthar in the Dreamlands, discovers that when she sleeps, she has certain abilities which she doesn’t possess in her waking life. She uses her newfound power of flight to explore the farthest reaches of the new world laid bare beneath her.

"Of the Doom of Irem" is a short Cthulhu Mythos work by Mexican author Luis F. Abbadie.

### Overview
The piece is written as a factual translation of a portion of the Necronomicon (although it is stated to have come from a Latin fragment, itself translated into Spanish and then English).

The excerpt concerns the building and subsequent destruction of the city of Irem, first mentioned in the Cthulhu Mythos in the short story "The Nameless City" (), but with a number of major differences; for example, Irem is stated to have been built by Shaddad (similar to the Encyclopedia Britannica entry of the builder, a man named Shedad) as opposed to the inhabitants described by Lovecraft.

### Publication History
"Of the Doom of Irem" was published in the online Mythos zine Nightscapes in September 1998.

"Of the Faceless Crowd" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Hungarian author Gábor Csigás, writing as Csigás Gábor. It was published in the Salomé Jones-edited anthology Cthulhu Lives! by Ghostwoods Books in August 2014.

### Synopsis
The story explores the emotional toll taken on a group of three unspecified entities as they pose undercover as a human family on Earth. For unknown reasons, the three must periodically switch roles within the family - mother, father, and young daughter - at the whim of their handlers, with some of the roles being more desirable than others.

### Mythos Connections
At one point, one of the entities thinks to itself that humans have "[n]o need to know about bio-engineered doppelgangers built on tech ‘stolen’ from a certain alien race from Yuggoth." Who these beings might be to steal from the technologically-advanced Mi-Go is never explored.

"Of the Fittest" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Evan Dicken. It was published in the Jason Andrew-edited anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods in October 2015.

### Synopsis
After serving a compulsory five-year term in Hastur's Yellow Guard, Sergeant Long returns home to his family in a world wracked by the conflict of warring abominations. He finds his wife and friends have formed a resistance to Hastur's reign, and agrees to help them strike back against an avatar of the Great Old One. However, at the last minute Long gets cold feet, and strikes a bargain with the being: hand over his friends to the Byakhee, and his family will be spared.

The Ogdru Hem were the spawn of the Ogdru Jahad and serve as major antagonists in the fictional universe of Hellboy by Dark Horse Comics.

### History
The Ogdru Hem were spawned originally by the Ogdru Jahad during the begining of time, and they assisted their parents during the battle against the Watchers. They lost and the Seven Gods of Chaos were imprisoned in a crystal prison in the heart of the cosmos, while the Hem were slain.

Despite their death, the spawn of the great dragon still continued to exist as spiritis and eventually managed to get physical forms back. Their main mission was to prepare the Earth for the coming of their parents, mainly by spreading destruction and turning humans into Frog Monsters.

Their numbers rose during the apocalypse, but were eventually destroyed by Liz Sherman as she burned the Earth to a crisp.

### Appearance
The Ogdru Hem are based heavily on the works of Lovecraft, resembling cephalopods, worms and crustaceans. In ancient times, some Ogdru Hem took the form of dragons, inspiring many myths on Earth.

### Members

*Katha-Hem
*Conqueror Worm

fullContent:
The Ogdru Jahad (aka, the Dragons of Revelation) are Lovecraftian reptilian entities in the fictional universe of Hellboy by Dark Horse Comics.

### Background
The Ogdru Jahad  are chaotic entities whose goal is subjugation and destruction. Beings whose appearance can induce madness. They were born on the newly created Earth, created out of mud and fire by great spirits. Whom were the Watchers, sent by God to oversee his new creation. Despite the efforts of the Watchers, the Ogdru Jahad did not awaken, appearing a failure. During the night the Ogdru Jahad awakened and began to breed abominations, the Ogdru Hem, the first lifeforms on Earth. A total of 369 were spawned before the outaged Watchers waged war against them. Most of the Ogdru Hem were slain and the Ogdru Jahad were imprisoned in a crystal prison in the heart of the cosmos. God looked toward the Earth and in fury punished the Watchers for ruining his creation. Those Odgru Hem which were slain, continued to exist as spirits which would attempt to free their imprisoned Ogdru Hem siblings.

Ever since the Ogdru Jahad have been attempting to break free from their imprisonment and return to Earth. In the early 21st century, one of them (Nunn-Jahad) finally did so, and returned to an apocalyptic Earth. Where it immediately destroyed part of the state of Kansas upon landing and began to breed hordes of Ogdru Hem. Despite the efforts of the U.S. military (barrage of nuclear missiles) and the Bureau for Paranormal Research & Defense (B.P.R.D), they were unable to stop his advance. Worldwide other Ogdru Hem were appearing, devastating cities alongside the Frog people and Hammerhead monsters which served them. He was finally stopped by Johann Kraus who sacrificed himself, channeling the infinite power of Vril to kill Nunn-Jahad. After which all the Ogdru Hem on Earth went still and silent. Though it did not save the Earth, as Hellboy soon afterwards fulfilled his prophecy, bringing about the end of the world (with the help of his lover Elizabeth Sherman who burned the world to a crisp). What remained of humanity survived within Hollow Earth, leaving the surface world to a new race created by Hellboy and the goddess Hecate, a race of amphibious humanoids (similar to Abe Sapien) with Elizabeth Sherman encased protectively in a crystal.

During this apocalypse, the demonic champion of Earth, Hellboy and the B.P.R.D. battled numerous Ogdru Hem, Frog Monsters, and Hammerhead-monsters. Among the Ogdru Hem they faced was the skyscraper-tall bipedal Katha-Hem that was invulnerable to conventional weapons and which emitted green grass that turned humans into frog people. Another one, Sadu-Hem was a tentacled monstrosity which converted a complete town into frog people. The Conqueror Worm was one which also turned humans into frog people with its gas and continued to grow in size, threatening the entire planet.

Olathoë is a great fortified city of marble in the far northern kingdom of Lomar in the Dreamlands. It lies on the Plateau of Sarkis in a hollow between the mountains Noton and Kadiphonek. Olathoë faces external threats from a horde of ruthless conquerors known as the Inutos that appeared out of the unknown west. The city is also threatened by the gradual encroachment of a great advancing ice sheet that long ago displaced the Zobnarians, the ancestors of the Lomarians. (: "Polaris") 

### Description
Olathoë's architecture makes extensive use of marble in its construction. The upper parts of the pillars are carved into the images of bearded men, and the public squares where people gather to converse contain many statues. As a city in a high northern latitude region, Olathoë experiences periods of continual daylight and darkness. (: "Polaris") 

Olathoë is a repository for the grimoire known as the Pnakotic Manuscripts, as well as books that contain the wisdom of the Zobnarian Fathers. (: "Polaris")

### Inhabitants
The people of Olathoë exhibit characteristics of nobility and wisdom, combined with a strong and honorable warrior tradition. They regard themselves as the bravest of the Lomarians. The commander of the army is Alos who is described as "a true man and patriot". (: "Polaris") 

### Notable Locations
The Watchtower of Thapnen is a tower that guards the narrow pass that comes up from behind Mount Noton, providing a defense against potential invaders that would use the pass to launch a surprise attack against Olathoë. In such a case, a signal fire would be lit at the top of the tower to warn the soldiers and thereby save the city from immediate disaster. (: "Polaris")

Olaus Wormius (13 May 1588 – 31 August 1654) is a historical figure, a 17th century Danish scholar who made significant contributions to medicine, natural history and literature. In his fictional "History of the Necronomicon", H. P. Lovecraft credits Olaus Wormius with making the first translation of the Necronomicon into Latin, but dates this event to 1228--360 years before the historical Wormius was born.

Brian Lumley's Cthulhu Mythos novella Lord of the Worms draws in-universe attention to this discrepancy, but leaves open whether the translator of the Necronomicon was a different person, or if Wormius was in fact a sorcerer who extended his life by unnatural means.

Similarly, in The Womb of Time, by Brian Stableford, it is claimed that the 1228 version of the Necronomicon was translated from Greek to Latin "by someone who signed himself Olaus Wormius, although that was a long time before the more famous scholar of that name was born".

Joan Stanley, in Ex Libris Miskatonici, a fictional catalogue of Miskatonic University's arcana collection, writes that the 1228 translation  is "incorrectly attributed by many to Olaus Wormius," and suggests that instead it was done by Accursius (c. 1182 – 1263), an Italian jurist "who was noted for being outspokenly blasphemous." Stanley adds that Wormius did produce a Latin translation of the Necronomicon--in 1624, not 1228--and that "his version is still the best of the Renaissance translations."

fullContent:
"Old Bugs" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, probably written shortly before July 1919. (EXP: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) It was first published in the Arkham House book The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces (1959).

The piece was written after Lovecraft's friend Alfred Galpin's suggestion that he wanted to try alcohol before Prohibition went into effect. In response, Lovecraft, a teetotaler, wrote a tale of an old derelict known as Old Bugs, who turns out to be Galpin himself, brought low by "evil habits, dating from a first drink taken years before in woodland seclusion." At the bottom of the manuscript, Lovecraft had written, "Now will you be good?" (EXP: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

The woman whose engagement to Old Bugs is canceled due to his drinking, Eleanor Wing, was a fellow student in Galpin's high school press club. (EXP: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

### Reaction
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia says of the piece, "It is not nearly as ponderous as it sounds, and is in fact a little masterpiece of comic deflation and self-parody." (EXP: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

The Old Gods are Lovecraftian-like entities in the fictional universe of the Warcraft video game by Blizzard Entertainment.

### Background
The Old Ones are eldritch parasitic horrors which were created by the Void Lords. The Void Lords desired to warp the universe into a realm of chaos and suffering. Opposing them were the Titans, planet-sized cosmic beings who spread life across the cosmos. They created the Old Gods to corrupt nascent Titans before they awakened.

From the Void, the Old Gods were hurled into the universe, in the hope that some of them would smash into worlds containing sleeping Titans. Their sole purpose being to locate and corrupt the sleeping Titan world-souls. The Old Gods being the physical manifestations of the Void, appear as colossal horrors, growing on those worlds like cancerous tumors. 
 
Several of them ended up on Azeroth where they established the Black Empire, spawned two servitor race, and ruled the planet. They were later defeated by the Titans' armies and imprisoned. Despite their sequestration, they were able to influence the world, corrupting races and individuals. Originally they waged war against each other, but ever since their imprisonment they have been working together, influencing the history of Azeroth. 

The greatest of their servants during their imprisonment was the great dragon, Deathwing who lived for over 10,000 years, led a flight of corrupted dragons, and was responsible for the recent global cataclysm which reshaped the world. Another great monster in their service is Ozumat, the patriarch of the krakens. Queen Azshara is another one, the queen of the night elfs who betrayed her people and attempted to summon to Azeroth the dark titan Sargeras, Lord of the Burning Legion. In the aftermath of her failure and the flooding of her city, she made a pact with the Old Gods, as she and her followers were transformed into the naga.

The Old Ones are Lovecraftian-like demons in the fictional universe of the Buffy the Vampire Slayer franchise by 20th Century Fox.

### Background
The Old Ones were pure-breed demons that ruled Earth prior to man, during the Primordium Age (liked they ruled many other dimensions). They warred endlessly with each other, were worshiped as gods, and turned Earth into a nightmarish world. Eventually mortal animals emerged, including humans, and the Old Ones were driven from Earth's reality by unknown powers. The Old Ones bred with or infected the mortal animals of Earth, creating hundreds of demon species. Cults were established which worshiped the Old Ones, anticipating their return to Earth which would result in the destruction of mankind. 

The greatest of the Old Ones could never be destroyed, and the most one could do was destroy their physical bodies. Their essence would live on though and thereby have the ability to eventually come into being again. Thousands of Old Ones were buried in the "Deeper Well", whose corpses or essences were contained within sarcophagi to prevent their resurrection. It ran across the Earth, nearly 8,000 miles, and could be accessed via an entrance in England and another one in New Zealand.

### Known Old Ones
*Illyria: During the Primordian Age, she ruled over what would become California, where she led an army of a thousand demons, and greatly enjoyed battle, once participating in a war that lasted a thousand years. She was eventually overthrown by her rivals and imprisoned. At the beginning of the 21st century, she was reincarnated in the body of Winifred Burkle of Angel Investigations, only to discover that her army was gone, mankind dominated the Earth, and her powers a pale shadow of what they once were. At first an antagonist of the vampire anti-hero Angel and his team, eventually she became an ally of theirs.
*Maloker: Was the progenitor of the demon races of vampires. He returned to Earth in the early 21st century, reincarnated within Dracula. His return was short-lived as Dawn (turned into a giant by Willow) staked his heart.
*Arsgomor: He was a rival of Illyria, who attempted to conquer her lands and upon his defeat was entombed by her, only to be accidentally freed by her in the early 21st century after which she defeated him again. 
*Quor'toth: Who ruled his own dimension, where he slumbered for millennia, a dimension with so much hate and negativity, that it made the witch Willow go dark.
*Baticus: He was a giant worm-like Old One, the last of his kind which had attempted to overthrow Illyria and failing were exterminated, after which he was entombed and temporarily freed in the early 21st century before being slain by Illyria.

fullContent:
The Old Ones are Lovecraftian eldritch titans in the fictional universe of Palladium's Rifts Megaverse, a pen-and-paper game. These beings are the personifications of chaos and evil.

### Background
The origins of the Old Ones are unknown and no one knows how long they have existed. What is known is that for millions of years they ruled numerous worlds and dimensions. Some believe that they created magic, and if not, that at the very least they contributed to its evolution. It is also believed that the Old Ones created many lifeforms, including elves and dragons. The reign of the Old Ones was one of despair and sorrow, having established psychic empires in which lesser lifeforms were their playthings.

Eventually an alliance rose in opposition against them, consisting of many races. The result of this was an epic war that ultimately doomed most of those races. The greatest and most powerful among the Old Ones (Xy, the Great Old One) was tricked by another Old One and disappeared. This turned the tide for the rebellion which eventually realized its goal of finally putting an end to the horrible supremacy of the Old Ones, all of whom were forced into a state of sleep, being imprisoned in the bowels of various worlds.

### The Race of Old Ones
The Old Ones are a race whose members do not have a set form. Rather, each member has a wholly distinct form, all of which are nightmarish in their manifestations, violating the known laws of physics and/or biology. Their bodies are so disturbing that most mortals would go mad upon seeing them. Incomprehensible combinations of ectoplasm, slime, flesh, mouths, eyes, teeth, heads, limbs, and tentacles. If any useful analogy of them might be made, it is that they are a race of psychic vampires, all of whom feed on the emotions of lesser lifeforms. As negative emotions are the strongest and most intense, those are the ones they prefer.

While the Old Ones are not omnipotent, their powers vastly exceed those of most cosmic and mystical races and entities. Old Ones are able to shapeshift, have a lifespan that is conservatively in the millions of years, and can regenerate. They have extensive knowledge of magic, and posses nearly god-like psionic powers. They possess such power that if one of them were to be destroyed, the cosmic energy released by its death would be catastrophic. Therefore the reason they were imprisoned rather than be destroyed upon their defeat. Nonetheless, though the Old Ones slumber, and in that slumber their powers be muted, sentient races and beings continue to be influenced by them. Escaping their imprisonment and conquering the Megaverse is their ultimate goal.

### Known Old Ones

*Ya-Blik

*Erva
*Tarm-kin-toe
*Ya-ahk-met

The Old Ones are a species or group of demonic-like cosmic beings in the Grimm Fairy Tales multiverse which are based on the Old Ones of the Cthulhu Mythos. They were first identified as Old Ones in issue #2 of the 1st volume of Call of Wonderland in 2012. The first Old One to appear was the Jabberwocky in issue #16 of the 1st volume of the Grimm Fairy Tales in 2007, though he wasn't identified as an Old One till years later.

### Background
The Old Ones are incredibly powerful entities that represent the forces of chaos in the cosmos. Their enemies are the Keepers, who represent the forces of order. In ancient times, these two factions waged a war across the realities that threatened to tear the multiverse apart. Defeated by the Keepers, the Old Ones were put into slumber and imprisoned for eternity. 

The Keepers spared only one, the youngest of the Old Ones, for all intents a baby, the Jabberwocky, who was put in the Realm of Dreams, to have its evil cleansed, which ended up being a spectacular failure. Early in the 21st century, the Red Knight tried to free the Old Ones, so that they would destroy the world.

Old Whateley, also known as Wizard Whateley, is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror".

### Biography
It can be assumed that he summoned Yog-Sothoth to impregnate his daughter or that she was a type of sacrifice.

He was the "aged and half-insane father of Lavinia Whateley, about whom the most frightful tales of magic had been whispered in his youth". Dunwich gossips recall that "the hills once shook when he shrieked the dreadful name of Yog-Sothoth in the midst of a circle of stones with a great book open in his arms before him."

He and his daughter occupy a large farmhouse on a hillside, four miles from the Village of Dunwich, Massachusetts, and a mile and a half from any other dwellings. When his daughter was twelve, his wife died, through ill-explained but violent means.

He has a large collection of "rotting ancient books and parts of books" which he inherited through two centuries of Whateleys. He uses these to "instruct and catechise" his daughter as well as his grandson Wilbur. One such book was an incomplete version of the infamous Necronomicon.

He died of natural causes on August 2, 1924. Just before his passing he left Wilbur with the responsibility of looking after his twin:



Wilbur observed that the whippoorwills dispersed shortly after his passing, signifying that the creatures did not take his soul. (: "The Dunwich Horror")

It is unknown if he is the same man as John Whateley (: Fungi from Yuggoth).

### Trivia
*In Stanley C. Sargent's short story "The Black Brat of Dunwich" Old Whateley's first name is given as Elezer.

Older Gods is a low budget British Lovecraftian horror film. Despite containing no direct references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, it features strong cosmic horror motifs, such as an ancient cult which worships a sleeping god, and the impact of dark knowledge on the sanity of mankind.

### Synopsis
In an attempt to come to terms with the disappearance of his friend Billy, American Chris rents the remote cottage where he was last seen, located far from civilisation in rural Wales. Uncovering a video diary and evidence of a doomsday cult left by his friend, Chris begins a descent into madness which culminates in the revelation that the cult has spread its insidious influence to all corners of the globe in anticipation of the awakening of a dark god.

### Behind the Mythos
Written, produced and directed by David A. Roberts, Older Gods was filmed on a budget of around $500,000, with filming being squeezed in between lockdowns during the Covid-19 pandemic. Released on the indie film festival circuit in 2023, although many IMDb users criticise it's slow pacing.

Olkoth, also known as The God of the Celestial Arcs, is a fictional entity created by user Danto for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game website Tentacules.net, which first appeared in the scenario "The Voice of Christ". The character was later given an in-print publication, being featured as the antagonist of Bryn Fortey's 2021 short story "Beneath the Pimple", published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine.

### Overview
Olkoth is an Outer God who appears as a demoniacal deity with the ability to manifest in the form of a human if certain conditions are met, such as in proximity to an eyeless, grotesque statue of the Virgin Mary. It is described as a cautious being, one which always waits to see which way the wind is blowing before taking sides in any conflict.

Olkoth has always played on the sidelines, aligning itself with whatever being it deems to be the potential victor. However, the Outer God Yog-Sothoth, losing patience with Olkoth's machinations, set in motion a plan to trick it into taking the wrong side and thus allowing Yog-Sothoth to wreak its vengeance upon it. This plan, enacted with the aid of D'endrrah and involving Mh'ithrha, resulted in Olkoth being imprisoned beneath Twymbarlwm, a culturally significant hill in Wales. (: "Beneath the Pimple")

"On Icy Kinarth" is a poem by Frank Belknap Long which was published in the April 1930 issue of Weird Tales.

The planet Kynarth (spelled with a "y") was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos in the short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price.

### Synopsis
The poem describes a dream the narrator has, in which they find themself standing at the edge of a cliff on "icy Kinarth", with bats and "lizard-birds" soaring through the sky above, and an agitated sea below. The narrator clings desperately to a tree while trying not to slip on the ice. To make matters worse, a predatory "fleshless thing" is drawn to and attacks the narrator, clawing their face while producing "sharp metallic cries". The narrator's fate is undisclosed.

fullContent:
"On the Death of a Rhyming Critic" is a satirical poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. It first saw print in the July 1917 edition of the Toledo Amateur.

### Poem
* My Muse attempts a doleful rune:
* Poor MACER Sunday afternoon
* Resign’d the cares of earthly strife,
* And reach’d his last eternal life!
* A curious fellow in his time,
* Fond of old books and prone to rhyme—
* A scribbling pedant, of the sort
* That scorn the age, and write for sport.
* A little wit he sometimes had,
* But half of what he wrote was bad;
* In metre he was very fair;
* Of rhetoric he had his share—
* But of the past so much he’d prate,
* That he was always out of date!
* He lean’d to mythologic matters,
* And sang of Gods and Nymphs and Satyrs,
* Till so unvary’d grew his art,
* You could not tell his works apart!
* The modern ear he’d often pain
* With rantings in heroic strain:
* And when the town would call them witty,
* ‘Twas mostly out of friendly pity.
* Tho’ much by ancient notions marr’d,
* He was a fairly clever bard;
* His numbers smooth enough would roll,
* But after all—he had no soul!
* His pen was ever keen to fight
* For manly virtue and the right—
* But somehow he was rather weak;
* Instead of slang he quoted Greek!
* He serv’d his purpose—to correct
* Each rising poet’s crude defect,
* And yet—he ne’er made life the sweeter,
* For all he knew was rhyme and metre.
* His even verses will be miss’d—
* Tho’ he was quite an egotist!
* Of all his views I can’t approve,
* But still, I mourn with tears of love.
* My grief is deep—since half past three
* I’ve worked upon an elegy,
* Yet cannot seem to get it done
* In time to reach the Morning Sun!
* The polish must my care engage,
* For I am promis’d the first page!
* Yes, he is gone! I feel the sorrow—
* The fun’ral will be held tomorrow—
* My broadcloth suit I’m having press’d
* To go and see him laid to rest.
* God speed his soul! I trust he’ll rove
* In peace ‘mid Seraphim above—
* And by the way, tho’ I’ve been told
* He had but little wealth in gold,
* I wonder what his heirs will do
* With all his books—they were not few!
* In truth, I know of two or three
* That could be nobly us’d by me!
* So many strugglers he befriended,
* That rougher bards on him depended:
* His death will still more pens than his—
* I wonder where the fellow is!
* He’s in a better land—or worse—
* (I wonder who’ll revise my verse?)
* He never left a stanza slack—
* But I could hardly wish him back.
* Tears for his loss do freely flow—
* Yet after all, ‘tis better so!

"On the Eastbound Train" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Darrell Schweitzer. It was published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express by Chaosium in December 2014.

### Synopsis
After promising young scholar George Henderson is invited by the Turkish government to study a newly-discovered manuscript unearthed at a historic monastery, he takes passage to Constantinople on the legendary passenger train the Orient Express. Aboard, he is approached by his former mentor Professor Augustus Lindsay, who inducts the naïve young man into a cult dedicated to gathering forbidden lore.

Although Henderson’s induction into the cult results in the loss of his sanity and the seeming death of Lindsay, much later it emerges that Henderson had continued his mentor's work for decades after the incident. He and his blasphemous acts were only exposed when the others of the cult were hunted down and destroyed, and Henderson himself committed to a mental health institution.

### Mythos Connections
The man who first inducted Lindsay into the sinister brotherhood went by the name of Jedediah Orne, and claimed to be over 200 years old; Jedediah was an alias used by Simon Orne, one of the primary antagonists in The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, who used dark magic is to extend his lifespan. An item of note is that Lindsay boarded the train at Vienna, the closest stop to Prague, where Orne was said to have relocated.

### Trivia
* A man consulted by Lindsay during his metaphysical research, "a noted specialist in mental diseases in Vienna … obsessed with earthbound, carnal explanations, and … quite unable to follow the path of Professor Lindsay’s brilliance," would appear to be a reference to pioneering neurologist Sigmund Freud.

On the Sending Out of the Soul is an occult text created by American author Henry Kuttner for his 1939 short story "Hydra".

### Description
A 4" by 5" pamphlet running to eight pages, On the Sending Out of the Soul contains seven pages of "banal sophisms of mysticism" with the last page giving instructions on how to project one's astral self. The instructional is deceptive, however, with those who follow the directions causing the beheading of others who are then fed upon by the extra-dimensional entity dubbed the Hydra, their souls forever trapped in a state of extreme anguish.

### History
On the Sending Out of the Soul was published in Salem in 1793 by worshipers of the Hydra, although whether it originated here is unclear. All copies of it are presumed destroyed in the modern age.

"On The Thing in the Woods by Harper Collins" is a poem by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. Although dated 29 November 1924, it remained unpublished until decades after his death, when it made its first appearance in the 2001 Night Shade Books anthology The Ancient Track: The Complete Poetical Works of H. P. Lovecraft .

### Overview
The poem is a commentary on the 1913 children’s novel The Thing in the Woods, a story concerning lycanthropy in rural Pennsylvania, by Margery Williams; when published in America, the book had been issued under the pseudonym Harper Collins. It has been speculated to have been an influence on Lovecraft's 1929 short story "The Dunwich Horror" , which may be supported by his writing of this piece.

"On the Threshold" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
Two scientists attempting to access other dimensions tear a hole in reality which allows something to come through and begin what appears to be a hostile takeover. Luckily for them, they figure out that the universe has a natural barrier to such events in place and, after they remove their system protections, an eldritch guardian banishes the thing back to its own world.

### Characters
*John, a scientist working on the practicalities of other-dimensional access.
*Connon, John's partner, far more zealous in his pursuit of knowledge.

### Publication History
*Ominous Realities: The Anthology of Dark Speculative Horrors (2013)
*Dread: A Head Full of Bad Dreams (2016)
*Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2019, 2021)
*Lab: Three Tales of Weird Fiction (2020)

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no references to either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Meikle's inclusion of "On the Threshold" in the collection Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates his belief that it follows in the spirit of such works. Additionally, the description of the entity which breaks through from another dimension (itself a common trope in Lovecraftian fiction) is virtually identical to that of a being from two of Meikle's other short stories, "Bats in the Belfry" and "The Last Quest", which was a manifestation of the Outer God Yog-Sototh.

"Once More, from the Top" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Adam Scott Glancy, which takes place in the Delta Green sub-setting for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. It was first published in the anthology Delta Green: Dark Theatres (2001, Armitage House) .

### Synopsis
A retired former U.S. marine, now semi-crippled and living in a retirement home, relates the story of his deployment as a young man to the coastal fishing town of Innsmouth during the late 1920s. His battalion was assigned to conduct door-to-door operations, separating those citizens who were obviously inhuman from the others. He and another marine bore witness to the vengeful retaliation of the Deep Ones and their Shoggoth servitors, and were instrumental in turning the tide against their aquatic opponents.

The story concludes with the man telling of how he went on to have a long career in the military, and had witnessed several enclaves of the same strange-looking people he saw in Innsmouth in various locations across the globe. When he asks his interviewers if humanity is winning the conflict against these creatures, the lead interviewer tells him yes, but privately reflects that the opposite is true.

The One Below All is a Lovecraftian-like eldritch entity in the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics.

### Background
The One Below All, is the multiversal counterpart of the multiversal One-Above-All. It resides in the deepest part of Hell called the "Below-Place" and is the source of the mutagenic form of Gamma energy. It uses those mutated by gamma energy to manifest itself in the material world. The entity spawns entities known as Qlippoths and disgorges legions of demonic monsters.

It can only possess one host at a time to directly influence the physical world, but from its realm it can subtly influence people and events in the material world. Anger and sorrow increases its power, and though it is prevented from accessing in full the physical world, its power in the physical world still greatly eclipses that of other demonic entities like Mephisto.

The Onga are a fictional Congo river basin tribe created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1920 short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family".

### Overview
The Onga were first encountered by Sir Wade Jermyn during his expedition to the Congo river basin in the mid-1700s. In the time "Arthur Jermyn" takes place, the titular character also travelled to the basin on a research expedition, where he too encountered the Onga.

The Onga retained cultural memory and legends regarding the "white apes" of the nearby jungle ruins.

### Possible Etymology
Real life Congo tribes and moieties predominantly belong to the Mongo or Anamongo language and cultural family. Since the "M" in Mongo is sometimes more of a hum or even a glottal sound, it is quite possible that in the first quarter of the twentieth century them any stories about the Congo could have had a wide variation in spelling and pronunciation of what is even today a disparate language group, especially since alien language terminology has been imposed on the Mongo moieties for over a century.

Others suggested that their name may be related to the Ngoe, or Nkongho language groups spoken by the Bantu peoples of what is now Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and Cameroon.

### Trivia
*Onga is a Congolese surname.

"Only the End of the World Again" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author and comic book creator Neil Gaiman, featuring the character Lawrence Talbot from the 1941 film The Wolf Man. First published in the thematic anthology Shadows Over Innsmouth in 1994, it has been reprinted many times, and has even been translated into Dutch, French, Portuguese and German.

### Synopsis
The story concerns a man named Lawrence Talbot, an "adjustor" [sic] who also happens to be a lycanthrope. Intended to be a blood sacrifice to allow the Deep Ones and their gods to rise and reclaim the Earth, his would-be murderers do not count on the ferocity of his canine nature, giving him the opportunity to kill them, and thus preventing the titular "End of the World".

### Characters
*Lawrence Talbot, a shapeshifter in an unknown but shady-sounding profession.
*Madame Ezekiel, an avatar of the racial will of the Deep Ones, destroyed by Talbot.
*The Bartender, a member of the Esoteric Order of Dagon, killed by Talbot.
*The Fat Man, another member of the Order, one whose agenda seems to run contrary to the others.

Oorn is a fictional entity created by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow for their 1933 short story "The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast". 

### Overview
A pudgy creature with short grey-colored fur and three small red eyes, Oorn is believed to have originated from the mysterious "outer abyss", and was found on the outskirts of the city of Zeth, located on an extraterrestrial planet, long before the dawn of humanity on Earth.

While it hasn't demonstrated actual intelligence, Oorn does have the ability to mimic speech. The shamith priests of Zeth have declared Oorn to be a god and oracle, and surreptitiously instruct it on what to answer every time the citizens ask questions to it, knowing that Oorn will flawlessly repeat the priests' words. (: "The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast")

Oorn is described as being the mate of the Great Old One Mnomquah.(source?)

### Behind the Mythos
Brian Lumley later created a different creature named Oorn for his 1987 Cthulhu Mythos novel Mad Moon of Dreams. As "The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast" was written in 1933 but remained unpublished until 1994, it seems extremely unlikely that Lumley was aware of the mention of this previous being.

Oorn is a fictional creature created by British author Brian Lumley for his 1987 Cthulhu Mythos novel Mad Moon of Dreams.

### Description
Oorn is the mate of the Great Old One Mnomquah, described as a huge tentacled mollusc-like being with appendages which are capable of spraying digestive acids. It is worshipped by both the Men of Leng and the Moon-beasts.

### Behind the Mythos
A creature also called Oorn was created by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow for their story "The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast". However, as this story was written in 1933 but unpublished until 1994, seven years after the publication of Mad Moon of Dreams, it seems highly unlikely that Lumley would have been aware of its existence when writing about his own creation.

"Ooze" is a short story by American author and editor Anthony M. Rud. It has been speculated that it was an influence on H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror".

### Synopsis
A wealthy scientist living in the Alabama backwoods discovers a way to allow amoeba to grow to any size. When a specimen grows to the size of a cow's liver, he instructs his son to destroy it. The son, seeing an opportunity to increase his father's fame, does not destroy the creature, and instead pays a local to bring meat to feed it. However, the amoeba grows too large and hungry, and devours the son and daughter-in-law. The father succeeds in burning the creature to death, but is driven insane with grief.

### Characters

*Unnamed Narrator, a friend of the Cranmer family who determines to uncover the truth of what happened.
*John Corliss Cranmer, an accomplished and extremely wealthy scientist.
*Lee Cranmer, John's son.
*Rori Pailleron, a dim-witted local drunk who strikes a bargain with Lee.

### Publication History
"Ooze" was the first story in the debut issue of Weird Tales, March 1923. It has since been reprinted in several publications, including more than one Weird Tales anthology.

shortDefinition: "Open Minded" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. Taking place in his dystopian Punktown setting, it was first published in the Chaosium anthology Eldritch Chrome: Unquiet Tales of a Mythos-Haunted Future in October 201...
fullContent:
"Open Minded" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. Taking place in his dystopian Punktown setting, it was first published in the Chaosium anthology Eldritch Chrome: Unquiet Tales of a Mythos-Haunted Future in October 2013.

### Synopsis
Fallon Ash, an up-and-coming technology designer in Punktown, is assigned by his company to design a prototype humanoid bionic armature for the extra-dimensional Ogim. The specifications for this device state that it must be capable of being piloted by an artificial brain, although their reasons for requiring such a function are kept secret.

During the course of his work, Ash stumbles across news reports of a series of murders where the victims have all been leaders in their respective fields, and whose corpses have all been discovered sans brain. At the same time he witnesses a secretive test by the Ogim utilising an "artificial" brain and the prototype device, and comes to the obvious conclusion: that the beings are stealing live human brains and implanting them in his machine. Unfortunately for Ash, a technical fumble alerts the Ogim to his snooping.

The story concludes with the Ogim ordering fourteen of the new armatures before departing Punktown. As they leave they thank Ash for his assistance, telling him that they may one day return for "further use of that clever mind of yours". Ash immediately recalls that he had only uncovered details of thirteen of the bizarre murders…

### Publication History
Since its 2013 debut in Eldritch Chrome, "Open Minded" has also appeared in the collections of Thomas's own works Flesh for Punktown (2019) and Punktown: Volume 1 (2021).

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly named as such, the alien Ogim are intended to be Mi-Go: their descriptions, their activities involving human brains, their home planet of Yuggoth, and their species name backwards, are all clear pointers towards their true nature.

shortDefinition: Operation Antarctica is a science fiction/horror novella by British-born author William Meikle which, while not prominently connected, is loosely linked to the Cthulhu Mythos.  ### Synopsis An elite group of soldiers are sent to investigate an abando...
fullContent:
Operation Antarctica is a science fiction/horror novella by British-born author William Meikle which, while not prominently connected, is loosely linked to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
An elite group of soldiers are sent to investigate an abandoned German research facility located within the Antarctic Circle which dates from the days of the Second World War. There they encounter Nazi zombies and an experimental flying saucer which is powered by an infernal creature imprisoned within during its construction. Only through the help offered by the journal of famed occult detective Thomas Carnacki are they able to defeat the enemy and escape with their lives.

### Characters
*Captain John Banks, leader of the expedition.
*Sergeant Hynd, Banks's second-in-command.
*Corporal McCally, another soldier.
*Private Wiggins, another soldier.

### Behind the Mythos
Thomas Carnacki, who has featured in several of his own Cthulhu Mythos stories, states in his journal that one of the texts he used to research the demonic entity was De Vermis Mysteriis, or The Book of the Worm.

### Publication History
Operation Antarctica was first published by Severed Press in 2018 in both paperback and ebook formats (in April and November, respectively). In the following year, European publisher Luzifer released a German-language digital translation.

### Trivia
*Operation Antarctica is the second book in William Meikle's S-Squad series of military action/fantasy novellas.

The Order of the Bloated Woman is a fictional cult created by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. It made its first appearance in the 1984 globe-spanning supplement Masks of Nyarlathotep. 

### Overview
An ancient cult devoted to a dark goddess, the Order of the Bloated Woman believe she an aspect of a primal deity worshiped secretly in many forms all over the world: one of the avatars of Nyarlathotep. This organisation is unique to China, and its rituals are practiced both on the mainland and on some uninhabited islands, such as Gray Dragon island, which houses a shrine as well as a village in which its inhabitants wear the cult characters of the Bloated Woman on medallions, belts, and so forth. At one time, it was much feared throughout the coastal regions of China; the dread Fukien pirates were said at times to take instructions from the Order, which reputedly wielded powerful magic against its enemies. Authorities now doubt that the Order still exists, but, in truth, it has grown in the last few years. Only a fraction of their victims have been found. 

Their high priest is a man named Ho Fong, a wealthy import/export businessman from Shanghai. The sect employs a signature weapon: a sickle which they use to mutilate the victim's trunk before severing the limbs, bleeding to death; unlike many gangs with access to them, the use of firearms is rare. The sect is in contact with a Deep One colony in the East China Sea, and human and Deep One hybrids are common amongst their membership. (: Masks of Nyarlathotep)

The ceremonial robes worn by the Order are a voluminous black and yellow silk garb, tailored to simulate the shape of the Bloated Woman. All members are marked with a tattoo on the left armpit with a symbol which allows identification. The ideograms are in kanji (the normal written Chinese language) and simply mean "Bloated Woman". Reflecting the cultists' range of interests, the Order normally holds only death rites and breeding rites. The former feature several hours of mad chanting and dancing followed by the slaughter of sacrificial victims and the summoning of the Bloated Woman, who devours the sacrifices and delivers a short homily encouraging self-sacrifice and unthinking obedience. The latter involve the ravishment of humans by Deep Ones, especially female ones. 

The Order is well known in Shanghai's extensive criminal underworld due to the reputation of its minions, with both nationalist and leftist underground movements also being vaguely aware of their existence.

On January l4, 1926, the Gray Dragon island holds as many members of the Order of the Bloated Woman as can get there. The god appears as the Bloated Woman, and her followers grovel. The god then freezes, not to move again until the Great Gate opens and she roars her horrible triumph. Its hunger is endless, requiring a constant supply of sacrifices to placate the voracious god. Its origins lay in the Land of Black Blood, being the first of the Charda to be spawned from the black blood.

Oriab is a large island located in the Southern Sea of the Dreamlands.

### Overview
Every month the people of Oriab trade "fragrant resin of Oriab’s inner groves, and the delicate pottery baked by the artists of Baharna, and the strange little figures carved from Ngranek’s ancient lava. For this they were paid in the wool of Ulthar and the iridescent textiles of Hatheg and the ivory that the black men carve across the river in Parg".

### Locations
*Mount Ngranek - A snow-topped mountain on which the gods of earth used to dance and carve images of themselves. The Southern side is made up of sheer crags over a valley of lava and caves occupied by Night-gaunts.
*Baharna - A mighty port city on the northern banks of the Yath.
* Yath - A large lake on the island.

The Orocoran are a fictional species created by Paizo Inc. in 2017 for the supplement Starfinder: First Contact of the role-playing game Starfinder. It is an intelligent race, indigenous to the planetoid Great Old One known as Aucturn for uncountable time.

### Appearance
Its appearance is that of a large wingless mosquito. They have excellent senses. Although they cannot speak, they understand the languages ​​spoken in the planet. They weigh about 68 kilos (150 pounds). Although they can stand almost two meters upright, they prefer to crawl on all fours.

### Culture and Society
Orocorans are the most numerous indigenous creatures on Aucturn. They are semi-intelligent predators. Orocorans do not have sex and reproduce by sharing genetic information with their tongues, nailing them to their torsos. Subsequently, they lay splinted eggs on ichor parts torn from Aucturn's skin and leave the site. Whilst they can be found in the Citadel of the Black (albeit in small numbers), most are often seen extracting the black ichor that flows through Aucturn's veins with their proboscis tongue. This ichor is also a psychotropic drug that leaves them drowsy. They can often be found scattered where the veins are larger, either defending them or lying next to them in an ichor-induced stupor, which they call the "womb mind". During the time that they are in this dream state, they believe that they can communicate with the planet's gestating consciousness and receive vague prophetic advice from the planet.

When they are not dreaming, they are irritable and unpredictable when suffering from withdrawal syndrome. Lazy by nature, they make little or no effort to create a civilization, except if forced by more powerful races or the rare Orocoran Ichor Lords. Due to their drug-addled lifestyle, orocorans are seen as little threatening nuisances because its members are often drugged and isolated. However, they can release vomit containing the black ichor, causing hallucinations. They also pose a threat when gathered in large swarms.

Orocorans shun the Suppurating Scarp, bearing an ingrained fear of the tiny wriggling worms that occasionally squirm out of the cliff to plop into the pus pools below. Orocoran rumors hold that a fresh corpse submerged in the pools of pus and left undisturbed for 11 days rises again as a horrid amalgamation of bloated yellowish worms bearing the creature’s memories but none of its kindness or mercy.

### The Ichor Lords

Although the higher faculties of most members are impaired by their addiction and they do not use their telepathy to communicate, ichor affects the intellectual capacities of one in every thousand individuals, giving them greater intelligence, cunning and magical powers.

He has also written tie-in pieces for traditional games such as Warmachine and Iron Kingdoms. In the works of H. P. Lovecraft, the Other Gods are a group of higher deities that protect the Gods of Earth. Their leader is Azathoth, and their "soul and messenger" is Nyarlathotep (: "The Other Gods", The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath). In the Expanded Mythos, these creatures are identified as the Outer Gods.

The role-playing game Call of Cthulhu acknowledges two meanings of the term "Other Gods". The first is the same as the Outer Gods, while the second is more specific, referring to a group of Outer Gods that dwell in the Court of Azathoth. The least prestigious of them are collectively referred to as the Lesser Other Gods. Additionally, the latter label also includes a collection of entities that are of a similar status but not part of the Court of Azathoth.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite Chaosium mentioning them, there are to date no known Lesser Other Gods which are not in some form associated with the Court of Azathoth. This seems to be due to the label "Lesser Outer God" being used by authors for any such entities normally, or at best, the Larva of the Other Gods, which are in-universe speculated to perhaps grow into Lesser Other Gods, but the only examples of such creatures, The Star Mother and The Messenger of Azathoth, are still in their larval stage (: Ye Booke of Monstres II).

Confusingly, Outer Gods that are part of the Court of Azathoth are also never labelled as regular Other Gods either, despite that being the probable intent of emulating Lovecraft's useage of "Other Gods" in the titular story of the same name.

With this many labels it should also be stated that in Chaosium's RPG, all instances of Lesser Other Gods, Lesser Outer Gods and Larva of the Other Gods do in fact go under the wider label of Outer Gods; the intent is that these are subgroups, not other types of entities entirely.

In Marvel Comics, the Other Gods are confused with the Great Old Ones often enough to be categorized the same, with Nyarlathotep being the only confirmed Other God.

### References

"Other People's Houses" is a short story by American author Sarena Ulibarri. It is inspired by the works of the late Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
A man obsessed with what other people hide behind closed doors one day discovers a neighbour's key lying in the street. While violating the man's house it’s tenant, along with an accomplice, returns home. The man then witnesses the partially-successful summoning of an extra-dimensional entity from the closet he is hiding in and, after returning to his own home, begins to metamorphose into something distinctly inhuman.

### Publication History
"Other People's Houses" was published in the anthology of H. P. Lovecraft-inspired works Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.

Othuum (The Oceanic Horror) is a Great Old One from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. It was first mentioned in Brian Lumley's short story "Rising with Surtsey", and was later incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. 

### Description
Othuum is an unknown entity who is theorised to resemble a twisting rope-like monstrosity covered in tentacles with a singular alien face in the middle of a squirming, ropy mass. It has been speculated that the entity may be a servant of Cthulhu, dwelling beneath the waves and striving for his master's return. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

*Othuum appears in the role-playing video game Shadow Hearts: From the New World. However, the character's name was changed to "Automaton" in the English version. 
*Othuum appears in the mobile game Yurudora, during the Cthulhu Festival event.

shortDefinition: Otis Adelbert Kline (1891 - 1946) was an American songwriter and author of fantasy and science fiction whose stories have been published in various magazines such as Argosy, Weird Tales, Amazing Stories, Strange Stories, and many others. Born in Chic...
fullContent:
Otis Adelbert Kline (1891 - 1946) was an American songwriter and author of fantasy and science fiction whose stories have been published in various magazines such as Argosy, Weird Tales, Amazing Stories, Strange Stories, and many others. Born in Chicago, Illinois, he is most well known for his planetary romance novels in the style of Edgar Rice Burroughs. He also acted as Robert E. Howard's literary agent and co-authored a number of stories with E. Hoffmann Price.

Kline holds the rather unusual distinction of being the only person mentioned by his real name in "The Battle that Ended the Century", a comedic story written by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow which features several of the authors' colleagues and acquaintances under humorous nicknames or pseudonyms. The story was mailed anonymously to the authors' friends. Lovecraft playfully denied having anything to do with it, and acknowledged the discrepancy of Kline's name being unaltered.



Since Barlow's typewritten draft mentions several other people by their real names, and it was Lovecraft who came up with the nicknames for them, it is possible that he might have simply forgotten to alter Kline's name and left it unaltered by mistake in the final version.

Oukranos is the name of a river in the Earth's Dreamlands (: "The Silver Key", "Through the Gates of the Silver Key"). It is also the name of a deity associated with the river (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, : H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands). 

When the King of Ilek-Vad was young, he lived in a cottage by the banks of the Oukranos, and the river's god sang to him. Once a year, the King travels from Ilek-Vad to a temple by the river and prays to the god of Oukranos. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

In Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, Oukranos is identified as a "Lesser Dreamlands Deity", a minor entity who is neither a Great One, Great Old One, Outer God, or Elder God. (: H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands)

fullContent:
Our Lady of Darkness is a Fritz Leiber novella published in 1977. It was used by Miskatonic River Press as a source for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game campaign "Our Ladies of Sorrow".

### Publisher summary
Our Lady of Darkness introduces San Francisco horror writer Franz Westen. While studying his beloved city through binoculars from his apartment window, he is astonished to see a mysterious figure waving at him from a hilltop two miles away. He walks to Corona Heights and looks back at his building to discover the figure waving at him from his apartment window—and to find himself caught in a century‑spanning curse that may have destroyed Ambrose Bierce, Clark Ashton Smith and Jack London. 

### Contents
This Fritz Leiber novella is a pioneering early work of urban fantasy. It introduces the concepts of Paramentals, Megalopolisomancy and also references the magical powers of music for good and evil. 

The novella is notable for taking the Lovecraftian approach of using real-world locations and parodies thereof to the logical extreme. Every element of contemporary 1976 San Francisco is described in detail, accurately and with affection. Fritz Leiber also creates in the figure of Franz Westen a very accurate autobiographical figure, to the point of almost being a self-insert. 

The main antagonist in the novella is a Paramental entity nicknamed Taffy.

### Behind the Mythos
Fritz Leiber, with all his skill as a writer, catalogues and comments on the whole Lovecraft Circle and its milieu in this work. He also catalogues and comments on San Francisco. Several people have made a "pilgrimage" out of visiting the places Leiber refers to in the novel, all of which are quite real. 

The sinister figure of "De Castries" who is the deceased antagonist in the story is lampshaded within the text as being based on Adolphe de Castro, a real life, and troublesome, ghostwriting client of H.P. Lovecraft. 

### External Links
*Mike Humbert's [http://www.mikehumbert.com/Fritz_Leiber-s_Our_Lady_of_Darkness_page_1.html website] provides a detailed review of the locations of Our Lady of Darkness.

Out of Mind: The Stories of H. P. Lovecraft is a 1998 Canadian TV movie  written and directed by Raymond St-Jean.

Its official tagline: "Haunted by disturbing dreams from an inherited book, a young man becomes interested in the writings of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Out of Mind is a fictionalised story about a modern-day (1998) young man who inherits a strange book from his deceased uncle. As the story unfolds the young man experiences vivid and horrible dreams of a past life from the 1910s and 1920s. People familiar to him appear in unfamiliar roles and the nightmares continue as he searches for answers and horror begins to emerge in his waking life as well.

Ultimately, he meets the man himself - H.P. Lovecraft - and clearly at least one of them is dreaming...

### Behind the Mythos
The film namechecks and plays with some of the elements of the Lovecraft works and the Mythos, but also looks at Lovecraft himself, with actor playing the writer, doing a mock radio broadcast using Lovecraft's own words from both his letters and his fictional writing.

shortDefinition: "Out of the Aeons" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald, a writer from Somerville, Massachusetts. It is one of five stories Lovecraft revised for Heald. It focuses on a Boston museum that displays an ancient mummy recovered from a sunk...
fullContent:
"Out of the Aeons" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald, a writer from Somerville, Massachusetts. It is one of five stories Lovecraft revised for Heald. It focuses on a Boston museum that displays an ancient mummy recovered from a sunken island.

### Plot summary
The story is told from the point of view of the curator of the Cabot Museum in Boston. In 1878, a freighter captain sighted an uncharted island in the Pacific, presumably risen from its sunken state due to volcanic activity. From it, he recovered a strange mummy and a metal cylinder containing a scroll. Early in November 1879, the mummy is put on display in the museum, and the island vanishes without a trace.

Over the years, the mummy garners a reputation as a possible link to an ancient tale of K'naa, from the Black Book by von Junzt, where a priest named T'yog, challenges the demon Ghatanothoa using the power of a magical scroll, written in Naacal on Yakith Lizard skin, and inspired by Great Old Ones opposed to Ghatanothoa. In his sleep, however, one of the cultists stole the true magical scroll and replaced it with a fake one, and T'yog was never seen again. When the possible link to the Black Book and T'yog reaches the general public, the narrator begins to notice more and more suspicious foreigners coming to the museum.

Soon, several attempts are made to steal the mummy. During one attempt on the 1st December 1932, two men, armed with the true scroll, die as the mummy seemingly springs to life, opens its eyes and reveals an image of the approaching form of Ghatanothoa. The image had retained the power of Ghatanothoa to mummify any who view it, turning one of the thieves into a mummy, but the image has significantly faded by the time the curator examines it ,and it only frightens him. Though he does not understand what he has seen, the curator is horribly shaken and orders the dissection of the mummy on 8th December. The curator and all present are shocked that the mummy is in fact the remains of T'yog with a living brain which is still aware of its surroundings.

### Characters
### The modern world
*Richard H. Johnson Ph.D. - The late curator of the Cabot Museum. Having thoroughly researched the mummy and its origins he died of heart failure under suspicious circumstances on April 22, 1933.
*Captain Charles Weatherbee - The captain of the Eridanus, the freighter that discovered the mummy.
*Curator Pickman - The curator of the museum when the mummy first arrived.
*Stuart Reynolds - A journalist from the Boston Pillar whose article published April 5, 1931, brought the mummy into the public eye.
*Swami Chandraputra - Appearing in a turban and a heavy beard, the Swami is one of many occult experts who visits the mummy. 
*Etienne-Laurent de Marigny - A New Orleans mystic who wrote for the Occult Review about the links between the mummy's scroll with hieroglyphs in Nameless Cults.

"Out of the Ages" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, originally published in the 1975 anthology Nameless Places, by Arkham House. It is part of Carter's Xothic Legend Cycle.

### Synopsis
The bulk of the narrative consists of several entries from the diary of Dr. Henry Stephenson Blaine, curator of the manuscripts collection at the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities in Santiago, California. In 1928, Dr. Blaine has been tasked with cataloging the objects and documents of the Copeland Collection, formerly belonging to the late Professor Harold Hadley Copeland, who died screaming in a mental institution two years before.

In the Copeland Collection, Blaine finds several statuettes and ceremonial masks from widely separated cultures across the Pacific, all seemingly depicting the same aquatic deity, known by names such as Zatamagwa, Sothamogha or Z'mog, which according to Copeland's annotations, are all variations of Zoth-Ommog. The main artifact is a skillfully sculpted jade figurine found by a diver off the coast of Ponape, which depicts Zoth-Ommog himself: a creature that combines aspects of starfish, squid and reptile. By reading Copeland's papers, Blaine finds evidence of a prehistoric civilization in ancient Mu which worshiped the Xothic gods, sons of Cthulhu, who were served by slug-like creatures called Yuggya. There is also record of a 19th century ship whose crew was attacked by the Yuggya, suggesting that the creatures remain active even today.

Feeling agitated and stressed by the things he has learned, Blaine starts to experience frightful dreams of prehistoric landscapes, followed by a recurring dream in which he stands at the local pier trying to communicate with the aquatic Yuggya. He also learns from his housekeeper that he has been sleepwalking.

One night, two police officers find Blaine in his pijamas, standing knee-deep in sea water by the pier, and also notice a large slug-like white creature in the water. Blaine screams maniacally about having seen a Yugg and is confined to an asylum.

fullContent:
"Out of the Belly of Sheol" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas, first published in the Delirium Books thematic anthology Dark Testament in 2002.

### Synopsis
The prophet Jonah, tasked with pronouncing God's judgement on the city of Nineveh, finds himself adrift in the middle of the ocean after attempting to ignore his creator's command. When the storm subsides, a colossal being breaches the surface and, recognising Jonah's unique gift - to hear the babbling of the many gods across the universe - swallows him whole to act as his new prophet.

Inside the belly of the beast, who he soon discovers is Great Cthulhu himself, Jonah begins to hear voices in his head telling him that he must put the god back to sleep or the world of man will be doomed. Opening his mind to the word of the Elder Gods, he begins to carve their warding symbols into the intestines of the monster, which regurgitates him before slipping back into the depths and a deep slumber.

### Behind the Mythos
"Out of the Belly of Sheol" parallels the Abrahamic story of Jonah, but substitutes the religious elements with Cthulhu Mythos ones instead.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Out of the Belly of Sheol" has also appeared in the anthology Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012, German-language translation) and Unholy Dimensions (2005).

### References

"Out of the Black" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author William Meikle. It was first published in the anthology Fading Light: An Anthology of the Monstrous by Angelic Knight Press in August 2012.

### Synopsis
An explorer searching for life-giving ores on a dying Earth discovers a seemingly-derelict habitation of other humans which his instruments indicate hold a cache of the material. However, when he enters the complex, he finds humans devolved into a feral state, their minds shattered by the star-dotted blackness of the infinite sky.

Returning to his own warren, he deletes the coordinates of the site, begging his friends not to go in search of that cursed place, before realising that the madness which had infected the others has also taken root in his own mind…

"Out of the Frying Pan" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
After a botched bank job, Jake Higgins runs off into the West Virginia backwoods to escape the law. Stumbling across the run-down cabin of the old madwoman Mother Shub and her beautiful young apprentice Dora, Higgins' overactive libido and penchant for strong liquor cause him to fall foul of the witch's magic.

### Characters

* Jake Higgins, a somewhat dim-witted career criminal.
* Mother Shub, a powerful witch and priestess of Shub-Niggurath.
* Dora McCain, Mother Shub's apprentice.

### Publication History
"Out of the Frying Pan" was first published in the anthology Eldritch Horrors: Dark Tales in 2009, and appeared in the collection of Shiflet’s own work They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in 2018.

fullContent:
"Out of the Jar" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Charles R. Tanner, originally published in the magazine Stirring Science Stories, in February 1941.

### Synopsis
In 1940, a collector of curiosities named James Francis Denning acquires an ancient jar sealed with a six-pointed star and decorated with strange symbols. The jar soon catches the attention of Denning's friend, Edward Barnes Halpin, a knowledgeable occultist of "the Miskatonic school", who has published papers on the Comte d'Erlette's Cultes des Goules and translated sections of the Gaelic Leabhar Mor Dubh. Halpin becomes fascinated by the jar, judging from the seal that it must have belonged to the legendary King Solomon.

Halpin repeatedly tries to purchase the jar from Denning, and when the latter refuses to sell it, the occultist proposes to break the seal to see what's inside, which Denning also forbids. One night, Denning is awakened by noises and is shocked to find that Halpin has broken into his house and is trying to open the jar. Halpin insists that he wasn't going to steal it, but couldn't resist the opportunity see if the legends are true. He hastily explains to Denning that, before the rise of humankind, the Earth was ruled by alien creatures called Jinn, and that some survived the ice age and persisted into the time of Solomon, who found a way to imprison them inside objects such as the jar.

From the damaged jar oozes a mass of luminous bluish fluid that forms itself into a tall creature, vaguely humanoid, with an eyeless tentacled face and a beak. Halpin addresses the entity as Psuchawrl and claims that, as the one who freed them from the jar, Halpin is entitled to a wish, which the Jinni is obliged to grant. Halpin wishes to know "the place of man in this universe, and the place of this universe in the cosmos". In response, Psuchawrl moves their hands and creates a small portal, and invites Halpin to peer into it. Halpin does so, staring into the portal for a few seconds, them quietly backs away. Psuchawrl dematerializes, and Denning recovers from the shock and turns on the lights. Halpin, who has looked into the portal, never recovers, and is interred in an asylum, where he meditates quietly with a look of constant despair on his face.

The Outer Gods are a category of fictional entities of cosmic significance used in certain systemisations of the Cthulhu Mythos. They may be distinguished from the Great Old Ones, although the distinction isn't universally acknowledged.

Generally speaking, they are located beyond the confines of Earth and the Solar System, exerting their influence from deep space or from beyond our dimension. However, some Outer Gods have taken up residence on Earth.

The term "Outer Gods" does not appear in H. P. Lovecraft's works, but was popularized by the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, where it refers to Chaosium's interpretation of the entities that Lovecraft referred to as the Other Gods from Outside, or simply the Other Gods.

In Lovecraft's fiction, these dwell in the outer voids (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) outside of thought and existence (: "Hypnos") in a "graveside" beyond Time. (: "Nyarlathotep") This Last Void transcending matter and universes is accessed by the Ultimate Gate, itself beyond time and space. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

### Evolution of the concept
The idea of Outer Gods, although not referred to by that name, can be traced back to Lovecraft's short story "Nyarlathotep", based on one of the author's dreams. The titular entity is identified as the soul of "the gigantic, tenebrous ultimate gods—the blind, voiceless, mindless gargoyles", which dwell in a nightmarish realm and dance to the sounds of pipes and drums originating "from inconceivable, unlighted chambers beyond Time".

In Lovecraft's Dunsanian fantasy "The Other Gods", the eponymous deities arrive to punish a sage named Barzai for the crime of trying to spy the Gods of Earth. These "other gods" are identified as "the gods of the outer hells that guard the feeble gods of earth".

The ultimate gods from "Nyarlathotep" and the beings that unleashed their wrath on Barzai in "The Other Gods" are explicitly identified as being one and the same in Lovecraft's posthumously published novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, which features the return of characters from both tales, and refers to the events of the latter.

Identified as "the Other Gods from Outside", these creatures dwell in the central void outside the ordered universe, beyond time and beyond the Dreamlands. They are again described as "gigantic", "tenebrous", "blind", "voiceless", and "mindless", dancing to the sounds of pipes and drums at the court of their sultan Azathoth. Their larvae drift through cosmic space in the Dreamlands. The Gods of Earth, a.k.a. the Great Ones, are protected by them. Their "soul and messenger" is Nyarlathotep, who negotiates with their many "agents", human and otherwise.

"Outposts" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
During the days of the Roman occupation of the British Isles, an old soldier with an occult background investigates the bizarre deaths of several men on the Antonine wall. As he delves deeper into the mystery, he finds a temple to Yog-Sothoth buried beneath the wall and encounters a crazed Pictish shaman using his dark magic to summon the ancient god.

### Characters
*Marcus Caelius, a former legionary with a degree of knowledge on the Elder cults.
*Flavius Butto, the centurion in command of the targeted wall fort.

### Publication History
"Outposts" was first published in the anthology Further Tales of Cthulhu Invictus by Golden Goblin Press in 2017. It was also included in the 2019 collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror.

"Overcome" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Jason Vanhee. It was published in the Jason Andrew-edited thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods by Simian Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
Amongst the wreckage of a ruined city, a group of believers attempt to attend church, even although humankind's new masters forbid religion. Standing firm in the face of the human collaborators which deny them access, the group's sanity is shattered by the sudden appearance of one of the masters, which leaves them easy prey for the mortal enforcers.

The Pabodie Expedition was a fictional scientific survey mission to Antarctica, undertaken in 1930-31, whose disastrous outcome is told in H. P. Lovecraft's novella At the Mountains of Madness.

### Overview
The primary objective of the Pabodie Expedition was to research the continent's geological history using a highly advanced (for the time) drilling apparatus alongside more traditional dynamiting techniques. They also expected to discover fossil evidence of Antarctica's previous inhabitants during this process. It was primarily funded by the Nathaniel Derby Pickman Foundation and organised by Massachusetts' Miskatonic University.

The organisers expected the expedition's duration to be one, or at most two, Antarctic summers; if it lasted for two, the intervening winter was to be spent "hunkered down" in a specially constructed base camp while their ships went back for supplies.

### Members
The party consisted of four professors, seven graduate students, and nine mechanics.
*William Dyer, Professor of Geology and expedition leader.
*Frank Pabodie, Professor of Engineering.
*Lake, Professor of Biology.
*Atwood, Professor of Physics and a meteorologist.
*Danforth, a graduate student.
*Carroll, a graduate student.
*Gedney, a graduate student.
*Ropes, a graduate student.
*McTighe
*Orrendorf
*Sherman
*Watkins
*Williamson
*Seven others

### Specialist Equipment

*A custom drilling rig designed by Pabodie.
*Blasting equipment.
*Devices to prevent the fuel and engines of their aircraft from freezing in the extreme cold.

### Transportation

*Two former whaling vessels -- the Arkham and Miskatonic, captained by J. B. Douglas and Georg Thorfinnssen, respectively -- reinforced against ice pressure.
*Five modified Dornier transport aircraft (four being used as forward exploring aircraft, with one being left at the initial basecamp at Mcmurdo Sound/Mount Erebus as backup). Custom-built to withstand extreme Antarctic weather conditions and for transporting crew and drilling/blasting equipment.
*Fifty-five Alaskan sledge dogs and at least four sledges.

### History

Pabodie's drill is a fictional technology featured in the cosmic horror novella At the Mountains of Madness, by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview
A revolutionary drilling apparatus invented by Miskatonic University engineer Frank H. Pabodie, the drill was employed in the Pabodie Expedition to Antarctica in 1930, to retrieve samples of ice, rock, and fossils.

According to Prof. William Dyer, Pabodie's drill combines "the ordinary artesian drill principle with the principle of the small circular rock drill in such a way as to cope quickly with strata of varying hardness". Its metallic parts are made of a "clever aluminium alloy" that renders the equipment surprisingly light and portable. Its components include "steel head, jointed rods, gasoline motor, collapsible wooden derrick, dynamiting paraphernalia, cording, rubbish-removal auger, and sectional piping for bores five inches wide and up to 1000 feet deep", the combined weight of which is still light enough to require no more than three seven-dog sledges for transportation.

It was the drill that enabled Prof. Lake's party to locate a cave where they found the bodies of dead and dormant Elder Things. (: At the Mountains of Madness)

The Pacific Ocean features in the Cthulhu Mythos mainly as the location of the sunken city of R'lyeh, where Cthulhu lies dreaming. H. P. Lovecraft gives R'lyeh's coordinates as  47°9'S 126°43'W  (: "The Call of Cthulhu"); August Derleth writes that it is instead at 49°51'S 128°34'W. (: "The Black Island"). 

The Pacific, the largest ocean on Earth, lies between North America, South America, Asia, Australia, and Antarctica.

### In the Mythos
### Lovecraft's Works
*As previously mentioned, the sunken city of R'lyeh is located beneath the waves of the Pacific Ocean.
*The Pacific Ocean is where Obed Marsh learns how to summon deep ones in The Shadow Over Innsmouth.
*The short story "Dagon" is set in "one of the most open and least frequented parts of the broad Pacific".
*The mummy that features in the story "Out of the Aeons" is discovered on an uncharted Pacific island.

"Pacifist War Song—1917" is a humorous poem by H. P. Lovecraft first published in The Tryout in March 1917. It later appeared in the 1977 collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems.

### Synopsis
The poem takes the form of a satirical song sung from the point of view of the Knights of Peace, a proud group of pacifists apparently spread worldwide from the Chautauqua Lake, New York, to Prussia, who refuse to engage in combat even when their homes are being invaded by tyrants and conquerors.

Pagan Publishing was a small publishing company whose focus was on Cthulhu Mythos games and related fiction.

### Overview
Founded by John Scott Tynes in 1990 when he was just 19, Pagan Publishing's first product was the Call of Cthulhu fanzine The Unspeakable Oath. As the company grew and expanded it began to produce actual sourcebooks for the game, perhaps the most famous being the Delta Green supplement written by Tynes, Adam Scott Glancy and Dennis Detwiller.

Since it’s formation, Pagan Publishing has mostly produced content in book form, although it has also dabbled in the field of card games with Creatures & Cultists in 1993 and even released a modular board game in the form of The Hills Rise Wild! in 2000.

Pagan also released a small amount of non-gaming work through their Armitage House imprint, the majority of which was devoted to Delta Green fiction.

As of July 2021 Pagan Publishing's website is no longer available to access, indicating that the company has ceased trading. All new Delta Green material is now handled by Arc Dream Publishing.
