Paighon is a fictional entity which appears in the Lovecraftian fiction of the late American author Walter C. DeBill, Jr.

### Overview
Described as a "nuclear force-creature" (: "The Barrett Horror"), Paighon is possibly a Great Old One or an Elder God.  In "Collector's Item", the earliest of DeBill's works it appears in, Paighon is said to have come from the Andromeda galaxy to the Solar System and settled inside the core of the Earth soon after it formed.

Paighon is the deadly enemy of Ngyr-Khorath and its servitor, 'Ymnar. (: "The Barrett Horror")

fullContent:
The Pale Night, aka the Mother of Demons, is a Lovecraftian-like demonic entity from the fictional universe of the Dungeons & Dragons pencil-and-paper roleplaying games by Wizards of the Coast.

### Background
The Pale Night is a member of the Obyrith, a demonic species. She has an incorporeal form, appearing as a flowing white shroud that appears to have underneath it the shapely body of a female human. It's true form though is so hideous and terrifying, that its rejected by reality. Glimpse what's underneath the shroud and you risk madness and/or death.

The Pallid Dancers, also known as Courtiers of the King in Yellow, The King's Demons, Masked Ones, and Yellow Horrors, are fictional entities created by games designer Chad Bowser for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. They made their first appearance in the 2006 monster manual Malleus Monstrorum. 

The Pallid Dancers were further developed for the 2020 edition of Malleus Monstrorum where they were renamed the Courtiers of the King in Yellow; this evolution was credited to "Mike Mason with Chad Bowser".

### Description
Pallid Dancers manifest as miniature humanoid entities that dance and caper like ballerinas. They accompany the Great Old One Hastur whenever he is summoned.

The Pallid Mask also known as the Phantom of Truth or The Stranger is a humanoid emissary of Hastur.

### Background
The Pallid Mask is a 6 foot tall slender figure in a voluminous yellow robe who walks around with a staff and has a genderless, featureless white mask covering his face. For millennia it has visited cities known for their nihilism and decadence to determine if they should be consumed by Carcosa.

The character takes its name from a being referred to in Robert W. Chambers' The King in Yellow.

### Behind the Mythos
The character was expanded upon in 2017 "Black Stars Beckon" by Jim Groves for Paizo Inc's Pathfinder roleplaying game.

Pan is an ancient Greek god often associated with pastoral scenery, music and fertility. He is typically represented as a humanoid figure with the legs and horns of a goat, similar to the mythic fauns. His name is the origin of the word panic.

### In the Mythos
In ancient times, the god Pan was said to dwell in Mount Maenalus, in Arcadia, and was accompanied by strange creatures named Panisci. (: "The Tree")

Later on, Pan and the other gods entered a death-like sleep, but shall wake up and reclaim their domains someday. (: "Poetry and the Gods")

In The Great God Pan, by Arthur Machen, the titular deity is unseen, but plays a pivotal role by impregnating a woman who took part in a scientific experiment to see beyond the fabric of reality (similar to H. P. Lovecraft's "From Beyond"). This union results in the birth of a deceptively human child named Helen Vaughan, who grows up to commit terrible acts (: The Great God Pan). In Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror", Henry Armitage mentions Machen's story in connection to the case of Wilbur Whateley.

In the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium, Pan is depicted as an avatar of Shub-Niggurath. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

fullContent:
Pandora Peaslee is a fictional character created by American author Peter Rawlik for his Cthulhu Mythos fiction.

### Description
Pandora is an unspecified descendant of the Peaslee line, which includes Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee and Wingate Peaslee, characters who made their first appearance in H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Shadow Out of Time.

A former Central Intelligence Agency operative, Pandora later came to work as a government liaison to Mister Ys, a member of the Great Race of Yith, thousands of whom were living quietly among us in the build up to a calamitous event. In the aftermath, Pandora found purpose in becoming a resistance fighter against the Yithians who had harnessed a biological weapon and used it to subjugate the human race. 

### History
Pandora was present at the fall of the human race, when an experimental biological weapon was unleashed on the populace, causing an outbreak of zombie plague. Fortunately for some, a recent influx of Yithians, come to witness the end of the world, had made preparations for a select group of humans with particular skill sets to have a chance at survival, Pandora amongst them (: "Time Flies"). 

Later, when the plague had brought the human race low, the Yithians used their advanced technology to control the zombie hordes, subjugating what remained of the population. Pandora used a special serum and invocation to the Great Old One Hastur to disorient the aliens, allowing her people to begin their reconquest of Earth (: "The Pestilence of Pandora Peaslee"). 

### Appearances
Note: appearances listed by in-universe chronology

fullContent:
Pantha is a hero in the fictional Dynamite universe, who was created in 1974 by Carl Wessler. She was a character for Harris Publications before Dynamite Entertainment. Pantha was originally an alien shapeshifter from the planet Drakulon, the same world as Vampirella, who was later retconned into an ancient cursed Egyptian shapeshifter.

### Background
Sekhmet was a high priestess of Ra in ancient Egypt whom was given the ability to turn into a panther and was worshiped as a minor deity. When Egypt was inflicted with famine and drought, bloodlust took over and she killed and devoured many, including her own son. For her crimes, she was condemned by Ra to walk the Earth for eternity. In the modern era, she has been a friend and ally of Vampirella.

One version fought alongside Vampirella, Red Sonja, Eva, Dracula, Athena, Herbert West, and Ash Williams against the sorcerer Kulan Gath and the Army of Darkness. Pantha is able to turn into a panther or half-panther. In her possession is the scarab of Atum-Ra, an object that only women can touch. Which protects her and is able to open doorways to other worlds.

Paramentals are elemental spirits which manifest through inanimate materials such as glass, concrete and steel. They are described in the novella Our Lady of Darkness by Fritz Leiber. Paramentals are not friendly, and to become aware of them is not a good thing. They are described as "about midway in nature between the atomic bomb and the archetypes of the collective unconscious."

### Notable Individuals
The paramental antagonist in Our Lady of Darkness goes by the name of "Taffy".

The Parapsychologist's Handbook: A New Occupation for Call of Cthulhu is a supplementary sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
The Parapsychologist's Handbook contains background information on running both parapsychologists as player characters and a parapsychology-themed campaign. Included are a potted history of the discipline and a rundown on the basic tenets, a guide to common phenomena, plot seeds, new psychic feats, and a list of recommended reading.

### Behind the Mythos
Running to a total of 112 pages, the Parapsychologist’s Handbook was written by Chris Jerome with cover art supplied by Meghan McLean and interior work by Simon Monk and Jessica Billman. It was published in November 2003 by Chaosium in both softcover and digital download formats.

The Parchments of Pnom were created by Clark Ashton Smith for his Hyperborean Cycle series of weird fantasy stories, and have also been incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Description
As their name may suggest, the Parchments of Pnom were written by a man named Pnom, who was a renowned prophet and the chief genealogist of ancient Hyperborea. 

The Parchments contain, at least in part, genealogical charts of the Great Old Ones and Outer Gods.

### Behind the Mythos
Clark Ashton Smith used the Parchments of Pnom as a means to more definitively integrate his own pantheon of gods with that created by H. P. Lovecraft. This was achieved through the use of family trees in which Smith's gods were shown to be related to, and in many cases the mates of, Lovecraft's creations.

### Trivia
*The sorcerer Evagh was seen to be unsuccessfully consulting the Parchments of Pnom in "The Coming of the White Worm", possibly in an effort to identify the nature of the threat posed by Rlim Shaikorth.

Parker is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Description
He was a crew member on the marine vessel Emma of Auburn, although his role is uncertain. After Donovan was successful in opening the vault discovered by the crew in R'lyeh, Cthulhu emerged, killing Donovan, Guerrera and Angstrom. Second Mate Gustaf Johansen recounts that during the slaughter, Parker slipped and was "swallowed up by an angle of masonry which shouldn't have been there; an angle which was acute, but behaved as if it were obtuse." (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

Parks is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft who first appeared in his fantasy short story "The Silver Key". He is the elderly servant of Randolph Carter, "who for years bore patiently with his vagaries".

### Biography
Parks is significantly older than Carter, having been employed by the family since Carter was a boy. In 1928, he helped Carter retrieve the Silver Key from the old box that belonged to Carter's grandfather. Parks was "strangely affected" by the mysterious carvings on the box. He never saw Carter again after the latter entered his car and drove off to his family's ancestral estate in the Arkham countryside. (: "The Silver Key")

Parks died in early 1930, and thus never saw how Carter returned to Earth in the body of the Yaddithian sorcerer Zkauba. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

Partridgeville is an imaginary town created by Frank Belknap Long, the setting of his stories "The Space-Eaters" (1928) and  "The Hounds of Tindalos" (1929). Long does not specify a state, but it is on a seacoast and near New York City, which suggests New Jersey or Connecticut.

### In Long's Fiction
Partridgeville has a newspaper, the Partridgeville Gazette; it is home to the Partridgeville Glue Works and the Partridgeville Chemical Laboratories. law enforcement is provided by the Partridgeville Reserve.

The town's financial district is built around Central Square, where the jewelry firm Smithwich and Isaacs is located. The First Baptist Church, designed in 1717 by the famous British architect Christopher Wren, is found on Angell Hill.

On the other side of Mulligan Wood is the nearby town of Brewster.

shortDefinition: "Passing of a Dreamer"  is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gary Myers.  ### Synopsis In the city of Ulthar, in a narrow windowless alley behind the Hall of Burgesses and the Woth the Baker's shop, there is a door with questionable exi...
fullContent:
"Passing of a Dreamer"  is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gary Myers.

### Synopsis
In the city of Ulthar, in a narrow windowless alley behind the Hall of Burgesses and the Woth the Baker's shop, there is a door with questionable existence holding an altar of bones (not merely human ones) where sits an idol of a winged salamander-like daemon called the Keeper of Dreams, offering infamous services only to an unknown fee. The story tells of a priest named Snireth-Ko, who prepared the incense burned at all hours in the left ear of the image Nasht to confound his perception and avoid Nasht's perception of his worshipers being sinful. But he was able to discern the supposed nonexistence of the gods and turned them away. He wandered the cat-filled streets with lost faith, and he was drawn into an alley and a secret doorway. He at first believed he was in Woth's shop until he realized he was in the den of the Keeper of Dreams, fearful of what fee the Keeper will demand. He had lost his blindness to this entrance when he lost his faith, and so he entered a veil of purple cosmic flames and into a clime of a viscous shore filled with polyp-like beaked tentacled creatures and vast continent of weeds.

Snireth-Ko walked through white mist, spires, emerald minarets, crystal ways between tall columns of figured glass, riven temple-domes and cyclopean ruins of brilliant green, into a wide court approaching an emerald demigod banded with mysterious runes stood staring at the stars. He was a dreamer who sought the stars guessing what cryptic messages they gave. But he darted into the darkness when the god shuttered. He arrived in a dark necropolis in the Plateau of Leng where he saw the lurid fires of spirits and followed a mysterious hooded figure. Though the figure vanished, Snireth-Ko managed to trace him down broken steps into an ancient dark tomb through a door that held some eldritch creature that deterred Snireth-Ko. But he gets a vision of being consumed into the aether and meeting a Messenger of Azathoth on the dark side of the moon. He soon broke free from his trance seeing that the Keeper of Dreams had taken something from him as payment for its service.

The story ends with the claim that what had been taken from Snireth-Ko as payment remains a matter of grim speculation. But the narrator claims that, in London, he found an old man cowering in an alley lamenting with fleshless fingers that he lost his faith and paid an undesired price.

shortDefinition: "Passing of Eric Holm" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by August Derleth. It was published in the December 1939 issue of Strange Stories, in which Derleth was credited by the pseudonym "Will Garth".  ### Synopsis An inquest is held to determine the c...
fullContent:
"Passing of Eric Holm" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by August Derleth. It was published in the December 1939 issue of Strange Stories, in which Derleth was credited by the pseudonym "Will Garth".

### Synopsis
An inquest is held to determine the circumstances of the death of Eric Holm, who was last seen alive on April 3, 1939, returning home with a newly-bought book. Mr. Sanderson, the bookseller, testifies that Holm had bought the Confessions of the Mad Monk Clithanus. A witness named Johnny Heckler claims to have seen some kind of creature sliding over the wall of Holm's garden, but this is largely dismissed due to Heckler's reputation as a drunkard. Finally, a respectable man named Lansing shockingly reveals that he and Holm used to purchase books on witchcraft and try out the spells, usually without results.

On the night of April 3, Holm had invited Lansing to see his new book, and claimed to be able to summon a kind of "animal" from the sea. Clithanus' book identified the creature in question as one of the Spawn of Cthulhu, and provided a formula for summoning one and sending it after the summoner's enemies, as well as another formula for banishing it back to the sea. Holm proposed to send the Spawn of Cthulhu after Lansing, who would then banish it back safely. Although skeptical, Lansing agreed to try it, and returned home. Once in his library, he heard the noises of something breaking into his house. Frightened, he recited the formula, and was relieved to hear the thing stop and turn back the way it came from. When he gathered enough courage to leave the library, Lansing saw the front door opened and a trail of large webbed footprints that emanated a noxious smell.

Lansing called Holm to tell him that the ritual had worked, but Holm in turn revealed that the creature was now coming for him. Over the telephone, a terrified Lansing heard Holm screaming, and the sounds of the beast breaking into the room and attacking him. Lansing promptly notified the police. Once in Holm's house, the police and Lansing found the same giant webbed footprints, and Holm's body torn apart and half-eaten. The trail of footprints revealed that the creature had left the house, climbed over the garden wall, and went back to the sea.

### Publication History
*Strange Stories (1939)
*Dwellers in Darkness (1976)
*The Cthulhu Mythos (1997)
*In Lovecraft's Shadow: The Cthulhu Mythos Stories of August Derleth (1998)

fullContent:
The setting of the Pathfinder role-playing game is one of high fantasy with a touch of sci-fi and elements of horror. It's a Tolkien-like world with the Cthulhu Mythos incorporated into the setting, which have been part of the game from the beginning and play a major role in the setting. Originally Paizo published the Dungeons & Dragons games under contract to Wizards of the Coast from 2002-2006. When Wizards of the Coast decided not to renew the contract in 2007, Paizo continued on with Pathfinder under the Open Game License of the older version of D&D.

### Background
In the world of Pathfinder there are several dozen sentient species (normal, magical, aberrant, and demonic) living on the world of Golarion, some native and others not. Which includes dragons, krakens, giants, elves, dwarves, lizardmen, 100+ ft kaiju, demons, necromancers, vampires, zombies, naga, aboleth, serpentmen, merfolk, kitsune, spirits, elementals, and gods among many other races and species. Humans are one of the races and there are analogs of the various ancient and medieval human civilizations of Earth, and it's believed that the humans on Golarion are actually immigrants and/or refugees of another world (Earth). The greatest human civilization on Golarion is that of the empires on the continent of Tian Xia. Empires and kingdoms which are very similar to those of China, Japan, and Korea on Earth, and populated by both humans and non-human sentient species. The humans of Tian Xia have a physical appearance similar to the peoples of East Asia and Southeast Asia on Earth, and similar cultures.

The planet Golarion is part of a solar system with a number of inhabited worlds, each of which has multiple sentient species and the presence of magic, which altogether have over 100 sentient species of which some are from the system and others elsewhere (outside the solar system or from other dimensions). Through the use of magic (e.g. portals) some of these species have spread to neighboring planets within the system. The eldritch entities and species of the Cthulhu Mythos (known as the Elder Mythos) have a strong presence in the multiverse. The pantheon of the Elder Mythos are one of many pantheons and deities in the cosmos, with a good number in Golarion alone (some of which consist of human-like gods). While magic is a strong force in the universe, among the stars there are many spacefaring civilizations with high technology (interstellar starships, robots, artificial intelligence, directed energy weapons) and a few of those races have visited Golarion, some of them with an agenda and others due to their ship crashing on the world or as refugees. Resulting in alien artifacts (e.g. robots), mysterious alien ruins, wrecked alien ships, and isolated colonies of aliens. The worlds of these solar system also have portals to other dimensions inhabited by elemental beings, demonic races, etc., and with the right magic, one can travel to and from those dimensions.

Patriarch Michael I (c. 1000 – 1059 AD), also known as Michael I Cerularius or Michael Keroularios, was a real-world archbishop of the church in Constantinople who was cited in H. P. Lovecraft's pseudo-historical "History of the Necronomicon" as having "suppressed and burnt" Theodorus Philetas' Greek translation of the Necronomicon in 1050 A.D., because it "impelled certain experimenters to terrible attempts."

The historical Michael was patriarch of Constantinople from 1043 to 1059, making him the most important figure in the Eastern church and a powerful figure in Byzantine politics. His conflict with Pope Leo IX over ritual, theology, and church hierarchy led to the Great Schism of 1054, which permanently separated Christianity into Roman Catholicism and Eastern Orthodoxy.

After the death of the Byzantine Emperor Constantine IX in 1055, Michael came into conflict with his successor, Empress Theodora, whose gender Michael found objectionable in a ruler. After her short reign ended in 1056, Michael help persuade the new emperor, Michael VI, to abdicate in 1057 in favor of the rebellious general who became Emperor Isaac I. Michael also quarreled with Isaac, who brought charges of treason and heresy against the patriarch. Michael died on January 21, 1059, before he could be brought to trial.

shortDefinition: Patrice Hathaway, the Violinist, was created by Fantasy Flight Games as a playable character for several of their Arkham Horror Files lines of games including Arkham Horror itself.  ### History Always a natural with the bow and string, as Patrice gre...
fullContent:
Patrice Hathaway, the Violinist, was created by Fantasy Flight Games as a playable character for several of their Arkham Horror Files lines of games including Arkham Horror itself.

### History
Always a natural with the bow and string, as Patrice grew up it became clear to all that she was something of a musical prodigy. Immersing herself in her sublime violin symphonies, upon reaching adulthood, her fame grew to worldwide proportions, and she played in venues across the globe.

However, something had always nagged at the back of Patrice's mind when she played, the thought that something was watching her and listening to her harmonies. And so it was that when she found herself playing a few melodies with an old gypsy woman one day, the crone's revelation that she was being stalked by something malignant was not as much of a shock as it should have been; she took notice and decided to do something about it. Thus, Patrice took her first steps on the path which would ultimately lead to the knowledge that there really are monsters lurking in the abyss beyond human sight.

### Behind the Mythos
Although initially conceived as a character for the Innsmouth Horror expansion of Arkham Horror Second Edition, Patrice has also made appearances in several of Fantasy Flight's companion games including Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and Elder Sign. In 2010 a plastic figurine designed to replace the cardboard tokens included with the games was created for her as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, although this is no longer in production (all ).

Paul Roulet is a fictional character who appears as the main antagonist in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Shunned House".

### Background
Paul is part of the Roulet family that moved from Caude, in France, to Rhode Island in 1686. The story suggests that the family be related to Jacques Roulet of Caude, a historical figure who was convicted of being a werewolf in 1598. The family is said to have "possessed an abnormal affinity for outer circles of entity—dark spheres which for normal folk hold only repulsion and terror"; Paul's father, Etienne Roulet, was noted for "reading queer books and drawing queer diagrams".

But Paul, remembered as "a surly fellow" with "erratic conduct", seems to have had a worse reputation; of all the Roulets, he "was particularly a source of speculation", with "old wives" saying "that his prayers were neither uttered at the proper time nor directed toward the proper object." So disliked was he that it's thought that he "probably provoked" a riot in the 1730s that "wiped out the family."

The story's narrator speculates that the riot "set moving certain kinetic patterns in the morbid brain of one or more of them—notably the sinister Paul Roulet—which obscurely survived the bodies murdered and buried by the mob, and continued to function in some multiple-dimensioned space along the original lines of force determined by a frantic hatred of the encroaching community[.]" 

This perpetuation of hatred beyond death--coupled with the fact that the Shunned House sits on the land that used to be the Roulet family graveyard--is offered as the explanation for the long series of tragedies that dogged the house. The suggestion is that the "titan elbow" of the "unthinkable abnormality" buried beneath the cellar floor belonged to Paul Roulet. (: "The Shunned House")

fullContent:
"Payback is a Bitch" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008, and later by Tenoka Press in 2017.

### Synopsis
Small-time hoodlum Morris Hodge, having had his illicit gambling winning stolen, decides to enact revenge on the man he believes to be responsible: the well-connected criminal Wendell Hawthorne. After murdering Hawthorne then burying him in a shallow grave, Hodge comes to believe that the ghost of the dead man is haunting him, following his every move in preparation for its vengeance.

In an effort to reassure himself that what he is seeing is simply a combination of paranoia and a guilty conscience, he revisits the gravesite, and is confronted by Hawthorne's twin brother Richard, the man who has been following him for days. A chance encounter with a copperhead snake gives Hodge the opportunity to kill Hawthorne, but then suddenly his dead brother rises from the grave and enacts his revenge on Hodge.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing little in the way of direct connections to the Cthulhu Mythos, "Payback is a Bitch" is loosely connected to the greater Mythos by way of Wendell Hawthorne's nickname: he is called The Professor by those who know him, due to having attended Miskatonic University before embarking on his criminal career. Hawthorne was rumoured to have been thrown out after stealing and copying some very ancient and valuable texts, possibly explaining how he was able to return from the dead.

fullContent:
"Pazuzu's Children" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the Robert M. Price-edited zine Cthulhu Codex by Necronomicon Press in April 1997.

### Synopsis
A downed American pilot during the Gulf War's Operation Desert Storm is captured by the group he was sent to attack: a mysterious cult living in caverns beneath the sands. He soon discovers that they are in service to an ancient entity - whose name they give as Pazuzu, but who he also hears being referred to as "Cth-" - and that they are protecting one of its "children", the severed tentacle of which he briefly glimpses.

When the Americans send a second strike to finish the job, the pilot's captors try to force him into persuading them to turn back; realising the danger these madmen and their pet monster present to the world, he takes the microphone and screams for his comrades to attack, whatever the cost.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Pazuzu's Children" has also been included in the collections Unholy Dimensions (2005), Hardboiled Cthulhu: Two-Fisted Tales of Tentacled Terror (2006), and Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012, German-language translation).

Pegasus Spiele Verlags - und Medienvertriebsgesellschaft mbH, as the full name of the enterprise goes (Pegasus Games Publishing and Media), has been active since 1993 when it was created by current directors and owners Karsten Esser and Andreas Finkernagel.

With the latest success and the nomination of "Pandemie (Pandemic)" (2009) for “Spiel des Jahres” (Game of the Year) and the further nomination of "Im Wandel der Zeiten – Das Würfelspiel: Bronzezeit (Roll Through the Ages: The Bronze Age)"(2010) as well the nomination for the "Kennerspiel des Jahres" (Connoisseur´s game of the Year) 2011 for "Strasbourg", the hessian enterprise has established itself not only as a distributor, but also as a publisher of popular games. In 2012 the success story so far has been crowned with the “Kennerspiel des Jahres” prize itself for "Village" by editorial partner eggertspiele which also won the "Deutscher Spielepreis" in the same year. Pegasus Spiele continues the tradition of well-known German publishers in this area. Today more than 5.000 games and toys are distributed through its commercial partners worldwide.

Pegasus Spiele titles are well-known at trade fairs and events in German-speaking Europe. Amongst its titles, Pegasus Spiele is famous for innovative board games like "Wunderland" and "Junta", as well as for releasing the German version of the cult card game "Munchkin" and the European Version of "Ultimate Werewolf". A network of 250 volunteer game-explainers support the publisher in releasing its products, like the export-hit "Mondo" and the party-hit "Pictomania". Dozens of temporary and 18 permanent employees at the headquarters in the hessian town of Friedberg work every day to create new gaming worlds and experiences.

In January 2015, Pegasus Spiele acquired children's game publisher Selecta Spielzeug.
Amongst many others, Pegasus Press printed the successful Worlds of Cthulhu Magazine.

fullContent:
"People of the Dark" is a short story by Robert E. Howard, first published in the June 1932 issue of Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror. It is notable as the first appearance of Howard's famous character Conan, though the "Conan of the Reavers" in this story seems to belong to a different continuity than "Conan the Barbarian".

### Plot
The plot centers on a love triangle between the narrator, John O'Brien; an Englishman, Richard Brent; and the woman they both love, Eleanor Bland. O'Brien plans to murder Brent out of jealousy, and plots to ambush him at a remote cavern on the English coast called Dagon's Cave, once known as the Cavern of the Children of the Night, reputed to have been carved by a hidden atavistic society known as the Little People. Howard describes these survivals in frankly racist terms:

O'Brien enters the cave, which he had overheard Brent saying he had planned to explore, musing on the Little People: "Legend said that this cavern was one of their last strongholds against the conquering Celts, and hinted at lost tunnels, long fallen in or blocked up, connecting the cave with a network of subterranean corridors which honeycombed the hills." The narrator slips and hits his head, giving him a vision of a past life when he was Conan of the Reavers, a black-haired Irish barbarian fighting with the Briton Vertorix over the love of the woman Tamera--earlier incarnations of Brent and Bland.

(This Conan is Irish, not Cimmerian, and hence is thousands of years more recent in fictional chronology than the more familiar version of the character--though both swear by the deity Crom. The Cimmerian would make his debut later the same year, in "The Phoenix on the Sword," published in Weird Tales in December 1932.)

Conan's attempt to kill his rival is interrupted by an attack of the Little People, one of whom is described at race-baiting length:

After Vertorix and Tamera throw themselves to their apparent deaths rather than allow themselves to be taken by the Little People, O'Brien returns to the present and realizes that Brent and Bland were always meant for each other, relinquishing his homicidal jealousy.

"Perchance to Dream" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, featuring his occult investigator character Anton Zarnak. It was first published in the May 1988 edition of Robert M. Price's long running fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu .

### Synopsis
A wealthy young man named Parker Winfield reluctantly consults occultist Anton Zarnak, and tells him about recurrent nightmares involving an undersea city named R'lyeh, and a mysterious portal. Winfield reveals that his grandfather was a merchant who operated on a ship in the Pacific Ocean and acquired all kinds of artifacts, some of which Winfield has unpacked recently to decorate his new apartment. Zarnak asks to see the collection and visits Winfield on the next day. He recognizes an idol of Ythogtha and asks Winfield's permission to take it home and examine it.

Back on River Street, Zarnak reads about Ythogtha and examines the idol, noting its unnatural weight and electromagnetic properties. When he places a five-pointed star-stone on it, the idol and the star-stone are both reduced to dust. Satisfied, Zarnak phones Winfield, who tells him that he was having a nightmare about a portal opening in sunken R'lyeh, but saw a golden light flash and woke up. Zarnak informs Winfield that he won't have any more dreams of R'lyeh from now on. Winfield is grateful enough that he doesn't mind the destruction of the idol, and plans to donate the rest of his grandfather's artifacts to the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities in California.

### Characters
* Dr. Anton Zarnak, an occult investigator.
*Ram Singh, Zarnak's loyal servant.
*Parker Winfield, a wealthy man who inherited several artifacts from his grandfather.
*Rufus, Winfield's butler.

"Perfect Toy for a Nine Year Old" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Bruce R. Cordell. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
When times are tight, doting father Charlie Tokarev illegally downloads a digital pattern for a much-in-demand "supertoy," the rat-like Mister Jenkin, before printing it using his home software and gifting it to his daughter Margaret.

At first everything goes swimmingly, Margaret falling instantly in love with the toy, but soon things in the Tokarev household begin to take a turn for the worse: Margaret’s attitude becomes more sinister and Max, the family cat, disappears.

Soon, Charlie comes to the realisation that Mister Jenkin is an unhealthy influence on his daughter, and resolves to take the toy away. However, Mister Jenkin has other plans and, after showing Charlie the mutilated remains of Max, tells the man of his desire to wear his face.

The story culminates with Margaret’s mother returning home and noticing that Mister Jenkin seems to be looking strikingly like her absent husband that day…

### Behind the Mythos
Although never actually named as "Brown Jenkin," Mister Jenkin is clearly a reimagined version of Keziah Mason's rat-like familiar from "The Dreams in the Witch-House."

fullContent:
"Periphery" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Paul Lewis. It was published by Screaming Dreams in the thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg in October 2013.

### Synopsis
Jason relates to his brother Richard the story of how, after believing there to be mice in his house, his fear and revulsion of the creatures somehow opened a portal allowing invisible somethings into his home- somethings which were now able to perceive him. As the portal grew larger, the entities began to attack him, causing physical wounds. In an effort to escape his tormentors, Jason left his house, where he experienced visions of an enormous being stalking the nearby coastline; worse, this terrible entity now seemed aware of him…

Richard is of a mind that his brother is delusional, but is unable to explain the wounds he has suffered. He returns home to consider the situation, but when he visits Jason the next day, finds that the poor man has been torn to shreds by an unknown force in the night. Shocked and terrified by this development, Richard quickly comes to the realisation that his emotions have opened another gateway, and the malevolent beings can now perceive him as well…

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly named as such, the description of the colossal entity witnessed by Jason - of a creature which "walked on two legs like a man … its head … akin to that of an octopus. Scales clung to its rubbery body and long slender wings emerged from its back. It had claws on all four of its limbs" would appear to suggest that it was intended to be Great Cthulhu himself.

Sergeant Pete Ivalu is a fictional character created by Troy Young for his Nyarlathotep Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos short stories.

### Description
A 6-year veteran in the Canadian Army Rangers, an organisation purposed with maintaining a military presence in the Arctic Circle, Pete Ivalu was a small man with an infectious smile. He was of Inuk (Inuit) descent, a trait which aided him during his deployment in the tundra.

### History
After his squad was tasked with the investigation of a missing tribe in the far north of Canada, Ivalu was assigned to assist Dr. Adele Kramer in preventing them from completing their purpose: awakening a malevolent entity trapped in the ice floes. In the aftermath of this operation, he was seconded to the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena, a black-ops government agency dedicated to protecting humankind from "The Other".

Ivalu's first mission saw him partnered with Joe Mills, an Inspector in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, and the two successfully eliminated a Nyarlathotep cult.

His second assignment, which would prove to be his last, saw Ivalu, Kramer and Mills sent to the site of a former incident. There, they encountered an avatar of Nyarlathotep going under the name of William Akeley which promptly killed Ivalu, seemingly for nothing more than the fun of it.

fullContent:
Pete Von Sholly is an artist, filmmaker, and author who has worked on a number of Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos works over the course of a long career and varied career. These include a wealth of artwork for PS Publishing's Lovecraft Illustrated series, as well as numerous non-fiction works on the genre, which have appeared in publications such as Crypt of Cthulhu and Fantastic Fictioneers: A History of the Incredible. He has also illustrated works for leading genre authors including Stephen King, Joe R. Lansdale, and Ramsey Campbell. His Lovecraftian art has been collected into Pete Von Sholly's Lovecraft Illustrated (Spanish edition pictured with the creator), published by Clover Press in the US and by Diablo Ediciones in Spain .

Von Sholly's History of Monsters mural features over 1100 monsters in a panoramic sweep. It is a comprehensive history beginning with folklore and mythology and evolving into early fiction, pulp fiction, comics, movies and television. 

Von Sholly's filmmaking credits include storyboard and graphic design work for franchises such as A Nightmare on Elm Street, Return of the Living Dead, Re-animator, Child's Play/Chucky, Puppet Master, Demonic Toys, Pumpkinhead (second film), and Hellraiser (seventh film), stand-alone movies including The Shawshank Redemption, The Green Mile, The Mist, Darkman, and Mars Attacks!, as well as many children's television shows, for which he has also provided character designs .

Von Sholly has also appeared as a guest speaker at the H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival three times between 2015 and 2016, and on at least two other Lovecraftian panels at Wondercon and Monsterpalooza in the same time period .

### Praise
Von Sholly's artwork has received praise from many people involved in Lovecraftiana, including scholar S. T. Joshi, filmmaker Brian Yuzna of Re-Animator and From Beyond fame, director Sam Raimi, British horror writer Ramsey Campbell, and members of the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society .

Peter Hughes Cannon (born 1951 in Palo Alto, California, United States) is an editor, H. P. Lovecraft scholar and an author of Cthulhu Mythos fiction.

Cannon's writings on Lovecraft include "The Chronology Out of Time: Dates in the Fiction of H. P. Lovecraft" and "Sunset Terrace Imagery in Lovecraft". He edited Lovecraft Remembered, a collection of reminiscences by friends and acquaintances of Lovecraft, and co-edited More Annotated H. P. Lovecraft with S. T. Joshi . He also wrote a personal memoir about another writer in the Lovecraft Circle, "Long Memories: Recollections of Frank Belknap Long."

His fiction includes Pulptime, in which Lovecraft, Long and Sherlock Holmes join forces to solve a mystery; Scream for Jeeves: A Parody, which retells some of Lovecraft's stories in the voice of P. G. Wodehouse's Bertie Wooster; and The Lovecraft Chronicles, a novel based on Lovecraft's personal life.

He has also written several short stories in the Cthulhu Mythos genre, often with an element of parody. These include the Forever Azathoth series, a six-part sequel to "The Thing on the Doorstep"; "The Undercliffe Sentences", a takeoff on Ramsey Campbell; and "The Madness Out of Space", originally presented as a "lost" story by Lovecraft.

Cannon works as an editor for Publishers Weekly, specializing in the horror genre, science fiction, fantasy, and mystery. He lives in New York City and is married with three children.

Cannon was also a member of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts and scholars active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s.

Pf'legmwad is a fictional monster from the Donald Duck comic book story "The Call of C'rruso", which parodies the Cthulhu Mythos. The story first appeared in the German comic book Lustiges Taschenbuch ("Funny Paperback"), published in October 2004. Its first US appearance was in IDW's Donald Duck #16, published in 2016.

### Description
While most of its inhabitants are blissfully unaware of it, all of reality is in fact a dream of Pf'legmwad, a cosmic entity that eternally dreams inside a white citadel in the sunken island of Sp'too.

While dreaming, Pf'legmwad's subconscious mind also manifests itself as a pair of humanoid figures known as C'rruso and D'mmingo, which identify themselves as psychic manifestations of the monster's conflicting impulses. C'rruso dresses in black and dislikes reality, so he tries to get Pf'legmwad to wake up, while D'mmingo dresses in white and finds reality pleasant, so he seeks to keep Pf'legmwad asleep and preserve it. Every 100 years, as Sp'too rises above the waves, the two personifications compete against each other to see which will prevail.

As an otherworldly entity, Pf'legmwad's perception of music differs from the norm, in that it regards tuneful music as irritating, and dissonant music as soothing. Singing a song in a melodious voice in its presence will readily cause Pf'legmwad to wake up enraged, erasing most of reality and transforming the remaining parts into something more akin to its own image. On the other hand, someone with a particularly bad singing voice (such as Donald Duck) can lull the titan back to sleep and restore reality to normal. (: "The Call of C'rruso")

### Gallery

Pf'legmwad2.jpg|Pf'legmwad emerging from Sp'too (art by Flemming Andersen)
C'rruso&D'mmingo.jpg|C'rruso and D'mmingo, manifestations of Pf'legmwad (art by Flemming Andersen)
RealityChanges.jpg|Reality starts to collapse (art by Flemming Andersen)


### Behind the Mythos
Pf'legmwad shares several traits with Cthulhu from H. P. Lovecraft's story "The Call of Cthulhu", which "The Call of C'rruso" is a parody of. Both are giant tentacled creatures which lie dreaming inside a sunken citadel at the bottom of the ocean.

Furthermore, the fact that Pf'legmwad is the creator of reality and must be kept asleep to prevent it from destroying it makes this entity similar to Māna-Yood-Sushāī from Lord Dunsany's The Gods of Pegāna.

C'rruso and D'mmingo are meant to be "Lovecraftian" renditions of the names of famous opera singers Enrico Caruso and Plácido Domingo.

Pharol is a fictional deity created by C. L. Moore for her Northwest Smith series of science fiction stories. He was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Henry Kuttner in his 1939 short story "Hydra".

### Description
Pharol is a black, fanged, cycloptic demon with arms like swaying serpents. The entity normally dwells in another dimension - a "seething and sub-dimensional chaos" beyond the mundane universe. The wizard Eibon of Hyperborea occasionally summoned Pharol to query him for arcane information. (: "Shaggai")

shortDefinition: Philip J. Rahman (1952-2011) is the co-founder of Fedogan & Bremer, an important publisher of Cthulhu Mythos and other weird fiction. With his brother Glenn Rahman, he wrote a handful of Mythos stories. In 1980-81, the brothers wrote "the first succe...
fullContent:
Philip J. Rahman (1952-2011) is the co-founder of Fedogan & Bremer, an important publisher of Cthulhu Mythos and other weird fiction. With his brother Glenn Rahman, he wrote a handful of Mythos stories. In 1980-81, the brothers wrote "the first successful transference of H. P. Lovecraft’s style of supernatural literature into a modern role-playing format."

Rahman was born February 18, 1952, in Wabasha, Minnesota, one of six children. He worked for more than 30 years as a business analyst for the University of Minnesota hospital. He founded Fedogan & Bremer with Dennis Weiler in 1985, the publishing house taking its name from the partners' college nicknames. It published books by Donald Wandrei, Robert Bloch, Hugh B. Cave, Richard A. Lupoff, Karl Edward Wagner, Robert M. Price, and Basil Copper, among others. The press won a World Fantasy Award in 1998.

With his brother Glenn, Rahman published "The Lovecraft Variant" in the Summer 1980 issue of Sorcerer's Apprentice, a set of rules for running Lovecraftian scenarios with the Monsters! Monsters! roleplaying system. It was later described as a " a full system for investigating strange occurrences and uncovering ancient secrets, all while struggling to maintain the characters' sanity in the face of unimaginable terrors." The Summer 1981 issue of Sorcerer's Apprentice included a sequel, "The Monsters of the Cthulhu Mythos." The two pieces were packaged together as The Lovecraft Variant by Bolt Thrower Press.

Rahman was given the Minnesota Fantasy Award for Life Achievement in 1999. He was married to Lynne Holden from 1986 until 2005, and married his second wife Diane Landon shortly before her death in 2006. He was survived by his son Clark Howard Rahman and his step-daughter Dana Madden.

Sir Philip Jermyn is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family".

### Background
Sir Philip Jermyn was the son of Wade Jermyn and the great-great-grandfather of Arthur Jermyn. Described as a "highly peculiar" person, he was the first of his father's descendents to exhibit the simian characteristics that originated from the union between Wade Jermyn and a female member of a race of African white apes.

Despite a strong physical resemblance to his father, his appearance and conduct were so coarse that he was universally shunned. He did not inherit the madness which was feared by some, but he was densely stupid and given to brief periods of uncontrollable violence. He had a small frame but was very powerful and had incredible agility.

Twelve years after gaining his hereditary title Sir Philip married the daughter of his gamekeeper, but before his son Robert was born he joined the Navy as a common sailor. After the end of the Revolutionary War he became a sailor on a merchant ship in the African trade, having a reputation for feats of strength and climbing. Philip eventually disappeared one night as his ship lay off the Congo coast. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

fullContent:
Philip José Farmer (January 26, 1918 – February 25, 2009) was an award-winning American science fiction and fantasy writer, known for his pioneering use of sexual and religious themes in his works. He is perhaps best known for his World of Tiers and Riverworld series.

He has written extensively in the worlds of other authors, expanding on the fictional worlds of characters such as Phileas Fogg, Tarzan of Greystoke, Sherlock Holmes, Doc Savage, and The Wizard of Oz's Dorothy. His Wold Newton shared universe incorporates events and characters from the works of dozens of authors, including H. P. Lovecraft.

Farmer's 1979 short story "The Freshman" explored the dark side of Miskatonic University and delved deeper into the fictional history of Arkham as a whole.

Phosphorescent Monsters are a species of creature developed for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu Mythos roleplaying game.

### Description
Relatively unintelligent beasts of the Dreamlands, Phosphorescent Monsters are nevertheless dangerous beings which take their name from the eerie green glow which they emit. Standing a full thirty feet tall at the shoulder, they possess wide, gaping mouths which are capable of sucking up smaller creatures and a pair of large bat-like wings which allow them to fly through space.

The Phosphorescent Monsters are frequently employed as mounts and working beasts by the piratical Wenelians, and they presumably originated on the same planet, Yundu.

### Behind the Mythos
Phosphorescent Monsters were created by Phil Frances for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands in 1986.

fullContent:
"Pickford's Model" is the 13th issue in Volume 2 of Zenoscope Entertainment's contemporary horror anthology Grimm Tales of Terror, published in October 2016. It was written by Joe Brusha, with artwork by Vincenzo Riccardi, and features a primary cover from Gregbo Watson. Two variant covers were also completed, by Noah Salonga and Ceci de la Cruz, and Maria Laura Sanapo and Vinicius Andrade; the second of these does not relate to the story within, but feature Keres, a goddess of death who acts as a "hostess" of sorts for the series.

The story is an updated and uncredited adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's short horror story "Pickman's Model."

### Synopsis
Struggling artist Edward Whitney is deeply envious of his former art school acquaintance Jeremy Pickford, a talented and highly successful painter whose imagery evokes the demonic. One evening Pickford, in a boastful mood after a lucrative gallery exhibition, takes Whitney to his basement painting studio to show him the secret of his success. What he reveals is that he is in fact painting his subjects from life: a well leading to unknown subterranean depths spews forth a group of demonic creatures which must be fed. Fortunately for Whitney, a slip on Pickford's part leaves him at the mercy of the creatures, and in the aftermath Whitney slides into Pickford’s shoes, posing as his protégé.

### Behind the Mythos
The story is an adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model," although no acknowledgement is given to the original author in the credits. The story's description of a talented artist of the macabre who falls foul of the creatures he paints clearly shows identical elements, and even the well in the basement from which the monsters issue forth in Lovecraft’s tale is represented.

### Publication History
Since it’s first release, "Pickford's Model" has also been included in the omnibus collection Grimm Tales of Terror Volume 2, published two weeks after the release of this issue, the final in its series.

"Pickman’s Madonna" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the October 2013 issue of Sirenia Digest (#93).

### Overview
The story introduces the characters of Isobel and Isaac Snow, albino, incestuous twins descended from ghouls, who raise an army to conquer the Dreamlands. The characters reappear in Kiernan's "The Peddler's Tale; or, Isobel's Revenge." The Snow family that they belong to is featured in Kiernan works like Low Red Moon and "Pickman's Other Model."

The story's title refers to an idol of a ghoulish goddess, first noted by humans in the 5th century, that was later in the possession of Richard Upton Pickman. It disappeared soon after his own disappearance, and was later rediscovered in a cave in Arabia.

### Publication History
The story was reprinted (revised and in part) in Cherry Bomb (2015, Roc/NAL), a novel Kiernan wrote under the name Kathleen Tierney. It later appeared in Kiernan's collection Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018).

fullContent:
"Pickman's Model" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft, written in September 1926 and first published in the October 1927 issue of Weird Tales. It has since become one of Lovecraft's most iconic works.

### Plot summary
The story revolves around a Bostonian painter named Richard Upton Pickman who creates horrifying images. His works are brilliantly executed, but so graphic that they result in the revocation of his membership in the Boston Art Club and he is shunned by his fellow artists.

The narrator is a friend of Pickman, who, after the artist's mysterious disappearance, relates to another acquaintance how he was taken on a tour of Pickman's personal gallery, hidden away in a run-down backwater slum of the city. As the two delved deeper into Pickman's mind and art, the rooms seemed to grow ever more evil and the paintings ever more horrific, ending with a final enormous painting of an unearthly, red-eyed and vaguely canine humanoid balefully chewing on a human victim.

A noise sent Pickman running outside the room with a gun while the narrator reached out to unfold what looked like a small piece of rolled paper attached to the monstrous painting. The narrator heard some shots and Pickman walked back in with the smoking gun, telling a story of shooting some rats, and the two men departed.

Afterwards the narrator realized that he had nervously grabbed and put the rolled paper in his pocket when the shots were fired. He unrolled the paper to reveal that it is a photograph not of the background of the painting, but of the subject. Pickman drew his inspirations not from a diseased imagination, but from monsters that were very much real.

### Inspiration

Pickman's aesthetic principles of horror resemble those in Lovecraft's essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature" (1925–1927), on which he was working at the time the short story was composed. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) When Thurber, the story's narrator, notes that "only the real artist knows the actual anatomy of the terrible or the physiology of fear—the exact sort of lines and proportions that connect up with latent instincts or hereditary memories of fright, and the proper colour contrasts and lighting effects to stir the dormant sense of strangeness", he is echoing Lovecraft the literary critic on Poe, who "understood so perfectly the very mechanics and physiology of fear and strangeness". (: "Supernatural Horror in Literature")

Thurber's description of Pickman as a "thorough, painstaking, and almost scientific realist" recalls Lovecraft's approach to horror in his post-Dunsanian phase. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

The story compares Pickman's work to that of a number of actual artists, including John Henry Fuseli (1741–1825), Gustave Doré (1832–1883), Sidney Sime (1867–1941), Anthony Angarola (1893–1929), Francisco Goya (1746–1828), and Clark Ashton Smith (1893–1961).

"Pickman's Model" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Max D. Stanton and published in the Ulthar Press thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery in 2018. The story functions as something of a prequel to H. P. Lovecraft's 1927 short story, also named "Pickman's Model".

### Synopsis
When struggling young artist Richard Upton Pickman meets enigmatic aristocrat Abigail Peters, he begins to develop an intellectual fascination with her, despite her apparent oddities. In the following months, the two get to know each other better, and a bond of trust grows between the two. As a result, Abigail makes a decision: to show Pickman her true form. As she changes into a monstrous ghoul, Pickman realises that he has at last found his model.

### Characters
*Richard Upton Pickman, a talented artist with a taste for the macabre.
*Abigail Peters, a woman of old money descended from a very peculiar stock.

"Pickman's Model Kit" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Cliff Biggers. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
When avid model kit collector Danny discovers a "Pickman's Model" kit of a ferocious ghoul in a run-down antiques shop, he is delighted, and snaps up the bargain, immediately rushing home to build his new prize.

Over the next couple of days, strange disappearances in his neighbourhood, along with subtle changes to the model which suggest it reacts in sympathy to the events, horrify Danny, and he attempts to destroy the artefact. However, this only succeeds in summoning a real ghoul who appears to be somehow linked to the model, and Danny quickly becomes its latest victim.

fullContent:
"Pickman's Modem" is a short story by Lawrence Watt-Evans set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
The narrator, a man named George, tells the tale of his online friend Henry Pickman who buys a new modem from Miskatonic Data Systems in Arkham, Massachusetts. The modem corrupts his online posts, infusing them with bile and vitriol, and Pickman believes it to be watching him.

The story concludes by stating that Henry Pickman's house is set ablaze and the man himself never heard from again, but just prior to this he sends George a message telling of his fear of the modem, and concluding with a burst of line noise which reads "Iä! FThaGN!Iä!CTHulHu!"

### Characters
*George - the story's narrator.
*Henry Pickman - George's online friend.

### Behind the Mythos
Watt-Evans was inspired to write "Pickman's Modem" after an online chat session which was interrupted by a burst of line noise which formed text "that looked rather like a Lovecraftian invocation of the Great Old Ones," and another member of the group commented that "Pickman's modem [was] at work."

After completing the work, Watt-Evans sold it to Gardner Dozois at Isaac Asimov's Science Fiction Magazine. It was later reprinted in Arkham House's anthology Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology, and again in Isaac Asimov's SF-Lite. It received an eBook release with the publication of the The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack by Wildside Press LLC in 2012. Watt-Evans also included it in his own collection, Celestial Debris.

### Trivia
*The serial number on the side of Pickman's new modem was #R1LYEH, a clear reference to R'lyeh, Cthulhu's resting place deep beneath the Pacific Ocean.

### References
*http://www.watt-evans.com/PickmansModem.shtml, the author recounts the inspiration behind "Pickman's Modem".

"Pickman's Muse" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author K. H. Vaughn. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
The story charts the development of Richard Upton Pickman during his student days as a young artist railing against the stuffy, unchanging nature of the artistic community in the early 20th century, to the tempering of his work in order to gain acceptance by the local art patrons, and finally to realise what he needs to release his potential.

At the same time it relates his relationships with two wildly different women, one the scion of a wealthy Boston family with a rebellious streak, the other a Ghoul working as entertainment in a disreputable speakeasy. Although both women provide him with inspiration for his work, in order to realise his true potential and become his muse, one must die at the hands of the other.

### Characters
*Richard Upton Pickman, a talented young artist who feels his work is directionless.
*Jane Channing, a young dilettante whose interest in Pickman leads to her gruesome demise.
*Althea, a stripper at a seedy nightclub, she uses a veil and strategically-placed feathers to hide her Ghoul nature.

fullContent:
"Pickman's Other Model (1929)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that serves as a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model". It first appeared in the March 2008 issue of Sirenia Digest, and was reprinted in Black Wings: New Tales of Lovecraftian Horror (2010).

The narrator of Kiernan's story, though referred to at one point as "Mr. Blackman", is identified with Eliot, the person to whom Thurber, the narrator of "Pickman's Model", tells his story. In Kiernan's continuation, Thurber has committed suicide, and now Eliot Blackman (to combine the names from each story) has become obsessed--with Richard Upton Pickman, with Thurber, and with Vera Endecott, a silent movie actress who had posed for Pickman--the "other model" of the story's title.

### Characters
Richard Upton Pickman: The master of macabre painting, and the title character from Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model". Kiernan's narrator refers to him as "that sick bastard Richard Upton Pickman," and says that his art "had never struck me quite so profoundly as it had Thurber," but admits that he had "a great and singular talent": "I always credited his success at capturing the weird largely to his intentional juxtaposition of phantasmagoric subject matter with a starkly, painstakingly realistic style." We learn that Pickman worked in a "dank cellar studio near Battery Street" in Boston's North End, that he showed regularly in galleries from 1921 to 1925, before he was ostracized, that he was connected to "theosophical and occult societies, from Manhattan to Los Angeles," and that he disappeared in 1927. Blackman reports "whispers in the Art Club" that Pickman was gay, to which Vera Endecott retorted: “Mister, I have yet to meet the beast –- male, female, or anything in between –- that degenerate...wouldn’t have screwed, given half a chance.” 

William Thurber: Kiernan gives Lovecraft's narrator a first name, and considerable backstory--an education at the Rhode Island School of Design, participation in specific battles in World War I--as well as a relative, "the only surviving member of his immediate family, Ellen Thurber, an older sister." Blackman says that after Thurber returned from the war, he "was hardly more than a fading, nervous echo of the man I’d first met." He takes a "close, rather shabby room" on Hope Street in Providence after leaving Boston, presumably in an unsuccessful attempt to escape memories connected to Pickman. His suicide there weighs heavily on Blackman and sparks his own possibly self-destructive obsession. 

Eliot Blackman: The narrator, a fellow painter and friend of Thurber's from the Rhode Island School of Design. (Only his last name is used, and that only once, in Kiernan's story; he's repeatedly called "Eliot" in Lovecraft's story, which Kiernan apparently takes to be a first name.) Blackman reveals that the conversation with Thurber that comprises "Pickman's Model" happened in a "dingy tavern" on Chatham Street near Faneuil Hall. Blackman does not drink,

"Pickman's Progeny: The Horrid Truth Below" is a very short (two and a half pages) Cthulhu Mythos story by author Robert Masterson. It was published in the November 2008 edition of Nathan Shumate's short-lived zine Arkham Tales.

### Synopsis
During the 1970s, a young man takes his date on a late night subway journey in an effort to impress her with the spectacle of the local graffiti scene. However, the nature of the art on display changes as the train moves deeper into the tunnels, becoming more like Neolithic cave art. At the story's culmination, he witnesses a bizarre and angry-looking creature feeding on something unidentifiable, its only clothing a loincloth made from a tanned human face.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite the story itself featuring no direct references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the title indicates that the creature glimpsed by the unnamed narrator is intended to be a ghoul, the carnivorous subterranean creatures depicted by Lovecraft in his short horror story "Pickman's Model."

Pierre is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Alchemist".

### Oveview
Pierre was the servant of the Comte Antoine de C--. After the deaths of the young Antoine's parents, his care and education became the responsibility of Pierre, the family's last remaining servant. Pierre was described by Antoine as "an old and trusted man of considerable intelligence." 

During Antoine's youth, Pierre restricted his interactions with the local peasant children in order to avoid exposing him to tales and gossip concerning the curse on Antoine's family. Upon the Comte's twenty-first birthday, Pierre gave to him a family document handed down from father to son through many generations which revealed the history and origin of the curse. 

Antoine was near the age of thirty when the elderly Pierre died, presumably of natural causes. He was buried beneath the courtyard of the family castle.

"Pigman" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Max D. Stanton. It was first published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
Jason Zuckerman, a struggling art gallery owner who is desperate to earn fame and fortune, makes the mistake of attempting to obtain works from the sociopathic "art-terrorist" Pigman, a highly-gifted but murderous creature who has in recent years perpetrated numerous atrocities against the human race across the globe.

Contacting Pigman, he is lured into the depths of the New York subway system, where he is led to an abandoned rail cart and imprisoned. There, Pigman makes him the subject of his latest work, tattooing his entire body with horrific images before infecting him with an incurable strain of swine flu and depositing his near-lifeless body at an active station to infect more of the populace.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never outright stated, Pigman and his inhuman clan are heavily implied to be Richard Upton Pickman and his pack of ghouls; descriptions of his sublime yet shocking artistic talent, his first attack being launched in Boston, and the manner in which his acolytes' bodies move beneath their concealing clothes, all point in this direction.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Pigman" has also been included in the collection of Stanton's own works, A Season of Loathsome Miracles, issued by Trepidatio Publishing in August 2020

"Pilgrimage" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Welsh author and editor Mark Howard Jones. It was published in the thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg by Screaming Dreams in October 2013.

### Synopsis
A man on a train journey's life devolves into a nightmare as Nyarlathotep, in his guise as the Black Man, boards and bends reality to his desires. As the other passengers melt, rot, or simply cease to exist, the man is brought by Nyarlathotep to his final destination where he is transformed into an inhuman monstrosity as a dark sacrifice.

### Behind the Mythos
A small group of fellow passengers - and the only ones to remain unaffected by the reality distortions cause by Nyarlathotep - are hinted to be non-human, perhaps members of the diminutive Tcho-Tcho species.

Pilot Demons are a species of extra-dimensional being created by American author and screenwriter Byron Craft for his 2014 novel The Alchemist's Notebook, and subsequently expanded upon in 2015's Cthulhu's Minions.

### Overview
Described as "ethereal puffs of smoke that sometimes take shape and solidify" , Pilot Demons can take a multitude of forms when they materialise, but are always diminutive in stature. Occasionally winged and always fast and vicious, they act as heralds and pathfinders when greater beings wish to worm their way into our plane of existence. They are highly intelligent creatures, being able to perform complex tasks such as constructing mechanical devices to enable them to operate automobiles.

### Appearances

*Cthulhu's Minions (2015)

"Planetfall on Yuggoth" is a very short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author James Wade. It was first published in the H. P. Lovecraft tribute fanzine HPL in March 1972.

### Synopsis
The story covers the landing of an expedition on Pluto, codenamed "Operation Yuggoth" after "the name for the planet used in pulp fiction by some obscure author of the last century", from a historical point of view. The expedition vanished, their ships destroyed, but not before one of the crewmen sent back a garbled radio message about "living fungi, like great clumsy crabs with membranous wings and squirming knots of tentacles for heads".

The entire occurrence was soon dismissed as one of the perils of space travel, with the crewman's radio transmission put down to some form of space madness, and future missions were revealed to be planned, both to Pluto and to a newly-discovered tenth planet. This latter venture was named "Operation Shaggai".

### Publication History
*HPL (1972)
*The Hastur Cycle (1993, 1997, 2006)
*Nightscapes (1997)
*Le cycle d'Hastur (2000)

### Trivia
*Written in 1972, Pluto was at that time still considered a planet; "Planetfall on Yuggoth" refers to it as such, although it does mention the controversy surrounding that designation. It has since been reclassified as a dwarf planet.

Leng is a fictional location created by H. P. Lovecraft, a cold, arid plateau whose location seems to vary entirely according to different accounts. Abdul Alhazred describes it as a place where different realities converge, which might explain why its precise location cannot be pinned down.

The Plateau of Tsang, referenced by Frank Belknap Long and other authors, may be a region of Leng.

### Locations
*The Necronomicon places it in Central Asia and says it is inhabited by a corpse-eating cult. (: "The Hound")
*The Plateau of Leng is located in the northern Dreamlands, an alternate dimension accessible only in sleep. It is inhabited by satyr-like degenerates known as the Men of Leng. It is also the dwelling place of the High Priest Not to Be Described in a prehistoric monastery. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) The plains of Leng are supposed to be located in Earth's Dreamlands. (: The Clock of Dreams Brian Lumley)
*Leng is a remote plateau in Tibet where the monks of a lone monastery serve what appears to be an ancient underground fungus and possible hive mind, similar to Ophiocordyceps sinensis, but which infects humans. (: "Leng", first printed in Lovecraft Unbound Marc Laidlaw)
*Leng is a demi-plane, or pocket dimension, that exists adjacent to the world of Golarion. It closely resembles the Dreamland's version of Leng. (: Pathfinder roleplaying game)
*The plateau of Leng is a projection into a higher mathematical space, which makes up the universe as observable by humans. (: Neonomicon, Alan Moore)
*Leng Avenue is a street in Innsmouth. (: "Only the End of the World Again", Neil Gaiman)
* The "Hall of Leng" is a location within the Imperial Palace on Terra (Earth). (: "Blood Games" [Dan Abnett, Warhammer 40,000, Tales of Heresy, Book 10 of the Horus Heresy series)

### Antarctica
An expedition from Miskatonic University explores a plateau in Antarctica and discovers an ancient and apparently abandoned city built by the Elder Things. It was discovered by geologist William Dyer and graduate student Danforth. One member of the expedition, who has encountered references to the Plateau of Leng in ancient texts, forms the hypothesis that the plateau they are exploring is Leng. (: At the Mountains of Madness) In common with the High Priest's abode, the walls of the buildings atop the plateau are covered with detailed frescos that are disturbing to read. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) Wilbur Whateley also had vision of cities at the poles when studying aklo. (: The Dunwich Horror)

The location in Antarctica is confirmed as the Plateau of Leng. (: "God Cancer", Greg Stolze)

The Plateau of Tsang is an area in central Tibet, now part of the Ü-Tsang region. The location was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Frank Belknap Long in his novel The Horror from the Hills.

### Description
The Plateau of Tsang is a remote region in central Asia that consists mostly of a cold, arid, thoroughly inhospitable desert. Among the men who died trying to cross it are explorers like Steelbrath, Talman, McWilliams, Henley and Holmes. Among the few who did manage to return alive is an American archaeologist named Richardson, who came across a cave in Tsang inhabited by Chaugnar Faugn worshipers, and guarded by faceless yellow creatures who also venerate the primordial elephantine deity. After days of torture, Richardson's endurance impressed the cultists enough that they allowed him to escape and return to America. He was followed by another explorer, Clark Ulman, who likewise managed to brave the plateau and find the cave, where Chaugnar Faugn fed on his blood. (: The Horror from the Hills)

Professor Harold Hadley Copeland, in his 1913 expedition to central Asia, crossed the Plateau of Tsang to get to the northern mountains, where he discovered the tomb of the Muvian wizard Zanthu (: "The Dweller in the Tomb", "Out of the Ages", "The Horror in the Gallery") who escaped the destruction of Mu. On September 24, 1913, Copeland wrote in his journal that "only poor Richardson and the unfortunate Clark Ulman have gone as far as I into this forbidden Tsang Plateau region". Copeland also noted the Plateau's dryness, utter sterility and incredibly ancient fossil strata with no sea life, suggesting that the region might have remained on dry land since Pre-Cambrian times. (: "The Dweller in the Tomb")

Water obtained from the Plateau's snows has a bad taste as if it was somehow contaminated (: "The Dweller in the Tomb"), forcing those who cross the desert to drink their own blood or that of their mount animals to survive (: The Horror from the Hills, : "The Dweller in the Tomb"). Copeland also reports having many encounters with the Mi-Go in this area (: "The Dweller in the Tomb"), but it's not known whether they correspond to the "faceless guardians" encountered by Richardson and Clark Ulman.

It is possible that the Plateau of Tsang might be dimensionally connected to the Plateau of Leng (: "The Dweller in the Tomb"), which the Necronomicon claims to be located in central Asia as well (: "The Hound", At the Mountains of Madness), but which might exist simultaneously in Antarctica (: At the Mountains of Madness) and the Dreamlands (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath).

### Behind the Mythos
The Tibetan region of Ü-Tsang is referenced in "The Last Test", by H. P. Lovecraft and Adolphe de Castro.

The Pnakotic Manuscripts (or Pnakotic Fragments) is a fictional grimoire from the Cthulhu Mythos, which first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "Polaris". It was extensively expanded upon by Lin Carter, who wrote a couple of "chapters" from the work; Chaosium has also added data.

### Background
The Pnkakotic Manuscripts were written by the Great Race of Yith and kept in their library-city of Pnakotus before being moved to frozen Lomar and the Dreamlands.

### Contents
The ~1,011 (MXI) Pnakotic Fragments make up several books that include:
*The "pre-Pleistocene" records of the Great Race; they were later added to by the prehuman worshippers of Tsathoggua (the Voormis) and then by the Pnakotic Brotherhood, right up to the flight from Lomar, when copies were carried into the Dreamlands, among other places. Each generation of the Brothers added to the text.
*The eighth fragment deals with Rhan-Tegoth. (: "The Horror in the Museum") In the 15th Century, the one public translation (into English) was made by an unknown author. This "pirate" version is known only as five bound manuscripts held by major libraries in Europe and America.
*The story of Sansu, who climbed the mountain Hatheg-Kla when the world was young, but found nothing (: "The Other Gods").
*An untranslatable section containing the symbol found carved atop Hatheg-Kla after the disappearance of Barzai the Wise (: "The Other Gods").

### In Other Media
*The Doctor Who novel Millennial Rites features a copy of the Pnakotic Manuscripts in the collection of the Library of St John the Beheaded.
*The Pnakotic Manuscripts appear in the Demonbane franchise, taking the form of a human girl named Etheldreda. She is the grimoire of Master Therion, who uses her to pilot Liber Legis. When the Black Lodge was unable to obtain Al Azif for the C Project, Etheldreda was used as a substitute during their ritual to summon Cthulhu. The city of Pnakotus was an ancient city on Earth. It appears in the story "The Shadow Out of Time".

### Location
In the remote past, Pnakotus was located in what is now known as the Great Australian Desert.

### Description
Pnakotus was built millions of years ago by the Great Race of Yith. It is known for its large library, which includes the Pnakotic Manuscripts. The Great Race inhabited the city under a system similar to the socialist one, governed by a vote of the citizens considered most capable in the face of psychological and cultural tests. From the underground cave system, the Flying Polyps fought back against the Great Race, taking over this place of cyclopean walls.

The Great Race collected information on all eras, both past and present, in the archives of the Great Library. To accomplish this, they sent their minds back and forth in time, occupying the bodies of the dominant races of each era. The minds displaced from the bodies of these species are sent to the body of the member of the Great Race that has supplanted them and, while they remain in Pnakotus, they are treated as kings in exchange for contributing their knowledge to the data in the Library. Once they are returned to their respective bodies, the members of the Great Race who have replaced them also return to theirs and complement the information left by the guests with their own intensive study of the historical moment they have occupied.

It is known that the Great Race has not only visited the bodies of Earth beings: it has also visited the bodies of inhabitants of other worlds.

### Fauna and Flora
Although initially this place was the home of the Great Race, nowadays in its ruins dwell the flying polyps, which have made them their territory.

Pnidleethon is a fictional planet first mentioned by Clark Ashton Smith in his story fragment "The Infernal Star" and later expanded upon by John W. Patterson in "Priestess of Nycrama".

### Description
Pnidleethon is a planet which orbits the binary star system comprised of Yamil Zacra and Yuzh. It is inhabited by an intelligent an magically-proficient race of alien beings whose name has not been revealed.

Every night, the planet is scoured by enormous flocks of red-eyed, bat-winged creatures called Pnumbrals, whose purpose is to "eliminate the foolish, the unwary, and the slothful of Pnidleethon" (EXP: "Priestess of Nycrama").

Pnidleethon is also home to a species of semi-animate flora called Khisanti trees, which appear to be benign in nature (EXP: "Priestess of Nycrama").

### The Royal Palace
Avalzant, one of Pnidleethon's rulers, maintains a royal palace, although little is known of this structure.
