fullContent:
"Poetry and the Gods" is a short story by horror writer and poet H. P. Lovecraft in collaboration with writer Anna Helen Crofts. The story is very different from the vast majority of Lovecraft's other work and collaborations. It does, however, bear similar themes regarding dreams as a doorway to magic realms, and slumbering gods.

### Synopsis
The narrative follows the dream-voyage of Marcia, a young woman filled with weariness of the mundane world and all its woes. She resolves to ease her troubled soul by reading a magazine of poetry. As she does, a dream-state unfolds in which the Greek god Hermes appears and bears Marcia to the court of Zeus and the Olympians. It is here that she sees Dante Alighieri, William Shakespeare, John Milton, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, and John Keats. The gods reveal that it is poets that sustain beauty in the world and whose work is reawakening the gods to bring wonder and magic back to the world. She is told that it's her destiny to meet the man who would be the world's next great poet. The story closes on Marcia, some time after, with her poet lover as he reads to her.

"Pokethulhu" is a whimsical Cthulhu Mythos story by author John Taloni. It made its first - and to date, only - appearance in the Jesse Dedman-edited anthology Ancient Ones II in March 2018 .

### Synopsis
Four former high school track stars who had made a pact with an elder entity in exchange for sporting success are mystically summoned back to their home town decades later. There, they must gather the shards of their dark lord which have crashed to Earth, in order that the being may become whole once again and rise from its slumber.

As the men collect the pieces, they begin to realise that pitting them against each other in combat strengthens the shards - which they dub Cthulhini - and, in turn, the entity which they serve.

### Behind the Mythos
The men are unable to fully pronounce the name of the being which they are indebted to, as it does not allow them to speak it aloud; instead, the word devolves into "Cthulhaaarrrggghhh" on every utterance.

The mystical balls which the men use to collect the shard, as well as the concept of battling creatures to evolve their skills, is taken directly from the Japanese multimedia franchise Pokémon , which is also the source of the story's title, a portmanteau of "Cthulhu" and "Pokémon".

### References

shortDefinition: "Polaris" is a fantasy short story by H. P. Lovecraft, written in 1918 and first published in the December 1920 issue of the amateur journal The Philosopher. It is noteworthy as the story that introduces Lovecraft's fictional Pnakotic Manuscripts, th...
fullContent:
"Polaris" is a fantasy short story by H. P. Lovecraft, written in 1918 and first published in the December 1920 issue of the amateur journal The Philosopher. It is noteworthy as the story that introduces Lovecraft's fictional Pnakotic Manuscripts, the first of his arcane tomes. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

Other elements introduced in this tale, such as the land of Lomar and the non-human Gnophkehs, would be referenced in other Lovecraft stories as well.

### Inspiration
Critic William Fulwiler writes that "'Polaris' is one of Lovecraft's most autobiographical stories, reflecting his feelings of guilt, frustration, and uselessness during World War I. Like the narrator, HPL was 'denied a warrior's part', for he 'was feeble and given to strange faintings when subjected to stress and hardships'".

Like many Lovecraft stories, "Polaris" was in part inspired by a dream, which he described in a letter: "Several nights ago I had a strange dream of a strange city--a city of many palaces and gilded domes, lying in a hollow betwixt ranges of grey, horrible hills.... I was, as I said, aware of this city visually. I was in it and around it. But certainly I had no corporeal existence." (: Selected Letters 1.034)

Lovecraft remarked on the peculiar similarity of the story's style to that of Lord Dunsany, whose work he would not read for another year.

It has been suggested that Lovecraft and Dunsany were both influenced by the prose poems of Edgar Allan Poe. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

### Plot summary
The story begins with the narrator describing the night sky as observed over long sleepless nights from his window, in particular that of the Pole Star, [Polaris], which he describes as "winking hideously like an insane watching eye which strives to convey some strange message, yet recalls nothing save that it once had a message to convey".

He then describes the night of the aurora over his house in the swamp, the night he first dreams of a marble city lying on a plateau between two peaks, with Polaris ever watching in the night sky. The narrator describes the progress of Aldebaran while observing motion within the houses. As robed men begin to populate the streets and converse to each other in a language that he had never heard before but still, strangely, understood. However, before he can learn any more about the city, he awakes.

Time and time again he dreams of the city and the men who dwell within. After a while, the narrator tires of merely existing as an incorporeal observer and begins to desire a place within the city, simultaneously beginning to question his conceptualization of what constituted reality and thus whether this was just a dream or whether it was real.

Then, one night, while listening to discourses of those who populate the city, the narrator obtains a physical form: not as a stranger, but as an inhabitant of the city, which he now knew as Olathoë, which was besieged by the forces of the Inutos.

Ponape, correctly spelled Pohnpei, is a real-world island in the Pacific Ocean, part of the Caroline Islands group and politically part of the  Federated States of Micronesia. Due to the ruined megalithic city of Nan Madol located on the island, Ponape has been incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos, particularly in the works of August Derleth and Lin Carter. 

### Nan Madol
Nan Madol is an extraordinary complex, constructed from large black lava columns placed on 92 artificial islands built atop coral reefs. It's the only ancient city built on a coral reef, and aside from the giant sculptures of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), its use of massive rock in construction is virtually unique in Oceania.

As visitors to the area will notice, there is amongst the literally cyclopaean architecture a broader pool or lagoon, formed from the surrounding blocks. Within this flooded area is a rectangular shaft, apparently sealed underwater with a block, preventing access to whatever well or tunnel might be below. This specific feature of Nan Madol (called Nan Matal in the story) features in Merritt's novella The Moon Pool, a favorite of H.P. Lovecraft.  

A complex of palaces, temples, and tombs built from 1200-1500 A.D., Nan Madol was the ceremonial center of the Saudeleur dynasty, which ruled Pohnpei from around 1100 A.D. to c. 1628. It is still unknown how the islanders managed to erect such huge pieces of stone on isolated islets; he mistakenly believed that Nan Madol was many millennia rather than several centuries old.  

### Other Mythos Writers
August Derleth made Ponape much more central to the Deep One mythology, which had the unfortunate effect of implicating the real-world residents of the island (with a population of nearly 37,000 in 2020) in a cult of Cthulhu-worshipping hybrid sea monsters.  

Thus in "The Survivor" (1954), the notes of Jean-Francois Charriere refer to "[c]onsiderable traffic between Innsmouth and Ponape," adding, "Some dark religious worship." In "The Shadow Out of Space" (1957), after the Innsmouth raid of 1928, there were "the most vaguely terrifying hints of a connection to certain batrachian people of Ponape." (In the story, Ponape is one of the places Amos Piper travels to when he is possessed by a Yithian.)  

Zebulon Whateley in "The Shuttered Room" (1959) speaks of "Obed Marsh's "wife that he faound in the trade—at Ponape, if ye know whar that is.” Later, a letter from Ariah Whateley discusses the Innsmouth look, noting, "Once I did see a native who had a similar appearance, but he was evidently not typical, for he was shunned by all the workers around the ships in the harbor where I saw him. I’ve forgotten now where it was, but I think Ponape."   

The story "Innsmouth Clay" (1971) features a Zadok Allen-style blabbermouth, Seth Atkins, who remarks, "“Cap’n Obed larnt a lot o’ things in Ponape an’ from the Kanakys—all abaout people they called t

The Ponape Scripture is a fictional document created by Lin Carter for his Cthulhu Mythos short stories, particularly those that make up the Xothic Legend Cycle.

### Description
An immensely old artifact, the Ponape Scripture consists of several sheets of palm-leaf parchment inscribed with metallic ink of various colours, and bound between boards of wood that some experts identify as coming from an extinct species of prehistoric cycad or tree-fern. The text is written in the Naacal language, although some passages are in an earlier idiom identified only as "the Elder Tongue" by Yogash. Some of the signs bear resemblance to pictographs found on a black stone in Zimbabwe. (: "The Dweller in the Tomb", "The Fishers from Outside")

### History
The Ponape Scripture was discovered on Ponape by Arkham ship master Captain Abner Exekiel Hoag in 1734. Captain Hoag took the book with him to his house in Arkham, Massachusetts, where the text was translated to English by his Ponapean servant, Yogash, a human/Deep One hybrid. (: "The Dweller in the Tomb", "The Fishers from Outside")

Yogash's translation circulated privately for many years among cultists and occultist in the USA, Europe, and Asia. (: "Out of the Ages")

At some point before 1911, both the original and the translation found their way to the Kester Library in Salem, where they were kept "hidden away in the archives", only made available to scholars. (: "The Dweller in the Tomb", "The Fishers from Outside")

The Wilmarth Foundation gathered most of its knowledge about Cthulhu's progeny from the Ponape Scripture and the Zanthu Tablets. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

### Contents
The Ponape Scripture contains the writings of Imash-Mo and other priests of Ghatanothoa who lived in the prehistoric continent of Mu hundreds of millennia ago. It also has information about Zanthu, including the directions to find his tomb, thus suggesting that parts of the text were written after Zanthu's death, over 11,000 years after the time of Imash-Mo. The Scripture condemns Zanthu and blames him for a catastrophic blasphemy that caused the Elder Gods to descend to Earth and destroy the Muvian continent. (: "The Dweller in the Tomb", "The Thing in the Pit")

The Scripture provides information about several Muvian deities, particularly the "Xothic Triad", which consists of Ghatanothoa, Ythogtha, and Zoth-Ommog. According to the Scripture, these three are sons of Cthulhu and Idh-yaa, born in the vicinity of the double star Xoth (: "The Thing in the Pit"). Other deities mentioned include Yig, Mnomquah, and Groth-Golka (: "The Fishers from Outside").

Pond Street is a street in the fictional town of Bolton, Massachusetts and mentioned in the story "Herbert West--Reanimator" by H. P. Lovecraft. After their graduation from the Miskatonic University Medical School and relocation from Arkham, Herbert West and his friend, the unnamed narrator of the story, set themselves up as general practitioners and bought a house on an isolated site at the end of Pond Street. There they built a laboratory in the basement for their continuing experiments involving the reanimation of the dead. 

### Geography
The house on Pond Street was deliberately chosen not only for its relative isolation but also its proximity to a local potter's field that served as a convenient source of bodies for use as test subjects. Separating the house and the potter's field is a stretch of uninhabited meadowland bisected by a narrow neck of the forest which lies to the north. The lack of people in that area meant that the two doctors could retrieve bodies without being observed. (: "Herbert West--Reanimator")

"Portents and Omens" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author John M. McCormick. It was published in Vol 5, Issue 3 of the Lovecraftiana zine by Rogue Planet Press in October 2020.

### Synopsis
A man out foraging in the wooded hills of West Virginia accidentally disturbs a nest of yellowjackets, which causes him to fall down a steep incline. As he lies dying, he is approached by a mysterious stranger who offers him insights into life, death, and the nature of the universe. Before the stranger departs, leaving the man to his fate, he imparts the knowledge that "he that slumbers in the great halls of R'lyeh is beginning to stir once more".

fullContent:
Portrait of Death is an uncredited comic book adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model." It was first published in Horrific #8 in 1953, from Harwell Publications. In a good update of the original story the antagonist of this tale uses movie camera footage on which to base his nightmarish and grotesque paintings. Story and art was by Rudy Palais.

The story is now in the public domain due to copyright having not been renewed.

### Synopsis
A young woman, ace reporter, Pat Carter ("ace girl reporter"), attends the scene of another in a series of unimaginably savage and grisly murders. After a brief conversation with her fiance, police detective Jim Young, she notices a middle aged man carrying a Jack the Ripper style doctor's bag heading to a nearby tenement. She follows the man, with her fiance and his police partner in tow.

The police officers identify the man to Pat as Gilman, a local artist a man considered a harmless crank.

Pat is not so sure and goes back to visit Gilman on her own.

In his studio the walls are covered with grotesque, graphic, bizarre and convincing paintings and sketches. Deranged, Gilman offers with little prompting a complete confession to Pat. He shows her the door to the underground in his apartment. Usually locked, he opens it to allow a monster out. Inducing the monster to drink a tasty but poisonous drink, Gilman then intends to film it with his camera. He explains that he then uses the footage as his model for his outsider artwork.

However, murderous fiend that he is, Gilman intends to feed Pat Carter to the creature at the same time to remove a snooper. Instead, due to the distraction, the creature although it has already drunk poison attacks Gilman and not Pat, allowing Pat to escape just as he fiance and other police arrive. Gilman is destroyed by the dying creature which returns below.

The story is so unbelievable that the authorities reject it, until a special screening is held at which Gilman's footage is shown. No one can argue against what it shows, and the story ends with Pat and her fiance discussing the reality of the horrors below. Her fiance says this new reality is the reason why he will never sleep easy again...

Poseidon is the name of the primary sea-god of Classical Greek mythology, later known to the Romans as Neptune. It has been mentioned in a handful of stories and poems, both those set in the Cthulhu Mythos and as reference to its real-world aspect.

### In Lovecraft's Works
Poseidon was briefly mentioned in "To Greece, 1917," a tribute to the people and mythology of Classical Greece. (: "To Greece, 1917")

Father Neptune once appeared to Thomas Olney, holding a trident and accompanied by scores of tritons and nereids, as well as the primal god Nodens. (: "The Strange High House in the Mist")

### Expanded Mythos Works
According to David Parker, Neptune, Dagon and Cthulhu are all different names for the same entity. (: "Dagon's Bell").

Poseidon is a powerful extragalactic entity, awed by 'Ymnar. It battled against the Elder God Paighon.(source?)

Poseidonis is the fictional last remnant of the lost continent of Atlantis, mentioned by Algernon Blackwood in his novella Sand (published in 1912 in his collection Pan's Garden) and also detailed in a series of short stories by Clark Ashton Smith.

In H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Strange High House in the Mist", the inhabitant of the titular house tells Thomas Olney about "how the pillared and weedy temple of Poseidonis is still glimpsed at midnight by lost ships, who know by its sight that they are lost".

In "The Black Kiss", by Robert Bloch and Henry Kuttner, Dr. Makoto Yamada refers to the Graham Dean's dreams of the oceanic depths inhabited by the sea-dwellers as "visions of Poseidonis".

Smith's Poseidonis series is also connected to his Hyperborean Cycle, with Hyperborea and the Serpent People mentioned in the Poseidonis story "The Double Shadow".

The name Poseidonis is from Late Antiquity, but of uncertain origin when used in connection with Atlantis, having been variously attributed to locations in North Africa, the eastern Mediterranean, the Canary Islands and the Caribbean. In more modern usage in fringe archaeology it has become settled usage for the Caribbean theorized location of one or more islands drowned by the sea rise in the Younger Dryas period approximately 11,600 years ago to 11,800 years ago. 

Smith based Poseidonis on the conceptualization of Atlantis within the Theosophy movement (such as Secret Doctrine by Helena Blavatsky), and his concept of "the last isle of foundering Atlantis" is echoed by the isle of Númenor in J. R. R. Tolkien's legendarium.

Poseidonis is the closest conforming part of the greater Cthulhu Mythos to the mainstream idea of Atlantis as an island continent that sinks as opposed to the repetitive losses by massive flooding of other regions across the last 150,000 years of geological time.

"Potential" is a short story by famed British horror writer Ramsey Campbell set in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. It was published by Arkham House in 1973 in the Campbell collection Demons by Daylight.

### Synopsis
Whilst searching for acceptance, Charles meets a man who introduces him to a secretive cult. The cult convince Charles to commit an unspeakable act, one which transforms Charles himself into the sacrifice necessary to summon forth a dark entity.

### Characters
*Charles, a man looking to belong somewhere.
*Cook, a cult member.
*Smith, the cult's enigmatic leader.

### Mythos Connections
*The story is set in Campbell's fictional Severn Valley setting, specifically Brichester, the backdrop to many of his Mythos-related stories.
*Both H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth are referenced in "Potential" as being the same people as in real life.

Potowonket, Maine is a fictional town created by Howard Phillips Lovecraft and Winifred V. Jackson as the setting for their short story "The Green Meadow".

### Overview
Located somewhere on the east coast of Maine, USA, Potowonket is described as a "small seaside village". On August 27, 1913, a meteorite landed in the waters off its coast. When the meteor was dredged from the ocean, it was found to contain a journal, written in Ancient Greek, that related the astonishing tale of a man adrift in the cosmos.

### Residents
The fishing party that dredges the meteorite from the ocean floor consists of John Richmond, Peter B. Carr, and Simon Canfield; it is Canfield who comments that the object resembles "a piece of slag." The "local scientific authority" is Richmond M. Jones, who identifies it as "an aerolite or meteoric stone"; it's Jones who discovers the manuscript embedded in the "semi-metallic mass," and retains possession of it.

fullContent:
"Prank Call of Cthulu" is the sixth episode of the fourth season of the animated comedy series The Grim Adventures of Billy & Mandy, and pits the protagonists against Cthulhu, whose name is spelled as "Cthulu" without the second "h" in the episode. It first aired on October 21, 2005.

The story was conceived by series creator Maxwell Atoms, along with Alex Almaguer, and Mike Diederich. Almaguer and Diederich did the storyboards, and the episode was directed by Russell Calabrese, Juli Hashiguchi, Eddy Houchins, Robert Hughes, and Sue Perrotto.

### Synopsis
The series' premise is that Billy and Mandy are two children who live in the town of Endsville and have successfully tricked the Grim Reaper into becoming their "friend" or glorified slave. In this episode, Billy wants to send prank calls, but finds that most phones have a caller ID that lets everyone know it's him. Searching in Grim's basement, he finds a mysterious phone, which Grim warns him not to use, as doing so will awaken an ancient monster named Cthulu, who can drive people mad by his mere presence, and who will destroy the world once he awakens from his slumber.

Ignoring the warning, Billy and his friend Irwin try to use the phone to prank call Cthulu, but are grabbed by tentacles that come from inside the phone and transported to the monster's native dimension. Grim thinks the universe is doomed, but Mandy convinces him to go after the boys, so they make a call and find themselves in a world inhabited by eldritch creatures. They soon find that Billy and Irwin have been hired as the new interns at Cthulu's company, where they have already started mutating into tentacled monstrosities. Their job is to make phone calls to the citizens of Endsville, who are likewise turned into monsters by the emanations coming from their phones when they answer them.

While Grim returns to Earth to watch TV, as he doesn't care about the imminent end of the world, Mandy asks Billy and Irwin to take her to Cthulu, who is out playing golf. Using a mirror to avoid looking directly at his madness-inducing visage, Mandy confronts Cthulu, who captures her with his tentacles and tries to eat her. Before he can do so, however, she uses her own phone to call the Phone of Cthulu, which is answered by Grim. She then handles her phone to Cthulu and disconnects the line. Cthulu is sucked inside Mandy's phone and transported to Earth, but Grim smashes the Phone of Cthulu before he can come through, thus trapping the monster between the phone lines with no way to get out.

Freed from Cthulu's influence, everyone who had been transformed reverts to their human forms. However, Billy, Mandy and Irwin realize that they're now trapped in Cthulu's realm with no means to get back. Billy laments that he misses Cthulu and is promptly attacked by an aquatic beast, while Irwin tries to woo Mandy and is rejected. "Priestess of Nycrama" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author John W. Patterson. It was first published in the December 1999 edition of Edward P. Berglund's online fanzine Nightscapes.

### Synopsis
Two explorers, Doctors Howard Phillips and Claude Farnsworth, explore a mysterious plateau in a remote region of Venezuela. During their researches, they are captured by a tribe of Nycrama cultists who send them through a portal to the pocket dimension inhabited by their master. There, they encounter a mysterious young woman named Endura who aids them in returning to their own world and destroying the malevolent creature, though the psychological strain costs one of them his life.

In the aftermath, Endura is revealed to be an alien woman who was planted into Nycrama's dimension with the goal of destroying it for good. The survivor, Farnsworth, travels to the dimension where Endura (whose real name is revealed to be Avrenim) dwells, and the two live in bliss together, while Phillips is reincarnated as none other than Howard Phillips Lovecraft himself.

### Behind the Mythos
In his afterword to the Kindle edition, Patterson dedicates the story to Clark Ashton Smith, H. P. Lovecraft, and H. Beam Piper. He further states that:



### Publication History
Since its debut appearance in Nightscapes, "Priestess of Nycrama" has also been independently published as a digital chapbook through Amazon's digital Kindle platform, with the release having two different covers.

### Trivia
*Virtually every name used in the story has been reused from elsewhere in the Cthulhu Mythos, although  not all of them are used to refer to their more usual subjects.

"Primavera" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. fullContent:
The Prime Reality (a.k.a. Earth-616) is a fictional universe created by Marvel Comics which is inhabited by the Many-Angled Ones and Lovecraftian Elder Gods. It is the setting for most of the comic series published by Marvel Comics, with a few comic series focused on the universe itself (the cosmic character or team series). It has also been the stage of two cosmic horror stories, the Infinity Gauntlet event in 1991 and the Chaos War event in 2010. There were also several other universal level events, such as the Infinity War and the Infinity Crusade.

Within "known space" (the local group of galaxies) there have been various events and crossovers, ranging from those focused on a particular character or team (e.g., the Dark Phoenix Saga, the Brood Saga, the Thanos War, and Emperor Vulcan: The Rise and Fall of the Shi'ar Empire) to the intergalactic wars that altered the region's geopolitics (the Kree-Skrull War, Operation Galactic Storm, the Second Kree-Skrull War, Annihilation, Annihilation: Conquest, War of Kings, The Thanos Imperative, and Infinity).

### Background
The Prime Reality (Earth-616) is the mainstream reality of the Marvel Multiverse that is still expanding and currently contains billions of galaxies. Its existence is occasionally threatened by the super-genius and super-powered Thanos the Mad Titan and sometimes by someone else (e.g., the Lovecraftian entity Dormammu) and on occasion its existence is threatened by an entity or faction from another reality. In this reality, during the late 20th century and so far in the early part of the 21st century, it is usually someone from Earth or an alien who favors Earth, who saves the universe or "known space". Most of the time it is either the Silver Surfer, the Fantastic Four, the Avengers, or the X-Men (the latter three being from Earth).

### Lovecraftian Cosmic Entities
The Old Ones have representation within the Prime Reality, either themselves or their minions. On occasion, those existing outside of the various universes (e.g., Shuma-Gorath and Slorioth) will manifest in the Prime Reality, though because of how incomprehensibly vast is their power, it is usually only the tiniest infinitesimal fragment of their being.

In the Prime Reality are various eldritch entities which are not one of the Many-Angled Ones, but in their own way pose just as great a threat to the cosmos whom spread their corruption, or attempt its conquest or, worse, its destruction. Among their ranks are Dormammu, Knull the Abyss, Glory, the Dragon of the Moon, the Chaos King, and Null the Living Darkness:

He has conquered many dimensions and is obsessed with conquering the Prime Reality due to his many defeats at the hands of Doctor Strange. The Primitive Snouter is a fictional species of small mammals created by Gerolf Steiner for his 1961 book The Snouters: Form and Life of the Rhinogrades. It has been incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, which identifies it as an ancestor of the Buopoth.

### Description
Primitive Snouters are, as their name indicates, the most basal members of the order of mammals known as the snouters, a.k.a. Rhinogradentia, which inhabited the Hy-yi-yi islands before their sinking. They are named for their extraordinary well-developed snouts. The Primitive Snouter is a mouse-sized forest animal which can balance itself on its snout while feasting on its favorite food: cockroaches. (: The Snouters)

Although once thought to be extinct, Primitive Snouter populations have been discovered to be alive and well in the Dreamlands, where they can be found along the trade routes to Mhor. They are known for their curious disposition and propensity to steal objects from distracted travelers. (: H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands)

Professor Bradley is a fictional character who appears in "The Green Meadow", a story written by H. P. Lovecraft based on a dream by Winifred V. Jackson. He is an academic from Columbia College. 

In the story, Bradley is an expert who studies a metallic rocklike object that lands off the coast of Potowonket, Maine, in the evening hours of Wednesday, August 27, 1913, and brought to shore four days later by a fishing crew. While Boston's  Dr. Richard M. Jones and Professor Mayfield of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology hold that it is a meteorite, and Dr. von Winterfeldt of Heidelberg maintains that it is not a meteorite, Bradley "adopts a less dogmatic ground," pointing out that as the object contains large quantities of utterly unknown ingredients, no classification is not yet possible. (: The Green Meadow)

### Behind the Mythos
Columbia College was the name of Columbia University, located in New York City, until 1896; it continues to be the name of one of Columbia's undergraduate schools.

fullContent:
"Professor Peabody's Last Lecture" is a horror comedy television sketch set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It is the final segment of the eighth episode of Season 2 of Rod Serling's anthology show Night Gallery, and aired for the first time on November 10, 1971. The sketch was written by series producer Jack Laird, directed by Jerrold Freedman, and stars Carl Reiner as the titular ill-starred academic.

### Synopsis
A professor of comparative religion gives a lecture on an ancient belief system centered around the Great Old Ones, who supposedly ruled the Earth before mankind. Far from taking the subject seriously, the professor repeatedly comments on how absurd and preposterous the cult of the Old Ones is, and makes several jokes about the deities. When a student points out that mentioning Hastur by name is a taboo, the lecturer dismisses his concerns and speaks the unspeakable's name aloud several more times.

At this point, a storm brews in the summer sky outside. The professor grows visibly nervous, but tries to hide it while continuing to make jokes. Finally, he produces a rare copy of the forbidden Necronomicon that he got from Miskatonic University and starts reading it, casually dismissing the book's warning about the "ghastly consequences". The storm rages while the professor continues to read the book aloud, until he is finally transformed into a monstrous creature before the shocked eyes of his students.

### Behind the Mythos
According to Prof. Peabody, the Great Old Ones include Nyarlathotep, 'Umr at-Tawil, Hastur, Cthulhu, Azathoth, Shub-Niggurath, and Yog-Sothoth. He mentions that their cult has been active as recently as 50 years ago in Arkham, Massachusetts.

The three students who ask questions during the lecture are named Mr. Bloch, Mr. Derleth, and Mr. Lovecraft, after seminal Mythos contributors Robert Bloch, August Derleth and H. P. Lovecraft. Fittingly, Mr. Derleth is the one who points out that Hastur's name should not be spoken, as it was the real Derleth who came up with the deity's epithet "the Unspeakable". Also fittingly, Mr. Lovecraft is the one who asks questions about the Necronomicon, as the grimoire was Lovecraft's creation in real life. The end credits reveal that another student is named Miss Heald, after Lovecraft's frequent collaborator Hazel Heald.

### Trivia
*"Professor Peabody's Last Lecture" was the only original Mythos story featured in Night Gallery, but not the only Mythos story overall, as the series also featured adaptations of "Cool Air", "Pickman's Model" and "The Return of the Sorcerer".

The Progeny of Yig, a.k.a. Spawn of Yig, are half-human, half-snake hybrid creatures that result from the curse of the snake-god Yig: either the humans turned into snakes for offending Yig, or else the offspring of such humans.

The child of Audrey Davis is the one such creature seen in "The Curse of Yig". Davis actually gave birth to four hydrid children, but only one survived into adulthood. Thirty-five years later, the doctor who cared for Davis' daughter claimed that she "doesn't seem to age", and believed that she would outlive all of her caretakers. This suggests that the Progeny of Yig might be very long-lived, even if some individuals die young.

### Description
The Progeny of Yig are humans who, as a result of a curse invoked by disturbing a Child of Yig, begin to develop snake-like features. They then lay eggs that birth hairless humans with beady black eyes.

"Prom Night, or Whateley Family Happiness" is a tongue-in-cheek Cthulhu Mythos story by author G. Large. It was published in the Lammas Eve edition of the Lovecraftiana zine by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
Told in the style of a frenetic sitcom episode, amidst the chaos of everyday life on the farm, young Eliza Whateley tries to get ready for her mystery prom date while trying to keep her clan quiet so as not to make a bad impression. The hazards include: constantly-growing brother Wilbur desperate to kill his mother Lavinia - a harlot intent on engaging in congress with Yog-Sothoth and his friends; a grandfather slowly losing his sanity and reciting passages from Favourite Sayings from the Necronomicon; younger brother Little Peaslee, a boy intent on declaring war on the Yithians who have inhabited the bodies of the neighbours; and the antics of H. W., another brother who spends his days in the basement tinkering with corpses. 

When finally Eliza's date does arrive, he is revealed to be Bob the Shoggoth, a lecherous creature intent on carnal relations with the girl.

Proto-Shoggoths are a subspecies of shoggoth.

### Origin
There is a theory that the Elder Things created life on Earth using the proto-shoggoths. However, according to the Book of Eibon, it was Ubbo-Sathla who created only terrestrial life. It is possible that the explanation for this inconsistency is that the proto-shoggoth was created using genetic material obtained from the plasma remains that Ubbo-Sathla left on the surface. Therefore, the proto-shoggoths would have arisen from Ubbo-Sathla and subsequently all life would have arisen as a result.

### Modern recreation
In "The Asylum", a Call of Cthulhu scenario included in the supplement The Asylum & Other Tales, Dr. Terence Freygan began creating an army of proto-shoggoths after studying a Greek copy of the Pnakotic Manuscripts in hand from a local cult of the Silent Shouter on the Hill and having studied the case of Jeffry Quarren, a boy abducted by the Great Race of Yith who maintained a mind of these beings. Since then, truck fleets have approached the Greenwood Asylum, the doctor's workplace. And, some time later, there were a series of deaths around the madhouse. The reason behind these events is that Freygan, using the manuscripts and a laboratory built in the building, began to transform human tissue into proto-shoggoth fabric using a catalyst in the asylum patients. These attempts resulted in the death of the patients, but subsequent attempts maintained the brain, which spread throughout the body. The doctor came to use himself as a guinea pig successfully, but he still seeks to refine the process to turn the cultists and the nearby village inhabitants into an army of these protoplasmic beings using a series of medications alongside the use of the catalyst.

### Characteristics
NOTE: taken in part from Dr. Freygan's description according to "The Asylum".



In combat, in addition to body movements (such as punches, firearms, prey...), they can use a crush move. Unlike true shoggoths, they can only attack one human victim at a time until death by crush or absorption.

Providence is a twelve-issue comic book limited series, written by Alan Moore and illustrated by Jacen Burrows, published by Avatar Press. It is set in the same continuity as the "The Courtyard" and the 4-issue Neonomicon series, both also written by Moore. 

The premise of Providence is that Lovecraft's stories are loosely based on the experiences of Robert Black, a queer Jewish journalist who is exploring New England in hopes of garnering material for a novel based on occult outsiders. This conceit allows Moore to rework Lovecraft's familiar fictions in his own unique style.

"Providence" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Written on 26 September 1924 , it was first published in The Brooklynite in November of the same year .

### Synopsis
Consisting of thirteen four-line verses, "Providence" conveys Lovecraft’s appreciation of the city of Providence, Rhode Island, his home town which held a special place in his heart, concluding with the lines " For thou art of the soul of me, And always at my side!"

fullContent:
The Providence Pals were a group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts who shared their mutual interest during the latter part of the 20th century. They were so named for their periodical meetings in Providence, Rhode Island. The group was formed by the members to allow them visit and re-visit sites related to Lovecraft's life and works in like-minded company.

Robert M. Price, in his introduction to the Michaelmas 1985 edition of Crypt of Cthulhu names the Pals as Marc A. Michaud, S. T. Joshi, Jason Eckhardt, Donald R. Burleson, Peter H. Cannon, Mollie Werba, himself, Ken Neily, and Sam Gafford, although his wording suggests that there may have been more whom he did not list. In the back cover text for his 2015 collection Providence Pals: Memories and Miscellany, Sam Gafford adds the names of Steven J. Mariconda, Will Murray, and Robert H. Knox.

Price states the group coalesced in the late 1970s, with Gafford stating that he was invited to come to Providence in 1982, when he joined .

fullContent:
Providence Pals: Memories and Miscellany is a selected collection of the works of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s. Edited by Sam Gafford, who was a member of the Pals from 1982 onwards, and featuring cover art by Jason C. Eckhardt, another member, it was published by Ulthar Press in July 2015.

Gafford states in his introduction that he "spread the word far and wide and asked for a contribution from each [of the Pals] and, when possible, a short memorial of the group and what it meant to them. What follows are their memories and also some samples of the fine work that each have done in this field."

Providence is H. P. Lovecraft's home town and is the capital and the most populous city of the U.S. state of Rhode Island, and one of the first cities established in the United States. Located in Providence County, it is the estimated third-largest city in the New England region.

The area which is now Providence was first settled in June 1636 by Roger Williams, and was one of the original Thirteen Colonies of the United States.

So strongly did Lovecraft himself identify with the place of his birth that he even stated,I am Providence, & Providence is myself—together, indissolubly as one, we stand   thro’ the ages; a fixt monument set aeternally in the shadow of Durfee’s ice-clad   peak!

(Letter to James Ferdinand Morton, 16 May 1926)As with Salem and Arkham, Providence and its locale served as inspiration for various locations in his stories. It was also the direct inspiration for its eponymous poem, "Providence" written by Lovecraft in 1924.

"Providence: Two Gentlemen Meet at Midnight" is a short Cthulhu Mythos poem by the late American author and friend of Lovecraft, August Derleth. It was first published in the Autumn 1948 edition of defunct magazine The Arkham Sampler.

### Synopsis
The piece is written as a conversation between two men, H.P.L. and E.A.P., as they discuss the city of Providence, Rhode Island.

### Behind the Mythos
The poem would seem to have inspired at least the germ of a story in Derleth, one which may have gone on to be developed in his "posthumous collaboration" "The Dark Brotherhood".

The character H.P.L. mentions the entities Dagon, Yog-Sothoth, and Cthulhu when discussing the evils which have befallen the world.

*Something About Cats and Other Pieces (1949)
*The Man Who Called Himself Poe (1969)
*In Lovecraft's Shadow: The Cthulhu Mythos Stories of August Derleth (1998)

PS Publishing is a World Fantasy Award-winning small press founded by Peter Crowther in 1999 and based in the United Kingdom. Specialising in novella-length works, as well as a number of anthologies and collections, it publishes horror, science fiction, and fantasy works in collectible editions, many of which are offered as signed copies upon their initial release.

PS has issued a number of Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos publications, including the Black Wings anthologies, and the Lovecraft Illustrated series, which reprints H. P. Lovecraft stories along with new artwork and a selection of related short stories and/or non-fiction.

### Selected Publications

### Lovecraft Illustrated
*The Dunwich Horror (2014)
*The Shadow Out of Time (2015)
*The Shadow Over Innsmouth (2015)

### Black Wings
*Black Wings (2010)
*Black Wings II (2012)
*Black Wings III (2014)
*Black Wings IV (2015)
*Black Wings V (2016)
*Black Wings VI (2017)

### Anthologies
*The Starry Wisdom Library (2014)
*Innsmouth Nightmares (2015)
*That Is Not Dead (2015)
*Through a Mythos Darkly (2017)
*Tales from the Miskatonic University Library (2017)
*Mountains of Madness Revealed (2019)
*New Maps of Dream (2021)
*Cold War Cthulhu (2025)

### Collections
*The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants (2011, Ramsey Campbell)
*The Dulwich Horror & Others (2015, David Hambling)
*Dark Gods (2021, T. E. D. Klein)

### Novels
*The Darkest Part of the Woods (2003, Ramsey Campbell)
*The Ceremonies (2016, T. E. D. Klein)

Psuchawrl is a fictional character created by Charles R. Tanner for his 1941 Cthulhu Mythos short story "Out of the Jar".

### Description
One of the alien Jinn who came to the Earth in prehistory, Psuchawrl cannot be killed by humans, but was instead imprisoned in a jar by King Solomon, and can only be freed by breaking the jar's seal. Their physical appearance is that of a 9 ft tall humanoid with an eyeless sea anemone-like face, a beaked grinning mouth, and a pronounced ridge running from the forehead to the nape of the neck. (: "Out of the Jar")

Psycho Re-Animated is a very short film which blends Alfred Hitchcock's acclaimed psychological horror Psycho (based on the novel by Robert Bloch) with Stuart Gordon's comedy-horror Re-Animator (which took its inspiration from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "Herbert West--Reanimator").

### Synopsis
The film contains no real plot, consisting of scenes recreated from Psycho to the backdrop of audio taken from Re-Animator.

### Behind the Scenes
Directed by Abner Pastoll, Psycho Re-Animated was released in the United Kingdom on 23 January 2021. Running to a total of only 2 minutes, it stars Barbara Crampton and Bruce Abbot, who played two of the three lead characters in Re-Animator. Pastoll has provided the film free to view on both YouTube and Vimeo.

shortDefinition: "Psychopompos: A Tale in Rhyme" is a narrative poem by H. P. Lovecraft. Originally published in 1919, in The Vagrant, it appeared again in the September 1937 issue of Weird Tales and was reprinted in several collections of Lovecraft.  ### Synopsis Se...
fullContent:
"Psychopompos: A Tale in Rhyme" is a narrative poem by H. P. Lovecraft. Originally published in 1919, in The Vagrant, it appeared again in the September 1937 issue of Weird Tales and was reprinted in several collections of Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Set in medieval Auvergne (the same setting that inspired Clark Ashton Smith's Averoigne), the poem tells of the reclusive Sieur De Blois, and his equally secretive wife, both of whom are feared by the villagers, who whisper about their evil deeds and the fact that they never attend church. At some points, the narrator seems to doubt the veracity of these rumours, reminding themself that people who tell them aren't particularly trustworthy.

On Candlemas Eve, the Dame De Blois stops by the bailiff's house and smiles in a sinister way when she sees the bailiff's young son, Jean. The next day, the healthy child inexplicably falls ill and dies. That night, a snowstorm rages, and the bailiff's wife sees a large reptilian beast crawling towards her son's coffin. She uses an axe to strike the monster's head and watches it escape into the night.

Over the next weeks, the villagers whisper about how agitated the Sieur De Blois seems to be. The misanthrope is uncharacteristically eager to hear about the incident in the bailiff's house, and disappears for days after learning of it. They also notice that the Dame De Blois hasn't been seen at all since the incident.

When the snows melt at spring, the body of the Dame De Blois is discovered, with her skull split open. When the body is brought to her husband, he reacts with anger and his servants with fear, but no one in the house shows surprise.

On the next Candlemas, another storm rages, and the village is invaded by a pack of wolves headed directly towards the bailiff's cottage. The wolf leader seizes the bailiff's wife, but the bailiff strikes the beast with an axe and rescues her. As the other wolves approach the couple menacingly, the house is destroyed by the storm, but the chimney and hearth remain intact, including the Lord's image and the cross. At the sight of this holy shrine, the supernatural wolves vanish and the storm dissipates.

The last two stanzas reveal that the story is being told by an old lady to her guest, who asks her what the Sieur De Blois had to do with the wolves. The old lady reveals that, from the track of blood left by the wounded wolf leader, the villagers concluded that it had perished in the quicksand swamp. The Sieur De Blois is never seen again, and his dog is seen howling in mourning on the same swamp.

Ptar-Axtlan (also spelled Ptar-Aztlan) is a fictional entity created by Gerald W. Page for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "Confession in Darkness".

### Description
Known as the Leopard That Stalks the Night, Ptar-Axtlan is a mysterious entity associated with cats. Like Cthulhu and other similar beings, Ptar-Axtlan can grant gifts of immortality and eternal youth to its followers. However, while Cthulhu's followers assume the traits of fish, Ptar-Axtlan's have a more feline appearance. Even a sadistic practitioner of the dark arts shuddered to think about what an entity like Ptar-Axtlan might ask in return for its gifts of unaging beauty. (: "Confession in Darkness")

fullContent:
Ptmâk is reported in an antehuman text to be the "immediate" parent of Cthulhu (Kthulhut) and his race (the Cosmic Octopi). It appears to have remained dwelling of Vhoorl and is thus quite obscure. Probably another name for Nug.

### Behind the Mythos
Ptmâk was created by Clark Ashton Smith in letters to R. H. Barlow. Lin Carter attempted to incorporate some of the information into his work.

The letter is written ambiguously about who is a child of Nug: "The immediate parent of Cthulhu and his race (child of Nug) was Ptmâk". Comparing Smith's letter with his and Lovecraft's Family trees of Azathoth suggests that Ptmâk and Cxaxukluth are the Hyperborean versions of Nug and Yeb.

### References

fullContent:
Pulptime is a historical mystery novella by Peter Cannon published by Weirdbook Press in 1984, with illustrations by Stephen Fabian. Set in 1925, it features the detective Sherlock Holmes joining forces with weird fiction writers H. P. Lovecraft and Frank Belknap Long, with the latter acting as the story's first person narrator. It also features the other members of the Kalem Club in supporting roles.

### Synopsis
In New York, 1925, young author Frank Belknap Long receives a phone call from his friend and literary mentor, H. P. Lovecraft, who has just came back from a trip to Washington, DC. Returning home after dining in an Italian restaurant, the two arrive at Lovecraft's boarding house to witness a new tenant, an elderly man named Altamont, being assaulted by ruffians. The two friends rush to help the gentlemen, who reveals his real identity while he recovers from his injuries. Altamont, it turns out, is actually the renowned British detective Sherlock Holmes, in a secret mission to America. Furthermore, his presence in Lovecraft's boarding house is not a coincidence. In fact, Lovecraft was recommended to Holmes by their mutual friend, magician and escape artist Harry Houdini. Holmes needs a guide to navigate the less reputable districts of the city and is willing to hire both Lovecraft and Long for the job, which the two eagerly accept.

The next day, following breakfast at Long's house, the three men meet up with Houdini, who briefs Lovecraft and Long on their mission. A wealthy bootlegger and smuggler of illegal migrants named Jan Martense has recently visited England, where he stole documents that could compromise an illustrious individual, whose identity cannot be revealed. Holmes and Houdini have strong reasons to believe that Martense has been sponsoring the career of celebrated spirit medium Cordelia Garrison, who Houdini wishes to debunk.

Over the next week, Holmes disguises himself as a deliveryman and befriends Martense's cook, which gives him and Lovecraft the opportunity to search the criminal's mansion, to no avail. One Wednesday night, Holmes uses his "Mr. Altamont" alias again to attend a meeting of the Kalem Club at Long's place. Later on, a visit to Martense's speakeasy proves fruitful when a chance encounter with poet Hart Crane accidentally leads to a bar brawl that serves as the distraction Holmes needed to steal a paper from Martense containing the schedule of ships due to bring in illegal migrants to Red Hook.

Two weeks pass by before Holmes, now disguised as a gentleman who lost his son in World War One, manages to arrange a séance with Cordelia Garrison, during which he uncovers (but keeps quiet about) her method of deception. Now with enough leverage to use against Martense, Holmes, Lovecraft and Long sneak into the subterranean tunnels where they witness illegal migrants being smuggled into the country, to confront the man himself, while the other members of the Kalem Club keep guard outside. Pulse Pounders is a 1988 horror anthology B-movie from American director Charles Band. One of the segments is an adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft short story "The Evil Clergyman".

### Overview
Intended for release in 1988, Pulse Pounders was believed lost after the collapse of distributor Empire Pictures. A copy was recovered in 2011: this was digitally restored and "The Evil Clergyman" received a world premiere at the Chicago Flashback Weekend. It stars screen Mythos regulars Jeffrey Combs, Barbara Crampton, and David Warner.

Paxton, whose inhabitants almost universally refer to it as Punktown, is a fictional metropolis created by American author Jeffrey Thomas as the setting for a series of dystopian science fiction stories of the same name. Making its first appearance in "The Reflections of Ghosts" in 1995, a number of other authors have since expanded upon its background and culture.

Although not initially created as a setting for Cthulhu Mythos fiction, in the years since its inception Punktown has played host to a number of stories both Lovecraftian and Mythos-related, and has even received its own setting book for Chaosium's  Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
The city of Paxton, or Punktown as it is more commonly referred to, is located on an alien planet named Oasis and is one of the group known as the Earth Colonies. Home to both high technology and savage barbarism, it is a large urban and commercial sprawl, the host to all types of lifestyles, from corporate business to rampant street thuggery.

### Species
As noted above, Punktown plays host to a number of alien species from across the galaxy, some of whom even maintain their own embassies. A selection of these is listed below.


*Choom, a humanoid species native to Punktown's planet, the Choom have wide mouths which extend all the way back to their ears. Some members of this species run in violent street gangs.
* Ogim, an insectile species from Yuggoth who disguise themselves as tall, cloaked humans, hiding their true appearance using synthetic hands and faces. Although they do not appear to maintain a permanent presence in Punktown, they have been known to visit in order to engage the services of Augmentation Concepts (: "Open Minded").
*L'lewed, a "putty-like extradimensional race" which were confined to small life-support containers transported by human helpers before receiving mechanical humanoid bodies from Augmentation Concepts. Looking down on humanity, and humanoids in general, several L'lewed have been deported from Punktown for practicing blood sacrifice as part of religious rituals (: "Open Minded").
*Mee'hi, another insectile species described as being "small as termites", the Mee'hi were similarly provided with mechanical armatures by Augmentation Concepts. They share the same disdain for humanoid beings as the L'lewed, and have also had several members deported for criminal activity, in this instance the parasitising of human hosts (: "Open Minded").
*Tikkihottos, another humanoid species, the Tikkihotos have nests of sea anemone-like feelers in place of eyes; these organs grant them enhanced vision.
*Kalians, a species of patriarchal humanoids with glossy grey skin and jet black eyes which are otherwise very similar in appearance to humans. Originating on the planet Kali, certain extremist sects are known to worship the ancient, powerful, and malevolent entity Ugghiutu.

fullContent:
Punktown: A Setting Book for Call of Cthulhu and Basic Roleplaying is a setting supplement designed for use with Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu and Basic Roleplaying game systems. It was published under license by Chronicle City in 2018.

### Overview


Primarily a setting supplement containing information describing how to play games in Jeffrey Thomas's dystopian Punktown milieu, Punktown also contains three ready-to play scenarios and a pair of short stories by Thomas set in his fictional universe. It was designed by Mike Tresca, Glynn Owen Barrass, and Brian M. Sammons, and runs to a total of 148 pages in both paperback and digital formats.

Punktown appears to have suffered setbacks in its release, having been first announced as part of a Miskatonic River Press Kickstarter campaign in November 2012, with publication delayed by the closure of the press in 2014. However, Miskatonic seems to have retained the licensing for Punktown, and Chronicle City took up the completion of the project, finally bringing the book to publication in 2018.

Pursuit to Kadath is a third-party scenario sourcebook for Chaosium's Mythos roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu.

### Overview
Published by Theatre of the Mind, usually refered to as T.O.M.E., under licence from Chaosium in 1983, Pursuit to Kadath was written by Bob Gallagher and E. S. Erkes with cover art supplied by Lawrence L. Flournoy. It ran to a total of 71 pages and contained two self-contained but linked scenarios.

### Synopsis

### Pursuit to Kadath
The primary scenario, the titular Pursuit to Kadath, involves a group of Miskatonic University students who are part of a paranormal-interest group named the Sunday Club. The group must travel to New York, Boston, Europe and Turkey in their search for a missing friend.

### "The All-Seeing Eye of the Alskali"
This second, far smaller, scenario is designed to break up the main adventure, although it can also be played as a stand-alone game with the correct setup. It deals with an encounter with the inhuman Alskali while investigating the disappearance of an archaeologist in Turkey.

"Pushing Back" is a Lovecraftian horror flash fiction piece by author J. C. Hemphill.

### Synopsis
The story follows a detective and his interrogation of a man found covered in blood next to the body of his friend. As the interview progresses, it becomes apparent that the man has become infected by whatever entity killed his friend.

### Characters
* Sikowitz, a man whose body has become host to a horrifying parasite.
* The Detective, a law-enforcement officer.

### Publication History
"Pushing Back" was published in the H. P. Lovecraft-inspired anthology Whispers from the Abyss in 2013.

Q'yth-az (also known as The Crystalloid Intellect) is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Scott David Aniolowski for his short story "An Early Frost", and was later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Ye Booke of Monstres)

### Background
Q'yth-Az is a Great Old One that lives on a lightless world known as Mthura. It's a stationary entity that extends and absorbs with frost-like tentacles. Anything living that is touched by the crystalline tendrils is transformed into formations of solid minerals. By generating large clusters of sharp, heavy minerals and crystals it crushes victims.

It is able to project its thoughts and influences across the cosmos via mineral formations. Humans that are psychically sensitive who come into contact with crystal formations can pick up its projected thoughts, its influence often manifesting in dreams.

The Qlippoths are a Lovecraftian-like race of chaotic beings in the fictional universe of the Pathfinder pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Paizo Inc.

### Background
The Qlippoths are an eldritch race of monstrous beings, whose sub-species come in a variety of forms with tentacles and fangs. Before there were demons, the Qlippoth ruled the Abyss. When they became aware of the Great Beyond (the material universe) they surged forth, doing battle with the Proteans (serpentine chaotic beings) which gave time for the establishment of order in the Great Beyond and the creation of other dimensions. When portals would open to the Abyss, they would swarm out and prey on all.

They would eventually lose their control of the Abyss to the demons, who though weaker vastly outnumbered them. The Qlippoth were almost exterminated and were driven into deeper planes. Qlippoths are currently a pale shadow of what they once were, the Qlippoth Lords haven been reduced in power to the level of a new demon lord (though there may still be a few in the depths of the Abyss with the powers of demigods). The Qlippoth have one goal, to regain control of the Abyss, exterminate the demons, and wipe out all mortals who can sin as they are the foodstuff of demons.

Quachil Uttaus (The Treader of the Dust) is a fictional entity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Treader of the Dust". The character was later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Background
Quachil Uttaus is a Great Old One who can reduce all living tissue he comes into contact with to dust (and is therefore similar to another of Smith's characters, Ubbo-Sathla). Quachil Uttaus is usually associated with age, death, and decay. Summoning this god is considered lethal, if one even subconsciously entertains thoughts of suicide.

It is noted for the acceleration of time that occurs in its presence. Appears as a mummified humanoid with withered, bone-thin arms and unnatural, ever-grasping hands. Also known as "The Ultimate Corruption". It may have been known in ancient Egypt as Ka-Rath, "The Keeper of the Dust".

### In Other Media
*In the light novel series Ultimate Antihero, Quachil Uttaus is one of the Evil Gods that Homura Kamishiro has the ability to summon. It has the power of time acceleration, which can be used to increase the speed of an entire army by making them move ten times faster.
*In the mobile game Yurudora, Quachil Uttaus appears during the Cthulhu Festival event.
*The survival horror game That's Not My Neighbor features a character named after Quachil Uttaus.

The Queen of Clubs is a character in the fictional Grimm Fairy Tales pastiche universe, who first appeared in 2013 in issue #13 of the 1st volume of Wonderland. The character was created by Patrick Shand & Raven Gregory. Despite the name of her home universe, the character is inspired by characters from the Alice's Adventures in Wonderland and Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There books by Lewis Carroll, and not the fairy tales compiled by the Brothers Grimm.

### Background
The origins of the Queen of Clubs is unknown. The Queen of Clubs and the Queen of Diamonds are lovers, and enemies of the Queen of Spades. After their most recent battle with her, they finally became free of Wonderland, retreating to Los Angeles, California.

The Queen of Hearts was created by Lewis Carroll in 1865, first appearing in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. In 2008, the character was reimagined for Zenescope Entertainment's Grimm Fairy Tales fictional universe, in the issue #0 of the 1st volume of Grimm Fairy Tales: Return to Wonderland.

### Background
In 1860, two sisters went to the Allen family home to visit their friend William, a boy they had a crush on. Playing a game of hide and seek, the two sisters got into a quarrel and accidentally fell through the Mirror to Wonderland. Frightened by the Jabberwocky, they clung to each other. Their bond of love was so strong that Wonderland was unable to break it, but it was able to twist their love, physically fusing them into one being: the Queen of Hearts.

The Queen of Hearts bears two equally insane and incredibly emotionally volatile halves (upper and beautiful and lower and ugly), and has a murderous temper. She sentences anyone who offends her to viciously sadistic deaths. Considering herself the Queen of Wonderland, she answers only to the Jabberwocky.

The Queen of Spades is a character in the fictional Grimm Fairy Tales universe, who first appeared in 2010 in Tales from Wonderland: The White Knight. The character was created by Raven Gregory, Troy Brownfield, Ralph Tedesco, and Joe Brusha.

### Background
Alone in the Realm of Dreams, the Jabberwocky desired companionship. He took down a sky whale, and ate the sacred, ancient entity. Its death shook the foundations of the realm, resulting in the birth of a new entity, the Queen of Spades which emerged from the Jabberwocky's shadow. An entity who controlled the shadows and desires to conquer all of Wonderland, the Queen of Spades has displayed both good and evil tendencies.

"Queen of the Vultures" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mark McLaughlin.

### Synopsis
A resident of the Dreamlands, tiring of his immortality, travels to the waking world where he retrieves the Queen of the Vultures, a forgotten god who he hopes can resolve his predicament. As it happens, the ability to turn his own flesh into that of a rotting corpse proves to be a particularly appealing one to the hungry Queen.

### Characters
*Gilles, a powerful magician who wishes to end his existence.
*Miss Thurin/The Queen of the Vultures, an unworshipped deity living a amnesiac existence in the waking world.
*Ignezzo Roman, a necromancer and Gilles' friend.

### Publication History
"Queen of the Vultures" was published in the collection The House of the Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares in 2019.

Quetzalcoatl is a deity in Aztec beliefs. It is a very inspirational and popular figure in Aztec religion and literature.

The name Quetzalcoatl is formed from two Aztec language (Nahuatl) words, quetzalli, "tail feather of the quetzal bird" and coatl, "snake", creating the compound word Feathered Serpent.

Quetzalcoatl was a major god and usually considered a benevolent one sympathetic to humans. He was one of the major deities of the ancient Mexican pantheon. Originally, Quetzalcóatl seems to have been conceived as a vegetation god, allied with the rain god Tlaloc.

In the Cthulhu Mythos, "Quetzalcoatl" is considered to be another name for Yig.

Quoggoth is a fictional entity created by Marvel Comics for the 2009 comic book Wolverine: First Class #12 "The Substitute".

### History
Quoggoth was created by Shuma-Gorath, lord of the Old Ones himself. Quoggoth served his creator for aeons, until hundreds of millions of years later, he perceived himself to be more powerful than his lord and rebelled against Shuma-Gorath. Although he was unable to destroy his rebellious disciple, Shuma-Gorath imprisoned him within a sunken sepulchre.

Millions of years later, the island upon which the sepulchre was located was brought up to the ocean's surface and used by Magneto as his base, until his defeat at the hands of the X-Men. When they found themselves stranded on the island, Quoggoth brought Cyclops and Shadowcat to the sepulchre. He attempted to make a deal with Shadowcat to get them to release him from his prison but failed to convince Cyclops. They fled and tried to escape, battling the pursuing spawn generated by Quoggoth. Neither Cyclops's optical blasts nor Shadowcat's phasing powers were able to get through the doors that were covered by mystic sigils. Wolverine heard their screams from the other side of the door, and freed them with his claws by prying off the crystal seal. Quoggoth attempted to follow after them but Cyclops managed to close the doors in time with his optic beams as Wolverine put the crystal seal back in place, thereby once again imprisoning Quoggoth.

### Powers and Abilities
Not even a telepath of Xavier's power was able to sense him, despite being on the same island. Quoggoth was able to produce spawn from its form, which varied from winged bat-like creatures to one that looked like a little human girl. It's touch was able to shock and stun Shadowcat and it could elongate its tentacles to great lengths. Blasts from Cyclops were unable to wound, much less destroy its tentacles. Considering the fact that Shuma-Gorath's power is such that it's aura-pressure alone could destroy multiple galaxies and it could even destroy a universe with it's most powerful blast, and yet could not destroy Quoggoth only imprison it, Quoggoth must be a cosmic and perhaps even a multiversal threat.

### Behind the Mythos
Quoggoth was seemingly inspired by the Shoggoths, regarding his name, appearance and origin: a servant formed as a mass of eyes and tentacles, created by an Old One, and who later rebelled.

Quumyagga is a fictional monster created by Lin Carter for his Cthulhu Mythos fiction. The first and oldest member of the Shantak species, it is the leader of all the Shantaks who serve Groth-Golka. As such, Quumyagga is considered the prototype of the race and one of the Lesser Old Ones. (: "The Descent into the Abyss", "The Fishers from Outside", "The Horror in the Gallery")

### Description
Quumyagga is a giant bird-like creature covered in both feathers and scales, with a single eye and a single leg, as well as a hooked beak. (: "The Descent into the Abyss")

According to the Book of Eibon, Quumyagga dwells either in the high peaks of the Plateau of Leng or in the chasm beneath Mount Antarktos. (: "The Fishers from Outside")

### Behind the Mythos
The original versions of the stories that mention Quumyagga claim that it is a servant of Gol-goroth, but this was later changed to Groth-Golka. Carter always intended it to be Groth-Golka, but confused the name of the two deities due to the fact that both were featured in "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth", by Robert E. Howard.

Quyagen is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Crispin Burnham and E. P. Berglund for their short story "The Thing in the Library".

### Description
Quyagen is the god of Yagothoggua, mentioned in The Black Book of the Skull, which takes the form of an enormous shadowy, horned creature with a mass of tentacles. The god is served by the Y'nathogguans and is worshipped by blood sacrfices, most famously through the "brides of Quyagen". It used the Eye of Zysl'm against the Great Race of Yith until it was imprisoned under the temple at Yagothoggua. It might be related to Othuyeg.

shortDefinition: Robert Hayward Barlow (May 18, 1918 – January 1 or 2, 1951) was an American author, avant-garde poet, anthropologist and historian of early Mexico, and expert in the Nahuatl language. He was a correspondent and friend of horror writer H. P. Lovecraft...
fullContent:
Robert Hayward Barlow (May 18, 1918 – January 1 or 2, 1951) was an American author, avant-garde poet, anthropologist and historian of early Mexico, and expert in the Nahuatl language. He was a correspondent and friend of horror writer H. P. Lovecraft, and was appointed by Lovecraft the executor of his literary estate.

Born at a time when his father, Lieutenant Colonel Everett Darius Barlow, was serving with the American Forces in France, Barlow spent much of his youth at Fort Benning, Georgia, where his father was stationed. Around 1932, Col. Barlow received a medical discharge and settled his wife (Sarah Barlow) and son in the small town of DeLand, Florida. Family difficulties later forced Robert H. Barlow to move to Washington, D.C., and Kansas. He received training at the Kansas City Art Institute, and subsequently at San Francisco Junior College. 

He went to Mexico in 1940-41, studied at the Escuela Nacional de Ciencias Biologicas, and upon his return to California received the B.A. degree at the University of California in 1942. Returning to Mexico as a permanent resident, he joined the staff of the Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico. In 1944, he received a Rockefeller Foundation Fellowship, and in 1946-48 a Guggenheim Fellowship. He became head of the Department of Anthropology at Mexico City College, a position he held at the time of his death by suicide on January 2, 1951.

According to fellow anthropologist Charles E. Dibble, "In the brief span of a decade, Barlow gave Middle American research an impetus and perspective of enduring consequence. His contributions in Mexican archaeology, classical and modern Nahuatl, Mexican colonial history, and what he preferred to call "Bilderhandschriften" are of lasting importance." Dibble compared Barlow's zeal for searching for and deciphering little known or dimly recalled codices and colonial manuscripts to that of Zelia Nuttall.

### Life and career

### Lovecraft associate
Barlow had been a friend of writers H. P. Lovecraft and Robert E. Howard since he was 13. He collaborated with Lovecraft on six stories (among them "The Battle that Ended the Century", "The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast", "Till A' the Seas" and "The Night Ocean"), and Lovecraft made several extended visits to the young Barlow at his home in DeLand, Florida.

Barlow attempted to bind and distribute Lovecraft's story The Shunned House (1928) but bound only a few copies. (Arkham House distributed some bound versions of the original Barlow project as late as the 1970s.)

Barlow aided significantly in the preservation of Lovecraft's manuscripts by typing texts in exchange for autograph manuscripts.

At his death, Lovecraft's will named Barlow his literary executor. Barlow came to Providence, Rhode Island, shortly thereafter, donating most of the manuscripts and some printed matter to the John Hay Library of Brown University.

R'llyeh is a fictional location in the Prime Reality of Marvel Comics. It is a clear pastiche of R'lyeh.
### Background
R'llyeh, the First Atlantis, the Seventh World of the Ancients, was built by ancient "things", hideous otherworldly beings from the stars, who ruled Earth ages ago, building great cities and working their magic in unfathomable ways. Their servants were kept chained, living and dying in the dark glory of their masters.

On the walls of the city, the magic of these ancient beings were carved into writings. It has been suggested that these are the source of all magic on Earth, imperfectly copied into such texts as the Darkhold, the Necronomicon, and the Oracles of Zoroaster. The sinking of Atlantis and the return of man to the sea awakened the ancient evil, who used the formless substance called "Sh'g'th tissue" to create unholy life, the first Aqueos (a race of sea-dwelling vampiric beings).

### Notes
*The name R'llyeh is very close to the name of Cthulhu's tomb / resting place R'lyeh.
*Much like Island M's and Quoggoth's story, R'llyeh and the Aqueos (created from "Sh'g'th tissue") were influenced by various elements from "The Call of Cthulhu" and At the Mountains of Madness, both about alien (extraterrestrial and/or extradimensional) beings creating cities before the dawn of man and horrific servants.
*It is possible that R'llyeh is actually the R'lyeh of the Cthulhu Mythos proper, in which case the "ancient things" are actually the Great Old Ones. Though the lore states it was created by Chthon billions of years ago when the Elder Gods walked the Earth, it is theorised that R'llyeh is the source of the Darkhold, the Necronomicon and other tomes of magic.(by who?)

R'lyeh (pronounced /ˈɹu.li.a/ or /ɹɪl.ˈai.ɛ/) is a fictional island city created by H. P. Lovecraft, which makes its first appearance in the 1928 short story "The Call of Cthulhu". R'lyeh is also referred to in Lovecraft's The Mound as Relex.

R'lyeh is a sunken city located deep under the Pacific Ocean and is where the Great Old One Cthulhu is interred. R'lyeh's bizarre architecture is characterized by its non-Euclidean geometry, colossal structures, and shifts in perspective that can make an observer unsure about what is vertical and what is horizontal. (: "The Call of Cthulhu")

The city is extraordinarily ancient, having been built on dry land in the Paleozoic era. It sank to the bottom of the sea along with all the other cities of the alien Cthulhi in a prehistoric cataclysm (: At the Mountains of Madness), which the K'n-yanians believe was caused by a race of "space-devils", inimical to Cthulhu (: The Mound).

### Description
When R'lyeh rises in Lovecraft's short story "The Call of Cthulhu", the only portion of the city that emerges is a single "hideous monolith-crowned citadel" in which Cthulhu is entombed. The human onlookers are awed by the sheer immensity of the city and by the frightening suggestiveness of the gargantuan statues and bas-reliefs.

The city is a panorama of "vast angles and stone surfaces [...] too great to belong to anything right and proper for this earth, and impious with horrible images and disturbing hieroglyphs." The geometry of R'lyeh is "abnormal, non-Euclidean, and loathsomely redolent of spheres and dimensions apart from ours." The strange architecture of the city makes navigation on foot disorienting and treacherous; surfaces that appear flat may actually be tilted, and angles of masonry that appear convex at first glance may actually be concave.

In Lovecraft's stories, R'lyeh is sometimes referred to in the ritualistic phrase "Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthulhu R'lyeh wgah'nagl fhtagn", which roughly translates to "In his house at R'lyeh, dead Cthulhu waits dreaming."

The R'lyeh Text is a fictional grimoire created by August Derleth. It first appeared in his short story "The Return of Hastur" and was later featured in many other works of the expanded Cthulhu Mythos, including Lin Carter's Xothic Legend Cycle.

### Contents
Written by author or authors unknown, the R'lyeh Text contains information on Cthulhu, Ghatanothoa, Zoth-Ommog, Cyäegha and other Great Old Ones.

### Known Copies
*In August Derleth's short story "The Return of Hastur", Amos Tuttle paid a hundred thousand dollars for a copy of the R'lyeh Text that came from "the dark interior of Asia". The book was bound in human skin.
*In Lin Carter's short stories "Behind the Mask" and "The Strange Doom of Enos Harker", a translation of the R'lyeh Text was produced by Bryant Hoskins based on the aforementioned Tuttle copy, and kept in the library of Miskatonic University.
*In Brian Lumley's short story "Lord of the Worms", Julian Carstairs has a copy that he keeps in his library at The Barrows.
*In Robert M. Price's short story "Down in Limbo", a copy is known to have been held by the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities. It was translated by a scholar named Jacob Maitland, who was so disturbed by what he learned from it that he destroyed both the original and the translation. It is unknown whether copies remain extant in other scholarly institutions.
*In James Ambuehl's short story "The Advent of Uvhash", a book titled The R'lyeh Text: Fragmentary Transcriptions is referenced, indicating that in Ambuehl's continuations, at least sections of the original writing remain in existence.
*In the Demonbane series by Nitroplus, the R'lyeh Text takes the form of a human girl and was located in Innsmouth, where she was guarded by Dagon and the Deep Ones. She was eventually retrieved by the Black Lodge, who used her as one of the key components for their ritual to summon Cthulhu.
*The R'lyeh Text appears in the Fate franchise by Type-Moon, most notably being featured in the Fate/Zero anime. Cthuvian, which is also called R'lyehian, is a fictional language created by H. P. Lovecraft in "The Call of Cthulhu" and expanded upon by various authors.

The name "R'lyehian" was first used in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", which claims that the language was brought to prehistoric Earth by the Spawn of Cthulhu.

### Introduction
R'lyehian is described as sounding strange and guttural, and is supposedly impossible for the human mouth to speak or pronounce. Humans have still tried and tired again to transcribe the language, leading to consonant clusters that sound relatively foreign to the English ear - such as mglw'naph or fhtagn.

### Phonology
As R'lyehian does not have any canonical spoken content and, even besides, is a language purely made to adapt something unspeakable to begin with, multiple phonological proposals exist.

### Grammar
R'lyehian is highly agglutinative and possesses free word order; it makes extensive use of prefixes and suffixes to alter and derive meaning from pre-existing words. Articles such as prepositions are prefixed - such as ph-, meaning "beyond," as in ph-shugg "extraterrestrial;" or nafl-, designating the past tense, as in nafl-sll'ha, "invited."

Plurals are formed within R'lyehian via reduplication of the final syllable - e.g. ngha-gha "deaths."(source?)

Linguist Paul Tuttle believed that the prefix nafl- denoted a negative construction. For instance, if "Cthulhu fhtagn" can be translated as "Cthulhu waits dreaming", the phrase "Cthulhu naflfhtagn" means "Cthulhu no longer waits dreaming" (i.e. has awakened). (: "The Return of Hastur")

Engineer Raabe is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Temple".

### Overview
As an engineer aboard the German submarine U-29, Raabe served under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich during the First World War. During the course of the supernatural events experienced by the crew, Raabe and fellow engineer Schneider were both killed by an explosion in the engine room. (: "The Temple")
