The Raandeese are a fictional species in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by Gregory Nicoll for his short story "From the Deep".

### Overview
The Raandeese are monstrous shark people who worship the god Raandaii-B'nk. Their known colony is within the Bermuda Triangle.

Once every two years, the females give birth to three young (two females and one male). At birth, the offspring resemble sharks before developing arms and legs within a few days. At 20 yeas old, they have grown to resemble humans in shape. Once they develop limbs, they can leave water, and once in humanoid form, may live wholly on land. This lasts for four years and then the process reverses itself, and the creature becomes increasingly shark-like. Certain ones, the more intelligent and powerful, retain limbs during these later years, although they become more batrachian in form. Raandeese tend to live for about 700 years. There are different "types" of shark among the Raandeese, with Hammerheads being leaders, followed by Mako sharks, then tiger sharks.

According to Les Enfants du Poisson, a book containing information about Raandeese, they sometimes travel via a gate known as "The Threshold of Yuggoth", which lies within the Bermuda Triangle area. Their relationship to the Deep Ones, and particularly the dolphin-like Laniqua Lua'huan, is unclear, but it may be that the Raandeese are a subspecies of Deep One.

term: Racism in the Works of H.P. Lovecraft
shortDefinition: One of the most controversial aspects of Lovecraft's works is the author's inclusion of racist ideas and themes, which "does not endear Lovecraft to the modern reader," and comes across through many disparaging remarks against the various non-Anglo-S...
fullContent:
One of the most controversial aspects of Lovecraft's works is the author's inclusion of racist ideas and themes, which "does not endear Lovecraft to the modern reader," and comes across through many disparaging remarks against the various non-Anglo-Saxon races and cultures within his work.

As he grew older, the more "jagged" aspects of his original Anglo-Saxon racial worldview softened into a universal classicism or elitism, regarding any fellow human being of self-ennobled high culture as of metaphorical "superior race." Lovecraft did not from the start even hold all white people in uniform high regard, but rather he held Anglo-Nordic people, and especially persons of English descent, above all others. While his racist perspective is undeniable, many critics argue this does not detract from his ability to create compelling philosophical worlds which have inspired many artists and readers.

In his early published essays, private letters and personal utterances, he argued for a strong color line, for the purpose of preserving race and culture. These arguments occurred through direct statements against different races in his journalistic work and personal correspondence, or perhaps allegorically in his work using non-human races. Some have interpreted his racial attitude as being more cultural than brutally biological: Lovecraft showed sympathy to others who pacifically assimilated into Western culture, to the extent of even marrying a Jewish woman whom he viewed as "well-assimilated."

While Lovecraft's racial attitude has been seen as directly influenced by the time, a reflection of the New England society he grew up in, his racism appeared stronger than the popular viewpoints held at that time. Some researchers also note that his views failed to change in the face of increased social change of that time. It is noted that in his last year, Lovecraft embraced socialism and Roosevelt's New Deal, while dismissing many of his old right wing views.1

Despite the unique and interesting nature of many of Lovecraft's works, several are marred by a racist streak deeply ingrained in the author's personality. A common dramatic device in Lovecraft's work is to associate virtue, intellect, elevated class position, civilization, and rationality with white Anglo-Saxon ethnicity, which he often posed in contrast to the corrupt, intellectually inferior, uncivilized and irrational, which he associated with people he characterized as being of lower class, impure racial "stock" and/or non European ethnicity and dark skin complexion who were often the villains in his writings.

Some of his most hostile racist views can be found in his poetry, particularly in "On the Creation of *******," and "New England Fallen" (both 1912). Lovecraft once took this to an extreme, explicitly characterizing black people as sub-human:

|"On the Creation of *******"}}

Radiant Dawn is the first novel by Cody Goodfellow, published in 2000 by Perilous Press.  Goodfellow has described it, along with its sequel Ravenous Dusk, as "a two-part modern epic based upon Lovecraft’s At the Mountains of Madness."

Goodfellow's short story "In the Shadow of Swords", anthologized in the collection A Mountain Walked, serves as a prequel to Radiant Dawn.

The novel describes a secret war between a renegade special forces team and a new age cult over the future of humanity.

### Organizations
Radiant Dawn: Once a New Age utopian commune in the California desert two miles south of Convict Lake; later reorganized as the Radiant Dawn Hospice Village. Dedicated to a radical advancement of trans-human evolution.

Spike Team Texas: A trio of mutant ex-Special Forces operatives affiliated with Radiant Dawn. They were defectors from Special Forces in Vietnam, who "radioed our boys into ambushes in the jungle.... The things they supposedly did over there made the Khmer Rouge look like the Salvation Army." They were captured by the Pentagon in 1978, and subjected to a test of the RADIANT SDI system in 1984 that was supposed to kill them, but instead turned them into nearly indestructible, shoggoth-like supersoldiers.

The Mission: Renegade military personnel and DARPA scientists dedicated to wiping out Radiant Dawn before it can replace humanity. They describe themselves as "a militia of human beings fighting a holy war against eugenic terrorists."

School Of Night: A cult based in Colma, California, that worships Mana Yood Sushai, the dreaming god. Serves as a surveillance network for The Mission.

### Characters
Stella Orozco, 29-year-old registered nurse with terminal liver cancer. After being rejected by Radiant Dawn, becomes a combination hostage/guinea pig/lab technician for The Mission. Described as having "bronze skin and ebony hair...with angular brow and cheekbones, deepset black eyes, an aquiline nose and an almost too-wide, generously lipped mouth".

### Thermopylae
Zane Ezekiel Storch, Gulf War veteran suffering from Gulf War Syndrome. Born in 1966, Storch enlisted in the Airborne Rangers in 1983; promoted to sergeant, he transferred to  Special Forces. He saw combat in Desert Storm, lost a thumb and was awarded the Silver Star and Purple Heart; he has repressed memories of an encounter with Spike Team Texas in the Tigris Valley that altered his physiology. Runs Sgt. Storch's Quartermaster Supply in Thermopylae, California.

Harley John Pettigrew, Sgt. Storch's assistant manager. Described by the FBI as "a convicted illegal firearms dealer with associates in both militant anti-government and organized crime circles." Secretly an agent of The Mission, codenamed Serapion.

Ely Buggs, computer programmer and conspiracy theorist who works as a cashier for Storch. Also does IT work for the School Of Night.

Ragnalla, also known as the Nest-Mistress of the Winged Ones and The Seeker in the Skies, is a fictional entity created by American author James Ambuehl for his 1985 poem "Ragnalla". The character was incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos via Ambuehl's Lu-Kthu Cycle.

### Overview
Described as a vulturine or raptorial being (: "The Stalker in the Snows"), she is also said to have a single, huge eye and a crown of tentacles (source?). She may also be capable of sending "loathsome visions" to her victims (: "Ragnalla").

Ragnalla and her brood are colossal in size, so much that a human being is but a "tiny morsel of food" to her "cycloptic and cyclopean" Winged Ones. (: "Correlated Contents")

The rakshassi (singular: rakshassa) are fictional creatures featured in Andy Lane's novel All-Consuming Fire, named after a type of demons from Hindu mythology.

In the novel, the rakshassi are not a naturally-occurring species, but the final result of a transformation process that all worshipers of "Azathoth" go through, regardless of whether they start off as human, shlangii, etc.

### Description
The rakshassi are winged crustacean-like creatures with crimson red armour and a long segmented tail ending in a spiked club. They are the servants of a massive slug-like alien who identifies herself as "Azathoth", although the Doctor believes that she is just using the name of a more powerful being to back up her claims of goddesshood.

Rakshassi walk around on their membranous clawed wings like a bat. Their heads are faceless, with no eyes or mouth to be seen, and covered in a multitude of mobile spikes. Despite the absence of a visible mouth, the rakshassi can produce high-pitched screams and even speak human languages when they want to. Conversely, they are completely incapable of singing. They can use their tails as a spring to leap at their victims, or coil the tail around them and lift off. Their blood is a pink water-like fluid.

The Doctor has speculated that the slug-like "Azathoth" might be the larval form of her species, and that the rakshassi might perhaps resemble the adult form of the race. (: All-Consuming Fire)

### Behind the Mythos
The physical appearance of the rakshassi is somewhat similar to the Mi-Go, another race of winged crustacean-like creatures with featureless heads covered in a multitude of antennae or protuberances. However, a notable difference is that the Mi-Go can't fly properly on Earth, being only suited for interstellar flight. The rakshassi, in contrast, can fly over long distances even while carrying the weight of an adult humanoid.

Ralph Eugene Vaughan (born 16 September 1954) is an American author, poet, essayist, editor and occasional artist based in Chula Vista, California, who has contributed a number of stories to the weird fiction genre. Perhaps best known for his extensive Sherlock Holmes output (and is credited with penning the first Holmes/Cthulhu Mythos story, "The Adventure of the Ancient Gods") he has written several stories combining the Baker Street universe with that of the Cthulhu Mythos. He has also written several non-fiction works on the topic, including the limited-run HP Lovecraft in the Comics, and his work has appeared in zines such as W. H. Pugmire's Tales of Lovecraftian Horror, Robert M. Price's Crypt of Cthulhu, and S. T. Joshi's Lovecraft Studies.

Vaughan's non-Mythos output includes the multi-volume series Paws & Claws, an urban fantasy about crime-fighting dogs, and The Steampunk Adventures of Folkestone & Hand.

Ram Singh is a fictional character created by the late American author Lin Carter for his Anton Zarnak series of occult detective stories.

### Overview
Ram Singh is a large yet cultured man of prodigious strength. He is a Sikh and wears a dastar (turban) as part of his religious observances. In India, Anton Zarnak saved Ram Singh from a were-tiger (the feline equivalent of a werewolf). After this incident, Singh spent much of his life, and met his death, in service to the accomplished mystic: as a result of this, he appears to be extremely well-educated in the ways of the occult.

### Appearances

### Lin Carter's Works

### Other Works

### Trivia
* Although Lin Carter gave Singh's first name as Ram, Robert M. Price refers to him as Akbar. One possible explanation for this is that Price's stories are set after the death of the original Singh, and that Akbar is Ram's replacement; as Singh, meaning "lion", is a common middle and surname in the Sikh religion, this explanation seems entirely possible.

Ramjet is a Decepticon and Herald of Unicron from the Transformers: Cybertron comics by Fun Publications.

### Background
Ramjet was once Unicron's most dangerous lieutenant and a sadistic monster who enjoyed helping his master destroy many realities throughout the multiverse. Ramjet was granted godlike interdimensional powers, often using them to torture and wipe out entire planets as a means of announcing the inevitable outcome of Unicron ending their universe. However, after Unicron's physical body collapsed into a massive black hole, Ramjet found himself stranded in unspace. Unfortunately for Ramjet, he was not alone there as he would encounter some ancient evil entities of indescribable power. Ramjet would endure an eternity of torment at their hands, repeatedly being destroyed and recreated countless times. Eventually growing bored of him, Ramjet would be sent back to reality. This experience would drive Ramjet completely insane, in addition to making him far more powerful than before and nearly indestructible due to being in a state torn between existence and non-existence.

fullContent:
Ramsey Campbell is a British writer considered by a number of critics to be one of the great masters of horror fiction. T. E. D. Klein has written that "Campbell reigns supreme in the field today", while S. T. Joshi has said that "future generations will regard him as the leading horror writer of our generation, every bit the equal of Lovecraft or Blackwood."

### Overview
Campbell's childhood and adolescence were marked by the rift between his parents and his mother's developing schizophrenia, an experience he has discussed in detail in the introduction and afterword to the restored text of The Face That Must Die. Although both parents lived in the same house, Campbell states, "I didn't see my father face to face for nearly twenty years, and that was when he was dying."

His early work was greatly influenced by the work of H. P. Lovecraft. His first collection, The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, is a volume of Cthulhu Mythos stories published by Arkham House in 1964. At the suggestion of August Derleth, he rewrote many of his earliest stories, which he had originally set in the state of Massachusetts locales of Arkham, Dunwich and Innsmouth, and relocated them to English settings in and around the fictional Gloucestershire city of Brichester, near the River Severn, creating his own Severn Valley milieu for Lovecraftian horrors.  Brichester was deeply influenced by Campbell's native Liverpool, and much of his later work is set in the real locales of Liverpool and Merseyside. In particular, his 2006 novel Secret Stories (published in the U.S. as Secret Story) both exemplifies and satirizes Liverpudlian speech, characters, humor, and culture.

With the collection Demons by Daylight (1973), Campbell set out to be as unlike Lovecraft as possible. In 1969, he had written "Lovecraft in Retrospect", an essay for the fanzine Shadow, "condemning [Lovecraft's] work outright." However, in his 1985 book Cold Print, which collects his Lovecraftian stories, Campbell disavowed the opinions expressed in the article, stating: "I believe Lovecraft is one of the most important writers in the field" and "the first book of Lovecraft's I read made me into a writer." Demons by Daylight includes "The Franklyn Paragraphs", which uses Lovecraft's documentary narrative technique without slipping into parody of his writing style. Other tales, such as "The End of a Summer's Day" and "Concussion", show the emergence of Campbell's highly distinctive mature style, of which S. T. Joshi has written:



Subsequently, Campbell has published a number of other collections; many of his most popular stories can be found in the 1993 collection Alone with the Horrors.

Campbell has written many novels, both supernatural and non-supernatural. They include The Face That Must Die (issued in a badly cut version in 1979 and in a revised edition in 1983), the story of a homophobic serial killer told largely from the killer's point of view. Randolph Carter is a fictional character in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character is semi-autobiographical, sharing several of Lovecraft's biographical aspects as well as his antiquarian tastes and mild nature.

### Biography
Randolph is the descendant of the Elizabethan magician Sir Randolph Carter, as well as another ancestor who fought in the crusades, and was captured by Muslims and learned their magical secrets. Another ancestor, Edmund Carter "the wizard", fled from the gallows during the Salem Witch Trials and resettled at Arkham; "tales of his sorceries were many." (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

Carter was born c. 1874. At the age of nine, he underwent a mysterious experience in the Snake Den, a cave at his great-uncle Christopher's Arkham farm, and thereafter exhibited a gift of prophecy.

Randolph Carter graduated from Miskatonic University. During World War I, he served in the French Foreign Legion, where he met Etienne-Laurent de Marigny, a New Orleans mystic who became a close friend. De Marigny took him to Bayonne to show him "certain terrible secrets in the nighted and immemorial crypts that burrow beneath that brooding, eon-weighted city". De Marigny later became Carter's literary and financial executor.  (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

Like Lovecraft, he is an under-appreciated horror writer. His story "The Attic Window" appeared in the January 1922 issue of the fictional magazine Whispers.

### Early Encounters with the Unknown
See: The Statement of Randolph Carter

His first appearance was in the short story "The Statement of Randolph Carter", in which he and his friend Harley Warren attempt to locate the door between the human world and a hellish dimension. Though Carter survives, Warren was killed by an unseen evil.

### Quest for Kadath
See: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath

### Revelation and Transformation
See: Through the Gates of the Silver Key

After obtaining the Silver Key, Carter performed the ritual of the Key in the hills behind Arkham, in the cave known as the Snake Den, on October 7, 1928. The ritual opened a gateway into a strange realm, which offered up visions of Earth's distant past before resolving into an unknown area of strange stone architecture. There Carter encountered 'Umr at-Tawil, The Most Ancient One, whom Carter knew from the writings of Abdul Alhazred in his Necronomicon. 'Umr-At-Tawil addressed Carter telepathically, telling him that he had unlocked the First Gate, and giving him the choice of proceeding to the Ultimate Gate or turning back the way he had come.

"Rapture of the Deep" is a short story by Cody Goodfellow that first appeared in Dark Discoveries #15 (Fall 2009). It tells the story of a corporate intelligence agency using a psychic operative to investigate a mysterious phenomenon in the Marianas Trench.

### Characters
Ingrid: An employee of a corporation based in Hong Kong, Moscow, and San Francisco. A psychic sensitive, she has the ability to see through the another's eyes--especially someone she's slept with. She has a doctorate in psychology. Her good looks are striking, but she grew up an unpopular fat girl.

Roger Mankiw: Ingrid's boss, a vested partner in the corporation. He is skeptical of psychic abilities, but demands that they get results.

Sergei Vasilievich Lyubyenko: A Russian psychic with the ability to project his mind for remote viewing. He can also psychically control those he touches, to the point of inducing suicide. An independent contractor, he formerly worked for the KGB, but defected after they forced him to view Opaque Zone 38A; his wife and two sons were subsequently killed by the Soviet government. A bald, moustachioed old man, Lyubyenko has three fingers on one hand, the others lost to wolves in a gulag. 

### Setting
The story takes place above and in the Marianas Trench, "the deepest hole in the earth." The trench is the source of "a steady warming trend with trace radioactivity that’s sweeping the whole South Pacific." 

The anomaly is centered on an area in the trench called Opaque Zone 38a. The Soviet Union sent the submarine Rybinsk to the zone to drop a tactical nuclear weapon on it (to "end the nightmares"); the sub did not return--nor did the submersible drones the corporation later sent to investigate. 

When Lyubyenko and Ingrid investigate psychically, they find a "plain of basalt slabs fragmented into disturbingly tessellated geometrical patterns." It's dotted with hundreds of towering hydrothermal vents, the smaller ones twelve stories tall, arranged "in a uniform field. A farm." The chimneys are "festooned with giant tubeworms and anemones," surrounded by "enormous shrimp," and tended by "monstrous arachnids" that "farmed globules of cooling heavy metals, and bore them off across the plain, like leaf cutter ants harvesting fungi."

Beyond the plain are "dozens of octagonal pits, each hundreds of yards across, and seemingly bottomless." Their walls are honeycombed with wormholes whose "hypnotic complexity suggested that they were inhabited by something utterly alien."

fullContent:
Rat God is a five-issues comic book series written and illustrated by Richard Corben. It was published by Dark Horse Comics in 2015.

The story is set in the vicinity of Arkham, Massachusetts, and concerns a strange community who worships a giant preternatural rat god.

### Synopsis
### Issue #1
In a prehistoric taiga, Achak and his sister Mak-Kitoto are fleeing from an enemy tribe who wants to kill or enslave them. As their pursuers approach, Achak is wounded by an arrow. He urges Mak-Kitoto to keep running, promising to meet her in three days by the river. As per her brother's instructions, she runs and hides in the forest. But when the three days pass and she hopes to meet her brother again, she instead sees something entirely alien to her time period: an automobile.

The driver also sees Mak-Kitoto, but when he comes out of the car, she is gone. The only person nearby is a man named Chuk, who looks like Achak and asks for a ride. Chuk recognizes the driver as Clark Elwood from Arkham, a friend of his sister Kito. However, Elwood refuses to believe that a native American like Chuk could be the brother of a white woman like Kito. Soon, Elwood's racist remarks and aggressiveness escalate into a fistfight, which he loses. Chuk steals the car and drives away, but Elwood is intent on heading north even on foot, to arrive at the small town of Lame Dog. On the way, he reminisces about how he first met Kito at Miskatonic University and fell in love with her.

Elwood loses his way in the woods and comes across mummified bodies covered in snow. A black panther attacks and almost kills him, but the beast is shot by two men traveling by dog sled. A wounded Elwood tries to signal to them, but they move on without him.

### Issue #2
Elwood staggers on through the snow, and continues to remember his dates with Kito in Arkham. She told him that her home town of Lame Dog prospered between 1860 and 1890, when Russian prospectors moved in and found gold. However, when the gold became scarce, most settlers left. A man named Zedon Peck allied himself with the Cthanhluk tribe, learned their religious rites, and eventually became their leader. With his Cthanhluk allies, Peck orchestrated the burning of Lame Dog's church, and converted the town's population to a new faith. Elwood also remembers the day he found out about Kito's job of posing nude for an anatomy class, and cut ties with her even as she confessed her love for him, which is the reason why he's going to Lame Dog now, to find her and apologise.

Weakened by the cold and exhaustion, Elwood falls unconscious, but wakes up inside a cabin. His saviour turns out to be Chuk, who tells him to take his car and leave. Elwood does so, and finally arrives in Lame Dog, a decrepit town inhabited by strange people with rat-like facial features. The Rat God is a fictional monster created by Richard Corben for his comic book series of the same name, where it serves as the mysterious deity venerated by the people of Lame Dog, Massachusetts.

### Description
Native to the woods in the vicinity of Arkham, the Rat God resembles a bear-sized rodent with a bare rat skull for a head. Its origins are unknown, but it has been alive since prehistory. This carnivorous beast devours humans and demands sacrifices of its cultists, which seem to be somehow linked to it. Many citizens of Lame Dog in the early 20th century displayed rat-like facial features themselves. The Rat God is also served by a swarm of oversized rats. Additionally, it might be associated with a type of fungus that revives the dead bodies of its followers, allowing them to live again for several generations.

The Rat God can dig under the ground at prodigious speed. It is strong enough to charge at an accelerating car and topple the vehicle, suffering no apparent damage from the collision. (: Rat God)

The Rat People are a race of rat-like quadrupeds created for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. They were tangentially inspired by the short story"The Rats in the Walls" by H. P. Lovecraft, although whether they are intended to be the same species of creature as those depicted is unknown.

### Description
The Rat People are rat-human hybrids who can be both bipedal and quadrupedal. They were all once human, but have degenerated due to inbreeding and the worship of gods such as Y'golonac.

### Bouchers
The Bouchers are an example of a human family that evolved into this species. Vicious semi-human creatures, Bouchers possess traits of both man and rat. Distant descendants of the degenerate worshippers of Y'golonac, they are subterranean beings with a powerful bite. 

Bouchers were created by Ed Gore in his Call of Cthulhu adventure Warren in the 1989 gaming supplement collection, Cthulhu Classics.

Rat-Things are a fictional species created for the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, based on the character Brown Jenkin from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Dreams in the Witch-House".

### Overview
Rat-Things are small creatures that closely resemble rats, albeit with human-like hands and faces. They have strong sharp teeth that can tear through flesh easily. These beings are spawned by dark magic, originating from deceased human cultists who have been revived in a new form so that they may continue to serve their deities. Populations of Rat-Things have been reported from Yorkshire, England, as well as Massachusetts. (: Call of Cthulhu)

shortDefinition: "Rats in the Cellars" is a 1920s-era prequel to the main events of Armand Rosamilia's Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.  ### Synopsis A man travelling across country finds himself in the backwards coastal town of Keyport, New Jersey. There, he discovers h...
fullContent:
"Rats in the Cellars" is a 1920s-era prequel to the main events of Armand Rosamilia's Keyport Cthulhu story cycle.

### Synopsis
A man travelling across country finds himself in the backwards coastal town of Keyport, New Jersey. There, he discovers his family heritage and witnesses his strangely-deformed grandfather as he sacrifices himself to a monstrous creature dwelling below the streets.

Cut to several years later, and the man's firstborn child is born with several strange abnormalities. He realises that he has not escaped his family curse, and wonders what he is to do about it.

### Characters
* Jeffry Ruggerio, an Italian-born Englishman travelling south.
* Mister Peabody, Jeffry's grandfather and a famed airship designer.
* Dylan Murphy, an antecedant of the Dylan Murphy featured in the main plot of Keyport Cthulhu.
* Douglas Grandon, a tailor and member of the Esoteric Order of Dagon.
* Toland, Peabody's manservant.

### Publication History
"Rats in the Cellars" was first published in the collection Keyport Cthulhu in November 2013.

### Trivia
* Although advertised as a steampunk story, aside from a few offhand references to a burgeoning dirigible industry the tale contains no steampunk elements.

Ravenous Dusk is a 2003 novel by Cody Goodfellow, a sequel to Radiant Dawn (2000). It was published by Perilous Press. Goodfellow has described the books as "a two-part modern epic based upon Lovecraft’s At the Mountains of Madness."

### Synopsis
The new age cult Radiant Dawn and the Mission, a coalition of renegade Special Ops officers and DARPA scientists, continue their secret war. Zane Storch and Stella Orozco, now transformed into meta-Shoggoths, try to figure which--if any--side that puts them on. And FBI analyst Martin Cundieffe tries to figure out what's going on, and where the Cave Institute, a secret society of ungendered illuminati, fits in.

fullContent:
Ravenstone Sanitarium, written by John Gary Pettit, is an adventure module for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game by Chaosium. It was released in 2008.

It provides game mechanics for dissociative identity disorder (multiple personality disorder) characters, and allows a player to create and play characters which are fragments of a mentally ill person's mind. It also adds a new rule and game mechanic, the Personality Check, modifying the standard and ubiquitous Sanity Check.

### Synopsis
There are two adventures provided. 

In the first, the player is playing a character who has already failed one too many Sanity checks and is in an asylum for the insane. The player generates characters that are fragments of their own mind.

In the second, set ten years later than the first sequence, the player characters are investigating the same asylum to find out what nightmarish secret it has hidden all along.

The adventure features the first appearance of the Great Old One Xchthol.

### Behind the Mythos
This adventure module, containing two adventures, was part of the Miskatonic University Library Association monograph series. These works featured rules, situations or other content that was either not standard to the published Call of Cthulhu RPG rules, much more adult in content, or both. Ravenstone Sanitarium was Monograph #0350. To quote Chaosium:

"MISKATONIC UNIVERSITY LIBRARY ASSOCIATION monographs are longer works by one or more authors on a subject of import to Call of Cthulhu roleplayers. On these products the author has also fulfilled the functions of editor and layout artist; we at Chaosium have done little in the way of editorial. We found these works compelling and thought that you would enjoy them. Through the publication of monographs we can offer our most loyal fans more information more easily, and evaluate the potential of these works for eventual release to the wholesale market."

Sheriff Raymond Dirk is a character created by American comic book creator Michael Alan Nelson as one of the primary protagonists for The Gray Man story arc of his Mythos series Fall of Cthulhu. He made his first appearance in issue #11 in March 2008.

### Description
A well built man somewhere in his late thirties, Dirk is Sheriff of the Arkham Police Department, and as of the end of the Gray Man story arc, apparently one of the last. He is a tough but fair officer with an open mind, and is well aware of the flaws of those who work for him.

Several years prior to the events of The Gray Man, Dirk lost his beloved wife in a car accident; his actions in trying to help the people of Arkham resulted in him losing all memory of her very existence.

Dirk comes from a family with a tradition of holding the title of Sheriff in Arkham, being at least the third in his line to occupy that position; the officers under his command expect that if Dirk ever has a son, then he too will take up the role.

### History
Dirk was involved in investigating the brutal murders of two innocent people when his station was attacked, the officers present all slaughtered. Partnering with the young thief Lucifer, he attempted to bring the supernatural perpetrator to justice, dealing with the Harlot in the Dreamlands and facing off against both a Cthulhu cult and the Gray Man in the process. Although Dirk and Lucifer could not kill the creature, they did manage to trap it in an inescapable prison, saving the people of Arkham, at least for a time (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 3: The Gray Man).

Later Dirk, along with Lucifer and escaped mental patient Cy Morgan, was instrumental in sending the newly-risen R'lyeh back beneath the waves, single-handedly defeating two of the Horsemen of Nyarlathotep. Although driven slightly insane by his time on R'lyeh, he later recovered, and a gift from Lucifer allowed him to recover the memories of his deceased wife (: Fall of Cthulhu Volume 4: Godwar; Fall of Cthulhu Volume 5: Apocalypse).

### Overview

fullContent:
Re-Animator is a 1985 American black comedy/horror/science fiction film loosely based on H. P. Lovecraft's serialized short story "Herbert West--Reanimator". Written by Dennis Paoli, directed by Stuart Gordon, and produced by Brian Yuzna, it was the first film in the Re-Animator film series. Its success caused a small boom in Lovecraft adaptations in cinema, and the film is still used as one of the benchmarks for appreciating and critiquing Lovecraftian cinema.

It was followed by two sequels, Bride of Re-Animator in 1990 and Beyond Re-Animator in 2003.

### Synopsis
A black comedy retelling of the original short story, Re-Animator is updated to a contemporary setting. It takes its plot and characters from the first two episodes of the story, depicting Herbert West--played by science fiction and horror legend Jeffrey Combs in his first screen Mythos appearance--as a medical student at Miskatonic University. The unnamed narrator in the story is called Daniel Cain, and is played by Bruce Abbott. Dean Alan Halsey, another character invented by Lovecraft, is played by Robert Sampson, first as an academic foil to West and later as a re-animated zombie. Halsey is given a daughter, Megan, played by Barbara Crampton; she is Cain's love interest. Dr. Carl Hill, played by David Gale, is a rival of West's who learns to use some of West's techniques--allowing himself to function even after his head has been separated from his body.

### Adaptations 
*In May 1997, a novelisation of the film written by Jeff Rovin and published by Pocket Books was released. It was reissued in 2020 by Encyclopocalypse Publicatios as part of their Retro Mass Market Series.
*The film was adapted for the stage as Re-Animator: The Musical, first performed in 2011. Stuart Gordon and Dennis Paoli, the original film's director and screenwriter, respectively, both played key roles in the theatrical production.

### Trivia
*The name of West's professor in Switzerland, a minor character who appears at the beginning of the film, is Hans Gruber - which is also the name of the villain in Die Hard, a film released three years later.

Re-Animator: The Musical is a stage show based on the low-budget 1985 horror movie Re-Animator, which was itself based on H. P. Lovecraft’s short story "Herbert West--Reanimator".

### Production
Inspired in part by the musical horror-comedy Little Shop of Horrors, Stuart Gordon, who directed the Re-Animator film, partnered with Dean Schramm to produce Re-Animator: The Musical. Music and lyrics were provided by Mark Nutter, while Gordon, Dennis Paoli (a long-term collaborator of Gordons) and William J. Norris wrote the script.

### Runs
The show premiered in March 2011 in Los Angeles, California, with later productions in New York in July 2012, and at the Edinburgh Fringe Festival in August 2012. A further run in Las Vegas, Nevada was announced, although it is unclear if this actually went ahead.

The Re'Kithnid is a fictional book created by C.T. Phipps for his Cthulhu Armageddon horror action adventure series, making its first appearance in the 2017 novel The Tower of Zhaal.

### Description
The Re'Kithnid is an occult tome written during the Middle Ages by the "Mad Nun" Brianna Lethder. It is a book of sorcery and mythology, depicting a conflict between the Great Old Ones and the Elder Gods. It associates both with alchemical principles of the time. The book is considered highly inaccurate but incredibly potent. The book associates the god Re with a hypothetical "good" brother of Cthulhu called Kithnid.

### Behind the Mythos
The Re'Kithnid is a tribute to both Brian Lumley and August Derleth with the fictional author's name being references to both. Kithnid being an homage to Kthanid.

fullContent:
Reader's Guide to the Cthulhu Mythos is an annotated bibliography of Cthulhu Mythos fiction. Originally published by Robert Weinberg in July 1969, it was released in an expanded edition in 1973 by Weinberg and Edward P. Berglund, published by Silver Scarab Press. 

The book attempts to list all Cthulhu Mythos fiction then published, arranged chronologically and cross-indexed alphabetically. It includes separate listings for nonfiction, poetry, and parody. 

The second edition incorporates Berglund's material from Biblioteca: H. P. Lovecraft, edited and published by David A. Sutton in 1971.

Berglund also ran an web site of the same name with updated bibliographical material, of which the fanzine Nightscapes was part.

Reanimated corpses are featured throughout various stories in the Cthulhu Mythos, spanning a broad cross-section of origins and purposes. There are some that would be defined as biological experiments, such as the work of Herbert West and Dr. Muñoz. Others such as the so-named "The Thing on the Doorstep" seem to be by-products of both magic and will.

The K'n-yanians, with their advanced science, keep the reanimated bodies of their slaves and enemies functioning as biological automatons named Y'm-bhi, which do nothing but obey the commands of their masters. (: The Mound)

Sorcerers like Joseph Curwen can recreate the body of a deceased person from their essential salts alone (: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward). Sometimes a sufficiently skilled sorcerer is even capable of reanimating themself after death, even after their  body has been cut to pieces (: "The Return of the Sorcerer").

Reanimated mummies, created from human and animal parts, dwell under the pyramids of Egypt and worship the Sphinx. (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs")

Some Mythos entities are capable of reanimating the dead, e.g. Bugg-Shash. (: "The Kiss of Bugg-Shash")

Reanimator is a 4-issue mini-series written by Keith Davidson and published by Dynamite Entertainment in 2015.  It is a pastiche that expands on the original Herbert West character created by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Working in New Orleans, Dr. Herbert West continues his experiments in reanimating the dead via chemical methods. The pharmacologist Susan Greene assists the doctor in his ghoulish experiments, while he finances his research in the narcotics trade by selling zombie brain fluid: the reagent from "Herbert West--Reanimator". Soon he ends up in a confrontation with drug gangs, Haitian Voodoo and the followers of the Elder Gods.

fullContent:
Reanimators is a novel by American author Pete Rawlik, first published by Night Shade Books in June 2013, as a paperback ; digital and audiobook versions were released in August of that year . The book was followed by a sequel of sorts, the Lovecraftian mash-up The Weird Company, in 2014.

### Synopsis
When his parents are murdered at the hands of a rampaging, reanimated Allan Halsey, gifted medical student Stuart Hartwell vows his revenge on mad scientists Herbert West and Daniel Cain.

First obtaining his medical degree and establishing his practice, he begins to investigate the processes employed by West and Cain in their work, becoming a reanimator whose skill surpasses that of his nemeses, and even managing to systematically sabotage their researches.

As the years pass, Hartwell's lust for vengeance waxes and wanes, and he is frequently distracted from his purpose by encounters with other characters from H. P. Lovecraft's fiction, his story weaving an interlinking narrative through many of his most popular works.

### Genesis
Author Pete Rawlik originally intended to write a novel mixing many aspects of Lovecraft's fiction, with Herbert West as a central character. However, his devotion to established timelines meant that he was unable to pursue this line of writing, and so he created a new character instead: Dr. Stuart Hartwell. This gave him a very similar character with which to do as he pleased .

The original idea of a "mash-up" novel was later completed as the sequel to Reanimators, The Weird Company .

### Behind the Mythos
Some of the characters encountered by Hartwell include Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee ("The Shadow Out of Time"), Dr. Muñoz ("Cool Air"), Wilbur and Lavinia Whateley and their father ("The Dunwich Horror"), Frank Elwood ("The Dreams in the Witch-House"), Erich Zann ("The Music of Erich Zann"), and many others.

Despite casting West and Cain in the roles of villainous - and occasionally incompetent - mad scientists, one chapter shows the two doing some real good in the hospitals of World War I France, and it is noted that their motives are generally well-intentioned, even if their methods may be at best morally grey.

"Recognition"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, first published in Weirdbook 15 (1981). It was written four years earlier, in January 1977. 

Lumley has said that he almost made this a Titus Crow story, but decided that Crow was "too bold, daring and…inquisitive" to be the protagonist of this story.

### Synopsis
An aristocrat gathers a team of occult specialists to identify and expel a malignant force that haunts one of his properties--while his friend argues that when it comes to the supernatural, sometimes the less one knows, the better.

### Characters
Lord David Marriot: A young, cultured upper-class gentleman with "fine and aristocratic" features. He seeks the identification and removal of a malignant influence from one of his family's properties, so that it might be resold.

Lawrence Danford: A retired clergyman, a "sprightly octogenarian." He is meant to exorcise the spirit that haunts the property, though when he hears its voice, he calls it “a monstrous presence" and declares, "I could not even try to exorcise … that!” He flees the estate.

Jason Lavery: A medium with the "alleged ability to speak in the tongue of the ghost, the possessing spirit. When he goes into a trance, he produces an "insane cough, whistle, and stutter of harshly alien syllables and cackling cachinnations," the only recognizable syllables of which approximated the name "Atlach-Nacha." Soon after this manifestation, he too abandons the project.

Jonathan Turnbull: Another medium, whose special skill is the ability to make an "automatic sketch" of an intrusive entity. He strikes the narrator as "damned arrogant...so sure of his theories and principles." He asks to be left alone in the estate; the next day, he is found "frozen, lying in a crystallized pool of his own blood," with a "thousand circular holes of about one-half inch in diameter penetrated deep into his body."

The Narrator: An "old friend of the family whose name does not really matter." The Marriot family has valued his advice "for many years, in all manner of problems."

### Setting
The estate, not named in the story, is "a large, ungainly, mongrel architecture of dim and doubtful origins, standing gaunt and gloomily atmospheric in an acre of brooding oaks." It's surrounded by "nine acres of otherwise barren moors borderland"--the "borderland" reference suggesting a location in the far north of England, near the Scottish border.

The building currently on the property is only 250 years old, a previous--and larger--structure on the site having burned to the ground in 1618. The older building "is given brief mention in texts dating back almost to Roman times," and the site had been inhabited much earlier, possibly by "a druidic order or some such." When the Marriot family bought the property some 80 years before the events of the story, an "extensive cellar—a veritable maze of tunnels, rooms, and passages—was discovered during renovation." The Red Coterie is a fictional organisation created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Cthulhu Mythos setting. They and their members are regularly mentioned in the 2022 Aconyte anthology Secrets in Scarlet, the title likely being a direct reference to the Coterie.

### Overview
The Red Coterie is a secret society dedicated to the acquisition of powerful mystical artefacts known as "Keys." What they intent to achieve with these items is unclear, but as the motives of their members appear to range from at least somewhat beneficial to actively malevolent, it is entirely possible that the Coterie is no more than an alliance of convenience.

All of the known members wear some item of clothing or accoutrement which is coloured a shade of red, most likely the source of the sect's name. They all appear to capable of utilising magical abilities to some degree, but it is heavily implied that these abilities are entirely conferred by the Keys which they possess rather than any innate natural abilities.

The Coterie is in regular opposition to the Foundation, a government agency dedicated to protecting mankind from the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos.

In Venice, Italy, the Coterie received an offer of alliance with the United States government's Cipher Bureau, although whether the proposition was accepted remains to be seen. (: "The Red and the Black")

### Known Members
* The Lady with the Red Parasol: Tzu San Niang, seemingly one of the most powerful of the Coterie. She has been sighted operating in such widely-separated locations as Shanghai (where she maintains a presence in both the criminal underworld and high society), San Francisco, and Cuba (: "City of Waking Dreams," "Brother Bound," "A Forty Grain Weight of Nephrite")
* The Claret Knight: a member possessed of prodigious financial means, the Knight possesses the power of disconnecting others from their magical abilities. (: "Brother Bound") The Knight has a ruthless streak, as shown when he had members of a rival - though seemingly harmless - group of occultists beaten and mutilated when they attempted to recruit one of the Coterie into their ranks (: "In Art, Truth")
* The Sanguine Watcher: one of the Coterie's more repugnant members, he is more than prepared to use violence in achieving his goals, and appears to have conducted experiments on living human subjects (: "Honor Among Thieves")
* La Chica Roja (the Girl in the Red Coat): Rosa Varela, a former high-society thief who, after the death of her sister decided to redirect her talents to help the Coterie (: "Honor Among Thieves")
* The Red-Gloved Man: a more reserved member of the group, little is known of the Red-Gloved Man, although he was responsible for recruiting Rosa Varela into their ranks (: "Honor Among Thieves")
* Ece Şahin: a scholar of ancient art and history at the Museum of Turkish and Islamic

Red Equinox is a Cthulhu Mythos horror novel by American author Douglas Wynne, the first in his SPECTRA Files series. It was published by JournalStone in both paperback and digital formats in January 2015, and re-released with a new cover in December 2022 .

### Synopsis
After the funeral of the grandmother who raised her, freelance photographer and urban explorer Becca Philips begins to uncover her family's history of involvement with the occult, and the events which led to her grandfather's incarceration and death in a mental health facility.

Shortly afterwards, when the Starry Wisdom Cult, a group devoted to the Outer God Nyarlathotep, attempt to summon forth Shub-Niggurath and, ultimately, Azathoth, Becca must use her family legacy to save the future of the human race. With the aid of her best friend and lover Rafael Moreno, adopted stray dog Django, and SPECTRA agent Jason Brooks, she utilises the power of an ancient counter to the Shining Trapezohedron to thwart the schemes of the Old Ones. However, not all of them survive the encounter…

### Characters
*Rebecca "Becca" Philips, a disturbed young woman with a previously-unsuspected connection to dark forces.
*Rafael Moreno, a young street artist, and Becca's closest confidant and lover.
*Jason Brooks, an agent of shadowy government agency SPECTRA, who appears to share a closer connection than most to the dark forces which fall under its purview.
*Django, a former street mutt adopted by Becca.
*Nereus Charobim, the Black Pharaoh of legend, an avatar of Nyarlathotep.

The Red Knight is a character which was created by Lewis Carroll in 1871, first appearing in Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There. In the fictional Grimm Fairy Tales universe by Zenescope Entertainment, he first appeared in the Wonderland Annual 2009, and would play a role in the Cthulhu Mythos crossover Call of Wonderland.

### Background
Ben was a child who was inflicted with severe combined immunodeficiency, forcing him to live behind a germ-free barrier. Unfortunately, his family decided to relocate and moved into the Liddle family's former home, where his family were murdered by his disturbing drawings which came to life, after which he ended up in Wonderland. In the Realm of Nightmares, his true potential was unleashed, becoming the Red Knight, a killer who planned to destroy Wonderland and Earth by freeing the Old Ones.

Red Sonja is a character in the fictional universes of Marvel and Dynamite, who was created in 1975 by Roy Thomas for Marvel Comics. The character is a free adaptation of Robert E. Howard's Renaissance swordswoman, Red Sonya of Rogatino, who appeared in 1934 in the short story "The Shadow of The Vulture". 

Red Sonja first appeared in issue #23 of the 1st volume of Conan the Barbarian, from Marvel Comics. A hero of the Hyborian Age, who at times was the companion, ally, and love interest of Conan of Cimmeria.

### Background
### Marvel
The red-haired Hyrkanian girl Sonja lived in the steppes with her parents and siblings, until a gang of mercenaries slaughtered them all and violated Red Sonja. A goddess answered her cry for revenge, bestowing unparalleled combat skills on her. With the condition that she would never have sexual relations with a man, unless said man defeated her fairly in combat. She would go on to become an adventurer and mercenary. During her adventures she clashed with the forces of the Mythos in the form of Varnae the Lord of Vampires and the sorcerer Kulan Gath, and had encounters with the Darkhold and the N'Garai demons.

### Dynamite
The red-haired daughter of a Hyrkanian chief, Sonjita was the only survivor of a vicious raid on her village. She escaped into the wild, and would use her hunting skills to track down the raiders, killing them one by one. Later she is captured by slavers and for three years, she was forced to fight in the arena. In the process gaining unparalleled fighting skills and earning the name "Red Sonja". Afterwards she becomes an adventurer, a lusty and hotblooded warrior who loves battle. Eventually becoming the queen of Sogaria, after liberating it from the oppressive Emoran Empire.
During her adventures she fought the sorcerer Kulan Gath and later was transported several thousands of years into the future, where she fought alongside various heroes and supernatural beings (Dracula, Eva, Vampirella, Athena, Pantha, Herbert West, and Ash Williams) against the time displaced Kulan Gath and the Army of Darkness. After which she was sent back to her own time.

shortDefinition: "Red Star, Yellow Sign" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Leigh Kimmel. It was published in the thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press in April 2011.  ### Synopsis In the aftermath of the unexplained assassination of ...
fullContent:
"Red Star, Yellow Sign" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Leigh Kimmel. It was published in the thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press in April 2011.

### Synopsis
In the aftermath of the unexplained assassination of a senior Soviet politician, man named Yezhov is tasked with uncovering the motive for this attack on the State. He soon uncovers a plot by mystical forces to interfere in the affairs of humankind and, after discovering the entity controlling the human assassin - a monstrous Lloigor - embarks on a course of action which he believes will result in the purging of all supernatural elements from his country.

The story is interspersed with a series of missives between R'lyeh and the Leningrad Operational Center. These reveal that the initial assassination attempt was the result of poorly-planned meddling in human affairs; the final one explains how the manipulation of Yezhov and the sacrifice of a Lloigor agent had resulted in a violent program which would keep the secrets of the supernatural puppet masters safe for centuries.

### Behind the Mythos
During the course of his investigations, Yezhov discovers a small statue in the apartment of the assassin which he describes as looking like "a bat-winged man with staring eyes and a beard of squidlike tentacles." This is a clear nod to the statuette recovered during Inspector Legrasse's 1907 raid of the Cthulhu Cult, and ties in with the R'lyeh communications which exposit the antagonist's motivations in "Red Star, Yellow Sign."

Although the entity encountered by Yezhov is named as a Lloigor, it bears no resemblance to the more commonly depicted members of that species, being described as having "vast eyes like glowing saucers, surrounded by a mass of squirming tentacles patterned in colours that shifted and shimmered," a much more generic Cthulhu Mythos description than its reptilian namesake.

The Yellow Sign mentioned in the title refered to symbols etched on the statue found by Yezhov and imprinted on sewer walls by the Lloigor. Usually associated with the Great Old One Hastur, in this story the Sign was tied to Hastur's half-brother Cthulhu, the two entities being more commonly depicted as antagonistic in later Mythos stories.

### Trivia
* The assassination of Sergei Kirov was a real-world event which occurred in the Soviet Union in December 1934. The killing would cause the already-paranoid state leader Joseph Stalin to initiate the Great Purge, a political cleansing which would result in the deaths of hundreds of thousands.

"Reeling Back" is a short story by American author and games designer Tom Lynch. It forms a part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by C. J. Henderson.

### Synopsis
Sheriff-turned-manhunter Sam Branson is hired by the Arkham Detective Agency to track down a number of missing teenagers. His search leads him a to psychic who directs him to the supernatural abductor: the cosmic being known as Atlach-Nacha. With the aid of the psychic, he tracks the Great Old One to her throne of silk in the Dreamlands and succeeds in saving the boys.

### Characters

* Sam Branson, a former cowboy thrown forward in time to the modern age. Hired by the Arkham Detective Agency for his skills in finding people.
* Frank Nardi, a partner in the Agency.
* Atlach-Nacha, a Great Old One.
* Suzanne Wvinch, last in a long line of legitimate psychics.
* Shirley Manning, a teenage girl who was either a puppet or avatar of Atlach-Nacha, killed during Branson's rescue.

### Publication History
"Reeling Back" was written for the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology Arkham Detective Agency, published by Dark Regions Press in November 2017.

fullContent:
"Regnar Lodbrug's Epicedium" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Introduced with the lines An 8th Century Funeral Song . . . Translated from Olaus Wormius, the seven stanzas describe in brief the career of Regnar Lodbrug, the legendary Viking warrior more commonly known in English as Ragnar Lodbrok. The spelling that Lovecraft uses is closer to the Danish spelling of his name: Regnar Lodbrog.

### Publication History
Although written by Lovecraft in 1914, "Regnar Lodbrug's Epicedium" did not see publication until several years after his death in 1937.

shortDefinition: This page offers a selection of useful online resources related to H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos.  ### General Resources  ### BoardGameGeek A catalogue for board and tabletop games of all types, including information on designers and artists...
fullContent:
This page offers a selection of useful online resources related to H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos.

### General Resources

### BoardGameGeek
A catalogue for board and tabletop games of all types, including information on designers and artists associated with the publications. Includes a large number of Cthulhu Mythos and Mythos-related games. Website link: https://boardgamegeek.com/

### Comic Vine
A website dedicated to cataloguing comic book releases of all kinds, as well as characters and creators. Website link: https://comicvine.gamespot.com/

### Cthulhu Files
With a focus on the first generation (Lovecraft’s friends and correspondents) of Mythos writers. Features include the "Librarium Cthulhuvius," a compendium of related works by these authors. Website link: https://www.cthulhufiles.com

### Deep Cuts in a Lovecraftian Vein
A deep-dive blog site run by Bobby Derie, which focuses on “writers and protagonists that are female or POC, LGBTQ issues, and related themes of sex, gender, race, and all the other bits and pieces that people don’t normally like to talk about.” Website link: https://deepcuts.blog

### DriveThruRPG
A website dedicated to digital roleplaying of every genre, the site hosts a large amount of Lovecraftian gaming resources, including the Miskatonic Repository player-driven initiative. Website link: https://www.drivethrurpg.com/en/

### Goodreads
A book review aggregate site which covers every conceivable genre from non-fiction to comic books, and allows users create community discussion groups and vote for their favourite books of the year. Offers publication histories and synopses amongst other things. Website link: https://www.goodreads.com

### The H. P. Lovecraft Archive
Featuring contributions from prominent Lovecraft scholars S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz, the Archive addresses every aspect of Lovecraft from his life to his writings to critical studies on his work. Website link: https://www.hplovecraft.com

### The H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society
The website of the global Historical Society, HPLHS is devoted to producing period-authentic products related to Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos, including films, audio releases, gaming material, and other merchandise. Website link: https://www.hplhs.org

### The Internet Movie Database (IMDb)
A film, television, web original, and video game site which offers information on cast, crew, and production details, as well as user reviews and lists. Includes many Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos releases. Website link: https://www.imdb.com

### The Internet Speculative Fiction Database (ISFDB)
A catalogue of speculative fiction books; although it covers an enormous range of genres, a wealth of Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos publications can be found here. Website link: https://www.isfdb.org

### League of Comic Geeks
A website dedicated to comic book releases of all types, including Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos works. Website link: https://leagueofcomicgeeks.com

fullContent:
"Return to the Mountains of Madness" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ran Cartwright.

### Synopsis
A trio of ghost hunters investigating a crypt in the side of an Ohio mountain uncover a portal which through time and space leading to the Elder Thing city described in At the Mountains of Madness. 

There, they discover that Elder Things have been enslaved by the few remaining Shoggoths, who are conducting medical procedures on captured humans. These procedures are designed to make humans look more like Elder Things, so that they can offer them as sacrifice to the Shoggoths in their own place. Unfortunately for the ghost hunters, the Shoggoths seem to have developed a fairly high degree of intelligence, and none of them survive the encounter.

### Characters

*Bernie Howe, a technical genius.
*Karl Mayburg, the team leader.
*Jenni Osborne, a psychic sensitive.
*Rick Forney, the local who alerts the ghost hunters to the presence of the crypt.

### Publication History
"Return to the Mountains of Madness" was first published in the second issue of fanzine E'ch Pi El in February 2007, and also appeared in the collection of Cartwright's own work Of Gods & Aliens in October 2011.

fullContent:
"Revelation" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft, first published in the March 1919 edition of The Tryout.

### Poem
* In a vale of light and laughter,
* —Shining ’neath the friendly sun,
* Where fulfilment follow’d after
* —Ev’ry hope or dream begun;
* Where an Aidenn gay and glorious,
* —Beckon’d down the winsome way;
* There my soul, o’er pain victorious,
* —Laugh’d and lingered—yesterday.

* Green and narrow was my valley,
* —Temper’d with a verdant shade;
* Sun-deck’d brooklets musically
* —Sparkled thro’ each glorious glade;
* And at night the stars serenely
* —Glow’d betwixt the boughs o’erhead,
* While Astarte, calm and queenly,
* —Floods of fairy radiance shed.

* There amid the tinted bowers,
* —Raptur’d with the opiate spell
* Of the grasses, ferns, and flowers,
* —Poppy, phlox and pimpernel,
* Long I lay, entranc’d and dreaming,
* —Pleas’d with Nature’s bounteous store,
* Till I mark’d the shaded gleaming
* —Of the sky, and yearn’d for more.

* Eagerly the branches tearing,
* —Clear’d I all the space above,
* Till the bolder gaze, high faring,
* —Scann’d the naked skies of Jove;
* Deeps unguess’d now shone before me,
* —Splendid beam’d the solar car;
* Wings of fervid fancy bore me
* —Out beyond the farthest star.

* Reaching, gasping, wishing, longing
* —For the pageant brought to sight,
* Vain I watch’d the gold orbs thronging
* —Round celestial poles of light.
* Madly on a moonbeam ladder
* —Heav’n’s abyss I sought to scale,
* Ever wiser, ever sadder,
* —As the fruitless task would fail.

* Then, with futile striving sated,
* —Veer’d my soul to earth again,
* Well content that I was fated
* —For a fair, yet low domain;
* Pleasing thoughts of glad tomorrows,
* —Like the blissful moments past,
* Lull’d to rest my transient sorrows,
* —Still’d my godless greed at last.

* But my downward glance, returning,
* —Shrank in fright from what it spy’d;
* Slopes in hideous torment burning,
* —Terror in the brooklet’s tide:
* For the dell, of shade denuded
* —By my desecrating hand,
* ’Neath the bare sky blaz’d and brooded
* —As a lost, accursed land.

Rexford T. Murphy, also known as The Reporter, is a fictional character in the Arkham Horror series by Fantasy Flight Games.

### History
An investigative reporter for the Arkham Advertiser, Rex had looked into many strange reports in his time, but had always managed to lose any evidence before these stories had gone to press. His photographs from Innsmouth had blown out to sea in a gust of wind, the bizarre tracks he found in Dunwich had washed away in a freak storm before anyone was able to verify them, and those were most certainly not the only incidents.

On Rex’s most recent excursion, this time to Lithuania, he had gone to see an old gypsy fortune teller, who had screamed him right out of her home, claiming that he was cursed. Soon afterwards, the diary that he had uncovered concerning cult activity in the area had mysteriously gone missing.

Returning to Arkham empty-handed, Rex quickly went to work trying to uncover what he believed was a global conspiracy.

### The Dark Waters Trilogy

### Ghouls of the Miskatonic
In Graham McNeill's 2011 novel, Murphy joined forces with a disparate group of petty criminals, reporters, private detectives and academics to put a stop to a cult of Cthulhu worshippers who were murdering young women in Arkham. Although the group were successful, Murphy suffered lasting psychological damage from witnessing the cosmic entity Cthugha burning the cultists to cinders. (: Ghouls of the Miskatonic)

### Bones of the Yopasi
In the sequel to Ghouls of the Miskatonic, Murphy once again teamed up with Professors Oliver Grayson and Alexander Templeton, along with George Gammell Angell and Silas Marsh, to do battle with a cultist hell-bent on awakening Cthulhu from his slumber in order to destroy the world. During the course of their adventures, Rex and the others travelled to the Dreamlands to save the life of an illuminated lunatic. Later, Rex was grievously injured in battle with a swarm of Deep Ones, and the group failed in their quest to prevent the Eye of Infinite Stars from falling into the cultist's hands. (: Bones of the Yopasi)

### "Strange Things Done"
In Lisa Smedman's short story, Murphy and a mysterious man named Thorne - who may or may not have been a member of the secret society known as the Red Coterie - confronted and defeated an extra-dimensional entity known as an "Outsider" while en route to Alaska, although due to certain magical effects the reporter retained no memory of the encounter. (: "Strange Things Done")

### Behind the Mythos
The character of Rex Murphy was first introduced by Fantasy Flight as part of their Kingsport Horror expansion for the Second Edition of adventure board game Arkham Horror in 2008. Since then, they have used him in several of their other releases - including Arkham Horror: The Card Game and Elder Sign - and released a (now discontinued) plastic miniature of him as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures line.

Rhan-Tegoth is a Great Old One in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald for their short story "The Horror in the Museum".

### Description
Rhan-Tegoth is an entity shaped somewhat like an enormous insect, with a tremendous, barrel-shaped trunk with six appendages ending in claws-like pincers and a near-spherical head covered with hair-like filaments or feelers, a tentacle-like proboscis and three small, beady eyes. The hair-like feelers function as additional mouths that perforate the skin of the creature's prey and secrete digestive acids. Similar to Chaugnar Faugn, Rhan-Tegoth feeds by sucking out the blood and liquefied innards of its victims, the bodies of which are crushed and disfigured by the great strength of the monster.

Despite being a deity of comparatively little power, it is vital for the return of the Old Ones. It lived in the warm seas of Yuggoth before coming to Earth.

Three million years ago, during the Pliocene epoch, it inhabited an area of Alaska before going into a hibernation-like trance. Rhan-Tegoth was the last god to sleep, and was probably meant to be the first to wake. Its body was found by George Rogers and moved to a museum in London, 1926 (: "The Horror in the Museum"), but was then lost track of until It turned up, firstly in Sheffield, UK in the 1980s (: "The Return of Rhan-Tegoth"), and then in Chorazin, New York in the mid-to-late 1980s. (: "Wilbur Whateley Waiting")​ It was worshipped by the prehuman, cannibal Gnophkehs, but few humans know of it in modern times. (​: "The Scroll of Morloc")

shortDefinition: Rhode Island is a state in the New England region of the United States. It is the home state of H. P. Lovecraft and the setting of several Cthulhu Mythos tales. Its capital and largest city is Providence.  Known as the Ocean State, it is the smallest...
fullContent:
Rhode Island is a state in the New England region of the United States. It is the home state of H. P. Lovecraft and the setting of several Cthulhu Mythos tales. Its capital and largest city is Providence.

Known as the Ocean State, it is the smallest state in the union. Despite its name, it is mostly on the US mainland. It was founded by Roger Williams, who was expelled from the Massachusetts Bay Colony over his advocacy of religious tolerance.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Providence appears as a setting in such Lovecraft stories as "The Call of Cthulhu", "The Shunned House", and "The Haunter of the Dark".

The Case of Charles Dexter Ward takes place in both Providence and in Rhode Island's Pawtuxet Village, where Joseph Curwen has his laboratory. The climax takes place at a private hospital on Conanicut Island.

The town of Pascoag, Rhode Island, appears in the prologue to "The Horror at Red Hook" as the place where Thomas Malone goes to recouperate.

Bristol Highlands, a neighborhood in Bristol, Rhode Island, is mentioned in "The Strange High House in the Mist" as Thomas Olney's vacation home goes after his time in Kingsport--a place "where no tall crags tower, and the neighbours are urban and modern."

In The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, the litany of beloved scenes from Randolph Carter's youth includes the "hushed stony slopes and low ivied cottages in the lee of huge boulders in Rhode-Island’s back country".

Richard Allen Lupoff (21 February 1935-22 October 2020) was a prolific American author who wrote fiction in several genres, as well as non-fiction. He has written a number of pieces set in the greater Cthulhu Mythos, including at least one which features a fictionalised version of H. P. Lovecraft himself, the 1985 novel Lovecraft's Book.

Lupoff was well-versed in the works of Lovecraft, as well as those of Tarzan and John Carter creator Edgar Rice Burroughs , and he wrote numerous pieces on both topics .

Richard Corben (1940 - 2020) was an American artist, writer, publisher, and animator, who authored several comic book adaptations of H. P. Lovecraft's works, including "The Rats in the Walls", "Herbert West: Reanimator" and the anthology series H. P. Lovecraft's Haunt of Horror. His original story Rat God is set in the Cthulhu Mythos as well. His other works notably include the graphic novel Bloodstar (based on "The Valley of the Worm", by Robert E. Howard) and DC Comics' adaptation of The House on the Borderland, by William Hope Hodgson.

Over the course of a long and acclaimed career, Corben has illustrated stories of Conan, Vampirella, Hellboy, John Constantine, Batman, and many others. He is perhaps most well known for his work in the Heavy Metal magazine, including the saga of Den, which features a Cthulhu-like deity called Uhluhtc.

Richard E. Dansky is an author of horror and non-fiction, as well as a games designer who has worked on both traditional and video game releases. His Lovecraftian output has appeared in anthologies such as Madness on the Orient Express (2014, Chaosium) and Dark Tales from the Secret War (2015, Modiphius), and periodicals including Lovecraft Studies (Necronomicon Press).  

Dansky's non-Lovecraftian output includes extensive work on White Wolf Publishing's World of Darkness games Wraith: the Oblivion, Vampire: The Masquerade, and Changeling: The Dreaming, as well as a long career in video games design, including work on franchises such as the Tom Clancy universe, Assassin's Creed, and Far Cry.

He has cited H. P. Lovecraft, T. E. D. Klein, and Algernon Blackwood as amongst his influences.

Richard Franklyn Searight (13 June 1902 - ? September 1975) was an American author and correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft's.

### Overview
Searight wrote a few stories set in the Cthulhu Mythos, and many of his works were published in pulp magazine Weird Tales. He was  the creator of the ancient mystic writings known as the Eltdown Shards, which were later used by Lovecraft in "The Challenge from Beyond", although the two authors created divergent histories for the texts.

Richard was the father of the late Franklyn Searight, who wrote a significantly larger proportion of Mythos pieces than his father, and appears to have attempted to complete some of the elder Searight's unfinished works.

Richard L. Tierney (7 August 1936-1 February 2022) was an American writer and poet. Tierney, a scholar of H. P. Lovecraft, wrote Cthulhu Mythos novels and was the coauthor (with David C. Smith) of a series of Red Sonja novels, featuring cover art by Boris Vallejo. 

He is best known for two series: one featuring Simon of Gitta, a first century Samaritan who uses both sword and sorcery to fight the Roman Empire, the other focused on John Taggart, a time-travelling ally of alien forces. The two series come together in the novel The Drums of Chaos.

Tierney was one of the first to challenge August Derleth's interpretation of Lovecraft's creations in his notable article "The Derleth Mythos", published in Meade and Penny Frierson's fanzine H.P.L. (1973). In an interview for Sword & Sorcery magazine, however,  Tierney said that he considers his own Mythos work to be in the Derlethian vein:

Richard Upton Pickman is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Pickman's Model". He was a renowned Boston painter notorious for his graphic works.

### Biography
### Lovecraft's Work
Pickman's origins are ambiguous. His artwork depicts the ghouls as having the habit of abducting human children and replacing them with "changelings": ghoul children that look deceptively human-like, left to be raised by humans. One of the children depicted bears an uncanny resemblance to Pickman himself, hinting that he might have been one of those changelings. If true, this could explain his close association with ghouls (: "Pickman's Model"), and the fact that he apparently transformed into a ghoul himself at some point after his disappearance (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath).

As an artist, Pickman had undeniable skill. "Boston never had a greater painter than Richard Upton Pickman," his one-time friend and devotee Thurber declared. His "morbid art was preëminently one of daemoniac portraiture," with "frightful pictures which turned colonial New England into a kind of annex of hell"--though he went on to do a series of "modern studies" that "brought the horror right into our own daily life." He was "a thorough, painstaking, and almost scientific realist," Thurber maintained, whose art "coldly and sardonically reflected some stable, mechanistic, and well-established horror-world which he saw fully, brilliantly, squarely, and unfalteringly." (: "Pickman's Model") 

Pickman came from "old Salem stock," and had a great-great-great-great-grandmother hanged during the Witch Trials in 1692. He had a studio on Newbury Street in Boston's Back Bay neighborhood, and another one in the North End that he rented under the name Peters. There he painted in the cellar, where he said he could "catch the night-spirit of antique horror and paint things that I couldn’t even think of in Newbury Street." (: "Pickman's Model")

"It’s my business to catch the overtones of the soul, and you won’t find those in a parvenu set of artificial streets," he claimed. It was his contention that "one must paint terror as well as beauty from life." (: "Pickman's Model")

Pickman's art grew increasingly shocking, to the point where several people in his social circle refused to associate with him. Dr. Reid, an acquaintance who studied comparative pathology, insisted that the artist "repelled him more and more every day...that the fellow’s features and expression were slowly developing in a way he didn’t like"; he told Pickman he was "a sort of monster bound down the toboggan of reverse evolution." fullContent:
Richard Watts (born 1967) is an Australian game designer, arts journalist and broadcaster who has been writing for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game for over three decades. He also contributed to Chaosium's out of print Stormbringer and Elric! game lines, as well as to White Wolf's World of Darkness games in the 1990s.

### Overview
After encouragement from his friend and former housemate Mark Morrison, as well as then-Line Editor Keith Herber, Watts' first contribution to Call of Cthulhu was the scenario "A Little Knowledge" in the first edition on Arkham Unveiled (1990). Two of his scenarios for the game, the Ramsey Campbell-inspired "Love's Lonely Children" in Cthulhu Now collection The Stars Are Right! and the 1920s-set "Behold the Mother" in Dead Reckonings (which introduced Watts' most significant contribution to the Cthulhu Mythos to date, the lesser Outer God known as the Mother of Pus) appeared on a list of "The Most Disturbing Call of Cthulhu Scenarios Chaosium Has Ever Licensed". Most recently he contributed to the second edition of Chaosium's Terror Australis (2018) and Golden Goblin Press' Cthulhu Invictus supplement Britannia & Beyond (2023), for which he wrote the chapter about Ireland/Hibernia.

Richard Joseph "Rick" Lai (6 October 1955 - 30 April 2024) was an American author of primarily horror and fantasy, whose career intersected with the Cthulhu Mythos and Lovecraftian horror on numerous occasions. Perhaps most notable to this wiki are his stories involving H. P. Lovecraft's Herbert West, David Conyers' and Brian M. Sammons' Harrison Peel, Lin Carter's Anton Zarnak, and Jeff Rice's Carl Kolchak.

Lai was a close friend of The Lovecraft eZine founder and editor Mike Davis, and has been described as possessing a "seemingly limitless wealth of knowledge about the history and mythology surrounding The Shadow, H.P. Lovecraft, Doc Savage, Robert E. Howard, Philip Jose Farmer and so many other characters and writers from the classic pulp era."

fullContent:
Rifts is a genre-spanning roleplaying game created by American designer Kevin Siembieda. First launched in 1990, it and its many supplements have remained in constant publication through Palladium Books ever since. In addition to the core roleplaying game, several tie-in novels, a collectible card game, and a video game have also been released .

### Premise
The world of Rifts is set several hundred years in the future in a world torn apart by nuclear war and subsequently reshaped by the opening of rifts, interdimensional portals which allow access to other planes of existence and, conversely, the denizens of said planes to access our own world. Due to the enormously varied locations made accessible by these rifts, the game can support virtually any type of roleplaying game, but has a strong focus on the cyberpunk, fantasy, science fiction, and horror genres.

### Mythos Connections
The setting describes a number of entities which many consider Lovecraftian in nature, including the Alien Intelligences, but notably contains no direct references to either the Cthulhu Mythos or the works of H. P. Lovecraft.

Originally published as part of the Miskatonic University Library Association monograph series (a precursor to the community content programs now common in the world of tabletop role-playing games, and which was retired in 2022), Ripples from Carcosa was republished by Chaosium in 2014, edited and developed by Mike Mason.
