"Ripples in the Ether" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle. It stars the character of Professor Challenger created by Arthur Conan Doyle.

### Synopsis
A Scotsman’s attempts to broadcast pictures using radio waves inadvertently attracts the attention of a bizarre alien entity whose very presence is inimical to life on Earth. Luckily for the human race, Professor Challenger is on hand to identify the source of the attractant and, once reversed, the entity departs with no further incidents.

### Characters
*Professor Challenger, a highly-intelligent scientist.
*Malone, a reporter and Challenger's friend.
*Logie Baird, an overly-enthusiastic inventor.

### Publication History
*The Alchemy Press Book of Pulp Heroes (2012)
*Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2017)
*Builders: Three Tales of Weird Science (2020)

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, "Ripples in the Ether"'s inclusion in the collection Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates the author's belief that the story is in the same spirit as these works.

"Rise of Thalhulla" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Joshua Robinson. It was first published in the Gavin Chappell-edited horror magazine Lovecraftiana Vol 8, Issue 2 (2023, Rogue Planet Press) .

### Synopsis
Horror writer William travels to a remote Spanish island after being drawn there by an image of an incredible painting he stumbled across online. At the island's only hotel, he finally manages to examine the painting, and is stunned by the level of detail. The hotel's owner Angela informs him that it depicts the upcoming return of a titanic alien being named Thalhulla.

Over dinner, Angela informs William of the island's history, of how the people once worshipped the star-born Thalhulla and were rewarded with protection and the ocean's bounty. However, after witnessing the horrific appearance of Thalhulla's only son, the people slaughtered him and turned their backs on their former god. Vowing vengeance, the being slunk back beneath the waves.

After being drugged by Angela, who reveals herself to be the last priestess of Thalhulla, William is put through a horrific procedure by the woman and her daughter where he is turned into a semi-cephalopod creature and thrown into the ocean; there, he unites with the many others who have undergone this treatment to form Thalhulla's army, and witness the rising of their god, now ready to wreak its vengeance on an unsuspecting world…

### Behind the Mythos
The story mentions that the painting seen by William remind him of H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth, establishing that Lovecraft exists in this universe. This is further reinforced when William is shown to have a tattoo of Cthulhu, acquired on his eighteenth birthday.

"Rising with Surtsey" is a short story by British author Brian Lumley set in the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Phillip Haughtree has to have his brother Julian committed to an asylum, as the latter is showing signs of severe mental distress. When Julian is released, he appears to have been rehabilitated, but is still displaying an obsession with the occult. When Phillip confronts him about his mania, Julian reveals that his mind has been taken over by a Minion of Othuum, and Phillip kills him accidentally before being himself committed for raving about ancient monsters.

### Characters
*Phillip Haughtree

*Gordon Walmsley
*Pesh-Tlen

### Publication History
"Rising with Surtsey" was first published in the 1971 Arkham House anthology Dark Things, edited by August Derleth. It was included in the revised edition of Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1990), and has appeared in Lumley's collections The Second Wish and Other Exhalations (New English Library, 1995), Beneath the Moors and Darker Places (Tor, 2002), and The Taint and Other Novellas (Subterranean Press, 2007).

Rita Young is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos-related content.

### History
Growing up as part of a poor family in the American South, Rita is well acquainted with persecution, but as a strong independent young woman never let it get to her.

Discovering from an early age that she possessed a natural ability as an athlete, Rita worked hard and managed to secure herself a track-and-field scholarship at Arkham's prestigious Miskatonic University.

### Ghouls of the Miskatonic
Graham McNeill's novel Ghouls of the Miskatonic expands on Rita's character considerably, showing that she has a certain knowledge of black magic, and perhaps even a degree of proficiency in its use.

In the story, Rita and her best friend, roommate Amanda Sharpe, are kidnapped by a sinister cult of Cthulhu worshipers and their pet ghouls, but are eventually rescued by a ragtag group of people investigating the disappearances, including Rex Murphy and Finn Edwards.

### Behind the Mythos
The character of Rita Young was first introduced in the Arkham Horror Second Edition expansion Dunwich Horror. She later appeared in Eldritch Horror, Mansions of Madness, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, the aforementioned Ghouls of the Miskatonic, and in the form of a gaming accessory as part of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line.

The River Skai is a river in the Dreamlands that originates on Mount Lerion. It flows through fertile plains, fields, and meadows, beautiful countryside, and peaceful farmland near the towns of Ulthar, Nir, and Hatheg. The river then continues all the way down to the city of Dylath-Leen on the Southern Sea. A smooth trade road used by merchant caravans runs along the river between the aforementioned towns and cities. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

Near Ulthar the river flows past the Enchanted Wood where a village of the zoogs is located in the central part of the forest. A great stone bridge also spans the river at Ulthar. The masons who originally built the bridge sealed a living human sacrifice within the central support thirteen hundred years before Randolph Carter first visited the Dreamlands. Rlim Shaikorth (The White Worm) is a fictional entity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Coming of the White Worm", which purports to be a chapter of the Book of Eibon.

### Description


Appearing as a gigantic, pale, white worm with a great gaping maw and empty sockets for eyes that drip blood continuously, Rlim Shaikorth was a being of unknown origin, although it is hinted that it originated in another world or dimension (Smith uses the word "ultraterrestrial", a term he often used in lieu of "extraterrestrial"). It fed on the bodies, souls and knowledge of the most powerful of sorcerers, and the more it consumed, the larger it grew. It was also capable of causing those within its immediate vicinity to fall into a deep sleep, and to control their actions whilst in the state.

Due to the great age and unrecognisable origin of some of the artefacts frozen within Rlim Shaikorth's iceberg-fortress Yikilth, it is assumed to be an entity of tremendous age.

### History
Rlim Shaikorth first came to Earth during the Hyperborean Age and it proceeded to roam the coastline on Yikilth, inflicting death and destruction on the land seemingly for the sake of it and inducting magic-users into its priesthood as a source of sustenance.

Rlim Shaikorth was destroyed by the mage Evagh, who caught it during a period of rest and was able to inflict a mortal wound on the creature, an act which also resulted in the destruction of Yikilth.

### Behind the Mythos
Rlim Shaikorth's place among the Great Old Ones is ambiguous. Although the "Old Ones" are mentioned twice in its debut story, there is no indication that Rlim Shaikorth is one of them. If anything, the sorcerers' urging Evagh "by the faith of the Old Ones" to destroy Rlim Shaikorth would seemingly imply that the Old Ones might be its enemies.

Conversely, in the greater Cthulhu Mythos, such an enmity might be explainable: in Smith's stories, the Old Ones venerated in Mhu Thulan are subterranean beings such as Tsathoggua and Atlach-Nacha (: "The Seven Geases"), which, according to the elemental theory of August Derleth, would be inimical to Cthugha (: "The Dweller in Darkness"). Since Lin Carter identifies Rlim Shaikorth as the Lesser Old One who serves Cthugha's son, Aphoom-Zhah, it makes sense that the "earth beings" would oppose it.

In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, Rlim Shaikorth itself is classified as a Great Old One. It is mentioned that it repeatedly appears and disappears on Earth and Dreamlands, and when it is defeated, it goes to another dimension along with Yikilth, and reform itself after a few hundred years.  (: Malleus Monstrorum: Cthulhu Mythos Bestiary Volume II)

shortDefinition: Robert Anton Wilson (January 18, 1932 – January 11, 2007) wrote 35 books and over 1,500 published articles. He coauthored, with Robert Shea, the underground classic The Illuminatus! Trilogy, which won the 1986 Prometheus Hall of Fame Award. His writi...
fullContent:
Robert Anton Wilson (January 18, 1932 – January 11, 2007) wrote 35 books and over 1,500 published articles. He coauthored, with Robert Shea, the underground classic The Illuminatus! Trilogy, which won the 1986 Prometheus Hall of Fame Award. His writings include Schrödinger’s Cat Trilogy, called “the most scientific of all science fiction novels,” by New Scientist, and nonfiction works of Futurist psychology and guerrilla ontology, such as The Cosmic Trigger Trilogy, Prometheus Rising, Quantum Psychology and The New Inquisition.

Bob worked as an associate editor at Playboy magazine from 1966 to 1971. 

In 1975, with his wife Arlen, he founded the Institute for the Study of the Human Future. 

In 1976, he created the Starflight Network to help implement Timothy Leary’s SMI2LE philosophy (Space Migration, Intelligence Increase, and Life Extension), and promote The Eight Circuit Model of Consciousness  (see Prometheus Rising). Bob regularly gave seminars at Esalen and other New Age centers, and lectures across North America and Europe. He made both a comedy record (Secrets of Power) and a punk rock record (The Chocolate Biscuit Conspiracy), and his play Wilhelm Reich in Hell was performed at the Edmund Burke Theatre in Dublin, Ireland. 

His novel Illuminatus! was adapted as a 10-hour science fiction rock epic and performed under the patronage of Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II at Great Britain’s National Theatre, where Bob appeared briefly on stage in a special cameo role. In 2006, as the unofficial write-in candidate for the Guns and Dope Party, Bob unsuccessfully ran in the election for Governor of California.

Robert Harrison Blake is the fictional alter ego of real-life author Robert Bloch. This alter ego was created by H. P. Lovecraft and placed as the protagonist of the story "The Haunter of the Dark". It is primarily based on Robert Bloch but also incorporates elements of the personality and history of H. P. Lovecraft himself, as well as author Clark Ashton Smith.

This alter ego creation was a friendly parody of Robert Bloch by Lovecraft following their correspondence by mail.

Lovecraft's tale "The Haunter of the Dark" names five stories written by Robert Blake: "The Burrower Beneath"; "Shaggai"; "The Stairs in the Crypt"; "In the Vale of Pnath" and "The Feaster from the Stars". These are all references to real published works written by Robert Bloch.

fullContent:
Robert Albert Bloch (April 5 1917, Chicago – September 23 1994, Los Angeles) was a prolific American writer. He was the son of Raphael "Ray" Bloch (1884, Chicago-1952, Chicago), a bank cashier, and his wife Stella Loeb (1880, Attica, Indiana-1944, Milwaukee, WI), a social worker, both of German-Jewish descent.

Bloch wrote hundreds of short stories and over twenty novels, usually crime fiction, science fiction, and, perhaps most influentially, horror fiction (Psycho and American Gothic). He was one of the youngest members of the Lovecraft Circle; Lovecraft was Bloch's mentor and one of the first to seriously encourage his talent.

He was a contributor to pulp magazines such as Weird Tales in his early career, and was also a prolific screenwriter. He was the recipient of the Hugo Award (for his story "That Hell-Bound Train"), the Bram Stoker Award, and the World Fantasy Award. He served a term as president of the Mystery Writers of America.

Robert Bloch was also a major contributor to science fiction fanzines and fandom in general. In the 1940s, he created the humorous character Lefty Feep in a story for Fantastic Adventures. He also worked for a time in local vaudeville, and tried to break into writing for nationally known performers. He was a good friend of the science fiction writer Stanley G. Weinbaum. He worked on assistant city attorney Carl F. Zeidler's successful 1940 campaign to become mayor of Milwaukee, and afterwards worked in advertising for several years.

### Early writing career
During the 1930s, Bloch was an avid reader of the pulp magazine Weird Tales. H. P. Lovecraft, a frequent contributor to that magazine, became one of his favorite writers. As a teenager, Bloch befriended and corresponded with Lovecraft, who gave the promising youngster advice on his own fiction-writing efforts. Bloch's first professional sales, at the age of just seventeen, were to Weird Tales with the short stories "The Feast in the Abbey" and "The Secret in the Tomb". Bloch's early stories were strongly influenced by Lovecraft, and a number of his stories were set in, and extended, the world of Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. It was Bloch who invented, for example, the oft-cited Mythos texts De Vermis Mysteriis and Cultes des Goules.


The young Bloch even appears, thinly disguised, as the character "Robert Blake" in Lovecraft's story "The Haunter of the Dark", which is dedicated to Bloch. In this story, Lovecraft kills off the Bloch character, repaying a courtesy Bloch paid Lovecraft with his tale "The Shambler from the Stars", in which the Lovecraft-inspired figure dies; the story goes so far as to use Bloch's then-current street address in Milwaukee. (Bloch even had a signed certificate from Lovecraft [and some of his creations] giving Bloch permission to kill Lovecraft off in a story.) Bloch later wrote a third tale, "The Shadow From the Steeple", picking up where "The Haunter of the Dark" finished.

fullContent:
Robert Ervin Howard was an American pulp writer of fantasy, horror, historical adventure, boxing, Western, and detective fiction. Howard wrote "over three-hundred stories and seven-hundred poems of raw power and unbridled emotion," and is especially noted for his memorable depictions of "a sombre universe of swashbuckling adventure and darkling horror."

He is well known for having created — in the pages of the legendary Depression-era pulp magazine Weird Tales — the character Conan the Cimmerian, a.k.a. Conan the Barbarian, a literary icon whose pop-culture imprint can be compared to such icons as Tarzan of the Apes, Count Dracula, Sherlock Holmes, and James Bond.

In the late 1920s and early 1930s, between Conan and his other heroes, Howard created the genre now known as sword-and-sorcery, spawning a wide swath of imitators and giving him an influence in the fantasy field rivaled only by J.R.R. Tolkien's creation of High Fantasy.

As a seminal figure in the history of modern fantasy, Howard remains a highly read author, with his best work endlessly reprinted. He has been compared to other American masters of the weird, gloomy, and spectral, such as Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville, and Jack London.

In August 1930 Howard wrote a letter to Weird Tales praising a recent reprint of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Rats in the Walls" and discussing some of the obscure Gaelic references used within. Wright forwarded the letter to Lovecraft, who responded warmly to Howard, and soon the two Weird Tales veterans were engaged in a vigorous correspondence that would last for the rest of Howard's life. He became a prominent member of "The Lovecraft Circle," a group of writers and friends all linked via the immense correspondence of Lovecraft, who made it a point to introduce his many like-minded friends to each other and encourage them to share stories, adopt each other's invented fictional trappings, and help each other succeed in the pulp field. In time, this circle of correspondents has developed a legend rivaling literary conclaves such as The Inklings, the Bloomsbury Group, and the Beats.

Howard was given the affectionate nickname "Two-Gun Bob" by virtue of his long explications to Lovecraft about the history of his beloved Southwest, and during the ensuing years he contributed several notable elements to Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos shared universe. Howard's Mythos stories include: "The Black Stone", "The Children of the Night", and "The Fire of Asshurbanipal". He also corresponded with other Weird Tale writers such as Clark Ashton Smith, August Derleth, and E. Hoffmann Price.

Throughout this time, Howard continued to be dogged by fits of increasing melancholy and depression, and he maintained his belief in suicide as an ultimate escape. His close friends had married and were immersed in their careers, Novalyne Price had left Cross Plains for graduate school, and his most reliable market, Weird Tales, had fallen far behind on his payments.

Robert H. Waugh is a scholar and occasional editor who has written numerous works on the life and career of H. P. Lovecraft, as well as a small number of Lovecraftian short stories. His Lovecraft scholarship has been published in a series of volumes by Hippocampus Press and Scarecrow Press, and has also appeared in publications including Lovecraft Studies, Lovecraft Annual, and An Epicure in the Terrible, while his Lovecraftian short fiction has seen print in Black Wings.

Outside of his Lovecraft-related written material, Waugh is a Professor Emeritus in the field of English at the State University of New York.

Sir Robert Jermyn is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family".

### Background
Sir Robert Jermyn was a noted anthropologist who explored Africa, and was the great-grandfather of Arthur Jermyn. He married a daughter of the seventh Viscount Brightholme in 1815 and had three children including his second son Nevil. The youngest and eldest are unnamed and were never publicly seen due to physical and mental deformities. 

When an explorer named Samuel Seaton visited Robert at his home in 1852 with a manuscript of notes collected in Africa, Robert discovered to his horror that there was a simian strain in his own family originating from a union between his grandfather Wade Jermyn and a female member of a race of African white apes. The unhinged Robert murdered Seaton along with his own three children, but his two year old grandson Alfred survived. 

During the second year of his confinement in an asylum, Robert died of apoplexy after repeated attempts at suicide. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

fullContent:
Robert McNair Price is an American theologian, writer, editor and artist. He has written extensively within the Cthulhu Mythos, and created a podcast discussing the Lovecraft Mythos which ran to more than a hundred episodes.

He is known for arguing against the existence of a historical Jesus (the Christ myth theory). He teaches philosophy and religion at the Johnnie Colemon Theological Seminary, is professor of biblical criticism at the Center for Inquiry Institute, and the author of a number of books on theology and the historicity of Jesus.

Price was also a member of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts and scholars active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s.

### H. P. Lovecraft Scholarship
As editor of the journal Crypt of Cthulhu (published by Necronomicon Press) and of a series of Cthulhu Mythos anthologies, Price has been a major figure in H. P. Lovecraft scholarship and fandom for many years. In essays that introduce the anthologies and the individual stories, Price traces the origins of Lovecraft's entities, motifs, and literary style. The Cthulhu Cycle, for example, saw the origins of the octopoid entity in Alfred Lord Tennyson's "The Kraken" and particular passages from Lord Dunsany, while The Dunwich Cycle points to the influence of Arthur Machen on Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror."

Price's religious background often informs his Mythos criticism, seeing gnostic themes in Lovecraft's fictional god Azathoth, and interpreting "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" as a kind of initiation ritual.

Most of the early Call of Cthulhu Fiction books by Chaosium were overseen by Price; his first book was The Hastur Cycle (1993), an anthology of short stories which traced the development of a single Lovecraftian element, and this was followed by Mysteries of the Worm (1993), a collection of Robert Bloch's Mythos fiction.

### Publishing
Price has been involved in the publication of numerous works, including several related to H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos. He has self-published under his own name, and under several others, including Miskatonic University Press and Cryptic Publications.

Robert Martin Olmstead (: "Notes for The Shadow Over Innsmouth") is the narrator of The Shadow Over Innsmouth. It is remarked that his eyes have the same strange quality seen in all descendants of Obed Marsh. In the story's final pages, he learns he himself is the great-great-grandson of Obed Marsh and a Deep One, and in time will become one of the amphibious monsters he witnessed in Innsmouth.

Growing up in Toledo, he journeys to Massachusetts and stops at Innsmouth almost by chance, as it is on the way from Newburyport to Arkham, while on a journey to discover more of his family roots.

Olmstead's name is never given within the original story, but is given as Robert Martin Olmstead in Lovecraft's notes for the story.

In "The Watcher from the Sky", by August Derleth, a character refers to the Shadow Over Innsmouth narrator as Williamson. In the original story, James Williamson was the name of Olmstead's maternal grandfather.

fullContent:
Robert Spencer Carr (1909 - 1994) was an American author and screenwriter who contributed several stories and poems to the pulp magazine Weird Tales between 1925 and 1928.

Carr was one of the many authors to be spoofed in the comedic short story "The Battle that Ended the Century", by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. The story tells of an absurdly violent boxing match in the then-future year of 2000, and features parodies of the authors' friends and colleagues. Carr appears as the referee, "Robertieff Essovitch Karovsky, the Muscovite Ambassador", referencing the real Carr's communist and Russian sympathies.

At the time "The Battle that Ended the Century" was written, Carr was actually living in Russia, where he stayed until 1938. Seeing the horrors of Joseph Stalin's regime led him to return to the USA and renounce his membership of the communist party.

Carr is also known for his involvement in UFOlogical research, including his claim that the US military has conducted autopsies on the bodies of extraterrestrials whose spaceship crashed in the vicinity of Aztec, New Mexico.

Robert Silverberg (born 15 January 1935) is an American author and editor, most active in the sci-fi and fantasy genres, who wrote the Cthulhu Mythos short story "Demons of Cthulhu". His work notably includes the Majipoor series, set on the eponymous planet populated by multiple sapient species. He is married to fellow science fiction author Karen Haber.

Silverberg's Lovecraftian works have been included in anthologies such as The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 and The Necronomicon: Selected Stories and Essays Concerning the Blasphemous Tome of the Mad Arab, as well as Robert M. Price's long running fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu.

Robert Suydam is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Horror at Red Hook".

### Overview
Robert Suydam is described as "a lettered recluse of ancient Dutch family, possessed originally of barely independent means, and inhabiting the spacious but ill-preserved mansion which his grandfather had built in Flatbush." Seen by most as "a queer, corpulent old fellow whose unkempt white hair, stubbly beard, shiny black clothes, and gold-headed cane earned him an amused glance", the police detective Thomas Malone knew of him as "a really profound authority on mediaeval superstition." On account of "certain odd changes in his speech and habits; wild references to impending wonders, and unaccountable hauntings of disreputable Brooklyn neighbourhoods," his relatives tried unsuccessfully to have him declared insane. He is about 60 in the time frame of the story. (: "The Horror at Red Hook")

fullContent:
Robert William Chambers was an American artist and writer.

### Biography
He was born in Brooklyn, New York, to William P. Chambers (1827 - 1911), a famous lawyer, and Caroline Chambers (née Boughton), a direct descendant of Roger Williams, the founder of Providence, Rhode Island. Robert's brother was Walter Boughton Chambers, the world famous architect.

Robert was first educated at the Brooklyn Polytechnic Institute,and then entered the Art Students' League at around the age of twenty, where the artist Charles Dana Gibson was his fellow student. Chambers studied at the École des Beaux-Arts, and at Académie Julian, in Paris from 1886 to 1893, and his work was displayed at the Salon as early as 1889. On his return to New York, he succeeded in selling his illustrations to Life, Truth, and Vogue magazines. Then, for reasons unclear, he devoted his time to writing, producing his first novel, In the Quarter (written in 1887 in Munich ). His most famous, and perhaps most meritorious, effort is The King in Yellow, a collection of weird fiction short stories, connected by the theme of a book (to which the title refers) which drives those who read it insane. Chambers' fictitious drama The King in Yellow features in Karl Edward Wagner's story "The River of Night's Dreaming", while James Blish's story "More Light" purports to include much of the actual text of the play.

Chambers' returned to the weird genre in his later short story collections The Maker of Moons and The Tree of Heaven, but neither earned him such success as The King in Yellow.

Chambers later turned to writing romantic fiction to earn a living. According to some estimates, Chambers was one of the most successful literary careers of his period, his later novels selling well and a handful achieving best-seller status. Many of his works were also serialized in magazines.

Chambers, for several years made Broadalbin his summer home. Some of his novels touch upon colonial life in Broadalbin and Johnstown.

On July 12, 1898, he married Elsa Vaughn Moller (1882-1939). They had a son, Robert Edward Stuart Chambers (later calling himself Robert Husted Chambers) who also gained some fame as an author.

|Selected Letters 2.282}}


He died at his home in the village of Broadalbin, New York on December 16th 1933.

A critical essay on Chambers' work appears in S. T. Joshi's book The Evolution of the Weird Tale (2004).

### In the Mythos
Chambers wrote The King in Yellow, influenced by the Necronomicon. (: "History of the Necronomicon")

He changed reality by the powers invoked by his writings, making his suicide chambers a real thing known as "exit gardens". (: Providence)

Robert Edward Weinberg (1946-2016) was an American author and editor who wrote horror, science fiction, fantasy, and superhero comic books, as well as numerous nonfiction works related to genre fiction. He wrote the Reader's Guide to the Cthulhu Mythos (1969), a comprehensive bibliography of Mythos-related writing, and several of his early short stories were set in the Mythos universe. He edited or co-edited dozens of anthologies, including  Lovecraft's Legacy (1990) and Miskatonic University (1996), both with Martin H. Greenberg. The Abominable Snowmen are robots created by BBC in 1967 for their long-running Doctor Who franchise.

### Background
The Robot Yeti are robots created and used by the Great Intelligence on Earth. The Great Intelligence is believed by some to be identical with Yog-Sothoth. 

Robot Yeti were deployed by the Great Intelligence in Tibet, where they formed its footsoldiers during a convoluted plan to conquer Earth. The robots were large and hairy, fur covering everything except the eyes, claws, and feet. Yeti robots had green eyes and yellow teeth. The Doctor encountered several types of Robot Yeti with the Mark I types being equipped with Web-guns, the Mark II types firing webs from their claws, and the New World types being impervious to bombs. All of them were were armed with fangs and claws, and possessed augmented durability and strength.

fullContent:
Robyn Hood: Dagon is a 40 page Cthulhu Mythos comic book written by Joe Brusha, and featuring artwork by Alessio Mariani (Artist, Penciller) and Juan M Rodriguez (Colorist). It was published digitally by Zenescope Entertainment on January 11, 2023 with three variant covers.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Robyn Hood is a female archer superhero living in 2020s New York. A swashbuckler and adventurer, she is attracted to a mystery in the sewers beneath New York. There, she encounters Deep Ones who worship the dread Old One Dagon, and in the process of teaming up with other street level heroes "in the shadows of New York" the girls battle the Deep Ones, a shantak, and ultimately - Dagon. The story is quite abrupt, a function of the edits imposed upon it, but it incorporates the Innsmouth part of the Mythos into the broader Zenescope universe, setting up the building confrontation between the female superheroes and antiheroes of Zenescope, and the horrors of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Behind the Mythos
The Deep Ones in this story have much more in common with the monsters from Humanoids from the Deep or The Creature From The Black Lagoon (see the article on this wikia "Deep Ones in Popular Culture") than the more squamous and blobby frog-men from the original Lovecraft story, The Shadow Over Innsmouth. Also of note, Dagon is the god of the fish-men in this story and very definitely of a significant power rank, not just an over-sized Deep One.

Roger William Corman (5 April 1926-9 May 2024) was a prolific American producer, director, and occasional actor with over 500 film credits to his name. Best known for his work in the B-movie horror genre, his output included film adaptations of the works of classic authors such as Edgar Allan Poe and H. P. Lovecraft.

In addition to the films which he had a hand in realising, in 1975 Corman was approached by Colombian writer Andrés Caicedo with pitches for, amongst others, adaptations of Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth and Clark Ashton Smith's "The Nameless Offspring." Roger Little is a fictional character created by Frank Belknap Long for his novel The Horror from the Hills.

### Biography
Roger Little is an occult detective and inventor known for having investigated various cases of supernatural phenomena. He has an interest in criminal psychology and a reputation as something of an eccentric.

At some point in his life, Little worked as a criminal investigator and psychologist who dealt in cases involving Fortean phenomena, including several cases of men and women abducted in broad daylight by the Fishers from Outside. Little has documented, as he puts it, "dozens of instances of possession, of return, of immolation, of divination, and of transformation", proved the existence of vampires, succubi and lamias, and "slipped not too unwillingly, into the warm and clinging arms of women five centuries dead". His research into the occult has led him to witness instances of other worlds impinging on ours, and to establish contact with noncorporeal entities "in the void a thousand billion light years beyond the remotest of the spiral nebulae". Little has had such experiences in both dreams and waking ours, the latter which he claims requires "infinite patience and self-discipline, and years of study".

While he eventually retired as a detective and became known as a recluse, Little continued to use his knowledge to fight abnormal threats, and to invent fantastic devices, chief of which is the entropy-reversing machine. He has also authored several books about the supernatural and expressed an interest in writing fiction.

Like Hsieh Ho, Little is an individual of above-average psychic sensitivity and had a dream prophesying the return of Chaugnar Faugn and its brothers from a long period of isolation. Archaeologist Clark Ulman had brought what was initially assumed to be a stone idol of Chaugnar Faugn to the Manhattan Museum of Fine Arts, and the idol emerged from stasis, revealing itself as the actual living god and brutally killing the museum's watchman to feed on his blood. At roughly the same time in the Pyrenees, the Brothers of Chaugnar Faugn descended from the mountains and killed fourteen people. The museum's Curator of Archaeology Algernon Harris and ethnologist Henry C. Imbert sought Little's assistance, which the retired recluse was at first reluctant to provide until Harris mentioned the name Chaugnar Faugn, leading Little to realize the real meaning of the dream he'd had earlier.

Roland Banks, the Fed, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror series of Cthulhu Mythos publications. He made his first appearance in the 2009 expansion Innsmouth Horror.

### Overview






### Description
As can be gathered from Fantasy Flight's various flavour texts, Roland is known for being something of a stickler for the rules. On occasion, however, in extraordinary circumstances, he is shown to be willing to throw procedure out of the window in the interests of serving justice, as seen when he tackled the case of a murdered orchestra (see "History," below).

### History
Banks had been a model agent for his entire career, but during one particular investigation had the bad luck to get caught up in a local situation in which corrupt local authorities had struck a deal with local bootleggers to supply their town with illegal hooch. Although Banks tried to bring the authorities to justice, it transpired that at least one of the perpetrators had had connections high in the federal bureaucracy. Immediately removed from the case, he was reassigned, and word went out within the bureau that Banks was now blacklisted.(: The Dirge of Reason)

Banks was subsequently assigned to investigate a case in the jurisdiction of Arkham, the case of a murdered orchestra which the Bureau had been pressured to solve by yet more meddling higher-ups, and which his superiors believed would be unsolvable - adding yet another black mark to his record. As it turned out, Banks was far more resourceful and open-minded than his superiors had counted on, and discovered that the orchestra's conductor had been putting ancient Sumerian texts to music, accidentally summoning an otherworldly entity which destroyed them all. Banks managed to defeat the being and close the gate torn open by the orchestra's music, and file a report which seemed plausible yet contained no mention of the supernatural causes which would have had him labelled as a kook.(: The Dirge of Reason)

At the conclusion of the Arkham orchestra case, Banks received word that he was being transferred to a clandestine division with a special remit involving unusual cases, although it was never explained what this unit actually was.(: The Dirge of Reason)

### Behind the Mythos
The division to which Banks was being transferred is likely a nod to "The Agency," a highly secretive government-mandated anti-Mythos department which appeared as a playable faction in Fantasy Flight Games' now-defunct Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

Lieutenant Ronald Hill was a minor character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1922 short horror serial "Herbert West--Reanimator."

### Overview
Little is known of Hill other than that he was a pilot who flew surgeon Major Sir Eric Moreland Clapham-Lee, D. S. O. over the battlefields of France in late March of 1915, during the bitter fighting of the Great War. Unfortunately for the two, their plane was shot down directly over their destination, St. Eloi: Clapham-Lee was nearly decapitated, while Hill's body was described as "unrecognisable." He had been previously said to have been "intrepid." 

Upon being reanimated by Dr. Herbert West, Clapham-Lee uttered the words "Jump, Ronald, for God’s sake, jump!", presumably the last thoughts on his mind being concern for his unfortunate comrade. (: "Herbert West--Reanimator")

fullContent:
"Ronnie and the River" is a short story by American author Christian Riley.

### Synopsis
Ronnie is a quiet, unassuming young man with Down's syndrome and a love of painting. He works a janitorial job at the local university and lives a peaceful life in his small apartment; the only upset in his quiet life is the local bully, a thug named Rick who delights in tormenting Ronnie.

One evening, while working at the university, Ronnie uncovers a secret trapdoor which he proceeds to investigate. When he emerges a little while later, something about him has changed, although he doesn’t realise it. 

Over the next few days, Ronnie begins to see strange symbols in the shapes of everyday objects. After a while, he paints one of these symbols onto his canvas: a great tentacle whips down from the sky and drags off Rick, while Ronnie quietly wanders off to who-knows-where.

### Characters

*Ronnie, a man who lives a quiet, solitary existence.
*Rick, a malicious bully.

### Publication History
"Ronnie and the River" was published in the Weirdbook Annual 2 by Wildside Press in February 2019.

fullContent:
"Rough Night in Innsmouth" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and poet Ron Shiflet. It was first published in the Edward P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes in December 1999.

### Synopsis
Max Peaster, a seaman on shore leave in the fishing town of Innsmouth in 1926, gathers a couple of his comrades with the aim of fleecing a little money from the locals by betting on himself in a local boxing competition.

When the time comes for his bout, Max finds himself up against a brute of an opponent dubbed "The Boston Mangler". When Max goes down after a punishing flurry of blows, the referee attempts to stop the fight, only for the Mangler to push him out of the way and attempt to attack Max again. Luckily for the sailor, his friends come to his rescue, but this only serves to enrage the Mangler: sprouting huge claws from beneath his gloves, the by-now obviously inhuman creature goes berserk, attacking any and all in its way before the barman blows a small bone whistle, summoning a nine-foot-tall fish-like humanoid which kills the Mangler. The sailors make their escape in the subsequent panic, stealing the purse on their way out.

### Behind the Mythos
The Boston Mangler is heavily implied to be a ghoul: the town from which he takes his title, the clawed hands and the description of looking "a little bit like "The Dog-Boy" [Max had] once seen in a carnival freak show" all point towards this conclusion.

Similarly, the creature summoned by the bartender - who himself was said to have the Innsmouth Look - matches that of a Deep One: "A creature about nine feet in height … It looked to be some hellish cross between fish and man … It walked on two legs like a man, but had gills, bulging eyes and scaly skin like a fish. It's huge hands were webbed and what passed for fingers ended in wicked-looking claws".

### Publication History
*Nightscapes (1999)
*Innsmouth Tales 2000 (2000)
*Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir (2008)

fullContent:
Rovagug, called the Rough Beast, is a Lovecraftian-like monster in the fictional universe of the Pathfinder pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Paizo Inc. On the world of Golarion, where it is imprisoned, Rovagug is worshiped as the god of destruction.

### Background
Rovagug is the greatest of all the Qlippoth, feared and hated by the gods and imprisoned deep within Golarion since the Age of Creation. Lying in a state of torpor, his sole goal is to destroy the gods and all of creation. Despite his imprisonment, he is restless and stirrings are increasing, some of which are believed to be the cause of earthquakes and volcanic activity. His avatar is that of a monstrous worm-like entity with innumerable teeth, limbs, claws, eyes, and other unmentionable parts.

Among his names are the Great Destroyer, the Rough Beast, and the Worldbreaker. In primordial times, from the deepest Abyss, the qlippoth lord Rovagug emerged seeking to destroy the world. Already an ancient being, he had destroyed countless other worlds. Upon turning his gaze on Golarion, a coalition of gods of all alignments stood in opposition against him. Many fell in battle against him, but in the end he was defeated and imprisoned.

Eventually, a tiny crack developed in his prison. Over the next 5,000 years, a dozen terrible monsters were unleashed by the Rough Beast onto the world, known as the "Spawn of Rovagug". Over the centuries and millennia, lesser qlippoth fed on his blood, skin, and other bodily fluids, and were forever transformed. It's believed that when the End Times arrive, the archdevil Asmodeus in desperation will release him to consume the other apocalypse. Rovagug will then devour creation and finally himself, leaving only Groetus the god of the apocalypse and one survivor to start all over.

### Known Spawn of Rovagug
All of Rovagug's Spawn are known to radiate an aura of terror in a 300 ft radius. They are likewise all immune to a wide variety of attacks and are able to regenerate, even being disintegrated. They cannot be truly destroyed, only imprisoned, put to slumber, or temporarily "killed" (until they regenerate). The spawn are all highly resistant to magic. After one of the spawn rampages it goes into hibernation for years, decades, or centuries.

### Greater Spawn
*Tarrasque: Known as the Armageddon Engine. The greatest of Rovagug's spawn, which is resembles a colossal dinosaur. It's a monster of incomprehensible power, with powerful claws, a mighty tail, and jaws which can swallow whole villages. The carapace deflects magical attacks and sometimes reflects it back on the spellcaster.

Has some magical spell-like powers, has razor-sharp long tongues, and fires eye rays. It's cry awakens blood fury and madness among those who hear it's song.

Roy Leakey was a fictional character created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Moon-Lens".

### Overview
Once a bookish man who enjoyed antiquarian pursuits, Roy Leakey had heard that there were many second-hand shops in the town of Exham in the Severn Valley, which he had never visited. One day he decided to take the train to Exham, although he had to do so via a very contrived route, as the town had only a single line which made its journey infrequently.

Upon reaching Exham, Leakey was tricked into thinking that there were no trips back out until the next day and so decided to spend the night in a local hotel. The hotel had only a single room on the second floor, one which overlooked an unusual hill fronted by a strange device resembling a tall, pylon-mounted lens.

Later that evening, whilst locked in his room by the hotel manager - a cultist of the Black Goat of the Woods, Shub-Niggurath - he saw an enormous monstrosity emerge from what Leakey saw was a door in the hillside. He was then offered the chance to become one of Shub-Niggurath's servants. However, he saw an opportunity to escape, and shimmied down the outside wall whilst the townsfolk lay prostrated in front of the aperture.

Not counting on the speed and agility of the portal's caretaker, Leakey found himself trapped by the creature's tentacles and jelly-like flesh. Accompanied by Shub-Niggurath's High Priest, he was drawn down into the depths of the temple. 

Once there, Leakey was released and, having control of his body again, punched the High Priest in the throat and ran through the realms of the Goat searching for a way out, eventually finding it, but being forever changed by the experience, both physically and mentally.

Years later, after discovering that his mind had adapted to be capable of processing the horrors he had witnessed in Shub-Niggurath's domain, and that his body could endure any form of self-termination that he could conceive, Leakey visited a physician in the hope that the man could help relieve him of his torment through assisted suicide. One good look at his cosmically-altered form drove the physician mad, and the last that anybody saw of the unfortunate Roy Leakey was a pathetic cloaked figure running from the scene whose hand looked like the talon of a bird, but made from obsidian. "It didn't look like a human's hand at all," said the only witness. (: "The Moon-Lens")

shortDefinition: Roy William Thomas Jr. is a prolific American comic book writer and editor, most notable to this wiki for expanding the world of Robert E. Howard's character Conan the Barbarian - who has been retroactively incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos since ...
fullContent:
Roy William Thomas Jr. is a prolific American comic book writer and editor, most notable to this wiki for expanding the world of Robert E. Howard's character Conan the Barbarian - who has been retroactively incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos since his early stories - in the 1970s.

As a man with a lifelong love of and strong participation in the fandom and fanzine culture of Weird Tales, including bringing out his own professional fanzine Alter Ego, Roy Thomas did more than many in driving the rediscovery and popular culture resurgence of H. P. Lovecraft and Lovecraftian fiction. Thomas is famous or notorious depending on one's point of view for being the first professional writer and editor in comics to really relentlessly mine the Golden Age of the 1930s and 1940s for pulp and comic book characters, and bringing them into the contemporary world of fiction. It is hard to imagine how revolutionary this was when he began the practice since it is now a commonplace. But it began with Thomas.

In a minor way, he began incorporating not just details of the Mythos into Marvel Comics where he was the assistant editor in chief and then editor in chief but also the sensibility of the style of story common to the Mythos, complete with repeated use of a mysterious location as a setting for stories. In the case of Thomas, this was Rutland. Vermont.

Rutland was where Thomas and his wife lived in the early 1970s and as a result Thomas used it to set spooky stories such as the original "Titans Three" team-up that would become The Defenders super team, as well as having a professor of mathematics from Miskatonic University show up there during a Halloween parade - notable in the case of that story as being the very first occasion cosplay made it into popular culture.

Thomas drove the Conan craze that began in the 1970s but he equally drove the heightened awareness of the works of Lovecraft and Derleth.

### Selected Bibliography
* The Horn of Azoth (1990)
* "Within the Mountain of Madness" (1995)

shortDefinition: "Rude Awakening" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Will Murray published in the 1996 anthology The Cthulhu Cycle: Thirteen Tentacles of Terror.  ### Synopsis In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, where warm and cold currents meet, a scientist named Ca...
fullContent:
"Rude Awakening" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Will Murray published in the 1996 anthology The Cthulhu Cycle: Thirteen Tentacles of Terror.

### Synopsis
In the middle of the Pacific Ocean, where warm and cold currents meet, a scientist named Carl Blackshear conducts an experiment aboard the research vessel Lemuria involving the use of undersea sound waves to measure global warming trends. After years of getting clearance from international organizations to make this test, Blackshear becomes increasingly annoyed when the proceedings are interrupted repeatedly, first by an environmental vessel, then by a Japanese whaling ship. Both interlopers are worried that the sound waves will disturb a gigantic cephalopod-like creature that the Japanese refer to as Tako-ika-taki-ika-ika, a name tentatively translated as "Devilfish-cuttlefish".

Instead of listening to them, Blackshear dismisses the monster as mere superstition and starts the experiment. The sound wave is followed by another noise, which Blackshear rationalises as an air pocked that has been dislodged from the sea floor. When he receives orders from the National Reconnaissance Office to halt the experiment, it's too late: the sound is already propagating. The NRO informs him that his vessel is standing over the sunken city of R'lyeh, where an entity named Cthulhu lies dormant. Blackshear witnesses the water become agitated while dolphins and flying fish leap frantically, trying to escape. Down in the sea, Cthulhu opens its gargantuan mouth and slurps water in, devouring masses of animals (from plankton to helpless whales), and creating a whirlpool that engulfs the Lemuria.

The Rue d'Auseil is a fictional street in an unnamed French city that is generally assumed to be Paris; it appears as the location of Erich Zann's apartment in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Music of Erich Zann".

Lovecraft's narrator describes the street as a "narrow, steep, and ancient street of steps and tottering houses":I have never seen another street as narrow and steep as the Rue d’Auseil. It was almost a cliff, closed to all vehicles, consisting in several places of flights of steps, and ending at the top in a lofty ivied wall. Its paving was irregular, sometimes stone slabs, sometimes cobblestones, and sometimes bare earth with struggling greenish-grey vegetation. The houses were tall, peaked-roofed, incredibly old, and crazily leaning backward, forward, and sidewise. Occasionally an opposite pair, both leaning forward, almost met across the street like an arch; and certainly they kept most of the light from the ground below. There were a few overhead bridges from house to house across the street.The street cannot be found on any map, but it "lay across a dark river bordered by precipitous brick blear-windowed warehouses and spanned by a ponderous bridge of dark stone.... Beyond the bridge were narrow cobbled streets with rails; and then came the ascent, at first gradual, but incredibly steep as the Rue d’Auseil was reached."

The inhabitants of the street at first seem "silent and reticent", and are "all very old".

Erich Zann lives in "the third house from the top of the street, and by far the tallest of them all"--a "tottering house" whose landlord was "the paralytic Blandot." Zann occupies a peaked garret on the sixth floor--whose "single gable window was the only point on the street from which one could look over the terminating wall at the declivity and panorama beyond."

After Zann's death and the narrator's escape from it, the street seems to vanish as if it had never existed. The narrator searches extensively, but is never able to locate it again, or to find anyone who's ever seen it.

### Behind the Mythos
"Auseil" is not a word in French, but it has been suggested that Lovecraft derived it from the phrase "au seuil," meaning "at the threshold."  Auseil is read like "oseille," meaning "sorrel" or, colloquially, "money".

### Other Writers
Fred Chappell wrote a short story called "In the Rue d'Auseil", which appeared in Song of Cthulhu: Tales of the Spheres Beyond Sound (2001).

fullContent:
"Running the Night Whiskey" is a short story by Evan Dicken and the first story in the anthology The Devourer Below. It is set in the popular Arkham Horror Fiction universe.

### Plot Summary
Leo De Luca, a local alcohol smuggler, is in his apartment, hungover from a night of drinking and gambling in the Nightingale Club. He notices at least two men approaching his apartment, attempting to break in. As they succeed, Leo smashes a bottle over the first man’s head, then drives him into a wall. The other man charges into him, and a fistfight on the floor ensues. Leo manages to grab his Colt 1911, and points it at the man. But a third man suddenly appears behind him, pressing a rifle between his shoulder blades and forcing him to drop the gun. He is surprised to see that this man is Donald Alighieri, a fellow veteran from the Great War. Donny dismisses the other goons, who were sent by Johnny V, a local mob boss, to rough up Leo due to an unpaid loan. Donny says he has a proposition for Leo: across the border in Canada, they will be picking up two cases of a booze called “night whiskey” for some local buyers. Johnny V will know nothing about it. Leo then finds the deal too good to be true, but Donny reassures him that if he wanted him dead, he would be already. Feeling that he has nothing to lose, he agrees to the deal. 

Later that morning, Leo and Donny are driving north towards Canada. Leo notices that they are being followed by a Green Model T car. He increases their speed, and manages to lose the car. During the drive, Donny talks relentlessly. Leo, listening, is reminded that Donny’s mood could suddenly turn from talkative to angry, and decides to remain silent. As they finally reach their destination near a lake, they decide to walk the final mile to avoid getting trapped in mud. Donny tells Leo that the lake used to be a town called Harrow, but was flooded after the Revolution, killing all of its residents. They reach a cabin and find a still next to it producing the night whiskey. There, they also meet the moonshiner, a man named Enoch. After a brief greeting, he points them towards two crates filled with bottles of whiskey. Donny warns Leo to be careful, as the whiskey is highly flammable. As they leave, Leo hears Enoch singing in a warbling voice, and believes he hears an answering song from across the lake.

As they start the drive back to Arkham, they encounter the Model T car again. Leo makes a turn and speeds up as the car starts to chase them. He turns off the headlamps and takes to the side roads, believing he has managed to shake off the driver. But the Model T appears again, so Leo decides to take a county road. There, they come across a patrol of prohibs, who are blocking the road with a truck. The Model T drives off as the prohibs start shooting at Donny and Leo. fullContent:
Russell's Guide to Interdimensional Entities is a Mythos book by J. Alan Russell and B. A. Lee.

### Overview
Presented as a kind of "field guide" to the creatures of the Cthulhu Mythos, Russell's Guide includes information on these beings, such as descriptions, behaviour and true names, along with original artwork to accompany each entry.

The book focuses on body and alien horror through the lense of B.A. Lee's own Cthulhu-inspired work and mythos, Merrow Tales (2012).

### Specificities

### Canon modifications
Most entries and descriptions are based on B. A. Lee's own work, Merrow Tales (2012). The bestiary's chapters also follow Lee's personal classification of beings and artifacts into five categories: Great Old Ones, Ascendency, Merrow, Star Spawn, and Subdimensional Entities.

The book offers new names for several entities such as the Dunwich Horror (called Dumgal Zi Yog-Sothoth, "Prince of Yog-Sothoth"), Shoggoth (called Gugalushargal, "All Devourer"), Flying Polyp (called Bydogalzul, "Great womb of evil"), Mi-Go (called Star Spawn Drones), and so on. While each entry differentiates between entities sourced from H. P. Lovecraft or Lee's work, it points to Lovecraft as the sole source for entries that offer modifications to the canon.

### Psionic Alphabet
Both Lee and Russell use a fictional alphabet named "psionic alphabet" in illustrations and occasionally in the text, mostly as a depiction of "true names". The alphabet is a phonetic collection of characters directly linked to English letters and diphtongs. Each letter, regardless of its use and placement in a word, possesses individual variations resembling small tentacles. Some letters are also adorned with dots with no apparent logic.

While entity names are translated sound by sound and their meaning is rooted in Lee's theorical psionic language, the use of the alphabet on the backdrop of illustrations appears to be random.

### Publication History
First published by CreateSpace Independent Publishing Platform in August 2015, Russell's Guide is written by B. A. Lee with artwork provided by J. Alan Russell, and runs to 96 pages.

### See Also
*Russell's Guide to Interdimensional Entities, Artefacts and Incantations, a follow-up book.

"Russian About" is an episode of the animated supernatural comedy series The Real Ghostbusters written by J. Michael Straczynski, and originally aired in 1990. It is the third episode of the series to incorporate elements from the Cthulhu Mythos, following "The Collect Call of Cathulhu" and "The Hole in the Wall Gang".

### Synopsis
The Ghostbusters, a group of American paranormal investigators consisting of Egon Spengler, Ray Stantz, Peter Venkman and Winston Zeddemore, as well as a friendly ghost named Slimer, are invited to give a talk at a Soviet institute of paranormal research in Dnepropetrovs, sponsored by tennis player Katarina Novachenka. The Institute houses a vast collection of occult artifacts, as well as a laboratory where scientists Vladimir Maximov and Dmitri Smerdyakov conduct their researches.

During the lecture, Egon's demonstration is interrupted by Vladimir, who announces that a theft has occurred and accuses the Ghostbusters. Among the stolen items is the "Nameless Book", a grimoire containing magic so powerful and dangerous that even mentioning its real name would lead to terrible consequences, hence the appellation. Ray describes the Nameless Book as a "leftover" from when creatures known as the Old Ones ruled the Earth.

Egon tells Katarina that the Ghostbusters previously fought one of the Old Ones, and she in turn reveals that Vladimir has often talked about these beings, making the Ghostbusters suspicious. Tracking the book's supernatural energy with the P. K. E. Meter, they drive through the forest at night while pursued by police inspector Faden, who considers them the primary suspects. When the car breaks down, the Ghostbusters and Katarina take a horse carriage, and finally arrive at the entrance of a subterranean complex where Vladimir and Dmitri, along with several other cultists, conduct a magic ceremony with the Nameless Book.

Egon asks Slimer to fly back to North America and retrieve a box labelled "big trouble". Meanwhile, the Ghostbusters and Katarina follow the cultists into the underground complex, descending a staircase with steps made for humongous creatures, and containing marks made thousands of years ago. Down in the tunnels, Egon and Ray advise caution, as the Old Ones often leave "guardians" in their lairs, listing shoggoths, shamblers and ghasts as examples. Sure enough, several flying monsters appear. The Ghostbusters fire their Proton Packs, but their ghost traps aren't designed to contain these entities, so the heroes are forced to run away. At last, they find the cultists and confront Vladimir and Dmitri, who reveal their plans to revive one of the Old Ones and rule the world after it has ravaged it.

As the ancient beast starts to emerge from a pit, Slimer returns with the package, a contraption that Egon claims can use the power of all their Proton Packs to create a rip in time and space. Peter volunteers to carry the devide to the edge of the pit and throw it. The plan works, as the spaceti

Ry'leh is a fictional alien planet created by Andy Lane for his novel All-Consuming Fire. It is the location where the supposed "Azathoth" has been imprisoned, in a city known as Kadath in the Cold Wastes.

### Description
Ry'leh is a cold icy planet with an extraordinarily odd appearance. It is speculated that, at some point in time, its sun cooled down to the point that its atmosphere was frozen. However, internal heat resulted in the creation of a habitable hollowed space between the planetary surface and the frozen upper layers of the atmosphere, which form an ice sheet supported by mountain ranges that serves as the "sky" of this world. Sunlight passes through the ice, supporting an ecology rich in mobile carnivorous plants and balloon-like animals whose flesh is edible and tastes like chocolate. The local fauna also includes 5 ft long tripedal rat-like creatures with bodies covered in greyish-green scales and a mane of black fur along their spines.

Ry'leh's gravity is similar to that of Earth, and the ground is mostly purple in colour. Although habitable for humans, it is an inhospitable world, uncomfortably cold, with a frigid constant wind blowing. Refracted through the ice sky, the sunlight is too diluted to cast shadows.

Despite being located hundreds of light-years apart from each other, Ry'leh and Earth are aligned in the folds of spacetime continuum in such a way that the chanting of specific spells can open up a gateway between the area of Ry'leh known as the Plain of Leng and the Earth region of Jabalhabad, India. (: All-Consuming Fire)

### Behind the Mythos
The name of this planet is an obvious reference to R'lyeh, the sunken city in which Cthulhu and his spawn are imprisoned in the works of H. P. Lovecraft. Coincidentally, the animated film Howard Lovecraft and the Frozen Kingdom similarly portrays R'lyeh as an ice-covered world which can be accessed from Earth by magical gateways.

Seppo Albert Kivinen (19 October 1933-13 August 2021) was a Finnish author and doctor of philosophy and docent emeritus of University of Helsinki, known for his occult interests. He is a onetime winner of the Atorox Award for best Finnish short story, for his Lovecraftian pastiche "Keskiyön Mato Ikaalisissa" ("The Midnight Worm in Ikaalinen"). He is one of the notable early Finnish Cthulhu Mythos authors.

### Kivinen Mythos
Kivinen's Cthulhu Mythos entries take place in Finland, often in the author's childhood home county of Satakunta and particularly the municipality of Ikaalinen. The stories also interconnect with the works of Boris Hurtta.

fullContent:
Shloyme Zanvl Rappoport (1863, Vitebsk –1920, Otwock), better known by the pseudonym S. Ansky (or An-ski), was a scholar who documented Jewish folklore and mystical beliefs.

He was born in Vitebsk, Belarus, then Russia, but travelled around much of the western part of the Russian Empire. Initially writing in Russian, from 1904 he also became known as a Yiddish author.

Initially under heavy influence of the Russian narodnik movement, Ansky was soon interested in ethnography. Between 1911 and the outbreak of the Great War in 1914 he headed ethnographical expeditions to various Jewish towns of Volhynia and Podolia.

He is best known for authoring the play The Dybbuk or Between Two Worlds, which was first staged in the Elyseum Theatre in Warsaw two months after the author's death in Otwock on November 8, 1920 . Ansky was also the author of the song Di Shvue (The Oath), which became the anthem of the Bund party, and several other pieces of literature, both in Russian and Yiddish.

His ethnological collections were locked away in Soviet vaults for years, but some material has come to light since the 1990s. The State Ethnographic Museum at St Petersburg holds a good deal of it. 

H.P. Lovecraft was very fond of his story The Dybbuk.

S. Petersen's Field Guide to Creatures of the Dreamlands is a sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
Collecting an assortment of creatures which inhabit the Dreamlands, the Field Guide features full-colour illustrations, size comparisons, monster habitats, behaviours and recognition guides, along with maps of the Dreamlands. It was written by Sandy Petersen with contributions from Lynn Willis and Tom Sullivan, and artwork by Mark J. Ferrari. 

Like its companion book S. Petersen's Field Guide to Cthulhu Monsters, Creatures of the Dreamlands contains only flavour text and images; no actual gameplay information is included.

### Publication History
S. Petersen's Field Guide to Creatures of the Dreamlands was published in 1989 and is currently out of print. However, Chaosium released a successor of sorts in 2015 with the publication of S. Petersen's Field Guide to Lovecraftian Horrors, a book which combines the contents of both Creatures of the Dreamlands and Cthulhu Monsters, along with some additional material.

S. Petersen's Field Guide to Cthulhu Monsters is a background sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
The book consists of an in-depth look at 27 of the most commonly-encountered monsters in the Cthulhu Mythos, with a full-colour painting of each and other details such as size comparison charts. It was written by Sandy Petersen and Lynn Willis with artwork provided by Tom Sullivan, and runs to 64 pages. It should be noted that while the Field Guide was marketed as a gaming aid, it features no actual game information such as monster stats, and is solely of use as a flavour guide.

### Publication History
S. Petersen's Field Guide to Cthulhu Monsters was first published by Chaosium in 1988. Although is is now out of print, a successor of sorts has been released in the form of S. Petersen's Field Guide to Lovecraftian Horrors., which features the same creatures in a similar format, but with a number of updates.

shortDefinition: Sunand Tryambak Joshi (born 22 June 1958), known as S. T. Joshi, is an Indian American literary critic, novelist, and a leading figure in the study of H. P. Lovecraft and other authors of weird and fantastic fiction. Besides having written what criti...
fullContent:
Sunand Tryambak Joshi (born 22 June 1958), known as S. T. Joshi, is an Indian American literary critic, novelist, and a leading figure in the study of H. P. Lovecraft and other authors of weird and fantastic fiction. Besides having written what critics such as Harold Bloom and Joyce Carol Oates consider to be the definitive biography of Lovecraft, I Am Providence: The Life and Times of H. P. Lovecraft (Hippocampus Press, 2010 [originally published in one volume as H. P. Lovecraft: A Life, 1996]), Joshi has prepared (with David E. Schultz) several annotated editions of works by Ambrose Bierce. He has also written on crime novelist John Dickson Carr and on Lord Dunsany, Algernon Blackwood and M. R. James, and has edited collections of their works, as well as collections of the best work of several other weird writers. Joshi has compiled, edited or written over 200 books, detailed in the recent publication 200 Books by S.T. Joshi (Hippocampus Press, 2014).

He is a significant bibliographer, having compiled bibliographies of Lovecraft, Bierce, Dunsany, Ramsey Campbell, William Hope Hodgson (forthcoming), Ray Bradbury and Clark Ashton Smith. He has been general editor of the Horror Classics series for Dover Publications.

Joshi is known for his acerbic style, and has been described by editor Ellen Datlow as "the nastiest reviewer in the field". Most recently he has turned his attention to collecting and editing the works of H. L. Mencken. He currently resides in Seattle, Washington.

Joshi was also a member of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts and scholars active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s.

### Literary Criticism
Joshi discovered Lovecraft when he was 13 in the public library in Muncie, Indiana. He read L. Sprague de Camp's biography of Lovecraft, Lovecraft: A Biography, on publication in 1975, and began thereafter to devote himself to the study of Lovecraft, guided in this by scholars such as Dirk W. Mosig, J. Vernon Shea, and George Wetzel. He also wrote some Lovecraftian fiction, such as the story "The Recurring Doom", which can be found in Robert M. Price's anthology Acolytes of Cthulhu.

Joshi elected to become a freshman at Brown University, where he received a B.A. (1980) and M.A. (1982) in classics, primarily because of the holdings of Lovecraft books and manuscripts in the John Hay Library. He later did graduate work at Princeton University from 1982 to 1984, where he was the recipient of the Paul Elmer More Fellowship in classical philosophy. 

Appalled at finding literally 1,500 textual errors in his favorite Lovecraft story, At the Mountains of Madness, he devoted years of research consulting manuscripts and early publications to establish the textual history of Lovecraft's works, in order to prepare corrected editions of Lovecraft's collected fiction, revisions, and miscellaneous writings, in collaboration with Jim Turner for Arkham House; they were published in five volumes between 1984

S.M.A.R.T., the Supernatural Military-Adjacent Response Team, is a fictional organisation in the Army of Darkness universe by Dynamite Entertainment.

### Background
S.M.A.R.T. is an organisation founded in 1300 AD by The Wise Man, Lord Arthur, and Sheila to protect the world from supernatural forces, especially those of the Necronomicon. They passed fighting styles and writings similar to those used by "The Promised One". It became widespread through history, and would eventually end up as a division of the National Security Agency. 

Ash William's first encounter was due to the machinations of its director Doctor Glen Friedrich, who had become tired of how the other divisions within the NSA looked down on them. He had a secret plan to create a Deadite army for S.M.A.R.T., and was using a high school in Dearborn, Michigan as a testing ground. Ash ended up joining forces with Commander Alexis Digges, S.M.A.R.T.'s field commander, once she discovered what the doctor was doing. SMART soldiers were equipped with chainsaws and double-barreled shotguns.

The S'glhuoans are a fictional alien race created by Ramsey Campbell for his 1964 short story "The Plain of Sound". They were later expanded upon by Chaosium in the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplements Ye Booke of Monstres II (1995) and Malleus Monstrorum (2006).

### Description
S'glhuoans are a race which exists in a world located in the Gulf of S'glhuo, a universe in which every world and inhabitant is made up of sound. Campbell describes them as "too thin and tall" to be human, with "huge pupil-less eyes, and a skin covered with tiny rippling scales." Their fingers are boneless.

They are shown to have the ability to mentally project messages which humans pick up as dreams, even across dimensions. But without the aid of a special device known as a "translator", they cannot travel outside their home universe. The "translator" must be activated on the planet they desire to visit, and it's built by those whom receive their dream messages--like the former Brichester University professor Arnold Hird, who makes such a device in 1930 in a house outside Severnford.

### In the Call of Cthulhu RPG
As they consist of living sound, Chaosium extrapolated that the denizens of S'glhuo cannot be harmed by physical attacks, only by magic and specific discordant sounds. They are given the ability to use bursts of sound waves in combat. The game invented Tru'nembra as a deity worshiped by the sound creatures.

S'ngac the violet gas is an alien character created by H. P. Lovecraft. They first appeared unnamed in the short story "Celephaïs" and are identified by name when they appear as a minor character in the novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Biography
S'ngac the violet gas is a member of a species of "coloured gases" which inhabit a distant region of space, where forms don't exist. This realm seems to be contained within the Dreamlands, but is far beyond Earth and outside infinity. The coloured gases are wise creatures which study the secrets of the universe. (: "Celephaïs", The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

The dreamer Kuranes met S'ngac while exploring the most distant areas of space in his dreams (: "Celephaïs"), and learned much about the Outer Gods from them. Specifically, S'ngac told Kuranes "terrible things" about Nyarlathotep and warned him never to approach the Court of Azathoth. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

When dreamer Randolph Carter was dragged against his will towards the central void by a Shantak under orders from Nyarlathotep, he desperately jumped into the cosmic abysses. At this point, both S'ngac and Nodens came to Carter's aid and helped to guide him back to the safety of the waking world. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

S'tya-Yg'Nalle (The Whiteness) is a fictional entity created by James Ambuehl and E. P. Berglund for their 1997 short story "Whiteout".

### Overview
S'tya-Yg'Nalle, also known as "The Whiteness", is an ally or avatar of Ithaqua, stated to be one of the most powerful servitors of the Great Old Ones. Manifesting as what appear to be "snowflakes", they are actually tiny white crawling forms with pincer claws, similar to crabs or spiders. Despite their snowflake-like appearance, the particles actually generate extreme heat.

The Whiteness is said to be a portion of Ithaqua, much like how the Blackness is a portion of Nyarlathotep. Such as with Yin and Yang, the Whiteness and the Blackness are not considered opposites and cannot be used against each other, as they are aspects of space and time as one, consorting as "brothers". The Blackness moves through the stream of time while the Whiteness fills the spaces.

The Whiteness can be summoned using the Nyarlathotep ritual of Ob-ran, the Dark Herald of the Angled Howler, if the name of Ob-ran is interjected with "S'tya-Yg'Nalle". Targeted by the summoner, the rival caster will become a gateway for the Whiteness to enter this dimension, devouring the fabric of the rival caster's flesh from the inside. However, it can also be turned against the summoner, if the rival caster shouts out the Vach-Viraj incantation, a protection spell against the Great Old Ones, while dousing the summoner in the Tikkoun Elixir, also known as holy water, leading to the summoner being devoured instead. Once the feeding is over, the Whiteness will melt away into the body, disappearing as the lifeless shell is reduced to a torn and ragged state. (: "Whiteout")

Saaitii is a fictional entity which made its first appearance in William Hope Hodgson's Thomas Carnacki story "The Hog", although it was unnamed in that work. It was given a proper title and classified as a Great Old One in Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game in 1994, incorporating it into the Cthulhu Mythos proper.

In the original Carnacki stories, the word "Saiitii" (sometimes spelled "Saaitii") is not the name of a single entity, but rather a dangerous class of supernatural manifestations, of which the titular monster from "The Hog" is identified as one. The word first appears in "The House Among the Laurels", and is also used in "The Whistling Room" and "The Hog".

### Background
Saaitii is a minor Great Old One that resides in an outer realm, full of darkness and labyrinth tunnels. It manifests as a nightmarish swine, with rhino-like flesh covering its bloated, cadaverous form. Which has a tiny cyclopean eye, at least a dozen cloven-hoofed legs, and three maws filled with boar-like teeth and tusks. Saaitii attacks the souls of its victims, first possessing them and then dragging them into its lair where they are devoured.

shortDefinition: Sacrifice is a 2020 Lovecraftian horror film based on a short story by Paul Kane and directed by Andy Collier and Tor Mian. It stars screen Mythos stalwart Barbara Crampton as the lead antagonist.  ### Synopsis A man who was brought to America as a y...
fullContent:
Sacrifice is a 2020 Lovecraftian horror film based on a short story by Paul Kane and directed by Andy Collier and Tor Mian. It stars screen Mythos stalwart Barbara Crampton as the lead antagonist.

### Synopsis
A man who was brought to America as a young child returns to his Norwegian family home after his mother's death, accompanied by his heavily-pregnant wife. Despite remembering nothing of his childhood, he is quickly introduced to a local cult which worships a sleeping sub-aquatic deity, and embraces them wholeheartedly.

The film culminates in the man’s murder in order to appease the water-god, as he was revealed to have been spirited away by his mother on the eve of his planned sacrifice as a child.

### Behind the Mythos
Sacrifice contains a number of themes consistent with Lovecraftian horror, such as the isolated backwater society and a secret cult in service to an ancient god. Is also gives several nods to the mythos, including:

*A small statuette which very much resembles the description of the idol recovered from the Cthulhu Cult in "The Call of Cthulhu" (see image below).
*A submerged sleeping god known as The Slumbering One which manifests to mortals in dreams is a clear reference to Cthulhu.
*The Norwegian family changing their surname to Pickman upon arrival in America likely refers to the titular character in the short story "Pickman's Model".

Sadu-Hem was the first Ogdru Hem to be encountered in Hellboy.

### History
### Origin
Sadu-Hem was put into the Gorinium, a temple dedicated to the Ogdru Jahad at the top of the Arctic circle, in order to guarantee that the Seven Gods of Chaos have always a foodhold on the Earth.

After the 2nd World War Grigori Rasputin found the being in the temple, and remained in a trance near the Sadu-Hem, until Trevor Bruttenholm and his exploration party discovered them. The Ogdru Hem devours most of the exploration party, save for Bruttenholm, who was allowed to return to America, and the two followed, hiding in Cavendish Hall.

He was later destroyed mostly, when Abe Sapien speared Rasputin to death and Liz Sherman set the Cavendish Hall on fire.

### Plague of Frogs
A small part of Sadu-Hem survived, and tried to turn humans into frog monsters, until he was killed again by Liz Sherman.

### Trivia

*Sadu-Hem was likely inspired by Cthulhu.
