Salem is a real-world town in Essex County, Massachusetts, infamous for its connection to the witchcraft hysteria of 1692. It is often cited in Cthulhu Mythos fiction; while Salem's historical "witches" were innocent victims of false accusations, those in Lovecraftian fiction tend to be genuine practitioners of cosmic evil. In her introduction to Tales of H. P. Lovecraft, Joyce Carol Oates wrote, "Lovecraft seems to have taken for granted that Salem 'witches' existed, not considering if perhaps they were simply victims of others’ malevolent misuse of power."

Salem, now a suburb of Boston, was founded in 1626. It was actually two communities at the time of the witch trials: Salem Town, the coastal settlement that's known as Salem today, and Salem Village, an inland farming village that is now called Danvers. Many of the accusers in the witch hunt were from the village, while some of the accused were from the town; some suggest that economic and political tensions between the village and the wealthier, more powerful town contributed to the hysteria.

Salem is often cited as a model for H. P. Lovecraft's Arkham. "My mental picture of Arkham is of a town something like Salem in atmosphere & style of houses, but more hilly...& with a college (which Salem hasn't)," Lovecraft wrote to F. Lee Baldwin. "The street layout is nothing like Salem's," he added. 

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
Attempting to explain what was distinct about American weird fiction in Supernatural Horror in Literature, Lovecraft concluded that  the United States was an environment "in which tales of witchcraft and unbelievable secret monstrosities lingered long after the dread days of the Salem nightmare." The town features more often as a background element than as the setting for narrative in Lovecraft's fiction.

In "The Dreams in the Witch-House", the villainous Keziah Mason is said to have fled from Salem Gaol in 1692, a feat "one was ever able to explain." Her jailer was driven insane, babbling of "a small, white-fanged furry thing which scuttled out of Keziah’s cell," and Cotton Mather was baffled by "the curves and angles smeared on the grey stone walls with some red, sticky fluid."

Lovecraft envisioned a considerable exodus from Salem in 1692: Randolph Carter's ancestor Edmund Carter fled from Salem to Arkham at that time, according to "Through the Gates of the Silver Key," as did "two or three armigerous families" who became the "old gentry" of Dunwich (in "The Dunwich Horror"). An ancestor of Richard Upton Pickman was not so lucky, said in "Pickman's Model" to have been hanged as a witch in Salem in 1692. (Perhaps this has something to do with Lovecraft's observation in "The History of the Necronomicon" that  no copy of the Necronomicon's Greek edition "has been reported since the burning of a certain Salem man’s library in 1692"--though in the same

Salem Hawley is a series of Cthulhu Mythos novellas by American author Michael Patrick Hicks. As of March 2024, there are only two books in the series, although in the "Acknowledgements" section of the first book, The Resurrectionists, Hicks states that there are another "two Salem Hawley books to follow."

### Overview
Taking place on America's east coast in 1788, the series follows the adventures of Salem Hawley, a freed black slave from New York, as he tackles the otherworldly forces of the Cthulhu Mythos and their human agents.

The first book puts a supernatural spin on the 1788 Doctors' Riot, a real-world event involving a spat of civil disobedience in the aftermath of a series of high-profile graverobbings , while the second concerns Hawley's search for the stolen Al Azif amidst a plague of supernatural beasts in the town of Arkham, Massachusetts.

Sally Compton, known late in her life as Grandma Compton, is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop who appears in two of their stories: "The Curse of Yig" and The Mound.

### Biography
Sally Compton was one of the first pioneers to settle in Caddo County, Oklahoma, where she lives in the town of Binger with her son, Clyde. She is extremely knowledgeable about local folklore. (: The Mound)

Originally from Arkansas, Sally and her husband Joe Compton moved to Oklahoma and settled down in the area before Binger was founded. At the time, their son Clyde was still an infant.

Sally had a reputation as a teller of macabre tales, including one which was considered her "masterpiece", about a man in Scott County who had been bitten by so many rattlesnakes at once that his body swelled and burst open.

In 1889, the Comptons helped their new neighbors, Walker and Audrey Davis, build their own cabin, about two miles away from the Comptons' land. Sally and Audrey became close friends, and would often visit each other, sharing stories of Arkansas, where they both grew up, as well as rumours about the new country.

Although she was sympathetic about Walker Davis' paralysing fear of snakes, Sally was apparently oblivious to her friend Audrey's own fear of the snake god Yig: a fear cultivated after Audrey killed a nest of rattlesnakes to spare Walker of the trauma of seeing them. Local folklore told of the terrible vengeance that Yig reserved for those who harmed the serpents, and Walker became obsessed with the idea that he and Audrey were cursed. When Sally told Audrey the tale of the Scott County snake victim, Audrey begged her not to let Walker hear of it. Sally and Joe respected her wish and refrained from sharing this anecdote with Walker or others.

On October 31, 1889, the Comptons attended the Davises' Halloween party, and noticed how their hosts seemed to forget all their worries on the dancing floor. However, on the next day's afternoon, Sally came over to visit them and found the tragic result of the curse of Yig: an insane Audrey hissing like a snake, and the bloody remains of Walker, whom Audrey had axed to death after mistaking him for Yig at night.

Joe Compton died at some point prior to 1925. (: "The Curse of Yig")

In 1928, Sally and her son Clyde allowed a Virginian ethnologist to stay in their house and assisted him in his research about local folklore, particularly the legend of a ghost man and a headless ghost woman that haunted a particular mound. (: The Mound)

The Salton Sea Monster is a Lovecraftian reptilian entity from the fictional universe of Hellboy. He was one of the Ogdru Hem, children of the Ogdru Jahad.

Originally his being was seen as an herald of the end-times, but it was quickly worshipped as a god by humans.

One of these key worshippers was Paul Nedin, a former Christian pastor from Atlanta, who formed the Church of the Living Earth.

Sam Gafford (1962 - 20 July 2019) was an American author, editor, comic book creator, and occasional artist who specialised in the horror, non-fiction and weird fiction genres. Much of Gafford's work focused on William Hope Hodgson's occult detective Thomas Carnacki.

In 1982, a 20-year-old Gafford was invited to Providence, Rhode Island by leading H. P. Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi, where he joined the informal group of Lovecraft enthusiasts the Providence Pals. In 2015, he would publish a collection of their works titled Providence Pals: Memories and Miscellany.

Gafford was also the founder of the independent publishing house Ulthar Press; following his death in 2019, the press is no longer active.

Samuel Marshall "Sam" Raimi (born 29 October 1959) is an American director, screenwriter, and producer who began his career in the low-budget film industry but has risen to direct blockbuster productions such as the Spider-Man trilogy (2002-2007) and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness (2022).

For the purposes of this wiki, Raimi is notable for his creation of the multimedia Evil Dead franchise, which follows the (mis)adventures of bumbling store clerk Ash Williams as he battles various forces thrown into his path by the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis, an evil grimoire possessed by a demon. During the course of his escapades, Williams has crossed paths with many elements of the Cthulhu Mythos.

fullContent:
Samuel E. Loveman (14 January 1887-14 May 1976) was a Jewish American author and critic.

### Overview
A close friend of Howard Phillips Lovecraft and member of his literary circle the Kalem Club, Samuel Loveman also provided a source of inspiration for Lovecraft: in addition to appearing in the dreams which inspired "The Statement of Randolph Carter" (in which he became the major character Harley Warren) and "Nyarlathotep, the story "Hypnos" was dedicated to Loveman and he was the subject of the poem "To Samuel Loveman, Esquire, on His Poetry and Drama, Writ in the Elizabethan Style". Loveman was also responsible for introducing Lovecraft to several authors and clients - the pair shared many literary acquaintances - and wrote two memoirs of his friend after his death.

Despite this, after Lovecraft's death in early 1937, Loveman was informed by Lovecraft's ex-wife Sonia Greene of her former husband's anti-Semitic beliefs and this discovery caused Loveman to burn all of his correspondence and write a scathing essay ("Of Gold and Sawdust") on the topic.

Samuel Nightingale is a fictional character who appeared in Peter J. Evans' 2013 novel Feeders from Within. It was his first and only appearance, having died during the story’s finale.

### Description
A slight and wiry man, Nightingale nevertheless had a coldness in his eyes which caused all who met him to be instantly wary; psychiatrist Dr. Carolyn Fern instantly recognised him as a sociopath with no regard to the fate of others. He worked for businessman/bootlegger Phillip Avery as his second-in-command and enforcer (and had been nominated to succeed Avery) until the two died in November 1926. He was also a member of the Silver Twilight Lodge, although doesn’t appear to have been particularly advanced in the hierarchy. (: Feeders from Within)

### History
Nightingale was responsible for dispatching the assassins who attempted to kill Carolyn Fern, and he himself tried to kill Mark Harrigan, but was interrupted by the arrival of Diana Stanley. When the group of Silver Twilight Lodge members travelled through Mr. Stone's portal to N'kai, he was one of the few lucky or cunning enough to make it back after the Formless Spawn attacked. In a fight shortly afterwards, Nightingale was killed by Diana who stabbed him through the neck. (: Feeders from Within)

Samuel Seaton is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family".

### Overview
Samuel Seaton was an explorer who was murdered by the noted anthropologist and fellow explorer Sir Robert Jermyn. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

On the 19th of October, 1852, Seaton visited the Jermyn home with a manuscript of notes collected in Africa. From these notes and other revelations, Robert discovered to his horror that there was a simian strain in his own family originating from a union between his grandfather Wade Jermyn and a female member of a race of African white apes. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

The unhinged Robert strangled Seaton to death and murdered his own three children in order to eradicate his stained bloodline, but his two year old grandson Alfred survived. Robert died of apoplexy during the second year of his confinement in an asylum after repeated attempts at suicide. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

San Francisco is a city in California that appears in a handful of stories by H. P. Lovecraft, and is the setting for Cthulhu Mythos stories by other writers.

Originally the home of the indigenous Yelamu people, San Francisco was founded as a Spanish mission in 1776. Claimed by the United States in 1846, it expanded rapidly following the Gold Rush of 1849. Its excellent harbor made it a central port for trade with Asia and the Pacific. The city survived a devastating earthquake in 1906, becoming the cultural center of Northern California with a strong Bohemian (and, later, LGBTQ) tradition. Its population was 506,676 in 1920, rising to 873,965 by 2020.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The Lovecraft story that features San Francisco most prominently is the 1928 revision tale "The Last Test," a reworking of Adolphe de Castro's "A Sacrifice to Science." The character Alfred Clarendon and his sister Georgina live in "the gloomy old Bannister place near Goat Hill, overlooking the bay...a rambling, French-roofed relic of mid-Victorian design and gold-rush parvenu display." Goat Hill is today better known as Potrero Hill, a neighborhood on the east side of the city, south of 16th Street and east of U.S. Route 101. The city is also mentioned in another story Lovecraft revised for de Castro, "The Electric Executioner," in which the narrator is "an auditor and investigator connected with the Tlaxcala Mining Company of San Francisco."

At the end of Lovecraft's story "Dagon" (1917), the narrator finds himself "in a San Francisco hospital; brought thither by the captain of the American ship which had picked up my boat in mid-ocean." An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia disputes the idea that the entity Dagon follows the narrator to the city, as "the notion of a hideous creature shambling down the streets of San Francisco is preposterous."

In "The Call of Cthulhu," Francis Wayland Thurston passes through San Francisco on his way to Dunedin, New Zealand, to investigate the Emma's encounter with the Cthulhu cult.

### Other Mythos Writers
"The Hunters from Beyond" (1932), by Clark Ashton Smith, takes place in San Francisco, featuring the fictional bookstore Toleman's and the studio of sculptor Cyprian Sincaul.

The recurring character of occultist Michael Leigh, who appears in Henry Kuttner's "The Salem Horror" (1937) and Kuttner and Robert Bloch's "The Black Kiss" (1937), is based in San Francisco.

Fritz Leiber's 1977 novel Our Lady of Darkness provides a detailed portrait of San Francisco.

Michael Shea's "Copping Squid" (2009) taking the reader on a journey through San Francisco, "down Sixteenth through the Mission," "under the freeway and down to the Bayside, hanging south on Third," and up into the hills that overlook the city. San Francisco is also home to Shea's Hyperion Hotel, where he set a number of stories.

The Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities is a fictional research facility created by Lin Carter for his Xothic Legend Cycle. 

### Overview
Mirroring H. P. Lovecraft's Miskatonic University in that, aside from their more mundane departments, the two have a particular specialisation in the occult, maintaining extensive libraries on the subject. However, Sanbourne seems to lean more towards the research aspect of graduate study rather than higher learning as with Miskatonic, specialising in the study of cultures in and around the Pacific Ocean. 

### History
Sanbourne was founded by the son of a tuna-packing magnate in Santiago, California. 

In Robert M. Price's short story "Down in Limbo", the institute is said to have been absorbed into "the University," although it is unclear which university is being referred to.

### Library
Sanbourne is known to be home to a large collection of occult literature, including: 

* A New Scrutiny of the Polynesian Genesis according to the Cthäat Aquadingen (Anton Zarnak) 
*The Bimini Glyphs (rubbings)
* The Livre d'Eibon (Gaspard du Nord edition) 
* The Necronomicon (Dee translation) 
* The Ponape Scripture 
* The R'lyeh Text 
* Die Unaussprechlichen Kulten 
* The Yuggya Chants

Alexander "Sandy" Antunes (born 1967 in Baltimore, Maryland) is an American games designer, astronomer, and gaming commentator. His roleplaying game credits include a number of supplements for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu investigative roleplaying game, largely focusing on settings for the town of Arkham, Massachusetts and in particular its premier institute of learning, Miskatonic University.

Antunes is also the co-founder of RPG.net, a site devoted to all aspects of gaming, both traditional and video, and plays host to his column on the business aspect of contemporary gaming, as well as being a past director of the Game Publishers Association.

Carl Sanford Joslyn "Sandy" Petersen (born September 16, 1955) is an American game designer. He is the principal designer of the Chaosium role-playing game Call of Cthulhu and drove its development for decades. After separating from Chaosium he continued to write and edit Mythos related game material such as the Malleus Monstrorum. He has now returned to Chaosium in the role of senior consultant and advisor with input into design, game balance and syncretising the disparate elements of different Mythos writers into the standardised and statistics based approach of the Chaosium games.

Prior to Call of Cthulhu Petersen worked long term on the rules for the RuneQuest games family as well as the Basic Role-Playing Game (BRG) universal rules, more recently released under an Open Games License (OGL).

Petersen also designed the lion's share of the levels for the video games DOOM and DOOM II.

Petersen was the Executive Producer for the 2011 movie The Whisperer in Darkness which received award nominations at the Chicago International Film Festival and Warsaw International Film Festival (Foreign Feature division). The film was produced by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society Motion Pictures team in the style of a 1930s black and white horror movie.

Petersen has very extensive video game credits but his primary relevant credits for Lovecraft related works remain Call of Cthulhu RPG and related rules-light supplements such as Malleus Monstrorum.

Sarah Monette (born November 25, 1974) is a writer of fantasy, horror, and science fiction. She wrote a series of short stories with Elizabeth Bear, the Boojumverse tales, that merge the universes of the Cthulhu Mythos and Lewis Carroll in a space opera setting.

Monette received a Ph.D. in English literature from the University of Wisconsin at Madison in 2004.

Her first novel, Mélusine, was published in 2003; she published three more novels in the Doctrine of Labyrinths series. She co-wrote three novels in the Iskryne series with Elizabeth Bear from 2007 to 2015.

Her novel The Goblin Emperor, which she published under the name Kathleen Addison, won the 2015 Locus Award for Best Fantasy Novel. She has since written two more novels set in the same world.

Sarah Newton is a traditional games designer, author, and editor based in France, whose works focus on the science fiction and fantasy genres. She is perhaps best known for her Mindjammer property, which explores transhumanism in a distant future setting ; since the original novel's publication, it has been developed into an award winning roleplaying game for two separate games systems .

Newton was also the author of the Zero Point campaign supplement for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, a pair of books which launched the Achtung! Cthulhu setting, and were the catalyst for the foundation of traditional games manufacturer Modiphius Entertainment. Her Lovecraftian short fiction has been included in anthologies such as Cubicle 7 Entertainment's tie-in collection World War Cthulhu .

Sarkomand is an ancient, ruined city found in The Dreamlands.

### Location
Situated in the northern Dreamlands, in a valley by the Plateau of Leng, above an entrance to the underground Abyss sections of the Dreamlands. It is beside the sea, but the rocks are jagged; human ships do not go there, although Black Galleys sometimes do.

Out in the water is a mountainous granite island, with windowless dwellings and paths carved into the rock, inhabited by Moon-beasts and their slaves. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

### Description
The city was "proud and pillared ... wondrous with high fanes and carven places", filled with pillars of black stone. It was a seaport. In modern times its stones and pillars are broken, and overgrown with weeds and grass.

The basalt cliffs of Leng beside which the city stands are carved with frescos, and there is an archway there leading up to Leng itself.

The underground entrance, a huge black stone staircase (of narrow steps and, in modern times, slippery with mold) in the central plaza, is flanked by two huge diorite sphinxes. The six gates of the city are likewise crowned by sphinxes. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

### History
A million years before the first true humans, Sarkomand was invaded by Moon-beasts and it's inhabitants conquered. The city was abandoned.

In modern times, Randolph Carter and an army of Ghouls and Night-gaunts fought the Moon-beasts there, in retaliation for them having captured and tortured some ghouls. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

Sarnath was a vast, majestic and powerful city in Mnar, an extremely remote land on Earth, some ten thousand years ago. Its dwellers were human empire builders of immense wealth; but their mighty city was built on blood, because not long after they laid its foundations, the people of Sarnath had destroyed the ancient city of Ib, where had dwelled the thuum'ha - non-human creatures who, while hideous by human standards, were peaceful enough.

For a thousand years Sarnath stood by the lake where it had been built and ever grew in size and beauty. Its splendor was impossible to overstate, as the city was resplendent with palaces, gardens and temples of immense size which seemed to compete with each other in opulence and grandeur. Its spires reached for the heavens and its streets stretches to the horizon; princes and kings travelled many miles to marvel at Sarnath's beauty and pay it homage.

But one day, on the one-thousandth anniversary of the destruction of the gray city of Ib, as the lake had swelled greatly, the entity Bokrug, whom had been the subject of worship by the people of Ib, meted out the fullness of his revenge on the proud people of Sarnath; it was witnessed how the revelers in the palace of the king seemed to be twisted into the likeness of the thuum'ha, and all fled in abject terror. And the next day, of the immense city in all its majesty, decadence and vanity, not a trace remained - all there was, was a muddy plain, a realm for water lizards.

Sarnath was never re-settled.

### Religion
The chief gods worshipped in Sarnath were Lobon, Tamash, and Zo-Kalar. All three were depicted as graceful bearded men. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

fullContent:
"Sarnath Centre" is a short Cthulhu Mythos poem by author Tony Daly. It was published in the Gavin Chappell-edited zine Lovecraftiana, Vol 8, Issue 2 by Rogue Planet Press in July 2023 .

### Synopsis
The eighteen lines offer a brief exploration of the doomed city of Sarnath, from its lofty towers, to its verdant gardens, to its lowest slums, as well as the moral burden weighed upon its people as a result of their actions against the Beings of Ib.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite the text containing no direct references to the Cthulhu Mythos or the writings of H. P. Lovecraft, the poem's title combined with the content makes it clear that the piece was intended to refer to the short story "The Doom That Came to Sarnath".

Satampra Zeiros is a character created by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith for his Hyperborean Cycle series of fantasy stories.

### Description
A life-long thief, Satampra Zeiros was good at his profession, although he stated to have never stolen from anyone who was not a robber themselves in some shape or form. He was described as a largish man, and later in life was missing his right hand, the result of a near-fatal encounter with a Formless Spawn of Tsathoggua during a calamitous expedition to the abandoned city of Commoriom.

Zeiros loved a woman named Vixeela, a former temple girl who later became his accomplice, but he outlived her by many years. Indeed, he appears to have outlived all of his friends and associates by some time.

shortDefinition: "Satan's Servants" is a horror short story by Robert Bloch, written in 1935 and first published in the 1949 Arkham House collection Something About Cats and Other Pieces. H. P. Lovecraft revised the original draft and made several suggestions that Bl...
fullContent:
"Satan's Servants" is a horror short story by Robert Bloch, written in 1935 and first published in the 1949 Arkham House collection Something About Cats and Other Pieces. H. P. Lovecraft revised the original draft and made several suggestions that Bloch would implement in the final version.

Upon publication in 1949, Bloch described "Satan's Servants" as the last story written with Lovecraft's input to be published; a claim that is no longer true today, as two of the Lovecraft-Barlow collaborations ("The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast" and "The Slaying of the Monster") would be published for the first time in 1994.

### Synopsis
In 1693, Gideon Godfrey travels to the village of Roodsford, Massachusetts. A devout Puritan, Godfrey has heard rumours of widespread witchcraft and devil-worship and, having studied the Necronomicon and other forbidden tomes himself, intends to use a combination of prayer and magic spells to exorcise all evil from the place, essentially fighting fire with fire.

Along the way, Godfrey stops in a glade to sleep, only to wake up alone, his two guides and horse having vanished along with all of his provisions. Noticing that the turf is remarkably smooth and that the stones are arranged in a pattern that corresponds to the stars in the night sky, Godfrey concludes that the glade is a gathering spot for sorcerers, and that only his fervent prayer has protected him. Still resolute, he resumes his trip and finally reaches Roodsford by night.

Exhausted after the long journey, Godfrey buries his bible and pistol under a rock to avoid suspicion. He finds shelter for the night with a man named Dorcas Frye, who invites him for supper, but the meal is interrupted by the opening of a trapdoor and the emergence of a hellish hound, which Godfrey recognises as a wizard's familiar.

Feigning interest, rather than fear, Godfrey asks his host to show him what lies under the trapdoor. They descend into a long tunnel and reach a subterranean chamber that is also accessible from the other houses of the village. At the center of the chamber there is an altar, where the sacrificed bodies of Godfrey's guides lie, surrounded by a horde of animal-shaped familiars.

With a supreme effort to hide his shock and fear, Godfrey pretends to be pleased by what he sees and boldly introduces himself as the demon Asmodeus, who came to prepare the way for his Master and oversee their Sabbat. His performance fools Frye and the others, who come to accept him for what he purports to be. In this role, he is allowed to stay and gains the trust of the villagers, who are indeed all powerful magicians and worshipers of Satan.

During his stay, Godfrey learns that Roodsford is more than a hundred years old, and that the village has neither children nor graveyards, having no need of either, since its inhabitants are all undead. More alarmingly, he learns that the coven is planning to summon their Master during the Sabbat at Hallow-Mass, after which they will seek to convert

Satha is a character created by H. P. Lovecraft’s close friend Robert E. Howard, appearing in the stories "The Scarlet Citadel" (1933) and the "The Valley of the Worm" (1934), Conan and James Allison stories respectively.

Satha first appeared in Marvel Comics in the adaptation of "The Valley of the Worm" in Supernatural Thrillers #3 (April, 1973). "Scarlet Citadel" was later adapted in Savage Sword of Conan #30. He also appeared in Darkhorse Comics (where?).

### Background
During the Hyborian Age, Satha dwelt in the southern jungles of the Country of the Worm, terrorizing the Picts. When a tribe of Aesir split from Niord's tribe (as part of their colonization of the place), they migrated to the area, where the eldritch creature known as the Worm killed them, urging Niord, the leader of the tribe who hunted it down and appeared to slay it. In this perspective, he trapped and killed Satha, using his poison to slay the Worm, but died during the battle.

Sometime before or after, Satha lived in Koth where it encountered the powerful sorcerer Tsotha-Lanti to whom it submitted. Conan of Cimmeria would end up in the sorcerer's citadel and encountered it two times, both times surviving though not because of his own actions.

Saturnalia and Other Poems by H. P. Lovecraft is the 21st issue of Robert M. Price's long-running Lovecraftian fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu. Edited by leading H. P. Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi and published by Cryptic Publications, it featured cover art by Rick Bryant, and ran to a total of 72 pages in an A5 format.

Satyrs are imaginary creatures from Greek mythology, often depicted as having the upper half of a man and the lower half of a goat. Though creatures resembling them have frequently been incorporated into Cthulhu Mythos fiction, they aren't actual Satyrs in the sense of the Greek legends, but rather beings related somehow to Lovecraftian origins.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
In the story "The Horror at Red Hook", H. P. Lovecraft describes a parade of horrific creatures led by Lilith in the catacombs below Red Hook, which includes "goat, satyr, and aegipan, incubus, succuba, and lemur, twisted toad and shapeless elemental, dog-faced howler and silent strutter in darkness".

In Lovecraft's "The Nameless City", the narrator's sight of the city's inhabitants evokes "comparisons as varied as the cat, the bulldog, the mythic Satyr, and the human being".

In his "The Music of Erich Zann", listening to the music of Zann--who is twice described as "satyr-like"--the narrator "could almost see shadowy satyrs and Bacchanals dancing and whirling insanely through seething abysses of clouds".

In The Whisperer in Darkness, Albert Wilmarth initially compares the legend of winged crustacean creatures of the Vermont woods to similar legends about Satyrs, Fauns and Dryads from around the world.

Though Wilbur Whateley in "The Dunwich Horror" is not explicitly called a satyr, he is frequently described as "goatish", and after his death it is revealed that below his waist, his "skin was thickly covered with coarse black fur."

In The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, Lovecraft depicts the Men of Leng as satyr-like humanoids with horns and hoofs.

### Other Writers
Satyrs are said to inhabit the French province of Averoigne (: "The Satyr", Clark Ashton Smith) and at least some of them are known to be servants of Sheila-Na-Gog, a possible avatar or alias for Shub-Niggurath (: "The Wedding of Sheila-Na-Gog", Glenn Rahman & R. L. Tierney). It's also been suggested that stories about satyrs might have been inspired by the Gof'nn hupadgh Shub-Niggurath (: "The Moon-Lens", Ramsey Campbell).

A passage from the Necronomicon claims that when the time comes, the Spawn of Shub-Niggurath will "take dominion over all wood nymphs, satyrs, leprechauns, and the Little People". (: "The House on Curwen Street", "The Keeper of the Key")

While hiding from the Hounds of Tindalos, Halpin Chalmers worried that his defenses against them might be insufficient if another race such as the Doels or the Satyrs help them break through. He notes that the Satyrs can "advance through the scarlet circles" and that the Greeks knew how to prevent that, but the knowledge has long been lost. (: "The Hounds of Tindalos")

"Saucers from Yaddith" is a short story by Robert M. Price featuring Arwassa. 

### Overview
In this story it is suggested that the Nug-Soth have visited Earth repeatedly from their homeworld of Yaddith to abduct humans and perform medical experiments upon the abductees. The experiments range from the swapping of a man's blood type from O to A to the swapping of eyes and hands to more nightmarish medical procedures. Obviously, this is a Mythos version of the Alien Abduction belief.

### Publication History
"Saucers from Yaddith" was first published in the Esoteric Order of Dagon APA. It has since appeared in Etchings & Odysseys #5 (October 1984), The New Lovecraft Circle (1996), and Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2008).

The eight fairly long verses in essence sing the praise of the Great Old One Chaugnar Faugn.

"Scarlet Obeisance" was first printed in the online zine Nightscapes in August 1999, and then in the Hallowmas 2000 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu. In 2008 it was included in the Robert M. Scat is a recurrent character who appears in the Cthulhu Mythos works of the late American author Michael Shea.

### Description
An intelligent, pretty young woman. Called a "nervy little minx, bright as a button," and a "bright kid, merry and invulnerable."   Scat is described as looking



She is a sex worker in a more run-down part of San Francisco, and has a voracious appetite for the work of weird fiction writers like H. P. Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith. She describes herself as "a hooker that reads."

### History
Scat first stumbled across the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos when she and Dee - the owner of a local bookstore which she frequented - accidentally ate cookies laced with cannabis. The ingestion of the drug brought the two to the attention of a supernatural killer in service to Dagon and, although they were able to defeat the creature, were forever changed by the encounter.

Scat currently lives in Dee's spare bedroom, where she presumably assists her friend in finding ways to combat the powers which she has recently become aware of.

Scathach is a character from Gaelic mythology introduced into the Cthulhu Mythos in the story "October Surprise" by Kevin L. O'Brien. In the Mythos story, she is described as the daughter of Hziulquoigmnzhah and Klosmiebhyx and the sister of Ysbaddaden.

### Folklore
In Gaelic mythology, Scathach was a warrior-queen and sorceress. She is considered to be the legendary founder of Scotland in some tales and also figures prominently in the Ulster Cycle of Irish history and folklore. Her name means "The Shadowy One" in Gaelic.

Seaman Schmidt is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his 1920 short story "The Temple". 

### Overview
Schmidt served aboard the German submarine U-29 under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich during the First World War. As a result of the supernatural events experienced by the crew, both Schmidt and Seaman Bohm became sick and lapsed into violent insanity. Their constant ravings concerning a "terrible curse" upon the submarine led Heinrich to execute them in order to maintain discipline. (: "The Temple")

The Scimitar of Barzai (also known as Barzai's Scimitar) is a fictional artefact in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. It was first mentioned in George Hay's anthology The Necronomicon: The Book of Dead Names, which describes the recipe for the item. 

It is named after Barzai the Wise from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Other Gods"; however, it is unknown if the Scimitar has any connection to its namesake.

### Description
According to the Necronomicon, the Scimitar of Barzai is a bronze scimitar that has the power to summon the Outer God Yog-Sothoth. In the day and hour of Mars, and when the Moon increases, the Scimitar should be made with a hilt of fine ebony, along with arcane symbols inscribed on each side of the blade. After the ritual is complete, the Scimitar must be wrapped in a cloth of black silk and set aside until it is used again. If anyone else tries to abuse the Scimitar's power, it will be rendered powerless.

### In the Demonbane Mythos
In the Demonbane series by Nitroplus, the Scimitar of Barzai is described to be a tool used as a medium for arcane rituals, similar to a wizard's staff.

The Scimitar appeared as one of Al Azif's missing fragments, taking the form of a large, crescent moon-shaped sword that was rampaging through Arkham city like a flying boomerang. During a fight between Daijuuji Kurou and the android girl Elsa, the Scimitar interrupted their confrontation by slicing through the nearby buildings. The Scimitar was caught by Kurou, but it broke free and flew away due to an attack from Elsa. The next day, Kurou managed to catch the Scimitar again, trapping it between his hands using the sword-catching technique, focusing magic through his palms to cause the Scimitar to explode into a whirlwind of paper. The pages were stolen by Doctor West, in order to activate his newest Destroyer Robot: an evil knockoff of Demonbane called "Demonpain". Al finally retrieved her missing pages, after Demonpain was destroyed by the real Demonbane.

While fighting the Anticross Tiberius at the Hadou Estate, Al gave Kurou access to the Scimitar, which increased his power many times over. Kurou used the Scimitar to slice Tiberius' body in half, and later repeatedly sliced his upper body, mutilating Tiberius beyond recognition; however, he managed to survive due to achieving immortality from the power of De Vermis Mysteriis. After Tiberius summoned his Deus Machina known as Belzebuth, Kurou summoned a gigantic version of the Scimitar while piloting Demonbane.

On an island near Innsmouth, Kurou used the Scimitar to fight off a pair of human-octopus hybrid monsters at the stone temple. fullContent:
"Scion of Chaahk" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tom Lynch.

### Synopsis
A pair of explorers on the Yucatan peninsula stumble across an underground chamber filled with what appear to be offerings and the statue of the previously-undepicted Mayan deity Gh'laahki. As they explore the chamber, it becomes obvious that the carving is more than it appears to be and the two men attempt to escape, only to find themselves trapped by an ancient cult dedicated to the dark god's worship.

### Characters
* Bill Taylor, a researcher of the Mayans who believes that their decline was due to religious reasons.
* David Anderson, Bills partner and best friend since college.
* Luisito, a local working for Bill and David as an assistant, who is also a secret cultist.

### Publication History
"Scion of Chaahk" was published in the thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

fullContent:
The Scions of Forever is a fictional organisation in the CthulhuTech pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Wildfire LLC.

### Background
The Scions of Forever is the most enigmatic group on Earth and one that is neutral in the multi-sided conflict. It's unknown what influence they wield, the fact that they are masters of the currents of time means that if wanted they could wield great power. Despite such power, they have chosen to use it in very unusual ways. An organisation of para-psychics and talented sorcerers who revere Yog-Sothoth. It's rumored that it's members can manipulate time and many of them are virtually immortal. Due to them knowing everything there is to know about the past and future, they are fabulously wealthy but are the world's most private and quiet citizens.

shortDefinition: Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated is a children's television show based on the long running Scooby-Doo! franchise which was launched by Hannah-Barbera Productions in 1969. Unlike other entries in the series, it features an overarching storyline which ...
fullContent:
Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated is a children's television show based on the long running Scooby-Doo! franchise which was launched by Hannah-Barbera Productions in 1969. Unlike other entries in the series, it features an overarching storyline which continues throughout both seasons, employs character development, features some villains who are actually supernatural in nature, and is much darker in tone.

### Premise
As with all of iterations of Scooby-Doo!, Mystery Incorporated features five main characters: Fred Jones, the trap-obsessed team leader; Daphne Blake, a socialite from a wealthy family; Velma Dinkley, a highly-intelligent yet socially awkward overachiever; Norville "Shaggy" Rogers, a food-obsessed slacker; and Scooby-Doo, Shaggy's talking pet dog. Together, they solve mysteries in their home town of Crystal Cove; these mysteries tend to appear supernatural in nature, but usually turn out to have more mundane explanations when looked into further.

The larger story involves Professor Pericles, a hyper-intelligent talking parrot, attempting to harness the power of the Evil Entity, an extra-dimensional being imprisoned aeons ago beneath Crystal Cove.

### Mythos Connections
Although containing few direct connections to H. P. Lovecraft or his works, there are many nods to the Cthulhu Mythos, as well as a scattering of Lovecraftian horror. Some examples of these include:

*Miskatonic University: appears in both the original timeline and the altered one in which the Evil Entity has been eradicated. In the series closing, the gang - including Scooby-Doo - are offered scholarships at Miskatonic by Professor of sub-nuclear sciences Harlan Ellison.
*The Evil Entity: an ancient being of incredible power and malevolence, the Evil Entity was imprisoned millennia ago beneath the Earth where it awaits its release. This recalls several of Lovecraft's creations, including Cthulhu himself.
*H. P. Hatecraft & Char Gar Gothakon: the episode "The Shrieking Madness" features a clear parody of Lovecraft, as well as his literary creation who bears more than a passing resemblance to a certain Great Old One; it is also mentioned in the episode "Menace of the Manticore," when Marcy "Hot Dog Water" Fleach remarks that her father's theme park, Creepy Spooky Terror Land, has around 5,000 surplus Char Gar Gothakon plushies in stock. Hatecraft, meanwhile, was voiced by Jeffrey Combs in two episodes of the show. Combs, a screen regular in Mythos-related screen productions, has also played the role of a fictional Lovecraft in at least two feature films.
*Howard E. Roberts: a superfan whose name is a play on Robert E. Howard.

Scott Dorward is a traditional games designer and podcaster who specialises in tabletop Lovecraftian roleplaying games. His gaming credits include material for Cthulhu Dark and the World War Cthulhu line of Call of Cthulhu supplements, the latter of which he line developed for Cubicle 7 Entertainment until 2017; he has also written Call of Cthulhu material for Chaosium, the game's creator company, and Pelgrane Press.

Dorward is also the co-creator, with Matthew Sanderson and Paul Fricker, of Good Friends of Jackson Elias, a podcast devoted to the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game and related topics, named for one of the primary characters in the Masks of Nyarlathotep supplement. Dorward, Sanderson, and Fricker have also worked together on written material for the game, including Nameless Horrors (2015, 2023) and The Two-Headed Serpent (2017).

The Scrag are a fictional race created by Ideas from the Deep Software for the First Person Shooter called Quake.

### Background
In Quake, a Scrag is a kind of floating creature resembling a white cobra snake combined with a human torso that spits small yellowish green globs of poison at their opponents.

Scrag floats by means of a gas bladder. If the Scrag is killed, it will fall to the ground.

"Scratching from the Outer Darkness" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tim Curran.

### Synopsis
A blind woman begins hearing a scratching coming from outside the boundaries of reality at the same time that random acts of madness take a firm grip on the Earth. Despite her lack of sight, as one of the last people to retain a hold on sanity she is gifted a front-row seat to the return of the Old Ones.

### Characters
*Simone, a self-sufficient woman who has been blind since birth.

### Publication History
"Scratching from the Outer Darkness" was first published in the thematic anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror in 2017. It was included in Year's Best Hardcore Horror Volume 3 the following year.

### Trivia
*One of the doomsayers on a public-access television channel references the prophecies contained in the Al-Azif, the Pnakotic Manuscripts, the Eltdown Shards, De Vermis Mysteriis and the Unaussprechlichen Kulten. Also, Simone's mother comments on how the fall of humanity will see the return of Cthulhu, Tsathoggua, and others.
*One of the other books mentioned is Azathoth and other Horrors by Edward Derby. This is likely a reference to Edward Pickman Derby, a character from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Thing on the Doorstep".

"Screaming Crawler" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Australian author David Conyers. It first saw print in Issue #1 of the short-lived Lovecraftian fanzine Dreaming in R'lyeh in January 2003.

### Synopsis
Aristocrat Lady Clare Heatherington and her faithful manservant Jake Morgan travel to the jungles of Africa and befriend a tribe of pigmies in their long-running quest to put an end to the cults of Nyarlathotep which plague the world. However, they are beset by both the Screaming Crawler, a creature sent by their enemies to end their lives, and a group of colonial militia whose masters may or may not be in league with the Outer God. Although Lady Clare manages to avoid the attentions of the Crawler, the militia are wiped out by the being, and Morgan is grievously injured. 

### Behind the Mythos
Although presented as a short story, the lack of explanation for Clare and Jake's crusade alongside the cliffhanger ending seems to imply that "Screaming Crawler" was intended to be part of a longer tale rather than a stand-alone work. 

### Trivia
*In its first appearance in Dreaming in R'lyeh, "Screaming Crawler" was credited to David Gonyers .

### Synopsis
: "Scritch, Scratch", Lynne Hardy}}

The story tells a short narrative about the cosy English rural town of Muscoby. Muscoby has always had a rat-catcher for as long as anyone can remember, the latest of whom is an eccentric man named Old Gurteen who catches the many rats which populate the surrounding countryside and hang them to rot in the nearby forest.

When the local council decides to try and turn Muscoby in to the latest tourism cash-cow, they find that many of the visitors are put off by Gurteen's activities. Their problems are solved when he is unexpectedly admitted to hospital and they are able to have him committed due to his mad ramblings about needing to take care of the rats. Cleanup crews are sent into both the town and the forest, and for a while all seems well.

However, what nobody had realised is that Gurteen's activities were not the result of a delusional psyche, but offerings to a dark force: now that the offerings are no longer being made, the forest begins to creep forward in search of its own sustenance…

The Scrying Stones of Chthon first appeared in Marvel Comics' "Doctor Voodoo: Avenger of the Supernatural Vol 1 #1" in 2009, appearing in 3 issues of that series.

### Background
It has not been revealed if the stones were created by Chthon himself or others using his magic such as the Darkhold. Via the stones, one can see the location of other beings, including Hell Lords, and use them to influence being observed. Through the stones others are able to transport themselves to the user's location (and likely vice versa).

Doctor Voodoo during his time as the Sorcerer Supreme used the Scrying Stones of Chthon to help him monitor extradimensional mystical threats to his home dimension. He used the Lost Spirits of Shuma-Gorath to guard the stones. Unfortunately for him, it was turned against him as Nightmare traveled through one of the stones to his location.

The Sea-dwellers are a fictional species created by Robert Bloch and Henry Kuttner for their short story "The Black Kiss".

### Description
The Sea-dwellers are a mysterious species that dwells in the depths of the Pacific Ocean. Although poorly-known to modern Westerners, the Japanese have known about them for a long time. According to Dr. Makoto Yamada, they have inspired myths about Nereids, Gorgons, Mermaids, and other legendary beings.

Sea-dwellers are vaguely seal-like creatures with a long sinuous undulating neck and an inhuman head. They have scaly skin and veined gills, and are almost entirely white. Even their bulging eyes and strangely human-like lips are white, with no pigmentation whatsoever. Instead of a nose, the center of their faces is occupied by a mass of blue worm-like feelers. They have seal-like bodies with four limbs, which seem to be taloned flippers. They also have sharp teeth, befitting their carnivorous nature.

Sea-dwellers can swim prodigiously fast. Their language sounds like cackling laughter and grunts. Apparently, they can live for much longer than a human.

Similar to the Great Race of Yith, Yekubians, Tunnelers Below, and Minions of Othuum, Sea-dwellers are adept at mind-transference. They long to experience the world through the bodies of other creatures, such as humans, and will forcefully transfer their minds into human bodies, thus trapping the victim's consciousness in the body of the Sea-dweller. In most circumstances, however, forcefully taking over the mind of a healthy human is beyond their abilities. Although they can exert some level of psychic influence in dreams and lure people towards the sea (corresponding to the siren's song of legends), this is rarely enough to claim the victim's body as their own. Instead, they often seek out people who are drowning and incapable of resisting them. Dr. Yamada claims that stories about shipwreck survivors who were "saved" by mermaids are actually about people whose bodies were taken over by them.

After performing the mind-transference, the Sea-dweller's consciousness inhabits the human's body until its natural death, at which point the Sea-dweller returns to its own body, casting out the mind of the human, which has no living body left to return to, and therefore perishes. (: "The Black Kiss")

### Behind the Mythos
The general description and habitat of the Sea-dweller is quite reminiscent of the Ningen, a Japanese cryptid known from folklore and a more recent controversial video. The Ningen is sometimes called the "White Godzilla" or "Marine Godzilla". Interestingly, a Japanese expert was featured in the original story "The Black Kiss".

fullContent:
Seabury Grandin Quinn (also known as Jerome Burke; December 1889 – 24 December 1969) was a government lawyer, journalist, and an American pulp magazine author, most famous for his stories of the occult detective Jules de Grandin, published in Weird Tales.

### Biography
He was born and lived in Washington, D.C. In 1910. He graduated from the law school of the National University and admitted to the District of Columbia Bar.

He served in World War I. After his Army service he became editor of a group of trade papers in New York, where he taught medical jurisprudence and wrote technical articles and pulp magazine fiction.

His first published work was "The Law of the Movies", in The Motion Picture Magazine, December 1917. (His story "Painted Gold" may have been written earlier.) "Demons of the Night" was published in Detective Story Magazine on March 19, 1918, followed by "Was She Mad?" on March 25, 1918. He published "The Stone Image" in 1919. He introduced Jules de Grandin as a character in 1925 (taking the character's surname from his own middle name), and continued writing stories about him until 1951. The longest of the de Grandin stories is the 1932 novel-length story The Devil's Bride, strongly influenced by Robert W. Chambers' 1920 novel The Slayer of Souls.

In 1937, he returned to Washington to represent a chain of trade journals, and there subsequently became a government lawyer for the duration of World War II. He alternated between law and journalism all his life. He published over five hundred short stories.

His first book, Roads (a surprising new origin for Santa Claus, drawn from the original Christian legends), was published by Arkham House in 1948.

Ten of the Jules de Grandin stories were collected in The Phantom Fighter (Mycroft & Moran, an imprint of Arkham House; 1966). A broader selection of the stories, including the novel The Devil's Bride, was issued in a six-volume Popular Library paperback edition in 1967–77. A three-volume omnibus reportedly including all the de Grandin stories was issued by Battered Silicon Dispatch Box in 2001.

Although the De Grandin stories were enormously popular on their initial publication, modern critics tend to regard them as the weakest part of Quinn's work, with Brian Stableford describing the De Grandin stories "as indeed rather undistinguished", claiming they are full of stereotyped characters and poorly resolved plots. Quinn wrote several non-De Grandin tales in the 1940s and 1950s; Stableford states Quinn's "best stories here are ironically perverted love stories", such as "The Globe of Memories" (1937) and "Glamour" (1939).

His writing was secondary to his career as a lawyer specializing in mortuary jurisprudence. He taught this subject at mortuary schools for many years, and for some 15 years was the editor of Casket & Sunnyside, a leading trade journal.  Quinn wrote articles for The American Funeral Director and other trade journals.

"Seafoam" is a short Cthulhu Mythos poem by author Alan D. Peschke, first published in the December 1997 edition of Edward P. Berglund's online zine Nightscapes .

### Synopsis
A man named Grimm relates to his friends how, during his college days, he came into possession of a pipe carved from a very unusual variety of meerschaum. Once he begins to smoke from the pipe, he is beset with bizarre dreams of capering fish-men and the octopoid god which is the object of their worship. Determined to uncover the provenance of the pipe, his research points him to answers which may be held in a forbidden text in the Poe’s session of Miskatonic University.

Immediately heading to Arkham, Massachusetts, Grimm is allowed access to the book, Cthulhu in the Necronomicon, when he shows the librarian the pipe and its bizarre carvings. Learning that the fish-men are known as "ones from the deep" or "deep ones," and their dark master Cthulhu, who sleeps beneath the waters of the South Pacific in his sunken city of R'lyeh, he begins to develop a yearning to visit the site of the creature's slumber.

Pursuing his new obsession, Grimm does whatever is necessary to get to the site of R'lyeh, eventually posing as an environmental activist aboard a ship travelling to protest underwater nuclear testing. When sailing over the location of the sunken city, he finds himself compelled to throw himself overboard and join dread Cthulhu beneath the waves, but is able to overcome the urge and throws the pipe over the side instead.

The story concludes with Grimm musing on how, if normal meerschaum - a German word which translates to English as "sea foam" - is created from "the compacted remains of tiny, fossilized sea creatures," then what must the dark, sinister material from which he inhaled be made of?

Sean Branney is an American actor, filmmaker, occasional author, editor, and games designer, and co-founder of the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society. His output to date has revolved almost exclusively around the creation of Lovecraftian works, and includes two full-length feature films based on the stories of H. P. Lovecraft, numerous audio drama productions, and roleplaying game material. He is also a regular attendee at the H. P. Lovecraft Film Festival .

Branney is also credited with coining the name of the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society: according to their website, when Branney and some of his friends were playing a Cthulhu Mythos live-action roleplaying game at college, passers-by who were unaware of the activity called police on the group. When officers attended the scene "a quick-thinking Sean … told them the group was the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society. The police were mollified, and the name stuck."

Sebek is a mythological crocodile-headed god of Ancient Egypt, incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Robert Bloch. Bloch first mentions the deity in "The Suicide in the Study", published in June 1935; the god himself makes an appearance in "The Secret of Sebek", which appeared in the November 1937 issue of Weird Tales.

### In Egyptian Mythology
Sebek was an Egyptian god worshipped in the form of a Nile crocodile, or of a man with a crocodile's head. He was a god of fertility and war, and was often invoked for protection.

Sebek was worshipped in Egypt from the Old Kingdom (c. 2700 BCE) through the Roman era (until 350 CE), and was a particularly important god during the 12th Dynasty (roughly 2000-1800 BCE). The center of Sebek's worship was the Egyptian region of Faiyum, with its capital at Crocodilopolis.

Sebek's name is also given as Sobek or Sobki; it is spelled SBK in hieroglyphics, and scholars can only guess at the actual vowels.

### Behind the Mythos
Bloch featured Sebek in the story "The Secret of Sebek", and mentioned him in "The Suicide in the Study" (where the wizard James Allington focuses his will using "the Soul Chant of Sebek as a focal point"), "The Faceless God", "Fane of the Black Pharaoh", and "The Eyes of the Mummy".

In these early Mythos stories, which Robert M. Price calls "The Egyptian Tales of Robert Bloch", Egyptian deities such as Bast ("The Brood of Bubastis"), Anubis ("The Opener of the Way"), and Sebek are treated as Great Old Ones alongside mythos deities, particularly Nyarlathotep.

### Description
Bloch describes Sebek in "The Secret of Sebek", when the god incarnates at a New Orleans Mardi Gras party: 


The incarnation wears a "long white robe" that "concealed a body whose contours were elusively problematical"; "taloned hands" with "jeweled fingers" held a rod of gold, marked with the Eye of Horus.

"Second Death" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Pierre V. Comtois, first published in his collection Goat Mother and Others by Chaosium in February 2015.

### Synopsis
Anton Zarnak is summoned by his friend Dr. Aaron Stillnor, director of the Pickerton Rehabilitation Hospital, requesting help on a case involving a patient, Charles Danforth, who had recently emerged from a coma.

The story focuses on the aftermath of the original expedition described in H.P. Lovecraft's At The Mountains of Madness, and reflects a view of Miskatonic University as having been passed by the evolution of other Ivy League schools, with the institution now patronizingly seen by the protagonist as hopelessly old fashioned.

The tale unfolds to reveal that the Shoggoths of Antarctica had developed biological sciences capable of telepathic influence and physical transformation, culminating in a confrontation with a half-human, half-Elder Thing monstrosity.

### Publication History
* Goat Mother and Others (2015, 2016)
* Beyond the Mountains of Madness (2015)

fullContent:
"Secret Santa" is a festive Cthulhu Mythos short story by American author Steven M. Vance. It was first published in the Jesse Dedman/William C. Marchese-edited anthology Cthulhu Christmas Special and Other Lovecraftian Yuletide Tales in November 2017.

### Synopsis
When small-time painter Nathan learns from his girlfriend Andi, an Arkham Police Department detective, of the existence of a seasonal serial abductor who dresses up as Santa Claus in order to procure his victims, he resolves to lend a hand.

Getting in touch with one of his mysterious contacts to obtain both support and bait, Nathan then sets about preparing his ambush site, using magic to divine where the killer dubbed Evil Santa is to be found. Collecting the bait - a small girl named Amity - he sets her up in the exact spot the killer will be. When the man attempts to take the girl away, she stabs him with a bone shiv, and her family - a pack of vicious ghouls - emerge from below ground to spirit the body away and feed. Leaving just enough evidence for the police to make the connection between what remains at the murder site and Evil Santa, Nathan heads off to enjoy Christmas.

shortDefinition: Secrets is a modern-day scenario supplement for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, published by Chaosium in 1997. Written by Brian M. Sammons, it features artwork by Paul Carrick and maps by Drashi Khendup. Lynn Willis and Shannon Appel wer...
fullContent:
Secrets is a modern-day scenario supplement for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, published by Chaosium in 1997. Written by Brian M. Sammons, it features artwork by Paul Carrick and maps by Drashi Khendup. Lynn Willis and Shannon Appel were also involved in the book's production .

### Overview


The book contains four stand-alone scenarios designed to be plated over the course of a single session. All necessary handouts are included but, unusually, no pre-generated investigator characters.

### Contents
*"Closed Casket": Robert Monroe-Tyler has just discovered that he is a ghoul, and fakes his own death to disappear and be with his people. When his casket is found to be filled with bricks, his distraught adoptive mother entreats the investigators to find out what became of him.
*"A Love in Need": the investigators stumble across a boarding house whose owners are killing their tenants in a ritual designed to save their disease-stricken son.
*"The Unsealed Room": when a bumbling occult investigator accidentally releases an imprisoned star vampire, its predations are mistaken by all involved for a vampire from folklore.
*"A Cult of One": when an ancient priest of Nyarlathotep has his organs implanted into unsuspecting donors to extend his life, the investigators must race to prevent the possessed victims from uniting and unleashing the evil magician's full power.

### Trivia
*The credits page states that "Paul Carrick's cover illustration for Secrets depicts the idea of secrets, not a particular scenario incident or situation"; however, every scenario includes an instance of a painting depicting a woman suspended over a swamp, though these pieces bear no relation to the story at hand.
*"A Love in Need" features an elixir which allows those who imbibe it to travel through the interstellar void on the back of a Byakhee. Referred to as "space mead" in the story, it would appear to be based on the Golden Mead created by August Derleth for his Trail of Cthulhu series.
*In a comment posted on review aggregate site Goodreads, author Brian M. Sammons stated that Secrets was the "first thing I ever wrote (other than reviews and some columns) to be published" .

"Secrets in Storage" is a Lovecraftian short story by American authors Greg van Eekhout and Tim Pratt.

### Synopsis
A man who buys the contents of old storage lockers for a living finds an ancient chest amongst the contents of his latest purchase. Inside, he finds a magical tunnel which descends into the bowels of the Earth, and there, a cave which houses several altars, a multitude of dead bodies, and a malignant entity which dwells in a pool. Fleeing the chest, he destroys it, although he is forever haunted by what he witnessed within.

### Publication History
"Secrets in Storage" was published in the anthology of Lovecraft-inspired works Whispers from the Abyss in 2013.

fullContent:
Secrets of Japan is an expansion book for the popular Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium.

### Overview
Containing information on how to play games of Call of Cthulhu in modern-day Japan, Secrets of Japan contains a potted history of the country, a guide to culture and traditions, additional character occupations, spells and combat rules, monsters of Japanese folklore, three stand-alone scenarios, and two flavour stories. Written by Michael Dziesinski, it is a softcover book with full-colour cover and black and white interior, and runs to a total of 360 pages in length.

### Publication History
First published in 2005 by Chaosium, Secrets of Japan is currently out of print.

Secrets of Morocco: Eldritch Explorations in the Ancient Kingdom is a supplement for Chaosium’s iconic roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu.

### Overview
Containing a general rundown on all aspects of 1920s and 30s Morocco, including political, social, geographical and cultural information, Secrets of Morocco also features a more detailed look at three of the country's more prominent cities: Rabat, Casablanca and Marrakesh. It also provides a briefing on the colonial situation with regards to the French and Spanish rulers, along with three ready-to-play scenarios to give players and Keepers a taste of what adventures in Morocco could feel like.

Secrets of Morocco was written by William Jones with cover art by Malcolm McClinton, and runs to 130 pages in total.

### Publication History
First released in July 2008, Secrets of Morocco is available in softcover print and digital (PDF editions). Both versions feature full-colour covers with black and white interiors.

"Seduced" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
A down-on-his-luck man vacationing with relatives in the West Virginia backwoods is seduced by an alluring young woman while hiking deep in Shub's Woods, the local name for the thick forest behind his family's property. He does not realise until it is too late that she is actually a witch in the service of Shub-Niggurath, and is intent on devouring both his body and soul.

### Characters

* Michael Simmons, a Texan enjoying a much needed vacation.
* Dora McCain, a beautiful but amoral girl who is in actuality a cultist of Shub-Niggurath.

### Publication History
"Seduced" was first published in mythos-dedicated fanzine Al-Azif #2 in March 1998. It has since appeared in Cthulhu Cultus #17 (2000), and the anthologies Eldritch Blue: Love & Sex in the Cthulhu Mythos (2004) and They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness (2018).

fullContent:
"Seeds From the Blasted Heath" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Brian Barnett. It was published in the Gavin Chappell-edited zine Lovecraftiana, Vol 8, Issue 2 by Rogue Planet Press in July 2023 .

### Synopsis
While returning home to Kentucky via the back country west of Arkham, the unnamed narrator stops off at a roadside stall selling the most incredible tomato plants he has ever seen. Unable to resist buying one from the oddly-afflicted vendor, he proceeds on his way, intending to cultivate the plant at journey's end.

On the way home, he notices a pungent odour coming from the tomatoes, but thinks little of it. At his house, he leaves the plants at his back door with the intention of attending to them in the morning. However, upon awakening, he discovers that the fruit has rotted overnight: determined to salvage what he can, he rescues as many seeds as possible, replanting them in a nursery. He then notices that he has begun to develop the same afflictions possessed by the stallholder, but quickly dismisses this as the compulsion to sell the seedlings on grows stronger…

### Behind the Mythos
The story is intended to be a continuance of H. P. Lovecraft's 1927 short story "The Colour Out of Space"; the title's reference to the "Blasted Heath" refers to the location contaminated by the alien entity's presence in Lovecraft's story, while the mutated flora and strangely-afflicted vendor are consistent with the effects generated by the being.

Seekers are a type of extradimensional creature which feature in the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Description
Created by the malevolent Adumbrali, Seekers are employed by their parent race to travel across dimensions and bring them living beings to torture and ultimately kill. To aid them in this task, they are able to change their shape to match that of the indigenous species, and possess extensive mental abilities which enable them to mesmerise other beings and transport them to their masters' dimension.

### Known Seekers
*Dureen, a Seeker which disguised itself as a physically-perfect human male before taking its prey, a young university student who dabbled in the occult (: "The Abyss").

### Behind the Mythos
Seekers were created by American author Robert A. W. Lowndes for his short story "The Abyss" in April 1941.

Seekers of Knowledge is a deluxe expansion for Fantasy Flight Games' Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

Released in 2011 and containing 165 cards (55 sets of three duplicates), the majority of the cards in Seekers of Knowledge relate to the Miskatonic University faction, although it also contains additional cards for the other factions as well as a handful of general-purpose cards usable by players of any faction.

With the demise of Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game (which was replaced by Arkham Horror: The Card Game, likely due to licensing considerations regarding Chaosium copyright), Seekers of Knowledge was discontinued.

Sefton Asylum is a fictional mental health institution created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his serial horror story "Herbert West--Reanimator."

### Overview
The asylum is located in the fictional town of Sefton, Massachusetts. After being captured in Arkham, the reanimated corpse of Dr. Allan Halsey was kept in the facility at Sefton where it beat its head against the walls of a padded cell for sixteen years. A group of zombies, further products of Herbert West's reanimation experiments, then arrived and broke Halsey out of the asylum, killing four attendants while doing so. (: "Herbert West--Reanimator")

Selected Letters, colloquially known as the Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft, is a five-volume compilation of extracts of Lovecraft's known correspondence published by Arkham House. It includes letters to key contributors to the Cthulhu Mythos like Clark Ashton Smith, Robert E. Howard, August Derleth, Frank Belknap Long, and Robert Bloch.

### Content

Selected Papers on Lovecraft is a collection of non-fiction works by prominent H. P. Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi.

### Overview
Containing five individual studies and running to a total of 75 pages, Selected Papers on Lovecraft was published by Necronomicon Press in June 1986. Cover art was supplied by Jason Eckhardt.

### Contents
*Introduction by Steven J. Mariconda
*Author's Note
*"Lovecraft's Alien Civilisations: A Political Interpretation"
*"The Structure of Lovecraft's Longer Narratives"
*"Lovecraft's Other Planets"
*"Lovecraft's Revisions: How Much of Them Did He Write?"
*"A Look at Lovecraft's Letters"
*Select Bibliography

Sentinel Hill is a location in the fictional town of Dunwich, Massachusetts, created by H. P. Lovecraft in his story "The Dunwich Horror."

The hill, located near the Whateley farm, features in the story as the site of the Whateley family's May Eve and Halloween rituals. At the climax of the story, it's where Henry Armitage confronts the Dunwich Horror--fulfilling Old Whateley's prediction that "yew folks’ll hear a child o’ Lavinny’s a-callin’ its father’s name on the top o’ Sentinel Hill!”

There is a "sizeable table-like rock" atop Sentinel Hill that serves as a ritual altar. There are also "deposits of skulls and bones," thought by Dunwich residents to be the buried remains of the Pocumtuck Indians, though ethnologists maintain they are Caucasian in origin.

There may also be one of the "great rings of rough-hewn stone columns" found on Dunwich hilltops. These structures are generally believed to be the remnants of the Native American cult which practiced religious rites on the mound before the colonisation of Dunwich, although some think that they predate even this. 

The elder Whateley was rumored to have performed a profane ritual atop Sentinel Hill before the birth of his daughter's children Wilbur and Yog.

Sergio Palumbo is an Italian author who has written a number of Lovecraftian stories, several of which have been included in Rogue Planet Press publications such as Swords Against Cthulhu, Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights, and Lovecraftiana.

Palumbo is an Italian civil servant, a law school graduate with a focus on public real estate. He is the co-editor (with Michele Dutcher) of the steampunk anthology Steam-Powered Dream Engines (2018) and the science fiction collection Xenobiology: Stranger Creatures (2020), both published  by Rogue Planet Press. In addition to numerous horror and science fiction anthologies, his work has appeared in outlets like Aphelion Webzine, Weirdyear, Quantum Muse, AntipodeanSF, Schlock!, and SQ Mag. He also designs and builds sci-fi dioramas.

In addition to H. P. Lovecraft, he credits horror writers Stephen King and and Edgar Allan Poe, science fiction's A. E. Van Vogt and Robert A. Heinlein,  and fantasist J. R. R. Tolkien as inspirations for his work.

### Selected Works

The Serpent Crown is a fictional item in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 1968 (as the Helmet of Power) in issue #101 of the 1st volume of the Tales to Astonish comic book series. It made its first appearance as the "Serpent Crown" in 1969 in issue #9 of the 1st volume of the Sub-Mariner comic book series.

### Background
The Serpent Crown (aka the Helmet of Power, Crown of Lemuria, Helmet of the Ancients, and Seven-Headed Serpent Crown of Lost Lemuria) is a mystical artefact created by mortals, per the instructions sent to them by the Elder God Set. They grant men a variety of powers but serve as tools for Set to control those individuals.

The powers which men receive vary depending on the individual, and have included mind reading, hypnosis, mental manipulation of matter & energy (e.g. creating earthquakes), superhuman strength & endurance, creating illusions, levitation, communication with others wearing the Serpent Crown (including those in other dimensions), and powerful destructive mystical bolts.

Serpent People are a fictional nonhuman species which, although possessing somewhat humanoid limbs, strongly resembles snakes. In Mythos stories by various authors, they once ruled the Earth before humanity before being in conflict with prehistoric humans.

They first dwelt in Shuggon in Mesozoic times, but when it was destroyed (circa 65 million B.C.E.) they moved first to Elder Valusia (the Thurian Continent), and then small pockets moved all over the world (America being a probable site). However they suffered several defeats when encountering Mankind. Both the goat-spawn and the shoggoths have functioned as their slaves. They had an advanced culture of science and sorcery, and are capable of impersonating any humanoid lifeform at will (a skill they use to infiltrate human sociopolitical systems and thus gain power).

Sometimes they are also called "Snake Men", "Serpent Men" "serpent folk" and "Valusians".

Named serpent people include: Ssrhythssaa, Zloigm, Sss'haa, Ssathasaa.

### Behind the Mythos
The serpent people were invented separately, but almost simultaneously by Robert E. Howard and Clark Ashton Smith; H. P. Lovecraft, Lin Carter, and John R. Fultz have all expanded the information. Richard L. Tierney added the goat-spawn and shoggoths in "The Temple of The Abomination" by Howard and Tierney.

The Servants of Glaaki are creatures created by the Great Old One Glaaki. 

### Description
The Servants of Glaaki are zombie-like beings that result from living victims who have been infected by Glaaki's toxic spikes. For the first 65 years, they retain their human appearance, and are still capable of independent thought and action when not receiving direct orders from Glaaki. After this period, however, they experience something known as the "Green Decay", which transforms them into undead creatures that can't withstand sunlight. (: "The Inhabitant of the Lake")

"Servant of the Dark" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by John Houlihan, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Synopsis
During the Second World War, an avaricious SS officer in the German-occupied Netherlands attempts to extort valuable gems from the Jewish population as they are being prepared for transportation to concentration camps.

His final target for the day, an elderly book dealer living in seeming seclusion named Jacob Rosenstein, directs the officer to a secret room concealed behind a bookshelf. Inside, he finds a magnificent jewel held in what appears to be some kind of containment field. Greedily reaching for it, he is surprised to find himself immobilised the second he lays his hand on it. Then, slowly, the gem begins to pull…

As the officer's body is inexorably sucked into the gem, Rosenstein explains that the gem is in fact a prison, containing "a creature, a being of the void, a cruel, savage, alien intelligence: hungry, voracious, a feaster upon men’s souls." His fate is to be utterly consumed by the entity, doomed to torment for all eternity.

fullContent:
"Servile" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was published in the Lammas 1997 edition of the Robert M. Price-edited fanzine Cthulhu Codex by Necronomicon Press.

### Synopsis
Gabrielle Rumsey returns to work for her old employer Dianna Wallace, a former explorer and researcher who was crippled several years previously during an attack by unknown assassins in Tibet. She finds her old friend has changed a great deal in the years since their last acquaintance and now, rather than physically searching for the occult truths which she once sought, now travels through dreams to achieve the same result. She is aided in this by a mysterious new servant, an ebony mute named Smith.

Over the following days, Gaby comes to learn that Dianna has become involved in the worship of an ancient, slumbering deity by the name of Tsathoggua. When Dianna orders her husband killed at the hands of Smith, who is in actuality a Formless Spawn masquerading as a man, Gaby flees the house, later learning that her old friend died of an apparent heart attack that very same night, with no trace ever found of the murdered man or Smith.

Although suffering from horribly vivid dreams in which she has knowledge of things which she should not possess, these eventually fade, and Gaby is eventually able to return to something approaching a normal life, but forever wonders if Dianna has perhaps sold her soul to a god which she did not fully understand.

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance, "Servile" has also been included in the collections Unholy Dimensions (2005) and Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012, German translation).
