The Servitors of the Outer Gods, also known as the Idiot Flute-players or Amorphous Flute-players, are a mysterious species expanded upon by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. They were first referred to by H. P. Lovecraft in "The Rats in the Walls", and are also featured in August Derleth's stories, such as The Lurker at the Threshold.

### Background
The Servitors of the Outer Gods are amorphous beings that resemble squids, frogs, and octopi which are constantly changing their shape and appearance. When needed they accompany the Outer Gods, though most of them are in the Court of Azathoth.

The music to which the Outer Gods dance to is made by these demonic drummers and flautists. On occasion they will also play for cultists to summon deities or to provide background music.

The "amorphous idiot flute-players" are often seen in the company of Nyarlathotep. (: "The Rats in the Walls", : "The Dweller in Darkness")

One "amorphous flute-player" also played music to summon the Byakhee in an ancient Yule ritual partaken by the Crawling Ones. (: "The Festival")

### Behind the Mythos
The Servitors of the Outer Gods share many similarities with the Moon-beasts from Lovecraft's novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. The Moon-beasts are also amorphous, toad-like with squid-like tentacles, are often seen playing flutes, and are also servants of Nyarlathotep.

A servitor race is a species that collectively serves another entity or entities. Typically, the entity they serve is a Great Old One, although species that serve Outer Gods, Great Ones, or Elder Gods aren't unheard of either. In many cases, the servitor race will venerate the entity that they serve as a deity, and dutifully perform ceremonies and even sacrifices to it.

While examples of servitor races can be found in the works of the earliest Cthulhu Mythos contributors, such as H. P. Lovecraft and Frank Belknap Long, the concept was first codified as an important aspect of the mythology by August Derleth, who laid a foundation that the expanded Mythos would build upon.

In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, most species are classified as either servitor races, independent races, or fabulous creatures. The game establishes that the Great Old Ones are often accompanied by their servitor species, representatives of which "may act as hitmen, messengers, spies, and delivery boys, frightening off investigators and bulking out confrontations".

### Definition
While alien entities are often worshiped as gods in Lovecraft's stories, the distinction between widespread cults and examples of species-wide servitude is not always clear. For instance, Cthulhu is identified as the leader of the cosmic octopi, also referred to as his "star-spawn", which are currently imprisoned in R'lyeh (: "The Call of Cthulhu", At the Mountains of Madness). Conversely, the Deep Ones are also known to offer tributes to Cthulhu, and are free to move about, rather than being imprisoned, although stones marked with a certain sign can repel them (: The Shadow Over Innsmouth). In the Dreamlands, the Shantaks, Moon-beasts and Men of Leng are all followers of Nyarlathotep, whereas the Night-gaunts serve Nodens, and the Ghouls owe allegiance to no deity (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath). Some species are also portrayed by Lovecraft as entirely irreligious, including the Elder Things and the Great Race of Yith.

It was Derleth who first established the notion that the Great Old Ones have "spawned" several species as "servants" or "minions", who are actively trying to free their masters from the imprisonment that the Elder Gods subjected them to, and preparing the terrain for their return (: "The Return of Hastur"). Unlike the Great Old Ones, the servitor races aren't themselves imprisoned. However, they are also defined by the fact that the sight of the Elder Sign can repel them. Species identified as servant races by Derleth include the "Abominable Snowmen" / "Abominable Mi-Go", the Byakhee, the Deep Ones, the Dholes, the Shantaks, the Shoggoths, and the Voormis (: "The Keeper of the Key", "The House in the Valley"). It's worth noting that some of these would later be classified by Chaosium as independent races, not servitors.

### Overview
An area in the United States, Pacific Nortwest similar in nature to New England's Miskatonic River Valley and the Severn Valley of the United Kingdom, the Sesqua Valley is a region steeped in the supernatural, with those who leave being said to struggle to recall details of the area.

### Sesqua Town
A reasonably-sized urban settlement complete with its own business district.

The base of operations for a cell of the Cult of Gla'aki, the lake appears to be one of the places outside of the Severn Valley where the Great Old One is capable of manifesting.

Set was a "dark" god (chaos, violence, fire, storms, etc) who was worshiped in historical pharaonic Egypt. In Egypt he was variously worshiped depending on the region of Egypt from which various cults originated as a red-haired storm god and uncle of Horus (Set), the destroyer of life, family and fertility (Sutekh) or as a violent but still ultimately benevolent god-pharaoh who was a member of the godly royal family descended from Ra.

In the Hyborian Age stories of Robert E. Howard, the god Set was originally known as Satha, the venomous giant serpent, who was worshiped by some cultures and demonised by others, becoming known not only as Set, but also as Leviathan and Satan (: "The Valley of the Worm"). He was the dark god / evil god who was worshiped by many of Conan the Cimmerian's sorcerer enemies as well as in the dark kingdom of Stygia. (: "The Phoenix on the Sword", et al)

According to one account, Set is a Great Old One, (: Nameless Cults, Conan: Adventures in an Age Undreamed Of sourcebook) but according to another, Set is the same entity that would later become known as Assatur or Hastur, whose name is derived from "Ah-Set-ur". (: "The Worm of Urakhu")

In the age of Conan, Set had already in times far distant even from that prehistoric era sired "monster-kings" known as the children of Set (: "The God in the Bowl"), described in Marvel Comics stories using Conan as the Man-Serpent species.

Father Set of the Underworld is also referenced in the Cthulhu Mythos stories of Robert Bloch, where he is identified as one of the seven main gods of Egypt, along with Osiris, Isis, Ra, Bast, Thoth, and Anubis. (: "The Opener of the Way")

Some sources depict Set as an avatar of Nyarlathotep which takes the form of a humanoid deity with the head of a Typhonian Beast. (: Lurking Fears, Malleus Monstrorum)

According to one source, Set is one of the many avatars of Nyarlathotep documented in the Great Library of Celaeno. (: Haiyore! Nyaruko-san)

### Background
Set who is known by many names (Great Dragon, Yig, and Quetzalcoatl), is a slavering hungry deity. Set originates from the Outer Dark, and is a being whose physical form is rejected by the world, twisting reality around it. Relics which have been blessed or touched by him are no longer completely part of the physical world, which is the reason that they are endowed with incredible powers. Any priest who draws on those powers does so at great personal risk, as the forces that are unleashed corrupt the flesh and tear at the mind.

Apostate Stygians who speak blasphemies against Set often meet sticky ends. They mysteriously disappear, are found hideously murdered via the most inhuman methods, or they end up slowly turning into serpent men as their eyes turn yellow and their skin slips away. Set is an Elder God in the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. Which also appears as the primary dark / evil god in the Conan mythos, worshiped by most of Conan's greatest sorcerer foes, being the god of the sinister decadent kingdom of Stygia, and the god / creator of the Serpent Men.

The Marvel adaptation of Set first appeared in the 6th issue of the 2nd volume of the Marvel Feature comic book series by Roy Thomas and Frank Thorne.

According to one account, Set is the same entity as Hastur, whose name is derived from Assatur or Ah-Set-ur. (: "The Worm of Urakhu")

### Background
Set was one of the Elder Gods of Earth, whose ranks included Gaea, Oshtur, and Chthon. At the dawn of life on Earth, they were created on Earth by Demiurge the sentient biosphere. Set discovered that he could increase his power by devouring other Elder Gods, thereby becoming the first murderer on Earth. Other Elder Gods then followed his example and soon the majority of his kind had become corrupted, as they degenerated into demons. Among the worst of them were Set and his "brother" Chthon. Gaea wept for what happened to her siblings, and to stop the corrupted Elder Gods she conceived a child with the Demiurge. Her son Atum had a secondary form, Demogorge, the God-Eater. He then set out to destroy the corrupted Elder Gods. Some of them managed to escape destruction, fleeing into parallel pocket dimensions, including Set and Chthon.

During the time of dinosaurs, Set formed a bond with the reptiles that ruled the Earth. Using their combined lifeforces, he merged several dinosaur bodies and reincarnated on Earth, making his first manifestation as a serpent. Atum intervened, resulting in an epic battle that lasted eons, a battle so cataclysmic that it resulted in the extinction of the dinosaurs. It was during this battle, that Set first revealed his hydra-like ability to grow two heads for every one that was destroyed. Eventually he was defeated by Atum and forced to retreat back to his dimension. From its pocket dimension it continued to exert varying levels of influence in the physical world via its worshipers and its spawn. Its influence reached 100s of alternate Earths and through its manipulations, on those worlds men create the infamous Serpent Crowns, mystical artifacts that granted men powers but which served as tools for Set to control those individuals.

fullContent:
Settler's Wall is a longer version of a short story by Robert Lowndes published as 'The Long Wall' in Stirring Science Stories, March 1942, under the pseudonym 'Wilfred Owen Morley'. The story was later expanded into 'Settler’s Wall' as a novella in Startling Mystery Stories, Fall 1968.

### Synopsis
In the countryside near Flagstaff, Maine, there is a wall ten feet high, dull, and has been there for as long as anyone can remember. There is no other side. If you try to climb over it, you will find yourself on the same side as you started. If you try to walk around it, you will get back to where you started. Objects thrown over are later found lying in the grass on your own side.

The novella is a puzzle tale work of what is now usually called Mathfiction, about a one-sided wall near Flagstaff, Maine, describing events that occurred around the year 1934. The narrator and his cousin, Arthur Gordon, and a friend, Will Richards, are headed for Summer camp when they encounter an odd wall which seems to stretch for miles, with a very odd atmosphere around it. It eventuates that the wall is in fact one-sided and in some preternatural manner loops around itself in the manner of Mobius Strip. This object which apparently interpenetrates into other, "higher" dimensions persists in the neighborhood where it is encountered until a mighty hurricane strikes the region in 1938. At that time the wall vanishes, or, if as the narrator speculates it was some sort of cosmic entity, it simply "swam away."

Seugathi were created by Paizo Inc in 2008, appearing in the Denizens of the Darklands sourcebook for the Pathfinder RPG.

### Physiology
The Seugathi are huge creatures, that resemble a cross between a worm and a caterpillar. Having bodies that stretch up to 14 ft in length. When threatened a Seugathi will rear up, using their caterpillar-like legs to support themselves. On their heads are three sharp bony jacks and insectoid eyes. At the end of the body, the torso splits into two long prehensile slender tentacles which are used to wield weapons.

### Backround
It's a subterranean race of sentient tentacled worms that serve the Neothelids who spawn hundreds of them in pits. Only a foot long when spawned, they begin to consume each other, until only one fully grown adult remains. At which time, the Neothelids begin to give it many missions which further the secret agendas of their makers. Each Seugathi is spawned for a single purpose.

While they are able to survive on subterranean fungus and creatures, a Seugathi's favorite food is the rational thoughts of the sane. Unfortunately for the victim, the siphoning of those thoughts drives them insane. Seugathi bites are also poisonous which makes the victim more pliable for feeding. Seugathi are solitary creatures which rarely interact with other lifeforms, though they occasionally are encountered in small groups of their own kind formed into as cults, or as a warband being led by creatures of a similar mindset.

The Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan are a collection of fictional occult grimoires created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Other Gods".

### Overview
Little is known of the contents of the Seven Cryptical Books, even where they come from: both the Dreamlands and the waking lands of Earth's prehistory have been suggested as their place of origin. Presumably written by a person or entity named Hsan, or in a place called Hsan, their contents also remain a mystery.

Despite the uncertainty of their history, copies of the Seven Cryptical Books are known to exist in the Dreamlands of the modern age.

fullContent:
"Seven Serpents Waiting" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
The demented Wendell Willis, having fled his home following the events detailed in "When in Leng…", seeks sanctuary in the Louisiana swamps with his old friend Tobias Jackson, a high priest of the snake-god Yig. 

When Willis discovers that Jackson knows the secrets of serpent stealth, powerful magic which would allow him to reintegrate himself into society anonymously, he kills his former friend and enacts the ritual. What he does not realise is that Jackson has laid a trap for any who might try to steal his secrets, and the story finds Willis held captive in his magic circle, safe from the serpent-followers of Yig which surround him, but with nothing to eat or drink.

### Characters

*Wendell Willis, a madman with a thirst for forbidden knowledge.
*Tobias Jackson, a swamp dweller who worships the Great Old One Yig.

### Publication History
"Seven Serpents Waiting" has been published in Imelod #17 (October 2000), Lovecraft's Disciples (June 2006), and They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness (2018).

shortDefinition: The Severn Valley is the setting of several fictional towns and other locations created by horror writer Ramsey Campbell. Part of the Cthulhu Mythos begun by H. P. Lovecraft, the fictional milieu is arguably the most detailed mythos setting outside o...
fullContent:
The Severn Valley is the setting of several fictional towns and other locations created by horror writer Ramsey Campbell. Part of the Cthulhu Mythos begun by H. P. Lovecraft, the fictional milieu is arguably the most detailed mythos setting outside of Lovecraft Country itself.

In his early writings, Campbell used the setting of Lovecraft's stories, in the fictional New England area of the Miskatonic River valley. Fellow Lovecraftian writer August Derleth suggested that instead of copying the older works, Campbell should instead use a setting that he knew personally: his hometown of Liverpool. Campbell's creation of Severn Valley is a reflection of the English countryside that he knew well. By the mid-60s, Campbell acknowledges that "my invented town of Brichester, originally intended as the Severn Valley equivalent of Lovecraft's Arkham, was Liverpool by now in all but name."

### Real-world location
The River Severn is an actual river in Wales and western England. Campbell's stories mention various real-world locales, including the Cotswold Hills, Berkeley (in "The Church in High Street"), and the A38 road ("The Room in the Castle"). These references place "Campbell Country" in the southern part of Gloucestershire, roughly between the cities of Gloucester and Bristol. This area is more correctly referred to as the Vale of Berkeley or the Severn Estuary; the real-world Severn Valley refers to an area around fifty miles (80 km) further north.

### Ramsey Campbell

Campbell invented his locales, when, as a 15-year-old Lovecraft fan, he submitted Lovecraftian pastiches, set in Lovecraft's New England, to Arkham House's August Derleth. "Derleth told me to abandon my attempts to set my work in Massachusetts," Campbell wrote in the introduction to his collection Cold Print, and he accordingly rewrote his stories with an English setting. His short story "The Tomb-Herd", for example, was originally set in Lovecraft's Kingsport, Massachusetts. It was transposed to the Cotswold town of Temphill when it appeared as "The Church in High Street", Campbell's first published story, in the 1962 Arkham House anthology Dark Mind, Dark Heart.

In that story, Campbell refers to hints "of actual worship of trans-spatial beings still practiced in such towns as Camside, Brichester, Severnford, Goatswood, and Temphill," indicating that he had already conceived of most of the principal locations of his Severn Valley setting. At the time, the teenage Campbell had never been to the actual Severn Valley; the imaginary landscapes he described may relate more to the post-World War II Merseyside scenes he was familiar with. He recalled in an interview:



Campbell's first collection of short stories, The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants (1964), was filled with stories that take place in the Severn Valley setting, including "The Room in the Castle", "The Horror From the Bridge", "The Insects from Shaggai", "The Render of the Veils", "The Inhabitant of the Lake",

Severnford is a fictional town created by Ramsey Campbell, part of his Severn Valley setting for Cthulhu Mythos stories. The place is introduced in Campbell's  short story "The Room in the Castle".

Severnford is a community located on the real-world River Severn, almost directly northwest of Brichester. Campbell summarizes it in the introduction to The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants:



It's described in Campbell's "The Plain of Sound" as a dull place to visit:



The "forced" is a reference to the fact there is only one bus-route daily from Severnford to Brichester, which leaves in the morning. If visitors miss it, walking may be the only alternative. It's a full morning's walk away, and the route is not well-marked.

One attraction is the Inn at Severnford, a facility in central Severnford which is said to be "one of the oldest (inns) in England". However, in 1958 it was found to be "temporarily" closed to the public, reportedly because of repeated vandalism.

Severnford and its outskirts are the main setting of Campbell's "The Room in the Castle", in which the Anglican church in Severnford is noted for having "a stone carving depicting an angel holding a large star-shaped object in front of a cowering toad-like object."

In "The Stone on the Island", Cambell gives Severnford a "Harrison Hotel at the edge of dockland", several bookshops, a "grimy library"--and a police officer, Inspector Blackwood.

Campbell returned to Severnford in the story "Potential", a setting in which "(t)he streets were lit by gas-lamps, reflected flickering in windows set in dark moist stone." The climactic scene of that story is set in a disused Severnford pub called The Riverside, used as a sort of clubhouse by cultists who listen to the avant-garde composer Penderecki, and read Roland Franklyn and Ultimate Press pornography. There is a suggestion that the Severnford authorities are complicit in the cult's activities: "Oh, the police know about this," one cult member says. "They're used to it by now, they don't interfere."

About two-and-a-half miles (by foot) out of Severnford, after passing a "thickly overgrown forest, where (one) would certainly have become further lost," and crossing "monotonous fields (without) seeing a building or another human being," one comes to "an area of grassy hillocks," followed by a region of "miniature valleys". It is in one of these that the title phenomenon of "The Plain of Sound" was encountered, next to a house once inhabited by former Brichester University professor Arnold Hird. This peculiar phenomenon can become a gateway into the Gulf of S'glhuo.

In the story "The Faces at Pine Dunes", Severnford is named by the fictional book Witchcraft in England as one of several centers of witchcraft activity—apparently the only place in the Severn Valley so listed.

fullContent:
Sex and the Cthulhu Mythos is a non-fiction book by Bobby Derie, published by Hippocampus Press in 2014, that looks at the role of sexuality and gender in the life and work of H. P. Lovecraft, and in the Cthulhu Mythos that he inspired. 

Derie first looks at the role sexuality and gender played in Lovecraft's life, particularly in the context of his marriage to Sonia Greene, and the ideas he expressed about sex and love. Lovecraft's views on homosexuality and miscegenation are examined.

He then turns to Lovecraft's fiction, first looking at the way sexuality was expressed in the literature that influenced him, particularly Edgar Allan Poe and Arthur Machen. Derie goes on to analyze the sexual content in various Lovecraft stories, including “Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family” (1920), “The Outsider” (1921), “The Lurking Fear” (1922), “The Rats in the Walls” (1923), “The Unnamable” (1923), “The Horror at Red Hook” (1925) The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath (1926–27), The Case of Charles Dexter Ward (1927), “The Dunwich Horror” (1928), “The Shadow over Innsmouth” (1931), “The Dreams in the Witch House” (1932), and “The Thing on the Doorstep” (1933).

Turning to the Lovecraft's legacy, Derie discusses a number of writers in the Mythos tradition whose work has dealt with sexual themes to a greater or lesser extent, including Robert E. Howard, Clark Ashton Smith, Robert Bloch, August Derleth, Ramsey Campbell, Richard A. Lupoff, Peter H. Cannon, Brian McNaughton, Robert M. Price, W. H. Pugmire, Caitlín R. Kiernan, Edward Lee, and Alan Moore.

The book makes note of the magazine Cthulhu Sex (1998–2007) and anthologies of erotic Mythos fiction such as Eldritch Blue: Love & Sex in the Cthulhu Mythos (2004), Cthulhurotica (2010), and Whispers in Darkness: Lovecraftian Erotica (2011).

While critical discussions of the Mythos generally focus on written fiction, Derie looks more broadly at the sexuality in the Lovecraftian occult, and in art, comics, and cinema.

Shabbith-Ka is a Lesser Outer God which appears in the H. P. Lovecraft-inspired Cthulhu Mythos. Created by Jeff Moeller, it appeared in the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game scenario "What Goes Around, Comes Around," first published in The Unspeakable Oath #8/9, and later included in the collection The Resurrected III: Out of the Vault.

### Description
Shabbith-Ka manifests as an amorphous blob of glowing purple energy; staring at the entity for long enough may allow the viewer to discern the outline of a rudimentary face, although what effect such an action might have on the person's sanity is enough to make one shudder.

The entity's worshippers summon it through the use of a particular spell, which is employed in the form of a song. When summoned, anyone not under the protection of an Elder Sign or actively singing the summoning spell will be attacked and consumed by it. It achieves this by absorbing the person into its "body," leaving nothing behind but a purple-tinged husk, which quickly disintegrates into ashes. Due to the nature of its form, physical weapons are useless against Shabbith-Ka.

When exposed to an Elder Sign, or if it has simply run out of viable prey, Shabbith-Ka retreats back to its lair at the centre of the universe, either by blasting through space at an incredible velocity or simply fading away into the void.

### Behind the Mythos
Due to the nature of the entity (Lesser Outer God) and its residence ("centre of the universe"), it may be the case that it is part of the Lesser Other Gods that reside at the Court of Azathoth. This isn't explicitly stated, however.

The Shadows are a Lovecraftian-like race in the fictional universe of the Babylon 5 live action television series. 

### Background
The Shadows are an ancient race, one of the First Ones. A race that is billions of years old. Known as the "Shadows" by the younger races, their actual name in unpronounceable to them, being over 10,000 letters long. It's a race whose form is that of an insectoid hexaped, a cross between a praying mantis and a spider. With seven pairs of pinpoint eyes on their small triangular head. They can cloak themselves from most of the visible wavelengths but can sometimes appear as figures of static in the infrared spectrum's upper end.

Shadows embrace chaos, seeing it as the universe's supreme force. They believe that a race cannot reach its full potential if it is not tested through conflict and war, pain and struggle. Therefore through their manipulations they bring about the aforementioned, to force evolution forward. The end result being that strong races become stronger and the weak race die off. The Shadows follow the First Principles: chaos through warfare; evolution through bloodshed; perfection through victory.

The Shadows are masters of organic technology, using it everywhere. They possess great ships that resemble black spiders known as Shadow Vessels, which use living sentient beings as their central processing unit. Their ships have the ability to phase in and out of hyperspace, unlike the other races which need to form a jump point or use a jumpgate. They are equipped with beam weapons that are vastly more powerful than those of the younger races, can fire jump point destabilizers, and launch swarms of shadow fighters. The Shadows have planet killers, called the "Death Cloud". It's a colossal movable latticework structure that is surrounded by a vast cloud of nanites, which surrounds a world and launches burrowing multi-megaton missiles which tear apart the world from the inside.

Serving the Shadows are a number of servitor races whom have pledged their service to the Shadows. They have been given access to Shadow technology and lived / worked right alongside the Shadows, including on their homeworld. Whenever the Shadows slept between the wars, their servitor races continued the work of the Shadows throughout the galaxy. Manipulating races, carrying out experiments, and preparing the way for the eventual return of the Shadows.

The Shadow is a Lovecraftian power in the fictional universe of the Supernatural television series, an "ancient cosmic entity" older than God who exhibits great destructive power when woken from eternal sleep.

### Background
The Shadow is the oldest entity in the Supernatural cosmos. Before God or even the Darkness existed, there was only absolute nothingness. This giant nothing is actually sentient, has a true form that even angels would go mad from seeing, and its mindset is noticeably more alien than that of any other deity or cosmic entity. Like Cthulhu or Lord Dunsany's Mana-Yood-Sushai, its normal state is eternal sleep, and becomes a destructive force to the cosmos when awakened.

"Shadow of the Black Sun" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author David J. Rodger which takes place in Modiphius Entertainment's Achtung! Cthulhu roleplaying game setting. It was published in the anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius in 2015.

### Synopsis
The story revolves around a squad of German soldiers stationed in occupied Norway during the Second World War. When they capture and kill a local witch, the act inadvertently opens a dimensional rift which allows the malevolent entity known as the Black Sun entry into our world. As the being begins to break through, the commander of the unit finds his body destroyed, his disembodied soul consigned to bear witness to the Black Sun for all eternity.

### Mythos Connections
Aside from the story's setting, the lost lands of Thule and Hyperborea are also made mention of.

The game is a third person single-player adventure following a photographer in the town of Illsmouth (a clear play on Lovecraft's Innsmouth) who must unravel a sinister conspiracy while surviving his three-day stay. It borrows many of its themes and devices from The Shadow Over Innsmouth and The Dunwich Horror.

### Release

"Shadow Transit" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Ferrett Steinmetz.

### Synopsis
When Michelle's daughter Lizzie begins to communicate with a colossal entity sleeping beneath the ocean, she is taken by a shadowy government organisation which specialises in training children in the use of their abilities. On one of her monthly visitations, Lizzie tells her mother a terrible secret: that the Dreamer is on the verge of awakening…

### Characters
*Michelle, a mother struggling to cope with the powers manifested by her ever-more eccentric daughter.
*Elizabeth "Lizzie", a young girl gifted - or cursed - with a mind which can communicate with an inhuman being.

### Publication History
"Shadow Transit" made its debut online on Buzzy Mag in July 2013. It was given an audio reading in Pseudopod #418 in December 2014, and was included in the Kat Rocha-edited anthology Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be in October 2015.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly stated, the slumbering behemoth referred to as the Dreamer is implied to be the Great Old One Cthulhu, as Lizzie knows the date of its awakening, presumably the date at which the stars are right.

fullContent:
"Shadows Dawning" is a short story by Georgina Kamsika and the second story in the anthology The Devourer Below. It is set in the popular Arkham Horror Fiction universe.

### Plot Summary
Lita Chantler is searching for clues for who murdered her husband John. She found a cultist and coerced them into giving her a name. Lita returns home, reminiscing about what had happened. Strangers had begun harassing her husband at his butcher’s store, demanding live meat, and Lita had insisted that they talk to the police. But they had refused to help them, and not long after John had been murdered. Lita had sworn to find the murderers and avenge his death. When returning home, Lita is greeted by her friend Priya Anand, whom she and her partner Emily have known for years. Priya brings Lita into the kitchen to stitch the wounds she got from meeting the cultist. Once Priya is done, they move to the living room. Lita pours herself some brandy, but Priya declines her offer to join her. Priya tells Lita that she has to stop and move on with her life. Lita asks if Priya could do the same if something similar had happened to Emily. As they continue to argue, Lita hears a noise from the front door. She goes to the hallway and arms herself with a poker. The door bursts open as a man breaks in and starts to attack Lita. She defends herself, and manages to hurt the man badly by striking him in the collarbone. Wounded, the man retreats and flees into the night. A policeman named Billy Cooper arrives almost immediately after, dismissing the assault as another animal attack before he leaves. Priya asks Lita why she didn’t tell the police officer about what had happened, and Lita responds that he is one of the cultists. She sends Priya home through the backdoor, and watches her go home.

Lita is too beaten up to sleep, and sits in the living room in the dark. She sees her old wedding pictures and, in a fit of rage, throws her tumbler against the wall. Finally falling asleep, she’s woken up by the grandmother’s clock at six am. Lita goes to the kitchen and makes coffee, as she is too nauseous to eat. As she thinks about how much she misses her husband, the phone suddenly rings. Lita picks up, but no one answers, making her believe it’s one of the cultists harassing her. She remembers how often the phone used to ring, with invites to dinner or simply to chat. But the police had helped spread the rumor that she was the primary suspect in John’s death, so her friends had stopped calling. Lita goes into John’s study, where she has set up a map with all of the information she had gathered about the cultists. The cultist she met gave her the name Ida Smith, and she finds an address for her in the telephone directory. Lita pours herself some scotch and lights a cigarette, thinking of her discovery of ghouls and the cultists that aided them.

fullContent:
The Shadows of Pnath by Josh Reynolds is a novel in the Cthulhu Mythos stories from Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting for Arkham Horror Fiction. It is the second book of the Countess Zorzi series. Paperback, digital and audio editions were released. It was adapted by Graphic Audio into an audio production with an entire cast of voice actors.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Infamous cat burglar Countess Alessandra Zorzi has left Arkham, Massachusetts with her protege, Pepper Kelly, in hopes of redeeming herself from her life of crime. She is now tracking down artifacts and volumes she stole for nefarious occultists in order to restore them to the "right" hands of Miskatonic University. However, Pepper is soon kidnapped by her former lover, the Comte Henri de Erlette, who ransoms her at a steep cost: the original copy of Cultes des Goules. Black Chamber agent, Trish, and a representative of the ghoul agent want the book for themselves. However, the Comte has his own plan for the tome that may shake the foundations of the universe.

### Characters
*Countless Alessandra Zorzi - An infamous Italian cat burglar from a family of con men and grifters. She is both beautiful as well as cunning. The Countess has made her career dealing in occult artifacts stolen from an eclectic and eccentric clientele. Her encounters in Arkham have caused her to reevaluate her belief in the supernatural.
*Pepper Kelly - A young woman masquerading as a boy to serve as an Arkham taxi driver. She has done some bootlegging work for the local gangs but is not a professional criminal. That is until the Countess offers her a lucrative and enjoyable side career as her guide.
*Trish: An agent of the Black Chamber (the predecessor agency for the NSA) that is in charge of investigating occult matters for the United States government. It is loosely allied with the Silver Twilight Lodge and wishes to acquire the book for themselves.
*Comte Henri de'Erlette: A French aristocrat whose ancestor wrote the original Cults des Goules. He is obsessed with his family's occult legacy and getting revenge on the entire ghoul race. He is the Countess' former lover.

### Synopsis
In the years following his Uncle Robert's disappearance, a man begins to develop an affinity with the ocean while undergoing strange physical changes. Slowly retreating from mainstream society, he finds acceptance amongst the local dock workers and the dour folks of Innsmouth. As his body metamorphoses, he eventually takes to the ocean, and assumes his birthright amongst the Deep Ones and reunites with his vanished uncle, now acting as the High Priest of the Esoteric Order of Dagon.

shortDefinition: "Shadows of the Evening" is a short story by Joyce Carol Oates that appeared in her collection The Collector of Hearts: New Tales of the Grotesque (Dutton, 1998). It was included in the anthology Dreams from the Witch House: Female Voices of Lovecraf...
fullContent:
"Shadows of the Evening" is a short story by Joyce Carol Oates that appeared in her collection The Collector of Hearts: New Tales of the Grotesque (Dutton, 1998). It was included in the anthology Dreams from the Witch House: Female Voices of Lovecraftian Horror (2015).

It tells the story of Magdalena Schön, a shy young woman from Buffalo, New York, who in 1928 goes to live with her wealthy, stroke-ridden great-aunt, Erica Kistenmacher, in Edmundston, Massachusetts. Taking a walk down to lower Edmundston, Magdalena hears and becomes obsessed by a young man with a beautiful voice, singing a hymn over and over in a decrepit church: "Now the day is over, night is drawing nigh… Shadows of the evening steal across the sky."

Oates has described "Shadows of the Evening" as "my Lovecraft story", indicating that it was based on  "The Music of Erich Zann":[I]t’s about somebody who hears someone singing at a distance. She hears a voice singing, and she’s drawn out of her house, and goes into the city, and goes into a strange place, maybe like a church, and she discovers who’s singing, so it definitely was evolved from the Lovecraft story.

### Reception
A New York Times review of The Collector of Hearts called "Shadows of the Evening" one of "the most striking stories in the collection....  It would be a disservice to this fine story to reveal how adroitly Oates spools together the aunt and the singer, how Magdalena is lost and then saved." Kirkus Reviews called it one of "two superbly imagined and skillfully constructed exercises in psychological horror" in the collection.

Shadows of Yog-Sothoth: A Global Campaign to Save Mankind is a campaign sourcebook for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
The first scenario supplement for Call of Cthulhu, Shadows of Yog-Sothoth contains a seven-part campaign and two stand-alone adventures. The campaign takes the players across the globe in pursuit of the cult of the Hermetic Order of the Silver Twilight, from America’s east coast to Scotland to the South Pacific. The two adventures consist of "The People of the Monolith", a trip to Hungary in search of a mysterious poet, and "The Warren", the hunt for a missing friend in Boston.

### Publication History
Released in 1982, the first edition of Shadows of Yog-Sothoth ran to 72 pages and featured artwork by Tom Sullivan. In 1989, it was collected along with other previously-published playing material and an all-new scenario in Cthulhu Classics, while in 2004, it was re-released in an updated format for the sixth edition of Call of Cthulhu along with new material and artwork. This version ran to 144 pages.

fullContent:
Shadows Over Baker Street is a thematic anthology in which the stories blend the cases of Arthur Conan Doyle's master detective Sherlock Holmes with elements of the Cthulhu Mythos. Unlike in Doyle's original stories, where the supernatural is only used as red herring plot devices, here it is all too real.

Neil Gaiman's "A Study in Emerald", which won the 2004 Hugo Award for Best Short Story, first appeared in this collection.

### Publication History
Edited by Michael Reaves and John Pelan, who both contributed stories, Shadows Over Baker Street contains eighteen shorts and runs to 464 pages. It was first published in September 2003 by Ballantine Books' science fiction/fantasy imprint Del Rey Books.

### Contents
* "A Study in Emerald" by Neil Gaiman
* "Tiger! Tiger!" by Elizabeth Bear
* "The Case of the Wavy Black Dagger" by Steve Perry
* "A Case of Royal Blood" by Steven-Elliot Altman
* "The Weeping Masks" by James Lowder
* "Art in the Blood" by Brian Stableford
* "The Curious Case of Miss Violet Stone" by Poppy Z. Brite and David Ferguson
* "The Adventure of the Antiquarian's Niece" by Barbara Hambly
* "The Mystery of the Worm" by John Pelan
* "The Mystery of the Hanged Man's Puzzle" by Paul Finch
* "The Horror of the Many Faces" by Tim Lebbon
* "The Adventure of the Arab's Manuscript" by Michael Reaves
* "The Drowned Geologist" by Caitlín R. Kiernan
* "A Case of Insomnia" by John P. Vourlis
* "The Adventure of the Voorish Sign" by Richard A. Lupoff
* "The Adventure of Exham Priory" by F. Gwynplaine MacIntyre
* "Death Did Not Become Him" by Patricia Lee Macomber and David Niall Wilson
* "Nightmare in Wax" by Simon Clark

### Behind the Mythos
In addition to Sherlock Holmes and the Cthulhu Mythos, there are many stories in this book that also feature additional crossovers.
*Thomas Carnacki, the fictional occultist created by William Hope Hodgson, appears in "The Adventure of the Antiquarian's Niece" (although his name is spelled 'Carnaki').
*The sinister Dr. Nikola from the works of Guy Boothby is featured in "The Mystery of the Worm".
*"The Drowned Geologist" references the mysterious fate of the ship Demeter from Bram Stoker's Dracula.
*The villainous Dr. Caresco from the works of André Couvreur is referenced several times in "Death Did Not Become Him", as his experiments are crucial to the plot.
*The narrative of "A Study in Emerald" is interspersed with advertisements for fictional products that reference Mary Shelley's Frankenstein, Robert Louis Stevenson's Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, Bram Stoker's Dracula, and the legendary Spring-Heeled Jack.

fullContent:
Shadows Over Scotland is a sourcebook for Chaosium's horror adventure game Call of Cthulhu. It is part of Cubicle 7 Entertainment's Cthulhu Britannica line.

### Overview
As it’s name might suggest, Shadows Over Scotland is a sourcebook for playing Call of Cthulhu games north of the border in the United Kingdom. It contains sections detailing the history of Scotland - including how the forces of the Mythos have shaped the country - an in-depth look at nine of her cities, a breakdown of the lowlands, Highlands and Islands, and six standalone adventures complete with player handouts. The book was written by Stuart Boon and runs to a total of 288 pages.

### Scenarios

*"Death and Horror Incorporated"
*"The Hand of Abyzou"
*"Uisge Beatha (The Water of Life)"
*"Heed the Kraken's Call"
*"The Forbidden Isle"
*"Star Seed"

### Publication History
Third-party content provider Cubicle 7 Entertainment published Shadows Over Scotland in August 2011 in a hardcover edition. It is currently out of print.

fullContent:
"Shaft Number 247" is a short story by Basil Copper. It was first published in Ramsey Campbell's anthology New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos by Arkham House in 1980. It has been reprinted several times, and French and German translations have since also released.

### Synopsis
The story describes a stealthy assault on a civilization consigned to a permanent underground existence. The assault is by something from Outside, outside the tunnels in which they lives and perhaps Outside normal time and space. Describing an underground dystopian society, the story features Driscoll, who oversees a watertight well circuit, who at the request of his superior has to question Wainwright, a junior in charge of well 247, about the disappearance of Deems, his predecessor in the post. The story has many Kafkaesque and Orwellian elements.

The entity hunting the surviving humans uses smell as one of its main weapons, producing a "heady perfume" that smells of... blue skies, grass, the beauty of the surface world.

The overall plot is one familiar to any fan of Doctor Who, that of the base under siege, with strong elements of a totalitarian society enabling essential elements of the story to work.

Whether the entities Outside are Shoggoths or something else even worse is never revealed.

### Publication History
* New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (1980, 1982, 1987, 1988)
* Le livre noir: nouvelles légendes du mythe de Cthulhu (1991, 1996, 2000)
* Cthulhu 2000 (1995, 1999)
* Spur der Schatten (2004)
* Darkness, Mist and Shadow: Volume 1 (2010)
* Darkness, Mist and Shadow: The Collected Macabre Tales of Basil Copper (2010)
* Darkness, Mist and Shadow: Volume 2 (2013, 2014, 2018)

Shaggai, also known as "Chag-Hai", is a planet orbiting a binary system with green suns. It was covered by thick inhabited jungles and dark seas. It was home to insects called the Shans, as well as a mysterious being known as "The Worm that Gnaws in the Night". According to Robert Blake, it is in the depths of the cosmos, even deeper than Yuggoth. However, it could somehow be reached by beings from other worlds, as related in the Book of Eibon by Eibon himself.

Shaggai was first mentioned in "The Haunter of the Dark", first as the name of a famous short story by the protagonist Robert Blake, and second in Blake's diary as so: "What am I afraid of? Is it not an avatar of Nyarlathotep, who in antique and shadowy Khem even took the form of man? I remember Yuggoth, and more distant Shaggai, and the ultimate void of the black planets..."

### Appearance
Shaggai orbited one of the two binary blue stars in a system located in Andromeda. Because of the peculiar gravitational forces at play in Shaggai's binary system, only two planets were able
to form there: Shaggai and Xiclotl. These two planet's orbits are filled with dust and asteroids, which filtered the light from the two blue stars, making them appear as green as emeralds.(: Delta Green: Countdown)

Due to the gravitation forces of the binary system, Shaggai has a complex orbital path, wobbling axis and drastic temperature changes, making life nearly impossible. The thick acidic atmosphere prevents almost all lights from reaching the surface, only allow X-rays and gamma radiation emitted by the twin stars to pass through, causing the surface to frequently build up and release static electricity in the form of lightning. (: Delta Green: Countdown)

The landscape of Shaggai was terrifying: black sea formed by plasma, deserts covered by glass particles, crystalline purple mountains and forests with dense vegetation.

### Inhabitants
The simplest life form on Shaggai is a black "sea", either a complex organic compound or a single protoplasmic organism. From the deep volcanic vents at the bottom of this sea that more advanced life forms were born. One of the life form to develop enough to reach the surface was the Shan, which feed on the radiation generated by the binary stars. (: Delta Green: Countdown)

Eons before the Shans first crawled out of the seas, there was a civilization on Shaggai that had erected cities consisting of pyramidal buildings made from green minerals unknown to Shaggai. They had long since departed or extinct. (: Delta Green: Countdown)

### History
In 592 A.D., Shaggai was destroyed by the Outer God Ghroth. (: Delta Green: Countdown)

fullContent:
"Shaggai" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, first published in the 1971 anthology Dark Things.

### Synopsis
In ancient Hyperborea, the wizard Eibon summons an alien entity known as Pharol, to ask him about a mysterious passage in the Pnakotic Manuscripts concerning "The Worm that Gnaws in the Night", the summoning of which means doom. Despite Eibon's insistence, Pharol gives no answer other than that the question must be asked to "The Dweller in the Pyramid", so Eibon prepares a potion that will allow him to travel to other worlds by astral projection, hoping to find the enigmatic entity.

His first stop is on Yuggoth, where he consults with a Mi-Go archimage who is unable to help him. Eibon then moves on from world to world until "the very rim of transdimensional gulfs", in which a luminous gas creature tells him that the being he is looking for dwells in the shunned planet Shaggai.

There, Eibon locates a mountain-sized pyramid standing on a boreal plateau. Its walls are made of an unknown metal and extraordinarily thick, as if designed to contain something. Passing through the walls, Eibon sees a dark abyss, with walls inscribed with symbols that he can read, as the language is similar to that of the Elder Records of Celaeno. He reads and gasps in horror, as he realizes the source of the faint luminescence from the abyss, and the very reason why Shaggai is shunned: a colossal worm that the native insectoid race once summoned, only to realize that there was no way to destroy or banish it, so they built the pyramid to try to contain it while it slowly gnaws away the interior of their planet.

A Shaggai dog is a sapient alien species created by Darrell Schweitzer for his comedic short story "The Last Horror Out of Arkham".

Their name is a play on "shaggy dog story", an expression used to refer to an intentionally pointless narrative.

### Description
Shaggai dogs are strange-looking creatures, about as tall as an elephant. They have four long, tapering legs, and no tail. Their bodies are covered in rope-like purplish hair. The head is neither at the front nor the rear end of the body, but in the middle.

Identified by Prof. Latham Knucklebury as a lower form of life on the planet Shaggai, comparable to a dog on Earth, this species is nevertheless sapient and has access to extraordinarily advanced technology. (: "The Last Horror Out of Arkham")

### History
Centuries ago, the Great Old Ones sent a lone Shaggai dog to Earth, where it assembled a large technological apparatus inside a building where Miskatonic University would eventually be built. The device could bend the fabric of space and duplicate objects from any point in time, which has been used to create countless genuine copies of the Necronomicon, the Book of Eibon, and other exceedingly rare grimoires, thus ensuring that, despite their great rarity, anyone could come across them by complete chance. Once its work was complete, the Shaggai dog went into suspended animation, waiting for the return of its masters. (: "The Last Horror Out of Arkham")

The Shans, also known as the Insects from Shaggai, are an insectoid alien race which appears in the Cthulhu Mythos and were also said to awe the plant-like deity Dzéwà.

### Description
Shan are described as having semi-circular ridged wings covered with triangular scales, huge lidless eyes, jointed tendrils covered with black shining tentacles, ten legs, and three mouths. Shans are parasitic and can phase into a human's brain, giving its host their memories while slowly taking over. They are made of alien matter that allows their atoms to exist conterminously with those of their host. Their nutrition comes from photosynthesis of the green rays of the double sun that Shaggai orbit. (: The Insects from Shaggai)

The Shans' brains have six lobes, containing three separate pairs of right and left hemispheres. An individual Shan can therefore entertain three separate trains of thought, three separate actions, or even three separate conversations. With highly developed mental powers, their primary means of communication between members of their own species is telepathy. They can also communicate telepathically with or even feel emotions of species other than their own, but only through direct physical contact with the central nervous system. They also developed an ability to slide their atoms through the electron shell of any organic substance (Kirlian phasing). (: Delta Green: Countdown)

The Shans are extremely-long lived organisms. An average Shan can be expected to live for as long as fifteen to eighteen centuries. The Shans are hermaphroditic and can fertilize themselves if need be, but usually two Shans will exchange reproductive materials. Both Shans will develop an "egg sac" containing hundreds of Shan embryos. When the egg sac ruptures, the Shan embryos consume their parent as their first meal, and then turn on each other; this ensures that only the strongest and most aggressive larva will survive. Because of the fatal nature of reproduction, Shans breed only when it is in the group's interests to increase its numbers. (: Delta Green: Countdown)

Without having to work for food, the Shans had sunk to an abysmal state of decadence. While on Shaggai, they would torture slave-races from other worlds for pleasure; and when on other planets, they sought the most terribly haunted localities to view their horrors (: The Insects from Shaggai). They also have an insatiable desire for new experience and its narcotic effect on their mind, not curiosity. (: Delta Green: Countdown)

They worship Azathoth and practice various horrible rituals. (: The Insects from Shaggai)

### History
Eons before the Shans first crawled out of the seas, there was a civilization on Shaggai that had erected cities consisting of pyramidal temple-ships made from green minerals unknown to Shaggai. fullContent:
Shane Ivey is an American games designer whose output has included numerous contributions to Cthulhu Mythos works. His gaming credits include the core rulebook for the Delta Green stand-alone horror roleplaying game as well as a large number of its supplements, and several books for Cubicle 7 Entertainment's Tolkenian fantasy The One Ring Roleplaying Game.

Ivey is also the co-founder, with Dennis Detwiller, of Arc Dream Publishing, through which they publish Delta Green and the resurrected roleplaying magazine The Unspeakable Oath, for which he is the editor-in-chief. He also worked for the now-defunct Pagan Publishing, several of whose works Ivey and Detwiller have continued through Arc Dream.

Shang is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Cats of Ulthar".

### Overview
Shang is a resident of the town of Ulthar where he works as a blacksmith. He was one of the town burgesses who helped pass the law that made it illegal to kill cats. (: "The Cats of Ulthar")

fullContent:
Shanghai is a coastal city located on the eastern edge of the Yangtze River estuary of China, one of the most populous cities in the world, and the most populous in the country. It has been linked with the Cthulhu Mythos on numerous occasions, perhaps most prominently through roleplaying game material such as Chaosium's iconic Masks of Nyarlathotep supplement for their Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game.

### Notable People and Factions
* The Order of the Bloated Woman: a cult dedicated to the Bloated Woman avatar of Nyarlathotep which maintains an extensive presence in Shanghai's criminal underworld, as well as in its import/export trade. (: Masks of Nyarlathotep)
* Victor Sassoon: a businessman with an impressive empire who stands in opposition to the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos. (: The Sassoon Files)

### Appearances
* Masks of Nyarlathotep (1984): globe-trotting Call of Cthulhu campaign which features Shanghai as one of the investigator's stop offs
* Masks of Nyarlathotep Companion (2013): Call of Cthulhu supplement which features a guide to, amongst other places, Shanghai
* The Sassoon Files (2019): Call of Cthulhu/Trail of Cthulhu campaign which focuses on a supernatural power struggle in the city. Also includes a potted history of the region and guide to political and underworld factions
* The Sassoon Files: The Brother of Jesus (2019): an expansion scenario for The Sassoon Files
* "City of Waking Dreams" (2022): Davide Mana's Arkham Horror Fiction short story tells of an operative of the Foundation who travels to Shanghai to investigate the disappearance of his partner

### External Links
* [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai Shanghai] at Wikipedia

Shannon Appelcline is a games designer and historian, computer scientist, author, and comic book creator who has written numerous works involved with the Cthulhu Mythos, although he is possibly best known for his lengthy treatise on the history of tabletop roleplaying, Designers & Dragons. Much of Appelcline's Mythos-related output was accomplished in supplements for Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game.

Appelcline's non-Mythos work includes writing for White Wolf Publishing, designers of the hugely popular World of Darkness setting. He is also the vice president of Skotos Tech, owners of the roleplaying game site RPGnet, where is the editor-in-chief.

Shantaks are a fictional species created by H. P. Lovecraft for his Dreamlands novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. Lovecraft depicts them as a flying bird-like creature larger than elephants, with heads resembling those of horses. They have scales rather than feathers, and lay eggs of colossal size and rich flavor. They are allied with Nyarlathotep, and fear the Night-gaunt minions of Nodens.

Lovecraft describes the Shantaks' speech as "tittering tones that rasped like the scratching of ground glass".

In the short story "The Gable Window", August Derleth presents a different image of the shantak via the notes of Wilbur Akeley: "Average height exceeding that of a man. Furred, bat-like bodies, bat wings, extending three feet above head. Face beaked, vulture-like, but otherwise resembling bat."

Derleth lists the Shantaks as one of the servitor races of the Great Old Ones (: "The Keeper of the Key"), and claims that they "flew from Kadath in the Cold Waste at the bidding of Wind-Walker, the Wendigo, cousin of Ithaqua" (: "The Seal of R'lyeh").

Lin Carter portrayed the Shantaks and the Fishers from Outside as being the same species (: "The Fishers from Outside"), although other media, such as the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, maintain that they are distinct. In Carter's works, the Shantaks / Fishers from Outside are led by Quumyagga, and are loyal to Groth-Golka.

### Description

### History
According to the Kulten der Antiken Welt, the Shard was utilised in Ancient Greece as a protective talisman by a man named Paenoestes, an Athenian scholar, who was a "self-proclaimed wielder of dark arts". Where it originated from is not revealed.

In the novel Feeders from Within, after a group of Mi-Go reconstructed the Shard using an arcane machine, it was once again shattered by a group of soldiers including Mark Harrigan. The alien Mr. Stone then once again pieced it back together before using it as a device to shield himself and his Silver Twilight Lodge acolytes from the attentions of the Great Old One Tsathoggua and his servants, the Formless Spawn. The artefact was once more smashed by Harrigan, and left in pieces in the subterranean realm of N'kai.

The Shatterer of Worlds is a Lovecraftian-like extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics.

### Background
The Shatterer of Worlds was a nigh-omnipotent eldritch entity from another reality whom was summoned to Earth by the Cult of Wrarrl during the Hyborian Age, to use its power to resurrect their master, the demon Wrarrl (aka, the Devourer of Souls) who had been slain by the Cimmerian barbarian Conan. Not realizing that its presence in their universe would tear the very fabric of reality and that within minutes of it being in their world the universe would cease to exist.

Realising what the foolish cultists had done, the resurrected Wrarrl was forced to end his fight with Conan. To prevent the destruction of the netherworld (the world of his demonic race), which was a parallel world to Earth, Wrarrl consumed the souls of the cultists. Using them to boost his eldritch powers, Wrarrl sacrificed himself to obliterate the entity.

Shaurash-Ho (The Prowler Among the Tombs, and Father of All Ghouls (source?)) is the progenitor of the ghoul species (source?), possibly through mating with Bast, as the goddess has also been associated with ghouls (: "The Brood of Bubastis"). Shaurash-ho is a descendent of Cthulhu and parent of Yogash the Ghoul (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft) and it has been postulated that it might itself have been a Deep One (source?). The Book of Eibon identifies Nug as the "grandfather of all ghouls on the earth-plane" (: "The Descent into the Abyss"), but other sources claim that Nug never inhabited the Earth (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft), although it might still have visited it. Friedrich von Junzt names Naggoob the "Father of Ghouls" (: "The Horror in the Gallery"), possibly suggesting a connection between Naggoob and Shaurash-ho.

This mysterious entity is mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's letter to James F. Morton as a descendant of Cthulhu which spawned Yogash the Ghoul. Yogash in turn is the ancestor of K'baa the Serpent and Ghoth the Burrower. The latter would have sired with a Roman noblewoman Viburnia the legendary ancestor of Lovecraft himself. The appearance of Shaurash-Ho has never been described.

fullContent:
"She Sleeps in the Depths" is a short story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
Two people who are tormented by a song which constantly plays in their heads discover each other whilst looking for an answer to their condition. Travelling to the islands off the north-west coast of Scotland, they feel that the source of the singing is coming from the waters around the base of the monolithic Old Man of Hoy. As they disturb an ancient statuette sunken beneath the waves something ancient and terrible begins to awaken, but when they restore the idol to its place the creature calms and returns to its slumber.

In the aftermath the two decide that the only thing they can do to ease the burden of the song is to put as much distance as they can between themselves and it’s origin, and plan a trip to New Zealand.

### Characters
*Fallon, a young man searching desperately for a solution to his unusual problem.
*Val Leyton, a woman who shares Fallon's condition.

### Publication History
"She Sleeps in the Depths" was first published in the anthology DarkFuse #1 by DarkFuse in 2014. It was also included in the collections of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in 2019 and Into the Mist in 2020.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no explicit references to either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Meikle's inclusion of the story in his collection Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror shows his belief that it follows in the spirit of such works. Additionally, the premise of the creature the protagonists encounter, that of an ancient creature kept sleeping beneath the waves, is very much in the same vein as the Derlethian vision of the Cthulhu Mythos.

"She Wore a Trench Coat" is a short story by American author Don Webb. Although it forms part of the Arkham Detective Agency series, it has little to do with the Agency itself.

### Synopsis
Beat cop Travis Mazoni is assigned to surveillance of the Arkham Detective Agency by a shadowy government department after he witnesses a bizarre death on the street: a woman who is literally consumed from within by small, dark, ephemeral creatures which disappear in the aftermath.

Investigating on his own time, Mazoni uncovers a link to the "Church of the Transformations", which is in reality a cult devoted to the Great Old One Eihort. Although nearly ensnared by their enchantments, Mazoni manages to break the spell and escape. He subsequently resigns from the Arkham Police Department and leaves town.

### Characters

* Travis Mazoni, a street cop who yearns to be with the wife who left him many years ago.
* Frank Nardi, a senior partner in the Arkham Detective Agency.
* Dr. Sebastian E. Phillips, leader of the Church of the Transformations.
* Constance Valetta, the woman described in the title, killed by Eihort's broodlings on her way to seek help from Nardi.

### Publication History
"She Wore a Trench Coat" was published in the Dark Regions Press anthology Arkham Detective Agency in November 2017.

Sheila (also known as The Chosen One) is a fictional hero created by Sam Raimi for the 1992 comedy-fantasy film Army of Darkness, the third installment of Raimi's Evil Dead franchise.

### Background
Sheila was a maiden in 1300 AD who first hated the time displaced Ash Williams and then fell in love with him. A Deadite possessed her and she turned into "Bad Sheila". Upon the defeat of Evil Ash and the Army of Darkness, she was freed of the Deadite and witnessed Ash's return back home to his own time.

Another version married Ash Williams who decided to stay in 1300 AD. This version had lost her right hand, and battled Deadites alongside her husband. Pregnant with his child, they married. Unfortunately during the reception party, a drunken Ash spoke the words "Klaatu Barada Nikto" which sent him to 1350 AD.

In another reality, after Ash returned to his time, she was convinced by the Wise Man and Lord Arthur to help them create a team to continue the teachings of the Promised One. She became a teacher to what would eventually become the 21st century's Supernatural Military-Adjacent Response Team (S.M.A.R.T).

Another version would be involved in his adventures, both in the early 14th century and in his own time. She would travel to the future and back, multiple times. Fighting alongside him against the forces of the Necronomicon, ending up trapped in the Mirror Dimension, for a time becoming Evil Sheila again, and helped Ash fight the Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse. The two of them went back one last time to 1300 AD and were going to get married. Only for Ash to call it off when the Wise Man told him she was destined to die if she stayed with him. Left in the care of her newly resurrected brother, Ash took a potion that put him to sleep for seven centuries.

Sheriff Engle is a character who features in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files series of games and fiction. He is the head of the Arkham Police Department.

### Origin
Engle made his first appearance as a Blight card for the Arkham Horror Second Edition expansion The King in Yellow.

### History
When unwilling cultist Diana Stanley attempted to break her ties with the Silver Twilight Lodge, she went to see Sheriff Engle in an attempt to blow the whistle on the cult's activities. At first, Engle seemed to believe her story, but soon mysteriously abandoned the case, and in doing so hinted that he may have in fact been in the pocket of Carl Sanford, the Lodge's high priest. (: Feeders from Within)

After Professor Norman Withers told Engle the story of how his colleague Claus Schmidt had been abducted by Hounds of Tindalos, Engle agreed to launch an investigation, but only under the condition that Withers change his statement to something more mundane. Engle further hinted that he knew about the strange goings-on in Arkham, but was unwilling to write about these occurrences in a report. (: Ire of the Void)

Sheriff Engle briefed Agent Roland Banks on an unsolved Arkham case to which Banks had been assigned: the mystery of an orchestra who had been murdered in an apparent bombing. Although the pair at first had something of a strained relationship, Engle was more than happy to have the problematic case taken out of his hands, and once again hinted that he knew the town played host to more than its fair share of inexplicable events (: The Dirge of Reason)

Sherlock Holmes is a fictional character created by the late British author Arthur Conan Doyle, who made his first appearance in the 1887 novel A Study in Scarlet. Since his first appearance, Doyle expanded on the character, with his works totalling four novels and dozens of short stories involving Holmes; in the years since, many other authors have also given their own takes on the character, and the body of fiction surrounding him likely numbers in the tens of thousands.

Sherlock Holmes has also been crossed over into several other properties, particularly those of the occult detective genre. These include the Cthulhu Mythos established by H. P. Lovecraft, William Hope Hodgson's Carnacki universe, and the Solar Pons mysteries of August Derleth.

### Overview
Holmes is considered to be one of the greatest detectives of his age, perhaps the greatest in history. He lived contemporary to the author's time, and shared much of his adult life with Dr. John H. Watson, his closest friend and partner throughout many of his cases.

The original Sherlock Holmes stories were very much grounded in reality; although several appeared at first glance to have supernatural elements, these were eventually all proven to be red herrings or explained by natural phenomena. In the works of some later authors, particularly in crossover pieces, the stories involve actual paranormal phenomena.

"Sherlock Holmes and the Mystery at Miskatonic University" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Zebulon Zachariah. It was independently published as a digital chapbook in June 2023; a paperback edition was released in August that year.

### Synopsis
Professor Henry Armitage sends for the world-renowned detective Sherlock Holmes when his colleague Dr. Herbert West goes missing. Their investigations reveal that during the course of his researches, Dr. West's involvement with the writings of the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred have caused him to become trapped in a prison devised by the Elder Gods. With the aid of Charles Dexter Ward and Dr. Randolph Carter, the men are able to free the wayward doctor.

Despite having freed West, Holmes is driven insane by the material he has read and incarcerated in Arkham Asylum for three long years, but emerges from his term a stronger man for it.

fullContent:
Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened (рус. Шерлок Холмс и секрет Ктулху; Sherlock Holmes and the Secret of Cthulhu) is an adventure quest developed by the Ukrainian company Frogwares and released by Focus Home Interactive in 2007. The game combines two fictional universes: the stories of Sherlock Holmes and the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft.

It is the third game in the series The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes. The tenth game in the series was the 2023 remake of The Awakened for Windows, Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S..

The name Cthulhu is never mentioned - neither in the original title of the game, nor in the characters' dialogues; however, the game itself contains numerous references to this fictional deity.

### Plot
Sherlock Holmes is once again left without a case to investigate. Dr. Watson reports that his patient, Captain Stanwyck, has lost an Indian servant. Sherlock investigates and discovers that a number of seemingly unrelated people have disappeared recently.

The detectives will have to visit the gloomy alleys of London, Switzerland and New Orleans to find traces of a mysterious sect that worships an ancient sea demon on the western shores of Scotland.

### Gameplay
Unlike the first two games in the series, the action takes place in a full 3D environment, unlike classic quests, where three-dimensional characters move through painted backgrounds. The view is from the first person, and both mouse and keyboard controls are possible, which brings the quest very close to shooters. The game features a traditional inventory, a folder for documents, and a map of visited locations.

The "Gold Edition" of the game in 2008 made it possible to play from a third-person perspective, as in classic quests.

### Reception
The game received positive reviews from critics and players. Gamers responded positively to the reduction of quizzes, which were not to everyone's taste in the second game in the series. They also noted the convenience and "charm" of both keyboard and mouse controls. Finally, some critics were pleased that the characters began to resemble real people, and not “such robots, mechanisms for investigating crimes”.

“Igromania” gave the quest 7.5 points out of 10, calling it “an ambiguous, but extremely interesting game”. The Russian localization was also assessed quite positively.

Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened is an adventure quest developed and released by the Ukrainian company Frogwares in 2023. The game combines two fictional universes: the stories of Sherlock Holmes and the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft. It is a remake of Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened (2007), part of the Sherlock Holmes series, and tells the story of the first major case of Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson. The Awakened was announced in July 2022 and released on April 11, 2023 on Microsoft Windows, PlayStation 4, PlayStation 5, XboxOne, Xbox Series, and Nintendo Switch.

The developers dedicated their game to the Ukrainian people, who were victims of the Russian genocide. Frogwares' message to players, translated into all available localization languages: On February 24, 2022, our Motherland, Ukraine, was brutally invaded and dragged into a full-scale war. In April 2022, we began developing Sherlock Holmes The Awakened. We dedicate this game to all the soldiers, volunteers, everyone who helps them, and in general, all the people who hold our country on their shoulders. This game is an act of defiance against the chaos and horrors that the enemy is trying to fill our lives with. Glory to Ukraine!

### Gameplay
Sherlock Holmes: The Awakened is a third-person action-adventure detective horror game. Like its predecessor, Sherlock Holmes: Chapter One, the game takes place in an open world, with the exception of some story locations. The inventory mechanics are almost identical to previous Frogwares games - players have access to Sherlock's "Notebook", which records the detective's main plot and secondary investigations, the evidence for them, as well as the thinking rooms, where the detective forms an imaginary picture of the crime and makes accusations based on it. What sets The Awakened apart from the studio's previous project is the lack of the disguise mechanic that was a key feature of Chapter One. The tab with the various costumes available to Sherlock and Watson is still located in the inventory, but it is now purely a cosmetic feature.

The mechanics of finding clues and evidence have also undergone some changes: eavesdropping on other people's conversations and taking photographs have disappeared, but a thorough examination of places and people to collect evidence, questioning witnesses, following clues, and recreating past events are still present in the game. The collected evidence is labeled according to what should be done with it - discuss it with someone, ask passersby, check the information in the archive, examine it with a detective's eye, or look for something additional at the location. A new lockpicking mechanic was introduced, presented here as a mini-game where players must manually bend a "lockpick" to fit the lock. Boating and gun shooting were also added.

### Description
Nothing is known about Shimba, other than that it is a benevolent god of shepherds worshiped in monasteries in ancient Hyperborea. A remarkably agreeable deity, the monks of Shimba are allowed to indulge in hedonistic consumption of food and drink, and live in great comfort. (: "The Stairs in the Crypt")

It's unknown whether Shimba is a real entity within the context of the Mythos.

The Shining Trapezohedron is a fictional artefact in the Cthulhu Mythos. It first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Haunter of the Dark", and Robert Bloch's sequel "The Shadow from the Steeple". 

### Overview
The Shining Trapezohedron serves as a window on all of space and time. By gazing into it, its wielder would summon the Haunter of the Dark, an avatar of Nyarlathotep, as well as (possibly) the other Outer Gods. In exchange for horrible sacrifices, the Haunter of the Dark would reveal other worlds and arcane knowledge.

The Shining Trapezohedron was a "crazy angled stone" created on the planet Yuggoth and brought to Earth by the Old Ones before the emergence of the human race. (: "The Haunter of the Dark") It was formed by the Mi-Go. (: Call of Cthulhu) It was held by the Elder Things, then the serpent-men of Valusia, and eventually the first humans on Lemuria. Later it came to Atlantis and the Pharaohs of ancient Egypt, specifically Nephren-Ka. Occultist and archaeologist Enoch Bowen discovered it within a box of alien construction while exploring the ruins of the tomb of Nephren-Ka in 1843. Bowen returned to his home in Providence, Rhode Island, with the Trapezohedron and its box the following year, where he founded the Church of Starry Wisdom. (: "The Haunter of the Dark")

The Shining Trapezohedron was researched by Robert Blake, who deciphered a number of ancient texts concerning the stone. He attempted to summon Yog-Sothoth with the stone, and saw him re-creating universes, but failed to do so. Following Blake's death, the stone was removed from the Starry Wisdom cult's sanctuary and thrown into Narragansett Bay by Dr. Ambrose Dexter. (: "The Haunter of the Dark") Unknown to Dexter, however, the constant darkness at the bottom of the bay ensured the Haunter of the Dark's perpetual freedom. For his trouble, Dexter was possessed by the Haunter, and eventually became one of the foremost nuclear scientists in the world, in charge of investigation of atomic energy for wartime purposes. (: "The Shadow from the Steeple")

According to one account, the Shining Trapezohedron can be used as a focal point to open gates between worlds and dimensions. Its light can heal, destroy, and transform, allowing entities such as Nyarlathotep and Cthulhu to shift between human and non-human form. (: Strange Eons)

"Shipping on the River" is a short story by Sergio Palumbo and Ivan Bertozzoni. It is unusual for a story in the Cthulhu Mythos genre in that it describes what appears to be a peaceful interaction between humans and the creatures of the Mythos.

### Synopsis
Glasgow, late 1800s: two men stumble across what at first appears to be a people-smuggling operation, or perhaps even an annual mass sacrifice being undertaken by the crew of a small ship. As they delve further however, they discover that the ship's captain is merely trying to help Deep One hybrids who are coming of age in their first steps towards realising their aquatic heritage.

### Publication History
"Shipping on the River" was published in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2020.

The Shlangii are a fictional alien species featured in Andy Lane's novel All-Consuming Fire, based on a line of dialogue from the 1978 Doctor Who serial The Ribos Operation, which mentions "mercenaries from Shlangii".

### Description
The Shlangii are strange-looking creatures with a sac-shaped body supported by five spindly legs. Each leg has five joints, which are composed of two hinges aligned on different planes, thus allowing the legs to bend on any direction. Their skin is mottled grey, with a network of blood vessels visible underneath, arranged like a cobweb. They don't have any visible eyes or mouth, but speak in a hissing voice, which is produced by a pulsating membrane on the underside of the body. They can move faster than the human eye can follow.

A ruthless mercenary species, a large group of Shlangii have been employed on the planet Ry'leh to guard an imprisoned being who presented herself as Azathoth (although the Doctor denied that she was the real deal). The Shlangii were selected for this task because their reluctance to accept new ideas makes them particularly resistant against the false Azathoth's psychic abilities. However, this didn't prevent some Shlangii from being brainwashed by the creature, and converted to her cult. Like all of Azathoth's worshipers, the converted Shlangii were eventually transformed into rakshassi. (: All-Consuming Fire)

Sho-Gath is a fictional cosmic entity created by August Derleth for his 1945 short story "The God-Box". It is depicted as a dark smoky column, with red malevolent eyes and a grotesque face, imprisoned inside a vintage box. Originally from Atlantis, the box eventually found its way to prehistoric Britain, where it was guarded by immortal druids in Stonehenge.

### Behind the Mythos
The name Sho-Gath is evocative of Shoggoth, a species created by the Elder Things in H. P. Lovecraft's novella At the Mountains of Madness. Both entities are black, amorphous, and extremely dangerous, although Sho-Gath's gaseous smoke-like constitution distinguishes it from the amoebic protoplasmic form of the Shoggoths.
