"Shocking Terrors #13" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Frank Forte, first published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
An avid pulp magazine collector develops an obsession with tracking down an elusive edition of horror magazine Shocking Terrors, an issue said to contain a story which drives all who read it insane.

After five long years of searching, he eventually manages to locate a copy, and settles down to read it despite the warnings of everyone who has heard of the curse. Predictably, his sanity immediately begins to degrade and he embarks upon a murderous rampage before trying to kill himself. He is eventually put out of his misery at the hands of the armed police officers who attend the scene of his last crime.

### Trivia

* Legendary pulp magazine Weird Tales is mentioned as being among those favoured by the collector.

Shoggoths are fictional creatures created by H. P. Lovecraft, first appearing in his novella At the Mountains of Madness (1936). They are depicted as amorphous, shapeshifting beings who were genetically engineered by the Elder Things as a race of servant-tools, but eventually rose up against their masters. The monsters were later mentioned in Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth (1936) and "The Thing on the Doorstep" (1937), and have become one of the most widely shared elements of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Description
A shoggoth is a sentient blob of self-shaping, gelatinous flesh, something like a giant amoeba. A shoggoth is some 15 feet in diameter if it shaped itself into a sphere, but larger and smaller versions exist. A shoggoth is capable of shaping itself into whatever organs or shapes it finds necessary at the moment; however, in its usual state it tends to sport a roiling profusion of eyes, mouths, and pseudopodia. When encountered at the South Pole, it moved at incredible speed. It was described as like watching a train closing in on someone standing on the tracks.

The shoggoth can kill its enemies by enveloping them and generating enough suction-force to decapitate their victims. That is specifically how they fought the Elder Things during their rebellion.

Apparently, they emit a horrible, overpowering stench that's strong enough to completely mask the alienating smell of the Elder Things.

A curious behavior of the shoggoth is their repetitive cry of "Tekeli-li! Tekeli-li!" Demonstrating their mindless mimicry, this is a phrase they copied from the Elder Things. Arthur Gordon Pym also encountered the phrase, as cries from flocks of large, white birds, in his journey in the Southern Ocean (: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket)

### History
The shoggoths were originally bred as servitor creatures by the Elder Things, who used them for underwater construction. Their ability to shape their bodies as needed made them ideal living construction machinery. Although created to be mindless, the shoggoths mutated through the aeons and slowly developed consciousness, and even became periodically rebellious. Eventually, they overthrew the Elder Things and killed them, and built their own cities (: At the Mountains of Madness) Their architecture mimics the five-pointed symmetry of the Elder Things.

Though rare, some shoggoths have managed to survive into the modern era, most notably in Antarcti

fullContent:
"Shoggoth Apocalypse" is a short story by authors Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. It is followed up by the story "The Glorious Return Of Herbert West".

### Synopsis
After the Earth is ruined by pollution and nuclear warfare, the American president decides to spearhead an initiative to colonise Mars. When the initial surveyors discover the relics of an ancient civilisation buried beneath the surface, they are transported to earth for further examination. 

Through an ancient tome which conveniently has a built-in translation system, the humans are able to piece together the history of life on Mars. The relics reveal that the Martians co-existed with the alien Elder Things for a time, before the Elder Things' servants, the Shoggoths, rose up and devastated the planet. The Elder Things fled to Earth, draining Mars's water supply in order to kill the Shoggoths.

A freak accident in the relic storage facility then triggers the sprinkler system which rehydrates the Shoggoths which, it transpires, were merely in a state of hibernation, and hidden amongst the other artefacts. As a result, all life on Earth is destroyed.

### Characters
*August Danforth, president of the United States of America.
*Brent Roman, director of Project Europa, the initiative to colonise Mars.

### Publication History
*Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (2018)
*The House Of The Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares (2019)
*Shoggoth Apocalypse & More Tales Of The Cthulhu Mythos

### Trivia
*The story directly conflicts with the background of the Elder Things established by H. P. Lovecraft in At the Mountains of Madness.
*The Martians were said to worship the insect-god Ghattambah, and the books referenced by the scientists in decoding the Martian history were The Seven Blasphemies of Ghattambah and Wyck'd Secrets Of The Infernal Beaste Ghattambah. How ancient Martians had come to utilise human texts is unexplained.
*The name of the American president, August Danforth, is likely a nod to August Derleth, a friend and contemporary of Lovecraft's, and Danforth, one of only two survivors from the Pabodie Expedition in At the Mountains of Madness.

Shoggoth Lords are a fictional species created by Michael Shea for his short story "Fat Face", depicted as being an evolved variety of Shoggoths. They were later expanded on by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. 

### Description
In their true forms, Shoggoth Lords resemble most Shoggoths, but are both more intelligent and have the ability to mimic the human form, although they use specially-crafted suits to assist in maintaining the shape. The only parts of their body which Shoggoth Lords will not allow to revert to its original form is the head, a precaution to ensure that they do not replicate the face imperfectly and rouse suspicion amongst the human population. 

### Notable Shoggoth Lords
*Fat Face, a Shoggoth Lord who operated a hydrotherapy clinic and pet refuge as a cover for his associates, eating the animals and relaxing in the therapy pools (: "Fat Face").
*Mr. Albert Shiny, who aimed to increase the human population for their eventual harvest. (: At Your Door)

"Shoggoth's Old Peculiar" is a satirical Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Neil Gaiman. It first appeared in print in 1998 in The Mammoth Book of Comic Fantasy, edited by Mike Ashley for Carroll & Graf. That year, it was nominated for the World Fantasy Award for Best Short Fiction .

### Synopsis
American tourist Benjamin Lassiter is walking the coastline of the United Kingdom when he comes across an unusual little village called Innsmouth. A night spent drinking with two locals - who claim to be cultists of Cthulhu - ends with Lassiter witnessing something horrific beneath the waters of the harbour before passing out in a field.

Unable to locate the town, he makes his way to the next village over, but despite questioning the locals, can find no evidence that such a place as Innsmouth exists. He promptly heads back to America on the next flight he can find, where he lives out his life under a cloud of intangible fear of whatever it was he saw beneath the waters of Britain.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Shoggoth's Old Peculiar" has been reprinted in nearly a dozen different publications over several editions. It has also been translated into Dutch, French, and Portuguese .

### Trivia
*The story takes its name from the beer which Lassiter and the cultists drink together, Shoggoth's Old Peculiar.

* "[https://lovecraftzine.com/2013/08/14/shoggoths-old-peculiar-read-by-neil-gaiman/ Shoggoth's Old Peculiar]" read by the author at the Lovecraft eZine

fullContent:
"Shoggoths in Bloom" is a short story by Elizabeth Bear that originally appeared in the March 2008 issue of Asimov's Science Fiction. The shoggoths of the title are the creatures introduced in H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, but unlike Lovecraft's shoggoths, Bear's have always been known to science. Bear's story won the 2009 Hugo Award for Best Novelette.

The story is set in November 1938 in the fictional town of Passamaquoddy, Maine. It focuses on Professor Paul Harding, a Black academic who is studying the little known life-cycle of the shoggoth. It occurs against the background of racism in the United States and looming war in Europe. 

### Characters
*Professor Paul Harding: A professor of some sort of biological science; his work focuses on the lifecycle of the shoggoth. He served in the Great War in a non-combat role because "colored soldiers mostly worked supply." Afterwards, he lives in Harlem, where "he remembers the riots and the music, and the sense of community," then goes to college in Alabama,  which he associates with segregated restaurants and "the excuses he made for never leaving the campus." He gets a Ph.D. from Yale, "the first school in America to have awarded a doctorate to a Negro." He is in a tenure-track position at Wilberforce University, a historically black school in Ohio. Harding is described as "an educated man, well-read," with a "close-cropped beard."
*Burt Clay: A Passamaquoddy fisherman hired by Harding to take him out on Passamaquoddy Harbor to study the shoggoths. Like Harding, he is a veteran of the Great War. He rescues Harding when the latter is forced to jump into the water to get back to the boat when the weather suddenly turns stormy. He is married; his boat is the Bluebird.
*Nathan Harding: Harding's grandfather, a "buffalo soldier"--that is, a soldier in one of the African-American US Army units formed in 1866 to fight in the Indian Wars, particularly the 10th Cavalry. He is described as an "African-born ex-slave who fought on both sides of the Civil War," having deserted after being sent to serve in his master's stead in the Confederate Army. His grandson "remembers beaded ridges of hard black keloid across his grandfather’s back, the shackle galls on his wrists."
*Professor John Marshland: Harding's colleague and mentor at Yale University.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Asimov's Science Fiction, "Shoggoths in Bloom" was anthologized is several "best of" collections, including The Best Science Fiction and Fantasy of the Year: Volume Three (Night Shade Books, 2009), The Year's Top Ten Tales of Science Fiction (Infinivox, 2009), Year's Best Fantasy 9 (Tor, 2009), The Year's Best Science Fiction & Fantasy, 2009 Edition (Prime Books, 2010), and The Hugo Award Showcase: 2010 Volume (Prime Books, 2010). It was also included in The Best of Elizabeth Bear (Subterranean Press, 2020).

The story was selected for the Lovecraftian anthologies The Book of Cthulhu (Night Sha

As one of the most iconic elements from the Cthulhu Mythos, the Shoggoths have had numerous appearances and references throughout popular culture.

### Books/Stories
*A Certain Magical Index: New Testament: In volume 14 of the light novel series, Patricia Birdway gets her body infested by a parasite known as "Sample Shoggoth". The creature was discovered during a research mission in Antarctica (a reference to At the Mountains of Madness).
*Andrea Doran: Shoggoths are a frequent opponent of the protagonist with him slaying several over the course of the books.
*Cthulhu Armageddon: Shoggoths have a big role as an ancestor of humanity and descendants of the Kastro'vaal race. The protagonist is frequently described as half-shoggoth.
*The Littlest Shoggoth: A Holiday Tale of the Cthulhu Mythos: a children's book, published by Otherworld Creations.
*Monster Girl Doctor: a light novel series featuring a Shoggoth named Molly Vanitas.
*Monster Girl Encyclopedia II: features the Shoggoths as a subspecies of the Slime Family.

fullContent:
"Shout / Kill / Revel / Repeat" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Scott R. Jones.

### Synopsis
Earth in the far future: the Old Ones have risen and destroyed the planet, decimating its population and sending waves of madness throughout the galaxy.

A coalition of beings utilising cannibalised Yithian and Elder Thing technology, and buoyed by successes against the Wind Walker and the inhabitants of the Severn Valley, attempt to bring their most powerful weapon to bear against the lord of R'lyeh: a biological weapon imbued with the essence of everything mankind can become. However, this being proves far more powerful than their previous targets, and destroys their device with a thought, sending the survivors into paroxysms of insanity, doomed to repeat their actions for all eternity.

### Characters
*Captain Deimos Strunk, starship captain and leader of the expedition. Species unknown.
*Silattha Parv, an evolved ghoul with the power to control or destroy lesser minions of the Old Ones.
*Piotr Tillich, science officer and Mi-Go meatpuppet.
*High Priest Grantha, head of the hexentechs, a type of metaphysical engineer.

### Publication History
"Shout / Kill / Revel / Repeat" was published in the Dark Regions Press thematic anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror in 2017. It was later included in the collection of Jones' own works Shout Kill Revel Repeat in 2019.

fullContent:
"Shreds of a Suit on a Library Floor" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author R. C. Mulhare. It was published in the Lammas Eve edition of Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
Elizabeth Corwin is a farm girl posing as a male student in order to be enrolled at the traditional-minded Miskatonic University, an institution which restricts the majority of its curriculum to men. During her journey to Arkham, she crosses paths with one Wil Whateley, and witnesses something which makes her suspect that all is not as it seems with the strange giant.

Later that day, she is awoken in her dorm by the sounds of one of the campus guard dogs going berserk; she and another student take it upon themselves to rubberneck through the library window, and her suspicions about Wil are confirmed when she sees his putrescent corpse liquifying on the floor.

Shterot, also known as The Tenebrous One, is a fictional entity created by Dominique Balczesak for the Call of Cthulhu scenario "Paris, Rêve ou Réalité", featured in the licensed gaming supplement Les Années Folles (1988).

### Description
Shterot is a Great Old One who takes the form of a colossal abomination that resembles a starfish. It possesses the ability to replicate when a part of its body is severed, creating duplicates of itself which can connect to and control other beings; while the duplicates are nowhere near the equal of their "parent" in power, the Tenebrous One can create these creatures ad infinitum, potentially granting it a limitless number of followers.

### History
First encountered by humans when it descended from the heavens in long ages past, Shterot proceeded to spawn millions of its duplicates which then attached themselves to fully half of the population of the unfortunate continent that it made landfall upon. This parasitic infestation granted Shterot telepathic control over those infected, and for many years it ruled the land as its regent.

Eventually, however, the Elder Gods took notice and intervened. Rather than killing it, they cut Shterot into many pieces and scattered them across the globe, where these parts continue to live individual existences to this day. It is said that if the pieces unite then Shterot will be whole once more, and free to do as it pleases once again.

### Family
*C'thalpa (mother)
*Five unnamed siblings

Shub-Niggurath, also known as The Black Goat of the Woods with a Thousand Young, is an Outer God in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was first mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's revision story "The Last Test" (1928); in Lovecraft's fiction, she is never actually described, but is frequently mentioned or called upon in incantations. Shub-Niggurath is also referenced in the works of other Mythos authors, including Robert Bloch, August Derleth, Ramsey Campbell, Lin Carter, and Brian Lumley.

### Background
Shub-Niggurath is an Outer God (or Outer Goddess) in the pantheon. She is a perverse fertility deity, said to appear as an "hellish cloud-like entity". (: "Selected Letters 5.875")

She has been described as an enormous mass which extrudes black tentacles, slime-dripping mouths, and short, writhing goat legs (: S. Petersen's Field Guide to Cthulhu Monsters). Small creatures are continually spat forth by the monstrosity, which are either consumed into the miasmatic form or escape to some monstrous life elsewhere. (source?)

Shub-Niggurath is the wife of the Not-to-Be-Named One (: The Mound) and of Yog-Sothoth which birthed the twins Nug and Yeb. (: Selected Letters 4.617, 5.875)

T'yog of K'naa, the High-Priest of Shub-Niggurath in ancient Mu, believed this entity to be benevolent, or at the very least willing to side with humanity against the tyranny of Ghatanothoa. (: "Out of the Aeons")

In the works of August Derleth, Shub-Niggurath is one of the Great Old Ones classified as an earth elemental, along with Yog-Sothoth, Tsathoggua, and Nyarlathotep. Derleth portrays them as inimical towards the fire elementals such as Cthugha and his flame creatures.

### Cult
Of all the Mythos deities, Shub-Niggurath is probably the most extensively worshipped. Her worshippers include the Hyperboreans, the Muvians, and the people of Sarnath, as well as any number of druidic and barbaric cults. fullContent:
Shubra Cabra is a short story by Dennis E. Power in which the supernatural anti-hero El Head battles Shub-Niggurath and a posse of supernatural carnivorous black goats with glowing yellow eyes.

It is available to read online [http://www.pjfarmer.com/secret/elhead/shubacabra.htm here].

### Behind the Mythos
Shubra Cabra is a deliberately confused version of the Mythos entity Shub-Niggurath, and El Head is itself a pastiche character on the edge of the Wold Newton shared universe, in which "crossovers" between for example pulp heroes or Sherlock Holmes and elements of other stories, in this case Lovecraft works, are a common staple. These stories are pastiche, in that they do not attempt to do more than emulate the original format or tone of stories from the original authors, and sometimes in their effort to do so the works verge on parody, intentional or not.

Shudde M'ell is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Brian Lumley for his short story "Cement Surroundings".

### Description
Shudde M'ell is a mile long great grey worm-like creature that burrows through the earth, melting all rocks in its wake. It is believed to be the supreme regent of the Chthonians as well as the largest and most powerful of the race. 

Shudde M'ell appears as a colossal worm with tentacles sprouting from its head, and is so large that it can cause earthquakes by simply moving. Although Shudde M'ell is thought to have lain dormant beneath Ethiopia for aeons, it is also suspected to have been the cause of the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.

### History
Millennia ago, when humanity as we know it was a thing still to come, Shudde M’ell sided with the Old Ones in their war against the Elder Gods. When the Great Old Ones were bested, the Elder Gods imprisoned their defeated enemies rather than destroy them. As such, Shudde M'ell found itself locked in a subterranean prison below the sands of Ethiopia, with the Elder Gods using their Star-Stone artefacts to keep them from escaping.

Over the aeons, humans evolved to their present condition, and sprung from the valleys of Africa. With time, tribes of humans reached Ethiopia, and with them came curiosity. The masters of the tribe, those known as shamans, began to excavate the unusual outcroppings that surrounded them, and eventually came across strange artifacts which they chose to wear as badges of office. As time went on, the shamans dug up further artefacts, and the number of these charms worn became a sign of seniority amongst others. Little did these men know how the taking of the star-stones would affect the world around them...

As the star-stones were slowly removed, so were their confining properties, and soon the Cthonians were free. With this, Shudde M'ell and his kind were free to roam the earth, and so they did for the next few millennia, excavating their lairs across the globe and eventually infesting nearly every part of the planet.

Come the 1960s, a group of humans known as the Wilmarth Foundation became aware of these creatures and began to plot ways to rid the planet of their foul taint. In conjunction with noted occultists Titus Crow and Henri-Laurent de Marigny, they launched simultaneous campaigns known as the Great Britain Project and the American Project which were ultimately successful in driving the bulk of the Cthonians from their respective domains.

Shuggob is a fictional character created by Lin Carter for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "In the Vale of Pnath".

### Description
Shuggob is an elderly ghoul sage who lives alone in a stone house surrounded by a garden of moss and lichens, with a hedge made of mottled fungi, in the part of the Dreamlands known as the Vale of Pnath. He is extremely knowledgeable about magic and skilled in the craft of potions.

Somewhat unusually for a ghoul, Shuggob is a soft-spoken individual of gentlemanly demeanor and scholarly inclinations. He is amicable and receptive to strangers, offering them food and drinks of the type generally consumed by his species, i.e. made from human flesh and blood.

In terms of physical appearance, Shuggob is tall and lean. His skin is grey, cold to the touch, and rubbery, and his hands are surprisingly strong. He is so ancient that parts of his face have been eaten away by maggots, making his speech difficult to understand at times. Eibon attributes this state of partial decomposition to Shuggob's extreme age and "questionable diet". (: "In the Vale of Pnath")

Shuggon is an ancient continent created by the late American author Lin Carter for his Cthulhu Mythos works.

### Overview
In the Cthulhu Mythos works of Lin Carter related to Hyperborea, Shuggon is the ancient continent of the Mesozoic serpent people destroyed in a cataclysm c.65 million B.C.E. which caused the surviving serpent people to migrate to Elder Valusia and aided in the extinction of the dinosaurs. Shuggon is named in the Necronomicon but goes unnamed in most other texts. It may also be the same as Altuas or Altuan.

Shugoran is an Avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep created by H. P. Lovecraft contemporary Henry Kuttner, although it has since been expanded on by several other authors, including T. E. D. Klein.

### Expanded Mythos

### "Black Man with a Horn"
In T. E. D. Klein's 1980 short story, Shugoran is associated with Tcho-tcho artwork of an oversized man with a long horn. However, sightings of the creature give the impression of a fish-like being with webbed feet, a gas mask-like trunk, and wings of some description, although these may in fact be catfish-like fins.

It is also hinted to have some kind of connection with strange yellow snails which are widely feared as supernatural in nature by Malayan tribesfolk.

### Chaosium
Shugoran was incorporated into Chaosium's Lovecraftian roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu, first appearing in 1992's Escape From Innsmouth by Kevin Ross. It later appeared in the Malleus Monstrorum (2006). It was Chaosium that introduced the idea that Shugoran was an avatar of Nyarlathotep.

### "The Boonieman"
In Edward M. Erdelac's short story "The Boonieman" (2014), Shugoran lies sleeping beneath a village in South Vietnam until it is woken by a raiding force of North Vietnamese soldiers. Erdelac describes it thus:


However, this description appears to differ somewhat from previous iterations, so it is possible that this is not the same entity.

Shuma-Gorath is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. He was first mentioned in a short story by Robert E. Howard from the 1920s (exact date unknown) called "The Curse of the Golden Skull", in which the "iron-bound books of Shuma-Gorath" are briefly mentioned in a single sentence.

He is a character which has been fully developed by Marvel Comics into a cosmic threat. The first appearance of Shuma-Gorath as the primary antagonist was in a story arc within Marvel Premiere #3–14 involving the super-hero Doctor Strange, and it was in issue #10 of that series when he made his first physical appearance in print.

Since then he has appeared in other Marvel comics and, during his incursions into Earth (of the Prime Reality), his manifestations have battled Doctor Strange, the Avengers, the Fantastic Four, the Invaders, and Salem's Seven. His minions have battled various heroes and teams, including the X-Men. Shuma-Gorath has also appeared in Marvel properties in both video games (Capcom and Zen Studios) and role-playing games (TSR).

### History
Shuma-Gorath is a member of the Great Old Ones (also known as the Many-Angled Ones), a race of malevolent cosmic entities that fed on the flesh and bones of mankind's ancestors. He is at least hundreds of millions of years old, having been on Earth at the time of the dinosaurs when he battled a rebellious Many-Angled One of great power whom he had created in the skies over the planet. He claims to be older than the universe itself, which would make him billions of years old. Shuma-Gorath once ruled over Earth, along with the other Great Old Ones, before Sise-Neg (a time-traveling sorcerer from the 31st century) defeated him by putting him to sleep and banishing him into another dimension, after which he destroyed and re-created the universe.

Millions of years later, Shuma-Gorath was able to re-establish himself in the Prime Reality (Earth-616), but his manifestation was imprisoned in a mountain by the Cimmerian god Crom. The barbarian warrior Conan would later battle a newly-freed Shuma-Gorath whom Crom would banish back to his home dimension. He would be summoned to Earth many times during the 20th century and early 21st century by sorcerers, an agent of Thanos, and a group of superhuman Nazis, though the heroes of Earth would successfully stop his incursion each time.

During the early 21st century, Shuma-Gorath and the rest of the Many-Angled Ones attempted the conquest of the Prime Reality via an invasion from one of the realities that they had conquered known as the Cancerverse. Shuma-Gorath's Ego Maze first appeared in Marvel Comics' Secret Avengers Vol 1 #33 in 2012. So far it has appeared in two issues of the same volume, #33-34.

### Background
When Captain Britain gave the Undead Avengers of Earth-666 the Orb of Necromancy to prevent its use elsewhere, they stored it in Shuma-Gorath's Ego Maze. It's not clear if it is actually located in their world or in another dimension, but Brother Voodoo of the Undead Avengers opened a mystical portal to get to Shuma-Gorath's Ego Maze.

They placed it in the "center tower", and before they went through the portal, Captain Britain was warned that a living man could end up dying of introspection in there. He also mentioned that he risked the fabric of his mind by taking him there. The "center tower" ended up being an Undead Celestial, the god of the planet's inhabitants, who held the Orb of Nercomancy which they planned to use to spread undeath throughout the cosmos.

The Sieur De Blois is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his narrative poem "Psychopompos: A Tale in Rhyme".

### Overview
The Sieur and his wife, the Dame De Blois, lived in a castle by the forest in the historical French province of Auvergne. Both were adept in the dark arts and capable of changing from human to non-human form. The Sieur was a werewolf who commanded a pack of supernatural wolves, while his wife could transform herself into a monstrous reptilian creature.

The Sieur De Blois descended from a "high and vast" lineage. His physical appearance was described as dark and lean, with "glossy hair" and "gleaming teeth". He was a taciturn man, rarely seen by his neighbours, and served only by elderly servants whose ancestors had been employed by his family for generations. He was sometimes sighted near the river at midnight with an "aspect so uncouth, and gaze so strange" as to frighten those who witnessed the scene. The De Bloises never attended church, had no use for their chapel, and employed no chaplain, monk, or priest in their household. (: "Psychopompos")

### Biography
After the Dame De Blois was killed in her reptilian form by the bailiff's wife, who struck her with an axe when the Dame was trying to devour the body of the bailiff's son, the Sieur De Blois waited until the next Candlemass for his revenge. In his wolf form, he led his pack through a snowstorm and broke into the bailiff's house to attack his wife's murderer. The bailiff, using the same axe his wife had used before, struck the wolf's head and rescued her. The injured wolf fled, but his pack continued to attack until the storm destroyed the house and a lightning strike revealed a crucifix in the hearth, the sight of which caused the demonic wolves to flee and the storm to dissipate. Later on, the trail of blood and footprints revealed that the Sieur had died in a quicksand swamp, where his loyal hunting-hound was found howling in mourning. (: "Psychopompos")

The Sign of Koth is a sigil described by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft in his novellas The Case of Charles Dexter Ward and The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Overview
In the Gugs' city in the Dreamlands, it is told that a central tower stands, which displays the Sign of Koth, "a monstrous symbol in bas-relief which made one shudder without knowing its meaning." (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

During the course of his investigations, Dr. Marinus Bicknell Willett notices the Sign of Koth engraved on a doorframe, and recalls his friend Randolph Carter drawing the symbol and explaining its usage. (: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward)

### Other Mentions of Koth
* Koth-Serapis is a sorcerer who features in Robert M. Price's stories set in Robert E. Howard's James Allison story cycle.
* In Howard's writings, including the Conrad & Kirowan and Conan cycles, Koth is a long-dead city (: "Dig Me No Grave"), a Hyborian kingdom (: "The Phoenix on the Sword", etc.), and possibly the name of a god (: "The Fire of Asshurbanipal").
* In August Derleth's short story "The God-Box", the druid guardian of the box where Sho-Gath is imprisoned mentions the Sign of Koth.

Silas Marsh, the Sailor, is a character who features in many of Fantasy Flight Games' Cthulhu Mythos-related games, and who has also appeared in some of their fiction.

### History
Growing up, Silas had always displayed a natural affinity for water, and for the ocean in particular. It therefore came as no great shock to anybody who knew him when he decided to pursue a career as a sailor. Signing up to a merchant shipping company, Silas took his leave and set off to explore the oceans.

As Silas sailed the world, visiting ports the world over, he began to have strange dreams, visions in which he walked through undersea cities and conversed with fish-like beings of nightmarish properties. Upon one of his rare trips home, he resolved to discover the source of these dreams, and was directed to the main branch of the family in Innsmouth.

### Behind the Mythos
First appearing as an Investigator for the Second Edition expansion of Arkham Horror, Innsmouth Horror, Silas has since made appearances in Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror: The Card Game and Mansions of Madness, in addition to the novella The Deep Gate by Chris A. Jackson, which is centered on the character. In 2010, Fantasy Flight released a plastic miniature of Silas as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, but this is no longer available.

### Trivia
*The Arkham Horror and Eldritch Horror biographies on Silas differ slightly, with the first relating that his family recommended that he travel to Innsmouth to meet the main branch of the Marshes, and the second stating that he had always lived there. The novel keeps with the Eldritch Horror version and has Silas born and raised in Innsmouth, having just recently returned to New England from the High Seas after news of his parents death.
*Silas is a Deep One hybrid, although he has not completely transformed.
*Another heroic Deep One hybrid is the viking warrior protagonist of the novella I Walk the World's Black Rim, by Mike Minnis.

### Synopsis
Three men, led by a warrior from Uzuldaroum, descend into the caves beneath a great mountain in search of a rare egg as part of a sacrifice to the Great Old One Tsathoggua. Although a foolish error causes them to lose their first prize and necessitates a retreat to the surface, they quickly about-turn and make their way back below again.

### Characters
*Klebmt, a skilled swordsman hailing from the great city of Uzuldaroum.
*Thuenk, an accomplished archer with a knowledge of the surrounding jungles.
*Meskshi "the Mute", a mercenary cursed by a witch to forever speak in a silly voice.

The Silent Ones were a group of creatures which appeared in Mark McLaughlin's 2004 short story "Toadface".

### Description
Each of the three Silent Ones were roughly eighty feet in length, with heads similar to that of a snake yet sporting fish-like faces. They had fat bodies, tentacles in place of arms, and massively thick legs akin to those of an iguana. Although they were stated to possess gills, they seemed to be capable of comfortably surviving on land, at least for a short period of time.

### History
The three Silent Ones slept in an ancient ruined temple (said to be reminiscent of a gladiatorial arena) within the aquatic Deep One city of Y'ha-nthlei just off Innsmouth harbour. The one known as G'hlaballa had its body inhabited by the ghost of a man known as John Masters who used it to kill the Deep One Toadface before heading back to the ocean to feed on whales.

The origins of the Silent Ones, how long they had lain dormant in their temple, or indeed how they even came to rest there, remains a mystery, although it is possible that they may have been either gods of the Deep Ones or Great Old Ones, as Toadface stated that by possessing G'hlaballa's slumbering form, Masters was committing an act of blasphemy.

"Silently, Without Cease" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Daniel Mills. It was published in the 2011 anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press .

### Synopsis
During the time of the Byzantine Empire, the dying Emperor Justinian is approached by a mysterious stranger who offers him salvation. All that he asks in return is that the Emperor opens the gates of the city and allows him to leave to spread his festering message across the entirety of the known world. He agrees, but is horribly scarred and his wife, who has guessed the reason for his miraculous recovery, turns her back on him.

### Behind the Scenes
Although "Silently, Without Cease" contains no direct references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft of the greater Cthulhu Mythos, in a commentary on the story author Daniel Mills states that as the plague was believed to have originated in Egypt, "[t]he connection to Nyarlathotep – especially the pharaoh-like herald of apocalypse described by Lovecraft’s early prose poem – came all-too-easily."

The Silurians (: Doctor Who and the Silurians), more properly known as the Eocenes (: The Sea Devils, : White Darkness), are a fictional species created by Malcolm Hulke for the sci-fi television series Doctor Who.

A race of sapient reptilian humanoids which evolved on the planet Earth in prehistory, the Silurians have placed themselves in hibernation chambers millions of years ago, in order to escape a catastrophic event that threatened their civilisation. They are evolutionarily related to the aquatic Sea Devils, both species being collectively known as Earth Reptiles.

### History
The Silurians figure among many species known to have worshiped the Great Old Ones long before the rise of humankind (: All-Consuming Fire). By the time the Great Old Ones placed themselves in stasis, following a great war that left the Earth's biosphere in ruins, the "reptile men" had already done so as well (: White Darkness).

The occultist Aleister Crowley owned an unexpurgated copy of the Necronomicon with at least one passage written in the Eocene language, containing instructions on how to raise the dead (: White Darkness).

### Behind the Mythos
The time period this species originates from is the subject of contradicting evidence in Doctor Who. The Doctor himself has stated that the name Silurian is a misnomer, as they are not from the Silurian period, suggesting Eocene as a more accurate name. In truth, neither the Silurian Period nor the Eocene Epoch are compatible with the fact that this species is known to have coexisted with Mesozoic dinosaurs, and that their representation of the world shows the supercontinent Pangaea, perhaps suggesting the Triassic as the most likely candidate. Further complications arise from the fact that they apparently coexisted with early hominids as well, and that the Doctor has speculated that the disaster they went into hibernation to escape from was the formation of the moon, which in the real world is believed to have happened long before the Earth was capable of harbouring complex life.

The Silver Key is a fictional artefact in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his eponymous short story.

### Overview
The Silver Key is an ancient magical artefact that unlocks gates of space and time, allowing access to remote times and places of the universe. It was last in the possession of Randolph Carter, who used it to travel through the Ultimate Gate.

It is described as "a huge key of tarnished silver covered with cryptical arabesques". Carter has a vision of his late grandfather, who tells him where to find the key: It's in a box in the attic of his Boston home, where it was placed by Edmund Carter, his ancestor who lived at the time of the Witch Trials. The key had been handed down to Edmund by ancestors further back: Randolph's grandfather mentions Sir Randolph Carter, an Elizabethan wizard, and another ancestor who lived at the time of the Crusades and learned secrets from the Saracens who held him captive. Randolph Carter eventually uses the Silver Key to go back in time, reverting from his adult self in 1928 to his child self in 1883. (: "The Silver Key")

To use the key, it must be held up to the setting sun and turned nine times, with some particular "syllables of ceremony" intoned on the ninth turn, at a location near a "dark polarity and induced gate". The Silver Key was created in prehistoric Hyperborea, and is attuned to "the personal consciousness-angles of human beings alone". When Carter found his consciousness transported to the body of Zkauba (an insectoid Yaddithian from millions of years in the past), he found that the Silver Key might assist him in travelling back to his own time, but would not have the power to return him to his original body. To do so, Carter would need a powerful spell that might give the key "limitless powers it otherwise lacked". (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

### In Other Media
*In the manga series Alicia Y, Randolph Carter used the Silver Key to free Alicia Y Armitage when she was trapped underneath a giant star-shaped stone.
*In the manga series D.Y.N. Freaks, Narukami Chikage is a wielder of the Silver Key. It can be used to seal the powers of Yoguruma Mugen, an avatar of the evil god Yog-Sothoth.
*In the mobile game Fate/Grand Order, the Silver Key is described as being a crucial ability for humans while facing off against the Outer Gods. Originally located in Salem, Massachusetts, the Silver Key was preserved by an English Thaumaturgist until it was eventually handed to Abigail Williams, a girl who met the conditions to inherit it. Abigail was turned into a living version of the Silver Key itself, after Raum tricked her into summoning and temporarily fusing with Yog-Sothoth. Randolph Carter is also implied to be a possessor of the Silver Key.

The Silver Twilight Lodge is a shadowy occult organisation created by Sandy Petersen for his Shadows of Yog-Sothoth campaign in 1982. It was included in Richard Launius's 1987 board game of Lovecraftian horror, Arkham Horror. It has since become something of a staple in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-based content.

### Overview
Originally conceived as something of a morally ambiguous cult whose aims were somewhat unclear, the Lodge did consort with malevolent entities, but also attempted to thwart the plans of the Great Old Ones and their minions.

However, later entries in the Arkham Horror Files series have portrayed it as a much more evil organisation who are in direct contact with various eldritch beings, and who actively try to assist their plans for world domination and the like.

### Arkham Horror
Debuting in Arkham Horror First Edition, the Silver Twilight Lodge has also appeared in the Second and Third editions of the game, where it has traditionally been a source of mystic knowledge and aid for the players, as well as something of a threat.

### Feeders from Within
In Peter J. Evans' 2013 novel, the Lodge was directly involved in the alien Mi-Go Mr. Stone's ultimately unsuccessful attempt to harvest creatures named the Feeders from Within, with the goal of bringing madness and chaos to the Earth.

### Members

*Carl Sanford, the Lodge's high priest.
*Phillip Avery, a high-ranking member, deceased. (: Feeders from Within)
*Diana Stanley, a former initiate who decided to leave the Lodge and attempt to expose their activities. (: Feeders from Within)
*Samuel Nightingale, criminal and Lodge enforcer, deceased. (: Feeders from Within)
*Hookie, criminal and Lodge muscle, deceased. (: Feeders from Within)
*Cable, criminal and Lodge muscle, deceased. (: Feeders from Within)
*Mulcaine, criminal and Lodge muscle, deceased. (: Feeders from Within)
*Perino, criminal and Lodge muscle, deceased. (: Feeders from Within)

### Behind the Mythos
The Silver Twilight Lodge was based on the Order of the Silver Twilight from Sandy Petersen's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game supplement Shadows of Yog-Sothoth, which in turn was loosely based on the real-life occult organisation of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn.

Simon Birks is a U.K.-based actor, producer, screenplay writer, comic book creator and author. In addition he, in partnership with Marielle Bouleau, founded Blue Fox Comics, an independent small press based in Linlithgow, Scotland, which was initially created to publish Birks's work. Due to the company's success, it has branched out to encompass the works of other authors and comic book creators, and has published dozens of works via successful Kickstarter campaigns.

Birks has adapted a number of H. P. Lovecraft’s stories into a comic book format, including "The Thing on the Doorstep" and "The Shadow Over Innsmouth", has written a sequel to At the Mountains of Madness in the same format, and was the creator of the Fighting Fantasy-style gamebook Innsmouth: The Stolen Child.

### Selected Works

fullContent:
The Simon Necronomicon is a grimoire attributed to "Simon", allegedly a pseudonym of occultist, conspiracy "researcher" and writer Peter Levenda.  

Materials presented in the book are a blend of ancient Middle Eastern elements, with allusions to the writings of H. P. Lovecraft and Aleister Crowley, woven together with a story about a man known as the "Mad Arab". The ritual magic elements of this work of fiction are directly taken from academic work on the Assyrian language meaning that all of the passages relating to exorcizing demons are in fact magical formulae to summon demons. Not everyone thinks this is an accident. The magical system and philosophy behind it exactly match those of the Brooklyn "magic shop" frequented by Levenda and others in the late 1960s and early 1970s and of the Process Church of the Final Judgement and its splinter groups based in New York. This book also directly references Pazuzu and other demons and devils who rose to popularity and notoriety in movies such as The Exorcist.

The book was released in 1977 by Schlangekraft, Inc. in a limited edition hardback printing, followed by a paperback release by Avon Books, and a subsequent paperback release by Bantam Books.

The book is cobbled together from a mishmash of recontextualized Sumerian and Babylonian texts peppered with added references to fictional deities created by Lovecraft and the orientalist magical system of Aleister Crowley. 

Simon’s text plagiarizes the work of pioneering Assyriologists like R.C. Thompson, from whose Devils and Evil Spirits of Babylonia many of the translations are lifted. In their original context, these texts were incantations against evil spirits and the problems and plagues they caused, not spells for conjuring them. 

The author of the Simon Necronomicon presents descriptions of the demons and their portfolios in English, but slips into transliterated Akkadian when the texts begin to call for the spirits to be cast out, leading to an implication that the demons are being invoked rather than exorcised. This is also the clearest evidence of the plagiarism from Assyriologists since there is no modification from the original sources in the material quoted in the book.

These ancient Mesopotamian incantations have come to be considered “satanic” through a centuries-long process of reinterpretation. The Simon Necronomicon reads its ancient sources through a combination of medieval demonology, 19th-century Theosophy, and 20th-century pulp fiction, predominantly that of the Mythos authors. It follows the Derleth adoption of the reconciliation of Old Ones with various Elemental forces and the Paracelsian Elements.

### Fictional Book, Real Life Murder

Simon of Gitta is the protagonist of a series of Cthulhu Mythos stories by Richard L. Tierney set in the days of Ancient Rome. Simon is an ex-gladiator turned sorcerer, using his skills with sword and sorcery alike to combat Mythos entities and the Roman Empire. He first appeared in "The Ring of Set", published in Swords Against Darkness #1 in 1977, though written in 1960.

Tierney based Simon of Gitta on the biblical figure of Simon Magus, inspired by the portrayal of the character by Jack Palance in the film The Silver Chalice (1954). The stories incorporate aspects of the historical religion of Gnosticism, meshing its lore with that of H. P. Lovecraft and his circle. 

Tierney's Simon of Gitta stories are collected in The Scroll of Thoth: Simon Magus and the Great Old Ones, a Chaosium publication edited by Robert M. Price, and in Sorcery Against Caesar: The Complete Simon of Gitta Stories, from Pickman's Press.

Simon Orne is a fictional character in H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, an associate and collaborator of the book's main villain, Joseph Curwen; over the course of the novel, Orne also goes by the names Jedidiah Orne and Joseph Nadek.

### Character Biography
Simon Orne was born in the mid-17th century, and lives in Salem, Massachusetts. His close friends were two disreputable characters, Joseph Curwen and Edward Hutchinson. While his associates left the area around the time of the witchcraft panic of 1692, Orne stayed in Salem until 1720, "when his failure to grow visibly old began to excite attention." He reappeared about 30 years later, using the name Jedidiah Orne and claiming to be his own son; it was remarked that the supposed son was the "precise counterpart" of the father. He left Salem for good in 1771, when "when certain letters from Providence citizens...brought about his quiet removal to parts unknown."

The intervention from Providence was the result of an intercepted letter from Orne to Curwen, who had been living in that city. The letter alludes to the necromantic efforts to raise the dead that the three associates had engaged in in Salem, and which Curwen was continuing in Rhode Island. Orne urges Curwen to "write me as Jedediah and not Simon," referring to his "Plan by which I came back as my Son," as "In this Community a Man may not live too long."

The letter also suggests that Orne's necromantic skills are not as great as Curwen's, as he confesses that  I have not ye Chymicall art to followe Borellus," and pronounces himself "confounded by ye VII. Booke of ye Necronomicon that you recommende."

More than a century and a half later, in 1924, Charles Dexter Ward travelled to Prague to visit "a certain very aged man supposed to be the last living possessor of some very curious mediaeval information." This was Orne, living in "in the oldest quarter of Prague" under the name Josef Nadek, "an evil old man" who had dwelt there "alone ever since anyone could remember." He had been keeping up his necromantic studies, as he later wrote a letter to the resurrected Curwen referring to something he had raised from Egypt that gave him a scar that he still had 75 years later.

In 1928, Nadek disappears--this time for good, as far as the novel is concerned--after a being raised by Marinus Willett (referred to as Number 118) destroys his house in Prague.

Simon Strantzas (born 1972) is a British Fantasy Award-nominated author of weird fiction from Ontario, Canada. He has written a number of works set in and inspired by both the Cthulhu Mythos and the Yellow Mythos. These have been included in anthologies such as Paula Guran's New Cthulhu 2: More Recent Weird, Joseph S. Pulver, Sr.'s A Season in Carcosa, and S. T. Joshi's Black Wings III and Black Wings IV.

Strantzas has also been named, alongside Thomas Ligotti, Laird Barron, and John Langan, as one of the more notable authors of recent weird fiction by True Detective writer Nic Pizzolatto .

Sinbad and the Great Old Ones is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by British author Gavin Chappell, which crosses Middle Eastern folk tale hero Sinbad into the Lovecraftian horror genre. It was first published in April 2016 by Schlock! Publications; paperback, hardcover, and digital editions have all received a release.

### Synopsis
When the Mad Arab Abdul Alhazred makes a bargain with Nyarlathotep to retrieve the four parts of the Sign of Koth and pave the way for the return of the Great Old Ones, legendary sailor Sinbad and a motley crew of heroic sidekicks are drawn into a race against time to stop the evil sorcerer. 

From the Indian Ocean to the Plateau of Leng, from Baghdad to Kadath, the group pursue their quarry across the known - and unknown - world, encountering such diverse threats as feralghouls, flying Shantak-birds, predatory Spiders of Leng, ravenous Tcho-Tchos, and marauding Star Spawn. Although successful in his quest, virtually all of his companions and the entirety of his crew meet a grizzly death at the hands of one monstrous being or another.

fullContent:
Sinkhole is a third-party (not written or approved by Chaosium) adventure module for the Call of Cthulhu RPG, written by Michael LaBossiere.

From the introduction to the module (and quoted by express permission of the author as per the terms of his website):

"Untold eons ago the earth was visited by strange and terrible beings. Among these was the horrid entity Tulushuggua. Tulushuggua found the water filled crevices of the earth to its liking and squirmed its way deep into the earth’s crust. There Tulushuggua spawned its brood of Tulush who spread out through the dark caverns in search of food. 

When man arose he encountered the Tulush. Some men, impressed by the power of the creatures, worshipped them and formed cults. Most of these cults eventually perished, but some lived on in various isolated parts of the world. 

Several years ago, a promising young graduate student named Hayes encountered one of these cults and found their activities appealing. With his abilities, Hayes was able to contact more sophisticated cults with a worldwide agenda. Drawn into the madness, Hayes agreed to work for the cults and chose to go back to his beginnings by reviving a Tulushuggua cult. Hayes needed a place to locate his cult and he was able to purchase a plot of land in Wakulla, Florida. Naturally, he selected a piece of land with a sinkhole so that he might contact the Tulush. Hayes selected Janet Reuben to aid him in his endeavors. When Hayes realized he needed help to lure people into his planned cult, he sought Pete Smith, a religious con man. Smith turned out to be something of a disappointment for Hayes, which is where the adventure begins."

Sirens, also spelled Syrens, are a species of unearthly female sea creatures in Greek mythology, known for their ability to enthrall men with their singing. Traditionally, they have been depicted as woman-headed birds who inhabit rocky islands and cliffs. The Sirens first appear in the Homeric epic poem, the Odyssey. 

They were traditionally believed to be sired by Phorcys who mated with the sea monster Ceto, immortal creatures whom use their voice to lure men to their deaths.

According to one source, the Syrens were banished from the Earth's surface in ancient times and exiled to the abyssal depths of the oceans, where their descendants became known as the Spawn of the Green Abyss, ruled by their queen Zoth Syra. (: "Spawn of the Green Abyss")

### In Marvel Comics
In the Marvel Multiverse, Sirens are the descendants of the Elder God known as Set. The Marvel Comics incarnation of these creatures were created in 1970 by Roy Thomas and Sal Buscema, making their first appearance in issue #29 of the 1st volume of the Sub-Mariner comic book series.

### In the Call of Cthulhu RPG
 (Cthulhu Invictus)]]
Sirens are a species of winged bird-like humanoids who originated on the planet that stood between Mars and Jupiter. When their homeworld was destroyed and turned into the Asteroid Belt, the Sirens fled to Earth. After many generations, they lost their advanced technology and their ability to fly through space, and eventually became "little more than murderous, if cunning, predators" which use their hypnotic voices to lure victims to a watery death and feed on their drowned corpses.

Sirens have deadly talons on their feet and are strong enough to fly while carrying twice their body weight. Despite their feminine appearance, they are hermaphrodite creatures with an alien method of reproduction that involves three parents, each impregnating the other two, so that all three will lay eggs. Each parent cares for their respective offspring for about three years, after which the young Sirens leave to establish their own territories. (: Cthulhu Invictus)

The Skinless One is an avatar of Nyarlathotep created by Geoff Gillan for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game.

### Overview
A relatively obscure avatar, the Skinless One manifests as a well-built humanoid creature a full 8 feet in height most notable for its completely exposed musculature and occasionally-visible third eye. Despite usually only manifesting to accept offerings from its followers, a small cult known as the Brothers of the Skin, the Skinless One is far from defenceless, possessing the horrific ability to flay those who displease it. Needless to say, this causes extremely painful and debilitating injuries, and any who witness the process are likely to come through with their sanity in tatters.

### Behind the Mythos
The Skinless One was designed by Geoff Gillan for the Call of Cthulhu campaign expansion Horror on the Orient Express. It was later included in the monster manual Ye Booke of Monstres II.

Based on the quotation included in Ye Booke of Monstres II, it would appear that the Skinless One was inspired by a passage from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Whisperer in Darkness": "To Nyarlathotep, Mighty Messenger, must all things be told. and He shall put on the semblance of men, the waxen mask and the robe that hides, an come down from the world of the Seven Suns to mock."

Penelope Love, another of the contributors to Horror on the Orient Express, used the Skinless One as an antagonist in her 2014 short story "Daddy, Daddy," included in the tie-in anthology Madness on the Orient Express, released to coincide with the revised edition of the original campaign.

fullContent:
"Skoptsy" is a short story by Jonathan Sharp, first published in the collection of Lovecraftian fiction Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be by 01Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
Two mob enforcers are dispatched to a remote farmhouse in the north of England with instructions to kill its occupants. What they encounter is a cult who practice self-mutilation led by a deathless old man with a tentacled abomination embedded within his torso.

### Behind the Mythos
The Skoptsy were a real-world Christian sect originating in Russia in the late 1700s. They were known for their practice of removing the sexual organs of members to inhibit notions of lust and remained in existence until as recently as the early 21st century.

fullContent:
Skull-Face is a fantasy novella by Robert E. Howard, originally serialized in Weird Tales in 1929.

While containing no direct references to the Cthulhu Mythos, the story shares several themes with "The Call of Cthulhu", and the character Kathulos of Atlantis has been incorporated in the expanded Mythos. The story is also included in the collection Nameless Cults: The Cthulhu Mythos Fiction of Robert E. Howard.

### Plot
In London, an American World War I veteran named Stephen Costigan, traumatized by his war experience, becomes addicted to hashish and spends his days at Yun Shatu's Temple of Dreams. In a drug-induced dream, he sees a man with a skull-like face, and a beautiful young woman behind him.

When Costigan finally runs out of money, the same woman from the dream actually appears in front of him and speaks to the bouncer, Hassim, who allows Costigan to continue to frequent the opium house. Costigan is vaguely aware that the girl must be paying for his hashish, but is so disinterested in life at this point that he barely gives it a thought.

Hassim takes Costigan to a secret room, telling him that "the Master" wants to see him. Although he remains hidden, Costigan recognizes the Master's voice as that of the skull-faced man from his dream. The man marks Costigan's hand with the image of a scorpion, and gives him a golden liquid that cures his addiction. Over the next days, Costigan notices that he's not only cured, but also seems to be endowed with physical strength and awareness beyond that of a normal man.

Feeling grateful for what the Master has done to him, Costigan accepts a job to impersonate a government commissioner. Before he can do so, Costigan prevents an attempt at the Master's life by a British secret agent named John Gordon, but also prevents the Master's agent, Yussef Ali, from murdering Gordon, and allows the latter to escape. The young woman, Zuleika, visits Costigan in secret, revealing that she too is an agent of the Master, and is worried about what Costigan has done. After she leaves, Hassim returns to announce a change of plans, and Costigan finds out from a newspaper that the commissioner he was supposed to impersonate has been found murdered.

The Master sees Costigan again and acknowledges that the latter saved his life, but chastises him for saving Gordon's as well. Costigan claims that his dept of gratitude is paid, but the Master counters that Costigan will always be in his service, no less of a slave than Hassim or Zuleika. As he reveals himself, Costigan is horrified to see the skull-like face, parchment-like skin and clawed corpse-like hands, confirming this as the same man that he had seen in his dream.

The Master reveals that he cured Costigan's hashish addiction with a far more addictive drug, the golden liquid that was also responsible for increasing Costigan's physical and mental capacity. shortDefinition: "Slaves for the Slaughter Sect" is a short story by prolific Mythos contributor Robert M. Price. It centres on the character of Frank Nardi, created by C. J. Henderson for his Arkham Detective Agency series.  ### Synopsis A man named Arlan Hellison, ...
fullContent:
"Slaves for the Slaughter Sect" is a short story by prolific Mythos contributor Robert M. Price. It centres on the character of Frank Nardi, created by C. J. Henderson for his Arkham Detective Agency series.

### Synopsis
A man named Arlan Hellison, claiming to be researching a book on satanic cults, approaches Frank Nardi for help in investigating a series of disappearances in Arkham. Despite finding his way to the truth of the matter, that a cult of deranged inbreeds has been abducting, killing and mutilating the missing people, Nardi is double-crossed by Hellison, who is secretly a cultist. Luckily for Nardi, the Arkham Police Department is able to locate him in time, and the ritual being practiced by Hellison backfires, killing him instead.

### Characters
*Frank Nardi, a former New York police detective turned private detective.
*Annabelle Sawyer, a librarian at Miskatonic University and victim of the cult.
*Arlan Hellison, a newcomer to Arkham who is investigating a supposed occult slave ring with a view to writing a novel. Is actually a cult initiate with a view to sacrificing Nardi and Sawyer.
*Sergeant Cerasini, an officer with the Arkham Police Department.
*Langer, another Arkham police officer.
*Hoffman, a student at Miskatonic University.

### Behind the Mythos
"Slaves for the Slaughter Sect" was written by Robert M. Price in response to a request from Brian M. Sammons for stories involving C. J. Henderson's hard-boiled detective Frank Nardi. It was published in the collection Arkham Detective Agency by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Mythos Connections

*The story is set in the fictional town of Arkham created by H. P. Lovecraft himself.
*An article in The Arkham Advertiser makes reference to a citizen who believes that the Windwalker is responsible for the recent disappearances. The Wind-Walker is an epithet of the Great Old One Ithaqua, who is known to abduct humans for his own purposes.
*A drug taken by Hoffman as part of a fraternity prank, the Black Lotus, was created by Robert E. Howard for his Mythos story "The Slithering Shadow."
*The cult is attempting to summon the Great Old One Rhan-Tegoth.

### Trivia
*The name of the character Arlan Hellison is a clear nod to noted science fiction author Harlan Ellison.

shortDefinition: The Slaves of the Flame Undying are an Egyptian cult that worships Cthugha.  Bret Kramer's "Baggage Check" first appeared on the scenario included in the first issue of "The Unbound Book", an irregular series of .pdf magazines created by New Zealand ...
fullContent:
The Slaves of the Flame Undying are an Egyptian cult that worships Cthugha.

Bret Kramer's "Baggage Check" first appeared on the scenario included in the first issue of "The Unbound Book", an irregular series of .pdf magazines created by New Zealand fans containing a series of scenarios for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Description
The cult dates back to pre-Roman Egypt, where a secret priesthood within the Nile River areas worshiped Cthugha under the name Kathigu-Ra. The worship of the cult and its god declined under the reign of the Ptolemaic dynasty and the cult completely disappeared from the records sometime during the 2nd century BC. Despite this, they continue with their activities to this day, doing everything possible not to attract attention and not carry out risky actions.

### Practices
The cult's ceremonies involve ritual orgies and ceremonial immolations, leaving its limbs with burn scars on the torso, arms and legs. The most fanatical cult members are often marked with symbols sacred to Cthugha. The high priestesses of the cult are able to divine and predict events that occur far from the place where they are staring at a ceremonial brazier.

### Scenarios
In "Baggage Check", four of the slaves (named Abd Higazi, Hasan al-Majub, Saad Khalidi and Zaynab al-‘Ashur) are in search of a stolen canopic vase. During a trip, and to avoid the authorities, the thief makes a change with the investigators' luggage. This is a ceremonial object of the Cthugha cult, and they will not hesitate to sacrifice to their god those who stand in their way. The slaves will keep a watchful eye on the investigators and then do their best to retrieve the vessel. If necessary, more slaves will appear, guided by visions from their god and orders from their priestess.

What no one knows is that within him is a fire vampire, trapped within him nearly two millennia earlier by these Cthugha cultists. Among other peculiarities, the vampire uses the possessor's dreams to encourage him to worship Cthugha, showing him the Egyptian cult of the slaves of the eternal flame. This is not always effective, and the effects can range from zero to pyromania.

fullContent:
The Sleepers are a fictional organisation in the CthulhuTech pencil-and-paper role-playing game by Wildfire LLC.

### Background
The Sleepers are a benevolent organization whose members walk the dreams of men. Who hold sway over the realm of dreams and potentially influence anyone they speak to in their sleep. It has been around for millennia and recruits from lucid dreamers, the most talented of them all. They recruit only those who have a protective or altruistic mindset, and quickly dismiss the greedy, selfish, or secretly malevolent. Once they roamed The Dreamlands, but ever since it has been cut off or possibly consumed by a Great Old One, that realm has been inaccessible to them. A good chunk of their members were lost at that time, though it's unknown if they were simply trapped in the cut off realm or worse, consumed by an entity.

"Sleepy Hollow To-day" is a short non-fiction work by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. One of his travelogues, it was written in the summer of 1928, and first saw print in an unknown publication in 1930.

### The real Sleepy Hollow
Sleepy Hollow is a village in the town of Mount Pleasant, in Westchester County, New York, United States. It was the setting of "The Legend of Sleepy Hollow" by Washington Irving, which tells the tale of Ichabod Crane, a local schoolteacher, and his struggles against his romantic rival for the hand of a fair maiden. Although usually treated in adaptations as a supernatural story the original tale strongly implies that in fact Ichabod has been the victim of a cruel hoax and his disappearance is not due to being killed by a phantom but rather to fleeing the area in shame, never to return.

### Publication History 
* Uncollected Prose and Poetry (1978)
* Collected Essays Volume 4: Travel (2006)

### Background
Sligguth was the offspring of the Elder God Set, who possessed superhuman durability and strength. He drained a victim's life force by generating a magical fungus which rapidly grew over the body. He was in the service of Shuma-Gorath, lord of the Great Old Ones.

Slorioth is a fictional entity created by Marvel Comics, who appears as the primary antagonist of the four-part story arc "Final Defense", featured in Secret Defenders Vol 1 #22-25.

### History
Slorioth was one of the Great Old Ones, and ravaged the Earth eons ago, until his soul and body were bound to the land by a cabal of sorcerers.

Thousands of years later, a town would be established nearby, in the state of Maine: Starkesboro. Near the end of the 20th century, he corrupted and manipulated the hero Dr. Druid into releasing him from his imprisonment. Slorioth's reemergence was felt throughout the world. Spider-Man's spidey sense went into overdrive. Daimon Hellstrom (The Son of Satan) sensed the disturbance of the Aether, threatening to shift the balance between Heaven and Hell. The powerful telepath Psi-Lord sensed danger everywhere, but was unable to pinpoint its location.

Beneath NY City, subharmonic tremors rippled through the Deviants underground realm. Waves of pure discord threatened to inundate mankind's subconscious minds. Throughout thne United States, reports of extranormal activity rose, building to an unholy crescendo. Upon is emergence, both the Defenders and Secret Defenders fought against him, with no success. The Vishanti arrived threatening Earth with its destruction if they did battle with Slorioth, therefore the Living Tribunal was summoned. Who agreed that Slorioth could not be contained by any dimension and so threatened the entire universe (Earth-616) with destruction, and therefore was drawn away from Earth and its reality.

### Powers
Slorioth is an eldritch being that disrupts temporal continuity. When it emerged from its imprisonment it was ripping and tearing at the fabric of reality, and clawing itself unbidden into the minds and hearts of mankind. Reveling in the self-destructive indolent nature of humanity. The Silver Surfer sensed that it was the the primal embodiment of the darkest nightmares that mankind had produced. A being of pure, unadulterated corruption, unrestrained malice, and power without reason. That they fought only the tiniest aspect of the being, which was a pan-dimensional gestalt that was beyond the comprehension of mortals.

The nature of Slorioth was to continually expand, making him an existential threat to any dimension or reality. His expansion in the universe would have eventually ended in a cataclysmic conclusion for Eternity, the cosmic abstract of time. When in corporeal form, he was resistant against any type of attack and possessed super strength. The tentacles corrupted the minds of those it touched and burned them with their acidic touch. They drained the lifeforce of those it touched, even a cosmic being like the Silver Surfer.

The Snake Clan is a fictional race in Marvel Comics created in 2001 by Juan Roman Cano and Fiona Avery. Making their first appearance in the 2001 issue of the 1st volume of Spider-Man Annual.

### Background
The Snake Clan are the offspring of Tartessus, daughter of the Elder God Set. Depicted as a primitive humanoid race they live in the jungles of Peru, using spears and blowguns and tattooing their heads with the image of an open mouthed snake head. They are long-time rivals of the Spider Clan, and had a hostile encounter with Spider-Man.

shortDefinition: "Snake Fever" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.  ### Synopsis Will Allison, a cowboy in America’s Wild West, takes refuge from a Comanche hunting party at an abandoned homestead said by the natives to be cursed land. Whi...
fullContent:
"Snake Fever" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
Will Allison, a cowboy in America’s Wild West, takes refuge from a Comanche hunting party at an abandoned homestead said by the natives to be cursed land. While there, he recalls the story of the previous occupants, who made the mistake of killing a nest of strangely-coloured snakes. Thereafter, the head of the household developed a deep-seated psychosis, causing him to believe that his family were transforming into serpent-like creatures and culminating in a brutal murder-suicide. Before going to sleep, Allison discovers a snake with odd markings in his camp and kills it before settling down for the night.

Awakened in the middle of the night by a strange noise, Allison is horrified to find a horde of snakes pouring forth from the old house, led by a grotesque creature which seems to be half man, half serpent: Yig, the creature believed by the indigenous people to be the source of the blight upon the land. Although managing to escape the creatures' clutches, he finds himself beginning to believe that everyone around him is undergoing a reptilian transformation . . .

### Characters

*Will Allison, a man on the run from from Comanches for unknown reasons.
*Yig, a Great Old One and the Father of Serpents.

### Publication History
"Snake Fever" appeared in the zines Dark Legacy (April 2004), Lovecraft's Disciples (July 2007), and E'ch Pi El #7 (December 2007), and most recently in the anthology of Shiflet's own work They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness (2018).

### Background
The Snakes of Many Colors are descendants of the Elder God Set. They are the offspring of his granddaughter Echidna. They are 50-75 foot long snakes with scales of multiple bright colors possessing human-level intelligence whom are are able to speak. Beings which are able to manipulate energy and have great magical powers, dwarfing sorcerers like Thoth-Amon. Which gives them the ability to banish their enemies across time and/or space. They have the ability to create a rainbow (no matter the weather or time of day), which they use to travel nearly instantaneously across vast distances.

Snireth-Ko is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his fantasy novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. The character is only mentioned once in passing, as a dreamer who might be the only "fully human person" to have seen the dark side of the Dreamlands' moon.

### In the Expanded Mythos
Snireth-Ko is featured as the protagonist of Gary Myers' Dunsanian story "Passing of a Dreamer". In this story, Snireth-Ko was a priest of Nasht responsible for preparing the incense that would be burned in the left ear of the Nasht image in the temple, to ensure the god would hear nothing else but his worshipper's prayers, which are whispered into his other ear. An erudite scholar, Snireth-Ko eventually came to the (erroneous) conclusion that the gods are not real, thus losing his faith and casting aside his priesthood.

While wandering the streets of Ulthar, Snireth-Ko came upon the altar of the Keeper of Dreams, an entity that can make men's desires come true, albeit for a terrible price. Longing for the wonder of his lost faith, Snireth-Ko was shown a string of fantastic and terrifying places, culminating in the dark side of the moon, where he beheld the Messenger of Azathoth and fled in terror. He was later sighted in an alley in London, mumbling about "the faith he had lost and a fee he had not wished to pay". (: "Passing of a Dreamer")

shortDefinition: "So Runs the World Away" is a short story by American author Caitlin R. Kiernan that introduces her setting of the supernatural underworld of Providence, Rhode Island, which she used as the milieu for several subsequent stories. It was first publishe...
fullContent:
"So Runs the World Away" is a short story by American author Caitlin R. Kiernan that introduces her setting of the supernatural underworld of Providence, Rhode Island, which she used as the milieu for several subsequent stories. It was first published in 2001 in The Mammoth Book of Vampire Stories by Women. It was later reprinted in Kiernan's collection To Charles Fort, With Love, and in their 2018 Cthulhu Mythos omnibus Houses Under the Sea.

### Overview
The story focuses on an undead creature known as Dead Girl who seems to have trouble fitting in to the societies of ghouls and vampires who dominate the Providence dark world. She is preoccupied with remembering the human life she had before her transition, an impulse discouraged by the character known as The Bailiff: “We forget for a reason, child,” he tells her. “Time is too heavy to carry so much of it strung about our necks.”

The story introduces characters and settings that will play important roles in later fiction by Kiernan, including The Bailiff, Madame Terpsichore, and the house on Benefit Street. It begins to sketch out Kiernan's vision of ghoul society, elaborated from the hints in H. P. Lovecraft's "Pickman's Model".

### Locations
The "big", "yellow" house on Benefit Street, described as "a house filled up with things that are pretty or broken or both." The aboveground portion of the house is occupied by vampires, described as "stiff and obsolescent beings... tragic waxwork shades sipping absinthe"; the basement is an entrance to the subterranean warrens of the ghouls. In Kiernan's 2007 novel Daughter of Hounds, its address is given as 135 Benefit Street--explicitly identifying it with the house that served as the model for the Lovecraft story "The Shunned House".

The bottom of Providence's Sekonk River is where Dead Girl, Bobby, and Gable sleep during the day--the latter "coiled like an eel in the roots of a drowned willow".

The Swan Point Cemetery has a mausoleum for the Stanton family where Dead Girl keeps a cigar box full of secrets. The story also contains a description of Lovecraft's gravesite in the cemetery, as well as a nearby tree where fans have carved the "unpronounceable names of dark, fictitious gods and entire passages from Lovecraft," as well "a scar in the shape of a tentacle-headed fish, a parody of the Christian ichthus."

### Characters
* Dead Girl, an undead woman who sleeps at the bottom of the Sekonk River. It's unclear whether she is a vampire or something else; she is acquainted with both vampires and ghouls but does not seem to be part of either society. She has memories, possibly stolen, of being a living human in the modern era, taking a boyfriend to see Lovecraft's grave, but she also has an attachment to a newspaper article about a suspected 19th century vampire named Mercy Lena Brown. (Brown was a real person who was actually accused of vampirism after her death.)
* Bobby, Dead Girl's companion. He is described as having "quicksilver eyes", which

"Soaked Shells" is a short Cthulhu Mythos comic book story written by Phil McClorey and illustrated by Jeff McComsey. It was published in the Arcana Comics horror anthology Velvet Rope in November 2010.

### Synopsis
When jaded big game hunter John Ford hears of bizarre humanoid creatures inhabiting the Amazon river basin, he sets out to add another trophy to his collection. Upon reaching the home territory of the creatures, he is dragged into the water by an aggressive fishman, where he witnesses the sleeping god Dagon, Lord of the Deep.

On his return home, Ford begins to develop gills and bulging eyes, and commits suicide rather than face the physical and mental changes his brief contact with Dagon tells him will soon be inflicted upon him.

Soames is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family".

### Overview
Soames is a butler who worked for Arthur Jermyn until Arthur took his own life by self-immolation in 1913. Described as a trustworthy man, Soames provided a factual account of the details of Arthur's suicide. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

In the Forever Azathoth series by Peter Cannon, Daniel Upton and his family have a British butler named Soames. It's unknown whether this is meant to be the same character from "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family". However, since Lovecraft's Soames was described as "aged" in 1913 and Forever Azathoth has him still active in the 1940s, it is possible that the Uptons' butler might actually be his son or relative. (: Forever Azathoth)
