Sodatha, also known as the Slithering God and the Hidden One, is a possible Great Old One by Marvel Comics, (: Official Handbook of the Marvel Universe A-Z #3) and a spawn of the Outer God Yog-Sothoth. (: The Appendix to the Handbook of the Marvel Universe)

Yog-Sothoth is known by the same name. (: "Valley Beyond the Stars")

### Background
Sodatha was a great tentacled subterranean monster, which lived within the walled city of Hanghrara in the kingdom of Zamora during the Hyborian Age. The Cult of Sodatha worshiped it as an elder god. It was a creature that possessed great strength, enough to destroy a city and it was capable of borrowing deep and fast. Guarding the tunnels to Sodatha were its spawn, miniature versions of itself. Both Sodatha and its spawn had a maw full of teeth, and many tentacles and eyes. Conan would encounter it in his adventures and during his fighting with its priests, boiling oil ended up on the abomination. Enraged with pain it burst from the ground into the city, toppling buildings and causing the populace to panic. Its inhabitants left the destroyed city in a mass exodus. (: "The Slithering God")

Solar Pons and the Cthulhu Mythos is a monograph written by Eric von Konnenberg and Pierre de Hammais. 

### Overview
The text focuses on the connections between August Derleth's fictional detective Solar Pons and the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. As Derleth's detective is a pastiche of Sherlock Holmes, the monograph itself is a mock scholarly article much like those written concerning the Sherlock Holmes 'canon', albeit referencing actual details provided by Derleth in various Solar Pons writings.

### Publication History
The article appeared in the Solar Pons Gazette in December 2013.

fullContent:
Many of the planets in our Solar System are referenced in H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. Lovecraft was a passionate amateur astronomer and enjoyed inserting references to celestial bodies into his tales.

### Mercury
Mercury is the first planet from the sun.

At some point in time, Mercury will be home to an intelligent species of "bulbous vegetable entities", whose bodies will be possessed by the Great Race of Yith after the fall of the coleopteran civilization on Earth. (: The Shadow Out of Time)

### Mercury's moon
In the past, Mercury also had a moon, which was inhabited by a hybrid polyp species with gestalt minds. At some point, however, Mercury's moon was plunged into the sun and destroyed. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

### Venus
Venus is the second planet from the sun.

According to the writings of Claes van der Heyl, at some point in history creatures known as "the lords of Venus" arrived in their spaceships to "civilise" the Earth. (: "The Diary of Alonzo Typer")

At some point in the future, the Crystal Company begins to colonise Venus from their base at Terra Nova and is locked in conflict with the native lizards over the planet's valuable crystal orbs that can be used as a source of electrical power. Venus' atmosphere cannot sustain human life, although a human equipped with supplementary breathing apparatus may spend most of his or her time unmasked, requiring only occasional use of this equipment to survive. Parts of the planet are covered in thick jungle which becomes almost impassable after a rain. (: "In the Walls of Eryx")

In the far distant future, over half a billion years from the present day, the cosmic time traveller Titus Crow telepathically communicated with a species of intelligent mollusc which had evolved there. Ten million years after that, all life on Venus had been extinguished. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

When Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee swapped minds with a member of the Great Race of Yith, one of the entities he met was a Venusian being "which would live incalculable epochs to come" (: The Shadow Out of Time). It's not known whether this Venusian was a member of the lizard-race, the intelligent mollusc race, or some other species entirely.

"The Vaults of Yoh-Vombis" mentions "the frozen, giant-builded battlements of Uogam on the glacial tundras of the nightward hemisphere of Venus". fullContent:
"Some Backgrounds of Fairyland" is a non-fiction essay by H. P. Lovecraft. It was originally part of a letter written to to Wilfred B. Talman, dated 23rd September 1932.

The essay was printed as part of the anthology Marginalia by Arkham House in 1944. It was reprinted in Jack L. Chalker's fanzine Mirage issue 8 in 1966 and has also been reprinted in Howard Phillips Lovecraft 1, a French-language collection edited by Phillipe Druillet and published by Robert Laffont. It has also been translated online into Spanish on several Spanish language blogs.

### Overview
In this essay, Lovecraft summarizes the then-current theories of the origin of belief in fairies, and suggests the confusion of three different strains of thought: the "Aryan" spiritual or religious beliefs in female nature spirits, the fearful superstitious dread of intangible female creatures of the night, and folk memories of ancient struggles and warfare between "Dwarfs" or Neanderthals and "true" humans who arrived as a later species.

Reference is also made to witch cult theories and it is clear that in all of this Lovecraft is following closely the theorizing of the author Arthur Machen, an admitted strong influence on Lovecraft and his writing.

shortDefinition: "Some Causes of Self-Immolation" is a non-fiction essay by H. P. Lovecraft. It was written on December 13, 1931. The essay was printed as part of the anthology Marginalia by Arkham House in 1944.   This is an essay of some 4,290 words, and was penned...
fullContent:
"Some Causes of Self-Immolation" is a non-fiction essay by H. P. Lovecraft. It was written on December 13, 1931. The essay was printed as part of the anthology Marginalia by Arkham House in 1944. 

This is an essay of some 4,290 words, and was penned under the pseudonym “L.Theobald, Jun., N.G., A.S.S.,” 

### Overview
The essay begins with a survey of the history of attempts to explain human behavior using methodological analysis and a Theory of Mind, beginning with Ancient Greek philosophy, then Descartes and Hobbes to Schopenhauer and Nietzsche. This section ends with a look at philosophers and psychologists of the then-contemporary era of 1900 to 1930.

Lovecraft suggests that there are eleven “Instincts” each of which is a driving force in the mind. These instincts include nutrition, escape ("flight" as in fight or flight), repulsion and their corresponding emotions (hunger, fear, disgust, etc.). The list of instincts is adopted from the work of William McDougall in the latter's book, Introduction to Social Psychology [1908].

Lovecraft expands this list with an instinct of his own, Symmetry. 

The purpose of the dissertation is to explain why humans do what they do, in a somewhat ironic but scholarly way.

It has been suggested that Lovecraft wrote this essay as a parody. He is sending up the prose and attempted analys of psychological Obscurantism. Evidence of this parody is found in the essay's subtitle (“Motives for Voluntary Self-Subjugation to Unpleasant Conditions by Human Beings”) and by the fact that L.Theobald, Jun. is cited as “Professor of Satanism of Applied Irreverence in Philistine University, Chorazin, Nebraska; Mencken Lecturer on Theology in Holy Roller College, Hoke’s Four Corners, Tennessee.”

### Behind the Mythos
Parodying the binary or dualistic approach to human motivation demonstrates somewhat of an antagonistic attitude to the often touted "Duality of Man" which in turn confirms Cosmicism as Lovecraft's dominant belief system. This puts him squarely at odds with the religious spirituality of August Derleth and in turn helps explain the jarring nature of the departure from Lovecraft's own version of the Mythos in the works of Derleth.

### Known Publication History

* Grimoire of the Aristocracy (2024)

fullContent:
"Something About Cats" is a non-fiction essay by H. P. Lovecraft, defending his ailurophilia (love of cats) as part of an ongoing debate about the virtues of cats versus the virtues of dogs. It was written on November 23, 1926 and published under the title "Cats and Dogs" in the Summer 1937 issue of the magazine Leaves.

According to August Derleth's introduction to the 1949 Arkham House collection Something About Cats and Other Pieces, the titular essay "grew out of a discussion at a meeting of the Kalem Klub and was carried into a Blue Pencil gathering".

### Contents
In this essay, Lovecraft explains that, although he doesn't dislike dogs, he favours cats for their self-sufficiency, aesthetic appeal, and "silent mystery", among other qualities. He accuses dog-lovers of judging the intellectual merits of a pet "by its degree of conformity to their own wishes", an attitude that Lovecraft perceives as absurd and self-centered. Conversely, it should be noted that Lovecraft exhibits his own bigoted elitism by likening the traits of cats that he admires to the aristocracy, at one point summarising his thesis with the classist statement: "The dog is a peasant and the cat is a gentleman".

### Publication History

* Grimoire of the Aristocracy (2024)

"Something Eating at You" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author R. C. Mulhare which was published in the Jesse Dedman-edited anthology Ancient Ones II in March 2018 .

The story is a reimagining of H. P. Lovecraft's 1927 short story "The Colour Out of Space," updated to a contemporary setting.

### Synopsis
After a meteorite makes planetfall on the property of the Gardners, whatever material it infuses the land with makes its way into the produce. When Norah Gardner makes a pumpkin pie for the local baking competition Laura, the only judge to actually take a bite, begins to hear a voice in her head, one which begs her to open her mind and let a force from outside enter. 

When she approaches Norah for help, the other woman encourages Laura to consume more of the contaminant: as she does so, the voice becomes more strident, and Laura's perception of reality begins to change… 

### Behind the Mythos
In addition to featuring the Gardners (Norah and Nate), "Something Eating at You" also mentions their neighbour Amelia Pierce, a clear nod to Ammi Pierce, the source of much of the story related in "The Colour Out of Space."

"Something Foetid" is a black comedy short story by Peter Cannon which retells the events of H. P. Lovecraft's "Cool Air" with the addition of the characters Bertie Wooster and Jeeves from the works of P. G. Wodehouse.

It is the second of Cannon's Cthulhu Mythos crossovers with Jeeves and Wooster, following "Cats, Rats, and Bertie Wooster", and followed by "The Rummy Affair of Young Charlie".

### Synopsis
During a sojourn in New York, young rich Londoner Bertram "Bertie" Wooster befriends an author named Randy Carter, who tells him about his fellow lodger, a Spanish doctor named Hector Muñoz who is permanently confined to his apartment due to some undisclosed illness. One day, Carter bursts into Wooster's apartment to request help, as Muñoz's condition is deteriorating rapidly, and while he steadily refuses to see a physician, he might not object to a visit by Wooster's valet, Jeeves, who is known for his astute and insightful nature. However, Jeeves treats Wooster coldly since the latter is wearing a tacky suit that the valet disapproves of, so Wooster and Carter end up going alone.

While Muñoz's landlady, Mrs. Herrero, insists that the doctor was renowned as a great man in her native Barcelona, Wooster is at first unimpressed by his lifeless appearance. To justify the visit, Carter pretends that Wooster had a heart attack recently, so Muñoz agrees to examine him. Once inside, Wooster notices the extreme cold, as well as the strong smell of spices and Egyptian incense. Muñoz explains that he is a sworn enemy of death, and has dedicated his life to figuring out how to conquer it.

Back home, Wooster relates the experience to Jeeves, who expresses his belief that Muñoz's ideas aren't as sound as they might appear. Jeeves also reveals that he has spoken to Carter's servant, Parks. It transpires that Carter is far wealthier than he lets on, and that living in a shabby New York boarding house is merely his "latest fancy". Concluding that Muñoz is "beyond all earthly assistance", Jeeves advises his master to accept an invitation by Miss Pauline Stoker to go to her father's estate in Long Island. Wooster does so, but unfortunately finds that he has caught a cold, no doubt after spending time in Muñoz's frigid room. To make matters worse, he receives an urgent phone call from Carter telling him that the pump piston from Muñoz's refrigerating machine is broken. Carter begs Wooster to return, ignoring Wooster's protests that he is not feeling well. He also reveals that Jeeves has been with them earlier, but right now he can't reach either Jeeves or Parks.

When Wooster arrives, Muñoz is in bad shape, bandaged like a mummy. Carter tells Wooster that they have to wait until the morning to purchase the replacement part they need, but asks him in the meantime to get as much ice as he can from every all-night establishment he can find in town. "Something from Out There" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author August Derleth, first published in the January 1951 issue of Weird Tales. The story references Cthulhu, R'lyeh, the Elder Gods and the Confessions of Clithanus.

### Synopsis
Rural English doctor William Currie is brought a man named Malvern, gripping a star-shaped stone and gibbering in the throes of madness. Looking into his movements prior to his delirium, the doctor learns that Malvern had been investigating a ruined priory and had prised the stone from an ancient casket which he had discovered there. 

Becoming aware of his past history as an occultist, Currie contacts two of Malvern's old acquaintances and begins to realise what he had been involved in. The occultists and the doctor then track down the creature before it is able to increase its power by through the consumption of human life-essence and use the star-stone to force it back inside its casket, sealing it once again and dropping it to the bottom of the ocean.

### Characters

* Dr. William Currie, a small-town physician.
* Geoffrey Malvern, the son of an aristocrat with an interest in the occult.
* Soames Hemery, a young occultist.
* Duncan Vernon, a young occultist.

fullContent:
"Something in the Moonlight" is a short story authored by accomplished Cthulhu Mythos author Lin Carter. It was first published in the paperback anthology Weird Tales #2 in December of 1980, a publication also edited by Carter .

### Synopsis
The story follows the statement of newly-qualified psychiatric councillor Charles Winslow Curtis, M.D., interspersed with notes from the journal of one of his patients, one Uriah Horby. Whilst Curtis does not believe Horby's paranoid tale of an ancient creature of immense power which wishes to take his soul, he sees no harm in acceding to the man's requests for access to portions of ancients texts which he thinks might protect him. Curtis later becomes something of a believer when Horby is found dead of terror on the night he had predicted, his window shattered, a foul slime spattering his room, and a visiting orderly driven half-mad.

### Characters
*Dr. Charles Winslow Curtis, M.D., a young doctor who obtained his qualifications at Arkham's Miskatonic University before landing a job at the Dunhill Sanatorium of Santiago, California.
* Uriah Horby, an occultist who has been committed to the Dunhill Sanatorium due to his belief that a reptilian moon-creature is seeking to consume his soul. He is described as "a small man in his mid-fifties, lean of build and going bald, clean-shaven and seemingly in good health," and "an exceptionally intelligent man of obvious breeding ... [who] had enjoyed an excellent education."
*Dr. Harrington J. Colby, a senior practitioner at the Dunhill Sanatorium, he is stated to be extremely well-regarded in his field.

### Mythos Connections
"Something in the Moonlight" is littered with references to the greater Cthulhu Mythos. Below are listed some examples. 
*The occult tome the Necronomicon makes an appearance in the story, as does the Cultes des Goules, the Book of Eibon and the Unaussprechlichen Kulten.
*Several locations relevant to the Mythos are discussed, including Sarnath, Mnar, Ib, Carcosa, Aldebaran, Fomalhaut and Mars.
*Although only one entity actually makes an appearance (this being presumably either a Thuum'ha or, more likely, Mnomquah) many others are made reference to in the text, including Bokrug, Cthugha, the Fire Vampires, Yhtill, Gla'aki, Azathoth, Aphoom-Zhah, Vulthoom and Tsathoggua.
*A handful of human characters are alluded to, such as Abdul Alhazred, Ludvig Prinn and Friedrich von Junzt.
*The Silver Key is also mentioned, as part of a ritual with which to communicate with otherworldly entities.
*The Zoan Chant is mentioned by Horby as a means to protect himself from the Great Old Ones.

### Publication History   
*Weird Tales #2 (1980)
*The Xothic Legend Cycle: The Complete Mythos Fiction of Lin Carter (1997)
*The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (2012)

fullContent:
"Something in Wood" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by August Derleth, originally published in the March 1948 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
Jason Wecter is an art critic/collector of weird and macabre artwork who lives in Boston. To balance his collection, he wishes to obtain something made of wood that would be evocative of the same exotic imagery of Clark Ashton Smith's stone sculptures that he already owns. A friend of Wecter, named Pinckney, locates a wooden bas-relief of an octopoid creature at a second-hand shop in Portland, Maine, and purchases it as a gift, which Wecter gratefully appreciates.

Pinckney is unable to identify the wood that the sculpture is made of, but notes that it's dark and surprisingly heavy. Neither can he identify the language of the inscription written on the base, which says: "Ph'nglui mglw'nafh Cthulhu R'lyeh wgah'nagl fhtagn". Wecter is fascinated by the incredible age of the relic and how closely it resembles some of the stone sculptures by Smith, wondering how an ancient civilization and a modern artist could have independently come up with something so similar.

For the next week, Pinckney notices an inexplicable change in Wecter's art reviews, which now unleash harsh criticism on artists that he had formerly viewed favourably, while celebrating others that he previously hated. The sole criterion for Wecter's judgment of art now seems to be how similar or dissimilar it is to ancient and occult sources. He chastises a sculptor for failing to follow "the cult-art of Ahapi or Armnoida", and applauds a musician whose work calls to mind "the music of the Great Old Ones".

When Pinckney questions Wecter about this, the latter tells him that he has no memory of writing these reviews, and is unfamiliar with the cultures or creatures mentioned in them, although he's convinced that they do exist. Since Pinckney brought him the sculpture, Wecter has been plagued with strange dreams that reveal new information to him, including the name of the creature depicted in the bas-relief: a shapeshifting monster called Cthulhu, who dwells in a sunken city named R'lyeh, at the depths of the Atlantic Ocean [not the Pacific, as in most depictions]. He is also aware that the sculpture was carved by ancient cultists in Ponape, and acts as a "point of contact" to another dimension through which Cthulhu can reach out to him, both mentally and physically.

As proof of what he is saying, Wecter points out to Pinckney that the tentacles of the sculpture appear to have moved, but Pinckney can't tell whether they have or not. Wecter claims that he went as far as to see Cthulhu materialize in his own room for the briefest of moments, before retreating and turning back into the sculpture, to which Pinckney reacts with skepticism.

"Son of Azathoth" is a horror comedy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It is the sixth and final installment of Peter Cannon's serialised novella Forever Azathoth, which serves as a humourous sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep". The series was published in Cannon's collections Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (1999) and Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches (2011).

### Synopsis
(Continued from "Bride of Azathoth"...)

The final part is narrated by Vartan Bagdasarian, Jr., who is just as passionate about the works of Edward Derby and Robert Blake as his father. His mother, in fact, is Blake's niece, Belinda Bagdasarian, née Blake. Like his father before him, Vartan Jr. enrolls at Miskatonic University with the express purpose of becoming the world's leading authority on Derby. There he befriends another enthusiast, young George Holden, whose great-aunt was the guardian of Derby's wife, Asenath Waite, during her high school years. From George, Vartan Jr. learns that Azathoth House, the publishing company where his father once worked, hasn't published any new material from Derby. Instead, the company has shifted its focus towards publishing mysteries and Derby-inspired fantasies by an author named Ephraim Waite. Nevertheless, the two boys attend an event at a local bookshop to honour the 30th anniversary of Azathoth House. They are happy to meet the company's owners, Jake and Wendy Derby, the former a distant cousin of Edward Derby.

When Vartan Jr. accidentally spills root beer over a copy of the latest Ephraim Waite book, Jake Derby forces him to buy it, while at the same time offering to sign it for him as publisher. His signature is eerily similar to that of the author. Later, Jake seethes with rage when the bookshop owner produces an unexpurgated Latin edition of the Necronomicon by a rival publisher named Bonanza Books. Jake insists that the Latin edition is dangerous, and that the expurgated Azathoth House version in English is far more user-friendly and safer. So offended is he by the man's ownership of the Latin book that he "solves" the issue by buying it from him. Meanwhile, Jake's wife Wendy is more agreeable and invites Vartan Jr. and George for tea, during which she politely listens to their ideas for future Derby projects.

After Jake turns down their idea to publish a collection of Derby's amateur journalism ventures, the boys decide to pursue the project themselves, using the university's Xerox machine. While looking for potential buyers, they visit Wendy again and offer her a copy while asking if they might be able to borrow Azathoth House's mailing list, or run an ad in their next catalogue. Sona-Nyl, also known as the Land of Fancy, is a coastal region in the Dreamlands of Earth. The dreamer Basil Elton lived there for a time before embarking on his doomed sea voyage aboard the White Ship in search of the fabled land of Cathuria. The harbor of Sona-Nyl is guarded by twin headlands of crystal that rise from the sea and meet in a resplendent arch. (: "The White Ship") 

### Description
According to Elton's description, "in the Land of Sona-Nyl there is neither time nor space, neither suffering nor death, and there I dwelt for many aeons. Green are the groves and pastures, bright and fragrant the flowers, blue and musical the streams, clear and cool the fountains, and stately and gorgeous the temples, castles, and cities of Sona-Nyl. Of that land there is no bound, for beyond each vista of beauty rises another more beautiful. Over the countryside and amidst the splendour of cities rove at will the happy folk, of whom all are gifted with unmarred grace and unalloyed happiness." (: "The White Ship") 

Elton continues, "for the aeons that I dwelt there I wandered blissfully through gardens where quaint pagodas peep from pleasing clumps of bushes, and where the white walks are bordered with delicate blossoms. I climbed gentle hills from whose summits I could see entrancing panoramas of loveliness, with steepled towns nestling in verdant valleys, and with the golden domes of gigantic cities glittering on the infinitely distant horizon. And I viewed by moonlight the sparkling sea, the crystal headlands, and the placid harbour wherein lay anchored the White Ship." (: "The White Ship")

### Fauna
In Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, the brightly-coloured creatures known as Butterfly-Dragons are stated to be found almost exclusively in Sona-Nyl .

"Song of Summoning" is a short horror story by Brian Willis which is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg in October 2013.

### Synopsis
The story is told for the most part through a series of journal entries made by composer Edward Raphael Holt, with a framing piece written by a historical biographer who is attempting to document Holt's life.

At the dawn of the 19th century, composer Edward Raphael Holt retreats to Brynteg, a village in rural Wales, in an attempt to lift his spirits and recapture his passion for music. There, while wandering the countryside he happens upon an ancient-looking flute which immediately ignites in him a strange passion, but brings with it darkest dreams accompanied by "angelic" music.

Over the following few weeks, his mental state devolves steadily as the dreams and his obsession with the music increases. He comes to the realisation that he has been somehow tricked by whatever is sending him the music, and that it is not in fact angelic, but demonic. As his psyche crumbles, he is taken into custody by the authorities as a violent psychopath and incarcerated in a London asylum.

### Mythos Connections
In the introductory section, the biographer states that Holt's surviving family donated his papers to Miskatonic University after relocating to Massachusetts, USA.

### Trivia
* At one point in the narrative, Holt notes that he believes there to be entities plotting against him "in the timeless spaces of the world, half-corporeal things, denied the rapturous transfiguration of the Winged Ones, shambling through dreams and shadows to work their influence upon mortal men." Whether these Winged Ones are any relation to the various entities described as such in the Cthulhu Mythos is unclear, although it would seem unlikely; the context suggests that Holt believes these to be more divine in nature.

fullContent:
Sonia Haft Greene Lovecraft Davis was a one-time pulp fiction writer and amateur publisher, a single mother, business woman and successful milliner who bankrolled several fanzines in the early twentieth century. She is best known for her two-year marriage to American weird fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. She was a president of the United Amateur Press Association.

### Biography
Some of Greene's biographical details are unclear – she was born as either Sonia Haft Shafirkin or as Sonia Shaferkin Haft in either Ichnia, Ukraine, Russian Empire or Konotop, Chernigov Province to Simyon and Racille (Haft) Shafirkin. It is known that she did come from a Jewish family. Her father apparently died when she was a child, and her mother emigrated to the United States, leaving Sonia and her brother in Liverpool at the Baron Maurice de Hirsch School. Sonia joined her mother in America in 1892, after her mother remarried to a shopkeeper named Samuel Morris.

At the age of sixteen, on 24 December 1899, Sonia married Samuel Greene, a Russian whose name may have originally been Samuel Seckendorff, who was ten years her senior. The following year she gave birth to a son, who died at three months of age. Her daughter, Florence Carol (later Carol Weld) was born on 19 March 1902. According to Lovecraft's correspondent Alfred Galpin Samuel Greene was "a man of brutal character". The marriage was turbulent, and Samuel Greene died in 1916, apparently by his own hand.

Greene was independently middle class, unusual for women of that time. She worked as a milliner at a department store and traveled frequently for her job. Her salary allowed her to rent a nice house for herself and her daughter in the then-fancy area of Brooklyn known as Flatbush. It also allowed her to donate money to several amateur press publications, as well as to travel to amateur press conventions.

Her daughter Florence became a successful journalist under the name of Carol Weld. The two women had a tense relationship, and stopped speaking to each other. Greene does not mention her daughter in her volume The Private Life of H. P. Lovecraft, an autobiographical work which details only the period of her relationship and marriage with Lovecraft.

### Relationship with H. P. Lovecraft
In 1921, a few weeks after his mother's death, she met Howard P. Lovecraft at an amateur press convention in Boston, having been introduced to the world of amateur journalism by Lovecraft's colleague James Ferdinand Morton, Jr. in 1917. In the following October she issued The Rainbow, a fanzine described by Rheinhart Kleiner as "a large and handsome affair, illustrated with half-tone reproductions of photographs of well-known amateurs of the day and containing excellent contributions by many of them." Lovecraft reviewed Greene's magazine at some length in The National Amateur (March 1922). A facsimile edition of the magazine was issued by Necronomicon Press in 1977.

Greene's best-known story is "The Horror at Martin's Beach

"Sorrow Road" is a short story by American author Tim Waggoner.

### Synopsis
Stuck on a highway as the Old Ones begin their return, a group of people witness the changes being wrought on the planet- and themselves. One woman, desperate to save her sick child, makes a deal with the nearest being: make the boy better, and she will serve it willingly. However, the woman doesn’t know what manner of being she is attempting to bargain with, and her choice of words results in a horrific transformation …

### Characters
*Kris, a devoted mother.
*Danny, Kris's son, victim of a malignant tumour.
*Sheri, Kris and Danny's neighbour.

### Publication History
"Sorrow Road" was published in the thematic anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

Sothoth is a fictional deity from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was first mentioned in Fred Pelton's occult text "The Sussex Manuscript". It is best known for being the father of Ulthar.

### Description
Sothoth is one of the Outer Gods who serves Azathoth. It is said to be the creator and master of the Great Old Ones, as well as being the one who created Yog-Sothoth; however, Sothoth might have been the result of faulty translation, suggesting that the deity may not actually exist. (: "The Sussex Manuscript" & The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana)

### In Other Media
*D.Y.N. Freaks: In DYN Memo, a list of supplementary materials for the manga written by Jin Haganeya, Sothoth was described to be the same entity as Yog-Sothoth; however, this is in contrast to Pelton's original depiction, where Sothoth was meant to be a different entity.

The Soul Worms are an extra-dimensional race from the fictional universe of the Rifts pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium.

### Background
The Soul Worms are a malevolent race of alien intelligences, a race of manipulators and enslavers. Larva-like beings with a great cyclopean eye surrounded by a dozen tentacles. Ranging in size from 25-30 ft in length and 5-7 ft in height. They have an average lifespan in the 1000s of years. 

It's a race with superhuman strength which is able to regenerate, have psionic abilities, and are able to use magic. Resilient enough to survive a 3.8 Megaton nuke though with grievous wounds. Soul Worms drain the life force and memories of their victims, though they must focus on their victim when doing so. Most of them become addicted to this activity, doing it at least once a week.

They used to serve a far more powerful alien intelligence which reigned over 100s of worlds, millennia ago.  Until one day it mysteriously disappeared, leaving its servants vulnerable to its many enemies which included the Splugorth. Their invasions combined with the slave uprisings resulted in 9/10ths of the Soul Worms perishing, the rest scattering across the Megaverse.

A few thousand Soul Worms have survivved. Some of them are now wanderers. Others have established dimensional kingdoms. Some of them lead dimensional raiders. Others are now in servicee to demon lords or evil gods. On the post-apocalyptic Earth which emerged after the cataclysmic return of magic, a Soul Worm has established himself. Inix who relocated his trans-dimensional city of Cibola to South America. A city of a million with over 40 permanent portals to other dimensions.

South Carolina is a state in the United States of America located on the eastern (Atlantic) coast of the country. One of the original Thirteen Colonies, it was notably the first region of what is now the United States to host a European settlement, although the pioneering colony was quickly abandoned.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
South Carolina's appearance in the fiction of H. P. Lovecraft is limited to a passing reference in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key," a story he co-wrote with E. Hoffman Price, when one character remarks of Harley Warren that he was a "South Carolina mystic whose studies in the primal Naacal language of the Himalayan priests had led to such outrageous conclusions."

### In the Real World
Lovecraft visited South Carolina at least twice, in 1930 and 1931, where he was apparently impressed with the level of preservation of the state. His observations were recorded in three essays, "Account of a Visit to Charleston, S.C." (written 28 April to 9 May 1930), "An Account of Charleston, in His Majty's Province of South-Carolina" (17 July 1930; 1995), and "Charleston" (January 1936).

The Space Eaters are entities created by the late American author Frank Belknap Long for his short story "The Space-Eaters", and were subsequently expanded upon by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. 

### Description
The Space Eaters appear as massive luminous beings that can create temporary limbs. Their appearance is heralded by an area becoming misty and wet. 

As the name suggests, they have the ability to "eat through space", which they use to travel between planets. 

The Space Eaters can bore holes into the skulls of human victims to feed on the victims' brains. Those who find themselves in the presence of these beings must not allow them to establish a mental link. Since the real form of the Space Eaters isn't recognizable by human senses, whenever they seem to assume a definitive shape, it is a sign that they're already influencing the observer's mind.

They can be repelled by the sign of the cross.

The space-devils are a fictional alien species mentioned by H. P. Lovecraft in the novella The Mound.

### Description
The K'n-yanians, who are worshipers of Tulu and Yig, claim that the space-devils are "hostile alike to men and to men's gods", and blame them for the great sinking that "submerged the gods themselves, including great Tulu, who still lay prisoned and dreaming in the watery vaults of the half-cosmic city Relex".

At some point much later in time, the space-devils returned to Earth and caused most of the world's landmasses to sink, with the only human survivors being the space-devils' own agents. This led the K'n-yanians to isolate themselves and cut off all traffic with the surface, as they believed all surviving humans were their enemies. (: The Mound)

### Behind the Mythos
Lovecraft's space-devils are similar to the Elder Gods, as portrayed by August Derleth and others. Like the space-devils, the Elder Gods are enemies of the Great Old Ones, deemed responsible for imprisoning Cthulhu in sunken R'lyeh.

Spawn of Azathoth: Herald of the End of Time is a campaign supplement for the Mythos roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu.

### Overview
A complete campaign in seven scenarios, Spawn of Azathoth takes a group of Investigators to locations across the globe and beyond on a quest to prevent the end of the world. It is unusual in that the first and last scenario are the only ones which need played in those slots; the order of the other scenarios is dependant on which order the Investigators uncover, and choose to follow, a series of clues.

The first edition of Spawn of Azathoth was written by Keith Herber and released in 1986 as a boxed set containing three booklets, the first two describing the scenarios and the third dedicated to player handouts; cover art was by Susan Sedona Boulet. The second edition came as a 200-page softcover book with new artwork and a cover provided by Tom Sullivan.

### Scenarios
*"Providence, Rhode Island"
*"Garrison, Montana"
*"St. Augustine, Florida"
*"The Andaman Islands"
*"Ulthar and Beyond"
*"The Eternal Quest"
*"The Tibetan Interior"

### Publication History
The first edition of Spawn of Azathoth was published in 1996 and is no longer available. The second edition was released in 2005; although the physical copy is no longer in print, it is available as a digital PDF download from Chaosium's website.

"Spawn of Dagon", sometimes issued as "The Spawn of Dagon", is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and Lovecraft contemporary Henry Kuttner. It is part of his Elak series about an Atlantean criminal.

### Synopsis
Elak the swordsman is made an offer by a mysterious stranger named Gesti: kill the wizard Zend, the power behind the Atlantean throne, and be rewarded with a princely sum of gold. He quickly accepts.

Close to completing his mission, Elak is interrupted by the arrival of Gesti and his cult, in actuality a race of creatures known as the Spawn of Dagon who wish to overthrow Zend and use his power to sink Atlantis beneath the waves. Fortunately, the timely intervention of Lycon allows Zend to regroup and direct his magic against the usurpers, saving the continent.

At the story's conclusion, Elak and Lycon escape, along with a comely wench whom Zend had intended to force into a life of servitude.

### Characters

*Elak, an Atlantean criminal and swordsman.
*Lycon, Elak's partner in crime.
*Zend, the Wizard of Atlantis, an amoral sorcerer who nevertheless is the only thing to stand between Atlantis and the Spawn of Dagon.
*Gesti, a Spawn of Dagon intent on the destruction of all human life on Earth.

### Publication History
"Spawn of Dagon" was first published in Weird Tales magazine in July 1938. It has since been reprinted many times in both periodicals and anthologies.

fullContent:
The Spawn of Dagon, also referred to as the Children of Dagon, are an ancient species which first featured in Henry Kuttner's short story of the same name.

### Description
Worshipers of the Great Old One Dagon, Kuttner described the Spawn thus:



They were said to have control over earthquakes, but proved to be vulnerable to the light emitted by the wizard Zend's red sphere which drew power from the stars, their bodies dissolving into puddles of slime upon exposure.

### History
Dwelling upon the Earth long before the rise of man, the Spawn of Dagon existed when the planet was covered by nothing but ocean. Jealous of the races which followed them, viewing them as usurpers, they spent the aeons working to ensure that no civilisation stood above the waves. Many of them were killed by Zend and his red sphere during a battle on the long-lost continent of Atlantis, although it is unknown if they were wiped out in their entirety.

### Trivia

*Although Kuttner refers to the Spawn as "a race which had not sprung from human or even earthly loins", there is no evidence that Dagon is an extraterrestrial creature.

Spawn of Madness is an expansion pack for Fantasy Flight Games' Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

### Overview
The first Asylum Pack in the Forgotten Lore Cycle series of expansions, Spawn of Madness is divided into the standard format of three duplicate sets of 20 unique cards for a total of 60, with the cards contained divided between the existing factions. First released in 2010, it was discontinued in 2015 with the demise of Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

 The Spawn of Nyogtha are a fictional race created in 1995 by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Background
The Spawn of Nyogtha are produced by the blasphemous unions between ghouls, humans, and Nyogtha. Within three-to-six decades, they degenerate into shapeless abominations. During the first decades they easily pass for a human. Running through their bodies is not blood but a viscous black ichor. They are charismatic, strong, and tough creatures whom serve Nyogtha and seduce others into its cult.

Once degeneration begins, within a few months they complete their metamorphosis. Which starts with hideous black splotches appearing on the flesh which quickly spread, while the spawn becomes ravenous. Its final form is one of squirming and writhing slimy flesh, skeletal hands with razor-sharp talons, hideously distorted features on a skeletal face with lupine fangs and bulging eyes, and bloated corpulent torso and limbs.

The Spawn of Othuyeg are creatures created by Crispin Burnham for his short story "The Seven Cities of Gold" and later used by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. 

### Description
The Spawn of Othuyeg appear as miniature versions of their creator Othuyeg, who they live with in the Seven Cities of Gold. They are most commonly seen flooding out of the ground after earthquakes.

The Spawn of the Green Abyss are a fictional species created by C. Hall Thompson for his eponymous short story. They were later incorperated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Ye Booke of Monstres)

### Background
The Spawn of the Green Abyss are a highly evolved and intelligent race which lives in the oceans and seas of Earth. Living in societies ruled by their queen, Zoth Syra. They appear as bluish slime whose various features are shifting. Limbs and sensory organs are created as needed. The songs of the spawn can influence those whom hear it. Though normal weapons cannot hurt them, they can be harmed by fire, chemicals, electricity, magical spells, and enchanted weapons.

The Spawn of the Green Abyss herald from outer space and came to this planet long ago to inhabit oceans and watery places. While similar to the Shoggoths, in some respects, the spawn are utterly alien and possess great intelligence, sometimes traveling in groups for undecipherable reasons. They tend to remain in deep waters, occasionally swimming to the surface to hold what appear to be strange rituals when certain cosmic alignments take place. Some fishermen—who claimed to have been taken down into the depths by the spawn—speak of the monsters dwelling in bizarre aquatic societies and that they are ruled by beings named Zoth Syra and Yoth Kala. Some have alleged the spawn are actually part of Deep One society and can be found deep within that race’s underwater cities.

The spawn appears as a bluish-black slime with various and shifting features, able to create limbs and sensory organs as needed. They are capable of speech, including human tongue, and use a form of “singing” that, akin to old sea tales of mermaid and siren song, is able to command the will of weak-willed folk.

fullContent:
"Spawn of the Green Abyss" is a short story by C. Hall Thompson, published in Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
This short story is similar to the Innsmouth leitmotif of sea dwelling monsters intertwining with humanity. 

A doctor taking restive time in a remote Mid-Atlantic town falls in love with the daughter of a cursed former sailor. As their relationship develops, he discovers that she is actually only part human, her father having been bewitched and seduced by an abomination from beneath the waves. As the girl begins to hear the calling of her blood, she begs her new husband to kill her rather than let her be drawn into the horrors thrust upon her by her inheritance. 

### Setting
The story is set in Kalesmouth, an "antiquated village sprawled on a forlorn peninsula off New Jersey’s Northeastern coast." It is described as  little more than a sprinkling of cottages with a single general-store and a population in the low fifties. The small white houses are scattered along a narrow finger of sand-and-rock land that juts defiantly eastward into the sea. There is water on three sides and a single highway to the mainland. Its most prominent landmark is an ancient mansion called Heath House, a "misty hulk" with "straggling, mossy embattlements." Behind it is a cove in which  stood four weirdly hewn pillars, placed so that each made the corner of a crude square; in the moonglow they had the aspect of sinister mediaeval altars of sacrifice, reared to noxious, unnameable gods. 

### Characters
*Dr. James Arkwright, a young brain surgeon.
*Cassandra Arkwright, née Heath, Lazarus' daughter, and the product of his unholy coupling. She is described as "slim and well-made; ebony hair flowing to her shoulders gave one a feeling of rich warmth. It matched the steady blackness of extraordinary eyes that protruded ever so slightly. Her skin was deeply tanned." 
*Lazarus Heath, a former sailor manipulated into breeding with a creature from the deep. His "skin, taut and dry, was the color of aged jade, covered with minute, glistening scales.... Lazarus Heath’s pale eyes bulged horribly," and he has "two faint bluish streaks, about four inches in length, running along each side of the scaly neck, just below the jawline."
*Dr. Henry Joyce Ambler, a provincial GP; a "florid, white-haired individual, full of shop-talk."
*Eb Linder, the "taciturn, wind-dried proprietor of the general-store."
*Solly-Jo, a "slow-witted, distorted brute, with matted blond-gray hair"; he is homeless and sleeps on Kalesmouth's beach.

### Publication History
"Spawn of the Green Abyss" was first published in the November 1946 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reprinted several times, including in Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos (Fedogan & Bremer, 1992) and A Mountain Walked (Centipede Press, 2014), and has also been translated into German.

### Connection to the Mythos
*The Spawn of the Green Abyss were added to the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium.

"Spawn of the Maelstrom" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by August Derleth and Mark Schorer. It was originally published in the September 1939 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
A Londoner named Bassett meets with his friend, Jason Warwick, who is obsessed with mysteries. Warwick tells him that he's going to the Lofoten Islands, Norway, to investigate a local legend about the uninhabited island of Vömma, and asks Bassett to notify their common friend Sir John Hardie. According to the legend, Vömma Island is inhabited by an immortal being spawned from a nearby maelstrom. Some say the being is a man, while others say it's an animal.

When Warwick returns, Bassett notices several differences in his voice, mannerisms and movements. His skin is cold to the touch, and he seems to have trouble recognizing people and remembering things. One night, when Bassett is visiting Hardie, they witness the latter's watchman yelling about a burglar and being attacked by a man they both recognize as Warwick, who steals several letters and escapes. The watchman, Sullatt, is now dead, and his body is inexplicably cold and rigid. Strangely, the letters that Warwick has stolen are his own, written to Hardie during Warwick's trip to Norway. Hardie believes that he himself was the intended victim, and that Warwick mistook Sullatt for him in the dark, as they are both of the same height and built.

Hardie shows Bassett the one letter that Warwick has failed to steal, as Hardie had kept it in his pocket. The letter, written by Warwick during his trip to Vömma, was found inside a bottle cast at the sea. It reveals that a Norwegian priest had pleaded Warwick not to go to Vömma, and given him a five-pointed star-stone as an amulet, which Warwick left in the boarding house, as he thought he wouldn't need it. According to the priest, the entity that inhabits Vömma is an immortal shapeshifter, which can assume the form of any man or animal, and feeds on the life force of humans, leaving its victims' bodies cold and rigid. Ever since it came out of the maelstrom, the monster has been confined to the island as its prison. However, by consuming the life of three humans, it would become strong enough to leave the island and roam through the world, consuming more and more people. Before Warwick, there had been two historical cases of men who went to Vömma and whose bodies were found cold and rigid. Once alone in the island, Warwick realized that he was being stalked by the shapeshifter, and about to become its third victim. He finished the message by asking whoever finds it to send both the letter and the star-stone he left in his boarding house room to Hardie. The star-stone, Warwick reveals, is an amulet forged by the Elder Gods, and has the power to defeat the deathless shapeshifter by banishing it back to "the ever damned depths from which he first came upon earth".

The Spawn of the Maelstrom is a fictional monster created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer for their short story "Spawn of the Maelstrom".

### Description
The Spawn of the Maelstrom is a shapeshifting immortal creature that gains strength by absorbing the life of humans. Its victims' bodies are always found cold and rigid, even when examined only a few seconds after death. As a shapeshifter, it can assume the form of any animal, as well as mimic the appearance of an individual human. However, the imitation is not perfect: the creature's skin remains abnormally cold to the touch, and even though its telepathy allows it to absorb some knowledge from the person it's mimicking, it isn't enough to fool a close acquaintance, who will readily notice some gaps in knowledge, as well as differences in the way the impersonator acts and moves around.

The origin of this creature is unknown, whether it was born in the ocean depths or came from another world. It emerged from a maelstrom near the uninhabited island of Vömma, which is part of the Norwegian Lofoten Islands. There it remained imprisoned for centuries. Only by consuming the life force of three humans would the monster become strong enough to escape its confinement and leave the island.

The only known way to destroy the Spawn of the Maelstrom is with one of the five-pointed star-stones carved by the Elder Gods. Contact with the star-stone will cause the shapeshifter's body to disintegrate, leaving only a few inhuman bone fragments. As a truly deathless entity, the destruction of its body doesn't kill it, but merely sends it back to the oceanic abysses it came from originally. (: "Spawn of the Maelstrom")

Spawn of the Winds, published in 1978, is the fourth novel in the Titus Crow series by Brian Lumley. Notably, Titus Crow is entirely absent from the story.

### Overview

### Plot Summary
Outraged by the killing of his brother by Ithaqua, psychic Texan Hank Silberhutte gathers a team together to try and find a way to permanently defeat or destroy the Wind Walker. Whilst en route in an aircraft, Hank and his team are swept to a world ruled by Ithaqua, and a planetary romance-style adventure unfolds.

Absent Titus Crow and friends, the action is of the two-fisted pulp variety, complete with an alien princess as ally.

### Publication History
Spawn of the Winds was originally published in paperback in July 1978 by Jove/HBJ (with cover art by Boris Vallejo). It was first published in hardcover by W. Paul Ganley in 1995. It was included in Volume 2 of an omnibus edition in 1997 by Tor and HarperCollins (UK).

The novel has been translated into French, Italian, and Japanese.

The Spawn of Yog-Sothoth are creatures derived from the Dunwich Horror by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Background
The Spawn of Yog-Sothoth are thoughtless squirming masses of flesh, tentacles, eyes, and tails, along with extra maws in places where joints or vertebrae would be expected. They are amorphous and can fit through most gaps, pulling themselves through with tentacles. 

They notably emanate an unpleasant scent, typical among old ones and relations. In addition, they possess a weak form of invisibility, allowing them to pass in the dark without drawing attention. They quickly grow to enormous size, and if they continue to feed, they will continue to grow but at a much slower rate. 

Despite this, their cognition never improves to be much more developed than that of a toddler. Due to this, they are not capable of complex decision making, more motivated by short term instincts than the  Child of Yog-Sothoth, a closely related species. 

They are capable of wielding magic, but rarely use it for more than fundamental rites. 

The ancient Spawn of Yog-Sothoth can be as large as buildings or small hills; however, they are generally dormant at this size to preserve energy. If killed, their flesh rapidly melts, and soon only a crusty stain remains. 

Creating a Spawn of Yog-Sothoth involves a blasphemous ritual in which a humanoid or animal is used as an incubator, a Child of Yog-Sothoth's seed combined with the blood of a member in a pact of Yog-Sothoth. The mother dies upon giving birth and usually gives birth to twins, a Spawn of Yog-Sothoth and a Child of Yog-Sothoth. If twins are not produced, the offspring are still birthed.

The Sphinx was an ancient entity known, among other places, in Egypt.

### Description 
The famous Great Sphinx of Giza was patterned after the true Sphinx, but the face was later replaced with the human one of the Pharoh Khephren. It seems that it was something close to life-size, for the real Sphinx's paws were the size of hippopotami. (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs")

The real Sphinx's paws were covered in yellow fur, and each toe was equipped with a retractable claw. Harry Houdini, who caught sight of the paw, but not the rest of the creature, mistook each of the five toes for a head, and the claws for rigid tentacles that extended forward to consume food. (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs")

The Sphinx-statues of Sarkomand resembled vast winged lions. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) However, the Great Sphinx of Giza has no wings.

### Nature
The Sphinx was kin to cats, such as the Cats of Ulthar, and they spoke her language, although the Sphinx was not as old as cat-kind. (: "The Cats of Ulthar")

The hybrid creatures which worshipped her were known as the Children of the Sphinx. (: Call of Cthulhu RPG)

The Sphinx encountered by Houdini has been identified as one of the Million Favoured Ones (: Ye Booke of Monstres II). The Great Sphinx of Giza is also associated with at least two avatars of Nyarlathotep: the Faceless God and the Beast, both of which have been sometimes represented as a faceless sphinx statue. (: "The Faceless God", : Call of Cthulhu - Day of the Beast)

### History
Sphinx statues adorned Sarkomand a million years before humanity was born. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath) However, it is unclear whether these were patterned after the true Sphinx or not.

The famous Great Sphinx of Giza was patterned after the true Sphinx. At some point, the Sphinx took up residence in a tomb deep beneath the Great Sphinx, where she was worshipped and fed by creatures resembling animal-human hybrids and the undead pharaohs Khephren and Nitocris.

In 1910, Harry Houdini glimpsed the creature while escaping from the tomb, having been kidnapped. (: "Imprisoned with the Pharaohs")

The Brotherhood of the Black Pharaoh also made use of the shallowest tunnels beneath the Great Sphinx. (: Call of Cthulhu - Masks of Nyarlathotep)

### Trivia
In real life, the Pharaoh Khephren (also transliterated Khafra, Khafre, Chephren etc) is credited by mainstream academia with constructing the Sphinx from scratch - although this attribution is quite speculative - rather than merely re-carving the face. There are indeed tales of tunnels beneath the Sphinx going back a long time. To date only one subterranean passage has been found, leading to or from a nearby ancient well and not containing anything very remarkable.

The Spiders of Leng, also known as the Leng Spiders, are sentient cannibalistic creatures in the Cthulhu Mythos, who first appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Description
Purple-colored arachnid creatures that appear somewhat similar to terrestrial spiders yet on a much larger scale, the smaller of the Spiders of Leng are the size of a Shetland pony; larger specimens would tower over an elephant. They possess a degree of intelligence far higher than that of regular animals, but are not above the cannibalisation of other Leng Spiders. Whilst they are capable of spinning webs to disable their victims, they also possess a venomous bite of great potency, and have the ability to climb sheer surfaces, much like their counterparts in the waking world. 

### History
Long ago, the Spiders controlled the entire Plateau of Leng in Earth's Dreamlands, until defeat after a long war with the Men of Leng forced them to abandon much of their homeland and retreat back to the southern mountains and vales of that strange land. There they dwell to this day, ready to prey on any creature foolish or unwary enough to stray into their territory.

Spot, also known as Thu Thu Hmong and who is later confirmed to be Cthulhu, is a character who appears in Arcana Studio's Howard Lovecraft series of children’s comics. He made his first appearance in the graphic novel Howard Lovecraft and the Frozen Kingdom.

### Description
When first encountered, Spot resembles common depictions of the Cthulhi: a large, humanoid being whose lower face is hidden by a mass of tentacles. Later, after his transformation, he takes on a more octopoid appearance, seemingly losing much of his body in the process.

### History
When young Howard Lovecraft accidentally used the Necronomicon to transport himself to the frozen kingdom of R'lyeh, he encountered the Deep One Thu Thu Hmong, who he saved from falling into a crevasse. In gratitude, the creature, who Howard calls Spot as he is unable to remember its full name, pledged itself to his service, and the two helped the citizens of R'lyeh to rid the land of its icy curse. However, the people had been lying to them, and were in fact cultists dedicated to awakening Great Cthulhu. As they conducted their ritual, Spot began to change, and was later revealed to have become Cthulhu.

Later, Spot accompanied young Howard on a series of adventures, travelling to such far-flung places as Antarctica and Yuggoth, and encountering a succession of Mythos luminaries including Dr. Herbert West and Azathoth.

"Squatter's Rights" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Josh Reynolds.

### Synopsis
When an amateur occultist buys the deeds to the houses of Lakeside Terrace but does not move in, he is attacked by the supernatural servants of Gla'aki. Surviving the attack, he enlists the aid of his friend, the serving Royal Occultist, who "persuades" the estate agent responsible for the sale to reverse the transaction and return the deeds. This causes the secretive Great Old One to lose interest in its murderous course.

### Characters
* Charles St. Cyprian, the Royal Occultist, a position first occupied by one John Dee.
* Philip Wendy-Smythe, an occultist with just enough knowledge to repeatedly get himself into trouble.
* Ebe Gallowglass, an enforcer in the employ of St. Cyprian.

### Publication History
"Squatter's Rights" was published in the Dark Regions Press thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki in 2017.

Squire Brewster is a fictional character from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Tomb". 

### Background
Brewster was a Boston man described by Jervas Dudley as rich and celebrated, and a maker of local history (though this is not elaborated upon). According to Jervas, the undertaker Goodman Simpson had robbed the recently dead body of the Squire, stealing various articles of clothing before burying him in 1711. Jervas acquired this information from spirits with whom he conversed during one of his nightly visits to a local cemetery. 

Jervas also stated that Squire Brewster had not been fully deceased at the time of his presumed death, for he had "turned twice" in his coffin on the day after burial. (: "The Tomb")

St. Dymphna's Orphanage: Azathoth's Children is an adventure for the 7th edition of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. Its setting is an orphanage in the 1920s and it features the confronting content of traumatized children making it unsuitable for some players. It is a third party publication released under the Miskatonic Repository imprint. It is available only as a digital download from DriveThruRPG. It is 27 pages long.

Written by Zachary Pagram, the adventure calls upon the players to take on the roles of orphan children who must solve mysteries after lights out in an oppressive orphanage in the 1920s, when orphans were, to put it mildly, treated more like prisoners in a medium security prison than children needing love and kindness.

St. John was a fictional character who appeared in H. P. Lovecraft's 1924 short horror story "The Hound". Whether St. John was his first or last name, or simply an affectation, is never revealed.

### History
St. John was a man with a twisted obsession for grave robbing, desiring nothing more than to steal perverse trophies from the dead. When he and his unnamed friend - who later told the tale of St. John's fate - heard the story of the resting place of a graverobber who had been dead for five hundred years, they knew that they had to have something of his for their collection.

Travelling to Holland on their depraved mission, St. John and his friend opened the man's grave and stole from him an amulet. Upon returning to England, a series of bizarre events and the sound of ghostly howls growing ever closer culminated in the bloody murder of St. John late one night by the amulet's owner. His last words as he lay dying were “The amulet - that damned thing - .”

### Trivia
*For the character of St. John, H. P. Lovecraft used the nickname he had given to one of his friends, a fellow named Rheinhart Kleiner.

Stanley Pickman is a fictional character created by Ian Davey for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "Black Letter Day". At the culminations of the events of "The Epiphany of Dissolution", he is revealed to be an avatar of Nyarlathotep.

### Description
At first appearing as an older man who claims a professorship in an unknown subject, after the fall of mankind and return of the Old Ones, Stanley Pickman looked considerably younger, as if the global catastrophe has somehow rejuvenated him. Later, in a confrontation with Glyph and Lucy, Pickman was obliterated when Nyarlathotep fully manifested and called forth his fellow Outer God Yog-Sothoth.

The Star Mother is a fictional entity created by Scott David Aniolowski for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

### Background
The Star Mother is one of the Other God's larvae, the size of an infant. Resembling a yellow-green stone whose shape is that of a huge-breasted faceless plump female figure with dozens of pencil-thin root-like strands. It lives in a sunken 18th century two-masted sailing ship. From the Star Mother countless small vines spread, as well as thin strands and larger tentacles.

Sprouting from the ship and within its hull are slimy sickly yellow-green plant-like growth as the entity's strands and tentacles have spread throughout the vessel. She can raise and sink the ship at will, animate the corpses of its crew, attack at long distances with her roots, and generate fog banks. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

The Star Vampires are a fictional extraterrestrial species in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by Robert Bloch for his short story "The Shambler from the Stars", and were later incorperated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Description
Star Vampires are creatures from outer space that are normally invisible. They are voracious blood suckers, becoming visible once their bodies are full of the victim's blood, a vivid red colour. Its form is like that of a jellyfish with neither a head or any visible facial features apart from its huge maw. Their bodies have multiple muscular tentacles, each strong enough to crush a man to death and on the tips are the suckers with which it drains the blood of its victims. From the star vampires comes nonstop eerie horrifying laughter.

It's possible that the Star Vampires might be in some way related to Tsathoggua, since the infamous grimoire De Vermis Mysteriis contains a spell to summon them which mentions "bufoniformis Sadoquae" (i.e. toad-like Tsathoggua). The book's author, Ludvig Prinn, was known to keep a number of Star Vampires as his loyal servants. (: "The Shambler from the Stars")

### In Other Media
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, the Star Vampires are invisible disc-shaped weapons of Tiberius' Deus Machina, Belzebuth. They are capable of draining the magical power along with the magic circuits of their enemies once attached. These weapons are summoned by the incantation "Tibi, Magnum Innominandum, signa stellarum nigrarum et bufaniformis Sadoquae sigillum……!" (English translation: "To thee, the great Not-to-Be-Named, the signs of the black stars, and the seal of the toad-shaped Tsathoggua……!").
*The Star Vampires appear in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X, under the name "Dusk-Awaiting Star, Shambler".
*The Star Vampire (also known as the Shambler) appears in the action puzzle video game Scribblenauts.

### Gallery

The Star-Warriors of Orion are a fictional species created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer for their short story "The Lair of the Star-Spawn".

### Description
The Star-Warriors are giant luminous beings which dwell among the stars of the Orion Belt and serve the Elder Gods. They have six flailing appendages described as "similar to arms, yet not arms", and ride through the sky mounted on limbless animals. The tube-like weapons they carry with them, supplied by their masters, fire destructive beams of energy that can harm even the Great Old Ones. (: "The Lair of the Star-Spawn")

### In Other Media
*The Star-Warriors appear in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
*The Star-Warriors appear in the Demonbane Mythos by Nitroplus, as sentient weapons created by the Elder Gods.
*The Ultra Warriors from the Ultra Series strongly resemble the description of the Star-Warriors, including the ability to shoot energy beams, being adept at fighting monstrous creatures, and their home planet being located in Nebula M78, a reflection nebula in the constellation of Orion. Although this was most likely coincidental, the Ultra Series has directly referenced the Cthulhu Mythos many times over the years, most prominently in Ultraman Tiga.

Starkesboro is a fictional town in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 1972 in issue #4 of the 1st volume of the Marvel Premiere comic series. It's a pastiche of the Innsmouth of canon.

### Background
15,000 years ago, the body and soul of Slorioth, one of the Old Ones, were bound to the land by a cabal of ancient sorcerers. Land which millennia later would be known as New England. At some point in time, N'Gabthoth (another Old One), established himself in a nearby cavern in the ocean, where he slept.

Centuries ago, in what would become the state of Maine, a village was founded by fisherfolk. Over time the village would become the town of Starkesboro. Later, a serpent-twined inverted cross was found floating in the sea. It was brought into town, which resulted in Sligguth's power infiltrating the population. Sligguth an agent of Shuma-Gorath, the ruler of the Old Ones, permitted one of its residents (Ebora) to remain completely human, and mutated the rest into semi-reptilian subhumans. Ebora, a magic user, became his high priestess. They desecrated the local church and performed various rituals to Sligguth, including human sacrifice.

Sligguth took up residence below the church in a cavern, and would come up to the surface to get his human sacrifice. It was a town with a dark magical aura which Dr. Strange was barely able to overcome while in astral form. Those who left were pulled back to the town by Sligguth's influence and the chants of its locals awakened their inner Serpent-Men. Upon the defeat of Sligguth and later N'Gabthoth whom they worshipped by Dr. Strange, they fled into the dark hills.

Two decades later, its new inhabitants were turned into werewolves by the criminal scientist Nightshade (whom was allied with the cult leader Dredmund Druid). They were stopped by Captain America and his allies, who forced them to cure the residents. A few years later, the superhero and ex-Avenger Doctor Druid was manipulated and corrupted by Slorioth into releasing him from his imprisonment. Slorioth burst from the land and battled both the Defenders and Secret Defenders whom were failing in their attempt to contain him much less defeat him. The godlike trio, the Vishanti, intervened and summoned the multiversal entity, Living Tribunal, who judged Slorioth a threat to the reality, and banished him.

shortDefinition: Starro the Conqueror is a Lovecraftian extraterrestrial entity from the fictional universe of DC by DC Comics.  ### Background Starro was from an alien race known the "Star Conquerors". He resembles a giant one-eyed starfish and enslaves entire plane...
fullContent:
Starro the Conqueror is a Lovecraftian extraterrestrial entity from the fictional universe of DC by DC Comics.

### Background
Starro was from an alien race known the "Star Conquerors". He resembles a giant one-eyed starfish and enslaves entire planets by sending millions of smaller Starro drones to attach to his victims' faces, mind-controlling them in the process. Starro attempted to conquer Earth several times, although he was defeated by the Justice League every time, usually by exploiting his weaknesses to extreme cold and garden lime. 

In the Post Infinite Crisis era, Starro's backstory was greatly expanded upon. Originally an alien boy named Cobi, he and his people encountered the Starro Motherstar when it arrived to enslave their planet Hatorei and give birth to a new queen. However, due to a telepathic link shared by all the inhabitants, the Starro drones' mind-controlled victims were still conscious and their collective outrage was sent to Cobi's brother Andrez. This caused their control over Andrez to be weakened long enough for him to attempt to destroy the queen before she can be born. Unfortunately, the queen defended herself by using Cobi to decapitate Andrez with an axe. Enraged by the death of his brother, the collective anger of the people was then sent to Cobi and he broke free from his Starro drone's control, ripping it off his face. Cobi then tried to kill the queen himself, causing her to fuse with him and giving him the power to control all Starros. Cobi, now renamed Starro the Conqueror, used his new powers to enslave all intelligent life he encounters which made him grow much stronger over time. During his conquests, Starro gained control over a grand total of nine galaxies.

### Mythos Connections
The character was created by Weird Tales contributor Gardner Fox as a homage to the Cthulhu Mythos. Starro's first appearance in The Brave and the Bold #28 even has a direct reference to H. P. Lovecraft's hometown.

fullContent:
"Starry Wisdom" is a short Cthulhu Mythos/Thomas Carnacki crossover story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
An expedition returning from the Antarctic inadvertently brings with it an active Shoggoth. When a deranged cult get their hands on a sample, they attempt to grow it into a full-fledged specimen, but the creature breaks loose and feeds upon the entire group, killing them all. Fortunately, occultist Thomas Carnacki is on hand. He successfully contains the beast, before it, and all evidence of it, are destroyed by Winston Churchill and his secretive team.

### Characters
*Thomas Carnacki, a learned man with a specialism in matters of the occult.
*Winston Churchill, a senior civil servant devoted to defending the shores of Great Britain.
*Richard Malcolm, one of the three members of the Antarctic expedition who ascended Mount Erebus and encountered the Shoggoth.
*Gerald Watkins, a senior cultist.
*Mr. Fitzwilliams, another cultist.
*Professor Andrew Kennedy, a scholar with the Royal Geographical Society.

### Publication History
"Starry Wisdom" was published in the collection of Meikle's Thomas Carnacki stories Carnacki: Starry Wisdom and Other Stories by Dark Regions Press in March 2021.

### Behind the Mythos
"Starry Wisdom" is a rewrite of Meikle's earlier story "Into the Black". Entire passages remain completely unchanged, although "Into the Black" lacks either Thomas Carnacki and any mention of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Trivia
*The Antarctic expedition mentioned in the story was an actual event led by Ernest Shackleton; the real-world team also succeeded in scaling Mount Erebus.
*Winston Churchill in his pre-British Prime Minister days is a recurrent character in Meikle's Carnacki stories.

The Starstone is a fictional item in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 1973 in issue #7 of the Marvel Premiere series of comics.

### Background
The Starstone was a football sized oval gem that was cold to the touch, as if it had been touched by the frigid cold of space. Within it was a strange shadow and those who touched it felt a chill of terror down their spines. Kathulos sent it to Earth, and when it was bathed in the light of the stars and moon, power was transmitted to the gem.

It was able to cast a spell on the inhabitants of the nearby town, controlling its inhabitants into drone-like slaves. From it a sentient slime came out which turned the Witch House into a living building that tried to kill its trapped inhabitants (by animating objects and overwhelming them with the flowing sentient slime).

"Static"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Will Murray that originally appeared in the anthology Beyond the Mountains of Madness (Celaeno Press, 2015). It is part of Murray's Cryptic Events Evaluation Section series of Mythos stories.

### Synopsis
A psychic on staff at the Cryptic Events Evaluation Section is sent to Antarctica to decipher mysterious prehuman inscriptions--and unwittingly unleashes a cosmic horror.

### Characters

* Banis Power: A CEES psychic operative. He started "as a Cartomancer First Class, back when Special Powers was a pilot program." The story's narrator.
* Kim Greene: Team leader at CEES's South Pole Station, head of a team of exo-archeologists. She is a Leo with Sagittarius rising.
* The Director: CEES's chief is said to be "a guy who requires regular exorcisms the way you and I need to scan our home computers for viruses." His office is at CEET headquarters in Chantilly, Virginia.

### Setting
A "fortress west of the great plateau" of Antarctica, built by "the race of star-headed beings called the Great Old Ones by their so-called discoverers, the members of the infamous Miskatonic University Expedition of 1930–31." It is dated to "the later period of habitation, during the Jurassic era." It is a "spiral black dome" roughly 12 stories tall, "looking like a basalt vault dusted with snow" with "a bulge at the top, like a Christmas ornament atop a domed mosque." CEET researchers ironically call it the Fun House. The bas reliefs that line the structure's single hallway are the major focus of the story.

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in Murray's collection The Wild Adventures of Cthulhu: Volume One.

Stealing Cthulhu is a roleplaying game aid written by Graham Walmsley and annotated by Gareth Ryder-Hanrahan, Kenneth Hite, and Jason Morningstar. It was published by CPI Anthony Rowe in January 2011.

### Overview


Stealing Cthulhu deconstructs H. P. Lovecraft's works and creations in order to provide insight for gamesmasters into how to make roleplaying games more "Lovecraftian" in feel. It also contains the full rules for Cthulhu Dark, a rules-light roleplaying game also designed by Graham Walmsley.

fullContent:
Stephen Hickman (April 9, 1949 - July 16, 2021) was an artist and sculptor who also occasionally worked as a writer.

Born in  Washington, D.C,  he has created cover art for writers including Stephen Brust,  Hal Colbatch, Tom Cool, Gordon Dickson, David Drake, Harlan Ellison, Robert Heinlein, Anne McCaffrey, Larry Niven, Andre Norton, Jerry Pournelle, and Steve Stirling.

Hickman won among other honors a World Science Fiction Convention's Hugo Award, 6 Chesley Awards from the Association of Science Fiction and Fantasy Artists and 2 Spectrum Gold Awards.

Hickman illustrated over 425 covers for Ace, Baen, Ballantine, Bantam, Berkeley, Dell, Del Rey, Doubleday, Phage Press, Tor, Warren Publications and others over a 44 year period beginning in 1976.

Hickman wrote The Lemurian Stone (Ace Books) (1988), which formed the basis for his Pharazar Mythos illustrations.

### Mythos Connection
In 1996, Hickman created a "Cthulhu Idol" statuette based on an earlier illustration he had created for the Baen Books edition of H.P. Lovecraft story The Call of Cthulhu. The statuette was produced and  distributed by Bowen Designs. He also sculpted a bust of H.P. Lovecraft. Limited edition replicas of both sculptures are sold at high prices to collectors.

Stephen Jones is the protagonist of H. P. Lovecraft's revision story "The Horror in the Museum". He visits a wax museum of horrors in the Southwark borough of London out of a languid decadent desire for stimulation, and ultimately is far from disappointed.

### Description
Jones is not physically described but his mien is that of quiet patronizing amusement bordering on disdain when listening to George Rogers rant about the arcane discoveries that Rogers claims to have made. By description he is called languid, relaxed and behaves in a diffident manner, initially. As the horror in the museum unfolds this inevitably changes. Jones is a somewhat dismissive skeptic of new thrills since he has become jaded with even gory displays of murderers and their victims. This deadening of his sensibilities is perhaps why he resists what might have driven a more typical Lovecraftian protagonist insane.

### History
Rogers met Stephen Jones, a decadent connoisseur of bizarre art, and dared him to spend the night in Rogers' wax museum. Initially this seems to arise from Jones skeptical and slightly contemptuous treatment of Rogers, but in fact Rogers has been hoping all along to make Jones or someone like him another sacrifice to Rhan-Tegoth. Rogers dresses up in the hide of a Dimensional Shambler to surprise Jones, but Jones manages to subdue Rogers and flees, leaving Rogers to himself become a sacrifice to the alien god.
