Stephen King is a world-renowned author, best known for his horror and fantasy work, who has made several contributions to the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. He has stated on multiple occasions that H. P. Lovecraft is one of his greatest influences, possibly due to having spent some of his childhood growing up in New England, the setting for many of his own works.

“Now that time has given us some perspective on his work,” King has written, “I think it is beyond doubt that H. P. Lovecraft has yet to be surpassed as the twentieth century’s greatest practitioner of the classic horror tale.” He credits his discovery about 1960 of a paperback copy of Lovecraft’s The Lurking Fear and Other Stories as a decisive moment in his development as a writer. “Lovecraft. . . opened the way for me, as he had done for others before me.... It is his shadow, so long and gaunt, and his eyes, so dark and puritanical, which overlie almost all of the important horror fiction that has come since.”

Critics have noted similarities between King's recurring antagonist Randall Flagg and Lovecraft's Nyarlathotep, and between the cosmic entity encountered in King's novel It and Cthulhu.

Stephen Mark Rainey (born 2 May 1959) is an American author and editor who has contributed numerous novels and short stories to the fictional Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Overview
Rainey began his writing career in the mid-1980s with a number of short stories set in or inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. Many of his early works were published in Robert M. Price's Crypt of Cthulhu and other magazines under Price's Cryptic Publications label, such as Revelations From Yuggoth edited by Shawn Ramsey and Tales of Lovecraftian Horror, edited by Wilum H. Pugmire. Many of Rainey's Mythos-related stories originally appeared in Chaosium's Cthulhu-Mythos "Cycle" anthologies, such as The Azathoth Cycle, The Shub-Niggurath Cycle, The Innsmouth Cycle, The Ithaqua Cycle, and others. He went on to edit his own Cthulhu Mythos anthology, Song of Cthulhu, published by Chaosium in 2001.

Rainey's Lovecraftian and Cthulhu Mythos stories have appeared in such anthologies as The New Lovecraft Circle (1996), Miskatonic University (1996), Singers of Strange Songs (1996), World War Cthulhu (2014), Return of the Old Ones (2014), Black Wings IV (2015), Through a Mythos Darkly (2017), Summer of Lovecraft (2019), and Tales from Arkham Sanitarium (2022), among others.

Many of Rainey's Lovecraftian stories are set in or around the fictional community of Aiken Mill, a rural community in the mountains of southwest Virginia. Most of these stories involve entities summoned by the music of one Maurice Zann, whose relationship to Lovecraft's Erich Zann remains undefined but absolute. Maurice Zann is the author of a grimoire titled The Spheres Beyond Sound, a book of music that, when performed, opens doors to a realm populated by entities both directly and indirectly related to those of the Lovecraft's pantheon. Pivotal works in what author/editor Robert M. Price calls Rainey's "Fugue Devil Cycle" include the stories "Threnody," "The Spheres Beyond Sound," "Fugue Devil," "Eye of the Devil," "The Herald at Midnight," and "Misfits."

Stephen Strange (aka, Dr. Strange) is a superhero in the fictional Marvel universe, who was created in 1963 and has been one of its main superheroes, a B-list hero with several of his own comic book series.

### Background
Doctor Strange is Earth's premiere mystical defender, its most powerful sorcerer and the one that Earth's other superheroes most often turn to when they need to consult on mystical questions or need a mystical heavy hitter. His greatest and oldest enemy is the eldritch dimensional conqueror, sorcerer god Dormammu. He has clashed with more Old Ones than any other of Earth's heroes (except possibly Conan), and has battled both Shuma-Gorath and Chthon several times.

Stephen Herbert Perrin (born January 22, 1946), often simply known as Steve Perrin, is a game designer. He has also worked previously as an editor, reviewer, publisher and technical writer. Perrin is best known for creating the tabletop role-playing game rules for RuneQuest for the tabletop gaming company Chaosium. He also worked on their most famous game, Call of Cthulhu.

He worked as a freelance game writer and designer for two decades before returning to Chaosium in 2020 as a consultant, primarily for the Call of Cthulhu game line.

Sthanee is a Great Old One created by the late American author Robert A. W. Lowndes.

### Description
Manifesting as a gigantic marine horror with twelve serpentine limbs equipped with suckers similar to those found on an octopus, Sthanee also has a beard of tentacles. It is served by a vicious race of merfolk known as the Children of Sthanee who worship it as a god.

### Behind the Mythos
Sthanee is mentioned in Robert A. W. Lowndes' short poem "Nyaghoggua" (1941), but its physical appearance was first depicted in the pages of Lowndes' comic book feature "When Sthanee Wakes" (pp. 32-33) which was published in Scienti-Comics #2.

fullContent:
"Sticks" is a short story by Karl Edward Wagner.  The story received first publication in the March 1974 issue of Whispers. It was reprinted in Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos, revised edition (Arkham House, 1990).

### Synopsis
Colin Leverett, an artist specialising in horror artwork, takes a fishing trip into the Adirondack Mountains in New York in the spring of 1942, where he finds an old abandoned house. The ruin has been encircled by weird arrangements of sticks, with bundles tied together in odd patterns. Leverett sketches the patterns before entering the house, where he is attacked by a lich in the basement. He narrowly escapes and flees the area. 

Around 1970, Leverett is contacted by his friend Prescott Brandon, a small-press publisher, who asks him to illustrate a collection of the works of noted horror author H. Kenneth Allard (based on H.P. Lovecraft). Leverett hits upon the idea of using his old sketches of the sticks as the basis of the artwork for the commissioned work. 

The artist is later approached by Allard's nephew, who wants him to do the art for a new volume of Allard's previously unpublished works--featuring all the images of the sticks he has. Accepting the job draws Leverett into a potentially world-ending occult conspiracy.

### Setting
Mann Brook is a real body of water in upstate New York, located, as in the story, between the towns of Ostelic and DeRuyter.

### Characters
*Colin Leverett, an artist for pulp magazines "whose fascination for the macabre was evident in his art." He fights in Italy's Appenine Mountains during World War II.
*Prescott Brandon, a friend of Leverett's and the editor/publisher of Gothic House, a small press based in Salem, Massachusetts, that specializes in weird fantasy.
*H. Kenneth Allard, a weird fiction writer. His books include Voices from the Shadow, Unhallowed Places and Dwellers in the Earth. His works feature the mythical Book of Elders of Alorri-Zrokros.
*Dana Allard, Allard's nephew, from Petersham, Massachusetts.
*Dr. Alexander Stefroi, an archaeologist, an "earnest scholar" of the occult history of New England and upstate New York. He lives in Pelham, Massachusetts.

### Behind the Mythos
It has been suggested that the protagonist is based on Clark Ashton Smith, due to biographical similarities. 

The twig lattices were directly inspired by the artwork of Weird Tales artist Lee Brown Coye. This artist illustrated two Carcosa Press volumes of which Wagner was the editor. 

### Legacy
"Sticks" has been surprisingly influential, despite its relative current obscurity. The similarities between the weird stick bundles in "Sticks" and those in The Blair Witch Project -- which also features an abandoned house in the woods -- have been repeatedly remarked upon. The first season of the HBO series True Detective also made use of Wagner's sticks motif.

Stonehenge is a prehistoric monument located on Salisbury Plain, England. Consisting of numerous megaliths arranged in a circular pattern, it is believed to have been built over a period of fifteen centuries, from about 3100 BC to 1600 BC.

### In the Mythos
The sacred Black Stone of the Children of the Night was kept in Stonehenge until the Picts came along and drove the Children of the Night to the underground. (: "People of the Dark")

The god-box containing the Atlantean monster Sho-Gath was also kept in Stonehenge by druids, under the guardianship of a Druidic priest. (: "The God-Box")

An archaeologist named Schneider from Miskatonic University believes that Stonehenge is older than the Egyptian pyramids, dating back at least to the Hyborian Age, and that it was originally a larger complex built in the shape of a gigantic star-stone to imprison some unknown entity. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

According to another account, Stonehenge can be used to summon Yog-Sothoth due to it being a ring-shaped circle of stones. (: Alicia Y)

"Stragglers from Carrhae" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Darrell Schweitzer.

### Synopsis
In the aftermath of the Roman defeat at Carrhae, two legionaries are plagued with dreams sent by the Outer God Nyarlathotep, who wishes them to lead his undead armies in the conquest of Earth. Despite one of the two giving in to Nyarlathotep's will, the other retains enough sanity to resist, and kills his comrade rather than allow darkness to descend over the world.

### Characters
* Unnamed Narrator, a Roman legionnaire who survived the Battle of Carrhae.
* Marcus Vibius, the narrator's best friend and fellow survivor.
* Nyarlathotep, an Outer God.

### Publication History
"Stragglers from Carrhae " was first published in the Dark Regions Press anthology World War Cthulhu in August 2014. It was included in the collection of Schweitzer’s own works Awaiting Strange Gods by Fedogan & Bremer in 2015.

Strange Eons is a 1978 novel by Robert Bloch that serves as an homage to the Cthulhu Mythos stories of H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in hardcover by Whispers Press, then released in paperback in 1979 by Pinnacle Books. It is "dedicated to HPL who dedicated himself to other outsiders and gave to them a silver key".

The book has been translated into French, Spanish, Italian, and German.

### Synopsis
Art collector Albert Keith finds a painting that his friend Simon Waverly assures him is one mentioned in horror writer H. P. Lovecraft's story "Pickman's Model". "The painting was inspired by Lovecraft's story," Albert suggests. 

"Suppose it was the other way around," Simon responds. "Suppose Lovecraft's story was inspired by the painting?"

Meanwhile, model Kay Keith, Albert's ex-wife, is hired to work for the Starry Wisdom Temple, now established in Los Angeles.

The final section of the novel deals with Mark Dixon--the child of Kay and Cthulhu--and the events leading up to end of the world.

fullContent:
"Strange Manuscript Found in the Vermont Woods" is a horror short story by Lin Carter, set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in 1988 in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
The narrative consists of the journal of Winthrop Hoag, which has been found inside a briefcase in Vermont in 1936. The briefcase was found partially buried into the frozen ground, as if it had fallen from a great height. It was damaged in some places, as if it had been exposed to both extreme heat and acid, and also had stains of a foul-smelling viscous black substance. The manuscript inside was, in some pages, damaged and unreadable, leaving a few gaps in the narrative.

The journal reveals how Winthrop Hoag inherited a cabin in the woods in the vicinity of Arkham, Massachusetts, after the disappearance of his cousin, Jared Fuller. Hoag moves in, hoping to take advantage of the isolation and work on his thesis. Taking a look at his cousin's books, he passes over foreign titles such as Unaussprechlichen Kulten, De Vermis Mysteriis and Cultes des Goules, and finally locates two which are in English. One is Prof. Copeland's translation of the infamous Zanthu Tablets. The other is an anonymous manuscript called Of Evill Sorceries Done in New-England of Daemons in no Humane Shape.

Seeing that the books are about occultism and witchcraft, Hoag tosses them aside and settles for reading his cousin's diary instead. From it, he learns that Fuller had heard people chanting deep in the woods, repeating the names Ossadagowah and Zvilpogghua, and found the body of a dead man, broken as if he had fallen from a great height and covered in foul-smelling black slime. The description corresponds to other bodies found in similar conditions in the area.

Hoag tries to sleep, but the light of the star Algol shines bright through his window and keeps him awake, as he hears (or imagines hearing) a distant chanting. On the next day, he goes for a walk in the woods and finds a barren spot where no vegetation grows, with a large stone at its center, carved with the image of a winged, tentacled toad-like creature. At night, Hoag sits by the window to try to hear the chanting, as the constellation of Perseus (which Algol is part of) rises in the sky. He glimpses the shadow of some large winged creature. On the next day, when he returns to the site of the great stone, Hoag finds several human footprints, intermingled with those of an enormous web-footed animal.

Frightened, Hoag reads through Fuller's diary and correspondence with a folklorist named Wilmarth. He learns that Ossadagowah and Zvilpogghua are the same entity, the former name meaning "child of Tsathoggua". The monster resides on a world in orbit around Algol, and can be summoned to Earth when the star is high in the night sky, at which point the beast will swoop down and capture prey. When it's done feeding on the prey's blood, it will drop the prey's body from the sky.

Strange Stories was a short-lived pulp magazine intended to be a competitor to Weird Tales. 

### Overview
The magazine ran for thirteen issues from 1939 to 1941.  It was edited by Mort Weisinger, assisted by Julius Schwartz, neither of whom were credited.  

Contributors during its short run included Robert Bloch, C. L. Moore, August Derleth, and Henry Kuttner. Strange Stories was a competitor to the established leader in weird fiction, Weird Tales.  With the launch, also in 1939, of the well-received Unknown, Strange Stories was unable to compete.  Publication ended in 1941 due to low sales.

Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror was a pulp magazine launched in 1931 by Clayton Publishing to publish supernatural fiction; it was one of the main competitors to Weird Tales. It published stories by Robert E. Howard, Clark Ashton Smith, and August Derleth before folding with Clayton's bankruptcy in 1933. It was briefly revived in the 21st century by Wildside Press, which published three issues under the editorship of Robert M. Price between 2003 and 2007.

shortDefinition: "Strange Things Done" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Lisa Smedman, which takes place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting. It was published by Aconyte in the thematic Arkham Horror Fiction anthology Secrets in Scarlet in...
fullContent:
"Strange Things Done" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Lisa Smedman, which takes place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting. It was published by Aconyte in the thematic Arkham Horror Fiction anthology Secrets in Scarlet in October 2022.

### Synopsis
Reporter Rex Murphy takes passage to Alaska aboard the fading liner Martha while pursuing a human-interest piece on the frontier poet Robert Service. During the course of the voyage, he encounters a mysterious man by the name of Thorne and begins to notice that the notes which he has taken during his interviews do not correspond to any of his memories; indeed, many of the people he has spoken to are not even registered as passengers aboard the Martha.

When Thorne becomes aware of this, he reveals to Murphy that he is aboard the ship in search of an extra-dimensional entity known as an "Outsider": a malevolent creature capable of not only taking on the form of those it encounters, but of erasing their very existence. Thorne and Murphy eventually succeed in tracking down and confronting the Outsider, but not before it has shipwrecked the Martha off the inhospitable Alaskan coastline. In a final showdown, the two blow the stricken ship, and the Outsider, to smithereens; in the aftermath Thorne vanishes, and Murphy is left with nothing but a sheaf of waterlogged notes which he has no memory of having written…

### Mythos References
Thorne is suggested to be a member of the Red Coterie, a recurrent element in the Arkham Horror setting. This is hinted at when he apparently utilises his bright red cravat to cast some manner of spell on the Outsider; all members of the Coterie utilise magical artefacts known as "Keys" to create or augment magical effects- usually in the form of clothing or accoutrements and invariably some shade of red.

Rex Murphy is an investigator character created by Fantasy Flight Games for the second edition of their popular board game Arkham Horror. At one point, he notes that Thorne reminds him of Professor Walters, another investigator and recurring character in the franchise.

### Behind the Scenes
The man who Rex Murphy plane on writing an article on, Robert Service, was a real-world poet who wrote numerous works about life in the nascent frontier societies of North America. The title of the story is a reference to the opening line in one of his best-known poems, "The Cremation of Sam McGee": "There are strange things done in the midnight sun, By the men who moil for gold."

"Stranger Crossings" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Welsh author Adrian Chamberlin. It was published in the thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg by Screaming Dreams in October 2013.

### Synopsis
When a dealer in antique books and artefacts identified only as "Taffy" is asked to evaluate a relic retrieved from a house clearance, he is unwittingly infected with the "spores of the Lloigor." As he looks into his worsening condition and the provenance of the artefact, he comes to the realisation that it is a part of a group of objects necessary to conduct a ritual which will bring doom to mankind.

When he attempts to locate and destroy the piece, Taffy finds that the removals man has sold it to a folk band; further investigation suggests that they are in fact a cult who possess the other two objects necessary for the ritual, and have the necessary knowledge to conduct it. In desperation, he confronts the band on stage, murdering them all, then returning home to commit his account to paper before the spores do their transformative work.

### Behind the Mythos
The name of the band which purchases the artefact is "Lloigor of Logres," and its members are Tarquin Leng (Plateau of Leng), Quentin Lemuria (continent of Lemuria), and Julian Kardath (Kadath in the Cold Wastes). Tracks from their albums which contain Mythos references include: "The Lament of Y’Ha Nthlei," (the Deep One city of Y'ha-nthlei) "The Cloak of Tawil at-Umr," (the avatar of Yog-Sothoth 'Umr at-Tawil) and "Tcho-Tcho  Llamas Day." (the malignant Tcho-Tcho people)

Stregoicavar, originally known as Xuthltan by its builders, is a fictional Hungarian village created by Robert E. Howard as the setting of his horror short story "The Black Stone". It was mentioned obliquely in "The Thing on the Doorstep", by H. P. Lovecraft, and also referenced in "The Second Wish" by Brian Lumley.

Xuthltan is also the name of an ancient Assyrian wizard in Howard's story "The Fire of Asshurbanipal". Any relation between this character and the people who built the village is unknown.

### Overview
Stregoicavar is a village located in the mountains of Hungary, adjacent to the mysterious monolith known as the Black Stone. The village was originally built by people of unknown origins and ethnicity who named the place Xuthltan. The name "Stregoicavar", which means "Witch-Town", was ascribed to it by the denizens of the valleys below, who feared the people of Xuthltan due to their habit of abducting girls and infants from neighbouring settlements to sacrifice them to their god, a monstrous toad-like creature perched atop the Black Stone.

When the Turkish army invaded Hungary in 1526, they were so horrified by the sacrifices that they massacred the entire population. Eventually, the village was rebuilt and repopulated by settlers from the valleys, who decided to keep the name Stregoicavar.

As of 1931, the inhabitants of Stregoicavar are a peaceful community who fear and shun the Black Stone. (: "The Black Stone")

### In the Expanded Mythos
Carl Earlman's ancestors came from Stregoicavar, Hungary. (: "The House of the Temple")

Strephon is a fictional character created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his 1918 poem "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin."

### Description
Little is known of Strephon, although it can be inferred from his behaviour that he is a devious character, and does not appear to have a particularly high regard for the thoughts and emotions of others.

### History
After a woman named Chloe failed to be swayed by his romantic overtures, in an effort to make her jealous Strephon took up with Hecatissa, who had an eye for the man. This ploy worked, and by merely batting her eyes at him Strephon rejected Hecatissa and the two fell into each others' arms. On the day they were wed, poor Hecatissa attempted to take her own life. (: "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin")

"Strident Caller" is a short story by American author Laird Barron, first published in the collection of Lovecraftian fiction Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be by 01Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
Craven, a drifter passing a few months as the kept toyboy of a wealthy but ageing actress, discovers that the woman's husband is not in fact entirely dead, and is the head of a cult seemingly operating in another dimension. Although Craven manages to escape their clutches, as a punishment for not offering himself to be sacrificed the cult take his dog from him and curse him to an existence of despair.

Dr. Stuart Hartwell is a fictional character created by American author Peter Rawlik for his Cthulhu Mythos stories, making his debut in the episodic novel Reanimators (2013, Night Shade Books).

### History

### Reanimators
Hartwell was a student and protégé of celebrated Miskatonic University physician Dr. Allan Halsey. When Halsey's corpse was reanimated by the misguided Herbert West, Hartwell's parents fell victim to the crazed beast during its murderous rampage. In the aftermath Hartwell, having deduced the cause of Halsey's condition, swore revenge on West.

In the following years, Hartwell obtained his medical degree and established himself as a respected practitioner, primarily through an association with neighbour Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee. However, this relationship soon soured when Peaslee's body was inhabited by the Yithian Mr. Ys, who coerced him into acting as his agent, and pressing him into his service with such other Mythos characters as Dr. Muñoz.

Despite these distractions, Hartwell remembered his vow and, although his zeal in pursuing his vengeance waxed and waned several times over the years, it was always in his mind. To this end, he developed an proficiency in the reanimation process; although this was initially solely for thwarting West, he soon came to be an accomplished practitioner in the art, his own versions of the reagent surpassing West's (although this may have been at least partially due to the acts of sabotage Hartwell enacted when West was absent from his laboratories).

### The Weird Company
After the resolution of his oath against West, Hartwell returned to the life of a general practitioner, merely dabbling in the art of reanimation. This would change when he was recruited by the enigmatic Asenath Waite, who was assembling a team of uniquely-qualified individuals to combat the deadly threat posed by a colony of Shoggoths unleashed by the ill-fated Pabodie Expedition in 1931. Hartwell's iteration of the reagent, which is revealed to be strikingly similar to the blood of the Elder Things, proved instrumental in defeating the protean menaces.

fullContent:
"Study for The Witch House (2013)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan, part of their Dandridge Cycle. It first appeared in the September 2013 issue of Sirenia Digest (#92).

### Synopsis
The story concerns the sale of a painting, called Study for "The Witch House," by the artist Albert Perrault. It depicts a "crooked, ramshackle house...clinging to the edge of a towering sea cliff," whose "gables and turrets seem...to claw at the sky." On the cliffs below the house, there's the suggestion of a "cave, half hidden in the violence of white-capped breakers and spray," with "something else, something not quite human, peering out."

The prospective buyer of the painting, Charlie O'Hara, argues about its authenticity with the gallery owner, and describes the history of the structure depicted:  Located between Anchor Bay and Point Arenas, California, it was built in 1890 by Machen Dandridge, "supposedly some sort of wizard," who worshipped "obscure gods and goddesses of the ocean," like Poseidon, Dagon, Mother Hydra and Father Kraken. He died in 1917 or 1918, after being accused of having "murdered his family, sacrificed them one by one to his pantheon.” 

An article about the house appeared in the April 1957 issue of Argosy. In the 1960s, the house became a mecca for "hippies and occultist types," and a "cult...supposedly met there every Halloween." It was largely destroyed in a fire in 2003.

### Publication History
The story was republished in Kiernan's collection Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018).

shortDefinition: Stygian: Reign of the Old Ones is a tactical role-playing game developed by Cultic Games and published by 1C Entertainment in 2019.  ### Summary Stygian: Reign of the Old Ones is described as "a supernatural horror role-playing video game which takes...
fullContent:
Stygian: Reign of the Old Ones is a tactical role-playing game developed by Cultic Games and published by 1C Entertainment in 2019.

### Summary
Stygian: Reign of the Old Ones is described as "a supernatural horror role-playing video game which takes place in the strange worlds of Howard Phillips Lovecraft". The game features a 2D graphical style with an art style "reminiscent of 20's illustrations". The setting takes place in the city of Arkham, displaced into an otherworldly dimension after the events of the "Black Day". The protagonist, either created by the player or pre-made, attempts to discover and follow clues leading to the mysterious "Dismal Man", In this endeavor they can recruit and be joined by other characters, aligned by common goals, circumstance, or as a paid henchman. 

This game features survival and crafting mechanics, in which the characters must manage health, hunger and sanity. Health and hunger are managed by food and medicine but sanity is managed by the choices made. Each character has a belief system, when that character makes decisions that align with that belief system they recover sanity. Sanity loss along with a host of other causes can inflict mental illness upon a character which can change dialogue options, alter the characters perception of reality and more.

Combat is turn-based and tactical: making use of a hex-grid, characters can use melee weapons, guns, and spells in combat with the various forces in Arkham including members of a Cthulhu-worshiping cult, the Mob, Mi-Go and other creatures. Combat results in angst accumulation, at particular thresholds of angst the character gains a permanent de-buff, incentivizing careful decision making and avoiding unnecessary combat. The majority of combat is optional and much of it can be escaped rather than fought to the death.

### External Links

"Suck It Up, Get It Done" is a short story by author Brandon Barrows. It is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
A recently-hired Boston sewer worker investigating a blockage discovers a juvenile ghoul trapped in one of the pipes. When he informs his supervisor, he is told that taking care of problems like these are all part of the job before being handed a heavy-duty revolver. The man decides to simply "suck it up, get it done".

### Publication History
"Suck It Up, Get It Done" was published in the Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in 2013.

Summanus is a fictional deity created by British author Brian Lumley for his short story "What Dark God?" (, 1975) and identified as a Great Old One in "The Fairground Horror" (, 1976). It is named after an obscure nocturnal thunder god referred to in the works of Ovid, Pliny the Elder, and Martianus Capella.

### Description
Appearing as a grotesque, mouthless humanoid with pale tentacles sticking out from under his robes, Summanus can use these appendages to siphon blood from his victims.

Summanus had a following in Roman times, but if he is worshipped today, his cult is even more secretive. The rites needed for the proper worship of Summanus are found in the Tuscan Rituals.

### Behind the Mythos
Brian Lumley based this Great Old One on the Roman deity of the same name mentioned in the poet Ovid's Fasti. It first appeared in the short story "What Dark God?" (1975), and was later incorporated into the greater Cthulhu Mythos by Lumley himself in "The Fairground Horror" (1976). Chaosium included it in the Malleus Monstrorum sourcebook for their Call of Cthulhu () roleplaying game.

shortDefinition: Summoned is a young adult Cthulhu Mythos novel by Anne M. Pillsworth, published by Tor (under its Tor Teen imprint) in 2014. It introduces Sean Wyndham, a teenager with Mythos-related magical powers, the central character of Pillsworth's Redemption's...
fullContent:
Summoned is a young adult Cthulhu Mythos novel by Anne M. Pillsworth, published by Tor (under its Tor Teen imprint) in 2014. It introduces Sean Wyndham, a teenager with Mythos-related magical powers, the central character of Pillsworth's Redemption's Heir series.

The novel is set in both Providence, Rhode Island, and in H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Arkham, Massachusetts, in the year 2006.

### Characters
Sean Wyndham: A 16-year-old boy from Providence. He turns out to have strong magical aptitude that attracts the interest of both a three-century-old wizard and of the wizard's master, Nyarlathotep. 

Rev. Redemption Orne: An immortal wizard who recruits Sean as a potential apprentice via an email address in a clipping from the Arkham Advertiser of 1895. Born in Cambridgeshire, England, on February 28, 1669, Orne emigrated with his family to Boston in 1681, where he attended  Boston Latin School. He graduated from and Harvard College in 1690, and the next year married Patience Bishop of Dunwich, who introduces him to magic. In 1692, Orne becomes head of the Third Congregational Church of Arkham, is granted immortality by Nyarlathotep, and falls afoul of the witch panic in Arkham. His whereabouts since then are not disclosed.

Jeremy Wyndham: Sean's father and sole caretaker since the death of Sean's mother.

Eddy Rosenthal: Sean's best friend, known for her practicality; she tries to warn Sean away from his magical recruitment, and offers naturalistic explanations for his supernatural experiences. A diligent student, she is also agile and wields a baseball bat effectively as a weapon.

fullContent:
Sundered is an indie video game developed by Thunder Lotus Games. The game rigidly follows the topics of the Cthulhu Mythos, from which it takes themes and characters, and the game designer considers that the game may even be considered an official part of its canon.

### Description
Sundered was originally released on July 28, 2017 for Windows, Mac OS X, Linux, and PlayStation 4 and already in 2018 for Nintendo Switch. It is described as "a chaotic hand-drawn metroidvania in which to resist or embrace arcane and supernatural powers." The story takes place in the ruins of the Eschaton civilization, followers of Nyarlathotep in which the protagonist, Eshe, enters guided by the Shining Trapezohedron, container of Nyarlathotep's consciousness, which serves as a weapon and companion. The Trapezohedron constantly insists that Eshe accept its dark power to obtain more power, before which the player can obey or ignore it, this decision conditioning which of the three available endings will be obtained. It is notable that the "corrupted" versions of weapons obtained by yielding to the dark power have names that refer to various Lovecraftian gods and beings, notably the Mi-Go, Tsathoggua, Ghatanothoa, Azathoth, and Atlach-Nacha.

### Synopsis
In an apocalyptic future, a theocratic civilization known as Eschaton managed to rise up thanks to the power of Mother Ishaela Bha'gor, a powerful priestess who made a pact with the Outer God Nyarlathotep, who promised that, in exchange for worshiping and preparing for their return, it would grant them great prosperity. At first the god appeared to keep his promise, but Eschaton's rise aroused the suspicion of General Waters, leader of the Valkyrie military group, who planned to invade them. Eschaton was quick to respond, precipitating the beginning of a major conflict. To prevent the situation from stalling, Waters himself decided to personally mobilize and capture or kill Mother Ishaela. What the general did not know is that she had already initiated the ritual to free Nyarlathotep and, by interrupting it, the supernatural energy that maintained the portal went out of control and unleashed a corrosive wave that shook the entire city, transforming both the devotees into abominations. of Eschaton as well as the Valkyrie military who fought there.

Some time after these events, a young woman named Eshe enters the ruins and, guided by the voice of the Shining Trapezohedron, must face the monstrous inhabitants of the ruins of Eschaton, standing up to those who were the leaders of both groups, now converted into giant spawn.

fullContent:
Supernatural is a TV series that ran from 2005-2020 on the CW network. The show had Lovecraftian elements, including in one episode an appearance by H. P. Lovecraft himself.

The show centered on the adventures of the Winchester brothers, Dean (played by Jensen Ackles) and Sam (Jared Padalecki), "hunters" who crisscross America destroying supernatural monsters. While much of the show's mythology derives from Christian tradition, involving struggles between demons, angels, and eventually God himself, it borrows from numerous folkloric and horror traditions, including the tropes of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### H. P. Lovecraft as Character
In the episode "Let It Bleed," H. P. Lovecraft (portrayed by Peter Ciuffa) appears in a flashback, killed by an unseen intruder on March 15, 1937, just after completing the manuscript for "The Haunter of the Dark." 

The episode goes on to reveal that Lovecraft had shortly before held a dinner party at which he and his friends tried to open a gate to another dimension--a ritual that succeeded in summoning an entity from Purgatory that possessed Lovecraft's maid Eleanor. (The Lovecraft of Supernatural is evidently more financially successful than the one in the real world.) 

In this episode, Sam and Dean consult with a Lovecraft expert named Judah, who says of Lovecraft, "This guy is literature. He should be be taught in schools. He's up there with Dickens and Dean R Koontz." 

The episode contains several Mythos references. Zeboyd Games' Cthulhu Saves the World is being played by Judah, who has a sticker that reads (reads what?). In another scene, the character Ben (who may or may not be Dean's son) is reading the graphic novel Cthulhu Tales Vol. 2: The Whisper of Madness when he is kidnapped by demons.  

Surprised that Dean hasn't heard of Lovecraft, Dean's mentor Bobby prompts him: "Horror writer. At the Mountains of Madness, The Call of Cthulhu?" Dean responds: "No, I was too busy having sex with women."  

### Leviathans

The Leviathans, the main villains in season 7, are shapeshifting monsters, a ravenously destructive race that sees other lifeforms as inferior, to be destroyed or treated as a food source. In the shows mythology, they predate the angels. Immortals that are virtually indestructible, they are able to fly, block angels' powers by their physical presence, regenerate from virtually any injury, have enhanced senses, possess venomous blood that can kill angels, and have super strength, agility, and speed. 

In their true forms, they are perceived by humans as balls of black goo with powerful jaws. When possessing human hosts, they dislocate their jaw, displaying a forked tongue and large teeth. Their society has a hierarchy based on strength and fear, in which they betrayal is the norm and those who fail or annoy others are eaten. Death referred to the Leviathans as "the Old Ones."

shortDefinition: Supernatural Horror in Literature is an essay written by H. P. Lovecraft. It traces the history and development of "Supernatural Horror" and "Weird Literature", highlighting key writers and works. He goes over their faults as well as the things that ...
fullContent:
Supernatural Horror in Literature is an essay written by H. P. Lovecraft. It traces the history and development of "Supernatural Horror" and "Weird Literature", highlighting key writers and works. He goes over their faults as well as the things that make them unique and worth reading. In many cases, the things that Lovecraft mentions as being good or of high quality were those things he himself wished to better emulate in his own writing; the essay serves as a guidebook to the most important influences on Lovecraft's fiction.

The essay was first published in August 1927 in the sole issue of the amateur press magazine The Recluse; portions of a revised and expanded version were published in The Fantasy Fan from 1933-35. The complete revised version appeared in the Arkham House collection The Outsider and Others in 1939.

### Summary
While noting that "[c]osmic terror appears as an ingredient of the earliest folklore of all races," and can be traced through Classical and Medieval literature, the essay points to the Gothic novelist Horace Walpole--author of The Castle of Otranto—as "the actual founder of the literary horror-story as a permanent form" (though Lovecraft criticizes his writing as "tedious, artificial, and melodramatic").

The essay devotes a chapter to Edgar Allan Poe, calling him the author to whom "we owe the modern horror-story in its final and perfected state." A chapter on "The Weird Tradition in America" concentrates on Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ambrose Bierce--though also giving special mention to Lovecraft's friend Clark Ashton Smith. A final chapter on "The Modern Masters" singles out  Arthur Machen, Algernon Blackwood, Lord Dunsany, and M. R. James.

### Chapters
*I. Introduction
*II. The Dawn of the Horror-Tale
*III. The Early Gothic Novel
*IV. The Apex of Gothic Romance
*V. The Aftermath of Gothic Fiction
*VI. Spectral Literature on the Continent
*VII. Edgar Allan Poe
*VIII. The Weird Tradition in America
*IX. The Weird Tradition in the British Isles
*X. The Modern Masters

Surama is a character created by H. P. Lovecraft and Adolphe de Castro for their short story "The Last Test".

### Biography
One of the most enigmatic characters in Lovecraft's fiction, virtually nothing is known about the real nature of Surama. Physically, he is a bald, clean-shaven and abnormally lean man. His skin is dark and parchment-like, and so tightly drawn as to make his head resemble a skull, even more so due to his deep-set black eyes. His anatomy is not entirely human, combining simian and saurian traits as well, although he manages to appear human when wearing the right kind of clothes (similar to Wilbur Whateley). He also has some form of psychic perception that allows him to pick up images and ideas from the minds of others, and to speak any language flawlessly without the need to learn it.

In terms of personality, Surama is noted for his keen intellect, but also for his sardonic demeanor, which is most often expressed by a deep guttural chuckle. He is also highly sadistic, as seen in the way he treats test animals and enjoys watching them suffer.

Of his early life little is known, although Dr. Alfred Clarendon's statements imply that he was originally an Atlantean priest who prolonged his life through unnatural means, and whose body was preserved in a sealed temple in an Atlantean colony in Northern Africa. After speaking to the Saharan Tuareg people, who are descendants of the Atlanteans, Dr. Clarendon somehow managed to revive the mummified body of Surama, hoping that the ancient man's knowledge would prove useful to modern medicine.

Surama promised Clarendon to share ancient secrets that would help in Clarendon's goal to find an ultimate cure to all disease, and thus Clarendon hired him as his assistant. For the next years, however, Surama had a negative influence over Clarendon, teaching him to worship ancient entities, and manipulating the American physician towards the fulfillment of Surama's own mysterious agenda, which involved introducing a new disease known as the black fever: actually an extraterrestrial pathogen obtained by Surama by unknown means, and for which there could be no cure.

Thanks in large part to his friendship with Governor James Dalton, Dr. Clarendon was appointed medical director of the California State Penitentiary at San Quentin, and used his position to test new forms of treatment on the inmates when an epidemic of the newly-discovered black fever took place. After a confrontation with the prison's director caused the aggressive and antisocial Clarendon to lose his position, Surama helped him continue his research by inoculating the lethal pathogen in numerous animal test subjects, a kidnapped Mexican boy, Clarendon's Thibetan servants, and the beloved St. Bernard that belonged to Clarendon's sister Georgina.

"Swami Chandraputra" is the alias used by Randolph Carter after his mind is trapped in an alien body. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key") He appears in H. P. Lovecraft's stories "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" and "Out of the Aeons".

### 'Through the Gates of the Silver Key'
In "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", co-written with E. Hoffmann Price, Chandraputra takes part in the settlement of Carter's estate at the New Orleans home of Etienne-Laurent de Marigny, with whom he has corresponded. The swami claims to be "an adept from Benares with important information to give" about Carter's disappearance. (Benares, now known as Varanasi, is considered the holiest city in Hinduism.)

Chandraputra's peculiar appearance is described--he isnon-committal in age—lean, and with a dark, bearded, singularly immobile face of very regular contour, bound with the turban of a high-caste Brahmin and having night-black, burning, almost irisless eyes which seemed to gaze out from a vast distance behind the features.,,, In general attire he was the normal European civilian, but his loose clothes sat peculiarly badly on him, while his bushy black beard, Eastern turban, and large white mittens gave him an air of exotic eccentricity.He later reveals that this face is a mask; what lies behind it is shocking enough to kill Carter's cousin Ernest Aspinwall  when he catches a glimpse of it.

Chandraputra speaks in a "queerly alien voice":His speech had an oddly forced, hollow, metallic quality, as if the use of English taxed his vocal apparatus; yet his language was as easy, correct, and idiomatic as any native Anglo-Saxon’s. At the meeting at de Marigny's house, he recounts what happened to Carter--revealing at the end that he and Carter are one and the same. In his travels with the Silver Key through the Ultimate Gate, Carter learned that he had and will exist in a multiplicity of forms throughout time and space. He becomes one of these forms, the wizard Zkauba on the distant planet Yaddith, thousands of years in the past. In this "clawed, tapir-snouted" form he is "rugose, partly squamous, and curiously articulated in a fashion mainly insect-like yet not without a caricaturish resemblance to the human outline." After struggling for control of this body with the "Zkauba-facet", Carter uses one of Yaddith's light-envelopes to return to Earth--traveling through time as well as space, aiming to arrive as close to the time that he departed from in 1928.

As it happens, he returns to Arkham in October 1930. Using the disguise that he had prepared (and gold brought with him from Yaddith), he adopts the Chandraputra identity and moves to Chambers Street in Boston's West End, where he works to decipher a parchment that will allow him to return to human form. fullContent:
Swan Point Cemetery is a cemetery located in Providence, Rhode Island. It is the burial place of Howard Phillips Lovecraft, as well as that of his parents, Winfield Scott and Sarah Susan Phillips Lovecraft, and his grandfather Whipple Van Buren Phillips. Lovecraft's gravestone there reads "I Am Providence".

Swan Point was started in 1846 as a 60-acre tract of land; it has now grown to 200 acres, and is still accepting interments.

It is the resting place of numerous prominent Rhode Islanders, including 23 governors. The second most famous horror writer buried there is C. M. Eddy, Jr., a friend of Lovecraft's who was also a frequent contributor to Weird Tales.

Lovecraft's short story "The Tomb" was inspired by a visit he made to Swan Point to see the grave of a distant relative.

Swarog is a fictional entity created for the German-language Call of Cthulhu supplement Berlin: Im Herzen der großen Stadt.

A hideous being appearing as a dark, gigantic, legless bird-like horror swathed in dark flames, Swarog has a long neck topped by a black lump, half of which endowed with a big glowing eye and the other being covered in innumerable tentacles.

It was revered by Slavic and Viking folks as the Solar god Svarog, though sharing almost nothing with the traditional deity.

"Sweet Despise" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Peter A. Worthy.

### Synopsis
A supernatural killer known as the Ghoul in the service of an entity named N'h'll tracks down and butchers the immortal members of a cult for an unknown transgression. Ultimately confronting a man named Oakes, the leader of the cult, the Ghoul dooms him to an eternity of torment by tricking Oakes into summoning Cynothoglys.

### Characters

*Professor Damian Oakes, the cult's leader.
*Matthias Tolliver, a senior cultist who is remorseful for his act within the group.

### Publication History
"Sweet Despise" was first published in the first issue of Nightscapes in June 1997, and then appeared in Dark Legacy #4 in March 1999.

### Trivia
*The events of "Sweet Despise" take place across much of Lovecraft Country, and the story namechecks many well-known Mythos elements, including Miskatonic University, Azathoth and the Necronomicon.

fullContent:
"Sweet Ermengarde" is a short comedic story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft under the pseudonym "Percy Simple". It was probably written between 1919 and 1921; Lovecraft scholars state it is "the only work of fiction by HPL that cannot be dated with precision." (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) It was first published in the Arkham House collection Beyond the Wall of Sleep (1943).

### Synopsis
The story is a parody of romantic melodrama, centering on Ermengarde Stubbs and her relationships with villainous mortgage-holder 'Squire Hardman, would-be rescuer Jack Manly and fiance Algernon Reginald Jones. Daniel Harms calls it "a take-off on the Horatio Alger 'rags-to-riches' genre". An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia suggests that a more precise target for Lovecraft's satire was writer Fred Jackson, whose novels often "have exactly the sort of implausibility of plot and sentimentality of action that is parodied in 'Sweet Ermengarde'."

### Reception
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia describes the story (with "A Reminiscence of Dr. Samuel Johnson" and "Ibid") as one of a trilogy of Lovecraft's "comic gems".

Harms describes it as "actually quite funny at places."

The Swine Things are a fictional species created by William Hope Hodgson for his cosmic horror novel The House on the Borderland. They were later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu by Scott David Aniolowski in the 2006 edition of the Malleus Monstrorum monster manual, under the name of Swine Folk.

### Background
The Swine Things are a barbaric species of porcine humanoids which dwell underground. They have pig-like ears and snouts, hoofed hind legs, clawed hands, and very pale skin color. Their mouths and jaws in turn are those of a human. Some of them have large curved tusks. Swine people are able to both walk upright and go on all fours. Usually they hunt in packs and are brutal fighters that will fight to the death. The species is attracted to space and time irregularities, being able to sense them.

### See Also
*Saaitii, another supernatural pig-like entity created by William Hope Hodgson

"Swinging" is a short story by Cody Goodfellow that first appeared in Rapture of the Deep and Other Lovecraftian Tales (Hippocampus Press, 2016). The mind-swapping, time-jumping tragic love story is a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Out of Time.

### Characters

* Lorna Orchard (born c. 1987): A young woman (born c. 1987) who learned the Yithian mindswapping technique from her father, whom she killed when she was 15.  As the story begins, she is a secret patient in Stockton State Hospital, part of California's mental health system. She goes on to found "the first doomsday cult to get everything right." She leads the cult from behind the scenes, manifesting as "One, the benevolent, bodiless sage of Celaeno."
* David Orchard (1959-2002): Lorna's father, born in 1959, who is possessed by a Yithian from 1992 until 1995. He is able to learn the mind-transfer technique for himself--which he calls "swinging"--and writes books about it, including The Mind-Snatchers, aka Beyond Time, Out of Mind. He works for a time at the Atwater Institute for Psychonautical Research. He is repossessed in 2002 "to stop me telling the world about them," at which point his body is killed trying to murder Lorna.
* Narrator: He meets Lorna (in a variety of other bodies) while in for a ninety-day observation at Stockton. He learns to swing from Lorna, and after he is released and she escapes from the hospital, he becomes the figurehead of her successful global cult. He describes himself as having a "creepy sociopathic charm."
* Adolph Sutro (b. April 29, 1830): A historical figure, an engineer who made a fortune extracting silver from Nevada's Comstock Load and later becomes San Francisco's mayor. In real life, Sutro served only one term as mayor (1895-97), and died two years later, but in the story, he serves two terms, and "a year after his first term, he disappeared for nearly four years on a strange world tour"--during which time he was possessed by a Yithian. Upon his return to his body, he constructs the device known as the Sutro Lenses in an effort to reconstruct the secret of mind-swapping. 

### Setting
The story opens at Stockton State Hospital, "the lowest tier of California’s public mental hospital system." When Lorna and the narrator get out, they open their first meditation center in the hills of Berkeley. The cult's main headquarters are at Aspen, Colorado, which doubles as a fallout shelter.

The cult funds archaeological expeditions to Australia to explore the "fossil remnants of the Great Race’s library city," and Lorna and the narrator later take a trip 50 million years in the past there to the time when the Yithian civilization is being destroyed by the flying polyps.

The Sutro Lenses are found at the De Young Museum, a real-world institution in San Francisco's Golden Gate Park.

"Sybarites", also titled as "Sybarites, or, Enmity of Perverse Existence" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Doug Rinaldi. It was published in the James Ward Kirk Publishing thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark in November 2015.

### Synopsis
A man searching for his missing daughter finds her enslaved by a cult who operate a den of debauchery beneath a hollowed-out mountain. The object of their worship is a colossal creature which appears to feed on their acts of depravity, and in attempting a rescue, the man interrupts these rituals of obeisance. Although he is unable to save his daughter, his actions result in the death of the cult members; he then sets the creature's lair - a great pool of methanol - alight, and waits for the flames to consume him.

"SymbiOS" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
In a dystopian future which much of humankind have been laid low, a new performance-enhancement product has appeared on the market: the biote, a symbiotic entity engineered from both flatworm and Shoggoth DNA. However, the benefits are paired with a downside which nobody is aware of: when the human partner sleeps, the biote claims control of their body and directs it to work on digging a tunnel to connect the underground to the ocean. What purpose this will serve is not revealed.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, a former down-and-out who gives everything he owned to purchase a biote in the hope of improving his lot in life.

### Publication History
"SymbiOS" was first published in the Chaosium anthology Eldritch Chrome: Unquiet Tales of a Mythos-Haunted Future in October 2013. It was also included in the collection of Meikle's own work Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in April 2017.

Syththunu is a Great Old One (Dark Giant) created by DC Comics which appeared in the 6-part Eclipso Rising story arc with its first appearance in 2011 in issue #54 of Volume 2 of the Justice League of America comic series.

### Background
Synththunu is an Elder God, who at one time was feared and revered on Earth. Its dark power was respected by the Atlantean Mage Arion. He was imprisoned in a crystal small enough to be held in the palm of a man's hand. He was awakened and released by Eclipso in the early 21st century. He is an intelligent god with whom Eclipso communicated and he participated in Eclipso's assault on Emerald City, which fell within a quarter-hour.

The Elder God's form is that of a 100+ ft tall humanoid squid with a humanoid torso on top of tentacles, two clawed hands with four fingers each and tentacles on the lower part of his face. Alongside Eclipso and others he recruited or enthralled, Synththunu battled the Justice League of America on the surface of the Moon, using its arms and lower tentacles (which could stretch great lengths).

Theodore Eibon Donald Klein is an American writer and editor.

Klein wrote his honours thesis on H. P. Lovecraft while attending Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island. He added "Eibon" to his name in part as a nod to the character created by Clark Ashton Smith.

Although his fiction output has been relatively scant, Klein has garnered praise for the construction in his work, which includes stories such as "The Events at Poroth Farm". He was, along with others, responsible for the creation of the World Fantasy Convention in 1975, and "The Events at Poroth Farm" was nominated for Best Short Fiction at the first event. 

Among the publications he has edited, the Twilight Zone magazine is perhaps the most notable. As an editor, he had a hand in encouraging Ramsey Campbell with his early work.

T'yog is a fictional character from H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald's story "Out of the Aeons", an ancient priest turned into a mummy by the sight of Ghatanothoa. T'yog first appeared in the April 1935 issue of Weird Tales.

### High-Priest of Shub-Niggurath
T'yog's history is recounted in the story as information the narrator gleans from reading Von Junzt's Nameless Cults--a book invented by Lovecraft's friend Robert E. Howard in the short story "The Children of the Night". In "Out of the Aeons", the book recounts a myth from the lost continent of Mu, which flourished in what is now the Pacific Ocean some 200,000 years ago. In Mu there was said to be a land called K'naa, dominated by the priesthood of Ghatanothoa, an alien entity living beneath the sacred mountain Yaddith-Gho, and kept quiescent by annual human sacrifice.

T'yog, Von Junzt relates, was the High-Priest of Shub-Niggurath, the "guardian of the copper temple of the Goat with a Thousand Young"; the cleric, a "heretic" noted for his "skill and zeal", had "thought long on the powers of the various gods, and had had strange dreams and revelations touching the life of this and earlier worlds." He resented the power of the cult of Ghatanothoa, and believed that with his own god, along with the twin gods Nug and Yeb, and the Serpent-god Yig, were "ready to take sides with man against the tyranny and presumption of Ghatanothoa."

T'yog prepared to confront Ghatanothoa in his "alien-angled citadel of Cyclopean stone" by creating a scroll, written in "hieratic Naacal" on pthagon membrane (the inner skin of a yakith-lizard) and encased in "a carven cylinder of lagh metal" brought from Yuggoth, that would neutralize the power of the Daemon-God. On the Day of the Sky-Flames in the Year of the Red Moon--estimated to be 173,148 B.C. by Von Junzt--the High-Priest set forth , with the blessings of K'naa's King Thabon and the hopes of the people, to "confront the shocking devil-entity in its lair".

Unbeknownst to T'yog, however, the High-Priest of Ghatanothoa, Imash-Mo, had switched his scroll with an ineffectual facsimile, rendering him powerless against the Devil-God. Rather than breaking the power of Ghatanothoa, he was instead petrified by the sight of the horrific entity, transformed into a living mummy. In that immobile form, T'yog survived through the aeons as Mu sank beneath the waves of the Pacific.

### The Eridanus Mummy
T'yog's mummy was found on May 11, 1878, when the freighter Eridanus, en route from New Zealand to Chile, encountered a "new island unmarked on any chart", "suddenly upheaved from the Pacific's floor." In a "massive stone crypt" on the island, formed of "prehistoric Cyclopean masonry", Capt. Charles Weatherbee found the "ghastly, inexplicable mummy", which he brought back to Valparaiso. There it was acquired by Boston's Cabot Museum of Archaeology, which put it on display in November 1879.

Ta-Vho-Shai is a fictional character created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "Vulthoom".

### Overview
Ta-Vho-Shai is an Aihai who lives in the Martian underground country of Ravormos, beneath Ignar-Vath. Like the other Aihais of Ravormos, they are a servant of Vulthoom, a powerful creature from a world outside the solar system whose spaceship crashed on Mars in prehistory. The powers of Vulthoom grant its servants immortality in return for their loyalty. Like Vulthoom itself, they sleep and stay awake for alternating periods of a thousand years. In Aihais, this great longevity results in tremendous growth, so Ta-Vho-Shai and their brethren stand about 10 ft., a full yard taller than the average Aihai. (: "Vulthoom")

In the Unaussprechlichen Kulten, Friedrich von Junzt identifies Ta-Vho-Shai as the leader of the Aihais who serve Vulthoom, and blames the Elder Gods for imprisoning them in Ravormos. (: "The Horror in the Gallery")

Taffy, also known as The Pale Brown Thing, is a paramental creature brought into being through the focused black magic of Megapolisomancy. Her first appearance is in the horror novella Our Lady of Darkness by Fritz Leiber.

Taffy takes its / her physical form from a vaguely woman-shaped piled of old pulp magazines strewn across the protagonist's bed. At the climax of the story the magazines shred themselves into paper dust and form a dry pale brown face figure with a long tangle of dark "hair" and a snout for sucking bone marrow from its victims after it has choked them to death and shattered their bones.

Taffy fixates on those who handle or are exposed to a book of tables and magical formulae, a kind of mathematical cursed grimoire, created by her original summoner. Taffy in some ways is like a possessive, jealous and destructive lover, and at one point is referred to as "Scholar's Mistress" as her physical form gradually takes shape from the cast off magazine and books. This pile of paper begins to resemble a reclining woman with dark hair.

"Take Your Daughters to Work" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Livia Llewellyn. It was first published in issue #6 of the Subterranean Press magazine Subterranean in January 2007 .

### Synopsis
The New Y'ha-nthlei Steelworks is an industrial facility dedicated to raising submerged city from beneath the depths, one piece at a time, for reassembly on land. On the company's "take your daughter to work" day, the staff send their female offspring who are of age into the deep water to be used as breeding vessels for their aquatic compatriots.

### Behind the Mythos
The New Y'ha-nthlei Steelworks would appear to be attempting to rebuild the sunken city of Y'ha-nthlei, which was attacked and damaged - but not destroyed - during the events recounted in The Shadow Over Innsmouth. Why an aquatic species such as the Deep Ones would wish to have Y'ha-nthlei rebuilt on land is not explored.

In the story, the girls sent beneath the waves are attached to chains and hauled back out later, their corpses used as hosts for the parasitic offspring of whatever lurks at the site of old Y'ha-nthlei; this would suggest that whatever is using them as breeding vessels is something other than Deep Ones.

### Publication History

*Engines of Desire: Tales of Love & Other Horrors (2011, Lethe Press)

As given away in the title, Taken by the Scholar's Choice… is a drinking game which in which participants must take a drink each time a particular motif from Lovecraftian fiction or Shakespearean play appears in a story. The Taker of Souls is a fictional demon created by Rodo Sayagues in 2013 for the remake of Evil Dead.

### Background
The Taker of Souls is a non-corporeal entity which is summoned by the Ex-Mortis. The demon is extremely aggressive and has a tendency to horrifically mutilate those it possesses. It creates Deadites which are different from the usual Deadites, being less intelligent and talkative than the norm. Which are somewhat zombie-like and masochistic. It's Deadites are far more durable, requiring the destruction of their brains to stop them.

The demon possess superhuman strength and is supernaturally durable, being able to easily flip an automobile and continue functioning with both legs sliced off. It is able to possess humans and physically manifest itself as a twisted version of a human and later a nude and bloody human female. The demon possesses a type of thermokinesis, burning a human's hand by simply touching it. To summon its true form, requires five souls.

fullContent:
Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos is a Lovecraftian anthology first published by Arkham House in 1969, edited by H. P. Lovecraft's friend and literary executor August Derleth. Arkham House released a revised edition in 1990, edited by James Turner, that omitted four stories and added seven others. 

### Overview
First published by Arkham House in a hardcover format in 1969, Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos contains twenty stories with an introduction by Derleth. It has since been translated into French, and has actually had more French editions than English.

Although many of the stories were written by authors considered to be a part of Lovecraft's circle, it also contains a handful from more recent contributors to the Mythos. Six stories appeared for the first time in the volume, including pieces by Ramsey Campbell, Colin Wilson, J. Vernon Shea, James Wade, and two by Brian Lumley.

The 1990 version dropped four of the six stories original to the 1969 edition, keeping only Campbell and Wilson's contributions. It substituted a different Lumley story, "Rising with Surtsey". The added stories included one by Lovecraft Circle member Fritz Leiber, and pieces by Joanna Russ, Karl Edward Wagner, Philip José Farmer, Stephen King, and Richard A. Lupoff. A new introduction by James Turner was also included.

fullContent:
Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos is an anthology of Cthulhu Mythos fiction edited by Robert M. Price and published by Fedogan & Bremer in 1992; it was reissued in October 2002 with new cover art by John Jude Palencar. In March 2010, Mondadori issued an Italian-language translation of the book, titled I miti di Lovecraft, featuring cover art by Franco Brambilla.

### Overview
In his introduction, Price describes the volume as:

The editor notes that the book "covers the pulp era, but extends no further. We are concerned here with the foundational generation of Mythos writers."  It also is an attempt to "assemble the stories in which certain important Mythos names or items are either first mentioned or most fully explained by the author who created them":

Several of the stories in the collection appear in earlier forms that differ significantly from later revisions--including "The Lord of Illusion", the original draft of the story that became the H.P. Lovecraft/E. Hoffman Price collaboration "Through the Gates of the Silver Key".

Price's subsequent anthology The New Lovecraft Circle serves as a sequel of sorts to Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos, collecting work from the next generation of Lovecraftian writers.

* "Preface," by Robert Bloch
* "Introduction," by Robert M. Price
* "The Thing on the Roof" by Robert E. Howard

Taran-Ish is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Doom That Came to Sarnath".

### Background
Taran-Ish was a high priest of the city of Sarnath in the land of Mnar. When Sarnath conquered the city of Ib and exterminated the nonhuman beings that lived there, the warriors brought back to Sarnath a green stone idol of Bokrug, the Great Water Lizard. There it was set up in the high temple as a symbol of conquest over the old gods and a sign of leadership in Mnar. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

On the night after the idol was enshrined, eldritch lights were seen over the lake, and by morning the idol had mysteriously vanished. The high priest Taran-Ish was found dead, having died from some nameless fear, but before he died he had scrawled upon the altar of chrysolite the Sign of Doom to serve as a prophecy of warning. A thousand years later the prophecy was fulfilled with the complete destruction of Sarnath as a result of the vengeance of Bokrug. (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

Taranushi (also known as Lord of the Jinn) is a jinn from North African mythology. It was later incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game by Chaosium. (: Cthulhu Invictus)

### Background
Taranushi is an Outer God who was summoned to Earth by Simoon, a Saharan sorcerer. Easily breaking free of his spell, Taranushi coerced Simoon to bring the jinn to Earth. Which Taranushi let loose on the peoples of the Arabian desert and eastern Libya.

For decades, the Earth was their playground, traveling back and forth from their home dimension. Upon Simoon's death, they found themselves unable to return home. Enraged, the jinn rebelled against Taranushi, who was able to fight them off, but lost control of the jinn. He is both worshiped and hated by the jinn.

His giant form appears insubstantial as if made of smoke. One with greyish skin and tusks coming out of its mouth. Taranushi can take a form that is human in shape, jinn, or a combination of the two.

### Behind the Mythos
"Taranushi" (more properly, Tarnush  (Farsi: طارنوش or طارنوس) or Jann (Arabic: جان)) is the "Father of the Jinn" in North African and Arabic folklore. He was born of the hot wind of the Sahara desert (simmum (سموم)). "Born of the Earth" he is cognate with the Nephilim of Judaeo-Christian beliefs (and the meaning is the same: "Earth-born" or "born of the Earth"). 

Tarnush symbolizes a clouded mind that sees nothing, arrogance, deceit and blasphemous false rulership.

fullContent:
"Tarbis of the Lake" is a horror short story by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price first published in the February 1934 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
The story takes place in the French city of Lourdes. A man named John Rankin seeks the knowledge of a wise priest, Father Peytral, asking him about a woman named Tarbis. Peytral tells him of an ancient Egyptian queen of that name, who was rejected by Moses and fled to France. There she founded the cities of Tarbes and Lapurdum, the latter of which would become "a den of necromancers" and other black magicians, until it was flooded and turned into a lake adjacent to modern Lourdes.

Frightened, Rankin confides to Peytral that he believes that Tarbis Dulac, a girl he fell in love with in his youth, is actually the immortal Tarbis, still alive and unaged after several millennia, and that she now haunts him by appearing in his dreams, dressed in ancient garbs and murmuring words that he cannot understand.

Peytral advises Rankin to face his fears by speaking directly to Miss Dulac. Rankin follows the advice, visiting her that night and asking about her real age and nature. After several attempts to evade his questions and seduce him, Dulac finally gives in and leads Rankin to her room, where she shows him a sarcophagous containing the mummy of the real Queen Tarbis. She leaves Rankin and the mummy alone and closes the door, telling him that she will be waiting downstairs.

 (Weird Tales).]]
Rankin finds a box of cigarrettes and smokes one. He comes to the conclusion that Tarbis Dulac (whose surname is French for "of the lake") is nothing but a physical body projected by the consciousness of the still-living mummified woman. He recollects how she avoids being seen under daylight, and wonders if this might be because she lacks a shadow. At last, unable to contain his curiosity, he opens the casket and tears off the bandages of the mummy. Despite her withered state, he recognises the features of Tarbis Dulac, down to the same knife scar on her breast.

Terrified beyond words, Rankin sets fire to the mummy. Immediately, he hears the agonising screams of Dulac down in the living room and realises that he has killed her. Unable to face what he has done, he escapes through the window and runs into Father Peytral, who has been watching from a distance and correctly guesses what happened. Peytral tries to comfort Rankin by claiming that Tarbis' soul is now free, but Rankin is still plagued by the guilt of having killed the woman he once loved. Rejecting the priest's offer to pray for their souls, Rankin walks away in shame.

She rules over her own dimension but is not powerful enough to cross dimensions on her own power. The Tatsu are the serpentine elemental and celestial dragons of the Far East which originated in Chinese mythology (Long) and spread to Korean (Yong), Vietnamese (Rồng), and Japanese (Tatsu) mythology. Whom were first used in 2005 by Chaosium as a fictional race for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Background
The Tatsu are a race of dragons, elemental beings whom possess incredible powers over nature. There are two earthly types of dragons, the kazu-tsuchi whom have an affinity with the element of fire and the wata-tsumi who have an affinity with the element of water. The kazu-tsuchi live deep below the earth and when awake, their playing in the molten rivers causes earthquakes. It can breathe a flames or spit lava, and cause volanic eruptions or earthquakes. The wata-tsumi in turn live in bodies of water, and control the rains. It can breathe a torrent of water and call forth tsunamis. The heavenly dragons live in the Palace of the Green Dragon. It breathes blasts of wind or shoots lightining bolts, and their aerobatics cause thunder and typhoons. They feed from their element (e.g. moisture, flame, etc).

They regenerate by siphoning Chi from their element and are able to communicae with humans via telepathy, projecting images. Dragons can also summon and consult with Mythos entities. Fire dragons usually call upon Cthugha or Tulzscha, water dragons contact Yig or Cthulhu, and heavenly dragons consult Nyarlathotep or Hastur. The water dragons use bodies of water, fire dragons will visit volcanoes or fires, and heavenly dragons will use electricity, Chi, and spirit. Dragons are the personification of Earth's life force, Gaia's living will. They are Earth's natural defense system, basically the bio-system's white blood cells which attacks non-terrestrial invaders.

Due to the human race, the Earth is slowly being killed by their overexploitation of its natural resources and the pollution they've generated. Which has kept dragons in a deep slumber and caused the some of them to disappear. It's in the Dreamlands, where the most active dragons are located. On Earth, their lairs are known as "dragon paths" (ley lines), with the dragon's lifeforce within the energy lines crisscrossing the planet.

The Tcho-Tcho people are a fictional species of hominids in the Cthulhu Mythos. They were originally created by August Derleth and Mark Schorer for their short story "The Lair of the Star-Spawn".

### Background
The Tcho-Tcho people are a group of tribes of near-human beings native to Asia. They can be found in Burma, The Anderman Isles, Tibet, and Malaysia. They are genetically from humans, but they are notably smaller, have livid red skin, and other marked physiological differences. Legends point to prehistoric genetic engineering of pre-human ancestors by the Great Old Ones Zhar and Lloigor. These legends purport they "grew from the 'seeds' of the Twin Obscenities".

The Tcho-Tcho people are feared by other tribes and appear to be inimical to Mankind, while worshiping various deities including Han, Chaugnar Faugn, Rhan-Tegoth, Hastur and his spawn. They appear to be the "corpse-eating cult of Leng" mentioned in the Necronomicon and have "lamas" as priests (cf. Elder Hierophant). One source suggests that only the warrior caste are bred small. They might be related to the Men of Leng in the Dreamlands. The name Tcho means "destroyer" or "sorcerer", thus the Tcho-Tcho people are the "destructive sorcerer people."

One of their delicacies is the Bak Bon Dzshow, or Human Ganglia Paste, a sauce spread over vegetables which takes days to prepare beforehand. The translation is generally given as "White Pork Sauce" with white pork meaning human flesh. As its real name suggests, it is made of pounded human ganglia and ordinary elements. It tastes like creamed artichokes with a hot peppery aftertaste. Humans eating it will dream of cannibalistic orgies. (: At Your Door)

One source claims that an offshoot of the Tcho-Tcho at one point interbred with the Miri Nigri, a species created by Chaugnar Faugn from amphibious flesh in early Earth history. This tribe, who reside "on the desert plateau of Tsang in the Far East near Tibet," worship Chaugnar Faugn, and believe in a prophecy which states that the coming of a "White Acolyte" will see the beginning of Chaugnar's ascendancy over the Earth .

### In the Marvel Multiverse
Though they have yet to appear, the Tcho-Tcho people were stated to exist in the Marvel Universe. At some point between his vampirification (circa 18,500 BC) and 1000 AD, Varnae, Lord and first of the Vampires, stated that the Tcho-Tcho had known him as Tsathoggua, presumably worshiping him. (: "Norse Blood")

### Behind the Mythos
Robert W. Chambers mentions a species called "Tchortcha" who might be the same as the Tcho-Tcho.

The Tcho-Tcho were also featured prominently in the story Black Man with a Horn by T. E. D. Klein.

The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles are fictional characters that were originally created by Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird. They first appeared in Mirage Studios' 1984 comic book series of the same name, which later spawned a multimedia franchise with numerous other comics, animated series, movies and video games that are still being produced to this day.

### Background
The Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles are a group of turtles that became anthropomorphic after being exposed to a substance known as Mutagen. Leonardo is the leader of the group with the other members including Donatello, Michelangelo and Raphael. They live in the sewers of New York City with their master Splinter, who is a mutant rat that trained them in Ninjutsu to fight crime. Some of their most notable enemies are the Shredder, Baxter Stockman and the Kraang.

In most of their incarnations, the Ninja Turtles wear different color bandanas to distinguish them. However, this was not the case in the original comic, as this concept was introduced in the 1987 animated series. Another notable change that also originated from the animated series is that Master Splinter used to be a human named Hamato Yoshi, while in the original comic, he was just Yoshi's pet rat before his owner died.

Mirage Studios' comic series features several encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos. While teaming up with Clark Ashton Allard (a nod to Clark Ashton Smith), the Ninja Turtles managed to fight off Dagon and his vampire cult. (: "Men of Shadow") The Norse god Loki summoned Nyarlathotep to attack them but the ritual was interrupted by Michelangelo. (: "Hall of Lost Legends") Leonardo once found a copy of De Vermis Mysteriis in an abandoned building. (: "Circle of Darkness") Savanti Juliet resurrected several famous people from the past to ambush the Ninja Turtles. However, after H. P. Lovecraft refused to help her, Juliet punished him by banishing his soul to R'lyeh. The ghost of Robert E. Howard also references Lovecraft when he mentions his nickname "Two-Gun Bob" to Raphael. (: "Juliet's Revenge")

When the Elder Gods broke free from unspace, the IDW incarnation of the Ninja Turtles had their universe invaded by Shub-Niggurath. (: Infestation 2)

Other incarnations also have some Lovecraftian themes. In the 1987 animated series, the Shredder cast a spell that accidentally summoned an extra-dimensional tentacle monster at a subterranean temple, with both the spell and the temple being used by a cult during the 1920s. (: "Splinter No More") In the 2003 animated series, the Ninja Turtles were forced to face their worst fears while under the influence of the Necro Monster, an extraterrestrial entity that resembles Cthulhu.
