Tekeli is a Lovecraftian entity from the fictional universe of the Uchi no Meido ha Futeikei light novel series. 

### Background
Billions of years ago, Tekeli's species were created by the Great Old Ones to be their servants. The Great Old Ones were very abusive towards their servants, forcing them to work nonstop with no breaks and even sending them to wars that got many of them killed. The servants eventually went on strike, which lead to their masters punishing Tekeli by sealing her away beneath Antarctica. Although her imprisonment was meant to last forever, Tekeli was freed in the present day after she was discovered by an archeologist. The archeologist sent Tekeli to Tokyo's Ninagawa Ward in Japan so that his son Tooru Araizawa could be her new master. Due to both Tooru and his father treating her with kindness, Tekeli willingly became Tooru's new servant and tried to her best to help him as much as she can. (: Uchi no Meido ha Futeikei)

### Powers and Abilities
Although she usually takes the form of a female human maid, Tekeli has been described as being a "formless entity" with her true form being a ball of amorphous slime. Her body is composed of something akin to embryonic stem cells, allowing her to generate new limbs and sensory organs at will. She is also capable of separating herself into multiple Tekelis, which explains why she always addresses herself as "we". This ability has no upper limit and each Tekeli's abilities are not hindered by the division, as they are all the same entity. Tekeli is also effectively immortal and has superhuman strength.

### In Other Media
*Haiyore! Nyaruko-san: Tekeli has made several cameos throughout the series. She is described as being "a legendary monster that isn't sold anywhere except in the Ninagawa Ward of Japan on Earth!".

fullContent:
"Tekeli-li, They Cry" is a Lovecraftian short story by Canadian author A. C. Wise. It was first published in the Broken Eye Books anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu in January 2016.

### Synopsis
On a future Earth where reality is broken and time has little meaning, a grieving mother takes a job at a near-abandoned Antarctic research station in the belief that somehow, in that place, she may be reunited with her daughter. As her colleagues succumb to madness and the voices in her head intensify, she does indeed meet her daughter, as something vast and terrible begins to stir beneath the ice.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to either Lovecraft's work or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the title of "Tekeli-li, They Cry", which is a reference to the vocalisation made by the Shoggoth in At the Mountains of Madness, is a clear statement of the author's intent for the story to be a part of the Mythos. Additionally, the theme of humans driven to insanity by forces utterly beyond their ability to understand is a core tenet of Lovecraftian horror.

### Publication History
*Tomorrow's Cthulhu (2016)
*The Dark, August 2017 (2017)
*The Ghost Sequences (2021)

Temphill is a fictional English town, created by Ramsey Campbell in his first published story, "The Church in High Street", which introduced the Severn Valley setting in which Temphill is located. In the introduction to The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, Campbell describes it as 

In "The Church in High Street", Temphill is called a "decaying Cotswold town" and "a place of ill repute." The story's narrator notes that

The region around Temphill is dominated by "grim, brooding plains, sparsely habited, where the only vegetation was a grey, diseased grass and an infrequent bloated oak." There is also a thickly forested marsh, however, and a "densely wooded hillside" that bears "the aspect of a primeval forest."

### The Church
The "shunned church"--a temple on a hill--inspired the name of the town, which grew up around it; in his introduction, Campbell notes that it is "reported to be other-dimensional". The church is said to exist "conterminously" with a temple of Yog-Sothoth:

It's said that "the majority of the people of Temphill still visit the church on the right nights." Those who penetrate the catacombs beneath the church, reached via a trap door beneath the first set of pews, find themselves unaccountably unable to leave the town, as if the streets were turning back on themselves. This is an effect of the Tomb Herd, extra-dimensional predators who dwell in the crypt.

Other than the church, the main attraction of Temphill seems to be Poole's General Store, on the ground floor of a three-storey building with a collapsed roof.

### Characters
In "The Church on High Street", Temphill is home to John Clothier, "a man possessed of an extraordinary amount of ancient knowledge," and formerly Albert Young, a young man working on a "book on witchcraft and witchcraft lore." In the subsequent story "The Horror From the Bridge," Temphill is where James Phipps acquires "extremely rare chemicals," as well as his mysterious wife.

"The Franklyn Paragraphs" lists Temphill as one of the places visted by "the circle of young men" around cult leader Roland Franklyn. Franklyn's widow, complaining about the horrors he had put her through, says: "He took me down to Temphill, and made me watch those things dancing on the graves."

The Temple of Chthon is a fictional temple in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 2016 in the #13 issue of the 2nd volume of Carnage.

### Background
The Temple of Chthon (aka, the Temple of the Darkhold) is located on the Chthonic Island. It's a massive temple with eldritch statuary and wall sculptures, which has a stairway that goes deep into the Earth. Deep under the temple is a nether region, between the material world and Chthon's reality. Where the rules of Euclidean geometry and Newtonian Physics no longer apply. The psychopathic supervillian Carnage entered the temple where he temporarily brought Chthon to Earth.

"Tender Is the Night-gaunt" is a comedy short story by Peter Cannon which parodically combines the worlds of F. Scott Fitzgerald's Tender Is the Night and H. P. Lovecraft's The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, featuring characters from both novels interacting in the Dreamlands setting. First published in 1998 in The Mammoth Book of Comic Fantasy, this story is also included in Cannon's 2011 collection Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches.

### Synopsis
In the French Riviera, young Rosemary Hoyt is madly in love with a psychiatrist named Richard Diver. When she learns from a hotel's concierge that Dr. Diver and his wife Nicole have moved to a place named Dreamland, she decides to follow them, descending the seven hundred steps to the Gate of Deeper Slumber.

In a peaceful villa near Ulthar ("peaceful" save for the ongoing war between the cats and the zoogs, that is), Rosemary sneaks into a party being hosted by Diver, with several distinguished guests in attendance. Diver sits her between Atal and Kranon. The guests notice that Nicole is not present, and Nasht announces that he saw something unbelievable in the bathroom. At this point, however, he is interrupted by the arrival of King Kuranes and Randolph Carter. The conversation moves to the topic of whether Carter should continue in his quest to Kadath. Atal in particular is firmly against it, claiming that it will spell doom for everyone. Another interruption comes when a pack of Ghouls arrive led by former artist Richard Upton Pickman.

The next day, the two Richards (Diver and Pickman) accompany Rosemary and the other survivors of the party through a trench while showing the sites where a terrible battle was fought, with the Ghouls and Night-gaunts on one side against the amorphous Moon-beasts and their allies on the other side. Rosemary confesses her love for Diver and he, in turn, confesses his own matrimonial problems. It is revealed that the scene Nasht saw in the bathroom the previous night was Nicole having a mental breakdown. Hoping that a long trip will help to cure her, the Divers have decided to travel to Kadath with Randolph Carter. Diver invites Rosemary to come along, which she accepts eagerly.

The journey is detoured by several misadventures, from getting captured by the black galleys and brought to the moon (from which they are rescued by friendly cats), to encounters with Gugs and Ghasts in the vale of Pnath (from which they are saved by friendly Ghouls), to Nicole crashing a galleon into a wharf off the shore of Celephaïs. After that last incident, the group meets King Kuranes again, but the visit turns sour when Diver notices the attention the king is directing towards Rosemary. The ensuing fight involves a waiter, a cab diver, and a viscous bhole. Kuranes, despite being a righteous king, loses his temper and sends Diver and the bhole to a dungeon, where they will await trial. The Tengu are part of Japanese folklore. In 2005 they were first used by Chaosium as a fictional race for the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

### Background
The Tengu are an alien race of bird-like humanoids that have crow-like features, talons, shiny black wings, a beak and bird-like feet along with human-like hands and a bipedal form. Its members can live for centuries, with elders growing long wiry beards. They cannot fly but travel via astral apportation, in which they turn into an energy state, travel via the astral plane, and reform physically elsewhere. Due to being multi-dimensional entities, they can regenerate by drawing ethereal energy from the astral plane. Tengu are incredibly agile and due to their ascetic training they are also highly skilled martial artists who are able to harness their Chi to increase the power of their strikes and able to use pressure points to stun, immobilize, or kill opponents.

The Tengu arrived on Earth over 50,000 years ago and have settled the mountainous regions of Asia, and since then have intermittently warred with the Mi-Go over territory. Tengu originally shared their home star system with the byakhee. Seeking to become the masters of Aldebaran, for many millennia they waged war against the byakhee. On the verge of defeat the byakhee appealed to Hastur for help, whom demenaded their servitude. To destroy the byakhee, the Tengu summoned Ghroth. It consumed the byakhee homeworld, which then plunged into its sun, resulting in a cataclysm. The Tengu fled and scattered across the cosmos, some of whom arrived on Earth. Because of this, the Tengu have become the sworn enemies of Hastur. Due to the influence on Buddhism by one of his avatars, the Emerald Lama, the Tengu are usually antagonistic toward Buddhist institutions. They enjoy tricking and tormenting Buddhist monks, leading them astray. They are a mystical race whose members can weave illusionary magics to fool the senses, communicate via telepathy and, if skilled enough, can possess the body of a human.

The Terrible Old Man is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story of the same name. He also plays a minor role in "The Strange High House in the Mist".

### Overview
The Terrible Old Man is an extremely aged man who lives alone in an old cottage on Water Street, in the coastal town of Kingsport. Feared and shunned by most of his neighbours, he is known to consort with supernatural forces or entities. His physical appearance is that of a frail and elderly man with long white hair and beard, and yellow eyes, who walks with the help of a cane. This apparent physical frailty, however, is highly misleading, as the robbers Angelo Ricci, Joe Czanek, and Manuel Silva learned the hard way. (: "The Terrible Old Man")

### Biography
The Terrible Old Man's family has been living in Kingsport for at least three generations, as he remembers stories his father and grandfather told about the One who has lived in the Strange High House in the Mist since the Terrible Old Man's grandfather was a little boy. (: "The Strange High House in the Mist")

In his youth, the Terrible Old Man used to be a sea captain, and is known to have amassed a treasure of gold and silver in his travels. By the time the stories take place, he is "so old that no one can remember when he was young" and still uses "Spanish gold and silver minted two centuries ago" to pay for his groceries. Dogs bark in his presence, suggesting an aura of danger. He has a collection of large painted stones arranged in a peculiar way in his front yard. Inside the house he has a bare room with a table, upon which are kept several bottles, each with a piece of lead suspended by a pendulum. Those who have peered through the window claim that they have seen the Terrible Old Man talking to these bottles, calling them names such as Jack, Scar-Face, Long Tom, Spanish Joe, Peters, and Mate Ellis, and the lead pendulums vibrate as if they were answering him. (: "The Terrible Old Man")

Although he is "not fond of strangers", the Terrible Old Man did invite Thomas Olney into his cottage and told him what he wanted to know about the One who lives in the Strange High House in the Mist. After Olney visited the One and returned, he talked to the Terrible Old Man again about the events that took place in that mysterious abode. The Terrible Old Man listened to him and came to the conclusion that the Olney who returned was "not wholly" the same. (: "The Strange High House in the Mist")

Terror Australis is a background and scenario gamebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, first released in 1987 and revised in 2018 to bring it in line with the contemporary version of the game.

### Overview




### Behind the Mythos
The first edition of Terror Australis, written by Penelope Love, Mark Morrison, Lynn Willis, Larry DiTillio, and Sandy Petersen, was published in a paperback format in 1987, and was reissued as a PDF download in 2004. 

In 2019, a full-colour revised edition was released, which replaced the three scenarios included in the original book with two new scenarios, and significantly increased the page count (from 136 pages in the first edition to 304 pages in the new edition). Additional material from contemporary Cthulhu Mythos authors and games designers such as Brian M. Sammons, Lynne Hardy, Dean Engelhardt, Geoff Gilan, Marion Anderson, Phil Anderson, Richard Watts and Mike Mason was also included, with new content including details about the cities of Perth, Adelaide and Brisbane accompanied by new maps, as well as significantly expanded coverage of the major cities of Melbourne and Sydney. The new edition of Terror Australis also includes expanded sections on Australian history, the LGBT+ community of the period, law and order, criminal activity, and more.

fullContent:
"Terror of Tribeč" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Martin Korda which takes place in Modiphius Entertainment's Achtung! Cthulhu roleplaying game setting. It was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius in 2015.

### Synopsis
A dying old man tells the story of how, as a child living in a  remote area of occupied Czechoslovakia during the Second World War, he assisted a covert team of British soldiers in tracking down and destroying The Book of Shadows, a mystical tome which had fallen into the hands of the Nazi-sponsored Black Sun.

The man, whose younger brother had been kidnapped by occupation forces barracked at a remote mountain castle, leads the British squad to the Nazi fortress via secret pathways known only to a handful of locals. There they find the entirety of the garrison dead, apparently slaughtered by their own hands, and the bodies of numerous little creatures known as Saldroth - entities capable of creating and magnifying the fear felt by others a thousandfold in order to feed upon it - scattered about. Also present is the man's young brother, Ondrej, apparently unharmed.

As the soldiers set charges to demolish the castle, they are picked off one by one by the stealthy Saldroth. It also soon becomes apparent that Ondrej's body has been taken over by Von Asberg, the camp's sorcerous commandant. Fortunately for the boy, Ondrej's sequestered consciousness manages to stall Von Asberg long enough for his brother to make his escape and allow the explosives time to do their work.

In the aftermath, the narrator is found by roaming hunters and taken to hospital, where he is approached by British agents who swear him to secrecy on the subject.

Tesla vs Lovecraft is a video game released in 2018 for PC by 10tons Ltd. It is a top-down shooter inspired by the creatures of the Cthulhu Mythos. The player controls Nikola Tesla as he tries to secure the Wardenclyffe Tower from H. P. Lovecraft and his hordes of eldritch creatures.

The player will battle with various creatures from Cthulhu Mythos (e.g Deep Ones, Shoggoths, Flying Polyps, Fire Vampires, Spiders of Leng) as well as some new creatures designed by developers (e.g. Awakener, Eldritch Tentacle) while possessing an armory consisting early 20th century weapons (Colt M1911, Thompson Submachine gun) as well as sci-fi weapons (e.g plasma gun, ray gun) as well as a battle mech and various upgrades.

fullContent:
"Testimony XVI" is a short story by American author Lynda E. Rucker, which is loosely tied to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
Presented as a found manuscript, "Testimony XVI" gives a view-from-the-ground perspective on the fall of humankind. Two young women take to the road in search of one of their boyfriends as colossal monsters emerge from beneath the ocean, heralding a rash of earthquakes and nightmarish dreams.

The manuscript is stated to have been found in the "Pacific Northwest Exclusion Zone," however, implying that the end of the world might not have been as complete as the author feared.

### Mythos Connections
The beginning of the story features the legend "Classified by: Hastur Project Team," although what this organisation's remit might be is not explored.

### References

The Teumessian Fox is a monster of Greek mythology, a gigantic fox sent to prey on the children of Thebes. In the Marvel fictional universe it is mentioned as being one of the offspring of Echidna but it has not yet made an appearance in Marvel Comics.

### Background
The Teumessian Fox is a descendant of the Elder God Set. It's the offspring of Set's granddaughter Echidna who mated with Typhon, one of the Titans. The giant fox which was destined never to be caught, was sent by the gods to punish the inhabitants of Thebes by preying on its children. The regent of Thebes trained Laelaps, magical dog which is destined to catch anything it pursues to hunt the fox. Resulting in the two ending up in an eternal chase.

fullContent:
Th'rygh, also known as The God-Beast, is a minor Great Old One created by Irish games designer Gareth Ryder-Hanrahan, which made its first appearance in his 2002 scenario supplement Verboten! Operation: FAUST for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Description
Little is known about Th'rygh, other than that it is a monstrous entity which manifests as a horrible patchwork of flesh, soil, and alien matter, and that it is capable of absorbing organic matter - including living creatures - with the slightest brush of its transparent tentacles.

### History
During the spring of 1945, elements of the SS enacting Operation: WEREWOLF under the direct orders of Adolf Hitler attempted to summon Th'rygh using a passage from the Necronomicon. Their goal: to destroy the Red Army which was inexorably driving towards Berlin. When the Allies got wind of this plot, agents of the American Office of Naval Intelligence department Delta Green were parachuted in to thwart their scheme.

Thalarion is a coastal city in the Dreamlands of Earth also known as the City of a Thousand Wonders.

### Description
A mighty city surrounded grey stone walls that hide most of the frieze covered buildings and alluring sculptures. Its temple spires however reach into the sky, far enough for their peaks to be invisible to the naked eye. Within the walls its streets are littered with unburied bones. 

A stone pier leads to the huge carven gate of Akariel.

### Geography

*South of Zar by sea.

### Residents
Though many men enter none leave and the streets are home to daemons and mad things that are no longer men.

*Lathi - An eidolon who rules the city and reduces those who see it to skeletons

Thana Niveau (born 1971 in Houston, Texas, USA) is an American-born author who has written a number of stories connected to and inspired by H. P. Lovecraft and the Cthulhu Mythos. These have appeared in anthologies such as Steampunk Cthulhu (2014, Chaosium), The Children of Gla'aki (2017, Dark Regions Press), and Lovecraft Mythos: New & Classic Collection (2020, Flame Tree Press).

Niveau has included Edgar Allan Poe, Stephen King, and Ramsey Campbell as amongst her early influences. She has also expressed a deep fascination with the literary genre of underwater horror, and several of her works incorporate an aquatic motif.

Thanaroa is a mysterious entity introduced in Abraham Merritt's fantasy novel The Moon Pool. Its name recalls that of Polynesian creator god Tangaroa.

Although unseen in the novel, Thanaroa is the primal god worshiped by the Murians, and is distinct from and greater than the Dweller in the Moon Pool (a.k.a. the Shining One).

### Description
Thanaroa is a creator god and the highest deity worshiped in the ancient continent of Muria in the South Pacific (cf. Lemuria or Mu), where the ruins of Nan-Matal in Ponape now stand. When most of the continent sank, its people migrated to an underground land that they also named Muria, and continued to worship the same gods, with Thanaroa as the greatest, albeit the most distant, indifferent to the affairs of man.

Dr. Walter T. Goodwin believes that Thanaroa is the original name of the Polynesian god Tangaroa, suggesting that its cult has persisted long after the sinking of Muria. The Russian scientist Marakinoff was familiar with it, and gained the confidence of the Murian ruler Lugur by making a gesture in praise of Thanaroa. The Silent Ones' handmaiden, Lakla, described Thanaroa as "the maker of all things, dwelling far away". (: The Moon Pool)

### Behind the Mythos
The Moon Pool was originally published in two parts, titled "The Moon Pool" (1918) and "Conquest of the Moon Pool" (1919). The novel is sometimes cited as an influence on "The Call of Cthulhu" by H. P. Lovecraft, which may in turn have itself influenced Merritt's later story Dwellers in the Mirage.

"That Tantalizing Taste You Will Never Forget" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A gifted advertising specialist is offered a lucrative position with an Innsmouth-based company which deals in fish-based products. After a while, he stumbles across the dark truth of the organisation: that it is run by Deep One hybrids, and their foodstuffs are in fact a catalyst which begins the transformation from human to Deep One in those who consume it.

### Characters
*Derek Prince, a highly-skilled publicist employed as the marketing director for foods manufacturer Sea Bounty.
*Minerva, a senior executive with Sea Bounty.
*Mrs. Hamogeorgakis, the managing director of Sea Bounty.
*Edie Prince, Derek's wife.

### Publication History
"That Tantalizing Taste You Will Never Forget" was published in the 2018 collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Trivia
*The title of the story, "That Tantalizing Taste You Will Never Forget", was taken from Sea Bounty's marketing slogan.
*A member of the Marsh family, Ezra, is mentioned to have worked for Sea Bounty near the end of the story.

fullContent:
"That Which Lurks" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Frank Forte. It was published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
When young scholar Robert Doleman meets elderly fanatic Jacob Reid, the two unite their separate goals through a common means: Doleman wishes to discover the hidden truth behind the universe, while Reid craves the return of his dead wife, killed by a supernatural force years before.

Abandoning their moral codes, the two use a ritual they uncovered in the cursed Necronomicon to summon the mighty Outer God Yog-Sothoth; their wishes are granted after a fashion, Reid being horrifically merged with his dead wife's reanimated corpse, and Doleman witnessing the coming to Earth of Cthulhu and his spawn before being driven to insanity.

term: Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-England Canaan
shortDefinition: Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-England Canaan is a fictional book invented by H. P. Lovecraft in notes that were incorporated into August Derleth's "posthumous collaboration," The Lurker at the Threshold. It is described as a book written by Rev...
fullContent:
Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-England Canaan is a fictional book invented by H. P. Lovecraft in notes that were incorporated into August Derleth's "posthumous collaboration," The Lurker at the Threshold. It is described as a book written by Rev. Ward Phillips, pastor of the Second Church of Arkham, that reports on supernatural phenomenon in New England.

In the novel a copy of the book is found by Ambrose Dewart. The copy, bound in black imitation leather, was printed in Boston in 1801, but this is not believed to be the first edition. Dewart reads a passage regarding one Goodwife Doten, who around Candlemas 1787 brought forth a child who looked "like a monstrous Bat with human face." The child was said to resemble the long-dead "Richard Bellingham or Bollinghan"--a reference to the wizard Richard Billington.

Alijah Billington, Richard's descendant, took offense at this reference to his relative, and wrote a short note to an Arkham newspaper advising Phillips that "there [are] things in existence better left alone and kept from the common speach." The paper printed a sharp retort to this from Phillips, but he later seemed to heed the advice, as he reportedly tried to gather up every copy of the book and burn them.

fullContent:
The Abbey: Resources for Cthulhu Dark Ages is a supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu offshoot Cthulhu Dark Ages.

### Overview
Split into three sections, The Abbey contains background allowing Keepers to run games in medieval France. The first section provides information on St. Bartholomew's Abbey, a pregenerated backdrop in southeast France of 982AD; section two takes a look at France during the period, giving some flavour for the region at the time; the final section offers a look at the priestly Order of St. Jerome, a set of non-player characters for investigators to interact with.

The Abbey was written by Michael Patty.

### Publication History
First issued as physical work in February 2004, The Abbey also received a digital release. It is currently unavailable in either format.

fullContent:
"The Abominations of Nephren-Ka" is a short story by authors Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. 

### Synopsis
When the High Priest of Horus, a man named Mnekh, discovers the existence of a city hidden near his home, he resolves to put an end to the evil festering within. Gathering about himself an army of the righteous, he marches on the City of Night, but is betrayed by one he saw as a friend and his men slaughtered. Despite this setback, he manages to cleanse the city by calling on the power of his god, who burns the evil with cleansing fire. 

### Characters
*Mnekh, a child born of Horus who grows up to become the head of his cult. 
*Tsoth/Nephren-Ka, a wicked king who has prolonged his life through sacrifices to his dark god. 
*The Living Shroud, an avatar of Nyarlathotep.
*Pash, Mnekh's mother. 

### Publication History
"The Abominations of Nephren-Ka" was published in the anthology Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in 2018.

### Trivia
*The story mentions that evil came to the City of Night through a strange artefact dubbed the Eye of Yuggoth. Given the description of the Eye and its function, this is certainly intended to be the Shining Trapezohedron from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Haunter of the Dark".

All of the stories were included in the later collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

fullContent:
"The Abyss" is a short story by American author and Lovecraft contemporary Robert A. W. Lowndes.

### Synopsis
A group of university friends dabbling in the occult unwittingly summon a being of great power which offers one of their number to its masters, a race of sadistic extra-dimensional creatures.

### Characters
*Unnamed Narrator, a member of a circle of friends with an interest in the occult.
*Graf Norden, another member of the group, and the one with the most learning in the subject.
*Dureen, a creature known as a seeker, sent forth by its masters the Adumbrali to fetch them fresh playthings.
*Colby, another member of the group, apparently quite foolhardy.

### Publication History
"The Abyss" first saw print in the February 1941 issue of Stirring Science Stories and has been reprinted many times in many different publications.

### Trivia

*"The Abyss" saw the first appearance of Lowndes' occult manuscript the Song of Yste, which is spoken of in the same context as the Necronomicon and the Book of Eibon.

fullContent:
The Acolyte was a fanzine edited by Francis Towner Laney assisted by Duane W. Rimel and Samuel D. Russell from 1942-1946 (a total of 14 issues), dedicated to articles about horror and fantasy fiction, with particular emphasis on H. P. Lovecraft and his circle, and occasional fiction and poetry. It has been widely considered to be the premier fanzine of the 1940s and was certainly the one with the best and closest connections to the Circle. It was nominated for the 1946 Retrospective Hugo Award for Best Fanzine, losing to Forrest J Ackerman's Voice of the Imagi-Nation.

fullContent:
"The Acolyte of the Flame (A Translation of Fragment MXI of the Pnakotic Manuscripts)" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Lin Carter, first published in the Yuletide 1985 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu by Cryptic Press.

### Synopsis
In the last days of Hyperborea, as the ice sheet advances and renders all the northern lands uninhabitable, a group of men known as the Pnakotic Brethren persist in their mission to preserve and expand upon the historical records first compiled by the Great Race of Yith.

One of the archivists, named Athlok, translates a passage which blames the ice age on Aphoom-Zhah, the Cold Flame, a son of Cthugha who descended to Earth from Neptune and was imprisoned by the Elder Gods under the ice mountain, Yarak, at the north pole. The passage also contains the prophecy of a Voormi shaman who claimed that a "Savior" would come bearing a mark on his chest like a grey flame. Athlok himself has a grey flame-shaped birthmark and concludes that the prophecy refers to him.

Despite being conflicted by the existence of another prophecy that claims that the whole of Hyperborea would indeed be engulfed by ice, Athlok hopes to be able to save his homeland. He drinks the golden mead and summons the Byakhee to take him to Yarak, then enters a cave at the base of the mountain that leads him to an abyss where he finds a star-shaped stone and breaks it. But rather than destroying Aphoom-Zhah as he expected, this act liberates the monster, causing Athlok to flee and the glaciers to expand before covering the entire continent. Too late does Athlok realize his error, in that the prophecy referred to the "Savior" of Aphoom-Zhah, not of Hyperborea.

Reasoning that no punishment could ever be proportional to the crime he committed, the Pnakotic Brethren simply order Athlok to write down his narrative and add it to the archives, so that history will know that he was the one who doomed the whole continent.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance in Crypt of Cthulhu, "The Acolyte of the Flame" has also been included in Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu Fiction anthology The Book of Eibon (2002).

### Trivia
*"The Acolyte of the Flame" marks the first appearance of the Great Old One Aphoom-Zhah.

fullContent:
"The Advent of Uhvash" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by American author and editor James Ambuehl.

### Synopsis
A man is invited to visit his friend, bringing with him some books on "Black Magic". It transpires that his friend has begun to experiment with intense Astral Projection, assisted by the Great Old One known as Gi-Hoveg, in defiance of another Great Old One, Uhvash. It ends very badly for the narrator's astrally projecting friend.

### Publication History
"The Advent of Uvhash" was first published in the anthology Mythos Tales & Others in 1996, and later appeared in Midnight Shambler #9 in August 1998.

### Behind the Mythos
The story features a laundry list of books related to the Cthulhu Mythos, some of which are creations of the author. The texts named are "the accursed Blood-Rituals of Rhylkos, Cultes des Goules, The R'lyeh Text: Fragmentary Transcriptions, the Confessions of the Mad Monk Clithanus, the Caelano Fragments,  the Clavicule Cosmopgraphicum, The Ultimate War, Devil-Gods of the Lu-Kthu Mythos, and the Book of Non Amya. 

The Marvel Comics superhero Doctor Strange is mentioned as a comics character, indicating that the story takes place in a universe where Marvel's own contributions to the Mythos are likely fictional.

term: The Adventure of the Voorish Sign
shortDefinition: "The Adventure of the Voorish Sign" is a Sherlock Holmes pastiche crossing over with the Cthulhu Mythos by Richard A. Lupoff. It was originally published in the anthology Shadows Over Baker Street, in 2003. Based on the characterization of Doctor Wat...
fullContent:
"The Adventure of the Voorish Sign" is a Sherlock Holmes pastiche crossing over with the Cthulhu Mythos by Richard A. Lupoff. It was originally published in the anthology Shadows Over Baker Street, in 2003. Based on the characterization of Doctor Watson in this story it is reasonable to conclude that it is the Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce version of Holmes and Watson, or characters very like them, that are intended to be portrayed.

### Synopsis
Holmes and Watson are visited by Lady Fairclough with a missing persons case. Her husband has disappeared and her brother has married a sinister foreign woman. Their marriage ceremony was off, too, being presided over by a mysterious priestess who made a bizarre hand gesture that Lady Fairclough is unable to replicate. However even the lady's description of the hand gesture, intended to be the Voorish Sign, is enough information for Holmes to begin formulating a theory. Sherlock Holmes then leads an expedition to Lady Fairclough's family home, a stately manor known as the Anthracite Palace.

Once there, her new sister-in-law unabashedly invites them all to take part in a ceremony sponsored by her religion, the Wisdom Temple of the Dark Heavens.  Everyone agrees with apparenty civility and amicability despite Lady Fairclough's deep disquiet and Holmes' suspicions. Holmes reveals to Watson that he, Holmes, has been maintaining a treasure trove of texts in his secret library of occult tomes. Holmes summarizes the works he has available, which avoid the usual namechecking of titles but does, Holmes notes, contain the complete works of Arthur Machen. And he explains his certainty that the mysterious hand gestures is surely the "Voorish Sign", a magical pass of great power and evil.  

Holmes and Watson sabotage the attempt to summon some extra-dimensional horror, and dynamite the castle, escaping in time with Lady Fairclough and her brother.

fullContent:
"The Alchemist" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft, written in 1908, when Lovecraft was 17 or 18, and first published in the November 1916 issue of The United Amateur.

### Plot summary
The story is recounted by the protagonist, Count Antoine de C-, in the first person. Hundreds of years ago, Antoine's noble ancestor was responsible for the death of a dark wizard, Michel Mauvais. The wizard's son, Charles le Sorcier, swore revenge on not only him but all his descendants, cursing them to die on reaching the age of 32.

The protagonist recounts how his ancestors all died in some mysterious way around the age of 32. The line has dwindled and the castle has been left to fall into disrepair, tower by tower. Finally, Antoine is the only one left, with one poor servant, Pierre, who raised him, and a tiny section of the castle with a single tower is still usable. Antoine has reached adulthood, and his 32nd year is approaching.

His servant, Pierre, dies, leaving him completely alone, and he begins exploring the ruined parts of the castle. He finds a trapdoor in one of the oldest parts. Below, he discovers a passage with a locked door at the end. Just as he turns to leave, he hears a noise behind him and sees that the door is open and someone is standing in it. The man attempts to kill him but Antoine kills him first. His dying words reveal that he is none other than Charles, who actually managed to successfully fabricate the Elixir of life, enabling him to personally fulfill the curse generation after generation.

### References

fullContent:
"The Alien Gardener" is a short story by Canadian author Troy Young. It is the second story in book 2 of his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
The bulk of the story is framed as field agent Mindy Nguyen relating the story of her most impactful encounter with "The Other" - a name given by Harjit Singh to the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos - to rookie Malcolm Mayweather whilst on a lengthy car trip.

Nguyen is tasked with investigating a cluster of incredibly dense vegetation in the centre of an expanding zone of barrenness. At the epicentre she discovers a greenhouse full of alien vegetation, and is overcome by a cloud of spores from one particular plant. Whilst in her fugue, she views from the periphery a series of scenes from the past and future.

As Nguyen emerges from her state, she hears the voice of an alien being in her head, which explains that it was intending to strip the Earth clean of the parasitic humans which are in the process of destroying it, but it will re-evaluate it’s course of action in light of the decision of the Star Flower of Uldalthmoon to bestow its gift upon her. 

As she departs the scene, the landscape is quickly beginning to revert to its natural state, but Nguyen is left with a lingering ability to sense the proximity of The Other.

The story concludes with an unrelated section involving events in one of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena's facilities: one of the cultists captured gives birth to a rat-like abomination which is accidentally killed, and doctors discover that Adele Kramer- last seen in "It Ends Where It Began" - is in a state of mental overdrive, despite being non-responsive to physical stimuli.

### Characters
*Mindy Nguyen, an experienced field agent with the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.
*Harjit Singh, the director of the Department.
*Malcolm Mayweather, a rookie agent.

### Publication History
"The Alien Gardener" was published in The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 2 in 2020.

### Connections
*The nature of the incident is highly reminiscent of H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Colour Out of Space", and the name of the disused farm at the story's epicentre, Pierce Family Farms, is a clear nod to Ammi Pierce, a primary character from that tale.
*Several of the visions which Nguyen is privy to are scenes from Lovecraft stories: a thief discovering a page of sheet music on the Rue d'Auseil ("The Music of Erich Zann"), an aquatic humanoid witnessing the destruction of an underwater city ("The Shadow Over Innsmouth"), a steam yacht ramming a colossal monstrosity risen from beneath the ocean ("The Call of Cthulhu"), a man assisting his friend in the hunt for the final resting place of one Joseph Curwen ("The Case of Charles Dexter Ward"), and a security guard's experience of a break-in at Miskatonic University ("The Dunwich Horror").
*The description of the rat-thing birthed by the cultist sounds very similar to that of Brown Jenkin, Keziah Mason's familiar from "The Dreams

### Synopsis
When Young Kelvin takes his Grampa Vezo's new cat Yarek to the vet to get its shots, he decides to have it neutered at the same time. When his grandfather finds out he is horrified, explaining that it is an ambassador for the Cats of Ulthar, come to spend some time exploring the wonders of Earth.

When Kelvin later falls asleep, he lives a life in the Dreamlands where Yarek has been his constant companion since early childhood. Upon waking, he discovers that Yarek has somehow switched bodies with him, and he is now destined to spend the rest of his life as a eunuch house pet.

fullContent:
"The Ancestor" is a short story by August Derleth, one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. It first appeared in Arkham House's 1957 collection, The Survivor and Others.

### Synopsis
The story describes experiments in recovering hereditary memory by Dr. Ambrose Perry, as recounted by his cousin Henry, who serves as his secretary. Perry is a successful Boston physician who retires to the wilds of Vermont to pursue his theory that a combination of food deprivation, drugs, and music can recover any memory--even memories of distant ancestors. Perry's fanatical investigations lead him to sequester himself in his lab--and eventually to physically regress to a subhuman creature that is killed by Perry's own dog.

### Behind the Mythos
The story closely follows the plot of Leonard Cline's The Dark Chamber, a novel praised by Lovecraft in Supernatural Horror in Literature. It also prefigures the central theme of the novel and film Altered States.

"The Ancient Track" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by the late American horror author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. 

### Synopsis
The two fairly lengthy stanzas describe the narrator's journey along a sinister and seemingly-abandoned pathway. At one point, it is mentioned that there is a sign posted which claims "Two miles to Dunwich", but whether the track leads to or from there, or merely passes it by, is unclear. 

### Publication History
"The Ancient Track" was first published in the March 1930 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reprinted a multitude of times, and has even been translated into French.

### Trivia

* The poem lends its name to a magazine dedicated to Lovecraftian horror.

fullContent:
The Annihilation Score is the sixth novel in Charles Stross's Laundry Files series, published by Orbit and Ace Books in 2015. Like other books in the series, it blends elements of the Cthulhu Mythos with spy fiction and bureaucratic office comedy; this volume adds a parody of comic book-style superpowers to the mix.

Set in 2013 after the events of The Rhesus Chart, the book is the first in the series not to have Bob Howard as its narrator/protagonist. Instead, the story is told by Bob's estranged wife, Dominique "Mo" O'Brien, who has been picked to head up a task force to deal with the sudden emergence of superpowers as the world heads closer to a Lovecraftian apocalypse. 

Joining Mo on this task force are two of Bob's former love interests: the human/deep one hybrid Ramona Random (from The Jennifer Morgue), and Mhari Murphy, who was introduced as Bob's girlfriend in The Atrocity Archive and turned into a PHANG (Stross's take on vampires) in The Rhesus Chart. Complicating things further, Mo develops romantic feelings for Officer Friendly, her superpowered liaison to the Metropolitan Police.

Mo finds herself involved against her will in a government plot to cast a mind control spell on the British public in the name of law and order. The scheme involves coercing Mo to play the score of an operetta based on The King in Yellow on Lecter, her sentient bone violin made by Erich Zahn--a performance that threatens to invoke the King in Yellow himself.

A subplot of the novel involves the task force recruiting and vetting potential superhero candidates; one such interview turns disastrous when the candidate, known as Fabian Everyman, turns out to have nearly irresistible powers of persuasion. Everyman is just barely neutralized and imprisoned--and turns out to play a very major role later on in the series.

fullContent:
The Apocalypse Codex is the fourth novel in Charles Stross's Laundry Files series, published by Ace Books and Orbit in 2012. Like other books in the series, it blends elements of the Cthulhu Mythos with spy fiction and bureaucratic office comedy.

### Synopsis
Set in 2010, the plot involves an American televangelist who worships the wrong gods cozying up to the British prime minister--a situation that the Laundry, the UK agency tasked with countering occult threats, is forbidden for political reasons from investigating. Bob Howard once again is the narrator and protagonist.

### Behind the Mythos
The book introduces the characters of Persephone Hazard, a freelance witch and secret agent, and Peter Wilson, a minister and expert in biblical apocrypha who gets sucked into the world of the Laundry when Howard is forced to ask him for advice about the cult's scriptures.

The Apocalypse Codex won the Locus Award for best fantasy novel in 2013.

### Inspiration
Stross describes the book as "a tribute to the Modesty Blaise comic strip and books by Peter O'Donnell."

### Publication History
The Apocalypse Codex was published by Ace Books in the United States: in hardcover and ebook format in July 2012, and in paperback in  July 2013. Orbit released it as a trade paperback and an ebook in Britain in July 2012.

fullContent:
"The Aquarium" is a short story by Carl Jacobi that first appeared in the Arkham House collection Dark Mind, Dark Heart (1962). It is notable for its introduction of several marine-themed eldritch tomes.

### Synopsis
In the story, a painter named Emily Rhodes and her friend, Edith Halbin, lease a house in the Knightsbridge section of London. The house contains a large aquarium, which houses a collection of rare shellfish that belonged to Horatio Lear, a conchologist who had some unorthodox opinions about mollusks. Halbin develops an unwholesome fascination with the aquarium—an obsession that ends with Halbin having her face eaten off by one of the conchs in Lear's collection.

### Characters
*Emily Rhodes: A 32-year-old painter who had lived in London a year before leasing the house in Knightsbridge. She is described as a "tall angular woman with black hair and metal grey eyes."
*Edith Halbin: Rhodes' friend from Bristol, who moves into the Knightsbridge house with her. Described as "a gaunt, prematurely grey woman." She has a Siamese cat name Kuching with four kittens.
*Horatio Lear: A conchologist who was "famous for his deep sea work", particularly for "exploring the Senarbin Deep off the coast of Haiti". Lear, who dies about a year before the story begins, believed that
somewhere in the unplumbed ocean depths there exists a highly developed kind of mollusk capable of emulating certain characteristics of those life forms it devours.... He believed that these super undersea species are the incarnation of those Elder Gods who ruled the antediluvian deep.... [C]ommanded by the great Cthulhu, they have lain dormant these eons in the sunken city of Flann, awaiting the time they would rise again to feed and rule.
*Edmund Lear: Lear's hated brother, who "publicly accused Horatio of falsifying reports as to the depths he had reached in the diving bell". He disappears and it's suggested that he became food for Horatio's collection. "Edmund’s refusal to accept Horatio’s theory concerning some forms of deep marine life" seems to have been at the root of the animosity between the brothers. They lived together for years, though there was "bad feeling between the two men"; one day Edmund "left", supposedly to pursue "interests in Haiti."
*Talbot Longeway: Senior partner in the firm Longeway & Longeway, which leases the house to Rhodes. Described as "a thin, cadaverous-looking individual with a completely bald pate."
*Lucius Bates: Rhodes and Halbin's neighbor.

### Mythos Tomes
"The Aquarium" introduces a handful of eldritch tomes with an aquatic theme. Lear's library contains, among other works,a copy of Gantley’s Hydrophinnae, containing some of the most hideous and horrible illustrations [Rhodes] had ever seen. There was a first edition of Dwellers in the Depths by Gaston Le Fe who, the foreword stated quite blandly, had died insane. And there was a pirated manuscript of the German Unter Zee Kulten, all copies of which had supposedly been destroye

fullContent:
"The Arctic Stone" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ross F. Bagby.

### Synopsis
"The Arctic Stone" introduces the titular item as an exhibit in the Witchcraft Museum in the fictional town of Granton, Ohio. Its use and purpose is made clear in a file entitled The Harrison-Elder Experience, which describes the tale of two anthropologists discovering the camp of an Inuit/Deep One tribe dedicated to worshiping their god of death and the deeps, Tornasuk, who is of course, Cthulhu, his servant-creation Dagon, and his son Leviathan.

### Characters
* John Harrison and Michael Elder, two anthropologists taken prisoner by the tribe.
* Y'holptr, the angekok of the tribe.
* Reston Mitchell, the curator of the museum housing occult items and files, including the "power-object of an [Inuit] shaman."

### Publication History
"The Arctic Stone" was first published by Yith Press in the seventh issue of Eldritch Tales in 1980.

### Trivia
* The Inuit tribe featured in the story is the same tribe mentioned by William Channing Webb in "The Call of Cthulhu."
* The curator's office displays an original piece by Richard Upton Pickman, titled Ghoul Sabbat.
* In the Inuit religion, Torngarsuk is a sea, death and underworld god, one of the more important deities in the Inuit pantheon. He is said to be the leader of the Tornat, a group of protective gods. Torngarsuk is listed as a demon or spirit in the Dictionnaire Infernal, a.k.a. Tornatik, Torngarsoak, Torngasoak, Tungrangayak, Tornasuk and is recorded there as a mischievous demon or spirit worshiped by the making of offerings with cults in Greenland and the northeastern regions of Canada.

fullContent:
The Arkham Detective is a series of Cthulhu Mythos stories by American author and filmmaker Byron Craft. Begun in 2015 with the novella Cthulhu's Minions, it runs to a total of 7 novellas and a short story, with the complete set later released in two collections.

### Premise
The series involves the protagonist, an Arkham Police Department detective whose name is never revealed, as he investigates cases in his home town, and sometimes in other Lovecraft Country locales, such as Innsmouth and Dunwich. The cases featured in the stories invariably involve the supernatural elements of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Genesis
The Arkham Detective was born from the novelisation of an unrealised film script, The Alchemist's Handbook. A group of malevolent creatures dubbed Pilot Demons, which featured in the novelisation, came to be the antagonists of the first of the novellas, Cthulhu's Minions.

### Recurrent Characters
*The Arkham Detective: a police officer in the Arkham PD's Mythos Division and, later, a private investigator.
*Matthew Bell: the Detective's partner, promoted to Detective Sergeant and put in charge of the Mythos Division after his superior's departure.
*Nora Bishop: the Detective's lover and later wife.
*Allison: the Detective's adoptive daughter.
*Alvin Nash: a former rail busboy, later the Detective's adoptive son.
*The Chief: the perennially-angry head of the Arkham PD.
*Esther Vinebeam: Arkham PD switchboard operator.
*Mrs. Trumble: the Detective's former landlady, later adopted as the family's de facto grandmother.

fullContent:
The Arkham Evil is a scenario supplement for Chaosium's horror roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu, consisting of three interconnected stories. It was first published by Theatre of the Mind Enterprises for the first edition of Call of Cthulhu in 1983; a French edition was also released, titled Terreur sur Arkham.

The Arkham Evil was designed by John Diaper, Bob Gallagher, C. Rawling, and Ed Wimble.

### Overview
The three scenarios consist of:

*"Into the Throat of the Beast": the group must investigate the mysterious disappearance of miners in Pennsylvania.
*"The Wanderer": a radioactive asteroid makes planetfall in Arizona.
*"And the Dogs Shall Know You": the adventure concludes at Miskatonic University's science department.

Also included are a timeline and calendar of events to allow the Keeper to track the story's progress.

### Reception
The Arkham Evil received mixed reviews, with commenters praising the potential of the storyline, but being generally critical of its execution .

The Arkham Gazette was a sporadically-released magazine dedicated to Call of Cthulhu roleplaying, specifically in the Lovecraft Country setting. Running for a total of five issues between August 2013 and November 2021, it was founded by Bret Kramer and published by Sentinel Hill Press.

The magazine was initially released as a free download but as of issue 3 in November 2015, after establishing a licensing deal with Chaosium, it was changed to a fixed-charge publication; this also enabled the Gazette to pay its contributors, the previous arrangement being on a voluntary-contribution system only.

fullContent:
The Arkham Sampler was a short-lived American magazine published quarterly by Arkham House which ran for eight issues between 1948 and 1949. Focusing on the fantasy and horror genres, The Arkham Sampler included a mix of fiction, non-fiction, and poetry, and contained pieces by Lovecraft and his contemporaries, as well as more recent writers. All issues were edited by August Derleth.

Contributors included H. P. Lovecraft, August Derleth, Clark Ashton Smith, Robert Bloch, Fritz Leiber, George T. Wetzel, Rheinhart Kleiner, C. M. Eddy, Jr., Samuel Loveman, Ray Bradbury, Frank Belknap Long, E. Hoffmann Price, John Wyndham, Jules Verne, A. E. van Vogt, and many others.

fullContent:
"The Arkham Town Musicians" is a short story by Christine Morgan, originally collected in the Kickstarter crowdfunded anthology A Mythos Grimmly. It is a parody of the folktale The Musicians of Bremen.

### Synopsis
A mutant donkey (albeit one with tendrils around its mouth) from a property near that of the Whateleys in Dunwich leaves home after its master dies. It is joined by an abandoned Hound which may or may not be a true canine, a many-colored and splendid Cat of Ulthar whose mistress Witch was beheaded, and an eldritch abomination resulting of the mating of a Night-Gaunt with a chicken. This last creature is a "rooster", due solely to its coxcomb.

With each of the four animals out of their original homes, they set off for Arkham, there to seek their fortune as musicians. Before their arrival in Arkham itself, they find a farmhouse. They anticipate encountering a kindly old farming couple who will shelter them for the night, but instead stumble on to a cult performing a ritual around a grimoire.

Accidentally disrupting the cult and frightening them off, when one member of the cult is sent back to retrieve their grimoire he provokes the cat and in return is savaged. The cult abandon the property, and the four animals take up permanent residence there. "And if no one has yet killed or banished them, then they must live there still."

term: The Assaults of Chaos: A Novel About H. P. Lovecraft
shortDefinition: The Assaults of Chaos is a supernatural novel written by S. T. Joshi. It was published by Hippocampus Press in August 2013.   ### Overview In the summer of 1914, a few months before his twenty-fourth birthday, H. P. Lovecraft receives a strange lette...
fullContent:
The Assaults of Chaos is a supernatural novel written by S. T. Joshi. It was published by Hippocampus Press in August 2013. 

### Overview
In the summer of 1914, a few months before his twenty-fourth birthday, H. P. Lovecraft receives a strange letter from his father, Winfield Scott Lovecraft — a father he thought had died sixteen years before — speaking cryptically of an urgent task that must be performed to save the world from a nameless fate. Meeting his father in Quinsnicket Park, Lovecraft is engulfed in an adventure that takes him across the water to his beloved England, where he encounters some of the titans of weird fiction. With this unusual but stalwart band of comrades, Lovecraft does indeed find himself facing a cosmic menace too horrible to contemplate.

In this story, the young Lovecraft is brought vividly to life. The shy, retiring, inward-looking recluse is brought out of his shell and brought into contact with such of his literary idols as Arthur Machen, Lord Dunsany, and Algernon Blackwood. Together, they must deal with a horror from beyond the stars with the only weapons at their disposal—their minds and imaginations.

### Reception
Published in hardcover with a very limited run of 500 copies, this little-regarded pastiche put Lovecraft in the company of many other weird fiction writers, many of whom are used to make long speeches that are little more than author-insert literary criticisms. It is not well regarded in general and has become collectible mainly for the Joshi completists.

Although described as a novel, about half of it is so descriptive and typical of literary criticism that the work is arguably of more interest in a non-fiction or criticism sense than as a work of fiction.

fullContent:
The Asylum & Other Tales is an adventure module supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, with the seven individual stories each supplied by a different designer.

### Overview


Consisting of seven unrelated short scenarios, The Asylum & Other Tales was only the second supplement released for the Call of Cthulhu game. Creation of the book was overseen by Sandy Petersen, Lynn Willis, and Charlie Krank, with cover and interior art by Tom Sullivan, and runs to a total of 80 pages.

### Contents
*"The Auction": A guide on how to run scenarios involving the auction of mystical artefacts. Also features a short scenario involving the theft of one of these items by ghouls. Written by Randy McCall.
* "The Madman": A young man has developed a split personality as a result of exposure to the Cthulhu Mythos, and his evil personality is attempting to enlist the aid of Hastur. Written by Mark Harmon.
*"Black Devil Mountain": When one of the investigators inherits a cursed property in the backwoods of Maine, they must deal with an undead shaman in service to dark powers, as well as a variety of his supernatural minions including zombies, ghouls, and Chthonians. Written by David A. Hargrave.
*"The Asylum": The deranged head of a psychiatric institution has discovered how to meld the DNA of Shoggoths with that of humans, and the investigators must find a way to put a stop to his malevolent machinations. Written by Randy McCall.
*"The Mauretania": More of a setting than a scenario, "The Mauretania" offers the investigators a chance to relax and watch the world go by while on a transatlantic voyage, as well as a number of plot hooks should they wish to join in on Cthulhu Mythos-related adventure. Written by M. B. Willner.
*"Gate from the Past": The investigators much deal with breaches in the fabric of time and space when a group of Old Ones, pursued by vengeful Shoggoths, open a gateway into the Late Jurassic. Written by John Scott Clegg.
*"Westchester House": Called in by an eccentric heiress to investigate a possible haunting in her sprawling estate, the investigators must deal with a mundane case of art theft and the various groups involved in trying to retrieve a stolen painting. The scenario contains no Cthulhu Mythos elements, but the group must navigate a labyrinthine mansion and deal with a group of dangerous art thieves. Written by Elizabeth Wolcott.

### Publication History
The Asylum & Other Tales was first released in 1983 and is currently out of print; however, the book was incorporated into a later release by Chaosium, the Cthulhu Casebook, in 1990.

### Trivia
*The credits page of the book states "by permission of Arkham House".
*The final scenario, "Westchester House," is clearly based on the real-world case of Sarah Winchester, the widow of firearms manufacturer William Winchester who spent many years building the Winchester Mystery House, an extensive building whimsically constructed and expanded by Sarah in the years following

shortDefinition: The Atrocity Archive is a novel by Charles Stross, the first novel in The Laundry Files, a series that blends Lovecraftian sci-fi horror, British spy fiction pastiche, and bureaucratic office comedy. It was originally serialized in Spectrum SF (2001-...
fullContent:
The Atrocity Archive is a novel by Charles Stross, the first novel in The Laundry Files, a series that blends Lovecraftian sci-fi horror, British spy fiction pastiche, and bureaucratic office comedy. It was originally serialized in Spectrum SF (2001-2002), then released as The Atrocity Archives (Golden Gryphon Press, 2004), accompanied by the Laundry Files short story "The Concrete Jungle". 

Like most of the Laundry Files books, The Atrocity Archive is narrated by Stross's character Bob Howard, an employee of the secret British occult agency known as The Laundry. It is set, according to the author, in 2002.

### Inspiration
In his acknowledgements, Stross writes: "Three authors in particular made it possible for me to imagine this book and I salute you, H. P. Lovecraft, Neal Stephenson, and Len Deighton." Neal Stephenson is a leading writer in the cyberpunk mode of science fiction, best known for his 1992 novel Snow Crash. Len Deighton is a British spy novelist known for novels like The Ipcress Files with a "sardonic working-class hero."

Stross has explained that the idea for the book began in 1992 with the question, "How do you put the horror back into H. P. Lovecraft?... You mate it with something that truly is horrifying." This led to his short story "A Colder War," a "sort of sequel to At the Mountains of Madness" in which various global powers sought to steal alien supertechnology, the tools of an extinct race, and put them to use as weapons.... World War Three breaks out, Cthulhu himself is deployed as a weapon from the crypt in the Urals, everybody dies horribly, or worse, wishes they could die.Stross felt that this merger of Mythos with Cold War paranoia "worked really, really well as a horror story....  But, while I wanted to do more with this idea, I couldn’t do it in that particular setting. It was too dark."

He decided he needed to leaven the horror by "add[ing] some snarky humor to it," leading him to the idea that he would take a somewhat grungy, down-at-heels, peeling-paint British government agency, dealing with something obscure and quite terrifying, and parachute into it somebody who is totally inappropriate, utterly unsuited to that sort of office culture.

### Premise
The Atrocity Archive introduces the premise of the Laundry Files series, which is that the eldritch horrors described by Lovecraft are real, they gain access to our reality through applied higher mathematics, and there is a branch of the British secret service dedicated to protecting an unsuspecting public from these occult threats. 

Howard explains:  Everything you know about the way this universe works is correct—except for the little problem that this isn’t the only universe we have to worry about.... We live in an Everett-Wheeler cosmology, all possible parallel universes coexisting. The opener of the gates to these other universes is maths: When we carry out a computation it has side effects that leak through some kind of channel underlying the structure

shortDefinition: "The Avatars of the Old Ones" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas, the second in a short series set in his futuristic Punktown setting. It was first published in the chapbook Avatars of the Old Ones by Imelod Publication...
fullContent:
"The Avatars of the Old Ones" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas, the second in a short series set in his futuristic Punktown setting. It was first published in the chapbook Avatars of the Old Ones by Imelod Publications in 1999.

### Synopsis
Having been exiled from Oasis for his murderous activities against cults devoted to the Old Ones, former law enforcement officer John Bell travels to Earth and takes a job as security at a soup kitchen where he can keep an eye on some of the 24 million near-mindless infected humans from the previous incursion, now dubbed "Afflicted".

While on shift one day, he observes the Afflicted initiate a new effort to bring about the return of their masters, beginning with the slaughter of any human which comes within reach. As he and one of the kitchen workers, a woman named H'anna, travel across the city, they become aware of a pattern in the Afflicted's activities, one which centres on the Museum of Fine Arts.

At the museum, Bell and H'anna are able to locate the nexus of the incursion, a now-living statue of the Outer God Nyarlathotep. Luckily for the human species, Bell's auxiliary sidearm, a plasma-launching handgun, is sufficient to destroy the abomination, as outside armed citizens and law enforcement launch a counter attack against the now-disorientated Afflicted.

In the aftermath of the attack, Bell and H'anna embark upon a relationship, but this is painfully cut short when Bell is recruited as part of an extra-planetary task force to combat future events initiated by the Old Ones.

### Publication History
*Avatars of the Old Ones (1999)
*Unholy Dimensions (2005)
*Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012 , German-language translation)
*Cthulhu Detective: A C. J. Henderson Tribute (2015)

### Trivia
*The name of the structure which houses the soup kitchen, the Ambuehl Building, is likely a nod to author James Ambuehl, a Cthulhu Mythos author contemporary with the publishing date of "The Avatars of the Old Ones.

"The Baby Downstairs" is a tongue-in-cheek short story by author Chad Fifer, first published in the Kat Rocha-edited anthology of Lovecraftian fiction Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be by 01Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
A man is threatened by a seemingly-intelligent baby living alone in the downstairs apartment, one which makes the police officers which he calls to deal with the situation disappear…

The story culminates with the man finding a bloodstained rattle outside his front door along with a note which reads "Don’t make me come up here again".

fullContent:
"The Baleful God", which has also seen print under the title "Yon Baleful God" is a very short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author W. H. Pugmire, writing as Wilum Pugmire. It was first published by Necronomicon Press in the May 1996 edition of fanzine Cthulhu Codex.

### Synopsis
In the Sesqua Valley, a man introduces his lover to the worship of the Great Old One Tsathoggua before the two share an unexpected sacrifice.

### Publication History
*Cthulhu Codex May 1996
*Dreams of Lovecraftian Horror (1999)
*Gathered Dust and Others (2011, as "Yon Baleful God")

### Trivia
*The fictional Sesqua Valley is a recurrent setting in the Cthulhu Mythos fiction of W. H. Pugmire, having been created by the author for this very purpose.

fullContent:
The Ballad of Bass Rock is a stand-alone adventure module sourcebook for Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
Consisting of a single scenario written by Stuart Boon, The Ballad of Bass Rock contains material which was originally intended to be in Cubicle 7 Entertainment's Shadows Over Scotland book, but was cut due to space issues. It runs to a total of 14 pages including the front cover and is part of Cubicle 7's popular Cthulhu Britannica line.

The plot involves a group of investigators being trapped on the Bass Rock in the Firth of Forth, Scotland, with a hungry shoggoth. The book contains all of the necessary handouts and information on a small number of NPCs.

### Publication History
The Ballad of Bass Rock was published by Cubicle 7 Entertainment in 2012 as an ebook-only release, but is no longer available to purchase.

### Gallery

fullContent:
"The Ballad of Black Bart" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by American author James Ambuehl. It is written in seven verses of eight lines each.

### Synopsis
The poem tells the story of a Wild West showdown between two men: Black Bart, a mean old gunslinger, and the Stranger, a creature disguised as a man who uses the power of the Necronomicon against its enemies. Despite being filled full of lead, the Stranger is unharmed and uses an arcane ritual to tear away Bart's soul before a man named Doc Jones counters his magic with a protective spell, casting the entity back to the abyss from whence it came; unfortunately, this act results in Jones's own death.

### Characters
*Black Bart, a cowboy "with a buzzard's eyes and a coyote's grin."
*The Stranger, an unknown monstrosity in the guise of a man.
*Doc Jones, a man with a certain knowledge of the Necronomicon.

### Publication History
"The Ballad of Black Bart" was published in the E. P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes in October 2006.

shortDefinition: The Ballad of Black Tom is a novella by Victor LaValle that retells H. P. Lovecraft's "The Horror at Red Hook" from a Black perspective. Published by Tor Books on February 16, 2016, it won the 2016 Shirley Jackson Award and the 2017 British Fantasy A...
fullContent:
The Ballad of Black Tom is a novella by Victor LaValle that retells H. P. Lovecraft's "The Horror at Red Hook" from a Black perspective. Published by Tor Books on February 16, 2016, it won the 2016 Shirley Jackson Award and the 2017 British Fantasy Award for best novella.

The novella was included in the Tor omnibus Reimagining Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
The Ballad of Black Tom tells the story of Tommy Tester, a Harlem hustler and street musician recruited by Robert Suydam as part of a scheme to raise the Great Old Ones--a scheme Tester ultimately foils.

### Adaptations
In 2017, AMC announced a television series adaptation of The Ballad of Black Tom, with LaValle as executive producer; as of January 2024, the series has not materialised .

### References

"The Balm of Sperrgebiet Is the Krokodil" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Steve Berman. It was published in the Jason Andrew-edited thematic anthology Flub by Simian Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
After an unspecified collapse of civilisation, a group of men take up residence in an abandoned town located in the Namib desert, killing those who stumble across their new home. When a group arrive muttering the name of something called "Ahtu", the group attempt to kill them, but are in turn attacked by the vicious parasites growing within their victims. After successfully fending off the beasts, most of the group sets off to seek answers about Ahtu, leaving one to grub out an existence in the derelict town, a changed man.

shortDefinition: "The Bank Job" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was first published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008, although Shiflet states in his afterword for the s...
fullContent:
"The Bank Job" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was first published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008, although Shiflet states in his afterword for the second edition that it was written before that book was a project in the works.

### Synopsis
When a bank robbery goes drastically wrong, cowpoke criminal Wayne Handley flees from the sheriff and his posse of angry citizens. Finding himself trapped in a local graveyard, he hides in the sole mausoleum, beneath which he discovers a secret passageway.

Fleeing through the catacombs beneath the old cemetery, Handley encounters a colossal half human, half serpent monstrosity which claims to be Dorffman, the mausoleum's former inhabitant and a powerful warlock. Dorffman and his inhuman "children" attempt to eat the man, but he is able to escape via an underground stream, bringing the chambers crashing down on the creatures in the process.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct connections to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos, Dorffman at one point mentions that he arrived at his position "having studied the Arab's book". This would appear to be a reference to Abdul Alhazred and the Necronomicon, both prominent elements of the Mythos.

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance in Looking for Darla, "The Bank Job" has appeared in the Rainfall Books zine Tales of the Weird West #2 in August 2015.

fullContent:
"The Barrens" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by F. Paul Wilson, first published in the collection Lovecraft's Legacy (Tor, 1990). It was later reprinted in Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology (Arkham House, 1995).

### Synopsis
Kathleen McKelston, a New Jersey accountant, is contacted by an ex-lover from college, Jonathan Creighton, who seeks her help investigating the folklore of Jersey's Pine Barrens. As she takes him farther into the Barrens, he takes her deeper into the Barrens' mysteries--putting her sanity and reality itself at risk.

### Characters

### Kathleen McKelston
The story's narrator is the proprietor of a small accounting firm, Kathleen McKelston and Associates, in New Jersey. Born in the Pine Barrens, her family moved when she was 14 to nearby Pemberton, so she could attend Pemberton High. In the Pines, she's remembered as "the one who got the college scholarship." She attended Rutgers University in the '60s, where she was "career-oriented" and was nicknamed Mac. She describes herself as "what you might call a feminist." At the time the story is set (ca. 1990), she is recently divorced.

Her hair has "a little gray tucked in with the red," but has "young face," with "high coloring and freckles."

### Jonathan Creighton
He grew up in North Jersey, near a rural town called Gilead. He attended Rutgers in the '60s, where he was known as "Crazy Creighton." He dated and for a time lived with Kathleen, though she objected to his Pickman prints. He graduated with a degree in anthropology, then got a Master's and a Ph.D.  in clinical psychology. He started a practice that failed--because he was using "a form of reality therapy, and "I don’t know—really know—what reality is." He went back to school, in the anthropology department of Miskatonic University, which he left because the “old farts in the antiquities department didn’t like where my research was leading me.” He now claims to have grants from Rutgers, Princeton, the American Folklore Society, and the New Jersey Historical Society to study “the origins of folktales." At the story starts, he's living in New York City (as he has a number with a 212 area code), but later is staying in Jersey at the Laurelton Circle Motor Inn.

He is described as a "plump, bearded, almost cherubic figure.... His hair was still thick and dark brown, but despite his round, rosy cheeks, his eyes were sunken and too bright."

### Jasper Mulliner
He's "some sort of an uncle" of Kathleen—"on my mother’s side, I think." He's thought to be "a descendant of the notorious bandit of the pines, Joseph Mulliner." Kathleen tells him that her father always said "there weren’t many folks in the Pines you didn’t know, and not much that went on that you didn’t know about.”

"His white hair was neatly combed and he was freshly shaved," Kathleen observes. "His skin was a weathered brown and looked tougher than saddle leather."

### Gus Sooy

fullContent:
"The Battery" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
Two couple, the Cejas and the Stones, live peacefully in a cliff-side apartment building by the ocean. When one day a mysterious stranger arrives, the older couple reveal that they are guardians of a sort, and that the stranger has come to begin the process of ending the world. Enlisting the help of the younger couple, the group awaken Tsathoggua who slumbers beneath the rock, and the Great Old One in turn contacts an even more powerful entity which puts an end to the threat.

### Characters
* Nolo Ceja, an average Joe living a quiet life.
* Adrienne Ceja, Nolo's wife.
* Ray Stone, an occultist with a concern for the safety of the Earth.
* Estella Stone, Ray's wife
* Mr. Ginunga, a supernatural entity masquerading as a man.

### Publication History
"The Battery" was included in the collections of Shea's own works Copping Squid and Other Mythos Tales (2009) and Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea (2017).

### Trivia
* At the climax of "The Battery", the Cejas take over the mantle of guardianship from the Stones.
* The story is titled "The Battery" as the setting was once the site of a coastal defence installation.
*The Shoggoths employed by the Stones as manual labour display similar traits to the  Shoggoth Lords created by Shea for his short story "Fat Face", although whether they are the same entities is unclear.
