fullContent:
"The Battle that Ended the Century" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow.

### Overview
Originally privately circulated amongst the Lovecraft Circle, this comedy short story is a plethora of in-jokes and references to the members of the circle under their nicknames, alter egos or other humorous names. H. P. Lovecraft wrote most of it, with additions and a Glossary of Names at the end of the short work provided by R. H. Barlow.  

### Glossary of Names
*Two-Gun Bob—Robert E. Howard
*Knockout Bernie, the Wild Wolf of West Shokan—Bernard Austin Dwyer, of West Shokan, N.Y.
*Bill Lum Li—William Lumley
*Wladislaw Brenryk—H. Warner Munn
*D. H. Killer—David H. Keller
*M. Gin Brewery—Miles G. Breuer
*A. Hijacked Barrell—A. Hyatt Verrill
*G. A. Scotland—George Allan England
*Frank Chimesleep Short, Jr—Frank Belknap Long, Jr.
* The Effjoy of Akkamin—Forrest J Ackerman
*Mrs. M. Blunderage—Margaret Brundage (artist for Weird Tales)
*Mr. C. Half-Cent—C. C. Senf (artist for Weird Tales)
*Mr. Goofy Hooey—Hugh Rankin (artist for Weird Tales)
*W. Lablache Talcum—Wilfred Blanch Talman
*Horse Power Hateart—Howard Phillips Lovecraft
*M. le Comte d’Erlette—August Derleth (author of Evening in Spring)
*J. Caesar Warts—Julius Schwartz
*H. Kanebrake—H. C. Koenig (employed by the Electrical Testing Laboratories)
*H. Wanderer—Howard Wandrei
*Robertieff Essovitch Karovsky—Robert S. Carr
*Teaberry Quince—Seabury Quinn
*Malik Taus, the Peacock Sultan—E. Hoffmann Price
*Sing Lee Bawledout—F. Lee Baldwin
*Ivor K. Rodent—Hugo Gernsback
*Rev. D. Vest Wind—Unknown
*Klarkash-Ton—Clark Ashton Smith
*Windy City Grab-Bag—Weird Tales
*W. Peter Chef—W. Paul Cook
*Smearum & Weep—Dauber & Pine
*Samuelus Philanthropus—Samuel Loveman
*Mr. De Merit—A. Merritt (author of The Dwellers in the Mirage)
*Wurst’s Weekly Americana—Hearst’s American Weekly

### Behind the Mythos
In addition to Barlow's Glossary reproduced above, some people appear in the story under their real names, including Lovecraft's friends Arthur Leeds, Harry K. Brobst, and Vrest Orton, and popular pulp writer Otis Adelbert Kline. The trio of musicians called De Silva, Brown, and Henderson are a reference to Buddy DeSylva, Lew Brown, and Ray Henderson. However, the references to Leeds, Brobst, and Orton are only present in Barlow's version of the text, and omitted in the final version, which was mailed anonymously to the authors' acquaintances with the subtitle "MS. Found in a Time Machine". Lovecraft denied any involvement in it, but wasn't able to fool August Derleth, Frank Belknap Long, or Clark Ashton Smith, as they all deduced that the authorship was his, with Smith correctly guessing Barlow's involvement as well.

Despite being little more than a series of affectionate jokes aimed at the authors' friends and colleagues, "The Battle that Ended the Century" does borrow a few elements from the Cthulhu Mythos. Namely, there is a reference to "the primal serpent-god of Valusia", and August Derleth and Clark As

"The Beard of Byatis" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
Years after the archaeological party which he was a part of accidentally released the monstrous creature known as Byatis from its prison beneath the Severn Valley, scholarly cleric Mr. Batchel returns to fix his mistake. Somehow deducing that the creature is hiding in plain sight at Brichester University, he uses a star-stone to banish it before it can turn him to stone, as it did with the leader of the original expedition.

### Characters

*Mr. Batchel, an educated and well respected pastor.
*Mr. Barlowe, Batchel's young assistant.
*Professor Ashdod, an archaeologist determined to prove the link between the Gorgon and the pagan deity Byatis.
*The Professor/Doctor Raines/Byatis, a supernatural being hiding amongst the faculty of Brichester University.

### Publication History
"The Beard of Byatis" was first published in the Scott David Aniolowski-edited anthology Made in Goatswood by Chaosium in July 1995. It later appeared in the collection of Price's own works Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2008.

### Trivia

*The story is set in the fictional Severn Valley, a setting created by Ramsey Campbell for many of his mythos stories.

fullContent:
"The Beast in the Cave" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft written in 1905, when Lovecraft was fourteen. It was first published in the June 1918 issue of the amateur press journal The Vagrant.

### Plot
A man touring Mammoth Cave in Kentucky separates from his guide and becomes lost. His torch expires and he is giving up hope of finding a way out in the pitch dark, when he hears strange non-human footsteps approaching him. Thinking it to be a lost mountain lion or other such beast, he picks up a stone and throws it toward the source of the sound. The cave beast is hit and crumples to the floor. The guide finds the protagonist, and together they examine the fallen creature with the guide's torchlight. The creature mutters in its last breaths and they see its face, discovering that it is in fact a pale, deformed human, who had also become lost in the cave.

### Popular culture
*Sapthuran's EP The Beast in the Cave (2007) is based upon the short story.
*H. P. Lovecraft's The Beast in the Cave (2016) is a short horror film adaptation.

### Behind the Mythos
This story is the first example of devolution in Lovecraft's work. Devolution is where more recent forms of a species are "degenerate" and more "primitive" or "savage" than earlier forms. This idea undermines any concept of progress, whether moral or biological, and of course removes humanity from its destined role as rulers of creation. As such, it is also an early example of Cosmicism.

Other works that explore the devolution of humanity are "The Lurking Fear", "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family", "The Rats in the Walls", and arguably even The Shadow over Innsmouth.

"The Beast of Averoigne" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, set in Averoigne, his semi-historical province of France. It first appeared in the May 1933 issue of Weird Tales.

It tells the story, through a series of manuscripts and letters, of an uncanny beast that ravages the province of Averoigne in the summer of 1369, particularly in the vicinity of the Abbey of Périgon.

The conclusion of the story strikes a particularly Lovecraftian note:


### Characters
* Abbott Théophile: The chief monk of Périgon, who leads the hunt for the beast, unaware that he is the host for the creature. Brother Gérôme notes that "a strange illness devours him as if with perpetual fever," leaving him with "hollow cheeks and burning eyes".
* Brother Gérôme: The "humblest monk of the Benedictine Abbey of Périgon," he is the first to see the beast in the woods outside the abbey, and writes an account of the sighting at the behest of Théophile. He is later killed by the beast in his cell.
* Sister Therèse: A nun of the Benedictine convent at Ximes, she is Théophile's actual sister, and he confides in a letter to her the strange spell that seems to come over her each night. She too is killed in her cell by the beast.
* Brother Constantin: The cellarer of Périgon, who saw the beast climbing the abbey wall near Théophile's window.
* Luc le Chaudronnier: A student of the occult who lives at Ximes, who knows "spells that summon or dismiss evil demons and other spirits." He is enlisted by Théophile and the town marshall of Ximes to defeat the beast, which he does by freeing the entity confined in the Ring of Eibon. His appellation means "cauldon-maker," used of a coppersmith or tinker. He seals his account in a brazen box in a hidden chamber of his house so that "the good renown of the holy Théophile should suffer no calumny."

### Locations
* Périgon: The center of the depredations of the beast, all attacks occurring within five hours' travel of the abbey there. The cloister of Abbott Théophile and of brothers Gérôme and Constantin.
* Ximes: A major town of Averoigne. Home to Luc le Chaudronnier and the Benedictine convent wherein Sister Therese lives. 
* Ste. Zénobie: The village Gérôme is returning from when he first sees the beast. The cemetery there is despoiled as one of the creature's first outrages; a peasant girl there is its final victim.
* La Frênaie: Another place where the beast hunted victims.
* Isoile: Averoigne's main river formed one edge of the beast's range.
* Faussesflammes: The ruined castle, reputed to be the haunt of vampires, is searched for signs of the beast.

"The Becoming" is a short story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
A young man has the magical ability to "become" the characters he reads about in books. He suffers a gruesome fate when an accident leaves him unable to leave the character he has become while reading H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep".

### Characters

*Danny Phillips, a teenager who has gained magical power from one of his estranged uncle's musty old books.
*Robert Phillips, Danny's father, an average Joe.
*Asa Phillips, Danny's uncle, apparently something of an occultist.

### Publication History
"The Becoming" was first published in the January 1998 edition of Nightscapes, and then again in April 1998 in Cthulhu Cultus #12.

shortDefinition: "The Bell in the Tower" is a short story by Lin Carter originally published in Crypt of Cthulhu #69, Yuletide 1989. It is sometimes also attributed to H. P. Lovecraft as co-author since Lin Carter wrote the story inspired by a fragmentary note left b...
fullContent:
"The Bell in the Tower" is a short story by Lin Carter originally published in Crypt of Cthulhu #69, Yuletide 1989. It is sometimes also attributed to H. P. Lovecraft as co-author since Lin Carter wrote the story inspired by a fragmentary note left behind by Lovecraft. However other than this one-line inspiration the story really is entirely written by Carter. It has a somewhat similar specific theme to Lovecraft's story, The Lurking Fear.

### Synopsis
An old man living in London is triggered into fits of screaming at the sound of church bells ringing.  Williams, a fellow tenant at Gray's Inn where the old man resides makes friends with the old man. In conversation with the old man Williams discovers that the man is Lord Northam, scion of an old Yorkshire family and inheritor of a crumbling ruin of an old ancestral home.

Williams has also found and purchased a copy of the Necronomicon having discovered it for sale at a ridiculously cheap price at a used book-store one night.   Thinking the old man may find it interesting, Williams shows it to him.  Seeing the book causes Lord Northam to tell his family's cursed history.

It transpires that the Northam family has always dabbled in the occult as far back as Roman times. Lord Northam himself was drawn to the grimoires in the Northam estate's library which included the range of Mythos books.  There he found a copy of the Necronomicon, many years prior.  He also discovered a sealed tower on the estate. Entering it he discovered that the tower's belfry houses a giant silver bell. The bell was inscribed with "Nug-Soth" runes.  Lord Northam discovered a forbidden ritual in connection with the ringing of this bell.

The ritual, involving hallucinogenic drugs and the tolling of the bell summoned a procession of human figures on the fields below the tower, from all eras of mankind.  Northam became addicted to viewing this procession and in the process addicted to the drugged ritual. Gradually and originally almost imperceptibly, less human figures began to join the procession during each ritual.

Finally, Lord Northam realized that the procession was making its way to the crypts underneath the castle.  He decides to visit the crypts himself. Intruding into the sealed mausoleums he discovers to his horror that an undead monstrosity is chained down there in perpetual captivity. The thing that turns his mind and gives him his terror bells is that the undead horror is obviously a member of the Northam family. He is of the same accursed and not entirely human bloodline as this monster.

fullContent:
"The Bells of Horror" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Henry Kuttner under the pen name of Keith Hammond.

### Synopsis
An expedition from the California Historical Society working near the town of San Xavier, California, unearths a trio of bells said to summon a dread entity when rung. Despite the horrific incidents which occur during their removal - including one of the local attendants gouging out his own eyes - the group brings the bells back to San Xavier and has them hung in the local Mission. There, an earthquake causes the bells to begin ringing, and a darkness  descends over the eyes of all who hear it. Only the members of the Historical Society, with their knowledge of the occult grimoire The Book of Iod, are able to stop the bells and restore sight and sanity to the town.

However, a solar eclipse two months later appears to precipitate a gruesome suicide, and brings the suggestion that the summoning of the bells was not as unsuccessful as the party had previously thought . . . 

### Characters

*Ross, secretary of the California Historical Society.
*Arthur Todd, president of the society.
*Denton, Todd's assistant.
*Zushakon, a demonic entity.

### Publication History
"The Bells of Horror" was first published in pulp magazine Strange Stories in April 1939. It was included in the Kuttner-focussed anthology The Book of Iod: Ten Tales of the Mythos by Chaosium in 1995.

The Best of Lovecraftiana is an anthology collection of works which have appeared in the Lovecraftiana horror zine over the then-seven years since its launch. Edited by Gavin Chappell, it was published by Rogue Planet Press in October 2023; both print and digital editions were released.

### Controversy
In his note "The Anthology they Couldn’t Cancel", editor Gavin Chappell tells of how, during the voting and finalisation of the pieces to be featured in The Best of Lovecraftiana on Facebook, he began to receive complaints about the inclusion of one author who had allegedly displayed right-wing leanings in the past. This prompted Chappell to contact all contributors with the information, and as a result a number of stories originally slated to appear in the collection were pulled from the final line up.

It should be noted that Chappell makes a point of stating that he was unaware of any political stances currently or previously held by any of the contributors, and that his policy is to publish based on the merit of the work rather than any other considerations.

"The Bicycle-Centaur" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Welsh author Rhys Hughes, set in a fantasy iteration of rural Wales. It was first published by Screaming Dreams in the thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg in October 2013.

### Synopsis
In a fantastical version of Wales, a bizarre wheeled creature named the Bicycle-Centaur roams the countryside, forever on the lookout for the one who created it.

When it stumbles across a small valley from which eldritch lights appear to be emanating, it finds the robotic monstrosity which created it, along with its minions who are in the process of summoning one of the Old Ones, a being known as Ootoo. Requiring a sacrifice, they attempt to use the Bicycle-Centaur for their nefarious purposes. However, the plucky being has other ideas and, in an effort to be the master of its own fate, drives itself headlong into the maw of Ootoo, only to find itself in the office of the Dean of the local university.

### Mythos Connections
When inquiring of the throng of monsters which Old One they intend to summon, the Bicycle-Centaur asks: "Cthulhu himself? Is it Azathoth, Nyarlathotep, Yog-Sothoth, Ithaqua, Aphoom-Zhar, Dagon, Zoth-Ommog, Tsathoggua, Yig, ShubNiggurath, Plonker, Ghatanothoa or Hastur the Unspeakable?"

fullContent:
"The Big Fish" is a thriller short story by Kim Newman set in his Diogenes Club universe. The series combines elements from several works of fiction, with the titular club originating from the Sherlock Holmes stories of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle. This story in particular is a mashup of Raymond Chandler and H. P. Lovecraft. It stars a detective heavily implied to be Philip Marlowe investigating a case connected to the Esoteric Order of Dagon.

"The Big Fish" was first published in the magazine Interzone in October 1993. It also appeared in the Cthulhu Mythos anthologies Shadows over Innsmouth (1994), Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology (1995), and The Book of Cthulhu II (2012), as well as the Diogenes Club collection The Secret Files of the Diogenes Club (2007).

### Synopsis
Bay City, California, 1942. A hard-boiled detective is hired by Hollywood actress and former Olympic swimmer Janey Wilde to find the whereabouts of her former lover, cassino owner Laird Brunette, who has apparently ditched Wilde for Janice Marsh, an actress with a peculiar appearance who is nevertheless quite popular. Apparently, Marsh somehow induced Brunette to join some sort of cult, to which he has since dedicated himself at the expense of his business. At the same time, a number of Brunette's employees have been found dead, one decapitated, another drowned.

The detective goes to the Seaview Inn for an appointment with mafia boss Gianni Pastore, a business associate of Brunette's. He finds Pastore dead in a bathtub and three people inside who hold him at gunpoint. One is a British man named Edwin Winthrop, the second a French woman named Geneviève Dieudonné, and the last one a burly FBI agent named Finlay. The trio ask the detective if he knows anything about a town named Innsmouth, the Esoteric Order of Dagon, Obed Marsh, the Deep Ones, Cthulhu, Y'ha-nthlei, or R'lyeh. Satisfied that he knows nothing, they allow him to go, telling him that they will take care of the investigation and pay him for his expenses so far. Back in his apartment, the detective does some research and finds that the Esoteric Order of Dagon is the cult that Brunette has joined. Janice Marsh was born in a town named Innsmouth and is a descendant of a Captain Obed Marsh.

On the next day, the detective meets with Wilde to explain what's happened. She wants him to continue the investigation and admits that Brunette has kidnapped their infant son, Franklin. She believes Janice Marsh to be behind this, and that she means the child harm for some reason, but can't contact the police because the baby was born out of wedlock and the ensuing publicity would damage Wilde's career. fullContent:
"The Black Brat of Dunwich" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Stanley C. Sargent, first published in issue #10 of the zine Cthulhu Codex in 1997. It retells the story of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror" from a different perspective, painting Wilbur Whateley in a far more sympathetic light, and conversely Henry Armitage as the story's villain.

### Synopsis
Two men writing the first definitive account of the Dunwich horror of 1928 encounter an old man who claims to have been employed for a time as Wilbur Whateley's tutor. He reveals the truth of those events: that Henry Armitage and Old Whateley were working together to bring about the return of the Outer God Yog-Sothoth, along with Wilbur's loneliness as a pariah and reluctance to be a part of the plot.

After his grandfather's death, Wilbur worked tirelessly to find a way to contain of perhaps even destroy his brother. However, requiring a copy of the Necronomicon to access the necessary spells, he was thwarted by Armitage, necessitating his fatal trip to Miskatonic University, whose watchmen Armitage had recently supplied with guard dogs- animals the Professor knew would attack the boy on sight.

The story ends with the revelation that Armitage had used his knowledge of magic not to destroy the Dunwich Horror, but to allow it to slip beneath the earth to join its kin: the source of the strange noises often heard near Dunwich, and the cause of the many hills and mounds to be found growing in the surrounding area…

The Black Goat of the Woods was the fifth expansion pack for Fantasy Flight Games' Second Edition of Lovecraftian adventure board game Arkham Horror, released in June 2008.

### Overview
A cards-only expansion, The Black Goat of the Woods did not include the optional game board seen in some of the larger packs. It included an additional 90 Investigator and 88 Ancient One cards to diversify games of Arkham Horror, and a new Herald, the Black Goat of the Woods, along with a handful of additional Monster tokens.

In addition, the expansion introduced two new optional mechanics to change how the core game plays, and a difficulty level selector system to allow for easier or more challenging gameplay. The new mechanics were Cult Encounters, which allowed Investigators to interact more deeply with Arkham's occult elements, and Investigator Corruption, a system by which Investigators slowly gain negative effects as their adventure progresses.

fullContent:
"The Black Kiss" is a short story by Robert Bloch and Henry Kuttner, originally published in the June 1937 issue of Weird Tales.

It features Kuttner's occult investigator character Michael Leigh, albeit in a small role.

### Synopsis
An artist named Graham Dean inherits the house that once belonged to his great-great-grand-aunt Morella Godolfo in San Pedro, California. After moving there, he starts to experience strange dreams in which he swims under the sea, and from which he wakes up exhausted.

Dean soon learns about the local legends concerning Morella Godolfo, who was rumored to practice dark magic and who disappeared one night into the sea in which she was often seen swimming in the company of unknown creatures.

After consulting with his doctor, who dismisses his dreams as the product of stress, Dean receives a telegram from his uncle, the occultist Michael Leigh, who is in Calcutta and has just received the news about Dean inheriting the Godolfo property. Leigh urges Dean to leave the house immediately and to seek help from Leigh's colleague, Dr. Makoto Yamada.

Feeling too tired to follow his uncle's instructions, Dean falls asleep and has a dream in which he sees visions from the ocean, culminating in a cave underneath the seashore cliff on which the house stands, and a serpentine sea creature with white lips who kisses him. As soon as he wakes up, he receives a visit from Dr. Yamada, who has been contacted by Leigh.

Yamada informs Dean of the existence of sea creatures that can mind-swap with humans in order to experience the exotic sensations of a land-based existence, which they find pleasurable. The body of Morella Godolfo had been inhabited by one of these entities, and when her body died, the creature was forced to return to its own. Longing to experience life as a human again, the same creature is now trying to establish a psychic link with Dean, explaining the dreams and the feeling of constant fatigue.

Dean feels drowsy and answers Yamada's questions automatically, as if a voice inside his head instructed him about what to say. Suddenly, he realizes that he's no longer in his house with Yamada, but in the ocean, swimming with the white serpentine creatures that no longer appear strange and repulsive, but perfectly mundane to him. He can understand the beings' language and accompanies them when they find a shipwreck and drag the sailors to the sea depths, which he finds perfectly natural. After that, he finds himself on a seashore and sees his own house on the cliff and two men running towards him, calling out his name.

Dean crawls away so they won't see him, and hides in the same cave where the white creature had kissed him. There, he finally realizes that he is inhabiting the body of the creature, and sees his own body inside the cave, as the creature is accustoming itself to it. Dean realizes that the sea-dweller is planning to impersonate him.

The two men, who turn out to be Leigh and Yamada, enter the cave and see Dean

"The Black Pool" is a short story by British author and games designer James "Grim" Desborough. It  was published in the thematic anthology Lovecraft after Dark by James Ward Kirk Publishing in November 2015.

### Synopsis
A young heiress in post-WWI Britain uses her vast fortune to indulge in her every whim and desire, searching for a way to lose herself in sensation. Despite her wealth, she is unable to find what she is looking for and eventually becomes jaded with life, until she meets a man who whispers to her of a place which may provide what she seeks.

Travelling to Iceland, she eventually locates a lodge for the rich and decadent, and is introduced to their secret. Led deep beneath the surface to a colossal cave system, she encounters a strange, tar-like being which takes her to the extremes of pleasure. Deciding that her life is no longer worth living, she resolves to surrender to the being one last time before allowing it to consume her.

### Behind the Mythos
The creature encountered in the bowels of the Earth is intended to be a Shoggoth, as evidenced by its soft call of "Tekeli-li".

"The Black Rapture" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

After finding a musty old tome in a the attic, a young loner murders his unloving parents during the opening stages of the return of the Great Old Ones, believing this act will grant him favour with the Earth's new masters. However, his parents are not quite what they appeared to be, and even death is not enough to stop them from finishing the scheme they have spent years nurturing.

### Characters
* Robert, a friendless teenager who wishes for little other than to watch the world burn.
* Robert's unnamed parents, two cultists of the dark gods.

### Publication History
First published in the September 1998 edition of Nightscapes, "The Black Rapture" was reprinted in Dark Legacy #7 in July 2000.

### Trivia

"The Black Recalled"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, first published in World Fantasy Convention 1983: Sixty Years of Weird Tales (Weird Tales, 1983). The story is a sequel to Lumley's "The Caller of the Black" (1971), which featured the occult investigator Titus Crow. Though Crow does not appear directly in this tale, it's still considered to be a part of the Titus Crow series.

The story is set eight years after the destruction of Blowne House and the disappearance of Crow--events depicted in Lumley's novel The Burrowers Beneath as occurring in 1968.

### Synopsis
Two occult gangsters meet up at the ruins of Blowne House to reminisce about their mentor James Gedney and his downfall at the hands of Titus Crow--and to attempt to use against each other the same eldritch force that Crow turned against Gedney: the animate blood of Yibb-Tstll, known as The Black.

### Characters
Geoffrey Arnold: He had been one of the "senior members of Gedney’s cult or coven"; after Gedney's destruction, Arnold "picked up the reins from Gedney—became ‘chairman’ of the society, so to speak, ‘donned the Robes of Office’"; it's said that he is "far more powerful now than Gedney ever was." Physically, Arnold is described as "small, thin-faced, his pale skin paper-thin," with "ears large and flat to his head. He seemed made of candle wax, but his eyes were bright with an unearthly mischief, a malicious evil."

Ben Gifford: Another of Gedney's leading disciples, Gifford left England after his leader's death for America, where "there are survivals even now in old New England...if a man knows where to seek them out. Cults and covens beyond even my belief when I first went there," he tells Arnold, "all of them integrated now—under me!" ("Loosely as yet," he hastened to add.) Gifford is called "huge...tall and overweight; his heavy jowls were pock-marked in a face lined, roughened and made coarse by a life of unnatural excesses." (His bulk turns out to be the result of a symbiotic relationship he's formed with The Black.)

James D. Gedney: Though long dead at the time of the story's action, Gedney is discussed at length by his former acolytes. He "had been no mere dabbler; his studies had taken him to all the world’s strange places, from which he rarely returned empty-handed.... [H]is occult library had been second to none," and he had the power, thanks to his "masterly erudition in matters of linguistics and cryptography," "to penetrate even the blackest veils of myth and mysticism," to turn the "merest fragments of time-lost lore" into "working spells and enchantments." He viewed magic as "simply the inconceivable science of alien abysses, the knowledge of dark dimensions beyond the powers of men even to perceive."

fullContent:
"The Black Stone" is a short fantasy/horror story by Robert E. Howard. It is notable for containing the second mention of Unaussprechlichen Kulten (Nameless Cults or The Black Book), a grimoire first referenced in Howard's "The Children of the Night" and mentioned later by many authors, including Lovecraft himself.

### Synopsis
The story opens with an unnamed narrator being gripped with curiosity by a brief reference to the Black Stone in the book Nameless Cults, a.k.a. The Black Book, by Friedrich von Junzt. He researches the artifact but finds little further information. The ancient (though its age is debated) monolith stands near to the village of Stregoicavar ("meaning something like Witch-Town") in the mountains of Hungary. There are many superstitions surrounding it; for instance, it is believed that anyone who sleeps nearby will suffer nightmares for the rest of their life, and anyone who visits the stone on Midsummer Night will go insane and die. Though the Monolith is hated and disliked by all in the village, it is said by the innskeeper that "Any man who lay hammer or maul to it die evilly", so that all of the villagers simply shun the stone.

The narrator decides to travel to Stregoicavar on vacation. Along the way he hears of the local history and sees the site of an old battlefield, where Count Boris Vladinoff fought the invading Suleiman the Magnificent in 1526. Local stories say that Vladinoff took shelter in a ruined castle and was brought a lacquered case that had been found near the body of Selim Bahadur, "the famous Turkish scribe and historian", who had died in a recent battle. The unnamed contents scared the Count, but at that moment Turkish artillery destroyed a part of the castle and he was buried in the rubble, where his bones still remain to the present day.

Reaching the village, the narrator interviews some of the villagers. The current inhabitants are not the original people of the village, who had been all wiped out by the Turkish invasion in 1526. They are said to have been of a different, unknown, race than the Hungarians, with a reputation for raiding other villages to kidnap women and children. A schoolteacher reveals that, according to legend, the original name for the village was Xuthltan, and the stone was at one time worshiped by pagans (although the stone probably predates them). The black stone is "octagonal in shape, some sixteen feet in height and about a foot and a half thick."


A week after arriving, the narrator realizes that it is Midsummer Night and makes his way to the stone. He falls asleep an hour before midnight, but wakes to find the chanting and dancing people around the stone. After much dancing, during which the narrator is unable to move or do anything but observe, a baby is killed in sacrifice. fullContent:
: King of Chicago
|created by   = Gary Sumpter
|affiliations=Outer God}}

The Blackness from the Stars is an extraterrestrial entity in the Cthulhu Mythos. Its only appearance is in Chaosium's supplement King of Chicago for their Call of Cthulhu RPG.

### Description
The Blackness from the Stars is an immobile blob of living, sentient darkness, torn from the primal fabric of the cosmos at the center of the universe. It is distinguishable in darkness only as a vaguely shimmering, oily patch.

The Blackness is immune to physical threats, and can regenerate itself upon harm by magical threats. Heat, cold, acid, and electricity have no effect. The entity can't endure light: direct sunlight will sear it to dust; even the dimmest light source (such as a candle) can still damage it.

The thing can enthrall nearby victims and make them slaves. Creatures within twenty miles of it can also suffer nightmares of the entity; those with histories of mental instability are most susceptible and therefore often targeted. To defend itself, it can also manipulate the air to create a vortex that spirals from itself to nearby areas.

Although intelligent, it speaks no known language and ignores attempts to communicate.

### Worshipers
The Blackness from the Stars can telepathically enthrall nearby humans, mostly derelicts like drug fiends, drunks, and borderline personalities. Soon they will become slaves with no will of their own.

Human servants of the Blackness are driven to mutilation; all bear the scars of self-inflicted wounds. Victims are always maimed before being sacrificed to the entity.

### In the Mythos
The Blackness from the Stars was summoned from the stars by a cult named Celestial Providence down to Chicago on Sunday, October 8, 1871 to the basement of an old Baptist Church. Its arrival caused a great conflagration that burnt down a large part of the city and trapped the thing itself in the basement in the process. While the church was demolished and turned into a vacant lot when the city was rebuilt, the basement and the entity inside is still intact.

In the 1920s, Johny Premoli of the North River Gang (probably based on the real-life North Side Gang) in Chicago along with the derelicts tried to stage a coup to overtake the gang and then used its resource to release the entity, but this plan proved unsuccessfully.

### Behind the Mythos
Although the entity was depicted as connected to a cult in the original source, it was never given any kind of deity status there. Later compilations of entities such as the Malleus Monstrorum books would go on to categorize the entity as a Lesser Outer God. This status, alongside its residence at the center of the universe, may then also put it amongst the Lesser Other Gods which reside at the Court of Azathoth.

shortDefinition: "The Blade of the Slayer" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney in which his sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta encounters an ancient warrior--who in one version of the story is another notable recurring fantasy character. The story first appeare...
fullContent:
"The Blade of the Slayer" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney in which his sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta encounters an ancient warrior--who in one version of the story is another notable recurring fantasy character. The story first appeared in Pulse-Pounding Adventure Stories #1, published in 1986; a significantly different version appeared in Tierney's collection The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997).

### Synopsis
Travelling between Persepolis to Susa on his way to Rome, Simon is set upon by vicious bandits. He escapes and takes refuge in a magus's lair in an ancient ruin--only to find that the sorcerer plans to turn him over to the bandits whom he is in league with. Simon survives by freeing an ancient warrior, known as "The Slayer," whom the sorcerer's order had kept magically imprisoned for ages. 

### Setting
The story takes place in January of 32 A.D., during the journey from Persia to Rome described in Tierney's story "The Seed of the Star-God." The ruins of the "First City" are in modern-day Iran.

### Behind the Mythos
The identity of the Slayer is different in the two published versions of the story: In the Pulse-Pounding version, he's the biblical character Nimrod; in the Scroll of Thoth iteration, he's Karl Edward Wagner's immortal hero Kane, who was inspired by the figure of Cain in the book of Genesis. 

Tierney originally wrote the character as Kane, then changed him at Wagner's request; although Wagner liked the story, he thought he might write more Kane stories, and didn't want to feel bound by Tierney's continuity. "Since the tragic death of Karl Wagner, that problem has vanished," Scroll of Thoth editor Robert M. Price wrote, allowing the original version of the story to be published "as a tribute to Karl Edward Wagner."

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Pulse-Pounding Adventures, "The Blade of the Slayer" was reprinted in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth  and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020). Both of the reprints feature Tierney's original conception in which the Slayer is Kane.

### References

"The Blue Canoe" is a short Lovecraftian story by author Ben Scotti.

### Synopsis
A letter from a dead man describes the day, many years ago, when his life was changed by a chance encounter with an alien entity. The man tells of when, while working as a bartender, a stranger entered the tavern. Revealing himself to be some form of malignant being, the stranger caused a wave of madness to sweep through the patrons before burning the building to the ground. Aside from the letter's author, none survived.

shortDefinition: "The Bone's Prayer" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan about a Providence writer whose life is upended by the discovery of a small carved stone on a Rhode Island beach. It first appeared in the February 2009 issue of Kiernan's ezine Sirenia Diges...
fullContent:
"The Bone's Prayer" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan about a Providence writer whose life is upended by the discovery of a small carved stone on a Rhode Island beach. It first appeared in the February 2009 issue of Kiernan's ezine Sirenia Digest (#39).

The stone that drives the plot is shaped like a teardrop and is the color of pea soup. The stone glistens wetly in the dim afternoon light, and...there are markings etched deeply into its smooth surface. One of them looks a bit like a left-facing swastika, and another reminds her of a Greek ichthus.

### Characters
*Edith: A writer who often suffers from writer's block; Edith is not the name that appears on the covers of her novels. She "is not an outgoing person.... She hates the thought of being seen."  Her hair is "an unremarkable dishwater blonde," and her eyes are "a dull brown.... Edith’s hands are thick, her fingers stubby. She keeps her nails chewed down to the quick."
*Sammie: Edith's closest friend and sometimes lover.  She is "two or three inches taller" than Edith, "and has striking jet-black hair just beginning to show strands of grey." Her "eyes are a bright hazel green," and she "has delicate hands and the long, tapered fingers of a pianist."

### Setting
The stone is found at Moonstone Beach, a real beach in South Kingstown, Rhode Island. Edith remembers, as a child, seeing a weird aquatic creature she identified as a "mermaid" near Beavertail Lighthouse--a real lighthouse on Conanicut Island. 

### Connections
Sammie recalls reading a book called Mysteries of the Sea that included an account of "a ship finding an uncharted island somewhere in the South Pacific, back in the twenties.... They found an island, complete with the ruins of a gigantic city, but then the whole thing sank in an earthquake."

### Publication History
"The Bone's Prayer" was reprinted in The Year’s Best Dark Fantasy & Horror 2010 (Prime Books, 2010). It subsequently appeared in Kiernan's collections Confessions of a Five-Chambered Heart (Subterranean Press, 2012) and Houses Under the Sea (Centipede Press, 2018). 

### References

fullContent:
"The Bones of the Old Ones" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. Part of a short series set in his dystopian sci-fi setting of Punktown, it was first published in The Bones of the Old Ones and Other Lovecraftian Tales by Necropolitan Press in 1995.

### Synopsis
Detective Inspector John Bell of the Paxton Police Department is called to the scene of a mass murder where the only survivor was a strange young child. He is soon informed that the perpetrator, an old friend of his by the name of Joshua Kaddish, is in custody and apparently spared the boy on purpose. Through questioning and a scan of Kaddish's memories, Bell is convinced that the murdered people were in fact a cult dedicated to bringing about the return of the Old Ones, employing supernatural means such as the Hounds of Tindalos to further their goals.

At this time, reports on the news networks begin to announce loss of contact with Earth; the phenomenon soon extends to Luna Colony, Mars, the Jovian colonies and Titan.

Shortly after, Kaddish escapes from police custody; he and Bell quickly deduce that the surviving child is in fact an avatar of Yog-Sothoth, a tool to be used to open the gates for the other gods to pour through. Confronting the boy, the being reveals his true nature and begins to transform into a dimensional portal; Kaddish is successful in closing the gate and killing the child, but it costs him his life.

The story concludes with transmissions slowly returning from Earth and the silent colonies, and the revelation that thousands of people across the galaxy have been horribly disfigured, their minds shattered by the events of the last few hours.

### Publication History
*The Bones of the Old Ones and Other Lovecraftian Tales (1995)
*Dreaming in R'lyeh Issue 1 (2003)
*Unholy Dimensions (2005)
*Voices from Punktown (2008)
*Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012, German-language collection)
*Punktown: Volume 1 (2021)

### Trivia
*The name of the murdered cult leader, Willy Pugmire, is likely a nod to the late American author W. H. Pugmire, with whom Thomas later collaborated on the 2013 Cthulhu Mythos collection Encounters with Enoch Coffin.

fullContent:
"The Book" is an unfinished short story by H. P. Lovecraft, believed to have been written in late 1933. It was first published in the journal Leaves in 1938, after Lovecraft's death. It has been posthumously completed by Martin S. Warnes as "The Black Tome of Alsophocus".

In the story fragment, the narrator is given an ancient book by a strange bookseller, and when he takes it home and examines it, weird and sinister events ensue.

Lovecraft considered "I am at a sort of standstill in writing--disgusted at much of my older work, & uncertain as to avenues of improvement. In recent weeks I have done a tremendous amount of experimenting in different styles & perspectives, but have destroyed most of the results." (HPL: Selected Letters 4.664)

The H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia suggests that "The Book" was one of the undestroyed experiments—an attempt to translate Lovecraft's poem sequence Fungi from Yuggoth into prose. (The completed fragment corresponds to the first three sonnets, which form more of a coherent narrative than the rest of the sequence.)(: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

"The Black Tome of Alsophocus", first published in New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (1969), turns the fragment into a tale of possession by Nyarlathotep.

### Notes

fullContent:
"The Book" is a short story with Cthulhu Mythos connections by author J. C. Weir. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 1 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in April 2018.

### Synopsis
Aging vicar John, a collector of rare and antique books, comes into the possession of an ancient volume of unknown provenance. Reading the book and perusing it’s almost-animate illustrations unnerves him greatly, and he resolves to be rid of it in the morning. However, whatever dark power the book contains has already done its work, and when his wife awakens the next day, she finds John in his library, bloody and inconsolable, and muttering the phrase "Tekeli-li! Tekeli-li!" over and over again.

### Behind the Mythos
Although the phrase "Tekeli-li! Tekeli-li!" is most commonly associated with the prehistoric Shoggoths in the context of Lovecraftian fiction, it would appear that in this instance it would be more likely to have been intended to be the cry of despair uttered by the Inuit in Edgar Allan Poe's The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket.

Further, it could be extrapolated that the grimoire received by John in "The Book" is one of the "unsuspected and forbidden sources to which Poe may have had access when writing his Arthur Gordon Pym" mentioned by Danforth in At the Mountains of Madness. This would explain the mournful recitation of "Tekeli-li" in both Arthur Gordon Pym and "The Book."

It was released digitally in May 2017 by Humanoids Inc. in partnership with comiXology. The Book of Chaos story was continued in a second volume, Infernum in Terra, later that month.

### Synopsis
When Miskatonic University Professor Jack Stanton returns to New York from an archaeological trip to China, he writes a book to reveal to the world the world-changing truths he discovered there: that the planet was inhabited by intelligent and technologically-advanced beings long before the rise of humankind.

Just prior to the launch of his book, however, Stanton is attacked by a religious zealot determined to prevent its release; subsequently, the crash of a supertanker into the New York cityscape triggers an event which transports him to a bizarre, nightmarish land where he must fight for survival against strange creatures and an environment which is inimically hostile to human life.

### Synopsis
Former Miskatonic University professor Jack Stanton is pursued across the hellish landscape that he comes to realise is a devastated future Earth. Joining a group of mutated survivors whose leader believes him to be a prophet capable of delivering salvation to the human race, they travel back to the group's hidden city, only to find it in ruins, the victim of one of the colossal beings which now stalk the planet. 

Believing that the key to the world's salvation may lie in a video cassette made by the man who attacked him in his own time, Stanton makes his way to his old apartment, where the tape reveals the cause of the destruction: a "stele" which acts as a cosmic beacon, calling the alien colossi to Earth.

fullContent:
The Book of Chaos, Vol. 3: Pater Tenebrarum is a short Cthulhu Mythos graphic novel written by Mathieu Lauffray and Xavier Dorison, with Lauffray also suppling the artwork. It was first published in French as Prophet 03: Pater Tenebrarum in 2005; an English translation has since been published.

### Synopsis
Former Miskatonic University professor Jack Stanton and his small group of survivors attempt to reach the stele which they believe might hold a chance for redemption. As the band dwindles in the face of the horrors which patrol the streets of New York, the revelation that Stanton was the cause of all that befell Earth threatens to tear the group apart, despite the growing realisation amongst them that he possesses certain abilities which hint that he may in fact be the true prophet.

### Trivia
During a discussion on his previous life, Stanton reveals that he knew a Professor West at Miskatonic University. However, given the context of the conversation, this is more likely to be a nod to Herbert West, rather than any intention for it to have been the good doctor himself.

The contents of the Book of Eibon are primarily the work of Clark Ashton Smith, one of the most famous contributors to Weird Tales and the creator of the Book of Eibon, as well as Lin Carter, esteemed fantasy and horror editor. Robert M. Price, Richard L. Tierney, Joseph S. Pulver, and a number of other authors have helped complete the text, resulting in a tome that reveals all the secrets of the Cthulhu Mythos, from the history of the first alien races to come to Earth, to the histories of the Elder Magi of Hyperborea, and the story of Eibon's life and death.

### Contents
Aiming to replicate the contents of the fictional tome it is named after, The Book of Eibon is divided into five parts, or "Books". Book One collects stories of ancient wizards. The stories in Book Two are about Eibon himself. Book Three is concerned with the history of the world, according to the Mythos, while Books Four and Five contain poetry and magic rituals.

Each story is preceded by an introduction by Robert M. Price.

fullContent:
"The Bookseller's Second Wife" is a short story by Walter C. DeBill, Jr. first published in the anthology collection The Disciples of Cthulhu II by Chaosium in February 2003. The story forms part of DeBill, Jr.'s Mlandoth Cycle, a myth cycle originally intended to run parallel to the Cthulhu Mythos, but later incorporated into the setting in the Call of Cthulhu monster manual Ye Booke of Monstres (1994, Chaosium).

### Synopsis
A college student gets a summer job working for an antiquarian bookseller. In reality, the bookseller is a necromancer and a supplier of grimoires to cultists and other evil magicians. He has a horde of half-rat humanoid servitors, which makes him extremely dangerous.

The college student attracts the attention of the necromancer's second wife, who is in reality an avatar of the energy vampire Yidhra. Rather than merely a conventional adulterous love triangle, Yidhra inveigles the young man into a lethal situation where his life force is devoured, the jealous necromancer has his revenge, and Yidhra simply regenerates into another of her seductive vampiric forms and continues her endless parasitic existence.

### Publication History
* The Disciples of Cthulhu II (2003, Chaosium)
* The Black Sutra (2006, Mythos Books)

"The Boonieman" is a short story by American author Edward M. Erdelac.

### Synopsis
When a remote American firebase during the Vietnam War receives word that a major North Vietnamese offensive may be in the offing, a small unit takes a helicopter to investigate. Landing at a friendly village, they find that they have arrived too late and it has already been burned out. However, amongst the survivors is a sorcerer who yearns for revenge, and he awakens the entity which sleeps beneath the village. As the abomination rampages across the countryside, the helicopter pilot and a local man use the power of a strange charm to send it back into slumber.

### Characters

*Lieutenant Jatczak, a special forces officer nearing the end of his tour of duty.
*Beo, a Vietnamese villager who has thrown his lot in with the Americans stationed nearby.
*Rin, a village shaman, actually a Tcho-Tcho sorcerer from Cambodia.
*Major Dyer, an American officer with knowledge of what lies beneath the hilltop village.
*Shugoran an Avatar of Nyarlathotep.

### Publication History
"The Boonieman" was included in the thematic anthology World War Cthulhu in 2014, published by Dark Regions Press and edited by Brian M. Sammons and Glynn Owen Barrass.

"The Bride of the Yellow King" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young. It is the fifth instalment of Book 3 in his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
As Mayweather drops into a coma from the effects of his cancer, Hines sets off on a rogue mission to confront the fears of her past: to destroy a cell of cultists of Hastur.

Travelling to Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, she attempts to tackle the small family of cultists but is quickly overpowered and prepared as a vessel for the children of Hastur. She manages to escape her bonds and kill the human vessel inhabited by the essence of the Great Old One, and is aided in her escape by a group of silent Mi-Go, presumably in service to Hastur's enemy, Nyarlathotep. The aliens pass her a mysterious artefact containing an enormous amount of Eldritch energy before disappearing into the night. 

During the debrief with Harjit Singh at the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena, Mayweather is found to have recovered considerably, and is speculated to have received assistance in the battle against his disease from none other than Nyarlathotep, and Adele Kramer suddenly awakens.

### Characters
*Malcolm Mayweather, a veteran agent with the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.
*Charlene Hines, Mayweather's junior partner.
*Harjit Singh, the Department's director.
*Josiah, Arleth, Ezekiel, and Gabriel Bain, inbred cultists of Hastur.
*Abida Bain, the youngest of the Bain family, who wishes to escape from the cult.
*Hastur, an alien entity of enormous power, who is yet unable to fully manifest in our world.
*Marie Hollis, Department of Extraordinary Phenomena field agent.
*Jim Barnes, Department of Extraordinary Phenomena field agent.

### Publication History
"The Bride of the Yellow King" was published in the collection The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 3 in 2021.

fullContent:
The Broken Hours: A Novel of H. P. Lovecraft is a gothic mystery novel by Canadian author Jacqueline Baker, first published in a paperback format by Harper Perennial in September 2015. Unusually for a story involving Lovecraft, it contains no supernatural elements, preferring instead to focus on the broken psyche of the main character.

### Overview


### Synopsis
When poverty-stricken Arthor Crandle takes a live-in position transcribing documents for the reviled and reclusive author Howard Phillips Lovecraft, he uncovers a family history of congenital madness as well as the tragic events which resulted in his employer's current condition. 

The story concludes with the revelation that Crandle - and the woman with which he began to fall in love with - in fact never existed, and was nothing more than another manifestation of Lovecraft's psyche, desperate to escape the knowledge that his newborn child, born hideously deformed, died in infancy. As he recalls this painful memory, he retreats once again into seclusion, presumably to begin the cycle of forgetting once again. 

### Publication History
The Broken Hours was rereleased in hardcover and digital editions by Talos Press in April 2016; a reissue of the paperback was released the following year.

fullContent:
"The Brood of Bubastis" is a horror short story by Robert Bloch set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in the March 1937 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
The American narrator travels to Cornwall, England, to visit his friend Malcolm Kent, who shares his interest in occultism. Kent makes the shocking announcement that, according to Ludvig Prinn's De Vermis Mysteriis and other sources, a group of Egyptian renegades once settled in Cornwall. Furthermore, he claims to have found a cave with Egyptian hieroglyphs in the countryside, which he invites the narrator to see. Only when they arrive at the entrance does Kent reveal that, according to Prinn, the Egyptian renegades were worshipers of the cat-goddess Bubastis, or Bast, exiled from their country for the atrocious sacrifices performed by their cult. The cave that Kent discovered accesses an underground temple built in honour of Bubastis, and he claims that the Priests of Bast experimented with the breeding of human / animal hybrids in an attempt to recreate their deity.

As he descends into the tunnels, guided by Kent, the narrator is horrified to find the mummified bodies of half-human, half-animal things, including some with horns, hooves, wings, and/or multiple heads. The walls are covered with sickening images of sacrifices and carnal rituals engaged in by the human priests and their creations alike. At last, they enter a large chamber with an altar covered in half-eaten bones, many of them recent and still clad in modern clothes. Kent reveals that after finding the cave, he has sacrificed several people to a monster that still inhabits these tunnels, a descendant of the priests' experiments known as the "Chewer of Corpses". The creature emerges while Kent and the narrator fight each other, and the latter manages to strike Kent and run away, but not before witnessing the Chewer of Corpses viciously devour Kent as its prey.

Since his return to New York, the narrator has been plagued by nightmares of his traumatic experience and a newly-acquired phobia of cats. He has written down the narrative as a suicide note, as well as to warn others away from the cave. As a final note, he reveals that the Chewer of Corpses is a 10 ft tall female humanoid with a feline head, created by the priests as a reincarnation of the goddess Bast herself.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite being referred to as a "ghoul", the Chewer of Corpses doesn't seem to be related to the canine-headed Ghouls found elsewhere in the Mythos.

fullContent:
"The Brown Tower" is a short story by author John Prescott. It first appeared online on Mike Davis's long-running blog / fanzine, "The Lovecraft eZine".

### Synopsis
The story describes two friends, Lane McKenzie and Mark Stillwater, who, out of boredom during the winter, in the small southern town of Brayton. Crossing the only bridge out of town they happen upon the eponymous Brown Tower and decide to press on and explore it. Doing so leads to a terrifying period in darkness as they ascend and then their horrible final moments as prey of the bat-like monstrosity  that dwells within.

The tower was constructed by a family of witches and sorcerers called the Billingsteins in the 1920s and already by the 1930s it enjoyed an evil reputation. It was ostensibly intended to be a feed store for the surrounding farms but the evil reputation of both the structure and the family responsible for it deterred its use. When Mark and Lane arrive at the tower the stench from inside is remarkably pungent and unpleasant. Ignoring this and all other ill omens, they press on and climb the tower, to their doom.

Before their untimely end, the two explorers discover walls covered in weird bas-relief carvings and a fragment of paper covered in bizarre writing, including the apparent name of the entity that ultimately destroys them:

### Synopsis
The sorcerer Eibon relates the story of how, in his youth, he sought the secret to eternal life despite the warnings of his elders, and how the revelation put paid to that quest.

On the trail of Koth-Serapis, an evil wizard said to have already learned and employed the secret, he travels first to Lemuria and consults with the spectre of Sharajsha, who guides him on his way with another dire warning.

Following the instructions which lead him to the Vale of Pnath, he encounters a colossal worm which devours the souls of the dead, but soon comes to the realisation that this creature is in fact Koth-Serapis, and that his transformation is the price which must be paid for the prize.

"The Burrower From the Bluff" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Beecher Smith. It was published in the Issue #4 of online zine The Three-Lobed Burning Eye in January 2000.

### Synopsis
A corrupt lawyer writes down the story of how, when in dire financial straits, he was persuaded to push through a legal motion which would allow an amoral development company to move sacred mounds to another location in order to construct prime riverside real estate, in spite of warnings from a Native American chief.

Unknown to the developers, moving the bluffs inadvertently released the underground monstrosity Dhumin, held captive in the hard rock for untold ages. Beginning with the ground crew, all involved begin to fall prey to freak accidents involving road collapses or cave-ins. The lawyer, last of the group, attempts to put everything to paper as he feels the tremors come closer…

### Mythos Connections
At one point, Native American Chief Russell Two Bears states that Dhumin was possibly a Great Old One, a type of entity mostly banished back to the stars by the Elder Gods.

The Burrowers Beneath is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by Brian Lumley, and the first in his series of Titus Crow novels.

### Overview


### Synopsis
The story follows occultist Titus Crow and his friend Henri-Laurent de Marigny as they uncover a plot by the Chthonians and their masters against the people of Great Britain. The two eventually join up with the Wilmarth Foundation, a group of humans with knowledge of the Cthulhu Cycle Deities, and participate in an operation to clear the island of their influence, killing the Chthonian leader in the process. The book ends with the Great Old One known as Ithaqua attacking Crow with his elemental minions. After the attack, Crow is believed dead.

*Cgfthgnm'o'th, the leader of the Chthonians.
*Ithaqua, a Great Old One.

### Behind the Mythos
The Burrowers Beneath was first published in 1975. It has since been re-released numerous times, and has been translated into a number of languages including German, French, Italian and Japanese.

fullContent:
"The Cairn on the Headland" is a short story by Robert E. Howard, a Mythos-adjacent tale in which a struggle between Norse paganism and Celtic Christianity is given a Lovecraftian twist. It was first published in the January 1933 issue of Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror.

### Synopsis
Two American academics, James O'Brien and Ortali, visit Grimmin’s Cairn, a centuries-old monument at Clontarf, near Dublin, Ireland--raised at the time of King Brian Boru's defeat of the pagan Viking invaders in 1014 A.D. Ortali, who holds a deadly secret over O'Brien, coerces him into a plan to loot the historical site for treasure. O'Brien agrees to the plan, though he is tempted to murder his blackmailer, though it would mean the gallows for him. 

O'Brien is met by an Irish woman wearing oddly dated clothing and speaking archaic Gaelic, who calls herself Meve MacDonnal. She warns him against his oppressor's plan, and offers him a priceless relic for protection: the crucifix of Saint Brandon the Blessed, believed lost since 1595.

Returning to his hotel, O'Brien has a vision of the Battle of Clontarf, apparently through the eyes of an ancestor, Red Cumal, an Irish fighter. After donning the armor and helmet of a slain enemy, he witnesses the death of a strange Norse warrior, a massive figure in grey armor with skin smooth as ivory. Mistaking Red Cumal for a comrade, the warrior reveals that he is a god trapped in a dying human body, and urges him to touch him with holly to liberate him. The Irishman recognizes the god as Odin, and instead of restoring him with holly, imprisons his corpse with the stones of the cairn.

Realizing that Ortali has decided to ransack the cairn without him, a night earlier than planned, O'Brien rushes to head him off--running across as he does so Meve McDonnal's gravestone, which reads "1565–1640." When he arrives at Grimmin's Cairn, he finds Ortali in the process of exposing Odin's uncorrupted body--and sees a sprig of holly that had been tucked into Ortali's lapel fall upon the corpse, liberating the god. Far from grateful to his rescuer, Odin slays Ortali with a bolt of lightning. O'Brien, meanwhile, confronts Odin with the cross of Saint Brandon--which sends the god back to the stars from which he came.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Cairn on the Headland" originally began life as "Spears of Clontarf," a historical fiction story that was rejected by Soldiers of Fortune magazine. (It was not published in this form until 1978.) He rewrote it with fantasy elements and submitted it to Weird Tales as "The Grey God Passes"--which was also rejected, eventually seeing print in the anthology Dark Mind, Dark Heart (Arkham House, 1962) as "The Twilight of the Grey Gods." Howard reworked it a second time by adding horror elements, and that substantially revised version was published by Strange Tales as "The Cairn on the Headlands."

fullContent:
The Call Number of Cthulhu is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author Tom Bruno. It was independently published on Amazon's digital Kindle platform in May 2018.

The book is the sixth in Bruno's L is for Librarian series, a thematic collection which features libraries and librarians as their core plot device. The series was brought about by the author's background as a librarian in the real world. The title is a reference to call numbers, a form of "address" in book cataloguing which allows the book to be more easily located.

### Synopsis
During the 1940s, Massachusetts Institute of Technology's Professor Vannevar Bush believes he has discovered a way to automate book cataloguing systems to make them more accessible to readers, but is unable to to persuade any to allow him to test his ideas at their institute. That is, until he gets a message from Harriet Kuhlthau, the progressive young director of Miskatonic University, Arkham.

Bush and Kuhlthau hit it off, and embark on a program of testing different methods of categorisation, beginning with the more mundane books, and eventually working their way through to the restricted collection. Simultaneously, a chance encounter with a Russian professor who has knowledge of a previous attempt to implement a similar system, along with his own researches, lead Bush to the slow realisation that the mere act of categorising such works may initiate a ritual to summon a dark god to our world.

Racing back to Arkham in an effort to prevent Kuhlthau from beginning the completed automation process, Bush finds to his dismay that she has started early, and arrives just in time to witness the enormous form of Great Cthulhu emerging from the depths of the Miskatonic River and consuming the entire city, erasing it not only from the face of the planet, but also from the collective consciousness of the human race.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly stated, Harriet Kuhlthau is heavily implied to have been a Cthulhu cultist, whose goal was to summon the Great Old One all along. It is also suggested that she was responsible for her predecessor's death, one Professor Henry Armitage.

"The Call of Cthulhu" is a short story by American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in August and September 1926 and originally serialized in the February 1928 issue of Weird Tales. It is the only story written by Lovecraft in which the extraterrestrial entity Cthulhu himself makes a major appearance. The story is written in a documentary style, with three independent narratives linked together by the device of a narrator discovering notes left by a deceased relative.

The narrator pieces together the whole truth and disturbing significance of the information he possesses, illustrating the story's first line: "The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents. We live on a placid island of ignorance in the midst of black seas of infinity, and it was not meant that we should voyage far."

### Summary
"The Call of Cthulhu" is presented as a manuscript "found among the papers of the late Francis Wayland Thurston, of Boston". In the text, Thurston recounts his discovery of notes left behind by his grand-uncle, George Gammell Angell, a prominent professor of Semitic languages at Brown University in Providence, Rhode Island, who died suddenly in "the winter of 1926–27" after being "jostled by a nautical-looking negro."

### "The Horror in Clay"
"The Horror in Clay" concerns a small bas-relief sculpture found among the papers, which the narrator describes: " [...] my somewhat extravagant imagination yielded simultaneous pictures of an octopus, a dragon, and a human caricature [...] A pulpy, tentacled head surmounted a grotesque and scaly body with rudimentary wings."

The sculpture turns out to be the work of Henry Anthony Wilcox, a student at the Rhode Island School of Design who based the work on his dreams of "great Cyclopean cities of Titan blocks and sky-flung monoliths, all dripping with green ooze and sinister with latent horror." These images are associated in the dreams with the words Cthulhu and R'lyeh.

Wilcox's dreams began on March 1, 1925, culminating in a period from March 23 until April 2 when Wilcox was in a state of delirium. During the same period, Angell's research reveals, there were cases of "outre mental illnesses and outbreaks of group folly or mania" around the world — from Paris and London, Africa and South America, Haiti and the Philippines, western Ireland and India. In New York City, "hysterical Levantines" mob police; in California, a Theosophist colony dons white robes to await a "glorious fulfillment."

### "The Tale of Inspector Legrasse"
In the second part of the story, "The Tale of Inspector Legrasse", Angell's notes reveal that the professor had heard the word Cthulhu and seen a similar image much earlier. At the 1908 meeting of the American Archaeological Society in St. Louis, Missouri, a New Orleans police official named John Raymond Legrasse had asked the assembled antiquarians to identify a statuette, made of an unidentifiable greenish-black stone

shortDefinition: The Call of Cthulhu is a 2005 independent silent film adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft short story The Call of Cthulhu, produced by Sean Branney and Andrew Leman and distributed by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society. It is the first film adaptat...
fullContent:
The Call of Cthulhu is a 2005 independent silent film adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft short story The Call of Cthulhu, produced by Sean Branney and Andrew Leman and distributed by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society. It is the first film adaptation of the famous Lovecraft story, and uses Mythoscope, a blend of vintage and modern filming techniques intended to produce the look of a 1920s-era film. The film is a length of a featurette.

### Plot
The film adheres very closely to Lovecraft's story, but there are a few changes. The sailors aboard the Emma first encounter the Alert abandoned at sea, rather than crewed by Cthulhu cultists and taken over by Emmas crew after a violent confrontation as in the original story. Additionally, the film depicts the narrator present at the time of his great-uncle's death, who dies peacefully in his sleep, rather than being summoned upon the mysterious death of his great-uncle, who was presumably killed by Cthulhu cultists in the original short story. The narrator (Matt Foyer) notes as well that Inspector Legrasse, who had directed the raid on cultists in backwoods Louisiana, had died before the narrator's investigation began.

In the original story, the narrator does not seem to end in a lunatic asylum or experience any mysterious nightmares himself.

### Production
Early on in production, Branney and Leman decided to film it as a black-and-white silent film. The official site says this was done to show what the film would have looked like had it been made in 1926, when the story was first published. In the DVD commentary the producers admit that shooting in black and white provided many other benefits. When using black-and-white cinematography, a filmmaker does not need to pay particular attention to the materials and decoration of sets, as the colors will not appear in the final product.

### Release
The Call of Cthulhu has been selected to appear at numerous film festivals, including the 2006 Slamdance Film Festival and North America's largest, the 2006 Seattle International Film Festival, where it sold out both screenings thanks in part to a glowing review from The Stranger, a local paper.

### Reception
Despite the long-standing conventional wisdom that this story was inherently "unfilmable", the film garnered mostly positive reception from genre reviewers. It holds 100% approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. Paul di Filippo of Science Fiction Weekly went so far as to call it "the best HPL adaptation to date," labeling the decision to adapt it as a silent film "a brilliant conceit."

In their book Lurker in the Lobby: A Guide to the Cinema of H. P. Lovecraft, Andrew Migliore and John Strysik write: "The Call of Cthulhu is a landmark adaptation that calls out to all Lovecraftian film fanatics — from its silent film form, its excellent cast, its direction, and its wonderful musical score ... this is Cthulhuian cinema that Howard would have loved."

The Call of Cthulhu is an adaptation from the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, released as part of their Dark Adventure Radio Theatre series. It is based on the short story of the same name. 

### Overview


As with all of the DART productions, The Call of Cthulhu is presented in the style of a 1930's radio broadcast. It runs to a total of 77 minutes and was issued in both Compact Disc and digital download formats with a set of period-authentic props available to enhance the immersive experience. These include: 

*A police document on the Cthulhu Cult member Castro.
*A page from the Sydney Bulletin detailing discoveries made aboard the yacht Alert.
*A photograph of the Cthulhu statuette possessed by the Eskimo branch of the Cthulhu Cult.
* A written record of one of his dreams by Henry Wilcox.

fullContent:
The Call of Ktulu is an epic instrumental song by Metallica. It was inspired by the works of H.P. Lovecraft, particularly The Call of Cthulhu. It was included on Metallica's second album, Ride the Lightning, released in 1984. It is the band's second instrumental, and the first to feature the entire band playing simultaneously.

This is one of the few songs in Metallica's career to be co-written by Dave Mustaine, the band's lead guitarist since its inception, and was originally titled "When Hell Freezes Over". The song's title was later changed, apparently at the instigation of the band's new bassist, Cliff Burton, who was a great fan of Lovecraft.

Michael Kamen arranged the classical instrumental accompaniment for "The Call of Ktulu" for the 1999 album S&M, and the version from that album won a Grammy Award for Best Rock Performance.

The song is also notable for being the longest on the album Ride the Lightning, at 8:53.

Dave's current band Megadeth used the same chord structure (00:05-00:32) in their song "Hangar 18" from the album Rust in Peace.

The song was written by James Hetfield, Lars Ulrich, Cliff Burton and Dave Mustaine.

fullContent:
"The Call of the Deep" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
In the near future mankind's destruction of the ecosystem has caused the "amphis", a species of aquatic humanoid, to rise up and declare war on the land-dwellers. In an effort to combat climate change and deter the aquatics, a group of scientists develop a sonic system designed to reduce the global temperature. Unfortunately, this has the side-effect of acting as an immense bell which calls the amphis in even greater numbers and awakens the slumbering Great Old One Cthulhu.

### Characters
*Sam Green, a highly-trained military operative.
*John Ridder, Green's subordinate.

### Publication History
"The Call of the Deep" was first published in the Dark Regions Press anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror in 2017. It was later included in the collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in 2019.

### Trivia
*The amphis are implied to have been the Deep Ones, with amphi simply being the name given to them by authorities ignorant of their nature. Amphi is of course a contraction and abbreviation of the descriptive noun Amphibian, itself an accurate of generic term for an entity such as a Deep One that can exist on both land and underwater.

"The Caller of The Black" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, part of a series featuring the occult investigator Titus Crow. Its first appearance was as the title story of Lumley's first collection, published by Arkham House in 1971.

Lumley later wrote of the piece, "One of my first stories, written in 1967 before any of my work had been published, 'Caller' is derivative not only of H. P. Lovecraft’s work but also the work of others, more especially of August Derleth."

In the story, Cabot Chambers comes to Titus Crow for help, having fallen afoul of James Gedney, an evil magician. Crow is unable to save Chambers, but  turns the malignant entity Gedney has summoned back upon him.

### Characters
Titus Crow: An occult investigator with an extensive library of arcane lore. He has "many friends in positions which...make them extremely useful ... when a bit of detective work is necessary."--including the curator of the Special Books Department at the British Museum. Crow lives near London in a place called Blowne House, a "sprawling bungalow." He is six feet tall.

James D. Gedney: The leader of a "Devil-Cult"; it's said that the "things that man does would make the Marquis De Sade in his prime appear an anaemic cretin." His "contacts were the worst sort of people and his favourite haunts were, in the main, very doubtful establishments"--including the "dimly lit Demon Club." He is described physically as resembling a thinner Bela Lugosi: "His hair is black as night and swept back from a point low in the centre of his forehead. His eyebrows are bushy above hypnotic eyes of the type you often find in people with very strong characters." The six-foot-tall Crow has to look up at him. Gedney has a country house not far from London.

Symonds: A "well-to-do" young man who joins Gedney's cult out of a boredom, then was killed by occult means when they had a falling out.

Cabot Chambers: Another wealthy thrill-seeker who was initiated into Gedney's cult; he lives "on the outskirts of town, near the old Purdy Water-mill". After the death of Symonds, he seeks Crow's help. Crow is unable to save Chambers, but learns that Gedney is using an entity known as "The Black" to eliminate his enemies.

### The Black
The supernatural threat faced in this story is "The Black", an emanation that can be used to kill enemies at a distance. It is referred to in the Necronomicon as the "blood of Yibb-Tstll, that which liveth apart from him and eateth souls, that which smothers and is called Drowner". It resembles black snowflakes, which cluster around a victim and kills by asphyxiation. It can be fended off by running water. 

According to the "legends of Hyperborea"_ the Ptetholites, a "prehistoric, sub-human race", used to send the Black against their enemies, including "Edril Ghambiz and his Hell-Hordes, ensconced on the pre-neolithic isle of Esipish in what was then the North Sea". ### Overview


### Synopsis
Four people, brought together through their connections to a series of bizarre deaths, look into a cult with connections to a monolithic pharmaceutical company. As their investigations proceed, the begin to realise that the company is in fact a front for the Cthulhu Cult, and that their plans to awaken their dark god have nearly come to fruition. 

A climactic confrontation aboard an oil rig in the middle of the Pacific Ocean results in the elimination of the cult as a threat, but leaves one of the group dead.

fullContent:
The Cards of Cthulhu is a cooperative Mythos-based cards-and-dice game.

### Gameplay
Designed for up to four players but optimised for solo play, gameplay involves the player attempting to prevent a certain number of Horror tokens from accumulating on four different Cult boards. This is achieved by collecting and playing Follower cards, each of which has its own associated special abilities and costs. If five Horror tokens accumulate on a single board, then the player loses as the Old One awakens; if the player exhausts the Cult deck, then he or she wins, having foiled the Old Ones' plans.

### Behind the Mythos
The Cards of Cthulhu was developed from a regular 52-card deck game created by Ian Richard in 2012. It was published by Dan Verssen Games following a successful Kickstarter campaign in 2014, with artwork provided by Christian Quinot.
