term: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward
shortDefinition: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward is a short novel (51,500 words) by H. P. Lovecraft, written in early 1927, but not published during the author's lifetime. Set in Lovecraft's hometown of Providence, Rhode Island, it was first published (in abridged fo...
fullContent:
The Case of Charles Dexter Ward is a short novel (51,500 words) by H. P. Lovecraft, written in early 1927, but not published during the author's lifetime. Set in Lovecraft's hometown of Providence, Rhode Island, it was first published (in abridged form) in the May and July issues of Weird Tales in 1941; the first complete publication was in Arkham House's Beyond the Wall of Sleep collection (1943). It is included in the Library of America volume of Lovecraft's work.

The novel, set in 1928, describes how Charles Dexter Ward becomes obsessed with his distant ancestor, Joseph Curwen, an alleged wizard with unsavory habits. Ward physically resembles Curwen, and attempts to duplicate his ancestor's Qabalistic and alchemical feats. He eventually uses this knowledge to physically resurrect Curwen. Ward's doctor, Marinus Bicknell Willett, investigates Ward's activities and is horrified by what he finds.

### Inspiration
In August 1925, Lovecraft's Aunt Lillian sent him an anecdote about the house at 140 Prospect Street in Providence. Lovecraft wrote back, "So the Halsey house is haunted! Ugh! That's where Wild Tom Halsey kept live terrapins in the cellar--maybe it's their ghosts. Anyway, it's a magnificent old mansion, & a credit to a magnificent old town!" (: letter to Lillian D. Clark, August 24, 1925; : An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​ Lovecraft would make this house—renumbered as 100 Prospect—the basis for the Ward house.

The following month, September 1925, Lovecraft read Providence in Colonial Times, by Gertrude Selwyn Kimball, a 1912 history that provided him the anecdotes about John Merritt and Dr. Checkley that he incorporated into his novel. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

A possible literary model is Walter de la Mare's novel The Return (1910), which Lovecraft read in mid-1926. He describes it in his essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature" as a tale in which "We see the soul of a dead man reach out of its grave of two centuries and fasten itself on the flesh of the living." (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

The theme of a descendant who closely resembles a distant ancestor may come from Nathaniel Hawthorne's The House of the Seven Gables, which Lovecraft called "New England's greatest contribution to weird literature" in "Supernatural Horror in Literature". (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

Another proposed literary source is M. R. James' short story "Count Magnus", also praised in "Supernatural Horror in Literature", which suggests the resurrection of a sinister 17th century figure.

The germ of inspiration came from Lovecraft reading Cotton Mather and running across a quote from Borellus. Borellus is Petrus Borellus aka Dr Pierre Borel, a well-known French doctor and alchemist. The quote refers to old experiments of the alchemists in creating life/rebirth from death using essential salts. fullContent:
"The Castle in the Window" is a fantasy short story by Steffan B. Aletti, set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally published in the July 1968 issue of the Magazine of Horror.

### Synopsis
The narrator, a British artist, visits an old bookstore and notices the diary of an early 19th century alchemist, Dr. Michael Gwynn, complete with references to extremely rare tomes such as the Necronomicon and the Song of Yste. They buy the diary as a gift to their roommate, Colin Black, who is himself an occultist and antiquarian. Black is fascinated by it, as the diary tells of how Gwynn made a glass window baptized "with the terrible rites of R'lyeh", and claimed that by looking through the window, he could see the past. Specifically, he saw a castle on the landscape that he knew hadn't been there for centuries. Gwynn never allowed anyone else to see the window, and was deemed insane by his physicians, who forced him to leave the house in 1807. Before doing so, he covered the window with paint and plaster.

Black is intent on finding this magic window, and convinces the narrator to accompany him on a trip to Cornwall. There, he successfully locates the house that once belonged to Gwynn, and obtains permission from the owner to look inside. Finding the window, the two carefully break the plaster and remove the paint. Sure enough, looking through the window reveals a medieval castle that has been destroyed centuries ago. Black is mesmerised, just like Gwynn before him, and the narrator finds him on the next day, still staring at the castle, wondering about a way to pass through the glass window and travel to the past.

The narrator tries to reason with him, but Black leans heavily on the window, and the glass breaks under his weight, causing him to plummet through. The narrator looks down, but sees nothing on the ground below, and can't find any sign of Black anywhere else. Later on, when researching about the castle in the local library, they come across the story of a man wearing strange clothes who appeared in the year 1243, speaking an unknown variety of English, and claiming to be from the future. The man was burned as a sorcerer.

fullContent:
"The Cats" is a horror poem by H. P. Lovecraft. It was written in 1925 and published posthumously in the 1977 collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems.

### Synopsis
The poem describes a crumbling urban scene overtaken by death and decay, including "cobwebs of cable" spun by "nameless things", and catacombs from which "streams of live foetor" leak to rot under the sun. There are references to crowds praying to "stranger-gods", and bats flying over the "weed-cumber'd streets", but apparently, the only creatures thriving in this place are hordes of lean cats that howl under the moonlight.

"The Cats of River Street (1925)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the July 2014 issue of Sirenia Digest (#102).

### Synopsis
The story presents vignettes of several human residents of Innsmouth, each of whom has found some way to ignore the Deep Ones' control of the town. Each human has one or more cats they take care of--cats that secretly play a crucial role in keeping the aquatic horrors of Innsmouth Harbour from invading the land.

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in the anthologies Innsmouth Nightmares  (PS Publishing, 2015) and The Year's Best Dark Fantasy & Horror: 2015 (Prime Books, 2015). It also appeared in Kiernan's collections The Dinosaur Tourist (Subterranean Press, 2018) and Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018).

shortDefinition: "The Cats of Ulthar" is a short story written by American fantasy author H. P. Lovecraft in June 1920. In the tale, an unnamed narrator relates the story of how a law forbidding the killing of cats came to be in a town called Ulthar. As the narrative...
fullContent:
"The Cats of Ulthar" is a short story written by American fantasy author H. P. Lovecraft in June 1920. In the tale, an unnamed narrator relates the story of how a law forbidding the killing of cats came to be in a town called Ulthar. As the narrative goes, the city is home to an old couple who enjoy capturing and killing the townspeople's cats. When a caravan of wanderers passes through the city, the kitten of an orphan (Menes) traveling with the band disappears. Upon hearing of the couple's violent acts towards cats, Menes invokes a prayer before leaving town that causes the local felines to swarm the cat-killers' house and devour them. Upon witnessing the result, the local politicians pass a law forbidding the killing of cats.

Influenced by Lord Dunsany, the tale was a personal favorite of Lovecraft's and has remained popular since his death. Considered one of the best short stories of Lovecraft's early period, aspects of "The Cats of Ulthar" would be referenced again in the author's works "The Other Gods" and The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. It was first published in the literary journal The Tryout in November 1920 and now resides in the public domain.

### Synopsis
An unnamed narrator, while gazing upon his pet cat, begins to reminisce about a law in the town of Ulthar that forbids the killing of cats and relates the story of how this law came to be. The tale begins with the introduction of an old cotter (farmer) and his wife who delight in trapping and violently killing any cats who venture onto their property. The people of the town are too afraid of the couple to speak against these acts, so they instead focus their efforts on keeping their felines from approaching the cotter's house. One night a caravan of travelers from a distant land arrives and passes through the village. They bring with them an orphan named Menes who, having lost his family to a plague, has only a small, black kitten to keep him company. After being unable to find his kitten on the third day of his stay, Menes hears the stories of the old cotter and his wife, and decides to take action.

Menes spends time meditating prior to unleashing a prayer that affects the shapes and movements of the clouds in the sky. The caravan leaves Ulthar that night, shortly before the townspeople notice that all of their cats have gone missing. The townspeople suspect both the old couple and the wanderers, but the innkeeper's son Atal claims to have witnessed the felines circling the property of the cotter. The next morning, the cats have returned to their owners well-fed, but the cotter and his wife have vanished. When the townspeople explore their abandoned house, they discovered nothing more than two skeletons that have been picked clean. The local burgesses, after reviewing the evidence and stories of the townspeople, decide to pass a law that forbids the killing of cats in Ulthar.

fullContent:
"The Cawl of Cthulhu" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Bob Lock. It was published in the 2013 thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg by Screaming Dreams.

### Synopsis
When Bryn Evans returns to his hometown in coastal Wales to take stock of his life after a bad breakup, he listens to Tom Jenkins, one of the town's hard-drinking old-timers, tell of how a recent fire has uncovered the ruins of a house belonging to Mamgi Folvercat, an elderly woman reputed to have been a witch.

Resolving to stay in the ruins overnight as something of a dare to himself, Evans is confronted by the descendant of the witch, a cultist of Cthulhu, who has been preparing a stew made from the mutilated remains of itinerant travellers who were later resurrected to serve the Great Old One even in death.

Although he makes his escape, Evans bears witness to a brief emergence on shore of mighty Cthulhu, and afterwards resolves to return to the big city where such occurrences are less likely.

### Behind the Mythos
In the old man's tales of Granny Folvercat, it is revealed that in 1925, H. P. Lovecraft secretly spent a period of several months staying with the woman, thus explaining how he came by his knowledge of the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Trivia
* In Jenkins' story, he recalls with disapproval how Lovecraft "drank shandy or light ale"; however, it is well documented that the real-world Lovecraft was a teetotaller.
* The cawl mentioned in the title is a type of meat-and-vegetable based stew widely regarded as one of the national dishes of Wales: this is the broth which both Granny Folvercat and her granddaughter had been preparing. Needless to say, human flesh is not one of the traditional ingredients.

fullContent:
"The Celery at the Threshold" is a short story which crosses the world of the Cthulhu Mythos with A. A. Milne's series of children's stories featuring Winnie-the-Pooh. Written by British author John Linwood Grant, it was published in the anthology The Call of Poohthulhu by April Moon Books in May 2022.

### Synopsis
When Christopher Robin, Pooh, Piglet, and friends decide to embark upon a search for the South Pole, they encounter a lost little creature which identifies itself as a Small Elder Thing. Despite their fears that a Shoggoth - or worse, a Woozle - might be on the prowl, they manage to return the fearful little creature to its parent. In return, the Huge Elder Thing gives them a metal rod which had been to the South Pole, as they had become so sidetracked with helping its offspring.

The story concludes with the group returning home for a spot of tea, and the glurping of a black tarry mass to whose attention they have come…

fullContent:
"The Cellar Gods" is a short story by American author Jeffrey Thomas which is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in the anthology New Mythos Legends by Marietta Publishing in September 1999.

### Synopsis
In 1944 America, the narrator , a young man medically excused from military service, develops a crush on a young woman who belongs to a group of labourers at a secretive warehouse, apparently all of Asian or Eskimo descent. When one night the bigoted locals put the warehouse to the torch and murder the workers, the young woman, whose name was Ng, fled unnoticed and sought sanctuary in the narrator's home.

The narrator hides Ng away in a secret room in his basement, a la Anne Frank, where she remains in happy, self-imposed solitude for many years, rebuffing any and all attempts to persuade her to go outside again.

One day, however, Ng begins to develop a facial deformity similar to one seen by the narrator on another woman of Ng's old group. When asked, she will only reply that she had been chosen, and must accept the gift. The deformity grows worse over the following months, until eventually something horrible burst from her body, and a mysterious statue emerges from the floor. The creature is swiftly killed by the narrator and his father.

The story concludes with the discovery of an odd little lens in Ng's room, one which shows visions of a nightmare worlds being consumed by colossal creatures very similar to that which was so violently birthed from Ng's body earlier. The narrator takes a hammer and smashes it to pieces, before noticing that the statue has vanished.

### Mythos Connections
The story is loosely tied to the Cthulhu Mythos through a vague reference to the labourers possibly having connections to places called Leng or the Dreamlands. This, along with their general description of stockiness and an faintly Asian appearance, may hint that they are intended to be Tcho-tcho people.

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance in New Mythos Legends, "The Cellar Gods" has also appeared in the collection Unholy Dimensions (2005, Mythos Books) and the anthology Zart wie Babyhaut (2010, Festa, German translation).

fullContent:
The Ceremonies is a Lovecraftian horror novel by T. E. D. Klein, published by the Viking Press in 1984. Klein's only published novel, it is an expansion of his 1972 short story, "The Events at Poroth Farm."

The book is in part an homage to "The White People" by Arthur Machen, quotes from whom appear as epigraphs before several chapters.

The Ceremonies won the 1986 British Fantasy Award for best novel. Stephen King has called the novel "the Moby-Dick of '80s horror," "the best of the best" of the genre from that decade.

### Publication History
After its initial publication in hardcover by Viking in June 1984, The Ceremonies was released in paperback by Bantam in July 1985. A British edition was published by Pan in 1986.

A limited-edition hardcover version came out from PS Publishing in June 2016, followed by a trade paperback by Drugstore Indian Press in November 2017.

A German translation was published by Goldmann in September 1986, titled MorgenGrauen, "Morning Grey." A Spanish version called Ceremonias macabras came out in 1987, from Martinez Roca, with another German translation (titled The Ceremonies) published by Piper in December 2022.

"The Chain of Aforgomon" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith. It is notable for introducing the time god known as Aforgomon, who may be an avatar of Yog-Sothoth. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Synopsis
A narrator recollects about the occult writings of an acquaintance of his named John Milwarp and how they have all mysteriously vanished from the libraries following his death, as even his recollection of him has become obscure. In his will, John made the narrator his executor and how he wanted him to spread interest in publishing for his newest novel, which is his diary, which he kept a while before his demise, and to the narrator, might explain how it happened.

Milwarp had returned to his house in San Francisco after a long sojourn in Indo-China into places that are obscured by the Occidentals. We who knew him gathered that he had gone into places seldom visited by Occidentals. Around the time of his death, he finished a novel dealing with more romantic and mysterious aspects of Burma. On the morning of April 2nd, 1933, his housekeeper noticed a glare of brilliant light which issued from the half-open door of Milwarp's study, and when investigating, she saw Milwarp sitting in an armchair at the table wearing Chinese brocade robes as a dressing-gown. When she confronted him, he removed the robe to find his body made of pure white fire in the form of linked chains. Though it stopped, the housekeeper, despite being frightened, saw that he was dead and scorch marks resembling long unbroken spirals were around his arms and legs, like he was being wrapped with chains. People have been figuring out the cause of death, chemists trying through a drug that Milwarp had been addicted to with an alkaloid whose source and attributes were obscure to Western science. They eventually gave up and memory of him has been obscured. His diary manuscript was given to the narrator, and he has been trying to decipher it before the ink of the text dissipates.

The text seemed to have unintelligible lettering but eventually he found that it told of the drug, called souvara, which is believed to restore, even for the uninitiated, the memory of other lives. Obtaining it from Buddhists he first took it on March 9th. His physical vision was extended into seeing through objects and in altered coloration and he soon saw the history of Earth in reverse, leading into the beginning of the universe and arriving in a mysterious city called Kalood on Hestan. Hestan was a planet with four suns, inhabited by jewel-colored insects. He saw  beautiful gardens, and noticed that he was dressed in an astronomy-themed robe. He was at an altar with symbols of Aforgomon, the omnipotent time-god, whom he was serving as his priest, while having the name Calaspa.

"The Challenge from Beyond" is a 1935 horror short story written by Howard Phillips Lovecraft, Frank Belknap Long, Robert E. Howard, C. L. Moore, and Abraham Merritt. It was published in Fantasy Magazine and is part of the Cthulhu Mythos.

This is actually the second of two round-robin stories named "The Challenge from Beyond", both commissioned by editor Julius Schwartz and published in the same issue of Fantasy Magazine, in September 1935. The first "Challenge" was written by Stanley G. Weinbaum, Donald Wandrei, E. E. Smith, Harl Vincent and Murray Leinster, and focuses more on science fiction, whereas the "Challenge" written by Moore, Merritt, Lovecraft, Howard and Long is more fantasy-oriented (although both contain elements from both genres).

### Summary
On an August night, a man named George Campbell was camping out in a Canadian forest until he heard a faint noise, and attempted to throw a rock at the creature. But he stopped and saw that the rock he picked up was a cube-shaped quartz crystal that held a disc inside inscribed with peculiar cuneiform writing. He began to think to himself where this unusual crystal came from, possibly from the times of Sumeria or back further, until he decided to get some rest, even when putting out the light revealed the crystal's own afterglow for a brief moment. However, the thought kept him awake. After hours unable to sleep, he saw that the crystal was still showing luminescence and felt like it was drawing him in. The crystal's markings began to change, and a voice was heard luring George in. Sounds were heard from it and with all the curious nature, he decided to gaze upon it for any change. Upon applying torchlight, the cube's cuneiform markings formed the shape of objects, music was heard, and the cube started slowly melting, and the disc was growing. Panicked, George attempted to look away but was dragged into the disc that had now become a globe.

He found himself sucked into the unknown grey misty void produced by the globe, and woke up in an incorporeal form unable to touch or feel cold. However, his thinking capability was heightened, as he recalled reading about clay fragments called Eltdown Shards from Pre-Carboniferous strata in southern England thirty years before, earning their name for how it baffled their discoverers for predating humanity and looking artificial. He then recalled a time in 1912 when Arthur Brooke Winters-Hall, an occultist Sussex clergyman, had identified the Eltdown Shards as consistent with 'pre-human hieroglyphs' cherished in certain mystical circles, publishing a translation that told a story about a race of worm-like beings with nigh-unlimited nature control, mastered interstellar travel very early, and inhabited every habitable planet in their galaxy while exterminating every other race they found. It originally ran from 1988 to 1993 in the Monthly Comic Nora magazine, with a total of 12 chapters. The series was collected into five volumes in 2014, which were later translated into English. "The Charnel God" is a Zothique short story written by Clark Ashton Smith. It was originally published in the March 1934 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
A young newly married couple Phariom and his lovely bride Elaith have unwisely traveled to the city of Zul-Bha-Shir, which is dominated by the cult of the corpse-eating god Mordiggian. This eccentric choice of a honeymoon destination leads to catastrophe.

Falling ill and apparently dying, Elaith is in fact in a coma. However, since she is deemed dead by the priesthood of Mordiggian, and since all corpses are claimed by the cult to feed to their dread god, Elaith is seized by the priests and taken to the underground lair of the monster god.

Phariom must embark on a desperate quest, racing against time before his bride is devoured alive by the voracious ghoul-god Mordiggian!

Fortunately, since Mordiggian is a just god who will feed only on the genuinely deceased, his priesthood allowed Phariom to rescue his wife and leave. The unscrupulous priest who stole her is himself fed to the ravening god-ghoul in her place.

fullContent:
The Children of Burma is a short story by American author Stephen Mark Rainey which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos. Aside from the final few paragraphs, it is told entirely as an extract from the protagonist's journal.

### Synopsis
Colonel Terusawa, a Japanese army engineer who is part of the force invading Burma in 1942, is tasked with taking control of former British airfield in the jungle and preparing it for occupation. Reaching the airfield, his small unit begins their work, but when one of his officers notices movement on the slopes of a nearby ridge, Terusawa sends out a patrol to investigate; the patrol fails to return, but gunshots and a scream are heard from the forest.

That night, a sentry notices lights from torches in the jungle accompanied by an unearthly thumping sound. When the lights and sound subside, the soldiers find the heads of the missing patrol mounted on spikes on the outskirts of their camp.

The next day, Terusawa mounts a watch but continues with the work, although he contacts his superior to inform him the the area may not be secure, and an armoured unit is dispatched to assist the engineers. The tanks do not arrive, and are never seen again.

Later that day, one of the men on watch catches a physically-degenerative native skulking on the edge of camp. Questioning proves futile as they are unable to understand his language, and the man is executed by one of the angry soldiers. Afterwards, the men spot a nebulous entity on the ridge and fire their artillery at it. Whilst it disappears, they do not believe that they have harmed it in any way.

That night sentries are again posted, but the sound and vibrations from the jungle return, and the whole group makes ready. Suddenly, several of the soldiers are dragged off screaming into the undergrowth by tentacles of black mist, and the rest retreat to the airfield to regroup, with the exhausted Terusawa falling asleep.

When he awakens the camp is empty, all of his command having vanished in the night. As the first of the aircraft begin to arrive at the almost-finished runway, a unit of American fighters ambushes them, and shoots most down, injuring Terusawa in the process. Before falling unconscious, he hears the words “Remember the children” whispered from the jungle. A transport is eventually able to land and airlift the colonel to safety, and he is discharged from duty on medical grounds.

At this point, the telling of the story shifts to an administrative note, presumably from a medical file, which states that Terusawa later killed his three children before mounting their heads on poles outside his house, and has since spoken only the words “Remember the children.”

* Colonel Kenjiro Terusawa, a Japanese Army officer and commander of the 212 Engineering Corps, XV Army in Burma, assigned to take and repair a former British airstrip.
* Captain Shindo, Terusawa's aide.
* Lieutenant Isao Tajima, chief engineer.
* Sergeant Ishida, scout.

The Children of Cthulhu:  Chilling New Tales Inspired by H. P. Lovecraft is an anthology of Lovecraftian horror edited by Benjamin Adams and John Pelan, and published by Del Ray/Ballantine in 2002.

The stories in the anthology may not all qualify as belonging to the Cthulhu Mythos, in the sense of  referencing the specific elements of the shared universe; in their introduction, the editors say they were not looking for writers who would "merely throw a few Lovecraftian beasties and the Necronomicon into their tales," but rather for writers with an affinity for Lovecraft's "terrifying vision of an indifferent and chaotic universe populated by beings that were, in their total alienness, completely inconceivable by mere humans."

The cover image is by Dave McKean, a British illustrator best known for the covers of Neil Gaiman's Sandman comic book.

The Children of Fear is a Chaosium campaign sourcebook for their Call of Cthulhu RPG. It provides maps, handouts, rules, monsters and other details for a multi-part adventure across India, Tibet and neighbouring locations in 1922 to 1923. It is written by Lynne Hardy "and friends".

In keeping with past Chaosium efforts, the players create characters or use past characters appropriate to the setting to go on a cross-country expedition to try and stop a cult and its servitors from destroying the world. In this case the gimmick is that the path taken by the characters imitates that in Pilgrimage to the West, a Medieval Chinese fairy tale based on the spread of Buddhism.

shortDefinition: "The Children of the Night" is a horror and science fiction short story by Robert E. Howard, first published in Weird Tales in the April-May issue of 1931.   This story introduced the recurring characters of John Kirowan and John Conrad, and directly...
fullContent:
"The Children of the Night" is a horror and science fiction short story by Robert E. Howard, first published in Weird Tales in the April-May issue of 1931. 

This story introduced the recurring characters of John Kirowan and John Conrad, and directly links them to H. P. Lovecraft’s Cthulhu Mythos.

The story is explicitly racist, asserting and celebrating the idea of innate racial enmity.

### Synopsis
The story is narrated by a man called John O'Donnel. He is part of a group of men at the home of John Conrad, among them Professor John Kirowan. (Both Conrad and Kirowan appear in other Howard tales, such as "Dig Me No Grave"). As the men talk, the conversation turns to cults. Various Mythos entities are namechecked, among them Cthulhu. The cult of Bran Mak Morn is mentioned. Talk then turns to the Picts, and to what degree the legends mentioning them might be accurate. A flint stone is produced, to discuss whether or not it is Pictish.

Two of the men present try the flint weapon out, swinging it around. As they do so, one of them, Ketrick, accidentally strikes O’Donnel on the head with the flint. He loses consciousness and experiences a vision of a past life. In this previous incarnation, O’Donnel was Aryara, a member of the tribe known as the Sword People.

In the past life O'Donnel is experiencing while he is unconscious, Aryara and his group have been attacked by the Children of the Night, a degenerate race that has fallen into subhuman savagery. They are considered beneath contempt by both Sword People and Picts.  

Aryara had fallen asleep on watch. When he awoke, he discovered that the rest of his group had been slaughtered by the Children of the Night. Disgraced by his failure to keep watch, Aryara becomes an exile who dedicates the rest of his life to hunting down and exterminating the Children of the Night. As O'Donnel regains consciousness, he understands that Aryara died in battle against the Children of the Night.

Awake once more, O'Donnel sees Ketrick, the man who accidentally struck him, as a descendant of, and throwback to, the Children of the Night. The other men present intercede, and stop O'Donnel as he tries to kill Ketrick. As the story ends, O'Donnel has vowed to hunt the man down and destroy him.

### Characters
John O'Donnel: The story's narrator, he is knocked out by an oddly balanced neolithic tool and has a vision of a past life when he was Aryara of the Sword People. 

Conrad: The story is set at his home. He has a "bizarrely fashioned study, with its queer relics from all over the world." He believes that "the unknowable is most tantalizingly fascinating.” His library is stocked with horror fiction as well as "works on witchcraft and demonology...Voodoo and dark magic," including von Junzt's Nameless Cults. 

Clemants: Described as "a tall, lean man, silent almost to the point of taciturnity." He is an author whose "swashbuckling novels furnish...him a generous income," and also an editor on a bohemian poetry magazine

fullContent:
The Chronicles of Thrang is a fictional occult text created by American author Walter C. DeBill, Jr. as part of the Mlandoth Cycle, a mythos created in parallel to that of the Cthulhu Mythos. The cycle was retroactively incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos, as is the case with so many other properties, via Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Description
The Chronicles of Thrang is an obscure text translated into English from some prehuman tongue and the language of the pre-Sumerian Ngarathoe. It possibly relates to the "Thrang Grotto of Tatary" mentioned in the Necronomicon to have been attacked by Nyogtha. One source claims it as a non-human chronicle, but this is unclear. The writings detail the cosmic entities Yidhra and Ngyr-Korath.

fullContent:
"The Church in High Street" is a short story by noted British author and Mythos contributor Ramsey Campbell. It was Campbell's first published story,  appearing in the 1962 Arkham House anthology Dark Mind, Dark Heart, edited by August Derleth. Derleth convinced a teenaged Campbell to transfer the first draft of his story, "The Tomb Herd", from Lovecraft Country to an English landscape he was more familiar with, thus sparking the creation of Campbell's Severn Valley setting.

### Synopsis
A man named Dodd travels to the dilapidated rural town of Temphill to take up employment with an old friend. After discovering his friend to be missing, Dodd comes across journal entries and the testimony of a presumably crazed neighbour which indicate that some dark presence dwelling beneath the church in High Street may be responsible. Investigating the tunnels which lead below the church, Dodd encounters a terrifying entity--one of the extradimensional predators known as the Tomb Herd--and escapes Temphill by the luckiest of flukes. Despite this, he subsequently feels a strange desire to return to the old church. The story is revealed to be a manuscript Dodd wrote before mysteriously disappearing.

### Characters
*Richard Dodd, a down-on-his-luck man looking for gainful employment.
*John Clothier, an elderly resident of Temphill with knowledge of the supernatural.
*Albert Young, Dodd's missing friend, known only by his writings and the accounts of Clothier.

### Behind the Mythos
After its initial appearance in Dark Mind, Dark Heart, "The Church in High Street" was later included in Campbell's own anthology Cold Print in 1985, and appeared in the 1994 collection Shadows over Innsmouth.

### Mythos Connections
*"The Church in High Street" is set in Campbell's fictional Severn Valley, England, the setting for many of his later Mythos stories; it makes the first mentions of the major Severn Valley locations--Brichester, Goatswood, Severnford and  Camside--as well as Temphill.  The locations Yuggoth and Leng are also referenced.
*Several Mythos entities are referenced, including Yog-Sothoth (to whom the temple beneath the church is said to be dedicated), Cthulhu, the Old Ones, Azathoth, Nyarlathotep and Dholes.

"The Circumstances of Ghostly Cats" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Mike Minnis.

"The Circumstances of Ghostly Cats" is a very brief short story set in the aftermath of the battle of Poitiers on September 19, 1325, in France. It touches upon the fictional Averoigne region created by Clark Ashton Smith but stands apart.

### Synopsis
The first part of the short narrative concerns Gasquet the Sorcerer and a brutish murderer of cats. Gasquet wanders war-ravaged France until he finds a suitable lair. Cats gather and become infused by his magics.

In a sequence similar to that of the "Cats of Ulthar," a brutish innkeeper "murders" cats sadistically until the shades of the cats return to destroy him. And it is said to this day that from the cellar of the inn ghostly cries of cats may be heard.

### Publication History
"The Circumstances of Ghostly Cats" was first published online in E. P. Berglund's digital zine Nightscapes in 1998.(source?) it has also been translated into French and included in the anthology Rêves d'Ulthar : 21 histoires de chats fantastiques in August 2002.

fullContent:
"The Cleaner's Tale" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Tom Johnstone. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
An immigrant cleaning lady named Maria Luisa, former employee at a rural New England research facility funded by Arkham's Miskatonic University, relates her story to an investigative reporter.

While performing her duties - largely ignored by the faculty - she overhears two of the senior researchers, men by the names of Marston and Thurber, discuss an old photograph which the latter had in his possession, an image of a strange creature which appears to be some kind of canine-human hybrid. As she is called away, she hears one last fragment: that the men may know of a technological way to replicate the creature in the picture.

Later, Maria Luisa comes across a scene of carnage: one of the restricted sections is awash with blood and human body parts, and one of the experimental machines, a kind of biological 3-D printer, has been destroyed from the inside out. Making an anonymous call to the police, she leaves the facility and never returns, although she later comes to believe that she is being followed by shadowy government agents.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly stated, the name of the Bostonian researcher and the subject of the photograph clearly implies them to be the narrator and final image described in "Pickman's Model".

fullContent:
The Clock of Dreams is a novel by British author Brian Lumley and is the third in his Titus Crow series of Mythos fiction.
### Overview

### Synopsis
After leaving Elysia in the space/time machine De Marigny's Clock, Titus Crow and Tiania travel to the Earth's Dreamlands in order to discover why so many of the allies of the Elder Gods there have suddenly gone quiet.

After investigating the situation, the two discover a plot by the entity known as the Fly-the-Light to enslave the people of the Dreamlands with the aid of the Men of Leng. After a series of events involving the capture of both Crow and Tiania, Crow's friend Henri-Laurent de Marigny travels to the Dreamlands and effects a rescue, after which the trio rid the land of the Fly-the-Light and are able to throw the Men of Leng out of the cities.

The book concludes with Crow, Tiania, and de Marigny forging alliances with some of the inhabitants of the Dreamlands - including Randolph Carter - in preparation for the upcoming war against the Cthulhu Cycle Deities.

### Characters
* Titus Crow, an occultist with a desire to rid the universe of the Cthulhu Cycle Deities.
* Tiania, Crow's lover and expert on the Cthulhu Cycle Deities.
* Henri-Laurent de Marigny, Crow's best friend and fellow occultist.
* Professor Wingate Peaslee, a senior member of the Wilmarth Foundation.
* Randolph Carter, a highly influential resident of the Dreamlands.

### Mythos Entities
*The Fly-the-Light, an avatar of Nyarlathotep.
*The Men of Leng, a race of horned, humanoid slave-traders and worshipers of the Fly-the-Light.
*The Keeper of the Cage, once a human sorcerer, later stripped of his free will and forced to serve the Great Old Ones.

### Behind the Mythos
The Clock of Dreams was first published in 1978. It has since been included in a number of collected editions along with other volumes of the Titus Crow series.

fullContent:
"The Cold Comes South" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Matthew Baugh. It was first published in the first and only issue of Ron Shiflet's Lovecraftian fanzine In Lovecraft's Shadow in March 2007.

### Synopsis
Fleeing from an unseasonable storm in the old west, Dave Mather and his group of buffalo hunters rescue a mysterious squaw from a group of thugs intent on violating her. The woman is revealed by one of the group to be a buffalo-spirit, and her cloak is taken away by the men, removing her access to her magical abilities. She in turn reveals the source of the storm: one of the group has offended the Great Old One Ithaqua, who is coming in vengeful pursuit.

Later, the group encounter the woman's would-be assailants, who have succumbed to the depredations of the storm: one has become a cannibal, subsequently consuming the others and becoming a malevolent Wendigo. Mathers is able to kill the creature with a pot of boiling water, and Billy, the man who stole Ithaqua's heart as a youth, decides the time has come to burn it. The squaw tells them that this is enough to end Ithaqua's hunt, and they return her cloak in gratitude. She immediately departs the camp.

Later, the survivors, too weak from their ordeals to travel, begin to starve in the wilderness. The buffalo-woman leads a group of white men to rescue them, but her selfless actions result in her own death.

fullContent:
"The Collect Call of Cathulhu" is an episode of the animated series The Real Ghostbusters that incorporates elements of the Cthulhu Mythos. It includes several in-jokes relating to Mythos authors. It was written by Real Ghostbusters writer Michael Reaves, and first aired October 27, 1987 on the ABC network.

### Synopsis
Miskatonic University professor Ted Klein and New York Public Library librarian Clark Ashton come to the Ghostbusters' New York City headquarters to report the theft of the only English translation of the Necronomicon, which was on loan from Miskatonic to the library. Egon of the Ghostbusters warns that the book could be used to open gates to the Old Ones, particularly Cathulhu: "He makes Gozer look like Little Mary Sunshine." The Ghostbusters are then attacked by the Spawn of Cathulhu, and barely escape.

Deciding they need more info on the Cult of Cathulhu, Ghostbusters Ray and Winston consult the Book of Dzyan and Pnakotic Manuscripts, while Egon and Peter fly to Arkham, Massachusetts, to consult with Alice Derleth at Miskatonic. Alarmed, she returns with them to New York.

Derleth and the Ghostbusters track the cult to Wagner's Occult Shop in East Greenwich Village. The cult sends a Shuggoth after them, which Derleth turns to stone with a spell.

Ray suggests that a friend's collection of pulp magazines may have the answer, and they find an old issue of Weird Tales in which Cathulhu is defeated. Hurrying to Coney Island, where the cult has already summoned Cathulhu, they follow the clue in the Weird Tales story that Cathulhu is vulnerable to electricity, and lure the entity onto the Cyclone roller coaster, where he is destroyed by a lightning strike. With their deity dispelled, the cult is defeated, and its leader is unmasked as--Clark Ashton!

At show's end, Alice Derleth and Peter are going on a date; she suggests an exhibit on the Eltdown Shards at the Natural History Museum, followed by a lecture on the  Zanthu Tablets at Columbia University.

### Namesakes
The guest characters in the episode are named after Mythos writers:

*Ted Klein is an homage to T. E. D. Klein.
*Clark Ashton is a reference to Clark Ashton Smith.
*Alice Derleth evokes August Derleth.
*Wagner's Occult Shop seems to be a call out to Karl Edward Wagner.

"The Collection of Gibson Flynn" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Pete Rawlik.

### Synopsis
When fanatical bibliophile Gibson Flynn is introduced to a run-down bric-a-brac store, he stumbles across a copy of the Revelations of Gla'aki, Volume 7: Of the Symbols the Universe Shows. Desperate to have the book, he strikes a deal with the shop's owner whereby he will run a series of errands in exchange for it. 

As he completes each of the tasks, they become more and more perverse, but Flynn is desperate to get his hands on the book. His shocking errands finally completed and his soul irrevocably corrupted, Flynn returns to the vendor who offers him a place in the cult of Gla'aki.

### Characters
*Gibson Flynn, an avid book collector and Teacher of Comparative Literature at Miskatonic University.
*Walter Pike, a proprietor of used goods and cultist of Gla'aki.

### Publication History
"The Collection of Gibson Flynn" was published in the thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

"The Color of Madness" is a DLC expansion pack for the roguelike horror roleplaying game Darkest Dungeon. It was first released by Red Hook Studios on 19 June 2018.

### Overview
"The Color of Madness" opens a new setting for the game in which a small farmstead has been struck by a comet which has laid a blight upon the land and transformed many of its inhabitants into twisted, malevolent creatures. 

### Behind the Mythos
Although the comet and its effects on the locals bear no direct relation to Lovecraft's works, the description of its incomprehensible colouration and repeated story references to "the blasted heath" show a clear inspiration from "The Colour Out of Space".

fullContent:
"The Color That Stole Christmas" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
On the 24th of December, a rural veterinarian is called out to a local farm to treat livestock afflicted with an odd green infection. Taking a sample before going about his daily business, he realises too late that he has spread the contagion to most of the town. As the people and animals are infected, they dissolve into an animate green sludge, and meteors begin to descend, delivering more of the substance to an unsuspecting world…

### Characters
*Tom, a small-town vet.
*Ellen, Tom's wife.
*Sam, Tom and Ellen's dog.
*John Millar, one of Tom's clients.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to either H. P. Lovecraft's works or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Meikle's inclusion of "The Color That Stole Christmas" in the collection Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates his belief that the story follows in the spirit of such works. Additionally, the premise - that of an alien lifeform falling to Earth and corrupting everything it comes into contact with - harks back to Lovecraft's short story "The Colour Out of Space"; in this context, its title is clearly intended to reference that piece.

### Publication History
"The Color That Stole Christmas" was published in the collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in May 2019.

A deformed but magically-gifted child in the house of Tutankhamen is raised in the catacombs beneath the palace where he forms his own cult to Nyarlathotep. Eventually, he stumbles across a group of undead worshippers of Azathoth and their monstrous guardian, which kills him when he displeases it.

### Characters
*Mupp, a severely deformed man whose appearance and powers are the result of interference by Nyarlathotep at the point of conception.
*Setek, the huge and deadly guardian of the cult of Azathoth, who was the inspiration for the Egyptian Sphinx.

shortDefinition: "The Colour Out of Space" is a short story written by American horror author H. P. Lovecraft in March 1927. In the tale, an unnamed narrator pieces together the story of an area known by the locals as the "blasted heath" in the wild hills west of Ark...
fullContent:
"The Colour Out of Space" is a short story written by American horror author H. P. Lovecraft in March 1927. In the tale, an unnamed narrator pieces together the story of an area known by the locals as the "blasted heath" in the wild hills west of Arkham, Massachusetts. The narrator discovers that many years ago a meteorite crashed there, draining the life force from anything living nearby; vegetation grows large, but tasteless, animals are driven mad and deformed into grotesque shapes, and the people go insane or die one by one.

Lovecraft began writing "The Colour Out of Space" immediately after finishing his previous short novel, The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, and in the midst of final revision on his horror fiction essay Supernatural Horror in Literature. Seeking to create a form of life that was truly alien, he drew his inspiration from numerous fiction and nonfiction sources. First appearing in the September 1927 edition of Hugo Gernsback's science fiction magazine Amazing Stories, "The Colour Out of Space" became one of Lovecraft's most popular works and remained his personal favorite short story. It was adapted into feature film versions in 1965, 1987, and 2019.

### Synopsis
Written in the first-person perspective of an unnamed surveyor from Boston, "The Colour Out of Space" tells the story of the narrator's attempts to uncover the secrets behind a shunned place referred to by the locals of Arkham as the "blasted heath". Unable to garner any information from the townspeople, the protagonist seeks out an old and allegedly crazy man by the name of Ammi Pierce who relates his personal experiences with a farmer who used to live on the cursed property, Nahum Gardner. Pierce claims that the troubles began when a meteorite crashed into Gardner's lands in June 1882.

The meteorite never cools, but begins shrinking and local scientists are unable to discern its origins. As the stone shrinks, it leaves behind globules of colour that are referred to as such "only by analogy", as they do not fall within the range of anything known in the visible spectrum. These remains eventually disappear but, the following season, Gardner's crops come in unnaturally large and abundantly. When he discovers that, despite their appearance, they are inedible, he accuses the meteorite of having poisoned the soil. Over the following year, the problem begins spreading to the surrounding vegetation and local animals, warping them in unusual ways. The plant life around the farmhouse becomes "slightly luminous in the dark", and Gardner's wife eventually goes mad, forcing him to lock her in the attic. During this time, Gardner begins to isolate his family from the rest of the town and Pierce slowly becomes his only contact with the outside world. As he wrote the tale, however, he was also typing the final draft of his horror fiction essay Supernatural Horror in Literature. Although the author himself claimed that his inspiration was the newly constructed Scituate Reservoir

"The Colour that Came to Chiswick" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle featuring legendary fictional detective Sherlock Holmes.

### Synopsis
Sherlock Holmes is asked to investigate the presumed sabotage of a London brewery. What he discovers is a glowing green slime which hungers to consume human flesh. Luckily for humankind, Holmes is able to devise a chemical means of destroying the creature, preventing it from preying on any more unsuspecting Englishmen.

### Characters
*Sherlock Holmes, a highly-accomplished detective.
*Dr. Watson, Holmes's best friend, a qualified physician.
*Inspector Lestrade, a senior police officer.

### Publication History
*Gaslight Arcanum: Uncanny Tales of Sherlock Holmes (2011)
*The Quality of Mercy and Other Stories (2013)
*Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2017)
*Spore: Three Tales of Weird Science (2020)

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no explicit references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the inclusion of "The Colour that Came to Chiswick" in Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates Meikle's belief that it is in the same spirit as these stories. Additionally, the description of the creature could possibly be compared to that of the Colour Out of Space from Lovecraft's short story of the same name.

### Trivia
*"The Colour that Came to Chiswick" bears a certain resemblance to another of Meikle's short stories, "Amoeboid", first published in 2016.

shortDefinition: "The Coming of the White Worm" is a short story by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith. It is the penultimate tale in his Hyperborean Cycle of fantasy works.  ### Synopsis When the dreaded entity Rlim Shaikorth arrives off shore in its iceber...
fullContent:
"The Coming of the White Worm" is a short story by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith. It is the penultimate tale in his Hyperborean Cycle of fantasy works.

### Synopsis
When the dreaded entity Rlim Shaikorth arrives off shore in its iceberg-fortress Yikilth, it destroys the sorcerer Evagh's village and forcibly recruits him into its small priesthood of mages.

Travelling the length of Hyperborea and devastating its coastline for many miles inland, Evagh slowly learns of his new master, an ancient entity which desires nothing more than to inflict destruction on whatever happens to lie in its path. However, as the days and weeks pass, the priesthood begins to dwindle: its members simply disappear during the night, and Rlim Shaikorth appears suspiciously larger in the morning.

The day arrives when Evagh is the only one left, and he comes across his master in a state of slumber. From within the beast, he hears the souls of his fellows calling to him along with the many, many others it has consumed over the aeons. The captive souls beg him to take his sword and slice open Shaikorth, although they warn that to do so will also mean his own death.

Evagh complies, and a black liquid gushes forth from the fatal wound in his former master, along with the souls of its victims, the liquid killing Evagh and melting Yikilth. Although it has cost him his life, the brave sorcerer has saved his land from certain destruction.

### Characters
*Evagh, a powerful Hyperborean wizard.
*Dooni, a member of Rlim Shaikorth's priesthood.
*Ux Loddhan, a member of the priesthood.
*Rlim Shaikorth, an ancient being of unimaginable evil.

### Publication History
"The Coming of the White Worm" was first published in the pulp magazine Stirring Science Stories in April 1941. It has since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into Spanish, Dutch, German, French, Italian, Hungarian and Portuguese.

### Trivia
*The story is presented as a tale related by the Hyperborean sorcerer Eibon, who learned it through questioning the spirit of Evagh.

fullContent:
The Compact Arkham Unveiled is a setting supplement for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game, which focuses on the fictional New England town of Arkham, Massachusetts. Written by Keith Herber, Lynn Willis, and John B. Monroe, it features a cover by Lee Gibbons and interior art by Tim Callender, and was published by Chaosium in 1995.

The book is in essence a reprint of the 1990 supplement Arkham Unveiled with the scenarios of the earlier book omitted and changes made to the maps included. A poster map of Arkham is also included, as is a four-page edition of fictional newspaper The Arkham Gazette.

The Compleat Crow is an anthology of short stories by British horror writer Brian Lumley. It forms part of his Titus Crow series of Mythos-set fiction.

### Overview
Collecting all eleven of the Titus Crow short stories in one volume, The Compleat Crow was first published by Hodder and Staughton in 1987. It has since received several reissues, the most recent being from Subterranean Press in both trade and limited editions. The stories were written by Lumley over the course of seventeen years, and follow Titus Crow's exploits outside of the events of the main six novels.

fullContent:
"The Connection" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Frank Forte, first published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
A mad doctor grafts another living human brain onto his own in an effort to make himself stronger, faster and more intelligent: in his words, "the perfect organism". Unfortunately, the original owner of the brain has other ideas, and before his individuality can be absorbed by the superior intellect of the doctor, he destroys the abomination they have both become.

fullContent:
"The Continent of Madness" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Japanese author Ken Asamatsu, translated by Edward Lipsett. It was published in the thematic anthology Beyond the Mountains of Madness by Celaeno Press in April 2015. It was later republished in Ken's collection Kthulhu Reich in 2019, under the title "In the Wasteland of Madness".

### Synopsis
The story details a 1939 Nazi expedition to the Antarctic wastes to establish a colony for the Third Reich in what Nazi Germany had claimed as its territory, named Neuschwabenland.

The expedition is equipped with tanks and military aircraft as well as a Mythos item, the platinum Mask of Yoth-Tlaggon. This metallic mask is flexible like rubber and gives the wearer visions of Mythos times and places. However it also acts a powerful psychic magnet to Shoggoths and Flying Polyps resulting in the annihilation of the Nazi expedition other than the narrator, who finishes his report, seals it in a metal flask and throws it out of his aircraft as he flies back over the Mountains of Madness to the lair of the Shoggoths, where he intends to crash his plane, carrying the Mask of Yoth-Tlaggon, and thus bind them to the location since they will go wherever the activated Mask resides.

"The Crawling Chaos" is a short story by American writers H. P. Lovecraft and Winifred V. Jackson, first published April 1921 in the United Cooperative. As in their other collaboration, "The Green Meadow", the tale was credited to "Elizabeth Berkeley" (Jackson) and "Lewis Theobald, Jun" (Lovecraft). Lovecraft wrote the entire text, but Jackson is credited since the story was based on a dream she experienced.

Despite the title's similarity to the character's epithet, Nyarlathotep (who is, indeed, harbinger of the apocalypse) does not appear in this story. The name was used because Lovecraft liked "the ring of it".

### Synopsis
The story begins with the narrator describing the effects of opium and the fantastical vistas it can inspire. The narrator then tells of his sole experience with opium in which he was accidentally administered an overdose by a doctor during the "year of the plague".

After a disembodied sensation of falling, the narrator finds himself within a strange beautiful room containing exotic furniture, where a sound of pounding from outside inspires an inexplicable sense of dread within the narrator. Determined to identify the origin of this sound, the narrator moves towards a window and observes a terrifying scene of fifty-foot waves and seething vortex three hundred feet below where he is standing, consuming the shoreline at an incredible rate.

Sensing imminent danger, the narrator quickly exits the building. Fleeing the waves, the narrator travels inland. The narrator eventually arrives in a valley with tropical grass extending above his head and a great palm tree in the center. Driven by curiosity despite considerable fear, the narrator crawls on his hands and knees toward the great palm.

Soon after arriving at the tree, the narrator observes an angelic-looking child fall from its branches. The child then smiles and extends its hand towards the narrator but before he can respond, he hears the sound of ethereal singing within the upper air followed by the child saying in an otherworldly voice:



As the child speaks, the narrator observes two youths, whom the narrator recognizes as the singers he had just heard, emerging from the leaves of the tree. They take the narrator by the hand and describe the worlds of "Teloe" and "Cytharion of the Seven Suns" which lie beyond the Milky Way.

As they speak, the narrator observes that he is floating in the upper atmosphere, with the palm tree far below, and now accompanied by an ever increasing number of singing, vine-crowned youths. As they ascend, the child tells the narrator that he must always look upward and never down at the Earth below.

As he rises further listening to the youths singing, the narrator is disturbed by the return of the sound of the waves, and, forgetting what the child said, looks downward and observes a sight of global destruction, with cities being consumed by the great waves until there is nothing left. The Creature Companion: A Core Game Book for Keepers is a gamebook supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Written by prolific American games designer Scott David Aniolowski, it was published in a paperback format in 1998.

### Overview
Running to a total of 112 pages, The Creature Companion combines the contents of two earlier "monster manual"-style gamebooks, Ye Booke of Monstres (1994) and Ye Booke of Monstres II (1995), with a selection of new entities and additional background material.

The Creature Companion was later developed into another sourcebook, Malleus Monstrorum, a greatly expanded version of the original, released in 2006 and again in 2020.

"The Creature in the Fog" (also "The Creature From the Fog") is a short horror story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
A man travels to visit relatives in the countryside where he finds that a recurrent nightmare may have been more of a premonition than a dream, and that his apparently mad old uncle was likely saner than any had ever suspected.

A shapeless horror approaches through the fog and is repelled from the door of the house in which the narrator is hiding. Its tentacular pseudopods bounce off the door despite the creature's immense power, due to a small stone embedded in the door inscribed with a star-shaped symbol.

Although never outright identified the creature's shapelessness but ability to change its form and manifest eyes or tentacles makes it likely that it was a Shoggoth.

### Characters

*The Narrator, a city man on holiday in West Virginia.
*Roger, the narrator's brother.
*Hoyt Thompson, the narrator's now-deceased uncle.
*Elvira Higgins, the lover of Hoyt, a suspected witch, also deceased.

### Publication History
"The Creature From the Fog" was first published in Dark Legacy #6 in April 2000, and again in Nightscapes in August 2001.

### Synopsis
A man living adjacent to a waxwork museum befriends an alien Mi-Go living surreptitiously in the building's basement. Despite developing a bond with the creature, the man is horrified when it transfers its brain into the body of the museum's owner and he chops up the Mi-Go's own body, forcing it to live out the remainder of its days as a regular human.

### Characters

*Aloysius Pickman, a former art teacher and grandnephew of Richard Upton Pickman. Owner of the Pickman Waxworks.

### Publication History
"The Creature In The Waxworks" was published in the collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

shortDefinition: "The Creeper in the Crypt" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the July 1937 issue of Weird Tales. It is notable as one of the first stories not written by H. P. Lovecraft to be set in the Lovecraft-created town of Arkham.  The pl...
fullContent:
"The Creeper in the Crypt" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the July 1937 issue of Weird Tales. It is notable as one of the first stories not written by H. P. Lovecraft to be set in the Lovecraft-created town of Arkham.

The plot involves a gangster from New York coming to Arkham with a scheme to kidnap members of prominent families, since the "local coppers are all stiffs". He picks a local haunted house to use as a hideout--not realizing that in Arkham, the ghosts are real--and carnivorous.

Bloch does not explicitly name the "creeper" of the story's title, but he provides its identity in the form of an easily answered riddle: "What lurks in graveyards, ancient and unseen, then creeps from crypts to feast?" In case the reader needed another hint, when the creature finally attacks, the narrator hears a "sudden ghoulish baying that conjured up worlds of nightmare horror in my shattered brain."

The story includes a considerable amount of lore about Arkham, some borrowed from Lovecraft and other aspects invented by Bloch.

### Arkham
In Bloch's Arkham, "where ancient gables point like wizard’s fingers to the sky," there is "a tale for every rotting ruin, a story for every little corpse-eye window that stares out at the sea when the fog comes up."  The story's narrator compares Arkham's old houses to "deserted palaces in a land where all but memories are dead," noting that "the streets of Arkham are bare at midnight, and over all hangs the age-old enchantment of days gone by."

Bloch mentions several Arkham streets, none of which appear on Lovecraft's map of the town:

* Blascom Street, where the narrator lives in his family's place.
* Sewell Street, the location of Tarleton's party.
* Pringle Street, the address of the Chambers house.
* Old Town Street, where Cyrus Hook's mansion was burned down.

### The Chambers House
The story's primary location is the Chambers house, also know as the Dark house, known as "the moldering house with the iron door in the cellar." Built on Pringle Street, it was originally owned by the colonial wizard Ezekiel Chambers, and then by the smuggler/graverobber Jonathan Dark. Dark was accused as using the door "as a passageway for bringing his stolen cadavers back to dispose of," but the door was not opened after his arrest; he made the "astounding and hideous claim that the key which locked it was on the other side." Dark also claimed that the tenants of the graveyard "would come to visit the house from below when a wizard invoked it with the proper spells and sacrifice."

### The Graveyard on the Hill
Next to the Chambers house is "the old graveyard on the hill"; this corresponds to the "Wooded Graveyard" on "Hangman's Hill" that appears on Lovecraft's map. in 1818, the U.S. president was James Monroe.) 

A "great immigrant panic" occurred in Old Town Street in 1869, "when the moldering mansion of Cyrus Hook was burned to the ground by fear-crazed foreigners."

fullContent:
The Creeping Kelp is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by British author William Meikle. Although a fairly straightforward creature-feature, it is also intended as a cautionary tale on mankind's mistreatment of Mother Nature.

### Synopsis
An experiment during the Second World War involving recovered Shoggoth DNA results in disaster and the results are destroyed. However, a U-Boat attack leaves a small sample extant beneath the waves of the North Atlantic, and the creature is released in the modern day.

Quickly reproducing, the Shoggoths overrun a boat full of environmentalists and begin construction of their own city, while simultaneously rampaging up and down the coast of England.

Fortunately, two of the surviving environmentalists come up with a plan to destroy the Shoggoth's guiding intelligence, and with their core destroyed the colony instantly devolves into mindlessness, ending their threat.

### Characters
*Dave Noble, a researcher studying the effects of plastic pollution in the North Atlantic.
*Suzie Jukes, a biologist aboard the same ship, the Earth Rescue.

### Publication History
The Creeping Kelp was published by Dark Regions Press in 2011, 2016 and 2018. It also received an ebook release in 2013. It runs to a total of 157 pages and features cover art by Wayne Miller.

### Trivia
*A segment of the book which describes the Spanish Inquisition's encounter with a Shoggoth was taken in its entirety and published as "Inquisitor" in 2011. A smaller part of this same section was also reused in the non-Mythos Thomas Carnacki story "Carnacki: Captain Gault's Nemesis" in 2013.
*One part of the story involving military records from the Second World War was later mostly rewritten by Meikle - though with the same characters - and published as "The Terror That Came to Dounreay" in 2015.

shortDefinition: "The Crime of the Century" is a short non-fiction work by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Although it was written in April 1915, it did not see publication until its inclusion in L. Sprague de Camp's 1976 collection To Quebec and ...
fullContent:
"The Crime of the Century" is a short non-fiction work by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Although it was written in April 1915, it did not see publication until its inclusion in L. Sprague de Camp's 1976 collection To Quebec and the Stars .

It is a tirade against World War I in racialist and racist terms, decrying the conflict for causing "unnatural" alliances.The present European war, occuring as it does in an age of hysterical sentimentality and unsound political doctrines, has called forth from the sympathizers of each set of belligerents an unexampled torrent of indiscriminate denunciation.

The effeminate idealist, half awaked from his roseate vision of universal brotherhood, shrieks at the mutual slaughter of his fellow-men, or singles out individualists of cruelty or treachery as the objects of his well-meaning rage; while the erratic socialist, saturated with false notions of equality and democracy, raves unendingly against cruel systems of government which sacrifice a peaceful peasantry to the greed and ambition of their warlike masters.

But though the sober philosopher perceives in war a phenomenon eminently natural and absolutely inevitable; though he realizes that the masses of mankind must remain subject to the will of a dominant aristocracy so long as the present structure of the human brain endures; he can none the less find in the colossal conflict an ample cause for the deepest regret and the gravest apprehension. High above such national crimes as the Servian plots against Austria or the German disregard of Belgian neutrality, high above such sad matters as the destruction of innocent lives and property, looms the supremest of all crimes, an offense not only against conventional morality but against Nature itself; the violation of race.

In the unnatural racial alignment of the various warring powers we behold a defiance of anthropological principles that cannot but bode ill for the future of the world.

-H.P. Lovecraft, "The Crime of the Century"It is very stark evidence of the deep and abiding racism of H.P. Lovecraft and something that should be faced squarely by any devotees of his work or students of his craft and its inspirations. Although he seemingly began to resile from this attitude in the final months of his life, this attitude inflected all his extant work.

### Publication History 
*To Quebec and the Stars (1976)
*Howard Phillips Lovecraft 3 (1992, 2016)
*Miscellaneous Writings (1995)
*Grimoire of the Aristocracy (2024; Ukrainian-language collection)

fullContent:
"The Crisis on Infinite Betties" is a comic book story arc published by Dynamite Entertainment, featured in the one-shot Bettie Page: Halloween Special and issues #1-5 of Bettie Page: Unbound Vol. 1, which were later collected into a trade paperback.

### Synopsis
In the fall of 1952, the secret agent Bettie Page was sent to investigate an artist named Richard Upton Pickman after one of his paintings depicted the mysterious entity known as "Unsub Ede 17". To defend herself from any extra-dimensional monsters that she may encounter, Page receives a briefcase containing a slip of paper with a chant written on it, as well as an A .22 pistol in case Pickman gets out of hand. Posing as an admirer of his work, Page enters Pickman's house and quickly finds out that he got the ideas for his artwork from the Necronomicon. The two of them get into a brief scuffle before Pickman uses a chant to send both Page and himself to an alternate dimension. There, it was revealed that the identity of "Unsub Ede 17" is actually Yog-Sothoth, who was angered by Pickman for saying his name too many times. As a punishment for his actions, Yog-Sothoth summoned a Shoggoth to devour Pickman. Before the eldritch monster can attack her too, Page recites the chant that she memorized from the piece of paper earlier, sending her back to her home dimension and seemingly ending the threat.

Shortly afterwards, Bettie Page encounters an alien and the Loch Ness Monster while also obtaining one of the five Keys to the Eternal Gates that need to be used to lock the Great Old Ones in their own dark dimension. During her quest to collect the other keys, Page travelled across several alternate realities and took the role of a different alter ego in each one. She first appeared as a barbarian known as "Bettie the Page" in Hyperborea, where she gained superior strength and swordsmanship to defeat Count Vizier, an evil sorcerer who was under the influence of Nyarlathotep. In the next reality, she becomes a vampire-lady from the planet Vampiron. When the chief inquisitor Benway tried to commit genocide against their race, the Ruling Council of Vampiron attempted to save their world by summoning Yog-Sothoth. In another reality, she becomes a princess of Xenon and encounters the genocidal Benway again, who ends up summoning Azathoth in order to destroy the city of the Puru. Finally, she takes the form of a tiny fairy who allies herself with a mermaid version of her best friend Melyssa and a group of pirates to fight off Cthulhu. With their help, she successfully used the five keys to banish the Great Old Ones, saving the entire multiverse from destruction and transporting Page back to her home world.

fullContent:
The Cruel Empire of Tsan Chan is a horror fiction role-playing game based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos set during the 51st century. The game is published by Chaosium and was published in 2010.

### Setting
The game is set in a nightmarish Earth, approximately 3000 years in the future. In which the awakening of Cthulhu led to a world gone mad. Throughout the world, most of mankind has gone insane and worship the Great Old Ones. They fight for them and die for them, pray to them and are sacrificed to them. Ruling over them are the Great Old Ones and their servitor races. In what used to the Far East, is a human empire of sorts, ruling over what used to be the Middle Kingdom which is under siege by the forces of the Mythos.

### History
When Cthulhu awoke, he returned to Earth not as a conqueror or destroyer, but as an evangelist. The high priest of fantastically powerful, mysterious, and dangerous gods. The shock of his rising and the power of his ministry resulted in what came to be known as the Dream. Humanity's psyche was damaged beyond repair by the rise of Cthulhu. The world became insane as humans turned into barbaric and immoral shrieking beings, who had zero scruples and acted without any thought to their consequences. Human culture and society collapsed, until every living human had onverted to a religion they barely understood, screaming Cthulhu's name. Vast teeming masses of humans who revel, kill, rut, and sing hymns to the Gods.

The only exception was in the Plateau of Leng within China, where the deathless sorcerers (the Kuen-Yuin) who were devoted to Nyarlathotep had taken precautions. They feared the rising of Cthulhu, as those immortals did not want to die nor did they wish to be converted. They relocated the plateau to a remote location in Northern China, near the Greater Khingan Range in Inner Mongolia. For unknown reasons, Nyarlathotep provided them with technologies, psychic drills, sorcerous knowledge, and memetic techniques to protect them from Cthulhu's rising. When Cthulhu returned, the only place in the world spared from the Dream, was a few square hundred miles in China. Nyarlathotep then left the sorcerers to their own devices, and ever since has had little interaction with Earth.

The Deathless quickly enslaved those humans who found themselves in the safe zone. After which they had their mountainous domain sealed by blocking every valley and passage into their stronghold. They planned to escape into the Dreamlands but discovered that Cthulhu's presence had turned it into a chaotic realm of madness. In the subterranean world, they found Abhoth who tried to consume them and Tsathoggua who would not aid them against Cthulhu but did provide them with gifts of magic in return for their homage.

fullContent:
The Cry of Cthulhu was a planned film which never made it past the pre-production phase. It was envisioned as being the first original Lovecraftian film to directly incorporate elements of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Production History
Author and screenwriter Byron Craft finished the final draft of The Cry of Cthulhu in 1976; the following year, he partnered with Bill Baetz as co-producers, and the two began pitching their ideas to various studios while engaging artist and special effects creator Tom Sullivan to produce concept art for the project. Around 1978, the pair also secured the blessing of Arkham House's then CEO April Derleth, although they acknowledged that legally they were under no obligation to.

Later in 1978, producer Dino de Laurentiis, apparently unfamiliar with the legal status of H. P. Lovecraft's work, attempted to secure story rights from Arkham House, but were rebuffed. De Laurentiis then contacted Craft and Baetz, claiming a desire to finance The Cry of Cthulhu, with the only caveat being an executive producer credit. This soon turned out to be false, with de Laurentiis offering $100,000 for full rights to the script and total forfeiture of creative control, royalties and future franchising from Craft and Baetz, which was promptly refused.

Subsequently, Craft and Baetz attempted to produce The Cry of Cthulhu independently, but a lack of finances and time to pursue the project led to its being shelved.

### Legacy
Craft decided to write a novelisation of his screenplay, which was eventually released as The Alchemist's Notebook in 2016. It's name was later returned to The Cry of Cthulhu to reflect its origins.

### External Links
*[https://2warpstoneptune.com/2014/10/23/cthulhu-calling-an-interview-with-byron-craft/ Interview with Byron Craft at 2warpstoneneptune.com] in which he describes the pre-production of The Cry of Cthulhu.

The Cthulhu Invictus Companion is a sourcebook for Chaosium's historical Call of Cthulhu offshoot, Cthulhu Invictus.

### Overview
Containing a trio of scenarios which take investigators to the far reaches of the Roman Empire - from Sinai in Asia to the Severn Valley in England - The Cthulhu Invictus Companion allows players to further explore the world as it was during the first century. Player handouts are also included for the scenarios, "Chuma Invictus", "Morituri Te Salutamus" and "Bacchanalia".

The Cthulhu Invictus Companion was created by Chad Bowser and Andi Newton, among others, and runs to a total of 64 pages.

### Publication History
First released in April 2011, The Cthulhu Invictus Companion has since gone out of print, but is still available as a digital PDF download from Chaosium's website.

fullContent:
"The Cthulhu X-Files" is a fairly long Cthulhu Mythos poem by Swedish author Mathias Jansson. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 1 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in April 2018.

Despite the title, it bears no relation to popular science fiction series The X-Files.

### Synopsis
The different sections offer snapshots into some form of Mythos-related activity or other, with all attributed to a deceased author. These vignettes are:

* Chan Hol X-Act 7: the burial of a child of Yig and mother of serpent people outside the gates of R'lyeh. The corpse is discovered and investigated by humans and must be reclaimed and reinterred.
* Ludwig Leichhardt (1813—1848)—Act #28: an explorer excavates a secret chamber beneath Uluru, also known as Ayers Rock, in Australia, where he finds information on aboriginal myths concerning the Great Old Ones. Also mentions Ayi'ig, Kurpannga, and Yog-Sothoth.
* Benjamin Spooner Briggs (1835-1872)—Act #95: a ship's crew salvages a lifeboat from the legendary Mary Celeste, writing scratched into the gunwales suggests the crew were taken by "octopoid monstrous men," a possible reference to either the Deep Ones or Cthulhi.
* Epilogue—Benjamin Spooner Briggs  (1835-1872)—Act #95b: describes a seance recording of Madame Blavatsky, who contacts Briggs, now held prisoner and tormented by Cthulhu in R'lyeh.
* Yda Hillis Addis (1857-1902)—Act #113: a patient in an asylum draws mysterious sigils on her cell walls, shortly before disappearing in a cloud of smoke. This recalls the escape of the witch Keziah Mason from her cell in "The Dreams in the Witch-House." Also mentions the Great Old One Ny-Rakath.
* Percival Harrison Fawcett (1867—1925)—Act #156: a man ends up dead near the peak of a mountain in Bhutan, and nobody knows how he came to be there. His notes have the phrase "Ph’nglui mglw’nafh Cthulhu R’lyeh wgah’nagl fhtagn" scrawled amongst them. Also mentions the scrolls of Cambuluc and Aiueb Gnsha.
