fullContent:
"The Curious Case of Miss Violet Stone" is a sci-fi mystery short story by Poppy Z. Brite and David Ferguson first published in the 2003 anthology Shadows Over Baker Street. As with most stories in the collection, it features the detective Sherlock Holmes and is set in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
In 1894, Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson receive a letter from Thomas Stone, a hotel cook who is worried about his sister and wishes to hire the detective to find out what's wrong with her. Three years ago, Violet Stone dived into a pond in the Greek island of Knoxos, fancying she saw a coin or another shiny object. Afterwards, she fell violently ill and was forced to return to England. Her symptoms included a bad case of amnesia, although she tried to disguise it by feigning familiarity with those around her. Following a period of intense fever, her body started to wither and she became unable to eat or drink, rejecting and spitting out everything that was forced down her throat. To the surprise of everyone, she didn't perish, and the case of the girl who hasn't eaten anything for the last three years made it to the London newspapers.

Despite Watson's skepticism, Thomas insists that his sister never lied before and would not benefit from such a ruse, as her illness is obviously real. Her body is still weak and withered. She spends her days in bed reading and making annotations on a notebook, and her interests have shifted away from the novels she enjoyed before the incident to strange tomes such as the Necronomicon. Holmes asks to see the girl right away.

At first, Violet Stone seems politely indifferent to her visitors, but her attitude changes when she hears Holmes' name, at which point she holds his wrist and begs for his assistance, claiming he has the "mental capacities" to help her. After confirming that he would have access to a lens grinder, a metallurgist, and a machinist, she gives Holmes her notebook, which contains the instructions for a machine that must be built. Holmes promises that he will do his best and departs in a state of shock. Back on Baker Street, he consumes some cocaine to deal with the shock and tells Watson that when Violet touched his wrist, she also communicated things to his mind directly. In truth, the entity inhabiting Violet Stone's body is a member of a sapient prehistoric species of giant limpet-like creatures which can send their consciousnesses across spacetime to switch bodies with other beings and learn about them. However, being still new to this technique, the alien's consciousness entered Violet's body by mistake and was imperfectly joined with her, resulting in unforeseen physical symptoms. To revert the process, a special machine will be needed, which the alien can't build themself while struggling to keep Violet's weakened body alive.

The Curse is a film based on the plot of H.P. Lovecraft's "The Colour Out of Space".

### Plot Summary
A meteorite lands on the property of Nathan Hayes (Claude Akins) and local physician Alan Forbes (Cooper Huckabee) is unable to explain why the rock keeps shrinking. He is dissuaded from contacting the authorities by Charlie Davidson (Steve Carlisle), a realtor who does not want the new arrival to discourage the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) from establishing a new reservoir in the area. As the rock disappears, a glowing colour seeps out and into the ground. Within a few weeks, the farm's crops bloom but are soon discovered to be inedible. Shortly after, the local animals, as well as Nathan's wife, begin to go mad and a previously unknown element is discovered in the property's well. Soon Nathan and his son Cyrus (Malcolm Danare) are driven insane as well and begin terrorizing those who come to the farm, including the other children Zack (Wil Wheaton) and Alice (Amy Wheaton). In the film's conclusion, they are saved by TVA representative Carl Willis (John Schneider) and the house collapses.

### Reception
Lovecraft scholar Charles P. Mitchell referred to the film as faithful to the author's original work, but claimed that "[t]he last twenty minutes of the film are so disjointed that they virtually ruin the entire film".

shortDefinition: "The Curse of Cthulhu" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Jake Webb, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphiu...
fullContent:
"The Curse of Cthulhu" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Jake Webb, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Synopsis
When high school pupil Jordan Turner begins to have visions of a grotesque, octopus-headed monstrosity, the people around him - at least those who appear to have been experiencing similar flashes - begin to disappear.

Jordan soon finds himself embroiled in a battle between two rival organisations: the Visitors, a group of sinister Men in Black-type characters who worship the Great Old One Cthulhu, and the Organisation, a loose-knit coalition of regular folks devoted to thwarting the Visitors and keeping mankind from falling to the depredations of their dark god.

During a series of nightmare clashes across suburban England and its surrounding countryside, Jordan uncovers one of the Visitors' secret lairs, as well as the horrific fate which befell his father and many of the others who have fallen into their hands over the decades.

### Mythos Connections
Aside from the setting and Cthulhu-dedicated cult, there is mention of a preserved alien species described in a historic letter concerning events at the Visitor base. Described as an Old One, and held in a cylindrical container around seven feet tall "tentacles, wings and all," is possibly intended to be an Elder Thing - a species which were referred to as Old Ones in H. P. Lovecraft’s novella At the Mountains of Madness - but is stated to be one of "Cthulhu's hordes" - which is contrary to Lovecraft’s own history.

Jordan's maths teacher at the beginning of the story is referred to as "Mr. Wilmarth"; however, after a few pages, his name is inexplicably changed to "Mr. Wilhelm."

A character named Küttner is a possible nod to Lovecraft’s friend Henry Kuttner.

### Behind the Mythos
Although the story is intended to take place in the Achtung! Cthulhu universe, the setting is almost entirely contemporary, with the only references to Achtung! Cthulhu being a handful of letters dating back to wartime Britain.

"The Curse of the Crocodile" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney that pits his sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta against the machinations of the cult of the crocodile-headed god Sebek--making it something of a prequel to Robert Bloch's story "The Secret of Sebek". Tierney's story first appeared in the Roodmas 1987 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu (#47).

### Synopsis
A forbidden alliance between the Roman ruler of Thebes and the Cult of Sebek, the crocodile-headed Egyptian god, aims to conquer Egypt and ultimately the Roman Empire. Simon, still evading Imperial agents, uncovers a plot orchestrated by the nefarious Nomarch of Thebes to resurrect the blasphemous rites of Sebek. Alongside his allies, Simon endeavors to sabotage the ritual and prevent a catastrophic manifestation. 

### Setting
The story is set in February, 38 A.D., in Memphis, Egypt.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Crypt of Cthulhu, "The Curse of the Crocodile" was reprinted in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997) and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

shortDefinition: The Curse of the Dark Pharaoh was the first expansion pack for Fantasy Flight Games' Second Edition of Lovecraftian adventure board game Arkham Horror, released in 2006.  ### Overview One of the small-box supplements, The Curse of the Dark Pharaoh wa...
fullContent:
The Curse of the Dark Pharaoh was the first expansion pack for Fantasy Flight Games' Second Edition of Lovecraftian adventure board game Arkham Horror, released in 2006.

### Overview
One of the small-box supplements, The Curse of the Dark Pharaoh was a cards-only expansion. Included were the soon-to-become-standard set of 76 Investigator cards featuring additional Items, Spells and Allies for players to select from, along with 90 Ancient One cards to diversify the ways in which the core game could be played.

In addition, The Curse of the Dark Pharaoh introduced rules to simulate the arrival of a travelling museum exhibit - complete with cursed yet useful artefacts - to Arkham.

The new mechanic provided with this set (nearly every subsequent expansion would feature the addition of optional game mechanics in some form or other) was that of being excluded from certain locations. This, like most of the subsequent optional mechanics, increased the difficulty of winning a game of Arkham Horror, an already tough game to beat.

### Revised Edition
In 2011, Fantasy Flight released a Revised Edition of The Curse of the Dark Pharaoh in order to bring its contents into line with later packs, as more recent expansions had introduced game concepts which were incompatible with the original. It also came with a sheet allowing the Dark Pharaoh himself to be played against as a Herald.

term: The Curse of the Golden Skull
shortDefinition: "The Curse of the Golden Skull" is a short story by Robert E. Howard, first published in Spring 1967 issue of The Howard Collector (#9). Featuring Howard's recurring character Kull of Atlantis, the story is notable for the first mention of Shuma-Gora...
fullContent:
"The Curse of the Golden Skull" is a short story by Robert E. Howard, first published in Spring 1967 issue of The Howard Collector (#9). Featuring Howard's recurring character Kull of Atlantis, the story is notable for the first mention of Shuma-Gorath, an entity later developed as a cosmic adversary by Marvel Comics.

### Synopsis
Rotath, a sorcerer who served and was betrayed by the king of Lemuria, lies dying, mortally wounded by the sword of Kull of Atlantis. With his dying breath, he curses Kull, the king, and "all men living and dead, and all the generations unborn for a million centuries to come." He curses them by various eldritch forces: "by Hotath and Helgor, by Ra and Ka and Valka... Vramma and Jaggta-noga and Kamma and Kulthas... by the fane of the Black Gods, the tracks of the Serpent Ones, the talons of the Ape Lords and the iron-bound books of Shuma-Gorath." He lays a curse upon his own bones "that they might bring death and horror to the sons of men" and, realizing that his bones would turn to dust before the curse would take effect, casts a final spell to turn his bones into solid gold.

Ages later, an explorer enters the ruins of a temple on a jungle island, once a mountaintop of Lemuria. There he finds a golden skeleton, which he first takes to be a fallen idol, then realizes was once living bones. He touches the skull and dies - as a venomous snake crawls out of the golden skull.

### Publication History
A manuscript discovered in Howard's storage trunk along with hundreds of other unpublished works, "The Curse of the Golden Skull"  first appeared in The Howard Collector, a magazine published by Howard scholar (and literary agent) Glenn Lord. It has since appeared in various collections of Howard's fiction, including The Book of Robert E. Howard (Zebra Books, 1976), The Gods of Bal-Sagoth (Ace Books, 1979), Kull (Baen, 1995), Kull: Exile of Atlantis (Del Rey/Ballantine, 2006), and The Best of Robert E. Howard Volume 1: Crimson Shadows (Del Rey/Ballantine, 2007).

The story has been translated into French, German, Italian, and Hungarian. Rotath then made several more appearances in Marvel's Conan stories.

### References

A young woman discovers that two scions of the Tillinghast family have been continuing the experiments of their ancestor Crawford. fullContent:
"The Curse of the Windsor Witch" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young. It forms the fourth part of Book 3 in his Nyarlathotep Cycle. 

### Synopsis
Agents Mayweather and Hines travel to Windsor, Canada on the trail of a serial killer believed to be supernatural in nature. There they uncover the spirit of a long-dead witch, recently released from imprisonment and intent on murdering the ancestors of the men who brought about her downfall. With the aid of a Catholic priest they are able to re-inter her spirit, but the man pays a terrible price as his body is used to contain her evil soul. 

### Characters
*Malcolm Mayweather, a veteran agent with the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.
*Charlene Hines, Mayweather's junior partner.
*Father Sean Doyle, pastor for a small Catholic parish.
*Harjit Singh, the Department's director.
*Gwen, a helpful local cab driver.
*Chief Winston, the head of the Windsor police department.
*Eliza Donaghy, a restless spirit with a hunger for revenge.
*Kirk, director of the Windsor Historical Society.

### Publication History
"The Curse of the Windsor Witch" was published in the collection The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 3 in 2021.

### Trivia
Although containing no direct reference to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the energy used by Eliza Donaghy to enact her vengeance is said to emanate from "The Other": Harjit Singh's catch-all term for the Cthulhu Mythos.

shortDefinition: "The Curse of Yig" is a 1928 short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop in which Yig, "The Father of Serpents", is first introduced.  ### Background Bishop supplied the story idea and some notes, paying Lovecraft to flesh them out in 1928. It c...
fullContent:
"The Curse of Yig" is a 1928 short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop in which Yig, "The Father of Serpents", is first introduced.

### Background
Bishop supplied the story idea and some notes, paying Lovecraft to flesh them out in 1928. It could be said the tale was "ghost-written"; however, others class it as a "collaboration". Bishop then sold the story under her own name to Weird Tales magazine. It was published first in the November 1929 issue (Volume 14, Number 5) on pages 625-36.

It was the first of three tales Lovecraft wrote for Bishop, the others being The Mound and "Medusa's Coil". In fact, The Mound might be regarded as a sequel to "The Curse of Yig", featuring the same first-person narrator and the same general setting, as well as the return of some secondary characters such as Chief Grey Eagle and Grandma Compton.

### Synopsis
Based in Oklahoma around 1889, a newly arrived couple learn about the local legends surrounding a "Snake God", Yig, who takes vengeance on anyone who kills a serpent by killing them or turning them into a half-snake monster. The husband has a snake phobia, which isn't helped by the wife disturbing a nest of rattlesnakes.

The husband and wife go through rituals to keep Yig away, but in the end it fails, and in fear the woman kills her own husband in the dark, thinking he is Yig. She is taken to an asylum, and dies there.... But not before giving birth to a half-snake creature.

### Plot Summary
.]]
While researching snake lore in 1925, the unnamed narrator finds that while most of the residents of Oklahoma are unwilling to talk, there is a rumor that Dr McNeill is keeping a terrible relic in the Guthrie Asylum.

He is well-received by the aging doctor, who reveals that the relic is in fact a living victim of the curse of Yig. After being taken to see it in the basement, the horrified narrator is gently led back to the doctor's plush office to hear the full story, from the afternoon till late at night. After explaining the local customs surrounding Yig, the Doctor moves on to the story of Walker and Audrey Davis.

In the spring of 1889, public land was opened in Oklahoma, and the Davises left Arkansas to settle north of the Wichita River, with all of their worldly possessions and Wolf (an ancient dog) in a covered wagon pulled by two mules. They made slow progress, but given the time of year, they were unaffected by Walker's crippling fear of snakes. However, after hearing the Legend of Yig from a settler in Okmulgee, he became obsessed with protecting himself against the Serpent god and his minions.

Twenty-two days in, they were forced to shelter from the wind against a cliffside. Searching the rocks, Audrey found a nest of newborn rattlesnakes, which she promptly crushed with a rifle butt. But rather than being reassured, Walker was petrified. He believed that she had angered Yig, and so sought out a Wichita Chief, Grey Eagle, who taught him a long protective charm to ward off evil.

The Curse of Yig is a collection of works by the late American author and H. P. Lovecraft's collaborator Zealia Bishop. Released in 1953, as with many of the older Arkham House publications, it was released in a limited hardback run, in this instance 1,200 copies. It has not been reissued.

shortDefinition: "The Cyprus Shell" is a Cthulhu Mythos-connected short story by Brian Lumley that first appeared in the Summer 1968 issue of The Arkham Collector. It was Lumley's first published story.  ### Synopsis A British officer explains his seafood phobia by r...
fullContent:
"The Cyprus Shell" is a Cthulhu Mythos-connected short story by Brian Lumley that first appeared in the Summer 1968 issue of The Arkham Collector. It was Lumley's first published story.

### Synopsis
A British officer explains his seafood phobia by recounting the story of a deadly encounter with a mysterious mollusc.

### Characters

*Maj. Harry Winslow: A British military officer with an embarrassing fear of seafood; the story's narrator.
*Jobling: A corporal under Winslow's command who is an avid collector of conch shells.
*Col. George L. Glee: A retired officer whose dinner party Winslow fled, requiring an explanation.

### Setting
The discovery of Murex hypnotica occurs in Cyprus, near "Kyrea, between Cephos and Kyrenia on the coast." Kyrenia is a good-sized town near the center of the island's north coast.

The dinner party that Winslow fled was in Redcar, Yorkshire--a real town on the North Sea coast, not to be confused with Radcar, Yorkshire, a fictional town that figures in Lumley's "Cement Surroundings".

### Mythos Connections
Winslow recommends a set of books to Glee for further information about the secrets of the sea: "Gantley’s Hydrophinnae, Gaston Le Fe’s Dwellers in the Depths, the German Unter-Zee Kulten and the monstrous Cthaat Aquadingen by an unknown author." This is the first mention in print of the Cthaat Aquadingen, and the first of several times that Lumley refers to the library of aquatic horror introduced in Carl Jacobi's "The Aquarium".

### Publication History
After its appearance in The Arkham Collector, "The Cyprus Shell" was reprinted in Lumley's collections The Caller of The Black (Arkham House, 1971) and Fruiting Bodies and Other Fungi (Roc UK/Tor, 1993). It also appeared in Matt Shaw Presents Masters of Horror (Matt Shaw Publications, 2017). It has been translated into French (as " Le coquillage de Chypre," 1986) and German ("Die Muschel aus Zypern," 2011).

### Trivia
* The Cypriot locations mentioned are all part of the Phoenician murex purple dye industry in ancient times, where seashells were collected and deep purple dye for textile coloration was extracted from the molluscs. This industry was a major source of revenue for the Phoenicians for thousands of years and is also the origin of the association of purple first with imperial Roman majesty and then with aristocracy and royalty in more modern times.

fullContent:
"The Dappled Egg" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Tim Mendees, first published in the Gavin Chappell-edited zine Lovecraftiana (year unknown, Rogue Planet Press).

### Synopsis
Claudia and her partner I are a young couple who run a pet store specialising in reptiles. When Claudia orders a new batch of iguana eggs from her supplier, she discovers an unusual dappled egg mixed in amongst the others; she attempts to incubate it, and as the days pass she becomes increasingly obsessed with the egg, turning almost feral at any perceived slight made by I against it.

When the egg comes to term, it hatches a bizarre creature which forms an immediate bond with Claudia, while displaying an overtly threatening demeanour towards I. The creature proceeds to eat many of the animals in their shared pet store, before Claudia gives herself to it and sacrifices I to assuage it’s dark appetites. She then goes on to send her freshly-laid eggs to unsuspecting recipients, presumably in an effort to repopulate the Earth in the image of her new lord Yig.

### Behind the Mythos
In the aftermath of I's sacrifice, Claudia renames the store Yig and Sons Reptiles, showing that the entity was intended to be a rebirthed Yig, or at least one of its avatars.

### Publication History
*Lovecraftiana (unknown year, Rogue Planet Press)
*The Best of Lovecraftiana (2023, Rogue Planet Press)

### Trivia
*Despite the entity from the egg being named as Yig, it bears a closer resemblance to common depictions of fellow Great Old One Tsathoggua, possessing a more frog-like appearance.

"The Dark Boatman" is a short story by British author John Glasby.

### Synopsis
A man named Dexter inherits his eccentric uncle's sprawling Cornwall mansion, and receives a mysterious letter from him a few days later. Along with a friend, Michael Ambrose, Dexter travels to his new property and uncovers a terrible family secret stretching back thousands of years.

### Characters

*Dexter (first name unknown), the last of his lineage, Dexter is a thirty-something man presumably from somewhere in either England or Wales.
*Michael Ambrose, a colleague of Dexter's, and something of a specialist in objects of antiquity. Ambrose is killed when he inadvertently assumes Dexter's place in his family's destiny.
*Andrew Forsythe, partner in the law firm Poulton and Forsythe and the Dexter family solicitor.
*Charon, the mythical boatman to the underworld.

### Behind the Mythos
The Dark Boatman was first published in Spectral Tales No. 2 in December 1989, was later included as part of Glasby's own collection The Dark Boatman: Tales of Horror and the Cthulhu Mythos in July 2012, and was released as part of the digital collection The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack later the same year.

shortDefinition: "The Dark Brotherhood" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth. One of the controversial "posthumous collaborations" between the two, it was in fact written almost entirely by the latter, based on a fragment by the former.  ### Synopsi...
fullContent:
"The Dark Brotherhood" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth. One of the controversial "posthumous collaborations" between the two, it was in fact written almost entirely by the latter, based on a fragment by the former.

### Synopsis
Arthur Phillips and Rose Dexter, a pair of friends whose habit is to explore the city of Providence, Rhode Island by night meet a mysterious stranger who appears to share their enjoyment of after-dark walks. As their relationship develops, the woman is beguiled by the stranger's charm while the man uncovers a cult who are scheming to draw something deadly to Earth.

### Mythos Connections
The extra-galactic species shown to Arthur Phillips by the strange group in an effort to convince him of the existence of alien life would appear to be members of the Great Race of Yith in the form of the Earth-native species which they took on: four limbed conical creatures with two pairs of claws and three eyes.

Additionally, aside from having his middle name, Arthur Phillips may have been an insert by Derleth of H. P. Lovecraft: a well-educated man from Providence, Rhode Island in poor general health.

The bodies used by "Mr. Allan" and the others of his group for their activities on Earth are exact duplicates of the late American author Edgar Allan Poe, although why they chose this particular mien is not explained.

### Publication History
"The Dark Brotherhood" was first published in the collection The Dark Brotherhood and Other Pieces by Arkham House in 1966.

### Trivia
* Although the story depicts the main characters exploring Edgar Allan Poe's burial site in Providence, Poe was in fact buried in Baltimore, Maryland.

fullContent:
"The Dark Demon" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the November 1936 issue of Weird Tales. It features a reclusive writer of weird fiction who is a thinly veiled portrait of H. P. Lovecraft.

The story's main character is Edgar Henquist Gordon, "the strange dark genius whose eldritch tales were once so popular among fantasy-lovers everywhere." 

His "later work...alienated the public" with its "nightmare hints and outlandish  fancies.... Many people branded the extravagantly worded tomes as the work of a madman." He is "a tall, thin, angular man with the pale face and deep-set eyes which bespeak the dreamer."

The narrator is "a hopeful (and at times, hopeless) amateur writer" who is "the last of all of [Gordon's] friends." Describing Lovecraft's relationship with Bloch, the story reports that Gordon exchanged letters with authors and editors all over the country; would-be writers, aspiring journalists, and thinkers and students everywhere.... What Edgar Gordon did for me in the next three years can never adequately be told. His able assistance, friendly criticism and kind encouragement finally succeeded in making a writer of sorts out of me.Gordon confides to the narrator that his stories--with titles like The Soul of Chaos and The Principle of Evil--all come from his dreams. In sleep, he has repeatedly visited the "[m]ountains of black stalagmites; peaks and cones amidst crater valleys of dead suns; [and] stone cities in the stars" that reoccur in his dreams. He admits that his stories echo "descriptive passages in such books as the Necronomicon, the Mysteries of the Worm, and the Book of Eibon," but insists that he had prior knowledge of Azozath [sic] and Yuggoth before learning that they appeared in such books, and could describe Nyarlathotep and Yog-Sothoth from "actual dream contact with these allegorical entities."

The narrator becomes concerned when Gordon becomes obsessed with an entity known as "the Dark One", the Demon Messenger, who has chosen Gordon "to be the Messiah; the messenger of His word." (As any fan of the Cthulhu Mythos would, the narrator wonders if this character is "remotely connected with the Nyarlathotep fable.") The Dark One appears to Gordon as "looking like Asmodeus--black all over, and furry, with green eyes, hog snout, and the claws and fangs of some wild beast." Gordon declares he has been promised that "I shall become incarnate with him!"

Increasingly worried for his friend, the narrator goes to his house on Cedar Street (in an unnamed city) to insist that he get help. He carries a revolver, with a premonition he "might meet with a violent response." Instead, he finds his friend asleep on the couch--transformed into the hog-snouted form of the Dark One. He shoots him three times; the police find only his empty clothes, and declare him a missing person.

shortDefinition: "The Dark Eidolon" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, set in Zothique, "the last continent on Earth." It was first published in Weird Tales in January 1935.  ### Synopsis Namirrha, an arrogant sorcerer, is destroyed by his own hubris. He makes w...
fullContent:
"The Dark Eidolon" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, set in Zothique, "the last continent on Earth." It was first published in Weird Tales in January 1935.

### Synopsis
Namirrha, an arrogant sorcerer, is destroyed by his own hubris. He makes war on the Emperor Zotulla and his Empire of Xylac. At a feast, he first summons female Ghoul dancing "girls", before summoning horse-like monstrosities from beyond, called the Coursers of Thamogorgos, to destroy the empire. Namirrha then mind-swaps with the Emperor. However, all does not go as planned for the prideful spellcaster....

### Behind the Mythos
The story begins with a passage that links Smith's Zothique stories--which take place on "the last continent" at the end of time--to his other stories set in prehistoric times, some of which have direct connections to the Cthulhu Mythos:[O]ut of the shadows, the older gods had returned to man: the gods forgotten since Hyperborea, since Mu and Poseidonis, bearing other names but the same attributes. And the elder demons had also returned, battening on the fumes of evil sacrifice, and fostering again the primordial sorceries.The passage suggests that in Smith's mind, his Zothique series belonged to the same continuity with his Mythos tales. It also implies that the gods of Zothique may be identified with the Mythos entities.

The "eidolon" of the title references both the ghostly form of the emperor after he is driven from his body and exists disembodied as a phantom over the dead body of the sorcerer, and of course the dark desires of Namirrha himself.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Weird Tales, "The Dark Eidolon" was first reprinted in Smith's collection Out of Space and Time (Arkham House, 1942). It has since appeared in numerous collections of Smith's work, including Zothique (Ballantine Books, 1970), The City of the Singing Flame (Timescape/Pocket Books, 1981), Ubbo-Sathla (Neo, 1985), A Rendezvous in Averoigne: The Best Fantastic Tales of Clark Ashton Smith (Arkham House, 1988), Tales of Zothique (Necronomicon Press, 1995), The Emperor of Dreams (Gollancz / Orion, 2002), The Maze of the Enchanter: Volume Four of the Collected Fantasies of Clark Ashton Smith (Night Shade Books, 2009), The Return of the Sorcerer (Prime Books, 2012), and The Dark Eidolon and Other Fantasies (Penguin Books, 2014).

It has also been included in multi-author anthologies, including The Spell of Seven (Pyramid Books, 1965), edited by L. Sprague de Camp; The Century's Best Horror Fiction 1901-1950 (Cemetery Dance Publications, 2012), edited by John Pelan; and Swords Against Darkness (Prime Books, 2017), edited by Paula Guran.

The story has been translated into German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Italian, and Portuguese.

"The Dark Horse" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author John Goodrich.

### Synopsis
In a post-apocalyptic New York where Cthulhu and his servants have awoken and subjugated the human race, a fugitive woman named Laura is approached by the mysterious Dornier who teaches her a spell which will destroy the Great Old Ones when recited by enough people at the correct time, which they will know when the sky is lit in green.

Laura spends the next few years teaching the spell to as many other survivors as she can find, before she is captured by the Lord of Manhattan, a servitor of Cthulhu. Later, while imprisoned, Laura sees the sky light up in green and begins the chant, which is taken up by all of those whom she has taught. However, Dornier has deceived them, and the spell is in fact a ritual used to summon Azathoth, and the sky opens to admit the Outer God before it reduces the Earth to ash.

### Characters
* Laura, a survivor living on scraps who was only a child when Cthulhu awoke.
* Travis Dornier, a cultist of Azathoth masquerading as humanity's last hope.
* The Lord of Manhattan, an (at least partially) human servant of Cthulhu.
* Azathoth, an Outer God.

### Publication History
"The Dark Horse" was published in the thematic anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu by April Moon Books in March 2014.

"The Dark Light" is a short Thomas Carnacki story by American author and scholar Robert M. Price. It is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
When a Member of Parliament disappears, supernatural sleuth Thomas Carnacki discovers that he has travelled to another dimension, one in which the human race was unable to evolve past the primitive caveman stage. Carnacki finds the man on the verge of death, the tribesfolk tending to him under attack from deadly predators, and is forced to abandon them all to their fate.

### Publication History
"The Dark Light" was published in the Sam Gafford-edited anthology Carnacki: The Lost Cases in June 2016.

### Trivia
* The drug used by the parliamentarian to travel between dimensions was the Black Lotus, a narcotic known to be harvested and used by the cannibalistic Tcho-Tcho people.

"The Dark Man's Assassin" is a short story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
A man who hears murderous voices in his head is recruited by his brother to perform a service for the evil entity known as the Dark Man; this act will allow the Dark Man's pawn to gain the US presidency. However, the voices persuade the man that this would be an incredibly bad idea, and he double crosses both his brother and the Dark Man, likely saving the world from a terrible fate.

### Characters
*The Narrator, a man who hears internal voices which may not be figments of his imagination…
*Frankie, the narrator's brother and cultist of the Dark Man.
*The Dark Man, an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep.
*Professor Markham Stiles of Miskatonic University, head of a cabal dedicated to thwarting the plans of the Nyarlathotep and the Great Old Ones.
*Senator Wilson, a rising star in the field of politics, and a pawn of the Dark Man.

### Publication History
"The Dark Man's Assassin" was first published in the online zine Nightscapes in April 1998, and then again in Cthulhu Cultus #14 in January 1999.

fullContent:
The Dark Rites of Arkham is a video game developed by Postmodern Adventures and published by enComplot based on the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
Detective Jack Foster rejoins the police department after a traumatic incident to take over the investigation of what appears to be mere political blackmail. Soon, however, he's faced with the discovery of a gruesome ritual murder that took place in a sealed room, from which no one could have gotten in or out without being seen. Along with his new partner, Harvey Whitman, an expert on cults, Foster dives deep into the shadows of the city of Arkham.

The case will get even darker when they find out it is related to three witches that escaped the Salem trials in 1693, and a conspiracy that could put an end to the world as we know it.

### Release
The Dark Rites of Arkham was released in 2026 on Steam by Postmodern Adventures.

fullContent:
The Dark Swamp is a real-world location near Glocester, Rhode Island that was one of the early inspirations for H.P. Lovecraft's story The Colour Out of Space.

Lovecraft with his friend and "adopted son" (a humorous reference by Lovecraft) C.M. Eddy, Jr. went hiking to try and find The Dark Swamp but met with no success. Lovecraft described their exploration in detail (and poetry) in a letter to Frank Bellknap Long a week later. C.M. Eddy, Jr. wrote a fictionalised version of the trip as the unfinished novella Black Noon.

The Dark Swamp is the location of many local legends going back to before white settlement. The location is believed to be the home of a foul-smelling creature with flaming eyes and clam shell scales. Some say it breathes fire. It is referred to simply as "IT". There have been, as of 2021, recent reports of a skunk ape type creature wading in the swamp. It should be noted that due to the depth of the liquid mud and the thick screening foliage, passage into the swamp itself is all but impossible even in winter. A final real-world phenomenon remarked upon by visitors is that The Dark Swamp is a zone of silence - no bird or animal sounds are heard within its boundaries although they are common beyond it.

Recently, Lovecraft fans have explored the region and found the Dark Swamp location. It has contracted in size but still has standing water and thick woodlands surrounding it. There are also abandoned and collapsed nineteenth century buildings and an abandoned cemetery. The explorers and bloggers have also discovered that the direct descendants of the family encountered by Lovecraft and Eddy, the Law family, still live in the area and have family oral history and memories of the visit. Ruth Scott, the grand daughter of the grand daughter of the man Lovecraft spoke to at the time, has commented on blogs to this effect.

Recent exploration of The Dark Swamp: https://stonewings.wordpress.com/2012/05/23/417/
Radio broadcast describing Dark Swamp and its legends as well as the Lovecraft link: https://www.wpri.com/video/the-haunted-tale-of-dark-swamp/5985746/

fullContent:
The Dark Wood is an adventure written Fred Behrendt for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG, released as part of the game supplement book Adventures in Arkham County in which it was the fourth of the five adventures provided. It is, as with all the adventures in that volume, set in the original 1920s Call of Cthulhu RPG setting in New England. The adventures all take place in the county of which Arkham forms part.

### Synopsis
Amateur archaeologists discover what at first seems to be a Viking burial ground but which proves in fact to be of Hyperborean origin.

It is a research and action combined adventure of relatively short duration in which the characters will also encounter the hideous, relentless and surprisingly quick and dangerous Desh.

fullContent:
The Darkest of the Hillside Thickets is a Canadian rock band dedicated to promoting the literature of H. P. Lovecraft and the Mythos, especially the Necronomicon.

The band was formed in January 1992 by lead singer and main songwriter Toren Atkinson and lead guitarist Warren Banks, who met at Fraser Valley College in Abbotsford, British Columbia. They were originally joined by bass player Quentin Rogers, though he was replaced by  Devon Presseau before their first show. The band's current lineup includes Atkinson, Banks, guitarist/bassist Mario Nieva, drummer Jordan Pratt, and bassist/backup vocalist Merrick Atkinson. Members live in British Columbia's Vancouver, Abbotsford, and Chilliwack.

Their music blends melodious punk and rock. They describe their song titles and lyrics as good-natured but macabre. The band's name comes from the Lovecraft story "The Tomb," which includes the line, "I will tell only of the lone tomb in the darkest of the hillside thickets."

### Discography
The Shadow Out of Tim concept album is an updated reimagining of Lovecraft's story "The Shadow Out of Time".

Spaceship Zero is not a Lovecraft-oriented album.

shortDefinition: "The Death of Vanessa Fell" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Tony Richards. It was published in his collection The Howling Terror and Other Lovecraftian Horror Stories by Weird House Press in November 2022.  ### Synopsis When success...
fullContent:
"The Death of Vanessa Fell" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Tony Richards. It was published in his collection The Howling Terror and Other Lovecraftian Horror Stories by Weird House Press in November 2022.

### Synopsis
When successful publisher Charles attempts to comfort and rehabilitate his best friend, the wealthy steel merchant David Cossett-Byrne, who has recently suffered the loss of his beloved fiancé Vanessa Fell, he comes to the shocking realization that David believes he is being haunted by the woman. Eventually managing to calm his friend and put him on the road to recovery, Charles decides to look into the background of the mysterious Miss Fell.

Questioning of the locals leads to some unsettling revelations on the propriety of Miss Fell's behaviour, as Charles breaks into her now-abandoned country manor in an effort to get to the bottom of things. There, he discovers a series of diaries which reveal that the Fells were a clan of cultists in service to many dark gods, including Cthulhu, Yog-Sothoth, and Dagon. They also tell of how Vanessa's death was no accident, merely the first part in a ritual which will allow her to join with her gods, as long as a sacrifice can be provided.

Shocked by the realization that his friend David is to be the undead woman's victim, Charles rushes back to warn his friend, just in time to witness David being lured through a magical portal and brutally murdered in the name of the Old Ones.

### Trivia
*Although the story touches little on this particular aspect, the Fells are implied to be Deep One hybrids, despite living in a landlocked English county. Mentions of certain familial characteristics recall the Innsmouth Look, while Vanessa herself wears an unusual necklace made of a peculiar metal which she states "a great-uncle of mine found … whilst travelling the South Seas"; this is reminiscent of the jewellery described in The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

When his wife is devastated by the loss of her brother, Peter Ingram resolves to go to any length to help ease her pain. Delving into evil texts, he creates a revolutionary radio set which he uses to plead with the dark gods of the cosmos in an effort to have his brother-in-law returned to them. His prayers seem to be answered, but what comes back is not what was lost, and one of them must pay a terrible price.

### Characters

*Harry Crandall, a coastal radio operator.
*Peter Ingram, Harry's friend.
*Elaine Ingram, Peter's wife.
*Yago, the Ingram's Seminole Indian manservant.

### Publication History

*Weird Tales (1939)
*Murgunstrumm and Others (1977, 2004)
*Cthulhu's Heirs: Tales of the Mythos for the New Millennium (1994)

### Trivia

*Amongst the deities beseeched for help by Ingram are Hastur the Unspeakable and Nyarlathotep.

"The Decorative Water Feature of Nameless Dread" is a short Cthulhu Mythos parody by Australian-born author James Brogden.

### Synopsis
A man in middle England listens to a radio show phone-in where one of the callers has inexplicably discovered a Deep One inhabiting his garden pond and attempting to mate with his wife, who appears to have fallen for the creature.

### Publication History
"The Decorative Water Feature of Nameless Dread" was first published in the anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014. It also appeared in the collection of Brogden's own works Evocations in July 2015.

### Trivia
* Namechecked in the text are Father Dagon, Mother Hydra, Y'ha-nthlei, the Great Old Ones, and the Elder Gods.
* The end of the story mentions that the listener had been stung by a triffid seedling, a species of carnivorous plant created by John Wyndham for his 1951 novel The Day of the Triffids.

fullContent:
The Deep Gate is a novella written by Chris A. Jackson and published by Fantasy Flight Games under their Arkham Horror Files label. The main protagonist of the story is Silas Marsh, a recurrent character within the setting.

### Synopsis
Silas Marsh encounters librarian Abigail Foreman who persuades him to perform some nautical calculations for him. Based on these calculations, and the prophecies contained in an ancient book of forbidden knowledge, the two travel to Innsmouth in an attempt to stop a cataclysmic event which may spell the end of the human race.

### Characters
### Main Characters
*Silas Marsh, a grizzled seaman and Deep One hybrid.
*Abigail Foreman, a librarian who has uncovered hidden knowledge.
### Minor Characters
*Martin, Silas's cousin.

### Behind the Mythos
The Deep Gate was first published as a hardback novella by Fantasy Flight Games in June 2018 as part of their Arkham Horror Fiction line of Mythos-related literature. In addition to the story, the release includes full-colour inserts detailing the evidence uncovered by Silas and Abigail during the course of their investigation, and a set of four exclusive cards for use with Arkham Horror: The Card Game.

### Trivia
*The antagonists of The Deep Gate are the aquatic Deep Ones, despite Silas himself being a hybrid member of the species.
*Although having been previously depicted by Fantasy Flight as an antagonistic character in their The Curse of the Dark Pharaoh expansion for Arkham Horror, Abigail Foreman is most definitely portrayed as one of the heroes of the story.

"The Deep Ones" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author James Wade.

### Synopsis
A parapsychologist working alongside a centre for dolphin research falls for one of his coworkers, a woman descended from Innsmouth stock. Hypnotising her in an effort to stimulate psychic contact with the dolphins results in her genetic heritage taking over, and the story's climax sees her leaving the land to be with her people.

### Characters
*Dorn, a parapsychologist and the story's narrator.
*Josephine Gilman, an animal specialist.
*Dr. Frederick C. Wilhelm, a highly-regarded marine biologist.
*Alonzo Waite, a scion of Innsmouth leading a small group in opposition to the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Publication History
"The Deep Ones" was first published in Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos by Arkham House in 1969. It has since been reprinted several times, and has also been translated into French.

fullContent:
"The Deprogrammer" is a short Mythos story by author and Lovecraft scholar Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
The story revolves around a man whose job is to kidnap and "deprogram" young people who have been brainwashed by their membership in cults. After taking on the case of Ginny Salamone who has joined the Church of Starry Wisdom, his hired muscle is brutally killed and Ginny has disappeared. Deciding to look into the mysterious organisation further, he is converted to their cause and starts his work as a recruiter.

### Characters

* Ted Brigham, a professional deprogrammer with a cynical attitude to religion.
* Ginny Salamone, a member of the Church of Starry Wisdom.
* Baruch Rowley, a senior member of the Church.
* Mitch Ames, a clergyman who runs a halfway house for former cult members.
* Mr. and Mrs. Salamone, Ginny's parents.
* O'Rourke and Graves, Brigham's hired muscle, both beneficiaries of his deprogramming skills.

### Publication History
"The Deprogrammer" was first published in the September 1989 edition of the magazine Deathrealm. It later appeared in the anthologies Quick Chills II (April 1992) and Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2008).

The Derelict is a scenario supplement for the Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Written by Sandy Petersen with Mike Mason, it featured artwork by M. Wayne Miller and cartography by Stephanie McAlea. The book was released as a digital download by Chaosium in June 2016 as part of the Free RPG Day initiative, with physical copies later being made available at Lulu.com.

### Overview


Set aboard a derelict freighter in the North Atlantic, the scenario is less of an actual story, and more of a sandbox setting where investigators are rewarded for improvising solutions in a desperate fight for survival against the Sciapod, a monstrous creature incorporated from Norwegian folklore.

shortDefinition: "The Derleth Mythos" is a half-page essay of criticism and scholarship by Richard L. Tierney. It critiques and analyzes the relative contributions of H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth to the body of work that has come to be almost universally accept...
fullContent:
"The Derleth Mythos" is a half-page essay of criticism and scholarship by Richard L. Tierney. It critiques and analyzes the relative contributions of H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth to the body of work that has come to be almost universally accepted as the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview


Tierney identifies the Derleth approach as essentially attempting to map Mythos entities and concepts to Christian ethics and morality, and the the Paracelsian concept of Elementals. He makes the excellent point that equating Cthulhu with the element of water is to ignore or miss the point that Cthulhu is a space alien who built his city on land and who became immobilized by water when his city sank in an ancient cataclysm. Clearly water is not a sympathetic element for Cthulhu in that case.

Further contradictions are highlighted: Hastur is meant to be an Air Elemental but lives on the bottom of a lake (water), and it is necessary for Derleth to invent out of whole cloth a Fire Elemental (Cthugha) to round out the four elements in the Mythos and provide the needed balance between opposing elements in the Paracelsus model of atomic structure.

In essence, Tierney identifies the difference and semiotics of pastiche as opposed to continuation or exploration of an author's work.

### Publication History

*Crypt of Cthulhu #24 (1984)
*Nightscapes (1997)
*Discovering H. P. Lovecraft (2001)

shortDefinition: "The Descendant" is a story fragment by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, believed to have been written in 1927. It was first published in the journal Leaves in 1938, after Lovecraft's death.  ### Inspiration Lovecraft may have been ref...
fullContent:
"The Descendant" is a story fragment by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, believed to have been written in 1927. It was first published in the journal Leaves in 1938, after Lovecraft's death.

### Inspiration
Lovecraft may have been referring to this attempt at a story when he wrote that he was "making a very careful study of London...in order to get background for tales involving richer antiquities than America can furnish."

### Characters
### Lord Northam
Lord Northam is a "harmlessly mad" Londoner who "screams when the church bells ring." Once a "scholar and aesthete" who studied at Harrow and Oxford, he has become "thin and grey and wrinkled" before his time and "seeks...not to think" through "books of the tamest and most puerile kind". He only begins to explain the fear he lives under when confronted with a copy of the Necronomicon.

The details of the character evoke two of Lovecraft's favorite British writers: He lives in Gray's Inn, where Arthur Machen lived for many years, and is the "nineteenth Baron of a line whose beginnings went uncomfortably far back into the past", recalling Lord Dunsany, who was the eighteenth baron of a line founded in the 12th century.

Northam's sampling of various worldviews is similar to Randolph Carter's quest for meaning in Lovecraft's "The Silver Key". Northam's description as "a dreamer who found life tame and unsatisfying" also links him to Carter.

Northam is also linked to Lovecraft's "The Nameless City," perhaps even being the main character therein: "He would travel leagues to follow up a furtive village tale of abnormal wonder, and once went into the desert of Araby to seek a Nameless City of faint report, which no man has ever beheld. There rose within him the tantalising faith that somewhere an easy gate existed, which if one found would admit him freely to those outer deeps whose echoes rattled so dimly at the back of his memory."

### Williams
A 23-year-old "dreamer" whose "love of the bizarre" has been manifest since he was 16, when he learned about the Necronomicon from a bent old bookseller in Chandos Street. He finally buys a copy at an "absurdly slight" price from a "gnarled old Levite" whose bookshop is in "the squalid precincts of Clare Market". He is attracted to the "breath of cosmic wind" he senses around Lord Northam.

### Lunaeus Gabinius Capito
The reputed ancestor of the Northam line, he was military tribune in the Third Augustan Legion, which Lovecraft places at Lindum in Roman Britain. (Lovecraft mentions the same Roman unit in "The Rats in the Walls", where it is based in the fictional town of Anchester; the Third Legion was actually based in Damascus.) Gabinius was "summarily expelled from his command for participation in certain rites unconnected with any known religion", rituals he had learned "in a cliffside cavern where strange folk met together and made the Elder Sign in the dark"—remnants of the people who fled an Atlantis-like lost continent and built Ston

shortDefinition: "The Descent into the Abyss" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter and Clark Ashton Smith, albeit written after the latter's death. Carter wrote the tale based on a story prompt by Smith, similar to the "posthumous collaborations" of Derleth ...
fullContent:
"The Descent into the Abyss" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter and Clark Ashton Smith, albeit written after the latter's death. Carter wrote the tale based on a story prompt by Smith, similar to the "posthumous collaborations" of Derleth and Lovecraft.

"The Descent into the Abyss" was first published in the 1980 anthology Weird Tales #2 (not to be confused with the magazine it is named after). At the time, the story was credited to Smith, with a note saying "completed by Lin Carter".

This story functions as a prequel to Smith's "The Seven Geases", as it reveals the backstory of the mysterious Haon-Dor.

### Synopsis
In ancient Hyperborea, at a time before the advent of humans, the antehuman sorcerer Haon-Dor goes through a crevice at the bottom of Mount Voormithadreth to find the way to the underground realm of grey-litten Y'qaa, which is rumoured to function as a dimensional nexus that connects several different worlds. Deep within the abyss, Haon-Dor hopes to locate the domain of Ubbo-Sathla, and retrieve the Elder Records: the stone tablets stolen from the Elder Gods.

Once inside the tunnels, Haon-Dor comes across Zushakon, one of the entities spawned by Ubbo-Sathla, and respectfully asks to be allowed passage while displaying the sigil known as the Elder Key. Later on, he enters a huge cavern, with alcoves gnawed into the stone wall. Inside each of these is a creature, which Haon-Dor recognizes as the "prototypes" of several races that serve the Great Old Ones. Quumyagga of the Shantaks, Nug of the Ghouls, etc., each being the first of their respective kinds to have been created. To each of them, Haon-Dor asks for passage and shows the sigil.

Leaving the Cavern of the Prototypes behind, Haon-Dor crosses a bridge over a colossal chasm and finds a luminous portal guarded by K'thugguol, the prototype of the Shoggoths. Unexpectedly, the Shoggoth allows Haon-Dor entrance even before the sorcerer has time to ask it. When he passes through the portal, Haon-Dor gazes into the pit and sees the primordial Ubbo-Sathla, as well as the Elder Records scattered around it. However, reading just one glyph of the tablets is enough to send the sorcerer running back the way he came from, terrified of the undisclosed cosmic truth he learned.

After this traumatic experience, Haon-Dor sets residence in the caves beneath Mount Voormithadreth and never returns to the surface.

In the "The Despised Pastoral", Lovecraft laments his perceived attitude of poets of the time to look down on the pastoral, a type of poetry which extolls the virtues of a rural lifestyle and the countryside in general. He also expresses his fondness for such works.

fullContent:
The Devil Came to Arkham is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author Byron Craft, the third in his Arkham Detective series. It was independently published through the CreateSpace platform in March 2017; both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Overview


### Synopsis
The coming of enigmatic stranger Corvus Astaroth to Arkham heralds the beginning of an unprecedented heatwave in the area which destroys local crops and saps the strength of the populace. As Astaroth establishes his political power over the city, those who cross him suffer mysterious deaths. Simultaneously, a bizarre wasting disease begins to afflict many of the residents, and Arkham is put under quarantine by the Federal authorities.

With the aid of a dying former policeman and Miskatonic University's Dr. Henry Armitage, the Detective is able to establish that Astaroth is in reality a shapeshifting Night Gaunt, somehow separated from his home in the Dreamlands, and now siphoning off the life-essence of the population for use in a scheme to get back. He and his new partner, rookie cop Matthew Bell, are soon able to defeat the creature using an iron broadsword and, although many have already fallen victim to the illness, those who have not yet succumbed quickly recover.

### Trivia
*Despite being set during America's Prohibition era (1920-1933 ), at one point the Detective notes that the entrance to Astaroth's mansion is large enough to "let in a parade of Sherman tanks"; the Sherman tank was not designed and put into production until 1940 .

"The Devil's Hop Yard" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Richard A. Lupoff. It was first published in Chrysalis, Volume 2 in August 1978.

### Synopsis
1928, Dunwich: a man named Sawyer and two members of the decayed branch of the Whateley family conspire to conduct a ritual similar to that planned by Wilbur Whateley ten years previously. Using the elder Whateley's daughter as a vessel for the offspring, they birth an abnormal and malevolent girl-child.

Once the girl comes of age, the three conduct a ritual atop the blasted hill known as "the Devil's Hop Yard". A handful of townsfolk and a local constable attempt to stop the process, but the girl is lifted off into the ether, presumably to join her "father" Yog-Sothoth, to whom the rite was dedicated.

shortDefinition: "The Diary of Alonzo Typer" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and William Lumley. It is Lovecraft's revision of Lumley's "The Diary of Alonzo Typer, Found After His Mysterious Disappearance". It first appeared in the February 1938 issue of Weird Ta...
fullContent:
"The Diary of Alonzo Typer" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and William Lumley. It is Lovecraft's revision of Lumley's "The Diary of Alonzo Typer, Found After His Mysterious Disappearance". It first appeared in the February 1938 issue of Weird Tales.

### Publisher's Summary
"Alonzo Hasbrouch Typer of Kingston, New York, was last seen and recognized on April 17, 1908, around noon, at the Hotel Richmond in Batavia. He was the only survivor of an ancient Ulster Country family, and was fifty-three years old at the time of his disappearance."

It features the Ancient One, as well as a passing reference to the city of Yian-Ho, seemingly referencing Robert W. Chambers' "The Maker of Moons," which references a mysterious city in China called Yian.

### Setting
"The Diary of Alonzo Typer" is set in the village of Chorazin, a six-hour walk from Batavia, New York. It's located in "a small, swampy valley of strange brown weed-stalks and dead fungi surrounded by scraggly, evilly twisted trees with bare boughs." Chorazin is the site of the Van der Heyl mansion, which "was very old, antedating the general white settlement of the region, and had formed the home of a strange and secretive family." Chorazin, a "straggling village", grew up around it, "populated by Indians and later by renegades from the surrounding country." 

Chorazin, like the settings of "Beyond the Wall of Sleep," "The Lurking Fear," and "The Man of Stone," is an Upstate New York genetic backwater: "Of the singular hereditary strains which afterward appeared in the mixed Chorazin villagers, several monographs have been written by ethnologists." The "decadent Chorazin villagers" are noted for their "stupidity and taciturnity," which "baffle all students of the region and its secrets." Typer's diary is found by John Eagle, a "swarthy, simian-faced, Indian-like villager."

Near Chorazin and the van der Heyl house is
a steep hill crowned with a peculiar ring of ancient standing stones which the Iroquois always regarded with fear and loathing. The origin and nature of the stones, whose date, according to archaeological and climatological evidence, must be fabulously early, is a problem still unsolved. 

### Characters
Alonzo Hasbrouch Typer: A student of the occult from Kingston, New York, born c. 1855 to an "ancient Ulster County family." He was educated at Columbia and Heidelberg universities, and was a member of the Society for Psychical Research until 1902. He has published privately on vampirism, ghouls, and poltergeist phenomena.

Claes van der Heyl: This first known progenitor of the van der Heyl line, though he's suspected of descent from "generations of evil heritage." He keeps a diary in "barbarous Latin" from 1560 to 1580, a commits a "nameless sin" in 1591 that his descendants may have to expiate.

Cornelis van der Heyl: Known as Cornelist of Leyden. The worst of the "accursed line," who "broke down the barrier after his father had found that other key"--his father from context app

fullContent:
"The Diary of Hannah Greeley" is a short Cthulhu Mythos piece by American author Jennifer M. Oaks, and a companion piece to her story "The Innsmouth Covenant". It was published with its parter digitally in the chapbook collection The Brides of Innsmouth in 2012.

### Synopsis
When Miskatonic University junior librarian Janet Poole is told by her boss Mr. Woolsey to place a new acquisition in the forbidden texts section, her curiosity gets the better of her, and she sneaks the book off to read it. What she discovers is the events recounted in "The Innsmouth Covenant": the story of a young girl gifted to the Deep Ones as part of a historic inter-species bargain.

However, unfortunately for Janet, Mr. Woolsey is not all that he seems and, after noticing her take the book and read it, arrives with his Deep One henchmen to spirit Janet and her sister off to fulfil the Innsmouth compact made long ago between man and amphibian.

### Trivia
*The text recounted from Hannah Greeley's diary is writing taken - for the most parts verbatim - from the companion story "The Innsmouth Covenant".
*"The Diary of Hannah Greeley" mentions that the events in The Shadow Over Innsmouth were "recounted" by H. P. Lovecraft, rather than created by him. This would seem to suggest that, in this timeline at least, the Innsmouth incident was a real event, rather than something written as a pulp fiction piece.

fullContent:
"The Dig" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Sean Rodgers.

### Synopsis
An archaeological expedition to uncover the ancient ruined city of Irem in Saudi Arabia achieves its goal. However, the two archaeologists who descend into its depths meet a deadly creature: only one survives to tell his tale, and even he is promptly incarcerated within the walls of Arkham Asylum on his return to America.

### Characters
*Professor Thomas Wilkins, professor of Archeology and Ancient History at Miskatonic University. Driven insane by his encounter beneath the sands.
*Michael Addison, leader of the expedition.
*Salim, foreman of the work party hired to accompany the expedition.

### Publication History
"The Dig" was first published in Cthulhu Cultus #8 in March 1997, and appeared in the online fanzine Nightscapes in August of the same year.

fullContent:
The Dirge of Reason is a novella written by Graeme Davis and published by Fantasy Flight Games under their Arkham Horror Files label. The story revolves around one of the setting's recurrent characters, Roland Banks.

### Synopsis
When out-of-favour Bureau of Investigation Agent Roland Banks is sent to Arkham to investigate the bizarre deaths of a 38-strong orchestra at a remote cabin, he uncovers a tragic tale of misplaced curiosity and hubris.

The orchestra's conductor had been attempting to put the contents of recently-discovered ancient Sumerian texts to music, and had inadvertently opened a tear in the fabric of reality which allowed an unspecified entity to reach through and swat the entire group like flies.

When this breach occurred, some other entity, a bizarre, protoplasmic flautist accidentally made its way through as well, and Banks was forced to join forces with a booze smuggler to put an end to the beast.

### Characters
### Main Characters
*Roland Banks, the protagonist and an agent from the Bureau of Investigation.
*Leo de Luca, a local bootlegger.
*Edie Talbot, a New York reporter.

### Minor Characters
*Sheriff Engle, head of the Arkham Police Department.
*Warren Rice, Languages professor at Miskatonic University's Classics Department.
*Vicky Serra, hired muscle for a rival Boston bootlegger.
*Maurizio Trappeto, Vicky's partner.
*Elmer White, a local moonshiner.

### Mythos Connections
When discussing the ancient texts with Roland Banks, Professor Rice states that the expedition "was a real feather in the Classics Department's cap. I hear Geology is planning to go to Antarctica, just to get even." This would appear to be a nod to the Miskatonic-funded Pabodie Expedition, whose fate was described in At the Mountains of Madness.

The Arkham Advertiser is mentioned in passing.

Agent Banks interviews moonshiner Elmer White while he is a patient at Arkham Asylum.

### Publication History
The Dirge of Reason was published by Fantasy Flight Games in 2018 as a hardback novella under the Arkham Horror Fiction imprint as part of their Arkham Horror Files line. The release includes a fifteen page full-colour insert featuring extras such as artwork of the items and locations featured in the story, as well as fake newspaper reports on the incidents. Also contained are a set of four exclusive cards for use in Arkham Horror: The Card Game.

In October 2021 Aconyte, the publishing arm of Asmodee (with which Fantasy Flight Games had merged in 2014), released an omnibus edition of Arkham Horror novellas which included The Dirge of Reason, although the gaming materials and extras were omitted.

The first edition of The Disciples of Cthulhu was released in paperback format by DAW Books in 1976. It was edited by Edward P. fullContent:
The Disinterment is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft and Duane W. Rimel, although Rimel later disavowed the collaboration.

### Synopsis
The story tells of a leprosy sufferer, who, instead of living with the debilitating condition, opts for death and resurrection at the hands of a witch doctor.

The sufferer contracts the disease whilst nursing his brother, also a leper, in the Philippines. Since leprosy, if discovered, would condemn the man to a lifetime of exile in a leper colony in appalling conditions, he embarks on a wild plan to conceal his condition and find an exotic "cure" with the help of his longtime friend who is a doctor of medicine and also an occultist. The story becomes a kind of reversal of Herbert West--Reanimator, told from the point of view of the victim, rather than the doctor...

### Publication History
"The Disinterment" was first published in the January 1937 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reissued many times, and has been translated into both Portuguese and German.

fullContent:
"The Disinternment of Venus" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, set in Averoigne, his semi-historical French province. It first appeared in the July 1934 issue of Weird Tales. 

Set in the year 1550, the story relates the unearthing of a pagan statue of Venus at Averoigne's Abbey of Périgon, and the unsettling effect its erotic qualities have on the monks there.

### Characters
*Paul: The eldest of three monks who discover the statue of Venus while digging in the abbey's vegetable garden. A "man of ripe years, hale and robust," he cleans the dirt off the statue when it is first unearthed, and polishes it with the hem of his robe. He is one of eight monks who is driven by lust to temporarily leave the abbey.
*Pierre: Another monk, "in his early prime," who helped to unearth the statue. He was also found absent without leave from the abbey.
*Hughues: The third monk involved with the discovery, he was "little more than a boy, and had but recently taken his final vows." Like the others, he was drawn from the monastery  by an unaccountable lechery.
*Augustin: the "saintly abbot" of Périgon, of "reverend age" and known for his "rigorous temper." He thinks the statue should certainly be destroyed, but feels "a queer and unaccountable hesitation which led him to defer the necessary orders for her demolishment." After Louis meets his grisly fate, he orders it reburied instead.
*Brother Louis: A monk known for his "comely face" (as "[h]andsome as Adonis") and his "his austere piety": "he was given to ascetic vigils and prolonged devotions." He resolves to destroy the offensive statue, but when he approaches it with a hammer, he is overcome by passion and ends up crushed to death beneath the toppled sculpture's embrace.

### The Statue
Smith describes the statue as "the masterpiece of an unknown, decadent sculptor":


### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Weird Tales, "The Disinterment of Venus" appeared in several collections of Smith's fiction, starting with Genius Loci and Other Tales (Arkham House, 1970). It is included in both The Averoigne Archives (Pickman's Press, 2019) and The Averoigne Chronicles (Hippocampus Press, 2021).

It is featured in 100 Wild Little Weird Tales (Barnes & Noble Books, 1994).

shortDefinition: "The Distortion Out of Space" is a short story by the late Canadian author Francis Flagg, a.k.a. Henry George Weiss, a correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft.  ### Synopsis A pair of men camping on a mountain witness a meteor fall one evening, and travel t...
fullContent:
"The Distortion Out of Space" is a short story by the late Canadian author Francis Flagg, a.k.a. Henry George Weiss, a correspondent of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
A pair of men camping on a mountain witness a meteor fall one evening, and travel to investigate the next morning. They discover that whatever was inside the meteor has occupied the homestead of their friends and created some kind of spatial distortion, within which the wife is lost.

The first man, Jim, enters the distortion but quickly becomes lost, and after a while the narrator, Bill, follows him, also losing his way. Eventually, in frustration, Bill fires his pistol at a shimmering cloud which turns out to be the alien entity. In its death throes, it communicates to Bill the story of its journey through the stars and its landing on Earth, making it known to him that it was not its intention to harm or upset the humans. When Bill realises that he has killed an innocent, sentient creature, he breaks down in tears.

### Characters
*Bill, the narrator.
*Jim Blake, Bill's friend, a local physician.
*Henry Simpson, a rural homesteader.
*Lydia Simpson, Henry's wife.
*The Distortion Out of Space, a highly-intelligent alien entity.

### Publication History
"The Distortion Out of Space" was first published in Weird Tales in August 1934, and has been reprinted in The Magazine of Horror (1965), Weird Legacies (1977), The Monster Book of Monsters (1988), and Crew's 13: Classic Tales of the Macabre & Fantastic (1997).

### Behind the Mythos
Francis Flagg was a self-confessed fan of H. P. Lovecraft's works (as he stated in a letter to Weird Tales in September 1937 titled "The Genius of Lovecraft"), and it would appear that he took at least some inspiration for "The Distortion Out of Space" from "The Colour Out of Space", particularly the story's setup.

While Donald A. Wollheim suggested that the inspiration for the story was his own "The Man From Ariel" (1934), Flagg responded that the original story (albeit with a different ending) had been presented for consideration to several publishers two years before the publication of Wollheim's story, in 1932.

"The Doctor" is the main alias of a space and time traveling alien, the protagonist in the fictional Doctor Who universe, who was created in 1963. Currently, the Doctor is in their 15th incarnation.

### Background
The Doctor is a mysterious alien scientist and renegade Time Lord who has vowed to do no harm and to help others. He has traveled using his alien time machine called the TARDIS (Time And Relative Dimensions In Space) across the cosmos, across time, and to other dimensions and realities. His two favorite worlds are his homeworld of Gallifrey (the home of his people, the Time Lords) and Earth, both of which he defends ferociously. The Doctor has saved numerous civilizations, species and worlds, the universe, and all of space-time itself throughout his many incarnations. It is unknown how old the Doctor truly is due to all the time traveling and temporal anomalies he has experienced, but the Doctor claims to be over 800 years old.

The Doctor has fought many tyrants, empires, alien invaders, organizations, criminals, races, and entities both on Earth and across space-time. His greatest enemies are the Daleks, a race of intergalactic genocidal xenophobic cybernetic mutants who pose the greatest threat to the universe, and the Master, an evil Time Lord who seeks the conquest of the whole universe. The Doctor has also fought several entities of the Cthulhu Mythos, including Hastur and Yog-Sothoth, prevailing every time so far.

### The Time Lords' True Nature
The true nature of the Time Lords themselves are also considered to be eldritch, with them known as god-like beings from outer space with enormous power and intelligence. One story even stated that the Time Lords have "another form" which is bigger than the sun itself that exists in subspace. The Time Lords themselves have experimented with and weaponized many eldritch life forms of their own creation throughout their history, such as during the massive temporal conflicts known as the "War in Heaven" and the Last Great Time War.

### Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos
The Doctor has encountered and defeated multiple entities of the Cthulhu Mythos in his many incarnations.

The Seventh Doctor in particular intentionally confronted both the Elder Gods and the Great Old Ones many times, and spent so much time defeating every eldritch abomination he met to the point that the gods consider themselves at war with him. He also teamed up with Sherlock Holmes against an entity claiming to be Azathoth. Although he hoped never to meet Nyarlathotep, one of his companions managed to convince a cultist that he was Nyarlathotep himself.

fullContent:
"The Dog Handler's Tale" is a bittersweet Cthulhu Mythos short story by Canadian author Donald Tyson. It was published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 by Titan Books in October 2014.

### Synopsis
"The Dog Handler's Tale" is told as the written account of one of the work team on the ill-fated Pabodie Expedition to the Antarctic, one Jack Hobbs, a Miskatonic University handyman who managed to secure himself a position on the team as senior dog handler.

Hobbs recounts from a different perspective the events of the trip from its setting sail, through the establishing of the initial base camps, the butting heads of Professors Dyer and Lake, to Lake's uncovering of the subterranean resting place of the sleeping Elder Things, and eventually the massacre of the entire party. Grievously injured, he and his favourite dog Sergeant found themselves trapped inside the cave with no food and water; Hobbs' final entry in the account tells of his wish that nobody blame Sergeant for what he was sure the starving dog would soon do, and the hope that it would somehow find its way out and be rescued by the survivors.

The story concludes with a postscript by Professor Starkweather, leader of a 1935 venture following in the footsteps of the Pabodie Expedition, which states that the Hobbs' body was found untouched, the emaciated corpse of his faithful dog Sergeant draped across his legs.

"The Dogs" is a short story by American author Jeffrey Thomas.

### Synopsis
A lonely man uses his library of esoteric books to create a device which allows him to peer into the Earth's future. What he sees is a planet ravaged by the arrival of enormous floating abominations who have wiped out the human race. 

As he looks farther ahead, he sees the descendants of Earth's dogs as they slowly evolve into something more intelligent, before devising a way to escape the planet as the Outsiders descend from the sky to render it completely uninhabitable.

### Characters
* March, a recently-divorced man with nothing to tie him to the world other than his beloved dog Snow.

### Publication History
"The Dogs" was published in the April Moon Books anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu in March 2014, and later appeared in the collection of Thomas's own works, The Endless Fall and Other Weird Fictions in February 2017.

fullContent:
"The Doom in the Room" is a humorous Cthulhu Mythos short story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was published in the collection Unholy Dimensions by Mythos Books in October 2005.

### Synopsis
A Miskatonic University professor in search of a mysterious Egyptian crystal finds his way to a decrepit Arkham townhouse wherein he believes his goal to lie. What he discovers is a monstrous creature from beyond, juggling the shards of the crystal which it has just accidentally dropped and shattered. The story's conclusion implies that he does not survive the encounter.
