fullContent:
"The Doom of Enos Harker" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story based on Lin Carter's unfinished tale "The Strange Doom of Enos Harker". It was completed by Laurence J. Cornford and published in 1997.

While Carter's fragment was already part of a loose trilogy continuing from August Derleth's "The Return of Hastur" and Carter's own "Behind the Mask", Cornford also makes it a direct sequel to Derleth and Mark Schorer's "The Lair of the Star-Spawn".

### Synopsis
### Fragment by Lin Carter
The story is narrated by Paxton Blaine, an anthropologist graduated from Miskatonic University in 1931, who is hired as a secretary by Arkham resident Dr. Enos Harker, a priest and former missionary who has spent years in India, Burma and Tibet, and who claims to be afflicted by a severe skin condition that forces him to keep his hands and parts of his face bandaged. Blaine's job consists of organizing Harker's notes on obscure Asian cults, and assisting him in his research, which involves books such as the Unaussprechlichen Kulten, the Cultes des Goules, and the Necronomicon, among others.

A lot of Harker's research concerns the mysterious Tcho-Tcho people, believed to inhabit both Burma and a place known as Leng, the location of which Blaine is not able to pinpoint. The grimoires tell of strange gods worshiped by the Tcho-Tchos, and of a Tcho-Tcho lama who wears a silken yellow mask over his face. Blaine is disturbed by how this mythology seems to be related to a number of recent events in the vicinity of Arkham, all of which appear to have been hushed up by the authorities. These include the destruction of the Tuttle house, the military operations in the nearby town of Innsmouth, and the case of Bryant Hoskins, who went mad in a cabin in the woods and died in an asylum.

Two passages from the Necronomicon interest Harker particularly, the first claiming that the Tcho-Tchos originate from the Dreamlands and first came to the Waking World via Sarkomand, and the second concerning an incoming event called the Great Awakening, in which gods such as Cthulhu and Shub-Niggurath will call to summon their followers and all those "who carry the Emblem" as well as all those who have seen it.

As the days go by, Blaine notices that Harker's health seems to be worsening. He speaks in whispers, his eyesight is deteriorating, his entire body seems to be bloated, and has a repulsive smell. The bandages now cover almost his entire face, as well as his hands, and he becomes increasingly dependent on Blaine to help him with the house chores, as well as handle his correspondence with scholars from other parts of the world. From them, Blaine learns more about the ancient deities, said to have been defeated by their enemies, the Elder Gods, who placed something called the Elder Sign to keep their foes imprisoned long before the evolution of mankind. The Great Old Ones' servants, however, are still free to move about and do their masters' bidding. Said servants include the fish-like Deep

fullContent:
"The Doom of Yakthoob" is a short story by Lin Carter that first appeared in the Summer 1971 issue of The Arkham Collector. It is the first of a series of short fiction pieces Carter offered as autobiographical sketches by Abdul Alhazred from the Necronomicon.

The story concerns Alhazred's education, in which he "learned the summoning-up of Evil Things." It introduced Yakthoob, the "notorious Saracen wizard" who served as Alhazred's mentor, as well as "the languid and dissolute Ibn Ghazoul," Alhazred's fellow student and closest friend. The plot explains how Yakthoob met a gruesome end due to Ibn Ghazoul's selfish indulgence of vices.

Carter describes Alhazred's initiation into esoteric knowledge as taking place in Egypt: He "conversed with ghouls in the rock tombs of Neb and even partook of the unnamed Feasts of Nitocris in loathsome crypts beneath the Great Pyramid," descended the Secret Stairs to the "black catacombs below the crumbling ruins of elder and ghoulhaunted Memphis," and performed "Blasphemous Rites" In the "noxious caverns of Nephren-Ka in the sealed and unknown Valley of Hadoth by the Nile."

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Arkham Collector (including the hardbound omnibus The Arkham Collector: Volume I), "The Doom of Yakthoob" was reprinted in the Yuletide 1985 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu (#36), and again in the Candlemas 1990 issue (#70). It was included in the Cthulhu Mythos anthologies The New Lovecraft Circle (Fedogan & Bremer, 1996) and The Necronomicon: Selected Stories and Essays Concerning the Blasphemous Tome of the Mad Arab (Chaosium, 1996).

shortDefinition: "The Doom that Came to Dunfield" is a short story by the British-born author William Meikle.  ### Synopsis A think-tank for the British government develops what they believe to be the technology to render a battleship invisible, and dispatch the nece...
fullContent:
"The Doom that Came to Dunfield" is a short story by the British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
A think-tank for the British government develops what they believe to be the technology to render a battleship invisible, and dispatch the necessary materiel to a remote bay off the coast of Newfoundland to test their theory.

Upon arrival, the first test is a failure, with the machine only running for a few seconds before shutting down. Soon thereafter, however, the strange occurrences begin. The walls and decks of the ship become semi-liquid at random, swallowing men whole - or worse, partially - before hardening once more, and clouds of thick fog which dissolves living flesh and seems predatory in its behaviour appears.

As the crew dwindles, the head scientist hatches a plan to modify his machine to "switch off" these phenomena. This appears to be effective for a time, and a lone lifeboat manages to escape, although it is pursued by a tendril of the malevolent fog. However, as the ship sinks, this last lingering effect also dissipates.

### Characters
*Duncan, a senior scientist on the project with specialties in Human Biology, Chemistry and Applied Mathematics. It is uncertain if Duncan is his first or last name.
*Professor Muir, the man in charge of the project, a brilliant and unconventional scientist.
*Captain Squire, commander of the test ship.

### Publication History
"The Doom that Came to Dunfield" was published in the 2017 collection Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror.

### Trivia
*Despite containing no direct references to Lovecraft's work or the Cthulhu Mythos in general, Meikle's inclusion of "The Doom that Came to Dunfield" in the collection Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror would seem to indicate that he believes it to be in the spirit of Lovecraft's work. The appearance of incomprehensible entities from another plane of existence (the fog clouds) may offer some support to this conclusion.
*"The Doom that Came to Dunfield" appears to have taken at least some inspiration from the conspiracy theory of the Philadelphia Experiment (which is directly mentioned in the story, although the ship's name is given incorrectly). The legend goes that in the 1940s the United States government experimented with turning the destroyer USS Eldridge invisible, with some of the side effects being the same as those described here.
*The title of the story is somewhat confusing, as it is unclear whether the "doom" that came was to the ship (which is never explicitly named) or to the bay in which the experiment took place.

"The Doom That Came to Dunwich" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Richard A. Lupoff. A sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror," it originally appeared in Lupoff's collection Before...12:01...and After (1996, Fedogan & Bremer).

### Synopsis
A scion of the undecayed Whateleys living in Canada travels to Dunwich to conduct some research on her distant family. There, she encounters an ancient and half-crazed Henry Armitage and the Dunwich Research Agency, a shadowy government agency in service to an Outer God. As the stars align, she witnesses the manifestation of this angry entity, and the final destruction of Dunwich, but the experience leaves on her a terrible mark.

### Characters
*Cordelia Whateley, an anthropology grad student from Montreal's McGill University, and a young member of the undecayed Whateleys.
*Henry Armitage, the protagonist of Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror," now president of the Dunwich Institute and nearly 150 years old.
*Yog-Sothoth, a being of indescribable power. It is described as resembling "a gargantuan jellyfish, literally miles in breadth," with "thousands — no, millions — of tentacles dangl[ing] from its underside, writhing and squirming,"

fullContent:
The Doom That Came to Innsmouth is a short story by American author Brian McNaughton which is set in H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
The plot concerns a descendant of Joe Sargent, one of the minor characters from Lovecraft's short story The Shadow Over Innsmouth, who travels back to Innsmouth on the promise of a governmental payout over historic claims of property destruction.

As the story progresses Bob Smith, the descendant, discovers that the payout story is merely a lure by the government to trap and study Deep One Hybrids like himself when he is incarcerated in a prison-like facility in his ancestral home.

Later, Smith is revealed to be a serial killer who practices Deep One rituals on his victims and, after escaping the facility, transcends to the next stage in hybrid evolution before taking to the sea with his new-found Innsmouth bride.

### Behind the Mythos
The Doom That Came to Innsmouth was first printed in Tales Out of Innsmouth, then in a revised format in Even More Nasty Stories by Wildside Press. It received an ebook release in another of Wildside's publications, The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack.

shortDefinition: "The Doom that Came to Sarnath" (1920) is an early short story by H. P. Lovecraft. It is written in a mythic/fairy tale style and is associated with his Dream Cycle. It was first published in The Scot, a Scottish amateur fiction magazine, in June 192...
fullContent:
"The Doom that Came to Sarnath" (1920) is an early short story by H. P. Lovecraft. It is written in a mythic/fairy tale style and is associated with his Dream Cycle. It was first published in The Scot, a Scottish amateur fiction magazine, in June 1920.

The Doom that Came to Sarnath is also the title for a collection of short stories by Lovecraft, first published in February 1971.

### Inspiration
The influence of Lord Dunsany on the story can be seen in the reference to a throne "wrought of one piece of ivory, though no man lives who knows whence so vast a piece could have come", which evokes the gate "carved out of one solid piece" of ivory in Dunsany's "Idle Days on the Yann". (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

Though Sarnath is a historical city in India --the place where the Buddha first taught-- Lovecraft said that he thought he invented the name independently. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

### Synopsis
According to the tale, more than 10,000 years ago, a race of shepherd people colonized the banks of the river Ai in a land called Mnar, forming the cities of Thraa, Ilarnek, and Kadatheron (not to be confused with Kadath), which rose to great intellectual and mercantile prowess. Craving more land, a group of these hardy people migrated to the shores of a lonely and vast lake at the heart of Mnar, founding the metropolis of Sarnath.

But the settlers were not alone. At the other side of the lake was the ancient, grey-stone city of Ib, inhabited by a queer race who had descended from the Moon. Lovecraft described them as "in hue as green as the lake and the mists that rise above it.... They had bulging eyes, pouting, flabby lips, and curious ears, and were without voice."

These beings worshipped a strange god known as Bokrug, the Great Water Lizard, although it was more their physical form that caused the people of Sarnath to despise them.

The people of Sarnath killed all the creatures inhabiting Ib, destroyed the city and took their idol as a trophy, putting it in Sarnath's main temple. The next night, the idol vanished under peculiar circumstances, and Taran-Ish, the high-priest of Sarnath, was found dead. Before dying, he had scrawled a single sign on the empty altar: "DOOM".

Ten centuries later, Sarnath was at the zenith of its power and decadence. Nobles from distant cities were invited to the feast in honour of Ib's destruction. That night, however, the revelry was disrupted by strange lights over the lake and heavy greenish mists, and that the tidal marker, the granite pillar Akurion, was mostly submerged. Not too much later, many of the city's inhabitants fled, maddened by fear, as the king and the people in the feast had been transformed into the original creatures from Ib.

After this some of the survivors reported seeing the long-dead inhabitants of Ib peering from the windows of the city's towers, while others refused to say exactly what they had seen. Those that returned saw nothing of those unlucky enough to be left b

fullContent:
The Doom That Came to Sarnath and Other Stories is a collection of fantasy and horror stories by H. P. Lovecraft, edited by Lin Carter. It was first published in paperback by Ballantine Books as the twenty-sixth volume of its celebrated Ballantine Adult Fantasy series in February 1971. It was the second collection of Lovecraft's works assembled by Carter for the series, the first being The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. The stories were written between 1919 and 1935, and originally published in various fantasy magazines, notably Weird Tales.

The book collects twenty tales from the author's two main series of short stories, the Dream Cycle of Dunsanian fantasies and the Cthulhu Mythos of science fictional horror, with a general introduction, notes, and a partial chronology of Lovecraft's works by the editor. The book is dedicated to Lovecraft's friend, correspondent and posthumous publisher August Derleth.

fullContent:
"The Door to Saturn" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith which forms part of his Hyperborean cycle. It was first published in Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror in January 1932. 

### Synopsis
When the sorcerer Eibon is declared a heretic by Morghi, the High Priest of Yhoundeh, he uses a magical artefact gifted to him by Zhothaqquah to flee to Cykranosh (the planet Saturn in modern parlance). However, Morghi follows him through the portal and, trapped together, the two form an uneasy truce.

As Eibon and Morghi explore Cykranosh, they encounter many strange creatures and realise that there is no way for them to ever return home. In light of this knowledge, they establish themselves as priests to a tribe of humanoid creatures known as the Ydheems, and attempt to enjoy the remainder of their lives as best they are able.

### Characters
*Eibon, a powerful Hyperborean wizard.
*Morghi, a High Priest of Youndeh.
*Zhothaqquah, an ancient god.
*Hziulquoigmnzhah, a relative of Zhothaqquah's.

### Publication History
After its first appearance in Strange Tales, "The Door to Saturn" has since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into Spanish, Dutch, French, German, Italian, Hungarian and Portuguese.

fullContent:
"The Dorm Mate Out of Dunwich" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author R. C. Mulhare. Published in January 2020 in the Deadman's Tome anthology Deep Fried Horror Cthulhu Cheese Burger, it is a reimagining of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror".

### Synopsis
In the modern day, the practice of magic and the worship of strange gods is, if not common, at least an accepted part of society. At Miskatonic University, student Wil Whateley is trying to secretly care for his brother, while simultaneously attempting to remove himself from his Dunwich connections and find a way to reunite with his mother. However, access to the University's copy of the Necronomicon, which he needs to accomplish his task, is denied him by Professor Robert Armitage.

Eventually, despite his best efforts, and as a direct result of the curiosity of his friends, Wil's brother escapes and rampages across the town of Arkham, killing many in its fear and panic. Enlisting the aid of two of his dorm-mates and assistant teacher Morgan Francis, the group are able to send first the brother then Wil himself through a tear in reality to be where he want to be: at home with his kinfolk.

### Behind the Mythos
Comparisons can be drawn between Mulhare's "The Dorm Mate Out of Dunwich" and Stanley C. Sargent's 1997 story "The Black Brat of Dunwich", although Sargent's take is in a much darker vein, and does not feature such a neat, happy ending.

"The Dragons of Mons Fractus" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney in which his sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta confronts an undead version of one of the main villains of Christian tradition. It first appeared in the Spring 1984 issue of Weirdbook (#19).

### Synopsis
In search of vengeance, Simon tracks Pontius Pilate to the hinterland of the Roman Empire, where he discovers an undead horror menacing Germania. He finds unlikely allies in two survivors of the ancient serpent people.

### Setting
The story is set in the autumn of 41 A. D. in what is today France and Switzerland. The Vienna in the story is not the city in Austria but modern-day Vienne in France. Mons Fractus is now known as Mount Pilatus, near Lucerne, Switzerland; the legends surrounding this mountain involving both Pontius Pilate and friendly dragons form the basis of the story.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Weirdbook, "The Dragons of Mons Fractus" was reprinted in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997) and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

fullContent:
The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath is a novella by H. P. Lovecraft (1890–1937) published by Arkham House posthumously in 1943 in the collection Beyond the Wall of Sleep. Begun probably in the autumn of 1926, it was completed on January 22, 1927 and was unpublished in his lifetime. It is both the longest of the stories that make up his Dream Cycle and the longest Lovecraft work to feature protagonist Randolph Carter. Along with his 1927 novel The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, it can be considered one of the significant achievements of that period of Lovecraft's writing. The Dream-Quest combines elements of horror and fantasy into an epic tale that illustrates the scope and wonder of humankind's ability to dream.

The story was published posthumously by Arkham House in 1943 in the collection Beyond the Wall of Sleep. Currently, it is published by Ballantine Books in an anthology that also includes "The Silver Key" and "Through the Gates of the Silver Key". The definitive version, with corrected text by S. T. Joshi, is published by Arkham House in At the Mountains of Madness and Other Novels and by Penguin Classics in The Dreams in the Witch House and Other Weird Stories.

### Plot summary
Randolph Carter dreams three times of a majestic sunset city, but each time he is abruptly snatched away before he can see it up close. When he prays to the gods of dream to reveal the whereabouts of the phantasmal city, they do not answer, and his dreams of the city stop altogether. Undaunted, Carter resolves to go to Kadath, where the gods live, to beseech them in person. However, no one has ever been to Kadath and none even knows how to get there. In dream, Randolph Carter descends "seventy steps" and speaks of his plan to the priests Nasht and Kaman-Thah, whose temple - the Cavern of Flame - borders the Dreamlands. The priests warn Carter of the great danger of his quest and suggest that the gods withdrew his vision of the city on purpose.

### The quest begins
Carter enters the Enchanted Wood and meets the zoogs, a race of predatory and sapient rodent-like creatures. For a novice, such an encounter could prove calamitous, but Carter is an experienced dreamer and so is knowledgeable of their language and customs. When Carter asks the zoogs about Kadath, they don't know where it is; instead, they suggest that Carter go the town of Ulthar and find a wizened priest named Atal who is learned in the ways of the gods.

In the cat-laden city of Ulthar, Carter visits Atal, who mentions a huge carving wrought on Ngranek's hidden side that shows the features of the gods. Carter realizes that if he can go to Ngranek, examine the carving, and then find a place where mortals share those features and are thus related to the gods, he must be near Kadath.

shortDefinition: The Dream-Quest of Vellitt Boe is a novella by Kij Johnson set in the Dreamlands created by H. P. Lovecraft, reexamining the world of The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath from a female perspective. It won the 2017 World Fantasy Award for Long Fiction, a...
fullContent:
The Dream-Quest of Vellitt Boe is a novella by Kij Johnson set in the Dreamlands created by H. P. Lovecraft, reexamining the world of The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath from a female perspective. It won the 2017 World Fantasy Award for Long Fiction, and was a Best Novella finalist for the 2016 Nebula Awards, the  2017 Hugo Awards, and the 2017 Locus Awards.

Johnson's Dream-Quest tells the story of Vellitt Boe, a native of the Dreamlands who was a far-traveller in her youth, but at 55 has long settled down as a professor of mathematics at Ulthar Women's College. When her best student, Clarie Jurat, runs off with a man from the waking world, Boe must relearn her travelling ways and bring her back--first to prevent Clarie's trustee father from shutting down the school, and later, when it turns out that Clarie's maternal grandfather is a sleeping god, to keep him from destroying Ulthar and the plains of the River Skai.

Vellitt journeys to Hatheg-Kla, in hopes of exiting through the Gate of Deeper Slumber; to Ilek-Vad, in hopes of obtaining the Silver Key; and through the Underworld to Sarkomand, where the ghouls have a secret staircase to the waking world; and to the fabled lands of Wisconsin and Montana, where people are "random and meaningful and beautiful."

Along the way, she is hunted by zoogs, attacked by shantak birds, menaced by night gaunts, guided by ghouls, captured by ghasts, and guarded by a faithful gug.

She meets up with former traveling companions, including Reon Atescre, who is now Nasht, high priest of the temple of Flame; and the waking-world man Randolph Carter, once her lover, now king of Ilek-Vad.

In the book's acknowledgements, Johnson writes of Lovecraft's Dream-Quest:I first read it at ten, thrilled and terrified, and uncomfortable with the racism but not yet aware that the total absence of women was also problematic. This story is my adult self returning to a thing I loved as a child and seeing whether I could make adult sense of it.

### Characters
* Reon Atescre: When he was Vellitt Boe's travelling companion, he "had been slim and laughing-eyed, a lighthearted, fearless man who was not attracted to women." 
* Vellitt Boe: In her youth, "she had been a far-traveller, a great walker of the Six Kingdoms, which waking-world men called the dream lands." Then she attended the Women’s College of the University of Celephaïs, where she received a Physical Studies degree in Mathematics. "The Dream-Verse of Robt. Olmstead of Oberlin, Ohio" is a trio of short poems by Patrick J. K. Gray, first published in Vol 3, Issue 1 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana in April 2018.

### Synopsis
The work consists of three short poems, judging from the title a record of the dreams experienced by Robert Olmstead, the narrator and protagonist of H. P. Lovecraft's 1931 novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

* "I.—Three introverted quatrains.": offers a description of a long-abandoned underwater city
* "II.—Sonnet.": the narrator sees himself transforming into something alien amongst others of his kind, and yearns for the change
* "Lines on a Ghoul": seemingly unrelated to the first two, depicts monsters grubbing in the dirt and eating dead flesh

The Dreaming Tower is an uncredited comic book adaptation of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Outsider." It was first published in The Strange World of Your Dreams #1 in 1952, from Prize Publications. The publishers paid $25 to readers for published contributions of their personal dreams. In the case of "The Dreaming Tower", they simply adapted "The Outsider" uncredited. Art was by Jack Kirby.

The story is now in the public domain due to copyright having not been renewed.

### Synopsis
A young man, John Sumpter, is plagued by a recurring dream, or nightmare, that he is the sole occupant of a mansion with a tower. He awakens each evening and wanders, alone, plagued by doubts.

Eventually he hears voices and blunders into a room where two middle aged people, a couple, are entertaining guests. All of the people surprised by his entrance look at him in horror and flee, except the older couple.

We finally see the character's reflection in a mirror and he has a grotesquely deformed face. The older couple are his parents; they sympathize with their son and his condition and he returns to his room in the tower, the mystery of his lonely existence solved. He is doomed to be alone other than his parents and it is no dream or nightmare, it is his sad reality.

"The Dreams in the Witch House" is an episode of the Netflix television series Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities. Although billed as an adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft short story of the same name, it has been so heavily altered as to be virtually unrecognisable.

### Synopsis
Walter Gilman, a man whose twin sister was dragged off by an unknown force as a child, searches for a way to contact her spirit. Discovering an elixir which allows him to travel to the strange realm in which she is trapped, he is subsequently tormented by the evil witch Keziah Mason and her minion Jenkins Brown. Although he manages to bring his sister back and destroy Mason, he is in turn killed by Brown, who then uses his body as a puppet.

fullContent:
"The Dreams in the Witch-House" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft, part of the Cthulhu Mythos cycle of horror fiction. Written in January/February 1932, it was first published in the July 1933 issue of Weird Tales.

### Inspiration
"The Dreams in the Witch-House" was probably inspired by the lecture The Size of the Universe given by Willem de Sitter which Lovecraft attended three months prior to writing the story. De Sitter is even named in the story; he is mentioned as a mathematical genius, and remarked among other intellectual masterminds, including Albert Einstein. Several prominent motifs—including the geometry and curvature of space, and a deeper understanding of the nature of the universe through pure mathematics—are covered in de Sitter's lecture. The idea of using higher dimensions of non-Euclidean space as short cuts through normal space can be traced to A. S. Eddington's The Nature of the Physical World which Lovecraft alludes to having read (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft III). These new ideas supported and developed a very similar conception of a fragmented mirror space that Lovecraft had previously developed in "The Trap" (written mid 1931).

An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia says that "The Dreams in the Witch-House" was "heavily influenced by Nathaniel Hawthorne's unfinished novel Septimius Felton".

### Plot summary
Walter Gilman, a student of mathematics and folklore at Miskatonic University, takes an attic room in "the Witch House", a house in Arkham thought to be cursed. The first part of the story is an account of the history of the house, which once harboured Keziah Mason, an accused witch who disappeared mysteriously from a Salem jail in 1692. Gilman discovers that for the better part of two centuries many of its occupants have died prematurely.

The dimensions of Gilman's attic room are unusual, and seem to conform to a kind of unearthly geometry. Gilman theorizes that the structure can enable travel from one plane or dimension to another.

Shortly after moving into the attic Gilman begins experiencing bizarre dreams, in which he seems to float without physical form through an otherworldly space of unearthly geometry and indescribable colors and sounds. Amongst elements both organic and inorganic, he perceives shapes that he innately recognizes as entities, which appear and disappear instantaneously and at random. Several times his dreaming self encounters bizarre clusters of "iridescent, prolately spheroidal bubbles", as well as a rapidly changing polyhedral figure, both of which seem sapient.

Gilman also has nightly experiences involving Keziah Mason and her rat-bodied, human-faced familiar, Brown Jenkin, which he believes might not be dreams at all. In other dreams Gilman is taken to a city of the "Elder Things", and even brings back evidence that he's actually been there - a miniature statue of an Elder Thing that he'd broken off a balustrade in the city, made of unknown materials and a strange kind of alloy. fullContent:
"The Drowned Geologist (1898)" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that combines the fictional worlds of H. P. Lovecraft, Arthur Conan Doyle and Bram Stoker. It was first published in Shadows Over Baker Street (Delrey, 2003).

The story reflects Kiernan's fascination with deep time, as when the narrator remarks:


### Synopsis
The story is narrated by Dr. Tobias Logan, in the form of a letter to Dr. John Watson, dated 10 May 1898. Logan is a paleontologist who has come to Whitby, England, where he plans to meet up with a geologist friend from London, Sir Elijah Purdy, to examine Whitby's famous fossil beds. While Logan is there, a schooner named Demeter runs aground, creating a to-do that he doesn't pay much attention to. (Logan notes, "I have a habit of becoming so intent upon my collecting that I may often neglect to glance about me for long stretches.")

Logan encounters a mysterious stranger whom he suspects is Watson's friend Sherlock Holmes, even though Holmes at the time was supposed to have died in Switzerland. The stranger tells Logan of mysterious artifacts that have been discovered on the Yorkshire coast, tablets that seem to have writing on them but which were found in strata countless millions of years too old.

Logan receives a note from his friend Purdy that refers to "unusual fossils" he found, and asks, "Are you familiar with Phoenician (?) god Dagon or Irish Daoine Domhain?" Purdy later turns up drowned. Only Logan notices that his corpse is holding "a small ammonite of the genus Dactylioceras"--a recently living specimen of a species long extinct.

Logan receives a note from the stranger--signed "S. H."--that reveals that the mysterious tablets have all disappeared. The writer tells Logan, "Dark and ancient powers, the whim of inhuman beings of inconceivable antiquity and malignancy, may be at work here"; he urges the paleontologist to forget the matter if he can. Logan notes that the ammonite specimen, too, was taken in a burglary.

The story ends with a note saying that the unmailed letter to Watson was found after Logan's death by hanging on May 11, 1898.

### Characters
*Dr. Tobias Logan: A paleontologist at the American Museum of Natural History from 1894-1898.
*S. H.: A mysterious stranger who appears to be the famous detective Sherlock Holmes.
*Dr. John Watson: A medical doctor and a veteran of the Afghan wars; Holmes' friend and biographer.
*Sir Elijah Purdy: A fellow of the Geological Society of London and a friend of Logan's.

### Connections
Sherlock Holmes and John Watson are, of course, the creations of Arthur Conan Doyle. Doyle killed Holmes off in "The Final Problem", published in 1893, and brought him back by popular demand in 1905's The Return of Sherlock Holmes, though by the internal chronology of Doyle's stories, Holmes had resurfaced several years before 1898.

The Demeter is the ship on which Dracula first arrives in England in Bram Stoker's novel; it arrives at Whitby on August 8, 1898, as in Kiernan's

"The Drowning at Lake Henpin" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Paul Tobin. It was published in the Ross E. Lockhart-edited anthology The Book of Cthulhu II by Night Shade Books in October 2012 .

### Synopsis
The book is told in the form of an account kept by the sole survivor of an encounter with a malevolent cult.

During the course of an investigation into a series of brutal crimes, a policeman reignites his friendship with an old school chum recently returned to town after years of esoteric research abroad. As their bond of trust deepens, the man reveals to the policeman that he had in fact been acting as a protector of sorts, defending the human race from the incursions of monsters from beyond our reality. Furthermore, he tells him that he believes the recent crimes are caused by the worshippers of an ancient evil entity known as Ubbo-Sathla.

Resolving to put an end to the threat, the two men travel to nearby Lake Henpin, the site of the events and the suspected resting place of Ubbo-Sathla. Although they mount a valiant attack on the creature's minions, their opponents' command over the laws of reality prove too much for them, and the cultists manipulate the policeman into accidentally killing his friend. As he descends into the depths of insanity, his last writings tell of his resolve to take his own life and spare his shattered psyche any more torment.

### Cthulhu Mythos Connections
In addition to the cultists of Ubbo-Sathla, the Cthäat Aquadingen, Cthulhu, and the Black Goat of the Woods are also made mention of.

Their testing takes the two from the highlands of Scotland to its capital Edinburgh, where they locate a cult to Yog-Sothoth hiding in plain sight. Although Mayweather is captured by the cultists, Urquhart calls in backup and the worshippers are brought to account.

"The Dulwich Horror of 1927" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author David Hambling. It forms part of his William Blake cycle.

### Synopsis
An innocent bet involves a group of Bright Young Things with an ancient evil beneath a London church. As their investigation into its origin progresses, their grip on sanity begins to slip, and in a climatic battle with the forces they have inadvertently allowed to cross dimensions, they all suffer gruesome deaths- or worse…

### Characters
*William Blake, a man with a deep interest in philosophy.
*Jessica, a peerless architect.
*George, a well-connected young man with designs on high political office.
*Sophie, a woman with an astonishing grasp of psychology.
*Tom, photographer
*Daniel, a brilliant mathematician.
*Daisy, the group's wallflower.
*Mr. Hall, William's landlord.
*The Vicar, minister for the local church.

### Publication History
"The Dulwich Horror of 1927" was first published in the collection of Hambling's own works Shadows from Norwood in August 2013. It has also received a self-titled digital chapbook release.

### Behind the Mythos
Elements of "The Dulwich Horror of 1927" are reminiscent of the H. P. Lovecraft story "The Dunwich Horror", such as the mysterious, hermitic father and daughter - by the name of Whatley - who call forth twin monstrosities into the world.

The narrator of the tale, William Blake, features in his own, self-titled, story cycle.

The work also functions as an origin story for the character of Jessica, who would go on to be the primary protagonist in Hambling's The War of the God Queen series.

### Trivia
*The creature which the group battle is heavily implied to be a hybrid Spawn of Cthulhu, and the realm which threatens to break through into our world is believed by them to be R'lyeh.

The Dunwich Dungeon is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author and screenwriter Byron Craft, the second in his Arkham Detective series of hardboiled pseudo-noir stories. It was first published independently through the CreateSpace platform in August 2017; both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Overview


### Synopsis
When OSS agent and friend of the Detective Ian Woodhead vanishes while investigating an Arkham seafood vendor, he and newly-promoted Sergeant Matthew Bell are assigned the case. What they uncover is the sole surviving member of an ancient, malevolent race, who is using a piece of arcane technology to re-propagate his species in the modern world. With the aid of their newest recruit, a stray mutt named Robber, the officers track the creature to Dunwich, where they kill it, destroy its laboratory, rescue Agent Woodhead, and retrieve Old Whateley's stash of gold.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, The Dunwich Dungeon has also been included in the omnibus The Arkham Detective Collection Volume 1 (2017).

### Trivia
*Being set as it is in Prohibition-era America (1920-1933 ), the story includes a number of historical inaccuracies, such as featuring operatives from the OSS, which was not established until 1942 , and references to the Sherman tank, which was not designed until 1940 .

shortDefinition: "The Dunwich Horror" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. Written in 1928, it was first published in the April 1929 issue of Weird Tales (pp. 481–508) and is 17,524 words total. It takes place in Dunwich, a fictional town in Massachusetts. It is cons...
fullContent:
"The Dunwich Horror" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. Written in 1928, it was first published in the April 1929 issue of Weird Tales (pp. 481–508) and is 17,524 words total. It takes place in Dunwich, a fictional town in Massachusetts. It is considered one of the core stories of the Cthulhu Mythos. "The Dunwich Horror" is one of the few tales Lovecraft wrote wherein the heroes successfully defeat the antagonistic entity or monster of the story.

### Inspirations
### Geographical
The action "takes place amongst the wild domed hills of the upper Miskatonic Valley, far northwest of Arkham, and is based on several old New England legends — one of which I heard only last month during my sojourn in Wilbraham," a town east of Springfield. (: letter to August Derleth, August 4, 1928, : The Dunwich Horror and Others)

One such legend is the notion that whippoorwills can capture the departing soul. (: The Dunwich Horror and Others) 

Dunwich is "a vague echo of the decadent Massachusetts countryside around Springfield — say Wilbraham, Monson and Hampden." (: Selected Letters 3.508)

It is noted that "much of the physical description of the Dunwich countryside is a faithful sketch of Wilbraham:"

|letter from Lovecraft to Zealia Bishop, : Robert M. Price, The Dunwich Cycle}}

The physical model for Dunwich's Sentinel Hill is thought to be Wilbraham Mountain near Wilbraham. (: The Dunwich Horror and Others)

Researchers have pointed out the story's apparent connections to another Massachusetts region: the area around Athol and points south, in the north-central part of the state (which is where Lovecraft indicates that Dunwich is located). It has been suggested that the name "Dunwich" was inspired by the town of Greenwich, which was deliberately flooded to create the Quabbin Reservoir, although Greenwich and the nearby towns of Dana, Enfield and Prescott actually weren't submerged until 1938.  Donald R. Burleson points out that several names included in the story—including Bishop, Frye, Sawyer, Rice and Morgan—are either prominent Athol names or have a connection to the town's history.

Athol's Sentinel Elm Farm seems to be the source for the name Sentinel Hill. (: The Dunwich Horror and Others) The Bear's Den mentioned in the story resembles an actual cave of the same name visited by Lovecraft in North New Salem, southwest of Athol. (: The Dunwich Horror and Others) (New Salem, like Dunwich, was founded by settlers from Salem—though in 1737, not 1692.)

The book Myths and Legends of Our Own Land, by Charles Montgomery Skinner, mentions a "Devil's Hop Yard" near Haddam, Connecticut as a gathering place for witches. The book, which Lovecraft seems to have read, also describes noises emanating from the earth near Moodus, Connecticut, which are similar to the Dunwich sounds decried by Rev. Abijah Hoadley. (: The Dunwich Horror and Others)

shortDefinition: As one of H. P. Lovecraft's most well-known tales, and considered by most to be one of the 'core' Mythos stories, "The Dunwich Horror" has inspired numerous works by other artists, and has simply been name-dropped in many others. This page offers a n...
fullContent:
As one of H. P. Lovecraft's most well-known tales, and considered by most to be one of the 'core' Mythos stories, "The Dunwich Horror" has inspired numerous works by other artists, and has simply been name-dropped in many others. This page offers a non-comprehensive alphabetical list of these.

### Comic Books & Manga

*Alicia Y: a sequel manga by Juan Gotō, which also incorporates many elements from Lovecraft's other works.
*H. P. Lovecraft's The Dunwich Horror: a four-issue comic book adaptation by Joe R. Lansdale. 

### Film & Television

*Armitage III (1995): scriptwriter Chiaki Konaka reported being influenced by this story when writing the 1995 series. Among the signs of influence are the characters named Armitage and Lavinia Whateley, and a location variously spelled as Dunwich or "Danich" Hill.
*City of the Living Dead (1980): Lucio Fulci movie which is set in a town named Dunwich.
*Fringe (2008-2013): In the episode "Grey Matters", a woman who had severe OCD, involving her constantly thinking about the number 28, was a patient in the Dunwich Mental Hospital.
*Haiyore! Nyaruko-san (2012): In episode 4 of the anime television series, Kuuko stated that she can make a sandwich called the "Dunwich", presumably made using meat from the Dunwich Horror.
*The Real Ghostbusters (1986-1991): In the episode "The Haunting of Heck House", Egon claimed the Whateley House in Arkham is one of the most haunted houses on record, with a total of thirteen ghosts.
*Teen Beach Movie (2013): children's film in which one of the protagonists is about to be sent to an "exclusive" Dunwich Preparatory School. This might also be a pun, as Dunwich in the original story is a regressive backwoods town.

### Radio

*The November 1, 1945 episode of the radio horror program "Suspense" featured a freely adapted version of The Dunwich Horror, starring Ronald Colman as Dr. Henry Armitage and featuring William Johnstone, Joseph Kearns, and Elliott Lewis. It was adapted, produced, and directed by William Spier. It is widely considered by connoisseurs of Old Time Radio to be one of the best of its kind, ever.

### Music

*Bob Drake: On his third album, Medallion Animal Carpet, Drake and a collaborator retell the story of "The Dunwich Horror" under the title "Dunwich Confidential".
*Electric Wizard: the stoner/doom metal band released a song on their 2007 album, Witchcult Today, entitled "Dunwich", based around the short story. Also, "We Hate You", from their 2000 album Dopethrone contains sound clips from the film.
*Iron Man: the doom metal band's 2013 album South of the Earth contains the song "Half Face/Thy Brother's Keeper (Dunwich Pt. 2"), which is based on the story.
*Lorelei: the symphonic deathcore act released a song named "The Dunwich Horror".
*Ningen Isu: the Japanese progressive metal band recorded a song "Dunwich no Kai" ("The Dunwich Horror") for their 1998 album Taihai Geijutsu-ten.

shortDefinition: "The Dweller in Darkness" is a Cthulhu Mythos story written by August Derleth that first appeared in the November 1944 issue of Weird Tales.   The story concerns mysterious Mythos-linked goings-on at Rick's Lake, a remote body of water in north-centr...
fullContent:
"The Dweller in Darkness" is a Cthulhu Mythos story written by August Derleth that first appeared in the November 1944 issue of Weird Tales. 

The story concerns mysterious Mythos-linked goings-on at Rick's Lake, a remote body of water in north-central Wisconsin. 

### In the Mythos
The "Dweller in Darkness" of the title turns out to be Nyarlathotep,  described as well as "the Blind, Faceless One" and "the Howler in the Night." The entity has some sort of special connection to the area around Rick's Lake, known as the Wood of N'gai. Pictographs found in the area portray him as a  vast, amorphous creature...bearing only a curious, cone-like head which even in stone seemed to have a fluidity which was unnerving; moreover, the creature was depicted as having both tentacle-like appendages and hands—or growths similar to hands, not only two, but several; so that it seemed both human and non-human in its structure. When the story's main characters encounter the god, the stone carving turns out to be a close likeness: [T]here was now a gigantic protoplasmic mass, a colossal being who towered upward toward the stars, and whose actual physical being was in constant flux … [F]rom its mass of amorphous flesh there grew at will before our eyes tentacles, claws, hands, and withdrew again; the mass itself diminished and swelled effortlessly, and where its head was and its features should have been there was only a blank facelessness. This depiction of a faceless, tentacled Nyarlathotep had a considerable impact on the popular image of the entity--one of the most iconic of his "thousand forms".

In the story, the only way to defeat Nyarlathotep is to summon the fire elemental Cthugha, the one being he fears, from his dwelling place at Formalhaut. Invented to complete Derleth's schema of the Mythos entities corresponding to elemental forces, Cthugha makes his first appearance in this story, manifesting as a "great being hovering like a cloud of living fire above the trees."

### Rick's Lake
Rick's Lake, the setting that the story centers around, is in "north central Wisconsin." It's described as "a clear blue lake around which century-old trees brood eternally, a country where the only sounds are the cries of the owls, the whippoorwills, and the eerie loons at night, and the wind’s voice in the trees." One gets there by taking "the left fork at the junction of the Brule River highway and the Chequamegon pike on the way to Pashepaho." (The Brule is a real river in Wisconsin; Chequamegon Bay on Lake Superior has been the site of a Native American village since the 17th century, and was the first place in Wisconsin where Europeans settled.) 

The land around Rick's Lake is depicted as "country so primitive that it would seem remote from all human contact.... [I]t is not desolate country, but an area thick with growth, and over all its expanse there persists an intangible aura of the sinister, a kind of ominous oppression of the spirit quickly manifest to even the m

shortDefinition: "The Dweller in the Gulf", originally titled "Dweller in Martian Depths", is a short story by American author and friend of H. P. Lovecraft Clark Ashton Smith. It forms the second part of his Mars series.  ### Synopsis While seeking shelter from a sa...
fullContent:
"The Dweller in the Gulf", originally titled "Dweller in Martian Depths", is a short story by American author and friend of H. P. Lovecraft Clark Ashton Smith. It forms the second part of his Mars series.

### Synopsis
While seeking shelter from a sandstorm, three human prospectors on Mars stumble across a seemingly-bottomless chasm at the cave's rear. Discovering a shelf leading down across the face of the chasm's edge they decide to explore, but after a time making what they feel to be no appreciable progress towards the bottom, turn back.

As they begin their ascent, the find their way blocked by a mass of Martian natives, the Aihai, blocking their path. Every one of the aliens is blind and displays an albinism suggesting a solely subterranean existence. The Aihai subdue them and carry them deeper into the chasm.

Eventually reaching the bottom, the three are confronted by the statue of a bizarre creature which seems to induce a soporific effect on both the humans and Martians. After a while, all present succumb to sleep.

A short while later, one of the humans awakens to the sight of a partially-devoured Aihai, and rouses his companions before making their way back up the ledge, although a strange noise appears to be drawing closer to them from somewhere on the face of the cavern. They are eventually confronted by the creature upon whom the statue was based. Its presence causes them to become sleepy and docile once more, and the creature plucks out their eyes, leaving them to join its band of alien worshippers.

### Characters
*Maspic, a human prospector.
*Bellman, a human prospector and the strongest-willed of the three.
*Chivers, a human prospector.
*The Dweller in the Gulf, an ancient creature which has dwelt in the chasm since time immemorial.

### Publication History
"The Dweller in the Gulf" was first published in the March 1933 edition of pulp magazine Wonder Stories. It has since been reprinted numerous times, and has been translated into Dutch, German, French, Italian and Polish.

fullContent:
"The Dweller in the Pot; Or, The Pasta Out of Space Eaters" is a short story by American author Robert M. Price. 

### Synopsis
When Frank is invited round to Howard's house to sample his most recent concoction, he has no idea that his friend has made his latest dish using directions from an occult cookbook. Mid-meal, the two are attacked by enchanted spaghetti, but Howard is able to defeat the menacing foodstuff by eating it. 

### Characters

*Frank Chimesleep Short, the story's narrator, named after Frank Belknap Long's counterpart from "The Battle that Ended the Century".
*Howard, an experimental cook who is clearly based on H. P. Lovecraft himself.

### Publication History
First published in Crypt of Cthulhu #74 in August 1990, "The Dweller in the Pot" was later included in the collection of Price's own works Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2008. It was also included in The Tindalos Cycle.

### Trivia

*Amongst the nods to the Cthulhu Mythos, "The Dweller in the Pot" mentions cookbooks named for mythos books, for example De Vermicelli Mysteriis (De Vermis Mysteriis), the Cultes des Goulash (Cultes des Goules) and the Unaussprechlichen Kuchen (Unaussprechlichen Kulten).
*Frank Chimesleep Short is also the pseudonym of author Robert M. Price.

shortDefinition: "The Dweller in the Tomb" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, originally published in the 1971 anthology Dark Things, by Arkham House. It is part of Carter's Xothic Legend Cycle.  ### Synopsis The story consists of several entries from the...
fullContent:
"The Dweller in the Tomb" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, originally published in the 1971 anthology Dark Things, by Arkham House. It is part of Carter's Xothic Legend Cycle.

### Synopsis
The story consists of several entries from the diary of Prof. Harold Hadley Copeland, who becomes the last surviving member of his 1913 expedition to find the legendary tomb of the wizard Zanthu, who escaped the destruction of Mu and fled to central Asia, and the Zanthu Tablets he authored.

To find the tomb, Copeland and his men are forced to travel through the arid Plateau of Tsang, and Copeland narrates how the men keep deserting and/or dying one by one, although the Professor has his mind fixed upon completing the journey even if he has to go alone, which he ultimately does. Conditions on the plateau are extremely inhospitable. Water obtained from the snows appears to be contaminated and is utterly undrinkable, forcing Copeland to drink the blood of his own camels. Clawed marks on the stones provide evidence of some unseen creature responsible for dragging away some of the men, although Copeland remains convinced that the marks were faked to provide cover for the men's desertions and try to dissuade him from continuing.

Further into the plateau, Copeland encounters strange crustacean beings that the natives call Mi-Go. Although these Mi-Go are much larger than their American brethren (bigger than a grizzly bear, in fact), they seem to be inexplicably afraid of Copeland. At the height of desperation, the starved Copeland actually drinks the foetid green blood of a dead Mi-Go.

When he finally finds the tomb of Zanthu, uneased by a growing sensation of inexplicable familiarity, Copeland sees the mummified wizard, still recognizable as the spitting image of Copeland himself, presumably his descendant and/or reincarnation.

shortDefinition: "The Dwellers Under the Tombs" is a short story by Robert E. Howard that first appeared in 1976, three decades after Howard's death, in the anthology Lost Fantasies 4. It appears to be a sequel to Howard's Cthulhu Mythos story "The Children of the Ni...
fullContent:
"The Dwellers Under the Tombs" is a short story by Robert E. Howard that first appeared in 1976, three decades after Howard's death, in the anthology Lost Fantasies 4. It appears to be a sequel to Howard's Cthulhu Mythos story "The Children of the Night" first published in 1931, and continues Howard's Lovecraftian theme of a secret subterranean and degenerate race.

### Synopsis
O'Donnel, staying at his friend Conrad's house in the Dagoth Hills, is awakened by a neighbor, Job Kiles, who reports that his twin brother Jonas, who died a week earlier, has come back as a vampire. The skeptical friends accompany Job to the Kiles family tomb, perched atop Smuggler's Point. Job goes in first, alone, and staggers out, fatally frightened. O'Donnel and Conrad explore the tomb, and find Jonas's lidless coffin empty--but discover a secret door that leads to an extensive series of underground chambers leading down into the hill. One chamber contains a room that had been used as a hideout by Jonas; they find his diary, which spells out a plan to fake his own death and scare his hated brother to death by pretending to be a vampire. The underground labyrinth, however, turns out to be inhabited by real monsters--a degenerate subterranean race forced underground by the Indians--who, it turns out, killed Jonas and then frightened Job to death in the tomb. Conrad and O'Donnel encounter them while exploring the tunnel complex, and barely escape with their lives.

### Characters
The story features characters--or at least names--that first appeared in Howard's story "The Children of the Night", though their roles are quite different here. While Conrad in the earlier tale was a student of the occult with an extensive library on the supernatural, here he laughs at the idea of believing in "this vampire nonsense!" At the end of "The Children of the Night," O'Donnel is obsessed with killing a former friend because of his suspected descent from a degenerate subterranean race quite similar to the "Dwellers under the tomb" -- but he makes no connection between the creatures encountered in this story and those he calls his "ancient enemy" in the other.

Conrad is said here to be "iron-nerved in the presence of human enemies"--and less so when confronted with nonhuman horrors. O'Donnel carries a .45 pistol--which Conrad jokes is a sign of his "Texas raising."

Job Kiles is introduced as "a sour, miserly old man who lived on the small estate which adjoined that of Conrad." Jonas Kiles is a "spendthrift" who liked to "boast about his knowledge of secret cults and black magic." He spent years "wandering in the Orient," where he apparently learned the secret of entering "a self-induced state of catalepsy, such as is practiced by Hindu Fakirs."

The Kiles are descended from "old Captain Jacob Kiles," a 17th century "buccaneer and a smuggler."

"The Eater of Hours" is a short story by noted American author and literary critic Darrell Schweitzer which is set in H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in Inhuman magazine #4 in the summer of 2009.

### Synopsis
The ancient entity known as the Chronophagos dreams through some of its stolen time-memories, and decides to release one of its captive souls back into the world.

### Characters
*The Chronophagos, a mysterious entity which consumes the time and memories of the lives of mortals, with the events subsequently running through its dreams.
*Jon, the sole human released back into the world by the Chronophagos.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Eater of Hours" was inspired by a quote by Lovecraft ("Chronophagos, the Devourer of Time, the Eater of Hours. What man remembereth even the hour of his death if the Chronophagos hath devoured it?").

The chronophagic devouring of memories and time is similar to the erasing effect suffered by John Milwarp in "The Chain of Aforgomon".

"The Eater Of Souls" is a horror science fiction short story by Henry Kuttner. 

### Synopsis
The story tells of Sindara of Bel Yarnak who sets off to face the Eater of Souls, a creature whose calls have been dragging his people to their deaths in the Gray Gulf of Yarnak. Forsaking the tools given to him by his necromancers and hydromancers he calls on the god Vorvadoss for help. Getting nothing but a cryptic message, he reaches the Gray Gulf of Yarnak and faces the Eater of Souls in battle. After "a timeless interval of eternity" he is badly wounded while his demonic opponent is unharmed. After another message from Vorvadoss he realises that he has to merge with the creature and sacrifices himself by hurling them both into the abyss.

### Characters

* The Sindara: The benevolent ruler of Bel Yarnak and a devoted follower of Vorvadoss. He, his people and the son he left behind are not anthropoids and aside from having "bone and flesh" are nothing like humans.
* Vorvadoss: A deity who watches over the Sindara but is also willing to sacrifice him knowing that the Sindara's son will remain a worshipper.
* The Eater of Souls: According to the hydromancers the titular Eater of Souls is a half demon half god, created by the Ancients and a Black Shining One in the dark sun,  with the ability to lure victims in with a hypnotic call to be killed and kept in eternal servitude. It is described as being "appallingly hideous" with a white, hairy body, a misshapen head, black eyes and huge spidery limbs. The trapped souls he keeps trail behind him lamenting.

### Settings
### Bel Yarnak
A city of Towers and silver minarets that sits on a "green and joyous world" "beyond Betelgeuse, beyond the Giant Stars". As well as temples and taverns it is home to the throne of chalcedony and two feuding schools of mages: the powerful hydromancers and the less favoured necromancers.
### The Gray Gulf of Yarnak
A vast rocky canyon west of Bel Yarnak where the Eater of Souls lives and the nearer of the planets 3 moons is said to have come from. The cliff face curves into a dim grey haze and eventually total darkness.

### Publication History
"The Eater of Souls" was first published in the January 1937 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reprinted in Crypt of Cthulhu #41 (August 1986), The Book of Iod (May 1995), and Terror in the House: The Early Kuttner, Volume 1 (November 2010).

fullContent:
The Elder Ice is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author and editor David Hambling. It is the first volume of the Harry Stubbs series, an occult detective novel series set during 1920s Britain.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Former boxer and World War veteran Harry Stubbs is sent to recover a debt for his law firm from a deceased Antarctic explorer, Sir Ernest Shackleton. It is speculated by some that he may have encountered a primordial pre-human civilization in his travels and brought back relics of their culture. Harry finds himself caught between multiple employers who are willing to do anything to see if there is any truth to their claim.

### Characters
*Harry Stubbs - A former professional boxer and World War 1 veteran, Harry is an intelligent and reasonable man who is, nevertheless, more concerned about his next paycheck than uncovering eldritch secrets. He frequently finds himself having to do odd jobs and skirt the law in order to make ends meet.
* Sir Ernest Shackleton - A famous treasure-hungry explorer who chased rumors of wealth across the globe. He has recently expired and left considerable debts that Harry's law firm employers wish to recover. He may have encountered the civilization of the Elder Things.
*Mrs. Crawford - The secretary at Latham and Rowe who is actually the individual who sets him on the trail of the Elder Things. She is intersted in harnessing their power to improve humanity.
* Mr. Harcourt - A British imperialist who believes the Elder Things would be interested in allying with the empire to take over the world.

fullContent:
The Elder Sister-like One (姉なるもの, Ane Naru Mono) is a Japanese Cthulhu Mythos manga series, written and illustrated by Iida Pochi. The first works in the series consisted of several individual pornographic doujin that were self-published by Pochi, with the series later being picked up and turned into a mainstream manga series by Kodakowa Publishing in 2016. The serialized story was originally published in the magazine Dengeki G's Comic until 2019; after the magazine's print run had ended, the series is now continuing on Kadokawa's ComicWalker service and Dwango's Niconico Seiga website. The plot involves an orphan boy named Yuu striking a deal with Shub-Niggurath to be his big sister, with the eldritch entity taking the name "Chiyo" and having struggles adapting to the human world. Other Mythos entities are also introduced as the series progresses.  

So far, the manga has been collected into six trade paperback volumes, which were also translated into English by Yen Press.

fullContent:
"The Eldridge Collection"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Will Murray that originally appeared in the anthology The Disciples of Cthulhu II (Chaosium, 2003). 

### Synopsis
The Cryptic Events Evaluation Section has been searching for years for a set of paintings of Mythos entities, and has finally found them in a private Rhode Island museum--but the paintings have powers that make finding them and keeping them two very different things.

### Characters

* Esau Eldridge (1904–1961): A commercial artist who turned to gallery art and "a series of paintings depicting the Great Old Ones and their remorseless train." He never signed his work. He worked in a "lighthouse garrett" on Smuttynose Island, an island off the coast of New Hampshire (though actually part of the state of Maine). He was a double Scorpio, which means he was born on November 7 or 8, 1904. After his death, rival factions of Cthulhu cultists vied to acquire a complete collection of Eldridge's work, in "a Mafia-style power struggle conducted with demons and grimoires instead of hit men and firearms."
* Oriel Malbone: Curator of the Malbone Museum (founded 1971) of Newport, Rhode Island. He's in CEET's database as a "low-level dabbler,” but that seems to be an underestimation. He is described as an "elderly man with a face like a dried turnip" and a "thinning goatee," resembling "a mummified sea captain of the 1800s."
* Del Justice: A CEES operative, described as a "cadaverous man in severe black."
* Justo Osorio:  Justice's partner, "a short, dusky man in a severe black suit and tie." He and Justice previously made an unsuccessful attempt to seize an Eldridge painting of Nyarlathotep in Milan.
* Morand: Head of the CEES's Intelligence and Enforcement section.
* James Anthony: An operative in CEES's Intelligence and Enforcement division, based in Washington, D.C. An Aries with Moon in Capricorn. Divorced, no kids. Carries a reservoir of holy ashes in his belt buckle.
* Gina Itri: In the Cartomancy Division of the CEES's Arts and Crafts section--a Tarot reader, derisively referred to as a "pasteboard princess." A native of South Boston, she's attached to the Boston office. She graduated from Miskatonic University with a Masters in Applied Cartomancy and a minor in Scrying. She's been on missions ranging from Foxfield, Massachusetts, to Irem. She's described as "a feline redhead who looked like a cross between Fran Drescher and a moderately high-priced call girl," who "smoked like a Black Mass." A Leo with her Moon in Scorpio, she calls herself "part Gypsy.” Gargles with holy water between missions.
* Irby: A CEES agent who disappeared in Moodus, Connecticut, and was "later found embedded in a 125-year-old swamp maple as if it had grown up around his undecayed remains since Teddy Roosevelt’s day." His death made the CEES stop buying round-trip tickets for its agents.

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in Murray's collection The Wild Adventures of Cthulhu: Volume One.

fullContent:
"The Electric Executioner" is the name of H. P. Lovecraft's revision of Adolphe de Castro's "The Automatic Executioner" previously published in 1893 in In the Confessional and the following.

### Plot Summary
The unnamed narrator is an investigator for an American mining colony operating in Tlaxcala, Mexico, and is called into the country in 1889, when one of the company's assistant superintendents, Arthur Feldon, vanishes, taking valuable company paperwork with him. Though initially sent via private car, delays put the narrator on a regular passenger train bound to Mexico City. The train includes European-style, private cabins, and the narrator takes what he believes to be an empty one, before discovering a giant of a man somehow hidden in the darkness of the opposite seat.

Sensing something is wrong about this stranger, the narrator eventually reaches for his gun, but the stranger strikes first, and overcomes him, taking his gun away, and using it to force the narrator to cooperate. The stranger then produces a strange device from his valise, which the narrator describes as a mask of wires attached to a strange collection of electric components that the stranger addresses as a battery. The stranger explains that he is going to test the device on the narrator as his first human subject, and explains that the device is designed to be put onto the victim's head, where it will deliver a violent electric shock, executing them. It appears that he submitted this device to officials in New York when the state was adopting the electric chair for use in capital punishment, but was rejected.

The stranger's motives are not simply about profit. He has grand dreams about killing everyone on the planet, "before Quetzalcoatl comes back." He begins to waver back and forth, between mad scientist and cultist, saying that soon, "I and Quetzalcoatl and Huitzilopotchli will rule the world alone," while also boasting that his battery is a technical marvel, atomic in nature, and so beyond human science that mankind might never rediscover it, even if they did survive his plans.

After evoking several Greek gods, the stranger moves to begin his test, but the narrator attempts to stall for time, knowing that if the train reaches Mexico City, the railroad police will be able to rescue him. First he writes an extended will, and then, he appeals to the stranger's vanity, saying that he can write a letter that will convince the newspapers to spread the word of the invention, finally making up for his humiliation in New York. The stranger agrees, and is even passionate about making sure the technical details are correct. The narrator continues to stall by doing a sketch of the device, and he even talks the stranger into wearing the mask to demonstrate how it would appear around a human head. Finally, the stranger puts the papers in his pocket.

fullContent:
"The Emerald Tablet" is a short story by Robert M. Price that brings Richard L. Tierney's sword-and-sorcery character Simon of Gitta together with Clark Ashton Smith's elder entity Ubbo-Sathla.  The story first appeared in the August 2017 issue of Strange Sorcery (#24).

The Emerald Tablet is a genuine occult text from the Middle Ages, regarded by Islamic and European alchemists as the foundation of their art.

### Synopsis
Simon, driven by his pursuit of ancient wisdom, uses the powerful Emerald Tablet of Thoth to travel millions of years into the past, where he encounters Ubbo-Sathla, the primordial god responsible for the creation of all life on Earth. He finds that Ubbo-Sathla's domain includes a treacherous trap.

### Setting
The story is set in the spring of 33 A.D., after the events of Tierney's novel The Drums of Chaos. Simon's mystic voyage starts from below the Great Pyramid of Egypt.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in  Strange Sorcery, "The Emerald Tablet" was reprinted in the anthology Lin Carter's Flashing Swords! #6 (Pulp Hero Press, 2020) and in the Simon of Gitta collection Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

fullContent:
"The Enchanted Fruit" is a short story by Ramsey Campbell that appears in his 1975 collection Demons by Daylight. It takes place in Campbell's Severn Valley setting, with scenes in Brichester and in the woods near Goatswood.

### Synopsis
The plot involves Derek, a Brichester librarian, who retreat from "the daily press of Brichester, the false harsh rainbow of packed cars", into the woods near Goatswood.  At first he finds them enticing--"Each corridor of trees seemed made to be explored, each green shadow promised mystery"--and later forbidding; "A screen of leaves seemed secretive; parted, it revealed only vistas of dim branches." In the forest, he finds a tree whose "rich trunk, dark yet warm, stood alone on a mound of autumn built high from the edge of the glade;" he eats the fruit of this tree, "large as apples, soft and shaped as peaches", to his immediate delight and eventual regret.

fullContent:
"The Enchantress of Sylaire" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, set in his pseudo-historical French setting of Averoigne. It first appeared in the July 1941 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
The story concerns Anselme, a romantic young man who has become a hermit in "the wild woodland of Averoigne" after being spurned by Dorothée, the woman he loves. After 13 months of solitude, Anselme comes upon a beautiful woman bathing in a forest pool fed by the river Isoile--accompanied by an enormous wolf. She introduces herself as Séphora, an enchantress, and invites Anselme to accompany her to her domain, Sylaire, "a land lying outside of time and space" and reached through a stone portal erected by the druids.

Anselme becomes Séphora's lover and dwells with her in Sylaire. The "wolf" reveals that he is the sorcerer Malachie du Marais, now a werewolf, a curse he claims was bestowed on him when she tired of him as her lover. Séphora's servants, he claims, are vampires, and Séphora herself "an ancient lamia, well-nigh immortal, who feeds on the vital forces of young men".

Séphora warns that Malachie has become a danger to herself and to Anselme, and gives him a glass vial that she suggests he should switch with a similar container Malachie has, which holds a potion that will cure his lycanthropy, and thus restore his full sorcerous powers. She also gives Anselme a sword enchanted to be "effective against such as Malachie".

Anselme goes to Malachie's lair to secretly makes the switch, and while there Malachie gives him the "mirror of Reality", in which "all things are reflected according to their true nature." He sees that Malachie's reflection in it is that of a long-dead corpse.

Dorothée comes to Sylvaine, and professes that she now loves Anselme--who finds that his love for her has quite expired. Before he can explain, a maddened Malachie attacks in wolf form, and Anselme slays him with the sword. A grateful Dorothée tries to embrace him, but he shows her the mirror, and upon seeing her reflection recoils in "manifest horror" and flees back to her own world.

Séphora asks if he would not like to see what she looks like in the mirror of Reality. “I am content with what my eyes tell me, without the aid of any mirror,” he declares, throwing the mirror into a deep pit.

### Characters
*Anselme du Framboisier: The second son of the Comte du Framboisier. He is "not so ill-looking" and has fair manners, but is an "addle-headed dreamer" who is suspected of writing verses.
*Dorothée des Flêches: The only daughter of the  Sieur des Flêches. She has blond ringlets, a "full-ripened mouth," "round arms and slender waist."
*Séphora: An enchantress and the châtelaine of Sylaire. Possibly a lamia. She has "thick-curling chestnut hair", and a "short oval face with slightly slanted eyes and lips red as pomegranate flowers." Her eyes are blue-grey.

The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana, later known as The Cthulhu Mythos Encyclopedia, is a reference book written by Daniel Harms, and first published by Chaosium in December 1994. Cover art was provided by Allen Koszowski .

Several editions of the Encyclopedia have been released: the first, second, and expanded and revised second editions were all published by Chaosium (1994, 1998, 2003, respectively); the third edition by Arc Dream Publishing (2008, 2018); and the fourth by Elder Signs Press (2012). A Japanese-language translation was also made available in 2007 .

shortDefinition: "The End of History" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mathew Chabin.  ### Synopsis In a dystopian future in which the Old Gods have returned and what remains of humanity serves as either their devotees or sustenance, a teacher attempts to ho...
fullContent:
"The End of History" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mathew Chabin.

### Synopsis
In a dystopian future in which the Old Gods have returned and what remains of humanity serves as either their devotees or sustenance, a teacher attempts to hold on to what little remains of his humanity. During the incursion of a minor deity on campus, he discovers one of his students has a talent for a kinder magic than that imposed by the antediluvians. Gifting her with a small spark of light which he himself carries, he vows to make the world a little better before taking his own life.

### Publication History
"The End of History" was published in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2020.

### Trivia
* Although most of the Mythos namechecks in "The End of History" are those from the works of Lovecraft and his circle, James Ambuehl's Lu-Kthu is also given a mention.

fullContent:
"The End of the Story" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, the first of his stories set in the pseudo-historical French region of Averoigne. It was first published in the May 1930 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
The plot concerns a young law student named Christophe Morand, who stays at the Abbey of Perigon in Averoigne. There, he reads a manuscript about Gerard de Venteillon, a knight who was seduced by a lamia who lives in the ruins of the Chateau des Faussesflammes, near Perigon. Reading the story, Morand becomes similarly obsessed and seems to meet the same fate.

### Characters

* Christophe Morand: A "young law-student of Tours" who unaccountably disappearance after a stopping at the abbey of Périgon on his way to his father’s estate near Moulins in November 1789.
* Hilaire: The abbot of Périgon, proud of the abbey's library. He rescues Morand from the lamia and warns of her seductive danger, to no avail.
* Nycea: A lamia that inhabits the Chateau des Faussesflammes. It's implied that she is one of those "abominable hags whose bodies terminate in serpentine coils," though she appears as "a woman of goddess-like beauty". The reader is left to wonder which is the truth.
* Gerard de Venteillon: The Comte of Venteillon, "a knightly youth of indisputably proven valor" and "a true Christian". After meeting a satyr, however, he becomes obsessed with finding "the pagan ecstasies," and disappears into the ruins of Faussesflammes.
* Eleanor des Lys: A "renowned and beautiful demoiselle" who is engaged to Gerard, she is stood up by him at the altar of the cathedral of Vyônes when he disappears.

shortDefinition: "The Epiphany of Dissolution" is a story by Ian Davey. It forms part of his Bh'Yhlun series of Cthulhu Mythos shorts.  ### Synopsis Glyph continues her journey to Glastonbury and on the road joins up with an older couple, Helen and Aaron, who have be...
fullContent:
"The Epiphany of Dissolution" is a story by Ian Davey. It forms part of his Bh'Yhlun series of Cthulhu Mythos shorts.

### Synopsis
Glyph continues her journey to Glastonbury and on the road joins up with an older couple, Helen and Aaron, who have been similarly drawn to the ancient site. On arrival they meet Lucy, who had arrived a few hours previously. 

Atop the Glastonbury Tor the three women mentally meld and draw on a mysterious power embedded within the mound, but this action awakens the Outer God Shub-Niggurath. The four attempt to flee but the arrival of Stanley Pickman, and the revelation that he is in fact an avatar of Nyarlathotep, results in the death of two of them.

The two survivors manage to reach Stonehenge where their power causes a shift in reality where the world is restored to a pristine state, with one exception: the tower of Bh'Yhlun remains …

### Characters
*Glyph, a thirteen-year-old orphan girl.
*Lucy, a pregnant woman who has witnessed the end of the world from its genesis.
*Helen, an older woman in a deteriorating mental and physical condition.
*Aaron, Helen's husband.
*Stanley Pickman, an avatar of Nyarlathotep.

### Publication History
"The Epiphany of Dissolution" was first published in the online fanzine Nightscapes in January 1998. It later appeared in Dark Legacy in October 2000, and was also included in the anthology The Best of Dark Legacy, Volume 2 in September 2016.
