shortDefinition: The Events at Poroth Farm is a short horror story by American horror author and editor T. E. D. Klein which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos.  ### Synopsis The story follows a soon-to-be teacher who rents an outbuilding at the Poroth family far...
fullContent:
The Events at Poroth Farm is a short horror story by American horror author and editor T. E. D. Klein which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
The story follows a soon-to-be teacher who rents an outbuilding at the Poroth family farm somewhere in New England for the duration of the summer. He unwittingly opens a tiny tear in the fabric of space-time which lets through a malevolent entity. This entity at first takes the form of a bizarre little creature the size of a large shrew, then inhabits one of the farm owner's cats before moving on to the owners themselves, killing the wife and attempting to then murder their lodger.

The story concludes with the narrator stating his belief that the entity remains loose, and may in fact be coming for him.

### Characters
*Jeremy, the narrator, a man in his late twenties who is to teach English Literature at Trenton State College the following semester. To this effect, he rents lodgings on the Poroth farm with the intention of using the peaceful environment to read the many books which he will be using in his upcoming lesson plan.
*Sarr Poroth, one of the farm's owners. In his early thirties, Sarr is described as a shy and gentle soul, although he can come across as somewhat dour and morose because of his shyness. Both Sarr and his wife are members of a highly-orthodox religious group, but are nevertheless considered to be young liberals by their sect. Earned a bachelors degree at Rutgers University when younger.
*Deborah Poroth, Sarr's wife, also in her early thirties. Stated to have been the polar opposite of her husband, Deborah is outgoing and bubbly, traits which are somewhat frowned upon in their faith. She is still however, considered an upstanding member of their small community. Attended two years of community college when younger.

### Behind the Mythos
Originally published in From Beyond the Dark Gateway #2 in December 1972, The Events at Poroth Farm received an eBook release in The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack by Wildside Press LLC in 2012. In this version, the original received something of a revision.

### Mythos References
*One of the books read by Jeremy is Robert W. Chambers' The King in Yellow.
*H. P. Lovecraft is himself mentioned in the story, but only when telling of Jeremy's reading. The essay referred to is Supernatural Horror in Literature.
*A passing comment by Jeremy on the nature of small communities, "the New England harbor town where fishermen feign ignorance and cast “furtive glances” at the traveller" is a possible nod to Lovecraft's short story The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

shortDefinition: "The Evil Clergyman" is an excerpt from a letter written by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft in 1933. After his death, it was published in the April 1939 issue of Weird Tales as a short story.  The letter, to his friend Bernard Austin D...
fullContent:
"The Evil Clergyman" is an excerpt from a letter written by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft in 1933. After his death, it was published in the April 1939 issue of Weird Tales as a short story.

The letter, to his friend Bernard Austin Dwyer, recounted a dream that Lovecraft had had. Although Lovecraft frequently based stories on his dreams, An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia notes that "[i]t is difficult to say how HPL would have developed this conventional supernatural scenario."

The story was later adapted into the unreleased 1987 anthology film Pulse Pounders.

### Synopsis
The story begins in the attic of an ancient house. The narrator’s companion refers to the former owner of the house and the presumably violent end that befell him. He advises the narrator not to stay after dark or touch anything, especially the small object on a table, which the companion seems to fear considerably.

The narrator is then left alone in the attic; he notes the many theological and classical books, and one bookshelf in particular containing books on magic. He feels a considerable curiosity for the forbidden object on the table. The narrator finds a strange flashlight-like device in his pocket that produces a peculiar violet glow. He attempts to illuminate the object on the table with this strange light, which he describes as being composed of particles. The object makes a crackling sound like a sparking vacuum tube, and takes on a pinkish glow with a vague white shape taking form from its center. The narrator, feeling that his surroundings are taking on strange new properties, realizes that he is not alone; the sinister newcomer is described as wearing clerical garb typical of the Anglican Church. The newcomer begins throwing magical books into a fireplace.

The narrator notices other men within the room, all dressed in clerical attire, including a bishop; they confront the first man, who reaches for the object on the table with a wry smile. The other men, looking terrified, make a quick retreat. The man then proceeds to retrieve a coil of rope from a cupboard and ties it into a noose as if to hang himself. When the narrator attempts to intervene, the man notices him and approaches threateningly. The narrator shines the strange light on the man as if it were a weapon, causing him to fall backwards down an open stairwell.

When the narrator proceeds towards the stairwell, he finds no body below, but rather three people approaching with lanterns. Two of them see the narrator and flee shrieking, leaving only the companion who had accompanied the narrator to the attic. The companion says that the narrator should have left the object alone, that interfering with it had altered him. The man then leads the narrator to a mirror, where he is presented not with his own reflection, but that of the evil clergyman.

### Behind the Mythos
This story is alluded to in Ramsey Campbell's "The Return of the Witch" from The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tena

fullContent:
The Evil Dead is a 1981 low-budget American horror comedy film written and directed by Sam Raimi, starring cult icon Bruce Campbell, and featuring special visual effects by Tom Sullivan. The film was a commercial and critical success, and led to the creation of an entire franchise, including several sequels, as well as tie-in media including video games, comic books, and a three-season television series.

### Synopsis
The film follows a group of college friends who travel to the backwoods of Tennessee on vacation. There, they accidentally summon a host of demons which proceed to possess them for their own amusement. Although one of the group, a man named Ashly Williams, apparently survives the onslaught by killing his possessed friends, the final scene of the film shows a demon racing through the forest towards him. 

### Behind the Mythos
The Evil Dead is most notable to this wiki for introducing the Naturan Demanto, an ancient Sumerian text inspired by H. P. Lovecraft’s Necronomicon and the titular book of the film's working title Book of the Dead. In later films in the franchise, the Naturan Demanto would be re-titled as the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis.

Expanded Mythos author and Lovecraft enthusiast Stephen King is at least partially credited with gaining the film enough media traction to attract a distributor after he attended a screening at the Cannes Film Festival In 1982.

Special effects artist Tom Sullivan would go on to work on numerous Lovecraftian productions, including the documentary film Lovecraft: Fear of the Unknown and the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

A man who believes himself to be conducting an autopsy on a mutated human finds that he has been slipped experimental drugs which cause him to hallucinate his own murder at the hands of a monstrous being. Their test successful, the creators of the drug then haul him off for dissection.

"The Extraordinary Lineage of Ethan McKay" is a short Lovecraftian story by James Carlson. It was published in the Deadman's Tome anthology Deep Fried Horror Cthulhu Cheese Burger in January 2020.

### Synopsis
Ethan McKay, a young man who feels detached from society, is working at a New Jersey clam joint when the destruction of humankind begins. As he watches, he sees aquatic creatures rise from the depths and slaughter all in their path, as well as a colossal creature with leathery wings and a tentacled head. The monstrous being recognises something buried deep within Ethan and spares him, taking him beneath the waves to reclaim his birthright.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly stated as such in the story, the enormous being encountered by Ethan is all but named as the Great Old One Cthulhu.

A Yithian on a survey mission to Earth takes over the body of a pharaoh in ancient Egypt, while his host's consciousness is questioned by its colleagues. When the pharaoh is returned to his own body, the only thing he remembers is a mental image of an eye, which he believes to have been a vision sent by Horus. He subsequently orders the symbol to be carved on monuments across his realm.

fullContent:
"The Eyes of the Mummy" is a horror short story by Robert Bloch and a direct sequel to his earlier tale "The Secret of Sebek", set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in the April 1938 issue of the magazine Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
Following the events narrated in "The Secret of Sebek", Prof. Weildan seeks the unnamed narrator once again to join him in another Egyptian venture. This time he intends to actually go to Egypt, having gotten word about a location where a priest of Sebek was mummified, along with precious jewels. The prospect of wealth and adventure finally convinces the narrator to assist Weildan.

They travel to Khartoun to meet Weildan's informant, but the meeting turns sour as the man seems extremely agitated, arguing with Weildan and trying to communicate something to the narrator, who doesn't speak Arabic. Weildan takes the man to another room. The narrator hears a scuffle and Weildan comes out claiming that the argument was about payment. The narrator silently notices Weildan cleaning out blood from his hands.

The next morning, the two head off into the desert and find the tomb. The narrator questions why a priest would be buried in such a secretive and isolated location, but Weildan explains that he was probably fleeing either from a persecuting government or an angry mob, as the priests of Sebek were practitioners of dark magic who sacrificed maidens to their deity. Despite that, Weildan is sure that even a priest on the run would still bring along his treasured jewels and be accompanied by followers who would mummify his body upon death. Furthermore, it would be a rare and valuable finding, as the priests of Sebek were mummified with their internal organs intact, which wasn't a common practice.

Venturing inside the chamber, the two men open the casket and peer at the mummy, whose eyes have been replaced by an extraordinary pair of bright yellow gemstones. Hieroglyphs reveal that the priest's eyes were removed and replaced with these stones while he was still alive. The narrator stares into the gemstones, even as Weildan tries to warn him about their hypnotic effect and their role in the priests' belief in reincarnation. While hypnotised, the narrator's consciousness trades places with that of the still-living mummified priest. Once he realises that he is now a prisoner inside the eyeless mummy's body, while the priest of Sebek inhabits his own, the narrator panics and uses his mummified hands to tear off the gemstones from his eye sockets, thus reverting the spell and sending his consciousness back into his own brain. He finds that Weildan has collapsed dead from the shock of seeing the mummy's arms moving. Despite his own traumatic experience, the narrator makes sure to take the valuable gemstones with him as he escapes the tomb.

"The Face" is a short horror story by E. F. Benson. It was first published in the February 1924 issue of Hutchinson's Magazine.

### Synopsis
Hester Ward, a young and beautiful married woman, has a nightmare about a hideous and terrifying face. This same face had appeared to her ten years earlier in a recurring nightmare, telling her that it will return for her when she is older. She tells her husband about her strange nightmares. Together they seek medical advice and their doctor recommends that she seek a rest cure somewhere quiet. The peace and quiet are soon disturbed...

### Behind the Mythos
"The Face" was one of several stories by E. F. Benson which H. P. Lovecraft spoke highly of.

### Publication History
"The Face" was first published in Hutchinson's Magazine in February 1924. It as since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into both German and French.

fullContent:
"The Face of Baphomet" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas, published in his 2005 collection Unholy Dimensions by Mythos Books.

### Synopsis
D'Urberville is a man who believes his family can trace their lineage back to the secretive order of the Knights Templar; in an effort to confirm this belief, he approaches Basil Rosier, an enigmatic collector of antiquities. Despite an initial incredulity that his ancestors committed any of the heresies of which they were accused by the Catholic Church, when confronted with one of Rosier's artefacts, he is quickly convinced otherwise, and with such a revelation is immediately welcomed into the folds of Shub-Niggurath's cult.

### Trivia
The Knights Templar were a real-world Order during the Middle Ages who were betrayed by the Catholic Church at the behest of King Philip IV, who was heavily indebted to them. Their members were tortured into giving false confessions of heresy before being burned at the stake.

shortDefinition: "The Faceless God" is a short story by American author Robert Bloch which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos.  ### Synopsis A ruthless black marketeer named Doctor Stugatche discovers that a caravan of traders have uncovered a potentially-pricele...
fullContent:
"The Faceless God" is a short story by American author Robert Bloch which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
A ruthless black marketeer named Doctor Stugatche discovers that a caravan of traders have uncovered a potentially-priceless statue in the desert. Torturing its location from one of the traders, he mounts an expedition to retrieve it.

Upon locating the statue, Stugatche finds that his hired group of locals are unwilling to touch the thing, and he has to resort to the threat of violence to force them to dig it from beneath the sands. Settling down for the night, he awakes in the early hours of the morning to find that the natives have all departed while he slept, and taken everything except the statue with them. 

Attempting the long walk to the nearest oasis, Stugatche begins to notice a dark presence stalking him. Panicking, he loses his way and, still pursued by the presence, travels in an enormous circle, eventually finding himself back at his original campsite. There, the sands open and engulf him, leaving only his head above ground, to slowly die in the heat of the desert while chanting the name 'Nyarlathotep'.

### Characters
*Doctor Stugatche, described as being around forty-five years old and heavy-set, except for his legs, which are almost comically spindly in comparison. He was formerly an attaché to an archaeological expedition in Egypt who went on to deal in black-market antiquities.
*Hassan, an elderly man who was a camel-driver for the caravan which discovered the statue. Later abducted, tortured and killed for information by Stugatche's henchmen.
*Nyarlathotep, one of the Outer Gods, is revealed to have been both the subject of the statue and the presence which followed Stugatche. He is stated to have been dwelling in the desert since before the building of the pyramids, when he and his cult were cast out from civilisation. He now waits for the time to be right to return to the world.

### Behind the Mythos
The Faceless God was originally published in the May 1936 edition of Weird Tales, and collected in Robert Bloch's collections The Opener of the Way and Mysteries of the Worm. It was later included as part of the eBook release The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack by Wildside Press in 2012.

### Mythos References 
*The lost continent of Mu is mentioned.
*Abdul Alhazred's Necronomicon, the Book of Eibon, and the Mysteries of the Worm by Ludvig Prinn are all referenced.

"The Faces at Pine Dunes" is a short Mythos story by British author Ramsey Campbell.

### Synopsis
As a young man reaches adulthood, his father reveals his family legacy of witchcraft, and sacrifices himself to let the boy claim his birthright as a scion of the Great Old Ones.

### Characters

*Michael, a twenty-year-old man on the cusp of learning his family’s heritage.
*Michael's father, a witch and descendant of the Old Ones.
*Michael's mother, a woman seemingly drawn into the family through deceit.
*June, Michael's new girlfriend and future mother of the next generation of witches.

### Publication History
"The Faces at Pine Dunes" was first published in the collection New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos by Arkham House in 1980. It was later reprinted in Campbell's own collection Cold Print in 1985, and again in Cthulhu 2000: A Lovecraftian Anthology in 1995.

### Mythos Connections

*One of the locations Michael recalls visiting to during his family's nomadic life is the Severn Valley, the setting for many of Campbell's Mythos stories.
*Michael's fathers notebooks refer to Great Cthulhu, as well as the Necro (Necronomicon), Revelations Glaaki (The Revelations of Gla'aki) and Vermis (De Vermis Mysteriis).

fullContent:
"The Fairground Horror" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, written in 1972 and first published in The Disciples of Cthulhu (DAW Books, 1976).

Two brothers run a house of horrors at a travelling funfair--and one brother seems to take the horrors far too seriously.

### Characters
* Hamilton Tharpe: Part owner of the freak show at Hodgson's Funfair. Raised in the carnival, then owned by his father, he had a "joy in old books and fancifully dubious legends," and a "lust for travel, adventure, and outre knowledge" that took him to the Pacific islands, from which he returned with an idol of Cthulhu, and then to Arabia. Afterwards, the "sensitive, mystery-loving traveller" became a reclusive cultist, and he began using the freak show to attract sacrifices to his god.  He wore a shaggy toupee to conceal an anemone-like growth on his head.
* Anderson Tharpe: Hamilton's older brother, whose interest in occult paraphernalia is strictly mercenary. He is a "a tall man, well over six feet in height but...thin and emaciated.... His hair was prematurely grey and purposely grown long in an old-fashioned scholarly style, so that he might simulate to the crowd’s satisfaction a necessary erudition."
* Hiram Henley: A professor of archaeology and ethnology at Meldham University, with a specialization in Hittite antiquities; he lost his position due to his obsession with "cycles of myth and aeon-lost legend." He is a "slight, middle-aged man" with a "thin figure," a "balding head and tiny specs through which his watery eyes constantly peered."  He was "conspicuously odd," yet his "intelligence was patent; the stamp of a 'higher mind' was written in erudite lines upon his brow." He wears gloves to conceal his worm-like fingers, the mark of his secret status as a priest of Cthulhu.
* Stainton Gamber: An "eminent explorer and archaeologist; one whose name...might be even higher in the lists of famous adventurers and discoverers but for a passion for wild-goose expeditions and safaris."
* Bella Hodgson: The owner of the funfair, who buys it after the Tharpes fall into financial difficulties.
* Madame Zala: A "young, single, dark-eyed Romany fortune-teller" associated with Hodgson's Funfair, "a Gypsy girl of genuine Romany ancestry." She lives in a horse-drawn caravan. Hamilton Tharpe had been "somewhat enamored" by her, but cooled to her after his travels, and she "had been seen to cross herself with a pagan sign" when he passed by. Leaves the funfair, only returning after Anderson Tharpe's disappearance.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Disciples of Cthulhu, "The Fairground Horror" was reprinted in the anthologies The Book of Cthulhu (Night Shade Books, 2011) and Beside the Seaside: Tales from the Daytripper (Things in the Well Publications, 2019). shortDefinition: The Fantasy Fan was a fan magazine published from 1933 to 1935, the first such publication for the weird fiction fandom. It is remembered as the first outlet to publish H. P. Lovecraft's stories "The Other Gods" (November 1933) and "From Beyond" (Feb...
fullContent:
The Fantasy Fan was a fan magazine published from 1933 to 1935, the first such publication for the weird fiction fandom. It is remembered as the first outlet to publish H. P. Lovecraft's stories "The Other Gods" (November 1933) and "From Beyond" (February 1934), and as the first publication to serialize the revised version of his Supernatural Horror in Literature (October 1933-February 1935; unfortunately, the magazine folded before the complete text could be serialized).

An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia reports that The Fantasy Fan was unique in serving at the same time as "a news organ, a forum for the expression of fans' views, and a venue for work by distinguished writers in the field."

The magazine was founded and edited by Charles D. Hornig, 17 years old when he put out the first issue in September 1933. It was typeset and printed by Conrad Ruppert, who had already been producing the fanzine The Science Fic-Digest.

In addition to publishing original stories by Lovecraft, the magazine reprinted "Polaris" (February 1934) and "Beyond the Wall of Sleep" (October 1934), which had appeared in the amateur press. It also published four sonnets from Fungi from Yuggoth.

Lovecraft encouraged his author friends to submit articles to the magazine; Clark Ashton Smith, Robert E. Howard, August Derleth, and Robert Bloch all saw first publication of one or more of their stories in The Fantasy Fan.

### External Links
*[https://isfdb.org/cgi-bin/pe.cgi?28910 The Fantasy Fan] at the Internet Speculative Fiction Database

"The Far Deep" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Josh Reynolds. It was published in the thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press in 2011.

### Synopsis
Prior to the Battle of Lepanto in 1571 the Maltese galley St. Elmo, a ship belonging to the Grand Fleet of the Holy League, captures a small Greek fishing vessel, looting it of a number of golden trinkets.

As the battle against the Ottomans progresses, the Holy League's flank collapses, and the sinking St. Elmo is boarded by murderous semi-human aquatic monstrosities who only retreat when the survivors return the stolen baubles.

### Behind the Mythos
Possible Cthulhu Mythos elements include the captured fisherman apparently possessing the Innsmouth Look; the description of the inhuman boarders matching that of the Deep Ones; and the golden trinkets resembling those described in The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Trivia
*The Battle of Lepanto was a real-world fleet action which took place between the forces of the Turkish Ottoman Empire and a coalition of Catholic powers under the banner of the Papal States in 1571.

"The Fate of the Jaquiths" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author R. C. Mulhare which first appeared in the Gavin Chappell-edited zine Lovecraftiana (unknown year, Rogue Planet Press). It proved popular enough to have been voted for by the fanbase on Facebook for inclusion in a Best of… collection (2023, Rogue Planet Press).

### Synopsis
A young woman who has spent the majority of her life as a paid companion to a wealthy American girl watches as her charge is first seduced, then wed by a mysterious Englishman whose intentions appear to be more sinister than would seem at first glance. As she looks into her former friend's new relationship, she discovers the existence of a debauched cult, and comes to the realisation that the man's origins may not be entirely of this Earth…

### Mythos Connections
"The Fate of the Jaquiths" mentions a number of characters who share surnames with those from H. P. Lovecraft's fiction, including the Waite and Wentworth families, a Mrs. Cabot-Pickman, and a Sylvia Tillinghast; places referenced include Manuxet, and Aylesbury. Additionally, the Great Old Ones are mentioned in passing.

fullContent:
"The Feaster from Afar" is a horror short story by Joseph Payne Brennan set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published by DAW Books in October 1976 in the anthology The Disciples of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
Professional author Sydney Mellor Madison rents a hunting lodge in the small village of Granbury, New England, to work on his next novel. Despite the terrible condition of the road, he finds the place comfortable enough at first. However, he notices that the countryside is barren, not only avoided by humans, but completely devoid of animal life. To make matters worse, he starts to experience nightmares and inexplicable fatigue. When conversing with Saines, the local storekeeper, who asks Madison if he's a hunter, another villager cryptically warns him to "be sure yew ain't the hunted!".

Madison's nightmares get worse, as he dreams of being pursued by some alien creature that glides over the ground. One day, he asks Saines why the hills are shunned, and learns that a hunter has been found dead with his skull punctured by numerous holes, and no sign of a brain inside. Long ago, Saines says, a branch of the Whateley family lived on these hills, and they summoned something from the sky that never left. When Saines explains that such things are spoken of in the Cthulhu Mythos, Madison indignantly retorts that this whole mythology is fiction made up by an old pulp-magazine writer whose name he can't recall.

The next morning, Madison opens a book and finds a note which claims that a cosmic entity named Hastur the Unspeakable has been summoned, and "shall find sustenance". Despite the visible age of the paper, Madison convinces himself that it must be part of a hoax, planted there by Saines or someone else to scare him.

At night, Madison experiences one last dream of dashing over the hills, trying to outrun his pursuer. Even though he cannot possibly escape, fear alone keeps him going, until he comes to realise that he isn't actually dreaming, but awake, having sleep-walked away from the lodge into the wilderness. He continues to run in his pajamas, indifferent to the wounds caused by the stones and branches, until he falls down and finds himself paralysed, unable to look away and forced to see the monster's visage. His dead body is found afterwards, with his empty skull drilled by several holes, as the creature has consumed his brain.

"The Feaster from the Stars: The History of Yzduggor the Eremite" is a horror fantasy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos, specifically in the ancient continent of Hyperborea. It was first published in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu #26 (Hallowmas 1984), billed as by Clark Ashton Smith and Lin Carter. Similar to the "posthumous collaborations" of Lovecraft and Derleth, "The Feaster from the Stars" was written entirely by Carter, based on an unused story note by Smith. When republished as part of The Book of Eibon (2002, Chaosium) it was credited solely to Carter.

### Synopsis
Vooth Raluorn, high constable of Commoriom, dedicates most of his spare time to the study of grimoires, many of which were confiscated from forbidden cults by his predecessors. When called to arrest a group of demon-worshipers, he finds an idol upon their altar shaped like a winged toad-like creature with a mass of tentacles for a face. Revolted, Vooth Raluorn smashes the idol to pieces.

From this point on, the constable finds himself tormented by increasingly terrifying nightmares featuring the abomination. At first unable to find any reference to it in his books, he eventually learns that the creature is none other than Zvilpogghua, the firtborn son of Tsathoggua, who can fly down to Earth when Algol is visible in the sky. The distraught constable also learns of an eremite named Yzduggor, rumoured to be a former cultist, and heads to the Eiglophian Mountains to speak to him.

Apparently satisfied by the gifts that Vooth Raluorn brings, Yzduggor offers him a formula to protect one against the wrath of Zvilpogghua. On his return, the constable procures the rare ingredients from his nephew, the merchant Nungis Avargomon, and performs the ritual at night, with Algol brightly visible. The protection fails, however, as Zvilpogghua swoops from the stars and carries Vooth Raluorn away. In the Eiglophian Mountains, Yzduggor celebrates another sacrifice to his deity. Nungis Avargomon inherits his uncle's wealth and rank, and silently congratulates himself on having sabotaged one of the ingredients.

"The Festival" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft written in October 1923 and published in the January 1925 issue of Weird Tales. It is considered to be one of the first of his Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Inspiration
The story was inspired by Lovecraft's first trip to Marblehead, Massachusetts, in December 1922. Lovecraft later called that visit



The narrator's path through Kingsport corresponds to a route to the center of Marblehead; the house with the overhanging second story is probably based on Marblehead's 1 Mugford Street. The church in the story is St. Michael's Episcopal Church on Frog Lane, built in 1714 and the oldest Anglican church building still standing on its original site in New England. The church, which stands on a modest hill, has a rare colonial crypt where early parishioners were interred, and had a steeple for most of the eighteenth century. Lovecraft would have discovered these facts from visiting the church and talking with the rector, a fact corroborated by his signing of the guest register.

Lovecraft cited a book as another inspiration for the story: "In intimating an alien race I had in mind the survival of some clan of pre-Aryan sorcerers who preserved primitive rites like those of the witch-cult--I had just been reading Miss Murray's The Witch-Cult in Western Europe." This is why Lovecraft refers to the narrator's folk as "an old people, and...strange, because they had come as dark furtive folk from opiate southern gardens of orchids, and spoken another tongue before they learnt the tongue of the blue-eyed fishers." The idea of "pre-Aryan" survivals was the basis of Arthur Machen's "The Novel of the Black Seal", which Lovecraft had recently read and been much impressed by.

### Synopsis
The story is set at Christmas time: "It was the Yuletide, that men call Christmas though they know in their hearts it is older than Bethlehem and Babylon, older than Memphis and mankind." An unnamed narrator is making his first visit to Kingsport, Massachusetts, an "ancient sea town where my people had dwelt and kept festival in the elder time when festival was forbidden; where also they had commanded their sons to keep festival once every century, that the memory of primal secrets might not be forgotten."

The town he comes to, which shows little sign of habitation, seems centuries out of date,



He locates his relatives' house, which has an overhanging second story, and is greeted by an unspeaking old man with "flabby hands, curiously gloved," and a "bland face" that he comes to suspect is "a fiendishly cunning mask". This mysterious greeter directs him to wait next to a pile of old books that includes a Latin translation of the Necronomicon, wherein he discovers "a thought and a legend too hideous for sanity or consciousness." fullContent:
"The Fillmore Shoggoth" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Harry Turtledove. It was published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu by Titan Books in October 2014.

### Synopsis
Spring 1968: in a world in which humankind awkwardly coexists with the Elder Ones following the discoveries of the Pabodie expedition, a drifting iceberg originating from the Antarctic beaches on the coast beside San Francisco zoo. Near the heart of the city, psychedelic rock band HPL bear witness to the murderous rampage of the Shoggoths which hid aboard the berg. Although destroyed with fire and napalm, their actions result in the annihilation of everything which has come into contact with the Elder Ones- including two of the alien creatures themselves, San Francisco zoo's entire population of albino penguins, and one Howard Phillips, a scholar who had spent his life documenting the Antarctic discoveries.

### Trivia
*In the story, Howard Phillips is accompanied by his wife, whose name is given as Sonia. This is a clear nod to Sonia H. Greene, an amateur writer and publisher who was married to H. P. Lovecraft for two years during the 1920s, although, due to a clerical error, their divorce was never legally finalised.

"The Final Door" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by authors Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A middle-aged man, bored with his life at home falls for the exotic femme fatale living across the hall who introduces him, through her magic, to worlds and times beyond his imagining. After encouraging his wife to drink herself to death, he spends increasing amounts of time with the woman, whose power causes him to de-age until, during a trip to the caverns beneath the Sphinx of Giza, a terrible accident occurs and the woman is killed. Although he is able to return to his own time, his ageing process drastically accelerates, and the story ends with him an old man in a nursing home.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, a disillusioned man seeking some excitement in his life.
*Selket, an ancient Egyptian sorceress who learned her arts from Nyarlathotep.
*Annie, the narrator's wife.

### Publication History
"The Final Door" was published in the collection The Blasphemy In The Canopic Jar & More Tales Of The Cthulhu Mythos in September 2016, and was later included in Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

### Trivia
*One of the places visited by Selket and the narrator is the realm of Egyptica, an extra-dimensional plane of existence created by the authors for their Egyptian-oriented Mythos stories.

fullContent:
"The Fire of Asshurbanipal" is a short story by Robert E. Howard that first appeared in the December 1936 issue of Weird Tales. Two versions of the story exist: the Weird Tales version from 1936, which embraces Lovecraftian cosmic horror, and an alternate draft published in The Howard Collector #16 in Spring 1972, in which the supernatural happenings end up having a rational explanation.

### Synopsis
The Fire of Asshurbanipal is a gem rumored to be in the clutches of a skeleton on a throne in a lost city in the Arabian desert--"the ancient City of Evil spoken of in the Necronomicon of the mad Alhazred." Although the jewel is supposed to be cursed, it's sought by Steve Clarney, "a lean and wiry American," and Yar Ali, his Afghan companion. When they find the city and its treasure, they are ambushed and held captive by an old enemy of Clarney's, Nureddin el Mekru. 

Nureddin claims the jewel for himself against the protests of his own men, but as soon as he touches it, the gem springs out his hand and rolls to the wall of its own volition. Nureddin chases it, and at the instant he grabs for it, a hidden door in the wall opens and a tentacled monster grabs him and drags him into the shadows. Nureddin's men flee from the chamber while Clarney and Yar Ali play dead, daring not to open their eyes until they hear the hidden door close behind the creature once more. When they open their eyes, they see that the Fire of Asshurbanipal has been placed back in the skeleton's claw, and Nureddin's severed head sits in front of it, staring blankly.

Clarney and Yar Ali leave the city without the gem. Clarney reveals he caught a glimpse of the creature, which appeared like a humanoid toad with tentacles and wings. They are left shaken with the knowledge that there are older and stranger things that ruled the world before mankind.

### Alternate Version
In the Howard Collector version, after capturing Clarney and Yar Ali, Nureddin seizes the gem and smashes the skull of its skeletal guardian. He is struck dead, an apparent victim of the curse--but after Nuredin's minions flee in terror, Clarney points out that Nureddin was bitten by an adder that had been sleeping in the skull.

### Publication History
After its appearance in Weird Tales, "The Fire of Asshurbanipal" was included in several collections of Howard's fiction, including Skull-Face and Others (Arkham House, 1946), Wolfhead (Lancer Books, 1968), Cthulhu: The Mythos and Kindred Horrors (Baen Books, 1987), Nameless Cults: The Cthulhu Mythos Fiction of Robert E. Howard (Chaosium, 2001), The Haunter of the Ring & Other Tales (Wordsworth Editions, 2007), The Horror Stories of Robert E. Howard (Del Rey / Ballantine, 2008), Black Hounds of Death (Cosmos Books / Dorchester Publishing, 2008), and The Cthulhu Stories of Robert E. Howard (WordFire Press, 2020). It's also been featured in Mythos anthologies like Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos (first edition, Fedogan & Bremer, 1992) and The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack: 4

"The Fire Vampires" is a short story by Donald Wandrei written in 1933. Alongside "The Tree-Men of M'Bwa", it was one of Wandrei's stories that were retroactively incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos. It appeared in the February 1933 issue of Weird Tales.

### Plot
In the distant future, a United Federation of Nations historian named Alan Marsdale reminisces on an apocalyptic event involving a comet. A man named Gustav Norby, an authority on cosmic lifeforms, warned of impending danger from a comet coming on July 7, 2321, but people laughed off his claims. Dubbed 'Norby's Comet', noted for its reddish-blue coloration, it was projected to arrive in 18 years. But on August 10th, on its arrival to Alpha Centauri, it mysteriously vanished, then appeared four days later a billion miles beyond Pluto, perplexing the astronomers and the public, and prompting theories that it was controlled by other lifeforms. The revelation that it would appear near Earth in 16 hours, its approach visible in the sky, prompted reactions from panic to wonderment. 

Later the comet mysteriously changed course, moving in the opposite direction of Earth's rotation. The comet orbited and illuminated the world, and after a complete orbit exited in the direction of Antares. On August 16th, Norby and his assistant, Hue, argued that, because the comet followed no natural laws, it could return again, as it might have merely been observing Earth like a satellite. Records showed that thousands died under the comet's orbit via spontaneous combustion after a strike of lightning, leaving nothing but bones, and that this phenomenon is still occurring.

Six years later in August, Norby and Hue, after photographing a new star in the Antares cluster, came across a sentient fireball in a tree, of the same color as the comet. They observed in horror as the new creature consumed people in fire with fingers of lightning, and forced them to hide in the observatory. The two realized that this predatory lightning and fire had arrived on Earth from Norby's Comet, and that the new star in the Antares cluster was the comet planning its next move. The two learned on the news that these Fire Vampires were killing people around the world, arriving through electric bolts of lightning.

Later that night, the comet returned, appearing first in China. The comet formed mile-long fiery letters in the sky, spelling a message in appropriate languages over each country:People of Earth, you are ours by right of conquest. Hence forth and forever you belong to us, of Ktynga, known to you as Norby's Comet. You cannot fight us, nor defeat us, nor evade us. We are superior to you in every way. At irregular intervals, we shall return and claim as our due from 20-50 thousand of your inhabitants. We desire nothing else. But we insist upon the payment, and we shall take it. If you resist, we shall take more. On our next visit, we shall claim John Hanby, the president of the Federated Nations, Axel Gruno, master scientist

fullContent:
"The Fishers from Outside" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, first published in 1988 in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu. It reappeared in the anthology The New Lovecraft Circle, and in the collection The Xothic Legend Cycle. In the latter, the identity of the story's Great Old One is changed from Gol-goroth to Groth-Golka, a correction that Carter himself intended to make before his death.

Although "The Fishers from Outside" marks the first actual appearance of the titular creatures (previously mentioned by H. P. Lovecraft in "The Outpost" and "Winged Death", and by Frank Belknap Long in The Horror from the Hills), Carter actually identifies them as being just another name for the Shantaks. While Chaosium's depiction of the Fishers is derived from Carter's, the company has instead opted to keep Fishers and Shantaks as distinct species in their bestiaries.

### Synopsis
Professor Mayhew has spent 20 years of his career studying the mysterious Fishers from Outside: alien creatures that colonized Earth in prehistory and built megalithic outposts in central Uganda. From the Necronomicon, he learns that the Fishers from Outside are servants of an old god (Gol-goroth in the original version, Groth-Golka in the revised version) worshiped in the island of Bal-Sagoth.

In 1946, the story's narrator, Harlow Sloan, is hired as Mayhew's assistant in the archaeological site of Great Zimbabwe. Among several idols shaped like monstrous birds, they also find the Black Stone: an object shaped like a dodecahedron with mysterious inscriptions, including, again, strange avian creatures. That night, Sloan has a nightmare in which he sees Great Zimbabwe as it was in prehistory, and witnesses humans being offered as sacrifices to winged reptilian creatures summoned from the skies, which would brutally tear the sacrifices apart with their beaks.

Mayhew recognizes the inscriptions of the Black Stone as being similar to some he had seen in the Ponape Scripture, discovered by Abner Exekiel Hoag and translated by his manservant Yogash, who was a Deep One hybrid. Back in the United States, he studies the book and has access to other papers of Hoag and Yogash. The same symbols are present, and refer to the same pantheon of gods, which seem therefore to have been worshiped in both the Pacific and Africa. When they manage to translate the Black Stone's inscriptions, Mayhew and Sloan find that they are instructions for summoning the Fishers from Outside, a.k.a. Shantaks.

Two days later, Mayhew sends Sloan away to the Kester Library to make some annotations from the Book of Eibon, claiming he will need them that same night. Once there, however, Sloan quickly realizes that the order was just a pretense to get him away. He returns just in time to hear Mayhew reciting the summoning, and sees the Fishers from Outside descend from the skies and tear the Professor apart, to the point that the body is only identifiable by his pince-nez glasses.

"The Flame in the Ice" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author DJ Tyrer. It was published in the collection Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights by Rogue Planet Press in January 2017.

### Synopsis
Swords-for-hire Olbur and Peltamash are engaged by a wizard named Temsol to protect his caravan on a trip into the cold north of Hyperborea, ostensibly on a mission to obtain trade goods. However, once they reach the frozen tundra, Temsol reveals to the two that his true intention is to steal the power of an entity ensconced in a city of ice. 

The group battles their way through Gnophkehs and other, less savoury, guardians before reaching their target: Teloth, the flame in the ice. Realising at the last moment that allowing Temsol to claim Teloth's power would be disastrous, Olbur and Peltamash release the being which proceeds to kill the sorcerer and make its way out into the larger world…

### Characters
*Olbur, a seasoned swordsman and mercenary.
*Peltamash, real name Minon-Azal, Olbur's protégé and lover.
*Temsol, an ambitious magic-user.
*Teloth, a being seemingly composed entirely of fire, imprisoned in a crystalline city.

"The Foul One Lives to Destroy: A Tale of the Dreamlands" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mark McLaughlin.

### Synopsis
After lying imprisoned beneath the sands of the Dreamlands for a thousand years, the Foul One, an Avatar of Nyarlathotep, is freed and returns to the city of Xambolei to take its vengeance on the descendants of those who turned their backs on its worship so many years ago.

### Characters
*The Foul One, an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep.
*Chabao, a Xamboleian trader with a penchant for strong wine.

### Publication History
"The Foul One Lives to Destroy: A Tale of the Dreamlands" was published in the 2019 collection The House of the Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares.

The Foulness Island Vanishings: A Corrupting Infiltration in a Time of War is a scenario sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview


Containing a complete stand-alone scenario including all necessary non-player characters, handouts and maps, The Foulness Island Vanishings was written by prolific Cthulhu Mythos author Glynn Owen Barrass. Published by third-party content creator Stygian Fox in 2010, it runs to a total of 84 pages.

fullContent:
"The Four Sealed Jars" is a 1975 short story written by Gary Myers, first published in his collection of short fiction The House of the Worm.

### Synopsis
A curio shop in the town of Nithy-Vash in the Dreamlands is operated by the mysterious gnome-like Getech. Getech is wrapped up in all-enfolding black robes exposing only his bald pate and his eyes, and he may not be human. Wesh, a curious shopper, is conducted to a back room where a gold-masked mummy and four sealed jars await. Wesh is a dreamy individual seeking excitement and wonder.

Three of the jars seem to emit faint sounds as if bats fluttered inside or someone was quietly tapping to be let out. The fourth was empty.

Wesh buys the golden mask of the mummy and leaves the shop.

It is implied but not stated outright that after wearing the mask he is somehow trapped in the fourth of the jars, which are then sold as a set by Getech to a merchant in Celephaïs.

fullContent:
"The Franklyn Paragraphs" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Ramsey Campbell.

### Synopsis
Using correspondence received by a fictionalised version of Ramsey Campbell, "The Franklyn Paragraphs" tells the story of an aspiring writer in Brichester, England, who stumbles across an unliving cultist of Eihort. He ultimately disappears, and is hinted to have fallen foul of the Great Old One himself.

### Characters
*Roland Franklyn, a cultist of Eihort
*Errol Undercliffe, a small-time writer with an insatiable curiosity.
*J. Ramsey Campbell, the narrator.

### Publication History
*Demons by Daylight (1973)
*Cold Print (1993)
*Cthulhu's Heirs: Tales of the Mythos for the New Millennium (1994)
*A Mountain Walked (2014)
*Visions from Brichester (2015)
*Lovecraft Mythos: New & Classic Collection (2020)

It was also translated for the German-language edition of Demons By Daylight, published in 1998.

### Trivia
*"The Franklyn Paragraphs" marks the first appearance of the Great Old One Eihort.
*In addition to Campbell being the story's narrator, many real-world authors are mentioned, including Arkham House co-founder August Derleth.

shortDefinition: "The Freshman" is a short story by Philip José Farmer, set at H. P. Lovecraft's Miskatonic University. It was first published in the May 1979 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. It appears in the Arkham House anthology Tales of the ...
fullContent:
"The Freshman" is a short story by Philip José Farmer, set at H. P. Lovecraft's Miskatonic University. It was first published in the May 1979 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. It appears in the Arkham House anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos.

"The Freshman" depicts Miskatonic University not as a stalwart bastion against the Great Old Ones, as it usually appeared in the work of Lovecraft and his immediate circle, but more like the Miskatonic of the popular imagination: a campus in league with sinister forces and relishing forbidden lore.

### Synopsis
The story centers on Roderick Desmond, a 60-year-old writer of occult novels, who is enrolling at Miskatonic as a freshman. He longs to escape the control of his domineering mother, but knows that she will follow him even if he enters college. He mainly interacts with two other characters: Wendell Trepan, an upperclassman who hopes to recruit Desmond into his fraternity, Lam Kha Alif; and R. Layamon, chair of the Committee of the Occult Arts and History Department, who pushes Desmond to cross a moral line to achieve his full potential as master of arcane forces.

### Behind the Mythos
In addition to painting a picture of a pro-cosmic horror Miskatonic, the story provides some back story for the Arkham area: The hills to the west of Arkham are named for the Tamsiqueg Indians, whose legends tell that the hills were once evil giants, turned to stone by the tribe's hero Mikatoonis. The largest of the giants, Cotoaahd--whose name is also the acronym for Layamon's department--is said to sometimes return to life, leaving a trail of destruction in his wake. The Tamisqueg wonder-worker Atechironnon had a ritual for waking Cotoaahd tattooed on his body--a formula preserved when Simon Conant, half-brother of the historical Roger Conant (founder of Salem), turned the Indian sorcerer's skin into a book, Ye Lesser Rituall of Ye Tahmmsiquegg Warlock Atechironunn.

shortDefinition: "The Frog" is a short story by Henry Kuttner, originally published in the February 1939 issue of the magazine Strange Stories.  This story introduces Monk's Hollow, a location featured in Kuttner's Cthulhu Mythos story "The Hunt". Both stories are in...
fullContent:
"The Frog" is a short story by Henry Kuttner, originally published in the February 1939 issue of the magazine Strange Stories.

This story introduces Monk's Hollow, a location featured in Kuttner's Cthulhu Mythos story "The Hunt". Both stories are included in the anthology The Book of Iod: Ten Tales of the Mythos.

### Synopsis
Norman Hartley, an artist from New York City, rents a house in the small town of Monk's Hollow to work on some paintings. On the garden there is a large stone inscribed with symbols, which Hartley regards as ugly. The caretaker, Dobson, tells him that centuries ago a witch named Persis Winthorp was buried there.

Although she looked human at first, Winthorp was the daughter of a humanoid frog-like monster from the local swamp. When the villagers tried to drown her, they found that she wouldn't die, so they buried her alive and placed the magical stone over the spot, so she would remain there. It is believed that she's still alive, but incapable of escaping, and that at this point she's no longer human, but has transformed into a batrachian creature like her father.

Dismissing Dobson's story as superstition, Hartley pays two passing truck drivers to remove the stone. That night, Winthorp digs her way out of her grave, breaks into Hartley's house and kills Dobson. Hartley hears the sounds of someone breaking in and grabs a knife from the kitchen, but flees in terror when he sees the creature. He runs a great distance through the countryside with the monster at his pursuit, and engages in a brief fight with it, until a farmer named Byram Liggett fires a musket and saves him. Winthorp sneaks into another farm and kills Anam Pickering and his sister Martha.

On the next day, the townspeople and Hartley take part in a hunt for the monster, organized by Liggett. Hartley continues to doubt that the frog-creature is Winthorp, believing it to be some kind of hybrid animal instead. That night, Winthorp attacks a gasoline station, but the townspeople arrive too late to capture her. Two days later, she breaks into Liggett's house, where Hartley is staying. Hartley manages to escape and shoot Winthorp, causing her to bleed a black ichor, but she doesn't stop the pursuit. The frog-woman pursues Hartley into the swamp, followed by neighbors who heard the first shot and follow them by automobile. The neighbors and Hartley shoot Winthorp, who falls and sinks into the quicksand while cursing them.

### Characters
*Norman Hartley, a painter from New York. He is described as having an obsession with aesthetics, finding the presence of a large stone in the middle of the garden to be intolerable.
*Dobson, an elderly caretaker with a wooden leg, who tries to prevent Hartley from removing the stone.
*Persis Winthorp, an immortal witch who, over the course of several decades, transforms into a croaking beast, half-frog half-human, much like her father. She is phenomenally strong, with sharp claws, and eats the flesh of those she kills.
*Byram Ligg

shortDefinition: The Fuller Memorandum is a mildly comedic detective / espionage novel by Charles Stross, the third full-length book in his Laundry Files series. It was first published in hardcover by Ace in 2010.  ### Synopsis The document that provides the book's t...
fullContent:
The Fuller Memorandum is a mildly comedic detective / espionage novel by Charles Stross, the third full-length book in his Laundry Files series. It was first published in hardcover by Ace in 2010.

### Synopsis
The document that provides the book's title describes a supernatural entity, the Eater of Souls, connected to the founding of the Laundry. Both the document and Bob Howard's boss, James Angleton, go missing, leaving Howard and his wife and fellow Laundry agent Dominique O'Brien to deal with the threat of a mole inside the agency. The mole turns out to be a cultist loyal to Nyarlathotep, who captures Howard and plans to bind the Eater of Souls to Howard's body--a plot that is foiled when it turns out that the Eater of Souls was bound to Angleton decades ago. 

### Behind the Mythos
The title is inspired by The Quiller Memorandum (originally The Berlin Memorandum), a 1965 spy novel by Elleston Trevor (writing as Adam Hall). Stross originally intended The Fuller Memorandum to be an homage to Hall's Quiller series, but ended up using the spy novels of Anthony Price as his model instead.

The Fuller referred to in the title is Major-General J. F. C. Fuller, a historical figure who was an influential popularizer of military doctrine. He was also a close associate of occultist Aleister Crowley, and an enthusiastic supporter of Adolf Hitler--even after World War II, which he believed was won by the wrong side.

### Publication History
The Fuller Memorandum was first published in hardcover in 2010 by Ace Books, a switch from the first two Laundry Files books, which were published by in hardcover by Golden Gryphon Press. Orbit put out a paperback edition in 2010 as well. 

### References

fullContent:
The Fungi from Yuggoth is a campaign supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, written by Keith Herber and first published in 1984.

### Overview
Consisting of 8 interlinked scenarios, The Fungi from Yuggoth runs to a total of 80 pages. First published in 1984, a second edition was published in 1987. 

### Contents
*"The Dreamer": involves the search for a missing psychic.
*"The Thing in the Well": a series of child murders in Boston involves the group.
*"Castle Dark": an excursion to Transylvania.
*"Sands of Time": an encounter with a Miskatonic University research team in Egypt.
*"Mountains of the Moon": an investigation into a mining company involved with cultists.
*"By the Bay: Part I": Chinese cultists in San Francisco attract the group's attention.
*"By the Bay: Part II": a San Francisco research facility.
*"Day of the Beast": the story's culmination in Egypt and Gaza.

shortDefinition: The Gable Window is a "posthumous collaboration" between August Derleth and H.P. Lovecraft. As with other Derleth posthumous collaborations, it's basically a Derleth story.  It was first published in May 1957 in Saturn magazine under the name "The Mu...
fullContent:
The Gable Window is a "posthumous collaboration" between August Derleth and H.P. Lovecraft. As with other Derleth posthumous collaborations, it's basically a Derleth story.

It was first published in May 1957 in Saturn magazine under the name "The Murky Glass". 

### Synopsis
Fred Akeley inherits a house from his late cousin Wilbur Akeley, a scholar from Miskatonic University who was “a student of archaeology and anthropology”. Wilbur spent years overseas and his travels included visits to “Mongolia, Tibet, and Sinkiang Province” and “South and Central America, and the southwestern part of the United States”.  

Fred Akeley moves into his inherited house, which has a great circular window of cloudy glass installed as a gable window. Wilbur’s papers mention how the window is made of a special glass from “Leng… possibly Hyadean in origins”.  

It transpires that the special window is a interdimensional portal, connecting the house directly across space and time with the vistas it shows.

Fred and Wilbur are related to Henry Wentworth Akeley, a character from H. P. Lovecraft's story "The Whisperer in Darkness", whom Fred refers to in "The Gable Window" as "our fathers’ cousin, Henry Akeley, of Vermont". Some of the books in Wilbur's library of Mythos-related tomes were sent to him by Henry.

### Behind the Mythos
As detailed in the posthumous collaboration controversy article, Derleth took several tiny story ideas or the briefest of notes, wrote stories related to them or somehow inspired by them, and used Lovecraft's name on them. These are not Lovecraft stories, albeit they are indeed Mythos stories.

### External Link

* [https://cthulhufiles.com/stories/derleth/lovecraft-derleth-the-gable-window.html "The Gable Window"] complete text at Librarium Cthulhuvius

shortDefinition: "The Game Changers" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Stephen Mark Rainey.  ### Synopsis October 29 1969, somewhere near Mai Loc, Vietnam: a squad of American GIs lost behind enemy lines make their way to the site of a downed B-52 bo...
fullContent:
"The Game Changers" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Stephen Mark Rainey.

### Synopsis
October 29 1969, somewhere near Mai Loc, Vietnam: a squad of American GIs lost behind enemy lines make their way to the site of a downed B-52 bomber. There, they discover an attempt to weaponise a hungry entity from another dimension, and a group of aliens in league with a black-ops colonel.

### Characters

*Timmons, a young soldier and sole survivor of his squad.
*Sergeant Christopher Van Buuren, squad leader.
*PFC Ronald Sultan, weapons specialist.
*Colonel Everett M. Boothe, a covert operations liaison.

### Publication History
"The Game Changers" was first published in the Brian M. Sammons/Glynn Owen Barrass-edited anthology World War Cthulhu in 2014.

### Synopsis
A first-person telling of how the unnamed narrator undergoes a horrific ordeal of pain and pleasure, one which brings their dead lover back to them, after a fashion…

fullContent:
"The Garden of Fear" is a short story by American author Robert E. Howard. Although containing no immediately obvious connections to the Cthulhu Mythos, it forms the second written instalment of the James Allison Cycle.

### Synopsis
James Allison recalls another of his past lives, this one that of a pre-human barbarian fleeing with his love from their wrathful tribe. When his mate is stolen away by a black, winged figure, the tribesman uses his animal cunning to defeat the foe and his plantlike guardians, and rescue the girl.

### Characters

* James Allison, a man who has lived through many, many reincarnations.
* Hunwulf, a semi-feral ancestor of modern-day humans who hails from the icy northlands.
* Gudrun, Hunwulf's love.
* The Winged Black Man, the sadistic last survivor of a race which once ruled the world.

### Publication History
"The Garden of Fear" was first published in Marvel Tales #2 (July-August 1934). It has since appeared in a large number of other publications, both periodicals and anthologies, and has been translated into French, German and Hungarian.

### Behind the Mythos
The winged man supposedly is the last survivor of a race who inspired legends of harpies and Demons. He resembles the harpies encountered by Howard's Puritan hero Solomon Kane in Wings in the Night.

shortDefinition: The Gardens of Lucullus is a novel by Richard L. Tierney and Glenn Rahman, part of Tierney's Simon of Gitta series that merges the Cthulhu Mythos with sword & sorcery adventure at the time of the Roman Empire. It was published by the Sidecar Preserva...
fullContent:
The Gardens of Lucullus is a novel by Richard L. Tierney and Glenn Rahman, part of Tierney's Simon of Gitta series that merges the Cthulhu Mythos with sword & sorcery adventure at the time of the Roman Empire. It was published by the Sidecar Preservation Society in 2001. 

### Synopsis
Simon of Gitta, captured and brought to Rome while helping the northern tribes resist the Empire, is released by the Emperor Claudius on the condition that he use his eldritch skills to find out who's behind a goddess cult that's trying to revive a demonic deity from the depths of time. Simon teams up with Rufus Hibernicus, an Irish barbarian turned gladiator, with Rufus' sword and Simon's sorcery (and sword) combating Mythos terrors. 

### Publication History
The Gardens of Lucullus was written in 1981 but not published until 2001, and has long been out of print. Pickman Press is reportedly planning to reissue the book in 2024. 

A sequel, Heir of Darkness, was written by Rahman, with a plot outline approved by Tierney. It ended up being published years before The Gardens of Lucullus, in 1989.

The Gaslight Equipment Catalogue is a sourcebook for Call of Cthulhu, a horror roleplaying game by Chaosium.

### Overview
Consisting of game stats and uses for a variety of items, vehicles and weapons from the Victorian Age, The Gaslight Equipment Catalogue is a part of Chaosium's Monograph line, a series of digital-only releases whose content is primarily generated by the fan base.

### Publication History
The Gaslight Equipment Catalogue was first released in June 2007. It is only available as a digital PDF download.

fullContent:
"The Gateway to Carcosa" is a short story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A man with a desire to vindicate his dead fathers belief in the existence of Carcosa travels to the Aylesbury Public Library to consult their copy of The King in Yellow, Arkham's Miskatonic University being sans a copy. The madness which results from his reading the book causes him to kill himself, whereupon the gates to Carcosa open and he is reunited with his father.

### Characters
*Ethan/Roger Clarence, a man who feels deep guilt over his father's death.
*Graham, Clarence's father, who read The King in Yellow before killing himself.

### Publication History
"The Gateway To Carcosa" was published in Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

### Trivia
*"The Gateway to Carcosa" is prefaced by a quote from Robert W. Chambers' short story "The Repairer of Reputations".
*Although introduced with the first name Ethan, the main character is consistently referred to as Roger throughout the remainder of the story.

The Gathering is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by Brian Lumley, published as part of his Earth, Air, Fire & Water: Four Tales of Elemental Mythos Horror! collection (Tor, 2017). In the collection, the novel represents the element of fire.

### Synopsis
Andrew Gilman returns to The Hamlet, a tiny village in Lovecraft Country, after the death of his father, a doctor. Andrew's visit coincides with an annual ritual celebrated by the community.

### Publication History
The Gathering has not been republished separately from the Earth, Air, Fire & Water collection.

fullContent:
"The Gentleman Caller" is a short story by American author Lucy A. Snyder.

### Synopsis
When a mentally and physically damaged woman is gifted a strange necklace by a mysterious stranger, it unlocks her natural ability to switch bodies with other people. The stranger then asks her to release a man from an on-ship prison: the man turns out to be a cultist who uses his newfound freedom to launch a cruise missile which will awaken an ancient entity from its sleeping place beneath the Pacific Ocean.

### Characters
*Janie, a woman who was severely crippled by childhood surgery.
*Brandon Wilks, an urbane and manipulative cultist.

### Publication History
"The Gentleman Caller" was first published in the Dark Regions Press anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror in 2017. It was also included in a collection of Snyder's own works, Garden of Eldritch Delights, in October 2018.

### Trivia
*The description of the necklace which Janie is gifted is highly reminiscent of the Deep One jewellery encountered by Robert Olmstead in H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth.
*The being awakened by the cruise missile strike is implied to have been Great Cthulhu itself.

shortDefinition: "The Ghost-Eater" is a horror short story by  C. M. Eddy, Jr. with H. P. Lovecraft, published in the April 1924 issue of Weird Tales.   ### Synopsis An unnamed narrator sets out on journey from Mayfair to Glendale, Maine, on foot, but must traverse a...
fullContent:
"The Ghost-Eater" is a horror short story by  C. M. Eddy, Jr. with H. P. Lovecraft, published in the April 1924 issue of Weird Tales. 

### Synopsis
An unnamed narrator sets out on journey from Mayfair to Glendale, Maine, on foot, but must traverse a dangerous forest on the way. He believes this trip will take only a day. When he can get no one to be his guide, he sets out on his own. However, he soon becomes exhausted from the afternoon heat and falls asleep until it is nearly sundown. Upon awakening, he sees a storm on the horizon and frantically searches for shelter.

He sees a light and follows it to a house built within a clearing. Inside is a kindly old man with a limp who offers him dinner, yet doesn't eat his meal alongside the narrator. The old man isn't talkative, so the narrator retires in an upstairs guest room. As he takes his lamp with him, he notes how the old man's eyes reflect in the light. Fearful about the possibility of being robbed, he poses the bed as if it were occupied and sits watch in a corner chair.

Late in the night, he's awoken by heavy footsteps on the stair, as the narrator's door begins to open. He hides behind a dresser, as a tall unfamiliar man enters the room and proceeds to lie down in the bed before going to sleep. Determined to rouse the man, he moves to touch him, but find his hand passes through the man's body.

He hides again in terror as more footsteps are heard, these with a limp. A huge gray wolf with luminous eyes and a lame paw comes into the room and proceeds to eviscerate the sleeping apparition. Frightened, the narrator flees in terror.

Finally arriving in Mayfair the next morning, he finds refuge at the Lafayette House but doesn't reveal his ordeal. The proprietor is amazed he would travel through the "Devil's Wood" on the night of the full moon. The proprietor proceeds to tell the tale of Vasili Oukranikov, a Russian immigrant who built a home in the woods.

Oukranikov was reported to be a werewolf and devil worshipper. People reported being chased through the woods by a huge gray wolf. After a local shot the wolf in the foot one night, the suspicious of the townfolk were confirmed when Oukranikov returned to town with a limp. In time, Oukranikov sent Feodor Tchernevsky, the so-called "Count", to pay him a visit. The Count was warned about the danger of Oukranikov and had compatriots follow in case of danger. At some unspecified point, they stormed the house and found a huge gray wolf feasting on the Count's corpse. They killed the wolf, buried it underneath an oak tree, and burned the house to the ground. The proprietor asks if the narrator saw anything on his journey, but he denies it.

shortDefinition: "The Ghoul" is a short fantasy-horror story by Clark Ashton Smith, published in January 1934 in the amateur publication The Fantasy Fan. It tells the tale of Noureddin Hassan, who is accused of murdering seven people to fulfill a ghoul's demand to pr...
fullContent:
"The Ghoul" is a short fantasy-horror story by Clark Ashton Smith, published in January 1934 in the amateur publication The Fantasy Fan. It tells the tale of Noureddin Hassan, who is accused of murdering seven people to fulfill a ghoul's demand to protect his wife's grave. The story explores themes of grief, horror, and moral conflict.

### Synopsis
"The Ghoul" follows the story of Noureddin Hassan, a respected man from Bussorah. After the death of his beloved wife, Amina, he is consumed by grief. Mourning at her grave, he encounters a ghoul who demands a horrifying bargain: Noureddin must bring the ghoul a body each night for eight nights, specifically those he has killed himself, to spare Amina's grave from desecration.

Although poetically described as a demon the creature in this story is clearly intended to be a classical Ghoul of Arabia.

### Behind the Mythos
The 1933 movie The Ghoul starring Boris Karloff was an Egypt-based story about a vengeful mummy, however the redolent influence of that popular piece of cinema should not be ignored.(relevance or source Smith saw the film?) The more proximate influence for this story is without question the body of Arab folklore compiled in the Arabian Nights, specifically by way of William Beckford's  novel Vathek (1786).  The historical figure on whom Beckford based Vathek is the Caliph Al-Wathiq (full name Abu Jaffar Harun al-Wathiq ibn Mutasim), who was born in AD 816, and reigned from AD 842 to 847, which sets "The Ghoul" in the mid-840's.

### References

shortDefinition: "The Ghoul's Portrait" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Joshua Reynolds. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.  ### Synopsis When a talented thief steals a portrait of ...
fullContent:
"The Ghoul's Portrait" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Joshua Reynolds. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
When a talented thief steals a portrait of the god Mordiggian, its priests dispatch Amina Algol, a woman raised with ghouls, and her adoptive siblings Arif and Bera to retrieve the piece. Tracking the thief to the home of a powerful sorcerer, the three learn that the man had been forced into the act by the evil magician who wishes to bind the will of the god to his own.

Attempting to re-acquire the stolen work, the group confront the sorcerer, but he proves too powerful. Fortunately, a gift supplied to Amina by their god to aid in the task proves more than capable of dispatching the man, and his soul is sucked into a painting by the talented artist King Richard, from where it can be dealt with at Mordiggian's leisure.

shortDefinition: "The Ghulistan Affair" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Sam Inabinet, first published in the Ulthar Press anthology Pickman's Gallery in 2018.  ### Synopsis The story is for the most part a conversation between two men, implied to be special...
fullContent:
"The Ghulistan Affair" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Sam Inabinet, first published in the Ulthar Press anthology Pickman's Gallery in 2018.

### Synopsis
The story is for the most part a conversation between two men, implied to be special agents in the employ of the British government, on the state of affairs regarding the various non-human humanoid creatures which inhabit a vague geographical region incorporating India to Central Asia. In particular, their discourse revolves around an ill-fated expedition to an area known as the Land of Ghouls, and their ultimate realisation that one of the few survivors was, most likely, a ghoul himself.

The story concludes with what appears to be noises of an attack on their safe house, and the implication that ghoul footsoldiers have come to wipe out all those who know of their existence.

### Behind the Mythos
One of the names mentioned by the men in connection with their topic is Swami Chandraputra, although both confess to having been an able to find anyone with knowledge on who that may be.

fullContent:
"The Glorious Return of Herbert West" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. It is a direct sequel to "Shoggoth Apocalypse" by the same authors.

### Synopsis
In the aftermath of the Shoggoth apocalypse, an isolated group of scientifically-minded survivors utilise the essential salts process described in "The Case of Charles Dexter Ward" to resurrect deceased geniuses in an effort to combat the incursion.

Unfortunately, the returned souls only last for a few weeks at most, and so the men resurrect the improbably-located remains of Herbert West with a view to using his reagent to extend the returnees' lifespans.

Once awakened, West has other plans on his mind, and takes over the facility, using the reagent and his own surgical skills to transform the returned humans into composite creatures capable of fighting the Shoggoths toe-to-toe.

### Characters
*Professor Vincent Andrews, a leading scientist with Curwen International Industries.
*Herbert West, a deranged physician obsessed with the thought of eternal life.

### Publication History
"The Glorious Return of Herbert West" was published in the 2019 collection The House of the Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares.

"The God Lurking in Stone" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Andrew Dombalagian. It was published in the 2011 anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press.

### Synopsis
In Neolithic Mesopotamia, a wandering trader dubbed the Black Pharaoh by the locals gifts idiot child Marduk with a mystical stone carving. His brother Tigranes, seeing the stone, is driven into a frenzy and murders Marduk, bashing his skull in and shattering the artefact. As he looks on in horror, a slug-like entity emerges from the shards and reanimates the body of Marduk, scooping up a glowing piece of stone which he calls the Trapezohedron, and declaring the birth of a new god.

### Behind the Mythos
Aside from the Shining Trapezohedron and Nyarlathotep in his Black Pharaoh guise, other Mythos elements made mention of are Leng, "the reptile and serpent men of Irem," and the Great Old Ones.

"The God of Dark Laughter" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Michael Chabon, first published in The New Yorker in April 2001 .

### Synopsis
A bereaved husband and father is involved in the investigation of a murder in his capacity as district attorney. The ritualistic killing, that of a circus clown, leads him to uncover the existence of two warring cults, each of which follow different gods and possess polarised outlooks on the nature of the universe.

### Behind the Mythos
The narrator's research leads him to a book on the occult written by Friedrich von Junzt, best known as the author of the blasphemous tome the Unaussprechlichen Kulten.
