shortDefinition: "The God-Box" is a horror short story by August Derleth connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the September 1945 issue of Weird Tales.  ### Synopsis In London, an archaeologist and smuggler of relics named Philip Caravel calls the emin...
fullContent:
"The God-Box" is a horror short story by August Derleth connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the September 1945 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
In London, an archaeologist and smuggler of relics named Philip Caravel calls the eminent Prof. Curtin to determine the value of an object. From his briefcase, Caravel removes a small copper box which Curtin immediately recognises as a God-Box, a Druidic artifact found originally in Stonehenge, which Caravel stole from a museum in Salisbury. Curtin is impressed and estimates the price at a thousand guineas, but urges Caravel not to open it. He explains that boxes like this were used by Druidic priests to hold entities such as demons and genies. The inscription on this one reveals that it contains an entity named Sho-Gath, which Curtin claims is Atlantean rather than Druidic, speculating that it might have been "called up out of the sea". The writings also refer to a "guardian", a druid priest responsible for keeping the box safe.

Caravel laughs off the professor's superstitions, pointing out that the guardian didn't prevent the box from being taken away from Stonehenge to the museum, although Curtin counters that in the museum there was no risk of anyone opening it. A heavy rain starts to fall as Curtin bids Caravel good-bye and the latter retires to go to sleep. At two o'clock in the morning, he is awakened by a knock at the door. Standing in the rain outside is an extraordinarily old man who tells Caravel to surrender the box to him. Caravel closes the door, alarmed by the thought that the theft has been discovered and that the old man might have already spoken to the police. He decides to break up the box to be able to hide it away, reasoning that he could easily restore it latter. Inside the box there is a small black stain, which instantly starts growing, expanding like it was made of smoke. Soon, the protoplasmic smoke creature fills up the entire room. A terrified Caravel notices that the creature behaves like a hungry animal.

On the next day, newspapers report that Caravel's house has been blown up as if by an explosion, although no signs of fire or powder were discovered. Caravel himself was torn apart, and not all of his remains were found. A woman who witnessed the event claims that, after the incident, she saw an old man accompanied by a cloud of smoke which followed him like a tamed animal, and that the old man placed something on the ground and spoke words in an unknown language, which caused the smoke creature to retreat inside the object. After that, the man picked up the object and went off in the direction of Salisbury.

### Connections
*The druid guardian tells Caravel "by the Sign of Koth" not to open the box. (: The Case of Charles Dexter Ward, The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

shortDefinition: "The Gods of Bal-Sagoth", also known as "The Blonde Goddess of Bal-Sagoth", is a short story by Robert E. Howard. It was first published on Weird Tales in October 1931.  ### Synopsis After a savage battle with Vikings and a subsequent shipwreck after...
fullContent:
"The Gods of Bal-Sagoth", also known as "The Blonde Goddess of Bal-Sagoth", is a short story by Robert E. Howard. It was first published on Weird Tales in October 1931.

### Synopsis
After a savage battle with Vikings and a subsequent shipwreck after being blown far off course, Turlogh O'Brien the Gael and his friend-enemy Athelstane the Saxon wash ashore on a mysterious island. Swiftly embroiled in rescuing a scantily clad blonde girl from a giant dinosaurian bird, they discover that the girl is actually a Viking princess, Brunhild. She explains to them that they have washed up on the Isle of the Gods, the "oldest land in the world". It transpires that the devil-bird the men killed was Groth-golka the bird god, the last of an ancient race that preyed upon the local people of the island's city-state for innumerable generations.

Having had the worst of it in the palace takeover she had plotted, Brunhild now enlists the aid of Turlogh and Athelstane to help her try and take power once more. Their main enemy is Gothan, an ancient priest who has enjoyed an unnaturally long life. Together with the menace of Gol-goroth the god of darkness, this is the countervailing political force the girl intends to overthrow.

In a tumultuous battle of champions, the Mesoamerican society of the island is conquered and Brunhild becomes their queen.

Gothan strikes from hiding, using his own hypnotic powers, ape-men assassins and a nameless Thing, a black-skinned demonic giant which is only killed with great difficulty. Then, whether from supernatural causes or sheer coincidence, Brunhild is crushed to death beneath the peculiar enormous statue of Gol-goroth and the local people rise up against the two fighting men. Turlogh and Athelstane slaughter their way to safety as the city burns around them and take to a boat, sailing from the lost island and on to new adventures.

### Notes
It is interesting perhaps to modern eyes that the bird monster Groth-golka clearly has dinosaurian traits - scale-like primitive feathers for example, which conform more to modern concepts of how dinosaurs appeared than the "giant lizard" versions current at the time the story was written.

The statue of the dark god Gol-goroth, as opposed to the putative dark god itself, seems to have electrical effects. In fact there are no "real" gods of any kind in this story, even though it does feature monsters and sorcery. Groth-golka is presented as the last of a species of prehistoric birds, centuries-old and worshiped by the people of Bal-Sagoth, but still a flesh and blood creature, as it's killed by Athelstane's sword. Both Groth-golka and the toad-like Gol-goroth have been elevated to the status of Great Old Ones by later authors (although it should be noted that Howard himself had already listed Gol-goroth alongside Cthulhu, Yog-Sothoth and Tsathoggua in "The Children of the Night").

In the first version of "The Fishers from Outside", Lin Carter confused the name of Groth-golka with Gol-goro

fullContent:
"The Gods of Earth" is a fantasy short story by Gary Myers set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the 1975 Arkham House anthology Nameless Places.

This story provides an alternative interpretation of the entities that H. P. Lovecraft referred to as the Gods of Earth in his fiction, positing that they are in fact the Elder Gods from Betelgeuse, as featured in the works of August Derleth.

It is also notable for incorporating elements from the woks of Lord Dunsany into the Mythos.

### Synopsis
Nath-Horthath, Nasht and Kaman-Thah are a trio of deities that currently hold the title of Gods of Earth, having come to Earth from the red star Betelgeuse in their ships of cloud before the advent of humanity. The people of the Dreamlands worship them as the "Elder Gods" and keep incense burning in their Temple so that the smoke may carry their prayers to this holy trio, which live in an onyx castle in unknown Kadath in the Cold Waste and occasionally spend time in other mountainous peaks.

However, these Elder Gods live in fear of the "Other Gods", a.k.a. the Great Old Ones, which are the spawn of Azathoth. When the Elder Gods arrived on Earth, they found the Other Gods asleep and imprisoned them under the Elder Sign to prevent their awakening. As mankind evolved and spread over the Dreamlands, the Other Gods have paradoxically protected the Gods of Earth against man's encroachments into the highest peaks. The reason for this is that the Other Gods want to keep their enemies confined to Kadath, waiting for when the Other Gods are ready to take their revenge. At one point, the Gods of Earth tried to escape to a sunset city dreamed by Randolph Carter, but the Other Gods forced them to return to Kadath to wait for their comeuppance.

On Mt. Hatheg-Kla, the Gods of Earth capture a dream of a city of rose-coloured marble. The dream bears "the trademark of MANA-YOOD-SUSHAI", with writings in the Yannish language that reveal it to be the dream of a drunkard named Peabody. Seeing an opportunity to escape their predicament, the Gods of Earth sail to the Waking World in their ships of cloud and find Peabody sleeping on a bench in a municipal park. They announce themselves to him, making flowers sprout from the concrete to prove their godhood, and propose to trade places with him. However, all the beauties of the Dreamlands fail to entice Peabody, who is content as long as he can have whiskey from "a certain tavern in Kingsport", and who is already king of his own dream-kingdom named Ong.

Faced with Peabody's unanticipated reluctance, the Gods try a different approach, visiting Peabody in his own castle in Ong, where he sits upon an ivory throne. They appeal to Peabody's tastes by pointing out that if he moves to Kadath, he will have all the wine in the cellars, as well as the fermented sap of a Moon tree, Gorgondy brewed by gnomes, etc. The purple wine convinces Peabody to seal the deal.

The Gods of H. P. Lovecraft is a collection of Cthulhu Mythos short stories.

### Overview
The Gods of H. P. Lovecraft contains twelve stories, each of which focuses on a different entity or species from the works of H. P. Lovecraft and comes accompanied by a brief essay on the beings as they appear in his fiction. Despite the title, not all of the featured monstrosities are actually gods in their original appearances.

Running to a total of 454 pages, The Gods of H. P. Lovecraft was published in December 2015 by JournalStone. It was edited by Aaron J. French with cover art from Chuck Killorin and additional material by Donald Tyson. It has also been given an ebook release through Amazon's digital Kindle platform.

A follow-up titled Azathoth: Ordo ab Chao was published in 2023.

fullContent:
The Gods of Pegāna is a book by the Anglo-Irish fantasy writer Lord Dunsany, his first; it was published in 1905 by Elkin Mathews, who also published works by W. B. Yeats, James Joyce, and Ezra Pound, among others. The book is organized as a series of sketches about an imaginary pantheon;  the concept was a key influence on H. P. Lovecraft, who said he "got the idea of the artificial pantheon and myth-background represented by 'Cthulhu', 'Yog-Sothoth', 'Yuggoth', etc." from Dunsany.

Dunsany published a sequel, Time and the Gods, in 1906.

### The Pantheon
The creator of the gods is MĀNA-YOOD-SUSHĀЇ, "the god of Having Done and of the Resting." After creating the gods, he went to sleep, and when he awakes again, it will be the end of the gods and all worlds. He is the one god man cannot pray to.

Skarl, the Drummer, attends MĀNA-YOOD-SUSHĀЇ, playing his drum to keep him asleep. When he stops playing, MĀNA-YOOD-SUSHĀЇ will be shocked by the silence and awaken, and it will be the end of gods and worlds.

### The Small Gods

* Kib, the "Sender of Life in all the Worlds." The god of beasts and men.
* Sish, "The Destroyer of Hours." The god of time.
* Slid, "whose Soul is by the Sea." The god of waters.
* Mung, "Lord of all Deaths between Pegāna and the Rim." The god of death.
* Limpang-Tung, "The God of Mirth and of Melodious Minstrels." The god of pleasure.
* Yoharneth-Lahai, "The God of Little Dreams and Fancies." The god of dreams.
* Roon, "The God of Going." The god of travel.
* Dorozhand, whose Eyes Regard the End. The god of destiny.
* Hoodrazai, the Eye in the Waste. The mirthless god who knows the secret of MĀNA-YOOD-SUSHĀЇ.
* Sirami, the Lord of All Forgetting
* Mosahn, the Bird of Doom
* Grimbol, Zeebol and Trehagobol, the three goddesses of the tallest mountains, mothers of the three broad rivers of the plains.

### The Thousand Home Gods
The " the little gods that sit before the hearth and mind the fire," they are "so small that they be lesser than men":

* Pitsu, who strokes the cat
* Hobith, who calms the dog
* Habaniah, the lord of glowing embers
* Little Zumbiboo, the lord of dust
* Old Gribaun, who sits in the heart of the fire to turn the wood to ash
* Kilooloogung, the lord of arising smoke
* Jabim, the Lord of broken things
* Triboogie, the Lord of Dusk
* Hish, the Lord of Silence, whose children are the bats
* Wohoon, the Lord of Noises in the Night
* Eimes, Zanes, and Segastrion, the three broad rivers of the plain, who once "rebelled against the law of the Worlds"
* Umbool, the Lord of the Drought
* Araxes, Zadres, and Hyraglion, stars in the south
* Ingazi, Yo, and Mindo, stars to the north

shortDefinition: The Golden Bough is an anthropology text across two volumes, written by by James George Frazer. It was first published in 1913. It aims to be a masterwork for a popular audience rather than a purely academic work and for many years in the twentieth c...
fullContent:
The Golden Bough is an anthropology text across two volumes, written by by James George Frazer. It was first published in 1913. It aims to be a masterwork for a popular audience rather than a purely academic work and for many years in the twentieth century following its publication it was a seminal reference work both for would-be real life magicians and magician orders and groups and also for fiction writers wanting not only inspiration but to play associative games between disparate cultures.

Frazer himself belonged to at least two different magical Orders, and was a keen student of the occult for many years prior to writing The Golden Bough. His work assimilated and compiled not only his own intensive scholarship but previously secret or overlooked folkoric traditions from across Europe. So began as it were a cottage industry of piecing together theoretical "lost survivals" of prehistoric beliefs, not only in witchcraft but in prehuman forces and powers.

### Inspiration for The Golden Bough
Frazer began his investigations into folklore, myth and history to try and solve the historical riddles surrounding an ancient mystery religion in Sicily. From this original aim grew a massive work on syncretism, the theory that many different cultures with their gods, superstitions and folklore, were expressing the "same" objectives and beliefs, so that for example Thor, Indra and Set were not just three different red headed storm gods but "the same" god under different names remembered by different cultures and peoples refracted through their local culture and experience. Another example is the Devas of India being the Devils of Medieval Christian Europe, and so on. 


### Influence on the Cthulhu Mythos
It is hard to overstate how enormous an influence The Golden Bough was on many Lovecraft inspired authors, and indeed in some ways on Lovecraft himself although Lovecraft's own erudition and research is often underestimated.

Frazer conceived, thanks to his ritual magic training, that the human mind could itself syncretize. In other words that the mind interfaced with something beyond itself that was a repository of what one might commonly call knowledge, but knowledge not obtained through learning but directly in what we might consider to be a process of "downloading." This is a homeopathic medicine concept and in magical terms is known as the Law of Sympathy, greatly expanded. Through this process, "one person could be related to almost any other across time and place and from within completely different histories and circumstances." This is a constant leitmotif, if not a plot point of countless Mythos stories.

Specific Cthulhu Mythos examples inspired by The Golden Bough include the conflating of the fictional deity Yig with the real world Quetzalcoatl and Kukulkan, and the "Black Goat of the Woods" obviously witchcraft-inspired name for Shub-Niggurath. fullContent:
"The Good Prince of Yron" is a short story by British author Gary Budgen, loosely linked to the Cthulhu Mythos through its setting in Zothique. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long-running horror magazine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
In the ancient land of Zothique, young Prince Artoon comes to the throne of Yron with a good heart and a desire to improve his kingdom, which had suffered under the rule of his black-hearted and selfish father. His actions steadily raise the realm from the depths of degeneracy to which it had fallen, but through time he comes to realise that what both he and his city are missing is a bride, a marriage which will strengthen them through political alliance.

Sending out invitations for nearby kingdoms to offer their candidates, the prince is immediately captivated by the beautiful Lady Mordalia, and sends for her straight away. Although she and her manservant Vaxhalen seem somewhat peculiar, the prince is delighted with his new bride, and the wedding proceeds without a hitch.

One evening, while standing on balcony overlooking Yron and the wastelands beyond, Artoon questions Mordalia on her eccentricities, to which she answers that her family descend from that of the rulers of Kallasser, a ruined city located on the shores of a sea turned to desert. Perhaps, she muses, her strangeness is down to the proximity of her former homeland, and that a trip there might help to soothe her quirks. Artoon readily agrees and assembles an expedition, which includes his loyal bodyguard Cark, and the mysterious Vaxhalen.

As the small party enter the distant ruins of Kallasser, calamity befalls as Mordalia lapses into unconsciousness. Cark, believing Vaxhalen has something to do with the tragedy confronts the old man, but runs in terror from a spell he casts upon him. Artoon, trapped by Vaxhalen and reduced to immobility, learns from the man that he is in fact the last survivor of Kallasser, an immortal sorcerer devoted to the annihilation of Yron after his own city's destruction at the hands of Yron centuries earlier. He reveals that he reanimated the body of a dead prostitute to pose as Lady Mordalia and lure Artoon to Kallasser, where the spilling of his innocent blood is the only thing which will activate an ancient curse and bring down the undead legions of Kallasser upon Yron. Fortunately for Artoon and Yron, the timely intervention of a recovered Cark saves the Prince and ends in Vaxhalen's death.

Artoon is however devastated by the passing of his bride, and theorises that if she could be reanimated once, then there is nothing to stop the process from working again. To this end he begins to study the dark arts of necromancy, and in doing so abandons the welfare of his city and blackens his soul with evil magics.

fullContent:
"The Gorge Beyond Salapunco: The Testament of Claiborne Boyd" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by August Derleth, part of his Trail of Cthulhu series. It was written in June 1946, but not published until the March 1949 issue of Weird Tales.

### Reception
Few people are enthusiastic about this story, starting with Derleth himself: "I am far from satisfied with it, believe me," he wrote to a correspondent. "I think it a very poor job." He complained of the difficulty of writing a story complete in itself that also serves as a transition between two parts of a novel. S. T. Joshi dismissed it as “a retelling of ‘The Call of Cthulhu’”, while Derleth specialist John Haefele calls it "subpar". Weird Tales initially rejected it in July 1946, saying "we like this latest Cthulhu the least of all our problem material," before agreeing to publish it three years later.

### Characters
*Claiborne Boyd: A scholar of Creole culture and the heir of a wealthy New Orleans family.
*Asaph Gilman: A retired Miskatonic University professor of nuclear physics and student of the Mythos, who dies under mysterious circumstances.
*Japhet Smith: An agent of the Cthulhu Cult.

shortDefinition: "The Graveyard Rats" is a Lovecraftian short story written by Henry Kuttner that appeared in the March 1936 issue of Weird Tales. Kuttner's first published piece, it caught the attention of H. P. Lovecraft and brought Kuttner into the Lovecraft Circl...
fullContent:
"The Graveyard Rats" is a Lovecraftian short story written by Henry Kuttner that appeared in the March 1936 issue of Weird Tales. Kuttner's first published piece, it caught the attention of H. P. Lovecraft and brought Kuttner into the Lovecraft Circle. 

### Synopsis
The old-timers of Salem, Massachusetts, speak of the dark and eldritch things which lurk beneath their town, guiding the huge rats and less-savoury creatures which plague Salem to do their dark bidding.

Old Masson, a cemetery caretaker with a sideline in graverobbing, doesn’t believe these tales. Aware of the rat problem, he wages a covert war with the beasts for years, as they keep dragging off the bodies which he is intent on looting.

When one night Masson unearths a body just as the creatures are dragging it off, he crawls down the oversized tunnel in an attempt to retrieve it. However, he is ambushed by the rats in the warren, and then attacked by an animated corpse before becoming trapped in a dead-end tunnel and suffocating.

### Connections
While the story has no explicit references to Mythos elements, its depiction of corpse-eating humanoids who tunnel below cemeteries, a "moribund, inhuman life that was said to exist in forgotten burrows in the earth," seems to owe a great deal to Lovecraft's ghouls, as they appeared in stories like "Pickman's Model."

Kuttner's suggestion of "blasphemous secrets and mysteries...said to be hidden in subterranean cellars and caverns, where forgotten pagan rites were still celebrated in defiance of law and sanity" by "evil cults that worshipped Hecate and the dark Magna Mater in frightful orgies" evokes stories like "The Rats in the Walls" and "The Horror at Red Hook." 

The setting of "ancient, witch-haunted Salem," whose "dark gabled houses still leaned perilously towards each other over narrow cobbled streets," strongly recalls Lovecraft's Arkham.

### Characters
*Old Masson, a graverobbing cemetery caretaker.

### Publication History
The Graveyard Rats was first published in the March 1936 issue of Weird Tales, and was subsequently reprinted in the short story collection The Gruesome Book (edited by Ramsey Campbell) in 1983, then again in Weird Tales: Seven Decades of Terror in 1997. The story was also included in Wildside Press LLC's eBook bundle The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack in 2012. 

### Adaptations

* Trilogy of Terror II (1997): A screen version was filmed for this TV movie anthology, although it bears little resemblance to the original story.
* "Graveyard Rats": An episode of the Netflix series Guillermo del Toro's Cabinet of Curiosities was based on the story, with a somewhat expanded backstory for Masson.

The Great God Pan is a horror novella telling of misogyny, miscegenation, rape and the crossing over of two worlds, written by Welsh writer Arthur Machen and published in 1890.

### Synopsis
The story is that of a woman violated by an extra-dimensional entity. She then gives birth to a daughter who is in fact the incarnated form of something from beyond. It is an experimental mix of science fiction and gothic horror.

### Connection to the Mythos
It is mentioned by Henry Armitage as a direct parallel to the Dunwich Horror (: "The Dunwich Horror") suggesting it was Lovecraft's inspiration for his story.

### Publication History
"The Great God Pan" was first published in the collection The Great God Pan and The Inmost Light in 1894. It has since been reprinted many times in many different publications.

The Great Old Ones: New Adventures Against the Cthulhu Mythos is a campaign supplement book for Chaosium's horror roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu.

### Overview
Consisting of a series of six scenarios thematically linked by the inclusion of Great Old Ones, the book's included adventures can either be played as stand-alone missions, or in sequence to form a loose campaign. The Great Old Ones was written by Marcus L. Rowland, Kevin Ross, Harry Cleaver, Doug Lyons, and L. N. Isinwyll, with cover art provided by Tom Sullivan. It includes a selection of player handouts and runs to 176 pages.

The Great Old Ones was nominated for, and won, the Origins Award for Best Roleplaying Adventure of 1989.

### Publication History
First published in 1989 The Great Old Ones was reissued as a digital PDF in 2004 which is still available at DriveThruRPG. The print version is no longer available.

"The Green Fireballs" is a short story by author Jason Radak which is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the Lammas Eve edition of Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
Told through two separate conversations, one between mall employees and the other involving agents from two shady government agencies, "The Green Fireballs" tells of how an ancient, dead-but-dreaming entity was discovered sleeping beneath the land which would one day become the town of Claremont, New Jersey. The being was left in place and experimented on, and eventually a shopping mall was allowed to spring up atop the putrefying corpse, with the agencies monitoring the strange effects it’s psychic emanations had on the shoppers and staff.

The story concludes with the being stirring in its sleep, and the first tendrils of its awakening form beginning to make their way into the outside world.

### Behind the Mythos
When one of the characters, an undercover agent named Hansen Murdoch, makes his appearance, he refers to the entity beneath the mall as "Cthulhu's cousin".

### Trivia
*The green fireballs of the title refers in part to the name of a fictional psychedelic rock band whose frontman was a man named G Large. This is a possible nod to Gerry Large - who writes as G. Large - an author who wrote the story "Prom Night, or Whateley Family Happiness", published in the same issue of Lovecraftiana as "The Green Fireballs".

fullContent:
"The Green Meadow" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Winifred V. Jackson written in 1918/19 and published in the spring 1927 issue of The Vagrant. As in their other collaboration, "The Crawling Chaos", both authors used pseudonyms — the tale was published as by "Elizabeth Neville Berkeley" (Jackson) and "Lewis Theobald, Jun." (Lovecraft). Lovecraft wrote the entire text but Jackson is credited, since it was based on a dream she had experienced.

According to critic Moreau Vazh, the story owes a rather large debt to “The Willows” by Algernon Blackwood. Vazh also suggests that the story, and the dream from which it took its existence, relate to the Afterlife, citing the phrase at the end of the story:I knew now the change through which I had passed, and through which certain others who once were men had passed! and I knew the endless cycle of the future which none like me may escape. . . . I shall live forever, be conscious forever, though my soul cries out to the gods for the boon of death and oblivion. . . . All is before me: beyond the deafening torrent lies the land of Stethelos, where young men are infinitely old.

### Synopsis
A rocklike object crashes into the sea and is hauled ashore to a nearby village by a fishing vessel for scientists and experts to examine. Within the object is a small notebook, made of some indestructible material and inscribed in classical Greek. The notebook is the first-person account of a man trapped on a small, disintegrating island, who seems threatened by shadowy forces, and ultimately discovers Stethelos, a city from Lovecraft's Dream Cycle Mythos.

### Plot Summary
The story begins by explaining how the text was discovered. On the evening of Wednesday, August 27, 1913, at about 8:30 o’clock the people of Potowonket, Maine, see a strange rocklike object land in the sea. Four days later large, a fragment is brought in by a fishing boat and is identified by Dr. Richmond M. Jones of Boston as a 360 lb. aerolite or meteoric stone. The identification of the object as a meteorite is controversial; Professor Mayfield of MIT concurs with this classification, while Dr. von Wintefeldt of Heidelberg rejects it; Professsor Bradley of Columbia maintains no categorization is possible, pointing out that the object contains utterly unidentifiable substances.

While collecting samples for a Boston specialist, Jones discovers a mysterious manuscript within, which he keeps. The cover of 5 × 3 inch 30 leaf book of made from a dark, unbreakable, stone-like substance that puzzles geologists. Though they are incredibly thin, the lighter pages are similarly invulnerable and cannot be removed. The undated writing within is determined as perfect second century B.C. cursive Greek, but during his analysis Prof. Chambers does irreparable damage to the writing on the last pages. The remaining document was transcribed into the modern Greek alphabet and presented for translation.

shortDefinition: "The Grinning Ghoul" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the June 1936 issue of Weird Tales. The plot, involving a psychiatrist whose attempts to treat a patient put the doctor himself in a sanitarium, reflects the fact that Bloch...
fullContent:
"The Grinning Ghoul" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the June 1936 issue of Weird Tales. The plot, involving a psychiatrist whose attempts to treat a patient put the doctor himself in a sanitarium, reflects the fact that Bloch was "long skeptical of the pretensions of psychiatrists...regarding them as little more than shamans in suits."

### Synopsis
The narrator is an "inmate of a sanitorium for mental cases" who six months earlier was a "well-known and moderately successful practicing psychiatrist". In an effort to treat Alexander Chaupin, a professor at Newberry College, who has recurring nightmares about ghouls living beneath Misericorde Cemetery, the doctor insists that the two of them visit the graveyard at night to demonstrate that the creatures he fears are imaginary. When Chaupin leads the doctor to a tomb, he is surprised to find that there is indeed a secret opening there--giving access to stairways that drop deep into the earth. At the bottom is a vast cavern system, where Chaupin leaves the doctor, saying he will bring back proof that his stories are true. Instead, the doctor hears a cry, then "the rustling scrape of frantic movement", then a "hoarse barking", a "bestial growling" that sickens him with "its semi-human tones". The doctor races up the stairs, and slams the secret portal shut in the face of the pursuing ghouls--but not before he sees that the leader of the pack is Professor Chaupin.

### Behind the Mythos
In an effort to convince the doctor of the truth of his claims, Chaupin cites a number of Cthulhu Mythos tomes: "Ludvig Prinn's Mysteries of the Worm", "the grotesque Black Rites of mystic Luveh-Keraphf, the priest of cryptic Bast", and "the mad and legendary Necronomicon of Abdul Alhazred". He makes mysterious references to "the banned and infamous Fable of Nyarlathotep", and the "Legend of the Elder Saboth"; he speaks of "fabled Leng, lightless N'ken, and demon-haunted Nis", as well as "such blasphemies as the Moon of Yiggurath and the secret parable of Byagoona the Faceless One."

Of course, the doctor dismisses all this as "incoherent ravings"--but he does prepare for their visit to the cemetery with "a hasty perusal of the expurgated edition of Comte d'Erlette's Cultes des Goules."

### References

fullContent:
"The Guardian of the Book" is a short story by Henry Hasse that appeared in the March 1937 issue of Weird Tales. 

It is narrated by a Doctor Wycherly, who haunts used bookstores out of a "desire to peruse those so-called ‘forbidden books’ which speak of the unthinkable things of evil." He is offered the chance by a strange bookseller to read "the most Damnable Book ever loosed upon an unsuspecting Cosmos"--though he learns that reading this book will carry the ultimate cost.

The story is included in the collection Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos (Fedogan & Bremer, 1992).

### Mythos Tomes
The story includes an early catalog of Mythos tomes:The various versions of Alhazred’s Necronomicon, Flammarion’s Atmosphere, Von Junzt’s Nameless Cults, Kane’s Magic and Black Arts, Eibon’s Book, and the mysterious King in Yellow—which, if it does indeed exist, must transcend them all—none of these will you find lying around in bookstores.Flammarion's Atmosphere is a real book, chiefly remembered today for the first appearance of the Flammarion Engraving, an image of a traveler poking his head through the dome of the sky. The work by Kane was created by Bertram Russell in "The Scourge of B'Moth", although in that work it was called Magic and the Black Arts.

"The Guy" is a short story by English author Ramsey Campbell which is connected to the greater Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published by Arkham House in his collection Demons by Daylight in 1973. Since then, a German-language translation has also been released.

### Synopsis
Denis and Joe, two boys from different sides of the tracks, form an unlikely friendship when Joe's family moves into Denis' middle-class neighbourhood. After a while, Joe tells Denis about the death of his brother, Frankie, in a bonfire accident years previously, which he believes himself at least partially responsible for. When Guy Fawkes Night rolls around, Joe's family agrees to allow him to have friends over for a bonfire celebration. However, a malicious act by Joe's father results in the Guy being possessed by the spirit of Frankie which claims the boy's life.

### Mythos Connections
Despite containing no direct references to Lovecraft's works, "The Guy" takes place in Brichester, a town located in Campbell's Severn Valley setting, which has been the backdrop for many of his Lovecraftian stories.

### Publication History
* Demons by Daylight (1973, 1975, 1979, 1980, 1990, 2017)
* Dämonen bei Tag (1998)

fullContent:
The H.P. Lovecraft Historical Society, or HPLHS, is an organisation created in 1984 that is devoted to the promotion of the works of Howard Phillips Lovecraft and the Mythos. They produce a wide range of media based on that material. Founded in Colorado, it is now based in Glendale, California. The society's motto is "Ludo Fore Putavimus," which translates to "We thought it would be fun."

### Formation
The society saw its roots with a group of friends and Call of Cthulhu gamers including Sean Branney, Andrew Leman, and Darrell Tutchton. As all were amateur drama enthusiasts, they decided to home-brew their own live-action roleplaying system; during one session, passers-by who were unaware of what was happening with the group called the police and "a quick-thinking Sean … told them the group was the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society. The police were mollified and the name stuck." 

In 1986, Branney and Leman, along with Phil Bell, formally established the group, and set it on the path to become what it is today .

### Community Engagement
HPLHS is the largest organization of Lovecraft enthusiasts globally, with members in over fifty countries. They offer props for role-playing games and provide resources for fans to engage with Lovecraft's universe.

### Conclusion
The H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society plays a significant role in preserving and promoting Lovecraft's legacy through various media, fostering a community of fans and creators dedicated to his unique brand of cosmic horror. They created the Cthulhu Lives Live Action Role Playing (LARP) game and produced film and audio pieces; usually adaptations of Lovecraft stories. They also ran the Strange Eons fanzine.

"The Half Made Thing" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story and poem by American author T. E. Grau. 

### Synopsis
Young Eliot, whose father has been bewitched by a wealthy witch-woman named Marsila, moves into an enormous estate in Northumberland, England. Ignored by his father and step-mother, he spends his days alone, exploring his new home, and comes across a derelict watermill, within which dwells a disgusting, malformed creature. Befriending the monster, Eliot agrees to help it, and spends the next few months learning the ways of magic from it. However, the Half Made Thing has tricked the boy, and the spells he has been casting ultimately result in the Thing becoming it’s fully-formed, inhuman self, while Eliot transforms into a hideous abomination. 

### Characters
* Eliot, an 11-year-old boy uprooted from his home by a witch with no interest in him. 
* The Half Made Thing, a being from beyond whose manifestation has not been fully completed. 
* Marsila, Eliot's new step-mother, a depraved witch who is not entirely human. 
* Nevill, Eliot's father. 

### Publication History
"The Half Made Thing" was published in the thematic anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu by April Moon Books in March 2014.

### Trivia
* Although the story comprises the majority of "The Half Made Thing", the final three pages consist of a poem giving a recap of the tale. This poem contains a reference to the Elder Things.

"The Hands That Reek and Smoke" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author W. H. Pugmire, first published in his collection Sesqua Valley and Other Haunts (2008, Mythos Books) .

### Synopsis
The narrator, a jaded and cynical artist, listens in contempt as his friends wax lyrical about a new personality on the scene, a mysterious man named Nyarlathotep. Finally persuaded to visit the newcomer and take him as their muse, the narrator falls under Nyarlathotep's spell as so many have before. However, on their return home, they witness what has become of one of their friends, and realises that there may be more to this charismatic stranger than meets the eye.

"The Happenings of December 13th, 2012" is a short story by Troy Young. It is the final instalment of Book 1 of the Nyarlathotep Cycle, but does little to add much, aside from finally revealing the name of the government organisation which employs the characters and elaborating upon Harjit Singh's backstory.

### Synopsis
Presented as a report written six months after the fact, the story details Harjit Singh's first encounter with The Other, Sinh's term for the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos.

Singh and his group are walking back from their shift on the Fort McMurray oil fields when they are splashed by a strange glowing goo dripping from the basket of a power shovel. Shortly thereafter, one of the group goes insane and murders his entire family, whereupon the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena steps in and euthanises the others, all except Singh (who was uncontaminated) who they recruit into their ranks.

### Characters
*Harjit Singh, a man working an unspecified job on the oil fields.
*Big Mike, one of Singh's co-workers.

### Publication History
"The Happenings of December 13th, 2012" was published in The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 1 in 2020.

The Hastur Cycle: 13 Tales that Created and Define Dread Hastur, the King in Yellow, Nighted Yuggoth, and Dire Carcosa is a thematic Cthulhu Mythos anthology by Chaosium as part of their Cthulhu Cycle series of fiction.

### Overview
As its name might suggest, The Hastur Cycle focuses on the Great Old One Hastur, first incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft from a short story by Ambrose Bierce. It also explores the mythology of the King in Yellow as invented by Robert W. Chambers and elaborated by other authors. 

Each of the stories had been previously published and features a short introduction by editor Robert M. Price, who also provided additional material. It features cover and interior artwork by Dreyfus, was first published by Chaosium in October 1993, and ran to 304 pages.

A second revised edition was issued in June 2006, with all new cover art by H. E. Fassl, an interior plate by Earl Geier, and a poem and short story not featured in the first edition. This edition ran to 300 pages.

fullContent:
"The Haunter of the Dark" is a short story by the late H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
The story takes place in Providence, Rhode Island and revolves around the Church of Starry Wisdom. The cult uses an ancient artifact known as the Shining Trapezohedron to summon a terrible being from the depths of time and space.

The Shining Trapezohedron was discovered in Egyptian ruins, in a box of alien construction, by Professor Enoch Bowen before he returned to Providence in 1844. Members of the Church of Starry Wisdom in Providence would awaken the Haunter of the Dark, an avatar of Nyarlathotep, by gazing into the glowing crystal. Summoned from the black gulfs of chaos, this being could show other worlds, other galaxies, and the secrets of arcane and paradoxical knowledge; but he demanded monstrous sacrifices, hinted at by disfigured skeletons that were later found in the church. The Haunter of the Dark was banished by light and could not cross a lighted area.

The Shining Trapezohedron is a window on all space and time. Described as a "crazily angled stone", it is unlikely to be a true trapezohedron because of the Old Ones' penchant for bizarre non-Euclidean angles. It was created on dark Yuggoth and brought to Earth by the Old Ones, where it was placed in its box aeons before the first human beings appeared. It has further history in Atlantis and with the Pharaohs of Egypt, until it was finally unearthed and brought to New England.

After the death of Robert Blake, who came to grief after discovering the Shining Trapezohedron and deciphering texts about it from ancient evil cults, the artifact was removed from the black windowless temple where it was found by a Dr. Dexter and thrown into the deepest channel of Narragansett Bay. It was expected to remain there, under the eternal light of the stars, forever.

### The Shadow from the Steeple
Yet, Robert Bloch's sequel, "The Shadow From the Steeple", proved that Nyarlathotep had cheated Dexter, forcing him to peer into the stone and actually throw the stone into the bay, where the eternal darkness of the depths gave the Haunter the power to remain perpetually free; it used this power to merge with Dr. Dexter and make him one of the world's leading nuclear scientists in charge of atomic investigation for warfare.

### Characters
*Robert Blake
*Enoch Bowen
*Ambrose Dexter

### Continuity
*The Shining Trapezohedron is mentioned as having being fashioned on Yuggoth, an outpost of the Mi-Go mentioned in The Whisperer in Darkness.
*The Shining Trapezohedron "was treasured and placed in its curious box by the crinoid things of Antarctica," suggesting a connection with the Elder Things from At the Mountains of Madness.
*The serpent-men of Valusia also held possession of the Shining Trapezohedron at one point, connecting it to the Kull tales of Robert E. Howard.

shortDefinition: "The Haunter of the Graveyard" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author and Lovecraft correspondent J. Vernon Shea.  ### Synopsis Elmer Harrod, a television presenter and scriptwriter, develops a morbid fascination with the sprawli...
fullContent:
"The Haunter of the Graveyard" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author and Lovecraft correspondent J. Vernon Shea.

### Synopsis
Elmer Harrod, a television presenter and scriptwriter, develops a morbid fascination with the sprawling graveyard which lies next to his home. His obsession first begins to manifest when he directs short films in the cemetery, later noticing aberrations which might be otherworldly creatures appearing in the final cuts.

As he slowly spends more and more of his time there, he takes to reading and, eventually, sleeping atop the graves. During these sessions, he starts to dream of a cult to the Great Old One Cthulhu and his sorcerous disciples whose activities are something of a historical scandal.

After a time Harrod disappears, his badly decomposed and partially eaten remains eventually being discovered in the area of the cemetery which he had come to think of as the Witches' Hollow.

### Characters
* Elmer Harrod, a curious man in the television industry.

### Publication History
"The Haunter of the Graveyard" was first published in the August Derleth-edited anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in 1969. It has since been reprinted several times, and has also been translated into French.

### Trivia
* Harrod was stated to have cast students from Miskatonic University in his short films, and remembers making the acquaintance of one Randolph Carter in his early years.

fullContent:
"The Haunter of the Ring" is a short story by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Robert E. Howard.

### Synopsis
The malicious Joseph Roelocke gifts a woman who rejected him a possessed ring, which causes her to attempt to murder her husband. Unfortunately for Roelocke, the evil entity which inhabits the ring turns on him instead and rends his soul from his body.

### Characters
*John Kirowan, a mysterious man who possesses a wealth of knowledge on the occult.
*Michael O'Donnel, Kirowan's friend.
*James "Jim" Gordon, a friend of Kirowan and O'Donnell.
*Evelyn Gordon (née Ash), Jim's wife.
*Joseph Roelocke/Yosef Vrolok, a black-hearted, if somewhat unskilled, occultist.

### Publication History
"The Haunter of the Ring" was first published in Weird Tales in June 1934 and has been reprinted many times in many different publications. It has also been translated into German, French and Portuguese.

### Trivia

* The ring gifted to Evelyn by Vrolok is the Serpent Ring of Set once possessed by the Stygian sorcerer Thoth-amon.

shortDefinition: "The Haunting", originally titled "The Haunted House", is a scenario for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium, written by Sandy Petersen. It was originally released as a part of the 1st edition, and has been repeatedly published to bring ...
fullContent:
"The Haunting", originally titled "The Haunted House", is a scenario for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium, written by Sandy Petersen. It was originally released as a part of the 1st edition, and has been repeatedly published to bring it in line with new editions. As a result, "More people have played this Call of Cthulhu scenario than any other", according to the 6th edition rule book.

The scenario's 7th edition incarnation is currently available as a free PDF, as a part of the Call of Cthulhu Quick-Start Rules.

### Summary
In Boston, Massachusetts in the 1920s, the investigators are hired by a landlord (called Mr. Knott in the 7th edition revision) to investigate a seemingly cursed house. The tenants, Vittorio and Gabriela Macario, have both gone insane and were committed within a two-year period.  The landlord had heard rumors about the house being haunted when he bought it, so he defers to the investigators' expertise.  

Looking into the matter, the investigators hopefully discover a long line of deaths and injuries attached to the house, and learn that it was built by a Mr. Walter Corbitt, a member of the a religious group called the Chapel of Contemplation. At some point after Corbitt's death, the Chapel was investigated by the police after the disappearance of several neighborhood children, leading to a gunfight and a fire.  The investigators can visit the ruins, and (most likely after falling through a patch of weakened floorboards), can find a hidden chamber containing the Liber Ivonis, and records showing that Corbitt had been buried by the church in the basement of his former house, "in accordance with his wishes and with the wishes of that One Who Waits in the Dark."

Finally braving the house, the investigators are likely drawn to Corbitt's former bedroom by a series of supernatural incidents, culminating with Corbitt's bed being hurled by an invisible force, frequently knocking an investigator out the window to their deaths. The apparent ghost can also attempt to stab the investigators via an enchanted knife. Ideally, the investigators will finally discover a secret crawlspace in the basement, where they discover Corbitt's body on a bier.  Described as an "Undead Fiend," who is "in the process of transforming himself into something entirely inhuman," Corbitt attacks the investigators with his magic. If given the opportunity, he may have already summoned a Dimensional Shambler to aid him before the battle begins.

If Corbitt is destroyed, the keeper is encouraged to use various clues throughout the scenario to link to their next adventure, potentially continuing the story of the Chapel, or of Corbitt's transformation and notes.  If the investigators find nothing or renege on their agreement, the landlord attempts to sleep in the house himself to see if is safe, and is killed.

shortDefinition: "The Haunting of Halton Grange" is a short Thomas Carnacki story by American author William Jeffrey Rankin which contains some minor Cthulhu Mythos references. The first in his Black Obelisk trilogy, it was published in the collection The Carnacki Ca...
fullContent:
"The Haunting of Halton Grange" is a short Thomas Carnacki story by American author William Jeffrey Rankin which contains some minor Cthulhu Mythos references. The first in his Black Obelisk trilogy, it was published in the collection The Carnacki Casebooks, Volume 1 in November 2019.

### Synopsis
Occult investigator Thomas Carnacki is called upon to look into the case of Lord Halton, who is being plagued by an unknown, violent force at his country estate. unknown to all, Halton's great-grandfather, a man named Edward, had been secretly practicing the dark arts and engaging in human sacrifice. When Edward’s brother Colin discovered his vile deeds, he resolved to put a stop to them, but was framed by Edward for a double murder and subsequently killed by the evil sorcerer.

Back in the modern day, Colin’s angry spirit returns to Halton Grange, where it contrives to put the evidence of his innocence into Carnacki's hands, and provide him with the means to end the evil which still permeates out from Edward's legacy. Making their way to the family sepulchre, Carnacki, Halton, and the butler Carlisle discover Edward’s secret place of worship and its source of power: the fragment of a black obelisk. Although Edward’s spirit attempts to resurrect itself by possessing Halton's body, Carnacki and Carlisle are able to remove the obelisk from its altar, banishing Edward’s black soul back into the void.

### Mythos Connections
In Edward’s hidden place of worship, Carnacki, Halton, and Carlisle discover a hoard of forbidden knowledge, including the Comte d'Erlette's Cultes des Goules and Von Junzt's Unaussprechlichen Kulten.

### References

shortDefinition: "The Heart of the Sea" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Mick Gall, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphiu...
fullContent:
"The Heart of the Sea" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Mick Gall, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Synopsis
An undisclosed location in the Pacific Ocean during World War II: an Australian commando unit and their civilian doctor are seconded to eccentric professor Raymond Blackburn. Their mission is to investigate a series of islands which have been recently reported to have spontaneously arisen following increasingly violent geological activity in the region. Although the indigenous tribes have avoided the new landmasses, believing them to cursed, German and Japanese forces have shown an unusual interest in them.

Making their way to the closest of these new islands, the group discovered that it is even larger than they had been led to believe, and plays host to what appears to be a building. Investigation reveals that it is some kind of artificial structure, one which plays host to an unusual object seemingly made from living seawater. Blackburn grabs hold of the artefact and it attaches itself to him just as a Japanese gunboat arrives offshore and enemy soldiers hit the beach.

Fortunately for all, Blackburn has come to the realisation that the artefact, which he has dubbed "the Heart of the Sea" is a living being which allows him to exert control over all forms of water- including that contained within the human body. Gruesomely killing most of their attackers and sinking the Japanese gunboat, the group are confronted by Black Sun operative Johann Klampt, who is intent on retrieving the prize. During the showdown, a rogue bullet smashes the artefact into two pieces; Blackburn and Klampt each retrieve one and the German retreats, his goal achieved. 

In the aftermath, Blackburn reveals to the rest of the squad that his half of the Heart of the Sea has regenerated itself into a complete organism once again, albeit one whose powers appear to be reduced. He then recruits the others permanently into his shadowy organisation with the prospect of interesting missions in their future. 

### Mythos Connections
Aside from "The Heart of the Sea"'s roleplaying game setting, when asked about the nature of the beings which created the structure and artefact, one of the solutions presented by Blackburn is "just another race that was here before mankind. Atlantis, maybe, or Hyperborea."

fullContent:
"The Hidden Door" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Brittany Groves. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long-running horror periodical Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
A few weeks after its purchase, real estate agent Charles Merryweather relates the story of an old house's former occupants to its new owner.

The Billingtons, Andrew and Catherine, plan to enjoy their devoted marriage in an expansive New England manse. However, at some point, Catherine is seduced by a dark cult dedicated to the Outer God Yog-Sothoth living within the walls of the building and begins to give birth to a horde of abominations as Andrew is driven to the depths of insanity before the pair disappear, never to be seen again.

The story concludes with the ominous news that the new owner's wife has mysteriously become pregnant…

fullContent:
"The Hill of the Beast" is a short story by Harry Turtledove originally published in the anthology Mountains of Madness Revealed (2019), edited by Darrell Schweitzer. The anthology collects stories that serve as sequels to H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness.

### Synopsis
The story is the first person account of Moishe Leutner, a New York City-born Communist and volunteer with the Abraham Lincoln Brigade who fought in the Battle of the Ebro during the Spanish Civil War. 

While Leutner was intrigued by the discoveries in Antarctica outlined in Lovecraft's work, his ideology prompted him to go to Spain and join the Spanish Republicans. After surviving fierce fighting in July 1938, Leutner's squad is assigned to take Hill 666, which he dubs "The Hill of the Beast". On the eve of the assault, Leutner hears the Nationalists holding Mass, but he also hears flute playing that he realizes is out of place. He suspects that the Nationalists may have obtained something from Antarctica. The next day, a shoggoth attacks the Republican advance.

The story includes a postscript that confirms that Leutner went on to serve with the United States Army in various theaters during World War II, and became a successful civil rights attorney in New York after the war, dying in 1991.

fullContent:
The Hills Rise Wild!, which boasted the tagline A frenzied fury of hillbilly horror!, was a tabletop combat game loosely based on the greater Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
The premise of The Hills Rise Wild! is that Old Wizard Whateley has died and left his occult possessions to be looted. As a result, four Clans have gathered in the small town of Dunwich to battle it out for Whateley's copy of the Necronomicon. 

This transfers onto the tabletop as a modular game board representing Dunwich, and six card tents to represent the members of each Clan. The object of the game was for the player to locate the Necronomicon and bring it back to their home building. A tape measure was provided for measuring movement and range, and a 20-sided dice to determine combat and magic.

### Behind the Mythos
The Hills Rise Wild! was created by Jesper Myrfors and John Tynes with artwork by Dennis Detwiller, and was published in 2000 by Pagan Publishing, Tynes' own label. It is currently out of print.

shortDefinition: "The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. It was written in 1933 but not published until 1994, in Necronomicon Press’s The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast and One Other.  ### Synopsis On an unnamed alien world, i...
fullContent:
"The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. It was written in 1933 but not published until 1994, in Necronomicon Press’s The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast and One Other.

### Synopsis
On an unnamed alien world, in the many-towered city-state of Zeth, the chief wizard-auditor of the city, Yalden, discovers that the city is bankrupt and its presumed treasure missing. To remedy this, he seeks the counsel of the oracle-god Oorn, a huge gelatinous mass covered in short grey fur. Oorn had slithered its bulk into Zeth one day from parts unknown, and become the de facto ruler of the city-state.

With an ambiguous phrase, it encourages Yalden to do what he was already considering, namely raid the powerful necromancer Anathas. Anathas is mysterious and no one has seen him; some suggest he cast a gigantic shadow, but there is no solid information on him. 

This being so, Yalden consults the Lord of Worms, Sarall. Sarall proves to be a tiny maggot and not a gigantic eldritch entity, one of many ironic touches in this tale.

Yalden goes to the lair of Anathas and discovers a fiery lake inhabited by fire elemental creatures: Salamanders and Wyvern. He discovers that the fire barrier is easy to cross, and beyond it lies the enormous treasure of Anathas.

While he is still admiring it, the passage through the fire closes of its own accord, trapping him. A huge seven-eyed creature heaves into view, looking down on him with amusement as the Salamanders slowly approach his position, preparing to devour him.

### Behind the Mythos
This two-page story was the second collaboration between Lovecraft and the sixteen-year-old Barlow, created during Lovecraft's visit to Barlow in his home in Florida. It is a light-hearted ironic twist on the traditional fantasy stories, full of pompous descriptions and weighty matters. Jack Vance would make a cottage industry of such writing decades after this tale was written, but this work was not published in Lovecraft's lifetime, and would have received only a narrow circulation at the time among his Circle.

"The Hog" is a short story by the late author William Hope Hodgson which first appeared in the collection Carnacki the Ghost-Finder in 1947, nearly three decades after Hodgson's death. Chaosium retroactively incorporated the story into the Cthulhu Mythos when they included the antagonist, which they dubbed "Saaitti", as a Great Old One in the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Synopsis
Thomas Carnacki takes on the case of a man plagued by a malignant supernatural swine. He is eventually able to banish the entity, but discovers that the creature may have entered our world through the man's mind.

"The Hole in the Wall Gang" is an episode of the animated series The Real Ghostbusters written by science fiction author David Gerrold and first aired in 1987. Taking place in the town of Arkham, Massachusetts, it is one of three episodes of the series connected to the Cthulhu Mythos, along with "The Collect Call of Cathulhu" and "Russian About".

### Synopsis
A rich cheesemaker named Limburger and his wife move into a new mansion in Arkham, where they find themselves plagued by paranormal activity, with ghosts and apparitions making noises, baying at the moon, and leaving trails of slime around the house. After enduring this situation for three weeks, the couple finally decides to hire the Ghostbusters: a team of paranormal investigators consisting of Egon Spengler, Ray Stantz, Peter Venkman, and Winston Zeddemore. Not wanting to interfere, the Limburgers leave the house while these consummate professionals do their job.

Egon's P.K.E. Meter traces the source of supernatural activity to a small hole in the wall that apparently leads to the realm of spiritual beings. When Peter fires his Proton Pack into the hole, a small creature comes out of it. While trying to capture it, the Ghostbusters fire several shots, resulting in several more holes from which small ghosts of all types and appearances start to emerge. Wacky hijinks apart, the little ghosts seem harmless enough. However, Egon's readings detect something much bigger on the other side of the main hole. To investigate, he sends a remote-controlled probe attached to a cable. Something from the other side captures the probe, and Ray is pulled into the hole as he holds the cable. The others attack the hole with axes in an attempt to save him. When Ray is returned, he seems shaken up by the experience, to the point that his hair has turned white.

Winston finds a tiny hole from which proportionally tiny ghosts emerge, prompting Egon to realise that the size of the hole determines the size the apparitions will take when they come through. This leads to concerns about the enormously enlarged main hole, and what might emerge from it. To counter this, the Ghostbusters cut off a section of another wall containing a smaller hole, and place it in front of the big one, reasoning that anything trying to come out of the large hole will shrink as it is forced to pass through the small one. Egon worries that placing two holes adjacent to each other might result in an interdimensional imbalance that could cause the universe to implode. Instead, it results in an explosion that completely destroys the Limburger mansion, and enlarges the original hole to 50 ft. across. As expected, a behemoth-sized monster emerges from the mansion's debris.

fullContent:
"The Holiness of Azédarac" is a short story by American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith. First published in the November 1933 issue of Weird Tales magazine, "The Holiness of Azédarac" was included in the 2012 ebook collection The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack by Wildside Press.

The story is key in linking Smith's Averoigne setting to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
A young monk in medieval France is on his way to alert his superiors to the existence of a subversive cult in the ranks of the Catholic Church. He is soon intercepted by one of his opponents and cast back in time seven hundred years. In the past, the monk falls for the charms of a beautiful sorceress and, after engaging in an abortive attempt to return to his own era, decides to accept his fate and stays in the arms of his new love.

### Characters
*Brother Ambrose, a pious Benedictine monk in service to the Catholic Church in 1175.
*Azédarac, Bishop of Ximes, a dark occultist and sorcerer, many hundreds of years old, who has infiltrated the church. Later canonised as Saint Azédarac.
*Jehan Mauvaissoir, Azédarac's manservant, who masquerades as the Sieur des Émaux of Touraine to ensnare his target, Brother Ambrose. Known as Melchire in the distant past.
*Moriamis, an enchantress in pre-Christian France and former lover of Azédarac.
*Archbishop Clément, a senior member of the Catholic Church (reference only).

### Mythos Connections
*The story is set in the province of Averoigne.
*Azédarac makes reference to the entities the Ram with a Thousand Ewes, Dagon, Iog-Sotôt and Sodagui.
*Brother Ambrose steals Azédarac's copy of the Book of Eibon for proof of the man's corruption.

shortDefinition: "The Horla" is a horror short story by Guy de Maupassant. It was originally published in the newspaper Gil Blas, October 26, 1886. The author then expanded it and it was published in revised short story form in 1887.  It has been suggested(by who?) t...
fullContent:
"The Horla" is a horror short story by Guy de Maupassant. It was originally published in the newspaper Gil Blas, October 26, 1886. The author then expanded it and it was published in revised short story form in 1887.

It has been suggested(by who?) that the name "Horla" is a portmanteau word created by the author from the French words for "outside" and "there" giving the meaning of Horla as "the Outsider, the outer, the one Out There" or "who goes there?" or "what's outside?"

The story is written in the form of a diary or journal by the author who describes a growing perception of an invisible hostile and parasitic entity. The entity causes a fever, nightmares and ultimately seems to control first the author's mind and then his physical actions.

The Horla is extraterrestrial, non-anthropomorphic, and holds power over man as easily as man holds power over non-sapient animals, making this an early example of cosmic horror fiction.

This story is considered a direct inspiration and influence for the aspect of H. P. Lovecraft's story "The Call of Cthulhu" in which Cthulhu disturbs the dreams of the human race and begins to exert an intangible but palpable effect on human behaviour.(by who?) It is also a more general influence on Cthulhu Mythos works, as would be obvious.(why?)

In his essay Supernatural Horror in Literature, Lovecraft describes "The Horla" as de Maupassant's "masterpiece".

### Adaptations
"The Horla" was adapted into the 1963 film Diary of a Madman, starring Vincent Price.

### References

Conan the Barbarian: The Horn of Azoth is a Marvel Comics graphic novel set in Robert E. Howard's fictional Hyboria.

### Synopsis
Conan is hired by the priests of Shadizar to retrieve a horn, not knowing that it is tied to a prophecy from the Scrolls of Skelos to awaken Azoth the Dreaming God, one of the Outer Gods which could doom the world. Betrayed, Conan allies with the enemies of Azoth's cult to prevent its return, and a cataclysmic battle ends with the cult in disarray and Azoth's death.

### Behind the Mythos
Written by Gerry Conway and Roy Thomas (using their initial script for the movie Conan the Destroyer), The Horn of Azoth was pencilled by Mike Docherty and inked by Tony DeZuniga. It was published in April 1990 by Marvel Comics.

fullContent:
"The Horror at Martin's Beach" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Sonia H. Greene (1883-1972). It was written in June 1922 and first published in November 1923 in Weird Tales (Vol. 2, No. 4, 75–76, 83), where it was originally titled "The Invisible Monster".

### Plot Summary
On May 17th, 1922, the crew of the Alma killed a 50-foot-long creature at sea after a lengthy 40-hour battle. Its preserved corpse bore strange anatomical irregularities such as a single large eye, rudimentary forelegs, and six-toed feet in place of pectoral fins. After inspection by marine biologists, it is revealed to be just a juvenile.

Captain James P. Orne toured the coast with a custom-made maritime museum in the hull of a huge ship. Sailing south, he stopped at Martin's Beach, where he made vast amounts of money from admission fees, until the ship was lost in a storm on the morning of July 20th. Despite an extensive search by Orne and the scientists who had hitherto swarmed the specimen, neither the wreck nor its cargo were ever found, and the hunt was abandoned on August 7th.

The next day, on the 8th, the account relies on conflicting eyewitness reports, including that of the narrator. Highlighted by a low moon, a distinct ripple rolled across the sea before the horror was heralded by a pained cry from the black reefs. Two lifeguards tossed out a life-preserver on a rope, only to be slowly dragged towards the sea. Captain Orne and others joined the effort, but soon decided that a whale must have swallowed the cushion.

Upon deciding to leave the rope in order to harpoon the creature, he found that his hands were held in place by some unknown force. The other good Samaritans immediately realised that they too were stuck, and despite their struggling, they were all pulled slowly beneath the waves--to the horror of an onlooking crowd, who were soon forced back to the hotel veranda by a storm. Alongside the vanishing line of heads, the narrator thought he saw a great cyclopean eye, which let off a last ear-splitting satanic roar.

### Characters
*The Narrator - A witness to the horror at Martin's Beach, who tries to make sense of what they saw.
*Professor Alton - Author of "Are Hypnotic Powers Confined to Recognised Humanity", an article that publicised the event.
*Captain James P. Orne - Captain of the fishing boat Alma and captor of the sea monster.

### Locations
*Gloucester - Home port of the Alma.
*Martin's Beach - A wealthy resort district.
**Wavecrest Inn - A fashionable hotel with grand towers and a large ballroom, perched on a cliff overlooking the beach.
**A cottage colony atop a hill to the north.

*The Horror in the Museum and Other Revisions. Sauk City, WI: Arkham House, 1970. As "The Invisible Monster" by Sonia Greene

fullContent:
"The Horror at Oakdeene" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley. Written in 1970, it first appeared as the title story of Lumley's second Arkham House collection, The Horror at Oakdeene and Others in 1977.

### Synopsis
A hospital nursing orderly at Oakdeene Sanitarium is disturbed by one of his colleagues' evident sadism--and indulges an inmate's fascination with a book.

A man named Martin Spellman takes a job as a nurse at Oakdeene Sanitarium. Spellman hopes to become an author and plans to use the cases as inspiration for a book. Spellman becomes interested in a patient named Wilfred Larner, who became obsessed with occult studies, especially involving something called "The Black Book", This resulted in Larner becoming permanently insane. The Black Book is actually Larner's own translation of the Cthäat Aquadingen. Spellman begins to explore this translation.  

Larner asks Spellman to bring him a portion of the book called "the Sixth Sathlatta", calling it "a matter of justice". Spellman tries out this ritual, and dreams of the being Yibb-Tstll, a cloaked, winged figure. Larner begins to arrange a ritual with the help of several other inmates, while Spellman continues to dream of Yibb-Tstll.    

The ritual finally takes place, with Spellman cooperating under the control of Yibb-Tstll. A sadistic ex-nurse named Barstowe is found dead on the grounds, mutilated.  Five of the thirteen participating patients are suddenly cured. Five others, including Larner, are found dead.  Spellman himself is found insane and becomes a patient.

### Publication History
"The Horror at Oakdeene" has been reprinted in Lumley's collection The Taint and Other Novellas (Subterranean Press, 2007).

It was translated into French as "L'horreur dans l'asile" in L'avant-poste des Grands Anciens (Néo, 1986).

fullContent:
"The Horror at Red Hook" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft. Written on August 1–2, 1925, it was first published in the January 1927 issue of Weird Tales.

### Inspiration
Lovecraft referred to the area's immigrant population by referring to Red Hook as "a maze of hybrid squalor". He spelled out his inspiration for "The Horror at Red Hook" in a letter written to fellow writer Clark Ashton Smith:

|Selected Letters 2.197}}
Lovecraft had moved to New York to marry Sonia Greene a year earlier, in 1924; his initial infatuation with New York soon soured (an experience fictionalized in his short story "He"), in large part due to Lovecraft's xenophobic attitudes. "Whenever we found ourselves in the racially mixed crowds which characterize New York, Howard would become livid with rage," Greene later wrote. "He seemed almost to lose his mind."

The story was also inspired by the apartment that Lovecraft lived in, which is actually located on Clinton Street in Brooklyn Heights, rather than Red Hook. In 2008, children's book marketer Nellie Kurtzman, the daughter of cartoonist and Mad magazine founder Harvey Kurtzman, heard of the apartment from a friend, saying, "A friend of mine lives on the top floor of this building, and I remember her saying, 'There's this huge apartment in our building where the people seem to have disappeared.'" When Kurtzman and several friends inspected the ground-floor, two-bedroom apartment, it had been left unlocked by the tenants who left mysteriously, without notice. They held a seance, during which they used a Ouija board. Kurtzman, who has a penchant for the unusual that she inherited from her father, moved into the apartment that April with a roommate, after which she experienced unexplained noises, objects moving or disappearing inexplicably and unusual dreams.

Much of the magical background to the story was lifted from the articles on "Magic" and "Demonology" in the 9th edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, written by anthropologist E. B. Tylor. Daniel Harms and John Wisdom Gonce note the spell Lovecraft quotes and describes as a "demon evocation", was actually an incantation used for treasure hunting.

The survival of a prehistoric cult based on "witchcraft" is a direct inheritance from the fictional works of Arthur Machen and the scholarly works of Margaret Murray, most significantly her central tome The Witch-Cult in Western Europe (1921).

### Plot summary

The story begins with Detective Malone describing an on-duty incident at Red Hook, Brooklyn, that gave him a phobia of large buildings. Back-tracking to where it all began, Red Hook is described in detail, with its gangs and crime, and suggesting at an occult underbelly.

The "case of Robert Suydam" is then told to be the driving force behind Malone's federally ordered involvement at Red Hook. Suydam's demeanor changes suddenly. Known as a shabby recluse, he is seen around town looking younger and more radiant. News arrives of his engagement to a well-

The Horror at Red Hook is an audio play of the story of the same name by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, released under their Dark Adventure Radio Theatre line of productions.

### Overview
The Horror at Red Hook is a lively dramatization of one of HPL's most controversial works. A Brooklyn police detective learns the dark secrets of the city's most dangerous neighborhood, where mysterious immigrants conspire with a crazed old occultist to satisfy their ancient god in nightmare caverns below the urban squalor.

Running to a total of 66 minutes, The Horror at Red Hook is available in both physical (compact disc) and digital downloads, with both versions released with a set of period-authentic props to enhance the immersive experience. Included are: 

*A newspaper article from the Brooklyn Daily Eagle including a report on the incidents at Red Hook and a local map.
*An I.D. card belonging to one of Thomas Malone's informants.
*An excerpt from Malone's personnel file.
*A magazine article penned by occultist Robert Suydam.

The Horror From the Bridge is a short story by Ramsey Campbell that appeared in his 1964 collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants. It is set in Clotton, part of Campbell's Severn Valley milieu, and is largely a pastiche of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror".

Clotton is described a small town located where the river Ton flows into the Severn. Only a "few leaning red-brick houses... remain of the uptown section of the once-prosperous town;" the rest of the town was deliberately destroyed in 1931, for reasons explained in the story. The town's most noteworthy feature, also dating to 1931, is a "20-foot high concrete building...on the bank of the Ton", with an "eldritch sign clumsily engraved on each wall", carvings that "were blurred by moss and weather." Outside of Clotton is a "pit on a patch of waste ground on what used to be Canning Road, near the river," containing "roughly-cut steps, each carrying a carven five-pointed sign, which led down into abysmal darkness."

In 1800, a man named James Phipps, "a gaunt pallid-faced man, with jet-black hair, and long bony hands," moved into a house in Clotton on Riverside Alley. He was forced to leave his previous home in Camside "because his unorthodox scientific researches were distasteful to the inhabitants." In 1805, he married a woman from Temphill--whose name no one knew--with a "corpse-like pallor, who...walked with a peculiarly stiff gait." (Later we learn that a "monstrous coven" met in the "artificial caverns beneath the graveyards" in Temphill, where "newly corpses" were "reanimated by certain horrendous formulae," and these "living cadavers were taken as wives".) A year later, a son, Lionel Phipps, was born to the couple; the story pointedly notes that the offspring of the reanimated mates "would have primal powers which properly belonged only to alien deities." The elder Phipps was preoccupied with trying to release a "hidden primal race" that had been imprisoned below the Ton. After his death in 1898--when he was well over a century old--his work was carried on by Lionel. 

Trying to thwart these activities was Philip Chesterton, a librarian at the British Museum who became suspicious when Lionel Phipps came to that institution in 1900 to consult the Necronomicon and the Book of Eibon. Chesterton took a job at the library of Brichester University to better keep tabs on the goings on in Clotton. 

Finally, on September 2, 1931, Lionel Phipps is able to release three river monsters, servitors of the Great Old Ones. Reciting passages from the Necronomicon, and with the help of a local gun club, Chesterton is able to kill Phipps and two of the monsters, and imprison the third under fast-drying concrete--upon which were hurriedly carved representations of the Elder Sign.
