fullContent:
"The Horror from the Depths" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story cowritten by August Derleth and Mark Schorer. It was first published in Strange Stories in October 1940 under its original title, "The Evil Ones", though written in the summer of 1931. "Derleth supplied the outlines and later polished the stories Schorer drafted from them," John Haefele reports of this and two other collaborations between Derleth and Schorer.

"The Horror from the Depths" was republished in the collection Colonel Markesan and Less Pleasant People in 1966, and was included in In Lovecraft's Shadow: The Cthulhu Mythos Stories of August Derleth in November 1998.

### Synopsis
A dredging operation in Lake Michigan in 1931 awakens a group of ancient beings which go on to slaughter and spread madness over the next few nights. Joining forces to combat the threat, an engineer and a university professor discover through their research that the beings were imprisoned beneath the lakes surface by the Elder Gods untold aeons ago.

In an effort to re-inter the creatures, the two locate a number of star-stones which the dredger had also brought up. During the course of their attempt, they unwittingly summon the full power of the Elder Gods which destroys the entities utterly.

### Characters

* Sharp, the narrator, a senior engineer working on the land reclamation project.
* Professor Jordan Holmes, a scholar at Chicago's Field Museum of Natural History.
* Tennant, Sharp's superior.
* Dr. Jameson, an anthropologist with an interest in ancient texts.
* Professor Morrison, an anthropologist.

### Trivia

* The creatures disturbed by the engineering project are described as being the "brood of Cthulhu" and having certain octopod traits. This may indicate that they were in fact a group of Cthulhi, also known as the Star-Spawn of Cthulhu. The story's accompanying artwork by C. A. Murphy depicts them as dragon-like creatures.

### External Link

* [https://cthulhufiles.com/stories/derleth/derleth-schorer-the-horror-from-the-depths.html "The Horror From the Depths"] complete text at Librarium Cthulhuvius

fullContent:
The Horror from the Hills is a horror novel by Frank Belknap Long, originally serialized in Weird Tales magazine in 1931 in the January and February-March issues. It was published by Arkham House in 1963 in an edition of 1,997 copies. It has come to form an integral part of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Algernon Harris, the curator of Archaeology at the Manhattan Museum of Fine Arts, has sent field works all over the world in the hunt for unusual and valuable artefacts. Some of these agents have returned injured and in two cases horribly mutilated. However another agent by the name of Clark Ulman has returned with a hideous stone idol. Incongruously, Ulman now conceals his face behind a scarf.

The strange and ugly idol most closely resembles, to the extent it resembles anything recognisable, an elephant. The pedestal is also described as ugly and made from an unidentifiable stone. 

Another agent had written of the tortures he had been forced to suffer at the hands of a secret cult of subhuman worshippers of the idol. It emerges that Ulman was sent with the the idol back to civilization so that ancient prophecy may be fulfilled. In the process of this revelation Ulman reveals that the idol is based on life and that the entity it represents, named Chaugnar Faugn, is a real living being. Ulman also reveals that Chaugnar Faugn, a monstrous vampire, has already feasted upon Ulman himself.

Chaugnar and his brothers, revealed to be all parts of the same alien superorganism, lived in a cavern in the Pyrenees between Spain and France. This cavern was inaccessible in normal circumstances to humans. Chaugnar created the Miri Nigri humanoids as servants, made from the flesh of toads. Chaugnar and his brothers were offered human sacrifices from the people of the nearby settlement of Pompelo until the Romans attacked Pompelo and ended the sacrifices. Chaugnar Faugn and his brothers then destroyed Pompelo. Since then the Chaugnar Faugn brothers have been resting hidden in Asia until the time comes for their rise, assisted by their "White Acolyte" - none other than the unfortunate Ulman, who has been forced into the role by the high-priest Chung Ga so that the prophecy can be fulfilled.

Revealing all this is Ulman's final act. He collapses and dies. On examination it is discovered that Ulman's face had undergone mutation. He had an elephantine trunk and huge ears, not the result of surgery or disease. 

The idol of Chaugnar Faugn was put on display in the museum by Algernon Harris. Shortly afterwards, a museum guard is murdered in mysterious circumstances. At the same time there are news reports of the discovery in the Pyrenees of 14 dead villagers. Their heads were missing and gigantic hoof marks were found in the area where they were killed.

Harris consults Roger Little, a criminal investigator turned hermit and mystic. He had past experience with the Mythos and could offer guidance as to what had happened- and what was going to happen.

shortDefinition: "The Horror from the Middle Span" is a short story by August Derleth based on the notes of H. P. Lovecraft and billed as a "posthumous collaboration."  ### Synopsis When Ambrose Bishop travels to Dunwich, Massachusetts to claim his missing great-uncl...
fullContent:
"The Horror from the Middle Span" is a short story by August Derleth based on the notes of H. P. Lovecraft and billed as a "posthumous collaboration."

### Synopsis
When Ambrose Bishop travels to Dunwich, Massachusetts to claim his missing great-uncle's property for himself, his arrival triggers the return of the sorcerous relative from imprisonment beneath the titular "middle span" and the resumption of his sacrifices to dark powers. Despite the intervention of the locals, the pair seem to survive to continue their work...

### Characters
*Ambrose Bishop, a young man on a mission to reclaim his family's estate.
*Septimus Bishop, an old wizard in the service of the dark gods.
*Tobias Whateley, the elderly proprietor of Dunwich's sole general store.

### Behind the Mythos
Written by August Derleth years after H. P. Lovecraft's death, "The Horror from the Middle Span" was based on story notes left by Lovecraft and presented as a posthumous collaboration. It was first published in the anthology Travellers by Night in a run of 2,486 copies by Derleth's own publishing house, Arkham House, in 1964. It was later included in the collection of posthumous collaborations between Lovecraft and Derleth The Watchers Out of Time and Others, also by Arkham House, in 1974.

### Mythos Connections
*The story is set in Lovecraft's iconic backwoods town of Dunwich, Massachusetts. The towns of Aylesbury and Arkham, other creations of Lovecraft, are also mentioned.
*The surnames of Bishop and Whateley are commonly used by both Lovecraft and others when discussing the inhabitants of Lovecraft Country.
*Wilbur Whateley, one of the primary antagonists of "The Dunwich Horror", is noted to have been a correspondent of Septimus Bishop's.
*The Outer God Azathoth is made mention of.
*Septimus Bishop was apparently held prisoner beneath the middle span through the use of the Elder Sign. The artefact known as the Shining Trapezohedron is also referenced.

"The Horror in the Burying-Ground" is a Hazel Heald short horror story, heavily revised by H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in Weird Tales in May 1937 shortly after Lovecraft's death, but evidence from Ms. Heald's correspondence seems to indicate that she had struggled with the story for several years, and that Lovecraft had in fact revised it several years before its date of publication.

fullContent:
"The Horror in the Gallery", originally published under the title "Zoth-Ommog" in the 1976 anthology The Disciples of Cthulhu, is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter, and part of his Xothic Legend Cycle.

For people interested in Mythos lore, it is perhaps most significant for including long passages that detail the history of the Great Old Ones and the Elder Gods, based on and including references to the works of several Mythos authors.

### Synopsis
The story is presented as a police testimony given by Arthur Wilcox Hodgkins in 1929, after a night watchman is found murdered in the South Gallery of the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities in Santiago, California. Hodgkins maintains that there were actually two bodies, the second being the body of the night watchman's murderer.

Hodgkins worked at the Sanbourne Institute as an assistant to curator Henry Stephenson Blaine, but assumed Blaine's duties following the latter' internment in a mental institution (see "Out of the Ages"). At the time of his mental collapse, Dr. Blaine had been cataloging the collection of files and artifacts belonging to the late Professor Copeland, including a mysterious jade figurine found off the coast of Ponape that represented the god Zoth-Ommog. Since Copeland himself had died raving in an asylum, the press reacts to the news of Blaine's madness with the sensationalist claim that the haunted figurine had made another victim. Hodgkins is told to resume the cataloging, as the directors want the Copeland Collection to be put on display in the South Gallery later that year.

A few months later, Hodgkins receives a call from the asylum telling him that Dr. Blaine is extremely agitated, asking to see Hodgkins immediately. Blaine tells Hodgkins to destroy the Ponape figurine rather than put it on display, and advises him to consult the Necronomicon at the Miskatonic University library. He makes Hodgkins promise to read the Copeland files marked as "Xothic Legend Cycle", which Hodgkins agrees to. From Copeland's files (and Blaine's annotations), Hodgkins learns about the Cthulhu Mythos and particularly about Cthulhu's son, Zoth-Ommog, imprisoned under the island of Ponape. That same night, he starts experiencing bad dreams in which the face of the Zoth-Ommog figurine watches him menacingly.

Studying passages copied by Copeland from books such as De Vermis Mysteriis, The Revelations of Glaaki and the Cultes des Goules, Hodgkins learns that the Great Old Ones can create psychic links with those who have been in contact with the idols and statuettes that represent them, and those who have been in contact with such objects will have their life force drained by these eldritch deities, and see them in their nightmares. Even more alarming, he also learns that the Great Old Ones' servants can use these idols to summon their masters. A note by Copeland points to a page of the Necronomicon where a method for destroying such statuettes can be found. Any skepticism Hodgki

"The Horror in the Genizah" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story from American author and theologian Robert M. Price. It made its print debut in the first issue of the fanzine E'ch Pi El in July 2006.

### Synopsis
An American scholar searching ancient mosques which show the original presentation of the Koran uncovers information which demonstrates that the underpinning of the religious text is in fact the heretical Kitab Al-Azif. As his mind is infected by the words of the Al-Azif, he is pursued across the globe by a group of mysterious assailants who seem determined to stop this information from reaching the public, and ultimately decides to take his own life.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, a scholar in the field of ancient theology.

### Publication History
*E'ch Pi El #1 (2006)
*Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos: Cthulhu's Creatures (2007)
*Blasphemies & Revelations (2008, 2019)

fullContent:
The Horror in the Lamplights is an upcoming novel by Christopher Michael, which forms the second instalment in his Danforth: Eldritch Tales of WWII series of Cthulhu Mythos stories.

Set during the Second World War, the novel continues the reinterpretation of H. P. Lovecraft’s characterDanforth, one of the main protagonists in At the Mountains of Madness, as he is drawn deeper into covert intelligence work intersecting with occult forces operating beneath the surface of wartime Romania.

### Overview
The Horror in the Lamplights shifts focus toward a more intimate and localized form of horror, emphasizing secrecy, paranoia, and the influence of ancient beliefs within isolated communities. Building upon the psychological and cosmic themes established in the first volume, the narrative explores the lingering consequences of Danforth’s earlier encounters while expanding on the occult.

fullContent:
"The Horror in the Museum" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald.

### Plot
Stephen Jones is an artist, looking for artistic stimulation, who comes to a certain wax museum, which specializes in the grotesque. He is impressed: the proprietor is a former employee of [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Tussaud Madam Tussaud], who was fired for mysterious reasons, but has turned his incredible talents to not just the gallery of conventional horrors (common in wax museums of the time), but to fantastic monsters, some of which Jones recognizes: "black, formless Tsathoggua, many-tentacled Cthulhu, proboscidian Chaugnar Faugn, and other rumoured blasphemies from forbidden books like the Necronomicon, the Book of Eibon, or the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Junzt." Later descriptions mention Yog-Sothoth, Gnoph-keh, and a night-gaunt.

Wanting to meet the creator, Jones is introduced to George Rogers.  Rogers is happy to have an audience, and while his stories are initially conventional, he soon lapses into bizarre tales about the things he has read ("monstrous and half-fabulous books as the prehistoric Pnakotic Fragments and the Dhôl Chants attributed to malign and non-human Leng"), and his trips around the world, trying to find the lost civilizations described in those works, though he is only able to corroborate some of his stories with photos. He insists that all the creatures in his museum are real, and the pair soon develop an odd relationship: Jones holds an open but amused fascination with his fellow artist, and Rogers' spends their meetings trying to convince Jones to change his mind.

One day, Jones is at the museum when Rogers is supposedly not, and hears a horrible noise that Rogers' employee and servant, Orabona, attempts to pass off as a dogfight outside. Investigating, Jones notes a light on in Rogers' workroom, and comes to suspect the strange, locked door at the back of that room, marked with an undescribed symbol that Jones recognizes from the Necronomicon.

Jones and Rogers meet later that night. Rogers is in a pique, and tells Jones about a particularly important expedition to Alaska. Rogers insists that "There were things in the north before the land of Lomar."  During the trip, Rogers frequently lambasted Orabona for his fear and caution, since he knew what they are hunting. Rogers continues to insult Orabona throughout the conversation. In the deep tundra, the pair and their hired crew discovered a ruin with a massive, ivory throne, housing a horrendous occupant which is either in a million-years long hibernation, or outright deceased.  Later identifying this creature as "Rhan-Tegoth," Rogers insists that it is a god, and all it needs is the right sacrifice to give it nourishment.  Rogers arranged for the thing to be sent to London, and shows Jones a photograph, which shocks him, but he insists it must have been staged. The Horror in the Museum is a Dark Adventure Radio Theatre production by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, adapting the story of the same name.

### Overview


Running to approximately 70 minutes, The Horror in the Museum is an audio drama produced in the style of a 1930s radio broadcast. It is available in both physical compact disc and digital download formats, with both versions including a series of thematic props linked to the story: a ticket to the titular wax museum, a photograph of Alaskan ruins, a page from the Pnakotic Fragments, and the (fictional) front page from a newspaper of the time.

The Horror in the Museum and Other Revisions is a collection of short works which were either revised by H. P. Lovecraft, or ghostwritten by him for other authors.

### Publication History
First published by Arkham House in 1970, the collection ran to 383 pages and was edited by Lovecraft's friend and contemporary August Derleth. A revised edition was released in 1989 by S. T. Joshi, featuring a number of additions, with this issue running to 450 pages. A trade paperback was then released in 2002, this time by Stephen Jones, and featured a new introduction by Jones along with a potted biography of Lovecraft.

fullContent:
"The Horror in the Stable" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author R. C. Mulhare. It was published in the Jesse Dedman/William C. Marchese-edited festive anthology Cthulhu Christmas Special and Other Lovecraftian Yuletide Tales in November 2017.

### Synopsis
On Christmas Eve, Dr. Herbert West, now hiding his experiments in plain sight, is called to attend two badly-injured small children, Molly and Mickey Dolan, who have been struck by an automobile and subsequently crawled off to a remote barn to nurse their injuries. Deducing that the boy has little chance of survival, but the girl may be helped, he nevertheless injects them both with his reagent under the guise of administering painkillers. Micky immediately runs off into the woods, while Molly remains comatose.

West then transports Molly to his surgery where he may keep an eye on her progress. Later that night, when the doctor is asleep, he is awoken by the sound of the window breaking and investigates, only to find the girl vanished into the cold, dark night. A few days pass before West, deciding to embark on an evening constitutional, sets foot outside his front door, only to be confronted by a small figure covered in blood, and holding the partially-eaten remains of a little girl's leg…

fullContent:
"The Horror in the Water Tower" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A strange creature which was stolen away from a temple in Peru ventures forth into the wide  world of Innsmouth on the day her owner dies in an accident. Meeting a young researcher, the creature and the man fall in love, and together they discover her extradimensional powers and origin, ultimately using them to escape the confines of this world.

### Characters
*Pet/Rapunzel, a bizarre yet kindly and compassionate being from another dimension.
*Kaleb, a medical researcher who befriends Rapunzel.
*Miss Thorne, a benevolent witch who raised and cared for Rapunzel until her death.

### Publication History
"The Horror in the Water Tower" was published in the collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

### Trivia
*The title "The Horror in the Water Tower" is something of a non-sequitur, as the creature is consistently described as beautiful, and possesses no malevolent characteristics.
*The creature Ghattambah is referenced several times, and its temple was the site from which Rapunzel was taken as a larva.

The Horror of It All: Encrusted Gems from the "Crypt of Cthulhu" is a collection of essays (along with selected fiction) on H. P. Lovecraft, the Cthulhu Mythos and related subjects that appeared in the fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu, edited by Robert M. Price. "The title is not, as one might expect, 'The Best of The Crypt of Cthulhu," Price noted in the introduction, "since there is simply too much to choose from. The contents of this collection are among the best, but that would be a peculiar title!"

The Horror of It All was published in 1990 by Starmont House (Mercer Island, Washington). A second collection of Crypt of Cthulhu material, Black Forbidden Things, was published in 1992.

fullContent:
"The Horror on the Beach" is a Cthulhu Mythos story written by prolific science fiction author Alan Dean Foster. It was first published as a chapbook in 1978.

### Synopsis
When a family moves into an old house on the California coast, it triggers a series of manifestations by the entity Cthulhu.

### Setting
The story is set at Casa de Rodrigo de Lima, an old Spanish house at Cabrillo Cove, part of the "wild Pacific coast" near Santa Barbara, California. 

### Characters
*David Corfu, a "slightly undersize" oil engineer.
*Julie Corfu, David's wife.
*Flip Corfu, David and Julie's eight-year-old son, fond of miniature dinosaurs.
*General Lee, the Corfus' cat, a "mutated Siamese."
* Martin and Evelyn Birch, the Corfus' nearest neighbors, fond of bridge. They have two young twin daughters.
*Joshua Whipple, an old beachcomber who warns the Corfus about Cthulhu. He comes from "somewhere on the coast" in Massachusetts.
*Bascomb, a real estate agent who fails to tell the Corfus the history of Casa de Rodrigo de Lima before selling it to them.
*Pedro Armendariz, a biochemist, and a friend of David's at the University. He has learned about Mythos horrors from "certain forbidden and well-sequestered tomes, such as the De Vermis Mysteriis of Ludvig Prinn, and even worse, the Necronomicon of the mad Arab, Alhazred”--as well as from associates at Yale and Miskatonic.
*Rosa Armendariz, Pedro's wife, "a plump but still vivacious little woman."
*Major Gomez, Pedro's "friend at the missile base."

### Publication History
"The Horror on the Beach" was first published in July 1978, part of The Library Lovecraftian series, in an edition of some 1,000 copies.  The back cover carried the misspelled blurb, ""CTHLULHU WAS IN CALIFORNIA."

The story was not reprinted again until 1996, when it was included in Robert M. Price's The New Lovecraft Circle (Fedogan & Bremer).

shortDefinition: "The Horror Under Warrendown" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author Ramsey Campbell, linked to the Cthulhu Mythos through its setting in the fictional Severn Valley. It was first published in the Scott David Aniolowski-edited anthology Made...
fullContent:
"The Horror Under Warrendown" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author Ramsey Campbell, linked to the Cthulhu Mythos through its setting in the fictional Severn Valley. It was first published in the Scott David Aniolowski-edited anthology Made in Goatswood by Chaosium in July 1995.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator, a travelling bookseller, is cajoled into offering one of his friends, a man named Graham Crawley, a lift to the remote village of Warrendown to meet with a local girl who he has gotten pregnant. En route, the narrator comes to the realisation that his friend is terrified of Warrendown; upon arriving, he himself feels an inexplicable sense of revulsion at the place. Dropping Crawley off, he proceeds to Brichester to pursue his work with the promise that he will pick him up before sundown.

Unfortunately, the narrator is held up by a client, and by the time he makes it back to Warrendown it is long past sunset. Although he manages to locate his friend, something is wrong with Crawley, and the man runs off, disappearing down a dark tunnel beneath the village's ruined church. Following, the narrator comes across Crawley and the degenerate residents of Warrendown enacting a frenzied ritual in front of their dark vegetable god, and he runs in terror, barely making his escape from the hideous revelries.

### Other Mythos Connections
Aside from Brichester and Warrendown, the abandoned town of Clotton is also mentioned.

### Publication History
* Made in Goatswood (1995)
* Dark Terrors 3 (1997, 1998)
* Terror Tales of the Cotswolds (2012)
* Visions from Brichester (2015, 2018)

fullContent:
"The Horror-Horn" is a short story by the late British author E. F. Benson.

### Summary
The story focuses on a man who vacations in the Swiss Alps, around the Ungehoerhorn Mountains. He is met by a friend who relates a tale of his meeting with a local barbaric tribe of semi-human things, primitive and ape-like in all but their human features.

Days later, the man wanders in the forest and meets one of these people, an old hag of a woman. He manages to escape it, but he is horrified beyond his wits.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Horror-Horn" was one of several stories by E. F. Benson of which H. P. Lovecraft spoke highly.

### Publication History
"The Horror-Horn" was first published in Hutchinson's Magazine in September 1922, and has been reprinted many times in the years since.

fullContent:
"The Hound" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft in September 1922 and published in the February 1924 issue of Weird Tales. Notably, it contains the first mention of Lovecraft's fictional text the Necronomicon.

### Inspiration
On September 16, 1922, Lovecraft toured the Flatbush Reformed Church in Brooklyn with his friend Rheinhart Kleiner, writing about the visit in a letter:



Lovecraft wrote "The Hound" shortly afterwards, using as the name of one of the main characters his nickname for his companion Kleinhart, "St. John". The grave that is fatefully robbed in the story is in a "terrible Holland churchyard"—perhaps a reference to Flatbush church being part of the Dutch Reformed Church (although the story is actually set in the Netherlands, as well as in England).

Critic Steven J. Mariconda suggests that the story is a tribute to the Decadent literary movement in general and in particular Joris-Karl Huysmans' A rebours, an 1884 novel that Lovecraft greatly admired. (Huysmans is mentioned by name in the story, along with Baudelaire.) Like "The Hound"'s protagonists, victims of a "devastating ennui", the main character of A rebours suffers from an "overpowering tedium" that leads him to "imagine and then indulge in unnatural love-affairs and perverse pleasures."

Mariconda also points to the heavy debt the story owes to Edgar Allan Poe, an influence acknowledged by several borrowed phrases: 

:The "oblong box" exumed, the mysterious "knock on my chamber door", and the "red death" brought by the Hound all echo Poe's phraseology.

### Reaction
Though Lovecraft chose "The Hound" as one of the five stories he initially submitted to Weird Tales, his main professional outlet, he later dismissed it as "a dead dog" and "a piece of junk".

Some critics have shared Lovecraft's deprecation; Lin Carter called it "a minor little tale" that is "slavishly Poe-esque in style". But the story has its defenders; Steven J. Mariconda says it is "written in a zestful, almost baroque style which is very entertaining",

The plot of the Poppy Z. Brite short story "His Mouth Will Taste of Wormwood" bears a strong resemblance to this Lovecraft story, albeit transplanted to a modern Southern Gothic Louisiana setting.

### Synopsis
The story focuses around the narrator and his friend St. John, a pair of friends in England who have a deranged interest in robbing graves They constantly defile crypts and often keep souvenirs of their nocturnal expeditions. Since they reside in the same house, they have the opportunity to set up a sort of morbid museum in their basement. Using the objects they collect from the various graves they have robbed, they organize the private exhibition. The collection consists of headstones, preserved bodies, skulls and several heads in different phases of decomposition. It also included statues, frightful paintings and a locked portfolio, bound in tanned human skin.

"The Hounds Below" is a short story by Josh Reynolds and the third story in the anthology The Devourer Below. It is set in the popular Arkham Horror Fiction universe.

### Plot Summary
A man by the name Mr. Holsten arrives at the Arkham Sanatorium. He is writing a book on the subject of cannibalism and seeks to interview one of the patients, Philip Drew, who has been admitted for such acts. After months of being denied multiple requests to meet him, Holsten is finally allowed to see Drew under the condition that a chaperone will be present during his visit. Holsten meets the chaperone, doctor Fern, who was strongly opposed to Holsten visiting Drew. She states that Drew is in a weak mental state and warns Holsten that she will escort him out if she believes his questions or behavior towards Drew is inappropriate. Holsten attempts to assure the doctor that his book will help people to understand Drew and those like him but she doesn’t quite believe him.

Drew is located in the secure wing of the Arkham Sanatorium, in which the chaperone is needed as no one without proper credentials can enter unescorted. Doctor Fern explains that Drew is not allowed to interact with the other patients as even under supervision he is a danger to himself and those around him. When Holsten asks if he has ever tried to escape, she replies that it has happened once or twice as Drew seems to be suffering from an irregular mania. They arrive at the secure wing, hearing the patients shriek, sob and pound on the walls of their cells. Only one door is silent: the one of Philip Drew's cell. Doctor Fern opens the door and calls out Drews name. Holsten notices that the cell is in darkness and doctor Fern explains that Drew has asked the lights to be turned off as he claims it hurts his eyes. As she calls out Drew’s name again, Drew sits up in the bed he has been lying in. He is naked, in which doctor Fern explains that it is due to him disliking clothes and ripping them to shreds. Drew rises and stares at Holton, asking him who he is. Doctor Fern introduces him and Holsten explains that he wants to talk to Drew and know his story as he is writing a book about people like Drew. After a moment of contemplation, Drew agrees and begins to tell his tale.

Philip Drew was an alumnus at the Miscantonic University who joined the Canadian Regiment during the great war. He told of the horrors at the front, fighting the Germans with both guns and whatever was at hand. fullContent:
"The Hounds of the Dawn" is a Lovecraftian short story by British-born author William Meikle. It was self-published in the chapbook collection Up from the Deep in May 2023 .

### Synopsis
"The Hounds of Dawn" is told in the form of an account written by a Roman slave, an unnamed man likely from Africa or the Middle East, who has committed his story to paper while interred in an Imperial cell.

In the aftermath of the British defeat by the invaders, Caratacus's wife lays a curse on the Roman governor Publius Ostorius Scapula, calling on her "hounds", creatures she dubs the Cwn Annwyn, to torment the man and ultimately kill him.

Over the following nights, more and more of Scapula's guards are found at dawn, brutally and silently murdered in the dark, their corpses all but hollowed out. As the tension rises and his men are killed off one by one, the governor makes the decision to flee to Rome, throwing himself on the Emperor's mercy for abandoning his station, while his servant is jailed.

The story ends with the servant finishing his account, his final lines telling of how he has begun to hear the scratching and snuffling noises which precede the arrival of the Cwn Annwyn…

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly named in the story, the creatures summoned by the vengeful British noblewoman bear a strong resemblance to the Hounds of Tindalos, a species of supernatural predator created by Frank Belknap Long for the eponymous short story. Their physical description closely matches common depictions of the Hounds, while their ability to manifest through angles also lends credence to this position. Another point of note is that William Meikle's 2019 Thomas Carnacki short story "A Body in the Library" features a Hound of Tindalos which the protagonist also identifies as a "Cŵn Annwyn", making it even likelier that the entities featured in "The Hounds of the Dawn" are intended to be one and the same.

Caratacus and Scapula were real people, the former a British tribal chieftain defeated in battle by the latter , the appointed governor of Britain , and subsequently sent to Rome for trial. In the story, one of the conditions Caratacus's wife sets out for calling off the Hounds is that her husband be released; ironically, the real Caratacus was in fact set free after making an impassioned speech to the Senate , with the country of Wales being situated on the West Coast of the British Isles; Caratacus and his people, the Catuvellauni, were located around modern-day Hertfordshire, Bedfordshire, and Cambridgeshire, which are far closer to the eastern coast .

"The Hounds of Tindalos" is a short story by early Mythos contributor Frank Belknap Long.

The story's narrator, "Frank", appears to be the same character from Long's previous Mythos tale, "The Space-Eaters", as both are set in the fictional town of Partridgeville.

### Synopsis
The story follows unconventional researcher Halpin Chalmers who believes that he can view the entirety of time and space through the use of a mysterious Eastern narcotic called Liao. Conducting an experiment with the drug under the supervision of his friend, a man named Frank, Chalmers sends his consciousness out into the depths of time. Unfortunately for him, he travels too far back in time and attracts the attentions of the Hounds of Tindalos, predatory creatures which inhabit the angles of time and space, rather than the curves, as most creatures do.

Despite Chalmers' efforts to stave off the Hounds, they come for him (perhaps with the aid of their allies, the Satyrs and the Doels) and his body is found in his home a few days after a localised earthquake, decapitated and bloodless, and covered in a mysterious blue ichor. When taken for analysis, the substance is found to represent a form of life previously thought impossible.

### Characters
* Frank, the narrator, and presumably a friend of Chalmers. He does not believe that Chalmers has experienced anything other than a bad trip caused by the untested drug. He appears to be the author, Frank Belknap Long, inserting himself into his own story.
* Halpin Chalmers, a traditional-minded researcher who is nevertheless willing to try folkloric solutions to modern problems, disagreeing with the dogma of modern scientific theory.
* Detective Sergeant Douglas, the police officer in charge of the investigation into Chalmers' death.
* James Morton, the chemist and bacteriologist who analysed the substance found coating Chalmers' body. He seems to be named after Long's friend and fellow Kalem Club member James F. Morton.

### Behind the Mythos
The Hounds of Tindalos was first published in the March 1929 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. Since then, it has appeared in numerous collections of horror and Mythos work, including the Wildside Press eBook issue The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack in 2012.

"The House" is a horror poem by H. P. Lovecraft first published on December 11, 1919, in the National Enquirer. It was republished posthumously in the March 1948 issue of Weird Tales, illustrated by Boris Dolgov.

### Synopsis
The poem describes an eerie old house in a grove by the hill. Over its walls grow vines, the roots of which are nourished by something buried deep beneath the ground. After sunset, a spirit stalks the house's gardens. The narrator stands there on a hot day at noon, yet still shivers with cold and gropes for light as the memory of the last time they've been there flashes before their eyes.

"The House at the Edge of Time and Space" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young. It forms the first part of the third book in his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
Adele Kramer, still tasked to watch over the sleeping god Azathoth, is granted a short interlude to visit another cosmic being who explains the goals and motivations behind her enforced vigil. Free for the briefest of moments, she uses her newfound mental capacity to plant the name of the last person required to fight Nyarlathotep in the mind of Department of Extraordinary Phenomena director Harjit Singh.

### Characters
*Adele Kramer, a former marine biologist, now a pawn in the plans of a cruel god.
*Grandfather/Yog-Sothoth, one of the greatest of the Outer Gods.
*Nyarlathotep, an Outer God who has spent so long manipulating humankind that he has begun to imprint human emotions on himself.

"The House at the End of the Street" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author and artist Frank Forte. It was published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator recalls all of the horrific urban legends associated with an ancient abandoned house which he has been terrified of wince early childhood. As an adult, he resolves to overcome his fear by entering the house alone and proving to himself that there is nothing to be afraid of. However, as he explores the derelict structure he discover, room by room, that the old tales were all too true.

As his mind degrades, he attempts suicide, and as his conscience fades to black he wonders if his will become the latest story associated with the terrible old house.

"The House in the Woods" is a short Mythos story by American author Ran Cartwright writing under the pseudonym R. S. Cartwright.

### Synopsis
A reporter is on the run from a horror which he cannot remember. Picking up a young female hitchhiker on the road, he unwittingly travels back to the location of his prior trauma. As his memory begins to return, he realises that he has been tricked by an otherworldly entity, before his mind once again descends into darkness. 

### Characters

*Eric Cantrell, a reporter who uncovers a sinister cult during his pursuit of a story.
*Anna "Anne" Circola, a fun-loving young hitchhiker with a fondness for illicit substances.
*Nyarlathotep, an Outer God.

### Publication History

fullContent:
"The House of Azathoth" is a horror comedy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It is the third installment of Peter Cannon's six-part novella Forever Azathoth, which serves as a humourous sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep".

"The House of Azathoth" was originally published in the August 1996 issue of the magazine Cthulhu Codex. The entire series would later appear in Cannon's collections Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (1999) and Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches (2011).

### Synopsis
(Continued from "The Revenge of Azathoth"...)

Part three of the saga is narrated by Judge Hand, an elderly man who was acquainted with Edward Derby, Daniel Upton, and his son Edward Upton. A lawyer by trade, Hand came to work for the younger Upton's widow, Wendy, who founded a publishing company named Azathoth House to make the works of Derby widely available. Along with Derby scholar and Azathoth House editor Vartan Bagdasarian, Hand also acts as a quasi-parental figure to Wendy's four-year old son, Ephraim "Eph" Upton, a peculiar child who has a "knack for exciting animals and for predicting bad weather". Hand, nevertheless, is fond of the boy.

Bagdasarian's plans for Azathoth House are ambitious, including a new corrected edition of Azathoth and Other Horrors, collections of Derby's prose, and the extensive correspondence between Derby and Justin Geoffrey. However, Hand informs him that they can't risk anything at the moment, as the relatives of Derby's late wife Asenath in Innsmouth are threatening to go to court, demanding their share of the rights. A meeting between Hand, Bagdasarian, and Wendy is interrupted by a distressed and traumatised young Eph, who has just witnessed the death of the librarian Henry Armitage. Apparently, the library guard dogs became so agitated by Eph that they accidentally trampled their master when he tried to intervene, causing the old man to have a heart attack.

To cheer the boy up, Hand takes Eph on a trip to Innsmouth, a town he always wanted to visit, but this too ends in tragedy when they witness a sudden sea storm that destroys a number of boats and claims the lives of many, including Asenath's relatives. This tragic incident puts an end to the legal disputes, which allows Azathoth House to proceed with their plans, although Bagdasarian is forced now and then to interrupt his work in order to indulge in Eph's whims, such as taking him to the library to read the Necronomicon, which is now available to the public following Armitage's demise.

At Wendy's insistence, Bagdasarian reluctantly agrees to take Eph on a Halloween trip to Chesuncook, Maine, a location formerly frequented by Asenath's father, Ephraim Waite, after whom the boy was named. The two stay with inventor Jacob Lamar Derby, a distant cousin of Edward Derby. fullContent:
"The House of Cthulhu" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Brian Lumley, first published in the magazine Whispers, in July 1973.

### Synopsis
In ancient Theem'hdra, the dreaded Zar-thule the Conqueror and his fleet of dragonships set sail towards the island of Arlyeh to loot its treasures. They have heard about the island from a priest named Voth Vehm, who revealed the information under torture, claiming that his brother, Hath Vehm, was the guardian of the city in which a god named Cthulhu lied sleeping.

Upon their arrival, the raiders see that Arlyeh is indeed home to a great city, with towers of black stone and peculiar angles, built by prehistoric alien creatures. Despite the crew's superstition and reluctance to go any further, Zar-thule orders then to land ashore and head straight towards the citadel known as the House of Cthulhu. They are surprised to find that there are no guards or even a human population, except for Hath Vehm: an old man whose skin is covered by some sort of grey fungus, and who warns them not to touch him.

Believing that the god Cthulhu is just something Voth Vehm created to try to keep the raiders away, Zar-thule demands entrance, but Hath Vehm informs him that the gigantic door can only be opened by certain magic words, which the priest refuses to enunciate.

One of the pirates, who had touched Hath Vehm, finds that his own skin is now infected by the fungus. In his panic he kills himself, making the other pirates even more nervous. Under Zar-thule's orders, the men torture Hath Vehm with burning swords for several hours.

Sensing his approaching death, Hath Vehm manages to spit on Zar-thule, but also proceeds to pronounce the incantation, which cause the gigantic door to open. While some of Zar-thule's men rush inside in search of treasure, Hath Vehm reveals that there is also a second set of magic words, created by the Elder Gods to be used in case the door was opened. These words would make the entire island sink back to the bottom of the sea, as it was once before emerging. Sure enough, as soon as Hath Vehm says the new words, the ground begins to shake. Zar-thule promptly decapitates Hath Vehm.

At this point, Cthulhu emerges from the citadel and devours Zar-thule's crew with his tentacles. Zar-thule alone manages to escape to his ship, while the island sinks behind him. He is found adrift off the coast of Theem'hdra, in a state of complete insanity, and is brought to the capital of Klühn, where a doctor named Teh Atht (revealed to be the story's narrator) sees to Zar-thule's recovery and hears his story. Teh Atht is familiar with the legend of Cthulhu and believes that Arlyeh shall rise again at some point in the future. At the end, he reveals that Zar-thule was also infected by grey fungus, and his body has now degenerated to the point that any physical movement is now controlled by the parasite.

### Behind the Mythos
The parasitic grey fungus might be an homage to "The Voice in the Night", by William Hope H

"The House of Haon-Dor" is a story fragment by the late American author and poet Clark Ashton Smith, apparently intended to form part of his Hyperborean Cycle series of Cthulhu Mythos-related fiction. It was first published in James Ambuehl's 1998 anthology The Sorcerer's Apprentices: New Tales in the Tradition of Clark Ashton Smith , where it was credited as being co-written with Laurence J. Cornford . It has also been translated into French .

### Synopsis
What little was written in "The House of Haon-Dor" tell of a promising young poet who decides to spend time camped on the edge of an old mining site while recuperating from a minor medical condition. There, he becomes fascinated by a dilapidated and apparently uninhabited shack which appears to be a relic of America's gold digging boom.

The story ends at this point, literally cutting off in mid-sentence .

fullContent:
The House of Nodens is a horror novel by the late American author Sam Gafford which is loosely related to the greater Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in July 2017 by Dark Regions Press; paperback, hardcover and digital editions were all released.

The story alternates, through flashbacks, between two separate but linked tales which take place in Connecticut, New England.

### Synopsis
In 1975, a group of outcasts in their early teens calling themselves the Cemetery League discover a strange clearing in the woods which contains the carvings of an ancient entity. Deciding to build their clubhouse there, the evil which hibernates within the land begins to awaken and insinuate itself into the minds of some of the boys. As their leader becomes increasingly unhinged, the boys begin to pay service to the being known as Nodens, and their escalating activities culminate in the sacrifice of a local girl.

Forty years later, a small police task force attempt to apprehend the serial killer known as the Deer Hunter. Their investigations lead them to the few surviving members of the Cemetery League, and they eventually uncover the existence of a worldwide conspiracy to bring about the return of Nodens, although the group is wiped out as a result. The last remaining member of the Cemetery League is sacrificed as a host to allow the return of Nodens, and the being makes its way into the world to begin its work.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite being named Nodens, and being a god of health and the hunt, the entity depicted in The House of Nodens bears little resemblance to the popular portrayal of Nodens in the greater Cthulhu Mythos, being seemingly a creature whose home is Earth. At one point, it grants a vision to one of the characters of the world which is to come, in which "[c]reatures the size of mountains would roam the earth, calling others to their service"; at the story's finale, after its rebirth, Nodens muses to itself how "[p]laces had to be visited, gateways prepared, wards broken, and paths opened." These sentences would suggest that this iteration of Nodens is more akin to the herald of other cosmic entities, rather than one itself.

### Mythos Connections
*During one of the rituals performed by the boys in 1975, one of them gives himself the title of Guide of the Great Abyss. This would appear to be a nod to an epithet given to Nodens by H. P. Lovecraft in his short story "The Strange High House in the Mist," the Lord of the Great Abyss.
*Later, the leader of the Cemetery League reveals to the others that "making the Voorish sign or making the marks of the dholes upon our bodies" has ceased to be effective in facilitating their communion with Nodens.
*In the final ritual to summon Nodens, the chant "Dhonas’s dholas ort, agus leat-sa!" would appear to be a nod to a line uttered by Delapore, the narrator of Lovecraft's short story "The Rats in the Walls."

### Synopsis
A young man stumbles across a group of Cats of Ulthar and Cat-People of Ulthar living a secluded existence in a mysterious townhouse. Befriending them using coffee and cookies, he convinces one to teach him how to travel to the Dreamlands.

fullContent:
"The House of the Temple" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, written in April 1980  and first published in the November 1980 issue of Kadath. 

### Synopsis
A man inherits his uncle's Scottish estate, Temple House, under the condition that he destroy it completely.

### Publication History
It what Lumley described as "a genuine error on my part—in no way my usual practice," he sent the manuscript simultaneously to the English-language Italian magazine Kadath and to the revived Weird Tales, published by Zebra as a paperback under the editorship of Lin Carter. Both outlets accepted it, and Kadath published it first, in November 1980, followed by Weird Tales in 1981.

It was later reprinted in The Mammoth Book of Terror (Carroll & Graf, 1991) and in Lumley's collections The Second Wish and Other Exhalations (New English Library, 1995), A Coven of Vampires (Fedogan & Bremer, 1998), and The Taint and Other Novellas (Subterranean Press, 2007). It was the title story of Lumley's collection The House of the Temple (Endeavor Press, 2004).

fullContent:
"The House of the Worm" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by American author Gary Myers.

### Synopsis
The story tells of a house resting in the five black pillars of a round hill in Vornai in the plain of Kaar called the House of the Worm. It is an abandoned house which at sunset comes alive as the windows open red like eyes. The narrator tells that it is older than any man remembers, possibly akin to the Great Ones of Kadath. The man who built the house, referred to as the Old Man Of Whom No One Likes To Speak, was the last to live in a banquet of the House and has since gone mad. When he first arrived at the house he had feared the legends of the pillar ring holding daemons and had thus decided to arrive at daylight and be gone by dusk, reminiscing on the pillars' shining light from the red star Betelgeuse. He spoke to none of the natives and went to his cottage, not seen for a week and a day. On the eve of the ninth day, the people locked themselves in their homes as an unseen entity creeped about the dark streets.

The narrator, having been told these events upon his arrival in the plain of Kaar, asks the last of three people who attended the last banquet of the House still alive. He recounts that it was the hundredth year of his residence at the House. The Old Man handed out invitations after being isolated in the House for a century. Some had doubts, but 20 went with some ounce of regret, as they were perturbed by the setting of Betelgeuse’s light on the pillars and the faint feeling of watching daemons. A gnome escorted them to a pentagonal table and met with the Old Man. They were disturbed by the symbol of the five-sided star everywhere. This ritual continued for many nights, but few returned each time. Those who did not return were haunted by the Old Man’s tales of the Night-gaunts and how they drive people mad within the Peak of Throk, the appearance of Dholes, the worship of the goddess N'tse-Kaambl and the fall of the Serpent priests, and the Old Man also told of forbidden things in the Pnakotic Manuscripts while drawing the Sign of Koth. Only the three men remained after these forbidden tales on the final night.

On the final night, the Old Man told stories of higher and older gods, including Azathoth, and about how weaker gods were imprisoned in the Abyss and should return if Nodens should sleep and cease his watch. He stopped telling his story as he listened for something. From one of the cellars came ominous sounds and the visions of daemons and horrid flute-players. The three guests followed the Old Man into a hall of carvings depicting horrid monsters and stars. They went through following the fluting sounds and found in a well of light as the Old Man’s candlelight went out. As he looked within the well, the man claimed that this was the seal of the Elder Sign which imprisoned Azathoth’s children long ago as the Old Man, its guardian, was sucked inside, never to be seen again.

"The House of the Worm" is a short story by author Mearle Prout.

### Synopsis
Two men on a hunting trip uncover the existence of a deadly supernatural force which is killing everything in a remote valley. Knowing that they will never be believed, and viewing media reports of the spread of the evil, they venture back to the valley, burning the cultists which summoned the power and killing it at its root.

### Characters
*Art, an author in need of a break from writing.
*Fred, a bank clerk and Art's housemate.

### Publication History
First published in pulp magazine Weird Tales in October 1933, "The House of the Worm" has since been reprinted several times in different publications, and has also been translated into German.

### Behind the Mythos
Although containing no direct references to Lovecraft's works or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, "The House of the Worm" has long been touted as a Mythos tale. Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi's inclusion of the piece in A Mountain Walked would seem to support this claim.

fullContent:
"The Hunt" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Henry Kuttner, originally published in the June 1939 issue of Strange Stories.

It is set in the fictional town of Monk's Hollow from Kuttner's earlier tale, "The Frog".

### Synopsis
A man named Alvin Doyle goes to the small town of Monk's Hollow to kill his cousin, Will Benson, as Doyle is next in line for Benson's grandfather's inheritance. Benson's reputation as a wizard doesn't discourage Doyle, who finds the fact that his intended victim is a recluse highly convenient to his plans.

Benson reluctantly allows Doyle to stay after the latter pretends that his car has broken down, but explains that he's in the middle of a dangerous experiment. There's a large pentagram traced on the floor and a censer in which Benson is mixing up ingredients. He believes that what the villagers refer to as sorcery is actually a kind of science that allows one to peek at hidden worlds beyond the familiar three dimensions, and make contact with "the old gods". While acknowledging the venture as a dangerous one, he tells Doyle that they should be safe as long as the lamps are burning and they remain inside the pentagram.

Benson utters the incantation to summon one of the ancient deities, the extradimensional being known as Iod, the Hunter of Souls, who came to Earth from the stars to be worshiped by many civilizations, and who, according to De Vermis Mysteriis, delights in hunting the souls of men through hidden dimensions of space, killing only their bodies while keeping their consciousnesses alive.

While Benson is uttering the incantation, Doyle shoots him from behind and steps back. Benson's body collapses and knocks down one of the lamps. Satisfied, Doyle exits the pentagram, steals several things and breaks the window so that the police will think the murder was committed by a burglar. He disposes of the loot in a lake several miles away.

While driving back home, Doyle feels inexplicably drowsy and is forced to stop the car before he falls asleep. He dreams of being back in Benson's cabin, which is now roofless, and witnessing a mysterious shadow descending from the stars upon him. When he tries to escape, he finds himself standing on an alien world. The dream repeats itself, with the creature chasing Doyle through various dimensions of eerie and exotic scenery, until Doyle seemingly wakes up, back in his car, confronted by the actual image of a luminous alien being: none other than Iod itself.

The monster extends a tentacle and touches Doyle's head, killing him instantly. Doyle remains conscious but paralysed as people start to gather around him. A doctor examines his pupillary reflexes and declares him dead. The story ends as Doyle realizes that he's in a coffin, being buried.

shortDefinition: "The Hunters from Beyond" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith that first appeared in the October 1932 issue of Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror.   The story's titular creatures were first incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos in "The Guardian of...
fullContent:
"The Hunters from Beyond" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith that first appeared in the October 1932 issue of Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror. 

The story's titular creatures were first incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos in "The Guardian of the Book", by Henry Hasse. The character Cyprian Sincaul is also mentioned in Lin Carter's Mythos stories "Out of the Ages" and "The Horror in the Gallery".

### Characters
* Philip Hastane: The story's narrator, "a professional writer of stories that often dealt with occult phenomena, with the weird and the spectral." He is a second or third cousin of Cyprian Sincaul.
* Cyprian Sincaul: A San Francisco sculptor who "wanted to do in sculpture what Poe and Lovecraft and Baudelaire have done in literature, what Rops and Goya did in pictorial art." He is described as "lean, harsh, vehement, with an air of pride and penetration that was almost Luciferian. His unkempt mane of hair was already shot with white, and his eyes were electrically brilliant with a strange knowledge."
* Marta Fitzgerald: Sincaul's model and lover. Half Irish, half Italian, she is described as "beautiful, in a dark, semi-Latin fashion," with a "sullen and reluctant" mouth and "wide, liquid eyes."
* Toleman: The owner of a San Francisco bookstore called Toleman's. He is "a tonsured gnome with shell-rimmed goggles."

### Publication History
After its appearance in Strange Tales, "The Hunters from Beyond" has appeared in numerous collections of Smith's work, including Lost Worlds (Arkham House, 1944), The City of the Singing Flame (Timescape/Pocket Books, 1981), The Emperor of Dreams (Gollancz/Orion, 2002), The White Sybil and Other Stories (Wildside Press, 2004), The Door to Saturn: Volume Two of the Collected Fantasies of Clark Ashton Smith (Night Shade Books, 2007), and The Klarkash-Ton Cycle: Clark Ashton Smith's Cthulhu Mythos Fiction (Chaosium, 2008).

The story was included in the Lovecraftian anthologies The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (Wildside Press, 2012) and Lovecraft Short Stories (Flame Tree Publishing, 2017). It also was selected for the general horror anthologies The Macabre Reader (Ace Books, 1959) and A Book of Weird Tales (Veevers & Hensman, 1960).

It as been translated into French (as "Les chasseurs de l'au-delà," 1986), German ("Verfolger von Drüben," 1988, and "Die Jäger aus der Tiefe," 2015), Italian ("I cacciatori dell'Aldilà," 1990), and Portuguese ("Os Caçadores do Além," 2020).

### External Link
* "[http://www.eldritchdark.com/writings/short-stories/93/the-hunters-from-beyond The Hunters from Beyond]" full text at Eldritch Dark

"The Hutchison Boy" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Darrell Schweitzer.

### Synopsis
In New Jersey during the End of Days, a family is befriended by a strange boy named Caleb who is actually a Deep One hybrid. When the creatures of the ocean call to Caleb to come to them, he believes he can take the family's son, Jackie, with him, but Jackie is unable to breathe beneath the waves and drowns. The parents then grieve while the world crumbles around them.

### Characters

*Unnamed narrator, the father, a struggling writer.
*Margaret, the mother, an out-of-work teacher.
*Jackie, the 12 year old son.
*Caleb, a Deep One hybrid.

### Publication History
"The Hutchison Boy" was printed in the non-Mythos anthology The Dragons of the Night in May 2016, and again in Weirdbook Annual 2 in February 2019.

"The Hymn" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, written in July/August 2003, that first appeared in the Fall 2006 issue of H. P. Lovecraft's Magazine of Horror. It is one of the last of Lumley's Mythos stories to appear, and serves as something of a final statement on the genre.

### Synopsis
As part of a secret government experiment, two individuals with psychic powers are housed in an underground chamber, constantly exposed to an eldritch artefact.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in H. P. Lovecraft's Magazine of Horror, "The Hymn" was reprinted in Lumley's collection Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008).

fullContent:
"The Ice-Demon" is a fantasy short story by Clark Ashton Smith, originally published in the April 1933 issue of Weird Tales. It is part of his Hyperborea series, connected to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
A hunter named Quanga, along with two jewelers named Hoom Feethos and Eibur Tsanth, travels north of his native land of Iqqua, into the frozen Mhu Thulan, to search for the lost rubies of King Haalor.

Fifty years before, Haalor had ventured into the frozen land with a small army, and had the wizard Ommum-Vog conjure an artificial sun in the sky to melt the ice and reclaim the lands. However, as the ice-sheet started to melt, the water was covered by a mysterious fog which encircled the men and behaved like a living being. Some of those who ran away glanced back and saw their companions, including Haalor and Ommum-Vog, frozen inside a wall of newly-formed ice. The incident recalls legends about ice that acts like a sentient entity, and kills men by freezing, impaling, or entombing them.

Quanga and the jewelers find an ice cave in which Quanga's late brother, Iluac, claimed that he had found the bodies of Haalor's party. The entrance is shaped like a maw, with icicles for fangs. Deep inside, they find the bodies of Haalor's men sealed within the translucent walls of ice, including the king himself, his robes decorated with rubies and other gems.

Working with a pickaxe, the men free the body of the king from the ice and retrieve the precious gems. However, a large icicle falls from the ceiling above and kills Eibur Tsanth. At this moment, Quanga and Hoom Feethos realize that the chamber has narrowed in size considerably since they got in, and the entrance of the cave appears to be much farther away and smaller than before.

Quanga manages to crawl through the small opening and leaves the cave, but Hoom Feethos gets stuck and moans about ice-teeth crunching him. Before Quanga can help him, he realizes that the icicles have grown, one of them now impaling Hoom Feethos' body, which bleeds profusely. In an impulse, Quanga grabs the pouch of gemstones that Hoom Feethos had dropped and runs away, but realizes that the ice-covered ground is changing, until the plain transforms into an upward slope. Even the sky appears different, and the sun seems more distant. Looking back, Quanga sees a mirrored image of what he could see in front of him: another slope and another, equally remote sun (the story identifies this as the real atmospheric phenomenon known as parhelia).

Despite his fear, Quanga continues to climb upward, assailed by frigid winds. The ice on the ground changes into several menacing forms, as if to mock him, and mixed into the ice he sees actual human body parts: the faces and limbs of all those who had disappeared in the northern country in the years before. At last, Quanga reaches the end of the slope and everything seems to return to normal, including the ground's inclination and the sun.

"The Idea of Fear" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author C. J. Henderson. It is the first in the Arkham Detective Agency series.

### Synopsis
Private investigator Frank Nardi and psychic Madame Renee conduct an investigation into an old house on behalf of its new owners. Despite an uneventful night in the mansion, something evil is lurking in its walls.

### Characters
*Frank Nardi, former New York Police Officer turned private detective.
*Madame Renee, self-professed clairvoyant and sensitive.
*Jedidiah Mortonson, a psychic vampire who has transcended death by implanting his consciousness into the walls of his former home.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Idea of Fear" was written by C. J. Henderson shortly before his death in 2014. It was first published in 2017 in the short story collection Arkham Detective Agency.

### Mythos References
*The story is set in H.P. Lovecraft's iconic town of Arkham.
*Nardi references famous cases whose stories did the rounds amongst the officers of the NYPD, including the events experienced by Detective Malone in "The Horror at Red Hook".

shortDefinition: The Illuminatus! Trilogy is a series of three novels written by Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson, first published as individual volumes in 1975 and collected as an omnibus in 1984.  ### Overview The books tell a satirical, postmodern science ficti...
fullContent:
The Illuminatus! Trilogy is a series of three novels written by Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson, first published as individual volumes in 1975 and collected as an omnibus in 1984.

### Overview
The books tell a satirical, postmodern science fiction adventure that explores various conspiracy theories, both real and imagined, related to the Illuminati. It has also spawned disparate spinoff novels, short stories and articles, many of them in men's magazines of past decades.

The trilogy consists of three main parts:

*The Eye in the Pyramid (first two books)
*The Golden Apple (third and part of the fourth book)
*Leviathan (part of the fourth and all of the fifth book)

The narrative is nonlinear and often shifts between different perspectives. It covers a wide range of themes, including conspiracy theories, counterculture, mythology, numerology, and discordianism.

### Plot Summary
The story begins with the bombing of a leftist magazine's office, leading detectives Saul Goodman and Barney Muldoon on a complex investigation. They uncover a web of conspiracies involving secret societies and historical events, including the assassinations of prominent figures such as US president John F. Kennedy.

### Legacy
The trilogy has influenced various modern writers, artists, and musicians. It has been adapted for stage and audio formats and is known for its unique humor and complex narrative style. The term "fnord" and the "23 enigma" are notable concepts popularized by the series.

### Mythos Connections
*Both Cthulhu and Yog-Sothoth are referenced, and in the case of Yog-Sothoth, he is the subject of a ritual magic summoning in which he appears as the evangelical preacher Billy Graham before being abjured into a different form.
*The Necronomicon also features in the story, appearing as a reference work used by cultists and as a source of both wisdom and misguided and pornographic illustrations.
*Atlantis and other drowned ruins also feature, with dolphins being the guardians of Secrets Men Were Not Meant To Know as well as tireless opponents of sea-based menaces including Cthulhu.
*There are also several cult groups which, while not directly part of the Cthulhu Mythos, are much like the most debased and orgiastic of those described in the works of H. P. Lovecraft and his Circle.

"The Incessant Drone" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British-born author Neil Baker.

### Synopsis
With the planet being slowly conquered by mile-high abominations dubbed 'Thrashers', what remains of the world's military unites to do what they can to stop the incursion. However, their air attacks are all but useless against the Thrashers, and the few successes they are able to achieve give way to a shocking revelation: whatever dark forces are behind the attack are using humankind's own warriors against them.

*Jasi "Hot Stuff", a skilled pilot with the Euro-Asia Coalition air forces.
*Group Captain Redcarr, a senior officer with the EAC air forces.

"The Incubus of Atlantis", which has also been published as "The Incubus of Atlantis (The History of Klarkash-Ton the Heirophant)", is a short story by American scholar and writer Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
When Klarkash-Ton is employed by Pharnabazus the King of Atlantis to chronicle his nation's history, he stumbles across magical knowledge which allows him to astrally project his consciousness and inhabit the bodies of others.

Abusing these newfound abilities by using them to engage in sexual congress with the wives of the royal court, he becomes complacent and his soul is caught in a mystical trap by the court wizard, condemned to spend the aeons confined to an amphora of wine at the bottom of the ocean.

### Characters

shortDefinition: "The Infernal History of the Ivybridge Twins" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Molly Tanzer, the first in her Ivybridge Twins series. It was first published in the Innsmouth Free Press anthology Historical Lovecraft in 2011.  ### Sy...
fullContent:
"The Infernal History of the Ivybridge Twins" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Molly Tanzer, the first in her Ivybridge Twins series. It was first published in the Innsmouth Free Press anthology Historical Lovecraft in 2011.

### Synopsis
The story charts the history of two children, Basil and Rosemary Calipash, the offspring of an English lord murdered by his cousin before their birth. The murderer, Mr. Villein, has a deep knowledge of forbidden sorcery, and curses the two at birth, resulting in a pair of children who are not only inherently adept at magic, but also absolutely callous about anyone other than themselves.

As the children grow, Villein takes an interest in Rosemary, who is blossoming with puberty. Witnessing the twins' incestuous relationship, he flies into a rage, and schemes to send Basil from the family estate while taking Rosemary as his bride. Over the years Rosemary, pining for her absent brother, uses her magical abilities to create a golem from the dead bodies of her ancestors to fulfil her carnal desires, in the process contracting gangrene.

Unfortunately for him, Villein has underestimated the cunning of Basil who returns ten years later, and the reunited twins murder him. Together they use their considerable magical powers to tackle the problem of Rosemary's disease by swapping their mother's consciousness with that of Rosemary before sealing the poor woman alive in a family crypt.

### Behind the Mythos
Mythos connections include Basil being able to speak the alien language of R'lyehian from birth, and a small statue used by Mr. Villein to kill the former Lord Calipash being heavily implied to be the entity from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Temple"; this implication is reinforced by Tanzer's statement in Historical Lovecraft that while writing "The Infernal History of the Ivybridge Twins" she "consider[ed] the bizarre, Apollonian elements of "The Temple.""

A parallel with Lovecraft’s work may also be seen is the mind-transferral magic enacted by Basil and Rosemary upon their mother; this recalls the spell used by Ephraim Waite on his daughter Asenath in the short story "The Thing on the Doorstep."

### Publication History 
* Historical Lovecraft (2011)
* The Book of Cthulhu (2011, 2022)
* A Pretty Mouth (2012)
* Nightmare Magazine (2013)

### References

shortDefinition: "The Infernal Star" is an unfinished short story set in the wider Cthulhu Mythos by author and Lovecraft Circle member Clark Ashton Smith. It was abandoned unfinished and never returned to by the original author although its elements were taken up by...
fullContent:
"The Infernal Star" is an unfinished short story set in the wider Cthulhu Mythos by author and Lovecraft Circle member Clark Ashton Smith. It was abandoned unfinished and never returned to by the original author although its elements were taken up by others, notably

It was written in early February 1933 and first published as a self-published pamphlet with a print run of 1,000 by Smith himself in June 1933. After this very limited but surprisingly influential publication it was not published again until 1989 when it formed part of "Strange Shadows: The Uncollected Fiction of Clark Ashton Smith," by Greenwood Press, which includes various works by the author.

### Synopsis
The surviving draft is very brief and largely scene-setting rather than a full narrative. It begins with an ominous description of a mysterious, baleful star appearing in the heavens — a celestial body of ominous appearance whose radiation extends malevolently to other worlds. The star is not charted by astronomers, but is associated with malign portents and dread. The star is described in Smith’s highly poetic, decadent style, likened to a burning coal in the sky, casting strange hues and oppressive influence over the Earth.

There are hints of cult activity and dark rituals tied to the star, aligning it with the broader Cthulhu Mythos theme of cosmic entities whose manifestations are heralded by astronomical phenomena. Unlike other Smith works of the same period, the setting seems to be contemporary (early 20th century) rather than in one of Smith’s far-future cycles such as Zothique. This aligns it closer to the kind of “Mythos tale” Lovecraft himself would write, such as The Haunter of the Dark.

Unfortunately, the story breaks off before characters, plotlines, or named entities appear. It remains mostly a mood piece, conjuring up an atmosphere of dread, and a cosmic-horror premise awaiting development. 

### Behind the Mythos
"The Infernal Star" features the binary star system comprised of the stars Yuzh and Yamil Zacra. These were used in the later story "Priestess of Nycrama" by John W. Patterson.

fullContent:
"The Inhabitant of the Lake" is a short story by British author Ramsey Campbell.

### Synopsis
Artist Thomas Cartwright rents a secluded lakeside property in England's Severn Valley, the dark beauty of the location intended to inspire his morbid work. There, nightmares and half-imagined happenings in the night begin to plague him, and he discovers a set of ancient manuscripts which detail the coming of an ancient entity to Earth and its activities thereafter. As the strange happenings escalate, Cartwright calls on his friend Alan Kearney for help, and the two attempt to escape the cursed lake. However, only one of them is fortunate to survive the climactic encounter with the creature which dwells in the lake.

### Characters

*Thomas Cartwright, a gifted artist specialising in paintings of the macabre.
*Alan Kearney, the narrator and friend of Cartwight's.
*Joseph "Joe" Bulger, a friend of Cartwright's, forcibly made a follower of Glaaki.
*Thomas Lee, one-time leader of the cult of Glaaki.
*Glaaki, a Great Old One.

### Publication History
"The Inhabitant of the Lake" was published in Arkham House's 1964 release The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, and was later reprinted in the collection of short Ramsey Campbell works Cold Print in 1985.

### Mythos Connections

*The story is set in Campbell's fictional Severn Valley setting, the backdrop for much of his Mythos content; Brichester, Goatswood, Temphill and Mercy Hill all feature to some degree.
*"The Inhabitant of the Lake" sees the first appearance of the Revelations of Glaaki, a source of occult information which would become prominent in the Mythos work of Campbell, among others.
*The name of Alhazred is name-dropped in a missive discovered by Cartwright, a nod to the mad Arab Abdul Alhazred, author of the Necronomicon, while Cartwright discovers an 11-volume copy of the Revelations of Glaaki in his new home.
*References to Yuggoth, Shaggai, Yifne and Tond are all uncovered by Cartwright during his reading of the Revelations of Glaaki.
*Mythos entities made mention of include Vulthoom, as well as the alien race named the yarkdao and the Tomb-Herd beneath Temphill.
*The Crystallizers of Dreams are alluded to, as is their guardian.

term: The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants
shortDefinition: The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants is a collection of short horror stories by British horror fiction author and Mythos contributor Ramsey Campbell published by Arkham House. As it was edited by August Derleth, the stories are conside...
fullContent:
The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants is a collection of short horror stories by British horror fiction author and Mythos contributor Ramsey Campbell published by Arkham House. As it was edited by August Derleth, the stories are considered by this wiki to be set in the Derleth Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
Collected from stories written from 1961 through to 1963, The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants contains eleven tales set in the fictional Severn Valley region of England conceived by Campbell for his expansions into the Mythos. The volume is also notable for introducing the fictitious book of lore The Revelations of Gla'aki, a tome which would feature in many of Campbell's later stories, and which would be extensively expanded on by Chaosium for use in their Mythos role-playing games.

The editor of the Inhabitant of the Lake, Lovecraft contemporary and Mythos contributor August Derleth, discouraged Campbell's use of the New England settings created by Lovecraft and employed by Campbell, instead suggesting that he base his stories in an environment more familiar to Campbell. This resulted in the creation of the fictional Severn Valley location, including the towns of Brichester, Goatswood and Clotton.

### Publication History
Originally published in 1964 by Arkham House, The Inhabitant of the Lake was later reprinted with new forewords as Cold Print in 1985 with three of the original stories removed and others added in their stead. However, the 1993 reissue of Cold Print saw the missing stories reinstated.

In 2011, PS Publishing released an expanded and illustrated print of the book which was promoted as the '50th Anniversary Edition,' counting from when the stories were first begun in 1961. This edition was titled The Inhabitant of the Lake and Other Unwelcome Tenants (which was to have been the first release title, but had to be changed at the last minute due to a miscommunication with the cover illustrator) and featured the original versions of Campbell's stories, before they had undergone revision by Derleth.

### Contents 
*"The Room in the Castle"
*"The Horror from the Bridge"
*"The Insects from Shaggai"
*"The Render of the Veils"
*"The Inhabitant of the Lake"
*"The Plain of Sound"
*"The Return of the Witch"
*"The Mine on Yuggoth"
*"The Will of Stanley Brooke"
*"The Moon-Lens"

"The Ink of the Slime Lord" is a short story by American author Jason Ray Carney. First published in the 2017 Rogue Planet Press anthology Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights, it contains no direct references to the Cthulhu Mythos, but features Lovecraftian entities in the form of Cax, Lord of Slime, and the Inmor, a species reminiscent of the Deep Ones.

### Synopsis
After three great sorceresses and their entire cult are murdered by a rival priesthood, one of the sisters named Mera manages to resurrect herself, subsequently setting out on a quest to obtain a phial of slime from the being known as Cax. 

Hiring a mercenary crew, she travels across the ocean, the band killing all who stand in their way before reaching the cursed island home of Cax. There, Mera manages to obtain her sample, barely escaping with her life. After returning to her homeland, she enacts a complicated and dangerous ritual using the slime, but is eventually successful in bringing about the rebirth of her two elder sisters.

"The Inner Spheres" is a short Cthulhu Mythos poem by author Jeff Remling. It was published in the Candlemas edition (Vol 3, Issue 4) of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in January 2019.

### Synopsis
The twelve lines see the author grapple with existentialism while contemplating the mind's ability to access the Dreamlands - and perhaps even beyond.

### Mythos Connections
Aside from the Dreamlands overtones, the poem mentions Mythos staples Alhazred and Kadath, the latter, unusually, as a desirable location to inhabit.
