fullContent:
"The Innsmouth Covenant" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jennifer M. Oaks. It was self-published in the chapbook collection The Brides of Innsmouth in 2012, along with a companion piece, "The Diary of Hannah Greeley".

### Synopsis
In 1846, thirteen year old Hannah Greeley and her widowed father move to the small coastal town of Innsmouth, Massachusetts in the hopes of starting a new life. Over the next few years, they settle in to their new home, and her father marries an Innsmouth woman. As she begins to reach her majority, Hannah begins to suspect that there is something wrong with the natives, and that monsters lurk amongst the townsfolk. On her eighteenth birthday, she is dragged off to Devil Reef and forced by her father to marry a man - who may not be entirely human - against her will. Held captive on the reef and forced to give birth to inhuman offspring, Hannah recounts her experiences in a diary.

### Trivia
*Hannah's diary is reused as a plot device for "The Innsmouth Covenant"'s companion piece "The Diary of Hannah Greeley"; indeed, much of that story consists of sections of text taken in their entirety from this one.

shortDefinition: "The Innsmouth Heritage" is a short story written by British author Brian Stableford based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.  ### Synopsis Geneticist David Stevenson travels to Innsmouth after receiving a letter from his old friend Ann Eliot, who ...
fullContent:
"The Innsmouth Heritage" is a short story written by British author Brian Stableford based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Geneticist David Stevenson travels to Innsmouth after receiving a letter from his old friend Ann Eliot, who has been willed much of the land and property in the town by her late father, informing him of a strange condition possessed by many of the residents known as the Innsmouth Look.

After agreeing that this abnormality deserves further study, Eliot introduces Stevenson to an old fisherman named Gideon Sargent who has one of the worst cases of the Innsmouth Look evident. Sargent consents to becoming a study case for Stevenson on the condition that he attempt to rid the sufferers of the horrific dreams which accompany the Look. He also convinces many of the other reclusive victims of the condition to participate in the research. At this point, Eliot confesses to having the same dreams as the others, despite showing no physical signs of the Look.

Although Stevenson's research progresses at a good pace, his test subjects begin to mysteriously die, beginning with Sargent himself, who apparently drowns out on Devil Reef. Despite this, he has acquired enough samples to continue. During this time, a romantic relationship has developed between Stevenson and Eliot, and he asks her to marry him but is turned down.

After the proposal, Eliot and Stevenson begin to drift apart, and Stevenson continues with his work, eventually locating a series of genetic anomalies which he believes are the root cause of the Innsmouth Look. After several months without contact from Eliot, Stevenson attempts to call her, only to be told that she has drowned off Devil Reef, and that her body was never recovered.

### Characters
*David Stevenson, an English geneticist working at Manchester University, New Hampshire, who embarks on a program of research into genetic abnormalities found in the town of Innsmouth.
*Ann Eliot, a distant scion of one of the old families of Innsmouth, who owns a large portion of the town, and is suffering from the strange dreams associated with the Innsmouth Look.
*Gideon Sargent, a fisherman who has the most pronounced case of the Innsmouth Look in town, and who agrees to assist Stevenson in his research.

### Publication History
"The Innsmouth Heritage" was originally published as a chapbook by Necronomicon Press in March of 1992, and has since been reprinted in other collections, including Shadows Over Innsmouth and Wildside Press LLC's 2012 eBook bundle The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack.

### Trivia
*Ann Eliot is believed to be the last of the Eliot Family in Innsmouth.
*Gideon Sargent is the grandson of Joe Sargent, Innsmouth's bus driver in H. P. Lovecraft's 1931 novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth.
*Zadok Allen, another character from The Shadow Over Innsmouth, and the Esoteric Order of Dagon, are both mentioned in the story as possible sources for the outlandish tales concerning the town's residents.
*Althou

fullContent:
The Innsmouth Look is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author and filmmaker Byron Craft. The second in his Arkham Detective series, it was independently published through CreateSpace in September 2016, and features cover art by Eric Lofgren. Both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Overview


### Synopsis
The Arkham Detective is assigned the case of a woman who has been brutally murdered, her seven-year-old child abducted by the killer. His investigations into the whereabouts of the young daughter lead him to the degenerate fishing town of Innsmouth, where he uncovers a plot by the Deep Ones to raise a powerful creature from beneath the waves (variously described as being a Shoggoth, Father Dagon, and even Cthulhu himself). 

A series of events lead the Detective into contact with members of the Office of Strategic Services and United States Navy, who have also learned of the Deep Ones' scheme, and plan to destroy the town using the heavy guns of a warship anchored just beyond Devil's Reef. He manages to evacuate the handful of humans left in the town and rescue the girl, who he later adopts, her companionship going some distance to filling the hole left when his wife left him with their son some years previously.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite being set in Prohibition-era America, as evidenced by the existence of Speakeasies, the Office of Strategic Services which aid the Detective in his mission was not established until 1942, by the presidential decree of Franklin D. Roosevelt .

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance, The Innsmouth Look has since appeared in the 2017 collection The Arkham Detective Collection Volume 1.

"The Insidious Doom" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Frank Forte, first published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
Paranormal investigator Davian Cooper travels to the virtually-abandoned and slowly decaying town of Thurmond to investigate reports of supernatural activity. Booking a room in the town's sole remaining hotel, he listens to the owner's stories of strange happenings, and experiences several inexplicable occurrences himself.

Cooper is eventually murdered by the innkeeper and his eldritch minion before the man sends his journals to the national press, which results in an influx of visitors and more victims for the town's strange practices.

shortDefinition: "The Interloper" is a short story by acclaimed British horror author Ramsey Campbell, which is set in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the 1973 Arkham House collection Demons by Daylight.  ### Synopsis Two teenage boys attempt to find...
fullContent:
"The Interloper" is a short story by acclaimed British horror author Ramsey Campbell, which is set in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the 1973 Arkham House collection Demons by Daylight.

### Synopsis
Two teenage boys attempt to find a trendy subterranean music venue while on a lunch pass from their school. In a dirty back-alley they find a secret door leading to a tunnel - "accidentally" revealed by a passing newspaper vendor - and and think they have found their place, but discover instead a catacomb of desiccated human remains, and the malevolent entity which calls the tunnels home. 

The creature corners and, presumably, captures one boy while the other flees, finding his way back to the surface and running back to the school. However, when he reaches this supposed safe haven, he comes to the shocking conclusion that the visiting school inspector is not who he seems to be, and that he too is doomed to become a meal for the creature…

### Mythos Connections
"The Interloper" is set in the fictional town of Brichester, as evidenced when the boys come across a vendor selling copies of the Brichester Herald. Brichester is located in the Severn Valley, a backdrop created by Campbell and used as the setting for many of his Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Trivia
* Although the nature of the creature is never revealed, it is capable of mimicking human form in order to procure human prey, as seen when it disguises itself as the school inspector, and when one of the boys realises that it was in fact the newspaper vendor who gave away the secret door's location.

shortDefinition: "The Invaders" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Henry Kuttner, writing under the pen name Keith Hammond.   ### Plot The tale tells of horror writer Michael Hayward who accidentally unleashes monstrosities from a forgotten age upon the Earth.  Haywa...
fullContent:
"The Invaders" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Henry Kuttner, writing under the pen name Keith Hammond. 

### Plot
The tale tells of horror writer Michael Hayward who accidentally unleashes monstrosities from a forgotten age upon the Earth.

Hayward, who lives in an isolated cottage on the beach north of Santa Barbara, California, finds the formula for a narcotic drug in Ludvig Prinn’s De Vermis Mysteriis. He creates the substance and begins taking it. This drug is a "time drug", allowing Hayward to read the akashic record and recover ancestral memories. Because he did not properly obey the instructions to use magical protections such as the Pnakotic pentagram, he exposed himself to the danger of the ‘the  dwellers in the Hidden World’ who now took notice of him. 

Hayward uses the drug to help him prepare a manuscript, which read:



-there the manuscript ended.

The creatures from beyond, resembling gigantic eyeballs with small tentacles on their underside and a small puckered mouth, begin to mutate plants and animals surrounding his beachside house, and eventually even abduct one of his acquaintances, sending a misshapen wrecked undead version of the man back to Hayward, crawling along the beach. The entities then begin to directly impinge upon Earthly reality, the implication being they will mutate and overwhelm normal existence if not somehow stopped.

Eventually, Hayward successfully invokes Vorvadoss of  Bel-Yarnak and the interdimensional creatures are banished once more.

### Publication History
First published in the debut issue of Strange Stories in February 1939, "The Invaders" has since been reprinted several times, and has also been translated into Italian.

The Investigators of Arkham Horror is a reference book for Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files range of Mythos-related products.

### Description
A 264-page full-colour hardback reference book featuring more in-depth information on the Arkham Horror investigators than can be found in the various games, Investigators includes 52 short stories, with each one focussing on a different character but forming a narrative when read as a whole. A pre-order premium was also available for a limited time, which contained the same book along with an exclusive gaming mat, four art prints - including one of Daisy Walker - and three cards for Arkham Horror: The Card Game, featuring investigator Marie Lambeau.

### Publication History
The Investigators of Arkham Horror was first published by Fantasy Flight Games in February 2017. An updated 288 page digital-only version featuring 55 short stories was released by Aconyte Books on May 1, 2024.

shortDefinition: "The Invisible Menace" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle.  ### Synopsis In 1955, a group of British scientists are inspired by the film The War of the Worlds to create a magnetic field generator capable of defending against inter...
fullContent:
"The Invisible Menace" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
In 1955, a group of British scientists are inspired by the film The War of the Worlds to create a magnetic field generator capable of defending against intercontinental ballistic missiles- or at least make the Soviets believe that it will. Unluckily for the people of London, its activation opens a gateway to another dimension through which a colossal, invisible, insect-like creature emerges and begins laying waste to the historical city.

The scientists are a quick-thinking bunch however, and manage to devise a plan involving reversing the magnetism of the field, which sends the beast back home and closes the gateway to its dimension permanently.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, project leader of the Rocket Research Group, a government think-tank. Referred to as "Prof" by Thornton.
*George Thornton, a junior engineer on the project.
*The Minister of Defence, a cabinet member in charge of the project.

### Publication History
"The Invisible Menace" has been published in the following collections of Meikle's own works:

*B.E.M. (2016)
*Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2017)
*Nursery: Three Tales of Weird Science (2020)

### Trivia
*Despite not containing any direct references to the mythos or any of Lovecraft’s work, Meikle's inclusion of "The Invisible Menace" in Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates that he believes it to be in the spirit of these stories, even if it is not materially connected. Additionally, the theme of unseen creatures from another dimension may be considered somewhat Lovecraftian, in the tradition of stories such as "From Beyond".
*Prof, Thornton and the the Rocket Research Group appear in another of Meikle's Mythos-inspired works, "Amoeboid". The nature of the menace they face and the fact their name contains "Rocket Research" indicates that they are intended to be a pastiche of Professor Bernard Quatermass and his British Rocket Group. This is a common influence on many British and especially English writers of a certain age.

shortDefinition: "Carnacki: The Island of Doctor Munroe" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle. It is part of the Carnacki series established by William Hope Hodgson and expanded upon by many others.  ### Synopsis Thomas Carnacki relates the story of...
fullContent:
"Carnacki: The Island of Doctor Munroe" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle. It is part of the Carnacki series established by William Hope Hodgson and expanded upon by many others.

### Synopsis
Thomas Carnacki relates the story of his experience with one Doctor John Munroe, a self-proclaimed man of science who invited Carnacki to spend time on his island, and inspect his inventions.

However, upon arrival Carnacki, a veteran occultist with many years of experience in dealing with dark entities, immediately recognises that the island is in fact a prison for malevolent entities from the "Outer Darkness" which have been polluting Munroe's mind with designs for machinery which will bring about their release and, ultimately, the downfall of humankind.

Carnacki is able to use an obscure passage from an ancient book to cause the destruction of the island and the demise of the entities, but in doing so becomes responsible for the death of Doctor Munroe, an act for which he feels tremendous remorse.

### Characters

*Thomas Carnacki, a highly-accomplished occultist.
*Doctor John Munroe, a scientist who has unwittingly fallen into the thrall of entities from another plane of existence.

### Publication History
"Carnacki: The Island of Doctor Munroe" was first published in Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu Fiction anthology Steampunk Cthulhu in June 2014. It was later included in the collection of Meikle's own work Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in April 2017.

### Behind the Mythos
Although not directly involving Mythos elements, the character of Thomas Carnacki has featured in several Mythos stories in the past (although none of these were written by the series creator, William Hope Hodgson). However, the premise of "Carnacki: The Island of Doctor Munroe", that of ancient malevolence lurking just out of sight of humanity, is most definitely Lovecraftian in theme.

shortDefinition: "The Isle of Dark Magic" is a horror fantasy short story by Hugh B. Cave, set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the August 1934 issue of Weird Tales.  ### Synopsis Father Jason is a missionary priest stationed in the island of Faikana, close...
fullContent:
"The Isle of Dark Magic" is a horror fantasy short story by Hugh B. Cave, set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the August 1934 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
Father Jason is a missionary priest stationed in the island of Faikana, close to the Marquesas, which has a very small native population. One day, a ship arrives bringing Peter Mace, a young recluse who paid the captain to take him to the most isolated isle available, so that he would not be disturbed.

Mace is extremely secretive, revealing nothing about himself, and spends the days locked in the second floor of his house, where he keeps something brought inside a large crate, and allows no one access to it. The rest of the time, Mace drinks and studies piles of books. One day, Father Jason finds the house open and is horrified to discover that the books are grimoires. Driven by curiosity and a desire to know what kind of sin Mace is committing, so as to be able to help him, Jason climbs the ladder to the second floor and sees what he assumes to be a naked woman, but is interrupted by the arrival of a drunken Mace, who violently kicks him out.

Several days later, Mace seeks out Jason while drunk, and invites him to his house to explain things. When he sobers up, he tells Jason that he was once a prestigious medical student, but was expelled from the university after performing some undisclosed experiments. He was also deeply in love with a young prostitute named Maureen Kennedy, and was devastated when she died. However, he figured a way to try to resurrect her, and asked his artist roommate to make a life-sized sculpture of her. This marble statue is what Jason saw when he peeked into the second floor.

Mace forces Jason to watch as he takes an inverted crucifix, pours a dark liquid into a dish, and recites a prayer to Hastur, Nyarlathotep, and other entities. Jason hears other voices joining Mace's, and watches incredulous as the marble statue becomes alive for a few moments and contorts in obvious agony, before returning to its inanimate state. Mace reveals that this is the fifth time he performs this ritual, and that the gods have promised him that on the seventh time, Maureen would be revived permanently.

Several days later, Mace's native servant, Menegai, comes to Jason for help, telling that he saw Mace go into the second floor and heard the voices of demons chanting, followed by the sound of a woman screaming in pain. At this moment, a ship arrives at the island: the same one that had brought Mace. This time, the passenger is a young woman, whose face is concealed behind a veil, and who came to Faikana to look for Peter Mace. Jason accompanies her to Mace's house, and arrives just in time to hear Mace's ritual, culminating in triumphant screams.

When Jason enters the house, he sees that the statue is alive, and Mace is embracing her. However, when Jason informs Mace that another woman has come to look for him, Mace soon recognizes the veiled lady as the real Mauree

"The Ithiliad" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Christine Morgan.

### Synopsis
Telling the story of the final days of the Trojan War in Ancient Greece but with a twist: the Trojans in "The Ithiliad" are half-breeds, some part Deep One, others the descendants of Azathoth, Shub-Niggurath and other dark entities.

### Characters
* Briseis, a Trojan maiden captured by the Achaeans, she is a Deep One hybrid.
* Achilles, the mightiest warrior of the Greek coalition.
* Agamemnon, the highest king among the Greeks, and leader of their armies.
* Hector, a Trojan prince and greatest of their warriors, he is a halfbreed descendant of Yog-Sothoth.
* Andromache, Hector's wife and mother of his child, she is also a half-breed of Yog-Sothoth.
* Paris, another Trojan Prince, cowardly and arrogant. 
* Helen, a Greek princess whose abduction by Paris is the cause of the war.

### Publication History
"The Ithiliad" was published in the thematic anthology World War Cthulhu by Dark Regions Press in 2014.

shortDefinition: "The Jar of Aten-Hor" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and editor Kat Rocha.  ### Synopsis When museum researcher Beth Stanton begins to study a new acquisition - a burial urn belonging to the high priest of pharaoh Khephren - she b...
fullContent:
"The Jar of Aten-Hor" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and editor Kat Rocha.

### Synopsis
When museum researcher Beth Stanton begins to study a new acquisition - a burial urn belonging to the high priest of pharaoh Khephren - she begins to develop an obsession. Despite the efforts of a mysterious man named Nathanial Hotep to obtain the urn, she resists, and is slowly possessed by a glamour originating from the artefact. As her sanity degenerates under the urn's hold, Beth commits ritual suicide under the approving gaze of Hotep.

### Characters
*Beth Stanton, an enthusiastic and dedicated anthropologist whose area of expertise is ancient Egypt.
*Nathanial Hotep, an enigmatic figure implied to be either an avatar of Nyarlathotep or perhaps even the being itself.
*Dr. Curtis, Beth's superior.

### Publication History
"The Jar of Aten-Hor" was published in the anthology of H. P. Lovecraft-inspired Fiction Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.

### Behind the Mythos
References related to Howard Phillips Lovecraft include the discoverer of the urn, a man named Dunsany, and Beth's place of work, the Ephraim Museum of Anthropology.

shortDefinition: "The Jealous God" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.  ### Synopsis When disgraced rockabilly star Billy ...
fullContent:
"The Jealous God" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
When disgraced rockabilly star Billy Ray Wildman meets a strange old man in the forest one afternoon, a series of events are set in motion by which he pledges his soul to a mysterious entity known as the Dark Man. In return, he is granted a second chance in the music industry on the condition that he forsake all other gods.

Later, when Wildman remembers his promise to his devoutly Christian mother on her deathbed - that he would "get right with God" - he makes the decision to end his most recent concert with a gospel song. The Dark Man, both enraged and amused by this turn of events, manifests and proceeds to wreak bloody mayhem on all present, leaving Wildman a broken wreck at the centre of the carnage.

### Behind the Mythos
In his story notes for the second edition of Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir, author Ron Shiflet reveals that Nyarlathotep is the real villain of the story, stating that he "sort of fills in for the Devil in this plotline of a man selling his soul for success".

### Trivia
* Billy Ray Wildman is nicknamed the "Tenoka Tornado" for his hometown in Texas. Tenoka is a milieu created by Ron Shiflet as the setting for several of his Cthulhu Mythos stories.

shortDefinition: The Jennifer Morgue is a novel by Charles Stross, the second full-length novel in his Laundry Files series. It was first published in 2006 by Golden Gryphon Press.  ### Synopsis In this book, set in 2005, Bob Howard, an operative of the British occul...
fullContent:
The Jennifer Morgue is a novel by Charles Stross, the second full-length novel in his Laundry Files series. It was first published in 2006 by Golden Gryphon Press.

### Synopsis
In this book, set in 2005, Bob Howard, an operative of the British occult spy agency The Laundry, is assigned to thwart the efforts of billionaire Ellis Billington to raise a Soviet sub that contains the Jennifer Morgue, a device that allows one to talk to the dead--and risks the awakening of the Great Old Ones. Howard is accompanied in this task by Ramona Random, an agent of the Laundry's US counterpart, the Black Chamber, who is also an emissary of the Deep Ones, who are referred to by the code name Blue Hades.

Howard and Random travel to the Caribbean island of St. Martin, which Billington has placed under an enchantment that only allows people to enter if they fit into spy genre stereotypes, so Howard tries to adopt a James Bond persona to allow him access. He and Random nevertheless are captured and held prisoner on Billington's yacht, where Dominique O'Brien arrives to save them--leading Howard to realize that it's actually O'Brien who embodies the Bond archetype, and he actually entered the island under the Damsel in Distress archetype. O'Brien kills Billington using the White Violin.

### Behind the Mythos
The submarine that drives the plot is the same one that the CIA tried to raise in 1975, using Howard Hughes' Glomar Explorer. The CIA's effort was referred to in the press as Project Jennifer.

While the first novel in the series, The Atrocity Archive, was an homage to British spy novelist Len Deighton, The Jennifer Morgue took James Bond as its model--"riffing off the Broccoli movie franchise version of Bond, not Iain Fleming's original psychopathic British government assassin," Stross notes.

### References

fullContent:
The Jest of Droom-Avista is a very short Cthulhu Mythos story by Henry Kuttner, first appearing in Weird Tales in August 1937.

### Synopsis
The story is orientalist, set in the city of Bel Yarnak where a would-be powerful wizard called Thorazor summons and binds Droom-avista to exact from this god the alchemical ability to transmute gold into iron. Gold was common in Bel Yarnak, and iron was unheard, of although through their telescopes the wizards knew that other worlds possessed it.

In a cruel trick, Droom-avista causes not merely a crucible of gold to transmute to iron but the entire city. Bel Yarnak becomes in an instant Dis, The City of Iron.

### Publication History
First appearing in the August 1937 issue of pulp fiction magazine Weird Tales , The Jest of Droom-Avista has been reprinted numerous times in a variety of publications.

### Trivia

*A similarly orientalist city called Dis, although this one named Dis The City of Brass, is home to the fire genies (Efreeti) in early editions of Dungeons & Dragons, a game which was well known to draw a great deal of inspiration from pulp authors such as Robert E. Howard and H. P. Lovecraft.

fullContent:
"The Keeper of Dark Point" is a short story written by John Glasby. It was originally published in the 1967 pulp magazine Supernatural Stories #107 before being printed in the anthology The New Lovecraft Circle by Fedogan & Bremer in 1996 and later in The Dark Boatman: Tales of Horror and the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
The story is set in the summer of 1936. A man named Stephen Delmore Ashton has disappeared, and Martin, our narrator, has some ideas as to where.

Stephen came from an ancient British family, who owned a crumbling ancestral manor, not far from an abandoned lighthouse on the Cornish coast.   Martin met Ashton in college, where they shared an interest in pre-human civilizations. They remained in touch as Martin became a historian/author and Stephen traveled the world in search of rare and odd things.

Stephen approached Martin one night and, after describing the Cthulhu Mythos in detail, explained his quest to find a specific sinister book of lore. Then he disappeared. Martin journeys to Stephen's home in the hopes of finding his friend. The family manor is in ruins, having been burned down 10 years ago by neighbors who had their fill of Ashton's occultism.  Discovering a trapdoor in the ruins, Martin follows its tunnel to some underground chambers, where he finds an ancient book, and a note from Stephen's mother. It seems Stephen's parents weren't mere followers but actual minions of the Great Old Ones.  

"Do not fear what lives beneath the manor", the book instructs Martin. Following this discovery, Martin journeys to the nearby lighthouse and, after a fleeting encounter with some hideous green scaly creature, too quick to be fully seen, he performs the rituals in the hopes of recovering his friend. Instead, something abominable comes for him.

"The Keeper of Memory" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Christine Morgan.

### Synopsis
In a far future where the Earth has been conquered by malevolent gods, an entity masquerading as an elderly woman travels the globe with her entourage encouraging the scattered survivors to renew themselves and rise against their oppressors. When one of the planet's new rulers takes notice of her, she transforms into something wholly inhuman, and kills the creature.

### Characters
*Mema, the Keeper of Memory, a non-human monstrosity which nevertheless seems invested in seeing Earth return to its former level of fecundity.
*Nemon, the great-granddaughter of Mema and heir to her title.

### Publication History
"The Keeper of Memory" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Trivia
Although never explicitly stated, it is possible that Mema is intended to be an avatar of Shub-Niggurath, as she seems devoted to the return of widespread life to Earth, and appears to know the location of bunkers filled with stored eggs and embryos from every species which were rendered extinct by the planet's new masters.

"The Keeper of the Gate" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle. 

### Synopsis
Two police officers, unhappy at the official explanation for a family annihilation to which they were the first responders, launch their own investigation into the crime. What they uncover is a cult dedicated to Yog-Sothoth who trade their lives for the gift of prophecy. 

### Characters

*Unnamed Narrator, an American police officer.
*Jake Rogers, the narrator’s partner.

### Publication History
"The Keeper of the Gate" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu in March 2013, and again in the chapbook of Meikle's work The Keeper of the Gate in June 2019.

"The Keeper of the Key, being the Statement of Nayland Colum" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author August Derleth, first published in the May 1951 issue of Weird Tales. It forms the fourth part of his series The Trail of Cthulhu.  It has since been included in numerous other collections, and has been translated into German, French and Italian.

### Synopsis
Professor Laban Shrewsbury, continuing his crusade against the Great Old Ones, recruits successful author Nayland Colum and the two embark on a trip to Yemen in search of something to aid them in the war. Searching the desert, they locate the Nameless City and the remains of Abdul Alhazred whose spirit directs them to the original, though fragmentary, copy of the Necronomicon. On the sea voyage home, they are attacked by an unknown entity, and the two escape by summoning Byakhee birds, although the rest of the world believes them dead.

### Characters

*Nayland Colum, a successful horror writer whose latest effort deals with the supposedly fictional world of the Cthulhu Mythos.
*Professor Laban Shrewsbury, a man with certain magical abilities and a desire to wage war against the entities which threaten the world from the shadows.

shortDefinition: "The King in Waiting" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Dan Griliopoulos, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Mo...
fullContent:
"The King in Waiting" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story which takes place in the Call of Cthulhu historical roleplaying setting Achtung! Cthulhu. Written by Dan Griliopoulos, it was published in the tie-in anthology Dark Tales from the Secret War by Modiphius Entertainment in 2015.

### Synopsis
A group of disparate agents from secretive British intelligence agency MI18 during the Second World War are brought together to track down and bring in Sir Oswald Mosley, a prominent British politician and leader of the country's small minority of fascists. Mosley has turned his back on his own country to support Nazi Germany, and worse, is in possession of arcane knowledge, under the protection of a mystical entity, and has the backing of German soldiers equipped with technologically advanced weapons.

Tracking Mosley to an abandoned church, the group confront Mosley, but are defeated by two German Nachtwölfe operatives bearing advanced energy manipulation weapons; one of the group is killed, as are both of the Germans, but Mosley makes his escape.

Receiving information that Mosley has relocated to a coastal town in North Wales, the surviving team members make their way there and discover that the fascist has been picked up by a German submarine. They attempt to stop the boat from departing using one of the captured energy weapons but are successful. Fortunately, just as Mosley's escape seems inevitable, reinforcements arrive in the form of MI18's "Met Office," a cabal of aging magicians who have the ability to control the weather. These witches use their power to wreck the submarine on the rocky Welsh coastline and take Mosley back into custody.

### Mythos Connections
Aside from the story's roleplaying game setting, an unspecified Old One is alluded to, and the entity protecting Mosley is described as being "the gatekeeper and the opener of the gate and the gate itself," a possible nod to the Outer God Yog-Sothoth. The "Severn area" is also mentioned, but given the Welsh setting in which the latter half of the story takes place, this is more likely to be in reference to the real-world River Severn rather than Ramsey Campbell's fictional district.

### Behind the Mythos
Oswald Mosley was a real-life British peer and member of parliament, possibly the most prominent figure in the field of British fascism of the time. He spent the majority of the Second World War either imprisoned or under house arrest.

### References

shortDefinition: The King in Yellow is a collection of short stories written by Robert W. Chambers and published in 1895. The stories could be categorized as early horror fiction or Victorian Gothic fiction, but the work also touches on mythology, fantasy, mystery, s...
fullContent:
The King in Yellow is a collection of short stories written by Robert W. Chambers and published in 1895. The stories could be categorized as early horror fiction or Victorian Gothic fiction, but the work also touches on mythology, fantasy, mystery, science fiction and romance. The first four stories in the collection involve a fictional two-act play of the same title: The King in Yellow.

Chambers' book borrows elements from the supernatural stories of Ambrose Bierce and weaves them into a new lore, which would in turn be incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by authors such as H. P. Lovecraft, August Derleth, and Hugh B. Cave, among others.

### Stories
The first four stories are loosely connected by three main devices:
* A two-act stage play in book form entitled The King in Yellow.
* A mysterious and malevolent supernatural entity known as the King in Yellow (associated in some way with Hastur).
* An eerie symbol called the Yellow Sign.

The color yellow signifies the decadent and aesthetic attitudes that were fashionable at the turn of the 19th century, typified by such publications as The Yellow Book, a literary journal associated with Oscar Wilde and Aubrey Beardsley. It has also been suggested that the color yellow represents quarantine — an allusion to decay, disease, and specifically mental illness. For instance, Charlotte Perkins Gilman's famous short story "The Yellow Wallpaper", involving a bedridden woman's descent into madness, was published shortly before Chambers' book.

These stories are macabre in tone, centering on characters that are often artists or decadents. The first story, "The Repairer of Reputations", is set in an imagined future 1920s New York City, whose history, being at odds with the knowledge of the reader, adds to the effect of its unreliable narrator. The next two are set in Paris, while the fourth, "The Yellow Sign", is again set in New York.

The other stories in the book do not follow the macabre theme of the first four, and most are written in the romantic fiction style common to Chambers' later work. Some are linked to the preceding stories by their Parisian setting and artistic protagonists.

### List of stories
The stories present in the book are:

* The Repairer of Reputations
* The Mask
* In the Court of the Dragon
* The Yellow Sign
* The Demoiselle d'Ys
* The Prophets' Paradise
* The Street of the Four Winds
* The Street of the First Shell
* The Street of Our Lady of the Fields
* Rue Barrée

### The Play The King in Yellow
The fictional play The King in Yellow has two acts, and at least three characters: Cassilda, Camilla, and the Stranger. The titular King in Yellow is generally assumed to appear in the play as well (at one point, Cassilda cries "Not upon us, oh King, not upon us!"), and may or may not be the same as the Stranger. The King in Yellow was a small-box expansion for the Second Edition of Arkham Horror, Fantasy Flight Games' board game of Lovecraftian adventure. It was the third expansion to be released.

### Overview
The King in Yellow contains 76 Investigator cards which feature additional Items, Spells and Allies for the player to choose from, 90 Ancient One cards which affect gameplay in new ways, and a sheet of tokens which features a new Spawn Monster, the Riot, representing groups of civilians engaged in civil disobedience.

This expansion was notable for introducing the Herald mechanic, with Heralds being minions of the Great Old Ones who are working towards the coming of their masters to Earth. This mechanic was subsequently incorporated into every future expansion, and the previously-released two were later revised to add it as well. The Herald introduced in this set was the titular character, the King in Yellow himself.

Also, The King in Yellow features a set of optional rules for “Performance Play,” intended to depict the coming of the stage play The King in Yellow to Arkham.

fullContent:
"The Kiss of Bugg-Shash"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley that first appeared in a pamphlet called Cthulhu 3: Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos, published by Spectre Press in 1978. It is a sequel to the short horror story "Demoniacal," by David Sutton.

### Synopsis
Two dabblers in the occult implicate a black magician in the curse they are under, in hopes that he can find a solution. He does--but his counterspell includes conditions that turn out to doom them all.

### Publication History
Lumley saw Sutton's "Demoniacal" in an anthology titled New Writings in Horror and the Supernatural, Vol 2 (Sphere Books, 1972). "This story seemed to me so very much a Mythos-story that I obtained David’s permission to write a sequel," Lumley later recalled. Sutton's and Lumley's stories were published together in Cthulhu 3, and were later reprinted in the Candlemas 1984 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu (#19), as well as in the anthology The New Lovecraft Circle (Fedogan & Bremer, 1995). The story appeared on its own for the first time in Lumley's collection Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008).

"The Knot" is a short story by American author Dennis Detwiller, first published in the collection of Lovecraftian fiction Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be by 01Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
The story of a mathematician who has, over the course of a long and storied career, witnessed a mysterious man whispering into the ears of those who have changed the course of human history. The story culminates with the mathematician exchanging bodies with a bizarre creature millions of years in the past.

### Behind the Mythos
Although never explicitly stated, the conical body which the mathematician finds himself inhabiting at the story's conclusion, along with the mind transferral, heavily hints towards the mystery man being a member of the Great Race of Yith.

"The Kraken" is a poem by Alfred Lord Tennyson, published in his collection Poems, Chiefly Lyrical (Effingham Wilson, 1830). It has been cited as a major influence on H. P. Lovecraft's story "The Call of Cthulhu" and on his conception of the entity Cthulhu.

### Text


### Interpretation
The critic Robert Preyer writes that Tennyson's poem describes "apocalyptic shapes unseen by the ordinary person," "mindless forces" that are capable of "exploding to the surface in a burst of irrational frenzy that marks the end of its peculiar life-in-death, the end of ordinary living, and also the onset of eternity." 

Robert M. Price points to the parallels with Lovecraft's creature: a huge, octopoid sea monster, sleeping for ages at the bottom of the ocean (either "dreaming" or "dreamless"), and destined to emerge from his slumber in an apocalyptic age.

### Form
The poem is a variation on the Petrarchan sonnet, with 15 lines rather than 14. Its rhyme scheme is ABABCDDCEFEAAFE.

### Kraken
The kraken was a giant sea creature that was believed to live off the coast of Norway. (Price suggests that this connection explains why Lovecraft's character Gustaf Johansen, the sailor who survives an encounter with Cthulhu, is Norwegian.) It's first mentioned as the sciu-crak in Viaggio settentrionale (Padua, 1700), an account by the Italian priest Francesco Negri of his travels in Scandinavia. Negri describes the creature as a massive "fish" with many arms or horns.

In his Description of Greenland (1729), the Danish missionary Hans Egede describes it as a creature "having many heads and a number of claws," many miles in length, that had the ability to drag ships down to the depths. The Danish bishop Erik Pontoppidan, in The Natural History of Norway (1752-53), suggests that the kraken was a giant octopus, or perhaps a sort of starfish or crab.

The French zoologist Pierre Denys-Montfort's Histoire Naturelle Générale et Particulière des Mollusques (1802) included the "kraken octopus," which it described as perhaps the largest creature on the planet.

shortDefinition: The Labyrinth is a Lovecraftian-like eldritch dimension from the fictional universe of the Hellraiser franchise. This realm is a place of extreme agony ruled by the Cenobites and their god, Leviathan. Existing outside our dimension, it's often compar...
fullContent:
The Labyrinth is a Lovecraftian-like eldritch dimension from the fictional universe of the Hellraiser franchise. This realm is a place of extreme agony ruled by the Cenobites and their god, Leviathan. Existing outside our dimension, it's often compared to Hell as it's a place of endless suffering. Described as a vast, complex labyrinth, this realm has no clear exit. At its core lies Leviathan, the entity controlling the Cenobites. While sometimes called Hell, its exact nature and relation to traditional religious concepts remain uncertain.

### Description
The Labyrinth is a complex, multi-story maze filled with countless rooms and passageways. Outsiders cannot find their way through it. Inside, countless souls are trapped and subjected to endless, personalized torment by demonic creatures. Above the Labyrinth, a massive, geometric entity called Leviathan supposedly reigns, though its exact role remains unknown.


Hell, once a chaotic and entertaining realm according to the character Pinhead, has transformed into a more structured place since Angelique's era. While naturally a labyrinthine dimension, Hell is capable of changing its form based on the pleasures and pains of its inhabitants. Many believe it's not the traditional Hell of religious texts but a separate dimension that can be interpreted as either heaven or hell, depending on the perspective of those trapped within.

Hell, as depicted in the franchise, has evolved from a chaotic, pleasure-pain dimension into a more structured and less enjoyable place. While originally a formless realm shaped by the inhabitants' experiences, it's now often portrayed as a traditional hell. There’s speculation that it might not be the biblical Hell but a different dimension entirely, experienced as heaven or hell depending on the trapped soul.

### Trivia

* Clive Barker's film adaptation of his terrifying novella, Hellbound Heart, incorporates Lovecraftian elements featuring ancient, powerful beings. Barker himself is often categorized as a Lovecraftian writer, and this influence is evident not only in the film he directed but also in the original novella, which shares stylistic similarities with Lovecraft's work.

"The Labyrinth of Sleep" is a short story by author Orrin Grey, first published in the anthology Future Lovecraft in November 2011.

### Synopsis
When professional dreamer McCabe attempts to commit suicide, his friend Kendrick, also a professional dreamer, travels to the recently-discovered labyrinth of sleep to find out why the now-comatose man chose such a course of action. He eventually locates his old colleague and learns the secret of the labyrinth: that it is a dream created not by humans, but by an ancient entity entirely incomprehensible to mankind.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to Lovecraft's work or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, "The Labyrinth of Sleep" does contain some nods to earlier works; the dreamers are mentioned as travelling through the "wall of sleep", while the machine which enables them to do so is referred to as a "silver key". Also, the leviathan glimpsed by Kendrick at the story's conclusion is clearly implied to be Azathoth, the Blind Idiot God.

### Publication History
*Future Lovecraft (2011)
*Whispers from the Abyss Vol. 2: The Horrors That Are & Shall Be (2015)
*Painted Monsters & Other Strange Beasts (2015)

fullContent:
"The Lady in Gray" is a horror short story by Donald Wandrei, originally published in the December 1933 issue of Weird Tales. It contains references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith, and Robert W. Chambers.

### Synopsis
For all his life, a man has been assailed by nightmares filled with esoteric imagery, cosmic abysses, and terrifying scenes of death and torture. Psychologists and psychiatrists have tried and failed to shed a light on his nocturnal terrors, as apart from them, his life has been entirely free from traumatic events or even financial struggles.

However, real tragedy strikes when the narrator's fiancée, a pale-skinned, grey-eyed young woman named Miriam, dies in an airplane crash the day before their wedding. On the night of her funeral, the narrator dreams that Miriam appears to him as a floating, luminous figure: the titular lady in grey. She takes him into a strange sea made of a black viscous slime-like liquid, and guides him back to bed before he drowns in it. When he wakes up, he finds that his body is indeed covered in black slime.

Several weeks pass by, during which only his "regular" nightmares plague him, until one night the lady in grey returns. This time she takes him by hand to a field covered in grey dust, where a large grey slug stands on a pillar. The narrator is disgusted by it, even though the slug's visage suggests a sapient creature. Still, he follows Miriam's instructions when she asks him to take the slug and carry it back to his room, where the mollusk kisses Miriam before she leaves.

When the narrator wakes up, he finds the slug in the room with him. Repulsed, he kills it with a fire poker and burns its body in the fireplace. He is even more disturbed to find the grey dust on his shoes, recognising it as the ash-like soil that covers the area of the cemetery in which Miriam was buried, where no vegetation grows.

Once again, several weeks of comparatively "normal" nightmares pass by, before the narrator experiences his third dream of Miriam. This time she leads him through a forest to the entrance of a cave which descends almost vertically to an underground world, although they simply walk on the vertical walls as if they were horizontal. The tunnel leads them to a crypt lit by candles, where Miriam's body lies in her grave, unconscious but alive, with a bowl filled with the slime of the black sea at her head, the grey slug at her feet, and a glowing gardenia in her hand.

The narrator rushes to get to Miriam, spilling the bowl and trampling the slug in the process, and carries her out of the crypt while the gardenia glows brighter, leading the way. Outside the crypt, the vertical tunnel is gone, and he finds himself standing on the field of grey dust under a sky with no stars. He carries Miriam back to his room, and when he wakes up, she is still there, seated besides him on his bed. Awakened, however, he can see that she isn't truly alive, but a reanimated corpse of rotten flesh.

fullContent:
"The Lair of the Star-Spawn" is a short story written by August Derleth and Mark Schorer on August 1932 and published in Weird Tales. It is notable as the first story to reference the Tcho-Tcho people and the entity Lloigor.

### Synopsis
Eric Marsh is part of a scientific expedition led by famed explorer and scholar Geoffrey Hawks to Burma, c. 1902, in search of the legendary city of Alaozar, to be found in the Lake of Dread on the Plateau of Sung. The natives are reluctant to provide guides, due to fear of the "Tcho-Tcho People" said to live there. 

When Marsh doubles back to retrieve a forgotten compass, the party is attacked by "a horde of little men, the tallest of them no more than four feet, with singularly small eyes set deep in dome-like, hairless heads." He can only watch as his colleagues are slaughtered by the people identified as the Tcho-Tcho.

Marsh decides that civilization is closer in front of him than behind, so he continues onward, taking the food and water left behind by the attackers. (The Tcho-Tchos took all the tools, leaving Marsh unable to bury the dead.) He comes upon "the walls and parapets of a city...rising alone in the plateau"--the "long-lost city of Alaozar." Later, in the night, he sees "a faint white line, flame-like, wavering up" from the city "toward the distant stars." As he watches, he is struck from behind and blacks out.

He wakes up, bandaged, in a bed in Alaozor.  He's greeted by Dr. Fo-Lan, a Chinese scientist who was thought to have died three years earlier. Instead Fo-Lan has been a slave of the Tcho-Tchos, forced to help them unleash an awful terror upon the world. Fo-Lan tells Marsh that the two of them can now thwart the Tcho Tchos' sinister plans.

Fo-Lan leads him down a secret passage, where they watch the Tcho-Tchos bow down to their leader, the priest E-Poh ("he is seven thousand years old," says Fo-Lan), and the tentacled monster that lurks in the shadows, which Fo-Lan informs him is named Lloigor. Fo-Lan asks Marsh to watch his body while he astrally projects to get help.  This goes off without a hitch. Once back in flesh, Fo-Lan informs him that he must convince E-Poh to open the gates to Zhar and Lloigor, at which time "the Star Warriors" can come and save them.

Fo-Lan goes to E-Poh and tells him that Zhar says the Tcho-Tchos must summon Lloigor and Zhar from the city, while he and Marsh go out onto the plateau and do a ritual of their own. Despite displaying incredulity that Zhar would communicate with Fo-Lan and not him, E-Poh is willing but sends four Tcho-Tchos to accompany them. They ride out onto the plateau, and Fo-Lan and Marsh promptly kill the four Tcho-Tchos. Giant, flaming humanoid figures—the Star-Warriors and their masters, the Elder Gods—descend from the sky and destroy the city of Alaozar. Satisfied, Fo-Lan and Marsh return to civilization.

"The Lakeside Cottages" is a short Cthulhu Mythos/Thomas Carnacki crossover story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
Paranormal investigator Thomas Carnacki lends his assistance when two boys from Brichester University who visited Lakeside Terrace come down with a strange malady. Unable to save the first boy, Carnacki is forced to confront the inhabitant of the lake, Gla'aki, to save the second.

Despite managing to fend off the evil creature, as the second boy heads off towards the water at stories' end - carrying with him a nine-volume set of the Revelations of Gla'aki - Carnacki detects a remaining glimmer of the supernatural taint…

### Characters
*Thomas Carnacki, a highly-intelligent occultist.
*Professor Coates, a scholar at the Severn Valley's venerable Brichester University.
*Perkins, a student
*Mrs. Dingle, landlady of a small hotel at Lakeside Terrace.
*Parkinson, another student.
*Gla'aki, a Great Old One.

### Publication History
"The Lakeside Cottages" was first published in the thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki in 2017, and also appeared in the collection of Meikle's Thomas Carnacki stories Carnacki: Starry Wisdom and Other Stories in 2021. Both were released by Dark Regions Press.

shortDefinition: "The Lamp of Alhazred" is a short story, first published in the October 1957 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction as a "posthumous collaboration" between August Derleth and H. P. Lovecraft. While most such "collaborations" were entire...
fullContent:
"The Lamp of Alhazred" is a short story, first published in the October 1957 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction as a "posthumous collaboration" between August Derleth and H. P. Lovecraft. While most such "collaborations" were entirely written by Derleth based on fragmentary story ideas from Lovecraft, "The Lamp of Alhazred" incorporates text from Lovecraft's final and unfinished piece of correspondence recounting hiking Neutaconkanut Hill in Rhode Island from Lovecraft's final and unfinished piece of correspondence. (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft 5.930). 

As the chronologically final piece of fiction by Lovecraft, its subject matter, featuring his alter ego Ward Phillips, is poignant indeed. 

### Synopsis
Ward Phillips is a pulp writer who has visions of and writes about Cthulhu Mythos locations and entities. He goes on imaginary journeys to places from the Mythos, but is currently weary of the work and struggling through revisions of a turgid poem with which he is unhappy. 

He receives from his elderly relative Grandfather Whipple a brass lamp. recovered from a tomb in Arabia dating back countless ages. Grandfather Whipple has disappeared so there is no one to give him more information about the lamp. 

Surrounded by his book lined shelves, Phillips works into the night, and lights the lamp. The lamp ushers him into visions of an entirely different, sun-drenched, landscape, that of fabled and fabulous Arabia. Enraptured by the visions, Phillips ultimately gives in to the urge to see more, and, pushing through his bookshelves, enters the fabled Arabian landscape, never to return. 

His books are eventually given away, his house torn down. But of Ward Phillips nothing is found or ever discovered to explain his complete disappearance. 

The "Lamp of Alhazred" clearly infers the Lamp's previously owner as having been none other than Abdul Alhazred, author of the Necronomicon, himself.

fullContent:
"Carnacki: The Larkhill Barrow" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle. It tells of an investigation conducted by Thomas Carnacki, a character created by William Hope Hodgson and expanded upon by many others.

### Synopsis
Famous occultist Thomas Carnacki is summoned to assist a military man with a problem his unit have been having at their training facility: every time they test a new machine gun atop a rise in the ground, it results in the shooter going insane (an effect which dissipates after a short time) and the whole camp suffering from dreadful dreams of drums - and something far more sinister - in the dark (which does not).

Carnacki's investigations revealed that the rise is in fact an ancient barrow designed as a kind of sonic prison for an ancient and malevolent entity, and the rhythmic drum of the machine gun has partially opened the gate.

Luckily for everyone, Carnacki is able to reproduce the effects of the prison through the use of phonograph recordings and many mystical charms, and even manages to re-incarcerate the entity on one of his phonograph cylinders, a fact he keeps hidden from everyone involved.

### Characters
*Thomas Carnacki, a renowned occult detective.
*Private Jimmy Carruthers, a brave 18 year old soldier who assists Carnacki in his efforts.
*Colonel George Blandford, commander of the Royal Artillery base.

### Publication History
"The Larkhill Barrow" has been published in the collections Carnacki: Heaven and Hell (2011), Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2017), and The Larkhill Barrow (2019).

### Trivia
*Despite never explicitly referencing the works of H. P. Lovecraft of the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the inclusion of "The Larkhill Barrow" in Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates the author's belief that this is in the spirit of such works. Additionally, the premise, that of an unfathomable entity imprisoned and attempting to break into our our dimension, is most definitely Lovecraftian in nature.

fullContent:
"The Last Feast of Harlequin" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Thomas Ligotti, first published in the April 1990 edition of The Magazine of Fantasy & Science Fiction.

### Synopsis
A university professor with a lifelong fascination with clowns, their history, and their social evolution heads to a small town after hearing about a festival centred around clown culture. Observing a strange subculture of sad-faced clowns lurking in the background and treated with contempt by the other townsfolk, he infiltrates the group, only to find a cult dedicated to a subterranean creature called "the worm". Although he manages to escape the group during a sacrificial ceremony, the cult leader's final words remain with him forever after: that he is one of them, and has always been one of them.

### Publication History
Since its debut, "The Last Feast of Harlequin" has been reprinted many times, and has appeared in a number of Lovecraftian anthologies, including Cthulhu 2000 (1995), Return to Lovecraft Country (1997), and A Mountain Walked (2014). It has also been translated into German, Italian, Serbian and Finnish.

### Adaptations
In 2007, an adaptation of "The Last Feast of Harlequin" was included in The Nightmare Factory, a collection of comic book adaptations of Ligotti's short fiction.

"The Last Quest" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
In an alternate history where the bloodline of King Arthur has ruled the city of Londinium for millennia, the current king faces annihilation at the hands of a technologically-superior foe. Seeking the aid of the Holy Grail, in fact a well connected to the Outer God Iog-Sototh, he is able to repel the invaders, but is grievously wounded in the process. He then uses the grail to cross dimensions, leaving with the promise that he will return when his land most needs him.

### Characters
*King Arthur, the latest in a long line of British kings.
*Merlin, the line of Arthur's closest advisor.
*Lancelot, an ageing knight with designs on he throne.
*Persifal, one of the few knights to take his duties and heritage to heart.

### Publication History
"The Last Quest" was first published in the anthology Through a Mythos Darkly by PS Publishing in June 2017. It also appeared in the collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in 2019.

The Last Ritual by S. A. Sidor is a novel in the Cthulhu Mythos stories from Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting for Arkham Horror Fiction. It is a standalone novel. Paperback, digital and audio editions were released. It was adapted by Graphic Audio into an audio production with an entire cast of voice actors.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Alden Oakes is a dillitente artist who has a strange encounter with the supernatural in Spain before returning to discover that his hometown of Arkham is even stranger. Witnessing an event that may have led to the death of Harry Houdini, he soon finds himself hunted by monsters and investigates the local artists' commune run by the mysterious Juan Hugo Balthazar. Balthazar is a cultist of Yog-Sothoth who believes his god can be summoned through art. Alden is not the kind of man who is a hero, though, and relies heavily on his girlfriend, Nina Tarrington, to push him forward.

### Characters
*Alden Oakes - Alden Oakes is a wealthy scion of a prominent Arkham family who dabbles in art. He is neither particularly intelligent or brave but he does have a great appreciation for beauty. He becomes swiftly enamored of Juan Hugo Balthazar.
*Juan Hugo Balthazar - A Spanish artist who is a cultist of Yog-Sothoth and a dabbler in magic. He is the leader of a new cult in Arkham that is attempting to summon their god with art.
*Nina Tarrington - A investigative reporter and son of a prominent publishing magnate. She and Alden begin a romance.

fullContent:
"The Last Test" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Adolphe de Castro that appeared under de Castro's name in the November 1928 issue of Weird Tales. It is a revision of de Castro's "A Sacrifice to Science," which had been published in 1893. "The Last Test" is notable as the first story in writing order to mention the Cthulhu Mythos entity Shub-Niggurath.

### Plot Synopsis
Dr. Alfred Schuyler Clarendon, a world leading biologist and physician, has returned home to America after a long trip abroad. He is vehemently welcomed back by his childhood best friend James Dalton, who has become the Senator for California. James appoints Alfred as the medical caretaker of San Quentin Penitentiary, where he studies to try and cure the recent epidemic of "black fever", but is forced out due to medical malpractice. 

Clarendon's sister Georgina witnesses Dr. Clarendon being goaded into continuing his studies into the "black fever" in private by his assistant Surama, first experimenting on animals and then on kidnapped children. After sending a telegram for help to Dalton, Georgina overhears Clarendon and Surama arguing with each other, both apparently well-versed in the occult. 

After Dalton's arrival to their estate, Clarendon tries to inject his sister with a deadly formula, but is wrestled off by Dalton. Clarendon instead injects himself with the formula, and repents to Dalton that his assistant Surama was in fact an Atlantean priest whom Clarendon has released from suspended animation, and that Surama had actually been the one spreading the "black fever" so that Clarendon could study it. In his dying words he invokes a being called the Nemesis of Flame, who burns the manor-house down killing Surama along with him. 

### Characters
Dr. Alfred Schuyler Clarendon: Medical director of California's San Quentin Penitentiary. "One of the greatest biologists and physicians" of the 1890s, he is an authority at twenty-five and an international figure at thirty.  Described as "lean and ascetic, with steel-rimmed pince-nez and pointed brown beard". He lives in "the gloomy old Bannister place near Goat Hill, overlooking the bay...a rambling, French-roofed relic of mid-Victorian design and gold-rush parvenu display."

James Dalton: A lawyer who has known Clarendon and his family since their childhood in New York. Moves to California to make his fortune after Clarendon's father refuses to approve of a marriage between Dalton and his daughter. He rises in California politics to become governor and eventually senator.

"The Last Tweet" is an extremely short Cthulhu Mythos flash fiction piece by author Charles Black.

### Synopsis
The nineteen words are, as the title might suggest, a partial tweet describing how the tweeter found the Necronomicon in Arkham, conducted an occult ritual, and awakened the Great Old Ones.

### Publication History
"The Last Tweet" was published in the Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss in 2013.

"The Last Witch-House" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mark McLaughlin.

### Synopsis
In the modern day, the witch Keziah Mason traps her unwitting husband in the prison of her soul as a punishment for his dismissal of their love. However, the man's attempts to break free of his confinement result in the irrevocable damage of her being, and the two die together, locked together for eternity.

### Characters
*Timothy, a man cursed to wander the corridors of his wife’s soul for as long as he lives.
*Keziah Mason/Cassandra, an ancient witch.
*Brown Jenkin, Mason's rat-like familiar.

### Publication History
"The Last Witch-House" has appeared in the collections Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos and The House of the Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares.

fullContent:
The Laundry Files is a series of novels and short stories by Charles Stross that centre on a secret British government agency--The Laundry--dedicated to fighting Lovecraftian horrors. The series combines the science fiction elements of the Cthulhu Mythos with the British spy thriller genre, with a generous helping of bureaucratic office comedy.

In the world of the Laundry Files, there are two primary espionage groups dealing with the paranormal--the British Laundry and the United States' Black Chamber, the latter of which is secretly controlled by an extra-dimensional force known as the Many-Angled Ones. Among the eldritch entities in this multiverse are Nyarlathotep and Cthulhu. As humanity increases in number and computational power, the Many-Angled Ones will be able to filter through the universe's walls, an event the Laundry codenames CASE NIGHTMARE GREEN and spends much of its energy attempting to postpone and prepare for.

### Characters
* Bob Howard: The main character and narrator of most Laundry Files stories, Howard is an IT consultant recruited into the Laundry after stumbling onto one of the equations that open a pathway for dangerous extradimensional entities. The name he uses in the books is not his real name or his actual cover name, but a pseudonym used in his work diaries, derived from Robert E. Howard.
* Dominique "Mo" O'Brien: Bob's main love interest and later wife, she becomes an operative for the Laundry after being rescued by Bob from apocalyptic kidnappers. She wields a sentient violin made of bone once owned by "Erich Zahn" as a weapon of mass destruction.
* James Angleton: Bob's boss and a senior official at the Laundry, Angleton (a pseudonym taken from a famously paranoid historical CIA officer) is the vessel for a powerful glad-he's-on-our-side entity known as the Eater of Souls.

The Legacy of Arrius Lurco is a scenario sourcebook for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game.

### Overview


Containing a complete four-scenario campaign for the Cthulhu Invictus time period of Call of Cthulhu, The Legacy of Arrius Lurco also features new rules for the main game, including character professions, artefacts, weapons, and creatures, as well as background information on cults and secret societies of the time.

### Behind the Mythos
Written by Oscar Rios with artwork provided by Alberto Guerra and Steff Worthington, The Legacy of Arrius Lurco runs to a total of 132 pages. First published in 2011 by Miskatonic River Press, it is currently available as a digital download from licensed third-party content provider Golden Goblin Press, who have also released an update to the rules to be compatible with the 7th edition of the game.

fullContent:
The Legacy of Erich Zann is a horror mystery novella by Brian Stableford, first published in 2011. It is set in the Cthulhu Mythos and features the amateur investigator character C. Auguste Dupin, created by Edgar Allan Poe. As its title indicates, it is also a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Music of Erich Zann".

### Synopsis
In the 1840s, the Prefect of the Parisian Police, Lucien Groix, seeks the help of C. Auguste Dupin to investigate the murder of Bernard Clamart, a lawyer who was in charge of the testament of the late musician Erich Zann. The circumstances of Zann's death haven't been disclosed to the public, and he was buried in an unmarked grave in a ceremony attended by only five people: Dupin, Groix, Clamart, a doctor named Fourmont who examined his body, and a musician colleague named Palaiseau. This makes the fact that Zann's coffin was recently violated significant.

Several years ago, Erich Zann fled from his native Austria, accused of being in league with devils. Zann's violin, given to him by his mentor Tartini, was made by the great Antonio Stradivarius, but rejected by its creator as a "strange" and "unreliable" piece, which Zann turned out to be the only one who could learn to play properly. Settling on a Parisian street informally known as Rue d'Auseil, Zann first sought Dupin to ask about a 14th century esoteric book he was interested in, Harmonies de l'Enfer, of which Dupin possessed the only known copy in Paris. Over the course of several further visits, the two men became friends. When Zann died, the only witness came straight to Dupin, having found the latter's name on a note written by Zann. While the witness' claim that Zann had died of fright while playing was confirmed by Dr. Fourmont, the claim that Zann was trying to fend off devils with his music, which his body continued to play after death, is dismissed as the result of the witness' apparent insanity. Nevertheless, Dupin, Groix and Fourmont see something through Zann's window which they vow never to tell anyone about.

According to his testament, Zann left his compositions to Dupin and his violin to Palaiseau: a musician who could appreciate it, even though he wasn't any more able to play it reliably than Tartini was. At the night of Clamart's murder, however, it transpires that Palaiseau was publicly playing Zann's violin in a stage play, the pamphlet of which advertised the instrument as a "lost" Stradivarius. Dupin pays Palaiseau a visit and calls him out about his indiscretion, as they had an agreement not to disclose such matters. Palaiseau believes that the violin has a mind of its own and demonstrates it by playing for Dupin and the narrator, showing that in certain pieces (and not others) the instrument will retune itself, forcing the musician to compose pieces that incorporate this mysterious tendency. Dupin reveals that after seeing Zann's compositions he forced himself to burn them.

The Legacy of Erich Zann and Other Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos is an anthology of Cthulhu Mythos-related stories by the late British horror and science fiction author Brian Stableford.

### Overview
Consisting of two novellas and two short stories, the collection is a thematic one in that all of the stories are written as sequels to original H. P. Lovecraft titles.

### Contents
*"The Legacy of Erich Zann", a follow-on to "The Music of Erich Zann" featuring Edgar Allan Poe's fictional detective Auguste Dupin.
*"The Truth About Pickman", a story which expands on the characters from Lovecraft's short story "Pickman's Model".
*"The Seeds from the Mountains of Madness", where a frozen member of Scott's expedition to the Antarctic turns up alive and with a mysterious agenda in England. The sequel to At the Mountains of Madness.
*"The Holocaust of Ecstasy", which depicts the human race in the far future, after the return of the Great Old Ones.

### Publication History
The Legacy of Erich Zann and Other Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos was published by Wildside Press in April 2012; both paperback and digital editions were released .

"The Light from the Pole" is a story fragment by Clark Ashton Smith expanded upon and finished as a complete short story by Lin Carter, and included in Weird Tales #1, the anthology edited by Carter.

It is essentially a re-telling of "The Coming of the White Worm," another Clark Ashton Smith story.

### Synopsis
The prophet Pharazyn in the prehistoric Hyperborian Age senses a growing threat from the far north, which it transpires is actually caused by a fellow spellcaster who has ventured north, fallen under the spell of Rlim Shaikorth and who eventually causes an elemental iceberg larger than a volcano to move southwards, freezing to death all life with which it comes in contact.

Cognizant of the baleful prophecy attached to this preternatural event, Pharazyn takes his own life rather than forfeiting his existence to the Great Old Ones who rule the freezing cold.

It is possibly implied that this event is the beginning of a global Ice Age.

### Trivia
*Reference is made to Pharazyn consulting the Pnakotic Texts.

fullContent:
The Lightless Beacon: When the Lights Went Out is a beginner-level adventure module for Chaosium’s Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. It is dedicated to the memory of Chaosium founder Greg Stafford, who died in 2018.

### Overview
Intended for groups of up to five players, The Lightless Beacon is specifically designed to build confidence in new players with a short adventure, and includes four pregenerated characters for quick-start play. The storyline involves a group of investigators who are shipwrecked and washed ashore on Beacon Island, a rocky outcrop in the Atlantic Ocean which is home to an ominously dark lighthouse. Unfortunately for the group, the island has been infested with dangerous servitors of the Deep Ones known as Younglings, and they now face a frantic battle for survival.

Written by Leigh Carr with Lynne Hardy, The Lightless Beacon was first released by Chaosium in 2019 for the 7th edition of Call of Cthulhu. It is available as a free digital PDF download from their website.

### Trivia 
* Although The Lightless Beacon is dedicated to the memory of Greg Stafford, the date on the front cover of October 10, 2019 is not the date of Stafford's death: he actually passed away on October 10, 2018 .

"The Likeness" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by American author Dan Perez. 

### Synopsis
The story begins with Mindy being dropped off by her boyfriend Jake at a tattoo store. Uninterested in the usual selection of designs, the tattooer Cal realizes that Mindy wanted to get something that is truly special so he decides to give her a full-body tattoo, based on an illustration of Vthyarilops the Starfish God from the Necronomicon. Taking almost an entire week to complete it, Mindy began to have some weird side-effects such as becoming more violent and having weird dreams about the Starfish God traveling through outer space. When it was finally finished, Vthyarilops manifested through Mindy and devoured her boyfriend.

fullContent:
The Litany of Earth is a novella by Ruthanna Emrys, published by Tor in 2014. It is the beginning of her Innsmouth Legacy series, which sympathetically explores the Deep Ones of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" and the aftermath of their persecution by the United States government.

### Synopsis
The story centers on  Aphra Marsh, a woman from Innsmouth with Deep One ancestry. After the 1928 government raid on her hometown, in which her father was killed, she was sent to a concentration camp in Oklahoma, where her mother disappears. The Innsmouth captives are later joined by Japanese-Americans interned during World War II. At war's end, the few survivors from Innsmouth are released, including Aphra and her brother Caleb; their mother died . After 17 years as a prisoner, she moves to San Francisco, where she lives with the Kotos, a Japanese-American family that she met in the camp.

Aphra works at a used bookstore run by Charlie Day, a gruff but protective man not much older than her, who has an interest in forbidden texts. He is unaware of her heritage, but when he learns of her familiarity with the ancient languages of Enochian and R'lyehn, he persuades her to begin teaching him the rudiments of magic.

At the bookstore, she encounters a customer who asks for books by the likes of Al-Hazred and Prinn; he turns out to be an FBI inspector named Ron Spector, who seeks to recruit her to help the Bureau investigate what are referred to as Aeonists--worshippers of Cthulhu and the Great Old Ones. Though Aphra is originally repulsed by the idea of working for a government that has subjected her family to atrocities, his pitch to her sums up the books attitude toward the Cthulhu Mythos:

As an example of the latter sort of Aeonists, Spector alludes to the New Orleans sect described in Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu":

Aphra rebuffs Spector, but after he shares information about her mother's fate--she died after being subjected to grisly experiments when she began to transition--and reveals that he has relatives that were victims of the Nazi Holocaust, she reluctantly agrees to check out an Aeonist group for him. It's led by a wealthy San Franciscan named Oswin Wilder; one of his chief followers is an older woman named Mildred Bergman, who is immediately suspicious of Aphra. It is soon evident that Wilder's cult has no real magic--but he does pose a threat to followers like Bergman, offering a false and deadly promise of oceanic immortality.

The title refers to a list of the various species, 13 in all, that in the past, present or future are dominant on Earth.  The litany starts with the "five-winged eldermost of Earth," followed by "the Shoggoth, who rebelled against their makers". fullContent:
"The Little Glass Bottle" is a short story by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Written when he was only seven years old, it forms part of his juvenilia body of work.

### Synopsis
The crew of a small boat happen across a bottle floating in the sea. Inside they find a note from the captain of a sinking ship loaded with treasure and map marked with his location, along with a note asking for assistance. Their minds filled with the thought of getting their hands on some booty, the crew hires a schooner and sets off with the map.

Upon reaching the spot marked off the coast of Australia, the crew finds to their chagrin that the whole venture has been a practical joke and that there is no treasure, only a bottle filled with a note apologising for tricking them and $25 to cover their expenses.

### Characters
*William Jones, the crew's captain.
*John Towers, a crewman.
*John Jones/anonymous note writer, the prankster. Apparently unrelated to Captain Jones.

### Publication History
Although written in 1897, "The Little Glass Bottle" did not see print until years after Lovecraft's death, when it was included in the anthology The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces in 1959. It has since been included in a number of collections, and has been translated into Italian, French and Ukrainian.
