The Littlest Shoggoth: A Holiday Tale of the Cthulhu Mythos is a children's book written by Stan! and published by Otherworld Creations in 2013.

### Overview


### Synopsis
After getting bullied by the other Mythos monsters in the undersea city of R'lyeh, Squammy headed towards the surface world to get some respect. When he arrived on the beach, a couple of kids initially mocked Squammy for his small size until he ate one of them, causing the other one to run away in fear. Shortly afterwards, a group of townspeople attacked him, only to get eaten alive as well, with Squammy growing bigger after each person he ate. Now having grown to be kaiju-sized, Squammy strolled through town and confronted some military tanks, before also eating them. Tired of all the fighting and chaos, Squammy headed to Santa's palace. Squammy explained to Santa that he didn't want to cause this much trouble and just wanted peace. However, Santa was not very helpful and just laughed at Squammy, causing him to eat Santa before eating everything else on Earth.

The story ends with the reveal that it was all just a dream, as Cthulhu wakes up to see all the other Mythos monsters (including Squammy) and exclaims "Happy Solstice to all, May your stars all be right!".

### Mythos Connections
*The creatures living in R'lyeh include the Deep Ones, Hounds of Tindalos, Byakhee, Elder Things, Mi-Go and other Shoggoths.

"The Longdock Air" is a short story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
A young man searching for a song, fragments of which he hears in his head constantly but cannot place, meets an old man in a dying small town. As he stays and begins to learn the song from the older man, he begins to notice the towns peculiarities, yet the power of the song makes him feel like he belongs there. As he fully comprehends the song, the old man names him as the new choirmaster before he and many of the towns original residents submit themselves to the river and the Dreaming Lord which uses it as a psychic conduit.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, a man searching not only for a song, but for a deeper meaning in his life.
*John Gilthrop, the curator of a song which brings the cult-like population of a small town closer to their god.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to Lovecraft's works or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the inclusion of "The Longdock Air" in the collection Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates the author's belief that it follows in the spirit of such works. Additionally, the description of the townsfolk (who possessed skin resembling that of a fish, protruding eyes, and mouths which seemed to frequently open and close) and their Dreaming Lord (an ancient sleeping entity which affects mortals through its dreams) are reminiscent of the Deep Ones and Cthulhu respectively.

### Publication History
"The Longdock Air" was first published in the thematic anthology Shadows Over Main Street: Volume 2 by Cutting Block Books in October 2017. It was also included in the collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in May 2019.

In a sequel to the Cats of Ulthar, the story details the further adventurers of the Dark Wanderers who visited Ulthar and who ultimately come to an untimely end.

Seeking the treasures of the lost and ancient city of Golthoth, called by some The Damned, they find the ruins, and dig deep down below them, to a layer of stinking corrosive mud. Removing what are surely meant to be Elder Signs from an entombed mass, they steal away treasures and depart.

When other nomads find them, the leader of the tomb robbers, Snid, has begun the transformation into ravening Ghoul, having eaten the rest of the tomb robbers when found...

shortDefinition: "The Lord of Illusion" is the E. Hoffmann Price short story written as a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Silver Key." It only exists in draft form because, at Price's relentless urging, Lovecraft reluctantly but successfully edited and expanded the ...
fullContent:
"The Lord of Illusion" is the E. Hoffmann Price short story written as a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Silver Key." It only exists in draft form because, at Price's relentless urging, Lovecraft reluctantly but successfully edited and expanded the original work into what amounted to an entirely new work of much greater length, although preserving the main conceits of the original, those being the further adventures and astral travels of Randolph Carter, the nature and endurance of ego and mind separate from any particular body, and the layered nature of perception and reality.

The original manuscript, with notes and critique by Price and Lovecraft, exists as part of the Brown Digital Repository. The original manuscript version of the story, with corrections, was published in Ashes and Others, the tenth issue of Robert M. Price's long-running zine Crypt of Cthulhu, in December 1982.

shortDefinition: The Lovecraft Investigations is a supernatural audio drama podcast based on the works of the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. Created, written, and directed by Julian Simpson, it was produced by Karen Rose and Sweet Talk Productions, and release...
fullContent:
The Lovecraft Investigations is a supernatural audio drama podcast based on the works of the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. Created, written, and directed by Julian Simpson, it was produced by Karen Rose and Sweet Talk Productions, and released in four series between January 2019 and October 2023 .

### Premise
The Lovecraft Investigations follows two podcasters, Matt Heawood and Kennedy Fisher (Barnaby Kay and Jana Carpenter, respectively), co-hosts of the true-crime podcast Mystery Machine, as they stumble across and subsequently investigate a far-reaching conspiracy involving many elements of the Cthulhu Mythos.

Each series revolves around the events of a particular H. P. Lovecraft story, with the events, characters, and locations updated to reflect a modern setting. Heawood and Fisher find themselves directly embroiled in the events of each story while conducting their investigations, and each story has been adapted to be intrinsically connected to the others; also, some of the characters are later revealed to possess some direct connections to the events through their family histories.

### Characters
In addition to the main characters listed below, the show features a large supporting cast, comprising antagonists, expert advisors, eyewitnesses, and shadowy government agents, amongst many others.

*Matt Heawood (played by Barnaby Kay), British co-host of the Mystery Machine podcast specialising in the research aspects of the work.
*Kennedy Fisher (played by Jana Carpenter), American co-host of the Mystery Machine who works as the podcast's field investigator.
*Dr. Eleanor Peck (played by Nicola Walker), introduced as a teacher with a particular interest in the history of the supernatural, Dr. Peck later becomes the podcast's primary advisor on occult matters. She is hinted at being the Department agent Marie Lairre in the final episode of series 4.

### Series
The Lovecraft Investigations ran for a total of four series between January 2019 and October 2023 .

### Links to Other Media
The Lovecraft Investigations is connected to Mythos, another supernatural podcast series created by Julian Simpson, through "The Department", a secretive British government agency dedicated to combatting supernatural threats (later disbanded), and the character of Marie Lairre, a former Department agent implied to having undergone voluntary memory erasure in order to conduct a deep-cover assignment .

### External Links

*[https://www.cartoongravity.com/building-the-lovecraft-investigations/ Blog post] by Julian Simpson on the creation and development of The Lovecraft Investigations

The Lovecraft Mysteries is a trilogy of pulp Cthulhu Mythos novels by American author Brandon Berntson, begun with The Night of Dagon in June 2018.

### Overview
The series follows Devlin Macky, a private detective operating out of the city of Innsport, and his secretary/love interest Millie Von Clydesburgh, as they tackle the various supernatural threats which come their way.

Exactly when the series is set is not stated, although references to Creature from the Black Lagoon and the films of Humphrey Bogart, along with fashion and automobile styles, would seem to suggest that it takes place in the mid-to-late 1950s.

Although The Lovecraft Mysteries uses people, places and entities from the Cthulhu Mythos, these are often adapted to a greater or lesser extent; for example, the Arkham depicted in Arkham: Reanimated is very different to the one depicted in Lovecraft’s fiction, being little more than a village which has fallen to degeneracy.

### Characters

### Main Characters
* Devlin Macky, private investigator.
* Millie Von Clydesburgh, Macky's secretary and, later, girlfriend.

### Recurrent Characters
* Creighton Capshaw, curator of the Innsport Natural History Museum.
* Inspector Duke Givens, a senior Innsport police officer.
* Lieutenant Newt Bardhoff, Givens' partner.
* Mr. Kalabraise, Millie's pet cocker spaniel.

### Books
*The Night of Dagon (2018)
*Arkham: Reanimated (2019)
*The Lurker at the Threshold (2021)

### Trivia
* In the world of The Lovecraft Mysteries, both H. P. Lovecraft and Weird Tales exist. Lovecraft is, as is often the case with his fictional appearances, implied to have written his stories about real beings and events, although how he came to possess that knowledge is left unexplained in this instance.

fullContent:
The Lovecraft Tarot is a unique version of the standard 78-card Tarot deck created by Daryl L. Hutchinson, and printed by the now-defunct  Lovecraftian small press publisher Mythos Books. The first edition was an “odious shade of blue” and was printed in an edition of 500 in 1997.  A second improved “sepia” edition of 1000 copies was published in 2002, also by Mythos Books. The second edition contains much new artwork. A third edition of all new unpublished artwork was published in January 2025 by Black Moon Publishing. It was not a limited edition and is now available.

### Overview
The Lovecraft Tarot deck contains 78 cards. These cards correspond to the Major and Minor Arcana of the traditional tarot. The Minor Arcana ("suits") of The Lovecraft Tarot are the Suits of Man, Artifacts, Tomes, and Sites. These replace the traditional wands, pentacles, swords and cups of the "normal" Tarot variants.

The Major Arcana or Trumps have all been replaced by Great Old Ones, creatures and characters from the works of H. P. Lovecraft and other authors of the Cthulhu Mythos. All the artwork is by the creator, artist Hutchinson, who produced them as a labour of love. The cards are printed in duotone sepia and white giving a very unusual "pulp" and occult appearance to the set. 

The Lovecraft Tarot comes with an 80 page book by Eric Friedman, to provide an introduction to the unique Lovecraft Tarot cards.  This book also gives a detailed explanation of each Major Arcana card in this deck and how this card relates to the Cthulhu Mythos, and where applicable to its corresponding card in the traditional tarot. For people intending to actually use these cards for fortune telling there are also more traditional explanations of each card's "meaning" in upright and reversed position.

The descriptions for the Major Arcana also include quotes from the writings of H. P. Lovecraft, Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop (for the "Yig" card) and one quote from August Derleth (for the "Ithaqua" card).

fullContent:
"The Loved Dead" is a story written by C. M. Eddy, Jr. and H. P. Lovecraft in 1923. A controversial tale of necrophilia, it was published in Weird Tales bumper issue for May/July 1924.

### Synopsis
The plot centres around an unnamed narrator living in the rural village of Fenham who is a necrophile. He describes his repressive childhood and what drove him to commit these crimes. He works for one mortuary/undertaker after another, in order to be near corpses. At the end of the story, with police hot on his trail, he commits suicide.

### Reaction
Due to the tale's grisly subject matter, style and descriptiveness, it caused a storm of controversy. Robert Weinberg has disputed this, saying he was unable to find evidence of such withdrawals.

Ramsey Campbell wrote in 1969 that this story consisted of "ludicrous melodrama" and that it was a "distastefully sensationalist revision" He later modified this view in a revision of his 1969 article.

Robert Weinberg described "The Loved Dead" as an "over-written and minor" story.

### Publication History

*The Arkham Sampler (Summer 1948).
*First collected in The Dark Brotherhood and Other Pieces

*The Loved Dead and Other Revisions. New York: Carroll & Graf Publishers, 1997, 149-58.
*The Loved Dead and Other Tales by C. M. Eddy, Jr. Rhode Island: Fenham Publishing, 2008, 1-15.

fullContent:
The Lurker at the Threshold is a Cthulhu Mythos novel, credited on its publication by Arkham House in 1945 to H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth, although almost all of it was written by Derleth, incorporating "notes and fragments" written by Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
The Lurker at the Threshold is divided into three sections. "Billington's Wood" focuses on Ambrose Dewart, an English man who reclaims an ancestral property near Arkham, Massachusetts, and learns the disquieting history of his ancestors Richard and Alijah Billington. Disregarding the latter's posthumous warning, he removes a stone from a round tower on the Billington property, and thus unleashes eldritch forces.

The second section, "Manuscript by Stephen Bates," is presented as an account by Dewart's cousin, who comes to realize that Dewart is under a malignant influence.

The conclusion, "Narrative of Winfield Phillips," describes the actions of Miskatonic University librarian Seneca Lapham to deal with the evil unleashed by Dewart--written from the perspective of Lapham's assistant.

### Characters
Richard Billington: The first Billington to lay claim to Billington's Wood. According to the fictional book Of Evill Sorceries Done in New-England of Daemons in No Humane Shape, in the early years of the Plymouth Colony, during the governorship of William Bradford (1621-1657), Billington  sets up "a great Ring of Stones" where he said "Prayers to ye Devil" and "sung certain Rites of Magick abominable by Scripture". After a series of mysterious deaths are linked to him, he disappears, and is said by the Wampanaug Indians to have been "eat up by what he had call'd out of ye Sky." 

Misquamacus: An "antient Wonder-Worker" of the Wampanaug nation.  According to the fictional book Of Evill Sorceries Done in New-England of Daemons in No Humane Shape, Misquamacus teaches "Sorceries" to Richard Billington and imprisons Ossadagowah, a spawn of Tsathoggua, in a ring of stones. He is later raised from the dead in the early 19th century by Alijah Billington to be a servant and the guardian of his son, Laban; in this form he is called Quamis and is described as a Narragansett Indian. He is finally shot by Seneca Lapham with a silver bullet and turns into dust.

Alijah Phineas Billington: He inherits Richard Billington's estate in the late 18th century. His wife is Lavinia Billington; they have a son, Laban. Alijah enters into a rivalry with Rev. Ward Phillips, who had accused Billington and his forebear of practicing sorcery. The feud culminates with the disappearance of John Druven, one of Phillips' supporters. Afterwards, Billington leaves for England with his son Laban and his servant Quamis, remaining there until his death. Seneca Lapham recalls him as "a man well ahead of his time, [and] more intelligent than most men of his generation." Lapham observes: "He practiced rites and ceremonies which undoubtedly harked back to the beginnings of mankind, but he knew how to escape the consequences." He

fullContent:
The Lurker at the Threshold was a small box expansion pack for Arkham Horror Second Edition, Fantasy Flight Games' board game of Lovecraftian adventure.

### Overview
As a small-box set, The Lurker at the Threshold was a cards-only expansion, featuring 56 Investigator cards including new Items and Spells, and 110 Ancient One cards whose special effects were intended to spin games of Arkham Horror in different directions from the core set.

In addition, this pack saw the introduction of the Relationship and Dark Pact mechanics to Arkham Horror. As its name might suggest, the Relationship mechanic allowed players to develop interpersonal relationships with one another, further enhancing the role-play aspect of the game, while the Dark Pact rules allowed players to make beneficial, but potentially highly costly, deals with the Lurker at the Threshold.

The Lurker at the Threshold is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author Brandon Berntson. The third and final book in his Lovecraft Mysteries, it was first published in a digital format through Amazon's Kindle platform in February 2021 .

### Overview


### Synopsis
When private detective Devlin Macky drunkenly encounters the evil sorcerer Abdul Alhazred, he unknowingly sets in motion the Mad Arab's plan to summon armies of monstrous creatures to Earth and bring about the return of Cthulhu, Yog-Sothoth, and Azathoth. He must recruit the help of a diverse bunch of characters, including one Henry Armitage, and travel through time and space to enlist the aid of Nodens and the Elder Gods to save his beloved Innsport - and the continued existence of the human race - from the depredations of the Outer Gods, while dealing with the machinations of the devious Nyarlathotep.

### Behind the Mythos
Amongst the many and varied Cthulhu Mythos elements which make appearances or are name-dropped in The Lurker at the Threshold are the legendary city of Sarnath, malevolent frog monsters, the demigod Wilbur Whateley, the alien Mi-Go, Kadath of the Dreamlands, the barely-human Asenath Waite, monstrous artist Richard Upton Pickman, the Witch House, Ubba-Sathla [sic], Brown Jenkin, the city of Arkham, and Miskatonic University. 

Another likely nod to the Mythos is a police officer named Jerry Danforth.

"The Lurker From the Kelp Forest" is a short story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A man whose mother vanished in the waters of an island in the Pacific Ocean returns to the site to search for her corpse. There, he encounters a malevolent creature from the Dreamlands which has been consuming the souls of unwary seamen and divers for unknown ages. After battling the creature and wounding it, he leaves the island and tries to ensure that nobody else will fall victim to it.

*Patrick, a man seemingly dying from terminal cancer.
*Yagdolak, a predatory entity from another dimension.
*Grace, Patrick's mother.
*Emerald, Patrick's daughter.

### Publication History
"The Lurker From the Kelp Forest" was published in the December 2018 collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos.

fullContent:
"The Lurker in Tunnel 13" is a story featured in Swamp Thing Vol 1 #8 which was written by Len Wein, illustrated by Bernie Wrightson, and published by DC Comics in 1974. The plot involves the Swamp Thing facing off against M'nagalah, an Elder God that was terrorizing the mining town of Perdition, Pennsylvania.  

### Synopsis
While on the run from the Batman, the Swamp Thing gets lost in a snow-swept Appalachian forest where he encounters Ezekiel, an old man who is being attacked by a grizzly bear in a cave. The Swamp Thing manages to fight off and kill the bear but Ezekiel has already been fatally injured, and only lives long enough to warn him not to go into Perdition, a mining town that has been cursed by occult practices after running out of coal. Not wanting to leave him in the cave, the Swamp Thing carries Ezekiel's body in the hopes of giving him a proper burial and notifying his family. 

After arriving in Perdition, some of the locals mistake the Swamp Thing for being the murderer of Ezekiel and attack him until Ezekiel's son, Jason, points out that it can not be the case, as he has been clearly clawed to death by a bear. Having also been injured during the attack, Jason brings the Swamp Thing to his house to give him some time to recover; however, this recovery is quickly interrupted when his son, Jody, goes missing. Along with the Swamp Thing, Jason and his family go out to search for Jody by following some footprints that lead to the forbidden Tunnel 13. As gratitude for his previous acts of generosity, the Swamp Thing decides to enter the tunnel for Jason and risk his own life to retrieve Jody. 

The whole thing turns out to be a ruse, however, as the townspeople's true intentions are to trick the Swamp Thing into going into the tunnel in order to use him as a sacrifice to M'nagalah. Upon his entering the tunnel, M'nagalah explains to the Swamp Thing that he was responsible for the creation of all life on Earth and bestowed mankind with the capacity for mindless violence, but was also generous to touch the minds of humanity's greatest scribes (including H. P. Lovecraft, Ambrose Bierce and Edgar Allan Poe). M'nagalah managed to do this from a distant place not of this world and would have stayed there if Abraham, father of Ezekiel and grandfather of Jason, had not spoken the spell that freed him from his distant prison. During his occult practices to restore the town's coal supply, Abraham allowed M'nagalah to slowly manifest in the human world as a growth on his arm that eventually consumed his entire body, before consuming many others in order to gain more mass. M'nagalah attempts to consume the Swamp Thing so that he can reach his full mass and conquer the entire universe. The Swamp Thing tears off a pillar of the tunnel and throws it into M'nagalah, causing the whole tunnel to collapse on him.

fullContent:
"The Lurking Fear" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft in the horror fiction genre. Written in November 1922, it was first published in the January through April 1923 issues of Home Brew, with accompanying illustrations by artist and fellow Mythos author Clark Ashton Smith.

### Origin
Like "Herbert West--Reanimator", earlier published in Home Brew, "The Lurking Fear" was solicited by editor George Julian Houtain expressly to be published as a serial. Unlike with "Herbert West", however, Houtain ran recaps of the story so far with each installment after the first, relieving Lovecraft of the need for objectionable repetition.

### Plot summary
The story is divided into 4 chapters:

### I. The Shadow On The Chimney
The narrator, a monster hunter, hearing tales of a "lurking fear" upon Tempest Mountain in the Catskills, takes his two strongmen with him to investigate. They camp inside the deserted Martense mansion as a lightning storm approaches, and feeling strangely drowsy, they all fall asleep. The narrator wakes up to find both his companions missing, and in a flash of lightning sees a demonic shadow cast upon the fireplace chimney from a grotesque monster like the other one.

### II. A Passer In The Storm
Continuing his investigation, the narrator teams up with Arthur Munroe, another journalist. The two find as much information as they can on the mansion and environs, until they find themselves trapped by yet another storm. Bunkered in a small cabin, they witness a bright flash of lightning. Arthur looks out the window to survey the damage. The narrator, curious as to why Arthur is still staring out the window, turns him to find his face chewed off.

### III. What The Red Glare Meant
As the narrator digs open the grave of Jan Martense, he describes the history of the Martense Family. Upon reaching the coffin, he continues to dig, and subsequently falls into a subterranean burrow. He crawls along, until he sees two eyes reflecting his torch-light in the darkness. Yet another lightning-strike causes the tunnel to cave in above the beast and the narrator has to dig his way to the surface. He spots a red glare in the distance that he learns was a cabin that the hillside squatters had set alight with one of the beasts inside.

### IV. The Horror In The Eyes
The narrator continues to search for more clues, until it occurs to him that peculiar mounds of earth lead out in lines from the mansion. He finds a burrow entrance in the basement as another storm approaches. Finding a hiding place, he watches as countless creatures crawl from the hole. The narrator then sees one of the weaker members of the grotesque mob get attacked and eaten by one of its compatriots. He shoots one of the creatures as it straggles behind the rest of the pack using a clap of thunder to disguise the muzzle blast, and upon closer inspection, notices the creature's heterochromia and realizes that the deformed, hair-covered creature is in fact a member of the Martense family, who

### Overview

*An Albany Evening News article regarding the gruesome Lefferts Corners deaths
*Arthur Munroe's press card
*A map of the Catskill Mountains
*A medical examiner's report on one of the bodies
*A handwritten letter from Jan Martense to Johnathan Gifford (pre-order exclusive)

"The Macabre and Blasphemous Horror of Chocolate Cake Twinkles" is a tongue-in-cheek Cthulhu Mythos story by American author M. Kelly Peach. It was published in the Deadman's Tome anthology Deep Fried Horror Cthulhu Cheese Burger in January 2020.

### Synopsis
The story describes the seductive pull of a new brand of cake bar on the market, and one man's struggle to remain abstinent. Eventually, however, their allure becomes too much, and he buys a pack, only to discover that there may be more involved in their manufacture than simple baking…

### Behind the Mythos
A number of Cthulhu Mythos elements are name-dropped in the story, including Shoggoths, Hastur, Cthulhu, the Yellow Sign, the Silver Key, and Tsathoggua.

"The Madness of Arthur Malbrey" is a short Thomas Carnacki/Cthulhu Mythos crossover story by author Brandon Barrows.

### Synopsis
Supernatural sleuth Thomas Carnacki is called in to help a friend whose sanity has been taken from him after reading the cursed play The King in Yellow. Although he and another friend attempt to help the man, he is ultimately carried off to Carcosa with his new lord, leaving Carnacki befuddled and the other man dead.

### Characters
*Thomas Carnacki, an occult investigator without peer.
*Arthur Malbrey, a friend of Carnacki's working in the publishing industry.
*George Jones, Malbrey's business partner and close friend.
*The King in Yellow, an avatar of the Great Old One Hastur.

### Publication History
"The Madness of Arthur Malbrey" was published in the collection of Barrows' Thomas Carnacki stories The Castle-Town Tragedy and Other Tales of Carnacki, the Ghost-Finder in January 2016.

### Trivia
*Friedrich Von Junzt's mystical grimoire Die Unaussprechlichen Kulten is mentioned as being one of the sources consulted by Carnacki in his search for information on The King in Yellow.

"The Madonna of the Abattoir" is a short story by Anne M. Pillsworth, published on Tor.com in 2014. It is a prequel to Pillsworth's Summoned. 

### Synopsis
The story features Redemption Orne, a supporting character in Summoned, and Patience Orne, who features in that book's background--both of whom are acolytes of Nyarlathotep, and effectively immortal. Having fled Arkham, Massachusetts, during the witch panic of 1692, they return in the 19th century, with Redemption using the name Rev. Horace Winthrop, and Patience appearing as Patience Crawford, Horace's cousin and amanuensis. Patience is soon asked to model by a talented and earnest young painter, James Pickman, and she agrees--seeing this as an opportunity to pervert and destroy an innocent.

fullContent:
"The Magical Fruit" is a short story by Jayaprakash Satyamurthy, originally collected in the Kickstarter crowdfunded anthology A Mythos Grimmly. It is a alternative ending to "The Colour Out of Space", combined with Jack and the Beanstalk.

### Synopsis
A simpleton living on or near the farm plagued by the Colour Out of Space swaps his farm's "Milk Glands" for strange multi-colored beans. Already affected by the surrounding alien radiation to some extent, the unnamed narrator murders his mother then climbs the beanstalk that springs up overnight from where he scattered some of the beans.

The narrator has also eaten more of the strange beans, and he mutates as he climbs, until at the top of the beanstalk high in the sky he finds an alien palace shaped from the fruiting body of the plant, producing still more alien plants.

As his transformation is complete he sits on his throne inside the alien vegetation palace, serene and newly intelligent, calmly knowing that he is only the first of a transformed species that will rule the planet.

fullContent:
"The Maker of Gargoyles" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, one of his stories set in Averoigne, a fictionalized province of France. It first published in the August 1932 issue of Weird Tales.

The story centers on Blaise Reynard, a master stonecarver of Vyones, who carves two gargoyles so lifelike that they begin attacking residents. The story has been credited with introducing the idea of gargoyles as monsters rather than mere architectural decoration.

### Characters
* Blaise Reynard: The story's epyonmous maker of gargoyles, a taciturn and saturine stonecarver.
* Ambrosius: The Archbishop of Vyones.
* Nicolette Villom: Daughter of a local taverner and the object of Reynard's unwanted advances.
* Guillaume Maspier: A respectable clothier of Vyones.
* Gerome Mazzal: A reputable cooper of Vyones.
* Jean Villom: Owner of the local tavern and father of Nicolette.
* Raoul Coupain: A mercer's assistant and Nicolette's suitor.

### Adaptations
### Comics
The story heavily inspired Dynamite Entertainment's Gargoyles: Demona #3 "For Not Everything With Wings..." by Greg Weisman and Frank Paur, published in 2025 and based on the 1994 Disney animated series Gargolyes.  In the comic, the titular Demona and her daughter Angelika are members of a race of living gargoyles who are stone by day but flesh by night. Feared and hunted by humanity, they 'hide in plain sight' among the sculpted gargoyles of Vyones Cathedral before coming into conflict with Blaise Reynard's magically animated constructs.

### References

fullContent:
"The Maker of Moons" is a fantasy short story by Robert W. Chambers originally published in 1896. It introduces the mystical city of Yian, which would be incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Synopsis
In 1896, in an American town close to the Canadian border, a goldsmith named George Godfrey acquires a lifelike gold sculpture of a small snake. Godfrey shows the piece to his friend, Roy Cardenhe (the narrator), telling him that he bought it from a man who lived in the vicinity of Cardinal Woods, near Starlit Lake. While Cardenhe admires the work, a creature crawls out of Godfrey's pocket, much to his friend's surprise. The animal looks like a strange combination of worm, crab, and reptile, and Cardenhe is utterly apalled by it, sensing something wrong about it. Godfrey recounts that he first saw the creature clinging to the box in which the gold snake was kept. The staff of the Natural History Museum couldn't identify the species, so he decided to keep it and use it as a model for his own art work.

Later that day, Cardenhe goes on a hunting trip to Cardinal Woods with two friends: a wealthy gold miner named Pierpoint and a government secret agent named Barris. The latter reveals that he's actually in a mission to apprehend a gang of "gold-makers". Recently, a scientist named La Grange has demonstrated that gold is not an element, but a composite metal that can be manufactured, and while the discovery has been kept secret for the fear of the economic consequences, some people have apparently learned how to make it. Pierpoint worries about whether Prof. La Grange will truly keep his discovery a secret, but Barris confirms it by revealing that La Grange has just been found murdered.

Five days later, Cardenhe's servant, David, tells him that he saw a Chinese man in the woods. When Cardenhe goes hunting with one of his dogs, he comes across a glade with a pool and meets a young woman named Ysonde. She caresses the dog gently and seems harmless, but also displays a puzzling unfamiliarity with the local settlements, and becomes serious when she notices a crescent-shaped mark on Cardenhe's forehead. She only relaxes again after Cardenhe assures her that it's not a scar, but a birthmark. She then reveals that she's a sculptor, and shows him a stone on which she has carved the images of moths and dragonflies. Cardenhe is impressed by her skill, but she vanishes just as suddenly as she appeared. On his way home, Cardenhe catches the sight of a Chinese man hiding among the trees, just like David had described.

The next day, Barris and Pierpoint have breakfast with Cardenhe and reveal that they have located the gold-makers' camp near the lake. Barris also shows him a small crab-like creature, which Cardenhe recognises as being the same species as Godfrey's new "pet". "The Man in  the Bubble" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author David Annandale which takes place in Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting. It was published in the anthology Secrets in Scarlet by Aconyte in October 2022.

### Synopsis
A presumed explosion which devastates a Manhattan city block leads Commissioner Qiana Taylor and her team of special investigators deep beneath the streets of New York. In an enormous cavern, they discover a tomb which has been violated by ill-advised explorers who have unleashed something terrible on the world above.

The group's investigations lead them to wealthy businessman Ryan Davenport, a man who has an unhealthy obsession with the occult. He reveals that he paid the explorers handsomely to recover an artefact known as the Coronal Prism from the tomb, despite having no real knowledge of what he was initiating. Taylor's attempts to reason with Davenport and offer him protection in return for the device fall on deaf ears, however, and the monstrosity from the tomb descends to take vengeance on the thief.

fullContent:
The Man of Stone" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald in October 1932. It is one of five stories Lovecraft revised for Heald. Heald had been introduced to Lovecraft by his Providence friend Muriel E. Eddy.

### Plot
The story describes the narrator, Jack, and his friend Ben Hayden as they search for the missing sculptor Arthur Wheeler, who disappeared in the Upper Adirondacks of New York State. Inspired by the discovery of lifelike statues of a dog and a man in Wheeler's style, Ben Hayden persuades the narrator to travel with him to the small, secretive village of Mountain Top. While there, they learn that Arthur fell foul of his landlord: the sinister "Mad Dan" Morris, who believed Wheeler was having an affair with his wife, Rose. None of the three had been seen in town since.

The pair go to search for the statues, find the cave, and instantly abandon their theory: the statues are so realistic that the pair instantly recognize them as living creatures that have somehow become instantly petrified. Wheeler's involvement is instantly discarded, not least when they discover the second statue, and Hayden recognizes it as the missing sculptor himself.

Hayden steers Jack towards Mad Dan's cabin, and they break in via a window and discover Wheelers things, still untouched despite months away. They then discover why, as they find both Mad Dan and his wife petrified inside, Dan tied to a chair with a leather whip, and Rose strangely smug in her final moments. The pair find Dan's diary on the table, which tells the story in great detail. Dan is the decedent of a certain Nicolas Van Kauran, a wizard once burned at the stake, though his copy of the Book of Eibon survived, and was passed down through the generations.  Dan continues to perform ancient rites into the present, including sacrificing to Shubb-Niggurath, and complaining that the villagers "always prevent my doing the Great Rite that would open the gate."  Rose also does not participate in his ceremonies, much to his complaints, and when Wheeler arrives and Dan notices their flirting, he contrives a horrible revenge. 

After several months of study (during which he discards ideas like, "the emanation of Yoth," or "The Green Decay") Morris finds a weapon with a poetic flourish: a potion to induce petrification, once used for murder by another ancestor. Admitting it has more to do with science than magic, he constructs a secret laboratory in the cave, testing his formulas on passing animals. Finally, he succeeds and simply has to confirm that the formula will petrify a larger animal, starting with his wife's pet dog, Rex, purely for the sake of hurting her, though he pretends he was killed by a wolf. Soon, he is certain he has what he needs.

Morris lures Wheeler away to the cave, and kills him quite easily, praising Tsathoggua for the victory. Rose, however, would prove more difficult: Dan is only able to safely hide the formula in wine, but is stonewalled by the simple fact that Ro

"The Man Who Was Lovecraft" is a non-fiction piece by H. P. Lovecraft's friend and correspondent E. Hoffmann Price. It was first published in the 1949 Arkham House collection Something About Cats and Other Pieces .

In their 2001 reference work An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia, leading Lovecraft scholars S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz describe "The Man Who Was Lovecraft" as "a substantial memoir."

shortDefinition: "The Man Who Went Too Far" is a short story by the late British author E. F. Benson. First published in June 1904 in Pall Mall Magazine, it has been extensively reprinted in the years since.  H. P. Lovecraft, a fan of several of Benson's works, is sa...
fullContent:
"The Man Who Went Too Far" is a short story by the late British author E. F. Benson. First published in June 1904 in Pall Mall Magazine, it has been extensively reprinted in the years since.

H. P. Lovecraft, a fan of several of Benson's works, is said to have spoken highly of the story.

In his 1912 collection The Room in the Tower and Other Stories, Benson tells of how "The Man Who Went Too Far" was eventually developed into his 1905 novel The Angel of Pain.

### Synopsis
"The Man Who Went Too Far" deals with a man who wishes to know all the secrets of nature and is often able to hear beautiful sounds of pipes, which he calls "the pipes of Pan". He draws ever closer to his "final revelation" until he is one day found dead, mangled by a strange shape that waddles off into the darkness. On his dead body are afterwards found prints as of hooves.

fullContent:
"The Mandrakes" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, set in his semi-historical French province of Averoigne. It first appeared in the February 1933 issue of Weird Tales.

It tells the story of a married couple, both sorcerers, who make a living selling love-philtres whose active ingredient is the root of the mandrakes that grow to unusual size in the swamps along the river Isoile. When he kills her out of jealousy, she returns as a mandrake root and exposes his crime.

### Characters
*Gilles Grenier: A sorcerer who is tolerated in 15th century Averoigne because of the usefulness of his love potions. He is thought to have been driven out of Blois, "where all persons bearing the name Grenier were popularly believed to be werewolves." His "hands were black with bristles and [his] beard grew almost to his eyes," but he shows no other signs of lycanthropy. He is middle-aged, as indicated by the fact that his "sable mane and beard were already touched with the white warp of time."
*Sabine Grenier: Gilles' much younger wife, "a comely woman with blue-grey eyes and wheat-colored hair."

### Publication History
Since its initial appearance in Weird Tales, "The Mandrakes" has appeared in several collections of Smith's fiction, starting with Other Dimensions (Arkham House, 1970). It was included in both The Averoigne Archives (Pickman's Press, 2019) and The Averoigne Chronicles (Hippocampus Press, 2021).

It was also featured in 100 Wicked Little Witch Stories (Barnes & Noble Books, 1995).

fullContent:
"The Mannikin" is a short story by Robert Bloch that appeared in the April 1937 issue of Weird Tales.  

### Synopsis
Simon Maglore is an intelligent young man described as "tall and thin, with massive stooping shoulders, and a crooked back. He was...afflicted with a peculiar tumorous growth beneath his left shoulder blade." He was otherwise "a very pleasant-looking fellow. Black-haired, gray-eyed, fair of skin, he seemed a fine specimen of intelligent manhood." 

Maglore has an "earnest belief in the occult and esoteric"; his family has an "interest in sorcery" going back to Italy at the time of the Medici; they came to America to evade the Inquisition. Maglore's deformity also runs in the family; his grandfather was a "crookback", and his grandfather's grandfather as well. 

Maglore seems to have a split personality, being perfectly pleasant at times, and at other times showing a "leering face" and a "smile of sly, lurking evil." At those times Maglore was known to bother strangers with peculiar questions about occult lore. 

When Maglore is found dead, his secret is revealed: The lump on his back was actually a conjoined twin, a malformed person with a "little, wrinkled face, like a monkey's", and "tiny, reddish eyes". This mannikin vied for control of his brother's body--and when Maglore tried to reveal his twin's existence in a letter, he killed his brother as well as himself by biting Maglore in the neck. 

### Behind the Mythos
Maglore's library includes Ludvig Prinn's "infamous" Mysteries of the Worm, as well as Mycroft's Commentaries on Witchcraft; a Greek translation of the "almost priceless" Cabala of Saboth, c. 1686; and Ranft's De Masticatione Mortuorum in Tumulis, from 1734. While the first three books are fictional, and Bloch's inventions, the last is a real book, written by Lutheran pastor Michael Ranft, whose title translates as On the Chewing of the Dead in their Tombs. His accounts of post-mortem feeding by corpses contributed to the modern legend of vampires. 

When under the control of his twin, Maglore asks a number of Mythos-related questions, querying people about Nyarlathotep and the "Black Messenger"--who seem to be a different entities, though elsewhere (e.g., "The Faceless God") Bloch uses the latter is a title of the former. He also asks about Shub-Niggurath, "beast-men", "the thirteenth covenant",  the "Feast of Ulder", the "Doel chants", and "the ritual of Father Yig". 

The story is set in Bridgetown, on Lake Kane, places whose location is not further specified. The Algonquin-sounding name of the Indians whose legends Maglore inquires into--the Pasquantog--suggests a New England setting. 

### Publication History
After its initial Weird Tales appearance, "The Mannikin" was frequently reprinted. It appeared in Sleep No More: Twenty Masterpieces of Horror for the Connoisseur, a 1944 anthology edited by August Derleth, as well as The Seventh Fontana Book of Great Horror Stories (1972) and The Sixth Mayflower Book of B

fullContent:
"The Mantle of Graag" is a short story by authors Robert A. W. Lowndes, Frederik Pohl and Dirk Wylie.

### Synopsis
The story follows a group of writers dabbling in the occult. They unearth a mysterious chest and break its seal, allowing an evil entity to enter the world and consume them.

### Characters
*Frank Hartley, a member of the collective and the story's expositor.
*Harvey, one of the last surviving members.

### Publication History
"The Mantle of Graag" was first published in The Unique Magazine in October 1941. It later appeared in issue #59 of fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu in September 1988, and then in the Robert M. Price-edited collection The Necronomicon: Selected Stories and Essays Concerning the Blasphemous Tome of the Mad Arab.

### Trivia
* H. P. Lovecraft is mentioned as being a friend of the group, although he does not appear in the story.

fullContent:
"The Mark of Yig" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
A brilliant man who has an obsession with expanding the consciousness decides that the best way to do this is to suppress the base of the brain: the oldest, reptilian part. Contacting a friend of his employed at Oakdeene Sanatorium, the two decide to conduct an experiment on one of the inmates. However, rather than removing the subject's baser instincts, the procedure goes horrifically wrong and results in the deaths of two orderlies.

Deciding that perhaps it would be better to enhance the reptilian part of the brain, and unwilling to try again on other people, the man goes about the business of experimenting on himself. Although his intellect is subsequently enhanced, a physical transformation also occurs, metamorphosing him into a human/reptile creature, and he crawls off to join the beings he now sees as kin below ground in the caverns of Yoth.

### Characters

*Colin Gilman, a genius and visionary man.
*Dr. Allen Enslin, a senior resident at Oakdeene Sanatorium.

### Publication History
"The Mark of Yig" was first published in issue #2 of digital fanzine The Black Book in August 2002, and later appeared in the collection Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2008.

"The Master of the Crabs" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith set in his world of Zothique. It was originally published in Weird Tales in 1948.

### Synopsis
The benevolent working wizard Mior Lumivix accompanied by his callow apprentice Manthar race against the malevolent Sarcand to obtain the chart of the ancient pirate Omvor, and with it the location of the pirate's long-lost treasure. In addition to conventional precious stones and metals, the treasure of Omvor also includes books of lore sacred to the Moon God containing knowledge invaluable to a wizard. 

The story shows what a civilized wizard such as Mior Lumivix does to earn a living in a settled area, such as creating love potions for sale. Manthar is a typical apprentice wizard, unsure of himself. Sarcand is a driven and ruthless antagonist, who is also a cannibal as was his mother. The magic demonstrated in this story clearly influenced the original conceptualization of spellcasting in Dungeons & Dragons.

At the climax of the story Sarcand uses a magic item found in the pirate's treasure, the Signet Ring of Basatan. This ring has several magical effects, one of which is the power to summon and control a horde of crabs. Sarcand has been using them to catch unwary visitors to the island on which he is shipwrecked whereupon he and the crabs eat the unfortunate person.

When Sarcand attempts to swarm crabs over Mior Lumvix and Manthar, Mior Lumvix chops off the hand on which Sarcand wears the magic ring. As is the way of such things, the enraged crabs, no longer controlled by Sarcand, swarm over him and eat him alive.

The story concludes with Mior Lumivix entreating his apprentice to build a stout fire in which to cook a dozen crabs for their dinner. The wizard tells his apprentice to make sure that their dinner crabs are fresh caught from the sea.

### Behind the Mythos
Of concern to some modern readers is the ancestry of the antagonist Sarcand. He is a negro, and his mother is described as a "black cannibal", the usual epithet Smith used for the inhabitants of Naat, for example in his letter describing the island to L. Sprague de Camp.

fullContent:
"The Medium and the Message" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author L. C. von Hessen. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
The story is told in the form of an arts Masters degree thesis by one H. Lee Upton, a distant descendant of Richard Upton Pickman. It charts the discovery and history of a previously-unknown Pickman work uncovered in a subterranean structure beneath the streets of Boston. Many of those who studied the painting, dubbed Untitled (Red Canvas), went insane, often fatally, and predictably this begins to happen to Upton. Later discovering a film reel created by Pickman, Upton projects the images onto Untitled (Red Canvas) and his sanity decreases further, even as the events depicted on the film begin to change.

Interspersed throughout the story is an expanded history of Pickman, including his relationship with one Helen Martense, a woman who seemingly acted as a muse for his more supernatural works.

"The Messenger" is a short poem by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
The two verses describe the unnamed narrator's wait for an unknown "thing" to come upon him at 3 o'clock in the morning.

### Publication History
"The Messenger" was first published in the July 1938 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since seen inclusion in a number of works, both anthologies and periodicals.

### Trivia
*Although not seeing print until after Lovecraft's death, "The Messenger" was written in 1929 and was dedicated to Providence Journal columnist Bernard K. Hart in response to a playful article written on Lovecraft's short story "The Call of Cthulhu".
*The poem mentions the Elder Sign, although in this context it appears to be a device used to call set free dark entities rather than contain them.

### Music
In 2008, russian horror-punk band Korol i Shut (Король и Шут) released the song "Вестник" ("The Messenger"), on the album "Тень клоуна" (Shadow of the Clown).

fullContent:
The Metal Monster is an Abraham Merritt fantasy novel, and a sequel to his earlier novel The Moon Pool, featuring the character Walter T. Goodwin.

The epic adventure starts with a foreword where Merritt is assigned the duty to relay Dr. Goodwin's incredible tale of his encounter in the Trans-Himalayan mountains to the world, to let everyone know the terrible fate Goodwin's group barely escaped and the possibility of other such monsters out there.

### Plot summary
Dr. Goodwin is on a botanical expedition in the Himalayas. There he meets Dick Drake, the son of one of his old science acquaintances. They are witnesses of a strange aurora-like effect, but seemingly a deliberate one. As they go out to investigate, they meet Goodwin's old friends Martin and Ruth Ventnor, brother and sister scientists. The two are besieged by Persians as Darius III led when Alexander of Macedon conquered them more then two thousand years ago.

The group is saved by a magnificent woman they get to know as Norhala. She commands the power of lightning and controls strange metal animate Things, living, metallic, geometric forms; an entire city of sentient cubes, globes and tetrahedrons, capable of joining together and forming colossal shapes, and wielding death rays and other armaments of destruction. They are led to a hidden valley occupied by what they name "The Metal Monster", a strange metal city occupied by the metal animate Things Norhala commands. This city is governed by what they call the Metal Emperor, assisted by the Keeper of the Cones. Ruth is slowly being converted by Norhala to become like her; her little sister. Martin, her brother, tries shooting the Metal Emperor, who retalliates with a ray blast, putting Martin in a comatose state. Closed in between the Metal Monster and the Persians, it falls to Goodwin and Drake to find a way to escape their predicament.

### Legacy
This book was a favorite of H. P. Lovecraft, though he at first avoided the revised version, at the suggestion of C. M. Eddy, Jr..

### Copyright
The copyright for this story has expired in the United States and, thus, now resides in the public domain there. The text of the revision is available via Project Gutenberg.

### Revisions
There exist 3 versions of the novel.

The second version is named "The Metal Emperor", appearing in 1927 in a magazine -an abridged version of the 1st novel, with the leading character's name changed to Louis Thorton.

The Midnight Eye Files is a series of hardboiled detective stories which contain supernatural elements, some of which are connected to the Cthulhu Mythos. Created by Scottish author William Meikle, and set in Glasgow where he attended university in his younger days, the series began with the novel The Amulet in October 2005.

The complete stories have been collected in two omnibuses, published in 2016 and 2019 respectively.

### Premise
The series follows protagonist Derek Adams, a hard-drinking, heavy-smoking private detective from Glasgow, Scotland, as he investigates cases with occult, alien, or supernatural elements. These have included an encounter with a group of Mi-Go intent on claiming the brains of a cult, and a liaison with fellow private eye Frank Nardi while investigating mysterious signals from the outer cosmos.

*"Eeny Meeny Miney Mi-Go" (2019)

fullContent:
"The Mindhouse" is a short story by American author Christine Morgan. It could be perceived as a metaphor for humanity's wilful blindness to the problems of nuclear waste, pollution, and many other issues.

### Synopsis
In a letter to her estranged sister, a woman incarcerated in a mental health facility tells how she has been cured of her acute schizophrenia by an unconventional doctor using a bizarre room known as the Mindhouse. Although the writer of the letter knows that the insanity which is being siphoned away by the treatments will one day be used to spell the end of humanity, she delights in the good it has done for the patients who participate in the doctor's procedures.

### Characters

*The Unnamed Narrator, a woman who has been incarcerated since a young age at Evergate, a mental health institution situated on a very special site.

### Publication History
"The Mindhouse" was published in the April Moon Books thematic anthology The Dark Rites of Cthulhu in March 2014.

### Trivia

*The name of the doctor treating the patients, Dr. Hasturn, is a clear nod to the Great Old One Hastur from Robert W. Chambers' The King in Yellow. Similarly, some of the phrases involved in Hasturn's ritual, such as Cthlotha Fthagnd, are reminiscent of those used by H. P. Lovecraft and others in earlier Mythos stories.

fullContent:
"The Mine on Yuggoth" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Ramsey Campbell, originally published in The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants (Arkham House, 1964).

### Synopsis
Expanding on elements from H. P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness, the story concerns the efforts of Edward Taylor (b. 1899), a former Brichester University student obsessed with the occult, to travel to Yuggoth to obtain the unique metal tok'l.

### Publication History
The story was later reprinted in The Spawn of Cthulhu, edited by Lin Carter, the 1985 edition of Cold Print, and Chaosium's The Hastur Cycle.

fullContent:
"The Mirror of Nitocris" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley that introduces the character of Henri-Laurent de Marigny--later better known as Titus Crow's chief companion and chronicler. It is the only story written by Lumley in which de Marigny is the main character. It first appeared in Lumley's collection The Caller of the Black (Arkham House, 1971).

### Synopsis
De Marigny acquires a legendary mirror that once belonged to the monstrous Egyptian Queen Nitocris--and just barely escapes its malign influence.

### Characters
*Henri-Laurent de Marigny: An occultist and self-described "romantic fool." He attributes his "love of dark mysteries and obscure and antique wonders" as an inheritance from "my world-famous father, the great New Orleans mystic Etienne-Laurent de Marigny." His library includes books by "Geoffrey, Poe, d’Erlette, and Prinn."
*Nitocris: "A sixth-dynasty Queen who ruled her terror-stricken subjects with a will of supernatural iron from her seat at Gizeh." She is the subject of a book by Wardle called Notes on Nitocris.
*Bannister Brown-Farley: An "explorer-hunter-archaeologist who, before his recent disappearance, was a recognized connoisseur of rare and obscure objets d’art."
*Abu Ben Reis: An "old Arab" whose "home tribe was a band of rovers wandering far to the west, beyond the great desert. He tells Brown-Farley of the tomb where the Mirror of Nitocris may be found.
*Baron Kant: The "witch-hunting Baron" whose silver pistol de Marigny possesses.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Caller of the Black, "The Mirror of Nitocris" was reprinted in the April 1984 issue of the magazine Imagine. It was later included in Lumley's collections The Compleat Crow (W. Paul Ganley, 1987), Fruiting Bodies and Other Fungi (Roc UK/Tor, 1993), and Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008).

A French translation appeared (as "Le mirroir de Nitoctis") in Phénix #41 (1997).

fullContent:
The Miskatonic Five is a scenario supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Written by Matthew Sincic and Alex Artang, and featuring artwork by Andrew Sincic, it was published in a digital-only format through DriveThruRPG as part of their Miskatonic Repository licensed player-driven initiative. The book was released in July 2021, and is available free of charge on the site.

### Overview


The scenario is a short one, coming in at only 17 pages long, and contains all necessary NPC stats as well as a set of pre-generated characters, but no handouts. A handful of images are scattered throughout the book, for the most part real-life photography with filters applied.

### Synopsis
The Miskatonic Five's linear storyline takes place amidst civil unrest on the University campus, where a small cult of students led by a faculty member-cum-Priest of Hastur attempt to summon a Byakhee in order to travel to Carcosa and join with their master. The players, a group of university attendees, must race against the clock to prevent this.

fullContent:
The Miskatonic Museum is the first Mythos Pack in The Dunwich Legacy cycle for Arkham Horror: The Card Game.

### Publisher's Description
Somewhere in the Miskatonic Museum, Olaus Wormius’s Latin translation of a book called the Necronomicon lies hidden away, kept locked and secret so that those individuals who shouldn't gain access to it do not gain access to it. When recent events at the university and Clover Club lead you to believe that someone may now be searching for this strange and ancient tome – someone who should not be permitted to delve its secrets – you make your way to the Museum. The hour is late, and the place is locked. But you know you must recover the book before anyone can access its arcane secrets for dark purposes.

The cards and adventure from The Miskatonic Museum grant you access to the Museum and its many exhibitions even while the expansion's twenty-six player cards (two copies each of thirteen different cards) vie for your attention. Will you make use of these cards? How will you make use of them? Several of the cards offer a remarkable focus on long-term benefits over short-term returns, and you'll have plenty of time to incorporate them into your Arkham LCG campaigns – provided you first succeed on the task at hand. After all, there's something else stalking the museum's exhibits…

### Overview
This expansion contains 60 cards, which include 29 Player cards and 11 Encounter cards. This expansion not a standalone product. A copy of the Arkham Horror: The Card Game Core Set and The Dunwich Legacy deluxe expansion to play.

"The Misplaced Masterpiece of Richard Upton Pickman" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young. It is the third instalment in Book Three of his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
The story is told in the main part through the journal entries of a small-time art dealer who accidentally comes into possession of a previously-unknown painting by Richard Upton Pickman. As the image begins to entrance him, his newfound paranoia leads him to believe that he is being monitored by government agents who wish to take it from him. Attempting to hide the picture, he finds himself increasingly enraptured by it, before mysteriously disappearing. 

The story's conclusion confirms the agents to in fact be Mayweather and Hines from the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena, who recover the painting for disposal. The art dealer is heavily implied to have been drawn into Pickman's painting. 

### Characters
*Cromwell, an art dealer  on the verge of making a name for himself.
*Malcolm Mayweather, a senior agent for the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.
*Charlene Hines, Mayweather's junior partner.
*Harjit Singh, the Department's director.

### Publication History
"The Misplaced Masterpiece of Richard Upton Pickman" was published in The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 3 in 2021.

"The Mission" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by author Frank Coffman. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 2 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2018.

shortDefinition: The Mist is a malevolent force that serves as the titular main antagonist in Stephen King's novella, its subsequent computer game adaptation, and the 2007 film. This eerie, impenetrable fog is home to various species of otherworldly, grosteque creatu...
fullContent:
The Mist is a malevolent force that serves as the titular main antagonist in Stephen King's novella, its subsequent computer game adaptation, and the 2007 film. This eerie, impenetrable fog is home to various species of otherworldly, grosteque creatures and deadly predators from another dimension, posing a deadly danger to anyone caught within it.

### Description
The novella and film suggest the mysterious mist is from another world that accidentally spilled into ours due to a failed experiment called the Arrowhead Project. Evidence supporting this includes the mist's origin in Shaymore, the project's location, and the sudden influx of law enforcement there just before the mist appeared. Early script drafts confirm this theory, detailing how the Arrowhead Project attempted to open a portal to another dimension. A lightning strike during the experiment caused a system overload, forcing the mist and its terrifying creatures into our world. In the aftermath of a severe thunderstorm that struck Bridgton, Maine, the Mist appeared. It then expanded rapidly, engulfing unknown territories across the nation or possibly the world.

### Powers and Effects

### Novella
The novella describes a dense, white mist that enveloped a New England region for at least three days. Its exact geographic reach is uncertain, but it seems to have extended southward to Connecticut. This eerie mist has a pungent odor and a strange effect on sound, making distant noises seem close and vice versa. As night falls, the mist takes on a darker, gray hue.

### Film
After about three days of terrorizing the population with monstrous creatures, the Mist abruptly disappears, seemingly eradicated by military intervention. The fog itself is a metallic gray color and does not affect sound. Interestingly, it darkens to a blue hue at night, but whether or not it has the same strong, unpleasant odor as described in the original story is unknown.

### Inhabitants
The mist is home to a diverse array of creatures that rely heavily on their sense of smell to hunt, as visibility is severely limited. While many of these animals are drawn to light, others are not. Most, but not all, of these creatures are nocturnal. They include:

* Arachni-Lobsters
* Behemoth
* Four Horsemen (TV series only)
* Giant Spider Creatures
* Gray Widowers
* Green Flies (novella only)
* Killer Kites (novella only)
* Leeches (TV series only)
* Owl (TV series only)
* Pterobuzzards
* Scorpion-Flies
* Shadow Creatures (TV series only)
* Terrorpedes (behind the scenes only)
* Tentacles (also called "Tentacles from Planet X")

### Mythos Connections
Stephen King's The Mist undeniably carries strong Lovecraftian undertones. Both authors delve into the realm of cosmic horror, where humanity is confronted by incomprehensible, otherworldly forces that shatter our understanding of reality. This shared thematic ground makes the Mist a compelling example of Lovecraftian influence in contemporary horror fiction.

* Cosmic Horror: Love

"The Monomaniacal Pursuit of Glanvill's Will" is a Lovecraftian short story by author G. Large, published in Vol 5, Issue 4 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2021.

### Synopsis
The story tells the tale of a 17th century man named Pennington through later discussion by biographers. Pennington develops an obsession with a woman who is likely a figment of his own imagination, and he attempts to prove the strength of his will in order to gain her affections. This quest ultimately leads him to defeat death through sheer strength of will, but leaves him as a broken and slowly degenerating corpse. The story suggests that he may still be alive somewhere in the world.

fullContent:
"The Monster-God of Mamurth" is a short story by the late American author Edmond Hamilton, his first published fiction. It was featured in the August 1926 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales and has been reprinted numerous times, as well as being translated into French, German, and Italian .

The story is now in the public domain in the United States .

### Synopsis
In the North African desert near the Atlas Mountains, explorers encamped around a fire encounter a bedraggled stranger who stumbles into their camp.

This stranger had left Mogador two years before, searching for surviving ruins of the empire of Carthage and with them any surviving artefacts or treasures.

Instead, as the survivor explains, he had eventually found a ruined inscription referring to the lost Carthaginian city of Igidi, and vague directions as to where it might be found. Setting off, the survivor had progressed through fields of ruins in the desert until he found black desert and white stone ruins. As he began his exploration, he was attacked by a multi-legged giant monster, and with quick thinking drove it off with fire. He continued his exploration, discovering a long still standing wall, with a break in it guarded by two huge black basalt statues of seated figures, weathered by time. Through the gap in the wall he discovers that what seemed to be an empty area of the ruined city was actually an invisible building. And the invisible building is guarded, as local carvings seemed to warn, by invisible giant spiders.

Barely escaping his explorations with his life, the survivor had stumbled through the desert, barely making it to the camp of the other explorers, there to tell his tale.

### Behind the Mythos
Kenneth Sterling, who wrote the original draft of the science fiction short story "In the Walls of Eryx" before presenting his work to H. P. Lovecraft for revision, credits the concept of an invisible maze to "The Monster-God of Mamurth," although in Hamilton's story the maze exists in the Saharan Desert rather than on the surface of Venus.

"The Monsters in the Park" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author David Hambling. It forms part of his William Blake cycle.

### Synopsis
When William Blake is enlisted by an old schoolmate to find out what strange malady afflicts his son, he discovers that the boy has been taken over by a highly-advanced alien entity. It’s mission is to affect its species aeons-long war with another race, but it has become trapped in a less-than-ideal shell. Although Blake manages to fulfil the conditions necessary for the alien to vacate the boy's body, it simply jumps to his father and proceeds with its mission, leaving Blake to ponder the future of the human race.

### Characters
*William Blake, a schoolteacher whose past history makes him uniquely open to the strange tale told by "Paul".
*Paul Webster/The Alien, a member of an extraterrestrial species inhabiting the body of an 8-year-old boy.
*Webster, a wealthy aristocrat and Paul's father.

### Publication History
"The Monsters in the Park" was first published in the collection of Hambling's own works Shadows from Norwood in July 2013. It has since received a digital release in a self-titled chapbook.

### Trivia
*The Pnakotic Manuscripts are mentioned as one source consulted by Blake.
*The alien creatures are all but outright named as the Great Race of Yith. Likewise, their nemeses are heavily implied to be the flying polyps.
*Set in London's Crystal Palace Park, the title has a dual meaning, referring to both the statues of prehistoric animals for which the park is famous, and the creatures encountered by the protagonist within.

fullContent:
The Moon Pool is a fantasy novel by Abraham Merritt, first published in 1919. The first and second parts of the narrative were originally published separately, as "The Moon Pool" and "Conquest of the Moon Pool", respectively. It was followed in 1920 by a sequel, The Metal Monster.

H. P. Lovecraft was delighted with The Moon Pool and elements of its purple prose and its concepts of lost civilizations literally buried underground (or underwater) made their way into his own fictional universes, such as in the novella The Mound or the underwater cities of Cthulhu and the Deep Ones.

### Synopsis
Dr. Walter T. Goodwin, an eminent botanist, is studying the flora of Papua when he sees an old friend, Dr. David Throckmartin, who has just returned from the ruins of Nan-Matal in Ponape. Throckmartin is in a state of obvious shock, and at night, he shows Goodwin a luminous creature in the sky that seems to have been following him, with a mist-like body and seven lights, each of a different colour. Throckmartin identifies the creature as the Dweller in the Moon Pool, claiming that it took his wife and assistants, and removes his shirt to reveal an area of his skin where the being has touched him. The skin in that area has turned pearl-white, cold, insensible to touch, and impervious to being burned by a cigarette. He tells Goodwin that the Moon Pool is located under Nan-Matal, accessible through a passage that only opens when the moon light shines over it. He plans to go back to rescue his wife and the others, but before he can do so, Goodwin witnesses the Dweller abducting Throckmartin.

Goodwin embarks on a ship to Nan-Matal in hopes of rescuing his friend. On the way, he comes across a derelict vessel with a single occupant, a Norwegian sailor named Olaf Huldricksson, whose wife and daughter were also taken by the Dweller. Soon afterwards, they locate a wrecked hydro-airplane and rescue its pilot, Lt. Larry O'Keefe, an eccentric Irishman who believes in mythical creatures, only as long as they're from Ireland.

In Nan-Matal, Goodwin, Huldricksson and O'Keefe find the entrance to the underground world that Throckmartin had described, and come across a Russian scientist named Marakinoff, who attacks them at first, but later proposes to join forces with them in exploring the tunnels. At last, the four come to a subterranean nation called Muria, a beautiful land filled with marvelous technology, but inhabited by an oppressed population that lives in fear of its god, the Dweller, who regularly demands sacrifices and keeps its victims alive in a zombified state. Muria is ruled by a council presided by Yolara, the high-priestess of the Dweller, and a man named Lugur, identified as the Dweller's "voice". Beyond Muria there is another land, inhabited by a friendly race of female frog-like creatures called the Akka, and ruled by a trio of benevolent beings called the Silent Ones, whose handmaiden is a young woman named Lakla. shortDefinition: "The Moon Bog" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in or before March 1921 and first published in the June 1926 issue of Weird Tales.  The story was written to order, as an after-supper "shocker" for a Hub Club...
fullContent:
"The Moon Bog" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in or before March 1921 and first published in the June 1926 issue of Weird Tales.

The story was written to order, as an after-supper "shocker" for a Hub Club gathering of amateur journalists in Boston on March 10, 1921. The meeting had a St. Patrick's Day theme. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

The unnamed narrator describes the final fate of his good friend, Denys Barry, an Irish-American who reclaims an ancestral estate in Kilderry, a fictional town in Ireland. Barry ignores pleas from the local peasantry not to drain the nearby bog, with unfortunate supernatural consequences. The story bears a similarity to Lord Dunsany's first Irish novel The Curse of the Wise Woman in theme, showing the influence of Dunsany on Lovecraft's works.

Like Barry, Lovecraft had dreams of buying back his ancestors' home in England. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) This same theme is treated with greater depth in Lovecraft's "The Rats in the Walls" (1923).

"The Moon-Bog" is described by S. T. Joshi and David E. Schultz as "one of the most conventionally supernatural in HPL's oeuvre." (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

shortDefinition: The Mound is a horror and sci-fi novella that H. P. Lovecraft wrote as a ghostwriter from December 1929 to January 1930 after he was hired by Zealia Bishop to create a story based on the following plot synopsis:  "There is an Indian mound near here, ...
fullContent:
The Mound is a horror and sci-fi novella that H. P. Lovecraft wrote as a ghostwriter from December 1929 to January 1930 after he was hired by Zealia Bishop to create a story based on the following plot synopsis:

"There is an Indian mound near here, which is haunted by a headless ghost. Sometimes it is a woman."

Lovecraft did not like this premise of what seemed to be a conventional ghost story. The outline was so brief it allowed for a great deal of license, so he made it into a 29,560 word story about a mound that conceals a gateway to a subterranean civilization, the realm of K'n-yan, which one of the main characters enters and lives in for a while. The story is one of only three by Lovecraft where a non-human culture is described in rich details, the other two being At the Mountains of Madness and The Shadow Out of Time. It is not as well known as the later two, as it was ghostwritten for another author, but is considered to possess the same high level of quality and imagination.I found Lovecraft diffident but very gallant, with a gallantry of an era we only read about in mid-Victorian literature. In our conversation we discusses among things my short novel, “The Mound”—an outgrowth of another tale told by the Comptons from their recollections of two old Indians living near Binger, Oklahoma […]

—Zealia Bishop, “H. P. Lovecraft: A Pupil’s View” in Ave Atque Vale 259

The mound in the story is located in Binger in Caddo County, which unlike the fictional towns and locations in the majority of his works is a real town about 60 miles (100 km) southwest of Oklahoma City. He places the mound about a third of a mile west of Binger, an area where there are no mounds, which seems to make this geographic detail the only fictional part of its location. However the real-life mounds in that region were subject not only of contemporary retelling of folklore by Native Americans such as those spoken to by friends of Zealia Bishop but were also the site of truly Lovecraftian discoveries during contemporary excavations. It was a natural subject for treatment in such a story even if the mundane reality fell short of the fantastical elements in the collaborative story.

There are several mounds in the area, but not as described in the story. One of them is called the Ghost Mound and according to a local legend is haunted by ghosts. It is located closer to Hydro, rather than Binger. It does not look like how Lovecraft described it, and is a natural formation. This is most likely the mound that inspired Zealia Bishop to present her story idea to Lovecraft. It is possible a second nearby mound, known as Dead Woman Mound, may also have inspired her. Unlike the first, there is no ghost story connected with it, though it gained its name when the buried body of a dead woman was found there.

"The Murder at the Motel" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Brian M. Sammons.

### Synopsis
Grigory the sorcerer, who has cheated death for many years, is pursued by creatures who wish to restore the balance of life. In order to buy himself a few more years of existence, he tricks stage magician Dennis into becoming a sacrifice in his stead. Dennis, however, proves to be surprisingly resourceful: he succeeds in breaking the enchantment protecting Grigory, and the wizard is dragged off by the beings.

### Characters
* Dennis/The Amazing Kraygen, a failing stage magician out on the road.
* Grigory/The Astounding Radu, and ancient sorcerer unwilling to give up his grip on life.

### Publication History
"The Murder at the Motel" was published in the Wildside Press collection The Dark Rites of Cthulhu in February 2019, which Sammons also edited.

### Trivia
* One of the books which Grigory uses to practice his magic is the Cultus Maleficarum; his spells also invoke the Outer God Yog-Sothoth.
