fullContent:
"The Music of Erich Zann" is a short story by American author H. P. Lovecraft. Written in December 1921, it was first published in The National Amateur, March 1922.

### Synopsis
 for Weird Tales.]]
A university student is forced, by his lack of funds, to take the only lodging he can afford. In a strange part of the city he had never seen before, on a street named "Rue d'Auseil", he finds an apartment in an almost empty building. One of the few other tenants is an old German man named Erich Zann. The old man is a mute cellist (: Selected Letters 3.503) with a local orchestra. He lives on the top floor and when alone at night, plays strange melodies never heard before. Over time, the student gains Zann's trust, and eventually learns of his secret, that the old man has discovered melodies and rhythms of sound of an almost otherworldly nature. Zann plays these sounds to keep back unknown and unseen creatures from Zann's window, which is said to look out into a black abyss, most likely another dimension. One night, Zann's music reaches a crescendo, and the student, staring out the window in hopes of seeing the normal world outside, instead stares into an infinite abyss. The window shatters, and an unnatural wind sweeps through the room, carrying away all of Zann's music notes into the darkness, despite the student's attempts at catching them. Fleeing the house after he finds Zann seemingly dead despite his body still playing the cello, the student escapes not just the house but the neighborhood entirely. Years later, he writes down his accounts, and tells that he has never been able to find Rue d'Auseil again, as it does not appear on any maps, and no one else seem ever have heard of it.

### Setting
 (H. P. Lovecraft's Haunt of Horror)]]
The setting of the story is presumably Paris, though the city is never named. "Auseil" is not a true French word, but it has been suggested that Lovecraft derived it from the phrase "au seuil," meaning "at the threshold." (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) Auseil is read like "oseille," meaning sorrel or, colloquially, money.

### Reaction
Lovecraft considered "The Music of Erich Zann" one of his best stories, in part because it avoided the overexplicitness that he saw as a major flaw in some of his other work.

An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia notes that it "might, however, be said that HPL erred on the side of underexplicitness in the very nebulous horror to be seen through Zann's garret window."

The story was frequently anthologized even during Lovecraft's lifetime, including in Dashiell Hammett's 1931 collection Creeps by Night. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

Ramsey Campbell has stated that "The Music of Erich Zann" was "the single Lovecraft story that the late Robert Aickman liked".

### Influence
### Literature
*James Wade wrote a sequel to the story, "The Silence of Erika Zann", first published in The Disciples of Cthulhu (1976).
*In Charles Stross's The Laundry Files novels series including The Jennif

The Music of Erich Zann is a comic book-format adaptation of the H. P. Lovecraft short story of the same name, by Canadian artist Nick O'Gorman. It was published through his independent label Target Destroyed Comics in 2021 after obtaining funding through a successful Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign .

The book was later included in the omnibus collection HPL Vol. 1: Comic Adaptations of the Works of HP Lovecraft, also published by Target Destroyed.

### Trivia
*Significantly, the adaptation of "The Music of Erich Zann" has been changed to feature a black protagonist, something unlikely to have ever been written by Lovecraft himself.

fullContent:
"The Mystery of the Grave-Yard, or "A Dead Man's Revenge": A Detective Story" is a short story by American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Written when he was only 8 years old, it forms part of his juvinilia.

### Synopsis
The story concerns the kidnapping of a man by a group of ne'er-do-wells and the thwarting of their plot by King John, a renowned western detective. The titular mystery in the grave-yard refers to a family tomb with a hidden room in which the abductee was held captive.

### Publication History
"The Mystery of the Grave Yard" was first published in The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces in 1959, and has seen inclusion in a number of publications in the years since.

### Trivia

* Despite being labelled as a detective story, King John does no actual detective work, his modus operandi being to make his appearance at the most fortuitous time with guns in hand. This can likely be attributed to Lovecraft’s age when writing the tale.

fullContent:
"The Mystery of the Worm" is a sci-fi mystery short story by John Pelan which serves as a three-way crossover between the Cthulhu Mythos, the Sherlock Holmes series by Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, and the Dr. Nikola series by Guy Boothby. It was first published in the 2003 anthology Shadows Over Baker Street.

### Synopsis
In 1894, Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson are visited by a man claiming to be Robert Beech, an entomologist, who asks the detective's opinion about three unusual items he found in Egypt. The first is a metallic cylinder covered in strange inscriptions, the second a star-shaped stone, and the third a vial containing a preserved worm-like creature. The animal resembles a centipede, although with fewer legs, and has a sort of proboscis surrounded by a pair of strong mandibles. Holmes notices several details about the man's appearance which prove that he isn't who he claims to be, and outs him as a fraud. A few minutes later, another man comes in, who introduces himself as Dr. Nikola. He has the eyes of a mesmerist, a black cat perched on his shoulder, and no modesty at all, outright describing himself as the world's greatest intellect.

Nikola explains that the man who claimed to be Beech is actually Persano, one of Nikola's assistants (the one whose aspect is "the least likely to cause alarm"), sent on the doctor's orders to test Holmes' skill. Despite looking no older than 35, Dr. Nikola is well over a hundred years old. His longevity is due to having once sampled an elixir offered to him by a Chinese man, the formula of which Nikola has been trying to replicate ever since. His ultimate goal is to use his eternal life and intellect to create a "perfect world" benefiting from all sciences, including the arcane ones.

So far, all Nikola has learned about the elixir is that it might be derived from the royal jelly of certain species of bees. However, his research has also led him to discover the ruins of the mythical City of Pillars in Egypt. Placed on top of each of the pillars was a metallic cylinder with a star-stone firmly bolted to it. At night, Nikola and Persano heard the sound of swarms of insects. Upon examining the site, they found that one of their bearers had removed the star-stone from one of the cylinders, which apparently summoned something from beyond the Earth. There was no trace left of the bearers, except for some suggestive red marks on the sand and the worm-like creature, which Nikola believes to be extraterrestrial.

After telling his story, Nikola makes his proposal: he believes that the aliens killed the bearers because the two sides couldn't communicate and the bearers might have attacked the aliens first. With a man of Holmes' deductive abilities, he believes dialogue might be established, and mankind would benefit from trade with a species advanced enough to cross the gulfs of space. Nikola wants to hire Holmes to help him in this experiment, which the detective cautiously agrees to.

shortDefinition: "The Nameless City" is a horror story written by H. P. Lovecraft in January 1921 and first published in the November 1921 issue of the amateur press journal The Wolverine. It is often considered the first Cthulhu Mythos story.  ### Inspiration Lovecr...
fullContent:
"The Nameless City" is a horror story written by H. P. Lovecraft in January 1921 and first published in the November 1921 issue of the amateur press journal The Wolverine. It is often considered the first Cthulhu Mythos story.

### Inspiration
Lovecraft said that the story was based on a dream, which was in turn inspired by the last line of Lord Dunsany's story "The Probable Adventure of the Three Literary Men", quoted in the story itself: "the unreverberate blackness of the abyss". (: Selected Letters I)

Another identified source is the 9th Edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica, whose description of "Irem, the City of Pillars" he copied into his commonplace book: "which yet, after the annihilation of its tenants, remains entire, so Arabs say, invisible to ordinary eyes, but occasionally, and at rare intervals, revealed to some heaven-favoured traveller." (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

Critic William Fulwiler argues that Edgar Rice Burroughs' At the Earth's Core was one of Lovecraft's primary inspirations for "The Nameless City", citing "the reptile race, the tunnel to the interior of the earth, and the 'hidden world of eternal day'" as elements common to both tales. More generally, Fulwiler suggests, the theme of "alien races more powerful and more intelligent than man", which recurs frequently in Lovecraft's writings, may derive from Burroughs' Pellucidar stories. However, both writers drew on an already existing and vast literature of "lost city" stories and novels.

### Synopsis
, which appeared in the November 1938 Weird Tales reprint.]]The Nameless City of the story's title is an ancient ruin located somewhere in the deserts of the Arabian Peninsula and is older than any human civilization.

In ancient times, the Nameless City was built and inhabited by an unnamed race of reptiles with a body shaped like a cross between a crocodile and a seal with a strange head common to neither, involving a protruding forehead, horns, lack of a nose and an alligator-like jaw. These beings moved by crawling; thus, the architecture of the city has very low ceilings and some places are too low for a human being to stand upright. Their city was originally coastal, but when the seas receded it was left in the depths of a desert. This resulted in the decline and eventual ruin of the city.

The protagonist of "The Nameless City" states:



Indeed, the reptilians still maintain some form of life in a vast, luminous paradise in a cavern beneath the Nameless City, preserved and placed along the walls in a subterranean chamber. Also within this chamber are hieroglyphs and reliefs that tell to the protagonist the story of the city's heyday of prosperity and its fall, as well as their eventual hatred of humanity.

### Connections
The story contains the first mention of Abdul Alhazred, a fictional authority on the occult who would later be mentioned in most of Lovecraft's major Cthulhu Mythos stories, including "The Hound" (1922), "The Festival" (1923), "The C

shortDefinition: "The Nameless Offspring" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith that first appeared in the June 1932 issue of Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror. It begins with a quote from the Necronomicon--about "that spawn which the hidden dweller in the vaults ...
fullContent:
"The Nameless Offspring" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith that first appeared in the June 1932 issue of Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror. It begins with a quote from the Necronomicon--about "that spawn which the hidden dweller in the vaults has begotten upon mortality"--identifying the story as belonging to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Characters
*Henry Chaldane: The story's narrator. Born in England, he was taken to Canada as an infant. He returns to take a "motorcycle tour of the English counties" in order "to execute a long-cherished dream of visiting [his] natal land and exploring its rural by-ways." He ends up at Tremoth Hall, home of his father's childhood friend, by coincidence.
*Arthur Chaldane: A schoolmate of Sir John Tremoth, he moves to Manitoba, Canada, to become a beekeeper. He dies some years before the story begins.
*Sir John Tremoth: The master of Tremoth Hall. He is "scarcely beyond middle life," but his "cadaverous pallor and feeble tottering walk were those of a man who is stricken with some fatal malady."
*Lady Agatha Tremoth: Within a year of marrying Sir John, she becomes "the victim of cataleptic seizures," and the third such attack apparently kills her. She is placed in the family vaults, but is discovered alive in her open coffin, with "recollections of a pale, hideous, unhuman face...stooping over her." The creature was "large and white, and ran like an animal on all fours, though its limbs were semihuman." Nine months later, she dies after giving birth to a monstrous child.
*The Unnamed Monstrosity: The child of Lady Agatha and her tomb assailant, he is identified as a "corpse-devouring demon of Oriental tales and legends…the ghoul." He is described as "a huge, whitish, hairless and semi-quadruped body, of canine teeth in a half-human face, and long hyena nails at the end of forelimbs that were both arms and legs.
*Harper: Tremoth Hall's "only servant—a combination of valet, butler, housekeeper and chef." He has loyally looked after Sir John and his offspring for 28 years. He is described as an old man whose "fingers trembled with palsy or decrepitude."

### Inspiration
In a 1931 letter to H. P. Lovecraft outlining the plot of "The Nameless Offspring," Smith noted that he got the basic idea for the story from Arthur Machen's "The Great God Pan," which similarly deals with the offspring of a daemonic creature. 

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Strange Tales, "The Nameless Offspring" has been included in several collections of Smith's work, The Abominations of Yondo (Arkham House, 1960), The Emperor of Dreams (Gollancz/Orion, 2002), The Maker of Gargoyles and Other Stories (Wildside Press, 2004), A Vintage From Atlantis: Volume Three of the Collected Fantasies of Clark Ashton Smith (Night Shade Books, 2007), and The Klarkash-Ton Cycle: Clark Ashton Smith's Cthulhu Mythos Fiction (Chaosium, 2008). It is also available in The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (Wildside Press, 2012).

term: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket
shortDefinition: The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, published in 1838, is Edgar Allan Poe's only completed novel. A story of Antarctic exploration, Arthur Gordon Pym is considered a major influence on H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness.  The ...
fullContent:
The Narrative of Arthur Gordon Pym of Nantucket, published in 1838, is Edgar Allan Poe's only completed novel. A story of Antarctic exploration, Arthur Gordon Pym is considered a major influence on H. P. Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness.

The novel tells the story of Arthur Gordon Pym, a young man whose stowing away on a whaler ship leads to a series of increasingly bizarre adventures as he travels further and further south, involving storms, mutinies, shipwreck, cannibalism, and a ghost ship. Eventually he and his party come to an island called Tsalal in waters near the South Pole, with a mild climate despite the extreme latitude, where water is viscous and strangely colored. His companions are betrayed by the inhabitants, and he and the only other surviving crew member take refuge in an underground labyrinth with strange carvings. Stealing a boat, Pym journeys even further south, into a milky white ocean. The narrative ends abruptly with the sighting of a gigantic hooded figure appearing in a gap in a mysterious mist.

The phrase "tekeli-li" reoccurs in the novel, first as a phrase of the inhabitants of Tsalal that they shout with "the strangest expressions of mingled horror, rage, and intense curiosity." At the very end of Pym's narrative, it's heard from the "gigantic and pallidly white birds [who] flew continuously" from beyond the wall of mist.

### At the Mountains of Madness
Lovecraft's story tips a hat to Poe when the character of Danforth is described as "a great reader of bizarre material" who "had talked a good deal of Poe." The narrator William Dyer says he is interested in Poe "because of the antarctic scene of Poe’s only long story—the disturbing and enigmatical Arthur Gordon Pym."

Poe's novel is mentioned again when Dyer and Danforth hear a mysterious sound:Of course common reading is what prepared us both to make the interpretation, though Danforth has hinted at queer notions about unsuspected and forbidden sources to which Poe may have had access when writing his Arthur Gordon Pym a century ago. It will be remembered that in that fantastic tale there is a word of unknown but terrible and prodigious significance connected with the antarctic and screamed eternally by the gigantic, spectrally snowy birds of that malign region’s core. “Tekeli-li! Tekeli-li!” That, I may admit, is exactly what we thought we heard conveyed by that sudden sound behind the advancing white mist—that insidious musical piping over a singularly wide range.

fullContent:
The National Amateur was for many years the official organ and regularly published magazine of the National Amateur Press Association (NAPA). Although now superseded by online resources for NAPA such as its official website and Facebook presence, The National Amateur was published for over a century. 

Celebrating the enduring legacy of H. P. Lovecraft as an enthusiastic amateur press participant from adolescence to his death, the June 1971 edition of The National Amateur featured an article entitled "Lovecraft Lives!".

fullContent:
"The Nature of Water" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Tim Waggoner.

### Synopsis
When 12 year old Mark throws an annoying child into the lake at their vacation spot, the boy fails to come back up again. Although nobody discovers what Mark has done, he is wracked with guilt for years to come.

Thirty years later Mark, still haunted by his childhood misdeed, returns to the lake in hopes of making some sort of peace. The young boy appears and grants Mark forgiveness, telling him of the wondrous society beneath the surface which he has since become a part of under the patronage of Gla'aki. Mark surrenders himself to the dark waters, and becomes a disciple of the creature which dwells there.

### Characters
* Mark Sutton, a middle-aged alcoholic in search of redemption.
* Dustin Page, a child prodigy and later cultist of Gla'aki.

### Publication History
"The Nature of Water" was published in the Dark Regions Press thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki in 2017.

term: The Necronomnomnom: Recipes and Rites from the Lore of H. P. Lovecraft
shortDefinition: The Necronomnomnom (full title The Necronomnomnom: Recipes and Rites from the Lore of H. P. Lovecraft) is a humorous horror fiction recipe book based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. The book is published by The Countryman Press, copyrighted by R...
fullContent:
The Necronomnomnom (full title The Necronomnomnom: Recipes and Rites from the Lore of H. P. Lovecraft) is a humorous horror fiction recipe book based on H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos. The book is published by The Countryman Press, copyrighted by Red Duke Games, LLC and illustrated by Kurt Komoda. The illustrated edition was first published on 1 October, 2019 and is available in Hardcover and Kindle.

### Setting
Similarly to the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game, the Necronomnomnom appears to be set in the world of the Cthulhu Mythos. The tome itself is presented as a modern translation of ancient rites and rituals decoded from an older unnamed codex.

### Main Body
The first part is broken into eight sections: Drinks, Appetizers, Soups and Salads, Main Dishes, Sides, Breakfast, Children's Meals, and Desserts. 

Within this section, the recipes are written in-world with accompanying illustrations. Various recipes are presented in the format of either a spell, a play (wherein ingredients are dubbed cast), the text of an investigation, or even part of a short story or fictionalized account each having been collected together and bound in the original codex.

### Appendix
The second part is the Appendix where the recipes are rewritten with the fictionalized versions presented in real world instructions.

### Design
The main design of the Necronomnomnom is presented in a parody, using fictional cooking humor to offer real-world recipes that can be made and enjoyed. The text presents the ingredients and the "rituals" involved in an embellished format as one would uncover them in the fictional Mythos world, with odd ingredients substituted for mundane real world items, and odd rituals substituted for everyday directions.

Examples of such ingredients include:
*"half-cup of the White Ichor of Hellman" which references Hellman's Mayonnaise 
*"two tablespoons mixture from the Ranch hidden in the Valley" referencing Hidden Valley Ranch dressing
*"one large egg of the fowl of the wood as Sadogui doth favor" referencing one large chicken egg
*"Wedges of the Citrus in Yellow are always welcome" for the optional use of lemon wedges

Examples of the rituals involved:
*"Lobotomize the fungi by removing their stems" meaning removing the stems from the mushrooms
*"Preheat the kiln to 425 degrees" meaning preheat your oven to 425
*"Serve with space mead for a pleasant journey." instructing the food be served with a specific drink
*"Rend cheese artfully to remove corners (always beware the corners)" referencing a Hound of Tindalos

Recipe titles will also often have parodies based in lore of the Mythos, such as
*"The Mounds of Tindalos"
*"The Cake in Yellow"
*"Great Old Buns"
*"The Custard Out of Space"

### See Also
*Lovecraft Cocktails: Elixirs & Libations from the Lore of H. P. Lovecraft

### Synopsis
In order to survive, a man living in a hellish future tries to barter with the creatures which now rule the world. Unfortunately, they see through his attempt to trick them with a dishonest trade, and the beings descend on him in a savage fury.

fullContent:
"The Nest of Pain" is a short story written by American author C. J. Henderson. It is the third in the Arkham Detective Agency series, and is a direct continuation of the first story "The Idea of Fear."

### Synopsis
When one of the owners of the house investigated by the Arkham Detective Agency in the first story begs him to take another look at their property, Frank Nardi uncovers the immortal evil lurking in its walls. Using all of the cunning at his disposal, he is able to destroy both the entity and the means by which it has survived the centuries.

### Characters
*Frank Nardi, a private investigator with a speciality in paranormal affairs.
*Mark Berkenwald, one of Frank's partners in the Arkham Detective Agency.
*Edward and Julie Douglas, the young owners of the sinister house, and victims of its vampiric needs.
*Madame Renee, a psychic on retainer for the Arkham Detective Agency.
*Galtoni, another of Frank's partners.
*Jedidiah Mortonson, an immortal psychic vampire and the story's antagonist.

### Publication History
*"The Nest of Pain" was written by C. J. Henderson prior to his death in 2014. It was first published in the collection Arkham Detective Agency by Dark Regions Press in 2017, and has since also received an ebook issue.

### Mythos References
*The story is set in the fictional town of Arkham created by H. P. Lovecraft.

fullContent:
"The Night Music of Oakdeene" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Joseph S. Pulver, Sr.

### Synopsis
Nick Garrett, a man with a dark past, is a security guard at Oakdeene Sanitarium. After coming across an old scrap of paper covered with strange phrases, he discovers that one of the words drives his hated charges insane. Deciding that the incarcerated deviants should suffer a little for their crimes, he records the word on a repeating cassette and plays it over and over. Unfortunately for Nick, this causes the inmates to begin a chorus which summons a black entity which needs to feed.

### Characters

*Nick "Quick Nick" Garrett, night-shift security at Oakdeene
*Martin Spellman, a guard-turned-inmate at Oakdeene
*Yibb-Tstll, The Patient One, an Outer God

### Publication History
Although it was written in May 1985, "The Night Music of Oakdeene" was not published until May 1998 when it appeared in short-lived Mythos magazine Al-Azif #3. In December 1999 it appeared in the online magazine Nightscapes. It was later included in the John B. Ford/Steve Lines anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos: Cthulhu's Creatures, and again in Pulver's own collection Blood Will Have Its Season.

### Trivia

*In Nightscapes "The Night Music of Oakdeene" carried the following dedication "For Brian Lumley -  Whose rich songs carry us to all to the strange lands of night." British author Brian Lumley wrote the short story "The Horror at Oakdeene."

fullContent:
The Night Ocean by R. H. Barlow with H. P. Lovecraft is a short story first published in The Californian vol. 4, no. 3 (Winter 1936).

Possibly able to be considered a prose poem rather than a conventional short story, this very short tale is about a man who spends most of a year at a small coastal town. A series of deaths occurs, disappearances of swimmers including those strong and skilled enough for such deaths to be most unlikely. During a mighty storm the unnamed narrator see humanoid but inhuman figures emerging on the deserted beach. After the storm, when the beach has been cleansed by the waves, he finds a decaying human hand and realises that the sea creatures, ghosts, sea ghouls or whatever they may be- are indeed destroying swimmers.

With a progressive melancholy the narrator watches the seasons pass until on the night of a preternatural full moon he sees the strange figures emerge again and is unsure if they are dogs, humans or diseased fish- but they are inhuman.

The Night of Dagon is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author Brandon Berntson, the first in his Lovecraft Mysteries series of supernatural detective books. It was independently published in June 2018, with both paperback and digital editions receiving a release.

### Synopsis
After taking on a job to steal an artefact with magical powers, private investigator Devlin Macky finds himself embroiled in a plot to summon forth the voracious Great Old One Dagon. Macky must find a way to thwart the evil sorcerer Mordred Haddonfield to save the town of Innsport and, maybe, the entire world.

### Plot
### Chapter 1
Innsport private detective Devlin Macky meets Mordred Haddonfield, a wealthy recluse with an interest in ancient artefacts. Haddonfield hires him to retrieve the Silver Bluebell, which he claims was stolen from him by museum curator Creighton Capshaw. Despite some police attention, Macky is successful, and hands the Bluebell over to his client.

### Chapter 2
Macky's secretary and love interest Millie Von Clydesburgh is introduced, police officers Givens and Bardhoff question him about the previous night's robbery at the museum, and he accepts the case of Mrs. Gloria Trelane, whose husband never returned home from work the evening before.

### Chapter 3
Haddonfield and his servant Borgas sacrifice the captive Casper Trelane to the monstrous Dagon.

### Chapter 4
Macky begins his investigation into the missing Casper Trelane, and eventually a stroke of luck sees him find a witness to the man's abduction. Deducing that the kidnapper was Borgas, he makes the resolution to investigate his sinister former client more thoroughly.

### Chapter 5
As the investigation progresses, Macky questions Haddonfield, his daughter Vivian, and Borgas. Although they give nothing away, he realises that they are lying about their involvement with the disappearance of Casper Trelane.

### Chapter 6
Sneaking on to Haddonfield's coastal estate, Macky discovers Dagon's sacrificial site, evidence that Trelane had been there, and the tracks of something hungry and terrible crawling from the ocean. Later, he interviews museum curator, a man named Creighton Capshaw, and the two form a pact, agreeing that they must put a stop to Haddonfield and Dagon.

### Chapter 7
Returning to his office, Macky and Millie share a personal moment and a kiss before the police arrive with more questions. Macky tells them everything he has discovered, and asks them to continue looking into Haddonfield and his scheme in his stead, as he believes that the authorities will be able to accomplish more with the cultists than he can alone.

### Chapter 8
Macky makes his way to Innsport's Shady District, a run-down slum, where he tracks down Bradley "Boom-boom" Denton, an old colleague and explosives expert, from whom he procures some dynamite with which to combat the awakening Dagon. He also learns that Boom-boom, in his pyromaniacal insanity, has rigged explosives across much of the city, hiding th

shortDefinition: "The Night Sea-Maid Went Down" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Brian Lumley, first published in his Arkham House collection The Caller of the Black, in 1971.  Along with "Cement Surroundings", it is one of the two stories that Lumley later incorpo...
fullContent:
"The Night Sea-Maid Went Down" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Brian Lumley, first published in his Arkham House collection The Caller of the Black, in 1971.

Along with "Cement Surroundings", it is one of the two stories that Lumley later incorporated into his 1974 novel The Burrowers Beneath.

### Synopsis
The story is told in the form of a letter from Bernard Jordan, nicknamed "Pongo", to his boss, explaining why he decided to quit the prospecting business after the sinking of the oil rig Sea-Maid in the North Sea.

About two months before that disaster, the Sea-Maid had retrieved a number of star-shaped stones buried in the sea floor, and Jordan recognized them as the same uncovered by another platform that had been mysteriously lost in a "freak storm".

One of the Sea-Maids crew, a superstitious man named Joe Borszowski, becomes extremely agitated at the sight of the five-pointed star-stones, the nature of which the geologist, Carson, is unable to identify. Jordan also notices that the rig is enclosed in mist and the fish are inexplicably aggressive, attacking fishermen and divers.

Borszowski quits the job and explains that there are monstrous gods imprisoned under the sea floor, able to control the weather and the minds of animals, and that the five-pointed star-stones are the seals that keep them imprisoned. He worries that the removal of the star-stones might set one of these creatures free. After he leaves, a thick fog emanates from the ocean, cutting off visibility. A worker falls into the sea and is heard screaming in agony, but the others are unable to locate him.

On the next day, as soon as the drill reaches what is assumed to be the oil deposit, the rig is caught in the middle of a storm and destroyed by a seaquake. Jordan is the only survivor, and sees something that convinces him that Borszowski's claims were true: the liquid jet emerging from the perforation site is not black as an oil blowout, but blood-red, as if the drill had perforated the hide of a colossal creature.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Caller of the Black, "The Night Sea-Maid Went Down" was included in Lumley's collection of Mythos short stories, Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008). It was also reprinted in Sea-Cursed: Thirty Terrifying Tales of the Deep (Barnes & Noble Books, 1994), The Starry Wisdom: A Tribute to H. P. Lovecraft (Creation Books, 1995), and Brighton Shock! (PS Publishing, 2010).

A French translation appeared under the title "La nuit où la Sea-Maid fut engloutie," in a French edition of Lumley's stories, Compartiment terreur (Néo, 1989).

"The Nightmare In Delapore Tower" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. It takes a clear cue from H. P. Lovecraft's "The Rats in the Walls".

### Synopsis
A writer checks in to a high-rise hotel in order to finish his latest novel. While there, he discovers a dark secret on the thirteenth floor: the Delapores have been kidnapping people and eating their flesh, an act which extends their lives and allows them control over the countless rats which secretly inhabit the tower. Although the evil Lisa sends the rats to kill the writer her kindly yet mentally-deficient brother is able to turn the tables on her and save the man's life.

### Characters
*The unnamed narrator, a man who writes novels in his spare time.
*Lisa Delapore, a centuries old scion of the Delapore family.
*Hector Delapore, Lisa's brother.

### Publication History
"The Nightmare In Delapore Tower" was published in Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

### Trivia
*Hector Delapore at one point states that he has a copy of the Necronomicon, and that if his sister found out she would use it to open a gateway and summon forth Yog-Sothoth, although it is never explained why she would wish to do this.

term: The Novel of the Black Seal
shortDefinition: "The Novel of the Black Seal" is a horror story by Arthur Machen, part of his 1895 novel The Three Imposters. In its account of a hidden society of malevolent "Little People", the survivors of ancient days, the story influenced Lovecraft stories like...
fullContent:
"The Novel of the Black Seal" is a horror story by Arthur Machen, part of his 1895 novel The Three Imposters. In its account of a hidden society of malevolent "Little People", the survivors of ancient days, the story influenced Lovecraft stories like "The Call of Cthulhu", "The Dunwich Horror",  "The Whisperer in Darkness", and "The Lurking Fear". Lovecraft wrote in "Supernatural Horror in Literature" that "Black Seal", along with "The Novel of the White Powder" (also part of the same book), "perhaps represent the high-water mark of Machen’s skill as a terror-weaver".

### Characters
*William Gregg, an authority on ethnology who lives in England near the Welsh border. He disappears after investigating the Little People.
*Jervase Cradock, a simple-minded boy who works for Gregg; his father was one of the Little People.
*Miss Lally, who works for Gregg as a governess; she is the narrator of much of the story.

### Behind the Mythos
Although "The Novel of the Black Seal" has often been published as a short story, it actually originates as a chapter of Machen's novel The Three Impostors. Within the context of the novel, the story's protagonist and narrator, Miss Lally, is merely one of the personas assumed by one of the titular tricksters. While this might lead the reader to question the veracity of the events narrated, it should be noted that the character William Gregg is indisputably real in-universe, as is his mysterious disappearance.

Central elements from "The Novel of the Black Seal" are echoed in H. P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness and Robert E. Howard's "Worms of the Earth". All three stories concern a species that inspired the folkloric Little People, and associated with a mysterious black stone inscribed with unknown symbols. Lovecraft's story mentions Machen by name, as does Howard's "The Children of the Night", which deals with the same species. The Little People and their black stone return in Howard's "People of the Dark" as well.

In Machen's story, the black stone is known as Ixaxar, a.k.a. Ishakshar or the Sixtystone. Henry Kuttner referenced it by these names in his Cthulhu Mythos stories "The Hunt" and "Hydra", respectively.

The character Jervase Cradock is similar to Wilbur Whateley from Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror" as well as Helen Vaughan from Machen's own The Great God Pan: all three were born from human mothers who were impregnated by non-human creatures, and as a result are only superficially human.

"The Nyarlathotep Event" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Jonathan Wood. It was published in the Ross E. Lockhart-edited anthology The Book of Cthulhu II by Night Shade Press in October 2012.

### Synopsis
A secret agent from the British government's shadowy MI37 tackles the supernatural threat of Nyarlathotep in the midst of the busy metropolis of London. Unfortunately, he has underestimated the power which the Outer God has brought to bear, and what started as a simple assassination attempt turns into a running battle with a horde of cultists through the streets of Oxford and, eventually, into the realm of chaos. Luckily for the fate of the human race, the agent realises that the only way to defeat Nyarlathotep is to show no fear, and a global catastrophe is averted.

shortDefinition: The Old One is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by prolific British author John Glasby. It was first published in the Michaelmas 1989 edition of Robert M. Price's long-running Lovecraftian fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu.   ### Synopsis An associate professor o...
fullContent:
The Old One is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by prolific British author John Glasby. It was first published in the Michaelmas 1989 edition of Robert M. Price's long-running Lovecraftian fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu. 

### Synopsis
An associate professor of archaeology named Sheldon, who has an interest in the unconventional theory that intelligent races inhabited the earth long before the coming of man, researches this topic in his spare time. Coming across an old volume in an antique book shop which alludes to his interest, he uncovers references to an ancient city named Yuth which may be located somewhere near the Bimini Islands in the Bahamas but, knowing that his peers will make a mockery of him should he share this information, decides to keep it to himself.

Later, Sheldon's university decides to mount an expedition to the Bimini Islands to study the work already taking place there. They equip two boats - one carrying a bathysphere and several sets of diving gear - with Sheldon, his superior Professor Dorman and two others named Conlon and Brown comprising the research team.

Upon arrival at North Bimini, the group decide that as there is already considerable work being done by other researchers, they will look outside of their immediate area. Travelling thirty miles north, they deploy the bathysphere, discovering a vast ruined city off the edge of the shelf, later confirmed by Sheldon to be Yuth. Observing a strange red glow in the far reaches of the city, they decide that the easiest way to investigate this would be by diving suit.

Sheldon, Dorman and Brown descend to the city, and as Dorman enters the building which is emitting the glow the city begins to tremble. Dorman is grasped by a long tentacle attached to a “lumbering, amorphous bulk” and dragged down into the depths, while the other two flee to the surface, Brown's mind completely shattered by the sight.

### Characters
*Professor Sheldon, an associate professor of archaeology at a small unnamed university who has an interest in the theory of intelligent life on Earth before the evolution of mankind.
*Professor Dormer, Sheldon's superior. He was dragged off by a submarine monstrosity, likely Tsathoggua.
*Simon Haworth, a wealthy heir in possession of letters to his grandfather concerning the existence of a city named Yuth.
*Jethro Haworth, a man with an interest in the city of Yuth. He is only present in the story through references and the letters read by Sheldon.
*Conlon, a senior university professor of archaeology.
*Brown, a senior university professor of archaeology. His mind snapped when he viewed the entity in Yuth.

### Publication History
*Crypt of Cthulhu Michaelmas 1989 (1989)
*The Tsathoggua Cycle (2005)
*The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (2012)
*Beyond the Rim and Other Tales of Cosmic Horror (2015)

### Continuity
*The lost continent of Atlantis is mentioned several times.
*The Great Old One Tsathoggua is spoken of, and is all but outright stated to be the entity encountered

"The Old One" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Milos Radovic. It was published in the Candlemas edition (Vol 3, Issue 4) of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in January 2019.

### Synopsis
After an up-and-coming young lawyer named Dylan is assigned a missing persons case from his enigmatic boss Mr. Smithson, he finds himself drawn into a world of bizarre fishmen (which he dubs "Water Dwellers") and ancient gods. Researching the missing man, a scholar named Darian Ashton, he begins to draw disturbing parallels between Ashton's experiences and his own.

After finding himself pursued by hordes of Water Dwellers, Dylan once again encounters Smithson, who takes him to a mysterious island filled with the ruins of ancient buildings. Making his way beneath the ruins, he uncovers a temple to the water deity Ygallo, and embraces his previously-unsuspected heritage, becoming one of the fish-people and joining his dark god beneath the waves.

### Behind the Mythos
The story draws direct parallels with H. P. Lovecraft's iconic novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth, with the Water Dwellers being analogous to the Deep Ones and Ygallo to either Dagon, Mother Hydra, or Cthulhu. Indeed, Ygallo is depicted in carvings as possessing "[a] squid-like head with silver eyes with banded tentacles and bat-like wings," a description which is very close to that of Cthulhu. 

### Trivia
* At one point, Dylan reflects on the views of H. P. Lovecraft and his philosophy of cosmicism, indicating that in this universe Lovecraft (and presumably his works) exist.

The One is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft in the short story "The Strange High House in the Mist". He is a mysterious hermit who has dealings with mysterious supernatural forces.

The One lives in the titular Strange High House, an "abnormally antique grey cottage in the sky" atop a crag overlooking Kingsport. He is never seen or heard from by anyone in the town, but "people say One dwells therein who talks with the morning mists that come up from the deep, and perhaps sees singular things oceanward at those times when the cliff’s rim becomes the rim of all earth." The universal Kingsport opinion is that "the same One has lived in the ancient house for hundreds of years"--at least since the time "when Belcher or Shirley or Pownall or Bernard was Governor of His Majesty’s Province of the Massachusetts-Bay", that is, between 1730 and 1769. They maintain that "he had communed with the mists of the sea and the clouds of the sky ever since there was any village to watch his taciturn dwelling from the plain below."

He is visited for the first time by Thomas Olney, a Rhode Island philosophy professor who dares to scale the precipice and is invited inside. He is greeted by 

The One tells Olney "tales of marvellous ancient things...rumours of old times and far places":  about "Kings of Atlantis" who battled "slippery blasphemies that wriggled out of rifts in ocean's floor"; about the "pillared and weedy temple of Poseidonis" and about the "Years of the Titans"; about the "other gods" who danced on Hatheg-Kla "in the stony desert near Ulthar, beyond the river Skai". 

The One bids Olney to be silent when an unwanted visitor comes to the door that opens onto a sheer drop. But he welcomes a visit from "all the dreams and memories of earth’s sunken Mighty Ones": "Trident-bearing Neptune", "sportive tritons and fantastic nereids", and "the grey and awful form of primal Nodens, Lord of the Great Abyss".

Olney returns to Kingsport, but leaves part of himself in the house with the One forever after: "old folk tell of pleasing voices heard singing there, and of laughter that swells with joys beyond earth’s joys; and say that at evening the little low windows are brighter than formerly,"

"The One That Got Away" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
Unaware that he is being watched from beneath the waters by a monstrous beast, fisherman Wade Herndon enjoys a quiet morning's relaxation. As the creature prepares to make the man it’s next meal, a surprise strike from a water moccasin triggers a series of unlikely events which end with the creature lying dead and Herndon celebrating the biggest catch of his life.

### Characters

* Wade Herndon, an average Joe out on a fishing trip.
* Edward Marsh, a Deep One hybrid from Innsmouth who owns the local bait shop, Ed's Beer and Bait, and preys on visitors who will not be missed.
* Lewis Marsh, Ed's fully-transformed Deep One cousin which inhabits the Big Moccasin River.

### Publication History
"The One That Got Away" was first published in the Winter 2000/2001 issue of Dark Legacy. It later appeared in Lovecraft's Disciples in February 2006, and was included in the collection of Shiflet's own work They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in 2018.

### Trivia

* "The One That Got Away" takes place in Tenoka, Texas, a frequent setting for the mythos works of Ron Shiflet.

fullContent:
The Open Cthulhu Mythos is a supplement for the Apocthulhu, Cthulhu Eternal, and Fhtagn Cthulhu Mythos roleplaying games. Designed by Frank Dudenhausen, Julia Knobloch, and Volker Rattel, it was published by Cthulhu Reborn in 2023.

### Overview
The book is an overall reference document designed as a play aid for Cthulhu Reborn's various Mythos-related games.

It is a System Reference Document (SRD) and released under an Open Game Licence (OGL) meaning that it is usable by anyone, whether basing their work on the games for which it was originally created or not. The only requirement when using an OGL source is that the OGL itself has to be included in whatever is published by whomever has chosen to make use of it. The OGL inclusion in such works in usually the final page(s) in the third part work. The SRD, as plain text with no artwork, is available for free on DriveThruRPG.

This SRD is based on the "d100" type systems but it is intended to be compatible with OSR (Old School Roleplaying, predominantly Dungeons and Dragons retroclones but including other 3d6 for stats / roll d20 for outcomes games).

Philosophically this is a competitor to the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game itself based on the Basic Roleplaying system common to Call of Cthulhu RPG, Runequest and related works.

The Open Cthulhu Mythos more or less completes the expansion of Mythos material to all the varieties of commonly used roleplaying game rules systems.

### Legal Clearance Considerations
A major objective of this publication is to provide a strict and strictly legal list of public domain works within the broader Mythos, thus providing a compilation of concepts, entities and items and so on that will definitely not require licensing or legal disclaimers.

Making use of relentless scholarship from the German Lovecraft Society, this SRD provides the only genuine and comprehensive list of ONLY public domain Mythos content.

### Design Team
* Written by: Frank Dudenhausen, Julia Knobloch, and Volker Rattel
* Production staff: Dean Engelhardt and Matt Wiseman

fullContent:
"The Opener of the Way" is a short story by Robert Bloch that appeared in the October 1936 issue of Weird Tales. It served as the title story of Bloch's first Arkham House collection, The Opener of the Way (1945). It is included in the third edition of his collection of Mythos fiction, Mysteries of the Worm (Chaosium, 2009).

### Synopsis
An embittered archeologist, Sir Ronald Barton, along with his son and assistant Peter Barton, finds a hidden tomb in Egypt. He is guided by a pilfered parchment written in Chaldean, which describes how to evade the tomb's elaborate curse. The last step involves projecting oneself into a strange statue of Anubis--which Sir Ronald is able to do, but he fails to heed the warning that this process will be deadly for nonbelievers.

### Characters
Sir Ronald Barton: A British archeologist who thirsts after power and wealth, he resents being a "poor man" after spending 20 years in Egypt toiling on other explorers' expeditions. Described as "a tall, thin man with a face as wrinkled as the papyrus parchment he clutched.... His white hair, sunken eyes and yellowed skin gave him the aspect of an old man." He had "dabbled in sorcery, a bit."

Peter Barton: A "younger replica" of his father, though his "voice was not nearly as loud or as firm". He "really loved his father," but is "more than a little afraid of Sir Ronald".

### Behind the Mythos
"The Opener of the Way" was not included in the first two editions of Mysteries of the Worm, reflecting its subtle connection to the Cthulhu Mythos. Referring to Sir Ronald's parchment and the Egyptian priest who wrote it, the story states: 

While in the parchment, the "names of these accursed ones were set forth", they are not specified in the story. The "Demon Messenger", however, is cited as a epithet of Nyarlathotep in Bloch's story "The Faceless God". (In "The Opener of the Way", Peter Barton recalls the "terrible rumors concerning the end of that unsavory adventurer, Doctor Carnoti"; "Carnoti" was the name of the protagonist in early versions of "The Faceless God", later changed to "Stugatche".)

There is one more explicit Mythos tie-in in the story, when Sir Ronald declares, "Now I know what Prinn must have meant in his chapter on the Saracenic rituals; the part where he spoke of the 'symbols on the gate'."

fullContent:
"The Orphanage at Trellaree" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Tony Richards, first published by Weird House Press in his 2022 anthology The Howling Terror and Other Lovecraftian Horror Stories.

### Synopsis
When jaded English doctor Bryant moves to the small Irish coastal town of Trellaree, he uncovers a bizarre secret hidden within the walls of the local orphanage: the director, a Dr. Ernst Zwiegler, has been raising the children of an unidentified species of oceanic humanoid, and using their blood in experiments to heal the ailments of the human race. The doctor's discovery prompts the staff - who are all involved in the project - and Zwiegler to join their kinfolk beneath the waves, transforming into the creatures themselves as they do so.

Many years later, and the doctor's health begins to fade, a degenerative nerve disease preventing him from continuing his practice. In desperation, he makes his way to the shore and begs for the beings to make him one of them and heal his degrading body. To his surprise, Zwiegler emerges from the ocean depths and grants his request, inducting Bryant into their ranks and granting him eternal life.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to the creations of H. P. Lovecraft, the accompanying artwork to "The Orphanage at Trellaree", a black-and-white painting by K. L. Turner, is titled "Orphanage Deep Ones", confirming the story to be set in the greater Cthulhu Mythos.

### Trivia
*Unusually for a Cthulhu Mythos story, "The Orphanage at Trellaree" would seem to portray the Deep Ones in a less-malevolent light than is the norm for such stories. However, the mention of the disappearance of several fishing boat crews may perhaps put a lie to this surface impression.

fullContent:
"The Other Gods" is a short story written by American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft on August 14, 1921. It was first published in the November 1933 issue of The Fantasy Fan.

### Synopsis
Barzai the Wise, a high priest and prophet greatly learned in the lore of the "gods of earth", or Great Ones, attempts to scale the mountain of Hatheg-Kla in order to look upon their faces, accompanied by his young disciple Atal. Upon reaching the peak, Barzai at first seems overjoyed until he finds that the "gods of the earth" are not there alone, but rather are overseen by the "other gods, the gods of the outer hells that guard the feeble gods of earth!" Atal flees and Barzai is never seen again.

### Characters
*Barzai the Wise - The high-priest of the Gods of Earth (the Great Ones) in Ulthar and one-time teacher of Atal. He often delved into the unknown, reading such works as the Pnakotic Manuscripts and the Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan. He is the son of an aristocrat, which makes him skeptical of commoners' superstitions. He is said to have advised the burgesses of Ulthar when they passed their ban on cat-slaying. He vanishes shortly after climbing to the top of Hatheg-Kla to see the gods revelling on its peak.
*Atal - The apprentice of Barzai the Wise who accompanies him on his doomed climb to the top of Mount Hatheg-Kla to see the gods.
*Sansu - An explorer who was described as being "written of with fright" in the Pnakotic Manuscripts, having once scaled the mountain of Hatheg-Kla "in the youth of the world" and found "naught but wordless ice and rock". He is the last person to have climbed the mountain before Barzai.

### Locations
*Hatheg-Kla - A "high and rocky" mountain in the "stony desert" thirteen days' walk from the village of Hatheg, for which it is named. It is one of the places where the "gods of earth" once dwelt and sometimes return to when they are homesick.
*Thurai - A white-capped  mountains where the gods of earth used to dwell. It is said that at Thurai men mistake the tears of the gods for rain.
*Lerion - Another mountain formerly inhabited by the gods where the "plaintive dawn-winds" are the in fact their eternal sighs. Lerion is later described as the source of the river Skai. (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)
*Ulthar - The hometown of the story's main characters, was introduced in the story "The Cats of Ulthar". It is said to lie "beyond the river Skai" and to be a neighbour of Hatheg.
*Hatheg and Mir - Neighbouring towns run by Burgesses.
*Kadath - The mountain to which the gods of earth retreated.

### Connections
The Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan (misprinted as "...of Earth" in the story's original publication) appear for the first time in "The Other Gods". The Pnakotic Manuscripts make their second appearance in "The Other Gods", having been introduced in "Polaris", along with Lomar. Both later reappear in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 1 is the first book in the Nyarlathotep Cycle by Troy Young.

### Overview
Introducing the reader to the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena and its long-running battle to protect humankind from the forces of "The Other" - a term used by one of the main characters to describe the creatures of the Cthulhu Mythos - Book 1 depicts the recruitment of three new agents, their early missions, and the death of two of the three.

Despite being presented as a series of shorts, the stories are in essence chapters in a novel; whilst some of the earliest stories can be read as stand-alone works, the later ones would make little sense out of the Cycle's context.

### Publication History
First released in 2020, The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 1 was released in both paperback and digital download formats.

In 2023, the stories contained in Book 1 were included in the paperback compendium The Nyarlathotep Cycle: The Other Omnibus.

fullContent:
The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 2 is the second book in the Nyarlathotep Cycle by Canadian author Troy Young.

### Overview
The second book picks up with Harjit Singh of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena recruiting a new field agent, firefighter Malcolm Mayweather, as he tackles assignments across the globe, from Canada, to Egypt, to Scotland. It details Mayweather's struggle to cope with the reality of the Cthulhu Mythos and the negative effects - both physical and psychological - that exposure to it has upon him. Additionally, the origins of the department and some minor details about its modern-day operations are also revealed.

shortDefinition: "The Outsider" is a short story by American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft. Written between March and August 1921, it was first published in Weird Tales (April 1926). In this work, a mysterious man who has been living alone in a castle for as long as ...
fullContent:
"The Outsider" is a short story by American horror writer H. P. Lovecraft. Written between March and August 1921, it was first published in Weird Tales (April 1926). In this work, a mysterious man who has been living alone in a castle for as long as he can remember decides to break free in search of human contact and light. "The Outsider" is one of Lovecraft's most commonly reprinted works and is also one of the most popular stories ever to be published in Weird Tales.

"The Outsider" combines horror, fantasy, and gothic fiction to create a nightmarish story, containing themes of loneliness, the abhuman, and the afterlife.

### Inspiration
In a letter, Lovecraft himself said that, of all his tales, this story most closely resembles the style of his idol Edgar Allan Poe, writing that it "represents my literal though unconscious imitation of Poe at its very height." The opening paragraphs echo those of Poe's "Berenice", while the horror at the party recalls the unmasking scene in "The Masque of the Red Death". (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

The story may also have been inspired in part by Nathaniel Hawthorne's "Fragments from the Journal of a Solitary Man", in which a man dreams that he is walking down Broadway in a burial shroud, only understanding the shocked reaction of passersby when he sees his reflection in a shop window. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

Another suggested literary model is Mary Shelley's novel Frankenstein (1818), in which the creature causes a shock when he enters a cottage: "I had hardly placed my foot within the door before the children shrieked, and one of the women fainted." The monster later looks in a pool of water and sees his reflection for the first time. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

Colin Wilson, in The Strength to Dream (1961), points to Oscar Wilde's short story "The Birthday of the Infanta", in which a misshapen dwarf is horrified to see his reflection for the first time. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

Some critics have suggested that "The Outsider" is autobiographical, and that Lovecraft was talking about his own life when he wrote, "I know always that I am an outsider; a stranger in this century and among those who are still men." An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia finds this analysis to be exaggerated, but suggests that the story "may possibly be indicative of HPL's own self-image, particularly the image of one who always thought himself ugly and whose mother told at least one individual about her son's 'hideous' face." (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

### Synopsis
"The Outsider" is written in the first-person narrative style and details the miserable and apparently lonely life of an individual who appears to have never had contact with another individual. The story begins with this narrator explaining his origins. His memory of others is vague, and he cannot seem to recall any details of his personal history, including who he is or where he is from. The Outsider and Others, published in 1939, is the first book issued by Arkham House and the first ever collection of H. P. Lovecraft's fiction. The stories included were selected by August Derleth and Donald Wandrei; the use of "The Outsider" as the title story had been suggested by Lovecraft for a proposed collection to be published by Weird Tales editor Farnsworth Wright.

The book was issued in an edition of 1,268 copies, which sold out by 1944; the collection has never been reprinted. The cover art was by noted fantasy artist Virgil Finlay.

The collection included Lovecraft's classic essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature", which appeared there for the first time in its complete revised form.

fullContent:
The Overseer is the overarching antagonist of the Kingdom Rush franchise, serving as the overarching antagonists of Vengeance, the main antagonist of Legends of Kingdom Rush and the main antagonist the sixth installment of the franchise, Kingdom Rush: Alliance. It is a Lovecraftian-like, eldritch being of unknown origins that seeks to enter the world of Linerea to consume it with the help of his army, the Unblinded Cult, which worship him as a god. 

### Description
Only the eye of the Overseer is usually seen with just that being as big as a human and having reptile like appearance.

His full body, however, seems to be more similar to an octopus, with a big main body that have several eyes on it, multiple tentacles that starts from the main body and also a moltitude of mouths with sharp teeths. After being the final fight at the end of Legends of Kingdom Rush, one of his eyes appears to be cut, but that doesn't seems to be much of a problem of the beast because of his several other eyes.

### Powers

### Iron Marines: Invasion
The Overseer is a powerful entity that reigns over a dark, energy-filled realm called the Void, which it uses to move between different worlds. It arrived in this galaxy after forming an alliance with the ambitious Dark Herald, who sought immense power. The Overseer plans to use the Herald until its own goals are achieved.

The Overseer has unique abilities linked to its eyes. It can protect the Herald or attack opponents with various effects, depending on the eye used. Before coming to this galaxy, the Overseer nearly destroyed another world inhabited by powerful heroes. However, these heroes united and managed to defeat it.

### Kingdom Rush: Alliance
The events of Legends of Kingdom Rush reveal that the malevolent Overseer had already begun infiltrating the realm of Linerea. A group of people, blinded by his influence, formed the Unblinded Cult. Their goal was to create an opening for the Overseer into their world, allowing him to consume it as he had countless others before.

### Trivia

* The Overseer bears a strong resemblance to Cyäegha, or arguably, Yog-Sothoth himself. Images of the tentacles, a Lovecraftian trademark, are also recurring throughout the series.
* The minions Cult Abomination and Taskmaster Abomination serving the Overseer are clearly inspired by the iconic Cthulhu himself.

shortDefinition: The Pale Brown Thing is an earlier shorter version of the Fritz Leiber novella Our Lady of Darkness. It was serialized in the January 1977 and February 1977 issues of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. It was later published in hardcover an...
fullContent:
The Pale Brown Thing is an earlier shorter version of the Fritz Leiber novella Our Lady of Darkness. It was serialized in the January 1977 and February 1977 issues of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. It was later published in hardcover and paperback on February 28, 2022 by Swan River Press. This later edition reprints The Pale Brown Thing for the first time in nearly forty years, with an introduction by the author’s friend, Californian poet Donald Sidney-Fryer.

This new, high quality edition contains the following:

* “Thibaut de Castries, Revenant” by Donald Sidney-Fryer
* “The Pale Brown Thing” by Fritz Leiber
* “Story-telling Wonder-questing, Mortal Me: The Transformation of The Pale Brown Thing into Our Lady of Darkness” by John Howard

Along with the change in title and slight alterations to the spelling of certain coined words, the shorter version does not include some of the digressions and character anecdotes of the longer novella. The title is a reference to the paramental entity the hero nicknames "Taffy" in the longer version.

The Pale Brown Thing novella stands as Leiber’s vision of 1970s San Francisco: a city imbued with an eccentric vibe and nefarious entities, in which pulp writer Franz Westen uncovers an alternate portrait of the city’s fin de siecle literary set — Ambrose Bierce, Jack London, Clark Ashton Smith — as well as the darker invocations of occultist Thibaut de Castries and a pale brown inhabitant of Corona Heights.

Fritz Leiber himself considered this short story an alternate retelling of Our Lady of Darkness rather than a draft.

"The Parkland Experiments" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British-born author William Meikle. It was first published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited anthology Shadows of an Inner Darkness by Golden Goblin Press in 2019 .

### Synopsis
During the 1920s, inmates at the Parkland Correctional Facility become unwilling test subjects of the crazed Dr. John Barnard, a man obsessed with his research into the field of eugenics. As the procedures progress, the subjects find themselves increasingly obsessed with a very specific rhythm, and this becomes the focal point of the doctor's efforts.

The inmates come to realise that the rhythm denotes a set of potential coordinates, one of which lies in the middle of the Pacific Ocean; with this realisation come dreams of "an island that shouldn't have been there, an island topped by a gargantuan city of tumbled ruins, strange angles and black stone" and "a giant doorway open[ing] revealing a colossal, shadowy, figure coming up from some distant watery depth."

Hearing this, the doctor becomes increasingly demented and, determined to experience these visions himself, undertakes the same procedures on himself. Gathering the men together, they involuntarily enact a ritual involving the beats but something goes wrong, and Barnard is transformed into something grotesque and inhuman before his former charges kill him.

### Mythos Connections
The coordinates which insinuate themselves into the test subjects' minds, 47°9'S 126°43'W, are those given by H. P. Lovecraft as the location of sunken R'lyeh; this is further reinforced by the visions experienced by the men, which offer a clear description of the city and the coming of its dark master Cthulhu: "something that might stand like a man, fly like a bat and swim like an octopus."

### Publication History 
*Shadows of an Inner Darkness (2019, Golden Goblin Press)
*Up from the Deep (2023)

fullContent:
"The Peabody Heritage" is a short story by August Derleth, one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in Arkham House's The Survivor and Others in 1957.

It tells the story of the great-grandson of Asaph Peabody, who returns to claim his ancestral estate northeast of Wilbraham, Massachusetts--only to unwittingly enable Asaph to resume the career of evil interrupted by his death 23 years earlier.

The story contains no overt references to the Cthulhu Mythos, though Asaph's witchcraft is associated with a Black Man who resembles the form taken by Nyarlathotep in "The Dreams in the Witch-House", and as in that story, magic allows one to travel through "a strange and extra-dimensional angle".  The story drops names from Christian demonology, like Belial, Beelzebub, and Sathanus.

### Characters
* The Narrator: A Boston lawyer and a Peabody, though his first name is never given. On his parents' sudden death, he retires from the law and resolves to live in the ancestral Peabody mansion in Wilbraham. 
*Asaph Peabody:  The narrator's great-grandfather, a warlock who is required to commit "the murder of a child, or some other homicidal act of sorcery," at regular intervals. He dies in 1907, and returns to life (after his upside-down bones are righted) in 1930.
* Balor: Asaph's familiar, a lesser devil who takes the forms of an enormous cat or a handsome imp.
*Jedidiah Peabody: Asaph's ancestor, who builds the Peabody estate in 1787 after relocating from Salem. He is a warlock, and inducts Asaph into the Peabody heritage the same way that Asaph inducts the narrator.
*Ahab Hopkins: A Wilbraham lawyer who looks after the Peabody estate. 
*George Taylor: A neighbor of the Peabody estate whose two-year-old daughter goes missing. 
*Jon Cieciorka: The foreman of a crew of Polish workers who find children's bones in a hidden room. 
* The Black Man: A supernatural figure who attends Asaph's Black Mass; "a man of such vivid blackness as to be literally darker than night, but with flaming eyes which seemed to be of living fire."

### Timeline
* 1692: A Peabody is accused at Salem, Massachusetts.
* 1787: Jedediah Peabody comes from Salem to build the Peabody mansion in Wilbraham, Massachusetts.
* 1907: Death of Asaph Peabody.
* May 7, 1915: An uncle of the narrator goes down on the Lusitania.
* 1919: Death of Asaph's son, the narrator's grandfather.
* 1929:  Death of the narrator's parents in an auto accident.
* February 24, 1930: The narrator moves into the Peabody mansion.
* March 1930: The narrator enters the Peabody tomb and disturbs Asaph's bones.
*April 1930: A two-year-old neighbour child disappears from her bed.

### Asaph's Library
The named books found in the Peabody estate are all  real works by historical authors--most if not all of whom wrote from an anti-witchcraft perspective:

* Malleus Maleficarum  
* Daemonialitas of Sinistrari  
* Vitae Sophistrarum of Eunapius 
* Anania’s De Natura Daemonum 
* Stampa’s Fuga

"The Peddler’s Tale, or Isobel’s Revenge"  is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that first appeared in the December 2013 issue of Sirenia Digest (#95). Set in H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands, it serves as a sequel to "Pickman's Madonna."

### Synopsis
The story takes the form of a tale told by a peddler woman to children of Ulthar--the tale of the rivalry between the incestuous albino twins Isaac and Isobel Snow, who became co-rulers of the Lower Dreamlands before they had a falling out. The peddler tells of how Isobel escapes her brother's betrayal with the help of a ghoul named Sorrow and Richard Upton Pickman--and how the twins' daughter Elspeth grows up to avenge her mother by overthrowing her father.

### Publication History
The story was republished in The Mammoth Book of Cthulhu (Prime Books, 2015) and The Red Brain: Great Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Dark Regions Press, 2017). It later appeared in Kiernan's collection Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018).

fullContent:
"The Peltonville Horror" is a Lovecraftian short story by the late American author Richard A. Lupoff. It was first published in the collection Visions by Mythos Books in July 2009.

### Synopsis
During the 1930s, Paul and Delia, a young couple on an evening drive, find themselves stranded far from home when the bridge home is washed out by a particularly fierce storm. Stopping at a roadside tavern for a bite to eat, they mention to bartender Mustafa Cristopolous their intention to travel to the next town over. Hearing this, the man warns them to be on their guard, as something evil has recently taken up residence there.

Making their way to the town, Paul and Delia are unable to find anywhere open; with the storm intensifying, they spot a light in a nearby business. Stumbling inside, they find themselves in the midst of a sinister cult: the very evil which the barman had warned them of. On the verge of being fed to a monstrous abomination, the couple are saved by the timely intervention of Cristopolous, who engages in a battle with the inhuman cult leader before both are dragged off and consumed by the entity.

The story concludes with the destruction of the cult at the hands of a freak lightning bolt, and Paul and Delia making good their escape.

"The People of the Monolith" is a fictional poem first mentioned in Robert E. Howard's horror story "The Black Stone". It is also referenced in "The Thing on the Doorstep" by H. P. Lovecraft, as well as in multiple stories by Brian Lumley.

### Overview
"The People of the Monolith" is the work of poet Justin Geoffrey, who wrote it during his 1921 trip to the Hungarian village of Stregoicavar, where he saw the Black Stone: a towering monolith carved with mysterious symbols. At some point after writing this poem, Geoffrey was committed to an asylum, in which he died screaming in 1926. (: "The Black Stone", : "The Thing on the Doorstep")

"The Pestilence of Pandora Peaslee" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Peter Rawlik. It was first published in the Jason Andrew-edited thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods by Simian Publishing in October 2015.

The story features Pandora Peaslee, a recurrent character created by Rawlik as the one of the main protagonists for a series of Mythos-related stories which revolve around the Great Race of Yith.

### Synopsis
In a future where the Earth has been quietly brought under the control of the Yithians, Pandora Peaslee and her resistance enact a plan to begin cleansing the world of their presence. Using a serum created by her mother, Megan Halsey, the Reanimatrix, they raise an army of the dead and bind them to their will by invoking the power of Hastur, an act which simultaneously blocks the Yithians from using their time- and dimension-hopping abilities while the humans begin their reconquest.

### Behind the Mythos
The leader of the Yithian strike team sent to stop Pandora is one Mister Ys, another recurrent character of Rawlik's.

### Publication History
Since it’s debut in Apotheosis, "The Pestilence of Pandora Peaslee" has also appeared in the collection of Rawlik's own works The Peaslee Papers, a fictional record of the activities of Pandora, her antecedents and her descendants throughout the ages.

fullContent:
"The Phantom of Beguilement" is a short story by Wilum H. Pugmire that originally appeared in his collection Tales of Love and Death (Delirium Books, 2001). It is set in Kingsport, one of the less-revisited corners of Lovecraft Country.

### Characters 
*Katherine Winters: a young poet who comes to Kingsport "in search of creative flow."
*Mrs. Keats: the owner of a "quaint shop of curios."
* Jeremy Blond: A poet and a painter who disappeared some time ago. "A nervous young artist, with dark wounded eyes and pale lifeless hair." A painting and accompanying poem by him fascinates Katherine Winters.
*Winfield Scot: Described as a "drunken lout" by Mrs. Keats and a "brother poet" by Katherine. He lives at the former home of the Terrible Old Man.
*The Terrible Old Man: The character from H. P. Lovecraft's "The Terrible Old Man" is referenced, though he died before the story begins at "an incredible old age." He is described as "a former sea captain" who "had learned strange rites and secret ceremonies during his sea journeys."

### Kingsport
Pugmire describes Lovecraft's fictional town of Kingsport as a "charming New England town where thrived a vigorous artistic community." The story notes its "misty air" and "strange, old-fashioned inhabitants." Points of interest include Central Hill, the "craggy silhouette of Kingport’s prehistoric cliffs," the "narrow cobblestones of Harborside," the "tall and dilapidated building that had once been Mariner’s Church" on Foster Street, and the "trickling water of Blake’s Creek." 

The deserted cottage of the Terrible Old Man on Water Street is noted for the "large oddly painted stones that leaned in the tall grass of [its] yard...positioned in esoteric groups, like primeval idols."

### Publication History
In addition to appearing in four collections of Pugmire's work, the story was reprinted in A Mountain Walked (Centipede Press, 2014), edited by S. T. Joshi.

"The Pickman Revival" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Steven M. Vance. It was published in the Matthew Carpenter-edited thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
At the pre-opening meeting for an art exhibition celebrating the works and legacy of the enigmatic Richard Upton Pickman, a mismatched group of organisers, artists and journalists decide to take a trip to see the supposed studio of their hero, which one believes to have located beneath an abandoned Boston warehouse.

Upon reaching the warehouse and breaking in, the group do manage to locate the studio, but are quickly set upon by a pack of ghouls which boil up from the well located in the basement's centre. Only two of the group survive the attack and make a successful escape.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Pickman Revival" features several nods to the Cthulhu Mythos in addition to the Pickman paintings on display. These include the location of the exhibition, Innsmouth; one of the artists having subtle signs of the Innsmouth Look, as well as painting pictures of fish-men hybrids and enormous creatures with cephalopod traits; and another who admits to being a ghoul himself.

The story also features several unfinished plot threads which make it feel more like part of an uncompleted novel than a stand-alone short.

shortDefinition: "The Picture in the House" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft. It was written on December 12, 1920, and first published in the July 1919 issue of The National Amateur—which actually was published in the summer of 1921.  ### Lovecraft Country...
fullContent:
"The Picture in the House" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft. It was written on December 12, 1920, and first published in the July 1919 issue of The National Amateur—which actually was published in the summer of 1921.

### Lovecraft Country
"The Picture in the House" begins with something of a manifesto for the series of horror stories Lovecraft would write set in an imaginary New England countryside that would come to be known as Lovecraft Country:

:Searchers after horror haunt strange, far places. For them are the catacombs of Ptolemais, and the carven mausolea of the nightmare countries. They climb to the moonlit towers of ruined Rhine castles, and falter down black cobwebbed steps beneath the scattered stones of forgotten cities in Asia. The haunted wood and the desolate mountain are their shrines, and they linger around the sinister monoliths on uninhabited islands. But the true epicure of the terrible, to whom a new thrill of unutterable ghastliness is the chief end and justification of existence, esteem most of all the ancient, lonely farmhouses of backwoods New England; for there the dark elements of strength, solitude, grotesqueness, and ignorance combine to form the perfection of the hideous.

As Lovecraft critic Peter Cannon writes, "Here Lovecraft serves notice that he will rely less on stock Gothic trappings and more on his native region as a source for horror." Lovecraft's analysis of the psychological roots of New England horror is echoed in his discussion of Nathaniel Hawthorne in the essay "Supernatural Horror in Literature". (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​

The story introduces two of Lovecraft Country's most famous elements:

:I had been travelling for some time amongst the people of the Miskatonic Valley in quest of certain genealogical data.... Now I found myself upon an apparently abandoned road which I had chosen as the shortest cut to Arkham.

Neither location is further developed in this tale, but Lovecraft had placed the foundations for one of the most enduring settings in weird fiction.

### Inspiration
The ending of the story, in which the narrator is saved by a thunderbolt that destroys the ancient house, may have been inspired by the similar ending of Edgar Allan Poe's "The Fall of the House of Usher".

Critic Jason Eckhardt suggested that the dialect the unnaturally aged man uses in the story is derived from one used in James Russell Lowell's Biglow Papers (1848–62). Even in Lowell's time, the dialect was thought to be long extinct. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)​ Scott Connors has stated that "the use of an archaic dialect in "The Picture in the House"...represents an early example of (the notion of plunging through time), transforming what might otherwise be a mundane tale of cannibalism into a meditation on the paradoxes of time." 

Peter Cannon has pointed to parallels between "The Picture in the House" and Arthur Conan Doyle's "The Adventure of the Copper Beeches".
