"The Pillars of Melkarth" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney featuring his sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta, the last short story Tierney published featuring the character, and the last adventure he wrote in in-universe chronology. It pits the character against worshippers of August Derleth's fire deity Cthugha. The story first appeared in Space & Time #78, published in 1990.

### Synopsis
A sinister cult in Tyre that kidnaps children turns out to be part of the High Priest Matan's plot to summon Ku-thuga, a malevolent fire deity, through the Pillars of Melkarth. The cult's army, bolstered by fiery supernatural entities, proves to be a formidable challenge for Simon and his allies, who need to summon an opposing god to stand a chance of averting the impending destruction of the Earth.

### Setting
The story is set in the spring of 50 A. D. in the city of Tyre, then a free city in the Roman province of Syria, now in the modern country of Lebanon.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Space & Time, "The Pillars of Melkarth" was reprinted in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997) and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

"The Plague of St. James Infirmary" is a short story by Ken Asamatsu, translated from the original Japanese by R. Keith Roller.

The story first appeared in English language translation in the anthology of Japanese Mythos writings, Night Voices, Night Journeys (Lairs of the Hidden Gods).

### Synopsis
In 1920s Chicago, Elliott Ness battles Al Capone as at the same time elemental forces of fire and water battle each other in the form of fire servants of Cthugha and water servants of Cthaat. Michael Leigh, a character originally created by Henry Kuttner, also makes an appearance.

### Behind the Mythos
The pitting of fire against water in this story is a direct attempt to blend the kami elementals of Japanese mythology into the different concepts of the Mythos, in a manner quite similar to the August Derleth approach.

shortDefinition: "The Plain of Sound" is a short story by Ramsey Campbell, originally published in The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants (Arkham House, 1964). It introduces the alien species called the S'gluhoans.  The story involves three university st...
fullContent:
"The Plain of Sound" is a short story by Ramsey Campbell, originally published in The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants (Arkham House, 1964). It introduces the alien species called the S'gluhoans.

The story involves three university students, returning to Brichester from Severnford, who stumble across the titular Plain of Sound, a flat area with strange, almost unbearable noises. In the midst of the plain is a small stone house, within which the sounds cease.

Inside the house is a strange machine and a collection of occult books, including a copy of the The Revelations of Glaaki. There is also the diary of Arnold Hird, a former professor at Brichester University who moved to the stone house around 1930. There he was contacted in his dreams by aliens from a dimension called S'gluho, where our sounds become objects and their objects become sounds to us. They convince Hird to build the weird device, following instructions in the Revelations and the Necronomicon, whose purpose is to allow the aliens to cross over into our world. 

### Characters

* Les: A Brichester University student and the narrator of the story. He is noted for always carrying a compass.
* Frank Nuttall: Another Brichester University student; it's his idea to go to Severnford to visit the old inn.
* Tony Roles: The third student in the story, a bibliophile; he is unenthusiastic about going all the way to Severnford to get drunk. He is driven permanently insane by something he saw in S'gluho.
* Arnold Hird: A Brichester University professor in the 1920s. He was "asked to leave the university because he attacked someone when they disagreed with him," according to Les. He said he would "return and astonish everybody some day, but was never heard of again." His experiments in 1930 in a stone house near Severnford succeeded in making contact with S'gluho, but apparently led to his demise. 

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in the 1985 edition of Cold Print and in The New Lovecraft Circle (1996), and edited by Robert M. Price.

fullContent:
"The Poe-et's Nightmare: A Fable" is a lengthy poem by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft, written in 1916 and first published in the July 1918 edition of The Vagrant .

### Synopsis
The poem relates the story of one Lucullus Languish who, after an evening of over-eating and reading the works of Edgar Allan Poe, is taken on a fever-dream tour of the universe in which he is shown the insignificance of the human race in the grand scheme of the universe. Upon waking, he resolves never again to mix his physical indulgences with poetry.

### Behind the Mythos
In An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia, S. T. Joshi and Peter Cannon describe "The Poe-et's Nightmare" as "perhaps HPL’s first enunciation of cosmicism, predating even his early stories," and note that "[i]n later years HPL found the rhymed framework dissatisfying, thinking that it detracted from the seriousness of the cosmic message."

fullContent:
"The Poem of Ulysses, or The Odyssey" is the earliest extant poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft . Written on 8 November 1897 , it did not see publication as its own work until its inclusion in the Night Shade Books collection The Ancient Track: The Complete Poetical Works of H. P. Lovecraft in 2001 .

### Synopsis
The first draft of the poem, a mere four lines long, is an outline of the Odyssey, an epic attributed to the classical Greek poet Homer. The Odyssey describes the ten-year homeward journey of the hero Odysseus after his participation in the Trojan War . A second edition would give a longer synopsis of the story, although still little more than a recap.

### Behind the Scenes
The poem was referred to by Lovecraft as "The Poem of Ulysses; or The New Odyssey" in his essay "The Brief Autobiography of an Inconsequential Scribbler," in which he includes the four lines which comprised the initial draft .

fullContent:
"The Pool" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
Set over the course of several nights, a San Franciscan construction worker first bears witness to the surreptitious summoning of a Shoggoth by an occultist masquerading as a contractor. Subsequently, the man begins to receive mental messages exhorting him to revisit the site of the incantation - a newly-installed private swimming pool - and looks on as the creature devours first the homeowner, and then all of the guests at her house party.

### Characters
*Daryl, an average Joe working several jobs to forge a better life for himself.
*Mike Love, a charismatic general contractor and secret occultist.
*Don, Daryl's friend and coworker.
*Amy Robideau, a wealthy homeowner and sacrificial victim.

### Publication History
"The Pool" was first published in the February-March edition of Weird Tales. It has also been included in the collections of Shea's own works Copping Squid and Other Mythos Tales (2009) and Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea (2017).

### Trivia
*At one point during the story, Daryl finds and reads a copy of At the Mountains of Madness by H. P. Lovecraft, suggesting that Lovecraft himself was subjected to the same psychic contact as Daryl has been.
*Daryl is stated to lodge in the Hyperion Hotel in exchange for working the graveyard shift on reception, the Hyperion being a recurrent location within Shea's works.

fullContent:
"The Posthumous Recruitment of Timothy Horne" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Pete Rawlik. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
After Timothy Horne dies on the battlefield while fighting a large-scale incursion of the Migou, he is offered a second chance to serve his species when he is inducted into a special detachment tasked with taking the war to the enemy on a different plane of existence.

Horne is guided to the Dreamlands by his commanding officer Major Carter - who reveals himself to be a cat - and upon his arrival is transformed into a bandersnatch, a form better suited to battling the Migou on their own terms. Around the moons of Phobos and Deimos, he bears witness as the people of the Dreamlands and their allies assemble a vast fleet with which to conduct the second phase of the war, and boards his ship to begin preparations.

### Behind the Mythos
The entrance to the Dreamlands utilised by Horne's battalion was described as a seemingly never-ending staircase, which would appear to echo Randolph Carter's entry in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, particularly considering Major Carter's transformation into a cat. Other entrances mentioned are one which requires walking a yellow brick road, and another in which the traveller must navigate a wardrobe containing a forest of overcoats, references to L. Frank Baum's Oz series and C. S. Lewis's The Chronicles of Narnia, respectively.

The Dreamlands is described by the Carter-cat as a manufactured dimension, created by the Q'hrell: a name occasionally used for the Elder Things, and stated by author Pete Rawlik to be their name in the old language.

The Cats from Saturn are shown to be allies of the Dreamlands concord, and are described as entities which can be integrated into certain technologies to act as powerful star drives.

The name of the ship to which Horne is assigned is the Tars Tarkas. This is a nod to the noble Martian war leader of the same name who appears in Edgar Rice Burroughs' Barsoom series, and becomes one of the protagonist's main allies.

shortDefinition: "The Presentation" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.  ### Synopsis A chance street encounter with a prophet of Cthulhu kickstarts a movement amongst the artistic community of San Francisco. As the prophet gains...
fullContent:
"The Presentation" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
A chance street encounter with a prophet of Cthulhu kickstarts a movement amongst the artistic community of San Francisco. As the prophet gains influence in the city, the artists are hired to paint an enormous mural, one which opens into a portal to another dimension. When the portal closes, another commission is made, and the community begins to realise what they have initiated, and that it is pointless to resist what is happening.

### Characters
*Rick Tindal, a gifted artist for the comic book Death Groan Comix, referred to at one point as Mr. Tindalos. A "reasonably compassionate guy" who "prides himself on being a see-er."
*Irving, aka Rat, Rick's friend and fellow Death Groan artist. He is "one of corporate America’s eternal adversaries."
*Mark, Rat's stepfather. An entrepreneur who owns the loft where Death Groan is published, along with seven other buildings in San Francisco's South-of-Market neighborhood. He has investments in popular videogames like Acute Angle II and Nano-Barbarians III, and "boardroom links with AOL and Time Warner."
*Zed, a street artist--a "spraycan commando capable of Carrivagian compositions"--and writer of half of Death Groan's stories. She is "small and angular," with "black-lidded eyes and purple lips."
*Jackie, Zed's friend and fellow street artist. She has "sharp green eyes and a delicately hawkish nose, like a young falcon."
*Chet Shugrue, aka Chet Shoggua, a prophet of Cthulhu, sent to prepare the Earth for its return. He "looked like some guy in Vogue: lusciously suited, alligator shoes, his face a handsome vacancy."
*Luke Cipher, who conducts a ritual that manifests Chet Shugrue on Earth, involving fire and a token monetary contribution from Rick Tindal. He has "dramatic bones in his brow and cheeks," a tightness in his face that "gave him a kind of skinned look," "remote, impatient eyes," and a "taut and balanced" body. He warns Rick, "You can never unsee what you have seen.”

### Publication History
"The Presentation" was first published in issue #3 of Allen K's Inhuman Magazine in December 2005. It has since been included in the collections of Shea's own works Copping Squid and Other Mythos Tales (October 2009) and Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea (December 2017).

fullContent:
"The Prince" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Anddre Valdivia. First published in the Jesse Dedman-edited anthology Ancient Ones II in March 2018, it has yet to be reprinted .

### Synopsis
When volcanic activity in Argentina unearths an ancient prehuman metropolis, the archaeologist sent to investigate the ruins is driven insane by the forbidden texts which he uncovers within.

Intrigued by the mystical writings, the man's grandson embarks on a quest to find the missing pages of the fabled al-Azif. Beneath the sands of Arabia, he discovers the final resting place of Abdul Alhazred, whose shade awakens from its slumber and relates the tale of how, as a young man, he made a pact with a demon for knowledge and power. The pact doomed Alhazred, and his final days were spent committing what he had learned to paper before dying mad and alone.

As the man attempts to return to civilisation, he finds that the curse which had afflicted Alhazred has infected him as well, and he wanders the sands, certain that the same fate which befell the Mad Arab lies in his own future.

fullContent:
"The Prodigy of Dreams" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Thomas Ligotti. It was first published in August 1986 in an anthology edited by David D. Deyo Jr. entitled All the Devils are Here.

### Synopsis
The protagonist is a young man who is absolutely obsessed with the past and incapable of seeing himself in terms of anything other than the family legacy symbolized by a large decaying mansion in which he lives. The mansion and its contents were assembled thanks to the business acumen of his forebears. He is surrounded by reminders of his family but also of a profound irreversible decay.

The story revolves around one Arthur Emerson, a solitary scholar from a long line of business-people who has reached the end of his life with no partner, no children, and seemingly no friends. At one point, he talks about how the next owner of his house will doubtless be some distant relative whose face he has never seen. While Emerson’s forebears assembled fortunes, Emerson has been quite content to be an obscure scholar… author of books with evocative titles such as In The Margins of Paradise, The Forgotten Universe of the Vicoli, and The Secret Gods and Other Studies, but the work he is struggling to finish before he dies is called Dynasties of Dust. Emerson is effectively waiting for death as is clear in the quote that is credited to him at the beginning of the story:“I conceived my final leave-taking from this Earth – a drama prepared by strange portents, swiftly developed by dreams and visions nurtured in an atmosphere of sublime dread, growing overnight like some gaudy fungus in a forgotten cellar.”Defeated by life and listless to the point of inactivity, he is assailed by the noise the swans of the nearby lake make. This noise intensifies as the Great Old One Cynothoglys, with whom he has made some past agreement finally arrives to foreclose on his life. The sense is that somehow it has all been foreordained in a melancholy irresistible way. Embalmed "alive" he has reached the point where even the half-life living death comes to its inevitable end.

### Publication History

* Crypt of Cthulhu (1989)
* Noctuary (1994, 1995, 2012)
* The Nightmare Factory (1996)
* In einer fremden Stadt, in einem fremden Land (2001; German-language collection)

"The Psychic Investigator" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author David A. Riley which first appeared in the Gavin Chappell-edited zine Lovecraftiana (unknown year, Rogue Planet Press). It proved popular enough to have been voted for by the fanbase on Facebook for inclusion in a Best of… collection (2023, Rogue Planet Press).

### Synopsis
A team of paranormal investigators look into historic and ongoing reports of spooks in an abandoned area of the English town Edgebottom named Grudge End. On the first night, the group splits into two teams, and soon one of the teams goes missing: reports to apathetic local law enforcement go largely ignored, and the remaining team is at a loss on how to proceed until the others miraculously reappear, relating a fantastical tale of having been transported to a blasted future wasteland before being inexplicably returned.

After a lengthy discussion, a number of the group decide to return to the site of the first team's disappearance in an effort to get to the bottom of things. As they had hoped, the investigators find themselves once again transported into the hellish landscape, but this time are confronted with a group of mutated cultists. Fleeing the fanatics, they take refuge overnight in a shattered library, hiding from not only the cult, but also the feral ghouls which stalk the world in darkness.

The following morning, the group make their way to the site where they were first transported from modern-day Earth and manage to find a way to return to their own time, but not before one of the cultists slips them a copy of the last issue of a local newspaper to be published before the calamity which befell the world- an issue which has a date very, very near at hand…

### Mythos Connections
In addition to the ghouls encountered by the explorers, one member of the team mentions his prior experience with books such as the Necronomicon and Unaussprechlichen Kulten.

### Publication History
*Lovecraftiana (unknown date, Rogue Planet Press)
*The Best of Lovecraftiana (2023, Rogue Planet Press)

"The Puppeteer" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Gary Budgen. It was published in the thematic anthology Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights by Rogue Planet Press in January 2017.

### Synopsis
Young Naj, son of a Hyperborean landowner, develops an obsession with reclusive puppeteer Ridwan, a tenant on his father's property. Following the man, he witnesses him capture a wild Voormi before shrinking the poor creature down into a doll-sized mannikin and carrying it off.

Both terrified and fascinated by what he has seen, Naj waits until Ridwan has left his home before breaking in. Inside, he discovers hundreds of shrunken creatures inhabiting a miniature town, but is caught red-handed by the returning wizard. The man reveals to the boy how as a young man he was taken from his family and brought into the service of the Great Old One Tsathoggua, whose work he continues to this day. To prevent the boy from revealing what he has seen, Ridwan then shrinks him down to puppet size and sets him among the others, playing out a nightly hunt through the streets of the tiny town.

"The Pyramid of the Black Pharaoh" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young, it is the third story in Book 2 of the Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
Investigator Malcolm Mayweather is seconded to an international team comprised of agents from counterpart organisations to the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena. Their mission: to investigate a newly-discovered pyramid which predates all others and has been established to have connections to the Outer God Nyarlathotep.

As the group explore the interior, it quickly becomes apparent that the pyramid is in fact a techno-arcane device designed to send a signal to Nyarlathotep's "father" Azathoth. As the party begins to dwindle - due to both the effects of madness and the pyramid's guardians - the signal is sent. Only Mayweather and the Egyptian representative manage to escape with their lives.

The story concludes with Adele Kramer, a former agent whose consciousness has been stripped from her body, beginning to rebuild her mind in the face of cosmic horror.

### Characters
*Malcolm Mayweather, a former firefighter turned paranormal field agent.
*Rana El Masry, a psychoanalyst for the Egyptian analogue of Mayweather's department.
*Russ Atwood, a former journalist with the American analogue.
*Werner Beck, an antiquarian with the German analogue.
*Noa Gabbai, a counter-terrorist agent for the Israeli analogue.
*Shiro Takedi, a cult infiltrator with the Japanese analogue.
*Guillermo Vega, a former surveyor with the Chilean analogue.
*Harjit Singh, director of the Canadian department.
*Nyarlathotep/The Black Pharaoh, an Outer God with a cruel sense of humour.

### Publication History
"The Pyramid of the Black Pharaoh" was published in the collection The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 2 in 2020.

shortDefinition: "The Quest of Iranon" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. It was written on February 28, 1921, and was first published in the July/August 1935 issue of the magazine The Galleon. It was later reprinted in Weird Tales in 1939.  ### Plot summary The st...
fullContent:
"The Quest of Iranon" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. It was written on February 28, 1921, and was first published in the July/August 1935 issue of the magazine The Galleon. It was later reprinted in Weird Tales in 1939.

### Plot summary
The story is about a golden-haired youth who wanders into the city of Teloth, telling tales of the great city of Aira, where he was prince. While Iranon enjoys singing and telling his tales of wonder, few appreciate it. When a disenfranchised boy named Romnod suggests leaving Teloth to go to the famed city of Oonai (which he thinks may be Aira, now under a different name), Iranon takes him up on his offer.

Iranon and Romnod spend years on their journey to Oonai. Along the way, Romnod grows up while Iranon remains exactly the same. Eventually they reach Oonai, which Iranon is disappointed (although not surprised) to discover is not Aira. Iranon is loved by the people in Oonai, however, so he stays there even though he still desires to return to Aira. As the years pass, people appreciate him less and less, and he is eventually upstaged by dancers from the desert. By this point, Romnod has grown old and has become a drunkard. After Romnod's death, Iranon decides to leave Oonai and continue his search for Aira.

Eventually Iranon comes across an old shepherd and asks him if he knows of Aira. The shepherd tells him that he has indeed heard of it, for in his youth there was a beggar's boy who had always talked about it. The boy, who thought he was a prince, was laughed at by everyone and ran away.

With the truth revealed, that Aira was merely a figment of his imagination, Iranon loses his eternal youth. Now aged significantly, Iranon wanders into the quicksands to his death.

### Characters
*Iranon - A vine-crowned, yellow haired wanderer dressed in a purple robe. Though he believed himself to be an exiled prince from Aira, he in fact grew up poor in the countryside.
*Athok the cobbler - A resident of Teloth.
*Romnod - A young man from Teloth who left the city to travel with Iranon. Growing old over the course of their journey he fell prey to the excesses of Oonai and died red and fattened, writhing in a banquet-couch.
*The King of Oonai
*The old shepherd

### Locations
The following places are listed in the order of Iranon's travels rather than their appearance in the story.
*Aira - A beautiful city of veined and tinted marble and beryl with golden domed palaces and painted walls, surrounded by green gardens with cerulean pools and crystal fountains. The city and perhaps its surrounding geography was imagined by Iranon.
**Nithra - A river that curves by the groves of Aira.
**Kra - A tiny stream with a small waterfall in the valley by Aira.
*The Xari - A long frigid river
**The valley of Narthos
**Sinara - A city on the southern slope of the river occupied by dromedary-men in the market-place. Iranon claims that the people of Sinara were all drunken and ribald.
**Jaren - A city surronded with onyx-walls.
*Steth

fullContent:
"The Randy Oswald Story" is a Lovecraftian short story by author and artist Dean Wirth. The third in a series begun with "The Dewey Mine Attack", it was published in Vol 5, Issue 3 of the Lovecraftiana zine in October 2020.

### Synopsis
1945, Los Angeles: investigative reporter Randy Oswald stumbles across the story of the Dewey Mine massacre of 1885, before tracking down and interviewing its sole survivor, Bryan Katz, now released from an asylum and living a quiet life. 

After hearing Katz's story, he is hired by a woman named Mina Luddox - whose husband was killed by creatures identical to those described by Katz - to look into similar incidents; his investigations lead him to visit the Dewey Mine himself. There, he witnesses a man being dragged into the black mouth of the shaft, leaving behind only the logbook of the USS Constitution, dated 1806; the book recounts an attack by "star-demons" similar in description to those encountered by Katz.

He eventually comes to the realisation that the Dewey Mine incident is most definitely not an isolated one, and that these creatures have been preying on other sentient species for unknown ages. The truth of this appears to drive him to depression and the story ends with a newspaper article on his suicide.

### Characters
*Randy Oswald, a journalist specialising in crime and the paranormal.
*Bryan Katz, a former miner and only survivor of an attack by malicious alien beings.
*Mina Luddox, a woman whose husband-to-be was killed by the star-creatures aboard the USS Connecticut shortly after the end of WWI.

"The Rat King" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Troy Young. It is the first story in Book 2 of his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
Newly-recruited Malcolm Mayweather and senior agent Mindy Nguyen investigate the appearance of strange rats in a dying farming community. They uncover a cultist dedicated to an entity named Meph’hibb’anauth, and the plan to use his control over a legion of rats to spread pestilence and destruction. Using their mundane-world skills, they are able to kill the man and blow up his rat minions in an abandoned grain elevator.

### Characters
*Malcolm Mayweather, a firefighter-turned-government agent.
*Mindy Nguyen, a seasoned veteran in the employ of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.
*Harjit Singh, Mayweather and Nguyen's director.
*Ned Parker, a local farmer.

### Publication History
"The Rat King" was published in The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 2 in 2020.

shortDefinition: "The Rats in the Walls" is a short story by American author H. P. Lovecraft. Written in August–September 1923, it was first published in Weird Tales, March 1924.  ### Plot summary Set in 1923, "The Rats in the Walls" is narrated by the scion of the d...
fullContent:
"The Rats in the Walls" is a short story by American author H. P. Lovecraft. Written in August–September 1923, it was first published in Weird Tales, March 1924.

### Plot summary
Set in 1923, "The Rats in the Walls" is narrated by the scion of the de la Poer family, who has moved from Massachusetts to his ancestral estate in England, the ruined Exham Priory. To the dismay of nearby residents, he restores the Priory, plainly revealing his ignorance of the horrific history of the place. After moving in, the protagonist and his cats frequently hear rats scurrying behind the walls. Upon investigating further (and as revealed in recurring dreams), he learns that his family maintained an underground city for centuries where they raised generations of "human cattle" (some regressed to a quadrupedal state) to supply their taste for human flesh. Maddened by the revelations of his family's past and driven by a hereditary cruelty, the narrator attacks one of his friends in the dark of the cavernous city and begins eating him. He is subsequently subdued and placed in a mental institution. At least one other investigator, Thornton, has gone insane as well. Soon after, Exham Priory is destroyed. The narrator maintains his innocence, proclaiming that it was "the rats, the rats in the walls," who ate the man. He continues to be plagued by the sound of rats in the walls of his cell.

### Inspiration
Long after writing "The Rats in the Walls", Lovecraft wrote that the story was "suggested by a very commonplace incident — the cracking of wall-paper late at night, and the chain of imaginings resulting from it." (: Selected Letters 5.795) which was described by "Wall paper cracks off in sinister shape—man dies of fright." in his notebook. (: commonplace book 107) Another entry in Lovecraft's commonplace book also seems to provide a plot germ for the story: "Horrible secret in crypt of ancient castle—discovered by dweller." (: commonplace book 79)

Steven J. Mariconda points to Sabine Baring-Gould's Curious Myths of the Middle Ages (1862–68) as a source for Lovecraft's story. The description of the cavern under the priory has many similarities to Baring-Gould's account of St. Patrick's Purgatory, a legendary Irish holy site, and the story of the priory's rats sweeping across the landscape may have been inspired by the book's retelling of the legend of Bishop Hatto, who was devoured by rats after he set fire to starving peasants during a famine. (: "Baring-Gould and the Ghouls", The Horror of It All) See the story of the Mouse Tower of Bingen.

Parts of Lovecraft's story bear a striking resemblance to Carl Jung's famous "house" dream (told to Sigmund Freud in 1909, though not well known before 1925): the descent through one's historically-stratified ancestral family home to a Romanesque cellar; lifting a hidden slab; descending stone steps to a prehistoric cave littered with bones, broken pottery, etc.

The Rats in the Walls is a production from the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society, released as part of their Dark Adventure Radio Theatre series.

### Overview


Adapted from H. P. Lovecraft's short story of the same name and following the standard format of DART productions, The Rats in the Walls is presented as a 1930s-style audio broadcast and is available with a set of period-authentic props related to the story. *A rubbing of Latin carved text.
*An invitation card from Matthew Delapore which includes the Delapore family crest.
*An ancient title deed for Exham Priory.

fullContent:
The Ravening Deep is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author Tim Pratt, the first in his Sanford Files series for Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Fiction setting. Published in August 2023 by Aconyte, an audiobook edition was released simultaneously by Tantor Audio/Tantor and Blackstone Publishing.

### Synopsis
When down-on-his-luck fisherman Abel Davenport is caught up in a freak storm, he finds himself washed ashore on an odd little island off the coast of New England. Exploring the rocky outcrop, he discovers a secret temple concealed within, and an ancient amulet belonging to the dead sea god Asterias, the titular Ravening Deep. This amulet grants him visions of how to restore Asterias to its former glory, and Davenport, enthralled by its magic, enthusiastically agrees to help.

Back in Arkham, the amulet shows Davenport how to create doppelgängers of living people, through the simple process of removing a finger and submerging it in saltwater. Davenport begins with himself, but the resulting clones, which they dub "comets," soon show their true colours and turn on their creator, taking the amulet and casting him aside. Free from the amulet's power, Davenport quickly comes to realise the evil represented by Asterias.

Later, Davenport meets Diana Stanley, a cultist of the Silver Twilight Lodge now dedicated to bringing the organisation down, and Ruby Standish, a talented thief who has her own reasons for wishing harm on the Lodge's leader, Carl Sanford. The three form a plan to break in to the lodge and steal a jar containing the last surviving piece of Asterias and destroy it, in order to save the world from being devoured once the comets take possession of the artefact.

However, not all goes according to plan, and their attempts to steal the fragment fail; however, during the process, the comets - now numbering in their dozens - mount an assault on the lodge in order to take possession of their dead god's remains, and Davenport, Stanley, and Standish are forced to ally themselves with Sanford in order to not only fight back, but simply survive.

Although the Lodge's defences are penetrated with ease by the army of comets, the allies escape and eventually find their way to Asterias' island-temple, where a final showdown results in the destruction of the temple, the slowly-awakening god, and the comets.

In the aftermath, Davenport and Stanley relocate inland to be as far from the open ocean as possible. In thanks for her assistance, Sanford forgives Standish for her previous trespass and offers her a job on retainer as a thief-for-hire. Alone and back at the newly-restored and fortified lodge, he he muses over the fact that he managed to retain a small piece of Asterias, as any source of magical power is useful to one such as he…

* Abel Davenport: a fisherman struggling to stay financially afloat
* Diana Stanley: a businesswoman who has become unwittingly caught up with the Silver Twilight Lodge, but whose experiences

fullContent:
"The Recruiter" is a short story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
An elderly man, on the verge of being thrown out onto the streets in San Francisco, is offered a helping hand by a seemingly kindly neighbour. However, this help comes with a price, and the man's soul is used to deliver a host of dead bodies to a gargantuan creature which lies beneath the surface of the bay.

Once he has completed the task and been released from his service, he vows to fight the threat by any means which he can.

### Characters
*Chester Chase, a 75-year-old widower who believes he has nothing left to live for.
*Mr. Canning, an even older man in service to some dark power.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to Lovecraft’s works or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the creature beneath the bay has a very Lovecraftian flavour to it. Additionally, Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi's inclusion of the piece in Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea indicates his belief that it is set within.

Chester is a long-term resident in the Hyperion Hotel, the Hyperion being a recurrent location in Shea's Lovecraftian works.

### Publication History
"The Recruiter" was first published in the anthology Lovecraft Unbound by Dark Horse Books in September 2009. It was later included in the posthumous collection of Shea's own works Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea by Dark Regions Press in December 2017.

"The Recruiter" was a rewrite of sections of the novel Mr. Cannyharme, which was completed in 1981 but remained unpublished until 2021, long after the author's death.

fullContent:
"The Recurring Doom" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by S. T. Joshi, first published in 1980.

### Synopsis
Jefferson Coler is a prestigious but controversial British archaeologist with a strong interest in arcane books and ancient languages. In 1940, after returning from an expedition to Arabia, he calls his colleague Collins (the narrator), to show him a strange object he had found while excavating the ruins of what might have been legendary Irem, the City of Pillars. The object is a green rectangular crystal, similar to a box, but with no openings, and made of an unknown material that laboratorial analysis failed to identify. On the next week, Coler contacts Collins again to show him that the interior of the crystal is now glowing, as if a small luminous object had formed inside it.

Faced with this inexplicable phenomenon, Coler and Collins search in several occult books for an explanation, but are unable to find anything about it in De Vermis Mysteriis, the Unaussprechlichen Kulten, the Civitates Antiquae Fantasticae, or the Necronomicon. However, Collins' attention is drawn by a newspaper article about a congregation of cultists performing some sort of ritual in the druidic megaliths of Sentinel Hill, Brichester.

At this point, their research is interrupted by the arrival of Joseph Meredith, head of the Archaeology Department at Miskatonic University, who traveled to Britain to ask for Coler's help in deciphering the language of a parchment found recently in Egypt. While Coler studies this new text and Meredith rests from the long trip, Collins returns to his studies. With Coler and Collins focused on their tasks, the house is invaded by a cultist bent on stealing the crystal. Collins attacks the intruder and prevents the theft, then follows the man all the way to Sentinel Hill, where he sees that the cultists are gathered again, and witnesses the would-be thief being severely beaten by the cult leader for his failure.

On the next day, Collins finds that Coler's house has been broken into again, the crystal has been stolen, and Coler is unconscious, a wound on his head showing that he's been knocked out. Collins revives him and tends to his wound. As soon as he recovers, Coler grabs a rifle and tells Collins that the cultists must be stopped at any cost. Collins asks about Meredith, and is told that he has gone back to Arkham after finding out that a number of young people, including Miskatonic students, have been found dead in the sea off the coast of Innsmouth, their bodies torn apart viciously as if by some clawed animal, and covered in foetid slime. A similar incident has also happened in Tahiti.

Armed with Coler's rifle, Coler and Collins rush to Sentinel Hill, where the cult leader is presiding the ceremony and the crystal is already in place, the glowing sphere in its interior having increased in size visibly. Coler shoots the cult leader, fights the cultists alongside Collins, and retrieves the crystal. After that, the two take C

### Synopsis
By means of a cleverly-faked mystical grimoire, international spy Trish Scarborough engineers a meeting with the occult organisation known as the Red Coterie. Its purpose: to propose an alliance between the Coterie and the American government's cryptanalysis division the Cipher Bureau, also known as the Black Chamber, to jointly combat supernatural threats to humankind. Although she is able to make the mysterious Crimson Cavalier hear her out, he promises nothing more than to bring her proposition before his colleagues.

### Behind the Mythos
The story's title is a reference to the two organisations - the Red Coterie and the Black Chamber - potentially working in concert.

fullContent:
"The Red Offering", originally published as just "The Offering", is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter. It was first published in 1982 in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu, and forms part of the Xothic Legend Cycle.

### Synopsis
The story purports to be part of the translation of the Zanthu Tablets, as published by Prof. Copeland in 1916.

In ancient Mu, the hierophant Zanthu recounts how from an early age he wished to become high-priest of Ythogtha, a god he believed spoke to him in dreams, in which he heard the same phrase repeated over an over: "you must make the Red Offering". However, the cult of Ythogtha has dwindled for centuries due to persecution from the more powerful cult of Ghatanothoa, so although the position of high-priest was vacant, there was no viable authority to cement Zanthu's claim to it. To rectify this, Zanthu plans to obtain the talisman known as the Black Seal of the wizard Iraan, with which he would be enabled to summon Ythogtha and establish his position indisputably.

Zanthu travels to the southern parts of Mu, and is accompanied by his younger brother Kuth, who Zanthu resents for having won the attentions of a young woman named Yeena, who Zanthu himself was in love with. In a temple of Shub-Niggurath, Zanthu consults the Ygoth Records, written by a disciple of Iraan, which reveal that the Black Seal was brought to Earth by the Outer Ones from Yuggoth, and is now buried in Iraan's own tomb in the Land of Yish. With this information, Zanthu, Kuth, and their Gyaa-Hua servants find the tomb of the mummified wizard, still holding the Black Seal. As soon as they touch the talisman, however, the mummy opens its eyes and grabs Kuth by the throat, strangling him. Given the choice between saving his brother or seizing the opportunity to take the talisman, Zanthu chooses the latter. Kuth dies and the mummy crumbles to dust. As he buries his brother and returns to his homeland, Zanthu realizes that he has made the Red Offering, and not only would have the power he craved, but also Yeena.

### Publication History

*The Xothic Legend Cycle: The Complete Mythos Fiction of Lin Carter (1997)
*Die Xothic-Legenden (2004, German language translation)

"The Reliquary" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author C. P. Webster.

### Synopsis
The story begins with a letter from a Miskatonic University scholar introducing the author of the second part: a French occultist with a gift for photography who was found dead of extreme fear in the early part of the 20th century.

The journal entries which follow detail the man's experiments in photographing a medium, his discovery that some bizarre entity haunts the woman, and that it may in fact be coming for him.

### Publication History
"The Reliquary" was published in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2020. It was later reprinted in Webster's anthology Lovecraft's Cat and Other Tales of Weird Fiction, published in 2025.

### Trivia 
*The language in which the entity speaks is clearly intended to be R'lyehian.

fullContent:
"The Render of the Veils" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story written by British horror fiction author Ramsey Campbell.

### Plot
When Kevin Gillman allows stranger Henry Fisher to share his taxi for convenience, Fisher begins to talk about occult practices, and a fascinated Gillman agrees to accompany him home to perform an unspecified ritual. 

Upon reaching Fisher's home, the man explains to Gillman that he had joined a witchcraft society while at university and, while the others had been expelled once the group was discovered, he had managed to keep his membership secret, and continued with the practices he had learned there. He further explains that he had used his copy of The Revelations of Glaaki to travel to other dimensions, and in one discovered a cult of priests who told him of their god, Daoloth. Looking in to the legends of Daoloth, Fisher decided that he wished to summon the deity and have it grant him the ability to perceive things as they truly are in all dimensions, including the past and the future.

Gillman agrees to participate in the ritual, but neither man is prepared for the outcome. Despite their preparations and safeguards, the ability to see in all dimensions drives the two completely insane, and Fisher kills Gillman before taking his own life.

### Characters
*Kevin Gillman, an average man with an interest in witchcraft.
*Henry Fisher, an occultist.
*The Priests of Daoloth, a group of religious beings.

### Publication History
The Render of the Veils was first printed in Ramsey Campbell's short story collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, and was subsequently reprinted in his collection Cold Print.

### Trivia
*Amongst the places Fisher claims to have visited on his interdimensional travels are Yuggoth and Tond.
*The story takes place in the town of Brichester in Campbell's fictional Severn Valley, the setting for many of his Mythos contributions.
*The name of Kevin Gillman is possibly a nod to the character Walter Gilman from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Dreams in the Witch-House", in which Gilman was a researcher in non-Euclidean calculus and quantum physics.

shortDefinition: "The Repairer of Reputations" is a short story published by Robert W. Chambers in the collection The King in Yellow in 1895. The story is an example of Chambers' horror fiction, and is one of the stories in the collection which contains the motif of ...
fullContent:
"The Repairer of Reputations" is a short story published by Robert W. Chambers in the collection The King in Yellow in 1895. The story is an example of Chambers' horror fiction, and is one of the stories in the collection which contains the motif of the Yellow Sign and the King in Yellow.

### Story
The story is set in New York City in the year 1925, 30 years in the future of the story's publication. The protagonist, one Hildred Castaigne, is a young man whose personality changed drastically following a head injury sustained by falling from his horse. He was subsequently committed to an asylum for treatment of insanity by a Dr. Archer. The story is told from his subjective point of view, and due to his accident, Castaigne is a prime example of an unreliable narrator.

While still recovering, Castaigne obtained and read The King In Yellow, represented as a universally censored play which deeply disturbed him. Once a wealthy dilettante and affable man-about-town, after his accident Castaigne became an eccentric recluse who spent his days poring over old books and maps and associating with a more eccentric character, a Mr. Wilde, the "Repairer of Reputations" of the story's title.

In this alternate history, the United States has apparently prospered, significantly improving its infrastructure. The rise of a new aristocratic elite in the United States has reduced the influence and immigration of foreigners, and this is particularly evident in the case of Jews. Suicide has been legalized, Castaigne experiences, and has been made generally and readily accessible in the newly established "Government Lethal Chambers" being rapidly rolled out across other towns and cities.

Wilde claims to be the architect of a vast conspiracy which uses, amongst other devices, blackmail to influence and command powerful men whose reputations the conspiracy has saved from scandal. Hildred believes that, with Wilde's help, he will become the heir of the "Last King" of "The Imperial Dynasty of America," which Wilde says is descended of a lost kingdom from distant stars in the Hyades. However, he perceives his cousin Louis Castaigne standing before him in the line of succession, he plans to force Louis to abdicate his claim to the throne, accept exile, and never marry.

Louis, who believes that Hildred is still mentally ill, humours him by agreeing to abdicate his claim, but becomes angry when Hildred insists that Louis cannot marry his fiancee, Constance Hawberk. Hildred shocks Louis by claiming that he has murdered Dr. Archer and had Constance assassinated. When Hildred runs back to the apartment of Mr. Wilde, he finds that Wilde's feral cat has torn out his throat, utterly wrecking his plans to conquer the United States with the help of Wilde's conspiracy. The police arrive, and Hildred sees Constance crying as he is dragged away. It is unknown whether or not Hildred actually committed any murders.

The story ends with a note that Hildred Castaigne died the previous day

fullContent:
The Resurrected (also known as Shatterbrain) is a film released in 1991. It is inspired by, rather than a direct adaptation of, The Strange Case of Charles Dexter Ward by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Private detective John March (John Terry) of Providence, Rhode Island-based March Detective Agency is hired by the beautiful wife of pharmaceutical executive and researcher Charles Dexter Ward (Chris Sarandon). Ward has become peculiar and secretive, and moved out of the matrimonial home to continue his odd research in the middle of nowhere in the country. Then, he is arrested and questioned by the police after the discovery that he is having human body parts delivered to him...

It transpires that "Charles Dexter Ward" has become possessed, mentally and spiritually, by his ancestor, a wizard. In the process he has become a ghoul, requiring fresh raw meat and fresh blood to feed upon and maintain control of his hunger.

### Behind the Mythos
Written by Dan O'Bannon, the plot of the film borrows from the Lovecraft original, and follows some of the concepts in the original story. It also tries to make Providence and Rhode Island into "characters" in their own right, which is true to Lovecraft's original vision in his cosmic horror work.

fullContent:
The Resurrectionists is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author Michael Patrick Hicks, the first in his Salem Hawley series of historical horror fiction. It was first published by High Fever Books, Hicks's own small press label, in June 2019; paperback, ebook and audio download editions were released, and it was also translated into French as a solely digital release .

### Synopsis
In 1788, New York City is in the grip of an epidemic of body snatchings targeting the black community, ostensibly for the purpose of medical research, but which also provide cover for a darker purpose: a cabal of occultists in possession of a copy of the Al Azif are conducting experiments on summoning the Old Ones spoken of in its pages.

As racial tensions in the city intensify, former slave Salem Hawley attempts to even the score with the graverobbers, despite the uncaring attitude of the local authorities. However, the cabal ramps up their efforts in the midst of a protest at the bodysnatchers, slaughtering dozens of young medical students and opening a portal which allows the Old Ones to break through. Only the intervention of Hawley and a small band of plucky protesters prevents the breach from remaining open and spewing forth monsters which would destroy the world.

At the story's conclusion, and providing a set up for the following book, Hawley is recruited by a senior medical man, Richard Bayley, to track down the stolen Al Azif, ostensibly to destroy the book in an effort to keep the Earth safe. However, Hawley is unaware that Bayley is in fact the cabal's leader, having escaped during the confusion caused by the breach in reality, and intent on retrieving his property from a traitorous cultist.

### Behind the Mythos
The background events described in The Resurrectionists are based around the real-world 1788 Doctors' Riots, a spat of civil disobedience in New York City triggered by the medical profession's proclivity for corpse-snatching . Some members of the occult cabal were also based on real people, including Richard Bayley himself, although with a great deal of artistic licence applied .

shortDefinition: "The Return of Rhan-Tegoth" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Laurence J. Cornford, first published in the April 1998 edition of online fanzine Nightscapes. As its title suggests, it is a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Horror in the Mu...
fullContent:
"The Return of Rhan-Tegoth" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Laurence J. Cornford, first published in the April 1998 edition of online fanzine Nightscapes. As its title suggests, it is a sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Horror in the Museum", featuring the monstrous Rhan-Tegoth.

### Synopsis
British artist Daniel Sykes is invited by his colleague Philip Goodwin to see his recently acquired "masterpiece": a 15 ft. tall wax sculpture of a monster chewing on the corpse of a horribly mutilated man. The piece is called "The Sacrifice to Rhan-Tegoth", by George Rogers. Goodwin reveals that it was briefly exhibited in a London museum in the 1920s, but removed due to public outcry. During the war, all the museum's sculptures were stored in a warehouse, but with the destruction of the museum and the death of the owners, the pieces ended up being auctioned.

Sykes is both impressed and repulsed by the piece. At night, he dreams of a mountainous landscape and a dark city. The scenery changes and Sykes dreams of being a white bear-like creature with multiple legs and a single horn, hunting humans in the ice plains along with others of his kind. Finally, he dreams of a submerged stone city and being a bladder-like aquatic creature known as a Pirrak. He sees Rhan-Tegoth sitting on a throne, and the Pirrak present themselves to it. Those judged worthy by Rhan-Tegoth would be infused with some of its "godly matter" while the rest would be devoured.

On the next day, Sykes returns to Goodwin's studio, which the latter has filled with several paintings of Rhan-Tegoth. Goodwin, to Sykes' surprise, has experienced the same dreams. He reveals that Rhan-Tegoth is not a wax sculpture, but a living creature in a state of suspended animation, which can send telepathic messages in dreams. By offering small animals to it, Goodwin claims to be nurturing it back to full strength, at which point he believes Rhan-Tegoth will be instrumental in orchestrating the return of the old gods, and reward those who have served him. When Sykes sees the dead animals on a tray, he assumes that Goodwin is insane and tries to take the tray from him, but is knocked out by Goodwin in the ensuing fight.

When Sykes resumes consciousness, he finds that Rhan-Tegoth is gone, and notices a stream of water mixed with some blood coming from under the washroom door. Standing close to the door, Sykes hears the sounds of someone inside, who he assumes to be Goodwin, although the latter doesn't answer him. Trying to find something to break the door open, Sykes stumbles upon an object that he soon recognizes as Goodwin's body, reduced to an almost empty skin. The washroom door bursts open, revealing Rhan-Tegoth. Sykes tries to defend himself with a fire extinguisher, but it has no effect on the creature. The monster grabs Sykes and leaves the warehouse to dive into a nearby river, on its way back to the sea.

### Publication History

* Nightscapes April 1998
* Cthulhu Codex Lammas 1998

fullContent:
"The Return of the Lloigor" is a story by Colin Wilson that first appeared in Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1969). The story turned Lloigor, August Derleth's minor Great Old One, into an alien species of psychic vampires--a depiction that has influenced subsequent writers, including Robert Anton Wilson, Alan Moore, and Grant Morrison.

### Synopsis
Wilson's story follows Paul Lang, a 72-year-old professor of English literature at the University of Virginia. Lang makes a breakthrough that allows him to decipher the Voynich Manuscript--a real-world tome written in an unknown script--and finds that it is the text of a book called the Necronomicon. This leads him to the (supposedly) fictional work of H. P. Lovecraft and Arthur Machen, and the Machen connection takes him to Wales, where he meets Colonel Lionel Urquart, author of The Mysteries of Mu. (Urquart is a fictionalized version of "Colonel" James Churchward, a Devonshire engineer who concocted the lost continent of Mu.)

Urquart tells Lang about the Lloigor, alien entities, probably from the Andromeda galaxy, that "existed as 'vortices' of power in their natural state." The Lloigor enslaved humanity on Mu before becoming weakened and retreating underground and beneath the oceans. They still have the power to cause great violence--they are responsible for the destruction of not only Mu but Atlantis, and for the ruin of various lost cities around the world, including the two great ruined cities of North America, Grudèn Itzà, now sunk beneath the swampland around New Orleans, and Nam-Ergest, a flourishing city that once stood on the land where the Grand Canyon now yawns.The Lloigor also have the power to incite violence in individual people--"[m]urder, cruelty, rape, every possible kind of sexual perversion"—and are particularly powerful in certain locales--notably Caerleon in Wales, and Cohasset, Massachusetts, which is presented as the real-life counterpart of Innsmouth. 

After being menaced by Ben Chickno, a "thorough degenerate" Romani allied with the Lloigor, Lang and Urquart become convinced that the aliens are "planning a major attack on the inhabitants of the earth." The story closes with a note from Lang's nephew, Julian F. Lang, explaining that his uncle and Urquart disappeared while flying in a small plane over Virginia, on their way to a meeting Lang's old classmate, Senator James R. Pinckney, had arranged with the Secretary of Defense.

### The Lloigor
Urquart tells Lang  that the Lloigor, although infinitely more powerful than men, were also aware that optimism would be absurd in this universe. Their minds were a unity, not compartmentalised, like ours. There was no distinction in them between conscious, subconscious, and superconscious mind. So they saw things clearly all the time, without the possibility of averting the mind from the truth, or forgetting.Urquart compares them to "those suicidal romantics of the nineteenth century, steeped in gloom, convinced that life

fullContent:
"The Return of the Sorcerer" is a short story written by American author and artist Clark Ashton Smith which is set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos. The story was first published in Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror in September 1931, then in the Arkham House anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos, and later received an eBook issue with Wildside Press's The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack in 2012.

### Synopsis
After a down-on-his-luck scholar takes a job as a live-in secretary, translator and general assistant to an elderly occultist, he begins to experience a sense of deep unease. Strange noises in the night disturb his sleep and the obvious state of fear in which his employer lives only enhance this feeling.

Soon, events cause the occultist to divulge the fact that he and his brother had been dark magicians before he killed his more-powerful twin, and that the noises are his sibling's dismembered body parts returning to drive the man insane with terror before murdering him. He further reveals that he brought the other man into his home in an effort to find a way to banish his brother's restless spirit.

The story culminates with the various body parts of the dead sorcerer rejoining themselves, then killing his treacherous brother and dismembering the corpse with the same tools that were used upon his.

### Characters
*Mr. Ogden, a well-educated man fluent in Arabic who goes to work for elderly occultist John Carnby.
*John Carnby, a lifelong occultist who grew jealous of his brother's superior knowledge, and killed him. He was later haunted by the vengeful spirit of his more-powerful sibling.
* Helman Carnby, John's brother and fellow occultist who was capable of delving deeper into the dark arts than his twin ever could, and was subsequently murdered for this. Later returned to wreak his revenge upon John.

### Mythos References
The volume consulted by Ogden and Carnby in the search for a spell to exorcise Helman's spirit was an original Arabic version of the Necronomicon.

### In Other Media
The story was adapted as an episode of the television horror anthology series Night Gallery (first aired 24 September 1972), starring Vincent Price and Bill Bixby, and an episode of the radio drama series Suspense, featuring Tucker Smallwood (first aired 2012).

"The Return of the Witch" is a short story by Ramsey Campbell that appeared in his 1964 collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants.

### Synopsis
The witch of the title is Gladys Shorrock, who in the late 1910s comes to live, with her son Robert, at 7 Victoria Road in Brichester's Mercy Hill neighbourhood. At first little things are amiss: Her shrubbery grows unnaturally quickly, and a neighbour complains that "it rains on’t garden at them Shorrocks, though there ain’t no wet ground anywhere else!” The windows on one room facing the street are permanently shuttered.

Later incidents are more uncanny:

One man says that he "followed her toward Severnford and fled a gigantic glowing figure which strode after him through the forest."

Her son Robert, who was once fired from a construction job for walling up a black cat "in imitation of an ancient street-christening ceremony", dies in 1924, and Gladys dies the next year, on Halloween, found staring out her window with glazed eyes.

The house remains empty for some 35 years, when on February 1, I960, Norman Owen, a novelist from Lancashire, moves in. He is not deterred by the warnings he receives--particularly from Stanley Nash, a doctor at Mercy Hill's hospital. When he enters the house's shuttered room--against Nash's advice--he suffers a dizzy spell, and finds a neon pentagram hanging from the ceiling, that seemed "as though it radiated darkness". 

Owen begins having bad dreams, including one involving grave robbing--the ends with him waking up fully dressed, with his shoes caked with mud. Nash diagnoses that "the— soul, spirit, life-force, whatever you like—of the witch has been co-existing in your body." His advice: "drink as much black coffee as you can hold.”

Owen has another dream, where he retrieves a three-foot round wooden chest from a passageway in a hill in the countryside--only to wake and find the chest in his living room. Fighting an urge to open the chest, he telephones Nash and has him smash the pentacle--which seems to dispel the possession. They burn the chest--"only a long white member fell out as the lid warped"--and then Owen moves back to Southport in Lancashire.

fullContent:
"The Return of Zhosph" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gary Myers.

### Synopsis
Snurd is a man who studies the Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan, and lives in the city of Zulan-Thek where necromancy is forbidden and bodies are not to be buried. As such, when the bodies of two people named Klotlei and Shek were dug up in the night by sextons from Gak, he left Zulan-Thek to follow them, believing that the bodies will be used for witchcraft. He followed them through the hippogryph-flanked vine-hidden stone gates and entered a series of catacombs where he discovered a vault where the sextons disposed of the bodies of malefactors from Zulan-Thek including Klotlei and Shek. He realizes through the story of a thaumaturge named Zhosph that he had a retinue of shadows that feasted on Zulan-Thek's palaces and fanes in the night, and that the sextons had some kind of unfinished business. But they discovered things were altered. The hippogryph statues were changed to look smug, He continued following the sextons, the vines misbehaved strangely, disturbing the dwelling rats and scarabs within, and even strangling them, and there was wailing within the catacombs. A man claimed that something has been brought back to life and shifted the tomb, seeing a bat signaling something horrid coming. The sextons approached the dead body of Zhosph, whose skull was split open and whose brain was missing, and a yellowish membrane found as Snurd's body turns inside out, confirming that Zhosph has possessed him.

### Publication History
First published in the March 1972 issue of the fanzine HPL, "The Return of Zhosph" has also been included in the collections The House of the Worm (1975) and The Country of the Worm: Excursions Beyond the Wall of Sleep (2013).

The Revelations of Glaaki is a fictional grimoire in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Inhabitant of the Lake". 

### Overview
The Revelations of Glaaki is a holy text containing the collected wisdom of Glaaki.

A 12-volume book in English, it was written by the members of the Cult of Glaaki atop Mercy Hill between 1800-1865. The book is fragmentary, with one cult member taking up where the last left off, and deals with the worship, powers and methods of summoning Glaaki, Y'golonac, Daoloth, and other Great Old Ones.

The book was published in a pirated and edited nine-volume version published in 1865 as a folio, which is the more common version of it. A rumour claims that originally there were only 11 volumes, but a man on Mercy Hill in the Severn Valley, England, dreamed of, and then wrote, the 12th volume. Copies of the nine-volume version are held by many major libraries and by private collectors. Handwritten 11-volume (a set of old type loose-leaf notebooks, the pages covered in archaic handwriting) and 12-volume versions are almost unheard of. There has been some talk of Volumes 13 and 14, but such volumes are unknown.

### Contents
* A history of Glaaki's travels amongst the stars in the many long years before he settled on Earth.
* The Daoloth formula, a ritual designed to invoke the presence of Daoloth.
* The Pentacle of Planes, instructions on how to create a magical barrier which will prevent entities such as the aforementioned Daoloth from manifesting in our universe.

### Volumes
* I. On Conjuration 
* II. On the Purposes of Night 
* III. Of the Uses of the Dead 
* IV. Of the World as Lair 
* V. Of the Secrets Behind the Stars 
* VI. Of Humanity as a Chrysalis 
* VII. Of Things Seen by the Moon 
* VIII. Of the Symbols the Universe Shows 
* IX. Of the Dreaming of Creation 
* X. On Preparing the Table 
* XI. On Passing From View (endnotes)

fullContent:
"The Revenge of Azathoth" is a horror comedy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It is the second installment of Peter Cannon's six-part novella Forever Azathoth, which serves as a humourous sequel to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Thing on the Doorstep".

"The Revenge of Azathoth" was originally published in the 1995 anthology The Azathoth Cycle along with the previous installment, "Azathoth in Arkham". The entire series would later appear in Cannon's collections Forever Azathoth and Other Horrors (1999) and Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches (2011).

### Synopsis
(Continued from "Azathoth in Arkham"...)

The second part of the saga is narrated by Vartan Bagdasarian, a fervent admirer of Edward Derby's work who moves to Arkham to study at Miskatonic University with the explicit purpose of learning as much as possible about his literary hero. Bagdasarian was one of the founding members of the Dead Edward Derby Society and became close to Edward Upton, in part due to the fact that Edward controlled the Derby literary estate. Eventually, he got Edward's permission to examine a cupboard in Derby's old study where he found piles of unpublished material.

After the group's nocturnal visit to Derby's grave, however, Bagdasarian notes that Edward's behaviour has changed drastically. Originally meek and gentlemanly, he suddenly became rude, crude, and boisterous, and started to engage in vicious arguments with the Society's newest member, the Innsmouth girl Wendy Babson, who actually resents the late Derby due to the fact that he forced his wife Asenath to fire her Innsmouth servants, including Wendy's older sister Eunice. The verbal fights between Edward and Wendy reach bizarre levels, in which the two antagonise each other by exchanging quips about shoggoths and quotes from the Necronomicon, alienating the rest of the Society. Bagdasarian, who doesn't know that Edward is now possessed by the mind of the wizard Ephraim Waite, speculates that the recent death of Edward's parents might have contributed to the change. Soon, the entire group cuts ties with Edward, except for Bagdasarian himself, who is still studying the manuscripts, and, ironically, Wendy, who ceases the hostilities and starts flirting with Edward instead.

Edward marries Wendy, albeit only to avoid being drafted. Unfortunately for him, as World War Two escalates, he ends up being drafted anyway. Edward collapses, apparently loses his mind, and is committed to an asylum, where he is found and strangled by his former butler, Soames. While being arrested, the butler is heard to repeat the word "Azathoth". Wendy confides to Bagdasarian that she is pregnant with Edward's child, who is to be named Ephraim.

(...The story continues in "The House of Azathoth".)

### Connections
*Some of Edward Derby's stories were published in the pulp magazine Whispers. (: "The Unnamable")

shortDefinition: The Rhesus Chart  is the fifth novel in Charles Stross's Laundry Files series, published by Ace Books and Orbit in 2014. Like other books in the series, it blends elements of the Cthulhu Mythos with the spy thriller and bureaucratic office comedy gen...
fullContent:
The Rhesus Chart  is the fifth novel in Charles Stross's Laundry Files series, published by Ace Books and Orbit in 2014. Like other books in the series, it blends elements of the Cthulhu Mythos with the spy thriller and bureaucratic office comedy genres; this entry expands the genre-blending to include modern vampire horror.

Set in spring 2013, the novel tells the story of Alex Schwartz, a programmer at a high-powered investment bank who turns himself into a vampire-like creature by feeding an advanced dataset into a fractal visualizer. He then transforms his colleagues--including Mhari Murphy, introduced in The Atrocity Archive as Bob Howard's sometime girlfriend. (Howard is the narrator but not the main character of The Rhesus Chart.)

The story's vampires are known as PHANGs--Photogolic Hemophagic Anagathic Neurotropic mumble-mumble, later explained as Person of Hemophagic Autocombusting Nocturnal Glamour--and are not undead, but rather are hosts for extradimensional parasites. These entities confer superhuman powers at the cost of inducing an inexorable drive to consume human blood, which has the unfortunate side effect of inducing dementia in the blood donor.

The vampire investment bankers are recruited by the Laundry (Britain's occult secret service) as special assets--and find themselves caught up in a struggle between ancient vampires, one of whom has cast a glamour on the Laundry that convinces everyone that there's no such thing as vampires. The confrontation that results when the agency realizes that not only do vampires exist, one has infiltrated the organization for decades, results in the death of Howard's boss, James Angleton.

### Inspiration
Stross has said that he wrote a vampire-based novel because he "got bored with British spy thriller authors" and decided to start a "new cycle remixing contemporary fantasy sub-genres."

### Publication History
The Rhesus Chart was released as a hardcover and an ebook in July 2014, by Ace Books in the United States and Orbit in Britain. The British paperback was published in April 2015 by Orbit, and the US paperback in July 2015 by Ace.

"The Riddle of Jeremy Roman" is a Lovecraftian short story by Canadian author Dean Wirth, and is the second in a series begun with "The Dewey Mine Attack". It was published in the Lammas Eve edition of Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in 2020.

### Synopsis
Told through a series of letters, news reports, medical charts, and government memorandums, "The Riddle of Jeremy Roman" begins by telling of the rehabilitation of Bryan Katz, the sole survivor of the previous story who had been driven to insanity by his experiences. It then goes on to describe the experiences of two brothers, Joshua and Jeremy Roman, seamen serving aboard the battleship USS Connecticut in 1919. These men were the sole survivors of an attack by the star-creatures encountered by Katz decades earlier, although they later died from bizarre and horrific complications as a result of physical contact with the beings.

fullContent:
"The Ring of Set" is a short story written by Richard L. Tierney, the first of his Simon of Gitta tales to be published. It appeared in Swords Against Darkness in 1977.

The story introduced Simon of Gitta, based on the biblical figure of Simon Magus and modeled on Jack Palance's portrayal of that figure in the 1954 film The Silver Chalice.

Set in March, 37 AD, the story involves the ex-gladiator Simon's attempt to retrieve the Ring of Set, a powerful and cursed magic item once owned by the Stygian sorcerer Thoth-Amon, that had fallen into the hands of the Roman Emperor Tiberius. Simon also comes into conflict with Tiberius' nephew Gaius, better known as Caligula.

In the story, Simon is described as:

The Ring of Set first appeared in Robert E. Howard's Conan story "The Phoenix on the Sword", and made a reappearance in Howard's "The Haunter of the Ring". Tierney describes the item as "a strange ornament, fashioned in the shape of a thrice-coiled serpent gripping its tail in its mouth. The eyes were small, bright yellow jewels that seemed almost to twinkle with an inner life of their own." The ring carries a curse that dooms any ruler who wears it; Tiberius ignores Simon's warning about the curse, to his later regret.

The ring allows the entity Set--described as "the most ancient and evil god ever worshiped by the race of man"--to fatally feed on Tiberius' life essence; the curse provides a fictional explanation for Tiberius' death, which in actual history did occur on March 16, AD 37. In the novel The Drums of Chaos--published three decades later but set earlier in the chronology of the series--Tierney identifies Set with the Cthulhu Mythos deity Hastur.

In "The Ring of Set", Simon cites the Book of Thoth--"written more than ten thousand years ago by Thoth-Amon"--as possibly holding the secret to negating the curse of the ring.

### Behind the Mythos
Tierney wrote "The Ring of Set" around 1960, after seeing The Silver Chalice and being struck by Palance's portrayal of the sorcerer Simon Magus. "I never intended it to be the start of a series," Tierney later said. The story remained unpublished for about 16 years, until Tierney's friend Kirby McCauley submitted it to Andy Offutt, who was preparing the first in a series of sword & sorcery anthologies. Its reception upon publication encouraged Tierney to write more stories featuring Simon.

### Publication History
*Swords Against Darkness (1977, 1990)
*The Scroll of Thoth: Simon Magus and the Great Old Ones (1997)
*Sorcery Against Caesar (2020)

fullContent:
"The Ring of the Demon God" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and editor Robert Weinberg.

### Synopsis
After being shipwrecked and captured by a group of "fishmen" (clearly intended to be Deep Ones), a small group of people use the power contained in a ring worn by of one of their number, the Seal of Nyarlathotep. The story culminates with a battle between Nyarlathotep and a colossal entity known as the "Dweller in the Deep" which Nyarlathotep easily wins, before the group settle down to wait for rescue.

### Characters

* Alan Young, a shipwreck survivor.
* Morgan Smith, a man who has lived for centuries using the power of his ring.
* Farrel, a former sailor in charge of the Deep One prison camp.
* Anise Van, a shipwreck survivor.
* Nyarlathotep, an Outer God.
* The Dweller in the Deep, the god of the fishmen, likely Dagon.

### Publication History
"The Ring of the Demon God" was published in the online Mythos zine Nightscapes in June 1997.

fullContent:
"The River of Night's Dreaming" is a haunting and mysterious short story by Karl Edward Wagner. It is redolent with the same kind of atmosphere, and some of the names and setting, as Robert W. Chamber's original King in Yellow novel. It was first published in the anthology Whispers III by Doubleday in August 1981. 

### Synopsis
The story begins with a bus crash. A bus transporting prisoners plunges down a cliff, leaving a nameless female prisoner from Coastal State Prison free to start her life again. Swimming across a bay to an unnamed city she finds it looks like it hasn't been developed since the turn of the twentieth century. Escaping an unknown, and apparently deformed, assailant, she finds shelter with Mrs Castaigne and her maid Camilla, adopting the name of 'Cassilda Archer' (in part after her therapist, Doctor Archer), as a cover. A daughter, Miss Constance Castaigne is mentioned but is not present, it later being revealed she'd been sent to a hospital with brain fever. Cassilda is engaged as a companion to Mrs Castaigne and is asked to read to her from The King in Yellow, from a copy of the play that used to belong to her daughter Constance. which she finds evil and disturbing, but compelling. 

In this possible dream-world, events become more mysterious and distubing. Finally, "Cassilda Archer" makes an escape from the city, to an unknown destination. 

A final scene with Doctor Archer at the hospital, finding a copy of the King In Yellow, reveals the patient's body has not been found. In the book is written the name 'Constance Castaigne'.

After first chasing it off with a heavy-caliber handgun, he then tracks it with a large-bore sniper rifle, killing the creature when it is backlit by nearby Fourth of July fireworks.

The Roof of the World is a Doctor Who audio play released in 2004 by Big Finish Productions. It pits the alien time-traveler known as the Doctor against the Great Old Ones in Tibet, 1917.

The play was written by Adrian Rigelsford, directed by Gary Russell, and stars Peter Davison as the Doctor, Nicola Bryant as Peri Brown, Caroline Morris as Erimem, Sylvester Morand as General Alexander Bruce, Alan Cox as John Matthews, Edward de Souza as Lord Mortimer Davey, and William Franklyn as Pharaoh Amenhotep II.

### Synopsis
### Part One
The Doctor lands his spacetime machine, known as the TARDIS, aboard a train in 1917 Tibet, where he expects to attend a cricket match that will be held at the Grand Imperial Hotel. His traveling companions are Peri, who is from 20th century America, and Erimem, the daughter of an Egyptian pharaoh from the 15th century BC. On the way to the hotel, they meet a man named Lord Davey, whose body, unknown to them, is inhabited by a servant of the Great Old Ones, as the original Davey was killed after finding a pyramid-shaped structure inside an icy cave in the mountains. When he approaches Erimem, she starts hearing ghostly whispers, leading him to realise that she might be the key to his masters' return.

Arriving at the hotel, the Doctor and his companions meet General Alexander Bruce and his assistant/chronicler John Matthews. Erimem, who has never seen snow before, seems to recognise one of the peaks as the "White Pyramid" she was warned about as a child: a place where the evils of the world are sealed. The cricket match is interrupted by a monstrous cloud-like entity which descends from the mountain and chases the terrified crowds, who seek shelter inside the hotel. Erimem receives a telepathic message from Davey. Instead of joining the others in the hotel, she moves outside and allows herself to be engulfed by the cloud monster.

### Part Two
As a disembodied spirit, Erimem witnesses the Doctor deliver an eulogy for her, as she is believed to be dead. She tries in vain to communicate with Peri, but Davey explains that she has moved to another level of existence and can't interact with the others. She then finds herself transported to a temple in her own native Egypt. After several distressing visions, fabricated to break Erimem's spirit, Davey shows her his own original body. He explains that before taking the body of Lord Davey, the servant of the Great Old Ones was a priest who discovered these ancient beings inside a pyramidal structure within the mountain. The cloud monster is merely the Old Ones' guardian, but the Old Ones themselves remain imprisoned. Since entering their service, he has used many bodies as vessels, human and animal, with Davey's body being merely the latest.

The vision then takes the form of the Doctor, who shows Erimem a scene from ancient Egypt. Erimem's father, Pharaoh Amenhotep II, came into possession of certain scrolls which described creatures older and more fearsome than the gods themse
