fullContent:
"The Room in the Castle" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Ramsey Campbell.

### Synopsis
A Londoner on an errand to the British Museum for a sick friend happens across the legend of a fearsome creature imprisoned beneath an ancient castle in the Severn Valley. Despite warnings from his friend about the danger he is putting himself in, he decides to travel to the castle and take a look for himself, not really believing that he would find anything.

Upon reaching the castle, the man, stumbling across a hidden room beneath the ruined structure, inadvertently awakens the sleeping behemoth Byatis, which has lain undisturbed for countless years. He is lucky to escape with his life.

Resolving to fix his mistake, he returns the following day equipped with several containers full of petrol, dumping them through the trapdoor and setting Byatis ablaze. However, a strange shape in the smoke may indicate that the entity did not perish as planned…

### Characters
*Parry, a well-educated man with an interest in English folklore.
*Scott, Parry's friend, a former sceptic now convinced of the existence of otherworldly forces in the Severn Valley.
*Sir Gilbert Morley, a long-dead practitioner of black magic.

### Publication History
"The Room in the Castle" was first published in the Arkham House collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants in 1964. It has since been reprinted in several volumes of Campbell's work, including Cold Print (1985) and Die Offenbarungen des Glaaki, a German-language collection of translations of several of his stories.

### Trivia
*The wizard Morley was said to have trapped Byatis in order to use its essence as a link to the "sendings" of Cthulhu, Glaaki, Daoloth, and Shub-Niggurath.

"The Rose of England" is a very short poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft, first published in the October 1916 edition of The Scot. As the title might suggest, it displays an example of Lovecraft’s anglophilia using the literary device of a rose.

Since its first publication, "The Rose of England" has been reprinted several times, and has also been translated into Portuguese as "A rosa da Inglaterra" for the Brazilian market.

"The Round Tower (Being the Narrative of Armitage Harper)" is a short piece by American author Robert M. Price. It is an alternate ending to August Derleth's The Lurker at the Threshold, replacing the third and final segment. "The Round Tower" first appeared in The Dunwich Cycle: Where the Old Gods Wait by Chaosium in November 1995.

### Synopsis
To be added

### Publication History
After being published in The Dunwich Cycle in 1995, the story appeared in both Der Cthulhu-Mythos: 1976 - 2002 (May 2003) and Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2008).

### Behind the Mythos
Price said that The Lurker at the Threshold was his favourite of Derleth’s weird fiction writings, but was deeply dissatisfied with the final segment, the "Narrative of Winfield Phillips", feeling it to was a drastic departure from the tone and style of the previous sections. As a result, he discarded it and wrote his own ending (: Blasphemies & Revelations).

"The Rummy Affair of Young Charlie" is a horror comedy short story by Peter Cannon. It is set in the Cthulhu Mythos and features Bertie Wooster and Jeeves from the works of P. G. Wodehouse, as well as "Mr. Altamont": an alias used by the detective Sherlock Holmes from the stories of Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

It is the third and final of Cannon's Cthulhu Mythos crossovers with Jeeves and Wooster, following "Cats, Rats, and Bertie Wooster" and "Something Foetid".

### Synopsis
Bertie Wooster is ordered by his frightful Aunt Agatha to go to Paris in order to look after the son of her American friends, the Wards. The young man in question is Charles Dexter Ward, an eccentric individual of scholarly inclinations, currently touring Europe. Knowing better than to refuse a request from his tyrannical aunt, Wooster and his dependable valet Jeeves duly embark to France to meet the young gentleman, who turns out to be teetotaller, uninterested in games or gambling, and dedicated solely to his undisclosed research, which involves ancient books and a laboratory. After several failed attempts to socialise, Wooster is about to give up when Ward disappears, forcing Wooster to search for him or face the wrath of Agatha.

The ever efficient Jeeves discovers that Ward is currently lodging on the Rue d'Auseil, a street that cannot be found on any map. There, Ward has befriended an elderly mute musician named Erich Zann. Jeeves' informant, an old man who introduces himself as Mr. Altamont of Chicago, is also currently a tenant in the same boarding house as Ward and Zann, and believes that the former has his eyes on a priceless manuscript authored by the latter, which Altamont himself also wishes to acquire. The only problem is that the "manuscript" hasn't been written yet.

As part of his plan to get Zann to write down the manuscript, Altamont arranges a concert in the boarding house, with Altamont himself playing the violin and Wooster singing. At the last minute, Ward insists and is allowed to join them, playing the zobo. The audience, consisting of landlord Blandot and a few other lodgers, gathers in Zann's room to listen to the show. At midnight, Altamont cues Jeeves to turn off the lights and the music commences. The songs are received with applause from all except Zann, who appears to be agitated and uncomfortable. After several numbers, Zann suddenly picks up his viol and joins in, playing wild music that Wooster can't describe properly. He then drops the instrument and sits down at a table where he frantically starts writing, while the band resumes playing. The next interruption comes from Ward, who springs at the table and tries to steal Zann's notes.

At Altamont's prompting, the audience and Jeeves jump on Ward and try to hold him down, while the American fights back viciously. "The Sacred House" is a short story by American author Brian Barr. It it the second of his King in Yellow stories, and was first published in the anthology Home Invasion by J. Ellington Ashton Press in March 2017.

### Synopsis
A drug-addicted criminal steals a copy of The King in Yellow while committing a home invasion which results in the death of the targeted family. After reading the play he is visited by the spirits of the family, devoted to the King, who tear his body apart before his soul is brought into the service of their master.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance in 2017, "The Sacred House" has also appeared in an independently-published chapbook to which it lends its name (2018), and the collection Brian Barr's King in Yellow (2019).

fullContent:
"The Saga of Hilde Ansgardóttir" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Jesse Bullington. It was first published in the thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press in April 2011.

### Synopsis
Inter-tribal conflict in Grænland causes young seeress Hilde Ansgardóttir to confront the monstrous Volund Deep-Friend and his deformed clan. She is, however, unsuccessful, and Volund's aquatic allies follow her back to her own settlement. Two different conclusions are given, one in which the humans fight off their assailants, and another in which Hilde slaughters her own people to claim leadership, apparently in the name of a slumbering god. In both instances, the survivors disappear into a series of caves, never to be seen again.

### Behind the Mythos
There are several elements in "The Saga of Hilde Ansgardóttir" which would appear to hint at Cthulhu Mythos connections: Volund Deep-Friend and his people are heavily implied to be Deep One hybrids, as illustrated in the line "That one has the Hymirbjarg look;" the Inuit who make war with Volund's people in Markland (continental North America ) are described as having "worshiped some hungry thing in the sky," a possible nod to the Great Old One Ithaqua; and the mention of "a father, The dreaming Lord, Who shapes the world in His sleep" would appear to be a reference to Cthulhu.

The story was inspired by the real-life abandonment of Greenland's Eastern Settlement , an event which remains a mystery to modern archaeologists.

### Publication History 
* Historical Lovecraft (2011)
* Grimdark Magazine (2022)

"The Salem Horror" is a short story by American author Henry Kuttner, a friend and contemporary of H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
The spirit of dark priestess Abigail Prinn, executed during the Salem Witch Trials, is awakened when a man moves into her old home and uncovers her secret "Witch Room" hidden beneath. In order to wreak her vengeance on the descendants of the townsfolk responsible for her death, Abigail attempts to summon forth a dark evil in the form of the Great Old One known as Nyogtha, using the Witch Room, but is ultimately thwarted by the intervention of occultist Michael Leigh.

### Characters
*Carson, a writer living in the former home of Abigail Prinn.
*Michael Leigh, an occultist.
*Abigail Prinn, a deceased High Priestess of Nyogtha.
*Nyogtha, a Great Old One.

### Publication History
"The Salem Horror" was first published in the May 1937 edition of pulp horror magazine Weird Tales.

"The Sandwin Compact" is a horror short story by August Derleth set in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in the November 1940 issue of the magazine Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
In 1938, a librarian named Dave, who works at Miskatonic University in Arkham, receives a phone call from his cousin Eldon asking him to come over immediately. While Eldon doesn't explain the situation, he uses a code the two cousins devised when they were children, to be used when one is in distress. As such, Dave drives hurriedly to the house where Eldon lives with his father (Dave's uncle) Asa Sandwin and a servant named Ambrose. For generations, the Sandwins have lived comfortably without any visible source of income. Whenever money ran short, Asa would go on a mysterious trip to acquire more. When he returned from the last trip, Eldon heard him talking to himself about how he "tricked them". Since then, there have been strange occurrences in the house, such as doorknobs turning up wet, as well as the sounds of footsteps and strange music. These incidents have had a strong effect on old Asa, who seems terribly frightened and apprehensive, yet refuses to acknowledge that anything is wrong. Eldon is at loss as to what to do, which is why he called Dave.

Asa Sandwin is a man with a peculiarly frog-like appearance. He is happy to see his nephew and converses amiably during dinner, until an ululating sound outside interrupts him. Asa reacts to the sound as if it conveyed some sort of meaning to him. He stands up, violently closes the windows, and excuses himself from the room. Dave thinks the sound was a bird, but Eldon attests that none of the local birds make this kind of noise. He confides to Dave that he is convinced that whatever is making these sounds is speaking to Asa. Sometimes the sounds seem to come from the sea, other times from the sky, and occasionally from the underground. Additionally, Eldon has also heard music at night, which makes him dream of strange places. When he retires to bed, Dave himself experiences the same dreams and, on the next morning, the cousins hear Asa conversing with creatures with inhuman voices inside his room. Asa tells these visitors that he has "closed the passage" that would allow Cthulhu to reach him, and taken precautions against Ithaqua, but when the creatures speak the name Lloigor, the old man has no response. Dave recognises these names from certain books he has read at Miskatonic.

fullContent:
"The Satyr" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, set in Averoigne, his semi-historical French province. It first appeared in the July 1931 issue of La Paree Stories.

### Synopsis
It tells the story of an encounter with a nature spirit in the woods of Averoigne. The satyr drives an unmarried couple into an act of uninhibited love, and provokes a husband into uncharacteristic jealous violence.

### The Satyr
A "portion of the forest of Averoigne where the trees were older and taller than all others" is "haunted by some entity inimical to man, some primordial spirit of ill that was ancienter than Christ or Satan." It is encountered in the story by two hitherto-chaste lovers:


### Characters 
*Raoul, Comte de la Frênaie: He is "by nature the most unsuspicious of husbands." Noted for his limited imagination, he divides nearly all his time between hunting and drinking.
*Adèle: Raoul's wife, noted for her "wine-dark tresses" and "her golden eyes."
*Olivier du Montoir: A young poet, an "erudite and comely youth" who is becoming known beyond Averoigne for his poems praising Adele's beauty. He "might in time have rivaled Ronsard as one of the most brilliant luminaries of the Pleiade."

### Publication History
"The Satyr" was the only one of Smith's Averoigne tales that did not first appear in Weird Tales. Instead, it made its debut in the July 1931 issue of La Paree Stories, a pulp magazine specializing in "spicy" stories.

Since then, "The Satyr" has appeared in several collections of Smith's fiction, starting with Genius Loci and Other Tales (Arkham House, 1948). It is included in both The Averoigne Archives (Pickman's Press, 2019) and The Averoigne Chronicles (Hippocampus Press, 2021).

"The Scales of Justice" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. It was published in his collection Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir by Elder Signs Press in September 2008.

### Synopsis
Tough Arkham private detective Bill Sweetan takes on the case of Warren Peasley, a man who has been receiving mysterious notes, notes which contain only the words "Return the child". During the course of his investigations, he learns that Peasley enjoys collecting and stuffing exotic snakes. His latest acquisition, a creature he encountered in Oklahoma, defies classification and bears a strange diamond-shaped marking on its head.

As the letters continue to arrive, Sweetan locates the man who has been sending them: a Native American fellow named Jim Thunderhawk, who informs him that unless Peasley returns the strange snake to its home, Great Yig, the father of serpents, will manifest to take its revenge. Predictably, Peasley ignores this warning, and the man is gruesomely murdered by his taxidermied collection of serpents.

fullContent:
"The Scourge of B'Moth" is a horror short story by Bertram Russell, first published in the May 1929 issue of Weird Tales.

The story's titular entity has since been incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by Henry Hasse in "The Guardian of the Book", and would go on to be portrayed as an avatar of Cthulhu in the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
A psychiatrist named Randall is called by his eminent friend and colleague, Dr. Prendergast, to assist in an unusual case. The patient appears to be possessed by an entity that he refers to as "the Master". On the way to the hospital, the road seems to be covered in fog and drizzle, and Randall feels a supernatural presence trying to control him. Even though the windows are closed, the interior of the car is strangely cold and humid. Randall feels better when he turns the heater on, but soon after turning it off he loses control of the car and crashes. He finds to his great surprise that the night is clear, with no fog whatsoever, and the grass and the windshields are dry, bearing no hint of the drizzle.

In the hospital, Prendergast shows Randall the patient, who seems to be inexplicably aware of Randall's experience in the car earlier. He also tells them of his own imminent death and how in death he will join the Master, who lives deep in the ocean and manifests itself through water, rain, and fog. After the patient dies, the two doctors are stunned to witness the water in a nearby glass shine with a bluish light and evaporate into mist.

Several days later, Randall reads a newspaper report from Peru about a man who tried to commit suicide by drowning and assaulted his rescuer, yelling that he had been called by the Master, B'Moth. Soon after reading it, Randall receives a call from the hospital informing him that Prendergast has gone insane.

Prendergast tells Randall that he's been struggling to fight off the Master's influence, and also refers to the Master's name as "B'Moth". For the past days, his mind has been plagued by the thought that civilization ought to collapse and mankind will return to the "days of the jungle". When Randall offers him a glass of water, Prendergast refuses and throws it away. He also informs Randall that B'Moth already has millions of followers throughout the world, and pleads Randall to find a way to deter them.

Dr. Prendergast escapes from the hospital and steals a tank filled with reptiles and amphibians: animals that are associated with B'Moth, and worshiped by its cultists. fullContent:
"The Scroll of Morloc" is a fantasy short story, first published in the October 1975 issue of the magazine Fantastic, where it was identified as being by Clark Ashton Smith and Lin Carter. When incorporated into the 2002 anthology The Book of Eibon, it was credited solely to Carter.

"The Scroll of Morloc" is a rare example of a Mythos story in which no humans appear (although they are mentioned).

### Synopsis
In ancient Hyperborea, a Voormi shaman named Yhemog is infuriated after his seventh failed attempt to be elected high-priest. Embittered, he abandons his faith in Tsathoggua and decides to get revenge on his own people by trespassing into their temple and stealing the scroll of Morloc, which the Voormis themselves had stolen from their hated enemies, the Gnophkehs.

Putting the guards to sleep with a spell, Yhemog violates the chamber where the idol of Tsathoggua is located, and takes the scroll that had been placed at the god's feet. Not satisfied with that, he mocks the idol by reciting the rituals of the Gnophkehs in praise of their own god and Tsathoggua's enemy, Rhan-Tegoth. As soon as he does so, Yhemog sees himself transformed into a Gnophkeh and screams, thus attracting the attention of the guards, who brutally deal with the intruder.

fullContent:
"The Scroll of Thoth" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney that pits his sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta against the most notorious villain of Ancient Rome--the Emperor Caligula. The second story about Simon to appear, it first saw print in Swords Against Darkness #2, published in 1977.

### Synopsis
The insane Emperor Caligula acquires the ancient and malevolent Scroll of Thoth, toying recklessly with its dark power. Simon vows to steal the scroll from under the watchful eyes of the Praetorian Guard before Caligula unleashes an eldritch force.

### Setting
The story is set in Rome in January, A. D. 41.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Swords Against Darkness, "The Scroll of Thoth" was reprinted as the title story of the Simon of Gitta collection The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997), and was also included in the expanded edition Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

fullContent:
"The Scuttler in the Dark" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ran Cartwright.

### Synopsis
Gary receives a mysterious bite whilst hiking in northern Arizona's Hualapai Mountains. Soon afterwards, the bizarre dreams begin, along with a voice in his head which imparts to Gary indecipherable knowledge. The voice quickly lures him into the long-abandoned Fire Mine, where he is confronted by a nest of the children of Atlach-Nacha, along with the fearsome being itself, who uses his body as a host to spawn more of her babies.

### Characters
*Gary, an average Joe with a love of hiking.
*Atlach-Nacha, a fearsome being from another reality.

### Publication History
*Cthulhu Cultus #15 (1999)
*Nightscapes #13 (2000)
*Thirteen Stories #3 (2002)
*Of Gods & Aliens (2011)

### Trivia
*Whilst speaking to Gary, Atlach-Nacha feeds him information on a variety of Mythos staples including Azathoth, Yog-Sothoth, R'lyeh and Kadath. Why she should choose to do this is not explained.

"The Sea Nymph's Son" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
At the conclusion of the Trojan War, after Paris kills the demigod Achilles in a cowardly manner, Achilles' mother Thetis calls forth "the Kraken" who lays waste to the doomed city of Troy.

*Achilles, demigod son of Thetis.
*Andromache, Hector's wife.
*Agamemnon, Greek king.
*Thetis, Achilles' mother.
*The Kraken, Great Cthulhu.

### Publication History
"The Sea Nymph's Son" was published in the thematic anthology World War Cthulhu, edited by Brian M. Sammons and Glynn Owen Barrass, in 2014.

*Neither Achilles not his mother Thetis appear to be human in this story.

fullContent:
"The Sea-Spider" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A writer moves to a seaside retreat for the dual purposes of finishing his book and escaping his psychotic ex-girlfriend. While strolling down the beach one day, he rescues a bizarre creature which he nicknames the Sea-Spider.

Eventually his former partner tracks him down and attacks him, but is stopped and killed by the Sea-Spider and it’s kin. Both the Sea-Spider and the writer then transform into hybrid creatures and run off to live together in subterranean caverns.

### Characters
*Malcolm, a man determined to finish his book over the summer.
*The Sea-Spider, a member of an unidentified species.
*Amy, Malcolm's crazy ex-girlfriend.
*Oscar, a local food vendor.

### Publication History
"The Sea-Spider" was published in the collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

fullContent:
"The Sea, Like Broken Glass", alternatively titled "The Sea, Like Glass Unbroken" is a Lovecraftian short story by Mexican-Canadian author Silvia Moreno-Garcia.

### Synopsis
A young woman in a coastal village has been promised as bride to an unspecified entity from beneath the waves. However, when she is seemingly rejected in favour of another, she takes her own life in an attempt to see her inhuman love one last time.

### Publication History
"The Sea, Like Broken Glass" was published in the anthology of H. P. Lovecraft-inspired fiction Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.

### Trivia
Despite containing no direct references to Lovecraft's work or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, the description of the small town and it’s inhabitants, and the vague references to an oceanic entity recall the titular setting for The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

fullContent:
"The Sealed Casket" is a horror short story by Richard F. Searight, first published in the March 1935 issue of Weird Tales.

This story is notable for introducing the Eltdown Shards, although they are only mentioned in the opening quote, which the original publication omitted altogether. The Shards would later be incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in "The Challenge from Beyond", and would also be mentioned in Searight's own Mythos story "The Warder of Knowledge".

### Synopsis
The story opens with a passage from the Eltdown Shards, which tells of an ancient entity named Avaloth, who threatened to cover the world with ice, but was seemingly defeated by the wizard Om Oris. Other wizards have prophesied that Avaloth would one day be destroyed by "a great heat".

In the present day, a man named Wesson Clark inherits a relic called the coffer of Alû-Tor from his recently-deceased archaeologist friend, Martucci. The coffer is a small casket made of an unknown metal and inscribed with unknown glyphs. Martucci has never opened the seal, and asked Clark not to do it. Clark is convinced that Martucci never found out about the affair that Clark had with Martucci's wife, and dismisses the dead man's insistence in leaving the seal intact as pure eccentricity. Believing that there might be something valuable inside the casket, Clark locks himself in his own study and opens it.

Despite the uncomfortably hot temperature inside the room, Clark feels a draft of cold air emanating from the seemingly empty casket, along with a putrid odor. He then hears the rustling sound of some invisible creature moving about the study, positioning itself between Clark and the door. The temperature drops perceptibly and the odor intensifies, as he feels the invisible being's tentacles coiling around his body.

As it turns out, the reason why the room was so hot in the first place is that Clark's servant, Simpkins, had forgotten to close the drafts of the furnace, and the house was engulfed by flames. Witnesses talk about hearing the high-pitched sound of a creature screaming in agony. Clark's body is found burned, but the coroner is unable to explain why his bones are all broken, as if he had been constricted to death by several snakes, or why his body has been completely drained of blood.

### Characters
*Wesson Clark: An amateur archaeologist and shameless womanizer.
*Martucci: An eccentric archaeologist with great knowledge, but a dubious reputation. Clark befriended him, but had an affair with his wife, which he believes Martucci was oblivious to. Martucci left the casket to Clark after death, possibly as a form of revenge.
*Simpkins: Clark's careless, forgetful old servant.
*Avaloth: An eldritch creature imprisoned inside the casket by the wizard Om Oris. Its name and backstory are revealed only in the opening quote, which was omitted by Weird Tales.
*An unnamed coroner, baffled by the circumstances of Clark's death.

The Second Cthulhu Mythos Megapack is an ebook anthology published by Wildside Press in 2019, a follow-up to its Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (2012). 

The anthology features several of H. P. Lovecraft's revision tales (including the overtly racist "Medusa's Coil") and multiple contributions from Robert Bloch and Lin Carter. Most of the stories were written in the 1930s and '40s, with only five published since 1970.

shortDefinition: "The Second Theft of Alhazred's Manuscript" is a short Cthulhu Mythos/Sherlock Holmes crossover story by American author Bradley H. Sinor. It was published in Innsmouth Free Press's 2011 thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft.  ### Synopsis Holmes a...
fullContent:
"The Second Theft of Alhazred's Manuscript" is a short Cthulhu Mythos/Sherlock Holmes crossover story by American author Bradley H. Sinor. It was published in Innsmouth Free Press's 2011 thematic anthology Historical Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Holmes and Watson are approached by Sir James Marsden, the representative of a shadowy organisation which has been protecting the world from dark forces from behind the scenes for centuries; Marsden's request: that Holmes track down a partial copy of the Necronomicon which was stolen from their vaults.

As the investigation progresses, it emerges that Marsden was himself the thief, and used the situation to force Holmes into producing a missing page taken from the Necronomicon during Holmes' previous rescue of the manuscript, seemingly intending to use the complete text to enact some evil ritual. Fortunately for the future of the human race, Holmes opts to destroy the missing page rather than hand it over, and the resulting explosion kills Marsden and burns the ancient text.

### Behind the Mythos
Aside from the obvious Necronomicon connection, Marsden mentions that his unnamed organisation "had come into possession of some small, star-shaped stones that could be used to command certain situations," a reference to the ubiquitous Star-stones of Mnar. Another element is Marsden's thug who, after his death, is revealed to resemble a "cruel cross between a human and a fish … [o]n the side of the neck were what might even be gills," implying that the man was perhaps a Deep One hybrid.

### References

fullContent:
"The Second Wish"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley, first published in New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1980). 

An homage not only to H. P. Lovecraft but to Robert E. Howard as well, Lumley calls it "a fully fledged Mythos tale with just about every Mythos prop"--and "one of my personal favourites."

### Synopsis
Harry and Julia, on holiday in Hungary, encounter a sinister old man who shows them a macabre relic. Harry is told to hold the mummy's hand and make a wish--but finds that he gets more than he wishes for.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in New Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (Arkham House, 1980), "The Second Wish" was included in Lumley's collections The Second Wish and Other Exhalations (New English Library, 1995), Beneath the Moors and Darker Places (Tor, 2002), and Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008).

fullContent:
The Secret Cave, or John Lees Adventure, is a short story by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Written in 1898 when he was only eight years old, it forms part of his juvenilia.

### Synopsis
Young John Lee and his sister discover a passageway hidden behind a false wall in the basement when their parents leave them alone. Exploring the cavern, they come upon some treasure but inadvertently start a flood, the water coming from an unknown source. John escapes, but his sister is killed.

### Characters

*John Lee, an adventurous ten-year-old boy.
*Alice Lee, John's two-year-old sister.

### Publication History
First published in The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces in 1959, long after Lovecraft's death, it has been included in several collections in the years since, and has been translated into both Italian and German.

fullContent:
"The Secret in the Tomb" is a short story by American author  Robert Bloch, a protege of H. P. Lovecraft. Bloch's first published Cthulhu Mythos story, it originally appeared in the May 1935 issue of Weird Tales. 

### Synopsis
The last scion of a bloodline which have devoted themselves to the search for eternal life -- rumoured to be hidden in the mausoleum of the family's progenitor -- immerses himself in the evil lore of the Necronomicon, Book of Eibon, and Mysteries of the Worm, among others, in an effort to unlock the secret of the tomb.

When the narrator receives an unexpected psychic calling one day, he follows it to the tomb which had swallowed his predecessors without a trace. Upon entry, he discovers the family's first patriarch, buried many long years ago yet not dead. This creature has been feeding off its descendants one by one across the decades, in order to extend its own life.

Fortunately for the man, he is able to break the thing's hold over him and escapes the tomb, before having it razed to the ground and buried.

### Characters
*Unnamed Narrator, last in a long line of practitioners of dark magic.
*Jeremy Strange, the undead progenitor of the family.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Secret in the Tomb" contains the first mentions of Ludvig Prinn and his Mysteries of the Worm, described here as a "pinnacle of literary madness".

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Weird Tales, "The Secret in the Tomb" was reprinted in Bloch's 1981 collection Mysteries of the Worm, and later appeared in The Second Cthulhu Mythos Megapack. It has been translated into French and German.

fullContent:
"The Secret of Kralitz" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Henry Kuttner. The tale, which first appeared in Weird Tales in October 1936, was described as follows: "A story of the shocking revelation that came to the twenty-first Baron Kralitz".

The story is notable for introducing the Great Old One known as Iod.

### Synopsis
The aristocratic Kralitz family has been the victim of a dire curse for generations, ever since a distant ancestor burned down a monastery and had the monks put to the sword.

When the latest baron comes of age, he is summoned by dark-cloaked figures, who escort him through a portal in the bowels of his castle where he meets the tortured souls of his forebears. After a night of revelry with the group, during which he learns many dark secrets, the new baron is then escorted back to the castle crypts where he learns the true nature of the curse: that no coffin has ever been set within the vaults unoccupied. There, before him, lies a sarcophagus with his own name etched upon it's lid…

### Behind the Mythos
The story's connection to the Cthulhu Mythos is contained in the line: "I learned of the fungoid, inhuman beings that dwell on far cold Yuggoth, of the cyclopean shapes that attend unsleeping Cthulhu in his submarine city, of the strange pleasures that the followers of leprous, subterranean Yog-Sothoth may possess, and I learned, too, of the unbelievable manner in which Iod, the Source, is worshipped beyond the outer galaxies."

fullContent:
"The Secret of Nephren-Ka" is a story by Robert M. Price that uses Richard L. Tierney's sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta to attempt a synthesis of the Cthulhu Mythos and Mormon tradition. The story first appeared in the anthology The Mighty Warriors (Ulthar Press, 2018).

### Synopsis
The spirit of the infamous Black Pharaoh, Nephren-Ka, beseeches Simon to save his devoted worshipers in a distant land from annihilation. Although Simon's instincts warn him of a darker motive behind the spirit's plea, he embarks on a journey to an enigmatic land on the other side of the world, where he is forced to confront the eldritch entity masked by Nephren-Ka's spirit.

### Setting
The story is set in 39 A.D., and takes Simon from Egypt to North America via magical means.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Mighty Warriors, "The Secret of Nephren-Ka" was reprinted in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997) and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

fullContent:
"The Secret of Sebek" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the November 1937 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
A writer of horror fiction visiting New Orleans is invited to a special costume party for Mardi Gras and encounters an all-too-real incarnation of the crocodile-headed Egyptian god Sebek.

### Characters
*The Narrator: A fiction writer who appears to resemble Robert Bloch. Like Bloch, he writes a great deal about Ancient Egypt. He is a stranger in New Orleans, and as the story begins he is lonely and bent on getting drunk.
*Henricus Vanning: A New Orleans "gentleman of means and leisure", and a student of black magic. He is the organizer of the Coffin Club, whose members include:
*Doctor Delvin: "one of this country's foremost ethnologists".
*de Marigny: "a well-known occultist" whose "connection with the Randolph Carter case" is mentioned.
*Royce: Vanning's personal assistant.
*Weildan: A famous Egyptologist.
*Sebek: The incarnate crocodile-headed Egyptian god.

### Connections
 (Weird Tales)]]
The character de Marigny is H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price's creation, Etienne-Laurent de Marigny, who is involved with the "Randolph Carter case" in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", also set in New Orleans. Bloch's version seems more feckless than the character in the original story.

Writing about Egypt, the narrator says he gives his mind over to "images of Nyarlathotep, Bubastis, and Anubis".

The narrator and Weildan show up again in "The Eyes of the Mummy", which appeared in the April 1938 issue of Weird Tales.

shortDefinition: "The Secret of the Sahara" is a Lovecraftian short story by the late American author Richard A. Lupoff. It was first published in The Mammoth Book of New Jules Verne Adventures by Carroll & Graf in 2005.  ### Synopsis In an alternative steampunk real...
fullContent:
"The Secret of the Sahara" is a Lovecraftian short story by the late American author Richard A. Lupoff. It was first published in The Mammoth Book of New Jules Verne Adventures by Carroll & Graf in 2005.

### Synopsis
In an alternative steampunk reality, the leaders in their fields from five different countries investigate the recent discovery of pre-human ruins, located beneath the surface of the man-made Sahara Sea. In the tunnels beneath the seabed, they awaken a giant alien creature which seems intent on devouring them, but the intervention of the ship's cat gives the group a brief reprieve, allowing them to kill it. With the being's dying breaths, it tells them that it’s mother and father will soon be coming for it…

### Publication History
Since its debut in 2005, "Secrets of the Sahara" has also appeared in the collections of Lupoff's own works Terrors (2008) and The Doom That Came to Dunwich (2017).

### Trivia

* The entities detected frozen in time during the expedition's preliminary scans could be interpreted as Elder Things and Cthulhi, two species stated to have engaged in a war on Earth in distant prehistory in At the Mountains of Madness. However, the descriptions are sufficiently vague to make this conclusion uncertain.

"The Secret Painting of Thomas Cartwright" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author W. H. Pugmire.

### Synopsis
Siobhain Cleary, a cultist whose cell is obsessed with the Revelations of Gla'aki, Volume IV: On the World as Lair, gifts a painting by deceased artist Thomas Cartwright to sorcerer Simon Gregory Williams before disappearing into a lake to join her dark god.

### Characters
*Simon Gregory Williams, a powerful sorcerer, possibly intended to be Simon of Gitta.
*Siobhain Cleary, a cultist of Gla'aki, and possibly one of its avatars.

### Publication History
"The Secret Painting of Thomas Cartwright" was published in the thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Trivia
*The story takes place in the Sesqua Valley, a locale created by Pugmire as the setting for many of his Mythos tales.

"The Seed from the Stars" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by American author James Ambuehl. It consists of ten eight-line verses, and functions as something of a prequel to Ambuehl's 1996 short story "The Star-Seed".

### Synopsis
The story describes how the narrator, hearing of the star-seed of Ei'lor which fell to Earth in the town of Laren, Minnesota, wishes to see this being for himself. Travelling to the destroyed farmhouse said to be the landing site he discovers a mummified old man, somehow still alive, who relays to him the events of that fateful day before imploring him to run. The ground shifts below the narrator, and he sees the developing seedling before running in abject terror.

The final verse gives a warning from the narrator that the Earth is in great peril from the vegetable-creature slowly growing beneath the ground.

### Publication History
"The Seed from the Stars" was published in the E. P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes in October 2006.

fullContent:
"The Seed of the Star–God" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney in which his sword-and-sorcery character Simon of Gitta thwarts an attempt to summon Shub-Niggurath. It first appeared as the cover story for the Lammas 1984 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu (#24). 

### Synopsis
Simon learns that his beloved Helen is dead--and that her father, a powerful and possessed sorcerer, is preparing to sacrifice her sister to manifest the sinister fertility goddess Shub-Niggurath into the mortal world. Simon and his allies hasten to Ephesos to interrupt his grisly ritual. 

### Setting
The story takes place in the years 31-32 A.D. in Persepolis, Antium and Ephesos--in modern day Iran, Italy and Turkey, respectively.

### Publication History
After its appearance in Crypt of Cthulhu, "The Seed of the Star-God" was reprinted in The Shub-Niggurath Cycle (Chaosium, 1994) and in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997) and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

shortDefinition: "The Seeder from the Stars" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian-Chilean author Julio Toro San Martin. It was published in the 2011 anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press.  ### Synopsis Years after a child prodigy in service to...
fullContent:
"The Seeder from the Stars" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian-Chilean author Julio Toro San Martin. It was published in the 2011 anthology Historical Lovecraft by Innsmouth Free Press.

### Synopsis
Years after a child prodigy in service to the temple of the gods turns his back on his masters, he returns to wreak revenge on his former people in the form of a monstrous abomination. However, he has underestimated the powers of the high priestess who casts him into the eternal void but, remorseful over what she has done to the man she once saw as a son, she follows him through the portal, determined to return him to his home.

### Behind the Mythos
Mythos references in "The Seeder from the Stars" include a mention of the narrator dreaming of being "a lute musician in the glorious palace of Olathoë, in doom-laden Lomar," and a likely mention of the Outer God Yog-Sothoth in the line "Yog-Saduk, the Keeper of the Gates."

In his commentary on "The Seeder from the Stars," Toro San Martin hints that the narrator may in fact be an avatar of the Outer God Nyarlathotep in his guise of the Black Pharaoh, and that an unnamed Clark Ashton Smith story may give a clue on the identity of the titular Seeder from the Stars. 

Furthermore, Toro San Martin states that the story was written "as a sort of companion piece" to H. P. Lovecraft's "The Other Gods."

fullContent:
"The Seen and the Unseen" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author and artist Tim Stevens. It was published in Vol 5, Issue 2 of Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
A man on vacation in a small coastal town decides to take a solo kayak trip out into the ocean with the aim of spotting whales, the major goal of his holiday. When a strange fog rolls in unexpectedly, however, he bears witness to a colossal tentacled creature rising from the depths, snatching a whale up in its enormous appendages, and killing it.

Discovered by a policeman on the shore many hours later, he is taken to the local station where his statement is taken. The officers, and a man revealed to be a high priest in a cult of Cthulhu, then decide to kill the man rather than allow him to spread word of what he has seen.

fullContent:
"The Sentinels" is a short story by prolific British author Ramsey Campbell which is set in the greater Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in the 1973 Arkham House collection Demons by Daylight, and has been translated into both French and German.

### Synopsis
One evening, a group of young adults on a trip to the nearby countryside decide to explore the site of local landmark Sentinel Hill, a place whose circle of stone statues is said to provide protection against evil. As the night progresses, the group slowly realises that something malevolent is watching them from outside the circle and begins to panic. When the tension becomes too much, one of them breaks from the protective ramparts and makes a run for her car: the others have no choice but to watch as the creature pursues her and chases her down.

### Mythos Connections
The story is set in the fictional Severn Valley, as evidenced by a characters' reference to a Brichester-based fan group which some of them are members of, and a mention of the Herald, presumably that town's local rag, The Brichester Herald. The Severn Valley is a locale created by Campbell, and used as the backdrop to many of his Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Trivia
* The name of the story's setting, Sentinel Hill, would appear to be a reference to the sacrificial site located outside of Dunwich, Massachusetts, mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft’s 1929 short story "The Dunwich Horror".

### Publication History
* Demons by Daylight (1973, 1975, 1979, 1980, 1990)
* L'homme du souterrain (1979)
* Dämonen bei Tag (1998)
* Fungi #20 (2011)

fullContent:
"The Serpent's Egg" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by English author Jonathan Green. It was first published in the John Prescott-edited digital anthology Dreaming in Darkness in June 2013.

### Synopsis
Nathan, a novelist with writer's block, books a room in a stately home in his ancestral homeland of County Durham, England. Although finding inspiration for a new book and a woman with whom he falls in love, he also uncovers a despicable cult dedicated to bringing about the rebirth of their master, the creature known as Shudde M'ell. Nathan, with help from a doomed gamekeeper, thwarts the cult and defeats the monstrous creature, but is forever after haunted by the things which he witnessed in the catacombs beneath rural England.

### Behind the Mythos
Shudde M'ell, a colossal burrowing abomination, is implied to have been the basis for the real-world legend of the Lambton Worm, a monstrous creature from English folklore said to have terrorised the area during the Middle Ages.

One of the ancient volumes encountered by Nathan during his researches is Ludvig Prinn's De Vermis Mysteriis.

### Publication History
Since its debut in Dreaming in Darkness, "The Serpents Egg" has been released as a self-titled digital chapbook through Amazon's Kindle platform.

"The Serpents of Tenoka" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet. As it’s title might suggest, it takes place in Tenoka, East Texas, an area created by the author for several of his mythos stories.

### Synopsis
The unnamed narrator inherits a cabin just outside of Tenoka, Texas when his uncle Henry, who had been suffering from a bout of intense paranoia over the local snake population, dies suddenly of a heart attack.

Deciding to take a short vacation to the property before selling it, the man kills a rattlesnake which strikes at him, bringing down the wrath of the snake-god Yig, who transforms him into one of his serpent followers as a punishment.

### Characters

*The Narrator, a man on vacation from his hated factory job.
*Henry Teal, the narrator's uncle, who incurred the anger of Yig after killing a snake.
*Sheriff Blair, a member of local law enforcement.
*Yig, a Great Old One and protector of serpents.

### Publication History
"The Serpents of Tenoka" was first published in the online fanzine Nightscapes #4 in October 1997 and was later printed in Horror Carousel #4 in Spring 2006. It has since appeared in the anthologies Worlds of Cthulhu (2012) and They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness (2018).

fullContent:
The Seven Blasphemies Of Ghattambah is an occult book created by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr. for their Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Description
Written in 1417 by Belgian warlock Adrian Mondrago, The Seven Blasphemies Of Ghattambahs contents are written in English, Greek, German and, inexplicably, ancient Martian, a Rosetta Stone-like feature which would allow humans to understand the Martian language. Although it’s precise contents are unknown, it was said to contain information which would assist in bringing about the return of Nyarlathotep (: "Shoggoth Apocalypse", "The Relic In The Egyptian Gallery").

It is likely the same book which the Dr. Xorthonos was attempting to steal from the Arkham Public Museum although that book was simply named The Blasphemies of Ghattambah (: "The Relic In The Egyptian Gallery").

A copy of The Seven Blasphemies is in the possession of the Mondrago family, a bloodline with a long history of Ghattambah worship, while a Cthulhu-worshipping Deep One cult in the town of Sea Dream has another (: "In The Chapel Of Ghattambah", "The Testament of Cthulhu").

### Synopsis
The seven verses - one for each "gate" - describe a series of nightmares suffered by the author, culminating in his awakening, screaming and soaked in sweat.

fullContent:
"The Seven Geases" is a short story by Clark Ashton Smith, and forms part of his Hyperborean cycle. It was first published in Weird Tales in October 1934.

### Synopsis
Ralibar Vooz the Commorian and his men go spelunking in a monster infested cave system. Their explorations require them to do a mighty feat of mountain climbing first, since the entrance to the cavern system is on the heights of Mount Voormithadreth.

The region is home to the Voormi as well as the rumored and paranormal half-Saturnian monstrosities who were the product of ancient interbreeding between human women and creatures that had come to earth from Saturn.

Entering the caves becomes what modern readers might well describe as a dungeon hack culminating in an encounter with the Archetypes: primordial globular floating humanoids who see the Commorian men as devolved monstrosities. These globular creatures threaten to cast the Commorians to Abhoth to rid the world of their contagion.

The geases of the title require action, bravery and endless combat against everything from cave dinosaurs to Serpent People but ultimately a confrontation with Abhoth leads only to a further encounter with the webs of Atlach-Nacha... And doom.

fullContent:
"The Shade of Pierre Girault" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young. It forms the second episode in Book 2 of his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
Director of the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena Harjit Singh recruits a new agent, prisoner Charlene Hines, explaining to her the existence of dark forces in the world, before partnering her with the now-seasoned investigator Malcolm Mayweather.

The pair are dispatched on assignment to investigate the mysterious case of a man who awakened from a 17 year long coma claiming he had been psychically abducted. Their investigation leads them to uncover a possessed journal which releases the spirit of a long-dead warlock, and only the destruction of the book is enough to destroy the evil entity.

### Characters
*Charlene Hines, a young woman with a troubled past involving the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos.
*Malcolm Mayweather, a firefighter-turned-paranormal investigator.
*Harjit Singh, director of a shadowy government agency.
*Pierre Girault, an 18th century sorcerer.
*Paul Witmer, Girault's victim.

### Publication History
"The Shade of Pierre Girault" was published in The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 3 in 2021.

### Trivia
*Girault is stated to have made pacts with at least two Outer Gods, Shub-Niggurath and Nyarlathotep, while working his magics.

"The Shadow by the Altar" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author David A. Riley, first published in the Spring 1983 edition of Dark Horizons.

### Synopsis
Small-time criminal Stephen Tibbets is hired by a pair of mysterious thugs to break in to the house of wealthy Barlow and pour a vial of liquid over a specific symbol chalked on the basement floor. When he arrives to complete his task, he realises that confined within the sigil is a terrifying entity made from living shadow. While he debates what to do, the house's owner returns home; fearful that the intruder may release the being, Barlow offers to pay him to leave the act uncompleted. Unfortunately, in his greed Tibbets accidentally releases the creature, which tears both men to shreds.

fullContent:
"The Shadow from the Steeple" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the September 1950 issue of Weird Tales. 

It is the third and final story in a trilogy by Bloch and H. P. Lovecraft started by Bloch in 1935 with "The Shambler from the Stars," and continued by Lovecraft in 1936 with "The Haunter of the Dark." The trilogy concluding in this short story is also the final exploration of the mystery surrounding the "Shining Trapezohedron" in the works of the Lovecraft Circle.

The plot of "The Shadow from the Steeple" follows Edmund Fiske, a friend of Robert Blake's, who spends years searching for Ambrose Dexter, the doctor who disposed of the Shining Trapezohedron, in hopes of explaining Blake's disappearance. Dexter turns out to have been turned by the weird crystal into an avatar of Nyarlathotep--and to have aided humanity's development of nuclear weapons.

### Publication History
"The Shadow from the Steeple" has been frequently anthologized, including in August Derleth's Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (1969). It has been translated into French, German, Dutch and Portuguese. 

### Adaptations
A comic book adaptation was published in Journey Into Mystery by Marvel Comics in 1973.

shortDefinition: "The Shadow in the Attic" is a short story by August Derleth, presented as one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. Though most such "collaborations" involve Derleth writing a story based on an unused story idea from Lovecraft's C...
fullContent:
"The Shadow in the Attic" is a short story by August Derleth, presented as one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. Though most such "collaborations" involve Derleth writing a story based on an unused story idea from Lovecraft's Commonplace Book, in this case no such plot germ has been identified. The story first appeared in the Arkham House collection Over the Edge in 1964.

### Synopsis
The plot involves the narrator, Adam Duncan, inheriting a 200-year-old house in Arkham from his great-uncle Uriah Garrison, a malignant sorcerer, under the condition that Duncan live in the house for three months. Though Garrison's lawyer, Saltonstall, insists that no one else has access to the house, Duncan discovers that his uncle's housekeeper is still in residence. She turns out to be a sort of succubus--referred to at one point as Lilith--summoned by Garrison as a servant and companion. Garrison's spirit plots to take over Duncan's body from beyond the grave--a scheme foiled when Duncan's fiancee, Rhoda Prentiss, sets fire to the house.

### Behind the Mythos
While set in Lovecraft's Arkham (in June 1928), the magic-related texts discovered in Garrison's home are traditional, non-Mythos works, chiefly related to witchhunting, including the Malleus Maleficarum, Anania’s De Natura Daemonum, De Vignate’s Quaestio de Lamiis and Stampa’s Fuga Satanae. He also has "very old books" by Olaus Magnus, Eunapius and de Rochas.

Though featuring a typically Derlethian inheritance plot, the story is unusual in that it features a strong, appealing female character in Rhoda Prentiss--something rare in stories by Lovecraft or his circle--and also in its PG-13 sexuality.

fullContent:
"The Shadow Kingdom" is a fantasy short story by Robert E. Howard, and the first in his Kull of Atlantis series. It was originally published in the August 1929 issue of Weird Tales and has been reprinted in several Howard collections.

In addition to being the first Kull story, "The Shadow Kingdom" is notable for introducing the Serpent People, a species that would also be featured in Clark Ashton Smith's Hyperborea series, and mentioned frequently in the stories of H. P. Lovecraft.

The concept of a reptilian race that can disguise themselves as humans and infiltrate society by replacing key political figures has since become a common motif in popular culture, and the subject of actual conspiracy theories.

### Synopsis
Kull, an Atlantean renegade who seized the throne of the ancient kingdom of Valusia, is invited to attend a banquet hosted by Ka-nu, ambassador of the Picts. The Pict messenger, Brule, asks to speak in private and tells the king to go alone. Despite obvious hostility fueled by the age-old enmity between Picts and Atlanteans, Kull agrees, reasoning that Ka-nu wouldn't want to risk the alliance with Valusia.

After the banquet, Ka-nu shows Kull a bracelet with the image of a winged dragon, and tells him that on the following night, Kull would be approached by Brule, who would be wearing the bracelet. He asks Kull to lay aside tribal prejudices and trust him, also insisting that Kull should trust Brule and follow Brule's instructions. As a sign of trust, he presents Kull with a gemstone stolen from the Temple of the Serpent, proof that Kull could use to ruin Ka-nu if the latter were to betray him.

On the following night, Brule infiltrates the palace and tells Kull to change his royal clothes for something less conspicuous. He asks Kull to observe the guards, then shows him secret passages where the bodies of the same guards lay unconscious, proving that the ones they'd seen before were impostors who could somehow look identical to the men they impersonated.

Brule reminds Kull of ancient legends about the original rulers of Valusia, who were not human, but serpent-men. The magic of the serpent-men allows them to disguise their appearance, and for generations they have used this ability to impersonate kings and priests, and rule over the human population in secrecy.

Kull is surprised to see his councilor, Tu, sneaking into the king's room with a dagger and obvious intent to assassinate him. Kull beheads Tu and sees the man's head transform into the head of a serpent. The incident confirms that the creatures are planning to kill and replace Kull, as they had done with previous Valusian kings.

Following a brief encounter with a serpent-man posing as Brule, the real Brule informs Kull of the means to set men apart from the reptiles: the  bracelet with the image of the winged dragons, who are the serpent-men's enemies, and the phrase "ka nama kaa lajerama", which the creatures can't pronounce. "The Shadow of the Phoenix" is a short Carl Kolchak/Cthulhu Mythos crossover story by the late American author Rick Lai. It was published in the anthology Kolchak the Night Stalker: Passages of the Macabre by Moonstone in February 2016.

### Synopsis
During the course of his investigations, roving reporter Carl Kolchak uncovers a deadly rivalry between two sinister cults and their head priestesses: one, an old adversary by the name of Angelica Whateley, seeks to recruit Kolchak into the service of her dark masters the Great Old Ones, while the other wishes to sacrifice her young daughter in order to extend her lifespan.

Through diligent research, Kolchak is able to identify the weaknesses of these two monstrous characters and destroy them; one by saving the little girl and incurring the wrath of the priestesses' vengeful god, the other by employing the magical properties of a powerful talisman.

### Mythos Connections
Angelica Whateley, the witch in service to the Great Old Ones, is stated to have been born in Dunwich, Massachusetts, making it more than likely that she was one of the decadent Whateleys mentioned in "The Dunwich Horror." Nyogtha and Dagon are amongst the Old Ones mentioned as being her masters, although they play no actual part in the story.

The other witch, Lorna Volny, is in service to a being which goes by the name Assurah-Ka, which is later revealed to be an aspect of Set who, in this iteration, is the entity behind human religious beliefs such as the Devil.

### Trivia
* As part of her cover, Angelica Whateley poses as an avid collector of Weird Tales memorabilia to gain access to Carl Kolchak's hotel.

"The Shadow Out of Space" is a sci-fi short story by August Derleth billed as one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. These were stories written by Derleth based on unused annotations from Lovecraft's Commonplace Book and other sources. It was published in the 1957 Arkham House collection The Survivor and Others.

### Synopsis
In Arkham, 1933, a woman named Abigail Piper seeks out psychoanalyst Nathaniel Corey in the hopes that he can help her brother Amos, an anthropologist from Miskatonic University. Three years before, Amos Piper collapsed suddenly and fell into a long period of amnesia, followed by an alteration of personality, from which he recovered only recently. However, his recovery also brought in new symptoms in the form of terrifying hallucinations and nightmares.

In his dreams, Piper sees himself as a captive mind within the body of a large, rugose, cone-shaped creature with crab-like pincers, living on a planet orbiting a dark star in the Taurus constellation. He sees several other bodies like his, some hosting captive minds originating from several points in time and space. There are also many warders and one elderly instructor, who converses with the captives. From the instructor, Piper learns about the Great Race, a species which once inhabited the Earth, but got caught up in the war between the Elder Gods and the Ancient Ones and were forced to escape, first to Jupiter, then to other planets. Every time they migrate to a new world, they leave their old bodies behind and move their consciousnesses into the bodies of other beings. Piper also learns that once the captive minds are sent back to their own original bodies, their memories are erased and they are kept under discreet observation. If the memories resurface, the Great Race will effect a second replacement.

Dr. Corey tries to help Piper, but finds that not only are his dreams getting more vivid, he also shows signs of paranoia, having become convinced that agents of the Great Race are following him. One day, Abigail calls Corey to inform him that Piper is "not himself" and has returned to the state of altered personality he had during the three year period following his collapse. When Corey visits his patient, he is pleasantly surprised to see a much more confident man with no signs of nervousness and who insists that he has experienced no more dreams. Over the next sessions, Corey becomes convinced that Piper is cured, but is taken aback when Piper suddenly announces his plans to join an expedition to the Arabian desert.

Two days later, Corey finds out that someone has broken into his office and stolen all documents pertaining to the Piper case. Luckily, Corey had made copies of them, but the incident makes him ponder about the things Piper told him, concerning the purported existence of the Great Race. shortDefinition: The Shadow Out of Time is a novella by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. Written between November 1934 and February 1935, it was first published in the June 1936 issue of Astounding Stories.  ### Plot summary The Shadow Out of Time indi...
fullContent:
The Shadow Out of Time is a novella by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. Written between November 1934 and February 1935, it was first published in the June 1936 issue of Astounding Stories.

### Plot summary
The Shadow Out of Time indirectly tells of the Great Race of Yith, an extraterrestrial species with the ability to travel through space and time. The Yithians accomplish this by body swap with hosts from the intended spatial or temporal destination. The story implies that the effect when seen from the outside is similar to spiritual possession. The Yithians' original purpose was to study the history of various times and places, and they have amassed a "library city" that is filled with the past and future history of multiple races, including humans. Ultimately the Yithians use their ability to escape the destruction of their planet in another galaxy by switching bodies with a race of cone-shaped plant beings who lived 250 million years ago on Earth. The cone-shaped entities (subsequently also known as the Great Race of Yith) lived in their vast library city in what would later become Australia's Great Sandy Desert.

The story is told through the eyes of Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee, an American living in the first decade of the 20th century, who is "possessed" by a Yithian. He fears he is losing his mind when he unaccountably sees strange vistas of other worlds and of the Yithian library city. He also feels himself being led about by these creatures and experiences how they live. When he is returned to his own body, he finds that those around him have judged him insane due to the actions of the Yithian that possessed his body. While he was experiencing a Yithian existence in Earth's ancient past, the Yithian occupying his body was experiencing a human one in the present day.

The narrator at first believes his episode and subsequent dreams to be the product of some kind of mental illness. His initial relief at discovering other cases like his throughout history is withered when he discovers that the other cases are too similar to his own to be without a connection. The narrator's dreams become more vivid, and he becomes obsessed with archaeology and ancient manuscripts (as was the Yithian)--but lacks any sort of proof that would demonstrate whether he was (or is) simply mad.

He discovers that the Yithians on Earth died out eons ago, their civilization destroyed by a rival, utterly alien pre-human race described as "half-polypous" creatures, but the Yithian minds will inhabit new bodies on Earth after humanity is long gone. His tenuously held sanity is challenged when he discovers the proof he seeks—and that not only do remains of the Yithians' past civilization still exist on Earth, but also still remaining are those who destroyed them. shortDefinition: The Shadow over Innsmouth is a horror novella by H. P. Lovecraft, written in November–December 1931. It forms part of the Cthulhu Mythos, using its motif of a malign undersea civilization. It references several shared elements of the Mythos, includin...
fullContent:
The Shadow over Innsmouth is a horror novella by H. P. Lovecraft, written in November–December 1931. It forms part of the Cthulhu Mythos, using its motif of a malign undersea civilization. It references several shared elements of the Mythos, including place-names, mythical creatures and invocations.

The narrator is a student on an antiquarian tour of New England. He sees a piece of exotic jewelry in a museum, and learns that its source is the nearby decrepit seaport of Innsmouth. He travels to Innsmouth and observes disturbing events and people. A local resident tells him a horrifying story of aquatic monsters who can interbreed with humans to produce amphibian hybrids. The student is tricked into staying overnight in the town, and he is attacked in his hotel. He flees, but finds that his pursuers are the hybrid monsters of his informant’s story. He alerts the authorities, who take drastic action. He then discovers that he has non-human ancestors and must eventually return to the sea.

It is the only Lovecraft story which was published in book form during his lifetime.

According to L. Sprague de Camp, Lovecraft distrusted his ability to narrate action, and the story is unusual in that Lovecraft includes in chapter IV a sustained and effective piece of action writing.

### Inspiration
Both of Lovecraft's parents died in a mental hospital, and some critics believe that a concern with having inherited a propensity for physical and mental degeneration, a common preoccupation among eugenicists of the time, which, along with paranoiac fears of miscegenation, is reflected in the plot of The Shadow over Innsmouth. It also shares some themes with his earlier story, "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family". Cthulhu, an entity from previous Lovecraft stories, is the overlord of the sea creatures. The mind of the narrator deteriorates when he is afforded a glimpse of what exists outside his perceived reality. This is a central tenet of Cosmicism, which Lovecraft emphasizes in the opening sentence of "The Call of Cthulhu": "The most merciful thing in the world, I think, is the inability of the human mind to correlate all its contents."

### Possible influences
Lovecraft based the town of Innsmouth on his impressions of Newburyport, Massachusetts, which he had visited in 1923 and fall 1931. The real Newburyport features as a neighbouring town in the narrative.

A likely influence on the plot is Lovecraft's horror of miscegenation, which is documented by de Camp  Lovecraft was evidently impressed by this tale, writing in a letter to Frank Belknap Long: "God! The Harbour-Master!!!" (: Selected Letters 3.430) 

"Fishhead" is the story of a "human monstrosity" with an uncanny resemblance to a fish: "His skull sloped back so abruptly that he could hardly be said to have a forehead at all; his chin slanted off right into nothing. His eyes were small and round with shallow, glazed, pink-yellow pupils, and they were set wide apart on his head, and th

fullContent:
The Shadow Over Innsmouth is a 2014 one-shot comic book published by Dynamite Entertainment featuring their vigilante hero Lamont Cranston, aka The Shadow. It is inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's original story of the same name. The name of the comic book is a play on words, with the protagonist's superhero moniker of "The Shadow" lending the title a dual meaning.

### Synopsis
The Shadow and his plucky girl assistant / love interest Margo Lane find themselves in a coastal town called Innsmouth during Prohibition, being warned off by a local eccentric of the waterfront, Zadok. Claims are made that weird fish-men have been seen coming from and going to the ocean, carrying treasure.

The Shadow investigates. He sees the fish-men, establishing that there is some sort of physical reality to the story he was told.

When The Shadow and Margo clash with the fish-men, it transpires, in a Scooby-Doo style denouement, that the "fish-men" are merely human bootleggers in costumes. Margo pulls the costume head from one of them, revealing him to be none other than the source of the original imprecations - Zadok.

In a final cameo epilogue, H. P. Lovecraft is seen, writing down notes on what has happened, implying that this is the source of his weird horror story.

### Behind the Mythos
Coincidentally or not, and although the Lupoff version features, amongst many other things, Nazi divers and a submarine base, there are basic plot similarities to the earlier Lovecraft's Book.

"The Shadow Over Innsmouth High" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author S. O. Green. It is an ironic take on H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth in a contemporary setting.

### Synopsis
New girl in town Cat meets some very strange characters on her first day at Innsmouth High. Befriended by one girl and bullied by another, she is taken to a remote cave after school where her new friend has prepared her enemy for sacrifice. Determined not to fall foul of their cultish ways, Cat makes her escape, only to discover from her mother that she shares some very exotic blood with the locals.

### Characters
*Cat, a girl who has recently moved into the small town of Innsmouth.
*Shell, resident school bad girl.
*Sally, a cliquish bully.
*Finn, Shell's partner.

### Publication History
"The Shadow Over Innsmouth High" was published in the thematic anthology It Calls From the Sea in 2020.

### Trivia
*Unusually for a story involving the denizens of Innsmouth, "The Shadow Over Innsmouth High" suggests a definite hierarchy amongst the unchanged hybrids of the community.
*All of the character names have some association with the ocean: Cat is nicknamed "Catfish" by Shell, with Sally's full name being Salmon.

fullContent:
"The Shambler from the Stars" is a horror short story by American writer Robert Bloch, first published in the September 1935 issue of Weird Tales.  It is the first story of the Robert Blake Cycle.

It was later included as part of his first published book, The Opener of the Way (1945), and his 1994 collection The Early Fears. A Cthulhu Mythos tale, it introduced the forbidden tome De Vermis Mysteriis (Mysteries of the Worm), although it had been earlier mentioned in the short story "The Secret in the Tomb". Later on in 1935, Lovecraft wrote the short story "The Haunter of the Dark" as a sequel and dedicated it to Bloch. Eventually, in 1950, Bloch wrote his own sequel "The Shadow From the Steeple".

### Creation
Robert Bloch's idea was to write a story in which he could "kill" a character inspired by H. P. Lovecraft, whom he considered his mentor and pen pal. Before drafting it, he sent a letter to Lovecraft himself asking for permission to do so, to which he replied:



Lovecraft, who signed it,  had the likes of Abdul Alhazred, Friedrich Wilhelm von Juntz, Gaspar du Nord and the Tcho-Tcho Lama of Leng appear as witnesses to the document. Although Lovecraft liked the story, he decided to continue the joke by killing the narrator of the story, inspired by Robert Bloch, in the sequel.

### Summary
The story focuses on a college student who hopes to become a writer of weird fiction pulp. As his works are repeatedly rejected, he seeks forbidden knowledge and begins correspondence with thinkers and dreamers. A "mystic dreamer" from New England tells him of tomes such as the Necronomicon and Book of Eibon. Soon afterwards, the narrator mails letters to various libraries, universities, and occult practitioners, hoping to secure the volumes. As he is only met with both hostility and threats of violence, he begins searching various bookstores around his hometown.

At first, he again meets with disappointment, but, in an old shop on South Dearborn Street, he obtains De Vermis Mysteriis, which he knows was written by a Belgian sorcerer named Ludvig Prinn, who was burned at the stake during the witchcraft trials. Finding it to be written entirely in Latin, and not being able to speak the language, he contacts the New England mystic, who agrees to aid him in translation. The narrator travels to his home in Providence, Rhode Island, where the mystic is initially hesitant to even open the volume, but eventually does so upon the narrator's insistence. While perusing the book, the mystic inadvertently stumbles across a spell or invocation which he believes to be a summoning towards one of the invisible "star-sent servants" spoken of in the stories surrounding Prinn.

The narrator doesn't stop the mystic from reading the inscription out loud, and immediately afterwards, the room turns cold. An unearthly wind rushes in through the window, followed by a hideous laughter, which heralds the arrival of an invisible vampiric monstrosity; a star vampire. The monster lift

fullContent:
The Shimmer is a mysterious and ever-changing phenomenon featured prominently in both Jeff VanderMeer's Southern Reach trilogy and Alex Garland's film adaptation, Annihilation. It is referred to as "Area X" in the Southern Reach trilogy. It's a sprawling, iridescent area that has appeared on Earth, seemingly out of nowhere, and has defied all attempts at understanding or containment.

### Description
The Shimmer is characterized by its iridescent, shimmering appearance, hence its name. It is a barrier to the outside world, distorting space and time within its confines. The flora and fauna within the Shimmer are mutated and often grotesque, with genestic properties of living beings randomly switched to each other, hibiting uncanny properties and behaviors. The environment itself is unpredictable and dangerous, with rapidly changing terrain and atmospheric conditions.

### Origin and Nature
The exact origin of the Shimmer remains a central mystery in both the novel and the film. Theories range from a natural anomaly to an extraterrestrial or even dimensional incursion. It is implied that the Shimmer possesses a degree of sentience or consciousness, capable of manipulating its environment and possibly influencing those who enter it.

Exposure to the Shimmer has profound and often terrifying effects on humans. Physical alterations, mental instability, and psychological breakdown are common. Those who return from the Shimmer are often changed irrevocably, with some experiencing accelerated aging, memory loss, or even a complete transformation. The Shimmer serves as a powerful symbol of the unknown, the uncanny, and the destructive power of nature. It represents a challenge to human understanding and control, forcing characters to confront their own mortality and the limits of human knowledge.

The Shimmer's depiction varies between the novel and the film, with the film taking a more visually striking and action-oriented approach compared to the novel's more psychological and atmospheric exploration.

### Trivia
* The Shimmer bears a strong resemblance to the eldritch Colour Out of Space from H. P. Lovecraft's story of the same name.

### Synopsis
A small-town preacher from Massachusetts wins a place in a Miskatonic University archaeological expedition to Egypt in search of the near-mythical tomb of Nephren-Ka. However, once there, he is lured into the desert where he encounters the Black Pharaoh, and becomes a herald of Nyarlathotep.

### Characters

*Reverend Enoch Bowen, an elderly Christian minister.
*Professor Daniel Aiken, an archaeologist from Miskatonic University.
*Doctor Alan Farrington, an archaeologist from Harvard University.
*Abu-Serif, a servant of Nyarlathotep masquerading as an Egyptian holy man.
*Nephren-Ka/The Black Pharaoh, an Avatar of Nyarlathotep.

### Publication History
"The Shining Trapezohedron" was first published in Lovecraft's Disciples #34 in October 2018. It also appeared in the Weirdbook Annual #2: Cthulhu and the Weirdbook Annual #2: The Third Cthulhu Mythos Megapack, essentially the same release, with the former being a physical publication and the latter an ebook.

fullContent:
The Shoggoths is a comic book series, begun in Skywald's adult horror magazine Nightmare issue #9. It was written by Alan Hewetson under several pseudonyms with black and white art by a variety of European artists. It is also the subject of the issue's cover.

Billed as "continuing the Lovecraft Cthulhu Mythos" it has some of the trappings of works from Lovecraft's Circle although with its violent lusty content including quite graphic scenes it is more on the Clark Ashton Smith or Robert E. Howard part of the Mythos spectrum rather than Lovecraft's own work.

The series begins with an origin story, "Skull-Forest of Old Earth" which describes the coming of a tribe of humans from Uranus to the primitive Earth. There, they encounter a subhuman race of humanoid cannibals called Shoggoths, who eat members of the Uranian tribe alive and interbreed with captured women. After the carnage of the first meeting the scene is set for an ongoing saga of prehistoric Earth.

As the introduction to the series puts it, 

"There was a time on this Earth, before human-man walked its surface - men such as us, upright, civilized men - when crawling things, ancient even in their own time, ruled and dominated this grey earth."

The series went on providing the same sort of graphic and at times quite poetic and surreal content until the cancellation of the Skywald line with the liquidation of Skywald as a publisher. "The Shoggoths" and all other Skywald content is in the public domain.

### Behind the Mythos
Other than the name, the subhuman cannibal ravager species has nothing whatsoever in common with the traditional Mythos entity called a Shoggoth. They are very much in keeping with the Picts from the original Conan stories or similar savage marauders and since they are part of the ancestry of all modern humans also are cognate to similar Parahuman miscegenations such as those in "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family."

Hewetson was a devotee of Lovecraft and consciously tried to update and use the type of content Lovecraft and his Circle created rather than simply adapting or retelling the traditional stories from the canon. This series is a prime example of his approach.
