"The Show Must Go On" is a short Cthulhu/Yellow Mythos story by author Scott Arbuckle. It was published in Vol 6, Issue 3 of Gavin Chappell's long-running horror magazine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in October 2021 .

### Synopsis
Stage manager Leviticus Holmes is required to step into the director's shoes when the man hangs himself during the opening night of a production of the cursed play The King in Yellow. As the show progresses, more of the cast and crew take their own lives as the remaining staff and audience slowly begin a slide into insanity and reality begins to lose all meaning. At the play's climax, Holmes takes on the role of The Stranger and the barriers between dimensions finally crumble before he is transported to the breathtaking city of Carcosa.

"The Shrieking Madness" is an episode of the animated children’s show Scooby-Doo! Mystery Incorporated. It is heavily inspired by H. P. Lovecraft and "The Call of Cthulhu" in particular.

### Synopsis
The Mystery Incorporated gang investigate attacks made by a fictional monster named Char Gar Gothakon, the creation of one H. P. Hatecraft. They uncover a crazed superfan who is dressing up as one of his favorite characters to exact revenge on those who have been in any way critical of his idol.

### Characters
*Mystery Incorporated: Fred, Daphne, Velma, Shaggy and Scooby-Doo, a gang of crime-solving teens and their talking dog.
*H. P. Hatecraft, a hack author pretending to be writing stories based on ancient texts to increase his sales.
*Howard E. Roberts/Char Gar Gothakon, a fan who will go to any lengths to protect what he sees as Hatecraft's professional integrity.

### Trivia
*The character of H. P. Hatecraft was voiced by B-movie legend Jeffrey Combs, who has starred in several adaptations of Loveecraft's work, and even starred as a fictionalised version of the man himself in the 1993 film Necronomicon: Book of the Dead
*The episode features many nods to both Lovecraft's real life and the Cthulhu Mythos, including:
**H. P. Hatecraft, clearly a parody of Lovecraft himself, both in name and character design.
**Howard E. Roberts, the villain whose name is a play on that of one of Lovecraft’s closest friends, Robert E. Howard.
** Char Gar Gothakon, Hatecraft's creation which bears more than a passing resemblance to Cthulhu.

"The Shunned House" is a novelette by H. P. Lovecraft in the horror fiction genre. Written on October 16–19, 1924, it was first published as a booklet by W. Paul Cook in 1928, but this edition was barely distributed; the story got its first real exposure in the October 1937 issue of Weird Tales.

### Inspiration
The Shunned House of the title is based on an actual house in Providence, Rhode Island, the Babbit House, built around 1763 and still standing at 135 Benefit Street; Lovecraft was familiar with the house because his aunt, Lillian Clark, lived there in 1919-20 as a companion to Mrs. H. C. Babbit.

But it was another house in Elizabeth, New Jersey, that actually provoked Lovecraft to write the story. As he wrote in a letter:



This location is at present the site of a plaza named in honor of Mexican-American War hero Winfield Scott, who was the namesake of Lovecraft's father.

### Plot summary
 (Weird Tales)]]
For many years the protagonist and his uncle, Dr. Elihu Whipple, have nurtured a fascination with an old, abandoned house on Benefit Street. Dr. Whipple has made extensive records tracking the mysterious, yet apparently coincidental sickness and death of many who have lived in the house for over one hundred years. They are also puzzled by the strange weeds growing in the yard, as well as the unexplained foul smell and whitish, phosphorescent fungi growing in the cellar.

After the protagonist discovers a strange, yellowish vapour in the basement, which seems to be coupled with a moldy outline of a huddled human form on the floor, he and his uncle decide to spend the night in the house, investigating the possibility of some supernatural force. They set up cots and chairs in the cellar, arm themselves with military flamethrowers, and outfit a modified Crookes tube in the hopes of destroying any supernatural presence they might find.

When Dr. Whipple naps while the protagonist keeps watch, he begins tossing and turning, and finally starts babbling in French until he suddenly awakes. He tells the protagonist he has had strange visions of lying in an open pit, inside a house with constantly shifting features, while faces stared down at him. Many of the faces were those of the Harris family, whose members died in the house.

When the protagonist sleeps, he is awakened by a terrible scream. He sees a revolting yellowish "corpse-light" bubbling up from the floor, which stares at him with many eyes before vanishing in a wisp through the chimney. He finds his uncle transformed into a monster with "blackened, decaying features" and dripping claws. He turns on the Crookes tube, but seeing that it has no effect, escapes the house through the cellar door as his uncle's body dissolves, transforming into a multitude of faces of those who died in the house as it melts. The protagonist returns the next day to find his equipment intact, but no body.

"The Shuttered Room" is a short story by August Derleth, presented as a "posthumous collaboration" with H. P. Lovecraft. It first appeared in The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces, an anthology published in 1959 by Arkham House.

### Synopsis
The story tells of Abner Whateley, a member of the Dunwich Whateleys who has long lived abroad, coming back to the old Massachusetts town because his grandfather, Luther Whateley, dies and left him the old family home on the Miskatonic River as inheritance, including an attached mill. In a letter found in the house, Luther urges him to destroy the mill and kill anything that he finds in it, "no matter how small". While investigating the mill, and in particular a shuttered room where his Aunt Sarah was kept locked up following her visit with relatives in Innsmouth, Abner catches sight of a "long-legged frog or toad". However, he makes no effort to kill it, despite his grandfather's admonition. Instead, he kicks open the shutters to let in fresh air, in the process breaking a small hole in a window pane.

After further warnings from Tobias Whateley, his distant cousin who runs Dunwich's general store, and from Zebulon Whateley, Abner discovers tracks around the window of the (formerly) shuttered room; tiny tracks leading out of the room, and slightly larger tracks leading back in. Both tracks resemble those made by miniature human hands and feet, but with webbing between the fingers and toes.

Abner finds an old correspondence to Luther from a cousin, Ariah, who relates what he has heard about their mutual cousin from Innsmouth, Obed Marsh, from H.P. Lovecraft's "The Shadow Over Innsmouth". Ariah relates the lore about Innsmouth's Human/Deep One hybrids, which Luther evidently dismisses as rigmarole grounded in racism, because Ariah replies:

Abner also finds notes from Luther about "punishing" Sarah following her visit to Innsmouth, where she had dallied with her cousin Ralsa Marsh, said to be "probably the most repellent of all the family". Luther also writes about a mysterious "R." who was "out again". The papers include the observation that "size commensurate with amt. of food." There are references to disappearing sheep and cows, and later people; Ada Wilkerson and Howard Willie, whose shoe was found with a foot still in it. The account concludes with: “R. back at last.... Nailed the shutters to the windows of Sarah’s room.... Once he has lost weight, he must be kept on a careful diet and to a controllable size.”

Meanwhile, animals begin disappearing in Dunwich again. There are also signs that something large is moving in and out of the once-shuttered room. Abner overhears a desperate phone call on the party line from his neighbor, Luke Lang, attacked and presumably killed by "some unairthly thing...a-hoppin’ raoun’."

The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces is a collection of works by and about the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Overview
Running to a total of 313 pages, edited by August Derleth, and featuring illustrations by Frank Utpatel, The Shuttered Room and Other Pieces was published in a limited run of 2500 copies by Arkham House in 1959. It has not been reissued.

The book contains a selection of works by Lovecraft - including several juvinilia and "posthumous collaborations" -along with a number of memoirs, reminisces and studies by both those who knew him and other, more contemporary, authors.

The Signalman is a ficitonal character in Caitlin R. Kiernan's Tinfoil Dossier series, the only character who appears in all three books. He is a senior agent of the shadowy organization known as Albany, a cynical and burnt-out alcoholic who is nonetheless one of the agency's most effective assets. He has a reputation as "the one who never flinched," and as "one of the last of Albany’s True Believers, a stone-cold MiB, the agency man through and through." He has an apartment in the hills above Santa Monica, California.

The Signalman and Vance in 2015 investigate a doomsday cult known as the Moonlight Ranch at the Salton Sea in California, and discover that the cult members have infected themselves with a virulent fungus brought from Yuggoth. Vance herself turns out to be infected.

"The Silent Garden" is a short story by author and artist Jason C. Eckhardt. It is loosely connected to H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Legendary paranormal detective Thomas Carnacki lends his assistance to an elderly woman whose quaint little garden has become overrun by a malignant presence, one which threatens to spill out and consume the entire world if not dealt with quickly.

### Characters
* Thomas Carnacki, an Edwardian occultist with a wealth of knowledge on the supernatural.
* Althea Bartely, a cultured woman in her twilight years.
* Davey Bartely, Althea's nephew.

### Publication History
"The Silent Garden" was published in the Sam Gafford-edited anthology Carnacki: The Lost Cases by Ulthar Press in June 2016.

### Behind the Mythos
One of the occult devices employed by Carnacki in his cleansing of the evil is a three-tined tuning fork inscribed with "intentions in the lost language of Lomar." Since Lomar is normally considered part of the Dreamlands this may be evidence either of a dreamer from Earth transcribing the language or that at some point in the past Lomar was once also in the waking world, in the same way Leng seems at times to straddle the Dreamlands the physical waking world.

shortDefinition: "The Silver Key" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1926, considered part of his Dreamlands series. It was first published in the January 1929 issue of Weird Tales. It is a continuation of The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, and was follow...
fullContent:
"The Silver Key" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1926, considered part of his Dreamlands series. It was first published in the January 1929 issue of Weird Tales. It is a continuation of The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath, and was followed by a sequel, "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", co-written with E. Hoffmann Price.

The story and its sequel both feature Lovecraft's recurring character of Randolph Carter as the protagonist.

### Synopsis
Randolph Carter discovers, at the age of 30, that he has gradually "lost the key to the gate of dreams." Randolph once believed life is made up of nothing but pictures in memory, whether they be from real life or dreams, and he highly prefers his romantic nightly dreams of fantastic places and beings, as an antidote for the "prosiness of life", believing his dreams to reveal truths missing from man's waking ideas, regarding the purpose of humans and the universe, primary among these being the truth of beauty as perceived and invented by humans in times past. As he ages, though, he finds that his daily waking exposure to the more "practical", scientific ideas of man, has eventually eroded his ability to dream as he once did, and has made him regretfully subscribe more and more to the mundane beliefs of everyday, waking "real life". But still not certain which is truer, he sets out to determine whether the waking ideas of man are superior to his dreams, and in the process, he passes through several unsatisfying philosophical stances. Discouraged, he eventually withdraws from these lines of inquiry, and goes into seclusion. After a time, a hint of the fantastic enters his dreams again, though he is still unable to dream of the strange cities of his youth, leaving him wanting more. During one of these dreams, his long-dead grandfather tells him of a silver key in his attic, inscribed with mysterious arabesque symbols, which he finds and takes with him on a visit to his boyhood home in the backwoods of northeastern Massachusetts (the setting for many of Lovecraft's stories), where he enters a mysterious cave that he used to play in. The key somehow enables him to return to his childhood as a ten-year-old boy, and his adult self disappears from his normal time. The story then relates how Randolph's relatives had noted, beginning at the age of ten, that he had somehow gained the ability to glimpse events in his future. The narrator of the story then states that he expects to meet Randolph soon, in one of his own dreams, "in a certain dream-city we both used to haunt", reigning there as a new king, where the narrator may look at Randolph's key, whose symbols he hopes will tell him the mysteries of the cosmos.

### Inspiration

"The Sinking City" is a short story by Greek author Konstantine Paradias. It contributes to the expanded Cthulhu Mythos by providing a story about events behind the original Mythos story of Cthulhu.

### Synopsis
The story of how R'lyeh came to be submerged beneath the waves. During the war between the Great Race of Yith and the Xothians and Deep Ones led by Cthulhu, a lone Yithian takes control of a human from the present and transports him into the distant past, using his body - which, due to being a creature which does not exist during that time period, cannot be detected by R'lyeh's defences - to infiltrate the great city. Although not making it as far as the centre, the Yithian detonates its displacement bomb, ripping a huge chunk from R'lyeh and causing it to sink. 

### Characters
*Unnamed Narrator: a Yithian infiltrator in control of a human body.
*Robert Bendis: the human vessel used by the Yithian, who unfortunately remains conscious throughout the majority of the mission.
*Cthulhu: a Great Old One and enemy of the Yithians.

### Publication History
"The Sinking City" was published in the Brian M. Sammons/Glynn Owen Barrass-edited anthology World War Cthulhu in August 2014.

fullContent:
The Sinking City is an action-adventure video game developed and published by Frogwares in 2019.

A sequel The Sinking City 2 is planned for 2026.
### Summary
Former U.S. Navy sailor turned private investigator Charles Winfield Reed travels to the largely unknown town of Oakmont, Massachusetts to investigate the nightmarish visions he has been experiencing, after correspondences with a resident of that town, Johannes van der Berg, promising answers. There he discovers the town to be in great tumult, as not only is the town flooded and experiencing an influx of refugees from the recently destroyed town of Innsmouth, but also an incursion of otherworldly creatures brought in with the rising tides.

In the course of his investigation, Reed discovers that some of the occult factions within Oakmont are attempting to unseal the sunken temple of Cthygonnaar, which imprisons Cthylla, in an effort to bring about the awakening of Cthulhu.

### Characters
* Charles Reed - A WWI veteran turned private detective who sails to Oakmont to investigate missing persons as well as his own tortured dreams. He provs to be the key to either restarting the Cthulhu Cycle or unleashing Cthulhu's daughter.
* Johannes van der Berg - A wealthy patron and associate of Charles Reed who is actually an avatar of Hastur and attempting to bring about the end of the world. He frames Charles for his murder at one point.
* Robert Throgmorton - A half-ape man similar to Arthur Jermyn that is one of the wealthiest and most powerful individuals in Oakmont. He is directly opposed to the Innsmouthers and Esoteric Order of Dagon. His son was recently murdered.
* Ebernote Blackwood - A Deep One human hybrid that has turned against his fellow Blackwoods and the Esoteric Order of Dagon because he was passed over for carrying the Dreamer's Seed.
* Cthylla - The daughter of Cthulhu that is imprisoned beneath Oakmont. She is attempting to influence Reed into releasing her so that she can bring about the end of the world.

### Trivia
The protagonist, Charles Reed, has a background that suggests that his character is based on the unnamed protagonist from "Dagon." The similarities to that character include:

* Served as a naval officer during World War I.
* Got stranded at sea. His ship was attacked and he escaped in a life boat, eventually getting lost.
* He awoke on a small island not found in any map, and theorized that it may have recently emerged from volcanic activity.
* He found horrors, ruins and a creature (Dagon, a Deep One) in that island.
* His rescuers didn't believe his tales and dismissed him as delirious.
* Since the incident, he's been haunted by horrific visions.
* He's addicted to narcotics (laudanum, in Reed's case).

"The Sister City" is a short story by Brian Lumley in the Cthulhu Mythos genre. One of Lumley's first stories, it was written in 1967 and first published in Arkham House's 1969 collection Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos. 

Lumley later incorporated this story into his novel Beneath the Moors.

### Synopsis
The story is mainly narrated by Robert Krug, an archaeologist with peculiar physical abnormalities who claims to have discovered the ruins of Sarnath and Ib--and, beneath the moors of Yorkshire, Ib's sister city, Lh-yib.

### Behind the Mythos
The story contains the first references to people and places that were to recur frequently in Lumley's Mythos fiction--including the archaeologists Sir Amery Wendy-Smith and Gordon Walmsley, the lost city of G'harne in Africa, and the Oakdeene Sanitarium.

"The Sky Above... the Pits Below!" is a comic story featured in Thor Vol 1 #230 which was written by Gerry Conway, illustrated by Rich Buckler, and published by Marvel Comics in 1974. 

It is a continuation of the previous issue, featuring the Dweller-in-Darkness as the main antagonist.

### Synopsis
(Continued from "Where Darkness Dwells, Dwell I!"...)

Taking the unconscious Hercules to the Avengers Mansion, Thor seeks the aid of his fellow hero Iron Man, in order to use his Memory Inducer to probe the mind of Hercules. Iron Man asks for an explanation regarding what's going on; however, Thor is not entirely sure himself, using the Memory Inducer to learn what happened to Hercules during the missing hour. After the device is activated, Hercules wakes up and begins freaking out, destroying the laboratory while being haunted by visions of the demons who attacked him earlier. Thor and Iron Man were unable to restrain Hercules but he snaps out of it when the young goddess Krista enters the room, with Hercules being unable to harm her due to his nobility being far too great. An hour later, Hercules fully recovers his sanity, revealing that he was attacked by a figure of utter blackness before being dragged into the depths of the Earth, to a place where no light reached at all. Although Hercules could not remember what happened after that, only feeling dread, both he and Thor headed towards the street where the incident occurred. 

Meanwhile in eternal Asgard, a woman named Hildegarde tries to figure out what's happening to Odin, finding it strange that he has been hidden for nearly seven days, even refusing to appear when his son Thor asked for his aid. Breaking into Odin's palace, Hildegarde finds out that his throne is empty, with his most trusted servant Vizier telling her that Odin has vanished.

Back on Earth, Thor and Hercules enter the manhole leading to the pits of darkness, where they seemingly encounter some demons that immediately disappear when Thor tries to attack them. Hercules explains that the power behind this mystery is something they can't touch, not only affecting their minds but having its will over their very souls. While searching for this power in order to destroy it, they get attacked by another group of demons, which were a lesser breed of the monsters from earlier. While Thor is being overwhelmed by the demons swarming him, Hercules figures out that their master cannot destroy them in a physical attack but seeks to crush them in a spiritual way by overwhelming them with incredible odds, making them despair and capturing their souls.

shortDefinition: The Slayer of Souls is a fantasy novel by Robert W. Chambers originally published in 1920. It mentions the mystical city of Yian, which would be incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in The Whisperer in Darkness.  ### Behind the Myt...
fullContent:
The Slayer of Souls is a fantasy novel by Robert W. Chambers originally published in 1920. It mentions the mystical city of Yian, which would be incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by H. P. Lovecraft in The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Behind the Mythos
The Slayer of Souls mentions the city of Yian, which would be mentioned in The Whisperer in Darkness as part of a list of names that Albert Wilmarth comes across in his occult studies. Said list also includes references to Chambers' The King in Yellow, as well as to the works of Clark Ashton Smith, Lord Dunsany, Robert E. Howard and Lovecraft himself.

Yian might also be related to, or even synonymous with, the city of Yian-Ho, which is mentioned in "The Diary of Alonzo Typer" (by Lovecraft and William Lumley), and "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" (by Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price).

Although The Slayer of Souls is not part of Chambers' more famous The King in Yellow series, it seems to share certain themes.

shortDefinition: "The Slaying of the Monster" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. It was written in 1933 but not published until 1994, in Necronomicon Press’s The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast and One Other. It is an incredibly short story, being only f...
fullContent:
"The Slaying of the Monster" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow. It was written in 1933 but not published until 1994, in Necronomicon Press’s The Hoard of the Wizard-Beast and One Other. It is an incredibly short story, being only five small paragraphs and a one sentence twist in the tail.

### Synopsis
The Slaying of the Monster is a satirical and playful story of a heroic quest to destroy a legendary beast that has terrified a local community for generations. However, when the "monster" is finally found, the truth turns out to be far less mythical—and far more ridiculous—than expected. The plot parodies classic monster-hunting tropes and is a playful and light-hearted take on Lovecraftian themes. Sometimes, slaying the monster reveals more about us than the creature itself.

The people of Laen live in their town in the shadow of what we can see by its description is an active volcano. Believing it to be a dragon, the Laen townsfolk send their bravest souls to climb the mountain to where the lava spitting fire breathing dragon must be hidden.

Arriving at the mouth of the volcano, it is too hot, too smoky and far too dangerous to do anything against.

The Laen people return to their town and erect a stone plint that reads,“BEING TROUBLED BY A FIERCE MONSTER THE BRAVE CITIZENS OF LAEN DID SET UPON IT AND SLAY IT IN ITS FEARFUL LAIR SAVING THE LAND FROM A DREADFUL DOOM.”The story ends with the following sentence:"These words were hard to read when we dug that stone from its deep, ancient layers of encrusting lava."

fullContent:
"The Sleeping One" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Frank Forte, first published in his collection Beyond Lovecraft by Asylum Press in September 2020.

### Synopsis
Veterinarian Dr. Nathaniel moves into the small coastal town of Rileh, Massachusetts, to try and make the fortune which he failed to earn in the big city. When one day he is asked to attend to a bizarre creature which washes up on the beach, he is assaulted by vivid visions of Cthulhu, surrounded by it's minions beneath the ocean and slowly awakening.

Later events reveal the townsfolk to be cultists of the Great Old One, and they cast dark magics on Nathaniel before sending him to be with their god, believing that this mere man will be the one to awaken the sleeping behemoth.

### Behind the Mythos
The name of the cultist's town, Rileh, is clearly intended to recall R'lyeh, the deep sea resting place of Great Cthulhu.

### Trivia
* The story is prefaced with a quote from Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu", specifically the "correlate its contents" paragraph.

fullContent:
"The Slime Girls" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Ambuehl.

### Synopsis
A patient in the care of Arkham Asylum recounts to his doctor the tale of how he came to be committed. Believing himself to be a Deep One radio DJ in the cloistered town of Innsmouth, he gets a chance to interview the world-famous Slime Girls (a clear take on real-life girl group the Spice Girls) only to discover that, rather than being Deep Ones like himself, they are in fact humans in disguise. 

### Characters
*Isaac "Icthyic Ike" Waite, the narrator and a mental patient.
*The Slime Girls ("Eldritch," "Squamous," "Rugose," "Fungoid" and "Non-Euclidean"), a band invented by the insane narrator.

### Publication History
"The Slime Girls" was first published in the short-lived The Ancient Track magazine in October 1998. It was later reprinted in Innsmouth Tales - 2000 in 2000.

### Trivia
*Despite being clearly insane, the man still seems to posses knowledge of not only the creatures of the Cthulhu Mythos, but also some of their language.
*The story is dedicated to real-life Spice Girl Melanie Chisholm, better known as Mel C.

fullContent:
"The Slimy Ones" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mark McLaughlin.

### Synopsis
A lonely man who has spent the most recent years of his life trying to warn the world of the dangers posed by humanoid fishmen and their space-borne allies discovers that he is in fact one of the creatures. As his transformation completes, he ambles off to find his lost kin.

### Characters
*Michael "Fishboy" Jarvis, an outsider who believes he has important knowledge which must be shared with the world.
*George Flicker, a trash radio talk show host and distant relative of Jarvis's.
*Lavinia Thragg, a fully-transformed Deep One.

### Publication History
"The Slimy Ones" has been included in the collections The Horror In The Water Tower & Five More Tales Of The Cthulhu Mythos and The House Of The Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares.

### Trivia
*The name Lavinia is likely a nod to H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Dunwich Horror", which features a degenerate cultist named Lavinia Whateley.

"The Smiling People" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Andrew Peregrine. It was published in the Jason Andrew-edited thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods by Simian Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
In a dystopian future city in which the human race is forced to perform soul-destroying tasks of drudgery under the watchful eyes of their new overlords, the titular Smiling People, one man attempts to find a degree of happiness with his co-worker. When this fails and he invokes the wrath of their masters, he attempts to escape the city, only to be confronted with a shocking revelation: the Smiling People care nothing for their subjects or their misery, and only watch them as a form of entertainment.

"The Son of Misharga" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author and editor F. C. Adams. It claims to be the real-world translation of a fragment of an occult volume titled the Book of Yng, and is the first instalment in a series of such.

### Synopsis
The account of a conflict between Shub-Niggurath and a high priestess of Set, as each attempts to secure the worship of the people of Ceryx. Shub-Niggurath eventually tricks the priestess into mating with it, with the union's product being the creature which would come to be known as the Chimaera.

### Characters
*Misharga, a "serpent-woman" and high priestess of Set.
*Shub-Niggurath/Ishmak, an Outer God.
*The Chi-maera, the progeny of Misharga and Shub-Niggurath.

### Publication History
"The Son of Misharga" was published in the online Mythos zine Nightscapes in September 1998.

### Trivia
*Unusually, Shub-Niggurath is portrayed as male in this story.

fullContent:
"The Sorcerer's Jewel" is a short story by Robert Bloch that first appeared in the February 1939 issue of Strange Stories. It appeared under the pseudonym Tarleton Fiske, as Bloch had another story appearing under his own name in the same issue, "The Curse of the House". 

### Synopsis
The story concerns the photographer David Niles, who is obsessed with the idea that "the modern camera could photograph dream worlds and blend fancy with reality." Himself a rationalist, Niles hires the narrator as a technical adviser because of his interest in mythology and the occult. Niles begins by photographing models made up to look like mythological subjects, then making elaborate papier-mache sets for clay models. Continually dissatisfied with his results, he turns to unusual lenses to get closer to what he calls the Fourth Dimension--and the narrator calls the Astral Plane. Finally the narrator hits on the idea of lithomancy--"divination by the use of jewels"--and goes to the occultist Isaac Voorden, whose antique store on South Kinnikinnic (a street in Milwaukee, Wisconsin) specializes in "paraphernalia of wizardry". 

Voorden proposes to sell him the Star of Sechmet. ("Very ancient, but not costly.") Originally set in the crown of a statue of the lioness-headed goddess Sechmet (or Sekhmet), it was stolen by the Romans and put in the vestal girdle of Rome's high priestess of Diana. Barbarians looted it and cut it into a round stone. Later Axenos the Elder "bathed it in the red, yellow and blue flames, and sought to employ it as a Philosopher's Stone"; he was able to use it to see "beyond the Veil" and command elemental forces. Other possessors included Gilles de Rais (c. 1405-1440) and the Count St. Germain (1691?-1784?). Voorden  claims to have "bought it in Amsterdam from a Russian priest whose eyes had been burned out by little gray brother Rasputin." 

Surprisingly, Voorden agrees to grind this irreplaceable millennia-old antique down to use as a photographic lens, but warns the narrator "to take care in using it. There is danger in invading the realms--" 


Taking the lens back to Niles, the narrator looks through it and sees first geometric shapes, and then "shapeless toadstools with tentacles ending in Cyclopean eyes" and other monstrous figures. Niles sees similar shapes, then "tall, eyeless creatures with heads all hair...and underneath the hair, little wrinkled pink-pulp mouths like the convolution slits of the human brain." And finally--"the Goat with the Hands!" 

Shaken but exhilarated, Niles is sure he's on the right track at last. The narrator warns him, "I wouldn't advise looking too closely into that lens," but Niles insists he'll use it to take photographs with it the next day. 

That day, the narrator goes to see Voorden, and finds him dead. The notes he leaves behind point to a sinister explanation: Through the centuries, everyone who has reset, cut, or misused the stone has died. (The notes mention Veno's History--an apparently imagin

shortDefinition: "The Sorcery of Aphlar" is a fantasy short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Duane W. Rimel first published in the December 1934 issue of The Fantasy Fan. At the time, it was credited just to Rimel.  ### Synopsis The wizard Aphlar is exiled from the city ...
fullContent:
"The Sorcery of Aphlar" is a fantasy short story by H. P. Lovecraft and Duane W. Rimel first published in the December 1934 issue of The Fantasy Fan. At the time, it was credited just to Rimel.

### Synopsis
The wizard Aphlar is exiled from the city of Bel-haz-en for spending too much time alone, brooding instead of working, and consulting the papyri of Elder aeons far too frequently. He moves to the mountains and becomes a cave-dwelling hermit, but continues to study the scrolls he brought with him, and preaches his wisdom to the wind, the birds and the snails.

Aphlar knows that other exiled intellectuals have been secretly assassinated at the orders of the council following their exile, and expects a similar fate. Over the course of many seasons, he converses with the snails, who seem to understand him, and spends the nights making offerings to the moon-god Ale and communing with nocturnal "winged things".

One day, Aphlar walks down the mountain and deliberately retrieves a small object from the river bank. He takes the object back to his cave and spends the day studying it. At night, he remains in his cave.

A few days later, seven assassins sent by the council arrive, only to find the cave empty, with no sign of Aphlar. They shudder at the sight of the magic scrolls and pick up a round stone covered in unknown symbols.

When they throw the stone over the cliff into the river, the assassins are surprised to hear no sound, as if the stone has floated away instead of falling into the water. After they leave the place, which they believe is cursed, a snail crawls over the grass and watches the river, as Aphlar used to do.

shortDefinition: "The Sothis Radiant"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Will Murray which originally appeared in the anthology Miskatonic University (DAW Books, 1996). Part of Murray's Cryptic Events Evaluation Section series, it's the first story in which Murray refers ...
fullContent:
"The Sothis Radiant"  is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Will Murray which originally appeared in the anthology Miskatonic University (DAW Books, 1996). Part of Murray's Cryptic Events Evaluation Section series, it's the first story in which Murray refers to the organization as a "Section" rather than a "Taskforce."

### Synopsis
A long-sealed observatory at Miskatonic University holds the key to detecting a cosmic threat.

### Characters
*David Webb: Acting dean of astronomy at Miskatonic University.
*Randall Vincent: An agent with the Cryptic Events Evaluation Section of the National Reconnaissance Office. He is described as "thirtyish, black eyes, black hair, his wiry body encased in a dark gray Brooks Brothers suit accented by a subdued charcoal tie. There was an edgy sharpness about him." (Vincent appears briefly in Murray's 1995 story "Rude Awakening.")
*Azor Sparhawk: A 19th century astronomy professor at Miskatonic, the first director of the Sparhawk Observatory, which he opened in 1891. "He developed an apochromatic lens which compensated for chromatic aberration in a way we still don’t understand. He discovered the universe was riddled with what he called tendrils," originating from a point he called the Sothis Radiant. Born c. 1847, he was committed to Arkham Sanitarium in 1897, and died in 1903. In a photograph, he appears as "a stern-eyed man with the pointed mustaches of the Gay Nineties."
* Pickman: A former CEES operative who had responsibility for monitoring the Sothis Radiant until his death in Antarctica. (Pickman's Antarctic death is featured in Murray's 1994 story "To Clear the Earth.")
*Francis Parkman: Miskatonic's dean of astronomy until he suffered a devastating stroke, which prevented him from explaining to his successor the Sparhawk Observatory's relationship to the CEES.

### Setting
Sparkhawk Observatory is located in "the southernmost corner of the sprawling Miskatonic Campus." A "jewel of a Victorian observatory," it's an "old brick structure" with a "verdigrised dome," covered with ivy that stops short of the dome. Opened in 1891 by astronomer Azor Sparhawk, it was seized by the U.S. Secret Service and padlocked in 1897. The National Reconnaissance Office took responsibility for it in 1965. 

### Publication History
The story was reprinted in Murray's collection The Wild Adventures of Cthulhu: Volume One.

Murray wrote three sequels to "The Sothis Radiant": “What Brings the Void” (2010), “The Hour of Our Triumph” (2011), and "Dark Redeemer" (2015). Together, according to Murray, these stories "form an overarching narrative in which the world that we know it is annihilated and the Great Old Ones come down from the dark stars beyond our reality to take possession." 

### References

fullContent:
"The Soul of Kephri" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney that pits his sword-and-sorcery character Simon of Gitta against enemies derived not only from the Cthulhu Mythos but from the mythology of Star Wars as well. Aiding Simon are a character and a magical weapon derived from the works of Robert E. Howard. Tierney's story first appeared in the Summer 1984 issue of Space & Time (#66).

### Synopsis
The Roman Emperor Tiberius' plan to attain immortality poses a threat not only to Egypt but to the entire world. Guided by visions of the deceased sage Epimetrius, Simon uses the broken sword of an ancient Aquilonian king to confront the ancient evil Tiberius has summoned from its tomb.

### Setting
The story is set in the spring of 34 A.D. in Egypt, with a prelude on the Italian island of Capri.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Space & Time, "The Soul of Kephri" was reprinted in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997) and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

fullContent:
"The Soul of the Devil-Bought" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Robert M. Price. It continues the Anton Zarnak series of occult detective stories begun by Lin Carter, for whom Price acted as literary executor.

### Synopsis
Anton Zarnak, with the aid of his manservant Singh and Jacob Maitland of the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities, investigate a pair of men who have recently inherited their rich uncle's estate - along with his extensive library of occult writings. What they find is that Hiram Stokely, the uncle, has in fact used been using black magic fuelled by the blood of humans to extend his life and control a population of Yuggs which live in the catacombs beneath his mansion.

After a fierce fight with a Yugg and Stokely himself - who has possessed the body of one of his nephews- the three emerge victorious, and burn Stokely's mansion to the ground.

### Characters

* Anton Zarnak, a highly-intelligent occultist.
* Akbar Singh, Zarnak's friend and servant.
*Jacob Maitland, a student working towards his doctorate at the Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities.
*Hiram Stokely, an occultist in league with dark powers.
*Winfield Phillips, one of the heirs to Stokely's estate; by the time of the story has been possessed by his uncle.
*Brian Winfield, the other heir to Stokely's estate, who is being used as a source of living fuel by his uncle.

### Publication History
*Cthulhu Cultus #5 (May 1996)
*The Xothic Legend Cycle: The Complete Mythos Fiction of Lin Carter (1997)
*Lin Carter's Anton Zarnak: Supernatural Sleuth (June 2002)
*Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2008)

shortDefinition: "The Sound and the Fungi" is a sci-fi comedy short story by Peter Cannon published in his 2011 collection Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches. A parody of William Faulkner and H. P. Lovecraft, it features the Compson family from Faulkner's The S...
fullContent:
"The Sound and the Fungi" is a sci-fi comedy short story by Peter Cannon published in his 2011 collection Forever Azathoth: Parodies and Pastiches. A parody of William Faulkner and H. P. Lovecraft, it features the Compson family from Faulkner's The Sound and the Fury interacting with the alien Mi-Go from Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Synopsis
The Compson children - Benjy, Caddy, Jason, and Quentin - find a "claw-print" in their property which tells them that they are still being visited by the Outer Ones: fungoid/crustacean creatures from the planet Yuggoth which are made of an alien type of matter that doesn't appear in photographs. They find that their father has invited the Outer Ones for a party, or possibly a funeral. Caddy climbs up a tree to spy on the party and sees the Outer Ones holding martini glasses with their pincers, while her mother lies on the divan with the top of her head sawed off. The mother's brain is extracted and placed in a metallic cylinder.

Several years later, as the siblings are now adults, the family is still doing business with the Outer Ones, much to the distaste of xenophobic Jason, who hates his job as a manager in one of the Outer Ones' mines and wants to become a professional novelist. His sister Caddy has married an Outer One named N'gah-Kthun, who divorced her and left her with their hybrid daughter Quen-Kthun (apparently named after Quentin). The girl is just human enough to be visible in photographs, albeit as a translucent figure, and still has functional wings and antennae. The other Compsons haven't fared so well: Benjy was selected for brain removal like his mother, but something went wrong in the operation, while Quentin killed himself in college and was revived by a lunatic colleague, but his reanimated corpse crashed into his sister's wedding and had to be torn to pieces by the Outer One guests.

In addition to all these events, which have soured his opinion of the aliens, Jason also resents his niece Quen-Kthun for being a published amateur author, while Jason's own novel remains unpublished. His paranoia apparently proves itself justified when Quen-Kthun steals Jason's typescript and flies away after one of their arguments. Jason contacts the police, but when the officers arrive, they reveal themselves as Outer Ones who arrest Jason, nominally for neglecting his job in the mines. Meanwhile, Quen-Kthun marries a fellow amateur author, rewrites Jason's novel, and publishes it under her own name.

"The Space-Eaters" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Frank Belknap Long, originally published in the July 1928 issue of Weird Tales. It was reprinted in Long's collection The Hounds of Tindalos (1946) and in August Derleth's seminal anthology Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos (1969), among others.

The story's narrator, Frank, appears to be the same character from "The Hounds of Tindalos", as both stories are set in the fictional town of Partridgeville. Frank and his friend Howard are also named and modeled after Long himself and his real life friend Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
The story opens as a mysterious fog envelops the town of Partridgeville at night. Frank and his friend Howard are discussing Howard's career as a horror author, and the challenge of describing in words something entirely alien to human experience. Their conversation is interrupted by the arrival of Frank's neighbor, Henry Wells, who tells them about a strange incident that happened to him while returning to town from Brewster.

While Wells was crossing the woods, an object similar to a calf's brain fell from the trees on his wagon, followed by a long thin white creature. Wells finds this creature difficult to describe, but compares it to an impossibly long thin arm coming out from the tree tops, complete with a hand. He notes, however, that it might not have looked like that at all. Wells and his horse are scared by the sight and run away, but Wells feels an agonizing sensation of frigid cold inside his head, as if his brain was being burned by ice. Although the pain soon fades away, Wells finds out that he now has a deep hole on his head.

Frank and Howard have little time to examine Wells' head before the pain comes back and the big man runs away, screaming about something inside his head that wants to return to the woods. Frank believes that Wells has been shot on the head and survived miraculously, but Howard points out that the flesh wasn't torn and there was no blood. As they hear Wells' tortured screams, the two venture into the woods and find him alive but barely conscious, telling them that he's been attacked again. And this time could see the being more coherently: it was not a hand, but some kind of many-legged creature which entered his head and was now feeding on his brain.

The three men hear a mysterious droning sound and Howard urges them to run. They arrive at the farm exhausted and shut the door, but Wells starts acting like a wild animal and bites Howard, prompting the latter to knock him unconscious. Frank ties Wells up, tends to Howard's wounds, and calls a doctor, Smith, who declares that Wells has a brain fever and will die if not operated on. Smith notices that Howard has a slight fever too, and gives him a glass of water with an opiate, so Howard falls asleep while Smith operates on Wells. Frank holds the lamp for him, but doesn't dare to look. When Smith is finished, he reveals that he couldn't do anything about the thing he saw inside Wel

fullContent:
"The Spaces Between" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Peter Rawlik.

### Synopsis
A library assistant helps a famous former musician suffering from a hereditary genetic disorder to research her family’s musical history. They slowly uncover a dark past to the family, and amendments made to the compositions of her forebears begin to take on a dark aspect. As they get to the bottom of the mystery, the musician discovers that her condition allows her to play in a way in which others cannot, but the melodies she creates summon forth a dark entity which consumes her.

### Characters
*Martin Andersson, the narrator, a man working in the Miskatonic University library while he works on his Masters degree.
*Bela “Madame Dogma” de Hond, a former world-famous performer forced into early retirement by the development of a disorder similar to Parkinson’s.

### Publication History
"The Spaces Between" was published in The Lovecraft eZine, issue 38, in October 2016.

### Trivia
*Pete Rawlik has stated that the entity which takes Bela at the end of the story is in fact Chaugnar Faugn.

Since then the series has expanded to encompass three full-length novels in the main series, as well as a prequel novel . The main trilogy was later collected as an omnibus edition .

The series follows the exploits of Becca Philips, a young photographer and urban explorer with  family history which is intertwined with the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos. The Spirits of London is a short setting supplement for the Cthulhu by Gaslight setting of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Written by Robert Grayson, it was published by third-party content provider Stygian Fox in 2017.

### Overview


The Spirits of London is part of Stygian Fox's Hudson & Brand, Inquiry Agents of the Obscure series of Cthulhu by Gaslight supplements, a milieu which "[takes] its inspirational cues from The Murders at the Rue Morgue, A Study in Emerald, This House Is Haunted, and the stories of Sherlock Holmes."

The lion's share of the book deals with areas of London which may be home to instances of the supernatural or paranormal, rather than the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos. However, it also includes sections on a Serpent Person posing as a human medium, a Tcho-Tcho mob boss, and Mythos elements which may be mistaken for the supernatural., such as the Colour Out of Space, Dimensional Shamblers, the Hounds of Tindalos, Rat-Things, and a Mi-Go technological artefact,

The Squire is a fictional character from H. P. Lovecraft's 1926 short story "He". He is depicted as a wizard who "flouted the sanctity of things as great as space and time".

### Description
The narrator of the story--as stand-in for Lovecraft himself--describes his first impression upon meeting a stranger in Greenwich Village who shared his fascination with Old New York:

The stranger wears a costume not of the time the story is set, but typical of two centuries earlier:


### History
The stranger leads him to his home, a private estate incongruously located in the heart of Greenwich Village, where taking off his cloak he is "revealed in full mid-Georgian costume from queued hair and neck ruffles to knee-breeches, silk hose, and the buckled shoes I had not previously noticed." He tells the narrator the story of an ancestor who is plainly meant to be understood to be the stranger making a thinly veiled confession:

These Native Americans for years had climbed over the wall of the estate to hold a ritual on the night of each full moon.

The story's narrator is told that he is "the first outsider" to be told of this secret--and this only shared with him because he is "so hot after bygone things".

The stranger insists, though, that what he learned from the Native Americans he subsequently murdered is only part of his arcane knowledge:

As the narrator learns of his host's depraved character, his perception of the Squire's appearance becomes more horrific:

The Squire shows the narrator visions of New York's past and future, the last causes him to scream--a sound that enrages the Squire and summons the spirits of the Native Americans whose magic he stole. In a panic, the wizard pulls curtains off a window that exposes him to the light of the full moon, which breaks the spell that has preserved his flesh from the effects of time:

The "head with eyes" is taken away by the collective spirit of the Indians, and the house collapses from the cumulative decay of centuries. The narrator concludes: "Of who or what that ancient creature was, I have no idea; but I repeat that the city is dead and full of unsuspected horrors."

shortDefinition: "The Stairs in the Crypt: The History of the Necromancer Avalzaunt" is a horror fantasy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos, first published in the August 1976 issue of Fantastic. The story is considered a "posthumous collaboration" between Lin Car...
fullContent:
"The Stairs in the Crypt: The History of the Necromancer Avalzaunt" is a horror fantasy short story set in the Cthulhu Mythos, first published in the August 1976 issue of Fantastic. The story is considered a "posthumous collaboration" between Lin Carter and Clark Ashton Smith, written by the former after the latter's death, but incorporating material from Smith's unpublished story notes.

### Synopsis
When the necromancer Avalzaunt dies, in ancient Hyperborea, his body is "preserved in a bath of bituminous natron" by his disciples, as per the deceased's own instructions, and interred in a crypt that he himself had designed. The eldest disciple, Mygon, inherits the tower in which his master lived.

A few years pass while Avalzaunt's mummified body gathers enough strength to revive itself. When he does so, he opens up a passage to the stairs that lead to the underground lairs of the canine Ghouls. In life, Avalzaunt was a friend of the Ghouls and a worshiper of their deity, Nyogtha, so when they finally enter the chamber, he asks them for some blood to drink. Offered a beverage made from a rotten corpse's fluids, the revived sorcerer finds that it does nothing to quench his thirst. Instead, he realises that he needs fresh warm human blood, straight from the veins of the living.

Avalzaunt and his Ghoul pack kill each of the sorcerer's former acolytes, starting with Mygon, and drink all their blood. The authorities inspect the necromancer's crypt, but conclude that it is unviolated and that Avalzaunt could't have escaped it, unaware of the hidden stairs that lead to the Ghouls' tunnels. Having ran out of acolytes, Avalzaunt moves on to other victims and continues to drink, becoming more and more swollen, as his mummified body is incapable of digesting the blood.

When Avalzaunt invades a monastery dedicated to Shimba and tries to attack a monk, the latter defends himself by stabbing the undead's stomach with a knife, causing litres upon litres of coagulated blood to pour out of the bloated body. Once Avalzaunt is drained, the other monks collect his remains and burn them, preventing him from ever rising from the grave again.

fullContent:
"The Stalker in the Snows" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Ambuehl, part of his Lu-Kthu story cycle. It was first published in the Eastertide 1997 edition of Robert M. Price's long-running Lovecraftian zine Cthulhu Codex.

### Synopsis
A small expedition goes into the mountains of Minnesota to try and catalog wolves. In a series of bizarre events the expedition suspects they have encountered a werewolf, as a member of the party begins to spontaneously spout Mythos lore, almost literally chapter and verse, before finally discovering a cenobium of monks from a secret monastery, more fitting for Tibet than rural America. The monks take the expedition prisoner.

After being unwillingly exposed to Mythos lore, the survivor of the expedition becomes a raving cannibal - or so it seems.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance in Cthulhu Codex, "The Stalker in the Snows" has also been included in Correlated Contents, a collection of James Ambuehl's Cthulhu Mythos works, by Mythos Books in December 2000.

shortDefinition: "The Star-Seed" is a short story by American author James Ambuehl. It takes place against the backdrop of his Braving, Minnesota mythos setting.  ### Synopsis A Royceton University professor with an interest in the occult investigates an abandoned ma...
fullContent:
"The Star-Seed" is a short story by American author James Ambuehl. It takes place against the backdrop of his Braving, Minnesota mythos setting.

### Synopsis
A Royceton University professor with an interest in the occult investigates an abandoned mansion in the woodlands near his hometown with an evil reputation. There he comes across a decaying library of dark knowledge, and a basement-dwelling plant-creature which he narrowly escapes.

Learning what he can from the books he took, and consulting others in Royceton's Rare Book room, he deduces this being to be Ei'lor, a Great Old One. Utilising the protection of the Elder Sign and an incantation to summon Yaggdytha, he is successful in ridding the planet of the being, but later comes to the realisation that it was not Ei'lor itself, but merely one of its invasive Star-Seeds.

### Publication History
Originally written for the Chaosium collection Made in Goatswood, for which it was rejected, "The Star-Seed" was later published in Cthulhu Codex #7 in May 1996. Ambuehl later rewrote the story to incorporate it into his Braving, Minnesota milieu, although this version appears to have only been published online.

### Trivia

* A book which the narrator references, Tales of Braving and it’s Insidious Environs, is stated as being written by one James Ambrel, a clear nod to the author's own name.

shortDefinition: The Starry Wisdom: A Tribute to H. P. Lovecraft is an anthology of Lovecraftian writing edited by D. M. Mitchell and published by Creation Books in 1995. In 2012, Elektron Books released The Starry Wisdom: Fiction Inspired by H. P. Lovecraft, which c...
fullContent:
The Starry Wisdom: A Tribute to H. P. Lovecraft is an anthology of Lovecraftian writing edited by D. M. Mitchell and published by Creation Books in 1995. In 2012, Elektron Books released The Starry Wisdom: Fiction Inspired by H. P. Lovecraft, which combined much of the contents of the 1995 volume with additional material.

In an introduction, Mitchell said he aimed to "bypass the superficial and access the subterranean channels of archetype and inspiration with which Lovecraft was connected." Mitchell presents Lovecraft--and the writers in his anthology--as part of a tradition not only of horror writers like Edgar Allan Poe, Algernon Blackwood, and Arthur Machen, but also of avant-garde writers like Comte de Lautréamont and Antonin Artaud, and occultists like Aleister Crowley and Helena Blavatsky.

Far from writing "escapist fantasies," Mitchell said, Lovecraft "crafted morbid and disturbing allegories of social and biological upheaval" that were "cryptically prophetic and spiritually exploratory":A large part of Lovecraft’s driving force came from the frisson he experienced between the patriarchal vision of order, logic and reason to which he adhered, and the intruding chaotic, female forces from "outside" –- forces both disruptive and ultimately redeeming.Lovecraft's "occasional misogyny and ill-considered racism both sprang from this gulf between these antagonistic sides of his personality," Mitchell asserts.

In 2009, Mitchell edited Songs of the Black Würm Gism: Hymns to H. P. Lovecraft, a collection of original Lovecraftian fiction published by Creation Oneiros as a sequel to Starry Wisdom. The 2012 version of Starry Wisdom fused the majority of the 1995 original with the bulk of the 2009 volume.

The Statement of Andrew Doran is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by American author and editor Matthew Davenport, the first in his Andrew Doran series. It was first published independently through the CreateSpace platform in February 2013; both paperback and digital editions were released.

### Synopsis
The protagonist, Dr. Andrew Doran formerly of Miskatonic University, is called upon by the Dean of that esteemed institute to recover the Necronomicon, which has been stolen by Nazis to be used in their plans for world domination.

### Plot

### Chapter 1: Miskatonic University
Dr. Andrew Doran is summoned to Miskatonic University by his nemesis Dean Brandon Smythe and informed of the loss of the Necronomicon, which has been stolen by Nazi infiltrators. He equips himself with a magical sword and handgun from the University's armoury and prepares to set off on his mission.

### Chapter 2: The Shadow Over Barcelona
Taking passage to Barcelona aboard a freighter, Doran encounters Deep Ones on a mission to establish a new colony off the coast of Spain. He strikes a deal with the creatures: he will ensure the coral vital to the new colony arrives intact in exchange for the ship and the lives of its crew.

### Chapter 3: The Whisperers in Andorra
After contacting the French Resistance in Andorra, Doran and his new allies are captured by the local Nazis, who are in league with the alien Mi-Go. Through judicial use magic and firearms, he and Olivia, the sole surviving member of the resistance, succeed in killing the Mi-Go liaison and begin the long journey to Lyon.

### Chapter 4: The Thing in Lyon
Hunted once again by the Nazis, Doran and Olivia make contact with Leo, another French Resistance agent, and flee their pursuers through the extensive tunnels beneath Lyon. After a brief encounter with an undying sorcerer, during which Doran has his mind and body swapped but uses his knowledge of magic to revert the spell, the group return to the surface and continue on their way.

### Chapter 5: Geneva-Reanimated
On the way to Geneva with the aim of meeting up with an old friend of Doran's, the group are attacked by a small horde of reanimated corpses seemingly in service to the Nazi party. After a lengthy road battle, they see off the dead fiends and arrive safely in Switzerland, meeting up with Father Blake, who directs them to the city of Bern, and a scientist who may be able to assist them on the next leg of their journey.

### Chapter 6: Cool Air in Berne
When Doran contacts Karl Freeman in Berne, the man reveals that he is in fact a secret Cthulhu cultist who has prolonged his life using arcane sciences. He also informs him that Olivia is not what she seems, and that Doran is destined to use the Necronomicon to awaken Great Cthulhu. Doran in turn kills Freeman for his troubles, before preparing the small group of freedom fighters for their next move.

"The Statement of Eeyore Carter" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Kevin Wetmore. As can be guessed from the title, it is a retelling of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Statement of Randolph Carter", with the characters swapped out for those of A. A. Milne's children's series Winnie-the-Pooh. It was published in the April Moon Books anthology The Call of Poohthulhu in March 2022.

### Synopsis
Eeyore tells detective Christopher Robin the story of how he and Pooh Bear investigated a secret tomb which they found in the Floody Place. Pooh travelled into its depths while Eeyore waited above. Although the two were able to communicate through a length of twine and two tin cans, eventually Pooh's voice was replaced by an alien one which proclaimed "You fool, Pooh is dead!"

### Behind the Mythos
Amongst the Cthulhu Mythos elements made reference to are Shoggoths, Shantak Birds, Cthulhu, R'lyeh, Dimensional Shamblers, De Poohis Mysteriis, and Ludvig Pooh.

### Synopsis
Henry Worthy's botanist nephew Matthew mysteriously disappears--and when he reappears, he is undergoing a horrific transformation.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in The Horror at Oakdeene, "The Statement of Henry Worthy" was reprinted in the August 1991 of the magazine Frighteners.

It was later included in Lumley's collections Dagon's Bell and Other Discords (New English Library, 1994), The Whisperer and Other Voices (Tor, 2001), and  Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008).

"The Statement of Jackson Palmer" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Thomas V. Powers. It was published in the March 1999 edition of E. P.  Berglund's digital zine Nightscapes.

### Synopsis
The story is narrated by someone who becomes fascinated by the Cthulhu Mythos and who then immerses themselves in research on the topic. By doing so they discover literary sources used by H. P. Lovecraft and others that attest to the reality behind the Mythos.

The story is a prolonged exercise in harmonizing real world myth and references to those of the Mythos, including "explaining" the real meaning of Mythos language words in terms of real-world religious or folklore elements to which they refer.

"The Statement of One John Gibson" is a short story by Brian Lumley in the Cthulhu Mythos genre. It serves as a sequel to "The Diary of Alonzo Typer", a story that H. P. Lovecraft revised for William Lumley (no known relation). It was originally published in Crypt of Cthulhu Candlemas 1984 (February), an issue dedicated to Brian Lumley.

### Plot
The story is presented as a transcript made by John Gibson, born April 30, 1957, of Surrey, England. On his father's side he is descended from the "Typers of New Hampshire," originally from Ulster County, New York, "known for the coarse, almost greenish cast of their features." On his mother's side he is from an old Dutch family, the Sleghts--thus linking him on both sides of his family tree to the narrator of Alonzo Typer, the narrator of the Lovecraft revision tale.

John's father was an obsessive student of "all manner of Earth’s elder horrors and mysteries",  a "delver in obscure myths and myth-cycles, a searcher of nighted crypts and beneath desert mastabas, and a pursuer of all things esoteric and exciting to his sort of super-imaginative mind." After the father's death, some time in 1982, from "some creeping organic malfunction which aged him well before his time", John inherits the contents of his locked bureau. Despite a dying warning from his father's solicitor, James Ogilvy--his last words, after inexplicably crashing into an oak tree on the Gibson estate, were “Glub . . . glub . . . look in . . . bureau . . . destroy . . . glub . . .”--John opens the forbidden cabinet of mystery and finds a collection of Mythos-related literature, specifically:

Perhaps more surprisingly, the father's secret texts include old copies of Weird Tales, a set of the Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft, and a copy of the Arkham House revisions anthology The Horror in the Museum, which reprinted "The Diary of Alonzo Typer".

The father's effects also included a medallion (later found to have originated in Yian-Ho) , "not quite circular, perhaps two inches across at its widest point." Despite its small size, the medallion bears a fantastically detailed engraving depicting "a burst of light beyond a horizon of strangely angled architectural structures, windowless towers and turrets whose unbalanced geometry made them seem both concave and convex." In the foreground are a host of figures who seem to be fleeing "the approach of some awesome event or Being":

He later identifies these as the entities Ithaqua and Cthulhu; others are left as an exercise for the reader:
There is as well a letter to the father from his great-uncle Victor Gibson (c. 1835-1920), who was "a Professor of Anthropology, specializing in Ethnology and Mythology, at Heidelberg" until he retired in 1895. It turns out that Typer was a student of his, and that he is the V__ mentioned in Typer's diary as the source of forbidden knowledge. shortDefinition: "The Statement of Randolph Carter" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. Written in December 1919, it was first published in The Vagrant, May 1920. It tells of a traumatic event in the life of Randolph Carter, a student of the occult loosely represent...
fullContent:
"The Statement of Randolph Carter" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. Written in December 1919, it was first published in The Vagrant, May 1920. It tells of a traumatic event in the life of Randolph Carter, a student of the occult loosely representing Lovecraft himself. It is the first story in which Carter appears, and is part of Lovecraft's Dream Cycle.

### Synopsis
"The Statement of Randolph Carter" is the first person testimony of the titular character, who has been found wandering through swampland in an amnesiac shock. In his statement, Carter attempts to explain the disappearance of his companion, the occultist Harley Warren.

Warren has come into the possession of a book written in an unknown language that he forbids Carter from seeing. Carter mentions that Warren has other "strange, rare books on forbidden subjects", several of which are in Arabic.

Based on something he has read in his mysterious book, Warren encourages Carter to travel with him to an ancient graveyard near Big Cypress Swamp. Upon arriving, Warren locates a particular tomb and opens it to reveal a staircase that descends into the earth. Taking a lantern, he leaves Carter on the surface and follows the stairs into the darkness, communicating with his companion by a telephone wire.

After several minutes of silence, Warren suddenly begins to make vague, panicked outbursts that culminate in a desperate plea for Carter to flee. Finally, after Warren is silent for several minutes, Carter calls to him down the line, only to hear an alien voice telling him that Warren is dead.

### Characters
### Randolph Carter

Randolph Carter is one of Lovecraft's most commonly recurring characters. An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia places the events of the story after those of "The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath" and before "The Unnamable" or "The Silver Key".

### Harley Warren

Harley Warren is a mysterious occultist who apparently perishes while exploring an underground crypt in Big Cypress Swamp. After his disappearance, Randolph Carter tells police that "I have for five years been his closest friend, and a partial sharer of his terrible researches into the unknown." Warren, he says, "always dominated me, and sometimes I feared him." He mentions a facial expression of Warren's that caused him to shudder. Warren himself suggests that he sees himself as someone with "ironclad sensibilities".

Carter describes Warren as having a "vast collection of strange, rare books on forbidden subjects," many of them apparently in Arabic, with one "fiend-inspired book...written in characters whose like I never saw elsewhere."

In the dream that inspired the story, the character of Warren was actually Lovecraft's friend Samuel Loveman. Loveman also figured in the dream that became the prose poem "Nyarlathotep".

fullContent:
"The Steel Plague" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Nate Southard. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
After a sophomore's science fair experiment into self-replicating robots goes disastrously wrong, the newly-created machines - who require only metal and plastic to recreate themselves - slowly begin the process of dismantling human civilisation.

In the aftermath, one woman survives long enough to witness an enormous swarm of the little mechanoids create a vast, temple-like construct from their own bodies, before something huge and terrible emerges from beneath the ground.

### Behind the Mythos
As the robots evolve over the course of the story, the noises which they emit begin to sound more and more like a language, albeit one unknown to humans. Near the conclusion, their chant becomes "R'lyeh! Ia! R'lyeh! Ia!," from which one could infer that the monstrous subterranean entity is intended to be the Great Old One Cthulhu.

"The Stocking" is a short story by British author Ramsey Campbell which is connected to the greater Cthulhu Mythos. It was first published in the anthology Tandem Horror 2 in 1968 by Tandem, and has also been translated into German.

### Synopsis
The flirtatious relationship between office workers Tom and Shiela, who appear to be mutually attracted to each other, takes a dark turn when Tom traps Shiela in an abandoned building for which she has long harboured a deep-seated fear.

### Mythos Connections
Despite containing no direct references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, "The Stocking" is tied to the Cthulhu Mythos by the short story "The Franklyn Paragraphs", which features a fictionalised version of Ramsey Campbell as its narrator. In the story, when Campbell sends author Errol Undercliffe a manuscript of "The Stocking", he replies that he did not like it, labelling it as "elaborately pointless".

fullContent:
"The Stone on the Island" is a short story by Ramsey Campbell in the Cthulhu Mythos genre, set in his Severn Valley milieu in 1962. It first appeared in 1964 in the Arkham House anthology Over the Edge.

### Synopsis
Michael Nash, a young man from Brichester, finds his father dead from suicide, leaving behind a mysterious warning about the Island Beyond Severnford, an island near Severnford in the Severn River. The warnings centers on a mysterious stone on the island, associated for more than a hundred years with mysterious deaths and mutilations (and spooky floating white ovals). Naturally, Michael goes to investigate, on October 28, 1962, and finds the stone:


He touches it, despite explicit warnings about  "going too near the stone": "Immediately he knew that he had done the wrong thing."

Michael finds himself haunted by floating faces: First one, then two and more. They watch him at home and at work; thinking he sees one in the storeroom at the office, he kicks at it viciously and find he has accidentally killed a new co-worker. He jumps on a bus to avoid arrest and finds himself back in Severnford. There he is set upon by the faces; when he is found by police from Brichester and Severnford, they discover that someone has "remove[d], cleanly in one piece, the skin of [his] face."

### Characters
*Michael Nash: A young civil servant who works in a modern office building in central Brichester. He knows just enough about eldritch matters to get himself into trouble: He is aware of the supposed protective qualities of "five-pointed stones", and knows to use the "Saaamaaa Ritual" as a last resort.
*Dr. Stanley Nash: Michael's father, a Brichester physician. He commits suicide, leaving his son a warning about the "Island Beyond Severnford." He also leaves behind a "secret library of rare books".
*Mr. Miller: Michael's boss.
*Gloria: Michael's co-worker.
*G.F.E Dickman: A disgruntled client.
*Jack Purvis: A friend of Michael's in Camside who owes him money.
*Inspector Daniels: A Brichester police officer.
*Inspector Blackford:  A Severnford police officer.
*Historical:
**Joseph Norton: A witchcult believer who worships at the island in 1803, and is later found in Severnford mutilated and raving about "going too near the stone".
**Nevill Rayner: A Severnford clergyman who goes to the island in 1826 to "rid my flock of this evil", and is later found mutilated in his church.
**Alan Thorpe: Removes the stone from the island in 1890 while "investigating local customs", and is then found "horribly wounded"--with the stone showing up back on the island.

### Connections
Michael Nash is aware of "the hidden forces which clustered about a house in Victoria Road, a demolished wall at the bottom of Mercy Hill, and such towns as Clotton, Temphill and Goatswood." The Victoria Road house and Mercy Hill wall are references to Campbell's story "The Return of the Witch", while horrors in the towns are explored in his "The Horror From the Bridge", "The Church in Hi

"The Storm Cellar" is a short story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
A man relates the tale of how, in 1966, a tornado forced him and his grandparents into their storm cellar, where they encountered a monstrous creature and were lucky to escape with their lives. Afterwards, all involved pretended that the whole incident was nothing more than a fever-dream.

### Characters

* Tommy, a young boy on vacation with his grandparents in Texas.
* Grandpa Tate, a retired oil field roughneck.
* Grandma Tate, a kindly old woman.

### Publication History

### Trivia

* Although never explicitly stated, the subterranean creature which the three people are attacked by is clearly intended to be a ghoul.

fullContent:
"The Strange Doom of Enos Harker" is an unfinished Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter. The fragment was published posthumously in the magazine Crypt of Cthulhu in 1989. It is both a continuation of Carter's "Behind the Mask" (itself a sequel to August Derleth's "The Return of Hastur") and tied into his Xothic Legend Cycle, as the protagonist, Paxton Blaine, is the nephew of Dr. Henry Stephenson Blaine from "Out of the Ages".

"The Strange Doom of Enos Harker" was later completed by Robert M. Price, and the finished version was published in the 1997 collection The Xothic Legend Cycle: The Complete Mythos Fiction of Lin Carter.

In the same year, Laurence J. Cornford also penned a different ending, and the resulting tale was published under the slightly altered title "The Doom of Enos Harker".

### Synopsis
### Fragment by Lin Carter
The story is narrated by Paxton Blaine, an anthropologist graduated from Miskatonic University in 1931, who is hired as a secretary by Arkham resident Dr. Enos Harker, a priest and former missionary who has spent years in India, Burma and Tibet, and who claims to be afflicted by a severe skin condition that forces him to keep his hands and parts of his face bandaged. Blaine's job consists of organizing Harker's notes on obscure Asian cults, and assisting him in his research, which involves books such as the Unaussprechlichen Kulten, the Cultes des Goules, and the Necronomicon, among others.

A lot of Harker's research concerns the mysterious Tcho-Tcho people, believed to inhabit both Burma and a place known as Leng, the location of which Blaine is not able to pinpoint. The grimoires tell of strange gods worshiped by the Tcho-Tchos, and of a Tcho-Tcho lama who wears a silken yellow mask over his face. Blaine is disturbed by how this mythology seems to be related to a number of recent events in the vicinity of Arkham, all of which appear to have been hushed up by the authorities. These include the destruction of the Tuttle house, the military operations in the nearby town of Innsmouth, and the case of Bryant Hoskins, who went mad in a cabin in the woods and died in an asylum.

Two passages from the Necronomicon interest Harker particularly, the first claiming that the Tcho-Tchos originate from the Dreamlands and first came to the Waking World via Sarkomand, and the second concerning an incoming event called the Great Awakening, in which gods such as Cthulhu and Shub-Niggurath will call to summon their followers and all those "who carry the Emblem" as well as all those who have seen it.

As the days go by, Blaine notices that Harker's health seems to be worsening. He speaks in whispers, his eyesight is deteriorating, his entire body seems to be bloated, and has a repulsive smell. The bandages now cover almost his entire face, as well as his hands, and he becomes increasingly dependent on Blaine to help him with the house chores, as well as handle his correspondence with scholars from other parts of the world.
