shortDefinition: "The Strange High House in the Mist" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. Written on November 9, 1926, it was first published in the October 1931 issue of Weird Tales.  ### Plot Summary Thomas Olney, a "philosopher" visiting the town of Kingsport, Ma...
fullContent:
"The Strange High House in the Mist" is a short story by H. P. Lovecraft. Written on November 9, 1926, it was first published in the October 1931 issue of Weird Tales.

### Plot Summary
Thomas Olney, a "philosopher" visiting the town of Kingsport, Massachusetts with his family, is intrigued by a strange house on a cliff overlooking the ocean. It is unaccountably high and old and the locals have a generations-long dread of the place which no one is known to have visited. With great difficulty, Olney climbs the crag, approaches the house, and meets the One, the mysterious man who lives there. The only door opens directly onto a sheer cliff, giving access only to mist and "the abyss". The transmittal of archaic lore and a life-altering encounter with the supernatural ensue, as Olney is not the only visitor that day. He returns to Kingsport the next day, but seems to have left his spirit behind in the strange, remote dwelling.

### Inspiration
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia suggests that the story may have been inspired by Lord Dunsany's Chronicles of Rodriguez, in which strange sights can be seen from a wizard's house on a crag. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

One model for the setting was Mother Ann, a headland near Gloucester, Massachusetts. (: Selected Letters III)

### Connections
, by Hugo Petrus (Mythos: Lovecraft's Worlds)]]
Kingsport, which is mentioned in several Lovecraft stories, first appeared in "The Terrible Old Man" (1920). The title character of that story makes an appearance in "The Strange High House in the Mist" as well, as the Old Man mentions that the House had been on the cliff even when his grandfather was a boy, which the main character comments "must be immeasurable ages ago".

The story features the Celtic god Nodens, who also appears in The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. This entity was later identified by August Derleth as one of the Elder Gods. In the same passage in "The Strange High House in the Mist", Lovecraft also mentions the arrival of the god Neptune, but that Roman deity has not similarly been adopted by Lovecraftian writers.

### Critical Reaction
The story was originally rejected by Weird Tales when submitted in July 1927. In 1929, Lovecraft agreed to let W. Paul Cook publish it in the second issue of The Recluse, but when it became clear that that issue would never appear, he resubmitted it to Weird Tales, which accepted it, paying him $55. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

Joanna Russ described The Strange High House in the Mist as "pleasing", and Robert A. W. Lowndes called it one of Lovecraft's "best short stories".

### Comic Book Adaptations
The story was adapted into webcomic book form by Jason Thompson. It is currently available [http://mockman.com/ online], and was later published as his collection The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath and Other Stories.

It was also adapted by Brandon Barrows and Hugo Petrus for their comic book series Mythos: Lovecraft's Worlds.

### Synopsis
After Crawford Tillinghast's body goes missing from the morgue and he has a lucid dream he is still alive in another reality, the narrator of "From Beyond", Lucien Holmes, resolves to do everything in his power to bring his friend back. After initial setbacks, he recruits the assistant of Miskatonic University quantum physicist Kaitlyn Davidson to help rebuild the resonator.

Holmes is successful in his attempts, and returns Tillinghast to his home reality, but he is not the same man he once was: possessed of superhuman powers and a malign intellect, he is intent on bringing the creatures he lived with on the other side to our world. To this end he abducts Kaitlyn to be used as a blood sacrifice; Holmes and Kaitlyn are able to stop his plans and cause Tillinghast's death, but in the process open a colossal portal through which pour the ravenous hordes from beyond.

fullContent:
"The Street" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written in late 1919 and first published in the December 1920 issue of The Wolverine amateur journal.

### Synopsis
The story traces the history of the eponymous street in a New England city, presumably Boston, from its first beginnings as a path in colonial times to a quasi-supernatural occurrence in the years immediately following World War I.

As the city grows up around the street, it is planted with many trees and built along with "simple, beautiful houses of brick and wood," each with a rose garden. As the Industrial Revolution runs its course, the area degenerates into a run-down, polluted slum, with all of the street's old houses falling into disrepair.

After World War I and the October Revolution, the area becomes home to a community of Russian immigrants; among the new residents are the leadership of a "vast band of terrorists" who are plotting the destruction of the United States on Independence Day.

When the day arrives, the terrorists gather to do the deed, but before they can get started, all the houses in the street collapse concurrently on top of them, killing them all. An observer at the scene testified that immediately after the collapse, he had seen visions of the trees and the rose gardens that had once been in the street.

### Inspiration
The Boston Police Strike of September–October 1919 inspired Lovecraft to write "The Street", as he declared in a letter to Frank Belknap Long:



The terrorism was also real, and had been going on since 1914 in a series of parcel bombs. In 1919 two campaigns of mail bombing were discovered. In 1920 there would be a major terrorist bomb attack on Wall Street.

The story's anti-immigrant stance echoes such earlier xenophobic poems by Lovecraft as "New England Fallen" and "On a New-England Village Seen by Moonlight".(EXP: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia)

The (real and unreal) news of the anarchy occurring during the Russian and German revolutions would, along with the story of Peter the Painter, also indubitably have effected a market for the story.

### Reaction
An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia describes this story as "manifestly racist". Daniel Harms, author of The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana, wrote, "If someone came up to me and said, 'Hey Daniel, I think H. P. Lovecraft was a wordy, overly-sentimental bigot whose stories don't make much sense,' this would be the last story I would hand to him to convince him otherwise."

### Notes

*S. T. Joshi and David Schultz, An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia

"The Studies of Dr. Reid" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Peter Rawlik. It was published in the thematic anthology Pickman's Gallery by Ulthar Press in 2018.

### Synopsis
Dr. Reid explains to Eliot, the silent "audience" from "Pickman's Model", how he had observed the artist Richard Upton Pickman for a time before his disappearance, noticing several unusual characteristics which he had been developing over time. 

Reid had later followed Pickman on his nightly jaunts, and watched his trysts with the ghouls which became the subject of his art. Fascinated, Reid began to study taxidermy in an effort to understand the biology of the creatures, and eventually worked up the courage to kill one, later dissecting it.

The story ends with the revelation that Reid has brought Eliot to a subterranean nest of ghouls, where he wants the poor man to aid him in procuring another sample for the dissection table.

### Characters
*Dr. Reid, a learned man with an unhealthy interest in the creatures which prowl the Boston streets at night. Studied taxidermy under one Will Minot at the Cabot Museum in pursuit of this interest.
*Eliot, the man who heard Thurber's account of the fate of Richard Upton Pickman in "Pickman's Model". Although an important part of both this story and the original, Eliot has no lines in either.

### Behind the Mythos
Dr. Reid was a character mentioned in "Pickman's Model" as one of the men who snubbed Pickman's art. Here, he explains that he did not turn his back on him as Thurber stated, but merely wished to distance himself a little from the artist's disturbing presence after a long time spent in close proximity together.

"The Substance in the Sound" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author W. B. Stickel.

### Synopsis
When a father and son fishing crew discover a strange lump of protoplasm floating off of America's east coast, they take it to an expert to be analysed. The scientist has the two take him back out to where they found it, only to discover many more of the masses.

The expert then reveals that he is of Innsmouth stock, and recites a chant which invigorates the creatures before sacrificing the fishermen and heading to Innsmouth to prepare for a coming war, one in which the newly-awakened monstrosities will play a central role…

### Characters
* Hammich Kellerman, a seasoned Bostonian fisherman.
* Edwin Kellerman, Hammich's son.
* Abe "Telly" Teller, a former sailor now working for the Northeastern University Marine Science Center.

### Publication History
"The Substance in the Sound" was published in the Kat Rocha-edited Lovecraftian anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in 2013.

### Trivia
* The creatures encountered by the seamen, whilst not actually named, are implied to be Shoggoths.

fullContent:
"The Suicide in the Study" is a horror short story by American writer Robert Bloch, first published in the June 1935 issue of Weird Tales.

The story is notable as the first appearance of the Mythos tome Cultes des Goules (described as "ghastly"), as well as its fictional author, the Comte d'Erlette. The count's name is a play on August Derleth's name, which has misled some into thinking that Derleth was the originator of the book. 

The story is also the first mention of Luveh-Keraph, a fictional priest of Bast from Ancient Egypt--whose name is of course based on H. P. Lovecraft, who was well-known for his love of cats.

### Characters
*James Allington - a 'modern day' wizard attempting to split his good self from his evil self, similar to the concept of Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde except he uses hypnotism rather than a chemical solution.
*Monstrous Figure - Allington's evil-half made real through physic manifestation. It was more powerful than Allington's good-half and resembled a great hairy black ape, whose head appeared as a rotting living skull with yellow fangs and little red eyes full of dark wisdom.

"The Survivor" is a short story by August Derleth based on an idea from H. P. Lovecraft, billed as one of the controversial "posthumous collaborations" between the two writers. It initially appeared in the July 1954 issue of Weird Tales, and then was the title story of a collection of Derleth/Lovecraft "collaborations" released by Arkham House in 1957.

### Synopsis
The story concerns the efforts of antiquarian Alijah Atwood to investigate the history of the Carriere House on Benefit Street in Providence, Rhode Island, which Atwood is renting. The owner of the house, Jean-Francois Charriere, a surgeon who supposedly died in 1927, was born in Bayonne, France, in 1636 after having achieved near-immortality by turning himself into a kind of human/reptile hybrid.

fullContent:
The Survivor and Others is a collection of short stories billed as "posthumous collaborations" between August Derleth and H. P. Lovecraft, released in 1957 by Arkham House. In fact, the stories were for the most part written by Derleth, based on unused story ideas jotted down by Lovecraft. With the exceptions of "The Survivor", published by Weird Tales in July 1954, and "The Gable Window", published (as "The Murky Glass") in the May 1957 issue of Saturn magazine, all the stories made their first appearance in this collection.  

Ballantine Books reissued the collection in paperback in 1962 and again in 1971, and a French-language version has also been produced.

fullContent:
The Sussex Manuscript is a text created by Fred Pelton in the 1940s, presented as a transcription of an occult text from the Renaissance called Cultus Maleficarum. The text is dedicated to the fictional Frederick I, Baron of Sussex, and is dated 1598.

Pelton described his creation:The manuscript contains four books: the first deals with the Mythos up to the time of the Coming of Cthulhu, the second with that Reign of Cthulhu and his overthrow, the third with the rites and ritual of the cult, and the fourth is a book of prophecy. It is now well established that the Sussex Manuscript will rank with the dreaded Necronomicon as one of the most reliable and detailed texts concerning the Mythos. The author of this masterpiece is unknown.  Pelton submitted the manuscript to August Derleth at Arkham House, who at one point planned to publish it; Derleth even included a reference to The Sussex Manuscript in his short story "The Gorge Beyond Salapunco" (written in 1946 and published in 1949). Derleth later wrote to Edward P. Berglund, who had expressed interest in publishing Pelton's work:THE SUSSEX MANUSCRIPT, I assure you, was not worth publishing—a hodgepodge of stuff, some from the published HPL & other Mythos stories, some made up to fill in the gaps. Pelton did a persuasive job in places, but the performance was very uneven. And certainly not a viable addition to the Mythos or we'd have published it. . . . Nor would other publication be likely, for we'd not permit the quotations from our stories to be used. So forget it. and Pelton's A Guide to the Cthulhu Cult (Armitage House, 1998).

Derleth also made reference to the Sussex Fragments in his short story "The Seal of R'lyeh," published in 1957. These are sometimes identified with the translation of the prehistoric Eltdown Shards, said to have been offered by the Reverend Arthur Brooke Winters-Hall, "a deeply learned Sussex clergyman of occultist leanings," in the round-robin short story "The Challenge from Beyond."

### A True Labor of Love
The original physical copy of The Sussex Manuscript was lost after Fred L. Pelton's death in 1950. However, his son John inherited and preserved his father's papers and books and later passed the original still-extant material to Edward P. Berglund. In Edward P. Berglund's own words:"John Pelton informed me that his father had died in 1950. He did have the Sussex Manuscript in his possession, although it was only partially complete. Of the four books or chapters, he had only the first three in their entirety, with the opening pages of the fourth. The manuscript in toto was in a large, 12" x 19 1/2", leather-bound book."

"The Tale of Nanok the Merchant" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Thomas V. Powers. It was published in the Gavin Chappell-edited anthology Swords Against Cthulhu II: Hyperborean Nights, by Rogue Planet Press in 2017.

### Synopsis
Avaricious Hyperborean merchant Nanok, his trusty business partner and swordsman Tochran, and ambitious magician Uhlmhaas gather together an expedition to search for a copy of the fabled Book of Eibon, rumoured to be hidden along with a fabulous stash of treasure.

Travelling to a remote island on their quest, the party encounter and defeat a cult devoted to Great Cthulhu, the guardians of the book and its hoard of valuables. Unfortunately for them, during the confrontation the book is destroyed, and they are forced to abandon their stolen treasure on the return voyage when they are attacked by wave upon wave of aggressive fish-men.

"The Tale of Satampra Zeiros" is a short story by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith, first published in the pulp magazine Weird Tales in November 1931, and part of Smith's Hyperborean Cycle. It is notable for containing the first description of the toad-god Tsathoggua.

### Synopsis
A pair of down-on-their-luck thieves in ancient Hyperborea decide that the best way to get their finances back on track is to raid the long-abandoned city of Commoriom, said to be cursed, and shunned by all sensible folk.

Upon their arrival, they investigate an ancient temple to Tsathoggua, and invite the wrath of one of the temple's guardians, a Formless Spawn. Although one of the adventurers manages to escape with merely the loss of a hand, the other is not so lucky.

### Characters
*Satampra Zeiros, an accomplished thief.
*Tirouv Ompallios, Satampra Zeiros's lifelong friend and partner-in-crime.

### Publication History
Since its first publication, "The Tale of Satampra Zeiros" has been reprinted many times. It has also been translated into Spanish, Dutch, French, Italian, Finnish, German, and Hungarian.

"The Tale of the Reanimator" is an episode of the children's horror anthology television series Are You Afraid of the Dark?, written by Kenny Davis and first aired in 2000. Rather than an adaptation, it is inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's short story "Herbert West--Reanimator".

### Synopsis
A young girl named Julie gets an after-school job at a botanical laboratory, owned by a scientist named Mr. Doyle. When Julie finds out that Doyle invented a serum that revives plant life, she speculates that he is working on one that can revive humans as well, in hopes of finding a way to bring back his deceased wife. Later, she tells her brother Peter and their friend Jake about it, but unfortunately, they do not believe her story, leading to Peter pouring a sample of the serum on a grave that says "Ian Kazex, May he be forgiven!", indicating that he was a bad person. The serum ends up reviving a violent criminal, who preceded to terrorize the children as a Reanimated corpse. Remembering how Doyle's plants immediately died from having water poured on them, Julie figures out that the effects of the serum can be reversed by extreme heat. The zombie is lured into a hot box, causing it to dry up and die again. Afterwards, Doyle finds out about what has happened and blames himself for trying to tamper with fate, canceling any further research for his experiment.

fullContent:
"The Tale of Toad Loop" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Stanley C. Sargent.

### Synopsis
A man incarcerated in a sanatorium relates a tale from his youth. The story concerns the arrival in town of a man from Innsmouth named Mulltree who proceeds to buy up a parcel of land including Toad Loop, an area avoided by the townsfolk and feared by the natives.  

After Mulltree marries a local girl by the name of Pritchy and puts her in the family way, he is witnessed summoning forth a dark entity through the old shrine at Toad Loop, although the creature breaks free and devours him. 

The doctor called to look after Pritchy shoots himself after witnessing the being that she gives birth to, and the teller of the tale is driven insane when he ventures onto the farm to help her. 

### Characters
*The Narrator, an unnamed man from Madlan County, currently residing in a mental institution.
*Mazrah Mulltree, a stranger from Innsmouth with a dark agenda.
*Pritchy Mulltree (née Kwik), a local girl who marries Mazrah.
*Steve Simmons, a rebellious young teenager.
*Doc Jefferys, the local physician.
*The Sheriff, the local lawman.
*Olivia "Oly" Johnson, a local woman hired to care for Pritchy.
*Toadaggwa, or Tsathoggua, a Great Old One.

### Publication History
First featuring in the online zine Nightscapes in January 1998, "The Tale of Toad Loop" was later included in the first edition of sporadic horror magazine Dark Legacy. It has since appeared in a number of anthologies including Ancient Exhumations and Ancient Exhumations +2, Eldritch Blue: Love & Sex in the Cthulhu Mythos and The Tsathoggua Cycle: Terror Tales of the Toad God.

### Trivia

*"The Tale of Toad Loop" is dedicated to American author Robert Bloch.

fullContent:
The Tales of Inspector Legrasse is a collection of Cthulhu Mythos fiction by the late American author C. J. Henderson. The stories centre around the activities of Inspector John Raymond Legrasse, a character created by H. P. Lovecraft for "The Call of Cthulhu", and the collection includes the original story. Published by Mythos Books in 2005, it runs to 217 pages and features cover art by Ben Fogletto with an introduction by Robert M. Price.

*"The Call of Cthulhu" by H. P. Lovecraft
*"Patiently Waiting"
*"To Cast Out Fear"
*"So Free We Seem"
*"Locked Room"
*"Where Shadow Falls"
*"Nothing to Fear but Dust"

fullContent:
"The Tall Grass" is an episode of animated science fiction/horror tv show Love, Death & Robots. It is based on the short story of the same name by Joe R. Lansdale.

### Synopsis
When a train breaks down in the middle of seemingly-endless fields, passenger Laird gets off to enjoy a quiet smoke. Hearing something moving in the tall grass, he wanders off to investigate and is attacked by deformed creatures from beneath the ground, narrowly making it back to the train just as it is pulling away.

As they are moving off, the railman explains to Laird that every so often the train breaks down, always in the same place, and that sometimes people wander off, never to be seen again. He believes that in some places, the barrier between worlds rubs thin, and that this allows creatures to come through from outside our own dimension.

### Characters
*Laird, a train passenger.
*The Railman, an ageing rail worker.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Tall Grass" was released on May 14, 2021, as the fifth episode, season 2 of the Netflix original series Love, Death & Robots.

The design of main character Laird clearly takes some inspiration from H. P. Lovecraft himself; also, the theme of the episode (that of monstrous creatures breaking through from another dimension) is very reminiscent of some of Lovecraft’s work.

fullContent:
"The Tattered Lady" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author Troy Young. It is the sixth episode in his Nyarlathotep Cycle.

### Synopsis
Department of Extraordinary Phenomena field agents Malcolm Mayweather and Mindy Nguyen are assigned to investigate the mass disappearance of homeless people in Winnipeg, Canada. There, they discover that an entity named the Tattered Lady has been abducting the street people and infecting them with a supernatural contagion in preparation for unleashing them en masse on an unsuspecting population.

Although Mayweather and Nguyen are ultimately able to destroy the Tattered Lady, Mindy is infected with the plague and asks her partner to kill her. In the aftermath, the Department is forced to destroy an entire residential block - and all of its occupants - to ensure the disease is contained.

### Characters
*Malcolm Mayweather, junior agent for the Department of Extraordinary Phenomena.
*Mindy Nguyen, senior agent and Mayweather's partner.
*The Tattered Lady, an unidentified supernatural being possibly linked to the cultist from "The Rat King".
*Harjit Singh, department director.

### Publication History
"The Tattered Lady" was published in the collection The Other: Encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos Book 2 in 2020.

shortDefinition: "The Temple" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1920, and first published in the pulp magazine Weird Tales #24 in September 1925.  ### Synopsis The story is narrated as a "found manuscript" penned by Karl Heinrich, Graf von Altberg-Ehrens...
fullContent:
"The Temple" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1920, and first published in the pulp magazine Weird Tales #24 in September 1925.

### Synopsis
The story is narrated as a "found manuscript" penned by Karl Heinrich, Graf von Altberg-Ehrenstein, a lieutenant-commander in the Imperial German Navy during the days of World War I. It documents his untimely end at the bottom of the ocean.

Altberg begins by declaring that he has decided to document the events leading up to his final hour in order to "set certain facts" before the public, aware that he will not survive to do so himself.

The manuscript states events from June 1917 to August 1917 in the North Atlantic ; after sinking SS Victory, a British freighter, and thereafter sinking its surviving crew's lifeboats, the cruel and arrogant Altberg commands his U-29 u-boat to submerge, surfacing later to find the dead body of a crew member of the sunken ship, who died clinging to the exterior railing of the sub. A search of the body reveals a strange piece of carved ivory. Because of its apparent great age and value, one of Altberg's officers keeps the object, and shortly thereafter, strange phenomena begin to occur.

An uncharted oceanic current pulls the sub southward, and several members of the crew suffer the sudden onset of severe fatigue and disturbing nightmares. One even claims to have seen the corpses of the dead seamen from the British freighter staring at him through the U-boat's portholes. Altberg has him brutally whipped, rejecting the pleas from some of his men to discard the ivory charm. He eventually resorts to executing a couple of them when it is clear that they have gone insane from fright, ostensibly to maintain discipline.

Next, a mysterious explosion irreparably damages the U-boat's engines, leaving them without the ability to navigate, only the ability to surface and dive. They soon encounter a United States warship, and several of the terrified crew plead with Altberg to surrender, but instead, Altberg has these "traitors" killed. Later, the submarine faces ominous waves from a violent storm and Altberg orders the u-boat to submerge. Afterward, it is unable to surface when its ballast tanks fail to repressurize, leaving the submarine being pulled southward without resistance while slowly sinking deeper into the ocean; they never see the light of day again.

With the U-boat's batteries running low, and their chance of rescue non-existent, the six remaining, delirious crewmen attempt a mutiny, successfully disabling the u-boat by destroying several key instruments and gauges, even as they rave on about the curse of the ivory talisman, but all are murdered by the venomous Altberg. His lone companion, Lieutenant Klenze, grows increasingly unstable and paranoid. Certain of their fate, the two pass the time in their drifting vessel by sweeping the sub's powerful searchlight through the dark abyss, noting that dolphins follow them at depths and for lengths previously unhear

fullContent:
"The Temple of Bones" is a pseudo-factual Cthulhu Mythos work by author and editor F. C. Adams. It is the second in his Translations from the Book of Yng series.

### Synopsis
The translation tells of a city named Ikhyr, built by the worshippers of Hastur. When Ikhyr was sacked by a horde of nomadic barbarians, the few survivors prayed to their god for vengeance, and Hastur sent the Zorkai, a "legion of bat-winged star spawn whose hunger for flesh and thirst for blood cannot be slaked." The Zorkai killed the invaders and stripped the flesh from their bones, which the surviving priests used to rebuild their temple.

### Characters

* Korba, high priest of Hastur.
* Hastur, a Great Old One.

### Publication History
"The Temple of Bones" was published in issue #9 of online Mythos zine Nightscapes in September 1998.

shortDefinition: "The Tenants of Ladywell Manor" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.  ### Synopsis A pair of unattached socialite sisters meet two dashing young naval men and are invited to a gathering at their house, Ladywell Manor. Wha...
fullContent:
"The Tenants of Ladywell Manor" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
A pair of unattached socialite sisters meet two dashing young naval men and are invited to a gathering at their house, Ladywell Manor. What the women do not realise is that, after a disaster at sea, the men and their companions are in thrall to C'thulhu, and are dedicated to calling forth his servants across the globe by means of ritual sacrifice.

Fortunately for the girls, the captain of the crew is not so deeply affected as his compatriots, and with the assistance of the older sister is able to break the hold C'thulhu has over him for long enough to free them and set the Manor ablaze, with all of the cultists and dark abominations still inside.

### Characters
*Anne, the eldest scion of a wealthy family.
*Captain Wentworth, former commander of the Royal Navy ship HMS Valiant.
*Lucy, Anne's younger, somewhat vapid, sister.
*Lieutenant Barclay, an officer in the Royal Navy fallen to the worship of C'thulhu.

### Publication History
"The Tenants of Ladywell Manor" was first published in the anthology Cthulhu Unbound, Vol. 2 in July 2009. It has since appeared in the collections of Meikle's own works Dark Melodies (2012) and Home From the Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2017).

shortDefinition: "The Terrible Old Man" is a very short short story (less than 1,200 words) by H. P. Lovecraft, written on January 28, 1920, and first published in The Tryout, an amateur press publication, in July 1921. It's notable as the first story to make use of ...
fullContent:
"The Terrible Old Man" is a very short short story (less than 1,200 words) by H. P. Lovecraft, written on January 28, 1920, and first published in The Tryout, an amateur press publication, in July 1921. It's notable as the first story to make use of Lovecraft's imaginary New England setting, introducing the fictional town of Kingsport.

### Reaction
Lovecraft scholar Peter Cannon dismissively describes the story as "little more than a polemic against the intrusion of people Lovecraft regarded as 'foreigners,' that is, the non-English immigrants who arrived in the nineteenth century as cheap labor to fill the factories of an increasingly industrialized America."

### Synopsis
The Terrible Old Man is a strange elderly man "so old that no one can remember when he was young, and so taciturn that few know his real name." He lives alone in an ancient house on Water Street in the town of Kingsport. Even among the locals, few know the details of the Old Man's life, but it is believed that he captained East Indian clipper ships in his youth and had accumulated great riches throughout his life. Those who had visited the property had seen bizarre collections of stones in the front yard and observed the Old Man carrying on conversations with mysterious bottles on his table, which make "certain definite vibrations as if in answer." Most locals take care to avoid the Old Man and his house.

The story focuses on three robbers (Angelo Ricci, Joe Czanek and Manuel Silva), who are "of that new and heterogeneous alien stock which lies outside the charmed circle of New England life and traditions." They take little heed of the locals' cautionary whispers about the Terrible Old Man, but are immediately interested when they learn about his supposed hoard of treasure. They act immediately on their avarice according to their natures, and go to the Old Man's house to commit robbery. Ricci and Silva go inside to "interview" the Old Man about the treasure and its hiding place, while Czanek waits outside in the getaway car. Czanek waits impatiently for a long time. He is startled at one point by an outburst of horrific screaming from the house, but assumes that his colleagues have been too rough with the Old Man during their interrogation. Soon after this, however, the gate of the house opens, revealing not Czanek's colleagues, but the Terrible Old Man, "smiling hideously" at him. For the first time, Czanek takes note of the Old Man's unsettling yellow eyes.

The mutilated bodies of the three robbers are later found by the seaside, "horribly slashed as with many cutlasses, and horribly mangled as by the tread of many cruel boot-heels." The people of Kingsport talk about the discovery, as well as about the abandoned car and the screams heard in the night, but the Terrible Old Man shows no interest in their gossip.

### The Terrible Old Man

shortDefinition: The Terrible Old Man is a reimagining of H. P. Lovecraft's short story of the same name. Despite being billed as a graphic novel, it is structured as a mix between a conventional short story and a comic book, with both elements combined to tell the s...
fullContent:
The Terrible Old Man is a reimagining of H. P. Lovecraft's short story of the same name. Despite being billed as a graphic novel, it is structured as a mix between a conventional short story and a comic book, with both elements combined to tell the story, and the artwork created using DALL*E 2 Artificial Intelligence software. It was published in a solely digital format by VoR Books in May 2023.

### Overview


The book is in essence Lovecraft's "The Terrible Old Man", rewritten and with a handful of minor elements changed and added to expand the narrative. For example, the story now takes place in Innsmouth rather than Kingsport, and three threads, one about a boy who delivers newspapers to the titular character, another about the criminal's ties to a Boston syndicate, and the last about a Vatican priest investigating the Old Man, were added, although ultimately none of these are significantly developed.

term: The Terrible Old Man of Keyport
shortDefinition: "The Terrible Old Man of Keyport" is a short story by American author Chuck Buda. It is essentially a rewrite of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Terrible Old Man" relocated to Armand Rosamilia's Keyport milieu, and with the titular character replaced by a Dee...
fullContent:
"The Terrible Old Man of Keyport" is a short story by American author Chuck Buda. It is essentially a rewrite of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Terrible Old Man" relocated to Armand Rosamilia's Keyport milieu, and with the titular character replaced by a Deep One hybrid.

### Synopsis
Three small-time criminals passing through the decaying New Jersey town of Keyport attempt to rob a supposedly wealthy old man. What they find is a den of monsters and magic, and none of the men survive to tell the tale.

### Publication History
"The Terrible Old Man of Keyport" was first published in the collection Keyport Cthulhu in November 2013.

### Trivia
* Dylan Murphy, one of the primary human protagonists of the first run of Keyport Cthulhu tales, plays a small part in "The Terrible Old Man of Keyport".

term: The Terror From Beyond-Or, Dick Cooper's Weird Tale
shortDefinition: "The Terror From Beyond-Or, Dick Cooper's Weird Tale" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Thomas V. Powers. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 2 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2018....
fullContent:
"The Terror From Beyond-Or, Dick Cooper's Weird Tale" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Thomas V. Powers. It was published in Vol 3, Issue 2 of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in July 2018.

### Synopsis
Richard Harlan Cooper, a brilliant private detective in the tradition of Sherlock Holmes, is engaged by Hope Hobbeson to track down her father, a scholarly old gent who she believes has been kidnapped by a malevolent cult named the Celestial Revelation Fellowship to translate their latest acquisition: a copy of the fabled Necronomicon.

Utilising his extensive network of agents, Cooper and his agents infiltrate a meeting of the Fellowship, but are unable to rescue the older Hobbeson; during a fracas caused by their discovery, Hoper herself is also kidnapped, to be used as a tool to force her father to comply with their demands.

After some intelligence gathering, Cooper assembles a posse and track the fugitive cultists to their underground lair where, in a final confrontation, the Fellowship is subdued, and their leader destroyed- but not before he enacts a ritual which shows a glimpse of what the power of the Necronomicon is capable of.

The story concludes with Cooper and Hope spending more and more time together, before entering into a relationship.

### Mythos Connections
"Dick Cooper's Weird Tale" is littered with references to the Cthulhu Mythos. These include:

* the Necronomicon, legendary book of dead names. It's history as the Al-Azif is alluded to, as is its author Abdullah Hazrat, and it’s connection to English polymath John Dee
* at one point, an astronomer named Flammarion is made mention of. This would appear to be a nod to Caitlin R. Kiernan's Cthulhu Mythos protagonist Dancy Flammarion
* one of Cooper's past cases involved an organisation known as the Brotherhood of Bahgoona (although the name later changes to the Brotherhood of Bygoona). This is a possible reference to James Ambuehl's Great Old One Byagoona
* Several references to various aspects of Nyarlathotep are made: the "Mighty Messenger" of the Fellowship is referred to as Nyarlat, and the avatars Black Beast and Black Man are mentioned in passing
* Enoch Bowen is spoken of, including his travels in Egypt, involvement with Nephren-Ka, and establishing of the Church of Starry Wisdom
* Cooper states that his past enemies have included "Tul-Hoo crazed Kanakas"
* The leader of the Fellowship, Archelaus Corvus, speaks of the trans-Neptunian planet of Yuggoth
* Hope Hobbeson and her father come from Massachusetts, New England, having just returned from that region's namesake

shortDefinition: "The Terror From the Depths" is a short story by Fritz Leiber, first published in the 1976 anthology The Disciples of Cthulhu. Leiber reportedly began writing the story in 1937, the year of H. P. Lovecraft's death, but did not complete it until 1975....
fullContent:
"The Terror From the Depths" is a short story by Fritz Leiber, first published in the 1976 anthology The Disciples of Cthulhu. Leiber reportedly began writing the story in 1937, the year of H. P. Lovecraft's death, but did not complete it until 1975.

### Synopsis
The story concerns Georg Reuter Fischer, a young poet and Miskatonic University dropout who dreams obsessively about strange winged worms flying through a network of tunnels under the Pacific Ocean. He seeks help from Miskatonic's Albert Wilmarth--who bears a striking resemblance to Lovecraft, who also figures as an offscreen character in the story.

### Behind the Mythos
"The Terror From the Depths" extensively name-drops elements of Lovecraft's works, referencing a host of characters and events which take place in his stories. Additionally, Lovecraft himself is said to have sensationalised real-world events in order to sell his stories.

### External Link

fullContent:
"The Terror of Emmett's Cove" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Lee Clark Zumpe.

### Synopsis
Two people on a mission to purchase a copy of the Pnakotic Manuscripts in a backwoods town in North Carolina discover that the writings are far more than mere script. They are in fact alive, and have possessed the body of a local man and begun to call forth terrifying entities which are terrorising the local population. Although the two manage to destroy the Manuscripts and close whatever portal they had cracked open, one of them must pay the ultimate price.

### Characters
*Celina, a woman working acquisitions for a rare artefacts dealer.
*Patan, a former Sherpa and Celina's assistant.
*Captain Neville, the caretaker of a Hyperborean copy of the Pnakotic Manuscripts.

### Publication History
*Lovecraft's Disciples #13 (2009)
*Lovecraft's Disciples #27 (2017)
*Lovecraftiana Vol 5 Issue 1 (2020)

The Terror of the Tides is an expansion pack for Fantasy Flight Games' Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

### Overview
The fourth Asylum Pack in the Summons of the Deep Cycle, The Terror of the Tides consists of three duplicates each of 20 unique cards for a total of 60, and focuses on expanding options in the Arcane Struggle sub-phase of the Story Phase. First released in 2008, it was discontinued with the demise of Call of Cthulhu: The Card Game.

shortDefinition: "The Terror of Toad Lake" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Ambuehl, part of his Lu-Kthu story cycle.  ### Synopsis Deep in the backwoods of Minnesota, a man stumbles across an ancient cult of toad-men and degenerate hillbillie...
fullContent:
"The Terror of Toad Lake" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author James Ambuehl, part of his Lu-Kthu story cycle.

### Synopsis
Deep in the backwoods of Minnesota, a man stumbles across an ancient cult of toad-men and degenerate hillbillies nearing the final night of a dark ceremony. After enlisting the assistance of his childhood best friend, the two tackle the cult and succeed in stopping their ritual; however, the sole survivor of this encounter discovers to his horror that the toad-men may have passed on some vile condition. 

### Characters

*John, the narrator, a member of Royceton University's security staff.
*Thomas Wynne, John's oldest and best friend.
*The Reverend Thomas Skyler, an old adversary of the cult.
*Sathogwa, the Great Old One Tsathoggua.

### Publication History
"The Terror of Toad Lake" was published in the first issue of online fanzine Nightscapes in June 1997, and appeared in James Ambuehl's collection Correlated Contents in December 1998. May 2003 saw its translation into German, and its inclusion in the anthology Der Cthulhu-Mythos: 1976 - 2002.

term: The Terror that Came to Dounreay
shortDefinition: "The Terror that Came to Dounreay" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle.  ### Synopsis During the Cold War, experiments at a secret military base in Scotland awakens the interest of creatures from between realities. As the tests int...
fullContent:
"The Terror that Came to Dounreay" is a short story by British-born author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
During the Cold War, experiments at a secret military base in Scotland awakens the interest of creatures from between realities. As the tests intensify, the power which the creatures draws from them increases, and it becomes more and more able to affect our world. A hasty decision by the base commander to bomb the base and thus annihilate the entities is undertaken, but an ancient folk song suggests that this is all that the beings need to manifest fully.

### Characters
*Dr. Ballantine, an alcoholic biologist.
*Professor Rankin, a brilliant physicist.
*The Colonel, the officer in charge of the facility.

### Publication History
"The Terror that Came to Dounreay" was first published in the Chaosium anthology Atomic-Age Cthulhu: Tales of Mythos Horror in the 1950s in March 2015. It was also included in the collection of Meikle's own works Home From The Sea: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in 2017.

### Trivia
* The story concludes with Ballantine becoming aware of the American nuclear tests in the Pacific Ocean, and hints that the entities encountered are somehow connected to either Cthulhu or R'lyeh.

shortDefinition: "The Testament of Athammaus" is a short fantasy story by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith. It forms part of his Hyperborean Cycle series of tales.  ### Synopsis Athammaus, headsman of the deserted city of Commori...
fullContent:
"The Testament of Athammaus" is a short fantasy story by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith. It forms part of his Hyperborean Cycle series of tales.

### Synopsis
Athammaus, headsman of the deserted city of Commoriom, relates the story of how his once-great city came to be abandoned overnight.

When the feared tribal reaver Knygathin Zhaum is captured by the Commoriom soldiery, the creature is sentenced to death. However, with each beheading, it simply reforms itself and goes on to consume another helpless civilian before re-submitting to its captivity. After the third reformation, it has changed beyond all recognition, and the citizenry flee their homes en masse, with Athammaus the last to leave.

### Characters
*Athammaus, the headsman, or executioner, of Commoriom.
*Knygathin Zhaum, an inhuman creature with a taste for human flesh.
*King Loquamethros, lord of Commoriom.

### Publication History
"The Testament of Athammaus" first saw print in the October 1932 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales. It has since been reprinted many times in many different publications, and has also been translated into German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Italian and Hungarian.

shortDefinition: "The Testament of Cthulhu" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.  ### Synopsis A man who believed his mother to have died in an accident stumbles across the small town of Sea Dream. There he discovers an enclave ...
fullContent:
"The Testament of Cthulhu" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
A man who believed his mother to have died in an accident stumbles across the small town of Sea Dream. There he discovers an enclave of Deep Ones in the process of transitioning from land to sea, helped in their journey by his alive and fully-transitioned mother. Together they travel to the city of Y'ha-nthlei to pursue their worship of Cthulhu.

### Characters
*Edgar Thane, the descendant of a very unusual bloodline.
*Carter Marsh, the mayor of Sea Dream.
*Lily Thane née Marsh, Edgar's mother, now a Deep One sea goddess.

### Publication History
"The Testament Of Cthulhu" was published in the 2018 collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Trivia
*"The Testament of Cthulhu" is prefaced with a quote from "The Call of Cthulhu" by H. P. Lovecraft.

The Thanos Imperative is a six-issue comic book mini-series written by Dan Abnett and Andy Lanning which was published by Marvel Comics. The mini-series was bookended by two one-shot comics, Thanos Imperative: Ignition and Thanos Imperative: Devastation. It follows up the events of the crossover story "Realm of Kings" which introduced the Cancerverse and the "War of Kings" crossover event before it. Which involved an intergalactic war that resulted in the creation of a tear in the fabric of the universe, creating "The Fault" in the void between the Milky Way galaxy, the Andromeda galaxy, and the Shi'ar galaxy.

### Plot
### Prelude
Concerned about the Fault, several groups take action to investigate the phenomena. The Nova Corps and Guardians of the Galaxy, send Quasar into the Fault. Who discovers a corrupted universe ruled by evil colossal organic entities. He is captured by the Revengers, corrupted versions of the Avengers and is informed by their leader Lord Mar-Vell of their plan to extend the rule of their gods, the Many-Angled Ones, to his reality (Earth-616). Meanwhile, the million-world Shi'ar empire sends a unit of its super-powered Imperial Shi'ar Guard to investigate the Fault. In the process they encounter insectoid refugees from that reality, who they are forced to battle, and afterwards encounter living bio-ships carrying abominations and the Ex-Men (mutated X-Men). They lose several team members in the process before they manage to escape and warn the Shi'ar and Kree empires of the coming threat.

### Invasion
Erupting from the Fault is an invasion of colossal starships (many of them with giant head or skull-like bows) and eldritch monsters, which tear through the forces assembled to stop the invasion. Opposing the invaders is a massive fleet of starships from the Kree and Shi'ar empires, the Rigellian colonists, and the Negative Zone Horde, among others. Assisting them were the Galadorian Spaceknights and the Nova Corps. Soon they were joined by Galactus the Devourer of Worlds, several Cosmic Heralds (including the Silver Surfer), and a good number of cosmic aspects (including Celestials). 

Despite the impressive force assembled, they were taking massive casualties, as they were being overwhelmed. Chthonic entities were able to tear through the starships and even kill cosmic aspects. The invaders brought through the Fault the Galactus Engine, an Eldritch weapon of mass destruction, and various cosmic aspects fell to the weapon. Soon the Negative Zone Horde withdrew from the battle, abandoning their allies, and due to the losses the defenders were suffering, they were forced to retreat. The invaders in turn were searching for the universe's Avatar of Death (Thanos) to kill, so that this reality's Death would cease to exist.

fullContent:
"The Theft of Thirty-Nine Girdles" is a short story by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith. It forms part of his Hyperborean Cycle, and is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
In his dotage, a master thief recalls a time in his youth when he and two companions stole a number of religious artefacts from a temple. Using a concoction dubbed The Powder of the Fetid Apparitions, the group are able to terrify the temple's occupants and patrons into leaving the group to go about their work, but unfortunately one of them is recognised. As a result, another of the group flees the city with the bulk of the treasure, leaving the others with but a single small gold ingot for their troubles.

### Characters
*Satampra Zeiros, a career criminal, and one of the greatest in his field.
*Vixeela, Zeiros's companion and accomplice, and a former servant at the temple.
*Veezi Phenquor, a highly-skilled alchemist and magician.

### Publication History
"The Theft of Thirty-Nine Girdles" was published in Saturn Science Fiction and Fantasy in March 1958. It has since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into Spanish, Dutch, Italian, French, German, and Hungarian.

fullContent:
"The Thing From Beyond The Living Door" is a short story by authors Mark McLaughlin and Michael Sheehan, Jr.

### Synopsis
Two tenants at a large Arkham boarding house uncover a plot by the landlady and one of the residents, a mad scientist, to extend their lives by sacrificing elderly people to a dark creature named G'hodloth which lives in the basement. The pair are discovered snooping by their adversaries, but are able to turn the tables on the evil conspirators, who are subsequently burned to death in their house of horrors.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, a student studying Cinematography at nearby Miskatonic University.
*Caspar, a construction worker and friend of the narrator.
*Dr. Brandywine, an insane yet gifted inventor.
*Mrs. Veng, the boarding house's landlady.
*G'hodloth, a strange being with the power to suck the life essence from living creatures and pass it on to others.

### Publication History
"The Thing From Beyond The Living Door" was published in the collection Horrors & Abominations: 24 Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos in December 2018.

### Trivia
*Brandywine mentions that a fever which he contracted many years ago was treated by a Dr. Muñoz, a character who appeared in the H. P. Lovecraft short story "Cool Air".

fullContent:
"The Thing from the Blasted Heath" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Brian Lumley that first appeared in his collection The Caller of The Black  (Arkham House, 1971).

Lumley says it was written in September 1967 "as an homage to HPL, and to the Mythos." Lumley calls the story a sequel to, "The Colour Out of Space," his favourite Lovecraft story, and his all-time favourite horror story--even though, as he points out, it "isn't a Mythos story".

The "thing" of the title is a mutant shrub from the shores of the Arkham Reservoir. Planted in his garden, it wreaks horrific changes.

### Publication History
Since its initial appearance in The Caller of The Black, "The Thing from the Blasted Heath" has been reprinted in Lumley's collections The Last Rite (Jwindz Publishing, 1992), A Coven of Vampires (Fedogan & Bremer, 1998), and Haggopian and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2008).

"The Thing from the Trenches" is a short story by Robert M. Price. It expands on a section of Lovecraft's short story "Herbert West--Reanimator".

### Synopsis
On the Western Front, Herbert West discovers the remains of two soldiers - one French and one German - whose diaries reveal them to have almost identical psychologies, and he convinces his friend to aid him in an experiment to create a composite entity. Although the resulting creature appears to be possessed of all its faculties, the experiment is ultimately unsuccessful as it literally tears itself apart due to conflicting national allegiances.

### Characters

*Unnamed Narrator, West's sidekick from the original story.
*Herbert West, a brilliant if unconventional physician.

### Publication History
"The Thing from the Trenches" was published in the collection of Price's own works Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2008.

fullContent:
"The Thing in the Jar" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Carlton Herzog, first published in Vol 5, Issue 3 of the Lovecraftiana zine in October 2020.

### Synopsis
Peter Knock, a man born with severe physical abnormalities - including a right arm which seemingly has a mind of its own - stumbles across an ancient organism buried in a jar in his back garden. Communicating telepathically with Peter, the being explains that it needs a human body with which to build a device which will allow it to return to its own people, and offers to construct Knock a new body if he will only provide him with a sacrificial form to begin the process. The desperate man agrees immediately.

When the entity demands a second body as it has worn out the first, Knock begins to realise that it has a more sinister agenda in mind. Deciding to act, he is horrified to discover that it has almost complete telepathic control over him, and renders him helpless against it. Luckily, Knock's arm decides to act of its own accord, allowing him to overpower the creature and destroy its host body.

The story concludes with Knock re-burying the creature, and wondering whether limbs with their own moral compass may be the next step in human evolution.

shortDefinition: "The Thing in the Moonlight" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft and J. Chapman Miske, and first published in the January 1941 issue (Volume 4, Number 1) of Bizarre magazine, a publication for which Miske was co-editor. It was solely credited...
fullContent:
"The Thing in the Moonlight" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft and J. Chapman Miske, and first published in the January 1941 issue (Volume 4, Number 1) of Bizarre magazine, a publication for which Miske was co-editor. It was solely credited to Lovecraft at the time of printing.

The story is notable for being the basis for the God of the Bloody Tongue, an iconic avatar of Nyarlathotep; however, the character would not be fully developed until the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Masks of Nyarlathotep.

### Plot Summary
The narrator recounts the story of Morgan, an illiterate man alone in his home, who suddenly began to write a letter under the name Howard Phillips of 66 College Street, Providence, Rhode Island, detailing a dream from November 24, 1927.

In the text, the dreamer finds himself in a reedy marsh and feels compelled to climb a cliff to the north. Reaching a moonlit plateau, he looks around and discovers a rusting tramway. Some way down the track, he finds a yellow 1900-10 tram car numbered 1852. He climbs aboard, and though the car stands empty, the conductor and motorman approach from the left before the latter begins to howl and the former charges on all fours. Seeing that the motorman's face is in fact a mere white cone tapering to one blood-red tentacle, the dreamer flees. Though he knows he's sleeping, he is trapped in the dreamland, involuntarily returning to the ancient tram car and the howling creature each night. He signs off by asking "God! When will I awaken?".

### Behind the Mythos
"The Thing in the Moonlight" was based on a 1927 letter from H. P. Lovecraft to Donald Wandrei, in which Lovecraft recounted one of his dreams. Later, Miske came into possession of the contents, and turned Lovecraft's description into the meat of a story, doing little more than adding three paragraphs to the beginning and five to the end to create a wraparound section.

### Publication
*Bizarre magazine, January 1941
*Dreams and Fancies, Arkham House 1962
*The Tomb and Other Tales, Ballantine Books 1970
*Dreams of Terror and Death: The Dream Cycle of H. P. Lovecraft, Ballantine Books 1995
*Shadows of Death, Del Rey Books 2005
*The Horror in the Museum, Wordsworth Editions 2010
*Eldritch Tales: A Miscellany of the Macabre, Victor Gollancz Ltd. 2011

shortDefinition: "The Thing in the Pit" is a horror fantasy short story by Lin Carter set in the Cthulhu Mythos, and part of his Xothic Legend Cycle. It was first published in Carter's 1980 collection Lost Worlds.  ### Synopsis The story purports to be part of Prof. ...
fullContent:
"The Thing in the Pit" is a horror fantasy short story by Lin Carter set in the Cthulhu Mythos, and part of his Xothic Legend Cycle. It was first published in Carter's 1980 collection Lost Worlds.

### Synopsis
The story purports to be part of Prof. Copeland's translation of the Zanthu Tablets, which narrate the life of the hierophant Zanthu, high-priest of the god Ythogtha in the ancient continent of Mu. Peppered through the text are Copeland's footnotes, which provide additional information about many beings and places mentioned by Zanthu.

About 11,000 years after the time of T'yog, the cult of the god Ghatanothoa becomes the sole official religion of the kingdom of K'naa, thanks to the influence of its high-priest Yaa-Thobboth over King Shommog. This results in all the other temples being sealed and the worship of other deities being banned. Given the political power of K'naa, Zanthu fears that the same law might be passed in his own kingdom, G'thuu.

Zanthu's palace is located next to the Abyss of Yhe, where Ythogtha himself is believed to be imprisoned by the Elder Sign placed there by the Elder Gods. Studying the Thirty-one Rituals, Zanthu finds a spell that could open the door of Yhe and liberate his god from its prison. Determined to do so, he secures the alliance of Ubb and the Yuggs, gathers his acolytes, and performs the ritual at the edge of a cliff overlooking the Abyss of Yhe.

At first, Zanthu is awed by the sight of a faceless, mountain-sized creature with a single black horn that emerges from the pit. But when a second identical "monster" emerges next to it, followed by many others, Zanthu cries in fear as he realises the sheer size of the creature. The things he mistook for individual monsters are nothing more than the tips of Ythogtha's clawed fingers.

Zanthu and his acolytes run away while the earthquakes caused by Ythogtha's movements destroy the continent of Mu. The Elder Gods descend to Earth from Betelgeuse as great towers of flame to push the monster back into the abyss and close the gate. Zanthu and a few others manage to reach a "sky chariot" and escape, but watch their homeland sink beneath the waves.

### Behind the Mythos
One of Copeland's footnotes mentions the wizard Malygris from Clark Ashton Smith's Poseidonis series.

### Publication History 
*Lost Worlds (1980, 2020)
*The Xothic Legend Cycle (1997)
*Al-Azif (1998, January-February edition)
*Die Xothic-Legenden (2004)
*The Xothic Cycle (2021)

fullContent:
"The Thing in the Pond" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author John R. Fultz.

### Synopsis
A man relates the tale of how, as a boy, he witnessed the taking of one of his friends from a local pond by an unknown creature. Later, his friend returned, reanimated and rotting, to try and entice the boy down to the city of Tsath where he claimed to live in contented servitude.

As an adult, the man comes back from the Second World War lame and traumatised, and returns to the pond. Desperate to belong, he begs the being which lurks beneath the surface to take him down to Tsath.

### Characters

*Ted, a war veteran with mental and physical scars.
*Johnny Haxton, a childhood friend of Ted’s.
*Jeb Carter, the man who dug the pond, and was the first victim of whatever lurks beneath its surface.

### Publication History
"The Thing in the Pond" was published in the anthology Weirdbook Annual 2 by Wildside Press in 2019.

shortDefinition: "The Thing in the Vault" is a short story by British author David Hambling.  ### Synopsis Prohibition-era private detective Edward Jones is hired by a wealthy man to investigate the progress of a venture in which he has invested: a new form of filter...
fullContent:
"The Thing in the Vault" is a short story by British author David Hambling.

### Synopsis
Prohibition-era private detective Edward Jones is hired by a wealthy man to investigate the progress of a venture in which he has invested: a new form of filter to produce higher-quality liquor. In this task, he is joined by the representatives of three powerful crime syndicates who also have a monetary interest.

Travelling to the man's underground complex, they find that he has indeed developed a revolutionary technology, with the aid of a mysterious group who may not be entirely human.

When the group attempt to leave the complex, the man's associates refuse to allow them egress, and are revealed to be alien abominations. Most of the representatives are killed, but Jones succeeds in escaping with a sample of the filter, which he returns to his employer. Two of the representatives also survive, although one of them is caught by the aliens and his still-living brain is placed in a tank, leaving him trapped forever as part of the aliens' "brain bank". 

### Characters
*Edward Jones, a Chicago private investigator.
*Dr. K, a talented chemist.
*Wilson, an experienced hustler and con-artist
*James Moran, a Chicago mob enforcer.
*Phil Ricca, a street thug.
*Louie Cristillo, Ricca's muscle.
*Spencer Wade, a wealthy businessman with a shady heritage.
*Estelle, the representative of an which appears to oppose the dark forces at work in the world.
*Pretski, a small-town bed-and-breakfast owner.

### Publication History
"The Thing in the Vault" was published in the 2013 collection of Hambling's own works Shadows from Norwood. It has also since received a digital chapbook release.

### Behind the Mythos
Although containing no direct references to either the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the Cthulhu Mythos, the chapbook's tagline for the story - A Hard-Boiled Tale of the Cthulhu Mythos - indicates the authors intention that it should be taken as part of that universe. Additionally, the creatures encountered by the Chicagoans, described as insectoid/crustacean beings with a fungal biology who are capable of transferring a human brain into a life-support cylinder, are clearly intended to be Mi-Go.

shortDefinition: The Thing in the Woods is a children’s horror novel by British-American author Margery Williams. It was first published in the United Kingdom by Gerald Duckworth & Co. in 1913; its American release by Robert M. McBride & Company credited the author t...
fullContent:
The Thing in the Woods is a children’s horror novel by British-American author Margery Williams. It was first published in the United Kingdom by Gerald Duckworth & Co. in 1913; its American release by Robert M. McBride & Company credited the author to the pseudonym Harper Williams . It was also included in the Robert M. Price-edited anthology Tales Out of Dunwich (Hippocampus Press, 2005).

### Synopsis
The story involves a case of lycanthropy in rural Pennsylvania, a place Williams lived from ages 9 to 19.

A weird murder mystery begins when a doctor takes over the practice of another doctor for three months whilst the other practitioner is on vacation. The locum practice is in the Pennsylvania woods. 

The relieving doctor is a new graduate of medical school and is unfamiliar with the local area, so he encounters difficulties from the beginning. 

The new doctor tries is entangled with the inexplicable murder of a cyclist. This first murder is followed by other brutal attacks and more murder. Ultimately, the murderer is found to be someone who believes themselves to be a werewolf. Whilst it is possible to accept the conventional explanation of insanity, the possibility is definitely left open that the murderer was actually a werewolf.

The setting is reminiscent of the more familiar Dunwich description and the melancholy gloom of a backwoods area of neglect and decay where mystery is more common and strange events more plausible within the darkness of the trees.

### Behind the Mythos
The Thing in the Woods has been speculated by some to be a possible inspiration for H. P. Lovecraft's 1929 short story "The Dunwich Horror" ; Lovecraft wrote a poem in November 1924 titled "On The Thing in the Woods by Harper Williams", a fact which may support this hypothesis.

In the autumn of 1924, J. C. Henneberger, owner of Weird Tales, owed H. P. Lovecraft some money. Unable to lay hands on the funds immediately, Henneberger instead transferred to Lovecraft his sizable credit at the prominent New York bookseller Scribner’s. Lovecraft hoped to convert this into cash, but unable to do this, he was left with $60 credit—so, Lovecraft and his friend Frank Belknap Long, Jr. decided to go on a buying spree, purchasing a number of books by Lord Dunsany, Arthur Machen, and works of history. Lovecraft even picked up a book for his friend:For Belknap (his own choice)

The Thing In the Woods (new horror novel)—Harper Williams

—H. P. Lovecraft to Lillian D. Clark, 6 Nov 1924, Letters to Family & Family Friends 2.185Before Lovecraft gave Long his gift, he read the whole novel himself.

fullContent:
"The Thing on the Doorstep" is a short story written by H. P. Lovecraft, part of the Cthulhu Mythos genre of horror fiction. It was written in August 1933, and first published in the January 1937 issue of Weird Tales.

### Inspiration
Two novels suggested as inspirations for "The Thing on the Doorstep" are Barry Pain's An Exchange of Souls (1911), about a scientist's invention that allows him to switch personalities with his wife, and H. B. Drake's The Remedy (1925; published in the U.S. as The Shadowy Thing), in which a character with the power of mind-transference comes back from the dead by possessing the body of an injured friend.

Lovecraft scholar Robert M. Price has suggested that the wizard Ephraim Waite is based on Arthur Edward Waite (2 October 1857 – 19 May 1942) , a British author, poet and occultist who helped create the popular Rider-Waite tarot deck. 

### Plot summary
The story is divided into 7 chapters:

### "I."
Daniel Upton, the story's narrator, begins by telling that he has killed his best friend, Edward Derby, and that he hopes his account will prove that he is not a murderer. He begins by describing Derby's life and career.

### "II."
He then tells of Asenath Waite, and how Derby and she wed.

### "III."
A few years later, people start to notice a change in Derby's behaviour. He confides in Upton, telling him strange stories of Asenath, and how he believes her father, Ephraim Waite, may not actually be dead.

### "IV."
Upton is called to pick up Derby who has been found in Maine, rambling incoherently. on the trip back, Derby tells of Asenath using his body, and suggests that it is in fact Ephraim who resides in the body of Asenath. Before finishing, he has a small seizure and rapidly changes personality, asking Upton to ignore what he might have just said.

### "V."


A few months later, Derby shows up at Upton's door and says he's found a way to keep Asenath away; to stop her using his body. Derby finishes renovations on his old family house, yet seems strangely reluctant to leave Asenath's old place.

### "VI."
One time, whilst visiting Upton, Derby starts and begins rambling again. Upton gets him to sleep, but with his condition getting no better, ends up committing him to Arkham Sanitarium. Upton gets a call, saying that Derby has regained normality, though upon visiting, Upton can see it's not the true personality of Edward Derby.

### "VII."
Upton, at home, is greeted by a fetid-smelling dwarf-like figure at the door carrying a letter from Derby. The letter explains that Derby had in fact killed Asenath and buried her body in their cellar. Despite this, Asenath had managed to take control of his body while he was in the Sanitarium, meaning that "the thing on the doorstep" was actually Derby inhabiting Asenath's liquefying corpse. The note implores Upton to go to the sanitarium to kill Derby, who has been permanently possessed by Asenath/Ephraim's soul and that he should cremate his body to prevent this happening aga

shortDefinition: "The Thing on the Roof" is a short story by Robert E. Howard, first published in the February 1932 edition of Weird Tales.   ### Synopsis A London scholar is contacted by Tussman, an academic enemy, who wants his help in finding an original copy of V...
fullContent:
"The Thing on the Roof" is a short story by Robert E. Howard, first published in the February 1932 edition of Weird Tales. 

### Synopsis
A London scholar is contacted by Tussman, an academic enemy, who wants his help in finding an original copy of Von Junzt's Nameless Cults. This allows him to return to the Temple of the Toad in Honduras and return with a toad-shaped jewel. He failed to heed Von Junzt's warning, however, and met his doom in the form of a hoofprint from a vengeful god.

### Characters
* Narrator: He lives in London and is the author of Evidences of Nahua Culture in Yucatan.
* Tussman: An academic who lives in Sussex, England, a rival of the narrator. Obsessed with finding the treasure of the Temple of the Toad.
* James Clement: A professor in Richmond, Virginia, who helps track down an original copy of Nameless Cults.
* Friedrich Von Junzt: Author of Nameless Cults. After "he spent the full forty-five years of his life prying into strange places and discovering secret and abysmal things," he was found mysteriously strangled to death in a barred and bolted room in 1840, six months after a trip to Mongolia. 
* Justin Geoffrey: Poet, author of Out of the Old Land.
* Juan Gonzales: Spanish traveler who saw the Temple of the Toad in Honduras in 1793.

### Behind the Mythos
Although the exact nature of the entity which kills Tussman at the climax of "The Thing on the Roof" is left intentionally vague - being described only as emitting a "hideous high-pitched tittering" and, presumably, possessing something akin to hooves - others have offered interpretations of what the entity may have been in the years since. Marvel, in their horror comic Chamber of Chills, suggested that it was the Toad God of Tussman's temple itself; in Ye Booke of Monstres II for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, J. Todd Kingrea instead stated that it was merely one of the temple's guardians, the Children of Tsathoggua.

### Adaptations
A comic book adaptation was published in Chamber of Chills by Marvel Comics in 1972.

shortDefinition: "The Thing That Walked on the Wind" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author August Derleth. It was first published in Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror in January 1933. It has since entered the public domain, and has been reprin...
fullContent:
"The Thing That Walked on the Wind" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author August Derleth. It was first published in Strange Tales of Mystery and Terror in January 1933. It has since entered the public domain, and has been reprinted many times in both periodicals and anthologies.

The story is notable as featuring the first appearance of the Great Old One Ithaqua, a creature which has been extensively reused in later Mythos works, perhaps most notably in Brian Lumley's Titus Crow series, where it acts as the main antagonist.

### Synopsis
The story is framed as a senior law enforcement officer's report on the disappearance of one of his constables, a man named Robert Norris, and the subsequent discovery of his frozen corpse. 

Norris had been investigating the disappearance of an entire village in the Canadian wilderness. During the course of his enquiries, three people who had gone missing the previous year miraculously appeared from the sky. Although one was dead on arrival, the two survivors related the tale of the missing townsfolk, revealing the secret of a community which worshiped an ancient and malevolent being which showed its displeasure with its followers by abducting them to enact an unknown punishment.

Whilst on the case, Norris glimpsed the creature, a colossal caricature of a man with glowing red eyes, and this marked him for a cold death at its hands.

### Characters

* Constable Robert Norris, a highly-trained officer in the Mounted Police.
* Dr. Jamison, a provincial doctor and friend of Norris's.
* Allison Wentworth, a traveller through the wilderness.
* James Macdonald, Wentworth's companion.
* Irene Masitte, a young woman chosen by the townsfolk as a sacrifice.
* John Dalhousie, a division chief in the Mounted Police and Norris's superior.
* Wind-Walker, a local name for Ithaqua, a Great Old One.

fullContent:
"The Third Eye" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas. It was first published in the Todd H. C. Fischer-edited fanzine Imelod in July 1997.

### Synopsis
A young boy grows up watching his father, an officer in the Arkham Police Department, slowly lose his mind from the bizarre things he has seen, finally deciding to use any means at his disposal to fight back against the supernatural forces ranged against mankind. However, the mystical texts he reads cause a horrific mutation to begin, and the man ends up taking his own life.

As an adult, the boy follows in his father's footsteps, also vowing to fight the minions of the dark gods. However, he has something his father did not: a protective amulet bearing the sign of the gods…

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance, "The Third Eye" has also appeared in the fanzine Tales of Lovecraftian Horror (1997) and the collection of Thomas's own works Unholy Dimensions (2005).

fullContent:
The Thirteen is a short supplement for the Cthulhu by Gaslight sub-setting of Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. Written by Tyler Omichinski, it was published by third-party content provider Stygian Fox in 2017 .

### Overview


The Thirteen details the activities and members of a secret society of immortals who have manipulated the course of human history across the millennia. The group, who no longer number thirteen due to the inevitable attrition caused by such a lengthy existence, gained their immortality by drinking the blood of an unidentified entity which fell to Earth around 12,000 years ago during the Stone Age.

Although the group for the most part avoids interaction with the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos, fearing that to reveal their existence to any of these various entities would invite their destruction, one of the members has studied these beings extensively, and been driven insane in the process. Another, long deceased by the time of Cthulhu by Gaslight, treated with these very entities, including the Deep Ones of Doggerland, as well as various beings which inhabit the Dreamlands.

### Design Team 
* Written by: Tyler Omichinski
* Artwork by: Jon Gibbons
* Production staff: Stephanie McAlea, Badger McInnes, and Jeff Moeller

shortDefinition: "The Thousand-and-Third Tale of Scheherazade" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan set in the milieu of the ghouls of Providence. It first appeared in the January 2009 issue of Sirenia Digest (#38), and was later reprinted in Kiernan's collection C...
fullContent:
"The Thousand-and-Third Tale of Scheherazade" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan set in the milieu of the ghouls of Providence. It first appeared in the January 2009 issue of Sirenia Digest (#38), and was later reprinted in Kiernan's collection Confessions of a Five-Chambered Heart (Subterranean Press, 2012).

The story is set in "the terrible old house on Federal Hill," a place used by the changelings, humans kidnapped as infants and raised to serve as servants of the ghouls:For more than two centuries now, this place has served as a refuge for the Children of the Cuckoo, those stolen as infants and raised up in the warrens below College Hill to labor and officiate for the Hounds of Cain, to walk abroad in the day-lit world where the ghouls dare not venture.It introduces a third class besides the ghouls and changelings: humans kidnapped as adults and treated as slaves by ghoul and changeling alike--described as "the men and women kept downstairs, inside the filthy cages built into the sub-basement of the old house."

The story describes the relationship between a changeling, a female assassin, and a male slave who "was a scholar, once." The unnamed changeling somewhat resembles Soldier, from Daughter of Hounds, but at one point she mentions a character named Pentecost; if that is Scarborough Pentecost, from Low Red Moon, then this story takes place before Soldier is born. 

The story also mentions the Bailiff, a character who plays a prominent part in Daughter of Hounds and appears in several other Kiernan stories. The changeling is getting ready to do a job for him in Warwick, a Rhode Island town to the south of Providence.

Like Scheherazade, the slave attempts to hold the changeling's interest by telling a story that ends with a cliffhanger--in this case, a story about a girl Ijbeyneh who is fostered by a ghul woman. (The story appears in the book Folk-Lore of the Holy Land.)

### Publication History
The story also appears in Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Centipede Press, 2018).

fullContent:
"The Three Enchantments" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gary Myers.

### Synopsis
Lir, the apprentice of an elder Lhosk carpet salesman named Dlareb, is aged and sitting on the shores of the Cerenerian Sea to reminisce his times as a boy playing in the white sands and the teak wharves of the shore, loving the sight of the rose-tinted sails that often distracted him from his duties. Back then he would find an old and tarnished silver ball with three cunning glyphs that belonged to Cthulhu, but he was whacked by Dlareb with his knotted stick noting that his rug from remote Sona-Nyl was infested with roung golden spiders, returning to Lhosk to clean the spiders off the rug. He always noticed that Dlareb was peeping out on the sea horizon and acted unusual. He found him one night with the silver ball altered and he traced the least of the ball's glyphs onto the Sona-Nyl rug.

Several of Dlareb's clients would end up falling ill with discomfort while others would claim of voodoo dolls resembling the clients with bamboo splinters penetrated them. Then one morning, gulls flew away from the fitful sea and the Moon gained a peculiar aura. When the sun set behind the Tanarian Hills behind Celephaïs, where Kuranes noted its shrunken appearance but did not inquire to the priests. That night dreams were not pleasant and a shadow of a city was cast upon the land, and Lhosk would be coated in a fog where large tentacles would slither about. Dlareb had removed the voodoo dolls of his clients, and replaced them with waxen images of inhuman creatures with pins in the pattern of a five-pointed star and/or pentagon. Dlareb had went to hide the silver ball and ended up undergoing a horrific flabby transformation that scared Lir away. Then his body would be wound in the blood-stained rug and not buried. But upon trying to close up Dlareb's shop, they learned that the pins came from and they cast the dolls into the sea, as an unseen beast chuckled, which dragged the body of Dlareb into the sea with it as Lir watched.

### Publication History
"The Three Enchantments" was published in the collections of Myers' own works The House of the Worm (1975) and The Country of the Worm: Excursions Beyond the Wall of Sleep (2013).
