shortDefinition: "The Warder of Knowledge" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Richard F. Searight, written in 1935 but not published until 1992, in the Fedogan & Bremer collection Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos. The story is notable for its explication of the Eltdown Shards...
fullContent:
"The Warder of Knowledge" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Richard F. Searight, written in 1935 but not published until 1992, in the Fedogan & Bremer collection Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos. The story is notable for its explication of the Eltdown Shards, pre-human records invented by Searight in his story "The Sealed Casket" and elaborated upon by H. P. Lovecraft in the round-robin story "The Challenge from Beyond".

Lovecraft read Searight's unpublished story in manuscript, and wrote to him about it on November 4, 1935:I like the story exceedingly, & hope you will not let [Weird Tales editor [[Farnsworth Wright|Farnsworth] Wright]]’s rejection discourage you....The references to the Eltdown Shards are fascinating—but woe is me! I’ve given a lot of dope in that composite story [“The Challenge from Beyond”] which conflicts directly with the true facts as here revealed!... I also fear that I described the shards in a conflicting way. Oh, well—in sober truth relatively few people will ever see the composite yarn anyhow.

### Synopsis
Gordon Whitney, chair of the chemistry department at Beloin University, a small Midwestern college, has always been impelled "by a restless, driving urge, without motive or practical goal, to crowd into one mind all the vast aggregation of discovered scientific fact as well as the limitless secrets still undisclosed to research." He becomes obsessed with the Eltdown Shards, fantastically old tablets reputed to record pre-human knowledge, and their apparent reference to an entity called the Warder of Knowledge. Whitney is able to invoke this being, and the ensuing flood of information he receives kills him.

### The Eltdown Shards
"The Warder of Knowledge" provides the fullest description of "the cryptic and half-decipherable Eltdown Shards" by the author who invented them. Searight's account conflicts in certain respects with their treatment by other Mythos writers, particularly H. P. Lovecraft.

In Searight's story, the Shards were discovered "some forty-four years before" the time of the story, which was written in 1935, so approximately 1891. They were found in an "early Triassic stratum" in a "gravel pit near Eltdown"; the "geologic stratum in which the shards had lain indicated an antiquity antedating by millions of years the earliest inscriptions previously known." (The Early Triassic is the geologic period from approximately 252-247 million years ago.)

The first experts to examine them, Dalton and Woodford, "had announced them to be untranslatable"; they were placed in the "small red-brick museum" at the obscure Beloin University, seemingly to prevent them from attracting more attention. There they are kept in a "high cabinet of black walnut".

"The Warm" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Darrell Schweitzer. It was first published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 in October 2014.

### Synopsis
"The Warm" is a retelling of H. P. Lovecraft's 1927 short story "Pickman's Model" but told from the perspective of the ghoul, itself something of an outcast from its own society, who first inspired Richard Upton Pickman's most controversial works. Pickman befriends the creature, persuading it to pose for him, then later encouraging it to tell him stories of its kin to be used as subject matter.

However, through extended contact, the ghoul begins to become more human as Pickman becomes more animalistic. Although the creature wants the man to introduce it to human society he refuses and, in despair, the ghoul summons its fellows who take Pickman below ground to join them, as shown in the finale of "Pickman's Model".

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance, "The Warm" has also been included in the collection of Schweitzer's own works Awaiting Strange Gods: Weird and Lovecraftian Fictions, published by Fedogan & Bremer in September 2015.

### Trivia
*The first picture Pickman paints of the ghoul is stated to be the infamous Ghoul Feeding; it is also the subject of the photograph seen by Thurber in "Pickman's Model".

"The Watcher from the Sky: The Deposition of Abel Keane" is the second part of August Derleth's The Trail of Cthulhu series, following "The House on Curwen Street" and followed by "The Gorge Beyond Salapunco". It was first published in the July 1945 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
Abel Keane is a divinity student living in Boston, Massachusetts, who has some experience as a stage hypnotist and has taught himself psychic abilities, including telepathy. One night, Keane returns to his apartment to find a man clad in strange robes sleeping in his bed. Since the door was locked, Keane can only conclude that the intruder somehow entered by the window.

Using his psychic sensitivity, Keane tries to learn something about the man, who responds mentally by calling Keane by name and telling him to be patient. He explains that he is Andrew Phelan, who had disappeared from this same room two years before, and has recently returned from Celaeno. When Phelan wakes up, he asks Keane to lend him a suit so he can go out. Keane tries to prevent him from leaving without further explanations, but when he attempts to hypnotise Phelan, he ends up falling asleep himself. Somehow, their minds are linked, and Keane experiences visions of Phelan leaving the apartment, taking a bus to Innsmouth, walking to the Marsh family refinery and the Esoteric Order of Dagon church, and being pursued by a batrachian creature until he escapes the town. Keane wakes up at the moment Phelan is returning to the room, and the latter confirms that what Keane witnessed did in fact occur.

While Phelan rests, Keane tries to find information that would elucidate what's happening. He finds out that Phelan, before his disappearance, had been a secretary of Prof. Laban Shrewsbury, and would often visit the Miskatonic University library on behalf of his employer. Keane takes a bus to Arkham and heads straight to the library to inquire about what kinds of books Phelan used to consult. Later on, Keane takes another bus to Innsmouth, where he talks to a shopkeeper (the only person he could find who doesn't have the Innsmouth look), asking him about the reason the town is shunned and the refinery owned by Ahab Marsh. The shopkeeper, Mr. Hendreson, tells Keane that Ahab Marsh's ancestor, Obed, had brought the church of Dagon to Innsmouth, but warns him not to let the locals know that he's been asking questions, as people who do so always end up disappearing.

At last, Keane returns to Boston and confronts Phelan, who explains that he and Shrewsbury are in a mission to try to prevent the return of the god known as Cthulhu, who ruled the Earth before being imprisoned. To protect themselves, they are armed with five-pointed star-stones that can repel Cthulhu's lesser servants, including the batrachian Deep Ones, but are not effective against the deity itself or its more immediate servants. "The Watchers Out of Time" is the final story in the collection of the same name. It is a "posthumous collaboration" between H.P. Lovecraft and August Derleth, meaning that in reality, it is a Derleth story inspired by jotted notes and fragments of stories left behind by Lovecraft at the time of his death.

"The Watchers Out of Time" is an unfinished work, it was not completed at the time of Derleth's death on July 4, 1971. It was published as the final story in the anthology The Watchers Out of Time and Others in 1974.

### Synopsis
Nicholas Walters of Surrey inherits the property of the vanished Whateley family in Dunwich. Not knowing of any connection by blood to this family, Walters travels to Massachusetts and begins investigating the past - and his own family tree. At the same time, ominous and foreboding shadows from the past begin to intrude into his life.

The Watchers Out of Time and Others is an anthology of "posthumous collaborations" between H. P. Lovecraft and August Derleth. Although described thus, the stories were actually written by Derleth, inspired by notes and fragments left behind by Lovecraft after his death in 1937. Many of the stories included here had been previously published by Arkham House in earlier anthologies.

### Publication History
First published by Derleth's specialist publisher Arkham House in 1974, the initial release was given a run of 5,070 copies. It has since had several reissues.

### Synopsis
The story tells of the employees of a small market store which harbours a dark secret: the waste chute in the warehouse blesses the town with prosperity, but must be fed and kept in the way in which it has always been. The arrival of a new manager with radical ideas on how to shake things up in the store forces the employees to take action to save their way of life.

The Web of Easter Island, also published as Dead Titans, Waken!, is a sci-fi horror novel by Donald Wandrei, first published in 1948 by Arkham House.

Concerning a gigantic race of extradimensional "titans" that will descend to the Earth when the stars are in the right configuration, the novel is an homage to the Cthulhu Mythos and is dedicated to Wandrei's friend and Mythos creator H. P. Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
In the British village of Isling, a young boy finds an idol in the old Devil's Graveyard and takes it home. Soon afterwards, the boy is found dead by his parents, his body inexplicably decayed, and the parents themselves suffer the same fate later. An archaeologist named Carter E. Graham, who has traveled the world gathering evidence of an ancient alien race that might have created humanity, reads about the case and gets interested.

Graham visits the Devil's Graveyard and starts digging, first finding an ancient statuette of a monstrous god. The statuette is made of a green substance that seems to change its nature, so it can't be properly identified as stone or metal. It is surprisingly heavy, so hard that the knife can't scratch it, and gives the impression of being alive, infused with energy. Digging further, Graham also finds a large slab made of the same substance, carved with unknown symbols. As soon as he touches it, the slab changes its shape and opens up a passage to an underground crypt. Graham buries the slab again, but takes the statuette with him, planning to examine it at the Ludbury Museum, of which he is the curator.

Traveling by train, Graham hears an inhuman voice chanting in an unknown language, and loses consciousness as the train crashes mysteriously. He wakes up in a hospital and finds out that his bag with the statuette is missing. Unbeknownst to him, the bag has been stolen by a fugitive who embarks on a ship to America. The statuette has a strange effect on the thief, which makes him incapable of tossing it overboard, and similarly seems to enchant a woman named Joane Marsh. The ship is enveloped by a mysterious green mist and vanishes.

Back in Isling, Graham photographs the symbols on the green slab and asks a linguist friend named Alton to translate them. While he's doing so, Graham, along with a colleague named Liska, returns to the Devil's Graveyard and touches the slab again to open up the passage, so the two can go down while tied up in ropes. They find that the passage leads down an unfathomably deep tunnel, at the bottom of which there are thousands of skeletal remains of modern and pre-modern humans. However, the opening turns out to be time-locked, so the slab automatically returns to its original configuration, severing the rope and trapping them.

fullContent:
"The Wedding of Sheila-Na-Gog" is a short story Richard L. Tierney wrote with Glenn Rahman that places Tierney's sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta in an ancient version of Clark Ashton Smith's Mythos setting Averoigne. The story first appeared in the Candlemas 1985 issue of Crypt of Cthulhu (#29).

### Synopsis
Handed over by treacherous Black Goat Druids to the Romans in Gaul, Simon faces imminent sacrifice to the druids' grotesque patron goddess Sheila-na-gog. Salvation comes from an  unlikely and disreputable source—the enigmatic Averoni tribe. 

### Setting
The story is set in Gaul in the summer of 42 A.D.

### Behind the Mythos
Although the identity of the goddess Sheila-na-gog is unknown, her physical appearance is seemingly identical to Abhoth from Clark Ashton Smith's "The Seven Geases": a pool of amorphous slime or flesh that continually gives birth to small monsters. On the other hand, the Black Goat motif of her cult suggests an association with Shub-Niggurath, and she has the ability to engulf humans and transform them into other creatures, such as Satyrs, Criosphinxes, and Rat-Things, which is an ability displayed by Shub-Niggurath in her Keeper of the Moon-Lens form from Ramsey Campbell's "The Moon-Lens". Conversely, Sheila-na-gog is also known for her rivalry with Tsathoggua, which might be inspired by Yhoundeh. The name "Sheila-na-gog" is based on the mysterious sheela na gig carvings of Medieval origin found throughout Europe, which portray female humanoid figures with massively exaggerated genitals. 

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Crypt of Cthulhu, "The Wedding of Sheila-Na-Gog" was reprinted in the January 2003 issue of The Black Book (#3) and in the anthology The Averoigne Legacy (Pickman's Press, 2019), as well as in the Simon of Gitta collection Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

The Weird Company: The Secret History of H. P. Lovecraft's Twentieth Century is a novel by Pete Rawlik, a follow-up to his 2013 book Reanimators. It features characters from various Lovecraft stories working together to defeat eldritch forces. It was published by Night Shade Books in 2014, with an audiobook version also receiving a release.

The novel is episodic, with several chapters having been previously published as short stories. The bulk of the novel takes the form of an account written by Robert Martin Olmstead, the narrator of The Shadow Over Innsmouth, but individual chapters are written from the points of view of other characters, including Asenath Waite from "The Thing on the Doorstep," Thomas Gedney from At the Mountains of Madness, Swami Chandraputra from "Through the Gates of the Silver Key," and others.

### The Weird Company
The novel's main narrative involves characters from Lovecraft forming a sort of superteam to deal with a threat unwittingly unleashed by the Pabodie Expedition to Antarctica. The team, who call themselves the Weird Company, is led by Asenath Waite and includes Olmstead, Chandraputra, Frank Elwood from "The Dreams in the Witch-House," and Dr. Stuart Hartwell, a character created by Rawlik to replace Herbert West, whose story had diverged from the narrative the author wanted to tell in his books. They are later joined by the Yithian who possessed Wingate Peaslee in "The Shadow Out of Time," now inhabiting the body of Thomas Gedney, who goes by the name of Mister Ys.

### Easter Eggs
The Weird Company features a number of quiet nods to other properties, as well as some in-jokes. These include:

*A member of an Antarctic expeditionary team named MacReady, MacReady being the main protagonist in John Carpenter's 1982 science fiction horror film The Thing.
*A chapter set in Kingsport mentions a sailing vessel named the Elizabeth Dane, also the name of a ship in one of Carpenter's earlier films, the 1980 supernatural horror The Fog.
*Chapter 6 features an interlude in a mental health facility. There are many characters who appear only in this chapter, and all are named for Cthulhu Mythos contemporaries of Peter Rawlik. These include a Dr. Willis Lynn (Lynn Willis), patients Mrs. Tanzer and Mr. Meikle (Molly Tanzer and William Meikle, respectively; Tanzer was described as "mad", while Meikle was merely "infirm"), orderlies Sammons, Davis, and Barrass (Brian M. Sammons, Mike Davis, and Glynn Owen Barrass), and a local hunter named Grau (T. E. Grau). An unfortunately-fated cat named Doc was possibly named for Keith "Doc" Herber.

"The Weird of Avoosl Wuthoqquan" is a short story written by Clark Ashton Smith. First printed in Weird Tales in June 1932, it is the third tale in his Hyperborean Cycle fantasy series.

### Synopsis
The story features the character of the title, the avaricious money-lender Avoosl Wuthoqquan, chasing a pair of ill-gotten emeralds that mysteriously rolled away from his possession, out of the city of Commoriom and into a far-away cavern. Inside this cavern he finds a great trove of precious gems, as well as its monstrous owner, the latter of whom devours Avoosl Wuthoqquan before he can sink beneath the pile of treasure.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Weird Tales, "The Weird of Avoosl Wuthoqquan"  has since been reprinted many times, and has been translated into German, Spanish, Dutch, French, Italian and Hungarian.

"The Well" is a Lovecraftian flash fiction piece by British author Tim Jeffreys.

### Synopsis
A man trapped at the bottom of a well is surrounded by a pack of sleeping beasts. As those at the top of the well attempt to make contact with him, their shouting awakens the creatures, dooming him to a grisly death.

### Publication History
"The Well" was first published in Grim Corps Magazine #1 in February 2013. Later that year it was also included in the Lovecraft-inspired collection Whispers from the Abyss.

shortDefinition: "The Well of Stars and Shadow" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-slayer. It was written at the end of October 2001 and published in November 2001 on Gothic.net-...
fullContent:
"The Well of Stars and Shadow" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-slayer. It was written at the end of October 2001 and published in November 2001 on Gothic.net--the first Dancy story (after Threshold) to appear, but the second one written (after "Les Fleurs Empoisonnées").

The story is set during Dancy's childhood in Shrove Wood in Okaloosa County, Florida. It describes her friendship with an elderly neighbor, Mr. Jube, who tries to protect her from the thing that fell from the stars and lives in the nameless lake Wampee Creek empties into.

### Characters
Dancy Flammarion: An albino girl who frequently appears in Kiernan's stories. While she usually appears as a teenager, here she is eight years old, described as a "strange albino child" with "bony shoulders." She claims to have never seen a schoolteacher, but knows how to read and has read the whole Bible. She wears a tarnished St. Christopher medal. She is told: “There were tears the day you were born, Dancy Flammarion. There are tears in your mother’s heart every time she looks at you.”

Mr. Jube: Dancy's elderly neighbor, who lives in a shack near the nameless lake. He has "skin the color of molasses," a bald head and "full white beard," and a "wide, false-toothed smile" with "tobacco-yellowed dentures." He has lived in New Orleans and St. Louis, and sells snakes, frogs, and turtles to men from Tallahassee. He likes to play checkers with Dancy, and buys her candy. He once saw a loup-garou. He has an understanding with the thing that lives in the lake that is threatened by Dancy's unexpected evening visit.

The Moon-Fell Whisperer: An entity that fell into the nameless lake during the great meteor shower of November 13, 1833: "Apalachee mothers told their children about the demons from the moon, the star-fall whisperers below the water."  Little of it can be seen except its eyes, which are "twin balls of the deepest, the most vivid blue...pupil-less eyes that shine bright enough to blind and somehow give off no light whatsoever." It does have an appendage that's described as a "jointed thing that isn’t an arm" and a "black tendril."

### Publication History
"The Well of Stars and Shadow" was republished as part of Trilobite: The Writing of Threshold (Subterranean Press, 2003), and later appeared in Kiernan's collection Alabaster (Subterranean Press, 2006).

fullContent:
"The Wendigo" is a novella by Algernon Blackwood that was first published in The Lost Valley and Other Stories (Eveleigh Nash, 1910). Lovecraft in Supernatural Horror in Literature called it "amazingly potent" (though "less artistically finished" than Blackwood's "The Willows"). "The Wendigo"'s depiction of an encounter with a supernatural creature in the Canadian wilderness deeply influenced August Derleth, and through him the broader Cthulhu Mythos.

The story is set in the wilderness of western Ontario, north of the real-life town of Rat Portage.

### Characters
* Dr. Cathcart: The author of a book on collective hallucination
* Simpson: Cathcart's nephew, a divinity student. 
* Hank Davis: Cathcart's guide.
* Joseph Défago: Simpson's guide, a French "Canuck" who loves the wilderness. 
* Punk: The party's First Nations cook.

fullContent:
"The Were-Snake" is a horror short story by Frank Belknap Long, published in the September 1925 issue of Weird Tales. It briefly mentions "the mad Arab Alhazred", a character created by Long's friend H. P. Lovecraft in "The Nameless City".

### Synopsis
An archaeologist named Arthur, accompanied by his lady friend Miss Beardsley and a local guide, explores a temple of the ancient goddess Ishtar, which he identifies as the Magna Mater, the mother goddess known throughout several parts of Asia as Inanna, Astarte, and other names. Arthur is a skeptic, but believes that superstitions must be investigated, and that spending the night inside a supposedly haunted temple will give him prestige. Miss Beardsley is reluctant, but willing to stay with him, while the guide believes mysticism to be a more prudent attitude than materialism, and advises Arthur to keep a knife close by to protect himself. Arthur would prefer a gun, but the guide insists that bullets would be useless, whereas a knife wouldn't.

At night, Arthur falls asleep and dreams of ancient sacrifices made to Ishtar, who took on the form of an impossibly beautiful woman, the mere sight of which would reduce men to submissive worshipers. When he wakes up, he sees two glowing eyes in the darkness and is convinced that someone is trying to frighten him. He yells at the unseen figure, threatening to go to the American consul and expose the hoax. When he approaches, however, he notices that the glowing eyes are compound, like an insect's. Frightened, he shoots at the monster several times, to no avail. The creature crawls towards him, and just as he's about to surrender to Ishtar's mental influence, he hears the voice of Miss Beardsley. He warns her not to approach, but the monster captures her and drags her away.

With no light to guide him, Arthur desperately stumbles through the interior of the temple, at one point coming in contact with the slime trail left by the entity, and follows it into a long tunnel. He calls out to Miss Beardsley, who shouts out that the creature is squeezing her, like a constricting snake.

Arthur crawls through the tunnel until he sees the beast. Its head is dog-like, but covered in reptilian scales, and its serpentine body is coiled around Miss Beardsley. When he finally manages to dominate his fear, Arthur decapitates the beast with a sharp stone and urges Miss Beardsley to leave the temple for a romantic breakfast. At noon, they meet the guide again, who tells them that a strange scene was found inside the temple: the decapitated body of a woman, and the head of a hooded cobra. The guide thanks Arthur for freeing the people from Ishtar.

### Behind the Mythos
The goddess Ishtar (a deity worshiped in real-world ancient Mesopotamia) is identified as being the same as Astarte and the Magna Mater. The latter would be referenced in Lovecraft's "The Rats in the Walls" and Henry Kuttner's "Hydra", and interpreted in the expanded Mythos as an avatar of Shub-Niggurath. Love

fullContent:
"The Whippoorwills in the Hills" is a horror short story by August Derleth, first published in the September 1948 issue of the magazine Weird Tales. Set in the Cthulhu Mythos, it derives elements from several H. P. Lovecraft stories, particularly "The Dunwich Horror", The Shadow Out of Time, and "The Rats in the Walls".

### Synopsis
On April 30th, 1928, a man named Dan Harrop takes possession of a country house in the vicinity of Arkham and Aylesbury. The house used to belong to Dan's cousin, Abel Harrop, who disappeared a few weeks before. Convinced that the local authorities are not doing anything to find out what happened to him, Dan decides to investigate on his own, but finds the other residents of the valley to be both suspicious and uncooperative, as Abel was regarded as a recluse with a bad reputation for reading books on occultism.

At night, Dan is kept awake by the incessant callings of a flock of whippoorwills, which are noticeably larger and noisier than usual. According to local folklore, whippoorwills can capture the soul of a person who's dying, so the birds' activity is taken as a bad omen.

On the next day, Dan speaks to a man named Amos Whateley, who reacts with hostility to him, but hesitates when Dan points out that he won't stay permanently, and would be willing to sell the house as soon as he finds out what happened to his cousin. Whateley tells him that Abel was taken by "Them from Outside", but regrets saying it when he realises that Dan has no idea what he's talking about. Instead of explaining, he urges Dan to burn Abel's books.

Back in the Harrop house, Dan decides to read some of the books to get to the bottom of the mystery. He finds some marked passages, one of which cautions the reader about summoning Yog-Sothoth and other entities, who demand blood when summoned, and will feed on the summoner themself if the latter has no other sacrifice to offer.

That night, Dan manages to fall asleep, despite the cacophony of the whippoorwills, but wakes up in the middle of the night by a different sound: that of a thunderous, pulsating chant in an unknown language which includes the name Yog-Sothoth. The whippoorwills seem to call rhythmically, as if responding to the chant. Although Dan is unable to identify the source of the chant, he feels that it is extremely close: inside the house, or even inside his room. He remains paralysed with fear until the strange ritual ends with the sound of earth-shaking footsteps moving away, and the fluttering of the whippoorwills taking off.

In the morning, Dan is still shaken by his experience. Before he can return to the study of Abel's books, he realises with some confusion that he seems to already know their contents, as if he had read them before. He goes as far as to recall a vision of tentacled, amoeboid beings with names such as Yog-Sothoth, Cthulhu, Hastur, etc., who wait in other dimensions for their followers to open the gates, so they can reclaim the Earth.

fullContent:
The Whisperer in Darkness is a novella by H. P. Lovecraft. Written February-September 1930, it was first published in Weird Tales, August 1931. Similar to "The Colour Out of Space" (1927), it is a blend of horror and science fiction. Although it makes numerous references to the Cthulhu Mythos, the supernatural does not figure in the plot. The story also introduces the Mi-Go, an alien race of fungoid creatures.

### Inspiration
In The Whisperer in Darkness, narrator Albert Wilmarth initially dismisses those who believe that nonhuman creatures inhabit the Vermont hills as "merely romanticists who insisted on trying to transfer to real life the fantastic lore of lurking 'little people' made popular by the magnificent horror-fiction of Arthur Machen."

This line, Lovecraft scholar Robert M. Price argues, is an acknowledgement of the debt Lovecraft's story owes to Machen's "The Novel of the Black Seal" (1895).

"I would go so far as to make Lovecraft's tale essentially a rewriting, a new version of Machen's," Price writes.

In both cases we have a professor, an antiquarian, following his avocational interests in what most would dismiss as superstition on a dangerous expedition into a strange region of ominous domed hills. He is lured by a curiously engraved black stone which seems a survival from an elder prehuman race now hidden in those mysterious hills.... Lovecraft splits the role of Machen's Professor Gregg between Professor Wilmarth and the scholarly recluse Akeley.... [I]t is Akeley, not the Professor, who eventually disappears into the clutches of the elder race. Wilmarth remains behind to tell the tale, like Machen's Miss Lally. 
Price points out parallel passages in the two stories: Where Machen asks, "What if the obscure and horrible race of the hills still survived...?"

Lovecraft hints at "a hidden race of monstrous beings which lurked somewhere among the remoter hills". Where Machen mentions "strange shapes gathering fast amidst the reeds, beside the wash in the river," Lovecraft tells of "certain odd stories of things found floating in some of the swollen rivers." Price suggests that Machen's reference to accounts of people "who vanished strangely from the earth" prompted Lovecraft to imagine people being literally spirited off the Earth.

As noted by critics like Price and Lin Carter, The Whisperer in Darkness also makes reference to names and concepts in Robert W. Chambers's The King in Yellow, some of which had previously been borrowed from Ambrose Bierce. In a letter to Clark Ashton Smith, Lovecraft wrote that "Chambers must have been impressed with 'An Inhabitant of Carcosa' and 'Haita the Shepherd', which were first published during his youth. But he even improves on Bierce in creating a shuddering background of horror--a vague, disquieting memory which makes one reluctant to use the faculty of recollection too vigorously."

fullContent:
The Whisperer in Darkness is a 2011 film adaptation of the 1931 H. P. Lovecraft short story of the same name, created by the H. P. Lovecraft Historical Society. The Society aims to produce adaptations of Lovecraft's work that appear to have been made when the stories were published; according to the Society's website, Whisperer is meant to evoke "the classic horror films of the 1930s like Dracula, Frankenstein and King Kong." 

The film was directed by Sean Branney, from a screenplay by Branney and Andrew Leman. It stars Matt Foyer as Albert Wilmarth, Barry Lynch as Henry Akeley, and Autumn Wendel as Hannah Masterson, the daughter of a cultist. The real-life paranormal investigator Charles Fort appears as a character played by Leman.

Scenes set at Miskatonic University were shot at Mount Holyoke College in South Hadley, Massachusetts.

"The Whisperers" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Richard A. Lupoff that first appeared in the September 1977 issue of Fantastic.

### Synopsis
When two high school journalists get a chance to interview a hot rock band with an occult shtick, it seems like a dream assignment--but it soon turns out to be a nightmare.

### Characters

*Mario Cipolla: A senior at Millbrook High School in Marin County, California, and a reporter for the school paper, the Millbrook Hi-Life.
*Annie Epstein: A Millbrook High senior and photographer for the Hi-Life. Hardly ever seen without a camera around her neck. Her father is Hal Epstein of Dagon, The Whisperers' record label.
*Karen Robertson: A Millbrook High senior and editor-in-chief of the Hi-Life. Friend to Mario and Annie.
*Johnny Kendrick: Singer and synth player for The Whisperers. "His hair was long, hanging in straight, glossy black planes on either side of his dark, serious face. He wore a dark moustache." He resembles "Omar Sharif...made up to look like a satanic priest."
*Olivia Oldham: Singer for The Whisperers. Her hair was a "glistening blonde that picked up each color in turn from the glaring lights.... Her face was thin and pale.... [S]he had a peculiar, fascinating way of holding her fingers as if she were grasping some invisible line for support."
* Bart Starke: Manager of The Whisperers. He's a "heavyset middle-aged man" whose "jowly face was ringed with a fringe of graying hair. He wore a rumpled gray tweed jacket and baggy brown flannel pants."
*Gooley: The gruff doorman at the Winterland in San Francisco.

### Singles

fullContent:
"The White People" is a horror-fantasy story by Arthur Machen, originally published in his 1906 collection The House of Souls.

The story marks the debut of elements that would later be incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos, such as the Aklo language referenced by Lovecraft in numerous stories and the Alala, referenced by Ramsey Campbell in "The Plain of Sound". Additionally, the mysterious Dôls mentioned briefly in "The White People" might be the source of Frank Belknap Long's Doels and/or H. P. Lovecraft's Dhôl Chants.

### Synopsis
The story opens up with a conversation between three men, one of which, named Ambrose, defends that the "great sinners" must be as far removed from the mundane aspects of man's social sphere as the great saints are. In other words, to be what he describes as a real sinner would involve breaking, not society's laws, nor even the commandments, but the laws of nature itself. One of the other men, named Cotgrave, is keenly interested, but insists that Ambrose provide an actual example. Reluctantly, Ambrose lends him a green book that turns out to be the diary of a 16 year old girl.

From this point on, the bulk of the narrative consists of the girl's writings, which reveal that she is strangely well-versed in occult languages, knows how to contact strange entities and has participated in secret ceremonies. She remembers a time when she was still an infant, and creatures with "little white faces" spoke to her and taught her their language. These beings lived in a "great white place", where the grass and the trees were white too, and a cold wind would blow through the tall hills.

When the girl was 5, she was left alone under a tree by a pool and saw a beautiful woman, with skin as white as milk and dark hair, who sang and danced until the girl fell asleep. When she woke up, she related the experience to her nurse, who seemed to be deeply frightened by it, even though the girl notices that the nurse looks a bit like the white lady herself.

At the age of 13, over a year after her mother's death, the girl finds a path over the countryside that leads to a strange place filled with "ugly stones", some of which seem to be shaped like people or animals. While frightened at first, she finds that she actually likes the stones. Later on, she locates a hidden valley where the ferns remain green throughout winter, and a stream made out of a liquid that looks like water but tastes much better. While trying to get back home, she finds herself at the bottom of a hollow pit and remembers a story her nurse once told her about another girl who went to the same pit and returned with what appeared to be beautiful jewelry, but a mysterious black man came to take her. Remembering this story, the girl gets frightened and utters some protective charms to keep the black man away.

shortDefinition: "The White Ship" is a short story written by science fiction and horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in The United Amateur (Volume 19) #2, November 1919.  Unlike many of Lovecraft's other tales, "The White Ship" does not exp...
fullContent:
"The White Ship" is a short story written by science fiction and horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in The United Amateur (Volume 19) #2, November 1919.

Unlike many of Lovecraft's other tales, "The White Ship" does not expressly tie into the Cthulhu Mythos. However, the story cannot be entirely excluded from Mythos continuity either, since it makes reference to preternatural, godlike beings, as well as several locations that would be mentioned again in Lovecraft's novel The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. The tone and temperament of "The White Ship" also speaks largely of the Dream Cycle literary structure that Lovecraft utilized in other stories such as The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath (1926) and "The Cats of Ulthar" (1920), showing the influence of Lord Dunsany.

### Plot summary
A lighthouse keeper named Basil Elton engages upon a peculiar fantasy in which a robed, bearded man is piloting a mystical white ship which appears when the moon is full. Elton walks out across the water on a bridge of moonbeams and joins the bearded man on this ship, and together they explore a mystical chain of islands unlike anything that can be found on Earth.

They travel past Zar, a green land where "dwell all the dreams and thoughts of beauty that come to men once and then are forgotten", then the majestic city of Thalarion, "City of a Thousand Wonders", where dwell frightful demons. They pass Akariel, the huge carven gate of Thalarion, and continue their voyage. Elton is informed that those who enter both places have never returned. During the voyage they seem to be following an azure celestial bird. They also pass Xura, the "Land of Pleasures Unattained", which seems pleasant from a distance but reeks of plague upon getting nearer. They finally settle in Sona-Nyl, the "Land of Fancy", where Elton spends a period of time which he describes as "many aeons", living in what seems to be a perfect society. In his time in Sona-Nyl, Basil learns of Cathuria, the "Land of Hope". Though no man truly knows where Cathuria is or what lies there, Elton is thrilled with the idea, fantasizing about it wildly, and urges the bearded man to take him there; a request which the latter reluctantly agrees to. They follow the celestial bird westward. After a perilous journey to where the crew believes Cathuria to be, the ship instead finds itself at the edge of the world, and plummets to its doom.

Elton awakens to find himself on the wet rocks next to his lighthouse, mere moments after he first departed on the white ship - and just in time to witness a catastrophic shipwreck caused by the light having gone out for the first time. Nothing remains of this wreck the next morning but the corpse of a bird familiar from his dream-journey, and a single brilliant white wooden spar. Elton does not see the white ship again.

fullContent:
"The White Sybil" is a fantasy short story by Clark Ashton Smith, first published in 1934. It is part of his Hyperborea series.

### Synopsis
After traveling through distant and fantastic lands, a poet named Tortha returns to his home city of Cerngoth in the ice-covered Mhu Thulan. Although he's seen many marvels in his travels, none was more remarkable than the woman he once saw on Cerngoth's own streets, the legendary White Sybil, who is rumored to descend from the northern mountains of Polarion and walk through the Hyperborean cities, sometimes giving out prophecies.

Obsessed with her exotic beauty, Tortha finds out more about the Sybil. He learns of her supernatural nature, as she has been sighted "on the same day in places hundreds of miles apart", and that when encountered on the mountains, she invariably "disappeared quickly, like a morning vapor that melts among the crags".

One day, while traversing a flowery meadow on the northern mountains, Tortha sees the Sybil, who gestures for him to follow her. She moves up the mountainous terrain with ease, while Tortha follows with difficulty, enchanted by the sight of her.

Just as he reaches the ice-covered summit, Tortha is engulfed by a snowstorm and loses sight of the Sybil, thus breaking the spell and reminding him of his fatigue. When he opens his eyes, he is no longer on the mountains, but in an alien valley where the turf and trees are covered in delicate flowers, and the sky is uniformly luminous, with no sight of a sun, moon, stars, or clouds. He notices that he has no shadow, and neither do the trees, which also have no reflection on the stream. The place is utterly silent and there is no wind.

He finds the Sybil again in an arbor and forgets much of what occurs afterwards, remembering that she "greeted him in thrilling, mellifluous words of a tongue that he knew well, but had never heard", and told him of wonders and secrets, but didn't reveal her name or nature. Tortha confesses his love for her and she kisses his brow. As he embraces her, however, her body seems to change, feeling first as a frozen corpse or mummy, then as a truly ethereal thing without form or substance, until she finally vanishes.

The scenery also begins to fade away, the flowers crumbling to dust before the trees, the stream, the sky and even the ground turn into a snowstorm, with Tortha suspended in the air within. When the snow fades, he finds himself high in the sky, falling to the icy ground below.

Tortha survives the fall and his injuries are treated, but now has a permanent white mark on his brow where the Sybil had kissed him. One of the people who tend to him is a fair young woman named Illara, whom he believes to be the Sybil. He marries her and the two live happily, despite his delusion.

fullContent:
"The Will of Claude Ashur" is a short story by C. Hall Thompson, one of two Cthulhu Mythos stories he wrote before being edged out of the genre by August Derleth. It originally appeared in the July 1947 issue of Weird Tales.

### Setting
The story is set in Inneswich, a town on the "lifeless, Atlantic-clawed stretches of the Northern New Jersey coast." It's said that "people who know that part of the country give wide berth to Inneswich and the legends that hang like a slimy caul over the ancient coastal village." Its main point of interest is Inneswich Priory, an "infamous" structure "that lies on the northernmost edge of Inneswich." The main social establishment is the Tavern at Inneswich.

The story also takes place in part at Miskatonic University, providing one of the first descriptions of Miskatonic and Arkham not written by Lovecraft or Derleth. It at first appears to be "a well-endowed college, abounding in charming tradition, nestled in the domed hills of Arkham, in Northern New England"; it later emerges that "obnoxious horrors lay hidden within the ivy-strangled walls of the Library of Miskatonic." The Dean of Men boasts that "our library is reputed to contain the most extensive collection of forbidden and esoteric lore in existence today," citing its holding "the only extant copies of such things as the Unaussprechlichen Kulten of von Juntz, and the loathsome Book of Eibon … Yes, even the dreadful Necronomicon …” A visitor is struck by "the distant, gray coldness of the hills that hemmed in Arkham," and "the sluggish winding ribbon of the Miskatonic." Claude Ashur has lodgings in the town in Pickham Square.

A description of one semester's course load gives a taste of the kind of education available at Miskatonic: "Medieval Lore; Ancient Cults and Sects; History of Necromancy; Examination of Extant Literature on Witchcraft.”

The story begins and ends at the State Asylum in New Jersey, which is in Trenton.

### Characters

*Claude Ashur: The story's main character, an individual of extreme willpower and malice; he is "coldly self-sufficient, and completely capable of getting anything he wanted." Claude was "always extremely delicate of health, and given to strange moodiness. His head seemed too large for the fragility of his body, and his face was constantly shadowed by a pallor.... His nose was long and thin with supersensitive nostril-volutes, and his eyes, set well apart in deep sockets, held a sort of mirthless brilliance." Later, when his brother meets him after several years apart, his "aquiline face was paler and more emaciated," but had "a certain regularity of feature that made it handsome in a striking, sardonic way."
* It's noted that "animals of every sort displayed an often vicious aversion to Claude." He attends Miskatonic University for a time, but is expelled for having "a decidedly unwholesome interest in subjects that are directly opposed to the concepts of medical science."

The Will of Stanley Brooke is a short story written by noted British horror author and Mythos contributor Ramsey Campbell.

### Synopsis
After elderly Stanley Brooke is diagnosed with terminal cancer, he turns to ancient books of lore in an attempt to find a cure, before summoning his lawyer, Ernest Bond, in order to dictate a new will. This terms of this will state that his four siblings and niece will no longer be beneficiaries of his substantial estate, and that William Collier, a man whom they have never before met, is to inherit his entire fortune. The will further lays out that Collier is the exact double of Brooke, and that he will have as identification a letter handwritten by Brooke in a sealed envelope.

When Collier arrives at Brooke’s house for the reading of the will, the family and Bond all remark on the uncanny resemblance Collier bears to the dead man. During the course of their meal and the reading of the will, some strange reactions by Collier to remarks such as "you are what you eat" and "You worm!" by the siblings cause the penny to drop for Bond. Under the pretext that the family is in a foul temper after discovering their disinheritance, Bond takes Collier away in his car, stopping at a disused quarry. Collier is never seen again.

When Terence Brooke, Stanley's brother, calls at Bond's house two weeks later, he finds him shovelling in his garden, and the lawyer remarks on how he cannot stand worms. When Terence asks Bond for the loan of a spanner to fix his disabled car, he claims to have lost it some time ago.

### Characters
*Stanley Brooke/William Collier, an old man dying of cancer who resurrects himself, the manner of which is hinted to be through the consumption of worms.
*Ernest Bond, Stanley's lawyer.
*Emily, Stanley's sister.
*Terence Brooke, Stanley's brother.
*Joyce, Stanley's sister.
*Barbara, Stanley's sister.
*Pamela James, Stanley's niece and former housekeeper.

### Publication History
First printed in the Ramsey Campbell collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants, The Will of Stanley Brooke was later reprinted in Cold Print, another collection of Campbell's.

### Trivia
*Both Brooke's house on King Edward's Way and Bond's on Almshouse Gardens are located in Brichester, a town in the Severn Valley which forms the setting for many of Ramsey Campbell's Mythos stories.

shortDefinition: "The Winfield Heritance" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter which originally appeared in the 1981 anthology Weird Tales #3 (named after but not to be confused with the Weird Tales magazine). It is part of Carter's Xothic Legend Cycle.  Rob...
fullContent:
"The Winfield Heritance" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by Lin Carter which originally appeared in the 1981 anthology Weird Tales #3 (named after but not to be confused with the Weird Tales magazine). It is part of Carter's Xothic Legend Cycle.

Robert M. Price wrote a sequel to it called "The Soul of the Devil-Bought".

### Synopsis
Set in 1936, the story is presented as a document written by Winfield Phillips to be sent to his boss, Dr. Seneca Lapham, in the event of Phillips' death or disappearance.

A resident of Arkham, Phillips travels to California to attend the funeral of his uncle, Hiram Stokely, and is pleased by the opportunity to resume friendship with his cousin, Brian Winfield. The two cousins are surprised to find out that Uncle Hiram, who had severed ties with the rest of the family, had named the two as the only heirs to his estate, including a library filled with rare volumes. Next to the house is an empty field where hundreds of human bodies, dating back to pre-colonial days, had been excavated.

Exploring the library, Phillips finds rare books of poetry and popular horror fiction, while Brian locates a secret passage and finds the Necronomicon as translated by John Dee. Reading from the old grimoire, the cousins learn about the Yuggya, which resemble oversized worms and have access to subterranean sources of gold and wealth, which they offer to men in exchange for sacrificial victims. The legend makes them think about their uncle's mysterious fortune and the field of dead bodies ranging from ancient to recent. Exploring further, they reach a staircase with steps littered with precious coins and gemstones, leading down to an underground pool where Phillips witnesses Brian being captured and dragged underwater by a Yugg.

Phillips flees the scene in terror, but later starts to hear the telepathic call of the Yuggya, telling him that he's given them a fresh sacrifice and is now in league with them. Rather than resisting them, Phillips wonders about all those bodies and how the "legacy" of serving the Yuggya must have passed from one to another for generations, and muses that he might move into his uncle's residence as it belongs to him now, part of "the Winfield heritance".

### Behind the Mythos
This story notably includes a sort of literary in-joke in which the authors of rare books discovered in Hiram Stokely's library are all protagonists or deuteragonists of other Mythos tales, including the likes of Robert Blake, Justin Geoffrey and Halpin Chalmers, among many others.

fullContent:
The Witch-Cult in Western Europe is a 1921 speculative anthropology book by the late English scholar Margaret Murray. Although receiving popular recognition on its release, it’s theories have since been largely discredited by the academic community.

### Overview
In essence, the book claims that until the early modern age, there existed a cult in existence across Western Europe which worshipped a horned god of pagan ancestry. This organisation was so successful in keeping its existence hidden from the ever-expanding influence of Christianity that it was not until the Reformation that the Church took any real notice of the group; the subsequent persecution of witches was the response, resulting in its virtual annihilation.

### Influence on H. P. Lovecraft
The Witch-Cult in Western Europe appears to have had a strong influence on Lovecraft's writing; he read it shortly after its release, likely sometime in 1923.

*"The Festival" (1923): In correspondence he wrote "In intimating an alien race I had in mind the survival of some clan of pre-Aryan sorcerers who preserved primitive rites like those of the witch-cult--I had just been reading Miss Murray's The Witch-Cult in Western Europe."
*"The Horror at Red Hook" (1925): again, the survival of a prehistoric cult based on witchcraft is central to the storyline.
*"The Call of Cthulhu" (1926): the story itself directly references the book, where it mentions "passages in such mythological and anthropological source-books as Frazer’s Golden Bough and Miss Murray’s Witch-Cult in Western Europe."

### References

fullContent:
"The Witches of Innsmouth" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author Stephen Hernandez. It was published in the Halloween edition of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in August 2018.

### Synopsis
The story is framed as the unnamed narrator, a former student of archaeology and ancient languages at the famed Miskatonic University, relates to an old friend how his fascination with the occult led to the damning of his very soul. During the course of his research, the narrator discovered the existence of Cthulhu and the Great Old Ones while studying the R'lyehian/Aklo language. This revelation awakened in him a deep desire to pursue arcane knowledge, and led him to become the apprentice of a powerful sorcerer from Innsmouth named Eleazar Caldwell.

For the next few months, he studied the dark arts under Caldwell's tutelage, believing that the old man wished him to join his coven. Ultimately, he was invited to a ceremony to confirm his membership, only to find out that, rather than becoming an acolyte, he was to be the cult's next sacrifice to their master: the Outer God Nyarlathotep. Fortunately for the man, a timely tantrum by Caldwell's familiar - a small black goat - allowed him to escape, interrupting the ritual and bringing Nyarlathotep's fury down upon his former devotees.

### Behind the Mythos
The titular Witches of Innsmouth, a coven dedicated to Nyarlathotep, are, unusually, no relation to the Deep Ones more commonly associated with that blighted town. The odd appearance of the town's denizens is, however, made mention of.

Nyarlathotep is portrayed as the least of the pantheon of eldritch entities of the Mythos, and is stated to have to grovel and beg before the others to avoid destruction at their hands. Strangely though, he is still able to curry their favour on behalf of mortals.

The story is littered with other references to the Cthulhu Mythos, although most of these are confined to name-checks of books and entities. These include:

* The Necronomicon is mentioned, as is its author Abdul Alhazred; other books namedropped are De Vermis Mysteriis, Book of Iod, Cultes des Goules, and the Pnakotic Manuscripts
* Several Mythos entities are listed, including Nug, Hastur, Idh-yaa, Ghatanothoa, Ythogtha, Zoth-Ommog, Cthylla, Shaurash-Ho, Yogash the Ghoul, and K'baa the Serpent
* Other elements alluded to are Devil's Reef and the Elizabeth Arkham Asylum
* Aleister Crowley is briefly spoken of, although he plays no part in the story

fullContent:
"The Witness in Darkness" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author John Shirley. It was first published in the S. T. Joshi-edited anthology The Madness of Cthulhu by Titan Books in October 2014.

### Synopsis
The story is told in the form of a transcript taken from a statement by scholar and explorer William Dyer. Dyer had returned to Antarctica years after the disastrous Pabodie expedition and had encountered an Elder Thing, this one conscious and active. The being then uses Dyer's mind and vocal chords to recount the history of its species, from their origins amongst the stars, to their coming to Earth, to their wars with the Cthulhi and Shoggoths, then finally to their eventual downfall and subsequent scattering.

The Elder Thing goes on to describe the expedition's discovery of it and its fellows in a hibernation chamber, and the role it played - unseen by any of the party - in the events related in At the Mountains of Madness. It ends its monologue by stating that intends to retreat to the oceans and propagate, before issuing a warning not to enter the ruined city again, as the Shoggoth may no longer be as hopelessly trapped as the Elder Thing left it…

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "The Witness in Darkness" has also appeared in the Hippocampus Press collection of Shirley's own works Lovecraft Alive!, published in 2016.

fullContent:
The Wolverine was an amateur press publication from Detroit, Michigan, that was appeared from the 1900s through the 1920s. Three of H. P. Lovecraft's short stories first appeared in the journal, including "The Nameless City," sometimes considered the first story set in the Cthulhu Mythos.

Described as "An Amateur Free-Lance" publication, The Wolverine was edited by Horace L. Lawson, later joined by Marjorie C. Lawson. They published Lovecraft's virulently xenophobic "The Street" in December 1920, followed by "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family" in March 1921, and "The Nameless City" in November 1921. 

The publication also published a column called "The Vivisector," featuring criticism of work appearing in The Wolverine and elsewhere in the amateur press, under the pseudonym Zoilus. (The name comes from a 4th century B.C. Greek writer known for his harsh criticism of Homer.) It was mostly written by Lovecraft, who contributed the columns that appeared in March 1921, June 1921, March 1922, and Spring 1923. The only "Vivisector" column not written by him was in the November 1921 issue, where his friend Alfred Galpin used the pseudonym to discuss "Arthur Jermyn."  

The Wolverine also published Lovecraft's poem "On the Return of Maurice Winter Moe, Esq., to the Pedagogical Profession" in its June 1921 issue. 

### References

fullContent:
The Womb of Time is a Cthulhu Mythos novel by Brian Stableford, first published in 2011.

Set in 1935 in the real village of Dunwich, England, the novel explores themes of ancestral memories and how the human mind might respond to the disruptive influences of external agents, both chemical and semiotic. It is also notable for connecting the Cthulhu Mythos to the legend of King Arthur, Merlin, and especially the vilified Medraut, better known today as Mordred.

### Synopsis
Every 114 years, a combination of astronomical phenomena results in the English village of Dunwich experiencing an "ultra low tide", exposing parts of the sea floor that had been continually submerged for over a century. In 1821, this event was witnessed by Thomas De Quincey, who had been invited to Dunwich by a Reverend Wychelow and an apothecary named Paston. During his stay, De Quincey started working on his most famous book, Confessions of an English Opium-Eater.

In 1935, Richard Halsted, a literary scholar from Arkham, Massachusetts, currently studying at Oxford, England, decides to visit Dunwich and stay at the Hidden Crown, the same inn where De Quincey, Wychelow and Paston stayed 114 years before. The other guests include another literary expert named Martin Rylands; an antiquarian named James Wychelow who descends from the Reverend; and a government biologist named Graham Ridpath with an interest in esoteric matters. A pair of quiet gentlemen, Vamplew and Conrad, are the inn's permanent residents. The innkeeper, Giles Crome, is also a peculiar character, apparently obsessed with the idea that Mordred (the man who killed King Arthur) was actually a hero, whose historical reputation has been tarnished.

When Halsted reveals that he works at Miskatonic University, all the others except Rylands react with great surprise and shock. It transpires that they are all familiar with Dunwich's American namesake in the Miskatonic River valley, which has recently been the site of certain events involving an esoteric book called the Necronomicon. Halsted himself is familiar with this tome, having studied it under the guidance of Miskatonic's librarian Henry Armitage. However, he claims that the book isn't a grimoire as commonly thought, but something of a catalogue of pre-Islamic deities, the text of which is barely comprehensible due to a history of consecutive translations and alterations. After the introductions are made, the group proceeds to the beach, where Halsted catches sight of a mysterious veiled woman who reminds him of his ex-lover.

While staying at the inn, Halsted learns that Vamplew and Conrad are former scientists who have been employed by the British government to develop chemical and biological weapons for the war; the same research which Ridpath is currently involved in. fullContent:
"The Wonderful Musician" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
A man uses modern technology in an effort to tune in to the frequency of the cosmos. In the process he opens a gate and allows something through, something which begins to repopulate the Earth.

### Characters
* Rickman, a man on a mission to connect to the music he believes underlies all of existence.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite lacking any direct reference to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Meikle's inclusion of "The Wonderful Musician" in his collection Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates his belief that it follows in the spirit of such works. Additionally, two of the beings summoned during Rickman's experiments bear a similarity to entities found within the Mythos: a winged crustacean resembling a Mi-Go, and a conglomeration of multiplying black eggs whose description is identical to that found in other stories by the same author, and has been revealed to be Yog-Sototh.

### Publication History
* A Mythos Grimmly (2015)
* Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror (2019)
* Lab: Three Tales of Weird Science (2020)

"The Wood" is a short fantasy poem by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft. First published posthumously in the September 1938 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales, it has since been reprinted numerous times, and has been translated into both German and French .

### Synopsis
The five four-line verses describe the destruction of an ancient woodland, the rise of a magnificent city of crystal and ivory, and the subsequent return of the primal forest after a careless word spoken in a magical tongue by a drunken reveller.

### Publication History

*Beyond the Wall of Sleep (1943)
*Collected Poems (1963)
*The World of H. P. Lovecraft (1971)

*Songs of Giants (2019)

fullContent:
"The World Ends in Neon Yellow" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author LA Knight. It was published in the thematic anthology Tomorrow's Cthulhu by Broken Eye Books in January 2016.

### Synopsis
Casilda Carter, a woman whose family has long stood in opposition to the dark forces which threaten humankind, uses her technological expertise to warn the citizens of New York City of the coming of Hastur, an event which she knows will precipitate the destruction of the species. Attempting to rejoin her father in Arkham, Massachusetts, she realises that her opponent has tracked her to the family home, and prepares to sell her life dearly for the cause.

### Mythos Connections
Mythos elements made mention of include the play The King in Yellow, nightgaunts, gugs, and Carcosa, as well as the real-world Essex County, Massachusetts. Additionally, during her escape from New York, Casilda mentions her desire to avoid the subway system, as she recalls a man named Pickman whose descendants released creatures from the sewers, a clear reference to the ghouls described in "Pickman's Model."

The Worlds of H. P. Lovecraft was a series of comic books which adapted several of Lovecraft's short stories into a more visual format. 

### Overview
Published by Caliber Comics for the first five issues between 1993 and 1996, the next four issues were released under Caliber's Tome Press imprint from 1997 to 1998. In 2020 Caliber released The Shadow Over Innsmouth. Most of the stories were collected together in two omnibus editions, with the stories divided by the label which they were originally published under.

All of the stories were adapted by Steven Philip Jones, and were released with full-colour covers and black-and-white interiors.

shortDefinition: "The Worm in the Wood" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story written by Laurence J. Cornford, first published in 1997 in the magazine Cthulhu Cultus #7.  ### Synopsis The story is told by a narrator who is trying to dissuade someone from venturing into the...
fullContent:
"The Worm in the Wood" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story written by Laurence J. Cornford, first published in 1997 in the magazine Cthulhu Cultus #7.

### Synopsis
The story is told by a narrator who is trying to dissuade someone from venturing into the wood in the vicinity of Arkham. Although no one has claimed the land after the death of the last owners, the locals take care to maintain the fence around the wood in good condition.

When pressed, the narrator reluctantly tells the story of how he used to visit the wood as a child thirty years before, in 1946, along with three young friends named Hubert, Seth, and Clyde. Due to the recent war, the fence had been somewhat neglected at the time, so the children found a place where they could easily get through. At first, they found the wood a peaceful place, and enjoyed the cool temperature and the supply of tasty apples, even though a good number of these had worms inside them. After their first ventures, they started to feel some kind of presence, and found signs such as trails and half-eaten animal carcasses, which they tentatively explained away as the work of a bear.

When the silence was broken by a sound betraying the presence of a large creature, the children decided to track the putative bear, and followed it to a place where the branches of gnarled trees grew close to the ground and formed a gigantic tunnel covered in some kind of web or membrane. They heard the sounds of the creature moving inside the tunnel, and Hubert urged the others to keep following, in spite of their fear.

At the end of the tunnel, they found themselves inside the lair of the beast: a chamber where many such tunnels converted to, all covered in phosphorescent mold and slime, and filled with apples, fish, and animal remains, which were being devoured by swarms of worms. The worms ranged from regular maggot-sized to cat-sized. Finally, they saw the monster: a pale thing larger than a bear, which attacked the kids. The four ran for their lives, out of the tunnel and towards the outskirts of the wood. The narrator looked behind and saw the thing charge at Hubert. Seth and Clyde reached the fence and escaped, as did the narrator.

Later on, the narrator learned from an old man that the creature was a Manitou, known as the "Spirit of the Trees", or the "Worm in the Wood". The locals retrieved Hubert's dead body from the wood, then proceeded to fix and reinforce the fence. The narrator finishes the story by revealing that he has since had the opportunity to consult a library in Arkham, and believes he knows the truth about the monster. He claims that if his ideas are correct, there must be a great number of such beings, but that they don't want anything from humans. In fact, they won't be a danger to anyone, as long as no one intrudes in their territory and starts killing the worms inside the apples again.

fullContent:
"The Worm of Urakhu" is a short story by Richard L. Tierney that uses his sword-and-sorcery hero Simon of Gitta to mesh the Cthulhu Mythos with the lore of Frank Herbert's Dune series. The story first appeared in the 1988 issue  of Weirdbook (#23/24).

### Synopsis
Relentlessly pursued across the barren Egyptian desert by a Roman cohort, Simon stumbles upon an ancient abandoned temple where he seeks refuge. What he finds therein may be more terrifying than the legions of Rome: The temple holds secrets tied to a colossal extraterrestrial horror.

### Setting
The story is set in the autumn of 37 A.D. in the Egyptian desert.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Weirdbook, "The Worm of Urakhu" was reprinted in the Simon of Gitta collections The Scroll of Thoth (Chaosium, 1997) and Sorcery Against Caesar (Pickman's Press, 2020).

The Worm that Gnaws in the Night is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Lin Carter for his short story "Shaggai".

### Background
The Worm is a massive polychaete worm-like fiend that was observed by the wizard Eibon, who noticed that it was slowly eating away at the planet Shaggai.

The Worm has immense durability and might be one of the most powerful Great Old Ones. The Elder Gods couldn't even handle it and the Worm has survived the radiation from Ghroth, the Outer God who destroyed all life on Shaggai. It was one of the only Old Ones on that planet, with the other being Baoht Z'uqqa-Mogg.

"The Woven Offspring" is a Lovecraftian short story by the late American author W. H. Pugmire, first published in issue #9 of Lore magazine in 1998.

The story is loosely connected to the Cthulhu Mythos through its setting of the Sesqua Valley, a locale created by Pugmire as the stage for many of his mythos stories.

### Synopsis
Young siblings Alma and Alexander find themselves embroiled in a love triangle with Thomas, a charming drug addict. When they find Thomas dead of an overdose one morning, Alexander enacts a ritual to bring him back. However, the magic of the Old Ones required by the process causes Alexander to brutally kill himself, leaving Alma to care for the tiny doll into which Thomas's soul has been transferred.

"The Wreck of the Charles Dexter Ward" is a short story by Elizabeth Bear and Sarah Monette, part of their Boojumverse setting that combines elements of the Cthulhu Mythos and creatures from Lewis Carroll in a space opera setting. The story concerns an attempt by the Arkhamers, a spacefaring sect of seekers of forbidden knowledge, to salvage a hospital ship that was once a living spaceship called a boojum. It was first published in audio form in two parts on the podcast The Drabblecast.

The story won the 2013 Locus Award for best novelette.

### Characters
*Cynthia Feuerwerker: A space doctor. After she is kicked off the liveship Richard Trevithick over "allegations of malpractice and unlicensed experimentation," she takes a job on the Arkhamer archive ship Jarmulowicz Astronomica. 
*Thomas Wandrei: A senior Arkhamer scientist. Described as "a bald old Arkhamer whose jowls quivered with every word he spoke. His skin was so dark [one] could just about make out the patterns of tattoos against the pigment, black on black-brown."
*Hester Ayabo Jarmulowicz:  An Arkhamer  crew member who studies extradimensional creatures "like boojums and cheshires and the dreadful bandersnatches." She is described as "tall and skinny and iron-black."
*Julia Filomela Fiorenzo: An disgraced Arkhamer doctor, following in the footsteps of Herbert West.
*Martha Patterson Snead: Feuerwerker's predecessor on the Jarmulowicz Astronomica. Described as "not very tall, wiry, freckled skin." Feuerwerker suspects she neglected her patients for her research.
*Doctor Belafonte: Patterson's predecessor.

### Ships

### Boojum Liveships
*Charles Dexter Ward: An ambulance ship, killed and then reanimated by Julia Filomela Fiorenzo.
*Richard Trevithick: Named for a British engineer who invented the first working steam locomotive.
*Lavinia Whateley:  Said to have "vanished without a trace after pirating a cargo of the Mi-Go's canisters of disembodied brains" (a story told in full in Bear and Monette's "Boojum")

### Arkhamer Ships 
* Jarmulowicz Astronomica: A "cumbersome, centuries-accreted monstrosity."
* T.H. White: One of the Jarmulowicz Astronomica's two landing crafts, a "lumbering scow." Named for the author of The Once and Future King.
*Caitlín R. Kiernan: The Jarmulowicz Astronomica's other landing craft, "an incongruously sporty little skimmer." Named for the weird fiction writer.
* Burlingame Astrophysica Terce

### Other Ships
*Veronica Lodge: A "sleek, busy tug." Named for Archie's black-haired girlfriend in the Archie Andrews comics. 
*Calico Jack, no doubt named after the pirate Calico Jack Rackham.

After first airing on the Drabblecast podcast, "The Wreck of the Charles Dexter Ward"'s first print appearance was in The Year's Best Science Fiction: Thirtieth Annual Collection (St. Martin's Griffin, 2013), followed by The Mammoth Book of Best New SF 26 (Robinson, 2013). fullContent:
The X-Files is a long-running American science fiction/paranormal police drama franchise created by Chris Carter which has been claimed by some to be Lovecraftian in nature. To date, eleven series, two full-length feature films, and a spin-off series have been produced, along with a host of associated media, such as novels, comic books, video games, and much more.

### Premise
The show follows two Federal Bureau of Investigation special agents, Fox Mulder and Dana Scully, who are assigned to a branch of the Bureau which investigates unexplained crimes and phenomena. The overarching story of the franchise involves a government conspiracy to cover up their involvement with aliens, and the agents' attempts to find the truth hidden by the shadowy figures ranged against them.

### Characters
* Fox Mulder: a brilliant psychological profiler who is driven to uncover the disappearance of his younger sister Samantha during childhood. Mulder has the tendency to believe in almost any paranormal activity unquestioningly.
* Dana Scully: a gifted medical doctor, Scully is a skeptic who is often used as a foil to Mulder's believer in earlier series. Later, however, she comes to accept that the world she lives in contains many inexplicable phenomenon.

### Inspiration
Carter has repeatedly mentioned the Kolchak series, amongst a handful of others, as having had a significant impact on his creation of The X-Files.

### Lovecraftian Themes
* The show frequently features themes of a greater knowledge lurking just out of sight, which is a very Lovecraftian concept.
*Some episodes, such as "Squeeze" and "Tooms" feature characters who will go to desperate lengths in order to extend their life spans. These recall stories such as "Cool Air".
*The two-part episode "Dreamland" features a case of body-swapping, which could be likened to the events of "The Thing on the Doorstep", although in The X-Files the story plays out in a far more lighthearted and upbeat way.

### Trivia
*Issue #7 (December 1995) of the Topps comic book series The X-Files, titled "Trepanning Opera," opens with H. P. Lovecraft’s "correlated contents" quote from his novelette "The Call of Cthulhu."
*The Season 5 episode "Chinga" was co-written by expanded Mythos author Stephen King.
*In the comic story "Hallow Eve" (The X-Files Annual #1, 1995, Topps), Mulder and Scully travel to Arkham, Massachusetts, to investigate the death of a professor at Miskatonic University.

shortDefinition: "The Yellow Sign" is a short story by Robert W. Chambers that appeared in his 1895 collection The King in Yellow. It's one of five stories in the book that are connected through their references to a fictional play called The King in Yellow, which ha...
fullContent:
"The Yellow Sign" is a short story by Robert W. Chambers that appeared in his 1895 collection The King in Yellow. It's one of five stories in the book that are connected through their references to a fictional play called The King in Yellow, which has an inevitably disastrous effect on those who read it.

### Synopsis
The story concerns an Greenwich Village artist named Scott and his favorite model, Tessie Reardon. While painting a nude portrait of Tessie, Scott glances out his window on Washington Square and sees the watchman of a nearby church, whose face gives the "impression of a plump white grave-worm"--an image so "intense and nauseating" that it spoils the painting. Tessie confesses that she has seen the "young man with the pasty face" in a dream--driving a hearse that carries Scott in a coffin. Scott later overhears the watchman muttering something that turns out to be "Have you found the Yellow Sign?"

The relationship between Scott and Tessie grows closer, and she gives him "a clasp of black onyx, on which was inlaid a curious symbol or letter in gold," as a symbol of her love, which she had found coming back from  Battery Park. He promises to wear it always.

Scott injures his wrists in an accident in his studio, rendering him temporarily unable to paint. Looking about for something to read to occupy himself, he comes upon "a book bound in serpent skin, standing in a corner of the top shelf of the last bookcase." It is, inexplicably, The King in Yellow, a book he has studiously avoided: "If I ever had had any curiosity to read it, the awful tragedy of young Castaigne, whom I knew, prevented me from exploring its wicked pages." Tessie playfully grabs the book, and despite Scott's entreaties, hides away and reads it: "I looked at Tessie and saw it was too late. She had opened The King in Yellow." Scott sits down and reads it too, from beginning to end. "Oh the wickedness, the hopeless damnation of a soul who could fascinate and paralyze human creatures with such words...!"

They now realize that the found onyx clasp is the Yellow Sign; Tessie begs Scott to throw it away, but he refuses, for reasons he doesn't understand. They sit discussing the play:[W]e murmured to each other of the King and the Pallid Mask, and midnight sounded from the misty spires in the fog-wrapped city. We spoke of Hastur and of Cassilda, while outside the fog rolled against the blank window-panes as the cloud waves roll and break on the shores of Hali.... I knew that she knew and read my thoughts as I read hers, for we had understood the mystery of the Hyades and the Phantom of Truth was laid.They hear wheels outside and see a hearse; they bolt the door but "knew no bolts, no locks, could keep that creature out who was coming for the Yellow Sign." The pallid watchman breaks in and retrieves the onyx clasp.

In the aftermath Tessie is dead, Scott knows he is dying, and a corpse that has been "dead for months" is discovered in Scott's room.

"The Yoth Protocols" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Josh Reynolds.

### Synopsis
A government agent and the enigmatic Indrid Cold descend into the darkness of K'n-yan when their K'n-yanian contacts suddenly go silent. There, they discover the survivors of a Soviet special forces team who have accidentally unleashed not only a deadly contagion, but also the denizens of the cavern beneath K'n-yan, Yoth . . . 

### Characters

*Indrid Cold, a mysterious and inhuman creature working with the United States government.
*Sarlowe, an agent working for an unspecified government organisation.
*Grigori Petrov, a Soviet soldier on a secret mission.

### Publication History
"The Yoth Protocols" was published in the Dark Regions Press anthology World War Cthulhu in August 2014.

### Trivia

*The character of Indrid Cold is something of a niche pop-culture icon, usually associated with stories of Earth governments in collaboration with aliens.

"The Young of the Old Ones" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas, first published in his 2005 collection Unholy Dimensions by Mythos Books. It is the third and final story in a series set in Thomas's Punktown milieu involving the character John Bell.

### Synopsis
When a man believed lost for the last eight years after an experiment in dimensional travel miraculously reappears, Colonial Security Agent John Bell is assigned to conduct an investigation at the R'lyeh research station.

Through interviews with the returnee and science staff there, he establishes that the man has been in the presence of a godlike being, most likely Cthulhu, and that while there his body was laced with thousands of microscopic creatures which the team have successfully removed. However, when Bell orders these organisms destroyed, a reaction is triggered which causes them to grow massively in size, attack all those they come into contact with, and attempt to re-initialise the dimensional portal.

Fortunately for the few surviving staff - not to mention the human race as a whole - other elder powers have been watching these events from the beginning, and have inserted a biological version of the star-stone into the facility, killing the invading creatures at a terrible cost to itself.

### Publication History
Since it’s first appearance, "The Young of the Old Ones" has also been included in the 2012 German-language collection Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos by Festa.
