"Theodore Roosevelt: 1858–1919", or simply "Theodore Roosevelt", is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft in honour of the late American president and New York governor Theodore Roosevelt. It was first published in January 1919 in The United Amateur, soon after Roosevelt's death. The poem also appeared in the 1977 collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems.

### Synopsis
This elegy expresses the author's admiration for Roosevelt, here depicted as a noble, wise, kind, just and valourous man and an outstanding leader to his people, whose memory will continue to inspire others after his death.

Theodorus Philetas is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft as the translator of Abdul Alhazred's Al Azif from Arabic into Greek, thus creating the first book actually called the Necronomicon rather than its previous Arabic title. He appears in Lovecraft's mock-scholarly "History of the Necronomicon" (1927).

According to Lovecraft's fictional history, Theodorus was a resident of Constantinople who "secretly translated" the work in 950 under the title Necronomicon. This translation "impelled certain experimenters to terrible attempts" over the next century, until it was suppressed and burnt by Patriarch Michael I in 1050. Though a print edition was published in Italy between 1500 and 1550, no copy of Theodorus' translation has been known to exist since one was burnt in Salem in 1692. Lovecraft later stated that Theodorus was a Byzantine monk who translated the Al Azif into late Greek in 900 (not 950), giving it the title Τὸ Νεκρονόμικον. (: Selected Letters 3.421)

Joan C. Stanley, in Ex Libris Miskatonici, suggests that character's Greek name would be more accurately transliterated as Theodoros Philetos. She points out that in medieval Greek, his surname would indicate that he was considered a heretic--an allusion to the Biblical character of Philetus (2 Timothy 2:16-18), who denied the bodily resurrection, a stance associated with Gnosticism.

shortDefinition: Theosophy is an occult movement originating in the 19th century with roots that can be traced to ancient Gnosticism and Neoplatonism.   The term theosophy itself is a portmanteau word derived from the Greek theos (“god”) and sophia (“wisdom”). It is ...
fullContent:
Theosophy is an occult movement originating in the 19th century with roots that can be traced to ancient Gnosticism and Neoplatonism. 

The term theosophy itself is a portmanteau word derived from the Greek theos (“god”) and sophia (“wisdom”). It is generally explained as and understood to mean “divine wisdom.” 

Forms of this doctrine were held in antiquity as genuine religious or spiritual beliefs by the Manichaeans, an Iranian dualist sect, and in the Middle Ages by two groups of dualist heretics, the Bogomils in Bulgaria and the Byzantine Empire, and the Cathars in Burgundy, southern France and Italy. 

In modern times, theosophical views have been held by Rosicrucians and by certain  Freemasons. The international New Age movement of the 1970s and 1980s originated among independent theosophical groups in the United Kingdom.

Theosophy freely borrows and in some cases distorts or misrepresents concepts from Buddhism, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism and the then-current understanding of ancient mystery cults. It refined itself as it went along, adapting to various fads and movements in popular culture throughout the late nineteenth and into the twentieth century.

Theosophy also found itself on the racist and eugenicist side of many debates since its teachings include highly bigoted concepts and teachings related to "Root Races" and the spiritual and physical corruption of life on Earth.

Theosophy has a relentlessly syncretistic and reductionist viewpoint. It teaches that all religions and spiritual teachings are corrupted from some prehistoric perfect form but that all contain at least a grain of truth. However real enlightenment can only come from esoteric teachings at the feet of a great teacher and through mystic experiences including ecstatic trances and meditation leading to contact with disembodied and in some cases completely non human intelligences (NHI).

One of the leading proponents of Theosophy was Helena Blavatsky who is variously considered an inspired teacher or a charlatan but whose work included popularizing various genuine mystical practices, albeit under bastardized or incorrect terminology, such as the thought-form (wrongly called a "Tulpa").

shortDefinition: "There is a Book" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and games designer Dennis Detwiller. It was published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express in December 2014.  ### Synopsis The story tells of a "book," which is i...
fullContent:
"There is a Book" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author and games designer Dennis Detwiller. It was published in the thematic anthology Madness on the Orient Express in December 2014.

### Synopsis
The story tells of a "book," which is in actuality an idea planted into the fabric of the universe as a tool by extra-dimensional entities to facilitate their entry into our plane of existence. Seeing humankind as a suitable vessel for itself, the idea gravitates towards the emerging human civilisations, where it implants itself into susceptible consciousnesses.

Despite early setbacks in which the idea failed to gain any real traction and was almost destroyed, it finds a suitable home in the mind of a madman by the name of Alhazred who transcribes its tenets into a book titled Al-Azif. Although Alhazred's book, which would later come to be known as the Necronomicon, finds a strong following amongst a certain type of person, the goal of opening a gateway to the other dimension never quite materialises, the entities finding themselves time and again opposed by unknown agencies amongst the humans.

In the modern day, a man travels to an obscure bookshop in Istanbul which he has discovered holds the only surviving intact copy of the Necronomicon, determined to destroy it and keep the world free from alien influences, at least for a while.

### Behind the Mythos
The unnamed man who visits the Turkish bookshop muses on how he had "recruited, fought beside, and lost too many people" in the pursuit of his mission against the alien entities. This is possibly a suggestion that the group to which he belongs is intended to be Delta Green, a franchise originating with the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game which author Dennis Detwiller co-created and has written for extensively.

"They Thrive in Darkness" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
Two recently-acquainted Arkham men investigate a mysterious door in one of their basements. After blacking out during an exploration of the tunnel which lies beyond, the man who was visiting wakes up alone in a nightmarish cavern system deep underground. Stumbling through the labyrinthine tunnels, he eventually happens across the other man, who is in the company of a pack of ghouls, a pack which includes a notorious figure from Arkham's past.

### Characters

* Owen Blake, a curious man on the road to becoming a meal for a pack of hungry abominations.
* Vincent Underhill, a rare book dealer with a dark family history.
* Richard, a ghoul.

### Publication History
"They Thrive in Darkness" was first published by Chaosium in the anthology Arkham Tales: Legends of the Haunted City in July 2006, and again in the collection of Shiflet's own work They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in June 2018.

### Trivia

* Vincent Underhill claims to be a descendant of the ghoul Richard, who is implied to be Richard Upton Pickman from the H. P. Lovecraft short story "Pickman's Model".

fullContent:
"Thick as a Brick" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Craig Brownlie. It was first published in Vol 8, Issue 2 of the Gavin Chappell-edited zine Lovecraftiana in July 2023.

### Synopsis
When young Carter is injured helping elderly relative Dominick declutter his house, the old man gives the boy a tincture of containing a strange black powder which may well be alien in nature. Although the substance makes his arm heal in a miraculous timeframe, the boy subsequently becomes obsessed with the rhythms of music, and accidentally triggers an event which causes him, his mother and sister, and a substantial portion of the family home to simply disappear into the ether.

Distraught and desperate to have his family returned to him, husband and father Nick does everything within his power to find out what really happened. Through correspondence with academic experts and extensive consultation and experimentation with Dominick, he finally comes up with a solution: activating a series of supercharged speakers and drinking as much of the black powder as he can stomach, Nick finds himself transported in the same manner as his family, although it is implied that he does not survive the trip.

### Mythos Connections
One of the correspondences Nick enters into is with a retired professor from Miskatonic University.

The Things are a fictional species created by John W. Campbell for his horror novella Who Goes There?. They were later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Malleus Monstrorum.

### Background
The Things are a race from a distant world that orbits a blue star. A deceitful race with the ability to shapeshift into the form of any creature that they consume. In the process, they absorb the mannerisms, skills, and memories of the victim, giving it the ability to perfectly imitate any organic life form. They can not only completely transform themselves, but they can also transform specific body parts, quickly creating claws or teeth. Every cell in their bodies acts as an intelligent independent organism, and even their blood will move to escape that which harms it.

Things have the ability to bud and create independent organisms, splitting into two. Dismembered body parts become separate creatures and its blood will attempt to enter a victim, consuming it from the inside and creating a new organism. They are a technologically advanced species that possesses interstellar ships, energy beam weapons, fusion power packs, anti-gravity packs, and possibly time travel technology.

"This Is How the World Ends" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author John R. Fultz, first published in the Darrell Schweitzer-edited anthology Cthulhu's Reign (DAW Books, 2010) .

### Synopsis
In a post-apocalyptic world where the human race has been overrun and virtually annihilated by a plague of extra-dimensional monsters, two survivors, one a pregnant woman, take refuge in an isolated cave. On the day she goes into labour, a tiny, winged, tentacle-faced monstrosity claws its way from her womb and utters a single word: "Cthulhu". The man quickly kills the little creature but the damage has already been done, and the woman lies dead.

As the months go by, the man becomes finds himself plagued by thoughts of the dead entity, and the name Cthulhu haunts his dreams nightly. Eventually, unable to locate any trace of other survivors and out of bottled water, he makes the decision to drink the tainted rainwater. This causes his body to metamorphose, changing him into one of the creatures which has infested the Earth and he flies off to join his new family.

### Publication History

*The Book of Cthulhu II (2012, 2022, Night Shade Books)

Thog the Ancient is a fictional entity created by the late American author Robert E. Howard for his 1933 short story "The Slithering Shadow".

### Description
An octopus-like monstrosity of the Hyborian Age, Thog is a man eating abomination which haunts the underground city of Xuthal.

### Background
Thog the Ancient is a Great Old One, residing within the subterranean city of Xuthal. It preyed on the city's Black Lotus addicted dreaming inhabitants whom were slowly being consumed by the hungry entity which roamed its dark corridors. They were also prey to its cosmic lusts, as Conan's companion Natala discovered to her horror. Xuthal's inhabitants whom lived for sensual pleasures, lived in terror of it, and would draw lots to see whom would be thrown to Thog to satisfy its lust and hunger.

### Marvel Comics
In the Marvel Multiverse, Thog the Ancient was seemingly the same (including his encounter with Conan, though it is unknown if he was one of the Great Old Ones, or a Lesser Old One.

He was possibly related to the demons Thog the Nether-Spawn (a Hell-Lord originated from the energies released by the culling of the Elder Gods by the Demogorge) and Thaug (ally of Salome, possibly a Great Old One).

### Behind the Mythos
The name Thog is also mentioned by H. P. Lovecraft in Fungi from Yuggoth, although the context suggests that it refers to a place, as opposed to a being.

Thomas Carnacki is a character created by the late British author William Hope Hodgson for his Carnacki series of detective stories. Other writers, notably William Meikle, have written stories in which he encounters the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Overview
A highly intelligent upper-class Englishman with a deep knowledge of the occult, Thomas Carnacki was active some time in the first quarter of the 20th century (possibly contemporary with the stories' publication in the early 1910s, but equally possibly a decade or so earlier). He is possessed of a deep-seated curiosity, and has been said to never turn down a challenge.

Carnacki has a small circle of friends to which he relates his stories, and it is in this way that each of the tales are presented. His friends are Dodgson, who relates the tale told by Carnacki to the reader, and Jessop, Arkwright and Taylor, who offer little but the occasional interruption, usually in the form of a question.

Carnacki is known to make use use of a number of mystical artefacts, perhaps foremost amongst them the Sigsand Manuscript, an ancient text with much information on the occult. He is also well-versed in certain magical arts, being aware of how to create defensive wards and and utilise mystic incantations. Other devices he employs include the Electric Pentacle, a protective technology of his own creation, and the Saaamaaa Ritual, a rite often used in conjunction with the Electric Pentacle.

### Behind the Mythos
William Hope Hodgson created the character of Thomas Carnacki independently of other works: he was never intended to have lived in the same universe as other literary creations. Since his inception, however, the character has been expanded upon by many other authors, some of whom have introduced Carnacki to other fictional universes, such as the Cthulhu Mythos. Other universes he has crossed over with include Doctor Who, Sherlock Holmes, Solar Pons, and The League of Extraordinary Gentlemen, all of which have crossed over into the greater Cthulhu Mythos at some point in their history.

Although H. P. Lovecraft was a self-confessed fan of Hodgson's work, he believed the Carnacki stories were his weakest efforts, describing the main character as "very weak, artificial and stereotyped".

Thomas Lee is a character created by British horror author Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Inhabitant of the Lake".

### Overview
Born some time before 1865, Thomas Lee was a Brichester resident who, as an adult, became a servant of the Great Old One Glaaki, and the leader of his cult. In this capacity Lee commissioned a row of houses, later known as Lakeside Terrace, in a remote part of the Severn Valley next to the body of water in which his master dwells. He and his fellow cult members were responsible for transcribing the volumes known as the Revelations of Glaaki. 

Having succumbed to the Green Decay, Lee is no longer able to tolerate the touch of sunlight, and now appears to spend his days inside one of the many stone sarcophagi which dot the landscape surrounding Lakeside Terrace.

fullContent:
Thomas Ligotti (born July 9, 1953) is a contemporary American horror writer. His writing has been predominantly in the genre of weird horror fiction influenced by gothic horror. His influences in the horror genre, according to his own description, include Ambrose Bierce, Arthur Machen, H. P. Lovecraft and Edgar Allan Poe, among others.

Ligotti is a sufferer from chronic anxiety as well as the condition known as anhedonia, a reduced or absent ability to experience pleasure of any kind. His Anhedonia has led to various problems including lack of motivation, depression and social anxiety.

Ligotti has written several Mythos stories, as well as poetry, and has also provided some quotes related to his nihilistic, atheistic and socialist beliefs.

### True Detective
"In 2014, the HBO television series True Detective attracted attention from some of Ligotti's fans because of the striking resemblance between the pessimistic, antinatalist philosophy espoused in the first few episodes by the character of Rust Cohle (played by Matthew McConaughey) and Ligotti's own philosophical pessimism and antinatalism, especially as expressed in The Conspiracy Against the Human Race. After accusations that dialogue from Cohle's character in True Detective were lifted from The Conspiracy Against the Human Race, the series' writer, Nic Pizzolatto, confirmed in The Wall Street Journal that Ligotti, along with several other writers and texts in the weird supernatural horror genre, had indeed influenced him."

-Writer Nic Pizzolatto on Thomas Ligotti and the Weird Secrets of 'True Detective'

Thomas F. Malone is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Horror at Red Hook".

### Background
Thomas F. Malone is an Irish-born New York police detective, "detailed to the Butler Street station in Brooklyn" before going on indefinite medical leave. A "Dublin University man born in a Georgian villa near Phoenix Park," he is said to have "the Celt's far vision of weird and hidden things, but the logician's quick eye for the outwardly unconvincing.... In youth he had felt the hidden beauty and ecstasy of things, and had been a poet; but poverty and sorrow and exile had turned his gaze in darker directions, and he had thrilled at the imputations of evil in the world around." This morbid streak is offset by a "keen logic and a deep sense of humour". 

At the age of 42, he investigates mysterious disappearances in the Red Hook neighbourhood of Brooklyn. At one point he questions the elderly recluse Robert Suydam, whom he suspects of skullduggery. His exploration of the catacombs below Red Hook leave him psychologically devastated. (: "The Horror at Red Hook")

Thomas Malone is one of the investigators sent by J. Edgar Hoover to investigate a series of bombing alongside Bureau of Investigation agent Miranda Keller (: Miskatonic). 

Thomas Malone is available as an Ally in the Second Edition of Arkham Horror.

Thomas Olney is a fictional character who appears in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Strange High House in the Mist". He represents the observation that "humdrum lives breed wistful longings of the unknown".

Lovecraft describes Olney as a "philosopher" who "taught ponderous things in a college by Narragansett Bay". He comes to spend a summer in Kingsport, and because "his eyes were weary with seeing the same things for many years, and thinking the same well-disciplined thoughts", he becomes captivated by the titular house on the crag overlooking the town. He gathers legends about the house from the Terrible Old Man and Granny Orne, two of Kingsport's oldest residents.

As he is "avid for new strange things", he resolves to visit the house--which is almost unreachable, but just barely possible from the landward side. There he meet the "nameless hermit" who lives there, the One, who introduces him to Elder Gods like Nodens and Neptune. 

Olney returns from the house "with the look of far places in his eyes", but the Terrible Old Man vows:

Indeed, he seems to have left something vital up in the house, for 
Olney never returns to Kingsport after that summer, instead spending his vacations in the prosaic Bristol Highlands, Rhode Island. But ever since Olney's visit to the Strange High House, "old folk tell of pleasing voices heard singing there, and of laughter that swells with joys beyond earth’s joys; and say that at evening the little low windows are brighter than formerly."

Thomas Slauenwite, M.D., is a fictional character from the horror short story "Winged Death", by H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald. A vengeful and callous physician who sees his murderous actions as justified, he is an example of an amoral narrator-protagonist, similar to Lt. Cmdr. Karl Heinrich from "The Temple" and the necrophiliac mortician from "The Loved Dead".

### Biography
Thomas Slauenwite was born on April 12, 1885, in Trenton, New Jersey. His father, Dr. Paul Slauenwite, was a South African physician from Pretoria, Transvaal, who died in 1916. At the time, Thomas was fighting in World War One in France as part of a South African regiment. Following his father's footsteps, he studied medicine at Columbia University and became an expert in African fevers. One of his classmates was the future biologist Henry Sargent Moore, who befriended Slauenwite and studied with him in both America and Africa, eventually becoming one of the world's most respected authorities on African flies and other dipterans. Meanwhile, Slauenwite's own research took him from Durban, Natal, to Mombasa, where he lived in the same house that had been formerly occupied by the late physician Sir Norman Sloane.

Slauenwite found Sir Norman's papers in the house and, after reading them, published a revolutionary theory about the transmission and development of remittent fever, which made him famous among his peers. He was promised a high position in the South African health service and a probable knighthood if he were to resign his American citizenship, which he agreed to. Unfortunately for him, it was at this point that his promising career was ruined by Moore, who had corresponded with Sir Norman. Moore accused Slauenwite of plagiarism and produced letters that proved that Slauenwite's theory was actually Sir Norman's.

Slauenwite was furious at what he perceived as a betrayal, claiming that he helped to propel Moore's career, and referring to Moore's accusations as "absurd". With the "half-promised appointment and knighthood" withheld and his reputation tainted (especially among those colleagues who had known Sir Norman in person), Slauenwite left Mombasa and found work as a general clinician at the small trading post of M'gonga, close to the Ugandan border. He resolved that someday he would find a way to kill Moore.

In January 1929, Slauenwite treated a hunter named Mevana, who had been bitten by a devil-fly in the Ugandan jungle. Slauenwite learned about the legend that if a man dies after being bitten by a devil-fly, his mind and memories will move into the body of the insect. While he dismissed this as superstition, he was interested in the flies' infectiousness and started to plan out how he could murder Moore. fullContent:
"Those Folk Below" is a short Mythos story by Josh Reynolds, and forms part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by C. J. Henderson.

### Synopsis
The Arkham Detective Agency is working security for an auction at Miskatonic University where the prized piece is a grimoire of ancient knowledge. As the proceedings come to a close, a pack of ghouls attack the attendees and steal the book. Frank Nardi, assisted by an aristocrat with knowledge of the occult, must descend into the tunnels beneath the city in order to retrieve it.

### Characters

*Frank Nardi, a former New York cop and co-founder of the Arkham Detective Agency.
*Count Anton Sforza, a Venetian aristocrat.
*Indrid Cold, a figure from real-world pop culture, often associated with conspiracies involving government collaboration with aliens.
*Mark Berkenwald, another Arkham Detective Agency operative.
*Madam Amina Bera, the head of a brood of inhuman ghouls.
*Harold Clemmens, president of Miskatonic University.

### Publication History
"Those Folk Below" was written for inclusion in the collection Arkham Detective Agency at the request of editor Brian M. Sammons for submissions. It was published in both print and ebook format in November 2017.

### Mythos Connections

*The book being auctioned was a rare 1839 Düsseldorf edition of the Unaussprechlichen Kulten.
*Ghouls were originally created by H. P. Lovecraft himself, although these appear to have been a lesser or hybrid breed, as they are able to pass themselves of as normal humans. It is worth noting that Richard Upton Pickman from "Pickman's Model" eventually becomes a full Ghoul, so at some point he may have been still able to pass for a human even though he had become a Ghoul.
*A large portion of the story is set in Arkham's Miskatonic University.

fullContent:
Those of the Air is a short story by American author and literary critic Darrell Schweitzer in collaboration with artist and author Jason Van Hollander which is set in H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
The story takes place on the day an estranged son returns to his family ten years after leaving. As he reminisces about his childhood, it is revealed that the family are descended from the Whateleys of Dunwich, and that the curse of that lineage has followed then down the years along with a copy of the Necronomicon. It is further revealed that since a young age, the boy's older brother has been kept locked in the attic, as he has been slowly mutating into a creature resembling the Dunwich Horror. 

The story concludes with the father giving himself as a living blood sacrifice to the transformed son, before the entities known as Those of the Air come to take him away.

### Characters
*Jerry, the youngest child who became disgusted with his family and left for ten years, only returning when his brother's time to ascend came about. He finished the story as a guardian of a copy of the Necronomicon written in an unspecified language which he could not speak.
*Jeffrey, the older sibling, who was mutated beyond recognition - he was possessed of foot-long tusks and additional limbs amongst other things - by the family curse. Jerry described him as being a playful, happy soul, despite his misfortune.
*Pappa, the children's father, and former guardian of the family curse and the Necronomicon.

### Behind the Mythos
Those of the Air was first published in the Mythos anthology Cthulhu's Heirs (Chaosium, 1994), and was subsequently included in the Wildside Press eBook collection The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack in 2012.

shortDefinition: "Those Who Seek" is a short story by the late American author August Derleth.  ### Synopsis The son of a rich landowner, a man named Arnsley, commissions artist Jason Phillips to paint an ancient ruined chapel which lies on his land and which he has ...
fullContent:
"Those Who Seek" is a short story by the late American author August Derleth.

### Synopsis
The son of a rich landowner, a man named Arnsley, commissions artist Jason Phillips to paint an ancient ruined chapel which lies on his land and which he has developed a fascination for. The two spend the night on location in order to complete the painting, and during the night Arnsley disappears. Whilst searching for his companion, Phillips discovers an open portal in the abbey and, looking into it is driven into a delirium. 

While in the hospital, Arnsley's body is discovered in a hidden room within the abbey, horribly mutilated. The police record an open verdict on the case.

After his discharge two months later, Phillips tracks down a priest with an interest in the history of places such as the abbey. The priest tells him that it used to be used as a place of worship by a cult devoted to an entity known as the "God of Blood", and that a tunnel beneath the abbey connected it to the ocean. This implies that some ancient and terrible creature travelled from the sea, murdered Arnsley, then returned.

### Characters
* Jason Phillips, an accomplished artist in the employ of Arnsley's rich father.
* Arnsley, the son of a lord, and a man with too much time on his hands.
* Father Richards, a local scholar.

### Publication History
"Those Who Seek" was first published in pulp magazine Weird Tales in January 1932, and has seen inclusion in a number of collections since.

### Trivia
* Despite containing no obvious connections, "Those Who Seek" is widely considered to be a part of the Cthulhu Mythos. This is likely due to the description of the God of Blood (like a huge black-green jelly, and seems equipped with minute suckers and tentacles, much like an octopus. It resembles a sea creature very much, giving off a blue-gray light, and flaring a bright green from its eyes) and the injuries inflicted on Arnsley being typical of the depiction of Mythos entities across the years.

"Thought He Was a Goner" is a short story by Christine Morgan that first appeared in the Herbert West-themed anthology Legacy of the Reanimator (Chaosium, 2015).

### Synopsis
The story is a scene from West's childhood, as the future mad scientist accidentally reanimates his first corpse, a freshly deceased schoolyard bully.

### Behind the Mythos
Anthology co-editor Peter Rawlik describes it as "a rather touching tale of schoolyard life (and death) that shows us how West may have got his start."

The title is a line from the song "The Cat Came Back," about a man whose cat keeps coming back despite all his attempts to get rid of it.

### Characters
*Herbie West: A quiet, studious schoolboy who hopes for early admission to the medical school of Miskatonic University; he "prefer[s] to be addressed as Herbert." His parents having recently died, he has come to live with his aunts Gertrude and Ludmilla.He "wasn’t a tall boy.,,thin, and quite pale, with fine hair the color of buttermilk. His eyes, behind spectacles, were a very light blue." He is seen as "polite and soft-spoken," though he is described by a teacher as “sharp as a tack, smart as a whip, cleverest student I’ve ever had … but insolent."

* Sarah Grantham: A classmate who has a crush on Herbie. She has "curls...as black and shiny and glossy as fresh ink."

* Sebastian Crewe: A schoolyard bully who fancies Sarah. His accidental death leads to West's first success with partial reanimation--accomplished with a pencil inserted into his brain.

The Thralls of Cthulhu are mutated cultists created by Brian Lumley for his short story "The Fairground Horror" and later expanded upon by Chaosium for their Call of Cthulhu horror role-playing game. 

### Description
The Thralls of Cthulhu are worshippers of the Great Old One Cthulhu that have been mutated into bloated grey-skinned forms through a ritual.

### Behind the Mythos
The Thralls were first incorporated into Call of Cthulhu by Doug Lyons in the 1989 supplement The Great Old Ones .

Threshold is a novel by Caitlin R. Kiernan, published in 2001, part of their Deep Time series. It introduces characters whose stories continue in Low Red Moon (2003) and Alabaster (2006). 

It won the 2001 International Horror Guild award for best novel. 

### Characters
* Chance Matthews: A 23-year-old paleontologist from Birmingham, Alabama. Her life has fallen apart since her then-lover Deacon Silvey and her best friend Elise Alden on a lark broke into the Birmingham Water Works tunnel on Red Mountain above the city.
* Deacon Silvey: A psychic who has become an alcoholic by self-medicating against the "crippling headaches" that come with his powers. He "dropp[ed] out of Emory halfway through an undergraduate degree in philosophy." He works "convenience store jobs, liquor store jobs, anything to pay the rent and enough left over to stay drunk whenever he needed to stay drunk." After dating Chance for three years, they broke up after Deacon slept with Elise after whatever happened inside the waterworks tunnel. He's now seeing Sadie Jasper.
* Dancy Flammarion: A 16-year-old albino girl from Florida who believes that angels instruct her to kill monsters. She escaped from the state mental hospital in Tallahassee. She comes to Birmingham to enlist Chance, Deacon, and Sadie's help to stop something that was released in the Red Mountain tunnel.
* Elise Alden: A friend of Chance's, she kills herself after being traumatized in the waterworks tunnel and blaming herself for the end of Chance and Deacon's relationship.
* Sadie Jasper: An aspiring writer and Deacon's lover. Known for her "callous goth-girl shtick." She has "coalblack hair"; her eyes are "heavy-lidded and her pale, blue irises surrounded by all that smudged eyeliner."
* Dr. Alice K. Sprinkle: An older paleontologist on Chance's thesis committee. She "has hands like a bricklayer."
* Soda: A friend of Deacon's who loans him a beat-up car.

fullContent:
"Through Obscure Glass" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Jeffrey Thomas, set in W. H. Pugmire's fictional Sesqua Valley locale. It was first published in the chapbook collection Avatars of the Old Ones by Imelod Publications in 1999.

### Synopsis
After the collapse of her new relationship, Judith seeks out her ex-husband Robert in a desperate attempt to rekindle their relationship. Robert, who has returned to his family home in the Pacific Northwest's Sesqua Valley, has taken up a mantle of guardianship which has been the responsibility of his bloodline for generations, a fact of which Judith is unaware.

Upon reaching her destination, Judith's attempts at reconciliation are rebuffed, although Robert allows her to spend the evening before she must leave. During the night, Judith hears strange noises coming from the basement and, upon investigating, discovers an enormous lens which offers viewers a look into the Dreamlands. Unfortunately, her observations attract the attentions of a tribe of Gugs, one of which passes through the portal in search of her. Although Robert is able to return the creature to its own plane and close the gateway, he is mortally wounded during the encounter; as the last of his line, there is now nobody left to protect the Dream Lens.

The following morning, Judith resolves to take up guardianship of the portal as both penance and tribute to her late lover.

### Publication History
*Avatars of the Old Ones (1999)
*Terror Incognita (2000)
*Unholy Dimensions (2005)
*Geschichten aus dem Cthulhu-Mythos (2012, German-language translation)

### Trivia
*Robert's family surname, Fuseli, and his being described as an unrecognised artist would appear to be a nod to Swiss painter Henry Fuseli, many of whose works involved supernatural elements and whom H. P. Lovecraft mentioned in at least two of his short stories.

term: Through the Gates of the Silver Key
shortDefinition: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" is a short story co-written by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price between October 1932 and April 1933. A sequel to Lovecraft's "The Silver Key", and part of a sequence of stories focusing on Randolph Carter, i...
fullContent:
"Through the Gates of the Silver Key" is a short story co-written by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price between October 1932 and April 1933. A sequel to Lovecraft's "The Silver Key", and part of a sequence of stories focusing on Randolph Carter, it was first published in the July 1934 issue of Weird Tales. Price's first draft of the story, titled "The Lord of Illusion", has also been published in the anthology Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos.

### Inspiration
The story has its origins in Price's enthusiasm for an earlier Lovecraft tale. "One of my favorite HPL stories was, and still is, 'The Silver Key'," Price wrote in a 1944 memoir. "In telling him of the pleasure I had had in rereading it, I suggested a sequel to account for [protagonist] Randolph Carter's doings after his disappearance." 

After convincing an apparently reluctant Lovecraft to agree to collaborate on such a sequel, Price wrote a 6,000-word draft in August 1932; in April 1933, Lovecraft produced a 14,000-word version that left unchanged, by Price's estimate, "fewer than fifty of my original words," though An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia reports that Lovecraft "kept as many of Price's conceptions as possible, as well as some of his language." 

Thus, many of the central ideas of the story like 'Umr at-Tawil, the talk of mathematical planes, and multiple facets of Randolph Carter throughout Time and Space, came from Price, who was well-read in neoplatonic thought, theosophy, and the occult. Even the quote from the Necronomicon is mainly by Price in outline, though put in more Lovecraftian language. (: An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia) The sub-plot about Yaddith was entirely Lovecraft's idea, however.

In any case, Price was pleased with the result, writing that Lovecraft "was right of course in discarding all but the basic outline. I could only marvel that he had made so much of my inadequate and bungling start." The story appeared under both authors' bylines in the July 1934 issue of Weird Tales; Price's draft was published as "The Lord of Illusion" in Crypt of Cthulhu No. 10 in 1982.

### Synopsis
At a gathering to decide the fate of Randolph Carter's estate, which has been held in trust since his disappearance, the mysterious Swami Chandraputra, who wears curious mittens and enveloping robes, tells Carter's acquaintances of his ultimate fate. He explains that the key took Carter to a type of higher dimension. There, Carter, on an ill-defined mission (or out of sheer curiosity), travelled strange sections of the cosmos by first meeting with 'Umr at-Tawil, a dangerous being warned of in the Necronomicon, saying that those who deal with it never return. 

'Umr at-Tawil offers Carter a chance to plunge deeper into the cosmos; Carter thus perceives the true nature of the universe before passing through the "Ultimate Gate." shortDefinition: Thule is a legendary land described in Classical Greek literature as being to the far north of Europe. The name was applied to ancient lands in the fiction of Lovecraft Circle writers Robert E. Howard and Clark Ashton Smith, and its role in the Cthul...
fullContent:
Thule is a legendary land described in Classical Greek literature as being to the far north of Europe. The name was applied to ancient lands in the fiction of Lovecraft Circle writers Robert E. Howard and Clark Ashton Smith, and its role in the Cthulhu Mythos was systematised in the tales of Lin Carter.

### In Classical Literature
Thule was first mentioned by Pytheas, the first documented representative of the Mediterranean world to visit the British Isles. Pytheas' writings do not survive, but he is cited by Strabo as describing Thoulē as an island six days' sail from Britain, near the frozen sea.

The Roman poet Virgil refers in his Georgics to Ultima Thule--"farthest Thule"--which became an expression for any place beyond the known world.

### Clark Ashton Smith
In Smith's "The Double Shadow," a short story published in 1933 and set in the Atlantean remnant of Poseidonis, the narrator Pharpetron wishes that his master, the sorceror Avyctes, "had contented himself with the lore preserved from Atlantis and Thule, or brought over from Mu and Mayapan." He notes that "this should have been enough: for in the ivory-sheeted books of Thule there were blood-writ runes that would call the demons of the fifth and seventh planets, if spoken aloud at the hour of their ascent."

In Smith's "Ubbo-Sathla" (1933), the protagonist Paul Tregardis is told that a crystal offered for sale, found by a geologist in Greenland, "may have belonged to some sorcerer of primeval Thule." Tregardis, a student of The Book of Eibon, links Thule to "Mhu Thulan, that northern  portion of ancient Hyperborea, [that] was supposed to have corresponded roughly with  Modern Greenland."

Mhu Thulan is mentioned in Smith's Hyperborean stories, including "The Coming of the White Worm" and "The Door to Saturn."

### Robert E. Howard
Howard set his Kull stories in the Thurian Age,  the pre-Cataclysmic period that preceded the Hyborian Age familiar from Conan. In the map of the continent of Thuria, Thule is the northernmost peninsula, in the approximate location of Scandinavia on the Eurasian continent. It is to the north of Valusia and west of Commoria.

### Fictional History
Originally the prehuman civilisation of Ultima Thule was inhabited by the pre-human ancestors and the Voormi, before being colonised by survivors from Zobna. Thule was overwhelmed by the same ice-sheet which destroyed Hyperborea. Survivors from Thule founded an new colony in the northern part of the Thurian Continent until the ice-sheet retreated, when some of them returned to the island.

Thurber (first name unknown) is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Pickman's Model", making his first appearance in print in the October 1927 edition of Weird Tales.

### Description
Thurber is the narrator of "Pickman's Model", who gets to know Richard Upton Pickman while working on "a monograph about weird art"; he describes himself as "fairly 'hard-boiled'", as well as "middle-aged and decently sophisticated". He is apparently a World War I veteran: "I guess you saw enough of me in France to know I'm not easily knocked out." (: "Pickman's Model")

### History

### In Lovecraft's Works
A friend of Pickman's, Thurber was invited to a tour of his gallery, during the course of which he bore witness to Pickman's fate and discovered the truth behind his inspiration (: "Pickman's Model").

### In Other Works

### Casefile: Arkham- Nightmare on the Canvas
In a slightly altered timeline, Thurber is one of the people interviewed by private detective Hank Flynn during his search for the missing Pickman. Thurber is by this point a wreck of a man, driven to the bottle by what he has learned.

### Behind the Mythos
Given Thurber's self-description, An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia finds his horror at Pickman's paintings "implausible...strained and hysterical". This can be accepted as a valid critique to an extent but it is worth remembering that Lovecraft's cosmic horror approach was always to vault into the extreme. On that basis, a battle-hardened man still being brought to the edge of madness emphasizes the nature of what confronts people in this short story. It is meant to be at the edge of sanity and natural experience. Referring to the horrors of trench warfare and the charnel house of World War I is also a means to evoke horror by comparison and implication, another strong suit in Lovecraft's writing.

Thurber is one of several Lovecraft characters to develop a phobia as a result of his horrific experiences; (Lovecraft Remembered) his fear of subways and other underground spaces resembles that of the narrator of "The Lurking Fear", who "cannot see a well or a subway entrance without shuddering".

Thuria is a fictional supercontinent created by Robert E. Howard. It first appeared in "The Shadow Kingdom" (Weird Tales in August, 1929), the first of his King Kull stories and, according to Lin Carter, both one of the first three stories contributing to the Cthulhu Mythos and written by others than H. P. Lovecraft, and the very first story of the sword and sorcery genre.

It is the setting for the his King Kull stories and the background history for the Hyborian Age of his more widely successful Conan the Barbarian stories.

It likewise featured in the King Kull line of comics published by Marvel Comics and Dark Horse Comics, and in the Conan: Adventures in an Age Undreamed Of roleplaying game of Modiphius Entertainment, the Mythos is involved in its history.

### History of the Thurian Age
### The pre-Thurian Age
Tens of thousands of years ago, elder monstrous races ruled the land. In what would later become the land of Valusia, the Serpent Folk established an empire.  The elder races were overthrown and for the most part exterminated, circa 100,000 BC, by the rising race of man, who would go on to establish their own kingdoms. This marked the beginning of the Thurian Age.

### Thurian Age
Over 20,000 years ago, on the Thurian super continent were seven great empires dominated most of the continent, of which the western empire of Valusia was the greatest. To the west of them was the small continent of Atlantis, and to the west of the Atlanteans were the Pictish Islands. On the eastern shore of the Thurian supercontinent was a human empire ruled by non-Thurians, a people who came from a continent far to the east across the sea. East of that empire were the large islands of Lemuria. South of the Thurian continent was a mysterious human civilization.

From the island continent of Atlantis, a barbarian who would start out as a pirate and then become a mercenary within the Valusian army would seize the decadent throne of Valusia. His name was known as Kull the Conqueror, and he not only revitalized the Valusian kingdom but crushed the last remnants of the Serpent Folk in those lands and it was thought he wiped them out.

### Great Cataclysm
Circa 20,000 BC, a great cataclysm devastated the world. Atlantis and Lemuria sunk beneath the waves. Parts of the Thurian supercontinent sunk or vanished under the waves, forming great inland seas and lakes. The Pictish islands were thrust up forming the mountains of a new continent. Cities were toppled and nations wiped out by earthquakes, volcanoes, and flooding.

### Post-Cataclysm
On the Thurian coast was an Atlantean colony to which surviving Atlantean refugees fled to in their ships. A great colony of Picts had survived untouched on Valusia's south. Many Lemurians made it to the eastern Thurian shores only to be enslaved by the non-Thurian empire and kept in servitude for 1000s of years. The Thuum'ha were - or possibly are - natives of the land Mnar, seemingly amphibious humanoids who share numerous physical characteristics with Deep Ones and those that have the hybridised Innsmouth look. Though their exact location is not specified they are stated to be as far from the waking lands as they are from the Dreamlands making it is difficult to determine whether they are near other known Deep One cities.

The Thuum'ha - a name apparently given them by the people of Sarnath, and which means no more than 'the Voiceless' - venerated a statue of the great water lizard Bokrug.

However, it is possible that Ibians are merely the name the Deep Ones are given in the Polaris Era, circa 24,000 B.C.

They seem far more docile than Deep Ones of Earth, in any case, being easily overcome by the human people of Sarnath, who routed them to the point of extermination. They are described as "weak, and soft as jelly to the touch of stones and spears and arrows".

According to Chaosium, who included the Beings of Ib in their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement Ye Booke of Monstres II, they survive to this day on the moon, as only a fraction of their species descended to Earth in prehistory. 

### Ib
Ib was a Thuum'ha settlement by the banks of a giant lake. It was claimed that the ancient stone city had been there as long as had the lake itself. Around ten thousand years ago the city was destroyed and the Thuum'ha driven out by the humans of Sarnath, who found their existence unacceptable.

Tiamat (aka, Beast II and Titan) is a Lovecraftian-like cosmic entity from the fictional universe of the Fate/Grand Order mobile game.

### Background
Tiamat is the Goddess of Chaos, who randomly designed life. She is the sea of life, circulating the True Ether of Genesis. An entity who enjoys being the mother of all, full of joy and love her children. She is also filled with hatred due to being abandoned by her children who turned on her and destroyed, exiled, or imprisoned the goddess. Millennia later she was awakened from her deep slumber by the collapse of the Human Order Foundation, the Grail's power, and Chaldea's attack. She returned to Earth to exterminate humanity and be reunited with her children.

She is a being who doesn't speak any human language, her voice sounding like a sound which can only be understood by her children. She has various abilities including being able to transform, alter her size, possess others, remaking other organisms into its minions, a barrier which subverts the theory of evolution, and monstrous strength. 

### Behind the Mythos
The name of Tiamat is taken from the Mesopotamian pantheon. She was believed to be a divine creatrix and primordial goddess of the sea. With her mate Apsu (also spelled Abzu), the god of groundwater, she created the younger gods. Tiamat was seen as the monstrous embodiment of the chaos of primordial creation. She is also referenced in the Judeo-Christian Bible, and a version of her depicted as a dragon goddess appears in Dungeons & Dragons.

fullContent:
Tiamat is a Lovecraftian-like entity in the fictional universe of the Ghostbusters comic by IDW Publishing.

### Background
Tiamat is a Sumerian goddess who is the embodiment of chaos and the ruler of her own dimension. Sister and rival of Gozer the Destructor, whom she surpasses in power. Over the millennia her power has been growing as she spread chaos across the multiverse. During the 4th millennium BC, her worshipers were engaged in a protracted war with Gozer's disciples, the Gozerians. A conflict which ended in victory for her followers and Gozer's banishment from Earth by Tiamat. She has recently taken an interest in Earth because of the Ghostbusters defeating her brother Gozer and ripping holes in the universes' fabric upon escaping from the Collectors' Limbo. Filled with curiosity she decided to go to Earth to play and toy with them.

She has a variety of powers including those of necromancy, warping reality, invading and influencing dreams, shapeshifting, illusions, speaking to the dead, extracting souls from other beings, manifesting on the moon's face and on mirrored surfaces, create inter-dimensional portals, remotely observe other dimensions, becoming intangible, and erasing the memories of a world's entire population.  Her presence alone can disrupt the fabric of an environment and disrupt it's rules of science. Among the forms she has taken are that of a multi-headed dragon and an attractive human female.

Tiania is a character created by Brian Lumley as part of his Titus Crow series of Cthulhu Mythos novels.

### Description
Tiania is a beautiful young woman who appears to be human. She resides in a floating palace in the other-dimensional realm of Elysia, and is the ward of the Elder God known as Kthanid.

### History
How Tiania came to be under the guardianship of Kthanid is unclear, but she has apparently lived her entire life in his care.

### The Transition of Titus Crow ()
During the events of the novel, Tiania guides Titus Crow, who has become lost in time and space, to Elysia. During his stay there, the two fall in love and begin a relationship, while Tiania shows him the wonders of her world.

### The Clock of Dreams ()
Accompanying Titus Crow and his companion Henri-Laurent de Marigny on a mission to investigate strange occurrences in the Earth's Dreamlands, Tiania is abducted by a Nightgaunt and held captive by a servant of the Cthulhu Mythos Deities known as the Keeper of the Cage. Despite this, she escapes with the aid of Crow and de Marigny, and the three rid the Dreamlands of the blight which plagues it.

fullContent:
"Tick Tock" is a Lovecraftian short story by prolific American author Don Webb.

### Synopsis
A conspiracy theory blogger decides to conduct a small experiment on the nature of reality. Unfortunately, his radical idea has drastic consequences and tears a small hole in space-time, allowing the first wave of ancient beings from beyond to pour through.

### Characters
*John Cardenas, a cynical man who one night receives a revelation on the workings of reality.
*Don Bowen, Cardenas's friend, a second-hand book dealer.

### Publication History
"Tick Tock" was published in the Brian M. Sammons-edited thematic anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror in 2017.

### Trivia
*Amongst the books noted to be held in stock by Bowen are works by H. P. Lovecraft, Ramsey Campbell and Stephen King.

The Tick-Tock Man is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Scott David Aniolowski for his short story "I Dream of Wires".

The entity was later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, depicted as being an avatar of Nyarlathotep. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Overview
The Tick-Tock Man takes the form of an artificial intelligence, with its true form being that of a machine; however, the entity can also create a humanoid form that usually appears as a black man with some mechanical body parts. It should be noted that the humanoid form cannot exist without the machine.

In order to manifest, the Tick-Tock Man will use some other beings to build a suitable machine to inhabit, usually either by sending inspirational dreams to its chosen builder or providing an adequate design. The entity can also take control of other machines against the original creator's will. The Tick-Tock Man can offer advanced calculations for weapons or other unsafe advanced technology. Due to it being an avatar of Nyarlathotep, the Tick-Tock Man is dedicated to spreading chaos, madness and destruction.

The avatar's actual size, construction and appearance varies depending on the time and place, including manifesting as an enormous steam-powered engine in the Victorian London, a high-tech computer in modern Tokyo, or an unimaginable machine in an alien world. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

At the Brichester University, the Tick-Tock Man manifested in the Dughall Computer Lab, run by a balding man and his female assistant. The lab contains numerous unconscious victims with their wrists and foreheads strapped to a metal table, and wires attached to their heads and chests like a hospital patient. The victims are surrounded by numerous monitors, keyboards and cables, with the wires attached to them plugging into the Tick-Tock Man's computer. Amongst the victims was a student named Christian Barnett, who had the Tick-Tock Man inside his mind, creating a whole world in his subconscious. (: "I Dream of Wires")

### In Other Media
*In the novel series The Dark Tower, written by Stephen King, the character Andrew Quick is nicknamed as the "Tick-Tock Man".
*In the anime series Haiyore! Nyaruko-san, the Tick-Tock Man is one of the many avatars of Nyarlathotep documented in the Great Library of Celaeno.

"Tidal Forces"  is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that originally appeared in the June 2011 issue of Sirenia Digest (#55).

### Synopsis
"Tidal Forces" is the story of a woman who, after being struck by a mysterious shadow, develops a growing hole in her abdomen--a hole that seems to be a portal to Azathoth.

### Publication History
The story was republished in the anthology Eclipse Four: New Science Fiction and Fantasy (Night Shade Books, 2011), and in The Best Science Fiction and Fantasy of the Year Volume Six (Night Shade Books, 2012). It also appeared in Kiernan's collections The Ape's Wife and Other Stories (Subterranean Press, 2013), Beneath an Oil-Dark Sea: The Best of Caitlín R. Kiernan (Volume Two) (Subterranean Press, 2015),  Houses Under the Sea: Mythos Tales (Subterranean Press, 2018), and The Very Best of Caitlín R. Kiernan (Tachyon Publications, 2019).

shortDefinition: "Till A' the Seas" is a short story by American horror fiction authors H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow, written in January, 1935 and published in Summer 1935 in The Californian.  ### Plot The story consists of two parts. The first describes the even...
fullContent:
"Till A' the Seas" is a short story by American horror fiction authors H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow, written in January, 1935 and published in Summer 1935 in The Californian.

### Plot
The story consists of two parts. The first describes the events which took place on Earth from a few thousand years after present to few millions years. The climate on Earth is getting warmer and warmer, oceans are slowly disappearing. People are gradually moving towards poles, becoming more and more barbaric. Mankind is steadily dying out because of the lack of water, until there is only a few decades left.

The second part starts in a small village in the desert. There is only one man left in the village: young Ull. A very old woman, the only company for the man, died just before. So, Ull starts a journey in search of other people, and he seems to know from old legends about the place. In a few days, extremely thirsty and tired, he finds a small settlement. Ull enters one of the houses and finds nothing, but a dried-up old skeleton. Depressed, he starts searching for water and finds a well with a little water in it. Trying to reach the string to pull up a dip-bucket, he falls into the well and dies. And after the death of the last man, mankind totally has vanished. A farce, named "evolution", faces a natural conclusion.

Tim Lebbon (born 28 July 1969) is a prolific British author whose work focuses on the horror, science fiction and fantasy genres. He has won several awards for his fiction, including the Bram Stoker Award for Short Fiction and the August Derleth Award, and is a New York Times bestselling author. His Lovecraftian fiction has appeared in anthologies such as The Children of Cthulhu, Shadows Over Baker Street, and Innsmouth Nightmares.

Many of Lebbon's works are franchise tie-in pieces; he has written for properties including The X-Files, Aliens, Firefly, Hellboy, Predator, Star Wars, King Kong, and 30 Days of Night.

Lebbon has also cited Arthur Machen - whose works had a major effect on those of H. P. Lovecraft - as one of his personal influences.

Tim Mendees is a British author, editor, podcaster, and DJ who specialises is weird fiction and cosmic horror. His short fiction has appeared in zines including Lovecraftiana - where his short story "The Dappled Egg" was voted by the fanbase for inclusion in a Best of… anthology - and collections such as Occult Detective Magazine Mythos Special; he also co-hosts two podcasts which specialise in the weird fiction genre. In addition to these accomplishments, he is the co-founder of the Innsmouth Literary Festival, a "one day festival celebrating weird and cosmic fiction."

Mendees has cited Algernon Blackwood, William Hope Hodgson, Ramsey Campbell, and Stephen King as among his literary influences.

Writing primarily in the science fiction, fantasy and horror genres, Tim Waggoner's output has included tie-in novels and stories for many major film, literary, and gaming franchises such as Conan and Dungeons & Dragons, as well as a number of Cthulhu Mythos works. fullContent:
"Time Flies" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Pete Rawlik.

### Synopsis
A mass migration of Yithians to Earth brings with it a wealth of new scientific knowledge, although it does not go unnoticed by the authorities - who are well aware of the nature of these aliens - that this time they have chosen to inhabit the bodies of the recently deceased.

After a series of catastrophic events signalling the return of the Old Ones and the downfall of humankind, the Yithians reveal that they are simply there as tourists, wishing to have a front-row seat to such an important event. Furthermore, they reveal that once they leave their bodies, a consequence of the process acting upon deceased brains will turn them into ravenous, highly-infectious zombies, although they have made preparations for a select group to survive in pre-prepared defensible locations, allowing the continuance of the human race after a fashion.

### Characters
*Pandora Peaslee, a former CIA agent working for the Yithians.
*Mister Ys, Pandora's Yithian assignment.
*Miss Trey, another Yithian.

### Publication History
"Time Flies" was published in the thematic anthology Return of the Old Ones: Apocalyptic Lovecraftian Horror by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Trivia
*The names taken by the Yithians appear to be plays on the word 'mystery'.
*The main character's surname, Peaslee, is shared with two of the characters from H. P. Lovecraft's short story "The Shadow Out of Time".

Running to a total of 303 pages, it was published in July 2020 by Mystique Press; both paperback and digital editions were released. It was updated and re-released with new content in July 2023. It is part of the Books of Cthulhu series.

Time Lords are a fictional alien species featured in the Doctor Who franchise. Hailing from the planet Gallifrey, they are notable for their time-traveling technology, psychic abilities, natural awareness of timelines and temporal phenomena, and regenerative capacity. They are one of the most advanced races in the Doctor Who universe.

Even the Great Old Ones fear the Time Lords, considering them a potential threat. (: White Darkness)

The Shobogans are a Time Lord faction that once formed a cult to venerate the Great Old Ones. The Doctor has described the Shobogans as "New Age Time Lord drop-outs". (: All-Consuming Fire)

### Behind the Mythos
While the Doctor and his granddaughter Susan were established as coming from another planet in the first episode of Doctor Who (1963), it was only in 1969 that the term "Time Lord" was first used and their homeworld first depicted, in the serial The War Games.

Tina (last name unrevealed, possibly Cecil) is a character created by American author Armand Rosamilia for his Keyport Cthulhu series of Mythos tales.

### Description
A somewhat plain-looking girl in her late teens, Tina is ever so slightly overweight, although given her age this may simply be puppy fat. She is devoutly religious as a result of her upbringing as the daughter of a Catholic minister.

### History

### Keyport Cthulhu
In the first book of the series, Tina happened across Father Rocco while on a date with her sleazy boyfriend Matthew DiNardo. Joining the ragtag band of people who were trying to thwart the Esoteric Order of Dagon and their plot to awaken Cthulhu, she was captured and offered as a human sacrifice. Fortunately, former criminal Bones arrived in time to rescue her, but the rising of an eldritch abomination from the depths at the story's conclusion left her fate uncertain.

Tindalos is a fictional location, shown in some works to be a dimension, in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was first mentioned, through the title of their most infamous denizens the Hounds of Tindalos, by American author Frank Belknap Long in his 1929 short story "The Hounds of Tindalos."

### Overview

### Lovecraft Circle Works
Assuming that Tindalos is in fact a location and not the master of the Hounds of Tindalos, it may be inferred from the actions of the Hounds that it is a separate dimension.

### Expanded Mythos Works
In Richard Lee Byers' novella Ire of the Void, Tindalos is an alien dimension, one inhabited by not only the Hounds, but also Satyrs and fearsome Dholes (in Long's story, it was already established that the Satyrs and the Doels are associated with the Hounds of Tindalos). Its geography consists primarily of floating roadways in bizarre geometric patterns, and the occasional land mass adorned with dome-shaped buildings. Despite the incomprehensible laws which govern this strange realm, it is not unnavigable by human beings, as shown when Norman Withers worked his way across the labyrinth of roadways and rescued the abducted Claus Schmidt.

The Tindalosian Hybrids are creatures from Roger Zelazny's 1981 novel The Changing Land, which borrowed heavily from the Cthulhu Mythos. They were later included in the Call of Cthulhu monster manual Malleus Monstrorum. 

### Description
Tindalosian Hybrids often resemble living cubist paintings that shift around regularly. They often hide by wearing long robes. When they are not trying to mimic human form, they grow gaping mouths with crystalline fangs and sharp, wolf-like claws. 

Tindalosian Hybrids are not a natural species, and are instead created whenever someone consumes the blue ichor that may be left behind by Hounds of Tindalos.

fullContent:
The Tinfoil Dossier is a series of novels by Caitlin R. Kiernan that blend the Cthulhu Mythos with conspiratorial spy fiction, following the operations of the agents of shadowy quasi-governmental organizations as they battle (or in some cases assist) eldritch horrors. The series comprises Agents of Dreamland, Black Helicopters, and The Tindalos Asset.

Black Helicopters was first published as a chapbook by Subterranean Press in 2013, before Agents of Dreamland was published by Tor in 2017. But Tor published an expanded version of Black Helicopters in 2018, so it is designated the second book in the series, and Agents of Dreamland the first. The Tindalos Asset was published by Tor in 2020.

All three novels unfold achronologically, and involve events that occur over considerable stretches of time, but Black Helicopters takes place largely in 2012, Agents of Dreamland in 2015 and The Tindalos Asset in 2017.

Each book tells a self-contained story, but they are interlinked by the rival agencies that try to contain or exploit the outbreaks of unnatural horror that feature in the plots. These are:

* Albany, also known as Dreamland, a US-based organization that functions like the Men in Black or the FBI's X-Files program to neutralize or contain supernatural threats. The group has no official name, but is referred to as Albany because its headquarters are based in Albany, New York, beneath the Erastus Corning Tower.
* Barbican Estate, also known as Y, a London-based group that is sometimes a rival and sometimes an ally of Albany. 
* X, a group with an affinity for chaos that is often an adversary of both Albany and Barbican Estate. They are sometimes referred to by the name of their leader, Julia Set.

Certain characters appear in more than one book, particularly The Signalman, an agent of Albany who appears in all three books. Other recurring characters include Julia Set and Barbican Estate's Immacolata Sexton.

Tisha Hewitt is a fictional character created by American author Lee Clark Zumpe for his Cthulhu Mythos stories.

### Overview
A woman somewhere in middle age, Tisha is a native of Arkham, Massachusetts. A former investigative journalist for the Arkham Gazette, she left this profession to author books on real-life ghost sightings, a field in which she became well respected. As well as writing, she founded a successful ghost tour business in her home town and still accepts the occasional contract as a freelance journalist. In addition, she is on the books of the Arkham Detective Agency as a consultant.

Tisha had a brother, Alex, five years older, who disappeared when he was seventeen. In her later life, she discovered that he had been sacrificed by a cult on the outskirts of Arkham.

Titus Crow is a fictional character created by Brian Lumley for the eponymous Cthulhu Mythos series Titus Crow.

### Description
Originally an occultist with a vast knowledge of the history, creatures, and motivations of the in-universe Mythos, Crow also had in his possession a number of artefacts related to the topic. He has displayed an unwavering resolution in stopping the schemes of the Great Old Ones and their minions, even to the point of apparent self-sacrifice.

Later rebuilt to be better in every way after a catastrophic accident, Crow became a persistent nemesis to the Cthulhu Cycle Deities, and Ithaqua in particular.

Lumley's 1987 short story "Inception" reveals the Crow's vast mystical knowledge to stem from being unwittingly baptised in a mind-expanding liquid.

Crow's best friend is a man named Henri-Laurent de Marigny, who assists him in many of his ventures, and shows an equal commitment to his cause, despite not being as knowledgeable as Crow himself.

### History
### The Burrowers Beneath
Crow and de Marigny uncovered a plot by the Chthonians against the people of Great Britain. During the course of their investigations, they were approached by a shadowy organisation known as the Wilmarth Foundation who had similar goals to them, and the two immediately joined. Subsequently aiding in the Great Britain Project, an operation designed to rid the British isles of the Chthonians, their combined strength was great enough to destroy the Chthonians inhabiting Britain and kill their leader, the being known as Cgfthgnm'o'th. 

Following this, the Great Old One Ithaqua retaliated, leaving Crow missing, presumed dead. (: The Burrowers Beneath)

### The Transition of Titus Crow
Having escaped Ithaqua's wrath in the cosmic time machine de Marigny's Clock, Crow travelled the universe, although he was lost in time and space, unfamiliar with the machine's controls. He visited past and future incarnations of Earth, before colliding with a virtually-uninhabited planet after a lengthy pursuit by the Hounds of Tindalos.

Luckily for Crow, the planet's sole resident was a highly-advanced robot who collected what was left of his body and reconstructed it using the memories and brain patterns stored in the Time Clock. Crow emerged better than before, physically superior to any other human.

Taking his leave of his saviour, Crow then wandered the cosmos again, before being guided to the domain of the Elder Gods, Elysia. There, he was enlisted by their leader Kthanid in the fight against the Great Old Ones, met and fell in love with the Lady Tiania, and enhanced his already-considerable knowledge of the Cthulhu Cycle Deities. (: The Transition of Titus Crow)

### The Clock of Dreams
Sent by Kthanid to investigate the strange silence which had descended over Earth's Dreamlands, Crow and Tiania travelled there and uncovered a plot by the Fly-the-Light to enslave the population.

fullContent:
The Titus Crow series, sometimes referred to as The Cthulhu Cycle Deities series, is a Cthulhu Mythos story arc by noted British author Brian Lumley. It comprises six novels and eleven short stories featuring the eponymous protagonist Titus Crow and those allied with him against the forces of the Great Old Ones, primarily Ithaqua, but including several other Mythos entities.

The books are heavily influenced by the interpretation of the Mythos forwarded by August Derleth, even citing his elemental classifications for the Great Old Ones, and are pulpish battles between good versus evil where the heroes triumph as often as fail. It also introduces good counterparts to the Great Old Ones in the Elder Gods, including Kthanid, who is Cthulhu's brother. The books also introduced the Chthonians, terrifying squid-like worms and their own Great Old One, Shudde M'ell.

### Novels

* The Transition of Titus Crow (1975)
* The Clock of Dreams (1978)
* Spawn of the Winds (1978)
* In the Moon of Borea (1979)
* Elysia (1989)

"To a Dreamer" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Synopsis
Consisting of six four-line stanzas which describe the narrator's encounter with a terrifying creature - seemingly masquerading as a man - previously seen only in his sleep: a denizen of the Dreamlands.

shortDefinition: "To Arkham and the Stars" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Fritz Leiber. It revisits H. P. Lovecraft's Miskatonic University setting and many of his characters in an affectionate tribute to a writer who served as a mentor to Leiber ...
fullContent:
"To Arkham and the Stars" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Fritz Leiber. It revisits H. P. Lovecraft's Miskatonic University setting and many of his characters in an affectionate tribute to a writer who served as a mentor to Leiber when he was just setting out on his literary career.

### Synopsis
An unnamed narrator revisits Arkham and Miskatonic University--as it turns out, to lay a wreath on the grave of Henry Armitage, the hero of "The Dunwich Horror", accompanied by Albert Wilmarth from "The Whisperer in Darkness". Along the way we see a version of the town and school updated to the 1960s, and meet many of the characters from Lovecraft's fiction--most of whom have been given happy endings.

Pulling into the "Arkham station of the Boston and Maine Railroad", our narrator finds that a "suburb of quite tasteful Modern Colonial homes now covers most of Meadow Hill," where Herbert West once experimented. He remembers that the Witch-House was pulled down in 1931, and the "moldering tenements of the Polish Quarter have largely been replaced by a modest housing development in Colonial urban style." 

Miskatonic has gained a new Administration Building and the Pickman Nuclear Laboratory--both designed, along with the Polish Quarter apartment development, by Daniel Upton (from "The Thing on the Doorstep"), who "has had a distinguished career ever since he was given a clean bill of mental health and discharged with a verdict of ‘justified homicide’". (The college buildings are deemed "magnificent structures, wholly compatible with the old quadrangle."

The lab is funded, like the expedition in At the Mountains of Madness, by the Nathaniel Pickman Derby Foundation. It's run by Professor Ellery, who discovered unidentifiable elements in a statuette brought back by Walter Gilman in "The Dreams in the Witch-House".

Other professors sighted include Upham of the Mathematics Department (from "The Dreams in the Witch-House"); Nathaniel Peaslee of of Economics and Psychology, and his son Wingate Peaslee, in Psychology ("The Shadow Out of Time"); and William Dyer of Geology (At the Mountains of Madness). Dyer is said to be "well through his ninth decade" and the oldest academic present, save for the elder Peaslee.

Francis Morgan, professor of Medicine and Comparative Anatomy, is "now the sole living survivor of the brave trio who had slain the Dunwich Horror"--meaning that Rice as well as Armitage are now dead. Morgan’s "research in mescaline and LSD" has led to the creation of anti-hallucinogens that allowed Danforth, insane since At the Mountains of Madness, to leave the asylum and become a professor of Psychology at Miskatonic.

### Publication History
"To Arkham and the Stars" was first published in the Arkham House anthology The Dark Brotherhood and Other Pieces, for which it was written, in 1966. It has since appeared in The Book of Fritz Leiber (DAW, 1974), Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos (Fedogan & Bremer, 1992), and Fritz Leiber and H.
