shortDefinition: "To Clark Ashton Smith, Esq., upon His Phantastick Tales, Verses, Pictures, and Sculptures" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft in honour of his friend and fellow weird fiction author, artist and poet Clark Ashton Smith. Written in December 1936, it...
fullContent:
"To Clark Ashton Smith, Esq., upon His Phantastick Tales, Verses, Pictures, and Sculptures" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft in honour of his friend and fellow weird fiction author, artist and poet Clark Ashton Smith. Written in December 1936, it was posthumously published in the April 1938 issue of Weird Tales under the simplified title "To Clark Ashton Smith".

Some collections, such as Fungi from Yuggoth and Other Poems, have also published it under the more fanciful title "To Klarkash-Ton, Lord of Averoigne".

This is the last poem that Lovecraft ever wrote, as he became ill and passed away a few months after writing it.

### Synopsis
The poem describes an ominous tower in the middle of the woods, where the Dark Lord of Averoigne creates frightening eidola and writes about things that lurk "beyond the star-gulfs", which he knows about because from his windows he can see "pits of dream no other gaze could bear".

### References

shortDefinition: "To Clear the Earth" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Will Murray that originally appeared in the anthology The Shub-Niggurath Cycle (Chaosium, 1996). The story introduces Murray's recurring secret government organization, the Cryptic Events Evaluation T...
fullContent:
"To Clear the Earth" is a Cthulhu Mythos story by Will Murray that originally appeared in the anthology The Shub-Niggurath Cycle (Chaosium, 1996). The story introduces Murray's recurring secret government organization, the Cryptic Events Evaluation Taskforce.

Murray wrote a sequel/prequel, "Black Fire," that was published in 1995.

### Synopsis
An agent of the Cryptic Events Evaluation Taskforce goes to Antarctica to investigate the emergence of an ancient artefact that threatens to destroy all life on Earth.

### Characters

* Pickman: An agent of the Cryptic Events Evaluation Taskforce, associated with ARCHINT--archeological intelligence. He describes the CEET as a branch of the National Reconaissance Office that conducts " other, super-classified, reconnaissance" on “any unexplained or unclassifiable phenomenon." His eyes are "the clear green of the Aurora Australis."
* Evan Stark: U.S. Navy glaciologist stationed in Antarctica. Comes from Kentucky.

### Mythos Connections
The artefact that emerges from the Antarctic ice, a "crackle-skinned sphere of pitted brown metal" 40 feet in diameter, is called the Furnace of Yeb. Depicted in the Necronomicon--"circa 738 A.D.”--it's "the Elder engine that’s supposed to clear the Earth.” 

Yeb is described in the story as one of the greatest of the Old Ones. The offspring of Yog-Sothoth and Shub-Niggurath, father to Tsathoggua. In ancient times, he was worshipped in underground shrines all over the world. In Rome, Luxor, Petra––even Teotihuacan. Two years ago when they uncovered the lost city of Irem in the Middle East, they found a cave shrine dedicated to Yeb.In the Irem shrine, the CEET found a "basalt wall tablet...the only complete surviving text of the Black Litany that is identified with Yeb." It describes something associated with Yeb called the Black Fire.
The reference to the discovery of Irem "two years ago" would seem to place the story in 1993.

### Publication History
Since its appearance in The Shub-Niggurath Cycle, "To Clear the Earth" has been reprinted in Murray's collection The Wild Adventures of Cthulhu: Volume One.

### References

term: To Edward John Moreton Drax Plunkett, Eighteenth Baron Dunsany
shortDefinition: "To Edward John Moreton Drax Plunkett, Eighteenth Baron Dunsany" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft, first published in The Tryout, 5, No. 11 in November 1919.  The piece is a tribute to the works of Lord Dunsany, a key i...
fullContent:
"To Edward John Moreton Drax Plunkett, Eighteenth Baron Dunsany" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft, first published in The Tryout, 5, No. 11 in November 1919.

The piece is a tribute to the works of Lord Dunsany, a key influence in H. P. Lovecraft’s writings, particularly those incorporating the Dreamlands.

### Poem
* As when the sun above a dusky wold
* Springs into sight, and turns the gloom to gold,
* Lights with his magic beams the dew-deck’d bow’rs,
* And wakes to life the gay responsive flow’rs;
* So now o’er realms where dark’ning dulness lies,
* In solar state see shining Plunkett rise!
* Monarch of Fancy! whose ethereal mind
* Mounts fairy peaks, and leaves the throng behind;
* Whose soul untainted bursts the bounds of space,
* And leads to regions of supernal grace;
* Can any praise thee with too strong a tone,
* Who in this age of folly gleam’st alone?
* Thy quill, Dunsany, with an art divine
* Recalls the gods to each deserted shrine;
* From mystic air a novel pantheon makes,
* And with new spirits fills the meads and brakes;
* With thee we wander thro’ primeval bow’rs,
* For thou hast brought earth’s childhood back, and ours!
* How leaps the soul, with sudden bliss increas’d,
* When led by thee to lands beyond the East!
* Sick of this sphere, in crime and conflict old,
* We yearn for wonders distant and untold;
* O’er Homer’s page a second time we pore,
* And rack our brains for gleams of infant lore:
* But all in vain—for valiant tho’ we strive
* No common means these pictures can revive.
* Then dawns Dunsany with celestial light,
* And fulgent visions break upon our sight:
* His barque enchanted each sad spirit bears
* To shores of gold, beyond the reach of cares.
* No earthly trammels now our thoughts may chain;
* For childhood’s fancy hath come back again!
* What glitt’ring worlds now wait our eager eyes!
* What roads untrodden beckon thro’ the skies!
* Wonders on wonders line the gorgeous ways,
* And glorious vistas greet the ravish’d gaze;
* Mountains of clouds, castles of crystal dreams,
* Ethereal cities and Elysian streams;
* Temples of blue, where myriad stars adore
* Forgotten gods of aeons gone before!
* Such are thine arts, Dunsany, such thy skill,
* That scarce terrestrial seems thy moving quill;
* Can man, and man alone, successful draw
* Such scenes of wonder and domains of awe?
* Our hearts, enraptur’d, fix thy mind’s abode
* In high Pegāna; hail thee as a god;
* And sure, can aught more high or godlike be
* Than such a fancy as resides in thee?
* Delighted Pan a friend and peer perceives
* As thy sweet music stirs the sylvan leaves;
* The Nine, transported, bless thy golden lyre,
* Approve thy fancy, and applaud thy fire;
* Whilst Jove himself assumes a brother’s tone,
* And vows the pantheon equal to his own.
* Dunsany, may thy days be glad and long;
* Replete with visions, and atune with song;
* May thy rare notes increasing millions cheer,
* Thy name beloved, and thy mem’ry dear!
*

shortDefinition: "To Greece, 1917" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Thought to have been written in May 1917, it did not see print until its inclusion in an unknown publication in November of that year.  The poem is a tribute to the pe...
fullContent:
"To Greece, 1917" is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Thought to have been written in May 1917, it did not see print until its inclusion in an unknown publication in November of that year.

The poem is a tribute to the people and mythology of Classical Greece, and the influence the culture had on future civilisations.

### Poem
* Ye sons of Greece! by true descent ally’d
* To Athens’ glory, and to Sparta’s pride;
* Heirs to the spark that set the world ablaze
* With new-born Freedom’s first awak’ning rays;
* Children of Hellas, from whose deathless heart
* Sprang all we have of wisdom and of art:
* Can ye, unblushing, bear upon your throne
* A slave of gods and cultures not your own?
* Heav’ns! would Pelides, foremost in the fray,
* Bow thus to Thor’s and Woden’s frost-mad sway?
* Would Agamemnon drop his glist’ning shield,
* And passive to barbarian Wilhelm yield?
* Shame on thee, Constantinos! Reign no more,
* Thou second Hippias of the Attic shore!
* Rise from your tombs, ye Marthonian slain!
* Ye shades of Salamis, adorn the main!
* Appear, ye martyrs of th’ embattled free,
* Whose sacred mem’ry guards Thermopylae!
* With ancient valour teach your native Greece
* To scorn the Goth, and spurn a coward’s peace!
* As once your hands, invincible and just,
* Smote tyrant Xerxes prostrate in the dust;
* Disarm’d th’ oppressor, and preserv’d the brave;
* Snatch’d infant Europe from a Persian grave;
* So may ye now against the despot stand,
* And stir the sleeping glories of your land!
* Need any tongue before your ears rehearse
* The monstrous menace of the Vandal curse?
* Need bard or prophet sound the mourning lyre,
* Or Delphic riddles rouse your smould’ring fire?
* Behold the Teuton, threat’ning in his guilt
* The laws and arts your matchless Athens built;
* Your laws and arts, by Roman prowess spread
* Thro’ grateful Europe, and to Britain led;
* By British pow’r sent o’er the ocean crest
* Where young Columbia rules th’ expansive West;
* Gaze on the Hun, his bestial cohorts hurl’d
* Against the freedom of a Grecian world!
* See great Italia soar again to fame,
* Till monarchs shudder at the Roman name;
* See fiery Gaul achieve a nobler height,
* And shew the neighb’ring nations how to fight;
* And proud o’er all the rest, with ties renew’d,
* See brother Saxons cow th’ invading brood!
* All these behold—these scions of your mind—
* Shall Hellas, source of all, remain behind?
* Say not, ye Greeks, that those bold men are gone
* Who yesteryear your conqu’ring hosts led on;
* Say not your plains of heroes are bereft,
* Nor cry that Clisthenes no heir hath left;
* False is the tongue that such a slander gives
* To Grecian soil, while VENIZELOS lives!
* With such a chieftain could your country know
* The fame and liberty of long ago;
* Once more would tyrants meet their well-earn’d fate,
* And Grecian freedom bless the Grecian state:
* A Cretan Pericles the helm would hold,
* That Greece might sail to glory as of old!
*

fullContent:
"To Hold Ye White Husk" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author W. H. Pugmire.

### Synopsis
Two sailors whose ship has been sunk wash ashore on an island which feels intrinsically wrong. There, they stumble across what appears to be some kind of dark fane, and the desiccated corpse of one of their former crewmates. As the corpse begins to chant, so does one of the sailors, and the two eventually lapse into madness as something evil circles the temple.

### Characters
*The Narrator, and unnamed seaman.
*Johnny Roberts, the Narrators' companion.
*Gustav Sturhman, a sailor who died from his injuries at sea. Likely a cultist to some dark god.

### Publication History
"To Hold Ye White Husk" was published in the thematic collection World War Cthulhu, edited by Brian M. Sammons and Glynn Owen Barrass, in 2014.

### Trivia
*Although the time period in which the story is set is never stated, the sailors ship was torpedoed and their lifeboat required rowing, so it most likely takes place at some point during the 20th century.

shortDefinition: "To Mars and Providence" is a science fiction short story that serves as a crossover between H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos and H. G. Wells' The War of the Worlds. It was written by Don Webb and published in the 1996 anthology War of the Worlds: Gl...
fullContent:
"To Mars and Providence" is a science fiction short story that serves as a crossover between H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos and H. G. Wells' The War of the Worlds. It was written by Don Webb and published in the 1996 anthology War of the Worlds: Global Dispatches.

### Synopsis
The story is set in 1898, at the beginning of the Martian invasion of Earth. An eight-year-old boy named Howard Lovecraft sees a Martian cylinder crash-landing nearby and leaves home to investigate. At first, he believes the invaders might be the night-gaunts that have appeared to him in dreams. Instead, the creature that comes out of the ship is a tentacled, octopus-like Martian, which Howard watches from a nearby church tower with his binoculars. The crowd surrounding the crash site is decimated by the Martian's heat-ray weapon, and Howard faints.

When he wakes up back home, his mother tells him that the Martians have spared him and took him inside their ship, from which he was rescued by a librarian named Armitage. At this point, most families are trying to get away from the chaos of the invasion, but the Lovecrafts will stay until grandfather Whipple comes home. Feeling a strange compulsion to return to the church near the crash-site, Howard observes the Martians with a telescope, admiring their machines and their oversized brains. He sees one of them deposit a golden box into the tower of the church.

At night, Howard sneaks out and enters the church, where he finds a shining trapezohedron. When he touches it, his consciousness expands, and he sees a living colour that reaches into his brain and communicates with him. As it turns out, the colour is a manifestation of the Martians' communal mind, and tells Howard about the race's history.

The Martians, Howard learns, are descended from the same ancestral species that colonised both Mars and Earth, the latter in Antarctica, but evolved in a completely different direction by modifying their bodies and their brains. They eliminated all their emotions except for fear (as the latter was deemed necessary for survival) and built an advanced civilisation, making contact with a fungoid species from a world at the outskirts of the solar system. Through them, the Martians discovered that they weren't the first species to settle on Mars, and eventually started to uncover artifacts of a mighty race of long-faced, ghoul-like creatures that they called the Elder Gods. Finding that the Elder Gods haven't died out, but are merely asleep, the Martians grew fearful of their return, and ultimately decided to abandon Mars and take over Earth, leaving the red planet to its dormant masters.

The colour also informs Howard that some years ago, some Martians have sent their minds through space to inhabit human bodies and gather information about the Earth. "To Pan" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1902 (when he was only 12 years old) as part of an illustrated manuscript he named his Poemata Minora, Volume II. It appeared under the title "Pan" in The Tryout in April 1919 and was later published by Arkham House in Collected Poems in 1963.

### Synopsis
The narrator falls asleep in the woods by the side of a reedy stream and dreams of an encounter with the god Pan, who plays music in his reed pipe while Nymphs and Satyrs gather around to dance. When the narrator wakes up, he longs to hear the song of Pan again.

"To Sea" is a Lovecraftian short story by author Josef Desade. It was published in the digital zine Lovecraftiana Vol 5, Issue 4 by Rogue Planet Press in 2021.

### Synopsis
A man commits to paper the story of how the world ended: watching from a coastal clock tower, he witnessed as a spore-transmitted contagion was washed ashore by something malevolent lurking in the ocean. Those touched by the spores - virtually everyone other than the narrator - drops dead to rot in the street as the cloud spreads outward. The letter ends with the man encouraging any survivors to join the creature, and himself, in what rapture he claims to have seen beneath the waves.

### Behind the Mythos
The theme of contagion suggests that the entity responsible for the fall of mankind may have been Hastur, however, the lack of any real evidence makes this conjecture at best.

"To Skin a Corpse" is a short story by Cody Goodfellow, a hard-boiled crime story about reanimated dead ala "Herbert West--Re-Animator." It first appeared (as “To Skin a Dead Man”) in Hardboiled Cthulhu (Elder Signs Press, 2006).

### Characters
*Tom Thorpe, a hoodlum and the story's central character. Once a boxer known as Three-Round Thorpe who was trained by Swede Magnussen.
*Helix, "a moon-faced torpedo" who is Thorpe's partner.
*Bogomil, former partner of Thorpe and Helix, who dies knowing where the loot from their last job is.
*Matilda Blau, "a hard-faced frail" who was Bogomil's lover.
*Swede Magnussen, once a trainer and now a re-animator of boxers. A dwarf with "feisty, icy eyes."
*Aubrey Dubois, the undertaker at Shady Glade Cemetery who has a special arrangement with the ghouls.
*Von Hohenheim, a "four-hundred-year-old alchemist," described as "fat, white-haired man in an impeccable white suit." Like Joseph Curwen, he has the ability to restore the dead from their essential salts. The loot whose location Thorpe and Helix are trying to learn came from the robbery of his estate,
*Carlos the Bewitched, formerly King Charles II of Spain (1661-1700), now Von Hohenheim's resurrected servant. Has "granulated gray skin like pressed ashes" and "mismatched limbs."
*Herbert West, who "ruined the sport" of boxing by introducing re-animation. Mentioned, but does not appear in the story.

### Publication History
After its initial appearance in Hardboiled Cthulhu, "To Skin a Corpse" was reprinted in Goodfellow's collection Rapture of the Deep and Other Lovecraftian Tales. It was translated into German in Tiefenrausch (Festa, 2022).

fullContent:
"To Swim in the Light" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Paul Lubaczewski. It was published in the Candlemas edition (Vol 3, Issue 4) of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction zine Lovecraftiana by Rogue Planet Press in January 2019.

### Synopsis
In rural America Amos Calhoun, a man who has been jealously guarding a very special location somewhere in the backwoods behind his house, is unexpectedly rushed to hospital. Taking advantage of the situation Rick and Mary, a pair of photography enthusiasts, take the opportunity to sneak onto Amos's land to take pictures of the wondrous waterfall hidden deep within the forest.

During the course of their shoot, the pair uncover an expansive cavern hidden behind the waterfall and within, a shrivelled old scholar inextricably enmeshed with an observation chair set before a silver portal. Curious as to what lies beyond the gateway, Rick and Mary make their way through, but are transformed into hideous alien monstrosities with no way to return to their previous selves - or even home…

### Behind the Mythos
Although unknown to Rick and Mary, the ancient city whose outer reaches they find themselves stranded in is named as Pnakotus. In light of this, and combined with certain hints given in the text on the nature of the creatures they have been transformed into - beings who use the clicking of their claws to communicate - would strongly suggest that navigating the portal has somehow switched their consciousnesses with those of Yithians. What has happened to the minds of the aliens whose bodies have been traded is not explained.

"On Receiving a Picture of ye Towne of Templeton, in the Colonie of Massachusetts-Bay, with Mount Monadnock, in New-Hampshire, Shewn in the Distance," more commonly referred to as "To Templeton and Mount Monadnock," is a poem by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. It first saw print in an unknown publication in June 1917 .

### Synopsis
The poem is an appreciation of Mount Monadnock, a geographical feature located in New Hampshire, USA .

### Behind the Mythos
"Mount Monadnock" is an early example of Lovecraft’s Anglophilia and the racist attitudes he possessed at the time, as seen in the lines "Can with’ring change ancestral shades o’er-ride, And aliens live where sturdy Saxons died?"

"To the Old Pagan Religion" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft as part of a manuscript he named his Poemata Minora, Volume II. This was written in 1902, when the author was only 12 years old. The poem was published in The Tryout in April 1919, under the title "The Last Pagan Speaks". It also saw print as part of the 1977 collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems.

### Synopsis
The poem is written from the point of view of someone who worships the Olympian Gods, including Jove and the nymphs, and regrets the spread of the new monotheistic Christian faith. Rather than accepting this new religion, the narrator chooses to pray to the old Gods one last time.

shortDefinition: "To Zara" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft on 31 August 1922, but never published during his lifetime. It first appeared on print as part of a letter to Maurice W. Moe in the first volume of Lovecraft's Selected Letters (1965). In 1990, it appear...
fullContent:
"To Zara" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft on 31 August 1922, but never published during his lifetime. It first appeared on print as part of a letter to Maurice W. Moe in the first volume of Lovecraft's Selected Letters (1965). In 1990, it appeared in the collection The Fantastic Poetry.

The poem was written as part of a prank that Lovecraft and Frank Belknap Long played on Alfred Galpin, who generally disliked Lovecraft's poetry. It was presented to Galpin as a recently discovered piece by Edgar Allan Poe, dated 1829 and inscribed to a Miss Sarah Longhurst. Galpin didn't believe that Poe was the author, but he did praise the poem, much to Lovecraft's amusement. It was only after Lovecraft told him the truth about the authorship that Galpin "began to see defects". (: Selected Letters 1.95)

### Poem
: I looked upon thee yesternight
: Beneath the drops of yellow light
: That fell from out a poppy moon
: Like notes of some far opiate tune.
: I looked and sighed, I knew not why,
: As when a condor flutters by,
: And thought the moonbeams on thy face
: Timid to seek thy resting-place.
: 0 sacred spot! Memorial bower!
: Unsuited to the mocking hour
: When winds of myrrh from Tempe’s lake
: Stir soft, yet stir thee not awake!
: Thy clear brow, Zara, rests so fair
: I cannot think death lingers there;
: Thy lip as from thy blood is red,
: Nor hints of ichors of the dead:
: Canst thou, whom love so late consumed,
: Lie prey to worms—dissolved, entombed?
: And he, whose name suffused thy cheek
: With ecstasies thou couldst not speak;
: Will he in fancy hold thee ever
: Fair as thou art, decaying never,
: And dreaming, on thine eyelids press
: A tribute to thy loveliness?
: Or will his fancy rove beneath
: The carven urn and chiselled wreath,
: Where still—so still—the shroud shall drape
: Grotesque, liquescent turns of shape?
: No, Zara, no! Such beauty reigns
: Immortal in immortal fanes;
: Radiant for ever, ever laden
: With beams of uncorrupted Aidenn,
: And naught that slumbers here tonight
: Can perish from a lover’s sight.
: Where’er thy soul, where’er thy clay
: May rise to hail another day,
: Thy second soul, thy beauty’s flame,
: The songs of passionate lutes shall claim;
: Pale, lovely ghost—so young, so fair,
: To flutter in sepulchral air—
: To flutter where the taper dies
: Amidst a mourner’s choking sighs!

The Toad God is a fictional entity, created by Robert E. Howard for his short story "The Thing on the Roof". 

### Background
The Toad God used to be worshipped by an ancient tribe in Central America, during the pre-Columbian era. A temple was built for the deity, where it laid dormant for thousands of years. However, the temple also contains a mummy wearing a toad-shaped jewel. If the jewel is removed and used to open the hidden door, the Toad God will awaken to curse whoever disturbed it. (: "The Thing on the Roof") 

After appearing in their adaptation of the original story, the Toad God was incorporated into the Marvel Multiverse, where it would be established as being either a Great Old One or Lesser Old One. (: Official Handbook of the Marvel Universe A to Z #3; Demons' profile)

fullContent:
Toadface is a short story by Mark McLaughlin set in H. P. Lovecraft's Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
Innsmouth accountant John Masters meets a strange-looking man whom he mentally dubs Toadface while having coffee with a coworker at the Pantheon Coffeehouse. Toadface has overheard their talk of dieting, and questions Masters about his regime, making veiled comments about the consumption of human meat during the consumption. Masters makes his excuses and leaves.

That night, Masters believes he is dreaming of an undersea city populated by bizarre aquatic humanoids when he sees Toadface, undressed and with the same fishlike attributes as the others. Toadface informs him that he is not asleep but in fact dead, his mind cut from his body by the creature while he slept. Toadface goes on to say that he is about to travel to the surface world to consume Masters' corpse, but lets slip that it may be possible for a ghost to inhabit the body of another sleeping creature.

Masters explores the underwater city - pursued by Toadface - and happens upon an ancient temple containing the slumbering forms of three creatures known as Silent Ones. He takes control of the largest one and sweeps Toadface up in its tentacle before carrying him off and burying him in the wet concrete of a construction site, presumably killing him. Hungry, Masters then heads back to the ocean with the intention of consuming an entire whale.

### Characters
*John Masters - An accountant with Innsmouth Quality Construction.
*Toadface - A psychic Deep One, heavily afflicted by the Innsmouth Look.
*Meg - John Masters' coworker.
*G'hlaballa - A Silent One possessed by Masters' discorporated spirit. Hinted to be some kind of deity.

### Behind the Mythos
Toadface was first printed in Mark McLaughlin's short story collection Motivational Shrieker, published in 2004 by Delirium Books, and was later included in the eBook bundle The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack (Wildside Press LLC) in 2012.

### Synopsis
The story takes place in an alternate version of Tokyo, where people known as Transients are summoned from 23 other worlds to participate in a game. Participants in these games are given a Sacred Artifact, armaments giving their users extraordinary power. These people form guilds within the 23 wards, one of which will reign above them all. One of these 23 worlds is home to the Old Ones, beings who hold eldritch attributes over reality.

Tom Lynch is an American author and games designer who has worked on a number of books for Chaosium's popular Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, as well as writing several separate Cthulhu Mythos tales. His Lovecraftian fiction has appeared in anthologies such as The Dark Rites of Cthulhu, The Children of Gla'aki, and Arkham Detective Agency.

Lynch was also the co-founder, with Keith Herber, of the now-defunct Miskatonic River Press, an independent publisher established in 2008 which specialised in Lovecraftian gaming material and fiction.

The Tomb Herd is a collective of extra-dimensional beings that feast in crypts by possessing statues. They are described in the Necronomicon as creatures that exist beyond the threshold of space. They were first described by Ramsey Campbell in his short story "The Tomb Herd", which later became known as "The Church in High Street".

### Trivia

* Interestingly, they are very similar in most respects to the Weeping Angels who appear in the BBC science fiction drama series Doctor Who much, much later.

Tomb of the Black Pharaoh is the first volume in Christopher Michael's Danforth: Eldritch Tales of WWII series of Cthulhu Mythos fiction. It was independently published in 2024; hardcover, paperback, digital, and digital audio editions were all released.

The story serves as a direct continuation of the fate of H. P. Lovecraft’s character Danforth following the events of At the Mountains of Madness. Set during the early years of the Second World War, the novel situates Danforth within the emerging world of Allied intelligence operations as occult activity tied to Nazi and Axis interests begins to surface across Europe and North Africa.

### Overview


The narrative follows Danforth as he becomes entangled in an investigation involving ancient artifacts, forbidden texts, and secret societies seeking to exploit powers associated with the Cthulhu Mythos. Drawing heavily upon Lovecraftian themes of inherited trauma, forbidden knowledge, and cosmic inevitability, the novel portrays Danforth as a man haunted by his Antarctic experiences and increasingly aware that the horrors he once believed buried beneath the ice persist in other forms.

The novel introduces recurring Mythos elements and entities, including references to the Necronomicon and manifestations associated with Nyarlathotep, while grounding its events within real historical settings and intelligence operations of the period.

The volume functions as both a character study and a foundation for the broader series, establishing Danforth’s psychological state, thematic trajectory, and the series’ approach to integrating cosmic horror within historical events.

Tommy Muldoon, the Rookie Cop, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for inclusion in their Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-related products.

### History
Straight after passing out of Boston City's police academy, Tommy found himself immediately sent out on secondment to the Arkham Sheriff's department.

At first, Tommy didn’t mind this, but the realities of working in Arkham were soon brought home to him, with bizarre reports of monsters stalking the outskirts of the city and horribly mangled corpses turning up all over town making him realise that there was something deeply wrong with the place.

However, Tommy had sworn an oath to protect and serve and so, with his trusty rifle Becky at his side, he set about the dirty business of cleaning up Arkham, whatever the personal cost might be.

### Behind the Mythos
Fantasy Flight originally created Tommy as a playable Investigator for their Second Edition expansion for adventure board game Arkham Horror, Innsmouth Horror. Since then, he has made appearances in other related products including Eldritch Horror, Mansions of Madness and Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and a plastic figurine of the character was released in 2010 as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, but this is no longer available to purchase.

Tony Balnco is a minor character created by American author C. J. Henderson for his Frank Nardi series of short stories.

### History

### Pre-Arkham
A police officer for the NYPD, upon retirement Balnco partnered with three other former detectives including Frank Nardi to form the Arkham Detective Agency, a private investigations company which specialised in cases with a supernatural aspect.

### Death
Whilst providing security for an exhibit on ancient Egyptian culture at Arkham's Miskatonic University, Balnco encountered a mysterious entity who had visited the display for reasons of its own. Inadvertently insulting the being, he suffered a gruesome fate at its hands, being turned into a great gobbet of living, suffering flesh. At the request of Frank Nardi, who seemed to have gained a measure of respect from the entity, he was transformed back to a human corpse upon his death (: "Cruelty" by C. J. Henderson).

### Resurrection and Final Death
Some months later the entity, now confirmed to have been the Outer God Nyarlathotep, returned to Balnco and gave him new life, encouraging him to seek out Frank Nardi and murder him. Why it chose to do this is not revealed. Luckily for Nardi, however, he was able to turn the tables on his would-be attacker and ended Balnco's life for good, granting his former friend the closure he so desperately sought (: "Closure" by Glynn Owen Barrass).

### Appearances

*"Closure" by Glynn Owen Barrass

Tony Morgan, the Bounty Hunter, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games for their Arkham Horror Files and appears in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
One day, while hard on the trail of a particularly elusive bounty, Tony cornered his quarry out in the countryside, near a large river. However, this time his prey turned out not to be human.

A humanoid creature covered in scales and coated in slime, the monster stank of the ocean, rotted fish and the offal of the unfortunate farm animals which it had slaughtered and devoured. Upon realising that it had a pursuer, the thing immediately made for the river, throwing itself straight in. Having never let a target escape, Tony shrugged off his revulsion, drew his knife, and went to work.

Everything from then on had gone by in a blur; Tony had a vague recollection of the nightmarish beast trying to tear his arm off at the shoulder before everything went black, and he passed out.

Waking up in the hospital three days later, Tony felt sick to his stomach after remembering what had happened. After spending a fortnight recuperating, he was finally declared fit enough to leave, and Tony once again took up his mantle of hunter. This time however, his prey is anything but human.

### Behind the Mythos
Although originally created as an Investigator for Fantasy Flight's Second Edition release of Arkham Horror, he has since made appearances in several of their other games including Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. He has also received a physical representation of the character through the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line, though this is no longer in production (all ).

### Trivia
*The creature first encountered by Tony whilst chasing a bounty is heavily implied to have been a Deep One.

Tony Richards (born 3 June 1956) is a British short story writer and novelist whose works fall primarily into the horror and supernatural genres. He has authored a number of Lovecraftian works, including the Weird House Press collection The Howling Terror and Other Lovecraftian Horror Stories; in addition to these, he has penned three ongoing literary series, including Raine's Landing and The Birchiam Chronicles. He is both a Bram Stoker and British Fantasy Award nominee.

Richards counts Ray Bradbury, Fritz Leiber, Harlan Ellison, and Poppy Z. Brite amongst his literary influences .

Tower of Shadows, later retitled to Creatures on the Loose, was a bi-monthly comic book anthology series which ran for six years between 1969 and 1975. It initially printed stand-alone horror stories, but after rebranding moved on to primarily fantasy works, and several Mythos stories appeared in its pages over the years.

### Adaptations and Mythos References
### Tower of Shadows
* "At the Stroke of Midnight", the lead story in the debut issue, was originally titled "The Lurking Fear at Shadow House" by writer-artist Jim Steranko as an homage to the works of H. P. Lovecraft, but was changed by editor Jim Lee before publication.
* "The Terrible Old Man" was adapted for issue #3.
* An adaptation of "Pickman's Model" featured in issue #9.

### Creatures on the Loose
* Issue #10 featured a short King Kull story.
* "Thongor : Warrior of Lost Lemuria!" appeared in issue #22.

"Toy Reanimater" is a short story written by the late Yasumi Kobayashi. Other than being his debut novel, it also won the short story category for the second Japan Horror Novel Award. In addition to the titular short story also included "The Drunken Man".

### Synopsis
The story of the Toy Reanimater is told from the perspective of the female patron to the male patron at a bar. During her childhood, children in her neighborhood often whisper of the legend of Toy Reanimater, a being whose presence is hidden from the adults. The Toy Reanimater has the ability to fix broken items and even deceased living beings.

The female patron's childhood self was bringing along her little brother Michio on her back while running errands for her parents. One day, she just so happened to came across another girl who had to carry her pet cat after accidentally killing it, hoping for the Toy Reanimater to resurrect it. Meanwhile, the female patron fell from the footbridge and accidentally killing Michio in the process. Her last vision before she succumb to the fall was seeing her little brother and his toy gun dismantled by a young boy.

By the time the woman reawakened, she sees the Toy Reanimater fixing the Word Processor (which has the soul of a living being, either Michio or the cat) while the deceased cat she saw before had its eyes replaced by toy bullets.

The flashback ended and returned to the present day with the grand revelation. The first being how the female patron losing part of her face and had to be repaired, with a cat's eye replacing her old one (hence why she keeps wearing sunglasses even indoors). The second one being the male patron was Michio all along, but lost his identity.

### Characters
*Toy Reanimator: The titular repairman who agrees to fix broken items, usually toys or video games for as long as he is instructed over the condition of the item before it was broken.
*Female Patron: A patron of the coffee shop who always wears sunglasses, even indoors as she carries a dark past.
*Male Patron: A fellow patron of the coffee shop who becomes the "audience" of the female patron's storytelling. He is said to be the female patron's younger brother Michio, revived and amnesiac.

### Mythos Connections
*The Kanji that make up the Toy Reanimater's name is "玩具修理者", as it was originally read as Gangu Shurisha per the novel's accompanying furigana. However, the titular character's name (also written in the same Kanji) is actually read as Yōgu Sōtohōtofu, implying that the elderly repairman is actually an avatar of Yog-Sothoth.
*While spewing enchantments to heal/repair, the Toy Reanimater spoke of corruptions of the words Cthulhu and Nyarlathotep, as well as mimicking the roars of Shoggoth.

The Toy Vault Cthulhu Collection is an American toyline released by Toy Vault, primarily focused on plush figures. It has also featured other products, including accessories, decorations, card games and other toys. The first Cthulhu plush was produced in 2000, and the line officially began in 2001, with the release of a medium and small Cthulhu plush.

In 2002, the Cthulhu line expanded with the release of more plushes including Dracuthulu, Summer Fun Cthulhu, Nyarlathotep, and Gothic Cthulhu. 

In 2003, the Cthulhu line would add Super Hero Cthulhu, Shoggoth, and Secret Agent Cthulhu. 

In 2004, the next wave included the Deep One, Cthulhu Slippers, Cthulhu Hand Puppet, Mini Secret Agent Cthulhu, Mini Shoggoth, Cthulhu the King, Moon Beast, and the Cthulhu Action Figure.

In 2005, the Cthulhu line added Gug, the Cthulhu Bust, Cthulhu Backpack, Night Gaunt, Miskatonic Cthulhu, Giant Cthulhu, Ithaqua, Santa Cthulhu, and the Hound of Tindalos.

In 2006, the Cthulhu line expanded with Valentino Cthulhu, Blue Velvet Cthulhu, Necronomicon Plush Book, Cthulhu Stocking, Cthulhu Pouch, and the Do You Worship Cthulhu? card came.

In 2007, the Cthulhu line expanded further with the Cthulhu Pillow, Cthulhu Hat, Screaming Cthulhu, Hallows Eve Cthulhu, Peeping Cthulhu, Cthulhu the Wicked, Cthulhu Wreath, Cthulhu Gloves, and Mounted Cthulhu.

In 2015, the Cthulhu line released the My First Cthulhu Plush, Cthulhu Ski Mask and Cthulhu Beach Towel, along with the memory matching card game Recall of Cthulhu and its supplement Dreamlands Expansion.

Trail of Cthulhu is an investigative tabletop role-playing game designed by Kenneth Hite using the GUMSHOE system designed by Robin D. Laws. The core rulebook was published by Pelgrane Press in March 2008.

The Trail of Cthulhu roleplaying game uses a rules-light approach where points are spent to obtain clues to the adventure's resolution and for combat. Similarly points are spent to use other skills.

Perhaps its most noteworthy feature is that this game does not provide dogmatic descriptions of Mythos creatures. Instead, it provides a summary of the various versions and interpretations that have been written over the many years since each entity was first created. Rather than using syncretism to try and reconcile the hundreds of iterations of a Mythos creature the different versions are simply offered as options that a referee running a game can choose from. This also serves to disarm players with encyclopaedic knowledge of the "settled" versions of the Mythos creatures. This is a radical point of difference from the "monster manual" approach taken by Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu RPG.

### Supplements

Trail of the Loathsome Slime is a contemporary scenario supplement for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, written by Marcus L. Rowland and issued by then-small press publisher Games Workshop in 1985. Little more than a booklet, it ran to a total of 16 pages, and also included player handouts and a handful of new skills for investigators to employ.

The base material from which Trail of the Loathsome Slime was developed first appeared in Games Workshop's hobby magazine White Dwarf #43 in June 1983.

fullContent:
The Trans-Galactic Empire is a totalitarian intergalactic empire controlled by a Lovecratian-like entity in the fictional universe of the Rifts pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium.

### Background
The Trans-Galactic Empire (TGE) is a totalitarian regime in the Three Galaxies, which is controlled from the shadows by an incredibly powerful colossal alien intelligence which is also completely insane, the Dweller Beneath. Ruling the empire as its servant is the Kreeghor Emperor, each of which has been chosen by the Dweller Beneath and bestowed with superhuman powers. It's an empire dominated by the Kreeghor, a warlike race of reptilian-looking mammilian humanoids who used to be one of the Splugorth's major servitor races. Who rose up against their masters and broke free, though unknown to them their rebellion and the establishment of their empire was all orchestrated by the Dweller Beneath. 

The elite of the empire are the Royals, a super powered caste of Kreeghor. It has a population in the trillions and controls 100s of thousands of worlds. The empire controls a third of the Corkscrew Galaxy (the southern part), and one third each of the Thundercloud and Anvil galaxies. A few of the conquered species have earned a higher position in the empire, proving themselves worthy in the eyes of the Kreeghor, including the Wolfen (humanoid lupines), the Machine People, and the Silhouettes (dark skinned humanoids).

It's an intergalactic empire with a vast war machine and sophisticated technology. Serving in the war machine are conscripts and volunteers whom come from all of the races within the empire, though the Kreeghor dominate positions of leadership. Though the military itself is feared and hated by the oppressed populace, the citizens hope to join as those who are in the military have far greater privileges, many more right, and receive benefits unlike the regular citizenry. It's armada consists of 100s of thousands of warships including over 10,000 capital ships, each nearly a km in length or larger. The legions are equipped with power armor, mecha, and directed energy weapons. It's shock troops are genetically-engineered super beings, who serve in the Invincible Guard. Who outrank all in the empire, except the Royals and the Kreeghor Emperor.

fullContent:
Transformers is a multimedia franchise developed by TakaraTomy and Hasbro, featuring alien robots that can be converted into other forms, such as vehicles and animals. It first appeared as an American toyline in 1984, which originally imported Japanese figures from Diaclone and Micro Change, before being accompanied with a comic book series, published by Marvel Comics. Shortly afterwards, an animated series was produced by Marvel Productions and Sunbow Productions, animated by the Japanese studio Toei Animation. The franchise would later spawn numerous other comics, animated series, movies and video games that are still being produced to this day.

The storyline primarily focuses on the endless conflicts between the heroic Autobots and the evil Decepticons (usually led by Optimus Prime and Megatron, respectively) from the planet Cybertron; however, the details can vary depending on the incarnation.

The alternate universe from the Hearts of Steel miniseries was featured in the crossover comic Infestation 2.

### Lovecraftian entities
In the Transformers multiverse, many entities are based on or inspired by the Cthulhu Mythos. 

Some of them include:
*D-Void 
*The Dweller 
*Ebon Knights
*Elder Gods 
*Hytherion 
*Ramjet 

### Trivia 
*In the book Transformers Animated: The AllSpark Almanac II, Vhoorl is mentioned as being a neutral planet in the Dark Nebula. Additionally, one of the many planets that was colonized by the Cybertronian race in the Hadeen System is named after Tsathoggua, which has a moon named Eibon.
*The animated series Transformers: Cyberverse features several references. Much like the original Generation 1 incarnation, the Dweller bears a strong resemblance to Cthulhu. In the episode "Bring Me The Spark Of Optimus Prime", when Megatron was live streaming Starscream's funeral, most of the usernames in the chat were based on familiar Mythos entities. In the episode "The Scientist", the titular Quintesson's laboratory is labelled the "Shub-Niggurath nursery", written in Cybertronix.

shortDefinition: Translations from the Book of Yng is a series of short Cthulhu Mythos stories from author and editor F. C. Adams. The individual works "The Debt of the Summoner," "The Fleece of Yaggar" and "The Punishment of Igharta" were published in Beyond The Dar...
fullContent:
Translations from the Book of Yng is a series of short Cthulhu Mythos stories from author and editor F. C. Adams. The individual works "The Debt of the Summoner," "The Fleece of Yaggar" and "The Punishment of Igharta" were published in Beyond The Dark Gateway, July 1973.  Later all the stories were printed in the Edward P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes in 1998.

### Overview
As the title suggests, the stories are each presented as a translation from an occult text named the Book of Yng, and are stated to be an English translation of a Spanish text, itself adapted from a Latin copy. Some are clearly intended to have been the inspiration for other mythological tales.

### Entries

* "The Son of Misharga" (1998)
* "The Temple of Bones" (1998)
* "The Debt of the Summoner" (1973)
* "The Punishment of Igharta" (1973)
* "The Fleece of Yaggar" (1973)

### Trivia

* The Outer God Shub-Niggurath, who appears in several of the stories, is portrayed exclusively as being male, when it is more usually associated with the opposite gender.

Seaman Traube is a fictional character in the story "The Temple" by H. P. Lovecraft. 

### Background
Traube served aboard the German submarine U-29 under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich during the First World War. As a result of the fear and stress suffered by the crew during the supernatural events that befell them, they started to become mutinous. When they sighted an American battleship the men were restless in their desire to surrender to it. Traube in particular insisted on this with such violence that Lieutenant Klenze shot him to death in order to maintain discipline. (: "The Temple")

The Travelers are a fictional species expanded upon by Chaosium in 1994 for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, which were based on creatures which appeared in Michael Shea's 1980 short story "The Autopsy".

### Background
Travelers are a spacefaring race whom travel across space using translucent ships the size of basketballs. When approaching a planet they use meteor showers as cover. If detected, the ship auto-destructs, creating an explosion large enough to take out a city block. The Travelers remain hidden until they can invade a suitable host. The alien parasites are a sadistic race which enjoy the pain and horror their host experiences, as the trapped consciousness is taunted and tortured.

A traveler's life cycle goes through four stages, of which only the earliest stage, the larval form, is mobile. Its adult form is a brain-like entity which controls a network of whip-like filaments which it uses to control the host. They are also used as weapons, projecting from an orifice a paralyzing tendril and another one that extends to the victim's ear to feed on its blood. The filaments can also be used to animate the dead.

"Treacherous Memory" is a short story by American author Glynn Owen Barrass.

### Synopsis
A private detective takes on the case of a man's wife who vanished for two years before returning claiming no memory of her whereabouts during this time. What she uncovers is a tale of alien abduction, one which she becomes all too caught up in.

### Characters
* Cassandra "Cassey" Bane, a private investigator.
* Ted Cruise, a man who has developed an obsession with alien abductions after the disappearance of his wife.
* Selene Cruise, Ted's wife and the victim of an extraterrestrial research program.
* Abe, a business associate of Cassey's.

### Publication History
"Treacherous Memory" was published in the Doug Draa-edited anthology Weirdbook Annual 2 by Wildside Press in 2019.

The Tree-Men of M'bwa are once-human creatures created by Donald Wandrei for his short story of the same name, incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the role-playing game supplement Malleus Monstrorum.

### Description
The Tree-Men were the unfortunate victims of an evil undead being named M'bwa, an entity in service to the alien God of the Red Flux.

Those who strayed into the valley occupied by M'bwa were accosted by the long-dead yet still animate creature who, by virtue of his dark magic, was invulnerable to harm. He quickly overpowered these poor souls before forcing them to drink an elixir which would allow him to work on them uninterrupted, amputating their legs and grafting what remained onto the stumps of trees. These living humans would then slowly transform into Tree-Men, serving as a macabre warning to others. For the first two decades or so, they remain capable of speech. As the transformation continues, they become silent, inanimate, and possibly insentient.

A man named Daniel Richards, who avoided this fate by having his legs amputated soon after the transformation started, forever after had to have the saplings which sprouted from the stumps of his legs trimmed on a monthly basis. (: "The Tree-Men of M'bwa")

"Treehouse of Horror XXIX" is an episode of the animated television series The Simpsons, which first aired on October 21, 2018. It was written by Joel H. Cohen and directed by Matthew Faughnan.

### Overview
The episode features three horror-themed segments, as well as an additional short in the opening sequence involving the Simpson family going on vacation to Fogburyport, a New England town inhabited by Deep Ones and their god Cthulhu. The residents attempt to sacrifice the Simpson family, which leads to Homer challenging Cthulhu to an oyster-eating competition.

fullContent:
"Tribute Band" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author John Goodrich.

### Synopsis
Two young musicians on a road trip investigate the mysterious disappearance of one of their inspirations years earlier. Coming into possession of the man's copy of the Revelations of Gla'aki, they are approached by his former compatriots, who trick the pair into enacting a ritual which frees the Great Old One from its tether to the Severn Valley.

### Characters
*Ron, guitarist in the Murderous Dwarfs, a tribute band to the now-defunct Goatswood Gnomes.
*Tommy McCandless, lead singer in the Murderous Dwarfs, obsessed with the disappearance of Goatswood Gnomes frontman Brian Brady.

### Publication History
"Tribute Band" was published in the thematic anthology The Children of Gla'aki by Dark Regions Press in January 2017.

### Trivia

* The name of the missing man's band, the Goatswood Gnomes, is a nod to the fictional entities created by British author Ramsey Campbell for his short story "Made in Goatswood," and later incorporated into Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game.

"Tricks no Treats" is a short story by the late American author Paul Dale Anderson.

### Synopsis
A patient in a lunatic asylum relates the tale of how he travelled to Arkham, Massachusetts on Halloween night with the hope of finding a mystic portal which would allow him to talk to his dead wife. However, the portal spews forth a gaggle of immature Shoggoths which pursue him through the city streets and rob him of his sanity.

### Publication History
"Tricks no Treats" was published posthumously in the Wildside Press collection Weirdbook Annual 2 in February 2019.

The Triffids are a fictional species created by John Wyndham for his 1951 novel The Day of the Triffids, depicted as being bio-engineered organisms. They were later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos by the Call of Cthulhu gaming supplement Malleus Monstrorum.

### Description
The Triffids are hostile plants with a straight stem from which its mouth appears and four stick-like protrusions which they use as legs. 

The Triffids were theorised to have been the result of a scientific program - possibly Soviet - but their seeds have spread throughout the world. They can grow in any environment, but take four to five years to mature.

Trish Scarborough, often simply referred to as the Spy, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files series of Cthulhu Mythos-related content. 

### History
Something of a prodigy, Trish excelled at everything she turned her hand to as a child, which caused eyebrows to raise when she settled down in a seemingly-mundane job with a commercial code company as an adult.  

What nobody had realised was that the company was in fact a front for something far more sinister: Trish had been recruited by "The Bureau", a shadowy organisation purporting to be part of the government, and she now works as a covert operative. 

However, recently Trish has begun to suspect the motives of her employers, and wonders who is really pulling their strings- the government, or perhaps forces from beyond our world… 

### Appearances
Trish was first introduced in the Arkham Horror Second Edition expansion box Innsmouth Horror. She has since appeared in other Fantasy Flight products, including Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. A now-discontinued plastic gaming piece was also released under the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line of accessories. In 2022, she was written as the primary protagonist of Josh Reynolds' short story "The Red and the Black," where she was working in the employ of the American government’s Cipher Bureau.

Troids are a fictional race in Marvel Comics, which were created in 1993 by Chris Cooper. Making their first appearance in issue #2 of the 1st volume of the Midnight Sons Unlimited comic book series. 

### Background
Troids are a race of immaterial parasitic beings created by Elder God Chthon. They are present in most humans, feeding on the fear and humiliation that is felt by their hosts. The hosts aren't physically effected by the parasite, which grow to maturity within. If an injury occurs to the host's skin, the parasite escapes. Outside of the host, its a 3 ft. long 10-legged winged insectoid that can talk. It can only be detected by those with mystical abilities, but if detected, normal physical means can injure the creature.

Tru'nembra, The Flautist of Azathoth, is an Outer God who resides eternally in the Court of Azathoth. Tru'nembra does not possess an instrument for he himself is an instrument. He is made entirely out of visible noise and is seemingly unintelligent, just like his master. When Tru'nembra is summoned, it brings along the maddening symphony it uses to keep its master asleep, bringing insanity to those who are unfortunate enough to hear its blaring chaos. Tru'nembra had only been summoned once which was during the time when the flying polyps escaped from the tunnels the Yithians had forced them in, possibly hinting that the two events are somehow connected.

fullContent:
True Detective is an HBO anthology series in the hard-boiled detective genre. Its first season, which aired in 2014, contained references to the King in Yellow stories of Robert W. Chambers. The character of Rustin Cohle, played by Matthew McConaughey, is based in part on the philosophies of Thomas Ligotti.

### Mythos Connections
Although the majority of the first season is dominated by Southern Gothic and Southern Noir elements, a continuing theme is references by the main antagonist in his writings and "decorations" to appropriations from The King In Yellow. Carcosa is mentioned, and there's some writing referring to it, as well as to the Yellow King, King in Yellow, and a general air of malaise and evil associated with it. The ritualistic sexual abuse and murder of a young woman has pagan overtones which in this show are tied to the Carcosa mythos created by the show. Later seasons don't really return to this subject at all, and it seems to have been, within the universe of the show, something arising from the madness of the first antagonist in the series rather than an overarching theme - other than the sense of a decayed world in a more general context.

The Tsan-Chan Empire is a fictional future Terran empire created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft and first mentioned in his 1919 short story "Beyond the Wall of Sleep".

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
During a conversation between the unnamed narrator and the cosmic being inhabiting the body of Joe Slater, the narrator is told that "we are all roamers of vast spaces and travellers in many ages. Next year I may be dwelling in the dark Egypt which you call ancient, or in the cruel empire of Tsan-Chan which is to come three thousand years hence" (placing that date in the year 4900 AD).

Whether Lovecraft intended Tsan-Chan to refer to an individual emperor, a dynasty, or even a geographical region is uncertain.

### In the Expanded Mythos

### The Cruel Empire of Tsan Chan
Chaosium's 2010 Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game supplement The Cruel Empire of Tsan Chan greatly expands on the Tsan Chan Empire. In this interpretation, it is an empire which rules what used to be China and Korea, plus great parts of Thailand, Vietnam, and Myanmar. Tsan Chan is not a Chinese empire but it does exist as if it was a fever dream of ancient China. The architecture is similar to that of ancient China, and so are the fashions and diet. The language has drifted due to mixing with other groups and the naming conventions are to a degree Chinese. The empire prosecuted several wars against the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos, including the Tcho-Tcho people and the Star Spawn, and have made such diverse allies as the Ghouls and Tsathoggua.

Using Deathless and Serpent magic in conjunction with the technology of the Elder Things, the Tsan Chang suceeded in forging a more powerful and effective Interdiction (a form of enormous Elder Sign), turning it into a colossal wall which surrounds the empire. God-Trap technology warns away those powerful predator races of the Mythos. Dreamers and Tcho-Tcho are kept away by mine-fields, barbed wire, and gun turret emplacements. Weapons that employ the technology of the Elder Things includes beam cannons that fire an invisible beam which creates an Elder Sign, lethal toward Mythos creatures.

The Mighty Children which survived the war became the Empire's nobility, it's new rulers. To prevent them from summoning their parents and other entities to the Earth, the Serpents closed every interdimensional and interplanetary portal within the empire. The Deathless became the priests of the empire. The Empire is presently campaigning in Antarctica against the Shoggoth, as part of their alliance with the Elder Things. It's currently ruled by the Empress, the greatest of the Mighty Children. The masses of the empire follow the "Way", a kind of philosophy, religion, and discipline created by the Deathless to keep the Dreamless sane, and prevent them from committing suicide or starting revolutions. Tsath is a fictional subterranean city that appears in H. P. Lovecraft and Zealia Bishop's "The Mound." Named after the once-worshipped Tsathoggua, it is the last occupied city in the underground realm of K'n-yan.

The story describes Zamacona's first sight of "the monstrous, gigantic, and omnipotent city of Tsath":It was a city of the plain, but fashioned of such heaven-reaching towers that its outline was truly that of a mountain. Above it hung a curious greyish haze, through which the blue light glistened and took added overtones of radiance from the million golden minarets.He is told that: the upper parts of the great towers were no longer used, and that many had been taken down to avoid the bother of maintenance. The plain around the original urban area was covered with newer and smaller dwellings, which in many cases were preferred to the ancient towers.Entering the city,  Zamacona finds "a network of strange and ancient streets." He is struck by thedizzy giganticism of its overawing towers, the monstrous surge of teeming life through its ornate avenues, the curious carvings on its doorways and windows, the odd vistas glimpsed from balustraded plazas and tiers of titan terraces, and the enveloping grey haze which seemed to press down on the gorge-like streets in low ceiling-fashion.Surrounding the outskirts are the great amphitheatres used for entertainment and drawn-out public executions.The gold- and stone-paved roads are thronged with ever-present caravans flowing noisily in and out. The maze of streets and ornate avenues that run below the great towers are filled with people and lined with curious carvings on its doorways and windows. 

The gn'agn of the supreme tribunal and the council of executives operate from the frescoed halls of a gold-and-copper palace behind a gardened and fountained park.

### L'thaa
A ruined suburb of Tsath leading to Nith.

### Inhabitants
Dressed in "tasteful robes and trappings and swords," the Men of Tsath are the dominant power in K'nyan.

### Slaves
Slavery is a common practice in K'n-yan and there are several forms of slaves used:

*The four legged gyaa-yothn.
*The bio-magical y'm-bhi.
*An unnamed, semi-human slave-class which could also be programmed with hypnotic impressions to be incredibly efficient. Inferior specimens provided the principal meat stock of K'n-yan.

### Language
The closest link to a human language is that it may have been corrupted into Aztec. In

Tsath-yo, also spelled Tsatho-yo, is a fictional prehistoric language first mentioned in the horror fantasy short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price.

It might be connected to the alien deity known as Tsathoggua, which was venerated in preglacial Hyperborea.

### Overview
Tsath-yo is a primal language that was used in Hyperborea millions of years ago, at the time the Silver Key was created. The parchment that was kept in a box with the Silver Key by Randolph Carter's grandfather contained inscriptions in R'lyehian which had been translated from the original Tsath-yo. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

Prof. Laban Shrewsbury cited Naacal, Aklo, and Tsatho-yo as examples of pre-human languages used by the cults of the Great Old Ones. (: "The House on Curwen Street")

Tsathoggua, also known as the Sleeper of N'kai, is a fictional entity in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Clark Ashton Smith for his Hyperborean Cycle.

Tsathoggua (or Zhothaqquah) is described as an Old One, a godlike being from the pantheon. He first appeared in Smith's short story "The Tale of Satampra Zeiros," written in 1929 and published in the November 1931 issue of Weird Tales. His first appearance in print, however, was in H. P. Lovecraft's story The Whisperer in Darkness, written in 1930 and published in the August 1931 Weird Tales.

Lovecraft mentioned Tsathoggua in nine stories, not counting the unfinished fragment that would later become The Lurker at the Threshold. This makes it one of the most oft-mentioned Mythos deities in Lovecraft's fiction, tied with Yog-Sothoth and losing only to Nyarlathotep (ten stories), Cthulhu and Shub-Niggurath (eleven stories each). Of these, Tsathoggua is the only one not created by Lovecraft himself.

Like Shub-Niggurath, however, Tsathoggua never appears physically in Lovecraft's stories, except for a possible appearance disguised as a wax sculpture in "The Horror in the Museum".

Other authors also mentioned Tsathoggua in their Mythos fiction, including Robert E. Howard and Robert Bloch. The short story "Death's Black Riders" in Crypt of Cthulhu Lammas 2000 by C. J. Henderson, completed from an unfinished story fragment by Robert E. Howard, features a confrontation between Tsathoggua and Howard's hero Solomon Kane.

Although Smith sometimes used the term "elder gods" to describe the Hyperborean pantheon, Tsathoggua included, it's not considered one of the Elder Gods in the Derlethian sense.

### Description
The first description of Tsathoggua in the Mythos occurs when the protagonists encounter one of the entity's idols:

: "The Tale of Satampra Zeiros")}}

In a later story, Tsathoggua is described again:

: "The Seven Geases")}}

Tsathoggua is often found asleep.

fullContent:
"Tsathoggua" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late American author Michael Shea. 

### Synopsis
The plot consists of two storylines whose characters intersect at the beginning and end. 

The first involves an old woman named Maxie trying to eke out an existence with her dying dog in the slums of San Francisco. She stumbles across a strange ooze which appears to be contaminating the locals, and is eventually shown that it’s origins lie with the Great Old One Tsathoggua. 

In the second, another elderly woman is infected by the creatures spawned from the ooze, turning her into one of them herself. While at first she believes her new condition to be a divine blessing, she soon comes to realise the horror of her predicament when she is swallowed alive by her new master. 

The story concludes with Maxie being introduced to a character from another of Shea's stories, Dee, who begins her education on the darkness which lies just out of sight of an unsuspecting population. 

### Characters
*Maxie, a woman in her twilight years who still mourns the death of her husband.
*Maureen, another aged woman, also suffering through bereavement.
*Leon Petrov, an old man with some knowledge of the Cthulhu Mythos.
*Dee, a middle-aged woman beginning her own induction into the supernatural.
*Vera, Maxie's friend.
*Tsathoggua, an ancient being of incredible power.

### Publication History
*The Autopsy and Other Tales (2008)
*Copping Squid and Other Mythos Tales (2009)
*New Cthulhu: The Recent Weird (2011)
*Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea (2017)

### Trivia
*Dee mentions Scat, a character from a previous Michael Shea story, in the final paragraph.

"Tuama" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author L. F. Falconer.

### Synopsis
After an esteemed professor's husband dies as a result of researching the fourth dimension, she gathers his notes, recruits a graduate student, and travels to a remote Scottish island to continue his work.

However, what the professor has not told her student is that she has deduced that the guardian to the fourth dimension needs a sacrifice, and plans to make the girl her victim. Unfortunately for her, her student proves more resourceful than she believed and turns the tables on her elder, leaving the professor to be sucked into a horror-filled inky blackness.

### Characters
* Diana, an entomology grad student.
* Dr. Miriam Chase-Whateley, a well-respected marine biologist with a secret obsession to complete her dead husbands work.
* Dr. Andrew Whateley, a former Miskatonic University professor of physics and Miriam's husband, deceased.

### Publication History
"Tuama" was published in the Wildside Press anthology Weirdbook Annual 2 in 2019.

fullContent:
Tulu-metal is a fictional extraterrestrial substance featured in the novella The Mound, written by H. P. Lovecraft based on a story prompt by Zealia Bishop.

### Description
Tulu-metal (named after the K'n-yanian god "Tulu", a.k.a. Cthulhu) is a heavy, dark, lustrous and "richly mottled" metal that doesn't occur naturally on Earth, but has been brought to the planet by Cthulhu. Tulu-Metal is paramagnetic meaning that it exhibits physical properties of magnetism but only insofar as it interacts with itself. Objects made of this material are attracted to each other, as if by magnetism, but have no such effect on common magnetic metals. Chemical analysis has identified it as "an amalgam of unknown metallic elements of heavy atomic weight".

The K'n-yanians always had a deep respect for this rare substance, which has grown to a quasi-religious veneration over the course of their history. Objects made of Tulu-metal include "Cyclopean idols" and talismans, as well as metallic cylinders used to store sacred scrolls. The manuscript of Zamacona y Nuñez, who was kept captive in K'n-yan in the 16th century, was found inside one such cylinder.

At one point in history, the currency of K'n-yan was made of Tulu-metal, combined with other elements such as iron, gold, silver, copper, or zinc, so as to greatly diminish its paramagnetic properties and make it more practical to use.

Since the K'n-yanians have cut off all trade with the surface world after the cataclysms caused by the "space-devils", Tulu-metal is almost unheard of outside K'n-yan.

A talisman made of this metal belongs to the Wichita Chief Grey Eagle, having been passed down from father to son for countless generations of his family. As all of Grey Eagle's ancestors lived for well over a century like him and perished only in battle, it has been speculated that the talisman might be responsible for their longevity, although it's not known whether it is connected to the K'n-yanians' own immortality.

Grey Eagle's talisman is about two inches in diameter and decorated with an image of Cthulhu on one side and Yig on the other, these being the two gods originally worshiped by the K'n-yanians. An identical talisman had previously been found by Zamacona at the entrance of K'n-yan, and worn by him when he first made contact with its inhabitants. Zamacona also found a large sculpture of Cthulhu made of the same metal. (: The Mound)

### Behind the Mythos
Although Tulu-metal only appears in The Mound, it might be related to the unnamed alien stone of which the idols of Cthulhu are made of in "The Call of Cthulhu". These are also stated to have been brought to Earth from the stars by the Cthulhi, and resemble no kind of mineral known to Earth, being described as soapy and greenish-black with iridescent striations.

Tulzscha, also known as The Green Flame, is a fictional entity created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his short story "The Festival". Although the being was unnamed in its first appearance, the name "Tulzscha" was applied retrospectively by Chaosium in their Malleus Monstrorum monster manual supplement for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Overview
Tulzscha appears as a blazing green ball of flame, dancing with its Lesser Outer Gods at the court of Azathoth. When summoned to the world of men, it manifests in a gaseous form, penetrating the planet to the core, then erupting from below as a pillar of flame. It is unable to move from the point at which it emerges.

The Tunnelers Below are a fictional race created by Fritz Leiber for his short story "The Terror From the Depths", and were later expanded upon by Chaosium in 1994 for their Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

### Background
The Tunnelers Below are a race of worm-like creatures which are as long as humans and as thick as their thighs. Along their bodies are numerous pairs of tiny translucent wings which vibrate continuously. Eyeless creatures with a circular mouth lined with shark-like teeth, they are creatures that possess great psionic abilities, especially telepathy, which they use to invade dreams, steal the memories and thoughts of the unwilling, and communicate with spirits.

The Tunnelers have an insatiable lust for knowledge of the Mythos and are drawn to every aspect of it. It is known that Tunnellers congregate below strong sources of psychic power, mystical energy, and locations which have been most influenced by aliens. They have a web of caves that spans the planet, which even extends below the seabed. One of their favoured spots is beneath the sunken city of R'lyeh, where they glut themselves on the death-dreams of Cthulhu.

The Tunnelers are not a hostile race, as long as they are not provoked. When angered or threatened, they attack with their maw of shark-like teeth or burrow beneath the target, creating fragile tunnels to collapse the structure. The primary threat they pose to humans is that they are continuously telepathically broadcasting Mythos concepts, findings, and knowledge. Unless the victim moves or the Tunnelers are driven away, he or she will either be driven completely insane or die.

"Two Black Bottles" is a short story written by American horror writers H. P. Lovecraft and Wilfred Blanch Talman. It was first published in the August 1927 issue of Weird Tales.

### Synopsis
The narrator is called into the town of Daalbergen after the death of his uncle, Dominie Johannes Vanderhoof, to inherit his estate. The locals recount the strange behavior of the Dominie, and his Sexton Abel Foster, which led them to suspect he was in league with unseen spirits. Though warned against going up at night, the narrator is unperturbed and crosses a swamp to reach the church so he can confront Foster. 

Passing the fresh grave of his uncle, he enters the church at sundown, before finding Foster sitting catatonic in a room lined with ancient symbols, occult manuscripts, and jarred animals. Despite having his eyes open, Foster was heavily intoxicated and only sensed the narrator's presence when he was tapped on the shoulder. Initially mistaking the narrator for the risen corpse of Dominie Vanderhoof, he begins babbling about how the Reverend isn't truly dead and will return for revenge. Initially unconvinced, the narrator realises that his uncle's cross has begun to topple.

After further interrogation, Foster reveals how he learned the secrets of demonology and occult rites from the long dead Dominie Slott. Using his newfound power, he cursed the townsfolk and manipulated Dominie Vanderhoof before trapping his soul inside a black bottle and burying the body. Convinced by the reality of the coming threat, the narrator demands that Foster return the Dominie's soul but without the formula the old Sexton explains that they'll both be killed. To prevent the narrator from getting the bottle, Foster attempts to extract his soul with a low chant but the narrator manages to tackle him before breaking the bottle that held his uncle's soul, killing Foster.

Fleeing the church, the narrator makes it back to Daalbergen where the locals seem not to believe him at first. However, an old man accompanies him back to refill the now abandoned grave and burn the cursed documents. To this day, a gigantic figure roams the graveyard clutching its bottle.

### Dominie Johannes Vanderhoof
The narrator's uncle is described as a large and imposing man with a weak heart. After the arrival of Foster (who'd stare at the Reverend through the eyes of a painting of the devil in the church) he quickly fell under his dark influence giving bizarre sermons about "region of hideous, unseen spirits" that scared off his congregation. Despite the efforts of the local deacons they couldn't afford to replace him and he continued to preach to an empty hall.

### Mark Haines
The cautious grocery store owner who called the narrator into town and explained his uncle's demise.

Father Ubb, or just Ubb, is a fictional monster created by Lin Carter in his Xothic Legend Cycle, where it is portrayed as the lord of the yuggs, and identified as one of the Lesser Old Ones.

### Overview
A large, aquatic entity similar to a chthonian, Ubb is pale gray and slug-like with a large mouth full of horn-like teeth, ringed with tentacles. Ubb dwells in the cold fastness of the Pacific Ocean, with the rest of his race, the Yuggs. The Yuggs are said to guard their gods, the Great Old Ones Ythogtha and Zoth-Ommog, whose tombs, legend tells, lie in the Abyss of Yhe and at the bottom of an abyssal trench near the island of Ponape, respectively.

Ubbo-Sathla, also known as the Unbegotten Source and the Demiurge, is a fictional amorphous monster created by Clark Ashton Smith for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "Ubbo-Sathla", in which it is identified as a primordial entity dwelling in the interior of the Earth, the source of all life on our planet, and guardian of the tablets that preserve the knowledge of primal gods. In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, it is one of the ancient beings known collectively as the Outer Gods.

August Derleth identifies Ubbo-Sathla as the "source" and "the unforgotten beginning" of the Great Old Ones, who rebelled against the Elder Gods of Betelgeuse. (: "The House on Curwen Street")

In the works of Lin Carter, Ubbo-Sathla is Azathoth's twin sibling, and the parent of Zushakon, Abhoth, Nyogtha, Yig, Atlach-Nacha, Byatis, and Han, among others. (: "The Horror in the Gallery")

### Overview
It is described as a huge protoplasmic mass resting in a grotto deep beneath the frozen earth. The being is of a monstrous fecundity, spontaneously generating primordial single-celled organisms that pour unceasingly from its shapeless form. It guards a set of stone tablets believed to contain the knowledge of the Elder Gods.

Ubbo-Sathla is said to have spawned the prototypes of all forms of life on Earth; though whatever its pseudopods touch is forever devoid of life. Ubbo-Sathla is destined to someday reabsorb all living things on Earth. Ubbo-Sathla possibly dwells in Y'qaa.

The being may also dwell in Mount Voormithadreth and may have spawned another of its residents, the being Abhoth, whose form and nature is very similar. This similarity has led some writers to speculate that Ubbo-Sathla and Abhoth are the same entity viewed at different epochs under different names. The tablets that Ubbo-Sathla guards have been oft sought by sorcerers, though no sorcerer has yet succeeded in acquiring them.

### In Other Media
*In the mobile game Morimens, Ubbo-Sathla is worshipped as a creator deity with its tablets being heavily associated with the Ten Commandments and gave its 'executor' Salvador the ability to use his own flesh and blood to perform miraculous acts of healing.
*In the mobile game Crash Fever, a character based on Ubbo-Sathla appears as a member of an organisation named Pnakotus. He is a failed copy of Azathoth that was created by Hastur, and the Tablets of Interstellar Stone would later be used to improve him.
*Ubbo-Sathla appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
