fullContent:
"Ubbo-Sathla" is a short story by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith. It forms a part of his Hyperborean cycle.

### Synopsis
A man stumbles across an unusual orb in a small curio stand, recognising it as the crystal of Zon Mezzamalech, a relic of lost Hyperborea. Upon bringing it home, he feels compelled to use it, and finds that it can transport him back in time. Over the coming days he travels farther and farther back, his consciousness merging with that of the sorcerer Zon Mezzamalech, and reaching the source of all life on Earth: the entity known as Ubbo-Sathla. There, his shattered mind and metamorphosed body settles down amongst the other amoeboid creatures excreted by the monster.

### Characters

*Paul Tregardis, a man with a deep curiosity about the history of life on Earth.
*Zon Mezzamalech, a long-dead sorcerer who created a crystal to allow him to travel in time.
*Ubbo-Sathla, a creature believed to have been the source of all life on Earth.

### Publication History
First printed in the July 1933 edition of pulp periodical Weird Tales, "Ubbo-Sathla" has been published many times in many different publications since. It has also been translated into French, Dutch, Spanish, Italian, Finnish, German and Portuguese.

fullContent:
Über H. P. Lovecraft is a collection of non-fiction works focused on the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft. Edited by Franz Rottensteiner, it runs to a total of 301 pages and was published by Suhrkamp in July 1984. It has not been reissued. Some of the essays are translated from English and French, while others are original to the collection .

### Contents 
*Vorwort (foreword) by Franz Rottensteiner
*"H. P. Lovecraft: Leben und Denken" by S. T. Joshi ("Life and Thought")
*"Lovecraft oder die Revolutionierung des Mythos" by Claude Ernoult ("Lovecraft ou le mythe en rêvolution")
*"Ein literarischer Kopernikus" by Fritz Leiber, Jr. ("A Literary Copernicus")
*"Strukturkonzepte des Phantastischen: H. P. Lovecrafts phantastischer Kosmos" by Hans Joachim Piechotta
*"Anmerkungen zur Erzählkunst Howard Phillips Lovecrafts" by Michael Koseler
*"Der erschrockene Erzähler" by Marek Wydmuch
*"H. P. Lovecraft: Mythenschöpfer" by Dirk W. Mosig ("H. P. Lovecraft: Myth-Maker")
*"Erzählungen des Wundersamen und des Lächerlichen" by Edmund Wilson ("Tales of the Marvellous and Ridiculous")
*"Die Fakten im Falle H. P. Lovecraft" by Barton L. St. Armand ("Facts in the Case of H. P. Lovecraft")
*"Lovecraftiana" by Uwe Japp
*"Vier Rezensionen" by  Jörg Drews
*Reviews by  Jörg Drews
*"Die rationale Handhabung des Irrationalen: Lovecraft im Kielwasser E. A. Poes" by Margit Hager
*"Die Stadt im Werk H. P. Lovecrafts" by Gilles Menegaldo ("La ville dans l'œuvre de H. P. Lovecraft")
*"Erste Liebe mit letzter Kraft" by Rudi Schweikert
*Bibliographie zu H. P. Lovecraft by Kalju Kirde

Uchi no Meido ha Futeikei (うちのメイドは不定形, My Maid is a Formless Entity) is a Japanese light novel series, published by the PHP Institute. The story was conceived by Ryou Morise and written by Tassou Shizukawa, featuring illustrations by Juu Ayakura. The first volume was released in 2010. Despite initially fading into relative obscurity, it eventually gained enough popularity for a second volume in 2013 (most likely due to it being referenced in Haiyore! Nyaruko-san). The plot involves a boy named Tooru Araizawa receiving a new maid, who is a Shoggoth named Tekeli. 

### Overview


### English Translations
Although the series was never officially released in the US, there are some fan-made translations to English. In 2013, a member in the Baka-Tsuki Translation Community (going by the name "Yog-Sothoth-chan") started working on translating the first volume. However, the project was seemingly abandoned the same year after the second chapter was only partially translated.

Uganda (whose geographic footprint roughly corresponds to the former Protectorate of Uganda, a British territory in H. P. Lovecraft’s time) is a landlocked country in East Africa, situated in the Great Lakes region. Inhabited by a variety of different peoples until its settlement by Bantu and Nilotic peoples around 3,000 years ago, it became a British protectorate in 1964. Gaining state independence in 1962, it experienced a series of regime troubles in the wake of the British departure.

Uganda is a geographically diverse country, whose features include volcanic mountains, the world's second-largest freshwater lake, Lake Victoria, and many national parks, including extensive forests and savannahs.

Although Uganda has received minimal representation in the works of H. P. Lovecraft and his circle, there have been a small handful of exceptions.

### Overview

### In Lovecraft’s Works

### "Winged Death"
H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald's 1934 short horror story, which describes an unstable scientist's use of a species of deadly fly as a murder weapon. The insects, dubbed "Devil-flies," originate in the jungles of Uganda, and the scientist undertakes an arduous trek through the untamed Ugandan wilderness to retrieve his specimens.

Also encountered in these remote jungles were cyclopean megalithic ruins which oral tradition held to have been a dwelling place or outpost of the "Fishers from Outside;" the site may have also held some connection to "the evil gods Tsadogwa and Clulu." (: "Winged Death")

### In the Works of Lovecraft’s Circle

### "The Tree-Men of M'bwa"
Donald Wandrei's story of western explorers who fall foul of an ancient being and its seemingly-immortal worshippers in the uncharted depths of the African bush. The events are stated to have transpired somewhere to the west of Uganda, between that country and the mighty Congo River. (/: "The Tree-Men of M'bwa")

Ugghiutu, also known as The Outsider, is an extra-dimensional entity created by American author Jeffrey Thomas for his dystopian science fiction/Lovecraftian horror setting of Punktown.

Ugghiatu is described in some detail in The Summoning of the Old Ones, a short collection of stories which form an arc in the Punktown setting, first published together in December 2019.

### Description
Originating from the same dimension as the Kalians who worship it, Ugghiatu is most commonly believed to appear in a similar manner to the symbol usually employed to represent it: a spiral depicting the nucleus of a gargantuan eye surrounded by a corona of black tentacles (: "Drawing No. 8").

It is said to lie sleeping beyond the stars, having been imprisoned countless years ago by a race of enemy gods (: "Drawing No. 8").

### Avatar
Black Temple is a known avatar of Ugghiutu, is a being grown from a seed birthed from the sacrifice of four highly-trained Kalian dancers. The seed is then planted, after which it grows into an enormous, ambulatory entity with the appearance of an alien tree or organic temple. As the avatar sends forth its tendrils to devour anything nearby, it slowly increases its size and composition until it is the size of a city. At this stage, it can be imagined that very little would have the power necessary to banish it (: "Drawing No. 8").

Dai-oo-ika is a clone created using the genetic map of Ugghiutu. It was produced by Fukuda Biofarm (: Deadstock).

### History
Virtually nothing is known of Ugghiutu's history prior to the appearance of Kalians on Oasis (the planet on which Punktown was founded), although it appears highly likely that some extremist sects called forth avatars of the god to wage war on their enemies (: "Drawing No. 8").

In the far-future colony of Punktown, a Kalian sect initiated the process of summoning Ugghiutu's avatar, despite the best efforts of an opposing group. Fortunately, for both Punktown and every being on Oasis, a group of Kalian priests employed their own biological weapon, a literal living book composed of heavily-tattooed acolytes, to thwart the manifestation, although the price paid by all was severe (: The Summoning of the Old Ones).

### Religious Artwork
A Kalian artist named Narik Guul depicted the rise of Ugghiutu in a series of eight pen-and-ink drawings collectively titled The Summoning of the Outsider. These images were designed to aid in the calling of the entity, and described the exact process necessary to evoke an avatar of the god, as well as the outcome of such an act. One of these pictures, the last, was destroyed by a Kalian woman in an attempt to avert the coming of Ugghiutu, and died in the process; unfortunately, the Kalian extremist group represented by Nhil commissioned talented but struggling artist Maxim Komaroff to create a replacement which rendered the poor woman's efforts in vain (: "Drawin

fullContent:
Uhluhtc is the primary god worshipped by the antagonists in the Den series of comics and graphics novels by Richard Corben. Human sacrifices are offered to it in the world of Neverwhere the stories take place and it is also the source of the Locnar or Loc-Nar, the single most powerful magical artefact of Neverwhere and in the film version of the story indeed the entire universe.

Uhluhtc's name is Cthulhu reversed, and the god is similar to the 1970s popular culture idea of Cthulhu as an alien monster and worshipped entity, looming as a shadowy presence over rituals carried out in his name rather than normally appearing as a physical being except in climactic battle. The attribution of a human concept of definite evil to Cthulhu may seem to be definitely in the same vein as August Derleth and his conceptualization of the Mythos however the world of DEN is an amoral one where most of the characters shift in attributes, attitudes and even appearance. Seen in this context the "evil" of Uhluhtc, at least in the original comic book version, is more along the lines of tyranny, The Establishment and a kind of wickedness and harshness. The most objectively "evil" aspect of Uhluhtc is its love of human sacrifice.

Ulthar is a village in the Dreamlands of Earth. Its people are known for their simplicity, superstitious nature and reverence of cats. In the village it was forbidden for any citizen of the land to harm or kill a cat, after the visit of mysterious dark people who resemble Romani from Earth, albeit overt worshippers of Ancient Egyptian style deities (: "The Cats of Ulthar").

### Description
For those wise enough to not anger the large population of man-eating cats, the cobbled streets of Ulthar seem to be some of the most pleasant in the mythos. Surrounded by suburbs of "little green cottages and neatly fenced farms" the centre of the town is composed of pink buildings, topped with old, peaked, red tiled roofs, overhanging upper stories and numberless chimney-pots". (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath)

### The Temple of the Elder Ones
Above the town on the area's highest hill is the modest, ivy-clad stone tower of the Temple of the Elder Ones, home to priests and their ancient records under the watchful eye of patriarch Atal.  Randolph Carter visited the temple during his search for Kadath.

### Geography
*Across a 1,300-year-old bridge over the River Skai from from the fertile plains around Nir. 
*7 days ride down river from Dylath-Leen.

### Residents
*The old cotter and his wife - Two elderly residents who spent their time killing local cats before being cursed by the dark people.
*Atal - The innkeeper's son who went on to become the patriarch of the Temple of the Elder Ones.
*Old Kranon - The Burgomaster of the town.
*Nith - The lean town Notary.
*Shang - Blacksmith
*Thul - Stonecutter
*Zath - Coroner
*Barzai the Wise - A priest born to a landgrave. He became obsessed with seeing the gods of earth atop Hatheg-Kla. (: "The Other Gods")

Ulthar (also known as Ultharathotep) is a fictional deity from the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was first mentioned in Fred Pelton's occult text "The Sussex Manuscript".

### Description
Ulthar is the son of Sothoth and an Elder God who was sent to Earth, in order to keep watch over the Great Old Ones. Every one thousand years, the rulers and priests of all the empires on Earth come together to visit the high temple located in the pre-human city of N'gah-Kthun, conducting a ritual that summons an avatar of Ulthar, known as Ultharathotep. (: "The Sussex Manuscript")

### In Other Media
*D.Y.N. Freaks: After awakening her Azathoth's power, Azana Hatsumi temporarily transforms Narukami Chikage into Ultharathotep, in order to finally defeat Sphinx. It should be noted that Narukami did not truly become Ultharathotep, only taking the name and form of the deity, due to all the Elder Gods being defeated by Demonbane the Vortex Blaster. In DYN Memo, a list of supplementary materials for the manga written by Jin Haganeya, Ultharathotep was described to be the Favored One of Sothoth, who is also known as Yog-Sothoth; however, this is in contrast to Pelton's original depiction, where Sothoth was meant to be a different entity.

fullContent:
Ulthar Press was an indie publishing house which largely published weird fiction, with a particular focus on the occult detective genre. As of 2019, it can be assumed to be inactive.

### Overview
Founded by the late American author and editor Sam Gafford, after Gafford's passing in 2019, his wife stated her intent to continue Ulthar Press in his honour. Unfortunately, this appears to have been impossible, and the company has not released any new material since 2018; their website is no longer hosted, and the last post on their Facebook account is dated January 2020 .

Ultraman Tiga is a Japanese tokusatsu television series, produced by Tsuburaya Productions. The series aired from September 1996 to August 1997, with a total of 52 episodes. It is the 12th installment of the Ultra Series (although it takes place in an alternate universe) and incorporates elements from the Cthulhu Mythos.

The film Ultraman Tiga: The Final Odyssey was released in 2000 as a direct sequel to the series.

### Synopsis
After protecting an ancient civilization 30 million years ago, Ultraman Tiga is resurrected in the present day by merging with Daigo Madoka, a member of the GUTS defense team. Meanwhile, an apocalyptic prophecy is unfolding involving kaiju and aliens threatening the Earth, with Ultraman Tiga being the only one who can stop them. Eventually, an ancient evil named Gatanothor is revealed to have been behind it all.

In ancient times, Gatanothor once ruled the Earth in an age of darkness. After destroying all of humanity, he returned to the city of R'lyeh and remained dormant there for millions of years until life repopulated the planet. Reawakened in the present day, Gatanothor attempted to wipe out humanity again. His first attempt was to make humanity destroy itself by getting them to be addicted to the plant kaiju Gijera's extract. When that failed, Gatanothor would send his Zoigers (a race of Lloigor-based kaiju) to spread chaos and destruction across the world. Eventually confronting Ultraman Tiga, Gatanothor proved to be invincible to all of his attacks and easily defeated Tiga by turning him to stone. However, the light of humanity managed to revive Ultraman Tiga and he defeated Gatanothor in the second round.

### Selected Episodes
*Episode 45: "Eternal Life" 
*Episode 50: "Take Me Higher!"
*Episode 51: "Master of Darkness"

shortDefinition: Uluath is a cephalopodic Lovecraftian deity in the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. Created by Justin Jordan and Sebastián Carrillo, it made its first appearance in Monsters Unleashed (Vol. 3) #10 in January 2018.  ### Background Uluath...
fullContent:
Uluath is a cephalopodic Lovecraftian deity in the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. Created by Justin Jordan and Sebastián Carrillo, it made its first appearance in Monsters Unleashed (Vol. 3) #10 in January 2018.

### Background
Uluath (aka the Destroyer and the Dread Lord) is an "Undergod". Which has been sleeping in the Pacific Ocean, in the City Below the Seas. Happyology, a cult founded by a man named McTavish, attempted to awaken Uluath via the use of an ultrasonic transmitter. Elsa Bloodstone attempted to stop them, but was unable to prevent its activation. Causing the city to rise to the surface and bringing forth a horde of fishmen. She ended up being captured by the cultists and fishmen. Kid Kaiju and Aegis one of his robot like monsters arrived on the island, attempting to rescue her, and in the process completely awakened Uluath, who was defeated and knocked out by Aegis, and went back into slumber.

### Behind the Mythos
It has been suggested that Uluath was inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's iconic creation Cthulhu or, less likely, Dagon. The similarities between these entities seem apparent: ancient godlike beings which rest in a sunken island-city beneath the Pacific Ocean and served by fish-like humanoid devotees.

Another connection may be a chant made by Uluath's cultists, which goes "Nyar' L'Hagopep," a possible nod to the Outer God Nyarlathotep.

"Un-Dhu-Milhuk Would (If He Could)" is a darkly comedic Cthulhu Mythos story by author Liam Davies. It was published in the thematic anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg by Screaming Dreams in October 2013.

### Synopsis
Beneath the valleys of the Welsh coal mining country, the Elder God Un-Dhu-Miluhk sleeps, dreaming of his love, Rhu-thmar-duhk. His mind lingers on all of the fond liaisons they will have once he is awoken by the inevitable delving of the humans into his resting place, and conjures romantic poems to the creature expressing his ardour.

As the story draws to an end, an announcement is made that the last of the coal pits is to close. Un-Dhu-Miluhk, oblivious, continues dreaming his idle fantasies, convinced that any day now the foolish humans will be by to rouse him from his resting place.

### Mythos Connections
Un-Dhu-Miluhk is said to be a descendant of Great Cthulhu himself, described as "nought but a spent abstraction of his forebear …  nought but a passing of gas from the vile passage of a worthier deity" in light of his love for another.

### Trivia
* Despite being spelled "Un-Dhu-Milhuk" in the title, the creature is consistently referred to as "Un-Dhu-Miluhk" in the story itself.

Unaussprechlichen Kulten, also known as Nameless Cults or the Black Book, is a fictional grimoire in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally created by Robert E. Howard for his short story "The Children of the Night".

### Overview
Written by Friedrich von Junzt with the help of numerous "blood-curdling and partly-suspected sources" including the surviving members of the cult of Ghatanothoa, Unaussprechlichen Kulten is an occult tome said to have been published in Düsseldorf in 1839.

The pages written in the last months of the author's life were found torn into pieces with his body after his death. When his friend Alexis Ladeau managed to reassemble the fragments and read what had been written, he burned them and cut his own throat with a razor.

The book was widely suppressed, and after von Junzt's death in 1840 many people burned their copies. Not counting the poorly executed Bridewall translation (London, 1845) or the heavily edited reprint by Golden Goblin Press (New York, 1909) there were not likely to be more than half a dozen copies in existence by the 1930s. One known copy can be found in the Miskatonic University's collection.

### Contents
Among other topics, the book contains:
*Occult objects from around the world such as a strange monolith in the mountains of Hungary. (: "The Black Stone")
*A description of the Hyborian Age. (: "Black Eons")
*A description of the prehistoric province of K'naa on the continent of Mu and the story of the High Priest T'yog. (: "Out of the Aeons")
*Recreations of hieroglyphs that appeared on the carved metal cylinder in the Cabot Museum (: "Out of the Aeons") and in the visions of Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee. (: The Shadow Out of Time)
*A passage detailing a Pictish "king who rules the Dark Empire, which was a revival of an older, darker empire dating back into the Stone Age; and of the great, nameless cavern where stands the Dark Man—the image of Bran Mak Morn, carved in his likeness by a master hand while the great king yet lived, and to which each worshipper of Bran makes a pilgrimage once in his or her lifetime. Yes, that cult lives today in the descendants of Bran's people—a silent, unknown current it flows on in the great ocean of life, waiting for the stone image of the great Bran to breathe and move with sudden life, and come from the great cavern to rebuild their lost empire." "Uncle Caesar" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Mark McLaughlin.

### Synopsis
After a strange man comes to treat his ailing father, a young boy notices not only a drastic improvement in the man's health, but also a disturbing change in his personality. When the boy grows up and has a family of his own, he must consider whether to ask for the man's help in order to save his own child.

### Characters
*The Unnamed Narrator, a once dutiful son, now doting father.
*"Uncle" Caesar Mason, an apparently-immortal relative of the witch Keziah Mason.

### Publication History
"Uncle Caesar" was included in the collections The Horror In The Water Tower & Five More Tales Of The Cthulhu Mythos and The House Of The Ocelot & More Lovecraftian Nightmares.

shortDefinition: "Unda; or, The Bride of the Sea" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1915. It was published in The Providence Amateur in February 1916 and was included in the 1977 collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems.  The poem is dedicated to Lovecraft's fr...
fullContent:
"Unda; or, The Bride of the Sea" is a poem written by H. P. Lovecraft in 1915. It was published in The Providence Amateur in February 1916 and was included in the 1977 collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems.

The poem is dedicated to Lovecraft's friend Maurice W. Moe.

### Synopsis
The narrator reminisces about falling in love with a woman named Unda, the Bride of the Sea, and the cherished days they spent laughing on a beach under a cliff. One day, however, while Unda was watching the ocean from the cliff, she suddenly became serious. She descended the cliff and walked over the sand to the ocean, where she disappeared without explanation, much to the narrator's despair.

The narrator travels through the world, both on land and sea, searching for Unda, until he returns at last to the same cliff shore where she vanished. There he sees a bridge forming from the Earth to the moon, made out of wavelets and beams, where Unda stands calling for him. The narrator walks into the sea trying to reach the bridge and is happy to be reunited with Unda.

An epilogue reveals that the narrator died by drowning. The last lines of the poem are used to warn young men about the dangers of falling in love.

After many years of corresponding with the mysterious Machteld, Gerald Voss is finally invited to a meeting where he will learn the secrets of Great Cthulhu and the Old Ones. "Under the Mound" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Robert M. Price. It forms the first chapter in the multi-author miniseries The Challenge from Below.

### Synopsis
A white man searching for the body of his old Native American friend Gray Eagle ventures into tunnels leading beneath an ancient burial mound. There he finds, much to his surprise, that Gray Eagle is in fact alive and well. His friend tells him the story of the destruction of Yoth, and how this fate may befall the entire world if the dark powers which brought about the catastrophe are not stopped. 

As a precaution to ensure that the knowledge of these events does not become lost to the winds of time, the man allows himself to be transported far into the future, into the body of an insectile being, where he may be in a position to help prevent the return of the old gods.

### Characters

* The Unnamed Narrator/Zkafka, a human scholar who makes a great sacrifice for his world.
* Gray Eagle, outwardly, a normal person, but in actuality the consciousness of a Yothian - a species of long-dead reptilian creature - inhabiting a human host.

### Publication History
"Under the Mound" was first published in Lore #3 in December 1995. it was later included in the collection Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2008, and again in the anthology LORE: A Quaint and Curious Volume of Selected Stories in November 2011. 2021 saw its inclusion in the Ramble House thematic anthology The Yig Cycle.

"Under the Shelf" is a short story by the late American author Michael Shea.

### Synopsis
Two sisters on an expedition to explore the waters beneath an Antarctic glacier discover a hidden valley inhabited by a deadly arthropod-like creature. Although they are nearly killed by the beast, the intervention of an ancient entity which has slept beneath the waves allows them to escape.

### Characters
*Belinda, an adventurous young woman with a desire to push the boundaries of contemporary knowledge.
*Melody, Belinda's younger sister and fellow explorer.
*Earl, the captain of the sisters transport vessel.

### Publication History
"Under the Shelf" was first published in the Titan Books anthology The Madness of Cthulhu: Volume 1 in October 2014. It also appeared in the collection of Shea's own works, Demiurge: The Complete Cthulhu Mythos Tales of Michael Shea in December 2017.

### Trivia
*Despite containing no direct references to either Lovecraft's works or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi's inclusion of the work in Demiurge indicates his belief that it should be considered a part of the Mythos. Also, the concept of an ancient, unfathomable being which sleeps beneath the waves and is capable of peering into the depths of a human soul would seem to be Lovecraftian in nature.

fullContent:
"Undersea Quest" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by the late British author John S. Glasby. It was published posthumously in Glasby's April 2012 collection The Lonely Shadows by Borgo Press, an imprint of Wildside Press.

### Synopsis
The story consists of three leaked reports from various government agents who were involved with the 1928 raid on Innsmouth. It is prefaced by a cautionary statement on the dangers posed by the Deep Ones and other potential inhabitants of the submarine city of Y'ha-nthlei.

# Narrative of Federal Agent James P. Curran: February 27, 1928: Agent Curran and a representative of the Treasury Department travel to Arkham to interview one Robert Olmstead. Although neither of the men believe the tale they are told, they submit their reports. Curran is then assigned to an Army unit during the Innsmouth raid, and witnesses the storming of the Esoteric Order of Dagon temple along with the rounding up of many of its inhuman citizenry.
# Testimony of Federal Agent William T. Darnforth: March 2, 1928: assigned to a detachment of Marines tasked with taking Innsmouth from a different angle to the Army complement, Darnforth and his unit patrol the old smuggling tunnels beneath the town in order to prevent the denizens from escaping. There, he sees firsthand the degeneracy which has befallen Innsmouth, before bearing witness to the burning of Innsmouth docks.
# Confidential Report of Federal Investigator Walter C. Tarpey: March 5, 1928: Tarpey is assigned to a submarine, part of a task force conducting a naval blockade on Innsmouth. After the boat is attacked by Deep Ones issuing forth from the town, they proceed to the next phase of their mission: the reconnaissance and destruction of Y'ha-nthlei. Tarpey sees an enormous creature, which he believes to be Dagon, approach the submarine before the torpedoes strike home, banishing the creature and devastating the undersea city.

shortDefinition: Underwater is an American science fiction/horror movie directed by William Eubank and starring Kristin Stewart, Vincent Cassel and T. J. Miller. Although filming finished in May 2017, due to issues with production company 20th Century Fox it did not ...
fullContent:
Underwater is an American science fiction/horror movie directed by William Eubank and starring Kristin Stewart, Vincent Cassel and T. J. Miller. Although filming finished in May 2017, due to issues with production company 20th Century Fox it did not receive a cinematic release until January 2020.

The film has received generally middling to mediocre reviews and was a box office flop.

### Synopsis
When a deep water drilling station at the bottom of the Mariana Trench is struck by a freak earthquake, the few survivors must scramble to reach safely. The soon come to realise that their access to the emergency pods is blocked, and that they must travel to an abandoned facility located on the ocean bed nearby.

Travelling deeper through the station, the group's numbers dwindle as a result of secondary damage to the station and contact with a species of aggressive humanoid creatures which have somehow infiltrated the tunnels.

When the last three survivors finally traverse the seabed and reach their destination, they find that only two of the escape pods remain serviceable. Two of the group use the pods, but as they do a colossal creature with wings and a tentacled face emerged from beneath the ocean floor. The last remaining survivor overloads the abandoned facility's nuclear reactor, defeating the creature and allowing the pods to make their getaway.

### Behind the Mythos
Although not originally envisioned as a Cthulhu Mythos film, after filming was complete, director William Eubank made the decision to redesign the creature encountered at the finale as the Great Old One Cthulhu. He also stated in an interview that the film is "a secret Lovecraft story". In light of this, the humanoid creatures encountered by the crew in the tunnels could be seen as Deep Ones, although this has not been confirmed.

### Trivia
*During the credits at the beginning and ending of the film, various news articles are shown depicting the deep water drilling station, named the Kepler 822; from the dates on the article, the story takes place sometime around August 2050.
*When Norah opens Lucien’s locker she sees strange drawings pinned to the inside. One of these pictures is a copy of Lovecraft's original drawing of the Cthulhu idol. 
*The screenplay was written by Brian Duffield, who also worked on the animated series Skull Island, which features King Kong fighting a kraken that has a strong resemblance to this film's depiction of Cthulhu.

"Unexpected Turbulence" is a short Lovecraftian story by British author David Purcell, first published in Vol 5, Issue 3 of the Lovecraftiana zine in October 2020.

### Synopsis
In 1927, a young pilot attempts to be the first to make the Atlantic crossing from New York to Paris. Mid-journey, he spies a colossal being striding through the ocean and sending waves of madness through his mind before knocking his small aircraft into the ocean. Swimming to a nearby island, he encounters a cult dedicated to the entity; as the entity approaches the shore, he joins them in their worship, sure that it’s coming means the end of them all.

Unfathomable is a Cthulhu Mythos game for 3-6 players by Fantasy Flight Games. Designed by Tony Fanchi and Corey Konieczka, it was released in 2021.

### Overview
A betrayal-style board game, Unfathomable represents a group of characters aboard the steamer SS Atlantica on a voyage to Boston, Massachusetts in 1913. During the course of the journey, a series of dark occurrences take place, such as a ritualistic murder in the ship's chapel, and the sighting of mysterious creatures trailing the vessel- in actuality Mother Hydra and Father Dagon at the head of a swarm of Deep Ones. The characters are each assigned a secret alliegiance, either human or hybrid, and must work to further the goals of that faction whilst trying to determine the loyalties of the other players.

Unusually, although Unfathomable is set in Fantasy Flight's Arkham Horror Files universe, it features a cast of ten characters which are new to this game. This is to represent the fact that the game takes place several years before the events depicted in the "primary" Arkham Horror Files setting of the late 1920s.

"Unfinished Business" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
A man named Balmer comes into the possession of a pair of authentic Pickman paintings and plans to launch an exhibition before selling them. To provide security he hires private detective Wade Kearney to watch the artwork overnight.

On his first night's watch, Kearney tackles a strange creature resembling those in the paintings which is trying to enter the gallery, although it runs off after being shot. Meanwhile, Balmer receives the first of a series of phone calls threatening him with death if he does not destroy the paintings. 

On the third night, Balmer has become so disturbed by the calls that he decides to spend the night at the gallery with Kearney for protection. In the early hours, a pack of ghouls led by Richard Upton Pickman himself break into the building, kill Balmer and destroy the paintings.

### Characters
* Wade Kearney, a private investigator.
* Balmer, a profiteer looking for a big score.
* Joe Brennan, an elderly book seller.
* Richard Upton Pickman, a former artist who has devolved into a very special ghoul.

### Publication History
"Unfinished Business" was first published in the anthology Hardboiled Cthulhu in July 2006. It later appeared in Lovecraft's Disciples #12 in May 2008, and was included in the collection of Shiflet's own work They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in 2018.

"Unholy Cosmic Terror" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author Cameron Walker.

### Synopsis
A veteran NASA mission controller stumbles across evidence of a secret mission involving a previously-unknown planet whilst conducting research for his memoirs. As he digs deeper, he uncovers video footage from a rover sent to explore the new world, which is in fact the Mi-Go colony of Yuggoth. Unfortunately for the man, the mere act of viewing the film catches the attention of the Outer God Nyarlathotep, who then manifests to consume him, body and soul.

### Publication History
"Unholy Cosmic Terror" was published in Vol 5, Issue 1 of the Lovecraftiana zine in 2020.

shortDefinition: The United States of America is the home country of H. P. Lovecraft, most of his correspondents and collaborators, and the setting of the bulk of his weird fiction.  ### Lovecraft's America Lovecraft was born into a nation with 44 states--six of thos...
fullContent:
The United States of America is the home country of H. P. Lovecraft, most of his correspondents and collaborators, and the setting of the bulk of his weird fiction.

### Lovecraft's America
Lovecraft was born into a nation with 44 states--six of those admitted in the previous 12 months--and saw it grow to 48 states, with the admission of Utah (1896), Oklahoma (1907), New Mexico, and Arizona (both 1912). In 1890, the year of his birth, the census recorded nearly 63 million people in the United States; by 1940, three years after his death, the population had more than doubled to 132 million. Over the same time period, average life expectancy advanced from 45 to nearly 63 years.  

There were ten American presidents during Lovecraft's lifetime:  Benjamin Harrison (1890-93), Grover Cleveland (1893-97), William McKinley (1897-1901), Theodore Roosevelt (1901-09), William Taft (1909-1913), Woodrow Wilson (1913-21), Warren Harding (1921-23), Calvin Coolidge (1923-29), Herbert Hoover (1929-33), and Franklin Roosevelt (1933-45). Cleveland, Wilson, and Franklin Roosevelt were Democrats; the other seven were Republicans. 

In Lovecraft's lifetime, the US fought in two major wars, the Spanish-American War (1898) and World War I (1917-1918), then known as the Great War. Other important events in his era include the passage and repeal of Prohibition (1920-1933), and the Great Depression (1929-1939). 

### Travels in the US
In the first three decades of his life, Lovecraft's travel was restricted to New England, specifically Rhode Island and its two neighbouring states of Massachusetts and Connecticut. His horizons then broadened considerably, starting with a six-day trip to New York City in April 1922. In August 1922, he visited Alfred Galpin and Samuel Loveman in Cleveland, Ohio. During his two-year residency in Brooklyn, New York, he visited Philadelphia; Washington, DC; New Jersey; and upstate New York. Returning to Providence, Lovecraft visited Vermont, New Hampshire, and Maine for the first time in 1927.  

In July 1928, he took a trip south as far as Virginia, documenting his travels in the essay “Observations on Several Parts of America”. He wrote up an April 1930 visit to Charleston, South Carolina, which he found wonderfully preserved, in “An Account of Charleston”. In 1931 he returned to Charleston; visited Savannah, Georgia; and spent considerable time in St. Augustine, Key West, and other Florida towns. A trip that started in May 1932 took him to Tennessee, Mississippi, and Alabama, and allowed him to visit E. Hoffman Price in New Orleans.

In the summers of 1934 and 1935, Lovecraft had extended stays with R. H. Barlow in DeLand, Florida, visiting or revisiting several cities on the way to and from those visits.  

### America in Lovecraft's Fiction

The Unknown Abomination is an eldritch abomination from the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics.

### Background
The Unknown Abomination resided in the cavern of a mountain in the Swamp of Mists in Atlantis during the Thurian Age. It was controlled by Lieutenant Khornah via a gem and with its energy, the abomination grew. It absorbed and consumed it's victims, seizing them with its tentacles. It's slimy ichor burned the skin of those it took, which within minutes would only be bones. King Kull of Valusia buried it in a crushing avalanche of boulders.

Unspace is an extra-dimensional location in the fictional universe of Transformers by Hasbro and Takara Tomy.

### Background
Unspace is a realm of kaleidoscopic madness and anti-matter, a timeless non-space that exists beyond all reality. Cybertronians often use space bridges to travel through unspace as a means teleportation. Some entities, such as Unicron and other multiversal singularities, can transverse through unspace at will.

It is also home to the Elder Gods, a race of ancient evil entities of indescribable power. If someone is unfortunate enough to be stranded in unspace, they will likely suffer a fate far worse than death at the hands of the Elder Gods. (: Hasbro Transformers Collectors' Club issue #5) Despite being trapped in unspace, the Elder Gods were able to influence the minds of sensitive beings in the material universe, including H. P. Lovecraft who used his horror prose to channel their call. Although, the clandestine organization Oblivion killed him before he can summon them, Lovecraft's stories continued to spread throughout popular culture and the Elder Gods eventually broke free to invade the multiverse. (: Infestation 2)

fullContent:
Unspeakable Cults: Azathoth was part of an intended line of d20 System Reference Document Pathfinder supplements, each of which would have focused on a different Cthulhu Mythos entity and its cult. Unfortunately the project was abandoned; however the Azathoth volume was released. It is 26 pages long and available only as a digital file on [https://legacy.drivethrurpg.com/product/269690/Unspeakable-Cults-Azathoth DriveThruRPG].

In keeping with the then-fashion for Pathfinder and Dungeons & Dragons, the electronic book has heavily colored parchment style pages and highly effective clip art provided under license by Matt Thomason, Lord Zsezse Works, Publisher’s Choice Quality Stock Art and Rick Hershey (as Fat Dragon Games).

The publishing line of which this was intended to be a part was abandoned in early 2020 and it was announced by the designer Christopher Bunge that there is no likelihood whatsoever of further publications in this line.

### Overview


### Contents
The book contains a summary of the Cult of Azathoth, the goals of both the entity and the church, rituals, objectives and new Feats: Azathoth's Conflagration (Invocation), Azathoth’s Smite (Invocation), Expanded Mysteries (Azathoth), Fire of Azathoth (Invocation), Grimoire of the Blind God , Rite of Supplication (Azathoth) and Secret Name (Invocation).

In addition, the book also specifies Azathoth's clerics as favoring the Warhammer as their holy weapon as well as providing new suitably named spells and rituals.

Rounding out the book is a new corruption "Dream Chosen."

The work cleaves closely to the "Monster Manual" approach and straddles the themes of Pathfinder and the more recent fantasy historical settings for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

The Unspeakable Possessors are a fictional species expanded upon by Chaosium in 1995 for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game which were based on August Derleth's "The Return of Hastur".

### Background
Unspeakable Possessors are a race created by the Great Old One Hastur, made from humans who have made the Unspeakable Promise. All of which are eventually possessed by Hastur and transformed. If the one who made the Unspeakable Promise is deceased, within a few days the nearest blood relative is possessed.

The victim's form remains humanoid but becomes bloated. It has boneless fluid limbs that end in tentacle-like jaw-tipped fingers and a gray-green skin with a scaly texture. The creature retains its intelligence and knowledge (e.g. the magical kind), but now is content in destroying, killing, and devouring.

fullContent:
Untold Tales by Clark Ashton Smith is the 27th issue of leading H. P. Lovecraft scholar Robert M. Price's long running Lovecraftian fanzine Crypt of Cthulhu. Edited by Price and featuring cover art by Ros Calverley, it ran to a total of 52 pages in an A5 format and was published by Cryptic Publications in November 1984.

The issue is a special dedicated to the works of Lovecraft's close friend Clark Ashton Smith, and includes a story credited to Smith in error. Included are several of Smith's stories set in his fiction French setting, Averoigne.

Interestingly, some of the interior text for issue 26 hints that Price may have been assisted in his role as editor by Clark Ashton Smith scholar Steve Behrends

The Upas tree (Antiaris toxicaria) is an Indonesian and Australian tree. It also grows in Africa.

In folklore it was believed to poison its surroundings and said to be fatal to approach. 

The London Magazine of 1783 described it in terms of its folklore, claiming to be translated from the Dutch original account.

It is a massive plant that can reach heights of 120 feet (40 meters).

### Mythos connections
It is mentioned by name in the poem Nyaghoggua by Robert A. W. Lowndes.

Ursula Downs, the Explorer, is a character who features in Fantasy Flight Games Arkham Horror Files range of Cthulhu Mythos-related games and fiction.

### History
Never one to follow the pursuits usually associated with young women of the time, Ursula enjoyed climbing trees, digging in the mud and exploring all of the places where others didn’t want to go. After showing a natural aptitude for languages, the sciences and history, she enrolled in Boston University where she graduated first in her class at Archaeology.

Using her inheritance to finance her trips across the globe, Ursula set about exploring the remnants of lost civilisations and the ritualistic practices of remote tribes which had never before seen a westerner, selling the pieces she wrote about these expeditions to various magazines and scientific journals in order to fund future excursions. In this manner, Ursula became the world's premier female archaeologist, and one of the few people on the planet able to make boasts such as having climbed a mountain on every continent and stolen a priceless relic from a savage tribe of cannibals.

Eventually Ursula's pursuits led her to Arkham, where she had tracked down the members of a shadowy cult and their shipping container full of mysterious artefacts. Resolving to get to the bottom of things, Ursula took her first steps on the road to discovering the dark truths of the city.

### Behind the Mythos
Ursula was first introduced as an Investigator character for Fantasy Flight's Second Edition of Lovecraftian board game Arkham Horror, debuting in the Innsmouth Horror expansion. In addition to Arkham Horror, she has made appearances as a playable character in both Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and a short-lived plastic miniature of Ursula designed to replace the stock cards included in these games was released as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures line (all ).

Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Joseph S. Pulver for his novel Nightmare's Disciple. Despite its relative obscurity, the entity has appeared in several other works over the years.

### Background
Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her takes the form of a huge faceless creature with various appendages sprouting from her head, a beard of oozing horns, many reddish teats, and fish-like fins sprouting from an egg-shaped body. 

Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her's true origins are unknown, although it's been speculated that she has a connection to Shub-Niggurath, possibly being the spawn or an avatar of the Outer God. Others have theorized that she may be the twin sister of Glaaki. She is known to dwell in the Cetus constellation, near the vicinity of a red giant star known as Mira (Omicron Ceti). There have been several claims of her being summoned to Earth but most of these cases remain unconfirmed. (: Malleus Monstrorum)  

One manifestation of the entity lives in the caverns below Antioch (a Hellenic colony in modern-day Turkey), where she is worshiped by an all-female cult known as the Daughters of Isolation. Twice a month, they wear masks which are made of flayed human skin and wear sheer gowns. The women lure men to the Paradise of Daphne, promising that they will fulfill their most outrageous sexual desires. The orgy is a cover, and three victims are taken underground, who have been drugged, becoming unable to either speak or move while still being semi-conscious. They are both raped and flayed before being fed to Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her. (: Cthulhu Invictus)

### In Other Media
*Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her appears as a yaoi fangirl in the anime Haiyore! Nyaruko-san, under the name Tsuruko. She is obsessed with Mahiro and illegally came to Earth in hopes of seeing him. However, the running gag involves something always interfering with her before she can actually meet him.
*Ut'Ulls-Hr'Her is featured in the collectible card game WIXOSS by Takara Tomy.

Uvhash, also known as The Blood-Mad God of the Void, is a fictional entity created by American author James Ambuehl for his short Cthulhu Mythos story " The Advent of Uvhash".

### Description
A gigantic, vampiric red mass of eyes and tentacles, Uvhash is the archenemy of the being known as Gi-Hoveg. It dwells in the realm of Rhylkos, which is linked to the planet Mars, and it is said that whoever summons Uvhash will meet with a terrible fate. 

Uvhash seems to have affinities with the Star Vampires and the Hounds of Tindalos, and is rumoured to have been one of the mad Roman Emperor Caligula's eldritch sponsors. (: "The Advent of Uvhash")

### History
In the short story "The Advent of Uvhash", Uvhash consumed the soul of a man who was attempting astral projection under the patronage of its arch-enemy Gi-Hoveg.

Uzuldaroum is a city created by the late American author and Lovecraft contemporary Clark Ashton Smith for his Hyperborean Cycle series of fantasy fiction.

### Overview
Built after the citizens of Commoriom were forced to abandon their former home, Uzuldaroum became the new capital of Hyperborea in the days of that great civilisation. Although an opulent city, it did not compare to its predecessor, which it lay but a day or twos travel from.

One of the gods worshipped there was named Leniqua, to whom a temple was maintained. The temple's priests maintained a harem of young and beautiful women who they sold to the wealthiest men of the city on certain nights of religious significance. They believed this act to be one of worship. Leniqua was a god of the moon.

### Notable People 
*King Loquamethros, the city's founder.
*Athammaus, the headsman, or executioner.

shortDefinition: "Valentia" (sometimes appearing as "Valentia (1994)") is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan in the Cthulhu Mythos genre, first published in the 2000 anthology Dark Terrors 5. The story, which involves the discovery of strange fossils on the real-lif...
fullContent:
"Valentia" (sometimes appearing as "Valentia (1994)") is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan in the Cthulhu Mythos genre, first published in the 2000 anthology Dark Terrors 5. The story, which involves the discovery of strange fossils on the real-life Irish island of Valentia, highlights Kiernan's interest in paleontology and deep time.

The destruction of the 385-million-year-old Valentia trackway advances a common theme in Kiernan's fiction: that paleontological evidence of the true history of Earth has been suppressed.

The anomalous artifact found in the trackway--a seven-sided metal disk, "ice cold to the touch"--displays "runes or an unknown cuneiform set around the image at the disc’s center –- the tentacled face, its parrot beak, the dragon wings". This may be interpreted as an image of Cthulhu.

The final phrase Maire utters, “Theena dow’an", is revealed by an invented quote from a real book (Lady Wilde's Ancient Legends of Ireland) to be a phoneticization of Daoine Domhain, Irish for deep ones, which Kiernan links to the Fomorii, giants from Irish folklore. "[P]erhaps the most feared of all the water fairies", the quote notes, they "dwelt in Ireland before the arrival of the Gael. They...are rarely spoken of aloud."

### Characters
*Morris Whitney, a paleontologist who discovered the Valentia trackway in 1993 and came to a mysterious and tragic end in 1994.
*Anne Campbell, the story's main character, a paleontologist at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, with an apartment in Tribeca. Long ago Whitney's lover, she travels to Ireland to see what she can learn about his death.
*Arthur Randall, a colleague of Campbell's at the American Museum. He is 60 years old.
*Maire, a student who worked on Whitney's dig. She is described as a "pale, coal-haired girl from Dublin with...tourist-brochure eyes". She is Catholic but is familiar with older religions.
*Billy, another Irish student who worked on the dig with Maire.
### Publication History
After its appearance in Dark Terrors 5, edited by Stephen Jones and David Sutton, "Valentia" was included in Kiernan's 2005 short story collection To Charles Fort, With Love, and their 2019 Mythos omnibus, Houses Under the Sea.

fullContent:
Valkyrie Crusade is a Japanese mobile game developed by Nubee in March 2013, and later acquired by MyNet in January 2016, before ultimately ending its service in May 2021. The game primarily focuses on collecting and evolving various types of cards in order to battle with other players, or to conquer different areas by defeating archwitches in the campaign mode. The game also allows the player to build a city inside their kingdom, spending resources to update important facilities, with the game running in real-time as it progresses.

The story involves the player getting sent to an alternate dimension, known as the Celestial Realm, where a Shinto priestess named Oracle asks for the player to help unify the realm after it was divided by warring kingdoms. Using the knowledge given by Oracle, the player rules over a small kingdom and summons the Valkyries to be their army for the quest to dominate other kingdoms. The Valkyries are "battle maidens" who take the form of cute girls, with several of them being familiar entities from the Cthulhu Mythos.

fullContent:
"Valley Beyond the Stars" is a story in issue #152 of the first volume of Savage Sword of Conan. Written by Charles Dixon, it was published in September 1988 by Marvel Comics. 

### Synopsis
The evil Queen Sullimma, ruler of the Set-worshipping kingdom of Stygia, and her hunchbacked crone hatch a plan to call forth the Elder God Yog Sothath when the stars come into their proper alignment. Conan joins up with a small band determined to stop her, including a holy man, a crippled seer, and the seer's sister.

Battling their way across the barren desert, the group must face down bandits, armed soldiers, and flying monstrosities in their quest, but are ultimately successful in closing Yog-Sothath's portal, killing Queen Sullimma and curing the young mystic of all his ails. In the aftermath, it is revealed that their actions have banished Yog-Sothath from the world for ten thousand years.

### Trivia

* Yog Sothath is given many names by the people of the Hyborian Age, including Yog Sothoth, Sodathat, Yathg Soggatha, Soggoth, Sodatha, Sothath, Sedoula, Sogotha, Yog Sothath, Yog the Mighty, and Yog the Fearsome.

Vampires are found in the mythology and folklore of many of mankind's cultures as creatures sustained by the blood or lifeforce of a human. Vampire-like creatures occur in H. P. Lovecraft's work, and appear more explicitly in works by other writers of the Cthulhu Mythos.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The vampire legend is a central theme in H. P. Lovecraft's "The Shunned House", but it is not clear whether the half-fungoid / half-incorporeal monster of that tale was supposed to be regarded as a vampire in the literal or merely the metaphorical sense. After a series of unexplained deaths in the house, the servant Ann White insiststhere must lie buried beneath the house one of those vampires—the dead who retain their bodily form and live on the blood or breath of the living—whose hideous legions send their preying shapes or spirits abroad by night. To destroy a vampire one must, the grandmothers say, exhume it and burn its heart, or at least drive a stake through that organ.The narrator notes that White comes from Exeter, Rhode Island, a "remote bit of backwoods" that was a seat of the most uncomfortable superstitions. As lately as 1892 an Exeter community exhumed a dead body and ceremoniously burnt its heart in order to prevent certain alleged visitations injurious to the public health and peace.This is a reference to the real-world case of Mercy Brown of Exeter, a suspected vampire whose body was exhumed and her heart burned in 1892. Still, the narrator says of himself and his uncle, Elihu Whipple: To say that we actually believed in vampires or werewolves would be a carelessly inclusive statement. Rather must it be said that we were not prepared to deny the possibility of certain unfamiliar and unclassified modifications of vital force and attenuated matter.The narrator concludes that the malign force in the house is "some exotic emanation; some vampirish vapour such as Exeter rustics tell of as lurking over certain churchyards."

).]]
Other Lovecraft stories feature characters that have been resurrected from death and display traits associated with vampirism: Joseph Curwen from The Case of Charles Dexter Ward was responsible for "revolting cases of vampirism" in which "a lean, lithe, leaping monster with burning eyes...fastened its teeth in the throat or upper arm and feasted ravenously." Surama from "The Last Test" could only be killed by fire or by a stake driven through his heart. 

Other blood-sucking entities include Rhan-Tegoth (: "The Horror in the Museum") and the Dunwich Horror (: "The Dunwich Horror"). Brown Jenkin, Keziah Mason's familiar in "The Dreams in the Witch-House," is reported by witnesses to have "nursed on the witch’s blood—which it sucked like a vampire."

Alonzo Typer, an expert on the occult in "The Diary of Alonzo Typer," privately published "papers on vampirism, ghouls, and poltergeist phenomena..

The Vampire Intelligence are a Lovecraftian-like eldritch vampiric race in the fictional universe of Rifts the pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium. They resemble some of the conventional conceptualizations of "Old Ones" and the Shoggoth.

### Background
Vampire Intelligences are a race of sadistic and malevolent alien intelligences, inter-dimensional conquerors and rivals of the Splugorth. Their horrifying eldritch form consists of a lump of slime covered flesh with a huge cyclopean eye surrounded with a hundred smaller eyes. The body itself can reach up to 200 ft in diameter. A dozen tentacles ending in fanged mouths protrude from the flesh and are able to stretch up to 200 ft. They are vampiric beings which live off of a world's magical energy and enjoy feeding on the blood of humanoids.

They are incredibly strong and are able to regenerate, even capable of surviving a 1.2 megaton nuke, though not without taking grievous wounds. Vampire Intelligences have formidable psionic abilities and are able to wield magic. As a supernatural entity it is vulnerable to weapons of wood or silver, and both holy and running water all of which can do more damage than conventional and energy weapons.

Vampire Intelligences can send fragments of their essence into other dimensions, bonding with willing hosts with whom they are able to communicate. Once it is in possession of a host, the lifeforce shard fragments further into thousands of tiny pieces which are used to create vampires. A Vampire Intelligence is able to physically enter and inhabit a dimension once a few thousand vampires are created. It then seizes control of a magical nexus (ley lines) which permits it to maintain a physical presence in that dimension. A fortress is then built at the location to prevent its use by inter-dimensional travelers or other magical users. As long as its in that dimension, the Vampire Intelligence is linked to all the vampires which its lifeforce created, up to several miles from its location. Several of them have established strongholds in the future post-apocalyptic Earth, most of them in what used to be Mexico, domains known as the Vampire Kingdoms.

Vampirella is a comic book hero created by Forrest J Ackerman, as the eponymous character for the horror comics magazine Vampirella, published by Warren Publishing. The Vampirella comics would go through several other publishers, including Harris Publications and later Dynamite Entertainment. Her background has changed depending on the publisher, starting as a space vampire from the planet Drakulon to being the daughter of a vampire from the dimension of Hell.

### Background
Vampirella is a vampire, who possesses most of the powers of vampires and none of the weaknesses. Therefore she is able to walk in daylight and is neither deterred or hurt by holy symbols / items (e.g. crucifix) and blessed / sacred materials (e.g. holy water). She defends humanity from the forces of the supernatural which would enslave, torture, feed, or kill them.

Among her enemies have been vampires, werewolves, demons, zombies, Dracula, the Gods of Chaos, Xenomorphs, and the Old Gods. Two incarnations of Vampirella have had encounters with the Cthulhu Mythos. One fought side by side with Ash Williams against the Army of Darkness, and another one encountered Herbert West who awakened a death god.

Vampirella vs. Reanimator is a four-issue crossover mini-series which pits the superhero Vampirella against H. P. Lovecraft's demented doctor Herbert West. Written by Cullen Bunn and featuring artwork by Blacky Shepherd, it was based on an original story by Bunn and Shepherd, and was first published by Dynamite Entertainment between December 2018 and April 2019; a trade paperback collecting all issues was released in August 2019. 

Although the series featured colour covers - and an extensive number of alternate covers showcased in the collected edition - the story itself is rendered almost entirely in black-and-white, including only a few splashes of colour here and there, mostly red to denote blood, and a sickly yellow or purple for West's reagents. 

### Synopsis
During the course of his quest to conquer death, crazed scientist Herbert West accidentally awakens the Aztec Goddess of Death Mictecaciguatl, in reality a powerful member of the species to which Vampirella belongs, the Drakulons.

When Vampirella becomes aware of what has transpired, she immediately reacts, knowing that whatever Mictecaciguatl has planned will be disastrous for the human race. However, the reagent used on the goddess by West has granted her a tremendous level of power, and Vampirella is easily defeated.

In an effort to gain an ally, Vampirella awakens Mictecaciguatl's husband, the Death God Mictlantecuhtl, believing that Mictecaciguatl's dalliance with West will drive him into paroxysms of jealousy sufficient to kill his errant wife. However, when confronted the goddess reveals to him that she had only been using West to construct a portal to Drakulon, one which will allow a dark energy to flow through and consume the Earth.

In desperation, Vampirella injects herself with a new version of West' reagent, and becomes even more powerful than the Death Gods. She easily overcomes them, killing Mictlantecuhtl outright, and cursing Mictecaciguatl to ten thousand years of torment in a limbo-like realm. When she returns to wreak her vengeance on West, he has already made his escape.

### Synopsis
The Voodoo Priestess Marie Laveau plans to resurrect Varnae, the original Lord of Vampires, with the Darkhold.

### Note
The vampires of Marvel Earth are part of the Mythos. Being created by the Darkhold (the source of the Necronomicon), which was created by the Elder God Chthon. The Darkhold not only has a spell which creates vampires but one that destroys them. Vampires have used the Darkhold to enhance themselves and Dracula, the Lord of Vampires was himself destroyed and restored by the Darkhold, and has used it to increase his powers.

Vârcolac is a fictional character in the Marvel universe which first appeared in 1988 in issue #2 of the 2nd volume of the Werewolf by Night comic book series.

### Background
Vârcolac was one of the Wolf Lords, created by the Elder God Chthon by conducting mystic genetic experiments on humans, twisting the flesh of demon, human, and beast. The most feared of the Wolf Lords was Varcolac, a relentlessly merciless hunter, from whom no prey could escape. He sired the bloodline that would give rise to the Midgard Serpent and Fenris Wolf, and spawned the Wolf-Men. When modern werewolves emerged due to the experiments conducted by aliens in the Savage Land, Varcolac spread his influence to the peaceful werewolves and over time helped make them a violent race.

He was a demon of great power that possessed a variety of powers including a psychic connection to o to all vampires, superhuman speed + agility + strength, shape shifting, and making those werewolves under its influence more feral and murderous. It ruled over a hell in which the souls of deceased werewolves ended up, where they are tormented for eternity. The landscape was a rocky one, with impaled or hung werewolf skeletons or decomposing sentient bodies scattered everywhere. In this domain he was omnipotent and used the souls to create a physical form.

Varnae is a fictional character created by Marvel Comics, first appearing in the story "Tomb of Dracula: The Blood Request" (Bizarre Adventures Vol 1 #33, December, 1982), written and penciled by Steve Bissette.

### Background
Varnae was an Atlantean sorcerer during the Thurian Age. Circa 19,000 BC, he participated in the Assemblage of Avatars, a congress of sorcerers associated with the four Elder Gods of Earth (Chthon, Oshtur, Set, and Gaea).

Circa 18,500 BC, after being mortally wounded by Kull, King of Valusia, Varnae volunteered to be the subject of a ritual held by his fellow or allied Atlantean Darkholders, followers of the Kull-slain Thulsa Doom, who used the Darkhold (the black book of Chthon) to create the first vampire. They tried to make him subservient to them, only for Varnae to slay the cultists and turn them into vampires, establishing himself as the "Lord of the Vampires". For centuries afterwards he was worshiped by the undead.

When Atlantis sunk circa 18,000 BC, Varnae went into suspended animation, though he received visions of what happened in the world during his sleep. He awakened during the Hyborian Age circa 10,000 BC, established himself in Koth, and clashed with Conan of Cimmeria.

He became known as Baal in Babylonia, and in Mesopotamia circa 2000 BC, Varnae forced Aamshed, a Sumerian sorceress, to create a ritual which would vastly increase his power, but she corrupted the spell in order to make it useless to him, and foiled his attempt to raise Atlantis. He later observed a group of Wise Men heading toward Bethlehem, and sent vermin hordes to attack them. A Timespirit came to their aid and fought the vermin and later Varnae, and the three remaining Wise Men continued on to Bethlehem. Along his travels and plots, he became known as Tsathoggua to the Tcho-Tcho People, and Croatoan to the Native Americans.

In AD 1000, vampires led by Varnae wiped out the Viking settlements in North America, whom were then avenged by Thor, who decimated the vampires. In the 12th century, he led an army fo vampires against Rome itself. He then trained a mystic who conquered the mystical Tibetan city of Kamar-Taj in the 15th century, who was later defeated by the Ancient One. Tired of an undead existence spanning thousands of years, he chose Vlad Tepes as his successor and manipulated him into becoming first a vampire and then the new Lord of the Vampires. He committed suicide by walking into the sunlight. In the late 20th century, he was brought back to life (as a vampire) by an incantation from the Darkhold. Immediately battling Doctor Strange, he embraced being once again a vampire, as Doctor Strange was a truly worthy foe. He later battled Blade the Vampire-Slayer and the Nighstalkers, and he was destroyed. His spirit ended up returning to Earth and possessed another vampire, turning it into his own body.

Vasili Oukranikov  is a fictional character who appears in the story "The Ghost-Eater", written by H. P. Lovecraft with C. M. Eddy, Jr. Oukranikov was a werewolf in life, and in death is a ghost who haunts the Devil's Woods between Mayfair and Glendale in Maine.

The character, a Russian immigrant, is described as "a tall, thin, handsome chap with shiny yellow hair and a wonderful manner"; he is  strikingly handsome, with thin, clean-shaven face, glossy, flaxen hair neatly brushed, long, regular eyebrows that met in a slanting angle above the nose, shapely ears set low and well back on the head, and large expressive gray eyes almost luminous in their animation. Oukranikov is of "impressive height", and walks with "long, limping steps"; he wears a "long lounging-robe of gray swathing his lean form." He has "a magnificently even set of firm white teeth," and a visitor is struck by "the fineness of his slender hands, with their long, tapering fingers whose ruddy, almond-shaped nails were slightly curved and exquisitely manicured"--in striking contrast to the "huge hairy arms that hung at his side".

He is a man of "engaging personality": "His voice was soothing and well modulated, and his eyes held a calmness almost hypnotic." But there is a "quality of strangeness in him; some subtle alienage that could hardly be analyzed." His eyes glow "almost phosphorescently" in a darkened room.

Oukranikov is remembered by a Glendale resident as "a servant of the devil—a werewolf and eater of men." When transformed, he takes on "the gaunt form of a great gray wolf." He walks with one hind foot...held in the air, as though wounded by some stray shot." In his wolf shape, he has the same "gray phosphorescent eyes" that he does in human guise.

Suspicions about Oukranikov were confirmed when "one night somebody took a pot shot at the wolf, and the next time the Russian came into Glendale he walked with a limp." When another Russian immigrant, Feodor Tchernevsky (known as the Count), went to confront him, he was killed by the werewolf; townsfolk "found the Count’s mangled body...and a gaunt gray wolf hovering over it with blood-slavering jaws."  The mob "killed it—filled it full of lead and buried it in the house, and then burned the place down." This happened 60 years before the present day of the story, which was published in 1924--so 1864 or earlier.

The Vaults of Zin is a fictional location created by the late American author Howard Phillips Lovecraft for his fantasy novella The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath.

### Overview

### Description
The veerla are thought of as spirits or as creatures from somewhere outside. They are nearly immaterial and immune to all weapons and most magic. (: Arkham Unveiled)

A veerla attacks its enemy by trying to possess it, whether it is a living creature or a dead body. If successful, the possession and animation can last indefinitely. A possessed victim behaves like a zombie, foraging afield and lacking any rational intelligence. (: Arkham Unveiled)

"Venice Burning" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by Canadian author A. C. Wise. It was first published in the Innsmouth Free Press anthology Future Lovecraft in November 2011.

### Synopsis
Ara is a hunter who specialises in finding people in a world in which sunken R'lyeh has risen and forever transformed the entire history of the human race. Engaged to find the son of a missing senator, a man named Marco, she uses her altered physiology to travel through time in search of her target, while confronting her own demons. When eventually Ara finds Marco, she is forced to make a choice on whether to continue to survive or, as Marco has chosen, face a long-awaited oblivion.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Venice Burning" has also been included in the thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods by Simian Publishing in October 2015.

In January 2013, a reading was featured on the digital audio magazine Pseudopod.

The Venusians, also known as Man-Lizards are a reptilian species that live in cities and towers in the thick jungles of the planet Venus and worship the Venusian crystals. Despite being initially peaceful they now defend their crystals with swords and poison darts. In addition to this they are viewed as primitive by their human opponents when in fact they are highly intelligent.

### Biology
Venusians are upright bipeds like humans, with a vaguely reptilian appearance. They stand about 7 ft (~ 2.13 meters) tall on average, although some individuals can be as tall as 8 ft (~ 2.43 meters). Their legs are proportionally short and their feet are shaped like suction cups. They have difficulty seeing in the dark and rarely attack at night. Kenton J. Stanfield believes that they must have some kind of sixth sense which allows them to detect the presence of crystals, as they are always able to identify humans who are carrying crystals with them, and only attack those that do. (: "In the Walls of Eryx")

### Language
They are said to communicate telepathically through the movements of the four tentacles on their chests.

### Venusian Crystals
The shining spheroid crystals hold a great religious significance to the Venusians and they construct elaborate mazes with invisible walls to protect them and trap potential thieves.

Upon finding one of these mazes and the human corpses within, the Crystal Company decides to step up their efforts to annihilate the lizardmen completely.

The Venusian crystals are a fictional type of extraterrestrial material featured in the science fiction short story "In the Walls of Eryx", by H. P. Lovecraft and Kenneth Sterling.

### Overview
The crystals are shining egg-like spheroids which occur in the jungles of Venus, being more commonly found scattered in streams and river-beds. The big deposits are guarded by the Venusians, who worship the crystals religiously, despite having no practical use for them. Humans, on the other hand, seek them out as a power source. A single crystal, despite being no larger than a chicken egg, can generate enough energy "to keep a city warm for a year".

While the crystals can be detected with a handheld device known, appropriately, as a crystal-detector, Kenton J. Stanfield has also speculated that the Venusians must have some natural means of detecting them, as they never fail to attack humans who are carrying them, no matter how concealed. (: "In the Walls of Eryx")

"Venusian Hell" is a short Yellow Mythos story by American author Brian Barr. The third instalment in his King in Yellow series, it was first published in the J. Ellington Ashton Press anthology Doorway to Death in September 2015.

### Synopsis
When her former crewmates begin to mysteriously die, grounded astronaut Alicia Meadows begins to look into the government coverup of derelict alien spacecraft which they had discovered on their last mission. Discovering a link between the strange symbol etched into the craft and an ancient play called The King in Yellow, she manages to track down a copy. After reading it, Alicia embarks on a murder spree across America, slowly paving the way for her new master to establish a hold on Earth.

### Publication History
Since its first publication in 2015, "Venusian Hell" has also appeared in an independently-published chapbook to which it lends its name (2019) and the collection Brian Barr's King in Yellow (2019).

Vermont is a state in the New England region of the United States. H. P. Lovecraft visited it twice, in 1927 and 1928, and later used it as the setting for his story "The Whisperer in Darkness".

Vermont's population in 1930, the year Lovecraft wrote his story, was 359,611. Its largest city at the time was Burlington, with 24,789 residents. Vermont's capital is Montpelier, which then had 7,837 people.

### Travels
Lovecraft first visited Vermont in August 1927, one of several New England locales he saw that summer. This visit produced the travelogue "Vermont--a First Impression", which first appeared posthumously in Something About Cats and Other Pieces (Arkham House, 1949).

He returned to the state at the invitation of his correspondent Vrest Orton, spending two weeks with him in Brattleboro in June 1928. The Mi-Go sightings occasioned by the flood occur in real Vermont rivers; one encounter is "connected with the Winooski River near Montpelier, another attached to the West River in Windham County beyond Newfane, and a third centring in the Passumpsic in Caledonia County above Lyndonville."

The only other mention of Vermont in Lovecraft's fiction is in The Shadow Over Innsmouth, where the Newburyport station agent--who is the first person to tell Olmstead about Innsmouth--mentions wild tales about devil worship there, then says,  "but I come from Panton, Vermont, and that kind of story don’t go down with me."

Lovecraft and Clark Ashton Smith, in which Cthulhu is the offspring of Nug (in Lovecraft's version) or Cxaxukluth (in Smith's version).

Vibur was created by Chaosium in 1995 for its Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Background
Vibur is a 12 ft tall Great Old One from another plane of existence which has been on Earth for a half-dozen millennia. Whose lumpy pear-shaped body is covered by a fur-like matted black covering. Lacking feet or limbs, it rarely moves but for convenience will shift from one point to another. Small tentacles will occasionally twitch or pass across its body. Radioactive glowing finger-length hexagonal and triangular stones are emitted like feces. Growing on its fur is a blue fungus-like substance which is dangerous to humans. The being's perception and metabolism are those of another universe, and is not fully within the material universe itself. It has incredible psionic abilities, can regenerate itself from a nuclear attack, and is able to teleport itself light years away from a nuclear strike.

Exposure to the fungus risks infection and inhalation of the spores results in infection, which starts with random instances of extreme pain, the loss of physical senses, and experiencing confusing odors, terrible visions, and seeing colors beyond what humans normally see. Vivid nightmares, clinical insanity, and profound depression are common. Eventually the victims loses physical sensation and access to voluntary muscles, and the eyeballs are eaten away by bluish fluid. Becoming a zombie which is completely controlled by Vibur, with the victim's memory and consciousness trapped and helpless within. A third die within 2 weeks, while the majority continue to be transformed by the blue fungus as it locks the consciousness in never ending pain. By this time they are for all intents and purposes dead though the body continues to eat and digest what it consumes. It takes several more months before its tortuous undead life finally ends.

Viburnia is a fictional character created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his tongue-in-cheek "Family Tree of Azathoth".

### Overview
Little is known of Viburnia other than that she was a Roman noblewoman descended from Nyarlathotep. She mated with the being known as Ghoth the Burrower, itself a descendant of Cthulhu, a coupling which Lovecraft described as a "hellish and nameless tragedy" and eventually resulted in the birth of himself and Owen Gwynedd, amongst many others.

fullContent:
Jean-Marie-Mathias-Philippe-Auguste, comte de Villiers de l'Isle-Adam (November 7, 1838 – August 19, 1889) was a French symbolist writer.

Villiers de l'Isle-Adam was born in Saint-Brieuc, Brittany, to a distinguished aristocratic family. His parents, Marquis Joseph-Toussaint and Marie-Francoise (née Le Nepvou de Carfort) were not rich, however, and were financially supported by Marie's aunt, Mademoiselle de Kerinou. His father became obsessed with the idea he could restore the family fortune by finding the lost treasure of the Knights of Malta, reputedly buried near Quintin during the French Revolution. Consequently, he spent large sums of money buying land, excavating it and then selling it at a loss when he failed to find anything of value. The young Villiers' education was troubled (he attended over half a dozen different schools) but from an early age his family were convinced he was an artistic genius: as a child he composed poetry and music. The most important occurrence in these Breton years was probably the death of a young girl with whom Villiers was in love, an event which would deeply influence his literary imagination.

### Writing
Villiers' works, in the romantic style, are often fantastic in plot and filled with mystery and horror. Important among them are the drama Axel (1890), the novel L'Ève future ("Tomorrow's Eve") (1886), and the short-story collection, Contes cruels (1883, tr. Sardonic Tales, 1927). L'Ève future greatly helped to popularize the term "Android" (Andréide in French).

Of his works, H.P.Lovecraft was very fond of the story A Torture by Hope.
