fullContent:
Vincent Price (1911 – 1993) was an American actor who became one of the most celebrated names in the horror genre. He starred in two adaptations of stories set in the Cthulhu Mythos. The first was The Haunted Palace (1963), directed by Roger Corman and based on H. P. Lovecraft's The Case of Charles Dexter Ward and Edgar Allan Poe's "The Haunted Palace". The second was "The Return of the Sorcerer" (1972), an episode of Rod Serling's anthology TV series Night Gallery, based on Clark Ashton Smith's short story of the same name. In both of these, Price did double-duty, playing Charles Dexter Ward and his ancestor Joseph Curwen in the film, and the twin sorcerers John and Helman Carnby in the episode.

Price's association with horror, fantasy, and science fiction spans over five decades, from playing the titular role in The Invisible Man Returns (1940) to the unnamed inventor in Edward Scissorhands (1990). Other memorable credits include The Fly (1958), The Last Man on Earth (1964), and The Abominable Dr. Phibes (1971), to cite but a few.

In addition to The Haunted Palace, Price starred in seven other films based on the works of Poe: House of Usher (1960), The Pit and the Pendulum (1961), Tales of Terror (1962), The Raven (1963), The Masque of the Red Death (1964), The Tomb of Ligeia (1964), and City Under the Sea, a.k.a. War-Gods of the Deep (1965). All except the last one were directed by Corman. He also played leading roles in adaptations of classics by Jules Verne (Master of the World, 1961), Thomas De Quincey (Confessions of an Opium Eater, 1962), and Guy de Maupassant (Diary of a Madman, 1963).

On television, Price played the brilliant and puntastic villain Egghead in Batman (1966), and the sinister but heroic sorcerer Vincent Van Ghoul in The 13 Ghosts of Scooby-Doo (1985), and made guest appearances on Alfred Hitchcock Presents, The Man from U.N.C.L.E., Voyage to the Bottom of the Sea, Daniel Boone, Columbo, The Bionic Woman, The Muppet Show, and The Love Boat, among others.

Charles Vincent Emerson Starrett (1886 - 1974) was a Canadian-American journalist, mystery and fantasy author, poet, and literary scholar who corresponded with H. P. Lovecraft. He is perhaps most well known for his pioneer works of Sherlock Holmes scholarship. He was also a fan of Arthur Machen and helped to popularise Machen's work in America.

Born in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, Starrett's family moved to Chicago, Illinois, USA. Some of his short stories were published in the earliest issues of Weird Tales in 1923. The 1935 movie The Great Hotel Murder was based on Starrett's story "Recipe for Murder".

Starrett wrote a poem about Lovecraft titled "HPL", which was published in the 1949 Arkham House anthology Something About Cats and Other Pieces. He also contributed to the Yellow Mythos with the poem "Cordelia's Song from The King in Yellow", which first appeared in Weird Tales and was reprinted in Lin Carter's 1971 anthology The Spawn of Cthulhu.

Virgil Warden Finlay (July 23, 1914 – January 18, 1971) was an American illustrator who specialized in fantasy, science fiction, and horror artwork. He began his career at the classic pulp magazine Weird Tales; H. P. Lovecraft called him "the best all-around artist Weird Tales has ever had." Finlay illustrated several of Lovecraft's stories, and provided the cover art for Arkham House's first collection of Lovecraft's work, The Outsider and Others. Finlay's depiction of Lovecraft as an 18th century gentleman, "The Old Gentleman From Providence" (1937), has become iconic.

### Biography
Born in Rochester, New York, the son of woodworker Warden Finlay, who died in 1935 at the age of 40. That same year, 21-year-old Virgil sent Weird Tales editor Farnsworth Wright six samples of his art. Wright was impressed with his talent, but only assigned him work after running tests to make sure Finlay's finely detailed style would translate to the pulp medium. Finlay went on to contribute interior art to 62 issues of Weird Tales, while also painting 19 covers. Finlay's art would accompany stories by several writers in Lovecraft's circle, including Robert Bloch, Henry Kuttner, Frank Belknap Long, A. Merritt, C. L. Moore, and Clark Ashton Smith. He was a convert to Judaism.

Finlay joined the US military during World War II, seeing combat on Okinawa and making poster and illustrations for the Morale Services.

"Visiting Rights" is a short story by author Joff Brown, which is loosely linked to the Cthulhu Mythos. It was published in the Salomé Jones-edited anthology Cthulhu Lives! by Ghostwoods Books in August 2014.

### Synopsis
Young Nate's parents are divorced, and his mum has started seeing an odd little man named Bernard. When one night He overhears his mum and Bernard talking about a rite they are planning to conduct upon him, he is convinced that he is to be sacrificed in some bloodthirsty ceremony.

When he tells his dad, he becomes immediately and understandably concerned, and it is revealed that both father and son are predatory, shapeshifting entities. His father tells Nate that he believes the rite is to remove the part of him that is not human, but tells him that he needs to return home anyway.

Later that week, Bernard attempts to conduct the Ritual of Severance, but young Nate manages to escape to the front door. Opening it, he finds his dad - fully transformed into his other form - waiting, along with a group of entities named the Authorities "draped tall and monstrous across the sky," amongst them his grandfather. The creatures have clearly taken offence at having one of their own threatened, and begin to move in on Bernard…

### Behind the Mythos
When discussing the Ritual of Severance with a colleague on the phone, Bernard mentions that they will be using "the Leshek Concordance … from Leng."

Later, during the course of the rite, Bernard says that "[w]e’ll cut out the part that belongs to the Old Ones." Which Old Ones he is referring to is unknown, although later comments confirm that the Authorities to which Nate and his father are related are not of this world.

Vitas Varnas is a fictional character who appears in numerous Cthulhu Mythos role-playing games and supplements. He first appears in Pax Cthuliana and then in the Call of Cthulhu supplement The Sassoon Files. Vitas is usually portrayed as an eccentric character that helps characters either with hints or assets.

### Biography
### Pax Cthuliana
Appearing in London 1927, he is first encountered at the Cleopatra's Needle obelisk where he helps guide the investigators with hints, either direct or vague, to discovering the Yellow Sign on it. Later throughout he continues to help guide them as well as free them from prison if needed. It is suggested that he could be an avatar of Nyarlathotep.

### The Sassoon Files
In 1920's Shanghai, Varnas is an actor with an interest in the occult and seeks adventure. He travels to Shanghai in hope of raising funds for his cinematographic masterpiece and build his network, and whilst there practices his art at the Great World Amusement Arcade. He gains critical acclaim for his vaudeville act "Arin & Danny - The Two Grumps" where he plays the role of Arin and his co-star Lauri O'Malley as Danny, which gains the attention of businessman Victor Sassoon. Victor pitches his idea to collaborate with Vitas on making a movie and through Victor he's able to access the secret occult scene in Shanghai.

### Other appearances
*Arkham Relic Hunt - He's mentioned on one of the Cultist Initiate cards which says "All! Hail! Magus Vitas Varnas!".
*Miskatonic University: The Restricted Collection - He appears as a graduate of Miskatonic University and a member of the Mu Pi Psi fraternity.

### Trivia
*Vitas Varnas is an insert of the real-life actor, producer and writer of the same name.

Dracula is a fictional character created by Bram Stoker for his 1897 novel of the same name. He was loosely based on the 15th century Wallachian prince Vlad III, a.k.a. Vlad Tepes (Vlad the Impaler) or Vlad Dracula. In the novel, Dracula is a centuries-old vampire who moves from Transylvania to England. Due to the novel's influence, his name has become almost a synonym for blood-drinking undead.

Vlad Dracula has appeared in Marvel Comics since 1951, usually as a B-list villain, although in the supernatural-related issues he was a A-list villain.

As of the start of the 21st century, Dracula has appeared in comics published by Dynamite Entertainment as the primary antagonist of Vampirella and an occasional antagonist or ally of Ash Williams, using the Necronomicon or in opposition to its forces.

### Background
Hailing from the Carpathian Mountains in Transylvania, Count Dracula is a powerful vampire who must sustain himself by drinking the blood of the living. He has the power of hypnotism and is able to form psychic links with his victims, as well as controlling animals and manipulating the weather. He can change his appearance and take the form of a bat, wolf, or mist. As a creature of the night, he loses some of his abilities during the day. He must sleep on soil from his homeland to regain his strength, and can be repelled by garlic or crosses. Those on whose blood he has fed will become vampires too after death, unless Dracula is destroyed first. (: Dracula)

### In Other Media
### Marvel Comics
Dracula was in his mortal life the ruler of the 15th century principality of Wallachia, Romania. Who fought the Ottoman Turks who were beginning their expansion into the Balkans. Due to a series of events orchestrated by Varnae the millennia old Atlantean Lord of Vampires, he became a vampire and then the new Lord of Vampires. Over the centuries he has been involved in various historical events and clashed with various supernatural beings, until the emergence of superhumans (mutants, mutates, and both mystical and technologically enhanced heroes).

Due to the role that the Darkhold played in the creation of vampires and the powerful dark magic within, the pages of the Darkhold have played an on and off role in Dracula's life. Sometimes he uses the spells in it for his purpose, other times he attempts to find a lost page and is stopped by heroes. Other times a rival or enemy of Dracula is the one attempting to use the Darkhold, and Dracula by hims

The Voors are a fictional ancient race created by Lin Carter for his short story "The Secret in the Parchment". They were later incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game.

Their name comes from the "kingdom of Voor" mentioned in Arthur Machen's "The White People", although in that story, the word didn't refer to any type of creature, but to something like a veil of darkness.

### Description
The Voors are a race of puffy worm-like dwarves with white skin and no eyes, but this was not their original appearance. 

The Voors were once the most prosperous species on Earth, but steady out-competition by the Hyperboreans forced them underground. They worship a pantheon of chthonic gods including Tsathoggua, Abhoth, Atlach-Nacha, and Ubbo-Sathla.

The Voormis are a fictional race of cave-dwelling humanoids who worship Tsathoggua. They are the primary focus of the short story "The Scroll of Morloc" by Lin Carter and Clark Ashton Smith.

### Description
They are referred to as the Voormi (plural: Voormis) in The Pnakotic Fragments.

The Voormis considered themselves the chosen minions of Tsathoggua, and his direct descendants.




The Voormis are described as three-toed, umber-colored, fur-covered humanoids though they are carefully differentiated from their traditional enemies (the shaggier-haired but superficially similar Gnophkehs who worshiped the Great Old One Rhan-Tegoth). Both of them are further differentiated from true humans. The Voormis communicate by dog-like howls.

They reside in the continent of Hyperborea, which will be known in the future as Mhu Thulan. The Voormi inhabit cave systems under the four-coned extinct volcano named after them - Mount Voormithadreth, the tallest peak in the Eiglophian mountains. Their ancestors, as described by Carter's narrative, were originally thralls of the Serpent People who escaped after the continent of the latter sank to the sea. They are shamanistic and apparently begun dwelling underground in an effort to imitate their deity, Tsathoggua, under the leadership of the eponymous Voorm.



The Voormis established a thriving culture in the surface Hyperborea before the coming of humans; establishing citadels in the island of Ta-Shon

The Vorlons are a Lovecraftian-like alien race in the fictional universe of the Babylon 5 live-action television series.

### Background
The Vorlons are an ancient race, one of the First Ones, and have been around for over a billion years old. It's a race of partly translucent, bioluminescent radially symmetrical multi-tentacled creatures. Thoughout history, they have manipulated the development of many of the younger races, appearing to them as divine beings. Through an actively projected telepathic image, any individual who descends from one of those races and sees a Vorlon outside of a container suit, perceives the Vorlon(s) as a divine being of their mythology and/or history.

Vorlons are connected to each other telepathically and have a telepathic connection to their own vessels. Their strongest influence on the minds of younger races is when the individual's mind is in an altered state, such as when exhausted or while sleeping. Vorlons also possess telekinetic powers, including flight. Like the Shadows, they too use organic technology, such as their sentient squid-like starships. Though unlike the Shadows they don't use sentient lifeforms as parts in their ships. The Vorlons possess miles-long planet killer starships that can shatter worlds with lightning-like streams of particles.

Unlike their long time rivals, the Shadows, the Vorlons believe that the evolution of races reach their fullest potential is via order and discipline. Younger races are to be guided and taught, and they in turn have to obey the Vorlons. Recently they orchestrated the emergence of telepaths among the younger races, to use them as weapons against the Shadows.

Vorvadoss (also known as The Flaming One) is a fictional deity in the Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Henry Kuttner for his short story "The Eater of Souls".

### Description
Cloaked in a silvery mist of darkness, only inklings of the face of the entity have ever been visible, described as utterly inhuman and only half-visible features arranged in non-human patterns following alien geometries. Its eyes are clear and black, with tiny green flickering flames seen within them. If inclined to help, despite its passionless alien expression, it can induce reassurance in one who beholds it. (: "The Invaders," Henry Kuttner)

### Worshippers
The only known worshippers dwell on Bel Yarnak, the inhabitants of which are only known to be non-anthropoid and utterly unlike mankind in countenance. Vorvadoss has forbidden its own worship to any but the Sindara, the rulers of Bel Yarnak, whom can call upon the deity for advice. Vorvadoss seems to respond in - perhaps manipulative - riddles, as suits its purposes. (: "The Eater of Souls," Henry Kuttner)

### Behind the Mythos
In Kuttner's works, Vorvadoss is an enigmatic and potentially dangerous god with no clear classification. Lin Carter would then place the entity amongst Yig, Shub-Niggurath, Nug and Yeb, a group of gods "known" as gods friendly to man (: "Out of the Aeons", : "Out of the Ages"), and the lesser gods of Mu, a group that includes Yig, Nug, Yeb, Iod, Dagon and Mother Hydra (: "The Thing in the Pit"). The intent seems to have been to group it into the Great Old Ones.

However, Scott David Aniolowski would give it a clear classification as an Elder God in his work for Chaosium (: Ye Booke of Monstres).

Playing off of this circumstance, James Ambuehl would classify Vorvadoss as "the only entity neither wholly Great Old One nor wholly Elder God", as well as making it the twin brother of Yaggdytha and the son of Nodens (named "The Lord of the Abyss" in another callback to "The Eater of Souls") (: "The Star-Seed").

Kenneth Vrest Teachout Orton (1897 - 1986) was a poet, editor, and artist from Hardwick, Vermont, USA, and founder of the Vermont Country Store. In 1925, he was living in New York, where he befriended H. P. Lovecraft and became a sporadic member of the Kalem Club. By 1928, he had moved back to Vermont and invited Lovecraft for a two weeks visit, which partially served as inspiration for Lovecraft's Vermont-based cosmic horror novella The Whisperer in Darkness.

A drawing by Orton appeared on the cover of the 1927 edition of The Recluse, in which Lovecraft’s essay Supernatural Horror in Literature first appeared. It would later be used on the cover of S. T. Joshi's scholarly work The Annotated Supernatural Horror in Literature .

"Vulcan's Forge" is a Lovecraftian short story by British author William Meikle.

### Synopsis
In 79 AD, at the height of the Roman Empire, a seismic upheaval unearths a chamber full of strange artefacts. As a local scholar and his team of construction workers explore the interior, more and more catacombs are brought to light. The arrival of a prominent general coincides with the discovery of a black, tar-like entity which appears to be in hibernation, and the soldier demands its weaponisation for the glory of the Empire.

As the exploration progresses, the group learn that the mountain was once the last refuge of an unknown species who fought a war against the black tar, and as their fortress was overrun, they activated their ultimate weapon: the volcano. Now that the black tar has begun to once more awaken, the Romans find themselves with no other option than to repeat this process, in the process dooming Pompeii and its inhabitants…

### Characters
*Septimus, a learned man assigned to the exploration of the chambers.
*Galvinius, the senior builder on the team.
*General Flavius Meranus, an old soldier.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite containing no direct references to the works of H. P. Lovecraft or the greater Cthulhu Mythos, Meikle's inclusion of "Vulcan's Forge" in his collection Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror indicates his belief that it follows in the spirit of such pieces. Additionally, the black tar is reminiscent of Lovecraft’s Shoggoths or Clark Ashton Smith's Formless Spawn, and the description given of one of the preserved corpses appears identical to that of a Mi-Go.

### Publication History
"Vulcan's Forge" was first published in the historical fiction anthology Tales of Cthulhu Invictus by Golden Goblin Press in 2015. It was also included in the collection of Meikle's own works Into the Black: Tales of Lovecraftian Terror in 2019.

Vulthoom (also known as Gsarthotegga) is a fictional entity created by Clark Ashton Smith for his eponymous short story, and later incorporated into the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Overview
In the story, Vulthoom is the Martian Aihai's equivalent of Satan; though most humans believe it to be a myth, it is nonetheless greatly feared by the natives. In truth it is an enigmatic being from another universe, exiled by its fellows for unknown reasons.

When Vulthoom first came to Mars in the distant past, its appearance caused a civil war, as those who fell for its promises fought to establish it as the planet's ruler. This faction was eventually defeated and Vulthoom, along with his surviving followers, retreated to the underground city of Ravormos where it remains.

Vulthoom plans to conquer Earth and take it as its trophy. Because of its vast intellect and advanced technology, it seems godlike, but is in reality merely a very powerful alien who must rest for millennia at a time and cannot travel to other worlds without a spaceship. (: "Vulthoom")

In The Revelations of Glaaki, mention is made of a mysterious alien race "of which Vulthoom is merely a child". (: "The Inhabitant of the Lake")

The Unaussprechlichen Kulten identifies Vulthoom as a Great Old One and one of the sons of Yog-Sothoth, along with Cthulhu and Hastur. Curiously, however, the same text also presents Vulthoom as a brother of Tsathoggua, who is described as the son of Ghizguth, not Yog-Sothoth, possibly suggesting that Vulthoom and Tsathoggua might be maternal half-brothers. (: "The Horror in the Gallery")

In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, Vulthoom attempted to manifest in Kingsport at some point. (: More Adventures in Arkham Country, Scenario: "Two Tales of Kingsport")

### In Other Media
*Vulthoom appears in mobile game Fate/Grand Order, sharing the name and body of the Foreigner-class Servant "Van Gogh". The power and influence of the Outer God that shares the vessel becomes more prominent as their host continues to gain strength.

### Trivia
*While under the influence of the hallucinogenic perfume of an alien blossom, one man envisioned Vulthoom as a gigantic, otherworldly plant with an elfin figure formed with exquisite beauty and symmetry grew from a vermilion cup on the top, but the being's true form is unknown.
*Smith previously featured another vegetable deity ruling over the planet Mars in the otherwise unrelated non-Mythos story "The Planet Entity", co-written with E. M. Johnston.

fullContent:
"Vulthoom" is a short story by the late American author and friend of H. P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith. It is part of Smith's "Mars Cycle" which is a set of three short stories set in a future period when humans have colonized Mars, but are menaced by eldritch horrors from the distant past. 

### Synopsis
Two men living on Mars encounter an incredibly ancient alien entity which has designs on the planet Earth. 

### Characters
*Bob Haines, a human pilot seeking employment. 
*Paul Septimus Chanler, a professional writer in search of inspiration. 
*Vulthoom, a semi-mythical alien entity dwelling deep beneath the surface of Mars. 

### Publication History
"Vulthoom" was first published in the September 1935 edition of Weird Tales. It has since appeared in a multitude of publications and has been translated into Dutch, German, French and Italian.

fullContent:
Vyônes (pronounced vee-OWN) is a fictional town created by Clark Ashton Smith, the major municipality of his imaginary French province of Averoigne. It was mentioned in the first Averoigne tale, "The End of the Story", published in the May 1930 issue of Weird Tales. But Smith did not use it as an actual setting until the third tale, "The Maker of Gargoyles", in Weird Tales' August 1932 issue.

### In Smith's Fiction
In "The End of the Story" (1930), the protagonist reads an account of Gérard de Venteillon, which says that his betrothed, Eleanor des Lys, "waited vainly for him at the cathedral of Vyônes, the principal town of Averoigne, where the wedding had been set." 

The town gets a slightly less glancing mention in "A Rendezvous in Averoigne" (1931) : "Visiting one day that quaint cathedral town, Vyônes, which lies so near to the ancient wood of Averoigne, Gérard had seen Fleurette, the daughter of a well-to-do mercer named Guillaume Cochin," the story relates; later, when lost in that wood, Gerard tells a stranger, "I should be profoundly grateful if you would direct me toward Vyônes"--to which the stranger replies, “Unfortunately, there are no paths from my château to Vyônes.”

"The Satyr" (1931) mentions the town briefly when Raoul, Comte de la Frênaie, "returned to the château from Vyônes, where he had gone on business."

Smith's first story that actually utilized Vyônes as a setting is "The Maker of Gargoyles" (1932), set in the year 1138, when "Vyônes was the principal town of the province of Averoigne." As in "Rendezvous", its closeness to the forest of Averoigne is noted: "On two sides the great, shadow-haunted forest, a place of equivocal legends, of loup-garous and phantoms, approached to the very walls and flung its umbrage upon them at early forenoon and evening." In the other directions, the view is more pastoral: "On the other sides there lay cultivated fields, and gentle streams that meandered among willows or poplars, and roads that ran through an open plain to the high châteaux of noble lords and to regions beyond Averoigne."

Vyônes is described in "Gargoyles" as "prosperous" and "sanctified by the presence of two nunneries and a monastery"--plus the cathedral whose construction sets the stage for the story. Despite this divine protection, Smith admits, "there had been occasional instances of alleged sorcery or demoniacal possession; and, once or twice, the perilous temptations of succubi had made their inroads on the pious virtue of Vyônes." The story goes on to recount a series of vicious gargoyle attacks.

In "The Holiness of Azédarac" (1933), Brother Ambrose is sent from Vyônes to Ximes by Clement, his uncle, who is also the Archbishop of Averoigne, with his seat at Vyônes' cathedral. Ambrose is tasked to investigate rumors that Ximes' bishop, Azédarac, has dealings with unholy powers--rumors that turn out to be all to true. The story turns on Ambrose's attempt to return to Vyônes with the evidence--a journey that turns

fullContent:
Wilum Hopfrog Pugmire (born William Harry Pugmire (3 May 1951 – 26 March 2019), was an American author and poet based in Seattle, Washington, USA. He specialised in the horror and weird fiction genres. 

Pugmire changed his middle name to Hopfrog as a tribute to the titular character in Edgar Allan Poe's short story "Hop-Frog", the story of a vengeful dwarf who enacts his wrath on a malicious king . 

He was heavily influenced by Lovecraftian horror and weird fiction in general, genres to which he devoted much of his output. In 2011, H. P. Lovecraft scholar S. T. Joshi described Pugmire as "the prose-poet of the horror/fantasy field; he may be the best prose-poet we have," and "perhaps the leading Lovecraftian author writing today." Bobby Derie wrote that Pugmire "wrote Lovecraftian fiction without the formulaic trappings of the mythos, wrapped in a sensuous prose and characters with easy, fluid sexuality".

In March 2019, Pugmire died at home from heart problems, a condition which he had been battling for many years .

### Sesqua Valley
Many of Pugmire's Mythos stories take place in the fictional Sesqua Valley, a Pacific Northwest equivalent to Lovecraft's New England which he created for this very purpose. Other authors have also adopted the Sesqua Valley as the setting to their Mythos tales, amongst them author and artist Jeffrey Thomas, who worked on a large number of stories with Pugmire, and provided artwork for several of his publications.

fullContent:
William Paul Cook (August 31, 1881 – January 22, 1948) was a printer, publisher, and editor in the amateur press movement. He was a friend and colleague of H. P. Lovecraft, encouraging his writing and publishing some of his first weird fiction.

Born in Mount Tabor, Vermont, Cook joined the United Amateur Press Association in 1901 and began publishing the Monadnock Monthly, a highly regarded amateur literary journal. In 1907, he was appointed the UAPA's official editor, though he resigned before serving his full term. After marrying Adeline Emmeline Smith in Connecticut in 1912, he moved to Athol, Massachusetts, the next year. 

Cook started publishing The Vagrant in 1915, which would continue to come out somewhat sporadically until 1927. He had a day job at the local newspaper, which allowed him to print The Vagrant and other amateur publications on its press; he got to know Lovecraft in 1917 when he agreed to print Lovecraft's journal The Conservative.

Cook and Lovecraft struck up a friendship; Cook read Lovecraft's juvenilia, publishing  "The Beast in the Cave" in the June 1918 issue of The Vagrant, and encouraged him to resume writing fiction.

Cook solicited Lovecraft to write a study of weird fiction that became Supernatural Horror in Literature; it was published in the only issue of Cook's journal The Recluse (1927).

In 1928, after "The Shunned House" was rejected by Weird Tales, Cook printed it as a chapbook; most of the 300 copies were not bound, however, until they were finished by Arkham House in 1959-61.

After Lovecraft's death, Cook wrote In Memoriam: Howard Phillips Lovecraft (Driftwind Press, 1941), which An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia called "still perhaps the best memoir of HPL."

### Selected Bibiography

Sir Wade Jermyn is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family", depicted as being the ancestor of the Jermyn family who mated with a white ape princess.

### Biography
Sir Wade Jermyn was an 18th century English explorer, one of the first Europeans to traverse the more distant parts of the Congo region, and authored books about the people, animals and things that he saw there. One of his books, Observations on the Several Parts of Africa, was met with ridicule by the scientific community, who refused to believe in Sir Wade's ideas about a prehistoric civilization in Congo.

Sir Wade was an erudite man with few friends, and infamous for the "wild stories" he told about his travels, which were often met with skepticism. He kept a large collection of unusual trophies and specimens from his voyages. During his second and longest expedition, he discovered the White Apes and their city, married their princess and had a son, Philip Jermyn. When he returned to the Jermyn House, he kept his wife hidden from the public and told others that she was the daughter of a Portuguese merchant, unaccustomed to English culture. He was very dedicated to her and to their son, and took care of all of their needs. Finally, seeing that his wife wouldn't adapt to life in England, Sir Wade returned with her to Africa, leaving young Philip under the care of a Guinean woman.

Sir Wade and Lady Jermyn lived among the White Apes and were worshiped as gods until Lady Jermyn's death, after which her husband arranged for her body to be mummified and kept in a stone temple where she would continue to be remembered and venerated. It was only after the death of his wife that Sir Wade returned home and assumed tutorship of his son.

At some point, Sir Wade's eccentricities gave way to signs of severe mental unrest. In 1765, he was confined to a mental institution where he died three years later. (: "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family")

Wade Kearney is a fictional character created by American author Ron Shiflet for his Cthulhu Mythos stories. He made his debut appearance in the short story "Unfinished Business" in July 2006.

### Overview
Kearney is a tough, hard-drinking private detective based in Arkham, Massachusetts. Despite having no desire to look into such matters, many of the cases which cross his desk involve supernatural elements: as a result, he is occasionally sought out by clients who have heard of his experience with occult investigations.

In addition to his detective services, Kearney has also been known to provide security services, although he appears somewhat reluctant to engage in such employment.

### Cases
*Arkham: Kearney had a run-in with a pack of ghouls while providing security for a pair of original Richard Upton Pickman paintings (: "Unfinished Business").
*Arkham: he attempted to locate a missing book, becoming embroiled in a web of deceit and deadly supernatural forces (: "Case of the Missing Grimoire").
*Arkham: Kearney witnessed a series of gruesome deaths when hired to locate a mutated lab animal. (: "Don't Monkey With a Monkey").
*Massachusetts: The PI faced down a reanimated Egyptian mummy in the swamps outside Arkham (: "Keeping it Under Wraps").

### Behind the Mythos
In his story notes for the 2017 edition of Looking for Darla: Stories of Mythos Noir, creator Ron Shiflet states that "The truth is that there was an ongoing mental tussle at the time as to whether I should focus on [Bill] Sweetan or Wade Kearney as an ongoing character in my fiction. They are pretty much the same person but I eventually seemed to settle on Kearney."

### Appearances
*"Unfinished Business" (2006)
*"Case of the Missing Grimoire" (2008)
*"Don't Monkey With a Monkey" (2008)
*"Keeping it Under Wraps" (2017)

The Wailing Writher is a fictional entity believed to be an avatar of Nyarlathotep, but with no known veneration. It made its first appearance in H. P. Lovecraft's 1920 prose poem "Nyarlathotep". Chaosium later incorporated it into their Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game in the supplement Escape from Innsmouth, and was included in the Innsmouth Horror expansion for Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror board game.

### Appearance
The Wailing Writher manifests as a cylindrical structure floating in the air full of tentacles and jaws that moan in agony. According to some, these mouths would be accompanied by eyes and nostrils, composing complete faces.

### Behavior
The creature moves by levitating. As it does so it emits screaming like the voices of madmen. If it catches a mortal in its tentacles, it is likely to eat them. However, its sole purpose may actually be to simply spread panic among mortals.

Wales is a small, mountainous country in north-west Europe, located on the west coast of the British Isles, and part of the United Kingdom. It borders England to the east, and is surrounded by both the Irish Sea and the Bristol Channel on its coastlines.

In H. P. Lovecraft’s day, Wales was known for its coal mining and steel industries, as well as livestock farming, although the former have since largely collapsed. In the modern era, it is perhaps better known as a tourist destination, its relatively low population affording visitors access to large areas of natural beauty.

### In Lovecraft’s Works
Although almost entirely absent in Lovecraft’s works, a notable exception is in a light-hearted letter to his friend James F. Morton, where he claims lineage from one Llunwy of Wales, Llunwy himself being a descendant of many infamous Cthulhu Mythos deities. (: Selected Letters 4.617)

### In Other Works
Wales plays a larger role in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos, albeit still not one which will likely spring to mind first when envisioning the setting, with mentions being largely confined to the occasional short story or roleplaying game supplement. However, the 2013 Screaming Dreams anthology Cthulhu Cymraeg features a selection of Lovecraftian works explicitly set in Wales. 

### In the Real World
One of Lovecraft’s major inspirations, author Arthur Machen, was from Wales, and his Welsh upbringing influenced much of his writing.

"Walking to the Abyss" is a short story produced by screenwriter Chiaki J. Konaka. Serving as a prequel to Ultraman Tiga, the story details a marine biologist's discovery of a mysterious plate that slowly drives him to madness, only for the plate to be just the start of a deeper mystery. 

### Synopsis
Katsumi, a marine biologist, travels aboard the research submarine Ryugu on a trip into the depths of the Pacific Ocean off the coast of the Ogasawara Islands, with a target depth of 1,000 metres below sea level. While en route, he talks with his co-pilot about the discovery of a mannequin head by the Shinkai 6500, perfectly preserved on the sea floor. As the submarine reaches its target depth, Katsumi notices a footprint in the sand, but is dismissed by his colleagues, who believe it to be just an optical illusion created by the lights of the Ryugu hitting the sea floor; however, Katsumi then finds an ancient plate, bearing writing in several unknown languages. 

The plate is recovered, taken to the surface and delivered by Katsumi to the research mission's client, a mysterious, dark-skinned man named Teppu Naiharato, who presents Katsumi with a riddle as to the plate's true identity. Katsumi speculates that the plate may have come from a rogue ship operating in Japan's territorial waters, but Teppu disagrees.

Days go by, and Katsumi begins to descend into madness. He begins periodically repeating a mantra and sees strange visions of Teppu appearing everywhere he goes, and a huge creature emerging from Tokyo Bay, which Katsumi identifies as a sea serpent. A report of an oarfish that washed up on the Izu Peninsula reaches Katsumi, and he travels to the area to see the fish for himself. When he arrives, he initially feels relieved, believing that the fish was the true identity of the sea serpent he saw in Tokyo Bay. However, the oarfish was then dissected, and Katsumi recoiled in horror when he believed that he saw the eyes of the other passengers in the bus he took after delivering the plate to Teppu, still alive yet disembodied, and all of them staring straight at him.

A few days later, Katsumi abruptly awakens in his office in the middle of the night - having fallen asleep due to the stress of being overworked and his growing hallucinations - and finds that a container that had been used to store the sand that had collected around the plate was spilled over the floor. He hears a knocking sound coming from outside, but when he looks through the window, he is met with only darkness, and can't make anything out through the gloom. Walking through the office, he encounters another oarfish, this time being alive, and realises that he has somehow been transported to the depths of the ocean.

"Walpurgis Night" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author John Michael Greer. It was published in the Walpurgisnacht 2018 edition of Gavin Chappell's long-running weird fiction magazine Lovecraftiana in April of that year.

### Synopsis
Sam, a young university graduate who has fallen on hard times and who feels his life is circling the drain, stumbles upon an odd little bar one evening while trying to drown his sorrows and avoid a persistent ex-girlfriend. Inside, he meets a mysterious and alluring woman who he feels may be something of a kindred spirit, and the two embark on a passionate, carnal relationship.

As Sam's life continues to deteriorate, he reflects on local legends which say that on Walpurgis Night every year, an ancient mother-deity named Shub-Niggurath chooses a human to become one of her Thousand Young. After losing his job, he comes to the realisation that the woman at the bar is one of these Thousand Young, and that becoming like her may not be as bad as the dithering local preachers might say. Making his way to the bar the woman, and a throng of others like her, take Sam into the nearby forest where they send him into the bosom of their goddess.

### Mythos References
Aside from the Shub-Niggurath connection, "Walpurgis Night" contains several references to the greater Cthulhu Mythos, including:

* the setting of Bolton, a town created by H. P. Lovecraft for his serial short story "Herbert West - Reanimator"
* Arkham is also made mention of, and Sam is stated to have attended St. Stanislaus Church as a child
* at one point, Sam makes his way across a train line which runs from Ipswich to Newburyport
* the Miskatonic River is mentioned in passing
* the beer drunk by Sam and the woman is called Kingsport Black
* a chant intoned by the assembled Thousand Young of Shub-Niggurath references Cthulhu and Tsathoggua

### Publication History
* Lovecraftiana Vol 3, Issue 1 (2018)
* Lovecraftiana Volume 3 (2020, omnibus)

Walter Brown is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his horror sci-fi novella The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Overview
Described by Henry Akeley as a "surly" man, Walter Brown was a farmer who lived alone in the deep woods in the vicinity of Townshend, Vermont, close to Akeley's own property. He worked as a spy and agent of the extraterrestrial beings known as the Mi-Go, who visited his farm and spoke to him occasionally. Akeley once overheard Brown's voice "in a very terrible conversation" with one or more of the creatures.

Akeley suspected that Brown was the one tampering with his letters to Albert Wilmarth when they investigated the activities of the Mi-Go. At the time, Brown was often seen loitering in Brattleboro, Bellows Falls, Newfane, and South Londonderry.

On the night of August 12th, 1928, Brown and a group of Mi-Go invaded Akeley's farm, shot many of Akeley's dogs and cut off his telephone wire. Similar incidents recurred in the following weeks. During one of these, Akeley shot at the invaders and later found both human and alien blood over the ground. Brown was never seen again after this incident. Since the Mi-Go are known to take away their dead and wounded, what ultimately became of Brown is unknown. However, the being that impersonated Akeley did refer to "the late Walter Brown", implying that he was killed. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

Walter de la Poer is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his horror short story "The Rats in the Walls".

### Biography
Walter de la Poer, eleventh Baron Exham, was a British nobleman who lived during the reign of James I and was described as a "shy, gentle youth". The third son of the master of Exham Priory, Walter was the only survivor of an undisclosed tragedy that claimed the lives of his father, three brothers, two sisters, and numerous servants. It is believed that after discovering his family's dark secret (namely that they raised human and human-descended beings as livestock) Walter himself conspired with four of his servants to kill the entire household while they were asleep. His neighbours approved of this deed, feeling that Walter had "purged the land of an immemorial curse".

As a murder suspect, Walter lost his property and immigrated to the American state of Virginia, where he became the founder of the Delapore family. The authorities didn't do much to try to prevent his escape. However, it is said that Walter was assailed by "some horror greater than that of conscience or the law", and desired nothing more than to never set foot on his birthplace again, thus he never attempted to prove his innocence or reclaim his family estate. A gentleman adventurer named Francis Harley, who knew Walter in America, described him as "a man of unexampled justice, honor, and delicacy". (: "The Rats in the Walls")

Walter Gilman is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his 1932 short story "The Dreams in the Witch-House".

### Biography
A man from from Haverhill, Massachusetts, Walter Gilman attended Miskatonic University to advance his research in non-Euclidean calculus and quantum physics which he linked to the "fantastic legends of elder magic". While there he came into contact with the Necronomicon, the Book of Eibon and the Unaussprechlichen Kulten but was later forbidden by his professors to further consult the university's collection of rare books, as they feared the deep mental tension brought on by studying such material too hard.

Gilman later took board in the reportedly haunted "Witch-House," which in the 1600's was home to the black magician Keziah Mason. She eventually entered his dreams with the Black Man, attempting to convince him to sign his name into the Book of Azathoth. He tried to refuse, recalling the description of Azathoth given in the Necronomicon, but may have succumbed as he went on to sleep walk into occult rituals and a kidnapping.

Though Gilman later managed to strangle Mason and confess his full story to fellow student Frank Elwood, he was himself killed when her demonic rat, Brown Jenkin, ate his heart. (: "The Dreams in the Witch-House")

### Trivia
*His acuteness of the senses in the opening paragraphs can be likened to that of some of Edgar Allan Poe's characters.

Wanda Maximoff (Scarlet Witch) is a fictional character created by Marvel Comics. Introduced as a minor villain in the X-Men series, Scarlet Witch soon became a popular hero, joining the Avengers and being featured as either a central character or key element in many core events of the Marvel Universe (including Avengers Disassemble, House of M, M-Day and Avengers vs. X-Men).

### Background
The Scarlet Witch is one of the most powerful beings on Earth, able to alter reality on a multiversal scale but is someone who is prone to mental breakdowns due to her mental illness, though usually it's under control. She has been a member of the Avengers superhero team for decades, and for a long time believed that she was a mutant who was the daughter of Magneto.

In reality, she is an orphan who was engineered by the High Evolutionary and her magical powers were amplified by the Elder God Chthon. Chthon has manipulated her several times and on occasion has been able to possess her, until her teammates broke his control over her.

Ward Phillips is the name of several characters in the Cthulhu Mythos, all derived from the name of Howard Phillips Lovecraft. 

There is a Ward Phillips in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" (1934), described as "an elderly eccentric of Providence, Rhode Island."  This "Providence mystic," who "enjoyed a long and close correspondence" with Randolph Carter, is said to be "lean, grey, long-nosed, clean-shaven, and stoop-shouldered.

The Rev. Ward Phillips is "Pastor of the Second Church in Arkham in the Massachusetts-Bay" in August Derleth's The Lurker at the Threshold (1945). He is the author of Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-English Canaan, published in Boston in 1801, and he has a vitriolic debate over the book with Alijah Billington in 1808.

Joan Stanley, in Ex Libris Miskatonici, says the Miskatonic University library was created in 1693 when another Ward Phillips--great-grandfather of the reverend--donated his library of 127 mainly religious books to the fledgling college.

The Ward Philips of August Derleth's "The Lamp of Alhazred" is the closest of all to Howard Phillips Lovecraft: a pulp fiction writer who makes extra money revising other people's stories; who goes on imaginary journeys to Arkham, Innsmouth, R'lyeh, and the Plateau of Leng; who writes of Cthulhu, Hastur, Yog-Sothoth, Shub-Niggurath, Hypnos, and Nyarlathotep; who lives on Angell Street in Providence. Ward Phillips is 46 when he disappears, the same age Lovecraft was when he died.

### In Games
The Lurker at the Threshold iteration of the Rev. Ward Phillips is mentioned in "The Asylum", a Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game module included in the 1983 supplement The Asylum & Other Tales. In the scenario, a copy of his pamphlet comes up for sale at an Austrian auction house during the 1920s .

Another Chaosium version of the character for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game, Ward Phillips is a pulp-horror author and a prominent dreamer. He is able to use a the Lamp of Alhazred, left to him by his grandfather, to travel between the Waking World and the Dreamlands. He now lives in Ennon where he aids fellow travellers like Nathaniel Elton (citation needed).

### Appearance
"Phillips appears as a sickly youth of perhaps 17 years of age. He has brown hair and eyes, stands about 5'6", and speaks with a distinct Boston accent."

### Behind the Mythos
The name Ward Phillips was used as a pseudonym by H. P. Lovecraft when writing "Ex Oblivione" and the character's description is clearly based on his own. Since Lovecraft has died in real life, and since this character is his alter ego, it is implied that, like Kuranes, H. P. Lovecraft himself is now a permanent resident of the Dreamlands.

In the 2019 movie adaptation of "The Colour Out of Space", the protagonist (unnamed in the original story) is named Ward Phillips.

fullContent:
"Waste Paper: A Poem of Profound Insignificance" is a satirical poem by H. P. Lovecraft written as a parody of T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land. It was first published in the 1977 collection A Winter Wish and Other Poems.

### Synopsis
The poem resembles a nonsensical stream of consciousness which parodies Eliot's work by alternating styles and themes in seemingly random fashion. The first few lines go from the formation of the planet to the price of a "dandy acetylene lantern" that the poet uses to ride his bicycle at night. What follows range from autobiographical bits about the author playing the zobo with two other boys as part of the Blackstone Military Band, to confessing a murder committed on Christmas, to rambling about Lord Byng (Governor-General of Canada) among many other equally unrelated statements, all mixed in with quotes, literary allusions, brief narratives such as that of a man named Jack who receives a message from his bootlegger family, and other bits of non sequitur.

### Trivia
*While otherwise unconnected to Lovecraft's Dream Cycle, this poem interestingly contains the line "Meet me tonight in dreamland . . . BAH".

fullContent:
"Waycross" is a short story by Caitlin R. Kiernan that features their recurring character Dancy Flammarion, the teenage albino monster-slayer. It was written in March 2002 and released as a chapbook by Subterranean Press in 2003. It takes place following the events in "Alabaster" (2006).

The story tells of Dancy's capture by and eventual defeat of the Gynander, a shapeshifting monster who steals the skins and the likenesses of its victims. Along the way, she kills the Gynander's friend Sinethella, a millennia-old godlike entity who has writhing tentacles in place of breasts. Dancy is forced to look into Sinethella's box, which shows her images of her abuse in the asylum in Tallahassee and at a county fair she attended with her mother, and what seem to be past-life memories of being hunted like an animal--in France, and much earlier, on the Ice Age landbridge between Siberia and Alaska.

### Characters
Dancy Flammarion: An albino girl who is used by an angel to hunt monsters. She was introduced in Kiernan's novel Threshold and has since appeared in numerous short stories and graphic novels.

The Gynander: A creature that wears the skins of people and animals that it's killed, taking on their appearance. In its true form, it's described as a "red thing" and "long, raw fingers." It refers to itself as a "two-bit, back-woods haint."

Sinethella: An entity that's lived at least 11,000 years, described by the Gynander, who is her friend, as "a goddess, almost.” She appears as "a woman in a yellow raincoat," with "shaggy black hair [that] fell about her round face in tangled curls," and "smooth and perfect" olive skin that "glinted wetly." She has eyes that are "very green and pupil less,"  and "long sharp teeth." In place of breasts she has "wriggling, tentacled masses instead, like the fiery heads of sea anemones, surrounding hungry, toothless mouths."

### Inspiration
In Kiernan's novel Threshold, which introduced Dancy, the character recalls previous encounters she's had with the supernatural. One of them was "the black-haired woman in Waycross with stubby, writhing tentacles where her breasts should have been." Kiernan's curiosity about just who it was that Dancy met grew into the story "Waycross." 

### Publication History
"Waycross" was reprinted in The Mammoth Book of Best New Horror 15 (Carroll & Graf/Robinson, 2004). It was later included in Kiernan's collections Alabaster (Subterranean Press, 2006) and Two Worlds and In Between: The Best of Caitlin R. Kiernan (Subterranean Press, 2011).

Wayne Douglas Barlowe (born January 6, 1958) is an American science fiction and fantasy illustrator, film concept designer, and author; probably most well-known for his book Expedition: Being an Account in Words and Artwork of the 2358 A.D. Voyage to Darwin IV (1990); which was later made into the documentary Alien Planet (2005).

Barlowe illustrated and wrote about the Elder Things in Barlowe's Guide to Extraterrestrials (1979, under the entry "Old Ones"), and the Gugs in Barlowe's Guide to Fantasy (1996).

He also designed the Lovecraft-inspired Ogdru Jahad for Guillermo del Toro's Hellboy (2004). Del Toro commented in an interview that he intended to bring Barlowe onboard in an undisclosed role on his abortive At the Mountains of Madness film project.

fullContent:
Weird Detective: The Stars Are Wrong is a Cthulhu Mythos comic book mini-series written by Fred Van Lente and illustrated by Guiu Vilanova. First published by Dark Horse Comics as a five-issue run between June and October 2016, in February 2017 it was collected as a graphic novel; both print and digital editions were released.

### Overview


### Synopsis
In the modern day, a Yithian impersonating New York City police detective Sebastian Greene is assigned a new partner, transferee Sana Fayez, who has been given the job of keeping tabs on his activities by the chief of detectives.

Tasked with investigating a bizarre series of murders in which the victims have had their innards sucked out in their entirety, Greene must balance pursuing his mission - to track down a rogue polyp which is attempting to bring about the return of the Old Ones - with keeping his secret hidden from Fayez. During the course of the investigation, the pair must deal with corrupt cops, apathetic citizens, Deep One Hybrid gangsters, and interpersonal issues.

Greene is ultimately able to track down the polyp and use his advanced technology to banish the monstrosity to the distant planet of Yuggoth, but doing so destroys the technology he needs to return himself to his former body, effectively trapping him on Earth in our time.

### Other Mythos Connections and References
* The corrupt Chief of Detectives is named Thomas Malone, a nod to the main protagonist from "The Horror at Red Hook." Similarly, all of the victims of the strange crimes are found in the neighbourhood of Red Hook.
* Greene has a poster of an Argosy cover hung in the wall of his houseboat. The Argosy was a pulp magazine which published certain works by H. P. Lovecraft and his circle.
* During one scene in a homeless camp, Yellow and Elder Signs can be seen daubed on various features among the surroundings.
* A character named J. Randall Carter, whose relationship to the story is for the most part not explored during the series' run, is an author who writes books with dream-related titles. This would appear to be a nod to Randolph Carter, a recurrent character in Lovecraft’s fiction.
* One of the Old Ones depicted in the story bears more than a passing resemblance to Great Cthulhu himself.

### Behind the Mythos
Despite the alien which Greene is tracking being described as a "polyp," it would appear to be a different entity from the flying polyps described in The Shadow Out of Time, as they are stated to have been a rebellious Yithian servitor species which turned on their creators, much like the Shoggoths in At the Mountains of Madness, rather than the pre-human alien species depicted in Shadow.

The alien "Greene" inhabits a body far more versatile and powerful than a regular human frame, with the human Greene held in a coma-like stasis while his consciousness resides among the Yithians. How the aliens managed to achieve this is not explained.

fullContent:
Weird Tales is an American fantasy and horror fiction pulp magazine first published in March 1923. The magazine was set up in Chicago by J. C. Henneberger, an ex-journalist with a taste for the macabre. Edwin Baird was the first editor of the monthly, assisted by Farnsworth Wright.

### Edwin Baird
Baird first published some of Weird Tales' most famous writers, including H. P. Lovecraft, Clark Ashton Smith and Seabury Quinn, author of the hugely popular Jules de Grandin stories. The magazine lost a considerable sum of money under Baird's editorship, however--running through $11,000 in capital and amassing a $40,000 debt--and he was fired after 13 issues.

Henneberger offered the job to Lovecraft, who declined, citing his reluctance to relocate to Chicago; "think of the tragedy of such a move for an aged antiquarian," the 34-year-old writer declared. (: Selected Letters 1.172)

### Farnsworth Wright
The publisher then gave the job to Farnsworth Wright, who became the magazine's best-known editor. Wright (who suffered from Parkinson's disease) continued to publish stories by Lovecraft, Smith, and Quinn, though he was more selective than Baird; he rejected Lovecraft's At the Mountains of Madness, The Shadow Over Innsmouth, and (initially) "The Call of Cthulhu", among other stories. Many of Smith's Hyperborean cycle stories were rejected as well.

Among the new writers Wright found for the magazine were Robert Bloch and Robert E. Howard, whose Conan the Barbarian stories, among many others, were hugely popular. Wright even put playwright Tennessee Williams into print for the first time (with his story "The Vengeance of Nitocris"). Edmond Hamilton's earliest science fiction stories also first appeared in Wright's Weird Tales.

Notably, Wright hired the former fashion designer and illustrator Margaret Brundage to produce the magazine's cover illustrations, starting in 1933--making Brundage the first and only female cover artist of the pulp era. She created many striking images, especially of nude or semi-nude young women in provocative poses (her whipping scenes attracted the highest attention). Though her art was far from flawless, Brundage's covers became a focus of extreme attention and controversy--which of course helped to sell the magazine. Wright also ignited the careers of two important fantasy artists, Virgil Finlay and Hannes Bok, by buying and publishing their work, first and frequently.

Weird Tales always struggled financially. In the 1920s and '30s, the magazine's business manager, William Sprenger, was crucial in keeping the enterprise afloat. It is estimated that the monthly circulation of Weird Tales never topped 50,000 copies per issue. (In the 1920s, circulation figures for the most successful pulps topped one million; even in the depths of the Great Depression, popular pulps like Doc Savage or The Shadow enjoyed circulations of 300,000 per issue, monthly or even semi-monthly.) Weird Tales #1 is a fantasy anthology licensed as part of the overall publishing operation under the Weird Tales imprint. It was edited by Lin Carter. Weird Tales #1 was the first in what was intended to be his paperback revival of the classic fantasy and horror magazine Weird Tales itself. 

Weird Tales #1 is also numbered vol. 48, no. 1 (Spring 1981) as a direct continuation of the numbering of the original magazine from the point where it had ceased publication. 

The anthology was first published in paperback by American publisher Zebra Books in December 1980, and reprinted in 1983.

fullContent:
Welcome to Neverbury is a collection of horror fiction by U.K.-based author Chris Lynch. It was self-published on Amazon’s digital Kindle platform in June 2023; an audiobook edition has since been released through Audible.

### Overview


Welcome to Neverbury contains a series of loosely-linked short stories which share the same fictional locale of Neverbury, a small town somewhere on the coast of England which is steeped in the supernatural. The individual tales run a range of horror genres, from black comedy ("Yes, No Refunds", "Bring the Thunder") to gothic ghost stories ("A Design for Living"). Although they contain no direct references to the Cthulhu Mythos, they all took their cue from H. P. Lovecraft (see "Inspiration", below), and at least one ("Bring the Thunder") has strong suggestions of a Mythos connection.

### Inspiration
Lynch states in his foreword to the book that the stories contained within were first written in response to a February challenge posted on the online Storytelling Collective website, wherein the authors were supposed to write a single flash-fiction piece every day for a month. To provide a springboard for the authors creativity, a prompt was given on the site for each day; these prompts were taken from H. P. Lovecraft’s Commonplace Book.

As all of his stories ran far in excess of the 500 word suggested target, Lynch compiled the first fourteen - plus one which acts as a gateway for a future volume - into Welcome to Neverbury. He also states that as there are still fourteen prompts whose stories were not used, he will return with another collection of stories about Neverbury.

Wendell Hunt is a character created by American author David Kenney for his Lost Archivist series of Cthulhu Mythos stories. He made his first appearance in the 2019 short story "The Lost Archivist."

### Overview
Hunt is the chief archivist of Miskatonic University's Armitage Memorial Library. In this capacity, he encounters a variety of supernatural forces, including covetous necromancers amongst the faculty and zombies, amongst others. He is assisted in his tasks by his boss Dr. Clara Pedrick and the insane researcher Dr. Shattuck, both of whom have extensive experience in the field.

During the course of his duties, hunt has suffered some serious and permanent physical disfigurements, including the loss of an eye on one occasion, and an ear on another.

### History
During his investigation of theft and murder at one of the library’s most dangerous departments, Storage Area B, Hunt confronted and defeated a magic-wielding professor and his zombie minion. He is able to overcome the threat and restore balance to the archives, but loses his ear to the zombie's hungry jaws in the process (: "Gnashing Whispers")

Wendell Willis is a character created by American author Ron Shiflet for his short story "When in Leng...".

### History
The last scion of a wealthy family with a sprawling estate outside Tenoka, Texas, Willis was a fantastic cook who had a lifelong fascination with the occult.

In his middle years, he undertook an expedition to the Plateau of Leng where, after having been driven quite mad by the tribe of Tcho-Tcho people who took him in, returned to the United States and fed human flesh to his horrified friend Robert Ballard. After Ballard fled the house, Willis came to the realisation that he would soon be in the sights of the local police (: "When in Leng…").

Fleeing to the backwoods Louisiana shack of another of his old friends Tobias Jackson who happened to be a priest in service to the Great Old One Yig, he killed Jackson and tried to steal his magical knowledge, but fell foul of a trap laid by the wily cultist. Trapped by serpent servants of Yig with no obvious means of escape, his fate appeared to have been sealed (: "Seven Serpents Waiting").

Somehow surviving the deadly trap, Willis later found himself incarcerated in the Hillsdale Asylum, an institution for the criminally insane. Obtaining the assistance of the minor deity Chor-Tal, he managed to escape, but immediately found himself in the sights of a gun-toting jealous husband (: "A God's Eye View").

### Behind the Mythos
Wendell Willis is a character with no linear storytelling: the order in which his stories appear may not even be his in-universe chronological timeline. Creator Shiflet has put him in a number of seemingly-impossible to escape situations which Willis has consistently found his way out of, always off-camera with no explanation of the means involved.

*"A God's Eye View" (2008)

The Wendigo is a supernatural creature originating from Algonquian myth and folklore. It is typically described as a gaunt, ghoulish humanoid associated with a foul stench and an insatiable craving for human flesh. In some traditions, its size is phenomenal, being taller than the tallest trees. In popular culture, Wendigos have been depicted in various ways, often as monstrous humanoids, sometimes with horns or antlers, associated with the Northern winds and/or cannibalism. In some depictions, humans can be possessed by or transformed into Wendigos.

The Wendigo featured in the Cthulhu Mythos is derived from Algernon Blackwood's 1910 novella The Wendigo. It was first incorporated into the Mythos by August Derleth, and is intimately associated with Derleth's creation, Ithaqua.

The exact relationship between Ithaqua and the Wendigo varies across media. Sometimes the Wendigo is seen as a "cousin" of Ithaqua (: "The Seal of R'lyeh"), sometimes as an avatar of it (: Born of the Winds), and sometimes as an entire species of creatures that serve the boreal giant. (: Ye Booke of Monstres)

### Description
In Algernon Blackwood's novella, the Wendigo is a large beast that takes up humans as companions, apparently affecting their minds in some way and forcing them to run through the forest side by side with the creature. The Wendigo's presence is signaled by a strong smell. The creature runs at extreme speeds, burning the ground with its footsteps and running over the treetops, possibly to the point of running in the air itself. The abducted human will be forced to run so fast to accompany it that their feet will burn away, and regrow in the shape of the Wendigo's feet. Once in the sky, the Wendigo will drop its human companion to the ground. Those who survive the experience may still find themselves physically and psychologically altered somehow. In contrast to the well-known tales about cannibalism, Blackwood's Wendigo feeds exclusively on moss. (: The Wendigo)

In the works of August Derleth, the Wendigo is identified as a cousin of Ithaqua, and master of the Shantaks that fly from Kadath in the Cold Waste to do its bidding. Both Ithaqua and the Wendigo are also known as "Wind-Walker". (: "The Seal of R'lyeh")

In the role-playing game Call of Cthulhu, the Wendigo is another name for Ithaqua itself, but the word is also used to refer to the humans and other creatures that have been physiologically transformed by it and forced to accompany it in its travels. In humans, it is claimed that "this transformation leads to the complete destruction of the feet, immunity to freezing temperatures, and unendurable cannibalistic tendencies which bring on madness". (: S. Petersen's Field Guide to Cthulhu Monsters)

Wendy Adams, the Urchin, is a fictional character created by Fantasy Flight Games who appears in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
When Wendy was very young, her Mama used to let her play with her old necklace, a piece of unusual design featuring an eye surrounded by a shiny star. Wendy was always fascinated by this bauble.

However, her childhood happiness ended when they received word that her father had been lost at sea. This caused a change in Wendy's Mama, and she began to scrawl bizarre symbols all over their house in white chalk, and read books with evil-sounding names. Soon, the authorities took notice, and Wendy's Mama was carted off to the asylum, while Wendy was sent to an orphanage, but not before her Mama gave her a parting gift: the necklace with which she had been so besotted as a child.

Spending several years in the orphanage, Wendy became completely disillusioned with the care given her and, deciding that she would be better off on her own, snuck away to live her life on the streets. Times were difficult for a little girl running with a pack of street kids, but somehow she made it work.

One day, Wendy was on the street begging when a stranger whose face she did not see dropped a photograph into her cup. The picture was one of her father, with the words “Soon the Red Tide rises. Stay safe, my little girl” scrawled on the back. What this means, Wendy has no idea, but since then she has spent all of her time not given over to mere survival searching for her missing father, encountering many nightmarish creatures along the way.

### Behind the Mythos
Originally created by Fantasy Flight for their Second Edition release of the Arkham Horror board game, Wendy has since appeared in several of their other games - including Eldritch Horror, Mansions of Madness, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, and the Third Edition of Arkham Horror - and has made appearances in several of their novels based on the Mythos. The company also released a pre-painted miniature of the character to replace the cardboard tokens given in their games, but this has since been discontinued.

The Wenelians are a species of extra-dimensional creatures developed for the Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game by Chaosium.

### Description
Originating on the planet of Yundu which lies somewhere in the depths of space within the Dreamlands, the Wenelians are a bizarre-looking species. Long and eel-like, they are capable of a degree of body-morphing, are covered in a dazzling array of colours and float in the air, wriggling their way along like flying snakes. Their heads somewhat resemble those of a seahorse, with eyes on stalks, large ears, and a proboscis through which they are able to project small calcite darts. In addition, they have the ability to release a cloud of vapour in the manner of a squid's ink-sac, blinding, or at least severely hampering, those in its immediate vicinity.

Wenelians are known to be a piratical species, and their raids take them far across the space of the Dreamlands. To this end, they employ the flying Phosphorescent Monsters as steeds and working-beasts, sailing the depths upon their backs.

### Behind the Mythos
The Wenelians were created by Phil Frances for the Call of Cthulhu supplement H. P. Lovecraft's Dreamlands in 1986, and their details were later reprinted in the monster manual Ye Booke of Monstres II in 1995.

fullContent:
"Wentworth's Day" is a short story by August Derleth, one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. It was originally published in the 1957 Arkham House anthology The Survivor and Others. Though it is set in the country north of Dunwich, it is arguably not a Cthulhu Mythos story; the magic involved is of the traditional sort.

### Synopsis
The story, set in the summer of 1927, is narrated by Fred Hadley, a Bostonian salesman delivering stoves in the country north of Dunwich.  Hadley is forced by a storm to take refuge in the home of Amos Stark, which is "one of those houses which are all of a piece—house, ell, summer kitchen, barn, all in one long structure, under roofs of various heights."  Hadley describes his host as 

Stark is clearly uneasy, and explains that it is Wentworth's day--the day that a five-year loan of $5,000 that Nahum Wentworth made to Stark was to come due. Only Wentworth can't collect: "because it warn’t no less’n two months after that day that he got shot out huntin’. Shotgun in the back o’ the head. Pure accident." To silence those who said he did it on purpose, Stark made out a will that left his whole estate to Genie Wentworth, Nahum's daughter.

Nahum Wentworth was evidently a wizard of some sort, as chief among the books he left to Stark is The Seventh Book of Moses, which "purported to offer all manner of spells, incantations, and charms." Waiting out the storm, Hadley idly copies out "the worst of the incantations which caught my eye...nothing less than an incantation for the assemblage of devils or spirits, or the raising of the dead." He then "say[s] it aloud several times, not for a moment expecting anything untoward to take place."

Imagine his surprise, then, when his spell summons the restless spirit of Nahum Wentworth, as Hadley discovers when he rushes to investigate a "terrible cry":


### Lovecraft Country
Derleth has an evocative description of the country "north of Dunwich":

Amos Stark's house is said to be 17 miles north of Dunwich--a distance that would put it well into New Hampshire, by most reckonings of the imaginary village's location.

### Adaptations
A comic book adaptation by Russ Jones was published in Christopher Lee's Treasury of Terror.

The Werewolf--a creature, also known as a lycanthrope, that can turn itself from human to wolf, or into a wolf/human hybrid--are part of the mythology and folklore of several cultures, and have long been a staple of horror fiction. H. P. Lovecraft mentioned werewolves occasionally in his fiction, as did other early writers of Cthulhu Mythos fiction. 

Chaosium recognized werewolves as part of the Mythos in 2007, when it added the creatures to the Malleus Monstrorum sourcebook for tthe Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game. Many of the werewolves in Marvel Comics have a Mythos-connected origin.

### In Lovecraft's Fiction
The most extensive treatment of the werewolf trope in Lovecraft's fiction comes in "The Ghost-Eater", a story he revised for C. M. Eddy, Jr., that appeared in the March 1924 Weird Tales.  The villain of the story is Vasili Oukranikov, a Russian immigrant in Maine who was said to be "a servant of the devil—a werewolf and eater of men." Travelers in the Maine woods would report "being chased by a big wolf with shining human eyes—like Oukranikov’s." Oukranikov's monstrous identity was confirmed when "somebody took a pot shot at the wolf, and the next time the Russian came into Glendale he walked with a limp." (This identification of a shapeshifter via an injury suffered in animal form is a common folkloric motif.) The story's narrator sees the werewolf's ghost in "the gaunt form of a great gray wolf" whose "hind foot was held in the air, as though wounded by some stray shot." An H. P. Lovecraft Encyclopedia describes the tale as a "conventional ghost/werewolf story".

Another werewolf reference occurs in a Lovecraft story that appears in the same issue of Weird Tales: "The Rats in the Walls". Delapore, the narrator, notes in that story that the modern residents of the neighboring village of Anchester "viewed Exham Priory as nothing less than a haunt of fiends and werewolves." While the villagers were certainly correct to associate Exham with monstrous activity, it's unclear whether, in the context of the story, this particular identification was accurate or not.

A more substantive account of lycanthropy occurs in the story "The Shunned House" (1928), in which the narrator notes the coincidence that the Roulet family, which is associated with the house's curse, shares both a name and a hometown (Caude, France) with Jacques Roulet, an actual character from French history who was tried and convicted of lycanthropy in 1598.  The narrator notes, as an "ominous item in the annals of morbid horror", that the historical Roulet "had been found covered with blood and shreds of flesh in a wood, shortly after the killing and rending of a boy by a pair of wolves. One wolf was seen to lope away unhurt." The story is equivocal about what this says about the reality

In this very short story, a traveler on a British train encounters a drunken Scot and a group of cultists bent of feeding their vampiric god Summanus.

"What Songs We Sing" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by author L. K. Whyte. It was included in the thematic anthology Apotheosis: Stories of Human Survival After the Rise of the Elder Gods by Simian Publishing in October 2015.

### Synopsis
In a future where humankind lives in a series of shanty-towns and are kept in servitude through the use of a mind-altering drug, Ikere meets a mysterious and beautiful woman named Jonny who belongs to no shanty. Jonny persuades Ikere to stop taking the drug, an action which leads her to join a resistance movement dedicated to fighting back against the Earth's malevolent masters.

### Mythos Connections
When wandering the cemetery outside her shanty, at one point Ikere worries that she has disturbed "one of the Mi-Goh, perhaps, or a nesting byahkee."

shortDefinition: "What the Moon Brings" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written on June 5, 1922. This story was first published in The National Amateur in May 1923. It is shorter than most of Lovecraft's other short stories, and is...
fullContent:
"What the Moon Brings" is a short story by American horror fiction writer H. P. Lovecraft, written on June 5, 1922. This story was first published in The National Amateur in May 1923. It is shorter than most of Lovecraft's other short stories, and is essentially a fragment. It is based on one of Lovecraft's dreams (a common technique of his).

### Synopsis
This story is told in the first person; the narrator is never named.
The story describes a surreal dreamscape. The narrator wanders through his garden one night and in the moonlight sees strange and bizarre things. He comes to a stream:
:Silent and sparkling, bright and baleful, those moon-cursed waters hurried I knew not whither; whilst from the embowered banks white lotus-blossoms fluttered one by one in the opiate night-wind and dropped despairingly into the stream, swirling away horribly under the arched, carven bridge, and staring back with the sinister resignation of calm, dead faces.
He sees that now the garden has no end, and where the walls used to be there are now more trees and plants and terrifying stone idols and pagodas. The dead faces urge him on farther and farther, as the stream becomes a river and leads him to the shore of a sea. Here the frightening moon makes the lotus-faces vanish:
:And as I saw therein the lotus-faces vanish, I longed for nets that I might capture them and learn from them the secrets which the moon had brought upon the night. But when that moon went over to the west and the still tide ebbed from the sullen shore, I saw in that light old spires that the waves almost uncovered, and white columns gay with festoons of green seaweed. And knowing that to this sunken place all the dead had come, I trembled and did not wish again to speak with the lotus-faces.

What the sea has uncovered are the ruins of an ancient city, a city of the dead. The narrator sees a black condor in the necropolis and wishes to ask it about the people he knows that have died. He watches the sea for a time and sees ripples in it, attributing them to sea worms. He suddenly feels a chill and notices something far off beneath the sea:
:Nor had my flesh trembled without cause, for when I raised my eyes I saw that the waters had ebbed very low, shewing much of the vast reef whose rim I had seen before. And when I saw that the reef was but the black basalt crown of a shocking eikon whose monstrous forehead now shown in the dim moonlight and whose vile hooves must paw the hellish ooze miles below, I shrieked and shrieked lest the hidden face rise above the waters, and lest the hidden eyes look at me after the slinking away of that leering and treacherous yellow moon.
Fleeing this monstrous thing, he dives into the city of the dead:



The speaker clearly prefers death among horrors to this perceived-even-greater-horror revealed in carven grandeur. The tale ends, but does not confirm whether this was the ending of the speaker's life.

"When in Leng…" is a short story by American author Ron Shiflet. It contains extensive name-dropping of Mythos stalwarts such as Dagon and the Necronomicon.

### Synopsis
When Robert Ballard's rich and eccentric friend Wendell Willis returns from his travels abroad, he jumps at the chance to sample his fine cooking. What Ballard does not know is that Willis has been living for months amongst the cannibalistic Tcho-Tcho people, and has picked up more than a few of their habits…

### Characters

*Robert Ballard, an assistant librarian at an unnamed university.
*Wendell Willis, Ballard's friend since college, driven quite insane by the time the story takes place.

### Publication History
"When in Leng…" was first published in the fanzine The Ancient Track in October 1998. It has since appeared in the collections Tales of the Cthulhu Mythos: Cthulhu's Creatures (November 2007) and They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness (June 2018).

### Trivia

*Alan Peschke, a real-world Mythos author, is mentioned to have been a friend of Ballard and Willis's.
*Ballard is stated to live in Tenoka, Texas, a frequently-referenced location in the Mythos works of Ron Shiflet.
