### Synopsis
Kanga, an unwitting avatar of the Outer God Shub-Niggurath, lives her life quietly in Hundred Acre Woods, watching her friends re-enact the stories of "the Authors" daily, and listening to the whispering voices in her head. When her child Roo is mortally wounded in an accident, Kanga lets the little being die rather than heal it again, and with this act her consciousness drifts back to rejoin its source.

fullContent:
"When the Dweller Awakes" is a comic story featured in The Adventures of the X-Men issue #4 by Marvel Comics. It is a crossover with the X-Men superhero team and the Cthulhu Mythos. 

### Synopsis
The story begins with Scott Summers (aka Cyclops) encountering a group of N'Garai, who had escaped through a dimensional drift at Salem Center. Cyclops fights off a few of them before discovering the only house in the town that wasn't being attacked. Upon entering, Cyclops encounters a man named Erich Zann, who explains that the invasion was prophesied in the R'lyeh Texts (aka the Book of R'lyeh) and the N'Garai will awaken the Dweller-in-Darkness to bring devastation to the world. Although Zann refuses to assist in ending the current threat, he informs Cyclops that there is a counterspell in the Book of R'lyeh that can banish all the N'Garai, at the cost of sacrificing himself as well.

Cyclops heads to the N'Garai dimension and, with the help of his fellow X-Men members, manages to successfully retrieve the Book of R'lyeh. Unfortunately, it was already too late as Cyclops was unable to decipher the language and one of the Dweller's tentacles had already burst from the ground; however, Zann ultimately comes back to save them, after his previous encounter with Cyclops helped him realize that the world is actually worth saving. Reciting the counterspell to banish the Dweller and N'Garai, Zann happily accepts his sacrifice as a form of atonement. Shortly afterwards, the Book of R'lyeh was also destroyed, crumbling into dust.

### Mythos Connections
*In this comic, the Dweller is explicitly stated to be "a true offspring of Great Cthulhu". However, this was later retconned in the Official Handbook of the Marvel Universe A to Z Vol 1 #3, which states that the Dweller is "considered a worthy scion of the Great Old One Cthulhu, though no direct relationship exists".
*While introducing himself, Zann references "the Hounds of Tindalos baying in the frozen wastes beyond Leng" and "the gibbering of Nyarlathotep at the center of Chaos". 
*The counterspell invokes the names of Cthulhu, Shub-Niggurath, Yog-Sothoth, Hastur and Dagon.

*Adventures of the X-Men: Clear and Present Dangers (2019)

"When the Stars Are Right" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by British author William Meikle. It is told in the format of a series of message transcripts from a woman to her husband.

### Synopsis
When humanity discovers that the manifestation of mythos creatures releases staggering amounts of energy, they develop technology capable of storing and utilising this untapped new source. Building a ship in orbit around Earth, they plan to use occult texts to summon a lesser creature in order to power a trip to Mars. Despite suffering horrific casualties in the ritual, the process is deemed a success, and the officials in charge of the project begin to make plans to harness an even greater source- perhaps even Great Cthulhu himself…

After hearing reports of similar burrows beneath the ground in Yucatan, the two go investigating. *Dr. Peter Worthy, a professor of palaeontology at Arkham State University and Ernest's lifelong friend.

shortDefinition: "Where Darkness Dwells, Dwell I!" is a comic story featured in Thor Vol 1 #229 which was written by Gerry Conway, illustrated by Rich Buckler, and published by Marvel Comics in 1974. It is notable for being the first appearance of the Dweller-in-Dark...
fullContent:
"Where Darkness Dwells, Dwell I!" is a comic story featured in Thor Vol 1 #229 which was written by Gerry Conway, illustrated by Rich Buckler, and published by Marvel Comics in 1974. It is notable for being the first appearance of the Dweller-in-Darkness; however, the character would not be properly identified until later on. 

### Synopsis
While the thunder god Thor was viewing the world of man with kindly amusement, the Olympian god Hercules stared at the city streets with despair, questioning how mortals could enjoy a life filled with pain and sorrow. Shortly afterwards, Hercules hears the cry of someone in danger, breaking into an apartment building to save an old man who was being robbed. Only caring about getting the money, the robber had no intentions of harming the old man; however, the old man ordered the robber to kill him, claiming that someone promised him that he would live after dying. By the time Hercules arrived, the old man had already been stabbed, but the injury was far from fatal, leading to Hercules chasing the robber to the top of the building. Hercules quickly defeats the robber, carrying his unconscious body back inside the building, where the old man commits suicide by causing the stove to explode. Thor arrives to put out the fire by summoning rain and wind, leading to Detective Sergeant Blumkenn inviting him to have a little talk, along with Hercules.

In a nearby cafeteria, Blumkenn explains that the old man was the fourth victim in a series of mysterious suicides. The first one was a college chemistry instructor named Theresa Mendall, who had been acting strange for several weeks before mumbling some kind of incantation and setting herself on fire. The second one was the construction engineer Moe Hartwell, who seemingly acted normal until detonating himself with dynamite, wiping out a block of abandoned tenements in the process. The third one was found on a jet into LaGuardia Airport, who caused the plane to crash by shooting the pilot and co-pilot. When Thor and Hercules denied the possibility of it being a conspiracy, Blumkenn walks away with disappointment; however, after Blumkenn was long gone, Thor and Hercules decided to team up for some further investigation.

Seeking his advice and wisdom to guide them, Thor tries to summon his father Odin, who decides to send someone else instead: Sif, Lady of Asgard. Thor was overjoyed to be reunited with his beloved lady, seeming distracting him from their current mission, leading to Hercules continuing by himself in anger. fullContent:
"Where Howls the Edgog" is a Lovecraftian short story set in the world of A. A. Milne's children's character Winnie-the-Pooh. Written by American author Pete Rawlik, it was published in the anthology The Call of Poohthulhu by April Moon Books in May 2022.

### Synopsis
After a fierce storm, Pooh decides to take a trip out to see his good friend Piglet. Upon arriving at Piglet's house, he finds that the little creature has barricaded himself inside, fearful of the monsters which have begun to creep through the hedge in the aftermath of the storm, monsters which he has dubbed Edgogs.

Deciding to confront the horrible beasts, Pooh and Piglet are astonished when they turn around and retreat through the breach in reality from whence they came. However, one makes a shocking revelation before it departs: Piglet is actually the hybrid offspring of the Edgogs and Piglet's distant  ancestor…

### Behind the Mythos
Two of Piglet's ancestors' names are given as Farnsworth and Hogson William. Farnsworth is likely a nod towards Farnsworth Wright, an editor of Weird Tales who was the first to publish several of H. P. Lovecraft's stories, while Hogson William is a clear reference to William Hope Hodgson, the creator of occult detective Thomas Carnacki and one of Lovecraft’s inspirations.

fullContent:
"Where Yidhra Walks" is a short story by American author Walter C. DeBill, Jr. Although originally written as part of his Mlandoth Cycle, it has since been incorporated into the greater Cthulhu Mythos through Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game.

### Synopsis
Kovacs is travelling across Texas on the way to visit his cousin when he becomes stranded in the small town of Milando as a result of hurricane flooding. Over the next few days he becomes aware of the existence of a cult to the Earth Mother deity Yidhra and his curiosity leads him to look into this phenomena.

As he finds out more, he realises that most of the town has been inducted into this cult, and that membership grants certain gifts- along with a price. When he discovers that he is to be the next inductee, he uses a tragic and violent incident between one of the last remaining human residents and some of the degenerate townsfolk as a cover to make a getaway. 

Although Kovacs manages to escape Milando, by the time he has alerted the authorities the whole incident has been covered up, leaving the cult and its master to continue their activities unhindered…

### Characters
*Peter Kovacs, an average Joe on a road trip.
*Wilhelm Kramer, a man who has married into the community of Milando.
*Yolanda Prentiss, an avatar of Yidhra and leader of the cult.

shortDefinition: Whipple Van Buren Phillips (November 22, 1833 - March 28, 1904) is the maternal grandfather of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.  Phillips was a successful businessman who owned much of the land in and around the town of Greene, Rhode Island. There he found...
fullContent:
Whipple Van Buren Phillips (November 22, 1833 - March 28, 1904) is the maternal grandfather of Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

Phillips was a successful businessman who owned much of the land in and around the town of Greene, Rhode Island. There he founded Freemason Ionic Lodge No. 28 in 1870. He had four children with his wife Robie Alzada Place Phillips: Sarah Susan Phillips Lovecraft (1857 - 1921), Emeline Estella Phillips (1859 - 1865), Edwin Everett Phillips (1864 - 1918), and Annie Emeline Phillips Gamwell.

After H. P. Lovecraft's father Winfield was committed to Butler Hospital for a nervous disorder, Lovecraft was largely raised by his mother and grandfather. Phillips heavily encouraged his grandson Howard's passion for reading, with a focus on classical literature and English poetry. After his death in 1904 he was buried in Swan Point Cemetery, Rhode Island. Though he left his family a substantial inheritance, it was greatly mismanaged.

"The Dunwich Horror" story by Lovecraft is frequently considered autobiographical to some extent, with Whipple van Buren being compared to Wizard Whateley.

### In the Mythos
According to one account, Lovecraft was raised by his Freemason father Winfield Lovecraft, instead of his grandfather. He was Egyptian and possessed Picatrix of Maslama ibn Ahma al-Magritit (a.k.a. pseudo-Magriti) and Godziher’s Book of the Essence of the Soul of which Lovecraft's Necronomicon is a mere portion. (: introduction to the Hay Necronomicon)

According to another account, Van Whipple was a Freemason and member of the Stella Sapiente and manufactured the creation of his grandson so that his writings would bring enough power to his creation that they could manifest in the future. This was done in a way similar to the real life counterpart of Old Whateley. (: Providence)

Whippoorwills are a type of bird with a distinctive call and a feature of several stories set in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos, including some by H. P. Lovecraft himself. They were most notably present at the death of Old Whateley, his daughter Lavinia, and his grandson Wilbur. The first's soul they failed to capture, the second's they apparently succeeded, and the third's fate is left unknown.

### Behind the Mythos
Lovecraft likely pulled this plot device from the Native American superstition that Whippoorwills were able to predict death as a sort of Banshee in Irish folklore or even being a sort of night spirit or grim reaper, but these stories can mostly be parallels to the 'Raven Mocker'.

Whippoorwills are common most often in the east coast and are considered a separate species from the Mexican Whippoorwill, Whippoorwills would have been a common sight in H. P. Lovecraft's life growing up in New England.

Whippoorwills were heard during the passing of several main characters in various works by numerous authors in the Mythos.

Though this concept of the whippoorwills acting as a sort of psychopomp may represent the final passing into nothingness, it was used by Fritz Leiber in a fictional telegraph on H. P. Lovecraft's death. It can also be assumed that H. P. Lovecraft's final sight in the Ghooric zone was his "Father" that died of pneumonia when Lovecraft was at a young age, it can certainly be assumed that there is a sort of afterlife in Lovecraft's universe. However, it could be argued that, keeping in line with the original stories of Lovecraft and their theme of an unkind universe, any "afterlife" within Lovecraftian stories would be a bastardization of most people's concept of such.

The Whisper Men are beings created by the BBC in 2013 for Doctor Who.

### Background
The Whisper Men are featureless beings who serve the Great Intelligence and may have been a manifestation of the entity itself. They could morph into the appearance of Walter Simeon and appeared to be unreal, hollow on the inside. The Whisper Men lacked features, moved slowly, had extremely white angular faces that lacked eyes, possessed mouths with sharp teeth, and had exaggerated chins and cheeks. When hit they evaporated and reformed, and they were able to pass their limbs into the flesh of others without leaving any visible wounds. The Whisper Men spoke in rhyming couplets, hissed at their victims, and were said to be able to kill with a whisper. When attacking they moved in small groups.

The Whispering Shadows is an eldritch abomination from the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics.

### Background
The abomination of the Whispering Shadows inhabited an eldritch fortress in the Black Kingdoms of the Hyborian Age. The Cimmerian barbarian Conan found himself in a storm and sought shelter in the ruins of a great fortress made of dense black stones which was built with odd angles in the arches, as if the builders weren't quite sane. It had corridors that were like a serpent's track, with some wide and low, and others so narrow that Conan was barely able to pass through. 

He could sense and later during his sleep hear the whispers of the ghosts of 1000s of sentients who had died within the fortress and hungered for his blood. While he slept a slaver band of 40 Stygians whom likewise sought shelter from the storm took shelter in the fortress. The ghosts merged and used their lifeforces to create a physical body of numerous malformed heads, limbs, and tentacle-like appendages. It then slaughtered the Stygians, tearing and rending them. While that was happening, Conan fled the citadel.

The white apes are a species created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family".

### Description
The precise appearance of the "white apes" is never clearly defined. Based on the context of the story "Facts Concerning the Late Arthur Jermyn and His Family" we know from their remains that they are habitually bipedal, have a roughly similar frame as anatomically modern humans, but would be recognized by elongated arms, an unusually robust strength and an inhuman facial structure.

We know that they are at least biologically and genetically compatible on some level with human beings, as Arthur Jermyn is revealed to be the descendant of a "white ape" female and a human male.

### Speculation
By virtue of a modern understanding of evolution, genetics, and anthropology, a great deal of insight may be had into the biological lineage of the "white ape." Based on information contained in the Arthur Jermyn family tree, the wife and mate of Arthur Jermyn's Great-great-great Grandfather, Sir Wade Jermyn, was a "white ape". Their child, Sir Philip Jermyn, went on to have his own family and children. This is significant, and indicates that Great-great-great Grandmother Jermyn was not in fact an "ape", but rather a member of an extant highly rare and isolated human sub-species, not unlike the extinct Neanderthals and Denisovans.

Sir Philip would therefore have been an intra-species hybrid. Had his mother originated outside the Homo sapiens species, Sir Philip would have been sterile or have yielded unviable offspring (the limited number of offspring in the Jermyn line may suggest genetic compatibility issues.) The fact that he did not suggests that while having marked morphological differences from AMHs (anatomically modern humans), the bride of Sir Wade Jermyn was human on a genetic level.

There then remains the question of the origin of the "white ape" human sub-species. There are three potential explanations: 
#Like Neanderthals and Denisovans, the "white apes" descend from a common Homo erectus ancestor, this sub-species then persisted in isolation in the Congo river basin.
#The "white apes" are actually surviving Neanderthals or Denisovans, and their white color is either a cultural body painting/dying or the result of albinism reinforced in the limited gene pool.
# The "white apes" are actually genetic descendants of AMHs, human settlers to the basin at some point in the ancient prehistoric past. The morphology and pigmentation variation is therefore the result of genetic abnormalities that became reinforced in this isolated gene pool.

Finally, and perhaps most problematically, there is the possibility that there were no "white apes" at all. In this scenario, the "inhuman" features of Jermyn are an exaggeration as seen through the lens of a rac

shortDefinition: White Darkness is a Doctor Who novel by David A. McIntee released in 1993 as part of the franchise's New Adventures series. It features the Necronomicon and introduces the concept of the Great Old Ones to the Doctor Who universe.  ### Synopsis The Do...
fullContent:
White Darkness is a Doctor Who novel by David A. McIntee released in 1993 as part of the franchise's New Adventures series. It features the Necronomicon and introduces the concept of the Great Old Ones to the Doctor Who universe.

### Synopsis
The Doctor is a Time Lord from the planet Gallifrey who travels through time and space in a ship called the TARDIS, accompanied by his two human companions: Prof. Bernice Summerfield and Ace. Seeking a nice holiday in Florida, they mistakenly land in 1915 Haiti, in the middle of a revolution, being promptly arrested and brought before the cruel General Etienne. Meanwhile, a powerful voodoo sorcerer named Lemaitre and an assassin named Carrefour are working in league with the crew of a secret German military base in a mysterious project.

The Doctor convinces Etienne that he and his companions are British intelligence agents, and they are allowed to go, but the TARDIS key is confiscated by Captain Petion, who is assigned as their guide and tasked with keeping an eye on them.

One of Lemaitre's agents, named Henri Duval, keeps himself mentally in touch with an alien entity, whose body remains underground in stasis while its disembodied consciousness flows through the time vortex. Henri uses a tarot deck to find out about the Doctor and how he's going to interfere with their plans, and warns Lemaitre and his German allies accordingly. The Doctor, who has psychic abilities of his own, detects something akin to distant voices, which his human companions can't hear, and becomes aware that something is amiss.

On the next day, while Captain Petion gives the Doctor and his friends a tour, the four of them find a horribly mangled corpse inside a warehouse. The Doctor's analysis reveals that the man was torn apart by several barehanded people, and the victim's journal describes his encounter with a horde of zombies. Petion reluctantly admits that similar incidents have been happening for some time, and arranges for the body to be examined by an American physician named Howard Phillips, who has experience treating zombified people.

Howard explains that most so-called zombies are victims of tetrodotoxin, a drug that puts the major organs of the body into a catatonic-like state, so the subject remains barely functional enough to be used as a slave. He insists that tetrodotoxin victims are weak and docile, but also reveals that lately there have been cases in which a different, unknown type of drug has been used to create strong and aggressive zombies, including at least one who miraculously returned to life after an autopsy.

While Ace and Petion head off to retrieve the TARDIS, which has been taken by Etienne, Howard shows his collection of archaeological artifacts and a copy of the unexpurgated Necronomicon which contains instructions for reviving the dead. "White Feather" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author T. E. Grau.

### Synopsis
During the American revolution a New England privateer recalls a time when he and his crew encountered a hamlet populated by Deep One hybrids. The men put the village to the torch, and later his ship was boarded by Deep One and all but the captain slaughtered. The privateer later returns to the waters outside the destroyed habitation and waits for the Deep Ones to once again come aboard before detonating the ships gunpowder stocks.

The story ends with a statement that the Deep Ones had subsequently begun to prepare themselves for a war with those of the land.

### Characters

*Captain Mark James Chilton, a successful American privateer.

### Publication History
"White Feather" was published in the Brian M. Sammons/Glynn Owen Barrass-edited anthology World War Cthulhu in 2014, and later appeared in the collection of T. E. Grau works The Nameless Dark in 2015.

The White Rabbit was created by Lewis Carroll in 1865, first appearing in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. In 2008, it first appeared in Zenescope Entertainment's Grimm Fairy Tales fictional universe, in the issue #0 of the 1st volume of Grimm Fairy Tales: Return to Wonderland.

### Background
The White Rabbit is a rabbit that was purchased by the scientist Henry Allen in 1860, the first test subject he used in his experiments with the portal to Wonderland. Forced through the portal, it ended up in Wonderland where it was transformed by the Jabberwocky into a creature of madness and corruption, which lured Calie Liddle into Wonderland, after which the rabbit returned to Alice Liddle whom he slowly drove insane, ending in her suicide.

Who Stole the Necronomicon? is a Cthulhu Mythos novella by American author and screenwriter Byron Craft. The sixth in his Arkham Detective series of Mythos noir stories, it was self-published in 2020.

### Synopsis
In the aftermath of Prohibition, the Arkham Detective has decided to use some of his recently-acquired wealth to leave the Arkham Police Department and establish himself as a private investigator, while using his past experiences as a basis for short horror stories with which to make some extra cash. Along the way, he has regained custody of his estranged son Elijah, and picked up another stray in the form of street urchin Alvin Nash.

Unfortunately for his peaceful existence, a murder at Miskatonic University, the theft of the Necronomicon, and a request for help from former colleague Detective Sergeant Matthew Bell draw the Detective into another dark conspiracy. Despite being forced to face down a deranged descendant of the witch Keziah Mason, the actual ghost of Mason herself, the vicious familiar Brown Jenkin, the Outer God Azathoth, and - inexplicably - a group of Elder Things, he defeats all of these threats and emerges victorious.

### Trivia
*The Detective is stated to have sold one of his stories, titled Cthulhu's Minions and based on the events described in that book, to legendary pulp magazine Weird Tales. The pen name that he used for this was Byron Craft, implying that the real-life author is in fact the Arkham Detective, relaying his experiences in the guise of fiction.
*Bizarrely, the pseudonym used by Camon Mason, Keziah's descendent, is Millicent Schuyler-Potts, a minor character from 1960s sitcom The Beverly Hillbillies, which aired some 30 years after the time in which Who Stole the Necronomicon? is estimated to be set .

Wilbur Akeley is a fictional character created by August Derleth for his short story "The Gable Window", one of his "posthumous collaborations" with H. P. Lovecraft. He is depicted as a scholar of occult lore who installs a dimensional portal in his house in Lovecraft Country.

Derleth describes Akeley as "a student of archeology and anthropology". After graduating from Arkham's Miskatonic University, Akeley spends  three years in Mongolia, Tibet, and China's Sinkiang (now Xinjiang) province, and another three years in South and Central America and the southwestern United States. Concluding his travels in 1921, he moves to the "old Wharton place", a 200-year-old farmhouse "in a pocket of the hills off the Aylesbury Pike".

Akeley almost entirely rebuilds the old farmhouse, most notably adding a gable with a circular window in which he installs "a most curious clouded glass", which his notes describe as "a work of great antiquity, which he had discovered and acquired in the course of his travels in Asia". He refers to the window as "the glass from Leng" and speculates that it is "possibly Hyadean in origin". Combined with a pentagram-like design and a spoken formula, the window can be used to see into other places and dimensions.

Akeley accumulates an impressive collection of Mythos-related literature at the Wentworth place, including copies of the Pnakotic Manuscripts, the R’lyeh Text, Unaussprechlichen Kulten, the Book of Eibon, the Dhôl Chants, the Seven Cryptical Books of Hsan, De Vermis Mysteriis, the Celaeno Fragments, Cultes des Goules, the Book of Dzyan, and "a photostat copy of the Necronomicon". Some of his library came from Henry Akeley, a Vermont relative, apparently the same character who appears in H.P. Lovecraft's "The Whisperer in Darkness".

Akeley lives only three more years after moving to the Wentworth place; in 1924, sometime before April, he is "struck down with a coronary ailment while he was at work in the stacks of Miskatonic University Library". His death is called "untimely"; if he graduated from Miskatonic at a typical age, he would have died in his early 30s.

Wilbur Whateley is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Dunwich Horror".

### Background
In the rural town of Dunwich, Massachusetts on February 2, 1913 at 5 a.m., Lavinia Whateley gave birth to a son named Wilbur Whateley. The date of his birth is noted for the night before the hills rumbled and dogs barked incessantly. Dogs continued to show an instinctual hatred for him for the remainder of his life. Wilbur was immediately recognized for his hideousness, described as a "dark, goatish-looking infant".

He displayed unnaturally rapid physical and mental development: At seven months he could walk unassisted and eleven months could speak. At four and a half, he appeared fifteen and he began to grow facial hair.

"Though he shared his mother's and grandfather's chinlessness, his firm and precociously shaped nose united with the expression of his large, dark, almost Latin eyes to give him an air of..well-nigh preternatural intelligence,.. something almost goatish or animalistic about his thick lips, large-pored, yellowish skin, coarse crinkly hair, and oddly elongated ears."

At a young age he takes to wearing very concealing clothes. He also has a revolting odor about his person, a defining characteristic of the Great Old Ones. Wilbur's voice is distinctive for its "Strange, resonant fashion which hinted at sound-producing organs unlike the run of mankind's". This presumably allows him to speak the language of the Great Old Ones. At 15 years he had grown to 9 feet tall and showed no sign of stopping. 

Prior to his grandfather’s death he left him with the responsibility of raising his twin as well as ensuring he opens the gates to Yog-Sothoth. He could only accomplish this by finding the summoning ritual on page 751 of the Necronomicon. He then travelled to the Miskatonic, Cambridge, and Widener libraries in search of a complete version of this book. They all, under the guidance of Dr. Armitage, denied him access. He was then forced to return to Miskatonic University to steal their copy. This attempt ultimately proves his downfall, when a watchdog savagely kills him. It succeeded solely because Whateley's revolver failed to fire. 

It is then that several disturbing truths of his biology were revealed. In place of blood he had a greenish-yellow ichor. Yellow and black markings covered his back. From the waist down his body was covered in coarse black fur. A sort of rudimentary eye was positioned on each hip. 

His final words were the excerpt from the Necronomicon which he had been searching. Immediately afterward his corpse disintegrated into a sticky white mass, apparently having no true skeletal structure. Out the window a swarm of Whippoorwills were heard shrieking in anticipation for his soul. They soon fled after witnessing their intended prey.

fullContent:
"Wilbur Whateley Waiting" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American scholar and author Robert M. Price.

### Synopsis
When he is resurrected by amateur magician Ezekiel Prinn nearly sixty years after his own death, Wilbur Whateley goes searching for a copy of the Necronomicon with which to awaken Rhan-Tegoth. Unable to locate one, he ends his travels in his home town of Dunwich. After several years on his old homestead contemplating what to do, he stumbles across a cave, inside of which is a door. The door is covered in arcane symbols which he recognises from his old grimoires, and the story ends with Wilbur opening the door and preparing to begin again. As for Prinn, he finds that he has the correct incantation after all and awakens Rhan-Tegoth, which kills him and goes back to sleep after no blood sacrifices are forthcoming.

### Characters

* Wilbur Whateley, the semi-human son of Yog-Sothoth, who is dedicated to bringing the Earth into his father's hands.
* Ezekiel Prinn, an aging but dedicated, if somewhat ill-informed, occultist.
* Rhan-Tegoth, a Great Old One which will summon the rest of its kind if successfully unleashed.

### Publication History
"Wilbur Whateley Waiting" was first published in the fanzine Revelations from Yuggoth #1 in November 1987. It later appeared in the anthologies The Dunwich Cycle: Where the Old Gods Wait (November 1995) and Blasphemies & Revelations (November 2008).

### Trivia

* Ezekiel Prinn claims to be of the line "of Abigail Prinn, and of Ludvig Prinn before her." Abigail Prinn was the antagonist in Henry Kuttner's short story "The Salem Horror" (1937), while Ludvig Prinn is the fictional author of the recurrent occult grimoire De Vermis Mysteriis (which was first mentioned in Robert Bloch's "The Secret in the Tomb", 1935).

Wildside Press is an American independent publishing company whose output includes work from H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos, amongst many other titles.

### Overview
Originally founded in 1989 by author John Gregory Betancourt and his wife Kim as an outlet for speculative fiction, Wildside's scope has since expanded to cover a number of genres, including mystery, science fiction, romance, and nonfiction. The company also produces a range of audiobooks (both in digital and compact disc formats) and downloadable eBooks, and maintains a print on demand service as well as a reprint project dedicated to publishing issues of old pulp magazines in their original format.

Wildside Press incorporates the imprints Borgo Press, Cosmos Books and Point Blank.

Wilhelmshaven is a real world town located on the northern coast of Germany, mentioned in the story "The Temple" by H. P. Lovecraft. 

Kriegsmarinewerft Wilhelmshaven was and is a massive German naval base. During both World War I and World War 2 it functioned as the main shipyard for the country as well as housing submarine bases for docking and repairing Germany's fearsome submarine squadrons. It operated as U-Boat central docks in real life between 1918 and 1945.

In "The Temple," the German submarine U-29 under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich had intended to return there at the conclusion of its mission before it was lost at sea.

William Patrick Murray (born April 28, 1953), who publishes as Will Murray, is a fiction writer and a historian of popular culture, with a specialization in pulp fiction and comic books. His Cthulhu Mythos-related fiction has appeared in such anthologies as  Miskatonic University, The Cthulhu Cycle, Disciples of Cthulhu II, Cthulhu's Reign, Worlds of Cthulhu, The Yig Cycle, and The Mountains of Madness. His Mythos fiction has been collected in The Wild Adventures of Cthulhu, volumes one and two.

Murray has written extensively for Marvel Comics; with Steve Ditko, he is the co-creator of the character Squirrel Girl. 

He has edited two collections of stories by Clark Ashton Smith, Tales of Zothique and The Book of Hyperborea, for Necronomicon Press.

Murray was also a member of the Providence Pals, an informal group of H. P. Lovecraft enthusiasts and scholars active from the late 1970s through to the 1990s.

Along with S. T. Joshi and Jon L. Cooke, Murray founded The Friends of H. P. Lovecraft to raise funds for a memorial plaque at Brown University's John Hay Library to mark the centennial of Lovecraft's birth, in August 1990.

Since 1979, he has been the literary executor for Lester Dent, the creator of Doc Savage.

William Adcock is an American traditional games designer and occasional author from Rochester, New York, best known for his work on Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. For Call of Cthulhu, he has written material in several of the game's settings, including Classic (1920s), Colonial era, and particularly Cthulhu Invictus (Roman empire). fullContent:
William Blake is a recurrent character in the works of British author David Hambling, and the primary focus of a story cycle to which he lends his name.

### Overview
Born in the early 20th century, by the 1920s Blake was one of the Bright Young Things, a term given to the post-World War I generation of the London party scene. While studying for his PhD, he made a living by tutoring promising lower-achievers, at that time renting a room in the house of an older couple by the name of Hall (: "The Dulwich Horror of 1927").

Blake was never to finish his degree, however, as a result of an encounter with an extra-dimensional entity; the same encounter left him with near-fatal injuries, killing most of his friends and putting the two other survivors forever beyond his reach (: "The Dulwich Horror of 1927").

Later in life, Blake would become a teacher, living a semi-itinerant life and moving regularly in an effort to leave his past behind him (: "The Monsters in the Park").

In late 1936, Blake was recruited by an old school friend to try and help his 8-year-old son, who had suddenly and inexplicably suffered a drastic personality change. During the course of his efforts, he discovered that the boy had been taken over by an advanced extraterrestrial being intent on finding ways to affect the course of an aeons-long war. Although he was successful in returning the boy to his own body, the being simply transferred itself to his father, an act Blake was helpless to affect (: "The Monsters in the Park").

The William Blake Cycle comprises a series of Cthulhu Mythos stories by British author David Hambling, based on the character from which it takes its name.

### Overview
The series follows William Blake, a former "Bright Young Thing" in 1920s London, later a teacher. Blake has a long and traumatic history with the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos, although fortunately for all, this puts him at a unique advantage when dealing with these beings and their minions.

The cycle spawned a spin-off series in Age of Monsters, begun with the novel War of the God Queen, which follows Jessica, an old friend of Blake's who was cast through time during an encounter with an ancient evil.

William Channing Webb is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his short story "The Call of Cthulhu". 

### Background
William Channing Webb is a professor of anthropology at Princeton University and "an explorer of no slight note." When Inspector John Raymond Legrasse conferred with a meeting of the American Anthropology Society about the Cthulhu Cult, Professor Webb was the only member of the assembly to be familiar with an idol found during the raid and the ritualistic chants used by the cult, based on his investigation of a "singular tribe or cult of degenerate Esquimaux" he encountered "high up on the West Greenland coast" in 1860. William Dyer is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft, who makes his first appearance in the 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness.

### Description
Dyer is a professor of geology at Miskatonic University in Arkham, Massachusetts, and the leader of the disastrous Pabodie Expedition to Antarctica in 1930–31. Only his last name is mentioned in the text of Mountains, though he is fully identified as William Dyer in Lovecraft's novella The Shadow Out of Time, where he accompanies an expedition to Australia's Great Sandy Desert.

Detective William L. "Billy" Sinclair is a fictional character created by Josh Finney for his Casefile: Arkham series of Cthulhu Mythos stories. He made his first appearance in the 2016 graphic novel Casefile: Arkham- Nightmare on the Canvas.

### Description
A man in his late middle age, Sinclair is a jaded cop working for Arkham Police Department's homicide division in post-WWII America. Slightly overweight and beginning to go bald, he appears to be one of the few officers in the division with any morals.

Sinclair has made the acquaintance of private investigator Hank Flynn and considers him to be "almost" a friend; however, their personal relationship has not stopped him from threatening Flynn with legal action when he refused to leave a case well alone.

### History
Sinclair was a detective working on the Arkham Slasher case in 1946, but without any leads was getting nowhere. When Hank Flynn shot dead Richard Upton Pickman, the fiend responsible for the murders, he sent an anonymous tip in to Sinclair, allowing him to claim credit for bringing the case to a close.

Three months later, when Flynn shot Edward Pickman Derby after the man attacked him, Sinclair interrogated Flynn about the crime, but did not believe him to be guilty of murder.

shortDefinition: William Lumley was a late associate of Howard Phillips Lovecraft for whom Lovecraft ghostwrote "The Diary of Alonzo Typer" in 1935. The story was only published after Lovecraft's death, in the February 1938 issue of Weird Tales. Like many of Lovecraf...
fullContent:
William Lumley was a late associate of Howard Phillips Lovecraft for whom Lovecraft ghostwrote "The Diary of Alonzo Typer" in 1935. The story was only published after Lovecraft's death, in the February 1938 issue of Weird Tales. Like many of Lovecraft's collaborators, little is known of his life. He is reported to have been from Buffalo, New York, but it is unclear if this was his birthplace. He worked as a watchman for Buffalo's Agrico Chemical Company. 

He corresponded with Lovecraft from 1931 until Lovecraft's death, though few of Lovecraft's letters to him survive.We may think we're writing fiction, and may even (absurd thought!) disbelieve what we write, but at bottom we are telling the truth in spite of ourselves. It is interesting that this euhemeristic belief on the part of William Lumley anticipates by thirty years the 1960s adoption of Mythos entities as credible and "real" supernatural entities and concepts with to purport to practice magic by people such as Kenneth Grant.

While there has been confusion, there is no known relation between William Lumley and Brian Lumley, another horror writer and contributor to the Mythos.

William Barclay Meikle (born January 25, 1958) is an  British author of horror and mystery who has made extensive contributions to the Cthulhu Mythos first established by H. P. Lovecraft, including several which cross other characters from classic works of fiction with those of Lovecraft: examples of these include Arthur Conan Doyle's Sherlock Holmes and Professor Challenger, and William Hope Hodgson's Thomas Carnacki. Born in Ayrshire, Scotland but currently living in Canada, Meikle can claim over 30 published novels and more than 300 short stories to his name. 

The association of music and, to a lesser extent, dancing with the supernatural is a common element of Meikle's works. 

### Thomas Carnacki
Perhaps more than any other author, William Meikle has expanded upon the character of Thomas Carnacki, the occult detective created in the early 1900s by English author William Hope Hodgson. Meikle's Carnacki writings include stories directly tied to the Cthulhu Mythos, those with more subtle inspirations, and more traditional paranormal tales.

William Yorick, the Gravedigger, is a character created by Fantasy Flight Games as part of their Arkham Horror Files line of Cthulhu Mythos-related games and fiction.

### History
William has had two differing versions of his character biography released, the first printed in the Innsmouth Horror expansion to Arkham Horror Second Edition, and the second in Eldritch Horror. In both versions he was a struggling actor who took a job as a gravedigger at Arkham's South Church, where inhuman corpses began to appear. After this, the accounts diverge.

### Innsmouth Horror Deluxe Expansion ()
Noticing strange men watching him wherever he went, William realised that taking the corpses to Miskatonic University would be a fatal error, and instead decided to talk things over with Father Michael before deciding on his future course of action.

### Eldritch Horror ()
Taking the corpses to Miskatonic University brought down the wrath of an unknown group of people on William's head and, fearing for his life, travelled to Sydney, where he once again landed a job as a gravedigger. Everything was going fine for him, until the bodies began to crawl from their resting places ...

### Behind the Mythos
William Yorick was introduced as an Investigator for the Arkham Horror expansion Innsmouth Horror, and has also made appearances in Eldritch Horror, Arkham Horror: The Card Game, Elder Sign and Mansions of Madness. Fantasy Flight's 2010 release of the Arkham Horror Premium Figures line included a miniature of the character, although this is no longer available (all ).

fullContent:
Willis Clark Conover, Jr. (18 December 1920 - 17 May 1996) was an American broadcaster and music producer who spent a time in his youth corresponding with horror author Howard Phillips Lovecraft .

### Overview
Conover had been interested in science fiction from an early age, and this brought him into contact with Lovecraft who, by this time, was reaching the end of his life. 

An avid science fiction fan from an early age, Conover published his own fanzine, the Science Fantasy Correspondent, as a youth . Their correspondence has been collected in the volume Lovecraft at Last (1975, Carrollton Clark).

Conover would go on to spend much of his life in the broadcasting and music production industries, being a prominent figure in promoting jazz in conjunction with an anti-segregation mindset. Despite this, his was a relatively unknown voice in the United States, his influence being felt far more keenly in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe, where access to jazz music was severely limited .

A lifelong smoke, Conover died of lung cancer in May 1996 .

The Wilmarth Foundation is a fictional organisation in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally created by Brian Lumley for his novel The Burrowers Beneath, part of the Titus Crow series.

### Overview
The Wilmarth Foundation is an organisation based in Arkham, MA dedicated to combating the Great Old Ones with hundreds of agents and connections all over the world. It was founded by Albert Wilmarth.

During the 1960s they organised both the Great Britain Project and the American Project to drive out the Cthulhu Cycle Deities from their respective countries. The Great Britain Project was particularly successful, clearing the island of subterranean monstrosities and resulting in the death of the creature referred to as Cgfthgnm'o'th.

fullContent:
"Windows to the Soul" is a Lovecraftian short story by American author Time Kane. It was published in Vol 5, Issue 2 of the Lovecraftiana zine by Rogue Planet Press in July 2020.

### Synopsis
In a city in which the vacant-eyed homeless population is dramatically increasing, two men find themselves stranded late at night after an evening's carousing. As they attempt to navigate their way home, they encounter a grisly murder scene where the victim's eyes have been removed. Cutting through a construction site to try and regain the main drag, they enter a pool of blackness which consumes one of the men and leaves the other a slack-jawed wreck destined to live his life on the streets, his mind shattered by what he witnessed while the rest of the city slept.

fullContent:
Winfield Scott Lovecraft (26 Oct 1853-19 Jul 1898) was the father of Howard Phillips Lovecraft and the husband of Sarah Susan Phillips Lovecraft.

Winfield was born October 26, 1853, in Rochester, New York, the son of George Lovecraft and  Helen Allgood Lovecraft.

Winfield was a traveling salesman for Gorham & Co., a manufacturer of silverware based in Providence, Rhode Island. In 1893, when Howard was three, Winfield became acutely psychotic in a Chicago hotel room while on a business trip, caused by neurological symptoms of syphilis, a sexually transmitted disease. He was brought back to Providence and placed in Butler Hospital, where he remained until his death in 1898. Lovecraft was falsely informed that his father was comatose during this period.

He died July 19, 1898, in Butler Hospital, from complications of syphilis.

Winfield Townley Scott (30 April 1910 - 28 April 1968) was an American poet, newspaper editor, broadcaster and occasional critic. He is most notable to this wiki for his early scholarly work on the late Howard Phillips Lovecraft.

### Overview
Scott was known to have engaged in a brief correspondence with Lovecraft, and after his death wrote a handful of non-fiction works in appreciation of his former associate. He also wrote a critique of H. P. Lovecraft (1890–1937) for The Providence Journal and Evening Bulletin, and edited a short memoir of Lovecraft by his former wife Sonia H. Greene.

Scott was a long-term resident of New England, living there from birth until 1954 when he and his wife left for Santa Fe, California, and attended Brown University in his younger days.

Professor Wingate Peaslee is a character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Shadow Out of Time. He has since been expanded upon by several authors, perhaps most notably Brian Lumley in his Titus Crow series of Mythos novels.

### In Lovecraft's Work
In The Shadow Out of Time, Peaslee was a Miskatonic University professor and the son of Nathaniel Wingate Peaslee, also a Miskatonic professor. He is described by his father as "the only member of my family who stuck to me after my queer amnesia of long ago, and the man best informed on the inner facts of my case."

### Titus Crow
In Lumley's Titus Crow series, Peaslee is now a member of the Wilmarth Foundation, an organisation dedicated to combating the forces of the Cthulhu Mythos on Earth. He is a key figure in the Foundation's highly-successful Great Britain Project, an operation dedicated to clearing these entities from the British Isles. Peaslee's primary participation in this endeavour was his plan to destroy the entity known as Cgfthgnm'o'th.

### In Other Works
In Peter Rawlik's short story "Cold War, Yellow Fever" features Colonel Doctor Peaslee, a senior covert operations commander with the United States military who specialises in dealing with contagion.

shortDefinition: "Winged Death" is a short story co-written by Hazel Heald and H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in Weird Tales in 1934. In a departure from typical Lovecraftian horror, "Winged Death" describes the use of flies as an instrument of torture and d...
fullContent:
"Winged Death" is a short story co-written by Hazel Heald and H. P. Lovecraft. It was first published in Weird Tales in 1934. In a departure from typical Lovecraftian horror, "Winged Death" describes the use of flies as an instrument of torture and death.

The narrative intertwines themes of transferred personality, death, science, and the supernatural. The story is largely narrated as a confession by Thomas Slauenwhite, a disgraced medical practitioner. It revolves around a scientist's obsession with the potential of infectious insects, particularly tsetse flies, to serve as a means of murder. It also focuses on the negativity and obsession that comes with a desire for revenge and the moral failings giving way to cruelty and desire to persecute that follow.

### Synopsis
"Winged Death" begins with a group of four men in a hotel experiencing terror due in equal amounts to a mysterious dead fly floating in a small bottle of ammonia, scrawled writing on the ceiling of the room they occupied, and a journal clutched in the hand of a corpse on the floor. This sets the scene for a murder story where a vengeful doctor uses disease-carrying stinging and biting flies as his murder weapon.

### Mythos References

* Thomas Slauenwhite, M.D. relates in his journal how, when searching for the flies in Uganda, his party stumbled across "Cyclopean ruins … megaliths … older than man and that … used to be a haunt or outpost of "The Fishers from Outside"—whatever that means—and of the evil gods Tsadogwa and Clulu. To this day they are said to have a malign influence, and to be connected somehow with the devil-flies."

fullContent:
Winged Ones is a general name for winged creatures.

It may refer to a number of different elements of the Mythos.
*The "Black Winged Ones" are bat-winged creatures summoned to the rites of the Cthulhu Cult (: "The Call of Cthulhu"). These may be the "black-snouted winged creatures" that evolved on Earth at some point in the Cenozoic (: The Shadow Out of Time). The Byakhee are also described as "black-winged bat-like creatures", but are unlikely to be the same species, as the Byakhee are enemies of Cthulhu (: "The House on Curwen Street"). They might also be the black-winged creatures that John Whateley is in league with (: Fungi from Yuggoth).
*The star-headed Elder Things are sometimes called Winged Ones prior to their losing the power of flight
*Cult doctrine has it that "the Winged Ones taught the elder lore to men" in Lomar. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")
*Hastur and his servants, notably the Mi-Go, have been called by this term. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)
*Ragnalla, Nest Mistress of the Winged Ones. (: "Ragnalla" [James Ambuehl])
*An Elder Race of the Thurian Age. (: Kull of Atlantis [Conan: Adventures in an Age Undreamed Of expansion])

### Trivia
*The term was used by H. P. Lovecraft and taken up by Fred Pelton and others.

"Wings in the Night" is a Cthulhu Mythos short story by the late American author Edward P. Berglund. It was first published in the first issue of Dark Messenger Reader in 1975.

The story is notable for featuring the first appearance of Mynoghra, a Great Old One who would go on to appear in several other properties, including a recurrent role in the Carpe Noctem series by Hashtag Comics.

### Synopsis
The story recounts the tale of Eric Moltone, an amnesiac former book critic confined to the Oregon State Mental Institution with an irrational fear of shadows.

On All Hallow's Eve exactly one year ago to the day, Moltone had sought an interview with Charles B. Griths, a reclusive but brilliant author. Sneaking onto Griths' private island, Moltone chatted with the writer until the sun went down. As darkness fell, the lights began to extinguish themselves, and the entity which had gifted Griths with his success arrived to claim its due. After witnessing Griths' gruesome demise, Moltone fled for his life, escaping by the skin of his teeth.

On Halloween the following year, the lights in Oregon State Mental Institution begin to go out, and Moltone realises that finally dread Mynoghra has come to take the unfortunate man as its next meal…

### Publication History
*Dark Messenger Reader #1 (1975)
*Dark Legacy, March 1999 (1999)
*Shards of Darkness (2000)
*The Best of Dark Legacy, Volume 1 (2016)

fullContent:
Winifred V. Jackson was a collaborator with Howard Phillips Lovecraft on the short stories, "The Green Meadow" and "The Crawling Chaos", under the pseudonym Elizabeth Berkeley. Details about her life are scarce, but there is speculation that she and Lovecraft were romantically involved during the period of their collaborations. Lovecraft was highly congratulatory of her work and praised her talent in his essay, "Winifred Virginia Jackson: A "Different" Poetess".

After her divorce from Horace Wheeler Jordan and during her maybe-romance with Lovecraft, she was romantically involved with the African-American poet and critic William Stanley Braithwaite. Some of the remaining examples of her poems appear in his collections.

### Selected Works

*"The Green Meadow" (1927)

shortDefinition: Winter Tide is a novel by Ruthanna Emrys, published by Tor in 2017. It continues the Innsmouth Legacy series begun in the 2014 novella The Litany of Earth, in which the Deep Ones of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" are not treated as hor...
fullContent:
Winter Tide is a novel by Ruthanna Emrys, published by Tor in 2017. It continues the Innsmouth Legacy series begun in the 2014 novella The Litany of Earth, in which the Deep Ones of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Shadow Over Innsmouth" are not treated as horrific monsters but as a different kind of human deserving of sympathy. Winter Tide extends and examines other Lovecraft stories, including "The Shadow Out of Time", "The Thing on the Doorstep", and "The Mound".

As with Litany, Winter Tide focuses on Aphra Marsh, a Deep One woman and one of only two survivors (with her brother Caleb) of the government raid on Innsmouth to make it out of the subsequent concentration camps alive. In this book, set largely at Miskatonic University in 1948, she continues working with sympathetic FBI agent Ron Spector, this time trying to learn whether Russian agents have used Miskatonic's resources to learn the mind-swapping techniques. She gains new allies--including a member of the Great Race of Yith who has appropriated the body of a Miskatonic professor, and a student from Miskatonic's sister school who appears to be descended in part from the people of K'n-yan--and butts heads with another FBI contingent that hopes to use Miskatonic's magic for their own ends. Aphra reconnects with her blood family at Y'ha-nthlei, and strengthens ties with her growing chosen family.

### Characters
*Aphra Yukhl Marsh: Aphra comes to Miskatonic University to help the FBI learn whether mind-transfer magic may have been learned by the Soviets--but also to get back in touch with her Deep One family in Y'ha-nthlei. She has the "bulging eyes, thick neck, and receding hairline" associated with her Innsmouth heritage.
*Caleb Nghadri Marsh: Aphra's brother, and with her the only known survivors of Innsmouth who still live on land. He is driven to recover Innsmouth's books, now held in Miskatonic's library. He is a "gangling man" with "long arms and legs"; like his sister, he has "the bulging eyes, the flat nose, the broad chin, and long fingers" that mark them as People of the Water.
* Neko Koto: A  19-year-old member of Aphra's adoptive Japanese-American family who accompanies her to Massachusetts. She serves as a secretary to the FBI mission, but chooses to join them out of a love of travel.
*Charlie Day: Aphra's boss at the San Francisco used bookstore he owns--and her student in the magical seminar she runs. Gruffly protective of Aphra, he is gay but not out of the closet, even to her.
*Ron Spector: Aphra's contact in the FBI, who sees Aeonism as a religion with followers both good and bad, and wants to protect the former and enlist their help to protect humanity from the latter. He is Jewish, which is seen as slightly suspicious in the Bureau, especially after the formation of Israel. He is also gay and deeply closeted, which Aphra figures out when she detects his secret relationship with Day.
*Dorothy Dawson: A Black FBI agent who is undercover as both maid and mistress of Miskatonic's

Wisconsin, also known as "The Dairy State," "The Badger State," and "America’s Dairyland," is a state located in the Upper Midwest region of the United States of America. Once home to many Native American cultures, European visitation began with French exploration during the 17th century; however, the French did not establish any permanent presence in the region, and the British created the first non-native settlements, eventually gaining control of the area before it became a United States territorial possession in 1783. It gained its statehood - being the 30th to do so - in 1848.

Although Wisconsin receives little representation in the works of H. P. Lovecraft himself, his literary circle have expanded on this somewhat, and a number of his real-life friends and correspondents were either born there or lived in the state at some point in their lives.

### Overview

### In Lovecraft’s Works

### "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin"
The events of Lovecraft’s 1918 romantic tragedy take place around the town of Appleton, Wisconsin, near the banks of the Fox River. (: "A Pastoral Tragedy of Appleton, Wisconsin")

### "Ibid"
In Lovecraft’s parodic short story, the skull of Roman scholar Ibidus ends its journey across time and continents in a prairie dog hole in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (: "Ibid")

### "Winged Death"
Dr. Henry Sargent Moore, Ph.D, penned the book Diptera of Central and South Africa, which was used in the University of Wisconsin. (: "Winged Death")

### In the Works of Lovecraft’s Circle

### "The Warder of Knowledge"
1935 story of a man driven to death by the knowledge inscribed upon the mystical Eltdown Shards by Richard F. Searight. At one point, the shards are sent to one Gordon Whitney of Beloin College, Hanover, Wisconsin (: "The Warder of Knowledge")

### "The Sorcerer's Jewel"
The events related in Robert Bloch's 1939 short horror story, concerning mysterious deaths surrounding a cursed gemstone, take place in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. (: "The Sorcerer's Jewel")

### "Beyond the Threshold"
August Derleth's 1941 horror short details the investigation of a Wisconsin house which conceals a portal to another realm. (: "Beyond the Threshold")

### "The Dweller in Darkness"
Derleth's 1944 short story concerns events which take place around Rick's Lake, a secluded body of water in north-central Wisconsin; several of the characters also have ties to the State University. (: "The Dweller in Darkness")

### In the Real World
As noted above, several of Lovecraft’s friends and contemporaries called Wisconsin their home at some point. These include:

* Robert Bloch (lived in Milwaukee, Wisconsin circa 1935)
* August Derleth (born in Sauk City, Wisconsin; earned B.A. at the University of Wisconsin-Madison; wrote the Sac Prairie Saga, a series of historical novels on the area)
* Alfred Galpin (born in Appleton, Wisconsin)

The Wish-Demon is a fictional demon in the prime reality of the Marvel universe of Marvel Comics. It was created in 1993 by Chris Cooper, first appearing in issue #8 of the 1st volume of Darkhold: Pages from the Book of Sins.

### Background
The Wish-Demon was summoned by the Darkhold. It was a tall greyish humanoid demon with three arms and three heads. The demon granted any wish that anyone asked for in its vicinity, though the wish was nearly always granted in the most brutally horrific method possible. While granting these wishes, the demon would be loudly laughing.

On a hijacked plane, one man wished he was back home and the demon sent him smashing through the door, flying toward his house, and crashed through the roof into his bedroom. Another wished that her husband would make the demon leave, and the demon vanished with him. One person wished for no more wishes and the demon killed the flight crew, so that all would die and therefore no more wishes would occur.

"Witch Fire" is a short story by American author Scott T. Goudsward. It forms part of the Arkham Detective Agency series created by C. J. Henderson.

### Synopsis
During Arkham Police Department's investigation of a series of bizarre incidents, rookie cop Eddie Suarez is given a glimpse of Arkham's dark underbelly before being recruited by Frank Nardi on behalf of the Arkham Detective Agency.

### Characters
*Eddie Suarez, recently graduated police officer who is new to the city of Arkham.
*Frank Nardi, retired New York cop turned private investigator.
*Tim Jackson, Eddie's partner.
*Stanley and Alice Rothington, members of a centuries-old coven of witches.
*Detective Rand, a member of the Arkham Police Department.

### Behind the Mythos
"Witch Fire" was written at the request of Brian M. Sammons who was looking for contributions for the upcoming anthology Arkham Detective Agency. The collection was first published by Dark Regions Press in 2017.

### Mythos Connections
*The story is set in H. P. Lovecraft's iconic city of Arkham.
*Miskatonic University is referenced twice in the story.

The Witch House is a fictional building in the Marvel universe which first appeared in issue #7 of the Marvel Premiere comic book series, first published in 1973. It can be used as a portal for Kathulos, a servant of the Great Old One Shuma-Gorath.

### Background
The Witch House was located near the town of Penmallow in Cornwall, England, whose residents lived in fear of the manor. Dr. Strange sensed within it traces of ancient blasphemies. Its housekeeper was Blondine, who was the latest reincarnation of the High Priestess of Dagoth, of the evil city of Kalumesh, which had been sunk beneath the seas.

The Witch House was actually a portal to Kathulos' living planetoid. Kathulos could animate the house, which nearly killed Dr. Strange and his companions. To destroy the house, Dr. Strange was forced to call on the assistance of the Vishanti, a godlike trio, whose intervention reduced the house to rubble.

fullContent:
Witch Hunt is a 1994 sequel to Cast a Deadly Spell. Most critics consider it a vastly inferior film (citation needed) and the continuity between both stories is tangential at best.

### Plot
The film takes place in a fictional Los Angeles where magic is real, monsters and mythical beasts stalk the back alleys, zombies are used as cheap labor, and everyone—except hardboiled private investigator H. Philip Lovecraft—uses magic every day. Yet, cars, telephones and other modern technology also exist in this world. The year is 1953, at the beginning of the Second Red Scare, but in this universe magic is substituted for communism and the McCarthy-esque proceedings are being run by Senator Larson Crockett.

Lovecraft is hired by film star Kim Hudson to dig up dirt on her husband, producer N.J. Gottlieb, who is about to replace her on his latest film with a young starlet he may be having an affair with. Gaining entry to the studio with the help of practicing witch Hypolita Kropotkin, his friend and landlady who is working for the studio, he encounters Finn Macha, a warlock and former private investigator with whom he had once crossed paths. When Gottlieb is murdered by magic, Senator Crockett uses the crime to make Kropotkin a scapegoat for use in his Anti-Magic crusade and uses newly-passed Congressional legislation to have her sentenced to death by public burning. Lovecraft must now not only save Kropotkin and uncover the real murderer, the motive behind the murder and the secrets Kim Hudson is hiding, but also confront the demons in his own past...a past that includes Finn Macha and the reason why Lovecraft will not use magic.

Dan, who is reeling from the suicide of his girlfriend, discovers a mysterious book which she had been keeping from him. Soon the book, or perhaps something using the book, begins to communicate with Dan, and promises to reunite him with his girlfriend if only he will perform one small ritual …

"With Eyes That See" is a short story by Cthulhu Mythos author J. B. Lee.

### Synopsis
When Megan Summers tries to take her own life over a bad breakup, a strange artefact grants her a glimpse of how she might gain a degree of magical power. Once recovered, she uses these abilities to make the people she believes have hurt her pay. What she doesn’t realise is that with every application, the magic is using her, and is straining to open a portal to call forth the Great Old Ones and Elder Gods. 

When the light finally dawns, Megan decides that to protect the world she must sequester herself from it, and enters a catatonic state, spending the rest of her life in a psychiatric institution, unaware of the dark, goatish child she miraculously gave birth to after the onset of her condition.

### Characters 
*Megan Summers, a teenage girl with a lust for vengeance.
*Lynn Robinson, Megan's best friend.
*Michael "Mike" Harrison, Megan's ex-boyfriend.
*Sherry Riley, Mike's new girlfriend.
*Joan Ryder, Megan's English Literature teacher.

### Publication History
"With Eyes That See" was first published in the August 1999 edition of online fanzine Nightscapes, and later appeared in print in Dark Legacy in July 2000 .

The Wolf Men are a fictional race in the Marvel Universe which first appeared in 1971 in issue #2 of volume 1 of the comic book series Kull the Conqueror.

### Background
The Wolf Men were the spawn of the Wolf Lords (which were created by the Elder God Chthon) who held Earth in terror millions of years ago. Among the Wolf Lords were Garmr, a mountain-sized beast who sired Garm, a 40-foot tall hellhound that would go on to guard the gates of Hel, the Asgardian realm of the dead. The greatest of the Wolf Lords was Varcolac the Wolf Demon. With his speed, no prey could escape this relentless, merciless hunter. Both the Midgard Serpent and the Fenris Wolf descend from him.

The Wolf Men were shapeshifters who could take the shape of various humans. They had superhuman strength and speed, and were invulnerable to ordinary physical injuries and blows from Thurian Age weaponry (e.g., swords). At least one of them had additional magical powers (e.g., optical bolts of fire), being a sorcerer. Wolf Men were vulnerable to fire and silver.
During the Thurian Age, their sorcerer leader manipulated the Atlanteans and the Picts into going to war against Valusia. It was King Kull who killed their leader and revealed to the others the machinations of the Wolf Men, which led to peace being established among the three factions.

Wonderland is a fictional country which appeared in the children's novel Alice's Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll in 1865. Zenescope Entertainment reimagined it in 2007 as R'lyeh in its Grimm Fairy Tales comic series and its spin-off Wonderland.

### Background
Wonderland is the source of the world's madness (Never-Ending Dream). To prevent the madness from infecting Earth, mankind made a deal with the sleeping entity. In every generation, children are sacrificed so that it doesn't wake. The innocents who end up in Wonderland feed the Jabberwocky's undying cravings. The monsters of the world (e.g. Hitler and Jack the Ripper) were influenced by Wonderland.

Down the generations, it has been the responsibility of one family to keep Wonderland at bay. In the modern era, the Liddle family has been sacrificing their offspring, one of which was Alice Liddle. One ancestor refused to sacrifice his son, resulting in the Great Depression and World War Two. The essence of Wonderland slips through occasionally, resulting in war, insanity, etc., but far less than it would without the sacrifices.

Wonderland was a continuity-heavy comic book franchise starring various female protagonists, who battled the forces of the Lovecraftian dimension of Wonderland. Published by Zenescope Entertainment, it spanned a little over a decade, from 2007 to 2018.

It consisted of one main comic series (Wonderland), eleven mini-series, an annual series, one series of one-shots, and two individual one-shots. Wonderland was the largest and most popular spin-off from the "Grimm Fairy Tales" line of comic books.

R'lyeh is mentionned in "Return to Wonderland"

The Mythos are alluded to, but not explicitly, in "Alice in Wonderland"

Lovecraft is involved in the narrative of "Call of Wonderland" and "The Madness of Wonderland"

term: Works inspired by H. P. Lovecraft
shortDefinition: There are numerous works of literature and other media which, while not authored by H. P. Lovecraft himself, were still inspired by him in some capacity.  ### Works based on Lovecraft's ideas Some authors have created original works based on a premis...
fullContent:
There are numerous works of literature and other media which, while not authored by H. P. Lovecraft himself, were still inspired by him in some capacity.

### Works based on Lovecraft's ideas
Some authors have created original works based on a premise supplied by Lovecraft. For example, "The Werewolf of Ponkert" (1925), by H. Warner Munn, was inspired by a comment made by Lovecraft in the letter column of the March 1924 issue of Weird Tales, in which Lovecraft suggested a werewolf story written from the point of view of the werewolf himself.

"Cassius" (1931), by Henry S. Whitehead, was inspired by entry #133 in Lovecraft's Commonplace Book, which collects story prompts and ideas. The entry is about a man with a tiny conjoined twin which is surgically removed and unexpectedly survives as a vengeful homunculus.

Two stories by Duane W. Rimel: "The Small, Dark Thing" (1944) and "Norton and I" (1942) are both inspired by Lovecraft's comments about the aforementioned "Cassius" (: Selected Letters 5.725). Specifically, Lovecraft told Rimel about how his friend Whitehead developed the idea, and suggested two radically different directions in which the plot-germ could have been developed instead, thus inspiring Rimel to use both (although "Norton and I" differs from Lovecraft's conception in that a preserved brain takes up the role of the homunculus).

Several stories in Ramsey Campbell's collection The Inhabitant of the Lake and Less Welcome Tenants (1964) were inspired by entries from Lovecraft's Commonplace Book. For example, "The Insects from Shaggai" is inspired by entry #221, about extraterrestrial insects which "penetrate a man's head and cause him to remember alien and exotic things".

### Works that quote or paraphrase Lovecraft
Some stories contain prose derived directly from Lovecraft's writings.

The Horror from the Hills (1931), by Frank Belknap Long, includes a long dream sequence that incorporates Lovecraft's description of one of his own dreams (the same one that would be used as the basis for "The Very Old Folk"). This was done with Lovecraft's consent and approval.

"The House of the Worm" (1933), by Mearle Prout, includes passages lifted almost word for word from Lovecraft's "The Call of Cthulhu".

### Sequels to Lovecraft's works
Many writers have crafted sequels to Lovecraft's works. Examples include, but are not limited to:
*"The Shadow from the Steeple" (1950), by Robert Bloch: a sequel to "The Haunter of the Dark".
*"The Thing from the Blasted Heath" (1971), by Brian Lumley: a sequel to "The Colour Out of Space".
*"Documents in the Case of Elizabeth Akeley" (1982), by Richard A. Lupoff: a sequel to The Whisperer in Darkness.
*Alicia Y (1994), by Juan Gotō: a sequel to "The Dunwich Horror".
*"Azathoth in Arkham" (1995), by Peter Cannon: a sequel to "The Thing on the Doorstep".
*"Gedney" (2015), by Laurence J. Cornford: a sequel to At the Mountains of Madness.

### Lovecraft parodies

fullContent:
World Kaiju Encyclopedia (世界の怪獣大百科, Sekai no Kaiju Dai Hyakka) is a Japanese reference book first published by Keibunsha in 1982. In addition to kaiju from tokusatsu films, such as Godzilla and Gamera, the book features a total of 500 entries covering monsters from various movies, anime, manga, legends, etc. A second edition would later be published in 1990.

Relevant to this wiki, it is technically one of the earliest works in the Japanese Cthulhu Mythos. The book contains an entry for Cthulhu from the short story "The Call of Cthulhu" by H. P. Lovecraft; however, Lovecraft's [https://lovecraft.fandom.com/wiki/File:Cthulhu_sketch_by_Lovecraft.jpg original depiction] was not available at the time, resulting in a new illustration based on Cthulhu's description of being an "octopus dragon", somewhat reminiscent of Godzilla in terms of design.

fullContent:
World War Cthulhu: A Collection of Lovecraftian War Stories is a Cthulhu Mythos anthology, first published in 2014.

### Overview
A collection of 22 short stories linked by the backdrop of war, the works in World War Cthulhu span millennia of conflict, from battles in ancient history, through the twentieth century, to space-age strife.

Edited by Glynn Owen Barrass and Brian M. Sammons, with cover art by Vincent Chong, World War Cthulhu also features 22 interior illustrations by M. Wayne Miller, one for each story. It runs to a total of 360 pages.

### Contents
*"Loyalty" by John Shirley
*"The Game Changers" by Stephen Mark Rainey
*"White Feather" by T. E. Grau
*"To Hold Ye White Husk" by W. H. Pugmire
*"The Sea Nymph's Son" by Robert M. Price
*"The Boonieman" by Edward M. Erdelac
*"The Turtle" by Neil Baker
*"The Bullet and the Flesh" by David Conyers and David Kernot
*"Broadsword" by William Meikle
*"Long Island Weird - The Lost Interviews" by Charles Christian
*"The Yoth Protocols" by Josh Reynolds
*"A Feast of Death" by Lee Clark Zumpe
*"The Ithiliad" by Christine Morgan
*"The Sinking City" by Konstantine Paradias
*"The Shape of a Snake" by Cody Goodfellow
*"Mysterious Ways" by C. J. Henderson
* "Magna Mater" by Edward Morris
*"Dark Cell" by Brian M. Sammons and Glynn Owen Barrass
*"Cold War, Yellow Fever" by Pete Rawlik
*"Stragglers from Carrhae" by Darrell Schweitzer
*"The Procyon Project" by Tim Curran
*"Wunderwaffe" by Jeffrey Thomas

### Publication History
First released by Dark Regions Press in August 2014, World War Cthulhu was reissued in November 2018. It is also available in digital format.

### Trivia
*World War Cthulhu is dedicated to the memory of C. J. Henderson who passed during the publication process.

The World-Eater is an extra-dimensional eldritch entity from the fictional universe of Marvel from Marvel Comics.

### Background
The World-Eater is an entity which feeds on dimensions. It uses a host that is native to that dimension to consume it before jumping to the next dimension. Its weakness was that it could not enter much less feed on that dimension without a native host body.

Worlds of Cthulhu is a collection of Lovecraftian short stories--some in the Cthulhu Mythos and some not--edited by Robert M. Price and published by Fedogan & Bremer in 2012, with an ebook release following in 2015. It is a follow-up to Price's collections Tales of the Lovecraft Mythos and The New Lovecraft Circle, featuring mostly original fiction in a Lovecraftian vein.

As with other Fedogan & Bremer Mythos collections, the dust jacket illustration is by Gahan Wilson. Endpaper illustrations are by Tim Kirk.

The Worm that Walks is a fictional entity created by Sandy Petersen for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror role-playing game. It made its first appearance in the 1982 campaign supplement Shadows of Yog-Sothoth. A variation on the creature exists in Dungeons & Dragons and Pathfinder, inspired by H. P. Lovecraft's "The Festival".

### Description
The Worm that Walks is an entity that appears as a rotting human corpse, but can disguise itself as any human. It has the ability to siphon the energy from those who interact with it.

The D&D and Pathfinder version of the Worm that Walks is a wizard whose mind has been absorbed into the worms that fed on their corpse. Appearing human at first glance, underneath its clothes it is actually an enormous mass of worms squirming together in the shape of a human, with a single mind controlling all of them. A Worm that Walks retains all its memories and magical abilities from its human life.

fullContent:
Worms of the Earth is a short story by American author Robert E. Howard which is set in H. P. Lovecraft's fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Synopsis
In ancient Britain, when a Pictish king disguised as an emissary witnesses an act of unspeakable cruelty by the ruling Roman governor against one of his people, he vows revenge by any means necessary.

Consulting a deranged witch-woman, the king strikes a bargain with her, learning the route to an underground cavern which houses a relic sacred to the subterranean creatures known as the Worms of the Earth before stealing the piece. Once again travelling beneath the Earth, he meets with the Worms and agrees to return the relic on the condition that they bring him the Roman governor alive. The Worms agree, but when the governor is presented to the king, he has been driven mad by what he has seen, and so the king puts him out of his misery.

### Characters
*Bran Mak Morn/Partha Mac Othna, a Pictish king disguised as an ambassador in order to spy on his Roman enemies. He is said to be descended from a tribe of men even more ancient than the Picts.
*Atla, a witch-woman who lives on the fens and has an extensive knowledge of the supernatural creatures of the area. She is only half-human, being the product of interbreeding with the Worms of the Earth.
*Titus Sulla, a Roman governor of Britain who crucified a Pictish man after a biased trial for striking a Roman trader. Died insane at the hands of Bran.
*Grom, Bran's manservant.
*Gonar, the Priest of the Moon and chief advisor to the king.

### Behind the Mythos
First published in the November 1932 edition of pulp magazine Weird Tales, Worms of the Earth was later included as the titular piece in a collection of Howard's work in 1975. In 2012, it was given an eBook release as part of Wildside Press LLC's The Cthulhu Mythos Megapack, then as an individual volume by Amazon Digital Services on 17 February 2018.

In December 1976 and February 1977 Marvel Comics released a two-part black-and-white comic book adaptation under their Curtis Magazines label. These were later issued together as a trade paperback in October 2000 by Cross Plains Comics/Wandering Star, this time in full colour.

### Mythos References
*Bran, when swearing his revenge, states that he would invoke even the "Black gods of R'lyeh." R’lyeh is also later used as part of an exclamation by Atla.
*The lord of the Deep Ones, Dagon, lends his name to several locations in the story, for example Dagon's Mere, a body of water, and Dagon's Ring, a sacrificial henge.
