fullContent:
Worse Things Waiting is a Cthulhu Mythos novel written by Brian McNaughton. It was originally published in 1980 as Satan's Seductress (Carlyle Books), and released under McNaughton's preferred title in 2000 by Wildside Press. It is a sequel to 1978's Downward to Darkness (aka Satan's Mistress). Like its predecessor, Worse Things Waiting combines McNaughton's trademark black humour, plentiful gore and pervasive sexuality.

The title comes from a quote from A. C. Swinburne that serves as the book's epigraph:At the door of life, by the gate of breath, 

There are worse things waiting for men than death.

### Synopsis
Four years after the events of Downward to Darkness, Amy Miniter has returned to Mt. Tabor, Connecticut--and has been identified by local Satanist Howard Ashcroft as a likely vessel for the reincarnation of 19th century witch Mirdath Hodgson. Meanwhile, hack writer Martin Paige has come to town to do a true crime story about the Mt. Tabor massacre--and ends up falling in love with Amy and risking everything to thwart Mirdath's scheme. 

### Characters

* Amy Miniter, a 20-year-old with a "dreamy nature." When she was a sophomore in high school, she survived the Mt. Tabor Massacre, which took the life of her mother, her only remaining parent. She's now returned to Mt. Tabor and finds herself an unexpected success at her mother's real estate business. She is blonde and blue-eyed, but "the only adjective that ever came to anyone's mind on first seeing her was pale"--so much so that "she began to dress, think, and act palely." She lives by herself in Brooksprite Gardens, a housing development built on the former site of the town dump--which earlier was the gravesite of a notorious local witch.
* Martin Paige, a hack writer from New York City. (He has an address on Great Jones Street in Manhattan's East Village.) He's described as "a bum living by his wits, one step ahead of lawyers, loansharks and tax men, two steps short of middle age." He observes that "he had really become a writer to impress girls, but they remained unimpressed."  A "seedy-looking man" at 36 years old, he's said to be "a lookalike for the young Don Knotts," with his "receding, curly hair, his inconsequential build, and...his crazy eyes"--though "he really did have more chin than Don Knotts." He wrote a play called The Wild Hunt (which is mentioned in Downward to Darkness), ghostwrote parts of the successful novel Behold Now Behemoth, and is working on an epic fantasy novel, Swords of Winbourne.
* Mordred Glendower, a wizard born near Cardiff, Wales, in 1560. He was John Dee's secretary when that historic wizard translated the Necronomicon. He later moved to Salem, Massachusetts, fleeing from there to North Berwick, Maine, in 1692--"one step ahead of the rope."  He moved from Maine to Mt. Tabor, Connecticut, in 1810, where he became a miller and married Purity Jennings, "the foremost belle of the town." Purity died shortly after giving birth to a daughter, Mirdath, in 18

fullContent:
Wrath of N'Kai by Josh Reynolds is a novel in the Cthulhu Mythos stories from Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror setting for Arkham Horror Fiction. It is the first book of the Countess Zorzi series. Paperback, digital and audio editions were released. It was adapted by Graphic Audio into an audio production with an entire cast of voice actors.

### Overview


### Synopsis
Infamous cat burglar Countess Alessandra Zorzi has come to Arkham, Massachusetts for the cause of stealing a newly uncovered mummy from Oklahoma. Recruiting a local taxi driver named Pepper Kelly, she soon finds herself implicated in the theft before she has a chance to steal it as local bootleggers make off with the mummy. The Silver Twilight Lodge tries to recruit her to recover the artifact while the mysterious undead monster, Zamacoma, seeks to return the mummy to its resting place. The Countess must play against forces she never imagined existing in order to not only survive but prevent an even greater tragedy.

Complicating her adventures is the fact that the Countess has made eye contact with the strange mummy, causing her to make telepathic connection with the entity behind the preserved corpse and in the process become exposed to visions from the Mythos.

### Characters
*Countless Alessandra Zorzi - An infamous Italian cat burglar from a family of con men and grifters. She is both beautiful as well as cunning. The Countess has made her career dealing in occult artifacts stolen from an eclectic and eccentric clientele. She does not believe in the supernatural, though, until forced to confront it.
*Pepper Kelly - A young woman masquerading as a boy to serve as a Arkham taxi driver. She has done some bootlegging work for the local gangs but is not a professional criminal. That is until the Countess offers her a lucrative and enjoyable side career as her guide.
*Carl Sanford- the Leader of the Silver Twilight Lodge and an occultist interested in seeking the mummy's secrets.
*Zamacona - A former conquistador turned into an undead horror by the supernatural forces he encountered. He is now the leader of an undead cult that will do anything to recover the stolen mummy that contains a horror unimagined of by mortals.

### Mythos Entities 
*Tsagourra
*K'n-yan
*Shoggoth

### Trivia
*One of the bootleggers who robs the museum of the mummy is named Phipps.

fullContent:
"Wrath of the Wind-Walker" is a short story by American authors Robert M. Price and James Ambuehl.

### Synopsis
In the first part of the story, reporter J.J. Hanley listens to an ageing Professor Winslow tell the story of how in his youth he led an expedition into the jungles of Cambodia in search of an anomalous cult of ice worshipers. Hiring a group of hardened mercenaries, he located the cult but they were almost immediately ambushed by a band of Khmer Rouge; although successful in fending off their attackers, the mercenaries in their bloodlust also murdered the cultists, with the leader placing a curse on the survivors before passing.

The second part covers Hanley's investigation into the veracity of Winslow's story. He succeeds in confirming the name of the being the cult worshiped - Ithaqua - and discovers the fate of five of the expedition's survivors, all killed in bizarre accidents which left the bodies utterly frozen. Ultimately Hanley receives news of Winslow's death - his body found encased in a block of ice at the centre of a house fire - and this concludes his interest in the case.

### Characters

*James Joseph "J.J." Hanley, a reporter for the Braving Bulletin.
*Professor Jonah Winslow, an elderly scholar.
*Ithaqua, a vengeful Great Old One.

### Publication History
"Wrath of the Wind-Walker" was first published in the Chaosium anthology The Ithaqua Cycle: The Wind-Walker of the Icy Wastes in July 1998, and later appeared in the collection of Price's works Blasphemies & Revelations in November 2008.

### Trivia

*Professor Winslow lived in a house outside Laren and worked at Royceton University, and Hanley works for the Braving Bulletin. These are all elements of Ambuehl's Braving, Minnesota milieu and the setting for several of his mythos stories.

fullContent:
The X-Men are a fictional team in the prime reality of the Marvel universe of Marvel Comics.

### Background
The X-Men are a team of superheroes made of up of mutants (Homo Superior). It's a team which has been around for decades, fighting to have mutants accepted by normal humans. They've defended humans from mutant supremacists, terrorists, killers, and criminals and have defended mutants from those humans who would enslave, sterilize, or exterminate mutantkind. The X-Men also defend Earth from both extra-dimensional and alien threats. At times it has consisted of only one team and at other times multiple teams.

Which have operated on Earth, the Moon, elsewhere in the Milky Way galaxy, neighboring galaxies (Andromeda, Shi'ar, etc), and other dimensions. Some of its members have traveled to the future or the past, or even other realities. The team has clashed with gods, demons, aliens, and governments. Some of its members have been involved in universal scale events. Recently they along with most of the world's mutants have migrated to the sentient living island of Krakoa, establishing a mutant nation.

### Relation to eldritch horrors
The X-men found themselves dragged into encounters against the Elder Gods and Great Old Ones among other kinds of demons:
*The team had a long history of conflict with the demonic N'Garai due to the dimensional barriers being weak in the area where the Xavier Mansion is located. N'Garai Cairn periodically appear on their grounds resulting in N'Garai attacking the X-Men. In their most recent clash with the N'Garai, it was a global battle, as N'Garai cairns were appearing in multiple locations around the world.
*Magneto dragged Island M from the depths in the Bermuda Triangle, which was inhabited by horrible creatures known as the Ancients, and where Shuma-Gorath imprisoned his rebellious creation Quoggoth. Many X-Men has been confronted to some of the perils left behind by those ancient horrors:
**Shadowcat and Cyclops encountered Quoggoth.
**Later, when the X-Men temporarily based themselves on the island they found themselves in combat with the reactivated ancient eldritch defenses.
*Once the X-Men found themselves trapped in a New York City where the reality altering magic of the sorcerer Kulan Gath had turned it into a Hyborian city in which all of its inhabitants (except Spider-Man who somehow was immune) believed themselves to be living in the Hyborian Age.

fullContent:
X-Men: Apocalypse vs Dracula is a 4-part mini-series written by Frank Tieri.

### Synopsis
The 3,000 year old mutant Apocalypse the Eternal One battles the demonic N'Garai and the Lord of Vampires, Dracula.

### Note
The vampires of Marvel Earth are part of the Mythos. Being created by the Darkhold (the source of the Necronomicon), which was created by the Elder God, Chthon. The Darkhold not only has a spell which creates vampires but one that destroys them. Vampires have used the Darkhold to enhance themselves and Dracula, the Lord of Vampires, was himself destroyed and restored by the Darkhold, and has used it to increase his powers.

Xada-Hgla is an avatar of Azathoth created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "The Insects from Shaggai", in which it's described as Azathoth's "original form". Its name comes from another Campbell tale, "The Mine on Yuggoth".

### Description
The so-called "original form" of Azathoth is not nearly as monstrous as its current form, but is nevertheless unpleasant for a human to look at. Its body is contained inside a clam-like bivalvular shell, supported by multiple pairs of flexible legs. From the interior of the sheel peeks a "mouthless face, with deep-sunk eyes and covered with glistening black hair". It can extrude a number of jointed cylindrical limbs, terminating in "polypous appendages". (: "The Insects from Shaggai")

This avatar is only worshiped by the Shans and the Mi-Go. (: Ye Booke of Monstres)

Xalafu (also known as The Dread One) is a fictional entity created by Peter Levi for his short story "The Life and Death of Zebros Santiago".

### Overview
Xalafu is a Great Old One who manifests as a great spherical bubble, shiftingly translucent and opaque, covered in colours of disturbing hue, with one gigantic eye seemingly dominating the whole. 

The entity is worshipped by a secretive cult operating in a small village near the Crist'bal Col'n mountain in Columbia. The disciples wear black robes while carrying either torches or long staves, and the wizard is garbed in gaudy white and gold robes. When conducting a sacrifice, a human is tied to an altar as the cult repeatedly chants "Ng'gai'ghl rai uflu ph-ngl dtuu v'hss Xalafu ght gai'lall" numerous times until the human starts incomprehensibly screaming. After being beaten by the staff-wielding disciples, the wizard will perform a hand-waving ritual, and pour out a vial of white power known as Diabolusaerugo to cover the human's body, followed by repeatedly chanting "Omm ug'luh vai Ufalax cn-cns'lgh mngl whglg ssi XALAFU!", before exclaiming the previous chants backwards and stepping back. 

When the ceremony is complete, the sky will turn a sickly red and the moon will become purple, as an orangish light gleams from a rift in the sky, allowing Xalafu to enter this dimension. Creeping down from the sky towards the altar, Xalafu smothers the area and gorges on the human sacrifice. Upon finishing, Xalafu slowly floats back into the rift and disappears. 

If any outsiders find out about Xalafu, they will be forced to worship it or suffer an untimely death. The only way to quell Xalafu's doom is through a human sacrifice, while using a vial of Diabolusaerugo and reciting the wizard's chants in the opposite manner. (: "The Life and Death of Zebros Santiago")

"Xathagorra" is a creature created by Fred C. Adams for his Cthulhu Mythos works.

### Overview
The son of the Outer God Azathoth, Xathagorra has leathery wings, webbed feet, and an unknown number of tentacles. He is purple in colour. He is stated to live in a "hall on the rim of earth" (: "The Fleece of Yaggar") although given that the material from which this description comes from is intended to be archaic, this is likely more due to the worldview of the times, rather than an actual guide to its location.

Xathagorra may be in the service of the Outer God Shub-Niggurath, although it is equally possible that he is simply willing to perform a favour for one of his father's compatriots (: "The Fleece of Yaggar").

shortDefinition: "Xélucha" is a short story by M. P. Shiel first collected in Shapes in the Fire published by John Lane in 1896. It was later collected in the Arkham House anthology Dark Mind, Dark Heart in 1962 and is therefore to be considered at least a Mythos-Adj...
fullContent:
"Xélucha" is a short story by M. P. Shiel first collected in Shapes in the Fire published by John Lane in 1896. It was later collected in the Arkham House anthology Dark Mind, Dark Heart in 1962 and is therefore to be considered at least a Mythos-Adjacent work. It is a decadent "yellow" work in the meaning contemporary to the time it is written and so forms a neat bridge between the original King in Yellow by Robert W. Chambers and the more typical Mythos works that followed later.

### Synopsis
A group of decadents seemingly have a debauched and drugged revel in a magnificent house of Romanesque appearance. The narrator chases an attractive woman through the house to the uppermost chamber, while remembering and reviewing various events such as an unexpected stabbing, a man drowning in milk and events at the orgy as it unfolded. However, at the same time, the narrator is initiated into the concept that Will is the prime moving force, and that three great religions each began with a single individual exercising their extraordinary will power, with the eruption of Mount Vesuvius an aborted fourth event, the overwhelming by lava of the surrounding region forestalling the establishment of this religion and killing the cobbler of Herculaneum whose act of Will set it in motion.

At the end of the story the narrator has caught up to the object of his desire at last and as she seemingly suffers a fit and he sees green foam bubble from her, he realizes that she is not a beautiful girl but rather this same initiatory figure that has dwelled behind and within history: Xélucha. Likewise the magnificence of the house in which their bacchanal is taking place is not real. In reality it is a filthy deserted hovel, its magnificence entirely an illusion. The narrator has been wallowing in dust and filth.

Xélucha thus anticipates in the decadent tradition the figure of Nyarlathotep in the Cthulhu Mythos, whether a direct inspiration or not.

Xena is a fictional character created by Robert Tapert and John Schulian in 1995, first appearing in episode 9 of the first season of the mythological fantasy series Hercules: The Legendary Journeys. From 1995-2001 she starred as the protagonist of her own spin-off television show, Xena: Warrior Princess, which surpassed Hercules in popularity. In 2008, Dynamite Entertainment published its first crossover starring Xena and the Cthulhu Mythos in the form of the Necronomicon Ex-Mortis.

### Background
Xena is a heroine who protects the oppressed, fighting tyrants, the corrupt, monsters, and gods in her quest to make amends for her past. For the atrocities that she committed during the years when she was a brutal, ruthless murderer, terrorist, pirate, and warlord. It was her encounter with the heroic demigod Hercules that made her see the "light" and change her ways, becoming a hero. She has had various companions and allies, but the most important one has been Gabrielle. One version of Xena would end up having multiple confrontations with the forces of the Mythos, alongside Ash Williams.

Xenomorphs are an extraterrestrial species and the cosmic horror element in the fictional universe of the Alien movie franchise.

Chaosium described them as not being part of the Mythos themselves, but described how easily they can fit in a Mythos campaign. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Background
Xenomorphs are a parasitic hostile extra-terrestrial species, a race of predators who kill or infect any lifeforms they encounter, as they expand their species. They are eusocial life-forms in which a queen rules over a hive, which is organized along a caste system which consists of the 15 ft tall queen, praetorians, warriors, and drones. Queen Mothers are above the Queens, ruling over the Xenomorph species, though they have only been seen in Hiveworld. Possessing telepathic and empathetic abilities that permit them to communicate with the members of their respective hives across vast distances. Though not a sentient species, they have displayed problem-solving skills and observational learning. Xenomorphs have learned to cut power to a section in a complex, operate machinery at the most basic level, and board an elevator. It's a species that possesses genetic memory.

They are asexual with eggs laid by fertile queens from which facehuggers emerge, parasitical forms that implant chestbursters in the host creature. It is the infant form of a xenomorph, bursting out of the host's chest upon maturing. Xenomorphs have a vaguely bipedal form, though usually they adopt a hunched quadrupedal stance. Their bodies have a skeletal, biomechanical appearance, one which is colored in muted shades of blue, black, or bronze. It is extremely resilient, and is unaffected by its acidic blood and is able to withstand some types of small arms fire. It has an elongated cylindrical skull with an inner pharyngeal jaw, blade-tipped segmented tails, and four-digit-clawed hands.

Xenomorph blood is acidic and able to corrode through nearly any material with horrifying speed, which they can also spit to blind or incapacitate victims. They can fire their inner pharyngeal jaw like a piston that can smash through metal. The tail is used both to impale and as a blunt weapon, being strong enough to easily lift an impaled Predator. Xenomorphs are able to run and crawl along both walls and ceilings. They possess great strength, being able to break through welded steel doors and even reinforced pressurized doors. They build their hives and cocoon victims with Hive Webbing, which is a strong thick resine vomited from their mouths. Sub-species and mutated forms have emerged due to the different host species they have taken, including flying xenomorphs.

The Hives they create could potentially corrode entire worlds. Each portion of Hive Webbings has a living core known as a Hive Node, which is made up of small organisms secreted by the Drones. The Hive Nodes' less injured xenomorphs regenerate back to full health as long as th

Xhamen-Dor is a fictional entity created by Paizo Inc for their role-playing game Pathfinder. The character first appeared in the gaming supplement Wake of the Watcher.

### Background
Xhamen-Dor is a Great Old One whose form is a monstrous hybrid of fibrous, twisted hair-like fungal tendrils and toadstool-like growths which emerges from a mass of bones or a great corpse. It has various incarnations and forms it has taken, one of which is that of a serpentine dragon. It originated in Carcosa, from the residue left behind by Hastur which fused with the remnants of the minds and souls of those consumed by Carcosa. Xhamen-Dor burrows into the minds of those who have learned either its name or the true nature of Xhamen-Dor, spreading within their bodies and turning them into undead servants. It has visited countless worlds, turning their inhabitants into the undead, and feeding them to Carcosa.

The Xiclotlans are a carnivorous race of low intellect and great strength, which were enslaved by the insects of Shaggai and were used by them for labor until they left the planet, although some Xiclotlan slaves were brought to Earth along with their insectoid masters. They are 16 ft tall with six tentacles and a maw at the top. On Xiclotl they are ruled over by the Zy'tl Q'ae, to whom they make periodic sacrifices.

Xitalu (also known as The Great Devourer) is a fictional entity created by DC Comics for their comic series iZombie. The character was heavily inspired by Cthulhu, described as being a "Lovecraftian monster" throughout the storyline.

### Background
Taking the form of a multi-eyed creature with many tentacles, Xitalu is a higher-dimensional entity that dwells across the void between other dimensions and devours all the souls of any world in its path. Xitalu is accompanied by smaller creatures known as the "Hounds of Xitalu", who feed on the souls of Xitalu's leftovers. Every world encountered by Xitalu is driven to complete chaos before being reduced to a lifeless husk that was drained of all vitality. 

Xitalu was once worshipped by a civilization located in South America, where the entity briefly manifested on Earth until it was driven away by the immortal mummy John Amon, sacrificing all the residents in the process. 

Five hundred years later, Xitalu returned to Earth while slowly manifesting through an inter-dimensional rip in the sky near Eugene, Oregon. Amon attempted to drive away the entity again by convincing the zombie heroine Gwen Dylan to consume all the souls in the town before being force-fed to Xitalu. Galatea, a long-time enemy of Amon, had different plans and attempted to harness Xitalu's power for herself by using a different zombie named Francisco as a vessel. 

Although both of their plans ultimately failed, leading to Amon and Galatea getting their souls consumed, Gwen found another way to get rid of Xitalu after figuring out that the entity had a soul itself. Gwen defeated Xitalu by absorbing its soul, causing its body to shrink until it was small enough to be crushed in her hand. Thereafter, Gwen became a higher-dimensional entity like Xitalu, at the cost of abandoning everything from her previous life. (: iZombie)

fullContent:
"Xiurhn" is a 1975 short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gary Myers.

### Synopsis
Skaa is a witch who lives in a house in the Street of the Pantheon of Hazuth-Kleg opposite the onyx Temple of Unattainable Desires. There she worships her carven idols and performs rituals with the Voorish sign. A thief named Thish arrives after traveling a long way to Vornai seeking the Dark Jewel of Mhor. He is told of the unknown East of endless night where he will find the Dark Jewel in a peak haunted by the mythical Xiurhn, which was made by the Other Gods as supplication for Azathoth. To protect himself from Xiurhn, he seeks a talisman made by the yellow-skulled priests of Yuth anointed for their goddess N'tse-Kaambl. After scamming Skaa by paying with pebbles instead of opals, Thish set out. But Skaa used a ritual to turn the pebbles into opals.

Thish went to Yuth and stole the talisman and framed a witch for the crime, arriving in the unknown East upon a zebra to Mhor. He witnessed the arrival of beasts from the viscid Pool of Night. He found himself pursued and managed to enter the tower of stone to safety. He found the Dark Jewel and met the amorphous Xiurhn, who wanted to punish the thief but also recognized the talisman of N'tse-Kaambl, and instead answered the door that the creature who pursued Thish was pounding on.

### Publication History
First printed in the collection The House of the Worm, "Xiurhn" has since been reprinted several times, and has been translated into German and Italian.

Xoth, also known as Zoth, is the green binary star where Cthulhu and his like once lived before coming to the Earth. According to The Xothic Legend Cycle, it is where Cthulhu mated with Idh-yaa to beget Ghatanothoa, Ythogtha, and Zoth-Ommog.

Xoth is also the native home of Ycnágnnisssz and Zstylzhemghi, and was the temporary home of the latter's "husband", Ghisguth, and their progeny, the infant Tsathoggua. Tsathoggua later went to live on Yuggoth. Afterward, he fled to Cykranosh to escape Cxaxukluth's cannibalistic eating habits.

According to Friedrich von Junzt, Xoth is located in the same star cluster as the planets Abbith and Ymar. (: "The Thing in the Pit")

shortDefinition: The Xothic Legend Cycle is a series of short stories by Lin Carter that are based on the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft, primarily on Lovecraft's stories "The Call of Cthulhu" and "Out of the Aeons".  The cycle is centered on a trinity of deities ...
fullContent:
The Xothic Legend Cycle is a series of short stories by Lin Carter that are based on the Cthulhu Mythos of H. P. Lovecraft, primarily on Lovecraft's stories "The Call of Cthulhu" and "Out of the Aeons".

The cycle is centered on a trinity of deities said to be the "sons" of Cthulhu: Ghatanothoa, Ythogtha, and Zoth-Ommog. The five stories that make up the cycle (in chronological order) are "The Dweller in the Tomb" (1971), "Out of the Ages" (1975), "The Horror in the Gallery" (1976), "The Thing in the Pit" (1980), and "The Winfield Heritance" (1981). All these stories are to be found collected, with others, in The Xothic Legend Cycle: The Complete Mythos Fiction of Lin Carter (Chaosium, 1997).

Originally Carter had assembled some of these stories for a volume he planned to call The Terror Out of Time. Stories to have been included in this collection included "The Dweller in the Tomb" (to have been renamed "Zanthu"); "The Winfield Inheritance"; "Zoth-Ommog" (to be renamed "The Terror Out of Time"); "Out of the Ages" and "Them From Outside." The collection was submitted to DAW Books and Arkham House but was unpublished in Carter's lifetime. "Zoth-Ommog" (originally titled "The Horror in the Gallery") was published in the original DAW Books edition of Edward Berglund, ed, The Disciples of Cthulhu, but was omitted from the Chaosium reprint of this anthology; however, the story appears under its original title in The Xothic Legend Cycle: The Complete Mythos Fiction of Lin Carter (Chaosium, 1997). "Them from Outside" was scheduled to appear in an issue of Crypt of Cthulhu as "Concerning Them from Outside".

The cycle introduces various mythos elements, such as the Zanthu Tablets, the Ponape Scripture, Father Ubb and the yuggs, and two new Great Old Ones: Ythogtha and Zoth-Ommog. The cycle also features the (fictional) Sanbourne Institute of Pacific Antiquities, perhaps Lin Carter's answer to Lovecraft's Miskatonic University. The lost continent of Mu also figures prominently in the cycle, as do the events that led to its sinking.

### The Demon Trinity
Carter's "Demon Trinity" (Ghatanothoa, Ythogtha, and Zoth-Ommog) were spawned on a planet near the binary star Xoth. They are the progeny of a mating between Cthulhu (Cthulhu and Ghatanathoa were originally the creations of Lovecraft, appearing in "The Call of Cthulhu" (1928) and "Out of the Aeons" (1935), respectively. While Lovecraft never established a connection between these beings, Robert M. Price, believes that Ghatanothoa is essentially a revised version of Cthulhu) and the quasi-female entity Idh-yaa.

### Ghatanothoa


Ghatanothoa is said to be the firstborn of Cthulhu. It is infamous for its horrid appearance and its fearsome medusa-like ability which causes a viewer's skin to become hard and leathery but preserves the brain, leaving the victim to go slowly mad trapped within an immobile shell. Among the myriad of deities worshipped in Mu, Ghatanothoa was the most respected as well as the most

Xotli (also known as The Demon from Beyond and The Lord of Terror) is a Lovecraftian extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of Marvel by Marvel Comics. It first appeared in the 1968 novel Conan of the Isles, by L. Sprague de Camp and Lin Carter.

### Background
Xotli is a Lovecraftian demonic god which was worshiped in Antilla during the Hyborian Age. It threatened all of humanity, and would have killed Conan at the Great Pyramid of Ptahuacan if it wasn't for the intervention of the god Mitra. Xotli did not fully manifest on Earth at that time, all that was visible were great tentacles emerging from a sinister black cloud.

Y'golonac (also known as The Defiler) is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Ramsey Campbell for his short story "Cold Print".

### Background
Y'golonac is the god of perversion and depravity – not just "average" human perversions or depravities, but any that can be conceived of by a sapient being (sane or otherwise). His demeanor is much like that of Nyarlathotep, but he is even more perverse and sadistic. Y'golonac can sometimes be summoned merely by reading his name in the The Revelations of Glaaki.

Y'golonac is imprisoned behind a wall of bricks in unknown ruins. His true form is uncertain, but when he possesses a human host to manifest, he appears as a grotesquely obese man, lacking a head or neck, with a mouth in the palm of each hand. Unlike other deities, Y'golonac is clearly capable of understanding humans, to the point of being able to conduct a conversation in English through his human host.

Y'golonac seeks humans who read perverse and forbidden literature to become his servants. When he is summoned, Y'golonac will offer to grant the summoner the dubious honor of becoming his priest, or simply kills them for food. (: "Cold Print")

According to some sources, Y'golonac has a servitor race of nearly mindless creatures that swarm their victims in packs, known as the Children of Y'golonac. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

### In Other Media
*In the light novel series Ultimate Antihero, Y'golonac is one of the Evil Gods that Homura Kamishiro has the ability to summon. Unless they have a considerable amount of self-restraint, anyone who hears Y'golonac's voice will be consumed by hatred and malice, causing them to attack their own allies. Because of this, Y'golonac is very effective when fighting against a large group of enemies. 
*In the mobile game Tower of Saviors, Y'golonac was spawned by the destructive nature of Azathoth. Due to the entity instinctively following its creator, Y'golonac was dedicated to causing destruction but this brought it less and less joy overtime, until having a confrontation with Mordiggian. After learning that its true desire was to destroy the "forever truth" (the balance between Daoloth's creation and Azathoth's destruction), Y'golonac and Mordiggian teamed up to initiate an evil scheme that would break the fate of the universe together, making an impossible annihilation possible through pure destruction.
*In the dark fantasy film Pan's Labyrinth, directed by Guillermo del Toro, the Pale Man appears to be at least partially inspired by Y'golonac. Both of them are malformed humanoid monsters that were sealed away in a brick wall lair and are known to devour their victims. However, the Pale Man has eyes on his hands, instead of mouths.
*In the animated series Justice League, some of Icthultu's minions bear a strong resemblance to Y'golonac.
*Y'golonac appears in the trading card game Z/X Zillions of enemy X.
*Y'g

Y'ha-nthlei is a fictional city created by H. P. Lovecraft for his novella The Shadow Over Innsmouth.

### Overview
Y'ha-nthlei is one of the undersea cities populated by the Deep Ones. The hybrid denizens of Innsmouth are known to migrate there after their transformation is complete. 

The city is a cyclopean hub of unearthly and terrible beauty, with many columns and palaces with hundreds of terraces filled with corals and phosphorescent brachiates. The city is located near Devil Reef, off the coast of Innsmouth, Massachusetts. Its location was revealed to the United States government by Robert Olmstead in the 1920s and the city was attacked by submarines and partially destroyed, but not completely.

### In Other Media
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, during the duel between Master Therion and Hadou Kouzou, Master Therion taunted Hadou that he will violate and feed his granddaughter to the fish of Y'ha-nthlei.

Y'lla is a fictional entity created by American author James Ambuehl for his 1998 short story "Correlated Contents."

### Overview
Very little is known of Y'lla, although it has been described as a "titanic tentacled sea worm," and it lies sleeping in an ancient fortress named K'hraa, now lost beneath the waves. (: "Correlated Contents")

Y'lla has spawned an unknown number of offspring, which are similar in attributes to their sire. When spotted by humans, they have been mistaken for whales or giant squid, but prefer to remain in the depths of the ocean. However, they are reputed to have been responsible for a number of particularly violent tropical storms and tidal waves throughout the course of history; one Davis Rault of Royceton University even speculated that they may have been responsible for the sinking of the Titanic and sightings of the Loch Ness Monster. (: "Correlated Contents")

The Y'm-bhi are corpses reanimated by the people of K'n-yan to perform basic physical labour. Most are taken from the mortal slave-class but some are the remains of disgraced Freemen and captured humans.

### Appearance

Described as being more manlike in shape than the gyaa-yothn slaves, the y'm-bhi are closely comparable to classic zombies with unnatural, mechanical movements. Despite many of them suffering terrible injuries before death they do not seem to decay as even after 400 years one example's body still retained most of its skin and hair.

### Creation
The y'm-bhi are mechanically reanimated with atomic energy and thought power by their K'n-yanian masters. As stated above most of the corpses belonged to the slave-class who had either died naturally or had been recovered from vast arenas of Tsath where they were mutilated and killed for public entertainment. A much smaller part of the y'm-bhi ranks were filled by criminal K’nyanians like T'la-yub and captured humans like Zamacona y Nuñez both of whom had tried to escape to the world above.

### Purpose
Though not able to understand complex thought-commands their loyal, dog-like nature means they can be put to work on farms or posted as sentries at the few remaining tunnels to the outside world. As such many could be found on the outskirts of Tsath and 12 were left to guard the mound near Binger in Caddo County, Oklahoma.

Grey-litten Y'qaa, a.k.a. the abyss of Y'qaa, or the Cavern of Y'quaa is an underground realm inhabited by the primordial being Ubbo-Sathla, and the current location of the Elder Records. The location first appeared unnamed in Clark Ashton Smith's story "Ubbo-Sathla", while the name was coined by Lin Carter for his Xothic Legend Cycle.

In Carter's "The Descent into the Abyss", the realm of Y'qaa can be reached by the tunnels deep inside Mount Voormithadreth in Hyperborea, which suggests that it might be intended to be the abode of Abhoth, the "Source of Uncleanliness", as featured in Smith's "The Seven Geases". This could be an allusion to the similarity between Ubbo-Sathla and Abhoth, proposed by Gary Myers to be two different names for the same deity.

The alternate spelling Y'quaa is used in the 2020 edition of the Malleus Monstrorum, in which the cavern is associated with both Abhoth and Ubbo-Sathla.

### Description
A grey-litten abyss identified as multidimensional, "coterminous with many worlds and planes of existence", including Yarnak. Nevertheless, Y'qaa can be accessed by the interior of Mt. Voormithadreth, past the cavern of the Prototypes. Its entrance is guarded by K'thugguol, the Grand Shoggoth. Ubbo-Sathla dwells there with the Elder Records it stole from the Elder Gods. The legendary power of these tablets has tempted many sorcerers to brave the abyss and try to retrieve them, but none has been successful so far. (: "The Descent into the Abyss")

Yaddith is a fictional planet in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally created by the late American author H. P. Lovecraft for his story Fungi from Yuggoth.

### Description
Yaddith is described as "a dim, fantastic world [with] five multi-coloured suns, alien constellations, dizzy black crags, clawed, tapir-snouted denizens, bizarre metal towers, unexplained tunnels, and cryptical floating cylinders." It is also inhabited by the burrowing Dholes. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

In the works of Lin Carter, Yaddith revolves around the star Deneb. (: "The Horror in the Gallery", "Dreams in the House of Weir") Conversely, Lovecraft places Yaddith is in a quintuple star system located in another galaxy, millions of light-years away from Earth. (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

Carter also identifies Yaddith as the dwelling place of the goddess Shub-Niggurath, who is worshiped by both the tapir-snouted Yaddithians (which Carter refers to as the "Nug-Soth") and the Dholes.

### History
Eons ago, Yaddith was inhabited by the Yaddithians (a.k.a. Nug-Soth), creatures with traits similar to mammals, reptiles, and insects. The Nug-Soth sought a way to prevent the destruction of their planet's crust by the Dholes, but to no avail. Eventually, the Dholes overwhelmed them and destroyed the Nug-Soth's civilization. Survivors of the catastrophe escaped, however, and hid on various planets.

### Notable Residents
*The wizard Zkauba is native to Yaddith.

### In Other Media
*The climax of the 2019 film Color Out of Space (an adaptation of the short story) features a vision of an alien planet overrun by huge worm-like creatures which may represent Yaddith and the Dholes.
*In the visual novel Deus Machina Demonbane, Yaddith appears as one of the worlds where Demonbane and Liber Legis fought through during their final battle at the Outerverse.

Yaddith-Gho is a fictional location created by the late American authors H. P. Lovecraft and Hazel Heald for their 1935 short story "Out of the Aeons."

### Overview
Yaddith-Gho was a colossal mountain located in the province of K'naa on the now-sunken continent of Mu, formerly located somewhere in the Pacific Ocean. Atop the mountain sits a Cyclopean stone fortress built by the "spawn of Yuggoth", while beneath it lies sleeping the Great Old One Ghatanothoa. Around it has sprung a powerful sect of Muvians who both fear and worship the entity. In an attempt to keep Ghatanothoa quiescent, the high priests of this religion annually sacrifice 12 young warriors and 12 young maidens upon their flaming altars, believing that this offering will appease the sleeping monstrosity. (: "Out of the Aeons")

### Behind the Mythos
Whether the "spawn of Yuggoth" who built the fortress which crowns Yaddith-Gho and left Ghatanothoa sleeping beneath were the Mi-Go or the original Yuggothians remains unknown. However, it would appear more likely that the Mi-Go were the culprits, as there appears to be no evidence that the now-extinct Yuggothians ever visited Earth.

In the fantasy short story "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price, the planet Yaddith is home to an intelligent species of clawed, snouted creatures. The wizard Zkauba is a member of this species.

Although not named in the original story, the Call of Cthulhu RPG refers to them as Yaddithians or Denizens of Yaddith. In Lin Carter's short story "Dreams in the House of Weir", they are called the Nug-Soth, which is also the name of a human magician from the year 16,000 AD in Lovecraft's The Shadow Out of Time.

### Background
The Yaddithians are a race of powerful wizards and brilliant scientists. Though their world was ravaged by the Dholes, some of them escaped to other worlds, dimensions, or times. One of their inventions was a device known as "light-wave envelopes", which were machines that could transport passengers across time and space.

fullContent:
Yaldabaoth, The Demiurge is a deity associated with Platonism and Gnosticism sects. According to some creeds of Platonic roots, at first matter did not exist and everything was spirit. However, Yaldabaoth, a proud and jealous god, tried to structure everything by recreating the spirit in a material world and confining everything on that plane. But he only succeeded in fabricating an imperfect world, a crude imitation of the original spirit. His arrogant personality prevented him from admitting his mistake.

Yaldabaoth, presumptuous and stupid, hates men because, unlike him, they have souls, which he lacks and which he wishes to obtain by any means, although it is impossible for him. Therefore, he mistreats, punishes and represses mortals to take revenge on them. (: Apocryphon of John, On the Origin of the World, Hypostasis of the Archons)

"Samaël" is one of the mystical words used by occultist Robert Suydam, along with "Sephiroth" and "Ashmodai". (: "The Horror at Red Hook") According to one account, Samael is an avatar of Nyarlathotep. (: "What Dark God?")

### Etymology
The term "Yaldabaoth", the name by which it is usually known, tends to be associated with the meaning son of chaos, although there is great controversy regarding this.

Demiurge comes from the Greek δημιουργός, which means "craftsman" or "creator".

Saklas is an Aramaic word that translates as "stupid".

Samael means "poison of God" in Hebrew. It can also be translated as "Severity of God" or "blind God".

Nebro means "rebel", which sometimes leads to associating him with Lucifer.

Ariel means "lion of God" or, perhaps, "divine lion". It should be noted that, iconographically, the lion is linked to excessive force, to the wild.

Satanael is a derivation of the name Samael.

### Appearance
The Demiurge usually appears with the appearance of a snake whose head would be a blinding fireball or that of a typical male lion. Another iconographic typology would show him as a man with the head of a lion or leopard, which would resemble the god Mithras, who is often represented in this way, especially in late times and sometimes assimilated to Saturn.

Other times the Demiurge is simply shown as an old and dour man, also having saturnal implications and later assimilating the imagery of the God of the religions of Judaic origin. This is mainly due to the neo-Gnostic currents considering that the God of monotheism is just another identity that the demiurge adopts to attract followers.

### Conceptual information and role
Despite not being a god created by the Lovecraft Circle, its integration into the bestiaries of the Mythos is undoubtedly due to its cosmic character. It is not uncommon for Yaldabaoth to be assimilated to Azathoth or Yog-Sothoth, and it is also typical for him to be associated with Nyarlathotep, since Samael, a name associated with the Demiurge, is one of the many identities that he adopts.

Yamil Zacra is a fictional star created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his 1933 story fragment "The Infernal Star". It was later mentioned by John W. Patterson in his 1999 short story "Priestess of Nycrama", which was inspired by Smith's earlier work.

### Overview
Smith reveals little about Yamil Zacra, other than that it is part of a binary star system along with its sister Yuzh, that the two are orbited by the planet Pnidleethon, and that it is somehow bound to a sorcerous amulet (: "The Infernal Star").

Although Patterson makes mention of Yamil Zacra in "Priestess of Nycrama", it plays no real part in the story, and no new information is revealed.

### Behind the Mythos
In his afterword to the digital edition of "Priestess of Nycrama", Patterson states that Yamil Zacra is one of the "fantastic names and places … [which inspired] me to write".

The yarkdao are an extraterrestrial species which appear in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos.

### Biology and Sociocultural Characteristics
Of their physical attributes, nothing is known about the yarkdao save that their bodies are humanoid and they possess a pair of retractable ears. They are an intelligent race, being the rulers of their world - the planet Tond - and are a polytheistic people, their priests of Chig conducting rituals which last for several years.

All that is known of the yarkdao comes from writings in the occult volumes of The Revelations of Gla'aki.

### Behind the Mythos
The yarkdao were created by Ramsey Campbell and introduced in his short story "The Inhabitant of the Lake".

Ycnágnnisssz is a fictional entity from the Cthulhu Mythos. The character first appeared in Clark Ashton Smith's 1934 "Genealogical Chart of the Elder Gods" answer to R. H. Barlow's now missing style sheet. (: Selected Letters of Clark Ashton Smith 189)

### Overview
Ycnàgnnisssz is a Hyperborean name for one of the progenitors of the gods (Azathoth being the other) according to the genealogy in the Parchments of Pnom and the related Book of Eibon. Not much is known about the entity but Ycnágnnisssz is an Outer God from the dark star Xoth, and it spawned Zstylzhemghi by fission. It is a fissionary being who is possibly either Abhoth or Ubbo-Sathla; however, these two names are also Hyperborean, so it may be a different entity. It might also be the Nameless Mist or the Darkness, or possibly it is the "Azathoth-Ubbo-Sathla", the bivalvular shape of Azathoth.

The Ydheem are a race of extraterrestrial creatures. They first appeared in the Clark Ashton Smith short story "The Door to Saturn", published in 1932.

### Description
The Ydheem are humanoid creatures (both male and female) with a hairless body. They have evolved to a stage where their head now inhabits the thoracic cavity, and although they are physically very similar to the Bhlemphroim, Ydheems have a slightly more pronounced skull.

They have a low level of technology and are interested in nothing more than the most basic forms of agriculture (one of their products being a wine made from mushrooms) and religion, whose main aspect seems to be the worship of the Great Old One Hziulquoigmnzhah. Although they are highly religious, their fervour is not intolerant of other forms of worship.

### History
Much of their past is unknown, but it is known that, at one point in its history, their largest city was destroyed by an avalanche. As this interfered with their worship, the Ydheem quickly rebuilt the metropolis and went straight back to their activities as if nothing had happened.

Yegg-ha, The Master of the Nightgaunts, is a faceless bat-winged giant that was "killed" by Roman soldiers near Hadrian's Wall in Britain, c.128 A.D. 

It first appeared in the Brian Lumley short story "An Item of Supporting Evidence."

Its connection as master of the Night-gaunts is given in the Necronomicon, although Yibb-Tstll is mentioned elsewhere as the "Lord of Gaunts." Presumably Yegg-ha is a servant of Nodens and its legend appears in the book The Frontier Garrison. While its physical body might be dead it endures in the Dreamlands.

The Book of Eibon describes Yegg-ha as a Lesser Old One, "immense and faceless", who "leads the night-gaunts in the service of the Crawling Chaos and his awful son, Yibb-Tstll". (: "The Descent into the Abyss")

Some sources identify Yegg-Ha as a Great Old One, albeit a "very minor" one. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Behind the Mythos
Yegg-ha was created by Brian Lumley in his The Caller of the Black anthology, published at the end of August Derleth's era by Arkham House, and expanded upon by Lin Carter, who associates it with "the Crawling Chaos", i.e. Nyarlathotep. This differs from H. P. Lovecraft's portrayal of the night-gaunts as Nyarlathotep's enemies, not servants (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath).

The Yekubians are a fictional alien species created by H. P. Lovecraft, Robert E. Howard, Frank Belknap Long, Abraham Merritt, and C. L. Moore for their 1935 short story "The Challenge from Beyond". In 1994, Chaosium incorporated them into its Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game in the bestiary book Ye Booke of Monstres (although here they were referred to as 'Inhabitants of Yekub').

### Background
The Yekubians are a race of worm-creatures whom invade worlds and exchange their minds with those of the natives in a manner similar to the Great Race of Yith. They employ four-inch square crystalline cubes and any intelligent creature who looks into the cube has its mind drawn into a Yekubian machine. The vacated body is taken over by a Yekubian mind which uses it to explore. Once this it has completed its task, the alien uses the cube to send its own mind back.

fullContent:
Yellow Dawn is a Cthulhu Mythos roleplaying game designed and written by British author David J. Rodger, and launched with the core rule book as a self published title in 2006. Since then, three further revisions or editions of the basic rules were released, along with a number of supplements.

Yellow Dawn was announced as being taken over by Modiphius publishing in the July 5, 2015 issue of the Forever Folio ezine but this seems not to have ever happened, or if it did, it attracted no notice and has since disappeared.

### Overview
Some time around the 2030s, the Earth is ravaged by a string of viruses after a corporate cargo ship, returning from an orbital lab, crashes into the atmosphere. Vast numbers of people die. Some are left altered by the pathogen, visibly changed on a molecular level. Others are affected in a more horrific way: turned into the living dead, unable to die without violence, locked in a state of perpetual fury, and with an infectious bite, they force most cities to be left abandoned. The event was called Yellow Dawn. Ten years on, and civilization has rebuilt itself. It is this new world into which the players venture out.

Those changed by the virus devolved into one of two states. Those altered horrifically in terms of looks, but better suited to adapt to the wilderness are known, unfairly, as orcs, looking much the part of the grotesque dark skinned creatures made famous from the Lord of the Rings trilogy. Those who remained human on the outside but became psychotic monsters are known as zombies, much in the style of those made popular by 28 Days Later. Also, very occasionally, you might find the robots - when the virus first appeared their response was to slaughter the infected, since then they appear to have pretty much disappeared.

Within the few cities that have survived the collapse of society intact, life goes on, pretty much as before but with fewer resources. Immediately outside the walls, and lurking in the shells of other once proud cities, vast numbers of zombies can be found. And it the wilderness between cities live those brave enough to make a living from the world around them, including the tribes of orcs that have banded together for self-preservation.

### System
The rules system was an unacknowledged adoption of the Basic Roleplaying games system as used in the original Call of Cthulhu, with the addition of Ranks, similar to levels in Dungeons and Dragons, reflecting a character's faith, willpower, training or sacrifices. This put it more in line with D&D type games and Warhammer 40K in that not only basic statistics but "levels" would improve in play.

The last announcements on the website for the game before the website disappeared were that a major campaign would be released adding diseased zombies as a major threat and a series of suggestions for how to directly add more Mythos elements to the game, since originally these were in the background and implicit rather than front and center as most peop

"Yellow Is the Color of Tomorrow" is a short story by American author Ron Shiflet.

### Synopsis
In an alternate reality, bibliophile Mr. Hollister buys an aged yet intriguing-looking book from an elderly bookseller. What he does not realise is that the book is in actuality a copy of the cursed play The King in Yellow, and it’s magic has taken a hold on his mind. After blacking out, Hollister realises that he has committed a sickening murder while in his fugue state, and he ends his own life rather than fully succumb to the power of the book.

### Characters

* Mr. Hollister, a political cartoonist with a deep love of books.
* Reuben Rothstein, Hollister's aged friend and owner of a failing bookstore.

### Publication History
"Yellow Is the Color of Tomorrow" was first published in Book of Dark Wisdom #4 in fall 2004. It later appeared in the anthology Rehearsals for Oblivion (Act I) in August 2006, and again in Shiflet's own collection They Thrive in Darkness: Mythos and Madness in June 2018.

"Yellow Labelled VHS Tape" is a short story by American author R. C. Mulhare.

### Synopsis
A young man comes across a box of video cassettes at a flea market. After watching one of the tapes - labelled "The King in the Tattered Cloak- Castaigne" - he begins a descent into madness.

### Behind the Mythos
The King in the Tattered Cloak and the name Castaigne would seem to be oblique but clear references to The King in Yellow.

* Lexus, Mason's girlfriend.
* Davan, a friend of Mason's.
* Dr. Archer, a psychiatrist.

"Yellow Labelled VHS Tape" was published in the Doug Draa-edited anthology Weirdbook Annual 2 by Wildside Press in February 2019.

shortDefinition: In the Cthulhu Mythos, The Yellow Sign is a symbol that is usually used by the Brotherhood of the Yellow Sign, a cult that worships the Great Old One Hastur. It is said that the symbol can bestow supernatural powers such as mind-control and possessio...
fullContent:
In the Cthulhu Mythos, The Yellow Sign is a symbol that is usually used by the Brotherhood of the Yellow Sign, a cult that worships the Great Old One Hastur. It is said that the symbol can bestow supernatural powers such as mind-control and possession, and is used to place individuals under the control of the King in Yellow.

### Behind the Mythos
The Yellow Sign first appears in Robert W. Chambers' 1895 anthology The King in Yellow. As is the case with many who use the Yellow Sign, its exact nature is not made very clear, appearing to act as either a catalyst or invocation of the aforementioned King in Yellow.  Within the context of the Mythos, the Yellow Sign (and Hastur himself) are only offhandedly mentioned once in H. P. Lovecraft's 1931 novella The Whisperer in Darkness.

In Robert W. Chambers' original work, the Yellow Sign comes to those who have somehow either become aware of the King in Yellow or of whom the entity known as the King in Yellow has become aware. It is mysterious, portentous, and fatal. This strongly suggests a poetic metaphor for infectious disease. The contemporary sign for contagious disease was a yellow flag.

Also contemporary with Chamber's original book was the practice by booksellers to censor provocative, sexual or outright pornographic books by selling them wrapped in yellow paper, concealing the contents but the bright color acting as a warning sign. An example of this is in Oscar Wilde's The Picture of Dorian Gray where The Yellow Book is given to the protagonist by a fellow decadent aesthete with the express intention of furthering his corruption. The book in question in Wilde's story was A rebours , a particular favorite of H.P. Lovecraft.

Thus the concept of a yellow book, was well established in popular culture and was shorthand for a collection of mature and challenging provocations to the accepted social order. Diseases of mind and body were sure to follow exposure to such material.

A final point that may provide amusement or intrigue is that conventionally, in current society, The Yellow Sign or a Yellow Sign is what a warning sign is usually referred to as being. The triangular, diamond shape or square hazard warning signs are the same shade of yellow as the yellow wrappers of provocative books of 150 to 100 years ago. The concept of yellow signs associated with danger persists in the real world, feeding back into the unquestionably eerie mystery of The Yellow Sign. A deliberate paranoid work of art has been created by Fallon Planning providing "warning signs from the future" thus juxtaposing the conspiratorial, hazard caution and anticpatory or fictional to create a new Yellow Sign subset. There is something powerful in the concept of The Yellow Sign, something that perhaps even Chambers himself could not fully articulate but of which he had nevertheless a clear artistic vision.

fullContent:
The Yeti, a.k.a. Abominable Snowman, or Migo, is a legendary creature and cryptid originating from the Himalayan mountains. They are usually described as anthropoids, comparable to the American Sasquatch. Although popular culture often portrays them as having white fur, this feature is rarely reported in actual sightings.

In the Cthulhu Mythos, the Yeti is most commonly associated with the Mi-Go, an alien species named after the Tibetan word for the creature. However, other interpretations have been proposed as well.

### In Lovecraft Circle works
H. P. Lovecraft refers to the Himalayan legend in his novella The Whisperer in Darkness, in which protagonist Albert Wilmarth skeptically dismisses reports about alien creatures in the Vermont hills by comparing them to similar legends of satyrs and dryads found around the world. Wilmarth specifically points out "the even more startlingly similar belief of the Nepalese hill tribes in the dreaded Mi-Go or 'Abominable Snow-Men' who lurk hideously amidst the ice and rock pinnacles of the Himalayan summits". After his correspondence with Henry Wentworth Akeley, who presents evidence that the Vermont creatures are real, Wilmarth and Akeley come to the conclusion that they are in fact the Mi-Go.

: The Whisperer in Darkness)}}

In At the Mountains of Madness, Lovecraft continues to refer to this species as Mi-Go and to liken them to the Himalayan Snow-Men. Protagonist William Dyer, who has spoken to Albert Wilmarth about the Mythos before, readily identifies the crustacean-like aliens from Yuggoth as "undoubtedly the same as those figuring in certain whispered hill legends of the north, and remembered in the Himalayas as the Mi-Go, or Abominable Snow-Men".

In the works of August Derleth, the Great Old Ones' servitor races include the "Abominable Mi-Go" (: "The House on Curwen Street", "The Whippoorwills in the Hills"), also referred to as the "Abominable Snowmen" (: "The House in the Valley"), which inhabit not just Tibet but the Plateau of Leng as well (: "The Seal of R'lyeh"). On at least one occasion, Derleth went as far as to call them "the Abominable Snow-Men of Mi-Go" (: "A Note on the Cthulhu Mythos").

### Other interpretations
The Cultes des Goules contains information about the Yeti, which are apparently a cult of degenerate nocturnal humanoids connected to Ithaqua. A Miskatonic University expedition to Mt. Sarn'a in the Himalayas encountered Yetis that looked like facultative bipedal anthropoids with no tail, only traveled at night, and chanted about Ithaqua. (: "They Only Come Out at Night")

In the Doctor Who universe, the Yeti are a real mammalian species that inhabit the Himalayas. However, the actual Yeti has only been featured briefly in the series, as the creatures that menaced the Doctor turned out to be Robot Yeti, modelled after the real animal and controlled by the alien entity known as the Great Intelligence (: The Abominable Snowmen, Downtime). Yhoundeh (also known as Y'houndeh, The Elk-Goddess) is a fictional entity created by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith for his short story "The Door to Saturn".

### Description
Although given the epithet of "the Elk-Goddess", Youndeh's true appearance is never given. However, in a letter to Robert H. Barlow dated 10 September 1934 Smith stated it to be the offspring of the "androgynous animal archetype" Zyhumé. The same letter also stated that the marriage of Yhoundeh and Nyarlathotep is mentioned in Parchments of Pnom.

### Worship
Yhoundeh was worshipped in the waning days of Hyperborea, where her priests displayed a fanatic zeal, outlawing the "heretical" worship of older gods and torturing and executing their followers. However, this would prove to be Yhoundeh's downfall as when Morghi, Yhoundeh's high priest, failed to return from an expedition to bring the sorcerer Eibon to trial for his worship of Zothaqquah, the masses believed that dark magic had saved him, and turned from Yhoundeh to once more venerate Zhothaqquah.

### In Other Media
*Black Souls II: Yhoundeh is featured in the role-playing video game, as a minor character named Mother Alice, based on Alice in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll. The game depicts Yhoundeh as a mature version of Alice and her main role in the story is to deceive the player for Nyarlathotep. She also has a descendant, known as the Jabberwock.
*Yurudora: Yhoundeh appears in the mobile game, during the Cthulhu Festival event.

Yian is a fabulous city created by Robert W. Chambers for his short story "The Maker of Moons". It is mentioned in The Whisperer in Darkness, by H. P. Lovecraft, and "The Isle of Dark Magic", by Hugh B. Cave, although in the latter it might be the name of a being, as opposed to a location.

### Description
A woman named Ysonde, raised in Yian for the first 16 years of her life, described it as a beautiful city, "sweet with perfume and the sound of silver bells all day long". She says that in Yian, "all the gardens are sweet and the river flows under the thousand bridges". Of the daily life of the inhabitants she knows little, as she was raised by her "stepfather", the legendary sorcerer Yue-Laou, who didn't allow her to leave her garden and interact with other people. From her garden, however, Ysonde could see the thousand bridges "and the white mountain beyond", and could see that millions of people lived in Yian.

The city's language is unknown, but it's not English. The main god worshiped in Yian is called Xangi, but there are also other deities, possibly including Yue-Laou and the Xin. The colour yellow is considered a symbol of faith in Yian.

According to Ysonde, Yian is located "across seven oceans and the great river which is longer than from the Earth to the moon". However, American Colonel Franklyn Barris, who has himself lived in Yian for years, dismisses this as "the allegories of another land". He claims that Yian "lies hidden in that gigantic shadow called China, vague and vast as the midnight Heavens,--a continent unknown, impenetrable". Nevertheless, Barris admits that Yian is the centre of activity of the Kuen-Yuin: a powerful society of sorcerers led by Yue-Laou, who appears to have the power to create and/or access places that are otherwise unreachable, including a house and a glade in Cardinal Woods that could never be found by anyone not allied with Yue-Laou (: "The Maker of Moons"). As such, the possibility that Yian might be only accessible by magical or supernatural means can't be ruled out.

Yian is one of the many things that Albert Wilmarth learned about while studying ancient myths that might be related to the Mi-Go or the entities worshiped by them. (: The Whisperer in Darkness)

### Behind the Mythos
It's not known whether Yian is related to the "shunned and dreaded" city of Yian-Ho, which is mentioned in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key" and "The Diary of Alonzo Typer". If so, it might also be associated with the Ancient One and the Plateau of Leng.

Yian-Ho is a fictional city mentioned in "The Diary of Alonzo Typer", by H. P. Lovecraft and William Lumley, and again in "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", by H. P. Lovecraft and E. Hoffmann Price.

### Description
Yian-Ho is described as a "shunned", "dreaded" and "abhorred" place, identified as "that lost and hidden city wherein brood aeon-old secrets, and of which dim memories older than the body lurk behind the minds of all men". Claes van der Heyl claims to have been to Yian-Ho "in the veritable flesh of this body, as none other among the living has been", and there learned the means to summon a monstrous tentacled entity. (: "The Diary of Alonzo Typer")

A clairvoyant Yogi that Harley Warren was acquainted with also claimed "that he alone of living men had been to Yian-Ho". The Swami Chandraputra described Yian-Ho as "the hidden legacy of sinister, aeon-old Leng". (: "Through the Gates of the Silver Key")

### Behind the Mythos
It's not known whether Yian-Ho is related to (or even synonymous with) the mystical city of Yian, mentioned in Robert W. Chambers' "The Maker of Moons" and H. P. Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness.

### A Speculation on Language

Allowing for the contemporary usage of transliterated Chinese, "-ho" as in Yian-Ho or indeed Gung-Ho! may be identical with -hua in modern Chinese transliteration, meaning "change" and often used to indicate that something has changed state, either becoming energized or losing energy. Since Lovecraft was a very erudite man in his writings it would be a mistake to think that he had not perhaps stumbled across the usage of "-ho" (or in modern Chinese notation "-hua") in relation to his naming of this place. Or, he may simply have liked how it sounded of course.

Yibb-Tstll (The Patient One) is a fictional entity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Brian Lumley for his short story "Rising with Surtsey".

### Background
Yibb-Tstll is an obscure god, said to watch at the center of all time as the universe revolves. Because of this insight, only Yog-Sothoth is said to be wiser. Its blood, The Black, is a weapon which takes the form of black snowflakes that stick to and smother a victim. The god's touch causes an instant change in the person affected, this change is usually fatal but occasionally brings some benefit.

Yibb-Tstll is sometimes described as an immobile, dark, tentacled entity with a pulpy, alien head, detached eyes, and large bat wings under which countless Night-gaunts suck black milk from its innumerable breasts.

### Notes
Yibb-Tstll makes its major appearance in "The Horror at Oakdeene", and also appears in "The Caller of the Black".

Some scholars suggest that, having a close connection to the Great Old One Bugg-Shash, (: Malleus Monstrorum) Yibb-Tstll should be regarded as a Great Old One - specifically in the Drowners group introduced by Brian Lumley, parasitic alien entities which thrive by vampyrizing the Great Old Ones themselves (: The Encyclopedia Cthulhiana) - though in Chaosium’s material she is classified as an "Outer God". (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### In Other Media
*In Wyrd Games' tabletop miniatures game Malifaux, a sub-faction of the Neverborn utilise a mechanic known as Black Blood to damage opponents when they are struck; this may have been inspired by Yibb-Tstill, as much of that game draws inspiration from other sources.
*In the role-playing video game Black Souls II, Yibb-Tstll appears as a minor character named Frumious Bandersnatch, who is connected to daughter Alice, based on Alice in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll. The game depicts Yibb-Tstll as a younger version of Alice and her role is to deceive the player.

Yidhra is a fictional deity in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was originally created by Walter C. DeBill, Jr. for his short story "Predator", part of the Mlandoth Cycle.

### Overview
Yidhra is an Outer God who is worshipped as a beautiful, awesome and terrible earth-mother, similar to Shub-Niggurath and might be connected to the Darkness. She has many avatar forms including Yolanda and Madam Yi since her "life-cycle" centres around absorbing other lifeforms and taking from them their evolutionary advantages (in the process she also takes memories). This cycle of "rebirths" makes her immortal. She has telepathic powers which gives her a link to her servitors, and can project illusions. Her servitors are "the Lurkers in the desert," Xothra and Y'hath, and "the Children of Yidhra" (her human cult).

### Avatars
### Madam Yi
Madam Yi appears as a beautiful human Asian female, dressed in billowing red, white, and black robes. This avatar has a delicate painted face that looks like that of a porcelain doll and possesses long razor-sharp fingernails. China is where this avatar is encountered, where it mates with and kills the young men provided to her by female led and dominated cults. The mating produces monstrous or deformed offspring, most of which are reabsorbed by her.

### Yolanda Prentiss
A semi-human reptilian creature which casts a glamour to appear as a beautiful, cultured young woman, Yolanda Prentiss ministers to the Yidhra cult located in Milando, Texas. She has the power to fuse humans and animals into new forms, which she employs as her servitors.

At least one iteration of Yolanda Prentiss was destroyed by a human named Wilhelm Kramer at the same time he murdered his family, who were malformed descendants of Yidhra; unfortunately for Kramer, Yidhra immediately sent a duplicate of Yolanda to deal with him.

Yig, the Father of Serpents, is a fictional deity introduced in the H. P. Lovecraft revision story "The Curse of Yig". He is introduced as "the snake-god of the central plains tribes," and "a shunned and feared object in central Oklahoma." 

The story describes him as: 


The snake-god's chief quality was "a relentless devotion to his children," making it taboo to kill snakes. Those "who flouted him or wreaked harm upon his wriggling progeny" would suffer the "curse of Yig," in which the deity would "turn his victim, after suitable tortures, to a spotted snake." 

Walter C. DeBill Jr.'s "A Movement in the Grass" describes Yig as the father of Ayi'ig and the mate of the outer god Yidhra. 

### Origin and beliefs
The serpentine Yig was one of the many gods worshiped in the ancient continent of Mu. (: "Out of the Aeons", : "The Invaders")

T’yog believed that Yig was one of the "gods friendly to man", along with Shub-Niggurath, Nug and Yeb, and that these deities would be willing to side with humanity against the tyranny of Ghatanothoa. (: "Out of the Aeons")

In the early 1920s, an "American Indian ethnologist" conducted extensive research into snake lore from Guatemala to Oklahoma. He described Yig as the dark prototype for the more benevolent Quetzalcoatl and Kukulkan. 

By the time of his investigation, the ethnologist found that the people of Oklahoma were often too afraid to discuss the legend, though this had not always been the case. Before the Land Rush of 1889, the plains tribes were more open than the Pueblo or desert nomads about their worship of Yig. The influx of white immigrants, however, led to a series of unnatural tragedies. Belief was more common in the west than it was in the transplanted south eastern tribes.

Unlike most of the Great Old Ones, Yig was rarely malicious, although he would enter a feeding frenzy in Autumn, leading the Pawnee, Wichita, and Caddo of Oklahoma to drum constantly from August through to October to drive him away. In addition to this, the Wichita would make offerings of corn to appease him (: "The Curse of Yig").

While researching other legends, the same ethnologist also came across the manuscript of Zamacona y Nuñez, and found about the subterranean world of blue-litten K'n-yan, where Yig is one of the two main gods worshiped by the K'n-yanians, alongside Tulu. (: The Mound)

Yikilth was a colossal iceberg-fortress created by Clark Ashton Smith for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "The Coming of the White Worm".

### Description


An enormous chunk of seaborne ice which followed the direction of its master Rlim Shaikorth, Yikilth emitted a pale light for many miles which froze solid anything it touched: living beings which fell victim to its lethal caress were forever transformed into marble-like statues which emitted an intense cold and could not be thawed by even the heat of a large bonfire.

Yikilth grew as its master consumed the bodies and souls of sorcerers, and absorbed the domiciles of these dead unfortunates into its mass. Thus, as the wizard Evagh witnessed  "dwellings such as men had never built … that might belong to other ages or worlds" in the deepest crevasses, it may be inferred that Yikilth and its master were both incredibly ancient and utterly alien.

### History
Yikilth appeared on Earth in the Hyperborean Age where it devastated Hyperborea's coastline with impunity. It was finally destroyed when the sorcerer Evagh inflicted a mortal wound on Rlim Shaikorth, releasing a seemingly endless stream of hot black "blood" which melted the iceberg and sent its frozen contents to the bottom of the ocean.

Yith is a fictional planet, an earlier home of the Great Race of Yith, a prominent species within the Cthulhu Mythos. (: The Shadow Out of Time) The name first appeared in Duane W. Rimel's poem cycle, "Dreams of Yith"; Rimel had originally written "Yid", but Lovecraft changed that when revising the poems, noting that Rimel's word was also a derogatory word for Jews.

The word "Yith" appears only once in Lovecraft's fiction, when he notes in The Shadow Out of Time that "the minds of the Great Race sped across the void from that obscure trans-galactic world known in the disturbing and debatable Eltdown Shards as Yith."

Yog-Sothoth is a fictional cosmic entity and Outer God created by H. P. Lovecraft, appearing as a core part of the Cthulhu Mythos (which Lovecraft would refer to facetiously as the "Yog-Sothothery"). Born of the Nameless Mist, he is the progenitor of Cthulhu, Hastur the Unspeakable, and the ancestor of the Voormi. He is also the father of Wilbur Whateley.

### Description
Like many Lovecraftian gods, Yog-Sothoth has many different appearances throughout the various stories of the Mythos, by various authors. However, there seems to be a common agreement that Yog-Sothoth visually manifests as a mass of glowing orbs, with eyes or tendrils in some versions, and in others simply the orbs. 

It is heavily implied that Yog-Sothoth is omniscient, and is locked outside the universe, meaning he can know and see all of space-time all at once, which means there is no secret hidden from Yog-Sothoth. 

### Appearances
Yog-Sothoth's name was first mentioned in : The Case of Charles Dexter Ward. He goes on to be the driving force of : "The Dunwich Horror," in which he fathers twin children with a human. (That story includes a lengthy quote from the Necronomicon about Yog-Sothoth: Yog-Sothoth is the key and guardian of the gate. Past, present, future, all are one in Yog-Sothoth....")

He is encountered by Randolph Carter in : "Through the Gates of the Silver Key", the only Lovecraft story in which Yog-Sothoth seems to speak.

The entity is described as "a congeries of iridescent globes" (: "The Horror in the Museum", : "The Lurker at the Threshold"). In the : Hay Necronomicon, 13 of these are named:

Yogash the Ghoul is a mysterious entity that is in the line of Azathoth, descending through Cthulhu, and producing the line which would produce H. P. Lovecraft. It's not clear if this degree of separation from Cthulhu and Azathoth renders Yogash the Ghoul mortal, or if his powers and capacity are significantly diminished compared to the Great Old Ones.

Yogash is the offspring of Shaurash-ho, who is a grandchild of Nug (: Selected Letters of H. P. Lovecraft). Since Nug has also been referred to as the "grandfather of all ghouls on the earth-plane" (: "The Descent into the Abyss"), it's possible that Shaurash-ho itself might have been a Ghoul, although this is pure speculation. It's also possible that Yogash was the first of the Ghouls, and the origin of that species. Due to the humanoid features and the capacity for the continued cross-breeding with the human species, it is likely that the "union" of Shaurash-ho, biological or otherwise, was with a human parent. This would have yielded a near human genetic variant, but with obviously bestial and monstrous features. This concept is supported by the seeming continual genetic compatibility with humans which would eventually yield Richard Pickman, who in most respects was indistinguishable from his fellow human peers.

However, it should be noted that some generations before humans start showing up in the family tree, Yogash's bloodline seems to have taken a more reptilian turn, spawning beings such as K'baa the Serpent and Ghoth the Burrower (one of the Little People). This is far from inconsistent, as even modern Ghouls have been described with reptilian traits, such as "scaly claws", as well as a preference for subterranean habitats, much like the Little People.

Another entity, Naggoob, has been identified as the "Father of Ghouls" (: "The Horror in the Gallery"), and thus might be related to Shaurash-ho and Yogash.

A character named Yogash the Black appeared in Nyarlathotep's retinue in the climax of the The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath. Given that the Ghouls owe no allegiance to Nyarlathotep, it's not known whether Yogash the Black is the same as Yogash the Ghoul.

### Behind the Mythos
In Lin Carter's Xothic Legend Cycle, Yogash is also the name of a Deep One hybrid who worked for Abner Exekiel Hoag, and was responsible for translating the Ponape Scripture. (: "Out of the Ages", "The Fishers from Outside")

Yogthulu is an extra-dimensional entity from the fictional universe of the animated series Iron Man: Armored Adventures by Marvel Comics, appearing in the episode "Doomsday".

### Background
Yogthulu is a demonic entity from an alternate dimension, who takes the form of a giant centipede-like creature. He is known to make bargains with lesser beings, but will forfeit the deal if the terms are not met.

The supervillain Doctor Doom used the power of the ninth Makluan Ring to open wormholes to other dimensions, summoning Yogthulu in hopes of reuniting with his family. Doctor Doom kidnapped the superhero Iron Man, along with his father Howard Stark and his adversary the Mandarin, planning to exchange those "three pure souls" for Yogthulu to bring back his family; however, Yogthulu was able to sense impurity in one of the souls, calling off the deal. Shortly afterwards, Doctor Doom was sealed away in Yogthulu's dimension for eternity.

### Mythos Connections
His name is an obvious reference to Yog-Sothoth and Cthulhu; however, it is unknown if Yogthulu has any relation to either of them.
