fullContent:
"Yohk the Necromancer" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Gary Myers. It first appeared in the Winter 1971 issue of The Arkham Collector.

### Synopsis
The narrator tells that in the land of Vornai, there was a fat-bellied clerk in the Street of Frogs called Yohk, who was a sorcerer of no little accomplishment that arrived from the mists and escorted by cautious cotters. When people mysteriously started vanishing, he was quickly blamed for it. But he was met by three men who came from the House of the Worm crying about the end of the world upon the house’s caretaker’s demise. Yohk took up residence inside an abandoned temple of a lesser god in the Street of Frogs. There he practiced thaumaturgies that called upon Nasht and Kaman-Thah and summoned some of their priests as he had taken something from them he keeps in an ebon box.

The narrator further explains that Yohk had travelled far and wide, meeting with the King in Yellow in Carcosa, and heard the fluting tunes of Bokrug in the ruins of Sarnath. He studied black magic in the Plateau of Leng, gazed with his soul into the Vale of Pnath, and approached the great city of Kadath. This gave him experience in magic that one quite possibly shouldn’t. His aim was to find a key to freeing the Great Old Ones to receive untold wealth beyond avarice. But since a spell never existed in the world, he sought to look ‘behind’ it. He approached the House of the Worm and entered, performing a ritual that he believed failed. He soon vanished and his former neighbors reported a foul smell and rats scurrying around the Street of Frogs at night. The mayor and his five augurers formed a posse to confront Yohk at the temple and discovered Yohk slimmed down in weight and performing a magic ritual with four globes of light. The people left abruptly out of respect.

### Publication History
*The Arkham Collector, Winter 1971 (1971)
*The Arkham Collector, Vol 1 (1971)
*The House of the Worm (1975)
*The Country of the Worm: Excursions Beyond the Wall of Sleep (2013)

fullContent:
The Yokai are part of Japanese folklore. In 2005 they were first used as a fictional species by Chaosium for the Call of Cthulhu RPG.

### Background
The Yokai are creatures whose appearances is bizarre and whom are visually frightening. They most often materialize in the hours around dusk and dawn, due to the veil between the dimensions weakening at that time. They are the manifestations of chaos incarnate. When the fabric of space-time is ripped or rended, tendrils of Azathoth seep through. As the tears "heal", they become cut off from their source. The beliefs of locals instantly shapes and molds the chaotic energies, creating what is known in Japan as yokai.

### Examples of Yokai
* Rokuro-Kubi: Whom are usually women and constrict their victims with their neck.
* Yuki Onna: Whom appear as women whom hungers for the warmth of humans. It's embrace paralyzes them and drains their warmth, unintentionally killing them.
* Iso Onna: From a distance she is beautiful, appearing as a mermaid. Up close it's all scales, fangs, a serpentine lower body, and claws. With which it tears its victims apart.
* Dora-ta-boh: It's a monster which lays hidden within muddy rice fields. Emerging after the rice has been harvest or the field has been left fallow. Victims are suffocated by pressing their faces into the mud.
* Iwami-no-ushi-oni: It's a which impales or rushes whomever intrudes into its domain.
* Kawa-aka-go Which are disguised as wailing drowning babies or toddlers. It's would-be rescuer is pulled underwater and drowned by it.
* Umi-Bozhu: It hunts the seafaring lanes, capsizing vessels and drowing the crew by crushing them under its massive body. It appears a a monstrous hovering black globe, which rises out of the sea.
* Oh-gumo: They are monstrous spiders whom feast on human fluids.
* Bake-neko: Shapeshifting great cats that appear as needy frail old women, whom transform into great cats which attempt to eat the would-be Samaritan.

### Gallery of Examples of Yokai

Yokoth & Glythur (the latter aka the Mother of Faceless Hordes, Ravager of Galaxies, & the Star of Madness) are Lovecraftian-like extra-dimensional entities in the fictional universe of the Supernatural television series.

### Background
Yokoth and Glythur together destroyed or consumed most of their universe, with the assistance of their offpsring, the "faceless hordes. Entities whose true form is amorphous and cephalopod-like. In 1925 a rogue group of Men of Letters opened a rift to that universe, desiring to bring the Old Ones through to "cleanse the world of hate and bring a new paradise". Yokoth came through and devoured most of the group, before they were able to close the rift and bound her. In 2018, she tricked the Winchester brothers into releasing her. She opened a rift for Glythur who began to come through, but the Winchesters managed to close the rift in time as Glythur took Yokoth back to its home dimension.

Yomagn'tho is a fictional deity created by Crispin Burnham and E. P. Berglund for their short story "The Thing in the Library". The character would later be incorporated into the Call of Cthulhu role-playing game. (: Malleus Monstrorum)

### Description
Yomagn'tho is an Outer God described as being equal to Cthugha in terms of power. The entity was sealed away in a world circling the star Pherkard, and when summoned to Earth, it takes the form of a flaming circle with three inner-petals and a dark interior with chaotic shapes. Some texts refer to it as "the Feaster from the Stars", although that title is more commonly associated with Zvilpogghua.

### In Other Media
*Haiyore! Nyaruko-san: The anime television series features a parody of the online shopping website Amazon.com, named after Yomagn'tho.
*Mobile Suit Gundam GQuuuuuuX: The anime television series features a space weapon known as the Solar Ray, Yomagn'tho being its codename. The weapon has already appeared since the original 1979 Gundam series, but the Yomagn'tho moniker is exclusive to the GQuuuuuuX divergent timeline. In reality, it's a specialized super weapon that uses "The Rose of Sharon", an alternate universe MAN-08 Elmeth with its pilot Lalah Sune still inside and in suspended animation, and the Mobile Suit GFreD to create a localized "Zeknova" at a target and destroy everything within it, scattering what's left across the multiverse.

### Behind the Mythos
Although its name is spelled slightly different, Pherkard was based on a real-life star located in the northern constellation of Ursa Minor.

### Synopsis
In twenty-six lines the narrator describes the lengths he would go to when trying to avoid a telephone call from the Great Old One Cthulhu.

### Publication History
Since its first appearance in 2 AM, "Yoo-Hoo, Cthulhu" has also been included in the 2005 collection of Thomas's own works Unholy Dimensions.

The Yorhi were a species of native Martian which appeared in the H. P. Lovecraft-inspired Cthulhu Mythos.

### Description
The parent race of the Aihai, to whom they bore a very strong resemblance, the Yorhi possessed three flared nostrils, a skin like tough leather, and long limbs with recurved, satyr-like legs. They had eyes which rested in peculiarly sunken sockets, a double row of sharp teeth, fingers with four joints, and a tendency to wear little to no clothing. Although they had the same angular chest as the Aihai, the arm which sprouted from it was of a far more practical use, and the Yorhi were said to have carried themselves with a grace not present in their descendants. The Yorhi were also a good deal taller than the Aihai, with adults all measuring over seven feet in height.

The technology of the Yorhi was of a far greater level than that of their descendants, although some of the Aihai still possess Yorhi artefacts, along with the knowledge of how to use them. Similarly, Yorhi architecture was of a more grand scope than than that of the younger race, and they were known to favour enormous pyramidal edifices featuring many buttressed terraces. Indeed, some Aihai still inhabit the ancient cities of their predecessors.

Why the Yorhi devolved into the Aihai is a mystery that has yet to be revealed.

Red-litten Yoth is a fictional subterranean location featured in the novella The Mound, written by H. P. Lovecraft based on a story prompt by Zealia Bishop. It is adjacent to blue-litten K'n-yan and black N'kai, and was formerly inhabited by a species of sapient quadrupedal reptiles.

Since The Mound wasn't published until 1940, the first mention of Yoth in print was in Lovecraft's The Whisperer in Darkness.

### Description
Yoth is a subterranean world deep inside the Earth, located beneath K'n-yan, but above lightless N'kai. It is filled with the Cyclopean ruins of a non-human civilization that existed long before the rise of humanity. Beneath the largest Yothic city are the vaults of Zin (: The Mound), which also exist in the Dreamlands (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath).

The source of the red light that illuminates Yoth is unknown. However, Pánfilo de Zamacona y Nuñez speculated that the blue light of K'n-yan might result from a phenomenon akin to the aurora borealis: an explanation that the American ethnologist who found Zamacona's manuscript finds reasonable, although he also suggests that radioactivity might be involved. (: The Mound)

### Inhabitants
When the K'n-yanians explored the Cyclopean ruins of red-litten Yoth, they came across reptilian horned animals believed to be the degenerate and unintelligent descendants of the sapient Yoth natives. These reptiles were cross-bred with a mammalian species to produce the creatures called gyaa-yothn.

Carvings and manuscripts found in the vaults of Zin, underneath the ruins of the largest Yothic city, confirm that the Yothics were reptilian and quadrupedal. However, they also reveal that these creatures (like the Elder Things) had the means to create and modify new species.

In the Dreamlands, the vaults of Zin are inhabited by the leaping Ghasts (: The Dream-Quest of Unknown Kadath), perhaps hinting at a relationship between them and the Yothics.

The Yothics explored black N'kai, containing the ruins of an extinct, even older civilization of sightless creatures. They found temples and idols of Tsathoggua, and brought the Tsathoggua faith to Yoth. After the Yothics' own extinction, the K'n-yanians likewise found the images and adopted Tsathoggua as a god, to the point of naming the K'n-yanian capital Tsath after their new deity. However, the Tsathoggua faith was abandoned by the K'n-yanians, and the passage leading from Yoth to N'kai was sealed, after they discovered the Formless Spawn.

Since the Yothic manuscripts claim that no life was found in N'kai, some K'n-yanians have speculated that at some point after the manuscripts were written, a natural disaster might have opened up a passage to unsuspected lower chambers, and allowed the Formless Spawn to return to their temples. Yoth-Tlaggon is an obscure Great Old One first appearing in Ken Asamatsu's 1994 short stories, "The Mask of Yoth-Tlaggon" and "Queen of K'n-yan."

Originally, the name was mentioned in the heading of a letter from Howard Phillips Lovecraft to Clark Ashton Smith.
"Yoth-Tlaggon ―at the Crimson Spring Hour of the Amorphous Reflection."

Although the inclusion of strange terms and cryptic references were very common in Lovecraft's letters, Yoth-Tlaggon does not appear to relate to any entity or concept present in the work of Lovecraft. Ken Asamatsu included Yoth-Tlaggon in his stories, depicting it as a slug-like being covered with wrinkles and scales, and endowed with innumerable eyes. It also appears that it has a mask shaped like an inverted triangle. The creature is worshiped in Yuggoth and served by the electromagnetic wave lifeform known as Illewik. A related artefact is the Mask of Yoth-Tlaggon, which grants the bearer knowledge of the past and future.

fullContent:
"You Will Never Be the Same" is a short Cthulhu Mythos story by American author Erica Satifka.

### Synopsis
A junior officer aboard a ship which crosses the stars by travelling through dimensions attempts to assist when the pilot and crew are driven insane by something they have seen during the course of their journey. Although successful in his endeavour, he is shown not only a truth - that the realities are unraveling in the face of the Great Old Ones' return - but a name: Cthulhu.

### Publication History
"You Will Never Be the Same" was published in the Kat Rocha-edited anthology Whispers from the Abyss by 01Publishing in November 2014.

### Behind the Mythos
The name of the starship, the Wong-Danforth, appears to be a nod to one of the two surviving characters in H. P. Lovecraft's novella At the Mountains of Madness, Danforth.

shortDefinition: "Young Goodwife Doten" is a short story by American author Robert M. Price. It is an expansion on events referenced in Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-England Canaan, a fictional book which appeared in The Lurker at the Threshold.  ### Synopsis A...
fullContent:
"Young Goodwife Doten" is a short story by American author Robert M. Price. It is an expansion on events referenced in Thaumaturgical Prodigies in the New-England Canaan, a fictional book which appeared in The Lurker at the Threshold.

### Synopsis
A young couple living near Arkham in what will one day become New England find that all of their attempts to have children result in stillbirth. In desperation they turn to a reclusive old woman who lives in the nearby woods, and is rumoured to possess arcane knowledge; after a visit to the woman, and coupling with what she believes to be an angel of heaven, the wife indeed becomes pregnant.

However, on the day of the birth the midwife runs in terror from the abomination which she sees brought into the world. It is quickly put to death, and the young couple burnt for witchcraft.

### Characters

* John Doten, a young farmer in the early days of American colonisation.
* Prudence Doten, John's wife.
* Goody Watkins, a worshipper of dark gods.
*Reverend Abijah Hoadley, a religious zealot with an apparently homicidal streak.

### Publication History
"Young Goodwife Doten" was first published in the 1995 anthology 100 Wicked Little Witch Stories. It was later included in Blasphemies & Revelations, a 2008 collection of Price's own works.

### Trivia

* The creature which impregnates Prudence recalls descriptions of the Black Man, an avatar of Nyarlathotep.
* The Reverend Abijah Hoadley made his first appearance in the opening chapter of H. P. Lovecraft's "The Dunwich Horror."

Younglings are a species of amphibious monstrosity created by Leigh Carr and Lynne Hardy for Chaosium's Call of Cthulhu horror roleplaying game. They made their first appearance in the scenario supplement The Lightless Beacon in 2019.

### Description
Distant relations to the Deep Ones, for whom they are known to act as muscle and shock troops, the Younglings make up for what they lack in size and intelligence with brute strength and animal cunning. They are somewhat smaller than an average human, but possess sharp teeth and claws with which to rend their victims, as well as poisonous spines which they are able to launch from their backs to disorient and paralyse their victims. They are protected by a thick, scaly hide which acts as a natural armour, possess a long-finned tail, and are equally at home in the water or on land (: The Lightless Beacon).

### History
When the Deep Ones of Innsmouth lost a ship off the coast of Beacon Island, they sent a number of Deep One Hybrids along with a cadre of Younglings to retrieve the gold coins which had been aboard the vessel and were now being washed up along the shore. Unfortunately, one of the lighthouse keepers had been surreptitiously collecting them, and this act resulted in the slaughter of all three of the men (: The Lightless Beacon).

Later, with the light from the beacon extinguished a passing ship, the SS Essex County, was shipwrecked, and a small group of survivors made it to Beacon Island. Unaware of the presence of the Deep Ones and Younglings, the group soon found themselves in a vicious battle for survival (: The Lightless Beacon).

Ysbaddaden, is a fictional extraterrestrial being created by American author Kevin L. O'Brien for his short Cthulhu Mythos story "October Surprise".

### Overview
According to The Book of Merlin, Ysbaddaden and its sibling Scathach were the offspring of Hzioulquoigmnzhah and Klosmiebhyx on distant Yuggoth. When the cannibalistic Cxaxukluth came in search of nourishment, Ysbaddaden and Scathach were whisked off to Cykranosh by Hzioulquoigmnzhah. What became if it afterwards is not recorded (: "October Surprise").

### Behind the Mythos
Ysbaddaden, Chief of Giants is the name of a character from Welsh mythology which is loosely related to the legend of King Arthur. According to the folklore, Ysbaddaden was killed by a nobleman named Goreu after it killed many of his siblings.

Ythogtha is a Great Old One in the expanded Cthulhu Mythos. The character was created by Lin Carter for his Xothic Legend Cycle.

### Description
Ythogtha is the second son of Cthulhu who resembles a gigantic, humanoid frog or Deep One, with but a single, huge eye in the center of his forehead like a cyclops. A dense mane and a beard of writhing tentacles grows from his head. Ythogtha is incredibly large; when the sorcerer-priest Zanthu attempts to free Ythogtha from his prison, he mistakes his god's clawed, slimy fingertips for mountainous heads. The Elder Gods imprisoned Ythogtha in the Abyss of Yhe. He is served by the planarian-like yuggs and their lord, Ubb, The Father of Worms.

Yuggs are a fictional species created by the late American author Lin Carter for his short story "Out of the Ages".

### Description
Yuggs, which may be extraterrestrial in origin, resemble enormous white flatworms.  Reaching a minimum of  12 feet in length, and up to 4 ft in diameter, they have mouths full of horn-like teeth and a half dozen tentacles which can be up to 2 ft long. Yuggs have unusual characteristics, such as the ability to shoot organic darts into humans to transmit genetic information. Though Yuggs can exist anywhere, they prefer to spend most of their time burrowing beneath the Earth's crust. Yuggs sometimes bestow great wealth to humans in exchange for their cooperation and for regular sacrifices.

### Yuggya
Yuggya is the name given to the progeny of a mating between a Yugg and a Deep One of the fish-like variety. The resulting being has the outward appearance of a human, however it is not remotely human but has characteristics of cnidarians, squids and insects. Although its mind is alien to normal human thoughts and emotions, a yuggya is nonetheless empathic and can use this ability to exploit the emotional weaknesses of its adversaries.

The Yuggya race is detailed and appears in the novel "Other Nations" by T&P Marsh. The term Ub-Bg-zth also appears in the novel "Other Nations." Both the Yuggs and Yuggya (Carter and Marsh) are direct offspring of Ubb.

(Note: The term "Yuggya" can also be used as the plural for "Yugg").

Yuggoth is a fictional planet in the Cthulhu Mythos. It was originally created by H. P. Lovecraft for his story Fungi from Yuggoth.

### Description
*Yuggoth is a planet located at the very edge of the Earth's Solar System in either the Kuiper Belt, Scattered Disk or even as far away as the Oort Cloud. It is the site of a Mi-Go colony, a race of fungoid, crustacean-like extraterrestrials.
*Yuggoth is a major stopping-off point for the Great Old Ones on their way to Earth.
*Yuggoth has its own mini-solar system including Zaman, Nithon, the binary planets Thog and Thok, and the Ghooric Zone. It orbits at ninety degrees from the plane of the elliptical. It is the natal home of an "Elder Race" of Yuggothians who died out (perhaps due to the cannibalistic habits of Cxaxukluth?) before the planet became an “outpost” of the Mi-Go territory. Relics of the Elder Race exist including, according to The Revelations of Gla'aki, a city of green pyramids, and a pit that might be “the Pit of Shoggoths”. A dark inhospitable world; its surface is ravaged by high winds, while its "seas" and "rivers" consist of a warm, oily substance that flows sluggishly under basalt bridges. Cities, towers, and mines exist on both land and sea.
*Yuggoth has been suggested to be Pluto.
*Na'morha is a named city on Yuggoth.
*The artifact known as the Shining Trapezohedron is stated to have been created on Yuggoth. The Black Seal of Iraan also comes from Yuggoth  (: "The Haunter of the Dark").
*The planet is a source of lagh-metal (: "Out of the Aeons").
*Yog-Sothoth is known as "The Beyond One" on Yuggoth. Daoloth is also worshipped.
*The Raandeese, according to Les Enfants du Poisson, sometimes travel via a gate known as "The Threshold of Yuggoth", suggesting that they may have been on Yuggoth at some stage too (: "From the Deep and Beyond" [Gregory Nicoll]).
*Several Great Old Ones settled on Yuggoth at one time or another Including: Rhan-Tegoth, Tsathoggua, Ghizghuth, Zstylzhemgni, Hziulquoigmnzhah and possibly Gla'aki.

### Trivia
*If Yuggoth is indeed Pluto it would presumably share Pluto's location in the Kuiper Belt. Pluto was the only Kuiper Belt Object to be discovered during Lovecraft's lifetime; the next KBO would not be discovered until 1992.
*The real Pluto has a region named the Cthulhu Macula shaped like a whale following an online poll from "creatures related to underworld mythologies."
*Russell's Guide interprets Yuggoth as a group of nine, Outer God-like entities who worship Azathoth, on top of which the Mi-Go have constructed an artifical surface.

"Yuggoth on the Rim" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by author Alan Peschke.

### Synopsis
The six four-line verses describe an encounter with the alien Mi-Go, and end with the statement that the narrator will shortly join them on their homeworld of Yuggoth.

### Publication History
"Yuggoth on the Rim" was first published in the online Mythos zine Nightscapes #7 in April 1998, and saw physical print in Imelod #11 in October of the same year.

"Yule-Thoughts in Kingsport" is a Cthulhu Mythos poem by American poet Ann K. Schwader. It was first published in the Summer 1992 issue of long-running weird fiction magazine Eldritch Tales.

### Synopsis
The fourteen lines describe the narrator's horror at the supernatural elements which lurk just below the surface of their small town, Kingsport. It makes reference to Cthulhu Mythos stories such as H. P. Lovecraft's "The Festival".

### Publication History
Since its first appearance, "Yule-Thoughts in Kingsport" has also appeared in the Keith Allen Daniels-edited anthology The Three Sonneteers (June 2000, Anamnesis Press), the collection of Schwader's own works The Worms Remember (2001, Hive Press), and the E. P. Berglund-edited online zine Nightscapes (December 2006).

fullContent:
Yuth is a ruined undersea city which features in the fictional Cthulhu Mythos.

### Description
Located around thirty miles north of the Bimini Islands beyond the chain's oceanic shelf and deep beneath water, Yuth is a gargantuan city composed of thin cones hundreds of feet in height engraved with enigmatic runes, and squat squarish buildings which have for the most part been knocked flat by seismic upheaval. Despite the ruined nature of the cones, many of them retain their sharp tips, and so remain a forest of hazards to those attempting to descend to the city.

Yuth is an entirely alien city to humans, with much of it's geometry said to be painful to look at. What is known is about its ground level is that it reaches farther than any human has explored, and has at least one - now broken - causeway which stretches for further than the eye can see. One end of this causeway terminates in a vast temple, home of the Great Old One Tsathoggua, who was believed to have lived there.

### Trivia 
*In John Glasby's short story The Old One, several humans attempted to explore Yuth and one, Professor Dorman, was snatched from there by Tsathoggua.
*Although Tsathoggua is stated to have taken residence in Yuth, this goes against most other sources which claim that he sleeps in the subterranean realm of N'kai.

Yuzh is a fictional star first mentioned by the late American author Clark Ashton Smith in his unfinished 1933 story "The Infernal Star". 

### Overview
In his story fragment, Smith reveals almost nothing of Yuzh, save than that it is a binary star in partnership with its sister Yamil Zacra, and that the two are orbited by the planet Pnidleethon (: "The Infernal Star").

John W. Patterson later states Yuzh to have become the prison for the soul of the monstrous being Nycrama after its death at the hands of Endura/Avrenim, although how or why this is the case is left unexplained (: "Priestess of Nycrama").

### Behind the Mythos
In his afterword to the digital edition of "Priestess of Nycrama", Patterson states Yuzh is one of the "fantastic names and places … [which inspired] me to write".

Z'toggua is a fictional entity created by Ran Cartwright for his eponymous short story.

### Overview
Z'toggua is a Great Old One worshipped by the Deep Ones. He is described as a green, scaly monster with bat wings, yellow insect-like eyes, tentacles hanging from his nose, a gaping mouth on his stomach, and three large tentacles emerging from his underbelly and is explicitly not Zothaqquah nor Tsathoggua. (: "Shog-E'yahg")

### In Other Media
*Z'toggua is referenced by name in the Thunder Lotus produced video game Sundered when the player chooses to corrupt their double jump skill; the double jump is given a new name (Z'toggua's Wings) and new feature that morphs Eshe (the player character) into a bat-like creature.

Zadok Allen is a character in H. P. Lovecraft's The Shadow Over Innsmouth, one of the few remaining humans in Innsmouth. After relating  the history of Innsmouth to traveller Robert Olmstead, he was captured and presumably sacrificed to the Deep Ones by the Esoteric Order of Dagon.

### Expanded Mythos
In Robert M. Price's short story "The Transition of Zadok Allen" (1995), Allen is depicted as having in fact been taken below the waves and transformed into a Deep One, where he presumably still lives.

Allen also appeared as an important non-player character in Bethesda Softworks' Call of Cthulhu: Dark Corners of the Earth video game in 2005.

Pánfilo de Zamacona y Nuñez, often referred to simply as Zamacona, is a fictional character who appears in The Mound, a novella ghostwritten in 1929-30 by H. P. Lovecraft for Zealia Bishop. He is a Spanish adventurer who uncovered the hidden land of K'n-yan in 1541.

### Biography
Born in Luarca, Spain, a quiet port on the Bay of Biscay, Zamacona was a wild young man, and at the age of 20 traveled to New Spain. Arriving in the Americas in 1532, he found himself surrounded by tales of adventure, and in 1540 he was picked to head north with Francisco Vázquez de Coronado's failed expedition to Cíbola. Eventually Zamacona was one of the few selected for a last-ditch attempt to discover something of worth. Though Coronado gave up at the Arkansas River in autumn 1541, Zamacona was still optimistic enough to believe the stories of Charging Buffalo, a native American who said he had navigated through a series of tunnels to a vast cavern that glowed with a strange blue light.

Enticed by promises of golden cities, he abandoned the camp under Charging Buffalo's guidance on 7 October 1541, and by October 13, the pair had found the tunnel's red sandstone entrance in a great ravine. Armed with a good stock of torches, Zamacona continued alone, agreeing to meet his fearful companion in a month's time. His progress took him past a series of carvings dedicated to Yig and Tulu, though his closest frame of reference came from the walls of Mexico. After three days' trek, the tunnel opened up into the blue-lit cave described by Charging Buffalo.

Roughly following a decaying highway, he stumbled upon a river with small deserted villages dotted along its bank, but also realises that he's being tracked. Reaching one of the abandoned settlements, he seals himself in to rest in a gold-lined temple with a dark metal statue of Tulu, which seemed to attract a talisman he found in the dirt. He was woken by his pursuers, a party of 20 K'n-yanians, and despite his knowledge of Wichita, Aztec, Spanish, French, Latin, Greek, Galician, Portuguese and Babel peasant patois, he was unable to communicate until they made psychic contact. They explained that they can't let him leave, and he rides with them to Tsath on a gyaa-yoth. His guide G'll-Hthaa-Ynn used the journey to catch Zamacona up on the history and culture of K'n-yan, indicating points of interest on the way.

In return for his knowledge of the outside world, he was offered an apartment in the city, unlimited access to the city's library, 10 slaves and a place in a high-class affection-group. Living in the lap of luxury for four years, Zamacona was able to explore the length and breadth of K’n-yan, from the plains of Nith to the ruins of Yoth. Zaman's Hill is an imaginary place mentioned in H. P. Lovecraft's poetry. It is the subject of the sonnet "Zaman's Hill" in the sonnet sequence Fungi from Yuggoth, and is mentioned in the poem "The Ancient Track."

### Fungi from Yuggoth
In "Zaman's Hill," the "great hill" was a "green, tall, and wooded" summit that hung over "the old town." It was a "man-shunned slope," because for 200 hundred years there had been whispers of "oddly mangled deer or bird" found there, and boys who got lost there did not reappear.

One day the unnamed village at the foot of the hill disappeared--people and houses both. A mail carrier was thought mad for saying he had seen  the "great hill’s gluttonous eyes, and jaws stretched wide."

### The Ancient Track
In "The Ancient Track," the hill is first a familiar landmark that reassures him that he well knows the place he's revisiting:I knew what shadows would be cast

When the late moon came up at last

From back of Zaman’s Hill, and how

The vale would shine three hours from now.Later, the hill signifies how unfamiliar his old haunts are:And over Zaman’s Hill the horn

Of a malignant moon was born,

To light the weeds and vines that grew

On ruined walls I never knew.

### Location
Zaman Hill appears to be part of Lovecraft Country; when it eats its neighboring village in "Zaman's Hill," the people who come to gape are from Aylesbury. In "The Ancient Track," after noting the moon rising above the hill, the narrator sees a milestone that says "Two miles to Dunwich." This suggests a location to the east of Dunwich, between Dunwich and Aylesbury.

Zar is a fictional coastal region in the Dreamlands of Earth and home to "the dreams and thoughts of beauty that come to men once and then are forgotten".

### Description
Its green shore is bright and beautiful with verdant tree-studded terraces rising up from the sea. The temples have gleaming white roofs and colonnades and stand amoungst a beautiful landscape of "forms and fantasies more splendid than any I had ever known; the visions of young poets who died in want before the world could learn of what they had seen and dreamed".
However those who go there can never return home.

The Zaratan are a fictional species which has its origins in the folklore and mythology of Islam . Chaosium incorporated the Zaratan into its Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game in the Cthulhu Invictus setting.

### Background
Zaratan are an ancient species which live throughout Earth's oceans and seas, and sometimes in its largest rivers. The race has existed for millions of years, perhaps billions of years. Drifting in the water as they sleep, and due to their size the water's current barely moves them.

Over the years, plant life grows on their shells and birds nest on them. Though its true nature is usually known to those who live close to it and therefore avoid it, unwary sailors may land on a Zaratan. If they dig too deeply or start a fire, they cause it pain. The enraged behemoth then submerges, dragging the sailors deep into the water in the undertow.

### In Other Works
*The Zaratan have also appeared in the Dungeons & Dragons roleplaying game  in its Arabian Nights / Ray Harryhausen Sinbad movie inspired setting Al-Qadim. Dungeons & Dragons has a long history of ties to the Cthulhu Mythos and Lovecraftian horror in general.

### References

The Zarbi are a species created by the BBC in 1965 for Doctor Who.

### Background
The Zarbi are an insectoid species on the planet Vortis whom are often controlled by the Animus. They resemble gigantic ants. Some move on human-like legs and others on six legs. Overall, they are simple-minded creatures of little intelligence with no individuality. They communicate via rubbing their legs together, screeching, and dancing. Their social structure is similar to that of Earth's ants and they live in nests consisting of millions. Like ants, their hives consist of giant, bloated queens, powerful warriors, and common workers.

Zarr is the name for a species of aliens created by the late American author Richard L. Tierney for his 1975 novel The Winds of Zarr.

### Overview
Originating from the planet Zarr, from which they take their name, the Zarr are a fanatical, ruthless race who had conquered most of their home galaxy, Xentilx. In the distant past, the god Zathog made a pact with the Zarr, granting them the power to travel through time and space, and thus giving them the opportunity to conquer the entire universe, on the condition that they actively sought to free the Great Old Ones and oppose the Elder Gods.

### Methodology
The Zarr's method of conquest is to first subdue their target planet through use of nuclear bombardment, then recruit indigenous collaborators to form a puppet government and overthrow any internal opposition.

### Unique Abilities
The Zarr possess the ability to manipulate the weather; in ancient times this led the Native Americans of Earth to fear them as demons.

### Trivia
*The Black Book of the Skull makes references to the Zarrians; this is an alternative name for the species.

Zarr is a planet created by the late American author Richard L. Tierney for his 1975 novel The Winds of Zarr.

### Overview
An ancient planet in the Xentilx galaxy, a body of stars adjacent to our own, Zarr is home to the warlike Zarr, a technologically-advanced species who sit at the centre of a galaxy-spanning empire and serve the malevolent Zathog.

At the centre of the planet Zathog makes his lair, a Great Old One who fled there after the war with the Elder Gods. It has since struck a pact with the Zarr, and gifts them with the power to travel through space and time in exchange for their aid against its ancient enemies.

Zathog, Dark Lord of the Whirling Vortices is a fictional character created by the late American author Richard L. Tierney for his 1975 short story "From Beyond the Stars."

### Overview
Zathog is a Great Old One who settled in the heart of the planet Zarr in the Xentilx galaxy after fleeing from the war with the Elder Gods and their "overweening" sphere of influence. It is one of the few gods not deep in torpor, and additionally still possesses its full powers (possibly because it moved to another galaxy, thus escaping the influence of the "star change"). It became the patron god of the Zarrians offering them rulership of the Universe in return for freeing the Old Ones, and the destruction of the Elder Gods (or Pain Lords), even at the cost of all time and space. It is said to be Ubbo-Sathla's brother and seeks to unite life on Earth into the Oneness of Ubbo-Sathla once more.

### Behind the Mythos
First created by Richard L. Tierney for his 1975 short story "From Beyond the Stars," Zathog has also been used in the fiction of Llewellyn M. Cabos.

### Trivia
*A reference to "Black Zathog, the master of the Zarrians" is made in the Necronomicon (source?). Whether this is the same entity remains unclear, although the reference to Zarrians makes it seem likely.
*The name is reminiscent of Zoth-Ommog.

fullContent:
Zealia Brown-Reed Bishop was an American writer of short stories.

Her stories appeared in the magazine Weird Tales. However, they were extensively revised by H. P. Lovecraft to the point of being ghostwritten.

Her name is sometimes spelled 'Zelia'.

Arkham House published her volume The Curse of Yig (1953) which contains three horror stories by Bishop (all revised by H. P. Lovecraft) and two profiles by Bishop, one about H. P. Lovecraft and the other about August Derleth. That on Lovecraft has been reprinted in Peter Cannon's collection of essays on Lovecraft, Lovecraft Remembered. The three Lovecraft-Bishop revision stories all appear in The Horror in the Museum and Other Revisions.

Bishop's preference was for romantic fiction, of which she wrote and published far more than she did of the weird. She lived in Kansas City with her husband D.W. Bishop, took an active role in the National Federation of Press Women, the New England Historic Genealogical Society and the Missouri Women's Press Club. She authored a historical series about Clay County, Missouri.

### Selected Bibliography

### Collections

* The Curse of Yig (collection)

### Short Fiction

* "The Curse of Yig" (1928, with H. P. Lovecraft)
* Medusa's Coil (1939, with H. P. Lovecraft)
* The Mound (1953, with H. P. Lovecraft)

### Non-Fiction

* "H. P. Lovecraft: A Pupil's View" (1953)

### References
*Sheldon Jaffery, The Collector's Index to Weird Tales (1985)
*S. T. Joshi, Sixty Years of Arkham House: A History and Bibliography (1999)

Zebulon Whateley is a fictional character in the Cthulhu Mythos. He is first mentioned by H. P. Lovecraft in "The Dunwich Horror" as a Dunwich resident who is a distant relative of Wilbur Whateley. He later appears in "The Shuttered Room", written by August Derleth, where he is the great-uncle of the story's protagonist.

### In Lovecraft's Works
In "The Dunwich Horror", written in 1928, Lovecraft describes "Old Zebulon Whateley" as coming from "a branch [of the Whateley family] that hovered about half way between soundness and decadence". When the Dunwich Horror is on its rampage, Zebulon "made darkly wild suggestions about rites that ought to be practiced on the hill-tops" to dispel or placate the entity. Lovecraft notes: "He came of a line where tradition ran strong, and his memories of chantings in the great stone circles were not altogether connected with Wilbur and his grandfather."

Later, when the party from Miskatonic observes the destruction wrought by the horror on Sentinel Hill and the "thick and foetid deposit of...tarry stickiness" it left behind, it's said that only Zebulon "could have done justice to the situation or suggested a plausible explanation."

After the Horror is dispatched, Zebulon "wanderingly remembered ancient things." It's Zebulon who recalls:  "Fifteen year' gone...I heerd Ol' Whateley say as haow some day we'd hear a child o' Lavinny's a-callin' its father's name on the top o' Sentinel Hill. . . ."

### In Derleth's Works
In "The Shuttered Room", Derleth's 1959 "posthumous collaboration" with Lovecraft, also set in Dunwich, Zebulon is called "Grandfather Luther Whateley's brother—the only living Whateley of his generation." and described as "an old, white-bearded man". He appears to deliver a warning about his family to protagonist Abner Whateley:


He offers to help Abner in dealing with the evil left behind by his brother Luther--"ef I can."

Zerubbabel Stubbs is a fictional character created by H. P. Lovecraft for his comedy short story "Ibid".

### Biography
Zerubbabel Stubbs was the son of Rest-in-Jehovah Stubbs, a pious 17th century drug dealer. In 1661, Zerubbabel left Ireland to the American continent to seek his fortune in New England. His father gave him the skull of Ibidus as a talisman, as he mistakenly believed Ibidus to have been a holy man. When he arrived in Salem, Zerubbabel built himself "a modest house near the town pump" and placed the skull in a cupboard beside the chimney. However, he became addicted to gambling and lost the relic to Epenetus Dexter of Providence, Rhode Island. (: "Ibid")

### Trivia
*Since he moved to America, it is possible that he might be an ancestor of Vermont bootlegger Hiram Stubbs from "Sweet Ermengarde".

Zhar and Lloigor are twin Great Old Ones from the Cthulhu Mythos. They first appeared in the short story "The Lair of the Star-Spawn" by August Derleth and Mark Schorer. 

### Background
Zhar and Lloigor are connected by the star Antares, from where they probably originated (although Rigel and Betelgeuse are also mentioned as origin points). Their mountainous ropy bodies lie in vast lightless caverns beneath the "Lake of Dread" on the Plateau of Sung's Isle of the Stars in Burma. Their enormous tentacles are entangled with each other's bodies, which lie in distant parts of the same cave. The two constantly emit strange humming sounds at each other as they have for millennia since being imprisoned there by the Elder Gods​​​​​​. The cavern appears to have been blown up and it is implied the bodies are killed, but as the caverns were also flooded by the lake, it's possible that their bodies might now be buried.

Zhar, "The Twin Obscenity" is the older and more powerful of the twins. The Tcho-Tcho of Sung worshipped it. Though his body is imprisoned on Earth, Zhar's mind is simultaneously said to live near Arcturus (although Rigel and Betelgeuse are also mentioned).

Lloigor, "The Star-Treader" is the possible progenitor of the lloigor species. His importance varies sometimes, he being seen as he "who walks the winds among the star-spaces," as a kind of cosmic Ithaqua, while at other times he is merely listed as a minor being subservient to his brother, Zhar. Nevertheless, he is worshipped by the Tcho-Tcho people in Tibet and Burma, and connected with Hastur (his father?) and Ithaqua (his elder brother?). He has the power to "draw the body [his body?] from the earth piecemeal" and his presence is signaled by sourceless winds. There is some suggestion that Lloigor's body was killed when Alaozar was destroyed, but if so then only the flesh substance was destroyed.

### In Other Media
*Demonbane: Zhar and Lloigor appear in the OVA episode that accompanied the PS2 release of Kishin Houkou Demonbane. However, they are very different compared to the versions from Derleth's story, as the entities are depicted as being some missing fragments of Al Azif.
*Haiyore! Nyaruko-san: Zhar and Lloigor appear as antagonists in the second season of the TV series. Their combined form is known as "ZharLloigor" and the combination resembles CycloneJoker from the Kamen Rider franchise. They run a sketchy environmentalist group that receives their funds by creating new endangered species to protect, with their latest one being a giant monkey deity named Alaozaru. However, ZharLloigor forgot to give Alaozaru enough intelligence to follow their commands, causing them to get defeated by their own creation.

The Republic of Zimbabwe is a landlocked country located in the extreme southeast of the African continent, much of its landmass consisting of high, arid plateaus and lowland veld. Like many regions of Africa, during colonial times it was a British territory, known as Rhodesia (a name it held in H. P. Lovecraft’s day); as a result of the dismantling of the British Empire in the decades following the Second World War, the country eventually gained sovereignty in 1980.

### In Lovecraft’s Works

### "Beyond Zimbabwe"
Presumably taking place in Zimbabwe, H. P. Lovecraft and R. H. Barlow's 1934 poem (one of two poems collectively known as "Bouts Rimés," the other being "The White Elephant") describes a ritual of human sacrifice by deranged cultists to a mysterious entity which takes place in the dark jungle. (HPL: "Beyond Zimbabwe")

Seaman Zimmer is a fictional character in the story "The Temple" by H. P. Lovecraft. 

### Background
Zimmer served aboard the German submarine U-29 under Lieutenant-Commander Karl Heinrich during the First World War. During the supernatural events experienced by the crew, both Zimmer and Boatswain Müller went missing. They were presumed by Heinrich to have committed suicide by jumping overboard while the U-29 was surfaced, victims of the fear that overcame them. (: "The Temple")

Zindarak, also known as the Fiery Messenger, is a fictional entity created by American author Llewellyn M. Cabos for his 1982 Cthulhu Mythos story "Dr. Dexter".

### Description
According to the Necronomicon, at the appropriate time in the appropriate year, Zindarak will arrive on planet Earth to release Cthulhu from his prison so that he may rise from the ocean to cause the death of humanity and take over the world. However, this can only occur when the stars are aligned, as nearly happened in 1982 (: "Dr. Dexter").

Zindarak's true alignment is unknown. It's believed that he is a representative of the Fire Vampires, a pyrokinetic race of alien beings that serves one of the Great Old Ones known as Cthugha. Other scholars believe he is a servant of the Outer God named Ghroth, which flies past the planets in different corners of the universe and, as a result of its voice, awakens any of the Old Ones nearby. So, Zindarak is likely to working on behalf of his masters.(source?)

fullContent:
Zllphyan are an eldritch-like race of energy beings in the fictional universe of the Rifts pencil-and-paper roleplaying game by Palladium.

### Background
During the Dark Ages, Earth was visited by a Zllphyan known as Zazshan who arrived after the fall of the Roman Empire. He planned to conquer the Earth and established himself on the British Isles. Where it used one of its meat puppets (Myrrlyn, aka "Merlin") to manipulate the Celtic-Roman tribes into creating the kingdom of Camelot.

Unfortunately for Zllphyan, the Atlantean cataclysm which occurred 1000s of years earlier was still playing havok with Earth's magic. Which resulted in Zazshan losing control of Camelot and its imprisonment in a crystal chamber deep within the Earth. Where it would lay trapped until the cataclysmic eruption of the ley lines a 1000 years later awakened him.

He reestablished his kingdom of Camelot and this time is using three meat puppets - a benevolent sorcerer (Myrrlyn), King Arr'thuu's beautiful queen (Lady Guinevere), and the goddess (the Lady of the Lake), to manipulate King Arr'thuu. Whom Zazshan chose to act as the unknowning figurehead of the realm. Zazshan is a patient entity, as he first "unites" the British Isles under Camelot, after which he plans to do the same to Europe and then the rest of the world.

### Zllyphan
Zllyphan are a malevolent race of manipulators, alien intelligences whom are beings of energy that appear as giant energy spheres the size of a house. Electric-like energy crackles on the sphere and around the body. Zllyphans on average live 120,000 years. Beings with formidable magical and psionic abilities. Which fire destructive energy blasts and are capable of surviving a 6.5 megaton nuke, though with grievous wounds. They can splinter their essence into smaller shards, and send those shards into other dimensions. All of which are directed and controlled by the core. 

They can possess those whom have recently died and resurrect them. The corpse which is controlled by the shard does not look, act, or smell like one of the undead. It breathes, talks, walks, eats, drinks, and so on just like any other living being. Magical items, psionics, magical creatures, and supernatural beings inflict far greater damage on a Zllyphan compared to a laser beam, a plasma cannon, explosives, poison gas, acid, steel swords, or any other type of conventional weapon.

Zoey Samaras, the Chef, is a fictional character who appears in several of Fantasy Flight Games' Arkham Horror Files products based on the expanded Cthulhu Mythos.

### History
God had spoken to Zoey ever since she was just a child- six years old to be precise, on the same night that He had also taken her parents away in a calamitous fire. He told her that she was to be His earthly warrior, protecting the innocent whilst making the evil answer for their crimes.

Ever since that day, God had continued to speak to Zoey, especially when times were hard; His presence gave her both comfort and the strength she needed to do the things He asked of her. On more than one occasion, He even pointed her in the specific direction of one who needed to be taught His justice, and every single time she prevailed.

Then one day, God told Zoey to gather her things and travel to Arkham; there, she would face the greatest challenge of her life. God did not speak to Zoey again but, doing as she was bid, she set her sights on Arkham, hoping that to rid the town of its festering evil would once again bring the voice of the Almighty back in to her life.

### Behind the Mythos
Making her first appearance as an Investigator for the Second Edition expansion of Lovecraftian adventure board game Arkham Horror, Innsmouth Horror, Zoey has since made appearances as a playable character in Fantasy Flight's related games Eldritch Horror and Arkham Horror: The Card Game. In addition a plastic miniature of the character was released in 2010 as part of their Arkham Horror Premium Figures release, but this is no longer in production.

Zokkar, known as Zokkar the Olden King, was a king of Sarnath who is remembered for the gardens of exquisite beauty that he made for the city during his reign. A description of the gardens is provided in "The Doom That Came to Sarnath"  by H. P. Lovecraft.

### Gardens of Zokkar
"In the centre of Sarnath they lay, covering a great space and encircled by a high wall. And they were surmounted by a mighty dome of glass, through which shone the sun and moon and stars and planets when it was clear, and from which were hung fulgent images of the sun and moon and stars and planets when it was not clear. In summer the gardens were cooled with fresh odorous breezes skilfully wafted by fans, and in winter they were heated with concealed fires, so that in those gardens it was always spring." (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

"There ran little streams over bright pebbles, dividing meads of green and gardens of many hues, and spanned by a multitude of bridges. Many were the waterfalls in their courses, and many were the lilied lakelets into which they expanded. Over the streams and lakelets rode white swans, whilst the music of rare birds chimed in with the melody of the waters. In ordered terraces rose the green banks, adorned here and there with bowers of vines and sweet blossoms, and seats and benches of marble and porphyry. And there were many small shrines and temples where one might rest or pray to small gods." (: "The Doom That Came to Sarnath")

Zombies are undead or walking dead creatures which are part of the mythology and folklore of several of mankind's cultures. Chaosium first made zombies part of the Mythos in 2007 when they were added to the Malleus Monstrorum sourcebook, and though supernatural are neither creations of the Mythos deities nor are they aligned with them in any way.

### Call of Cthulhu Roleplaying Game
Zombies vary from those created by witch doctors and sorcerers to be their slaves and servants to those that are uncontrollable ravenous flesh-eating zombies. Which can be created a variety of ways including malevolent spirits that possess and animate corpses, using voodoo or black magic, extra-terrestrial material which animates corpses, or zombies created by radiation or toxic chemicals. They are mostly immune to firearms (save for shotguns) and impaling though the appearance of the corpse worsens. Ideally, zombies must be either hacked apart or set aflame.

### Doctor Who
Historically in Haiti, voodoo sorcerers have devised a process to create zombies by using a combination of tetrodotoxin from puffer fishes and a plant called the zombi concombre. The first slows the metabolism and places the body in a death-like state, whereas the latter is described as a datura-related psychotrope that "blanks out the will, making the victim a mindless vegetable who'll obey any order at all". It should be noted that zombies created by this method are not actually dead, and are usually non-violent. In 1915, however, a Cthulhu follower named Gilles Lemaitre managed to perfect the formula with a third ingredient, which resulted in zombies capable of extraordinary strength and aggressiveness, albeit still susceptible to mental commands. Lemaitre's zombies could also survive multiple gunshot wounds and extensive damage to their interior organs, to the point of coming back to life even after an autopsy has been performed. (: White Darkness)

### Marvel Comics
Chthon and Sagbata the Vodu god of death and plague made a pact in which they created the first true zombies, animated undead corpses which had no free will to serve the witch-doctors of Sagbata. Other demonic entities have directly or indirectly created zombies including the Great Old One Lloigoroth who gave the supervillain Grim Reaper the power to reanimate the dead, creating sentient flesh-eating undead which had all the abilities they had in their mortal lives. In at least one alternate reality, the Darkhold contains a spell to create a plague of flesh eating zombies, the Gospel of Hunger. Which creates sentient undead corpses that are sadistic and even have a sense of humour, and are able to alter their corpses (e.g. growing a head in a beheaded body or projecting organ like tentacles from the abdomen).

fullContent:
ZombieWorld was a horror comic book series published by Dark Horse Comics between September 1997 and October 1999.

### Overview
The series contained several stories, most of which spanned more than one issue. The majority of these stories were of the more traditional "zombie apocalypse" genre, albeit with some unusual twists, but the two which formed a bookend story arc explaining the source of the outbreak - "Champion of the Worm" and "Tree of Death" - featured direct connections to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### "Champion of the Worms"
The three-issue introductory story, written by Mike Mignola of Hellboy fame, tells the story of a small-town museum which receives delivery of a mummy from a previously-unknown human civilisation named Hyperborea. This arrival precipitates the return of powerful Hyperborean necromancer Azzul Gotha, who plans to bring about the return of his dark gods. As part of his preparations, he unleashes a green mist on the Earth, which causes the dead to rise and enact his will.

In opposition to Gotha stand a small band of talented individuals led by the enigmatic Major. However, despite their best efforts, they are unable to prevent the Hyperborean sorcerer from initiating his plans.

### "Tree of Death"
In the final tale, a four-issue story written by Pat Mills, the Major and his small band of survivors attempt to fight back against the evil Azzul Gotha. Aided by the reincarnation of the mighty warrior who thwarted Gotha's plans 42,000 years ago, the group track down the legendary grimoire known as the Necronomicon Hyperborea. Although Gotha has already begun to transport the demonic Qlipoth to our dimension using the great worm Crom-Cruach to dig a tunnel network dubbed the "Tree of Death," the powerful magic contained within the Necronomicon proves sufficient to reverse his magics and save the world- at least from the Qlipoth; the planet is, after all, still overrun with zombies…

Zon Mezzamalech is a fictional character created by Clark Ashton Smith for his Cthulhu Mythos story "Ubbo-Sathla".

### Biography
An ancient Hyperborean sorcerer, Zon Mezzamalech lived in Mhu Thulan and possessed a mysterious crystal that allows one to experience visions of the past, all the way down to the beginning of all things.

The Book of Eibon records that Mezzamalech disappeared mysteriously without a trace, and the crystal was lost afterwards. In truth, Mezzamalech used the crystal to send his mind back in time to the source of all life on Earth, the amorphous Ubbo-Sathla, hoping to study the stone tablets guarded by this unbegotten entity, and gain the knowledge of a race of gods who had died or abandoned the material universe "before the Earth was born". Zoogs are a race of sentient forest-dwelling creatures that inhabit the Dreamlands of Earth. They are mortal enemies of cats, as they prey upon kittens and are preyed upon in return by adult cats.

Randolph Carter enlisted the aid of the Zoogs during his quest for Kadath.

They are small and curious, and usually unseen. One sees their weird eyes long before one can discern their slippery brown outlines. The Zoogs' speech consists of fluttering sounds. Although they eat mostly fungi, they are not above occasionally eating animals or visiting dreamers. The zoogs make a wine from the fermented sap of a moon-tree (a tree grown from a seed dropped down by someone on the Moon of the Dreamlands).

The Zoogs dwell in the enchanted wood, just past the Gate of Deeper Slumber in the world of dream. They cannot travel far outside the world of dream, but range freely over the nearer parts of dreamland.  One of their villages is near an old circle of mossy stone, where elder beings danced and sacrificed. The Zoogs fear and shun a stone slab set with a huge iron ring. This slab if opened reveals a path that leads down to the realm where the Gugs were banished in the underworld of the Dreamlands.

The Zoog Council of Sages at one point recognized Randolph Carter as an old ally. Some Zoogs who followed Carter to Ulthar were slain by the local cats, after at least one of the Zoogs tried to eat a kitten. Later Carter overheard the Zoogs planning a war of revenge against the cats. After Carter warned the cats, they launched a pre-emptive strike and secured the surrender of the Zoogs, along with tribute and hostages. Thereafter the cats provided Carter an escort, to protect him from the justifiedly resentful Zoogs.

Interestingly, the Zoogs have the means to visit the waking world of Earth, travelling physically to and from the Dreamlands at two places kept secret from the general public. They don't range far from these crossover points between the two worlds on the Earth side, but it is fascinating that this is another example of the Dreamlands being not just an "astral" dimension but in some respects more of a physical parallel world or different vibrational level of the "same universe". This is also illustrated by the Cats from Saturn and the mentions of other planets having their own Dreamlands -or perhaps simply their own "local" areas of the same Dreamlands.

Zoth Syra is a ficitonal entity created by C. Hall Thompson for his short story "Spawn of the Green Abyss". The character was later incorporated into Chaosium's role-playing game Call of Cthulhu. (: Ye Booke of Monstres II)

### Description
Zoth Syra, known as the Queen of the Green Abyss or Empress of the Abyss, is the ruler of a species of amorphous creatures that dwell deep within the Earth's oceans, being descended from the mythical Syrens.

Like her subjects, Zoth Syra enchants humans with her hypnotic singing and can somehow convert them into scaly gilled humanoids (similar to Deep Ones) so that they can live in her abyssal empire: a vast underwater city of bizarre geometry, whose architecture somehow seems "all wrong" (similar to R'lyeh). The hypnotized victims, even while feeling terrified and revolted, are incapable of offering any resistance to the amorphous enchantress.

After converting humans into aquatic humanoids, Zoth Syra can mate with them and bear deceptively human-like children. (: "Spawn of the Green Abyss")

Zoth-Ommog is a Great Old One and the third son of Cthulhu, featured in the Xothic Legend Cycle by Lin Carter.

He has a tapered cone-shaped body, a razor-fanged reptilian head like a Tyrannosaurus rex, four broad, flat, starfish-like arms with suckers, and a mane of tentacles. How he swims or walks on the ocean floor is unknown, but he may have a slug-like foot similar to the Great Race of Yith.

The Elder Gods imprisoned Zoth-Ommog beneath the seabed near Ponape and R'lyeh. Like his older brother Ythogtha, Zoth-Ommog is served by Father Ubb and the Yuggs.

Zoth-Ommog's legend is chronicled in the R'lyeh Text and the Ponape Scripture.

Zothique is an imagined future continent in a series of short stories by Clark Ashton Smith. Zothique is also the title of the cycle of tales which take place there. In terms of number and extent, the Zothique Cycle is the largest collection of stories written by Smith. The cycle belongs to the fantasy genre, and more precisely to the Dying Earth subgenre.

August Derleth in "The Dweller in Darkness" mentions Zothique, and thus ties this far future continent to the Cthulhu Mythos.

### Zothique Cycle
Clark Ashton Smith himself described the Zothique cycle in a letter to L. Sprague de Camp, dated November 3, 1953:Zothique, vaguely suggested by Theosophic theories about past and future continents, is the last inhabited continent of earth. The continents of our present cycle have sunken, perhaps several times. Some have remained submerged; others have re-risen, partially, and re-arranged themselves. Zothique, as I conceive it, comprises Asia Minor, Arabia, Persia, India, parts of northern and eastern Africa, and much of the Indonesian archipelago. A new Australia exists somewhere to the south. To the west, there are only a few known islands, such as Naat, in which the black cannibals survive. To the north, are immense unexplored deserts; to the east, an immense unvoyaged sea. The peoples are mainly of Aryan or Semitic descent; but there is a negro kingdom (Ilcar) in the north-west; and scattered blacks are found throughout the other countries, mainly in palace-harems. In the southern islands survive vestiges of Indonesian or Malayan races. The science and machinery of our present civilization have long been forgotten, together with our present religions. But many gods are worshipped; and sorcery and demonism prevail again as in ancient days. Oars and sails alone are used by mariners. There are no fire-arms—only the bows, arrows, swords, javelins, etc. of antiquity. The chief language spoken (of which I have provided examples in an unpublished drama) is based on Indo-European roots and is highly inflected, like Sanskrit, Greek and Latin.Darrell Schweitzer suggests the idea of writing about a far future land may have come from William Hope Hodgson's novel The Night Land, noting that Smith was an admirer of Hodgson's work. However, this theory was conclusively disproven by Scott Conner's "Dust and Atoms: The Influence of William Hope Hodgson on Clark Ashton Smith" in Sargasso #2 (2016), the scholarly journal devoted to Hodgson. Conner establishes with evidence that Smith did not read Hodgson until 1934, when Smith had already slowed his writing output.

Zug is a fictional Lovecraftian entity from the Hyborian Age. First mentioned by Robert E. Howard in his 1933 short story "Black Colossus," the character was more fully developed by Marvel Comics in their Conan the Barbarian comic book in 1991.

### Background
Zug was worshipped by the priests of Thugra Khotan in Stygia during the Hyborian Age. A great dome was built over its chamber. The dome was impenetrable to Hyborian weaponry and could only be opened by specific unlocking mechanisms. Inside the dome was a huge amount of gold. Zug itself was dozens of feet in diameter and had a great maw full of sharp teeth, and numerous eyes and tentacles, the latter as strong as human beings and dozens of feet long. The creature apparently slumbered and its body was mistaken to be the chamber's floor. The creature attacked and consumed any who were within reach. Conan and his companions encountered the beast, and were barely able to escape it.

Zushakon, The Dark Silent One, appears as a swirling, black vortex, revered by the Mutsune Native Americans as a dire death god. He is also worshipped by the mysterious servitors known as the Hidden Ones. It is a descendent of Ubbo-Sathla. The name is also given as Zul-Che-Quon (by West Coast Indian tribes) and Zushakon (in Mu and Xinian).

"Zushakon" is an alternative spelling of Zulchequon used by the Elder Hierophant Yogmosh-Voth in Mu and it is also used in the Book of Iod. A variation of this name, Zyshakon, was used by some of the American Natives.

### Behind the Mythos
The original name variant Zushakon was invented by Henry Kuttner in "The Bells of Horror"; Lin Carter used this name and other variants in his fiction.

Zulchequon was created by Henry Kuttner and expanded upon by Lin Carter.

Logic suggests that Zushakon is the "father" of Cyäegha.(source?)

Zvilpogghua, a.k.a. the Feaster from the Stars, is a fictional monster created by Clark Ashton Smith in his letters to R. H. Barlow. Smith identifies it as a child of Tsathoggua.

In the expanded Cthulhu Mythos, it is regarded as another name for Ossadagowah, a child of Tsathoggua featured in a story fragment by H. P. Lovecraft.(source?)

August Derleth, using Lovecraft's unfinished work, developed Ossadagowah in The Lurker at the Threshold.

### History
Zvilpogghua is the son of Tsathoggua and Shathak, and is the father of Sfatlicllp. (: "The Family Tree of the Gods")

Zvilpogghua was conceived on the planet Yaksh, known to earthlings as Neptune. (: "The Feaster from the Stars")

Zvilpogghua is known to the Native Americans as Ossadagowah and is mentioned under this name in the book Of Evill Sorceries Done in New England of Demons in No Humane Shape. He usually takes the form of an armless, winged, bipedal toad with a long, rubbery neck and a face completely covered in tentacles. He currently dwells on Yrautrom, a planet that orbits the star Algol, in the Perseus Constellation. Zvilpoggua is an alternative spelling.

“The Star Beast” is the avatar form of this god (sometimes called the minion of “the Great Old One”) and was sometimes summoned by Native Americans, although they rarely did this because it could only go back to the stars of its own free will.

### Marvel Ultimate Universe
In Earth-1610, Zvilpogghua, the Feaster From the Stars, was one of the Great Old Ones. It was cast into "The Abyss" (or "N-Zone"), by the ancestors of Atlantis and their "Old Gods", and slumbered there for millions of years. It was mentioned by Lovecraft.

It manifested in modern days when the Fantastic Four entered the N-Zone, possessing the Human Torch, until it was removed using ancient magical texts from Atlantis, then trapped into Doom's body and carried into the Marvel Zombies Universe.

### Behind the Mythos
Ossadagowah and Zvilpogghua are confirmed to be different names for the same entity in "Strange Manuscript Found in the Vermont Woods", by Lin Carter, which also identifies the monster's current dwelling place as Yrautrom in the Algol system.

However, in "The Feaster from the Stars", Carter referred to Zvilpogghua's Algolian abode as either Ymar (in the Crypt of Cthulhu version) or Abbith (in the Book of Eibon version), the latter being Carter's name for the World of Seven Suns from which Nyarlathotep can be summoned to Earth as well.

The Zy'tl Q'ae are a fictional race created by Ramsey Campbell for his Cthulhu Mythos short story "The Insects from Shaggai" in which they are unnamed. Their name originates from Chaosium's roleplaying game Call of Cthulhu, first used in the 1994 supplement Ye Booke of Monstres.

### Background
The Zy'tl Q'ae is a species which consists of sentient carnivorous plant-things who are the dominant lifeform on Xiclotl. From the other inhabitants of Xiclotl they demand periodical sacrifices of their own. Prey are lured to the plant creatures via clouds of pollen-like spores which produce a hypnotic effect on those whom inhale the spores.

Their victims are captured and consumed using their snapping purple blossoms and grasping tendrils. Reproduction is via seeds the size of human skulls, which are discharged with such force that some of them escape the atmosphere. The seeds can survive in the vacuum of space, and some of them end up on other worlds, spreading the species.
